# Patrologia Latina, volume 1 — English translation

## Patrologia Latina, Volume 1

## The Complete Works of Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullian, Presbyter of Carthage

### Part One

### List of the contents of this volume

[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF TERTULLIAN]

[Col. 0009]

## Preface

### Preface to Tertullian

[Col. 0009A] As we undertake, with the favor of God and of the blessed Virgin Mother of God, to publish anew all the Fathers and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin tongue, we asked—after weighing chronology, subject matter, and works—which man should march first as standard-bearer before so great a host of witnesses to the Christian cause. A man of better reputation and a name of holier omen could indeed readily have been found among the earliest cradles of the Church; yet no one, apart from our QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, was more outstanding in intellectual power and abundance of learning.

His genius must indeed be praised, but his heresy condemned; and the last [Col. 0009B] and greater part of so great a man’s long life, spent in foul errors, must certainly be lamented. Yet since the other and better part was vigorously devoted to battles for the faith, let him at least, in view of chronology and the right of seniority, be granted first place. Let the Western Church deservedly claim him as her first champion. Protected, therefore, by the shadow and patronage of his great name, may this new and complete series of all the testimonies by which Catholic Tradition grew arise and flourish. It is to be assembled from every work, great and small, produced and still surviving throughout the Christian world for the defense of the faith, from the apostolic age to the last of the Fathers. It will republish everything already printed; supply the place of old books that disappear day by day or are rarely found; answer the earnest and longstanding desire of many; fulfill what was announced long ago; and begin late so as to begin more prudently. For the undertaking is arduous and immense; yet by tireless effort and continuous labor, if only good and favoring [Col. 0009C] God assists us, it is to be carried through to its final end.

As we make such a beginning, may it be happy and auspicious for us to reread what is impressed upon the very first steps, and to learn from Tertullian’s miserable fall: no support from even the most fertile genius has ever been necessary for planting or preserving the faith, nor must this pillar and foundation of truth be propped up by the frail and perishable hand of men in order that the Church’s foundation may stand firm and unshaken [Note: [Col. 0009D] 1 Tim. 3:15]. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is CHRIST JESUS [Note: [Col. 0009D] 1 Cor. 3:11]. God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone [Col. 0009D] who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0009D] 2 Tim. 2:19].

Meanwhile, the character of this first witness who meets us is so varied and equivocal that something must be said by way of preface about his proper [Col. 0010A] use and true authority. Others will each contribute what must be discussed about him in the course of this work:

First PAMELIUS will construct the Septimian annals through twenty-four consular years.

Then Johann August NOESSELT and Dom Gottfried LUMPER will expressly discuss the occasion, date, and authority of each book, how many there are, and when each was written, whether before or after its author embraced Montanism.

Next Tertullian’s Paradoxes, together with their antidote, will be reviewed through the renewed labor of Pamelius.

Along with these will follow Beatus RHENANUS and ANDREAS [Col. 0010B] HOYUS of Bruges, explaining the proverbial expressions Tertullian uses most frequently, from which no small light is cast over the whole work.

Then, in a very rare and deeply learned dissertation on the apologetic books, Dom NICOLAS LE NOURRY will explain all the difficult points of Septimius’s doctrine at greater length and fullness.

Meanwhile there is appended a brief and lucid investigation by LAURENCE MOSHEIM on the date of the *Apology* and the beginning of the Severan persecution.

There follows the complete text of Tertullian, illustrated with variant readings from the Rhenanus, Pamelius, Franeker, Rigault, Paris, Venice, Halle, and Würzburg editions; corrected also by the emendations of Junius, Latinius, Wouwerius, Salmasius, Ciacconius, Scaliger, Semler, Ritter, and Leopold; and furnished with the extensive commentaries of Rhenanus, [Col. 0010C] Pamelius, Pancirolus, La Cerda, Albaspinaeus, Havercamp, Muratori, Dom Corbinian Thomas, and various others.

When the labors of so many and such men have been completed, there will be added, as a crowning abundance, a very full index of Tertullian’s Latin usage, arranged chiefly through the work of Gottfried Schutz.

Everyone may therefore see how small a province remains for the new editors and how nearly nothing must be added from their own store, except perhaps the matters we resolved above to undertake: first, what must be said about Tertullian’s use and authority—though even here we are not wholly left to ourselves, since an excellent shorter [Col. 0010D] essay by Dom Corbinian Thomas on the same subject is available; then, what principal labors have been devoted to Tertullian in the republic of letters down to our own time, which we shall in turn receive as carefully investigated by the very learned Ceillier, Lumper, Schram, and Schoennemann; and finally, as a crown, it remains to indicate more fully in this introduction by what ordering of subjects, sequence of books, addition of dissertations, variety of collated readings, abundance and selection of commentaries, and culmination of appendices and indexes this new edition is to be distinguished from others.

[Col. 0011A]

## Article I. On the Authority of Tertullian

Authority in one who possesses the power to teach others is rightly derived from two sources: esteem for his knowledge and confidence in his truthfulness.

Supreme authority belongs to God alone, since he alone possesses supreme truth in knowing and supreme truthfulness in speaking.

[Col. 0011B] Every other authority becomes greater in proportion as it approaches that authority more nearly and participates in it more perfectly.

Hence for us Catholics there is no greater authority under the sun—indeed none greater in heaven or on earth, and none other than that of God himself—than the teaching power of the Church. It rests, is guided, and is confirmed by the word of the power of God [Note: [Col. 0011D] Heb. 1:3], in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0011D] Heb. 1:3], and by the infallible assistance of the Holy Spirit, which will never fail even to the consummation of the age.

Blessed Vincent of Lérins teaches that all Catholics who strive to prove themselves legitimate children of the Church must cling to, fasten themselves upon, and die in the faith of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0011D] Col. 2:3]. With the consent of the whole Tradition, he lays down this rule for assenting [Col. 0011C] to the Fathers: whatever you know to have been held, written, and taught openly, frequently, and perseveringly, not by one or two alone but by all alike with one and the same agreement, understand that this must also be believed by you without any doubt.

To Fathers taken individually no authority belongs except private authority, to be discerned from various signs, some peculiar to each and others drawn from without.

In the men themselves we must consider both what belongs to a rightly formed intellect and what belongs to a sound will: on one side, the force of their genius, abundance of learning, and manner and customary usage of speech, from which it may safely be believed that they are not deceived; on the other, uprightness of morals and holiness of life, by which every [Col. 0011D] suspicion that they deceive or wish to deceive is removed.

To these, as it were, intrinsic signs of authority are added the various circumstances of times, places, ranks, and all else amid which authors wrote, and especially the judgment of such great weight by which the Church approves and evaluates certain writers through a title tacit or solemn, special or most special.

Yet ecclesiastical writers who have not attained the highest and legitimate peaks of holiness, or have not trodden the straight path of faith with an unwavering foot, should not all be cast aside or rejected. Since they remained at least for a time in the bosom of orthodox faith, it is neither fair nor lawful to deny them all credit. Indeed, wherever they agree with Catholics, confidence in them is all the greater, since no sane person will think that collusion and a friendly conspiracy occurred on both sides.

[Col. 0012A] With these Catholic criteria of patristic study established, we must now come to our subject. QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN must now be weighed with an even and steady balance: deeply skilled in so many ancient disciplines; powerful in philosophical, historical, legal, oratorical, and poetic learning; renowned before accepting the faith for his distinction at the bar, and more renowned after receiving it, as defender [Col. 0012B] and advocate of the entire Christian cause before the emperors in the forum of the Roman world; herald of the second Christian era, nearest that of the Apostles; first witness and champion of the Latin Church, indeed the one man whose defenses have come down to us; distinguished first-fruits of the African faith; pupil of apostolic men; himself teacher of martyrs, bishops, and doctors; advanced to holy orders at Rome and enrolled among the presbyters at Carthage; thoroughly versed in mysteries; conqueror of all the heretics of his age, indeed a notable overthrower of Montanus; and yet—would that it were otherwise!—a Montanist, a heretic, and the dead head of a heresy, at last no longer a man of the Church!…

Since he underwent so many changes, our estimate of him must be manifold, becoming different according to the different character which he, so unlike himself, assumes. Above all, in him as in the other doctors of the Church, it is of some value to distinguish secular learning from sacred equipment, the private writer from the Catholic or Montanist author, and a merely literary or historical matter from a dogmatic cause.

[Col. 0012C] But what reason would there be to linger long over Septimius’s secular reputation in this preface and threshold to a purely patristic work? I shall therefore state briefly what sort of rhetorician, grammarian, dialectician, or cultivator of literary form he was, and what sort of philosopher, philologist, investigator of antiquity, master of history, jurist, and man practiced in every kind of knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium* II, 20.]

What judgment should be made of his manner of speaking, discussing, and arguing you will find a little below, elegantly and expressly explained by the very learned Dom Lumper [Note: [Col. 0012D] See below, vol. I, cols. 89–96]. It is useful to add only a few words, lest a highly fastidious [Col. 0012D] reader and devotee of more polished learning stumble and stick upon the rough places of Tertullian’s Latin. Tertullian, almost the first of all to transmit dogmas and mysteries hitherto wholly unknown to Latin speech, could—and indeed had to—introduce new formulas and unheard words, or at least words used in another sense. That ecclesiastical Latin was being born and was almost wailing in its cradle. From the beginning it had its own modes and its own laws, whether in prose speech or rhythmic measure, especially suited to treating heavenly mysteries; it established and preserved them. No small part of Tertullian’s praise is that he contributed wonderfully to forming and spreading them through men’s mouths. [Col. 0013A] For all who came after him, and especially the many produced by the African Church—most fertile in illustrious men in those days—marveled at his genius and imitated even his difficult and harsh language. Led by Cyprian, an assiduous admirer of the man he called his most deserving master, they eagerly fashioned themselves and their speech after Tertullian’s diction.

It will not be irrelevant to observe in passing that Tertullian’s genius suffered a certain decline after his departure from the true faith. In books apparently written in his last period amid the dregs of Montanism, he either becomes harsher and more uneven, swept away by an uncontrollable itch to speak and a restless combativeness, or deliberately wraps himself in obscurer meaning and speaks only through tangled riddles. These faults may be almost touched with the finger especially in *On the Pallium* and *Against the Valentinians*.

[Col. 0013B] Perhaps the same change for the worse may be found when, forgetting the harshness of his unadorned and ill-composed diction, you look deeply into the subject and the inward substance of his thought. The majesty and grand eloquence of the *Apology*, the *Prescription*, and the books *On Prayer*, *On Baptism*, and *On Repentance*, sometimes restrained by extremely sharp and Laconic brevity, declines into shapeless and diffuse eloquence that tosses out whatever comes to hand, even tasteless things, and does not disdain buffoonery or rather impudent jokes.

But since these points, as I have said, belong more to secular criticism than to Tertullian’s dogmatic authority, we now set our sails toward that subject, unwilling to be carried elsewhere.

[Col. 0013C] By sacred learning, says Walch [Note: [Col. 0013D] *Bibliotheca Patristica*, new ed., Jena, 1834, ch. 7, §46], we mean that which treats matters disclosed not by nature and knowable by human faculty, but divinely manifested and contained in the most holy code (to which venerable Catholic Tradition is also added). Knowledge of these matters consists in various disciplines: exegetical, dogmatic, polemical, moral, symbolic, catechetical, and homiletic theology, together with ecclesiastical history.

Since Tertullian is commended under almost all these titles, from them must be drawn the principal signs of authority that are proper and peculiar to him.

To begin with the Word of God, Tertullian makes a by no means contemptible contribution to its interpretation and to exegetical science. Whether Catholic [Col. 0013D] or Montanist, he always taught that the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments were inspired [Note: [Col. 0013D] Cf. *On the Dress of Women* I.3, vol. I, col. 1307; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 22, vol. II, col. 823; *Against Marcion* III.6, col. 325; V.7, col. 485; *On the Soul* 2, col. 648]. He adores the plenitude of Scripture no less than its divinity [Note: [Col. 0013D] *Against Hermogenes* 22, vol. II, col. 217]. In adoring it he does not remove tradition; rather, he openly declares that interpretation of Scripture must be referred to tradition—that is, to the Apostles and disciples of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0013D] *Scorpiace* 12, vol. II, col. 146]. Although he nowhere formally discussed the canon [Col. 0014A] of Sacred Scripture, it can nevertheless be gathered from various passages of his works that books cast out of the canon in our age by pseudo-critics were numbered by him among the sacred and divinely inspired books [Note: [Col. 0014D] Cf. Gottfried Lumper, *Historia theologico-critica de vita, scriptis atque doctrina SS. Patrum*, vol. VII, ch. 6, art. 1, p. 242 ff.].

Yet Tertullian’s authority as an exegete is utterly overturned if his latest editor and most insolent detractor, J. Salomo Semler, is to be believed. With brazen front Semler asserted that this writer never used with his own eyes and hands any Greek codex of the Gospels, Epistles, or other sacred books, and never wished to use Greek codices because they were corrupted; and that this same man, willingly ignorant of Greek codices, corrupted the Latin books and enlarged them with interpolated glosses and opinions still [Col. 0014B] surviving, of which Tertullian himself was the first and sole certain author [Note: [Col. 0014D] Dissertation on the varied and uncertain character of these books, reprinted with the works of Tertullian, Halle-Magdeburg, 1828, vol. V, pp. 176–313]. But, I ask, what credit belongs to an itch for innovation so insolent that the same man dares declare that all Latin writers in these first centuries never consulted Greek books, and all conspired to insert deliberately into their own books, against the witness of the Greek codices, new glosses—while the first beginnings and recent rudiments of that Latin translation arose in Tertullian’s time, if not from Tertullian himself? But why recount these things, when in this same dissertation Tertullian’s detractor reached such audacity that, after dispersing the darkness of so long a time—as that exceedingly novel and perverse man puts it—he discovered an association, unheard of in all preceding antiquity, of conspirators dwelling at Rome, both Greek [Col. 0014C] and Latin, from whose workshop there secretly issued many works of Tertullian, some of Clement of Alexandria, and all of Irenaeus, entirely counterfeit and spurious? When first published, these claims were deservedly regarded as monstrosities and attacked and routed by the most learned men of Germany itself [Note: [Col. 0014D] Cf. Johann Daniel Schumann, *Observationes in veteres Ecclesiae scriptores*, specimens III and IV, on interpolations wrongly imputed to Tertullian’s New Testament codex, Hanover, 1776–1777, quarto; C. W. F. Walch, on the authenticity of Irenaeus’s books against J. Sal. Semler, in *Novi Commentarii Societatis Regiae Gottingensis*, vol. V, part II, p. 3]. To expose them is enough to make them rejected with ridicule [Note: [Col. 0014D] Cf. the points briefly touched below, vol. I, cols. 55–56 n.; vol. II, cols. 548–49, 551–52, 554, 538, 565, 594].

The dogmatic authority of Tertullian the Catholic, however, rises high; even that of Tertullian the Montanist must sometimes not be despised. Our author embraces in a remarkable way the three methods used by the Fathers in expounding the faith: the symbolic, in which the weightiest linked dogmas of faith are recited continuously in a few words; the polemical, adapted to refuting Gentiles, Jews, or heretics; and the discursive or catechetical, which for the use of Christian believers [Col. 0014D] explains now one point of doctrine and now another.

[Col. 0015A] For he has three formulas of faith: one, the shorter, in *On the Veiling of Virgins* [Note: [Col. 0015D] Ch. 1, vol. II, col. 888]; another, longer, in the *Prescription against Heretics* [Note: [Col. 0015D] Ch. 13, vol. II, col. 26]; and a third and later one in *Against Praxeas* [Note: [Col. 0015D] Ch. 2, vol. II, col. 156].

He was the first among the Latins to attack every enemy of the newborn Church with polemical and apologetic writings. Against the nations he wrote the seven books we have entitled apologetic: the two books *To the Nations* and the great *Apology*, the latter addressed to governors and the former to the people; likewise *On the Testimony of the Soul*, a fuller treatment of chapter 17 of the *Apology*; and the book *To Scapula*, in which he complains of unjust and cruel persecution and extols the virtues of Christians. To these are added *To the Martyrs*, an apology on the glory of martyrdom; *On the Shows*, an exhortation to Christians to avoid [Col. 0015B] the shows of the heathen; and *On Idolatry*, addressed to all worshipers either of Christ or of the gods, on the great gravity of that crime.

Following the footsteps of Justin the philosopher, Irenaeus the martyr, and others whose names he himself displays, he demonstrates to the Jews that the Messiah foretold by the prophets has come [Note: [Col. 0015D] Cf. G. H. Scharffenberg, academic commentary on Justin, Tertullian, and Cyprian against the Jews, Lund-Gothenburg, 1820, quarto]. He slays all heretics generally in the *Prescription*, not even excepting Montanus, and then pierces them individually, as if in single combat. Thus he assails, conquers, and crushes the disordered troop of Gnostics ten times [Note: [Col. 0015D] In *Scorpiace*, *Against the Gnostics*, *Against Hermogenes*, the five books *Against Marcion*, *Against the Valentinians*, *On the Flesh of Christ*, and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh]; and he apparently did not quit this battle line, like a discharged veteran soldier, until the enemy had been scattered and put to flight. He also opposed Praxeas, who asserted one God but not a triune God, and Montanus, to whom he miserably defected, [Col. 0015C] in the elegant and charming little book *On Repentance*. Finally, he explodes the sophists’ tasteless philosophizing *On the Soul*. With this tireless labor and ceaseless contest Tertullian fought; and when, advanced in age and stricken by an incurable wound, he deserted to Montanus’s side, far from relaxing his assault, he armed himself more fiercely for battle and seemed to say to himself: “Woe to me if I do not fight!”

Again, he was the first to offer Latin ears a distinct treatise on a particular dogmatic topic, composed in lucid speech. Indeed, he excelled so greatly in treating these dogmas separately that I dare say that, through the boundless passage of years, nothing has yet appeared that can deservedly be thought to surpass Tertullian’s books *On Prayer*, *On Baptism*, *On Repentance*, *On Patience*, and the other works [Col. 0015D] we judged should be styled dogmatic.

Meanwhile I shall not deny that even Tertullian’s best writings suffer here and there from many errors and are disfigured by much poisonous corruption. I would have you see these treated to some extent with the best and most wholesome antidote, reviewed again through the labor of the old editors and placed at the front of this volume.

[Col. 0016A] Another praise of Tertullian remains more intact and cannot be sufficiently celebrated: his moral and hortatory excellence, to be gathered from his many books concerning Christian conduct. These form two series, the first written before the author embraced Montanism, the second after he was already a Montanist. In both, the mirror of Christian life is vividly expressed: in its perennial fountain, private and public prayer [Note: [Col. 0016D] *On Prayer*]; in its most abundant streams, namely the sacraments [Note: [Col. 0016D] *On Baptism*, *On Repentance*, *On the Eucharist*, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, *On Marriage*, *To His Wife*]; in its ordinary acts [Note: [Col. 0016D] *On Patience*, *On the Dress of Women*] or its most excellent ones [Note: [Col. 0016D] *On the Veiling of Virgins*]; in the liturgical rites that give it outward form [Note: [Col. 0016D] *On Prayer*]; in avoiding the enticements of the world or flesh, where the Christian soul is endangered [Note: [Col. 0016D] *On the Shows*]; in undertaking works by which [Col. 0016B] it revives [Note: [Col. 0016D] *On Repentance*, *On Fasting*]; or in entering the bloody arena of martyrdom by which it is glorified [Note: [Col. 0016D] *To the Martyrs*, *Scorpiace*]. In treating these matters, the more rigid harshness of the Montanist is certainly carried beyond legitimate bounds rather often, and provision has carefully been made against the error hidden in our books. Besides, one must frequently note the impulse of a fervent genius that urges men toward great things and exceeds the common measure of mankind.

You have, then, TERTULLIAN commended solely from his own writings and his peculiar resources. He is further commended by the ancient times in which he wrote: the first among the Africans, the first among the Latins after the Roman Pontiffs who is at least known and preserved. They were blessed times of teachers and disciples, when in the new seed of the Christians the blood [Col. 0016C] of Christ and the martyrs still ran warmer, when the Apostles’ voice still sounded and their faces were still represented, when their authentic letters were publicly read [Note: [Col. 0016D] *Prescription* 36, vol. II, col. 49]. He is commended also by his native city and the Church of which he was the first priest known to us: Carthage, Rome’s rival as conqueror, yet conquered by faith; won by Peter’s disciples as Rome was by Peter; new, if you will, but already the happy and exultant mother of her infants. Its noble offspring had only lately been announced to the world: the Scillitan Martyrs and the company of Perpetua, Felicity, and their companions, whose contemporary our Septimius was—indeed, as some think, their witness and panegyrist [Note: [Col. 0016D] Cf. J. A. Noesselt’s dissertation below, vol. I, col. 85 ff.]. This Church long flourished in the holiness and learning of men who followed Tertullian in unbroken succession, as though our author had roused their talents, trained their hands for battle, marshaled their ranks [Col. 0016D] for the field, and bestowed and fashioned for them a new idiom, like a military watchword, afterward to be spread throughout the whole Christian West. He is commended by the very holy men with whom he lived, conversed, or was joined by circumstance [Col. 0017A] or shared studies: Irenaeus, whom he mentions with reverence; Gaius and Hippolytus, disciples of that same Irenaeus; his contemporary Clement of Alexandria; Origen, whom he perhaps met at Rome; and finally the supreme bishops of bishops, who instilled in him the most uncorrupted doctrine, the whole of which the Apostles poured out at Rome with their blood [Note: [Col. 0017D] *Prescription* 36, vol. II, col. 49]. He is commended by the hundreds of authors of every kind whom he kept before his eyes—sacred and profane, historians, philosophers, poets, jurists, and masters of every discipline—whose volumes he handled by night and by day, and whose testimonies he set at the head of all his tablets. He is commended by posterity, both those nearest to him and the most recent: his fellow Africans, led by St. Cyprian, who, when asking for Septimius’s [Col. 0017B] books, used to say, “Give me the master” [Note: [Col. 0017D] St. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*]; and our own countrymen, heralded by the illustrious Bossuet of Meaux, who whenever he summons Tertullian seems to burst forth with these or like words: “A great man, a weighty man, powerful in authority and force.”

Great, then, is the name of QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN. But how much greater it would have been had that Lucifer of the African Church, who rose in the morning, not fallen like lightning from heaven; had he who wounded nations not crashed to earth; had he not said in his heart, “I will ascend above the height of the clouds” [Note: [Col. 0017D] Isa. 14:12, 14]! For like Satan, cast down by the lightning of pride, he fell; and once fallen, whether he rose again no one even dares ask. Solomon is questioned; Origen is debated; Tertullian is passed over in silence. Yet he wasted away in prolonged old age, and he lacked no long interval for repentance [Col. 0017C]. His last writings all too strongly persuade and convict us that he remained miserably obstinate and, as if maddened by the single blow that felled him, continued for almost forty years—until nearly his eightieth year—fierce in hostile anger against the Church and threatening missiles even with a failing hand.

Who, then, would not fear and shudder at God’s unsearchable judgments? Who would have thought that so auspicious a beginning for TERTULLIAN would end thus? Once the *Apology* had been issued at the beginning of the century and the other addresses for the Christian cause delivered; once confessors had thereby been strengthened or martyrs raised to the laurel; once the heat of persecutions had cooled and the Church breathed a little; and once she had at last been settled in peace for almost forty years, a new order of affairs and a more pleasant face of the times were dawning. With eager ears, both Gentiles and Christians attended [Col. 0017D] those who preached peace and good things. What Irenaeus was to do in Gaul, Clement in Egypt, and Hippolytus in Latium, Tertullian seemed about to do in Africa and throughout the West: so that, the common people having been won, nobles and wise men too might be won, and the Church built from bottom to top and the Christian world established. This, unless I am mistaken, was the splendid role for which Tertullian was destined. What more? He fell, dragged down to hell, into the depth of the pit [Note: [Col. 0017D] Isa. 14:15]. This, then, was contained in God’s unsearchable [Col. 0018A] decree: that this new Church, growing through so many wounds, after at last triumphing over Jews, pagans, and Gnostics, should strike against this stumbling-stone; that when she deserved to be refreshed by the aid of so great a spirit, she should lose him through his fall, endure him as an enemy, and mourn him as he resisted and insulted his mother’s bosom for forty years. We should no longer ask, as many have wished, whether he benefited the Church more than he harmed her, but rather whether or not he benefited himself unto life. He is not a man of the Church, though returned from so many labors and battles! Yet would that we might trust more confidently in the pious prayers scattered repeatedly through his works and fulfill his wish when he said to catechumens: “Therefore, blessed ones whom the grace of God awaits, when you ascend from that most holy bath of new birth and for the first time spread out your [Col. 0018B] hands before your Mother with your brethren, ask of the Father, ask of the Lord, special riches of grace and distributions of charisms,” adding, “‘Ask and you shall receive,’ he says. For you have sought and found; you have knocked, and it has been opened to you. I ask only that, when you pray, you remember also TERTULLIAN the sinner” [Note: [Col. 0018C] *On Baptism* 20, final words. Judgments concerning the greatest men often vary so much that some raise them to heaven while others thrust them to the bottom. So it has generally happened to our Tertullian: as he has not lacked detractors, so he has found many champions and exceedingly generous admirers. Some have thought all his surviving works written during his Montanism, while others deny that he fell into the criminal communion of Montanus. There have even been those who celebrate Tertullian as a martyr, said to have suffered under Decius. On these and other matters concerning Tertullian’s history and authority, cf. *Magdeburg Centuries*, cent. III, ch. 12; Joachim Zentgrav, *Exercise on Tertullian’s Fall to the Montanists*, Strasbourg, 1704, quarto; Timann Gessell, *Sacred and Ecclesiastical History of the New Testament*, p. 299; Pierre Allix, *Dissertation on the Life and Writings of Tertullian*, Paris, 1680, octavo; De la Motte, *History of Tertullian and Origen*, Lyon, 1701, octavo; Nicolas Le [Col. 0018D] Nourry, dissertation on Tertullian’s *Apology*, books *To the Nations*, and *To Scapula*, below, vol. I, col. 705 ff.; Johann W. Hopfmann, dissertation arguing that all surviving works of Q. S. F. Tertullian appear to have been written during Montanism, Wittenberg, 1738, quarto; J. A. Noesselt, Dissertation III on the true date and teaching of the surviving writings of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, Halle, 1757; the same author’s three commentaries concerning ecclesiastical history, Halle, 1817; Giuseppe Antonio Cantova, two dissertations on Septimius and St. Epiphanius, Milan, 1783, octavo; H. Chr. Baltenstedt, *Tertullian’s Intellectual Abilities, Religious Knowledge, and Theology*, three commentaries, Helmstedt, 1785, octavo; August Neander, *Antignostikus: The Spirit of Tertullian and Introduction to His Writings*, Berlin, 1825; Friedrich Münster, *Beginnings of the African Church*, Copenhagen, 1829, quarto; C. Joseph Hefele, “Tertullian as Apologist,” in Drey et al., *Tübingen Theological Quarterly*, 1838; J. A. Möhler, *Patrology, or History of Christian Literature*, edited by D. F. X. Reithmayr, Regensburg, 1840.]

## Article II. On the Use of Tertullian

We think that a still sharper judgment is altogether required for the proper use of this most ancient Father than was just required for discerning TERTULLIAN’s true authority. In his writings, therefore, one must again consider both the author’s condition, now Catholic and now Montanist, and the books’ doctrine or historical information, each either [Col. 0018C] sacred or profane. His sacred doctrine concerns dogmas [Col. 0019A] of faith, while his historical information concerns the practices then customary in the Church, that is, matters of discipline.

Lest these preliminary warnings grow beyond measure, it is not our task to traverse each item separately or enumerate exactly everything he said rightly or rashly concerning sacred exegesis, dogmatic or moral theology, the Church’s rites and customs, or the history of times and opinions.

Only some principal heads of Tertullian’s doctrine and his gravest errors must be indicated in summary, and the more notable passages of his works chiefly useful for exegetical, dogmatic, moral, liturgical, and ascetical purposes must be pointed out. Thus anyone devoted to patristic study may more eagerly equip himself to examine them fully, and a safer and easier road may especially be opened to younger students of theology and [Col. 0019B] patrology.

Before all else TERTULLIAN proclaims in a full voice that the whole edifice of Christian faith rests upon the firmest historical truth and the venerable authority of tradition. These are the inescapable facts upon which the whole Christian reality hangs, as by a chain of bronze and gold: God the Father sends his Son into this world to build the Christian Church. Jesus Christ, for the same end, sends his Apostles and teaches them all the truths that supply this building with its foundation and growth. The Apostles hand on the doctrine received from the Lord to all the churches to which they are sent. Those churches hold that apostolic doctrine most firmly and communicate it to others that saw none of the Apostles [Col. 0019C]. All those churches, united with one another, constitute one and the same body in the unity of the same doctrine and the same faith. Who, then, will desert this Church, the immovable pillar of truth, to embrace sects separated from her? This is Tertullian’s celebrated argument from prescription, the chief weapon of all Christian polemic, surely the most beautiful and invincible ever employed among disputants,
Thus, says that great man, “so many and such great churches are that one first Church from the Apostles, from which they all come” (*Prescription* 20).—“We have the Lord’s Apostles as our authorities. They themselves chose nothing by their own judgment to introduce, but faithfully assigned to the nations the teaching received from Christ” (ibid. 6).—“No nation is now [Col. 0019D] foreign to God, since the Gospel flashes over all the earth and to the ends of the world” (*On the Soul* 49). “Taught innocence by God, we know it perfectly, as revealed by a perfect teacher, and guard it faithfully, as commanded by a judge who cannot be despised” (*Apology* 45). Yet this sect will not fail; know that it is built up more when it seems to be cut down (*To Scapula* 5). “We become more numerous whenever you mow us down: the blood of Christians is seed” (*Apology* 49, vol. I, col. 535A).

But remember that here the Lord left his keys to Peter and, through him, to the Church (*Scorpiace* 10). “You have Rome, from which authority is ready for us too. How blessed is that Church, upon which the Apostles poured out their whole doctrine together with their blood!” (*Prescription* 36, vol. II, col. 49).

[Col. 0020A] This one, apostolic, catholic, holy, immortal, and visible Church—that is, the Roman Church—to which belongs the right to teach all nations, receives her doctrine from one source, namely the word of God, whether written or handed down. By her own right it belongs to her both to discern, confirm, and sanction traditions and to establish the Scriptures, their inspiration, interpretation, and canon. “For where it shall appear that the truth of Christian teaching and faith resides, there will also be the truth of the Scriptures and their expositions and of all Christian traditions” (*Prescription* 19, vol. II, col. 31).

Little need be added to what we said earlier from Tertullian about the inspiration of Scripture, its adorable fullness, its apostolic interpretation, and the legitimate canon. We note only that sacred books [Col. 0020B] must be used so that heretics, abusing parables, do not fashion from them the very substance of doctrines; one should not therefore appeal to them or establish the contest in matters where victory is either nonexistent, uncertain, or no better than uncertain (*Prescription* 19, vol. II, col. 31). One must first examine to whom the Scriptures belong, by whom, through whom, when, and to whom was delivered the teaching by which men become Christians. God permitted—indeed willed—the Scriptures to be arranged so as to supply material to heretics, who cannot exist without Scriptures (ibid. 39, col. 53). Also notable and very famous in Tertullian is the passage about the authentic writings of the Apostles, on which highly learned men have offered various conjectures (ibid. 36, col. 49) [Note: [Col. 0020D] See Pamelius’s notes at the cited passage; Hugo Grotius, *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* III, notes; Dodwell, dissertation, vol. I, §41; Richard Simon, *Critical History of the New Testament*, ch. 4, p. 40; Nathaniel Lardner, *Credibility of the Gospel History*, part II, ch. 27, §8, pp. 501–508; Lumper, “Life and Writings of Tertullian,” in *Historia theologico-critico-literaria SS. Patrum*, vol. VII, pp. 257–262]. Nor should we omit what he discusses in many places concerning both the translation of the Seventy [Note: [Col. 0020D] Cf. Christoph Cellarius, Dissertation XIII on the Seventy Translators; Simone de Magistris, dissertations appended to the edition of the Septuagint version of Daniel from the Chigi codex; Lumper, cited work, p. 666 ff.; consult below Dom Le Nourry’s dissertation, ch. 6, arts. 2–3, p. 787 ff.] and the most ancient Latin translations of the Bible, already current in the West [Col. 0020C] and received with greater or equal authority than the Greek codices.

Having laid these foundations of the Church, Tertullian then incidentally overturns the perishable structures of the heretics: now reproaching their crimes against God’s word and their slaughter of the Scriptures; now showing that heresy, idolatry, and profane philosophy differ little from one another; now describing marks of heresy utterly alien to the true Church (*Against Marcion* V.17; IV.19; *Prescription* 7, 17, 37, 40, 41, 44). By the single argument from prescription he pierces and crushes with an incurable wound all heresies, present or future, including Montanism and Tertullianism themselves.

[Col. 0020D] This mode of argument is invincibly valid not only against the Gnostics, as Neander wished in a recent work [Note: [Col. 0020D] *Antignostikus: The Spirit of Tertullian*, etc.], [Col. 0021A] but even against all heretics, without excepting the newest Protestant sects. Modern and ancient heretics display the same chief errors: they desert the unity and authority of the apostolic Church; despising tradition, they appeal to Scripture alone; they interpret and break up the canon at will. The leaders of new sects display no more lawful signs of divine authority than Marcion or Valentinus once did; before or after them they have not a trace or jot of apostolic succession. Moreover their doctrines are rejected alike by the Roman Church and by all churches throughout the world, whether Greek or Asian [Note: [Col. 0021D] See J. A. Möhler, *Patrology, or History of Christian Literature*, vol. II, p. 354, French trans., Paris, 1843].

Next, to return to Tertullian, one of the three formulas of faith Septimius inserted in his books would have to be recited, or at least compared with the creeds published by Irenaeus, Gregory Thaumaturgus, and others, were we not constrained by the limits of a preface.

[Col. 0021B] We shall deal briefly with Septimius on God and his attributes, since we give below Dom Le Nourry’s very rich and extensive dissertation. Go there, therefore, and see by what sixfold argument Tertullian proves that God exists (ch. 7, art. 1, col. 804 ff.); in what sense he says God is known to men although invisible, incomprehensible, and beyond estimation; what he says of this true and living God’s knowledge, wisdom, and eternity (col. 809 ff.); and what Septimius means by his often repeated phrase that God is a body, though God is spirit (col. 811 ff.) [Note: [Col. 0021D] Cf. Noël Alexandre, *Ecclesiastical History*, second century, art. VIII, vol. III; Cantova, dissertation on the anthropomorphism of Septimius and Epiphanius, Milan, 1773, octavo]. Tertullian likewise declares clearly that God is nothing if not good (*Scorpiace* 5). Against Marcion he defends God’s justice as well as his goodness (*Against Marcion* II.11), though he calls goodness innate in God and justice accidental—that is, adapted to the creature in its effect and subsequent to sin (ibid.). Hence he argues splendidly against Hermogenes that God created everything from nothing and that matter is not eternal (*Against Hermogenes* 19 ff.).

[Col. 0021C] Tertullian speaks so clearly and exactly of the Trinity of divine Persons and their consubstantiality that nothing further could be desired. As clearly as the theologians and doctors of our age, he distinguishes three divine persons and predicates actual existence of each in the unity of one and the same nature. From these points the Catholic Church’s doctrine concerning this mystery is surely constituted.

[Col. 0021D] (Cf. *Against Hermogenes* 45, vol. II, col. 237; *Against Praxeas* 2, col. 156; 3, col. 157; 4, col. 159; 8, col. 159; 11, col. 166; 12, col. 167; 13, col. 168; 26, col. 188; 30, col. 195; 31, col. 196.)

For the Son’s divinity, generation, consubstantiality, sonship, and eternity, and for Christ as God and man foretold by the prophets, clothed in flesh and dwelling in Judea, dead, restored to life, and assumed into heaven, we again refer [Col. 0022A] to Dom Le Nourry’s excellent work (below, ch. 9, cols. 853–867), which splendidly crushes the obstinate inventions of Marcion, Apelles, and the other Gnostics.

The same author explains with precision what Tertullian says about angels and demons, ibid., ch. 10, cols. 868–891.

Discussing man in various writings, Tertullian first teaches that man is the handiwork of God the creator; consists of two substances, body and soul; was made as a work in the likeness of the Son and Spirit and as God’s image; is possessor of the whole universe; and was constructed in it by God so that he might be lord while made by the Lord (*Against Marcion* IV.37; V.17; *Against Praxeas* 12; *On the Shows* 2; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 5–6).

[Col. 0022B] Although to some who taste his writings only in fragments Tertullian seems to philosophize about man and the soul in a rather coarse and material way, anyone who looks deeply into his thought will rightly judge that his acute gaze penetrated the difficult and most subtle mysteries of anthropology and psychology [Note: [Col. 0022D] See this lucidly explained in J. A. Möhler’s already praised work, *Patrology*, vol. II, p. 364, French trans.].

Like Plato, he distinguishes a twofold part of the soul, one intelligent and the seat of wisdom, the other blind and devoid of understanding (λόγικον (“rational”) and ἄλογον (“irrational”)). But he denies, in the Gnostic sense, that soul and spirit are distinct: “If you separate spirit and soul, separate their works too; let both perform something apart, the soul by itself and the spirit by itself; let the soul live without the spirit and the spirit breathe without the soul.… Therefore they will not be two things that cannot be divided” (*On the Soul* 10, vol. II, col. 663).

[Col. 0022C] Since soul is the same as spirit, it necessarily follows that the soul’s properties are the same as the spirit’s. Hence the soul is simple and separable from the body: they are two things and diverse. One should therefore not stumble over the fact that he also calls it corporeal and shaped—that is, subsisting in form and reality. Elsewhere he confesses that it was born from God’s breath, Christian by nature, simple in substance, endowed with free will, rational, and immortal—not by grace, as almost all the ancients held, but by its own nature—and that after this present life it either suffers in the underworld or rejoices in heaven (*On the Soul* 58). Yet elsewhere he teaches that before the universal resurrection the soul is neither punished nor rejoices, and further that certain sins must be expiated by us immediately after death while awaiting the resurrection.

[Col. 0022D] Tertullian wonderfully glorifies man’s flesh itself, and perhaps no Father can be found who said more remarkable things about it. “Whatever shape the clay was taking, Christ was being contemplated as the man who was to be.… Thus that clay, already then putting on the image of Christ who was to come in the flesh, was not only God’s work but also his pledge” (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 6, vol. II, col. 802).

[Col. 0023A]

Again he sketches in these outlines the same flesh recreated from sin and rising again with the revivified soul: “When the soul is joined to God, it [the flesh] is what makes it possible for the soul to be joined. The flesh is washed so that the soul may be cleansed; the flesh is anointed so that the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is signed so that the soul too may be fortified; the flesh is overshadowed by the laying on of hands so that the soul too may be illuminated by the Spirit; the flesh feeds upon Christ’s body and blood so that the soul too may be fattened upon God” (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 8). “When the soul marries the Spirit, the flesh follows as part of the dowry, and is now no longer the soul’s servant but the Spirit’s. O blessed marriage, if it admits no adultery!” (*On the Soul* 41). Finally, he splendidly describes the triumph of the flesh exulting with Christ: “He [Jesus Christ] … keeps the deposit of the flesh also in himself, the earnest of the entire sum. For as he left us the earnest of the Spirit, so he received from us the earnest of the flesh and carried into heaven the pledge of the whole sum that is one day to be brought there. Be confident, flesh and blood: in Christ you have taken possession of heaven and the kingdom of God” (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 51, vol. II, col. 869).

[Col. 0023B] He is no less successful in describing the soul in its fallen and stained state than in its whole and innocent state. He admits original sin and teaches admirably how widely the primal stain crept and infected all: “The human soul, like a shoot derived for propagation from the rootstock Adam and entrusted to the woman’s generative furrows, will sprout with all its equipment,” etc. (*On the Soul* 19). “You pronounce Satan … by whom man was deceived from the beginning into transgressing God’s command and therefore delivered to death, and who thereafter made the entire race, infected from his seed, the transmitter also of his condemnation” (*On the Testimony of the Soul* 3, vol. I, col. 618).

[Col. 0023C] Let us now hear him sing, as if in a new song, of Christ’s birth on earth: “The inaugurator of a new birth had to be born in a new way.… This is the new birth, when man is born in God—in that man in whom God was born—having taken flesh of the ancient seed without the ancient seed, so that he might reform it by new seed, that is spiritually, purified by the exclusion of its ancient stains” (*On the Flesh of Christ* 17, vol. II, col. 781).

[Col. 0023D]

To Tertullian the humanity and kindness of the Savior appeared in flesh, the Word made flesh, as the beginning and end of all mysteries of faith, the summit and foundation of the new creation, the unique center of the dawning world, from which every good flows to us and to which all things that bind God and men return and are joined. Hence Septimius’s vehement and ardent impulse, by which he is swept into wonder at the incarnate Word and attacks and repels the impious attempts of anyone who assails even lightly this great mystery of godliness; through excessive amazement at Christ born and suffering he seems to go mad. “But now,” he says to Marcion, “answer here, murderer of truth: was God not truly crucified? Did he not truly die, since he was truly crucified? Was he not truly raised?… Spare the one hope of the whole world. Why destroy the shame necessary to faith? Whatever is unworthy of God profits me. I am safe if I am not ashamed of my Lord. ‘Whoever is ashamed of me,’ he says, ‘of him shall I also be ashamed.’ I find no other occasions of shame that, through contempt for shame, prove me rightly shameless and happily foolish. The Son of God was born: it causes no shame, because it is shameful. And the Son of God died: it is wholly credible because it is absurd; and, buried, he rose again: it is certain because it is impossible” (*On the Flesh of Christ* 5, vol. II, col. 763).

[Col. 0024A] Let this suffice to make known how greatly Tertullian can aid the exposition of dogmatic faith. There are very many other dogmas which he asserted with equal abundance and the very learned Dom Le Nourry commented upon more abundantly; you will find them brought to light again in the course of this volume.

Nothing shows us better how admirably and correctly Septimius understood the true and sincere notion of our active, practical faith than the extensive description of liturgical discipline and dense abundance of ancient rites scattered throughout his writings. Since passages displaying the discipline and customs of the first centuries are of the greatest value, we shall present as accurately as possible each liturgical document mentioned in Septimius’s writings.

[Col. 0024B] To begin with baptism, this ancient doctor first teaches the laborious works to be undertaken before baptism: frequent prayers, fasts, kneelings, and vigils, with at least private confession of all past sins. Next come the things belonging to the conferral of baptism: triple immersion and invocation of the three persons of the most holy Trinity. Last come those that follow: anointing after the washing, laying on of hands and, as many have rightly thought, the conferral of the Holy Spirit through the sacrament of confirmation, and even participation in the Eucharist [Col. 0024C] (cf. *On Baptism*).

Tertullian composed a particular treatise *On Repentance*, so beautiful and elegant that some have wrongly dared deny it to him. In it he admirably describes all the rites and dispositions of penance, public or private, performed before or after baptism, as may be seen to some extent below, where he speaks of *exomologesis*, which “when it casts man down, raises him all the more; when it makes him squalid, renders him the more cleansed; when it accuses, excuses; when it condemns, absolves” (*On Repentance* 9, vol. I, col. 1244).

Discussing the Eucharist, Tertullian teaches that Christians customarily assembled very early in the morning to celebrate this mystery; that laypeople received the sacrament from the hand of those presiding; that they received it into their own hands and carried it into their homes so as to partake fasting under one species; and that the newly baptized, whether infants or adults, were granted the same benefit.

[Col. 0024D] Tertullian professes everywhere, especially in that golden book *On Prescriptions*—which he perhaps wrote while still Catholic but published when already a Montanist—that the ecclesiastical hierarchy is distinct from the laity, furnished with various orders having their own duties and proper names, disrupted or utterly extinguished among heretics, but preserved unshaken among Catholics in perpetual succession from the Apostles to the latest times. There he censures the heretics of his time because “their ordinations are rash, frivolous, and inconstant: one man is bishop today and another tomorrow; today a deacon is tomorrow a reader; today a presbyter is tomorrow a layman” (ibid. 41, vol. II, cols. 56–57).

[Col. 0025A] With the Apostle he calls marriage a great sacrament; but he teaches that secret unions, neither first professed before the Church nor requested from a monogamous bishop, priests, and deacons, are to be reckoned alongside adultery and fornication (*On Modesty* 4, vol. II, col. 987). Everyone knows this passage: “How shall we suffice to recount the happiness of that marriage which the Church joins, the offering confirms, the blessing seals, angels announce, and the Father ratifies?” (*To His Wife* II.9, vol. I, col. 1302).

Finally, Tertullian records the following about prayer, private and public, sacred assemblies, and the Lord’s Supper. Christians prayed looking toward heaven, [Col. 0025B] with hands extended in the image and form of Christ fixed to the cross, head uncovered, face and voice lowered, turned toward the east. Before prayer they commonly washed their hands and removed their cloak. Some sat while praying; others, in the sight of God and while the angel of prayer still stood, thought it more reverent to stand themselves. They refreshed one another with alternating psalms and hymns and did not withhold the kiss of peace after prayer. They prayed without a prompter leading aloud, from the breast and the heart’s inward affection. They gathered with joy on Sunday, then attended to readings from the sacred books, reciting both writings of the Prophets and memoirs of the Apostles, and heard the president’s admonition. Then they received corrections and divine censure, offenders being banished from participation in prayer [Col. 0025C] and assembly and every sacred fellowship. Bishops presided over these assemblies and, under their authority, approved and elected presbyters and deacons, called elders. From these men and no others they received, at mealtime and even in gatherings before dawn, the sacrament of the Eucharist, either to consume or to reserve for consumption at home. Besides Sunday there were days of fasting and stations, on which they prayed longer, bending their knees with all other signs of humility and remaining longer at the altar after receiving the Lord’s body. There were also more solemn hours of the day—the third, sixth, and ninth—besides the appointed prayers owed at the coming of light and night; these customarily preceded food and bathing and interrupted the night watches. Otherwise nothing at all is prescribed, [Col. 0025D] except prayer at every time and place. Nothing, however, is more famous than the supper called the *Agape*. They do not recline until prayer to God has first been tasted. They eat as much as the hungry and temperate take; they drink as much as benefits the chaste. After supper water is offered for washing hands and lamps are lit until daylight. Then, the table removed, each person is invited to stand in the midst of the whole gathering and circle and sing a hymn, whether drawn from Holy Scripture or elicited from his own talent. Prayers then return thanks to God, and they depart with the same care for modesty and chastity, as men who have eaten discipline rather than merely supper. Christians offered this victim—devoted from the heart, fed by faith, tended by truth, whole in innocence, pure in chastity, crowned with agape, led to God’s altar with the procession of good works amid psalms and hymns—one that would obtain all things from God.

[Col. 0026A] We proceed more closely and rapidly, as promised, through Tertullian’s use in moral and ascetical matters. First one should investigate what the Christians’ morals were. “That we live by the discipline of divine patience,” says our author, “can be sufficiently plain to you, since so great a multitude of men—almost the greater part of every city—conduct ourselves in silence and modesty, perhaps better known individually than collectively, recognizable from nothing but the correction of our vices” (*To Scapula* 2, vol. I, col. 700).

[Col. 0026B] How great was Christian charity, which swept even pagans into admiration: “‘See,’ they say, ‘how they love one another, and how ready they are to die for each other!’ For the pagans themselves are readier to kill each other” (*Apology* 39, vol. I, col. 471). How great the chastity of Christian spouses, the integrity of many celibates, and the innocence of virgins! “For what distinction do we display except the first wisdom, by which we do not adore the frivolous works of human hands; temperance, by which we abstain from another’s property; chastity, which we do not defile even with our eyes; mercy, by which we bend over the needy; truth itself, by which we give offense; and liberty itself, for which we know how to die?” (*To the Nations* I.4, vol. I, col. 961). Who has not heard how invincibly Tertullian compares the finest examples of philosophers’ modesty, equanimity, fidelity, and simplicity [Col. 0026C] with Christian conduct (*Apology* 46)? Among the other Christian virtues there shone especially the observance of fasts, as diligent as it was severe, by which Christians differed from pagans no less than by their other virtues. It did not satisfy them to placate God’s wrath by such stern and austere fasting only in public calamities, but “rolling even in sackcloth and ashes,” says Tertullian, “we assail heaven with our importunity” (*Apology* 40). Here should be mentioned the beautiful things our author composed in special books about prayer, the virtue of patience, women’s vain dress and adornment, unlawful attendance at shows, idolatry and its various forms, and the magnanimity of martyrdom, surpassing all others.

[Col. 0026D] As a crown, let selected ascetical teachings from Tertullian’s works be appended.

**The Christian fears God, not men.**—“We who are judged under God, the watcher of all, and foresee eternal punishment from him, rightly are the only ones to seek innocence: because of the fullness of his knowledge, the impossibility of concealment, and the magnitude of torment—not prolonged but everlasting—fearing him whom the judge of those who fear must himself fear; fearing God, not the proconsul” (*Apology* 45, vol. I, col. 500).

**God urges us to repentance.**—“Is it good to repent, or not? Why ponder it? God commands it. Yet he does not merely command; he also exhorts. He invites with salvation as reward; when he swears, even saying ‘As I live,’ he desires to be believed. O blessed are we, for whose sake God swears! O most wretched, if we do not believe even the Lord when he swears!” (*On Repentance* 4, vol. I, col. 1233).

[Col. 0027A] **God kindly receives the sinner returning to him.**—“Who must we understand this Father to be? God, surely: no one is so much a father, no one so tender. Therefore he will receive you, his son, although you have squandered what you received from him and returned naked, because you returned; and he will rejoice more in your return than in another’s sobriety. But only if you repent from your soul … if you leave the swine, the unclean herd, if you seek your Father again though offended, saying, ‘I have sinned, Father, and am no longer worthy to be called yours.’ Confession of sins lightens as much as concealment aggravates. Confession is the counsel of satisfaction; concealment, of obstinacy” (ibid. [Col. 0027B] 8, vol. I, col. 1243).

“*Exomologesis* is the discipline of casting down and humbling a man, prescribing a manner of life that entices mercy. Concerning dress and food it commands lying in sackcloth and ashes, covering the body with filth, casting down the soul with sorrows, and changing by mournful treatment those things through which it sinned. It bids one know only plain food and drink, for the soul’s sake rather than the belly’s; generally to nourish prayers with fasts; to groan, weep, and cry out day and night to the Lord your God; to cast oneself at the presbyters’ feet, kneel before God’s beloved, and enjoin upon all the brethren the embassy of one’s supplication” (ibid. 9, vol. I, col. 1242).

**Repentance that does not cast off delicacies deserves ridicule.**—“Add to the expense; seek out the enormous fattening of game birds; clarify old wine. When someone asks for whom you lavish these things, say, ‘I have sinned against God and am in danger of perishing eternally. Therefore I now hang in suspense, waste away, and torment myself, that I may reconcile to myself the God whom I injured by sinning’” (ibid. 11, col. 1216).

[Col. 0027C] **To a Christian the world is like a prison.**—“If we reflect that the world itself is more truly a prison, we shall understand that you have gone out of prison rather than entered one. The world has greater darkness, which blinds men’s hearts; it puts on heavier chains, which bind men’s very souls; it breathes out worse uncleanness, the lusts of men. Finally, the world contains more accused persons, namely the entire human race. In the end it awaits the judgments not of the proconsul but of God” (*To the Martyrs* 2, vol. II, col. 622).

[Col. 0027D] **Riches are to be despised after Christ’s example.**—“In almost every place the Lord’s Scriptures admonish us to despise the age. No greater exhortation to contempt for money is available than that the Lord himself is found amid no riches: he always justifies the poor and condemns the rich. Thus he prepared disdain for wealth in advance against the loss that tries patience, showing through the rejection of riches that injuries to them too must be reckoned as nothing” (*On Patience* 7, vol. I, col. 1260).

**Why one should not grieve at the death of friends.**—“Since the resurrection of the dead is certain, grief of mind is needless, and so is the impatience of grief. Why grieve if you do not believe he has perished? What you think death is a departure. One who goes ahead is not to be mourned, though certainly to be missed. [Col. 0028A] That longing too must be tempered by patience. Why bear immoderately the departure of one whom you will soon follow? Moreover, impatience in such a matter both bodes ill for our hope and betrays faith. We injure Christ when we fail to accept calmly those he has called away, as though they were to be pitied” (ibid. 9, col. 1264).

**Praises of patience.**—“God is a fully competent trustee for patience. If you deposit an injury with him, he is avenger; if a loss, restorer; if pain, physician; if death, reviver. How much is patience permitted, since it has God as debtor? And deservedly: it protects all that pleases him and intervenes in all his commands. It fortifies faith, governs peace, assists love, teaches humility, awaits repentance, ratifies *exomologesis*, rules the flesh, preserves the spirit, bridles the tongue, restrains the hand, tramples temptations, drives away scandals, completes martyrdoms, consoles the poor, moderates the rich, does not overstrain the weak or consume the strong, delights the believer, invites the Gentile, commends servant to master and master to God, adorns woman and approves man; it is loved in the child, praised in youth, revered in age; in every sex and every age it is beautiful” (ibid. 15, col. 1270).

[Col. 0028B] **Against shows and theaters.**—“We are commanded to put away all immodesty. In this way, then, we are also separated from the theater, which is the private council-chamber of immodesty, where nothing is approved except what is disapproved elsewhere” (*On the Shows* 17, vol. I, col. 649).

[Col. 0028C] **Stage performers are always infamous.**—“They exclude stage performers from all honors and ornaments alike.… What a confession this is of an evil thing, when its most popular agents are not without a mark of disgrace!” (ibid. 22, col. 654).

**Christians are forbidden to attend comedies.**—“Will he think about God at that time, placed where there is nothing of God?… Will he learn chastity while staring at mimes? Indeed, at every show no greater stumbling-block will occur than the more elaborate dress of women and men, the very agreement, alliance, or dissension in applause, fanning between them the sparks of lust through their interaction. Finally, no one entering a show first thinks of anything except seeing and being seen.… May God turn from his own people so great a desire for deadly pleasure” (ibid. 25, col. 656).

[Col. 0028D] **The true pleasures of Christians in this age.**—“Now, if you think this span of life must be spent in delights, why are you so ungrateful that you neither account sufficient nor acknowledge the many great pleasures God has given you? What is more delightful than reconciliation with God the Father and Lord? Than revelation of truth? Than recognition of errors? Than forgiveness of so many former crimes? What greater pleasure than disgust with pleasure itself, contempt for the whole age, true freedom, a whole conscience, a sufficient life, and no fear of death?” (ibid. 29, col. 659).

**Evil priests are worse than the Jews.**—“What wickedness! The Jews laid hands on Christ once; these impious priests [Col. 0029A] assail his body daily. O hands that ought to be cut off! Let them consider whether it was already said by way of likeness, ‘If your hand scandalizes you, cut it off.’ What hands should be cut off more than those by which the Lord’s body is scandalized?” (*On Idolatry* 7, vol. I, col. 669).

**A Christian woman neglects—indeed dreads—pleasing men.**—“You who are perfect, that is, Christian and chaste, should know that a desire to be desired must not merely be undesired but abhorred: first, because the effort to please through beauty does not come from an uncorrupted conscience, for we know beauty naturally invites lust. Why, then, arouse that evil against yourself? Why invite what you profess yourself a stranger to? Further, we must not open a path to temptations, which sometimes—may God keep this from his own—prevail by pressing upon us, or at least move a stumbling-block in the spirit” (*On the Dress of Women* II.2, vol. I, col. 1517).

[Col. 0029B] **What kind of crime it is to use cosmetics.**—“In adorning the body one must not go beyond what simple and sufficient cleanliness desires, beyond what pleases the Lord. For women sin against him when they anoint the skin with preparations and stain the cheeks with rouge.… Evidently God’s workmanship displeases them: in themselves they convict and criticize the craftsman of all. For they criticize when they correct, when they add, taking those additions, of course, from the rival craftsman—that is, the devil” (ibid. 5, col. 1327).

**Image of the Christian woman.**—“Come forth now, you who are arrayed in the preparations and ornaments of the Apostles.… Submit your head to your husbands and you will be adorned enough; occupy your hands with wool and plant your feet at home, and they will please more than if clad in gold. Clothe yourselves in the silk of uprightness, the fine linen of holiness, the purple of chastity. Painted in this fashion, you will have God as your lover” (ibid. 13).

[Col. 0029C] **A Christian must flee the pleasures of the world.**—“You are a stranger to this world, a citizen of the Jerusalem above.… You have nothing to do with the joys of the age; indeed, you owe the contrary. ‘For the world will rejoice, but you will mourn.’ And he calls those who mourn blessed.… Everything in the age is imaginary and nothing true” (*On the Soldier’s Crown* 13, vol. II, col. 96).

**No prescription runs against truth.**—“No one can prescribe against truth: neither length of time, patronage of persons, nor privilege of regions. From these, indeed, custom generally takes its origin in some ignorance or simplicity, is strengthened into use through succession, and so is asserted against truth. But our Lord Christ called himself truth, not custom” (*On the Veiling of Virgins* 1, vol. II, col. 889).

[Col. 0029D] **Faith is not proved from persons, but persons from faith.**—“We do not prove faith from persons, but persons from faith. No one is wise unless faithful; no one great unless Christian; and no one Christian unless he has persevered to the end” (*Prescription against Heretics* 3, vol. II, col. 15).

**No knowledge other than that of Jesus Christ is to be sought.**—“We have no need of curiosity after Christ Jesus, nor of inquiry after the Gospel. When we believe, we desire to believe nothing further. For this we believe first: that there is nothing further which we ought to believe” (ibid. 17, vol. II, col. 20).

[Col. 0030A]

### On the continence of clerics

“How many men and women, then, in the ecclesiastical orders are esteemed for continence—those who have preferred to be wedded to God, who have established the honor of their flesh, and who have now dedicated themselves as children of that modesty, killing within themselves the desire of lust and all that could not be admitted within paradise. . . . . . . . Accordingly, among us it is prescribed more fully and explicitly that those chosen for the priestly order ought to have been married only once” (*On the Exhortation to Chastity*, vol. II, ch. 7, col. 922; ch. 13, col. 930).

### Man is the image of God through free will

“Man was not fashioned in the likeness of God in respect of his face, but in respect of the substance which he drew from God himself, that is, the soul, [Col. 0030B] which corresponds to the form of God and is marked by the freedom and power of its own choice. The law itself also confirmed this condition of man. For a law would not be imposed upon one who did not have in his own power the obedience due to the law; nor, again, would the threat of death be attached to transgression if contempt for the law were not also attributed to the freedom of man’s choice. . . . And otherwise, what sense would it make for man, possessing the whole world, not first to rule over the passion of his own mind—to be lord of others but the slave of himself?” (*Against Marcion*, book II, chs. 5–6, vol. II, cols. 290–291).

### God is to be loved as Father and feared as Lord

“The justice of God is the fullness of his divinity itself, presenting God as perfect, both Father and Lord: Father in clemency, Lord in discipline; Father in gentle power, Lord in stern power; Father, to be loved dutifully; [Col. 0030C] Lord, to be feared necessarily. He is to be loved because he prefers the repentance of the sinner to his death, and feared because he does not will sinners who no longer repent to belong to him. The law therefore defines both: ‘You shall love God,’ and ‘you shall fear God.’ It set the one before the obedient person and the other before the transgressor. In everything God meets you, the same God striking and healing, putting to death and giving life, humbling and exalting, creating evils and making peace” (*ibid.*, chs. 13–14, cols. 300–301).

Thus far, from all that we have gathered about Tertullian’s doctrine, we seem to have wished earnestly to prove that using him is good and very profitable. But we would now rightly be blamed if we offered no advice for guarding against a bad use of him. Just as we have established how much benefit his doctrine can bring, so from his [Col. 0030D] errors we must infer how much harm they may cause and with what keen judgment his writings must be sifted. Some paradoxes he shares with the Montanists; others are so peculiarly his own that he thereby became a founder of heresy and produced followers of those errors who were called Tertullianists after their author.

It is certain and beyond doubt that Tertullian not only assented to the errors and ravings of the Montanists, but also promoted them with the utmost ardor. Of this kind are all the passages in which he everywhere and shamelessly advertises his Paraclete; those in which he not only condemns second marriages but calls them an enormity greater than every crime; and those in which he teaches that, when persecution rages, it is unlawful either to flee or to buy oneself free with money. Yet my spirit recoils from recounting the insults that arrogant doctor poured out against the Church of God, attacking Catholics, whom he repeatedly calls “psychics,” that is, animal and carnal men. He charges them with indulging their bellies and practicing indecencies while celebrating agapes, and with driving confessors held in prison to intemperance. Here you have the chief errors of Tertullian the Montanist, from which he himself seized an occasion to reveal his hatred and his bitterly hostile disposition toward Catholics.

We come to the errors proper and peculiar to Tertullian as a heresiarch. He teaches that, when persecution rages, it is unlawful either to flee or to redeem oneself with money [Col. 0031A]. To avoid extending the discussion without limit, we refer the detailed weighing of these points to the notes of Pamelius, Rigaltius, and the other commentators that will be appended below [Col. 0031B]. It will suffice to bring forward the more notable ones. First, he dares to profess that the Virgin Mother of God lost her virginity in childbirth. Then, concerning the soul, although we judge that some things should be interpreted favorably, many remain wholly inexcusable—for example, his teaching that the more substantial properties, those in every way proper to corporeality, are also present in the soul; that the soul is distinguished by its own sex, namely male or female; that, like bodies, it has a threefold dimension of length, breadth, and depth; that it displays the form and figure of the human body; and that it is not an empty and void quality, but something tangible, airy in color and luminous. Tertullian errs notably besides when he teaches that the Church exists even where there are two or three, though they be laymen: “Where there are three, there is the Church [Col. 0031C], even though they are laymen!” A truly dreadful proposition, from which many far more ruinous consequences follow for the Church.

I pass over in silence other errors that he did not defend alone, but together with some other early writers, on matters not yet defined by the Church—for example, that those baptized by heretics must be baptized again. To the same class belongs the millenarian opinion and the description of paradise which in *Apology*, ch. 47, he calls a place of divine delight, appointed to receive the spirits of the saints and separated from knowledge of the ordinary world by a kind of wall of the fiery zone. To these must be added what he says about the apostate angels who knew the daughters of men [Note: [Col. 0031D] These and other paradoxes of Tertullian you will find below, supplied with Pamelius’s antidote and elsewhere cured by other commentators’ notes. Tertullian is defended against certain errors wrongly imputed to him by Lumper, *Bibliotheca historico-critica Patrum*, vol. VII, ch. 11, p. 709 ff.].

But, says one author of a life of Tertullian, this seems equal to a prodigy: that a man endowed with so lofty a genius [Col. 0031D] could have lent credibility to errors of this kind because of the visions of women, to which he gave complete faith just as though they were revelations of the Holy Spirit.

Hence we must conclude with the author just praised [Note: [Col. 0031D] Corbinian Thomas, concluding dissertation, work cited, p. 192] that fallen Tertullian now warns us how slippery a thing is the human understanding when it presumes too much upon itself, attributes everything to itself alone, believes itself too much, and disregards [Col. 0032A] the authority of others and especially that of the Church herself; how quickly any private person’s talent can be overthrown; how prone it is to fall into errors; and how truly Blessed Vincent of Lérins pronounced upon Tertullian in chapter 18 of his *Commonitorium*: “Tertullian, insufficiently tenacious of Catholic dogma—that is, of the universal and ancient faith—and far more eloquent than fortunate, afterward changed his opinion and finally did what the blessed confessor Hilary writes of him in one place: ‘By the error that followed,’ he says, ‘he destroyed the authority of his approved writings.’”

## ARTICLE III. THE LITERARY ANNALS OF TERTULLIAN

Having now weighed, as far as was possible, Tertullian’s manifold authority [Col. 0032B], and having offered such counsels as we ventured to give and judged most important concerning the right use of him, we think that we ought not to depart from this order of treatment. We therefore undertake to review briefly, year by year through the course of the centuries, what strenuous labors learned men devoted to him—whether in transcribing manuscripts, producing editions, translating the text into modern languages, or separately elucidating particular points of Tertullianic studies. Nothing shows more clearly than the laborious and tireless rivalry of so many men over the same author how highly all past antiquity and more recent scholarship valued Tertullian, how great his authority was, and with what diligence and prudence each man used his writings. Freely making use, according to our custom and right, of earlier studies on the same subject, especially C. T. G. Schoenemann’s exceedingly rare *Historico-Literary Library*, [Col. 0032C] we shall first touch briefly on the manuscripts whose existence has become known to us; then, as far as possible, give an extensive series of editions, translations, and commentaries under their respective years [Col. 0032D] [Note: [Col. 0032D] Material that we judged should be added to Schoenemann’s most learned notices has been marked by prefixed brackets; the rest we have distinguished only by new headings or a different arrangement.].

### § I. THE MANUSCRIPTS OF TERTULLIAN

“After the very ancient testimonies of Cyprian, Lactantius, Hilary, Eusebius, Rufinus, Jerome, Augustine, and Vincent of Lérins concerning Tertullian’s books, genius, and authority, no traces of him remain for several centuries; he seems buried beneath the celebrated decree of Pope Gelasius, who indiscriminately banished his works among the apocrypha. At last, awakened from that darkness of the apocrypha, he came into the light again around the fortunate age of Charlemagne, when literary studies reemerged from the monstrous flood of the barbarians. These flourished especially at Lyons, the ancient seat of Gallic learning and eloquence, and the archbishops of Lyons, among whom Leidradus and Agobard are named, are remembered as giving them considerable support. Agobard in particular must be thought to have cherished Tertullian above all others, since several manuscripts bearing his name survive. Hence:

[Col. 0033A] **Ninth century**

“**1. Between 814 and 840. I.** The first Agobard manuscript, on parchment, written in elegant, neat lowercase uncials and bound in quarto in 204 folios, torn by great age and gnawed and mutilated at the margins by prolonged damp, survives in the Royal Library under no. 1622. It could scarcely be handled safely when that outstanding codex was at last recently repaired; nevertheless, several translucent scraps of leaves were not preserved, upon which some letters once glimmered but now disappear because the margin is missing or an opaque binding obstructs them.
