On the second folio, beneath a title written by a more recent hand in square letters, these words appear in an ancient script: ‘BOOK OFFERED AT THE ALTAR OF ST STEPHEN [Col. 0033B] BY VOW OF BISHOP AGOBARD.’ On the verso of the same folio: ‘HERE ARE TWENTY-THREE BOOKS OF TERTULLIAN.’ The following list appears: *To the Nations*, book I; likewise *To the Nations*, book II; *On the Prescription of Heretics*, book I; *Scorpiace*; *On the Testimony of the Soul*; *On the Crown*; *On the Spectacles*; *On Idolatry*; *On the Census [Origin] of the Soul*; *On Prayer*; *On the Dress of Women*; likewise *On the Dress of Women*; *To His Wife*; again *On the Dress of Women*; *To His Wife*; again *To His Wife*; *On the Exhortation to Chastity*; *On the Hope of the Faithful*; *On Paradise*; *On the Veiling of Virgins*; *On Flesh and Soul*. In the other column of the same folio: *On the Flesh of Christ*; *On Patience*; *On Repentance*; *On the Submission of the Soul*; *On the Superstition of the Age*; ‘READ IN CHRIST IIIY.’ The manuscript ends in *On the Flesh of Christ*, at these words of chapter X: ‘likewise, since they presume it to be not of our flesh but of our soul.’ Nothing survives [Col. 0033C] of the books that follow, nor a single word of the four preceding works named in the list. On the red parchment cover, distinguished by golden lines and letters, one reads: ‘JACQUES GODEFROY, JURISCONSULT, A NATIVE OF PARIS, TO THE ROYAL LIBRARY OF PARIS.’ For this is the famous manuscript first handled by Godefroy, from which he first published the two books *To the Nations*, and which, after publishing them, he dedicated as a gift to the Royal Library.

“**II.** The Agobardine manuscript, different from the preceding, in the Leiden Library, praised but not described by Havercamp. See below, Havercamp’s preface to the *Apology*, col. 250 ff.

**Tenth century**

[Col. 0033D] “**III. About 900.** The manuscript of Claude Dupuy, in a very beautiful hand, with elegant uncials, 80 folios bound in quarto, preserved in the Royal Library, formerly no. 3971 and now marked 1623, containing only the *Apology*; it was in the hands of, and consulted by, Dom Nicolas Le Nourry and Rigaltius.

**Eleventh century**

“**IV. About 1000.** The manuscript of Pierre Pithou, assigned by Dom Nicolas Le Nourry and other learned men to the eleventh century from the form of its letters; once given from Pithou’s papers to the College of the Fathers of the Oratory of Jesus at Troyes, it is now preserved in the library of Montpellier. It is on parchment, in folio, and contains all Tertullian’s works. [Col. 0034A] Cf. Haenel, catalogue, p. 245. Rigaltius used it for his edition.

“**V. Same period.** The Harley manuscript, in elegance of hand not inferior to the Dupuy and, in Dom Le Nourry’s judgment, not a hundred years later. He received it from Achille de Harlay, president of the Parlement of Paris, and found in it both good and bad readings.

“**VI. Same period.** The Turin manuscript, which Mabillon testifies that he encountered in *Italian Journey*, vol. I, p. 8.

“**VII. Same period.** The first Colbert manuscript, which Dom Le Nourry received, by order of Abbot Colbert, from Charles Duchesne; it seemed to him to have been written about seven hundred years before.

**Twelfth century**

[Col. 0034B] “**VIII. Before 1050.** The Murbach manuscript, at whose end a later hand writes, ‘Pray for the lord abbot of Murbach,’ who is none other than Bartholomew of Andlau, appointed to the monastery in 1455. Dom Nicolas Le Nourry carefully excerpted its variant readings and believed it had been written six or seven hundred years earlier.

**Thirteenth century**

“**IX.** The later Colbert manuscript, brought from Tulle in 1687 by Étienne Baluze, marked no. 5271 in the Colbert Library, formerly 3973 in the Royal Library and now 1689; in Dom Le Nourry’s judgment, it was no more recent than four hundred years. Its first part contains Didymus’s treatise on the Holy Spirit and the letters and works of St Cyprian; its latter part [Col. 0034C] contains Tertullian’s *Apology*.

**Fourteenth century**

“The manuscripts that J. Trithemius saw in the exceedingly rich library of Hirsau Abbey and mentions in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* under Tertullian must be assigned at least to the years 1462–1500. The book *On Ecstasy*, now lost, is there reported as still surviving.

“On 12 January 1481, Angelo Poliziano wrote a letter about Tertullian as though he had in his hands all the books that we still possess.

“**X. By 1492** there appeared a manuscript of the Royal Library in Paris, formerly no. 4313-3 and now bearing no. 2616, a modest volume of fifty parchment folios, [Col. 0034D] in a neat and elegant recent hand, transcribed by Girolamo Varadeo for the use of a certain knight, Bartolomeo Calco, ducal chief secretary at Milan. The text is of the best quality despite being later. After passing through various events and owners, as the notes attached to the first folio show, it belonged to Antoine Faure under no. 178.

“Certain declamations of Tertullian assigned to the fifteenth century were found by Haenel in the catalogue of the Middlehill Library under no. 2377 and inserted in his library of manuscripts.

**Manuscripts of uncertain date**

“**XI.** The unidentified old manuscript from which the *Apology* was first copied.

[Col. 0035A] “**XII–XIII.** The Hirsau and Payerne manuscripts were the first from which Tertullian, with Rhenanus acting as midwife, came forth.” Even now, in Sélestat, from Beatus Rhenanus’s own library, certain writings of Tertullian survive in parchment manuscript. Cf. Haenel, p. 437.

**XIV–XV.** The Gorze and Fulda manuscripts—the latter afterward examined more carefully by François Modius—were of very great service in correcting Tertullian.

**XVI.** We do not know the manuscript of Gagneius from which he produced a fuller Tertullian.

**XVII.** The British manuscript of Malmesbury Abbey, communicated to Gelenius by John Leland, was plainly excellent. It supplied books of Tertullian not previously possessed, though it lacked others already extant.

**XVIII–XXIV.** The manuscripts of Pamelius: three Vatican manuscripts collated for his use by order of Cardinal Sirleto, [Col. 0035B] two belonging to the monasteries of Saint-Amand and Saint-Bavo in Belgium, and one English manuscript formerly owned by John Clement.

**XXV.** The Bongars manuscript used by Heraldus.

**XXVI.** The manuscript that Salmasius professed to have used in polishing the book *On the Pallium*.

**XXVII–XXVIII.** Two parchment manuscripts, nos. 324 and 376 in the Leiden Library, containing *On the Pallium* and used by Havercamp.

We should also note the variant readings that Fulvio Orsini had collected from various manuscripts, which Rigaltius employed after Wouwerius.

“**XXIX.** A Vatican manuscript containing, together with the chronicle of the Venerable Bede, many other things, among them a fragment of Tertullian [Col. 0035C] *On the Gods to Be Abominated*. It was first published in 1630 by J. M. Suárez, keeper of the Vatican Library, and, not reprinted since, is presented again in our edition, vol. II, col. 1114. Suárez says that the manuscript, written in Lombardic letters, appears to have been written seven or eight hundred years ago.

“**XXX.** The Ambrosian manuscript from which Muratori extracted the final part of the treatise *On Prayer*; it is ancient in his judgment, but he nowhere described it or assigned it a date.”

Two Paris manuscripts are wrongly inscribed with Tertullian’s name, one preserved in the Royal Library as no. 1656 and the other in the Sainte-Geneviève Library as no. 694; neither contains the slightest trace of Tertullian.

### § II. INDIVIDUAL EDITIONS, TRANSLATIONS, AND COMMENTARIES ON TERTULLIAN BY VARIOUS AUTHORS

[Col. 0035D]

**Fifteenth century**

**1483.** *The Apology of Q. Septimius Florens Against the Gentiles*. Printed at Venice by Bernardino Benali, without year, folio. It boasts an elegant typeface, with initials painted in red. This separate work of Tertullian survives in the Royal Academic Library at Göttingen and is mentioned in the Pinelli Library catalogue, vol. I, Latin Fathers, no. 683. Unless I am mistaken, however, it belongs to an edition of Lactantius produced by the same Bernardino Benali and mentioned by Fabricius. Since it may perhaps be rather rare, I would not immediately call it into doubt with Bunemann, [Col. 0036A] and there are signs in the form of the volume to alert an attentive observer: first, a table of chapters preceding it, copied in the same fashion customary in nearly all other editions of Tertullian’s *Apology* with Lactantius, occupying nearly half of the second page of the first folio; next, the absence of a date, scarcely encountered in editions from this place and printer; and then the item appended after the colophon, “Sermon on Eternal Life” [Note: [Col. 0036D] Its exact heading is: “Likewise, Sermon on Eternal Life, chapter 47”], which similarly appeared for the most part in later editions of Lactantius that included Tertullian’s *Apology*. These points may at least prompt learned men to examine the matter more closely where possible.

[Col. 0036B] **1493.** Milan, by Ulrich Scinzenzeler, folio: *Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, Apology Against the Gentiles*. Catalogue of the Pinelli Library, Latin section, no. 682, vol. I.

**1494.** Venice, through the care and at the expense of the nobleman Lord Ottaviano Scoto of Monza, 11 October 1494, by Boneto Locatello: *The Apology of Q. Septimius Tertullian*, with Lactantius.

**1500.** Paris, at Jean Petit, quarto: Tertullian’s *Apology*, with Lactantius, if conjecture may be trusted.

**Sixteenth century, 1501–1600**

Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* appeared repeatedly with Lactantius: 1502, Venice, folio; 1509, Venice, [Col. 0036C] folio; 1509, Paris, quarto; 1511, Venice, folio; 1513, Paris, quarto; Florence, octavo, at Filippo Giunta. Copies of the Giunta edition can also be found separately. See Pinelli Library catalogue, Latin Fathers, no. 684.

**1515.** Venice, in the house of Aldus and his father-in-law Andrea, April 1515. On the front: *TERTULLIAN*. Preceding the text, in addition to the dedicatory letter of Giovanni Battista Egnazio of Venice to Gasparo Contarini, Venetian patrician and eminent philosopher, are Jerome’s life of Tertullian and a table of chapters.

**1521. FIRST BASEL EDITION.** Tertullian’s works, Basel, at Froben, folio. “The works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, first among the Latin writers of the Church, [Col. 0036D] once read every day without fail by the divine Cyprian, brought out of darkness by BEATUS RHENANUS of Sélestat and rescued from decay to the best of his ability; with summaries of the individual books and, in places, conjectures added, by which this most ancient author is somewhat illuminated. You will find their catalogue on the next page. He flourished under the emperors Severus Pertinax and Antoninus Caracalla, very near the time of the apostles, about the year 160 after Christ’s Passion. Therefore these writings should be received favorably if in some places they differ from the accepted dogmas of our times, since he preceded all councils except those apostolic councils mentioned by Luke in Acts. [Col. 0037A] Rejoice, reader, obtain this rare and new treasure for yourself, and farewell.” At the end, on the folio immediately before the index: Basel, at Johann Froben, July 1521. The works in this volume, catalogued on the page facing the title, are: *On Patience*; *On the Flesh of Christ*; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*; *On the Prescription of Heretics*; *Against All Heresies*; *Against the Jews*; five books *Against Marcion*; *Against Hermogenes*; *Against the Valentinians*; *Against Praxeas*; *On the Soldier’s Crown*; *To the Martyrs*; *On Repentance*; *On the Veiling of Virgins*; *On Female Dress*; *On the Adornment of Women*; two books *To His Wife*; *On Flight in Persecution*; *To Scapula*; *On the Exhortation to Chastity*; *On Monogamy*; *On the Pallium*; and the *Apology Against the Gentiles*.

[Col. 0037B] Rhenanus conceived the plan of editing Tertullian when he happened upon an old manuscript from the Transjurane monastery of Payerne, and was soon assisted by the Hirsau manuscript as well. Yet he found both so corrupt and full of errors, and their script so similar, that one seemed copied from the other. He states that he would have abandoned the work altogether had the books, once announced, not already begun to be printed while Froben’s presses were free. He therefore followed this method in completing the labor: “Whenever he found corrupt passages and manuscripts did not come to his aid, knowing that authors’ writings must be treated reverently like sacred things, he changed nothing, but added in the margins [Col. 0037C] the conjectures that happened then to occur to him. Some of them,” he says, “do not greatly please even me, but I wished to assist the reader who would be in doubt. If it did not succeed everywhere, the attempt should not for that reason be condemned.” He continues: “Would that I had had access to the copy preserved at Gorze Abbey, three miles from Metz, and likewise to the one at Fulda or the one said to be at Rome. But shut out by the constraints of time, we could not obtain them. Yet I fear that none is more correct than ours, since the Hirsau and Payerne manuscripts we used agreed so consistently in all respects, though brought from different libraries and copied at different times. We shall entrust the labor of comparing them to others.”

Besides summaries prefixed to the individual books with brief annotations, Rhenanus prefixed a life of Tertullian [Col. 0037D] and a discussion, under the title *Admonition to the Reader Concerning Certain Dogmas of Tertullian*. There follow *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, later attributed to Gennadius, and finally an index of words, propositions, and dogmas. He dedicated the work to Prince Stanislaus Thurzo, bishop of Olomouc. Typographically this edition is quite distinguished, both by its large, clear type and by emblematic, mythological, and historical woodcuts, some surrounding the margins of the title, the first page of the dedication, and then the first page of the text itself, and others incorporated into the larger initials.

[Col. 0038A] **1525, 1528** [Note: [Col. 0038D] The British Museum catalogue, vol. II, cites *Works—with annotations of B. Rhenanus and F. Junius!* Basel, 1528, folio—absurdly! SCHOENEMANN.] **1536.** Basel, at Froben, folio: reprints of the first edition.

**1539. SECOND BASEL EDITION.** Basel, folio. “The works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian of Carthage, first among the Latin writers of the Church, once read every day without fail by the divine Cyprian; brought out of darkness by Beatus Rhenanus of Sélestat and rescued from decay to the best of his ability, with summaries of the individual books and conjectures throughout; and now, after comparison with the Gorze copy brought from Metz, made not only far more correct but also, as occasion required, expounded and illuminated by new and revised annotations. You will find their catalogue on the next page. He flourished under the emperors Severus [Col. 0038B] Pertinax and Antoninus Caracalla, very near the times of the apostles, about the year 160 after Christ’s Passion. BASEL, MARCH 1539.” Concerning this second edition let us hear Rhenanus himself in the prefixed letter dated at Sélestat on 1 March 1539: “We give Tertullian again, but more correct than before. The reason is that we finally obtained a collation of the manuscript preserved at Gorze in the region of Metz, performed with care and skill by Hubert Custine—with the help of his colleague Domenico Fiorentino—through the efforts of the jurist Claude Chansonette, counselor to Emperor Ferdinand. Yet that collation, though very useful, helped less than this discovery toward a more exact correction: we found that Septimius [Col. 0038C] sometimes writes in a Greek fashion, using Greek figures and constructions. It is clear that our author was constantly engaged in reading the ancient Greeks, who were very numerous at that time and were the sole sacred interpreters, so that even when writing Latin he could not forget the Greek turns of speech absorbed and impressed upon his memory. We have pointed out such tropes, often rather broadly so long as it was clear, for we wished to help students. The opportunity of this collation also furnished reason to revise the annotations wherever the later reading differed at times from the earlier. Since this had to be indicated, the changed words also required a different explanation. I could not be present in Basel while the work was being printed. But Sigismund Gelenius, a man of great literary judgment and the highest learning, acted in my place in correcting [Col. 0038D] it at the shop, and must not be deprived of his deserved praise.” The new preface is followed by *Proverbs, or Expressions Resembling Proverbs, Used Here and There by Septimius Tertullian in His Writings, for the Most Part Taken from Common Speech*; then the dedicatory letter and life of Tertullian repeated from the first edition. The admonition concerning certain dogmas of Tertullian was moved to the end; the definitions of ecclesiastical dogmas were omitted entirely. The index is new and altogether different. Notable sayings and propositions are carefully marked in the text’s margins. [Col. 0039A] A woodcut table representing Valentinian doctrine was added to the annotations on *Against the Valentinians*. Finally, *Against All Heretics*, which had formed a separate work in the previous edition, returned to its body here as a section wrongly detached from *On Prescriptions* [Note: [Col. 0039D] All Catholics should know that the censorial observations of Rhenanus were marked with a stroke by the Spanish Inquisition and placed at Rome by Pope St Pius V on the Index of Prohibited Books because of this edition’s freer comments on the Church’s laws, rites, and institutions. EDITORS].

**1545. FIRST PARIS EDITION.** Paris, folio, by Gagneius. Through Gagneius’s work eleven [Note: [Col. 0039D] Pamelius wrongly counts fifteen in the dedicatory letter prefixed to the 1579 papal edition. SCHOENEMANN] books of Tertullian were added: *On the Trinity*, book I; *On the Testimony of the Soul*, book I; *On the Soul*, book I; *On Spectacles*, book I; *On Baptism*, book I; *Scorpiace Against the Gnostics*, book I; *On Idolatry*, book I; *On Modesty*, book I; *On Fasting Against the Psychics*, book I; the epistle *On Jewish Foods*; and *On Prayer*, [Col. 0039B] book I. Of these, *On the Trinity* and *On Jewish Foods* were afterward vindicated for Novatian. Since I have not had the chance to see this edition, I cannot say whence Gagneius obtained these books, nor could I find anyone who took the trouble to give an account of it. In the catalogue of the Thott Library, vol. I, part I, p. 62, I find two editions of this year and place, likewise in the largest format: one, Tertullian’s works revised by Beatus Rhenanus, at Charlotte Guillard; the other, by the same editor, at Hugues de la Porte and the heirs of Aymon de la Porte. I do not know which is Gagneius’s, or whether both are.

**1550. THIRD BASEL EDITION.** Basel, folio. “The writings of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, priest of Carthage, a most ancient and learned author [Col. 0039C], both more numerous than before and more diligently revised through the industry of several well-lettered men against several ancient manuscripts sought from French and German libraries, foremost among which was one, by far the least corrupt, procured from remotest Britain; without omitting the careful annotations of Beatus Rhenanus. The facing page will reveal the catalogue. A fuller index has also been added. Basel, 1550. At the end: BASEL, AT HIERONYMUS FROBEN AND NICOLAUS EPISCOPIUS, MARCH 1550.” Sigismund Gelenius prepared this edition; we have already praised his part in Rhenanus’s second edition. Besides the books published in the previous Basel editions, it contains those recently produced by the Paris edition, but from the British manuscript in which those individual books survived; among the previously edited works, however, only these three were found there: [Col. 0039D] *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, *On Prescriptions Against Heretics*, and *On Monogamy*. Moreover, Francesco Zephyrinus of Florence’s commentary was added to the *Apology*, now first published. Here too are repeated Rhenanus’s dedicatory letter, life of Tertullian, proverbs, and admonition on the dogmas. From the elegance [Col. 0040A] of its paper and type, this edition must be counted among the handsomest. In the Baluze Library the *Apology* in one copy of this edition had been collated with a manuscript.

**1561.** Paris, at Andreas Wechel, quarto. Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian’s *Book of Prescriptions Against Heretics*, with scholia by Jean Quintin of Autun.

**1562. FOURTH BASEL EDITION.** Basel, folio. Reprint of the 1550 edition. At the end: Basel, in the Froben shop, by Hieronymus Froben and Nicolaus Episcopius, September.

**1562. FIRST FRENCH TRANSLATION.** Tertullian’s treatise *On the Prescription of Heretics*, published at [Col. 0040B] Paris by Aubert de Macère.

**1563. FIRST FRENCH TRANSLATION.** *On the Soldier’s Crown*, by the same, there.

**1566. BASEL–PARIS EDITION.** Paris, at Oudin Petit [Note: [Col. 0040D] Sandius wrongly says this appeared at Robert Estienne. SCHOENEMANN], under the sign of the Golden Lily, rue Saint-Jacques. An accurate reprint of Gelenius, in two octavo volumes. At the end of each: printed at Paris by Andreas Wechel, 1566. Gelenius’s index (“compiled by J. G.”—what that may mean I do not know) was reshaped to fit the contents of each volume.

**1572. FIRST GERMAN TRANSLATION.** *The Certain, Just, and Necessary Prescriptions of Q. S. F. Tertullian Against All [Col. 0040C] Heresies*, translated into German by Lorenz Albert of Franconia and printed at Dillingen.

**1579.**
### 1579

**PAMELIUS EDITION—FIRST ANTWERP EDITION, folio.** “All the works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage, that have been found up to the present. Now at last revised as accurately as possible after comparison with manuscript copies, and enlarged by several books; now first divided into chapters and arranged in a fixed order, with attention, so far as possible, to chronology, and distributed into five volumes, with the summaries and annotations of Jacques Pamelius of Bruges, theologian and archdeacon of Saint-Omer, interspersed throughout the whole work. By them the more obscure passages are explained and everything pertaining to ecclesiastical antiquity is illustrated. Newly added by the same [Col. 0040D] Pamelius are a life of Tertullian, a very full index of the Scriptures cited, and other prolegomena.”

The author of this new recension, Jacques Pamelius (van Pamele), was assisted chiefly by three parchment manuscripts from the Vatican, compared with the printed text through the care and by the order of Cardinal Sirleto, then prefect of the Vatican Library. He also had manuscripts from the monasteries of Saint-Amand and Saint-Bavo and an English manuscript owned by John Clement, an Englishman; also the conjectures of the Italian Latino Latini and the Englishman John Harris, communicated to him by the men themselves, and finally various observations of numerous [Col. 0041A] learned men. With these aids he certainly accomplished so much that he believed himself to have corrected innumerable places, filled lacunae, and rightly excised certain superfluous matter that had crept from the margin into the text. He was also the first to divide all the books into chapters and to add new summaries suited to those divisions and composed in Tertullian’s own words.

He then divided the whole work into five volumes: the first contains books against the Gentiles and Jews; the second, hortatory writings; the third, writings against heresies; the fourth, poems together with fragments of lost works; the fifth, works written against the Church and certain spurious works. Within each part the books are ordered according to the time at which they are thought to have been written. He also published an [Col. 0041B] *Admonition on Tertullian’s Dogmas or Errors*, far richer than Rhenanus’s treatment, arranged alphabetically and supplied with what he calls an “Antidote” [Note: [Col. 0041D] The first edition of Pamelius is not at hand, and we could not discover the printers and booksellers through whom it appeared; these particulars are therefore taken from the Paris edition of 1598, whose further additions are recorded in their proper place. SCHOENEMANN.].

Its contents are arranged thus: (1) a dedication to Pope Gregory XIII, dated at Douai on the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, 1579; (2) a second dedication to Philip II, king of Spain, written there on the same 14 September; (3) indexes of the books contained in each volume, with an account of the authors and manuscripts used in correcting Tertullian; (4) a life of Tertullian by Pamelius; (5) Tertullian’s paradoxes with Pamelius’s antidote; (6) rescripts of laws by Tertullian the Roman jurist; and finally (7) indexes to Tertullian—of passages, of other authors cited by him, and of subjects.

Pamelius was the first to insert into Tertullian’s works the [Col. 0041C] poetic books and fragments—or rather notices—of lost books that form the fourth volume and are encountered in other authors or in Tertullian himself. As to the poems, in vindicating for Tertullian the books *Against Marcion* and the poem *On the Judgment of the Lord*, he followed the authority of George Fabricius in his *Christian Poets*; for the poem *On Sodom*, that of Sixtus of Siena in *Sacred Library*, book IV. *Genesis* and *To a Senator*, which he had formerly attributed to Cyprian together with the poem *On Sodom*, he now at last assigned to Tertullian because of similarity of style and edited them anew.

These are followed by fragments of Greek works: *To a Philosopher Friend, on the Difficulties of Marriage, or On Virginity*; *On Fate*; *On Clean and Unclean Animals*; *On Circumcision*; [Col. 0041D] *On the Vestments of Aaron*; *On the Trinity*; *On the Origin of the Soul Against Hermogenes*; *Against the Apelleans*; *On Paradise*; *On the Hope of the Faithful*; six books *On Ecstasy*; *Against Apollonius*; several other and falsely attributed works. Volume V contains: *On the Exhortation to Chastity*; *On Monogamy*; *On Flight in Persecution, to Fabius*; *On Fasts Against the Psychics*; *On Modesty*; Novatian’s *On the Trinity*; the same author’s *On Jewish Foods*; and notices of his letters *On True Circumcision* and *On the True Sabbath*.

[Col. 0042A] **1580. THE BARRÉ EDITION.** Paris, at Michel Julien, on the hill of Saint-Hilaire under the sign of the Crowned Star: “The works of Tertullian and Arnobius, as many as could be rescued from destruction by the industry of eminent men, restored through comparison both with ancient copies and with more recent ones, supplied with passages of Scripture, and illustrated by commentaries able to bring no slight light to authors otherwise somewhat obscure and exceedingly difficult. All through the study and labor of René Laurent de la Barré. With very trustworthy and extensive indexes added.” At the end: “Printed by Pierre Le Voirrier, royal printer in mathematics, in the year of human salvation 1580, in the month of June.” [Note: [Col. 0042D] Cave cites this among reprints of Pamelius without the editor’s name; wrongly. SCHOENEMANN.]

Laurent de la Barré was the first to gather what various learned men—especially Beroaldo, Alciati, [Col. 0042B] Crinito, Turnèbe, Vertranius, Hotman, Cujas, and Scaliger—had contributed here and there in their writings to correcting or explaining Tertullian, and to write those excerpts, together with his own annotations, alongside Rhenanus’s commentaries. Where Rhenanus’s notes failed—that is, in the books added after Rhenanus—he supplied material of his own. He was nevertheless troublesome to readers because he nowhere distinguished his own material from that of Rhenanus or others. He had Rhenanus’s dedicatory letter and *Admonition on Certain Dogmas of Tertullian* reprinted, added a life of Tertullian of his own, and also prefixed an extensive catalogue of the authors on whose authority the annotations were composed. He dedicated this edition to his teacher, De La Bigne, doctor of theology. As regards outward appearance, the edition is very handsome and is quite conveniently furnished with annotations [Col. 0042C] placed beneath the text and printed in different typefaces.

**1582. FIRST GERMAN TRANSLATION.** The book *On Patience*, by Lucas Maius, Schmalkalden, octavo.

**1583. FIRST PAMELIUS–PARIS EDITION.** Paris, under the Basel shield; a reprint of Pamelius. It appears that this edition first added [Note: [Col. 0042D] Sandius cites a Paris edition of this year with notes by Rhenanus and Junius, folio; on what authority I dare not affirm] *Proverbial Expressions Contained in the Tertullianic Work, Illustrated with Brief Scholia*, by Andreas Hoyus of Bruges. Pamelius himself had entrusted this task to him, as we learn from Hoyus’s prefixed letter to Pamelius, dated at Arras, 1 January 1583 [Note: [Col. 0042D] In these matters I necessarily judged from the Paris edition of 1598, as I have already once declared. SCHOENEMANN.]. Whether Hoyus’s *Epigram on Tertullian’s Work Restored by Pamelius* [Col. 0042D], which indicates in order the subjects of the individual books contained in this five-part work, was also first added in this edition or had already been published, I do not know. In the Baluze Library, the *Apology* in a copy of this edition had been collated with a manuscript.

**1584. SECOND PAMELIUS–ANTWERP EDITION.** Antwerp, at [Col. 0043A] Plantin, folio, the same work reprinted. The Leiden Library catalogue (Leiden Batavian no. 716) describes it: *Works of Tertullian, corrected by Jacques Pamelius, with a collation of Agobard’s manuscript by Jean Mercier*. Antwerp, 1584, folio.

**1585. SECOND PAMELIUS–PARIS EDITION.** Paris, at Michel Sonnius, folio: *All the works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, revised by comparison with manuscripts and enlarged with several books, from the edition and with the annotations of Jacques Pamelius; added are a life of the same Tertullian and other prolegomena*. Catalogue of the Royal Library, vol. I, p. 363. I do not now remember where I found cited Tertullian’s works with notes of Jacques Pamelius, Paris, at Michel Sonnius, 1548; it is evident from the present entry that this is a typographical error.

[Col. 0043B] **1594. SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION.** *On the Soldier’s Crown*, by Florimond de Raemond (Louis Richeome), Bordeaux.

**1595.** Leiden, from the Plantin press, quarto (so the Leiden Library catalogue) and octavo (Catalogue of the Royal Library, vol. I, p. 364): Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, from the edition and with the notes of François du Jon (Junius).

**1596. FIRST HEIDELBERG EDITION.** Heidelberg, at Commelinus, folio, corrected by Rhenanus, Pamelius, and Junius. Cited by Sandius, Dupin, and Cave.

[Col. 0043C] **1597. FIRST PAMELIUS–FRANEKER EDITION.** Printed at Franeker by Aegidius Radaeus, printer to the States of Friesland: “All the works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage and a most ancient author, that have yet been found, from the edition of Jacques Pamelius of Bruges. To these have been separately added the annotations of Beatus Rhenanus of Sélestat, augmented by the censure of the Spanish Inquisition [Note: [Col. 0043D] In the catalogue of expurgated books published at Madrid in 1584 by order of Cardinal Gaspar de Quiroga, archbishop of Toledo and inquisitor general of Spain. SCHOENEMANN]; likewise the corrections and lucid, brief notes of FRANCIS JUNIUS of Bourges, collected both on the authority of manuscripts and from the contributions of Latino Latini of Viterbo and others, and perfected by weighty and choice conjectures. Common indexes have also been added: of passages of Holy Scripture and of other authors, and a very rich index of words and subjects.”

Junius preserved Pamelius’s text and order with scrupulous fidelity, [Col. 0043D] except that in volume IV he entirely omitted the fragments and notices of lost books. Pamelius’s annotations are also wholly absent [Note: [Col. 0043D] Fabricius wrongly cites it “with notes of Rhenanus, Pamelius, and F. Junius” (*Delectus scriptorum pro veritate religionis Christianae*, p. 213). SCHOENEMANN.]. After the text, the observations first of Junius and then of Rhenanus are appended separately. The former are prefaced by Junius’s dedication to the States of Belgium, dated at Leiden on 1 March 1597, together with a life of Tertullian newly composed by Junius himself; for he judges that Pamelius intended to weave not a life of Tertullian but a detailed history of that [Col. 0044A] age.

At the front they bear this title: “Corrections and notes on all the extant works of Q. S. F. Tertullian, as lucid and brief as could be made for so ancient and weighty a writer (c). In these, almost all the necessary readings, corrections, and interpretations of all the most learned men of our century are gathered from manuscript authority and probable conjectures and ascribed to their authors, even those being recorded that did not seem wholly contemptible; and from comparison of copies very many passages are drawn out of the deepest darkness of antiquity into the truth of things and the proper force of words, supplied, corrected, illustrated, and confirmed.”

After Rhenanus’s annotations there was added a small index of variant readings in the *Apology* [Col. 0044B] and *Against the Jews*, which François Modius of Bruges had formerly observed from comparison of parchment manuscripts, especially the Fulda manuscript. After they had long lain hidden with Marcus Welser of Augsburg, he communicated them to the young Gaspar Schoppe, who finally transmitted them to Junius. Junius especially praises the fact that many of Pamelius’s corrections were confirmed by the authority of the Fulda manuscript. The collation itself had been made against Barré’s Paris edition of 1580 [Note: [Col. 0044D] The observations that appeared brief and lucid to Junius himself were judged by Scaliger most worthy of correction and by Schoenemann mere divinations. “The most learned Gretser published a vindication of certain Tertullianic passages from the corruptions of Francis Junius the Calvinist,” in Gretser’s works, vol. V, part V, p. 305, Regensburg ed., 1735, folio. EDITORS], and was not changed by Junius; only the pages of the new edition were added. Two copies survive in the Leiden Library: one annotated by Joseph Scaliger’s own hand, and another to which Dominicus Baudius added Scaliger’s corrections from the autograph [Note: [Col. 0044D] Junius writes that René Laurent published this edition at Paris in 1580 with Barré as author. See what we said in its proper place. SCHOENEMANN.].

[Col. 0044C] **1597. FIRST PAMELIUS–GENEVA EDITION.** Geneva, with Pamelius’s notes (Sandius, Dupin, Cave).

**1598. THIRD PAMELIUS–PARIS EDITION.** Paris, at Laurent Sonnius, rue Saint-Jacques, at the Golden Compass, 1598. See the title of the 1579 edition, with these additional words: “There have also been added passages restored by conjecture by LATINO LATINI of Viterbo, and the learned commentaries of JEAN MERCIER, professor of law at Bourges, on *On the Pallium*. The reader will find the catalogue of the whole work after the dedicatory letters, and in each volume brief prefaces on the order of the books.” Latini’s corrections or conjectures, composed after Pamelius’s 1583 edition (Latini’s own preface is dated at Rome, 1 [Col. 0044D] November 1584), had been separately printed at Rome in 1584 by Francesco Zanetti and were afterward repeated more accurately by Carlo Macri in Latini’s *Sacred and Profane Library*, p. 191. Latini had no manuscripts, but used the variants of manuscripts cited by others. There are also [Col. 0045A] certain contributions of Pedro Chacón of Toledo, partly from conjecture and partly from a Vatican manuscript. Moreover, this edition is highly recommended to the learned by the brilliance of its type and paper.

**1599. SECOND PAMELIUS–HEIDELBERG EDITION.** Heidelberg, at Commelinus, folio. A reprint of Pamelius, according to Dupin.

**1599.** Cologne, at Arnold Mylius, duodecimo: Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian’s *Book of Prescriptions Against Heretics*, from the edition and with the annotations of Jacques Pamelius.

**1599. SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION.** The book *On the Crown*, again published by the same Florimond, at the end of his treatise on [Col. 0045B] Antichrist and the female pope Joan.

## SEVENTEENTH CENTURY, 1601–1700

**1600.** Paris, by Ambroise Drouart, octavo: Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, with a French translation and Latin notes by Edmond Richer (Catalogue of the Royal Library, vol. I, p. 364).

**1601. THIRD PAMELIUS–HEIDELBERG EDITION.** Heidelberg, folio, with Pamelius’s notes (Sandius, Cave). Dupin notes that the same appeared at Geneva in this year.

**1601.** Cologne, duodecimo: *Three Most Weighty Witnesses to the Constancy of the Perpetual Catholic Faith: Tertullian, On [Col. 0045C] Prescriptions; Vincent of Lérins, Against the Profane Innovations of All Heresies; Ten Reasons for the Contest Offered by Edmund Campion in the Cause of the Faith*. Catalogue of the Royal Carthusian Library of Saint Martin, Naples, 1764, folio.

**1602.** “Justus Calvinus published notes on *On Prescriptions* in a book published at Mainz under this title: *Six Treatises of Perpetual Prescriptions Against Heretics*.”

**1603.** “Theodore Petreius’s *Tertullianic and Cyprianic Confession*, arranged in four books. Paris, octavo.”

[Col. 0045D] **1603.** Frankfurt, octavo: Janus Wowerius, *Demonstrative Emendations on the Works of Q. S. F. Tertullian*. “Janus Wowerius to the reader: This whole little book, prepared less for display than for use, promises emendations by which Tertullian’s works are freed from countless faults. Following the ancients’ example I have entitled them *Demonstrative*, because they are a specimen and *prelude* (*προκυθάρισμα*) of a larger work, which I shall undertake as soon as the varied state of my affairs permits. Yet, lest you be mistaken, you owe the benefit of them not so much to me as to the most learned Fulvio Orsini. I excerpted them from his book preserved in the Vatican Library; and, that my assurance might not be doubtful to you, the learned Domenico Rinaldi, prefect of that library, granted me the use of the book. I can never [Col. 0046A] sufficiently proclaim his kindness and singular favor toward me. Although I very much wished that they had lain hidden with me longer, until a more becoming refinement from my own ability had been added to them, some unknown outcry has now spurred me, already running of my own accord, to hasten their publication and satisfy the curiosity of those who could not bear that this slender and fleeting gleam of little glory should reach me.”

**1605.** Kraków, in the shop of Andreas Petricovius: Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian’s *Book of Prescriptions Against All Heretics*, divided into chapters and illustrated with brief notes from the commentaries of Jacques Pamelius.

**1607. THIRD PAMELIUS–FRANEKER EDITION.** Franeker, folio, [Col. 0046B] a reprint of the 1597 edition (Sandius). Geneva, folio, with Pamelius’s notes (Dupin).

**1608. FOURTH PAMELIUS–PARIS EDITION.** Paris, folio, a reprint of the Paris Pamelius edition of 1598. Sandius, Fabricius, Cave, catalogues of the Barberini Library and British Museum.

**1609. THIRD PAMELIUS–ANTWERP EDITION.** At Commelinus, folio, a reprint of the 1583 Antwerp Pamelius edition. Fabricius.

**1610. FIFTH PAMELIUS–PARIS EDITION.** Paris, folio, the same, cited by Oudin, *Commentary on Roman Writers*, vol. I, p. 218.

[Col. 0046C] **1612.** Frankfurt am Main, at the Richter press: Janus Wowerius’s *Demonstrative Emendations on the Works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian*. Catalogue of the Royal Library, p. 365.

**1612. SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION.** The treatise *On Prescriptions*, translated by Brossaeus, Paris, octavo.

**1613.** Paris, from the Plantin press, at Adrien Périer, rue Saint-Jacques: *The Apology of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian*. Desiderius Heraldus corrected it from ancient books, illustrated it with a book of commentary, and added two books of digressions in which many passages of Tertullian and other writers are in part [Col. 0046D] corrected and in part explained and illustrated. *The Octavius of M. Minucius Felix*. Desiderius Heraldus corrected it with the aid of the Royal manuscript and added notes (a separate title, however, is prefixed to Minucius Felix’s book; see it in its proper place).

In correcting this book of Tertullian, Heraldus used two manuscripts, one belonging to the elder Dupuy but communicated to him by Dupuy’s sons, the other belonging to Jacques Bongars. Although Pamelius had used the first long before, he seemed to Heraldus, deprived as he was of the support of other books, to have left not a gleaning but a whole harvest. Besides those manuscripts he also used a book annotated by Cujas, which he obtained through Bongars’s care, and from it drew what seemed useful, naming the author.

“In our commentary,” he says, “we sought to observe this moderation: [Col. 0047A] neither to illuminate matters sufficiently clear to moderately learned men—that is, to light a torch for the sun—nor wholly to omit without explanation matters that might delay men otherwise learned but occupied in other disciplines. This book has such a mixture that its reading belongs not only to students of humane learning but especially to theologians and even jurists; its subject and disputes are such that the book ought to be in the hands of everyone wishing to guard against the leaven of the age. These considerations caused me sometimes merely to touch points that, without this reason, I would have wholly omitted—to touch them only, and only so far as sufficed for clarity.

“But since we see the custom has become established that, at the occasion of some word, rite, or [Col. 0047B] ancient practice, men very often range rather far afield and treat many things that contribute absolutely nothing to explaining the author before them, we wished both to satisfy custom and to escape the disadvantages that follow from it. We therefore decided to cast into other books matters lying outside *the work* (*τὸ ἔργον*); for that reason we gave them the name *Digressions*. In the first we included matters belonging to humane literature; in the second, matters illustrating ecclesiastical rites.” His dedicatory letter to Nicolas Brûlart, chancellor of France, deserves reading because of the events of those times. It is dated at Paris, 1 December 1613. In the copy of this book owned by the Royal Academic Library, variant readings from a Balliol College, Oxford, manuscript have been entered [Col. 0047C].

**1614.** Paris, at Jean Libert, octavo: Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, from the edition and with the translation and critical and historical notes of Théodore Marcile. Catalogue of the Royal Library, vol. I, p. 364, note b, no. 462; ibid., no. 465; and catalogue of a library at Utrecht, no. 776, vol. I, p. 557. It is also cited thus: *Satire on the Pallium, with a Familiar or Glossarial Interpretation and Other Notes by Théodore Marcile*.

**1616. SIXTH PAMELIUS–PARIS EDITION.** Paris, folio, a reprint of the Paris Pamelius edition. Sandius, Cave.

**1617. FIRST PAMELIUS–COLOGNE EDITION.** Cologne, [Col. 0047D] folio, at Antonius Hierat, the same as the preceding. Sandius, Fabricius, Cave, British Museum.

**1620.** “Hermann Rathmann’s *Theosophy of the Ancient Fathers Tertullian and Cyprian, Presenting Sure and Saving Instructions for the Ancient Faith and Truly Christian Life, Rendered and Recited from Their Own Monuments*.”

**1622.** “Albaspinaeus published notes on *On Prescriptions*, annexed to his two books of *Ecclesiastical Observations*. Paris, 1622; Helmstedt, 1672.”

[Col. 0048A] **1622.** Paris, at the expense of the late Jérôme Drouart, rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of the Sun Shield: Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*. Claude Saumaise (Salmasius) revised and explained it and illustrated it with notes. The book of notes has its own title. These facts are sufficiently certain; it is useful only to note that, besides the old editions, Salmasius inspected a fairly old and excellent manuscript and everywhere faithfully presented its text, which agreed in nearly everything with Rhenanus’s first and second editions. The editor dedicated the book to his father Bénigne Saumaise, royal counselor in the high court of Dijon.

Against this edition of Salmasius there appeared in the same year, at Rennes, from the press of the sworn printer Yvon Halec, Antoine Kerkoet the Armorican’s (Denis Petau the Jesuit’s) *Book of Observations on Claude Salmasius’s Notes on Tertullian’s On the Pallium*. To this [Col. 0048B] was opposed *A Refutation of Antoine Kerkoet’s Observations on Claude Salmasius’s Notes on Tertullian’s On the Pallium*, by François Franc, jurist, Middelburg, 1623. When the attack soon appeared again as *Antoine Kerkoet the Armorican’s Second Scourge-Bearer, or Refutations of the Refutation Which Claude Salmasius, under an Assumed Name, Opposed to the Kerkoetian Observations, Part II*, Paris, 1623, it was answered in the same year at Paris by *Refutation of Both Refutations of Cerco Petavius*, by François Franc, jurist; and against that was again issued *The Third Scourge-Bearer, or Refutations of the Salmasian Refutation, Part III*, in the same place and year. Little profit for Tertullian resulted from this flood of reciprocal abuse.

### 1624–1630

[Col. 0048C] **THE INCOMPLETE LA CERDA EDITION.** *The Works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, Presbyter of Carthage, Illustrated with Summaries, Explanations, and Notes, by Juan Luis de la Cerda, S.J., with a Very Full Index*. Paris, at the expense of Michel Sonnius, rue Saint-Jacques, under the Basel Shield; vol. I, 1624; vol. II, 1630.

The first volume includes sixteen books, in this order: *On the Pallium*, book I; *Apology*, book II; *On the Testimony of the Soul*, book III; *To Scapula*, book IV; *On Repentance*, book V; *On Prayer*, book VI; *To the Martyrs*, book VII; *On Patience*, book VIII; *On Spectacles*, book IX; *On Idolatry*, book X; *On Female Dress*, book XI; *On the Adornment of Women*, book XII; *To His Wife*, books XIII and XIV; *On the Soldier’s Crown*, book XV; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, book XVI. Nothing preliminary concerning the editor’s work or Tertullian occurs; there is only [Col. 0048D] a dedicatory letter to the most illustrious hero Don Antonio de la Cerda, lord of Atanzón, Pioz, and Olmillos, master of Pioz and its castle, his patron and most loving brother.

The other volume is prefixed by a dedication to the excellent lord Gaspar de Guzmán, Count of Olivares, etc. These letters are so wholly occupied with praising patrons that Tertullian’s name is scarcely mentioned once. The second volume contains the following five books: *On Prescriptions Against Heretics*, book I; *On Baptism Against Quintilla*, book II; *On the Soul*, book III; *On the Flesh of Christ Against Four Heresies*, book IV; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, book V. The remaining books of Tertullian are lacking, and it is regrettable that this edition [Col. 0049A]—generally disdained with unjust hauteur—remained incomplete.

In both published volumes, the text is divided into the chapters received from Pamelius’s edition and also into a great many sections. Each book is prefaced by a brief, excessively meager summary; each chapter has a fuller title in the manner of a synopsis. Each section is followed by an explanation in which the text’s meaning, paraphrastically (*παραφραστικὼς*), is unfolded; after the chapter is completed there follow very extensive notes, growing more abundant as the work progresses. Many concern the illustration of words and style, fewer the investigation of subjects and dogmas; in both respects they are somewhat prolix, yet by no means wholly superfluous.

At the end of volume I are added exercises on *On the Pallium*, in which Salmasius’s book is brought before the strict points of a judge’s scrutiny, approved in some things, condemned in many, and [Col. 0049B] weighed most learnedly in all. It is worth praising the Reverend Author’s concluding words: “It has often happened to me, when considering Salmasius’s readings beforehand, to rejoice that we possess Holy Scripture so whole and uncorrupted that no room for doubt remains. Were it otherwise and were it handed over to Salmasius or another, how many things would they change, delete, and transpose, when in Tertullian alone the readings vary so much in the letter?”

These two volumes of La Cerda rarely occur even in the best-stocked libraries, and more rarely still is the first joined to the second. Hence, at the beginning, compilers of library catalogues admitted many errors, as did even authors most expert in patristic bibliography. Thus both volumes are assigned to 1624 in the catalogues of the Barberini Library, vols. I and II. Thus Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 218, falsely asserts that [Col. 0049C] all Tertullian’s works, and Fabricius, *Selections of Sacred Writers on the Truth of the Christian Religion*, p. 213, that most of them, appeared in two volumes in 1624 and were repeated in as many volumes in 1630. Ittig had already warned of Oudin’s error in his *Ecclesiastical History of the Second Century*, p. 69, and Schoenemann of Fabricius’s in *Library of the Latin Fathers*, vol. I, p. 36. So the most learned Schoenemann, a strict corrector of errors of this kind, himself erred in describing volume I, which he had not seen, when he asserted, with insufficient basis, that it contained only thirteen books.

### 1625

**FIRST EDITION OF THE BOOKS TO THE NATIONS.** Geneva, at Pierre and Jacques Chouet, quarto: *Two Books of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian to the Nations, from the Copy of Agobard, Bishop of Lyons, with Notes, through the Labor and Study of Jacques Godefroy*. This edition itself is [Col. 0049D] not at hand. Concerning the manuscript called Agobard’s—certainly very ancient and undoubtedly the sole witness to these books—the editor later gave the Royal Library in Paris a witness to his fidelity and diligence. Rigaltius writes in the next edition of Tertullian that many pages had been so foully gnawed and corrupted by the injury of age, or rather the neglect of barbarians, that gaps frequently occur even in Godefroy’s edition; he entirely despairs of filling them without the aid of a more complete manuscript.

“Besides the gaps,” he continues, “there are other places where the copyist’s own hand not rarely erred. Some of these at least seem capable of correction by our conjectures. Yet we admit that conjectures unsupported by traces of the old writing are poorly trusted; we did not permit this to ourselves [Col. 0050A] except in very few places, and never without preserving the old manuscript reading.” This edition is sometimes said to have been produced in 1624; we therefore suspect that the dates of both years were printed on different copies. I dare not say whether, and in what way, the edition said to have been printed in the same year (1625) at “Aureliopolis” differs from the Geneva edition. In a copy of this edition in the Leiden Library, certain things were entered by Salmasius.

**1626.** Lyon, folio: Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, with La Cerda’s commentary.

**1628, 1629** [Note: [Col. 0050D] In the Catalogue of the Royal Library, p. 364, the title is given thus: “Nine books or various treatises of Tertullian, corrected in very many places and published from the Royal Library, revised and supplied with observations by Nicolas Rigaltius, 1628.” The year is elsewhere transcribed in varying ways, so it must have been found thus in different copies. In the 1641 Rigaltian edition of Tertullian’s works it is expressly said that Rigaltius’s dedication to the Duke of Richelieu was repeated from the 1629 edition of the nine books. SCHOENEMANN.].

Paris, at the press of Robert Estienne, with the widow of Olivier de Varennes, octavo: *Nine Books of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, Corrected from the Agobard Manuscript in the Royal Library and Illustrated with Observations*. Nicolas Rigaltius, whose [Col. 0050B] name is suppressed here, wished through this edition of the minor works to make a prelude to his later outstanding services to Tertullian. The nine works are: *On Prayer*; two books *To His Wife*; two books *On the Adornment of Women* [Note: [Col. 0050D] On the authority of the cited manuscript, he combined the works *On Female Dress* and *On the Adornment of Women* into one treatise of two books. SCHOENEMANN]; *On the Exhortation to Chastity*; *On the Crown*; *On the Prescription of Heretics*; and *Scorpiace*.

The Agobard manuscript had contained twenty-four books: besides those nine, books I and II *To the Nations*, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, *On Spectacles*, *On Idolatry*, *On the Origin of the Soul*, and *On the Flesh of Christ*; and the following writings of Tertullian now lost: *On the Hope of the Faithful*, *On Paradise*, *On the Submission of the Soul*, and *On the Superstition of the Age*. Rigaltius dedicated these writings of Tertullian to Cardinal Armand, Duke of Richelieu.

[Col. 0050C] **1630.** “A fragment from Tertullian’s books *On the Abominable Gods of the Gentiles*, drawn from the Vatican Library through the study of José María Suárez. Rome, 1630; Paris, the same year, octavo.”

**1632.** “Jean Crouzet published at Oxford, in octavo, a *Specimen of Conjectures on Certain Passages of Origen, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Epiphanius*.”

**1634.**
**FIRST RIGALTIAN EDITION.** Paris, at the expense of Mathurin Du Puis, rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of the Crown, folio. “The works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, corrected in very many places according to the oldest copies, and illustrated with observations and notes by the jurist Nicolas Rigault. With a glossary-index of the African style.” It is worth hearing in Rigault’s own, somewhat lengthy words what he achieved—or at least intended—by this new recension of all Tertullian’s works, which even now [Col. 0050D] holds first place.

“Readers of Tertullian’s [Col. 0051A] writings, even those by no means poorly educated, encounter many difficulties of language and text. The lofty African diction, surpassing almost every teaching by its endowment, demanded readers keenly attentive to its every movement. When it afterward fell into very different hands, it began to be altered by men unable to understand it, and the shamelessness of an adulterating hand scattered spurious expressions for genuine ones. Once the author’s words were intercepted, the ruin of the native text, like a battered body, destroyed its very sense and mind with it. Thus the worst correctors destroyed what was most correct. What limit could there be to complaints? What could remain beyond despair after so old and great a calamity?

“This plague had long ago so persuaded Homer that, when Aratus asked where an original copy [Col. 0051B] of the *Iliad* might be found, Timon son of Timarchus replied: ‘It must be sought in ancient copies,’ and added, ‘but copies not yet corrected.’ That dreadful tribe has long treated our Septimius’s books so foully that the antiquity of falsehood now bars truth by prescription of long time. If you appeal to the authority of old books, utterly false readings are produced on the authority of old books; for some old books have been most corruptly corrected. There is no hope of restoring truth unless books are found so old that they precede every antiquity of correctors.

“Our grandfathers’ age saw Rhenanus’s praiseworthy labor, worked out in three editions. Had partisan zeal not begrudged a man of such fidelity, judgment, learning, and diligence access to better copies, he would undoubtedly have achieved what would greatly lighten our [Col. 0051C] labor today. The next age produced Fulvio Orsini, who had examined manuscripts far better than Rhenanus’s. Content to note extracts from their readings in the margins of Pamelius’s edition, he did not even name their owners. Orsini’s readings, copied from the autograph into the book of the most distinguished and learned archbishop of Toulouse, Cardinal Montchal, also enabled us to establish the credit of Wouwer’s edition, perfected by his *Demonstrative Notes, and even of the extracts from Fulda and the Vatican on the *Apology* and *Against the Jews*, made public by Junius from Schoppe. Their credit should everywhere be strongly attested, especially because we derived many excellent readings from them that give this edition much [Col. 0051D] light and ornament.

“This will be our age’s glory among posterity. Vast distinction was added when at last we discovered the codex said to have been offered by vow of Agobard, bishop of Lyons, at St Stephen’s altar. The many passages restored by its aid to their original splendor will prove that this book was copied from manuscripts not yet corrected. To indicate each would have been extremely wearisome and worthless: Tertullian eagerly received his own words, and what had been badly torn apart now coheres so well that one would not believe it ever could have been separated. It will suffice to collect the chief restorations, thus showing what we are prepared to accomplish, but so that notable matters are finally included [Col. 0052A] and smaller yet not contemptible ones are left to scrupulous reckoning, someday to form an immense total.

“We added observations to illuminate certain obscure passages and trace remnants of ancient custom long forgotten or hidden learning. If some points seem stated or investigated somewhat freely—perhaps those on punishment of secret crimes, the form of the Lord’s face, and lamps lit by day—they must be understood as remarks for examining Septimius’s opinions, not for attacking Catholic teaching or rejecting decrees of Fathers later than Septimius [Note: [Col. 0052D] In these words Rigault excuses freer opinions sometimes inserted in his notes on both Cyprian and Tertullian. I do not know whether he satisfied everyone. Some passages plainly show that he speaks from his own mind rather than the author’s and even strays from the matter, sometimes writing notes insufficiently consonant with present Church usage. So Dupin, who adds that Rigault is reproached for excessive boldness in conjecture, insufficient care in revising his author from ancient manuscripts, and inserting his or others’ conjectures into the text without manuscript authority. EDITORS.]. Indeed, we always opposed to Tertullian the judgments and decrees of Fathers most accepted in the Church, so that those who stumble over those African [Col. 0052B] rough places immediately have somewhere safe to set their foot.

“We also inserted notes weighing ambiguous variants, investigating truth, and sometimes explaining or confirming conjectures. Finally, by comparing many passages, we compiled glosses of African style, the surest method of interpretation. We called them ‘glosses’ with the Greek word by which Fabius says unusual words of a more secret language are designated. We know the shorter observations and notes will not satisfy many, but we do not therefore excuse ourselves. This African admits no reader unless already learned.”

So Rigault in the dissertation entitled *On Tertullian and His Writings, Their Various Editions, and What Is Accomplished by This Edition*, which, together [Col. 0052C] with the dedicatory letter to Cardinal Richelieu, precedes the text in the edition of nine books of 1529 (so printed). It is followed by ancient testimonies on Tertullian, the series of works in the volume, and an account of the manuscripts from which each was notably corrected and how often—from at least four to as many as 250 times in the *Apology*, commonly thirty, twenty, or seventy times, but also eight hundred or 130 times, and sometimes in nearly every clause. He says *On the Pallium* is corrected in almost every line according to Salmasius’s most exact edition from old copies, except in six or seven places.

After the text comes an index of Holy Scripture; then, under the title “uncertain author,” poems once customarily ascribed to Tertullian [Col. 0052D]: five books *Against Marcion*, *On the Judgment of the Lord, Genesis,* and *Sodom*; finally an index of memorable subjects. The observations have their own title [Col. 0053A], with an excellently planned index of Tertullian’s glosses. Its elegant, brilliant type greatly commends this edition, assuming the first was no worse than the second before us. The bookseller added substantial utility by publishing in a separate volume many scholars’ notes on Tertullian: *James Pamelius of Bruges, theologian, etc., Arguments and Annotations on the Works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, with Annotations of Various Writers Added; All Corresponding to the Text of the Edition of the Distinguished Jurist Nicolas Rigault.* Paris, Mathurin Du Puis, rue Saint-Jacques, at the Crown, 1635.

Besides Pamelius’s annotations, arguments, life, etc., occupying most of the volume through p. 781, it contains [Col. 0053B] Latino Latini’s conjectures and corrections and notes by Jean Mercier, Edmond Richer, Théodore Marcile, Jan van der Wouwer, and Gabriel de L’Aubespine, bishop of Orléans, with an excellent index. The title’s claim that the annotations correspond to Rigault’s text was effected by marginal page numbers, except that *On the Pallium* and the *Apology*, which appear wholly transformed in Rigault, were reprinted according to Pamelius’s recension. This notes volume is separately listed in many catalogues, including those of Thott, the Bodleian, Firmian, and d’Estrées, vol. I.

**1636.** “FIRST FRENCH TRANSLATION of the *Apology*, by Louis [Col. 0053C] Giry, Paris, duodecimo.”

**1636.** “Hermann Rathmann’s *Theosophy* under the new title: *Speculative and Practical Theology Collected from the Fathers by a Distinguished Theologian and Published*, Wittenberg.”

**1639.** “FIRST SPANISH TRANSLATION of Tertullian’s books *On Patience, On the Testimony of the Soul, To Scapula*, etc., by José Pellicer, Barcelona.”

**1639.** “Paganino Gaudenzio, *Tertullianic Difficulties*, with his comparison of Origen’s doctrines with Platonic philosophy, Florence, quarto.”

**1639.** [Col. 0053D] “SPANISH TRANSLATION of *On Patience, On the Testimony of the Soul, To Scapula*, etc., by José Pellicer, Barcelona.”

**1610.** “FIRST FRENCH TRANSLATION of *On Prayer*, Paris, duodecimo; and *On Patience*, same place and format, by Hobier.”

**1640.** “SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION of *On the Pallium*, by Titreville, Paris.”

**1641.** Paris, with the device of a great ship, folio, two volumes: *The Works of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, Illustrated with Arguments, Explanations, and Notes*, by Jean-Louis de La Cerda. See the first edition.

[Col. 0054A] **1641. SECOND RIGALTIAN EDITION.** Paris, Mathurin Du Puis, etc., folio, enlarged with observations, notes, and glossary. A copy frequently collated with manuscripts, including a printed Agobard manuscript, existed in the Baluze Library. Oudin says Rigault’s edition was reprinted at Paris in 1644, 1646, 1650, and 1658.

**1644.** “Paganino Gaudenzio, three minor works, the last investigating many matters about Tertullian in treating the philosophical opinions of the ancient Fathers, Pisa, quarto.”

**1644.** “SECOND SPANISH TRANSLATION. Madrid, folio: Tertullian’s *On Patience* with Orio’s commentary; Pinelli Library catalogue I.89.”

**1644.** [Col. 0054B] “SECOND SPANISH TRANSLATION of *To Scapula*, translated by Pedro Manero, Zaragoza.”

**1645. SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION.** Antoine Arnauld translated *On Repentance* into French with other patristic treatises on the subject and published it at Paris; it appears in his works, vol. XXVIII, Paris 1779.

**1646.** “SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION of the *Apology*, by Louis Giry, duodecimo.”

**1646, 1648, 1650** [Note: [Col. 0054D] So Ceillier II, p. 526 and the Chigi Library catalogue under Amiens. Scholars differ: Fabricius gives 1646 and 1648; Dupin 1648 and 1650, so we followed both. Sandius wrongly cites a reprint in 1650 unless he carelessly meant distinct editions: P. Georges’s in 1648 and another, a reprint of Rigault, in 1650. SCHOENEMANN.]. Paris, Michel Soly, rue Saint-Jacques, at the Phoenix, folio, three volumes: *Tertullian Revived, Illustrated with Scholia and Observations, in Which the Form of Both Laws Is Traced to Its Origin and a Norm of Inquiry Is Prescribed for Lovers [Col. 0054C] of Ancient Piety*, by Father Georges of Amiens, Capuchin friar minor and professor of theology at Paris.

Rigault wittily wrote of this huge Capuchin work in the preface to his notes on Cyprian: “As for Tertullian, scarcely can any mortal call him ‘revived,’ since he is now buried and crushed beneath horrible loads of huge commentaries.” Before illustrating Tertullian’s works, Georges prefixes *Tertullianic Vindications*. Part I treats his birthplace, education, studies, and natural life. Part II asks, among other things, what moved him to Christianity, whether he was baptized immediately after [Col. 0054D] conversion, brought his wife to faith, and was a Doctor, priest, monk, or martyr. Part III treats his doctrine and apologetic, polemical, and exhortatory writings. He professes to interpret [Col. 0055A] Tertullian’s errors favorably. Ittig gives more in *Church History of the Second Century*, p. 71 ff.

**1650.** London, octavo: various works of Tertullian, in Francis Rous’s *Honey of the Fathers*, pp. 293–468. Buneau catalogue.

**1651.** “Andreas Rivinus edited Tertullian’s poetic works and added brief notes after Pamelius, Junius, and Barthius, Gotha, octavo.”

**1655.** “Hermann Rathmann’s *Theosophy*, third edition under the new name *Theological Marrow of the Fathers*, a harmonious consensus of the Fathers on ancient faith and truly Christian life, arranged in conclusions under theological topics and giving sure, salutary instruction against every adversary. At the end is added *Practical Theology*, confirmed and brought to light from Tertullian’s and Cyprian’s own words by M. Hermann Rathmann, Wittenberg.” [Col. 0055B]

**1656.** Leiden, Jan Maire, octavo: Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, revised, explained, and annotated before his death by Claude Saumaise, with his true portrait from life.

**1657.** “Strasbourg, octavo, Tertullian’s works edited by Boecler,” according to Sandius. Oudin instead records a reprint of Rigault at this place and year without format.

**1658.** [Col. 0055C] Paris, Jacques Dallin at St Stephen and Thomas Joly at the Shield of Holland, rue Saint-Jacques, folio, three volumes: *Tertullian’s Alphabetical, Rational, Tripartite Omniloquium*, all his works arranged, expounded, and illustrated in a new, unprecedented, easy order useful to advocates in both forums and professors and writers of human and divine matters, by Brother Charles Moreau, Augustinian Hermit of the Bourges community, convent of Queen Marguerite in the Faubourg Saint-Germain. The next page indicates its novelty: a summa of scholastic, positive, and moral theology excerpted chiefly from Scripture, the Fathers, Tertullian, and Augustine. [Col. 0055D] We omit the equally long titles of volumes II and III; the editor’s genius is sufficiently revealed by his summary:

“This new tripartite work is completed in three volumes. The first contains three parts. The first presents all Tertullian’s books alphabetically, supplying four notable defects omitted in every edition, identified in the prefatory notice [Note: [Col. 0055D] What defects? I found them neither there nor in the detailed preface to which he refers. Since that preface reduces the edition’s virtues chiefly to six points—and expressly says the others lack three, apparently not granting them the fourth—namely: a more correct text; scriptural passages distinguished in the text by type; not only chapter numbers but individual verses checked against the original and placed in the margin [Col. 0056C]; plain, brief arguments prefixed where other editions lack them [Col. 0056D]—I think Moreau, blessed with ample awareness of his own merits, called precisely these ‘defects.’ SCHOENEMANN.].

[Col. 0056A] “The second part, peacefully and without contentious controversy, and suppressing every adversary’s name out of regard for truth, piety owed to St Augustine, and protection of the work woven from his choicest judgments, refutes an alphabet of errors wrongly imputed to Augustine, Tertullian’s illuminator in sound matters and corrector in perverse ones. His whole doctrine, especially on predestination, grace, and free will, is reduced exactly through twenty-seven questions to the rules of Scripture, Fathers, councils, popes, above all Trent and Innocent X’s condemnation of five propositions, and proved wholly orthodox.

[Col. 0056B] “The third part alphabetically unfolds Tertullian’s erroneous, heretical, and harsher judgments, separated from his sound doctrine, explains them, and refutes them by Augustine’s Catholic teaching, with two indexes. Volumes II and III distribute all Tertullian’s sound works into commonplaces in a new alphabetical and rational order, explaining every obscurity literally in brief scholia and illustrating them from the marrow of Scripture, councils, Fathers, especially Augustine, and approved authors in every discipline [Col. 0056C], with three rich indexes—of more than three thousand explained scriptural places, matters and words, and sermons.

“On the title [Note: [Col. 0056D] ‘I called this an *Omniloquium*, both because I omitted no sentence or line from this sole work of Tertullian, great in every field of speaking, and because I supplied every speaker and writer with abundant material.’ SCHOENEMANN.], arrangement, usefulness, solidity, curiosity, clear brevity amid abundance, and the emblematic frontispiece [Note: [Col. 0056D] Parisians laughed at engraved images of Augustine in a cowl and Tertullian in his pallium, prefixed with: ‘Two African monsters of genius, spirits of all learning and eloquence, contending for the palm.’ Moreau says Cachin mocked them. He therefore thinks himself obliged to conform to Tertullian and write an apology for Augustine’s hood and sack as Tertullian did for his pallium. SCHOENEMANN.], together with a synopsis of Tertullian’s and Augustine’s lives, their symbolic and discordant [Col. 0057A] properties and praises, and the use and practice of the whole work, the reader has a general preface immediately after the dedicatory letter, which he should examine as necessary.”

He further promises innumerable corrections even to the best editions, supplied punctuation and accents obscuring the author, and many corrected misspellings, so that if the printer matches his purified autograph and obeys the vigilant corrector, even the severest censor will find nothing to blame. [Col. 0057B] Enough, though not too much, we hope, for the rarity of this paper bulk. He dedicated it to Pomponne de Bellièvre, knight and first president of the Parlement of Paris.

**1662. FIRST PAMELIAN–ROUEN EDITION.** Rouen, folio: Tertullian’s complete works, etc., with Pamelius’s arguments and annotations and Latini’s conjectures, reprinting the 1597 edition.

**1662.** “*The Genius of Tertullian*, by de Fayolle, Paris, quarto.”

**1664. FIRST PAMELIAN–RIGALTIAN EDITION OF LE PRIEUR.** Paris, at the expense of the Typographical Society for Liturgical Books [Col. 0057C]. Tertullian’s works diligently corrected from the oldest copies by Nicolas Rigault, with his complete notes and previously separate commentaries of various writers; Philippe Le Prieur added new arguments and notes to every book and a useful dissertation. Novatian’s *On the Trinity* and *On Jewish Foods* with notes are added as in Pamelius.

The text is Rigault’s second; it includes all his notes, both terminal and those appended to his Cyprian notes; selected annotations of Pamelius; learned observations of Rhenanus, Zephyrinus, L’Aubespine, and La Cerda; leading notes of Saumaise on *The Pallium*; Mercier’s, Wouwer’s [Col. 0057D], and others’ illustrations and corrections; and Le Prieur’s own notes and arguments. Regrettably the booksellers’ plan to publish Latin Fathers illustrated by scholars failed. This edition deserved universal applause for the order and arrangement of notes beneath the text in smaller divided columns and for its paper and type. Le Prieur’s notes have little value, though his editorial diligence is praiseworthy. Novatian follows Pamelius and has only his notes [Col. 0058A]. Besides Pamelius’s prefatory life, *Paradoxes with Antidote*, and proverbial formulas, it adds Rigault’s judgment and ordering and Le Prieur’s new dissertation on Tertullian’s life, opinions, and errors.

**1664.** “Fourth edition of Hermann Rathmann’s *Theosophy*, newly entitled *Theological Gold-Mine of the Fathers, Speculative and Practical*, arranged in conclusions by theological topics and offering salutary teaching against all adversaries, long desired and now published by a distinguished theologian highly deserving of Christ’s Church [Col. 0058B]. It is unclear whether the shifting titles and removal of the author’s name were designed to deceive buyers or because of the serious Rathmann controversy in Germany; no one now need regret not knowing.”

**1665.** “FRENCH TRANSLATION of *On the Pallium, On Patience,* and *Exhortation to the Martyrs*, by Mannessier.”

**1673.** “Paul Colomiès translated *To the Martyrs* into French, La Rochelle, octavo.”

**1675.** Brussels, quarto: *On Prescriptions against Heretics*, with scholia and notes by Christian Lupus.

**1675. SECOND PAMELIAN–RIGALTIAN EDITION OF LE PRIEUR.** [Col. 0058C] Paris, Pierre Le Petit at the Golden Cross, Edmond Couterot at the Good Shepherd, and Charles Angot at the Golden Lion, rue Saint-Jacques. A corrected reprint of 1664, adding the poem *Jonah and Nineveh*.

**1675.** “De La Motte, *History of Tertullian and Origen*, Paris 1675; Lyons 1702, octavo.”

**1680.** “Pierre Allix, *On Tertullian’s Life and Writings*, Paris, octavo.”

**1680.** “Natalis Alexander, dissertation on Tertullian’s doctrine and confirmation, in his *Ecclesiastical History of the Old and New Testaments* III, century II, article VIII, p. 293, Venice 1778.” [Col. 0058D]

**1682.** “*Jonah and Nineveh*, with comments by Juret, Barthius, and Gronovius, at the end of Paulinus of Périgueux, edited by Christian Daum, Leipzig, octavo.”

**1682.** “FIRST GERMAN TRANSLATION of *To Scapula* by Abraham Hinckelmann, Lüneburg, duodecimo; by him also *To the Martyrs*, duodecimo.”

**1683.** “THIRD FRENCH TRANSLATION of *On Prescriptions* by D. Hébert, who also translated *Veiling of Virgins* and the women’s dress books, Paris.”

[Col. 0059A] **1686.** Cambridge, John Hayes for Henry Dickinson and Richard Green, duodecimo: Tertullian’s *Apology* and *To Scapula*, with Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*. The *Apology* follows Heraldus with chapter arguments from La Cerda; *To Scapula* follows La Cerda.

**1695. THIRD PAMELIAN–RIGALTIAN EDITION OF LE PRIEUR.** Reprint of the Rigault–Le Prieur edition (Ceillier).

**1699.** “E. Salomon Cyprian, academic disputation examining Tertullian’s statement ‘Philosophers are the patriarchs of heretics,’ Helmstedt, quarto.”

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

[Col. 0059B] **1701. FIRST VENETIAN EDITION.** Venice, folio: Tertullian’s works with selected notes at the volume’s end. Fabricius, from Pfaff, says it is not very correct.

**1701.** “Salomon Cyprian, commentary on Tertullian’s evangelical doctrine, among his dissertations, Coburg.”

**1702.** “John Croy, conjectures on passages of Tertullian, Oxford, folio.”

Giry, advocate in the Parlement of Paris (1665), had published this version several times since 1636 without Latin.
