Muratori published the notes of the once-famous jurist Panciroli from fuller commentaries on all Tertullian’s works then hidden in the library of the Franciscan Giambattista Cattaneo, to whet his countrymen’s appetite for these long-neglected delights.

[Col. 0060B] **1714.** “Laurids Brorson, on *infantarii* in Tertullian, *To the Nations* I.2, Copenhagen, quarto.”

**1714–1715.** “SECOND FRENCH TRANSLATION of the *Apology* by Vassoult, with notes, Paris, Colombat, quarto, twice published. Both contain an excellent preface on Christian apologists and Tertullian in particular, with valuable especially historical notes.”

**1715.** Tertullian’s poems among ancient Latin poets, edited by Michael Maittaire, London, two folio volumes.

**1715.** “Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, dissertation on Tertullian’s *Apology*, two books *To the Nations*, and *To Scapula* [Col. 0060C], in his apparatus to the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum* II, pp. 1574–1590, Paris, folio.”

**1715.** “August Heumann, correction of *Prescriptions*, *Acta Eruditorum* 1715, pp. 299–305.”

**1717.** “Anonymous exposition of ‘booted military service’ in *Idolatry* XIX, in Archimbaud’s collection IV, pp. 116–119, Paris.”

**1718.** Leiden, Isaac Severinus: Tertullian’s *Apology*, most carefully revised from manuscripts and old editions and furnished with a continuous commentary explaining authors and Scripture, by Sigebert Havercamp, minister of the divine word, with chapter arguments, three rich indexes, figures and coins, and Tertullian’s portrait and epigram. [Col. 0060D] This is the finest edition of the work. Havercamp possessed a rich apparatus: nearly all editions; two Leiden parchment manuscripts, nos. 324 [Col. 0061A] and 376; Modius’s Fulda variants, first published with Junius in 1597, later known chiefly to Godefroy and selectively used by Rigault, leaving Havercamp a rich gleaning; and a collation of an Agobard manuscript distinct from the one that restored many other writings. Josias Mercier’s 1625 collation against Pamelius survives in Leiden, p. 71; Paul Colomiès copied it into Rigault’s margin, and François Fabricius lent it to Havercamp [Col. 0061B]. Because work was advanced before it arrived, variants for the first nine chapters and a full collation of the second Leiden manuscript were placed among the additions. He also had Scaliger’s conjectures in Junius and Scriverius’s old-manuscript corrections.

With these resources Havercamp confirmed Rigault’s text more than he created a new recension. In explaining words and matters of ancient history, rites, and religion, he displayed exceptional, judicious learning. He rejoices especially to have shown that Tertullian issued this work twice with slight verbal changes [Col. 0061C]. He promised annotated editions of the other anti-pagan works, especially a much-corrected *To the Nations*, and learned prolegomena on Tertullian’s life and writings; we do not know why they never appeared. Coins and engravings, following universal scholarly fashion, serve ornament more than use. They occasioned the dedication to Walter Block, owner of a splendid treasury.

**1719.** “Anonymous notes on *On Prayer* [Col. 0061D], *Mémoires de Trévoux* 1719, p. 1202; *Journal des savants*, December, p. 663.”

**1721.** “Lorenzo Magalotti, letter on a passage of Tertullian, in his scientific and learned letters, pp. 192–198, Florence, quarto.”

**1722.** “FIRST ENGLISH TRANSLATION of *Prescriptions*, by Joseph Betty, with notes, Oxford, duodecimo.”

**1722.** “Arnold Greve, Tertullian’s testimony concerning Ἀποθεώσει (‘deification’) decreed to Christ by Tiberius defended, Wittenberg, quarto.”

**1729.** “FOURTH FRENCH TRANSLATION of *Prescriptions*, Paris, duodecimo (*Journal des savants* LXXXVIII, p. 499). The Trévoux journal for March records a fifth translation in the same year.”

**1730.** “Dom Rémy Ceillier, O.S.B., *General History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, II.”

**1733.** “Anonymous observations on Tertullian and Cyprian, *Miscellaneous Observations on Authors* III.1, Amsterdam, octavo, pp. 45–54.”

[Col. 0062C] “Johann Heinrich Blumenbach, book on the senatorial decree concerning Quintus Septimius Florens the presbyter and the jurist Tertullians, Leipzig, quarto.”

**1743.** [Col. 0062D] “Justus Karl Wiesenhauer, disputation on the jurist and Q. Septimius Florens Tertullian, Hildesheim.”

**1744. SECOND VENETIAN EDITION.** Venice, Gaspare Girardi, folio: Tertullian’s works. A reprint of Le Prieur’s edition (see 1675), adding Sigebert Havercamp’s commentary on the *Apology*. A splendid production, with notes beneath the text. The *Apology* has Havercamp’s commentary purged, as stated, of certain errors, and Mosheim’s chronological-critical inquiry on its true date and the beginning of Severus’s persecution, dedicated to Havercamp. Regrettably [Col. 0063A] the edition is stained by so many printing errors.

**1744.** “J. Martin Chladenius, commentary on the stations of ancient Christians, chiefly designed to illuminate Tertullian, Leipzig.”

**1752.** “Dom Corbinian Thomas, O.S.B., observations and notes on *Prescriptions*, Salzburg, octavo.”

**1753.** “J. E. Immanuel Walch on authentic apostolic letters mentioned by Tertullian, Jena, quarto.”

**1755.** “Dom Corbinian Thomas, O.S.B., observations [Col. 0063B] and notes on Tertullian’s *Baptism* and *Repentance*, Salzburg, octavo.”

**1756. FIRST ITALIAN TRANSLATION.** All Tertullian’s Catholic and moral works translated by Selvaggia Borghini, a Pisan noblewoman, Rome, Niccolò and Marco Pagliarini. Other works—*Against the Jews, Prescriptions,* and *Against Hermogenes*—were promised; I do not know whether published. Florentine literary sheets say Bottari translated the works Borghini omitted (Lumper from Argelati and Paitoni’s bibliography of translators).

[Col. 0063C] **1756.** “Johann Georg Geret, program on a Tertullian passage concerning earthquakes, Ansbach, quarto.”

**1757.** “Johann August Nösselt, dissertation on the true date and doctrine of Tertullian’s surviving writings, Halle; also his three ecclesiastical-history dissertations, 1817.”

**1758–1759.** “August Heumann, appendix to various notes on Tertullian, with a fuller analysis of *Prescriptions*, *Acta Eruditorum*, supplement VI.5.”

**1758.** “Christian Wilhelm Franz Walch on Satan’s pomps in *Spectacles*, Göttingen, quarto.” [Col. 0063D]

**1759.** “C. G. Samuel Bernhold, program defending the *Apology* against unfair censure, Erlangen, quarto.”

**1762.** “J. Daniel van Hoven, sample notes on Tertullian, *Musaeum Criticum* II.26.”

**1764.** “C. A. Beger, letter on the sense in which Tertullian called God a body, Leipzig, quarto.”

**1766.** “J. Wernsdorf on the palm-embroidered robe, *Apology* 50, Wittenberg, quarto.”

[Col. 0064A] **1769–1776. FIRST HALLE EDITION.** Halle-on-Saale, Johann Christian Hendel, six volumes: Tertullian’s works edited by Johann Salomo Semler. Five books *Against Marcion* first appeared separately; the remaining works followed in four volumes, and volume VI supplies indexes and glossary. Semler began *Against Marcion* to make this outstanding work affordable for academic study; this became a complete edition. He restored Rhenanus’s first-edition text, corrected by his judgment and other editions, adding variants in doubtful places and rarely conjectures [Col. 0064B]. He used Rhenanus; Gagneius’s Paris 1566 octavo; Pamelius 1597; Junius’s Franeker edition; first Rigault; latest Venice; Latini; and Wouwer’s 1603 notes.

Volume II contains most polemical writings: *Prescriptions, Against Hermogenes, Valentinians, Praxeas, Jews; Scorpiace; Against the Psychics*. III: *Veiling of Virgins, Female Dress, Adornment of Women, To His Wife* I–II, *Exhortation to Chastity, Monogamy, Flight, To Scapula, Resurrection of the Flesh, Flesh of Christ*. IV: complete *Prayer* from Muratori’s Ambrosian supplements, *Testimony of the Soul, Repentance, Martyrs, Patience, Spectacles, Idolatry, Baptism, Soul, Soldier’s Crown, Modesty* [Col. 0064C]. V: *Apology, To the Nations* I–II, *Pallium*, and Semler’s dissertation on the variable, uncertain character of Tertullian’s books. VI: Semler’s preface and indexes of Scripture, memorable matters and opinions, and Tertullianic Latin, serving as a continuous commentary.

From volume IV Christian Gottfried Schütz managed the edition and prefaced it. Having gathered variants for earlier volumes, he continued but chose only the better ones [Col. 0064D], omitting useless readings, including many of Junius’s guesses. Where Rhenanus failed he followed Pamelius’s old reading unless intolerable. In V the *Apology* follows Havercamp, *Pallium* Salmasius, and *To the Nations* Rigault. Would that Schütz’s promised history of Tertullian’s works and editions had accompanied Semler’s illuminating dissertations. The Göttingen reviewer inaccurately calls chapter division peculiar to this edition; it had prevailed since Pamelius.

[Col. 0065A] **1770.** “J. C. Wernsdorf, program on the Church as the Dove’s simple house, *Against the Valentinians* III, Helmstedt, quarto.”

**1772.** “H. A. Zeibich, program on Tertullian’s view of the dove descending upon Christ, Gera, quarto.”

**1774.** “Engelbert Klüpfel, Tertullian’s view of the indissolubility of a marriage contracted in unbelief when one spouse converts, Freiburg, quarto.”

**1776.** “Christian F. Rössler, *Library of the Church Fathers in Translations and Extracts* I ff., III, Leipzig.” [Col. 0065B]

**1776–1777.** “Johann Daniel Schumann, observations on Church writers of centuries III–IV, conjecturing certain New Testament interpolations wrongly attributed to Tertullian, Hanover, quarto.”

**1780. WÜRZBURG EDITION.** Würzburg, Stahel: complete works, volumes I–II, also titled *Complete Works of the Holy Latin Fathers*, I–II. Oberthür followed Halle while comparing the Paris 1608 reprint of Pamelius, placing its variants below and rarely correcting the text. In volume II he acted somewhat more freely, substituting from Paris or Halle’s variants occasional words and, more rarely, sentences [Col. 0065C]. He adopted Nösselt’s chronology, but kept the books against Marcion together. He added poems once ascribed to Tertullian: *Against Marcion, Judgment of the Lord, Genesis, Sodom, Tree of Life* (omitted by Pamelius), and *To a Senator*.

**1780.** “All poems ascribed to Tertullian in the Pesaro collection of ancient poets, V.”

[Col. 0065D] **1780.** “Schütz, explanation of *Prescriptions* XVI–XVII on upsetting the stomach or brain by scriptural encounter, Jena, folio.”

**1780.** “FIRST ENGLISH TRANSLATION of *To Scapula*, by D. Dalrymple, Edinburgh.”

**1781.** “Dom Dominik Schram, O.S.B., analysis of Tertullian’s works in his great work III.”

**1783.** “José Antonio Cantova, two theological-critical dissertations on Septimius and Epiphanius, showing neither suffered anthropomorphism, Milan, octavo.”

[Col. 0066A] **1784.** “Schütz, program on Tertullian’s rule of faith, Jena.”

**1784.** Assisi, octavo: *Observations on the Analysis of Tertullian’s Book of Prescriptions*. It is preceded by an Italian version and Pamelius’s Latin text from Franeker 1597 (misprinted 1697), with Rigault’s variants from Venice 1744. The analyzed book appeared at Pavia in 1783; Oelrichs will, I think, inform readers about both.

**1785.** “H. C. Ballenstedt, *Tertullian’s Mental Powers, Religious Knowledge, and Theology: An Essay*, Helmstedt, octavo.” [Col. 0066B]

**1790.** “C. C. Birch, dissertation presenting and explaining theological passages collected from Tertullian, Copenhagen, quarto.”

**1791.** “J. G. A. Oelrichs, commentaries on Latin Church writers of the first six centuries, edited by A. H. L. Heeren, octavo.”

**1792.** “SPANISH TRANSLATION, *Apologist of the Ancient Christian Religion*, by Manuel Ximénez de Urieta, Madrid, quarto.”

**1792–1797.** “C. T. G. Schoenemann, *Historico-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers* I, pp. 2–53.” [Col. 0066C]

**1829.** In Caillau and Guillon’s select Fathers appeared nearly all Tertullian, except six partly printed works: *Soul, Flight, Modesty, Fasting, Exhortation to Chastity,* and *Monogamy*, volumes VI–VII.

**1832.** “FIRST FRENCH TRANSLATION of *Testimony of the Soul*, an especially elegant work fortunate in its first translator, *Annals of Christian Philosophy*, June 1832, no. 24 [Col. 0067D]. The index deservedly reveals the name unfairly hidden from readers: Melchior du Lac de Montvert.”

**1839.** E. G. Gersdorf’s selected Latin Fathers [Col. 0068A] published nearly all Tertullian in two classes: I, apologetic works—*To the Martyrs, Spectacles, Idolatry, Apology, To the Nations* II, *Testimony of the Soul, Soldier’s Crown, Flight, Scorpiace, To Scapula*; II, Christian rites and morals—*Prayer, Patience, Baptism, Repentance, To His Wife* II, *Adornment of Women* II, *Exhortation, Monogamy, Modesty, Fasts, Veiling of Virgins, Pallium*. Leipzig 1839, two duodecimo volumes, edited by E. F. Leopold. Its pure text and fine paper and type deserve praise [Col. 0068B]; it has variants but no commentary.

**1839.** “Leopold on causes of corrupt Latin after Augustus, chiefly the Fathers and especially Tertullian, in Illgen’s journal VIII.1 ff., Leipzig.”

**1842.** De Genoude lately published the newest and fullest French translation of almost all Tertullian in *The Fathers of the Church Translated into French* XII, Paris, octavo. H. Denain’s version contains twenty-two principal works [Col. 0068C], has no notes or commentary, and is elegant rather than exact, adorning African harshness with brilliant language and sometimes reproducing it vividly.

**1843.** These literary annals conclude with this new PARIS EDITION. After so many labors we undertake it confidently because we offer nothing not borrowed: we omit nothing useful from earlier elucidations [Col. 0068D] and claim nothing novel. We must explain its additions, preferred text, and commentaries.

## ARTICLE IV. The new Paris edition

It has three components: prolegomena, appendices, and the complete text between them with variants and commentary [Col. 0069A]. First we preserve Pamelius’s *Life of Tertullian through Twenty-Four Years*, adding brief notes and correcting the badly disordered consular list, though its persistent one-year anticipation could not be removed without upheaval. Pamelius’s annals remain imperfect and erroneous; Nösselt’s learned dissertation on the true dates and doctrine of Tertullian’s surviving writings, excerpted from Lumper [Col. 0069B], supplies needed aid, though we reserve judgment on some doubtful opinions of both.

We retain Pamelius’s *Paradoxes with Antidote* and proverbial formulas explained by Rhenanus and Hoye, more from precedent than evident usefulness. After the *Apology* we reproduce Mosheim’s inquiry from Venice II on its date and Severus’s persecution.

Nothing fuller exists than Le Nourry’s Maurist apparatus [Col. 0069C]. Though examining only three books, he enters all Tertullian’s doctrine, confidently illuminates difficulties, restores the author’s sense, vindicates him from false charges, marks real errors and spurious works, and rejects bold fictions even when supported by editors. We reprint this rare treasury.

Five appendices conclude the work. I contains genuine or spurious poems with brief notes [Col. 0069D]. II gives the Vatican fragment published about 1630 by Suares and forgotten for two centuries. III gathers what Septimius spoke, translated, or wrote in Greek. IV lists lost works, fragments, and spuria. V supplies Corbinian Thomas’s rich notes on *Baptism* and *Repentance*, received too late for their place but in time to conclude the work. We thank J. B. Malou of Louvain [Col. 0070A].

The body has text, variants, and commentary. Following Lumper, Schoenemann, and Walch, we chiefly use Le Prieur’s 1664 Pamelius–Rigault edition, collating Rhenanus, Pamelius, Rigault, Paris, Venice, Halle, Würzburg, and Leopold’s recent Leipzig recension [Col. 0070B]. Continuous variant lists represent the Agobard, Leiden, Fulda, Vatican, Ambrosian, Wouwer, Latini, and Gelenius manuscripts and principal editions. Some will disdain these trifles; fairer readers will judge no smallest aid useless in recovering Tertullian’s voice from scribal license [Col. 0070C], since one rejected word may yield more light than a long note.

We also add interpreters. We omit some Paris notes that merely give variants or oppose Catholic faith, drawing especially on Pamelius. We use fuller special commentaries [Col. 0070D]: Thomas on *Baptism* and *Repentance*; much of Havercamp on the *Apology*, removing undigested professorial and heretical matter; Salmasius on *Pallium*; Muratori and Panciroli on the enlarged *Prayer*. Against Semler’s impious dispute over Irenaeus, parallel passages show clearly that Irenaeus’s Greek works and old Latin translation preceded Tertullian [Col. 0071A].

Editions have imposed many orders: La Cerda and Oberthür chronology; Rhenanus and Rigault manuscript lists; Pamelius theological synthesis; Semler a mixture suggesting all works Catholic and Montanist alike are one Montanist mass [Col. 0071B]. We preserve familiar order where possible but adopt a partly chronological, partly systematic sequence: volume I Catholic, volume II Montanist; each divided into apologetic/polemical and moral/dogmatic works. Catholic apologetics are *Apology, To the Nations, Testimony, Martyrs, Spectacles, Idolatry*, with the Montanist *To Scapula* appended for affinity [Col. 0071C]. Catholic dogmatics are *Prayer, Baptism, Repentance, To His Wife* II, and *Adornment of Women* II; comparison with Lumper shows the chronology is preserved [Col. 0072A].

Montanist polemics are *Soldier’s Crown, Flight, Against the Psychics, Scorpiace, Praxeas, Hermogenes, Marcion, Valentinians, Jews, Soul against Philosophers, Flesh of Christ,* and *Resurrection*. Moral works are *Veiling, Exhortation, Monogamy, Fasts* [Col. 0072B], *Modesty,* and *Pallium*. The disputed *Prescriptions* stands between Catholic and Montanist works at the front of volume II, leading the twelve polemical books.

We conclude by imploring God, the Virgin Mother of God, mother and delight of angels and men, and the triumphant Church’s crown—festively celebrated on the day we finished—to make this long work acceptable to God, pleasing to the Church, useful to many, and eternally profitable to us [Col. 0072C].

Written at Paris, 1 November 1843.

## Life of Q. S. F. Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage, by James Pamelius

[Col. 0041]

## THE LIFE OF Q. SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, PRESBYTER OF CARTHAGE, BY JAMES PAMELIUS, CONTAINING THE HISTORY OF TWENTY-FOUR YEARS OF HIS AGE

[Col. 0041A] **§ I. A preliminary twofold controversy is set forth.—1.** As, God favoring, we write Tertullian’s life—he who, remarkably, flourished as an African under the African pope St Victor and the African emperor bearing his name, Septimius Severus—two very difficult controversies arise. The first concerns the consul Tertullus, our Tertullian, Tertylian the jurist, and St Tertullinus the martyr, four men whom some through error tried to make one. The second concerns the author’s period and age when, as a new recruit of Christ, he was initiated into the mysteries of faith.

[Col. 0041B] **2. And first, concerning the consul Tertullus, our Tertullian, Tertylian the jurist, and St Tertullinus the martyr.**—As regards the first, Rhenanus was above all misled by a corrupt reading in Regino, which must also be corrected in the *Chronicle* of Hermannus Contractus: in place of Tertullinus the martyr—whom the martyrologies list, from the Acts of the Passion of Pope St Stephen, on 4 August—he read TERTULLIAN. Those, moreover, have hitherto erred no less who confuse Tertullus, the Roman consul, with the jurist Tertylian, on account of the *senatus consultum Tertullianum*, concerning which several [Col. 0041C] rescripts were issued and are cited in Digest, book 38, title 17, and Code, book 6, title 55.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] See, at the end of that dissertation of Pamelius, the opinions of Tertylian the jurist that survive in the books of the Digest. Cf. Johann Blumenbach, *De Senatusconsulto Q. Septimio Flor. presbytero et Jureconsulto Tertulianis*, Leipzig, 1735, quarto; Justus C. Wiesenhauer, dissertation *De Jureconsulto et Q. Sept. Flor. Tertullianis*, Hildesheim, 1743, quarto; Maiansius, book IV, letter II, Valencia, 1732, quarto. EDD.]

For no consul named Tertullianus or Tertylianus can be found, but rather Q. Flavius Tertullus, who was consul with Licinius Sacerdos in the year 910 of the City; upon his report the said senatorial decree had already been promulgated earlier, during the reign of Hadrian Augustus. For, in the said title, law 21 of the Digest, the deified Pius decreed that in a certain factual case the *senatus consultum Tertullianum* did not apply; it is therefore established as earlier than he. Tertylian the jurist, however, as will presently be explained more fully, flourished many years later under the emperor Alexander, together with most of the other pupils of Papinian who devoted themselves to administering law. So that nothing may be lacking here, after this Life of our author we have appended his rulings from the Books of Questions and his single book *On the Soldier's Private Property*. Since these alone survive, [Col. 0042A] and no one else mentions any other books published by this Tertylian, Conrad Gesner appears mistaken when he further attributes to him legal rescripts from books *On Senatorial Decrees* and *On the Libonian and Orphitian Decrees*. On these matters the more learned are sufficiently agreed.

Whether, however, that Tertylian is the same man as our TERTULLIAN remains a question still under judgment, particularly because some jurists of great name and learning affirm it. We, certainly, subject to sounder judgment, consider them different: first because, according to the truer reading of the Florentine Pandects, as Augustine Justinianus attests, the former is everywhere called Tertylian, [Col. 0042B] whereas ours is TERTULLIAN; second because François Baudouin, in letters sent to me, acknowledged that their style and diction differ; and finally because their dates do not sufficiently agree. For if, with Bernardino Rutilio, we say that Tertylian published his books in the reigns of Hadrian and Antoninus—Hadrian having died in the year 890 of the City and Severus, under whom our TERTULLIAN first became prominent, having begun to reign in 945, with fifty-five years thus intervening—our author must have been more than fifty years old when he became a Christian, especially if we attribute to him those opinions which jurists customarily gave only after attaining great authority. Yet St Jerome establishes the contrary, writing that he fell into heresy in middle age after having already been a presbyter for a long time.

But if, according to others (whose view we followed above), he lived under the emperor Alexander along with the other jurists whose opinions were incorporated into the Pandects, it is clearer than daylight that he was not the same man. For our TERTULLIAN had embraced the faith of Christ about thirty years before Alexander and, if still alive at that time, was then entangled in heresy. [Col. 0042D] Nor do the arguments of those who think otherwise carry enough weight to draw me to their side. Ulpian, in Digest 38.17, *On the senatus consultum Tertullianum*, book 1—a passage that perhaps occasioned this controversy—mentions a rescript of “the Emperor and the deified Father” (that is, Antoninus and Severus) addressed to a certain Tertullian. Yet this Tertullian is first named either Junius or Ovinius according to manuscript codices, whereas ours is called Q. SEPTIMIUS TERTULLIANUS; furthermore, the Florentine Pandects read Tertullus, perhaps the same Q. Flavius Tertullus who [Col. 0043A] held the consulship with T. Flavius Clemens in Severus's third year.

The other argument on which they chiefly rely—that our TERTULLIAN was most exact in retaining the language of law and therefore, on Eusebius's testimony, a Roman jurist—proves no more than if we were to say that the orator Caecilius, whom Minucius Felix introduces conversing with him in his *Octavius*, was the same as our Caecilius Cyprian because both practiced oratory; or, to take a case closer to the present matter, if we judged the emperor Septimius Severus the same man as another Septimius Severus because both were Africans and historians, the former writing his own life and the latter that of the emperor Alexander; or finally if we confused that Septimius whose verses in praise of Janus survive in Crinitus, or Quintus Septimius Romanus, who rendered Dictys of Crete's six books on the Trojan War into Latin, with our SEPTIMIUS TERTULLIAN, because both were Africans and poets. Perhaps to distinguish himself from them, our author placed at the head of his books the designations Q. SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS OF CARTHAGE, [Col. 0043B] not being content with the two names SEPTIMIUS TERTULLIANUS, as were the other African writers after him: Minucius Felix, Caecilius Cyprian, Lactantius Firmianus, Marius Victorinus, and Aurelius Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] Thus, besides the manuscripts, Angelo Poliziano already designated our author in book IV, letter V, *On Names*. So too our author himself, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, last chapter: “To those who read this in good peace and place usefulness before custom, may peace and grace overflow from our Lord Jesus, together with SEPTIMIUS TERTULLIAN, whose little work this is.” The conclusion of the book *On Baptism* is similar: “I ask only that, when you pray, you remember TERTULLIAN the sinner as well.” The conclusion of the book *Exhortation to Chastity* is similar: “Remember in your prayers TERTULLIAN who exhorts you.” So the Paris, Frankfurt, and Venetian editions. Rigault, however, omitted these last words; hence both Salomon Semler and E. F. Leopold held it wholly certain that they were added by another hand, although no manuscript supports this. Cf. Lumper, *Historia theologico-critica SS. PP.*, part VI, chapter 1, article 1, note b. EDD.]

## § II. The time at which our TERTULLIAN was converted to the faith

**3.** As for the other controversy, concerning the time when our TERTULLIAN was converted to the faith, a far greater difficulty [Col. 0043C] presents itself. Some who think that he flourished around the year of Christ 160 were deceived by the author's words in *On Monogamy*: “about 160 years having since elapsed” (*On Monogamy* 3). How those years are to be counted—whether from Christ's Passion or rather from the period when the apostle Paul wrote his First Epistle to the Corinthians—will be discussed more fully below under the year of the Lord 214. Thus Eusebius, the Venerable Bede, Freculphus of Lisieux, Martin of Poland, Conrad of Lichtenau, abbot of Ursperg, Vincent of Beauvais, Hermannus Contractus, and Trithemius write much more correctly that TERTULLIAN flourished around the year of Christ 200. Yet all are silent about the year in which he gave his name to Christ, except TERTULLIAN himself, and he does so in exceedingly obscure words.

It is indeed clear [Col. 0043D] that immediately after his baptism he composed the book *On the Pallium*, on this occasion: when, in Christian fashion, he laid aside the toga and put on the pallium, some friend objected, “So, from the toga to the pallium?” Among other things he replies: “But I now also bring to it fellowship with the divine sect and discipline. Rejoice, pallium, and exult: a better philosophy has now deemed you worthy, since you began to clothe a Christian” (*On the Pallium* 5, 6, and 3).

It is not equally easy, however, to understand what these words of the same book mean: “But antiquity is now vain, when our own courses lie before us. How greatly has this age transformed the world! How many cities has the threefold power of the present Empire either brought forth, enlarged, or restored, God favoring so many Augusti in union! How many census lists have been transcribed! How many peoples driven back! How many orders ennobled! How many barbarians shut out! Truly the world is the most cultivated estate of this Empire: every aconite of hostility, every cactus, and every thornbush of treacherous intimacy has been uprooted; it is planted and delightful beyond the orchard of Alcinous and the rose garden of Midas.” Rhenanus, the Magdeburg Centuriators, and others following them interpret “the threefold power of the Empire” as Severus Augustus and the Caesars Pescennius Niger and Clodius Albinus—Severus and Niger having been proclaimed by their armies in Pannonia and the East, and Albinus in Gaul. But Rhenanus contradicts himself when he admits that Niger's proclamation occurred against Severus's will and that Severus judged both men enemies and afterward killed them. Hence, amid such hostility among three Caesars, the words “God favoring so many Augusti in union” cannot apply, still less “every aconite of hostility having been uprooted.” Moreover, because the choice of the three Caesars in different provinces occurred at the very beginning of Severus's reign, it can hardly agree [Col. 0044C] with the following words: “How many census lists have been transcribed!” and so forth, “how many barbarians shut out!” This last raises the greater difficulty, since it establishes that the book was composed only after the barbarians had been shut out—that is, after the Arabs, Parthians, and Adiabenians had been defeated.

We therefore later discovered that what, in our summary and notes, we assigned to about Severus's fifth year should rather be applied to the third, since Albinus began to defect from Severus in the fourth year and was killed in the fifth. At that time, therefore, Severus Augustus, his son Antoninus, and the said Albinus ruled together, and the Empire had already been pacified, since both Julianus, who had seized it after Pertinax was killed, and Pescennius Niger had already been defeated and slain.

**4.** All indeed agree [Col. 0044D] that Albinus was a partner in the Empire. According to the consular fasti, immediately after Severus received all the imperial titles, “D. CLODIUS ALBINUS WAS NAMED CAESAR BY IMPERATOR CAESAR L. SEPTIMIUS SEVERUS AUGUSTUS”; and in the next year Severus entered the consulship with Albinus, who from then on was also called SEPTIMIUS, apparently in honor of Severus. Severus furthermore honored him by ordering, as Spartianus attests, coins to be marked with his image. These still [Note: [Col. 0044D] That is, around 1579, when this Life of Tertullian by Pamelius was first published.] survive with both Greek and Latin inscriptions in the collections of the noble lords Marcus and Guido Laurinus, lords of Watervliet, along with many others that will be mentioned below. Supporting our view are these, issued after Niger had already been killed: “IMP. CAES. D. CLODIUS SEPT. ALB. COS. II. / MONETA AUG.,” “CS. VICT. AUG.,” “MINERVA THE PEACE-BEARER / A FERTILE AGE,” and finally “HAPPINESS.” All seem to relate to the phrase “every aconite of hostility having been uprooted.”

**5.** As for Antoninus, Severus's son, two things confirm our conjecture that he too had already been distinguished with the title Caesar: first, Code 3, *On Undutiful Wills*, law 1, which Severus and Antoninus rescripted on 1 July in the consulship of Falco and Clarus, a consulship falling in Severus's first year; and second, this coin legend: “THE UNCONQUERED PIOUS EMPERORS AUGUSTI” (with the effigy of Severus and Antoninus still a beardless boy), “THE GREATEST PARTHIAN VICTORY.” [Col. 0045B] This may indeed refer to the words “how many barbarians shut out!”, as may this: “L. SEPT. SEV. PERT. AUG. IMP. II. ARAB. PAR. ADIAB. COS. II. P. P. S. C.” Spartianus agrees especially in these words about the period after Niger's death: “He then conducted many operations around Arabia, reducing the Parthians too to submission, as well as the Adiabenians, all of whom had sided with Pescennius. On his return he was therefore called Arabicus, Parthicus, and Adiabenicus; but he refused a triumph lest he appear to triumph over a civil victory.” Eusebius agrees too—or rather St Jerome, who inserted much relating to the Latins into Eusebius's *Chronicle*—placing the Jewish, Samaritan, and Parthian war before the killing of Albinus, as do Orosius, John Zonaras, and Hugh of Fleury.

It is no objection that Herodian [Col. 0045C] writes that the Parthian war was still postponed: greater trust should be placed in a Latin than a Greek writer who observed no historical order; and Spartianus later writes that Severus again set out against the Arabs, Parthians, and Adiabenians and, after finishing the war against them, celebrated a triumph—the same triumph discussed below under Severus's tenth year. Especially pertinent are surviving inscriptions on marble and coins in which he is twice styled Parthicus. One, from his eleventh year, is on the Arch of Septimius at Rome: “TO IMP. CAES. L. SEPTIMIUS, SON OF MARCUS, SEVERUS PIUS PERTINAX AUGUSTUS, FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND, PARTHICUS ARABICUS, PARTHICUS ADIABENICUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, HOLDER OF TRIBUNICIAN POWER XI, CONSUL III, PROCONSUL; AND TO IMP. CAES. M. AURELIUS, SON OF LUCIUS, ANTONINUS AUGUSTUS PIUS FELIX, HOLDER OF TRIBUNICIAN POWER VI, CONSUL, PROCONSUL, FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND; THE BEST AND BRAVEST [Col. 0045D] PRINCES, FOR THEIR DISTINGUISHED VIRTUES AT HOME AND ABROAD; THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF ROME.” Another, from his fifteenth year: “L. SEPT. SEV. AUG. IMP. XII. PARTH. ARAB. PARTH. ADIAB. AA. X. / DEPARTURE OF THE AUGUSTUS,” apparently for Britain.

The former also in part explains “how many peoples driven back!” Likewise “how many orders ennobled!” refers to military orders or legions, as shown by these inscriptions of Severus's second, third, and fourth years: “IMP. CAES. L. SEV. ... TRIB. POT. II. IMP. IV. COS. II. PROCOS. P. P. / THE ORDER OF CLUSIUM”; “TO THE VIRGIN DIANA, SACRED, FOR THE SAFETY OF IMP. L. SEPT. SEV. ... TRIB. POT. III. IMP. V. / THE ORDER OF CLUSIUM”; and “IMP. CAES. ... IMP. VIII. TRIB. POT. IV. / LEGION VII OF CLUSIUM.” Nevertheless [Col. 0046A] we shall begin our history with Severus's first year, and with TERTULLIAN already a Christian from Severus's third year, once we have prefaced certain remarks on his designations Q. SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS OF CARTHAGE, and consequently on his people, family, stock, parents, homeland, education, studies and youthful writings, state of life, and age when Severus began his reign.

## § III. His praenomen, nomen, cognomen, and agnomen

**6.** All antiquarians know that Q.—which Vincent of Beauvais, Trithemius, Poliziano, and a manuscript codex long ago attributed to our author—is a praenomen, perhaps because he was born fifth, since Roman praenomina were generally taken either from an event or from grandfathers, great-grandfathers, or more remote ancestors [Col. 0046B] (in whose place today each person's given names have succeeded). Such too is QUINTA SEPTIMIA, which Onuphrius lists among female praenomina.

SEPTIMIUS is the designation of a clan that among the Romans was first royal, then plebeian, and finally consular and patrician. First there is found SEPTIMIUS MESIUS, KING OF THE AEQUI; then, in various marble inscriptions, partly among the epigrams of the ancient City and partly in Aldus Manutius's *Orthography*, the female names SEPTIMIA ANNIA, FL. HORATIA SEPTIMIA OCTAVILLA, SEPT. FELICISSIMA EURESIA, SEPT. SECUNDA, and SEPT. EXORTA; and, among men of the military order—which is more relevant to our purpose—T. SEPTIMIUS FELICISSIMUS OF THE SECOND COHORT; L. FLAVIUS L. F. SEPTIMIUS AFER OCTAVIANUS, C. V., OF THE SECOND CAVALRY SQUADRON, DECEMVIR FOR JUDGING LEGAL DISPUTES; L. SEPTIMIUS ANTIGONUS, SOLDIER OF THE SIXTH PRAETORIAN COHORT; T. SEPTIMIUS, SON OF GAIUS, SERGIAN TRIBE, MILITARY TRIBUNE; and finally L. SEPTIMIUS SEVERIANUS and SEPT. CARITO, V. P.

Among men of consular rank there were, under Julius Caesar Augustus, P. SEPTIMIUS; under Caesar Trajan, SEPTIMIUS AGNIDINUS, V. C., ACTING THROUGH THE SPANISH PROVINCES, V. C., P. T., HEARING CASES AS IMPERIAL DEPUTY; under Marcus, SEPTIMIUS SEVERUS; under the emperor Verus, L. SEPTIMIUS SEVERUS, SON OF M. SEPTIMIUS GETA, later emperor; under that very Severus, D. CLODIUS SEPTIMIUS ALBINUS, proclaimed Caesar with him as stated above; P. SEPTIMIUS, SON OF MARCUS, GETA, Severus's brother; Q. SEPTIMIUS PLAUTIANUS, father-in-law of his son Antoninus; and—strangely, since his elder son Antoninus omitted the name SEPTIMIUS—P. SEPTIMIUS GETA, SON OF SEVERUS AUGUSTUS, IMPERATOR CAESAR AUGUSTUS.

Whether our African author himself belonged to their clan is not so clear. Meanwhile he gives himself that name in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, last chapter, no. 140: “May peace and grace overflow from our Lord Jesus, together with SEPTIMIUS TERTULLIAN, whose little work this is.” Hence Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* 5.1, and St Jerome, letter 188 to Fabiola, call him SEPTIMIUS TERTULLIAN; Trithemius, Poliziano, and all manuscript and printed codices to date agree with them.

The cognomen FLORENS signifies a particular family of the Septimian clan, though one unknown among the Romans; yet it is attributed to the author not only in printed editions but also in a manuscript codex and long ago by Trithemius and Poliziano. Besides all other writers who mention him, he calls himself by the name TERTULLIAN in the words already cited and also in these: “I ask only that, when you pray, you remember TERTULLIAN the sinner as well,” and “Remember in your prayers TERTULLIAN who exhorts you to these things.” The name seems derived from Tertullus, just as Octavianus from Octavius and Septimius from Septimius, and to signify a branch of the Florens family. Perhaps of that branch is the man named in this inscription surviving at Mainz near St Maurice and at Milan near St Victor by the Vercelli gate: “C. SARTORIUS, SON OF LUCIUS, OF THE OUFENTINE TRIBE, TERTULLIANUS, VETERAN OF LEGION XI, [Col. 0047B] CURATOR OF ROMAN CITIZENS AT MOGUNTIACUM,” or MUNGOTIARIUM. At least this much is established from Eusebius's *Chronicle* and St Jerome's *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*: our TERTULLIAN was an African, the son of a proconsular centurion. St Isidore, the Venerable Bede, Nicephorus, Freculphus of Lisieux, Marianus Scotus, Ado, and Vincent of Beauvais also affirm it.

## § IV. What sort of education did he receive, and what was his knowledge of letters and the sciences?

**7.** The agnomen OF CARTHAGE indicates Carthage as his homeland. These authors agree here too when they say “of the province of Africa, of the city of Carthage,” as does St Optatus of Milevis in book I *Against Parmenian*, and Nicephorus expressly when he writes that Tertullian was born at Carthage in Africa. What is more, [Col. 0047C] the author himself indicates it abundantly clearly.

[Note: [Col. 0047D] Eusebius seems to have written that Tertullian was Roman and noble, *Ecclesiastical History* II.2: “Tertullian [relates] these things—he who had an exact knowledge of Roman laws, a man distinguished in other respects as well, and one of the most illustrious at Rome.”. His report that Tertullian was skilled in Roman laws led some to believe that the author was the jurist, and there is indeed a jurist of the same name. It is established, however, that he is a different man from our Tertullian; Eusebius does not report that he was a jurist, but that he was skilled in Roman laws. What Eusebius adds about his country and nobility cannot be defended unless it is understood of Roman writers, the sense being that Tertullian was one of the most illustrious Latin authors. Rufinus understood this passage of Eusebius in this sense, translating it “very illustrious among our writers.”]

At the beginning of *On the Pallium* he says: “First always in Africa, Carthaginian men, noble through antiquity, happy through novelty.... Yet once your dress too was different.... But after the benefit conferred by the injury upon you..., after the obscene omens of Gracchus..., after Pompey's three altars and Caesar's long delays—when Statilius Taurus set up the walls and Sentius Saturninus explained the rites—when concord assists, the toga was offered.... Yet you denounce the pallium generally, even though unmindful that it was yours. I indeed do not wonder, in view of the earlier lesson. For that Carthage too is called the Ram, fiercest in its pursuit of war, the first of all to take up arms. Yet when the final times of the homeland arrived” (behold, he calls Carthage his homeland) “and the now-Roman Ram dared assail its former walls, the Carthaginians were immediately astonished as at a new and foreign disposition. So powerfully can remote antiquity change with time. Thus, finally, even the pallium is not recognized.” We have treated this at somewhat greater length because of the opinion of Vadianus, who on his map of Palestine assigns Tertullian as his birthplace a certain town near the Altars of the Philaeni brothers.

**8.** How fortunate TERTULLIAN'S education was is attested by his books against the Gentiles, which, as St Jerome testifies in his letter to Magnus, contain the whole learning of the secular world. From these books alone it is evident that he had read every sort of author—historians, poets, and grammarians. As for the jurists, the matter is too well known to require proof; and the same may be inferred of physicians and philosophers from the book *On the Soul*. The reader will find a catalogue of all these, Greek as well as Latin and divided into their classes, among our indexes. Hence Lactantius calls him skilled in every kind of literature; Eusebius, illustrious for his knowledge of laws and Roman affairs; St Jerome, a man of sharp and vehement intellect, than whom none was more learned or acute; St Augustine, most eloquent, swelling his speech with sounding cheeks; and Nicephorus, exceptionally powerful in eloquence, very sharp and ingenious.

Vincent of Lérins develops all this much more fully: “Among the Latins,” he says, “this man must readily be judged the chief of all our writers. For who was more learned than he? Who more practiced in divine and human affairs? With a certain marvelous capacity of mind he embraced all philosophy and all the sects of the philosophers, the authors and champions of those sects, all their branches of learning, and every variety of history and study. Did he not also excel in an intellect so weighty and vehement that there was scarcely anything he proposed to overthrow which he did not either penetrate with acuteness or crush by force? And who could adequately celebrate the praises of his style? It is woven with such a density of arguments that those whom it could not persuade it compels to agreement; nearly as many words as judgments, as many senses as victories.”

Nevertheless, compelled by experience itself, we must admit what Lactantius writes of him: that he is not very accessible, less polished, and extremely obscure; and, according to St Jerome, dense in thoughts but difficult in expression. It is therefore unsurprising that Nepotian could easily distinguish his style, and that of other Africans too—as the same St Jerome testifies in Nepotian's Life—the styles, I mean, of Minucius Felix, St Cyprian, Arnobius, Lactantius, and Victorinus. Rhenanus somewhere noted the chief cause of his obscurity: through constant reading of Greek authors he absorbed Greek modes of expression so thoroughly that, even when writing Latin, he could not forget them.

St Jerome himself is an ample witness that Tertullian wrote certain things in his youth, even before accepting the faith of Christ. “This,” he says in *Against Jovinian* I, “is the place to describe the hardships of marriage and, as though in a rhetorical commonplace, to exult in speech. TERTULLIAN too, certainly, when he was still a young man, made sport of this subject.” In letter 22 to Eustochium he gives the book's argument and title: “If it pleases you to know how many troubles a free virgin escapes and to how many a wife is bound, read TERTULLIAN TO A PHILOSOPHER FRIEND.” Hence we judge that even from that time he observed the chastity he held in such esteem throughout his whole life. We therefore understand these words of the author as spoken not so much in his own person as in that of others, by way of example: “I know that I neither committed adultery with one flesh nor now strive for continence with another” (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh* 59).

## § V. His conduct in paganism; his marriage

**9.** That TERTULLIAN nevertheless entered into marriage is clear from his two books *To His Wife*. Perhaps he did so because the Papian, Poppaean, and Julian laws had not yet been abolished: these, as he himself admits, compelled people to beget children and forbade the unmarried and childless to receive a whole inheritance under a will. More will be said below about their repeal by the emperor Severus. The legislation fixed a definite age for marriage—thirty-five according to Plato—and thus confirms our conjecture that he married before accepting the faith, although no mention of any children of his occurs anywhere.

Trithemius writes that he gloriously taught rhetoric at Carthage for some years; we shall presently establish that he was afterward also an orator, or advocate in legal causes. That he was also learned in law is evident from the various legal phrases and juristic terms he employs. Perhaps at Rome he had Cervidius Scaevola as his teacher and the emperor Severus and Aemilius Papinian as fellow students. Yet he was younger than Severus, who was born in AD 146, so that Tertullian was forty at the beginning of Severus's reign. From then until the end of the reigns of Severus and his son Antoninus Caracalla, under whom the author flourished, there were about twenty-four years, making TERTULLIAN about sixty-three. From that year—which physicians call climacteric—the decrepit old age to which he lived is customarily reckoned to begin. Supporting this is the statement of St Jerome and Nicephorus that after middle age he fell into the heresy of Montanus: in our view, around his fifty-third year, in Severus's fifteenth year, a full decade before his death. But enough of these matters. Let us proceed to the history of those twenty-four years.

## The Year of Jesus Christ 194

**10.** In the year of the Lord 194, when C. Sosius Falco and C. Julius Erucius Clarus were consuls; in the eighth year of St Victor, son of Felix the African and Roman pontiff; and in the first year of Imperator Caesar L. Septimius, son of Marcus, the African, Pius Pertinax Augustus, TERTULLIAN, still a pagan, practiced as an advocate at Carthage. This is established by his own words, written about himself in the person of the pallium after he had become a Christian: “I owe nothing to the forum, nothing to the parade ground, nothing to the senate-house; I keep watch for no office, seize no rostra beforehand, haunt no praetoria, worship no railings, wear down no benches, disturb no laws, and trumpet no causes. More harm has been done to the state by togas than by breastplates” (*On the Pallium* 5).

He certainly admits that he had been a pagan. Speaking of the last judgment, eternal life and fire, and the raising of the dead, he says: “We too once laughed at these things; we were of your number. Christians are made, [Col. 0050A] not born.”

[Note: [Col. 0050D] Tertullian himself expressly attests in his own words that, together with the superstitions of the Gentiles, he served lust, in *On the Resurrection* 59: “I know that I neither committed adultery with one flesh nor now strive for continence with another.” At that time he also delighted in spectacles, of which he says, “I prefer not to supply the full measure rather than to remember” (Tertullian, *On Spectacles* 19), that is, to say little of them rather than remember what he saw. In the book *On Repentance* he admits that he was the greatest of all sinners and, urging repentance upon the fallen, says (*On Repentance* 4 and 12): “You sinner like me—indeed, less than I, for I acknowledge my own preeminence in offenses—seize upon repentance and embrace it as a shipwrecked man trusts some plank.” In chapter 12 he says of a life spent in vice: “What more can I say about these things”—that is, repentance—“since I am a sinner of every mark and born for nothing but repentance?”]

In the author certain matters pertaining to this year may be found. First, concerning the murder of the emperor P. Helvius Pertinax, son of Publius, killed on 28 March, there is this passage of the *Apology*: “Whence come those who train in the wrestling-school to squeeze throats? Whence those who burst armed into the palace, bolder than all the Sigeriuses and Partheniuses? From among the Romans, unless I am mistaken” (*Apology* 35). For he was killed at the palace gates by armed Praetorian soldiers through the conspiracy of Laetus, his own praetorian prefect; at the latter's command the emperor Commodus had shortly before been strangled by the athlete Narcissus, with whom he was accustomed to practice wrestling.

Then, concerning Imperator Caesar Pescennius Niger, who, after Imperator Caesar M. Didius, son of Marcus, Commodus Severus Julianus Augustus had been killed on the senate's orders, seized imperial power on 1 May, the same passage says: “To be sure, the other orders, religious according to their authority, in good faith breathe nothing hostile against Caesar—from the senate itself, the equestrian order, the camps, and the palaces themselves. Whence came the Cassiuses and the Nigers?” The first refers to Avidius Cassius, of the family of those Cassii who killed G. Julius Caesar, who attempted to wrest the principate from the emperors Antoninus Pius, Marcus, and Verus; the second to Niger's conspiracy against the emperor Severus.

In the same place he describes the solemnities of the Caesars—such as were celebrated on 1 June at Severus's new inauguration, after he had already been acclaimed emperor by the army on 15 May—in these words: “Why on a joyful day do we not shade our doorposts with laurels or break into daylight with lamps?” And shortly afterward: “I address the Quirites themselves, the native rabble of the seven hills: does that Roman tongue spare any Caesar of its own? The Tiber is witness, and the training-schools of the beasts. If nature had stretched some transparent material over our breasts so they could be seen through, whose inmost heart would not appear engraved with the scene of Caesar after Caesar presiding over the distribution of a largess—even at the very hour when they shout: ‘May Jupiter add years to you from ours’?” Herodian indicates this in book II, writing among other things that the Praetorian soldiers laid aside their weapons and advanced crowned with laurels in ceremonial dress. Spartianus and the consular fasti likewise record that on 2 July, thirty days after coming to the city, Severus departed for the East against the usurper Niger, after first giving a largess to the people and a donative to the soldiers. Finally there is this coin inscription: “IMP. CAES. L. SEPT. SEV. PERT. AUG. COS. / THE GENEROSITY OF THE AUGUSTUS.” The omitted continuation belongs here too: “To bring hearths and couches out into public, to banquet street by street, to turn the city into a tavern, and to make mud with wine.”

We further judge that this passage from the book *To Scapula* belongs to this year: “Severus himself, the father of Antoninus, was mindful of Christians. For he sought out the Christian Proculus, surnamed Torpacion, steward of Euodia, who had once cured him with oil, and kept him in his palace until Proculus's death. Antoninus too knew him very well, having been reared on Christian milk” (*To Scapula* 4). That a grave illness befell Severus at the beginning of his reign is evident from Aelius Lampridius, if only because he wrote that, since Severus's sons were not yet of an age to rule, Severus intended that, should some human misfortune happen to him, Pescennius Niger and Clodius Albinus would succeed him. Niger was killed in the following year. [Col. 0051B] And because, as will be explained more fully below, Antoninus was named Caesar Augustus in Severus's fourth year, when he was thirteen, the author's statement about his upbringing must be referred to this year. Similar is Spartianus's account of him: “Whenever he saw condemned men exposed to beasts, he wept or turned away his eyes. When he was seven years old and heard that a boy who was his playmate had been severely beaten because of the Jewish religion, for a long time he would not look at his own father, the boy's father, or the man responsible for the beating.” That he was reared on Christian milk is further confirmed by his birth at Lyon, where the Christian faith flourished.

## The Year of the Lord 195
**11.** With IMP. CAES. L. SEPT. SEVERUS PERTINAX AUGUSTUS II and D. CLODIUS SEPT. ALBINUS CAESAR II as consuls, in the ninth year [Col. 0051C] of St Victor, Roman pontiff, and the second year of Severus himself, it is likely that TERTULLIAN was still practicing as an advocate at Carthage. To this year must be referred his words in the book *To Scapula*: “Thus we are also defamed in matters concerning the emperor's majesty; yet no Christian could ever be found among the Albinians, Nigrians, or Cassians. The very people who until the day before had sworn by their guardian spirits, and who had both sacrificed and vowed sacrifices for their safety, were discovered to be their enemies” (*To Scapula* 2).

For in this year Imperator Caesar C. Pescennius Niger Justus Augustus was killed near Cyzicus—or Issus according to Herodian. After this Severus immediately killed those senators who had supported Niger's party and had served with Niger under the title of generals or tribunes. He killed all the others as well, except the soldiers, whom he received after offering them impunity, [Col. 0051D] and for the same reason deprived the Antiochenes of their privileges and the Neapolitans of civic rights. Several kings of barbarians, according to Onuphrius, who had aided Niger were afterward defeated by Severus; hence he was acclaimed imperator II, III, and IV. Our author calls them all Nigrians. This last point confirms our opinion that the Arabs, Parthians, and Adiabenians were defeated in this year; the ancient inscriptions on coins and marble quoted above therefore belong here, as do the author's words “the barbarians shut out” (*On the Pallium* 2).

Indeed, constitutions issued under these consuls in the names of Severus and Antoninus Augusti, dated 25 February, 21 April, 7 July, 26 September, and 22 October, confirm what we said above about Antoninus as colleague in the Empire from the beginning. They survive in Code 8.14.1; 6.2.2; 2.1.2; 2.24.1; and 8.16.1. We judge that the Jewish and Samaritan war, which we mentioned above from Eusebius and which Freculphus of Lisieux also reports, belongs to this year; Severus was accordingly offered the cognomen Judaicus. Our author seems in part to look back to it when speaking of the Jews: “Scattered, wandering, exiles from their own sky and soil, they roam through the world, without man, without God as King; they are not permitted even under the law of strangers to greet their native land with so much as a footprint” (*Apology* 21). From this I infer that the occasion of the war was their desire to return to Judaea, from which the emperor Hadrian had barred them.

Here too belongs what Nicephorus writes in *Ecclesiastical History* 5.2: “At the beginning of Severus's reign our affairs were in a fairly good condition, and the profession of the faith received daily increase, advanced by the writings and teaching of the ecclesiastical doctors whom we have named. This occurred especially in all the greatest cities: Alexandria, Antioch, Aelia, and throughout Palestine; Ephesus and Caesarea; and toward the West, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth, Gaul, and especially Rome. Whole multitudes and entire households were coming to the faith, ready to do and suffer anything rather than act or innovate against our religion.” This gives occasion to list here the ecclesiastical writers of this age whom both Nicephorus and Eusebius mention, especially since our author undoubtedly owed his conversion to their writings and teachings: at Alexandria, Demetrius, the twelfth bishop, and the presbyters Pantaenus and his pupil Clement of Alexandria; at Antioch, Serapion, the ninth bishop; at Jerusalem, Gordius, the thirty-fourth; Theophilus of Caesarea in Palestine; Polycrates of Ephesus; Palmas of Pontus; Beryllus and Bacchylus of Corinth; Agrippinus at Carthage in Africa; St Irenaeus at Lyon in Gaul; and finally St Victor, pontiff at Rome.

Thus our reading from the manuscript codex is confirmed in the author's words: “What kind of laws, then, are these that only the impious, unjust, disgraceful, savage, vain, and mad enforce against us—laws which no Pius and no Verus ever imposed?” (*Apology* 5), that is, down to the time when he published the *Apology*.

## The Year of the Lord 196

## § VI. When, on what occasion, and by what considerations he became a Christian

**12.** With Q. Flavius Tertullus Scapula and T. Flavius Clemens as consuls, in the tenth year of St Victor, Roman pontiff, and the third year of Severus, TERTULLIAN, in my opinion, gave his name to the Christian faith.

[Note: [Col. 0052D] This opinion of Jacques Pamelius is rejected by Pierre Allix in his dissertation *On the Life and Writings of Tertullian*, Paris, 1680, and by Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. III, article 2, p. 87. Some, as the distinguished Fr Berti reports, *Dissertationes historicae*, vol. II, century III, dissertation 4, §2, p. 413, think that he converted to the Christian faith around the time when he wrote *On the Pallium*, namely after the year 208. But many works of Tertullian written earlier survive and display the faith he professed. Fabricius places Tertullian's conversion in 196, Oudin in 170, and Cave in 185, though they hesitate and rely only on conjectures. See Lumper, ibid. EDD.]

The Empire had now been completely pacified, Antoninus, Severus's son, and Clodius Albinus ruling as Caesars with Severus; hence Tertullian calls it a threefold Empire in the words quoted above, to which we refer the reader, for several details there pertain to this year. His conversion occurred not at the beginning of the year but near its end, after “every aconite of hostility had already been uprooted” (*To Scapula* 3; *Apology* 23)—that is, after the destruction of Byzantium. Herodian, Zonaras, and Michael Glycas attest that, after a three-year siege begun in Severus's first year while Niger was still alive, the city was finally taken by famine. It was stripped of all freedom and assigned to the Perinthians, who had suffered much from Niger; its walls were demolished and it was reduced to the status of a village. Our author also mentions it: “Caelius Lapella, at the fall of Byzantium, exclaimed, ‘Christians, rejoice!’” (*To Scapula* 3).

He himself apparently indicates the occasion of his conversion: the testimony of some god who, adjured by Christians, confessed that it was a demon (*Apology* 23). “These testimonies of your gods,” he says, “are accustomed to make Christians; by trusting them most of all, we believe in Christ the Lord. They themselves kindle faith in our writings; they themselves build confidence in our hope.”

[Note: [Col. 0053C] Pamelius attributes Tertullian's conversion to the answer of an oracle, George of Amiens to a vision; both [Col. 0053D] appear to savor of fable. From the author's own testimony it is pleasing to draw out three principal causes of his conversion. First, the unconquered constancy of the martyrs amid the cruelest torments: “Everyone,” he says, “who beholds so great an endurance is struck by some doubt and is set afire to inquire what its cause may be; once he has learned the truth, he immediately follows it himself” (*To Scapula*, final chapter). Second, their astonishing power over demons and the demons' images and oracles: “What is more manifest than this work? What proof more trustworthy? The simplicity of truth stands openly before you: from bodies too they depart at our command, unwilling and grieving, and put to shame in your presence” (*Apology* 23). Third, fear of divine judgments: “We fly over to this discipline,” he says in *On the Soul* 2, “through fear of the judgment foretold.” To these I would add what Pamelius gives above: the authority of Scripture and the divine majesty of predictions confirmed by their truth; indeed, the calamities of the Empire, raging more fiercely as mad brutality against Christians grew more savage; and finally apologetic discourses, weighty in substance no less than sharp in words, published by many teachers who flourished during that storm of the Church. EDD.]

Nor did this arise from that alone, but also from faith in the sacred Scriptures, whose credibility the gods approve by their testimony. In particular, as he himself testified when already a Christian, the greatest antiquity vindicated their authority, because “the repository of the single prophet Moses preceded by several centuries all the substances and materials, the origins, orders, and veins of every ancient style; most peoples and cities; the notable subjects of histories and records; finally, even the very forms of letters, the indicators and guardians of things; the gods themselves, the temples themselves, the oracles and rites themselves.”

The truth of their predictions also confirmed their divine majesty: “Whatever happens,” he says, “was foretold. That earthquakes swallow cities; that seas rob away islands; that foreign and civil wars tear peoples apart; that kingdoms strike against kingdoms; that famine and pestilence, every local disaster, and the great frequency of deaths lay waste; that even the functions of the seasons and the tasks of the elements go astray; that the form of nature is disturbed by monsters and portents—all were providently written” (namely Matthew 25). “While we suffer them, they are read; when we recognize them, they are proved.” All these matters are treated more fully both in *On the Pallium* 2 and *Apology* 40, to which and to our notes we refer the reader.

**13.** Here we shall add only that, among other things, he alludes to the great plague at Rome and in many provinces, and to the earthquake in which Smyrna, a city of Asia, collapsed—events Eusebius records in the *Chronicle* under the emperors Marcus and Verus—and to the lightning that struck the Capitol under Commodus and set fire to the library, and to the civil wars of that age, which we have already mentioned. He likewise alludes to the famine, of which he writes in *To Scapula*: “Likewise under the governor Hilarianus, when they had shouted concerning the open spaces used for our burials, ‘Let there be no burial grounds,’ their own threshing floors ceased to be; for they did not gather their harvests” (*To Scapula* 3).

Finally he alludes to the portent mentioned in the same place: “For that sun too, in the assembly at Utica, with its light almost extinguished, was such a portent that it could not have suffered this from an ordinary eclipse, being situated in its own elevation and domicile” (*On the Testimony of the Soul* 1).

We also think that the writings against the Gentiles of many Fathers since Christ contributed to his conversion. Elsewhere he alludes to them: “Some among us,” he says, “in whom the labor of curiosity and the continuity of memory from their former literary culture endured, composed little works recalling and calling to witness, in order to censure, the origins, traditions, and grounds of opinions by which it can be recognized that we have embraced nothing new or monstrous for which common literature does not also act as advocate in our support, whether we have cast out some error or admitted some equitable thing” (*Against the Valentinians* 5). Among these should be named Quadratus, Aristides, Anaxagoras, Melito, Theophilus of Antioch, Apollinaris, Tatian, Clement of Alexandria, and Apollonius the Senator; and finally those cited somewhere by the author: Justin, philosopher and martyr; Miltiades, ecclesiastical sophist; and Irenaeus, “the most inquisitive investigator of every branch of learning.” That Tertullian labored through all their writings both before and after accepting the faith is evident from the *Apology*, in which from time to time he imitates them almost word for word.

Converted to faith in Christ with all these supports and already initiated, he put on the Christian pallium, as we touched upon earlier. When a friend reproached him with inconstancy because he had passed from the toga to the pallium, he delivered a speech at Carthage, which he entitled *ON THE PALLIUM*. In it he commends the pallium's antiquity, simplicity, ease, carefree freedom, philosophical gravity, and holiness, and shows through various examples that he should not be blamed for changing his attire. On that occasion he attacks the various kinds of lust through which nature is altered and the indecent adornment of matrons; he applies the cautery to the vices of the forum, judges, and soldiers, and also to ambition and gluttony.

A constitution of Severus and Antoninus dated under these consuls on 11 March and surviving in Digest, book 9, title 1, law 1, further confirms our opinion that Antoninus the son was a colleague in the Empire.

## The Year of the Lord 197

## § VII. From what sources he drew his comprehensive knowledge of Christian teaching

**14.** With C. Domitius Dexter II and L. Valerius Messalla Thrasea Priscus as consuls, in the eleventh year of St Victor, Roman pope, and the fourth of Severus, the writings of TERTULLIAN, which will be treated later, bear more than sufficient testimony to the occupations to which, now a Christian, he devoted himself wholly. From them it is first evident that he was so practiced in reading the sacred writings and had so committed every passage of Scripture individually to memory that he sometimes embraced several in a single period; this may readily be discovered from our Index of Scriptures by comparing it with the author.

In citing them, as regards the Old Testament he everywhere follows the edition of the Seventy translators, which, as he himself attests, was restored by Ezra (*On the Apparel of Women* 3; *Apology* 18). He does so not only in the Pentateuch of Moses and the other historical books, but also in the predictions of the prophets. “Those whom we have called preachers,” he says, “are called prophets from their office of foretelling. Their voices, and likewise the miraculous works they produced as evidence of divinity, remain in the treasuries of literature, and these are not now hidden. The most learned of the Ptolemies, surnamed Philadelphus, also most keenly interested in every kind of literature, when in his enthusiasm for a library he emulated Pisistratus, as I think, among other records supported in fame by either antiquity or some curiosity, at the suggestion of Demetrius of Phalerum, then the most approved of grammarians and the man to whom he had entrusted its administration, also requested books from the Jews—namely their own native writings, which they alone possessed. For the prophets had always spoken from among them and to them, that is, to the household nation of God by the grace of their fathers. Those formerly called Hebrews are now called Jews; hence both their letters and speech were Hebrew. But lest knowledge be lacking, this too was supplied to Ptolemy by the Jews, seventy-two translators being granted; Menedemus the philosopher, defender of Providence, also admired them because of their agreement in judgment. Aristeas likewise affirmed these things to you. Thus the records were openly left in Greek form. Today they are displayed in Ptolemy's library at the Serapeum together with the Hebrew writings themselves.” We have cited this at somewhat greater length against those who do not shrink from diminishing the authority of the Seventy translators.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] Johann Salomo Semler, a man sometimes daring in counsel and rather impatient of the well-trodden path, published at the end of his edition a dissertation *On the Various and Uncertain Character of Tertullian's Books*. One may see especially with what vehemence he dares to assert that Tertullian neither used Greek codices nor wished to use them; that his entire concern was to prefer his Latin reading to any foreign one, as if Greek books had already at that time been corrupted by heretics; and that the conviction thus more easily became fixed in Latin minds that Latin books possess especial excellence and greater antiquity, because Latin exemplars had their first beginnings and recent rudiments earlier. He even asserts that various new interpretations and glosses survive of which Tertullian was the first and certain author, and that from him they flowed into all [Col. 0056D] Latin codices. However that may be, one must diligently guard against the two aims this author sets before himself: to discredit the commonly received reading of the sacred books, and further to assert that certain books of the ancients—those of Irenaeus or Clement—came from one and the same workshop, so that there is no longer sufficient reason to continue dividing them among different authors, since they were composed by one. See *Tertulliani opera*, ed. Semler, Halle, 1828, vol. V, pp. 185–211. EDD.]

In the New Testament, however, it is evident from his distinctive rendering—often greatly different from all others—that our author, deeply learned in Greek, used not so much Latin translations as old Greek codices. For the benefit of professors of sacred literature, we have everywhere noted this divergence. [Col. 0055D] St Ambrose—or whoever wrote the commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Romans—long ago pointed it out at Romans 5: “It is established,” he says, “that certain Latins in former times translated from old Greek codices, which the simplicity of those times preserved and approved as uncorrupted. But after disagreement among dissenting minds and the disruptions of heretics began to twist questions, many things were altered according to human judgment, so that the letters would contain what seemed right to a man. Hence the Greeks themselves possess differing codices. I judge true, however, that reading in which reason, history, and authority were observed. For what is today censured in the Latin codices is found so placed by the ancients: TERTULLIAN, Victorinus, and Cyprian.” Thus far that author.

Our author further spent night and day examining not only the writers of apologies for the Christian faith whom we cited above but, without doubt, other ecclesiastical writers as well. Apart from Apollonius the Senator and St Victor, all were Greek. I mean Philo; Josephus, whom he calls “the native champion of Jewish antiquities” (*Apology* 19); Apion and Hegesippus, Jews; Clement of Rome and St Polycarp, whom he recognizes as ordained bishops, the former of the Romans by Peter and the latter of Smyrna by John (*On the Prescription Against Heretics* 32); St Ignatius of Antioch; St Dionysius the Areopagite of Gaul; Papias, bishop of Hierapolis; Agrippa Castor; Dionysius of Corinth; Pinytus and Philip, bishops of Crete; Musanus; Modestus; Pantaenus of Alexandria; Rhodo of Asia; Serapion; and a certain Proculus, whom he calls “the dignity of Christian eloquence,” about whom more will be said later; and finally Sextus, Apion, Candidus, Arabianus, Maximus, and Heraclitus (see also *Against the Valentinians* 5; *Song Against Marcion* 9; *On the Prescription Against Heretics* 38; *Apology* 35).

To these I add the other earliest successors of the Roman pontiffs in the chair of Peter, whose decretals survive and whom the author mentions together with Linus and Cletus: Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, likewise Soter—whom he omitted because no occasion offered itself—and Eleutherius, whom he calls Blessed. I think all these wrote in Greek, judging from the same Latin style, which appears to belong to one translator; for they knew Greek better than Latin, as did St Irenaeus. Consequently, as even Rhenanus notes, no one should wonder at the author's Greek manner of speaking: even if some works had been translated into Latin, he preferred, as they say, to drink from the springs rather than the pools.

Certain writers say that in this first year, on 15 May, the anniversary of the beginning of the reign, Severus named his son Antoninus Caesar Augustus at Viminacium before setting out for war against Albinus. Nevertheless, the rescripts of the preceding years in the names of Severus and Antoninus Augusti show that he had already once been called Augustus from the beginning. Meanwhile, the author too mentions Albinus's conspiracy against Severus in this year in the words: “Whence came the Cassiuses, Nigers, and Albini?”

## The Year of the Lord 198

## § VIII. When and amid what circumstances he composed certain poems

**15.** With T. Sextius Lateranus and M. Marius, son of Marcus, Cuspius Rufinus as consuls, in the twelfth year of St Victor, Roman pontiff, and the fifth year of the emperor Severus, it is likely that TERTULLIAN, to exercise his memory, composed in verse *GENESIS* and *SODOM*—indeed, in my opinion, the complete history of the sacred books of the Old Testament. The former poem is mutilated, and the opening of the latter sufficiently suggests that he also described the flood of the whole world. He also composed the poem *TO A SENATOR WHO RETURNED FROM THE CHRISTIAN FAITH TO THE SERVICE OF IDOLS*, five books *AGAINST MARCION* in verse, and a book *ON THE JUDGMENT OF THE LORD*.

In this year, on 19 February, Imperator Caesar D. Clodius Septimius Albinus Augustus was defeated in battle by the emperor Severus and killed near Lyon. Because Lyon had previously received Albinus, as Herodian attests, it was plundered and burned. In that campaign, as various inscriptions establish, Severus was acclaimed imperator VIII, IX, and X. Once Albinus had been defeated, Severus first ordered the execution of all the nobles of Gaul, Spain, and Britain who had aided him; then, returning to Rome, he sought out Albinus's friends everywhere and ordered forty senators among them to be killed, together with all who had conspired against Pertinax. The author accordingly calls them Albinians in the words quoted above.

He indicates that the investigation of them lasted from AD 195 through several years: “Even now,” he says, “the accomplices or applauders of criminal factions are revealed daily, a surviving gleaning after the harvest of parricides”—apparently as far as the Parthian triumph, and thus Severus's ninth year, as is explained there more fully. Elsewhere he likewise alludes to the murdered senators: “There is no one who cannot suffer for the sake of a man what he hesitates to suffer for God's cause. Let the present times themselves be our proof: how many and what sort of persons meet unexpected ends for the sake of a man, ends unlooked-for in view of their birth, rank, physical condition, and age—either at his own hand if they acted against him, or at the hand of his enemies if they stood for him” (*To Scapula* 2; *Apology* 35; *Against Marcion*, final chapter).

One of the said consuls, Lateranus, was so great a friend of the emperor Severus that he built him the most magnificent residence in Rome, which we still call the Lateran Palace. St Jerome later writes in the *Epitaph of Fabiola* that Lateranus was slain by a Caesarean sword, perhaps that of Antoninus Caracalla, who punished many of his father's friends.

Under these consuls the second letter of St Victor, Roman pontiff, was written to the African bishops and dated 1 September; the letter of his predecessor St Eleutherius was dated 11 July under the consuls Maternus and Bradua. We have therefore necessarily designated this as the twelfth, not the preceding, year of Victor's pontificate, especially because St Damasus writes that Victor occupied the pontifical seat from the consulship of Commodus V and Glabrio—under whom his first letter to Theophilus of Alexandria was dated 20 July—until Lateranus and Rufinus. From 1 June of that consulship, the day he was created pontiff, until 28 July of the following year, there are twelve years, one month, and twenty-eight days.

In the said second letter, rebuking the Africans' disagreement in the sacraments, Victor seems to me to allude to the observance of Easter. In his first letter he had commanded that, according to what his predecessors had also decreed, Easter must be celebrated on a Sunday, whichever Sunday fell between the fourteenth and twenty-first moon of the first month. In this matter some Africans perhaps at first followed the contrary custom with Polycrates of Asia, though they afterward came to one agreement. For of Blastus, a Quartodeciman heretic, the author writes: “In addition to all these comes Blastus, who secretly wishes to introduce Judaism. For he says that Easter must be observed only according to the law of Moses, on the fourteenth of the month. But who does not know that evangelical grace is nullified if he brings Christ back under the Law?” (*On the Prescription Against Heretics* 53, heresy 22; *On Fasting* 14 and 13).

This passage of the same author concerns the same observance: “We celebrate Easter in the first month in the annual cycle”; as does this: “Moreover, throughout the Greek lands councils drawn from all the churches are held in fixed places.” Although he speaks generally, we think this chiefly refers to the councils celebrated shortly before in Palestine under Theophilus of Caesarea, in Pontus under Palmas, at Corinth under Bacchylus, among the churches in Osrhoene, at Alexandria also under Theophilus, and finally in Asia. Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History* 4, final chapter, writes that at the Asian council the Fathers followed the said judgment of St Victor and the Roman Council, with which the council of the Gauls under Irenaeus also agreed.

## The Year of the Lord 199

## § IX. The publication of the books Against the Jews

**16.** With T. Haturius, son of Titus, Saturninus and C. Annius, son of Appius, Trebonianus Gallus as consuls, in the first year of St Zephyrinus as pope at Rome and the sixth year of the emperor Severus, there seems to us to have occurred that disagreement between TERTULLIAN and a certain Jew on account of which he indicates that he wrote the book *AGAINST THE JEWS*. “Very recently,” he says, “a disputation took place between a Christian and a Jewish proselyte. By turns, each pulling on the contentious rope, they prolonged the day into evening. Some spectators also shouted interruptions, and the truth was overshadowed by a kind of cloud surrounding each man's arguments. It therefore seemed good to examine more carefully what could be elucidated less fully through the clamor of the debate, and to settle in writing the questions considered anew” (*Against the Jews* 1).

Among other things, it should be noted how beautifully he traces the spread of the faith through almost the whole world even at that early date: “In whom else have all the nations believed except Christ, who has already come? ...
