Parthians, Medes, Elamites,” and so forth, as is read in Acts 2, “and the other nations, including the various peoples of the Gaetulians and the many territories of the Moors; all the boundaries of Spain and the diverse nations of Gaul; places among the Britons inaccessible to the Romans but subject to Christ; the lands of the Sarmatians, Dacians, Germans, and Scythians; many hidden nations and many provinces and islands unknown to us and which we can scarcely enumerate—in all these places the name of Christ, who has already come, reigns” (*Against the Jews* 7).

His account of the limits of the Roman Empire at that time is also memorable: “The Germans are still not permitted to cross their frontiers. The Britains are enclosed within the circuit of the Ocean. The nation of the Moors and the barbarity of the Gaetulians are blockaded by the Romans so that they do not pass beyond the boundaries of their lands. What shall I say of the Romans, who fortify their Empire with the garrisons of their legions and cannot extend the power of their kingdom beyond these nations?” Herodian touches on this very matter concerning the Germans in *History* 2, when he says that Severus was chosen by all the armies that, keeping watch against the barbarians along the banks of the Danube and Rhine, protected the Roman Empire.

We place this as the first year of the pontificate of St Zephyrinus—Habundius, son of Habundius, a Roman by birth—because, after St Victor died and the see had been vacant twelve days, he was created pontiff on 10 August under these very consuls. St Damasus himself attests this, writing that Zephyrinus occupied the see in the times of Severus and Antoninus, from the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus to the consuls Praesens and Extricatus.

How St Victor is nevertheless reckoned fifth among the martyrs when the persecution of the Christians had not yet begun is not without difficulty. This moved Eusebius and other chronographers to extend his pontificate into Severus's eighth, ninth, or tenth year. Yet my statement, and St Damasus's opinion on the dates of both pontiffs, is confirmed by Zephyrinus's decretal letters issued under these same consuls Saturninus and Gallus, the former dated 20 September and the latter 9 November. Nor was it unusual in the primitive Church for persecution to begin with the Roman populace or the prefects of the City.

What is more, the author expressly asserts this concerning the present time: “Severus knew that women and men of the highest rank belonged to this sect; not only did he not harm them, he even adorned them with his testimony and openly resisted the raging populace to its face” (*To Scapula* 4; *Apology* 1–2). Before the following year, moreover, the law of the deified Severus and Antoninus must have been issued that no absent person should be punished; it is mentioned in Digest, book 1, title *On Searching for Accused Persons*. Without doubt the author alludes to it in these words: “What loss do the laws suffer in their own dominion if the truth is heard? Or will their authority boast more if they condemn truth unheard?” And again: “Since it is not lawful for people wholly undefended and unheard to be condemned.”

## The Year of the Lord 200

## § X. The Apology, The Testimony of the Soul, and Fate, against the Gentiles; TERTULLIAN's priesthood and the books arising from it: On Repentance, On Prayer, On Circumcision, On the Garments of Aaron, On Clean and Unclean Animals, On the Trinity, and On Baptism

**17.** With P. Cornelius Anullinus II and M. Aufidius, son of Marcus, Fronto as consuls, in the second year of St Zephyrinus, Roman pontiff, and the seventh of the emperor Severus, the emperor departed with his sons Antoninus and Geta—whom before his departure he had declared Caesars, Augusti, and imperatores—for the second Arab, Parthian, and Adiabenian war discussed more fully above, after again giving a largess to the people and a donative to the soldiers. Meanwhile, the Roman magistrates and priests continued to persecute the Christian religion, a persecution begun by St Victor the pontiff. In imitation of others who had done so before him, and especially Blessed Justin Martyr, TERTULLIAN sent to Rome an *APOLOGY FOR THE CHRISTIANS*, in which, as even Lactantius attests, he argued this case fully.

The author himself indicates that, even before Severus's departure, the emperor had both amended and published many laws: “Do you not yourselves daily, as experiments illuminate the darkness of antiquity, lop and cut down that whole old and squalid forest of laws with the new axes of imperial rescripts and edicts? Did not Severus, most steadfast of the Caesars, only yesterday abolish after so venerable an old age the utterly vain Papian laws”—here he alludes to the *lex Papia Poppaea*, so called from its proposers, the consuls M. Papius, son and grandson of Marcus, Mutilus and Q. Poppaeus, son and grandson of Quintus, Secundinus—“which compel people to beget children before the Julian laws compel them to contract marriage?” (*Apology* 4).

How the abolition of those laws can be attributed to Severus although it is afterward ascribed to the emperor Constantine, we have treated more fully in our notes on this passage. If our conjecture concerning Digest, *On Sexual Violation and Adultery*, law 1, is accepted—that it establishes that sexual violation and adultery can be charged and punished even in the case of a betrothed woman—then that law must have been enacted under these consuls.

Our author also supports the fact that the second Parthian war had not yet been completed—a war Cassiodorus too records as begun under these consuls—when he counts the Moors and Marcomanni and even the Parthians among the enemies of the Roman Empire (*Apology* 37). Again he celebrates the spread of the Christian faith in these words: “We are of yesterday, and we have filled all that is yours: cities, islands, fortresses, towns, market-places, the camps themselves, tribes, decuries, the palace, the senate, the forum.” Shortly before, he confirms what we said under the preceding year concerning popular persecution: “How often, even apart from you, does the hostile mob attack us in its own right with stones and fires? In the very frenzy of the Bacchanals they do not spare even dead Christians, but tear them from the repose of burial, from a kind of asylum of death—already altered, no longer whole—and cut and rend them apart” (*Apology* 37).

To the same matter belongs this: “None demand Christians for punishment more than the mob,” and the popular cry so often quoted by the author: “The Christians to the lion!” Many other matters in the *Apology* deserve mention, but lest we grow too lengthy here, we refer the reader to our notes. We shall add only that the occasion of the persecution arose from false accusations, which Tertullian refutes magnificently, especially three charges: infanticide, feeding on human blood, and incest. “We are called,” he says, “the most criminal of men because of the sacrament of infanticide and the meal made from it, and because of incest after the banquet, since dogs overturn the lamps—as procurers, of course, of darkness—and provide for the shamelessness of impious lusts” (*Apology* 7).

## The Year of the Lord 300 [as in the source]

Restoration notes: E004 preserves the recovered legends verbatim; their corrupt or abbreviated forms make the supplied English interpretation uncertain.  

18. In the consulship of Tiberius Claudius Severus (not, as some incorrectly say, the emperor Severus III) [Col. 0061A] and Gaius Aufidius Victorinus, the third year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the eighth of Severus: although, while the emperor was still absent on his Parthian and Adiabenian campaign—having received the submission of the Arabs and of Abgar, king of the Persians, in the preceding year—the persecution of Christians at Rome seemed to abate somewhat, perhaps through the aid of his *Apology*, Tertullian nevertheless saw that neither he nor other writers had achieved anything, or very little, toward the conversion of the Gentiles through their apologies for the Christians. He therefore assailed them with another kind of work, demanding testimony against idols from the still-pagan soul itself, and consequently entitled the book *On the Testimony of the Soul*. In it he presses those common expressions: “As God shall grant”; “If God wills”; “God bless you”; “God sees all”; “I commend it to God”; “God will repay”; and [Col. 0061B] “God will judge between us.” It seems very probable to me that in this same year he also composed the book *On Fate*, of which only a single fragment survives, though it is mentioned by the author himself in these words: “Powers indeed preside: according to us,” he says, “the Lord God and his rival the devil; according to common opinion, providence, fate, necessity, and freedom of choice. For the philosophers too distinguish these, and we already know that they must be discussed according to faith under a title of their own.” To this year we also assign the author’s new condition of life, in which he was admitted to the order of presbyters,

> **Note [Cols. 0061B–0061C].** There is certainly no passage in Tertullian’s writings from which it can be concluded that he was a presbyter in the Catholic Church. A passage is indeed produced from *On the Soul*, ch. 9, where the author speaks of a certain sister who was accustomed to be carried into ecstasy and to prophesy. From this passage it could, though only laboriously, be inferred that Tertullian preached in a church—something that at that time belonged only to bishops, or at least to presbyters—but only in a Montanist church. There such a right was readily allowed to those who boasted of prophetic gifts, and especially to Tertullian, since virtually the whole authority of that church had come to rest upon the name of a man otherwise so celebrated. But St Jerome asserts Tertullian’s presbyteral office so positively that there is no longer any room for doubt on the point.

perhaps by Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage.

> **Note [Cols. 0061C–0062D].** Since Tertullian excelled equally in sacred and secular letters, he was afterward ordained a presbyter. Ancient writers disagree whether this was in the Roman or Carthaginian Church, and modern critics likewise do not agree. After Ceillier (*Histoire générale des auteurs*, vol. 2, p. 376), Semler defends the common opinion that he was enrolled among the presbyters at Rome, on the following grounds (Semler, vol. 5 of the works of Tertullian, diss. 1 on Tertullian, §2, pp. 222–227). Tertullian, as Jerome writes, remained until middle age a presbyter of the Church—of Africa, or of Rome? We think of Rome, [Col. 0061D] as we shall presently explain more fully. Afterward, however, through the envy and insults of the clergy of the Roman Church—that is, after being attacked and expelled from that Church—he fell into the doctrine of Montanus, etc. Jerome’s account may plainly appear to embody a history not unknown to him, even if he did not wish to describe it more fully and precisely. Unless, indeed, we suppose that Jerome himself discovered these things by conjecture from various passages in these writers, such as the beginning of *Against Praxeas*. From those statements it might appear that Tertullian himself was then at Rome when Praxeas, coming to Rome from Asia, told the Roman bishop such things about the Montanists that the bishop decided it was in the interest of the Roman ecclesiastical community to maintain no further relations with them.
>
> Tertullian certainly writes (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 1): “The bishop of Rome had already acknowledged the prophecies of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and by that acknowledgment was bringing peace to the churches of Asia and Phrygia. By making false assertions about the prophets themselves and their churches, and by defending the authorities of the bishop’s predecessors, [Praxeas] compelled him both to recall the letters of peace already issued and to desist from his purpose of receiving the charisms. Thus Praxeas managed two works of the devil at Rome: he expelled prophecy”—that is, the supporters of Montanus [Col. 0062A] who were then commending those churches of Asia to the bishop, among whom Tertullian himself was doubtless included—“and brought in heresy”—Tertullian now thinks that the Roman Church itself had fallen into heresy, and accordingly withdrew from it. “He put the Paraclete to flight and crucified the Father.” A little later he adds plainly: “And afterward acknowledgment and defense of the Paraclete separated us from the Psychics.” Here, as we think, Tertullian indicates clearly enough that he had previously lived in ecclesiastical communion with those Romans whom he here calls Psychics.
>
> From this passage, then, Jerome could have inferred as though it were history that envy and insults from the clergy of the Roman Church caused Tertullian to pass over to the Montanists. No more precise-looking account survives in other writers to persuade us that Jerome received these details from elsewhere. The words “expel” and “put to flight” signify clearly enough that this writer suffered an ecclesiastical affront and was removed and cast down from a sacred place and rank—namely, that of presbyter—[Col. 0062B] by the Roman clergy, as Jerome puts it more mildly. It is easy to understand that this was done by the Roman bishop himself through the clergy’s improper zeal. [Col. 0062D: Since Jerome wrote that catalogue at a later date, he seems to have written this judgment against the Roman clergy without the light of true history, in order to avenge himself upon those whose malicious judgments he had experienced after the death of Damasus.] Perhaps this cause may be examined more carefully elsewhere.
>
> That by “presbyter of the Church” Jerome means presbyter of the Roman Church is sufficiently certain even from Eusebius’ account, book 2, ch. 2. For he writes of Tertullian that he was “one of those especially illustrious at Rome”. Tertullian himself also states most clearly that he lived at Rome. [Col. 0062D: *On the Dress of Women*, book 1, ch. 6. Ceillier already used these passages against the *Praedestinatus*, which says that Tertullian, a presbyter of Carthage, wrote against the Montanists.] “At Rome too,” he says, “we saw the nobility of gems blushing before matrons at the disdain shown them by the Parthians, Medes, and the rest of their own Gentiles.” I should like to add other statements here which confirm that Tertullian lived as a cleric in the Roman Church. Chief among them is this passage (*On Prescription*, ch. 30): “Where then was Marcion, the Pontic shipmaster and student of Stoicism? Where Valentinus, the follower of Plato? For it is agreed that they lived not so long ago, about the reign of Antoninus, and at first believed the Catholic doctrine in the Roman Church, until under the episcopate of the blessed Eleutherus, because of their always restless curiosity by which they also corrupted the brethren, they were expelled once and again—Marcion indeed together with his two hundred sesterces which he had brought into the Church. Finally banished into permanent separation, they scattered the poisons of their doctrines. Later Marcion professed repentance and, when he had met the condition imposed upon him—namely, that he would receive peace if he restored to the Church (that is, the Roman Church) the others whom he had instructed for perdition—death overtook him.” [Col. 0062C]
>
> It is sufficiently clear that one who knew these things so precisely had himself been at Rome and had been among the clergy who were present when they occurred. If he had still been at Rome when he wrote this book, he would not have written “in the Roman Church” as though he himself did not belong to it. He had therefore already been expelled from Rome and was living in Africa. This appears still more clearly from chapter 36 of the same book: “Run through the apostolic churches—Achaia is nearest; you have Corinth—if you are near Italy, you have Rome, whence authority is available to us also.” He is addressing Africans who use the Latin language. “That Church (the Roman)—let us see what it learned and taught, and what fellowship of tokens it exchanged with the African churches.” It is altogether plain here that the writer was then in Africa; he must therefore previously have been at Rome, in that Roman Church, among the clergy. No others than clerics could have known such internal ecclesiastical affairs and histories. [Col. 0062D] Many other historical and political details of this kind—*Τοπικὰ* (“local matters”)—readily reveal a man long resident at Rome among other clerics.
>
> Such are Semler’s arguments for Tertullian’s Roman presbyterate. Dupin and Schroeck defend the opposite opinion. Yet their position, as it seems to me, is not sufficiently firm either, since it rests solely upon the testimony of the author of the *Praedestinatus*, who, because of his countless errors, has scarcely any authority among most discerning critics. It matters little for our purpose whether he was presbyter at Rome or Carthage or, as the distinguished Johann Georg Walch prefers (*Church History*, sect. II, ch. I, p. 643), presbyter of no particular church.

That he was distinct from Agrippinus [Col. 0062A], or Agrippa, the bishop whom Eusebius and Nicephorus mention under the emperor Marcus Aurelius, Zonaras under Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, and the abbot of Ursperg under Antoninus Verus, seems to me to follow from the fact that blessed Cyprian, in Epistle 70 to Januarius, indicates that Agrippinus was one of his predecessors, and blessed Augustine, in book 2 *Against the Donatists*, ch. 7, calls him Cyprian’s predecessor. This is especially so because Egypt, where that Alexandrian held his episcopate, was a province distinct from Africa, and Cyprian, Epistle 71 to Quintus, writes that Agrippinus of blessed memory, together with his fellow bishops—whom he also calls his predecessors in Epistle 70—issued a decree concerning the baptism of heretics.

It also seems probable to me that immediately upon receiving the priesthood the author, by mutual consent with his wife, abstained from marital relations, in accordance with the custom of the Latin Church dating from the decree of Pope St Clement. These words to his wife especially appear to tend in that direction: “Do not suppose that, from resentment at the injury of your bodily integrity having to be reserved for me, I am already insinuating to you a plan of widowhood.” Again: “The time,” he says, “has been shortened; it remains that those who have wives should act as though they had none. If those who have them must forget what they have, how much more those who do not?” (*To His Wife*, book 1, chs. 5–6.) He plainly indicates there that this practice was common among many at the time: “For how many are there who immediately after the washing seal their flesh? How many likewise, by mutual agreement, cancel the marital debt? For voluntary eunuchs, out of heavenly desire, abstinence is endured while the marriage remains intact” (*On Baptism*, ch. 15; vol. I, *To Scapula*, ch. 3).

> **Note [Col. 0063D].** Tertullian’s marriage is beyond doubt. The matter is established, as we have already said, by his books *To His Wife*, preserved to our time. Writers disagree, however, over whether he was exercising priestly office when in those books he urged his wife to preserve continence in widowhood. These words indicate that he did not then wholly abstain from marital relations: “Let us cherish the capacity for continence as far as we can; as soon as it comes, let us drink it in, so that what we could not achieve in marriage we may pursue in widowhood” (book 1 *To His Wife*, ch. 7). He surely would not have said “what we could not achieve in marriage” if they had imposed perpetual continence upon themselves within it, as the distinguished Samuel Basnage rightly observes (*Annales politico-ecclesiastici*, vol. II, p. 215). Some therefore contend that presbyters at that time were not yet bound by the bonds of continence. Yet even if this were true—which remains unproved—the Reformers would still boast in vain, with Dallaeus, of Tertullian’s example while insulting the Catholic Church for prescribing continence to priests. For since the discipline of continence was introduced more by custom and practice than by laws, it is in no way overthrown by one or two examples from that age.

Now that he had become a presbyter, and was mindful of the power granted to him both to absolve penitents and to offer sacrifices, [Col. 0063C] he composed the books *On Repentance* and *On Prayer*. In them he prescribes both the manner of repentance for catechumens and fallen Christians and the rites the faithful must observe in the sacrifice. To this year may also be assigned writings mentioned by blessed Jerome but now lost: *On Circumcision*, *On the Garments of Aaron*, *On Clean and Unclean Animals*, and finally *On the Trinity*; perhaps also the Greek book *On Baptism*, since it seems to have been composed after Agrippinus’ council. The author indicates that it treated the same subject: “But what must be observed concerning heretics,” he says, “someone worthy should reconsider. It is addressed to us; heretics have no fellowship in our discipline,” etc. “But this matter has already been treated more fully in Greek.” More on this point, on Agrippinus, and on the author’s own paradox [Col. 0064A] in the Prolegomena.

In this year too must have occurred what he wrote in the following year in *To Scapula*: “Moreover, the rain of last year showed what the human race deserved; there had also been a deluge in ancient times because of human unbelief and wickedness.” Perhaps also this: “Those who saw them know what the fires lately suspended over the walls of Carthage throughout the night threatened, and those who hardened themselves know what the earlier thunderings proclaimed. All these are signs of God’s impending wrath, which we must, in every way we can, announce and proclaim, while praying that it may be local. Those who interpret its examples otherwise will in their own time experience its universal and final form.”

## In the Year of the Lord 202

### [Col. 0064B] § XI. On other writings composed in good faith: *To Scapula*, *To the Martyrs*, *On Patience*, and *On Prescription against Heretics*

19. In the consulship of Lucius Annius Fabianus and Marcus Nonius Mutianus, the third year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the ninth of the emperor Severus: Scapula, a man of consular rank, governor of Carthage and therefore proconsul of Africa, had not yet received a decree of persecution from the emperor—and perhaps persecution had even been forbidden at Rome—but nevertheless raged more cruelly against the Christians at Carthage than did the other governors. Tertullian therefore wrote the book *To Scapula* (*To Scapula*, chs. 2–4). First he seeks goodwill by appealing to the Christians’ innocence and to their concern for the emperor’s safety not only through prayer but also through their sacrifices, from which it is clear that he was already a presbyter. [Col. 0064C] He then attributes the portents of the time and the destruction of Byzantium, already mentioned above, to the shedding of Christian blood. He adduces examples of punishment: Valgius Saturninus, Hilarianus, and Scapula himself in Africa, and Claudius Herminianus in Cappadocia, all persecutors of the Christian faith. He next urges that such cases be overlooked, citing the examples of the emperors Severus and Antoninus given above and Marcus Aurelius on his German expedition, as well as those of the governors and proconsuls Servilius Pudens under Antoninus Verus, Vespronius Candidus under Commodus, Cincius Severus, afterward killed by Severus, and Aper and Arrius Antoninus (the latter called Arrius by Lampridius and Brusius the governor by others), who were consuls under the emperor Antoninus.

[Col. 0064D] Finally he complains that although from the beginning the command had been to punish only by the sword, and this was observed by the governors of Numidia and Mauretania, Christians were also burned at Scapula’s order. To this belongs the statement in the *Apology*: “You call us faggot-men and half-axle-men, because, bound to a stake of half an axle’s length, we are burned within a ring of brushwood.” There too he records the kind of sentence by which a Christian woman was condemned “to the pimp rather than to the lion” (*Apology*, final chapter). Likewise, in the book *To the Martyrs* held in prison, composed at the same time, he adds to the sword and the supreme penalty of fire “the savage fury of beasts and every ingenuity of the executioner in torture” (*To the Martyrs*, ch. 4). He also mentions the custom by which those who did not possess peace in the Church, namely the lapsed, would ask it from martyrs in prison [Col. 0065A] (ch. 1). Although near the end of his life, when already a heretic, he did not approve this custom, it continued in the Church until the time of blessed Cyprian, as we discuss more fully in Cyprian’s *Life*.

He repeats all these punishments of martyrs in *On Patience* (*On Patience*, ch. 13; *To Scapula*, ch. 3; *On the Many Heresies*, ch. 7), which he also composed on the occasion of this persecution. There he even counts flight in persecution as a good belonging to patience, and thus he had not yet become attached to the Montanists, according to whose doctrine he later wrote, though in vain, the contrary work *On Flight in Persecution*. The author expressly attests that under Scapula St Mavilus of Hadrumetum was condemned to the beasts.

That the author was at Rome in this year appears from these words: “At Rome too we saw the nobility of gems blushing before matrons at the disdain shown them by the Parthians, Medes, and the rest of their own Gentiles—except that they are scarcely even displayed. Emeralds lie hidden singly, and only the sword beneath the cloak knows the cylinders on its sheath, while pearls on boots long to emerge from the mud.” [Col. 0065B] We interpret this as having occurred at the triumph of the emperor Severus, concerning which the consular fasti for this year report: “The emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus, son of Marcus, Pius Pertinax Augustus, Arabicus, Adiabenicus, Parthicus Maximus, pontifex maximus, holding tribunician power for the eighth time, consul twice, father of the country, proconsul, acclaimed imperator eleven times; and the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, son of Severus Augustus, Pius Felix Augustus, holding tribunician power for the third time, [Col. 0065C] consul-designate and imperator, triumphed together over the Arabs, Parthians, Adiabenians, and King Artabanus.” Spartianus and Herodian also mention this triumph. Our view is supported by the fact that the author describes as an eyewitness the custom observed in triumphs: “Even as he triumphs in that most exalted chariot,” he says, “he is reminded that he is a man. For it is whispered to him from behind: ‘Look behind you; remember that you are a man’” (*Apology*, ch. 33).

## In the Year of the Lord 203

20. In the consulship of the emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius, son of Marcus, Arabicus, Adiabenicus, Parthicus for the third time, and the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, son of Severus Augustus, in the fourth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, [Col. 0065D] and the tenth of Severus—or certainly in the preceding year—when not only ancient heresies but also several recent ones were already raging even in Africa, Tertullian published that truly golden work *On Prescription against Heretics*. That it was written before all his other books on the same subject is clear from the author’s words: “For the present we have dealt generally with all heresies, rejecting them from debate over the Scriptures by definite, just, and necessary prescriptions. Hereafter, if God’s grace permits, we shall also answer certain of them individually” (*On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 45, nos. 293–294).

Near its end he reviews a catalogue of the heretics who had torn the Church up to that time, following blessed Irenaeus, though without sufficiently observing chronological order; we have set that order forth as far as possible. First come four kinds of Jewish heretics: Dositheus the Samaritan, the Sadducees, Pharisees, and Herodians. Second come those who wished to be heretics on the basis of the Gospel (ch. 46, heresies 1, 2, 5, 10, and 11), twenty-five in all: Simon Magus, Menander, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, and Ebion (ch. 46, heresies 3–4; ch. 47, heresies 6–8; ch. 48, heresy 6), who spread their heresies under the apostles, and thus under Tiberius, Claudius, Nero, and Trajan. Third come Saturninus and Basilides, the Ophites, Cainites, Sethians, and Carpocrates, under the disciples of the apostles down to the emperor Hadrian. Fourth come Valentinus and his followers Ptolemy and Secundus, [Col. 0066B] Heracleon, Marcus, and Colorbasus. The author relates that Valentinus, their leader, first believed the Catholic doctrine among the Romans under Pope Hyginus, about the reign of Antoninus, and that under the episcopate of Eleutherus, because of his perpetually restless curiosity, he was expelled from the Church once and again together with Marcion (references in the source: ch. 30; chs. 49–53; *On Spectacles*, ch. 27; *On Idolatry*, ch. 25). His followers flourished under the Pius pontiffs and emperors.

Fifth come Cerdo and his disciple Marcion, and among Marcion’s disciples the teachers Lucanus and Apelles. The former began with Valentinus; Marcion and the others flourished under Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherus, while Pius and Aurelius were emperors. [Col. 0066C] Sixth comes Tatian, whom Clement of Alexandria also says established his school around the twelfth year of Antoninus Pius. What is more, Tertullian explicitly calls the Cataphrygians heretics, into whose heresy he later incautiously fell. Seventh, some of these were called *κατὰ* “according to Proclus” (of whom more below), others “according to Aeschines.” He charges them not only with heresy but also with blasphemy: they said that the Holy Spirit had been in the apostles but not the Paraclete, and that the Paraclete had said more, better, and greater things in Montanus than Christ uttered in the Gospel. More will be said presently about their period. Eighth, finally, come Blastus, discussed above; Theodotus of Byzantium and Theodotus the leather-worker, the Melchizedekian, under Pope St Victor and the emperor Commodus; Praxeas, discussed later; and Victorinus, who tried to strengthen Praxeas’ heresy. [Col. 0066D]

In the same book, from the apostle Paul, mention is also made of other heretics: ninth, Phygelus and Hermogenes, Hymenaeus and Philetus; and tenth, a certain Nigidius, of whom I know nothing, and Hermogenes. More on the latter shortly. The author further alludes to the persecution of Christians proclaimed by the emperor Severus in the same year when, speaking of the amphitheatre, he says: “There daily the lions are demanded against us; thence persecutions are decreed; thence trials are sent forth.” Again: “They naturally want to know the time of the persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the identity of the governor,” with several other remarks in the books listed below.

Here we have proved only that the beginning of the said persecution should be assigned to this tenth year of Severus’ reign rather than to the seventh or eleventh. First, blessed Jerome in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Origen, and after him Sophronius and Nicephorus the Greek, write that when persecution was stirred up against the Christians in the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, Origen’s father Leonides was crowned with Christ’s martyrdom. Eusebius, *Church History*, book 5, lists Leonides among the first martyrs who suffered at Alexandria, where the persecution raged most intensely. Second, Judas continued his chronography down to this year because, on account of this extremely severe persecution, he thought the coming of Antichrist imminent. Finally Spartianus expressly indicates that Severus went to Alexandria only after entering upon his consulship with his son in Syria, which fell in this year, undertaking the journey for devotion to the god Serapis. “On this journey,” he says, “he forbade anyone to become a Jew under severe penalty; he likewise decreed the same concerning Christians.” In this persecution very many martyrs suffered at Alexandria under the prefect Laetus; in Egypt, Libya, and the Thebaid under the tyrant Aquila; and in Gaul, Saints Irenaeus, Andeolus, Benignus, Andochius, and Thyrsus. Most writers also assign to this year the inscription: “Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, built this. The emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, consul, restored the Pantheon, damaged by age, with all its adornment.” We thought it appropriate to recall this here for the history of the Church.

## In the Year of the Lord 204

### [Col. 0067C] § XII. *On Baptism against Quintilla*

21. In the consulship of Publius Septimius Geta, son of Marcus, and Lucius Septimius Plautianus for the second time, the fifth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the eleventh of Severus: although persecution was already in force, Tertullian did not cease writing books against heresies. First among these, we think, should be placed *On Baptism against Quintilla*, since it is established that it was written before he began in any way to incline toward heresy: Quintilla belonged to the Montanist faction, from whom, on Epiphanius’ evidence, we derived there the so-called Quintillians. Whether the author wrote anything else against Montanus himself cannot be proved equally well. It is nevertheless probable both from Augustine’s words in *On Heresies*, “He passed over to the Cataphrygians, whom he had previously destroyed,” and especially from Nicephorus, book 4, ch. 34. Nicephorus relates that until settled middle age the author was a presbyter in the Catholic Church and composed many works against the doctrine of Montanus, but afterward fell into his error and in turn wrote many books in his defense. Since Nicephorus treats the history of the Montanist heresy at length in chapters 18 and 20–25 of the same book, drawing on Apollinaris of Hierapolis, Rhodo, Miltiades, Serapion, and Apollonius, who opposed it in their writings, and following Eusebius, book 5, chs. 3–4 and 14–18, we thought it proper—besides what we noted on *Prescription against Heretics*—to reduce it here to a compendium in fulfillment of our promise (*On Baptism*, no. 2).

### [Col. 0068A] Excursus on Montanism, which Tertullian first attacked in writing

22. There is said to have been a village in Mysian Phrygia called Ardabau, where, according to report, a certain Montanus (*On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 52, heresy 21), recently converted to the faith, first became inflamed—when Gratus was proconsul of Asia—with an insatiable desire to obtain primacy. As soon as he opened an entrance to the devil, he was seized by an evil spirit and suddenly driven by frenzy and madness. He began to pour out strange utterances and to prophesy contrary to the Church’s custom derived from the tradition and succession of the apostles. Some recognized these utterances as counterfeit and reproved him so that he would chatter no longer. [Col. 0068B] Among them were the bishops Zoticus of Comana, or Ostrenus, and Julian of Apamea, and the martyrs Gaius and Alexander; they refused, to their last breath, to commune with him and his insane prophetesses Maximilla and Priscilla, former prostitutes whom the demon had filled with the same spirit. Yet a few Phrygians began to adhere to him, and the Theodotus mentioned above assumed, as it were, the management of his fabricated prophecy.

Advancing thence into Galatia, Pontus, and Asia, they also attached to themselves a certain Alexander, whom Maximilla habitually received as an intimate table companion, and a certain Alcibiades and Themiso, who falsely boasted that they were confessors and martyrs of Christ. This occurred—with blessed Jerome also agreeing with them—under the emperor Marcus Aurelius, at the beginning of the pontificate of St Eleutherus. Blessed Irenaeus had carried letters to Eleutherus from Gaul, having been sent by the Christians of Lyons with letters from St Attalus and the other martyrs then still confined in prison, to convey to him in Asia and Phrygia the judgment of the Gallic Church concerning their pseudoprophecy. In my judgment, this same Roman bishop, relying on the authority of his predecessors, refused them letters of peace (vol. 3, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 1). Whether Praxeas, then still Catholic, assisted in this is for the author’s reliability to answer. Certainly not only the bishops at Rome and in Gaul, but also those living in Asia, repeatedly assembled in many places, examined their prophecy, showed it to be false and detestable, and deprived the Montanists of communion. [Col. 0068D]

Montanus and his insane prophetesses died by hanging, like Judas, not by martyrdom. That Alexander was condemned for robbery at Ephesus by the proconsul Aemilius Frontinus; when he falsely represented himself as a martyr, he was not received even by his own people, since he was a robber. Finally, that Theodotus, lifted aloft by a demon like Simon Magus, suddenly fell headlong and ended his life miserably. More on the errors of Montanus, into which the author afterward fell, among his paradoxes.

Before the Kalends of June in this year, when Severus’ eleventh year began, I think there occurred what the author describes: “How eagerly this age celebrates those contests, the contentious solemnities and superstitious rivalries of Greek religions and pleasures, Africa too has learned. Even now the individual cities harry Carthage with congratulations because, after the long decline of its stadium, it has been granted the Pythian contest” (*Scorpiace*, ch. 6). [Col. 0069A] For this seems to be the point of the ancient coin inscription “Severus Pius Augustus, pontifex maximus, holding tribunician power for the tenth time,” or “Antoninus Pius,” on one side, and on the other “The indulgence of the emperors; by decree of the senate; at Carthage”; likewise the Greek legends “ΑΥ; ΚΑΙ ΖΕΟΥΑΡΟΣ ΠΕΡΤ; ΚΑΡΤΑΓ ΜΗΤΡΟΠΟΛΙΟΣ” (“AU; and Severus Pert[inax?]; Carthage, metropolis”—the recovered legends are corrupt or abbreviated, so this interpretation is uncertain), signifying that these games were instituted at Carthage by the emperors Severus and Antoninus.

## In the Year of the Lord 205

### § XIII. On certain books of doubtful reliability: *On Spectacles*, *On Idolatry*, *On Female Dress* and *On the Adornment of Women*, the two books *To His Wife*, *Against the Apelleians*, *Against Hermogenes*, *On Matter Coeternal with God*, *On the Origin of the Soul from That Same Matter*, *Against the Valentinians*, *On the Soul*, and *On the Hope of the Faithful*

23. In the consulship of Lucius Fabius Septimianus, son of Marcus, for the second time, and Marcus Annius Libo, son of Marcus, the sixth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the twelfth of Severus: partly on the occasion of the Pythian games and other contests held at Carthage, and partly because the Secular Games had already been proclaimed at Rome—games to which heralds customarily summoned everyone on the ground that they had never been seen before and would never be seen again—Tertullian wrote, in both Greek and Latin, that distinguished book *On Spectacles* (*On Spectacles*, no. 1 ff.) in order to deter Christians from making that journey. In it he beautifully derives all four kinds of public entertainment from idolatry and therefore declares them forbidden to Christians. [Col. 0069C] That Severus celebrated the eighth Secular Games in this year is mentioned not only by Censorinus in *On the Birthday* and by Dio and Herodian—the latter says he saw them—but also by the consular fasti: “The eighth Secular Games were held by decree of the senate.” A coin inscription is likewise found: “Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Pius Augustus; the Secular Rites; by decree of the senate.” Poliziano and Onuphrius also think the triumphal arch of Severus, which still survives, was erected on this occasion in this year; its inscription is given above, and both authors treat at great length the origin and every rite of the Secular Games. Indeed, the author discusses so fully all the entertainments customarily exhibited at these games that the curious reader needs no other commentary, especially if he consults our annotations.

It is established that *On Idolatry* was composed at almost the same time, since it mentions both this book and the persecution (*On Idolatry*, ch. 13, no. 164; book 1 *To His Wife*, ch. 7, no. 44; book 2 *To His Wife*, ch. 1), and argues that imperial festivals belong to idolatry, together with many other things in which the worship of idols directly consists. To the same year we assign the books *On Female Dress* and *On the Adornment of Women*: in the former he censures excessive ornament, and in the latter especially superfluous care of the hair and skin. [Col. 0069D]

The two books *To His Wife* also seem to have been composed in this year. Since in the first he merely discourages a second marriage and in the second only forbids marriage with Gentiles, it appears that they were written before the author’s heresy, perhaps at Rome, where he frequently traveled, or at least to his wife while absent. He was apparently in poor health, since he calls the first admonition a legacy and trust made as though he were already dying. [Col. 0070A]

## In the Year of the Lord 206
24. In the consulship of the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Bassianus Antoninus Augustus, son of Severus Augustus, for the second time, and Publius Septimius Geta, son of Severus Augustus, the seventh year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the thirteenth of Severus: as various heresies were raging in Africa, Tertullian seriously devoted himself to writing against them. [Col. 0070B] First among these comes the book *Against the Apelleians*, though it is now lost—that is, against the followers of Apelles, Marcion’s disciple. Of them the author says: “There still survive in this world those who remember them, even their own disciples and successors, so that those who come later cannot deny them.”

We think that in the same year he composed two books *Against Hermogenes*: one *On Matter Coeternal with God*, and another *On the Origin of the Soul from That Same Matter*. It is not sufficiently established when Hermogenes began to spread his heresies. Blessed Jerome, however, seems partly to indicate it in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* when he relates that Theophilus of Antioch was the first to write against the heresy of Hermogenes. Although Theophilus flourished under the emperor Verus, it is proved from book 3 *To Autolycus* that he survived him, for there he computes the years both of the world and of Roman consulships and Caesars down to the death of the emperor Verus. We therefore think that Hermogenes spread his errors rather under the emperor Commodus, though he was still alive in the author’s day, as Tertullian himself testifies: “These”—speaking of Marcion, Valentinus, and Apelles, already dead—“we name as the more notorious and frequent adulterers of truth. But a certain Nigidius, of whom I know nothing, and Hermogenes, and many others, still walk about perverting the ways of the Lord” (*On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 30). Philastrius, *On Heresies*, testifies that Hermogenes flourished in Africa, while the author adds a certain Nigidius as though he were his teacher. [Col. 0070C]

Since swarms of Valentinian heretics also still survived, led—besides the first men named above—by Theotimus, Axionicus, Alexander, and Prodicus, Tertullian composed the book *Against the Valentinians*, following blessed Irenaeus almost word for word. Of the first two the author says: “Theotimus labored much over images of the Law. Valentinus nowhere does so, yet the Valentinians do, because they act through Valentinus. Axionicus alone at Antioch, down to the present day, consoles the memory of Valentinus by preserving his rules intact” (vol. 3, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 4, nos. 32–34; *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 15, no. 127; ch. 16, no. 131). Of the third he says: “For, as I read in a certain member of Valentinus’ faction, they do not at first think that Christ’s earthly and human substance was formed” (ibid., ch. 17; vol. 3, *Scorpiace*, final chapter). He then adds whom he means: “Besides, through a passion for argument and the shape of a heretical intellect, that Alexander made a place for himself.” And again: “But dismissing Alexander with his syllogisms” (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 3; *On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 21). [Col. 0071A]

Finally, two passages concern the last: “But if Prodicus or Valentinus had then been present”; and “When another God is introduced against the Creator, it is evil; still worse when several are introduced, according to the Valentinians and Prodicans” (*Against the Valentinians*, ch. 5; *On Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 3 and ch. 52, heresy 52, no. 327; *On the Soul*, ch. 55). The reading cannot be *Procli* there, as it was in the printed copies. Besides what we proved in its proper place, this is demonstrated by the fact that Proclus or Proculus was not a Valentinian but a Montanist; some followers of Montanus were therefore called κατὰ, “according to Proclus.” Tertullian, while still Catholic, had written against Valentinus.

Indeed, since the author calls Proculus “the dignity of virginal old age and Christian eloquence,” we seem to have reached what they call the first stumbling stone against which he struck when he began to favor Montanus’ party. He was apparently seduced by admiration both for Proculus’ virginal old age—Proculus must then have been elderly, since even by Tertullian’s testimony he was a contemporary of the Valentinian founders—and for the Christian eloquence he discovered in his writings. The wretched man little remembered what he had written earlier, perhaps on the occasion of this very great man: “These simpletons are also accustomed to build themselves up toward ruin by certain persons captured by heresy: Why did she or he, most faithful, prudent, and experienced in the Church, pass over to that side? Whoever says this does not answer himself: those whom heresies could change should be judged neither prudent, faithful, nor experienced. What then if a bishop, a deacon, a widow, a virgin, a teacher, even a martyr, has fallen from the rule? Will heresies therefore seem to possess the truth? Do we prove faith from persons, or persons from faith?” [Col. 0071C] Otherwise it is hardly probable that the author would have fallen into so absurd a heresy except through some such occasion, perhaps even through familiar association with Proculus during his repeated visits to Rome. We shall later show that Proculus lived at Rome. This is especially striking because Tertullian had earlier called it blasphemy to say that the Paraclete promised by Christ first appeared in Montanus, yet in his subsequent writings he did not hesitate frequently to ascribe the name Paraclete to him.

## [Col. 0071D] In the Year of the Lord 207

25. In the consulship of Nummius Senecio Albinus and Fulvius Aemilianus, the eighth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the fourteenth of Severus: most writers say that Perpetua and Felicity suffered martyrdom, according to the Venerable Bede on Severus’ birthday, assigned by the martyrologies of Usuard and Rome to March 7. They also number with them Revocatus, Saturninus, and Secundulus, who suffered together in the Mauretanian city of Thuburbo.

Since the author mentions the most courageous martyr Perpetua in the book *On the Soul*, that book, written *Against the Philosophers and Heretics*, cannot have been composed earlier. In it he also alludes to the book *On Paradise*, which we conjecture was written on the occasion of what St Perpetua says she saw in paradise. [Col. 0072A] To strengthen the faithful in this persecution of Christians, which also extended throughout Africa, we think that at almost the same time he wrote the book *On the Hope of the Faithful*. Nevertheless we find the proverb entirely true that one error draws another after it: the subject of each book is a paradox, and in the said book *On the Soul* one can find not a few further opinions that are insufficiently sound. These are discussed more fully among the author’s paradoxes, together with the antidote. We add only this here: the book was written *On Every Condition of the Soul*, as Tertullian himself testifies, for he even calls it a commentary on the soul, treating whatever philosophers and heretics had ever discussed concerning the soul, so that neither philosophers nor theologians today require another commentary. [Col. 0072B]

## In the Year of the Lord 208

### § XIV. On books already savoring of Montanism: *On the Flesh of Christ against Four Heresies*, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, five books *Against Marcion*, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, *Scorpiace against the Gnostics*, and *Against Praxeas*

26. In the ninth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the fifteenth of Severus, in the consulship of Marcus Flavius Afer, son and grandson of Marcus, and Quintus Allius Fabius Catullinus Maximus, it is established from these words that Tertullian wrote the first book *Against Marcion*: “But now, how can it be that the Lord was revealed in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, yet no substance of him has been discovered even by the fifteenth year of the emperor Severus?” (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chs. 2 and 45; book 1 *Against Marcion*, ch. 15; vol. 3, *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 7). It follows that at this time he must have published together *On the Flesh of Christ against Four Heresies*, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, and the five books *Against Marcion* (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 2; book 5 *Against Marcion*, ch. 10, no. 150; *On the Soldier’s Crown*, final chapter), since they were written at the same time. As we have said elsewhere, the fourth book *Against Marcion* is cited in *On the Flesh of Christ*; books 2 and 3 *Against Marcion* are cited in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*; and in book 1 *Against Marcion* the work *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* is cited. I therefore think that the first four books *Against Marcion* were written first, then the two intermediate works, and finally the fifth *Against Marcion*. [Col. 0072C]

If, as Onuphrius relates, the decennalia of Antoninus, the emperor Severus’ son, were celebrated in this year—perhaps anticipated by a whole year because of his departure for the British war, which Cassiodorus says occurred under these consuls—then the book *On the Soldier’s Crown* was also written in this year. If both events occurred in the following year, as seems more probable to me from the coin inscription “Antoninus Pius Augustus, consul for the third time; vows discharged to the god,” the reader may assign it there, provided he agrees with us that it preceded the British expedition. The inscription given above, with the image of a horseman holding a javelin—“Departure of the emperors”—also belongs to this expedition, for Severus took both sons with him. Since Publius Septimius Geta was first called emperor, Caesar, and Augustus and received tribunician power in the following year, as the consular fasti state, our conjecture is confirmed. [Col. 0073A] The inscriptions and consular fasti can indeed be reconciled with Onuphrius and with another inscription in which Antoninus is called “Augustus, holding tribunician power for the tenth time, consul for the third time designate,” by saying that his tenth year began under these consuls on May 1 and ended on May 1 in the following year; but we have preferred to assign it to the following year, lest we become more prolix here.

## In the Year of the Lord 209

27. In the tenth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the sixteenth of Severus, in the consulship of the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, son of Severus Augustus, for the third time, and Publius Septimius Geta, son of Severus Augustus: we think that after Antoninus’ decennalia were celebrated at Rome, Tertullian wrote the book *On the Soldier’s Crown*. [Col. 0073B] That it was written at Rome is clear from the words, “Blush, his Roman fellow-soldiers,” and its opening appears to refer to the decennalia: “Very recently there was a largess from the most excellent emperors.” We have thought it proper to append what follows, since it indicates the occasion for writing this book, in which he maintains—contrary to what others were muttering—that Christians were forbidden to wear crowns.

“The soldiers crowned with laurel were being paid off in the camp. One among them approached more truly a soldier of God, alone with uncovered head, holding his unused crown in his hand. One by one they point him out, mock him from afar, and gnash their teeth at him close at hand. A complaint reaches the tribune, and the man had now moved forward out of rank. The tribune immediately asked, ‘Why are you so different in dress?’ He denied that it was lawful for him to act with the rest. Asked his reasons, he answered, ‘I am a Christian.’ Then came consultations, adjournment of the case, and the accused man before the prefects. There he laid aside his cloak, took the military boot from his feet, and returned his sword”—for Herodian, book 2, makes clear at the beginning of Severus’ reign that soldiers customarily laid aside all military insignia when discharged. “And now, clothed in the red of hope for his own blood, he awaits Christ’s donative in prison.” [Col. 0073C]

“Then came opinions about him—I do not know whether from Christians, since there were no others from pagans—that he was rash, headstrong, and eager to die, because when questioned about his clothing he created trouble for the Name. Plainly it remains for them to plan also to refuse martyrdoms. Finally they mutter that so good and long a peace is being put in danger. I do not doubt that some are removing the Scriptures, packing their baggage, and preparing to flee from city to city. I know their shepherds too: lions in peace, deer in battle. But elsewhere we shall teach concerning the trials of confessions.”

By this he points either to the book *On Flight in Persecution* or, as is more pleasing, to *Scorpiace against the Gnostics* (*Against the Gnostics*, ch. 1), namely Prodicus, Scorpianus, and other Valentinians who opposed martyrdom and had already begun to break into Africa (on whom the reader may consult our annotations). Perhaps that work too was written at Rome. In it he explains at greatest length the question of confession—that is, that it is necessary to confess Christ—and describes in these words the most severe of all persecutions, which seems on the stated occasion to have flared up again after a long peace, since few martyrs under Severus are recorded at Rome and in Africa down to that time: “At present the heat is at its height, the very dog-days of persecution from this dog-headed creature” (by whom he means either the emperor Severus or, more probably, the prefect of the city of Rome during the emperor’s absence after his departure for Britain). “Fire has proved some Christians, the sword others, wild beasts others; still others, after tasting martyrdom under clubs and claws, hunger in prison.” [Col. 0074A]

We said Severus was absent in Britain because Eusebius in his *Chronicle*, Orosius, book 7, ch. 11, Paul the Deacon, book 8, ch. 1, and before them Spartianus, Herodian, and Dio in his life of Severus, mention the British expedition undertaken in this year, as we proved above. Tertullian himself indicates in the words cited above that Britain had not yet entirely submitted to the Romans: “Places in Britain inaccessible to the Romans [Col. 0074B] but subject to Christ” (*Against the Jews*, ch. 7), since Lucius, king of the Britons, had shortly before been converted to the faith with the aid of Pope St Eleutherus. Likewise: “The Britains are enclosed within the bounds of the Ocean.”

## In the Year of the Lord 210

28. In the eleventh year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the seventeenth of Severus, in the consulship of Marcus Aurelius Claudius Pompeianus, son of Marcus, and Lollianus Avitus: while still at Rome, Tertullian seems to me to have written the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. In these words he acknowledges that it had also been written in Greek: “Now that the issue peculiar to my opinion has arisen, I shall show in Latin too that our virgins ought to be veiled” (*On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 1). More on this subject in the following year.

It is also probable that shortly afterward, having returned to Carthage, he wrote the book *Against Praxeas*. Of Praxeas the author says: “He was the first to bring this kind of perversity from Asia to Rome, a man otherwise restless and, besides, swollen with boasting of martyrdom merely because of the ordinary brief weariness of imprisonment. The tares of Praxeas, sown here also”—that is, in Africa—“had borne fruit; then, having been exposed by one through whom God willed” (apparently Pope Zephyrinus, since blessed Optatus of Milevis, book 1 *Against Parmenian*, relates something of this kind concerning him), “they even seemed to have been uprooted. Finally the former teacher had given security for his correction, and the written bond remains among the Psychics, in whose presence the matter was then transacted; hence the silence. But those tares had everywhere shaken out their seed. Thus for some time he lay hidden through hypocrisy with deceitful vitality, and now he has broken out again” (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 1). [Col. 0074C–D]

From these words it is sufficiently clear both that Praxeas at one time retracted his heresy after being corrected by someone’s disputation, but relapsed and broke out again, and that he was still alive when this book was written. Yet if what Tertullian adds is true—that the prophecy of Montanus was expelled through Praxeas’ aid—then, since Praxeas is known to have flourished under Pope St Eleutherus, he must already have been old. We can scarcely think the author reliable in what has just been said. First, St Pacian writes these true statements about the Cataphrygian heretics: “First, they rely on several authorities: for example, the Greek Blastus belongs to them; Theodotus and Praxeas also once taught your people.” Second, the author himself elsewhere joins Blastus, Theodotus, and Praxeas as disciples, together with Victorinus, attributes to those called “according to Aeschines” the same heresy, and attacks it in this book. [Col. 0075A]

## In the Year of the Lord 211

### § XV. The time and cause of his defection

29. In the twelfth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the eighteenth of Severus, in the consulship of Marcus Acilius Faustinus, son and grandson of Marcus, and Gaius Caesonius Triarius Rufinius, son of Gaius, what Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle* and the Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, ch. 5, write about Severus after the authors cited above was completed: in Britain he extended from sea to sea, for a hundred and more miles, a rampart fortified with frequent towers, so as to make the portion of the province recovered by very severe battles safer from the rest. This is also supported by a law of the Augusti Severus and Antoninus, issued at York under this consulship on May 7, extant in the *Code*, book 3, title 32, law 1. [Col. 0075B] Indeed, inscriptions first appear then in which Severus is called “Britannicus Maximus, holding tribunician power for the eighteenth time,” Antoninus “Britannicus, holding tribunician power for the thirteenth time, acclaimed imperator twice, consul three times,” and finally one reading on one side “Publius Septimius Geta Pius Augustus Britannicus, holding tribunician power for the third time, consul twice,” and on the other “To the victory in Britain.” For this was only the third year since Geta had received tribunician power with the other insignia of imperial rule.

We think it was about this year that what blessed Jerome, Sophronius in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Nicephorus, book 4, chs. 12 and 34, write about Tertullian took place: after he had remained a presbyter in the Catholic Church until middle age, he fell into the doctrine of Montanus. [Col. 0075C] There is nevertheless great difficulty in Jerome’s statement that this happened through the envy and insults of the clergy of the Roman Church, and in Sophronius’ words φθόνῳ καὶ προπηλακισμοῖς τῶν κληρικῶν τῆς ἐν Ῥώμῃ ἐκκλησίας (“through the envy and insults of the clergy of the Church in Rome”), and Nicephorus’ translator’s phrase, “because of the envy of the Roman clergy.” This is especially difficult because the author nowhere complains of it, even in books written against the Church, and because Vincent of Lérins, though later than Jerome, omits this cause and says only that Tertullian, insufficiently tenacious of Catholic doctrine and the ancient faith, far more eloquent than fortunate, changed his opinion and fell into error, becoming a great trial in the Church. Abbot Trithemius follows him. [Col. 0075D]

30. One writer thinks the cause of envy toward the author was his eloquence. Some Catholics also follow Rhenanus’ conjecture, however suspect, and suppose that when Tertullian first began to favor Montanus’ heresy, he was immediately deprived of the Church’s communion before giving himself wholly to it; angered by this, he passed completely into Montanus’ party. But I do not see how Jerome could describe ecclesiastical excommunication not only by the term envy but also by that of insults. The author calls excommunication a divine censure and a preliminary judgment of the future judgment (*Apology*, ch. 39); blessed Jerome, in his letter to Heliodorus, calls it “a judgment before the day of judgment, by which one expelled from the Church is torn apart by the rabid mouth of a demon.” Jerome even acknowledges envy in saints when it means zeal (letter to Damasus on the prodigal and frugal sons). [Col. 0076A]

Therefore, if conjecture is permitted in an uncertain matter, we suppose that after Agrippinus’ death Tertullian was rejected in his attempt to obtain the bishopric of Carthage, perhaps through the envy of certain clergy of the Roman Church. After also suffering insults from them, he defected to Montanus’ party. Several passages in his preceding books could certainly have supplied fuel for their envy, since he tacitly censured the faults of certain clergy, perhaps Roman, just as later happened for the same reason to blessed Jerome and Paulinus (*On Spectacles*, ch. 25).

First, concerning attendance at spectacles: “While the tragic actor shouts,” he says, “that man”—namely someone from the clergy—“will reconsider the exclamations of some prophet. Amid the modes of effeminacy he will devise a psalm within himself; and while the athletes perform, he will say that one must not strike back. He may even be moved to mercy while gazing at the bites of bears and the nets of gladiators. May God avert from his own people so great a lust for deadly pleasure. What sort of thing is it to pass from the Church of God into the church of the devil, from heaven, as they say, into filth? To weary afterward in applauding an actor those hands you raised to the Lord? With the mouth by which you uttered Amen over the holy thing, to bear witness to a gladiator? To say εἰς αἰῶνας (“forever”) to anyone at all except God and Christ?” [Col. 0076B]

Again, concerning makers of idols: “All day faith’s zeal will plead this point with groaning: that a Christian comes from idols into the Church; that he worships with hands which outside are worshipped against God; that he lays upon the Lord’s body hands which furnish bodies to demons. Nor is this enough. Let it be a small matter that they receive from other hands what they contaminate: those same hands deliver to others what they have contaminated. Makers of idols are chosen for the ecclesiastical order. O crime! The Jews laid hands upon Christ once; these men assault his body daily. O hands that ought to be cut off!” (*On Idolatry*, ch. 7; *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 1.) [Col. 0076C]

Again, concerning pastors who flee in persecution: “Clearly it remains for him to plan even to refuse martyrdoms, since he rejects the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit. I know their pastors too: lions in peace, deer in battle.” Finally, concerning the veiling of virgins: “No one would have approved that custom which denies virgins while displaying them, except men of the same sort as the virgins themselves. Eyes such as the virgin has who wishes to be seen will wish to see a virgin. The same kinds of eyes desire one another. To be seen and to see belong to the same lust” (*On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 2). [Col. 0076D]

The author of the commentary on Paul’s epistles ascribed to St Ambrose seems to interpret that envy as though it were the author’s own envy toward the Roman clergy. “Corrupting charity through envy,” he says, “they reduced knowledge to nothing. For Tertullian and Novatian were men of no small learning; but because through jealousy they broke the bonds of charity, they turned to schism and created heresies for their own destruction.” These words also make my conjecture more probable from the fact that Novatian fell into schism and heresy because he was rejected for the Roman episcopate. [Col. 0077A]

If Tertullian had been excommunicated—and for entirely just causes—Pope St Zephyrinus perhaps pronounced the sentence even against him in his absence. First, in all books written before the fourteenth year of Severus’ reign, he frequently mentions the Paraclete’s new prophecy, and even the Holy Spirit of Montanus in the words cited above. He likewise occasionally mentions a female prophet, meaning at one time Priscilla and at another Maximilla, and says not a little about ecstasy in passages cited among the author’s paradoxes (*Against Praxeas*, ch. 1). Second, he began to call Catholics “Psychics,” that is, soulish people, both *Against Marcion* and *Against Praxeas*, as discussed more fully there. Finally, joining all these things together in *Against Praxeas*, [Col. 0077B] he slanders the Roman bishop—apparently Eleutherus—as though, having already acknowledged the prophecies of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, he had been ready by that acknowledgment to bring peace to the churches of Asia and Phrygia, had not Praxeas, by making what Tertullian calls false assertions concerning the prophets and their churches, forced him to recall letters of peace already issued and to desist from the purpose of receiving the charisms. He further says that Praxeas carried out the devil’s work by expelling prophecy and putting the Paraclete to flight. Certainly the author himself approves excommunication of heretics in more than one passage (*Scorpiace against the Gnostics*, ch. 1).

## In the Year of the Lord 212

### § XVI. On the final books of Tertullian the Montanist: *On Flight in Persecution*, *Exhortation to Chastity*, *On Monogamy*, *On Fasts against the Psychics*, *On Modesty*, *On Ecstasy*, and the seventh book *Against Apollonius*

31. In the thirteenth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the first of the reign of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus Pius Felix Augustus Britannicus Germanicus, in the consulship of Quintus Epidius Rufus Lollianus Gentianus, son of Lucius, and Pomponius Bassus, we think Tertullian composed the book *On Flight in Persecution*. He did so before the death of the emperor Lucius Septimius Severus Pertinax Augustus, who died at York on February 4 of that year, more from grief than illness—being punished by God even in this, according to Orosius, book 7, ch. 11—before the eighteenth year of his reign had elapsed. For from May 15, AD 194, to the said day of this year there are only seventeen years, eight months, and twenty-one days. We therefore make this the first year of Antoninus, [Col. 0077D] or at least place the work before Antoninus’ return from Britain with his brother Publius Septimius Geta Felix Augustus Britannicus, his partner in the empire, while the persecution was still continuing (*To Scapula*, ch. 4).

Antoninus—“imbued with Christian milk,” as we said above from the author—put an end to this persecution, as even Sulpicius Severus attests (*Sacred History*, book 2), for he writes that from the death of Severus until Decius the churches enjoyed peace, except that Maximinus raged against the bishops. Blessed Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, calls this a very long peace. Nevertheless the edicts of Severus appear to have remained in force for some time from the author’s words: “Unless perhaps we sin against senatorial decrees and imperial commands opposed to assemblies” (*On Fasts*, ch. 13; *On Flight in Persecution*, ch. 5). [Col. 0078A]

Since blessed Jerome, Sophronius, and Nicephorus assert in the places cited above that this work was written against the Church, it is probable that the Fabius addressed in it was a Roman presbyter. That he held some ecclesiastical ministry can certainly be inferred from these words: “But when the very leaders—that is, deacons, presbyters, and bishops—flee, how will the layman understand?” In our annotations we discuss more fully when, contrary to the author’s view, they are permitted to flee. He also mentions in this work the most holy martyr Rutilius. What Eusebius and Nicephorus write about Origen’s first and most severe persecution at Alexandria, before he castrated himself, should doubtless also be assigned to the reign of Severus.

For understanding the author, it is relevant that he says [Col. 0078B] it is “accursed before ἀποθέωσιν (“deification”) to call Caesar a god” (*Apology*, ch. 34). Herodian, book 3, recounts at length the rite observed when Severus was enrolled among the gods at Rome after death by his sons, once his ashes, brought with them from Britain in an alabaster urn according to Herodian, or a bronze one according to Spartianus, had been placed in the tomb of Antoninus.

We have also thought it should not be passed over here that, since Severus died on February 4, two laws in the *Code* should be corrected. In the first, book 6, title 45, law 1, “the fifth day before the Kalends of February” should be read instead of “January.” The other, book 6, title 37, law 3, should be ascribed to Antoninus Augustus alone, not to Severus and Antoninus Augusti, since it was issued on April 26, long after Severus’ death—especially as a law of Antoninus alone, issued on May 1, and several others issued under these consuls survive.

## [Col. 0078C] In the Year of the Lord 213

32. In the fourteenth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the second of Antoninus, in the consulship of Marcus Pomponius Asper for the second time and Asper—that is, the two Aspers, under whose consulship various laws of Antoninus are found to have been issued (we think the elder was the same man discussed above under AD 202)—Antoninus alone, according to Herodian and Spartianus, seized the empire. He had killed his brother Geta against their mother’s breast after Geta had reigned one year and twenty-one days, buried him in the Septizodium—which Severus had built, according to Eusebius, and which was named from the seven zones of heaven—and enrolled him among the gods. Antoninus also ordered many others put to death, however dear they had previously been to his father and himself. Among those to be mentioned are Papinian, teacher of Antoninus, Julian, and the jurist Tertullian, surnamed by Spartianus “the sanctuary of law,” and Sammonicus Serenus, whose numerous surviving books Spartianus mentions and who was afterward tutor to the Caesar Gordian. [Col. 0078D]

To this year we assign Tertullian’s book *Exhortation to Chastity*, since Nicephorus, book 4, ch. 54, lists it among the works written against the Catholic Church. In it Tertullian seems to have reached such madness as to think that the Church could exist even among three lay people—namely Montanus and his insane prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla—as he insists more fully elsewhere (*Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 7; *On Modesty*, ch. 21).

To this year we also assign the disputation of the ecclesiastical writer Gaius against Proclus, mentioned by Eusebius, book 6, ch. 14, and blessed Jerome in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, and more fully by Nicephorus in the place just cited: “Gaius flourished,” he says, “under Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, while Antoninus, son of Severus, was emperor.” Gaius held and composed a very ample disputation against Proclus, defender of Montanus, reproving and refuting him for his rash audacity in introducing a new prophecy. [Col. 0079A]

We once thought that this disputation gave Tertullian the occasion to defect to Montanus’ party. It seems probable that Proclus, convicted in the disputation and refusing to repent, was excommunicated by Zephyrinus, together with all his followers. Among them was doubtless the author, since he followed Proclus’ group among the Montanists, those called κατὰ (“according to”) Proclus, rather than those called “according to Aeschines,” whom he attacked in *Against Praxeas*. But it is clear from the preceding discussion that Tertullian had already begun to defect and had even written against the Church.

Perhaps around this time also occurred the journey to Rome under Zephyrinus of Origen’s disciples Clement of Alexandria and Ammonius, mentioned by Eusebius and Nicephorus. Eusebius, book 6, ch. 12, says that Clement’s reason was his desire to visit that most ancient Church. At this period they also enumerate other ecclesiastical writers: Beryllus of Bostra in Arabia; Hippolytus, according to some bishop of Portus; and Alexander, first bishop of Cappadocia and afterward of Jerusalem. Blessed Jerome also inserts among them Minucius Felix, [Col. 0079C] who imitated the author’s *Apology* in many respects.

## In the Year of the Lord 214 [the source prints “CCX V,” evidently an OCR or typographical corruption]

33. In the fifteenth year of St Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, and the third of Antoninus, in the consulship of the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Britannicus Germanicus, son of the deified Severus, for the fourth time, and Publius Caelius Balbinus, son of Publius, for the second time, the emperor Antoninus, holding tribunician power for the sixteenth time, triumphed over the Britons. In this year we think Tertullian also wrote against the Church the book *On Monogamy*. Among other things it reads: “Since now the time has been still further shortened, about 160 years having elapsed since then” (*On Monogamy*, ch. 3).

Anyone wishing to reckon these years from the Passion of the Lord would go completely astray, as is more than sufficiently clear from the foregoing. Even if, according to the author’s erroneous calculation, only twenty-two years were counted from Christ’s Passion to the devastation of Jerusalem—others count twenty-five—not merely 160 but 188 years would have elapsed by the present year. [Col. 0079D] Some begin this reckoning from the apostles, because the words “after the apostles” precede it; we too held this view when writing our annotations on the passage. But Saints Peter and Paul first suffered in Nero’s final year, which fell in AD 69, from which only 146 years are counted to this point; and St John the Evangelist lived down to Trajan, dying only around AD 100, from which there are no more than 114 years.

Those who count these approximately 160 years from the time of the apostle Paul come closer, and we accept their opinion. But since he first suffered martyrdom together with the apostle Peter, as already stated, we think they should be counted from the time when he wrote the First Epistle to the Corinthians, namely around AD 54. First, it is clear from the epistles themselves that both letters to the Corinthians were written after Paul had converted them to the faith. That conversion is thought to have occurred in AD 51, when he remained there for a year and six months. Second, if the letter was written from Ephesus, as certain Greek manuscripts—more correctly—have it, it is sufficiently clear from the accounts of Paul’s journeys that he was at Ephesus in the said year, which fell in the twelfth year of the emperor Claudius. If it was written from Philippi, as more Latin and Greek manuscripts profess, Acts of the Apostles, chapter 20, testifies that he traveled through Philippi in AD 55 after leaving Ephesus around the feast of Passover. [Col. 0080A–B]

That the author should be understood in this way is also gathered from the cited words, which he had read at approximately 1 Corinthians 7:29: “Since now the time has been shortened.” That this falls in the present year, not the fifteenth of Severus—as some learned men conjecture—is clear from the fact that Severus’ fifteenth year is the same as AD 208. From the year stated above to that date only 155 years are completed, and the calculation cannot be extended farther because the Corinthians were first initiated into the Catholic faith in AD 51.

This year was also distinguished by the consulship of three men of imperial rank. Besides Antoninus and Balbinus—the latter reigned fourth after him jointly with Pupienus—Marcus Antonius Gordianus, son of Marcus, was appointed suffect consul from the Kalends of March; he was afterward called emperor, Caesar, and Augustus, and was killed by Balbinus. Likewise, from the Kalends of May, Publius Helvius Pertinax, son of the deified Pertinax and his grandson, entered office and was killed not long afterward by Antoninus. [Col. 0080C]

## In the Year of the Lord 215
**34. The sixteenth year of St Zephyrinus, Roman pontiff; the fourth of Emperor Antoninus; consuls Silius Messala and Q. Aquilius Sabinus.** The emperor returned to Rome from the Gallic expedition mentioned by Spartianus and was called Caracalla from the ankle-length garment brought from there and distributed to the people, so that he might be greeted in that attire. We judge that about this year TERTULLIAN wrote against the Church his book *On Fasting against the Psychics* [Col. 0080D] (*On Fasting* 1, 13, 16). From it especially, the likelihood arises that after the aforementioned debate Pope Zephyrinus excommunicated Tertullian together with Proclus and the other Montanists, from these words: “While from every side we hear anathema because we announce otherwise.” He also testifies that various councils were then celebrated throughout Greece: “Moreover, in fixed places throughout Greece councils are held from all the churches, in which all the more profound matters are treated in common, and the representation of the whole Christian name itself is celebrated with great reverence. Those assemblies first performed stations and fasts.” I think these met chiefly against the Montanists, since that heresy seems to have begun creeping like a cancer even among certain bishops, from the author’s words [Col. 0081A]: “These will be examples both for the people and even for spiritual bishops”; for he opposes the “spiritual,” Montanus’s followers, to the “psychics,” as he slanderously calls Catholics (*On Fasting* 15).
