Furthermore, if the reading in Blessed Jerome’s Letter 54 to Marcella concerning the Montanists is true—that they kept three Lents a year, as though three Saviors had suffered—the author begins to differ somewhat from them by observing only two, as is clear from these words, also according to the manuscript: “You say that we offer God two weeks a year of dry fasting, and not even whole weeks, Saturdays and Sundays excepted, abstaining from things we do not reject but postpone.” More on this in our annotations.

## In the Year of the Lord 216

[Col. 0081B] **35. The seventeenth year of St Zephyrinus, Roman pontiff; the fifth of Antoninus; consuls Aemilius Laetus** (whom Spartianus says Antoninus killed shortly afterward) **and Anicius Cerealis.** In the same year in which Antoninus, on a German expedition, killed many barbarians near Raetia (Spartianus), and was chiefly for this called GERMANICUS, TERTULLIAN is thought to have written *On Modesty* (*On Modesty* 7, 10). In it the following words confirm St Damasus’s statement in the *Pontifical* about glass vessels appointed for the sacrifice by St Zephyrinus: “If perhaps that Shepherd whom you depict on the chalice will patronize him”; especially what follows: “But I drink in that Shepherd’s scripture, which cannot be broken.” Glass chalices can very easily be broken; [Col. 0081C] hence it is also plain that they were then customarily painted. Here too he differs from the Montanists. According to Blessed Jerome’s letter cited above, Montanus held that the fallen could not be restored through repentance and Jerome therefore joins him with Novatian; the author denies the Church’s peace only to adulterers and fornicators—wrongly, and contrary to what he had earlier written in *On Repentance*—deliberately opposing this decree of Zephyrinus (whom, even as a heretic, he calls Pontifex Maximus and bishop of bishops): “I remit the sins of adultery and fornication to those who have performed repentance” (*On Modesty* 1). This, in my judgment, is what Blessed Augustine writes about him in *On Heresies*: that, afterward divided from the Cataphrygians, he propagated his own conventicles [Col. 0081D], perhaps because, when those called followers after Proclus (whose follower he was) had died, the followers of Aeschines gained the palm. Against them he tacitly wrote *Against Praxeas*, on the Father and Son not being the same. We have also noted his disagreement concerning only two Lents. Those therefore err who infer from that passage that he returned to the Catholic Church, especially since Blessed Augustine assigns a twofold cause of his heresy: both because, passing to the Cataphrygians, he began to condemn second marriages, and because he propagated his own conventicles.

## In the Year of the Lord 217

**36. The eighteenth year of St Zephyrinus, pope of Rome; the sixth of Antoninus; consuls Q. Aquilius Sabinus II** (to whom Ulpian wrote the fifty-one books of the *Digest*) **and Sextus Aurelius [Col. 0082A] Anullinus, son of Publius.** We judge that TERTULLIAN’s six books *On Ecstasy* and a seventh *Against Apollonius* were written then (among the fragments). Blessed Jerome, Sophronius, and Nicephorus testify that these too were written against the Church. It is no objection that Blessed Jerome in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers places Apollonius before our author, since, as he elsewhere commonly does, he assigns him to no emperor’s reign. Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* V.17), and Nicephorus after him, numbers Apollonius among those who wrote against Montanus but sufficiently indicates by these words that the work was composed some time later: “Moreover, the ecclesiastical writer Apollonius, when the heresy called Cataphrygian was still seen to flourish in Phrygia, separately composed a book refuting its patrons.” What follows proves it [Col. 0082B]: “This same Apollonius in the same book records that it was now the fortieth year since Montanus began his fabricated and counterfeit prophecy when he applied himself to writing this work.” Yet from the beginning of St Eleutherius’s pontificate, when Montanus spread his heresy as stated above, to this year are forty-two years. Eleutherius sat from after the consulship of Cethegus and Clarus (having been created on 14 May, while a decretal letter of St Soter dated 23 May survives under those consuls) until the consuls Maternus and Bradua; he died 26 May—that is, from AD 172 to 186, fourteen years and thirteen days. St Victor, as stated above, sat twelve years, one month, twenty-eight days; with the eighteen years of St Zephyrinus [Col. 0082C], these make forty-two years.

## In the Year of the Lord 218

### § XVII. The latest time at which he flourished

**37. The nineteenth and last year of St Zephyrinus, pope of Rome, and the seventh and last of Antoninus; consuls Bruttius Praesens and Messius Extricatus.** Here we end our history of Tertullian. We do not assert with certainty that TERTULLIAN did not survive longer—Trithemius writes that he lived into old and extreme age—but only that he ceased writing. When composing our annotations we once thought *On Fasting* was published under Pope St Callistus, because it mentions fasts apart from the days on which the bridegroom was taken away (*On Fasting* 13 §78; 4), that is [Col. 0082D], outside Lent, thinking this alluded to the Ember fasts instituted by Callistus. But on closer inspection it can refer to what follows, “interposing the half-fasts of stations” (Wednesdays and Fridays until the ninth hour), and “sometimes living on bread and water”; or to the Saturday fast observed by decree at Rome, though not in Africa (which he mentions shortly afterward); or to the fasts of penitents and even catechumens, of whom before his heresy he had said: “Those about to enter baptism must pray with frequent prayers, fasts, kneelings, and vigils” (*On Baptism* 20); or, finally, to fasts on vigils of ecclesiastical feasts. We therefore accept the opinion of Blessed Jerome, Sophronius, and Nicephorus, who testify that our author flourished and wrote not under Macrinus or Heliogabalus but under Severus [Col. 0083A] and Antoninus Caracalla; especially since all write that he was renowned under St Zephyrinus, not Callistus, except one modern writer who had already made him contemporary under Hadrian with Terty[l]ianus the jurist. That this was Antoninus Caracalla’s final year, not the following (as Cassiodorus has it), is clear from the more correct consular fasti: “This year, on 8 April, IMPERATOR CAESAR MARCUS Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Britannicus Germanicus, son of the divine Severus, was killed” (*Apology* 15). For, says Spartianus, when he wished again to make war on the Parthians and winter at Edessa, and had gone thence to Carrhae out of devotion to the Moon-god (what he adds aids understanding of our author, who somewhere mocks the Moon as masculine), he was killed on his birthday during the Megalensian games through snares set by Macrinus, prefect of the Praetorian Guard, who seized the empire after him; yet Macrinus enrolled him among the gods, built him a temple, and added Salian priests. My view is confirmed because no laws survive under the consuls Antoninus and Adventus, but two bearing the title Antoninus Augustus under Praesens and Extricatus: one in book IX of the *Code*, dated 22 February, the other in book VIII, title 38, law 3, from the Kalends of March shortly before his death. He therefore reigned from 4 February AD 212 until the said day, seven years, two months, four days. No more than nineteen years and sixteen days can be assigned to Pope St Zephyrinus, whom St Damasus and all others say ended his life under these consuls, since precisely that interval is counted from 10 August AD 189 to 26 August, when he died. Because the Church honors him among the martyrs, persecution of Christians must have been stirred again at Rome by the pagan priests when Antoninus was already absent, and perhaps continued by Macrinus (who accordingly was himself punished by death after a year, a month, and some days); but because it was merely local, historians did not count it.

### And how he ended

**38.** For historical truth it must also be added that some vainly think he returned to the Catholic faith. We showed two years above that this cannot be gathered from St Augustine. We also noted at the very beginning that not TERTULLIAN but Tertullinus should be numbered among the martyrs (*On [Col. 0083D] Repentance*, end of the Argument, and at the relevant places). Finally, St Pacian’s words to Sympronianus against the Novatians do nothing for them: “Tertullian,” he says, “after his heresy” (which we judged should be added), “is yours, for you have taken much from him. You will hear him confessing in his own epistle, and precisely one he published as a Catholic, that the Church can forgive sins.” He does not speak of an epistle [Col. 0084A] published after his heresy, but of one issued earlier while he was still Catholic, namely *On Repentance*, from which we have noted elsewhere that Pacian copied much. Surely, had his return been believed, St Vincent of Lérins would not have lamented this good man’s heresy so greatly. We thought Vincent’s words should meanwhile be added as an antidote, lest anyone be scandalized by him: “He too was a great trial in the Church” (alluding to Origen, of whom he had written similarly, who survived from the end of Severus’s reign to Decius). “But I do not wish to say more of him; I shall recall only this: contrary to Moses’ command, by asserting that Montanus’s new frenzies arising in the Church and the mad dreams of mad women concerning a novel dogma were true prophecies, he deserved that it should be said of him [Col. 0084B] and his writings: ‘If a prophet rises in your midst,’ etc., ‘you shall not hear the words of that prophet.’ Why? ‘Because,’ he says, ‘the Lord your God tests you, whether you love him or not.’ From these many and weighty masses of ecclesiastical examples, and others like them, we must plainly perceive and understand more clearly than light, according to Deuteronomy’s laws, that if any ecclesiastical teacher ever strays, divine providence permits it as our trial—whether we love God or not with all our heart and all our soul.”

### § XVIII. On the Tertullianists

**39.** Finally, as a crown, we must not pass over what we learned from Blessed Augustine: the heretical TERTULLIANISTS survived to his own times and only then passed into the Catholic Church. We judge that to them, more than to Tertullian himself, must be imputed the utterly absurd heresy that the worst souls of men turn into demons after death, especially since Tertullianists who held this are first placed in Augustine’s age after Donatists and Jovinianists, both by Augustine and by St Isidore, Honorius of Autun, Rabanus, and Gratian in their catalogues of heretics. Augustine says to Quodvultdeus in *On Heresies*: “The Tertullianists, named from Tertullian, whose many most eloquently written works are read, gradually dwindled to our time and could not survive (for so we emend the text) in their final remnants in the city of Carthage. When I was stationed there some years ago, as I think you too remember, they were wholly consumed. Even the very few who remained passed into the Catholic Church [Col. 0084D] and handed their basilica, still very well known, to the Catholic Church.” Would that, by their example, the failing heretics of our own time in Belgium might soon do likewise, with God’s help, to whom be honor, power, and glory forever and ever. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0084D] The pious prelate says this of his contemporaries and fellow citizens.]

[Col. 0083]

## Opinions of Tertylianus, the Roman Jurist, Extant in the Books of the Digest

### From the Eight Books of Questions

[Col. 0083D] *Digest*, book I, title 3, *On Laws and Decrees of the Senate*, law 27.

Since it has always been customary to extend earlier laws to later cases, it must be believed to be implicit in laws that they also apply to those persons and things which at any time will be similar.

[Col. 0085A] *Digest*, book 29, title 3, *On Acquiring or Losing an Inheritance*, law 82, according to Baldus’s manuscript.

If the slave of one who cannot take an inheritance is appointed heir, and before entering upon it at his master’s command is manumitted and transferred to another, and nothing was done to evade the law, he himself is admitted to the inheritance. If his master can take only a share, the same must be said of the share he cannot take. It makes no difference whether the inquiry concerns the whole that he cannot take or a portion.

*Digest*, book 41, title 2, *On Acquiring or Losing Possession*, law 28.

If I possess something and afterward lease that same thing, do I lose possession? In such matters the intention makes a great difference. First it matters whether I know or do not know that I possess it, and whether I lease it as though it were not mine or as mine; and, knowing it mine, whether with regard to ownership or possession only. For even if you possess my thing and I purchase from you possession of it, or stipulate for it, both purchase and stipulation will be valid. It follows that a *precarium* and a lease also are valid, provided there is a specific intention to lease possession alone or request it as a *precarium*.

### From the Single Book on Military Peculium

*Digest*, book 29, title 1, *On Soldiers’ Wills*, law 23.

The same applies if a soldier who is head of a household, having made a will only concerning his military property, gives himself in arrogation; but if he does so after discharge, the will is invalid.

Ibid., law 33.

If a son under paternal power serving as a soldier made a will under military law and then, after his father’s death, a posthumous child was born to him, his will is certainly broken. But if he persisted in wishing that will still to be valid, it will be valid as though made anew, provided he was still serving when the posthumous child was born. Yet if a soldier under paternal power made a will and afterward, while he and the grandfather were still alive, a posthumous child was born to him, his will is not broken, because, since the child would not come under his power, he is not regarded as a direct heir; nor, when born during the son’s lifetime, does this posthumous grandson immediately become his grandfather’s direct heir. Therefore the grandfather’s will is not broken either, since although the child immediately begins to be under the grandfather’s power, the son precedes him. Accordingly, if a soldier under paternal power makes a will and mistakenly omits a posthumous child whom he did not wish disinherited, and the child is then born after the grandfather’s death while the son—his father—is still alive, he will altogether break that will. [Col. 0086B] If born after the soldier has become a civilian, the broken will does not recover validity. If born while he is still serving, it is broken; but if the father then wishes it ratified, it recovers validity as though made anew. If the posthumous child is born during the grandfather’s life, he does not immediately break the father’s will. If he survives after the grandfather’s death while his father still lives, he breaks it, because only then is a new direct heir born to him. Thus he can never break the wills of two persons at once, grandfather and father.

*Digest*, book 49, title 17, *On Military Peculium*, law 4.

A soldier ought to have as his own the things he took with him into camp with his father’s permission. A son always has an action and right of pursuit regarding military property even against his father’s will. If a head of household, while serving or after discharge, gives himself in arrogation, it must be considered whether administration of things acquired in camp before arrogation is also understood to be permitted to him. Although imperial constitutions speak of those who served from the beginning as sons under paternal power, this conclusion must be admitted.

## Dissertation on the True Date and Doctrine of the Surviving Writings of Q. S. Tertullian, by Dom Gottfried Lumper and Johann A. Noesselt

[Col. 0085]

### Dissertation on the True Date and Doctrine of the Surviving Writings of Q. Septimius Tertullian

[Note: [Col. 0085D] By Father Gottfried Lumper, Benedictine monk of the imperial monastery of St George in the Black Forest, then prior at Villingen. This dissertation is taken from volume VI of the work entitled *A Theological-Critical History of the Life, Writings, and Doctrine of the Holy Fathers and Other Ecclesiastical Writers of the First Three Centuries, Collected from the Literary Monuments of the Most Learned Men*.]

### Outline of the Dissertation

**Article I** [Col. 0085D] — On Tertullian’s genius, style, and reputation, p. 89.

**Article II** — On Tertullian’s books whose date and orthodoxy are established [Col. 0086D], p. 96.

§1. Rationale of the undertaking, ibid. §2. Certain general questions proposed, p. 97. §3. In what year did Tertullian defect to the Montanists? Did he afterward leave them and return to the orthodox? p. 98. §4. How a Montanizing Tertullian may be distinguished from a Montanist; defense of this distinction against Hoffmann, p. 99. [Col. 0087A] §5. First class of books, written during the earlier persecution of Christians under Severus Augustus, p. 101. §6. Discussion of that persecution, demonstrating that it existed before Severus’s edict; new arguments are added to Mosheim’s, and its beginning is placed in AD 197, ibid. §7. Causes of this earlier persecution, p. 104. §8. Its beginning is demonstrated from the year Albinus died; that he was killed in 197 is proved first from the order of Severus’s war with Pescennius Niger. Certain legends on Severus’s coins are explained in passing and Mosheim’s reasons corrected [Col. 0087B], p. 105. §9. The year 197 is proved secondly from the date of Byzantium’s capture, p. 108. §10. Thirdly, from the year Caracalla received the rank of Caesar by decree of the Senate, p. 109. §11. A passage of Tertullian *To Scapula*, compared with another of Spartianus, shows that this earlier persecution began in 197, ibid. §12. The same is further demonstrated from the date of Tertullian’s *Apology* and the books preceding it, p. 110. §13. The date of this class is fixed: *To the Martyrs* was written in 197 [Col. 0087C]; Hoffmann’s conjectures rejected, p. 111. §14. *On the Shows* written in 198; doubts of Tillemont, Hoffmann, and Dupin answered, p. 113. §15. *On Idolatry* assigned to the same year; conjectures of Tillemont and Hoffmann dispelled, p. 115. §16. *Apology* demonstrated to have been composed in 199, p. 117. §17. Two books *To the Nations* written in 199, p. 120. §18. *On the Testimony of the Soul* assigned to that year, p. 121.

**Article III** [Col. 0087D] — On Tertullian’s books whose date and Montanism are established, p. 122.

§1. *On the Crown* shown written in 201, ibid. §2. Contrary opinions examined, especially Hoffmann and Orsi, who assigned it to 198, and Pagi, who assigned 202, p. 126. §3. Baronius’s arguments for 199 overturned, p. 129. §4. Finally, the decisions of Pamelius and Allix, who placed it in 209, rejected, p. 130. [Col. 0088A] §5. Both books *On the Dress of Women* shown to have been published together, against Pamelius and Tillemont, p. 130. §6. In 201 or 202, p. 132. §7. *On Flight in Persecution* vindicated for 202, ibid. §8. The common opinion that *Scorpiace* is later than Tertullian’s books against Marcion examined, with discussion of his lost books against Marcion, p. 133. §9. *Scorpiace* concluded to have been written in 204, p. 135. §10. The five surviving books *Against Marcion*: the first assigned to 207 or 208, the others shown of uncertain date [Col. 0088B], p. 136. §11. Tillemont’s contrary opinion corrected, p. 137. §12. *On the Pallium*: discussion of the threefold excellence of the present empire and inquiry into the year Geta received the dignity of Augustus, p. 139. §13. The opinion of Basnage and Walch, who place it in 211, rendered doubtful; the work assigned to 208, p. 141. §14. *To Scapula* proved to have appeared at the beginning of Antoninus Caracalla’s reign, in 211, p. 143.

**Article IV** — On Tertullian’s books whose date or doctrine [Col. 0088C], or both, is unknown, p. 144.

§1. Third class: books of uncertain date but certainly written before his defection, ibid. §2. *On Prayer* written before the defection, ibid. §3. *On Baptism* composed by Tertullian while Catholic; contrary arguments refuted, p. 148. §4. Pamelius and Dupin corrected; the book’s freedom from Montanism demonstrated, p. 152. §5. Two books *To His Wife* composed before Tertullian’s fall, p. 156.

**Article V** [Col. 0088D] — Fourth class: books whose Montanism alone is clear, p. 157.

§1. *On Patience*, ibid. §2. *On the Veiling of Virgins*, easily the first Montanist book, p. 159. §3. *Exhortation to Chastity*, p. 160. §4. *On Monogamy, Fasting,* and *Modesty*, p. 161. §5. *Against Hermogenes, Against Praxeas,* and *On the Soul*, p. 162. §6. *Against the Valentinians, Prescriptions, On the Flesh of Christ,* and *On the Resurrection*, p. 164.

**Article VI** [Col. 0089A] — Fifth class: books whose date and doctrine alike are uncertain, p. 168.

§1. *On Repentance*, ibid. §2. *Against the Jews*, p. 170. §3. The Acts of Perpetua and Felicity and their Montanism, p. 171. [Col. 0090A] §4. The Artotyrite Montanists, p. 174. §5. Whiston’s arguments that Tertullian authored these Acts weighed, p. 176. §6. Use of the entire discussion demonstrated by examples from Christian history, p. 177.

## Article I. On Tertullian’s Genius, Style, and Reputation

[Col. 0089A]

[Col. 0089B] Tertullian’s writings clearly declare his great power in letters and learning. In Dupin’s judgment, “His genius was vigorous and acute, though not sufficiently exact and sound. His reasonings often have more brilliance than solidity. He affects and strikes by novel and unusual expressions rather than convinces by force of argument. His matter is studied and sometimes rather inflated. He expresses it with great but not wholly natural charm. He often speaks beyond measure, and in almost everything seethes and is carried away. He abounds in figures and hyperboles. He was filled with great knowledge and learning, which he used very aptly. He excelled in satire; his wit was urbane and biting. He attacked adversaries skillfully and overwhelmed them with a multitude of connected arguments. Finally, if he does not persuade by reasoning [Col. 0089C], he at least extorts assent by his brilliant manner of speaking. His discourse is Laconic, his expressions powerful; in his writings there are nearly as many thoughts as words. Yet Lactantius rightly criticizes three considerable faults: ‘Tertullian,’ he says, ‘was highly skilled in every kind of literature, but in speaking he was insufficiently fluent, insufficiently polished, and very obscure’ (*Divine Institutes* V.1). These three faults occur in most African authors, except Minucius, Cyprian, and Lactantius, who departed from the African style, although something remains even in Cyprian. In Tertullian, however, they exist in the highest degree; no writer’s style is harsher, less polished, or more obscure. Each work suffers from them, some more and some less. He is clearer and more fluid, though less elegant, in polemical books; obscurer and harsher in commonplaces, as in *On the Pallium*, one of antiquity’s most obscure works. *On Repentance* is the most elegant of all. His finest and most useful works are the *Apology*, *Prescriptions*, the books *On Repentance, Baptism,* and *Prayer*, and the exhortations to patience and martyrdom.” Thus Dupin (*Bibliothèque des auteurs*, I, p. 165, Latin trans., Cologne, 1703). But John Cave must also be heard. After quoting Lactantius’s words, he adds: “Yet Tertullian’s style has a certain majesty proper to itself, and lofty eloquence highly seasoned with wit and point, which at once exercises the reader’s intellect and sweetly delights his mind” (Cave, *Literary History*, I, p. 92, Basel ed.).

“From the foregoing,” Dupin continues, “it is not difficult to judge Tertullian’s character. Yet it is no easier to assert whether he deserves more praise or blame. First, if he is judged according to his service to the Church, it is difficult to say whether he harmed her more than he benefited her. On one side he vigorously defended her teaching against many heretics, maintained in certain works important heads of her discipline, and everywhere taught morals beautifully; on the other, besides always being infected by many errors, he openly attacked the Church’s discipline after deserting her. If he is next judged from his genius, it is so powerful for good and evil that it is hard to say which prevails. Finally, if from his style, it is uncertain whether he should be praised and admired for sublimity or blamed for faults. Opinions have therefore always differed, and men still vary considerably in their judgments of this author. I am thus led to believe [Col. 0090C] that it is better to praise what is good in him and blame what was evil than to issue an absolute judgment that would always be exposed to a thousand disputes.”

Here are some ancient and modern judgments on Tertullian. According to Jerome—who learned it from a presbyter, who had learned it from Cyprian’s secretary—Cyprian customarily read something of Tertullian every day and, when asking for one of his books, said: “Give me my master” (*Ecclesiastical Writers* 53). He truly imitated him and drew much from him. He also composed most of his works on Tertullian’s plan: his *On Idolatry* after the *Apology*, and his books *On Discipline and Women’s Dress* [Col. 0090D], *On Jealousy and Envy*, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and *On Works and Alms* in imitation of Tertullian. Eusebius says Tertullian was among the most learned Latin writers and renowned in every church (*Ecclesiastical History* II.2). Lactantius’s judgment, quoted above, does him little honor. Hilary writes in his commentary on Matthew that the error into which Tertullian fell diminished the authority of books otherwise deserving some approval. Jerome sometimes speaks honorably of him: in the *Catalogue* he calls him a man of vigorous and vehement genius; in his letter to Magnus he says every author is inferior to him in learning and subtlety. Elsewhere, however, he rebukes his errors and faults. In the *Apology against Rufinus* [Col. 0091A] he says: “I praise his genius; I condemn his heresies”; and against Helvidius, who cited Tertullian’s authority: “Of Tertullian I say that he is not a man of the Church.” Augustine praises his style and everywhere condemns his errors; in *Literal Commentary on Genesis* he says Tertullian’s acute genius sometimes perceived truth and could not avoid setting it down occasionally even against his own mind.

Vincent of Lérins paints him thus: “The same principle applies to Tertullian. As Origen among the Greeks, so he among the Latins must easily be judged chief of all our writers. What man was more learned, more practiced in divine and human matters? With wonderful mental capacity he embraced all philosophy, all philosophical schools, the founders and opponents of schools, all their disciplines, and every variety of history and study. Did he not excel in a genius so weighty and vehement that he proposed almost nothing to overthrow which he did not penetrate by acuteness or crush by weight? Who can recount the praises of his speech? It is packed with some compelling necessity of reasons, so that it drives to assent those it cannot persuade; almost every word is a thought, every perception a victory. Marcion, Apelles, Praxeas, Hermogenes, Jews, Gentiles, Gnostics, and the rest know this; their blasphemies he overthrew with the many great masses of his volumes, like thunderbolts. Yet after [Col. 0091C] all this, Tertullian, insufficiently tenacious of Catholic dogma—that is, universal and ancient faith—and far more eloquent than fortunate, changed his opinion and finally did what the blessed confessor Hilary writes: ‘By subsequent error he deprived his worthy writings of authority’” [Note: [Col. 0091D] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium* 18].

I pass over the judgments of Trithemius, Rhenanus, Politian, Pamelius, Rigault, and other moderns, whom readers may consult, and end with two French authors who painted Tertullian differently. The first is the famous Balzac, Letter 2, book V, to Rigault: “I await the Tertullian you are publishing, that he may teach me the patience he transmits.… Your preface would have reconciled me to that author had I hated him [Col. 0091D] and had his harsh diction and the faults of his age deterred me from reading him. But I have long esteemed him; though covered with thorns and somber, he does not seem unpleasant. In his writings I encounter that black light of which the old poet sings, and his obscurity delights me like polished ebony. I have always thought African forms, though unlike ours, do not lack their own charm; and as Sophonisba eclipsed many Italian women, so minds of that region please by their foreign eloquence, and I rank him above many imitators of Cicero. Let us concede to the fastidious that his style is iron; let them concede that from this iron he forged excellent weapons [Col. 0092A], defended the honor and innocence of Christianity, fiercely pursued the Valentinians, and utterly pierced Marcion.”

The second is Father Malebranche, author of *The Search after Truth* II.3: “Tertullian was undoubtedly cultivated in every learning, but stronger in memory than judgment; keener and vaster in genius than in mind. There can be no doubt that he was a fanatic in the sense explained above and possessed nearly all fanatic qualities. His reverence for the visions of Montanus and his prophetesses proves weak judgment. That sharp genius, impulses inspired by trifles, and unbridled mind plainly reveal it. How many irregular movements in his hyperboles and figures! How many brilliant, magnificent reasons which prove only by brilliance and persuade merely by stunning and dazzling the mind” [Col. 0092B]. Malebranche then tries to prove this portrait by excerpts from *On the Pallium*, which he thought especially suitable.

If we consider this portrait drawn from learned men, one may ask whether Tertullian benefited or harmed religion and the Church more; whether he brought greater losses or advantages; whether he deserves more blame or praise. Given scholars’ varied judgments, a decision is difficult and delicate. Yet according to the elegant Schröckh [Note: [Col. 0092D] Johann Matthias Schröckh, *Ecclesiastical History Written Theologically*, vol. III, p. 321 in my copy], if we question Tertullian’s writings, the answer may generally favor him. The Montanist errors he championed did not greatly attack the Church, much less overthrow Christianity’s foundations, but arose rather from excessive religious fervor that commonly rejected rational examination. Even in defending them he departed little, if at all, from Catholic faith and the Apostles’ Creed. Why should the name Montanist harm his reputation more than other ancient Fathers’ errors harmed theirs? He spent the better part of his life among sectarians, yet the Church of that age has no man comparable in learning and merit. I think even Tertullian the Montanist benefited Catholics considerably, both because his invectives sharpened their prudence [Col. 0092D] in action and because, by commending principles of stricter ethics so ardently, he called them away from allegorical games in explaining Scripture and ingenious questions about faith toward more useful matters.

His faults—unavoidable in one so merciless in exposing and refuting others’—do not obscure his conspicuous virtues. His writings abound in signs of a fervent and profound mind distinguished by its own genius: now it rises vehemently, now sinks as though ill and crawls anxiously; rich in its own inventions and thoughts, rarely calm, somewhat sad even in exultation. An extensive apparatus of learning, abundantly and aptly scattered in its places; a manifold imaginative power enjoyable and profitable to readers; and the resulting fertility of genius spread everywhere through refined thoughts, acute maxims, vivid images, merry wit, biting jests, and every kind of diction. When these powers are repeatedly driven rapidly and turbulently, judgment stumbles; hence his arguments often have much brilliance and show, but little weight and solidity. He flares even over trifles. Besides readily believing any little tale, he often views or invents things greater than truth and, himself swept away, carries the reader with him instead of inviting him by reason. More often than the bare teaching or proof of a matter requires, he delights in ornaments. He says many things more harshly and emphatically than he intended them understood. He knew Greek philosophy exceedingly well, yet abstained from using it both from hatred, condemning it among Christians as the mother of heresies, and from a temperament that abhorred slow thought freed from beloved digressions. Thus he philosophized less often and successfully than his capacity allowed.

[Col. 0093B] This did not prevent his becoming an outstanding apologist for Christianity against the Gentiles. Excepting a few peculiar opinions of no great moment, especially Montanus’s familiar dogmas, his writings everywhere present pure Catholic faith gravely, without artificial explanations and formulas of comparison attempted by some doctors. In moral teaching, where he so often turns to rigor, the stricter he is, the more excellent he often becomes. His zeal for advancing religion kindles readers and inflames them to noble actions. He treats moral questions and assertions with such force and grace that one readily forgives him when he errs. He uses Scripture frequently and interprets it learnedly, though not impartially, being over-eager to elicit his own opinions from it. He is a most vigorous athlete in restraining false teachers and corrupters of Christian doctrine, pursuing them with innate impetuosity, deadly hatred, taunts, and reproaches scarcely worthy of a gentleman. To defeat them strongly on every side he uses unfamiliar argumentative weapons, most of which strike hard rather than miss.

His style smells of hardness more than African—or, precisely, Tertullianic. Everywhere appears his singular effort to find words matching the magnitude and force of his thoughts. Ideas crowd ideas and words crowd words, so that clarity only rarely flashes from darkness. Obsolete, newly coined, or affected words; harsh constructions; varied abuses; uneven flow; compressed brevity; bold metaphors; frigid maxims, antitheses [Col. 0094A], and empty wordplay everywhere reveal Tertullian. He expresses what thought sits in his mind, but in words so obscure it is extracted by conjecture rather than clearly seen. His chosen phrases are rarely penetrated fully, and he is rightly blamed for deliberately wrapping his thoughts in darkness and verbal coverings. Yet the Oedipal labors of one who skillfully searches these stylistic riddles will not be empty. The author compensates for the doubtful light scattered through his works by the abundance of truths he reveals to the careful searcher. How delightful for a student of antiquity to labor through the carefully heaped mass of words to deeper knowledge and often uncover splendid truths by investigating almost a single little word! How unlike the many writers whose swollen method pours mere floods of words and offers empty nuts to nauseated readers. As many difficulties as our author contains, making reading hard for his devotees, so many charms fill his books; their varied, choice thoughts and truths make them more useful and pleasant. Besides treasures of recondite learning, his writings give an account of Christian faith, ecclesiastical discipline, ceremonies used in worship, attacks by heretical sects against Catholic doctrine, and contemporary heretical opinions so candid, clear, and pleasant as one would vainly expect from others of that age.

[Col. 0094C] There is no need to fear a confusion of Montanism—his private opinion—and Catholicism, as many scruple to do. He professed it in few and lighter matters, and we have means to distinguish his opinions from the common view. Some say his account of Gnostic errors is inaccurate because he was ignorant of Eastern philosophy, but that is not fairly believed. Should one who studied their writings with such diligence and acuteness, and discussed their errors more abundantly than anyone, be thought ignorant of their origin? He derives their absurd ideas solely from Greek philosophy; one must rather concede, then, that Eastern philosophy was not their sole source.

Moreover, Tertullian founded ecclesiastical Latin, the speech used in public Church affairs, joining words and thoughts of ancient Latium to new notions drawn from Christian dogmas, persons, and customs. Though the orthodox did not number him in their communion, they everywhere praised his genius and style and had no equal among Westerners. Soon afterward Cyprian, most celebrated among bishops, wholly fashioned himself and his speech after Tertullian’s diction; others attempted it less openly. As Montanus’s faction gradually failed, danger from reading him also disappeared, especially because the advantages drawn from him were altogether singular. His commentaries and interpretations of Scripture are illustrious monuments for the history of biblical theology and exegesis, though it is difficult to decide how much he used a Latin translation already existing then.

The number and variety of Tertullian’s works require ordering into classes. By subject they fall into three. The first contains writings against the Gentiles and Jews, sworn enemies of religion: the *Apology*, two books *To the Nations*, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, *To Scapula*, and *Against the Jews*. [Col. 0095B] The second contains writings against heretics: *Prescription against Heretics*, *Against Praxeas*, *Hermogenes*, *Valentinians*, and *Marcion*; *On the Flesh of Christ* against Apelles, Marcion, and Valentinus; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* against Sadducees and resurrection-denying heretics; *Scorpiace* against Gnostics; and *On the Soul* against philosophers’ and heretics’ opinions. The third concerns discipline and morals: first *On Baptism*, whose former part proves against the Cainites baptism’s necessity and efficacy and whose latter describes discipline; *On Repentance*, first among works concerning ecclesiastical discipline alone; *On Prayer*, concerning morals and discipline; and *On Idolatry*, *Crown*, *Flight*, *Pallium*, *Shows*, women’s dress and adornment, *Veiling of Virgins*, *Patience*, *To the Martyrs*, and *To His Wife*. By critical and chronological considerations, five classes will be established in the next chapter. Finally note the four works written for the Montanists against the Church: *Modesty*, *Monogamy*, *Exhortation to Chastity*, and *Fasting*.

Learned men dispute much about the time and order of Tertullian’s works, and the controversy cannot be resolved with complete precision [Col. 0095D]. Among Protestants, Samuel Basnage (*Political-Ecclesiastical Annals* II, p. 215) and Pierre Allix (*Dissertation on Tertullian’s Life and Writings* IV ff., p. 28) investigated their dates; William Cave judges Allix’s chronology nearest truth (*Literary History* I, p. 92) and chiefly follows it, though differing sometimes. Among Catholics, Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (*Mémoires* III, p. 300 ff., Brussels 1732), Ellies Dupin (*Bibliothèque des auteurs* I), and Rémy Ceillier (*General History of Ecclesiastical Authors* [Col. 0096A] II.28) devoted their powers to the question. But, in Schröckh’s judgment, none performed the task more successfully than Johann August Noesselt, doctor and public ordinary professor of theology at Halle, in his 1757 dissertation *On the True Date and Doctrine of the Surviving Writings of Q. Septimius Tertullian*, more correctly reprinted at Halle-Magdeburg in 1768. Because of both its excellence and rarity—for almost a year I wrote booksellers everywhere urging them to procure it, and at last obtained a copy with great effort—I decided to append it here, not without scholars’ gratitude.

## Article II. On Tertullian’s Books Whose Date and Orthodoxy Are Established

[Col. 0096B]

### §1. Rationale of the undertaking

After the darkness of the preceding barbarism was dispelled, the ancient elegance of the liberal arts and disciplines restored, and every kind of literature increasingly illuminated, men of great genius appeared who, deterred neither by lengthy art nor immense difficulties, devoted every effort to illustrating Christian history. Holding that neither literary elegance, the art of thinking well and accurately, nor sacred disciplines could be adequately served without rigorous reading of ancient writers [Col. 0096C], they believed those authors especially should be examined whose reading greatly aided understanding of Christian doctrine and discipline. But opinions, like times, change. This manner of learning from antiquity gradually fell into contempt among us, especially when men appeared who believed common sense alone, inherited from the Fathers and constrained by geometrical subtlety, made a scholar. They treated theological preliminaries as theology itself and, content with meager knowledge, despised studies lacking novelty or requiring intense, laborious thought. Hence most now disdain anything marked by antiquity and think matters concerning Scripture, early Christian teachers, and Christian history worthier of cloistered pedants than acute minds.

Reflecting often on this and lamenting our age with lovers of sound judgment, we chose to emulate the diligence of the former rather than the obscure wisdom of the latter. Once we began considering how to dedicate something to others’ use, we deemed it wrong to follow the popular road, which gradually leads our people back to ancient barbarism, and resolved to resume studies of antiquity closely joined to diligent cultivation of divine letters. Having applied myself continually, as opportunity allowed, to early doctors, Tertullian seemed especially worthy of accurate reading. I doubt whether all antiquity contains another from whom ancient Christian doctrine and morals may be learned who joined greater divine and human knowledge and subtlety in writing to so great a genius [Note: [Col. 0097D] Lest we seem partisan, add Jean Daillé’s testimony, unsuspected here because of his excessive severity toward early doctors. He calls Tertullian “a writer marvelously learned, acute, diligent, copious, and an exceedingly rich witness to his age’s ecclesiastical affairs” (*On the Religious Worship of the Latins* I.11, p. 50)].

Yet using him to learn ancient Christian institutions is chiefly hindered by uncertainty whether each book was written before or after his defection to the Montanists. This question greatly exercised scholars, who sought the books’ dates so that Tertullian could reliably show what ancient Christians thought. Unfortunately, some excellent men treated only one or two works, others treated the task lightly, and others were led astray by preconceptions, though they might have attained truth had they followed it unencumbered. After repeatedly reading his books and observing matters concerning their dates and doctrine profitably disputable but unmentioned by others, and that most could be dated more accurately, I resolved to submit to learned judgment evidence drawn from Tertullian’s books, compared with ancient writers and monuments. We shall proceed by first premising general points; then treating books whose date and doctrine are established; next those lacking definite dates but demonstrably Montanist or free from that suspicion; and finally candidly examining those whose date is no clearer than their doctrine.

### §2. Certain general questions proposed

The whole discussion concerns two matters, date and Montanism, and therefore has two considerable difficulties: neither doctrinal character nor reliable chronological signs can always be found [Col. 0098A]. Whether a work preceded or followed his defection may be understood from its date or its Montanist teachings. The first method has three uncertainties: some books show no chronological traces; some permit only conjecture; some suggest a date but leave uncertain whether Tertullian had then separated from the Church or returned. The second method, besides not applying everywhere, leaves doubt whether he had fully embraced Montanus or merely shared one or two errors without yet renouncing the orthodox Church. Where evidence is absent or doubtful, we shall sometimes state the reason and enter the ancients’ *non liquet* (“not clear”), and elsewhere give probable grounds for conjecture. In the remaining cases we shall briefly discuss three general points: the year of his defection, which dates books known chronologically but not doctrinally [Col. 0098C]; whether he ever returned to a sounder mind or remained permanently Montanist; and signs distinguishing books by an orthodox Tertullian leaning toward Montanism from those by one wholly alienated.

### §3. In what year did Tertullian defect to the Montanists? Did he afterward return to the orthodox?

Neither Tertullian nor another writer tells the year. Jerome’s statement (*Illustrious Men* 53, in Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, p. 125) that Tertullian remained a presbyter of the Church until middle age provides no sound route, since his birth, death, and attained age are uncertain. Some basis is found in chronologically successive books, some without Montanist traces and others with many. We shall show that no work before *On the Soldier’s Crown*—the latest being *On the Testimony of the Soul*—shows Montanism, while its first traces appear in *Crown*. We shall establish that *Crown* was written in AD 201 and *Testimony* near the end of 199; hence Tertullian probably joined the Montanists about AD 200.

The second question, whether he ever returned after embracing their errors, is harder, but there is no adequate basis for affirming it. His austere, excessively rigid weakness made him love stricter moral demands more and regard them as more pleasing to God and consonant with Christian perfection. As those afflicted by melancholy cling more firmly to what feeds sadness and their opinions strengthen with years, it is unlikely that he abandoned these opinions and the arena where he could practice them. Add the silence of all who wrote about him concerning a return, Augustine’s express testimony (*On Heresies* 86), and the consensus of those refusing his doctrinal authority because he joined the perversely minded. Nor do the books we shall show he wrote last oppose our judgment; almost all are stained with Montanist errors. Let this therefore be the rule: all books evidently composed after works undoubtedly convicted of those errors should be considered written after his separation.

### §4. How Tertullian Inclining toward Montanism May Be Distinguished from a Montanist; Defense of This Distinction against Hoffmann
But there are very many of Tertullian’s books whose date eludes the acumen of investigators and which bear upon themselves nothing but certain traces of Montanist errors; yet from these it can scarcely be determined which books he wrote before, and which after, his defection to [Col. 0099D] the Montanists. Hence it has come about that those who investigate these matters more subtly have said, not inaptly, that Tertullian as a Montanist must be distinguished from Tertullian as Montanizing. But John William Hoffmann, formerly a most learned professor of history at the Academy of Wittenberg, thought otherwise. Since he held the opinion that all the surviving works of Tertullian had been written during his Montanism, he undertook to demonstrate this in a separate dissertation (Wittenberg, 1739). He, indeed, clearly perceived that, if this subtle distinction were admitted, his demonstration would suffer some loss, and therefore denied that the distinction could be admitted. “For it lacks definite boundaries,” he says (§ IV, p. 17), “and the appearance of one who is becoming a Montanist and of one who is a Montanist is no less ambiguous than that of a person beginning to fall ill and one who is ill.”

[Col. 0100A] For my part, however, I very much doubt whether Hoffmann understood—or wished to understand—what those who speak in this way mean. “The books of Tertullian as Montanizing,” he adds (p. 18), “are perhaps those which are indeed infected with the doctrines of Montanus but do not assail those who hold the correct view; while those of Tertullian as a Montanist are those which not only contain the heresy but also defend it against the ‘Catholics.’” But among us and, so far as I know, among all those who speak in this way, μοντανίζειν (“to Montanize”) is the term applied to one who indeed shares either all or some errors with the Montanists, yet has not, after rejecting communion in the same rites with his own Church, already gone over to the rites of that community with which he agrees in certain doctrines; whereas a Montanist is one who has done both. Hoffmann, however, says that these distinctions [Col. 0100B] lack definite boundaries. Let it be so. Let the appearance of Tertullian as a Montanist and as μοντανίζοντος (“one who Montanizes”) be exceedingly ambiguous. What follows, then? Evidently, it cannot be judged from Tertullian’s appearance whether he had already been confined to bed by the disease or had merely been lightly touched by one of its attacks. And this is precisely what we maintained: that one cannot safely infer from certain slight indications of errors shared by Tertullian with the Montanists that he had already embraced the Montanists’ rites themselves.

Yet we do not wish this to be understood as though every argument drawn from Montanist doctrines encountered in this or that book of Tertullian, in order to assign those books to his Montanism, were spurious or suspect. For in this matter there are boundaries and, as it were, landmarks which I think must be employed, [Col. 0100C] lest we appear to reason either too little or too much about recognizing Tertullian’s Montanism from his books.

We therefore wish the first rule for judging this matter to be the following: a book of this kind should be numbered among those which he composed after he had already been enrolled in the Montanist family if the name “Psychics” occurs in it. For this was, as it were, the watchword by which he distinguished the members of the orthodox Church from the members of his own sect, whom he calls “spiritual” (see Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, chap. I, ed. Nicolas Rigault, II, p. 673 R.); and it seems to have been coined at approximately the time when he began to attack those who did not accept the austere discipline of Montanus. Nor does it occur in any other book which considerations either of chronology or of doctrine itself show to have been written before his defection. Accordingly, there is no reason to doubt that all those books which contain this name were written [Col. 0100D] after he had embraced Montanism.

Let the second canon be this: every book of Tertullian which treats doctrines not indeed peculiar to the Montanists, but nevertheless confirmed by the authority of a certain Paraclete, should be regarded as having come from the workshop of Montanus. For this was the Montanists’ principal error: they boasted that in their own age a Paraclete had come who would both guide them into all truth and imbue his hearers with a new knowledge of divine things, so that they might know what had been revealed to no person of an earlier age and might now aspire to the highest perfection (see the same author in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chap. I, and book IV *Against Marcion*, chap. 22, p. 537 C). He says that it was his acknowledgment of this Paraclete that separated him from the Church (*Against* [Col. 0101A] *Praxeas*, chap. I, p. 634 D). Nor did members of the orthodox Church ever allow themselves to be persuaded of this error, because it was the principal doctrine of those who followed Montanus as their teacher, although all the other errors of the Montanists were accepted in some measure by certain members of the ancient Church, either during the controversy itself or shortly afterward.

But since we have said that Tertullian never abandoned the errors which he had once learned in the school of the Montanists, it follows of itself from what we have just stated that those books of Tertullian in which he advanced other [errors], undoubtedly tainted by Montanist tenets, belong to the same class. Other rules could be added to these, identifying books as Montanist with the utmost certainty, such as Tertullian’s own explicit declaration; [Col. 0101B] but rules of that sort are generally so constituted that they either require no discussion or are not of the most certain reliability. If, however, something is found in a particular book of Tertullian that can be referred to one of these rules, it may be judged without danger of error that the book was published at a time when Tertullian had already entered into hostility with the orthodox Church. But let us now come to the books themselves.

§ 5.—The First Class of Books, Written During the Earlier Harassment of the Christians under the Emperor Severus

Of these, we promised first to examine those whose date and doctrine were not especially doubtful. First among them must be placed those which are known [Col. 0101C] to have been written at the time when, during the reign of the Emperor Severus, Christians were afflicted with many calamities by the worshippers of the gods because of their doctrine. Since their date cannot properly be determined unless we fix, as it were, the precise point in time at which the savagery against the Christians began, we must make it clear to everyone when this occurred.

But because this harassment arose twice—first before, and then after, Severus’s laws hostile to the Christians—we have learned from observation that the two-hundredth year after Christ’s birth divides Tertullian’s books into, as it were, two classes: one comprising those completed by him while orthodox, the other those completed by him as a Montanist. Since, therefore, our purpose is first [Col. 0101D] to consider that class of Tertullian’s books whose date is sufficiently clear, we shall conduct this treatment by demonstrating first that Christians were already being harassed because of their doctrine before Severus’s edict; then, after offering a few observations on the character of this earlier storm itself, we shall inquire precisely into the year in which this affliction began.

§ 6.—This Harassment Itself Is Discussed, with a Demonstration That It Existed before Severus’s Edict; To Mosheim’s Arguments on This Point New Ones Are Added, and It Is Shown to Have Begun in A.D. 197

The reason many have erred in determining the date of those books of Tertullian which were written during the Severan harassment is undoubtedly that [Col. 0102A] they failed to see that, even before Severus’s law forbidding the adoption of the Christian religion, the worshippers of the gods had harassed Christians. Thus it happened that, since everyone agreed that this law had not been issued by Severus until A.D. 202, all these books were absurdly placed after that year. From time to time there were some who perceived that this conflicted with the books themselves; yet even they did not arrive at the truth, because they had not followed the ancient records of these events candidly and prudently as their guides.

John Laurence Mosheim, a man of immortal memory, ὁ μακαρίτης (“the man of blessed memory”), therefore deserves the highest praise. After investigating the matter more carefully with his characteristic acumen and the greatest candor of mind, he demolished that error with most carefully devised arguments.

> **Note [Col. 0102D].** In the *Dissertation on the Date of Tertullian’s Apologeticum and the Beginning of the Persecution of the Christians under Severus*, which is included in vol. I of his *Dissertations Pertaining to Ecclesiastical History*, pp. 1 ff. He had also promised to provide a life of Tertullian and a chronology of his books more accurate than that offered by Allix (see *Thesaurus Epistolicus Lacrozianus*, vol. I, p. 284); but more serious concerns belonging to his sacred office later deprived him of the opportunity to carry out that plan, as he admits in the additions to vol. I of the *Dissertations on Ecclesiastical History*, p. 752.

[Col. 0102B] By his diligence this great man ensured that we need not labor extensively in demonstrating the matter. Nevertheless, so that those who have not been able to read that most elegant dissertation may not be deprived of the weightiest arguments by which he assigned the Christians’ calamities to the period preceding Severus’s edict, we shall recite them in a kind of summary. We assent to them entirely, and shall add two others which appear to possess some force in confirming them.

His first argument was drawn from the fact that Tertullian himself, in the *Apologeticum*, and especially throughout that entire discussion of the laws, produced so many indications that Severus had not yet fought against the Christians by legislation that no room for doubt whatsoever remains.

His second came from the book *To the Martyrs*, chap. 4, in which Tertullian recalls [Col. 0102C] the punishments Severus inflicted upon the friends of Albinus—an event which Mosheim most correctly observed to have occurred in A.D. 196, or, as I should prefer, 197.

The third was supplied to him by the words of Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata*, book II, Cologne ed., p. 414 B), in which Clement acknowledges that Christians were already being subjected to torture when he was composing the books of the *Stromata*, which he did at approximately the same time we have mentioned.

The fourth was supplied by the date at which the most severe punishments suffered by the Scillitan Martyrs occurred, in the second consulship of Claudius, who held the fasces together with Gaius Aufidius Victorinus in A.D. 200. Finally, he thinks that some additional authority is lent to these arguments by the testimony of Orosius and Freculphus themselves.

We are certainly not among those who think that these arguments [Col. 0102D] are insufficient to demonstrate the point, for we believe that, taken together, they place the matter beyond every doubt. Nevertheless, lest we appear to have omitted anything that could contribute in some way to its confirmation, we have resolved to add two other arguments. Although we readily concede that they are weaker than Mosheim’s, they nevertheless do not appear deserving of complete rejection.

One is what Aelius Spartianus says about [Col. 0103A] Caracalla (*Life of Antoninus Caracalla*, chap. I): when he was a boy of seven and heard that a boy who was his playmate had been severely beaten on account of the Jewish religion, for a long time he would look neither at his own father nor at the boy’s father, nor at those who had ordered the beating. From this passage it appears that the boy’s father had not himself punished him because of the Jewish religion, but that Severus himself had ordered others to punish the boy. For how could Caracalla have been angry with his father Severus unless Severus himself had wished this to be done? There is accordingly some ground for suspecting that violence was already being employed against Christians when Caracalla was seven years old, although Severus did not issue laws against the religion of the Christians and Jews until A.D. 202.

Caracalla passed through his seventh year in A.D. 195, which is easy to demonstrate. For everyone knows that Severus died in A.D. 211 and that Caracalla, succeeding him, was killed after he had reigned for more than six years (Cassius Dio, *Roman History*, book LXXVII, ed. Reimar, vol. II, p. 1314), in A.D. 217. But when he died he had reached his twenty-ninth year. When that number is subtracted from the year of his death, [Col. 0103B] the year 188 emerges, in which he must have been born; whence it follows that Caracalla passed through his seventh year in A.D. 195, long before Severus’s edict.

Nor do I think anyone will object that the situations of the Christian and Jewish religions were altogether different, and that it cannot be demonstrated that Christians were harassed by the worshippers of the gods merely because those who had attached themselves to the Jewish religion were punished. For those who think thus [Col. 0103C] must imagine that even the common people already distinguished Christians sufficiently from Jews—for we say that this disturbance was instigated by the common people. Yet since, before the time when Severus took possession of the empire, this distinction was not observed even by those who were best able to know both religions, and since I do not know how anyone could prove that people in Severus’s time were more perceptive than before, shall we suppose that an excited mob under Severus’s rule took care over this point and distinguished them sufficiently? But even if that inference may be very doubtful, it is nevertheless evident that there were examples of pagan hatred against those who were estranged from the worship of the gods, and that Severus himself was not altogether averse to that hatred.

If Severus acted in this way toward [Col. 0103D] children, to whom we very often forgive things that are by no means conceded to adults, I scarcely doubt that governors, driven by greed and popular unrest, were induced to proceed more severely against Christians.

I shall take the second argument from the book Tertullian wrote *To Scapula* (chap. 4, p. 87 D): “Severus, knowing that most illustrious women and most illustrious men belonged to this sect”—that is, the Christians—“not only did not injure them, but even honored them with his testimony and openly resisted the people when they raged against us.” Severus cannot be said to have openly resisted the people when they raged against the Christians after he had already enacted an edict against Christians. The harsh and almost iron character of Severus prevents us from believing this; certainly no one could have prevailed upon him to rescind a law once enacted. And does not [Col. 0104A] the very fact that Tertullian says that the common people harassed the Christians, indeed against Severus’s wishes, demonstrate that this did not occur under Severus’s laws? Here, therefore, we have another by no means obscure testimony that, before his edict, the Christians were afflicted with the greatest calamities.

§ 7.—What Were the Causes of This Earlier Harassment?

But now we must examine that other question concerning the time at which this earlier storm occurred, after I have first stated what appear to have been the causes of this outrage by the common people against the Christians. It is established concerning every popular disturbance against the Christians that the people attributed to them, as public enemies of the human race, every kind of calamity sent by the gods. [Col. 0104B] It is, moreover, clear from Tertullian’s writings that this was the reason Christians were especially persecuted at this time (cf. *Apologeticum*, chap. 40; *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 9, etc.).

Indeed, the rivalry over the greatest matters which existed between Severus and Niger appears not only to have displeased certain people who had demanded Niger, rather than Severus, as emperor against Didius Julianus (see Herodian, book II, chap. 8; III, chap. 5; Spartianus, *Life of Niger*, chap. 2), but the war he undertook against Albinus also greatly agitated everyone’s minds (see Dio in Xiphilinus, book LXXV, chap. 4, p. 1258 B). Accordingly, after both had been overthrown and Severus was preparing to destroy all those whom he knew to have supported Niger and Albinus, [Col. 0104C] an excellent opportunity presented itself to the common people to attack the Christians as enemies of the commonwealth and of the emperor. These people imagined that they could do this all the more justly because they believed that the Christians were hostile even to the gods themselves, toward whom they thought they could render good service after the gods had created this period of comparative peace for them.

The Christians themselves further persuaded the common people of this very opinion by their complete unwillingness either to participate in the games and celebrations instituted on account of Severus’s victory over his enemies (see Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chap. 1 and elsewhere), or to swear by the genius of the prince (the same author, *Apologeticum*, chap. 32, and book I *To the Nations*, chap. 17), or to make supplication to the gods for his safety (idem, *Apologeticum*, chaps. 10, 29 ff.).

Through this very disturbance the common people could easily drive the governors to the same course, since the governors themselves were not especially averse [Col. 0104D] to this kind of cruelty. For they prescribed to themselves a rule handed down, as it were, from hand to hand: Christians who had once been summoned before the court were by no means to be released unless they abandoned their own rites (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 21, ed. Reading, p. 240). As a witness to this we have Tertullian himself, who for this reason undertook a formal disputation against them concerning the correct interpretation of these laws (*Apologeticum*, chaps. 4 ff.).

Profit-seeking governors seized this opportunity to harass the Christians all the more readily because they clearly saw that it would bring no small advantage to their treasury. I know that I have not invented this from the example of the martyr Rutilius (in Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*, chap. 5, p. 693 A), whom I suspect to have been dragged before the court [Col. 0105A] while judgment was still being rendered not under Severus’s law but under the ancient laws.

> **Note [Col. 0105D].** This book was evidently written at a time when Christians had to expect more serious calamities from the worshippers of the gods (compare chap. 1), that is, as will be stated later, when Severus’s edict had been published and the Christians feared for their safety. But when Tertullian composed that little work, Rutilius had already been slaughtered. At first he had several times sought safety in flight; later he had purchased peace for himself with money; but, captured again, he returned to punishment. This must therefore have happened before Severus’s unjust law, and it supplies a new argument for what we have said: that under Severus Christians were condemned to death before that law.

For many Christians who feared for their wealth and their lives were thereby induced to ward off with an offer of money a danger which they could not avoid by another means. If we comprehend in our minds these causes of the cruelty of the governors and the common people, we shall indeed be able to determine the time at which this earlier storm arose once we have demonstrated when, and in what year, this specious opportunity to injure the Christians presented itself.

§ 8.—The Beginning of the Harassment of the Christians Is Determined from the Year in Which Albinus Perished; That He Was Killed in A.D. 197 Is Proved, First, from the Sequence of the War Which Severus Waged against Pescennius Niger. Along the Way, Certain Marks on Severus’s Coins Are Explained and Mosheim’s Arguments Are Corrected

[Col. 0105B] In investigating this date, let us first employ the very causes of the calamities which we have enumerated. For what provided the common people, as it were, with handles for attacking the Christian community was Severus’s eagerness to seek out all those whom he had learned to have sided with Niger or Albinus against him. Since he did this when, after Albinus had been destroyed, he returned victorious to Rome—for it was then that he decreed the most severe punishments against them (see Dio, book LXXV, chap. 7, p. 1262 D; Herodian, book III, chap. 8; and Spartianus, *Severus*, chaps. 12–13)—it is worthwhile to see in what year Albinus lost both his life and his rule.

We see that Mosheim has already devoted so much labor and care to determining this point (*Dissertation* cited above, § XX ff.) that we might almost dispense with the labor, were there not certain readily available considerations which appear capable of being urged against him. [Col. 0105C] Accordingly, since an opportunity here presents itself to call a certain popular opinion into question, and since the subject itself requires the calculations to be made somewhat differently, we shall retain the same class of arguments employed by that eminent man and candidly discuss what accords with the truth itself. Where we differ in opinion, we shall note below the reason for our disagreement, while preserving the reverence due to so great a man, whose name remains venerable to us even after his death.

When Severus came to power and saw Pescennius Niger preparing forces in Syria with which to oppose him, he first, lest he be pressed from both sides, made Albinus commander of the army in Britain, and decreed both coins and other tokens of honor for him. Afterward, having levied troops [Col. 0105D] throughout Italy and equipped a fleet, he set out against Niger in A.D. 193, when approximately the month of June had elapsed.

> **Note [Col. 0105D].** For Severus came to Rome at the beginning of June A.D. 193. This becomes clear when we count the sixty-six days which Dio assigns to the rule of Didius Julianus (book LXXIII, final chapter, p. 1240), or the two months and five days assigned to him by Spartianus (*Julianus*, chap. 9), beginning from the fifth day before the Kalends of April—that is, March 28—the day on which Julius Capitolinus reports that Pertinax was killed (*Life of Pertinax*, chap. 15). It is no less apparent [Col. 0106D] from this that Severus assumed control of the supreme power approximately on June 2. I shall not demonstrate at greater length that the terms of his tribunician power must likewise be reckoned from that day, since I recall that C. G. Schwarz, a most accomplished man, has done so in his dissertation *On Reckoning the Tribunician Power of the Roman Emperors and Caesars*, Observation IV. This being so, the time at which Severus departed from Rome is by no means obscure, provided Spartianus correctly records (*Life of Severus*, chap. 8) that he left Rome within thirty days of arriving there.

[Col. 0106A] When Severus’s generals engaged Niger’s soldiers in A.D. 194, they prevailed at Cyzicus. They enjoyed the same good fortune in the following year, when battle was joined in the narrows of Nicaea and Cius. Finally, in approximately A.D. 196, after the Severan forces had by chance occupied the fortress in the Taurus and broken into Cilicia, Niger’s army was defeated at the Cilician Gates, and not long afterward Pescennius himself was killed.

But here I suspect that some will wonder what moved me to set down calculations altogether different from those of others, since those who think that this last battle was fought in A.D. 194 are virtually unanimous. I therefore consider it incumbent upon me to produce sound arguments by which it can be proved that our calculations have been made entirely correctly.

First, then, I should like [Col. 0106B] the appellations *Imperator* III, IV, V, VI, VII, and VIII, which Severus is shown by the coins to have received, to be observed. He must have been honored with these during the interval which elapsed from the beginning of his reign to the time when he defeated Albinus, because we read that on assuming power he was styled *Imperator* II on the coins (see Vaillant, *Coins of the Roman Emperors*, vol. II, 3rd ed., Paris, p. 238), whereas, after Albinus was defeated, he was styled *Imperator* IX (in Mediobarbus, *Coins of the Roman Emperors*, under the year 197, ed. Milan, 1730, p. 271).

Now, since the Roman emperors were honored with the name *Imperator*, distinguished by numbers on coins, whenever they had accomplished something in war worthy of that title (on this subject see Cassius Dio, *Roman History*, book XL, chap. 44, p. 372), come, let us see [Col. 0106C] to what events this title of *Imperator*, repeated six times within that interval, must be referred. Within this period, of course, we read that Severus won three victories over Niger’s soldiers and subjected three peoples—the Osroenians, Adiabenians, and Arabs—to Roman power. Since he subdued the latter after Pescennius had already been defeated, let us refer the appellations *Imperator* VI, VII, and VIII to the defeat of these peoples.

> **Note [Col. 0106D].** On the coins cited by Mediobarbus under the year 196, p. 270, the appellations *Imp.* VI and VII are combined with *Tr. Pot.* III and the names *Parth. Arab.*, *Parth. Adiab.*, and other indications of victory. Likewise, *Imp.* VIII, p. 271, is combined with the Parthian victory and *Tr. P.* IV; and it appears with the same designations and the titles *Arabicus* and *Adiabenicus* in an inscription in Muratori, *New Treasury of Ancient Inscriptions*, vol. I, p. 244.

Let us say that the title *Imperator* III was granted to Severus because of the battle of Cyzicus, IV because of the battle in the narrows of Nicaea and Cius, and finally V because Niger was overthrown at the Cilician Gates. Let us now determine with what number of the tribunician power the individual marks of the imperial title are combined; for once we know this, the year to which [Col. 0106D] each battle must be assigned will present itself of its own accord.

> **Note [Col. 0106D].** But perhaps someone will say that these coins were not struck at the time when Severus returned victorious from the battles with Niger, but only afterward, and that Spartianus himself, in the *Life of Severus*, chap. 9, indicates that Severus did not write to the Senate about the matter until after the second battle in the narrows of Cius and Nicaea. But apart from the fact that Spartianus differs somewhat in his account from the other and more important historians, and in that passage speaks only of the first and second battles, it can scarcely be denied—since the appellations *Imp.* III, IV, and V are combined with entirely different numbers of *Trib. Pot.*—that this designation of tribunician power indicates the years in which he three times won victory over the enemy.

Yet the appellation *Imp.* [Col. 0107A] III, which we have said was a token of the victory at Cyzicus, is found combined with *Trib. Pot.* II (in Laurentius Berger’s continuation of the *Brandenburg Treasury*, p. 690; Vaillant, *Coins of the Roman Emperors*, vol. I, pp. 221–22; and Mediobarbus under the year 194, p. 269). This tribunician year must be reckoned from June 2, A.D. 194, to the same day of the following year (compare note y of this section and Observation II of Schwarz’s dissertation cited above). It follows, therefore, that this first battle must be assigned either to the latter part of A.D. 194 or to the earlier part of A.D. 195.

Moreover, a coin in Vaillant presents Severus bearing the title *Imp.* IV and holding tribunician power III, and there are several coins of this kind in Mediobarbus. Therefore, the second battle in the narrows of Nicaea and Cius fell either in the latter part of A.D. 195 or the earlier part of the following year. [Col. 0107B] Consequently, the appellation *Imp.* V and the final victory won over Niger can scarcely, it seems, be claimed for any year other than the one we have stated, A.D. 196.

Since Severus had therefore overthrown Pescennius approximately at the beginning of that year, he proceeded into Mesopotamia and from there led his army against the Osroenians, Adiabenians, and Arabs (Dio, book LXXV, opening). All these events must have been accomplished in approximately six months—unless one prefers to suppose that the last part of the preceding year brought death to Niger—since chronological considerations themselves suggest that, as will appear in its proper place, Severus had already set out against Albinus before this year ended.

But how could it have happened that in so few months he subdued so many great and highly warlike peoples? This can, in fact, readily be conceived. Dio himself, chap. 2 of the book cited, says that the cities of these peoples were captured by three of Severus’s [Col. 0107C] generals, not by Severus himself. This perhaps occurred when Severus had already gone to meet Albinus; for after his departure Laetus opposed these adversaries, as appears from Dio himself, chap. 9. Or it may have happened somewhat earlier, while Severus was pursuing Niger, for at that time he accomplished a great many things through his generals. Alternatively, Severus may have been content with some limited suppression of the barbarians.

Certainly Severus appears not to have wished to subject these peoples entirely to himself, nor to have done so at that time, since, after sending his generals against the enemy, he was occupied with other matters at Nisibis, and only after Albinus had been defeated did he at last assail these provinces with the utmost force. This could be confirmed by Herodian’s silence, for he has nothing whatsoever about the defeat of these peoples at this time.

Let this first rule therefore be established: Severus did not [Col. 0107D] set out against Albinus before the end of A.D. 196.

> **Note [Col. 0107D].** Here we do not venture to infer anything further from the sequence of events which we have related, but shall do so later. From what has been said, however, one may judge Mosheim’s view τῷ μακαρὶτῇ (“of blessed memory”) (*Dissertation* cited above, § 21): that Niger perished in A.D. 194; that in A.D. 195 Severus sent envoys into Gaul to kill Albinus; and that near the end of that year their plot was detected, whereupon Severus came to Gaul with the greatest speed in A.D. 196. I could scarcely believe—for I have already stated what must be thought about the dates of the battles—that those envoys remained inactive for almost an entire year before delivering the letters to Albinus; or that, when the plot was finally detected near the end of A.D. 195, Severus, whom Mosheim correctly describes as resembling one running rather than one merely setting out, either passed almost the whole of the year 196 in idleness or allowed Albinus enough time to gather his forces. It is much closer to the truth to say that Severus set out against Albinus near the close of A.D. 196 and allowed little time to pass before he could contend with Albinus in war.

§ 9.—That Albinus Was Killed in A.D. 197 Is Proved, Secondly, from the Date of the Capture of Byzantium

[Col. 0108A]

The date at which Byzantium was captured must be regarded as another and by no means insignificant weapon for accomplishing this demonstration. Dio says, book LXXIV, chap. 14, p. 1254, that it was occupied by Severus’s soldiers while Severus was staying in Mesopotamia—that is, after he had defeated Niger and before he proceeded against Albinus. The same Dio records, in the book cited, chap. 11, p. 1252, that the Byzantines were finally reduced by famine to surrender after they had been under siege for three complete years.
