We shall therefore know the year in which Severus was in Mesopotamia once we determine when that siege began.

I think its beginning coincided [Col. 0108B] with the beginning of Severus’s own expedition against Pescennius in A.D. 193. This can be understood from the fact that it is scarcely credible that Severus, when going to meet Niger, would have left in his rear a very strongly fortified city which Niger’s own soldiers held and to which they would have withdrawn if events turned against them. This also agrees very well with the events themselves. Suppose, then, that Severus began the assault through his soldiers in approximately September A.D. 193—for he had left Rome when June was almost over (§ VIII, note y). If the actual capture took place after three complete years, it will indeed fall in September A.D. 196, at which time it appears from what was said above that Severus was in Mesopotamia.

Consequently, there is no need for us to depart from the natural force of the words Ἐπὶ ὅλον, τριετῆ χρόνον (“for a full period of three years”), as Mosheim ὁ μακαρίτης (“of blessed memory”) allowed himself to be induced to do by Tillemont, whose interpretation, unless I am mistaken, does not adequately satisfy the force of the words. Accordingly, since Severus was in Mesopotamia in approximately September, he could not have arrived in Gaul until A.D. 196 was already drawing toward its close.

Nor do we read anywhere that, after Severus had been in Mesopotamia, he set out against the Osroenians, Adiabenians, and Arabs; for, according to Dio, book LXXV, chap. 3, p. 1257, these peoples were subdued by Lateranus, Candidus, and Laetus, Severus’s generals, while Severus was resting at Nisibis, a city of Mesopotamia. It follows from this that news of Albinus’s revolt was brought to Severus in Mesopotamia. Indeed, it is not improbable that Severus, who was especially accustomed to act with speed in his counsels, immediately after Niger’s defeat sent men to lay a trap for Albinus under the pretext of delivering letters, and that this plot was suddenly detected. It is therefore all the more apparent that Severus went into Gaul approximately as the year 196 was ending.

> **Note [Col. 0108D].** Mosheim entered upon another line of argument in § 22. He says that the city of the Byzantines was captured in A.D. 196; but that, according to Herodian, book III, chap. 6, it had not yet been brought under the emperor’s power when he went to meet Albinus; therefore Severus set out against Albinus in the year 196. I do not deny that this argument would have greater force than mine if Herodian’s words did not conflict with what was reported by Cassius Dio, who says that Severus received news of the capture of Byzantium in Mesopotamia. Dio is deservedly to be heeded, and Herodian’s authority rejected, as the most distinguished H. S. Reimar has already excellently observed in his notes on Cassius Dio, p. 1252 § 70 and p. 1256 § 1.

§ 10.—It Is Proved, Thirdly, from the Year in Which Caracalla Received the Rank of Caesar by Decree of the Senate

[Col. 0109A]

But although these considerations do not yet provide a sure means of determining precisely the year fatal to Albinus—because it is not yet apparent how long that contest for supreme power lasted—the date on which the dignity of Caesar was conferred upon Caracalla will, I think, more fully remove our uncertainty; from it, it will follow that Albinus perished in A.D. 197 [Note: [Col. 0109D] To establish this point we have used Caracalla’s dignity as Caesar, whereas Mosheim preferred to employ the dignity of Augustus conferred upon Caracalla. But here it seemed better to depart from the position of that most distinguished man. For on p. 66 he says: “Caracalla was adorned with the dignity of Augustus in the year following the battle of Lugdunum. Therefore, since it is agreed that he received this dignity in A.D. 198, Albinus fell in A.D. 197.” I rather doubt whether the first premise of this argument is evident from all the writers available to us, unless it is regarded as identical with the other proposition concerning his assumption of the dignity of Augustus in A.D. 198, which agrees with all the monuments that record the event.]. For there are certain monuments of antiquity, such as Pagi cited in his *Critique of the Ecclesiastical Annals of Caesar Cardinal Baronius*, century II, at A.D. 197, no. 2, Paris ed., 1689, p. 88, and which Mosheim, following Gutherius, adduced in the cited dissertation, § XXIII, in which, during the consulship of Lateranus and Rufinus, Caracalla is called “Caesar Designate by decree of the Senate.” Yet although Caracalla had already been adorned with that title by his father [Col. 0109B] when Severus set out against Albinus (see Spartianus, *Severus*, ch. 10), we nowhere find that it was confirmed by the Senate before the victorious Severus returned to Rome after Albinus had been overthrown; for then we read that Severus ordered his son Bassianus, Caesar, to be called Antoninus (in Spartianus, loc. cit., ch. 14). But all the consular lists teach that Lateranus and Rufinus were consuls in A.D. 197. Let it therefore stand that Albinus lost both life and imperial power in that same year—indeed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, as Spartianus has it, loc. cit., ch. 11. Since this is so, what we promised to establish is clear: from this opportunity for harassing the Christians that arose among the populace after Albinus’s death, those earlier calamities of the Christians began in A.D. 197.

## § 11.—From a passage of Tertullian’s *To Scapula*, compared with another in Spartianus, it is shown that this earlier harassment of the Christians began in A.D. 197.

[Col. 0109C]

We come to the second argument by which we wished to determine the beginning of that disturbance raised by the populace: the passage already quoted above, § 6, from Tertullian’s *To Scapula*, in which Severus is said “not only not to have harmed very distinguished women and men of the Christian sect, but even to have honored them with his testimony, and to have resisted the populace when it raged against the Christians.” Since Severus did not do this at a time when he had already issued an edict against the Christian religion, [Col. 0109D] as we argued there, the event must be assigned to a year in which Severus had not yet become hostile through this law. [Col. 0110A] Nor does he seem to have wished to show favor in this manner to certain very distinguished persons of this household at the time when, after defeating Albinus, he carried war against the Parthians and other peoples of the East—a war from which he did not return until after he had promulgated this same edict against the Christians. For at that time he was so entangled in wars with so many very warlike nations that it can scarcely be believed that he gave thought to matters of this kind.

But Tertullian’s words are also such that it readily appears that Severus, while not harming these particular women and most distinguished men, nevertheless harmed others from whom he wished the Christians to be distinguished. And I do not see to what time the violence inflicted upon those others can be referred except that in which Spartianus reports (*Severus*, ch. 12) that innumerable supporters of Albinus were killed, among whom were many leading men [Col. 0110B] of the state and many illustrious women; for in this matter there is even a certain verbal similarity between these writers. Indeed, I scarcely doubt that Severus assumed, as it were, the protection of these Christians and honored them with testimony intended to show that they were not among Albinus’s friends, lest the populace, under the pretext of supporting the Emperor’s cause, persecute and drag to trial these adherents of the Christian religion, against whom nothing could be charged except that they were Christians. Let it therefore be accepted as true that immediately after Albinus’s death and before Severus’s expedition against the Parthians—that is, in A.D. 197—the populace violently attacked the Christians.

## § 12.—The same is further demonstrated from the date of Tertullian’s *Apology* and of the other books that preceded it.

[Col. 0110C]

Finally, this too is no slight argument for our position: it appears that Tertullian’s *Apology* cannot have been committed to writing except before those laws of Severus—a matter about which no one who has examined this little work thoughtfully can doubt. But from what we shall argue later, it will readily be understood that this defense of the ancient Christians is later than his books *To the Martyrs*, *On the Shows*, and *On Idolatry*. In turn, I hope to establish so firmly that this vindication of the Christian religion was written at the beginning of A.D. 199 that no one endowed with even moderate judgment in these matters can doubt it. [Col. 0110D] It will therefore become apparent that the books *On the Shows* and *On Idolatry* cannot be assigned to any year other than A.D. 198.

Tertullian, however, had exhorted the martyrs to steadfastness and harmony in a separate little work before he prepared himself to write those two books just mentioned. It is therefore necessary to say that the book *To the Martyrs* was published about A.D. 197. This single fact places our position concerning the year in which this earlier harassment of the Christians began beyond all doubt. For those to whom he offered the book had already been cast into chains because of the Christian religion, and these martyrs-designate are proof that the worshippers of the gods were then inflicting violence upon the Christians. But these remarks are merely incidental; we shall now say more about these books themselves.

## § 13.—The dates of books of this kind are determined, so that *To the Martyrs* was written in A.D. 197. Hoffmann’s conjectures are rejected.

[Col. 0111A]

The first among books of this kind, therefore, is that which Tertullian addressed to the martyrs. The very subject of the book demonstrates that hostilities against the Christians had already been undertaken, for it is dedicated to martyrs-designate (compare ch. 1). It remains only to determine whether they were cast into prison before or after Severus’s edict; and for several reasons the former view pleases me more.

First, because in ch. 2 he says that the Christians were enduring the judgments not of the Emperor but of the proconsul. I do not deny that Tertullian could have said this even if the governors had been employed [Col. 0111B] by an Emperor who was waging war against the Christians by means of laws, since the governors executed those laws in the provinces. Nevertheless, from this there first arises a not unreasonable suspicion that at this time the governors themselves, rather than the Augustus, were chiefly exercising this violence.

But if this type of argument seems capable of being disputed in either direction, the controversy is undoubtedly settled by what stands at the end of our little work, where he says: “For this purpose”—namely, suffering in the cause of God—“let even the present times serve us as lessons: how many persons, and of what rank, encounter ends unforeseen in view of their birth, dignities, physical condition, and age, for a man’s sake—either at his own hands, if they have acted against him, or at the hands of his adversaries, if they have stood for him.” [Col. 0111C] That this pertains to the time when Severus was making the Roman world secure from his rivals for the empire cannot possibly be doubted. For only those who have failed to understand the passages adduced above are unaware that, once Albinus had been removed, Severus most especially punished those who had stood on the side of Niger or Albinus.

From this it is no less possible to understand how Tertullian could say (ch. 2) that those martyrs-designate, to whom he wished to bring some relief by composing our little book, did not share in the nations’ festival days and were not buffeted by the shouting at the shows. For although I am not altogether unaware that games were also presented when Severus later returned from the Parthians and the other barbarians, nevertheless the very argument [Col. 0111D] which he draws, for raising the martyrs’ spirits, from the most distinguished men who had experienced the same fate leads us to understand the games as those which we know were presented because of the victory gained over Niger, and still more over Albinus.

Moreover, I do not hesitate to claim first place for our little book among those whose date is discerned by some definite reasoning. For Tertullian not only recalls the mutual violence of the contenders for the imperial power against the adherents of the opposing side—an event which cannot be said to have occurred except in the very year in which Albinus perished, that is, A.D. 197—but also mentions the calamities undergone by the Christians as though they had only now begun; whereas all the other books whose composition was occasioned by this disturbance of the times show that the Christians [Col. 0112A] had already been harried by many tortures and torments.

Nor do I now fear that some may number this little book among those Tertullian composed after he withdrew himself from communion with the orthodox Church. For the very date of the book does not permit this, if what we said elsewhere, § 3, is true: that Tertullian did not make war upon it before A.D. 200. On this matter we see Hoffmann disagreeing with us, as usual, but employing in confirmation of his opinion an argument from which the very contrary of what he intended appears more clearly (*cited dissertation*, § 10). He supposes, namely, that the martyrs to whom Tertullian’s discourse is directed were partly orthodox and partly Montanists, and that this caused dissension to arise among them, which Tertullian attempts to remove from their minds [Col. 0112B] at the beginning of the book.

“But to unite them,” says Hoffmann, “there was need of an exhorter who wished well to both parties, such as Tertullian the Montanist, who was often very bitter against the Catholics, yet did not hate them as he did heretics.” I hear him. But in order that both parties may lay aside their hostility, it certainly is not necessary that the man who seeks to reconcile peace should favor both parties to the dispute. Rather, it is necessary that those who disagree with one another should be in agreement with the person who reconciles peace. I shall speak more plainly.

It is established from some writer whose identity I do not know, whose words are preserved by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.16, p. 232, Reading’s Cambridge edition, that those devoted to the purer Church so despised the Montanists that, if by chance they were cast into prison with them, they always remained separate from the Montanists and refused their fellowship. [Col. 0112C] But the same cannot be said of the Montanists, since no trace whatever of such a thing exists; indeed, Tertullian himself, even in those books which he opposed to the teachings of the general Church, carefully distinguishes the “Psychics” from heretics and affirms that the Montanists and the orthodox were not at variance over any matter touching the rule of what Christians must believe.

Assume, therefore, that Tertullian had already separated himself from the decrees of the orthodox when he composed the book. Could he then have attempted with any good hope to restore peace among the divided prisoners? I hardly think so. For those among the prisoners who called themselves associates of the orthodox Church would generally have recoiled from following the precepts of a man whose sect they vehemently detested. Conversely, if Tertullian is said to have written these things as a member of the purer Church, that hatred certainly cannot be said to have prevented the Montanists also from receiving amicably the admonitions given to them. [Col. 0112D]

Indeed, I can scarcely persuade myself that Tertullian, in commending peace to the martyrs, would have used the argument in chapter 1 that, if they pursued peace with others, they might perhaps one day be able to confer peace upon others also; for everyone who has read his book *On Modesty* (ch. 22) knows how harshly he judged that custom of issuing letters of peace.

Finally, there is no reason to dwell long on the example of the contracted gladiator found in our little book, ch. 5, no less than in the first book *To the Nations*, ch. 18. Let it indeed be granted [Col. 0113A] that our book is later than that one: who will on that account pronounce our book suspect of Montanism, unless it has already been certainly established—which we shall later convict as false—that the books *To the Nations* were composed by Tertullian after he had entered into association with the Montanists? Besides, if Hoffmann thought himself entitled to say that our little book was later than those books, we have an equal right to consider those books later than ours; and all the more because it is certain that this one appeared at the beginning of the harassment, whereas those appeared, as it were, in the very heat of the disturbance.

## § 14.—The book *On the Shows* was composed in A.D. 198. The doubts of Tillemont, Hoffmann, and Dupin are resolved.

[Col. 0113B]

There is no doubt that Tertullian published the book *On the Shows* during the same period. Even if, in establishing this, we employed no argument other than the fact that he cited that book in chapter 13 of the work he wrote *On Idolatry*, it would be very easy to understand that the former was made public at the latest in A.D. 198, since Tertullian communicated the latter to the Christians in approximately the same year.

But his very purpose in composing this book—to overthrow the opinion that Christians were permitted to attend shows—teaches that shows were being presented especially at that time. The worshippers of the gods said that Christians, by despising them, were choosing what they regarded as an easy kind of death (*On the Shows*, ch. 1). I very much doubt whether these shows can be understood as any other than those which we read were presented not only at Rome but also throughout the provinces (compare ch. 7) because of Severus’s [Col. 0113C] return and his victory over Albinus; Spartianus records such shows for this period in *Severus*, ch. 14.

For if we see Tertullian recalling games (ch. 16) held on the birthdays and festivals of kings and on occasions of public prosperity, and saying that none of them were free from the worship of the gods, under whatever name and title they might be presented, we naturally suspect what we have said—being especially led to this by his statement (ch. 30) that the governors, persecutors of the Lord’s name, would one day melt in flames fiercer than those with which they themselves had raged against the Christians; and by his statement elsewhere (ch. 26) that lions were demanded daily against the Christians and persecutions were decreed. [Col. 0113D] Thus the governors were already harassing the worshippers of Christ, whose obstinacy in rejecting the pleasure of the shows was commonly made an accusation against them (ch. 1).

We said in § 7 that one of the reasons for violating the Christians was held to be their religious scruple against attending the games, and that this very savagery against them already existed in A.D. 197. For this reason, we doubt that anyone will judge the book *On the Shows* to have been written in any year other than that one or the next.

I am not unaware that many have held the opinion that in our little book Tertullian had in view rather the Secular Games, whose commemoration we know to have been celebrated on so many coins; and Tillemont himself, the most accurate interpreter of these matters if one sets aside chronological reasoning, inclined toward this view (*Mémoires pour servir à l’Histoire Ecclésiastique des six premiers siècles*, vol. III, Paris ed., 1701, quarto, p. 210). [Col. 0114A] But we are prevented from assenting to that opinion, first, by Tertullian’s statement that the governors were the authors of the Christians’ calamities; for he thus appears to depart from his customary caution and concern to remove from Christians every suspicion that they had neglected their duty toward the Emperor. Consequently, by this very caution employed everywhere else by Tertullian, but which we see absent here, we are brought to the conclusion that, when this little book was published, Severus had not yet become a participant in this crime against the Christians, although he certainly was such in A.D. 204, when those Secular Games were presented.

Second, the very opinion of those who dissent would entail that this book was written by Tertullian after he had gone over [Col. 0114B] to the Montanist party. This is far otherwise, as will shortly appear, and is rejected by the very men who think differently.

Nor is it proper to refer this book to any time other than approximately the beginning of the year 198. For it is scarcely credible that Severus returned to Rome before May of the preceding year, since after the battle of Lugdunum (§ 10) many matters still remained to be settled by him (see Herodian’s *History*, book III, ch. 8, Boecler’s ed.). Hence it follows that even the little book *To the Martyrs*, which precedes ours, can be said to have been written only toward the end of that year. If we add to this what we shall demonstrate in its proper place—that *On Idolatry* is later than *On the Shows* and was composed in the same year—our opinion concerning the date of *On the Shows* will necessarily follow.

This same date of the book sufficiently demonstrates that [Col. 0114C] it cannot be numbered among those which Tertullian composed as an adherent of the Montanist sect; for we argued above that he joined it in A.D. 200, and the book itself bears no mark of a mind imbued with Montanist errors.

“But this little book is nevertheless later than *On the Crown*, which no one denies bears signs of Montanism.” Thus, approximately, Hoffmann in the cited dissertation, § 7. If one asks him the reason for this, he answers that our book appeared “when the peace of the Church had been destroyed, not indeed by Severus’s edicts, but by the cries of the populace and the authority of the governors.” But I hold that, when Tertullian was led by precisely this argument to apply his mind to writing *On the Shows*, he was plainly still a member of the orthodox community. [Col. 0114D]

For I see the entire force of the contrary argument to consist in the fact that, in chapter 1 of *On the Crown*, Tertullian says that the Christians had still enjoyed a good and lengthy peace. What must be answered to this will find a more convenient place later. But the claim that *On the Shows* was written after *On the Crown* is contrary to the truth. For on this point we have the wholly contrary testimony of Tertullian himself, who says in chapter 6 of the little book *On the Crown*: “We have dealt with this subject, because of our pleasure-loving brethren, in a Greek work also.” We are speaking, however, of the shows, which he regards as derived from the teaching of the devil. This very passage had already moved Allix to decide that our book *On the Shows* was earlier than the other work. Hoffmann attempts to break the force of this argument by declaring that Tertullian is speaking of a Greek little book, [Col. 0115A] and denies, for reasons he has adduced, that the same conclusion should be drawn concerning the Latin work.

I do not deny that Tertullian was speaking of a book which he had formerly composed in Greek concerning the shows; but neither can it be obscure that before that Greek work he had also discussed the same subject in Latin. For surely the man who admits that he had spoken about the shows “in Greek also” must be understood to have meant that he had previously treated that subject in another language as well. As for Hoffmann’s arguments to the contrary, I have already indicated that I shall discuss them later.

Nor should Dupin be heard, who thinks that this book, together with *On Idolatry*, was written about A.D. 202 or 203 by Tertullian when he was already inclining toward the errors of the Montanists (*dans la nouvelle* [Col. 0115B] *Bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, Paris ed., 1693, quarto, vol. I, pp. 91 and 108, note 1). I suspect that in this matter he was misled by the birthday of Geta Caesar, which I recall is mentioned in the *Acts of Perpetua and Felicity*, who are believed to have suffered death in that year. He thinks that this birthday was indicated by Tertullian in *On Idolatry*; but there is no trace of such a thing, at least in the passage he cited. And even if there were, the question would then arise whether Tertullian meant the anniversary of Geta Caesar’s accession or of his birth. Let it therefore remain established that *On the Shows* was published approximately at the beginning of A.D. 198.

## § 15.—The book *On Idolatry* is assigned to the same year. The conjectures of Tillemont and Hoffmann are dispelled.

[Col. 0115C]

The little book *On Idolatry* follows this one. When Tertullian wrote it, the Romans were plainly occupied in displaying the greatest joy at the happy condition of those times, and for that reason had adorned their very doorways with laurels and many lamps (compare ch. 15). That this was done in honor of the Emperor is demonstrated by the entire discussion which Tertullian adds concerning this question: whether the loyalty owed to the Emperor requires Christians to join the worshippers of the gods in various displays of rejoicing, in order to declare their joy at Caesar’s well-being.

If anyone asks to what period these things refer, I have no hesitation in saying: to the various signs of rejoicing with which the Romans applauded Severus, as it were, when he returned from the war against his rivals for the imperial power. For three times [Col. 0115D] we read in the ancient writers that something of this kind occurred under Severus’s rule: first, in A.D. 193, when Severus entered Rome to assume the imperial power after Julianus had been killed (Dio in Xiphilinus, book LXXIV, ch. 2, p. 1242 C); afterward, when he returned victorious from Gaul after Albinus had been overthrown (Herodian, book III, ch. 8; Spartianus, *Severus*, ch. 12); finally, at the decennial celebration of his reign, when he returned from the East (Dio, book LXXVI, ch. 1, p. 1272; and Herodian, book III, ch. 10). Every instance of this kind can be confirmed by many coins.

The first of these cannot have been meant by Tertullian. For, to say nothing of the fact that, while there was still a rival for the empire whom very many preferred, as Niger was after Julianus’s death, it could scarcely have been alleged against the Christians [Col. 0116A] that their failure to display loyalty toward the new Caesar was impious—as nevertheless appears from Tertullian’s entire discourse—Tertullian certainly refers to his book *On the Shows*, which we have said was not written until A.D. 198. Nor should anyone hesitate because he speaks not of the Greek book on this subject but of the Latin one. Since he wrote our little book in Latin, I do not doubt that, had he wished to indicate the Greek book *On the Shows*, he would have identified it by adding some qualifying word; and we have already said that one may argue without error from the Greek work to the Latin one as already written.

Nor does the final opinion seem admissible, which seeks to refer that public rejoicing to Severus’s decennial celebration. I do not now wish to discuss the fact that the very ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxy) of this book, which we shall later vindicate for it, conflicts with this opinion; [Col. 0116B] yet there is some room for suspecting that public offices were still being conferred upon Christians at that time. For I doubt whether Tertullian would have discussed the question of how far such an office ought to proceed in adopting some religious custom that came at least somewhat close to the worship of the gods, if Christians were not then being admitted to magistracies. Yet I do not deny that I am somewhat doubtful whether public offices continued to be shared with Christians after Severus had issued his edict forbidding the adoption of the Christian religion.

There remains, therefore, the second type of celebration we mentioned, which clearly occurred after Severus’s return from Gaul. A new argument for this view, and certainly not a negligible one, may be drawn from [Col. 0116C] Tertullian’s recollection that, at the time when he wrote this book, astrologers had very recently been banned from the City and Italy, ch. 9. When this happened can be learned from Spartianus no less than from Tertullian himself.

First, let us hear our author, *Apology*, ch. 35: “But even those who are now daily revealed as associates or supporters of criminal factions . . . with what very recent laurels did they cover their doorposts? With what lofty and brilliant lamps did they cloud their vestibules? . . . Not in order to celebrate public joys, but to proclaim their own wishes within another’s festival . . . changing the prince’s name in their hearts. The same duties are discharged by those who consult astrologers, haruspices, augurs, and magicians concerning the lives of the Caesars.”

But in this passage of the *Apology* [Col. 0116D] Tertullian says that these signs of public joy had formerly been displayed by criminals, whereas in our book he indicates very plainly that they were being displayed at that very moment. The little book *On Idolatry* was therefore written before the *Apology*, and consequently before the beginning of A.D. 199, as will appear later.

It seems to me not unreasonable to suspect that astrologers were expelled from Rome and Italy when many people had consulted them concerning Caesar’s safety. Those who had inquired of magicians about such a matter were being condemned to death at approximately the time when Severus set out against the Parthians, that is, in A.D. 198. This is understood from a passage of Spartianus’s *Life of Severus*, ch. 15, which, because it has not been sufficiently examined by others, I append here:

“After Severus had undertaken the Parthian war, he transported his army from Brundisium and, continuing his journey, came into Syria and drove back the Parthians. [Col. 0117A] But afterward he returned to Syria, so that he might prepare himself and carry war against the Parthians. Meanwhile, at Plautianus’s instigation, he persecuted the surviving remnants of Pescennius’s party.—He also put many to death on the charge that they had consulted Chaldaeans or soothsayers concerning his safety, especially anyone whom he suspected and considered capable of ruling.”

If we compare this passage with the one we have just quoted from Tertullian, it appears that each writer, when speaking of the search for the remaining supporters of Severus’s adversaries, also defines the very time when these things occurred. This is otherwise in the account of the second matter, concerning the astrologers who had been summoned for consultation. But just as the former gives us a sure means of discovering the true date of the *Apology*, so the latter teaches us that those who had questioned magicians concerning Caesar’s safety were put to death at approximately the same time. From this, at least, [Col. 0117B] what we wished to establish is understood: in our book Tertullian was speaking of the second type of celebration under Severus.

Although, if we wished to investigate this matter more subtly and apply the principle by which experience has taught us to judge the order generally observed by Spartianus in narrating events—a principle which it would take too long to explain more fully here—we could determine that the punishments of those who employed magicians to learn the fortunes of Severus’s reign need not be regarded as later than the punishments imposed upon Niger’s surviving friends. Accordingly, since the latter occurred in A.D. 198, as we shall say in its proper place, the former may not unreasonably be assigned to the preceding year.

Since this is so, it is clear that the book *On Idolatry* belongs to A.D. 198. Here I do not think it necessary to answer [Col. 0117C] Tillemont’s contention that this book was written by Tertullian after he had himself become the founder of some new sect. This is maintained without any reason whatever and was refuted by Hoffmann in the cited dissertation, § 8, p. 31. Hoffmann agrees with us approximately concerning the arguments from which the book’s date must be elicited, yet nevertheless considers it to have been written by Tertullian as a Montanist. That opinion cannot stand if what we demonstrated above is true: that he did not attach himself to the discipline of Montanus until A.D. 200.

Nor did Hoffmann properly employ in support of that view Tertullian’s own passage (*On Idolatry*, ch. 22): “Many say that no one ought to disclose himself.” He thinks Tertullian meant to indicate that a question had already arisen between Montanists and orthodox Christians [Col. 0117D] concerning flight in persecution. Yet the very sequence of the discourse teaches that he is speaking about every form of denial of the faith, not solely about flight; and from the most ancient history of the early Christians—for example, from the cases of Ignatius and Polycarp—it appears that differing opinions on this matter existed even among Christians of the purer doctrine themselves.

But to claim that this controversy between the orthodox and the Montanists arose from the action of the soldier who refused the laurel crown, and consequently that this book was written after *On the Crown*, is conjecture, not proof. Such a mode of argument ought to be kept entirely apart from all scholarly discussion.

## § 16.—The *Apology* is demonstrated to have been composed in A.D. 199.

Next comes the most elegant *Apologeticus*, which I venture to call the most outstanding of Tertullian’s books [Col. 0118A] both in learning and in candor. Although its date has been discussed at length by everyone—even by those who did not address his other books—and especially by Mosheim, that most accomplished man, to whom first place in this field is owed, it is nevertheless permissible, after that harvest, to gather a few ears of grain and, passing over what he has said with the greatest learning, to set forth as briefly as we can, ascending as it were step by step, what we have to say on this subject.

First, then, it cannot be obscure to anyone who has treated this book with any care that at that time Severus’ law against the Christians had not yet been issued. For who could believe that, by presenting this book to the provincial governors, Tertullian could have expected them not only to mitigate the anger conceived against the Christians, [Col. 0118B] but to put it aside altogether and release them as innocent, if the governors had been obliged to act according to Severus’ laws, from which they were not permitted to deviate even a finger’s breadth—especially since it was well known how harshly he had formerly dealt with those whom he learned had not properly discharged their judicial office (see Spartianus, *Severus*, ch. 8)?

Nor should anyone find it surprising that, if the governors together with the common people alone were inflicting injuries upon the Christians, Tertullian did not appeal to Caesar himself, and that the Christians did not take refuge under his protection. For if, at the instigation of Plautianus, the Christians endured every kind of calamity on the occasion of the punishment of those implicated by friendship with Niger and Albinus, such an appeal to Caesar would have had no prospect of success because of the supreme authority of Plautianus, prefect of the Praetorian Guard; [Col. 0118C] nor would it have done so even if made to Plautianus himself, a man of utterly unrestrained power and cruelty. Besides, even if Plautianus was by no means the author of so great an outrage against the Christians, how, I ask, could assistance against the assaults of the frenzied populace have been obtained from Severus, who had an insatiable appetite both for gold and for the slaughter of innocent men and of those suspected of sedition? There was rather every reason to fear that, although he had not yet undertaken public hostilities against the Christians, once alerted by their petitions he would go so far as actually to increase their sufferings by using his authority to confirm the governors’ fury.

This point being established, it must certainly be said that the occasion for writing the *Apologeticus* was a disturbance against the Christians stirred up by the populace. The force of certain passages of Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0118D] *Apol.*, ch. 37: “How often does the hostile mob invade us on its own authority with stones and fires? In the very frenzy of the Bacchanals they do not spare even dead Christians, but tear them from the repose of burial, cut them apart, and rend them limb from limb.” And ch. 35: “No one clamors more loudly for the punishment of Christians than the mob. Clearly the other orders, in keeping with their authority, are religiously observant in good faith: nothing hostile breathes from the senate itself, from the equestrian order, from the camps, or from the palaces themselves.”] is so manifest that it is plainly absurd to seek anything else there than this very circumstance. Hence Tertullian cannot be said to have delivered this defense of the Christians to the governors before the year 197 had fully run its course, because we have assigned the origins of these disturbances to that year by suitable arguments.

Accordingly, there is no need to use the passage (*Apologeticus*, ch. 35) [Col. 0119A] in which Tertullian included Cassius, Niger, and Albinus among the enemies of the empire in order to establish that the *Apologeticus* was later than the death of Albinus. Nevertheless, that very passage contains certain not particularly obscure traces by following which we can determine more precisely the date that we assign to the *Apologeticus*. We shall now say nothing of distributions of money given by the emperor to the people, nothing of the solemn day of the prince celebrated with every apparatus of luxury, nothing of vows undertaken for the emperor’s safety; for these considerations are either insufficiently suited to settling the matter, or have already been discussed most elegantly by Mosheim.

Let us examine a single passage, namely the one already brought forward above (§ 15), both because it settles the matter most clearly and because it moves us to depart slightly [Col. 0119B] from the opinion of that most learned man. Tertullian says, then, that associates in or applauders of criminal factions—surviving gleanings after the harvest of the parricides—were being revealed daily; he also says that certain astrologers, augurs, and magicians had taken counsel concerning the life of the Caesars. Spartianus coupled these same matters together, and the resemblance between the cited passages of the two authors led me to say that both had precisely the same period in view. But since neither does Tertullian expressly place the consultation of the magicians in the very same period as the search for the remaining friends of Niger, nor does Spartianus, where he does not explicitly define the time, follow the order of events with perfect exactness, we now set aside what is said in both authors about consulting magicians.

Let us instead follow the other indication of the time when the *Apologeticus* was written, namely [Col. 0119C] Plautianus’ zeal in dragging forth all those whom he declared suspect of hostility toward Severus. Spartianus says that Plautianus persecuted them during the period when Severus had attacked the Parthians and had returned to Syria to prepare himself to wage war against them with greater force. It is indeed credible that Severus set out against the Parthians approximately after the middle of 198 [Note: [Col. 0119D] The emperor’s departure is associated by Mediobarbus, under A.D. 199, p. 172, and by Vaillant, *Numismata Imperatorum*, vol. I, p. 113, with the sixth tribunician power, which ended in the middle of 199. But another coin in the former author, p. 273, has Severus’ sixth tribunician power together with the surname *Par. Ar. Ad.* and other emblems of victory.]; after checking their attacks to some extent, he returned to Syria, perhaps to pass the winter there. While he was preparing there what seemed necessary for prosecuting the war against the Parthians, Plautianus tracked down those whom he knew to survive among Niger’s friends; this therefore occurred approximately at the beginning of 199.

Consequently, I have no doubt that Mosheim’s opinion that this book was written in the middle of 198 [Col. 0119D] must be abandoned on this point, because it was only then that Severus set out against the Parthians, while Tertullian speaks not of the eliminated friends of Albinus but of Niger’s friends, who were still surviving after the Albinian affair. Yet this search for Severus’ enemies does not appear to have occurred later than the time we have stated; for that would conflict with the fact that Tertullian had already joined the Montanist party in 200, and that before this secession from the Church he wrote the books *Ad Nationes* and *De Testimonio Animae*, [Col. 0120A] which do not give even the slightest grounds for suspicion of Montanism and are earlier than the *Apologeticus*. This is beyond doubt regarding the book *On the Testimony of the Soul*, and highly probable regarding the books *To the Nations*.

Nor do I think anyone will now suppose that Tertullian was already a Montanist when he composed the *Apologeticus*. For unless they prefer, with the distinguished Havercamp (preface to his edition of Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*), to invent the claim that Tertullian issued this *Apology* twice, slightly altered, they must yield to our arguments by which we have proved it earlier than Severus’ edict. I do not approve Havercamp’s opinion, since certain variant readings in the text of this book do not sufficiently establish the point. From Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, ch. 2, I indeed know that Tertullian’s *Apology* [Col. 0120B] was written in Latin and afterwards translated into Greek; but that it was issued twice, and altered at that, I do not know at all.

If, therefore, they concede that the *Apologeticus* predates Severus’ edict, then surely, if they can, they must contest our position with surer arguments than those with which Hoffmann attacked the opinion demonstrated by Mosheim—arguments which Mosheim excellently showed to possess no solidity in the Addenda to vol. I of his *Dissertations on Ecclesiastical History*, pp. 741–48. We ourselves shall answer Hoffmann’s other argument in its proper place; of the remaining one, however, we point out that it conflicts with Hoffmann’s own position, for I am pleased to add these observations to Mosheim’s reply. For even if what Hoffmann says about Severus’ restoration of the cult of Serapis at Rome is true—that it occurred only [Col. 0120C] when he had toured Egypt after defeating the Parthians, that is, in 202—then what he had previously determined, namely that the *Apologeticus* was written before Severus’ edict, collapses; for Severus did not return to Rome before 203, and yet no one at all can call into question that the edict against the Christians was promulgated in 202.

## § 17.—The Two Books *To the Nations* Written in the Year 199

Tertullian relates in his *Apologeticus* (ch. 16) that very recently a certain man had put on display an image clothed in a toga, furnished with ass’s ears, and having one hoofed foot, with the added inscription, “The Christians’ God, *onochoetes*.” He reports [Col. 0120D] in the first book *To the Nations*, ch. 14, that the same thing had happened not long before. This may serve as evidence that both books *To the Nations* were published at approximately the same time as the *Apologeticus*, and, as I think, in such a way that they appeared after it. I say both; for the words with which he begins the second book at once show that it followed the first after the *Apologeticus*. This is so, first, because “very recently” appears to designate a shorter interval of time than “not long before”; and secondly, because it is more likely that Tertullian first addressed the governors, whose authority was greater and whose disposition was more tractable, than the people.

Besides these, there are not a few indications from which it may be understood that their date was much earlier than Severus’ edict. I refrain from enumerating them now, but nevertheless employ two [Col. 0121A] arguments for this purpose. One is that these books were intended primarily for the people; the other, that they indicate the victory over Niger and Albinus as having been won not very long before. Nowhere does he address the governors, as he did in the *Apologeticus*, but solely the people, from whom I recall that Tertullian somewhere even expressly distinguished the governors (e.g., book I, ch. 3). Next, he says that those to whom he dedicated these books had accused the Christians (book I, ch. 20); while I see that this may indeed fit the governors, it refers far more naturally to the common people. Finally, it is evident that the designation “Nations,” which stands in the title of these books, was applied by Tertullian to those devoted to the worship of the gods; but here it doubtless designates, properly speaking, the superstitious populace, because he had already placed before the governors for their consideration in the *Apologeticus* almost the same matters [Col. 0121B] as were discussed in these two treatises.

But he introduces mention of the recent slaughter of Niger and Albinus in such a way as to say that Syria breathes with the odors of corpses and that the Gallic provinces have not yet washed themselves clean in their Rhône. What else can this mean than that Severus’ war with Niger and Albinus had scarcely been brought to an end? All these considerations clearly show that the books *To the Nations* were published not after Severus’ edict but before it, and can teach everyone that we have not without reason assigned these books as companions to Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, since for this very reason they must have been written when half of 199 had already elapsed. From this it appears at the same time that their author had not yet gone over [Col. 0121C] to the Montanist position, since that happened only in 200, nor is anything found in these books that can raise any appreciable suspicion of Montanism.

Yet this one point in Hoffmann’s arguments seems to me worthy of notice. Relying on the same similarity of subject matter that exists between the *Apologeticus* and these books, he incorrectly pronounces in the opposite direction. For his opinion—that the books *To the Nations*, together with the treatise *On the Testimony of the Soul*, differ from the *Apologeticus* only in length and set forth somewhat more fully the same defense which Tertullian had compressed, as it were, into a fist in the *Apologeticus*—is neither altogether correct nor sufficiently adapted to proving the point. Nothing need be said about the conclusion of the argument itself, for this has been sufficiently discussed [Col. 0121D] by us, and will still be discussed in several places. And although in the *Apologeticus* Tertullian presents matters generally similar to those set forth in the books *To the Nations*, there are nevertheless many things in the former that do not occur at all in the latter, and conversely things in the latter that are sought in vain in the *Apologeticus*. Anyone wishing to perceive this more fully is referred to the whole of the second book, which is occupied with refuting the gods of the Gentiles; there, if one leaves aside the final sections of the book, one will find nothing that is treated in the *Apologeticus*.

## § 18.—The Book *On the Testimony of the Soul* Assigned to the Same Year

I hold the same opinion concerning the treatise that Tertullian composed *On the Testimony of the Soul*. I certainly do not deny that it is contemporary with the books *To the Nations*. [Col. 0122A] But I doubt whether Hoffmann is right to say, at the place cited, p. 34, that it is, as it were, the second part of a commentary that Tertullian issued on the *Apologeticus*, the books *To the Nations* having constituted the first. For the words of *Apologeticus*, ch. 17, “Do you wish us to prove it from the testimony of the soul itself?” which gave Hoffmann occasion to think so, do not seem to me framed in such a way that they can bring all readers to acknowledge the truth of this opinion, since in that same passage Tertullian also says that he can demonstrate the one God from his works; yet I do not recall him ever discussing that subject systematically, at least in a book of the kind written at the same time as the apologetic works.

That this book is contemporary with the *Apologeticus* is taught more securely by the words Tertullian uses in section five, p. 81: “The divine Scriptures, which are in our possession or that of the Jews, by far precede secular literature, not merely by some modest span of time, as we demonstrated in its proper place.” [Col. 0122B] But where did he demonstrate this, if not in the *Apologeticus*, ch. 18 ff.? Since he composed that work at the beginning of 199, but the books *To the Nations* somewhat later, he must be judged to have published our treatise when that year was nearly complete. Nor is this inconsistent with the task that Tertullian undertook to accomplish in the treatise: that the rivals and persecutors of the Christians should be convinced of the truth, and convicted of error in themselves and of injustice toward the Christians (ch. 1).

But I do not think this book should be assigned to another year, and one later than that which we have stated. For besides the fact that no indication of Montanism appears in this book, one might not inaptly say that it was added as a kind of appendix to the *Apologeticus* and the books *To the Nations*, because Christian doctrine is discussed in it somewhat more fully. Nor did Tertullian compose any book of this kind against the absurd worship of the gods [Col. 0122C] that could be assigned to another time than this, when the very violence against the Christians demanded a demonstration of the supreme injustice conspicuous in propagating superstition by sword and flame.

# ARTICLE III

## On the Books of Tertullian Whose Date and Montanism Are Established

### § 1.—The Book *On the Crown* Shown to Have Been Composed in the Year 201

In the preceding part of the discussion, we believe that enough has been set forth concerning those books whose date and purity of doctrine seemed capable of being established with a certain degree of certainty. [Col. 0122D] There now follows a second topic, which will treat those books whose date is no less established than the fact that they were published by Tertullian after he had abandoned his former discipline and gone over to that of Montanus. Among these the first place is occupied by the book *On the Crown*. It seems worthwhile to investigate its date somewhat more fully, all the more because this is, as it were, a παράπηγμα—that is, a fixed chronological benchmark, the standard against which all the other books must be measured if it comes into dispute whether they were written before Tertullian’s defection or not.

Since we see learned men disagreeing among themselves in various opinions on this matter, by which they have hindered rather than facilitated the discovery of the truth, we shall state candidly what seems probable to us, and shall employ the first section of the book alone, from which both the writer’s actual doctrine and the time [Col. 0123A] when he brought this book before the public can be elicited. Anyone may recognize the former from that entire discussion concerning the avoidance of things that might arouse even the slightest suspicion of worshiping fictitious gods. There one will hear Tertullian speaking, not calmly, modestly, and yielding, but austerely and vehemently, inflamed with extraordinary anger against those who thought otherwise, as generally happens with those who, having only recently advanced into some discipline, imagine themselves to possess exceptional wisdom.

For when he says that the pastors of the other sect are lions in peace and stags in battle, and that they have rejected the prophecies of the Holy Spirit, it plainly appears that a disciple of Montanus is speaking here, not a member of the common Church. For by these words he both declares himself to belong to a different flock from those whose teachers he attacks, and clearly indicates what had provoked his mind against [Col. 0123B] them: namely, that they had not joined him in following the same decrees of the Montanists’ Paraclete.

He begins this same section of the book with words that are like a fountain from which all knowledge of its date must be drawn. Thus he writes:

> Very recently there took place a largess of the most excellent emperors; in the camp the soldiers were receiving their gratuities crowned with laurel. One man there, more truly a soldier of God—alone with his head uncovered, the crown held idly in his hand.—The murmuring is reported to the tribune. The tribune at once asks, “Why are you so different in your dress?” He denied that it was lawful for him to do as the others did. When pressed for his reasons, he replied, “I am a Christian.”

When the other Christians condemned this soldier’s deed, thinking that so good and long-lasting a peace was thereby endangered, Tertullian strove against them, extolling it with the highest praise. [Col. 0123C] In this passage we first see him commemorate a largess of the emperors made very recently, and I doubt whether anyone would say that these were any other than Severus and Caracalla, both Augusti. Now above we said that Caracalla was adorned with the rank of Augustus when Severus was preparing his eastern expedition against the Parthians, on which he departed approximately after half of the year 198 had passed; and later we shall show that the peace which some believed was here being put at risk was the peace enjoyed by the Christians before they were publicly harassed by Severus’ law, which all agree was issued in 202. This book, therefore, must have been written in the interval that elapsed from Severus’ sixth to his ninth [Col. 0123D] year.

Within this period I have observed three years marked by imperial largess: the first, shortly before Severus set out for the East in 198 [Note: [Col. 0123D] Spartianus, *Severus*, ch. 14: “He set out for the Parthian war after presenting a gladiatorial show and giving a distribution of money to the people.”]; the second, the year 201, when, because the soldiers had proclaimed Caracalla Augustus and Geta Caesar, he handed Ctesiphon over to them for plunder [Note: [Col. 0123D] The same author, ch. 16: “On account of these titles he gave the soldiers a most lavish donative, granting them all the booty of the Parthian city, which the soldiers demanded.”]; the third, 202, when Severus and Caracalla were planning their journey to Egypt [Note: [Col. 0123D] The same author, ibid.: “After this—when he had designated his elder son consul with himself—he gave the soldiers an increased stipend and proceeded to Alexandria.”].

[Col. 0124A] I maintain that the first of these years cannot be intended here. For it may be debated whether the gladiatorial show and distribution recorded by Spartianus are the same as those which Herodian reports (*Book III*, ch. 8, ed. Boecler, p. 145) were given by Severus to the people when he returned to Rome after defeating Albinus. Nor should it be objected that Spartianus elsewhere (*Severus*, ch. 12) commemorated the same thing that Severus provided immediately after his return. For, not to mention that Spartianus often repeats the same things as though they were different, in that passage he does not speak of a donative granted to the soldiers, but of Severus’ giving the soldiers an amount of pay greater than that given by any prince. If, therefore, each author had the same distribution in view, it is certainly understood that Tertullian did not mean that distribution, since only in 198 was the rank of Augustus conferred upon Caracalla by the Senate.

But even if it is granted that Herodian means one distribution and Spartianus another, the event cited from this first passage cannot be referred to Tertullian’s passage, because Spartianus speaks only of a distribution given to the people and of spectacles presented, whereas Tertullian speaks of an entirely different benefit granted to the soldiers in camp. [Col. 0124B] Nor should the last interpretation be admitted, namely that this largess took place in Syria in 202, after the war in the East had ended and both Augusti had entered upon the consulship. For Aelius Spartianus, the only writer who mentions that event, says that the soldiers were given an increased stipend, and I doubt whether this can be called a donative of the sort Tertullian appears to indicate. [Col. 0124C]

But even if there are those who prefer to understand a donative in this passage of Spartianus, I hope that they will not entirely scorn my opinion that the largess described by Tertullian refers to the one concerning which I said Spartianus spoke when he related the events that occurred after the capture of Ctesiphon. When we examine the circumstances in this way, we observe not only that all the details accord well, if a comparison is made, but also that one passage can be excellently explained by the other. First, no one can fail to see that at this time there were two Augusti; for Caracalla had already been made Augustus before the Parthian expedition in 198, and was now also declared a partner in the empire by the soldiers. Next, Spartianus commemorates a donative given to the soldiers, [Col. 0124D] which explains the emperors’ largess in the camp. Finally, at the beginning of this year 201 Severus had not yet promulgated a law barring everyone from the Christian religion, whose community will soon appear to have been disturbed by it.

But since the claim that this donative was distributed to the soldiers at the beginning of 201 admits of some doubt, we shall briefly explain how the reckoning should be made. To begin, we ask that it be observed that, as we argued elsewhere (above, § 16, col. 119, note), Severus set out for the East after the first part of 198 had elapsed. He brought this war undertaken against the Parthians approximately to an end with the capture of Ctesiphon. For although Dio Cassius reports that only afterwards did Severus twice attack Hatra in vain, Severus does not appear—if Dio is correct—to have spent much time on this, [Col. 0125A] since the second and most violent assault upon that city was completed in twenty days (Dio, book LXXV, ch. 13, p. 1265), and Severus’ journey into Palestine and Egypt immediately followed it.

However this may be understood, Spartianus confirms in *Severus*, ch. 16, that Ctesiphon was captured near the winter season. This cannot be said to have happened in 198. For even if we say that Severus left Rome immediately after Caracalla assumed the rank of Augustus, how, I ask, could he in so short a time complete so long a journey to what were almost the remotest regions, equip a fleet, traverse Armenia, capture Seleucia and Babylon, and devastate Arabia? Nor is it any more credible that this occurred in the following year. For after the capture of Ctesiphon and the two sieges of Hatra, [Col. 0125B] Severus came to Syria, where he afterwards assumed the consular fasces. But all who have consulted the consular lists know that he held them with his son in 202. It would therefore have to be said that for nearly two or three years Severus did nothing to prosecute the war against his remaining enemies, which is wholly implausible.

It remains, therefore, to say that Ctesiphon was captured by Severus approximately as the year 200 was drawing to its close. Since its capture was immediately followed by the conferral of the rank of Augustus upon Caracalla by the soldiers and by the granting of a donative to them for that reason, this certainly occurred at no other time than the end of 200 or the beginning of the following year. This conclusion is excellently confirmed by those monuments of antiquity that have preserved for us the memory of both events. For, to begin with the Parthian victory, not only Eusebius—whose judgment some may perhaps refuse to accept—assigns this victory over the Parthians, Adiabenians, and Arabs to the year 200 (*Chronicle*, book II, at this year, Scaliger’s edition, p. 172); [Col. 0125C] but the consular lists as well (in Pamelius, *Life of Tertullian*, p. 18.II) and coins (in Mediobarbus, under A.D. 201, p. 274) attribute the surname *Parthicus Maximus* to Severus while he held the tribunician power for the eighth time, which everyone knows extended from the middle of 200 to the middle of the following year.

Next, that the rank of Augustus was conferred by the soldiers upon Caracalla, and that of Caesar upon Geta, in 201 may in some measure be understood from Spartianus, who says that this occurred when Caracalla was in his thirteenth year (loc. cit., ch. 16); and he undoubtedly was of that age in that year, as appears from what we have argued elsewhere concerning his birthday [Col. 0125D] (§ 6). If perhaps Spartianus’ authority seems worthy of rejection because he is not sufficiently consistent with himself in determining Caracalla’s age, this scruple is certainly removed by a most elegant coin from the treasury formerly at Schwarzburg and now at Gotha, which cannot be doubted to have been intended to preserve the memory of this event.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] Polycarp Tentzel communicated it to the learned world in a dissertation held under the presidency of Johann Andreas Schmidt, in which he explains selected gold, silver, and large-module bronze coins from the Amstadt-Schwarzburg treasury, pp. 22 ff. Scaliger, in his *Annotations on Eusebius*, p. 228, has another inscription in which the names of those three are joined with the ninth year of Severus’ tribunician power and the fourth year of Caracalla’s.]

One side presents the head of Severus encircled with laurel, with the added inscription: “Severus Aug. Part. Max. P. M. Tr. P. IX.” [Col. 0126A] The other presents the bare head of Geta and the laureate head of Caracalla, indicating that the latter was Augustus and the former Caesar, with the legend: “Aeternit. Imperi.” For the coin not only confirms what Spartianus reported concerning the time when they assumed these ranks, but also supports what we said before, that this event occurred in the year 201, since Severus assumed his ninth tribunician power in that year.

But let us return to the book *On the Crown*. We say that the passage examined above can be understood best if the opinion that we believe ourselves to have sufficiently proved is admitted. For it makes it particularly intelligible why the soldiers marched crowned with laurel—a circumstance that should surprise no one who knows that soldiers likewise wore crowns in triumphs, and something of that kind can readily be discerned here. For by now almost all those against whom Severus had led his army had been subdued, especially the most warlike nation of the Parthians; [Col. 0126B] and Severus himself, since an ailment of the joints prevented him from celebrating a triumph over the Parthians, nevertheless assigned his son a triumph to celebrate over the Jews, and perhaps, to compensate for the Parthian triumph, granted the soldiers the insignia of triumphants.

If we hold to these points, it also becomes clear how a fear that peace would now be disturbed could arise among the Christians. For all the emperor’s enemies had now been laid low, and Severus’ harshness, now that he was free from other business, threatened the utmost severity, which, while he was still occupied by graver affairs, he had been unable to pursue. And the soldier’s example seemed especially well suited to inflaming that harshness, since the worshipers of the gods, in their customary manner, believed that by rejecting the crown he had committed parricide and declared himself a public enemy of Caesar. [Col. 0126C]

### § 2.—The Opinions of Those Who Think Otherwise Examined, Especially Those of Hoffmann and Orsi, Who Assigned the Book to 198, and of Pagi, Who Assigned It to 202
But, although, led by these arguments, I contend that the book *On the Crown* was written in A.D. 201, I see that most scholars disagree, though they pronounce judgments that diverge entirely from one another. For Orsi, the most learned monk of the Dominican order, and his supporter Hoffmann assign it to A.D. 198; Baronius to A.D. 199; Pagi to A.D. 202; Pamelius and Allix to A.D. 210; and finally Tillemont thinks that it was [Col. 0126D] published under the emperor Maximinus, in A.D. 235. But all of these men, if one excepts Tillemont, erred without exception in understanding the soldiers’ donative given by Severus to be something other than the one that ought to be understood here. We might therefore refrain from refuting them, since we have shown what sort of donative Tertullian indicated here. Yet because the chronology of very many of his books depends upon the date of this little work, and because refuting those who think otherwise contributes greatly to confirming our judgment, come, let us examine these opinions as briefly as possible.

Here there is no need to say anything about Tillemont’s opinion, because the whole matter appears to have been adequately treated by Hoffmann (*In the Dissertation on All Tertullian’s Writings Composed during His Montanist Period*, § 6, p. 26 ff.); moreover, it plainly follows that hypothesis which maintains that Tertullian went over to the Montanists neither in A.D. [Col. 0127A] 199 nor shortly afterward—a matter we have discussed elsewhere. In this part of the discussion, indeed, Hoffmann handled the matter more correctly than when he advanced his own opinion. For he maintains that this book was composed at a time when the Christians’ peace had not yet been disturbed even by provincial governors, much less by an imperial edict, and specifically in the year after the birth of Christ 198. He believes the former to be established by the fact that Tertullian reports that the Christians believed their peace would be disturbed by the imprudent act of the soldier whom he defends here; the latter, he says, was demonstrated by Orsi with the most powerful arguments.

When Hoffmann employed these considerations in order to undermine Mosheim’s opinion—of blessed memory—concerning the true date of the *Apologeticum*, Mosheim indeed (*Additions to vol. I of his Dissertations Pertaining to Ecclesiastical History*, p. 741 ff.) [Col. 0127B] concedes that the matter had been correctly explained by Orsi; but he denies the correctness of the inference that Christians could not at the same time enjoy peace and nevertheless be subjected to various injuries by their enemies. And although I do not agree with Orsi, and indeed shall refute him below, I nevertheless acknowledge that Mosheim judged wisely when he said that, while Christian affairs were tranquil in some provinces and cities, they were very frequently disturbed by the governors in others, and that such was in fact the condition of Christianity when this book was written. This can be understood very well from Tertullian’s book *To Scapula*, which most of those who have attempted anything in this field acknowledge to have been published during Caracalla’s reign; and this will indeed become evident from what we shall demonstrate below.

Now who does not see from that book [Col. 0127C] that the Christians were then exposed to the greatest calamities? And yet there is not a single ancient writer who relates that Christians were persecuted under Caracalla. Why is this? Clearly because they then enjoyed a peace disturbed by no imperial edict, although they were not everywhere free from the cruelty of the governors. That matters stood in precisely this way when Tertullian committed these opinions *On the Crown* to writing can best be seen if what we ourselves think about the date of this book is admitted. For this deed of the soldier occurred in the East, perhaps even in Parthia, where we nowhere read that Christians were harassed before Severus’ edict; but the events narrated by Tertullian in the *Apologeticum* and his other books of that kind occurred chiefly in Africa, and therefore other Christians in the East could certainly fear that they would be deprived of peace because of the soldier’s deed.

But perhaps Orsi’s arguments will make a more powerful impression upon people’s minds; let us therefore see what they are and how strong they are. There are three passages in Orsi’s excursus in which he described this matter [Note: [Col. 0127D] In the historical dissertation demonstrating that the Catholic Church in the first three centuries by no means denied peace and absolution to persons guilty of capital crimes, sect. II, chap. 3, digression 2, pp. 104, 113. It appeared at Milan in 1730, quarto.]. First he observes that this book must be assigned to A.D. 198 and discovers traces of Severus’ generosity among the ancient writers; next he replies to Pagi, who had thought that this book was written in A.D. 202; then he shows that all the circumstances adduced by Tertullian concerning this act of generosity [Col. 0128A] agree excellently with the events of A.D. 198 but conflict with every other year. We too, therefore, shall follow in the footsteps of this most learned man, since we fear that we may otherwise confuse matters which he has already confused sufficiently; and, passage by passage, we shall indicate what he said correctly and what incorrectly, adding a briefer examination of Pagi’s arguments.

In that first passage, which concerns the number of the emperor Severus’ largesses, he says—I do not know whether quite correctly—that the soldiers were given donations by him five times, since some coins commemorate this seven times (see Vaillant, *Coins of the Roman Emperors*, vol. II, p. 234); but this may be conceded without prejudice to the point in dispute. Yet Orsi is not even consistent with himself in judging that Tertullian spoke of the donative of the year 198 (p. 104), while afterward saying nevertheless [Col. 0128B] that he spoke of the fourth largesse listed by Orsi himself (p. 106). For, as he himself observed, this fourth largesse is precisely the one that followed the capture of Ctesiphon.

The second passage, which he devoted to examining Pagi’s opinion, we do not reject in itself; yet there are some things in that discussion which must by no means be admitted. For, first, he absurdly says that Tertullian is speaking of the soldiers stationed in the city, whose praetorian camp was at the Viminal Gate for the protection of Rome. There is not even the slightest indication of this; and who could doubt that, outside Rome during wartime, Severus had military camps? Next—and this we see as especially contrary to our opinion—he says that every largesse was issued in time of peace and after a return from war; but Spanheim, whom he cites in passing on this matter, says absolutely nothing of the kind. [Col. 0128C] Even if I were to concede that this could be said of distributions to the people, I certainly doubt very strongly that it can be said of military donatives, as this undoubtedly was. Indeed, can the very largesse issued after the capture of Ctesiphon, which Orsi admits, be understood from Spartianus’ words in any other way than as one issued outside Rome during the war?

Finally, in replying to Pagi’s second argument, Orsi reasons badly that Pagi’s opinion cannot be granted because the Christians would have feared that their peace was to be disturbed either by the governors or by the emperor. Of these alternatives, he says, the former cannot be defended because the Christians had already been persecuted in A.D. 201, nor the latter because Severus was absent and extremely occupied in that year. The latter point is utterly trivial. For donatives were given to soldiers outside Rome as well, and in that same year 201 Severus brought the eastern war to an end. [Col. 0128D] But I admit that no weight should be assigned to Pagi’s arguments [Note: [Col. 0128D] He advanced them in his *Critique of Baronius’ Annals*, at A.D. 199, no. 3, in my edition pp. 91–92.]. For Caracalla’s quinquennalia, on account of which Pagi wishes the largesse mentioned by Tertullian to have been issued, belong to A.D. 203, when, as everyone knows, the Christians had already been torn apart by every form of outrage because of Severus’ edict. Furthermore, in the second argument it is also wrongly said that these hostilities were begun by the soldiers, as in the time of Diocletian; and that entire position is defended on the basis of the opinion that Christian affairs had not yet been disturbed before Severus’ tenth year—an opinion sufficiently refuted above.

Finally, the third passage of Orsi’s discussion, [Col. 0129A] in which he maintains that Tertullian’s words cannot refer to any year except 198, was not handled under a more favorable Jupiter. For his belief that this largesse of Severus occurred before the Parthian expedition does indeed contain some ambiguity. If it was issued twice—first in A.D. 197, after Severus’ return, as Herodian recorded, and then in A.D. 198, before the war against the Parthians was undertaken, as Spartianus relates—the latter, as we have said, cannot possibly be so understood, nor does it appear to have been so understood by Orsi, who cited Herodian to confirm the matter; while the former has absolutely no bearing upon the issue, because in that year Caracalla had not yet received the dignity of Augustus. But there is no need to linger at length over the passages he brought forward from Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, chap. 35, and the book *To Scapula*, chap. 4. [Col. 0129B] For we have assigned these to that same year 198 and to the following year, without any injury to our case; and all the rest collapses of its own accord once we know that donatives were distributed outside Rome.

### § 3.—Baronius’ Arguments for A.D. 199 Are Overthrown

There remain the conclusions of Baronius and Pamelius concerning the year in which this little work was written, and they are so constituted that they can be overthrown without difficulty. For Baronius (see his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, at A.D. 201, vol. II, Cologne ed., 1609, p. 299), in order to prove that this book was composed in A.D. 201 before Severus departed for the East—that is, as we more correctly customarily speak, in A.D. 199—[Col. 0129C] adduces a coin, one side of which shows Severus with *Tr. P. XI*, and the other *Liberalitas V*; and he adds, even more emphatically: “Know for certain that this coin pertains to the matters which we are about to discuss.” This seems to me to have been said in precisely the manner in which the Pythagoreans of old, when asked why something was so, used to interpose their formula, “The master himself has said it”; for nothing is further removed from the truth than this assertion of Baronius. For although he clearly relates that the seventh year of Severus’ tribunician power began in that year, he nevertheless adduces a coin bearing *Tr. P. XI*, which must plainly be referred to A.D. 204—or, if one prefers to follow Baronius himself, to A.D. 206. Does he not therefore contradict himself?

And what shall I say of his second argument, which he derived from the claim [Col. 0129D] that no calamities befell the Christians before this Parthian expedition, while many befell them after it? Here he erred twice: first, because he denied that any had occurred before Severus set out against the Parthians; and second, because he did not consider that the book *On the Crown* was later than the book *On the Spectacles*. We refuted the former claim in its proper place. As for the latter, no one can deny it unless it is pitch-dark for him at high noon—for this too has been sufficiently discussed. Consequently, there can be no mention in *On the Crown* of a persecution of Christians preceding Severus’ law, since there Christians are said to fear these calamities as events yet to come, whereas by the time Tertullian committed the book *On the Spectacles* to paper, the worshippers of the gods had already turned their assault against the Christians. Therefore, according to Baronius’ own reasoning, [Col. 0130A] the book *On the Crown* will have to be assigned to Severus’ tenth year.

### § 4.—Finally, the Conclusions of Pamelius and Allix, Who Had Placed This Book in A.D. 209, Are Rejected

I come to Allix, a most learned man, whom I am surprised to find so compliant toward the opinion of Pamelius—a scholar than whom, I doubt, anyone approached the task of determining the dates of Tertullian’s writings under less favorable auspices. Since Tertullian introduces mention of a largesse, Pamelius thinks that the little book must plainly be assigned to A.D. 209 and to Antoninus’ decennalia (*Life of Tertullian*, prefixed to Tertullian’s works published by Pamelius, Cologne, 1617, p. 22 E). But Pamelius does not prove [Col. 0130B] that a largesse was issued at those decennalia; he simply fabricates it at his pleasure. Yet elsewhere (*Notes on This Book*, p. 210, no. 1), merely for form’s sake, he appeals to a coin bearing this legend: *Imp. Caes. L. Sept. Sev. Pert. Aug. . . . Liberalitas Augg. SC.* Here let someone first tell me where the marks of the decennalia are. Next, although I am well aware that Severus and Caracalla jointly gave something to the soldiers and the people at the decennalia, were no other distributions to the people or military donatives issued besides these? No one, surely, could say so without rashness or ignorance. Indeed, since Pamelius ventured to foist the year 208 upon others without any adequate reason, it cannot in turn be held against us if we understand the year to be 201; for in that year too a largesse was issued, and issued by both Augusti.

Yet although Pamelius has exposed himself altogether disgracefully, [Col. 0130C] Allix nevertheless (*On the Life and Writings of Tertullian*, a very rare dissertation, chap. VI, p. 49) went over to his opinion. “For in the book *On the Crown*,” he says, “the little book *On the Spectacles*, which was written in A.D. 204, is cited.” Anyone who reflects upon what we stated above concerning that little work will readily understand that Pamelius, whom alone Allix follows, spoke absurdly. Nor, even if this claim concerning *On the Spectacles* were especially true, do we perceive any reason why the book *On the Crown* would have to be assigned to A.D. 208 rather than to some other year. Nor did he more correctly employ, in defense of that conclusion, the Montanist errors occurring in the book *On the Crown*. I do not deny that such errors are present in this book; but that this argument can establish the required conclusion will never be perceived except by [Col. 0130D] those who think that Tertullian went over to the Montanists only in that year.
