### § 5.—Both Books *On the Dress of Women* Are Shown, against Pamelius and Tillemont, to Have Been Published Together

But our inquiry into the book *On the Crown* has detained us long enough. We must therefore hasten on to certain other books, namely those which Tertullian composed *On the Dress of Women*. Here it does not seem foreign to the discussion we are undertaking to explain briefly at the outset what the title of these books once was, and to consider whether the latter little work was published by Tertullian at the same time as the other. Those who published Tertullian’s books before Nicolas Rigault called the one *On Women’s Apparel* and the other [Col. 0131A] *On the Dress of Women*. But Rigault, after obtaining that very ancient manuscript of Agobard, was the first to venture to entitle both *On the Dress of Women*. We therefore have no doubt that these books were never separate, but constituted, as it were, a single volume. We are moved not only by the authority of the Agobard manuscript, but also because the very plan and subject of these books suggest that the latter was published by Tertullian not very long after the former.

Pamelius, who followed the title otherwise received, could scarcely digest the fact that although Tertullian had carefully distinguished *cultus* from *ornatus* in the first book, he nevertheless treated women’s *ornatus* in the second, which was entitled *On the Cultus of Women*. But once the different titles of the two books are removed and their subject carefully understood, that difficulty vanishes in a remarkable way. For Tertullian had said that a woman’s appearance consists of *cultus* and *ornatus*. As examples of the former category he gives women’s finery, gold, silver, precious stones, garments, and things of the same kind; as examples of the latter, [Col. 0131B] the care of the hair, the skin, and those parts of the body which, as he says, attract the eyes. Now in the first book he treats gold and silver (chap. 4), precious stones (chap. 5), and garments (chap. 7); in the second he deals generally with the observance of modesty in the regulation of *cultus* and *ornatus* (chaps. 1–5), then with the coloring and adornment of the hair, and concludes the whole book with certain admonitions concerning adornment contrary to modesty. It is therefore clear that in the former he dealt with women’s *cultus*, in the latter with their *ornatus*, and that both, as parts, constituted a single book.

For Tillemont’s statement (*Mémoires pour servir à l’Histoire ecclésiastique*, vol. III, p. 662, note 12) that it is manifest that these two books were separate and cannot in any way be related to one another [Col. 0131C] is easier asserted than proved and does not even deserve refutation; it is the statement of an ignorant man. There is also another proof of our position. For in the latter book Tertullian makes unmistakable mention of evils impending over the Christians, while in the former there is no indication of them. Now if they had then been afflicted by hardship, how could Tertullian have refrained from mentioning it in order to dissuade Christian women from luxury, when elsewhere he frequently employs this argument? But since that first little work is later than *On the Spectacles*, as will presently appear, let someone tell me whether the Christians enjoyed peace in any year that elapsed from the year in which we said that *On the Spectacles* was written down to A.D. 202, when hostilities against the Christians began—unless perhaps in A.D. 201 or 202. [Col. 0131D] For both the order of the books established by us in the earlier part of this discussion and the history of the Scillitan Martyrs (see above, § 6) show that Christians were severely persecuted from Severus’ return from Gaul until A.D. 201. Accordingly, since Severus’ first edict was issued at approximately some point after the beginning of A.D. 202, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place, it can scarcely be said that the first little work *On the Dress of Women* was published at any other time than approximately that at which the later book on the same subject appeared.

### § 6.—Specifically, in A.D. 201 or 202

[Col. 0132A]

What is the point of all this? Clearly, that if the date at which either of the two books was written is established, the date of both is discovered. Therefore, to follow the surest indication of that date in the books themselves, we shall make use of the calamities to which Tertullian says the Christians were then exposed, and which his words show had approximately begun at the time when he was composing the second little book *On the Dress of Women* (book II, chap. 13): “The times for Christians are always, and now most especially, passed not in gold but in iron. The robes of martyrdom are being prepared.”

These words cannot be understood of the earlier persecution of the Christians by the populace, because in the first book on this subject he refers to the book [Col. 0132B] *On the Spectacles* (chap. 7). For I cannot persuade myself that Tertullian, in citing it, intended to indicate the Greek book on a similar subject, since we have shown (§ 14) that the Latin book is earlier than the Greek, and since this admonition of Tertullian—in which he states that something may come from God even though God is not the author of its abuse—certainly occurs in the Latin book *On the Spectacles* (chap. 2). Indeed, when he wrote *On the Spectacles*, the Christians had long been afflicted by the greatest evils, of which he does not speak even a word in that first book *On the Dress of Women*; and at the time of the later little work those evils were again impending. Therefore, these books can in no way be referred to the earlier persecution under Severus, but rather to the year after the birth of Christ 201 or 202, according as one prefers to believe that the Christians’ sufferings had then arisen or were still impending. [Col. 0132C]

Nor should we listen to Tillemont, who thinks (*loc. cit.*, p. 210, art. VI) that the first book was published only after A.D. 203, but the second much earlier, specifically in A.D. 197. For in the passage he cited [Note: [Col. 0132D] Book I, chap. 6: “We have also seen at Rome the nobility of precious stones blushing before matrons at the disdain of the Parthians and Medes and the rest of their countrymen.”], Tertullian may equally well have had in mind Severus’ earlier return from Parthia or some embassy of the Parthians as that later victory over the Parthians. As for his assertion that there is some reason for believing that the book which we call the latter was written long before he published the other: because Tillemont did not see fit to provide the basis for his opinion, we in turn see fit to remain doubtful until we see something of that kind produced by someone else.

### § 7.—The Book *On Flight in Persecution* Is Assigned to A.D. 202

[Col. 0132D]

The book *On Flight in Persecution* likewise owes its origin to the same period. Tertullian had already promised elsewhere, in *On the Crown*, to discuss this subject (chap. 1). Although some have thought that the words of that passage ought rather to be referred to the *Scorpiace*, others have already observed that they cannot be so understood, because he opposed the *Scorpiace* to heretics, but the treatise *On Flight* to the timidity of those who were [Col. 0133A] members of the orthodox Church. It is therefore evident that the little book *On Flight* was published by Tertullian only after A.D. 201. And I have no doubt about assigning that book to the following year.

I shall not, indeed, make use of that mildness and moderation of Tertullian which deserves notice in a book where he raises a question that separated the Montanists from the purer Church, although no one will doubt that he was then attached to them [Note: [Col. 0133D] The mention of the Montanists’ Paraclete may serve as evidence: he says that the Paraclete was not received by those to whom belonged the brother to whom he dedicated the book (chap. 1). Furthermore, he cites as testimony an utterance of the Spirit (chap. 9) which, since it does not occur in the sacred text, undoubtedly belongs to the Montanist spirit; of this spirit he also speaks in chaps. 1 and 14.]. For one might say that, in writing these things to a man who stood with the orthodox party, Tertullian restrained himself from harsher language. Certainly a weightier argument lies in the fact that, when he published our little work, he said that certain outrages against the Christians had already begun.

For he opens as follows: “You recently asked, brother Fabius, whether one should flee during a persecution, because something or other was being announced.” [Col. 0133B] And a little afterward: “Both your inquiry has commended this subject, and the condition of the times has now imposed it under its own name. For the more frequent the persecutions that threaten, the more carefully we must examine how faith ought to receive them.” Finally: “This is that chaff which even now cleanses the Lord’s threshing floor, namely the Church, by winnowing the mixed heap of the faithful—the grain of the martyrs and the chaff of the deniers.”

But no one who has observed that the earlier persecution befell the Christian community in A.D. 197 and the later one in A.D. 202, and that our little work was written after Tertullian had adopted Montanist opinions, can fail to see which persecution of the Christian body must be understood here. We therefore say that this discussion *On Flight* was published approximately toward the end of A.D. 202, [Col. 0133C] chiefly because Severus was still staying in Syria at the beginning of the year; hence it can scarcely be said that he enacted his law against the Christians before the middle part of that year had passed.

### § 8.—The Common Opinion That the Book *Scorpiace* Is Later Than Tertullian’s Books against Marcion Is Examined, and His Lost Books against Marcion Are Discussed

We now come to Tertullian’s *Scorpiace*, which we have resolved to assign to A.D. 204 and to explain the basis of that judgment. As we undertake this task, we do not doubt that there will be very many who say that our opinion does not deserve the least consideration. For nearly all those whom we know to have discussed this matter hold that Tertullian’s *Scorpiace* was written [Col. 0133D] only after the publication of the books against Marcion which survive to our own time. They seem to regard themselves as bound, as though by prescription or command, to defend this position because in the fifth section of the *Scorpiace* Tertullian says that the Marcionites learned from him that their God is good—a matter which he certainly discussed systematically in the first and second books against Marcion.

I am well aware that Tertullian published the books against Marcion—or at least the first—in A.D. 207 or 208, and that it therefore seems consistent [Col. 0134A] with the truth that he published the *Scorpiace* only in A.D. 208 or later. But since I always inquire what is most probable in any matter, I should like in some measure to weigh how much force this argument possesses. When Tertullian was composing the first book against Marcion which we possess, he had already opposed Marcion twice in writing; but one of these treatises he afterward suppressed when he undertook a fuller discussion of the subject, while the other he lost through the fraud of a certain man who had copied it and shared it with others. To make good this loss, he composed the books against Marcion which now survive, the first specifically in the fifteenth year of the emperor Severus, as he himself acknowledges in that book (chap. 15), where he also explained the matters we have just mentioned (chap. 1).

When I reflect upon these facts, [Col. 0134B] it certainly appears doubtful whether, in the book which he called *Scorpiace*, Tertullian referred to those books against Marcion which have not reached our age, or rather to those which we know to survive, since the lost books dealt with the same subject. I am not now arguing which of these alternatives must be chosen; that will become evident in its proper place. But everyone sees that the mode of argument employed by those who think otherwise is doubtful and finds little support in the argument that, from that mention, the book could be assigned to A.D. 208 or later.

Nor does Hoffmann’s reply to Tillemont, who prudently hesitated here, prevent us from doubting the matter. [Col. 0134C] He says (*dissertation cited*, § 14, p. 44):

> “The first little work, being slight, he suppressed himself; the second was published through another man’s fraud against Tertullian’s will, while it was still rough and insufficiently polished, and was not acknowledged by Septimius; the third does not survive. Now, since it is scarcely probable that Tertullian referred readers to a treatment of the Marcionite controversy which he himself had suppressed or never acknowledged, it follows that the books now in our hands must be understood.”

I have no desire here to dwell at length upon Hoffmann’s insufficiently accurate discussion of the second treatment of that subject, as if, when it was published, it had neither been sufficiently worked out nor acknowledged by Septimius. I certainly do not understand how this can be inferred from Tertullian’s words:

> “This one too,” he says, “not yet supplied with copies”—that is, not yet transcribed into several manuscripts—“but existing in only one, which he took away, I afterward lost through the fraud of a man who was then a brother but later an apostate; he had happened to copy certain passages most incorrectly and presented them to the public.”

[Col. 0134D] Yet even if I grant that everything Hoffmann has said here is correct, no one will deny that his entire argument accomplishes nothing if it assumes what first had to be proved. Thus, if we wish to be held bound by the opinion that the surviving books against Marcion are earlier than the *Scorpiace* before we have judged what is most correct in this matter, I admit that it is hardly probable that Tertullian commended in the *Scorpiace* a book which had been suppressed or never acknowledged. But suppose that this has not yet been established—as in truth it has not—and that the *Scorpiace* was perhaps written before those surviving books. In that case he could quite suitably cite the first and second volumes against Marcion, although they are now lost; for the first little work, as Tertullian himself says, he suppressed only later, when he produced a fuller composition, and it could therefore be cited before he had treated these matters in a more exact discourse.

Accordingly, Hoffmann’s argument either assumes as already true the very things that are plainly in controversy, [Col. 0135A] or else leaves them undecided. If the former, his argument clearly moves in a circle; if the latter, our opinion is no weaker than Hoffmann’s. But now that this difficulty, which might have worked to our disadvantage, has been removed, come, let us determine the date at which the *Scorpiace* was written.

### § 9.—It Is Established That the *Scorpiace* Was Written in A.D. 204

When Tertullian committed to writing the points concerning the dignity of martyrdom which he wished to discuss in this *Scorpiace*, the worshippers of the gods were occupied in utterly destroying the Christians. This is shown by the entire argument of this little work, directed against those heretics who, when faith was in the heat of trial and the Church was being burned in the figure of the bush, regarded it as disgraceful to suffer evils on account of religion (chap. 1). [Col. 0135B] Such evils must already have been extremely atrocious, as is shown by Tertullian’s words immediately added in the same section:

> “And now the present state of affairs is the very midpoint of the heat, the very dog days of persecution—proceeding, plainly, from the dog-headed one himself. Fire has tested some Christians, the sword others, wild beasts others,” etc.

There is no doubt here that the persecution which blazed forth after Severus’ edict must be understood, since he composed this book after *On Flight in Persecution*. For nowhere do we read Tertullian maintaining that God is acknowledged as the author of such calamities suffered on account of religion except in that little book *On Flight*, and especially in its third section; yet in the fourth section of the *Scorpiace* he says that he had already discussed this matter previously.

But to speak more precisely about the date of this book, I consider it to have appeared definitely in A.D. 204. [Col. 0135C] My first argument is this: when Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* VI.2, Cambridge ed., p. 257) had said that calamities were inflicted upon the Christians by Severus with the greatest violence, so much so that many already thought the advent of Antichrist was approaching, neither Eusebius himself nor any other ancient writer recorded any evils other than those which befell the Christians in Severus’ tenth year under Laetus, governor of Africa, and in the following year at the instigation of Aquila, governor of the same province (Eusebius, *loc. cit.*, chap. 3, p. 261).

Eusebius himself teaches that these latter events occurred in that year. He confirms that Origen was then placed in charge of instructing catechumens while Aquila opposed the growth of the Christian religion by injuring its adherents, and that Origen was eighteen years old, whereas he had said that he was in his seventeenth year when his father Leonides was put to death (chap. 2, p. 258), which occurred in Severus’ tenth year. [Col. 0135D] Now if some nevertheless persist in thinking that our little work was written in A.D. 208, let them tell me by what right they can assign to that year the Christians’ greatest calamities, of which no memory survives among the ancient writers.

At this point one may well marvel at the frivolity of so many extremely learned men. Once they had imbibed the opinion that the *Scorpiace* was later than our surviving books against Marcion, they forgot that nothing is more disgraceful in history than to believe rashly. For if I see two opinions advanced, one plausible but incapable of being established by the testimony of any ancient writer, the other so constituted that it displays this support of truth, why should I not abandon the former and follow the latter?

And this argument is at hand and must be pressed again and again, provided that we later show that Tertullian’s book *On the Pallium* must be placed in A.D. 208. For in that book (chap. 1) he says: [Col. 0136A]

> “I am glad, Carthaginians, that you enjoy such prosperous times, since you have sufficient leisure and inclination to find fault with clothing. These are the idle pursuits of peace and plenty; all is well from both the government and the heavens.”

How could Tertullian there have commemorated the prosperity of the times, or descended because of the leisure afforded by peace to matters of no importance at all, such as these trifles about the pallium, if the Christians were then suffering the extremely grave calamities which he depicts in the *Scorpiace*? Consequently, although others have thought that the *Scorpiace* was written nearly five years later, I certainly judge that it appeared before the surviving disputations against Marcion, specifically in A.D. 203 or 204. For this conclusion we have in Eusebius a most reliable witness. Although he nowhere states it expressly, what he does say, as we have seen, shows approximately the same thing.

For my part, I prefer the latter year because of the games which Tertullian says had been celebrated very recently [Note: [Col. 0136D] Chap. 6: “How greatly the world celebrates those contests, the contentious solemnities and superstitious competitions of the Greeks, both in religion and in pleasure, Africa too has had the opportunity to see. Even now the individual cities keep Carthage in a state of agitation with their congratulations, because, after the old age of its stadium, it has been presented with a Pythian contest.”]. [Col. 0136B] If anyone prefers to believe that they were celebrated during Severus’ decennalia and Caracalla’s quinquennalia, I shall not strongly object, since Spanheim—a man assuredly respected and highly distinguished in this field of scholarship—has adequately demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0136D] In *Letter I to Andreas Morell*, appended to his *Specimen of a Universal Account of Ancient Coinage*, Leipzig ed., p. 12 f.] that Pythian games were held elsewhere than at Delphi, and not only in honor of Pythian Apollo but also in honor of the emperors.

Nevertheless, I would prefer the other alternative because the Pythian games in Greece were celebrated in every third year of an Olympiad, and the third year of the 245th Olympiad itself falls in the year after the birth of Christ 204. [Col. 0136C] In this way no violence is done to Tertullian’s words; for if they are taken to mean that those games were held at Carthage—where Carthage itself could not be presented with the prize—they do not appear to cohere very well.

### § 10.—It Is Shown That of the Five Surviving Books against Marcion, the First Belongs to A.D. 207 or 208, While the Dates of the Others Are Uncertain

[Col. 0136D]

Besides this work of Tertullian, there survive, among those written after he had already fallen away from orthodoxy, the five books Against Marcion, which may unquestionably be charged with Montanist errors. For even if Tertullian’s own declaration (IV.22), where he says that his own party and the “Psychics” [Col. 0137A] disagree on the subject of ecstasy, were considered highly doubtful, and even if one were unwilling to take account of the visions by which, he says, those doctrines were confirmed (III.24; V.8), nevertheless—since all these books Against Marcion were not published at the same time—in the first book devoted to that subject he calls the discipline of Montanus his own, and represents himself as defending, on the authority of the Paraclete, his own decrees against repeated marriages (ch. 29); and the chronology itself shows that this book was written after he had already begun to belong to the Montanist party.

Since many of those who have labored to determine the date of Tertullian’s books have never even thought to doubt the latter point that we have undertaken to discuss, while others have said much about it incorrectly, we believe that, after repeated consideration of the matter, we ought to discuss it more precisely. And, to speak first [Col. 0137B] of the first book, no one says that its date is disputed. Quite rightly and properly; for there is an explicit and decisive declaration on the matter by Tertullian himself (I.15), who acknowledges that he composed this book in Severus’s fifteenth year. But when scholars say nothing about the date of the others, by their very silence they imply that they belong to the same period. This is far from being the case. For from the words with which Tertullian concluded the first book—[Note: [Col. 0137D] “If anyone thinks that we have accomplished too little, let him hope that what remains has been reserved for its own time, as has also the examination of the Scriptures used by Marcion.”]—it is fairly clearly inferred that this book was published separately and the others composed at a different time.

Although we do not venture to say whether he wrote the second, third, and fourth books separately or together, or at what time, we nevertheless affirm as beyond doubt that Tertullian did not publish the fifth book at the same time [Col. 0137C] as the others. For the book On the Resurrection is later than the one he composed On the Flesh of Christ (On the Resurrection, ch. 2), in which latter work (On the Flesh of Christ, ch. 7) he cites a passage from the fourth book Against Marcion, which we shall discuss below. Yet in the fifth book Against Marcion, ch. 10, he refers back to the work he had written On the Resurrection; from this it is clear that Tertullian brought the fifth book to light at a different time from that at which he published the fourth. Likewise, in the first book Against Marcion, ch. 1, he promises that he will someday complete a work On the Prescription of Heretics; but in On the Flesh of Christ, ch. 2, he says that such a work had already been written by him. This too therefore shows that the first book was not published in the same production as all the others.

Since this is so, we may confidently affirm that the first book Against Marcion appeared in A.D. 207—or, if one prefers, 208—[Col. 0137D] since Severus’s fifteenth year falls within both; but as to when the others were written, nothing can be said except that the fifth is not of the same date as the rest.

## § 11.—Tillemont’s Contrary Opinion Corrected

We had feared that some might raise against these arguments of ours an objection like the one we discussed in connection with the Scorpiace: namely, that the books Against Marcion cited there are not those still surviving, but other books that had, so to speak, been withdrawn and had long since been lost. We see that Tillemont has in fact done approximately this (Mémoires pour servir à l’hist. Eccl., [Col. 0138A] vol. III, p. 666, note 19), for he defends that view most vigorously. We must therefore set forth what can be answered in support of our position and examine what Tillemont argued on the other side—but both very briefly, and in such a way that we now entirely pass over those points which we established by Tertullian’s own explicit testimony.

Thus only this question can be disputed: whether, in On the Flesh of Christ, Tertullian cited the fourth book Against Marcion that still survives. I certainly think that he did: first, because in that book he examined Marcion’s scriptural text, and there (IV.19) is found precisely what he touched upon in On the Flesh of Christ; secondly, because, when he was producing against Marcion the first book that still survives, he had not yet published On the Prescription of Heretics. But just as the latter had already appeared publicly when Tertullian composed On the Flesh of Christ, as we have just proved, so it is plainly necessary that by then the first of the surviving books Against Marcion had also already been published. [Col. 0138B] Indeed, when he wrote this book, Tertullian had withdrawn and discarded the two little works in which he had formerly attacked Marcion; hence it is evident that in On the Flesh of Christ he could not have referred his readers to them.

But let us nevertheless hear Tillemont’s argument to the contrary. He says first that the following works of Tertullian—the Scorpiace, On the Flesh of Christ, On the Soul, and On the Resurrection—may be said to precede the surviving books Against Marcion, and that the books cited in them under that title are those which perished long ago. As regards the Scorpiace, I do not object, [Col. 0138C] for that question has been sufficiently treated; but concerning the others I do not agree. We have just stated what judgment must be made about the work entitled On the Flesh of Christ; if anyone wishes to resist that judgment, we shall hear him. And when we demonstrated this, it simultaneously became clear that what Tillemont maintained to the contrary was even further from applying to On the Resurrection—which is undoubtedly later than On the Flesh of Christ.

Finally, in On the Soul, ch. 21, Tertullian says that he had taught Marcion that the human soul is moved from no external source. Since he said much about this matter in the second surviving book Against Marcion, ch. 6 ff., it is not absurd to say that he had that book in view in the former work. Yet we shall not insist upon this stubbornly, since we have not used the testimony of On the Soul.

The second objection is positively childish. In the passage from On the Flesh of Christ that we cited [Col. 0138D] as evidence, Tertullian called the book Against Marcion to which he referred a “little book”; consequently, he cannot have meant to cite the fourth of the surviving books, which is not a little book but a large volume. What a foolish conclusion! As though Tertullian had not called the whole work Against Marcion a “little work” (I.1; I.31; II.1; etc.), or as though something that constitutes part of a larger work could not be called a “little book.” But on that reasoning, it must be said that Tertullian cited a work not yet completed! Could this truly have caused scruple to so eminent a man, who has a thousand times invoked in his commentaries his own books that had not yet been completed? And who will deny that Tertullian acted in the same way, if he has read our defense of our argument?

Finally, Tillemont says that Tertullian gives one account of the place in which holy men are kept from [Col. 0139A] death until the day of the Last Judgment in On the Soul, ch. 55, and On the Resurrection, ch. 43, but another in Against Marcion IV.34. I hear him. But do those books conflict in the passages that Tertullian says he had treated in his disputation against Marcion? Tillemont has never proved this; nor will anyone say that such a conclusion can be admitted merely because Tertullian departed from himself in other matters that do not pertain to the specific issue.

## § 12.—The Book *On the Pallium*. Discussion of the Threefold Power of the Present Empire, and Inquiry into the Year in Which Geta Assumed the Dignity of Augustus

Let us now take up the little book On the Pallium—obscure indeed and sufficiently confused, yet filled with a vast knowledge of all antiquity. [Col. 0139B] Since the opinions of the most learned men concerning its date diverge so greatly, we must either examine them candidly or present our own.

Here, however, there first arises a question that is easily resolved: what is that “threefold power of the present empire, with God favoring so many Augusti as one,” to which Tertullian attributes the prosperity of those times? [Note: [Col. 0139D] Ch. 2: “How many cities has the threefold power of the present empire either brought forth, enlarged, or restored, with God favoring so many Augusti as one! How many census rolls have been transcribed!”] Some (Jac. Gutherius, De officiis domus Augustae, Leipzig ed., p. 277) maintain that these words indicate Severus alone, because he had overcome those three rivals for the empire, Julianus, Niger, and Albinus; others understand Severus together with Niger and Albinus (the Magdeburg Centuriators, cent. III, p. 241); others Albinus, Severus, and Antoninus (Pamelius, Life of Tertullian, p. 10 D, 14 F); and still others understand Severus with his two sons Bassianus [Col. 0139C] and Geta.

But I approve none of the first three opinions. Gutherius’s view is so contorted and utterly foolish that I scarcely know whether anyone has ever followed things so plainly perverse and false. I shall not dwell upon the fact that the good man failed to see that this is called the threefold power of the present empire, that God is said to have favored so many Augusti as one, and that they too are said to have brought forth, enlarged, and restored many cities. Let someone tell me whether these things can be affirmed of Julianus, Niger, and Albinus—especially when they had already been killed. Nor shall I say how badly he applied Herodian’s words, III.7, where Herodian marvels that Severus ἕνα ἄνδρα τρεῖς καθελόντα βασιλέας ἤδη κρατοῦντας (“one man having overthrown three emperors who were already in power”); for these matters were already sufficiently discussed by Boecler (Annotations on Herodian, p. 420).

[Col. 0139D] I wish to examine only this one point, which is especially relevant to our subject: whether Geta was never made Augustus while Severus was alive. Since Gutherius maintains this, he first fails to distinguish Geta, Severus’s brother, from Geta Caesar, Severus’s son, as he ought to have done. For when Spartianus (Severus, ch. 10) says that Severus called his son Bassianus Caesar in order to remove his brother Geta from the hope of imperial power which the latter had conceived, is it not reasonable that he was speaking of Geta, Severus’s brother? Secondly, the fact that in many headings of the Code the names of the Augusti Severus and Antoninus are found, but never Geta’s, [Col. 0140A] contributes absolutely nothing to the matter. For from the time when Geta assumed the dignity of Augustus, as will be shown below, he was always his father’s companion in the war; no one should wonder that in wartime he was unable to devote thought to laws affecting the commonwealth.

What is altogether intolerable, however, is that Gutherius denies that Geta was called Augustus during his father’s lifetime and uses, to prove this, coins on which Geta’s second tribunician power is recorded. For since he himself adds that after his father’s death Geta reigned with his brother for only ten months and fifteen days, it is plainly necessary that Geta had been called Augustus before his father’s death.

The second opinion, that of the very learned men who composed the Magdeburg Centuries of sacred history, holds that Severus together with Niger and Albinus constituted that threefold power. To speak with Tillemont, it is rightly [Col. 0140B] convicted of error because it treats the source of the Roman Empire’s evils as the source from which flowed that great imperial prosperity of which Tertullian speaks.

And am I to think more favorably of Pamelius, from whose case the truth is usually as far removed as possible? He could even call Albinus an Augustus—although everyone knows that Albinus undertook hostilities against Severus because the dignity of Augustus had been denied him (see Dio Cassius, LXXV.4, p. 1258)—and make Caracalla his colleague in imperial power, though Caracalla was not granted the honors of Augustus until Albinus had long since been killed. If, with Scaliger, I were to say that he asserted these things in jest, I should be saying too little: he has cast such darkness over the truth.

It therefore remains only that we understand this threefold power as Severus together with his sons, now Augusti. [Col. 0140C] Of them God can be said to have favored many “as one,” to use Septimius’s expression, since, if we wish to speak properly, Severus alone reigned, while the other two were Augusti more in name than in reality. Hence, if we establish in what year Geta was raised to the dignity of Augustus, these words will contribute no more to knowledge and understanding of the book’s date [reading uncertain; the context may require “contribute not a little”].

Dodwell, indeed, shrewdly observed, as he did many other things (Camden Lectures XIX, § 21, p. 621 ff.), and confirmed with many examples, that the Roman emperors took care that the tribunician powers of their sons should be reckoned from their imperial quinquennial or decennial anniversaries. But who does not know that A.D. 208 marked Severus’s fifteenth anniversary and Caracalla’s tenth? Accordingly, scarcely anyone can doubt that in the same year the dignity of Augustus was conferred upon Geta; and what prevents us from saying that, according to the custom of the Roman emperors, the same thing befell Geta on the very same day on which it had once befallen Severus and Caracalla?

[Col. 0140D] And if this fact might perhaps seem doubtful because it could have happened earlier, or because emperors had not followed this one rule everywhere—although that is not likely in the case of Severus, who was an ardent student of Chaldaean astrology and carefully observed favorable days—the coins nevertheless place it beyond all doubt. For if we attend to the numbering of Geta’s tribunician power, by which the years of this dignity can be determined with the greatest accuracy, it does not advance beyond the fourth on Geta’s coins. But Geta held supreme rule jointly with Caracalla until approximately February [Col. 0141A] A.D. 212. [Note: [Col. 0141D] It is not so necessary for us to confirm this with many arguments, for Tillemont has sufficiently performed that task in his work entitled Histoire des empereurs, vol. II, part I, Brussels ed., p. 185, and in the notes, p. 391.] The fourth year of Geta’s tribunician power must therefore rightly be assigned to the middle of A.D. 211; if we count backward from it, it follows that Geta assumed the dignity of Augustus after half of A.D. 208 had elapsed. From this it is also evident that Tertullian’s On the Pallium is later than the middle of that year.

## § 13.—The View of Basnage and Walch, Who Maintained That This Book Was Published in A.D. 211, Is Rendered Doubtful, and the Little Book Is Assigned to A.D. 208

But because a more precise account is required of the year in which this book was written, those who discuss the matter more minutely, so far as I can see, adopt the view that it must be placed in the year 211. We need not concern ourselves [Col. 0141B] with the others, who state more generally that this work was composed toward the end of Severus’s reign. But those who have subjected the matter more strictly to chronological precision—Samuel Basnage (Annales politico-ecclesiastici, vol. II, p. 217), and the venerable Walch of Göttingen, who follows him (Antiquitates pallii philosophici veterum Christianorum, p. 227 ff.)—these men, I say, determine that this book was written in the year we have named, since there are certain similarities between that year’s events and the matters Tertullian mentioned here.

Yet after carefully examining the matter, my mind has inclined more toward the view that this little book was composed approximately in the year 208. Therefore, with the permission of that venerable man—who, I hope, will readily pardon an honest person who wishes to discover the truth without any contentiousness—[Col. 0141C] I shall explain very briefly both the considerations that move me to doubt somewhat the truth of his opinion and those that appear in some measure to commend the view I would like to adopt.

The entire opinion of those who think otherwise is evidently established by the similarity between what Tertullian says and what we know happened in A.D. 211. But although this argument does not seem objectionable in itself, it nevertheless possesses little strength, I think, if the same similarity exists between Tertullian’s statements and what occurred in A.D. 208; and it loses all probative force if it can be shown that what occurred in A.D. 211 was entirely different from what he recorded in our book. Both conditions are plainly present here.

[Col. 0141D] For, to speak first of the latter point: when Tertullian committed our little book to writing, Africa was already free from earthquakes (ch. 2); there was the repose of peace and abundance, and all was well through both the empire and the heavens (ch. 1). Yet at the time when he wrote to Scapula the words with which he sought to turn him away from cruelty toward Christians—a work composed approximately in A.D. 211, as we shall show below—the Africans had already been terrified for a year by rains, fire, thunder, an eclipse of the sun, and other events. Since Tertullian maintains that all these things were punishments inflicted upon the worshipers of the gods because they had kindled so many blazes of misery [Col. 0142A] against Christians, it is plainly necessary that this persecution of the Christians had already extended throughout an entire year.

Suppose, then, that the little book On the Pallium was written in A.D. 211: does not Tertullian contradict himself by ascribing both the highest prosperity and the gravest calamities to the same period? I do not deny that it might perhaps be said that, when these calamities had abated for a while, quiet and tranquil intervals, as it were, intervened. But since the records of ancient history have transmitted absolutely nothing from which this circumstance might in some way be inferred, would it be permissible to invent it in order to assist an opinion that seems almost to have reached its end?

Let those calamities, meanwhile, have been intermittent for a time; shall we nevertheless also say that the extreme injuries committed against Christians were interrupted? [Col. 0142B] You will say yes, for how could prosperous times have existed unless these too had ceased somewhat? But I have learned that Tertullian pursued his enemies, as it were, into every hiding place, and used even the slightest circumstance to convict of error and wickedness those who opposed the cause of the Christians. Would I then suppose that this same Tertullian would have argued against them simply by saying that, just as the gravest calamities had followed the adversaries’ injuries against Christians, so in turn the happiest times had followed their goodwill toward them?

There is still another point readily at hand. For when Tertullian composed this little book On the Pallium, there was the repose of peace, and in truth the world was “the empire’s most cultivated estate, tilled and delightful beyond Alcinous’s orchard and Midas’s rose garden” (ch. 2). How was this so? [Col. 0142C] “Every aconite of hostility” had been rooted out. Let this book, then, have been written at the beginning of A.D. 211; for at the beginning of February Severus ceased to be among the living, and the “threefold power of the empire” also ceased. Yet at that time the war against the Britons had not yet ended, nor did it ever end thereafter while Severus lived; only after his death did Antoninus finally make peace with the Britons (see Herodian, III.15, p. 173). Since, therefore, in that year there was certainly neither the repose of peace nor a world that was the empire’s most cultivated estate, a more suitable setting must be assigned to this book—namely, the closing part of the year 208—especially because everything Tertullian relates here agrees perfectly with it.

For if you ask about the threefold power of the present empire, [Col. 0142D] Geta had indeed only just assumed the dignity of Augustus. If you ask about the Carthaginians made happy by a new favor, the coins had already long since revealed them as such. [Note: [Col. 0142D] See Spanheim in his immortal work De praestantia et usu numismatum, diss. XII, vol. II, p. 443, who says that those coins of Severus and Antoninus bearing *Felix Karthago* relate to the restoration to that city of the right to strike coins. If the very common coins that celebrate *Indulgentia Augg. in Carthag.* refer to this same matter—or at least to a related one, as seems to me—this occurred approximately in A.D. 204 or 205, because on some of them it is combined with Caracalla’s sixth tribunician power. They were certainly issued before the little book On the Pallium was written, for nowhere on them is Geta’s name found, but only those of Severus and Caracalla.] If you ask about the “cactus and bramble of treacherous intimacy,” Plautianus, Severus’s closest intimate, had already been removed from the scene in A.D. 204 (see Tillemont, Histoire des Empereurs, loc. cit., p. 413 ff.). If you ask about “the hope of scorched Campania from its mountains” (ch. 2), Dio [Col. 0143A] Cassius expressly recorded it (LXXVI.2, p. 1272) at the time when Plautianus perished. Finally, if you ask about every aconite of hostility being rooted out and the repose of peace, these things certainly existed before Severus departed for Britain.

But where, then, had the barbarians been shut out? At that time they had not yet been kept out by the British wall, but they were nevertheless held back from the very frontiers of the Roman Empire by the defenses of the Roman legions. And since Tertullian speaks of many barbarians, what reason is there for us to understand the Britons alone? Therefore, since in A.D. 208 all those things mentioned by Tertullian were present; since no other year can be proposed to which they might be attributed with any greater right; and since, finally, the very recent memory of Geta’s dignity appears to have provided Tertullian with the occasion to mention it, [Col. 0143B] our conclusion—that On the Pallium belongs to A.D. 208—appears to fall little short of certainty.

## § 14.—It Is Proved That the Book *To Scapula* Appeared at the Beginning of the Reign of Antoninus Caracalla, in A.D. 211

The last book of this class—and, I believe, perhaps the last of all Tertullian’s works—is the one he wrote to Scapula, governor of Africa, whose cruelty against Christians undoubtedly occurred after the edict of the emperor Severus. For Hilarianus, whom Tertullian mentions in our little book, was governor of Africa at the time when Felicitas and Perpetua were put to death with their companions—an event which all acknowledge to have occurred after the laws enacted by Severus.

Moreover, from the very words with which Tertullian charges Scapula [Col. 0143C] with the greatest injustice, judging (ch. 4) that he could have discharged the duty of his jurisdiction while nevertheless remembering humanity, since nothing more was commanded than that those who confessed should be condemned, while those who denied should be recalled to torture—from these words, I say, it is fairly clearly inferred that certain laws of Severus hostile to Christians then existed. For before those laws had been issued, when the governors acted solely by the authority of those measures by which earlier emperors had harassed Christians, Tertullian argued vehemently against their force in the Apology.

[Col. 0143D] This point might indeed seem slight and need no distinct argument, had not Pamelius (Life of Tertullian, p. 13 C) thought that this book should be assigned to A.D. 195. How carelessly he argued is shown by the very words with which he says he was induced to think so: namely, that Tertullian included the supporters of Albinus among the emperor’s enemies (ch. 2).

Now, if it is true that the calamities by which Scapula persecuted the Christians came after Severus’s law, it is no less evident that they did not occur during Severus’s reign, although I see that this has pleased some scholars. For in the passage (On the Pallium, ch. 4) where Tertullian says that Severus, Antoninus’s father, had been mindful of Christians, and that Antoninus himself, nourished on Christian milk, had known Proculus, let someone tell me why he called Severus “Antoninus’s father,” a detail plainly irrelevant to the matter, or why he cited Antoninus himself as a witness, unless these words were written during Antoninus’s reign.

Nor indeed should this be doubted because we find no tortures of Christians under Caracalla recorded by other authors, or because such tortures could also be later than Caracalla’s time. [Col. 0144A] [Col. 0144A] The reason why no one else recorded them undoubtedly lies in the fact that they neither lasted long nor occurred outside Africa. For Tertullian now says that the Christian household was being attacked by the governor of the legion and of Mauretania, and he asks Scapula at least to spare Carthage and the province and to imitate the example of Arrius Antoninus, who in Asia had once diverted Christians from torture rather than dragged them to punishment.

[Col. 0144B] That these events were not later than Caracalla’s reign is established by the fact that Jerome (On Illustrious Men, ch. 73, Fabricius ed., p. 126) says that Tertullian did not live beyond the time of Antoninus; that, moreover, no hostilities against Christians of every kind are found down to Decius [Note: [Col. 0144D] Samuel Basnage sufficiently defended this against Scaliger and others, loc. cit., p. 218, no. 11.]; and that what is related in our little book agrees excellently with Caracalla’s period.

Although it has not been established with complete certainty in what year this defense of the Christians was composed, it nevertheless seems possible, by a measure of probability appropriate to such a matter, to claim it for the first year of Antoninus’s reign. For the solar eclipse which Tertullian says occurred in the previous year (ch. 3) was assigned by Antoninus Lalovera to A.D. 210. [Note: [Col. 0144D] In his letter to Joannes Bessonus, published by Petrus Possinus in the notes to the Acts of Perpetua and Felicitas, in Ruinart’s Acta primorum martyrum sincera, Amsterdam ed., p. 119.] Although Tillemont resists this on the ground that Tertullian said the sun could not have suffered this through an ordinary eclipse, since it was positioned at its own *hypsoma*, nevertheless Scaliger, the most expert in these matters, long ago ridiculed this method of argument employed by Septimius, who knows how repeatedly to turn everything—even things foolish enough—to his own purpose [Col. 0144C] (Animadversions on Eusebius’s Chronicle, p. 10).

Secondly, since Caracalla never enacted any law against Christians, these calamities inflicted upon them by Scapula must surely have been remnants of Severus’s cruelty. They appear to have been wholly extinguished when Caracalla, seeking to secure the empire for himself, recalled those who had been sent into exile (see Dio Cassius, LXXVII.3). Since he did this shortly after killing his brother Geta at the beginning of A.D. 212, we do not unreasonably say that Scapula acted against the Christians in A.D. 211.

# ARTICLE IV. On the Books of Tertullian Whose Date, Doctrine, or Both Are Unknown

[Col. 0144D]

## § 1.—The Third Class of Tertullian’s Books: Those Which, Although of Uncertain Date, Are Nevertheless Known to Have Been Written Before His Defection

This third discussion will bring to a close the Septimian studies that we have undertaken. Since we have thus far treated those books whose date and doctrine could be demonstrated by some definite method and reasoning, we must now append the others, which do not reveal their date [Col. 0145A] with sufficient precision, although their doctrine is nevertheless not very obscure—except in a few cases that appear to possess an equivocal character.

We shall therefore first adduce those earlier works which show that Tertullian was not yet wholly committed to the Montanist party; next, those upon which the marks of Montanism are by no means lightly impressed; and finally, those which leave the reader in doubt whether Tertullian, when he composed them, had been separated from the common Church or not.

When we say that the date of these three classes of Septimian works cannot be assigned with sufficient certainty, we do not mean that the date to be attributed to each is entirely unknown—for something can also be argued about it with probability—but rather that the precise year in which the books were written cannot be determined. This we venture [Col. 0145B] to deny, because there are in them no certain indications that can be assigned to a particular and definite year. But let us come to the matter proposed.

## § 2.—The Book *On Prayer*, Written Before the Defection and Published in 196 or 197
The work *On Prayer* may undoubtedly be said to belong to the first class. Unless I am greatly mistaken, it is the earliest of all Tertullian’s works that have survived; and by the broad consensus of all—if Hoffmann is excepted (*Dissertat. citat.* § 11, p. 37 sq.), whose interest it was to refer all Tertullian’s writings to his Montanist period—it is numbered among the works of purer doctrine. And even if the testimony of Hilary of Poitiers is perhaps suspect, though he indicates clearly enough that this little work was written before Tertullian’s defection, [Col. 0145C] nevertheless the book itself contains so many indications of opinions differing from those which he later defended in writings infected with Montanist errors that the doctrine of this book cannot be difficult to ascertain for anyone willing to compare the opinions expressed in the two groups of writings.

For first, how great are the praises bestowed here upon the work of Hermas entitled *The Shepherd*! When Tertullian shows that the practice of sitting down after prayer has ended, as observed by Hermas, does not conflict with his own position, he calls the work “almost Scripture,” and later—lest that “almost” furnish anyone with grounds for resenting our conclusion—he calls it “Scripture.”

> [Note: [Col. 0145D] Ch. 16. We use the edition of Lodovico Antonio Muratori, who published our little work, previously mutilated, in complete form from a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library in his *Anecdota Latina*, vol. III, p. 9 sq.]

Although I do not understand this, with Muratori (*loc. cit.*, note 3, p. 31) and others, as though Tertullian were placing the books of Hermas among the canonical books of the New Testament—for he is speaking more according to the customary language of his opponents than according to his own—he nevertheless does not scorn the authority of Hermas, [Col. 0145D] but brings it into agreement with his own position. This is very different from what he does in *On Modesty*, chs. 10 and 20, where he not only rejects the pronouncements of Hermas but calls that work spurious by universal consent, and calls him “the Shepherd of adulterers.”

I am therefore surprised that Hoffmann found this argument in Allix surprising. He supposed that Tertullian did not assail the *Shepherd* of Hermas in our little work because the authority of Hermas had not obstructed him so greatly as it did when he wrote *On Modesty*, and that there had consequently been no need to depreciate its worth. For even if we do not deny that the authority of Hermas was more adverse to Tertullian [Col. 0146A] in the matters discussed in *On Modesty*, his judgment concerning Hermas in our *On Prayer* is not merely much gentler but is even expressed in such a way that he himself appears not to have scorned the authority of Hermas altogether.

Moreover, the phrase “almost Scripture,” which Hoffmann thinks diminishes the force of this argument, has been explained by him quite ineptly, as though Tertullian had meant rashly to say that the title *Shepherd* was given to the little book of Hermas although it in no way deserved that title. For “almost Scripture” must certainly be understood to mean that the authority of the little work of Hermas was regarded as almost equal to that of the sacred books. This is clear from the fact that he afterward calls it “Scripture” without qualification; nor, in my opinion, would he have called it so if Hermas had been as contemptible to him as he was [Col. 0146B] at the time when *On Modesty* was written.

But there are also other statements of Tertullian here that differ greatly from those which he advanced in his Montanist works, and these show most clearly that Tertullian’s discipline was then very different from what it became afterward. In section 18 (p. 35 Murat.), for example, when disputing against those who, while abstaining from food, were also accustomed not to receive others with a kiss, he says that only on the day of Passover, on which there is a common and, as it were, public observance of fasting, may the kiss rightly be denied to others. This certainly shows that Tertullian then belonged to that sacred society which observed no day with public and common abstinence from food except the day on which Christ had died; for the Day of Passover is the day consecrated to the commemoration of Jesus’ death.

> [Note: [Col. 0146D] See, for example, *Against the Jews*, ch. 10.]

Indeed, the ancient Christians in Tertullian’s time [Col. 0146C] commonly observed only this day by fasting, because they said that the bridegroom had then been taken away. Yet Tertullian, in *On Fasting*, ch. 2—which undoubtedly belongs among his Montanist works—severely censures this custom of observing this one day alone through the common religious practice of fasting; and it is sufficiently clear that the Montanists observed several other days besides the anniversary of Christ’s death. From this the following conclusion is elicited: when Tertullian composed *On Prayer*, he had not yet withdrawn to the Montanist party.

This can be confirmed by a new argument drawn from the two little works. If anyone can reconcile their passages in any way other than that which we have stated—namely, from the difference in Tertullian’s discipline at the times when the two works were written—we shall hear him. For when, in [Col. 0146D] *On Prayer*, ch. 25, he turns to the question of the times at which prayers should be offered to God, he says that it is indeed good to assign certain fixed and settled hours, as it were, to prayer—namely the third, sixth, and ninth hours, which were also observed by the Apostles. But he adds that this is done without any prescribed observance, and that no prayers are commanded by law except the prescribed prayers, that is, those uttered at the rising of daylight and of night. And at the end of ch. 23 he says: “Concerning the times of prayer, absolutely nothing has been prescribed, except, of course, that one should pray at every time and in every place.”

But in *On Fasting* he assails with great bitterness the adherents of the orthodox Church [Col. 0147A] (ch. 2), because they said that abstention from food should be undertaken by free choice, not by command of the new discipline, according to the circumstances and reasons of each person, and because they generally concluded their prayers at the ninth hour, following Peter’s example. He adds expressly in ch. 10 that, while the liberty to pray always and everywhere and at every time remained entirely intact, those three hours were nevertheless more solemn occasions for divine prayer. And in ch. 13 he appeals to the very law given by the Paraclete, by which the latter had confirmed this Montanist custom. All these points undoubtedly prove that Tertullian’s opinion was entirely different when he composed *On Prayer*.

Finally, to omit many other considerations, this seems to me a powerful argument for assigning to our book orthodoxy: although he frequently discusses fasts and stations in this book, [Col. 0147B] he makes no mention of xerophagies, which he defends with such ardor in *On Fasting*, chs. 2, 5 sq. I doubt whether any other explanation of this omission can be given than that, when our little work was written, he belonged to that Church which, as he says in *On Fasting*, ch. 2, called xerophagies “a novel name for an affected duty, bordering upon pagan superstition.”

All these considerations seem to me far more worthy of attention than those which Hoffmann advances in defense of his opinion, to which we ourselves could, if necessary, add some others not wholly devoid of weight. He says, for instance, that the precepts given here in ch. 22 concerning the veiling of virgins are very similar to those defended by Tertullian in his book on that subject. But the case is quite otherwise. [Col. 0147C] For although he wishes virgins to be covered with a veil in both books, the mere agreement of the books on this point does not demonstrate that both proceeded from the same discipline. If anyone compares the passages of the two works carefully, he will find a great disagreement within Tertullian himself, one that confirms our judgment much more than Hoffmann’s.

In *On the Veiling of Virgins*, he defends this custom vehemently and above all from the law of the Montanists. But in our little work *On Prayer*, ch. 22, p. 43, he does not command this custom to be observed and says that even a law imposing the veil upon virgins can be excused; while at the beginning of that discussion, ch. 21, he treats as an uncertain question requiring reconsideration what is variously observed throughout the Churches: whether virgins ought to be veiled or not. The learned man’s argument is therefore slight. [Col. 0147D] He could more properly have cited ch. 6 as testimony for his opinion. There, after saying that the fourth petition of the Lord’s Prayer is to be understood not literally but figuratively of the sacred supper, Tertullian adds: “But also because this expression is understood carnally, it cannot be fulfilled without regard for religion and spiritual discipline.” Here “spiritual discipline” might give rise to some suspicion of a Montanist author, since the Montanists called themselves “spiritual” and others “psychic.”

Tertullian, however, could also have meant by “spiritual persons” any upright people and Christians, and I prefer this interpretation because not much later he explains these persons as “the faithful.” He contrasts them not with the orthodox, or “psychics,” but with the nations—that is, those who did not believe in Jesus. Nor have I found that Tertullian, even in his Montanist [Col. 0148A] books, denied the name “faithful” to the orthodox.

Since it is now established that this book belongs among those which contain the purer doctrine, it makes no difference what particular place one assigns it among Septimius’ writings of this kind. Since it has offered us not even the slightest suspicion of Montanist errors, we think it best to place it first within this class.

## § 3.—The Book *On Baptism* Written by Tertullian While a Catholic. The Arguments of Those Who Disagree Are Refuted

But it is more difficult to say what doctrine should be assigned to the book *On Baptism*. I am indeed aware that everyone judges the orthodoxy of this book to be placed beyond all doubt, with Hoffmann offering only slight opposition, as in the other cases. [Col. 0148B] Yet in this matter the levity of many learned men is astonishing. They have attributed to Tertullian the Montanist other books whose subject provides a definite indication of purity, while safely excluding from that class this book, even though its passages are so obscure that, if one searches in them for even the chief opinions either of the Montanists or of the orthodox, the mind, after examining everything, can scarcely see in which direction it should turn.

Nevertheless, so far as possible, let us determine whether the doctrine prevailing in our book inclines more toward the one side or the other. First I propose to examine the passages which create a suspicion of Montanism concerning this book, and then those—though more rarely advanced—which point in the contrary direction. To omit the objections hesitantly advanced by Baronius, whom Allix sufficiently refuted (*in Vit.* [Col. 0148C] *Tert.*, p. 29 sqq.), Hoffmann brings forward the following arguments in favor of the former position.

First, he argues that in *On Baptism* Tertullian uses statements similar to those he defended in *On Modesty*, since he assails those who assumed for themselves the power to grant pardon for offenses, though that power belonged to God alone. Unless I am mistaken, Hoffmann finds an indication of this in the words: “Neither does anyone forgive sin nor grant the Spirit except God alone.” I do not perceive how these words could have been uttered only by an author devoted to the discipline of Montanus. For the members of the orthodox Church did not deny this, nor was it a matter disputed between them and the Montanists. Rather, although those orthodox Christians assigned the power of forgiving sins to God alone, they did not think that peace should be denied to those who had been [Col. 0148D] cast out of the sacred society on account of sins, provided that they promised to reform their lives.

The learned man next says that this book belongs to a time filled with calamities inflicted upon Christians by the worshipers of the gods. This is certainly a slight conjecture. For the statement in ch. 16 of our book, which he calls as a witness—“We also have a second washing, namely that of blood”—in no way indicates that danger was then immediately present. Even if such danger had actually been mentioned by Tertullian, the book could not on that account be relegated among the writings filled with the errors of Montanus. For there are many writings of Tertullian which, as we showed in Dissertation I, were contemporary with these calamities but were composed before his defection.

Nor does the very manner of speaking by which Tertullian calls suffering a kind of baptism immediately reveal a Montanist, unless we wish to say that Origen also and others—whose passages are collected by Dodwell (*Dissert. Cyprian.* XIII, on the second baptism of martyrdom, especially § 2)—though they were never accused of Montanism, must on this account be regarded as adherents of the Montanist society. [Col. 0149A]

> [Note: [Col. 0149B] But someone might say that Christian authors who lived after Tertullian, once the highest esteem had arisen for those who had publicly confessed Christ by undergoing either death or torture, adopted this form of speech, like many other things, from the Montanists. Consequently, their passages would not be suitable for freeing this language from suspicion of Montanism, especially since it first appears in Tertullian and in the writings of other Montanists, as in the *Acts of Perpetua and Felicity* (§ 22).
>
> I may perhaps dispel this suspicion with another conjecture, if I show that Marcion himself had already employed the same manner of speaking. Epiphanius, *Haeres.* XLII, § 3, Cologne ed., p. 304, says that Marcion defended three baptisms (οὐ μόνον παρ` αὐτῷ ἓν λοῦτρον δίδονται, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἕως τριῶν λούτρων, “with him not only one baptism is given, but as many as three”).
>
> Although, in relating this, we grant that Epiphanius [Col. 0149C] mingled falsehoods with truth—as when he says that Marcion devised a threefold baptism in order to purify himself from an outrage committed with a virgin, which, as many have shown, is sheer calumny; and also when he says that Marcion administered baptism three times, a statement which in no way agrees with the argument by which this threefold baptism was confirmed, as will become clear below—I nevertheless judge that Epiphanius’ testimony should not be wholly despised. It will therefore be worthwhile briefly to show what this threefold baptism of Marcion was.
>
> I. There are many features in Marcion’s discipline similar to Manichaean discipline, and it is established that Manes divided his followers into Hearers and Elect. Therefore I am inclined to think that the same division may perhaps be assigned to the Marcionites, since Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, ch. 7, appears to indicate that Marcion denied permission to marry only to the more holy among his followers, in these words: “Marcion removes all sexual intercourse from the Faithful; as for his catechumens, they may see to themselves.” Here he could have called the less perfect “catechumens” in the same manner in which Epiphanius and others also use this name for the Hearers of the Manichaeans. Nor is it credible that Marcion abolished all marriage universally among his followers, since, as is established, he regarded the author of marriage not as the evil God but as that intermediate God whom he called just. [Col. 0149D]
>
> From this, II, it may reasonably be conjectured with Beausobre (*Histoire du Manichéisme*, vol. II, p. 122) that one baptism of Marcion was conferred upon everyone, while the Marcionites admitted to the inner circle were initiated by a second. This is especially so because Epiphanius expressly adds: ἔξεστι διδόναι, “it is permitted to give” (namely, λοῦτρον, “a baptism”) παρ` αὐτοῖς τῷ βουλομένῳ, “among them, to anyone who wishes”. This would conflict with all Tertullian’s passages on that subject, in which he says that everyone wishing to be washed in the sacred laver by the Marcionites had to renounce marriage (book IV, *Against Marcion*, ch. 11; book I, ch. 29; etc.), unless we admit this double baptism.
>
> But now, III, it remains to say what Marcion understood the third baptism to be; and this is the matter properly at issue for us. The manner in which it should be understood is taught most clearly by the argument with which Epiphanius says Marcion confirmed his threefold baptism. It was drawn from the passage in Luke (ch. XII, 50) where Christ undoubtedly speaks of his own suffering and of a certain baptism still impending over him—a passage which we see was also adduced by others to defend a second baptism of martyrdom. Moved by this consideration, I conclude without any doubt that Marcion also gave the name of a kind of baptism to the sufferings undertaken by Christians after the example of Jesus Christ.]

Finally, Hoffmann says that in the same passage Tertullian indicates clearly enough that the Montanists were wrongfully expelled from the society of the universal Church, since they and the other Christians had one God, one baptism, and finally one Church in heaven, while there was no fellowship with the other heretics (ch. 15). This argument certainly lends no support to his opinion. For Tertullian does not say a single word about the agreement of the Montanists with the orthodox in that doctrine. Rather, he contrasts that faith of the Christians with the heresy of the Caians, and shows that the latter were spurious Christians because communion with the other Christians had been taken away from them. [Col. 0149B]

And if what Hoffmann supposes were true, Tertullian would be so far from defending himself against the wrong inflicted upon the Montanists that he would instead have confessed that he and the Montanists were heretics. For in that very ch. 15 he says that heretics are outsiders—that is, non-Christians—as the very removal of communion testifies. Therefore, if Tertullian had indicated in this passage that the orthodox had expelled the Montanists from the Church, he would certainly have called himself and his associates heretics, which is wholly inconceivable. [Col. 0150A]

Here we must also address another difficulty advanced by Allix against the accepted opinion concerning the doctrine prevailing in this book (*Diss. de Tertulliani vita et scriptis*, ch. 4, p. 33). He says that we might suspect that Tertullian’s mind was already inclined toward the discipline of Montanus because he called Christians “little fishes” and Christ “the FISH” (ΙΧΘΥΣ, “FISH”). These names, he says, were drawn from the Sibylline books, [Col. 0150B] composed by some Montanist or even by Montanus himself. Moreover, in ch. 20 Tertullian mentioned certain charisms, which seemed to savor of Montanism, particularly when those statements are compared with what is taught in ch. 29 of *On the Spectacles*. But Allix did well not to regard this suspicion itself as excessively subtle or acute.

For even if we granted that the books now passed off under the name of the Sibylline books were fabricated either by Montanus or by one of his disciples—though I would rather assign them to some Gnostic—and that Tertullian also derived from them this name “Fish” given to Christ, nevertheless this argument could no more make Tertullian suspect of Montanism when he composed this book than it could Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and others [Col. 0150C] who frequently cite certain Sibylline books as testimony. And even if those books existed in general form at this very time, who can guarantee that they were not later interpolated so as to assume the form which they now possess?

This is especially to be feared in the acrostic of the eighth book, Ιησοῦς Χρίστος Θεοῦ υἱὸς σώτηρ, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior”, from which the common people suppose that this very surname ἰχθύος, “of the FISH” was taken. For it was not set forth by any of the ancients before Constantine the Great (*Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, ch. 18). From the very fact that he says Virgil sang of the birth of Jesus Christ (ch. 19 sqq.), it is clear how easily he could be deceived by men fabricating religion.

> [Note: [Col. 0150C] It may perhaps seem strange that our most learned Author, so highly knowledgeable in the ancient discipline, should hesitate [Col. 0150D] anxiously, as it were, upon an open road and doubt uncertainly whether the well-known token ΙΧΘΥΣ, “FISH” was more peculiar to Christians or to Montanists; and even that he should assert that the same symbolic acrostic had been set forth by none of the ancients before Constantine the Great.
>
> Many things occur that might be said on the contrary side. Until we reach the book *On Baptism*, however, it is better to postpone their treatment to the proper place. For now it is pleasing to anticipate only a few points, briefly and in readiness.
>
> Indeed, more than enough innumerable monuments answer the first point—monuments fully sufficient, of unquestionable antiquity, and genuinely produced and dedicated by Christian hands. In them the aforesaid token stands out, whether cut by a chisel, cast in bronze, carved in ivory, depicted in colors, expressed in letters, or adorned with verses; and, as generally happens, it is mingled with other signs and sigla from which one may infer the pure and unalloyed integrity of the sounder faith. Thus the fish is very frequently depicted with the dove (Aringhi, vol. I, 580; vol. II, 258), or joined to an anchor or to Christ’s monogram, which, as everyone knows, had come into common use long before the Constantinian *labarum* (Boldett., 370, 366, 453; Aringhi, I, 520; II, 327, 620; Bottari, III, 19). At one time it is placed at the feet of figures in prayer, [Col. 0151C] at another beside the Good Shepherd (Bold., 573; Bolt., pl. XXXV. See also and compare Costadoni, *dissertazione sopra i pesce come simbolo de primi cristiani*; *Raccolta d’opuscoli scientifici da Calogera*, vol. XLI, 1749.—Lupi, *dissert. ad Severae Epitaphium*, Palermo, 1734, pp. 103, 136, 145, 153, 165, 185.—Fabretti, *Inscript. antiq.*, book VIII, p. 569, nos. 124–126; p. 590, no. 107.—Münter, *Sinnbilder und Kunstvorstellungen der alten Christen*.—Thiersch, *Jahres-Berichte der Koeniglich Bayerschen Akademie der Wissenschaften*. Munich, 1829.)
>
> Nor are the written and sculpted testimonies proving the use of the Sibylline acrostic to be far older than Constantine the Great either fewer in number or of suspect credibility. Indeed, one may marvel at how great a host of witnesses concerning this matter rises from the apostolic age down to our own times. They seem, as it were, to join hands with certain traditions from the earliest age of humankind, diffused in every direction and, once the Church had arisen in the midst of the ages, renewed and revived within her own bosom; until, when peace had been established throughout the world, the fish and the dove, and all the other symbolic signs or sigla that had flourished in concealment, came openly into the light. [Col. 0151D]
>
> For now, therefore, concerning the ΙΧΘΥΟΣ, “of the FISH” acrostic, let it suffice merely to refer to certain Fathers: namely Clement of Alexandria in four passages, vol. I, pp. 260, 312, 289, and 787, Potter; and our own Tertullian in *On Baptism*, *On the Resurrection*, and *On the Spectacles*, as there will be an opportunity to discuss more fully below.
>
> Nor should we omit to add two ancient marble inscriptions recently excavated and published: one through the care of D. Raoul-Rochette, *Mémoires de l’Académie royale des inscriptions*, vol. XIII, p. 98, and D. Thiersch, at the place cited; the other dug up from the most ancient cemetery of St. Peter near the city of Autun, beside the paved road, and printed in the work entitled *Annales de philosophie chrétienne*, vol. XIX.
>
> Compare further Costadoni, §§ 23–27, 30, 33; Secchi, *epigramma greco cristiano de’ primi secoli trovata preso l’antica Augstoduno*, Rome, 1840.—Franz, *Christliches Denkmal von Autun erkloït*, Berlin, 1841. EDD.]

And [Col. 0151A] even if I concede everything he wishes, not even the points gathered in this learned man’s argument can stand or agree with one another. The earliest Christian writers, as William Beveridge (*In codice canonum Ecclesiae primitivae*, book I, ch. 14, § 4 sqq.) and William Whiston demonstrate at length, acknowledge that the books they call Sibylline are exceedingly ancient.

> [Note: [Col. 0151D] In easily the best of his books: *A Vindication of the Sibylline Oracles*, Proposition 10, p. 36 sq.]

From this it follows necessarily that those books were very different from the writings which falsely claim their name in our time, and which appear even to our opponent to have been composed in the second century after the birth of Christ. What is more, the very Tertullian about whom we are inquiring, at the time when he was very near to his defection, calls the Sibyl’s pronouncements exceedingly ancient in ch. 12 of the books *To the Nations*. Could he therefore have thought the Sibylline books to have proceeded from Montanus or from anyone belonging to that flock? [Col. 0151B]

Nor does the second point which Allix adds concerning a charism prove anything. I confess that in the cited ch. 20 I do not find a sufficiently clear mention of it. Even if it were found, it would no more follow that *On Baptism* had issued from the workshop of Tertullian the Montanist than the same could be said of *On the Spectacles*, which was undoubtedly written before his defection, as I demonstrated elsewhere.

And lest we pass over in silence anything by which someone might in some way lend truth to this opinion adverse to our book *On Baptism*, he might perhaps appeal to ch. 20 of this little work, where Tertullian says that abstinence from food is highly useful for avoiding the solicitations of sin. This might seem to agree with the praises of fasting [Col. 0151C] which he celebrated in *On Fasting*. Still more suspect is his statement at the end of ch. 8: “The person who renews his offenses after baptism is destined for the fire.” [Col. 0152A]

Yet neither of these two propositions was so alien to the discipline of those who held the correct faith as to be peculiar to the Montanists. For in the former there is nothing that could not be admitted, even if in other passages Tertullian attributes too much to this abstinence. The latter was either defended—though in an inept sense—even by certain adherents of the orthodox Church, as will be shown later, or it could properly be said of those who, after baptism, had fallen into an impious life and gave no thought to reforming it.

## § 4.—Pamelius and Dupin Are Corrected. The Book’s Freedom from Montanism Is Demonstrated.

But come, let us also hear the far more numerous scholars who unanimously acknowledge that the book *On Baptism* was written before Tertullian’s separation [Col. 0152B]. Among these, the error of those such as Pamelius is foolish: following Epiphanius, as it were (*Haer.* 42, nos. 1–2), they suppose that the Quintilla who furnished the occasion for composing this book belonged to the Montanist school. Since Tertullian opposed this woman even with insults, it would follow that, when he wrote this book, he still stood with the party of the purer Church. That argument would certainly settle the entire matter, had not Epiphanius—a man most careless in expounding the opinions of heretics—here too surrendered himself, in his usual fashion, to error. For Tertullian himself says in chapter 1 that this woman belonged to the sect of the Cainites, whose doctrines and customs differ greatly from Montanist discipline; nor do we ever read that baptism was rejected by the Montanists, [Col. 0152C] but rather that it was defended in many places by Tertullian as a Montanist, as in *On Modesty*, chapter 19.

Dupin, however (*Nouvelle bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. I, p. 91), has two other arguments by which he places this book in the catalogue of writings of sounder doctrine.
