The first is that no Montanist errors are scattered through the book; the second, that Tertullian says the power of conferring baptism belongs only to bishops and that it is even unlawful to grant it to women. These words of Tertullian appear to him contrary to Montanist discipline. Yet anyone can easily evade the former argument by saying that this book was not directed against the doctrines of the orthodox Church. It would therefore be nothing surprising if Tertullian professed no disagreement with that Church here, [Col. 0152D] since he did not do so in other works either when he saw no need to contend with the Psychics, as in the book *On the Pallium* and the other works discussed above.

But in Dupin’s second argument falsehood is mixed with truth. Accordingly, we shall discuss later what may rightly be drawn from it in support of the uncorrupted doctrine of this book, and here we shall note only one error of that learned man. He evidently suspects that the Montanists gave women the power to teach publicly; and because Tertullian denies them this license in our treatise, he thinks that the work is not among the Montanist writings. In this he is undoubtedly mistaken. We would establish the contrary here from Tertullian’s own Montanist-infected writings—for example, from *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 9—had not that discussion already been undertaken by the distinguished Theophilus Wernsdorf (*Commentatio de Montanistis saec. 2. vulgo creditis haereticis*, [Col. 0153A] Gdańsk, 1751, § 19).

We must therefore explain what moves us to think that judgment concerning our book should incline toward the more honorable rather than the worse conclusion. There are two grounds for this judgment. First, when Tertullian treats the question of those who possess the right to confer baptism (chapter 17), he says that the chief priest, who is the bishop, possesses that power in the highest degree, and after him the presbyters and deacons, though not without the bishop’s authority, because of the honor of the Church. “Otherwise,” he continues, “the right belongs even to laymen”—but since these matters belong to superiors, laymen should not assume for themselves the office of the episcopate, which is assigned to bishops.

From this it follows that Tertullian wrote our book while he belonged to some sacred assembly which both regarded bishops as the highest [Col. 0153B] governors of sacred affairs and granted laymen the right to wash someone in the sacred laver only when they found themselves in the utmost necessity. But a very different custom appears to have prevailed in the conventicles of the Montanists. For although I do not deny that they too had their own presbyters and deacons, Jerome bears witness that a different order was observed in appointing their teachers (*Letter to Marcella*, no. 27 in the edition of Jean Martianay, vol. IV, part II, p. 65):

> Among us, he says, the bishops hold the place of the apostles; among them, the bishop ranks third. For they have first the patriarchs of Pepuza, second those whom they call *Cenones*, and thus bishops are relegated to the third—that is, almost the last—place.

If anyone wishes to say that this Montanist custom was invented by Jerome [Col. 0153C] or was later than Tertullian’s age, I neither see what could have moved Jerome to invent things that could not be charged against the Montanists as a grave offense, nor is it in any way improbable that those who had separated themselves from the common Church by their doctrines or institutions should also have established an order of priests different from common custom—especially since Montanus himself had already called Pepuza, a town in Phrygia, Jerusalem (see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 18).

And now observe how much honor Tertullian claims for bishops in our treatise, since he derives from them all power of baptizing with sacred water and teaches that the honor of the Church itself is most closely joined to their dignity. But in the book *On Modesty*, that most vehement assault upon the custom of the orthodox Church, [Col. 0153D] how sharply, I ask, does he ridicule (chapter 1) “the Supreme Pontiff, the Bishop of Bishops,” and his peremptory edict! How little he grants to so great a man—to one upon whom, as he says here, the dignity of the Church depended!

And if anyone thinks—as I do not deny—that Tertullian brought great emotional agitation to the cause in that book, I shall offer another passage from the undoubtedly Montanist book *On the Exhortation to Chastity*. This passage, as it seems to me, grants laymen far greater license to confer baptism than he had defended in our book, as I now see that a great man, whom I name with honor, Justus Henning Böhmer, acutely observed (*Dissertatio IX Juris Ecclesiastici antiqui*, § 5). There, after Tertullian had said that repeated marriages were permitted neither to the priests of the Old Testament nor to the priests of the Christian [Col. 0154A] Church, he says that laymen ought not to contract them either, since they themselves had been constituted priests by Christ, and for that reason they too possessed the power of offering and baptizing and were priests to themselves.

Although he says that this should not be done except where no assembly of the ecclesiastical order is present, nevertheless he neither introduces any mention of the authority of bishops or the other public teachers, as he does in our book, nor derives this power of laymen from the reciprocal character of duties and rights, as he does here:

> **Note [Col. 0154D].** Thus in *On Baptism*, chapter 16: “Laymen too possess the right to confer baptism; for what is received on equal terms may be given on equal terms.”

Rather, he derives it entirely from the mystical priesthood of all Christians. From this, unless I am mistaken, a strong suspicion may be drawn that Tertullian’s discipline when writing those books infected by the errors of Montanus was entirely different from his discipline when he applied his mind to writing our book. [Col. 0154B]

And to confirm this further, I shall propose here a conjecture of my own—not because I think that I cannot be mistaken in it, but in order to offer those capable of judging the matter something by which they may determine whether it has any force in commending our case to learned men. In chapter 17 of our book Tertullian refutes an argument which the persons against whom he was contending were accustomed to take from certain *Acts of Paul*, in order to claim for women the power of teaching publicly. If I can show what these *Acts of Paul* were and who their author was, then it seems to me that Tertullian could scarcely have rejected them if he had written this book *On Baptism* after already devoting himself to Montanist discipline.

I suspect that these *Acts* were those which we know existed among the ancients under the title *Acts of Paul and Thecla*. They were not, indeed, in the condition and form in which they appear in the edition published by Johann Ernst Grabe (*Spicilegium SS. Patrum et Haereticorum*, vol. I, section 1, p. 95 ff.), for those texts were undoubtedly corrupted in later times. Nevertheless, in Grabe’s version there are certain traces or fragments, as it were, of those *Acts of Thecla* which were famous among the ancients—for example, on p. 115, the passage in which Paul confers upon Thecla the power to communicate Christ’s doctrine publicly to others. [Col. 0154C]

This very circumstance, I think, shows that in the passage cited Tertullian had these *Acts of Thecla* before his eyes, because he mentions a certain fictitious writing which falsely claimed the name of the apostle Paul and in which women were granted this license to teach. We shall confirm this further below. But if it is asked who fabricated these spurious acts under the name of the apostle Paul, I have no doubt that the heretic Leucius—whom people commonly, but wrongly, consider a Manichaean—was the author of the *Acts* cited by Tertullian. The reasons for this judgment should be explained briefly.

First, it cannot be denied that Leucius fabricated certain *Acts* of Paul, just as he did of the other apostles. This is attested by Photius (*Bibliotheca*, section 114, p. 156 in my edition), who had often examined such writings. Second, the exceptionally learned and highly discriminating Isaac de Beausobre demonstrated admirably that Leucius belonged not to the Manichaean but to the Docetic or Encratite school (*Histoire critique de Manichée et du Manichéisme*, book II, chapter 2, § 2 ff.). [Col. 0155A] Their principal error consisted in contempt for marriage; and the entire purpose of the *Acts of Paul and Thecla* is to extol with the highest praises a life lived without marriage. Many other works were likewise fabricated by Leucius under the names of the apostles in order to confirm that error by the apostles’ own teaching and practice.

Furthermore, Beausobre demonstrated by many arguments, in the place cited, that Leucius already existed in the second century; and Epiphanius (*Haer.* LI.6, p. 427) most plainly calls Leucius a disciple of the apostle John. Therefore these *Acts of Paul*, which we have said had Leucius as their author, existed in Tertullian’s time; and [Col. 0155B] it is highly probable that Tertullian intended to designate none other than the *Acts* of Leucius. For he says that the author of these *Acts* was a presbyter who, after being convicted of fraud in the matter, was removed from his place—that is, deposed from his sacred office.

If anyone adds to this Jerome (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 7, p. 104), who expressly says that according to Tertullian this presbyter was convicted before John and removed from public office because of the fraud he had committed, he will surely see that the author of the *Acts of Paul and Thecla* was subject to the authority of the apostle John—which, as I have just shown, can very well be said of Leucius.

Finally, it happened most conveniently for me that I found some indication of this matter also in Philastrius (*On Heresies*, chapter 55, Fabricius’s edition, p. 112), in the passage where he discusses the heretic Seleucus and his [Col. 0155C] doctrine. All acknowledge that the heretic Seleucus and our Leucius are the same person. Now observe, I ask, what Philastrius says about Seleucus and his followers:

> They do not use baptism because of this saying spoken by John the Baptist: “He will baptize you in spirit and fire.”

Nothing could be more similar to the errors that Tertullian refutes in the book *On Baptism*. The heretics against whom he argues there denied that Christians ought to be baptized in the sacred laver; and one of them adapts John’s own words about baptism through spirit and fire to his position. What, therefore, is more probable than that Tertullian’s adversaries adhered to the opinion of Leucius, who, according to Philastrius, had said precisely the same thing?

Let no one object to me that Seleucus, or Leucius, of whom Philastrius speaks was a Manichaean and was different from Leucius, the disciple of the apostle John; or that Philastrius was a man of no authority, [Col. 0155D] and that therefore we ought not trust this witness, whose credibility walks so unsteadily. For Beausobre, in the place cited, § 3, has sufficiently maintained against Fabricius that this distinction is fictitious and nonexistent. Nor am I unaware that Philastrius is indeed a trifler in very many matters, even in enumerating Seleucus’s errors themselves, not all of which can certainly be attributed to Leucius, the disciple of John. Yet who would dare to say that no seeds of truth lie concealed among those Philastrian trifles?

Let this therefore be established: when Tertullian rejected the *Acts of Paul* in our book, he rejected a writing fabricated by Leucius, who defended in every way the righteousness of a life passed without marriage. I now wish to appeal to Pacian, bishop of Barcelona [Col. 0156A] in the fourth century, who writes (*Letter I to Sympronian the Novatian*, published in the *Bibliotheca maxima Patrum*, Lyon edition, vol. IV, p. 305G):

> The Phrygians—that is, the Montanists—falsely claim that they were inspired by Leucius.

Nor does that testimony appear to depart from the truth, because it is certain that the Montanists, just like the Encratites, to whose school Leucius belonged, attributed excessive merit to those who recoiled from marriage. From this I believe the following conclusion may be reached: if Tertullian had written our book while established among the disciples of Montanus, he would have spoken more cautiously about a book whose author was Leucius and would not have accused him of fraud, since Leucius himself agreed with the Montanists.

But if anyone replies that the force of our case escapes us because it is not sufficiently established whether Tertullian knew the author of these *Acts*—although ignorance of this is scarcely credible in so inquisitive an investigator of all antiquity—I shall grant that, if one prefers. Yet in turn everyone should grant me this: unless someone establishes the contrary position, this suspicion should at least prevent us from casting this book of Tertullian into the class of works that he composed after his separation from the orthodox. [Col. 0156B]

## § 5.—The Two Books *To His Wife* Written Before Tertullian’s Fall

I now come to the books that Tertullian addressed to his wife. That they were published together is placed beyond doubt by the beginning of the latter book:

> **Note [Col. 0156C].** “Most recently I explained to you … what a holy woman ought to pursue.”

Although these books contain things that appear consonant with Montanist errors, I would nevertheless venture to place them rather among the works that he wrote before that defection. This appears to me to be confirmed, first, by the fact that Tertullian nowhere boasts of his Paraclete in matters in which that figure’s pronouncements would have possessed great authority. For, to use this example, at the end of chapter 7 of book I, where he argues that it is better to avoid second marriages, he does not invoke the Paraclete—whom he never fails to invoke in books proceeding from the Montanist school—but appeals solely to the authority of the Church’s discipline and the law of the Apostle, by which, he says, those who had contracted a second [Col. 0157A] marriage were excluded from public office.

> **Note [Col. 0156C].** Unless I am mistaken, this passage, and that other passage cited from *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 7—not to mention many others—plainly teaches that the ancient Christian Church understood Paul’s words in 1 Timothy 3:3 concerning a bishop, “μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνδρι (“a husband of one wife”),” in such a way that Paul was speaking of the second marriages of teachers.
>
> For in that passage of Tertullian, after he had said that such marriages were forbidden to the priests of the Old Testament, he says: “For Christ was reserving, in this matter as in the others, [Col. 0156D] the fullness of the law. Hence among us it is prescribed more fully and explicitly that those chosen for the priestly order must be of one marriage. Indeed, I remember some twice-married men being deposed from their place.”
>
> Here he neither intends this to be understood of priests who used some prostitute in addition to a wife, as Heumann thought in *Erklärung des N. T.*, part IX, p. 179, nor speaks in the manner of the Montanists. For Tertullian’s entire purpose opposes Heumann’s interpretation: he plainly speaks of the curtailed license to marry repeatedly, and in chapter 6 of God’s twofold dispensation—the first, “Increase and multiply,” and the second, “The time is now shortened,” etc.—by which God abolished the former.
>
> Nor does he mention an opinion peculiar to the Montanists, but one common to them and the Catholics. For first, in similar passages of *On Monogamy*, chapter 11, he convicts his adversaries of the inequity of repeated marriages by saying that they request such a marriage from persons who are not permitted to have one: from a monogamous bishop; from presbyters and deacons under the same sacramental rule; from widows as well; and from laymen. He also argues that the Apostle forbade such marriages because he orders the entire rank of the Church—that is, the priests—to be drawn from the once-married. [Col. 0157D]
>
> All these things show that the Catholics rejected second marriages among priests, since from the Catholics’ own opinions he concludes that marriages of this kind cannot be permitted even to laymen. And in chapter 12 he says most plainly that the Catholics argued as follows: “He bound only those who are in the clergy to the yoke of monogamy; therefore he does not prescribe it for everyone.”
>
> Next, he attributes this institution, by which second marriages were abolished, not to the Paraclete but to Christ, and adduces the Apostle’s words, who prescribed more fully and explicitly than in the Old Testament that those chosen for the priestly order must be of one marriage. Then he immediately adds: “Indeed, I remember twice-married men being deposed from their place.” This must be understood of Catholics, for the Montanists would not have tolerated even a layman guilty of a second marriage.
>
> In our present passage, however, he speaks as follows: “How greatly second marriages detract from faith, how greatly they obstruct holiness, is declared by the discipline of the Church and the Apostle’s prescription, since it does not permit the twice-married to preside, and does not allow a widow to be chosen for the order unless she has been the wife of one man.”

I am inclined to think that these words are less suited to a Montanist writer than to one who followed the doctrines of the more rightly believing Church. Next, in the same section, he does not say that his wife would act wrongly if she entered a new marital union; and he adds, in accordance with the thought of the apostle Paul, not that second marriages are dishonorable, but that they nevertheless bring considerable anxiety and misfortunes. Nor in book II, chapter 1 does he commend abstinence from a new marriage on any other ground than that it brings greater advantage. This is excessive leniency in a Montanist writer, whose discipline ranked every second marriage among the gravest vices.

Finally, in book II he permits his wife to enter a new union after his death, and imposes no stricter law than that she marry a Christian; and in chapter 1 he says that difficult circumstances readily obtain pardon. [Col. 0157B] But how did the Montanists receive those who returned to marriage?

> “We keep the twice-married outside,” says Tertullian at the end of *On Modesty*, chapter 1; “we fix the same boundary for adulterers and fornicators as well … they will receive from the Church no more than the public exposure of their disgrace.”

This, evidently, is what it means to grant pardon readily.

It is now not difficult to judge whether such clear passages, which support the case we have proposed, can be overthrown by some resemblance between certain statements in these books and the positions that Montanus’s more severe discipline persuaded Tertullian to adopt elsewhere. Hoffmann, in the place cited, § 12, has only one argument: that these books were written after the question of flight in danger on account of religion had been debated, and after Tertullian, together with the Montanists, had denied that anyone ought to seek safety by that means. Yet this single argument is so far from moving us to adopt his opinion that it draws us still further from it. For the very passage that he produces from book I, chapter 3—

> “Even in persecutions it is better to flee from the town, when permitted, than to be caught, tortured, and deny”—

sufficiently teaches that Tertullian did not consider every flight in such a crisis unlawful. It therefore confirms that, at the time when he composed these books, he agreed less with the Montanists than with the others. [Col. 0157C]

# ARTICLE V  
## The Fourth Class of Books, in Which Nothing but Montanism Is Evident

## § 1.—The Book *On Patience*, Written in A.D. 200 or 201

[Col. 0157D]

For this reason let us remove these books as well from the number of Montanist works [Col. 0158A] and consider those which may more properly be referred to that class. Among them I do not hesitate to place first the golden book *On Patience*. For although Tillemont (*Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire ecclésiastique*, vol. III, p. 262) wishes to join it to those works that precede Tertullian’s defection to the Montanists, because it neither rejects flight amid public calamities inflicted upon Christians on account of religion nor abandons great moderation, I consider neither argument at all suitable for establishing this conclusion.

As for that moderation, I do not see why Tertullian could not have employed it even after he had adopted hostility toward the orthodox, since it is not a virtue peculiar to the rightly believing. And the other argument does not even possess the truth attributed to it. For in the passage from which Tillemont attempts to derive Tertullian’s permission to flee (chapter 13), flight is by no means permitted. Rather, patience itself is affirmed to supply strength to human weakness, and fire, the cross, wild beasts, and the sword are said to be conquered by steadfastness itself. [Col. 0158B]

Yet even in this splendid little book there are several things which show that Tertullian’s mind was by no means lightly tinged with Montanist errors; indeed, almost all the errors of the Montanists are presented there. The indication of the Paraclete is admittedly rather obscure, yet there is some indication in this passage, chapter 1, where the grace of divine inspiration alone works toward comprehending and fulfilling these things.

Further, the excellence of marriages not repeated is presented in approximately these terms in chapter 13:

> “Patience also ministers continence of the flesh to holiness; it keeps the widow, dedicates the virgin, and raises the voluntary eunuch to the kingdoms of heaven.”

Likewise, in chapter 12 he stigmatizes second marriages with the name of adultery. The highest praise of fasting undertaken by one’s own decision appears in the following passage, chapter 13:

> “The affliction of the flesh is a propitiatory victim to the Lord through the sacrifice of humiliation, when, amid squalor and restricted nourishment, it makes an offering to the Lord, content with simple food and a pure draught of water; when it joins fasts together; when it becomes habituated to ashes and sackcloth.”

I have already spoken of flight. Finally, is the denial of pardon to sinners excluded from the sacred fellowship not contained in the words of chapter 12, where he places all the sinners’ hope not in pardon obtained from members of the Church, but in that salvation which Christians, awaiting their amendment, would either desire or obtain by prayer? Beyond this, nothing was to be expected from the Montanists’ sacred community (see [Col. 0158D] *On Modesty*, end of chapter 1).

Although these Montanist errors can be discerned in this book only through certain coverings, as it were, nothing follows from that except that this little book belongs to a period when Tertullian’s zeal in defending Montanist doctrines had either not yet blazed up or had somehow subsided. The date of this work is therefore insufficiently certain. I would not greatly doubt that it was written when danger to the Christians was already imminent, since a not unreasonable ground for this opinion is to be sought in the book’s very subject. But whether Tertullian wrote it amid the fears aroused by Scapula against the Christians during Caracalla’s reign, as Allix believed, or at the beginning of the public calamities under the emperor Severus—when that equally calm and temperate treatise *On Flight in Persecution* also appeared—no one could easily say. [Col. 0159A] Let us therefore pass to another work.

## § 2.—The Book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, Which Is Very Probably the First of the Montanist Books

This is the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, which I scarcely doubt belongs among the first works filled with Montanus’s errors. The extremely frequent mention of the Paraclete and of his new discipline does not allow us to hesitate about it; thus it is not even necessary to cite either the similarity of this book to the works *On the Dress of Women*, which belong to the Montanist school, or its rather obscure defense of single marriage in chapter 3.

For what is signified by those revelations by which, as Tertullian says in chapter 17, [Col. 0159B] the Lord measured out the dimensions of the veil? What is that novelty of correction which, while the rule of faith contained in the Apostles’ Creed remains fixed, the other matters of discipline and conduct admit through the grace of God working and advancing to the end (chapter 1)? What is that Paraclete whom the Lord sent so that discipline might gradually be directed and brought to perfection (ibid.)? What is that account of the ages of Christian discipline, in which righteousness is finally to be brought to maturity through the Paraclete? What, I ask, do all these things attest except that Tertullian was a disciple of Montanus?

Nor is it any more obscure that this was approximately the first offspring he produced after joining the Montanists. For—to begin with this—among all his Montanist books there is scarcely one in which he employs greater force to defend Montanist discipline against the charge of novelty than the book under consideration, especially in sections 1 and 2. [Col. 0159C] This certainly provides reasonable grounds for suspecting that Tertullian composed it as soon as he joined the Montanists, in order to remove from himself the accusation of innovation.

Nor in any other work does he seem to defend more strongly the Paraclete and the divine origin of his discipline than in this one. Since elsewhere (*Against Praxeas*, chapter 1) he says that not only his acknowledgment of the Paraclete but his defense of him separated him from the Psychics, it is easy to understand that our book, in which he certainly defends him vehemently, was written during the opening period of his life among the Montanists.

This may be confirmed by many arguments not lacking in probability. First, the books *On the Dress of Women* were written at precisely that time, as we argued elsewhere, and they treat almost the same subject as our book. Second, although Tertullian had a sufficiently suitable opportunity to inveigh more severely against the custom—contrary to his own—followed by at least some adherents of the orthodox Church in the veiling of virgins, he nevertheless argues here far more moderately than in his other works directed against the orthodox. [Col. 0159D] Anyone who has learned elsewhere of Tertullian’s extremely vehement emotional agitation in defending Montanism will say that this is difficult to understand unless our proposal is admitted.

Finally, although it would have greatly benefited the cause whose defense he had undertaken in our book if he had mentioned the public calamities and dangers to which Christians were exposed by the worshipers of the gods—and although Tertullian, who habitually omits nothing useful to his cause, employed that argument in the books *On the Dress of Women*, which resemble our book—he nevertheless does not say here, even in a single word, that such calamities existed. From this it may be concluded that it was written at a time when Christians were not oppressed by such evils. [Col. 0160A]

But since we have said that it was composed after Tertullian joined the Montanists, it is evident that our book cannot be earlier than A.D. 200, because we demonstrated elsewhere that Tertullian went over to the Montanists in that year. Nor can it be much later, since by A.D. 202 the calamities stirred up by Severus had already begun. We have nevertheless declined to place that book among those whose date is most certainly established, because the circumstances of its birth could be determined more by conjecture than by the employment of entirely certain arguments. [Col. 0160B]

## § 3.—The Book *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, Written in A.D. 201

Not much later, it appears, were written those books in which Tertullian sought to vindicate the Montanists’ distinctive doctrines from the contempt and assault of the opposing party: the treatises *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, *On Monogamy*, *On Fasts*, and *On Modesty*. No one doubts that all these works are full of Montanus’s errors; and it can scarcely be doubted any more that they appeared at approximately this time—that is, near the beginning of Septimius’s Montanism. We shall demonstrate both points briefly by surveying these individual books, [Col. 0160C] lest this part of our work, although also treated by others, appear to have been omitted.

If I see the matter correctly, these books were published in the same order in which we have listed them, so that the first of them may be regarded as *On the Exhortation to Chastity*. It is true that Jerome (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 53) does not include it among the books that Tertullian composed in defense of Montanus’s doctrines. There are also things in this book which might persuade someone who had not examined the matter sufficiently that Tertullian did not yet belong to that school at the time; but those considerations are comparatively slight.

The reason Jerome does not include our book in his catalogue of these writings may be that he intended to enumerate only those books that Tertullian designed to oppose to the orthodox. But the book *On the Exhortation to Chastity* was not directed against them; rather, it was written to instruct some brother or other, whom Tertullian wished not so much to refute when he was contemplating remarriage as to exhort to refrain from it. [Col. 0160D]

Moreover, I certainly do not deny that there is considerable moderation here—indeed, more than in the other books that discuss some doctrine of the Montanists. In this book Tertullian himself recommends one marriage and calls it useful and honorable more than he defends an absolute necessity of abstaining from second marriages. From this someone might conclude that he was perhaps inclining toward the Montanists but had not yet attached himself to their party, just as we said above concerning the books *To His Wife*.

Yet this moderation [Col. 0161A] and leniency appears even in other books undoubtedly written at a time when he had already devoted himself to Montanus’s discipline. Nor is it particularly surprising in a book of this kind, which has the character of a letter of persuasion, in which we customarily employ a more subdued and tranquil style. It also appears to have been written not to a Montanist, who would have delighted in a more severe discipline, but to a certain man belonging to the orthodox Church.

There is a clear indication of this at the beginning of the book, where he says that this brother was undoubtedly contemplating an end to his solitary state—that is, the restoration of marriage. I am inclined to think that this would not apply to someone who, together with the Montanists, regarded second marriages as unlawful.

Nor am I unaware of Tillemont’s scruple (place cited, p. 202). He both imagines a great difference between this work and *On Monogamy*—a difference that scarcely exists for anyone who attends correctly—and is surprised that Montanus is not mentioned. But, even without invoking the passage that Rigaltius restored because it was not printed in our books (*note ad hunc locum*, p. 114), which contains the highest praises of Priscilla, the Montanist prophetess, it would not have been prudent for Tertullian to praise Montanus to a man who appeared to reject his discipline. [Col. 0161B]

But if any other doubt remains, one may oppose to it not only the extraordinarily close similarity, extending even to the wording, between this book and *On Monogamy*—which one could almost call the παράφρασιν (“paraphrase”) of our book—but also the following statement in chapter 6:

> “In the beginning God cast forth the seed of the race, the reins of marriage having been loosened, until the world should be filled, until material for the new discipline should advance; but now, at the ends of the ages, he has restrained what he had released and recalled what he had permitted.” [Col. 0161C]

Nor is it more remote from the truth to call our book approximately the first of those whose very subject consists in defending Montanist errors. We cannot suppose the book *On Monogamy* to have been written at the same time as our book because, as we have said, it treats precisely the same subject. It therefore appears that Tertullian wrote our book before the other. Had *On Monogamy* already existed when he set about writing this one, there would have been no need to write the present book; instead, he could have referred that brother to the treatise *On Monogamy* as a publicly published discussion.

But if we judge that our book was written first, it could not have been commended to the Psychics, since it was not public but addressed to a private individual. [Col. 0161D] Finally, we shall show below that the book *On Monogamy* was written approximately at the beginning of the calamities stirred up by Severus himself in A.D. 202, and that the other works deliberately directed against the Psychics are later than *On Monogamy*. It is therefore necessary to believe that our book *On the Exhortation to Chastity* precedes them in date.

## § 4.—The Books *On Monogamy*, *On Fasts*, and *On Modesty*, Written in A.D. 203
Our discussion therefore turns to the book *On Monogamy*. Since throughout it Tertullian refutes the Psychics, celebrates the Paraclete as his authority (ch. 4, beginning; ch. 14; etc.) together with the new prophecy, and repeatedly proclaims his own adherents to be “spiritual”—so called because they acknowledge the charisms [Col. 0162A]—and, finally, devotes the whole work to attacking second marriages, there is no need of lengthy argument to assign this book to his Montanist writings. It is nevertheless useful to inquire briefly into the date at which this treatise was written. After Tertullian had turned to his own purpose that passage of Paul in which the apostle recommends abstinence from marriage because of the distress of that time, when Christians were continually exposed to danger, he adds, “Now still more the time has been shortened” (ch. 3). By these very words he indicates, with sufficient clarity, that a great storm of calamities had fallen upon the Christians when he was writing *On Monogamy*. Even if someone were to say that Tertullian could have written this while no public calamity had yet overtaken the Christians, the other conclusion is nevertheless far more probable, [Col. 0162B] because it is highly credible that, immediately after embracing Montanism, Tertullian applied himself to defending the doctrine of that discipline. If this is true, the book unquestionably falls within the period when the fire of public calamities had already broken out among the Christians. If, then, we ask what persecution of the Christians is meant here, the answer can be demonstrated without difficulty. For shortly after Tertullian’s separation to the Montanists there arose that upheaval which the Emperor Severus had stirred up by his edict. Since this persecution, which began in A.D. 202, ceased around 204, and since the books *On Fasting* and *On Modesty* were written after our book, there is no difficulty in assigning our book approximately to the year 203. [Col. 0162C]

Nor do I hesitate to place after it the book *On Fasting*. The beginning of that book sufficiently shows that it is later than *On Monogamy* and is, as it were, a second part of the controversy against the Psychics; it also teaches that Tertullian published it not very long after the former work. It too, therefore, was produced during some public persecution, which it seems to indicate here and there, as, for example, in the final part of the book. Nor can it be cleared of suspicion of Montanism, not only because of the period to which it belongs, but also because of its defense of the Paraclete in chapters 10, 11, and 13, and because war is publicly declared upon the Psychics in this book.

After this there remains a single treatise deliberately directed against the Psychics, namely that entitled *On Modesty*. No one has ever doubted that it was written against the opponents of the Montanists, [Col. 0162D] nor can anyone doubt it, because Tertullian himself states this and professes that he has separated himself from the fellowship of the Psychics (chs. 1, 6, 10, 16, etc.). There are also many indications, either stamped upon the book itself (ch. 22) or established from elsewhere, of the kind produced by Orsi (*Dissertation on the Peace and Absolution Not Denied by the Catholic Church to Those Guilty of Capital Sins during the First Three Centuries*, ch. 4, digression 3, p. 120 ff.), which show that this book was written not much later than the calamities inflicted by Severus upon the Christian community, and that its approximate year of birth was therefore 204 or the following year.

## § 5.—The Books *Against Praxeas*, *Against Hermogenes*, and *On the Soul*, Published in the Year 204 or 205

Tertullian had scarcely finished these books against the orthodox Church [Col. 0163A] when he turned to another kind of controversy, against heretics. It is not far from the truth that Tertullian attacked their doctrines in the books immediately following those just discussed, because these books themselves betray approximately the same date, shortly after the great calamity of the Christians under Severus. And if conjecture may be admitted, it would not be unreasonable to say that by defending these doctrines against heretics Tertullian wished to confirm his agreement with the true Church in matters pertaining to faith.

Among these books, no controversy seems earlier than that *Against Praxeas*. It also appears to have been written shortly before the book *Against the Valentinians*. For in this work against Praxeas, although Tertullian frequently mentions the Valentinians, he nowhere refers to the book written against them, [Col. 0163B] as he otherwise customarily does—a practice familiar to everyone who reads him. More particularly suited to confirming what we have said is the fact that Praxeas was a heretic whom the Montanists were bound to regard as especially troublesome to them. For, besides disseminating a contrary error concerning the doctrine of the most holy Trinity, he had also persuaded the Roman Pontiff—whom learned men have with good reason identified as Victor—to revoke the peace that had already been prepared for the Montanists (see ch. 1). It is therefore not difficult to believe that Tertullian began his controversies by skirmishing with Praxeas.

No one will deny that this dispute was undertaken by Tertullian as a Montanist. The very name “Psychics” (ch. 1), the Paraclete himself, by whom Tertullian professes that he was more fully instructed in the truth of the mystery of the supreme and greatest Trinity (ch. 2; [Col. 0163C] ch. 8; etc.), and, finally, his own declaration that recognition and defense of the Paraclete had separated him from the Psychics, place this beyond all doubt. Yet we do not venture to pronounce confidently upon the precise date of this book, although, if the controversy against Praxeas was the first of his contests with heretics, and these contests immediately followed the books directed against the orthodox Church, it may reasonably be assigned to approximately A.D. 204 or 205.

I would not hesitate to say that it was followed by the book *Against Hermogenes*. For that book is earlier than *On the Soul* and *Against the Valentinians*, as will be shown below. Since these latter works were composed approximately after the Severan fury had passed, our little book should apparently be assigned to the same year as the work *Against Praxeas*. [Col. 0163D] That it proceeded from Tertullian as a Montanist is made sufficiently clear by the exceedingly bitter attack upon Hermogenes’ repeated marriages (ch. 1).

To this, as a sort of appendix—as the beginning of the book and many other passages show—he added the book *On the Soul*, a work filled with innumerable fantasies and bearing unmistakable marks of Montanism.

> **Note [Col. 0163D].** For example, in chapters 55 and 58 he invokes the counsels and testimony of the Paraclete; there and in chapter 9 he says that his own party acknowledges spiritual charisms and has been deemed worthy, even after John, to receive prophecy.

It may, however, be debated whether it was written in approximately the same year as *Against Hermogenes*, or only after A.D. 208. For in chapter 2 he says: “That τὸ αὐτεξούσιον (“free will”) exists in us naturally we have already shown even to Marcion.” This controversy appears in the extant second book *Against Marcion*, chapter 6; [Col. 0164A] but Tertullian could also be referring to one of the lost books against Marcion. If the former is assumed, *On the Soul* will have been written after A.D. 208; if the latter, it may be placed even before that year. Of these opinions I prefer the second. For just as it is more customary to append works of the nature of our little book to their parent works immediately rather than after a long interval, so too in the *Scorpiace* he refers in the same manner to the books against Marcion that had already been lost. Moreover, if this opinion is accepted, the order of Tertullian’s books will be much more coherent.

For in the *Scorpiace*, which we have shown to have been written in A.D. 204, he complains that the heretics, Gnostics, and Valentinians attack the sufferings voluntarily endured by Christians for the sake of religion (chs. 1, [Col. 0164B] 4, 3). But in *On the Soul*, chapter 55, he discusses at length the glory of the martyrs; and, as will appear below, he immediately followed this work with *Against the Valentinians*, in which, at the beginning of chapter 30, he says that the Valentinians had attacked the necessity of martyrdom. It therefore seems sufficiently consonant with the truth that *On the Soul* and *Against the Valentinians* were composed not long after the *Scorpiace*, approximately in A.D. 205.

## § 6.—The Books *Against the Valentinians*, *On Prescriptions*, *On the Flesh of Christ*, and *On the Resurrection*, Written after A.D. 203

The order of the books therefore requires that we now discuss this refutation of the Valentinians. It certainly belongs after [Col. 0164C] Tertullian’s defection to the Montanists. Admittedly, the remarks scattered throughout the controversy do not demonstrate this with complete clarity, since there is nothing doctrinal in the little book that could not also have proceeded from an orthodox author. Nevertheless, it is apparent in two ways.

First, near the end of chapter 16 Tertullian says that he had already engaged Hermogenes on the same subject as that disputed with the Valentinians; and we have just assigned that anti-Hermogenian controversy to Tertullian as a Montanist writer. Secondly, at the end of chapter 5, he ardently wishes that it might be granted to him to equal Proculus in every work, whom he calls “the dignity of virginal old age and Christian eloquence.” I do not doubt that this Proculus was the Montanist Proculus mentioned by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 20. This identification rests both upon the praise of his virginity, [Col. 0164D] which Tertullian commends as an outstanding virtue in him, and upon the fact that he calls him “our own,” distinguishing him by this designation from the writers of the orthodox Church whom he had just praised: Justin Martyr, Miltiades (“the sophist of the Churches,” as he calls him, perhaps inflamed by hatred of this man, who, as Eusebius reports, loc. cit., book V, chapter 17, had also opposed the Montanists), and Irenaeus.

But if anyone inquires more closely into the actual date of the book, it seems sufficiently reasonable to say that it was composed not very long after the cruelty against the Christians had in some degree subsided. For there would have been little need to defend the confession of Christian truth before the authorities of this world and at the tribunals of governors—as he urges in chapter 30—unless either that calamitous period itself [Col. 0165A] or a vivid memory of it still existed. Furthermore, as we have just said, this book was written approximately at the same time as the *Scorpiace*, after the fury of Severus had been extinguished, as the history of the period teaches.

We may therefore proceed to the book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, which we do not hesitate to place after it, whatever Tillemont (*loc. cit.*, part III, p. 203, and note 6 on Tertullian, p. 656) and Whiston (*The True Origin of the Sabellian and Athanasian Doctrines of the Trinity*, p. 3 ff.) may have argued to the contrary. For in book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 1, Tertullian promises that he will sometime compose a controversy on prescription against the heretics. From this it follows by necessary inference that our book was not published until after A.D. 208. And that very fact [Col. 0165B] demonstrates most clearly that Tertullian’s mind was not free from Montanist errors at the time when he wrote our book—not to mention that there are distinct traces of these errors in the book itself, as in chapter 40, where, while teaching that even an evil spirit emulates divine institutions, he says: “What of the fact that it appoints its supreme pontiff to a single marriage? It too has virgins; it too has the continent,” and other things of the same kind.

But let us disclose the passages from which those who take the contrary view derive their entire argument on this question. First, they say that the passage we have cited from *Against Marcion* may also signify a book already written. Whiston even adduces another example of this manner of speaking from book V, chapter 19—an example both unnecessary in a matter known to all and in no way appropriate. [Col. 0165C] But that interpretation cannot adequately be defended. Whenever Tertullian cites a book already composed by him, he never employs the future tense, but always the past; and Tertullian would, I think, likewise have used a past-tense form here—as he did elsewhere concerning this book (*On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 2)—if he had intended to say that he had already composed it.

No less strained is Tillemont’s opinion that the passage in the work against Marcion could have remained from those books which Tertullian had written against him before the extant work. For that is a mere conjecture and wholly improbable, because, when Tertullian set about writing our books against Marcion, he states that one preceding controversy against him had been canceled and another lost. Moreover, Tillemont’s argument is inherently inept. [Col. 0165D] As for his statement that *On the Flesh of Christ* is earlier than our books *Against Marcion*, while the latter is later than *On the Prescription of Heretics*, I shall not attempt to discuss it here. The matter has been sufficiently argued above, from which it may be understood that the first book of our anti-Marcionite work, which is in question here, was not published with the others and is in no way later than *On the Flesh of Christ*.

But at the end of *On Prescription* Tertullian says: “For the present, indeed, we have treated the matter generally against all heresies, which must be repelled from comparison of the Scriptures by definite, just, and necessary prescriptions. Hereafter . . . we shall also reply specifically to certain of them.” I hear the objection. What follows, then? Are all Tertullian’s books against heretics later than *On Prescription*? [Col. 0166A] But Tillemont, as it seems to me, has not understood this passage correctly. For Tertullian does not say there that in this book he has refuted the heretics merely in a general way; he adds that he has done so universally by definite, just, and necessary prescriptions. Accordingly, in the other books he is not promising separately to refute the doctrine of each individual heretic, but to show that individual heretics and their tenets must yield in antiquity to the doctrines of those who hold right belief.

But Whiston again, *loc. cit.*, p. 4, says: “The treatise *On Prescription* is earlier than Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*.” Why, I ask? He answers that in *Apologeticum*, chapter 47, Tertullian says: “We readily prescribe against our adulterators that the rule of truth is that which comes from [Col. 0166B] Christ, transmitted through his companions, to whom these various later commentators will be proved subsequent.” What an acute man, who, when he hears of “prescription,” immediately sees a book written on the subject!

That objection was indeed more pertinent to the date of the book. The remaining arguments by which they say they were driven to expel this work from the number of Montanist writings are as follows. First, Whiston adduces the small book appended to ours, which lists the heretics who arose within the Christian community and in which the οἱ κατά φρύγας (“Phrygian”) heretics are very plainly condemned. That argument could not be evaded if this little book could be vindicated for Tertullian, as Whiston undertakes to prove. But let us nevertheless hear what he argues in favor of an opinion now utterly rejected by learned men.

“The style in this piece,” he says, “is the same as in Tertullian’s writings.” [Col. 0166C] How so? The little book frequently mingles Greek words with Latin; it speaks in the manner customary among Africans, in that rough and nearly barbarous style; it pursues the heretics with clever little conclusions; it also takes much from Irenaeus; finally, it recounts heretics mentioned by Tertullian, including even those whom he alone mentions, such as Ebion and Praxeas. But what if the author of this little book was an African by birth, or copied Tertullian? Whiston has no answer to this. Let us proceed, then.

Augustine states most clearly in *On Heresies*, no. 86: “Tertullian passed over to the Phrygians, whom he had previously destroyed.” Where, then? “Nowhere,” says Whiston, “so fully as in this appendix.” I should certainly like to hear how Whiston [Col. 0166D] learned this. Jerome, in *Against the Luciferians*, draws many things from the little book in question as from an ancient writing; Epiphanius does likewise. Let it be so; let them, then, have copied many things from it. Therefore this little book possesses great antiquity. Indeed it does, and may even be contemporary with Tertullian; but whether Tertullian was also its father I do not yet see Whiston’s testimonies to have established.

They next think it inconsistent that Tertullian, after separating from the common Church, should have written so fine and powerful a book against all who had separated themselves from the Church by their errors. Although truth possesses such force that it offers itself to be perceived and defended even by the unwilling, and although Tertullian himself repeatedly insists upon prescription against heretics in books undoubtedly composed during his Montanist period, [Col. 0167A] they nevertheless bid us observe that nowhere did he wield this weapon with such deliberation and fullness. This argument is subtler than is fitting. For the Montanists, including Tertullian himself—as is established (*On Fasting*, ch. 1; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 2)—never professed themselves estranged from the orthodox in doctrines pertaining to faith. Nor does Tertullian anywhere number the Psychics among the heretics; on the contrary, he distinguishes them very plainly from heretics (for example, at the beginning of *On Monogamy*). They merely said that their discipline had been corrected and brought to perfection; and they maintained that, in matters falling under faith—disagreement concerning which alone constitutes heresy—they did not differ from the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles. There is therefore no reason to marvel that he drew from the more recent age of the doctrines defended by heretics an argument for attacking them. [Col. 0167B]

Tillemont’s second argument is nothing. Even if I grant that Tertullian discusses this rule for judging doctrines deliberately here but only incidentally in his other books, he nevertheless sets it forth not obscurely but with sufficient clarity in his books against heretics. He had designed our book to discuss the matter systematically, while in the remaining works he refutes the absurdities of the heretics in a different manner.

These same considerations may also be opposed to another argument of our adversaries—by no means a slight argument, but one so strong that it could almost appear capable of drawing us over to the opposing side, although Tillemont, surprisingly, did not elucidate it sufficiently. In chapter 36, Tertullian sets forth the complete agreement of his own doctrines with those of the apostolic Churches and their vehement disagreement with those of the heretics. What is far more significant, in chapter 21 he sharply attacks the heretics because they were accustomed to say that the Apostles did not know everything, [Col. 0167C] something they thought Jesus Christ himself had told them in John in these words: “Many things remain for me to say to you, but you cannot yet receive them.” Tertullian then refutes them by the words of Christ that followed the preceding statement: “When that Spirit comes, he will lead you into knowledge of everything that is true.” From this Tertullian thinks it can be inferred that the Apostles had been taught everything, since he says that it is undoubtedly evident from the Acts of the Apostles that they subsequently received that very Spirit from Christ in full.

Yet would someone reflecting upon these words and considering the tenets of the Montanists—who, appealing approximately to that same latter passage of John, defended the Paraclete’s discipline as more perfect even than the discipline of Christ and the Apostles—think that Tertullian here pronounces so clearly against the Montanists themselves that there could be no doubt about the ὀρθοδοξίᾳ (“orthodoxy”) of this book? [Col. 0167D] I certainly do not think so. For although this passage carries great weight, it could nevertheless have been put forward even by one who stood with the Montanist party.

For, as we have said, Tertullian nowhere admits that there is any disagreement between the Montanists and the orthodox followers of the Apostles concerning those things which must be accepted by faith; and any Montanist could grant his contention that the Apostles lacked no true doctrine. What they maintained was that discipline had at last been perfected by the Paraclete, and that Christian doctrines were not new but the old ones more firmly confirmed. Indeed, in many passages Tertullian strives to prove from Holy Scripture, and even from the customs or precepts of the Apostles themselves, those very rites which the orthodox protested had been more recently introduced among Montanus’ followers. [Col. 0168A]

But those heretics against whom Tertullian’s controversy in *On Prescription* is directed continually asserted that the Apostles were either ignorant of many of Christ’s doctrines or that Christ had not transmitted everything to everyone, as our author says in the very passage under consideration. Since, therefore, the passage in dispute could have been employed no less by a Montanist than by an adherent of the orthodox Church, the question is which opinion or interpretation is more inclined toward the truth. Here I have little hesitation in saying that this very book proceeded from Tertullian as a Montanist.

First, there are works of Septimius derived from Montanist discipline in which he insists upon prescription in the case of heretics, yet nowhere—as was his usual practice with all his books to which he could refer readers—does he cite his own work *On the Prescription of Heretics* in advance as his authority; examples are *Against Praxeas*, chapter 2, and *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 1. [Col. 0168B] Secondly, if the meaning of the passage from our book discussed above were such as Tillemont imagines, it is scarcely credible that, after writing this book, Tertullian could have fallen into Montanism, since he had pronounced so clearly against the school of Montanus; or that, in books written by him as a Montanist, he could even have praised this book, in which Montanus’ enterprises had been condemned with such force, as he does near the end of *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 2.

Nor should anyone wonder that Tertullian so closely attached himself to the defense of doctrines accepted in the Christian Churches in a book written at the time of his defection from those Churches. For by that time Tertullian’s fury against the orthodox members who thought otherwise had already been extinguished in some degree; after his spirit had been pacified for a while, he turned against the heretics, whence there arose greater agreement with the orthodox and a milder judgment concerning them.

> **Note [Col. 0168D].** Difficult indeed, if any controversy ever was, and entangled in straits, is this question concerning the date of *On Prescriptions*. In the course of this work there will again be an opportunity to examine it to some extent and to explain our own opinion, such as it is, even if we are not permitted to settle such great disputes. For the present, however, it is useful to say only in passing that the opinion intimated by Tillemont is no longer displeasing to us: namely, that this book was conceived and begun before Tertullian’s defection, while he still flourished in sound faith and perhaps while, residing at Rome, he was examining the apostolic traditions deeply; yet it was not published until after the books against Marcion, when its author was already clinging to the dregs of Montanism. —**Editors**

## ARTICLE VI  
### The Fifth Class of Books, Whose Date and Doctrine Are Both Uncertain

[Col. 0168D]

## § 1.—The Book *On Repentance*

There is no reason to say much about the books *On the Flesh of Christ* and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, since the latter’s citation of the former sufficiently [Col. 0169A] shows it to be later (ch. 2), while the former was composed only after *On the Prescription of Heretics*, as is likewise evident (see art. 4, § 6). The precise year of these books, however, is not established.

There remain, therefore, those books for which, as it seems to me, no account can be given either of their date or of their doctrine—for this was the third topic of our work. Since others, who believed that they had settled the matter, have thought themselves able to decide with some certainty concerning them, we, who prefer to speak more cautiously in this question, must finally examine briefly whatever they have argued on the subject.

To this class belongs the book *On Repentance*. Erasmus went so far as to deny that it was Tertullian’s, and on this matter he was at one time approved by Dallaeus and also by Hoffmann, chiefly because of the dissimilarity of style between this and Tertullian’s other books. I confess that I cannot adequately detect that dissimilarity, [Col. 0169B] although here the involved and compressed manner of speaking that predominates in the other works is less apparent. For the dissimilarity is not so great as is supposed: the same broken and interrupted expression found here also occurs in other books whose style is somewhat moderated, such as *On Patience* and *On Flight in Persecution*.

Let this book, therefore, be the work of our Septimius; but I do not venture to say to which sect he belonged when he wrote it. Here almost everyone intervenes and says that it is absolutely certain that Tertullian then agreed with the orthodox. For, they argue, he grants to the sacred assembly the power to forgive the sins of those who had committed graver offenses—a power he completely destroyed in the book *On Modesty*—and in that work he expressly professes that he now wishes to refute the book which he had formerly written in favor of that power while devoted to the heresy of the common Church. [Col. 0169C]

In this entire controversy Hoffmann seems to me much wiser than in the others. At *loc. cit.*, § XIII, he aptly observes that the question proposed in *On Repentance* is very different from that posed by Tertullian in the treatise *On Modesty*, and that the Montanists too could have defended everything set forth in *On Repentance*.

The question between the orthodox and the Montanists was not whether those who had relapsed into their former impurity through graver sins could, after performing repentance, obtain pardon for their offenses from God. Neither party—not even the Montanists—denied this. Indeed, it is established that the Montanists required ἐξομολόγησιν (“confession”) from the guilty, though not in such a way that the sinner thereby obtained pardon from the Church and restoration to union with it; rather, the upright were to be moved to supplicate God that he might at some time finally grant pardon to that sinner. [Col. 0169D] The question was instead whether the Church might exercise the power which it itself believed it possessed, of receiving sinners who had been separated from its fellowship back into their former friendship and communion in sacred rites. The Montanists denied that this ought to be done; the orthodox said that it could be done.

Tertullian sharply and wittily attacks the exercise of this liberty by the orthodox in *On Modesty*. In *On Repentance*, however, he neither confirms nor attacks it, but speaks of that pardon before God to which access was not barred even to those immersed in the gravest crimes, provided that they returned to a sound mind. From this it also follows that in *On Modesty* Tertullian does not retract what he had once written, while adhering to the orthodox opinion, in a separate little book. He admits only that he now thinks differently concerning that pardon granted by the sacred assembly from what, while among the orthodox, he had formerly—not indeed written, but nevertheless thought.

What, then? Should we suppose that Tertullian wrote this book during his Montanist period? I do not venture to say that either. For although in chapter 8 he seems to promise sinners who return to their former and perverse life only one final hope of obtaining pardon from God, [Col. 0170A] he nevertheless teaches nothing in that matter which we read to have been peculiar to the Montanists. Rather, it is something that we find was also vigorously defended by others among the orthodox (see the *Shepherd* of Hermas, Mandate 4, in Fabricius’ *Apocrypha of the New Testament*, vol. III, p. 845 ff., and the passages cited there by Fabricius): that there is no hope of salvation for those who, after receiving baptism, again sin gravely and to the loss of true piety. This later introduced into the Church the most pernicious custom of deferring baptism. And what might appear too harshly stated Tertullian himself mitigates by adding these words: “But the spirit must not at once be cut down and overthrown by despair.”

Accordingly, since this book contains no indications capable of deciding the question, I frankly profess that I am entirely ignorant of the period or doctrine to which it should be assigned.

## § 2.—The Book *Against the Jews*

[Col. 0170C]

Nor am I ashamed to confess the same concerning the book which Tertullian wrote *Against the Jews*. It contains nothing savoring of the absurdities of Montanus; but neither is that surprising, since Tertullian had scarcely any occasion in this book to mention such matters. We must therefore determine whether any indication of its date can be found there.

There is indeed a rather obscure indication in two passages. The first is in chapter 7, where he mentions regions of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans, and shortly afterward the Britons “enclosed within the circuit of their own Ocean.” This led Baronius (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, at the year 212), Allix, and others to believe that the book was written after Severus’ victories over the Britons, and thus approximately in A.D. 209. [Col. 0170D] I would not say so. For how could regions of the Britons then have been called inaccessible when the Romans had gained access to them? And how could Tertullian have said that the Romans could not extend the power of their empire beyond those peoples, when they had done precisely that among the Britons?

Herodian confirms all too clearly (*History*, book III, ch. 14, p. 170 in my edition) that Severus not only left Geta in those regions of Britain which were subject to Roman rule, but also that Severus himself, he continues, advanced farther. Nor is the wall constructed by Severus in Britain—which deceived Baronius and the others—the boundary by which Tertullian means that the Britons were enclosed within their own territory. For he states with complete clarity that the Britons were enclosed not by a wall but within the circuit of the Ocean. [Col. 0171A]

The things that other writers record concerning the Britons belong only to Severus’ expedition against them, which is established to have been undertaken in A.D. 208. Tertullian’s book is therefore earlier, and indeed much earlier, if I see correctly.

Tertullian also argued rightly in a second passage, chapter 13. For at the time this book was written no Jew was permitted access to Bethlehem, the surrounding countryside, or Jerusalem. Yet it is established that Severus enacted many laws favorable to the Jews, which Jacob Basnage briefly enumerated (*History of the Jews*, vol. VIII, p. 49 ff.); and Spartianus says (*Life of Severus*, ch. 16) that these rights were established for them when Severus, after capturing Ctesiphon, was proceeding into Egypt, that is, approximately in A.D. 202. [Col. 0171B] It is therefore not credible that, after granting them many rights, he continued to prohibit anyone from entering either Jerusalem or any other place in Palestine. Nor can it be said that the exile of the Jews, or Tertullian’s book *Against the Jews*, arose only after that year; it must rather have been earlier.

I seem to be confirmed in this opinion by a passage from Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, chapter 21, where, among other things, he tells the Jews that they are not permitted even under the right of strangers to greet their ancestral land with so much as the sole of the foot. Although this is false of the whole territory of Palestine—from which the Jews do not seem to have been expelled even by Hadrian, as Joannes Masson demonstrated especially from many passages of ancient writers (*Historical Collection appended to the works of Aristides*, edited by Samuel Jebb, § 6, no. 8)—Tertullian must nevertheless have held that opinion when writing the *Apologeticum*. [Col. 0171C] From this, together with the other considerations we have presented, it may in some degree be inferred that *Against the Jews* belongs approximately to the same period.

But since neither the precise year of this book can be determined nor is it clear whether Tertullian already agreed with the Montanists at that time, I have chosen to append this book too to those whose date and doctrine are not apparent. When all the points thus far proposed have been collected, the order of Tertullian’s books may be established approximately as follows.

### Before His Adoption of Montanism

*On Prayer*. *To the Martyrs*. *On the Shows*. *On Idolatry*. *Apologeticum*. *On the Testimony of the Soul*. [Col. 0171D] Two books *To the Nations*. *On Baptism*. Two books *To His Wife*. (*Against the Jews*.)

### During His Montanist Period

*On the Crown*. *On the Veiling of Virgins*. *On the Dress of Women*. *On Flight in Persecution*. *Exhortation to Chastity*. *On Monogamy*. *On Fasting*. *On Modesty*. *Against Praxeas*. *Against Hermogenes*. *On the Soul*. *Scorpiace*. *Against the Valentinians*. *Against Marcion*, book I. *On the Prescription of Heretics*. *Against Marcion*, books II, III, and IV. *On the Flesh of Christ*. *On the Resurrection*. *Against Marcion*, book V. *On the Pallium*. (*On Patience*.) *To Scapula*. (*On Repentance*.)

## § 3.—On the Acts of Perpetua and Felicitas, and Their Montanism
And here we might end our discussion, since it is not our purpose to examine Tertullian’s other writings, which have either been wrongly attributed to him or no longer survive. But it occurred to me to say something about those Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity, which some have also attributed to Tertullian. Among these I propose to challenge Whiston alone, who made every effort to vindicate these Acts for Tertullian [Col. 0172A] (*In the Sacred History of the Jewish and Christian Church*, part II, vol. 6, pp. 477–78). He does not indeed think that those holy martyrs belonged to the Montanist discipline, as some have maintained, Samuel Basnage among them (*Annales politico-ecclesiastici*, vol. II, p. 224 ff.); but he plainly thinks that the man who collected these materials was not only a Montanist but Tertullian himself.

On this matter I hold the contrary opinion. For, first, there are many things in the memoirs left by Perpetua herself which show beyond doubt that she belonged to the Montanist community. Basnage has already made this argument, but he found an opponent in Joseph Augustine Orsi, who, although he considers the compiler of these Acts a Montanist, nevertheless labors strenuously to defend the orthodoxy of these martyrs [Col. 0172B] (*Dissertatio apologetica pro SS. Perpetuae, Felicitatis et sociorum martyrum orthodoxia, adversus Sam. Basnagium*, Florence, 1728, quarto). I remember that, when I once read his arguments, they did not persuade me of this point, but contained a great many matters wholly foreign to the present discussion. The work, however, is not now at hand; let us therefore pursue Whiston alone.

He says that there is not even a single letter savoring of Montanism in these memoirs of Perpetua and Saturus, from which those Acts are almost entirely composed. How far this is from the truth we shall show later. He then thinks this single point sufficient to settle the whole controversy: that Tertullian was the first to introduce the errors of the Montanists into Africa, at approximately the time when these martyrs suffered punishment. Therefore, since those doctrines had scarcely been brought into [Col. 0172C] Africa at that time, it cannot be said that persons unlearned in letters and living far from Carthage, as these people were, had already embraced that discipline.

More than one error is found in this argument. First, he undoubtedly assumes that these martyrs died at Thuburbo. I know that this city is mentioned in spurious copies of these Acts, and Whiston likewise expressly names it; but this has been sufficiently rejected both by the better απογραφα (“copies”) and by the arguments of Valesius and Ruinart (*Notes on the Acts of the Martyrs*, pp. 90–91, Amsterdam ed.). Accordingly, if we believe, as those scholars demonstrated, that they were killed at Carthage, they could easily have learned of the errors of the Montanists, since everyone knows that Tertullian lived at Carthage [Col. 0172D]. But from what source will Whiston prove that Tertullian was the first to spread these errors in Africa, and that he did so at approximately the time when these martyrs suffered? And even if I grant this too, what, I ask, is incredible in supposing that these martyrs had learned of errors disseminated in Africa by Tertullian and already defended by him in writing before the year 205—for Whiston assigned the death of the holy martyrs to that year—especially since very many who joined the society of Montanus were without literary education, and therefore resembled these martyrs?

Still farther from the truth is the assertion that none of Montanus’s delusions is sprinkled through the memoirs of Perpetua and Saturus themselves. For, first, there is strong reason to suspect a merely human character in the very appearances presented to these persons. Perpetua not only declares that immediately [Col. 0173A] with baptism she received the gift of foretelling future events [Note: [Col. 0173D] *Acts of Perpetua and Felicity*, in Ruinart’s *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, Amsterdam ed., p. 93, § 3: “Within the space of a few days we were baptized. But the Spirit dictated to me that nothing else was to be sought in the water except endurance of the flesh.”]; she also speaks so confidently of that gift that at will she could predict the future and even release the dead from the very punishments of hell [Note: [Col. 0173D] Ibid., p. 94, § 4: “My brother said to me: Lady sister, you are now in great dignity, so great that you may request a vision and it may be shown to you whether there is to be suffering or a reprieve”—that is, whether it would come to pass that she escaped the danger of death. See Holstenius’s note on this passage, ibid., p. 106; he aptly observes a passage of Tertullian in which he records that the sisters obtain from the Lord a *dignatio*, that is, a singular favor, whenever they desire it. She continues: “And I, knowing that I conversed with the Lord, whose benefits I had experienced in so great measure, confidently promised him, saying: Tomorrow I shall report to you….” Then, p. 96, § 7, “the name Dinocrates came forth from her lips,” her brother, who was already dead, “and she immediately understood herself to be worthy and bound to petition for him…. That very night it was shown to her in a vision that the dead Dinocrates was in distress.” But in § 8, after frequent prayers, she understood that he had been transferred out of punishment. We have never read that even the prayers of the Apostles, or of any great envoy of God, possessed such power.].

I shall not now examine this last presumption, but I nevertheless strongly doubt whether, in the period in which Perpetua lived—that is, toward the close of the second century after the birth of Christ—that miraculous faculty and, as it were, indwelling power which had been given to the Apostles and the Apostolic Church ought rightly to be attributed to her. To be brief, I shall offer two reasons for this opinion.

The first is that it cannot in any way be shown that anyone apart from the Apostles either received such a faculty except through the laying on of their hands, or could in turn communicate it to others [Col. 0173B]; by contrast, there are several sufficiently striking passages that may be argued in support of the opposite view. To use this example, why were the Apostles Peter and John finally sent by the others to Samaria (Acts 8:14 ff.)? Why would you say that, through the laying on of hands, they distributed to the new Christians the power to perform miracles, when Philip the Evangelist himself had already won renown in Samaria through many miracles? Why could the Ephesian Christians (Acts 19:2 ff.), whom the Apostle Paul was now visiting for the first time, have said both that they had not received the Holy Spirit and that they did not even know what this was, unless matters stood as we have said? If this is so, I do not venture to affirm that toward the end of the second century there was any Christian who shone with a faculty of this kind; for at that time [Col. 0173C] none who could have received it from the Apostles was still living.

The second reason is contained in Ephesians 4:7 ff. After Paul had argued at length above, vindicating for those who had previously followed the worship of the gods the same share and divine grace as the Jews, in order to reconcile the disagreements between Jewish and Gentile Christians, he then observed that miraculous faculties greatly contributed to fostering discord between the two groups. He therefore plainly affirms both that these faculties were most wisely distributed at Christ’s discretion, what end they served, and that they would not continue to exist except for a fixed period. In this passage no one, I think, will doubt that the faculties to be understood are not those spiritual faculties common to all Christians, but those suited to certain [Col. 0174A] Christians for producing actual miracles, provided that he compares these statements with what the Apostle discusses in Romans 12:3–8 and 1 Corinthians 12 ff.

Paul further adds in Ephesians 4:13–14 that they were given μέχρι καταντήσωμεν οἱ πάντες εἰς τὴν ἑνότητα τῆς πὶστεως, καὶ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον, εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ χριστοῦ (“until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”). κ. τ. λ. From this it follows that these faculties became extinct when both those who had become Christians from among the Jews and those from among the Gentiles (οἱ πάντες (“all of them”)) had agreed in believing the same things and acknowledging that one Son of God, and when the entire society of Christians gathered from both groups—which here, by a comparison drawn from the Mosaic tabernacle filled with divine splendor, is called πλήρωμα του (“the fullness of”) [Col. 0174B] χριστοῦ (“Christ”); compare 1:22–23—had been brought, as it were, to mature manhood and no longer allowed itself to be tossed about by the deceits of teachers ἰουδαιζόντων (“Judaizing”).

But I suspect that this point was reached not very long after the death of all the Apostles, or around the middle of the second century. For when Hadrian had forbidden the Jews to celebrate public worship in Jerusalem, Sulpicius Severus says (*Sacred History*, book II, ch. 31) that, with few exceptions, the Christians whose minds had still inclined toward the religion of the Jews both abandoned this error and appointed Mark, a Gentile, bishop of Jerusalem. Their example was doubtless followed by others of the same kind; for after this we never find the Christian community torn apart by the former disputes over observance of the Mosaic law [Col. 0174C]. For although someone might object by citing the groups of Cerinthians, Ebionites, Nazarenes, and Elcesaites, nevertheless, after the first half of the second century had passed, very few joined them; nor can there ever exist such complete concord among Christians that absolutely no one professes disagreement with the rest [Note: [Col. 0174D] This decidedly ill-omened opinion of Valesius and Basnage, so ungrateful to such great martyrs, which our present author improperly revives, has been vigorously routed and driven from the field in the decisive apologetic dissertation of Joseph Augustine Orsi, afterward Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, *On the Orthodoxy of Saints Perpetua, Felicity, and the Holy Martyrs*, Florence, 1728.
