In it the following points in particular are established: (1) that the most weighty testimonies prove that honor has in every age been rendered to our holy martyrs in the Church; (2) that even if the Acts of the holy martyrs flowed from Montanist sources, no prejudice against the martyrs themselves arises from this; (3) that in the Acts themselves nothing in fact occurs that smacks of Montanus’s workshop, or that does not agree perfectly with the genuine Acts of the other martyrs; (4) finally, that the virtues of our martyrs, the fruits of their visions, the fulfillment of their prophecies, and the marks of their miracles, teaching, and entire conduct are such as to make it plain that they were inspired by the divine Spirit and wholly removed from Montanist practices. These matters may be seen below in volume III of this *Bibliotheca*, where the Acts of St. Perpetua and the saints are to be published in their proper place, together with the notes of various ancient and modern scholars. EDD.].

§ 4.—On the Montanist Artotyrites

There is, moreover, a vision of Perpetua which had aroused strong suspicion of Montanism, and from which she acknowledges that she understood that a violent death was imminent for her (§ 4). In the vision, a morsel of cheese is offered to her by a certain shepherd; she eats it, and all who stand by say “Amen.” What is this? Surely a signification of violent death. [Col. 0174D] How does this follow: a piece of cheese, [Col. 0175A] an “Amen,” and a violent manner of death? If I see the matter correctly, these things do not appear connected in any way unless I say that this virgin belonged to the Montanist community; for Epiphanius (*Haer.* 49, § 2) and others say that they—or at least some of them—used cheese in the sacred supper (perhaps those less-than-precise writers meant in the agapes).

Now it had become customary among Christians for those present from the congregation to add “Amen” at the sacred meal, as is evident from Justin Martyr (*Greater Apology*, chs. 85 and 87, Grabe ed., pp. 125, 131–32); and that meal was also ordinarily distributed in prison to those destined for death. Everything is therefore perfectly clear if that virgin is thought to have belonged to the discipline of Montanus; if this is denied, the details cannot, as it seems to me, be explained in any way [Note: [Col. 0175B] Certain points arise from this account of Perpetua which may with considerable reason be argued against what I have said; they have also been employed with much ingenuity by the highly esteemed historian of the Montanists, Theophilus Wernsdorf, § 18. I propose to answer them briefly and modestly.

The statements of some ancient writers that the Montanists employed cheese in their sacred meals, from which they derived the name Artotyrites, seem to me by no means negligible. For even if this is wrongly said of the form of their sacred Supper, and even if that distinguished learned man much more correctly refers it to the Montanists’ agapes and offerings, our case requires nothing more than that the use of cheese be established for these agapes of theirs. This can readily be done, not only because no other explanation can be given for the origin of so ridiculous a charge and appellation, but also because it is agreed that the Montanists were especially devoted to dry fasts. It may therefore readily be understood that their sacred banquets were not sumptuous; nor will anyone who has learned from those Acts how wretched the martyrs’ lot was in prison readily doubt that Perpetua and the other martyrs also used such meager food as cheese in prison when they held what were, as it were, agapes.

But our employment of this circumstance to establish the Montanism of these martyrs [Col. 0175C], and especially of Perpetua, seems to be overturned by the arguments which that most learned man has presented in the passage cited. First he appeals to the authority of Augustine and Tertullian: the former praised that vision of Perpetua, while the latter did not mention it in his book *On the Soul*. Neither point, I think, is surprising. In Tertullian’s case, it may be doubted whether he referred to the very vision now in question, since he says only that martyrs were seen by Perpetua in paradise; one might perhaps miss any mention of this in our vision. Nor, for the purpose of his argument—which is concerned exclusively with asserting that perfect happiness before the final day of judgment belongs only to martyrs—would he suitably and relevantly have mentioned the cheese received by Perpetua.

As for Augustine, who is wholly occupied in praising Perpetua and interprets the morsel of cheese given to her in another way, who would be surprised that he nevertheless praised this circumstance? But the second objection is weightier. Augustine thought that the morsel of cheese was a sign of the sweetness of Perpetua’s happiness, and this interpretation persuaded that distinguished man, who appears to find the entire signification of violent death in the ladder fortified with thorns, swords, and other objects which Perpetua had to ascend. He says [Col. 0175D] that the reason cheese was used to foreshadow everlasting happiness lay in consistently pursuing the metaphor drawn from the image of the Shepherd.

But if this alone had been the significance of receiving the cheese, I would ask why cheese had been offered to Perpetua by the Shepherd as he was milking, rather than some milk, which would have been far better suited to foreshadow the happiness of the heavenly Canaan, flowing as it were with milk and honey. Next, let someone tell me why Perpetua records that it was presented to her mind that she received that morsel of cheese with joined hands—in accordance with the custom adopted at the sacred supper among the ancient Christians—and that all those standing around said “Amen.” I doubt whether anyone can give a reason for this unless he favors our case.

Finally, if receiving that cheese signifies something that was to happen to Perpetua in the heavenly kingdom, and perhaps foreshadows the supper of the Lamb described in John’s Apocalypse—from which nearly all those visions in the Acts under discussion were drawn—then, if you call Perpetua a Montanist, it is much easier to understand why a morsel of cheese was given to her to signify this, since, as we have said, the Montanists used cheese in their agapes. But if you say that the cheese does not refer to anything heavenly, but to some other circumstance connected with Perpetua’s violent death, the vision can be explained from the free meal which those Acts [Col. 0176D] (§ 8) report that the martyrs took as an agape on the day before they underwent punishment.].

§ 5.—Whiston’s Arguments for Tertullian as the Author of These Acts Are Examined

[Col. 0176A]

But let us come to the second question, which consists in this: whether the person who collected these Acts was either a writer from the Montanist sect or Tertullian himself. Whiston accepts both propositions—correctly, indeed, if the former is in question, but very differently if Tertullian himself is meant.

I therefore agree completely with Whiston on the former point, because that writer says in the preface that he acknowledges and honors new prophecies and visions, and consequently admits that he has added these new records of martyrs and revelations. He also boasts (§ 26) that, since the Holy Spirit permitted—and by permitting willed—the course of this contest (that is, the martyrs’ combat with beasts in the theater) [Col. 0176B] to be written down, he composed this account. I hardly know whether this does not disclose a writer who could only have been Montanist, principally because the orthodox did not customarily esteem Montanist martyrs highly, and much less would they have committed to writing their sufferings and steadfastness together with visions which they assuredly despised.

But on the principal point of this discussion—that Tertullian was that very writer—I shall not yield to Whiston’s arguments, which he sets forth more fully in this manner. First, as the preface shows, these Acts were composed not very long after the event itself. Next, they were written in Latin, and by an African, of which the harsh African style employed here is no slight evidence. Likewise, many words occur which are familiar to Tertullian [Col. 0176C] (as Holstenius’s notes on these Acts prove by several examples). Finally, the writer undoubtedly belonged to the school of Montanus, which Tertullian was the first to propagate in Africa at approximately the time when these martyrs were killed. These Acts must therefore also be Tertullian’s.

If I see the matter correctly, all this proves nothing except that Tertullian could be the man to whom the collection of these memoirs was owed; Whiston has not established by these arguments that he actually composed them. Indeed, among these premises are assertions which, being arbitrarily fabricated, either prove more than he wishes or prove nothing at all. For, as we have said, the claim that Tertullian was the first author of Montanism’s dissemination in Africa is fictitious; and the words common to Tertullian and these Acts do not come from his own distinctive style but [Col. 0176D] from African usage. For if the presence of many words customary in Tertullian’s speech showed that Tertullian himself composed such a work, it would certainly follow that the memoirs of Perpetua and Saturus themselves were composed not by them but by Tertullian; for, as Holstenius’s observations show, many words occur in those very memoirs which may also be found in Tertullian’s writings.

Whiston’s suspicions can also be met by contrary arguments. In *On the Soul*, ch. 55, Tertullian mentions a vision of Perpetua narrated in these Acts and adduces it to confirm a certain doctrine; [Col. 0177A] but there is not even a word there by which he indicates that he was the writer of these Acts. I do not doubt that, as is his habit, he would have done so had he been the author of this history. Furthermore, it seems to me that no one who knows Tertullian’s writings and manner of expression ought to dare say that the style found at the end of these memoirs is the same as that found in Tertullian’s other writings. These Acts must therefore be removed from the corpus of Tertullian’s works, and consequently there is no need to discuss their date itself.

§ 6.—The Usefulness of This Entire Discussion Is Demonstrated by Examples Drawn from Christian History

And as we bring our writing to an end, we do not doubt that there will be some to whom all the labor spent in discussing [Col. 0177B] these matters will seem trivial and badly applied. For there are some who think that every discussion concerned with matters that are uncertain and, in a manner of speaking, bloodless should be despised; others pronounce wholly useless those subjects whose utility does not offer itself at first glance, as it were, but lies deeply concealed.

We could meet them with the examples of great men who did not consider it disgraceful to engage in discussions of this kind, and with the splendid words of the venerable Ernesti, who certainly knows, if anyone does, what value is to be assigned to every discipline. He maintains (*Prolusio on the Use of Engraving*, p. 5) that each art should be judged in such a way that we measure its dignity and excellence not so much by the magnitude and necessity of its usefulness as by the difficulty of discovering and practicing it, and that we should consider not [Col. 0177C] how useful each art is, but how much each is worth—unless, because it is more necessary and useful to bake loaves than to paint pictures, we are therefore to prefer the craft of bakers to the art of painting.

I myself think it far more proper to apply industry to elucidating somewhat obscure matters than to other subjects already widely traversed, even though the latter may appear better adapted to common use; for in these there is little or nothing that has escaped the diligence of many, while in the former there is always something that can be discussed further. In matters that are not certain but must be established by probability, there is far greater usefulness for acquiring the faculty of understanding and writing than in matters that are certain and, as it were, necessary, because the former possess many [Col. 0177D] different shapes, so to speak, and can be conceived and argued on either side. The ancients long ago taught, and most correctly, that this has great power to cultivate subtlety of understanding itself.

But why should I gather together every consideration, when I have also taken pains to interpose matters extraneous to the immediate case, as far as this could be done, yet not too remote from the purpose, in order to relieve somewhat the weariness produced by similar topics, and to employ examples showing that the arguments we have offered, although perhaps comparatively slight, are nevertheless necessary if anyone wishes to examine questions of greater importance in sacred history? In presenting these I am not one who wishes to criticize learned men; rather, I shall adduce a few examples that occur without much searching, so that the usefulness of this discussion may nonetheless be understood in some measure.

To begin with this example, learned men debate [Col. 0178A] what caused Tertullian to join the Montanists. Many among them think Jerome should be heard, who says that Tertullian, inflamed by hatred of the teachers of the Roman Church, took leave of the common Church. Passing over other considerations, this is scarcely credible because in the Montanist book *On Prescription*, as we have said, he continues to extol the Roman Church with high praises (ch. 36); nor in *Against Praxeas*, ch. 1, where he fiercely assails Praxeas for corrupting that Church with errors, does he cast any insult upon that Church itself or its bishop.

Again, in the history of the Montanists, how many mistakes could have been avoided and how many arguments corrected if it had been determined more precisely which books were written before Tertullian’s defection and which afterward! [Col. 0178B] To take one example, some have numbered among Montanus’s disgraceful practices a ridiculous and effeminate devotion to adorning the eyes, hair, and other things, led by the matters which Apollonius recorded in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.18. If I see correctly, his words in no way confirm this point, and everyone has erred in believing that the prophet mentioned there was Montanus; for Apollonius’s words must be understood generally of vices which ought to have been absent from prophets, of whom the Montanists boasted that they had many. But that slander can also be refuted by Tertullian’s very severe statements in the books *On the Veiling of Virgins* and *On the Dress of Women* against excessive concern for feminine adornment.

Moreover, Epiphanius, *Haer.* 49, § 14, says that the Montanists brought a hand to the mouth while praying, whence [Col. 0178C] they earned the name Tascodrugites. Wernsdorf, that distinguished man, wishes to refute this charge, loc. cit., § 21, by a passage of Tertullian from *On Prayer*, ch. 13, where Tertullian says that it is inconsistent with modesty to raise the hands too high during prayer. Since that passage comes from a book written while Tertullian was still orthodox in belief, it has no force for repelling the charge—not to mention that Epiphanius reports this only of certain Montanists.

Furthermore, how confused are the discussions of Tillemont and others concerning the calamities of Christians under Severus, and how disorderly and inverted the arrangement of all their passages, for this one reason: that they did not correctly distinguish the books Tertullian wrote during the earlier persecution under Severus, when he agreed with the orthodox, from those written during the later persecution, when he had separated himself from them [Col. 0178D].

Finally, nothing is more effective than our discussion for overthrowing Whiston’s fantasies, which he proposed in the book cited above (*The True Origin of the Sabellian and Athanasian Doctrines of the Trinity*, London, 1720, octavo). In it he imagines that the doctrines of the Sabellians and of those whom he calls Athanasians concerning the most holy Triad were invented by Simon Magus and revived by the Montanists. He therefore attempts to demonstrate that Tertullian’s opinion on this matter was threefold, from three classes of books written by him: those composed when he believed correctly, those written when he inclined toward Montanus’s errors, and those written when he had been wholly imbued with them. Yet within each class he assigns books which we have established plainly belong to another class, and by this fact alone Whiston’s entire argument is reduced to nothing.

[Col. 0179A] But at long last we must stop, lest we appear excessive in these matters, and entrust our little book to the judgment of learned men. We ask that their judgment be all the more equitable toward us, insofar as either the very nature of the matters discussed, or the other labors by which we were burdened while presenting them, prevented us from furnishing a more exact treatment. [Col. 0180A]

Tertullian’s Paradoxes, with the Antidote of Jacobus Pamelius

[Col. 0179]

TERTULLIAN’S PARADOXES, WITH THE ANTIDOTE OF JACOBUS PAMELIUS

[Col. 0179A] 1. On the Rebel Angels Who Took the Daughters of Men. Vol. II, book *On Idolatry*, ch. 9, no. 47; book [Col. 0179B] *On Women’s Dress*, ch. 1, no. 17; book *On the Apparel of Women*, ch. 10, no. 56; and book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 7, no. 32. Likewise vol. III, book V *Against Marcion*, ch. 18, no. 291. (According to Pamelius’s edition, Antwerp, 1579; Paris, 1583.)

Tertullian was neither the first nor the last author of this paradox. As we have observed in part on the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, where he treats it most deliberately, before him it was held by Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I; St. Justin Martyr in both *Apologies*; Athenagoras in the *Apology*; and Clement of Alexandria in books III and V of the *Stromata*; after him by Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book II, ch. 15; St. Cyprian, *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, no. 54; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book V; and Methodius, discourse *On the Resurrection*.

The occasion for the error was that the old Greek Septuagint edition which they followed [Col. 0179C], following Philo, read οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ (“the angels of God”), and the Latin Itala, as Saints Ambrose and Augustine and Procopius attest, read “angels of God,” in place of what is found to have been read later, οἱ υἷοι τοῦ Θεοῦ (“the sons of God”), or in Latin, “sons of God.” St. Augustine and Procopius were acquainted with both readings in their time.

But St. Chrysostom admirably refutes that opinion by reducing it to absurdity in homily 22 on Genesis, asserting that nowhere else in Scripture—namely, according to the Septuagint edition, the only one he knew—are angels called sons of God. So too do St. Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, ch. 4; St. Augustine, question 3 on Genesis, and more fully in *The City of God*, book XV, ch. 15; St. Epiphanius, *Epitome of Divine Dogmas*; and Procopius in his *Commentary*. Of these, Chrysostom and Augustine also contest the authority of the Book of Enoch, on which Tertullian appears to rely [Col. 0179D]. They all interpret both the “angels” and the “sons of God” as the descendants of Seth, inasmuch as they were worshipers of God; so likewise does Blessed Jerome in the book *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis*. Finally, the Venerable Bede, our Rabanus, and Haymo, writing commentaries on Genesis, state that faithful and righteous men are frequently called “angels” in Holy Scripture. What of the fact that Philastrius, in his book *On Heresies*, ch. 108, numbers among the heresies those who assert that angels had intercourse with women before the Flood and that giants were born from this union?

2. On the Apparitions of Angels in True Human Flesh. Vol. III, book III *Against Marcion*, ch. 9, no. 61, and ch. 11, no. 72.

Those words of Tertullian do indeed appear to express something of the kind: [Col. 0180A] “Then know that not even this is conceded to you—that the angels’ flesh was merely apparent—but that it was of true and solid human substance.” [Col. 0180B] Yet in other books written at the same time he explains himself, as we noted on *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 6, no. 60, in such a way that he did not intend to assert anything certain on this matter; otherwise he would appear to contradict himself. “It is agreed,” he says there, “that angels did not bear flesh of their own, since they are by nature of spiritual substance; and even if they possess some sort of body, it is nevertheless of their own kind, though capable of being transformed temporarily into human flesh, so that they may be seen and associate with human beings.”

He speaks still more clearly in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 62: “For the angels too,” he says, “were sometimes as though human beings, eating, drinking, and extending their feet for washing; for they had put on a human outward appearance while preserving inwardly their proper substance.” It everywhere seemed sufficient to the Author that he did not agree with the doctrine of Apelles [Col. 0180C], who said that angels had been created from an airy substance; thus he would not appear to agree with him also in holding that Christ’s body derived its origin from ethereal matter.

But what kind of bodies were assumed by angels, and whence they were taken, remains controversial even today in the *Master of the Sentences*, book II, distinction 8, § 4. In the passage already cited, we preferred, with St. Bernard, to suspend our judgment on this matter rather than define anything as certain. Whether, however, the Author believed—as certain persons charge against him—that angels and demons are corporeal may not unreasonably be doubted. For although the Author here seems to attribute a body of their own kind to angels, he nevertheless makes them of spiritual substance, just as he also repeatedly does in the *Apologeticum*, and specifically in ch. 22, where he attributes spiritual powers both to angels [Col. 0180D] and to demons and calls them spirits. More generally accepted, however, and pleasing to me, is the opinion of those who make them incorporeal. Among these should be mentioned St. Dionysius the Areopagite, *Celestial Hierarchy*, ch. 2; Athanasius, *On the Common Essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*; Chrysostom, homily 22 on Genesis; and Cyril, book IV, on John, chapter.

3. On the Soul of the First Man Being from the Substance of God. Vol. III, book IV *Against Marcion*, ch. 38, no. 611.

The following words of the Author, explaining Luke 20, “Render to God the things that are God’s,” do indeed appear pertinent here: “He therefore commands that man be rendered to the Creator, in whose image, likeness, name, and substance he was fashioned.” This passage was perhaps the reason why Gennadius wrote thus of him [Col. 0181A] in the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “Let us not believe that anything from the essence of the Trinity was derived into the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian did.”

But since St. Augustine, who so often demonstrates that the soul cannot be called a part of God, attributes nothing of the kind to him, I too think that he should be cleared of so absurd a heresy. Indeed, he meant to say nothing other than that the soul takes its origin from the breath of God, in accordance with Genesis 2: “And God breathed the breath of life into the face of man, and man became a living soul,” as he himself very frequently insists, but especially in *On the Soul*, ch. 11. In that passage, as also in *On Baptism*, ch. 5, no. 43, we showed that this interpretation agrees with Saints Irenaeus, Prudentius, Chrysostom, Augustine, and Theodoret.

The last of these says: “By the term ‘breath’ we do not understand any part of the divine essence [Col. 0181B], according to the madness of Cerdo and Marcion, but signify by it the nature of the soul, because the soul is a rational and intellectual spirit.” These words also suggest to me another conjecture: that the Author speaks not according to his own opinion but according to Marcion’s, especially since it is clear from the fragments of the book *On the Origin of the Soul Against Hermogenes* that he believed the soul to be far inferior to God, as being passible, although immortal.

Indeed, one must also repeat what we noted in both places: St. Augustine rightly judged in his book *On Heresies* that Philastrius had listed many heresies which are not heresies. Of this kind is the interpretation of the breath, or breath of life, as the rational soul, which is not a heresy but the catholic opinion of the Fathers.

[Col. 0181C] 4. On the Souls of Adam’s Descendants Being Derived by Propagation. Vol. III, book *On the Soul*, ch. 9, no. 123; ch. 19, no. 256; ch. 22, no. 294; and the entirety of chs. 27 and 36.

This paradox is attributed to Tertullian by Rufinus, in his *Apology for Origen*, and by St. Jerome, in Books II and III of his *Apology against the Same*. The former thinks that nothing should be definitively settled; the latter speaks with considerable hesitation, although he seems more inclined to regard the opinion as condemned. For in his *Apology to Pammachius against the Errors of John of Jerusalem* he declares in express terms that the ecclesiastical opinion is that God daily creates new souls and infuses them into bodies already conceived, citing in support of this John V, Zechariah XII, and Psalm XXXII. Meanwhile, however, in Epistle [Col. 0181D] 99, addressed to Marcellinus and Anapsychia, he speaks more cautiously, writing that this indeed seems true to him, but referring the matter to St. Augustine, since he is unwilling to define anything with certainty, having read that Augustine still held his judgment in suspense: he alludes to Augustine’s letters written to him, and to Epistle 157, addressed to Optatus, *On the Origin of Souls*. In that letter Augustine condemns Tertullian not so much for deriving souls by propagation as for making them corporeal—concerning which paradox more will be said shortly. For he says:

> Even those who assert that souls are propagated from that single soul which God gave to the first man, and who thus say that they are derived from parents, if they follow Tertullian’s opinion, certainly contend that they are not spirits but bodies, and that they arise from corporeal seeds. What more perverse statement could be made? Nor is it surprising [Col. 0182A] that Tertullian imagined this, since he believes that even God the Creator himself is nothing unless he is a body.

But more will be said below about that paradox also, from the same Augustine. Gennadius, however, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*—which this passage alone makes clear is not by St. Augustine—after recounting Origen’s opinion and the opinion already mentioned, which he calls that of the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain Latins, among whom Tertullian was undoubtedly included, defines that, once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused by God. Nor does the author of the *Dialogue on the Origin of Souls*, among the works of Sts. Jerome and Augustine, teach otherwise. We, however, have preferred to teach nothing on this point as an article of faith, since the Church, even after so many councils have since been celebrated, has, so far as I know, left nothing expressly defined. It will suffice that we added certain remarks in the Annotations, in which we indicated, first, that St. Jerome’s opinion is no more conclusively proved, [Col. 0182B] and, secondly, briefly answered from St. Augustine and Lactantius the absurd arguments of Tertullian, who thinks that the soul arises from corporeal seeds.

### 5. On the Sex of the Soul  
*Ibid.*, chapter 36.

Tertullian indeed deduces this from the foregoing paradox. For if the soul is sown together with the body, that conclusion seems to follow. But St. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 4, and St. Augustine, Book I of *The Soul and Its Origin*, addressed to Vincentius, chapter 8, expressly define the contrary opinion. We have reproduced some of Augustine’s words in our annotations, to which we refer the reader. Augustine writes as follows:

> All souls, those of men as well as those of women, are beautiful and alike; only the members of the body create the distinction.

### [Col. 0182C] 6. That the Soul, Rather Than the Flesh, Is Sinful  
Vol. III, *On the Soul*, the whole of chapter 40, and chapter 58, no. 650; and Book V *Against Marcion*, chapter 10, no. 165.

Peter Lombard alludes to this paradox in the following words and refutes it at the same time; we also cited his words there, from Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 31:

> Some believed that original sin is derived through the soul, and not only through the flesh, because they thought that not only the flesh but also the soul is derived by propagation. And therefore, just as flesh is generated from corrupted flesh, so too they held that from a sinful soul a sinful soul, infected by original corruption, is derived from those who beget it. But this, he says, the Catholic faith rejects and condemns as contrary to the truth, for it admits that not souls [Col. 0182D] but the flesh alone is derived by propagation.

At the same place, no. 455, we cited, in support of the contrary opinion, passages from Sts. Ambrose and Augustine quoted by the same Lombard.

### 7. On the Corporeal Soul  
Vol. I, *Apology*, chapter 48, nos. 608 and 609; Vol. III, *On the Soul*, the whole of chapters 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 22, 36, and 37; *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 11, no. 98; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 17, no. 131, chapter 45, no. 320, and chapter 53, no. 384; Book V *Against Marcion*, chapter 10, no. 158, and chapter 15, no. 248. That it is therefore not properly a spirit: *ibid.*, *On the Soul*, chapter 11; and Vol. IV, in the fragments of the book *On the Origin of the Soul against Hermogenes*.

St. Augustine, [Col. 0183A] in Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, the final two chapters, and in his book *On Heresies*, and Fulgentius, in Book II of *On Faith, to Peter*, charge the Author with this paradox. Augustine, however, reproves him not so much because he makes the soul corporeal—which, in a certain sense, some interpret acceptably in Hilary, Cassian, and the Commentary on Job attributed to Jerome—as because he calls it shaped and colored. Thus he writes in the former passage:

> Finally, Tertullian believed the soul to be a body for no other reason than that he was unable to conceive it as incorporeal, and therefore feared that it would be nothing if it were not a body. And although he is certainly acute, he is sometimes overcome by the truth when it appears contrary to his own opinion. For when he assigned the soul an airy and luminous color, he came to the senses, with which he attempted to furnish it member by member, as though it were a body, and said: “This will be the inner man, [Col. 0183B] another than the outer, one man in twofold form. He too has his own eyes and ears, with which the people ought to have seen and heard God; he also has the other limbs, through which he acts in thoughts and functions in dreams.” Behold the ears and eyes with which the people ought to have heard and seen God: those which the soul employs in dreams! Yet if anyone were to see Tertullian himself in a dream, Tertullian would never say that he had been seen by someone whom he himself had not in turn seen, or that the man had spoken with him when he had not spoken with the man. Finally, if the soul sees itself in dreams, when the members of its body are plainly lying in one place while it wanders through the various images which it sees, who has ever seen it in a dream as airy and luminous in color, except perhaps as he sees other things which he similarly sees falsely? For he can see this too, [Col. 0183C] but far be it from him to believe, once awake, that the soul is such. Otherwise, whenever he sees himself differently—as happens more frequently—either his soul will have been changed, or even then it is not the substance of the soul that is seen, but an incorporeal image of the body, which is formed in a wondrous manner, just as it is in thought. For what Ethiopian does not almost always see himself as black in dreams? Or, if he saw himself in another color, was he not all the more astonished, if his memory remained with him? Yet I do not know whether he would ever have seen himself with an airy and luminous color if he had never read or heard Tertullian.
>
> What of the fact that people are led by such visions and wish to dictate to us from the Scriptures that something of this sort is not the soul but God himself, such as he was figuratively shown to the spirits of the saints, and such as he is also represented in allegorical discourse? For those visions are like such [Col. 0183D] sayings. Thus they err, setting up in their hearts images of vain opinion, and failing to understand that the saints judged such visions of their own in the same manner as they judge when they read or hear such things divinely spoken in figures: just as the seven ears of grain and the seven cows signify seven years; and just as the linen sheet tied at its four corners, like a dish full of various animals, signifies the world with all its nations. So too with the rest, and much more with those things in which incorporeal realities are signified by corporeal things—not by actual things, but by images.

And again in the following chapter:

> Tertullian nevertheless refused to allow the soul to grow in substance as the body does, even stating the reason for his fear: lest, he says, it should also be said to diminish in substance and thus be believed destined to fail. Yet because he extends it locally through the body, he found no way out concerning the growth [Col. 0184A] of the soul, which he wishes to expand from a tiny seed until it equals the body in size. He says: “But its force, in which its natural endowments remain implanted, while the measure of the substance with which it was breathed forth from the beginning remains intact, is gradually extended with the flesh throughout the limbs.” Perhaps we would not understand this unless, by employing a comparison with things we see, he had made his meaning clear. He says: “Take a fixed weight of gold or silver, as yet an unworked mass. Its form is compact and for the present smaller than what it will be, yet it contains within the boundary of its measure the whole nature of gold or silver. Then, when the mass is spread into a sheet, it becomes greater than its original form through the expansion of its fixed weight, not through addition, since it is extended but not increased. Yet in this manner too it is increased while being extended; for it may increase in form, though not in quantity. Then also [Col. 0184B] the brightness of the gold or silver itself is enhanced. It had indeed already been present in the mass, but more obscurely, though not altogether absent. Then other forms and shapes are added according to the pliability of the material and the direction given to it by the craftsman, who contributes nothing to its measure except its form. Thus the soul’s growth must also be understood as not substantial but elicitive.”
>
> Who would have believed that a man with such a mind could have been so eloquent? But these things should inspire fear, not laughter; for he would never have been driven to this if he had been capable of conceiving something which both exists and is not a body. What, moreover, could be more absurd than to suppose that a mass of some metal can grow in one part while it is being hammered unless it diminishes in another, or increase in breadth unless it is reduced in thickness? Or that there is any body which, while retaining the quantity proper to its nature, grows in every direction without becoming rarer? How, [Col. 0184C] then, will the soul fill, from that drop of seed, the full size of the body which it animates, if the soul itself is also a body whose substance grows by no addition? How, I ask, will it fill the flesh which it gives life unless it becomes rarer in proportion to the greater mass that it animates? He was evidently afraid that it would fail by diminution if it grew, yet was not afraid that it would fail by becoming rarer while not growing.
>
> But why should I linger any longer, when both the discussion is proceeding to greater length than the need to conclude permits, and my opinion is already sufficiently clear—both what I hold with certainty, and where I still hesitate, and why I hesitate?

Again, in the latter passage:

> He calls the soul immortal indeed, but contends that it is a shaped body.

Thus far St. Augustine. In our own Annotations [Col. 0184D] on chapter 6, we also confirmed, from St. Gregory, Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory Nazianzen, and Claudianus’ *On the State of the Soul*, the Platonists’ arguments concerning the incorporeal soul. In chapters 7 and partly 8, we showed from Sts. Justin Martyr, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Epiphanius, and the aforementioned Claudianus that some of the Author’s own arguments, including certain arguments from Scripture, do not establish his conclusion. In chapter 9, nos. 109 and 110, we cited both Plato and Clement of Alexandria against the soul’s having a bodily form. Then in chapter 11 we quoted a passage from the Author’s *On Repentance*, chapter 3, no. 12, where he had previously held the contrary, calling the soul a spirit brought to completion by the breath of God. Nor can it truly be concluded from Isaiah XLII and LVII, which he cites there in his support, that the soul is not called a spirit in other passages of Scripture. Moreover, the sense in which the soul may be [Col. 0185A] called a body is explained by him in *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 35, no. 124, in these words:

> Even if I grant, he says, that something among substances is incorporeal, nevertheless the substance itself is the body of each thing.

It seems, therefore, that he was led into the absurdity of assigning the soul an airy and luminous color through certain false revelations of a Montanist woman—not Priscilla or Maximilla, as we once thought, for they had long before perished by hanging, but one of their disciples—as is clear from the aforementioned *On the Soul*, chapter 9, no. 111. St. Jerome somewhere attributes this same paradox to Origen, and so this Antidote may also be useful for Origen’s works.

### [Col. 0185B] 8. That the Soul Can Suffer Nothing without the Body  
Vol. I, *Apology*, chapter 48, no. 609; *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 4, no. 14.

The Magdeburg Centuriators place this not among the paradoxes but among the dogmas of faith, and they confirm it from the passage of Tertullian just cited, but in vain. For the Author himself, as though retracting what he had declared without sufficient caution at the beginning of his faith, and having afterward been better instructed in the Catholic faith, develops at length and eloquently, throughout the final chapter of *On the Soul*, the doctrine that souls suffer in the underworld in the meantime—that is, until the Last Judgment. Among other things he writes:

> What, then, will happen during this interval? Shall we sleep? But souls do not sleep even in the living. How exceedingly unjust it would be if, even in the underworld, offenders should still fare well! Does not the soul by itself suffice to establish a claim to suffering? [Col. 0185C] How often, while the body is unharmed, is the soul alone tormented by bitterness, anger, and often by a weariness whose cause it does not itself know? Thus the soul knows how to suffer in the underworld without the flesh, because even while in the unharmed flesh it suffers, if it so wills. If it does this by its own choice in life, how much more by the judgment of God after death? For divine judgment pursues even thoughts alone and bare intentions. Therefore it is most fitting that the soul, even without awaiting the flesh, should be punished for what it committed without the flesh as its partner. In short, since we understand that prison which the Gospel presents (Matthew V) to mean the underworld, and interpret the last farthing as every smallest offense that must be paid for there, no one will doubt that the soul makes some payment in the underworld.

He also repeatedly teaches the same thing in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 17, nos. 133 and 134. At that [Col. 0185D] chapter we also adduced similar testimonies from the Author of the *Questions and Answers* among the works of St. Justin Martyr, from Lactantius, and from St. Augustine, and indicated that this opinion accords with that of the Fathers.

### 9. That the Souls of the Saints Are Cherished and Rejoice in Abraham’s Bosom, or Paradise, or beneath the Altar—that Is, in a Place Not Heavenly, but Nevertheless above the Underworld—until the Day of the Lord’s Judgment  
Vol. I, *Apology*, chapter 47, no. 601; Vol. III, *On the Soul*, chapter 7, nos. 94, 95, 96, and 97; chapter 9, no. 124; chapter 55, nos. 606, 608, 610, and 611; chapter 56, no. 622; and the final chapter, no. 644; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 17, nos. 132 and 134; Book III *Against Marcion*, chapter 34, nos. 548, 549, 550, and 551; and *Scorpiace against the Gnostics*, chapter 12, no. 95; Vol. IV, *On the [Col. 0186A] Judgment of the Lord*, chapter 11, no. 15; and in the fragments of the book *On Paradise*. Finally, Vol. V, Novatian’s *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, no. 10.

This paradox, not only in Tertullian and Novatian but also in other ancient writers, was occasioned both by the account or parable of Lazarus (Luke XVI), whom the rich man saw in Abraham’s bosom, and by the vision of St. John the Apostle in Revelation VI, in which he saw the souls of the martyrs beneath the altar, clothed in white robes, and they were told to rest until the number of their fellow servants should be complete, and finally by Christ’s words to the thief (Luke XXIII): “Today you will be with me in paradise.” For since they saw that the state of souls without bodies until the future Judgment had to be distinguished [Col. 0186B] from the more perfect state of souls with their bodies after the universal resurrection, they designated the former by the terms “Abraham’s bosom,” “peaceful rest beneath the altar,” and “paradise”; and, by contrast, the latter state as “the heavenly bosom,” “the higher altar,” and “the heavenly harbor.” They did not, however, suppose that the souls of the saints were meanwhile deprived of the glory of beholding God, as today’s Anabaptists and Cornelius Agrippa, their follower, maintain, since they had read in the Apostle (Philippians I): “I have a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” Likewise (II Corinthians V): “We are willing to be absent from the body and to be present with the Lord.” And concerning the very vision of God: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.”

Certainly the Author himself seems to indicate his opinion [Col. 0186C] in the following words of the aforementioned *On the Soul*, chapter 56, no. 622:

> Until that perfection, proportioned to the measure of angelic fullness, is promised.

If, meanwhile, any passage is found in him or in other Fathers which does not admit this reasonable interpretation, the reader should remember that this error does not detract from the learning and piety of such illustrious writers, since in their time the Church had not yet determined anything certain to be believed concerning this article. But after the Ecumenical Council of Florence—which, following the first condemnation issued in the decretal letters of Innocent III and Benedict XII, defined the matter—it is not permissible to hold otherwise. Its decree against the errors of the Armenians contains these words:

> We define that the souls of those who, after receiving baptism, incurred no stain whatsoever [Col. 0186D] of sin, and also those souls which, after contracting the stain of sin, have been purified either while in their bodies or after being divested of those bodies, as was said above, are immediately received into heaven and clearly behold the triune and one Lord himself as he is, although one does so more perfectly than another according to the diversity of their merits; but that the souls of those who die in actual mortal sin or in original sin alone are to be punished, although with unequal punishments.

What is more, the cited passages of Scripture do not support the other opinion if examined more diligently. First, although it is sufficiently agreed that Lazarus and the other Fathers of the Old Testament were in Abraham’s bosom, and that the thief was there also, or in paradise, for some time, they were nevertheless led from there into heaven by Christ, according to Psalm LXVII and Ephesians IV: “Ascending [Col. 0187A] on high, Christ led captivity captive”—that is, as the Apostle himself interprets it, “above all the heavens.”

Secondly, in his Fourth Sermon *On the Solemnity of the Saints*, St. Augustine interprets the white robes in the cited passage (Revelation VI) as the reward of baptism, the prize of martyrdom, and the joy of the heavenly homeland. In support he cites the following words (Revelation VII): “They shall stand before the throne in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and palms in their hands.” From this he concludes: “They stand crowned in the sight of the Lamb, before the throne of God, and cannot in any way be separated there from the contemplation of his glory.”

We therefore cited similar passages from Cyprian and from the same St. Augustine, as well as from Sts. Ambrose and Chrysostom—among whom certain obscure passages are also found—in our Annotations on St. Cyprian’s Epistle 16, no. 19. Feuardentius likewise [Col. 0187B] noted several passages in St. Irenaeus in our favor, contrary to the opinion of others, Book I, chapter 2, no. 3, and elsewhere. If anyone desires more, let him consult Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library*, Book VI, Annotations 264 and 345.

Meanwhile we shall add that, where the Author says in *On the Soul*, chapter 55, that paradise stands open only to the martyrs, although elsewhere he calls it the common receptacle of all the saints, Blessed Cyprian, his disciple, explains the matter thus in Epistle 32, addressed to Antoninus:

> It is one thing to stand awaiting pardon, another to attain glory; one thing, after being sent to prison, not to come out from there until one has paid the last farthing, another immediately to receive the reward of faith and virtue; one thing to be cleansed from sins by the torment of prolonged suffering and to be purified for a long time by fire, another to have purged one’s sins through suffering; one thing, finally, to remain in suspense on the Day of Judgment awaiting the Lord’s sentence, another [Col. 0187C] immediately to be crowned by the Lord.

At the same place, no. 59, and on Tertullian’s *On the Soul*, chapter 55, no. 611, we noted that this same passage serves to confirm the tradition of the Church concerning Purgatory. Moreover, that affirmation of Blessed Augustine in Book XX of *The City of God* is altogether contrary to the Author, who wishes all souls, even those of the faithful of earlier times, to be kept apart until the Day of Judgment:

> From the time when Christ’s blood delivered the ancient saints from the underworld, good believers thereafter, redeemed by the shedding of that price, know nothing whatever of the underworld.

### 10. That Every Incorporeal Manifestation of the Souls of the Dead Is a Deception  
Vol. III, *On the Soul*, chapter 57, no. 643.

[Col. 0187D] At first sight this indeed seems a paradox, but Tertullian is arguing deliberately against the heretical disciples of Simon Magus, who even promised that they could summon the souls of the prophets from the underworld. Tertullian thinks that in the case of Samuel’s soul (I Kings XXVIII), this could have been permitted to the divining spirit only by falsehood: it was Satan transfigured as an angel of light. We noted there, no. 638, that certain other Fathers also doubted this. He then explains himself by adding that the underworld lies open to no soul, proving this from Abraham’s words to the rich man (Luke XVI).

Since, meanwhile, he admits that certain souls can be recalled into bodies by God’s power, why could they not also, by a special privilege of God, be manifested outside the body—especially since, as we also observed there, no. 643, we possess in the Books of Maccabees the example of the apparitions of Onias [Col. 0188A] the priest and Jeremiah the Prophet? However the matter may stand, St. Augustine wrote beautifully on this subject in *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapters 10, 11, 15, and 16:

> Certain visions are related; it is reported that some dead persons appeared to the living, either in dreams or in some other manner, and showed the places where their bodies lay unburied to people who did not know, warning them that the burial which they lacked should be provided for them. If we reply that these things are false, we shall seem shamelessly to contradict both the writings of certain faithful persons—for example, St. Ambrose’s Sermon *On the Discovery of the Bodies of Sts. Gervasius and Protasius*, St. Lucian’s *On the Discovery of the Body of St. Stephen the Protomartyr*, and those of others—and the experience of those who affirm that such things happened to them. I should therefore believe, he says, that they occur through angelic operations, whether permitted [Col. 0188B] or commanded from above. This is sometimes done to good purpose, whether for some kind of consolation of the living, or so that through such admonitions humanity may be commended to the human race in the matter of burial.

Then, after presenting many arguments on both sides, he concludes as follows:

> Divine Scripture also testifies that some of the dead are sent to the living, just as Paul, conversely, was taken up alive into paradise. For the Prophet Samuel, though dead, foretold future events to the living King Saul—although some, among whom, as I have said, is our Author, think that it was not Samuel himself, who could not have been summoned by magical arts, but that some spirit suited to such evil works represented his likeness—since the book of Ecclesiasticus, which tradition says was written by Jesus son of Sirach and which, because of a certain similarity of style, is declared to be Solomon’s [Col. 0188C] even by Tertullian himself in one place, states in the Praise of the Fathers (chapter XLVI) that Samuel prophesied even after death.
>
> But if this book is rejected because it is not in the Hebrew canon, what shall we say of Moses, who is certainly said in Deuteronomy to have died, and in the Gospel to have appeared to the living with Elijah, who had not died (Matthew XVII)? This also resolves the question how martyrs show, through the very benefits granted to those who pray, that they take part in human affairs, if the dead do not know what the living are doing. For we have heard, not from uncertain rumor [Col. 0188D] but from trustworthy witnesses, that Felix the Confessor appeared not only through the effects of benefits but also to the very sight of men when Nola was being attacked by barbarians—a fact which St. Paulinus himself also attests in his Poem on Felix.
>
> But these things are manifested by divine agency in a manner far different from the customary order assigned to each class of creatures. Yet this question, he says, surpasses the powers of my understanding: namely, how the martyrs assist those whom it is certain are assisted through them. This matter is too lofty for me to reach and too hidden for me to investigate. Therefore I do not dare to determine which of these two explanations is true, or whether perhaps both are: that sometimes these things occur through the actual presence of the martyrs, and sometimes through angels assuming the person of the martyrs. I would prefer to inquire about these matters from those who know them.

The author of the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 26, extant among the works of Blessed Augustine, condensed these very words.

### [Col. 0189A] 11. That the Souls of the Worst Men Are Changed into Demons after Death  
St. Augustine, *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus.

This paradox should be attributed not so much to Tertullian as to the Tertullianists. Above, at the end of the Author’s Life, we noted that Blessed Isidore, Honorius, Rabanus, and Gratian expressly attribute it to them in their Catalogues of Heretics. Consequently, we judge that in Blessed Augustine also one should read “they say” and, a little later, “they believe,” instead of “he says” and “he believes”; especially since nothing of the sort is found in Tertullian’s writings, and since the Epistle 59 of Blessed Jerome to Avitus and Book II *Against Rufinus* attribute it not to Tertullian anywhere, but to Origen.

The opinion is so absurd that it needs no other refutation than the fact that [Col. 0189B] it was condemned under the name of heresy both by the aforementioned writers and, though somewhat less explicitly, by the Sixth Synod in Origen and his accomplices, Act 11, in the Epistle of Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem. It arose from the school of Plato, who, as the Author himself testifies in *On the Soul*, chapters 23, 24, and 28, said that souls depart from here to the heavens whence they came and afterward return here again. Origen and the other heretics plainly attributed something further to him, so that what the Author repeatedly says is most true: the philosophers are the patriarchs of the heretics.

Indeed, he himself expressly denies what would follow by the same reasoning, namely, that good men are changed into angels. Thus he writes in *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 32, no. 362:

> And yet I must turn aside to that place where, after death, there is no marrying at all; where one is clothed upon rather than stripped; where, even if I am stripped of my sex, I am reckoned among the angels, [Col. 0189C] but am not an angel, male or female.

Finally, in *On the Soul*, chapter 56, no. 622, he promises human beings not the substance of angels, but “that perfection proportioned to the measure of angelic fullness.” Then, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 62, no. 428, he says:

> Finally, he did not say, “They shall be angels,” lest he deny that they are human beings, but “Like angels”—“so as to deny men” [as printed; reading uncertain]. He did not remove the substance to which he attributed the likeness.

I therefore cannot sufficiently express my astonishment—as I also noted on Book III *Against Marcion*, chapter 9, no. 68—that Guido the Carmelite, in *On Heresies*, chapter 36, attributes both these heresies to Tertullian. Philastrius more correctly places them, in *On Heresies*, chapter 36, among the unnamed heresies without any certain author.

### 12. On Baptizing Heretics, Because among Them Everything Is [Col. 0189D] Foreign and Contrary to the Truth  
Vol. III, *On Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 12, nos. 78 and 80; *On Baptism*, chapter 15, no. 106; Vol. IV, among the fragments of the Greek book *On Baptism*; Vol. V, *On Modesty*, chapter 19, no. 162.

Concerning this paradox of Agrippinus of Carthage and the other fellow bishops, of Tertullian, and afterward of St. Cyprian and the other bishops of Africa and Cappadocia, lest I be too lengthy here, the reader should consult our Annotations on St. Cyprian’s Epistles LXX to Januarius, LXXI to Quintus, LXXII to Stephen, LXXIII to Jubaianus, LXXIV to Pompeius, and LXXVI to Magnus; likewise the Council of Carthage celebrated under Cyprian himself; his Life at the years of the Lord 252 and 256; likewise Firmilian’s Epistle to Cyprian, LXXV among [Col. 0190A] his works; and finally our Annotations on the fragments of Tertullian’s book *On Baptism*, and in our Life of Tertullian at the year of the Lord 201.

To these I add that no one should find it surprising if Agrippinus and his fellow bishops issued such a decree concerning the baptism of those returning from heresy to the Catholic Church, and if Tertullian approved it in the already mentioned book written in Greek. For most heretics down to that time did not confess the same Christ and therefore did not agree upon the Rule of Faith handed down by the Apostles—which the later Fathers even to this day call the Creed—although it had always been customary to “seal,” as the Author says, faith in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, with mention of the Church necessarily added. This may be seen at greater length in our Annotations on [Col. 0190B] *On Baptism*, no. 2, among the ceremonies of Baptism, and chapter 6, nos. 45, 46, and 47.

Charles Bovius certainly interprets in the same manner Apostolic Canon 47 and chapter 15 of Book VI of the *Apostolic Constitutions* of Clement of Rome. Hence the First Council of Nicaea, canon 19, the contemporary Council of Laodicea, canon 8, and the Second Council of Arles, canon 17, define that the Paulianists and Cataphrygians must be baptized. To these the Second Council of Constantinople, canon 7, adds the Eunomians, Sabellians, and Galatian heretics; and finally the Sixth Synod, celebrated in Trullo, adds the Manichaeans, Valentinians, Marcionites, and similar groups.

But in Tertullian’s time the Hermogenians chiefly flourished—whom St. Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapters 41, 44, and 45, reports as holding the same opinions as the Praxeanists—along with the Praxeans, Cataphrygians, Valentinians, Marcionites, [Col. 0190C] the Apelleians who followed Marcion, and finally the Quintillianists. Against the latter the Author expressly composed the Latin book from which the fragments of the Greek book *On Baptism* were taken.

Concerning them, the Author’s statement in *On Prescription against Heretics* is true: “Among them everything is foreign and contrary to our truth”; and likewise his statement in *On Baptism*: “We and they do not have the same God or the same Christ; therefore neither do we have the same baptism, because he is not the same.” This is sufficiently clear concerning the Hermogenians, Praxeans, Cataphrygians, and Quintillianists, who either acknowledged only one person in the Godhead or were Patripassians.

Concerning the Marcionites, Valentinians, and Apelleians, Augustine himself doubts, in Book III of *On Baptism*, chapter 15, whether they baptized with the Gospel words “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” [Col. 0190D] because they held erroneous opinions both about God and about Christ. Therefore we too may believe—as Blessed Augustine writes of the Paulianists—that they did not retain the rule of baptism and, as the Second and Sixth Synods phrase it, baptized with only one immersion.

Meanwhile, however, St. Augustine, in Book VI of *On Baptism*, chapter 25, acknowledges as true baptism even that in whose prayers certain statements contrary to the Catholic faith are inserted, provided it is consecrated with the Gospel words. Accordingly, in his seven books *On Baptism against the Donatists*, who attacked the baptism of all heretics, he customarily supplies an antidote to statements of St. Cyprian similar to those of the Author, because Cyprian had cited them generally against all heretics.

In particular, to the statement that there is one baptism and that the baptism of heretics is not the baptism of truth—which occurs in *On Modesty*, [Col. 0191A] Book II, chapter 3—St. Augustine responds in Book V, chapters 21 and 29, and Book VI, chapters 8, 9, 12, and 13. To the statement, “No one can be built up by that whereby he is destroyed; no one is enlightened by him through whom he is darkened,” he responds in Book IV, chapters 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17; and likewise to the aforementioned words, “We and they do not have the same God or the same Christ,” in the same place and in Book V, chapter 26. To the statement, “Among heretics everything is foreign or contrary to the truth,” he responds in Book VI, chapter 40. Finally, to the statement, “Since they do not rightly possess baptism, neither can they receive it, because they do not possess it,” he responds in Book VII, chapters 29, 33, 35, and 47.

Moreover, this one point must be repeated here: Augustine more than once admits that neither Agrippinus nor Cyprian and his associates would have issued so general a decree against the baptism of heretics if anything had been defined by any plenary council, as afterward it was [Col. 0191B] by the First General Council of Nicaea, with the Paulianists alone excepted, as has already been said.

### 13. On Christ as the Spirit of God  
Vol. I, *Apology*, chapter 21, no. 314; Vol. II, *On Prayer*, chapter 1, no. 2; Vol. III, *Against Marcion*, Book I, chapter 19, no. 127; Book III, chapter 6, nos. 38 and 39, and chapter 16; Book IV, chapter 21, no. 314; and *Against Praxeas*, chapter 26, no. 155.

Concerning this phrase of the ancients, we noted the words of St. Jerome on chapter IV of the Epistle to the Galatians, and in his Epistle to Pammachius and Oceanus *On the Errors of Origen*, in the book of St. Cyprian *On the Vanity of Idols*, no. 71:

> Many, through ignorance of the Scriptures—as Firmianus also does in the eighth book of his Epistles to Demetrianus—assert that the Holy Spirit is often called the Father and often the Son.

This is true to such an extent that, besides Lactantius, the same usage may be found [Col. 0191C] in the authors of the books *On Mounts Sinai and Zion* and *Against the Jews Who Persecuted Christ*, among our works of St. Cyprian. Undoubtedly related to this is the fact that Tertullian so often calls Christ the Spirit of God, doing so in the same sense in which God is called spirit in John III and I John IV.

Otherwise, it is clear from the same book *Against Praxeas*, chapter 2, no. 24; chapter 4, no. 40; chapter 8, no. 90; chapter 9, no. 61; chapter 13, nos. 75 and 78; that same chapter 26, no. 158; chapter 30, no. 183; and finally chapter 30, no. 182, that he, like the other ancients, distinguished three persons in the Godhead: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Among these passages by far the clearest is that in which he calls the Holy Spirit “the third divine power of the Godhead” and “the third name of the Majesty.”

### [Col. 0191D] 14. That Christ Was Revealed through Preaching in the Twelfth Year of Tiberius Caesar, and Suffered in His Fifteenth Year  
Vol. I, *Against the Jews*, chapter 8, no. 82; and Vol. III, Book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 15, no. 102.

Restoration notes: The recovered isolated Greek ῶ occurs inside the mixed-script source spelling allegoricῶs; the existing English ‘allegorically’ fully represents its semantic function, while the exact hybrid orthography remains uncertain.; δευτερώσεις is rendered ‘secondary traditions’; literally it may suggest ‘repetitions’ or ‘second traditions.’  

Although the manuscripts of Tertullian vary in the former passage, Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, asserts that this was his opinion, and it is evident from the latter passage—indeed, also from the former, in the same chapter, no. 92, where he places the Lord’s Passion in the consulship of Rubellius Geminus and Rufius, or Fusius, Geminus, whose consulship fell in the fifteenth year of Tiberius. In this he was followed by Julius Africanus, in the *Book of Times*, cited by St. Jerome in his *Commentary on Daniel*; Lactantius, book IV, chapter 10; and Paulus Orosius, book VII, chapter 10. Yet since this is contrary to the express words of the Gospel in Luke III, where Christ is said to have been baptized in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, it must be admitted [Col. 0192A] that some human error befell the Author and those others here. Clement of Alexandria, therefore, writes more correctly near the end of book I of the *Stromata*, as do Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, Jornandes in the *Annals*, the Venerable Bede, and Nicephorus in the *Chronicle*, that Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, when the thirty-third year of his life had already begun.

Not all agree so well concerning the consulship in which Christ’s Passion occurred. St. Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, final chapter, and Severus Sulpicius, book II of the *Sacred History*, perhaps led by Tertullian’s authority without examining the Consular Fasti, place it under the two Gemini, as do the aforementioned Authors in the former passage. Some more recent writers, who state that the Lord suffered in the thirty-fourth year of his life, name Galba and Sulla as consuls; they held the consulship in the nineteenth year of Tiberius. But more consonant with the Gospel is the opinion [Col. 0192B] of those—and specifically of the more accurate Cassiodorus—who assign the year of the Passion to the consulship of Gnaeus Domitius, son of Lucius, grandson of Lucius, Ahenobarbus, and Aulus Vitellius, son of Publius, grandson of Quintus. All those named above who write that Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius agree with them. Anyone desiring more should consult Paulus of Middelburg, Bishop of Fossombrone, in his thirty-three books *On the Year and Day of the Lord’s Passion*.

I shall add only this passage from St. Augustine, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*: “Ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born, or in which he suffered, compelled some to err by thinking that the Lord suffered at the age of forty-six, because the temple, which bears the image of the Lord’s body, was built over that many years.” Here perhaps he tacitly refers to St. Irenaeus, book II, chapters 39 and 40, who endeavors to prove that Christ suffered at approximately [Col. 0192C] the age of fifty, and at least after the fortieth year of his life, from John VIII: “You are not yet fifty years old.” And indeed it is likely that this ignorance concerning the consulship arose from divergent copies of the Consular Fasti. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 51, citing certain Fasti entirely different from those now extant, writes that the Savior suffered when Vinnicius and Cassius were consuls; according to the more accurate Fasti, however, their consulship fell only in the thirteenth year of Tiberius. The same is supported by that manuscript book of consulships on which Cuspinianus noted, in Cassiodorus, that the two Gemini were placed in the eighteenth year of Tiberius.

### 15. On God Being Corporeal, Because Nothing Is Incorporeal

Vol. II, *On Repentance*, chapter 3, no. 12. Vol. III, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 35, no. 124; *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter [Col. 0192D] 2, nos. 97 and 98; book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 16, no. 100; and, most explicitly, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 7, no. 54.

Long ago St. Augustine, in passages to be cited immediately, St. Fulgentius, book II of *On Faith, to Peter*, and Gennadius, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, attributed this error to Tertullian. But St. Augustine excuses him in these words, in book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, final chapter:

“Fearing that a thing would be nothing if it were not a body, he was unable to think differently even about God. Yet although he is indeed acute—for so I read, instead of ‘since’—he is sometimes overcome by the truth when it appears, contrary to his own opinion. For what could he have said more truly than what he says in a certain passage”—namely, *On the Soul*, chapter 7, no. 98—“‘Everything corporeal is passible’? He ought therefore to have changed the opinion by which he had said elsewhere”—namely, [Col. 0193A] in *Against Praxeas*—“that even God is a body. For I do not think he was so foolish as to believe that the divine nature too was passible, with the result that Christ should now be believed passible and mutable not merely in the flesh, nor in flesh and soul, but in the very Word through whom all things were made—an idea far removed from the Christian heart.”

And again in the same place, in words also cited above: “But these things are to be trembled at, not laughed at. For he would never have been driven to them if he could have conceived of something that both exists and is not a body.”

Again, in *On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus*, heresy 86:

“He also says that God himself is corporeal, though not shaped”—where he appears to allude to book II *Against Marcion*. “Yet he is not therefore believed to have become a heretic. For it might somehow be thought that he called the very divine nature and substance a body—not the kind of body [Col. 0193B] whose parts must or can be conceived as some larger and some smaller, as are all things that we properly call bodies, although he entertains some such opinion concerning the soul; but, as I have said, it might be thought that he therefore called God a body because God is not nothing, is not emptiness, is not a quality of body or soul, but is everywhere the same, is not divided by any spatial extension, and yet remains immutably in his own nature and substance.”

Certainly the Author himself explains his meaning sufficiently. Thus he says in *Against Hermogenes*: “Granting that something is incorporeal, I speak only of substances, since substance itself is the body of each thing”; and in *On the Soul*, chapter 7, no. 96: “For it is nothing if it is not a body.” Likewise, in *On the Flesh of Christ*: “But since it exists, it must have something through which it exists. If it has something [Col. 0193C] through which it exists, this will be its body. Everything that exists is a body of its own kind; nothing is incorporeal except what does not exist.” Finally, in book II *Against Marcion*: “For,” he says, “we also read of God’s right hand, eyes, and feet; yet they will not therefore be compared with human ones merely because they share the same appellation. How great will be the difference between the divine body and the human body beneath the same names of limbs,” etc.

All the other Fathers, however, teach that God is incorporeal, and class the contrary assertion among the heresies, as is evident from Philastrius, St. Augustine, Epiphanius, Theodoret, Damascene, Isidore, and Rabanus in their catalogues of heretics, when they mention the Audians, or Anthropomorphites.

### 16. On the Wrath of God

Vol. I, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 2, no. 7. Vol. III, *On the Soul*, chapter 16, no. 211; [Col. 0193D] *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 26, no. 181; book II, chapter 10, no. 94; book IV, chapter 15, no. 195, and chapter 31, no. 507.

At first sight Tertullian does indeed appear to attribute wrath to God in the passages cited, but almost everywhere he interprets it as God’s vengeance or retribution. And in truth he had to insist on this so often, not only against the Gentiles, as in the first passage, but especially against Marcion, who asserted that God was merely good, and not an avenger or judge. Hence Tertullian disputes against him at very great length and proves the contrary from the Scriptures, repeatedly employing passages that mention God’s wrath and thus his vengeance, especially in book I *Against Marcion*, chapters 25, 26, 27, and 28, and book II, chapters 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16.

There is indeed one passage where [Col. 0194A] he appears to acknowledge emotions in God; but besides the fact that there he interprets “to be jealous” and “to be angry” as “to condemn” and “to afflict,” in the final passage of all he explains himself more fully, taking “God to be moved” and “motions in God” to mean wrath. Finally, in the said chapter 16 of book II he explains himself completely in these words: “Whether wrath, or jealousy, or severity, all these are due to sternness, just as sternness is due to justice.” Then, after citing Marcion’s objection—“If God is angry and jealous, and is elated and provoked, then he will also be corrupted, and therefore he will die”—he answers very aptly:

“Most foolish are those who predicate divine things from human ones, so that, because passions of this kind are found in man, who is of a corruptible condition, they therefore suppose them to have the same condition in God. Distinguish the substances and assign to them their respective affections, as diverse as the substances [Col. 0194B] require, even though they appear to share the same terms. For we also read of God’s right hand, eyes, and feet; yet they will not therefore be compared with human ones merely because they share the same appellation.”

### 17. That the Church Exists in Three Persons, Even Laypersons

Vol. V, *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 7, no. 40, and *On Modesty*, chapter 21, no. 191.

Tertullian had spoken properly in *On Repentance*, chapter 10, no. 60, since this was before every heresy: “In one and another the Church exists.” For there he was alluding to Matthew XVIII: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,” having shortly before premised: “Tell the Church.” Yet all the ancients interpret this of the rulers of the Church, [Col. 0194C] the bishops, not of laypeople; so too does Tertullian himself in the same passage, where he speaks of the priests before whom public confession was made. Entirely catholic too is the statement in *On Baptism*, chapter 6, no. 47: “Where the three are—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—there is the Church, because it is the body of the three.”

But the following statement in *On the Exhortation to Chastity* belongs to his heresy, as we also noted in his *Life*: “But even where three are, there is the Church, though they be laypeople. For each person lives by his own faith.” This is especially so because he repeats precisely the same thing in almost the same words in *On Modesty*. From that passage it is gathered that he had reached such a degree of madness as to think that the Church existed in three persons—namely Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. To the same point belongs the fact that he also denies there that the Church is a number of bishops.

But we demonstrated the contrary at length in our Notes [Col. 0194D] on the former passage, even from Tertullian himself while he was still a catholic, and likewise against the Magdeburg Centuriators, who inferred from it that the Church exists among a few. Anyone desiring more should read all the books written by St. Augustine against the Donatists. He gathered together Scriptures from every quarter, from both the Old and New Testaments, establishing that the Church is not in one place alone in the world—Africa, for example—but is dispersed throughout the entire world, in accordance both with the prophecies of the Prophets and with the testimonies of the Apostles, which are clearer than the sun. To him we refer the Reader, lest we be more prolix here. We shall add only this: it pertains to the same heresy of Tertullian that he says in volume II, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 4, no. 47: “Or do you not think that every believer is permitted to conceive and establish something, provided only that it accords with God?”

[Col. 0195A] ### 18. On the Ecstasy, or Madness, or Prophetic Spirit, of Montanus and of the Insane Prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, and Similar Persons

Vol. II, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 1, no. 12. Vol. III, *On the Soul*, chapter 9, no. 111; chapter 45, no. 488; chapter 47, no. 543; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 11, no. 98, and the final chapter, no. 436; *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 22, no. 325, and book V, chapter 8, nos. 135 and 136; *Against Praxeas*, chapter 1, nos. 7, 8, and 10, and chapter 15, no. 93, and chapter 30, no. 183. Finally, in the fragments of the seven books *On Ecstasy*.

Long ago St. Pacian, St. Jerome, and Nicephorus charged Tertullian with this heresy in the passages cited in connection with the fragments of his books *On Ecstasy*, volume IV. There, from Jerome and Epiphanius themselves, we showed that the ecstasy in Adam [Col. 0195B] (Genesis II) was a deep sleep, not a displacement of the mind; and that the ecstasy in the Apostles (Matthew XVIII and Luke IX)—Peter, John, and James—was not madness, but an ecstasy of wonder, nor was it joined with any prophecy.

Next, from the Apostle (1 Corinthians XIV), however much the Author draws the contrary conclusion by wrongly adding the clause “in ecstasy,” it is established that the spirits of the Prophets are subject to the Prophets. For, according to the words of Jerome cited there, and Origen, Homily 6 on Ezekiel, prophecy is called a vision, which the Prophets therefore understood; for this reason they were called Seers. They did not, like madmen, speak involuntarily or produce sound without the mind. From this it may be gathered that what existed in Montanus and his false prophetesses was truly madness, not prophecy [Col. 0195C]; and thus, by God’s ordering, it came about that by this very designation the Author contradicted himself.

Before them, Apollinarius, Bishop of Hierapolis, beautifully established the same point against Montanus, as cited by Eusebius, book V, chapter 15. He writes that they were seized by a certain evil spirit and suddenly convulsed by frenzy and insanity of mind—which they called ecstasy—and began to utter strange sounds and to prophesy, contrary to what was required by the Church’s custom, handed down both by tradition and by succession from ancient times, from the age of the Apostles down to that day. He also cites—in Eusebius, the following chapter—the book of Miltiades against the same man, in which Miltiades shows that no one should believe any Prophet to have been accustomed to prophesy when struck by frenzy. For, as Eusebius quotes him, “they will not be able to allege any Prophet of the Old or New Testament [Col. 0195D] who was ever convulsed in this manner by an insane spirit—through ecstasy. Nor will they be able to boast concerning Agabus, Judas, Silas, Philip’s daughters (Acts XI, XV, XXI), Ammia of Philadelphia, Quadratus”—whom Jerome mentions in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*—“or any others besides, that they ever prophesied in that respect after the frenzied manner of these people.”

He afterward indicates that he had listed their names because they boasted that the women of Montanus had immediately succeeded all of them in the prophetic office. In the same manner, according to Jerome in the passage already cited, Tertullian, in the seven books *On Ecstasy*—the seventh of which he wrote against Apollonius—in confirmation of the same false prophecy of those women, wrote [Col. 0196A] that Melito was regarded as a prophet by his party, thus tacitly insinuating a kind of succession of prophecy as though it were genuine.

Finally, Apollonius, in his book against the Cataphrygians—as Eusebius records in the same book, chapter 17—testifies that when Zoticus, Bishop of Comana, came to Pepuza, where Maximilla was pretending to prophesy, he detected an insane spirit in her. Similarly Serapion, Bishop of Antioch—in the same work, chapter 18—says that blessed Sotas at Anchialus wished to cast the demon out of Priscilla, but those crafty hypocrites by no means permitted it.
