Moreover, it does nothing for the Author’s case that in book V *Against Marcion* he contends that women too possess the right to prophesy, on the ground that in 1 Corinthians XI the Apostle imposes a veil even upon a woman who prophesies. For it has already been proved that [Col. 0196B] in those insane prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla there was not true prophecy, but madness of mind. I pass over the fact that Tertullian himself, while still a catholic, attacks this practice in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter XLI, in these words: “How brazen are the heretical women themselves, who dare to teach, to dispute, to perform exorcisms, to promise cures, perhaps even to baptize”—as we demonstrated there at greater length, nos. 260, 261, 262, and 263—and in *On Baptism Against Quintilla*, herself a woman of the Montanist faction, no. 2.

### 19. That Christ the Son of God Was Always Seen by Human Beings in Real, Though Unborn, Flesh

Vol. I, *Against the Jews*, chapter 9, nos. 114 and 115. Vol. III, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 6, no. 58; *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 27, no. 187; book III, chapter 6, no. 39, chapter 9, no. 65; book V, chapter 19, no. 296; *Against Praxeas*, chapter 14, nos. 86 and 87, chapter [Col. 0196C] 16, nos. 96, 98, 100, and 101; and volume IV, the metrical book V *Against Marcion*, chapter 5, no. 8.

What Tertullian writes—that the Son of God, not the Father, was seen or heard by human beings whenever Scripture records such a thing—does not seem paradoxical. He refers, namely, to when God appeared to Adam, Genesis III; Noah, Genesis IX; Abraham, Genesis XII, XVII, and XVIII; Lot, Genesis XIX; Hagar, Genesis XXII; Jacob, Genesis XXIX, XXXII, and XXXV; and Moses, Exodus III and following, XXXII, and XXXIII. He derived this almost word for word from St. Justin Martyr’s *Dialogue Against Trypho*, and in part from St. Irenaeus, book III, chapter 6, and book IV, chapter 23. They were followed by Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chapters 25, 26, and 27; Blessed Cyprian, book II of the *Testimonies Against the Jews*, chapters 5 and 6; and from these passages they proved [Col. 0196D] that Christ was called not only man or angel but also God. St. Ambrose in the preface to Luke, St. Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*, Prudentius against the Anthropomorphites, and Arnobius on Psalm CIV do not teach otherwise.

They seem to have been led to this conclusion both by the words, “No one shall ever see God the Father”—as the Author reads—“and live,” Exodus XXXIII, and similar words in John VI, “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except him who is from God”; and, conversely, by Christ’s words in John VIII: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

Nevertheless, St. Augustine, in book III *Against Maximinus*, chapter 26, and book II *On the Trinity*, chapters 10–17, preferred to assert that God the Father and the entire Trinity were seen in the aforesaid passages through created things placed at their service, lest he agree with the Arian Maximinus. It was not enough for Maximinus to interpret those apparitions [Col. 0197A] as referring to Christ; he also endeavored to infer from them that Christ appeared to human sight through the substance of his divinity. The Author was certainly far removed from this heresy, however much some charge him with it.

But this is paradoxical and peculiar to Tertullian: in several passages he says that Christ was seen in true and solid flesh, although flesh not yet born. He did so through zeal not according to knowledge, in order to prove all the more strongly, against Marcion and his other followers, that the flesh of Christ which he afterward received from the Virgin was not phantasmal but true and solid, if he could be said to have been seen long before in real flesh.

Elsewhere, certainly, in *Against Praxeas*, following the opinion of St. Justin Martyr, who affirms that these apparitions were figurative, he explains himself:

“For we say,” he states in the former passage, “that the Son, under his own designation, [Col. 0197B] was invisible insofar as he is the Word”—which Maximinus nevertheless denied—“but was visible before the flesh in the manner in which he says to Aaron and Miriam (Numbers XII): ‘If there shall be a prophet among you, I shall be known to him in a vision, and in a dream I shall speak to him.’”

After citing the words of Exodus III, “Mouth to mouth I shall speak to him in visible form,” he adds:

“Therefore, when he reserves for Moses the sight of himself and conversation face to face for the future—for this was afterward fulfilled in the retirement upon the mountain, as we read in the Gospel, Luke IX, where Moses was seen conversing with him—it appears that previously God, that is, the Son of God, had always been seen in a mirror, and in an enigma, and in a vision and a dream, both by the Prophets and Patriarchs and by Moses himself up to that point.”

Nor does he speak very differently in the latter passage: “For he himself always descended to converse with human beings, from Adam down to the Patriarchs and Prophets, in [Col. 0197C] a vision, in a dream, in a mirror, and in an enigma.”

St. Augustine, however, in the passages already cited, prefers the view that Christ was indeed prefigured by these visions, but that God appeared through angels only figuratively. He proves this from Hosea XII, where the one who wrestled with Jacob is said to have been an angel, and Hebrews XIII, where certain persons are said unknowingly to have received angels as guests. To these may be added the fact that the God whom Moses said had appeared to him in the bush and on Sinai is testified by St. Stephen in Acts VII to have been an angel.

### 20. On Flight During Persecution Being Unlawful

Vol. II, book I *To His Wife*, chapter 3, no. 17; *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 1, no. 18; and volume V, the complete book on this subject.

We have refuted this error of Tertullian’s—which he expounds at length in the book [Col. 0197D] *On Flight in Persecution*, written, according to St. Jerome, Sophronius, and Nicephorus, against the Church—so extensively in our Notes on that work that there is no need for many words here. See there the antidote we appended to the end of the argument, drawn from the Author himself while still a catholic, volume II, *On Patience*, chapter 13, no. 88; from several passages of St. Cyprian; from St. Athanasius’s *Apology for His Flight*; and from St. Augustine, Letter 180 to Honoratus. From these we also answered almost every opposing argument, especially those in chapter 4, no. 35; chapter 5, no. 39; chapter 6, nos. 43, 47, and 49; chapter 7, no. 54; chapter 8, nos. 55, 57, and 58; chapter 9, no. 60; and chapter 18, no. 75.

The Author’s words cited are these: “The patience of the flesh fights in persecutions. If flight presses upon it, [Col. 0198A] the flesh serves as a soldier amid the hardships of flight; if prison overtakes it as well, amid that deprivation of light there is patience with the world.”

What of the fact that, from chapter 11 of the aforesaid book, he seems chiefly to condemn the flight of the superiors of the Church? For, according also to St. Athanasius’s letter to Dracontius and the cited passage of St. Augustine, they are not permitted to flee unless their flock flees, or does not seek its superior—that is, does not need his ministry—when the persecution is directed personally, so to speak, against bishops or pastors. Yet St. Athanasius demonstrates at length in his aforementioned *Apology*, both from many examples and from Scripture, that even in such a case they may flee. To it we refer the Reader, lest we be more prolix here.

Nor does it do anything for the Author’s case that Christ invites men to suffer, the contrary of flight: “Whoever is ashamed of me, of him shall I also be ashamed” (Mark VI), however much [Col. 0198B] in the *Scorpiace Against the Gnostics* he appears to infer from this that martyrdoms are commanded. For Tertullian acknowledges that this too is equally commanded: “When they begin to persecute you, flee from city to city.” Neither passage appears to be a command except according to persons, times, and causes: the latter, in a time of persecution on account of faith in Christ, for those whom the care of souls permits to be absent; the former, if we are apprehended, even in the very course of flight. Furthermore, since both are contained in the same chapter of Matthew, each must receive a sound interpretation, lest the Evangelist appear to contradict himself.

### 21. On Job Having Suffered the Voluntary Loss of His Children, Because They Were Not Restored to Him

Vol. II, *On Patience*, chapter [Col. 0198C] 14, no. 98.

It appears that the copies of the book of Job which Tertullian had seen lacked the statement, found in the Hebrew, Chaldean, Greek, and Latin copies, that seven sons and three daughters were restored to him. From this, I think, it came about that he followed this peculiar paradox, which I have been unable to find in any of the Ancients. It would certainly be superfluous to refute it at greater length, since Origen, who lived at approximately the same time, indicates in Homily 6 on Ezekiel that he had read this, as do all the Fathers after him, ancient, medieval, and more recent.

The Author would agree with them if he had said only that Job possessed twice over the other things he had lost, except his children, since he received only seven, and thus precisely as many as before. [Col. 0198D] Philip the Presbyter, St. Gregory the Pope, Bede, and Rupert, in their commentaries on Job, therefore interpret this to mean that the seven former children were considered still to be living with God.

### 22. On the Virgin Mary Having Given Birth to Christ by the Common Law of the Body’s Opening

Vol. III, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 4, no. 31; chapter 20, no. 155; chapter 23, nos. 174 and 175; *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 11, no. 78; book IV, chapter 21, no. 311; and book V, chapter 19, no. 304.

It is sufficiently clear that Tertullian wrote something of this kind, as did Origen, Homily 14 on Luke, and St. Ambrose on the same Gospel. Yet they may be understood, in accordance with St. Thomas Aquinas’s interpretation somewhere, to refer to such an opening [Col. 0199A] of the womb as did not violate the enclosure of virginity. We too noted this regarding Luke II, cited in his own support by the Author: “Every male opening the womb,” in the aforesaid *On the Flesh of Christ*, no. 175. In support of this we adduced the testimonies of a certain Greek interpreter and of St. Jerome, who acknowledge that Christ supernaturally opened the virginal womb, which had not yet been opened, and naturally preserved its closure, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy concerning the closed eastern gate through which the High Priest alone goes forth, yet which nevertheless remains closed forever.

To this also pertains St. Ambrose’s comparison in Letter 81, where he writes that Christ came forth from the Virgin’s womb just as waters flowed from the rock. Finally, there is the Author’s statement in the second passage cited from the aforesaid book: “What was novel in Christ’s birth [Col. 0199B] from a Virgin is clear: namely, solely that it was from a virgin.” He thereby signifies, both there and in the other passages cited here, that he pressed this point so far in order to prove Christ’s true birth from the Virgin against Marcion, who called it phantasmal. Later, however, when that heresy had been sufficiently refuted, the Fathers preferred to define that the Virgin Mother of God gave birth incorruptibly, with her womb closed.

### 23. On the Virgin Mary Marrying Once After Giving Birth

Vol. II, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 6, no. 48. Vol. III, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 23, no. 174; and volume V, *On Monogamy*, chapter 8, no. 55.

The Author does indeed appear to fall into this heresy rather obscurely, so that his words might in some manner admit a sound [Col. 0199C] sense. Yet since St. Jerome, when the heretic Helvidius cited Tertullian in his own support, does not deny that he wrote something of the kind, I too did not think Tertullian should be excused from it. It would be enough to reply with what Blessed Jerome says of Tertullian: “I say nothing except that he was not a man of the Church.”

But because he was likely misled by the same words of the Evangelists that misled Helvidius—Matthew XII, Luke VIII, and John VII, concerning the Lord’s brothers, whom in the aforementioned *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 7, no. 67, he asserts to have been true brothers, just as Mary was truly Christ’s mother, in order thereby to prove the truth of Christ’s flesh all the more—something must be added concerning the meaning of this expression.

Origen, Hilary, Euthymius, and Theophylact on Matthew; [Col. 0199D] Eusebius, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1; St. Epiphanius, book III of the *Panarion Against the Antidicomarianites*; St. Ambrose and Oecumenius in their commentaries on Galatians II, think that those called the Lord’s brothers were Joseph’s sons by Mary of Cleophas, the widow of his brother, by whom he had six children: James, Joseph, Simon, Judas, and their brothers. This, according even to Origen’s testimony, followed the Gospel bearing the title of Peter or James.

But St. Jerome speaks more correctly in his commentary:

“Some suspect that the Lord’s brothers were Joseph’s sons by another wife, following the ravings of the apocryphal writings and inventing a certain petty woman named Escha. We, however,” he says, “as is contained in the book we wrote against Helvidius, understand the Lord’s brothers to be not Joseph’s sons but the Savior’s cousins, the children of Mary, the Lord’s maternal aunt, who is said to have been [Col. 0200A] the mother of James the Less, Joseph, and Judas, whom we read in the Gospel to have been called the Lord’s brothers; for all Scripture demonstrates that cousins are called brothers.”

Here he alludes both to the Scriptures concerning Lot, the brother of Abraham, Genesis XIII, and to Matthew XVII, where Mary, the mother of James and Joses, or Joseph, is said to have stood by the cross. Euthymius rightly noted that this cannot be understood of the Lord’s mother. Furthermore, see the ecclesiastical definition on this matter in St. Fulgentius, *On Faith, to Peter*, among the works of Blessed Augustine.

### 21. On the Thousand Years After the Resurrection of Bodies

*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 25, no. 203; *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 29, no. 203; book III, chapter 24, no. 191 and following; book IV, chapter 29, no. 471; and volume IV, [Col. 0200B] in the fragments of the book *On the Hope of the Faithful*.

What Tertullian thought on this subject I believe I have sufficiently set forth in volume IV, in connection with the fragments of the book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, from his own words: namely, that a kingdom of Christ is promised to us on earth before heaven, after the first resurrection, but in such a manner that in it the saints are refreshed with an abundance of all spiritual goods.

Although erroneous, Blessed Augustine nevertheless admits this opinion to be tolerable in some measure, in book XX of *The City of God*. I think this is because it may also be found in St. Irenaeus, book V *On Heresies*, chapters 32–35, in St. Justin Martyr’s *Dialogue Against Trypho*, and in Melito, who in this matter followed Papias, at least according to St. Jerome. They are also joined by Apollinarius, who vainly attempted to attack the books of Dionysius of Alexandria against Nepos; [Col. 0200C] Lactantius, book II, chapter 13, and book VII, chapter 24; Victorinus on the Apocalypse, before his work was corrected by St. Jerome; and, on Jerome’s testimony, Severus in the dialogue *Gallus, on the Life of St. Martin*.

Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, nevertheless charges them—as he does Tertullian, but apparently incorrectly—with believing that the saints would enjoy the delights of drink and food. It is certainly evident that the heresy of Cerinthus, Marcus, and Nepos—whom Gennadius himself discusses in the same place, as does Eusebius in book III, chapter 22, and book VII, chapter 20, and, after Eusebius, Nicephorus somewhere—was very different, as was that of the other Chiliasts or Millenarians, against whom St. Epiphanius writes in *Heresy* 76. For they—like certain Anabaptists of the present day—expected even marital intercourse in that kingdom; indeed, Cerinthus and Marcus expected every kind of lustful indulgence. And, as [Col. 0200D] St. Jerome states, in accordance with the Jews’ δευτερώσεις (“secondary traditions”), they expected the disgrace of circumcision, the restoration of the temple, sacrifices of bulls and rams, Sabbath rest, the servitude of all nations, and consequently wars, armies, triumphs, the slaughter of the vanquished, and the death of a hundred-year-old sinner.

Moreover, because they based all these things upon the passage in the Apocalypse of St. John the Apostle—for all those writers attribute it to him—in chapter XX, “This is the first resurrection; blessed is the holy person who has a part in the first resurrection; in these shall be priests of the Lord and of Christ, and they shall reign with him for a thousand years,” something must be added here concerning the meaning of that passage.

Blessed Jerome, in the preface to book XVIII on Isaiah, says that the Apocalypse must be expounded not according to the letter, as the Judaizers do, but spiritually, as it was written. He does this himself in express words [Col. 0201A] in Victorinus’s manuscript commentary on the Apocalypse as corrected by him, following, I think, Dionysius of Alexandria in the aforementioned books against Nepos. St. Augustine, more explicitly, in *The City of God*, book XX, chapters 7, 8, and 9, interprets the first resurrection as the resurrection of souls, which is also recognized in Scripture, and the second as that of bodies. He interprets the thousand years either as the time of grace, which will remain until the end of the age, according to that mode of speech by which a part is signified by the whole, or as all the years of this age, so that the fullness of time itself is designated by a perfect number. He is followed by the commentary attributed to Ambrose, Primasius, Andrew, and Bede in their commentaries on the Apocalypse.

Nor does what is read in Apocalypse XXI concerning the city of Jerusalem descending to the new earth support them. For the Apostle John himself indicates that he is speaking not of an earthly Jerusalem when he adds: “And [Col. 0201B] I saw no temple in it”—although some of them, as stated above, believed that the temple too would be restored—“for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.” Accordingly, the other Fathers interpret it more correctly of the Church, both as militant in this age, whose foundations are the twelve Apostles, and as afterward reigning in heaven.

The same applies to Galatians IV concerning the free Jerusalem, which is our mother, where there is a contradiction in the very addition “which is above”; and also to Philippians III, “our citizenship (πολίτευμα) is in heaven,” and consequently not on earth. It is therefore remarkable that these passages should be cited by our Author in favor of the aforesaid opinion.

The passages in Isaiah LXV and LXVI, Jeremiah XVI and XXXI, and finally Ezekiel XX, XXVII, and XXVIII, concerning the [Col. 0201C] restoration of Judea—to which the Author alludes only in these few words—seemed to support him more strongly. They are explicitly cited partly by St. Irenaeus and partly by St. Justin Martyr. But Jerome, in his commentaries, beautifully interprets all these things allegorically of the Church confessing Christ and of her mysteries, everywhere ridiculing those fables of the thousand years. For brevity’s sake we refer the Reader to him.

The response is easier regarding Genesis XIII and XV, which the Author, following Irenaeus, cites in his own support, concerning the first and second promises made to Abraham’s seed: first that it would be as numerous as the sand, and then also like the stars, as though these were the beginnings of an earthly and a heavenly dispensation. For it is established that the first promise was fulfilled by the multiplication of the children of Israel in the land of the Canaanites, or Palestine; while the Apostle [Col. 0201D] Paul interprets the second of the Church of the Gentiles in Romans IX and Galatians III. In the same manner our Rabanus also distinguished these two promises in his commentary on Genesis.

No less easy is the response regarding Genesis XXVII, where the first promise to Jacob—whose figure we know Christians from among the Gentiles to bear—is of heavenly dew, and the second of the richness of the earth. For Jacob himself interprets that blessing as earthly in the words he afterward addressed to Esau: “With grain, wine, and oil I have established him.” And if we wish to understand it allegorically, Procopius, in his commentary, interprets the heavenly dew as what is instilled into the souls of the devout, and the richness of the earth as that possessed by the earth which receives seed and renders it back a hundredfold.

Finally, the response is easiest regarding Luke XII: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and the remaining things shall be added to you.” [Col. 0202A] For the beginning of Christ’s discourse makes it clear that Christ is speaking of this life, not that future life after the resurrection: “Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious for your soul about food, or for your body about clothing.”

Furthermore, we noted in connection with *On the Soul*, chapter 30, no. 376, that this error of the Millenarians was derived partly from Plato’s dialogue *On the Republic* and from the *Phaedrus*. Since the Author there regards such things as fables, it is remarkable that he afterward fell into the same error. But, as St. Jerome demonstrates sufficiently, he followed Papias, Melito, and the other aforementioned Authors, and especially St. Irenaeus.

### 25. On Second Marriages Condemned as Acts of Fornication

Vol. II, book I *To His Wife*, chapter 1, no. 11; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 10, no. 84, and chapter 11, [Col. 0202B] no. 98. Vol. III, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 11, no. 7; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 8, no. 82; *Against Marcion*, chapter 15, no. 245. Finally, volume V, the complete books *On the Exhortation to Chastity* and *On Monogamy*, and *On Modesty*, chapter 1, no. 15.

Restoration notes: S000067’s second expression, ἀπροσδιόνυσα, appears textually corrupt; it has been preserved verbatim and identified only from the surrounding reference to Bacchus/Dionysus.; The final words ὧν ἄγε in S000074 appear corrupt or uncertain; they have been preserved verbatim rather than silently emended.; S000079–S000080 contain several unusual recovered accents or forms; they have been preserved verbatim because the existing English translation supplies their sense.; S000067’s second expression, ἀπροσδιόνυσα, appears textually corrupt; it is preserved verbatim, while its contextual sense is supplied from the accompanying reference to Bacchus.; The final words ὧν ἄγε in S000074 appear corrupt or uncertain; they are preserved verbatim and identified contextually with the cry “Attend to this.”; S000079–S000080 contain unusual or apparently corrupt recovered accents and forms. They are preserved verbatim, with concise renderings supported by the existing translation that follows them.  

Into this Montanist heresy Tertullian gradually fell. First, from a love of chastity, he wrote to his wife a book on single marriage, in which he indeed discourages second marriages, but does not condemn them as fornication. Indeed, since in Book II *To His Wife* he argues at length that, if women wish to marry, they ought at least to marry “in the Lord,” that is, a Christian, he does not appear at that time to have condemned second marriages altogether. Nevertheless, these two books are not entirely free from error. Most notably, in Book I, chapter 1, no. 11, he calls second [Col. 0202C] marriages “confusion”; in chapter 4, no. 23, “an affront”; in chapter 5, no. 34, “detestable”; and elsewhere also “filthy” and “a voluptuous disgrace.” Such too are those passages already cited from the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. That he was speaking in these passages of second marriages, not first marriages, is established by these words of St. Augustine, Book I *On the Good of Widowhood*, which are also offered here as an antidote:

> Because the Apostle called the good of the unmarried honorable, we ought not therefore to suppose that the marriage bond is disgraceful; otherwise we shall condemn even first marriages, which neither the Cataphrygians nor the Novatians, nor Tertullian, their most eloquent supporter, dared to call disgraceful.

Thereafter, in the book *Against Hermogenes*, he discloses his error more openly in these words:

> He defends the law of God in lust; and, wholly an adulterer both in preaching and in flesh, [Col. 0202D] he reeks of contact with those who marry.

Finally, in the books *On the Exhortation to Chastity* and *On Monogamy*, following Montanus, he not only calls second marriages fornication, adultery, and illicit intercourse, but also attempts to prove this by various arguments—though in vain, as will be evident to the reader from the antidote supplied by our annotations on both works. To these, lest we become too lengthy here, we refer the reader. There, in support of the catholic position that second marriages are not forbidden, we have cited at intervals Blessed Jerome’s letter *On Monogamy* to Ageruchia, commonly called Gerontia; his writings *On Widowhood* to Salvina and to Pammachius; St. Augustine’s book *On the Good of Widowhood* and Book II *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*; St. Epiphanius *Against Montanus*, Heresy 59, and *Against the Cathari*; and the ancient commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, Romans 7, 1 Corinthians 7, and 1 Corinthians 5. To these [Col. 0203A] may be added that statement of Blessed Jerome in Letter 54 to Marcella—although elsewhere he sometimes appears rather unfavorable toward them—in defense of second marriages:

> We do not so much seek second marriages as permit them, since Paul commands young widows to marry; they, however—namely, the followers of Montanus—regard repeated marriages as so criminal that anyone who has done this is considered an adulterer.

Likewise there is the statement in his commentary *On the Epistle to Titus*, also cited by us elsewhere:

> Tertullian too wrote a heretical book *On Monogamy*; no one who has read the Apostle will fail to know that it contradicts the Apostle.

Likewise St. Augustine, in *On Heresies*, heresy 126:

> Tertullian therefore became a heretic because, passing over to the Cataphrygians whom he had previously destroyed, he also began, contrary to apostolic teaching, to condemn second marriages as fornication.

[Col. 0203B] **26. On Montanus as the Paraclete.** Vol. II, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 1, no. 6. Vol. III, *On the Soul*, chapter 51, no. 613, and chapter 58, no. 652. *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 11, no. 98, and the final chapter, final number. *Against Marcion*, Book I, chapter 29, no. 203, and Book V, chapter 15, no. 247; and *Against Praxeas*, chapter 1, no. 11; chapter 2, no. 22; chapter 8, no. 59; chapter 13, no. 78. Vol. V, *On Monogamy*, the whole of chapter 2, and more than once in the following books: *On Flight in Persecution*, *On Fasts*, and *On Modesty*.

Against this exceedingly absurd heresy, Tertullian’s own words from before his heresy may suffice. In *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 52, heresy 21, no. 327, he calls it a blasphemy of those heretics who were [Col. 0203C] called Cataphrygians that they said that the Holy Spirit had indeed been in the Apostles, but that the Paraclete had not; and that they said the Paraclete had spoken more through Montanus than Christ had set forth in the Gospel. And yet the wretched man—perhaps led astray by them because they detested second marriages—in so many passages already cited calls Montanus the Paraclete and repeatedly cites his words under the title of “the Paraclete.” Indeed, he twists to support this heresy of his the passage in John 16:

> I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth has come, he will teach you all truth and will announce to you the things that are to come.

Yet he himself interprets this passage in a catholic sense in the aforementioned book *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 8, no. 62, speaking of the Apostles:

> They were soon to receive the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who was to lead them [Col. 0203D] into all truth.

And again:

> The Apostles, destined for the nations, were themselves also to receive the Paraclete as their teacher.

There he treats the Holy Spirit and the Paraclete as the same, whereas they wrongly distinguished the Holy Spirit from the Paraclete, as has been stated from Tertullian himself. The very context of the Evangelist establishes this; and thus all the ancients interpret that passage, while St. Augustine expressly argues against this heresy in three tractates on the Gospel of John. For the sake of brevity, we refer the reader to them.

**27. On the denial of penance to adulterers.** Vol. V, the entire book *On Modesty*.

As we noted in the Life of the Author, Montanus and his followers, the Cataphrygians, entirely abolished [Col. 0204A] all penance—as is attested by Blessed Jerome in his often-cited letter to Marcella and by St. Pacian in his treatise *Against the Novatians*. Tertullian differs from them in this respect: he believed it ought to be denied only to adulterers. Perhaps at first he was led astray by certain bishops of his own age who, as St. Cyprian attests in the book *On the Lapsed*, did not think that penance should be granted to adulterers. Yet, apart from the fact that Cyprian there proves the contrary position from Scripture, namely, the Church’s power to grant pardon for every kind of sin, the Author, while still catholic, in Vol. II, in the book *On Penance*—which Cyprian there imitates—expressly demonstrates that penance is necessary for all offenses.

And this is what he says in *On Modesty*, chapter 1, no. 9:

> In opposition even to the former fellowship of [Col. 0204B] my own opinion with theirs.

St. Pacian speaks in much the same way when addressing the Novatians, in words also cited more than once elsewhere:

> Tertullian after his heresy belongs to you, for you have taken many things from him. You will hear him confessing in his own letter, and in one which he published while a catholic, that the Church can forgive sins.

Likewise St. Jerome says that Tertullian, in the book *On Modesty* which he wrote against penance, overturned his former judgment by a new opinion, in this following his own insane and blasphemous women.

To these the reader may add all those writings of the ancients on penance of which we have made mention in Vol. II, in the aforementioned book *On Penance*, chapter 1, and what we have said both on that book and on the other, *On [Col. 0204C] Modesty*. There, in response to each of the Author’s arguments to the contrary, we have generally answered from Pacian, adding for this purpose an exposition of several passages of Scripture, often from Tertullian himself.

At chapter 9, nos. 72 and 73, we also cited St. Jerome’s letter to Damasus *On the Two Sons*, where he expressly argues against the Author and, among other things, defends the position that the publicans were not Gentiles, as Tertullian wished, but Jews. He proves this by the examples of Matthew, an Apostle from the circumcision; of the publicans baptized by John; and of the publican praying in the temple, Luke 5, 7, and 18. If they had been Gentiles, Christ would not have dined with them, lest he break the law, nor would this publican have been admitted into the temple. Indeed, whenever it was noted as a fault in Christ that he associated with publicans, sinners [Col. 0204D] and publicans are almost always joined together; and thus he was not reproached because he dined with Gentiles, but because he dined with sinners.

To this pertains the Pharisee’s murmuring in Luke 7 concerning the sinful woman, in whom Tertullian himself recognizes both penance and pardon in Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 18, no. 265. Yet the Author nowhere dares to call her a Gentile, because it is established that her village was near Jerusalem, John 11.

Nor does the statement, “There shall be no one paying tribute among the sons of Israel,” do anything for the Author’s case. For even if they were not obliged to pay tax before, by God’s disposition, they were subjected to the Romans—and although it is sufficiently established that the occupation of the publicans was hateful and infamous—it nevertheless appears from the words of John the Baptist to them, Luke 3, that it could also be practiced without sin:

> Do nothing beyond [Col. 0205A] what has been appointed for you,

or, as it is translated from the Greek:

> Exact nothing beyond what has been appointed for you.

For the rest, let the diligent reader consult the aforementioned annotations of ours.

**28. On “Psychics,” the name with which he slandered Catholics.** Vol. III, *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 22, no. 325; *Against Praxeas*, chapter 1, no. 17. Vol. V, *On Monogamy*, chapter 1, nos. 4 and 5; chapter 11, nos. 86, 87, and 88; and chapter 16, no. 120; the entire book *On Fasting Against the Psychics*; and *On Modesty*, chapter 1, no. 8; chapter 6, no. 47; chapter 10, no. 83; and chapter 21, no. 190.

We have sufficiently demonstrated, even from the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 2, at the beginning of *On Fasting Against the Psychics*, no. 2, that “Psychics” means “animal” or “natural men.” After he had fallen into heresy, [Col. 0205B] Tertullian fastened this name upon Catholics, while on the contrary calling his own Montanists “spiritual,” because they followed Montanus as the spirit and Paraclete. He thereby slandered Catholics as if they were wholly animal men, following *passivitas*, that is, license in life, because they entered into second marriages, avoided martyrdom by flight, and rejected the Montanist fasts.

But the wretched man failed to notice that Montanus had led an animal life, since Priscilla and Maximilla, who abandoned their husbands and followed Montanus, were harlots; that their followers escaped martyrdom by denying Christ; that, if they suffered anything, they endured it because of robberies previously committed; and finally that, although they observed three Lents—on which more presently—they nevertheless indulged their appetites during the rest of the year.

Nor, however, was it new for heretics to call Catholics [Col. 0205C] “Psychics” and themselves “spiritual”; for the Author himself, following St. Irenaeus, ridicules precisely this practice among the Valentinians in *Against the Valentinians*, chapters 29 and 30. After them Blessed Epiphanius also wrote of it in his book *On Heresies*.

**29. On the two Lents.** Vol. V, *On Fasting Against the Psychics*, written in their defense, especially chapter 15, no. 90.

Since the Montanists annually observed three full Lents of seven weeks each, Tertullian appears to have differed from them in this respect after he began to hold separate assemblies apart from them: he observed only two. For thus he writes:

> How slight is our prohibition of foods? We offer to God two weeks of xerophagy in the year, [Col. 0205D] and not even the whole of those, since Sabbaths and Sundays are of course excepted.

Yet they are not on that account to be judged heretics. For Amalarius, Book I *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 36, and Book IV, chapter 37, describes the fasts of certain devout persons who observed three Lents: one before Easter, according to apostolic tradition; another from devotion before St. John’s feast—or rather after Pentecost; and a third before the Nativity of the Lord. Similarly, our *Micrologus*, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 35, records a second Lent for penitents, which even today is customary among certain monks.

To this also pertains the statement of St. Jerome in his letter to Lucinius of Baetica, cited by Amalarius:

> Would that we could fast at all times, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Apostle Paul and the believers with him did on the days of Pentecost and [Col. 0206A] on the Lord’s Day.

Likewise relevant are those extremely rigorous fasts of the early monks, described at length by Jerome as well as by Theodoret and Nicephorus.

But what was condemned as heresy among the Montanists was their insistence upon the necessity of observing these Lents, whether three or two, to such a degree that for this very reason they slandered Catholics with the name “Psychics”—that is, as has already been said, “animal men”—because Catholics were unwilling to observe them together with the Montanists. And this is what St. Jerome urges in Letter 54 to Marcella against Montanus:

> We fast for one Lent, according to the tradition of the Apostles, at the season appropriate to us; they keep three Lents in the year, as though three Saviors had suffered. It is not that [Col. 0206B] one may not fast throughout the whole year, except during Pentecost, but that it is one thing to offer a gift under necessity and another to offer it voluntarily.

Hence Eusebius—according to the more accurate translation from the Greek, previously corrupted by certain persons so that they might condemn ecclesiastical fasts generally as Montanist—in Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17; Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, Book III, on the Montanists; and Nicephorus, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 22, write that Montanus introduced and sanctioned new laws of fasting contrary to the custom of the Church.

**30. On divorce as lawful for Christians on account of adultery, so that they may marry another.** Vol. II, Book II *To His Wife*, chapter 1, no. 4. Vol. III, Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 34, no. 537.

[Col. 0206C] At first sight Tertullian indeed appears to hold some such position when he compares divorce to the death of a husband, in order to prove more strongly that after the latter it is not lawful to marry another, just as it is not lawful after divorce except on account of adultery. But he explains himself in Vol. V, *On Monogamy*, chapter 9, no. 70, and chapter 11, no. 89. In the former passage he speaks as follows of a divorced wife:

> So that the admission of another man, whether through marriage or promiscuously, may be pronounced by God to be altogether adultery.

And soon afterward, more clearly:

> The dissolution was effected, of course, by death, not by divorce, because the Apostle would not permit divorced persons to marry contrary to the former commandment.

Away, then, with Erasmus and his followers, who wrongly cite the Author in their own support. Certainly the contrary has now been defined by the Council of Trent, session 34, canon 9.

[Col. 0206D] **31. Concerning the Trinity.** Vol. I, Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 21, no. 316; *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 3, no. 15; *Against Praxeas*, chapter 3, nos. 29 and 34; chapter 4, no. 39; chapter 8, nos. 55, 59, and 60; chapter 9, nos. 62 and 63. Likewise Vol. V, Novatian, *On the Trinity*, chapter 11, no. 56; chapter 22, no. 98; chapter 24, no. 106; and chapter 31, no. 141.

That Tertullian did not doubt the faith of the Trinity—that is, of three Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but of one essence—is clearer from very many passages of his than to require proof, especially from his entire book on that subject and, according to our edition, bearing that very title, *Against Praxeas*. There, against Praxeas and his Montanist followers, who were called Aeschinians, he proves not only that the same person [Col. 0207A] cannot be called both Father and Son, but also expressly asserts:

> The rule of faith which has run down from the beginning of the Gospel orders unity into a Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Novatian speaks no differently in his book *On the Trinity*. In chapters 1, 3, and 29, he sets forth the rule of faith by which we believe in God the Father and almighty Lord, the supremely perfect Creator of all things; in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, our Lord and God; and also in the Holy Spirit.

But when we ascribe to them paradoxes concerning the Trinity, we mean only that they sometimes speak obscurely on this subject, since they lived before every heresy concerning the Trinity. And lest anyone should perhaps take from such passages an occasion for his own error or heresy, we add how they may be explained according to a sound understanding.

We now omit, first, [Col. 0207B] Rhenanus’s slanders against the scholastic theologians, contained in his admonition to the reader concerning certain doctrines of Tertullian—especially since he slanders Tertullian himself as well, both regarding certain corrupted or misunderstood passages, on which more presently, and because he falsely ascribes to him the heresy of those who think that in the Eucharist the body of Christ is present only figuratively. We vindicated Tertullian from this charge in our annotations on Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 40, no. 662. He also places among Tertullian’s doctrines or paradoxes those things which Tertullian most admirably develops at length, not only concerning public penance but also, as Rhenanus himself admits, concerning secret confession, in the book *On Penance*. Rhenanus did not hesitate even to doubt whether that book was Tertullian’s, although St. Pacian copied many things from it.

For this reason I am all the more astonished that, in the latest Paris edition of the year 1580, not only was [Col. 0207C] that entire admonition retained, but all of Rhenanus’s errors—many of them savoring of heresy—were also retained without any antidote being added. Thus the catholic reader must be warned that he should avoid those annotations no less—even when Rhenanus’s name is omitted—than those which were prohibited by the Roman pontiffs Pius IV and Pius V in earlier editions until they should be expurgated.

But let us come to the matter itself. First, where Tertullian speaks as follows in the *Apology* and *Against Praxeas*:

> They are three, not in condition but in degree; not in substance but in form; not in power but in kind; yet of one substance, one condition, and one power, because there is one God, from whom are [Col. 0207D] those degrees and forms and kinds.

By “condition” he means what the scholastics—and he himself also—call “substance”; by “degree,” what they call “notion”; by “form,” what they call “properties”; and by “kind,” what they call “mode of possessing.”

Next, the statement in *Against Hermogenes*—

> There was a time when neither sin nor the Son existed—

was spoken more forcefully out of zeal according to knowledge, to show that matter is not eternal. By it he intended to signify only what St. Hilary says in Book XII *On the Trinity*: that the Father alone is eternal, but that the Son is coeternal with him. I omit that in the same place Hilary answers similar words proposed to himself in the person of an Arian:

> This exceeds human sense and the understanding of the world; the reasoning of human understanding does not grasp it, but it is the profession of faithful wisdom.

The Author explains himself in the same sense [Col. 0208A] in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 5, no. 43 and following, and throughout chapters 6 and 7.

Thereafter, in these words from the same book *Against Praxeas*—

> assigning the second and third places of rank to the Son and the Holy Spirit, who share the substance of the Father—

he means what the scholastics say: that the Son and the Holy Spirit are produced by two emanations from the unproduced Father; or that the Son is the second Person and the Holy Spirit the third, as he afterward says more than once.

But Rhenanus wrongly charges him there with calling the Son and the Holy Spirit members, chief agents, and instruments, since those words refer rather to the angels, who are alien to the Father’s substance yet do not overthrow the monarchy of God. Similarly, when Tertullian calls the Holy Spirit the third degree, by “degree” he means origin.

Again, what in *Against Praxeas* προβολήν (“procession”) he attributes not only [Col. 0208B] to the Holy Spirit but also to the Son from the Father, Saints Hilary and Augustine, in their books *On the Trinity*, and other later Fathers prefer to distinguish in such a way as to attribute generation to the Son and procession to the Holy Spirit.

When in the same place he interprets this as the bringing forth of one thing from another, he understands the Persons as really, but not essentially, distinct; for he continues:

> Because we say that the Son was brought forth from the Father, but not separated.

Those propositions must also be interpreted suitably:

> Every origin is a parent, and everything brought forth from an origin is offspring;

and likewise:

> The Trinity, descending from the Father through connected and interwoven degrees.

Now, where he says:

> The Father is the whole substance, while the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole,

he takes “whole” to mean “full” or “fullness,” no differently from the scholastic doctors when they say: The Father possesses the fullness [Col. 0208C] of deity in the first moment of origin, because he has it from himself; the Son in the second moment of origin, because it is communicated to him by the Father through generation from one; and the Holy Spirit in the third moment, because from two through spiration he receives the same numerically identical essence.

And this is what the Author afterward expressed in other words:

> From the one Father are all things which are in God through unity of substance, and in the unity is a Trinity of one substance.

Likewise:

> Unity, deriving the Trinity from itself, is not destroyed by it but administered,

so that “the whole substance” is the same as “one undivided substance in three.”

Finally, the Son appears to be called a “portion” by the Author because he is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, although the three Persons are one God, and the Son is not the one who is the Father, nor the Father the one who is [Col. 0208D] the Holy Spirit.

When, however, he says in the same place that the Father is greater than the Son, this must be understood not with respect to the deity, as though it were lesser in the Son, but insofar as—as the following words indicate—the Son, begotten by the Father, is begotten.

And although the following statement is expressed rather obscurely—

> The very fact that they are called Father and Son: is not the one something other than the other?

—he afterward explains himself admirably, so that he agrees with the scholastics that the Father is called one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, but not one thing and another thing, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not the same Person, yet are of the same substance.

If there are any other statements in the aforementioned book *Against Praxeas* that are expressed too harshly or obscurely, let the reader remember that this entire book must be read cautiously and understood favorably.

Let us return to Novatian’s book *On the Trinity*. First, his statement [Col. 0209A] in chapter 11—

> with the divinity of the Word mingled in the very union—

even if something similar is found in the aforementioned book *Against Praxeas*, must be understood of a mingling by union, not of a mingling of the divine and human natures. We noted this there at no. 56, confirming it from several other passages of that book. The right faith, according to the Athanasian Creed, is that we believe and confess that Christ is one, not by conversion of the divinity into flesh, but by assumption of humanity into God; altogether one, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person.

Next, the statement in the same place—

> Before whom there was nothing except the Father—

must be understood in the same sense as what we cited above from Tertullian’s *Against Hermogenes*, in accordance with what [Col. 0209B] we noted on that same book, chapter 31, no. 141.

[Col. 0210A] Nor is his statement there that the Son is lesser than the Father to be understood otherwise than we have already explained: he is lesser insofar as he is the Son. The passage which appears to interpret the unity of the Father and Son as no more than a concord of fellowship must also be read cautiously, since for this position he wrongly adduces 1 Corinthians 3; for catholic faith and Scripture also recognize the reality of essence in the Father and the Son.

Finally, if he does not appear to agree with the catholic tradition of the Fathers from Scripture concerning the Holy Spirit, we think this occurred not because he denied that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son, but because, before the matter had been defined, the ancient Fathers customarily spoke more obscurely on account of the subject’s supreme obscurity—yet in such a way that their words admit some suitable sense.

## Proverbial Expressions Contained Throughout This Tertullianic Work, by Blessed Rhenanus and Andrew Hoy of Bruges

[Col. 0209]

# PROVERBIAL EXPRESSIONS CONTAINED THROUGHOUT THIS TERTULLIANIC WORK, ILLUSTRATED WITH BRIEF SCHOLIA, BY BLESSED RHENANUS AND ANDREW HOY OF BRUGES

[Col. 0209B] **1. He has gone away now, and must return.** Vol. I, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 4, no. 22.

Tertullian himself explains at great length the use of this proverb, which is also customary among Germans and Gauls: for a man “to have gone away” is for the soul to have departed from the body, [Col. 0209C] and thus for him to have ceased to be among the living. Thus the Greeks customarily use these words, οἴχεσθαι, κατοίχεσθαι, ἀπέρχεσθαι, ὑπογίνεσθαι (“to depart,” “to go down,” “to go away,” “to pass under”), that is, “to die”; all these expressions signify departure and withdrawal.

The entire force of the proverb appears to reside in the little word “now,” which suggests a long interval of time. Such was the force of the truth concerning the resurrection and the immortality of the soul that, handed down as though from hand to hand by their ancestors, it could not be torn from human minds even amid such profound darkness of vain opinions. Instead, it was preserved in a familiar and commonly used proverb concerning those who had long since died, as though people presumed—that is, anticipated and grasped beforehand in their minds—the resurrection of bodies, or the return to their bodies of the souls that had departed: ἀναστροφὴν, ἀνάστασιν (“a return, a resurrection”), that is, “to return,” ἐπαναστρέφειν, ἢ αναβιοῦν (“to turn back again, or to return to life”).

[Col. 0209D] **2. To leap across a very wide chasm.** Vol. III, Book V *Against Marcion*, chapter 14, no. 231.

“To leap,” in the sense of “to leap over” or “cross by a jump.” The full meaning is to omit something altogether, or at least to pass over the intervening words. It is taken from those who prefer to shorten a journey by a leap rather than incur loss by taking the easier walk. Thus Scaliger to Cardan:

> You fly across the broadest field with the lightest leap.

Tertullian soon explains himself:

> You have removed so much from the Scriptures,

that is, you have cut out, rejected, and broken off so much that very large gaps remain in the continuous text of the books. In Book V against the same opponent:

> What great pits he has made in the Epistle by removing what he pleased.

Virgil, Book IV:

> With these words she breaks off her speech midway.

[Col. 0210B] **3. To transfix with one’s gaze.** Vol. I, *On the Pallium*, chapter 4, no. 84.

It means to look sharply, with one’s eyes intent upon and, as it were, fastened upon the object: ἀτενὲς ὁρᾷν (“to gaze intently”). Virgil:

> . . . . . . His eyes fixed upon the dreadful maiden.

Thus those who are clothed in garments alien to nature’s moderation—garments which drive men [Col. 0210C] obliquely from an upright condition—offer themselves openly to be looked at, or rather laughed at, and seem to wish to turn everyone’s eyes upon themselves. Yet this kind of inspection or spectacle, which they court, is joined with the disgrace and insult of those who wear such garments, so that it counts not as praise but as blame.

To this are appended: “To point out with the finger” and “To betray by a nod.” On these below.

**4. The drawn edge of the sword.** Vol. V, *On Modesty*, chapter 14, no. 115.

This is said when the reins, as it were, of full right, authority, and power are let loose in open rebuke. In Virgil:

> He went with his sword enclosed.

The opposite is Cicero’s statement in the First Oration *Against Catiline*:

> But we have now allowed the edge of this authority to grow [Col. 0210D] dull for twenty days. For we possess a decree of the Senate, but it is enclosed in the records, like a sword hidden in its sheath.

Thus in Apuleius:

> Teeth bared, sharpened and thrusting forth to inflict wounds.

**5. Nothing to do with Andromache.** Ibid., chapter 8, no. 65.

This appears to allude to a play by some ancient tragedian entitled *Andromache*. From Tertullian it may be gathered that this proverb means nothing other than the expressions “Nothing to the verse,” “Nothing to Bacchus,” and οὐδὲν πρός ἕπος, ἀπροσδιόνυσα (“nothing relevant to the verse,” followed by an uncertain recovered expression that the context equates with “nothing to do with Bacchus”), that is, something foreign to the subject.

For he compares heretics to stage performers. The performers, adapting allegorical gestures to songs, represent things entirely foreign to the present play and scene—as though he had in view the Greek proverbs ἐκτός χοροῦ ὀρχεῖσθαι (“to dance outside the chorus”), or τὸ ἀπορχεῖσθαι (“to dance away”), [Col. 0211A] “to dance outside the chorus” and “to dance away from it.” The heretics, for their part, assign the same parables wherever they please and do not set them forth where they fit most aptly.

**6. To bring forth to the wrestling ground.** Vol. II, *To the Martyrs*, chapter 3, no. 44.

**RHENANUS.** The place of contest in which athletes meet is called σκάμμα (“wrestling ground”) by the Greeks, because it was customarily surrounded by a trench, παρὰ τό σκάπτειν (“from ‘to dig’”). Hence Blessed Jerome proverbially says “to leave the wrestling ground and the place of contest,” meaning “to depart from the subject proposed” or “to leap beyond the lines.” For thus his text should be read where he writes to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem:

> Since these are the questions at issue, why do you abandon the matters over which the contest is being waged and, leaving the wrestling ground and place of contest, [Col. 0211B] linger over foreign and utterly irrelevant disputes?

Moreover, he explains himself when he adds, “and the place of contest.” For *and* here has the same force as “that is.”

It must not be overlooked that Tertullian speaks very pointedly. Athletes and gladiators are said to be “brought forth” in public spectacles by the very sponsors who present the games. Thus shortly afterward:

> So that, well trained by every hardship, we may be brought forth to the stadium of the tribunal.

According to Tertullian’s meaning, it is to lead someone into the theater, the arena, or the public place of contest, for the sake of displaying and testing his skill and strength and of carrying away the prize, or βραβεῖον (“prize”); it is to descend into the arena.

Paulus Leopardus, Book I of the *Miscellanies*, chapter 22, explains the meaning of the word and rejects the interpretations of Erasmus and Caelius concerning *scamma*. Blessed Ambrose, Book I *On Duties*:

> The athletes are still on the wrestling ground,

also speaks proverbially, as though to say: [Col. 0211C] The prize is still being contested, and the palm remains uncertain.

**7. Attend to that for which we have come.** Vol. III, Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 7, no. 65.

During sacred rites silence was customarily commanded by the words:

> Keep silence,

and, in Greek, σῖγα πᾶς ἴστω λεώς (“Let all the people keep silence”). For the same reason it was customary to cry:

> Attend to this.

Plutarch appears to say this in his *Numa*: ὧν ἴχνός τι μέχρι νῦν διασὼζοντες, ὃταν ἄρχων πρὸς ὅρνισιν ἢ θυσίαις διατρίβῃ, βοῶσιν ὧν ἄγε (“Preserving some trace of these things even to the present, whenever a magistrate is occupied with omens or sacrifices, they cry ‘ὧν ἄγε’”; the final recovered words are uncertain and apparently correspond to “Attend to this”). Muretus, *Various Readings*, Book 15.

It will therefore be a proverb by which we command someone to pay attention to the matter undertaken, so that he applies his whole mind to that alone, neither speaking of anything else nor considering anything else within his mind.

[Col. 0211D] **8. From contributed money.** Vol. III, *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 12, no. 136.

**RHENANUS.** Although mention is made here of a common contribution—for Tertullian says, “They contribute to a common fund,” and shortly afterward, “All contributed one good thing”; Irenaeus likewise says, “Each one contributed that which he possessed within himself as best and most flourishing, and they made a contribution”; and again shortly afterward, “The construction of the second Christ, whom they call the Savior, composed from a contribution”—nevertheless, since the manuscripts consistently have “from contributed money,” I see that one might read not so much *collatitio*, “contributed,” which is obvious to everyone, as *collocatitio*, “money invested,” in the sense of loaned and foreign money. Good men, contributing such money into a common fund and placing it with a friend engaged in business, [Col. 0212A] would thereby both enrich and assist him, first obtaining security from him.

Hence perhaps arose a proverb commonly used among Africans at that time: something was said to be done “with invested money,” or someone boasted of being rich, although he possessed no resources of his own, but only borrowed and foreign resources. Indeed, in Irenaeus elsewhere, concerning this same Savior, we read:

> They deposited upon him, as it were, their own flower, as something invested.

Here perhaps *deposititium*, “something deposited,” should be read. The meaning will be the same if you read *collatitio*, “contributed,” or at least not greatly different.

Certainly among the ancients many things were made with contributed money; upon such works were inscribed the letters:

> AERE COL.

Perhaps Tertullian had this custom in mind here. There is a charitable contribution disbursed for the use of the poor; and a contribution or collection, also called an assessment, which is a kind of monetary taxation; and [Col. 0212B] σύμβολον (“contribution”), a contribution toward the furnishing of a dinner, either in money or provisions. Hence a “contribution dinner” is a banquet of companions or messmates, at which each person brings his own food.

ἔρανος (“a contributed feast”): the proverb will apply to those who are of no worth by themselves but depend entirely upon the resources of others, so that, when these are withdrawn, they collapse and lose both credit and fortune. They are rich in borrowed money, as Horace said:

> In my own money I am poor.

**9. Aesop’s jackdaw.** Ibid., chapter 12, no. 139.

**RHENANUS.** An apologue about this is found among those commonly attributed to Aesop. From it arose the Greek proverb Ἀισώπιος κολοιός (“Aesop’s jackdaw”), that is, “Aesop’s jackdaw.” It was customarily said of those who display other people’s possessions as their own.

Horace, *Epistles*, Book I, 3:

> How is my Celsus doing? He has been warned, and must often be warned,  
> To seek resources of his own and avoid touching  
> Whatever writings Palatine Apollo has received,  
> Lest, if one day the flock of birds should come  
> To reclaim their feathers, the little crow provoke laughter,  
> Stripped of its stolen colors.

The μυθολόγου τὸ ἐπιμύθιον (“the fabulist’s moral”) of Gabrias is altogether suited to Tertullian’s meaning:

Ἀλλοτρὶοις πτεροῖσιν ἠμφιεσμένος


Ηὐχεῖ κολοιὸς ὀρνέων ὑπερφέρειν·


Πρῶτον δὲ δῶρον ἡ χελιδὼν ἡρπάκε (“Clothed in others’ feathers, the jackdaw boasted of surpassing the birds; but first the swallow snatched back her gift”; recovered accents or forms are uncertain).

Μεθ` ἢν ἂπαντες εἶτα· γυμνὸς εὑρέθη (“After her, all the others did likewise; he was found naked”; recovered wording and accents are uncertain).

Ἐπιμύθιον· τὸ ἐξ ἐράνου κάλλος διαλύεται (“Moral: beauty assembled from contributions falls apart”).

We translate it thus:

> While the little crow, arrayed in borrowed feathers,  
> Boasts that she excels the other birds,  
> The swallow first snatches back her gift;  
> Then the others do the same, and at last the crow is seen naked.

**10. The ass from Aesop’s well.** Vol. III, Book IV *Against Marcion*, chapter 23, no. 349.

The words “you have only just come” or “you have only just appeared” are to be understood. It is said of someone who has arrived from elsewhere unknown, distinguished by no renown of name, and who, as though emerging only now from some corner, has hitherto lain hidden—or, to use Horace’s word, escaped notice—and then suddenly dares to boast of something great and illustrious, indeed to claim authority, favor, and reputation for himself.

Since this apologue is not found among the Aesopic fables, it would be futile to offer anything here by conjecture concerning the origin of this proverb, whatever nonsense others may speak: περὶ τῆς τοῦ ὄνου παρακύψεως (“concerning the ass’s peeping out”).

[Col. 0213A] **11. The middle balance-point, or to be borne at the equilibrium of the balance.** Vol. III, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 41, no. 142; and Vol. V, *On Modesty*, chapter 9, no. 73.

In *On Modesty*:

> For an equation of examples will not be admitted, even though it agrees most perfectly at the balance-point, if it is most harmful to salvation.

If, as Rhenanus says from Festus, the *agina* is that opening into which the beam of a balance is inserted—that is, in which the balance moves or turns—and if the balance is said to rest “in the middle *agina*” whenever the weights are equal, so that neither side inclines downward, then it will be the same in proverbial use as the *ansa*, which is λαβή (“handle”), the point upon which the tongue of the balance turns, or in the middle of which the pointer moves to and fro until, when the scales are equal, it corresponds to the highest point; [Col. 0213B] that is, it inclines to neither side but divides the distinction with equal weight.

The proverb may be applied to those who belong to neither party and therefore offend neither side; to those who embrace the virtues, which are certain means situated between extreme vices; to impartial judges; and to similar cases. See the annotations of Pamelius.

**12. More exalted than Alexander.** Vol. I, *Apology*, chapter 11, no. 173.

Restoration notes: S000105: The recovered phrase πρὸς τῆς οἴμου appears textually uncertain; its contextual sense is “before the song.”; S000116: The recovered Aristophanic wording appears uncertain, so its English rendering is approximate.; S000117: The recovered Greek may be corrupt; the contextual rendering “a cord of grievous cares” is approximate.; S000105: The recovered phrase πρὸς τῆς οἴμου is textually uncertain; the context indicates the sense “before the song.”; S000116: The recovered Aristophanic wording is corrupt and syntactically uncertain, so only its identifiable elements can be rendered approximately.; S000117: The recovered χοινίον may be corrupt; the contextual rendering “a cord of grievous cares” is approximate.  

For men of proud and lofty spirit. The loftiness of spirit in Alexander the Great is exceedingly celebrated, having shone forth in deeds no less than in words. As a boy, he grieved that his father might leave him nothing to accomplish himself; he refused to run in the Olympic stadium unless his competitors were kings; [Col. 0213C] while his fortunes were still unimpaired, he refused to divide the kingdom of Asia with Darius; and when he heard from Anaxagoras that there were innumerable worlds, he burst into tears because he had not yet become master of even one.

### 13. Bolder than an Amazon. Vol. III, Book I against Marcion, ch. 1, no. 14.

“The Amazons, or Amazon women, are a singular example for all ages,” says Justin, Book II. Their deeds, wars, and expeditions, full of more than masculine boldness, are commemorated. But since boldness in the female sex is generally joined with shamelessness, the proverb will apply to those who are shamelessly bold and rash. See the annotations of Pamelius.

[Col. 0213D] ### 14. A ram is poised against us, by which the flesh is battered. Vol. III, On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 5, no. 43.

A ram is a beam stretched and suspended by ropes, its head clad in iron so that it may appear to have a very hard forehead like a ram’s; it is also drawn backward in the manner of a ram so that it may strike with greater force and undermine walls. Hence the verb *to be poised*, because skill and a precise balancing were required in preparing and counterbalancing it for its intended blows. Tertullian adds the verb *is battered*. Virgil: “They were pounding the walls with the ram”; “The door totters under the repeated ram”; “He batters at the gates.” Cicero: “The ram has struck the wall.” It may be said proverbially when a powerful argument is raised against us which is difficult to refute. We are attacked by open force. Thus rams and mines may be set against one another in arguments.

[Col. 0214A] ### 15. More just than Aristides. Vol. I, *Apology*, ch. 11, no. 173.

So celebrated among the Greeks, and especially among the Athenians, were the justice and equity of Aristides that he earned the surname τοῦ δικαίου (“the Just”). So great was this man’s observance not only of the laws but also of equity and goodness that he was banished by the wicked for this name alone, and governed the commonwealth with Themistocles despite their opposing political allegiances.

### 16. The asp borrows venom from the viper. Vol. III, Book III against Marcion, ch. 8, no. 53.

Pliny speaks thus of the asp in Book VIII, ch. 23: “The necks of asps swell up, and there is no remedy for their bite except the immediate amputation of the affected parts: so rapidly acting is their venom.” Of the viper he says in the same book, [Col. 0214B] ch. 29: “Of serpents, the viper alone is said to conceal itself in the earth; the rest hide in hollows of trees or rocks.” But Aristotle, Book V of *The Nature of Animals*, reports the contrary: that the viper conceals itself beneath rocks, while the other serpents hide in the earth; during their period of retirement they all lie dormant bereft of venom. In Book VII, ch. 2, he says that the inhabitants of Mount Athos feed upon the flesh of vipers. This is surely evidence that their venom is less effective. This proverb will therefore signify that the most pestilential person is instructed in wickedness by one who is less evil.

### 17. Attalic riches. Vol. V, On Fasting, ch. 15, no. 93.

If the reading is *Attalic*, there is no difficulty: the wealth of Attalus, king of Pergamum, is well known, and the Roman people received it by inheritance. Horace speaks of him in the *Odes*:

[Col. 0214C] Neither through wealth nor as the unknown heir  
Of Attalus have I occupied a royal palace.

And: “On Attalic terms.” Thus those magnificent and superfluous riches and luxuries are contrasted with bread, that is, with the simplest food. But if the reading is *Atellan*, it will mean those masked refinements of dress and adornment. For the very famous Atellan actors, named after Atella, a town of Campania, had been granted the right not to be compelled to remove their masks on stage. Hence masked plays were called Atellan κατ` ἔξοχην (“par excellence”). It will be said of superfluous clothing procured for luxury and display.

### 18. From the toga to the pallium. Vol. I, On the Pallium, ch. 5, no. 94, and ch. 6, no. 116.

[Col. 0214D] RHENANUS. The pallium belonged to the Greeks and the philosophers. Romans too put it on after casting aside the toga. Hence that taunt of the wondering populace concerning more powerful men who had passed over to the Christian religion: “From the toga to the pallium.” Tertullian was thereby prompted to write his book in defense of the pallium. Ammianus Marcellinus, on Julian Augustus: “For in time of peace,” he says, “his frugality was an admirable standard to those who judged rightly, as though he were shortly to return to the pallium.”

### 19. A blind man led by a blind man into the same pit. Vol. III, Book III against Marcion, ch. 7, no. 44.

A proverb used even by the Savior, Luke XVI, whenever an unlearned man attempts to teach another unlearned man, or an imprudent man to advise another imprudent man, and thus hurls him together with himself into the same errors or corrupt opinions. [Col. 0215A] Tertullian interprets it thus: “To borrow from the same man both the rationale of one’s errors and one’s guidance.”

### 20. A blind man stumbles against a rock. Vol. III, Book V against Marcion, ch. 7, no. 119.

Tertullian speaks allegorically of Marcion, who, blinded by the depravity of his errors, held a wrong opinion of Christ, the spiritual rock. Not dissimilar is: “To strike against a reef,” in *On the Trinity*, ch. 28: “Deprived of both those eyes, as though they had been gouged out, he is utterly overcome in the blindness of his doctrine.” It will be applied to one whom the perversity of his opinions drives headlong into every kind of absurdity.

### 21. To strike at close quarters. Vol. III, Book II against Marcion, final chapter, no. 205, and Book III, ch. 5, no. 14.

[Col. 0215B] “To strike at close quarters,” “to fight at close quarters,” συστάδην μάχεσθαι, καὶ ἐγγύθεν (“to fight in close combat and at close quarters”), whose contrary is πόῤῥωθεν, διὰ δορὰτων ἢ βέλων (“from afar, with spears or missiles”). It is transferred from war, in which men sometimes fight with swords in close engagement and are said to “join” or “bring together hands,” while at other times they discharge missiles against the enemy from afar by machines or even by throwing-thongs. We shall use it when we wish to indicate that we intend to examine or discuss a matter more closely or at close range, and to bring forward arguments drawn from the nature of the thing itself, rather than assumed from external considerations, in order to weaken someone’s position.

### 22. From the lime-shop to the charcoal-shop. Vol. III, On the Flesh of Christ, ch. 6, no. 52.

RHENANUS. A lime-shop is a shop in which lime is stored or sold. So too a charcoal-shop takes its name from charcoal. It will be used [Col. 0215C] when a filthy or troublesome condition is exchanged for one equally filthy or troublesome. It is an elegant proverb whenever we retreat from an unclean place to one no cleaner, or fall from one evil into another of a different kind. After Tertullian had answered Marcion’s most impure heresy, he prepared to refute the equally impure heresy of Apelles. Not dissimilar are: “From Scylla into Charybdis”; “Out of the smoke into the flame.” Yet the former proverb appears to signify a certain diversity, and almost an opposition, between the evils, just as lime and charcoal are opposed by reason of their contrary colors. It is taken from those who abhor stains and do not readily allow their clothing to be soiled, which the dust of both substances causes.

[Col. 0215D] ### 23. To spread out over its own plains. Vol. V, On the Trinity, ch. 6, no. 26.

Novatian sets these things in opposition: “To enclose the measure or shape of the divine majesty within these outlines of our body,” and “to spread it without limit over its own plains of boundless magnitude.” The open expanses and immensities of plains are familiar in the proper meaning of the word. So too Virgil’s line:

Messapus, a horseman in arms,  
And Coras with his brother—spread out over the broad plains.

Κατὰ τὴν μεταφορὰν (“By metaphor”) are these expressions: “the plains of rhetoricians”; “for an orator to range over some field”; “to force an orator from a certain vast and immeasurable field into a narrow circle”; and “these matters [Col. 0216A] are accustomed to open a very broad field of discourse to the rhetorician.” From these the use both of this proverb and of the next is evident.

### 24. A broad and spacious field is opened. Ibid., ch. 28, no. 127.

Its contrary in Cicero is “not to have a sufficiently large field in which to range.” Novatian likewise says elsewhere in the same book: “Let these things be stated briefly by us and set down concisely, without being extended through a long disputation. For they could have been extended more broadly and drawn out in a fuller discussion.”

### 25. To speak with the eyebrow of the head. Vol. III, Against Hermogenes, ch. 27, no. 91.

Pride is marked in the eyebrows, by which we either refuse or assent. Tertullian undoubtedly borrowed [Col. 0216B] this from Homer, *Iliad* α (“Book 1”). Thetis says to Jupiter:

Νημερτὲς δὴ μοι ὑπόσχεο, καὶ κατάνευσον (“Promise me truly, then, and nod your assent”).

“Promise me without ambiguity and nod your assent.” Jupiter replies:

Εἰ δ` ἄγε τοι κεφαλῇ κατανεύσομαι, ὂφρα πεποίθῃς;


Τοῦτο γὰρ ἐξ ἐμέθεν γε μετ` ἀθανάτοισι μέγιστον


Τέκμωρ` οὐ γὰρ ἐμὸν παλινὰγρετον, οὐδ` ἀπατηλὸν,


Οὐδ` ἀτελεύτητον γ` ὅ, τι κεν κεφαλῇ κατανεύσω (“Come, I shall nod to you with my head so that you may trust; for this is the greatest pledge from me among the immortals: whatever I nod to with my head is neither revocable, deceitful, nor unfulfilled”).

Ἦ, καὶ κυανέῃσιν ἐπ` ὀφρύσι νεῦσε Κρονίων (“He spoke, and the son of Cronus nodded with his dark brows”). That is:

I shall nod to you with my head, that you may rest in sure confidence;  
For this is the greatest pledge from me among the immortal gods,  
Since whatever I nod to you with my head is neither revocable,  
Nor deceitful, nor left unfulfilled.

“The son of Saturn nodded assent to her words with his dark brows.”

Hence Pliny, Book I, in his letter to Octavius Rufus: “See to what height you have raised me, since you have given me the same power and the same sovereignty that Homer gave Jupiter:

Υἱῷ δ` ἕτερον μὲν ἔδωκε πατὴρ, ἕτερον δ` ἀνένευσεν (“The father gave one thing to his son but refused another”). The father granted one request; to one he nodded assent.

For I too can answer your request with a similar nod of assent or refusal.” I should not rashly judge the expression “the censorial eyebrow” to be irrelevant here, as though one condemned or approved by the eyebrow alone—an expression others interpret as grim severity.

### 26. To give a cathartic. Vol. I, On the Pallium, ch. 5, no. 111.

Καθαρτικὸν ἢ καθαρτήριον φάρμακον, ἢ κάθαρσις (“a cathartic or purgative medicine, or a purgation”), a medicine that causes evacuation, or that empties the bowels. Hence ὑπήλατον (“a medicine administered from below; a purgative”) was said of Hippocrates. Tertullian explains himself: [Col. 0216D] “By discourse you have persuaded me with a most wise medicine,” from a Greek senarius:

Λόγῳ μ` ἕπεισας φαρμάκῳ σοφωτάτῳ (“By discourse you persuaded me with a most wise medicine”).

Καθαιροῦν (“to cleanse or purify”) means to cleanse and expiate. Horace alludes to this in Book I, *Epistles* 1, when speaking of the vices of the mind:

There are words and utterances with which you may soothe this pain  
And drive away a great part of the disease.

And:

. . . . . There are certain expiations that could  
Restore you after you had read the little book in purity three times.

“To purge with hellebore,” and similar expressions, belong here.

### 27. Wiser and graver than Cato. Vol. I, *Apology*, ch. 11, no. 173.

The Sabines called an acute man *catus*, whence the name of the Catos. An encomium of this Cato—Tertullian’s first Cato and the Censor—may be found in Pliny, Book VII, ch. 27, [Col. 0217A] and in Cicero’s *On Friendship*, where Laelius says of Cato: “Either no one was wise, or, if anyone was, he was.” It may also be found in *On Old Age*, which is inscribed with the name of this Cato.

### 28. More rugged than the Caucasus. Vol. I, Book I against Marcion, ch. 1, no. 15.

The Caucasus is an immense mountain of Scythia. As Pliny says, Book VI, ch. 5, its ridges in the Colchian region of Pontus turn toward the Riphaean mountains, descending on one side toward the Euxine and Lake Maeotis, and on the other toward the Caspian and Hyrcanian Sea, under various names. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:

The bristling Caucasus begot you  
From its hard crags, and Hyrcanian . . .

By these words “rugged” is explained. It is applied to a coarse and hard person, intractable and inhospitable.

[Col. 0217B] ### 29. To have neither brain nor heart. Vol. III, Book IV against Marcion, ch. 10, no. 118.

In the human brain, the receptacle of the vital spirits, lies the supreme and, as it were, royal power of reason; in the heart lies the very source of all life and the seat of wisdom. Hence the senseless and foolish are said to be empty of brain and heart. Indeed, physical disorders themselves, if they affect either brain or heart, undermine the mind and conduct as well. Aesop’s familiar fable tells of the fox admiring the head of a theatrical mask: ὦ οἱα κεφαλή, καὶ ἐγκέφαλον οὐκ ἔχει· πρὸς τοῖς κατὰ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀλογίστοις (“O what a head—and it has no brain; besides those who are irrational in soul”). “O what a head! Yet it has no brain.”

### 30. Deer in battle. Vol. II, On the Soldier’s Crown, ch. 1, no. 18.

[Col. 0217C] RHENANUS. It has the flavor of a proverbial figure, arising, as it appears, from that saying of Chabrias, who said that an army of deer led by a lion was more formidable than an army of lions led by a deer. Plutarch mentions it. The deer is a simple animal of proverbial timidity, whose entire security lies in flight, since it is exceedingly swift. Hence men are called deer-like when they trust more in flight than in strength, and are fearful. To them Mars is, as Virgil says in Book II, “in their boastful tongue and fleeing feet.” And in Homer, *Iliad* α (“Book 1”), Achilles reproaches Agamemnon for cowardice in martial encounters:

Οἰνοβαρὲς, κυνὸς ὃμματ` ἔχων, κραδίηντ` ἐλάφοιο (“Wine-besotted, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer!”) Drunkard, with the heart of a deer and the eyes of a dog.

### 31. Chrysippus to the hellebore. Vol. III, On the Soul, ch. 6, no. 89.

[Col. 0217D] Chrysippus, the pupil of Cleanthes, was a man of exceedingly keen intellect, concerning whom there is the little verse:

Εἰ μὴ γὰρ ἦν Χρύσιππος, οὐκ ἄν ἦ Στόα (“For had Chrysippus not existed, neither would the Stoa”) . . . .

Had Chrysippus not existed, neither would the Stoa.

Valerius Maximus, Book VIII, ch. 7, reports that Carneades, when preparing to dispute with Chrysippus, used first to purge himself with hellebore so that he might express his own thought more attentively and refute Chrysippus’ more sharply.
