Yet just as African hunters in particular were urgently demanded to moderate the delight of the Eternal City—for by that false name Rome flattered herself—men who, powerful in strength [Col. 0251A] and skilled at frustrating the bites of beasts, might evade their assaults and kill the beasts themselves, so too the truly eternal City of the true God saw a sufficiently great defense born for itself from this same Africa against Valentinians, Gnostics, Arians, and similar monstrosities of nature.

For why should I praise Augustine’s subtlety and learning? Why commend the honey-flowing eloquence of Lactantius? Why pursue the learned inquisitiveness of Arnobius? Why admire the piety that shines everywhere in Cyprian’s writings, which he himself sealed with his blood? Finally, why should I marvel at the rounded and gently flowing eloquence of Minucius, who earned much true glory even from a single little book? TERTULLIAN alone is the equivalent of them all: Augustine takes great delight in him; Lactantius recognizes his mastery of every kind of literature; Arnobius sets him before himself as a model to follow; Cyprian, [Col. 0251B] whenever he asks for his books, calls him “the Master”; and finally Minucius, in his own Dialogue—which is like a small curving bay enclosed from the vast sea of this *Apologeticum*—all but transcribes him.

Although it is not my purpose to reproduce here all that ancient and modern authors have thought about this TERTULLIAN, with no small accumulation of praise, I nevertheless cannot refrain from sampling a few judgments. Vincent of Lérins, a writer of the fifth century—not without eloquence—according to the date assigned to him by du Cange, condensed the highly honorable testimonies of the ancients into these words:

“He must readily be judged the chief of all our Latin writers. For what man was more learned than he? Who was more thoroughly versed in matters divine and human? Indeed, with a certain marvelous capacity of mind, he embraced all philosophy and all the schools of the philosophers, the founders and champions of those schools, all [Col. 0251C] their disciplines, and every variety of history and learning. And did he not excel in an intellect so weighty and forceful that he set himself almost nothing to conquer which he did not either penetrate by acuteness or crush by sheer weight? Furthermore, who could adequately recount the merits of his style? It is woven together with so great and, as it were, so dense a mass of arguments that those whom it could not persuade it compels to agree with it. Almost every word of his is a maxim; every thought, a victory.”

Among more recent writers, the illustriously noble Joseph Scaliger knew no one in the learned world more elevated or more accomplished in every kind of learning and science. See, then, how great it is to be praised by one who is himself praised. These are his words in the first [Col. 0251D] *Scaligerana*, p. 96:

“TERTULLIAN must always be kept at hand and read carefully, both because of the distinctive character of the Roman language and because of his knowledge of every discipline and branch of literature. For he was an all-knowing and acute teacher, who must not be handled with unwashed hands or read in passing, since everywhere he makes the reader pause. TERTULLIAN is certainly a most excellent author in every respect.”

There also survives the highly learned and exact letter of Lipsius, Book IV, Epistle IX, to Jacobus Pamelius, to this effect:

“I hear, most distinguished Pamelius, that you are engaged in correcting TERTULLIAN. Whether you have undertaken a greater task or a more useful one, I do not know. To correct a writer filled with ancient and recondite learning is arduous; for that same writer to be published in corrected form concerns not only you theologians but all of us who handle Greek [Col. 0252A] and Roman literature.”

With good reason, therefore, among Barthius—a noble scholar of wide-ranging learning—he bears the title **FATHER OF LEARNING**, *Adversaria*, Book XIII, chap. XVI. In the same author, Book XIX, chap. I, one may also read the following:

“Of the writers who have come down to us, no one is more learned, and there is no one from whom you can learn more, than TERTULLIAN. There is not a single stroke in him that was not placed with care, so that, just as others sometimes seem to err through poverty of learning, he sometimes appears to err through its abundance.”

To these should deservedly be added the testimony of Thomas Campanella, a man whose intellectual force and acuteness of judgment I have often admired. In his little work *On His Own Books and the Right Method of Study*, chap. IX, Crenius’s edition, p. 216, after enumerating the virtues and faults of certain writers who treated theological subjects, he concludes his discussion of our author as follows: [Col. 0252B]

“TERTULLIAN, finally, as the Master of Theologians, proves more in two words than the others do with a thousand arguments: weighty, difficult, keen, effective, brief, elegant; a cultivator of philosophical, though not civic, grammar, who by his African manner of speech attracts men as though to foreign wares.”

What wonder, then, if so great an author found not only such distinguished eulogists but also commentators from every nation? Consecrated to eternity together with the name of TERTULLIAN, the names of RHENANUS, PAMELIUS, JUNIUS, DE LA CERDA, HERALDUS, GOTHOFREDUS, SALMASIUS, and RIGALTIUS will remain, drawn from every condition and discipline. I shall now pass over ZEPHYRUS, BARRAEUS, GAGNAEUS, LATINIUS, GELENIUS, MERCERIUS, WOUWERIUS, and the quite numerous [Col. 0252C] company of other scholars who wished to leave posterity public monuments of their devotion to this author.

Most of these men gave us all the works of TERTULLIAN adorned with their explanations. First among them was RHENANUS—to whom a grateful posterity owes both this author and very many others brought into the light—in editions repeated two or three times; GELENIUS and BARRAEUS followed him, then PAMELIUS and JUNIUS, and LOUIS DE LA CERDA, a man of outstanding learning. After them, a man of recognized learning, NICOLAS RIGALTIUS, all but brought Tertullian back alive from the dead; I omit a certain GEORGE AMBINAS, who, despite the gaping bulk of the three volumes of his laborious *Omniloquium*, accomplished nothing worthy of note. Rigaltius’s editions were very frequently returned to the press at Paris under the auspices of PHILIPPE LE PRIEUR, but in a form much more corrupted than that of Rigaltius himself, as we have often demonstrated in this one little book.

The rest proceeded by parts, or left behind corrections and brief notes published separately from the author’s work. Among these the industry of DESIDERIUS HERALDUS stands out. He composed a commentary full of varied learning upon this *APOLOGETICUM*—the work to which we too first chose to apply our mind and thoughts—as well as some truly learned books of digressions. But long before him FRANCIS ZEPHYRUS had also, in some fashion, illustrated this work with a kind of paraphrase; and ALDUS, following the editorial care of Baptista Egnatius, had published it separately at the end of Lactantius in the years 1515 and 1535. Yet Joannes Tacuinus had anticipated him, having likewise appended it to Lactantius at Venice in 1509.

And yet, after so many men of such distinction, I have ventured to appear before the public, [Col. 0253A] not in order to advertise my zeal and diligence or to weave for myself a garland of praise from censuring and excerpting the flowers of others—a practice I detest and hate—but so that, as a theologian, I might render whatever service I could to the theologian TERTULLIAN and to our own theologians; so that I might contribute to the understanding of an author who, by universal acclaim, was supremely skilled in Greek and Roman antiquities and disciplines, should anything relevant to this work of his present itself to me in the writers of either language while I happened to be continually handling him. I do not deny that from my earliest years I have taken very great pleasure in, and been captivated by, reading and engaging with those writers. Finally, my purpose was to provide some treatment for this author who, if any man ever was, remains, after so many physicians, exceedingly corrupt and in the worst condition.

As for this last purpose, [Col. 0253B] since I was well aware how difficult it is—especially with this author—even from the following words of the great Scaliger in the *Scaligerana*, p. 47:

“Beza had done some work on Tertullian, but he did well not to publish it. It is difficult to publish anything upon that author without manuscripts,”

I began to look about for that kind of assistance which scholars certainly cannot do without and from which they ought not to be barred. Yet I did not think I needed to travel as far as Turin, where Mabillon, in his *Italian Journey*, p. 8, testifies that he encountered a manuscript of this *APOLOGETICUM* dating back six hundred years. Let those to whom it is granted to enjoy such good fortune consult those parchments.

For our part, an outstanding parchment manuscript presented itself to us, containing, besides this little book, many writings of TERTULLIAN. [Col. 0253C] It occupies the second place among the manuscripts of the very well-stocked Leiden Library and is catalogued there on p. 324. Although we do not venture to assert that it is extremely ancient, we affirm that comparison has clearly established for us that it was derived from a very good and very ancient exemplar, and that in many places it agrees with the Fulda manuscript and other excellent witnesses.

For I do not think that anywhere on earth there exist manuscripts of this *APOLOGETICUM* comparable in singularity and excellence with the one formerly kept in the Fulda Library. Francis Modius of Bruges, a most diligent and learned man, had written the variant readings of this manuscript into a copy of the edition published at Paris in 1580 by Michael Julianus under the editorship of RENATUS LAURENTIUS BARRAEUS—not by RENATUS LAURENTIUS himself, as JUNIUS writes, since he had not examined that edition, which has also been carefully reviewed by us on this basis. [Col. 0253D] When these readings subsequently came into the hands of Gaspar Scioppius, he transmitted them to JUNIUS. But since Junius’s entire edition had already been prepared, he relegated them to the end of his notes on TERTULLIAN.

What has always seemed especially remarkable to me is that neither DE LA CERDA nor HERALDUS himself cast his eyes upon this exceedingly distinguished collation. It remained hidden after those notes of JUNIUS, known to scarcely anyone except GOTHOFREDUS, until NICOLAS RIGALTIUS, a man of penetrating learning, used it in the more correct of his earlier editions—but in such a way that he took from it those readings that pleased him, without mentioning in his notes any of the others, though they were quite numerous. He therefore left us a sufficiently abundant gleaning from that very collation. Throughout our notes we have faithfully reproduced its readings just as Modius, a most trustworthy excerptor, recorded them. [Col. 0254A]

In addition, there came to us an exact collation of an Agobardine manuscript—not indeed of that manuscript from which the remaining writings of TERTULLIAN are now read, all but raised from the underworld, and in which alone are found the two hitherto exceedingly corrupt books *To the Nations*; but nevertheless a manuscript of quite good quality, which, like the Leiden manuscript just mentioned, had not hitherto been examined by any editor of TERTULLIAN.

Three arguments persuade me that these two Agobardine manuscripts are distinct. First, RIGALTIUS corrected a great many of Tertullian’s books from a very ancient Agobardine manuscript written more than eight hundred years ago; before each book he noted from which manuscript and in how many places he had corrected it, yet before the little book of the *APOLOGETICUM* he does not mention this manuscript. [Col. 0254B]

Second, in the extremely exact collation of that most ancient Agobardine manuscript which JOSIAS MERCERUS made in his own hand against the Pamelian edition—in 1625, as he himself recorded, for Agobard—not JOANNES MERCERIUS, as is printed in the library catalogue, p. 71, unless my memory altogether deceives me, though I have used that book very often—the margins of the *APOLOGETICUM* are not covered with any notes. That book may still be seen today in the Leiden Library, p. 71.

Third and especially, JACQUES GOTHOFREDUS, editor of the books *To the Nations* and himself the distinguished owner of this treasure before it was transferred into the library of the king of France, carefully drew up in his preface to those books a catalogue of the works contained in that manuscript, but did not number the *APOLOGETICUM* among them. [Col. 0254C]

The collation of the other Agobardine manuscript which we now publish likewise resulted from the diligence of JOSIAS MERCERUS. He must be distinguished from JOANNES MERCERIUS, who was a professor of law at Bourges, composed notes on Tertullian’s book *On the Pallium*, and lived much earlier. The hand of PAUL COLOMESIUS, who had attached the following words to the margin of the Rigaltian edition, testifies to this:

“In the margin of this volume you have the notes of JOSIAS MERCERUS and variant readings extracted by him from the Agobardine manuscript. PAUL COLOMESIUS copied them at Souldley, near Windsor, in the house of Vossius, in the year 1682.”

FRANCIS FABRICIUS, the most celebrated Doctor and Professor of Sacred Theology at the University of Leiden, had mentioned this book to me and said that he possessed it. When I then asked for it, he ordered it to be brought out and, with his characteristic kindness, made it available. But the work had already advanced as far as the end of Chapter XI; therefore it seemed necessary to me that the collation of the first eleven chapters should be inserted among the Addenda. [Col. 0254D]

The same procedure had to be followed with another parchment manuscript, catalogued on p. 376 of the Leiden Library and bound together with writings of Cyprian and others. At first this book escaped our diligence, but very recently we collated it with the greatest care and inserted its variant readings into the same Addenda. It was certainly an excellent manuscript. Although in the quality of its script it was less elegant than the first Leiden parchment, it surpassed it in age and accuracy.

I also used JUNIUS’s edition, in which JOSEPH SCALIGER had written certain conjectures. Throughout, these have been acknowledged with the honor due to the name of so great a man. I likewise used a copy of the same edition in which PETRUS SCRIVERIUS had added certain corrections from ancient manuscripts, a volume which I had long ago acquired from the Almeloveen library when it was dispersed. [Col. 0255A] These corrections should perhaps be referred to the manuscripts of Heribert Rosweyde, a learned Jesuit and friend of Scriverius. Certainly the following words, once prefixed by the most learned SCRIVERIUS to his book, concern him:

“Heribert Rosweyde, in a letter written to me on the sixth of May 1603: ‘I have lately obtained two manuscript copies of TERTULLIAN’S *APOLOGETICUM*. They agree wonderfully and defend the ancient readings against the acuteness of the critics. I was indeed astonished that the great Scaliger devised *Gomphosin* for us in TERTULLIAN—a plausible conjecture, certainly, but by no means necessary, etc.’”

Nothing further appears there.

Besides this accession of manuscripts, I diligently sought out and compared every edition hitherto published of the works of TERTULLIAN or of this *APOLOGETICUM*, and noted the points at which they differed, [Col. 0255B] so that no one may say that I approached so great an author and so distinguished a work of his—such as this *APOLOGETICUM* above all—unprepared. What I have accomplished will be for the fair-minded reader to judge. If I have slipped anywhere—something which very often happened even to the greatest men before me in this very work, and which cannot be avoided in this kind of writing—he will, I think, readily pardon it.

Certain matters still remain for me to discuss: matters pertaining to the life, character, and opinions of TERTULLIAN, not all of which agreed in every respect with the orthodox Church; the time at which he wrote this *APOLOGETICUM*; the party to which he then belonged, and whether he was devoted to Montanus; and why, following, as I have observed, the example of Justin Martyr, he made his two books *To the Nations* into a kind of advance guard for this *APOLOGETICUM*. [Col. 0255C] Some of these matters, however, have been treated more fully by others; some are touched upon in this commentary itself; and some will also be set forth by us in the Prolegomena to the remaining books which he composed under various titles against the Gentiles. If it pleases God, the arbiter of human affairs, I intend shortly to publish these books, illustrated by my own and others’ brief notes.

Indeed, that no moderate amount of diligence has been devoted by us to them is evident even from the fact [Col. 0256A] that in these two small books *To the Nations*, when the opportunity was not sought but presented itself spontaneously, we have removed more than twenty corruptions in this commentary of ours. Since no assistance from manuscripts remains in their case beyond the single surviving witness, it was necessary to allow some freedom to conjecture.

Yet I wish it to be known that TERTULLIAN not only applied great care to this *APOLOGETICUM*, but also issued this same work to the public twice, altering the words and style a little here and there. This will, we think, appear evident to the reader if he compares the passages cited by us on pp. 292b, 313a, 409b, and especially 439a–b. Nor should this seem surprising, even if no one before us has observed it, since it is easy to show that the same thing happened to both Lucretius and Lucan. [Col. 0256B] Thus Hugo Grotius not undeservedly renders the same judgment concerning Lucan at Book VI, verse 187; Conrad Rittershausen acknowledges that the phenomenon may be observed in many authors in his commentary on Oppian—his words are excerpted from it by Gaspar Scioppius, *On the Critical Art*, p. 87—and finally the great Salmasius demonstrated it by invincible arguments in his notes on Achilles Tatius.

So much for these matters. If they please you, kindly reader, we promise that our labor will continue to advance your benefit. For we have many works begun, half completed, and even finished, which we shall freely draw from our store so long as spirit and leisure remain, and so long as

> —within this vigorous age  
> Blood remains, and strength stands firm in its own power.

[Col. 0256C] For, as the sweet Muse of the Syracusan Theocritus soberly counsels, *Idyll* XIV, final verse:

> —ποιεῖν τι δεῖ ὅς γόνυ χλωρόν—“one must act while one’s knee is still vigorous”.

Written in my study in the village of Stad aan ’t Haringvliet, on the island of Overflakkee, on the very Kalends of June, in the year 1718.

**THE FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, CONTAINING THE BOOKS WRITTEN BEFORE THE AUTHOR EMBRACED MONTANISM.**

**First Series. APOLOGETIC BOOKS. THE APOLOGETICUM AGAINST THE GENTILES. TO THE NATIONS, TWO BOOKS. ON THE TESTIMONY OF THE SOUL. TO THE MARTYRS. ON THE SPECTACLES. ON IDOLATRY. THE BOOK TO SCAPULA, BY WAY OF AN APPENDIX.**

**The Apologeticum against the Gentiles.**

**[APOLOGETICUM.]**

[Col. 0257]

# THE APOLOGETICUM AGAINST THE GENTILES, IN DEFENSE OF THE CHRISTIANS. (C)

## ARGUMENT OF THE ENTIRE WORK

[Col. 0257A]

While Septimius Severus was emperor and administered the Roman state together with his son Antoninus, Tertullian, burning with zeal for the true religion, whose sacred rites he had of course embraced, was distressed—as he ought to have been—that a religion which had begun in some measure to raise its head was being oppressed. This occurred at the beginning of the fifth persecution, during whose fury innocent Christians everywhere, without regard for sex or age, were tormented with punishments unheard of before that day.

With the supreme eloquence in which he then excelled, he undertook the defense of the Christians. Their condition was so deplorable that they were condemned without their case being heard and solely by a prejudgment founded upon their name. He judged it his duty to confront the common and public evil and, so far as lay within him, to restrain the storm that was daily breaking forth. For this reason he sent an apology to the Roman governors and for a time broke and weakened the unbridled assaults of his adversaries. For he pleaded the case with such vigor and learning that, if the dispute had been decided by reasons and truth, he would have driven [Col. 0257B] all the Gentiles into an impasse. He could have followed in the footsteps of Justin Martyr and Aristides; yet he imitated their eloquence in such a way that he appears to have surpassed them both in character of expression, weight of argument, and variety of learning.

# CHAPTER I

**ARGUMENT.—Since under Severus Christians had been denied permission to defend themselves in court, the author offered this work to the governors of the Roman Empire. In this chapter he demonstrates the injustice of that judicial procedure by which a defense is denied to the innocent and the truth is concealed. Meanwhile, the very many and very considerable persons who daily pass over to this sect make it worthy of some consideration; all of them, being free from any guilt of depravity, plainly show that they have assumed a disposition far different from that which is always discovered in criminals.**

If it is not lawful for you, governors of the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 0258B] **Governors of the Empire.** Francis Zephyrus says—in his scholia, which we have joined to our own—that he calls the pontiffs themselves *governors*, since their authority administered sacred affairs, ceremonies, and, in short, the whole of religion; and the highest interest of the commonwealth was engaged in the interpretation of these things. Hence Cicero also calls them leaders of public counsel and governors of the immortal gods. It is also established from ancient inscriptions that the emperors themselves were among them, since in those inscriptions they are called Supreme Pontiffs. PAMELIUS.], while presiding to judge in the open and elevated place [Col. 0259A] [Note: [Col. 0259A] “And in the place itself,” Paris edition. “And in the elevated place itself,” Rigaltius.] almost at the very summit [Note: [Col. 0259B] **Almost at the very summit of the city, presiding to judge.** He means the Capitol. Chalcidius also, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, says that reason has its seat in the head, [Col. 0259C] as though in the Capitol of the whole body. RIGALTIUS.] of the city, openly to ascertain [Note: [Col. 0259A] “To describe,” Barraeus, Leiden manuscript. “To look down upon,” Rhenanus, Junius.] and investigate face to face what clearly lies in the case of the Christians; if [Note: [Col. 0259B] Others read “but.”] in this matter alone [Note: [Col. 0259C] **In this matter alone.** Since the Christians’ case seems deplorable because of prejudgments and various decrees—so much so that no one does not dread speaking in their defense—and since they therefore need open advocacy, let it at least be granted us to argue privately on behalf of the Christians. By means of letters given to you as witnesses of our grief and love, preserve some assistance for tongues. LE PRIEUR.] your authority [Note: [Col. 0259C] **Your authority.** By *authority* he understands the supreme act of administration, the highest power and authority in governing the empire. Thus authority belongs to an institutor, dispenser, or procurator. Just as these men need supreme authority, therefore, so he says that these governors possess that authority and need fear or blush before no one, so that they may judge in safety. LA CERDA.], in its public concern for justice, either fears or blushes to inquire; if, finally, as recently happened, the hostility toward this sect, [Col. 0259C] being excessively occupied with domestic [Note: [Col. 0259C] **As recently happened, in domestic judgments.** He indicates a recent example of cruelty by certain men whom he calls governors of the Roman Empire. In a domestic judgment they had evidently decreed something unusually severe against their children or slaves because they had enrolled themselves in the Christian sect. As though they had thereby contracted harshness and brought prejudgments from home, they approached the tribunals themselves with greater hostility when the cases of Christians were to be judged. LA CERDA.] judgments [Note: [Col. 0259B] Thus Heraldus, Rigaltius, Havercamp. “Indications,” Fulda manuscript; old edition of Gelenius.] [Note: [Col. 0259B] “Burdened,” Paris edition. “In minds,” Modius, Fulda manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0259D] **Occupied.** A Greek usage; and Virgil likewise, *Georgics* I: “engaged upon the glad fields.” He says that the heathen attempted to investigate the crimes popularly imputed to Christians by questioning those who associated familiarly with them—I mean their male and female servants—but that nothing was ever discovered. LA CERDA.], blocks the way [Note: [Col. 0259D] **Hostility toward this sect.** Chalcidius uses *sect* in the same sense in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, where by the “holier sect” he signifies the Christian sect originating among the Hebrews: “That this is indeed true is attested by a certain eminent teaching of a holier sect.” LA CERDA.] to a defense [Note: [Col. 0259B] Thus Pamelius, La Cerda, Rhenanus. Junius, Heraldus, [Col. 0260A] Rigaltius, and Havercamp omit “the way,” on the authority of the manuscript; the Fulda manuscript reads “the mouth to a defense.”], let the truth be permitted to reach your ears at least by the hidden [Note: [Col. 0259D] **By the hidden way of silent letters.** He speaks similarly of this same matter in *To Scapula*, chap. 1: [Col. 0260B] “It is necessary, even in this way, to break forth and set before you the things that you are unwilling to hear openly.” Similar to this is Martial’s remark in the preface to Book XI of the *Epigrams*: “I see why actors in tragedies receive a letter: because they are not permitted to speak for themselves.” HAVERCAMP.] way of silent letters.

She asks no indulgence [Note: [Col. 0260A] Junius reads *Nilus* for “nothing concerning.”] for her cause [Note: [Col. 0260A] “Would ask indulgence,” Rhenanus, Paris edition.], because she is not surprised at her condition. [Col. 0260A] She knows that she lives as a foreigner [Note: [Col. 0260B] **Thus, as a foreigner upon the earth.** Prosper of Aquitaine, in his book of *Epigrams*, where he expresses Augustine’s saying, “Everyone who belongs to the heavenly city is a foreigner in the world, and while he uses temporal life he lives in an alien homeland,” sings as follows:

> Called, through Christ’s redemption, to his heavenly homeland,  
> He passes the span of fleeting life as a guest.  
> And while he strives toward the promised rest by no road of his own,  
> He endures the many dangers of the worldly way.  
> Now beset by adversity and now filled with prosperity,  
> It either breaks the fearful or binds the wavering.  
> Amid these snares, the world shall not capture the man  
> Who runs toward life’s joys, if Christ shall be his way.

HAVERCAMP.] upon the earth; among strangers she readily finds enemies. Yet she has her race, her dwelling place [Note: [Col. 0260C] **Dwelling place.** That is, the homeland which she seeks, cares for, and desires. When the supreme philosopher Anaxagoras, who had been highly neglectful of both public and private affairs, was addressed by someone in this manner, “Have you no concern at all for your homeland?” he replied, ἐμοὶ γὰρ καὶ σφόδρα, μέλει τῆς πατρίδος, δείξας τὸν οὐρανόν, that is, “Indeed I have concern for my homeland, and the greatest concern,” pointing his finger toward heaven. Diogenes relates this in his *Life* of Anaxagoras. Chrysostom, *Homily on Saints Bernice and Prosdoce*: “But the women enjoyed profound tranquility, since hope of future things fortified them on every side; because, even while living abroad, they were not living abroad. For they had faith as their true homeland, confession as their own city, and, since they were sustained by the best hope, they were affected by none of the things present, for they looked only toward those to come.” [Col. 0260D] Thus they could glory with Diogenes, the freest of all the Greeks: Ἔχειν πατρίδα ἀδοξίαν καὶ πενίαν ἀνάλωτον τῇ τύχῃ, that is, “that they possessed as their homeland contempt for glory and poverty, things which would never fall under the power of fortune.” HAVERCAMP.], her hope, favor, and dignity in heaven. Her one desire, meanwhile, is that she not be condemned without being known. What is thereby lost [Note: [Col. 0260A] “Here,” Paris and Venetian editions.] to the laws [Note: [Col. 0260D] **Is lost to the laws.** A rare word, and one which you will scarcely find in other authors. It does occur, however, in Lucretius, whom our Septimius read attentively. He, Book XI, 296:

Restoration notes: S000206 contains two distinct textual readings; E010 receives φλὰβιον (“Flavian”) and E011 receives φὰβιον (“Fabian”), as required by the surrounding correction.; S000228 ends mid-expression with κάκ; the continuation ἔμμεναι occurs in S000229 and is represented separately at E034 without duplication.; S000230 is legible as Οὺδὲ μὰγιον θυτιοδὴ but appears textually corrupt; it has been preserved verbatim and explicitly marked uncertain.; S000206 contains two distinct textual readings: E010 receives φλὰβιον (“Flavian”), the proposed restoration, and E011 receives φὰβιον (“Fabian”), the reading being replaced.; S000228 ends within an expression at κάκ; S000229 continues it with ἔμμεναι at E034, so the two markers together represent the passage once without duplication.; S000230 is legible as Οὺδὲ μὰγιον θυτιοδὴ but appears corrupt; it is preserved verbatim and marked uncertain.  

For nothing thereby increases or perishes. But if Festus collected certain testimonies, they have perished, and his epitomator Paulus has left us only this mutilated statement: *deperire* means “to perish utterly.” HAV.]

—if it is heard, under laws exercising dominion in their own realm? Their authority will glory all the more in this, that they will condemn the truth even after hearing it. [Note: [Col. 0260B] “That even,” Rhenanus, La Cerda, Pamelius. “That unheard,” the Puteanus manuscript, Jacobus Bongarsius, and Hugolius. Heraldus, Rigaltius, and Havercamp preferred to write: “Whereby even the truth, once heard, they will condemn”; but … [the supplied note is defective:] “of them, because the truth.”] But if they condemn it unheard, besides incurring the odium of injustice, they will also deserve the suspicion of a guilty conscience, since they refuse to hear what, once heard, they could not condemn.

We therefore lodge before you [Col. 0261A] this first ground of our case: [Note: [Col. 0261B] “We follow this reading as preferable to the others,” says de Gourcy, “for it certainly excels them in elegance, obvious meaning, and force. To ‘lodge a case before judges’ is the same as to summon one to appear before a judge and to explain the matter point by point; it certainly does not mean to assign the cause of a thing. Nor is Tertullian’s entire purpose in this passage to assign the causes of hatred toward Christians; rather, he is reviewing the principal heads of their case. In this first chapter he undertakes to assert that condemning them is the height of injustice. Then, at the beginning of chapter IV, he himself plainly discloses the genuine sense here when he says: ‘And so, having set these things out by way of preface, as it were, to stigmatize the injustice of the public hatred toward us,’ etc.” [Col. 0261C] EDD.] the injustice [Note: [Col. 0261A] “Of injustice,” Rigaltius, Semler, Leopold, Havercamp; “hatred,” Pamelius, Barr.] of the hatred directed against the name “Christian.” That very designation both aggravates and refutes the injustice which it seems to excuse—namely, ignorance.

For what is more unjust than that people should hate what they do not know, even if the thing deserved hatred? It deserves it only when it is known whether it deserves it. [Note: [Col. 0261A] “Deserved,” Pamelius, Fran., Semler.] But when knowledge of its deserts is absent, how can the justice of hatred be defended, since that justice must be established not from the outcome but from the conscience? Since, therefore, people hate [Note: [Col. 0261A] “They confess,” Paris.] because they do not know [Note: [Col. 0261A] “We are shaped,” Rhenanus, Heraldus, Rigaltius, Havercamp; “they are predisposed,” [Col. 0261B] Pamelius, Barr.] the nature of what they hate, why may it not be something of a kind that they ought not [Col. 0262A] to hate? Thus we refute each fault by means of the other: they are ignorant while they hate, and they hate unjustly while they are ignorant.

Evidence of this ignorance—which, while excusing their injustice, condemns it—is that all who formerly hated because they did not know the nature of what they hated cease [Note: [Col. 0262A] Pamelius and Semler, among others: “But what likeness has a Christian?” Rhenanus in his edition: “What likeness among Christians?” The Lyons manuscript B has “of Christians”; but Havercamp rightly determined that the reading of the Fulda manuscript should be restored, and what follows does not conflict with it.] to hate as soon as they cease to be ignorant. [Note: [Col. 0262A] “The nature of the evil,” Rhenanus, Barr., Semler, Leopold.] From among these people Christians are made, plainly as a result of discovering the truth; and they begin to hate what they had been and to profess what they had hated. They are as numerous [Note: [Col. 0261C] “And they are as numerous.” It is as though he had said: “Their multitude is so great that it does not escape your notice; instead, you judge them, and lament with loud public outcry—grieving under the pretext of justice and as though you had suffered a loss—that the world is besieged by this Christian religion and that all people are taking refuge in this name.” Thus that saying of Horace could deservedly be sung of the Church: “Plunge it into the deep: it emerges more beautiful.” PAM.] as we are noted to be. [Note: [Col. 0262B] “They are marked out,” Paris, Barr., Rhenanus, Heraldus, La Cerda, Gangnaeus-Gelenius.]

They cry aloud that the city is besieged— [Note: [Col. 0261C] “They cry aloud that the city is besieged,” etc. Barr reads: “They cry aloud that the city is besieged.” From the multitude of people flowing from every quarter toward the truth, Septimius seeks to prove that the Christian religion is not so wicked as they supposed, since everywhere so many of every sex and station flocked to it; not merely the unstable common crowd, therefore, but also men distinguished by illustrious birth and reputation were passing over to that sect. Below, chapter III: “Gaius Seius is a good man—except that he is a Christian”; and in the same place: “I am astonished that Lucius, a wise man, has suddenly become a Christian.”

Those enslaved to the darkness of the Gentiles could not endure this; hence even the indignation of Tacitus, *Annals* XV.44: “Repressed for the moment”—that is, by the execution of Christ, killed by Pontius Pilate—“the deadly superstition broke out again, not only throughout Judaea, the source of that evil, but even throughout the city, where everything atrocious or shameful flows together from every quarter and is celebrated.” He is speaking of Nero’s time.

Pliny, *Letters* X.97: “For many of every age, every rank, and both sexes are being summoned into danger and will continue to be summoned. For the contagion of this superstition has spread not only through the cities, but even through villages and rural districts.”

Hence that bitter passage of Rutilius, who flourished in the time of Honorius, *Itinerary*, verse 395:

> And would that Judaea had never been subdued  
> By Pompey’s wars and Titus’ sovereign power!  
> The contagion of the slaughtered people spreads more freely,  
> And the conquered nation weighs upon its conquerors.

[Col. 0262B] For those who were ignorant of both religions confused Jews and Christians. Hence Dio says, in his account of Domitian, that Domitian punished his own relatives Clement and Domitilla—the former with death, the latter with deportation to the island of Pandataria—because they had “εἰς τὰ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἤθη ἐξοκέλλοντας,” that is, lapsed into the rites of the Jews; but in fact they were Christians. The same author reports that Nerva, the tyrant’s successor, forbade anyone thereafter to be accused “οὒτε ἀσεβείας οὒτε ἰουδαικοῦ καταιτιᾶσθαι,” that is, either of contempt for the gods or of observing Jewish rites.

Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II: “At that time Hadrian, supposing that he could destroy the Christian faith by desecrating the place, set up idols in the temple and on the site of the Lord’s Passion. And because Christians were believed to be primarily Jews [Col. 0262C]—for at that time the Church at Jerusalem had no priest except one from the circumcision—he ordered a cohort of soldiers to maintain a permanent guard which would bar all Jews from access to Jerusalem. This, indeed, advanced the Christian faith, because at that time almost everyone believed in Christ as God while observing the law. Doubtless this was arranged by the Lord’s ordinance, so that servitude to the law might be removed from the freedom of faith and of the Church.”

Hence perhaps Arrian also fails to distinguish them in *Discourses of Epictetus* II.9, where he censures those who assume the character of philosophers when in reality they are not. “Τί οὖν,” he says, “στοικόν λέγεις σεαυτὸν; τί ἐξαπατᾷς τοὺς πολλοὺς; τί ὑποκρίνῃ, ἰουδαῖος ὦν, ἕλληνας; οὐχ ὁρᾷς, πῶς ἕκαστος λέγεται ἰουδαῖος; πῶς σύρος; πῶς αἰγύπτιος; καὶ ὄταν τινὰ ἐπαμφοτερίζοντα ἴδωμεν, εἰώθαμεν λέγειν· Οὐκ ἔστιν ἰουδαῖος, ἀλλ` ὑποκρίνεται, ὃταν δὲ ἀναλαβῃ τὸ πάθος, τὸ τοῦ βεβαμμένου, τότε καὶ ἐστι τῶ ὂντι, καὶ καλεῖται ἰουδαίος”; that is: “Why do you call yourself a Stoic? Why do you deceive and mislead so many? Why do you wish to be regarded as one of the Greeks when you are a Jew? Do you not [Col. 0262D] know why someone is regarded as a Jew, a Syrian, or an Egyptian? But when we see someone wavering between parties and equivocal in faith, we customarily say, ‘He is not a Jew, but is pretending.’ Yet when he assumes the disposition of one who has been baptized and admitted among the adherents, then he both truly is and is called a Jew.”

Nevertheless, Jewish proselytes were not unknown to him, as appears from that frenzy which Christ attributes to the Pharisees in Matthew XXIII.15. He employs the elegant word “ἐπαμφοτερὶζειν,” which denotes inclining so much toward each of two sides that one cannot tell to which the subject belongs. Aristotle, *On the Soul* II.8: “ἔνια δέ τῶν ζὼων ἐπαμφοτερίζει τὴν φύσιν, τῷ τε ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ τοῖς τετράποσιν, οἳον πίθηκοι”; that is: “There are creatures of an equivocal nature which imitate partly the human being and partly the quadruped, such as apes.” And again, IV.10: “ὁ δὲ πίθηκος, διά τον τὴν μορφὴν ἐπαμφοτερίζειν, καὶ μηδετέρων τ` εἶναι καὶ ἀμφοτέρων, διά τοῦτο οὒτε οὐρὰν ἔχει, οὒτε ἰσχία”; that is: “The ape, because its status between bipeds and quadrupeds is disputed, [Col. 0263A] at least with respect to form, has neither a tail nor buttocks: for as a biped it lacks a tail, and as a quadruped it lacks buttocks.”

Ausonius expressed this prettily in *Epigram* 105, about a beautiful boy:

> While Nature doubted whether to make a male or a girl,  
> A boy was made so beautiful that he was almost a girl.

And Horace, *Odes* II.5, verse 21, on the similar subject of Gyges of Cnidus:

> If you placed him within a choir of girls,  
> He would marvellously deceive discerning strangers;  
> The distinction would be obscure, with his flowing  
> Hair and ambiguous countenance.

[Col. 0263B] But to return to the point from which I digressed: beyond doubt the following fragment of Seneca, preserved for us by Augustine in *The City of God* VI.11, speaks of Christians. Speaking of those very Jews, he says: “Meanwhile, the custom of this most criminal nation has gained such strength that it has now been received throughout every land. The conquered have given laws to their conquerors.” Behold the man whom they imagine to have exchanged letters with Paul!

I have cited this passage all the more willingly so that I might correct what follows there. “They nevertheless,” Augustine says in Seneca’s words, “knew the reasons for their own rite; the greater part of the people does what it does without knowing why.” So the best manuscripts written in Lombard letters read—I possess a collation of them—and not “and the greater part,” as is everywhere printed. For although Seneca, in that work of his—such as it was—which has now perished, condemns this superstition as hateful to him, he nevertheless admits that they knew the reason for their rite, while the greater part of the Roman people, whose folly and sloth he censured in that same place, did not know why it did what it did.

And indeed, [Col. 0263C] besides the authority of the manuscripts, the preceding words in Augustine prove this: “He plainly added a statement signifying what he thought of the rationale of their sacred rites. For he says, ‘They nevertheless,’” etc. A passage in Suetonius, *Domitian* XII, also supports this: “Besides all others, the Jewish tax was administered with the greatest severity. Those were reported to it who lived a Jewish life within the city as though they had professed it, or who, concealing their origin, had not paid the tribute imposed upon that nation. I remember that, when I was a young man, a ninety-year-old man was examined by a procurator before a very crowded council to determine whether he was circumcised.” You see that the distinguishing mark of circumcision was necessary in order to identify them.

Indeed, Aelius Spartianus makes so little distinction between these sects that, at the beginning of the *Life of Caracalla*, he writes of him: “When he was seven years old, having heard that a boy who was his playmate had been severely beaten because of the Jewish religion, for a long time he would not look upon either his own father, the boy’s father, or those responsible for the beating.”

Hence also Lampridius writes of the emperor Alexander Severus: “He frequently proclaimed what he had heard from certain persons, whether Jews or Christians, and retained in his memory; and whenever he corrected someone, he ordered it to be announced by a herald: ‘Do not do to another what you do not wish to be done to you.’” He relates that this same emperor wished to enroll Christ among the gods and build him a temple, but was prevented by those who, after consulting the sacred rites, had discovered that, if this came about as desired, everyone would become Christian and the remaining temples would have to be abandoned. On the multitude of Christians, see also our Author below, chapter XXXVII, and the notes there. HAV.]—

in the countryside, in fortresses, and on islands; they cry that people of every sex, [Col. 0263A] age, station, and even rank [Note: [Col. 0263D] “And now rank.” Rigaltius and the Leiden manuscript rightly read thus. Others have “even.” The Fulda manuscript reads otherwise. Xiphilinus, in his epitome of Dio, on Domitian’s cruelty: “Καὶ τῷ αὐτῷ ἔτει ἄλλους τε πολλοὺς, καὶ τὸν Φάβιον Κλήμεντα, ὐπατεύοντα, καίπερ ἀνεψιον ὄντα, καὶ γυναῖκα καὶ αὐτὴν συγγένη ἑαυτοῦ Φαβίαν Δομιτίλλαν ἔχοντα κατέσφαξεν ὁ Δομιτίανος, ἐπηνέχθη δὲ ἀμφοῖν ἔγκλημα ἀθεότητος, ὑφ` ἧς καὶ ἄλλοι ἐς τὰ τῶν ἰουδαίων ἤθη ἐξοκέλλοντες πολλοὶ κατεδικάσθησαν. Ἡ δὲ Δομιτίλλα ὑπερωρίσθη μόνον εἰς Πανδατερίαν”; that is: “In the same year Domitian put to death many others, but especially the consul Flavius Clement [although he was his cousin and had married Flavia Domitilla, a kinswoman of Domitian], bringing against them both a charge of atheism [for this was the name given to the Christian religion, which mocked the gods]. For this reason many who had adopted Jewish customs were condemned: some were killed, some stripped of their property; Domitilla alone was banished to Pandataria.”

Observe here also that Jews and Christians are confused, and restore “φλὰβιον” in place of “φὰβιον,” as Suetonius expressly says in *Domitian* XV; for otherwise he could not have been the emperor’s cousin unless he belonged to the Flavian rather than the Fabian family. His wife appears to have acquired this name [Col. 0264B] in honor of Domitian’s mother, who was so called; her namesake daughter died prematurely.

Xiphilinus adds in the same place that the distinguished Glabrio died on the same charge: “Τὸν δὲ δὴ Γλαβρίωνα τὸν μετὰ τοῦ Τραιάνου ἄρξαντα, κατηγορηθέντα τά τε ἄλλα καὶ οἷα οἱ πολλοὶ, καὶ ὃτι καὶ θηρίοις ἐμάχετο ἀπέκτεινεν”; that is: “He also ordered Glabrio, who had held office with Trajan, to be killed, being accused—besides other matters—of the foregoing charge and also of having fought with wild beasts.” For Domitian had exposed him to a most ferocious lion, which he killed by God’s aid and his own courage.

Also remarkable is the inscription found in the cemetery of St. Agnes on the Via Nomentana, as reported by Aringhi, *Subterranean Rome* III.22, p. 340:

> THUS DO YOU PRESERVE REWARDS, VESPASIAN! O SAVAGE CITY, WHERE THE AUTHOR OF YOUR GLORY WAS REWARDED WITH DEATH. REJOICE, GAUDENTIUS: CHRIST, WHO PREPARED ANOTHER THEATER FOR YOU IN HEAVEN, HAS PROMISED AND GIVES YOU ALL THINGS.

[Col. 0264C] Aringhi refers it to Domitian, who had entrusted the architect Gaudentius with the construction of a theater and had promised to grant him, among other things, citizenship; but when the work was finished and Gaudentius was denounced to the emperor as a Christian, Aringhi thinks that he received martyrdom as his reward.

Reinesius attacks this conjecture in *Inscriptions*, p. 955, reading “VE. PASIANI. DIRE. CIVILITAS. UBI.” and treating it as an interjection of menace and detestation; and he refers it to Antoninus Bassianus Caracalla, the author of the sixth persecution. He also denies that Domitian was ever distinguished by the name Vespasian—something nevertheless proved by ancient bronze monuments cited by Hermolaus Barbarus on Pliny’s *Preface*, on which is written:

> IMP. CAES. DOMITIANUS VESP. AUG. GERM. JOVI VICTORI.

Hence it is doubtful to whom that name ought to be referred on the extremely rare large bronze coin in Patin’s *Thesaurus*, p. 148, which bears on one side the structure of a most magnificent amphitheater and on the other a figure seated upon spoils, with an olive branch and this inscription:

> DIVO AUG. DIVI VESP. F. VESPASIAN.

It may be referred to Titus, with *Vespasiano* understood, or to Domitian, who may have dedicated it to his brother’s memory; although I think it belongs rather to the former, since otherwise the emperor’s name is not expressed.

Whichever emperor the words should be assigned to, the building of a theater is certainly understood rather obscurely from the words “AUTHOR OF YOUR GLORY,” in contrast with the theater in heaven. But if you refer it to Domitian, I would prefer to read in the second line: “CIVILITY, WHERE THE AUTHOR OF YOUR GLORY …” For Suetonius says of him in chapter XVIII: “He was so conscious that his modest facial expression commended him that he once boasted in the Senate: ‘Until now, at least, you have approved both my disposition and my countenance.’”

The word “ANOTHER” also troubles me in the final line; it was perhaps wrongly transcribed for *AGION*, that is, “of the saints.” HAV.]—

are going over to this name, as though grieving over some loss. Yet even this fact [Col. 0264A] does not stir their minds to consider some hidden [Note: [Col. 0263A] “Hidden,” Paris.] good; they are not permitted to form a more reasonable suspicion, [Col. 0265A] nor do they desire [Note: [Col. 0265A] “They desire,” Paris; “they are permitted … they desire,” Rigaltius.] to examine it more closely. [Note: [Col. 0264D] “Yet even this,” etc. So many and such people passing over to that sect provide a powerful spur to inquiry. [Col. 0265B] Therefore the guilt of their ignorance is increased, because they are not moved by these examples to investigate more deeply. For men who are thought wise, and who possess good things which they stand to lose, would not pass over so suddenly, as the common crowd does—whose ears and eyes are often witnesses to evil, as Publilius says—unless some previously hidden and unknown good had presented itself to them. Below, in the final chapter: “That very obstinacy which you reproach us with is a teacher. For who, by contemplating it, is not shaken into investigating what lies within the matter? Who does not join us once he has inquired? Who, once he has joined us, does not long to suffer?”]

Only here does human [Note: [Col. 0265A] Rhenanus: “Only here does urbane curiosity”; others: “Thus urbane curiosity.”] curiosity grow numb. They love to remain ignorant, though others rejoice to have gained knowledge. How much more would Anacharsis have stigmatized these men as the unwise judging the wise than as the unmusical judging musicians! [Note: [Col. 0265A] “Non-musicians,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0265B] Anacharsis. Laertius in his *Life*: “Θαυμάζειν δὲ ἔφη πῶς τοῖς ἕλλησιν ἀγωνίζονται μὲν οἱ τεχνίται, καὶ κρίνουσι δὲ οἱ μὴ τεχνίται,” that is, in Rhenanus’ translation: “He said that he wondered how, among the Greeks, artisans competed but those who were not artisans judged them.” PAM.]

They prefer not to know [Note: [Col. 0265C] “They prefer not to know.” He explains why the example of others and human curiosity do not advance any farther in them: because they prefer not to know, etc. Minucius, p. 31: “Thus people begin to hate before they know, lest, once they know, they should either be able to imitate us or be unable to condemn us.” Seneca’s remark in *Letter* XXIX, concerning a certain Marcellinus, also applies: “He rarely comes to us, for no reason other than that he fears to hear the truth. But he is now free from that danger; for nothing should be said except to one willing to hear it.” HAV.], because they already hate. Thus they prejudge what they do not know to be such that, if they knew it, they could not hate it. [Note: [Col. 0265A] “For prejudging,” Rigaltius.] [Note: [Col. 0265A] “Will not be able,” Junius.] For if no debt of hatred is discovered, the best course will surely be to cease [Col. 0266A] hating unjustly; but if its guilt is established, not only will nothing be subtracted from the hatred, [Note: [Col. 0265C] “Be subtracted from the hatred.” The Fulda manuscript reads “be subtracted from hatred.” The argument closely resembles that used by Prometheus before Jupiter in Lucian when he seeks release from his chains and freedom from the Caucasus: “Οὐ γὰρ ἀγνοήσεις αὖθις ἔνθα ὁ Καύκασος ἕστιν, οὐδ` ἀπορήσεις δεσμῶν ἤν τι τεχνάζων ἀλισκωμαι”; that is: “For you are not ignorant where the Caucasus is, and you will have no need of chains if I am caught somehow practicing my tricks.” And the fictitious robber in Apuleius’ *The Golden Ass* VII says: “Especially if this opinion of mine displeases you, you may return to the ass again.” The sense is that the Christians’ cause certainly ought to be examined. If it is innocent, they may nevertheless hate it if they wish, although the man in Curtius VI.10 says that one ought not to plot against those who deserve well; but if the examination of the charge turns out otherwise, there is just cause for hatred, since it then rests upon the authority of justice. The same Curtius, VI.11, at the end: “Thus the inquiry was uncertain: while he denied the deed, he seemed to be tortured cruelly; after his confession, Philotas did not deserve the pity even of his friends.” HAV.] but more will be acquired to sustain it, even by the authority of justice itself.

“But it is not therefore good,” someone says, [Note: [Col. 0266A] “They say,” Junius.] “because it converts many.” [Note: [Col. 0265D] “Because it converts many.” Above, the Author had turned this consideration to his own advantage—that so many of every kind, sex, and locality were passing over to the Christians. But since, according to that saying of Publilius, verse 148,

> The crowd is always evidence of the worst,

he answers this objection splendidly in what follows by appealing to the virtue of Christians. He had also said before that not only people of every sex, but even persons of rank, passed over to this name; here too the same Publilius, verse 489, readily shows the path of defense:

> Strive not to please many, but to please people of worth.

HAV.]

For how many are predisposed [Note: [Col. 0265D] “Are predisposed to evil.” The editions of Barraeus and Pamelius have “are predisposed,” as though he were referring to those whom Cebes says drink more deeply from the cup of Error and Ignorance offered by Deceit and so are predisposed to evil, while those whom Tertullian calls deserters are those who are dragged sideways from the straight path by Opinions, Pleasures, and so forth. But Cebes himself deserves to have his words recorded. “Ὁρᾷς,” says the interpreter of the tablet there, “παρὰ τὴν πύλην θρόνον τοῦτον, καθ` ὃν εἰσπορέυεται ὁ ὂχλος, ἐφ` οὗ κάθηται γυνή πεπλασμένη τῷ ἤθει, καὶ πιθανὴ φαινομένη, καὶ ἐν τῇ χειρὶ ἔχουσα ποτὴριόν τι; Ὁρῶ. Ἀλλὰ τίς ἐστιν αὐτὴ, ἔφην. Ἀπάτη καλεῖται, φησὶν, ἡ πάντας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους πλανῶσα. Εἶτα τί πράττει αὐτὴ; Τοὺς εἰσπορευομένους εἰς τὸν βίον ποτίζει τῇ ἑαατῆς δυνάμει. Τοῦτο δὲ τί ἐστι τὸ ποτόν; Πλάτη, ἔφην, καὶ Ἄγνοια. Εἶτα τί; Πιόντες τοῦτο, πορεύονται εἰς τὸν βίον. Πότερον οὖν πάντες πίνουσι τὸν πλάνον, ἢ οὒ; Πάντες πίνουσιν ἔφην. ἀλλ` οἱ μὲν πλεῖον, οἱ δὲ ἧττον. Ἔπι δὲ οὐχ` ὁρᾷς ἔνδον τῆς πύλης πλῆθός τι γυναικῶν, ἐταιρῶν παντοδαπὰς μορφὰς ἐχουσῶν;. Ὁρῶ [Col. 0266C] Αὐταὶ τοίνυν, Δόξαι καὶ Ἐπιθυμίᾳ, καὶ Ἡδοναὶ καλοῦνται. Ὃταν οὖν εἰσπορεύεται ὁ ὄχλος, ἀναπηδῶσιν αὐτὰ, καὶ πλέκονται πρὸς ἕκαστον, εἶτα ἀπάγουσι. Ποῦ δὲ ἀπὰγουσιν αὐτοὺς; Αἱ μὲν εἰς τὸ σώζεσθαι, ἒφη, αἱ δὲ εἰς τὸ ἀπόλλυσθαι διὰ τὴν Ἀπὰτην”; that is:

“‘Do you see,’ he says, ‘beside the gate through which the crowd enters, a throne upon which a woman sits, with a counterfeit face and a cunning appearance, holding a certain cup in her hand?’

“‘I see her,’ I said, ‘but who is she?’

“‘Deceit,’ he said, ‘who leads all people astray.’

“‘And what does she do?’

“‘She gives those entering life a draught of her power.’

“‘And what is that drink?’

“‘Error,’ he said, ‘and ignorance.’

“‘What then?’

“‘After drinking it, they enter life.’

“‘Does everyone, then, drink Error?’

“‘Everyone drinks,’ he said, ‘but some more and some less. Besides, do you not see within the gate a certain crowd of women furnished with the various forms of prostitutes?’

“‘I see them.’

“‘These, then, are called Opinions, Desires, and Pleasures. As the crowd enters, they rush forward, embrace each person, and lead them away.’

“‘But where do they lead them?’

“‘Some lead them to salvation,’ he says, ‘and others, through deceit, to destruction.’”

[Col. 0266D] It continues there: “Οἱ δὲ διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν, καὶ τὸν πλὰνον, ὅν πεπώκασι παρὰ τῆς Ἀπάτης, οὐχ εὑρίσκουσι ποία ἐστιν ἡ ἀληθινὴ ὁδὸς ἡ ἐν τῷ βίῳ, ἀλλὰ πλανῶνται”; that is: “Because of the ignorance and error which they drank from Deceit, they do not find the true path of life, but wander rashly.”

The ancient sages often had this tablet in view, so much so that it appears not to have been unknown to the apostle Paul, both in other passages and in Ephesians IV.22: “Τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν φθειρόμενον διὰ τὰς Ἐπιθυμίας τῆς Ἀπάτης.” Hence Lucretius, II.9:

> From there you may look down upon others and see them everywhere  
> Wandering and straying as they seek the path of life.

How greatly this reading, “are predisposed,” would enrich the sense in our Tertullian: not only are many drawn away by Opinions and so forth from the good path upon which they had entered, but most, having drunk too deeply from Deceit’s cup, wander from the path from its very beginning. HAV.] to evil, and how many desert to the opposite side? [Note: [Col. 0266A] Rhenanus, Heraldus, Rigaltius, and Havercamp, from the Puteanus, Bongarsianus, and Lyons manuscripts, read “are shaped”; the Fulda manuscript, “are reshaped”; Pamelius and Barraeus, “are predisposed.”] Who denies it? [Note: [Col. 0266A] Wouwer prefers to write from a manuscript: “Who nevertheless denies that what is truly evil … those whom it seizes dare defend?”] Yet not even those whom genuine evil seizes dare to defend it as good.

Nature has suffused every evil with either fear or shame. [Note: [Col. 0266D] “Nature has suffused.” The Leiden manuscript reads “suffuses.” [Col. 0267A] The use of this word, transferred from liquids, is elegant; in it, as often, he followed that most idiomatic Latin author Lucretius. The latter, IV.80:

> All these things, the more they are inwardly suffused with charm,  
> Smile brightly, seized by the light of day.

The same author, describing the power of death in that book, verse 921:

> For the body would lie  
> Suffused with the eternal cold of death.

Because the mind is thus disturbed by passions, it often displays outwardly what kind of monster it nourishes within. Sallust, concerning Bocchus, king of Mauretania, while he was hesitating whether to hand Sulla over to Jugurtha or Jugurtha to Sulla, chapter CXIII: “The Moor, having summoned his friends and then immediately changed his mind and dismissed the rest, is said to have debated much with himself, variable alike in bodily countenance and in mind—his face, though he himself was silent, plainly revealing what was hidden.” Read “of the breast,” from the manuscript of my former teacher Petrus Francius. HAV.]

In short, criminals are eager to remain hidden; [Note: [Col. 0267B] “Are eager to remain hidden.” Horace beautifully describes their prayers, *Epistles* I.16.60:

> Fair Laverna,  
> Grant me the power to deceive; grant me to appear just and holy;  
> Cast night over my sins, and a cloud over my frauds.

The impious poet Lucretius has pious verses against the wicked, V.1153:

> Nor is it easy for one to lead a tranquil and peaceful life  
> Who violates by his deeds the common covenants of peace.  
> For though he deceives the race of gods and humankind,  
> He must nevertheless distrust that it will remain secret forever.

Hence Cicero’s wholesome counsel: “We ought to be fully persuaded that, even if we could conceal ourselves from all gods and human beings, we still must do nothing greedily, unjustly, lustfully, or without self-restraint.” HAV.] they avoid appearing, tremble when detected, deny when accused, and do not easily or always confess even under torture; [Note: [Col. 0267C] “Even under torture.” Likewise, the criminal in Apuleius, in the same place, as his cunning fully revived, did not cease most steadfastly to deny the crime and to call in falsehood as his physician. And shortly afterward, though still more clearly convicted, the wheel and rack had already been prepared for his torture after the Greek custom; but, hardened by astonishing presumption, he yielded to no scourging, not even to fire itself. Cicero, *Partitions of Oratory* L, where he argues against torture: “Others,” he says, “whether through bodily constitution, habitual endurance of pain, or fear of punishment or death, have withstood the force of tortures.” HAV.] when condemned [Col. 0268A] they certainly grieve; [Note: [Col. 0267A] “Sentenced,” Semler; “condemned,” Paris and others.] they charge against themselves [Note: [Col. 0267C] “Within themselves they count over.” That is, they recollect, inspect, and review inwardly themselves—that is, their deeds; they truly examine themselves. For *numerare* means “to review,” as Virgil testifies, *Georgics* IV:

> And he counted the gods’ numerous loves from Chaos onward.

But if you explain *dinumerant* more deeply, it may mean “they assess themselves”; for whatever is numbered and assessed possesses some value and standing. LAC.] the impulses of a guilty mind, [Note: [Col. 0268A] The Fulda manuscript: “the sloth of the mind.”] or impute them to fate [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Or to fate.” This is the first object upon which a person casts blame to remove it from himself. Once, when the Stoic Zeno was punishing a slave who had been caught stealing, the slave cried out in self-defense, touching upon his master’s doctrine: “It was fated for me to steal.” Zeno replied, not without wit, “καὶ δαρῆναι”—“and to be beaten.”

For such is human nature: “We reproach fate daily,” says Seneca in that excellent *Letter* XCIII. The same author, *On Providence* V, expresses their position: “Why, nevertheless, was God so unjust in the distribution of Fate that he assigned poverty, wounds, and bitter deaths to good men?” This comes from the school of Aristotle, as Theodoret teaches us in that most beautiful little book entitled *The Cure of Greek Affections*, or *Knowledge of Evangelical Truth from Greek Philosophy*, p. 86 of Sylburg’s edition.

Add Lucian, *Dialogue* XXV. Since his discourse is rather irreligious, let Prosper of Aquitaine succeed him. His words are: “For belief in fate is empty and conceived from falsehood; but faith in predestination is fortified by the authority of many holy Scriptures. To it the evil deeds of human beings may in no way be attributed; for they came into their propensity to fall not from God’s constitution but from the transgression of the first father.” *Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls* I. And in the same work: “No Catholic denies God’s predestination; but many, including non-Christians, refute fate or necessity.”

Tertullian himself, *On the Soul* XX: “Over and above these, if there are also other ruling powers—and indeed there are—according to us there are the Lord God and his rival the Devil; according to common opinion there are Providence, Fate, Necessity, and Freedom of Choice. For the philosophers distinguish these, and we already know that they must be discussed according to the faith under their own proper heading.”

Thus, wisely and in accordance with our Author’s thought, mighty Homer has Jupiter say in *Odyssey* I.32:

> Ὦ πόποι, οἷον δή νυ Θεοὺς βροτοὶ αἰτιοωνται.  
> Ἐξ ἡμῶν γάρ φασι κάκ. ἔμμεναι· οἱ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ


Σφῇσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὑπὲρ μόρον ἂλγέ ἔχουσιν.
>
> Alas! How unjustly mortals now blame the Deity!  
> They say that evils come from us; but they themselves,  
> Through their own wickedness, produce evils beyond Fate.

HAV.] or to the stars. [Note: [Col. 0268B] “Or to the stars.” He refers to the empty opinion of those who believed that the prosperous and adverse events of their lives depended upon the stars. This art was commonly called genethlialogy. There still survives a very ancient poem on it by the Egyptian Manetho, whose *Apotelesmatics* my teacher, that great man Jacobus Gronovius, was the first to bring to light and rescue from destruction. Much on this subject may also be read throughout Manilius, Fulgentius, and others.

Christians, who had been taught better, rightly regarded this as ridiculous, and their writings everywhere assail this most empty opinion. Our author, *On Idolatry* IX: “We need not even speak of astrologers. But because someone has challenged us on the subject in these days, defending his perseverance in that profession, I shall say a few words. I do not allege that he honors idols, whose names he has inscribed upon heaven and to whom he has assigned all God’s power; or that people consequently suppose there is no need to seek God, presuming that we are driven by the unchangeable judgment of the stars,” etc. In the same place he says, following Suetonius, that astrologers had once been expelled from the city and from Italy.

Valerius Maximus I.4: “When Marcus Popillius Laenas and Gnaeus Calpurnius were consuls, Gaius Cornelius Hispallus, praetor for foreigners, ordered by edict that the Chaldaeans depart from the city and from Italy within ten days, because by their deceitful interpretation of the stars they cast a profitable fog over frivolous and foolish minds through their falsehoods.”

I have thought it proper to record the verses of that outstanding ancient theologian Prosper of Aquitaine concerning this vanity. They come from the golden poem *On the Providence of God*:

> But where does your headlong course carry you? Do you wish to be good  
> Without labor of your own? Do you believe that this can happen  
> If the stars of your birth are changed—the stars whose course,  
> You say, drives you to wickedness? Why seek vain refuges  
> For ancient error in the Chaldaeans’ stars?  
> Although with anxious care you approach the heavenly things  
> And search deeply into the revealed causes of things,  
> One does not refuse to know God more fully [the syntax of the supplied Latin is uncertain]: what nature  
> He gave to each element, by what law  
> He commanded the sea to move, what power he sowed in the tender breezes,  
> And for what motions he created the starry fires.  
> Since he is the pure source of justice and goodness,  
> Did he prescribe a pitiless law with unjust commands,  
> If he had first bound human conduct to the stars?  
> For these things oppose and contradict one another utterly:  
> To demand innocent actions, to punish offenses,  
> And to call everyone to the same promises,  
> [Col. 0269A] Yet on the other hand to fasten upon those born a violent star  
> Which yields neither to human will nor power, while from above  
> Virtue and error alike lead everyone unwittingly.  
> Therefore either the fires of heaven have no authority over us,  
> Or, if they possess some part of us, they can lose it.

In the seventh verse, I think the sense requires *opertas*, “hidden,” to be written instead of *apertas*, “revealed.”

Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* XXXIX, *On the Holy Lights*: “Οὺδὲ μὰγιον θυτιοδὴ [recovered wording uncertain and apparently corrupt],” etc.; that is: “the Magi’s power of sacrifice and foreknowledge from the cutting open of entrails; nor the astrology and observation of nativities practiced by the Chaldaeans, which turns our affairs in the same motion as the stars, although they cannot know even what they themselves are or will be.” Here the scholia of Nicetas, p. 601, should be consulted. HAV.]

They do not wish what they recognize as evil to be their own doing. But Christians are entirely different: [Note: [Col. 0269B] Pamelius, Semler, and others: “But what likeness has a Christian?” Rhenanus in his first edition: “What likeness among Christians?” The Lyons manuscript B: “What likeness of Christians?” But Havercamp rightly determined that the reading of the Fulda manuscript should be restored; nor does what follows conflict with it.] no one is ashamed, [Note: [Col. 0269C] “No one is ashamed.” Pliny in that most celebrated letter: “I asked them whether they were Christians. Those who confessed I questioned a second and third time, threatening punishment; those who persisted I ordered to be led away. For I did not doubt that, whatever the nature of what they confessed, their stubbornness and inflexible obstinacy certainly deserved punishment.”

Our Tertullian displays this constancy of spirit still more strongly in *To Scapula* I: “We neither shrink from nor dread the things we suffer from the ignorant, since we have entered this sect under the accepted condition of its covenant: that, having pledged even our lives, we enter these contests, desiring to obtain what God promises and fearing to suffer what he threatens against a contrary life. In short, we contend against all your savagery, even bursting forward of our own accord; and we rejoice more when condemned than when acquitted.” HAV.] no one repents, except plainly that he was not one earlier. [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Except plainly that he was not one earlier.” They are so far from grieving altogether that they grieve only because they were not made such people sooner and long ago. Thus Lucretius used *de plano* for “certainly” or “altogether,” I.412:

> This I can promise you with certainty, Memmius.

HAV.]

If he is publicly marked out, he glories; if accused, he does not defend himself; when questioned, [Note: [Col. 0269B] “Is questioned,” Paris.] he confesses, even of his own accord; when condemned, he gives thanks. What kind of evil is this [Note: [Col. 0270B] “What this evil is,” manuscript Ago b Lugd.] which does not possess the natural characteristics [Note: [Col. 0269D] “The natural characteristics of evil.” Thus the Fulda manuscript and Pamelius, followed by Junius and Rigaltius. Other manuscripts, Barr., and Rhenanus have “the nature of evil,” a reading Scriverius prefers, but I do not. For our author used the singular *naturale* in this way in *On the Soul* XLI: “The soul’s evil, apart from what is built upon it by the arrival of an evil spirit, precedes from the defect of its origin and is in a certain sense natural. For, as we have said, the corruption of nature is another nature, having its own god and father—namely, the author of corruption himself; yet good also remains within the soul, that original, divine, genuine, [Col. 0270B] and properly natural element.” The Leiden manuscript reads: “another nature of evil.” HAV.] of evil— [Note: [Col. 0270B] “The nature of evil,” Rhenanus, Semler, Leopold.] fear, shame, evasion, repentance, and lamentation? What kind of evil is this [Note: [Col. 0270B] Others: “What this evil is.”], whose culprit rejoices, whose accusation is his desire, and whose punishment is happiness? [Note: [Col. 0270B] The Fulda manuscript: “whose punishment is victory.”] You cannot call it madness when you are proved ignorant.

## CHAPTER II.

Now, if they wished to treat Christians as criminals, they ought at least to have proceeded in court in the same manner with both groups, and not to have denied them the opportunity of defending themselves by any means whatever, [Col. 0269B] since a charge is ordinarily either disproved or [Col. 0270A] established from the circumstances. Indeed, the innocence of this sect is shown even by the fact that Trajan formerly forbade Christians to be sought out, although he wished those who were brought forward to be condemned. Tertullian ridicules this judgment as self-contradictory and proceeds both to demolish it and to rebuke the perverse conduct of the judges and correct their treatment of Christians, while at the same time investigating the cause of this evil which makes them fight against the bare name of Christians.

Finally, if it is certain that we are the most guilty of criminals, why are we treated by you yourselves differently from our peers, that is, from other criminals, when the same treatment ought to be applied to the same offense [Note: [Col. 0270B] “Guiltiness,” Rigault, Havercamp.]? Whatever we are said to be [Note: [Col. 0270B] “We say,” Paris manuscript.], when others are said to be the same [Note: [Col. 0270B] “When others are said to be the same.” The sense is: when other defendants are accused of the crime laid against us, whatever that crime may be, they are allowed to use their own voice, etc. HAV.], they employ both their own voice and hired advocacy [Note: [Col. 0270B] “And they employ hired advocacy.” Barraeus reads “hired advocates.” Cicero, *Letters* VII.2: “I would have given this advice, that they should request two advocacies from each interrex.” See Seneca in the preface to the *Controversiae* and in the *Play on the [Col. 0270C] Death of Claudius*. The Fulda manuscript reads: “both their own and a hired voice, and they employ advocacy.” For *advocatio* is what is now called consultation. Cicero to Trebatius, *Letters* VII.13: “In military affairs he is much more cautious than in consultations”; and *Against Verres* III.12: “There the senate is very frequently summoned; there consultations on the greatest matters are held daily.” Thus defendants have a threefold protection: either in their own eloquence—for, as Publilius, maxim 71, says:

> He who speaks for the innocent is eloquent enough.

Suetonius, on Claudius’s censorship, chapter XVI: “Nor did he allow anyone to give an account of his life except in his own voice, however well each man could, and without an advocate.” Diogenes Laertius relates of Aristippus that, when he was reproached for having hired an orator in his own case, he replied that he was also accustomed to hire a cook when he gave a dinner; or in the hired tongue of an advocate, whose

> eloquence sends forth a voice to defend  
> [Col. 0270D] sorrowful defendants,

as the author of the panegyric to Piso says—neither Ovid nor Lucan, but some other not inept poet, as I shall show elsewhere; or, finally, in advocacy, when a defendant is furnished with arguments by which to defend his case. Such a hired advocate was Tertullus in Acts XXIV.1, while Paul defended himself in his own voice. HAV.] to commend their innocence. The opportunity of answering and disputing [Col. 0270B] [Note: [Col. 0270D] “Of answering and disputing.” This nearly always obtained in Roman trials, and, as the ancients attest, Marcus Tullius Cicero was a marvelous craftsman of biting wit in such disputations. Apuleius likewise joined these things together in Book X of *The Golden Ass*: “But with what words the accuser proceeded, by what arguments the defendant refuted him, and, in short, their speeches and disputations, I myself, being absent at the manger, could neither know nor relate to you what I did not know.” No one describes it better than Quintilian himself, who treats this art expressly in *Institutes of Oratory* VI.5: “Nothing different is said in disputation from what is said in the speech itself, but it is said differently, either by questioning or by answering.” [Col. 0271B] And a little later: “Thus, in those cases—and they are the most frequent—which depend either solely on proofs external to the art or on mixed proofs, the contest is fiercest in this part, and nowhere else could one say that men fight more at sword-point. For all the strongest points must be impressed upon the judge’s memory; whatever we promised in our pleading must be fulfilled; and falsehoods must be repelled. Nowhere, finally, is the examiner more attentive. Nor was it without reason that certain men, although mediocre in speaking, nevertheless earned the name of advocates by their excellence in disputation.” In the same place he shows that this does not belong to everyone: “What is needed, therefore, above all is a quick and flexible talent, and a mind alert and keen. For one must not deliberate but speak immediately, and almost while the opponent is making his attempt one must raise one’s hand.” Rudolph Agricola, a careful vindicator of all secular learning, once boasted in *On Dialectical Invention* III.15 and II.12 that he possessed one book of Marcus Fabius’s *Disputations*. Peter Pithoeus suspected his reliability on this point. Yet, if such a work really existed—[Col. 0271C] for today, so far as I know, it is nowhere to be found—it was of the kind of Seneca’s *Controversiae*, and perhaps the same work; or a little book of the declamations still attributed to Quintilian today may have borne that title. HAV.] lies open to them, since it is not even lawful for persons wholly undefended [Col. 0271A] and unheard to be condemned [Note: [Col. 0271C] “Since it is not even lawful,” etc. In Livy, Titus Quinctius cries out that a man accused on a capital charge ought not to be harmed without condemnation and without his case being heard. Yet Christians were treated in that way. See chapter XXXI. “For you allow us to prove whatever we defend.” Ironically. HAV.].

But Christians alone are permitted to say nothing that might clear their case, defend the truth, or prevent the judge from becoming unjust [Note: [Col. 0271C] “Prevent the judge from becoming unjust.” Elegantly expressed; thus above, chapter I: “Moreover, if they condemn us unheard, besides the odium of injustice they will also incur the suspicion of some guilty consciousness, since they refuse to hear what, once heard, they could not condemn.” Alexander in Curtius VII.2: “If I had not investigated the allegations, my dissimulation might have appeared highly suspicious.” Likewise:

> The judge who crushes an innocent man condemns himself.

[Col. 0271D] Publilius, maxim 602. HAV.]. The only thing expected [Note: [Col. 0271A] Avercamp corrects this to “observed.”] [Note: [Col. 0271D] “Expected.” For a better sense, I think, read “observed.” A similar error beset the manuscripts of Augustine, *City of God* VI.10: “A learned leading mime, now an aged and decrepit man, acted a mime daily on the Capitol, as though the gods gladly expected the man whom those people had mocked.” There I read: “as though the gods gladly watched the man whom perhaps those men had once,” etc. But even so the passage is unsound. Therefore read the end from a collation of an excellent Fulda Library manuscript, written in Lombard letters, which is in my possession: “whom men had ceased to watch for them,” for he was now decrepit. This is the truest reading. In Virgil II.102 Sinon says:

> If you hold all the Greeks in one rank,

“and it is enough to hear that.” Tertullian means that the judges take care not that the laws should be observed, but that the mad [Col. 0272B] and senseless populace should not be provoked. Hence at the beginning of this *Apology*: “If it is not lawful for you, governors”—for the hatred against Christians was public. Indeed, I seem to see here judges like Pontius Pilate, as you will acknowledge if you compare John XIX.12. HAV.] is what public hatred requires: confession of the name, not examination of the crime. For when you investigate any criminal, you are not content to pronounce judgment the moment he has confessed the name “murderer,” “sacrilegious person,” “incestuous person,” or “public enemy”—to speak in terms of our indictments [Note: [Col. 0271A] Semler reads “another.”] [Note: [Col. 0271A] Semler and others read “your.”] [Note: [Col. 0271A] Paris manuscript: “from our selections.”] [Note: [Col. 0272B] “Our indictments.” The same editors correctly read “our,” not “your,” for these were the indictments of Christians, as will be sufficiently clear from what follows. Tertullian often delights in repeating this word in the sense it bore in judicial affairs. It was customary to append to the names of condemned persons a brief written statement or title showing the particular crime of which they were guilty.
