This appears most clearly from Suetonius, *Caligula* 27: “Reviewing the line of prisoners, without inspecting anyone’s indictment, he stood only in the middle of the colonnade and ordered them to be led away, from one bald man to the next.” And in a striking passage in Vulcacius Gallicanus’s *Life of Avidius Cassius*: “You see that many swords and many indictments are needed if the public order is to be restored to its ancient condition.” Spartianus speaks especially well concerning Severus: “During this legateship, when a certain Leptitanus, one of his fellow townsmen, himself a commoner, embraced him as an old tent-companion while the fasces went before him, he had the man beaten with rods under an indictment proclaimed by the same herald: ‘Commoner, do not rashly embrace a legate of the Roman people.’” Hence our author must be understood in this sense when he writes in *To Scapula* IV: “Pudens also released a Christian sent before him, when he perceived from the indictment that the man had been shaken down; he tore up the same indictment and refused to hear the man without an accuser.” And in *The Soldier’s Crown* V: “Everything contrary to nature deserves among all people the mark of monstrosity, but among us also an indictment for sacrilege against God, the Lord and author of nature”; and in *On the Soul* XVII: “Indeed, an indictment for deception ought no longer to be assigned even to the causes themselves.” HAV.]—unless you also demand the attendant particulars: the nature of the deed, its number, place [Note: [Col. 0272A] “Number” is absent from the Paris manuscript and Rigault.], manner, time, accomplices, and associates.

Nothing of this kind is done concerning us, although everything falsely bandied about ought equally to be extorted from us: how many infanticides each man had already tasted; how many incestuous acts he had hidden beneath the darkness [Note: [Col. 0272A] Rhenanus in his first edition and Gelenius read “celebrated together.”]; which cooks and which dogs had been present. Oh, how great would be the glory of that governor if he had unearthed [Note: [Col. 0272A] Paris manuscript: “found.”] someone who had already eaten a hundred infants!

And yet we find that even an inquiry into us has been forbidden. For Pliny the Younger [Note: [Col. 0272C] “For Pliny the Younger.” The nephew, through his sister, of that great investigator of nature, now sufficiently well known to all; his ten polished and elegant books of letters still survive, the last of which also contains the rescripts of Caesar Trajan, together with the Panegyric addressed to Emperor Trajan, “divine,” as Scaliger called it. His Letter 97 in Book X and Trajan’s reply, Letter 91, are most worthy of reading and should be committed to memory, not merely for knowledge of ancient Christianity. Scaliger notes in his *Labors on Eusebius* that Jerome had read them in his own time. Orosius, *Histories* VII.8, on Trajan: “Deceived by error in persecuting Christians, he was the third after Nero to order that those found everywhere be compelled to sacrifice to idols and that those who refused be killed; and when very many were being killed, he was admonished by the report of Pliny the Younger, who had been appointed a persecutor among the other judges, that these people did nothing contrary to Roman laws except confess Christ and hold honorable assemblies, and that, through confidence in an innocent confession, death indeed seemed neither grievous nor terrifying to anyone. He immediately moderated his edict by milder rescripts.” Jerome’s words in his Eusebian *Chronicle*, compiled from Eusebius and Tertullian, appear [Col. 0273C] at the year of the world 2031: “When Pliny the Younger governed a certain province and in his magistracy had killed very many Christians, terrified by their multitude he asked Trajan what ought to be done, reporting that, apart from their obstinate refusal to sacrifice and their meetings before dawn to sing to a certain Christ as God, he had found nothing among them; moreover, that, to bind their discipline together, murders, thefts, adulteries, robberies, and similar acts were forbidden by them. Moved by this, Trajan wrote back that persons of this kind were indeed not to be sought out, but that those brought forward ought to be punished. Tertullian reports this in the *Apology*.” HAV.], while governing a province, after condemning some Christians and depriving others [Col. 0273A] of their rank [Note: [Col. 0273C] “Depriving others of their rank.” Namely, some of those of more honorable station who inclined toward that sect; for every condition, even high rank, passed over to this name, as he said above. Since this also happened [Col. 0273D] in the time of Severus, our Tertullian proclaims that prince’s clemency and justice in *To Scapula* IV: “But Severus, though he knew that most distinguished women and most distinguished men belonged to this sect, not only did not injure them, but even adorned them with his testimony and openly opposed the people when they raged against them.” HAV.], was nevertheless disturbed by their very multitude and then [Note: [Col. 0273B] “Then” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] consulted Emperor Trajan about what he should do thereafter. He alleged that, apart from their obstinate refusal to sacrifice, he had discovered nothing else concerning their solemn obligations [Note: [Col. 0273B] Heraldus from a manuscript, and Havercamp from the Fulda manuscript, read “solemn obligations”; Semler and others read “sacred rites.” Compare Pliny, *Letters* 10.96.] except meetings before dawn [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Meetings before dawn.” Concerning “meeting,” note that this word was customarily applied to sacred matters. Hence Meursius translates the following passage of Constantine Manasses in his annals:

> Οὗτοι καὶ γὰρ ἀθροίσαντες ἄνδρας θεοφορήτους — “For indeed these men, having gathered God-bearing men…”

as follows: “For, when these men had gathered an assembly of religious men.” Dionysius Exiguus uses this word when translating the *Life of St. Pachomius*: “He enrolled him among the assemblies of monks.” LAC.] to sing [Note: [Col. 0273D] “To sing.” A pious exercise, concerning which see also *To His Wife* II.9: “No furtive signing, no trembling thanksgiving, no silent blessing: psalms and hymns resound between the two, and they challenge each other as to who will sing better to his God.” Write *cantet* or *canat*. And he exhorts in *On Exhortation to Chastity* X: “If he makes prayer to the Lord, he is near heaven. If he applies himself to Scripture, he is wholly there. If he sings a psalm, he pleases himself.” HAV.] to Christ as [Note: [Col. 0273B] Thus the Fulda manuscript; Rhenanus reads “and Christ and God”; others: “Christ and God.”] God, and that, to bind their discipline together [Note: [Col. 0273B] Paris reads “to impart.”], they forbade murder, adultery, fraud, treachery, and all other crimes.

Trajan then wrote back that persons of this kind should indeed not be sought out, but that those brought forward ought to be punished. O judgment confounded by necessity! He forbids them to be sought out as innocent and commands them to be punished [Note: [Col. 0273B] Paris reads “to be punished.”] as guilty. He spares and rages; he overlooks and chastises. Why do you entangle yourself [Note: [Col. 0273C] Wouwer, Rigault, and Havercamp read the feminine form “yourself.”] in your own judgment? If you condemn them, why do you not also [Note: [Col. 0274B] “Also” is absent from the Frankfurt edition.] [Col. 0273B] seek them out? If you do not seek them out, why do you not also acquit them?

A military post is assigned throughout all the provinces for tracking down [Note: [Col. 0274B] Paris reads “investigating.”] brigands. In the case of persons accused of treason and public enemies, every man is a soldier; the inquiry extends even to their associates and accomplices. A Christian alone may not be sought out, but may be brought forward—as though an inquiry would accomplish anything other than his being brought forward [Note: [Col. 0274B] Semler reads “the bringing forward.”]. You therefore condemn [Col. 0274A] a man who has been brought forward, though no one wished him to be sought out; and he, I suppose, has now deserved punishment not because he is guilty, but because he was found despite not being one who should be sought out [Note: [Col. 0274B] “Was” is absent from other witnesses.].

Accordingly, you do not deal with us in accordance with the established procedure for judging criminals even in this respect: to all others who deny, you apply tortures to make them confess; to Christians alone, to make them deny. Yet if our profession were an evil, we for our part would deny, while you would compel us by torture to confess. For you would not suppose that crimes need not [Note: [Col. 0274B] Rigault reads “you would not suppose that they must be investigated.”] be investigated [Note: [Col. 0274C] “You would not suppose for this reason.” La Cerda reads as follows: “For you do not therefore suppose that crimes need not be investigated by examinations because you are certain that they are committed from the confession of the name—who today, in the case of a confessed murderer, knowing what murder is, nevertheless . . . the sequence of the act?” He adds a question mark and explains *qui* as *quomodo*, “how.” Closely related to this is a passage in *To the Nations* II.13, which I shall elucidate and emend for the benefit of jurists. The text, badly treated by the injury of time, reads: “How . . . . . when a public announcement has been made concerning a runaway, we are accustomed both to . . . his labor by inquiring . . . to advertise it for abuse.” The eminent Rigault and Gothofredus did not dare touch it. Supply it at my risk and write: “Just as, when a public announcement has been made concerning a runaway, we are accustomed, by inquiring into his labor, to advertise it for abuse.” No one who examines the passage will doubt it. For just as we jurists, he says, act far too badly by investigating and thereby teach the method [Col. 0274D] of accomplishing an escape, so too do the poets in their fables about the gods. He said above in this same chapter: “For when you investigate any criminal, you are not content to pronounce judgment the moment he has confessed the name ‘murderer,’ ‘sacrilegious person,’ ‘incestuous person,’ etc., unless you also demand the attendant particulars: the nature of the deed, place, manner,” etc. HAV.] by judicial examinations merely because you were certain from the confession of the name that they had been committed. For today, even in the case of a self-confessed murderer, although you know what murder is, you nevertheless extort the sequence of the act.

How much more perversely, then, although you presume our crimes from confession of the name [Col. 0274B] [Note: [Col. 0274B] The Latin edition reads “from confession.”], do you force us by tortures to withdraw from that confession, so that by denying the name we may of course also deny the crimes which you had presumed from confession of the name! But, I suppose, you do not wish us to perish, though you believe us to be the worst of men. For this is how you are accustomed to speak to a murderer [Note: [Col. 0274B] Frankfurt reads the plural “murderers.”]: “Deny it” [Note: [Col. 0274C] Frankfurt reads “to deny.”] [Note: [Col. 0274D] “For this is how you are accustomed to speak to a murderer: ‘Deny it.’ You order a sacrilegious man to be mangled.” The man presiding over the torture of a Christian was accustomed to say, “Deny that you are a Christian,” as though suggesting the means by which the man could escape. The same official nevertheless ordered a confessing Christian to be tortured, although one who confesses is tortured in vain. Tertullian therefore attacks this perverse and absurd judicial procedure: “That is to say,” he says, “this is how you are accustomed to speak to a murderer who confesses: ‘Deny that you are a murderer’; that is to say, you order tortures to be applied to a sacrilegious man who admits that he is sacrilegious.” Tertullian himself, *To the Nations* I: “Indeed, you exert yourselves and tear all others apart for this purpose, that they may deny that they are what they are said to be,” etc. Here, however, the following should apparently be read: “If you do not deal in this way with criminals.” PAM.]; you order a sacrilegious man to be mangled [Note: [Col. 0274D] “To be mangled.” By tortures, namely, such as those suffered by Philotas in Curtius VI.11: “But after his body, swollen with sores, could no longer endure the strokes of the lash driven against his bare bones”—Curtius used *lacerari*, “to be torn,” where our author has *laniari*, “to be mangled.” “Then, through the final tortures, since he had been condemned and his enemies were torturing him to win the king’s favor, he is torn apart.” This word is properly used of gladiators; hence the senate’s acclamation concerning Commodus’s corpse in Lampridius: “Let the enemy of his country, the parricide, the gladiator, be mangled in the stripping-room.” Heraldus alone grasped Tertullian’s meaning here: “In conducting an examination, you admonish a murderer to deny the murder; thus, even if he confesses the very matter for whose sake you conduct the examination, you nevertheless torture him as though he had not yet confessed. The laws certainly prohibit that, and you do not do it. Therefore, if we are criminals, deal with us as with criminals.” That he speaks ironically is obvious. The Fulda manuscript reads “ought to be mangled.” In the rest, the Leiden manuscript, Barraeus’s edition, Heraldus, and Rigault agree; Junius also reads so, but interprets it badly. Pamelius, La Cerda, and Rhenanus read very badly: “whom you believe to be the worst—for this is how you are accustomed to speak—murderers. You deny that you order a sacrilegious man to be mangled,” etc.; as though the judges suggested a means by which they might escape, and Tertullian wished to imply something like what he refers to in *To Scapula* IV: “How many governors, both more steadfast and more cruel, have dissembled in cases of this kind? Cincius Severus, for example, who at Thistrus himself supplied the Christians with a remedy—how they should answer so that they might be released.” There “more cruel” does not please me; I correct it to “and the same men were better,” a corruption that could easily have arisen from the shape of the letters. Suetonius described Augustus himself as such—unjust, but from mercy—in his *Life* XXXIII: “He administered justice not only with the utmost diligence but also with leniency. Thus, in order that a man accused of manifest parricide should not be sewn into the sack—a punishment inflicted only upon those who confessed—he is said to have questioned him in this way: ‘Surely you did not kill your father?’” But observe here also Septimius’s vinegar-like sharpness and the peculiar language of tyrants, such as Gallienus in punishing a revolt even to the slaughter of old men and infants: “Tear apart! Kill! Cut down!” in Trebellius Pollio. HAV.] if he persists in confessing.

If you do not act in this way toward [Col. 0275A] criminals, then you judge us utterly innocent, since, as though we were utterly innocent, you do not wish us to persist in that confession which you know must be condemned by you from necessity, not justice. A man cries out: “I am a Christian.” He says what he is; you wish to hear what he is not. You who preside over the extortion of truth labor to hear a lie from us alone. “I am,” he says, “what you are asking whether I am. Why do you torture me into falsehood? I confess, and you torture me. What would you do if I denied?” Plainly, when others deny, you do not readily give them credence; when we deny, you believe us at once.

Let this perversity appear suspicious to you [Note: [Col. 0275A] Barraeus reads “to you”; Pamelius and Semler, “to us”; all the rest, “let it be to you.” Perhaps one should read “let it be among you.”], lest some power lie hidden in secret [Col. 0276A] [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Lest some power lie hidden in secret.” He means Satan. Similarly Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II.1: “What cause should we suppose produces this, unless there is some perverse power that is particularly hostile to truth?” etc. Below our author calls it “the principle of a rival operation.” HAV.], which employs you against the established form, against the nature of judging, and even against the laws themselves [Note: [Col. 0275A] Wouwer reads “assails.”] [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Which employs you against the laws themselves.” That is, which uses your service against the laws themselves. PAM.]. For, unless I am mistaken, the laws command that evildoers be brought to light [Note: [Col. 0275D] “They command them to be brought to light.” Tertullian favors this verb in judicial investigations of criminals. Above: “Oh, how great would be the glory of that governor if he had unearthed someone who had already eaten a hundred infants!” And below, chapter VII: “Yet we are always so called, and you do not take care to bring to light what we have so long been called. Therefore either bring it to light, if you believe it, or cease to believe it, since you have not brought it to light.” HAV.], not concealed; they prescribe that those who confess be condemned [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Those who confess be condemned.” From the most ancient law. Sallust, *Catiline* LII: “Punishment must be exacted, according to ancestral custom, from those who have confessed, just as from those manifestly guilty of capital offenses.” Curtius, above. Add the passage from Suetonius cited shortly afterward, and hence Matthew XXVI.65:

> Ὅτι ἐβλασφήμησε· τί ἔτι — “He has blasphemed; what further…”  
> χρείαν ἔκομεν μαρτύρων; — “…need have we of witnesses?”

For, as Publilius rightly says, maxim 473:

> Unless you punish offenses, you assist wickedness;

and, according to the same witness, maxim 642:

> He who pardons the guilt of one encourages many;

indeed, maxim 99:

> Whoever spares the wicked harms the good;

finally, maxim 215:

> Successful wickedness is the calamity of the best.

Tertullian, *To Scapula* IV: “For what more are you commanded to do than to condemn the guilty who confess and recall those who deny to torture?” For, as the same author says in *On the Spectacles* XIX: “It is good when the guilty are punished.” HAV.], not acquitted. This is what decrees of the senate, mandates of princes, and the imperial authority whose ministers you are determine. Yours is a civil, not a tyrannical, dominion [Note: [Col. 0276A] Rigault reads: “They determine. This . . . is dominion.”]. For among tyrants tortures are also employed as punishment; among you they are confined solely to examination [Note: [Col. 0276C] Thus an examination does not proceed beyond confession. Cicero, *For Milo* LVII: “What need is there of a torturer? What are you asking? Whether he killed him? He did. Lawfully or unlawfully? That is no concern of the torturer. For the rack investigates the fact; the court, its lawfulness.” Meanwhile the mild and humane custom of Roman rule is commended to us here. Livy praises it in Book I, chapter 18, where, after describing the cruel punishment of the traitor Mettius Fufetius, he adds: “That was the first and last punishment among the Romans that showed too little regard for the example set by humane laws. In other cases we may boast that no nation has approved milder punishments.” Just as our author said “to set limits to an examination,” so Sallust also appears to have said “to set limits to victory”; I would not dare explain it, as is commonly done, as though *obtemperare*, “to submit to,” had been written, as several inferior manuscripts present it. The passage is *Catiline* XI: “Thus those soldiers, after they had won victory, left nothing to the conquered. Indeed, prosperity wears down the minds of the wise. Much less would those men, with their corrupted morals, set limits to victory”—that is, those utterly wicked and ruined men were so far from moderating their victory that they conducted themselves not as victors but as brigands and marauders. HAV.].

Preserve your law for them up to confession; and if confession forestalls the examination [Note: [Col. 0276A] Others read: “up to the necessary confession; and now, if they confess,” etc.], the tortures will cease. Judgment is required: the guilty man must be struck from the account by payment of the debt [Note: [Col. 0276D] “Must be struck from the account.” This verb too is characteristic of Tertullian. *Against the Jews* IV: “It therefore follows that, just as the abolition of fleshly circumcision and of the old law is shown to have been completed in its proper times, so too the observance of the Sabbath is shown to have been temporary.” Throughout his works it means “to complete, finish.” Here, however, it has the same meaning as in Persius, *Satires* II.12:

> If only I might strike off the ward whose next heir  
> I press to become! For he is scabby and swollen  
> with acrid bile.

There the ancient scholiast notes that the expression is taken from soldiers, who are said to be “struck off” when they are discharged from military service. Likewise, the metaphor is from war, in which, when the man first in line falls, another is substituted. Thus “to be struck off” is to be erased and removed from the midst. Add Rigault’s note, which rightly teaches that the expression is taken from accounts. HAV.] of punishment [Col. 0277A], not exempted [Note: [Col. 0277B] Paris and Rhenanus read “must be overcome.”] [Note: [Col. 0277B] “The guilty man must be struck from the account by payment of the debt of punishment.” Every guilty person owes penalties. Condemned persons are called slaves of punishment; once punishment has been exacted, they are understood to have paid the penalty. Accordingly, in completing the judicial inquiry, the collector of penalties, after calling from the tablet or register the name of each condemned person together with his indictment or charge, struck it off once the punishment had been exacted. Thus, when the inquiry had been completed, the names of all the condemned could be seen struck off in the register, and the guilty were struck off by payment of the debt of punishment. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0277C] “Not exempted.” Alexander Severus, according to Lampridius in his *Life*, always deferred to his prefects, asserting that one who deserves to suffer punishment must be condemned by the emperor, not released. Pythagoras—or someone else—in Stobaeus, *Discourse* XLIV, likewise says gravely:

> Καὶ οἱ φυγῆς ἄξια — “And those who commit deeds deserving exile…”

etc.; that is: “Those who commit something deserving exile, imprisonment, or another punishment must be condemned, not acquitted. But if anyone acquits them rashly for the sake of gain or pleasure, he acts unjustly, and injustice must necessarily be dear to his heart.” Tertullian uses *eximere*, “to exempt,” just as Livy does, in whom Papirius says of Quintus Fabius, later Maximus: “Quintus Fabius is not exempted from guilt, but, though condemned for guilt, is granted to the Roman people.” Horace, *Odes* II.2.21:

> Phraates, restored to Cyrus’s throne,  
> though the people disagree, Virtue excludes  
> [Col. 0277D] from the number of the blessed. HAV.].

Finally, no one eagerly desires to acquit such a man [Note: [Col. 0277B] Wouwer adds “among you.”]; it is not lawful even to wish it. Therefore no one is compelled to deny. You regard the Christian—a man guilty of every crime [Note: [Col. 0277D] “A man guilty of every crime.” Tertullian notably clears them of all these charges in this *Apology*. He calls them enemies of nature because they were believed to be infanticides, incestuous, and unproductive in commerce. Thus Cicero says of Dolabella, formerly his friend, in *Philippic* XI.10, that perhaps he would not even now be estranged from him had Dolabella not, in addition to his many other crimes, finally proved an enemy of nature and humanity; enemies of the emperors, because the charge of treason and injured majesty was brought against them. Suetonius, chapter XVI, calls them “a class of men belonging to a new and wicked superstition.” As such they were persecuted by impious princes. An ancient inscription from the age of Diocletian and Maximian, in Gruter, p. 280: “THE CHRISTIAN SUPERSTITION DESTROYED EVERYWHERE.” Hence also the inscription of those same emperors in Baronius’s *Annals* and Spanheim’s *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*: “THE NAME OF THE CHRISTIANS, WHO HAD OVERTURNED THE COMMONWEALTH, ERASED.” Enemies of laws and [Col. 0278B] customs, because they neglected public festivals and the worship of idols. Tacitus, *Annals* XV.44: “Accordingly, those who confessed were arrested first, and they were convicted not so much on the charge of arson as of hatred of the human race.” From Tertullian, chapter XXXV, you will learn the source of the hatred charged against them as a crime and why they were called public enemies. Place a comma after “Christian.” HAV.], an enemy of the gods, the emperors, the laws, customs, and all nature—and you compel him to deny so that you may acquit him, although you cannot acquit him unless he has denied [Note: [Col. 0277B] Thus Wouwer.].

You betray the laws [Note: [Col. 0278B] “You betray the laws.” Thus reads the learned manuscript whose owner consulted Scriverius, and not badly. Festus: “Betrayers are named from stepping past.” Thus “to betray the laws” is to step past them. Asconius Pedianus, in the little book included among the ancient grammarians: “He who rejects the bad and retains the good is understood to be a true accuser. But one who does the contrary, so as to impede others and cunningly conceal the matter, is understood to be a betrayer.” These words illuminate Tertullian’s meaning perfectly. For “you wish,” therefore, the Fulda manuscript soon reads “you wish him to deny.” Barraeus’s edition deletes “now.” HAV.]. You therefore wish him to deny that he is guilty so that you may make him innocent—and indeed innocent against his will, and no longer guilty concerning the past. Whence comes this perversity, that you do not even reflect that greater credence should be given to one who confesses voluntarily than to one who denies under force? Or perhaps, after being compelled to deny, he may not have denied in good faith [Note: [Col. 0278C] “May not have denied in good faith.” He falsely pretended that he was not a Christian by supplicating gods whom he rejected in his heart. Emperor Trajan to Pliny, Letter XCVIII: “Nevertheless, anyone who denies that he is a Christian and makes this evident by the act itself—that is, by supplicating our gods—shall obtain pardon through repentance, although he may have been suspected concerning the past.” Not only did the gentiles attempt in this way to persuade Christians to deny their God, as will appear more fully, but there also arose the perverse heresy of the Ossenes, which Epiphanius arraigns for this crime in Book I, Heresy 19:

> ὑποκρίτας δὲ διδὰσκει — “Moreover, he teaches them to be hypocrites…”

etc. “He teaches them, moreover, to be hypocrites, saying that it is not a sin even if they happen to worship images when persecution is at hand [Col. 0278D], provided only that they do not worship them in conscience, and if they confess merely with the mouth but not in the heart.” Such is Hippolytus in Euripides, whose detestable saying is:

> Ἡ γλῶσσ` ὀμώμοχ` ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀνώμοτος — “My tongue has sworn, but my mind is unsworn.”

which Grotius translated in his *Excerpts*, p. 214:

The tongue has sworn; in mind I have sworn nothing. But this is a wicked counsel. Tertullian speaks truly, and from a better frame of mind, in *On Idolatry*, ch. XIII: “Why indeed should you conceal yourself, when through another’s ignorance you defile your own conscience? If you are not recognized for what you are—a Christian (so read)—are you therefore not put to the test? And do you act against another’s conscience as though you were not a Christian? Indeed, even if you have dissembled, once tested you stand condemned.” HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0278D] “He may not have denied in good faith.” Particularly noteworthy is this man’s peculiar expression; for in law “not I” is something midway between denying and truly affirming. He therefore assigns that formula to the Christian who does not deny from the heart. LAC.]

may not have denied in good faith; and, once acquitted there before the tribunal, may laugh at your zeal, once more [Col. 0278A] a Christian [Note: [Col. 0277B] Others read, “among the Christians.”]. Since, therefore, in every respect you deal with us differently from other accused persons [Note: [Col. 0277B] Semler and others: “you deal differently with us” (Rhenanus: *you may deal*), [Col. 0278B] “than with the rest.” But the reading of the Fulda codex must be defended, for the verb *disponere* corresponds to the Greek διατίθεσθαι (“to arrange” or “dispose”).], striving for this one thing alone, that we should be excluded from that name—for we are excluded from it if we do what non-Christians do—you can understand that no crime is at issue, but the name, which a certain principle of hostile rivalry pursues. Its first aim is that men should refuse to know for certain what they know for certain that they do not know. Hence they both believe about us things that have not been proved and refuse to have them investigated, lest it be proved that those things do not exist which they prefer to have believed to exist; so that the name, the enemy of that hostile principle [Note: [Col. 0278B] Fra­nequer reads *aemulationis*, “of rivalry.”], may be condemned upon presumed, not proven, charges, merely by its own confession. Hence we are tortured when we confess, punished when we persevere, and acquitted [Col. 0279A] when we deny, because the battle is over the name.

Finally, why on the tablet [Note: [Col. 0279C] “Why on the tablet.” Formerly, says Rhenanus, a sentence imposing capital punishment was read from a tablet. This is confirmed by Pontius’s *Life of St. Cyprian* and by Paul the Deacon. PAM.] do you pronounce him a Christian, but not also a murderer? If [Note: [Col. 0279B] Wouwer adds “and.”] a Christian is a murderer, why not also incestuous, or whatever else you believe us to be? In our case alone you are ashamed or reluctant to pronounce the actual names of the crimes [Note: [Col. 0279C] “The actual names of the crimes.” Cicero, *On the Laws* II: “I shall proclaim the laws of the laws aloud.” Since all other accused persons have their indictment written on the tablet—“sacrilegious,” “murderers,” and so forth—why, he asks, are Christians, whom you consider guilty both of those and of every crime, presented under this name alone, with no crime added? Hence this name occurs as the distinctive designation of that offense in a most elegant passage of the Author, ch. XLIV: “For we call your own records to witness—you who preside daily over the trial of prisoners and mark off the indictments by your sentences: so many accused persons are listed by you under indictments for various crimes. Which assassin there, which cutpurse, which temple-robber, corrupter, or thief from the baths, is also entered among them as a Christian? Or, when Christians are presented under their own designation, which of them is also such as all those accused persons are?” Pamelius and Rhenanus place a question mark after “pronounce”; Rigault, Barr., the Fulda codex, and Heraldus place a full stop. Either is correct, but under the latter punctuation the words must be delivered ironically, as though he had written, “In our case alone, of course.” HAV.]? If a Christian is guilty of no [Note: [Col. 0279B] Paris adds “name”; Rigault reads “is a name.”] crime, the name is exceedingly hateful if the crime consists solely in the name [Note: [Col. 0279B] This is the common reading. Rhenanus: “if he is guilty under the name of no crime, it is exceedingly hateful,” etc. The Fulda codex: “If Christian is the name of no crime, it is exceedingly inept”; the Puteanus and Bongars codices read “incestuous”; the Agobardinus and Lyon codices, “the ineptness of incest,” “if the crime consists solely in the name.” Havercamp adopted this reading, adding at the end the words “exceedingly hateful,” and Jos. Ign. Ritter followed him.].

## CHAPTER III

He demonstrates the blindness of the hatred of those who, by the very characterization with which they reproach Christians, are compelled to praise them, but who are so savage that they would rather suffer their wife and household to be laden with disgrace than to be Christian—that is, reformed. Since, therefore, that bare Name provokes such quarrels, [Col. 0279B] he investigates it: it is nowhere deserving of contempt; even when wrongly pronounced by them, it contains something lovable; and it shares with the other Schools the fact that its Name is borrowed from its Founder, although no School is ever persecuted merely because of its Name. Christians, however, upright and just both as regards their School and their Name, are condemned unheard and unknown merely because the Name is hated.

[Col. 0280A] What of the fact that most people stumble into hatred of it with their eyes so tightly closed that, even while bearing favorable witness to someone, they mingle with it a reproach against the name: “Gaius Seius [Note: [Col. 0279D] “Gaius Seius.” These words occur very frequently among the jurists when, for the sake of example, they wish to make some point concerning persons in general. LAC.] is a good man, except that [Note: [Col. 0279D] “Except that.” An expression familiar to our Author. Suetonius likewise, in *Nero*, ch. VI, concerning the time of his birth: “just as the sun was rising, so that he was almost touched by its rays before the earth was.” The sense is that Nero intercepted the sun’s rays, which illuminated him before they illuminated the earth. Suetonius borrowed this, as he did many things, from Lucretius. The latter, book II, line 220:

> except that you might say the name had changed.

The early printed editions have here, “but he is bad except that,” [Col. 0280C] an insipid reading recognized by none of the better manuscripts and deleted by Salmasius, Rigault, La Cerda, and Scaliger. *Tantum quod* is equivalent to the Greek πλὴν ὄσοι (“except as many as”) or πλὴν ὅτι (“except that”). Synesius, as cited by Stephanus: πλὴν ὅσον ηὐξὰμην (“except insofar as I prayed”). Aristophanes likewise said in the *Clouds*: πλὴν ὅτι (“except that”). HAV.] he is a Christian.” Another says likewise: “I am amazed [Note: [Col. 0279C] Rigault and Havercamp, from the Fulda codex: “I am amazed that Lucius,” etc.; [Col. 0280B] the others: “I report Lucius … as a Christian”; the verb *defero*, absent from most codices, is no more required than “I am amazed.” But compare *To the Nations*, ch. 4. Leop.] that Lucius, a wise man, has suddenly become a Christian.”

No one reconsiders: “Is Gaius not therefore good, and Lucius prudent [Note: [Col. 0280B] Most codices read *Lucius*, *Lutius*, or *Lusius*; the codices of Ursinus and Scriverius read “wanton.”], because he is a Christian? Or is he therefore a Christian because he is prudent and good?” They praise what they know and condemn what they do not know, and they corrupt what they know by what they do not know, although it would be more just to form a preliminary judgment about hidden things from manifest things than to condemn manifest things beforehand on the basis of hidden things.

Others whom, before they bore this name, people had known as promiscuous, contemptible, and wicked [Note: [Col. 0280C] “Promiscuous, contemptible, and wicked”: promiscuous because of lust, contemptible because they cheapened themselves through indiscriminate availability, and wicked because of their evil conduct. The emperor Hadrian expressed those promiscuous people by “wandering about” in that epigram addressed to Florus in Spartianus:

> I do not want to be Florus,  
> Wandering through the taverns,  
> Lurking in eating-houses,  
> Enduring rounded cups.],

from this very fact characterize them [Note: [Col. 0280C] “From this very fact characterize,” etc. Pamelius and Rigault read: “from the very thing by which they characterize them, they praise them; in the blindness of hatred they stumble into giving their vote. What a woman! How wanton! How charming! What young men! What a Lucius!” Rigault: “how playful!” [Col. 0280D] “How lovable! They have become Christians.” The Fulda manuscript: “from this very fact they characterize them, by which they praise them; in the blindness of hatred, while recounting their testimony: what a woman, how wanton, how charming! what young men, how playful, how lovable,” etc. Rhenanus: “from the very fact they characterize them, they praise them together,” etc. The manuscript consulted by Scriverius reads: “from the very thing by which they characterize them, they praise them,” another “they praise them together,” and soon afterward: “that a woman, that wanton, that charming; that a young man, that wanton, that lovable,” etc., which Scriverius approves. Finally, Scaliger conjecturally corrected it more smoothly: “by that very thing by which they characterize them, they praise them.” Diogenes Laertius similarly says of Aristophanes and the comic poets that, while attempting to traduce and condemn Socrates, they praise him by that very act. His words in the *Life of Socrates* are: οἵ λανθάνουσιν ἑαυτοὺς, δι` ὧν σκώπτουσιν ἐπαινοῦντες αὐτόν (“who, without realizing it, praise him through the very things by which they mock him”); and concerning Zeno: οἵ γε μὲν κωμικοὶ ἐλάνθανον ἐπαινοῦντες αὐτὸν διὰ σκωμμάτων, that is, “yet the comic poets, without realizing it, praise this man while condemning him.” These observations look toward the following words of our Author in *To Scapula*, ch. II: “recognizable by nothing other than the amendment of their former vices.” HAV.],

by the very thing by which they praise them [Note: [Col. 0280B] Wouwer, from the old books, reads thus: “from the very thing by which they characterize them, they praise them; in the blindness of hatred they stumble into giving testimony. That a woman, that wanton, that charming! That a young man, that wanton, that lovable—they have become Christians.”]; [Col. 0280B] in the blindness of hatred they stumble into giving testimony: “What a woman! How wanton! How charming! What a young man! How wanton! How lovable! They have become Christians.” Thus the name is charged with their reformation.

Some even strike a bargain with this hatred at the expense of their own interests, content to suffer injury provided that they do not have in their own home what they hate. A husband who is now [Note: [Col. 0280C] “Now” is absent from the Paris codex.] possessed of a chaste wife [Note: [Col. 0280D] “A now-chaste wife.” Rhenanus and the Leiden manuscript read “a chaste wife.” [Col. 0281B] Thus in *To Scapula*, ch. III: “Claudius Herminianus indignantly resents his wife’s conversion to this sect.” This arose from the perverse presumption evident in the sacrilegious words of Apuleius, *The Golden Ass*, book IX: “Then, scorning and trampling upon the Divine Powers, in place of a definite religion, with the sacrilegious presumption of a counterfeit god whom she proclaimed as the only one, and with fabricated and empty observances, deceiving all men and deluding her wretched husband, she had enslaved her body to morning wine and continual adultery.” He is speaking there about the Christians’ morning assemblies, sacred and innocent though they were, but burdened by the Gentiles with lies and slanders.

According to ancient practice, however, all these expressions should be written with a hyphen: *now-chaste*, *formerly-patient*, *now-faithful*, *formerly-gentle*. So in Virgil, *Eclogue* I:

> For he shall always be a god to me;

and *Georgics* III.92, concerning a noble horse who, like Ennius, worn out by old age, rests:

> Him too, when heavy with sickness or now more sluggish with years,  
> [Col. 0281C] When he fails, hide within the house and pardon his not-shameful old age.

In interpreting this, Gifanius disgraces himself in his Lucretian index. Lucretius himself likewise, book I, line 125:

> Whence he records that the form of ever-flourishing Homer  
> Arose before him.

Nor otherwise Publilius, verse 731:

> Innocence always follows its own light.

The Senate’s acclamation to the emperor Probus in Vopiscus must be understood in the same manner: “Probus Augustus, may the gods preserve you. Long-worthy, courageous, and just,” etc. Finally, that *formerly-gentle master* is Terence the African’s *master’s constant-gentleness*. Failure to observe this here and below, as will be stated in the proper place, has deprived our Author of elegance and the magnificent poet Lucan of polish; for book IX, line 158, must be read thus:

> From the tomb I shall disclose Isis, now-a-divinity, to the nations. HAV.]

has driven her out, though now no longer jealous; a father, formerly patient, has disowned his now-submissive son; [Col. 0281A] a master, formerly gentle, has banished his now-faithful slave from his sight. As each person is reformed by this name, he gives offense. The good is not valued as highly as Christians are hated.

Now, therefore, if it is the name that is hated, what guilt can there be in names? What charge can be brought against words, unless some word in a name sounds barbarous, ill-omened, abusive, or indecent? “Christian,” however [Note: [Col. 0281C] “Chrestian.” Thus learned men have long since shown that this designation was altered in antiquity; most recently Michael Rossal published at Groningen an elegant and learned little book concerning this alteration. The statements made by Suetonius and Tacitus are well known. The former, in *Claudius*, ch. XXV: “He expelled from Rome the Jews, who were constantly rioting at the instigation of Chrestus.” Orosius doubts whether the Christians too were expelled: “I am more troubled,” he says, book VII, ch. 4, “by Suetonius, from whom it cannot at all be determined whether Claudius ordered the Jews who were rioting against Christ to be restrained and suppressed, or whether he wished Christians also, as men of a related religion, to be expelled at the same time.” The cause of the disturbance—as Suetonius calls it—was the clash between the two groups, since the Jews denied that Christ had come, while the Christians affirmed it. But Orosius doubts in vain, for the edict of Claudius in Acts XVIII.2 must be referred to this: διὰ τὸ διατεταχέναι Κλαύδιον χωρὶζεσθαι πάντας τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἐκ τῆς Ρώμης (“because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to depart from Rome”).

Tacitus, again, *Annals* XV.44: “Those whom the populace called Christians, hated for their abominations. The originator of the name was Chrestus,” etc. Finally, Lucian openly calls them Χρήϛον (“Chreston”) in the *Philopatris*. Indeed, the same Lucian barks with blasphemous mouth in the *Philopatris*, p. 1003: εἰ τύχοι γε Χρηστὸς καὶ ἐν ἔθνεσι, “if indeed Chrestus has also existed among the nations.” Nor is it surprising that this appellation became prevalent among the Gentiles, since many persons named Chrestus are found among them, but none named Christus. It is worthwhile to add a few examples.

In Appian’s *Mithridatic Wars*, not far from the beginning, a certain Socrates surnamed Chrestus is mentioned, whom Mithridates, king of Pontus, placed upon the throne of Bithynia after expelling Nicomedes. A certain Chrestus is also mentioned by Aurelius Victor in his account of Hannibalianus: “Some soldiers conspired to murder him, with Chrestus and Marcellinus as their leaders, together with Magnentius.” Martial’s epigrams against a certain Chrestus are still extant, book VII.54 and IX.28, as also one against Chrestillus, book XI.91. A Chresta is also mentioned in an ancient inscription located in the vineyards of Vall.:

> Here, virtue, the glory of fate and a lovable name,  
> Celebrated for the dowry of chastity and the labors of her life,  
> Chresta now lies enclosed within the tomb.

[Col. 0282C] Fulgentius likewise, in the little book he composed *On Archaic Speech*, under the expression *unjoined oxen*, mentions a certain Manilius Chrestus, whom he says to have written a book on hymns to the gods; there too he quotes a fragment from it. Finally, Ausonius plays elegantly upon the meaning of the word in epigram XXXIX:

> Χρῆστος, Ἄκίνδυνος, εἰσὶν ἀδελφοί, οικτιὰ δὲ τέκνα (“Chrestos and Acindynos are brothers, and the children are pitiable”; the recovered οικτιὰ is uncertain).  
> Both bear false names because of their evil characters.  
> Ουδὲ οὗτος χρηστὸς, οὐδὲ, οὗτος ἀκίνδυνός ἐστιν (“Neither is this one good, nor is that one free from danger”).  
> A single letter can correct them both.  
> Αἴκεν Χρῆστος ἕλῃ, καὶ Ἀκίνδυνος ἄλφ` ἀπολέσῃ (“If Chrestos takes an alpha and Acindynos loses his alpha”); here one will become Κίνδυνος (“Kindynos,” meaning “Danger”), brother; the other will be Ἄχρηστος (“Achrestos,” meaning “Useless”).

And epigram XL:

> They are full brothers: one is Chrestos, the other Acindynos.  
> Each has a false name; but for each name to become true,  
> Let Acindynos give his alpha to Christos and himself remain without alpha:  
> Then each will bear a true name.

Rigault’s edition wrongly has “or Christian.” The Leiden manuscript, too, wrongly reads “Christian.” In the same manuscript [Col. 0282D] *quantum interpretatione* appears instead of *quantum interpretatio*. Rhenanus reads: “But since it is wrongly pronounced ‘Christian.’” HAV.],

so far as its interpretation goes, is derived from anointing. But even [Note: [Col. 0281A] “Even” is absent from the Paris codex.] when you wrongly pronounce it “Chrestian” (for among you there is not even certain [Note: [Col. 0282A] “Certain” is absent from the Paris codex.] knowledge of the name), it is formed from pleasantness or kindness. Thus, among innocent men [Col. 0282A] even an innocent name is hated.

“But,” you say, “the school [Note: [Col. 0282D] “But the school is hated,” etc. Both here and throughout our Author, *secta*, like the Greek αἵρεσις (“school” or “sect”), is taken in a favorable sense; it is enough to have noted this once. So likewise in Acts XXVI.5 the Apostle Paul says ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἳρεσιν τῆς ἡμετέρας θρησκείας ἔζησα φαρισαῖος (“that according to the strictest sect of our religion I lived as a Pharisee”). Our Author expands this passage somewhat in ch. XLVI: “Why, then, are those with whom we are compared in discipline not likewise placed on our level as regards the freedom and immunity of their discipline? Or why are they too, as our equals, not pressed to discharge duties for failing to perform which we are placed in peril?” etc.

Thus Donatus teaches that Terence used a distinctive expression in *Phormio* I.II:

> To follow, to lead to school and lead home again,

adding: “He has mocked the young man aptly and humorously, since his age was suited to following philosophers.” HAV.] is hated under the name of its founder.” What novelty is there if some discipline imposes upon its followers a designation derived from its teacher? Are not philosophers named after their founders—Platonists, Epicureans, Pythagoreans? Even from the places of their meetings and stations come the Stoics and Academics; physicians are named after Erasistratus, grammarians after Aristarchus, and even cooks after Apicius [Note: [Col. 0282D] “Apicius.” A notorious glutton. Books of Apicius *On Cookery* still survive, though not written by this Apicius—as we likewise falsely possess *Macer on Herbs* and other works—but composed, in confirmation of our Author’s statement, to suit that man’s palate and according to his judgment.

Our Author mentions him not only in *On the Pallium*, ch. V: “I pass over the Neros, Apiciuses, and Rufuses,” but also in *Against the Psychics*, ch. XII: “Why, then, do you delay believing in Apicius as the Paraclete whom you deny in Montanus?” Hence the *Apician seasonings* in *On the Soul*, ch. XXXIII: “Will not that soul receive more consolation than punishment because it finds its funeral among the costliest cooks, because it is buried with Apician and Lurconian seasonings, because it is brought to Ciceronian tables and carried forth on the most splendid Sullan platters?” etc. For “equally moderate,” Barr., the Leiden manuscript, and Rhenanus read “and”; Heraldus, “neither”; but the Fulda manuscript, Rigault, and Pamelius more correctly read “equally.” HAV.]?

Yet no one is offended by the profession of a name transmitted together with the institution from its founder. Certainly, if anyone proves a school evil and thereby its founder evil, he will also prove its name evil and deserving of hatred because of the guilt of the school and its founder. Therefore, before hating the name, it was proper first to examine the school from its founder, or the founder from the school. But now [Note: [Col. 0283C] “The name is detained.” I do not agree with De la Cerda and Junius, who read “is branded.” For he shows that the name alone is dragged into court and, as though it were a malefactor and parricide, is hauled along with a chain placed about its neck, just as Curtius VII.5 depicted Bessus, the murderer of Darius, being brought in by Spitamenes. HAV.], with inquiry into and knowledge of both neglected, the name is detained, the name is assailed; a mere word condemns beforehand both an unknown school and an unknown founder, because they are named, not because they are proved guilty.

## CHAPTER IV

He now prepares himself for the defense against the crimes with which Christians were burdened. But since, even after the most just defense, the violence of the law nevertheless demands obedience, he skillfully and forcefully demonstrates that laws, just as they can be enacted, can also be rejected and altered—indeed, that sometimes they ought to be—and that this is not without precedent, namely when they have been found cruel or unjust. For a law is determined to be just after its validity has been investigated; but a wicked law is found to be no law at all, but tyranny.

[Col. 0284A] And so, having offered these words by way of preface to brand [Note: [Col. 0283C] “To brand.” That is, not merely to convict it, but to burn into it a mark of shame, a bruise, and a welt, so that it may be publicly displayed. Thus he uses *branding* in ch. XI: “Your justice is branded in heaven.” Less correctly, the Leiden manuscript and Junius’s conjecture from the manuscripts read “to seal.” [Col. 0283D] In the same sense one may find in the Anonymous *Aesopic Fables* in Nevelet, fable XVI, concerning the now-aged lion:

> The sluggish ass rages and seals his forehead with a kick,

that is, marks it. HAV.] the injustice of the public hatred against us, I shall now take my stand [Note: [Col. 0283D] “I shall take my stand.” Tertullian likes to speak in this way. Thus *On Idolatry*, ch. XIII: “On this point, indeed, I shall first take my stand”; and in *Apology*, ch. XLVI: “We have taken our stand, I think, against the charge of every crime that demands the blood of Christians.” The manner of speaking is drawn from athletes and gladiators, who plant their foot in the arena so that they cannot easily be tripped or thrown down. In warfare too, when it is time to engage hand to hand, an army is said to halt or take its stand. Lucretius speaks similarly in book VI, line 454, where he explains how clouds are condensed and the sky is darkened:

> These things first cause small clouds to take their stand;

and shortly afterward:

> Because, when the clouds first take their stand.

Or, finally, the expression may have been transferred from judicial proceedings. Psalm I, final verse: [Col. 0284B] “Therefore the sinner shall not stand in the judgment, nor the wicked man in the assembly of the righteous.” HAV.]

on the issue of innocence. I shall not merely refute the charges brought against us, but shall also turn them back against those who [Note: [Col. 0283B] Paris reads “which.”] bring them, so that from this too everyone may know that the things which they are well aware exist among themselves do not exist among Christians [Note: [Col. 0284B] “Which they are well aware exist among themselves.” So that our adversaries may know that we are not merely free from those crimes, but that they themselves openly perpetrate them, if they are willing to look at the truth. This is the reading from the Collation of Modius adopted by Rigault and others; another reading is “which they do not know exist among themselves.” HAV.]. At the same time they may blush when, being not merely the worst, as I say, accusing the best, but already—as they would have it—accusing their equals [Note: [Col. 0284B] “Their equals.” Thus *equals*, that is, persons like the Christians, against whom they bring—though falsely—charges concerning things which they themselves actually do. Tertullian is sharp in lashing the Gentiles with a mocking false equivalence. Thus, in words closely agreeing with this passage, ch. XVI: “But he who thinks us devotees of the cross will be our fellow-votary.” The Author again uses the word *compar* for “equal” in *On Prayer*, ch. X: “No one receives an adversary; no one admits anyone except his equal”; and *Against Marcion*, book I, ch. XVI: “Some members are strong, others weak; some honorable, others dishonorable; some paired, others single; some corresponding, others dissimilar.” HAV.]—we shall answer every charge we are said to commit in secret, which we find them committing openly [Note: [Col. 0283B] Thus manuscript 2616 of the Royal Library; Rigault reads “which would openly be discovered.” [Col. 0284B]], and because of which we are deemed [Note: [Col. 0284C] “We are deemed.” That is, we are emphatically thought or considered so, for the prefix *de-* intensifies the verb. Elsewhere *deputari* in our Author means “to cut off.” Thus *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. VI: “There was an Old dispensation, which is cut off in the New Gospel, in which,” etc., “the axe is laid to the root of the tree.” HAV.] criminal, vain, condemnable, or ridiculous.

But since, whenever our truth meets every charge, the authority of the laws is finally erected as a barrier [Note: [Col. 0284C] “The authority of the laws is erected as a barrier.” Pamelius and Rhenanus read “is established,” which is less elegant. The Leiden manuscript reads “may be obstructed,” which is unnecessary. He speaks elegantly of laws being set as an obstruction before a defense, like an unconquerable mass through which it would be unlawful for truth to break. The comparison is drawn from that source, as in Lucan, book II, line 495:

> You block the fields and prepare to restrain them with rivers;

and line 661:

> But with massive works he blocks the waves  
> And the broad sea with rocks thrown down.

Our Author speaks even more plainly in ch. I: “He blocks the defense,” using a similar expression. Lactantius seems to have imitated this passage, *Divine Institutes* II.20: “But now a greater and more difficult contest with the philosophers lies before us, whose consummate learning and eloquence are set against me like some massive structure.” HAV.]

against it, so that either it is said that nothing may be reconsidered [Col. 0284B] [Note: [Col. 0284D] “Nothing may be reconsidered.” It is as though he said: “The defense is futile; for either the judge will reply that nothing contrary to the laws ought to be done and that they cannot be reformed, and will therefore send the defendant away unheard, as the law commands; or, even if inclined to hear the defense, sympathetic, indeed convinced, he will nevertheless tell himself, willingly or unwillingly, that the laws must be obeyed.” The Author frequently uses the terms *retractare* and *ingratis* or *ingratiis*, Greek ἀκουσίως (“unwillingly”). In *Against Hermogenes*, [Col. 0285B] ch. XVI: “Therefore, in laying the groundwork for this point, which may perhaps also have to be reconsidered elsewhere, I for my part define,” etc.; immediately afterward: “You prescribe this without any more humane reconsideration.” Below in *Apology*, ch. XXVI: “We resist unwillingly.” Add Plautus and Terence, and finally Lucretius, who elsewhere and especially in book III, line 1082, seems to describe our judge:

> He cannot escape; unwillingly it clings to him and torments him. HAV.]

after the laws have spoken, or the necessity of obedience, however unwilling, is preferred to truth, I shall first contend with you over the laws, as with their guardians. To begin with, [Col. 0285A] how harshly [Note: [Col. 0285A] Another reading: “when harshly”; Rhenanus, Fr. Junius, and Wouwer: “how harshly”; Havercamp: “when lawfully.”] you lay down the rule by saying: “You are not permitted to exist!” And you prescribe this without any more humane reconsideration. You openly profess violence and an unjust domination from the citadel [Note: [Col. 0285B] “An unjust domination from the citadel.” Phaedrus: “The tyrant Pisistratus occupies the citadel.” Juvenal, X:

> No tyrant in his savage citadel  
> Castrated an ugly youth. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0285A] “From the citadel”: Paris and Rigault.], if you deny that it is permitted simply because you so will, not because it ought not to have been permitted.

But if you do not wish it to be permitted because it ought not to be, then without doubt that which is done badly ought not to be permitted [Note: [Col. 0285A] Paris deletes “which is done badly.”]; and by that very principle it is already judged permissible when it is done well. If I find that what your law has prohibited is good, can it not be prevented by that prior judgment from prohibiting me in a case which, if it were evil, it would rightly prohibit? [Note: [Col. 0285B] Thus the Lyon codex, Heraldus, and Semler. Gelenius: “The law prohibited the name; on that basis it cannot prohibit me.” Rigault and Havercamp: “Do I not judge from that principle that it cannot prohibit me?”] If your law has erred, it was, I suppose, conceived by a human being; for it did not fall from heaven [Note: [Col. 0285B] “It fell from heaven”: Διοπετής (“fallen from Zeus,” hence “fallen from heaven”), as the commentators note. He plainly touches upon and ridicules the Romans’ sacred shields and the Palladium of the descendants of Aeneas, with its Trojan origin; in imitation of these came what we read in Acts of the Apostles XIX.35 concerning the city of Ephesus and its temple-warden: τῆς μεγάλης θεᾶς Αρτέμιδος καὶ τοῦ Διοπετούς (“of the great goddess Artemis and of the image fallen from heaven”). He likewise appears to brand the nymph Egeria’s conversation with Numa Pompilius. HAV.].

Are you astonished that a human being [Col. 0286A] could [Note: [Col. 0286A] Paris deletes “could.”] have erred in framing a law, or have come to his senses [Note: [Col. 0286A] Paris reads “have recovered himself.”] when rejecting one? Were not even Lycurgus’s laws amended by the Lacedaemonians, thereby inflicting such grief upon their author that in retirement [Note: [Col. 0285C] “That in retirement,” etc. Plutarch affirms the fact, though for another reason: when Lycurgus, on the pretense that he was about to set out again for the Oracle, had bound the Lacedaemonians by oath to preserve his laws uncorrupted until his return, he never returned, so that they might remain forever unchanged, but at Crissa killed himself by starvation. The same Cragius, III.1, shows that afterward many other laws were added to Lycurgus’s laws.] he passed judgment upon himself by starvation?

And do not you yourselves [Note: [Col. 0285C] “And do not you yourselves,” etc. He passes from foreigners to the Romans themselves, whom he teaches to repeal and correct old laws daily and to introduce and enact new ones. Relevant here are the words in our Author’s *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. VI: “But I suppose that a later human enactment and decree prevails over earlier ones.” [Col. 0285D] The Orfitian decree of the Senate, enacted in the consulship of Orfitus and Vettus, is also well known. Jerome must be understood as referring to it under the year 179: “The emperors bestowed many things upon many persons; and, remitting to the provinces money owed to the treasury, they caused the tablets of debtors to be burned in the middle of the Roman Forum; and lest anything should be lacking [so read] from their benevolence, they moderated every harsh law by new constitutions.”],

as experience daily illuminates the darkness of antiquity, cut down and hew away that whole old and squalid forest of laws with the axes of new imperial rescripts [Note: [Col. 0285D] “Imperial rescripts.” Again a phrase of the jurists. *Digest*, law I, *On the Origin of Law*, law II, concerning which Zephyrus says: “Imperial rescripts were called the emperor’s mandates, by which an emperor, either on his own initiative or moved by petitions, either granted something to or withheld something from a private person or community. They derived their name from the fact that [as Tacitus writes] it was customary to approach any prince who was present by a written request. Martial calls such writings petitionary booklets; in our time they are ‘supplications.’” PAM.] and edicts? [Note: [Col. 0286A] Pamelius, Heraldus, and others read “cut down”; Scaliger and Scriverius, “weeded”; Rigault, “rusted”; Havercamp, “cleared of brush.”]

Did not the utterly foolish Papian laws [Note: [Col. 0285D] “The utterly foolish Papian laws.” He makes a witty allusion to these even in the generation of the gods, book II, ch. 12: “How, then, were they long unmarried and childless before becoming husbands and parents?”

[Col. 0286B] Since the most illustrious and learned Gothofredus, however, writes in his notes at the end of ch. 6 of book II of *To the Nations* that the emperor Severus derogated from the Papian laws but did not repeal them—he says that he remembers having refuted elsewhere the contrary claim, falsely handed down by many—I thought that I would perform a welcome service by inserting here the great man’s note from his commentary on the Julian law *On Regulating Marriage*. Thus he writes on ch. XXIII of the Julian and Papian Law:

“Spouses were not subject to penalties for childlessness if the husband was not yet twenty-five years old and the wife not yet twenty. ‘Sometimes,’ says Ulpian at the beginning of the fragments *On the Papian Law*, title XVI, ‘husband and wife can receive the whole of each other’s estate, as, for example, if both or either one of them has not yet reached the age that requires children—that is, if the husband is less than twenty-five years old or the wife less than twenty.’

“And lest anyone hereafter be able to doubt that the age for begetting children was specifically defined by the Papian law, Tertullian, compared with Ulpian, *Apology* IV, will establish it: ‘Did not the utterly foolish,’ etc. For begetting children, therefore, the age I have stated was fixed beforehand by the Papian Law. Severus, however, established a more generous limit, namely the one stated by Ulpian. Sozomen, while discussing the Julian and Papian Law in book I, ch. 9, mistakenly transferred this to the age for contracting marriage. Νόμος (“A law”), he says, ἢν Ρομαίοις παλαιὸς, ἀπὸ εἴκοσι καὶ πέντε ἐτῶν, τοῦ ἴσων ἀξιοῦσθαι κολυων τοὺς ἀγάμους μὴ τοιοῦτοις (“There was an ancient law among the Romans which, from the age of twenty-five, prevented the unmarried from being accorded equal standing with those who were not such”; the recovered Greek is irregular). Sozomen should have said ἀτεκνους (“the childless”) or ἄπαιδας (“those without children”), not ἀγάμους (“the unmarried”).

“Thus an age for begetting children was defined by the Papian Law: namely, the twenty-fifth year for a male and the twentieth for a female. Before that age the Julian laws did not even compel marriage to be contracted, as Tertullian teaches in the earlier passage. But from what age the Julian laws compelled marriage to be contracted, or the Papian laws compelled children to be begotten, cannot be clearly stated.

“Accordingly, the third uncertainty remaining in Tertullian’s words—namely, what he means when he writes that Severus excluded the Papian Laws, which compelled people to beget children prematurely—has this clear meaning, which has nevertheless thus far escaped even the most acute minds: Severus permitted and defined a more generous age for begetting children than the Papian Law had established, restoring, as I think, the legal rule of the Julian laws. I therefore judge that the three matters in the foregoing passage of Tertullian which until now have remained undiscovered not merely by others but even by the most learned scholiasts on the *Apology* must be understood in this manner.” HAV.]

which compel people to beget children before the Julian laws compel [Note: [Col. 0286B] Wouwer, from a manuscript: “before the Julian laws permit marriage,” etc.] marriage [Note: [Col. 0286D] “The Julian laws permit marriage to be contracted.” La Cerda and Scriverius, following Wouwer’s Collation, wrongly wish “permit” to be added. For the sense is that the Papian Law compelled the begetting of children before the time at which marriage and conjugal intercourse were enjoined upon those already betrothed by the Julian Law; and therefore that the former law imposed penalties for childlessness τοῖς ἀτέκνοις (“upon the childless”) before the time at which the latter imposed penalties for celibacy τοῖς ἀγάμοις (“upon the unmarried”). The Papian Laws could therefore be called utterly foolish, especially since the Christians were already then expecting the end of the age.

Since betrothals took place early among the Romans, the Julian Law granted several years before marriage and intercourse necessarily took place, while in the meantime the betrothed enjoyed the legal rights of married persons. But under the Papian Law they were compelled to devote themselves earlier to having children, whereas the Julian Law granted a longer exemption from this obligation. This must be properly understood, since he looks back to it again in *On Monogamy*, ch. XCI: “It is another matter if they believe that proceedings under the Julian laws exist even under Christ and think that unmarried and childless persons cannot receive the whole under God’s testament.” Add Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* III.25, concerning these laws. HAV.]

to be contracted, [Col. 0287A] after an antiquity of such great authority [Note: [Col. 0287B] “So venerable an antiquity.” Cicero, *On the Laws* I.21: “There are set formulas of the laws, Quintus, not indeed so ancient as those found in the old and sacred laws, yet somewhat more archaic than our present conversation, so that they may possess greater authority.” Arnobius likewise spoke of “long-established religions” at the beginning of his first book.]—only yesterday Severus, most steadfast [Note: [Col. 0287B] “Most steadfast of emperors.” I think that Tertullian adorned him with this praise because he is the very man in whom, in *To Scapula*, ch. IV, he praises that virtue of mind which Horace requires in his steadfast man when he says:

[Col. 0287C]

> The just man, tenacious of his purpose,  
> Not the fury of citizens commanding wicked things …

[The supplied source breaks off here.]

Shakes [it] with a steadfast mind. And there is a most elegant passage in Aelius Lampridius, than which none can better illustrate this statement of the author. He speaks as follows of the emperor Alexander, son of Mamaea, whose surname was Severus: “Because of the immense vigor of his spirit and his marvelous and singular steadfastness against the insolence of the soldiers, the name Severus was bestowed upon him by the soldiers; this won him immense respect at the time and great glory among posterity, since he had acquired his name from a virtue of character.” Victor says of our Severus: “Keen in intellect, persevering to the end in everything to which he had applied himself. His benevolence, wherever it inclined, was marvelous and constant; diligent in acquiring, liberal in giving; equally vehement toward friends and enemies.” But the passage which Rigault adduces from Spartianus pertains not so much to Severus’s praise as to his disgrace and cruelty [Col. 0287D]; for the complete passage reads thus: “Many, however, were condemned because they had made jokes, others because they had remained silent, and others because they had said many things figuratively, so that he was indeed an emperor true to his name, truly Pertinax, truly Severus.” Capitolinus likewise says of Macrinus: “For he had wished to be called Severus Pertinax—two names which seemed to him to signify harshness.” Yet the name in which some perceived harshness could by others be bestowed for virtue of character. HAV.]

—of the emperors, excluded it? Yet the laws formerly provided that those adjudged to their creditors should be cut into pieces [Note: [Col. 0287D] **Formerly to be cut into pieces.** Rigault inserted from the Fulda manuscript the word *retro*, that is, “before” or “formerly.” It lies beyond our proper sphere to determine whether so cruel an example was actually carried out in antiquity, or whether instead the man himself was sold and the proceeds obtained from him divided among his creditors. Besides the distinguished jurist who treats this law in a separate chapter, Salmasius, *De Usuris*, p. 544, may also be consulted. Our author, austere by nature, adhered to the harsher interpretation. Accordingly I again illustrate and explain him from this when he writes in *On Patience*, chap. VII: “Now, as for one who has determined not steadfastly to endure the loss of some small portion of his property, whether through theft, violence, or even negligence, I do not know whether he could readily and sincerely lay hands upon his own possessions [Col. 0288A] for the sake of almsgiving. For how can one who cannot at all endure being cut by another himself apply the knife to his own body?”

This distinguished passage reminds me to use it to illustrate what is read in Matthew 24:51 and Luke 12:46: καί διχοτομησει αὐτον καὶ τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ μετὰ τοῦ ὑποκρίτων θήσει, “and he will cut him in two and assign his portion with the hypocrites”, where I think there is certainly a reference to the bodily punishment prescribed by this law, although I do not deny that it can thence be transferred to a spiritual sense, and thus that an allusion is made to this law. That punishment was surely [Col. 0288B] more severe than either reducing his daily allowance, as Beza would have it, and separating him from the rest, or even beating and tearing him with scourges, as Casaubon holds on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chap. XIII. There he adduces the law itself—as Junius also does here—from the very well-known passage of Gellius, but only to show that cutting men to pieces had already been practiced in antiquity, not to illuminate from it the passage of Holy Scripture, which, so far as I think, the other has not yet explained in this way.

Who else is this faithless servant in the Evangelists but a squanderer of his master’s goods, over which he had been placed while the master was absent? This is evident because, in his absence, ἄρξηται ἐσθίειν τε καὶ πίνειν μετα τῶν μεθυόντων, “he begins to eat and drink with the drunkards”, and, turning from drunkenness to violence, his fellow servants, who gave him sound admonitions, τύπτειν, “to beat”. What could he thereby have done but contract a great debt to his master? Once the master had returned, this squanderer of his master’s reputation and goods could deserve the penalty even of the strictest law. If these things too must be transferred solely to the mind, why did they not use the most elegant [Col. 0288C] word διχοθυμέω, “to be of two minds”—though I would not dare assert that this was actually written—which they could have formed from διχόθυμος, “double-minded”, a word known among lexicographers?

Finally, if I could in any way obtain support from antiquity, I would gladly explain what follows thus: καὶ τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ μετὰ τοῦ ὑποκρίτων θήσει, “and he will place his portion with the hypocrites”, that is, “he will hang up his severed parts [as is still done today in England] in that place where the bodies of criminal and, under the law, dismembered hypocrites—

> Who pretend to be Curii and live in Bacchanalian revels,

and thus swindle their creditors of their money, are buried.” In the same way, the servant in Plautus joked about the cross, the customary punishment of slaves, in which his father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather had been buried. Certainly Cicero’s severed head and right hand hung upon the Rostra, and likewise the heads of the proscribed were displayed there and in other places; the custom is sufficiently well known especially from Appian. I know that this last clause can nevertheless be understood otherwise, but these considerations do not seem contemptible either. For thus our author says of [Col. 0288D] Severus himself: “Severus also knew that certain most illustrious women and most illustrious men belonged to this sect; yet not only did he refrain from harming them, but he even honored them with his testimony and openly withstood the raging populace to its face.” HAV.] by their creditors; nevertheless, by public consent the cruelty was afterward erased and the capital penalty converted into a mark of shame [Col. 0288A] [Note: [Col. 0288D] **And the capital penalty was converted into a mark of shame.** This entire passage is absent from the Leiden manuscript and is not free from suspicion. For it has, somehow, the savor of another hand, officiously but ineptly at work in another man’s composition.]; through the employment of confiscation of property [Note: [Col. 0287A] *Proscriptio*, Rigault.], it preferred to suffuse a man’s face with blood rather than to shed his blood. How many laws still lie hidden among you that must be cleansed [Note: [Col. 0288A] *To be opposed*, Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0288D] **It preferred to suffuse a man’s blood rather than to shed it.** Optatus, book II: “Shedding blood, not of the body, but of shame.” But what other blood of shame is there than bodily blood? Gregory of Baetica—or whoever else wrote the book *On Faith against the Arians*: “That shameless forehead of theirs, which is without the sign of the Lord, must be crushed by the repeated stones of testimonies, so that, even if their flesh, pierced by many wounds, does not shed gore, shame may at least blush through a suffusion of blood.” RIG.], laws commended neither by the number of their years [Note: [Col. 0288D] **Laws commended neither by the number of their years.** Τὸ, “which,”, “which,” must not be referred precisely to “laws that must be cleansed,” but generally to “laws,” as if he were saying: Laws are commended neither by the number of their years nor by the dignity of their founders, but by equity alone. Hence in Livy, book XXXIV, L. Valerius, tribune of the plebs, says that some laws are mortal, others eternal: “Of those laws which were enacted, not for some limited period, but for the sake of perpetual utility and for all time, I admit that none ought to be repealed unless either experience has proved it defective or some condition of the commonwealth has rendered it useless. Thus I see that laws which particular times require are, so to speak, mortal and changeable together with the times themselves.” The same.], nor by the dignity of their founders, but by equity alone? And therefore, when [Col. 0289A] they are recognized as unjust, they are deservedly condemned, though they themselves condemn [Note: [Col. 0289A] “Though they are condemned,” Paris.].

How do we call them unjust? Indeed, if they punish the name, we call them foolish as well. But if they punish deeds, why [Note: [Col. 0289B] Wouwer adds “in our case.”] in our case do they punish deeds solely on account of the name—deeds which in others they defend as proved by the offense and not by the name [Note: [Col. 0289B] Wouwer and Rigault: “determine that they must be proved”; Havercamp: “maintain that they must be proved”; Heraldus: “defend them as proved.”]? I am incestuous: why do they not investigate? I am an infanticide: why do they not extort a confession? I commit some offense against the gods or the Caesars: why am I not heard [Note: [Col. 0289B] “Why am I not heard, if I have anything to say,” Wouwer.], when I have the means to clear myself [Note: [Col. 0289B] “that I may clear myself,” Paris.]? No law forbids examination of what it forbids to be committed; for neither does a judge justly avenge an offense unless he knows that what is unlawful has been committed, nor does a citizen faithfully obey the law while ignorant of the nature of that which it punishes. No law owes the consciousness of its justice to itself alone, but also to those from whom it expects obedience. Moreover, a law which does not wish to be tested is suspect; but it is wicked [Col. 0289B] if it rules without having been tested.

## CHAPTER V

He investigates the origin of laws of this kind and, taking occasion from Alburnus, whom Aemilius wished to have enrolled among the gods, shows that by those laws divinity was subjected to human decision [Col. 0290A]. He then sets forth Tiberius’s judgment concerning Christ and the Senate’s opposition. He shows that none but Nero and those most like him afflicted the Christian name, whereas Marcus Aurelius—having even been admonished by a miracle—together with Verus, and before them Vespasian, Trajan, Hadrian, and Pius, allowed Christians to exist. Finally he concludes that, since Christians were approved by good men and afflicted by evil men, they ought, from the similarity of their conduct, to be regarded as good rather than evil.

To [Note: [Col. 0289B] “But,” Paris.] reconsider something of the origin of laws of this kind, there was an ancient decree [Note: [Col. 0289C] **That no god should be consecrated by an emperor unless approved by the Senate.** The statement we read in the fragments of Ulpian has the same sense: “Gods cannot be instituted as heirs except those whom it has been permitted by decrees of the Senate and constitutions of the emperors to institute.” RIG. **An ancient decree.** You have the law itself in Cicero, *On the Laws*, II: “LET NO ONE HAVE GODS SEPARATELY, NOR NEW GODS; BUT LET THEM NOT WORSHIP FOREIGN GODS PRIVATELY UNLESS THEY HAVE BEEN PUBLICLY ADOPTED.”], that no god should be consecrated by the emperor [Note: [Col. 0289C] **By the emperor.** He provides an example in Tiberius, who attempted to include Christ himself among the gods. HAV.] unless approved by the Senate. [Note: [Col. 0289D] **Unless approved by the Senate.** Prudentius elegantly censures this folly of theirs as well, *Against Symmachus*, book I, verse 223:

> Believing true whatever is done by authority of the Senate,  
> He transferred his faith to statues, and regarded as lords  
> Of heaven those who stand in dreadful ranks of countenance.  
> There is Alcides, etc.

Rhenanus: “should be approved.” On the authority first of the Senate and afterward of the emperors’ consent in admitting someone among the gods, consult Petrus Faber, *Semestria*, book III, chap. 1. There is in Cassius Dio an elegant passage concerning the demolition of the temples of Serapis because they had been built on private initiative. We have produced it at the end of chap. 6. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0290B] “Should be approved,” Paris.].
