Marcus Aemilius knows this from the case of his god Alburnus. [Note: [Col. 0290B] Heraldus and Havercamp: “knows”; Pamelius and Semler: “as”; Rhenanus: “as—he did concerning Alburnus”; Gangnaeus: “as—he does concerning Alburnus.” Etc.] This too supports our case: among you divinity is weighed according to human judgment. Unless God has pleased man, he will not be God [Note: [Col. 0289D] **Unless God has pleased man, etc.** An elegant statement, matched by what he says in chap. XIII: “For, as we remarked above, the status of each god depended on the Senate’s estimation. He was not a god whom man, when consulted, had refused and by refusing had condemned.” Lactantius treats the matter fully in *Divine Institutes* I.15: “For who is so mad as to imagine that heaven is opened to the dead by the consensus and decision of innumerable [Col. 0290B] fools? Or that one can give another something which he himself does not possess? Among the Romans Julius is a god because this pleased the criminal Antony; Quirinus is a god because this seemed good to shepherds, although the one proved the murderer of his own brother, the other the murderer of his fatherland. But if Antony had not been consul, Gaius Caesar, for his services to the commonwealth, would have lacked even the honor accorded to a dead man.” HAV.]; man will now have to be gracious to God.

Tiberius, therefore, in whose time the Christian name entered the world, referred to the Senate what had been reported to him from Syria Palaestina concerning events that had revealed there the truth of that divinity [Note: [Col. 0290B] Heraldus: “received a report—which—had revealed”; Rigault and Havercamp: “the things reported—which—they had revealed.”] [Note: [Col. 0290C] **Tiberius.** Eusebius copied this entire account and inserted it into book II, chap. 2 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Junius cites Eusebius’s Greek words, inasmuch as Eusebius attests that he translated them from Tertullian, after first prefacing them with these words: “Meanwhile, when already throughout every place,” etc.

Especially memorable is what we read in Aelius Lampridius’s *Life of Alexander Severus*: “He wished to build a temple to Christ and admit him among the gods. Hadrian also is said to have contemplated this; he had ordered temples without images to be built in every city. Because they have no divine images, they are today called ‘Hadrian’s temples,’ and it was said that he had prepared them for this purpose. But he was prevented by those who, after consulting the sacred rites, discovered that all men would become Christians if his wish were fulfilled and that the other temples would have to be abandoned.” Indeed, the same Severus, when Christians had occupied a certain place that had been public property, while tavern keepers maintained that it ought to belong to them, issued a rescript that it was better for God to be worshiped there in some fashion than for the place to be given to tavern keepers. The same Lampridius relates this.

Concerning our Tiberius, however, it is worthwhile to compare Tanaquil Faber, vol. II, Epistle XII, who attempts through many arguments to prove that Tertullian was deceived and casts doubt upon the truth of the matter. He uses four arguments: that the story was drawn from a spurious book, namely the *Acts of Pilate*; that Tiberius displayed no concern for religion, for which reason Suetonius calls him “rather negligent concerning the gods and religions”; that the Roman Senate under Tiberius had sunk into the basest flattery and would not even have dared utter a word against the emperor; and that chronology makes it evident that the Christian name was scarcely known at Rome at that time.

To these I add that Tiberius was hostile rather than favorable to the Christian name just as he was to the Jewish, as is clearly apparent from Suetonius, chap. 36: “He suppressed foreign ceremonies and the Egyptian and Jewish [Col. 0291A] rites. Under the pretext of military service, he distributed the Jewish youth among provinces with a more oppressive climate; the rest of that nation, or those who followed similar practices, he expelled from the city under penalty of perpetual slavery if they did not obey.” Here by “those who followed similar practices” none but Christians can be understood.

And though Tiberius, while still a private citizen living at Rhodes, had once been eager to hear Diogenes the grammarian, who was accustomed to lecture on Sabbaths, as Suetonius relates in chap. 32, this can contribute nothing—as Torrentius at least supposed—to the opinion about Christ. For Suetonius teaches the contrary. And indeed those ancient Fathers were excessively credulous and simple; eagerly seizing whatever was offered them, they often fought with leaden swords. HAV.

Havercamp, becoming rather more audacious and, contrary to his custom, carried away by a sudden impulse to quarrel with the ancient Fathers, did not hesitate to press this charge. By what right, I ask? Let the dispute be submitted to the reader as judge. Moreover, there are many excellent testimonies of the ancients—testimonies which can by no means now be despised on account of excessive credulity or simplicity, or as a contemptible leaden sword—by which this report sent by Tiberius to the Senate concerning Christ’s astonishing death is confirmed.

The first witness preserved in human memory is St. Justin Martyr, in his *First Apology to the Emperors*, presented at Rome and almost before the doors of the Senate House, exposed to the watchful envy of hostile hearers. An author so great and so highly commended for his exceptional knowledge of affairs could not have given them so easy an opportunity to refute him and convict him of falsehood. The second witness, and no unequal one, is this very Tertullian of ours [Col. 0291C], by everyone’s admission an accurate investigator of ancient affairs and so peculiarly well informed about the aforesaid tradition that he recorded the same thing once and again in writings intended for the broadest circulation and to be read by the bitterest hostility. Compare St. Justin, *Apology* I, no. 35; Tertullian, *Apologeticum* V and XXI.

We have, moreover, had witnesses continuously succeeding one another and adding their approving vote in each century: namely Eusebius of Caesarea, St. John Chrysostom, Orosius instructed in Augustine’s school, our Gregory of Tours, then Cedrenus and Nicephorus, and a great many others of a later age. Compare Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 2; St. John Chrysostom, Homily 26 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians; and the other ancients collected in Natalis Alexander, sect. I, chap. IV, and J. C. Otto, *On the Writings and Doctrine of St. Justin*, I, p. 110, note 45.

Indeed, the pagan writers themselves support the account: first Pliny, since from his letter to Trajan it is established that governors customarily reported to the emperor whatever memorable events had occurred in their province [Col. 0291D]; then Suetonius, from whom we learn that Tiberius, although rather negligent concerning the gods and religion, was nevertheless eager to hear Jews or Christians disputing; and finally Lampridius, praised by Havercamp himself, who indicates with sufficient clarity how diligently several Caesars investigated matters affecting Christians.

Nor, furthermore, is it difficult to demolish each of the foregoing arguments of Tanaquil Faber and Havercamp. For in answer to the first, the immediate reply is that this opinion of Tertullian is not extracted from the fraudulent *Acts of Pontius Pilate* that are in circulation, but rather drawn from the Senate’s public records and journals. He would certainly not have ventured to assert this so boldly unless he had thoroughly ascertained it.

As to the second, enough seems to have been established by the pagan authors just praised; and in addition we know from Suetonius himself that nothing, small or great, occurred even during Tiberius’s reign, whether concerning public or private affairs, that was not immediately reported to the Senate.

As to the third, I would have you remember that Tiberius had already rejected temples and divine honors, although the Senate advised and entreated him otherwise; consequently, while he was alive, it was not fitting for the Senate to confer them upon anyone.

It is clear that chronology has no bearing on the matter here, since the discussion concerns Christ himself, who suffered in Judaea and rose again before so many witnesses, and by no means the name “Christians,” whether it was adopted earlier or later.

Finally, there is no need to inquire whether Tiberius’s disposition was favorable or hostile, provided that it is established in fact that he was changeable, inclined toward novel and unusual things, and therefore not averse to hearing with pricked-up ears the astonishing report of events accomplished in Judaea.

But whether, says the most learned Mansi, these writings of Pilate to Tiberius still survive is uncertain. For Pseudo-Hegesippus, who recites Pilate’s letters to Tiberius in his epitome of Josephus’s book *On the Jewish War*, is not an authority so securely established as to compel our belief [Col. 0292B]. It is far more uncertain, if such writings perhaps survive among the many and various documents of this kind published from ancient manuscript codices, what is genuine and what spurious. Johann Albert Fabricius collected several examples of these acts in the *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, part I, p. 298, and part IV, p. 456. I myself discovered in a very ancient codex of the eighth century another text entirely different from those of Fabricius, so far as I was able to inspect it with a hurried glance. God willing, when leisure permits me, I shall transcribe it and in due course publish it among the unedited pieces I am preparing. EDD.]

[Col. 0291A] together with the prerogative of his own vote [Note: [Col. 0292B] **Together with the prerogative of his own vote.** Certainly this is astonishing—if true—in a prince who wished to appear to do everything on the Senate’s authority and was a marvelous master of dissimulation, as Tacitus describes him throughout books III and IV of the *Annals* [Col. 0292C], and whose judgment prevailed in a similar case concerning the Sibylline books. Quintilianus, tribune of the plebs, thereupon made a reference to the Fathers concerning a Sibylline book which Caninius Gallus, one of the Board of Fifteen, had sought to have admitted among the other books of the same prophetess, requesting a decree of the Senate on the matter. When this had been passed by division, Caesar sent a letter mildly rebuking the tribune as ignorant of ancient custom because of his youth. He reproached Gallus because, although long experienced in sacred knowledge and ceremonies, he had brought the matter before a sparsely attended Senate despite the uncertain authorship, before obtaining the judgment of the college and without having the poem, as was customary, read and evaluated by its officials. *Annals* VI.12. Christoph Cellarius adheres to Tertullian in Dissertation XIV. HAV.].

The Senate rejected it because it had not itself approved it; Caesar persisted in his judgment, threatening danger to the accusers [Col. 0292A] of Christians. Consult your own records; there you will find that Nero was the first [Note: [Col. 0292C] **Nero was the first.** Eusebius copied this too word for word and transferred it into his accounts of ecclesiastical history, as Junius noted, adding a notable testimony concerning our author. After showing that Nero was infamous for every crime, Eusebius begins thus: “To all these things, therefore, this remained lacking: that he should be the first of the Roman emperors to turn the arms of impiety even against God himself, as Tertullian, a man most renowned for his writings, relates, saying: ‘Consult,’ etc.”

Jerome in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius: “Nero, in addition to all his crimes, is the first to institute a persecution among the Christians.” Our author likewise says again in chap. XV *Against the Gnostics*: “We read the lives of the Caesars; Nero was the first to stain with blood at Rome the rising faith.”

From this understand the statement of Orosius, who, after speaking in book VII, chap. 8 of the persecution carried out under Trajan, adds: “Nevertheless, immediately afterward at Rome the Golden House, built by Nero at the cost of so many private and public resources, suddenly burned in a conflagration, so that it might be understood that a persecution, though dispatched by another, was punished especially in the monuments of the one from whom it had first arisen, and in its very author.” He had in fact instituted it to remove the hostility which, after Rome was burned, he saw gathering against himself. HAV.] to rage with the imperial [Col. 0293A] sword [Note: [Col. 0293B] **With the imperial sword.** Certainly “sword” is here understood as every instrument by which death is inflicted. For there is no doubt that Tertullian speaks with reference to Peter and Paul; yet Peter did not end his life by the sword. LAC.] against this sect just when it was rising most vigorously at Rome [Note: [Col. 0292D] **Just when it was rising most vigorously at Rome.** The Fulda manuscript has “at greatest Rome.” Rhenanus and Pamelius: “then especially at Rome,” that is, in Nero’s time. This does not please me. The sense is that this sect found its followers nowhere more than at Rome, which Tacitus, *Annals* XV.44, seems to indicate: “Though suppressed for the moment, the deadly superstition broke out again, not [Col. 0293A] only throughout Judaea, the source of that evil, but also throughout the City, where all things atrocious and shameful from every quarter flow together and become celebrated.” HAV.].

Yet we even glory in having such a man as the inaugurator [Note: [Col. 0293B] **Such an inaugurator of our condemnation.** He used *dedicator* to mean the author or first institutor. Thus “he inaugurated repentance,” that is, first instituted it, in *On Repentance*, chap. 2; and in this *Apologeticum*, chap. 12, “the body of your god is first inaugurated on a gibbet,” that is, its beginning is made there.

Sulpicius Severus had regard to these words of our Septimius when he writes in book II of the *Sacred History* that Paul was taken to Rome in Nero’s reign: “I will not say the vilest of kings, but of all men and even of savage beasts, he proved worthy to be the first to begin a persecution of the Christians.” And shortly afterward: “He was the first to attempt to abolish the Christian name; for vices are always hostile to virtues, and all the best men are regarded by the wicked as though reproaching them; for at that time the divine religion had grown strong in the City.” HAV.] of our condemnation. For anyone who knows him can understand that nothing but some great good [Note: [Col. 0293C] **Nothing but some great good.** He praised nothing except some great evil. Suetonius says of him in chap. XXIX: “I have learned from certain persons that he was entirely persuaded that no one was chaste or pure in any part of his body, but that most concealed the vice and covered it by cunning; and therefore, to those who confessed obscenity before him, he forgave their other offenses as well.” Indeed, when that monster had recently been born, an ominous remark of his father Domitius was noted amid the congratulations of his friends: he denied that anything could be born of himself and Agrippina except what was detestable and a public evil, as the same author relates in chap. 6. HAV.] was condemned by Nero.

Domitian too had attempted it, a portion of Nero [Note: [Col. 0293A] “By the first name Nero,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0293A] “By Nero’s prior warning,” Wouwer.] in cruelty [Note: [Col. 0293C] **In cruelty.** This is the true and genuine reading, which our author confirms in chap. XI: “Yet how many more excellent men have you left in the underworld: some Socrates for wisdom, Aristides for justice, Themistocles for military skill, Alexander for sublimity, Polycrates for good fortune, Demosthenes for eloquence,” and elsewhere.

He did not add “in cruelty” without reason, for in cruelty Domitian showed himself a portion of Nero; in his remaining vices he was more of a human being, as the author immediately added. His nature is plainly shown by that episode involving his hour spent catching flies. Suetonius, chap. 3. In chap. 10 Suetonius likewise speaks of him thus: “But he did not persist in a course either of clemency or of abstinence; nevertheless, he declined somewhat more quickly into cruelty than into greed.” And chap. 11: “He was, moreover, possessed not only of great cruelty, but of cunning and unexpected cruelty,” etc. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0293A] “The same cruelty,” Wouwer.]; but, insofar as he was also human [Note: [Col. 0293A] “Because,” Paris; “what?” Wouwer.] [Note: [Col. 0293D] **Insofar as he was also human.** This is the best reading, acknowledged by the printed editions and the better manuscripts, including the Leiden manuscript, although the Fulda manuscript has “because a human being,” and Rhenanus “because also a human being,” less accurately. For this wording is confirmed by the author himself below, chap. 30: “They know who gave them their empire; they know by whom they are human beings.” Petronius: “For I too am a human being.” Tertullian means that Domitian, who unlike Nero had not entirely cast off all humanity, finally changed his judgment. HAV.], he readily suppressed what he had begun [Note: [Col. 0294A] “What he had received,” Paris.], even restoring those whom he had banished [Note: [Col. 0293D] **Even restoring those whom he had banished.** From Hegesippus—whom our author followed—Eusebius repeats this at *Ecclesiastical History* III.20: “In addition to this, Domitian, since he found no crime in them and regarded their usefulness as utterly contemptible, ordered them to depart freely. Moreover, through new edicts he suppressed the persecution which he had ordered to be conducted against the churches” [Col. 0294B]. Thus Hegesippus.

After Eusebius, Zonaras and Nicephorus rehash his words, writing that Domitian κατα παῦσαι διὰ προστάγματος τὸν κατὰ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας διωγμόν, “put an end by an edict to the persecution against the Church”, that is, “after issuing an edict, suppressed the persecution of the Church.” Among these banished persons Eusebius—and Jerome after him—also relates that Flavia Domitilla, niece on his sister’s side of the consul Flavius Clemens, was banished to the island of Pontia because she had professed herself a Christian, in the year 2110. Concerning this Flavius Clemens, who himself was not alien to the rites of Christ and was the emperor’s cousin, we have more at chap. XLII.

Orosius, however, more correctly attributes this to Nerva in book VII, chap. 7: “By his first edict he recalled all the exiles. Hence John the Apostle too, freed by this general indulgence, returned to Ephesus.” And Xiphilinus on Nerva: ὁ Νερούας τούστε κρινομένους ἐπ` ἀσεβείᾳ ἀφεῖκε, καὶ τοὺς φεύγοντας κατήγαγε, “Nerva acquitted those who had been charged with impiety and restored the exiles”, that is, “Nerva acquitted those who had been charged with impiety”—he means the Christians, as we note above somewhere from Dio—“and restored the exiles.”

Since it is therefore established that it was not Domitian, that savage and bloodthirsty man, but the most gentle old man Nerva Cocceius who recalled the banished, the great Scaliger, in his notes on Eusebius, p. 205, not undeservedly marks this as an σφάλμα μνημονικόν, “a lapse of memory” of Tertullian or of those whom he follows [Col. 0294C]. You will free the most learned Father from this fault if, with the Vatican codex, you delete this entire passage.

If my own judgment is to receive any consideration, however, the author wrote *restituistis*, “you restored,” rather than *restitutis*, “having restored”; the following words confirm this: “those condemned by whom you have been accustomed to restore.” Thus he would be saying that Domitian did not continue persecuting Christians with equal severity to the very end; indeed, that the Roman people afterward permitted the exiles to return.

The matter would certainly be clear if the manuscripts read as follows: “But the good Nerva readily suppressed what had been begun, even restoring those who had been banished.” He was assuredly a most highly praised prince, who changed all things for the better and was called “peaceful and most gentle” by Martial, book VIII, epigram 70:

> As great as peaceful Nerva’s repose, so great is his eloquence;

and XII.6:

> Nerva, gentlest of its princes, has fallen to the Ausonian court;  
> Now it may enjoy the whole of Helicon.

Nerva is expressly called “good” by Symmachus I.13. The same poet aspires in his thoughts to those happy times when, in the episode of the dove that had flown down into Aretulla’s lap, he plays among other things with these lines, book VIII.32:

> If it is right for a devoted sister to hope for better things,  
> And if prayers have power to bend the lord of the world,  
> This [dove], perhaps, for you from the Sardinian shores of exile,
When the brother was about to return, a bird came as messenger. HAV.]

Such have always been our persecutors [Note: [Col. 0294A] “Persecutors,” Wouwer]: unjust, impious, disgraceful—men whom you yourselves have also been accustomed to condemn, and whose condemned victims you have been accustomed to restore. Moreover, from among all the rulers since then [“down to” [Note: [Col. 0294A] “Down from” is absent from the Paris manuscript.]] and down to the present, men wise in divine and human matters [Note: [Col. 0294D] **Wise in divine and human matters.** The highest praise, which Pompeius Trogus, a most distinguished writer, ventured also to bestow upon Joseph, son of the patriarch Jacob—if the words read in Justin XXXVI.2 are his: “For he was both exceptionally skilled in prodigies and the first to establish an understanding of dreams, and nothing concerning divine or human law seemed unknown to him.” HAV.], produce a single vanquisher [Note: [Col. 0294D] **Vanquisher.** By contrasting this with “protector,” he shows what he means by “vanquisher”: not, namely, an exterminator, but an assailant, a persecutor. Theodoret likewise places in the same order the emperors here named by Tertullian, except that, by a contrary reckoning, he calls them all persecutors of the Church, though they were unable to vanquish and extinguish it. The accounts will agree, however, if you say—as is in fact the case—that all of them acted covertly, but not with open violence like Nero or Domitian. Thus he says on p. 126: Τὼν δὲ ἀλιέων τε καὶ τελωνῶν, etc., that is: “But the laws which our fishermen and publicans, and which the tentmaker, enacted and promulgated, neither Gaius nor Claudius was able to annul, nor Nero, who succeeded them. For although Nero in his savagery struck down two excellent lawgivers—for he ordered Peter and Paul to be killed—he certainly did not abolish the laws they had promulgated. Nor, finally, did Vespasian, Titus, or Domitian, although Domitian strove to attack them with many and various devices; for he removed many who had devoted themselves to those laws, directing every kind of torture against them. Trajan and Hadrian, moreover, equipped themselves with a great apparatus against those laws. Trajan indeed dissolved the power of the Persians, subjected the Armenians to the Roman bridle, and compelled the Scythian nations besides to obey his scepter; yet he could not abolish the laws of the fishermen and of our tentmaker. [Col. 0295C] Hadrian utterly destroyed and overthrew the city of the Jews, by whom Christ was crucified; yet he could not draw those who believed in Christ away from the service of Christ.” HAV.] of the Christians.

[Col. 0295A] We, on the contrary, produce a protector, if the letters [Note: [Col. 0295C] **The letters of Marcus Aurelius.** Jerome, under the year 174 of the Christian era: “When many wars arose against him, the emperor Antoninus often took part in person and often appointed the most distinguished generals. On one occasion, when Pertinax and the army fighting with him in the territory of the Quadi were oppressed by thirst, rain was sent by divine agency; meanwhile thunderbolts pursued the Germans and Sarmatians and killed a great many of them. Letters of Marcus Aurelius, that most serious emperor, are extant in which he testifies that the German thirst was dispelled by rain obtained through the prayers of soldiers who happened to be Christians.” On this passage Scaliger must certainly be consulted, as must his judgment concerning the spurious documents circulated under this emperor’s name at the end of Justin’s *Apology*, pp. 222–223. He also adduces this passage from Orosius: “Letters of the emperor Antoninus are still extant among many people, in which he admits that, through the invocation of Christ’s name by Christian soldiers, both that thirst was driven away and victory was granted.” HAV.] of the most serious emperor Marcus Aurelius are consulted; in them he testifies that the German thirst [Note: [Col. 0295A] “That” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0295D] **The German thirst.** A calamity hostile to an army, though one that often occurs. Curtius mentions it in more than one place, and Lucan in Book IX concerning Cato’s army in the Libyan desert; in Spain Afranius and Petreius, because of the same misfortune, were forced to surrender their camp to the victorious Caesar, as the poet treats at greater length in Book IV. Our author again recalls this German thirst, when Marcus was leading his forces against the Marcomanni, in *To Scapula* 4: “Marcus Aurelius too, during the German expedition, obtained rain amid that thirst through prayers offered to God by Christian soldiers. How often have droughts also been driven away by our kneelings and fasts! Then even the people, acclaiming ‘the God of gods’ and ‘the only mighty one,’ bore witness to our God under the name of Jupiter.” Yet the pagans, envying the Christians’ glory, attempted to remove this honor from them. Thus Capitolinus, in his *Life* of Aurelius, attributes it to the emperor’s own holy character: “By his prayers he wrung thunder from heaven against the enemy’s contrivance, while rain was obtained for his own men when they were suffering from thirst.” This is relevant to that Jupiter Pluvius whose image we have reproduced from the Column of Antoninus, and about whom we shall shortly send to press a separate dissertation; compare it, if you please. (I should like you to see this image, which has been published widely, namely in Baronius.) HAV.] was dispelled by rain obtained through the prayers of soldiers who happened to be Christians. Just as he did not openly remove punishment from men of that kind [Note: [Col. 0296B] **Not openly.** Marcus Aurelius wished both to satisfy his conscience and to detract nothing from the laws. Accordingly, to prevent their being readily accused, he established crucifixion as the penalty for informers, although, under the laws, certain death still awaited those who had been accused and convicted and refused to deny the faith. Some, such as Rhenanus, have therefore very badly taken τὸ (“the”) to mean “they did not abolish.” Closely akin to this is what occurs in Esther 8.8, 11, concerning the utterly desperate condition of the Jews and their fortunate escape from danger, and likewise in Daniel 3.29. HAV.], so in another way he openly frustrated it [Col. 0296A] [Note: [Col. 0296B] **Frustrated.** That is, rendered it ineffective, annihilated it, scattered it to the winds. HAV.], by adding condemnation, and indeed a more dreadful condemnation, for the accusers [Note: [Col. 0296B] **By adding also.** This emperor’s rescript to the Asians is extant in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.13. Since it is rather lengthy, students should seek it there. At the end it contains the following: “But if anyone persists in making trouble for men of this kind without any charge, then the person denounced under this name is to be acquitted, even if it is proved that he is what is charged against him—a Christian. The person who advances the charge, however, is to be held liable to the very penalty he proposed.” Add Hadrian’s letter, which will shortly be presented. Yet in that rescript of Aurelius the acquittal of a Christian is falsely stated. For he was not acquitted if he steadfastly defended the faith, but was killed, as is evident from the example of Apollonius in the same Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.21, and as may be seen in Heraldus. But accusation was not readily made, since the informer feared a most certain penalty. Much fraud, however, prevails in these rescripts. Therefore, to use Pliny’s words from that celebrated *Panegyric* addressed to Trajan: “But you, Caesar, what a splendid spectacle you presented to us when it was possible to look down from above upon the upturned faces and twisted necks of the informers! We recognized them and rejoiced when, like expiatory victims offered for the public anxiety, they were led over the blood of the guilty to lingering torments and heavier punishments,” etc. This emperor spoke more truly than that ruined man in Suetonius, *Caligula* 16, who denied that he had ears for informers. [Col. 0296D] For, as Domitian—when not yet brutalized—beautifully says in the same author, chapter 9: “A ruler who does not punish an informer encourages him.” Tacitus truly affirms of them that they are “a class of men devised for the public destruction and never sufficiently restrained by punishments,” *Annals* IV.30. HAV.].

What sort of laws, then, are these which against us are enforced only by the impious [Note: [Col. 0295A] “Are enforced,” Havercamp.], unjust, disgraceful, savage, empty-headed [Note: [Col. 0295A] “Various,” Paris; “savage” is absent from Havercamp.], and mad? Laws which Trajan partly frustrated by forbidding Christians to be sought out; which no Hadrian [Note: [Col. 0296D] **No Hadrian.** The Modian *Collatio* places Hadrian after Vespasian, with Junius’s approval. Yet men who from antiquity were always joined as a distinguished pair of good rulers should not be separated. Gregory Nazianzen, in his second invective against Julian, says that Julian set before himself those Trajans and Hadrians whose caution in avoiding dangers and greatness of spirit in despising them were alike customarily admired: πρὸς τοὺς, he says, βλέπων ἐκείνους, καὶ τοὺς Ἀδριάνους, ὧν οὐχ ἧττον τῆς ἀνδρείας, τὸ ἀσφαλὲς ἐθαυμὰζετο. And so they are commonly joined. Metius Falconius Nicomachus, in his speech to Tacitus upon his election as emperor: “Imitate the Nervas, the Trajans, the Hadrians,” in Flavius Vopiscus’s *Life of Tacitus*. Likewise, in the *Life of Florian*, concerning Probus: “a man to be preferred to Aurelian, Trajan, Hadrian, the Antonines, Alexander, and Claudius.” Indeed, if Lampridius is trustworthy, [Col. 0297B] Hadrian was not entirely averse to the sacred rites of Christ, as we have shown elsewhere in this commentary. Lampridius also joins him, as does our author, with the best emperors in his *Heliogabalus*: “The attentive reader will make compensation for himself when he reads of Augustus, Vespasian, Titus, Trajan, Hadrian, Pius, and Marcus, as against these monstrous tyrants.” Again Flavius Vopiscus, among the acclamations addressed by the Senate to Tacitus, includes this one: “Trajan too came to imperial power as an old man; Hadrian too came to imperial power as an old man; Antoninus too came to imperial power as an old man.” Finally Sextus Aurelius Victor, on Cocceius Nerva: “For what was more prudent or moderate than Nerva? What more divine than Trajan? What more excellent than Hadrian?” This indeed had to be granted both to the reputation of that most learned emperor, which some have assailed, and to the true reading of Tertullian. HAV.], although an investigator of every curiosity [Col. 0297A] [Note: [Col. 0297C] **An investigator of every curiosity.** Appian praises such an interest also in Brutus at the end of Book IV: Ὁ μὲν Κάσσιος, etc. “Cassius, intent upon the single war like a gladiator upon his opponent, regarded nothing else; Brutus, however, wherever he was, was eager to see and hear things, since he had also pursued philosophy in a liberal manner.” This curiosity of Hadrian is certainly noted by Epiphanius in his little book *On Weights and Measures*. When treating of his travels in Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine, he calls him ἄνδρα Φιλοΐστορα (“a man eager for knowledge”). Our author uses this term again in *On the Testimony of the Soul* 1: “Some in whom both the labor of inquiry and the continuity of memory from their earlier literary culture have persisted.” The manuscript glosses used by Barthius, *Adversaria* XIX.1, give: “Curious: accommodating, sharp-tongued, witty, teachable, urbane”—all of which Hadrian was. But if Hadrian was such a man, he had also thoroughly investigated the Christian religion, which by not persecuting it he tacitly commended. Indeed, if Orosius and others, VII.13, are trustworthy, Hadrian was instructed and educated through books composed about the Christian religion by Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, Aristides the Athenian, a man full of faith and wisdom, and Granius the legate, concerning whom see above; and by a letter addressed to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, he commanded that no one be permitted to condemn Christians without a specified and proven charge. HAV.], no Vespasian, although a conqueror of the Jews, no Pius, and no Verus [Note: [Col. 0297B] “Severus,” Paris manuscript.] brought to bear [Note: [Col. 0297D] **Brought to bear.** The expression is taken from military affairs, where cohorts are said “to make an assault” when they charge into the enemy’s battle line and throw it into confusion. Passages are common in the historians, and especially in Caesar. HAV.]. Certainly the worst men would more readily be judged fit to be eradicated by all the best, as their rivals, than by their own associates [Note: [Col. 0297B] “Accordingly,” Semler.].

## CHAPTER VI

**ARGUMENT.—He shows, moreover, that those very noisy champions of the laws and of antiquity have departed as far as possible from their ancestral institutions: since they have become prodigal, extravagant, pleasure-seeking, immodest, arrogant, given to wine, and haters of marriage. Even in religion they have not observed the decrees of the ancients, but have brought foreign religions into Rome and restored those that had been condemned. In pursuing novelty in all things, they have neglected their own gods more than the Christians themselves have. Since he intends to treat this last matter more fully elsewhere, he prepares at the end to refute the false accusations of secret crimes.**

Now I should like these most religious [Note: [Col. 0297D] **Now these most religious.** After showing that laws themselves are corrected, altered, and abolished for public advantage and benefit, he proceeds to teach that even those laws which deserve praise are everywhere badly observed, and that these very men sin against the laws which they so loudly proclaim. “Most religious” must be pronounced ironically, just as in chapter IX he calls Rome “the most religious city of the descendants of Aeneas.”] protectors [Note: [Col. 0298B] Some, including the Fulda manuscript, read “avengers,” and manuscript L.B. has “as avengers,” meaning executors of the punishments threatened by the law. Thus the law itself is said “to avenge,” that is, to punish: “not knowing what it is that the law avenges”; and likewise, “to see the wrongdoer and watch him with an avenging eye.” Publilius Syrus, verse 348:

Tertullian describes this splendidly in *On the Apparel of Women*, chap. IX:

“A tender neck bears forests and islands. The delicate skin of the ears expends a whole account-book, and the left hand plays upon each separate finger with the contents of separate moneybags. Since women’s minds are therefore enslaved to such things, Cato inveighs against them in Livy, book XXXIV:

“What honorable object, even in words, is put forward as a pretext for this women’s agitation? ‘That we may glitter in gold and purple,’ they say”; and shortly afterward: “That there may be no limit to expense or luxury.”

In the same passage Lucius Valerius judges that indulgence should be granted them in these matters:
