> A woman who marries many men does not please many.]

Even regarding your gods themselves, you yourselves, most obedient as you are, have repealed those far-sighted decrees of your fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0304A] Rhenanus: *perspecte*; Rigaltius, Havercamp, and Semler: *prospecte*; the Fulda codex: *specte*.]

By authority of the senate, the consuls had banished Father Liber with his mysteries not only from the city but from all Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0304A] The Paris manuscript deletes “his.”]

Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates, with their Cynocephalus, had been forbidden admission to the Capitol—that is, expelled from the senate-house of the gods. The consuls Piso and Gabinius, who certainly were not Christians, had repudiated them and even overturned their altars, restraining the vices of shameful and idle superstitions.

[Note: [Col. 0305B] **Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates.** The Fulda manuscript and Barraeus’s edition delete the first “and.” These foreign divinities appear joined in this manner on gems in Gorlaeus, vol. II, nos. 468 and 470; the first two appear together in no. 466.]

[Note: [Col. 0305C] **Cynocephalus.** He is everywhere joined to Isis on gems, marbles, and coins.]

[Note: [Col. 0305C] **Forbidden admission to the Capitol.** Their temples were placed outside the city boundary. Dio Cassius, book XL: καὶ ὃτι γε (“and indeed that …”), etc.; that is: “When the resolution prevailed that they should now begin to be worshiped publicly, they placed those gods outside the *pomerium*.” Hence Avienus says of Serapis in Macrobius I.7: “I hear that you admitted him reluctantly.” “To be admitted” is absent from *To the Nations* I.10, as it is here from the Fulda manuscript, and it may be omitted. By all means see Gothofredus’s note on *To the Nations* here.]

[Note: [Col. 0305C] **Even overturning their altars.** This happened more than once. Dio Cassius, in the passage cited: τοὺς γὰρ ναοὺς αὐτῶν (“for their temples …”), etc.; that is: “The senate ordered the shrines of those divinities, which certain private persons had erected, to be demolished, because it did not greatly count them among the gods.” The same author, book XLII: ἔδοξε γνώμη (“the resolution was adopted …”), etc.; that is: “Accordingly, the haruspices ordered all the temples of Isis and Serapis to be demolished.” Valerius Maximus I.III.3: [Col. 0305D] “When the senate had decreed that the shrines of Isis and Serapis should be destroyed, and none of the workmen dared touch them, the consul Lucius Aemilius Paulus laid aside his bordered toga, seized an axe, and struck it into the doors of the temple.”]

You restored these gods and conferred upon them supreme majesty.

[Note: [Col. 0305D] **You restored these gods.** Augustine mentions this in *The City of God* II.14: “Surely even to Priapus or some Cynocephalus, and finally even to Fever—divinities which the Romans partly received from abroad and partly consecrated as their own.” This happened in Caesar’s time, as Dio notes in book XLVII: καὶ νεὼν τῷ τε Σεράπιδι, καὶ τῇ Ἴσιδι ἐψηφίσαντο (“and they decreed a temple for both Serapis and Isis”); that is: “They decreed a temple to Serapis and Isis.”

Ovid, *Art of Love* I.77, speaks of many abominations there:

> Nor shun the Memphite rites of the heifer of the Nile;  
> She makes many women what she herself was to Jupiter.

And III.635:

> Though she sits attending the sistrums of the Pharian Heifer,  
> And where her companions are forbidden to go, let her go.

Accordingly Lucan, VII.83, indignantly addresses Egypt:

> We have received your Isis into Roman temples,  
> And demigod dogs, and sistrums that command mourning,  
> And Osiris, whom by your lamentation you attest to have been a man.

[Col. 0306B] In the second line I would rather read “the half-dog gods.” I do not know whether Ovid says of Pan:

> Both a half-god goat and a half-goat god.

Certainly, concerning the Minotaur, *Art of Love* II.24:

> When Daedalus enclosed the offspring conceived through the mother’s crime,  
> A man half bull and a bull half man.]

Where is religion? Where is the reverence owed by you to your ancestors? In dress, manner of life, furnishings, thought, and finally in speech itself, you have renounced your forefathers.

[Note: [Col. 0306C] **Furnishings.** He means splendid and invidious domestic equipment and apparatus. Isidore, *Origins* V.25: “Equipment is that which is produced through an implement, such as a staff, book, or tablet.” Barraeus and Rhenanus also read “furnishings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0305B] Thus all the manuscripts; Rigaltius reads “property,” and the Paris manuscript adds “and.”]

You are always praising antiquity, yet every day you live in a novel fashion.

[Note: [Col. 0305B] Rigaltius reads “the ancients.”]

From this it is shown that, while you abandon the good institutions of your ancestors, you retain and preserve the things you ought not to have preserved, since you did not preserve those you ought to have preserved.

[Note: [Col. 0305B] Havercamp reads “you preserve.”]

Even the very thing which you appear most faithfully [Col. 0305B] to protect as handed down by the fathers—the matter in which you chiefly mark Christians as guilty of transgression—I mean the zeal [Col. 0306A] for worshiping the gods, concerning which antiquity was most deeply mistaken: although you have rebuilt altars to Serapis, now become Roman, although you have sacrificed your frenzies to Bacchus, now become Italian, I shall show in the proper place that it is likewise despised, neglected, and destroyed by you, contrary to the authority of your ancestors.

[Note: [Col. 0305B] Junius reads “was concerned for.”]

[Note: [Col. 0306C] **To Serapis, now become Roman.** Thus the native brilliance of our author’s antiquity must be restored, as I have also shown above. Shortly afterward read, as printed, “now become Italian.” Lucan elegantly says in I.63, addressing Nero:

> But to me you are a god already;

and in IX.158 the fierce Pompeian, intending to avenge his ancestral ashes, threatens in these words:

> I shall cast forth from her shrine Isis, now a goddess to the nations.

These passages—and many others like them throughout all the ancient writers—must be corrected in this fashion. Seneca the tragedian likewise says in *Hercules Furens*, line 2, “the ever-foreign [Col. 0306D] Jupiter.”

What Spartianus reports of Hadrian in his *Life* is pertinent here: “He most diligently observed the Roman rites; foreign rites he despised.” By contrast, the same author says of Bassianus Caracalla in his *Life*: “He brought the rites of Isis to Rome and everywhere built magnificent temples for that goddess. He also celebrated her rites with greater reverence than they had been celebrated before.” Here it seems strange to me that the rites of Isis are said first to have come to Rome through this man, since Antoninus Commodus celebrated them in such a way that he even carried Anubis and made way for the procession—unless perhaps Caracalla added to their solemnity rather than first introducing them. Lampridius likewise says of Alexander Severus: “He fittingly adorned Isis and Serapis, adding statues, Delian objects, and all the mystical equipment.”]

[Note: [Col. 0305B] The Paris manuscript reads “likewise.”]

For now I shall answer that infamous charge of secret crimes, so that I may clear my way to matters more openly manifest.

[Note: [Col. 0306B] Junius, from Havercamp’s manuscript: “so that I may clear my way to matters more manifest.” Heraldus, Rigaltius, Havercamp, and others restored the passage thus from the codices. The older editions read: “so that from there I may proceed to matters more manifest.”]

## CHAPTER VII

**ARGUMENT.—He therefore challenges them to prove that those whom they consider guilty of the gravest crimes are indeed infant-killers, devourers of children, and finally incestuous persons, and urges them no longer heedlessly to believe rumor, whose origin is often false and whose report uncertain.**

[Col. 0306B] We are called the most criminal of men because of a sacrament involving infanticide, the meal that follows from it, and incest after the banquet—an incest procured by dogs that overturn the lights, acting, of course, as pimps for the darkness and for the shamelessness of impious lusts.

[Note: [Col. 0306B] Junius omits “because of.”]

[Note: [Col. 0306B] Rhenanus reads “a meal of raw flesh.”]

[Note: [Col. 0306D] **And the meal that follows from it.** Some books read, “And a meal of raw flesh,” as though Christians had been charged with feeding upon the raw flesh of a slaughtered infant. Tertullian himself seems to indicate this in *To the Nations* I, when he says: “Yet who ever came upon his own child half eaten?” Here, however, he speaks only of feeding on blood and of bread by which the blood’s gore is gathered up; nor, among what he afterward presents as the instructions of the father of the rites, does he say anything about devouring raw flesh. Nor does he do so in the corresponding passage of *To the Nations*, but speaks of “bread broken in blood, and blood in which the bread is saturated.” Indeed, he says that to convict the Christians they ought to have produced not only child-killers but also cooks: “Let the child-killers and cooks be produced, and the very dogs that procure the unions; the case would be settled.” RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0307B] **Dogs that overturn the lights.** People believed that candlesticks were tied to the dogs and were overturned when the animals leapt toward bones thrown before them. See the following chapter. Among Christians of a later age we read of candles being cast down and extinguished during excommunications, a practice illustrated by Lord Du Cange with many examples in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*. But I do not think this custom was in use in Tertullian’s age.]

[Note: [Col. 0307A] Rigaltius emended from a manuscript: “procure darkness, and then the shamelessness of impious lusts.” Junius deletes “impious.”]

[Note: [Col. 0307C] **Procure shamelessness.** Lucian in *The Lapiths*: ἀλλὰ πολλὰ ἐπράχθη, καὶ δεινὰ ἐν τῷ σκότῳ (“but many dreadful deeds were committed in the darkness”), etc.; that is: “And many serious offenses were committed in the darkness. When at last someone brought a lamp, Alcidamas—for he was a Cynic philosopher—was caught lifting the flute-girl’s garment and preparing to assault her by force.”]

[Note: [Col. 0307A] Wouwer and Havercamp read: “darkness, then the shamelessness of impious lusts they procure.”]

Yet we are always merely *said* to do these things, and you take no care to discover the truth of what has so long been said of us. Therefore either discover it, if you believe it, or cease believing it, since you have not discovered it. From your own deliberate neglect we enter the preliminary objection against you that what even you yourselves do not dare to investigate does not exist.

You prescribe a very different task for the executioner in dealing with Christians: not that they should say what they do, but that they should deny what they are.

[Note: [Col. 0307C] **That they should deny what they are.** “But,” says Tertullian, “do not claim that Christians are condemned after confessing their own shameful conduct. That is so false that by torture you compel them to deny this name, whereas, if they were participants in a crime, its confession ought by every means to be extorted.” Cyprian, following in the footsteps of his master Septimius, says to Demetrianus, p. 256:

“Accused persons who deny that they are implicated in the crime charged against them are tortured, so that the truth of the offense, which is not brought forth by the informer’s voice, may be expressed through bodily pain. But now, when I voluntarily profess and cry aloud, and repeatedly attest again and again that I am a Christian, why do you apply torture to one who confesses? I ought to have been tortured if I denied it.” HAV.]

The origin of this teaching, as we have already stated, is from the reign of Tiberius. Truth began together with hatred of itself; as soon as it appeared, it became an enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0307D] **The origin of this teaching.** “Origin,” “assessment,” “profession”; our author often uses the word thus. See chap. V.]

[Note: [Col. 0307D] **Truth began together with hatred of itself**, etc. The sense is: as soon as truth appeared, it began together with hatred of itself and became an enemy. They therefore not only hold it in hatred but also persecute it as hostile. Junius punctuates thus: “It is from Tiberius, together with hatred of itself.” The Montpellier collation: “Truth began together with hatred of itself, and at the same time is an enemy.” Barraeus: “Truth took hold; as soon as it appeared to exist.” The Leiden parchment manuscript reads: “From Tiberius”; it deletes τό (the Greek article introducing the quoted word “is”) “is.” “Truth began together with hatred of itself; at the same time it appeared and is an enemy.” I read: “Truth began with hatred of itself: as soon as it appeared, it is an enemy,” that is, the moment it appeared. It may also be punctuated thus: “The teaching began together with hatred of itself; truth, as soon as it appeared, is an enemy.”]

It has as many enemies as it has outsiders: the Jews are enemies in consequence of rivalry, the soldiers through extortion, and even the members of our own households through nature.

[Note: [Col. 0307B] The Paris manuscript reads “strictly speaking.”]

[Note: [Col. 0308B] **The soldiers through extortion.** Thinking that they are currying favor with their emperors, they betray, expose, and denounce their fellow soldiers. Tertullian again uses the term “extortioner” in *On Flight in Persecution*, chap. XII: “For what does that extortioner say? ‘Give me money’—surely so that he may not betray him.” And in chap. XIII: “Since you know it is unlikely that our extortioners, once brought into friendship by Mammon, will then receive us into the eternal dwellings.” Likewise, as here he uses “extortion,” so in *To Scapula*, chap. IV: “Pudens also, when a Christian was sent to him, understood from the written charge that the man had been subjected to extortion; he dismissed him after tearing up that same charge.”

Florus too, book III, in the epitome of the Jugurthine War: “Yet Numidia did not lightly suffer itself to be shaken.” And Flavius Vopiscus, in his *Tacitus the Emperor*: “Tacitus himself was deeply moved by this speech, and the whole senatorial order was shaken.” Indeed, Sallust himself, *Catiline*, chap. XXII: “This deed had at first shaken his fellow conspirators.” He has similarly used “rivalry” for “hatred,” as explained above. In place of “as many outsiders as,” the Montpellier collation has “so many outsiders,” an evident corruption. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0308C] **Through nature.** Through the natural hostility which they bear toward us, as Zephyrus says. Certainly, a slave angered against his master because his freedom has been taken away is everywhere conceived as harboring a hostile disposition toward him. “For it is natural both to hate the man whom you fear, and, if you can, to attack the man whom you dread,” says Minucius Felix, p. 31 of Ouzel’s edition. Long before him Seneca had said the same in *On Benefits* IV.19: “No one loves those whom he fears.”

He may be thought to have had regard to that saying of our Savior by which he reveals the lot of the Gospel, Matthew X.36: Καὶ ἐχθροί τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὶ οἰκιακοί αὐτου (“And a man’s enemies are the members of his own household”). Relevant here also are the words of Chrysostom in his homily on Saints Bernice and Prosdoce, whom their own father betrayed together with his wife Domnina, their mother. His words are:

“For this war was twofold”—he is speaking of the condition of the Church—“one part arising within, the other without; the former from members of the household, the latter from enemies; one brought upon them by strangers, the other by relatives,” etc.]

Every day we are besieged; every day we are betrayed; most often we are seized in the very midst of our assemblies and congregations. Who ever came upon an infant wailing in such a manner? Who ever disclosed to a judge bloodstained mouths of Cyclopes and Sirens just as he had found them?

[Note: [Col. 0308A] The Paris manuscript reads “Sirens” in a variant form.]

[Note: [Col. 0308D] **Reserved.** Thus the Puteanus manuscript and the Montpellier collation. The preceding words, “bloodstained, just as he had found them,” show this to be the true reading. Nevertheless, I do not wholly condemn *reseravit*, “unbarred,” which Barraeus, Pamelius, and La Cerda have; for it can mean that the savage maw of a beast-like human being, closed as though by the bolt of its row of teeth, was forcibly broken open, so that pieces of human flesh not yet sent down into the stomach might be discovered in the mouth. He joined Sirens to Cyclopes because it was thought that both men and women were allied in this crime among the Christians. Rhenanus wrongly has “evidence” in place of “judge.”]

[Note: [Col. 0308A] The Agobardinus and Lyons codices read “reserved the evidence”; Heraldus, Rigaltius, and Havercamp, “reserved it for the judge”; Rhenanus, “reserved the evidence”; Gangnaeus and Semler, “disclosed it to the judge.”]

Who ever detected any unclean traces of such things even upon their wives?

[Note: [Col. 0308B] Havercamp conjectures: “ever any.”]

Who, on discovering such crimes, concealed them or sold his silence, while nevertheless dragging the people themselves to trial?

[Note: [Col. 0308D] **Who, on discovering such crimes, concealed them or sold his silence.** Investigators of crimes are said to “sell” offenses when, after discovering wicked deeds through investigation, they are bribed not to report them before the tribunals. Yet who could believe that criminals were able to buy off their crimes when they themselves were being dragged before the proconsul every day? PAM.

**Or sold his silence, while dragging the people themselves.** The interpreters are silent, or—with the exception of Rigaltius—are variously confused and agitated, as is Heraldus, whose note La Cerda, as often, made his own. Yet the sense is very simple. Tertullian says, “Who, on discovering such crimes, concealed them or sold them?”—not the people, as La Cerda absurdly says in the exposition he placed before his notes, but the crimes themselves, concealing them for an accepted payment—“while dragging the people themselves,” that is, while nevertheless hauling the accused themselves into court for those crimes? Others have “had discovered” in place of “had found.”

Minucius, looking back to this passage, says:

“Nor did we understand that these tales were always being bandied about by the same men and were never investigated or proved, and that throughout so long a period no one came forward to betray the deed, though he would have obtained not only pardon for the act but even favor in the judgment.”

Rhenanus reads “while selling the people themselves.” HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0308B] The Paris manuscript reads “selling.”]

If we are always in hiding, when was what we commit ever betrayed? Indeed, by whom could it have been betrayed? Certainly not by the guilty themselves, since by the rule of all mysteries an obligation of silence is owed.

[Note: [Col. 0309C] **Since by the rule.** The Leiden manuscript gives *cum vetus ex forma*, so that it may be referred to *fides*, “obligation,” which follows. Julius Firmicus, *Astronomica* VII, Preface:

“When Orpheus revealed the ceremonies of the rites to unknown men, at the first threshold he demanded of those whom he initiated nothing other than the necessity of an oath, and demanded it with a certain terrible religious authority, lest the secrets of the religion he had devised and composed be betrayed to profane ears.”

“And Plato constantly kept Timaeus frequently with him, lest he should ever disclose the venerable records of secret discussions to the unskilled; for all these things suffer loss when they are thrust upon ruined and desperate minds.”

Among the Pythagoreans, our Porphyry consecrated religious silence for our feasting mind. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0309B] Semler reads “of every mystery.”]

The Samothracian and Eleusinian mysteries are kept secret. How much more should such things be concealed, when their betrayal will meanwhile provoke even human punishment while divine punishment is being reserved?

[Note: [Col. 0309D] **Samothracian.** “On the island of Samothrace,” says Zephyrus, “certain initiations are said to have existed as remedies against particular dangers. There too the mysteries of the Corybantes and the rites of Hecate were celebrated, and dogs were sacrificed to her at the cave of Zerinthus.” PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0309D] **The Eleusinian mysteries are kept secret.** Nothing is better known, especially since the Eleusinian rites were made more familiar through Meursius, who treats this silence at greater length in chap. XX, from which source everyone drinks. Hence Horace’s familiar lines, *Odes* III.2:

> I shall forbid the man who has divulged  
> The sacred rite of Ceres to remain beneath  
> The same roof with me, or to launch  
> A fragile boat with me.

Our author, however, attributes their silence to shame when he exposes their nakedness in *Against the Valentinians*, chap. I: “For those Eleusinian mysteries too, themselves the heiress of Attic superstition, are silent out of shame.” [Col. 0310C] HAV.

Nearly all the Fathers mention these rites. They were rites dedicated to Ceres and Proserpina, instituted by Musaeus and customarily celebrated in a certain district of Attica called Eleusis. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0309B] The Paris manuscript reads “will destroy them now.”]

[Note: [Col. 0309B] Franciscus reads “are reserved.”]

If, therefore, the guilty themselves are not their own betrayers, it follows that outsiders are. And how do outsiders possess the knowledge, when even pious initiations always exclude the profane and guard against witnesses—unless impious people are less afraid?

[Note: [Col. 0309B] Franciscus reads “impious.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310C] **Pious initiations.** Thus Rigaltius from the Fulda manuscript, and before him Heraldus and La Cerda; so too Tertullian himself in *To the Nations* I.7. One must have an iron mouth and a leaden heart not to approve it. The text used to read “impious initiations.”

“For,” he says, “since pious initiations”—that is, those which are considered pious and sacrosanct among you—“exclude outsiders, is it not much more fitting that impious ones should do so, since they are also terrified by fear of the law?”

At the end the Montpellier collation reads “unless the impious,” with *si* deleted, incorrectly; for above, in chap. III, he likewise spoke elegantly: “unless perhaps some word in the name sounds barbarous or ill-omened,” where *si* is likewise redundant, as it is in the passage La Cerda cited there from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* V.20:

> Unless perhaps, cruel man, this very thing  
> You demand—that he perish.

Likewise in another passage from Pliny, which may be seen there. Shortly afterward the Fulda manuscript reads “unless perhaps the inconsiderate man.” HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0309B] Franciscus reads “and witnesses.”]

The nature of rumor is known to everyone. It is one of your own sayings:

> Rumor is an evil swifter than any other.

Why is rumor an evil? Because it is swift? Because it reports? Or because it is very often false? Even when it conveys some truth, it is not without the vice of falsehood, for it subtracts from, adds to, and alters the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0309B] The Paris manuscript reads: “The nature of rumor is known to everyone. It is rumor …”]

[Note: [Col. 0309B] Semler reads “the evil of rumor.”]

What of the fact that its condition is such that it persists only while it lies, and lives only so long as it does not prove its report? For once it has proved it, it ceases to exist and, having as it were completed its function of reporting, hands over the fact. From that point it is the fact that is held and the fact that is named. No one says, for example, “They say this happened at Rome,” or, “Rumor has it that he was allotted a province,” but rather, “He was allotted the province,” and, “This happened at Rome.”

[Note: [Col. 0310B] The Paris manuscript reads: “Rumor has it that this happened at Rome.”]

Rumor, the name of uncertainty, has no place where there is certainty. Would anyone believe rumor except an inconsiderate person? A wise man does not believe what is uncertain.

[Note: [Col. 0310B] Havercamp emended the passage thus; others read: “because a wise man does not believe what is uncertain.”]

Everyone must judge that, however widely it has been spread through self-display and however strongly constructed through assertion, it must once have arisen from a single originator and thereafter crept through the offshoots of tongues and ears.

[Note: [Col. 0310B] Rigaltius reads “will be.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310B] The Paris manuscript has a variant form of “judge.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310D] **Everyone must judge**, etc. He wishes it to be understood that, however great the display with which rumor is spread and however openly it is affirmed, it nevertheless has only one originator, and all those others are no more to be regarded than if only one person were speaking. Indeed, through enlargement, alteration, subtraction, and addition, the truth is lost. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0310B] The Paris manuscript deletes “it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310D] **The offshoots of tongues.** Thus he elegantly calls what the Hebrews termed “another tongue.” Hence “the offshoot of incest” in chap. I; and in *Prescription Against Heretics*, chap. XXXII, the disciples and successors of the apostles are called offshoots of those whom the apostles appointed to the episcopate—“offshoots of the apostolic seed.”]

Thus the defect of a tiny seed obscures all the rest of the report, so that no one reflects whether that first mouth may have sown a lie, as often happens either from a disposition toward rivalry, from the caprice of suspicion, or from a pleasure in lying which is not newly acquired but innate in certain people.

[Note: [Col. 0310B] The Paris manuscript reads “obscure.”]

But it is well that time reveals all things—as even your own proverbs and maxims testify—through the arrangement of nature, which has so ordered matters that nothing remains hidden for long, even what rumor has not spread.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] **Time reveals all things, as even your own proverbs testify.** Aulus Gellius, book XII, chap. 2: “Another of the ancient poets, whose name I cannot now recall, said that Truth was the daughter of Time.” There are also verses of Sophocles to this effect:

Πρὸς πάντα κρύπτε μηδὲν, ὡς ἁπανθ` ὁρῶν

Καὶ πάντ` ἀκούων, πάντ` ἀναπτύσσει χρόνος (“Hide nothing in any matter, since Time, seeing everything and hearing everything, reveals everything”). RIG.]

Rumor, therefore, has deservedly remained for so long the sole party privy to the Christians’ crimes. This is the informer you bring forward against us—the informer who has not yet been able to prove what it once proclaimed and, over so long a span of time, strengthened into accepted opinion.

[Note: [Col. 0311B] **Christians’ crimes.** The following words occur here: “What is said always exists, because what exists ceases to be said.” Only the Fulda manuscript supplies them. Scioppius wrote beside them, “A witty saying, worthy of Tertullian’s claw.” Rigaltius passed them over; La Cerda rejects them and admits that he cannot grasp the sense, which here might be that what is said always “exists”—that is, Christians are always regarded as impious because this is said of them—whereas what truly exists is not said but simply exists. But this is a remarkable sophism, like that in Aristophanes’ *Frogs*, Act V, scene 1, where Aeschylus catches Euripides out:

ΕΥ. Εἶτ` ἐγένετ` αὖθις ἀθλιώτατος βροτῶν (“EURIPIDES: Then again he became the most wretched of mortals”).  
ΛΙ. Μὰ τὸν Δί` οὐ δήπον παύσατο (“ΛΙ [uncertain speaker label; the context identifies Aeschylus]: No, by Zeus! Surely he did not cease [to be wretched]”).

EURIPIDES: “Afterward he suddenly became the most wretched of men.”

AESCHYLUS: “No, by Jupiter! For he never ceased to be wretched.”

They are speaking of Oedipus. Apart from this, the sense here would be excessively strained. Accordingly, after a pause for reflection, I confidently pronounce that these words belong with those found earlier in this chapter: “And it lives only so long as it does not prove its report.” HAV.]

## CHAPTER VIII

[Note: [Col. 0311] This note appears at the foot of column 313, but the callout letter, (a), has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0313D] It is astonishing how greatly commentators sometimes labor over the easiest matters, since “harsh grimaces” mean nothing other than a certain disagreeable manner of laughing or an ungenerous contraction of the mouth, while “clothed in hides” means the same as “clothed in skins.” EDD.]

**ARGUMENT.—He shows that the charges are not merely false but, as contrary to the testimony of nature, incredible, and does so in vehement language. He then removes the objections that new Christians are supposedly led astray through ignorance and imposture and afterward do not dare to denounce them for fear of punishment, since, on the contrary, they are people who prefer death to shameful acts.**

[Col. 0311B] To invoke the testimony of nature itself against those who presume that such things ought to be believed, behold, we set before you the reward of these crimes: they promise eternal life. Believe it for the moment. For what I ask concerning this is whether even you who believed it would value eternal life so highly that you would attain it with such a thing upon your conscience.

[Note: [Col. 0311C] **To invoke the testimony of nature itself.** After showing that empty and very often false rumor ought not to be believed, he attempts to demonstrate from human nature itself that the crime charged against Christians cannot apply to any human being. HAV.]

Come, plunge the blade into an infant who is no one’s enemy, guilty before no one, the child of all.

[Note: [Col. 0311D] **Come, plunge the blade.** He presents this as though it were the law of Christianity by which a person about to be initiated into its rites is prepared. He says “plunge the blade” with reference to the wounds which people believed were made in the infant with needles thrust through the surface of a layer of meal. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0311D] **The child of all.** Born from a promiscuous and uncertain union. Learn from Epiphanius concerning the Gnostics, Heresy XXVI:

ἐὰν δὲ καὶ προληφθῇ τις αὐτῶν (“But if any one of them should also be overtaken …”), etc.

“But if someone has been overtaken so that the emission of the natural discharge enters and the woman becomes pregnant, hear what still more grievous and horrible deed such people commit. At whatever time they finally undertake the act, they remove the fetus, receive it, and pound it in a kind of mortar with a pestle. After mixing in honey, pepper, and certain other spices and ointments to avert nausea, they all assemble—the companions of these swine and dogs—and partake of the crushed child. When they have thus completed the eating of human flesh, they afterward pour out prayers to God. ‘We were not mocked by the prince of desire,’ they say, ‘but have gathered up our brother’s transgression.’” HAV.]

Or, if this is another person’s office, simply stand beside a human being dying before he has lived.

[Note: [Col. 0312B] **A human being dying before he has lived.** Frequent darts—sharp ones: he presses on and drives the point home. Lucan likewise, II.109:

> By what crime could little children deserve slaughter?  
> Yet it is enough that they are now capable of dying.

On an ancient marble, where the funeral of an old woman and a little boy is lamented, there is this conclusion:

> Barely to have seen the light was enough for one who might have lived.]

Restoration notes: S000305 is syntactically fragmentary because its implicit subject is absent; the replacement marks this uncertainty.; S000307 contains the recovered accentuation μέγὰ, and S000309 has unaccented καθιερευον; both are preserved verbatim.; In S000305, the recovered opening verb Ἓθέτο is syntactically uncertain and does not clearly support the Latin sense that follows; it is therefore preserved verbatim and marked as possibly corrupt.  

She who did not wish to live could scarcely have died. Nor is Job’s dreadful imprecation far removed from this, 10:18–19: “Why did you bring me forth from the womb? Would that I had breathed out my life, and no eye had seen me! I should have been as though I had not existed; from my mother’s womb I should have passed to the grave.” HAV.]; wait for the new soul as it flees [Note: [Col. 0311B] “Watch,” Paris.]; receive the raw blood, soak your bread in it, and eat gladly. Meanwhile, as you recline at table, count the places: where your mother is, where your sister is; mark them carefully, so that, when the dog-induced darkness falls, you do not make a mistake. For you will have committed a sacrilege unless you have committed incest [Note: [Col. 0311B] Havercamp conjectures: “For [it will be] a sacrilege unless you have committed or admitted incest” [syntax uncertain].]. Initiated and sealed by such rites, you live forever. I want you to answer whether eternity is worth so great a price—or, if it is not, whether it is therefore not to be believed. Even if you believed it, I deny that you would wish it; even if you wished it, I deny that you could do it. Why, then, can others do it, if you cannot? Why can you not, if others can? We have, I suppose, a different [Note: [Col. 0312B] “You,” Wouwer.] [Col. 0312B] nature: [Note: [Col. 0312B] “Cyclopes,” Wouwer. “Cynophanes,” Franeker.] are we dog-faced men [Note: [Col. 0312C] **Cynopaene.** The old manuscripts agree overwhelmingly. *Cynopenne*, in place of *Cynopaene*, that is, *Cynopesne*. Tertullian calls the *Cynopes* *Cynopae*, as he calls the Sirens *Sirenae*, p. 308A, and the Amazons *Amazonae*, vol. II, *Against Marcion*, book IV. The *Cynopes* or *Cynopae* are the Cynocephali, men with dogs’ heads, concerning whom Pliny speaks, from the Indian accounts of Ctesias, book VII, chapter 2; and he also places the Sciapods next to them. Tertullian, moreover, has borrowed not a little from Pliny. Augustine too, in *The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 8, lists the Sciapods, and immediately afterward the Cynocephali. It should be noted in passing that the same Augustine reports that such races of men—or quasi-men—[Col. 0312D] were depicted in mosaic on the seaside promenade at Carthage, from books, as he himself says, drawn as though from the storehouse of a more curious history. RIG.] or Sciapods [Note: [Col. 0312D] **Sciapods.** Pliny, book VII, chapter 2: “They are likewise called Sciapods because, lying supine on the ground in the greater heat, they protect themselves with the shadow of their feet.” Hesychius: Σκιάποδες οἱ ἐν Λιβύῃ πλατεῖς ἔχουσι τοὺς πόδας καὶ ποιοῦσι σκίαν αὐτοῖς ἐν τῷ καύματι. “The Sciapods are peoples in Libya who have broad soles to their feet and use them to make shade for themselves in the heat.” Stephanus of Byzantium likewise says of them: Σκιάποδες, ἔθνος Αἰθιοπικὸν, ὡς Ἐκαταῖος ἐν περιηγήσει Αἰγύπτου. “The Sciapods, an Ethiopian people, as Hecataeus says in his *Description of Egypt*.” HAV.]? Do others have different rows of teeth [Note: [Col. 0312D] **Different rows of teeth.** Like the dragons of Cadmus. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book III, near the beginning:

> Their teeth stand in a triple row.

Solinus, chapter 52, says the same of those furnished with dogs’ heads: “Megasthenes writes that throughout the various mountains of India there are peoples with dogs’ heads, armed with claws, clothed in coverings of hides, possessing no voice for human speech but sounding only with barks, with savage jaws.” For I maintain that Solinus wrote *rictibus*, “jaws,” not *ritibus*, “customs,” as Salmasius emends it: Maltese lapdogs have one kind of mouth, Molossian hounds another. Lucretius, V.1062, is perfectly clear:

> When first the great soft jaws of the Molossian dogs,  
> Provoked, begin to growl, baring their hard teeth,  
> With a far different sound, drawn tight in rage, they threaten  
> When now they bark and fill everything with their voices.

Lucretius calls their jaws “soft” with respect to the skin and flesh covering the mouths of the Molossians, which are extremely soft to the touch; Solinus calls them “savage jaws” with respect to their teeth. In the same passage of Solinus, where that great scholar is very anxiously perplexed, I do not doubt that one should read: “clothed in coverings of tigers or panthers”; for this is what Pliny calls “the skins of wild beasts.”], or different sinews for incestuous lust? You who believe these things of a human being are also capable of doing them. You yourself are a human being, as is the Christian. If you cannot do them, you must not [Col. 0313A] believe them. For the Christian too is a human being, just as you are. But the ignorant are deceived and imposed upon. For people knew nothing of anything of this kind being asserted about Christians—something surely to be guarded against and investigated with every vigilance. And yet it is customary, I suppose, for those wishing to be initiated first to approach that father of the rites [Note: [Col. 0313C] **That father of the rites.** He who was called ἱεροφάντης (*hierophant*); concerning him, see many things worth knowing in Meursius’s delightful little book *Eleusinia*, chapter XIII. In *To the Nations* I.7: “to approach the master of the rites, or the father.”] and set down what must be prepared [Note: [Col. 0313C] **Set down.** Namely, from the ritual books, which were contained between two stones fitted together with the greatest exactness, something they called πέτρωμα (*petrōma*, “stone case”), as may likewise be learned from Meursius’s *Eleusinia*, chapter X. Pausanias, *Arcadia*, p. 249 in the Wechel edition, where he discusses the Pheneatae, who share all their customs with the Athenians: Φενεάταις δὲ καὶ Δήμητρος ἔστιν ἱερόν Ἓλευσινίας, etc.; that is: “Among the Pheneatae there is also a sanctuary of Demeter surnamed Eleusinia, in which the initiations are performed according to the same rite as at Eleusis, although they themselves believe that those rites were first instituted among them.” And immediately afterward: “Near the sanctuary of Eleusinia stand two very large projecting stones, one fitted exactly upon the other. They call these stones *Petroma*. When the annual sacred day of the rites which they call the Greater Mysteries approaches, they separate them and take from them written documents in which the order of the procession and everything that must be done are recorded. After arranging for this register to be read aloud in the hearing of the officiating priests, they replace it in its former position that very night.”]. Then he says: “You need an infant, still tender, one who does not understand death and will smile beneath your knife; likewise bread with which you may collect the gravy of its blood [Note: [Col. 0313B] Rhenanus, Barraeus, and the Agobardine manuscript read “poisonous matter.”]; besides this, lampstands and lamps, and some dogs and morsels of food which will make them stretch themselves out so as to overturn the lights [Note: [Col. 0314B] “Made them stretch themselves out.” At first I thought of *incendant*, “set them alight”; but Tertullian certainly wrote it this way. For he says that dogs “stretch themselves out” when, throwing themselves onto their feet in hope of prey, they loosen the joints of the body and extend their coils; for the expression denotes the length of a dog’s body, which expands in motion. Ovid is perfectly clear in *Metamorphoses*, book XII, verse 476, concerning the centaur Latreus, killed by Caeneus:

> As he boasted thus, Caeneus  
> With a cast spear pierced the flank stretched out in running,  
> Where the man was joined to the horse.];

“above all, you must come with your mother and sister.” What if they are unwilling, or if you have neither? What, finally, of Christians who are alone? There will be no legitimate Christian, I suppose, unless he is a brother or a son. [Col. 0313B] What, then, even if all these things are prepared without their knowledge? Surely afterward they come to know, endure, and condone them. They are afraid of being punished—though, if they proclaimed them, they would deserve protection, and though they would even prefer to die voluntarily rather than live with such a conscience. Come now, let them be afraid; why do they also persevere? For it follows that you should no longer wish to be what, had you known beforehand, you would never have become.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0314A]

**ARGUMENT.—That, in truth, all those crimes falsely alleged against Christians are found actually to exist among their Gentile accusers: among them human sacrifices are committed, formerly openly and now secretly; murders are watched in the theater with delighted eyes; infanticides are committed every day by exposing newborn children, even by killing the offspring or inducing abortion; the blood of newly slain gladiators is also thirsted after; human food is sought from men condemned to wild beasts; indeed, they mutually inflame one another against themselves. Christians, by contrast, recoil from all bloodshed, even that of animals. Among the Gentiles incest is committed every day because, through indiscriminate fornication and the exposure of offspring, children are unknown even to their parents. All these things are utterly foreign to Christians, since they are chaste and continent, and some among [Col. 0314B] them are strangers even to lawful sexual intercourse. Nor can these charges against Christians be believed by anyone except those who believe and themselves commit such acts, and who judge others by themselves.**

To refute these things more fully, I shall show that they are done by you [Note: [Col. 0314C] **I shall show that they are done by you.** Porphyry, in Theodoret, pp. 108–109, *Cure of the Greek Affections*: Ἓθέτο γὰρ, φησὶν, ἐν Ῥόδῳ [the recovered opening verb may be corrupt; as recovered, approximately, “For [someone] set it, he says, in Rhodes”], etc. “For,” he says, “on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November a man was sacrificed among the Rhodians in honor of Saturn. After this practice had been observed for a very long time, it became customary. For they kept alive until the Saturnalia one of those who had been condemned by public sentence to capital punishment.” In the same place he adds other peoples who agreed to this unspeakable rite. Indeed, Lactantius notes in *Divine Institutes* I.13 that it was once written in the *Sacred History* of Ennius that Saturn and Ops, and the other people of that time, were accustomed to eat human flesh, but that Jupiter was the first to give human beings laws and customs and prohibited by edict [Col. 0314D] the eating of that food. What modesty—or rather, what shamelessness—is it to reproach another for something you see yourself doing? To make those things a reproach and charge which may be turned back against you in reciprocal retaliation? So Arnobius speaks in book II. HAV.], partly openly and partly secretly—the very fact on account of which, perhaps, you also believed them of us. Infants in Africa [Note: [Col. 0314D] **Infants in Africa.** If anyone desires the testimonies of the ancients, let him consult Elmenhorst and others on that passage of Minucius, p. 34: “Rightly, in some parts of Africa, infants were sacrificed, with caresses and a kiss suppressing their wailing, lest a tearful victim should be sacrificed.” Plutarch too, in the *Sayings*, relates that the tyrant Gelon, after defeating the Carthaginians at Himera, compelled them to write into their treaty that they would cease sacrificing their children to Saturn. HAV.] were sacrificed publicly to Saturn down to the proconsulship [Note: [Col. 0314D] **The proconsulship of Tiberius.** Heraldus, in his notes, attests that Scaliger solved—or rather cut—the knot which had greatly tormented scholars. And indeed his Letter 66 to Casaubon is worth reading, where he argues that these sacrifices were abolished by a propraetor or proconsul of Tiberius, who, according to Pliny, had also abolished the bloody sacrifices of the Gauls. Though I believe this to be true, I nevertheless cannot approve that distinguished man’s emendation, “down to the proconsul of Tiberius”; for so he reads, although the printers, contrary to his opinion, produced “proconsulship.” For he offended against Tertullian’s idiom, which certainly required “proconsulship,” but in such a way that by it he meant “proconsul,” just as he often speaks in this book: for example, when he said “shipwrecks” for the shipwrecked themselves in chapter 39, and elsewhere “ministries” for ministers. HAV.] of Tiberius, who exposed those very priests, alive, upon votive crosses among the same trees of their temple that cast their shadow over its crimes [Note: [Col. 0315B] **Trees of their temple that cast their shadow over its crimes.** He says that the trees concealed in their own darkness the crimes of the temple and its rites, just as in chapter VII he said of the dogs that they were pimps of darkness. From this appears the extremely ancient custom of shading temples with trees, both because of the awe of religion and to ward off the force of the winds, as is done today. And since a particular tree was dedicated to each god, that tree accordingly shaded the temple of its own god. In Virgil, *Aeneid* II.713, Aeneas says to his companions:

> As you leave the city there is a mound and an ancient temple  
> Of deserted Ceres, and beside it an aged cypress.

Here Servius learnedly notes that the poet appropriately placed a funeral tree before the temple of the mourning goddess. A noble monument to this antiquity [Col. 0315C] is presented by the engraving upon a gemstone displayed in Gorlaeus’s *Dactyliotheca*, vol. II, no. 321, where there is a sacred rite and a tree beside it; it will presently be reproduced by us at note ten. Moreover, just as our author says “upon the same trees,” so Seneca, speaking of a certain man’s obscene lust in *Natural Questions* I.17, says of that monster: “He ought to have been sacrificed to his own mirror.” And Nazianzen says that those who threw disemboweled Christian women stuffed with barley to pigs deserved to feed their own demons. See the passage itself below at the words “still belching from indigestion,” in this chapter. Pamelius omitted a comma after “crimes.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0315A] Havercamp adds “alive” from the Fulda manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0315C] **He exposed them alive upon votive crosses.** We have supplied the word “alive” from the Fulda manuscript; Rigaltius certainly ought not to have neglected it as he did. I explain “votive crosses” with the same Rigaltius as follows: this Tiberius made votive crosses from the votive trees, upon which those criminal priests hung handsomely like votive offerings. Lucian relates a certain sacrificial rite not far removed from this in *The Syrian Goddess*, p. 910: Δένδρα μεγάλα ἐκκόψαντες, etc. “They place large felled trees in the courtyard; afterward they bring goats, sheep, and other living livestock, and hang them from those trees. Among them are also birds, garments, and works of gold and silver. After they have arranged everything completely and carried the images of the gods around the trees, they kindle the pyre, and suddenly everything is burned.” HAV.], as the soldiery of our own country testifies [Note: [Col. 0315D] **The soldiery of our own country.** Since Tertullian was born to a father who was a proconsular centurion, someone might suspect that “of our father” should be restored, as indeed the Fulda manuscript is said to present it. But since his father could not have lived as early as the time of the emperor Tiberius, one would have to posit a different Tiberius from this one, a proconsul of whom he was speaking here; and I do not believe that. Soon afterward the same manuscript reads *quae ad ipsum manus* [a materially uncertain phrase], that is, “in his presence”; see the index. But since *illi* follows immediately here, this reading cannot stand. Proconsuls and higher magistrates were accustomed to execute such measures through centurions or tribunes. In an almost similar case, a splendid testimony appears [Col. 0316A] in Prosper of Aquitaine, *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, part III, chapter 38: “Under Constantius and Augusta Placidia, whose son, the pious Christian Valentinian, now [Col. 0316B] reigns, when the tribune Ursus pressed the matter, all those structures were razed to the ground and left the field as a burial place, plainly, for the dead; and now the Vandal hand destroys the very road, leaving no memorial of itself.” HAV.], which discharged that very duty for that proconsul. But even now this sacred crime persists in secret [Note: [Col. 0316B] **It persists in secret.** The offering of a little boy of this kind over a dish held by a Pythian priestess is set before the eyes in the engraving upon this gemstone, once published by Leonardus Augustinus, vol. I, no. 107, where it is shown that a similar sacrifice was offered to Apollo among the Cretans. See plate 1, no. 1. HAV.]. Christians are not the only ones who hold you in contempt [Note: [Col. 0316B] **Christians are not the only ones, etc.** The sense is that Christians are not alone in adhering to their own religion in contempt of idols, since those secret sacrifices to Saturn, although publicly rooted out and forbidden, persist among certain people. HAV.]; no crime is ever rooted out forever, nor does any god change his customs. Since Saturn did not spare his own children, he certainly persisted in not sparing those of others, whom their own parents offered, responding that they did so willingly [Note: [Col. 0315A] The manuscripts of Puteanus, Bongars, Fulda, and Lyon, and the editions of Rhenanus, Pamelius, and Semler have a term solemnly used in sacred rites: “they presented them.” But in the Agobardine manuscript and the other Lyon manuscript the words “and responding willingly” and, below, “they caressed” are absent.] [Note: [Col. 0316B] **They responded willingly.** A familiar term in sacred rites and one found in the best manuscripts—those of Heraldus, Fulda, and Leiden. Barraeus, Rhenanus, and Pamelius wrongly read “they presented them,” which signifies the vow of those wretched parents. Plutarch, at the end of his book *On Superstition*, where he censures this Carthaginian custom, quotes these verses of Empedocles:

> Μορφὴν δ` ἀλλάξαντα πατὴρ, φίλον υἱὸν ἀείρας,
>
> Σφάζει ἐπευχόμενος μέγὰ νήπιος
>
> (“A father, having lifted his beloved son, changed in form, slaughters him with a prayer—the great fool”).

He adds: ἀλλ` εἰδότες, καὶ γινώσκοντες αὐτοὶ τὰ αὐτῶν τέκνα καθιερευον (“but knowingly, and themselves recognizing their own children, they offered them in sacrifice”). HAV.], and caressed their infants so that they would not be sacrificed in tears [Note: [Col. 0316C] **So that they would not be sacrificed in tears.** It is well known that this was especially required in sacrifices: the victims were not to be sacrificed while resisting. Hence the noble words of the martyr Romanus to the tyrant, as Chrysostom reports them at the end of his *Homily on Saint Romanus*: “Cut my neck, and do not defile the altar; you have a willing victim—why bind a captive bull that resists?” Tertullian himself likewise says in *To Scapula*, chapter II: “Thus, even if you compel us to sacrifice, you will render no service to your gods, for they did not desire sacrifices from the unwilling, unless they are quarrelsome.” Add the passage below, chapter XXVIII.]. Yet parricide differs greatly from homicide. Among the Gauls, people of more advanced age were sacrificed to Mercury [Note: [Col. 0316A] “Are sacrificed.” Rigaltius, Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0316C] **Were sacrificed to Mercury.** The commentators on Minucius have said enough about this too. Rigaltius printed the reading in this way from the Modian collation. According to Nonius, the *prosecta* in sacrifice were the entrails cut from the organs of the victims and given upon the altars; Varro, in the same author, called them the “offering of entrails.” From this comes *prosecare*, “to present in sacrifice to a god,” a usage found frequently in our author. Thus in chapter XLVI he says of Socrates: “Yet at the very end he ordered a cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius.” Similarly, in chapter XXIII: “One force is pronounced to be in the man who cuts off his genitals or arms, another in the man who cuts his own throat.” The Modian reading is confirmed by these words of Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter XXV: “He utterly abolished the religion of the Druids among the Gauls, a religion of dreadful savagery which had under Augustus been forbidden only to citizens.” Pomponius Mela, book III, chapter 2, likewise attests that it had indeed ceased: “The Gauls were once so savage that they believed a human being the most pleasing victim to the gods. Traces remain of the ferocity now abolished: although they refrain from the final acts of slaughter, nevertheless, after bringing those dedicated to the altars, they draw blood from them.” Hence the Gallo-Greeks, descended from these people and retaining both the rites and the name, in Justin XXVI.2 slaughter victims for the omens of battle. When the entrails predict great slaughter and the destruction of all, [Col. 0317A] they are turned not to fear but to frenzy, [Col. 0317B] and, hoping that the threats of the gods can be expiated by the slaughter of their own people, they butcher their wives and children. The earlier reading was “they sacrifice.” HAV.]. I leave the Tauric tales [Note: [Col. 0317B] **Tauric tales.** Here belongs that *Orestes*, written even on its reverse and not yet finished. Concerning these matters, see the many observations on Minucius. Lucian too does not cease ridiculing them in the *Dialogue of Juno and Latona* and that of *Apollo and Bacchus*. HAV.] to their own theaters. Behold, in that most religious city of the pious descendants of Aeneas [Note: [Col. 0317B] **The pious descendants of Aeneas.** He calls them this by reason of the founder of their family and origin, who is everywhere introduced by the Poet with this commendation, but also so that he may scourge their impiety under such a name. He imitates Lucretius, who similarly calls the Athenian people “pious” in VI.1277, though without irony:

> Nor did that custom of burial remain in the city,  
> By which this pious people had always been accustomed to be buried.], there is a certain Jupiter [Note: [Col. 0317B] **A certain Jupiter.** The Leiden manuscript does not recognize the final word. He means Jupiter Latiaris, concerning whom others have said enough. The very learned Desiderius Heraldus adduces a notable passage of Cyprian in his notes; see [Col. 0317C] further material among the commentators on Minucius. Scaliger, in his notes on Eusebius, p. 56, demonstrates at length that this truly was once customary; and, from Pliny, he shows when restraint was first imposed upon this cruelty, after which the blood shed by beast-fighters took the place of this sacrifice. Prudentius, verse 379 of book I *Against Symmachus*:

> Behold the criminal sanctuaries of terrifying Dis,  
> For whom, upon the ill-fated arena, a gladiator falls and pours out his blood—  
> Alas, a victim for Phlegethon offered to Rome, so wickedly purified!

Why, then, should we not apply these words of Seneca at the end of *Octavia*, verse 978?

> Our city is gentler than Aulis  
> And the barbarous land of the Taurians.  
> There the deity above is appeased  
> By the slaughter of a stranger; at Rome  
> It rejoices in the blood of a citizen.], whom at their games they drench with human blood. “But it is the blood of a beast-fighter,” [Note: [Col. 0317C] **But it is the blood of a beast-fighter.** The edition of Barraeus reads “of beast-fighters.” These were those who fought with beasts in the arena, whether criminals or, when criminals were lacking, others matched against savage wild animals. A generous table was set before these men when they ate their final meal. *Apology*, chapter XLII: “I do not recline at table publicly during the Liberalia, as is customary for beast-fighters eating their last supper.”] you say. This, I suppose, is something less than a human being. Or is it [Note: [Col. 0317A] Perhaps *ut hoc* (“that this”), Havercamp.] more disgraceful because it is the blood of an evil human being? Certainly it is nevertheless shed through homicide. O Jupiter, a Christian, and the only son of his father [Note: [Col. 0317D] **O Jupiter, a Christian, and the only son of his father in cruelty!** Certain initiatory rites bloody with the murder of an infant were imputed to the Christians, as though our God and Lord delighted in blood and were worshiped by homicide. Tertullian first shows that this is utterly false and then turns the charge itself back upon the accusers. For infants were sacrificed to their Saturn, and he indeed had not spared his own children, only Jupiter escaping the teeth of his impious father by flight. Yet Jupiter too was worshiped at Rome with human blood. Hence Tertullian draws his conclusion and exclaims in mockery, “O Jupiter, a Christian!”—that is, one who wished to be appeased with human blood, like Christ; for slanderous rumor had spread this falsehood about Christ. “And the only son of his father,” as though this too were something Jupiter shared with Christ, and as Christian faith believes Christ to be the Father’s only-begotten [Col. 0318A] Son, so Jupiter also might be regarded as Saturn’s sole [Col. 0318B] and only son. Both are so called with respect to cruelty: Jupiter is “a Christian” because people falsely said that Christ, like their Jupiter Latiaris, was propitiated with human blood; Jupiter is “the only son of his father” because he alone survived his father, all the others having been most cruelly devoured by that glutton Saturn. RIG.] in cruelty! But since, where infanticide is concerned, it makes no difference whether it is perpetrated as a sacred rite [Col. 0318A] or at private discretion—even though parricide differs from homicide [Note: [Col. 0317A] So the editions of Rhenanus, Heraldus, and Semler; the Agobardine manuscript reads “homicide differs from parricide.” Rigaltius and Havercamp read: “although it makes a difference in the case of parricide.” But the entire sentence appears not to have proceeded from Tertullian.]—I shall turn to the people. How many, as you please, among those standing around and gaping for Christian blood—even among you yourselves, the governors most just and severe toward us—might I strike upon their consciences, who put their own newborn children to death [Note: [Col. 0318D] **Who put their own newborn children to death.** O cruel, inhuman crime: to draw the sword against infants who are enemies to no one, guilty before no one, who would smile beneath the knife even before enemies! Yet nothing was more common among them. Hence the simultaneous admiration expressed in that passage on the Germans in Tacitus, chapter XIX: “To limit the number of children, or to kill any of one’s later-born offspring, is regarded as a disgrace.” Lactantius too gravely censures this impiety in VI.20: “Therefore let no one suppose that even this is permissible: that one may crush newborn children, which is the greatest impiety. For God breathes souls into life, not into death. But human beings, lest there be any crime with which they do not pollute their hands, deny to souls still undeveloped and simple a light which was not given [Col. 0318C] by them.” Barraeus clearly, and consequently the Fulda manuscript, prefer “kill.”]? If, indeed, there is also a difference in the manner of death [Note: [Col. 0318A] Havercamp, from the Modian collation: “And what if there is also a difference in the manner of death? There is. Surely, etc.” Semler too preferred this text, while preserving the same word order, to the authority of the remaining books.]: surely it is more cruel [Note: [Col. 0318C] **And what if there is also a difference in the manner of death? etc.** Thus the Modian collation, altogether better than the others, which read: “If indeed there is also a difference in the manner of death, surely, etc.” Although parricide and homicide remain such in whatever manner they are perpetrated, nevertheless, if you also consider the manner of death, one kind is more cruel than another. The sword, which quickly destroys a person and which older people therefore choose when killing themselves, is a gentler kind of death than long tossing in the waters, consumption by cold or hunger, or, finally, living bodies being buried in a living tomb, as Lucretius says. In what follows, some editions read: “You wrench away the spirit, or expose them to cold and hunger and dogs; for even old age has preferred to die by the sword.” I therefore punctuate: “And what if there is also a difference in the manner of death? There is. Surely it is more cruel in water, etc.” HAV.] when you wrench away their breath in water, or expose them to cold and hunger and dogs [Note: [Col. 0318C] **You expose them to cold and hunger and dogs.** Lactantius, book V: “Those who either strangle children born to them or, if they are excessively dutiful, expose them.” Again, VI.20: “What of those whom false dutifulness compels to expose their children? They cannot be considered innocent when they cast their own flesh and blood as prey to dogs; and, so far as lies in them, they kill more cruelly than if they had strangled them.” Hence he deservedly says of Saturn in *To the Nations* II.12: “And so he devoured his male children; better himself than the wolves, had he exposed them.” Worthy of note is what I observed while reading Isidore, in whom these words of Tertullian are found, though in his usual manner he conceals the names of the authors from whom he drew them and slightly reverses their wording. Thus he says of the penalties established by laws in V.27: “There is also a difference in the very manner of death. For it is more cruel for the breath to be extinguished through torment in water; to be burned by fires; to be killed by cold and hunger; to be exposed to dogs and beasts. For even greater age would choose to die by the sword.” He adds from another source: “For the sword knows how to end life with an expeditious death and without more grievous torment.” To this belongs that fragment of Sallust’s *Histories*: “If violence should oppose them, they would more fairly perish by the sword than by hunger,” which Pompey in the same passage calls the most wretched of all deaths, book III. HAV.]; [Col. 0319A] for even old age would choose to die by the sword [Note: [Col. 0319A] **To die by the sword.** Hence Aeneas’s indignation in Virgil, book I, line 130:

> O Diomedes, bravest of the race of Danaans,  
> That I could not have fallen upon the fields of Ilium  
> And poured out this life beneath your right hand!

That this death devised by the sword was called “Roman,” as though brave and manly, may be gathered from these words of Martial, I.79, concerning Festus, who was suffering from a disease of the throat. HAV.]. [Note: [Col. 0319B] **Once it has been forbidden.** The elegant but not universally familiar usage of this word has corrupted many passages in good authors. Thus here, before the better manuscripts, *semper*, “always,” was invariably read; and in Lucretius it has today been changed to *simul*, “together.” Intending to free him from many errors which still remain, on the basis of the Vossian manuscripts in the Leiden Library, we restore:

> Since it has once been mingled among things.

And I had already corrected it in this way, led by Lucan VIII.707, where he speaks of Pompey:

> Once Fortune, pushing him with her delaying hand,  
> Dashes him against the sands; he is torn upon the rocks,  
> The sea sucked through his wounds—  
> The plaything of the deep.

Our author, finally, says again in chapter X: “It will follow that for the same reason we do not sacrifice for others either, because we do not even do so for ourselves, since once and for all we do not worship the gods.” HAV.] But as for us, since homicide has once and for all been forbidden, it is not permitted even to destroy what has been conceived in the womb [Note: [Col. 0319C] **What has been conceived in the womb.** By taking a potion to induce abortion. Juvenal, *Satire* VI.594, whom see. Ovid likewise abominates it in book II, etc., as also at verse 29. Thus it is done to pander to beauty and is common among prostitutes. Hence Prosper of Aquitaine, *On the Promises and Predictions*, book II, chapter 15: “So that she may now be a wife who shortly before had been a harlot, and may have children who had been eager not to have children, and may now serve not lust but the begetting of offspring.” But indeed, as Augustine rightly says, “Let no woman take potions to procure an abortion, nor kill children conceived or born. A woman who takes death-dealing potions so that she may not conceive is guilty of as many homicides as the number of children she could have borne.” *Tantorum* means “so many,” “such a multitude,” as often in our author too. The matter was indeed forbidden to physicians. Theodorus Priscianus, in book III addressed to Victoria: “It is never lawful to procure an abortion for anyone; for, as the statement of Hippocrates attests, the innocent duty of physicians ought not to be stained by the consciousness of so grave a charge.” Indeed, it was prohibited by law: Paulus, *Si quis aliquid*, section *Qui abortionis*, under *On Penalties*: “Those who give an abortifacient or love potion, although they do not act with malicious intent, nevertheless, because the act sets an evil example, are sentenced—persons of lower rank to the mines, persons of higher rank to relegation to an island with the loss of part of their property. But if a woman or man dies as a result, they are subjected to the highest penalty.” There is a similar law of Moses at Exodus 21:22. The Fulda manuscript reads “the conceived womb,” and Scioppius notes that the expression comes from legal usage. HAV.], while the blood is still being drawn out into a human being [Note: [Col. 0319D] **Is being drawn out into a human being.** Junius wrongly reads “is being deliberated”; other editions more correctly read “is being drawn out.” Blood is said to be “drawn out into a human being” while the embryo is nourished from the most excellent fluid of the human body. Lucretius:

> As bees sip everything in flower-bearing glades.

And it is the very same thing as Job 10:13: “Did you not milk me like milk, and curdle me like cheese?” Theodoret, p. 78, to which King David alludes in Psalm 139:15: “Was not my bone hidden in secret, when I was artfully embroidered in the lowest parts of the earth?” Rigaltius, however, printed “is being deliberated” from the Puteanus manuscript, as I too did from [Col. 0320A] the Leiden manuscript, and this is not to be rejected. It receives no little illumination from Ausonius’s well-known distich:

> While Nature hesitated whether to make you male or female,  
> You were made, O lovely boy, almost a girl.

But let that most elegant passage of Varro *On Human Origins*, preserved in Censorinus, *On the Natal Day*, [Col. 0320B] chapter IX, according to the doctrine of Pythagoras, stand in place of all others. These fragments, full of recondite antiquity, corrected and enlarged, illustrated with notes, and accompanied by a vocabulary of all the words, we have prepared for publication. But Varro himself says: “The numbers which bring some change in each birth, while either seed is converted into blood, blood into flesh, or flesh into the form of a human being.” Finally, Tertullian himself says again in *Against Marcion* IV.21: “not brought to completion by the torment of ten months.” For there too the better manuscripts read “brought to completion,” where others have “drawn out.” The sense is that Nature deliberates in the womb whether she wishes to form the conceived and mingled seed into a human being or to allow it to flow away and suffer a natural abortion. HAV.]. To prevent a birth is to hasten homicide; nor does it matter whether one snatches away a soul already born [Col. 0320A] or disrupts one in the process of birth: he is a human being [Note: [Col. 0320B] **He is a human being who is going to be one.** Martial, book IX, epigram 42:

> Believe that Nature herself is telling you the truth.

What you destroy with your fingers, Ponticus, is a human being.

For although among the jurists an offspring not yet brought forth is said not yet to be a human being, Paul nevertheless rightly testifies, in the section *On the Status of Human Beings* [Col. 0320C], that one who is in the womb is protected just as though he were already among human affairs. How such an offspring is spoken of by the jurists before birth is evident from comparison with the words of Papinian on the *Lex Falcidia*, *Digest* XXXV, tit. 2, § 9:

> Under the Falcidian law it was settled that fruits subsequently gathered, if they were ripe at the time of death, increase the valuation of the inheritance on account of the farm, which is deemed to have been more valuable at that time. In the case of a pregnant slave woman, no distinction based on time has been admitted; and rightly so, because an offspring not yet brought forth is not properly said to have been a human being.

The discussion concerns legacies and inheritances. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 25, calls that unformed thing, not yet a human being, *pecus*; and the membrane enclosing the fetus was called by the ancients ἂμνιον (“lambskin”), as though one were to say “the skin of a lamb.” Aristotle, therefore, must not be listened to either: wishing to discourage an excessive multitude of citizens in a single state, he proposes that the seed be destroyed and made abortive before it can be called a human being. His words are in *Politics* VII, ch. 16.]

—and so too is one who will be; for every fruit is already present in the seed.

[Note: [Col. 0320C] **For every fruit is already present in the seed.** On Zeno [Col. 0320D] the Stoic, Theodoret, p. 73: τὸν γὰρ τοι ἀνθρώπινον σπορόν, ὑγρόν ὂντα καὶ μετέχοντα πνεύματος, τῆς ψυχῆς ἔφησεν εἶναι μέρος τε καὶ ἀπόσπασμα (“For he said that human seed, being moist and partaking of spirit, is a part and offshoot of the soul”). For he believed that the generative seed of a human being, which is observed to be endowed with moisture and spirit, is a part of the soul and, as it were, a cutting from it. Thus Plato’s impious laws, in the same author, p. 131: Ὃταν δὲ αἱ γυναῖκες (“But when the women …”; the recovered quotation is incomplete), etc.:

> But when men and women have passed beyond the age for procreation, we shall allow them to associate as they please, warning them only not to bring any further conceived fetus into the light. But if anyone violates this ordinance and carries the fetus to birth, he must then expose it in such a way that it is entirely deprived of nourishment.

Others read: “and every fruit is already in the seed.” Rhenanus: “and the fruit of a human being.”]

Concerning nourishment by blood and tragic dishes of this sort, read whether it is reported anywhere [it is in Herodotus, I think] that certain nations established a covenant by tasting blood poured from the arms of each party.

[Note: [Col. 0320D] **Concerning nourishment by blood.** He turns back upon his adversaries the charge concerning the eating of raw flesh and drinking of blood; on this custom the commentators on Minucius have collected much.]

[Note: [Col. 0319A] All editions read: “read lest it be reported anywhere” (the Agobardinus and Lugdunensis manuscripts have *est*), except Scriverius alone, who correctly has “read whether it is reported anywhere.” The words enclosed in brackets, which are absent from Rhenanus’s edition, [Col. 0320A] may perhaps be due to the ill-directed diligence of a copyist. Herodotus describes this Scythian rite at IV.70.]

[Note: [Col. 0320A] Semler: “poured out.”]

[Note: [Col. 0320D] **Blood poured from the arms.** See Lydius’s *Sacred Treatise on Military Matters*, p. 203, and the notes on Minucius. [Col. 0321B] Athenaeus, II, relates the custom of the Carmanians, who used to offer one another blood to drink at banquets in order to confirm friendship. The Fulda manuscript has “from one or the other”; manuscript L.B. and Pamelius read “diffused.”]

Something of this sort, I know not precisely what, was also tasted in Catiline’s time.

[Note: [Col. 0321B] **Something of this sort, I know not precisely what.** The Modius collation adds “of this sort,” and the author rightly expressed himself in the manner of one who doubts, since Sallust himself does not assert it but presents it as a rumor: “There were at that time some who said that Catiline,” etc.; on which the very learned Putschius should be consulted. Something similar is said to have occurred under the tyrant Magnentius.]

They also say that among certain Scythian peoples every deceased person is eaten by his own relatives.

[Note: [Col. 0321B] **Eaten by his own relatives.** *Against Marcion* I:

> They devour at a banquet the corpses of their parents, slaughtered together with livestock. Those who have not died in such a way as to be fit for food are considered to have suffered an accursed death.

The Massagetae have a similar gluttony. Jerome, *Against Jovinian* II:

> The Massagetae consider those who die of sickness most wretched, and when parents, blood-relations, and kinsmen have reached old age, they slaughter and devour them.

τὸ (the isolated Greek article “the”; its referent is unrecoverable here) [Col. 0321C] Barraeus’s edition did not recognize this.]

I am ranging too far afield. Here today, blood caught in a small shield from a slashed thigh and given to its own devotees marks those consecrated to Bellona.

[Note: [Col. 0321A] Wouwerius: “And here.”]

[Note: [Col. 0321A] Wouwerius: “is consecrated.” Barraeus: “sucked out.”]

[Note: [Col. 0321A] Franeker edition: “into the palm.”]

[Note: [Col. 0321C] **Taken into a small shield.** So Rhenanus’s edition, and correctly; for what is that *palmula* which all the others substitute? The hollow of the hand, or wood from a palm tree? For the thing itself—the actual rite, with the priest of Bellona in the very act—see, at the goddess’s altar, the engraving of this remarkable gem in Gorlaeus’s *Dactyliotheca*, vol. II, no. 664, and here p. 91. There I would have you note the little shield, or buckler, leaning against the altar and intended to catch the blood. Yet that the palm of the hand too was employed in these rites is clear from a notable engraving of a gem produced by the very learned Leonardo Agostini, I.171. There a naked priest of Bellona is seen piercing his side with the blade he holds in his left hand, while raising before Bellona’s image his right hand filled with the gore flowing from his slashed thigh. But to one who looks more carefully, a different form of this rite appears: as the first gem depicts the consumption of blood, so the second depicts an act of devotion.]

[Note: [Col. 0321A] The Lugdunensis manuscript reads: “Here today the blood consecrated to Bellona, taken from a slashed thigh into the palm and given to her devotee, marks him.” The Fulda manuscript: “Here today Bellona’s cutter—the blood from the slashed thigh being received in the palm and given for use—marks him.” The Puteanus and Bongarsianus manuscripts: “received and given to his devotee marks him.” Rhenanus: “small shield.”]

Likewise, where are those who, when treating the falling sickness, drank with greedy thirst the fresh blood of slaughtered criminals in the arena, [caught as it flowed from the throat]?

[Note: [Col. 0322A] The Fulda manuscript reads “bandagers.” Perhaps “watchers.” Havercamp.]

[Note: [Col. 0321C] **Of the slaughtered.** The Fulda manuscript has *rigulatorum*; in all [Col. 0321D] the others it is *jugulatorum*. Scioppius approves the former and explains it as referring to the bandage with which they wrapped a wound and stopped the blood. Accordingly, he calls Nonius to his side under the word *rica*. Festus too might be cited. He says:

> *Ricae* and *riculae* are small coverings, like little cloaks made for use on the head. Granius, however, says that it is a woman’s headband, with which the Flaminica is bound in place of a fillet.

And Isidore XIX.31:

> A *rigula* is the maidenly headdress of the head.

For I do not like the repetition of “the slaughtered,” followed immediately by “throat.” What if, from the traces of the manuscript reading, you were to make *rigidulorum*, “the slightly stiffened,” so as to suggest gladiators or criminals who, already trained to offer their throats bravely when ordered, grew pale and stiff from the wound—a bodily state accompanying the soul’s flight? The dying emperor Hadrian, according to Spartianus in his *Life*, poured forth these verses:

> Little wandering, charming soul,  
> Guest and companion of the body,  
> To what places will you now depart,  
> Pale, stiff, and naked,  
> Nor, as you are accustomed, make your jests? [Col. 0322B]

Finally, Tertullian himself says below, ch. XLII: “I can stiffen and grow pale after the bath when I am dead.” For the throat is bandaged in vain in the arena, where the wound is mortal and where, as is well known, the defeated were required to offer it. The same collation shortly afterward deletes “caught,” which may indeed be absent. But I cannot tolerate that Rigaltius too removes from his edition the words “flowing from the throat”: plainly, this collision of a repeated word displeased him, and no remedy was found except a savage one—burning and cutting. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0322B] **The falling sickness.** Minucius:

> I believe Jupiter himself, the son of Saturn, cures the falling sickness with human blood—that is, cures one disease by a more grievous disease.

There Wouwerius, from the physician Scribonius Largus, ch. XII, notes that sufferers consumed a small piece of the liver of a slain gladiator, administered nine times. Note also the story of Faustina, wife of the philosopher-emperor Antoninus: when she was in love with a gladiator, the blood of that same man after he had been killed was offered to her as a remedy for her passion, as Julius Capitolinus relates. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0322A] Paris edition: “carry away.”]

Likewise, where are those who dine on wild-beast dishes from the arena, who seek meat from the boar or the stag? That boar wiped away, while struggling, the blood of the man whom it had bloodied; that stag tossed itself about in a gladiator’s blood.

[Note: [Col. 0322C] **They dine on wild-beast dishes.** Minucius, p. 34, sketched this whole passage:

> No different are those who devour from the arena beasts smeared with gore or fattened on human limbs and entrails.

How would Ovid characterize them, when in his *Metamorphoses* XV, verse 88, Pythagoras speaks against even the eating of beasts?

> Alas, what wickedness it is for entrails to be buried in entrails,  
> For a greedy body to grow fat upon an accumulated body,
