> And for one living creature to live by another living creature’s death!]

[Note: [Col. 0322A] Paris edition: “trampling.”]

[Note: [Col. 0322C] **While struggling.** The Fulda manuscript has “struggling”; Barraeus, “fighting.” But Rhenanus and manuscript Lugd. Bat. read “trampling,” which I think more correct, as being more characteristic of boars. Thus Christ speaks from their nature in Matthew VII.6: μήποτε καταπατήσωσιν αὐτοὺς ἐν τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῶν (“lest they trample them under their feet”). HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0322A] Paris edition: “lay.” Havercamp: “That stag tossed itself in a gladiator’s blood.”]

[Note: [Col. 0322C] **Lay in a gladiator’s blood.** So manuscript L.B. and the editions of Rhenanus and Rigaltius. Barraeus, Heraldus, and Pamelius, however, have “tossed”; much the same appears in the Fulda manuscript, or Modius collation: “tossed the blood.” I think the text should be restored as: “that stag refreshed itself with a gladiator’s blood.” Caecilius, cited by Nonius under *lactare*:

> What an overflow, what pleasure, what liberality delights you?

That is, soothes, delights, affects; or: “refreshed itself in gladiatorial blood.” Cicero, in the same place: “Malice delighting in another’s misfortune”; and this is most true. For if it merely tossed or lay in it, once the bloody hide had been removed no crime remained, nor any trace of human blood; but if it drank the gore, the matter is now different.

I judge that it will not be unwelcome to insert here why the Egyptians are said by some to have abstained from pork. Aelian, *On Animals* X.16, censures the gluttony of swine, which do not abstain even from eating human flesh: Ἡ ὑς καὶ τῶν ἰδίων τέκνων (“The sow even [does not spare] her own offspring”; the recovered quotation is incomplete), etc. That is:

> The swine is so devoted to filling its belly that it does not spare even its own offspring, nor does it restrain its voracity from the human body. This is why among the Egyptians an animal of this sort is held in the greatest hatred as unclean, detestable, and exceedingly voracious.

[Col. 0323B] The argument of our Septimius must be understood as follows: These animals, whose flesh you greedily devour, killed many of their opponents before they themselves were laid low in the arena by beast-fighters. Thus the boar wiped away and drank the gore which it drew from a wound with its tusks while trampling a half-dead man; the stag, wearied and thirsty, greedily gulped it down as a drink; and the bear even buried the man himself within its belly. Martial I, epigram 44:

> After such deeds let no boar be served to you;  
> Rather, let you be served to the boar, Charidemus.

Tertullian, *On the Shows*, ch. XII: “unless human bodies were also torn apart by wild beasts.” And ch. XXI: “In the same amphitheater the same spectator, with the most enduring eyes, leans over from above to view bodies gnawed and torn apart and befouled in their own blood.”]

The bellies of bears themselves are eagerly sought while they are still suffering indigestion from human entrails.

[Note: [Col. 0322A] Junius: “while slaughtering.” Havercamp: “while battering” or “thrusting.”]

Thus flesh fed upon a human being is belched up by a human being.

[Note: [Col. 0323A] Paris edition: “then.”]

[Note: [Col. 0323C] **Fed upon a human being.** Prudentius also uses this expression in *Against Symmachus* I, verse 383, rebuking the pleasure [Col. 0323C] taken by the eyes in gladiatorial slaughter:

> What pleasure fed on blood?

Understand this from Seneca, *Natural Questions* II.3:

> The hand, bones, sinews, and eyes are part of us; their material is the fluid of digested food, destined to pass into those parts.

HAV.]

You who eat these things—how far removed are you from the banquets of Christians? Do those who, with savage lust, gape after human limbs do any less because they devour them alive? Are they any less consecrated to filth through human blood because they lick blood that is yet to be?

[Note: [Col. 0323A] Junius: “by which.”]

[Note: [Col. 0323A] Paris edition: “from filth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0323C] **They lick blood that is yet to be.** Epiphanius on the Gnostics, Heresy XXVI: Οἱ δὲ τάλανες, μιγέντες ἀλλήλοις, καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ ἀληθείας αἰσχύνομαι εἰπεῖν τὰ παρὰ τοῖς αὐτοῖς αἰσχρὰ πραττόμενα, κατὰ τὸν ἅγιον Ἀπόστολον, καὶ τὰ παρ` αὐτοῖς γινόμενα αἰσχρόν ἐστι καὶ λέγειν· ὅμως οὐκ αἰσχυνῶ λέγειν, ἃ αὐτοὶ ποιεῖν οὐκ αἰσχύνονται, ἵνα κατὰ πάντα τρόπον φρίξιν ἐργὰσωμαι τοῖς ἀκοοῦσι τὰ παρ` αὐτῶν γενόμενα αἰσχρουργήματα (“But after the wretches have coupled with one another—and truly I am ashamed to tell of the shameful acts practiced among them, since, as the holy Apostle says, even to speak of what is done among them is shameful—nevertheless I shall not be ashamed to tell what they are not ashamed to do, so that I may in every way make those who hear of their obscene deeds shudder”). μετὰ γὰρ τὸ μιγῆναι πάθει πορνείας, προσεπιτούτοις ἀνατείνοντες τῆν ἑαυτῶν βλασφημίαν εἰς οὐρανὸν, δέχεται μὲν τὸ γύναιον καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ῥύσιν τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄῤῥηνος εἰς ἰδίας αὐτῶν χεὶρας (“For after coupling in a passion of fornication, and further raising their blasphemy toward heaven, both the woman and the man receive into their own hands the discharge from the male”), etc., καὶ οὓτως αὐτὸ ἐσθίουσι, μεταλαμβάνοντες τὴν ἐαυτων ἀκαθαρσίαν, καὶ φασι· Τουτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ (“And thus they eat it, partaking of their own impurity, and say, ‘This is the body of Christ’”). Above: “He is a human being who will be one, and every fruit is already present in the seed.” HAV.]

No, they do not eat infants, certainly, but rather adults. Let your error blush before the Christians. We do not include even the blood of animals among edible banquet foods; for that reason we also abstain from strangled animals and carrion, lest we be contaminated by blood in any form, even when it is buried within the entrails.

[Note: [Col. 0323D] **Blood among edible banquet foods.** Elmenhorstius illustrated this with many observations on the passage in Minucius, explaining from it Acts XV.27, which we explained differently above. In the same place he teaches that Christians of a later period sometimes abstained from meat altogether, from this passage of Prudentius’s *Cathemerinon*:

> Far removed be that hunger, etc.,  
> That delights in tearing bloody meals  
> From the slaughtered bodies of livestock.  
> Let feasts derived from the death of quadrupeds  
> Belong to untamed nations;  
> Let the foliage of vegetables and the pod,  
> Pregnant with many kinds of pulses,  
> Feed us with harmless banquets.

Hence Blandina in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.1, in Rufinus’s words:

> You are greatly mistaken, gentlemen, in supposing that those who do not even eat the flesh of dumb animals feed upon the entrails of infants.

Note particularly the phrase “edible banquet foods.” Minucius says *edulium*, terms signifying the more sumptuous feasts to which Christians sometimes invited one another as circumstances permitted. If, then, even in their delicacies they did not consume the blood of beasts, how could they gulp down human blood? Domitian too won praise among the Romans for clemency on this account—but only at the beginning of his reign—when he quoted Virgil’s verse:

> With what impiety has mankind feasted upon slaughtered bullocks!

He went so far as to intend to issue an edict forbidding the sacrifice of oxen, as Suetonius relates in his *Life*, ch. IX. Evanthius the Abbot, a pious and ancient writer, composed a treatise on this subject. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0323A] Franeker edition: “in any way”; manuscript L. Bat.: “also.”]

Finally, among the ordeals of Christians you even bring sausages swollen with blood to them, perfectly well aware, of course, that among them the very thing by which you wish to drive them beyond bounds is forbidden.

[Note: [Col. 0324B] **Even sausages swollen with blood.** On these one should certainly consult Emperor Leo’s Constitution LVIII, which forbids the eating of sausages and of blood altogether. This kind of food was already known in Homer’s time, as is evident from *Odyssey* Σ (“Book 18”), verses 44 and 117. Just as the Greeks called gluttons γαστέρες (“bellies”) and γαστριμάργους (“belly-mad,” that is, “gluttons”), a matter which Eustathius treats more fully on the passage cited, so our author too calls such people “sausages” in *Against the Psychics*, ch. 1: “the outer and inner sausages of the Psychics.”

Here, however, on the basis of the Modius collation, I read more forcefully: “among the tortures of Christians you even bring sausages swollen with blood,” etc. For in order to torment the wretched people, they stuffed sausages into their mouths, having ascertained that they abstained entirely from blood. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0323B] “Perfectly well aware”—“Moreover” is absent from the Paris edition.]

What kind of thing is it, moreover, that you believe people whom you trust to recoil from the blood of cattle to be eager for human blood—unless perhaps you have found it sweeter by experience? That blood itself, surely, ought therefore to be employed as a test of Christians, just like the sacrificial hearth and incense-box.

[Note: [Col. 0324A] Wouwerius, on Minucius p. 39, reads “to initiate.”]

[Note: [Col. 0324C] **Like the sacrificial hearth and incense-box.** By these means those who held life dearer than their soul sometimes purchased their lives. *Against Marcion* I.27:

> Why, in persecutions, do you not immediately gain your life by denial when the incense-box is offered?

Manuscript L.B. transposes the words: “ought to be employed like the sacrificial hearth and incense-box.” Pure piety breathes from the verses read among Ausonius’s poems. They occur in the *Parecbasis*:

> I do not demand incense to be burned,  
> Nor cakes of honeyed pastry;  
> The hearth of living turf [Col. 0324D]  
> I leave to empty altars.]

For they would therefore be proved Christians by seeking human blood, just as they are proved Christians by rejecting sacrifice.

[Note: [Col. 0324A] Paris edition: “likewise.”]

[Note: [Col. 0324D] **Just as sacrifice.** I would prefer the reading of the Fulda manuscript: “by seeking it, Christians who reject sacrifice.” The meaning is that those who are proved Christians by refusing sacrifice would be proved members of that sect still more decisively by consuming blood, since this is supposedly customary among them. But Rigaltius omitted this and many other readings of that manuscript. HAV.]

Otherwise they would have to be killed if they tasted it, just as if they had not sacrificed.

[Note: [Col. 0324D] **They would have to be killed if they tasted it.** Heraldus, Wouwerius, and Rigaltius prefer this reading; the Fulda manuscript approaches it, reading “they would have to be killed if they did not taste it.” Yet the other reading also rests on no feeble support: “they would have to be denied as Christians if they did not taste it, just as if they had sacrificed.” Pamelius, La Cerda, and Junius accepted this, and before them Barraeus and Gelenius; manuscript Lugd. Bat. also supports it. That is, those who do not seek blood are to be denied as Christians, just as those who sacrifice are now denied to be Christians.

I explain the former reading thus: only after proving their conduct by tasting blood should they be punished with death as perpetrators of infanticide and seekers after human blood, just as those who refuse to sacrifice are put to death. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0324A] Thus Heraldus, Wouwerius, Rigaltius, and Havercamp from a manuscript. The Fulda manuscript reads “they would have to be killed” (Pamelius and others: “denied”) “if they did not taste it, just as if they” [Col. 0324B] “had sacrificed.”]

[Col. 0325A] And in any case human blood would not be lacking for you amid the examinations of prisoners and the condemnation of defendants.

[Note: [Col. 0325B] **Would not be lacking for you.** He refutes the tacit objection concerning where this blood might be obtained—as though murder for that very purpose, or the opening of veins, were necessary, when among them the prison was always overflowing with criminals and each day the blood of human beings, or of Christians, was shed. HAV.]

Again, who are more incestuous than those whom Jupiter himself taught?

[Note: [Col. 0325B] **Jupiter himself taught.** Seneca, in the *Apocolocyntosis*, on Claudius:

> That man a god, and from Jupiter? Jupiter, so far as it lay in Claudius’s power, was condemned by him for incest. For he killed L. Silanus, his own son-in-law. Why, I ask? He preferred to call the most charming sister of all young women—whom everyone called Venus—Juno.

I punctuate and explain this as follows: Can that man become a Jovian god, so to speak—the expression resembles Lucretius’s “Ceres from Iacchus,” that is, the mother of Iacchus, and Tertullian’s frequent “concerning prudence,” “concerning justice,” etc.—who condemned Jupiter for incest in the person of Silanus, whom he killed because Silanus was said to have treated his sister Junia Calvina as Jupiter treated Juno, that is, to have taken her as his wife? And just as our author adds the example of the Persians, so Lucian wittily says that Jupiter married several other wives, but finally his own full sister Juno, and did so according to the custom of the Persians and Assyrians. His words occur in the dialogue *On Sacrifices*: Ἔγημε δὲ πολλὰς μὲν ἄλλας, ὑστάτην δὲ, τὴν Ἤραν τὴν ἀδελφὴν, κατὰ τοὺς Περσῶν τοῦτο, καὶ Ἄσσυρίων νόμους (“He married many others, but last of all Hera, his sister, doing this according to the laws of the Persians and Assyrians”). HAV.]

Ctesias reports that the Persians have intercourse with their own mothers. But the Macedonians too are suspect, because when they first heard the tragedy of Oedipus, they laughed at the anguish over incest and used to say ἥλαυνε (“he drove”), εἰς την μητέρα (“against the mother”).

[Note: [Col. 0325A] In the manuscripts: μέμηνε, ἔμινε, ἔμηνε (variant manuscript readings, approximately “has gone mad,” “remained,” and “was raging”; the readings are textually uncertain) or ἔμεεν (an apparently corrupt variant; literally perhaps “was vomiting,” but its intended sense here is uncertain), “they said,” εἰς τὴν μητέρα (“against the mother”). Gothofredus, on *To the Nations* I.16: ἤλαυνε (“he drove”), “they said,” τὴν μητέρα (“the mother”); and so [Col. 0325B] Havercamp, Semler, and Ritter. But the word εἰς (“against”) must not be deleted.]

[Note: [Col. 0325C] “Ἤλαυνε (“he drove”), they used to say, τὴν μητέρα (“the mother”).” Since this passage in the manuscripts of the *Apology* is variously expressed, learned commentators have extracted many ridiculous offspring from it, as can be seen in their notes. The text of the manuscripts is as follows. Barraeus: μέμηνε (“has gone mad”), “they used to say,” etc. Aldus and the Bongarsianus manuscript: ἔμινε (“remained”; possibly a corrupt spelling). Rhenanus and others: ἔμηνε (“was raging”; a variant reading) or ἔμεεν (an apparently corrupt variant; literally perhaps “was vomiting,” but its intended sense here is uncertain), “they used to say,” εἰς τὴν μητέρα (“against the mother”); others differently.

At last Rigaltius [Col. 0325D] fashioned his own ἔλαυνε (“drive on!”), “they used to say,” εἰς τὴν μητέρα (“against the mother”), as though they had shouted to Oedipus as their leader and king, “Come, lead the attack upon your mother,” as though he were about to storm a city or fortress; and he inserted the same reading into *To the Nations* I.16 against the authority of the Agobardinus manuscript. Finally Priorius, wishing to contribute something of his own but having nothing, stole Heraldus’s conjecture, the worst of all, ἐμίηνε (“he defiled,” that is, “he committed incest”), that is, “he committed incest,” and was so drowsy as to foist it upon us as though it were the reading of manuscripts, not one of which he appears ever to have used.

The sole true reading is that supplied by the book *To the Nations* and approved there by Gothofredus: “And then you said to one another, *elaune ten matera*.” Translated, this means “he drove his mother,” since that verb is commonly used of driving and urging on horses. It is also confirmed by the Fulda manuscript, in which you will not find τὸ εἰς (“the word εἰς,” ‘against’); for the Lugd. Bat. manuscript has nothing sound here: “the anguish, they said *epala*.” That the Macedonians could not have said otherwise is evident from the fact that they turned and spoke to one another, rather than turning to the tragic actor [Col. 0326B] or to Oedipus himself, as Rigaltius supposed. Those who had received the spectacle of Oedipus’s gouged-out eyes with such loud laughter plainly gave their companions in the same theater this disgraceful reason for their mockery.

This passage of Minucius may bear upon the matter:

> Your historical traditions and tragedies glory in acts of incest, and you gladly both read and hear them.

In the Fulda manuscript it was: ἐλάγταε (an apparently corrupt manuscript reading whose meaning is uncertain), “they said,” μετέραν (an apparently corrupt spelling of “mother”). HAV.]

Now consider how much opportunity errors provide for incestuous unions when the promiscuity of lust supplies the material.

[Note: [Col. 0326B] **The promiscuity of lust.** This is his name for that wandering Venus which roams indiscriminately through lawful and unlawful objects. The same term occurs frequently, and also in *Against Hermogenes*, ch. XLI:

> This is not unrest, this is not turmoil and promiscuity, but moderation and modesty.

Rhenanus therefore wrongly reads: “to supply materials, with lust everywhere inviting.” The Greek term is εἰκαιότης (“randomness” or “indiscriminate license”), whence εἰκαῖα πρόβατα (“sheep roaming at large”), “sheep at large.” See Scaliger on Manilius, p. 68. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0325B] Rhenanus: “to supply materials, with lust everywhere inviting.”]

First and foremost, you expose your sons so that they may be taken up by some passing stranger’s compassion, or emancipate them for adoption by better parents.

[Note: [Col. 0326A] Paris edition: “by an unrelated mother”; Franeker edition: “of an unrelated act of compassion.”]

[Note: [Col. 0326C] **A stranger’s compassion.** So the manuscripts generally read, much better than certain printed editions’ “of an unrelated act of compassion,” or Rhenanus’s “by an unrelated mother,” which Barraeus also has. The jurist Paul, elegantly quoted by Wouwerius on Minucius, says:

> Not only the person who suffocates a newborn child is deemed to kill it, but also the person who exposes it in public places to the compassion which he himself does not possess.

I cannot refrain from citing a passage from Lactantius, but in a more emended form. At VI.20 the common editions have:

> Who can doubt that he is impious who leaves no place for another’s compassion? Indeed, even if what he wished should occur, so that the child is nourished, he has certainly sentenced his own blood either to slavery or to the brothel.

At least in my copy, this says anything but what it appears to intend. Restore: “those who grant a place to another’s compassion, not their own”; the words that follow there require this. One may see such compassion from a stranger extended to Chariclea in Heliodorus’s *Aethiopica* II, p. 118, Commelinus’s edition. But we have said more about this cruelty at the beginning [Col. 0326D] of this chapter; to it may be added Kippingius I.1, p. 13 of the new edition. HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0326D] **To be adopted by better parents.** By people who embrace another’s children with paternal love, although their own parents, by sending them away, have openly declared their hatred of them. Yet this custom of adoption has not lacked praise among writers. There is a notable passage at the beginning of Philo Judaeus’s treatise *On Agriculture*; see it. HAV.]

The memory of an estranged family line must at some point be dispersed; and once an error has struck, thereafter the hereditary shoot of incest will spread, as the family line creeps onward together with the crime. Then, wherever one may be—at home, abroad, or beyond the seas—lust is his companion, and its everywhere-roaming excursions can easily somewhere beget children upon women who do not know him, even from some portion of scattered seed. Thus the family stock dispersed throughout human intercourse may encounter its own kindred, while failing to recognize in them unions of incestuous blood.

[Note: [Col. 0326A] Paris edition: “by an unrelated mother”; Franeker edition: “of an unrelated act of compassion.”]

[Note: [Col. 0326A] Rigaltius and Havercamp: “beget children, as though from some scattering of seed,” [Col. 0326B] etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0326B] Franeker edition: “so that the sprinkled stock.”]

From that eventuality the most diligent and faithful chastity has fenced us off; and as far as we are removed from adulteries and every transgression after marriage, so far are we secure from the accident of incest.

[Note: [Col. 0326D] **From that eventuality.** A most beautiful encomium of Christian continence. Minucius, p. 85:

> But we display modesty not in the face but in the mind; we gladly adhere to the bond of a single marriage; as for the desire to procreate, we know either one wife or none.

And shortly afterward in the same place:

> So far removed, indeed, is the desire for incest that for some even a chaste union is a source of shame.

But most relevant is the passage of Origen, *Against Celsus* I, which Elmenhorstius taught me, and I am bound in conscience not to suppress his name: Οἱ δ` ὑπ` αὐτῶν ἐπὶ ἰδιωτίᾳ ἐξουθενούμενοι (“But those who are despised by them for being uneducated”), etc. That is:

> Moreover, although uneducated people are treated by them as worthless, foolish, and illiberal, if only they entrust themselves to faith in God and receive the teaching of Jesus, they are so far removed from all wantonness, filth, and shameful lusts that, after the manner of perfect priests who shrink from every sexual union, many of them live altogether chastely and purely, abstaining even from lawful intercourse with women.

The words “and most faithful” are absent from Rhenanus onward. [Col. 0327C] HAV.]

Some, much more securely, ward off the entire force of this error by virginal continence: children in years, but old men in purity.

If you considered that these things exist among yourselves, you would accordingly perceive that they do not exist among Christians. The same eyes would have reported both facts. But two kinds of blindness easily coincide, so that those who do not see what exists seem to see what does not exist. I shall demonstrate this throughout every charge. For now I shall speak of the more evident matters.

[Note: [Col. 0327B] The words “I shall demonstrate this throughout every charge” are absent from Rhenanus’s edition, and the following words, “For now I shall speak of the more evident matters,” are assigned to ch. X. Rigaltius: “For now, concerning matters that are also evident.” Havercamp.]

## CHAPTER X

**ARGUMENT.—He now proceeds to the charge of irreligion and says that Christians refuse the worship of the gods because they are not gods, though they should be worshipped if their divinity could be demonstrated. He therefore appeals to the conscience of the Gentiles, which cannot deny that all those gods were once human beings—a point he now clearly demonstrates by the example of Saturn alone.**

[Note: [Col. 0327C] **You say, “You do not worship the gods.”** This occurs frequently in Arnobius, as in Book I:

> Are we therefore accused among you of an impious religion, and are we called ill-omened and atheists because we approach the Head and Pillar of all things with reverential homage—to use your abusive language?

Book V:

> You dare to call any of these men an atheist, irreligious, and sacrilegious because they either deny altogether that the gods exist or doubt it.

And Book VI:

> For on this point you are accustomed to stir up the most turbulent hostility against us, to call us atheists, and to say that we grant the gods very little.

See more in the commentators on Arnobius. HAV.]

You say, “You do not worship the gods, and you do not offer sacrifices on behalf of the emperors.” It follows that for the same reason we do not sacrifice on behalf of others, since we do not sacrifice even on behalf of [Col. 0328A] ourselves, once we have ceased to worship the gods. Accordingly, we are arraigned on charges of sacrilege and treason.

[Note: [Col. 0327C] **Sacrilege.** An abusive charge immediately cast at Christians; above, ch. II: “When you conduct an inquiry concerning some criminal,” etc.; and in the same place: “to order the sacrilegious man to be torn apart if he persists in confessing.” Also *To Scapula*, ch. II:

> Yet you have never caught us, whom you consider sacrilegious, even in theft, much less in sacrilege.

Indeed, the customary cry of the populace when demanding the punishment of innocent people was: [Col. 0327D] “Away with the sacrilegious!” Rufinus, from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV, has the judge say to Polycarp:

> Show respect for your age and spare your extreme old age; swear by Caesar’s fortune, repent of your former conduct, and cry out yourself as well: “Away with the sacrilegious!”

In the same place, concerning Polycarp’s death:

> When the assembled multitude had been struck with amazement by so remarkable a death and had begun to marvel at the courage of the whole Christian people in despising death, they all cried out: “Away with the sacrilegious!”

From comparison with these, light may be cast upon what we read concerning the Jews’ cry against the Savior in Luke XXIII.18: Ἁνέκραξαν δὲ παμπληθεὶ, λέγοντες· Αἶρε τοῦτον (“But they cried out all together, saying, ‘Away with this man!’”). The same happened to Paul in Acts XXI.36: Ἠκολούθει γὰρ τὸ πλῆθος τοῦ λαοῦ κράζον· αἶρε αὐτόν (“For the multitude of the people followed, crying, ‘Away with him!’”), and much more so in XXII.22: Αἶρε ἀπὸ τῆς γὴς τὸν τοιοῦτον· οὐ γὰρ καθῆκον αὐτὸν ζῇν (“Away with such a man from the earth, for he ought not to live!”). HAV.]

This is the chief ground of the case—indeed, the whole of it—and certainly one worthy of investigation, provided neither prejudice nor injustice passes judgment, the one because it despairs of the truth, the other because it rejects it.

[Note: [Col. 0328B] Paris edition: “despairs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0328B] Paris edition: “rejects.”]

We have ceased to worship your gods from the moment we recognized that they are not gods.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] **We have ceased to worship.** An excellent declaration of repentance, matched by the bold freedom of Subrius Flavus, a tribune convicted of participating in the conspiracy against Nero, in Tacitus, *Annals* XV [Col. 0328B].67. When Nero asked him for what reasons he had proceeded to forget his military oath, he answered:

> I hated you; yet no soldier was more faithful to you while you deserved to be loved. I began to hate you after you became the murderer of your mother and wife, a charioteer, an actor, and an incendiary.

HAV.]

This, then, is what you ought to require: that we prove they are not gods and therefore must not be worshipped, since they ought to have been worshipped only if they had been gods. Christians would then also deserve punishment if it were established that those whom they did not worship, because they supposed them not to exist as gods, really were gods.

“But to us,” you say, “they are gods.” We appeal from you to yourselves, and summon your own conscience. Let it judge us; let it condemn us, if it can deny that all those gods of yours were once human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0328B] **Were human beings.** Cicero has this in *Tusculan Disputations* I.12: [Col. 0328C]

> Is not almost the whole heaven—to avoid pursuing more examples—filled with the human race? Indeed, if I were to scrutinize ancient accounts and attempt to draw out from them what the writers of Greece have handed down, those very gods who are regarded as belonging to the greater nations would be found to have departed from us here into heaven. Ask whose tombs are displayed in Greece; recollect, since you have been initiated, what is handed down in the mysteries; then at last you will understand how widely this extends.

Diodorus Siculus likewise reports these things concerning the gods of the Egyptians and other peoples, Book I, p. 17: Περὶ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἐν οὐρανῳ θεῶν, καὶ γένεσιν ἀΐδιον ἐσχηκότων τοσαῦτα λέγουσιν Αἰγύπτιον (“Thus much, then, the Egyptians say concerning the gods in heaven who have an eternal origin”; the recovered final Αἰγύπτιον is grammatically anomalous). Ἄλλους δὲ ἐκ τούτων ἐπιγείους γένεσθαι φασὶ· ὑπάρξαντας μὲν θνητοὺς, διὰ δὲ σύνεσιν καὶ κοινὴν ἀνθρώπων εὐεργεσίαν τετυχηκότας τῆς ἀθανασίας (“They say that others of these became earthly gods: though originally mortal, they attained immortality through their wisdom and their beneficence toward humanity generally”). ὧν ἐνίους καὶ βασιλεῖς γεγονέναι κατὰ τὴν Αἴγυπτον (“Some of whom had also been kings in Egypt”). Μεθηρμηνευομένων δ` αὐτῶν τινὰς μὲ ὁμωνύμους ὑπάρχειν τοῖς οὐρανίοις, τινὰς δὲ ἰδίαν ἐσχηκέναι προσηγορίαν, Ἣλιόντε, καὶ Κρόνον, καὶ Ῥέαν, ἔτι δὲ καὶ Διὰ τὸν ὑπο τινων Ἄμμονα προσαγορευόμενον (“When their names are translated, some are namesakes of the heavenly gods, while others have distinctive appellations: Helios, Cronus, Rhea, and also Zeus, who is called Ammon by some”; the recovered Greek contains apparent textual errors).

> The Egyptians relate these things concerning the gods who are in heaven and whose race is eternal. Of these, they say, some were born from the earth and were mortal at first, but later attained immortality because of their abilities and the benefits they conferred upon all humanity. Some of them had been kings in Egypt. The names of certain of them were either changed so that they became similar in sound to those of the heavenly gods, or preserved without alteration according to their earlier form—namely, the names of the Sun, Saturn, Rhea, and Jupiter himself, whom some called Ammon.

EDITORS.]

But even if conscience itself should deny it, it will be convicted from its own records of antiquity, from which it learned about them: cities down to the present day bear witness—the cities in which they were born—and so do the regions in which they performed some deed and left traces behind, and in which they were even buried.…

[Note: [Col. 0328D] **In which they were born.** Not only Apollo, Diana, Bacchus, Hercules, and others, but Jupiter himself, father of gods and men and eternal king, concerning whose native soil our author himself employs his customary mockery in ch. XXV:

> But Jupiter would not immediately have allowed his own Crete to be shaken by the Roman fasces, forgetting the Idaean cave, the Corybantian bronze, and the most delightful fragrance of his nurse there.

HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0328D] **Buried.** Hence the statement below, ch. XII:

> Are we banished to islands? One of your gods too is customarily either born or dies on islands.

Who, certainly, does not know Jupiter’s cradle—

[Col. 0329B]

> and that  
> Crying which, they say, the Curetes once concealed in Crete, when  
> Armed and keeping rhythm, they struck bronze against bronze,  
> Lest Saturn should seize him and consign him to his jaws—
“And would inflict an everlasting wound beneath his mother’s breast,” as Lucretius sang, book II, verse 633. Add Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*, somewhat before the end: Οὗ τὸ μνῆμα οὐκ ὀλίγοις ἐστι δῆλον, ἐν Κρήτῃ γὰρ τῇ νήσῳ, ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ λεγομένῳ Λασίῳ, ἕως δεῦρο δακτυλοδεικτεῖται, that is: “His tomb is known to no few people; for on the island of Crete, on the mountain called Lasium, it is pointed out with the finger even to this day.” Callimachus, though indignant at this, nevertheless confirms the ancient tradition in Hymn I, verse 8. HAV.] are pointed out. Nor shall I run through them one by one [Col. 0329A]—so many and so great [Note: [Col. 0329B] So many and so great, etc. Augustine treats of these expressly in *The City of God*, book III, ch. 12: “Under the protection of so many gods—who can number them?—native and foreign, heavenly, terrestrial, infernal, marine, belonging to springs, [Col. 0329C] woodland, riverine; and, as Varro says, certain and uncertain; and, in every class of gods as among animals, males and females.” Here perhaps one should read even better *tot ac tanto*, as was entered from a manuscript into my copy of Augustine, by Vives himself, I think. Minucius Felix likewise, p. 6: “While they seek guest-gods from every quarter and make them their own; while they erect altars even to unknown divinities.” HAV.], new, old, barbarian [Note: [Col. 0329C] Barbarians, Greeks. Antisthenes, whose mother was Thracian and who was therefore mocked by the Greeks, is said to have replied: Καὶ ἡ μήτηρ τῶν Θεῶν, Φρυγία ἐστιν, that is, “The mother of the gods, too, is Phrygian.” Laertius, in his *Life*. HAV.], Greek, Roman, foreign, captive [Note: [Col. 0329C] Captive. Wretched as they were, when they wished to remove this disgrace from themselves, they first attempted to summon the gods away, and, when a city was under siege, to transfer to themselves the favor of its tutelary gods. Servius notes this on Virgil, *Aeneid* II.351:

> All have departed, abandoning their shrines and altars—  
> The gods by whom this empire had stood.

“For,” he says, “before a city was stormed, its divinities were summoned away by the enemy, in order to avoid sacrilege.” And from this comes Macrobius III.9: “When they were besieging an enemy city and had become confident that it could now be taken, they would summon away its tutelary gods with a prescribed formula; either because they did not believe that the city could otherwise be taken, or because, even if it could, they deemed it sacrilege to hold gods captive.” To this I perhaps refer the counsel of Balak and Balaam, Numbers XXIII.3, 23. That passage in Livy, book V, ch. 22, is noteworthy; see it. Yet what confidence could the blind pagans place in those gods, who were powerless to defend their own possessions, as the Author will show below? Hence Alexander also followed Philotas’ advice in Curtius V.2, when he was just about to order the sacred table of the gods—at which Darius had been accustomed to dine and which, as circumstances suggested, had been placed beneath him as a footstool for his higher royal seat—to be removed, after being admonished in these words: “By no means should the king do this; rather, take it as an omen that the table from which your enemy poured libations at his feasts lies beneath your feet.” Thus it is uncertain whether the Philistines placed the Ark of the Covenant in the temple of their god Dagon as a trophy taken from a defeated enemy, or out of reverence for and hope of assistance from the divine power; concerning this, see 1 Samuel ch. V. It is certain, at any rate, from verse 7 of ch. IV and verse 6 of ch. VI, that they thought no slight things about the God of the Israelites. But God took it most grievously when they received among their divinities the gods of those whom they had conquered and of the peoples whom they had eradicated, as is clear from 2 Kings XVI.3 and XVII.7–8. HAV.], adopted, personal, common, male, female, rural, urban, nautical, military. It would be idle even to pursue their titles, so as to gather them into a compendium [Note: [Col. 0330B] Gather them into a compendium. Note the expression of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, who says in a letter, “that we may briefly bind everything tightly with a girdle.” From this it becomes clear that the expression *briefly to bind tightly*, common among Latin authors, was taken from clothing, and especially from the girdle. Hence Tertullian says pointedly here, “I shall gather them into a compendium,” as though gathering up garments with a girdle so that they do not flow loose. Seneca’s expression in Epistle 76 likewise does not depart from the image of clothing: “that I may draw what has been said into a narrow compass.” LAC.]; and this not so that you may learn, but so that you may recognize them again—for you are certainly acting as though you had forgotten.

Before Saturn there is no god among you; from him dates the entire register of divinity, or at least its more important or better-known portion. Accordingly, whatever is established concerning its origin will hold good concerning its posterity. Thus, as for Saturn, if we follow what [Note: [Col. 0329A] The Lyon manuscript has *si quantum*; the others, *quantum*. And in the second part of the sentence, in place of what Gelenius and others had substituted—*si quaeras rerum argumenta*—Heraldus and Rigault restored from the manuscripts: *si quantum rerum argumenta*, etc.] literature teaches, neither the Greek Diodorus nor [Col. 0330A] Thallus, neither Cassius Severus nor Cornelius Nepos, nor any commentator on antiquities of this kind, has represented him as anything other than a man. If we follow the evidence of facts, nowhere do I find evidence more trustworthy than in Italy itself, in which [Note: [Col. 0330B] In which Saturn. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book I, verse 42, should be consulted here, where he begins:

> Is Saturn believed to have ruled the Latin forefathers better—  
> He who by such edicts instructed  
> Their rustic minds and the barbarous hearts of men?

HAV.] Saturn settled after many expeditions and after enjoying Attic hospitality, having been received by Janus—or Janes, as the Salii will have it. The mountain he had inhabited [Note: [Col. 0330C] The mountain he had inhabited. He seems to have taken this passage from Varro, book IV, *On the Latin Language*, also cited by St. Augustine, book VII of *The City of God*, ch. 2: “The mountain,” he says, “on which the Capitol stands was formerly called Tarpeian. They relate that this mountain was previously called Saturnian, and that the surrounding country was extensively called the Saturnian land, as Ennius also calls it. It is written that an ancient town named Saturnia once stood on it. Three traces of it still remain: the shrine of Saturn in the pass; the Saturnian Gate, which Junius records and which they now call Pandana; and the fact that behind the temple of Saturn, in the building regulations, the rear walls of buildings are recorded as ‘walls.’” On this passage Scaliger adduces Ennius’ own verses, and similar verses of Maro concerning the Janiculum. PAM.], was called Saturnian; the city whose boundaries he had marked out is called Saturnia to this day; and, finally, all Italy, after being called Oenotria [Note: [Col. 0330C] Oenotria. Italy was called Oenotria ὑπὸ τοῦ οἴνου, from wine, not from some king of that name. This opinion agrees with Aristotle, *Politics* VII, and with [Col. 0330D] Strabo, book VI, who identify it without making any mention of an Oenotrian king. LAC.], was surnamed Saturnia [Note: [Col. 0330A] Rhenanus and Gelenius: “The mountain which Saturn had cultivated was called Saturnian; the city which he had conquered was surnamed Saturnia.”]. From him first came tablets and a coin stamped with an image [Note: [Col. 0330D] Coinage marked with an image. Isidore, *Origins* XVI.17: “Afterward bronze coinage was invented by Saturn. For he ordained that coins should be stamped and inscriptions made. For this reason the treasury was also consecrated to Saturn by the pagans.” See more in Elmenhorst’s notes on Minucius, and also in Lipsius’ excerpts, appended to the new Kipping edition, p. 597, and in that great ornament of letters and true glory of Germany today, Johann Albert Fabricius, *Bibliographia Antiquaria*, p. 525. It should not, however, be left unmentioned that the collation of the Fulda manuscripts presents the reading *et imagine et signatus nummus*. From this I had conjectured that perhaps the text was *et imagines, et signatus nummus*. Minucius certainly, who diligently copied our author, has only “to stamp coins,” as do the others. Yet since others add the pruning of trees, wreaths, and ships, our Author may have ascribed the invention of the arts of statuary and sculpture [Col. 0331B] to Saturn, since previously images had consisted of a rough and unshaped stake. HAV.], and for this reason he presides over the treasury [Col. 0331A].

Yet if Saturn was a man, then he was surely born from a human being; and because he was born from a human being, he was surely not born from heaven and earth. But since his parents were unknown, it was easy for him to be called the son of those whose children we all may seem to be [Note: [Col. 0331B] Whose children we all may seem to be. From this it is clear how the corrupted passage in *To the Nations* II.12 should be restored. It reads there: “But he whose parents . . . . to some it was easy for him to be called the son of the Gods, whose . . . . seem.” The supplements *unknown*, and either “all can” or “we all can,” are correct. But the initial letter of τὸ, “Gods,” also ought to have been made lower-case. There too follows: “For who, indeed, does not call Heaven and Earth,” etc. HAV.]. For who does not call heaven and earth his mother and father, out of reverence and honor, or in accordance with the human custom by which unknown persons, or those who appear unexpectedly, are said to have arrived from heaven?

Consequently, because Saturn was everywhere sudden and unexpected [Note: [Col. 0331B] Thus Heraldus and Havercamp from the manuscripts; Wouwer: “because of Saturn’s sudden arrival.”] [Note: [Col. 0331B] Sudden and unexpected everywhere. So the Leiden manuscript, Heraldus, and Rigault. [Col. 0331C] Others less correctly inserted the word “arrival.” Wouwer’s “because of his sudden arrival, surely,” should therefore not be approved. For Tertullian says of Saturn what Tacitus, *Annals* II.39, says of the suborned and false Agrippa: “he left rumor behind, or arrived before it.” Laertius similarly notes in his *Life of Empedocles* that Empedocles obtained divine honors from the Selinuntines by his sudden appearance. But in a single stroke I shall also cure the passage in *To the Nations* II.13 which others have abandoned as hopeless. There, on the same subject, it reads: “Consequently . . . always need . . . sudden and unexpected everywhere, he became accustomed to be called a heavenly being.” Tertullian had written: “Consequently, because Saturn was always needy, sudden, and unexpected.” For Saturn, driven from his kingdom by his son Jupiter, is said in the same work to have wandered through many lands; for which reason Tertullian compares him to a beggar who nowhere remains long. HAV.], it happened that he was called a heavenly being. For the common people also call those whose lineage is uncertain “sons of the earth.”

I pass over the fact that men then behaved with such crudeness [Note: [Col. 0332B] The Fulda manuscripts have “then”; compare *To the Nations* II.12. The others have “still.”] that they were stirred by the sight of any new man as though by something divine [Note: [Col. 0331C] As though divine. In Justin V.4, the Athenians marvel when Alcibiades is suddenly restored to them with a victorious army: “The whole city turned its eyes toward him, every face hanging upon him; they gazed upon him as though sent from heaven and [Col. 0331D] as though he were Victory herself.” Lactantius, in the passage mentioned above: “Minucius Felix, in the book entitled *Octavius*, argued as follows: when Saturn had been driven out by his son and had come to Italy, he was called the son of Heaven, because we are accustomed to say that those whose virtue we admire, or those who arrive suddenly, have fallen from heaven.” Hence that familiar saying:

> A third Cato has fallen from heaven.

It is therefore no longer astonishing why the people of Lystra thought Paul and Barnabas to be Mercury and Jupiter, and heavenly beings who had descended, Acts of the Apostles XIV.12; just as in XXVIII.6 the Maltese, barbarians and islanders, believed Paul to be a god when he was unharmed by the viper. HAV.], whereas today, though already civilized, you consecrate as gods those whom only a few days before you confessed had died amid public mourning [Note: [Col. 0331D] Had died amid public mourning. The Fulda manuscript gives the final words thus: “dead and buried,” which could be attributed to the custom of copyists who, upon finding two variant readings, restored both by joining them together—unless one prefers to write: “dead and buried.” It may easily be seen that Tertullian here drenches the consecration and adoration of the Caesars with biting vinegar: for they were not merely dead, but had also been formally mourned and buried. One might also read “had died as human beings,” that is, in the manner of human beings, in contrast with “you consecrate them as gods.” A similar mockery of foreign divinities whose worship had gained strength at Rome appears in Lucan VIII.833:

> And Osiris, whom by mourning you attest to have been a man.

Rhenanus’ reading “we show” immediately afterward is wrong. HAV.].

Enough now concerning [Col. 0331B] Saturn, though said in few words. We shall also show that Jupiter was as much [Col. 0332A] a man [Note: [Col. 0332B] As much a man, etc. Sanchuniathon, a most ancient writer, as quoted by Theodoret, Discourse III, p. 42, relates that Saturn [Col. 0332C] was a man, and Rhea a woman and Saturn’s wife; that they begot Jupiter and Juno as children; and that all of them, on account of the benefits they conferred, were afterward regarded as gods by the Phoenicians. Lactantius likewise, after recounting Jupiter’s entire genealogy from the sacred books of Ennius, concludes as follows in I.14: “This, as it has been written, is the stock and kinship of Jupiter and his brothers, handed down in this manner from the sacred writing.” HAV.] as born from a man, and thereafter that the whole brood of his line was mortal and like its own stock.

## CHAPTER XI

**ARGUMENT.—Since men are said to have been enrolled among the gods after death because of the excellence of their merits, this chapter investigates the reasons that required this. No such reasons can be found with respect to the supreme God, since he does not need the help of others; with respect to the men themselves, those reasons are either empty or of such a kind that, because of them, the men deserve rather to be thrust down with criminals into the lowest Tartarus, where you have placed men who far surpassed them both in inventions and in merits.**

And since, just as you do not dare deny that they were men, so you have undertaken to assert that they were made gods after death, let us reconsider the reasons that required this. First of all, you must concede that there exists [Col. 0332B] some higher God [Note: [Col. 0332C] A higher God. One who is not merely Ἀρχαιότατος (“most ancient”)},{, as Herodian says of Janus in book I, ch. 16, but also Αὐτοκράτωρ (“sovereign”)},{, as Gaius is called on the coin that we shall produce at ch. XXXIV—namely, in relation to the Sun and Moon, who are called θεοῖ αὐτοκράτορες (“sovereign gods”)},{ in Philo, *On Monarchy* I, p. 812—and thus “God of gods,” as Janus is again called by Macrobius I.9. Δημιουργὸς καὶ θεὸς θεῶν (“Creator and God of gods”)},{, as Hierocles describes the supreme God in his *Golden Verses*: “the sole Creator-God, whom one might call the God of gods, and the highest and best God.” τον δημιουργὸν μόνον ὃν θεὸν θεῶν ἂν εἴποι τις, καὶ [Col. 0332D] θεὸν ὓπατον καὶ ἄριστον. HAV.] and a certain contractor [Note: [Col. 0332D] Contractor. Luctatius—or Lactantius—the scholiast on Statius, *Thebaid* IV, indicates what sort of being should be understood when he writes: “Countless philosophers and Magi, and likewise the Persians, affirm that besides these recognized gods who are worshipped in temples there truly exists another ruler and supreme God, the ordainer of the other divinities.” Tertullian again, *On the Shows* X: “But those activities conducted by voice, rhythms, instruments, and lyre have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their contractors.” HAV.—A certain contractor of divinity. As though he were some wholesale dealer in the commerce of divinity. Asconius interprets *mancipes* as “chief tax-farmers and public contractors.” Thus juristic authors speak of contractors for roads, saltworks, etc. So too Tertullian, in *On Idolatry*, spoke of “contractors for idols.” RIG.—A certain contractor. Rhenanus says that he wittily calls that higher and more powerful God, who shared divinity with the others, a “contractor of divinity,” just as Pliny calls the master of a shoemaker’s workshop a contractor, and those who are foremost in any matter are called contractors. PAM.] [Col. 0333A] of divinity [Note: [Col. 0333B] “A certain.” The Barraeus edition has “indeed,” as does the Leiden manuscript. HAV.], who made gods out of men. For they could neither have assumed for themselves the divinity [Note: [Col. 0333B] Assume divinity. Below, ch. XXII: “They rival divinity while they steal divination.” See our notes there. HAV.] that they did not possess, nor could anyone confer it upon those who did not have it except one who properly possessed it [Note: [Col. 0333B] “They possessed,” Paris manuscript.].

But if there were no one who made gods, you groundlessly presume that gods were made while removing their maker. Certainly, if they had been able to make themselves gods, they would never have been men, since they would obviously have possessed within themselves the power of a better condition. Therefore, if there is one who makes gods, I return to examining the reasons for making gods out of men. I find none, unless that great God desired their services [Note: [Col. 0333B] “Mysteries,” Paris manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0333B] Unless he desired their services. Observe that Tertullian constructs a dilemma. The great God sought an assistant for himself either because he needed someone’s help and service, without which the machinery of this world could not exist, or because some god’s merits demanded it. The first is not the case, because there is no basis in merit for raising them to heaven, whereas there are many merits for pressing them down into Tartarus; and this constitutes the entire force of this chapter. LAC.] and assistance for divine functions. First, it is unworthy that he should need anyone’s labor, and indeed the labor of a dead man, since, if he was going to need a dead man’s labor, it would have been more fitting for him to have made some god from the beginning.

But I see no place for such labor either. For this whole body [Col. 0333B] of the world—whether unborn and unmade according to Pythagoras, or born and made according to Plato—was surely discovered to have been disposed, equipped, and ordered once and for all in that [Note: [Col. 0334B] “In its own arrangement,” Havercamp.] construction, together with the whole apparatus of reason’s governance [Col. 0334A]. That which brought all things to completion could not have been imperfect [Note: [Col. 0333C] It could not have been imperfect. La Cerda teaches that these words should be understood not of that contracting God, but of the world: once it had been made or created, all things had been completed. Thus that which completed all things—that is, which brought to an end the making of any further new creature—cannot be regarded as imperfect; nor did any part of it await Saturn or the others, by whom it would be created as by gods, since it had already been perfected at its beginning. I too agree with this explanation, for it is fully required both by the preceding words, “But I see no place for such labor either,” and by what will shortly follow, “that from the beginning rains had already fallen from heaven,” etc. HAV.]. Nothing awaited Saturn and the Saturnian race.

Men will be foolish unless they are certain [Note: [Col. 0333C] Unless they are certain that from the beginning, etc. Manilius, book I, ch. 5:

> Even then, when the Greek peoples overturned Pergamum,  
> The Bears and Orion moved with opposing fronts:  
> The former content to bend their circuits at the pole,  
> The latter rising opposite from the contrary quarter,  
> Meeting the revolving sky and always coursing through the whole heavens.

God, of course, established the order of things once and for all; instituted together with the world and then beginning to be observed, it will endure together with it. Hippodamus the Pythagorean, in the fragment *On Happiness* that remains to us: Αἴτε γὰρ μὴ ἦ ὁ κόσμος, οὐδ` ἃν ὁ ἥλιος ἦν, οὐδ` ἁ σελανα, οὐδ` οἱ πλανᾶτες ἀστὲρες οὐδ` οἱ ἀπλανέες. Ὄντος δὲ γε τοῦ κοσμοῦ, καὶ τούτων ἕκαστον ἔστι. That is: “For if the world did not exist, neither the sun nor the moon nor either the fixed or wandering stars would exist. But since the world exists, each of these things too is seen.” HAV.] that from the beginning rains had fallen from heaven [Note: [Col. 0333D] The lights had blossomed. As often elsewhere, he has imitated Lucretius, book IV, verse 451. HAV.], the stars had emitted their rays, the lights had blossomed, thunder had bellowed, and Jupiter himself had feared the thunderbolts which you place in his hand [Note: [Col. 0334B] In Rhenanus and Gelenius the words “and Jupiter himself—had feared” are absent.]; likewise, that every crop [Note: [Col. 0333D] Likewise every crop. Either he alludes to the age of Saturn, whom Macrobius writes was the first to teach agriculture in Latium and also demonstrated the use of wine—Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII—or certainly to the history of Genesis, where in ch. III Adam is said to have been sent out of the paradise of pleasure to till the earth, and in ch. 2 Abel is said to have been a shepherd of sheep and Cain a farmer, with whom Josephus agrees, *Jewish Antiquities* I. PAM.] had sprung abundantly from the earth before Liber, Ceres, and Minerva—indeed, before any first man whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0334B] Man. The *Collatio Modiana* has “men.” I do not approve it, but I shall explain the passage briefly. He says that every kind of crop ought to have sprung from the earth before Bacchus, Ceres, and Minerva—indeed, even before the first man, whoever he was—because after man already existed, nothing by which provision might be made for him to persist in life could or ought to have been created.], because nothing intended to preserve and sustain man could have been introduced to provide for him only after man’s appearance.

Finally, they are said to have discovered these necessities of life, not to have instituted them. But whatever is discovered [Note: [Col. 0334C] But whatever is discovered existed. Septimius presses the etymology of what is called an “invention” too hard. For in this discussion *invented* is the same as *devised*, and those are called inventors of arts who were the first to devise arts and mechanisms: for example, those of ploughing the earth; grinding and baking bread; trenching and propagating vines; making, storing, and preserving wine; and other things of this sort that are necessary, useful, and pleasant for life. RIG.] existed; and what existed will not be assigned to the one who discovered it, but to the one who instituted it, for it existed before it was discovered.

But if Liber is therefore [Col. 0334B] a god because he revealed the vine, Lucullus was badly treated [Note: [Col. 0334C] Lucullus was badly treated. St. Jerome makes precisely the same point to Marcella no less wittily than truly [doubtless following Pliny, *Natural History* XV.25]: “We have received,” he says, “a basket filled with cherries of such a kind, blushing with such virginal modesty, that I might think them now brought by Lucullus. For, after Pontus and Armenia had been subdued”—namely in the Mithridatic War, in the year 680 from the founding of the city—“he was the first to bring this kind of fruit from Cerasus to Rome, whence the tree also received its name from its native place.” The words “revealer and discoverer” are absent from Puteanus’ book. PAM.], for he was the first [Note: [Col. 0334D] Who was the first to bring cherries from Pontus. The Fulda manuscript reads, “who was the first for the Romans to bring cherries from Pontus,” a reading which, since it could not be tolerated because of the “to Italy” that immediately follows, found no approval. Perhaps he wrote: “who, the first Roman, brought cherries,” etc., in the manner in which Lucretius, whom he often imitates, once spoke of the magnificent poet Ennius, who was the first of the Romans to merit the laurel, book I, verse 118:

> As our Ennius sang, who first brought down  
> From lovely Helicon a crown of everlasting foliage;

that is, the first of our people. Thus “the first Roman” means “the first of the Romans.” The same Lucretius, book V, verse 37:

> Whither none of our people approaches, nor does any barbarian dare.

This very act is attributed to Pompey by our Tertullian himself [Col. 0335B] in *To the Nations* II.16: “Gnaeus Pompey was the first to make the cherry from Pontus widely known in Italy.” HAV.] to make cherries from Pontus widely known in Italy, yet was not therefore consecrated as the originator of a new crop merely because he discovered and revealed it.

Therefore, if from the beginning the universe stood established, both equipped and administered according to fixed principles for the exercise of its functions, on this score there is no ground for alleging that humanity was elevated into divinity. For the stations and powers that you distributed among them existed as much from the beginning as they would have existed even if you had never created those gods.

But turn now to another reason, replying that the bestowal [Note: [Col. 0335B] The bestowal of divinity was the means of rewarding merits. Pliny, book II: “This is the most ancient custom of returning thanks to those who have deserved well: that such persons should be enrolled among the divinities.” RIG.] of divinity was the means of rewarding merits. And from this, I think, you will concede that this deifying God must excel in justice, since he did not dispense so great a reward rashly, unworthily, or prodigally. I therefore wish to review [Note: [Col. 0335B] “You wish,” Rigault.] their merits, to determine whether they are of such a kind that they should have raised them into heaven, and not rather plunged them into the lowest Tartarus, which you affirm, together with many others, to be the prison of infernal punishments [Col. 0335B].

For there are customarily thrust [Note: [Col. 0335B] The impious are customarily thrust there, etc. Lucian similarly enumerates these in the *Necromancy*: ἑτέρωθεν δὲ, he says, προσήγοντο, [Col. 0335C] etc.; that is: “From the other side there were brought in order many persons bound with a long chain, who were said to be adulterers, pimps, tax collectors, flatterers, informers, and crowds of that kind—men who had thrown everything into confusion during life.” Our Tertullian quite plainly has in view Virgil’s majesty, which, while describing the place of infernal punishment, sets forth these things among others in book VI, verses 608, 614, and 621–24. See the passage.], all who are impious toward their parents, commit incest with their sisters, commit adultery with married women, ravish virgins, defile boys, act with cruelty [Col. 0336A], kill, steal, deceive, and all who resemble any one of your gods. You will not be able to prove any one of them [Note: [Col. 0335C] Not one of them. Latinius should not have disturbed this reading, nor should others have commended it as corrupt. For our African wrote in perfectly good Latin, and precisely as Suetonius writes of Nero in ch. XXXIX of his *Life*: “I have learned from some that he held it as entirely certain that no human being was chaste or pure in any part of his body; but that most concealed their vice and covered it with cunning.” In the same manner he said above, ch. X: “Before Saturn there is no god among you.” But I cannot approve what the Aldine edition and Rhenanus have, “man,” as though Tertullian were beginning a new argument here; nor should the passage be written [Col. 0335D] with a question mark, as Barraeus does, in whose edition you will seek the following words in vain: “But since you cannot deny that those men existed.” HAV.] innocent of crime or vice, unless you deny that he was a man [Note: [Col. 0335B] Rhenanus and Gelenius: “What man among them will you deny?”].

But since you cannot deny that they were men, these marks are added as well, and do not permit the belief that they were afterward made gods. For if you preside over the punishment of such persons; if all upright people among you reject intercourse, conversation, and companionship with the wicked and disgraceful; yet that God has received their equals into fellowship with his majesty—why, then, do you condemn those whose colleagues [Note: [Col. 0335D] Colleagues. As below: “I discover nothing other than that the substances of vessels and common implements are sisters.” Psellus on Nazianzen, p. 1084: “In what manner shall I ridicule such acts of worship”—that is, the worship of idols and images—“and mock those who worship such things and who assign worship and honors to creation and matter, if I myself adore fellow servants and things that differ little or not at all from those regarded as gods among them?” He speaks of the fabrication concerning the Son of God as the first of created beings. HAV.] you adore? Your justice is a reproach in heaven [Note: [Col. 0335D] “It is a reproach in heaven.” So the *Collatio Modiana*, which I have found most excellent and follow throughout. Nearly all the others have “in heaven,” with much the same sense. The passage in *To the Nations* II.7 is not far removed from this: “You disgrace heaven with the tombs of your kings.” Moreover, this is an elegant passage, full of biting mockery. For while they justly punish criminals, adulterers, murderers, and thieves on earth, they do not see that by the same judgment they condemn their gods, whom they have placed in the heavens. He demonstrates what was certainly everywhere acknowledged by all: that not one of them is free from incest, adultery, theft, homicide, and the rape and corruption of virgins and boys. Thus, when they punish those who are their gods’ equals and colleagues in crime, their gods will certainly reckon this an insult, as he says at the end of ch. XIII. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0336B] The Fulda manuscript and Havercamp: “against heaven.”].

Make gods [Note: [Col. 0336B] “You make gods,” Semler.] [Note: [Col. 0336C] Make gods, etc. As wave follows wave, so shaft follows shaft in our Author. Having now virtually become an advocate for impiety, he will defend it—though it certainly enjoys neither this assistance nor this defender. You will find a similar sarcasm in ch. XIII: “But you worthily assign the honor of divinity to deceased emperors, since you assign it to them even while they are alive. Your gods will place it to your credit—indeed, they will congratulate themselves that their masters are made their equals.” Pamelius’ edition gives the extremely bad reading “You make gods.” For the meaning is: “Why do you not make the worst offenders among those in chains into gods? By this deed you will render a pleasing service to your gods, for like rejoices in like.” The Leiden manuscript, Heraldus, La Cerda, Rigault, Rhenanus, and the rest therefore correctly write “Make.” HAV.] of all the most criminal men [Note: [Col. 0336C] The most criminal men of all. Arnobius, book V: “If some despiser of the divinities, raging with the savagery of a sacrilegious heart, had set his mind on speaking evil of your gods, would he have dared to say anything more serious against them than what that history discloses, which you have gathered into an established form in your records as though it were something marvelous? And lest the force of time [Col. 0336D] and the long course of antiquity should render it obsolete, you honored it with perpetuity. For what is stated there about the gods, or what is written, which—if you said it of a man reared in shameful morals and harsher disciplines—would not render you liable for abuse and injury, and bring upon you hatred from irreconcilable feuds in proportion to the offense?” HAV.], so that you may please your gods. The consecration of their equals is an honor to them.

But let me omit reconsidering this indignity [Note: [Col. 0336D] You have left better men in the underworld. Equally outspoken was Diogenes, who, when the Athenians asked him to be initiated and told him that those who had been initiated held the chief places among the dead, replied Γελοῖον, ἕφη, εἰ Ἀγησὶλας μὲν καὶ Ἐπαμινώνδας ἐν τῳ βορβόρῶ διάξουσιν, εὐτελεῖς δέ τινες μεμνημένοι ἐν ταῖς μακάρων νὴσοις ἔσονται, that is: “It is utterly ridiculous, if Agesilaus and Epaminondas dwell in the mire, while every worthless person who has been initiated will inhabit the Isles of the Blessed.” HAV.], on the assumption that they were upright, blameless [Col. 0336C], and good. Yet how many better men have you left among the dead below? A Socrates in wisdom [Note: [Col. 0336D] Socrates. To whom he rightly assigns the first place among the wise, since Apollo himself called him the wisest of mortals. HAV.], an Aristides in justice [Note: [Col. 0336D] Aristides. His patience in enduring adversity was so great that, when votes were being gathered by which he was to be sent into exile, he complied when a man unknown to him—Aristides himself being unknown to that man—asked him to write the name “Aristides” on the voting shard for him because he was illiterate, the man giving no other reason than that he disliked hearing Aristides called “the Just” so excessively. His integrity was so great that, after returning from exile, although he had always discharged the greatest offices in the republic, he died in poverty, was given a public funeral, and his daughters received dowries from the public treasury. He was praised under this title by others and also by Nazianzen in his *Swan Songs*. O happiness of that age! HAV.], a Themistocles in military ability [Col. 0337A] [Note: [Col. 0337B] Themistocles in military ability. Themistocles’ glory shone forth in the Persian War at the battle of Marathon under the command of Miltiades; and a few years afterward he himself, as commander of the Athenians, fought Xerxes’ naval forces at Salamis with memorable distinction. LAC.], an Alexander in grandeur [Note: [Col. 0337C] Alexander. His μεγαλοψυχία (“greatness of spirit”)},{ fills every page in Arrian and Curtius. HAV.], a Polycrates in good fortune [Note: [Col. 0337C] Polycrates. He does not proceed at an equal pace, since at the end of his life he was cast down from every good fortune and miserably killed upon a cross; nevertheless, Fortune’s excessive indulgence and the ring which he had thrown into the sea and which was brought back by a fish secured for him the name “fortunate.” HAV.], a Croesus in wealth [Note: [Col. 0337C] Croesus in wealth. I am surprised that these words do not appear in the Junian edition, since Aldus also recognizes them, although “Crassus” is wrongly printed there. The temples of the gods in Lydia, enriched with his gold, demonstrated his opulence. Rhenanus also omitted it. HAV.], a Demosthenes in eloquence [Note: [Col. 0337C] Demosthenes. Astonished Greece stood in awe of the thunderbolts of his fluent tongue. HAV.]?

Which of your gods is more dignified and wiser than Cato [Note: [Col. 0337C] Cato. The man who was said to have fallen from heaven, who preferred to be good rather than to appear so. HAV.], more just and more soldierly than Scipio [Note: [Col. 0337C] Scipio. In him Tertullian combines these two virtues and sets him against Aristides and Themistocles—what great men! And certainly in the glory of warfare Lucian ranks him before everyone except Alexander, in that delightful dispute between Hannibal and Alexander among the *Dialogues of the Dead*. He also holds the first place in Theodoret’s enumeration of the Roman emperors, *To the Greeks*, p. 121: Οὐχ οἱ Ῥωμαίων περιφανέστατοι στρατηγοὶ, ὁ Σκιπίων ὁ πρῶτος, etc.; that is: “The most illustrious commanders of the Romans—Scipio the Elder,” etc. The name of Scipio likewise earned the epithet “just” through that famous deed by which he restored to her betrothed, untouched, a maiden of surpassing beauty who had been taken as spoil. Livy relates the story at the end of book XXVI, and Valerius Maximus in IV.3. Even now an ancient shield speaks of this deed because of its remarkable rarity—for Tertullian confuses the Scipios, all very similar to one another, just as he does the two Catos. A reproduction of it is now widely known and hangs, among other places, in the Leiden Library. HAV.]? Which is grander than Pompey [Note: [Col. 0337D] Pompey. That Pompey the Great who emulated all the deeds and sayings [Col. 0338B] of Alexander. Sallust is witness in the fragments that survive from book III of the *Histories*: “But Pompey, believing from early youth, because of the talk of his supporters, that he would be like King Alexander, was indeed an emulator of his deeds and counsels.” HAV.], more fortunate than Sulla [Note: [Col. 0338B] Sulla. Hence he was called by the surname *Felix*, “Fortunate”; and, something that rarely befalls the bloodthirsty, he was carried off by a peaceful death, for:

> Few kings descend without slaughter and wounds,  
> And few tyrants by a bloodless death.

Lucan concerning him, book II, verse 221:

> Was this the salvation of the state? Did Sulla merit by these deeds  
> To be called Fortunate, and by these to raise  
> His tomb for himself in the midst of the Field?], wealthier than Crassus, more eloquent than Tullius [Note: [Col. 0338C] Tullius. Juvenal, Satire X, verse 114:

> The eloquence and fame of Demosthenes or Cicero
Restoration notes: S000374 begins with an isolated Δ and an uncertain word division; both are preserved and the uncertainty is noted in E004.; S000388 contains uncertain recovered wording (ἐμείνων … εἰσεῖναι); it is preserved and translated according to the demonstrated context in E018.; S000394 contains the apparently corrupt reading τἢν σνμφορὰν; it is preserved and identified in E024.; S000395 contains the apparently corrupt word ἄτλα; it is preserved and identified in E025.; S000374 begins with an isolated Δ, and the remainder is not securely intelligible as recovered; both the text and a qualified approximate sense are represented in E004.; S000388 contains corrupt or uncertain recovered wording, especially ἐμείνων … εἰσεῖναι; E018 gives only the apparent contextual sense.  

Begins to desire, etc.]? How much more fittingly would he have waited for those gods to be taken up, since he surely had foreknowledge of better gods? He was in haste, I suppose, and closed heaven once and for all; and now he surely blushes while better men mutter in the underworld [Note: [Col. 0338C] **Muttering.** Perhaps *musinantibus* should be written, which comes closer to the reading of the Leiden manuscript and the Aldine edition, namely *musitantibus*. As Isidore teaches, *Origins*, book XII, ch. 1, the *musino* is an animal born of a she-goat and a ram; this verb could therefore have been formed from it. Thus he says satirically that those brave souls in the underworld nod together and, like rams, threaten with their horns on account of the injury inflicted upon them, intending, if opportunity is given, to charge the heavenly gods who are inferior to themselves. He had in view, I think, as often, that passage of Lucian in *Twice Accused*, p. 309, where Mercury says to Father Jupiter: Πάνυ ἀγανακτοῦσιν, ὦ πάτερ, καὶ σχετλιάζουσιν (“They are exceedingly indignant, father, and take it bitterly”)“. καὶ ἐς τὸ φανερὸν μὲν οὺ τολμῶσι λέγειν, ὑπογογγύζουσι δὲ συγκεκυφότες (“and they do not dare speak openly, but mutter with bowed heads”)“, that is: “They are exceedingly indignant, father, and bear it resentfully; they do not dare declare it openly, but bow their heads and mutter among themselves.” Or certainly that passage of Seneca in his most amusing jest on the Apotheosis of Claudius: “It is reported to Jupiter that someone of good stature and well gray-haired has arrived, who seems to be threatening something; for he is continually moving his head.” But if anyone considers the old reading safer, let him know that Tertullian similarly coined his own *mussitare*, as Homer has μύζειν (“to mutter”)“ in the *Iliad*, Δ


αὐ δὲ τὲ μύξαν Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἤρη (approximately, “… Athena and Hera muttered”; the isolated initial Δ and the recovered wording are uncertain); and from this Lucretius has *mussare*, book II, verse 658:

> But because they see many things contrary to themselves, they mutter;

and book VI, verse 1177:

> Medicine muttered in silent anguish.

Nor was Virgil ashamed to imitate it. He says in *Aeneid* XII:

> King Latinus himself mutters.

Thus *mussare* here means not daring to open one’s mouth, not even daring to utter μῦ (“mu,” the sound or syllable mū), as Dionysius Lambinus, a man most learned in Greek and Latin, rightly concludes from Varro.].

## CHAPTER XII

**ARGUMENT.—He next shows that those divinities are nothing but the empty names of dead men, whose images, in view of their material and manufacture, deserve the utmost [Col. 0337B] contempt, so much so that they may even console [Col. 0338A] the Christians who are punished on their account. For, in order to become gods, they are fastened to crosses like Christians, hewn with adzes, and finally mutilated. They are also surrounded by lions, dwell in quarries, and come from islands. Just as they themselves do not perceive these things, neither do they perceive the honors paid to them. Christians who reject them are therefore no more deserving of condemnation than Seneca formerly was, since he similarly condemned empty superstitions: for those gods are ridiculous who are exposed to injury even from the vilest little creatures—indeed, since they do not exist, they can neither benefit those who do exist nor be harmed by them.**

I shall now leave these matters, knowing that from truth itself I shall demonstrate what they are not when I have shown [Col. 0338B] what they are. So far as your gods are concerned, I see only the names [Col. 0339A] of certain ancient dead men [Note: [Col. 0339A] **Ancient dead men.** Similarly Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book II, ch. 2: “And therefore they set up images which, because they are representations of the dead, resemble [Col. 0339B] the dead, for they are devoid of every sense.” And in the same author, the Sibylline verses, book I, ch. 11:

> Δαίμονας ἀψύχους, νεκύων εἴδωλα καμόντων,


Ὦν Κρήτη καύχημα τάφους ἡ δύσμορος ἴσχει·

> Lifeless demons, images of the departed dead,  
> Whose tombs wretched Crete boasts of possessing.

that is: “Lifeless demons, images of dead corpses, whose wretched tombs Crete boasts of possessing.” Prudentius likewise, *Against Symmachus* I:

> And in Rome one may count as many temples of gods  
> As tombs of heroes in the city.

HAV.], I hear stories about them, and I recognize rites derived from those stories. As for the images themselves, I find nothing other than that their materials [Note: [Col. 0339A] Heraldus and Rigaltius: *materias sorores*; Havercamp, from one manuscript [Col. 0340A]; Aldus: *matres sorores*; Semler: *matre sorores*.] are sisters of ordinary vessels and implements [Note: [Col. 0339B] **That their materials are sisters.** For both gods and household vessels were commonly fashioned from the same material; and even objects that had previously been vessels were transformed into gods after being broken up and crushed with a pestle. Hence the material is their “sister,” that is, συγγενής (“kindred”)“, and as George Palamas has it: ἀδελφά φασι, και ὁμόχωρα, καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς κεραμείας (“they call them siblings, from the same place and the same pottery”)“. LE PR.], or that, being made from those very vessels and implements, they change, as it were, their destiny through consecration, while the license of art transforms them—and does so most insultingly and sacrilegiously in the very process of manufacture. Thus it may truly afford the greatest consolation in our punishments, we who are punished on account of the gods themselves, that they too undergo the same things in order to be made. You place Christians upon crosses and stakes [Note: [Col. 0339B] **Upon crosses and stakes.** He finely argues that they subject their gods to the same punishments with which they chastised Christians: crosses, stakes, claws, [Col. 0339C] capital punishment, beasts, fires, and condemnation to the mines. Here too Minucius imitates Tertullian throughout, distinguishing among images: for a wooden one it is appropriate to be suspended, cut, dressed with an adze, planed, and assembled; a bronze or silver one is melted, cast, soldered with lead, beaten with hammers, and shaped on anvils; and a stone one is cut, carved, smoothed, and erected. As for the statement, “What image is not first given rough form by clay built over a cross and stake?” Joseph Scaliger, on Festus, explains that the author is alluding to the derivation of *stipes* from *stipa*, properly the cross upon which modelers lay their clay. PAM.]: what image is not first given rough form by clay built over a cross and stake [Note: [Col. 0339C] **A cross and stake.** When modelers wish to rough out an image, they necessarily erect a stake around which the body is built, and a transverse piece of wood to form the arms. Minucius similarly develops this entire argument, p. 26: “If anyone considers with what torments and machinery every image is formed, he will blush to fear material that an artisan has mocked in order to make a god of it. [Col. 0339D] For a wooden god, perhaps a portion of a funeral pyre or an ill-omened stake, is suspended, cut, dressed, and planed; and a bronze or silver god is melted down from a filthy vessel—as was more than once done to an Egyptian king—beaten with hammers, and shaped on anvils; and a stone god is cut, carved, and smoothed by an unclean man.” See Elmenhorst there. Arnobius, book VI: “Baked in potters’ furnaces; scraped on anvils and under hammers and lathes, and rasped with files; cut with saws, drills, and adzes, dressed and hollowed out; excavated by the turning of augers and smoothed on their surfaces by planes.” HAV.]? The body of your god is first inaugurated upon a gibbet [Note: [Col. 0339D] **Your god is inaugurated.** Above he similarly called Nero the “inaugurator” of the condemnation of Christians, using *dedicare* in the sense of “to begin”; in this St. Cyprian also imitates him, Epistle 33. PAM.].

You scrape the sides of Christians with claws [Note: [Col. 0339D] **You scrape away with claws.** With the Fulda manuscript I should prefer *eraditis* to *deraditis*.
