Chrysostom, *Homily on St. Romanus the Martyr*: “For, like certain savage beasts surrounding his body, the executioners dug into his sides, scraped away his flesh, laid bare his bones, and penetrated even his innermost entrails.” Theodoret also enumerates these kinds of punishment in *Against the Greeks*, Discourse VIII, p. 112: Καὶ (“And”)“ [Col. 0340B] οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἔπεισεν (“did not persuade merely superficially”)“, etc.; that is: “Nor did they establish a shallow faith floating on the surface, but one fixed by roots so deep that a great multitude of people, in order to retain these doctrines, most willingly endured death; and when others wished them to deny them, they offered not their tongues in defense but their shoulders to scourges, their sides to torches and iron claws, and their necks to swords; they were stretched upon drums and racks, fixed upright upon stakes, saw themselves torn apart by savage beasts, and were burned alive.” From this it is clear that “to place upon stakes” here denotes that most cruel form of punishment in which a person’s lower parts are set upon a sharp stake erected in the ground, so that it protrudes almost through the shoulders and up to the neck. The Greeks called this ἀνασκινδυλεύεσθαι (“to be impaled”)“, which Hesychius explains as ἀνασκολοπισθῆναι (“to be impaled upon a stake”)“, “to be raised upon a stake.” Likewise, σκινδαλάμος (“splinter” or “stake”)“ or σκινδάλμος, σκὸλοψ (“splinter, pointed stake”)“, that is, “stake.” Seneca too, among the terrifying apparatus of punishments, writes in Epistle XIV: “Another evil has a mighty display about it: it has around it steel and fires and chains and a horde of beasts to be let loose upon human entrails. Think here of the prison, crosses, racks, the hook, the stake driven through the middle of a man so as to emerge through his mouth, limbs torn apart by chariots driven in opposite directions, and that tunic smeared and woven with fuel for fire.” And in *Consolation to Marcia*, ch. XX: “I see there crosses, not indeed all of one kind, but differently constructed by different people: some suspend their victims with their heads turned toward the ground; some drive a stake through their private parts; others stretch out their arms upon a crossbeam.” I also cite the exceedingly effeminate verses of the effeminate Maecenas, quoted by the same author in Epistle CI:

> While life remains, it is well.  
> Sustain this life for me, even if  
> I must sit upon a sharp cross.

Later Greeks called it πατταλεύειν (“to impale”)“. Procopius also mentions this punishment in book III of the *Gothic War*. HAV.]; but adzes, planes, and rasps bear more vigorously upon every limb of your gods [Note: [Col. 0340C] **Rasps.** These implements too served for finer ornamentation. The Glossary has Κοσμητήριον (“ornamenting implement”)“; for they used *scoba* in place of *scopa*, and hence *scobina* and the verb *scobere*. Guido II, prior of the Carthusians, who died in 1188 and was published by Chifflet in the statutes of that order, ch. XX, §2: “Let Martha therefore possess a ministry that is indeed praiseworthy, yet not without care and disturbance; and let her not trouble her sister, who cleaves to Christ’s footsteps and, because he is God, beholds him by remaining at leisure, polishing her spirit and turning her prayer into her own bosom.” HAV.].

We lay down our necks [Note: [Col. 0340D] **We lay down our necks.** He has in view the ancient practice whereby those to be beheaded were struck with an axe, as they are even today in England; for among the earliest peoples, as Lucan says in book VIII:

> It was not yet an art to whirl off a head with a sword.

This manner of death was later considered more honorable, as is clear from Bassianus’ indignation in Spartianus’ *Life of Geta*: “Papinian himself was struck with the axe,” Bassianus expressing disapproval because the affair had not been accomplished with a sword. HAV.]: before the lead, glue, and pegs [Note: [Col. 0340D] **Pegs.** Scaliger corrected the margin of his copy thus: “We lay down our necks before the lead; glue and pegging serve as a head for your gods.” He proposes this in his notes on Manilius, p. 509, and was so pleased with himself that he repeated it with praise in his notes on Eusebius, p. 226. But that most illustrious man is mistaken. The text must be written as in the editions of Rhenanus, Junius, La Cerda, and Rigaltius, and in all copies; the sense is simple and elegant. P. Scriverius also noted this in the margin of my codex, writing: “Scaliger on Manilius: ‘We lay down our necks,’ etc. Heribert Roswey rejected it in a letter to me in 1602 and in a small book published in 1607. ‘We lay down our necks,’ etc. It seems that it should be punctuated thus, which is the slightest possible change. [Col. 0341B] I ask, when the passage reads with excellent sense in this way, why are we stirring up waves in a ladle? Thus far Scriverius.” Tertullian enumerates three things done about the heads of gods when these were placed upon statues: lead—our *soudeerzel* or *soldarzel*—used for joining images of gold, silver, tin, and lead; glue, used for wooden and clay images; and pegs, used in colossi, where the head was fastened to the neck with iron nails, or with two or three leaden ones, because the joint would not be very visible at the viewing distance produced by the height. This can still be seen today at Rome in the most ancient statues, according to Scaliger on Eusebius, verse 226. The prophet Jeremiah has this in view when he says of them at 10:4, “They fasten them with pegs and hammers so that they do not fall apart”; compare Isaiah 41:7. The method of joining with glue and lead is taught in more than one place by the distinguished craftsman Pomponius Gauricus, in his elegant little book on sculpture or statuary, most recently appended to Vitruvius after having been published two or three times. The Greek-Latin Glossary of H. Stephanus II has: Γόμφος, ἐπίουρος (“peg or joint; stake”)“. “Joint, stake.” There is a notable passage in the *Acts of St. Thyrsus*, no. 21, concerning images: “Because they themselves are covered rather with iron pegs, lead, and stone.” I do not know what *Coll. Mod. Glutini et correptos* is meant to signify. Aldus and Heraldus read thus, but punctuate badly: “the necks before the lead, and glue,” etc. HAV.] your gods are without heads [Col. 0341A] [Note: [Col. 0341C] **Without heads.** For they commonly removed one god’s head in order to set another upon it. Thus Vespasian removed Nero’s head from his colossus and set upon it the head of the Sun with seven rays; after that in turn had been removed, Commodus sacrilegiously placed his own head upon it, as Spartianus relates in his life. In Suetonius, *Tiberius*, ch. LVIII: “He had removed the head from a statue of Augustus in order to set another’s upon it.” There the great Casaubon notes that this was common among the Rhodians, concerning whose statues witty men were accustomed to say that they resembled actors; and he adduces this passage of Dio Chrysostom’s *Rhodian Oration*: Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐμείνων ἔκαστον ἄλλοτ` ἄλλον εἰσεῖναι, καὶ τοὺς ἀνδρίαντας αὐτοῖς ἄλλοτε ἄλλα λαμβάνειν πρόσωπα, καὶ (approximately, “For just as each could be one person at one time and another at another, so their statues assumed different faces at different times, and”; the recovered wording ἐμείνων … εἰσεῖναι is corrupt or uncertain) [Col. 0341D] μικροῦ δεῖν ὑποκρινομένους ἷστάναι (“to set them up almost as actors playing roles”)“. Appropriately to the present passage, Scaliger, in the place cited above, quotes Jerome on Habakkuk 3: “Whenever a tyrant is beheaded, his images and statue are also taken down; and merely by changing the face and removing the head, the features of the victor are placed upon it, so that, while the body remains, the heads are cut off and another head substituted.” Thus, for as long as the god’s head is being changed, he is without a head; indeed, he is so from the beginning of his manufacture, before his head is fitted to his shoulders and neck with lead, glue, or pegs. HAV.].

We are driven to the beasts—surely the very beasts harnessed to Liber [Note: [Col. 0341D] **Liber and Cybele.** For tigers and lynxes draw Bacchus’ chariot. Of Cybele, Lucretius, book II, verse 600, says:

> The ancient, learned poets of the Greeks sang  
> That she drives a pair of lions harnessed to her chariot.

The fact is evident from Boissard’s plate, *Antiquities* III, 47; Gruter, *Thesaurus* I, 27; and the splendid coins once published by Patin in his *Thesaurus*, pp. 82 and 158, though note that four harnessed lions appear there. The name *Coelestis* [Col. 0342A] was used among the Asians for Carthage’s tutelary divinity; and even today, on coins of Severus and Caracalla, who were of African origin, she is seen seated upon a running lion, holding a thunderbolt in her right hand and a scepter in her left, her head encircled with a diadem. She is also represented in this way upon carnelian gem no. 566 in Golius Gronovius’ *Dactyliotheca*. The engraving must be noted, because Antonio Agustín suspected that the object on the coins was a rattle rather than a thunderbolt. A highly memorable statue of this goddess surrounded by two lions also occurs [Col. 0342B] in Boissard, *Antiquities* IV, p. 95, and the same may be viewed in the new edition of Gruter’s *Thesaurus*, vol. I, p. 86. More concerning this goddess at ch. XXIV. Other editions wrongly read “Ceres.”], Cybele, and Coelestis [Note: [Col. 0341A] Rhenanus and Semler: “Ceres.”]. We are burned with fires: so were they, even from the first stage of their material [Note: [Col. 0342B] **From the first.** Certainly while the still-rough material dug from the mountain is melted by fire, and not merely when it is poured into molds. HAV.]. We are condemned to the mines [Note: [Col. 0342B] **We are condemned to the mines.** Hilary complains of this against the emperor Constantius, who condemned even bishops themselves to this labor: “The bishops whom no one dared condemn, yet whom you ordered to be condemned, still bear upon their ecclesiastical brows, as we read, the sentences condemning them to the mines.” And Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, in book I *For Athanasius, to the Same Constantius*. LAC.]: from there your gods derive their lineage [Note: [Col. 0342B] **Your gods.** For some are made of metal, others of stone or marble. Lucian, *On Sacrifices*: ὅμως δ` οὖν οἱ παριόντες (“Nevertheless, those who enter”)“, etc.; that is: “Nevertheless, those who enter the temples no longer suppose that they see ivory imported from India or gold dug from Thracian mines, [Col. 0342C] but the very son of Saturn and Rhea, brought down to earth as a guest by Phidias.” Our author below, ch. XXIX, on statues of the gods: “I suppose that these very materials also come from Caesar’s mines.” HAV.]. We are banished to islands [Note: [Col. 0342C] **To islands.** Thus the Fulda manuscript and Rigaltius; but Aldus has “on an island,” Heraldus “on islands.” Others soon read “someone,” contrary to our author’s custom. In former times they commonly forbade certain condemned persons fire and water, with the result that, since no one dared provide these necessities of life, they perished miserably. Banishment to an island—or, as the jurists say, deportation—subsequently took the place of this cruelty. The island was generally barren, since most necessities of life were unavailable there, so the punishment was not very different. Law II of the *Digest*, *On Punishments*: “Deportation to a place succeeded interdiction from fire and water.” Law I of the *Code*, *On Repudiations*: “Marriage is not indeed dissolved by deportation or by interdiction from fire and water.” Tacitus, on Cassius Severus, *Annals* IV.21: “Stripped of his possessions and forbidden fire and water, he grew old upon the rock of Seriphos.” HAV.]: it is also customary for one of your gods [Col. 0342A] either to be born or to die on an island [Note: [Col. 0342D] **Either to be born or to die.** Apollo and Diana on Delos; Juno on Samos, by the river Imbrasus, beneath a grapevine, as is evident from a most singular coin in Seguin, p. 171; Jupiter himself on Crete, above ch. X and below ch. XXV: “But Jupiter did not immediately surrender his Crete to the Roman fasces,” etc. Lactantius too, *Divine Institutes* I, ch. 2: “Wasted by age, he exchanged life in Crete and departed to the gods. His sons, the Curetes, cared for him and adorned him. His tomb is in Crete, in the town of Knossos; and Vesta is said to have founded this city, in which his tomb bears the inscription ὁ Ζεὺς τοῦ Κρόνου (“Zeus, son of Cronus”)“, in Latin, ‘Jupiter, son of Saturn.’” Accordingly, the Cretan city of Hierapytna stamped the figure of an eagle upon its coins as a sign of Jupiter’s birth and upbringing, as may be seen in Patin, *Thesaurus*, p. 22, and Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, p. 475, who also mentions from Tristan Jupiter’s ΚΡΗΤΑΓΕΝΟΥΣ (“of the Cretan-born [Zeus]”)“. HAV.].

If any divinity is established through these things, then those who are punished are consecrated, and punishments will have to be called divinities. But clearly your gods do not perceive [Note: [Col. 0342D] **They do not perceive.** Jeremiah, in the book of Baruch, ch. VI.23: “Nor did they perceive when they were cast.” Equally absurdly, [Col. 0343B] though in another sense, Aeacus says of Bacchus being beaten in Aristophanes’ *Frogs*, act II, scene VI: Ἐίπερ θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν, οὐκ αἰσθήσεται (“For if indeed he is a god, he will not feel it”)“, that is: “For if he is a god, he will feel none of the blows.” HAV.] these injuries and insults attending their manufacture, just as they do not perceive the services rendered to them.

O impious [Col. 0343A] words! O sacrilegious insults! Gnash your teeth; foam at the mouth! You are the same people who censured a certain Seneca for declaiming at greater length and with greater bitterness against your superstition [Note: [Col. 0343B] **You are the same people who approve a certain Seneca when he declaims at greater length and with greater bitterness against your superstition.** This occurred, of course, in the books he composed on Roman superstition, which Augustine cites in book VI of *The City of God*. Septimius said “a certain Seneca,” just as elsewhere he commonly says “some Dido,” “a certain Licianus,” and “a certain Lazarus.” There is therefore no reason for us to be troubled by the authority of the Pithoean codex praised by Nicolas Le Fèvre in his preface to the edition of Seneca published at Paris in 1587. I believe that when that edition of Seneca appeared, Tertullian still read: “you censured him for declaiming at greater length and from greater authorities,” a reading not free from corruption. In the very ancient manuscript of the Putean library we read with perfect clarity: “You are the same people who censured a certain Seneca for declaiming at greater length and with greater bitterness”; the last copies wrongly omitted the word preserved by the Pithoean manuscript, which is certainly superior in that respect. The Fulda manuscript reads “you approve.” RIG.—**A certain Seneca.** Seneca wrote a volume on the superstition of the gentiles, which Aurelius Augustine mentions. [Col. 0343D] RHENANUS.—**A certain Seneca.** A fragment of his work *On Superstition* survives, which Lipsius adduces in *Selections* II, ch. 18, having taken it from Augustine, *City of God* VI, ch. 10. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0343B] Heraldus, from the Putean and Borgian codices: “than one declaiming at greater length and with greater bitterness—you censured.” Wouwer, from the codices of Pithoeus and Fulvius Ursinus: “you did not censure.” The Leiden codex and the editions of Rhenanus and Aldus: “at greater length and from greater authorities—you censured” or “you censure.” The Fulda codex: “you approve one declaiming.” Rigaltius and Havercamp: [Col. 0344B] “you approve a certain one—declaiming.”].

Accordingly, if we do not adore cold statues and images closely resembling their dead originals—images which kites [Note: [Col. 0343D] **Which kites, mice, and spiders understand.** That is, they know that these are not gods, but bronze, stones, or wood. They therefore nest in them; indeed, they do not fear to defile with every kind of insult the very things you worship as gods. They evidently understand that they will suffer no punishment from them for doing so. To this belongs the amusing oath of Horace’s Priapus:

> If I lie in anything, may my head be fouled  
> With the white droppings of crows.

RIG.—**Kites, mice, and spiders.** Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, and other very ancient defenders of the Christian religion demonstrated the foolishness of the gentile gods from the neglect and filth with which they abounded, since mice nested in them and spiders stretched out their webs. Thus that Roman emperor who, through the labor of older men, had collected ten thousand pounds of cobwebs adequately showed how much squalor resided in idols, since spiders were accustomed to live in them. LE PR.], mice, and spiders understand for what they are—does not our rejection of a recognized error deserve praise rather than punishment? For can we be thought to injure those whom we are certain do not exist at all? What does not exist suffers nothing from anyone, because it does not exist [Note: [Col. 0344B] “It suffers from him who does not exist,” Semler.].

## CHAPTER XIII

**ARGUMENT.—If, nevertheless, they wish these divinities to be so regarded, they ought surely to worship rather than despise them. Yet he shows that they commonly despise them: individuals worship several gods; divinity depends upon human judgment; and their images, like household implements, are pawned and sold—not only private but also public images—so that majesty itself becomes a source of profit. The same honor accorded to gods is also accorded to the dead, and is of course bestowed with even greater justification upon emperors while they are still alive, since emperors themselves make gods. Yet that honor can assuredly be assigned to prostitutes, pathics, and similar victims of public lust—not without signal insult to the gods, although the gods themselves are no more noble.**

“But they are gods to us,” you say. How, then, are you found, on the contrary, to be impious, sacrilegious, and irreligious toward your own gods—you who neglect those whom you assume to exist, destroy those whom you fear, and mock those whom you even avenge? Consider whether I am lying.

First, since different people worship different gods, you necessarily offend those whom you do not worship [Note: [Col. 0344B] **You offend those whom you do not worship.** Miserable people therefore had to expect their anger and vengeance. Curtius, on Alexander’s killing of Clitus, book VIII, ch. 2: “As he inquired whether he had been driven to so great a crime by the anger of the gods, it occurred to him that the annual sacrifice to Father Liber had not been performed at the appointed time; and therefore, since the killing had been committed amid wine and feasting, the god’s anger was manifest.” After Arrian related the same events in book IV, p. 163 of Gronovius’ edition, he prudently added, as a philosopher: Ἐπεὶ οὐδ` αὐτῷ ἄκοντι ἦν ἐς μῆνιν τοῦ θείου, μᾶλλον ἢ τὴν αὐτοῦ κακότητα, ἀναφέρεσθαι τἢν σνμφορὰν (“For it was not against his wishes that the misfortune should be attributed to the divinity’s wrath rather than to his own wickedness”; τἢν σνμφορὰν is apparently corrupt): “For it was not unwelcome to him that the event should be attributed to the divinity’s anger rather than to his own crime.” Hence the extraordinary admiration for the valor of Gaius Fabius Dorsuo in Livy, book V, ch. 46: when the Gauls were besieging the Capitol, he passed through the enemy’s lines and performed upon the Quirinal Hill the sacrifice traditional in his family. Lactantius rightly ridicules these empty fears, book XI, ch. 17: “Whenever dangers threaten, they declare that the gods are angry over some foolish and trivial cause: as Juno was with Varro because he had stationed a handsome boy in Jupiter’s temple to hold the vestments; and for this reason the Roman name was almost destroyed at Cannae.” Likewise, with sufficient absurdity, in Lucian’s *Philopseudes*, a certain bronze Hippocrates, after his customary sacrifice had been neglected, throws all the boxes and medicines into disorder, as is related there at p. 483. For *procedere*, the Fulda manuscript shortly afterward has *esse*. HAV.]. Preference for one cannot occur without insulting another, because there can be no choice without rejection. Thus you already despise those whom you reject, and by rejecting them you do not fear to offend them.

For, as we briefly indicated above [Note: [Col. 0344B] *praestruximus*, Semler.], the status of each god depended upon the senate’s appraisal. He was no god whom a man, when consulted, had refused to recognize and had condemned by that refusal. You treat your household gods [Note: [Col. 0344D] **Household gods.** Jerome likewise calls the Lares by this name in his commentary on Isaiah 58: “There was no place that was not defiled by the filth of idolatry, to such an extent that they even placed idols behind the doors of their houses, calling them household Lares, and shed the blood of their animals both publicly and privately.” See Gijsbert Cuper, III, in the *Inscriptions and Ancient Marbles* appended to the *Apotheosis of Homer*, p. 279, where he learnedly discusses Silvanus, Phoebus, and Jupiter himself as household gods, and summons this passage of our author in support. HAV.], which you call Lares, under the power of the household: pawning them, selling them, sometimes changing Saturn into a chamber pot [Note: [Col. 0344D] **Chamber pot.** The Fulda and Leiden manuscripts plainly read *caccabulum*, not *cacabulum*. Although this word does not commonly occur with a filthy meaning, it is readily apparent that it was employed together with the other word, *trulla*, to denote vessels used to receive the burden of the belly and bladder. Just as our author says that gods are changed into vessels destined for unclean uses, Minucius likewise derives the gods themselves from such vessels, p. 26: “A bronze or silver god is melted down from a filthy vessel, as was more than once done to an Egyptian king.” [Col. 0345B] That these are indeed their sisters is taught by an elegant passage of Philo’s *On the Contemplative Life*, p. 610, cited by Elmenhorst: ὧν τὰ ἀδελφὰ μέρη καὶ συγγενῆ λουτροφόροι γεγόνασι καὶ ποδονίπτρα, καὶ ἄλλα ἄτλα τῶν ἀτιμοτέρων, ἃ πρὸς τὰς ἐν σκότῳ χρείας ὑπηρετεῖ μᾶλλον, ἤ τὰς ἐν φωτί (“whose sibling and kindred parts have become water jars and foot-basins, and other baser objects serving uses performed in darkness rather than those performed in the light”; ἄτλα is apparently corrupt), that is: “Parts related to them [namely, the images] have been turned into jars, washbasins, and other dirty vessels employed for private uses.” These words are absent from Rhenanus. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0344B] In the editions of Rhenanus and Gelenius, the words “sometimes into a chamber pot from Saturn” are absent. The Fulda and Leiden codices read *caccabulum*.], sometimes Minerva into a close-stool, as each one is worn down and battered through long worship, and as each master [Note: [Col. 0345A] “Master,” Paris; “god,” Havercamp.] has found household necessity holier [Note: [Col. 0345B] **As each one [has found] God.** Rigaltius reads thus from the Fulda manuscript. But Latinius, Rhenanus, Aldus, and Pamelius prefer “as each master has found household necessity holier,” with either *vel* or *et*—the latter in Aldus. Although this produces a good and appropriate sense, I greatly prefer the Fulda reading. Scaliger had also seen it, and corrects it to “master.” For Tertullian says that they recognize that nothing good comes to them from these gods, which are subject to a greater power, namely household necessity. Thus Martial addresses his Priapus, VIII.40:

> Guardian, Priapus, not of a blessed garden  
> Or vine, but of a sparse grove,  
> Since you were born from it and can be born again,  
> I warn you to repel thieving hands  
> And preserve the woodland for your master’s hearth.  
> If it runs out, you too are wood.

To this pertains the jest of Diagoras in Epiphanius’ *Ancoratus*. Lacking wood, he shook down his wooden Hercules and mockingly said to him: “Come, Hercules, be present to undertake a thirteenth labor and cook our dinner.” “And indeed,” says Epiphanius, “taking him up, he split him into shingles, mocking his own god as though he were nothing; and after putting his meal upon him, he ate while deriding him.” In my Greek edition, p. 512: Οὐκ ἀκούουσι γὰρ Διαγόρου (“For they do not hear Diagoras”)“, etc. Aldus has “and as each master.” Pamelius, Heraldus, and La Cerda: “as each master has found household necessity holier.” But perhaps the original text was: “as each master [has found] God,” [Col. 0345D] etc. HAV.].

You likewise defile public gods under public law, keeping them as taxable entries in the auction register [Note: [Col. 0345D] **Whom you keep as taxable entries in the auction register.** He himself had said in book I *To the Nations*: “Whom you have entered in the auction register.” The *hastarium* is therefore the auction book, or the archive and register of taxes, which were commonly leased to contractors every five years under the spear and at the herald’s proclamation. Thus latrines were leased out; so too the vegetable market and other such public properties, for the Serapeum and Capitol were advertised under the same law. In short, the Capitol and vegetable market were leased beneath the same spear to the contractor who sought them. But what passed to the contractor through this award? Evidently, when the vegetable market was leased for five years, he might collect fixed payments from the merchandise offered there throughout that period. Similarly, when the Capitol was leased, he might demand payments for the things Tertullian himself notes in book I *To the Nations*, ch. 10: for the temple ground, for access to the sanctuary, for offerings, and for sacrificial victims. RIG.]. Thus the Capitol, thus the vegetable market [Note: [Col. 0346A] **Thus the vegetable market.** So Rigaltius correctly reads, supported by the Leiden manuscript, the book *To the Nations*, and the Aldine edition; others read, “whether the Capitol, whether the vegetable market.” Of all the interpreters, who have labored greatly to extract a suitable sense, Nicolas Rigaltius alone correctly explained this entire passage; see him. Tertullian is not discussing the sale of gods or statues taken as spoil and booty from enemies, as La Cerda imagines, but their leasing or rental, from which the public treasury’s revenue increased. The learned men evidently failed to notice the remarkable information about antiquity disclosed to us here. Rome was everywhere so full of statues that they constituted, as it were, another population; hence the character in Petronius says with good reason: “Our district is so full of present divinities that you can more easily find a god than a man.” There were so many temples of gods that the little Greek here too could have exclaimed, “Hear me, temples!” The Capitol was especially adorned with them, and was leased by the tax farmers so that the temple attendants and custodians received enormous profit from access to the sanctuary, the temple ground, and similar things—hence Tertullian says that one could not become acquainted with the gods without payment. Thus, in the same way as the vegetable market where vegetables were sold was sought under lease, the Capitol and the sacred temples were also eagerly bid for by some for their private and the public profit. HAV.] is solicited: beneath the same herald’s proclamation, beneath the same spear [Note: [Col. 0346C] **Beneath the same spear.** On the origin and practice of spears and auctions, see Alexander ab Alexandro III.16 and Junius Rabirius, whose book from the Paris edition of 1554, quarto, was inserted in volume V of Graevius’ *Thesaurus*. With these should be compared the words from *To the Nations* I.10, which alone fully illuminate the passage: “First of all, those whom you have entered in the auction register, subjected to tax farmers, and advertised among your sources of revenue, you lease out every five years. Thus the Serapeum, thus the Capitol is solicited; divinity is awarded and leased beneath the same herald’s proclamation and through the same exaction of the quaestor.” There too, before Rigaltius, the most learned jurist Gothofredus admirably explained everything pertaining to this subject and showed that it was leased to tax farmers for five years. HAV.], beneath the same registration by the quaestor, divinity is awarded [Col. 0346A] and leased.

Yet lands burdened with tribute are of lower value, and persons assessed for taxation are of meaner status, for these [Note: [Col. 0346A] “These,” Paris.] are marks of captivity. But among gods, the more tributary they are, the more sacred they are—or rather, the more sacred, the more tributary. Majesty becomes a source of profit. Religion goes begging around taverns [Note: [Col. 0346C] **Goes around taverns.** He censures the gentiles’ most shameful profit, among whom Cybele’s priests demanded alms door to door; hence Juvenal, Satire 8:

> Among executioners and makers of funeral biers,  
> And the idle drums of a reclining eunuch-priest.

LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0346D] **Begging religion.** The *Codex Modius* has “begging religion.” Lucretius writes not without a barb, book II, verse 624:

> Therefore, when first she is borne through mighty cities,  
> Silently enriching mortals with mute salvation,  
> They strew the entire course of the streets with bronze and silver,  
> Enriching her with lavish offerings.

Our author again, ch. XLII: “For we do not have sufficient means to bring aid both to men and to your begging gods.” Minucius, p. 26: “They lead begging gods through the streets”; see the interpreters there. Yet the present passage must be understood not of itinerant priests and religion begging door to door, but of a public invitation to lease, as is abundantly shown in *To the Nations* I.10: “Commerce is advertised by religion; sanctity begs for a lease.” Pamelius is therefore mistaken. HAV.].

You exact payment [Note: [Col. 0346D] **You exact payment.** It had to be paid to the tax farmers, for the passage concerns leasing, as is apparent from *To the Nations* I.10: “Majesty is established for profit; commerce is advertised by religion; sanctity begs for a lease. You exact payment for the temple ground, for access to the sanctuary, for offerings, and for sacrificial victims; you sell the whole divinity. It is not permitted to worship it without payment; in the end, more is paid to the tax farmers than to the priests.” For *sacri*, the Fulda codex reads *sacrarii*, and in the same place *inhonorandos* for *honorandos*. HAV.] [Col. 0347A] for the temple ground and for access to the sanctuary [Note: [Col. 0347B] **For access to the sanctuary.** What wonder, then, if the Jews too were compelled to pay an annual charge for the place in which they performed their rites? See below, ch. XVIII, at the words “the taxable Jew, of course,” as Juvenal, Satire III.15:

> For every tree has been ordered to pay rent to the people,

The tree, and, once the Camenae have been cast out, the grove goes begging. What, in short, do you do to honor them that you do not also bestow upon your dead? Temples in the same way, altars in the same way [Note: [Col. 0347A] “Temples likewise, altars.” Paris.]. The same attire and insignia appear on their statues. As the dead man’s age, craft, and occupation were, so is the god. How does Jupiter’s banquet differ from a funeral feast for an old man [Note: [Col. 0347C] “From Jupiter’s banquet,” etc. The *epulum* is a dinner sacred to Jupiter, now a god advanced in years; the *silicernium* was properly a funeral banquet offered to old men. The *simpulum* or *simpuvium* was a vessel with which wine was poured as a libation in sacrifices, while the *obba* was a kind of bulging vessel with which offerings were made to the spirits of the dead. LE PR.], the *obba* from the *simpulum* [Note: [Col. 0347B] Rhen. and Gelen.: *simpuvium*.] [Note: [Col. 0347C] “The *obba* from the *simpulum*.” The commentators have treated these matters carefully. He says that Jupiter’s banquet, now that Jupiter is advanced in years, differs in nothing from a funeral banquet for old men, nor do the vessels and utensils used in each, nor the services—which he names individually—differ. They did, however, say both *simpulum* and *simpuvium*, as in Rhenanus. The distinction may perhaps have been that the latter was made of wood and the former of earthenware. Nonius: “A *simpuvium* is a wooden vessel.” Festus: “A *simpulum* is a small vessel not unlike a cup, with which wine was poured as a libation in sacrifices.” Apuleius: “To this day the Roman people sacrifice to the immortal gods with a *simpulum* and an earthenware dish.” Kippingius has assembled a great many references in *Antiq. Rom.*, p. 209 of the new edition. On the *silicernium*, see Donatus on Terence, *Adelph.*, p. 299. HAV.], or the undertaker from the soothsayer? For the soothsayer also attends upon the dead [Note: [Col. 0347D] “Attends.” From this it is clear how this verb should be understood in Book II, *Ad Nat.*, ch. 5. I shall correct that passage at the same time: “whom the entire commerce of the world, arising for the benefit of the human race, may seem to attend, and . . . . onem.” Godefroy supplies “or accession”? I, however, suggest “and injury”? What precedes and what follows teach this. HAV.]. But you appropriately dedicate the honor of divinity to deceased emperors, since you assign it to them even while they are alive [Note: [Col. 0347B] “Add it,” Paris.]. Your gods will take it as received—indeed, they will congratulate themselves—that their own masters are made their equals [Note: [Col. 0347D] “Their own masters.” Admirably put! For those who previously commanded even the gods and made gods are now themselves enrolled in the order of divinities. Manilius, Book IV, on Augustus:

> Now he himself makes gods and sends to the stars a divinity  
> Greater still, and heaven grows beneath Augustus’ rule,

because of the consecration of the deified Julius. Hence the emperor and philosopher Julian, mocking him in the *Caesars*, calls him a maker of dolls, because, just as modelers fashion nymphs, so he fashioned gods. There is also Nero’s impious utterance—yet one worthy of such gods—in Seneca’s *Octavia*, verse 450:

> Foolishly would I fear, when I myself make gods.

This hints at Claudius’ mushroom. Ald. has *ferrent* for *ferent*. HAV.]. But when you worship Larentina [Note: [Col. 0347B] Rhen., Ald., Scaliger: Larentia. Cf. Minucius Felix, *Oct.* ch. 25.], a public prostitute—if only it had at least been Lais or Phryne!—among Junos, Cereses, and Dianas; when you consecrate Simon Magus with a statue [Note: [Col. 0348B] The same statue is mentioned by St. Justin, *Apol.* I.26 and also ch. 56; besides Eusebius, he was followed by Irenaeus, *Adv. haeres.* I, ch. 23, §1, p. 99, ed. In 1574 a stone, formerly the base of a statue, was dug from the ruins on Tiber Island (see Baronius, *Annals*, at the year 44, vol. I, Cologne, 1624, p. 363 f.; compare Montfaucon, *Diarium italicum*, etc., p. 268), bearing this inscription: “Sacred to Semo Sancus, the God of Good Faith,” etc. (in Gruter, *Inscriptiones antiquae totius orbis Romani*, ed. Graevius, vol. I, p. XCVI, no. 5). This *Semo* could also be called *Simo*, just as *Mircurius*, *Camina*, *Gimina*, and other forms often occur. Sancus—or Sangus, as in Gruter, loc. cit., no. 6, and Sanctus, as in Ovid, *Fasti* VI.213 f.—was a god of the Sabines (cf. Ovid, loc. cit., 217, and Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I, ch. 15, ed. Le Brun and Dufresne, vol. I) who presided over agreements and treaties and was named from “sanctioning”; for this reason he was also called *Deus Fidius* (Ovid, loc. cit., 213, and Gruter, nos. cited), from good faith. EDD.] and the inscription “Holy God”; when from among the court pages [Note: [Col. 0348A] Paris adds “or.”] you make some person or other [Note: [Col. 0348B] “A catamite,” Semler.] a god of the synod [Note: [Col. 0348D] “God of the synod.” From this too the superiority of the Leiden manuscript is apparent: although it is not ancient, it seems to have been derived from an excellent exemplar. In it the reading was plainly *sinodi*, just as the older spelling in the Fulda manuscript is *Cinhothi*. All editors except Rigault wrongly print *cinaedum*. He alludes not to the Romans’ Consenting Gods, or *συμβουλεύοντας* (“those who counsel”), and the Greeks’ *Παρέδρους* (“assessors”), but to those of higher rank and dignity who were called *σύνθρονοι* (“co-enthroned”). An ancient inscription teaches the point more than adequately and confirms the reading:

ΟΥΛΠΙΟΣ ΑΠΟΛΛΟΝΙΟΣ ΠΡΟΦΗΤΗΣ (“Ulpius Apollonius, prophet”) HAV.]—although the ancient gods are not more noble, they will nevertheless reckon it an insult from you that others too have been permitted what antiquity conferred upon them alone [Note: [Col. 0348B] Hav., from the Fulda codex: “what they alone had prescribed from antiquity.” Rig.: “had received.”].

## CHAPTER XIV

**ARGUMENT.—**After incidentally censuring their greed in offering proper victims, he attacks Homer and the other poets and shows what shameful things these teachers say about the gods, although they are presented to the young as models of language and conduct. He likewise attacks the tragic and comic poets, and even the philosophers, of whom the foremost, Socrates, together with Diogenes and Varro, mocked and demolished the gods.

I do not wish [Note: [Col. 0348B] All the codices except the Lyon manuscript read “I wish”; Semler and Ritter, on Havercamp’s authority, approved the Lyon reading “I do not wish.”] to review your rites too; I do not say [Col. 0349A] what you are like in sacrificing, when you slaughter every worn-out [Note: [Col. 0349A] “Worn-out.” He marks such contempt for the gods that they offered either the worst victims to the gods, or the worst and most contemptible parts, although by law and ancient ritual it was proper to give all the best things to the gods. On this subject Jerome Magius collected much in *Miscellanies* IV, ch. 4, as did others. For it had to be:

> A victim free from blemish and of surpassing form,

as Pythagoras indignantly says in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.130. The attendants and petty sacrificers therefore made careful inquiry, examining a victim from head to heel. Lucian, *On Sacrifices*: Καὶ πολύ γε πρότερον ἐξετάσαντες ἐκ ἐντελὴς εἴη ἵνα μὴ δὲ των ἀχρήσσων τι κατασφάττωσι, that is: “And long beforehand they examine whether it is lawful and suitable for sacred rites, lest perhaps they slaughter one of those creatures that religion rejects.” Hence, in the *Passion of St. Victor of Marseilles*, which Du Cange reports exists in manuscript in the Vatican Library, where he explains the verb *occare* in volume III of his *Glossary*, a pagan addresses the martyr thus:

> Arise and call upon the gods; taking it by the back of the head, examine  
> Whatever from the herd you please.

A victim selected in this way and duly qualified was called *mystica*. Tibullus, Book I, Elegy II:

> But from us, Lares, repel bronze-pointed weapons.  
> A full-grown pig from the sty shall be the mystic victim.

[Col. 0349C] Pan is therefore indignant in Lucian’s *Twice Accused*, p. 315, that an aged he-goat is offered to him. His words are: ὅμως δὲ δὶς ἢ τρὶς τοῦ ἔτους ἀνίοντες, ἐπιλεξάμενοι τράγον ἔνοχον θύουσί μοι, πολλῆς τῆς κινάβρας ἀπόζοντα, that is: “Yet two or three times each year they climb up and sacrifice to me some castrated goat selected from this herd, reeking most foully.” Jupiter himself is even more disappointed by the hecatombs Mnesitheus had promised the gods if they rescued his ship from the rocks of Caphareus; but he ἑκκαίδεκα θεοὺς ἐστιῶν, ἀλεκτρυόνα μόνον κατέθυσε, γέροντα κἀκεῖνον, ἤδη καὶ κορυζωντα, that is: “While providing a banquet for sixteen gods, sacrificed a single cock—and that one old and already suffering from a catarrh.” Below, ch. XXX: “Nor the blood of a rejected ox longing to die.”

Indeed, among the Israelites it was proper that nothing be offered to God unless complete in every part; hence the just indignation of Malachi 1:8: “When you bring a blind creature to sacrifice, does it not seem evil to you? And when you offer something lame or diseased, does that too not seem evil to you?” To the same point belongs what Chrysostom says against those who give alms from plunder, in Homily LXXXVI on Matthew 26: “For if those who offered lame victims were accused, when you do worse things, how will you obtain pardon?” That the same custom prevailed even in pagan times, at least among the greedy, can be inferred both from the preceding material and from a similar passage in Athenaeus XII, ch. 13, p. 551, where Hermippus addresses Bacchus thus:

νῦν οἱ γὰρ πενόμενοι

Ἀνάπηρά σοι θύουσιν ἤδη βοΐδια

Λεωτρεφίδου λεπτὸτερα καὶ Θουμάντιδος, that is: “But now poor little men sacrifice to you mutilated little cows, leaner than Leotrophides and Thaumantis.” Mythographers also write that Pasiphaë’s unspeakable passion for the bull arose because her husband Minos, though he had vowed the most beautiful bull to his father Jupiter, the god himself being overseer of the herds, sacrificed another instead. Most elegantly, however, as Joseph Scaliger noted before me, he describes by circumlocution what Festus and the ancients call *ablegmina*, that is, the parts presented to the gods. PAM.], which at home you would have assigned even to children or dogs; [Col. 0350A] when from Hercules’ tithe [Note: [Col. 0350B] “Hercules’ tithe.” In fragment XXXIX: “The accountants will calculate the expense of the Herculean tithes”; see Junius there. It is clear from this that a tenth part of one’s profit was vowed to Hercules, as also from the festive joke of Geta, the Plautine slave, in the *Truculentus*, Act II, scene VII, verse 10, who also did himself a good turn from the little basket his master had ordered carried to a prostitute:

> For just now, from this provision—from the single mina—I deducted

Relevant too is the Reatine inscription under the name of Semo Sancus in Gruter, p. XCVI, no. 7:

HAVING ALWAYS JUDGED IN HIS MIND THAT THIS SHOULD BE GIVEN, HE COMPLETED IT WITH YOUR AID, ASKING YOU TO MAKE EASY THE COLLECTING AND DISCHARGING OF DEBTS, AND TO BRING IT ABOUT THAT HE MAY PAY THE TITHE OF THE TRUE ACCOUNT; AND IN RETURN FOR THIS GIFT AND OTHERS, MAY YOU GIVE THINGS WORTHY TO ONE WHO DESERVES THEM.

A costly god indeed, who had to be worshiped at so great an expense. On this subject there are some verses by Antipater in Book I of the *Anthology*, at once extremely elegant and extremely truthful:

These gods, of course, belong among those dead persons of whom that wise mime-writer—I mean Publilius—says in verse 608:

Thus the dispute between Carion and Mercury in Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, Act V, scene I, is not unpleasant:

Flavius Vopiscus does indeed relate that the emperor Tacitus wished to dedicate a [Col. 0355B] silver statue to the deified Aurelian in the Temple of the Sun, and likewise ordered a temple of the deified emperors to be built, in which statues of good rulers were to stand. But these were divinities of the Romans, to whom both victims and vows were offered. Laertius says that a statue ἔν Πομπειῳ (“in the Pompeion”) was erected in a public building—as Casaubon observes from Pollux—in which, as he thinks, τὰ πομπεῖα (“the equipment for processions”), that is, the equipment for processions was preserved. Hence perhaps more precious images stored there could also be brought out on feast days to enhance the solemnity. Tertullian therefore wrote *in a temple* straightaway—a reading I approve on the basis of Laertius, who says that the Athenians, seized with remorse, εὐθὺς (“immediately”), immediately proclaimed public mourning, destroyed the accusers, and honored Socrates with a statue. But that statues of distinguished men were also erected in temples of the gods is shown by the honor accorded to Gorgias of Leontini in the temple of Pythian Apollo; similarly, statues of distinguished women were also set up in places dedicated to some divinity. Thus in his will [Col. 0355C] Theophrastus desired not only that an image of Aristotle be placed in a similar shrine. He says “some jest or other,” however, because those final words rather darkly suggested the force and violence of Hercules, which those Cynics imitated: if anyone refused what they asked, they took it by force, and they used a staff just as Hercules used his club, as may frequently be seen in Lucian. Thus, when Diogenes is asked by a buyer in Lucian’s *Auction of Lives* whom he imitated, [Col. 0355D] he answered, “Hercules.” So too we read of Hercules in Lactantius, in a passage which we shall cite not far below: “Hercules, employing his customary violence, because he could not obtain one, carried off both.” Indeed, they boasted of Hercules as the founder of their sect. The conversation between Diogenes and Hercules among the *Dialogues of the Dead* of Lucian of Samosata is exceedingly witty. There the Cynic mocks Hercules; see the passage and what follows. There is therefore nothing surprising if, among so many representations of Hercules—as a youth, an old man, bearded, and beardless—there is also room for one of him as a Cynic. The most distinguished antiquarian Leonardo Agostini reproduces, from an ancient gem, his bare and unkempt head, bristling with beard and hair, in *Ancient Gems*, part I, no. 6. PAM.], the Cynic, introduces three hundred [Col. 0356A] Joves, or Jupiters [Note: [Col. 0356B] **Jupiters.** See Priscian. For *Jovis* is not the genitive of τοῦ (“of the”; the recovered text is an isolated Greek genitive article) *Jupiter*, but the nominative *Jovis* used by the ancients, as may frequently be seen from examples of the poets cited by the grammarians. Hence Varro expressly says in Book VII of *On the Latin Language*: “Now it is customary to speak otherwise: *Jupiter* for *Jovis*, *bos* for *bovis* and *bus*, and *strues* for *struis*.” *Jupiter*, moreover, is as it were *juvans pater*, “helping father,” like *Marspiter*, and according to the same author it has only the direct cases. On this subject one may consult that universal scholar Gerardus Joannes Vossius, in the additions to Book II, chapter 8 of *On Analogy*. The Leiden manuscript reads *Jupitros dicendos*; the Fulda manuscript, *Jupiteros*. Their shipwrecked planks have been gathered by Riccobonus, Stephanus, and Popma; we too have devoted some effort to them. [Col. 0356C] Junius adduces something from Festus, but I cannot rest content with it. He is deservedly mocked for this by La Cerda, whose note reads: “*Without heads*, that is, diminished in civil status; Varro mentions neither their condition, family, nor citizenship, by which the threefold diminution of status is expressed.” So much for him. Varro also indirectly censured, as I at least think, the Stoic god—the world, round and globular. Seneca, *Letter* XCVI: “If they gave him a round shape, such as they gave to God.” The same author, in that ridiculous *Apocolocyntosis*, which I never read without laughter, says of Claudius: “What kind of god do you wish this fellow to become?” “A Stoic one.” “How can he be round”—as Varro says—“without a head and without a foreskin? There is something of the Stoic god in him: now I see it; he has neither heart nor head.” Just as some maintained that there were innumerable worlds, so Varro introduced three hundred gods, or Jupiters, in the work which both Seneca and Tertullian seem to have had in view.

There remains a reading in the manuscript of *To the Nations* I.10 that may detain us: there it has *inducit*. Unless he used this in place of [Col. 0356D] *introducit*, it seems to signify the erasure of these gods, who, as La Cerda says, were “diminished in status”—as though Varro had there examined the solidity and value of the divinity of each Jupiter and found three hundred whom he excluded from that name. If this interpretation is preferred, *inducit* ought to have been written here as well. This conjecture is supported by what is read in chapter XII of the same book concerning the multitude of gods: “So many households and so many nations are honestly seeking registration that they cannot be examined, distinguished, and entered upon a list.” Indeed, the Fulda manuscript reads so clearly in this passage as well that there is scarcely room for doubt. Aldus prefers *capidibus*. But *capis*, as Pompeius Festus observes, was a kind of cup, named from *capere*, “to take.” Nonius Marcellus joins it with the *armillum*; in his citation from Varro, *On the Life of the Roman People*, Book I: “Even now there is the coupling of what they call *capulae* and *capides*, which is a kind of connected vessel; likewise the *armillum*, which is a kind of wine-jar.” Now just as *armillum* was so called because it was carried *armo*, that is, on the shoulder, according to Festus, so the *capis* was a vessel of smaller form which could be grasped and lifted by the hand. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book [Col. 0357A] IV: “And the smaller vessels, *capides*, from *capere*, because they have handles so that they can be grasped, that is, taken.” Even now we see their shapes among [Col. 0357B] sacred vessels, both ancient wooden ones and earthenware ones. Livy too joins the *capis* with the augural staff, Book X, chapter 7, when speaking of pontifical dress: “If he is seen with the *capis* and augural staff, with his head veiled, let him sacrifice the victim or take the augury from the citadel.” It is therefore apparent that it was an implement connected with sacred rites, for according to Festus the *armillum* too was a wine-vessel used in sacrifices. It is as though Varro had somewhere in the *Menippean Satires* introduced this enormous phalanx of Jupiters and mocked them because no sacred equipment appeared around them. But I prefer to rest content with the reading of the Fulda manuscript and of *To the Nations*. Add that the subject here is the abolition of divinity, which can hardly be expressed more aptly than by the verb *inducere*, “to strike out.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0355A] The Paris manuscript reads “introduced.”]

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0357A]

**ARGUMENT.—He further demonstrates how shamefully the deeds and names of the gods are distorted by the pagans themselves in theatrical entertainments for the pleasure of eyes and ears, so that divinity is violated amid the people’s applause; how cruelly the gods are also employed in the amphitheater and theatrical games, where that majesty is treated with utter baseness; and finally, how irreverently the gods are regarded by them when they gratify their lust in the gods’ presence. Such a religion indeed shows its worshipers [Col. 0358A] to be foolish and insane, but its opponents sensible and wise.**

The other contrivances of wantonness also serve your pleasures by dishonoring the gods. Examine the elegant productions of the Lentuli [Note: [Col. 0357B] **The Lentuli.** *On the Pallium*, chapter IV: “and deservedly mentioned by Lentulus, the writer of mimes, in his *Catinians*.” Jerome too mentions him more than once. HAV.] and the Hostilii [Note: [Col. 0357B] **The Hostilii.** A most noble family among the Romans, several of whose names antiquity has preserved for us. The first is Hostius Hostilius, who fought with Romulus [Col. 0357C] against the Sabines and is mentioned by Livy, Book I. Cicero too mentions the Hostilian legal proceedings in *On the Orator*, Book I, chapter 245, and Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, ibid., chapter 238. In Reinesius too we encounter Gaius Hostilius, who was sent with Gaius Popilius Laenas as envoy to Syria to settle the war between the kingdoms of Syria and Egypt, *Inscription* IV.8; and Lucius Hostilius Fortunatus, with his daughter Hostilia Januaria, XII.45. In the same author, XVI.24:

C. HOSTILIO. C. F. FRUGIONI  
C. HOSTILIO. C. F. NEPOTI.

And again, XVII.154: HOSTILIAE ATTHIDI. Who the Hostilius in this passage was is unclear to me, and the mimes have long since perished together with their inscriptions. He is called Hostius in the book *To the Nations*. On the lust of a certain Hostius, see Seneca, *Natural Questions* II.1.16. HAV.], and consider whether it is actors in mimes [Note: [Col. 0357C] **Actors in mimes, or your gods.** Lactantius, Book V, chapter 21: “Could anything be worse than that these very same men, although they claim to worship the gods, nevertheless ridicule them publicly and shamefully, and allow them to be represented by actors in mimes amid laughter and pleasure? What kind of religion is this, or how great should that majesty be considered which is adored in temples and mocked in theaters?” Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter XXVII: “There the name of God is blasphemed.” HAV.] or your gods whom you mock in jests and tricks [Note: [Col. 0357D] **Tricks.** It is plain what the author means by this word, since he joins it with “jests.” Properly it means a cunning device employed in deception. Martial, on an adulteress, XI.8:

> Now such a trick passes away.

It comes from the word στρέφω (“I turn”), to which our proverb concerning something cunningly stolen is akin: *yts donker groen verwem*. For I certainly scarcely think that La Cerda’s observation concerning strophes and antistrophes in lyric poetry is intended here in connection with the mime. Rather, both *stropha* and *mimus* appear to have been names given to the type of entertainment from its subject matter. Jerome, *Apology Against Rufinus* II: “And as though it were a mime by Philistion or Lentulus, or a trick of Marullus, [Col. 0358A] composed in elegant language.” For Marullus was a distinguished writer of mimes; this saying of his to a [Col. 0358B] gluttonous parasite survives: “You imitate Hector: you never depart from Ilium”—playing on the double meaning of *Ilium*, which denotes both the city of Troy and an intestine. Servius reports this on Virgil, *Eclogue* VII.26 and *Aeneid* VII.499. It frequently signifies what is commonly called *raillerie*, *een loop je*. He uses this word again in *On the Soul*, chapter XXVII, mocking Pythagoras the son of Panthous: “For he who devised such a trick,” etc.; and in *Against Marcion*, Book III, chapter 10: “How deserving of faith is a necessity that had contrived such a trick?” Jerome too, *Against Rufinus*: “Do you wish to know all the tricks of your clever devices, or the ambushes of your watchtowers?” Hence also the expressions in Papias: “*Strophus*: twisted, a deceiver. *Stropha*: wickedness, fraud. *Stropharius*: impostor, deceiver.” The Agobard manuscript has “tricks” at the beginning. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0357A] “Whom you mock” is absent from the Paris manuscript.]:

**ANUBIS THE ADULTERER** [Note: [Col. 0358B] **Anubis the adulterer.** The god Anubis is the same as Cynocephalus; hence Virgil said, “and barking Anubis.” Mercury was worshiped under both forms. These, moreover, are titles of plays. Thus *Anubis the Adulterer* was performed, [Col. 0358C] just as *The Male Moon*, etc. LAC.], **THE MALE MOON** [Note: [Col. 0358C] **The Male Moon.** So all the manuscripts and printed editions. Meursius prefers *Lumus*, but there is no need for it. Whatever may be said about knowledge and worship of this divinity, collected from stones, coins, and other ancient monuments, we shall present in a special dissertation *On the God Lunus and Hermaphroditic Gods*. HAV.], **DIANA FLOGGED** [Note: [Col. 0358C] **Diana flogged.** “The poet,” says La Cerda, “invented this epithet as an insult to Diana.” I rather think that it was the title or inscription of a mime and should therefore, like the others, be set in capital letters. HAV.], the recitation of **THE TESTAMENT OF THE DEAD JOVE**, and **THREE HUNGRY HERCULES** [Note: [Col. 0358C] **Hungry Herculeses.** Whatever it was is now unknown; yet it seems not unlike what may be read in Lactantius, Book I, chapter 21. There, from the writings of the nations, he gives the following explanation of the rites of Hercules which were celebrated with curses and execrations at Lindus, a town of Rhodes: “When Hercules had arrived there and was suffering from hunger, he saw a certain plowman at work and began to ask him to sell him one ox. [Col. 0358D] The man, however, denied that this was possible, because his entire hope of cultivating the soil rested upon those two draft animals. Hercules, employing his customary violence, because he could not obtain one, carried off both. But the unhappy man, when he saw his oxen being slaughtered, avenged the injury by curses, which greatly delighted that elegant and urbane person. For while Hercules prepared a banquet for his companions and devoured another man’s oxen, he listened with laughter and guffaws as the owner abused him most bitterly. But afterward, when it was resolved that divine honors should be paid to Hercules in admiration of his valor, the citizens erected an altar to him, which from the event he named βουζυγον (“ox-yoke”), that is, ‘the yoke of oxen.’ At this altar two yoked oxen were to be sacrificed, like those he had taken from the plowman; and he appointed that same man as his priest, directing him always to employ the same curses in celebrating the sacrifices, because he declared that he had never dined more agreeably.” These titles of mimes about Jove and Hercules were absent from the Fulda manuscript. HAV.], who are held up to ridicule.

Moreover, the texts of the actors [Note: [Col. 0358D] **The texts of the actors.** Arnobius sketched all these things [Col. 0359A] at the end of Book V: “But you wished poets alone to be permitted to devise unworthy stories and scandalous mockeries concerning the gods. [Col. 0357D] What of your pantomimes, your actors, and that multitude belonging to the class of mimes and effeminates? Do they not misuse your gods for the profit of their trade, and draw inducements to pleasure from injuries and insults to the divine?” [Col. 0359B] The reading of Rhenanus, *sides*, deserves notice, as though referring to the body stretched into effeminacy and the notorious swaying of the sides. Yet in *To the Nations* I.10 you will read, as here, “theatrical texts.”] [Note: [Col. 0358A] Rhenanus: “sides”; but compare *To the Nations* I.10.] [Col. 0359A] portray every shameful deed [Note: [Col. 0359B] **Their shameful deeds.** Their loves, adulteries, quarrels, and the like. Relevant here is what follows in the same passage of Arnobius: “What it would be impious even to hear, Venus—the mother of the race of Mars, the progenetrix of the ruler and of the people—is danced as a lover and, through every passion of meretricious baseness, is represented in an immodest imitation as raving.” HAV.] of theirs. The Sun mourns his son, hurled [Note: [Col. 0359B] **Hurled.** The Fulda manuscript has “dragged down from heaven,” as though Septimius were ridiculing even the manner in which the striking of Phaethon by lightning was represented: after being raised aloft by some machine, as though riding high in his chariot, he was then dragged down again by another and thus hurled to the ground. The other manuscripts, as well as the Agobard manuscript, have “hurled.” HAV.] from heaven, while you rejoice; and Cybele [Note: [Col. 0359B] **Cybele.** Arnobius continues in the same vein in that passage: “The Great Mother too is danced, adorned with sacred fillets; and, contrary to the dignity of her age, that lady from Pessinus and Dindymus is represented as leaping with shameful desire for the embraces of a single herdsman.” That mocker of the gods, [Col. 0359C] Lucian, furnished material for laughter here; I recognize that our Septimius borrowed this and many other things from him. In the *Dialogues of the Gods*, Lucian introduces Venus speaking thus to her Cupid: Ἀλλὰ σὺ, ὧ τολμηρότατε (“But you, most audacious one”), etc., that is: “But you, most audacious one, even compelled Rhea herself, already an old woman and the mother of so many gods, to love a boy and desire that Phrygian youth. Driven mad by you, with her lions yoked and the Corybantes accompanying her—for they too are inspired by a kind of frenzy—she now wanders up and down throughout Ida, wailing because of Attis,” etc. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0359A] “And afterward Cybele—while you do not blush” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] sighs after a disdainful shepherd [Note: [Col. 0359C] **Sighs after a shepherd.** This is elegantly placed before our eyes in a most beautiful gem worthy of notice for Endymion’s pastoral dress, volume II of Gorlaeus’ *Dactyliotheca*, no. 498. Lucian, moreover, describes in *The False Prophet* the notorious impostor Alexander: Καὶ ὀ μὲν καθεύδων δῆθεν (“And he, supposedly sleeping”), etc., that is: “While he lay sleeping in the midst of them, there descended upon him from the roof’s highest point, as though from heaven and [Col. 0359D] playing the part of the Moon, a certain most beautiful Rutilia, wife of one of the officials of the imperial household. Just as she loved Alexander, so she was loved by him in return. Before the eyes of that utterly depraved husband, embraces and kisses were exchanged openly. Had there not been numerous torches, perhaps something of what is customarily done beneath the bosom would also have been accomplished.” Thus the phrase “sighs after a shepherd” means “desires him,” as in the *Curses* attributed to Valerius Cato:

> Fields, I envy you, and beautiful meadows;  
> More beautiful for this reason: that my beautiful girl  
> Is yours. Silently she sighs for your love.

Lindenbrogius correctly observed this there, except that I prefer the reading of the Manutius edition:

> Silently she too sighs for your love.

Lucan VI.370 is quite different:

> [Col. 0360A] Nor does the Anauros breathe out gentle winds. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0360A] **Disdainful.** Disdaining her love. Virgil, at the end of *Eclogue* II:

> You will find another Alexis, if this one disdains you.

For the Latin should read *Alexin*, not *Alexis*, as Servius’ note also indicates: [Col. 0360B] “Another Alexis,” another most beautiful boy, who will by no means disdain you. HAV.], while you do not blush.

And you endure the titles concerning Jove [Note: [Col. 0360B] **The titles concerning Jove.** I explained this word above. Arnobius, in the passage so often mentioned: “Indeed, in the plays that greatest ruler of heaven himself is introduced, without any fear for divine majesty or dignity, as playing the part of adulterers; and so that he may deceive the chastity of other men’s matrons, he changes his deceitful face and assumes the shapes of their husbands by simulating a substituted body.” The “titles concerning Jove,” therefore, are these: *Jupiter as Amphitryon*, *The Gold* or *The Golden Shower*, *The Feather* or *The Swan*, *The Bull*, and the many other shapes adopted for his illicit loves. Arnobius indeed recounts these titles again in Book VII: “Does Jupiter lay aside his wrath if the Plautine *Amphitryon* has been performed and declaimed? Or will he restrain the movement of his anger if Europa, Leda, Ganymede, or Danaë has been danced?” Concerning Cybele sighing for Attis, he says in the same place: “Does the Great Mother become calmer and gentler if she sees the ancient story of Attis revived by actors?” (Id.)] being sung, and Juno [Note: [Col. 0360C] **Juno.** See this judgment among the *Dialogues* of Lucian of Samosata. Venus herself appears there as the victor, displaying the golden apple and gazing at it with an appearance of joy. Gorlaeus, *Dactyliotheca*, vol. II, nos. 24, 77, 79, 166, 272, and on the coins of Plautilla and Faustina. But the actual scene of the judgment appears most clearly from this cast of an ancient gem and from the coin formerly published by Morellius. (See the frontispiece to Hugo’s volume.)], Venus, and [Col. 0360A] Minerva being judged by a shepherd.

What of the fact that the image of your god clothes an infamous and notorious head [Note: [Col. 0360C] **The image of your god clothes a most infamous and notorious head.** These words mean that the actor’s entire head was clothed with the mask of the very god whom he represented. Gavius Bassus makes this perfectly clear in Aulus Gellius, Book V, chapter 7: “For the head,” he says, “and face are covered on every side by the covering of the mask, which has only a single passage through which the voice may be emitted.” And in ancient illustrations of comic actors we see masks depicted in precisely this form. Boethius, in his book *On the Two Natures of Christ*, where he discusses the word *persona*: “But if the antepenultimate syllable is accented,” he says, “it will very plainly appear to have been named from sound. It is named from sound because the sound must necessarily be magnified by the hollow itself.” RIG.—**It clothes a most infamous and notorious head.** He has in view the stage apparatus, and particularly the masks into which actors inserted their heads. For they represented not only Socrates and others, as may be seen in the gems of Gorlaeus, vol. II, nos. 205, 311, 509, 539, but even the faces of the gods themselves. Thus a noteworthy mask of Pan appears there, no. 506. The eloquent Gregory of Nazianzus also refers to this custom in his *Oration Against Women*, where he teaches that it is unworthy of respectable women to color their faces with cosmetics. The Agobard manuscript reads “infamous,” and “that very thing” for “what.” HAV.]? What of the fact that a body impure and trained for that art by effeminacy [Note: [Col. 0360D] **Trained for the art by effeminacy.** Similarly Jerome to Marcella, vol. I, letter 8: “On theatrical stages the same actor, robust, now exhibits Hercules, and now, made soft, collapses into Venus.” Elmenhorst adduces this passage, as well as others from Cyprian, Lactantius, and Augustine, [Col. 0361A] on the words of Arnobius, Book VII, “men enervating themselves into feminine softness.” The manuscript of Modius corruptly has “citadel.” The abbreviated writing in the Leiden manuscript seemed to suggest “theatrical art.” HAV.] represents some Minerva or Hercules? Is not majesty violated and divinity prostituted [Col. 0361A] while you applaud [Note: [Col. 0361A] **While you applaud.** Thus Rigault printed from the Fulda manuscript, and so too the Agobard manuscript. Previously it read “while you praise.” Arnobius, Book IV, expresses it thus: “All the colleges of priests and magistrates sit at public spectacles: the chief pontiffs and the chief curiones sit there; the crowned quindecimvirs sit there,” and what follows. [Col. 0361B] Cyprian too: “A man weakened in every limb and dissolved into softness beyond that of a woman—whose art it is to express words with his hands—sets the whole city in motion on account of some single person, neither man nor woman, so that the legendary lusts of antiquity may be danced out.” HAV.]?

Clearly you are more religious in the amphitheater, where, over human blood and the filth of punishments, your gods dance accordingly, supplying plots and stories for condemned criminals—except that condemned criminals [Note: [Col. 0361B] **Condemned criminals assume their roles.** He means that, according to Roman custom, those criminals not only played the parts of the gods, but were often also forced as punishment to represent in reality what was feigned concerning those gods: to be castrated or burned. Relevant here are the words of Martial [see Book I.5, 7; XI.X.25]:

> Laureolus hanging upon no counterfeit cross.

Ausonius likewise alludes to this in *Letter* XXXIII:

> Happy chance mingled with the art that had been deceived.  
> The actor who danced Capaneus fell;  
> The same man who danced Niobe became stone, so that then  
> The spectator believed her the true Niobe.  
> In Canace he seemed much more fortunate than she herself,  
> Because he did not here cut open his entrails with the sword.] often assume the roles of your gods themselves? We once saw Attis castrated [Note: [Col. 0361C] That god from Pessinus, where he first obtained divinity and where his body is consecrated. See the history or fable in Arnobius, Book V. The Fulda manuscript reads, “your god from Pessinus”; Rhenanus, *Atten*. HAV.], that god [Col. 0362A] from Pessinus; and a man who was burned alive had assumed the role of Hercules [Note: [Col. 0361C] **Hercules.** Arnobius, Book IV: “That offspring of Jove too, Hercules, is introduced by Sophocles in the *Women of Trachis*, ensnared by the deadly garment, uttering pitiable wails, broken by the violence of his pain, and consumed to utter dissolution as his entrails liquefy and waste away.” The same author, Book VII: “Will the indignation of Alcides grow faint if Sophocles’ tragedy called the *Women of Trachis*, or Euripides’ *Hercules*, is performed?” Lactantius therefore rightly mocked him in Book I, chapter 9: “Men think him a god. But Philoctetes, his heir, did not think so: he placed the torch beneath him when he was about to burn; he saw his limbs and sinews burned and dissolved; he buried his bones and ashes on Mount Oeta.” Thus Hercules is falsely mocked by Aesculapius in Lucian’s *Dialogues* and disappointed of the first place as one who died later. Lucian has Aesculapius himself say: Εὖ λέγεις (“You speak rightly”), etc., that is: [Col. 0361D] “You speak rightly, since I also treated your burns when you came up to us a little while ago half-burned, your body corrupted and ruined on both sides, first by that tunic and afterward by the flame as well.” Jupiter settles the dispute by ordering Aesculapius to recline in the first place, not because he had been made a god earlier, but because πρότερον ἀποθανόντα (“as having died earlier”). HAV.].

And amid the playful cruelties of the midday spectacles [Note: [Col. 0361D] **The cruelties of the midday spectacles.** These were not regular gladiators, but generally those who remained from the morning spectacle and the beast-fighters. Although they had escaped the beasts, they were nevertheless not granted discharge; after the meal they were matched against one another, naked, to fight to the death—a spectacle abominable to human eyes and deservedly denounced by Seneca. On these see Lipsius in that excellent little work entitled *Saturnalian Discourses*, Book II, chapter 15, and Leonardo Agostini, *Ancient Gems*, vol. I, nos. 167 and 168, where he thinks he presents such men to you. From this single passage of Tertullian, however, we may infer that, if none or few of the morning combatants survived, [Col. 0362A] such things were performed even upon corpses. HAV.], we laughed at Mercury testing the dead with a cautery [Note: [Col. 0362A] **Mercury testing the dead with a cautery; Jove’s brother escorting corpses with a hammer.** The poets give a staff both to Mercury and to Dis, or Pluto. The former escorted souls; the latter, corpses. Thus, for sport and laughter, the man who played Mercury tested the dead with a red-hot iron rod: this was his cautery for rousing whatever remnants of their souls might perhaps be faint and sluggish. The man who played Pluto also proceeded with a staff, but one fitted with a hammer, so that he could more easily crush [Col. 0362B] anything of a hidden soul which might perhaps rebel in the corpses of those gladiators fresh from combat. The Greeks call the hammer and club ῥάβδον (“rod” or “staff”) and νάρτηκα (“fennel-stalk” or “cane/club”; the contextual sense is uncertain), etc. RIG. **Testing with a cautery.** This part was assigned to Mercury because it was his function to send the souls of the dead to gloomy Tartarus. Laertius, in his *Life of Pythagoras*, recounts this doctrine as Pythagorean also, though in a more restricted form: Τὸν δὲ Ἑρμῆν, ταμίαν εἶναι τῶν ψυχῶν καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Πομπέα λέγεσθαι, καὶ Πελαῖον, καὶ Χθόνιον, ἐπειδήπερ οὗτος εἰσπέμπει (“Mercury, moreover, is the steward of souls and is therefore called the Conductor, Gatekeeper, and Earthly One, since it is he who sends them in”), etc., that is: “Mercury, moreover, is the steward of souls and is therefore called the Conductor, Gatekeeper, and Earthly One, because he sends forth souls from bodies and from the earth and sea; the pure and purified souls he leads on high, but the impure he does not even permit to approach them or one another; instead, they are bound by the Furies with unbreakable bonds.” Most people, however, assigned the care of all souls to Mercury. There is a witty epigram by Nicarchus on the physician Zopyrus in Book II of the *Anthology*. It enumerates [Col. 0362C] several souls whom that physician sent down to gloomy Tartarus, and says that this is no wonder, since, equipped like Mercury with caduceus and winged sandals, he conducts to the underworld those whom he undertakes to treat:

Κηρύκιον γὰρ ἔχων ξύλινον, καὶ πλαστὰ πέδιλα,


   Ὡς Ἑρμῆς κατάγει τοὺς θεραπευομένους (“For, bearing a wooden caduceus and imitation sandals, like Mercury he leads those being treated down to the underworld”).

But since

> It is impious to carry living bodies in the Stygian boat,

Mercury was introduced as first testing with his cautery whether they were truly dead. Aldus has “with a cautery.” HAV.].

We have also seen Jove’s brother escorting gladiators’ corpses with a hammer [Note: [Col. 0362C] **Jove’s brother.** This passage is illustrated by *To the Nations* I.10, where it is worded thus: “Because Dis Pater, Jove’s brother, conducts the funerals of gladiators with a hammer; because Mercury, with little wings upon his bald head and a little flame upon his caduceus, tests with a cautery bodies already lifeless or pretending to be dead.” From this it is clear that the tip of the caduceus was heated and glowing and served this cruelty. It is also clear that *deducere*, “escort,” must be retained against Junius, who prefers *diducere*, “tear apart,” a reading Scaliger too approved. From this [Col. 0362D] one may understand that concluding line of a mime and the gesture of the actor who, pointing to the senate, pronounced the words reported by Suetonius in *Nero*, chapter 39: “Orcus leads your feet.” For although Pluto might perhaps tear apart those corpses by pounding them with his hammer-headed staff, he first took them by the feet and dragged them away. I believe this scene was represented because they imagined that nothing of us except faint shades and images,

> Pallid in wondrous forms,

passed down to Orcus.

Pluto, then, was introduced with a hammer so that he might pound those gleaming and well-fed bodies of gladiators—especially if any portion of the soul had been roused by Mercury’s cautery and some hidden spirit appeared—and, like goldsmiths working metals, draw them out until nothing remained but “the thread of a form,” to speak with Persius, which could readily enter Pluto’s kingdom. The learned man who attempts to correct this passage in his exceedingly laborious [Col. 0363C] *Lexicon of Roman Antiquities* applies an unfortunate remedy, because he did not compare Tertullian’s book *To the Nations* or attend to the consistent reading of the manuscripts. HAV.].

Who could continue to investigate every single one of these things? [Col. 0363A] If they disturb the honor of divinity, if they wear away the traces of majesty [Note: [Col. 0363B] Rigault and Havercamp, from the Fulda manuscript: “if they raze the summit of majesty,” as it is also written at the end of *To the Nations* I.10.], they are surely reckoned as contemptuous—both on the part of those who repeatedly do such things and on the part of those to whom they do them.

But these are theatrical amusements. Yet suppose I add things which everyone’s conscience will recognize no less readily: that adulteries are arranged in temples [Note: [Col. 0363C] **In temples.** Minucius likewise expressed this, p. 28: “Where, moreover, are illicit affairs more commonly procured by priests than among altars and shrines? Where are acts of pimping managed and adulteries plotted? Finally, where is burning lust more frequently discharged than in the chambers of temple-keepers, rather than in the brothels themselves?” See Elmenhorst there, and add to his notes this verse of Ovid, *Art of Love* I.77:

> Nor shun the Memphite rites of the heifer of the Nile.

> She makes many women what she herself was to Jove.

That is, as the same poet says, III.635:

> When they attend upon the heifer of Pharos with rattles,  
> Though her companions are forbidden to go, may she go?  
> When the Good Goddess drives men’s eyes from her temple—  
> [Col. 0363D] Excepting those whom she herself bids come?

Observe the gradation of the discourse: from temples to altars, from altars to the chambers of the temple-keepers, and thence to the sacred dress itself and the administration of the rite, while incense offered by ostensibly pure hands burns in the brazier. The story of Clodius is well known: he violated Caesar’s wife during the rites of the Good Goddess. A deed not dissimilar, on account of which God’s wrath was kindled against the household of Eli, is related in 1 Samuel 2:22. HAV.], that acts of pimping are managed among the altars, and that lust is commonly discharged in the very chambers of temple-keepers and priests, beneath those same fillets, peaked caps, and purple robes, while incense burns [Note: [Col. 0363D] **Lust is discharged**, that is, completed, consummated. Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius*, chapter XLIV: “It is also said that once, while sacrificing, he was captivated by the appearance of an attendant carrying the incense-box before him, and could not refrain from immediately taking him aside on the spot and violating him, almost before the divine rite had been completed, and at the same time his brother, a flute-player.” HAV.]: I do not know whether your gods have more cause to complain about you than about the Christians.

Certainly those caught committing sacrilege always belong to your own people. Christians do not know the temples even by daylight; perhaps they too would plunder them, if they too adored them. What, then, do those worship who do not worship such things?

It is now surely open to understanding that those who do not belong to falsehood [Col. 0363B] are worshipers of truth, and that they no longer err in that wherein, by recognizing that they had erred, they have ceased to err. Grasp this first, and from it imbibe the entire order of our sacred teaching—but only after the false opinions have first been refuted.

## CHAPTER XVI

**ARGUMENT.—Now intending to show what God the Christians worship and how they worship him, he first prepares to overthrow the false opinions concerning that worship: namely, concerning an ass’s [Col. 0364A] head, the cross, the sun, and that fictitious two-formed divinity which bore the inscription ONOKOITIS. He disposes of all these charges with laughter and biting wit, and shows that they apply more closely to the accusers themselves. In this way he clears a path for himself toward the demonstration of our religion.**
