For, as some of you have dreamed, an ass’s head is our god [Note: [Col. 0363D] **An ass’s head.** Excellent and learned collections on this passage may be seen in the commentators on Tacitus; to these should be added Lydius, *De Re Militari*, book II, [Col. 0364C] at the end of chapter 2. Instead of *ejusmodi*, the Fulda codex has *hujusmodi*. HAV.]. Cornelius Tacitus implanted a suspicion of this sort [Note: [Col. 0363B] Rhenanus, Aldus, Barraeus, and Gangnaeus: “For some,” etc.; Gelenius, François du Jon, and La Cerda: “Now, as some”; Havercamp and Rigault: “For some also” (the edition of 1754: “For even some”). Havercamp: “For, as some of you have dreamed, an ass’s head—our god, [Col. 0363C] this—implanted a suspicion of this sort.” François du Jon: “implanted it in Judaism.” But we have retained the older punctuation of the words; with this arrangement, the word *hanc* is not to be deleted, as Heinrich and Ritter wished, but *insevit* should be written in place of *inseruit*.]. For in the fifth book of his *Histories*, beginning his account of the Jewish war with the origin of that people, and making whatever arguments he pleased both about that origin itself and about the name and religion of the people [Note: [Col. 0364B] Du Jon: *argutatus*, “quibbling.”], he relates [Note: [Col. 0364B] The Paris manuscript: “introduces.”] that the Jews, having been released from Egypt [Note: [Col. 0364C] **Released from Egypt.** In the book *To the Nations* he had written: “He relates that the Jews, during their expedition,” etc.; and in the Glosses, *expeditio* is said ἔξοδος εἰς πόλεμον. In other copies, ἐξοδος ἐκδημητικὴ στρατιωτῶν. Here, however, he says that the Jews had been *released from Egypt*, as though liberated from the grievous yoke of the Egyptians—not driven out or exiled, as Tacitus thought. RIG.], or, as he supposed, expelled [Note: [Col. 0364B] Havercamp: “exterminated.”], were tormented by thirst in the vast and exceedingly waterless regions of Arabia; and that they employed as guides to a spring some wild asses which, happening to be returning from pasture, were believed to be seeking water. In gratitude for this, he says, they consecrated the likeness of a similar beast. And from this, I suppose, the presumption arose that we also, as closely related to the Jewish religion [Note: [Col. 0364C] “Religion” is absent from the Paris manuscript.], are initiated into the worship of the same image.

Yet that same Cornelius Tacitus—that most loquacious purveyor of falsehoods [Note: [Col. 0364C] **That most loquacious purveyor of falsehoods.** This is unsurprising when he treats the Jews, since every historian who has dealt with this subject has groped blindly and wandered along the same string of error. Read Tacitus and Justin, and you will laugh. The cause was the custom of the Jews, of whom Tacitus himself says in *Histories* V, chapter 5: “But toward all others they bear hostile hatred. They keep apart at meals and sleep separately.” Juvenal speaks more freely, *Satires* XIV, verse 101:

[Col. 0364D] Accustomed to despise the laws of Rome,  
They learn, observe, and fear the Jewish law—  
Whatever Moses handed down in his secret volume:  
Not to show the way except to one who worships the same rites,  
And to lead only the circumcised to the sought-for spring.

Therefore ridiculous and intolerable is the statement that La Cerda foisted upon Tacitus, as though Sidonius had said it about his prolixity:

> With what pomp Tacitus must speak, never reaching an end.

Since Tacitus is there joined with Varro, Sallust, and Plautus, even a blind man could see that the passage contains praise of him and should read: “must speak, never without praise.” Vopiscus, however, passes this judgment on all writers in his *Aurelian*: “No writer, so far as history is concerned, has failed to tell some falsehood; thus Livy, Sallust, Cornelius Tacitus, and finally Trogus have each been convicted of manifest errors.” Among these writers, indeed, the eloquent Muretus vigorously, [Col. 0365B] extensively, and expressly defends Tacitus from the accusations of both Vopiscus and Tertullian, *Works*, volume I, Oration 14. La Cerda, however, rightly observes our author’s wit in branding Tacitus as “most loquacious” and as one who exercises very little restraint over his tongue, contrary to what his very name, *Tacitus*, professes. HAV.]—relates in the same history that Gnaeus Pompey, after capturing Jerusalem and therefore entering the temple to investigate the mysteries of the Jewish religion, [Col. 0365A] found no image there [Note: [Col. 0365B] **Found no image there.** This is true, as even blindness itself bears witness. Did any pagan ever dare to offer greater testimony concerning Moses, the Jewish religion, and its earliest founders than this: “δικαιοπραγοῦντες καὶ θεοσεβεῖς ὡς ἀληθῶς ὂντες, just and truly religious”? These are the words of Strabo from his sixteenth book. His testimony there concerning Moses and the worship of the Deity precedes it in the following form: Μωσῆς γὰρ, etc., that is: “For Moses, one of the Egyptian priests, possessed a certain part of the country; but, being dissatisfied with the existing state of affairs, he migrated from there to this place, accompanied by many who had divine concerns at heart. For he affirmed and taught that the Egyptians were mistaken in attributing to God images of wild beasts and cattle, and likewise the Africans and the Greeks in ascribing human nature to the gods. Rather, that alone is God which encompasses us, the land, and the sea—which we call heaven, the universe, and the nature of all things. No sane person would surely dare to fashion an image of him resembling any of the things that exist among us. Therefore, all fabrication of images should be rejected; a temple and shrine worthy of him should be established, and he should be worshipped without any figure.” HAV.].

Certainly, if anything represented by an image had been worshipped there, nowhere would it have been displayed more readily than in its own sanctuary—especially since that worship, vain though it was, did not fear [Note: [Col. 0365A] Du Jon: “does not fear.”] the judgment of outsiders [Note: [Col. 0365A] “The judgment of outsiders” is absent from the Paris manuscript.]. For only the priests were permitted to enter [Note: [Col. 0365C] **Only the priests.** Worth noting is what Lucian writes concerning a similar Eastern temple and the ritual of its sacred rites in his dialogue *On the Syrian Goddess*, p. 901. After relating that it contained a more sacred chamber and an inner room, he adds: Εἰς μὲν οὖν τὸν μέγαν νηὸν πάντες εἰσέρχονται, εἰς δὲ τὸν θάλαμον οἱ ἱερέες μοῦνον. οὐ μὲν τοὶ πάντες ἱερέες, ἀλλά τοὶ μάλιστα ἀγχίθεοί τέ εἰσι, καὶ τοῖσι πᾶσα εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν μέλεται θεραπείη, that is: “Accordingly, everyone enters the great temple; only the priests enter the inner chamber, and not even all of them, but those who approach nearest to the god and upon whom all care of the temple is bestowed.” HAV.], while everyone else was denied the sight of it by a curtain drawn across [Note: [Col. 0365A] The Paris manuscript has *oppanso*; others, “was cut off by a curtain drawn across.”].

You, nevertheless, will not deny that you worship both all beasts of burden and whole geldings together with their Epona [Note: [Col. 0365A] Rhenanus and others: *Hippona*; compare *To the Nations* I, 11.] [Note: [Col. 0365D] **Together with their Epona.** So read the ancient manuscripts, not only of Tertullian but also of Minucius Felix and Apuleius; so too the ancient inscriptions. Finally, in Juvenal we read:

> He swears by Epona alone, and by the faces painted in the foul-smelling stables.

The populace introduced this exceedingly foolish goddess and at the same time corrupted her name. I would mention in passing that in Minucius the text seems to require: “You consecrate even whole asses in your stables, together with your lovely Epona.” In the very ancient Royal Library codex it reads: “Together with your—or Epona.” RIG. —Some read *Hippona*, as in Minucius; I would nevertheless agree with Rigault that *Epona* should be read. As Juvenal’s scholiast says, she is the goddess of muleteers. The whole matter is clear from Plutarch’s *Parallel Stories*: καὶ ὠνόμασεν Ἔποναν· ἔστι δὲ ἡ Θεὸς πρόνοιαν ποιουμένη ἵππων. LE PR.]. Perhaps we are condemned for this: that, among the worshippers of every kind of livestock and wild beast, we alone are worshippers of the ass.

But whoever believes us devoted to the cross [Col. 0366A] [Note: [Col. 0366A] The Paris manuscript has “a follower”; Wouwer and Du Jon, *consacraneus*.] will be our fellow-worshipper [Note: [Col. 0366B] **Fellow-worshipper.** Du Jon’s emendation *consacraneus* is not bad. For that is plainly how it was written in *To the Nations*, and likewise in several inscriptions in Gruter, such as 18.6 and 867.5: “A fellow-priestess of the goddess Ceres.” The passage in Capitolinus should likewise read *consacranei*, not *consecranei*, where he reports Maximinus’ words to the soldiers. Finally, as the distinguished Charles du Fresne rightly emends it, the Anonymous Writer of Bari says in his *Chronicle* for the year 1048: “Tornikes rebelled with the Macedonians, and Botazzi proceeded to Constantinople with his fellow-worshipper, to make himself emperor”—instead of “brother-in-law.” Our text in the Aldine edition has “will be”; Rhenanus, “a follower.” HAV.]. When a piece of wood is propitiated, never mind its outward appearance, provided the quality of the material is the same; never mind its shape, provided that very material is the body of the god. And yet how little do Attic Pallas and Pharian Ceres differ from the upright timber of a cross [Note: [Col. 0366B] **Attic Pallas.** She whom the Greeks call Ἀθηναίη. But no one thus far has been able to show that she stood displayed in this form; indeed, the commentators on our Septimius admit their ignorance. I think, however, that he is alluding to the goddess whom the Greeks called Ἐργάνη. Pausanias, that eminent preserver of Greek antiquities, alone recalls her image, made from a square stone—stones of this kind, as may be seen among the Athenian images of Mercury, were generally rough and tapered into a certain length—in his *Arcadica*, in these words: Εἰσὶ δὲ ὑποκαταβάντι ὀλίγον θεοὶ· παρέχονται δὲ καὶ οὗτοι σχῆμα τετράγωνον. Ἐργάται δὲ ἔστιν αὐτοῖς ἐπίκλησις, Ἀθηνᾶ τε Ἐργάνη, καὶ Ἀπόλλων Ἀγυιεύς, that is: “A little farther down, gods fashioned from square stones appear; they are surnamed *Ergatae*, or Workers: Athena Ergane and Apollo Agyieus.” She is the very goddess mentioned by Plutarch in περὶ Τύχης, where he quotes the iambics of someone unknown:

Βᾶτ` εἰς ὁδὸν δὴ, παῖς ὁ χείρώναξ λεὼν,

Οἱ τὴν Διὸς γοργῶνιν Ἐργάνην στατοῖς

Δίκνοισι προστρέπεσθε [recovered wording appears corrupt; its approximate sense is given by the translation that follows],

that is: “Come forward, you working multitude who seek your livelihood with your hands, who worship the Gorgonian goddess Ergane with baskets.” And he adds: τὴν γὰρ Ἐργὰνην καὶ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν αἱ τέχναι πάρεδρον ἔχουσιν: “For the crafts have obtained Ergane, who is also Minerva, as their patroness.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0366D] **Pharian Ceres.** Although what some produce from Aelian and coins in favor of “Ceres of Grain”—an interpretation supported by Meursius—deserves no consideration, the alternative reading is far better, if only because it is confirmed by the excellent Fulda manuscript; Minucius knows no other reading, nor, finally, does Tertullian himself in book I of *To the Nations*: “But if there is a difference in this matter, how little do Attic Pallas and Pharian Ceres differ from the upright timber of a cross? She is consecrated without form, as a rough stake and merely a small upright support of shapeless wood.” Read this last clause thus with the great Salmasius on Solinus, p. 94. The Leiden manuscript has *Farina*, so that it is doubtful whether its scribe intended “Pharian” or “made of flour.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0366A] Rhenanus, Heraldus, and Semler: “Ceres of grain”; Rigault and Havercamp: “Pharian,” for the manuscripts have *Faria*, *Fariam*, and *Farina*.], who stands exposed without an image, as a rough stake and a shapeless piece of wood [Note: [Col. 0366A] The Paris manuscript: “stands exposed.”]? Every piece of hard wood fixed in an upright position is a part of a cross [Note: [Col. 0366D] **Fixed in an upright position.** *Against the Jews*, chapter X or XI: “For even on a ship’s yard, which is part of a cross, the extremities are called horns, while the pole, supported at its center, is single-horned.” HAV.]; we, if anything, worship a god who is entire and whole.

We have said that the origin of your gods is fashioned by the modelers from a cross [Note: [Col. 0366D] **By the modelers from a cross.** The reading of the Montpellier Collection is “upon a cross.” A comma may also be placed after “your gods.” “We spoke above,” he says, “of the origin of your gods”; and what origin do they have? They are fashioned by the modelers from a cross, in this passage: “Does not the modeler first form the image from clay laid over a cross and stake? The body of your god is first consecrated upon a gibbet.” Chapter XII; see our notes there. But the common reading is good: “We have said that your gods, when they are formed by modelers, take their beginning from a cross.” *To the Nations* I, 12: “The modeler first sets up the wood of the cross, since the posture of our own body also possesses the silent and hidden outline of a cross.” In the same place: “If, therefore, you worship the cross as the origin of the class of gods.” Aldus has “from carts,” very badly. Scaliger emends “we have learned.” HAV.].

But you also adore Victories [Col. 0367A] [Note: [Col. 0367B] **But you also adore Victories.** This is certainly ridiculous, since in this way they venerated the weapons of conquered enemies. Yet he presents it as an unquestioned fact in *To the Nations* I, 12: “Now to obvious matters”—read thus, not “but.” “You venerate Victories as divine powers, and indeed the narrower they are, the more delightful. Whatever the framework raises aloft will be crosses—the innards, so to speak, of a trophy.” The figure of Victory itself, together with trophies, may sometimes be seen on coins, as on those of Hostilius and Aurelius and others. HAV.], although in trophies the crosses are the trophies’ internal framework [Note: [Col. 0367A] Havercamp emends: “although in them crosses are the internal framework—but of trophies.” I would prefer to transpose the individual words so that it reads: [Col. 0368A] “But you also adore Victories in trophies, although crosses are the internal framework of trophies.”].

The entire religion of the Roman camp venerates the standards [Note: [Col. 0367B] **Venerates the standards.** The Montpellier Collection continues: “adores the standards.” Tacitus therefore calls them “the peculiar divinities of the legions,” *Annals* I, chapter 19. Indeed, they did not merely adorn them—as the author will presently say—but even anointed them like images of gods. Pliny condemns this as barbaric and effeminate in *Natural History* XIII, chapter 3: “Most astonishing of all, however, is that this honor has penetrated even into the camps. Eagles and standards, though dusty and bristling with guards, are anointed on feast days; would that we could say who first established the practice.” So it is, of course: corrupted by this bribe, the eagles conquered the world. Among the many commentators who demonstrate this well-known rite, there is the remarkable passage of Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* I, chapter 4, where he says of the Labarum: Σημεῖον δὲ τοῦτο τιμιώτατον, καθότι ἀεὶ τοῦ βασιλέως ἡγεῖσθαι, καὶ προσκυνεῖσθαι νενόμιστο παρὰ ϛρατιωτῶν [ϛρατιωτῶν is recovered with ϛ, apparently for στρατιωτῶν, “soldiers”], that is: “This standard was especially venerable, because it was accustomed both to precede the emperor and also to be adored by the soldiers.” Lipsius should be consulted on Tacitus; he treats their worship, religious character, and form in *On the Roman Military*, book IV, chapters 3, 5, and 9; also Causeus, volume X, *Antiquities of Rome*, p. 1528. Hence an eagle standing upon an altar or thunderbolt appears between two standards in Gorlaeus II.44, I.161, and I.122, and in a noteworthy cultic representation in Seguin, p. 109, of which more shortly. HAV.]; it swears by the standards and sets the standards before all the gods [Note: [Col. 0367C] **Before all the gods.** The author means nothing other than that soldiers would more readily profane everything sacred and secular than violate their military oath. In the same way below, chapter XXVII: “Indeed, among you, perjury is committed more readily by all the gods than by the single Genius of Caesar.” Laelius says to Scipio in Livy, book XXXVI, during the dispute over the mural crown between Quintus Trebellius and Sextus Digitius: “On one side stand the legionary soldiers, on the other the marines, ready to swear by all the gods to what they wish rather than to what they know to be true, and to bind by perjury not only themselves and their own lives, but also the military standards and eagles and the sanctity of their oath.” Rhenanus omitted the word “standards” here. HAV.]. All those tiers of images upon the standards [Note: [Col. 0367D] **Upon the standards.** This is the brilliant emendation of Lipsius, *Epistolary Questions* V, letter 15, which I would urge you to inspect. Previously the absurd reading was “distinguished.” But the noteworthy Montpellier Collection also has “upon the standards,” though Rigault’s editions neglected it. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0368A] Lipsius emends “upon the standards,” *Epistolary Questions* V, 15.] are necklaces of crosses [Note: [Col. 0367D] **Necklaces of crosses.** There is a most beautiful passage in Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration I *Against Julian*: Τολμᾷ δὲ ἤδη καὶ κατὰ τοῦ μεγάλου συνθὴματος, etc., that is: “Indeed, he burst forth to such a degree of audacity that he rushed headlong against that great standard.” He is speaking of the Labarum, marked with the cross, concerning which Prudentius says in *Against Symmachus* I.483:

[Col. 0368A] Christ, embroidered in purple upon jeweled gold,  
Marked the Labarum; Christ had inscribed  
The emblems upon the shields.

That standard, together with the cross, leads the army magnificently and with splendid pomp, raised high aloft; it possesses the power of ending labors and derives its name among the Latins from that fact. It holds primacy, so to speak, over all the other standards—both those adorned with images of the emperors and with outspread fabrics in various dyes and painted lettering, as though exulting, and those which, flying from the dreadful gaping mouths of dragons raised upon the tips of spears, and fluttering along expanses patterned with woven scales, offer the eyes a spectacle at once most delightful and terrifying. From this you may charmingly understand why Solomon adds the terror of military standards to the Bride’s beauty in *Song of Songs* VI.10. Indeed, what Tertullian here calls “necklaces of crosses” is beautifully expressed and may even help to elucidate Holy Scripture.

Our author calls the little shields or bucklers hung in a circle from the standards “tiers of images.” Thus there might be many levels, some higher and others lower, like the stories and galleries seen on towers; upon them were painted the images of emperors who had been consecrated and enrolled among the gods, or who were still reigning—as is clear from Lipsius’ passage concerning the image of Vitellius. The same was also done with small gold and silver objects [*incunculis*; reading uncertain], as may still commonly be seen from marbles, paintings, gems, and so forth. Accordingly, magnificent and regal is the comparison appearing in Solomon’s highly elaborate nuptial song, chapter IV.4: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built for defense; a thousand shields project from it, all the bucklers of heroes.” For that is how the passage should be translated, though commentators go astonishingly astray there. He praises not merely the smooth, rounded elevation of his beloved’s neck; through this comparison he also describes and commends its ornamentation. For just as the tower of David, when strong defenders stand all around upon its platforms, gleams encircled by shields shining on every side, so precious necklaces add immense splendor to natural beauty. Thus in Lucan, book X, verse 140, adornment injures beauty by disguising it:

> Laden with the spoils of the Red Sea, upon her neck and hair  
> Cleopatra wears riches and labors beneath her adornment.

Not so Cato’s Marcia:

> No jeweled belt confined her flowing robe,  
> No graceful necklace adorned her neck,

in the same poet, book II, verse 362.

While engaged on another subject, I shall explain in the same operation the earlier passage in *Song of Songs* VII.5: “Your head upon you is like Mount Carmel, the ribbon of your hair is purple; the king is bound in its tiers”—so one may render it in Latin. The Greeks call it πλοκάμους. Hesychius explains it as κονδύλους τῶν τριχῶν πεπλεγμένων, that is, locks of hair curled with the fingers. This is how Juno adorns herself to entice Jupiter into love in Homer’s *Iliad*, ξ (book 14), verse 176:

ἰδὲ χαίτας

Πεξαμένη, χερσὶ πλοκάμους ἔπλεψε φαεινοὺς [the opening recovered wording may be corrupt; its approximate sense is given by the translation that follows],

that is: “And, combing her hair, she arranged its beautiful curls with her hands.” Thus our author’s “tiers of images.” To these passages you might add those of Statius and Juvenal, which are known to everyone. Less familiar is the passage of Nazianzen, who begins his Invective against Women thus: “Beware, women, lest you fortify your heads with false and counterfeit hair as though with towers, daintily displaying soft necks from rocky heights.”

We have written *crucum*, not *crucium*, following the Fulda and Leiden manuscripts and the book *To the Nations*. Those tiers [Col. 0369A] of images appear excellently as necklaces of crosses on the coin of Tiberius published by the celebrated Seguin in *Selected Coins*, p. 109, which we reproduced above when discussing the eagle. Two very similar coins, one of them belonging to Germanicus Caesar, occur in the distinguished Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, p. 120. Indeed, a different example appears in the same author at p. 558, on a denarius of the Valerian family. HAV.].

Those hanging fabrics [Col. 0369A] of the standards and *cantabra* [Note: [Col. 0369A] Rhenanus: “Those *sypara* of the standards and lampstands,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0369A] **Cantabra.** So Minucius reads, and our author again in [Col. 0369B] *To the Nations*. Learned men therefore dispute in vain when they alter it to *candes labarorum*, as Scaliger does, or to *cantabrorum*, *candelabrorum*, or *labarorum*, as others, including Barraeus and Aldus, do. For it was a type of standard whose name has an unknown origin. This origin can perhaps no more be referred to the Persians, Romans, or Spaniards than to the Africans themselves, who, because they shared many words with the Hebrews, perhaps possessed a term similar to the Persian *Kanatb* or the Hebrew *Kendes*, and closer to these *cantabra*. I have also found that among later writers *cantabrarii* are numbered among the standard-bearers, as Dom du Cange teaches me from book 2 of the Theodosian Code, *On Guild Members*. Editions commonly have *sypara*, but Rigault correctly reads *syphara*. The Fulda and Agobard manuscripts have *sypharant*, which the Leiden manuscript also favors, though it has *sifara*. Id.] are robes of crosses [Note: [Col. 0369B] **Are robes of crosses.** This is beautifully displayed to the eyes on certain coins commonly found among those of Aarschot: a gold coin of Augustus, where the form of the cross appears splendidly; a silver coin of Maxentius, where the figure of an eagle may be seen woven into the robe; and likewise a silver coin of Constans, which displays the very form of the Labarum—though the Christian Labarum, marked with the sacred name. Id.]. I commend your diligence: you have refused to consecrate naked and unadorned crosses.

Others, to be sure, believe more humanely and plausibly that the Sun is our god [Note: [Col. 0369C] **Our god.** Juvenal says of the Jews, whom they confused with Christians:

> They worship nothing except the clouds and the divinity of heaven.

Hence our author says below, chapter XXIV: “Let one worship God, another Jupiter; let one raise suppliant hands toward heaven, another toward the altar of Faith; let one, if this is what you think, count the clouds while praying, another the ceiling panels.” HAV.]. If so, we shall perhaps be classed with the Persians—although we do not worship the Sun painted upon a linen cloth [Note: [Col. 0369C] **Painted upon a linen cloth.** The commentators say much about the worship of the Sun among the Persians; worthy of addition are the materials collected by the distinguished Brissonius in his short work *On the Kingdom of the Persians*, book II, chapter 1. The painted Sun assumed different forms according to the different kinds of worship. I learn this from a memorable passage in Flavius Vopiscus’ *Life of Aurelian*, where, among other things, he records that the following portent of future imperial power befell him: “Moreover, when he went as legate to the Persians, he was given a garment of the kind customarily presented to emperors by the Persian king, upon which the Sun was engraved in the form in which he was worshipped in the temple where Aurelian’s mother had been a priestess.” Therefore, I understand the words “painted upon a linen cloth” not only of Persian standards, but of any pictures and linen cloths upon which that divinity was painted and worshipped by them within the walls of its temple.

Among the Egyptians, certainly, the Sun was depicted in various forms—as an infant, boy, young man, adult, and old man—as Macrobius notes in *Saturnalia* I.18. His words are: “These differences of age are referred to the Sun: at the winter solstice he is represented as a little child, such as the Egyptians bring forth from the inner shrine on a fixed day, because then, on the shortest day, he appears as though small and infantile. Thereafter, as the increments advance, he acquires the strength of an adolescent at the vernal equinox and is adorned with the figure of a young man. Afterward, at the summer solstice, his age is represented in its fullest maturity by the likeness of a beard, since at that time he attains his greatest increase. From then on, as the days diminish, the god is depicted in a fourth form, as though growing old.”

Maximus of Tyre, Oration XXXVIII, also writes that the Paeonians worship the Sun, and that among them its image is a small disk fastened atop an exceedingly long pole. Hemelarius suspected that this very object was represented upon a gold coin of Trajan Decius bearing the inscription *PANNONIAE*. HAV.]—since we possess the Sun himself everywhere in his own shield [Note: [Col. 0370A] *Sic* in the Paris manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0370A] **Everywhere in his own shield.** This is a noteworthy passage. Since earlier commentators had not understood it, La Cerda was the first to show correctly that it pertains not to the Persians but to the Christians themselves. Yet he will not disdain to receive some light from us as well. For I cannot agree with the very learned La Cerda and Rigault in taking “in his own shield” to mean the actual orb of the sun, as though it were “the shield of God,” as Ovid calls it in *Metamorphoses* XV.192. Heaven must be meant here. In its orb, besides the moon and the lesser stars, the illustrious Sun stands prominently forth.

When Homer, with poetic art, engraved heaven itself upon Achilles’ shield as though it reproduced the shield’s shape in one of its halves, he did not neglect to place the Sun upon it as well. His verses are in the *Iliad*, Σ (book 18), verse 483:

Ἐν μὲν γαῖαν ἔτευξ`, ἐν δ` οὐρανὸν, ἐν δὲ θάλασσαν·

Ἡέλιόν τ` ἀκάμαντα, σελήνην τε πλήθουσαν,

Ἐν δὲ τὰ τείρεα πάντα τά τοῖς τ` οὐρανὸς ἐστεφάνωται,

that is: “Upon it Vulcan fashioned the earth, heaven, and sea, the tireless Sun, the full Moon, and all the stars with which heaven is crowned.” What follows is gathered into a summary by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIII, verse 110:

> Nor the shield engraved with the image of the vast universe.

You now encounter heaven described by the word “shield” in those most ancient verses of Ennius, from Euripides’ *Iphigenia*, which the most Latin of authors, Varro, preserved for us around the middle of book VI of *On the Latin Language*:

> What time of night does it seem to be? In the loud-resounding  
> Shield of heaven the Wagon’s Pole rises above  
> The stars, driving aloft again  
> And again the journey of night.

“He wishes to indicate the advanced hour of night from the movement of the Wagon’s Pole,” says Varro. Accordingly, these two coins of the emperors Trajan and Alexander deserve inspection; upon them the Sun and Moon, together with the twelve signs of the zodiac, appear engraved upon the shield, as though upon heaven.

Finally, it is clear from this that the reading should not be *utique*, as Wouwer wishes and Rigault follows in his edition, but *ubique*, “everywhere,” as not only other manuscripts but also the Agobard manuscript exhibit it. Septimius says that we do not look up to that Sun painted by a human hand upon some tablet, but to God’s own finger in its own place and throughout every land, since it shines everywhere. Indeed, I say that *ibique*, “there,” should be read, as the very words of Lucian can show. I have found that in many respects Lucian appealed remarkably to our Septimius—excluding his impiety and blasphemies. Thus, on p. 904 of *On the Syrian Goddess*, Lucian gives the following reason why images of the Sun and Moon are not found there alongside the other gods represented in visible form: Λέγουσι, he says, τοῖσι μὲν ἄλλοισι θεοῖσι, ὅσιον ἔμμεναι ξόανα ποιεῖσθαι· οὐ γὰρ σφέων ἐμφανέα πάνσι τὰ εἲδεα. Ἡέλιος δὲ, καὶ σεληναίη πάμπαν ἐναργέες, καὶ σφέας πάντες ὁρεουσὶ, ποίη οὖν αἰτίη ξοανουργίης, τοῖσι ἐν τῷ ἠέρι φαινομένοισι·, that is: “They say that it is lawful to make images of the other gods, whose forms are not visible to everyone. But the Sun and Moon are entirely manifest, and there is no one who does not see them. Why, then, should I fashion an image of them when they appear in the air?”

On the engraving of shields, in addition to what Heraldus presents in his digressions on this author, one may consult Johann Albert Fabricius’ *Bibliographia Antiquaria*, p. 562, a storehouse of antiquity and of all more refined literature. HAV.].

Finally, the suspicion arose because it became known that we pray toward the region of the east [Note: [Col. 0370D] **Toward the region of the east.** There survives a special dissertation on this rite by Jacob Thomasius, published at Leipzig in 1670. Cosmas Indicopleustes V, p. 202, may also be consulted, as may Menardus and others cited by Johann Albert Fabricius, *Bibliographia Antiquaria*, p. 361. That the pagans also looked up toward heaven and prayed facing east can be shown, among many others, by Kippingius, pp. 178 and [Col. 0371B] 180. HAV.]. But many of you also, at times, with a pretense of worshipping heavenly things, quiver your lips toward the sunrise [Note: [Col. 0371B] **Quiver your lips.** With a silent murmur. > After saying aloud, “Father Janus,” and aloud, “Apollo,”  
> He moves his lips, afraid of being heard: “Lovely Laverna,  
> Grant me the power to deceive,” etc.

But La Cerda says more than enough, as does Brouwer concerning the Persians in *On the Adoration of the Ancients*, pp. 195 and 199—a diligent and learned man. HAV.].

Likewise, if we devote Sunday to rejoicing, for a reason far removed from worship of the Sun [Note: [Col. 0371B] **From worship of the Sun.** Restore the text thus, not “the worship of S.”, on the authority of the excellent Fulda manuscript. “From worship” is used just as above “from justice,” “from wisdom,” and very often in our author, in the sense of “because of wisdom” or “on account of justice.” Christians were not reluctant to retain this name, though borrowed from the pagans, in the designation of that day, since, as Ambrose writes in Sermon LXI, “on that day the Savior, like the rising Sun, scattered the darkness of the underworld and shone forth with the light of the resurrection.” HAV.], we rank second to those [Note: [Col. 0371C] **We rank second.** Septimius says that it cannot be demonstrated that we worship the Sun, as the Persians do, from the fact that a Christian turns toward the east in the posture of prayer—a practice maintained in the early Church because Christ is compared to the rising Sun, Malachi IV.2, and because it was also believed that on the final day he would appear from there in judgment. Nor can it be demonstrated from the fact that the day which is festive for us was consecrated to the Sun among the nations. They may foolishly have suspected this, just as Tacitus fell into a humorous error when thinking about Saturn, *Histories* V, chapter 4: “Others say that this honor is paid to Saturn, either because the Idaeans who transmitted the beginnings of their religion—whom we have learned were expelled together with Saturn and became the founders of the nation—or because, among the seven stars by which mortals are governed, the star of Saturn moves in the highest orbit and possesses the greatest power, and because most heavenly bodies complete their influence and course through the number seven.”

What now follows—“we rank second to those who devote Saturn’s day,” etc.—is likewise splendidly sprinkled with satirical salt. For he touches here not upon the Jews, as commentators commonly persuaded themselves, but upon the pagans themselves. They had so degenerated from their ancestral institutions that there was no nation from whose rites they had not plucked some portion and made it their own, as Gothofredus beautifully demonstrates in his highly learned notes on Tertullian’s book *To the Nations*. I am indignant that this truly learned man is not generally valued more highly.

It will be worthwhile to append here the passage from *To the Nations*, since our author must be understood from it. In book I, chapter XIII, he says: “It is certainly you who have also received the Sun into the register of the seven days. From among their days you selected the day on which you either abstain from bathing, postpone it until evening, or devote yourselves to leisure and feasting. You do this by deviating from your own religions toward alien ones. For the Jews have feast days, Sabbaths, the pure supper, and the Jewish rites of lamps, fasts accompanied by unleavened bread, and prayers upon the shore—all of which are certainly alien to your gods. Therefore, to return from my digression: you who reproach us with the Sun and its day, acknowledge the proximity. We are not far removed from your Saturn and your Sabbaths.” Thus what he says there—“acknowledge the proximity,” etc.—is expressed here as “we rank second to them.”

As for the reading of the Agobard manuscript, which has “Hebrews,” I cannot approve it; nor, I think, despite its plausibility at first sight, will it please anyone. HAV.] who devote Saturn’s day to idleness and feasting [Note: [Col. 0372A] **To idleness and feasting.** The pagans did indeed charge the Jews with this fault, just as that people’s supreme Lawgiver often complained through his prophets that they violated his sacred ordinances by devoting their leisure to themselves rather than to God. Juvenal, *Satires* V, verse 106:

> But his father was to blame: for him every seventh day  
> Was idle and touched no part of life at all.

Tacitus perhaps draws from the same source in *Histories* V.4: “They say that idleness on the seventh day found favor because that day brought an end to their labors; then, as indolence proved alluring, the seventh year also was given over to sloth.” But here the passage concerns the pagans themselves, to whom those lines of Persius, *Satires* V, verse 18, must also be referred:

> But when  
> The days of Herod have come, and the lamps arranged  
> In the greased window have disgorged a rich cloud of smoke,  
> Bearing violets, while the greasy window embraces a red dish.

For certainly the pagans themselves spent certain days in idleness, as though in accordance with Jewish custom, caring for nothing but food. He says this in the book *To the Nations*: “the day on which you forgo bathing, [Col. 0372C] or postpone it until evening, or devote yourselves to leisure and luncheon.” Seneca, Josephus in *Against Apion*, and Clement of Alexandria report the same thing. HAV.] decree, themselves also deviating from the Jewish [Col. 0372A] [Note: [Col. 0372C] **From Jewish custom.** Gothofredus considers the passage corrupt and wishes *a* (“from”) to be deleted. I do not agree. For this is the sense: Why do you delight in mocking us as though we spent Sunday dissolutely in merriment and pleasure? We tread upon your heels; we are not far removed from you, for you yourselves dedicate Saturday, which precedes our day, to more cheerful gluttony and idleness, according to a custom received from the Jews, whom you do not understand. Thus you not only depart from the customs and institutions of your ancestors, who did not wish foreign rites to be introduced, but also deviate from the true purpose of the Jews, which requires rest on that day, not indolence. For, as it is said in the book *To the Nations*: “Those festivals—the Sabbaths, the pure supper, the Jewish rites involving lamps, the fasts with unleavened bread, and the prayers upon the shore—are certainly foreign to your gods.” HAV.] custom, which they do not understand.

But quite recently a new representation of our God was publicly exhibited in this city, when [Note: [Col. 0371A] Some editions: *quidam* (“someone”).] a certain criminal, a hired performer in the business of eluding [Note: [Col. 0371A] La Cerda: *infrustrandus*.] wild beasts, [Note: [Col. 0372C] **A criminal hired performer.** Neither Gothofredus’ interpretation nor Rigaltius’, much less those of the others, is satisfactory. The former takes *noxius* to mean “liable”; the latter says that the man acted dishonestly because he had so often evaded the teeth of the beasts, and was therefore “criminal.” But what could be simpler than to understand a man who, although under no necessity to fight wild beasts and not sentenced to them as one of the condemned, nevertheless, from desire for a little profit and for an agreed payment, had handed himself over to the trainer? He elegantly calls combat with wild beasts an “eluding,” because the greater part of that daring art consisted in evading the beasts’ attack. The Agobardinus manuscript has *noxiis*, as though it referred to the pagans, whom he would be calling guilty; I do not think so. HAV.] displayed a picture bearing an inscription of this sort: **THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONOKOITHS**. [Note: [Col. 0372D] **THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONOKOITHS.** This monstrosity has been variously deformed by monstrous readings. Some editions have *onochoisitis*, which Baptista Pius emends by reshaping it into *ononychites*; this pleased Barraeus, Pamelius, and others. He nevertheless continues to conjecture *ononychotitis*, so named from ass, hoof, and ear, or *ononychottis*, in his annotations after chapter XIX. Junius, from the Vatican manuscript, [Col. 0373A] prefers *Onocorsites*. Finally, Rigaltius printed: “The god of the Christians, *Onochoetes*. He was,” etc. In his notes he also excellently explains *onocoitis* as something conceived from an ass and a human being. We have therefore admitted this reading into the text. For the Leiden manuscript clearly supports that reading; in it there stood *Onochoitissis erat*. So too the Aldine, which had *Onochoitis erat*, and the excellent Agobardinus manuscript itself, which clearly has *Onochoitis. Is erat*, etc. Finally, the Fulda manuscript, which nevertheless punctuates badly: “THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS. *Onochoites is erat*.” From this someone might perhaps suppose that the word *Onochoites* did not belong to the inscription itself devised by the buffoon, but was an explanation added by Tertullian himself, who, because he had aptly expressed the matter in Greek with a single word, was compelled by the poverty of the Latin language to describe it at greater length—were it not that he immediately adds, “We laughed both at the name and at the figure.”

Yet the word ὀνοκοίτης (“one who lies with an ass”), which was represented in Latin manuscripts in the manner formerly customary among copyists, is nowhere found among Greek writers in the sense of denoting offspring conceived from an ass and another animal, but does denote one who copulates with an ass, just as παρακοίτης (“husband” or “bedfellow”) is said of one who lies with his wife, and ἀκοίτης (“husband” or “bedfellow”) or ἄκοιτις (“wife” or “bedfellow”) of a woman who lies beside her husband. A similar usage is nevertheless found in the Septuagint translators, who frequently employed the word κοίτης (“coupling” or “offspring”) for offspring; from this Grotius explains the passage of Paul to the Romans, chapter IX, verse 10: Ἀλλὰ καὶ Ῥεβέκκα ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα Ἰσαάκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν (“And Rebecca also, having conceived by one man, Isaac our father”).

This very passage still seems to me not to have been sufficiently understood. For I do not refer ἐξ ἑνὸς (“from one”) to Isaac, as is commonly done—it would be absurd to imagine foreign assistance in the case of so chaste a wife as Rebecca—but to marital intercourse, the act of copulation itself. [Col. 0373C] And certainly this increases the force of the Apostle’s argument: speaking of Rebecca, hitherto barren, he observes that she conceived twins in her womb from a single intercourse, thereby excluding all superfetation, which Hippocrates discusses in his book *On Regimen* and which the sons of physicians know. Indeed, still more does he do so to show that Jacob and Esau issued from a single womb, were conceived and born at one and the same time, and yet found utterly different fortunes with God. Thus Persius’ saying, received in a sound sense, is altogether true, *Satire* VI, verse 18:

> For twins, O horoscope, you bring forth  
> With diverse genius.

Furthermore, the word Ἰσαάκ (“Isaac”) should not be referred to ἐξ ἑνὸς (“from one”), but to Ῥεβέκκα (“Rebecca”), so that the comma is placed before *and* Ἰσαάκ (“Isaac”), as though it were written Ῥεβέκκα, Ἰσαάκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα (“Rebecca, wife of Isaac our father, having conceived offspring from a single intercourse”), that is: “When Rebecca, the wife of our father Isaac, had conceived offspring from a single intercourse”—offspring which he states in what follows to have been twofold.

Accordingly, from the appearance of the body, [Col. 0373D] the Jewish buffoon represented this fictitious God as a kind of ὁνοκοίτην (“one who lies with an ass”; the recovered initial spelling is uncertain), as though he had been born from a shameful adulteress. Such is the bestial lust described in Juvenal, *Satire* VI, verse 330:

> If there is nothing else, recourse is had to slaves; should you remove  
> The hope of slaves, a hired water-carrier will come. If he  
> Is sought and no men are available, nothing will delay her  
> From lowering her rump beneath the ass mounted upon her.

That Roman eyes dared, under those most impure beasts Nero and Domitian, to watch something of this kind represented to the life in the story of Pasiphaë is attested by Suetonius, chapter XII, and Martial, book V. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0371A] Rhenanus, Heraldus, and Gangnaeus: *Ononychites*; the Bongarsian [Col. 0372A] and Leiden manuscripts: *Onochotasis*; the Vatican manuscript: *Onochorsites*; the Agobardinus, Puteanus, Fulda, and second Leiden manuscripts: *Onochoitis*; Rigaltius: *Onochoetes*; Havercampus: *Onokoitis*.]

For while he was offering incense, [Col. 0374B] they say, he saw a certain man standing there who had the form of an ass. When he had gone out and wished to say, ‘Woe to you! This is taught by Philostratus in books II and IV of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*; by the scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius, book III of the *Argonautica*; and also by Aristophanes in the *Frogs*, where Xanthias and Bacchus descend to the Underworld, Act I, Scene VI: καὶ βολίθινον θάτερον (“and the other is asinine,” referring to the other leg; βολίθινον is uncertain or corrupt in the recovered text), that is, “the other leg is asinine.” There the learned scholiast, explaining that apparition, says that it is therefore called ὀνὸκωλον (“ass-limbed,” or “an ass on one foot”), that is, “an ass on one foot.” The same scholiast calls it ὀνοσκελίδα (“ass-legged”), “ass-legged,” in his note on the *Assemblywomen*, not far from the end.

From Aristophanes’ description I recognize that very Empusa [Col. 0374C] among the gems in Gorlaeus, *Dactyliotheca*, vol. II, no. 41; learned men, I think, have hitherto failed to understand that it is represented there. HAV.] carrying a book and dressed in a toga. We laughed both at the name and at the figure. But they ought [Note: [Col. 0373A] Havercampus: *debuerant*.] immediately to have worshipped this [Col. 0374A] two-formed deity, [Note: [Col. 0374A] Paris edition: *nomen* (“name”).] since they have admitted gods compounded [Note: [Col. 0374C] **Compounded.** Porphyry had already seized upon this point in his highly subtle work *On Abstinence from Animals*, book IV, teaching that every kind of animal was formerly combined with the human form in the construction of images—as when the face of some bird or of a lion was joined to a human body—and that it was therefore impious to eat or consume any such creature. Read thus, following the emendation of the best manuscript. The others are Pans, Satyrs, Cynocephali, and Mithras. Add Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, p. 349. HAV.] gods that are goats from the loins downward; gods that are serpents from the legs; [Note: [Col. 0374C] **Serpents from the legs.** Does he allude to Erichthonius, the son born from Vulcan’s assault upon Pallas? Pausanias thinks that he is represented by the serpent at the feet of Phidias’ Minerva. Because of the sublimity of his origin and the brilliance of his deeds, temples, altars, and statues may have been erected to him, although I do not remember reading anything about his being worshipped as a god. Yet that could have happened, since Euripides observes that in his honor a custom remained among the Athenian women, where he had reigned, of adorning little children with golden serpents. Νὸμος τίς ἐστιν, ὄφεσιν χρυσηλάτοις


Τρέφειν τέκνα (“Hence there among the Erechtheids is a custom of rearing children with golden-wrought serpents.”)

Some think him represented in a certain engraving in Gorlaeus, *Dactyliotheca*, vol. II, no. 489. But my teacher Gronovius, a very great man, more correctly taught that it represents a serpent-footed giant.

Or does he instead allude to Serapis, whose head appears on the reverse of Antoninus Pius, with a serpentine body in many coils with which he entwines an ear of grain, as Montfaucon records in his *Italian Diary*, p. 443? I see no other deity to whom almost all these features could be applied than Mithras, concerning whom Ph. a Turre wrote a separate work. Among the Abraxas gems in Gorlaeus he is likewise almost always accompanied by serpents, and may also be seen with a lion’s head. ## CHAPTER XVII

**ARGUMENT.—He asserts that Christians worship the true God, who made all things, and describes his nature. He teaches that knowledge and recognition of this God are naturally implanted in the human being, so that he is not ignorant of God’s greatness, goodness, kindness, assistance, and justice, and believes that he acts in heaven, not on earth.**

The God whom we worship [Note: [Col. 0375B] *Nos* (“we”) is absent from the Paris edition.] is one. He brought forth this entire mass, together with all the equipment of elements, bodies, and spirits, out of nothing, [Col. 0375B] by the word with which he commanded, the reason with which he ordered, and the power with which he was able, as an adornment of his majesty. Hence the Greeks also applied to the world the name κόσμον (“ornament,” hence “world”). He is invisible [Note: [Col. 0375B] Paris edition: *et si*.], although he is seen; incomprehensible, although he is presented to us through grace; inestimable, although he is appraised by human [Col. 0376A] senses. [Note: [Col. 0375B] Paris edition: *sensibilis* (“perceptible”).] [Note: [Col. 0375D] **By human senses.** Tacitus, *Histories* V: “The Jews conceive of one deity, and that with the mind alone. They regard as profane those who fashion images of gods from mortal materials in the likeness of human beings.” Relevant here is the passage of Paul to the Ephesians, chapter V, verse 17: Διὰ τοῦτο μὴ γένεσθε ἄφρονες, ἀλλὰ συνιέντες τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Κυρίου (“Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is”). HAV.] For that very reason [Note: [Col. 0376B] Franeker edition: *adeo*.] he is true and so great.

Indeed, whatever can ordinarily be seen, comprehended, and appraised is less than the eyes by which it is occupied, the hands by which it is contaminated, and the senses by which it is discovered. [Note: [Col. 0375D] **It is less.** A most beautiful discourse, by which we are taught not to desire wisdom beyond measure, since God alone is conscious of his own mysteries, while to us there remains, from those things that he has revealed and in accordance with them—to use the words of Tacitus—only the glory of obedience. Indeed, the foremost of the Apostles derives from this the glory of the age to come and the excellence of our more perfect nature: that a fuller and clearer knowledge of God has been reserved for us. For thus he writes in 1 Corinthians XIII.12: Βλέπομεν γὰρ ἄρτι δι` ἐσόπρου ἐν αἰνίγματι, τότε δὲ πρόσωπον (“For now we see through a mirror, obscurely, but then face…”; ἐσόπρου appears corrupt in the recovered text) [Col. 0376C] πρὸς πρόσωπον· ἄρτι γινώσκω ἐκ μέρους, τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι καθὼς καὶ ὲπεγνώσθην (“…to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, even as I was fully known”; the initial accent in ὲπεγνώσθην is anomalous in the recovered text).
