Latinius prefers *dum* (“while”) to *et* (“and”); the Fulda manuscript deletes it. *Pati*, like the Greek word which he wished to imitate, πάσχειν (“to experience” or “to suffer”), is used both of something joyful and of something adverse. *Suam* (“its own”) is not without emphasis here, but is used as in the opposite and more sorrowful sense of that very famous saying:

> Each of us suffers his own shade,

in Virgil, book VI. The Agobardinus manuscript has *pascitur* (“is nourished”), which I cannot approve. HAV.] it names **GOD** by this name alone, because it is the proper name of the true God. “**GOD IS GREAT**,” “**GOD IS GOOD**,” and “**WHAT GOD SHALL GIVE**” are on everyone’s lips. It also calls upon him as judge: “**GOD SEES**,” “**I COMMEND IT TO GOD**,” and “**GOD WILL REPAY ME**.” O testimony of the soul, Christian by nature! [Note: [Col. 0377C] **Christian by nature.** *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 1: “But I do not summon you, soul, when formed in the schools, trained in libraries, and belching forth wisdom acquired in the academies and Attic porticoes. I address you as simple, untrained, uncultivated, and ordinary, such as those possess who possess you alone,” etc.] Finally, in uttering these words it looks not toward the Capitol but toward heaven. For it knows the dwelling place of the living God; from him and from there it descended.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**ARGUMENT.—He shows that this God, not content with the knowledge of himself implanted in human beings, wished to teach them by word and writing when they went astray. Accordingly, he sent prophets overflowing with the divine Spirit, who were to teach his people about himself, his worship, and his power. Since this was the prerogative of the Jews, these things required the Hebrew language; but because the records had been translated into Greek at Ptolemy’s command, they could readily be consulted, flashing with such force of truth that anyone who read or heard them would be compelled even to believe.**

But so that we might approach both God himself and his ordinances and purposes more fully and more deeply, he added a written instrument, in case anyone should wish to inquire about God, to find him after inquiry, to believe after finding, and to serve after believing. [Col. 0378A] For from the beginning he sent forth into the world men worthy through righteousness and innocence to know and reveal God, men overflowing with the divine Spirit, so that they might proclaim that God is one, who founded the universe and fashioned the human being from the earth—for he is [Note: [Col. 0377B] Franeker edition: *non est* (“is not”).] the true Prometheus; that he ordered the age by fixed arrangements and conclusions of time; and thereafter that he displayed signs [Note: [Col. 0377C] **Thereafter that he displayed signs.** The passage has been variously handled by learned interpreters, as may be seen in Wouwerius, La Cerda, and others. Pamelius, the Leiden and Agobardinus manuscripts, Heraldus, and finally Rhenanus read: “Thereafter what signs of his judging majesty he displayed, first,” etc.; so too the Aldine, except that it has “of his indicating majesty.” Rigaltius more satisfactorily reads: “Thereafter that he displayed signs of his judging majesty.” Barraeus has “of his majesty to be vindicated,” which Wouwerius follows. The excellent Fulda manuscript reads: “of his majesty he displayed, by judging he displayed.” It is therefore evident that it intended the reading: “Thereafter that he displayed signs of his majesty by judging through rains,” etc. Perhaps one should read: “Thereafter that he displayed signs of his majesty to be vindicated, judging through rains,” etc. What he says here—“thereafter,” etc.—is what he calls in chapter XIX, and again shortly afterward, “the avenging force of the flood against the iniquity of that age.” HAV.] of his judging majesty through rains and fires; [Note: [Col. 0377D] **Through rains.** He refers to the judgment upon the first world and the punishment of Sodom. These two are joined in exactly the same way by Peter also, Second Epistle, II.5–6: καὶ ἀρχαίου κόσμου οὐκ ἐφείσατο, ἀλλ` ὄγδοον Νῶε δικαιοσύνης κήρυκα ἐφύλαξε, κατακλυσμὸν κόσμῳ ἀσεβῶν ἐπάξας (“and he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, as the eighth, bringing a flood upon the world of the ungodly”). Καὶ πόλεις Σοδόμων καὶ Γομόῤῥας τεφρώσας καταστροφῇ κατέκρινεν, ὑπόδειγμα μελλόντων ἀσεβεῖν τεθεικώς (“And, reducing the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes, he condemned them to destruction, making them an example for those who would thereafter act impiously”). HAV.] that he established teachings for earning his favor, which you either do not know or have abandoned; [Note: [Col. 0377D] **Which you either do not know or.** Rigaltius is entirely correct in reading thus. Others wrongly have “which you do not know and have abandoned,” or “which, being unknown or abandoned.” For the nations either did not know these teachings, such as the word of God delivered to his Jews, [Col. 0378C] or they abandoned them. I mean not only those teachings that they ought to have inferred from the creation of the world and the marvelous order of all things, as the Apostle Paul argues from this in Acts XVII.27, compared with XIV.16–17—a point Moses impresses upon Israel in book V, chapter 17.19, teaching the prerogative of those whom God had personally undertaken to instruct, while distributing heaven, sun, moon, and stars to the remaining peoples so that only after long wanderings might they attain a crude knowledge of some deity—but also, and this is what he chiefly has in view here, the teachings now offered to them through the indulgence of the New Testament. HAV.] and that he appointed rewards for those who observe them [Note: [Col. 0377B] Paris edition: *observationibus*.], as one who, when this age has been brought to its end [Note: [Col. 0377B] Franeker edition: *producto*.], will judge his worshippers for the recompense of eternal life, and the profane for equally perpetual and unceasing fire, after all who have died from the beginning have been raised, restored, and reviewed, [Note: [Col. 0378C] **Reviewed.** The Fulda manuscript has *recensis*. The expression that follows, *dispungere*, is taken from financial business and from ledgers of income and expenditure. Hence also the expression in Revelation III.5: μὴ ἐξαλείψω τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἑκ τῆς Βίβλου τῆς ζωῆς (“I will not erase his name from the Book of Life”; ἑκ is an anomalous recovered spelling). HAV.] for the settling [Col. 0378B] of the accounts of the deserts of both groups.

We too once laughed at these things. We were among your number; [Note: [Col. 0378C] **We were among your number.** Diogenes Laertius, on Diogenes the Cynic: When someone reproached him for once having counterfeited money, he said, Ἦν ποτε (“There was once”), χρόνος ἐκεῖνος (“that time”) [Col. 0378D] ὅτ` ἤμην ἐγὼ τοιοῦτος ὁποῖος σὺ νῦν· ὁποῖος δ` ἐγὼ νῦν, σὺ οὐδέποτε (“when I was such as you are now; but such as I am now, you will never be”), that is: “There was a time when I was such as you are now; but such as I am now, you will never be.” HAV.] Christians are made, not born. [Note: [Col. 0378D] **They are made, not born.** *On the Soul*, chapter 1: “For you are accustomed to be made, not born, Christian.” For it is not generation but regeneration that makes Christians, according to Augustine, book III, *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 9—differently, of course, from poets, who are born, not made. There exists a short commentary on this saying of Tertullian by Matthaeus Zimmermann, Leipzig, 1662, quarto. HAV.]

Those preachers whom we have mentioned [Note: [Col. 0378B] Junius: *dicimus* (“we mention”).] are called prophets from their office of foretelling [Note: [Col. 0378B] Paris edition: *prophetandi* (“of prophesying”).]. Their words, and likewise the mighty works [Note: [Col. 0378D] **Mighty works.** The interpreters understand this as referring to their conduct, whereas it indicates rather the miracles performed through them, which are everywhere called “mighty works” in Holy Scripture. Immediately afterward, for *ad fidem* (“for establishing faith”), the Aldine edition, Heraldus, and Rhenanus have *ad finem* (“to the end”). Wrongly. HAV.] which they performed to establish faith in the divine character of their message, remain in the treasuries of writings, and those writings are not now hidden.

The most learned of the Ptolemies, [Note: [Col. 0378D] **The most learned of the Ptolemies.** If this is the true reading, as all editions hitherto display it, he wishes to suggest that the entire Ptolemaic family was very devoted to study, just as the entire line of Caesars descending from Julius is also said to have been sufficiently well educated. And certainly Ptolemy son of Lagus, not only the founder of the empire, also committed to writing the deeds of his king and commander Alexander, from which Arrian testifies that he benefited; while, even when the royal name came to an end, the woman Cleopatra was vigorously trained in the knowledge of languages.

The Fulda manuscript, however, supplies another reading: “Ptolemy [whom they surname Philadelphus], a most learned king and of all,” etc. Thus Scioppius corrects its corrupt *rexit omni*. His teacher was the philosopher Strato, who was presented by him with eighty talents. Diogenes Laertius, *Life of Strato*. HAV.] whom they surname Philadelphus, [Col. 0379A] and the most acute investigator of all literature, [Note: [Col. 0379B] **The most acute investigator.** With this concluding description he adorns him truthfully, suggesting that, like a hunting dog, he searched every corner of the libraries that existed in Greece and elsewhere and carried off an enormous quarry from them. Athenaeus likewise says of him in book XII, p. 536: παιδείας, εἴ τις ἄλλος, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπιμεληθείς (“himself likewise devoted to learning, if anyone ever was”), that is, “most devoted to literature, if anyone ever was.” He also calls the same king, in the highest praise, πάντ` ἄριστον (“excellent in every respect”), that is, “excellent in every respect,” book V, chapter 5; and in book XII, πάντων σεμνότατον γινόμενον τῶν δυναστῶν (“becoming the most dignified of all rulers”), that is, “the most dignified of all rulers.” [Col. 0379C] Philo Judaeus, book II of the *Life of Moses*, proclaims that he was distinguished by royal virtues above all the rulers of his own age and of earlier centuries. HAV.] when in his zeal for libraries [Note: [Col. 0379C] **In his zeal for libraries.** His father, the son of Lagus, had begun to collect them at Alexandria. He was persuaded by Aristotle, or moved by his example, according to Strabo, book XIII: Ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης, πρῶτος ἂν ὣν ἴσμεν, συναγαγὼν βιβλία, καὶ διδάξας τοὺς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ Βασιλέας Βιβλιοθήκης σύνταξιν (“Aristotle was the first of those known to us to collect books, and he taught the kings in Egypt how to organize a library”; ἂν ὣν is anomalous in the recovered text), that is, “Aristotle was the first of all those known to us to assemble a library, and he taught the kings of Egypt to do so.” Diodorus Siculus, book II, chapter 49, commends the Egyptians’ zeal for libraries, just as it was eager for every kind of wisdom. There he relates that Osymandias, a most ancient king of the Egyptians, built a library in addition to his other monuments, and ordered the inscription ΨΥΧΗΣ ΙΑΤΡΕΙΟΝ (“THE MEDICAL WORKSHOP OF THE SOUL”) to be placed above its threshold—that is, as Lipsius translates it, **THE MEDICAL WORKSHOP OF THE SOUL**.

Both of the Ptolemies, the son of Lagus and Philadelphus—the former with Berenice and the latter with Arsinoë, his sister and wife—may be viewed on ancient gold coins published by Spanheim. He displays them in his outstanding book *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, pp. 406 and 404; before him, Seguin likewise displayed a third in *Selected Coins*, p. 47. But the illustrious Spanheim is mistaken in thinking that the inscription should be translated “of the Brother Gods.” For Tertullian says distinctly in a notable passage, book II of *To the Nations*, chapter 13: “You have now admitted Ops and Saturn, siblings joined in incest.” Immediately afterward the Agobardinus manuscript has *aemulatur*. HAV.] was emulating Pisistratus, I believe, he asked—among other records whose antiquity or curious interest afforded them some claim to fame—at the prompting [Note: [Col. 0379D] **At the prompting of Demetrius.** Josephus, and before him, unless I am mistaken, Aristeas, also state this in express words in the passages cited above. Vives, in his note on St Augustine’s *City of God*, adds that this Demetrius, having previously held the highest offices at Athens, was driven out by the envy of his fellow citizens, received by Ptolemy, and appointed keeper of the library. He took this from Diogenes Laertius’ *Life of Demetrius*, where he says that Demetrius also wrote a book entitled *Ptolemy* and another *On Rhetoric*. The latter perhaps [Col. 0380A] gave Tertullian occasion to call him the most highly esteemed grammarian of that time, although in the next chapter below he cites him as [Col. 0380B] a writer on antiquities. PAMEL.] of Demetrius of Phalerum, [Note: [Col. 0380B] **Demetrius of Phalerum.** On this distinguished man the Eusebian notes of Joseph Scaliger, greatest of scholars, p. 133, certainly deserve consultation. There Scaliger thinks that Tertullian spoke too meagerly of him under this designation, although in Tertullian’s time the word was held in the highest esteem and signified that noble critical learning by which we judge the writings of the ancients. Thus he spoke with the greatest propriety; hence Donatus, book II, explains *litteratum* (“a man of letters”).

Scaliger is more correct when he teaches that this opinion is false, because Demetrius was banished by Philadelphus as soon as the latter began to reign, since he had advised the king’s father to transfer the royal succession to a son born of another mother. Accordingly, in exile he died from the bite of an asp. He could, however, have rendered his service to the father, the son of Lagus, and an error could have arisen concerning the name.

Let the most elegant testimony of Muretus concerning this man stand for us in place of all others. In *Oration* XXIII he says: “The Athenian people had erected three hundred and sixty bronze statues to Demetrius [Col. 0380C] of Phalerum within one year, and not even a full year; Demetrius himself outlived them all. But the monuments that he had erected for himself through the greatness of his intellect and learning flourished for many centuries after him; and when afterward a certain dense and murky night had extinguished almost all the light of learning, they were taken from sight and left an incredible longing for themselves in the minds of all learned people.” HAV.] then the most highly esteemed of grammarians and the man to whom he had entrusted supervision of the library, for books [Note: [Col. 0380C] **He asked the Jews for BOOKS.** Josephus, book XII: τὰ τὴς Ἰουδαίων νομοθεσὶας βιβλὶα (“the books of the Jews’ legislation”; the recovered accents are anomalous). Thereafter he always calls these books Νὸμον (“the Law”; the recovered accent is anomalous), so that it appears that the Seventy brought nothing but the Pentateuch from them, or translated nothing else into Greek. Hilary likewise says in the prologue to the Psalms that King Ptolemy entrusted to seventy elders the task of translating the whole Law from Hebrew into Greek. But Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, reports that they translated into the Latin language: τὰς γραφὰς, τὰς τοῦ νόμου καὶ τὰς προφητικὰς (“the Scriptures, those of the Law and the prophetic writings”). Irenaeus [Col. 0380D] likewise relates that the Apostles, and afterward their followers, proclaimed all the prophetic writings just as the elders’ translation contains them. Yet Jerome observed that the Apostles cited certain things from the prophets that are not found in that translation of the Septuagint; concerning this there is a weighty complaint by that most learned man in his prefaces to the Pentateuch and his *Hebrew Traditions*. RIG.] from the Jews also: their own [Note: [Col. 0379A] Junius and Havercampus delete *scilicet* (“that is”).] native writings, which they alone possessed. For the prophets had always spoken from among them and to them—that is, to God’s household nation by the favor shown to its fathers. Formerly they were Hebrews, who are now Jews; therefore both their writings and their language were Hebrew.

But lest knowledge of them remain unavailable, this request of Ptolemy was also granted by the Jews: seventy-two translators were supplied, whom the philosopher Menedemus also, a defender of providence, [Note: [Col. 0380D] **A defender of providence.** He evidently perceived in these things the divine providence of God, because all the translators had agreed upon the same meaning. This certainly would not have been remarkable unless they had translated the same Scripture separately. The Seventy translators were therefore separated, as Irenaeus reports in book III, chapter 25. LAC.] regarded with wonder because of their agreement in meaning. Aristeas also confirmed these facts for you. Thus he left the records publicly available in Greek style. [Note: [Col. 0380A] Havercampus: *exaperto*; Scioppius conjectures *exaperta*.]

To this day they are displayed at the Serapeum, in Ptolemy’s library, [Note: [Col. 0380D] **To this day at the Serapeum.** This place is either the temple of Serapis mentioned by Theodoret, book V, chapter 22, or a place near both the temple of Serapis and Alexandria in which Ptolemy’s library was preserved. LE PR.] together with the Hebrew originals. [Note: [Col. 0380D] **The Hebrew originals.** From this it is evident that this monument was bilingual, although the Alexandrian Jews, and afterward others as well, were generally content with the Greek translation alone. Add Scaliger’s Eusebian note, p. 134 of the best edition. The Fulda manuscript deletes the word *litteris* (“writings”), with which I readily agree. The Leiden manuscript also deletes it, as does the Agobardinus, which additionally omits *cum ipsis* (“together with the originals”). HAV.] [Col. 0381A] [Note: [Col. 0381B] *Litteris* (“writings”) is absent from the Fulda manuscript.]

But the Jews also read them openly; [Note: [Col. 0381B] **But the Jews also read them openly.** Since the journey to the temple of Serapis in Egypt was long, he points out a nearer, public source convenient for everyone. From this it is evident that at Carthage also, and elsewhere, the Jews freely attended their synagogues upon payment of an annual tax. At Rome, certainly, and in Italy, I think that they were obliged to purchase the right of residence, since after Titus’ command each of them also paid δίδραχμον (“a two-drachma tax”) to Capitoline Jupiter. They were treated more harshly and severely by Domitian, and more gently by Nerva, as is shown by his coin inscribed **THE ABUSE OF THE JEWISH TAX REMOVED**, in the distinguished Patin’s *Treasury*, p. 155. HAV.] this taxed liberty [Note: [Col. 0381C] **Taxed liberty.** Aldus and Rigaltius correctly punctuate thus. Others read: “the taxed liberty is commonly approached [La Cerda: ‘the liberty of the common people’] on every Sabbath.” See the observations of Isaac Casaubon on Suetonius, *Domitian*, chapter 12. We add Juvenal, *Satire* III.13:

> Now the grove and shrines of the sacred spring are leased  
> To the Jews.

Thus Jeremiah could truly have uttered an almost similar lament in *Lamentations* V.4: “We drink our own water for payment, and our own wood comes to us at a price.” HAV.] is commonly accessible on every Sabbath. Whoever hears will find God; whoever also takes pains to understand will be compelled to believe as well.

## CHAPTER XIX
### Argument.—

He shows that the true knowledge of this God, handed down in writings, is older than all secular literature—indeed, older than all the pagans’ gods themselves, since they were only subsequently enrolled among the gods. For since Moses was approximately contemporary with Inachus himself, he therefore leaves Danaus, the Trojan War, Homer, and anything else reputed ancient far behind him. He sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, shows that, if he wished, he could confirm this from the chronologists.

Thus the highest antiquity vindicates for these documents [Note: “These” is absent from the Paris edition.] their primary authority [Note: *Vindicat*, Junius]. Among you [Col. 0382A] also, it is virtually a religious principle to establish credibility [Note: *Finem*, Fran.] by chronology.

(The material that follows, enclosed in brackets, was first published from the Fulda manuscript by Havercamp; but, attributing it to a second revision by the author, he arranged for it to be removed at the end of his edition.)

[Note: [Col. 0381C] This notable fragment belongs to the beginning of Chapter XIX; for immediately after the words “to establish credibility by chronology,” this entire passage, whatever its extent, is inserted in the excellent Fulda Codex, and in that manuscript alone; as we have often noted, it differs greatly in other places as well from the remaining [Col. 0381D] manuscripts. Francis Modius of Bruges, a man renowned for his learning and his zeal in seeking out ancient manuscripts everywhere, was the first to observe this after carefully collating that codex. Gaspar Scioppius, a man exceptionally learned in Latin, subsequently obtained that collation and shared it with Francis Junius, adding his own minor corrections here and there. But since Junius’ work—through which a much better text of this work of Tertullian might have emerged—had already been brought to completion, the entire collation was relegated to the end of the book. What one may rightly find astonishing, however, is that those who followed Junius—Heraldus, La Cerda, and even Rigaltius himself, all of whom rendered excellent service to our author—made absolutely no mention of this fragment; to say nothing of the Paris editors, who published this author for us so many times. I myself believe that all of this is certainly from Tertullian’s own hand, but that he polished and altered it in the second edition of his *Apology*, something we have also observed elsewhere in this little work, namely on pp. 293 and 313. Since it was in the interest of scholars that this material should both survive and be read, we have wished to reproduce it here. HAV. [Col. 0382B] There are some who deny that this fragment is genuine. Semler removed it from his edition. The author of a recent French translation of the *Apology*, D. Allard, supplies many words rather than arguments in rejecting it. For our part, since we regard it as a religious duty to preserve all fragments of ancient authors, even doubtful ones, we have taken this passage for publication from Leopold’s careful edition. EDD.]

[For Moses was the first [Note: [Col. 0382B] “For the first.” Not, to be sure, the first among those who foretold future events, but the first among those who, as he says elsewhere, defended in writing the renown of truth that would endure forever. Note that the Greek word *prophetes* is retained here. (The following notes are all by Havercamp.)] prophet. Beginning with the creation [Note: [Col. 0382C] “Creation.” He regularly uses this word for both creation and creature. *On the Soldier’s Crown*, Chapter VI: “You ask whether nature ought to precede us in enjoying His creation, lest we be swept away by that nature through which God’s rival corrupted the whole creation, assigned to human beings for certain uses, together with humanity itself.” Shortly afterward the manuscript incorrectly has *pullatione* for *pullulationem*.] of the world and the propagation of the human race, and then with the retrospectively described force of the flood that avenged the wickedness [Note: [Col. 0382C] “Avenged wickedness.” Chapter XXVIII: “judging by rains, by fires.”] of that age [Note: [Col. 0382C] “Retrospectively.” According to Homer, the mark of a true seer is to know present, future, and past alike. Thus, concerning Calchas, *Iliad* I.80:

Ὅς ἤδει τά τ` ἐόντα, τά τ` ἐσσόμενα πρό τ` ἐόντα (“Who knew the things that are, the things that will be, and the things that were before”).

Apollo combines these in himself in Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I, verse 17:

> Through me what shall be, what has been,  
> And what is, lies revealed.

And of Proteus in Virgil, *Georgics* IV, verse 392:

> [Col. 0382D] For the seer knows all things:  
> What is, what has been, and what the coming future draws along.

They also note that the tripod was dedicated to Phoebus for this reason: because he prophesies according to the three times—present, past, and future. Suidas under that word: Τρίπους, κατὰ τοῦς τρεῖς χρόνους μαντευόμενος, ἐνεστῶτα, παρεληλυθότα καὶ μέλλοντα (“Tripod: prophesying according to the three times—present, past, and future”). These three are therefore most fully united in Moses.], he produced, through prophecy extending down to his own age and afterward, images of future events by means of actual occurrences [Note: [Col. 0382D] “By means of actual occurrences.” I think this should be corrected to “most truthful.”]. In his writings the order of times, arranged from the beginning, also furnished a reckoning of the world’s age [Note: [Col. 0382D] “A reckoning of the world’s age.” Among the most ancient pagan authors it is impossible to ascend beyond Danaus and Agamemnon; the Greeks count by Olympiads and the Romans by years from the foundation of the City. Lucretius therefore prudently refutes belief in the eternity of the world in Book V, verse 327:

> Why, before the Theban war and Troy’s destruction,  
> Did other poets not also sing of other events?  
> Where have so many deeds of men so often perished? Why do they nowhere  
> Flourish, implanted in eternal monuments of fame?].

He is found to be approximately three hundred years older than the time when Danaus, considered your most ancient figure, crossed over to Argos [Note: [Col. 0382D] “Crossed over.” It seems that the reading should be: “crossed over, and.”]; [Col. 0383A] indeed, he precedes the Trojan War [Note: [Col. 0383B] “The Trojan War, indeed.” The manuscript here incorrectly has “us” for “you.”] by a thousand years, and consequently Saturn himself as well. For according to the history of Thallus [Note: [Col. 0383B] “Thallus.” A celebrated chronographer—would that we possessed his work! Tertullian mentions him twice more: in the middle of this Chapter XIX and above in Chapter X. But take care not to suppose that he composed a history of the Assyrian war, since that war merely had to be mentioned in his *Chronicle* and assigned to a definite period.], in which it is reported that the Assyrian war occurred and that Saturn, king [Note: [Col. 0383B] “King.” For after Jupiter had driven him from his kingdom and scepter, he attempted, with the aid of the Titans—of whom Thallus made him the leader—to recover his kingdom; defeated, he fled to Italy. [Col. 0383C] See the mythographers. The manuscript incorrectly has “kings.”] of the Titans, fought with Jupiter, it is shown that the war [Note: [Col. 0383C] “The war.” The word “that” appears to have dropped out, or “the war” should be changed to “that one,” so that it refers to Saturn himself.] preceded the destruction [Note: [Col. 0383C] “Destruction.” This must plainly be restored in place of the manuscript’s “departure.”] of Troy by 322 years.

Through this Moses, too, that Law peculiar to the Jews was sent by God. Afterward, many things [Note: [Col. 0383B] Havercamp, against the manuscript: “many men”; but it is more likely that some verb has dropped out.] [Note: [Col. 0383C] “Many things.” Perhaps “many men” would be better; or he means that, just as Moses foretold various future events, so the other prophets after him foreshadowed many similar things.] and other prophets were older than your literature. For even the one who prophesied last either slightly preceded or was at least contemporary with the founders of wisdom and even with lawgivers. Zechariah lived in the reigns of Cyrus and Darius. At that time Thales, the founder of natural philosophy, when questioned by Croesus [Note: [Col. 0383B] Manuscript: Cyrus.] [Note: [Col. 0383C] “Croesus.” The manuscript incorrectly has “Cyrus,” as Scioppius also observed.], gave no certain answer concerning the Divinity, plainly because he was confounded by the words of the prophets; and Solon declared to that same king that the end of a long life must be kept in view, in no other way than the prophet [Note: [Col. 0384B] Psalm 39:5.] [Note: [Col. 0383C] “Than the prophet.” He has in view David’s prayer in Psalm 39:5: “Lord, make known to me my end and what is the measure of my days, that I may know how frail I am.” He said “the prophet” by the same figure whereby, in Chapter XXI, he says “Proculus regularly,” although there was one prophet and one Proculus who said it.]. Thus it can be seen that both your laws and your intellectual pursuits were conceived from the Law [Note: [Col. 0383C] “Pursuits—from the Law.” He says both that the laws established for you and the method of the studies through which a man was regarded as wise [Col. 0383D] were borrowed from the divine writings. Our author therefore appears to affirm that Thales and Solon had at least some knowledge of these writings, since they apparently wished to investigate true virtue while despising worldly things and those that dazzle earthly eyes.] and from divine teaching.

Whatever comes first must necessarily be the seed [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Must be the seed.” Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 6: Φασὶ δὲ αὐτοὺς (“They say that they…”), etc.; that is: “They say that those philosophers in Egypt received the doctrine and knowledge of the true God not only from the Egyptians themselves, but also from Hebrew teachers.” The same author writes nearly the same thing about Plato and the other philosophers, p. 31 ff.]. Hence you possess certain things in common with us, or close to what we possess. From *sophia*, the love of it was called philosophy; from prophecy, the imitation of it [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Imitation of it.” Emulation, assimilation. “They affect truth, and by affecting it corrupt it.” Concerning the same men, Chapter XLVII.] appropriated poetic divination [Note: [Col. 0383D] “Assigned.” It appropriated it, but in the way a branch is violently torn from a tree and then withers when its sap fails; hence he shortly afterward says, “they adulterated it.” *Exhortation to Chastity*, Chapter VI: “There was an old arrangement, which is assigned a place in the new Gospel.”].

Men hungry for glory [Note: [Col. 0384B] “Men hungry for glory.” Philosophers especially, of whom Cicero elegantly says in *For Archias*, Chapter XXVI: “Those very philosophers inscribe their names even on those little books they write about despising glory: in the very work in which they despise public acclaim and fame, they wish themselves to be acclaimed and named.” Our author likewise says below, Chapter XLVII: “Philosophers theatrically affect truth, and by affecting it corrupt it, since they seek glory.” See there much more to the same effect.], if they had discovered anything, adulterated it in order to make it their own [Note: [Col. 0384BC] “To make it their own.” By adding, subtracting, and altering. [Col. 0384C] Horace, *Art of Poetry*, verse 47:

> You will have spoken excellently if a skillful combination  
> Has made a familiar word new.

But when this is done to truth and perfection itself, its nature is ruined.]; even fruits sometimes degenerate from their seed [Note: [Col. 0384C] “Sometimes.” Perhaps the present tense, “degenerate,” but I nevertheless alter nothing.].

I could still take my stand [Note: [Col. 0384C] “Take my stand.” The same form of expression occurs in Chapter IV: “Now I shall take my stand upon the cause of innocence,” and elsewhere. The sense is the same as if he had written, “I could still take my stand in many ways upon the antiquity of the divine writings,” if not, etc.] in many ways upon the antiquity of the divine writings, had they not possessed, for establishing belief, a greater authority arising from the power of their truth than from the annals of their age. For what will support their testimony more powerfully than the daily settlement of accounts [Note: [Col. 0384C] “Settlement of accounts.” He rather frequently uses this term, taken from account keeping. Chapter XVIII: “for the settlement of either desert”; *On the Testimony of the Soul*, Chapter IV: “We affirm that you remain after the settlement of life”; and *On the Soul*, Chapter XXXIII: “Although, if any judgment awaits souls, it ought to be believed more serious in the settlement of life than in its administration.” Add also our Index. The daily settlement of the whole age is therefore that state of the world and outcome of events which daily [Col. 0384D] fulfills the truth of prediction through the event itself, as he treats more fully in what follows.] of the entire age, when the arrangements [Note: [Col. 0384B] The codex has the singular: “with the arrangement of kingdoms,” etc.] of kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0384D] “Arrangement of kingdoms.” The corrupt passage must be emended thus: “than the daily settlement of the whole age? When the arrangements of kingdoms, when the falls of cities,” etc. For the arrangements of kingdoms are their changes and successions, which the disposer of kingdoms and King of kings freely orders: “Until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of men and gives them to whomever He wishes.” These are Daniel’s threats to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4:24. “The emperors themselves know who gave them their empire,” below, Chapter XXX.], when the falls of cities, when the extinctions of peoples, and when the conditions of the times correspond in every respect to what was foretold thousands of years [Note: [Col. 0384D] “Thousands of years.” Note the expression, like “the steep places of mountains” in Apuleius and countless others in other authors.] ago?

From this our hope, which you ridicule, is given life, and our confidence, which you call presumption [Note: [Col. 0384D] “Presumption.” Because Christianity is believed to be some sect resting on human opinion, which he discusses in Chapter XLVI.], is strengthened. [Col. 0384B] For the verification of past events is sufficient [Note: [Col. 0384D] “Is sufficient.” That is, we already see so many things fulfilled which God foretold through the prophecies; therefore those that remain will also receive their fulfillment.] to establish confidence in future events: the same voices [Note: [Col. 0385B] “Voices.” Living voices; and, he adds, the things they said did not pass away, but were also committed to writing.] foretold both parts [Note: [Col. 0385B] “Both parts.” Both what has already been fulfilled and what will yet be fulfilled.], and the same writings recorded them. In their perspective there is a single time [Note: [Col. 0385B] “There is a single time.” Understand it thus: what comes before us separately and over different expanses of time, the Holy Spirit represented to the prophets in a single view and act. Indeed, just as present and future differ in no respect within God’s knowledge, neither do they differ for those inspired and illuminated by God.], though to us it appears divided. Thus everything that remains unproved [Note: [Col. 0385B] Scioppius: “already proved”; Havercamp: “are in the proved”; but I determine that the reading should be: “what remains unproved has been proved for us,” etc.] has been proved [Note: [Col. 0385C] “Has been unproved.” This is plainly corrupt, and Scioppius therefore corrected it to “has already been proved.” But it would accord better with Septimius’ thought and the traces of the letters if one read “are in the proved,” that is, “are easily proved.” His point is to show that future time appeared to the prophets as though it were a single present time. For us, however, it is divided, since we can prove only one part from its occurrence, while the part that is to be proved from future events remains. Thus, he says, both what has already been fulfilled and what remains to be fulfilled had to be regarded as future at the time of the prediction itself, since nothing had then yet been fulfilled. Since events have corresponded to the former part, we therefore also have the certainty of future events ready to hand and established.] for us, because it was foretold, together with the things that have been proved, when both were still future.

You possess, so far as I know [Note: [Col. 0385C] “You possess, so far as I know.” This entire passage is extraordinarily corrupt and admits of no sound sense; indeed, it requires correction in four places. I restore it thus: “We too, so far as I know, have a Sibyl, insofar as this appellation has been established by usage for a true prophetess of the true God, everywhere above the other women who appeared to prophesy. Your sibyls know that they falsely assumed their name from truth, just as your gods did.” Thus above, Chapter V: “Marcus Aemilius knows about his god Alburnus.” He means the Chaldaean or Erythraean Sibyl, whom Lactantius and other Fathers frequently praise, being easily deceived by excessive credulity. On the Sibyls one may consult, besides Suidas, Johann Albert Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. I, p. 167; Petit, van Dale, and others. Semler also testifies in the *Bibliotheca Gesneriana* that fourteen books of the Sibyl are kept in Rome in the Vatican Library, perhaps different from the rhapsody we possess. A volume is mentioned there under this title: Ἐκ τῶν προφητικῶν, Σιβύλλης λόγος θ (“From the prophetic writings: the Sibyl’s ninth discourse”). μέχρι τοῦ Ιέ (“through the fifteenth”). There is also a discourse on the Sibyls by the most humane and learned Jensius. The Fulda Codex now continues thus: “All substances, therefore,” etc., which may be seen in Chapter XIX.], and you too, a Sibyl, insofar as the designation was everywhere applied in this way to a true prophetess of the true God above the others who seemed to prophesy—just as your Sibyls falsely took their name from truth, in the same way as your gods [Note: [Col. 0385B] The manuscript reads: “You possess, so far as I know, and we too a Sibyl, insofar as this appellation—of our God.” Havercamp restores the passage thus: “We too, so far as I know, have a Sibyl, insofar as this appellation has been established by usage for a true prophetess of the true God, everywhere above the other women who appeared to prophesy. Your [Col. 0386B] sibyls know that they falsely assumed their name from truth, just as your gods did.”].]

Thus all the substances, all the materials, origins, [Col. 0386A] orders, and sources of each of your ancient literary traditions; most nations as well, and distinguished cities; the hoary records of histories [Note: [Col. 0386B] Rhenanus and Gangnaeus: “histories and causes of remembrances,” etc.; Aldus: “the histories and causes, the hoary records themselves and remembrances”; Heraldus: “the causes of histories and remembrances”; Fulda Codex: “the histories and hidden things of remembrances”; Put. and Lugd. Codices: “the histories and hoary records of remembrances.”] and of remembrances; finally, even the representations [Note: [Col. 0385D] “Representations of letters, signs.” He means not only the invention of letters, which that clever Cadmus brought from [Col. 0386B] Phoenicia into Greece—a people to whom settled opinion ascribes the credit for it. Hence Lucan, Book III, 220:

> The Phoenicians first, if tradition may be believed, dared  
> To mark with crude figures the voice that would endure.

Plutarch, in his book *On the Genius of Socrates*, relates that letters of this kind were found in Alcmena’s tomb, most ancient characters which he calls τοὺς τύπους (“the characters”), or forms of that writing which Hercules learned while Proteus was reigning. But they also used letters by means of carved and figured animals to express the mind’s meaning. Porphyry, also called Malchus, in the *Life of Pythagoras*, p. 15 of the new edition, reports that Pythagoras learned the language of the Egyptians thoroughly, and that their writing was of three kinds: epistolary, hieroglyphic, and symbolic. Τῶν μὲν κοινολογουμένων κατὰ μίμησιν, τῶν δὲ ἀλληγορουμένων κατά τινας αἰνιγμούς (“Some conveying ordinary speech by imitation, and others expressing it allegorically through certain riddles”), that is: “The first of these imitates their proper and common manner of speech; the others express meaning through allegories, beneath certain coverings of riddles.” Again Lucan:

> Memphis did not yet know how to weave papyrus from the river;  
> Only upon stones did birds, wild beasts,  
> And carved animals preserve magical languages.

“They preserved”—and hence our author calls them “guardians of things.” They were called hieroglyphics, on which Horus composed a special little book, elucidated by Johann Mercer and others. In this field the diligence of Lorenzo [Col. 0386D] Pignoria stands out above all others. HAV.] of letters, the signs and guardians of things—and I think I am still saying too little—even your gods themselves, the temples themselves, the oracles, and the sacred rites: the archive [Note: [Col. 0386D] “Archive.” La Cerda shows that Prudentius also used the word in this way. The reading in Persius, *Satire* I, verse 106, is inept and tasteless:

> Nor does it strike the bookcase, nor taste bitten nails.

Horace himself uses the word, as our author does, for writing, *Satires* I.1.120:

> Lest you suppose that I have plundered  
> Blear-eyed Crispinus’ archives, I shall add not another word.

The Agobardine Codex reads: “within, meanwhile, the prophet’s archive conquers the ages.” HAV.] of a single prophet, I say, surpasses them all in age. In it appears to have been stored the treasure of the entire Jewish mystery, and therefore [Note: Variant: “therefore.”] of ours as well.

If in the meantime you have heard of Moses, he is contemporary with Inachus of Argos; by almost four hundred [Note: [Col. 0386D] “Four hundred.” Thus also the Fulda Codex, writing the number out in words, though elsewhere it uses “CCCC,” and connecting this without punctuation to the preceding words. Aldus reads: “almost eight hundred years before the City was founded, he preceded Danaus, himself considered your most ancient figure, by 170 years.” This is certainly not absurd. For however one begins the computation, Moses and Danaus cannot be four hundred years apart. And he appropriately mentions the very ancient city of Rome. Therefore, since Moses himself did not live in the age of Inachus, but somewhat later, as is established, I punctuate the Fulda Codex thus: “He is contemporary with Inachus of Argos by almost four hundred years.” Then, with the Aldine edition: “Eight hundred years before the City was founded. By 170 years he preceded Danaus,” etc. For Inachus founded the Argive kingdom about the year 2093; Moses was born [Col. 0387C] in 2373 and led Israel out of Egypt in 2450. HAV.] years—for seven years are lacking—he preceded Danaus, himself [Col. 0387A] considered your most ancient figure [Note: [Col. 0387B] Rhenanus, Gangnaeus, and Aldus: “If indeed you have heard of Moses, he is contemporary with Inachus of Argos” (“is contemporary,” Franek), “almost eight hundred years before the City was founded; for he precedes Danaus, himself considered your most ancient figure, by 170 years, and the destruction of Priam by approximately three hundred years.”]; he precedes the destruction of Priam by approximately a thousand [Note: [Col. 0387B] “Three hundred,” variant.] [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Approximately a thousand.” Aldus: “approximately three hundred,” which agrees better with the chronologists, since the event occurred in the year 2767. HAV.] years. I could even say that he preceded Homer by more than five hundred [Note: [Col. 0387C] “I could even say, by five hundred.” The Fulda Codex has “could even say.” Aldus deletes the word “more.” In the same way Theodoret, among others, argues. In *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, Discourse II, p. 29: Εἰ τοίνυν τούτων μὲν (“If, therefore, of these…”), etc.; that is: “Since, therefore, as Porphyry says, Moses is a thousand years older than these poets—Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, Thamyris, and Philammon—and these are the most ancient of the poets (for after them Homer and Hesiod were born, who preceded Thales and the other philosophers by many spans of years), and since Thales and Thales’ hearers are older than the philosophers who followed, why, I ask, do we not leave all these behind and pass over to Moses, the ocean of theology, from whom, to speak poetically, all rivers and all seas are derived?” You see here the same mention [Col. 0387D] of Thales as above in the fragment. HAV.] years, and I have authorities whom I could follow.

The other prophets too, although later than Moses [Note: [Col. 0388B] “Even if,” Paris.], are nevertheless found to be, even the very last among them, no less ancient [Note: [Col. 0387D] “No less ancient.” Meursius: “no farther backward.” For the ancients used *retrorsus, -a, -um*, whence the neuter substantive—as grammarians call it—used adverbially, *retrorsum*, remained in use; just as ἀπὸ τοῦ (“from the word”), *prorsus, -a, -um*, produced *prorsum*. So he says. But they also used *prosum*, ἀντὶ τοῦ (“in place of”), for *prorsum*. Thus *retrosum* could likewise be used for *retrorsum*. Varro, indeed, said *prosis lectis*. Scriverius wrote this in the margin of my book. Yet with Junius and La Cerda I would prefer to derive it from *retro*, which occurs frequently in our author, so that he also derived his comparative *retrosior* from it: one who is farther back, that is, older or more ancient. I therefore leave it for consideration whether the negative τὸ (the Greek article marking the following *non* as a quoted word) should not rather be deleted, contrary to Junius, La Cerda, and Rhenanus. He would then be saying, not that the latest of the prophets were no later than their sages and lawgivers, but that they were in fact older. Above, in the fragment at the beginning of this chapter: “Afterward, many things and other prophets, older than your literature. For even the one who prophesied last,” etc. Those who are called “older” there are here called “farther back.” HAV.] than the earliest of your sages, lawgivers, and historians.

It is not so difficult for us to explain the chronological sequences by which these facts can be proved as it is immense; not arduous, but for the present lengthy. One must sit down with many documents, employing the counting gestures of the fingers. The archives of even the most ancient peoples—the Egyptians, Chaldaeans, and Phoenicians—must be opened. Their own countrymen, through whom knowledge has been supplied, must also be summoned as witnesses: such as [Note: [Col. 0388B] “Otherwise,” Junius from the manuscript.] Manetho the Egyptian and Berossus the Chaldaean, as well as Iromus [Note: [Col. 0388B] “Iromus.” Joseph Scaliger, the foremost scholar of all literature, showed in the prolegomena to his book *On the Emendation of Time*, p. 38, and in the fragments appended to the same work, p. 26, how this should be read, namely “Hieromus.” He is the same Hiram mentioned in Sacred History—for he too was called Εἰραμος (*Eiramos*) by a certain ancient writer—2 Chronicles 2:3, a man eminently worthy of the friendship of David and Solomon, to whom he appears to have been dear no less for his wealth than for his devotion to wisdom; he also bore witness to his learning for posterity in writings. HAV.—“Iromus the Phoenician.” In the fragments of Menander of Ephesus published by Scaliger, where the kings of Tyre are discussed: Τελευτήσαντος δὲ Ἀβιβὲνου διεδὲξατο βασιλείαν ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ Εἴρωμος (“When Abibenus died, his son Eiromus succeeded to the kingdom”). RIG.] [Col. 0387B] the Phoenician, king of Tyre [Note: “Hieronymus,” Fran.]; and their followers as well: Ptolemy of Mendes, Menander of Ephesus, Demetrius of Phalerum, King Juba, Apion, and Thallus; [Col. 0388A] and the Jewish Josephus, the native defender [Note: [Col. 0388B] “And Apion and Thallus, and—if anyone proves or refutes them—the Jew,” Junius from the manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0388C] “Native defender.” Take care not to think of the author of the *Josippon*. Tertullian calls Josephus a native defender—or, as Scaliger and the Fulda Codex have it, Josippus—because he, being a Jew himself, described the origins of his fellow Jews and their wars with the Romans, although he wrote in Greek. Scaliger shows, in his notes on Eusebius, p. 186, that Jerome imitated this usage: “Josephus, however, a native writer”; and Paula and Eustochium to Marcella in Jerome: “Finally, even Jophus, who is a native writer”; and again Paula and Eustochium to Marcella in Jerome: “Finally, even Josephus, [Col. 0388D] who is a native writer of the Jews.” Concerning the Jews’ document, see above, Chapter XVIII: “their own, that is, their native documents.” Thus the Trojan race is called native to the goddess Cybele in Chapter XXV. The Greeks said οἰκεῖον (“one’s own” or “native”). Concerning the celebrated sophist Prohaeresius, Eunapius of Sardis, p. 109, says: Προαιρεσίῳ δὲ ὁ Πόντος ὅλος καὶ τὰ ἐκείνῳ πρόσοικα τοὺς ὁμιλητὰς ἀνέπεμπον, ὥσπερ οἰκεῖον ἀγαθὸν τὸν ἄνδρα θαυμάζοντες (“The whole of Pontus and the regions neighboring it sent pupils to Prohaeresius, admiring the man as a worthy native”), that is: “The whole of Pontus and the neighboring peoples sent pupils to Prohaeresius, admiring the man as a worthy native.” Junius correctly adds in his translation, “and as one born among themselves.” Our author again, in Chapter XXXV, calls the Romans “the native populace of the seven hills.” The Agobardine Codex gives the passage thus: “and if anyone approves them,” etc.; but this was afterward corrected to “disapproves.” HAV.] of Jewish antiquities, who either confirms or refutes those authors.

The official record-keepers [Note: [Col. 0388D] “Official record-keepers.” He appears to mean those who compiled diaries, annals, and public records, whom he designates by a term from his own age, as the commentators note. HAV.] of the Greeks must also be consulted, as must the records of which events occurred when, so that the chronological chains may be disclosed through which the numbers in the annals become clear. One must travel through the histories and literatures of the world.

And yet we have already introduced what is virtually a portion [Note: “Father,” Junius.] of the proof, since we have indicated the means by which it can be proved. But it is better to postpone the matter, lest in our haste we pursue it less fully, or in pursuing it wander too far afield.

### Chapter XX

[Note: [Col. 0388] This note appears at the foot of columns 389 and 390, but the callout letter, (b), has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0389C] “Most of the numerous creatures of the mountains.” He means the wild beasts numerous in the mountains and inhabiting them, such as lions, bears, and so forth, as Wouwer and Rigaltius correctly understand it. For Africa had always abounded in wild beasts, so much so that Strabo, Book II, says that the Numidians were οὐ δυναμένους γεουργεῖν, διὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν θηρίων τὸ παλαιόν (“unable in ancient times to cultivate the land because of the multitude of wild beasts”), “in ancient times unable to cultivate the land because of the multitude of wild beasts.” Those regions became still more deserted through the continual shocks of war; the wild beasts consequently multiplied and wrought widespread destruction. Other editions have different readings: the Gelenian, “most of the numerous things are dead”; the Aldine, “generally of populous mountains”; Barraeus, “generally of seething mountains”; so too Rhenanus in his second edition, though in the first he printed “of populous mountains.” If that reading seems plausible to anyone, I would prefer to correct it thus: “and generally the seethings of mountains.” Certainly in Chapter XL, where he treats all these matters more fully: “But neither Etruria nor Campania was then complaining about the Christians, when fire poured down upon Volsinii from heaven and upon Pompeii from its own mountain.” Accordingly, I myself do not strongly oppose this reading; but my reason for preferring the other is that in the conclusion he says, “They were written down by providence.” He thus intimates that all those events which occur today, and which he now enumerates, were foretold beforehand in the sacred writings. But where are we to look for burning mountains belching out God’s avenging flame? Certainly not in Revelation 8:8, where that great mountain burning with fire is cast into the sea; nor in Psalm 83:15: “As fire burns the wilderness, and as flame sets the mountains ablaze.” For the passage there concerns trees which, shaken by the wind on mountains, sometimes catch fire. Lucretius is a witness, Book I, 896:

> But often, you say, it happens on great mountains that the neighboring tops  
> Of lofty trees rub against one another,  
> When strong south winds compel them to do so,  
> Until they flash, with a flower of flame arisen.

The same author, Book V, 1095:

> And yet, when struck by the winds, one branching tree sways  
> [Col. 0390A] And surges, leaning into the branches of another tree.  
> Fire is struck out by the mighty force of their rubbing,  
> And sometimes the fervent heat of flame flashes forth.

[Col. 0390B] Thucydides, who is older than Lucretius, likewise says in Book II: Ἤδη γὰρ ἐν ὄρεσιν ὓλη τριφθεῖσα ὑπ` ἀνέμων πρὸς αὐτὴν ἀπὸ ταὐτομὰτου πῦρ καὶ φλόγα ὑπ` αὐτοῦ ἀνῆκε (“For before now, a forest on the mountains, rubbed against itself by the winds, spontaneously sent up fire and flame from itself”), that is: “For before now, when a forest on the mountains was rubbed together by the winds, it spontaneously sent fire and flame upward from itself.” Both Lambinus there and Casaubon cite this passage in their notes on Suetonius’ *Tiberius*, Chapter VI, where Tiberius, traveling by night, encounters mortal danger: a flame suddenly arose everywhere from the woods and so completely surrounded his whole retinue that part of Livia’s clothing and hair was scorched.

There is also the passage in Isaiah 34:9, though it concerns the land of Canaan: “Their land shall be turned into burning pitch.” Likewise Deuteronomy 32:22: “A fire is kindled in my anger and shall burn to the lowest depths of hell; it shall devour the earth with its produce and set fire to the foundations of the mountains.” Here, indeed, the expressions are taken from burning mountains; but they concern the land of Canaan, which Strabo and other writers teach is now as though scorched by barrenness. Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, Book VI, Chapter [Col. 0390C] 7, notes the following on the words of Psalm 107:34: Ἃ καὶ νοήσεις ἀναδραμὼν (“These things you too will understand if you retrace…”), etc.; that is: “You will certainly have full knowledge of these things if you traverse that Jerusalem of the Jewish nation which was renowned in ancient times, together with its glory and the produce of its divine harvest—that is, those holy men and friends of God who lived in it—which you will now find deprived and stripped of all these things. For after Christ’s advent it truly became fruitless, without water, and wholly deserted, and, as the prophet says, turned into salt land because of the wickedness of those who inhabited it.”

Unless perhaps the author has in view Jeremiah’s threat against Babylon in Chapter 51:25: “I shall make you a mountain of fire,” that is, “I shall turn you into a burning mountain.” But I have no doubt that the author had in view Ezekiel 5:17. All these things are enumerated there; and although they properly concern the Jews, no more striking passage was readily available in which God’s manifold vengeance through His plagues against any enemies of His name could be expressed. The Fulda and Agobardine manuscripts [Col. 0390D] and the editions of Heraldus and Pamelius prefer “the frequency, for the most part, of deaths,” but in vain, since individual calamities are being enumerated here, such as famine, pestilence, wild beasts, and so forth. HAV.]

### Argument.—

Leaving aside antiquity, which can be subject to error, he shows the divinity of Sacred Scripture from its confirmation by the outcome of events. For whatever happens is found to have already been foretold in it, so that it is therefore necessary to believe the things that still remain in the future, since they too are contained and foretold in it.

We now offer more in compensation for that postponement: the majesty [Col. 0389A] of the Scriptures, if not their antiquity [Note: “By antiquity,” Paris.]. We prove them divine, if their ancientness [Note: “Antiquity,” Paris.] is doubted. Nor [Note: “Not,” Paris.] must this be learned more slowly or from some other source. The things that will teach it are before your eyes: the world, the age, and events. Whatever is happening was foretold; whatever is seen was once heard.

That the earth swallows cities; that seas deprive islands of their land; that foreign and civil wars tear apart; [Col. 0390A] that kingdoms clash against kingdoms; that famines, pestilences, and all manner of local disasters [Note: [Col. 0389A] “All manner of local disasters.” I think he means regions of such a kind that, notorious for the harshness of their air and marshes, [Col. 0389B] they carry off many mortals, especially those unaccustomed to those lands.

> What quarter of the world, what mists and malignant  
> Jupiter oppress,

in the words of Horace, *Odes* I.22. Martial says:

> In the midst of Tibur is Sardinia,

showing that death can be found even in the most healthful places, for:

> Human beings are always at the same distance from death,

according to Publilius, verse 1. Nor did Lucretius, that most eloquent investigator of nature, neglect this. After showing that places with pestilential air are hostile to birds and quadrupeds, he teaches that the same holds true for human beings, Book VI, verse 769:

> First I say this, which I have often said before as well:  
> That within the earth there are forms of things of every kind—  
> Many that are life-giving to human beings, and many diseases …]

To inflict, and which can also hasten death.

[Col. 0389C] Earthquakes, eruptions of mountains, inundations of rivers, and the like may also be understood. HAV.] and that repeated disturbances devastate most mountain regions [text uncertain] [Note: [Col. 0389A] Rhenanus, in ed. I: *frequentium* (in ed. II, and Barraeus: [Col. 0390A] *efferventium*) *plerumque montium*; Heraldus and the Lyon codex: *frequentiae plerumque mortium*; Gelenius: *frequentiae pleraeque mortuae*; Gangnaeus: *Frequentiae plerumque montium*; Wouwer, Rigaltius, and Havercamp: *frequentiae pleraque montium*.]; that the lowly are changed into the exalted, and the exalted into the lowly; that justice grows scarce, injustice more frequent, and concern for every good discipline becomes sluggish; that even the functions of the seasons [Note: [Col. 0390D] **The functions of the seasons.** Since neither spring, summer, nor autumn adequately performs its function in producing crops, which formerly used to turn out more abundantly, while either excessive rains or the heat of the sun injure them. Tertullian speaks of God in *On Patience*, ch. II: “who permits the functions of the seasons, the services of the elements, and the dues of the whole creation to fall alike to the worthy and the unworthy.” There is a notable passage in Flavius Vegetius, book I of *On Military Matters*. There he discusses the destruction of the world and writes, among other things:

“To speak of Italy, very many parts of it which were once inhabited by extremely numerous peoples now appear almost deserted. Likewise, very many places which in the time of the ancient Romans were inhabited by very few people have been so transformed that nothing could surpass them. There can be no doubt that this has also occurred in every other part of the world. Accordingly, if in our times we see that the air which was once exceedingly wholesome has commonly become [Col. 0391B] pestilential, why should we not affirm that many regions long celebrated for military glory have degenerated in human courage because of an altered condition of the air, which derives its quality from the state of the heavens?”

Lucretius ascribes the cause of this [Col. 0391C] to the declining age, when he wishes the earth to be regarded as a parent who has, as it were, exhausted her fertility. His verses are in book II, line 1149:

> And now the age is so enfeebled, and the earth exhausted,  
> That she scarcely creates small creatures—she who created  
> All generations and gave birth to the huge bodies of beasts.

Read thus with the Voss manuscripts in the Leiden Library. Sallust likewise speaks in precisely this manner in *Catiline*, ch. LIII, concerning the Roman Republic: “And as though the stock of parents had become exhausted, for many generations scarcely anyone at Rome was truly great in virtue.” The same Lucretius, after introducing the farmer’s complaints at line 1170, concludes thus:

> Nor does he grasp that all things gradually waste away and go  
> Toward the tomb, worn out by the long passage of age.

And here, following the elegant correction in those manuscripts, write *ad capulum*, that is, “toward burial.” HAV.] [Col. 0391A] and the duties of the elements depart from their courses [Note: [Col. 0391C] **Depart from their courses.** Barraeus and Aldus: *exorbitantur*. Prosper of Aquitaine beautifully sketched all these things in his book of [Col. 0391D] epigrams:

> The fields no longer have the same condition, nor do any cities;  
> All things rush headlong toward their end.  
> By sword, plague, famine, chains, cold, and heat,  
> Death, though one, snatches wretched mortals in a thousand ways.  
> Wars roar on every side; human fury stirs them up;  
> Kings fall with arms upon innumerable kings.  
> Impious discord rages throughout a world in confusion;  
> Peace has departed from the earth: you see the final things. HAV.];

that the form of nature is disturbed by monsters and prodigies—all these things were written providentially [Note: [Col. 0391B] Semler: *providentiae*, “of providence.”]. While we suffer them, they are read; while we recognize them, they are proved. The truth of prophecy is, I think, adequate testimony of divinity [Note: [Col. 0391B] Paris: *veritatem*, “truth.”]. Hence among us confidence in future events is also secure, since they have already been proved: for they were foretold together with those things which are proved daily. The same [Note: [Col. 0391B] *Eaedem eadem*. Junius.] voices resound, the same writings signify, the same Spirit impels. For prophecy, which foretells the future among human beings, there is only one time—if perhaps it is distinguished only as it is erased, when from future it is reckoned present [Note: [Col. 0391B] Paris: *futura*, “future things.”], and then from present, past. What fault do we commit, I ask you, by believing future events also, when we have already learned to believe those same events through two stages?

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 0391] This note appears at the foot of column 392, but the callout number, (8), has not been printed in the text.] [Note: [Col. 0392B] Havercamp: *Ut quos*.]

[Col. 0391B] **ARGUMENT.—In this remarkable chapter a most complete history of Christ, the Son of God, is presented; he is described extensively and forcefully, insofar as he ought to be known for the salvation of souls. Meanwhile it is shown what befell the Jews when they refused to recognize in him [Col. 0392A] the fulfillment of the divine Word. Once his divinity has been perceived, it is surely proper to renounce false religion, since he sometimes exacts testimony to his power even from the malignant spirits whom he commands.**

21. But since we have stated that this sect is supported by the most ancient records of the Jews, although most people know it to be somewhat recent [Note: [Col. 0391D] **Somewhat recent.** Another reading, found in the Fulda codex, gives a different sense to this passage. It reads *quam scient aliquando*, “which they will someday know,” referring this to the Jews. I think it more likely that, because of the following *sciunt*, that word was duplicated here. According to the Fulda manuscript, the alternative sense that seems to disclose itself here is this: those very Jews will someday know this sect—that is, will understand and approve it, casting themselves into our camp in accordance with Hosea 3:5—when they know and recognize him, Jeremiah 31:34, crying: “My God, we, your Israel, know you,” Hosea 8:2. Others read differently: Barraeus, Aldus, Heraldus, and Rhenanus, *quam aliquando novellam*; La Cerda, *quam aliquanto novellam*, as do the Leiden manuscript, Agobardinus, Pamelius, and Rigaltius. HAV.], as belonging to the time of Tiberius [Note: [Col. 0392C] **Belonging to the time of Tiberius.** Thus clearly the Agobardinus and Leiden manuscripts; likewise Pamelius, Rigaltius, and Rhenanus, who, since they do not place punctuation after *temporis*, seem to understand this as referring to writers of the time of Tiberius, which is false here. For he says that most people know that the entrance of this new sect into the world occurred in the time of Tiberius, and therefore might perhaps suppose that this novel presumption wished to hide behind that ancient and firmly established Jewish religion, as behind the shield of some Ajax. Others read *ut Tiberii temporibus*, “as in the times of Tiberius”; since that makes no sense, *ortam*, “arisen,” was added in the Fulda codex: *ut Tiberianis temporibus ortam*, “as having arisen in the time of Tiberius.” In Rigaltius’ Priorian edition the last form is corruptly printed *Tiberini*. Above, ch. V: “Tiberius, therefore, in whose time the Christian name entered the world.” HAV.], as we ourselves also acknowledge [Note: [Col. 0392B] Franciscus: *vobis*, “you.”] [Note: [Col. 0392C] **As we ourselves also acknowledge.** Thus Rigaltius, Aldus, and Junius. Others have *vobis*, “you,” as Pamelius does, which is corrupt; for we readily concede to the Jews and Gentiles that it is a new sect, yet one supported by the most ancient records even of the Jews themselves—a sect which does not abolish [Col. 0392D] the discipline pleasing to God, but illuminates and reforms it. La Cerda: *nostris*, “our people.”], perhaps its standing is disparaged on this account [Note: [Col. 0392D] **Is disparaged.** When he says that its standing is *retractari*, I think the word intimates the malice and envy with which they judged religion. For *retractare* indeed commonly means in our author “to treat and examine carefully”; but since one whose own eyes are inflamed is unwilling to look fairly upon the uprightness of others, and therefore carefully searches for material for disparagement wherever he may be able to kindle the torch of envy and abuse, I take it here in the sense of “to carp at.” He uses it in much the same way, certainly in a bad sense, in *On Fasting*, ch. XV: “Yet in writing to the Romans he now pricks you, the *retractatores* of this duty”; that is, its detractors, the disobedient, its mockers. HAV.], as though, beneath the shelter of a most distinguished and certainly lawful religion [Note: [Col. 0392B] Franciscus: *certe licentiae*, “certainly of license.”], it were concealing something of its own presumption. Or is it because, apart from its age, we share with the Jews neither restrictions concerning food, nor observances of days, nor the very mark upon the body, nor fellowship in name—as surely we ought to do if we were bound in service to the same [Col. 0392B] God?

But even the common people now know Christ as, of course, some human being, such as the Jews judged him to be; and so someone might all the more readily suppose us to be worshipers of a human being [Note: [Col. 0392B] Others, Junius: *Qui—existimaverint*.] [Note: [Col. 0392D] **Someone might suppose us.** The Aldine copy has: *qui nos h. c. existimaverint*. The true sense is that human intelligence ought at least to have been granted enough reason that, if people wished to fabricate and falsely devise something consistent with and resembling a truth, they would at least have fashioned the God of the Christians in human form, not in a bestial and monstrous one, as they had done with the donkey-hoofed god [*Onochoites*], [Col. 0393B] of whom he spoke a little above—as though some hybrid from the race of Centaurs, Chimaeras, and Sphinxes were worshiped by us. In this they would surely have acted as the Jews did long ago, who thought that God himself, our Jesus, was nothing but a mere man; and as those among the Gentiles also certainly acted who accused Christians of worshiping a crucified man. HAV.].

Yet we are not ashamed of Christ, since it is our delight to be reckoned and condemned under his name; nor do we hold a different conviction concerning God. It is therefore necessary that we say a few things [Note: [Col. 0393B] We have accepted the word *dicamus*, “let us say,” on the authority of the Fulda codex.] about Christ as God [Note: [Col. 0393B] Franciscus: *Ut de Deo totum*, “entirely as concerning God.”].

The Jews possessed such great favor with God because of the remarkable righteousness and faith [Note: [Col. 0393B] Rigaltius and Havercamp: “because of the remarkable righteousness and faith,” etc.] of their original founders; from this the greatness of their nation and the loftiness of their kingdom flourished [Note: [Col. 0393B] **The loftiness of their kingdom flourished.** Similar are these words of Justin the historian, though proceeding from one in error: “And ever afterward this was the custom among the Jews, that the same men were both kings and priests; through the mingling of righteousness with religion, they grew strong to an incredible degree.” Likewise Strabo, book XVI: “The successors continued for some time in the same ways, acting justly and being truly devout”, that is: “The successors of Moses continued for some time in the same institutions, being just and truly religious.” This, therefore, was the Jews’ true glory, which the Romans falsely assigned to themselves as though, by the merit of their most scrupulous religiosity, they had been raised to such loftiness; see below, ch. XXV. HAV.], and their happiness was so great that they were warned beforehand by the voices of God, through which they were instructed how to earn God’s favor and not offend him [Note: [Col. 0393B] The Fulda codex: “and such great happiness came from the voices of God, by which they were instructed and warned beforehand both to earn God’s favor and not to offend him.”].

But how greatly they transgressed [Note: [Col. 0393B] Franciscus: *dereliquerint*, “forsook.”] [Note: [Col. 0393C] **Transgressed.** All the books which Pamelius and I have seen read *dereliquerunt* or *dereliquerint*, “forsook.” Rigaltius, however, Scaliger, the old editions, Rhenanus, and Aldus read *deliquerint*, “transgressed”—and not without reason. It is from *delinquere*, from which later writers formed *delinquentia* for “offense”; see Paschasius Radbertus, *Epitaph of Wala*, book I, ch. 28. And in Papias’ glossary *deliquio* is explained as “forgetfulness.” HAV.], inflated by confidence in their fathers [to the point of madness] [Note: [Col. 0393B] Wouwer: *ad delirandum*, “to the point of madness,” which Havercamp accepted from the Fulda codex; Rigaltius deleted it. Rhenanus and Heraldus: *ad declinandum*, “to the point of deviation.”], turning away [Note: [Col. 0394B] *Derivantes*: thus the Lyon codex and most editions; Gelenius: *declinantes*; Rigaltius and Junius, from the Ursinus codex: *deviantes*.] from discipline into a profane manner of life, even if they themselves would not confess it, their present outcome would prove. Scattered, wandering, [Col. 0394A] exiles from both their own sky and their soil, they roam throughout the world, without [Note: [Col. 0393D] **Without a man.** Scaliger acutely emended in the margin of his book: “without a name, without God as king.” I think he wished to interpret Hosea 3:4 in this way: “For many days the Israelites shall remain without a king, without a prince.” For although there may be no king, there may nevertheless be a title of government, such as that of the Judges after Moses, of the Princes in the time of Ezra, or of Commanders when the Maccabees rose against the oppressors of the Jews.

Nevertheless, I do not depart from the common reading, which is more forceful. For they no longer have God as king, whom they had already rejected long ago when, after the example of the nations, they sought a human being as king for themselves and a visible kingdom in which a form worthy of a tyrant might gratify their eyes, 1 Samuel 8:5. Nor do they have even a man by whose appearance they might be strengthened against the accidents of fortune—rather as I think Tacitus speaks somewhere.

The Leiden manuscript nevertheless supports Scaliger’s conjecture and enlarges its sense, reading: “without a man, without God, without a king.” If this reading is preferred, it should be corrected thus: “without a Name, [Col. 0394B] without a King, without God”; that is, they now have neither a commonwealth, nor a kingdom, nor a theocracy. HAV.] a man, without God as king [Note: [Col. 0394B] Scaliger emends: “without a name, without God as king”; Lyon codex II: “without a man” (Lyon I: “without honor”), “without God, without a king.”]. They are not permitted, even under the right of foreigners, so much as to greet their native land with their footsteps [Note: [Col. 0394B] **To greet it with their footsteps.** Hadrian as victor prescribed the law of a dreadful sentence. Jerome, in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, year 2250: “From that time even permission to enter Jerusalem was taken from them.” Eusebius, from Aristo of Pella: “The whole nation from that time onward…”, etc.; that is: “From that time the whole nation was utterly barred from every region adjoining Jerusalem, both by the sanction of divine law and especially by Hadrian’s constitutions [Col. 0394C] and decrees, so that they were not permitted even from a higher vantage point to gaze from afar upon their ancestral soil with their profane eyes”; *Ecclesiastical History* IV.6. The great Scaliger presents more from Justin Martyr, Hilary, Jerome, and others in his *Annotations on Eusebius*, p. 216 of the best edition. HAV.].

Since the sacred voices threatened them beforehand with these things [Note: [Col. 0394C] **Foretold.** Deuteronomy 32:26; Psalm 59:12: “Make them wander by your power”; and especially verse 15: “Let them snarl like a dog and wander about the city.” Surely no one can now doubt how this passage received its fulfillment, especially since the eye of the true theologian ought to look toward the Messiah’s kingdom, prefigured by David’s reign and fortunes. See also Isaiah 1:7; Ezekiel 5:10; Hosea 3:10 and 10:3; Amos 9:9. Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 163: “And how throughout the whole inhabited world…”, etc.; that is: “It would also come to pass that the Jews, who were going to fasten him to the wood of the cross, would be exiled from their ancestral soil and dispersed throughout the whole world. Come then, let us see whether this prediction [Col. 0394D] has reached its fulfillment. As for the Jews, I do not think that you will be in doubt. For they have now been expelled from their native city and have migrated to other lands”; and what follows.

Tertullian himself says in his excellent book *Against the Jews*, ch. XI: “For because of these deserts of yours, Ezekiel announces your future calamity—not only the one in this age, which has already occurred, but also that on the day of tribulation which will follow.” And most clearly in ch. XIII: “And elsewhere it is said thus through the prophet”—it is Isaiah 33:17—“‘You shall see the king in glory,’ that is, Christ performing mighty works in the glory of God the Father, ‘and your eyes shall see the land from afar.’ Because of your deserts, after the conquest of Jerusalem, you were forbidden to enter your land and were permitted only to see it with your eyes from afar.” In the same place: “When they had committed these things and had not understood that Christ was to be found at the time of their visitation, their land was made desolate and their cities burned with fire.”

Jerome, in the passage cited above: “first by God’s command, as the prophets foretold, and then by Roman prohibitions.” See Scaliger there as well. HAV.], nearly all of them repeatedly insisted that, at the final courses of the age, God would choose worshipers for himself from every nation, people, and place—worshipers far more faithful, to whom he would transfer his grace, and indeed a fuller grace because of their capacity for a more advanced discipline [Note: [Col. 0394B] Franciscus Junius emends this passage thus. The common text reads: “would transfer it, and a fuller one indeed because of their capacity for the author’s discipline” (Gorze codex: *altioris*, “higher”; Puteanus codex: *auctoris*, “of the author”).].

[Therefore he came who had been foretold as destined to come from God to reform and illuminate it: that Christ, [Col. 0395A] the Son of God] [Note: [Col. 0395A] Rigaltius and Havercamp delete the words enclosed in brackets.].

Accordingly, the arbiter and master of this grace and discipline, the illuminator and guide [Note: [Col. 0395A] **Guide.** The one whom the Greeks in this sense would call δαδοῦχον (“torchbearer”), and Sacred Scripture ἀρηγὸν (“helper”). For in the Eleusinian rites this was the proper designation of the person who, holding a torch in his hand, went before others and, lighting the road, conducted them, as Eustathius teaches on Homer, *Iliad* I, line 279. In Arrian’s *Discourses of Epictetus* III.21, a certain despiser of the gods says: “There is a temple at Eleusis—behold, there is one here too; there is a revealer of the sacred rites there…” [Col. 0395B] “…and I shall appoint a revealer of the sacred rites; there is a herald there, and I shall establish a herald; there is a torchbearer there, and I too shall be a torchbearer”, that is: “There is a temple—and indeed one at Eleusis—and there is one among us also. There the president of the rites exists, and I shall arrange for one to be here; there is a herald there, and I shall establish a herald here; there is a torchbearer there, and I shall be the torchbearer.” Peter calls Jesus Ἀρχηγὸν τῆς ζωῆς (“the Author of life”) in Acts 3:15. The Leiden manuscript, as well as Agobardinus, deletes the following words, “Son of God.” HAV.] of the human race was announced as the Son of God—not, indeed, begotten in such a way that he should be ashamed of the name of son [Note: [Col. 0395B] **Of the name of son.** Restore this with the Fulda codex.
