The common editions have “in the name of son.” However much those heroes among the ancient poets might boast of gods as their fathers and parade their forefathers, they nevertheless ought, after the peacock had spread its tail, to have looked upon their muddy and scabby feet and been truly confounded by their origin, which could have been nothing other than fornication or adultery.

Nor did Virgil—poet of marvelous learning as well as supreme artistry—neglect decorum here. Since he was rightly ashamed of the origin of his Aeneas, he veils adultery under the specious name of marriage. In his work Helenus addresses the aged Trojan in book III, line 475, thus:

> Anchises, deemed worthy of Venus’ proud marriage.

And so, in his own words under the person of Dido, he condemns Aeneas in book IV, line 172:

> She calls it marriage, and with this name veils her fault.

**From his father’s seed.** He seems to say the same thing, though it is by no means the same. For he is now speaking of the manner of generation, which among them was monstrous and shameful: by the embrace of a dragon, the mounting of a bull, a goat, or a ram, the lascivious movement of a swan, and similar things. Hence it is evident that the reading in the Fulda codex, “from his father’s seed,” comes from a marginal gloss, just as “from intercourse with a bull” does, though it is based upon a suitable and learned interpretation. He may appear at the same time to have had the story of Caelus and Saturn in view, but only in passing. HAV.], or of his father’s [Col. 0396A] seed, nor as the offspring of incest with a sister [Note: [Col. 0395C] **Incest with a sister.** Juno; though he also united himself with his daughter Venus, and likewise with Proserpina, being called Pluto among the dead but Jupiter among those above. Indeed, he is believed not even to have abstained from his mother Rhea. Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 43: “For not only his sister…”, etc.; that is: “For he joined to himself as wives not only his sister, but also his mother and daughters; and besides these he corrupted almost innumerable women and goddesses through intercourse in fornication.” Hence Theodoret’s just indignation against this bestial frenzy of thought, p. 53: “But those afflicted by this passion…”, etc.; that is: “Those who fell into adulteries nevertheless spared women closely related to them by necessity and blood. If anyone was found who had been captivated by love for his sister, he did not also rage against his mother or become mad for his daughter; instead, he showed the regard for human nature and dignity that he owed, and did not put on the senselessness of brute animals.” And shortly afterward: “But this one, whom Θεῷν (as recovered; apparently θεῶν, ‘of gods’)…”, etc.; that is: “But this one, whom Homer called the father of men and gods, made Juno, his own full sister, his wife. In a frenzy of lust he even coupled with Rhea herself—whom they also call Deona and Demeter, that is, Ceres—although she was his mother; and he took Phersephatta, that is, Proserpina, born of that violation, as his wife, becoming the husband of his own daughter.” Our author therefore rightly says in ch. IX: “Accordingly, who are more incestuous than those whom Jupiter himself instructed?” HAV.], or of the violation of a daughter or another man’s wife [Note: [Col. 0396A] **Wife.** The Fulda codex incorrectly reads *de conjugis*, “from a wife’s.” For he was the husband of all women. Epiphanius: πασῶν γυναικῶν ἀνήρ (“the husband of all women”), as Suetonius says of Caesar.]; he did not have as father a god who was scaly or horned [Note: [Col. 0396A] **Horned.** The same author in his book *Ancoratus*: “For he corrupted Penelope, for whose sake he had become a goat; and he became a goat, I think, because of the pointed interweaving of the beard”, that is: “For he corrupted Penelope, having become a goat for her sake. He became a goat, I think, because of the resemblance of its pointed and intertwined beard.” For thus this passage should be translated and understood.

**Especially a bull.** In the same place: “He also became a bull for Pasiphaë, and likewise for Europa”: “He also became a bull for Pasiphaë, and likewise for Europa.” Hence the coin of Gortyna, a city on the island of Crete, which the very distinguished Patin published and explained in his *Thesaurus*, p. 21, also deserves to be mentioned here. On one side Europa is seated in a plane tree, or beneath its shade, mourning the flower of her virginity that had been carried off; on the other Jupiter, her ravisher, is seen in the wanton form of a bull.

Pliny, book XII, ch. 10: “At Gortyna on the island of Crete, beside a spring, there is a single plane tree famous in the records of both languages, which never sheds its leaves; and Greek mythology immediately supplied the story that Jupiter lay with Europa beneath it.” The girl carried off by the bull is also elegantly depicted on a gem by Leonardo Agostini, vol. I, plate 185; and again on a coin of Geta struck by the Byzantines, published by Patin in his true *Thesaurus*, p. 192. There is likewise a coin of the Sidonians in Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, p. 780.

An exceedingly delightful epigram of Moschus refers to this; and why should I not add it? Its title is εἰς Ἐρωτα ἀροτριῶντα (“On Love Plowing”):

> Having laid aside his torch and bow, he took up an ox-driver’s goad;  
> destructive Love had a pouch hanging from his shoulders.  
> And, yoking the labor-enduring necks of the bulls beneath the yoke, he sowed Demeter’s grain-bearing furrow.  
> Then, looking up toward Zeus himself, he said: “Burn the fields, lest I put you, Europa’s bull, beneath the plow.”.

That is: “Having laid aside his torch and bow, destructive Love took up the ox-driver’s goad. A pouch hung from his shoulders; and, having placed the neck of the labor-enduring bulls beneath the joined yoke, he sowed Ceres’ fruitful furrow. Then, looking upward toward Jupiter himself, he said: ‘Burn the fields, lest I place you, Europa’s bull, beneath the plow.’”

So it is commonly translated. But the use of the expression μή σε (literally “lest [I put] you,” but idiomatically here a threat: “indeed, I shall [put] you”) is more elegant; for it signifies “indeed I shall,” understanding “you,” with [uncertain abbreviated grammatical remark in the source]. The Aldine and Brodaeus editions also incorrectly read βοηλάτην (“ox-driver,” an erroneous reading here) and πλῆσον (“fill,” an erroneous reading for “burn”).], or a feathered lover [Note: [Col. 0396D] **Or feathered.** Since he had become a swan for Leda. *On the Shows*, ch. VIII: “They are not ashamed of Jupiter as a swan.” Ancient gems commonly display those adulteries of Jupiter. Gorlaeus I.26 and Leonardo Agostini II.19 depict the intercourse with Leda, as does a marble in the Giustiniani Museum.], or changed into gold [Note: [Col. 0396D] **Changed into gold.** Aldus, Pamelius, and other editions read “changed in gold.” Rigaltius and La Cerda, however, read as in the text. With Rigaltius and Rhenanus I have deleted the following word *Danaidis*, “of Danaë,” for it comes from a gloss, of which there are several in this chapter. And why should he connect Danaë herself with gold rather than Leda with feathers, or Penelope, Pasiphaë, or Europa with horns?

Aldus reads: “and these are your divine powers.” Epiphanius, in the same passage: “For Danaë he became χροσὸς (as recovered; apparently χρυσός, ‘gold’)…”, etc.; that is: “For Danaë he became gold, in order to corrupt the chaste virgin enclosed in her chamber. Yet he could never have become gold; rather, he was an impostor and deceived the virgin by lavish gifts of gold. For Leda he again became a swan, signifying the kindling heat of his lust”; for ἀναπτερούσθαι (“to be stirred into flight,” hence “to be inflamed with desire”) means “to be inflamed by desire for something.”

Theodoret, p. 51: “And mingling with Leda in the form of a swan, and indeed being borne into Danaë’s lap like gold”: “Intertwined with Leda in the form of a swan, and slipping into Danaë’s lap in the likeness of gold.” Parmenio the epigrammatist, book VII of the *Anthology*:

> Into Danaë you flowed as gold, Olympian, so that the girl might be persuaded as by a gift and not tremble at you as the son of Cronus.

[Col. 0397B] That is, in Petreius Tiara’s translation:

> Into Danaë, Jupiter, you flowed as gold, so that  
> You might not terrify her with lightning, but capture her with a price.

Therefore the same poet thinks he must seek the same path for himself in the little verses that immediately follow and which, I think, should be joined to those above. They are:

> Zeus won Danaë with gold, and I too shall win you with gold;  
> for I cannot give more than Zeus..

> With gold I shall win you, since once Jupiter himself  
> [And what more can I give you?] won Danaë.

For already long ago, as Horace himself bears witness in this very tale, *Odes* III.16.12:

> Gold can pass through the midst of guards  
> And break through rocks, more powerful  
> Than the stroke of lightning. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0396A] Franciscus: “Or changed into the gold of Danaë.”]: for these are the divine powers of your Jupiter [Col. 0397A] [Note: [Col. 0397A] One manuscript: “the names of your Jupiter”; another reading: “your divine powers.”] [Note: [Col. 0397B] **For these are the divine manifestations of your Jupiter.** This reading seems to me entirely correct, and I have reproduced it from the Leiden manuscript. Scriverius found in the manuscripts a reading not far removed from it: “For these are the names of your Jupiter.” Thus in *On the Shows*, ch. VIII: “Observe, Christian, how many unclean names have taken possession of the circus.” If anyone wishes to prefer that reading, I would not oppose him, for it is full of biting wit. But the other reading has greater force, and the varied testimony of manuscripts and editors favors it more. Barraeus: “Jupiter’s—and these are your divine powers”; likewise Aldus. Pamelius, Heraldus, Rhenanus, and the Agobardinus codex: “These things are Jupiter’s, and your divine powers.” The Fulda codex reads, rather neatly: “These are the human things of yours.” Finally, Rigaltius indeed printed: “For these are the divine manifestations of your Jupiter”; but in his notes he nevertheless thinks one should read: “For these are all the deeds of your Jupiter.” Less convincingly.].

The Son of God, however, has no mother from unchastity [Note: [Col. 0397C] **The Son of God, however, has no mother from unchastity.** The reading which Latinius and Pamelius testify is written in certain copies—“He has no mother from chastity”—is correct and should not have been altered. The Son of God, our Lord, was born from no marriage, not even a chaste or legitimate one. Therefore he has no mother “from chastity.” That is, the Virgin Mary became his mother not through the bond of any marriage, however chaste, but through the Word of God alone. Yet our Lord was commonly regarded as the son of Joseph and Mary. Hence Tertullian says: “Even the woman whom he appears to have as mother—that mother had not married.” RIGALTIUS.

**From chastity.** Rigaltius rightly supports this reading in his notes, and, in addition to the reasons he gives, it is confirmed by Rhenanus’ edition. He therefore means that our Jesus was born not only without impure and unlawful intercourse, but not even through pure and lawful marriage, by the power of his Spirit and the capacity of the divine nature, which built itself a dwelling among human beings and stirred the leaven of human generation in a virgin womb.

Those who did not understand this substituted “from unchastity.” Yet the Jews dared to assail his chastity, as is evident from the final chapter of *On the Shows*: “This is that son—I shall say it—of the carpenter or of the prostitute.” Thus Rigaltius emended it, though Prior dares to criticize him, while La Cerda chooses the common reading, “of the male prostitute.” What else is that but to eat acorns after grain has been discovered? For Rigaltius did not find this only in the Agobardinus copy; Josias Mercerus also noted it in his own book, which he compared most diligently with that codex. That book is today preserved in the Leiden Library. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0397A] Rhenanus, Latinius, Pamelius, and Havercamp read “from chastity,” a wording which [Col. 0398A] Rigaltius also defends.], even the woman whom he appears to have [Note: [Col. 0398B] **Had not married.** Barraeus and Aldus very incorrectly read “had married.” For although in Matthew 1:19 Joseph is called ἀνὴρ αὐτῆς (“her husband”), it must be understood that this is by prolepsis, just as Choroebus in Virgil, *Aeneid* II.344:

> As a son-in-law he brought aid to Priam and the Phrygians,  
> Unhappy man, who did not—his frenzied betrothed’s commands [the source breaks off here].

Restoration notes: E005/S000583 is only an incomplete opening phrase, so its incompleteness is stated in the replacement.; E010/S000588 contains apparently corrupt recovered spellings; the exact script is preserved and the contextual sense is rendered cautiously.; E011/S000589 contains uncertain or corrupt readings, especially the opening and final “Λία”; these are preserved and flagged.; E018/S000596 consists only of the isolated Greek article τὸ, whose intended contextual function is uncertain.; E005/S000583 contains only an incomplete opening phrase; its incompleteness is stated in the replacement.; E010/S000588 contains corrupt recovered spellings, especially in the final clause; the exact script is preserved and its contextual sense rendered cautiously.; E011/S000589 contains corrupt or uncertain readings at the opening and in the final name Λία; the contextual Latin supports the rendering “one and the same” and “Jupiter.”; E018/S000596 consists only of the isolated Greek article τὸ, whose contextual function is uncertain.; E021/S000599 has recovered θεὸν (“god”), while the surrounding English and Latin explain the word as “daemon”; the discrepancy is preserved and noted.  

He had heard. He is already called a son-in-law, although Cassandra had only been betrothed to him. Likewise Silanus is called Claudius’ son-in-law, although Octavia had been betrothed to him, in Suetonius, *Claudius*, ch. 27. That Mary herself was still immature and not yet of marriageable age in completed years may be inferred even from the fact that, although she could have answered the angel, “οὐκ ἔχω ἅνδρα (“I have no husband”),” as Christ was answered by that Samaritan woman at John 4:7, she preferred to say, “ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (“I do not know a man”),” perhaps because her very age precluded childbirth. For among the Jews not only were minors destined for the bond of marriage, as everyone knows, but even among the Romans Caesar [Col. 0398C] could provide an example: having put away Cossutia, who came from an equestrian family but was extremely wealthy and had been betrothed to him while he still wore the bordered toga, he married Cornelia, the daughter of Cinna, consul for the fourth time, as Suetonius attests, ch. 1.] she had not married.

But first I shall explain the substance, [Note: [Col. 0398A] “And” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] and thus the character of his birth will be understood. We have already declared that God fashioned this universe [Col. 0398A] of the world by the Word, Reason, and Power. Among your own sages also [Note: [Col. 0398C] Sages, “Λόγον (“Word” or “Reason”).” Besides those whom he names, there are Plutarch and Numenius, Plotinus, and Plato himself. Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 96, in the words of Plotinus: “Οὕτω δὴ ἐξ ἑνὸς νοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἀπ` αὐτοῦ λόγου, ἀνέστη τόδε τὸ πᾶν καὶ διέστη (“Thus, then, from one Mind and from the Word proceeding from it, this entire universe arose and was set apart”),” that is: “Thus, therefore, from the one Mind and from the Word that proceeded from it, this entire universe emerged and was set apart.” And again, p. 39, where he has defended quite admirably the truth of the Most Holy Trinity from the books of the Old Testament, he also adduces the following: “Αὐτίκα τοίνυν τὴν Πλάτωνος (“Immediately, then, Plato’s …”; the recovered phrase is incomplete),” etc.; that is: “Plotinus, therefore, and Numenius, in explaining Plato’s meaning, say that Plato posited three things which are above time and eternal: namely, the Good itself, Mind, and the soul of this universe. For he calls the GOOD the one whom we call the FATHER; MIND or Intellect the one whom we call the SON and WORD; and the POWER [Col. 0398D] that animates and gives life to all things he calls the SOUL—that very one, namely, whom Holy Scripture calls the HOLY SPIRIT.” There also survives in Hesychius Illustrius of Miletus a remark of Numenius about Plato, censuring him with this charge: “ὡς έκ τῶν Μωσαικῶν βιβλίων τὰ περὶ Θεοῦ καὶ κόσμου ἀποσυλήσασαν (“as having plundered from the Mosaic books what concerns God and the world”),” that is, that he had, as though by plagiarism, stolen from the Mosaic books what he taught about God and the world; hence he was called by the same author “Moses speaking Attic Greek.” “Τί γάρ έστι Πλάτων, ἢ Μωσῆς ἀττικίζων (“For what is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?”)”: “For what else is Plato than Moses speaking Attic Greek?” See Illustrius in the *Life of Numenius the Pythagorean Philosopher*. He adduces further testimonies there.] it is agreed that “ΛΌΓΟΝ (“WORD” or “REASON”),” that is, the Discourse and Reason, is regarded as the artificer of the universe. Zeno, indeed, [Note: [Col. 0398D] “Zeno defines him as the active maker.” We learn from Laertius that Zeno said something further, namely that there are two principles of all things, the Creator and Matter: “τὸ ποίουν καὶ τὸ πάσχον (“the active principle and the passive principle”).” And that Matter is substance devoid of quality, while the Creator is “τὸν ἑν αὐτῇ λόγον τὸν θεόν· τοῦτον γὰρ ὄντα ἀΐδιον κια πὰσις ταὑῆς δημιουργεῖν ἕκαστα (“the God who is the Word within it; for, being eternal, he creates each thing throughout all of it”; several recovered spellings are corrupt, and the rendering of the final clause is consequently uncertain).” RIG.] defines him as the maker who formed all things in ordered arrangement, and says that the same is called Fate, [Col. 0399A] God, the Mind of Jupiter, [Note: [Col. 0399C] “The same is called Fate and God and the Mind [Col. 0399D] of Jupiter.” The same words occur in Lactantius. Laertius, however, reported Zeno’s opinion thus: “ἐν τε εἰσθαι Θεὸν καὶ Νοῦν, Εἰμαρμένην, καὶ Λία (“and that one and the same is God and Mind, Fate and Jupiter”; the recovered opening and final name are corrupt or uncertain).” RIG.] and the Necessity of all things. Cleanthes gathers all these into the Spirit, whom he affirms to pervade the universe.

We too assign Spirit as the proper substance of the Word, Reason, and Power through which, as we have declared, God fashioned all things: a Spirit in whom the Word inheres when he speaks, Reason attends when he orders, and Power presides when he brings things to completion. We have learned that he was brought forth from God, was begotten by that bringing forth, and for that reason was called the Son of God and God by virtue of the unity of substance. For God also is spirit. And when a ray is extended from the sun, it is a portion from the whole; yet the sun will be in the ray [Note: [Col. 0399C] Junius reads “proceeds.”], because the ray belongs to the sun, and the substance is not separated but extended. So Spirit comes from Spirit and God from God [Note: [Col. 0399C] “So Spirit … God” is absent from the Fulda manuscript and Rhenanus’ edition.], as light is kindled from light. The matrix of the substance remains whole and undiminished, even though you derive from it several offshoots [Col. 0399B] endowed with qualities. [Note: [Col. 0399C] In the Paris manuscript. The Fulda manuscript and Pamelius read “of quality”; Lyons II, “qualities of the offshoot.”] So too [Note: [Col. 0399C] “And” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] that which proceeded from God is God and the Son of God, and the two are one. Thus Spirit from Spirit and God from God became another in measure, not in number; [Note: [Col. 0399D] “Another in measure, not in number.” The Father is other than the Son insofar as he is Father, not insofar as he is God. The Son is other than the Father insofar as he is Son, not insofar as he is God from God. The Spirit is other than the Father and Son insofar as he is Spirit, not insofar as he is God with God the Father and the Son. For since there is one Spirit from the Father and the Son, the Father, Son, and Spirit are one in one spirit and one substance, and that one is God. RIG.—“Another in measure.” Thus in *Against Praxeas*, p. 640: “Yet the Son is not other than the Father by diversity, but by distribution; nor other by division, but by distinction, because the Father and Son are not the same, or because one is other than the other in measure.” And p. 645: “But let us acknowledge the Son as visible according to the measure of his derivation.” Accordingly, “mode” and “measure” are the disposition, ordering, and economy of particular things according to the principles of their kind. The same.] in degree, not in condition; [Note: [Col. 0399C] The Paris manuscript reads “not in degree but in condition.” Franeker reads: “an alternate in measure, number in degree, not in condition.”] and he did not withdraw from the matrix but issued from it.

This ray of God, therefore, as had always been proclaimed beforehand, [Note: [Col. 0399C] Scriverius’ old manuscript reads “foretold.”] descended into a certain virgin and, formed as flesh in her womb, [Note: [Col. 0399C] “Formed”: Junius, Havercamp; the Fulda manuscript reads, “a certain virgin, and in her womb he is formed as flesh”; Semler, “formed,” feminine.] is born as a man mingled with God. The flesh, furnished with spirit, [Note: [Col. 0399C] “Constructed,” Fulda manuscript.] is nourished, grows to maturity, speaks, teaches, acts, and is Christ.

For the moment, accept this tale: it resembles your own, while we show how Christ is proved. Those among you who supplied rival tales of this sort in advance, for the destruction of the truth, also knew it. [Note: [Col. 0399C] Scriverius, Rigault, and Havercamp restored the passage thus; previously it read, “is proved, and those who … may have supplied in advance.”] The Jews too knew that Christ was to come, for it was to them, of course, that the prophets spoke. Even now they await his advent, and there is no greater dispute between us and them than their disbelief that he has already come.

For two advents of his were signified: the first, which has already been accomplished in the lowliness of the human condition; the second, which threatens at the close of the age in the sublimity of revealed divinity. Because they did not understand the first, they supposed the second—the one which they hope for because it was more clearly proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0399C] Gelenius: “foretold.”]—to be the only one. For their transgression deserved that they should not understand the former, since they would have believed had they understood, and would have obtained salvation had they believed. [Note: [Col. 0399C] Rhenanus in his first edition, Aldus, Pamelius, Barraeus, and Gangneius read [Col. 0400C] “was the desert of their transgressions.”] They themselves read that it was written that they had been punished by deprivation of wisdom and understanding and of the fruit of eyes and ears.

Since, on account of his lowliness, they had presumed him to be merely a man, [Note: [Col. 0400C] Semler: “a man only in respect of measure.”] it followed that, on account of his power, they should regard him as a magician, [Col. 0400B] when by a word he drove demons out of men, restored sight to the blind, [Note: [Col. 0400C] The Paris manuscript reads “illumined.”] cleansed lepers, restored paralytics, and finally by a word restored the dead to life; when he subjected the very elements to himself, [Note: [Col. 0400C] “Subjected.” Because they did not understand the use of the verb, in the Aldine and Agobard manuscripts they substituted the plural, “served.” Our author wished to express the Greek “δουλοῦν (“to enslave” or “reduce to servitude”),” meaning “to reduce to servitude”; interpreters note that others too spoke in this way.] restraining storms and walking upon seas; and when he showed himself to be the “ΛΟΓΟΝ (“WORD”)” of God—that is, that primordial and first-begotten Word, [Note: [Col. 0400C] The Fulda manuscript reads: “showing himself to be the Son and that Word of God long ago proclaimed by God and born for the salvation of all, that,” etc.; it omits the words “the same who … had made.”] attended by power and reason and supported by spirit, [Note: [Col. 0400C] Rhenanus, Heraldus, and Gangneius read “furnished”; the Lyons manuscript, “sustained.”] the same one who by his word both performed all these things and had made all things. [Note: [Col. 0400C] Rigault deletes this “ῥῆσιν (“phrase” or “wording”),” “the same … had made”; Havercamp defends it as revised thus: “the same who both made all things and had made them.”]

But at his teaching, by which the teachers and leaders of the Jews were refuted, they grew so exasperated—especially because an immense multitude was turning toward him [Note: [Col. 0400C] The Fulda manuscript reads “flowing together.”]—that in the end they used the violence of their votes to extort from Pontius Pilate, who was then administering Syria on Rome’s behalf, [Note: [Col. 0400C] The Leiden manuscript reads “from the Roman populace.”] [Note: [Col. 0400C] The Leiden manuscript reads “from the Roman populace”; Fulda, “Syria as a Roman part.”] [Note: [Col. 0400D] “On Rome’s behalf.” Manuscript L.B. reads “from the Roman populace,” as though suggesting that the Pontian clan was plebeian. Fulda, however, reads “Syria as a Roman part,” as though the author were unwilling to number Commagene and Judaea among the Roman provinces in Syria, since they were subject to their own dynasts and petty kings. It was customary among the Romans at that time to involve themselves, amid political disturbances, in the dissensions of peoples and kings, so that the more powerful men, who governed the commonwealth by their nod and gathered armies by stamping their feet, might grow rich from plunder and bestow kingdoms and powers upon whomever they wished. Those beholden to their patrons did not dare even to mutter against them.] that he be delivered to them for the cross. [Note: [Col. 0400C] Thus the Fulda manuscript; others read: “that Jesus be delivered to them for the cross.”] [Note: [Col. 0400D] “Administering.” Tacitus on Christ’s death, *Annals* XV.44: “Who, while Tiberius was ruling, had been subjected to punishment through the procurator Pontius Pilate.” Jerome, in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, no. 2042: “Pilate is sent by Tiberius as procurator of Judaea.” Since these matters are astonishingly confused everywhere by certain writers, it must be understood that Vitellius, a man of consular rank, was at that time governor of all Syria, but had his own procurators, who were generally Roman knights, whom he sent either into the smaller provinces or into the kingdoms of allies, so that there they might administer the affairs of the Roman people—whether in exacting tribute and preserving treaties made with Rome, or generally in seeing that the commonwealth suffered no harm. Thus among those territories Pontius Pilate received Judaea, a part of Syria, to administer. HAV.]

He himself had foretold that they would do so. That would be little, unless the prophets had also foretold it long before. And yet, when fastened to the cross, he voluntarily dismissed his spirit with a word, forestalling the executioner’s office. [Note: [Col. 0401B] The editions before Rigault and Havercamp read: “the prophets long before also. Yet, when fastened, he displayed many distinctive marks peculiar to his death. For his spirit,” etc. The words “many … For” are absent from the Fulda manuscript. Rigault emends: “And at last, when fastened.”] [Note: [Col. 0401C] “Forestalling the executioner’s office.” I wish to append two passages that especially illuminate this, one from Suetonius and the other from Seneca. In the *Life of Tiberius*, ch. 61: “Those wishing to die were forcibly kept alive. For he regarded death as so slight a punishment that, when he heard that one of them, named Carnalius, had anticipated it, he exclaimed, ‘Carnalius has escaped me.’” Seneca, *To Marcia*, ch. 22, speaks of her father Cremutius Cordus, who under the same emperor resolved to die by starvation lest he perish as a defendant: “At Sejanus’ prompting the accusers approach the consuls’ tribunals; they complain that Cordus is dying, interrupting what they had compelled. So truly did Cordus seem to be escaping them. A weighty question was under discussion: whether defendants should be prohibited from dying. While they deliberate, while the accusers approach again, he had acquitted himself.”]

At that same moment daylight was withdrawn, when the sun was marking midday over the world. [Note: [Col. 0401C] “The daylight, the middle.” Tertullian himself confirms this in *Against the Jews*, ch. 10: “For what happened during his passion, that the day grew dark at midday, the prophet Amos announces, saying: ‘And it shall be on that day, says the Lord, that the sun shall set at midday, and the daylight shall grow dark over the earth.’” In the same place: “So that the prophecies might be fulfilled, the day hastened to make evening.” From this he likewise explains Jeremiah 2:12: “Heaven was astonished at this.” “And how and when was it astonished? Undoubtedly when Christ suffered. ‘And it shuddered,’ he says, ‘exceedingly, and the sun grew dark at midday.’ And when did it shudder exceedingly, except during Christ’s passion?” He records a similar marvel in *To Scapula*, ch. 3: “For that sun too, at the assembly at Utica, when its light was almost extinguished, was so great a portent that it could not have suffered this from an ordinary eclipse, being situated at its own altitude and station.” He said “the sun marking off the globe,” that is, hiding and sealing away its light. For the ancients used *signare*, “to mark,” in the sense of sealing and concealing. Nonius says: “Antiquity meant an untouched virgin by ‘a sealed virgin.’” Hence Song of Songs 4:12: “You are an enclosed spring, a sealed fountain.” Indeed, concerning the very light of the heavenly spheres this expression occurs in Job 9:7, of God “who gives his command to the sun and it does not rise, and seals the stars.” I think the wording here alludes to that passage.] [Note: [Col. 0401B] Semler reads “the middle.”] Those who did not know that this also had been foretold concerning Christ naturally supposed it to be an eclipse; [not having discovered the reason, they denied it]. [Note: [Col. 0401B] The words enclosed in brackets are found as an addition only in the Fulda manuscript.] And yet you have that cosmic event recorded in your secret records. [Note: [Col. 0401B] Thus Rigault and Havercamp from the Fulda manuscript; the others read “in the archives.”] [Note: [Col. 0402B] “They naturally supposed it to be an eclipse.” Namely Phlegon and Thallus, distinguished chronologists, of whom the former is believed to have benefited from the name and scholarly interest of the widely learned Emperor Hadrian when publishing his works. Their testimonies are well known and worth reading in Eusebius, *Chronicle*, p. 202. On those testimonies and the miraculous nature of this event, the illustrious Scaliger should certainly be consulted there, where he adduces several passages, p. 186, and in *On the Emendation of Times*, p. 561. To him may be added Bynaeus, Book III, ch. 8, *On the Death of Jesus Christ*. HAV.]

The Jews then had him taken down and laid in a tomb, and with great vigilance surrounded it with a military guard, [Note: [Col. 0402B] Franeker and Paris read “with a military force as guard.”] [Note: [Col. 0402B] The Agobard manuscript reads “enclosed.”] lest, because he had foretold that he would rise from death on the third day, his disciples should secretly remove the body and deceive those already suspicious. But behold, on the third day [Note: [Col. 0402B] The Fulda manuscript reads “by the third day.”] the earth was suddenly shaken, the mass that had blocked [Col. 0402A] the tomb was rolled away, and the guard was scattered by fear; although no disciples appeared, nothing was found in the tomb except the grave-clothes of the buried man. [Note: [Col. 0402B] The Fulda manuscript reads “except the wrappings of the burial.”]

Nevertheless, the leaders—whose interest it was both to spread a tale of criminality and to recall from the faith a people who paid them tribute and rendered them service [Note: [Col. 0402B] Franeker reads “to the faith.”]—gave out that he had been stolen away by his disciples. For neither did he bring himself before the general public, lest the impious be freed from their error, and so that faith, destined for no ordinary reward, might be established by difficulty. But he remained for forty days with certain disciples in Galilee, a region of Judaea, teaching them what they were to teach. Then, after appointing them to the duty of preaching throughout the world, he was taken up into heaven with a cloud surrounding him, [Note: [Col. 0402B] Franeker reads “received.”] far more truly than the Proculi among you are accustomed to affirm concerning Romulus. [Note: [Col. 0402B] The Fulda manuscript, Rigault, and Havercamp read “Romuluses.”] [Note: [Col. 0402C] “Concerning Romuluses by Proculuses.” Thus Rigault from the Fulda manuscript—a familiar manner of speaking. Others read “concerning Romulus by Proculus.” Augustine, *City of God* III.15, shows from Cicero that Romulus’ reception among the gods was believed rather than accomplished. Nor is that surprising, since even his tomb existed, if Varro is to be trusted. Porphyrio, on Horace’s *Epodes*, at the poem beginning “Another generation is now being worn away,” notes this: “For Varro says that Romulus’ tomb was behind the rostra.” Augustine therefore speaks truly: “Certain writers may look to it, even those who said that because of his ferocity he was torn to pieces by the Senate, and that some Julius Proculus or other was suborned, who said Romulus had appeared to him and had through him commanded the Roman people to worship him among the divine powers; and that in this way the populace, which had begun to swell with anger against the Senate, was restrained and pacified.” Aurelius Victor certainly shows, in the *Epitome*, under Marcus Antoninus, that prayer was sufficient to obtain divinity: “And what was reluctantly believed concerning Romulus, all assumed with equal sentiment—that Marcus had been received into heaven.” Perhaps also relevant here is that half-naked young man in Bellori, *Vestiges of Roman Antiquity*, [Col. 0402D] plate 36, who gazes up in wonder as Faustina, wife of Marcus, in the garb of Diana Lucifera, is carried into heaven—unless, rather, from his dress and the diadem adorning his head he should be judged to be the god Genius; such madness for glory had evidently seized mankind. Suetonius, on the soul of Augustus, ch. 100: “Nor was there wanting a man of praetorian rank who swore that he had seen the likeness of the cremated emperor going to heaven.” But hear Tertullian, at the end of *On the Shows*, on the punishment of hell: “Watching so many mighty kings, who were announced as received into heaven, groaning in the deepest darkness together with Jupiter himself and those witnesses of theirs.” More truly do we apply to Jesus, our conqueror of death, what Valerius Maximus could say of Julius Caesar only in flattery, IV.5: “In this manner it is not men who expire, but immortal gods who return to their abodes.” I think Tertullian alludes to this when he says in *To the Nations* I.10: “Before the people, the beholder of the heavenly one received into heaven would not perjure himself.” But this passage reminds me of the remedy that this little book badly needs in that chapter. We read there: “Who might excuse that insult, which, so that it may either reckon the dead among the gods?” Godefroy rightly pronounces the passage unsound but applies no remedy. Rigault notes nothing and changes nothing. Delete one letter, and the truest reading will emerge by writing *utut mortuos*, “however they may finally have died”—as, for example, that ill-omened Romulus, whose members were scattered and who did not even find a tomb intact. See more in the commentators and Elmenhorst on Minucius, p. 56. HAV.]

All these things concerning Christ Pilate—himself already, in his conscience, a Christian [Note: [Col. 0403C] “A Christian in his conscience.” Since his conscience told him that Christ had been unjustly accused, that no fault, not even the slightest, could be found in him, and that he had proceeded to punish him under compulsion rather than willingly, where there was no offense, he necessarily had to favor his memory just as he had favored him while alive. Pilate is therefore called a Christian by our author in precisely the way that Augustus used jokingly to call Livy a Pompeian, as appears in Cremutius Cordus’ splendid defense in Tacitus, *Annals* IV.34: “Titus Livy, pre-eminent especially in eloquence and reliability, extolled Gnaeus Pompey with such praises that Augustus called him a Pompeian; nor did this impair their friendship.” It is therefore tempting to exclaim to Pontius, as our author does to Trajan in ch. 2: “O judgment confounded by necessity!” and, with a slight adaptation: “Why do you ensnare yourself by your own censorship? If you condemn, why do you investigate? If you investigate, why do you not also acquit?” HAV.]—reported to the emperor, who was then Tiberius. But the Caesars too would have believed concerning Christ, if either Caesars were not necessary to the age, [Note: [Col. 0403D] “If Caesars were not necessary to the age.” That is, to the Roman Empire, which they said would endure as long as the age itself. This derives, of course, from Paul’s “Only let him who restrains continue to restrain.” Flavius Vopiscus says of Aurelian: “This was the end of Aurelian, an emperor more necessary than good.” RIG.] or Christians could also have been Caesars. [Note: [Col. 0403D] “Or Christians could also have been Caesars.” Christians’ thinking was very different under Constantine, [Col. 0404C] whom they said could be both ruler of the age and a Christian—and with what resources of Greek ingenuity did they not prove it! Even under him, while he was still ignorant of Christian affairs, the heretics insulted the Catholics with a taunt of this sort: “What have Christians to do with kings? Or what have bishops to do with the palace?” Optatus, Book I. RIG.]

The disciples also, dispersed throughout the world, obeyed the command of God their teacher. They themselves suffered many things at the hands of the Jews who persecuted them—willingly, of course, because of their confidence in the truth—and finally, at Rome, through Nero’s savagery, they sowed the seed of Christian blood. But we shall show you [Note: [Col. 0403B] Semler reads “demonstrate.”] suitable witnesses to Christ: those very beings whom you worship. It is a great thing if I employ them so that you may believe Christians, when it is because of them that you do not believe Christians. [Note: [Col. 0403B] Franeker reads: “employ them so that you may believe, Christian.”]

Meanwhile, this is the order of our instruction; this is the origin we have set forth [Note: [Col. 0403B] Franeker reads “have issued.”] both of the sect and of its name, together with its founder. Let no one now cast infamy upon us; [Col. 0403B] let no one suppose anything else, since it is not lawful [Note: [Col. 0403B] Others read “unlawful.”] for anyone to lie about his own religion. For by saying that he worships something other than what he does worship, he denies what he worships, transfers both worship and honor [Note: [Col. 0403C] The words “and worship” are absent from the Fulda manuscript. The Agobard manuscript reads [Col. 0404B] “unto honor.” Both appear to have been added by an interpreter.] to another, and by transferring them no longer worships what he denied.

We say—and say openly—and, while being tortured by you, mangled and bloodied, we cry aloud: “We worship God through Christ.” Suppose him to be a man: through him and in him God wishes himself to be known and worshiped. To answer the Jews: they too learned to worship God through [a man,] [Note: [Col. 0404B] The Fulda manuscript and Havercamp read “through Moses.”] Moses. To meet the Greeks: Orpheus in Pieria, Musaeus at Athens, Melampus at Argos, and Trophonius in Boeotia bound men by initiatory rites. To look also to you, the rulers of the nations: Pompilius Numa was a man, and he burdened the Romans with the most laborious superstitions.

Let Christ too have been permitted to devise a scheme for divinity, a matter properly his own—not, as Numa did, to temper to civilized humanity men who were rock-dwellers [Note: [Col. 0404C] He calls rustic and uncultivated men *rupices*, “rock-dwellers,” from the Greek “ῥύπαξ (“a filthy or uncouth person”)” and “ῥύπος (“filth”).” *On the Pallium*, ch. 4: “That man, instructed in a rocky school under a rock-dweller, a forest-dweller, and a monstrous teacher.” In the same place: “rock-dwellers in urban affairs, buffoons in the forum, civilians in the army.” And *On the Soul*, ch. 6: “But what will so many mighty souls of rock-dwellers and Varrones do, when they lack the nourishment of wisdom?” Read the passage thus, not “of barbarians.” For he had in view Lucilius’ verse:

> The bristling, uncouth mouths of Varrones and rock-dwellers.]

and still savage, stupefied by the multitude of divine powers that had to be propitiated; but to give sight to men already cultivated, yet deceived by that very urbanity, so that they might recognize the truth. [Note: [Col. 0404C] “Give sight.” “Ἐξωμμάτωσε (“he gave sight” or “restored the eyes”),” says Scaliger, whom by all means see on Manilius, p. 118. Our author seems to employ the word *oculare* as though it meant “to restore sight,” as in his *On Repentance*, ch. 12: “The swallow, if it has blinded its chicks, knows how to give them sight again with its celandine.” Pacianus transcribed this in his *Exhortation to Repentance*: “The swallow knows how to give sight to its blinded chicks with its celandine.” Cyprian, that assiduous reader and admirer of our author, likewise seems to have taken it thus. He says in *On the Vanity of Idols*: “That they might lead men from the error of darkness to the way of light and give sight to the blind and ignorant, so that they might recognize the truth.” It differs from *inoculare*, “to graft,” which is borrowed from arboriculture and is known to everyone under this very term, *oculeeren*. For the “eye” in trees is that bud from which shoots must sprout. Cato, *On Agriculture*, ch. 6: “There plant eyes of reed three feet apart from one another.” Tertullian himself, *On the Soul*, ch. 19: “Or whence are shrubs immediately grafted upon them, leaves formed, and buds swollen?” HAV.]

Investigate, therefore, whether this divinity of Christ is true. If it is the kind by knowledge of which a person is reformed toward the good, [Note: [Col. 0404B] Semler reads “is reformed.”] it follows that every other divinity found to be contrary must be renounced as false—above all that one which, by every means, [Note: [Col. 0404C] Havercamp conjectures: “found contrary to every rational consideration—that one by every rational consideration.”] lurks beneath the names and images of the dead and contrives belief in its divinity by certain signs, [Col. 0404B] miracles, and oracles.

## CHAPTER XXII

**ARGUMENT.—**He now explains the nature of demons, knowledge of whom, he teaches, was imparted even by philosophers and poets. He next expounds their spiritual substance and thence deduces their manner of acting upon men so as to harm them. It is shown that by its deceits this activity aims solely to make credulous mortals abandon the true God and become enslaved to false religion.

Accordingly, we say that there are certain spiritual substances; [Col. 0405A] nor is the name new. Philosophers know demons, since Socrates himself waited upon the judgment of his daemon. Why not? For a daemon is said to have attached itself to him from childhood—plainly one that discouraged him from the good. [Note: [Col. 0405B] “Discouraging. Plainly from the good.” Previously the passage was everywhere read and punctuated thus: “is said. All poets know that Orpheus discourages from the good.” But Rigault rightly emended it and placed a comma after “is said”; we also place a full stop after “discouraging.” For that genius or daemon of Socrates was celebrated as discouraging him if some evil threatened or confronted him; indeed, Tertullian says mockingly, “from the good,” namely as turning him away from it. I therefore punctuate thus: “is said to have been discouraging. Plainly—from the good”; that is, he certainly had a daemon, but one that discouraged him from the good. Thus “τὸ (“the”; an isolated Greek article whose contextual function is uncertain)” frequently means “plainly,” and in *To the Nations* I.10: “Plainly, since heaven lies open to them,” that is, “indeed, rightly.” Thus Lactantius aptly says, Book I, ch. 14: “But although they are themselves destroyers of men, they nevertheless wish to appear their guardians, so that they themselves may be worshiped and God may not be worshiped.” The passage might also be punctuated: “is said to have been discouraging. Plainly from the good.” But however the punctuation is arranged, no other meaning is possible than the one we have given. Caspar Barth, certainly misled from the truth by bad punctuation, goes astray; after considering these words in his *Adversaria*, Book V, ch. 5, he wishes the reading to be, “The poets know that Orpheus discourages from the good,” so that those poems and hymns, which survive even today under his name and are quite ancient, might thus be indicated. But the wiser pagans who spoke of Socrates’ daemon understood nothing other than his provident mind, which was discerning in future matters. Hence Xenocrates the philosopher, in Aristotle’s *Topics* II, calls each person’s mind “δαίμων ἑκάστου ἡ ψυχὴ (“each person’s soul is a daemon”),” a daemon; in the same place he calls a person to whom a good mind had fallen “εὐδαίμονα (“fortunate” or “blessed”).” Euripides too, imbued with Socratic wisdom, said in Theon, *Progymnasmata*, p. 60, “τὸν νοῦν ἡμῶν ἑκάστου θεὸν (“that the mind of each of us is a god”; the recovered θεὸν, “god,” conflicts with the surrounding explanation, which says “daemon”)”—that each person’s mind was his daemon. HAV.]

Poets know demons; even the uneducated populace commonly uses the word as a curse. For from the same intrinsic consciousness of the soul it also utters, with the same word of execration, the name of Satan, [Note: [Col. 0405B] Wouwer from a manuscript, and Rigault, read “demons”; the others, “all.” Havercamp and others read “commonly uses Satan.” But the words “for also,” which occur in the Gorze and Lyons manuscripts, are neither superfluous nor to be rejected.] the prince of this evil race. [Note: [Col. 0405D] “For it also utters Satan with a word of execration.” What? Did the Romans ever use the word *Satan* in curses or execrations? Certainly not. But they designated Satan, the prince of evil demons, by uttering “Evil.” RIG.—The meaning of the words here seems to me to be this: “Even the uneducated populace now commonly employs as a curse Satan, the author of this race”—namely, of demons; hence, with the best witnesses, I placed the punctuation after “race.” Since he appeals here to the consciousness of the soul, he necessarily treated it more fully in the little book *On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 3. Its words indeed receive illumination from this passage. They are as follows: “You call a man a daemon because of uncleanness, malice, insolence, or any blemish whatsoever which we attribute to demons, or because he is intolerably hateful. Finally, in every aversion, disdain, and detestation, you utter ‘Satan,’ whom we call the angel of malice,” etc. For just as among Christians “the Evil One” stands absolutely for the Demon and Satan, so here in Tertullian “Satan” and “daemon” stand for an evil being. HAV.]

Plato did not deny the angels either. Even the magi serve as witnesses to both names. [Note: [Col. 0405B] Thus the Fulda manuscript; Rhenanus, Pamelius, and others read “even the magicians assert”; [Col. 0406B] the Puteanus manuscript, “even the magi are present,” which Rigault, Havercamp, and Semler adopted.] [Note: [Col. 0406B] “Even the Magi are present as witnesses to the existence of both names.” This is certainly the reading of the ancient Puteanus manuscript, and I consider it truer than the Fulda reading, “even the magi assert.” Septimius says that the names “demons” and “angels” are not unknown even to men alien to God’s city: “Philosophers know demons,” he says; “poets know them. Plato does not deny angels either.” He then adds: “Even the Magi are present as witnesses to the existence of both names.” That is: witnesses are present; they are present to testify; they are present to give evidence—namely, that both demons and angels exist. On the following page he himself says that magicians possess a power of invited angels and demons standing beside them. RIG.]

But how from certain angels, corrupted by their own choice, there emerged the still more corrupt race of demons, [Note: [Col. 0406C] “Concerning angels.” Tertullian too held that foolish opinion that demons were born from the mingling of angels with human beings, through a misunderstanding of Genesis 6:2. Thus again in *On Idolatry*, ch. 9: “Those angels were deserters from God, lovers of women.” Lactantius too, Book II, ch. 15: “Accordingly, while they were dwelling with human beings, that utterly deceitful ruler of the earth gradually enticed them into vices through the very intimacy and defiled them by intercourse with women,” etc. But Augustine was wiser; see him in *City of God* XV.23.] [Note: [Col. 0406D] “Race of demons.” Lactantius in the same place: “But those who were begotten from them, because they were neither angels nor men but bore a certain intermediate nature, were not received into the lower regions, just as their parents were not received into heaven.”] condemned by God together with the founders of their race and with the one whom we have called their prince, [Note: [Col. 0406D] “And with the one whom we called their prince.” The Fulda manuscript reads: “and the order which we called prince—or the holy writings—is known.” Lactantius again: “These are the unclean spirits, the authors of the evils that are committed, whose prince is likewise the devil.” Hence Trismegistus calls him “δαιμονάρχον (“ruler of demons”).”] is known in due order from the sacred writings. [Note: [Col. 0406B] Semler reads “the order.”]

For now it will be enough to explain their activity. Their activity is the overthrow of man: [Col. 0405B] thus spiritual malice took its beginning from the very first for the destruction of man. Accordingly, they inflict upon bodies both diseases [Note: [Col. 0406D] “And inflict diseases.” He seems to me to have in view public officials who punish men, inflict blows, and torture them. In the same manner John Chrysostom, in his discourse *On the Devil the Tempter*, calls the devil himself “ἀσὼματον δήμιον (“an incorporeal executioner”),” as though saying “an incorporeal executioner.” And he applies here God’s statement to the devil, “ἄψαι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ (“touch his flesh”), touch his flesh.” That is: “I appoint you public executioner for the infliction of wounds.” LAC.] and certain bitter accidents; upon the soul, violent, sudden, and extraordinary derangements. Their own marvelous [Note: [Col. 0406B] “Marvelous” is absent from Franeker and Rigault.] subtlety and tenuity provide them access to both substances of man.

Spiritual powers are capable of much, so that, being invisible and imperceptible, they appear in their effect rather than in their own action. It is just as when some hidden corruption in the air brings fruit or crops prematurely to the ground in blossom, kills them in the bud, or wounds them in their maturity; or as when the air, attacked by some unseen cause, pours out its pestilential breaths. By the same obscurity of contagion, therefore, the breath of demons and angels also produces corruptions of the mind through frenzies and foul madnesses, or savage lusts accompanied by manifold errors. Chief among these errors [Col. 0406B] is the one by which it commends those gods to the captivated and ensnared [Col. 0407A] minds of men, so that it may also procure for itself its proper nourishment of sacrificial smoke [Note: [Col. 0407B] “Of sacrificial smoke and blood, may procure.” The commentators have learnedly and industriously assembled very much here, to which may be added what has been noted on similar passages of Minucius and Arnobius. For those fools believed that their gods were marvelously delighted by that sacrificial smoke, so much so that what was stench to themselves and to us was nectar to the gods. Hence in Homer, Jupiter, not ungrateful to the Trojans, commends their generosity, *Iliad*, “Δ (“Book 4,” denoted by the Greek letter delta),” verse 48.]

Restoration notes: S000607 reads δηλακρίων, but the recovered form and its precise meaning are uncertain.; S000611 is corrupt or severely truncated; only ἀλλ` (‘but’) is securely intelligible.; S000612 is corrupt or severely truncated and cannot be translated securely.; S000613 is only a truncated word beginning κῶλ-, so its meaning is uncertain.; S000607 reads δηλακρίων, but the recovered epithet’s precise form and meaning are uncertain.; S000608 appears corrupt, though the surrounding Latin securely gives the intended sense “pursuing meat.”; S000611 is corrupt or severely truncated; only ἀλλ` (“but”) is securely intelligible.; S000613 contains only a truncated word beginning κῶλ-, so its meaning is uncertain.  

Οὐ γάρ μοί ποτε βωμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐίσης,
Λοιβῆς τε, κνίσσης τέ (“For my altar was never without its due feast, libation, and savor”). That is: “For my altar was never without its due feast, libation, and savor.” This folly is often censured by Lucian, but especially notably by Theodoret, *Discourse* VII, p. 104, which I recommend that you consult. Σφόδρα γὰρ αὐτοὺς χαἰρείν (“For they take exceedingly great delight in them”), etc. It is in this sense that Tertullian says in *To the Martyrs*, ch. II: “You are not lashed by filthy savors.” Theodoret, again in the same place, p. 110, shows from the words of Socrates that God is indeed unworthy of nothing, and that sacrifices of this kind possess nothing beyond smoke and, in fact, an exceedingly offensive stench [Col. 0407C]: καπνοῦ δὲ πλέον οὐδὲν ἔχουσιν αἱ τοιαῦται θυσίᾳ, καὶ καπνοῦ δυσοσμίας μεστοῦ (“Such sacrifices possess nothing beyond smoke—and smoke full of foul odor”). And yet they believed that their gods had an extraordinary appetite for this savor. Hence Nonnus, on *Oration II of Nazianzen against Julian*, p. 818: “All demons, rejoicing in the savors of sacrifices, are gluttons”; but Mercury is especially branded by this name. Hence he is also called δηλακρίων (the recovered Greek epithet; its precise form and meaning are uncertain), as though δήων κρέα (“pursuing meat”; the recovered spelling appears corrupt), that is, “one who pursues meat.” And so those wretched gods were wretchedly starving when no sacrifices were offered. Thus Mercury in Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, Act I, Scene I, 21:

Καὶ τῶν μὲν ἄλλων μοι Θεῶν ἧττον μέλει (“And I am less concerned about the other gods”).

Ἐγὼ δ` ἀπόλωλα κα` πιτέτριμμαι (“But I am ruined and utterly worn away”).

That is: “I am less anxiously concerned about the other gods; but as for myself, I have perished, utterly consumed by hunger.” Jupiter fears the same thing in Lucian’s *Menippus*, p. 302, and in the same author’s *Twice Accused*, p. 307: ἀλλ`α`στ (corrupt or truncated recovered Greek; only ἀλλ`, “but,” is securely intelligible), etc.; that is: “But the temples will be without garlands, the streets without savor, the mixing bowls without libations, and the altars everywhere cold—in short, everything will be without [Col. 0407D] sacrifices and victims, and there will be great hunger.”

Again Aristophanes writes wittily in *The Birds*: ἀντισρ (corrupt or truncated recovered Greek; meaning uncertain). κῶλ (truncated recovered Greek, apparently the beginning of a word; meaning uncertain). In the same work, verse 32, where Prometheus says: Ἀπόλωλεν ὁ Ζεὺς (“Jupiter is ruined”), etc. Ανεν θυηλῶν (“Without sacrifices”).

**PROMETHEUS:** Jupiter is ruined.  
**PISTHETAERUS:** How long is it since he was ruined?  
**PROMETHEUS:** Ever since you settled the air. For no mortal now sacrifices anything further to the gods, nor has the savor from thigh-bones risen to us since that time; instead, although it is the festival of Ceres, we fast without sacrifices.

Accordingly, when even the Jews had passed over to this foolish opinion, God rebuked them in Ps. 50:13; Isa. 1:11; Jer. 6:20; Amos 5:22; and elsewhere. Obviously God, the creator of the universe, has no need of any odor or blood. For these are the foods of demons, as our author rightly says in *To Scapula*, ch. II. “For what is more foolish, what feebler, than God’s exaction of bloody sacrifices and reeking burnt offerings?”—to use his own words in *Against Marcion*, book V, ch. 5. How, then, is he to be worshiped? In the manner in which Tertullian, in another sense, addresses idolaters in *On Idolatry*, ch. V: “You worship, however, not with the breath of some utterly vile savor, but with your own; not by expending the life of a beast, but your own life.” **HAV.**]

—and procures blood through what is offered to statues and images; and, as a choicer nourishment for them, they turn a human being away from reflection upon the true divinity through the tricks of false divination [Note: [Col. 0407A] Most manuscripts read *a cogitatu*; some, *e cogitatu*. Rigalt reads *a recogitatu*; Havercamp, *recogitatu*. Before the word “humanity,” Rhenanus inserted *qua*; Heraldus, *quam ut*; Rigalt, *nisi ut*, adding a question mark after “divination.”]. I shall explain how they perform these very things.

Every spirit is winged; such are angels and demons. They are therefore everywhere in an instant: the whole world is for them a single place [Note: [Col. 0408A] Havercamp reads “where.”]. What is happening everywhere they know [Note: [Col. 0408B] “They know as readily as they announce.” The Fulda and Leiden manuscripts read “announce,” but he says that immediately afterward. Relevant here is an elegant jest of Lucian in the work entitled *The Ship*. There, among those foolish wishers, the last wishes for the ring of Gyges, by putting on which he could be seen by no one; and so, among other things, he says: “And, what would be most delightful of all, on one and the same day I could report in Babylon who had won at Olympia; and if by chance I had eaten luncheon in Syria, I could dine in Italy.” “And to what purpose is all this?” he adds shortly afterward: “And I should seem a god to all the rest”: καὶ Θεὸς ἐδόκουν τοῖσ ἄλλοις (“And I should seem a god to the others”). **HAV.**] as readily as they announce it [Note: [Col. 0408A] Junius, from the manuscripts, reads “announce.”]. Their speed [Col. 0408A] is believed to be divinity because their substance is unknown.

Thus, too, they sometimes wish to appear the authors of the things they announce; and they plainly are sometimes the authors of evils, but never of good things. They both intercepted God’s arrangements when the prophets formerly proclaimed them [Note: [Col. 0408A] Franeker reads, “Now they excerpt them.”], and now gather them from the readings when they are recited. Thus, taking from these sources certain allotments of future times, they rival divinity while stealing divination [Note: [Col. 0408B] “They steal divination”—that is, snatch it. Vincent of Beauvais, a writer not to be despised for his period, speaks quite aptly with regard to the force of this word: “Man, when he was held in honor, did not understand, because he swelled with pride against the truth that illuminated him. For, armed with a fat neck, he ran against God with head held high; and while he wished to seize Divinity itself, thwarted and mocked by his own assault, [Col. 0408C] he collapsed upon himself under a certain weight of his iniquity.” So he writes in those immense volumes that he entitled the *Fourfold Mirror*, in the *Doctrinal Mirror*, book II, ch. 1.

How elegantly, moreover, Paul spoke of our Savior in the opposite and true sense in his *Epistle to the Philippians*, ch. 2:6: Ος ἐν μορφῇ
Θεοῦ ὑπάρχων, οὐχ ἀρπαγμ
ὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἷσα Θεοῦ (“Who, existing in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized”), denying that he rivaled divinity, because he could take from his own whatever he wished. Thus tyrants or emperors created through wrongdoing were said among the Romans to “seize” imperial power. A passage of Aelius Lampridius in his *Alexander Severus* fits beautifully: “For it suited neither the dignity of the senate to confer all honors at once, nor a good emperor to rush upon so many dignities at once and seize them.”

To this I also refer the following passage of Vopiscus in his *Life of Tacitus*: “Then, from hatred of the present rulers, the army, which had been accustomed hastily to create an emperor, sent a letter to the senate asking it to choose a prince from its own order.” Ausonius, in *The Caesars*, epigram XX, beautifully veils the ambition of Severus the African under an honorable title:

[Col. 0408D]  
The gods be praised that Didius does not enjoy rich spoils,  
And that the rewards were quickly snatched from the perjured old man.  
And you, father Severus, do not shrink from the title of innovator:  
Your might does not seize imperial power, but receives it back.

So too we may say that Christ did not seize the heavens, but that the heavens received him. Certainly Peter says in Acts 3:21: Ον δεῖ οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι ἄχρι χρόνων ἀποκαταστὰσεως πάντων (“Whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things”). In place of *dum*, the Leiden manuscript wrongly prefers “of God.” **HAV.**].

But Croesus knows, and Pyrrhus knows, with what ingenuity they adjust the ambiguities in oracles to suit their outcomes [Note: [Col. 0408D] “They adjust ambiguities to outcomes.” Lactantius II.15: “And therefore they are accustomed to adjust their answers to ambiguous outcomes,” drawing from our author. Hence I do not approve “the outcome,” which the Fulda manuscript has, although I also found it thus in the Leiden manuscript.

Theodoret, p. 193; Lucian, in the *Dialogue of Juno and Latona*: Ο δὲ Απόλλων προσποιεῖται (“But Apollo pretends”), etc.; that is: “Apollo pretends that he knows everything, can shoot arrows, play the lyre, practice medicine, and prophesy. And after setting up his shops of prophecy here at Delphi, there at Claros and [Col. 0409B] Didyma, he deceives those who consult him by answering obliquely and in terms bent toward either side of the proposed question, so that, of course, he cannot be convicted of error.”

And in the *Auction of Lives*, the buyer says to Heraclitus: Αἰνίγματα λέγεις (“You speak riddles”), etc.; that is: “Ho there! Are you speaking riddles, or composing puzzles? For, just like Apollo, you explain nothing.”

And Momus cleverly says to Apollo himself in *Jupiter Tragoedus*: Τοῦτο μὲν ὁρθῶς ελέξας (“This, indeed, you have said correctly”), etc.; that is: “Indeed, Apollo, you spoke correctly in praising those who employ clarity in their speeches, although you yourself are not usually much accustomed to employ that very quality in issuing and delivering oracles, but confidently cast forth many double-edged statements entangled in ambiguity, so that those who hear them need another Pythian to interpret the oracles.”

There are many similar passages in Arnobius, Minucius, and others. Nor did Lucian himself neglect the subject in *The False Prophet*. **HAV.**].

The Pythian announced that a tortoise was being boiled with the flesh of an animal [Note: [Col. 0409B] “With the flesh of an animal.” The Fulda manuscript reads “with the flesh of cattle”; and immediately afterward the same manuscript has “they had been” instead of “he had been.” Soon afterward the Leiden manuscript reads “denounced” instead of [Col. 0409C] “announced.” Nor did Lucian neglect to ridicule this. In him Momus again says to Apollo in *Jupiter Tragoedus*, p. 212: Λέγε, μόνον σαφῆ δὲ (“Speak—but only clearly”), etc.; that is: “Speak, Apollo, but only in language so clear that it needs neither advocate nor interpreter. For sheep’s flesh or a tortoise is not being cooked in Lydia; you know perfectly well what the consultation concerns.” **HAV.**] in the manner we stated above: in an instant he had been in Lydia [Note: [Col. 0409C] “In an instant he had been in Lydia.” As though he said that, at the very moment when the tortoise was being boiled by Croesus, he had been in Lydia—[the following words are corrupt: “which in Pyrrhus he was announcing”].

But, as Zephyrus notes in his paraphrase, “They possess,” etc., means “they are capable of knowing the preparations.” It is a Greek mode of expression, which our own writers do not avoid, as in “I have many things to say,” that is, “I can say them.” And Cicero to Lentulus: “Concerning the Alexandrian affair and the royal cause, I have only this to promise: that I, in your absence,” etc.

I do not recall having read the noun *paratura* elsewhere. Yet it is formed by the same analogy as *scissura* and *commissura*; Pliny used *divisura*, and *volatura* for *volatus*, which can appear no less novel. **PAM.**].

From their dwelling in the air, their proximity to the stars, and their commerce with the clouds [Note: [Col. 0409D] “They possess, from dwelling in the air.” Others have noted the phrase “they possess the capacity to know.” He says that, because they inhabit and have their dwelling in the air, are near the stars, and are accustomed to the clouds, they can know the condition of the air and thus predict rain, drought, pestilence, and famine. For they imagined these demons suspended in the air like spiders.

Lactantius II.15: “Those who were begotten from these, however, because they were neither angels nor men but bore a certain intermediate nature, were not received into the underworld, just as their parents were not received into heaven. Thus two kinds of demons arose, one celestial, the other terrestrial. These are unclean spirits, the authors of the evils that are done, and the same Devil is their prince.”

On Pythagoras’ opinion, Diogenes Laertius says in his *Life*: Εἶναί τε πάντα τὸν ἀέρα ψυχῶν ἔμπλεον· καὶ τούτους δαίμονάς τε καὶ ἥρωας νομίζεσθαι (“The whole air is full of souls, and these are considered demons and heroes”), that is, “Indeed, the whole air is full of souls, and they are considered demons and heroes.” He derived this from the teaching of the Chaldeans, concerning whom the same Diogenes says in his *Proemium* that they assert εἰδώλων πλήρη εἶναι τὸν ἀέρα, κατὰ ἀπόῤῥοιαν ὑπὸ ἀναθυμιάσεως εἰσκρινομένων ταῖς ὄψεσι τῶν ὀξυδερκῶν (“The air is full of apparitions, which enter the sight of keen-eyed observers by an efflux arising from evaporation”), that is, “that the air is full of demons, which subtly flow into the eyes of those who see them, as though from evaporation.” **HAV.**], they possess the capacity to know celestial preparations, so that they promise rains which they already sense. They are plainly poisoners [Note: [Col. 0409B] The Fulda manuscript reads “poisoners”; the others, “benefactors.”], even in their treatment of illnesses. For first they inflict harm [Note: [Col. 0410B] “For first they inflict harm.” Above: “They also inflict injuries upon bodies and health,” etc. Pythagoras himself does not deny this: Ὑπὸ τούτων (“By these”), he says, πέμπεσθαι ἀνθρώποις τούς τε ὀνείρους, καὶ τὰ σημεῖα, νόσους τε καὶ ὑγιείας· καὶ οὐ μόνον ἀνθρώποις, ἀλλὰ καὶ προβάτοις, καὶ τοῖς ἀλλοις κτήνεσι (“Dreams and signs, diseases and health, are sent to human beings—and not only to human beings, but also to sheep and other livestock”), that is: “By them dreams and signs, diseases and health as well, are sent upon human beings; and not only upon human beings, but upon cattle and beasts of burden.” This occurs in his *Life* by Diogenes Laertius. The Leiden manuscript reads “first of all.” **HAV.**]; afterward they prescribe remedies that are astonishingly new or even contrary, and after these they cease to inflict harm [Note: [Col. 0410B] “After these they cease to inflict harm”—that is, once those new and unusual remedies have been applied. But Rhenanus and Aldus [Col. 0410C] read: “or even contrary; after they cease,” etc.; that is, when they no longer inflict harm, they wish to appear benefactors and saviors.

John of Salisbury, a bishop exceptionally learned in his age, had this passage in view when he left the following written about the priests and prelates of his own time, in the book he entitled *Policraticus*, book VI, ch. 24: “They more often do harm, and in this imitate the demons, because they are thought to benefit people when they cease doing harm.” That writer lived in the eleventh century. **HAV.**], and are believed to have effected the cure.

Why, then, should I discuss the other devices or even powers of spiritual deceit—the apparitions of the Castors, water carried in a sieve, a ship [Col. 0410A] moved by a girdle [Note: [Col. 0410C] “And a ship moved by a girdle.” Herodian relates in book I of his *History* that the vessel by which the goddess of Pessinus was being conveyed along the Tiber suddenly stopped by some divine power and could not thereafter be moved by any force, until a Vestal priestess came forward. Herodian does not name her, but Ovid celebrates her as Claudia in the *Fasti*, and Livy writes of her in book 29.

Since she was accused of having violated her virginity and feared condemnation, she asked the people to entrust judgment concerning her to the goddess of Pessinus. When this was granted, she prayed aloud to the goddess that, if the goddess knew her to be undefiled, she should command the ship to proceed. Having said this, she unwound her girdle and tied it to the ship, which at once followed the maiden as she drew it by hand. Lactantius, book II, ch. 7. **LAC.**], and a beard turned red by a touch [Note: [Col. 0410D] “A beard turned red by a touch.” All these matters are well known from historians and commentators: the messengers of the Macedonian victory; the Vestal maidens Tuccia and Claudia; and Domitius Ahenobarbus, with reference to whom Martial writes in book VIII, epigram 52:

A young barber, but so great in skill  
As not even Nero’s Thalamus was—  
To whose lot fell the beards of the Drusi.

For Nero belonged to the Domitian clan and the family of the Ahenobarbi; see Suetonius in his *Life*, ch. 1 and following. Through his mother Agrippina, however, he was connected with the Drusi. **HAV.**]—which caused stones to be believed divine powers and the true God not to be sought [Note: [Col. 0409B] The Fulda manuscript reads: “did not accomplish by what means”; hence Havercamp suspected the true reading to be: “they accomplished that he should not be sought.”]?

## CHAPTER XXIII

**ARGUMENT.—Although the power of demons is great, he teaches that it is subject to a greater power, namely Christ’s. Christians therefore triumph even over that power when, by Christ’s might, they cast out unclean spirits, even against their will. In obeying Christ’s command, these spirits themselves deny their own divinity and acknowledge his alone.**

Moreover, if magicians produce apparitions [Note: [Col. 0410D] “Magicians produce apparitions.” Whatever they do, they do through the power of demons who minister to them. How much more easily, then, can the demons themselves accomplish the same thing while acting in their own cause? Apuleius says of them [Col. 0411B]: “Each of their number takes care, according to the province allotted to him, either of confirming dreams, examining the fissures of entrails, directing favorable birds, inspiring prophets, hurling thunderbolts, and all the other means by which we foreknow the future.” **HAV.**], malign the souls of those already [Col. 0411A] dead [Note: [Col. 0411A] Franeker reads “call upon.”] [Note: [Col. 0411B] “Malign the souls of the dead.” This is a most excellent reading restored by Rigalt from the Fulda manuscript and praised also by Junius. I too found it in the Leiden manuscript, as did Heraldus in his manuscripts. Our author himself writes in *To the Nations* I.5: “who malign the truth by the outward appearance of the word”; and II.7: “You malign heaven with the tombs of your kings.”

Nor, with Pamelius and others, would I prefer “call upon.” For it is to malign the souls of the dead when the shades of brave and distinguished men are raised, or are pretended to be raised, at the pleasure of a most impure witch; for they are nothing but mere trifles and deceptions. Hence Samuel’s righteous indignation is represented as rebuking Saul: “Why have you disturbed me, causing me to be raised?” 1 Sam. 28:15.

In the *Life of Aedesius* by Eunapius of Sardis, one may read that when a certain Egyptian summoned Apollo, and an apparition appeared, astonishing those present by its appearance, Iamblichus said: “Cease wondering, my friends; for it is the specter of a gladiator who died in single combat.”

Nor is a more attractive reward offered by the Thessalian witch to the corpse raised for the benefit of Sextus Pompey—that it would never again be exposed to any similar dishonoring—in Lucan, book VI, 762:

“Speak,” says the Thessalian, “what I command,  
And gain a great reward from me; for if you speak the truth,  
We shall make you forever immune throughout the world  
From Thessalian arts. With such a tomb,  
And with such wood and a Stygian spell, I shall burn your limbs  
That your enchanted shade will hear no sorcerer.  
Let it be worth so much to have lived again: neither words nor herbs  
Will dare to break for you the sleep of long oblivion  
After the death I give.”],

if they strike boys down to produce the utterance of an oracle [Note: [Col. 0411A] So the Fulda and Leiden manuscripts and those of Heraldus, and the editions of Rigalt, Havercamp, Semler, and Ritter. All the others read: “call upon—draw forth.”] [Note: [Col. 0411C] “They strike them down to produce the utterance of an oracle.” This reading of Junius’ Fulda manuscript, the manuscripts of Heraldus and Leiden, and Rigalt is entirely correct; others read “draw forth.” Junius interprets it of the sacrifice of boys, a kind of divination called βρεφομαντεία (“infant-divination”), or paedomancy. See Elmenhorst on Gennadius, pp. 195 and 210, and Boniface, *Playful History*, book VIII, ch. 21. La Cerda, Heraldus, and Rigalt understand it as causing the boy to fall after the fashion of a prophet. Both interpretations are true.

Lucan, in the same work, verse 554, acknowledges the practice in magical rites:

Nor does she shrink from slaughter, if the sacred rites demand  
Living blood and entrails quivering  
Upon the funereal table.

Effective, therefore, is the speech by which the witch wishes the gods below to recognize their due, verse 707:

If I never chant these spells fasting from human flesh,  
If often I have given you breasts filled with blood,  
And washed entrails cut out in a still-warm brain;  
If any infant whose head and inward parts  
I placed upon your dishes was destined to live—  
Obey my prayer.

Yet I think the latter meaning more suitable here, in the sense in which, in the same poet, book I, 695, a Roman matron, ceasing to prophesy,

Lay abandoned by her exhausted frenzy.

Read from the manuscripts, “abandoned by frenzy.” To “strike down” is to suffocate the breath. Lactantius, or Luctatius Placidus, in his *Epitome of Ovid’s Metamorphoses*, book VII, ch. 2: “that she might restore Aeson, crushed by old age, to youth.” Flavius Vopiscus says in his *Florian* that this was done by straining the limbs: “A certain fanatic in the temple of Silvanus cried out with limbs strained.” **HAV.**];

if they perform many miracles through the tricks of conjurers; if they also send dreams, since they have permanently at their service [Note: [Col. 0412B] “At their service,” etc. Diogenes Laertius says of the Chaldeans in his *Proemium*: Ασκεῖν τε καὶ μαντικὴν καὶ πρόῤῥησιν καὶ αὐτοῖς Θεοὺς ἐμφανιζεσθαι λέγοντας (“They also practice divination and prediction, asserting that gods appear to them”), that is: “They also practice divination and prediction, asserting that gods appear to them.” **HAV.**] the power of the angels and demons whom they have invited, through whom goats and tables [Note: [Col. 0412B] “Goats and tables.” Diodorus writes in book XVI that goats first gave an oracle at Delphi. Tables too were enlisted by the pagans for the same divination, and spoke through the work of demons. Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

Here from every side was the wealth of Troy,  
Snatched from the burning sanctuaries, and the tables of the gods.] have been accustomed to divine—how much more will that power, of its own choice and on behalf of its own business, strive with all its strength to perform what it supplies to the business of another?

Or if both angels and demons perform the same things [Col. 0412A] as your gods, where then is the preeminence of divinity, which surely ought to be believed superior to every power [Note: [Col. 0411A] Thus the Fulda manuscript; the others read: “which surely ought to be believed to be superior.”]? Is it not therefore more fitting to presume that these themselves make themselves gods, since they produce the very effects that cause gods to be believed in, than to suppose that the gods are equal to angels and demons?

A difference of places creates the distinction, I suppose, so that from their temples you consider them gods [Note: [Col. 0412B] “It creates the distinction, I suppose, so that from their temples.” Wouwer restored this excellently from a manuscript, with La Cerda’s approval. So too the Fulda manuscript, except that it reads “in temples.” I wonder that Rigalt did not follow it. Scriverius’ collation does not differ greatly: “distinguishes, as I suppose, from temples”; if this were restored, it would have to read: “It distinguishes, as I suppose; from their temples you consider them gods,” etc. One might also read “it is distinguished, I suppose.” But because of what follows, I prefer Wouwer’s text.

The printed editions read: “It is distinguished, I suppose, so that from their temples.” There is a passage in Minucius, p. 30, that commentators compare with this one: “These are the frenzied men whom you see running out in public; they too are prophets without a temple, and are mad in this way,” etc. Heraldus did not understand this passage, and while it escaped him, he corrupted it by reading: “they too are prophets in the temple itself.” His error arose because he punctuated it wrongly.
