But without doubt Tertullian had in mind the witty jest of his Lucian, whom Minucius follows everywhere. In Lucian’s *Jupiter Tragoedus*, the wretched Apollo is challenged by Momus—since he was regarded as the greatest prophet—to predict, then and there in the council of the gods, which of the sophists disputing about the gods and their worship would be victorious. He has no reply except this ridiculous one: Πῶς (“How”), [Col. 0412D] ὧ Μῶμε, δυνατὸν ποιεῖν ταῦτα, μήτε τρίποδος ἡμῖν παρόντος, μήτε θυμιαμάτων, ἢ πηγῆς μαντικῆς, οἵα ἡ Κασταλία ἐστιν (“O Momus, could these things be done when neither a tripod nor incense is present for us, nor a divinatory spring such as Castalia?”), that is: “How could this possibly be done, Momus, when neither my tripod nor incense is present, nor a divinatory spring such as Castalia?” **HAV.**] [Note: [Col. 0412A] Wouwer, from a manuscript, and Havercamp read “distinguishes”; the Fulda manuscript reads: “distinguishes, I suppose, as in temples,” etc. Latinius and Rigalt read “you consider”; the others, “you regard.”], though elsewhere you do not call them gods; so that one who flies over sacred towers may appear to be mad in one way [Note: [Col. 0412D] “To be mad.” Rigalt restored this from the Fulda manuscript, a reading Pamelius and others also embraced. I found it thus in the Leiden manuscript. The Basel, Aldine, and Rhenanus editions read “to make mad.” The Latin-Greek Glossary gives: “he makes mad,” ἐξίστησιν (“he makes mad” or “drives out of one’s senses”). ιδιωτικῶς (“in ordinary usage”). Hence in later Latin *dementatus* and *dementator* mean, respectively, a person alienated from his mind and one who perverts another’s mind. The word “to make mad” appears to signify rather a force inflicted upon another; “to be mad” means to be insane.

In *On the Soul*, ch. XVIII: “For when the man is mad, the soul too is mad.” Indeed Lucretius himself, III.464:

Indeed, amid diseases of the body, the mind often  
Wanders astray; for it is mad and speaks deliriously.

So nearly all the manuscripts, including the Vossian and Leiden copies. Lambinus should not have attempted to substitute “makes mad.” **HAV.**] [Note: [Col. 0412D] “One who flies over sacred towers,” etc. To this I refer the leap from the Leucadian rock near the shrine of Apollo, by which lovers believed that they were freed from love—as though any other rock would not accomplish the same thing, giving death in return for life. Ovid, in *Sappho’s Epistle*:

That place maintains this law: seek lofty  
Leucas at once, and do not fear to leap from the rock.

The folly of Elagabalus differs little. Lampridius says of him: “He had therefore prepared ropes twisted from purple silk, silk, and scarlet, with which, if necessary, he might end his life by hanging. He had also prepared golden swords with which to kill himself if some violent necessity pressed him. He had also prepared poisons in thunderstones, hyacinths, and emeralds, with which to kill himself if anything more serious threatened. He had also constructed a very high tower, with gold and jeweled tablets laid beneath it, from which he might throw himself, saying that even his death ought to be costly and display luxury, so that it might be said that no one had ever perished in this manner.” **HAV.**], and one who leaps across neighboring rooftops in another; and so that one kind of power may be declared present in him who cuts off his genitals or his arms, another in him who cuts his own throat. The outcome of the frenzy is alike, and there is one cause of the instigation.

But enough of words thus far. From this point comes a demonstration of the thing itself, by which we shall show that the character of both names is one and the same.

Let someone be brought forward here before your tribunals who is known to be driven by a demon. If commanded to speak by any Christian, that spirit will as truthfully confess itself a demon as elsewhere it falsely professes itself a god. Let someone likewise be produced from among those who are thought to suffer from a god—those who, breathing over altars, conceive the divine power from the savor; who are healed by belching [Note: [Col. 0413C] Thus all the manuscripts; Rigalt emends it to “attempt”; Havercamp, “bend.” I do not know whether one should read “are seized” or “rush forward.”], and who utter prophecies while panting [Note: [Col. 0413D] “They utter prophecies while panting.” This did not occur without confusion of the voice and extremely forceful breathing. Lucan, V.148:

From a tranquil breast she reports invented  
Words, with no murmur of a confused voice  
Bearing witness that her mind is impelled by sacred frenzy.

And shortly afterward:

No words broken by a trembling  
Sound, no voice sufficient to fill the space  
Of the capacious cavern, etc.

Add verse 170 and those that follow. But these matters cannot be learned better than from Donatus’ note on Terence’s *Phormio*, Act IV, Scene IV, on the words “The soothsayer forbade it.” There that very ancient and excellent interpreter writes: “A soothsayer is one who prophesies under divine inspiration. He is called *hariolus*, as though *fariolus*, from fate and from speaking, since F is used for H, and likewise H for F, in many expressions. Or is it because they imitate aspiration in exhaling? For by their breath they are accustomed to expel, as it were, their mortal soul, so that they may receive a divine one; hence they also utter a sound of this kind, OE, because the sound OE conveys the force of exhalation.” **HAV.**].

That very Heavenly Virgin [Note: [Col. 0414C] “The Heavenly Virgin.” Junius understands Juno, the principal divinity of the Carthaginians, concerning whom we have spoken above at ch. XII. La Cerda also discusses her excellently at the following chapter, showing that she is called the Virgin, and that the mention of rains, which descend from the air, is not inappropriately joined to her here. Hence Orpheus certainly says in his hymn to her:

Ὄμβρων μὲν διερῶν, ἀνέμων τροφὲ, παντογένεθλε (“O nourisher of drenching rains and winds, all-generating one”).

“Mother of rainstorms, producer of winds of every kind.”

Fabulous antiquity did not pass over Juno the Virgin in silence; Pausanias is my witness, near the end of his *Corinthian Matters*: Καὶ πηγὴ Κάναθος καλουμένη· ἐνταῦθα τὴν Ἤραν φασὶν Αργεῖοι κατὰ ἔτος λουμένην παρθένον γίνεσθαι· οὗτος μὲν δή σφισιν ἑκ τελετῆς ἣν ἂγουσι τῇ Ηρᾳ, λόγος τῶν ἀποῤῥήτων εϛίν (“There is also a spring called Canathus. The Argives say that Hera, bathing there every year, becomes a virgin again; this is one of their secret accounts from the rite they perform for Hera”), that is: “And a spring whose name is Canathus. Among the Argives it is commonly reported that whenever Juno bathes in that spring each year, she becomes a virgin again.” This account flowed from the mysteries of the initiatory rites performed for Juno according to solemn custom. The Aldine manuscript very badly reads “the heavenly voice,” as does Rhenanus, “the heavenly power.” **HAV.**], who promises rains; that very Aesculapius, who reveals medicines and supplies life to Socordius, Thanatius, and Asclepiodotus, though they are to die on another day [Note: [Col. 0414D] “Though they are to die on another day.” Rigalt excellently restored this from the Fulda manuscript, which has “though he is to die on another day,” while Heraldus’ manuscripts have “though they are to die.” For he ridicules that grant of life [Col. 0415C] which must nevertheless be exchanged for death shortly afterward. The common reading is “though otherwise they are to die.” Aldus, however, reads “though they are to die on another,” as do the Leiden and Agobardine manuscripts, making it clear that τὸ (the Greek article “the”), “day,” dropped out.

In the *Jugurthine War*, ch. 106, Sallust makes Sulla, undaunted amid dangers, reason with Volux in this way: “Even if certain destruction were at hand, he would rather remain than, by betraying those whom he commanded, preserve by a shameful flight a life that was uncertain and perhaps destined shortly afterward to perish by disease.” **HAV.**]—unless they confess themselves demons, not daring to lie to a Christian, then and there shed the blood of that most insolent Christian!

What could be more manifest than this deed? What more trustworthy than this proof? The simplicity of truth stands in full view; its own power supports it. No suspicion will be possible. You will say that it is done by magic or some deception of that sort [Note: [Col. 0413C] Rhenanus and others read: “No suspicion will be possible; that it is done by magic,” etc. “Do not stand by the statements, if,” etc. Rigalt and Havercamp accepted the reading of the Fulda manuscript. The Bongars manuscript has: “that it is done by magic in what is said.” The Puteanus, Leiden, and Agobardine manuscripts read: “You say it is done. You will not say so, if,” etc.], if your own eyes and ears permit you. But what objection can be maintained against that which is shown in naked sincerity?

If, on the one hand [Note: [Col. 0413C] The Leiden manuscript reads “of nature”; hence Havercamp suspects “by nature,” or “truly by nature.”], they truly are gods, why do they falsely call themselves demons? Is it in order to obey us? Then your divinity is already subject to Christians; and that which is subject to a human being, and indeed to its own rivals—which adds to the disgrace—must certainly not be regarded as divinity.

If, on the other hand, they are demons or angels, why do they answer elsewhere that they act as gods? For just as those who are regarded as gods [Note: [Col. 0414C] The Paris manuscript reads “are called.”] would have been unwilling to call themselves demons if they truly were gods, precisely so as not to divest themselves of majesty, so too those whom you know directly as demons would not dare elsewhere to act as gods if there were any gods at all whose names they use. For they would fear to misuse the majesty of beings undoubtedly superior [Note: [Col. 0414C] Franeker reads “superior majesty”; the Paris manuscript, “a superior majesty.”] and therefore to be feared.

Thus the divinity that you maintain does not exist at all, because, if it existed, it would neither be laid claim to by demons [Note: [Col. 0414C] Rhenanus and others read: “would neither be laid claim to in confession,” etc. Rigalt and Havercamp deleted the two words “in confession,” which had been added for purposes of interpretation.], nor denied by gods. Since, therefore, both parties concur in a confession denying that they are gods, recognize that both are one kind of being—that is, demons.

But now seek gods in both places [Note: [Col. 0414C] Franciscus Junius, Havercamp, Semler, and Ritter punctuate: “demons indeed. In both places now seek gods,” etc.], for you have learned that those whom you had presumed to be gods are demons. By the same operation of ours, however, through which those same gods of yours disclose not only that they themselves are not gods [Note: [Col. 0414C] The Paris manuscript adds “are.”], nor are any others [Note: [Col. 0414C] The Paris manuscript adds “but.”], you also learn immediately who truly is God; whether it is he, whether he is the one God whom we Christians profess; and whether he is to be believed and worshiped as the faith and discipline of Christians have established.

Then and there they will say who this Christ is, together with his “fable”: whether he is a human being of ordinary condition; whether a magician; whether after death [Note: [Col. 0415C] Havercamp reads “cross.”] he was stolen from the tomb by his disciples; whether he is now, in short, among the dead; or whether he is not rather in heaven [Note: [Col. 0415C] Semler reads “more swiftly.”], and destined to come from there amid the convulsion of the whole world, amid the terror of the earth, amid the mourning of all—but not of Christians [Note: [Col. 0415C] Franeker reads “if not.”]—as the Power of God and the Spirit of God and the Word and Wisdom and Reason and Son of God.

Whatever you ridicule, let them ridicule it with you. Let them deny that Christ will judge every soul from the beginning of time when its body has been restored. Let them say before the tribunal that, if they please, Minos and Rhadamanthus [Note: [Col. 0415D] “Minos and Rhadamanthus.” St. Justin Martyr, *Apology* II, records Plato’s agreement with the poets on this matter in these words: “Plato,” he says, “taught that Rhadamanthus and Minos would punish those who came to them unjustly; we say that this same thing will happen, but through Christ.” Athenagoras adds in his *Oration for the Christians*: “But we say that whether it be Minos or Rhadamanthus, or the father of either of them, not even he will escape the judgment of God.” **PAM.**], in accordance with the common view [Note: [Col. 0415C] The Paris manuscript reads “meaning.”] of Plato and the poets, obtained this office.

Let them at least refute the mark of their own disgrace and condemnation [Col. 0415B]. Let them deny that they are unclean spirits—something that should have been understood merely from their food: blood and smoke and the stinking pyres of cattle [Note: [Col. 0415D] “The stinking pyres of cattle.” It is well known that the ancients loaded demons with abuse. Sulpicius, concerning St. Martin: “Why do you stand here,” he says, “bloody beast? You will find nothing in me, accursed one.” **LAC.**], as well as the utterly impure tongues of their own prophets. Let them deny [Note: [Col. 0415C] Franeker and Rigalt read “let them declare.”] that because of their malice they have been condemned in advance to that same day of judgment, together with all their worshipers and agents [Note: [Col. 0415C] The Puteanus and Leiden manuscripts, Rhenanus, Aldus, and Franciscus Junius read “operations.”].

Yet all this dominion and power of ours over them derives its efficacy from the naming of Christ [Note: [Col. 0416C] “All this dominion and power of ours over them derives its efficacy from the naming of Christ.” A notable passage of Irenaeus, book II, ch. 5, expresses this view: “All things,” he says, “are subject to the name of our Lord. And for this reason the Jews even now drive demons away by this very invocation.” **PAM.**], and from the recalling of those things which they expect to befall them from God through Christ as arbiter. Fearing Christ in God, and God in Christ, they are subjected to the servants of God and Christ.

Thus, when by our touch and our breath they are seized by the contemplation and representation of that fire, they depart from bodies at our command, unwillingly and in pain, blushing in your presence. Believe them when they speak the truth [Note: [Col. 0415C] “Truth” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] about themselves, since you believe them when they lie. No one lies to his own disgrace, but rather to his honor. Credence more readily inclines toward those who confess against themselves than toward those who deny in their own defense.

Indeed, these testimonies of your gods have been accustomed to make Christians, [Col. 0416A] because by believing them very deeply we believe Christ the Lord [Note: [Col. 0415C] Wouwer prefers “the Lord in Christ.”]. They themselves kindle faith in our writings; they themselves build up confidence in our hope.

Yet, as far as I know, you worship them even with the blood of Christians. They would therefore be unwilling to lose you, who are so profitable and so dutiful to them, or to be driven out someday by you after you have become Christians [Note: [Col. 0416C] Franeker reads “to be driven out someday by Christians”; Wouwer, from a manuscript, “lest they be driven out.”] [Note: [Col. 0416D] “If they.” The sense is rather obscure, but nevertheless it is this: Believe them when, adjured by us, they speak the truth. For if they were permitted to lie when a Christian wishes to prove the truth to you, they would certainly do so, lest they lose you, who are so profitable to them—indeed, lest they should be driven from some possession of theirs by you yourselves, perhaps Christians one day. **HAV.**], if they were permitted to lie under examination by a Christian who wished to prove the truth to you.

## CHAPTER XXIV
Restoration notes: In S000646, the recovered form ὥϛε appears corrupt or typographically confused; it has been preserved verbatim and interpreted as probable ὥστε (“so that”).; In S000646, the recovered form ὥϛε appears corrupt or typographically confused; it is preserved verbatim and interpreted as probable ὥστε (“so that”).; The ending of S000641 literally appears to refer to pouring a libation upon Caesar while Caesar is being sacrificed, which conflicts with the surrounding account and may reflect corruption; it is preserved and translated without silently emending it.; S000649 is only the opening, grammatically incomplete portion of the sentence, so E014 preserves its fragmentary form.  

**ARGUMENT.—**The charge of irreligion is therefore false, and applies to the Romans rather than to the Christians. For even from this subjection of the demons it is evident that the Christians worship a God greater and [Col. 0416B] more exalted than they; and accordingly they ought at least to be allowed freedom of religion, since this is granted to others and is not denied even to the Egyptians. Yet among the Romans anything whatever may be worshipped except the true God.

That entire confession of theirs, by which they deny that they are gods and answer that there is no other God except the one to whom we are bound in service, is quite sufficient to repel the charge of having injured the public, and especially the Roman, religion. [Note: [Col. 0416D] *Having injured the public and the greatest Roman religion.* It is surprising that Rigaltius and the others did not notice this reading, but printed *having injured especially the Roman religion*. For he refutes three charges: first, the charge of injuring the religion observed everywhere by the Gentiles; then, most particularly, the Roman religion, which certainly differed from the dog-headed gods and defilements of the Egyptians, although these too were sometimes received at Rome; third, the charge of injuring the more august majesty of Caesar, namely that discussed in chapter XXVIII, to whom both the gods of the Gentiles and those of the Romans are subject. We owe [Col. 0417B] this and many other readings to the Fulda codex, which has *laesae publice et maximae R. r.* But it is well known that in many manuscripts diphthongs are not marked very accurately. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0416C] Thus Havercamp on the authority of the Fulda codex; the others: *having injured especially the Roman religion*.]

For if they certainly are not gods, then it certainly is not religion; if it is not religion, because they certainly are not gods, then we certainly are not guilty of injuring religion. On the contrary, the reproach will rebound upon you [Note: [Col. 0416C] *Resultavit*, Fran.; Reista; *resultabit*, V; Fulda codex.], who worship falsehood and, by not merely neglecting but actually attacking [Note: [Col. 0416C] *Oppugando*, Junius.] the true religion of the true God, commit against the true God the crime of true irreligion. [Note: [Col. 0416C] Thus the Fulda codex, Rigaltius, and Havercamp; the Lyons codex: *against the true*; all the others: *against God*.]

Now, even if it were established that those beings are gods, do you not concede, according to the common estimate, that there is someone more exalted and powerful, as it were the ruler of the world, possessed of perfect power [Note: [Col. 0416C] *Knowledge*, Fran.] and majesty? For most people arrange the divine order in such a way that they wish the sovereignty of supreme dominion to belong to one, while its offices belong to many; thus [Col. 0417A] Plato describes great Jupiter [Note: [Col. 0417B] *Pluto.* I think Lucian had these people in view in the *Icaromenippus*, p. 277: Οἱ δὲ ἔμπαλιν ἐπιδαψιλευόμενοι, πολλούς τε αὐτοὺς ἀπέφαινον, καὶ διελόμενοι, τὸν μέν τινα πρῶτον θεὸν ἐπεκάλουν, τοῖς δὲ τὰ δευτερα, καὶ τρίτα ἔνεμον τῆς θεότητος (“Others, conversely, being more liberal, declared them to be many; after dividing them, they called one the first god and allotted to the others the second and third ranks of divinity.”), that is: “Others, on the contrary, being more liberal, created many gods; after dividing them into ranks, they named this one the first god, while assigning to the others the second or third portions of divinity.” Hesiod multiplied them to thirty thousand:

Τρὶς γὰρ μύριοί εἰσιν ἐπὶ χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ

Ἀθάνατοι Ζηνὸς φύλακες θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων (“For upon the bountiful earth there are thirty thousand immortal guardians of mortal men belonging to Zeus.”).

Thus Varro, not without reason, recorded both certain and uncertain gods, [Col. 0417C] and Prosper of Aquitaine after him, *Promises and Predictions* III.38. But to what purpose are they, when Socrates had already declared that God had no need of them or of their οἰκείας λειτουργιαις (“their own proper offices”), the offices proper to each, as Theodoret observed from Plato himself, *Cure of the Greek Affections*, p. 110. HAV.—*Plato, great Jupiter.* Athenagoras relates this passage of Plato as follows: “That great leader in heaven, Jupiter, you find adorning his winged chariot”—these very words are cited by D. Justin in his *Address to the Gentiles*—“ordering and caring for all things. He is followed by the army of gods and demons.” This, he says, does not refer to the one said to be the son of Saturn, namely Jupiter; for by that very name the creator of the whole universe is designated. Plato himself makes this clear. For since he had no other name by which to designate him meaningfully, he used the common and customary name of God, though it was by no means God’s proper name, for the sake of a clearer designation; he further added the word *Great*, to distinguish the heavenly from the earthly, the unbegotten from the begotten. The same point is briefly repeated by Arnobius, [Col. 0417D] book I *Against the Gentiles*, or may be inferred from the title by which Jupiter is called and regarded as “Best and Greatest.” PAM.] in heaven, accompanied by an army of gods and demons alike. Accordingly, they hold that agents, prefects, and governors must also be received. [Note: [Col. 0417B] Rhenanus and others: *received*.]

And yet what crime does a man commit who, in order to earn Caesar’s favor more fully, transfers both his service and his hope to him, and acknowledges the title “god,” just like that of “emperor,” in no one other than the prince—when it is judged a capital offense either to call or to hear another person called Caesar besides Caesar himself?

Let one man worship God, another Jupiter; let one stretch suppliant hands toward heaven, [Note: [Col. 0417D] *Toward heaven.* Demonax in Lucian, when invited by a friend to accompany him to the shrine of Aesculapius to pray for his son’s health, said: πάνυ, ἒφη, κωφὸν ἡγῇ τὸν Ασκληπιὸν εἰ μὴ δύναται κᾀντεῦθεν ἡμῶν εὐχομένων ἀκούειν (“You consider Asclepius very deaf,” he said, “if he cannot hear us praying even from here.”). “You describe a very deaf god,” he said, “if he cannot hear us even from here.” HAV.] another toward the altar of Faith; let one, if this is what you think, count the clouds while praying, [Note: [Col. 0417D] *Let another count the clouds while praying.* Christians generally assembled in open courts and, when praying there, looked up to heaven without altars and without statues. The pagans therefore mocked them as though they were counting the clouds while praying; and so Tertullian refutes one absurdity with another. “We,” he says, “count the clouds; you count the recessed panels of the temples—that is, of the Capitols.” Thus he himself, book I, p. 37: “You seek heaven at the Capitol; you await clouds from coffered ceilings.” PAM.] [Col. 0418A] another the ceiling panels; [Note: [Col. 0417D] *Another the ceiling panels.* This refers to the Gentiles, among whom the coffered ceilings of temples were gilded. See Lipsius, book III *On the Greatness of Rome*, chapter 5; Meursius, *On Luxury*, chapter XII; and Rycquius, *On the Capitol*, p. 200. Against them rebounds the accusation they made against Christians and Jews, that they counted the clouds. For when sacrificing at the Capitol, they themselves stood upright not only with their hands raised, but also balanced upon their toes, [Col. 0418B] as though counting the ceiling panels. Martial writes of Aethon, book XII, epigram 78:

> While greeting Jupiter with many prayers,  
> Standing, bent backward, high upon his toes,  
> Aethon hung suspended in the Capitol.

HAV.] let one dedicate his own soul [Note: [Col. 0418B] *Another his own soul.* Prosper, in his book of epigrams:

> Whoever carefully considers in his heart what he should vow to the Lord,  
> Let him prepare and vow his entire self.  
> For no greater victim can be offered upon the altar of the mind,  
> Nor does a sweeter fragrance issue from Christ’s temple.

He expressed Augustine’s thought: “Whoever carefully considers what he should vow to God and what vows he should discharge, let him vow and render himself. This is required; this is commanded: let Caesar’s image be rendered to Caesar; let God’s image be rendered to God.” But, as Philo the Jew beautifully says in the treatise *That the Worse Is Wont to Attack the Better*, etc.: Πεπλάνηται καὶ οὗτος πρὸς ἀσέβειαν ὁδοῦ (“This man too has strayed from the path, toward impiety.”), etc.; that is: “That man has strayed from the life of piety who locates holiness in ceremonies and gives gifts to one who is not won by them and never accepts any other gifts, and who flatters one who cannot be cajoled, because he delights in true worship, in which the soul offers truth as its sole and unique sacrifice; but he turns away from counterfeit worship, such as displays of external wealth.” HAV.] to his God, another the soul of a goat. [Note: [Col. 0418C] *Another a goat’s soul.* The Fulda manuscript has *another a he-goat*. He is referring to sacrifices. Compare *On Idolatry*, chapter VI, though in another sense: “You worship, however, not with the vapor of some utterly worthless odor, but with your own spirit; not by expending the life of a beast, but your own life.” A he-goat or billy-goat was customarily sacrificed both to Pan and to Bacchus. The familiar little verse about Domitian, who was destroying vineyards, appears in Suetonius, chapter XIV:

Κἤν με φὰγῃς ἐπὶ ῥίζαν, ὅμως ἔτι καρποφορήσω,

   Ὅσσον ἐπὶ σπεῖσαι Καίσαρι θυομένῳ (“Even if you devour me down to the root, I shall nevertheless still bear enough fruit to pour a libation upon Caesar when he is sacrificed”—the recovered final wording is contextually doubtful.).

As one might say in Latin:

> [Col. 0418D] Gnaw the vine, billy-goat; yet when you stand at the altar because of it,  
> There will still be wine enough to pour upon your horns.

Gems illustrate the matter, one borrowed from du Choul and another from Gorlæus. *Dactyliotheca* I.21.]

Take care lest it also contribute to the indictment of irreligion [Note: [Col. 0417B] *Excurrat*, Leiden manuscript.], that you take away freedom of religion and forbid a choice of deity, so that I am not permitted to worship whom I wish but am compelled to worship whom I do not wish. No one will wish to be worshipped by an unwilling person [Note: [Col. 0418B] *Would wish*, Fran.], not even a human being. And yet even the Egyptians have been granted the power to practice so empty a superstition: to consecrate birds and beasts, and to condemn to death anyone who kills any god of that kind.

Every province and city likewise has its own god: Syria has Atargatis; [Note: [Col. 0418D] *Syria has Atargatis.* I have thus restored the text from the excellent Fulda codex, which has *Adargatis*. This reading is supported by testimony from book II *To the Nations*, chapter 8: “How many are there who know by sight or hearing even Argatis [read: Atargatis] of the Syrians, and the Heavenly Goddess of the Africans,” as Gothofredus correctly reads there and uses that passage to correct this one. For this goddess received various names. Strabo, at the end of book XVI: Αἱ δε τῶν ὀνομάτων μεταπτώσεις, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν βαρβαρικῶν πολλαί καθάπερ τὸν Δαριήκην Δαρεῖον ἐκάλεσαν, τὸν δὲ Φάρζιριν Παρύσατιν, Αταργατὴν δὲ τὴν Αθάραν (“Changes of names, especially barbarian names, are numerous: for example, they called Dariaces ‘Darius,’ Pharziris ‘Parysatis,’ and Atargatis ‘Athara.’”)—Casaubon corrects Ἀθάραν (“Athara”) at Athenaeus, book VIII, chapter 8—Δερκετὼ δὲ αὐτὴν Κτησίας καλεῖ (“Ctesias calls her Derceto.”); that is: “Changes of names are very numerous, especially among barbarians: thus they called Dariaces ‘Darius,’ Pharziris ‘Parysatis,’ and Atargata ‘Athara’; Ctesias called her Derceto.” She is also called Derceto or Dercetis by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.45, and Pliny, *Natural History* V.13; and in Hyginus the mother of Semiramis is called by this name in Fable CCXXIII, where he made Semiramis the daughter of Dercetis. But that god Atargatis [Col. 0419A] was worshipped under this name especially in the Syrian city of Bambyce. Strabo, book XVI: Ὑπέρκειται δὲ τοῦ ποταμοῦ, σχονους τέτταρας διέχουσα ἡ Βαμβύκη, ἣν καὶ Ἔδεσσαν καὶ Ἱερὰν πόλιν καλοῦσιν: έν ᾗ τιμῶσι τὴν Συρίαν θεὸν τὴν Αταργατιν (“Beyond the river, at a distance of four schoeni, lies Bambyce, which they also call Edessa and the Sacred City; there they honor the Syrian goddess Atargatis.”); that is: “Four schoeni beyond the river is Bambyce, which they also call Edessa and Hierapolis, that is, the sacred city. In it they worship Atargatis, the Syrian Goddess.” She provided the hungry little Greeks with a witty tale in Athenaeus, book VIII, chapter 8: Ὄτι Γάτις ἡ τῶν Σύρων βασίλισσα οὕτως ἦν ὀψοφάγος, ὥϛε κηρύξαι ἄτερ (“That Gatis, queen of the Syrians, was so fond of delicacies that she proclaimed, ‘apart from—’”; the recovered ὥϛε is uncertain, probably ὥστε.) [Col. 0419B] Γάτιδος μηδένα ἰχθὺν ἐσθίειν, ὑπ` ἀγνοίας δὲ τοὺς πολλοὺς αὐτὴν μὲν Ἀτέργατιν ὀνομάζειν, ἰχθύων δὲ ἀπέχεσθαι (“—Gatis, no one should eat fish’; but through ignorance most people called her Atergatis and abstained from fish.”); that is: “Gatis, queen of the Syrians, was so greedy for delicacies that she issued a proclamation through a herald forbidding anyone ἄτερ Γάτιδος (“apart from Gatis”), that is, anyone except Gatis, to eat fish; and through ignorance of the facts many called her Atergatis and abstained from fish.” Add Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*, p. 884. Concerning Astarte and the deities that follow, consult at this passage Junius and la Cerda—from whom the commentators on Minucius took most of their material—as well as Pithoeus, *Subseciva* I.V, chapters 3 and 4; Floridus Sabinus, *Subseciva* II.7; Scaliger, *On the Emendation of Time*, among the fragments, p. 27; Kippingius, *Roman Antiquities* I.6; and above all Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*. The common editions have *Astartes of Syria*; the Aldine, *Astartis*. HAV.]

Arabia has Dusares; [Note: [Col. 0419B] *Dusares.* Write it thus with the Fulda manuscript, which has *Duzares*. For the Arabs seem especially to have worshipped two deities, Obodas and Dusares, as Gothofredus correctly observes when emending the form *Obodanedussirem* that occurs in the book *To the Nations;* he likewise shows from Hesychius that Dusares is [Col. 0419C] Bacchus. Barræus and Rhenanus have *Diasares*; the common text, *Disares*. HAV.]

the Norici have Belenus; [Note: [Col. 0419C] *The Norici have Belenus.* The Aldine incorrectly has *Norico Tibelenus*, and Pamelius, *Norici Belenus*. But perhaps one should write *Norico Belenus*, to agree with the others. Mention of this god occurs frequently in inscriptions collected by Gruterus and Reinesius. The latter, commenting on inscription 51 of book I, notes that Belenus is assigned to the Norici by Tertullian because the people of Aquileia were situated on the border of Noricum and Illyricum, in the territory of the Carni; they were a part of, and once rivals to, the Veneti, but are now their subjects. For this was the tutelary deity of the city of Aquileia, as is very clearly evident both from the passage in Capitolinus’ *Maximini* cited by the commentators and from inscriptions found there, which the very learned Reinesius examines and explains there together with their god Belenus. To him should deservedly be added Jacobus Nicolaus Loensis, who collected numerous inscriptions from the ruins of Aquileia and discussed Belenus, the Norici, and the people of Aquileia at length in *Miscellanea Epiphyllides* V.15. The indefatigable defender of antiquity Gruterus included this work in his *Critical Lampas*, in the supplement to volume five. See also Scaliger, *Ausonian Readings* I.10; Le Moyne, notes on *Varia Sacra*, p. 622; and finally Philippus a Turre, *Monuments of Ancient Antium*. HAV.]

Africa has the Heavenly Goddess; [Note: [Col. 0419D] *Africa has the Heavenly Goddess.* Nor are writers silent about this goddess. She was in fact Juno, the tutelary deity of Carthage. See what we noted above on chapters XII and XXIII. Various inscriptions concerning her also occur in Gruterus and Reinesius; and the Loensis just praised assembled a most excellent chapter on her, though plundered by later writers, book VII, chapter 13. Monuments of her also survive on the gems of Gorlæus II.566 and on coins. Prosper of Aquitaine also mentions her in *Promises and Predictions* III.38, describing her memorable temple and a marvelous event he himself witnessed with his own eyes. Since the complete passage is highly worthy of reading and was not noticed by the commentators on Tertullian, I shall not hesitate to transcribe it:

“In Africa, at Carthage, there was said to be a temple of the Heavenly Goddess, exceedingly large and surrounded by shrines of all their gods. Its paved court, adorned with a mosaic pavement, precious columns, and walls, extended for nearly two miles. When, through neglect, it had long remained closed and become buried beneath thorny thickets growing around it, and the Christian people wished to reclaim it for the use of the true religion, the pagan populace cried out that dragons and asps were there to guard the temple. All the more inflamed with zeal by this, the Christians easily removed everything without injury, [Col. 0420B] in order to consecrate the temple to their own true heavenly King and Lord.

“For when the holy solemn festival of Easter was being celebrated, a multitude had assembled there, including many priests and people arriving from every direction out of curiosity. Our father and bishop Aurelius, worthy of remembrance and now a citizen of the heavenly homeland, held and sat upon his chair there in the place of the Heavenly Goddess. I myself was present at the time with companions and friends; and while—as the impatient nature of youth turned us about in every direction—we curiously inspected every single thing in accordance with the building’s vast size, something marvelous and incredible presented itself to our sight: an inscription written in large bronze letters upon the temple’s façade: ‘The pontiff Aurelius dedicated it.’ The people who read this marveled. The event had been accomplished by a prophetic spirit, and God’s foreknowing order had brought it to completion with this definite end.

“And when a pagan prediction, supposedly issued by that same Heavenly Goddess, was produced by someone, declaring that both the road and the temples would be restored again to the ancient rite of worship, that true God, I say, whose prophetic predictions know neither how to lie nor to deceive, under Constantius and Augusta Placidia—whose son Valentinian, a pious Christian, now reigns—and through the insistence of the tribune Ursus, [Col. 0420C] had all those structures razed to the ground, leaving the site, naturally, as a burial ground for the dead. And now a Vandal hand has destroyed the road itself, leaving no memory of it.”

Trebellius Pollio, in his account of Celsus, who is numbered among the Thirty Tyrants, teaches that this same goddess was customarily adorned with a robe: “They proclaimed Celsus emperor, adorned with the robe of the Heavenly Goddess.” Likewise, in Ammianus, the philosopher Asclepiades is said to have carried a small image of the Heavenly Goddess with him everywhere, so that he was recognized by it. Nor can there be any real doubt about the source from which her worship became established at Carthage, since Phoenician Dido is known to everyone and Pausanias writes so explicitly in his *Attica*: Πρώτοις δὲ ἀνθρώπων Ασσυρίοις (“First among mankind, to the Assyrians…”; the recovered clause is incomplete.), etc.; that is: “The Assyrians were the first of all mortals to worship the Heavenly Goddess. The Paphian people in Cyprus received the rite of her worship from them, together with the Phoenicians who inhabit the city of Ascalon in Palestine; the Phoenicians communicated it to the people of Cythera.” *Attica*, p. 14, Wechel edition, 1583.

Although she is celebrated there as Venus, nothing prevents the Africans from applying the same title to their own Juno, [Col. 0420D] for Juno, Luna, and Venus alike are called “Heavenly.” Lucian, *Dialogues of the Courtesans*, dialogue VII: Αν ἔτι τοιουτον εραστήν εὕρωμεν (“If we find another such lover in the future.”), etc.; that is: “Therefore, Musarium, if in future we find a lover like this Chaereas, we must sacrifice: to Public Venus a white she-goat, but to the Heavenly Goddess and to her who is in the Gardens, a heifer, certainly.” HAV.]

Mauretania has its own petty kings. [Note: [Col. 0420D] *Mauretania has its own petty kings.* Lactantius I.15: “For this reason, of course, the Romans consecrated their Caesars, and the Moors their kings”; and shortly afterward: “The Moors consecrated Juba.” There is a similar passage in Cyprian, but Minucius is more polished than either: “And Juba, because the Moors so willed it, is a god.” To this I relate the passage in Spartianus where he notes the cruelty of the emperor Severus: “The slayer, therefore, of so many and such illustrious men is regarded by the Africans as a god.” For he was African by birth. Hence Ausonius writes of him:

> Punic was his origin, but by his excellence he proved  
> That birthplace is no impediment when talent is strong.

HAV.]

I have listed Roman provinces, I think, yet not their Roman gods, [Col. 0420A] since these are worshipped at Rome no more than those who are enrolled as deities by municipal consecration throughout Italy itself: Delventinus of the people of Casinum; [Note: [Col. 0419A] This is the reading of the Fulda codex, approved by Havercamp. For *Casiniensium* others have *Casianensium*, *Casianentium*, or *Crustuminiensium*; for *Delventinus*, *Belventinus*; for *Narniensium Visidianus*, *Narnensium Viridianus*; for *Aesculanorum*, [Col. 0420A] *Asculanorum*—Reinesius conjectures *Faesulanorum*; for *Nortia*, *Norsia*, *Norcia*, *Nursia*, *Nurscia*, or *Nersia*; for *Ocriculanorum*, *Otriculanorum* or *Cericulanorum*; for *Sutrinorum Hostia*, *Sutrinorum Nortia*.]

Visidianus of the people of Narnia; [Col. 0421A] Ancharia of the people of Aescula; [Note: [Col. 0421B] *Of the people of Aescula.* Some, including Rigaltius, read *of the people of Asculum*. But book *To the Nations*, the Aldine edition, Heraldus, Rhenanus, and the Leiden manuscript read otherwise. Restore *of the people of Faesulae*, from Reinesius’ emendation. For Ancharia or Ancaria was a local deity of this Etruscan people, who worshipped her image or statue. This is very clearly evident from an inscription discovered at Faesulae, an ancient town of Etruria, which states that a noble citizen restored at his own expense the goddess’s image after it had fallen through age or some other accident:

> L. MAGILIUS L. F. PAVLLINVS VARISCUS III VIR SIGNVM ANCHARIAE [Col. 0422C] SVA PEC. RESTITV. L. D. D. D.

Reinesius published it in *Inscriptions* II, inscription 23. Turnebus, *Adversaria* XVII.24, thinks that those inspired by this goddess’s divine power, or perhaps her ministers, were called *Ancarii*. HAV.]

Nortia of the people of Volsinii; [Note: [Col. 0421C] *Nortia of the people of Volsinii.* I have preferred to write it thus with the Leiden codex, supported by the Fulda manuscript; the Agobard manuscript has *Norsia*, the Puteanus manuscript *Norcia*, and Tertullian himself has the clearer reading *Vulsiniensium Nortia* in *To the Nations*. Barræus, the Aldine, Heraldus, and Rigaltius read *Nursia*; Pamelius, Rhenanus, Junius, and la Cerda, *Nersia*. The manuscripts of Livy and Juvenal vary among *Nursia*, *Nortia*, and *Nurscia*; but an old inscription found at Florence, produced by Reinesius I.131, clearly calls her Nortia:

> TO THE GREAT GODDESS NORTIA.

Livy teaches that this was certainly the peculiar deity of the people of Volsinii; in him Cincius records that nails marking the number of years were fixed in her temple. And Juvenal, Satire X:

> That same populace, if Nortia had favored her Etruscan,  
> If the old age of the prince had remained secure and unoppressed,  
> Would at this very hour have called Sejanus Augustus;

as Lipsius observed on book IV of Tacitus’ *Annals*, where Tacitus reports that Sejanus was born at Volsinii. HAV.]

Valentia of the people of Ocriculum; Hostia of the people of Sutrium; [Note: [Col. 0421D] *Hostia of the people of Sutrium.* I have reproduced the reading of the Fulda codex. For some names of tutelary goddesses and gods are quite unknown to us, as this one is. Perhaps Juno Lucina herself was called by some such name. For according to Isidore, book VIII, chapter 11, some say *Juno* as though *Janona*, that is, “the door,” in reference to the purifications of women, because she opens, as it were, the doors of mothers’ offspring—that is, of married women—to their husbands. Correct this to: “she opens the doors of nature or for offspring, and of married women to their husbands.” Thus she might have been called *Hostiaria*, or *Hostia*, or by some similar term, though I would not venture to assert it. The common text has *Nortia of the people of Sutrium*. But I do not think that Nurscia belonged to the people of Volsinii and Nortia to the people of Sutrium, since the varied manuscript readings in all the authors sufficiently show that it was the same goddess, though her name was pronounced in different ways. HAV.]

and, among the people of Falerii, Juno succeeded to the honor of Father Curis and from him received her surname. [Note: [Col. 0422B] *To the honor of Father Curis, and from him Juno received her surname.* Junius and Rigaltius restored even these words, almost buried by antiquity, from the manuscripts; thus also the Agobard codex. Junius reads from Puteanus, “Among the people of Falerii, Juno possesses the honor of Father Curis, and from him received her surname.” Yet the Leiden manuscript is perhaps still better; in these names it demonstrates its remarkable quality. In it I found the following written: “Among the people of Falerii, Juno succeeded to the honor of Father Curris and received his surname.” For throughout this work scribes confuse *in honorem* and *in honore*. I believe that they also pronounced the name *Curris*, as Rigaltius wrote in the text, although *Curis* is printed in the notes. Unless one wishes to explain it with Junius: “Among the people of Falerii Juno possesses the honor of Father Curis, and indeed received her surname from him.” Rigaltius was also assisted by the Fulda codex, which has: “to the honor of Father Chumis, and from him Juno received her surname.” All the common texts have: “In honor is Father Curis, whence Juno received her surname.” But it is sufficiently clear that Tertullian intimates that the Juno of the people of Falerii succeeded to the honor of Father Curis—the name by which Jupiter is thought to have been called as prince of the Curetes—and acquired a similar name. I think that she was called *Curitis*, as Festus clearly teaches, although his mutilator Paulus Diaconus supplies another reason for the designation. Under the letter C he says: “They called Juno Curitis because they believed that she bore a spear.” On tutelary and local gods, consult also Johann Albert Fabricius, *Sciagraphia*, p. 256. HAV.]

But we alone are excluded from possessing a religion of our own. We injure the Romans and are not regarded as Romans because we do not worship the Romans’ god. It is well that there is one God of all, to whom we all belong whether we wish it or not. Yet among you there is a right to worship anything whatever except the true God—as though he were not more truly the God of all, to whom we all belong.

## CHAPTER XXV

**ARGUMENT.—**It is therefore without justification that the vast expansion of the Roman Empire is reckoned a reward for the Romans’ piety toward the gods—as though those gods had been able to confer it upon them and thus were the only gods. Yet these gods are ridiculous, shameful, or even foreign; and, if they possessed any power, they ought instead to have defended their own peoples against the Romans—a point pursued here with much wit. He also says that some of their gods had been kings, although at the time neither human beings nor those kings themselves had been without gods. Moreover, the gods were formerly worshipped with meager rites. It therefore appears that the Romans did not become great because of their religious devotion, but became religious because of their greatness. Indeed, they are not to be regarded as religious at all, since they became great by injuring religions: for they conquered the gods of other peoples together with the peoples themselves, devastated their temples, cast down their statues, and abolished their rites. Yet those peoples had been no less devout toward their own gods; nevertheless they were conquered by the Romans and absorbed into the sum of their empire.

I believe that I have sufficiently proved the nature of false and true divinity, since I have shown how the proof is established not only by discussions and arguments, but also by the testimony of the very beings whom [Col. 0422B] you believe to be gods. Nothing more, therefore, need be reconsidered in this case.

Yet since particular mention has arisen of the Roman name, I shall not omit the encounter invited by the presumption of those who say that, as the reward of their most scrupulous religious devotion, [Note: [Col. 0422C] *Of their most scrupulous religious devotion.* Thus Rigaltius and others correctly read from the manuscripts; the Leiden manuscript also reads thus. Some manuscripts, [Col. 0422D] as well as certain printed editions, have *religionis diligentissime*. The Fulda manuscript also has *of religion*, as though the phrase ought rather to refer to the gods, who had exercised particular care for the Roman commonwealth. In *To the Nations* II.17—which should be compared with Augustine, *City of God* IV, and Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, as well as with this chapter—the phrase is: “because by their observance of religious duties they earned dominion over the world.” Here too he presently repeats “to ascribe it to the merits of their religious devotion.”

Concerning this religious devotion of the Romans and the favor they believed they consequently received from the gods, there survives a splendid testimony of Cicero, Oration XXX, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, chapter 19:

“For who is so senseless that, when he looks up to heaven, he does not perceive that gods exist, but thinks that those things which are accomplished by such great intelligence that scarcely anyone can, by any art, follow the order and succession of events, happen by chance? Or who, once he understands that gods exist, does not understand that by their divine power this mighty empire was born, enlarged, and preserved? However much we may wish to love ourselves, Conscript Fathers, we have surpassed neither the Spaniards in numbers, nor the Gauls in strength, [Col. 0423A] nor the Carthaginians in cunning, nor the Greeks in arts, nor even the Italians and Latins themselves in that native and domestic intelligence peculiar to this race and country; but we have surpassed every people and nation in piety, religion, and this one wisdom—the recognition that all things are ruled and governed by the divine power of the immortal gods.”

Thus Cicero speaks as an orator. Polybius, however, called it rather what it was—superstition—adding the following political digression in book VI, chapter 54, which it will suffice to give in Latin:

“But,” he says, “I think that in no respect do the Romans surpass other peoples so much as in the opinion they hold concerning the gods. Indeed, the very thing that among other mortals is counted a fault appears to me to hold the Roman commonwealth together: I mean superstition. For, to a degree that many may deservedly find astonishing, superstition has been magnified among them and introduced both into private life and into public counsels as far as it possibly could be; and I believe they did this for the sake of the multitude. For if a commonwealth could be composed solely of wise men, that entire class of things would perhaps be unnecessary. But since every multitude is fickle, filled with unlawful desires, seething with headlong anger, and driven by rage to violence, nothing remains but that the common people be restrained by hidden terrors and terrifying fictions of this sort.”

True religion is constituted otherwise: worshipping God not from fear of punishment but from love of the good, it possesses a favorably disposed Deity of its own accord. Hence in Deuteronomy IV.6–8 Moses even makes Israel’s enemies proclaim its happiness, saying: “This people truly is wise and great.” For, as he himself adds: “What people is so great that its gods are so near to it?” etc.

The Jews may therefore argue from religious devotion to success in affairs: Rabbi Lipmann in book N, section 122, p. 158, and Rabbi Albo, discourse III, chapter XXV, *Sepher Ikkarim*, p. 14, from Genebrard’s translation: “Truly great is the people of God, the ruler of the world, since all kingdoms must be subjected to the Lord, whose scepter, sent forth from Zion, lays waste the boundaries of the Moabites and conquers the sons of Seth.”

Here, then, that enormous crowd of certain and uncertain gods whom Varro records—those eminent and chosen gods too, together with their king Jupiter himself, brandishing thunderbolts, formidable in counsel and power, as their worshippers declare, and terrible in arms—here, here they ought to have done something, if not for the world, at least for themselves, lest, indeed, one crucified man should destroy them. That they did perish we ourselves know, and the prophet David confirms it, saying: “Their memory has perished with a crash, but the Lord remains forever.” These are the words of Prosper of Aquitaine, [Col. 0423D] *Promises and Predictions* III.38.

Accordingly, our author rightly says of the Romans below in this chapter: “But how vain it is to ascribe the summit of the Roman name to the merits of religious devotion.” He refutes the same claim at the end of the chapter: “It certainly cannot be consistent with faith that those should appear to have grown through the merits of religion who, as we have suggested, either grew by injuring religion or injured it by growing.” HAV.]

the Romans were raised to such a height of greatness [Col. 0423A] that they occupied the world. [Note: [Col. 0423D] *That they occupied the world.* That is, because of this religious devotion of theirs. Havercamp refers to this an elegant relief in which the mother of the descendants of Aeneas is seen among the victorious standards of her Romans, accompanied by the gods Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, and Mercury, who appear to confirm for her the empire of the world.

Also worthy of notice is this ancient inscription, recorded by Gruterus, p. 83, no. 45, and Boissardus, part III, *Roman Antiquities*, plate 120:

> IN THE HAPPY AGE, PHISIAS, PRIEST OF ISIS THE SAVIOR. AT THE CONSECRATION OF THE PONTIFF, MAY THE GODS FAVOR THE VOWS, [Col. 0424A] THE SECRET POWERS OF THE ROMAN COMMONWEALTH AND THE DEFENSES OF THE CITY. MAY THOSE BY WHOSE WILL KINGDOMS HAVE YIELDED TO ROMAN RULE GIVE THEIR FAVOR.

Hence, in that elaborate letter which Symmachus wrote to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius in support of dedicating the Altar of Victory, Rome is introduced speaking thus: “This worship brought the world beneath my laws.”

Plutarch, however, was not so credulous: he ascribes it to the vicissitude of events [Col. 0424B] and attributes it to Fortune. Thus book I, chapter 4: “For what is peculiar to our work, and what has happened in our own time as a cause of wonder, is this: just as Fortune inclined nearly all the regions of the entire inhabited world in one direction and compelled all things to converge upon one and the same goal, so by this history we set before our readers, as though under a single view, the manner in which Fortune herself conducted herself toward the completion of this universal work.”

Rather, it was their pursuits in war and peace that placed them at so lofty a summit, together with their integrity of character, as Augustine argues in *The City of God* V.1. Indeed, Prudentius judges more reverently and truly that God softened the barbarians through the Romans and bound all peoples together by that single bond of Roman dominion, so that they might be subjected together to Christ the Lord, the stone cut out without the work of hands, and that their pride might be crushed by him. His verses in the *Passion of Saint Lawrence*, from verse 419 onward, deserve notice, as do these verses *Against Symmachus* II.582:

> Shall I tell you, Roman, what cause raised your labors  
> [Col. 0424C] To such a height? From what springs your glory grew  
> So famous that it curbs the world with imposed reins?  
> God, wishing to unite peoples discordant in language  
> And kingdoms dissonant in worship, caused whatever  
> Was tractable in manners to be subjected to a single  
> Empire, and with harmonious bonds of gentle iron  
> Established restraints by which he might hold human hearts joined,  
> Through love of religion; for no union with Christ is formed—
Worthy, unless a single mind unites the entangled nations. HAV.], and indeed that they are gods to such a degree that those who render them service beyond all others flourish beyond all others. That reward, no doubt, was credited by the gods to the Romans’ account [Note: [Col. 0423A] Fr. Jun. Rig. and Hav.: “by the Roman gods”; Cod. Fuld.: “This reward was, of course, credited by the gods as a prerogative to the Roman name.”]: Sterculius, Mutunus [Note: [Col. 0424A] Others read Sterculus, Stercutius—Mutinus, Mucunius.], and Larentina advanced the empire. For I cannot suppose that foreign [Col. 0424A] gods wished to favor an alien people [Note: [Col. 0424C] “To have favored more.” Worthy of inclusion are the observations Pomponius Laetus drew from the ancients in his *Compendium of Roman History*, chapter “On the Greatness of the Roman Empire,” at the end: “In the Second Punic War, M. Marcellus, after conquering Syracuse, displayed its wealth and brought in its statues and images of the gods. For this Q. Fabius Maximus censured him, saying that he ought to have left the gods angry with their own people, as he himself had previously done with those of Tarentum. But Marcellus’ practice prevailed. For long before, when Veii had been captured, M. Furius Camillus had brought the Juno of Veii into the city.” [Col. 0424D] For this they employed a fixed interrogative formula, as is clear from Livy, V.22: “When the human wealth had already been carried out of Veii, they then began to remove the gifts of the gods and the gods themselves, but in the manner of worshippers rather than plunderers. Young men selected from the whole army, their bodies ritually washed and dressed in white, to whom Queen Juno had been assigned for conveyance to Rome, reverently entered the temple, at first religiously laying hands upon her. Then, when one of them, whether touched by divine inspiration or in youthful jest, asked, ‘Do you wish to go to Rome, Juno?’ the others cried out that the goddess had nodded. The story was afterward embellished by saying that her voice also was heard declaring that she wished to go.” Although Livy thinks this was done here either in jest or by divine agency, it may nevertheless be gathered from Book I that it also became established as a rite. For in chapter 55, where he discusses the god Terminus, who refused to yield even to Jupiter himself, he says, “The birds did not give their assent in the shrine of Terminus”; in the *Epitome* this appears more simply: “Terminus and Juventas did not give their assent.” From this one might infer that the very images of the divinities were asked whether they wished to yield, and that their answers were divined from the auguries.] more than their own, or that they gave their native soil—in which they were born, raised, ennobled, and buried—to people from overseas.

Let Cybele see to it whether she cherished the city of Rome as a memorial of the Trojan race, namely of her own native people protected against the arms of the Achaeans; whether she foresaw that she should pass over to their avengers [Note: [Col. 0425A] “To those beyond,” Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0425A] “To their avengers.” Thus Junius from the Put. MS., and Heraldus from his manuscripts. Rig. follows Fuld., which soon afterward has *transferre*, “transfer,” for *transire*, “pass over.” Pam. reads “to those beyond,” as does La Cerda; Barr., “of her own accord to them”; Ald., Rh., MSS. L.B. and Agob., “adulterers.” The sense is that Cybele acted rightly in passing with her cult to the Romans, because perhaps she knew that avengers of Ilium would arise from them. Yet how could she foresee the fortune of so distant a time when she could not discern a few days in the fate of Aurelius? This is the sense of the passage. By subjugating Greece, the Romans indeed avenged Ilium’s destruction, and they had always held these cradle-lands of their nation in the highest honor. This is clear from Tacitus, *Annals* XII.59, and the learned observations of Justus Lipsius there. Lucan also ranges widely over this field in the person of Caesar at the end of Book IX. Appian records the impious deed of Fimbria, whereby this kinsman devastated the remains of that pitiable name more cruelly than any Agamemnon, although the city had been accepted under the protection of Sulla himself. His words in *The Mithridatic Wars* are: Ἰλιοῖς δὲ πολιορκουμένοις (“When the Ilians were being besieged”), etc.; that is: “The Ilians, when besieged by him (Fimbria), took refuge with Sulla. Sulla promised that he would come and warned Fimbria to abstain from attacking those who had surrendered to him. Fimbria congratulated them on having now returned to friendship with the Roman people, but nevertheless asked them to receive him also, since he too was a Roman; quibbling somehow about the kinship claimed by the Ilians, he finally broke in, killed everyone he encountered, and burned everything.” HAV.], whom she knew would subdue Greece, the conqueror of Phrygia.

Accordingly, she offered even to our own age a mighty proof of the majesty she had transferred to the city: when Marcus Aurelius was removed from the commonwealth at Sirmium on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, that most holy Archigallus [Note: [Col. 0425C] “Archigallus.” *On the Resurrection*, ch. XVI: “infected with the spirit either of an Archigallus, a gladiator, or an executioner.” An ancient inscription in Gruter, p. 308: “C. CAMERIUS CRESCENS, ARCHIGALLUS OF THE GREAT IDAEAN MOTHER OF THE GODS AND OF ATTIS OF THE ROMAN PEOPLE.” Thus the chief of Cybele’s eunuchs is designated. Just afterward Cod. Fuld. reads “most impure,” from a gloss intended to interpret τὸ (“the”), “most holy.” Virgil:

> To what do you not drive mortal hearts,  
> Accursed hunger for gold?]

on the ninth day before the same Kalends—the day on which, by cutting even his arms, he offered impure blood—issued the customary commands [Note: [Col. 0425C] “Issued the customary commands.” Did this Archigallus, in the customary manner, ask or command the goddess to guard Marcus’ health? I think an antiquity not yet adequately investigated lies concealed here. Just as in the Eleusinian rites there was a ruler (ἄρχων), who was king or prefect of the mysteries—Hesychius: Βασιλεὺς, ἄρχων τις Ἀθὴνησι μυστηρίων προνοῶν (“King: a certain magistrate at Athens who oversees the mysteries”)—and under his authority were joined the Overseers (οἱ Ἐπιμεληταὶ) and the Sacred Officials (Ἱεροποιοί), concerning whom see Pollux VIII.8.3 and 26, and the excellent Meursius, *Eleusinia*, ch. XV; so here also, in Cybele’s ministry, there is indicated such a king of the Galli, or Archigallus, who had under him his own sacrificers and lesser Galli, whom he likewise commanded to make vows and cut their arms for Aurelius’ safety. HAV.] for the safety of the emperor Marcus, who had already been taken from them [Note: [Col. 0425A] “Killed,” Seml.].

O tardy messengers! O drowsy dispatches [Note: [Col. 0425D] “O drowsy dispatches!” I wonder what drove Pamelius to resort metaphorically to magical dispatches of demons. Public messengers and official dispatches are meant quite simply; Tertullian is, as it were, angry with them for not having reached Cybele and her Archigallus sooner. Still less relevant are the oracles Pamelius dreams of, and the passage of Macrobius, which he did not understand, *Saturnalia* I: “Those who are absent consult this god by sending sealed dispatches, and he writes answers in order to the matters secretly contained in their inquiry.” Macrobius means what Lucian relates at length in the *Pseudomantis*. People used to send sealed notes to oracles and believed that they received them back intact, together with the god’s answer to the questions written within. But it was sheer fraud: by an artifice the wax was removed and then replaced without damaging the impressed seal, so that the questions could easily be answered. Lucian, observing this, sent a more carefully devised seal that could not be opened without an evident break, and always received ridiculous answers unrelated to his questions. HAV.], through whose fault Cybele did not learn of the emperor’s death sooner, lest the Christians laugh at such a goddess!

But surely Jupiter too would not have allowed his Crete to be shaken by Roman fasces [Note: [Col. 0426A] “Torches,” Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0426B] “That Crete by Roman fasces.” Heraldus correctly reads thus in his notes and explains it from African speech imitating Hebrew; he also adduces a similar passage from Apuleius. Virgil himself recognized a certain majesty in this pronoun and employed it for elegance where others might regard it as superfluous. Thus *Aeneid* X.707:

> And as that boar, driven from the high mountains  
> By the biting of dogs;

and Book XI:

> And as that wolf, before the hostile weapons pursue,  
> At once hid himself, pathless, in the high mountains,  
> After killing the shepherd;

and Book XII:

> That lion, wounded in the breast by the hunters’ grievous wound,  
> Only then sets his weapons in motion.

The most elegant Guilielmus Canterus, *New Readings* III.26, abundantly shows that later poets—Statius, Valerius Flaccus, and Claudian—imitated this usage. Why say more? Here is a passage of Tertullian beyond all objection, from *To the Nations* II.4: “But if that name is the proper and simple name of Divinity, and not interpretative, in that God.” Aldus, Junius, Scaliger, and Rigalt should therefore not be heard here when they read, “to be shaken by Roman fasces,” nor Pamelius, “that it should be shaken by Roman torches.” Crete was subdued by Metellus. Lucan III.163, on Caesar seizing the Roman people’s treasury:

> And Minoan Crete surrendered to victorious Metellus.

The cause of the war was impious enough, as Florus himself admits, III.7: “The Cretan War, if we wish to know the truth, was made by us solely from a desire to conquer that famous island. It seemed to have favored Mithridates; it was resolved to avenge this with arms.” Hence Mithridates himself speaks truly enough in his letter to Arsaces, preserved entire for us among the fragments of Sallust’s *Histories* IV: “For why should I speak of myself?” and shortly afterward: “the Cretans alone of all peoples free at that time, and King Ptolemy?” MS. L.B. reads “to be shaken by torches.” HAV.], forgetting that Idaean cave, the Corybantian bronzes [Note: [Col. 0426D] “Corybantian bronzes.” These are sufficiently well known from Lucretius and others. Ovid, in Lactantius I.21:

> Some strike shields with clubs, some empty helmets;  
> This is the work of the Curetes, this of the Corybantes.

The further details that may be seen there are excellently illustrated by these two coins, one of Trajan and the other of Maximinus, published by the distinguished Seguin in *S.N.*, pp. 116, 186. There the Curetes or Corybantes beat their shields so that Saturn cannot hear either the groans of Rhea bending in childbirth or the cries of the newborn Jupiter. Not merely swords but clubs are clearly visible there. Patin likewise presents a third coin of Maximinus in his *Thesaurus*, p. 123.], and the most delightful odor there of his nurse [Col. 0427A] [Note: [Col. 0427A] “The most delightful odor there of his nurse.” Germanicus likewise says in his *Aratea*:

> [Col. 0427B] She is believed  
> To have been the nurse of Jove—if Jupiter as an infant  
> Truly sucked the faithful udders of the Cretan goat.

For there was once a time when the world lay under a Jupiter not yet bearded, and he himself was reared on goat’s milk. Hence on coins and gems we sometimes see him as a boy or youth, accompanied by his she-goat. To this I refer the engravings in Gorlaeus, vol. II, no. 495, where he carries his nurse into heaven in reward for those services; no. 103, where there is only a she-goat, as on Philip’s silver coin; and vol. I, no. 189, where he sits playfully upon her, exactly as on Valerian’s silver coin. A youthful Jupiter occurs among the coins of Commodus, and Pausanias, *Eliaca* V, records a beardless image: Ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἄλλος Ζεύς οὐκ ἔχων πωγώνια (“There is also another Zeus who has no beard”); there is also another Jupiter in the same place, but beardless.

It is useful here also to defend the received reading of *To the Nations* I.10, which everyone fruitlessly disturbs by substituting “than by any Jupiter,” when the sole surviving MS. correctly reads “the little Jupiter.” This is supported not merely by the presumption afforded by the little Jupiter, who was known to all antiquity and is repeatedly mocked here in the *Apology* by Septimius, but also by the passage itself in *To the Nations*, where the little Jupiter is contrasted with Caesar. It was a solemn oath to swear by Caesar’s Genius, as is clear from the *Apology*; these Genii, commonly represented as little boys, may still be seen in marbles, whence the comparison between the little Jupiter and Caesar’s Genius is evident. But if the august divinity of Caesar, whether dead or living, is meant there, the reading is equally coherent: for what is little Jupiter beside great Caesar?

There are still many things in that little book for me to annotate and emend. Thus a little earlier in the same work: “although among you acts of perjury, because each man is pure.” Whoever enjoys raising storms in a ladle may consult the interpreters Gothofredus and Rigaltius, although changing one little letter restores the author’s entire hand. We therefore read, “as though,” etc. What, then, is to be hoped from such a god, who spent the rudiments of his life among goatherds? How finely Jesus son of Sirach, XXXVIII.26–27, says: “What wisdom can you expect from him who holds the plow, who boasts in the goad with which he drives the oxen, who is reared in their labors and speaks of young bulls? He will apply his heart to making furrows and keep watch to feed the herds.” Our author stings in his customary fashion, perhaps with an eye to Theocritus, *Idyll* VIII.76, where the cowherd Daphnis is worthy of the kisses of his calves:

> Ἁδεῖ` ἁ φωνὰ τᾶς πόρτιος, ἁδὺ τὸ πνεῦμα,  
> Ἁδὺ δὲ χώ μόσχος γαρύεται, ἁδὺ δὲ χἁ βῶς; that is: “Sweet is the heifer’s voice, sweet her breath; sweetly the calf lows, and sweetly the cow.” HAV.].

Would he not have preferred that tomb of his to the whole Capitol, so that the land which covers Jupiter’s ashes [Note: [Col. 0427D] “The land [should excel] the world.” Thus Barr., Pam., Rhen., and Rigaltius, more conveniently than “before the lands of the world,” as Aldus, Heraldus, MSS. Fuld. and L.B. read. Certainly in Seguin’s most elegant *Select Coins*, p. 114, Crete is called by the very proud title ΓΗ ΓΩΝ, that is, “land of lands,” as that noble antiquarian divides and explains the word. The coin in question bears Tiberius on one side and Augustus on the other, and was struck under the strategos Cornelius Lupus. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0428A] “Covers Jupiter’s ashes.” No one, I suppose, is unaware that in the latest period of pagan antiquity there flourished a certain philosopher, thought to have been Sicilian—Euhemerus, namely—a blind forerunner, as it were, of the apostolic preaching. He sharply attacked the old wives’ tales of a mythology already collapsing of itself, when, as Lactantius says, “he collected the deeds of Jupiter and the others who are regarded as gods, and composed a history from the sacred titles and inscriptions preserved in the most ancient temples” (*Institutes* I.11). Since the mythographers of our age and every symbolical pantheist leave no stone unturned to overturn the Euhemerian opinion completely, it will be worth some effort here to confirm more fully at least what he teaches concerning Jupiter’s death and burial as a man on the island of Crete. Although Callimachus opposed that opinion, even against his will he supports it in these verses dedicated to Jupiter:

> Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται· τὐν γὰρ τάφον, ὦ Ἄνα, σεῖο  
> Κρῆτες ἐτεκτήναντο· σὺ δ` οὐθάνες

(“Cretans are always liars; for the Cretans fashioned your tomb, O Lord—but you did not die.”). Porphyry, *Life of Pythagoras*, ch. XVII, testifies that the philosopher himself accepted this Cretan opinion, poured out many libations, and caused a poem to be inscribed upon this tomb: Εἰς τὸ Ιδαῖον καλούμενον ἄντρον καταβὰς (“Having descended into the cave called the Idaean cave”) … καθήγισε τῷ Δϊὶ, τόν τε στορνύμενον αὐτῷ κατ` ἔτος θρόνον ἐθεάσατο, ἐπίγραμμά τ` ἐνεχάραξεν ἐπὶ τῷ τάφῳ, ἐπιγράφας· ΠΥΘΑΓΗΡΑΣ ΤΩ ΔΙΙ, οὗ ἡ ἀρχὴ (“he performed sacred rites for Zeus, viewed the throne spread for him each year, and engraved an inscription upon the tomb, writing, ‘PYTHAGERAS TO ZEUS,’ whose beginning is”).

Ὧδε θανῶν κεῖται ζὰν, ὃν Διὰ κικλήσκουσι (“Here lies dead Zan, whom they call Zeus”). EDD.] should excel the whole world?

Would Juno [Note: [Col. 0428C] “Would Juno.” Cod. Fuld.: “Would Juno too.” Correctly; likewise above, “But surely Jupiter too.” Lactantius II.17: “For Juno could not dare either to defend Carthage, where her arms and chariot were, or to harm the Romans, because she had heard that a race descended from Trojan blood—

> Would one day overthrow the Tyrian citadels.”

HAV.] have wished the Punic city she loved above Samos to be destroyed by the race of Aeneas? For if:

> Here were her arms,  
> Here was her chariot; that this should be the kingdom  
> Of the nations, if only the fates permitted, even then the goddess both strove and cherished.

(VIRGIL, *Aeneid* I.16 ff.) [Col. 0428A]

That wretched wife and sister of Jupiter was utterly powerless against the fates:

> Jupiter himself stands subject to Fate.

[Note: [Col. 0428C] “Jupiter himself stands subject to Fate.” Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 85, on Jupiter and Homer: Καὶ γὰρ τούτων ὁ κορυφαῖος τὸν τῶν Θεῶν κορυφαῖον ὀλοφυρόμενον δείκνυσιν, ὡς ἐπαμῦναι τῷ παιδὶ μὴ δυνάμενον (“For even the chief of these poets represents the chief of the gods lamenting that he is unable to help his son”), etc.; that is: “When even the prince of poets introduces the prince of the gods plaintively complaining that he cannot avenge his son, because he is inferior to the son of Clotho; that he indeed wishes to undo her decree, but is prevented by Atropos and Lachesis, and therefore mingles his words with lamentations, tears, and much wailing. He likewise says that Neptune wished to take vengeance upon the leader of the Cephallenians, who put out Polyphemus’ eye, but was unable to overcome Fate, since Fate had already decreed that Ulysses son of Laertes should return to his native Ithaca.” The loquacious Lucian says innumerable things to this effect. Herald.: “to be subject to Jupiter’s Fate.” HAV.]

Yet the Romans did not consecrate so much honor to the fates [Note: [Col. 0428D] “The Romans dedicated to the fates.” Rig. transposed the words thus; others read “Romans concerning the fates.” Spanheim has this passage in view when, from the words of Procopius which he adduces, he concludes that a temple was erected to these goddesses at Rome, though after Tertullian’s time, perhaps by Diocletian. He explains a unique coin of that emperor bearing an equally unique inscription. It depicts three clothed women armed with torches, with the inscription *FATIS VICTRICIBUS*, “To the Victorious Fates”; that is, the Christian race having been conquered, subdued, and extinguished. It may be seen in the never sufficiently praiseworthy work *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, p. 838.] for surrendering Carthage to them against Juno’s purpose and desire as they did to the most prostituted she-wolf Larentina.

It is certain that several of your gods reigned. Therefore, if they possess the power to confer empire, from whom had they received that favor when they themselves were reigning? Whom had Saturn and Jupiter worshipped? Some Sterculius, I suppose, [but afterward at Rome] [Note: [Col. 0429B] “But afterward at Rome with his native gods.” There is extraordinary disorder and variation in the printed editions and MSS. Lugd. Bat. and Agob.: “but afterward the Roman woman with her unworthy ones”; Fuld.: “but afterward at Rome with his *inditamenta*.” Heraldus and Rigalt are silent; La Cerda turns elsewhere and, in the paraphrase appended to his edition, puts forward something or other about the aborigines, some of whom reigned and some did not, reading: “but afterward at Rome with his native gods; even if some did not reign, nevertheless,” etc. Aldus has: “but afterward Rome with his native worshippers”; Pam. and Rhen.: “but afterward at Rome with his native gods”; Herald. and Rig.: “but afterward at Rome with the natives.” Scioppius had written *induamentis* beside the reading of Cod. Fuld.; I read *indigitamentis*, that is, “with his pontifical books,” which serve Sterculus: a witty remark. The Glossary gives: *Indigitamenta*, Βιβλία ἱερατικά (“priestly books”). So the books and interpreters read; their great diversity amply shows that the passage was already corrupt long ago.

Do you ask, then, what I think? The words “but afterward at Rome” must be deleted and banished to Morbonia. Who does not see that they crept in from a gloss? I therefore judge that the text should read: “some Sterculus, I suppose, with his native gods”; or rather, if the MS. Fuld. does not supply *inditamentis* in vain—which I do not think it does—thus: “some Sterculus, I suppose, with his native gods and his *inditamenta*.” The interpreters erred in referring τὸ (“the term”), “native gods,” to the Romans rather than, as they ought, to Sterculus. For these are the native gods who, together with Sterculus, are the Romans’ indigenous and peculiar gods, such as Mutunus, Tutunus, and the like. He wished to call them “native gods” in the form used by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI.330:

> Yet I asked whether it were an altar of Naiads and Fauns,  
> Or of a native god.

Now some glossator, observing that these were finally worshipped at Rome long after Jupiter had been enrolled by his people among the gods, noted that this worship was rendered to Sterculus at Rome afterward; more foolish men accepted it into the text as though it had proceeded from Tertullian. HAV.], together with his own native gods [Note: [Col. 0429A] “His own” is absent from Havercamp.]. Even if some did not reign, nevertheless others reigned who were not yet their worshippers, since those gods were not yet regarded as gods. Therefore it belongs to others to bestow kingship, because kingship existed long before these gods were carved.

But how vain it is to attribute the eminence of the Roman name to the merits of religious devotion, when religion advanced only after the empire—or while it was still a kingdom, [its fortunes having already increased] [Note: [Col. 0429A] “While it was still a kingdom, did religion advance?” Fran.: “Come now, when its fortunes had increased, religion advanced.”]. For although superstitious fussiness was conceived by Numa, divine worship among the Romans did not yet consist in either images or temples. Religion was frugal and its rites poor; there were no Capitols competing with heaven, but makeshift altars of turf, vessels still of Samian ware [Note: [Col. 0429D] “Vessels still of Samian ware.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III: “I shall show that I have learned better things concerning the worship of the immortal gods from pontifical law and the custom of our ancestors, from the little sacrificial bowls Numa left us—which Laelius mentions in that little golden speech—than from the arguments of the Stoics.” Mention of that speech of Laelius also occurs among the fragments of Cicero’s *Republic* VI: “There survives a speech of Laelius which we all have in our hands, saying how acceptable to the immortal gods are the *sympina* of the pontiffs and the Samian *capedines*,” as Hadrianus Junius emended it. Samian vessels are earthenware pottery.

Indeed, Pliny expressly testifies, *Natural History* XXXIV.7, that until Asia was conquered—bringing wealth and luxury together—even the Romans’ images of the gods were only wooden or earthenware: “And it seems remarkable to me, although the origin of statues in Italy is so ancient, that wooden or earthenware images of the gods were dedicated in shrines until the conquest of Asia, from which luxury came.” Tibullus, I, Elegy 1, says of Samian vessels:

> Be present, gods, and do not disdain gifts from a poor table  
> Nor from small vessels of clay.

That old, and no less proverbial, verse of our people illustrates this:

> When chalices were made of wood,  
> Then priests were made of gold.  
> But now chalices are made of gold,  
> Now priests are made of wood.

For after clean baths were invented, those who bathe became filthier, as Seneca already said long ago, *Epistle* XXV. I have observed, however, that this proverb was taken from a saying of Boniface, bishop and martyr, preserved in the *Decretum*, Part III, *On Consecration*, distinction I, canon 44: “When,” he says, “we used wooden chalices, we had golden priests. Now we have golden chalices and wooden priests.”

John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus* VI.24, rebukes his age very sharply. There, among other remarks about priests and presbyters, he says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit in her, placing unbearable burdens upon men’s shoulders which they do not touch with a finger.
