They lord it over the clergy and do not become an example to the flock that proceeds by the straight path to life” (perhaps “that it may proceed,” etc.). “They amass costly furnishings and load their tables with gold and silver, while being excessively sparing toward themselves only in respect of avarice. For no poor man, or scarcely any, is admitted—one whom sometimes not so much Christ as vainglory introduces. They shake the churches, stir up lawsuits, set clergy and people against one another, show no compassion for those afflicted by labors and miseries, rejoice in the spoils of churches, and account every gain godliness,” etc. A little afterward in the same place: “Moreover, everyone censures him because, while the churches built by the devotion of the fathers fall and collapse, and while even the altars are neglected, he builds palaces and himself walks abroad not merely clad in purple but gilded. The priests’ palaces glitter, while in their hands Christ’s Church is befouled.” Thus far he. HAV.], smoke from them—and the God himself nowhere.

For the talents of the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0430C] “For the talents of the Greeks and Tuscans in fashioning images had not yet…” Varro related that the ancient Romans worshipped the gods without an image for more than 170 years. “Had that practice continued,” he says, “the gods would have been worshipped more chastely.” Among other things, he calls the Jewish nation as witness to his opinion. “Nor,” says Augustine, *City of God* IV, “does he hesitate to conclude that passage by saying that those who first set up images of the gods for peoples both removed fear from their cities and added error to them,” prudently judging that gods could easily be despised because of the stupidity of their images. PAM.] and Tuscans [Note: [Col. 0430D] “Tuscans.” From them the Romans borrowed many things in their sacred rites. Our author, *On the Shows*, ch. 5: “Thus in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, they also establish shows under the name of religion. From there the Romans borrow the artists they summoned, the season, and the designation.” Pliny also says of images, *Natural History* XXXIV.7: “Tuscan statues are also dispersed throughout the lands, and there is no doubt that they were commonly made in Etruria.” HAV.] had not yet flooded the city with fashioned images. Therefore the Romans were not religious before they were great; consequently they were not great because they were religious.

But how could they be great because of religion, when their greatness arose from irreligion [Note: [Col. 0430D] “From irreligion.” Thus MS. L.B., Rig., Ald., and Herald. La Cerda says that this is certainly how it must be written. Others read “from religiousness.” Cod. Pith. even has “truly from irreligion,” for which perhaps one might better substitute *revera de irreligiositate*. Mithridates, in his letter to Arsaces, Book IV of Sallust’s *Histories*, denies that from the beginning the Romans possessed anything that was not stolen—home, wives, fields, empire…; “no human or divine consideration prevents them from dragging off and destroying allies and friends, those dwelling far away and nearby, the powerless and the powerful; and they regard everything not enslaved—especially kingdoms—as hostile.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0430A] “From religiousness,” Fran.; “from true irreligion,” Jun.]? For unless I am mistaken, every kingdom or empire is acquired by wars and extended by victories. Furthermore, wars and victories are secured chiefly by capturing and overthrowing cities. That business cannot be conducted without injury to the gods [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Injury to the gods.” Livy, concerning Marcellus, the conqueror and destroyer of Syracuse, XXV.40: “He carried to Rome the ornaments of the city, the statues and paintings in which Syracuse abounded. They were indeed spoils of the enemy, acquired by the law of war; yet from that came both the first beginning of admiration for the works of Greek art and the license thereafter indiscriminately to despoil everything sacred and profane. This practice finally turned against the Roman gods themselves, and against that very first temple which Marcellus had magnificently adorned. The temples dedicated by Marcellus near the Porta Capena were visited by foreigners because of the outstanding ornaments of that kind, of which a very small part remains visible.” For thus it seems the text should be read, not “it does not seem,” etc. See Plutarch concerning the same Marcellus. HAV.]. The destruction of walls and temples is the same, the slaughter of citizens and priests alike, and the plunder of sacred and secular wealth indistinguishable.

The Romans therefore committed as many sacrileges as they raised trophies; they celebrated as many triumphs over gods as over nations; they possess as much booty as there remain images of captive gods. These gods consequently endure being worshipped by their own enemies and decree an empire without end to those whose injuries they ought to have repaid rather than their flatteries [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Flatteries,” Paris.]. Yet beings who feel nothing are harmed with as much impunity as they are worshipped in vain.

Certainly it cannot accord with credibility that those who, as we have suggested, grew by injuring religion or injured it by growing should be thought to have increased through the merits of religion. Even those whose kingdoms were fused into the sum of the Roman Empire were not without religions when they lost those kingdoms.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**ARGUMENT.—That God alone should rather be understood to reign and to dispose, as his own possessions, of empires, cities, human beings, and the very periods of time; that even before Rome was known he gave dominion to the Babylonians, Egyptians, and Assyrians; and that he long preserved even the kingdom of the Jews unharmed, although they destroyed all those gods whom the Romans and the nations regard as bestowers of kingdoms.**

Consider, therefore, whether it is not he who distributes kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0431D] “Distributes kingdoms.” The emperors themselves acknowledged that they understood this in so many coins inscribed *PROVIDENTIA DEORUM*, “The Providence of the Gods,” as is clear from those of Pertinax, Severus, Balbinus, Pupienus, Aurelian, and Antoninus Pius. Hence on a coin of Severus published by Tristan, Jupiter is even called *Imperator*, as though that title belonged to him alone. HAV.], to whom belong both the world that is ruled and the human being who rules. Consider whether it is not he who arranged the successions of dominion in their appointed times within the age: he who existed before all time [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Before all things, nor time,” cod. L.B., Agob.] and made the age [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Who made the age,” cod. Fuld.] the body of times [Note: [Col. 0432C] “Who made the age.” I prefer this with Cod. Fuld. to the reading of the others, “and the age.” Zephyrus understands it of that indeterminate age in which neither earlier nor later could be discerned, once it had been reduced to order and succession. Heraldus, however, prefers to understand it of the world; for the world is the body of times, and from its creation we number ages, years, months, and days. Beyond it we cannot distinguish the successions of times; there is eternity itself, and God himself is found to be both time and all things to himself. *Saeculum* may also be taken simply as a body of one hundred years.—HAV. “And he made the age the body of times.” A body of times is a collection or comprehensive total of many years or ages. Thus “the corpus of Homer” means all Homer’s writings, *On Laws* III. Augustine said that the order of ages was composed by God like a most beautiful poem, adorned even with certain seeming antitheses, *City of God* XI.18. LAC.]. Consider whether it is not he who exalts or lowers cities.

Under whom did the human race once exist without cities [Note: [Col. 0431C] “The human race,” Rhen., Paris; “the nation of men,” cod. Lugd.]? Why do you err? Woodland Rome is older than some of her own gods [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Her own disciples,” Rhen.]; she reigned before she built the Capitol with so vast a circumference [Note: [Col. 0431C] All codices read “before the Capitol was built”; Rhen. and Rig., “before she built.” I do not know whether the text should read: “before the Capitol was built with so vast a circumference.” Leop.].

The Babylonians too reigned before there were pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0432D] “The Babylonians before pontiffs.” Varro says in *On the Latin Language* IV that, according to Q. Scaevola the chief pontiff, they were so called from *posse* and *facere*, “to be able” and “to do.” I derive *pontifices* from *pons*, “bridge”; for the Pons Sublicius was first built and often restored by them, because sacred rites are performed on both this and the farther side of the Tiber. PAM.]; the Medes before the Fifteen; the Egyptians before the Salii; the Assyrians before the Luperci; and the Amazons before the Vestal Virgins.

Finally, if the Roman religions bestow kingdoms, Judaea—who despised these common divinities [Note: [Col. 0432C] “All,” Jun.]—would never have reigned in former times. Yet you Romans for a while honored both her God with victims, her temple with gifts, and her nation with treaties [Note: [Col. 0432C] V. Rig. deleted “Romans”; Wauwer, from a MS., reads, “sometimes, O Romans, you honored.”]; nor would you ever have become her masters had she not ultimately sinned against Christ [Note: [Col. 0432C] Thus read MSS. Fuld. and Agob.; the others have: “had she not sinned against God, ultimately against Christ.”].

## CHAPTER XXVII

**ARGUMENT.—He therefore considers that he has sufficiently refuted the charge of injuring a Divinity which, because it does not exist, can suffer nothing. He says that Christians refuse to propitiate it by redeeming their lives with incense because they know this to be the scheme of the devil, who rivals and envies them and who, although subjected to them by Christ’s power, nevertheless resists out of hatred and treachery, after the manner of penal servitude, and is never more completely triumphed over by them than through a bloody death for the faith.**

These observations are sufficient against the accusation that we injure religion and divinity [Note: [Col. 0432C] Havercamp added the words “of religion and” from Cod. Fuld.], so that we may not appear to injure that which we have shown not to exist.

Therefore, when challenged to sacrifice, we block the entrance for the sake of the faith [Note: [Col. 0433B] “For the faith.” The reading of Cod. L.B., “through treachery,” is not to be despised; it is supported by Rhenanus’ edition and MS. Agob. Tertullian would thus imply that Christians refuse to seek the escape of merely slaughtering victims, eating sacrificial meat, and burning incense without examining the occasion upon which it is done, because they would thereby render their conscience treacherous. They must oppose that treachery—that is, evil persuasion—and close every entrance into their hearts against it. In that case the following *qua*, which is now referred to “faith,” relates to conscience itself, as though he had written, “through which we are certain.” Compare Paul’s discussion concerning the eating of things sacrificed to idols (εἰδωλοθύτων) in 1 Corinthians 8:1, 8, 10. HAV.] of our conscience, through which we are certain to whom those services reach beneath the prostitution of images and the consecration of human names.

But some consider it madness that, although we could sacrifice for the moment and depart unharmed while retaining our purpose within our mind, we prefer obstinacy to safety. You are giving us, of course, advice by which we might deceive you. But we recognize the source from which such suggestions come, who sets this entire affair in motion, and how he labors—now through the craftiness of persuasion, now through the harshness of cruelty—to overthrow our steadfastness.

It is, of course, that spirit of the demonic and angelic host, who is our rival because of our separation from him and envies us because of God’s grace. From your minds he wages war against us by secret inspiration, tuning and suborning them toward every perversity in judgment and every injustice in cruelty [Col. 0433B] with which we began our discussion at the outset.

For although the whole power of demons and spirits of that kind is subjected [Col. 0434A] to us [Note: [Col. 0433B] “Spirits,” Paris, Rig.], nevertheless, like wicked slaves, they sometimes mingle defiance with fear [Note: [Col. 0433B] “Fear with occasional defiance,” Cod. Fuld.] and desire to injure those whom at other times they dread. For fear also inspires hatred [Note: [Col. 0433B] Thus Havercamp and Fuld.; the others read “breathes.”] [Note: [Col. 0433C] “Fear inspires.” I restored this from Fuld.; not “breathes,” as the others read. That is: enslaved servitude dares not openly display hatred, but fear inspires hatred in it, because one does not love the person one fears. Ennius, in Cicero, *On Duties* II: “Whom they fear, they hate; everyone desires the death of the person he hates.” Relevant here is that tyrannical saying:

> Let them hate, provided that they fear.

Seneca attacks this in *On Clemency* I.12, writing: “For he is hated because he is feared, and he wishes to be feared because he is hated.” Clearly—]

“He whom many fear must fear many,” as Publius Syrus declares, verse 435. HAV.], apart from the fact that [Note: [Col. 0433B] “Apart from and,” Fran.; “and apart from,” Rig.] their desperate condition, arising from their prior condemnation, [Note: [Col. 0433C] “From prior condemnation, consolation.” *Against Marcion*, book II, ch. 10: “Whom, nevertheless, by condemning him beforehand, he testified to have deviated through self-conceived desire from the form of his creation into voluntary wickedness.” The meaning is that unclean spirits, knowing that they are being reserved for punishment on the Day of Judgment, seek consolation for their punishment in that very interval of delay, so that meanwhile they may glut themselves with every kind of affliction of the good and enjoy their own malignity. For:

> It is a comfort to the wretched to have had companions in misfortune.

Hence also that spiteful speech of Pothinus concerning the fugitive Pompey, addressed to Ptolemy in Lucan, VIII.504:

> He asks  
> With what nation he may fall.

In Lucian, *Dialogue on the Syrian Goddess*, p. 897, some say ὡς ἡ Ἣρη φιλέουσα Κομβάβον, πολλοῖσι τὴν τομὴν ἐπὶ νόον ἒβαλλεν, ὅπως μὴ μοῦνος ἐπὶ τῇ ἀνανδρείῃ λυπέοιτο (“that Hera, because she loved Combabus, put castration into the minds of many, so that he alone might not grieve over his emasculation”), that is, that Juno, because she loved Combabus, impelled many to castrate themselves, so that he alone would not mourn having been emasculated. For he had castrated himself. “Thus assuredly he who seeks companions in his own perdition does many things throughout various lands,” says Prosper of Aquitaine, *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, dimid. temp., ch. VI. HAV.] regards the delay of punishment as a consolation for meanwhile enjoying their malignity.

And yet, when seized, they are subdued and succumb to their condition [Note: [Col. 0434B] “Sing along,” Paris.], and those whom they attack from afar they beseech when close at hand. Accordingly, when, in the manner of rebellious workhouse-slaves [Note: [Col. 0434B] Havercamp and Fuld. add “of those who resist.”]—whether from prisons, mines, or some such form of penal servitude—they break out against us, in whose power they are, they know that they are unequal to us and for that very reason all the more ruined. [Note: [Col. 0434B] “Workhouse-slaves.” There is no doubt that he speaks with reference to Roman history, in which it is a commonplace that servile men frequently rebelled. Plutarch should be consulted in his *Life of Crassus*, where the conspirators are men συρνειχθέντες (“bound together”; the recovered spelling may be corrupt), “in chains.” He uses “workhouses” for men confined in workhouses, just as below he uses “mines” for men condemned to the mines. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0434C] “Penal servitude”—the punishments commonly inflicted upon slaves. Hence Suetonius, ch. XXVII, numbers among the monstrous crimes of Gaius Caligula that “he condemned many men of honorable rank, after first disfiguring them with brands, to the mines, to road-building, or to the beasts”; such punishments were everywhere those of slaves. Hence the man in Plautus, *Poenulus* IV.II.5:

> So may the gods love me, I would rather spend my life  
> In the stone-quarries or the mill,  
> With my sides fettered fast in sturdy iron.

And the threatening Hegio in *Captivi* III, v. 64:

> Take him away  
> Where he may receive weighty, heavy fetters.  
> From there you shall go onward to the stone-quarries:  
> There, while others quarry eight measures each,  
> Unless you complete a measure and a half every day,  
> “Six-hundred-lashes” shall be the name imposed on you.

From this passage one may also nicely calculate the stonecutters’ daily assigned labor. Tyndarus, who had experienced the extremely onerous work there, testifies in V.IV.1:

> I have often seen many pictures of the torments  
> That take place in Acheron; yet no Acheron is equal  
> To the stone-quarries where I was.

[Col. 0434D] These kinds of punishments are also enumerated by our author below, ch. XLIV: “Your prisons are always seething with your people; your mines are always sighing with your people; the beasts are always fattened on your people; the providers of public shows always feed their herds of criminals from your people.” “But indeed, as for those condemned to the gladiatorial school, what sort of thing is it that, as correction for a lesser offense, they should advance to becoming murderers?” he says in *On the Shows*. Note, however, that *metalla* also signifies veins of stone. Lucan IV.303:

> Then the young men, exhausted by so much sweat,  
> Are brought out, wearied by the hard quarries of flint;

and VI.34:

> Enormous crags and rocks torn from the quarries. HAV.]

Despite their reluctance, we resist them as equals, and, persevering in that which they attack, we fight back; nor do we ever triumph over them more completely [Note: [Col. 0434D] “Nor do we ever triumph over them more completely.” Prosper, *Epigram*:

> That the wicked are very often permitted to rage against the saints,  
> And that the depraved can frequently harm the good,  
> Does not occur without God’s command: he proves that the hearts of his own  
> Are to be glorified even through these wars.  
> The palms of virtue grow, and crowns increase;  
> The battles of the world are changed into the peace of God.

] than when we are condemned for our obstinacy in the faith.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0435A]

**ARGUMENT.—**Hence, after briefly demonstrating the injustice of compulsory religion—since such coercion cannot be pleasing to the divine power, to whom, even in their opinion, the willing mind ought to be devoted—he proceeds to a second charge of injured, and indeed greater, Divinity. For they were accustomed to venerate the divine power of living emperors above all their gods, who were of course dead; and thus they are discovered to be irreligious toward their own gods, whom they never cease to despise in comparison with their Caesars and to pollute by perjuries.

But since it would readily appear unjust [Note: [Col. 0435B] “Appears,” Fran.] for free men to be forced against their will to sacrifice—for on other occasions too a willing mind is enjoined for the performance of a divine rite—[Col. 0436A] [Note: [Col. 0435B] “Is induced,” Rhen., Paris.] it would certainly be considered absurd if someone were compelled by another to honor gods whom he ought voluntarily to propitiate for his own sake, lest he should have ready at hand the right, by virtue of his freedom, to say: “I do not want Jupiter to be favorable to me. What is it to you? Let Janus meet me, angry from whichever face he pleases; what have you to do with me?” [Note: [Col. 0435B] “Who,” Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0435B] “From whichever face he pleases.” Him, therefore, I shall safely mock, and he will not see me:

> O Janus, whom no stork’s beak has pecked behind your back,  
> Nor a nimble hand mimicked with white donkey’s ears,  
> Nor a tongue as long as that of a thirsty Apulian dog,

in Persius, *Satire* I.5. This Janus, in that ridiculous *Apocolocyntosis of Claudius* composed in sport by Seneca, is called “a man, however shrewd, who always sees ἅμα πρόσω καὶ ὀπίσω (“both forward and backward at once”).” Accordingly Statius presents him as two-tongued in *Silvae* IV.2.15, on Domitian’s consulship:

> Behold, he raises upturned hands on either side  
> And speaks forth with this twofold voice.

Here the Fulda manuscript deletes τὸ (“the,” the Greek definite article); whence Junius’ conjecture, “and from whichever face he pleases,” may perhaps be correct. HAV.]

You have surely been fashioned by those same spirits so that you compel us to sacrifice for the emperor’s safety; and upon you has been imposed the necessity of compelling us, just as upon us the obligation of risking our lives. We have therefore arrived at the second charge of offending a more august majesty, since with greater dread and more calculating [Note: [Col. 0435B] “Warmer,” Havercamp from the Fulda manuscript.] timidity you observe Caesar more scrupulously than Jupiter himself from Olympus, [Note: [Col. 0435C] “Warmer timidity.” This is expressly read in the Fulda manuscript, with the Aldine edition also supporting it, although in the others the word “more calculating” is read and has generally occupied the passage. That word seems less suitable here; for the author wishes to express the fervor and zeal for religion which the Gentiles professed and which, he shows, was far more ardent toward emperors, who were merely men, than toward the gods whom they believed immortal. And just as Tertullian calls that flattery which is offered to Caesar under the appearance of religion and honor, with many foolish words, a “warm timidity,” so Lucretius too, with a most appropriate term, calls a mistress whose tongue is never silent but always and everywhere pours forth verbose trifles “blazing,” book IV.1159:

> But the blazing, hateful chatterbox becomes λαμπάδιον (“a little torch”).

Thus Asia easily imposed Rome and Caesar over its gods, erecting temples to them that may still be seen on coins bearing the legend **ROM. ET AVG. COM. ASI.** Consult Patin, who reproduces them in the *Thesaurus*, pp. 48 and 52. The Leiden manuscript has “with greater and more calculating.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0435D] “Jupiter from Olympus.” He speaks elegantly in this way, although he could have said “Olympian Jupiter.” But he wished to imitate his Lucretius, who similarly called Ceres “large-breasted from Iacchus,” meaning either the friend of Iacchus or Bacchus or, as Salmasius notes in the dedication of Regilla’s statue, p. 36, the mother of Iacchus, who was Proserpina’s brother. The poet’s passage is IV.1162:

> But if she is twinned and large-breasted, she is Ceres herself from Iacchus.

[Col. 0436B] With reference to this Arnobius writes in book III: “My mind longs and burns to behold, in those great halls and palaces of heaven, gods and goddesses with uncovered and naked bodies: Ceres, ‘large-breasted from Iacchus,’ as the Muse of Lucretius proclaims,” etc. HAV.] and deservedly so, [Note: [Col. 0436B] “And deservedly.” The particle “and” is deleted by the Leiden manuscript, Aldus, Barr., and the first edition of Rhenanus; others read “even.” That is, as Juvenal, *Satire* V.132, says, the god was the one who could be useful:

> If some god—or a little man like the gods  
> And kinder than the Fates—were to give you four hundred thousand.

He was ἐπιφανέστατος (“most manifest”), one whose help was immediately present. Hence that piece of flattery in Valerius Maximus’ preface to Tiberius, whom he places before the gods: “For whereas the divinity of the others is inferred from opinion, yours is evident by present proof and appears equal to the star of your father and grandfather.” Why then should we marvel at Ovid’s prayer when he speaks of Augustus?

> As I wish the gods to favor me, he is a god more manifest than they themselves. HAV.]

if only you knew it. For who among the living is not superior to any dead man of yours? [Note: [Col. 0436C] “Is not anyone superior to every dead man?” I have printed the reading of the Fulda manuscript, in place of which Rig. prefers: “Is anyone not superior to a dead man?” This is also how the Leiden parchment manuscripts and Heraldus represent it: “not anyone.” Wouwer from a manuscript and Scaliger prefer “not superior to any dead man.” Pamel. and others, finally: “not superior to every dead man.” Yet I think our author wrote: “Is not anyone superior to every dead man?” The saying is proverbial, and was beautifully expressed by the wisest king Solomon in the book entitled *Ecclesiastes* IX.4: “A living dog is better than a dead lion.” Since the dead man feels nothing, the speaker in the *Anthology*, book II, ch. XLVII, epigram 3, wittily desires that gifts be offered not to his tomb but to himself while alive, seeing and feeling:

Μὴ μύρα, μὴ στεφάνους λιθίναις στήλαισι χαρίζου (“Bestow neither perfumes nor garlands upon stone monuments”)  
[Col. 0436D] Μηδὲ τὸ πῦρ φλέξῃς· εἰς κενὸν ἡ δαπάνη (“Nor kindle the fire; the expense is in vain”).  
Ζῶντί μοι, εἴτε θέλεις, χάρισαι· τέφρην δὲ μεθύσκων


   Πηλὸν ποίησεις, κ` ούχ ὁ θανὼν τίεται (“If you wish, show me favor while I live; by drenching ashes with wine, you will make mud, and the dead man is not honored”; the recovered sequence κ` ούχ is textually uncertain).

Buchanan, among others, elegantly translated this as follows:

> Let no one heap my shade with fragrant violets,  
> Nor build my tomb with the mass of pyramids.  
> If anyone loves me, let him show himself generous to his living friend,  
> While there is still room for such services.  
> But when Lachesis ends my spent years,  
> Let my shattered urn bristle amid uncultivated brambles.

Opsopoeus rendered it somewhat more closely:

> Do not encircle marble statues with garlands,  
> Nor choose to pour pleasing wines into the flames.  
> Whatever pleases you, give it to your companion while he lives;  
> By drenching ashes, friend, you merely moisten mud.  
> By doing so, at least, your vain expenditure is wasted,  
> And no honor is bestowed upon me when dead.

Nor did the sophist Anaxarchus neglect this argument in Arrian, *The Expedition of Alexander*, p. 165, [Col. 0437B] book IV, when he maintained that divine honor should be paid to Alexander while he was alive. He said Καὶ γὰρ (“For indeed”), οὐδὲ ἐκεῖνο εἶναι ἀμφίλογον, ὅτι ἀπελθόντα γε ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ὡς θεὸν τιμήσουσι, πόσῳ δὴ δίκαιότερον ζῶντα γεραίρειν ἢπερ τελέυτήσαντα, ἐς οὐδέν ὄφελος τῷ τιμωμένῳ (“nor was this in dispute: that after he had departed from among mankind, they would honor him as a god; how much more fitting, then, to honor him while alive than after his death, when it would be of no benefit to the one honored”), that is: “There was no doubt that after Alexander departed from among the living they would worship him as a god; it was therefore far better to confer divine honors upon him while alive than when dead, since no benefit from the worship would reach him then.” Thus Publius Syrus the mime speaks most truly in verse 808: “He who sends a gift to a dead man gives him nothing and takes it from himself.” Indeed, little account is taken of all the dead; hence, when that Mnesilochus of Plautus is ordered by Pistoclerus in *Bacchides* IV.III.16 to take courage, he replies:

> Where am I to get it? A dead man is worth more than I am.

[Col. 0437C] And so, just as hares insult a dead lion, the dead Megapenthes is likewise safely despised, beaten, and spat upon by his own petty slave. See Lucian, *The Tyrant*. For “you,” the Agobardine manuscript has “to you” below. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0436B] Wouwer from a manuscript and Scaliger: “superior to a dead man?” Havercamp: “What then? Is anyone among the living not superior to every dead man?”—from Rigault’s conjecture. Heraldus: “Is not anyone among the living superior to a dead man?” Pamel. and others: “Is not anyone among the living superior to every dead man?”]

But even this you do not from reason so much as from regard for immediately effective [Col. 0437A] power; [Note: [Col. 0437A] “Immediately effective,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0437C] “Representatively present power.” Aldus and Rhenanus prefer “immediately effective,” as though the other term were either less Latin or unsuitable here; Heraldus also testifies that this reading appears in his manuscripts, yet he rightly establishes the ancient reading of the best codices. For “representatively present power” here is power which represents divine authority and performs its office on earth. Tertullian says that they worship such power not because it performs God’s office, but out of regard for itself, as though it were divine in itself—especially since it could also “represent” punishments, that is, exact them immediately, and was therefore more to be feared than the power of those wretched gods who, themselves subject to fate, are often compelled with Juno to bewail unavenged griefs; or, if at last and belatedly they hurl a thunderbolt, were believed sometimes to miss the target and strike those innocent of the offense, since they saw how, according to the Epicurean thought of Lucretius II.1102, Jupiter’s own missile:

> Often passes by the guilty  
> And kills the undeserving and innocent.

Lucian imitated this passage in *Jupiter Confuted*, where he makes the Cynic speak thus in dispute with Jupiter: Τί δήποτε τοὺς ἱεροσύλους (“Why ever [do you pass over] the temple-robbers …”; the verb is supplied from the surrounding translation because the recovered Greek is fragmentary), etc.; that is: “How then does it happen that, passing over so many sacrilegious men, robbers, criminals, violent men, and perjurers, you generally strike some oak, stone, or the sail of an innocent ship with your thunderbolt, and sometimes even an upright and holy traveler?” Seneca did not neglect this in *Natural Questions* either. There, ch. XLII, he says: “For whether, when he discharged the fires with which he struck innocent heads and passed over the guilty, he did not wish to aim more justly or failed to do so?” Therefore that torch of learning, Isaac Casaubon, similarly interprets the passage of Suetonius, *Claudius*, [Col. 0438B] ch. XXXIV, “and he represented the punishments of parricides,” as “he exacted them without delay.” Suetonius reproaches Claudius on this account, because he both wished to brand his age with such a mark and greedily endured to watch it in person, unlike Augustus, the founder of the empire, of whom the same author says in ch. XXIII of his *Life*: “He administered justice not only with the greatest diligence but also with mildness. Thus, to keep a defendant guilty of manifest parricide from being sewn into the sack—a punishment inflicted only upon those who confessed—he is said to have questioned him as follows: ‘Surely you did not kill your father?’” Casaubon also adduces Valerius Maximus VI.5 concerning Charondas of Thurii. After enacting a law that no one should attend the assembly wearing a sword, he inadvertently violated his own law and, as its avenger, killed himself. Although he could either have concealed his fault or defended it as an error, “he nevertheless preferred to represent the punishment,” lest justice be defrauded. Concerning Augustus, [Col. 0438C] Suetonius, final chapter: “He ordered that the sum be paid immediately, for he had always kept it confiscated and set aside”; he is speaking of Augustus’ will. The same author says of Nero in ch. V: “But in his praetorship he also defrauded the charioteers of the reward for their palms. Censured for this and mocked by his sister, when the owners of the factions complained, he decreed that thereafter prizes must be paid immediately.” HAV.]

and thus in this matter too you are detected as irreligious toward your gods, because you dedicate more fear to human dominion. [Note: [Col. 0437A] “You will be detected,” Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0437A] “Since more,” Fran., Paris., Rig.] In short, among you men swear falsely more readily by all the gods than by the single Genius of Caesar.

## CHAPTER XXIX

**ARGUMENT.—**Nor should this cause surprise, since those very gods acknowledge Caesar as their lord: it is he who keeps them safe by his guards, not they who preserve him unharmed by their divine power, for they have experienced him both angry and benevolent. Christians therefore ought not to be regarded as irreligious or as Caesar’s enemies because they do not subject him to his own possessions. [Col. 0438A] Rather, those people should be so regarded who expect both Caesar’s safety and their own from gods of such a kind, who cannot bestow it, and who also persecute those who know both how to request and how to obtain it from the true divine power.

Let it first be established, therefore, whether those to whom sacrifice is offered can bestow safety upon the emperor [Note: [Col. 0437B] “Emperors,” Fran., Rig.] or upon any human being; and then condemn us for the crime [Note: [Col. 0438A] Fran. adds “of treason.”]. If angels or demons, spirits utterly evil in substance, perform any beneficent act; if the ruined preserve, the condemned deliver; if, in short—as is in your own consciousness—the dead protect the living, [Note: [Col. 0438C] “The living by the dead.” A remarkable sarcasm, comparable to Lucretius, who does not hesitate to make a similar pronouncement concerning Cybele, the mother of the gods, book II.625:

> Therefore, as soon as she is borne through great cities,  
> Mute, she silently enriches mortals with safety.

For what can a shapeless, mute stone furnish to a human being? HAV.] then surely they would first protect their own statues, images, and temples, [Note: [Col. 0438C] “Their images and temples.” The Fulda manuscript reads “vindicate,” as though unwilling to repeat “protect,” which he has just used. Yet these wretched gods are so far from protecting them that they do not even spare them themselves, nor can they vindicate them from even their own thunderbolt once it has slipped from their hands. Lucretius is witness, book VI.416:

> Finally, why does he strike the gods’ holy shrines  
> And his own glorious dwellings with hostile thunder,  
> Shatter the gods’ well-fashioned statues, and by a violent wound  
> Strip honor from his own images?

The same author, book II.1100:

> Then let him hurl thunderbolts and often destroy  
> His own temples.

The speaker in Aristophanes ἑν Νεφέλ (“in the Clouds”; the recovered Greek is truncated or corrupt) complains of this: although Jupiter ought to strike perjurers, he neglects them and Ἀλλὰ τὸν αὐτοῦ νεὼν βάλλει, καὶ Σύνιον ἄκρον Ἀθηνῶν (“but strikes his own temple and Sunium, the promontory of Athens”), “instead strikes his own temple and Sunium, the promontory of Athens.” Marcus Tullius attests that he was no more favorable to Roman religion, in his *On His Consulship*:

> For the high-thundering Father, resting on starry Olympus,  
> Himself assailed his own citadels and renowned temples  
> And cast fire upon the Capitoline precincts.

The testimony of the ancients shows that this happened very frequently; Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 142, records that it also befell Apollo, and indeed by way of punishment, when he wished the ashes of the martyr Babylas to be removed from their place: Καὶ ὁ Δαφναῖος Ἀπόλλων τὸν ἡμέτερον παρασκευάσας μετατεθῆναι νεκρὸν, οὐρανόθεν ἐδέξατο τὸν σκηπτὸν (“And Apollo of Daphne, after causing our dead man to be removed, received a thunderbolt from heaven”).

Indeed, they are also vulnerable to human beings, not merely when, after a city is captured by enemies, the same destruction engulfs walls and temples and the same plunder sacred and profane things, but when some burglar, thief, or robber carries off the very statues and ornaments of the gods. Diogenes Laertius notes a certain philosopher Demetrius surnamed Ixion because he had wronged Juno; Hesychius of Miletus teaches what that wrong was: Δημήτριός τις ἕτερος Ιξίων ἐπεκλήθη, διότι λεπίδας χρυσᾶς κλέπτων τοῦ ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ τῆς Ἣρας ἀγάλματος ἐφωράθη (“A certain other Demetrius was surnamed Ixion because he was caught stealing gold plates from the statue of Hera in Alexandria”), that is: “Another Demetrius was surnamed Ixion because he was caught stealing gold plates from the statue of Alexandrian Juno.” In Lucian’s *Icaromenippus*, p. 294, Menippus asks Jupiter whether those who sacrilegiously plundered the temple at Dodona had been captured. Thus Baruch speaks truly, ch. VI.56: “Gods of wood, silver, and gold cannot protect themselves against thieves or robbers.” In the same manner the priests of the Syrian goddess are caught stealing in Lucian’s *Ass*, p. 154, concealing in the bosom of their goddess a golden bowl, a votive gift snatched from her shrine. In Lucian’s *Charon*, Solon mocks Croesus for preparing golden bricks for Apollo—namely, a rich and ready spoil for others. The Cynic says wittily to Jupiter in Lucian’s dialogue entitled *Jupiter Confuted*: Ἐῶ γὰρ λέγειν (“For I pass over mentioning …”), etc.; that is: “I pass over the fact that you, just like us, are plundered by sacrilegious men through robbery and sacrilege, and in a moment become utterly poor after being extremely rich; for many of you are fashioned from gold or silver.”

Apollo experienced this himself. Lucian exhibits him miserably stripped bare in *Jupiter Tragoedus*, where Mercury says: Καὶ γὰρ καὶ τὸν Ἀπόλλω ὁ αὐτὸς πολύχρυσον (“For that same man also called Apollo rich in gold …”), etc.; that is: “Yet that very man—Homer, namely—said that Apollo possessed much gold and wealth; nevertheless, you will see him sitting in utter poverty, his crown pillaged by robbers and the tuning-pegs stolen from his lyre.” These words were undoubtedly taken from Varro, whose relevant fragment from the *Menippean Satires* Arnobius presents to us in book VI: “Where, finally, is divine Apollo, when he was so plundered and burned by pirates and sea-robbers that, out of all the masses of gold amassed by countless ages, he did not possess even a single scruple to show to his hospitable swallows?”

It remains only for these wretches to be mocked with insulting words as well, as Lactantius amply shows in the case of Dionysius, that Sicilian robber of theirs, book II, [Col. 0440B] ch. 4, concluding: “Since human beings could not avenge these sacrileges, the gods themselves ought therefore to have been their own avengers.” Yet this did not happen, either in the case of Dionysius or in others. Hence in Lucian Cyniscus once more safely barks at Jupiter, declaring that he fears nothing from him: ἐπεὶ οὐδ` αὐτοὺς (“since not even those men themselves …”), etc.; that is: “Because I do not see even those sacrilegious men themselves being punished; rather, very many escape your hands.”

Prosper of Aquitaine develops all this beautifully in *On the Promises and Predictions*, book III, ch. 38, showing that all the gods of the Gentiles possess no power to defend their authority against the one crucified Son of Man, Christ. His words are: “Here that great multitude of definite and indefinite gods reported by Varro, together with those eminent and select gods and with their own king Jupiter—who, as their worshippers maintain, are formidable in counsel and power as they brandish thunderbolts, and terrible in arms—here, here they should have done something, if not for the world, at least for themselves, lest one crucified man should destroy them. That they have indeed perished we both know, and the prophet David confirms when he says: ‘Their memory has perished with a crash, but the Lord remains forever.’” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0438A] “Vindicate,” Fulda manuscript.], which, I suppose, [Col. 0439A] Caesar’s soldiers keep safe by their guards. [Note: [Col. 0439A] “Their,” absent from Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0440C] “Keep safe by their guards.” Aldus and Rhenanus do not recognize the word “their.” From this you may meanwhile learn that the more precious statues were guarded by soldiers, as may also be learned very clearly from a passage of Justin Martyr cited by La Cerda; but it is instead a passage of Lactantius. In book II, ch. 4, he discusses these statues as follows: “They therefore worship mortal objects, since they were made by mortals; for they can be broken, burned, and destroyed. They are often crushed when roofs collapse from age, and when consumed by fire they dissolve into ashes; and very often—unless their own size protects them or careful custody surrounds them—they fall prey to thieves.” This certainly happened to that marble Priapus in Martial VI.72. One may therefore exclaim concerning all these trifles in the words of Firmicus concerning the Palladium, in his little book *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “Troy was burned by the Greeks, Rome by the Gauls, and the Palladium was rescued from both fires. But it was rescued not by its own powers but by human protection; for men delivered it from both places, and it was carried away lest it burn in a human fire.” HAV.]

I think, moreover, that these very materials come from Caesar’s mines, and entire temples stand at Caesar’s command. [Note: [Col. 0440D] “Entire temples stand at Caesar’s command.” Concerning Caligula, Suetonius, ch. XXII: “Having given orders that statues of the gods distinguished for sanctity and artistry—including that of Olympian Jupiter—be brought from Greece, so that their heads might be removed and his own placed upon them, he extended part of the palace as far as the Forum; and, having transformed the temple of Castor and Pollux into its vestibule, he would often stand between the brother gods and present himself for worship to those who approached.”] In short, many gods have had Caesar angry with them. It makes for the case if he is also favorable and confers some act of generosity or privilege upon them. [Note: [Col. 0439A] Paris reads: “if, being favorable, he confers something upon them.”] How, then, will those who are in Caesar’s power and belong wholly to him have Caesar’s safety in their power, so that they may appear capable of bestowing upon him what they themselves obtain more easily from Caesar? [Note: [Col. 0439B] “May obtain,” Lyons manuscript.]

Is this why, then, [Note: [Col. 0440A] “For,” Fulda manuscript.] we commit treason against the majesty of the emperors—because we do not subject them to their own possessions; because we do not play games with the duty of securing their safety, [Col. 0440A] since we do not suppose that it lies in lead-fastened hands? [Note: [Col. 0440D] “Lead-fastened.” Lead-fastened hands are soldered with some support of lead so that they may not easily slip or split apart, as the commentators rightly explain. This was especially necessary in the bending of arms and extension of hands. HAV.] But you are the religious ones—[Note: [Col. 0440A] “Irreligious,” Fran.]you who seek it where it is not, ask it from those by whom it cannot be given, and pass over him in whose power it lies! Moreover, you assail those who know how to ask for it and who are also able [Note: [Col. 0440B] “Are able,” Fran.] to obtain it, because they know how to ask.

## CHAPTER XXX

**ARGUMENT.—**For Christians alone invoke on behalf of the emperor the true God, the living God—that God whom the emperor himself knows by nature to be greater than himself, to whom he owes everything, and from whom he expects everything. In a most weighty discourse he shows that they piously, truly, and rightly request and obtain from this God those things which ensure the safety of the emperor, the world, and themselves, [Col. 0441A] unlike the prayers of the Gentiles. “Slaughter them,” he says, “in the very posture of supplication; wrench out the soul as it entreats God on the emperor’s behalf; charge truth and devotion to God with irreligion, if you can.”

For the safety of the emperors [Note: [Col. 0441B] “For the safety of the emperors.” *To Scapula*, ch. II: “Thus we pray all the more for the emperor’s safety, asking it from the one who can provide it.” Indeed, a notable confirmation of this is the engraving on a gem, a cast of which Dom Du Cange, in his *Dissertation on the Coinage of the Later Age*, p. 20, testifies to be preserved in Louis Chaluc’s manuscript *Dactyliotheca*, which belongs to Sainte-Geneviève in Paris. The gem bears the monogram of Christ, with A and Ω (“Omega”) at the sides, and around them these characters: **SAL. DO. N. ALEX. FIL. LUCE**; that is, as they explain it: “The salvation of our lord Alexander, son of Mamaea, shines.” Such a monogram inscription is also found on coins of Constantius and Decentius. Yet the most illustrious Du Cange doubts whether it was engraved in the time of that Alexander, because the phrase “our lord” raises a suspicion against it; this phrase, however, can be taken in its ordinary sense, not as a designation of God, as our author says in ch. XXXIV. But I think that gem should instead be referred to one of the Byzantine emperors named Alexius, so that it reads: “The salvation of our lord Alexius, son of Manuel, shines.” Otherwise the gem’s owner was already a Christian under Alexander Severus.

Indeed, the Gentiles invoked no other than Jupiter himself, their supreme god, for Caesar’s safety. Martial VII.59, with considerable flattery:

> Ruler of the venerable Tarpeian hall,  
> Whom we believe to thunder while our leader is safe,  
> Though each man weary you with prayers  
> And ask you to grant what you gods can give,  
> Be not angry with me, Jupiter, as though  
> I were proud: I ask nothing for myself.  
> I must petition you on Caesar’s behalf;  
> On my own behalf, I must petition Caesar.

Thus the gem must either be referred to Alexius, or its owner was already a Christian under Alexander Severus. HAV.] we invoke the eternal God, the true God, [Note: [Col. 0441B] Paris adds “and.”] the living God, whom the emperors themselves desire to be favorable to them above all others. They know who gave them their empire; [Note: [Col. 0441D] “Gave them their empire”—something the false gods cannot do, since, as Jeremiah says in the book of Baruch, ch. VI.33, “They cannot set a king upon a throne or remove him.” Pliny also says significantly in his *Panegyric to Trajan*: “Even if it had previously been doubtful whether rulers were given to the earth by chance and fortune or by some divine power, it would nevertheless be clear that our emperor was divinely appointed. For he was not discovered by the hidden power of the Fates, but was openly and manifestly found and chosen by Jupiter himself.” HAV.] they know who made them human beings and who gave them a soul. [Note: [Col. 0441B] “Who,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0441B] “Souls,” Paris.] They perceive that he alone is God, in whose power alone they stand, in relation to whom they are second and, after whom, first—before and above all the gods.

Why should they not? [Note: [Col. 0441B] “Why should they not? Since—human beings,” absent from Paris.] Since they are above [Col. 0442A] all human beings, who are surely alive and take precedence over the dead. [Note: [Col. 0441B] In the Fulda manuscript and Rhenanus’ edition, the words [Col. 0442B] “Why should they not?—human beings” are missing. Lyons manuscript I and Gelenius: “gods, human beings who,” etc. Aldus: “Who for a long time, since,” etc. In place of “live,” Havercamp, from the Fulda manuscript, reads “living.”] They reflect upon the extent to which the strength of their empire avails, and thus they understand God: they recognize that they prevail through him against whom they cannot prevail.

Let the emperor, in short, conquer heaven; [Note: [Col. 0441D] “Let the emperor conquer heaven.” The argument of Callisthenes proceeds in the same fashion in Curtius, book VIII, ch. 5, where he refutes Cleon’s foul flattery concerning the worship of the living Alexander as a god: “Would you like to test your power? Make someone a king, if you can make a god: it is easier to bestow an empire than heaven.” For “that they prevail,” Rhenanus has “they themselves prevail.” HAV.] let him carry heaven captive in his triumph, [Note: [Col. 0442B] “Carry heaven in his triumph.” The ancient custom is well known whereby triumphing generals had representations of captured cities, and also paintings of memorable battles and victories, carried around on ceremonial carriages. Tertullian alludes to this. Rhenanus’ manuscript did not recognize the next six words. HAV.] let him send guards to heaven, let him impose tribute upon heaven. [Note: [Col. 0442B] “Heaven—impose,” absent from Paris.] He cannot. He is therefore great because he is less than heaven. For he himself belongs to the one to whom heaven and every creature belong. The source from which he is emperor is the source from which he was also a man before becoming emperor; the source of his power is also the source of his breath.

Looking up toward that place, Christians pray with outspread hands, [Note: [Col. 0442B] “Looking there, Christians, with outspread hands.” Lucian’s Tryphon very aptly accords with this Christian meaning and practice: ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸν ἐν Ἀθήναις Ἀγνώστον ἐφεύροντες καὶ προσκυνήσαντες, χεῖρας εἰς οὐρανὸν ἐκτείναντες, τούτῳ εὐχαριστήσομεν (“But having found and worshipped the Unknown One at Athens, and having stretched our hands toward heaven, we shall give thanks to him”). Moreover, we learn from a verse of Lucretius, book V, that even pagans worshipped with outspread hands:

> Nor to fall prostrate upon the ground and spread one’s palms  
> Before the temples of the gods.

[Col. 0442C] RIG.—“Looking upward toward that place.” That very posture, raised toward heaven, signifies contempt for the world. Clement of Alexandria writes beautifully in *Stromata* VII, p. 231 E: “We are raised toward heaven, endeavoring together with the word to draw the body away from the earth; and by desire for better things we compel the upright and elevated soul to advance courageously into holy things, despising the bond of the flesh.”

Maurice of Sens, *On the Mass*, which the often-praised Johann Albert Fabricius appended to his *Bibliography*, writes in verse 60 concerning the congregation standing during the sacred service, etc.:

> That you should be attentive, patient, and upright against the foe  
> Your head, your staff, and the very act of standing teach.  
> For, uncovering your head, you are admonished to listen attentively;  
> When you put aside your staff, you are instructed to be forbearing.  
> Standing, you learn that we are accustomed to fight while standing,  
> Because a grievous battle beneath a watchful enemy awaits you.

John Chrysostom, on Psalm CXXIX, concerning Elijah: “But if you wish also to see him standing upright in prayer, behold him again stretched out toward heaven, and stretched so far that he even brought fire down from heaven.” Thus, while the body stands upright, the spirit bows down; and God demands the rending not of a cloak but of the heart. Hence Jerome, book II, on *Ephesians* ch. 3: “Just as external genuflection edifies the simple, so we teach that true bending of the knee lies in the mind, because many have bent the bodily knee without in any way bending the knee-joint of the soul; and conversely, others, while beseeching God with the body upright, have bowed themselves more deeply in mind.” HAV.

“With outspread hands.” Apuleius, in his translation of Aristotle’s *On the Cosmos*, notes that this is natural to a human being in every crisis of life; but especially is the servant of God, who expects both life and safety from him, commanded by Jeremiah, *Lamentations* III.41, to raise his hands to heaven and God together with his heart. On this practice the following deserve consultation: John Philoponus on the *Hexaemeron*, p. 43; Joachim Hildebrand, who published three laborious books on the prayers of the ancient Christians, book II, ch. 9; John Price; Claude d’Espence on 1 Timothy 2; Barthius, *Adversaria* III.2; Hoornbeek, *Miscellanies*, p. 297; Adam Rechenberg on the New Testament and *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 145; Brouwer [Col. 0443B] van Nidek’s elegant little book *On Acts of Adoration*, ch. XXI; and finally Adam Rechenberg once again, whose separate dissertation on this subject was published at Leipzig in 1688. HAV.] because they are innocent; with head uncovered, [Note: [Col. 0443B] “Uncovered”—not veiled, as among the Gentiles. Consult the commentators Heraldus and La Cerda. The Fulda manuscript reads “bared.” Consult also Brouwer, cited here, p. 144, and Calvoer, *Ecclesiastical Ritual*, vol. II, p. 555. HAV.] [Col. 0443A] because we do not blush; and finally without a prompter—[Note: [Col. 0443B] “Without a prompter.” Among the pagans a prompter led the prayers, indeed from a written text, lest any words be omitted or spoken in the wrong order; there was in turn another observer who paid attention, and another who commanded that silence be observed. Pliny, book XXVIII, ch. 2. RIG.—“Prompter.” Plautus in the *Mostellaria* may be added to the commentators’ notes:

> When they take their place in the legion,  
> They will give him some relative as a support.

Servius teaches that such prompters were assigned to Roman youths in their first year of military service; and in Valerius [Col. 0443C] Flaccus, *Argonautica* I.475, Iphiclus accompanies the Argonauts, not in order to fight,

> but to impart counsels, so that the keen … [source breaks off]

And one who may fire men with the praises of great ancestors. These were called μνήμονες (“remembrancers” or “prompters”) among the Greeks, as Meursius duly observed on Lycophron’s *Cassandra*, p. 158. Thus in sacred rites there were prompters who whispered the formula of the prayers and went before in reciting the formula of the prayers, or the premeditated hymn. Aristander, in Curtius, book IV, chapter XIII, dressed in white, carrying sacred boughs in his hand and with his head covered, went before the king in reciting the prayers. Pliny treats many details of this religious rite in book XXVIII, chapter 2; add Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days* II.14 and IV.17, and Barnabas Brissonius—most worthy of a better fate—in book I of *On Formulas*, p. 61. Such a formula was certainly necessary amid so many familiar and unfamiliar names, by the invocation of which they believed their gods were delighted; our Savior, the prompter of a better formula, calls this βαττόλογίαν (“vain repetition”), Matthew 6:7, 9, and his Holy Spirit prays with us and for us with inexpressible [Col. 0443D] groanings. HAV.], because we pray from the heart.

We are all always praying for all the emperors: for them a long life, a secure empire, a safe household, valiant armies, a faithful senate, an upright people, a peaceful world, and whatever else constitutes the wishes of a man and of a Caesar. I cannot ask these things from any other than him from whom I know [Note: [Col. 0443A] “May know,” Paris.] that I shall obtain them, since he himself is both the one who alone grants them and I am one to whom their attainment is due: his servant, who worships him alone, who because of [Note: [Col. 0443A] Rhenanus, Gelenius, and Gangnaeus: “him alone”; the others: “alone.” In what follows, Havercamp, from the Fulda codex, reads *because of his discipline*. The words “who because of [Col. 0444A] his discipline am killed” are not found in the editions of Rhenanus, Aldus, or Heraldus, or in Leiden codex II.] his discipline am killed [Note: [Col. 0444A] “Who—am killed” is absent from Paris.], who offer him the rich and greater sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0443D] “Who offer him the rich and greater sacrifice.” Since the Magdeburg Centuriators distort this passage against the sacrifice of the altar, it would require a fuller treatment; but we refer the reader to the book *To Scapula*, below, which they also wrongly cite in their own support, since there he expressly uses the word “we sacrifice.” PAM.—Some offerings were called “greater,” others “suckling.” On the greater, that is, the greatest, there is a passage in Cicero’s second speech *On the Agrarian Law*: “Greater victims will be stationed in the Forum.” Further, the greater offerings or victims—for thus everyone freely calls them—were bulls; for I am not now drawing that distinction between sheep and bulls. LAC.], which he himself commanded: prayer proceeding from chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and a holy spirit. Not grains of incense [Note: [Col. 0443D] “Not grains of incense.” It would be futile to say that this passage opposes the practice of the Church, which uses incense in its sacrifices. For it is employed by apostolic tradition and institution. Apostolic Canon 3 has μή ἐξὸν δὲ ἔστω προσάγεσθαί τι ἕτερον πρὸς τὸ θυσιαστήριον, ἢ ἔλαιον (“Let it not be permitted to bring anything else to the altar except oil”) [Col. 0444A] εἰς τὴν λυχνίαν, καὶ θυμίαμα, τῷ καιρῷ τὴς ἀγίας προσφορᾶς (“for the lamp, and incense at the time of the holy offering”). LE PR.], worth a single as [Note: [Col. 0444B] “Worth a single as.” That is, of trifling price. For scarcely so much was given as two or three fingers could grasp. Lactantius V.19, speaking from the Gentiles’ point of view: “For to prefer to be tortured and killed rather than throw into the fire incense grasped with three fingers seems as foolish as, when another’s life is in danger, to care for his soul more than one’s own.” Jerome likewise, in the *Letter to Heliodorus*: “Servitude to an idol does not consist only in someone’s throwing onto the altar’s pyre incense pinched between two little fingers,” etc. Lactantius again, I.20: “For with incense and the tips of their fingers they worship things which they ought to have worshiped with their inmost senses.” Hence King Numa, in Livy I.21, wished the fingers to be free from their wrappings when sacrificing: “And to perform the divine rite with the hand wrapped up as far as the fingers.” Relevant here also is Curtius, book VIII, chapter 5, where Cleon the flatterer wishes divine honor to be accorded to Alexander even while he is still alive: “Gratitude could be returned to them in one way only: if they acknowledged as a god the man whom they understood to be one, repaying benefits so great at the slight expense of incense.” Lucian too mocks this in his customary manner, not only in *The Ass*, p. 122, where [Col. 0444C] the sorceress χόνδρους δύο λαβοῦσα, τὸν μὲν λιβανωτὸν, τῷ πυρὶ τοῦ λύχνου ἐπέθηκε (“having taken two grains, she placed the incense in the flame of the lamp”), that is, “having taken two grains, placed the incense in the flame of the lamp,” but especially in *Zeus Tragoedus*, p. 200, where Jupiter complains of the stinginess of Menesitheus, who had sacrificed an elderly cock: “In addition, four grains of incense, covered in decay, so that they were extinguished upon the coals and the smoke offered not the slightest scent even to the tips of the nostrils.” The most learned Brodaeus also adduces passages from Porphyry and Ovid in *Miscellanies*, book V, chapter 8, which Janus Gruter inserted in volume II of his *Lampas*. Alexander, that “Great” man, is said to have worshiped the gods magnificently, especially from early youth. Thus, when during a certain sacrifice he tossed incense into the flames with a lavish hand, Leonidas, a frugal and austere man, rebuked him as follows: “You will burn incense so freely when you have subdued the regions where it grows.” Remembering this remark, when he later gained Arabia by conquest, he is said to have sent Leonidas a great quantity of aromatics with this message: that henceforth he should not wish to be so sparing in honoring the gods, since he might understand that they repay gifts cheerfully offered with so [Col. 0444D] lavish a hand. Plutarch relates the story in *Alexander*, chapter XLIV, and *Apophthegms*, XXXVII; Pliny XII.14, 17. Finally, marbles and coins set the matter before our eyes, as may be seen in Choul’s ancient Roman marble, which he adduces and depicts in his book *On the Religion of the Ancient Romans*, in the place where he discusses priests’ linen garments; and on a coin of Lucilla Augusta, where she, in the guise of Piety, holds an incense-box in her left hand and casts incense with her right, taking the flower with three fingers. Thus Scaliger emends a passage of Pliny, book XXIV, chapter 10, in Epistle XVIII, adducing that passage of Ovid:

> And beneath the threshold she places three portions of incense with three fingers.

The same appearance and dress of Piety is seen on a coin of Lucius Aelius, except that there she also holds a libation-dish in her left hand. HAV.], the tears of an Arabian tree [Note: [Col. 0444D] “The tears of an Arabian tree.” Barr., Rhenanus, Heraldus, and Rigault himself write “not the tears of an Arabian tree,” as does the Leiden manuscript. But this is less correct; for the Fulda codex and Pamelius omit “not.” [Col. 0445B] He calls these grains of incense “the tears of an Arabian tree”; for, as Pliny discusses at length in *Natural History* XII.14, “On the incense-bearing tree of the Arabs”: “It used to be tapped once a year, because there was less opportunity for selling it. Now profit produces a second harvest. The first and natural harvest occurs around the rising of the Dog Star, in the fiercest heat, by making cuts where the tree seems most pregnant and the bark stretched thinnest. There the wound is opened, but the bark is not removed. From it a rich foam bursts forth. When this coagulates, it thickens; where the nature of the ground requires, it is caught upon a palm mat, elsewhere upon a beaten floor. By the former method it is purer, by the latter heavier. What adheres to the tree is combed off with iron; hence it contains bark.” Arnobius likewise, book VII: “Yet, O piety! How great or what sort of honor is this, which is produced from the odor of fire and procured as resin from trees?” See also what follows there. Thus every liquid dripping from trees is called a tear, especially that which comes from a vine. The same Pliny, book XXXIII, in the preface: “The tear of vines, which resembles a lump, heals leprosy, ringworm, and mange previously treated with soda.” The Aldine edition reads “not tears from the root of a tree,” as though that sap flowed from the roots. For the use incense afforded Christians, see below at chapter XLII. HAV.], nor two drops of unmixed wine [Note: [Col. 0445D] “Two drops of unmixed wine.” Besides the custom that Heraldus noted from Arnobius, this may also be referred to the practice by which, after drinking a cup of wine, they poured the residue at the bottom as a libation to the gods and dashed it against the pavement. This may be illustrated from Tacitus, *Annals* XVI, final chapter, where Thrasea, about to die, having opened the veins of both arms and shed his blood, sprinkled it upon the ground and, calling the quaestor nearer, said: “Let us pour a libation to Jupiter the Liberator.” The Greeks called this κατταβίζειν (“to cast as a libation in the cottabus fashion”), and the actual splash κονταβισμὸς (“the cottabus splash”). Xenophon, concerning Theramenes, one of the Thirty Tyrants, who was killed by order of Critias, *Greek History*, book II: Καὶ ἐπεί γε ἀποθνήσκειν ἀναβκαζόμενος τὸ κώνειον ἔπιε, τὸ λειπόμενον ἕφασαν ἀποκοτταγίσαντα εἰπεῖν αὐτὸν (“And when, compelled to die, he drank the hemlock, they say that he tossed out the remainder like a cottabus throw and said”). Κριτίᾳ τοῦτ` ἔστω τῷ καλῷ (“Let this be for handsome Critias”). That is: “At last, when he was compelled to meet death and drank the hemlock, it is related that he threw out what remained in the cup so that it rang, and at the same time said: ‘Let handsome Critias have this.’” In Plautus, *Curculio*, Act I, [Col. 0446B] Scene II:

> “Venus, from my little I shall give you this tiny bit,” says the lover.

But since here it is joined with incense, what Virgil says in *Georgics* IV, [Col. 0446C] 384, seems more likely to be intended:

> Three times with liquid nectar he sprinkled the blazing Vesta.

Suetonius, book VII, chapter 18: “He found nothing except lukewarm ashes on the altar and, beside it, an old man dressed in mourning, holding incense in a glass dish and unmixed wine in an earthenware cup.” How ancient this rite was is evident from Jotham in Judges 9:13, where the vine rejects the kingship offered to it, saying: “Should I forsake my new wine, which cheers God and men?” HAV.], [Col. 0445A] nor the blood of a condemned ox [Note: [Col. 0445B] “Of a man,” Franeker.] longing to die, and, after all these defilements, an unclean conscience as well. Hence I wonder, since among you victims are approved [Note: [Col. 0445B] “May be approved,” Paris.] by the most vicious priests, why the entrails of the victims are examined rather than those of the sacrificers themselves [Note: [Col. 0445B] Junius and Havercamp prefer “may be examined.”].

Thus, while we are stretched out toward God, let claws tear us, crosses suspend us, fires lick us [Note: [Col. 0446C] “Fires lick.” Let them burn the body by wrapping around it. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.684, concerning Iulus:

> Flame licking his hair and feeding around his temples.

From this Persius transferred the expression in his Prologue:

> Whose images the clinging  
> Ivy licks.

In the same way fire is also called “devouring” by Virgil in the same book, verse 758:

> At once the devouring fire, driven by the wind,  
> Rolls to the rooftops.

In Lucretius, book II:

> The fires leap up to the roofs of houses,  
> And with swift flame taste the beams and rafters.], swords sever our throats, beasts leap upon us: the very posture of a praying [Note: [Col. 0446D] “The posture of a praying Christian.” Eusebius wonderfully describes this posture in *Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapter 13. LAC.] Christian is ready for every punishment. Do your work, good governors; wrench out the soul that is supplicating God for the emperor. Here will be the crime, where there are the truth of God and devotion [Note: [Col. 0445B] So the Fulda codex; others: “the truth and devotion to God are.” Rigault deleted the whole sentence: “Here will be—the devotion.”].

## CHAPTER XXXI

[Col. 0445B] **ARGUMENT.—If the prayers of Christians should be called into doubt, he shows that the Holy Scriptures are readily available, and are not unknown to the Gentiles, owing to various accidents. From them it can be made clear that Christians are there commanded to pray for kings, rulers, authorities, and public tranquility. [Col. 0446A] This also accords with nature, because when the commonwealth is disturbed, Christians themselves are disturbed as well.**

So now we have flattered the emperor and lied about the wishes we expressed, plainly in order to escape [Note: [Col. 0445B] “For escaping,” Paris.] violence [Note: [Col. 0445B] “Violence” is absent from Paris.]. To be sure [Note: [Col. 0446B] “Nevertheless,” Fulda codex.], this deceit is profitable. For you permit us to prove whatever we defend. You, therefore, who have supposed [Note: [Col. 0446B] “Suppose,” Franeker, Paris.] that we care nothing for the safety of the Caesars, inspect the utterances of God, our writings, which we ourselves do not suppress and which many accidents convey to outsiders. Know from them that, as the superabundance of benevolence, we have been commanded [Note: [Col. 0446B] “I know from them that we have been commanded,” Franeker, Paris, Rigault.] even to pray to God for our enemies and to invoke blessings upon our persecutors. Who are more the enemies and persecutors of Christians than those on whose account we are arraigned on a charge of violating majesty? But it is also said by name and explicitly: “Pray,” he says, “for [Col. 0446B] kings, and for rulers and authorities, that all things [Note: [Col. 0446D] “That all things.” Likewise “and all things.” He has in view the passages of Paul, Romans 13:1; Titus 3:1; 1 Peter 2:13; and especially Paul, 1 Timothy 2:2. Magistrates, of course, are our parents: to be loved if good, endured if evil. Prosper of Aquitaine:

> Whatever the good order of the world demands must be rendered,  
> Provided it does not violate the purpose of devout faith.  
> No authority is to be despised by the gentle and the holy:  
> It is right to serve kings and masters,  
> So that for Christ’s servants it may advance true honor  
> To have loved the good and endured the evil. HAV.] may be tranquil for you.” For when [Note: [Col. 0446B] “May be tranquil. With you,” Franeker, Paris.] the empire is shaken, and with it all its other members, assuredly we too, although outside the disturbances [Note: [Col. 0446B] So it is read in the Fulda codex and in the editions of Rigault and Havercamp; all the others read: “although we are considered outside the disturbances.”], are found somewhere amid the catastrophe.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0447A]

**ARGUMENT.—He further shows that the safety of the emperor and the empire is dear to Christians, since they know that dreadful things threaten the world once the Roman Empire has ceased to exist, and that the very end of the age is therefore delayed by its continuance. He also maintains that those who swear by the safety of Caesar—which is more august than all the Genii—must not be compelled to swear by his Genius, since they are accustomed to adjure Genii, that is, demons, so as to harm them, not to swear by them so as to honor them.**

There is also another, greater necessity for us to pray for the emperors, and even for the entire condition of the empire and Roman affairs: we know that the tremendous force threatening the whole world, and the very conclusion [Note: [Col. 0447B] “Ending,” Paris.] of the age [Note: [Col. 0447C] “The conclusion of the age, threatening dreadful calamities, is, we know, delayed by the continued passage of the Roman Empire.” When Paul wrote to the church of the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord would not come before the Roman Empire had fallen, he veiled a matter most abhorrent to that age in carefully chosen words. With the same design, when Tertullian was about to signify this same matter to the Roman nobles in this *Apology*, he so ingeniously laid on his colors that it could even give pleasure. And in a similar figure, in *To Scapula the Proconsul*: “A Christian,” he says, “is no one’s enemy, much less the emperor’s; knowing that he was appointed by his God, he must love, revere, honor him, and desire his safety together with that of the entire Roman Empire, for as long as the age shall stand—for that long it shall stand.” But the Roman commonwealth long ago went to ruin, and the procession of the Roman Empire passed away; the apostasy came, and what was said to stand in the way was removed from the midst, and yet we read that the world has endured and perceive that the age still stands. What then? Do we say that Paul’s assertion is false—the assertion of so great an apostle, chosen so exceptionally by the Lord? Far be it. For we believe it most true, and have long been treading upon the scattered ruins of the Roman Empire. What then? Do we also say that the man of sin, the man of perdition, whose mystery was already at work when Paul wrote, came long ago? He came long ago, I say; but if we ask into what times that “long ago” of ours is to be extended, we accomplish nothing—indeed, we ask with considerable impiety. The Lord has placed before curiosity a cloud that we must adore, not remove. Let it suffice to contemplate what Peter reveals: one day with the Lord is the same as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. Suppose that most wicked man—or a multitude of most wicked men—has come, and that the years have already risen beyond a thousand. What are a thousand years in comparison with a hundred times a hundred thousand years extended into immeasurable eternity? If the ancients promised themselves anything in this matter concerning a period very short even to human thought, they were deceived well [Col. 0448C] and wisely. And we are well deceived if we too are deceived after their fashion, so that we remain watchful for that day as though it were always most imminent—a day known to the Father alone—in order that the concern of faith may be tested by suspenseful expectation. RIG.]—which threatens dreadful calamities—is delayed by the continued passage of the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 0448C] “By the continued passage of the Roman Empire.” He speaks of the duration of the Roman Empire as though it were a span of time through which a triumphal procession passes. Thus in the book *On Repentance*, p. 143, he called the time that catechumens spend in sinning between their acknowledgment of the truth of the Faith and the sealing of baptism “leave for sinning,” as though for conveying the column of offenses. RIG.]. Thus, by praying for the postponement of what we do not wish to experience, [Col. 0447B] we favor the prolongation of Rome.

But we also swear [Note: [Col. 0448C] “But we also swear.” Although Christians understood that every oath had been forbidden them, they nevertheless took particular care not to swear by the Genii or Fortune of the Prince. Hence, in the celebrated martyrdom of blessed Polycarp, in Eusebius, book IV, when the proconsul said to him, ὄμοσον (“Swear”) [Col. 0448D] τὴν Χαίσαρος τὺχήν (“by Caesar’s Fortune”), the blessed martyr replied most steadfastly: εἰ κενοδοξεῖς, φησὶν, ἵνα ὀμὸσω τὴν Χαίσαρος τύχην, ὡς λέγεις προσποιούμενος ἀγνοεῖν ὅστις εἰμι, μετὰ παῤῥησιας ἄκουε· Χριστιανός εἰμι (“If you vainly imagine,” he says, “that I will swear by Caesar’s Fortune, while pretending, as you say, not to know who I am, hear me plainly: I am a Christian”). LE PR.], not by the Genii of the Caesars, but by their safety [Note: [Col. 0448D] “By their safety.” There is an elegant passage in Arrian, the expositor of Epictetus, book I, chapter 14: τούτῳ θεῷ ἔδει καὶ ὑμᾶς ὀμνύειν ὅρκον οἶον οἱ στρατιῶται τῷ καίσαρι (“It was fitting that you too should swear an oath to this God, just as soldiers do to Caesar”). Ἀλλ` ἐκεῖνοι μὲν τὴν μὶσθοφορίαν λαμβάνοντες ὁμνύουσι πάντων προτιμήσειν τὴν τοῦ Καισαρὸς σωτηρίαν (“But they, on receiving their pay, swear to prefer Caesar’s safety above all things”). That is: “For it was fitting that you too should be bound to God by an oath, just as soldiers are to Caesar. But they, on receiving their pay, swear to prefer Caesar’s safety to all things.” Suetonius gives the formula itself in *Caligula*, chapter XV: concerning his sisters, he ordained that this should be added to every oath: “NOR SHALL I HOLD MYSELF AND MY CHILDREN DEARER THAN GAIUS AND HIS SISTERS.” From this it is evident that it was a military oath and therefore permissible even to Christians. HAV.], which is more august than all the Genii. Do you not know that Genii are called demons, and hence, by a diminutive term, *daimonia*? We revere in the emperors the judgment of God, who has set them over the nations. We know that in them is what God has willed, and therefore we also desire the safety [Note: [Col. 0447B] “Safety” is absent from the Fulda codex.] of what God has willed [Note: [Col. 0447B] The words “and therefore—has willed” were adopted by Pamelius from the manuscripts and by Rigault from the Fulda codex; they are lacking in the remaining handwritten books and editions.], and we regard this as a great oath.

As for demons, [Col. 0448A] that is, Genii, we are accustomed to adjure them, so as to drive them out of human beings, not to swear by them, so as to confer upon them divine honor.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**ARGUMENT.—Indeed, Christians necessarily look up to the emperor, since they know that he has been given to them by their God, and therefore truly regard him as their own. If they do not call him a god, they do so because they do not wish to lie or mock him: he himself is subject to God and rules beneath him; it is also in his interest to yield to God. Even amid the envy-provoking honor of a triumph he is admonished to do this, shining with such glory that he must be recalled to himself lest he falsely think himself a god.**

But why should I say more about Christian religion and devotion toward the emperor? We must look up to him [Col. 0448B] as the one whom our Lord has chosen [Note: [Col. 0448B] “Chose,” Semler.]. And rightly might I say: Caesar is more truly ours, as one appointed by our God. Therefore, in this respect too [Note: [Col. 0448B] Wouwer, from a manuscript: “in this respect too”; Rhenanus, Aldus, and Gangnaeus: “so that in this respect”; the others: “as toward my own.”], I labor more effectively for his safety, not only because I request it from him who [Note: [Col. 0448B] “Since I not only request it from him who,” Franeker.] can grant it, or because I, being such a person, request it and so deserve to obtain it, but also because, by keeping Caesar’s majesty below God, I commend him more effectively to God, to whom alone I subject him. I subject him to one whom I do not make his equal.

For I shall not call the emperor a god, either because [Col. 0449A] I do not know how to lie [Note: [Col. 0449B] “I do not know how to lie.” As a Christian can appropriate Terence’s saying, “Lying is not my way,” so Septimius wishes to indicate that he was not born for flattery, and could neither make himself ridiculous nor endure blows, like that man in the same author, *Eunuch* II.2. Juvenal, Satire III, verse 41:

> What am I to do at Rome? I do not know how to lie;  
> If a book is bad, I cannot praise it.

A splendid falsehood of Ovid, certainly, though one that could be of no benefit to his master, appears in *Letters from Pontus* IV, Elegy IX:

> Nor is my piety unknown: this hospitable land sees  
> That Caesar is sacred within my house.  
> His dutiful son and priestly wife stand together,  
> Divine powers now no lighter than the god already made.

He means Augustus and Livia, worshiped while still alive as living divinities and with no less honor than the deified Julius himself. [Col. 0449C] HAV.], or because I do not dare to mock him [Note: [Col. 0449C] “I do not dare to mock him.” For this is so absurd that in this manner I myself would become ridiculous and would seem to mock him both openly and inwardly. Hence the hesitation of Apelles the tragedian over what to answer Caligula was justified. Suetonius, chapter XXXIII, says of him: “Among his various jests, while standing beside a statue of Jupiter, he asked Apelles the tragedian which of the two seemed greater to him, and when he hesitated, had him torn with scourges.” Vitellius similarly averted death from himself by a witty response, in Cassius Dio, book LIX: καὶ ποτε τοῦ Γαίου συγγένεσθαί τε τῇ σελήνή (“and once [he said] that Gaius had intercourse with the Moon”), etc.; that is: “On one occasion Gaius said that he had intercourse with the Moon, and asked Vitellius whether he had seen him meeting the goddess. Then Vitellius, lowering his eyes to the ground, trembling, and speaking very faintly, said: ‘Only you gods, lord, are permitted to see one another.’” I discovered that this expression was reproduced, or rather borrowed, by Martial VII.60, where he compares Domitian with Jupiter in these words:

> [Col. 0449D] While each man wearies you with his prayers,  
> And asks you to give what you gods can give.
