For thus Paris, the edition of Colinaeus, and others correctly read; in place of this Hadrianus Junius reads “what power can give.” But this same Caligula, because of fear of his cruelty, was named heir by certain persons in their wills; he called them mockers because they persisted in living after naming him, and sent many of them poisoned delicacies. Suetonius, *Life of Caligula*, chapter XXXVIII. HAV.], or because he himself will not wish to be called a god [Note: [Col. 0449D] “He himself will not wish to be called a god.” When foolish Caligula aspired to such madness, he was deservedly mocked by a shoemaker. For the same Dio relates in the same book—and I am not reluctant to set down the passage—καὶ πότε τις ἀνὴρ γαλάτης ἰδῶν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ βήματος ὑψηλοῦ ἐν Διὸς εἴδει χρηματίζοντα (“and once, when a certain Gaul saw him administering justice upon a lofty tribunal in the guise of Zeus”), etc. That is: “It happened by chance that a certain Gaul saw him administering justice from a lofty tribunal in the guise of Jupiter, and burst into laughter. When Gaius summoned him and asked what he thought he looked like, the man replied—I shall give his very words—‘A great fool.’ He suffered no punishment for this, [Col. 0450B] because he was a shoemaker; for freedom of speech is more readily tolerated in ordinary people of this sort than in those distinguished by some rank.” The Leiden manuscript omits the little word “himself,” as though “God” ought to be read. HAV.]. If he is a man, it is in man’s interest to yield to God; let it suffice for him to be called emperor. Even this is a great name, one bestowed by God. He denies that he is emperor who calls him a god. Unless he is a man, he is not emperor.

Even while triumphing in that most exalted chariot, he is reminded that he is a man. For it is suggested to him from [Note: [Col. 0450B] “For it is suggested.” Besides La Cerda and others, see what the great Casaubon has on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter XCI.] behind: “Look behind you [Note: [Col. 0450B] “Look behind you.” Barr. reads “Look at yourself.” The Leiden manuscript, however, has “Look behind,” which is perhaps the true reading, for brevity is favored in admonitions of this kind. Two admonitions are mentioned: “Remember that you are a man,” and “Look behind you.” By the latter, I do not think that what Zonaras supposes is intended, *Annals*, volume II: that by being ordered to look backward he was admonished to consider the remaining course of his life and not to be made arrogant by that honor. Perhaps, rather, he was obliquely ordered to contemplate the instability of the wheels, just as one of the captive kings who drew the golden chariot of Sesostris, that most fortunate king of Egypt, is said once to have taught him that Fortune’s wheel turns all things. Or, more probably, by looking at the slave who rode in the same chariot behind him, he was to learn that he too, if affairs went badly, could be sent under the yoke by his enemies, and so recognize the saying of Publilius, verse 792:

> Alas, how wretched it is to learn to serve when one has been trained to rule!

For a public slave rode in the same chariot as the triumphator and, so that he should not appear idle, supported in his hand the triumphator’s golden crown, which was of considerable weight, as Pliny teaches in book XXXIII, chapter 1: “And although an Etruscan crown of gold was supported from behind, the ring upon the finger was nevertheless iron—perhaps both that of the triumphator and that of the slave supporting the crown.” Isidore rather comically calls this man an executioner, *Origins* XVII.3: “The fact that he was touched by an executioner served as a sign, so that those raised to so great a height might be reminded of the mean condition of humanity.” This was also done to avert envy, which the ancients believed to avenge excessive prosperity, as learned men have rightly taught. There is an especially noble passage in Livy V.2, where, after Veii had been captured, Camillus prays that, if his own fortune appeared excessive to any god or man, he might be permitted to appease that envy by some personal misfortune to himself that entailed the least possible public loss to the Roman people. Callisthenes also speaks appositely when opposing the decree to make Alexander a god, in Curtius VIII.5: “Do not draw envy upon deeds most successfully performed by such flattery.” And shortly afterward in the same place: “May the gracious gods hear without envy what Cleon has said, and permit events to proceed in the same course in which they have flowed.” Hence Suetonius relates that Augustus solicited small contributions. HAV.], remember that you are a man.” And certainly he rejoices all the more to shine with such great glory that a reminder of his condition is necessary for him. [He would have been lesser if he were then called a god, because he would not truly have been called one [Note: [Col. 0449B] Havercamp does not doubt that this sentence, which is absent from the Aldine edition, was inserted by some copyist.].] He is greater when he is recalled to himself, lest he suppose himself a god.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

[Col. 0450A]

**ARGUMENT.—Moreover, Augustus himself abhorred the name “lord” as that of a tyrant. Though Christians, following common usage, may use it, when spoken in place of “God” it is an insult to divine lordship. One who is called Father of the Fatherland should not be called Lord, much less God, which is rebellion against God and a curse upon Caesar, since among the Romans a Caesar is customarily made a god only after death.**

Augustus, the founder of the empire [Note: [Col. 0450D] “Augustus, the founder of the empire.” Everyone knows that the emperor Augustus, as Suetonius relates, rejected and abhorred the title “lord”; and when an actor in the public games called him lord, he took it so badly that on the following day he prohibited by edict the bestowal of this title upon him. LE PR.], did not wish even to be called lord, for this too is a surname of God. I shall certainly call the emperor “lord,” but according to common usage, and only when I am not compelled to call him lord in [Col. 0451A] God’s place. Otherwise, I am free in relation to him; for my one Lord is God, almighty and eternal, who is likewise the emperor’s Lord. How is one who is Father of the Fatherland its lord? But the name of affection is more pleasing [Note: [Col. 0451B] Thus Leiden codex II and the Aldine edition; others: “But the name is also more pleasing,” etc.; or “but a more pleasing name is,” etc.; or “but also a more pleasing name,” etc.] than that of power; even within a household men are more often called fathers than lords.

So far is it [Note: [Col. 0451B] Franeker adds “however.”] from being right for the emperor to be called a god [Note: [Col. 0451B] “To be called a god.” Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, pp. 418–419, shows, by producing the actual coins on which one reads “TO AURELIAN AUGUSTUS, BORN GOD AND LORD,” and “TO CARUS AUGUSTUS, GOD AND LORD,” that Aurelian and Carus appropriated this name while alive. Indeed, besides Domitian, Gaius too aspired to it, as is evident from his remarkable coin presented by Spanheim, p. 417. Although the Egyptian nation itself, born to flattery and servitude, worshiped its kings while they were still alive with the honors of gods, it did so without the appellation “God,” an honor which Diodorus, book I, relates was granted only to Darius, father of Xerxes. HAV.] that this cannot be believed without not merely the most disgraceful but also [Note: [Col. 0451B] “Unless not through,” Franeker.] destructive flattery. If, when you already have one emperor, you call another by that name, will you not incur the greatest and implacable [Note: [Col. 0451B] “Inexplicable,” Agobard codex.] resentment of the one whom you already had—a resentment to be feared even by the man whom you so addressed?

Be religious toward God, if you wish him to be favorable to the emperor. Cease worshiping or believing in another God, and consequently cease calling this man a god, since he has need of God [Note: [Col. 0451C] “God.” Fulda: “gods.” There is an elegant passage in Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander the Great* IV, p. 166, where among the other arguments by which Callisthenes advises against adoration of the king, this in particular appears: Οὔκουν (“Accordingly, neither”), he says, οὐδὲ Ἀλέξανδρος (“would Alexander”), etc.; that is: “For Alexander would not permit some private person to usurp royal honors through an illegitimate election and vote. Much more justly, therefore, would the gods be indignant if any mortal arrogated divine honors to himself or endured their bestowal by others.” HAV.]. If flattery of this kind does not blush for its falsehood in calling a man a god, let it at least fear the ill omen. To call Caesar a god before his apotheosis [Note: [Col. 0451D] “It is a curse.” Altogether excellent are the points Heraldus makes in this chapter, especially here, where he teaches the true sense of the passage from Tacitus; Lipsius also did not neglect to summon this passage of Tertullian in support. Lest I plunder other men’s storehouses, I shall add what I have observed from Arrian, Curtius, and others. There, in Arrian IV, p. 165 of the edition of my teacher—in whom I glory—Jacobus Gronovius, Anaxarchus, flattering Alexander, tries to persuade the Greeks to worship him as a god in the Persian fashion. He therefore says: Καὶ γὰρ οὐδὲ ἐκεῖνο εἶναι ἀμφίλογον, ὅτι ἀπελθόντα γε ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, ὡς θεόν τιμήσουσι πόσῳ δὴ δικαίοτερον ζῶντα γεραίρειν ἢπερ τελευτήσαντα, ἐς οὐδὲν ὃφελος τῷ τιμωμένῳ (“For this too was not in doubt: that after he had departed from among men, they would honor him as a god. How much more fitting, then, to honor him while alive than after his death, when it would bring no benefit to the one honored”). That is: “There was no doubt that, after he had departed from the living, they would worship him as a god. It was therefore much better to render him divine honors while alive than when dead, when no benefit from the worship could reach him.” Callisthenes wisely answers him there; Curtius also makes him argue to the same effect in this manner, [Col. 0452B] book VIII, chapter 5: “No fruit is both lasting [Col. 0452C] and premature; you are not giving celestial honors to the king, but taking them away. For an interval is needed before he may be believed a god, and posterity always renders this favor to great men. But I pray for a late immortality for the king, that his life may be long and his majesty eternal. Divinity sometimes follows a man; it never accompanies him. You were just now citing Hercules and Father Liber as examples of consecrated immortality. Do you believe that they were made gods by the decree of a single banquet? Nature first removed them from mortal sight before their fame carried them to heaven.” Pliny rather openly mocks the apotheosis of the Caesars in *Natural History* VII.55, where, babbling much against the immortality of the soul, he writes: “At other times by giving sensation to those below, worshiping the shades, and making into a god one who has now even ceased to be a man.” To him one may oppose the impious flattery of Valerius Maximus, who speaks thus to Tiberius in the Prologue: “For we have made the Caesars the remaining gods.” The Fulda codex has the faulty reading “handed down before, viciously.” HAV.] is a curse [Note: [Col. 0451B] The Agobard codex, both Leiden codices, and Pamelius’s edition read “to be called.” In the Fulda codex the following words ensue: “I know that by that name you wish him evil and invoke evil upon him, when you call an emperor a god while he is still living, although that name befalls him only when dead.” Havercamp corrects the final words to: “is applied to him when dead.”].

## CHAPTER XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0451] This note appears at the foot of column 456, but the callout letter (e) has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0456B] “From our years.” Heraldus admirably investigates the occasion on which this acclamation was probably used. That acclamations of this kind were often composed in verse may be illustrated by what Suetonius notes in *Caligula*, chapter VI: when Germanicus was thought to have been restored to his former health, the whole people acclaimed:

> Rome is safe, the fatherland is safe, Germanicus is safe,

for this is a complete trochaic verse. Corippus also states it openly in the poem he wrote in praise of the emperor Justin, book II, verse 317:

> They arrange songs and add measures to their voices.

There he wished to express Suetonius’s statement in *Caligula*, chapter XVI: “with boys and girls of noble birth singing his praises and virtues in a measured song.” This same prince, at the beginning of his reign, as the son of the excellent Germanicus, aroused such hope and love for himself that, when he fell ill, some were not lacking who vowed to fight with arms for the patient’s safety, while others vowed their own lives under a publicly displayed declaration; ibid., chapter XIV. That cruel tyrant later compelled them to fulfill their vows, chapter XXVII.

Violent indeed is that ardor of love whereby one desires to die for another so that the latter’s life may be prolonged; and therefore it is all the more wicked to wish his death even in expressions of this kind. This was frequently on the lips of lovers, whence Horace writes beautifully in *Odes* III.9.9:

> [Col. 0456D] Thracian Chloe now rules me,  
> Skilled in sweet measures and mistress of the lyre;  
> For her I should not fear to die,  
> If the Fates would spare her surviving soul.

Lydia answers still more beautifully:

> I am inflamed by a mutual torch  
> For Calais, son of Thurian Ornytus;  
> For him I would suffer death twice,  
> If the Fates would spare the surviving boy.

And in Plautus, *The Comedy of Asses* III.3.18, when the mistress complains:

> Why, I beg you, do you desire without cause on my part to consign me to death?

the young lover replies:

> I? Desire that for you? Why, if I knew your life was failing, I would at once  
> Bestow my own life upon you and add from mine to yours.

Yet those may much more deservedly use such words among whom love does not dissolve, before the final day, a union unbroken by bitter quarrels, as does Arimetus, this grieving freedman of the emperor Titus:

> [Col. 0457A] If the cruel Fates permitted souls to be weighed,  
> And one person’s safety could be purchased by another’s death,  
> Whatever little time of life was owed to me,  
> I would gladly have weighed out for you, dear Homonoea.

The inscription survives at Rome in the gardens of Cardinal Coelius, and Gruter and others reproduce it among the inscriptions. Many printed [Col. 0457B] codices, such as Aldus and Rhenanus, and manuscripts such as the Fulda and Leiden codices, have:

> From our years may Jupiter add years to yours.]
