### ARGUMENT.—

Christians are therefore wrongly called public enemies merely because, though in all other respects dutiful toward the emperors, they celebrate the emperors’ solemn festivals in accordance with conscience rather than wantonness, observing them modestly, decorously, chastely, and piously. The Romans themselves behave otherwise: among them not only does the common people often tear Caesar apart with abuse, desire a new emperor day after day for the sake of profit—and this during the very distribution of the largess—but the senators themselves, the knights, and the leading men of the city and the camps threaten Caesar’s life and conspire with the Cassii, Nigri, and Albini, meanwhile concealing their treason, until it breaks out, beneath a grand display of rejoicing. No Christians are found among these men. Nor do Christians consult astrologers about the safety of the Caesars, since that cannot be done except from a desire for political revolution, from which Christians wholly recoil.

Christians, then, are public enemies because they do not pay the emperors vain, deceitful, or rash honors; because, as men of true religion, they celebrate even the emperors’ solemn festivals in accordance with conscience rather than wantonness. A splendid duty, to be sure: to bring hearths and couches out into public, to feast street by street, to turn the city into the likeness of a tavern, [Col. 0452A–B] to make mud with wine,

> **Note [Col. 0452B–0453B].** Rhenanus, Gelenius, and Scaliger read *obole facere*; for *habitu*, Havercamp preferred to write *habitu*. The Fulda codex has: “to change the city into the likeness of a tavern.”
>
> “To make mud with wine.” The copyists did not understand this either. They therefore altered it to “to compel the drunken,” as in the Leiden codex, or “to produce drunkenness,” as presented by the Fulda codex. But “to make mud with wine” means to soak and intoxicate the ground with a great quantity of wine, as a sign of insolence and luxury. Horace touches upon this when censuring the miser, of whom Publilius Syrus says in verse 59:
>
> > The miser does nothing rightly except when he dies.
>
> For thus Flaccus, *Odes* II.14:
>
> > A worthier heir will consume the Caecuban wine  
> > guarded by a hundred keys, and with unmixed wine  
> > will stain the splendid pavement,  
> > wine finer than at pontiffs’ banquets.
>
> Cicero too, *Philippic* II: “Everything resounded with the voices of drunken men; the floors swam with wine; the walls were wet.”
>
> This, at any rate, seems to me to be the meaning of the present passage. La Cerda refers it to the novel custom of making fountains of wine, but I doubt that he can prove that this was also practiced among the ancients. There was also a festival of Venus at which much wine was poured out before the goddess’s temple. Plutarch, *Roman Questions* XLV, names Aeneas as the author of its institution and adds the reason for the pouring:
>
> > Ἦ καὶ τοῦτο σύμβολόν ἐστι τοῦ χρῆν νήφοντας ἑορτάζειν, ἀλλα μὴ μεθύοντας, ὡς τῶν θεῶν μᾶλλον τοῖς ἐγχέουσι χαιρόντων τὸν πολὺν ἄκρατον, ἣ τοῖς πίνουσι — “Or is this too a sign that festivals should be celebrated soberly and not drunkenly, since the gods delight more in those who pour out abundant unmixed wine than in those who drink it?”.
>
> For this signifies that festivals should be celebrated soberly, not drunkenly, since the gods take far greater pleasure in the pouring out of wine than in human drunkenness. This may perhaps also have given rise to the custom in question. The Greeks would call it πηλὸν ποιεῖν (“to make mud”), as does the man in *Anthology* II, chapter XL, epigram 3, who wished to be given while alive what is done uselessly for the dead:
>
> > Ζῶντί μοι εἴτε θέλεις, χάρισαι· τέφρην δὲ μεθύσκων,
Πηλὸν ποήσεις, κοὔχ ὁ θανὼν τίεται· — “If you wish, show me kindness while I live; but by making my ashes drunk, you will make mud, and the dead man is not honored.”.
>
> That is: “Give me, while I live, whatever you wish to offer; but by making the ashes drunk you will merely make mud, and the dead man receives no honor.” **HAV.**

to run about in bands committing outrages and shameless acts and pursuing the enticements of lust. Is public joy expressed in this way, through public disgrace? Are these things fitting for the solemn days of rulers [Col. 0453A], though they are not fitting on other days?

> **Note [Col. 0453C–0454B].** “Are fitting for rulers.” The manuscripts are extraordinarily confused here. Where Pamelius and others have, “Are these things fitting for the solemn days of rulers, though they are not fitting on other days?” the Fulda manuscript most strangely has: “I have said these things on the solemn days of rulers, and they decree that it is not fitting on other days.” These words, which are manifestly corrupt, acquire a new sense in the Leiden manuscript: “Will these things proclaim the solemn days as the beginning, which they will not proclaim on other days?” In the last phrase *decent*, “are fitting,” should be read. “To proclaim a beginning” is to provide an omen for what remains. For these vows were made chiefly on the Kalends of January, so that they might thus extend throughout the whole year.
>
> Tacitus, *Annals* IV: “Caesar, in a letter, offered vows for the Kalends of January, the solemn beginning of the year.” La Cerda cites a parallel passage from the jurist Gaius. In Dio, book LIX, p. 742 of Stephanus’s edition, we likewise read that under Gaius Caligula, on the first day of the year, a certain slave named Machaon ascended to the sacred couch of Jupiter Capitolinus, uttered many dreadful prophecies there, killed the puppy he had brought with him, and afterward killed himself. This certainly constituted a dreadful beginning and portent of the future, since it signified that Gaius—who, like a good physician, ought to have healed the wounds inflicted on the Roman commonwealth by Tiberius—would both destroy the commonwealth and himself perish by a bloody death.
>
> Thus that day was, to speak with Petronius, the “title” of the year; in Petronius the stork is the “title” of warm weather. The emperor was also said to “open the year.” Statius, *Silvae* IV, poem I.2, concerning Domitian:
>
> > Germanicus opens the distinguished year.
>
> And there, verse 20:
>
> > Thus is it fitting to enter the years.
>
> On this rite one may consult the learned short commentary by Giovanni Pietro Bellori, *On the Auspices of the New Year*, concerning a unique coin of Antoninus Pius inscribed: **S. P. Q. R. A. N. F. F. OPTIMO PRINCIPI. PIO**, that is, “a new, auspicious, and happy year.” It was published first at Rome, and afterward at the end of Cardinal Carpegna’s *Selected Coins*, Amsterdam, Wetstein.
>
> I have nevertheless not ventured to alter the reading of the Agobardine manuscript: “which are not fitting on other…,” with “days” deleted. **HAV.**

Will those who observe discipline out of respect for Caesar abandon it on Caesar’s account, and will license in evil behavior be piety, and an occasion for luxury be reckoned religion?

O we who deservedly ought to be condemned! For why do we, chaste, sober, and upright men, efface the vows and rejoicings made for the Caesars? Why, on a festive day, do we not overshadow our doorposts with laurels, nor interrupt the daylight with lamps?

> **Note [Col. 0453A].** “We desert”? Franciscus.
>
> **Note [Col. 0453A].** “We shade,” Paris.
>
> **Note [Col. 0454B–C].** “We overshadow our doorposts with laurels.” Rhenanus reads “we shade,” less correctly. Tacitus, writing of the discovery of the conspiracy against Nero’s life, says in *Annals* XV.17:
>
> “Meanwhile the city was being filled with funerals and the Capitol with sacrificial victims. One man, after the killing of his son; another, of his brother; another, of a relative or friend, gave thanks to the gods, adorned his house with laurel, threw himself at Nero’s knees, and wearied his right hand with kisses.”
>
> Our author, *On Idolatry* XV: “But if these things belong to those who are worshiped at doorways, the lamps and laurels will also belong to them. Whatever you have done to the doorway, you have done to the idol.”
>
> Pliny, *Natural History* XVI.30, commends the laurel under this description: “The laurel is properly dedicated to triumphs, and is the most welcome doorkeeper of the houses of Caesars and pontiffs: it alone adorns their houses and keeps watch before their thresholds.”
>
> Likewise, when applying themselves to incantations in their vows for the purpose of appeasing the gods, men fastened laurel to their doorposts, as is clear from Diogenes Laertius’s epigram on Bion of Borysthenes, who, during an illness,
>
> > Ράμνόντε καὶ κλάδον δάφνης
Ύπἐρ θύρην ἐθἤκεν — “He placed buckthorn and a branch of laurel above the door” [the recovered Greek contains uncertain spacing and diacritics].,
>
> that is, “placed buckthorn and a branch of laurel upon the door.” **HAV.**

It is an honorable thing, when a public solemnity demands it, to dress your house in the guise of some newly opened brothel.

> **Note [Col. 0454A].** “To bring in,” Paris.

Yet in this religion also of a secondary majesty—a religion on whose account we Christians are arraigned for a second sacrilege, because we do not celebrate the Caesars’ solemn festivals with you in a manner which neither modesty, decorum, nor chastity permits, but which an opportunity for pleasure rather than any worthy reason has recommended—I should like to demonstrate your loyalty and truthfulness, lest perhaps even here those who refuse to regard us as Romans, but call us enemies of the Roman rulers, should be found worse than Christians.

I summon the Quirites themselves, the native common people of the seven hills themselves, and ask whether that Roman tongue spares any Caesar of its own.

> **Note [Col. 0454C–0455B].** “Whether that Roman tongue spares him.” Although such conduct is readily to be expected from the common rabble and dregs of humanity, who possess neither a reputation they can stain nor property they can lose, those jesters in Trebellius Pollio’s *Gallienus* teach the point sufficiently. Peering with astonishing eagerness into the face of every person, they said that they were looking for the emperor’s father. This was Valerian, who had been captured by the Persians, whom Gallienus absurdly paraded in a procession while neglecting vengeance for his father.
>
> No one described such things more precisely than Suetonius Tranquillus, who committed the conduct of the Caesars to writing with freedom equal to that with which they themselves had lived. In *Nero* XXXIX: “As Nero passed by, Isidorus the Cynic had rebuked him in public with a loud voice because he sang well of Nauplius’s misfortunes but managed his own prosperity badly.”
>
> In the same passage, an actor in Atellan farces, when given the words ὑγίαινε πάτιρ, ὑγίαινε μήτερ (“Farewell, father; farewell, mother”) [πάτιρ is an uncertain recovered form]. in a certain song, had illustrated them by gestures representing drinking and swimming, thereby signifying the deaths of Gaius, Claudius, and Agrippina; and in the final line,
>
> > Orcus guides your feet,
>
> he indicated the senate by a gesture. Suetonius there records even the most notorious verses posted against Nero; Claudius before him and Domitian afterward continually suffered the same treatment.
>
> Even Vespasian, the best of the emperors and himself sufficiently witty, did not escape the sharpness of this tongue. Since his strained expression resembled that of a man exerting himself—that is, needing to defecate—he wished to hear some witty remark about himself from a certain man of polished wit. He had to hear: “I shall speak when you have finished emptying your bowels.”
>
> Indeed, even at Vespasian’s funeral, when mimes were employed according to custom, the dead man could not be spared. As Suetonius notes in chapter XIX, Favor, the chief mime, wearing Vespasian’s mask and imitating, as customary, the deeds and sayings of the living man, openly asked the procurators how much his funeral procession cost. When he heard “ten million sesterces,” he cried out that they should give him one hundred thousand sesterces and throw him into the Tiber if they liked.
>
> Here the jester seems to me to have had in mind that saying and action of Vespasian which Suetonius likewise relates in chapter XXIII. When envoys informed him that a colossal statue of no moderate cost had publicly been decreed to him, he ordered them to set it up immediately, holding out his cupped hand and saying that the base was ready. **HAV.**

The Tiber is witness,

> **Note [Col. 0455B].** “And the Tiber is witness.” The Fulda manuscript and Heraldus have “is” in place of “and.” The most distinguished Gothofredus, in his notes on *To the Nations* I.17, refers this to the Tiberian house, or palace of the Caesars. But in ancient times, as I think, the common people lived along the banks of the river, while the more powerful occupied the hills, safe from floods. Since Tertullian is speaking of the common people, he could indicate nothing more suitably than the place where they lived.
>
> The French translator Giry dreams of some statue of the Tiber—I do not know which: “the placards that are attached to the statue of the Tiber.” Finally, the Leiden manuscript seems to suggest a third possibility: “There, Vesta, the Tiber, and the schools of beasts are witnesses”; perhaps it intended “and the statues,” since in *To the Nations* he also speaks of statues. **HAV.**

and so are the schools of beasts.

> **Note [Col. 0455C].** “Schools of beasts.” Rigault reads “school.” Some, including Scriverius, take “schools of beasts” to mean that Roman enthusiasm by which men gathered for combats of beasts and spectacles of hunting as though attending a school. There was much license of speech there, as in all spectacles. Or he indicates the place where those condemned to the beasts were trained; there was room for abuse there, since nothing more dreadful than that death could be feared. Chrysostom also condemns the theaters under this heading, *Homily I on Isaiah* VI.1: “Is it from the insults, abuse, and mockery with which the spectators of such things bespatter one another?” **HAV.**

Now, if nature had drawn some transparent material over human breasts so that they could be seen through, whose inmost heart would not appear engraved—

> **Note [Col. 0455C–0456B].** “Now, if over breasts.” The Fulda manuscript shapes the reading in this way: “Now if, for the purpose of seeing through human breasts, nature had drawn over them some transparent material….” Hence Scriverius, in the margin of my book, and Meursius, in his *Critical Exercises*, emend it from Juvenal and others to “some transparent material.”
>
> I, adhering more closely to the traces of the manuscript’s reading, prefer: “Now if nature, when it first formed them, had drawn over human breasts some transparent material, etc.” For the word “human” seems to need adding from the Fulda manuscript, and τὸ (“the [word]”) signifies that ancient time when the human being received the form which all his descendants preserve.
>
> Momus, of course, had long before found fault with this and had wished the human breast to be furnished with windows, so that its more hidden thoughts could not remain concealed. From this philosophy Euripides wished men to be double-tongued, so that the sound of truth and falsehood might be disclosed in each man. For in *Hippolytus*, verse 925, Theseus speaks thus:
>
> > Φεῦ, χρὴν βροτοῖσι τῶν φίλων τεκμήριον
Σαφές τι κεῖσθαι, καὶ διάγνωσιν φρενῶν,
Ὅστις τ` ἀληθής ἐστιν, ὅστε μὴ φίλος — “Alas! Mortals ought to have some clear token of their friends and a means of discerning their minds—who is a true friend and who is not.”.  
> > Δίσσας δὲ φωνὰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ἔχειν,
Τὴν μὲν δικαίαν, τὴν δ` ὅπως ἐτύγχανεν,
Ὡς ἡ φρονοῦσα τ` ἄδικ` ἐξηλέγχετο
Πρὸς τῆς δικαὶας, κοὐκ ἂν ἠπατώμεθα — “And every person should possess two voices, one truthful and the other whatever it happened to be, so that the voice devising injustice might be exposed by the truthful one and we should not be deceived.”.
>
> That is: “Alas! Men ought to have some visible mark of their friends and a means of discerning the mind, showing who is a true friend and who is not; and every man should possess a double voice, one truthful and the other answering circumstances, so that the voice which devised unjust things might be convicted by the truthful voice, and we should no longer be deceived.”
>
> For already in Euripides’s time even the Spartans were such, as he says in *Andromache*:
>
> > Εὖ λέγοντες ἄλλα μὲν — “Speaking one thing plausibly”.  
> > Γλώσσῃ φρονοῦντες δ` ἄλλ` ἀνευρισκεσθ` ἀεὶ — “with the tongue, but thinking another, always to be found out”.
>
> Our Publilius, as though interpreting this, expressed it thus in verse 265:
>
> > A man always bears one thing upon his lips and thinks another.
>
> Sallust too, in his customary brief and vigorous manner, said in *Catiline*: “To have one thing shut within the breast and another ready upon the tongue.” For sometimes, beneath the human form—these are Seneca’s words—lurks the spirit of a beast, indeed one more fickle and savage than the beasts themselves. **HAV.**

with the scene of one new Caesar after another presiding over the distribution of a largess?

> **Note [Col. 0455A–0456A].** Pamelius and Heraldus read “might prepare”; Franciscus Junius, from the Puteanus codex, “appear”; the rest, “might appear.” Gelenius, Wouweren, and Gangneius have “stage.” The Fulda codex reads: “engraved, it might produce one new Caesar after another. A stage presiding at the distribution of the largess,” [uncertain text], against which Scriverius objects. Scriverius reads: “might appear upon this stage of a new Caesar.”
>
> **Note [Col. 0456B].** “At the distribution of a largess.” A *congiarium* is a gift and sum of money with which an emperor favored the entire populace; the corresponding gift to soldiers was a *donativum*. If anything other than money was ever given as a *congiarium*, it was specifically stated. **LAC.**

Even at the very hour when they acclaim:

> [Col. 0456A] May Jupiter increase your years from our years.

A Christian no more knows how to utter these words than he knows how to desire a new Caesar. “But,” you say, “it is the common people.” Granted that it is the common people, they are nevertheless Romans; and no one demands the punishment of Christians more vehemently than the common people.

> **Note [Col. 0456A].** The Fulda codex reads “destroyers” instead of “those demanding punishment.”

The other orders, clearly, are dutiful in proportion to their authority and loyal from conviction: nothing hostile breathes from the senate itself, from the knights, from the camps, or from the palaces themselves.

> **Note [Col. 0457A].** Thus emended by Rigault and Havercamp; all the others have the plural “breathe.”

Whence, then, came the Cassii, the Nigri, and the Albini?

> **Note [Col. 0457B].** “Whence the Cassii?” Similarly in *To the Nations* I.17: “We certainly recognize Roman loyalty toward the Caesars! No conspiracy has ever broken out; no Caesar’s blood has ever fixed a stain in the senate or in the palaces themselves? No imperial power has ever been usurped in the provinces? Syria still breathes with the stench of corpses; Gaul still does not wash them away with its Rhône.”
>
> Relevant too are the words which he adduces in *To the Martyrs* VI: “For this purpose, let even the present times serve us as evidence of how many and what sorts of persons meet ends unexpected in view of their birth, rank, bodies, and ages, for the sake of a man: either at his own hands, if they acted against him, or at the hands of his adversaries, if they stood for him.” **HAV.**

Whence came those who besieged Caesar between the two laurels?

> **Note [Col. 0457B–C].** “Between the two laurels.” He means the laurel grove to which Commodus had withdrawn for the sake of healthier air while a plague was raging in the city. Herodian relates the story in book I. Publius Victor, in the thirteenth region of the city, mentions the Greater Laurel Grove and the Lesser Laurel Grove. They were two groves.
>
> In the ancient martyrologies one also reads: “On the third day before the Ides of August, at Rome, between the two laurels, the martyr Tiburtius.” The *Alexandrian Chronicle*, concerning the murder of the emperor Valentinian: ἐσφάγη ἐν Ρώμῃ μέσον δύο δαφνῶν (“He was slain at Rome between the two laurels”). So too in Livy, book I: “a place between two groves.” **RIG.**

Whence came those who practiced their wrestling technique by squeezing his throat?

> **Note [Col. 0457A].** Rhenanus and Aldus read “his fasces.”

Whence came those who burst armed into the palace, more audacious than all the Sigerii and Parthenii?

> **Note [Col. 0457C–D].** “Sigerii.” Many learned men wrongly altered this to “Stephani,” although not only do all the manuscripts agree on the former name, but Xiphilinus also clearly numbers Sigerius among the conspirators against Domitian’s life; Martial too joins him with Parthenius in book IV, epigram 88:
>
> > And ten times you revisit the palace on the sacred hill,  
> > and sound nothing but Sigerii and Parthenii.
>
> Gothofredus rightly noted this on *To the Nations* I.17. They enjoyed intimate access to Domitian, as Xiphilinus teaches, and were men of great authority who had received the greatest favors from Caesar. Tertullian therefore preferred to name them rather than the obscure Stephanus, who was brought in to kill the tyrant merely because of his physical strength.
>
> Hence I also agree with Hadrianus Junius, who emends Martial’s *Apophoreta*, epigram CLXXXII, to “A clay statuette of Sigerius,” though there I would prefer “of Sigerius” in place of “of Giberius.”
>
> Moreover, with Franciscus Junius I readily persuade myself that this Sigerius was a German, since it is established that the Batavians in particular held a place among those peoples in the emperor’s guard. Indeed, I suspect that he may have been a Frisian. Among the Frisians, or the neighboring Groningers, not only are compound names such as Sigefridus and Sigebertus still frequent, but there also remains a very noble and ancient family of the Sigeri, or Sigerii—Sigers.
>
> Since almost all the manuscripts have “so many Sigerii,” whence the Leiden reading “so many signs” was corrupted, then—unless it was substituted as a variant reading for “all”—the expression includes, besides the two men named, every other person who violated the emperor’s majesty by a similar crime. **HAV.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0458A].** Gelenius, Gangneius, and Heraldus read “Stephani”; the manuscripts have either “all the Sigerii” or “all those many Sigerii.” Compare Martial, *Epigrams* IV.78.

They were Romans, unless I am mistaken—that is, non-Christians.

And thus all those men, right up to the actual outbreak of their impiety, both offered sacrifices for the emperor’s safety and swore by his Genius,

> **Note [Col. 0457D–0458B].** “They offered sacrifices,” in place of “S. I.” This is altogether relevant to Lucian’s elegant dialogue entitled *The Tyrant*. There Megapenthes replies to Clotho concerning his false friends:
>
> > Καὶ μὴν σπενδοντες ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις (“And indeed, when they poured libations at their banquets”), etc.
>
> That is: “Whenever at banquets they poured a libation of wine according to custom, they prayed aloud for every blessing upon me, to such an extent that, if it were possible, each of them was even prepared to undergo death for me. In short, they swore by nothing other than my name.”
>
> Clotho replies:
>
> > τοιγαροῦν παρ` ἑνὶ αὐτῶν (“Therefore, at the house of one of them”), etc.
>
> That is: “That is why you died immediately after the supper which you ate with one of them yesterday.”
>
> Lucian says the same of legacy-hunters in the dialogue *Pluto and Mercury among the Dead*, where he shows that their prayer is for the rich old man to die quickly. “What is most wicked of all,” he says, “is that meanwhile, while praying for such things, they nevertheless plainly watch over and honor him. No one is ignorant of what they deliberate among themselves when he falls ill; yet they promise to offer sacrifices if he recovers again.” **HAV.**

some outside,

> **Note [Col. 0458B–C].** “Some outwardly.” This may serve to illustrate and emend *To the Nations* II.11, where after a lacuna one reads: “…Spare them, shameless gods; no one intervenes between struggling spouses…those whose wish it is rejoice outwardly and blush.”
>
> Gothofredus does not touch the first lacuna; he supplies “those men” in the second and explains τὸ (“the [expression]”), “outwardly,” of those who labor outside at the wedding celebration. Wrongly. Restore the passage thus: “Spare human modesty, shameless gods, etc.; those very persons whose wish it is, etc.”
>
> For he says that those very persons who anticipate that nuptial joy in their minds and silently rejoice are nevertheless outwardly suffused with a blush at suggestive words and wanton jokes, like the deflowered girl in Theocritus, *Idyll* XXVII.68:
>
> > Ἡ μὲν, ἀνεγρομἐνη διέστιχε μάλα νομεύειν,
Ὄμμασιν αἰδομένη, κραδὶη δὲ οἱ ἔνδον ἰάνθη· — “And when she had risen, she went to pasture the sheep, her eyes suffused with shame, but her heart rejoiced within her” [the recovered μάλα is uncertain; the contextual sense is “sheep”].,
>
> that is: “And when she had risen, she went to pasture the sheep, her eyes suffused with shame, but her heart leapt within her.” **HAV.**

others inside, and of course they gave Christians the name of public enemies.

But those who are now discovered every day as accomplices or supporters of criminal factions—the gleaning that survives after the harvest of parricides—how freshly and luxuriantly did they barricade their doorposts with laurels?

> **Note [Col. 0458C–0459C].** “Supporters,” that is, favorers, helpers, or at least men desiring the same thing. In *On Repentance* X: “Why do you flee the sharers of your misfortunes and their supporters?” Read thus, not “as supporters.” For there he is discussing Christians’ mutual love and the military oath which we have all sworn to Christ.
>
> Publilius Syrus forbids the cruel practice of medicine which destroys much of nature—something to which Severus sufficiently testified—in verse 365 of our edition:
>
> > Bad is the medicine by which some part of nature perishes.
>
> Likewise, verse 247:
>
> > Certain remedies are more grievous than the dangers.
>
> Sufficient testimony may be furnished by the wise counsel of Geta, Severus’s son, who was more worthy of life and empire than his brother Bassianus. I shall append the words of Spartianus in his *Life*, for they deserve to be known:
>
> “This remarkable saying is reported of him when he was a boy. Severus wished to kill men belonging to opposing factions and said among his own people, ‘I am taking your enemies away from you.’ Bassianus agreed so completely that he said even their children should be killed, if Severus wished to provide for his own security. Geta is said to have asked how many were to be killed. When his father told him, he asked: ‘Do those men have parents and relatives?’ When the answer was that many of them did, Geta said: ‘Then more people in the city will be saddened than gladdened because we have conquered.’”
>
> Spartianus adds there that Geta’s opinion would have prevailed if the prefect Plautianus, or Juvenalis, had not pressed the contrary view in hope of the confiscations by which they were enriched.
>
> In the words “but those who,” Aldus deletes τὸ (“the [word]”), “and”; shortly afterward, instead of “survives,” the Fulda manuscript has the corrupt reading “surpasses”; and the Leiden manuscript has “always who” instead of “than.” **HAV.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0459C].** Havercamp, from the Fulda codex, reads “they clouded”; Rigault and Junius, from the Puteanus codex, “they obscured.” The words “how highly…they clouded” are absent from the second Lyon codex.
>
> **Note [Col. 0459C].** “Freshly.” Observe the ancient custom of employing especially fresh laurels, and so great a quantity and bulk of them that the entrances of the doors were virtually barricaded.

With how lofty and brilliant an array of lamps did they cloud their vestibules?

> **Note [Col. 0459C–D].** “Lofty.” I understand this of the rows of lamps and the raised structure, as our author spoke above: it seems that rows of these lamps were constructed in vestibules or on doorposts in several levels, as though upon platforms.

With what richly adorned and splendid couches did they divide the forum among themselves?

> **Note [Col. 0459D–0460D].** “Richly adorned and splendid couches.” Scriverius notes from an old manuscript the reading “bulls,” referring the passage to sacrifices. This does not please me, for the word must be taken as at the beginning of this chapter: “A splendid duty, to bring hearths and couches out into public.” See Heraldus there.
>
> Tertullian says that they “divided” the forum, evidently seizing the most convenient and desirable place like so many greengrocers or shopkeepers. No one describes the luxury and ornamentation of couches or litters better than Martial, book XI, epigram 16:
>
> > Zoilus is ill; his coverlets cause this fever.  
> > If he becomes well, what will his scarlet fabrics do?  
> > What will his couch from the Nile do, or the linen dyed with fragrant purple?  
> > What but illness displays his foolish wealth?  
> > What have you to do with physicians? Send away every Machaon.  
> > Do you wish to become well? Take my coverlets.
>
> The same poet also teaches us at what time of day this spectacle was dismantled and the couches brought home, book IV, epigram 8:
>
> > The ninth hour commands the erected couches to be broken up.
>
> For after that hour a respectable man did not readily roam through the streets but withdrew home for dinner and study. Prostitutes, however, customarily opened their brothel then, and were consequently called *women of the ninth hour* by Persius at the end of *Satire* I:
>
> > If a wanton woman of the ninth hour plucks a Cynic’s beard. **HAV.**

They did so not to celebrate public rejoicings, but to proclaim their own wishes already, and in another man’s solemn festival to inaugurate an example and image of their own hope, changing the ruler’s name in their hearts.

> **Note [Col. 0459C].** Rigault and Havercamp read “proclaim” in other editions, followed by “and an example,” etc. Others read “learn by heart”; the second Lyon codex reads “expound, lest in another’s solemnity both an example,” etc.
>
> **Note [Col. 0459C].** Rhenanus and Gelenius read “imitating”; the Lyon codex, “inviting.”

The same duties are also paid by those who consult astrologers, soothsayers, augurs, and magicians concerning the Caesars’ lives—arts which Christians, because they were disclosed by apostate angels and forbidden by God, do not employ even for their own affairs. But who needs to search into Caesar’s safety except one by whom something against it is being devised or desired, or by whom something following it is hoped for and awaited?

> **Note [Col. 0459C].** Havercamp reads “separated” instead of “awaited.”

For one does not consult concerning loved ones in the same frame of mind as concerning masters. The anxious curiosity of blood relationship is one thing; that of servitude another. [Col. 0459B]

## CHAPTER XXXVI

> **Note [Col. 0460D].** “And those who consult astrologers.” Tertullian touches upon this charge because under Severus many men perished on account of astrologers. Spartianus, in *Severus*. **LAC.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0460D–0461B].** “Thus piety and religion.” Up to this point he has refuted them from their own opinion; now he states clearly that the piety, religion, and loyalty owed to emperors do not consist in those duties and practices by which hostility is veiled, covered, and disguised—as the gentiles do, who openly say that they are Romans but secretly lay plots. **LAC.**

That those Christians may be regarded as enemies who breathe nothing hostile against either the Roman Empire or the Roman emperor—indeed, who are toward others just what they are toward the emperor, since they are not permitted to wish evil, devise evil, against others, much less against the emperor, who has been raised by God to so great a height.

If these things are so, so that men who were called Romans are discovered to be enemies, why are we, who are deemed enemies, denied the name of Romans?

> **Note [Col. 0460C].** “Why should we be denied,” Paris.

Can we not both be Romans and not be enemies,

> **Note [Col. 0460C].** Pamelius and others read: “both not be Romans and be enemies.”

when men who were regarded as Romans are found to be enemies?

Thus the piety, religion, and loyalty devoted to the emperors do not consist in duties of this kind—duties which hostility can more readily employ as a covering for itself—but in those forms of conduct which civic duty must display as truly toward the emperor as toward everyone.

> **Note [Col. 0460D].** “Changing in their hearts.” Rhenanus reads “imitating”; the Leiden manuscript, “inviting.” Neither pleases me. This is very well illustrated by the accusation with which Valerius Omulus burdened Marcus Antoninus’s mother before Antoninus Pius. Julius Capitolinus relates in his *Life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*:
>
> “Marcus was held in the highest favor by his adoptive father, although there were some who whispered things against him, particularly Valerius Omulus. When Omulus saw Lucilla, Marcus’s mother, in a garden venerating an image of Apollo, he whispered: ‘She is now asking that you end your day and that her son become emperor.’” **HAV.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0460C].** Wouweren restored this reading from a manuscript, and Rigault, Havercamp, and others accepted it. The earlier editions read: “in those things which divinity commands, as truly as,” etc. Havercamp and Ritter, however, transposed the words to read: “civic duty must display as truly toward the emperor as,” etc.
>
> **Note [Col. 0460C].** “Must” is absent from the Paris edition.

For these works of a good mind are not owed by us to emperors alone. We perform no good with partiality toward persons, because we render it for our own benefit, since we seek credit for neither praise nor reward from man, but from God, the exactor and remunerator of impartial kindness.

We are the same toward emperors as we are toward our neighbors.

> **Note [Col. 0460C].** Havercamp emends this from the reading: “from himself, because also toward our neighbors.”

For we are equally forbidden to wish evil, do evil, speak evil, or think evil concerning anyone. Whatever is not lawful against the emperor is not lawful against anyone; and what is lawful against no one is perhaps all the more unlawful against the emperor himself, who is so great through God. [Col. 0460B]

## CHAPTER XXXVII

> **Note [Col. 0460].** This note appears at the foot of column 462, but the callout letter, (d), has not been printed in the text.
>
> **Note [Col. 0462B].** “From the repose of burial.” A notable passage against the heretical followers of the Donatists in our own age, who dug up the buried bodies of Christians, indeed of kings, although burial is rightly called by Tertullian an asylum of death. And certainly the most severe penalties against violators of tombs were established long ago even by the pagan emperors themselves. **PAM.**

That nothing evil is to be expected from the Christians may be evident from this: among them it is not lawful to repay evil with evil. Yet if they wished to avenge unjust hatred and insults, they could do so very easily, both because of their enormous numbers, with which the world has been filled in a short time, and because of the contempt for death which they display even under torture for the Faith—whether they preferred to act by fires, by wars, or finally by mere withdrawal, thereby laying waste the commonwealth. But now, having actually become benefactors of their enemies, they deliver from the assaults of demons those whom they have nevertheless preferred to call enemies of human error rather than of the human race.

If, as we said above, we are commanded to love our enemies, whom have we to hate?

> **Note [Col. 0461A].** “Whom shall we have,” Paris.

Likewise, if, when injured, we are forbidden to retaliate, lest we become equal to them in deed, whom can we injure?

> **Note [Col. 0461A].** The Fulda codex adds “likewise.”

For consider the matter yourselves. How often do you rage savagely against Christians, partly obeying your own passions and partly the laws? How often, even bypassing you, does the hostile mob attack us on its own authority with stones and fires?

> **Note [Col. 0461A].** “When you have passed by,” Paris.
>
> **Note [Col. 0461B–C].** “With stones and fires.” Such punishment is familiar to the mob; compare John 8:59; 10:31; 11:8; Luke 20:6; Acts 5:26; 14:19. Eusebius, bishop of Samosata, was killed in this manner by an Arian woman, who threw a roof tile upon his head. On this deed see Nazianzen, *Oration XI against the Arians*, and concerning himself:
>
> > ὃν ἐκ τῆς ὑπερορίας ἀχθέντα λίθοις ὲδῖδαξασδε μεσούσης ἡμέρας, ἐν μέσῃ πόλει — “Whom, when he had been brought back from exile, you received with stones at midday, in the middle of the city” [ὲδῖδαξασδε is corrupt in the recovered text; its rendering follows the clear context].,
>
> that is: “When I was brought back from exile, you received me with stones, at midday itself and in the middle of the city.”
>
> In Petronius: “Some of those strolling in the porticoes threw stones at Eumolpus while he was reciting.” In the same work: “And so I am not surprised if the people pursue you with stones.”
>
> Indeed, even images of emperors and gods, and the temples themselves, were stoned by the raging mob, as Suetonius teaches in *Caligula* V concerning the death of Germanicus.
>
> Cyprian, book IV, epistle 10, presents a remarkable example of both kinds of fury in Numidicus, whom he commends to the presbyters of Carthage. By his exhortation Numidicus sent before him a great number of martyrs killed by stones and flames; and he joyfully watched his wife, who clung to his side, burned together with the others—or, I would rather say, preserved. He himself, half-burned, overwhelmed with stones, and abandoned for dead, afterward remained behind against his will when his daughter, seeking her father’s body with the anxious devotion of piety, found him half alive, revived him, and drew him away from the companions whom he himself had sent ahead. **HAV.**

In the very frenzy of the Bacchanals they do not spare even dead Christians, but tear them from the repose of burial, from that asylum, as it were, of death—by then altered, by then no longer whole—and cut and drag them apart.

> **Note [Col. 0461C–D].** “In the very frenzy of the Bacchanals.” He alludes to the description of Bacchus, whom afterward, as blessed Justin Martyr says in his book *On Monarchy*, they call “raving.” As for the rites of Bacchus—how shameful and how full of frenzy they were—let the reader consult Augustine, *The City of God* VII.21, and the annotations of Vives there. **PAM.**
>
> **Note [Col. 0461D–0462B].** “From the repose of burial.” Yet he says almost the same thing immediately afterward in “from a certain asylum of death.” For just as temples of the gods made those who fled into them safe and inviolable, preserving their lives, so death and the tomb can furnish corpses with nothing but repose.
>
> The reading of the Fulda codex, “from the remains of burial,” might therefore be preferred, were he not again saying virtually the same thing immediately afterward in “now others, now not even whole.”
>
> Nazianzen severely censures the Arians in the passage cited because they exposed the naked bodies of the saints to wild beasts and forbade burial of the dead:
>
> > τίνας (“what [beasts]”), he says, ἐπαφήκαμεν θῆρας ἁγίων σώμασιν; ἅς τινες τὴν ἀπάνθρωπον φύσιν δημοσιεύσαντες — “did we set upon the bodies of the saints?—beasts which certain men did set upon them, publicly displaying their inhuman nature” [the recovered construction is incomplete and ἅς is grammatically uncertain]..
>
> That is: “What wild beasts have we set upon the bodies of the saints? Certain men did this, publishing and prostituting human nature.”
>
> And shortly afterward: “Whom have we charged with a crime because they buried the dead—dead whom the very beasts themselves would have revered?”
>
> Certainly, as the same author says in praise of Hero, *Oration* XXXIII, burial should not be denied even to impious and criminal men. **HAV.**

Yet what retaliation for injury have you ever detected among men so closely united, so resolute even unto death, when a single night and a few little torches could abundantly accomplish vengeance, if it were lawful among us to balance evil with evil?

> **Note [Col. 0461A].** “Do you detect,” Franciscus.
>
> **Note [Col. 0461B].** “Repaid,” Franciscus.
>
> **Note [Col. 0461B].** Havercamp conjectures “little torches.”
>
> **Note [Col. 0461B].** Thus the Fulda codex, Rigault, and others; another reading is “for the abundance of vengeance.”

But far be it from us either that a divine sect should be avenged by human fire or that it should grieve to suffer the very thing by which it is proved.

If we wished to act as open enemies, rather than merely hidden avengers—

> **Note [Col. 0462A].** “Excluded,” Paris.
>
> **Note [Col. 0462B–C].** “Hidden avengers.” As Christians are now, entrusting vengeance to God. Or does he mean treacherous supporters of opposing factions? Elsewhere those too may be called hidden avengers who, being presently prevented from avenging themselves by lack of strength, seize a suitable time for vengeance, as Theognis urges in verse 362:
>
> > Εὗ κώτίλλε τὸν ἐχθρὸν — “Soothe your enemy well”.  
> > ὂταν δ` ὑποχεὶριος ἔλθῃ,
   Τίσαί νιν, πρόφασιν μηδεμίαν Θέμενσς — “but when he comes under your power, take vengeance upon him, admitting no excuse” [Θέμενσς is corrupt in the recovered text; the rendering follows the clear contextual sense]..
>
> That is: “Soothe your enemy well; but after he has come under your power, take vengeance upon him, admitting no excuse.”
>
> The sharp saying of Publilius Syrus, verse 156, teaches the same:
>
> > Do not speak evil of an enemy, but think it.
>
> On this passage one may consult the observations from the posthumous works of Janus Gruter which we have published. This political advice is fitting for gentiles, however, not for Christians. Sophocles speaks humanely, of course, in *Ajax the Flagellifer*, verse 747.

Restoration notes: S000732 and S000737 contain apparent textual or extraction corruption; their recovered readings have been preserved verbatim, and the renderings follow the clear sense supplied by their immediate contexts.  

Οτ` ἐχθρὸς ῆμην ἐς τοσὁνδ` ἐχθραντέος,


   Ὡς καὶ φιλήσων αὗθις (“When I was an enemy, I was to be hated only so far as one who might later become a friend.”). That is: “When I was an enemy, I was to be hated in such a way that I might become a friend again.” **HAV.**]—if we wished to act, would we lack the strength of numbers and forces? The Moors and Marcomanni, surely, and even the Parthians—or any peoples whatever, confined nevertheless to a single region and their own territories—are more numerous than the whole world? We are but of yesterday, [Note: [Col. 0462B] Thus Heraldus from the Put. MS., Aldus, Rigaltius, Havercamp, Junius, and La Cerda; the others: “foreigners.”] and we have filled everything you possess: [Note: [Col. 0462C] “We have filled everything you possess.” The swift course of the Gospel and the mighty scepter of his strength, which the Lord sent forth from Zion, quickly shattered the eternal gates of the world and its brazen doors. Striking testimony to this, even in the second century after Christ’s birth, may be obtained both from this passage and from chapter 1: “They cry out that the state is besieged,” etc. Also *To Scapula*, chapter 2: “Although so great a multitude of people, almost the greater part of every city, we conduct ourselves in silence and modesty; as individuals, perhaps, we are better known than as a whole”; and chapter 5: “What will you do with so many thousands of people, so many men and women, of every sex, every age, and every rank, offering themselves to you? How many fires, how many swords will be needed? What will Carthage itself suffer when decimated by you, when everyone recognizes among them his relatives and household companions, when he perhaps sees among them men and matrons of your own order, and all the foremost persons, and either relatives or friends of your friends?” *To the Nations* I.8: “But take notice, lest those whom you call the third race should occupy the foremost place, since there is no nation that is not Christian; and so whatever nation is foremost is nonetheless Christian.” Likewise, *Against the Jews*, chapter 7, where, after expounding the passage from Acts 2:9–11, he adds: “So now the various tribes of the Gaetulians, the many territories of the Moors, all the bounds of the Spains, the diverse nations of the Gauls, and the regions of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans but subject to Christ; and of the Sarmatians, Dacians, Germans, and Scythians; and of many hidden peoples, provinces, and many islands unknown to us, which we are scarcely able to enumerate—in all these places the name of Christ, who has now come, reigns: for before him the gates of all cities stand open, and none are closed; before him iron bars have been shattered and brazen doors opened. Although these things are also to be understood spiritually, insofar as the hearts of individuals, besieged by the devil in various ways, have been unlocked by faith in Christ, they have nevertheless been manifestly fulfilled, since in all these places a people bearing the name of God dwells.” And to the same people, chapter 12: “Behold all the nations emerging thereafter from the abyss of human error toward the Lord God the Creator and toward his Christ. And if you dare, deny that it was prophesied; immediately the Father’s promise confronts you in the Psalms, saying,” etc. Finally, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 12: “For Christ is also among the barbarians.” And that impostor in Lucian’s *Pseudomantis* cries out that Pontus is filled with impious men and Christians. **HAV.**] cities, islands, fortresses, [Col. 0463A] towns, meeting places, the camps themselves, tribes, decuries, the palace, the senate, and the forum. We have left you only the temples.

We can count [Note: [Col. 0463D] “We can count your armies: the Christians of a single province will be more numerous.” This entire passage is found only in the Fulda manuscript, and yet it plainly smacks of Tertullian. He says: We know how many armies the Romans maintain today and what their proper number is; but the multitude of Christians is so great that even a single province could furnish from them greater forces. The following words correspond beautifully with this. I can scarcely tolerate the fact that others, and Rigaltius above all, passed it over. I nevertheless think that the word “Christians” has fallen out. **HAV.**] your armies: [Christians] from a single province will be more numerous. [Note: [Col. 0463B] Havercamp received the words “We can—more numerous” from the single Fulda manuscript; he thought the word “Christians” had fallen out.] For what war would we not have been fit and ready, even though unequal in forces—we who are slaughtered so willingly—[Note: [Col. 0464C] “We are slaughtered so willingly.” For, as Publilius Syrus truly says in *Mimes*, verse 259:

> Alas, how much must he be feared who thinks it safe to die.

And the same author, verse 422:

> Once you despise death, you have conquered every fear.

From the same source comes Seneca’s saying *To Helvia*, chapter 13: “Into the heart from which you have cast out the fear of death, no fear of anything will dare to enter.”

> Those whom that greatest of fears, the fear  
> Of death, does not constrain: hence their minds are eager  
> To rush upon the sword, and it inspires men capable  
> Of death;

thus Lucan’s mighty spirit sings of the Druids in Book I, where instead of *capaces* (“capable”) I read *rapaces* (“eager to seize”): they seize their own death, as it were. **HAV.**] if under this discipline it were not more lawful to be killed than to kill?

We could also, unarmed and not rebellious but merely estranged, have fought against you through the resentment caused by our mere separation. For if so great a mass of people had broken away from you into some remote corner of the world, the loss of so many citizens, whatever their character, would surely have overwhelmed your dominion [with shame], [Note: [Col. 0463B] Havercamp received “with shame” from the Fulda manuscript; the Lyons edition has: “would surely have poured out.”] or rather would even have punished it by the very fact of abandonment. Without doubt you would have been terrified at your solitude, at the silence of things, and at a kind of stupor [Col. 0463B] belonging to a world as though dead; [Note: [Col. 0463B] Thus Rigaltius and Havercamp on the authority of the Fulda manuscript; the Put. and Bong. manuscripts have: “as though dead, you would have sought cities”; Pamelius: “as though of a dead city, you would have sought those whom you might rule in it”; Rhenanus [Col. 0464B], Aldus, and Gangneius: “as though the remains of a dead city, you would have sought,” etc.] you would have sought people to rule. More enemies than citizens would have remained to you.

For now you have fewer enemies in comparison with the multitude of Christians, since nearly all the citizens of nearly all cities are Christians. [Note: [Col. 0464B] Thus Havercamp; all the manuscripts have “citizens.” Rigaltius deleted the words “nearly all—of the human race,” to which others add: “rather than of human error.”] But you preferred to call us enemies of the human race, [Note: [Col. 0464B] “Rather than of human error” added by Franciscus, the Paris edition, and Rigaltius.] although who would rescue you from those hidden enemies that everywhere devastate your minds and health? I mean from the attacks of demons, which we drive away from you without reward and without payment. This alone would have sufficed for our vengeance: that from then on you would have lain open, an unoccupied possession, to unclean spirits. [Note: [Col. 0464B] “Would lie open,” Franciscus and the Paris edition.] Yet, giving no thought to compensation for so great a protection, you preferred to judge as enemies a race not merely harmless to you but even necessary. Enemies we certainly are—not, however, of the human race, but rather of error.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0464] This note appears at the foot of column 466, but the callout letter, (g), has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0466D] “There is nothing for us to speak, see, or hear.” The Fulda manuscript has: “For nothing.” The others have: “There is nothing.” But Rigaltius deleted τὸ (“the”) “there is,” perhaps rightly. Yet I cannot—indeed, I refuse—to follow him and Rhenanus in ordering the words “to speak, see, or hear” also to be banished. All the manuscripts acknowledge them, as do all the other editions, and finally they do not conflict with the sense. “To speak” refers to the disorderly shouts of the partisans, who, while contending and rioting among themselves over the charioteers whom they favored, each encouraged his own faction with acclamations. Hence that famous charioteer Scorpus is called by Martial:

> The glory of the clamorous circus.

[Col. 0467C] “To see” refers to the indecent gestures and nudity of the theater and the exercise-ground; “to hear” pertains to the arena, since it is certainly not humane to drink in with pleasurable ears the groans of the falling and the howling of those torn apart by beasts. **HAV.**]

Since these things are so, a sect that does no evil ought to be tolerated; for there is no reason to fear that people of this kind will assemble in unlawful factions, seeing that they avoid the places of faction and long ago learned to renounce the spectacles, the circus, the theater, the arena, and the exercise-ground—from which people commonly return cruel, mad, wanton, frivolous, turbulent, and for that reason fit for conspiracy. If, therefore, Christians choose other pleasures, and choose them harmlessly, they ought not to be disturbed, since they in turn leave the nations undisturbed in theirs.

Accordingly, and with no less leniency, this sect ought to have been counted among lawful associations, since it commits nothing of the kind ordinarily feared from unlawful factions. For, unless I am mistaken, it is agreed that factions are prohibited out of concern for public order, [Note: [Col. 0464C] Pamelius and others: “and public order.”] lest the state be split into parties—a circumstance that would readily disturb elections, assemblies, councils, public meetings, and even spectacles through the rival collisions of partisan enthusiasm, [Note: [Col. 0464D] “Through the rival collisions of partisan enthusiasm.” Such were those well-known factions of the net-fighters and shield-fighters, and of the Blues, Greens, and similar groups, known especially from Suetonius and other writers; concerning them, see Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, Book II, chapter 24. Chrysostom also alludes to them in the homily on Isaiah 6:1, where he forbids collisions in church: “Nor do we forbid a voice of praise, but a voice of absurdity and disorder, and your mutual contentions, hands rashly and idly raised into the air, stamping feet, and indecorous and effeminate behavior—the practices of those who frequent theaters and circus games, entertainments, and diversions. From there destructive examples are brought among us; from there irreligious and vulgar cries; from there foolish gesticulations of the hands, contentions, contests, unstable behavior, and tasteless, disorderly shouting.” Thus the whole city would be divided into parties, like the crowd at the spectacles. In the same passage: “From countless contentions, from rashly uttered oaths by those who speak evil,” etc. **HAV.**] since by then men had also begun to hold their venal and mercenary service of violence as a source of profit. [Note: [Col. 0465A] “Men—the venal and mercenary service of their violence.” In place of “venal,” the Leiden manuscript presents “they might wish,” while the Fulda manuscript deletes the word “men.” But I think the text should read: “since everyone had already begun to regard the base and mercenary service of his violence as a source of profit”; the meaning would be that people of every rank and condition, driven by factions, exposed themselves and their property to danger and destruction. For the condition of the commonwealth is most wretched when avarice has overthrown good faith, integrity, and the other good arts, and in their place has taught arrogance, cruelty, contempt of the gods, and the treatment of everything as venal, as Sallust rightly observes in *Catiline*, chapter 10; when friendships and enmities are no longer judged according to the thing itself but according to advantage, as he teaches in the same place. **HAV.**]

[Note: [Col. 0465A] Havercamp corrects the text to: “everyone—the base and mercenary service of his violence.”]

But for us, who are cold toward every burning desire for glory and office, [Note: [Col. 0465B] “Toward every burning desire for glory and office.” He elegantly called the desire for glory a “burning desire,” since it virtually sets people on fire; hence poets use the verb “inflame” and similar words. Thus Iphiclus, added to the Argonauts in Valerius Flaccus, Book I.75, was added not to labor:

> But, having been admonished, to impart keen counsels,  
> And to inflame the heroes with their great ancestors’ praises.

Thus, when he says in the proper terminology that Christians are “cold” toward that burning desire, he shows from the inner sanctuary of philosophy that they are wise men, holding that they ought not to administer a commonwealth whose morals are corrupt. These words, moreover, seem to have been sketched from Plato, whose most beautiful relevant passage you may see below at chapter 46, on the words “and necessarily desire.” Sallust also says of himself in *Catiline*, chapter 3: “And although I dissented from the evil conduct of the rest, nevertheless the same desire for office, with the attendant ill repute and envy, tormented me as it did the others.” The Fulda manuscript reads “glory,” while Aldus deletes τὸ (“the”) “from.” **HAV.**] there is no necessity for an assembly, and no concern is more foreign to us than public affairs. We acknowledge one commonwealth shared by all: [Note: [Col. 0465C] “One commonwealth shared by all.” This too comes from the definition of the wise, for whom the whole world is a home and every place a native land. The words of John Chrysostom concerning Saint Lucian are not far removed from this. When questioned under torture, he was asked: ποίας εἰ πατρίδους; Χριστιανος εἰμι φησι (“What is your native land? ‘I am a Christian,’ he says.” The recovered Greek is grammatically corrupt, but its sense is clear.). Τί ἔχεις ἐπιτήδευμα; Χριστιανὸς εἰμι (“What occupation do you have? ‘I am a Christian.’”). Τίνας προγόνους; ὀ δὲ πρὸς ἅπαντα ἕλεγεν, ὄτι Χριστιανὸς εἰμι (“Who were your ancestors? But to every question he said, ‘I am a Christian.’”). That is: “‘What is your native land?’ ‘I am a Christian,’ he replied. ‘What trade do you profess?’ ‘I am a Christian.’ ‘Who were your ancestors?’ But to everything he said, ‘Do you hear that I am a Christian?’” [Col. 0465D] Thus Aristippus said εἶναί τε πατρίδα τὸν κόσμον (“and that the world is his native land”), and Crates of Thebes, loftier than he, says in the tragedy:

Οὐχ εἷς πάτρις μοι πύργος, οὐ μὶα στέγη,


Πάσης δὲ χέρσου καὶ πόλισμα καὶ δόμος


Ἔτοιμοις ἡμῖν ἐνδιαιτᾶσθαι πάρα (“No single tower or dwelling is my native land; rather, every land’s city and home are available for us to inhabit.”).

That is:

> No single tower or house is my native land,  
> But all the earth’s strongholds and homes  
> Offer us a ready dwelling and supper-room.

It is, of course, as Aristophanes says in *Plutus*, verse 1:

Πατρὶς γὰς ἐστι πῶσ` ἒν` ἅν πράττῃ τὶς ἒυ (“For one’s native land is wherever one fares well.” The recovered Greek is textually corrupt, but the supplied context makes the sense clear.).

That is: “Each man’s native land is wherever he fares well.” I have written the passage with Rigaltius, with the Leiden manuscript agreeing; for Aldus and all the others—the source text is incomplete here. Barraeus, Rhenanus, and others have “we know.” The Leiden manuscript presents the entire passage thus: “For us, etc., who are cold, no concern is more foreign than public affairs, since we acknowledge one commonwealth shared by all: the world.” Just as here he calls the world the one commonwealth of all, so in the following chapter he calls nature the one mother of all. **HAV.**] [Col. 0466A] the world.

Equally, we renounce your spectacles [Note: [Col. 0466A] “Equally, the spectacles.” Junius wished the word “equally” to be attached to the preceding words and a full stop placed after it. Unfairly. For if anything had to be changed, it would be preferable to read: “We are fair toward your spectacles,” which can be reconciled with what follows. But the old reading is entirely sound. For just as Christians renounced the forum and senate-house because they did not desire praise and glory, so [Col. 0466B] they also renounced spectacles, since these both arose from idolatry and violated human and divine laws. The Fulda parchment reads: “And indeed.” Christians rightly renounced spectacles, since they themselves, having been made a spectacle to the world with Paul in 1 Corinthians 4:9, possess spectacles in abundance in the word of God. Let us hear Prosper of Aquitaine, *The Promises and Predictions of God*, “On the Glory of the Saints,” in the peroration: “If there is pleasure in watching,” he says, “you have here Christ as a spiritual charioteer, and Elijah, who was conveyed in a fiery chariot as far as the turning-posts of heaven, and Pharaoh’s chariots drowned in the deep. In the contest you have holy Daniel, conquering the lion not with steel but with prayer; and the bears attacking those who assailed the prophet Elisha with insults. In the holy spectacle you also have, not the indecencies of mimes, but virgins consecrated to Christ. In place of trick-riders you have Rebecca’s twins mystically at play. You have David dancing before the ark, and Christ stripped naked in his passion, presenting that very history of his before his servants and handmaids. [Col. 0466C] Finally, you have Jeremiah’s weeping and lamentations sung, not with tragic but prophetic art.” Add our author’s *On Spectacles*, chapter 29. **HAV.**] to the same extent that we renounce their origins, which we know were conceived from superstition; and we stand apart from the very things with which they are concerned. [Note: [Col. 0466A] “We presume,” Latinus; “we prefer,” the Paris edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0466C] “The things with which they are concerned—we stand apart.” This is the consistent reading of all the manuscripts, which the old editions of Barraeus, Aldus, and Rhenanus had corrupted into “we pass over the things exacted—or transacted.” Pamelius and others restored the true reading. But where they had placed “and from the very things,” Aldus printed “from the very things.” Rigaltius has “which very things,” contrary to the manuscripts. Tertullian elegantly says that Christians “stand apart from” those very things with which spectacles are concerned—that is, the things forming their subject matter, namely madness, lust, and cruelty—because Christians renounced these when they became Christians and consequently no longer live to them, but are dead, as Peter speaks in 1 Peter 2:24, and Paul likewise in Romans 6:2 and Colossians 3:7. Indeed, they are nothing to worldly things, just as in chapter 47 he aptly calls the god whom the Epicureans fashion for themselves a nobody in relation to human affairs. **HAV.**]

We have nothing to do, in speech, sight, or hearing, [Note: [Col. 0466D] “Since we stand apart from the very things with which they are concerned.” He says “stand apart from” as one says “survive.” We therefore stand apart from the things that we pass over and omit, and from which we are wholly estranged: namely, from the madness of the circus, the immodesty of the theater, etc. Marcus Cato likewise used “pass by” for what is commonly called “spurn” or “despise”: “I passed by their arguments,” he says. For so the manuscripts of Pliny’s preface addressed to Vespasian read, where those words of Cato are cited near the end. **RIG.**] with the madness of the circus, [Col. 0467A] [Note: [Col. 0467C] “The madness of the circus.” Chrysostom, among others, taught in the passage quoted above that disorderly shouts were uttered there. Tertullian shows in *To the Martyrs*, chapter 1, that the same practice also prevailed in the arena: “Nevertheless, not only their trainers and overseers, but even ignorant and entirely superfluous people encourage the most accomplished gladiators from afar, so that commands dictated by the crowd itself have often proved useful.” **HAV.**] the immodesty of the theater, [Note: [Col. 0467C] “The immodesty of the theater.” Elsewhere he calls it by its proper name, “the council-chamber of lust and immodesty.” There the plots of the plays, the characters, the words, and everything else are obscene, shameful, and unworthy of a good man’s hearing and sight. Chrysostom therefore inveighs sharply against them everywhere, along with others. Thus in his thirteenth homily on 1 Corinthians 4: “They assemble theaters and lead there choruses of prostitutes, boys who prostitute themselves, and those who outrage nature itself; they make the whole populace sit in an elevated place and so provide recreation for the city.” And on Matthew 11, Homily 37: “For absolutely everything done there is most shameful: words, dress, hairstyle, gait, voices, songs, melodies, rolling and movement of the eyes, flutes, pipes, and the very plots of the plays—all, I say, are full of shameful wantonness,” etc. For these reasons those sitting there ought not to dissolve in laughter, but to groan with tears and grief. He therefore severely rebukes Christians who dared to watch these abominations, in Homily 7 on Matthew 2: “For even when you have seen him”—Christ—“you leave him so that you may run from him to the theaters and desire instead both to see and to hear a mime. You leave Christ lying in the spiritual manger, but hurry to watch a prostitute lying on the stage.” And soon afterward: “Yet from this table flows the fountain of spiritual blessings, and immediately abandoning it you run to the theater to gaze at swimming women and at that sex exposed to the public eye.” And in the same place: “You abandon the fountain of this blood and the venerable cup and hasten to that diabolical fountain, so that you may watch a prostitute swimming and suffer the shipwreck of your soul; for she is a kind of immense sea of lust, in which bodies are not submerged but souls suffer shipwreck. She plays naked, swimming amid the waters, while you, looking down from the lofty tier, sink into the depths of lust.” See also the much more extensive discussion to the same effect that follows there. Again, the same author in the homily *On David and Saul*: “Do you not fear, do you not tremble, when with the same eyes with which you look there upon the bed set in the orchestra, where detestable tales of adultery are performed, you behold this sacred table where the awe-inspiring mysteries are celebrated? When with the same ears you hear both a prostitute speaking obscenely and the Prophet and Apostle introducing you to the mysteries of Scripture?” Finally, in the homily *That All Vices Originate from Idleness*: “At the very time when we were discussing these things here, others idly watched the devil’s pageant in the theaters. They then heard the songs of prostitutes; but you feasted upon the sweetest spiritual teaching. They fed upon the devil’s most impure dishes; but you were anointed with spiritual ointment.” Hence Cyril of Jerusalem rightly says in *Mystagogical Catechesis*, or *Catechesis* I.4, when explaining the devil’s pageantry that we renounced in baptism, that it is θεατρομανίας καὶ ἰπποδρομία, κυνηγορίαν καί πᾶσαν τοιάυτην ματαιότητα (“a passion for the theater and horse-racing, hunting, and every such vanity”).] the savagery of the arena, [Note: [Col. 0468D] “The savagery of the arena.” There nothing else is done but that men, laying aside humanity, may become rabid beasts. And so let Chrysostom also come forward here, in Homily 13 on 1 Corinthians 4: “What need is there to mention the frauds and deceptions that occur in horse races, and those that occur in contests of beasts? For all these things are full of stupefaction and madness. They continually teach the people to be merciless, savage, and inhuman, and train them to watch men torn apart and mangled, blood pouring out, and the cruelty of beasts throwing everything into confusion.”] and the emptiness of the exercise-ground. [Note: [Col. 0468D] “The emptiness of the exercise-ground.” The same Chrysostom, in a homily on Psalm 118: “You, children of the Church, ought not to be corrupted by the vanities of spectacles.” Bulengerus, Panvinius, Vellerus, Faber, and innumerable others have written about these games. Relevant also to the savagery of the arena just mentioned is an elegant saying of the philosopher Demonax to the Athenians, which Lucian recounts in his *Life*. The Athenians were deliberating about establishing a gladiatorial spectacle in imitation of the Corinthians. There the philosopher uttered this sound judgment: Μή πρότερον ταῦτα, ὧ Ἀθηναιοι ψηφίζεσθε, ἀν μή τοῦ Ἐλέου τὸν βωμον κατέλητε (“Athenians, do not enact these measures before you have overthrown the altar of Mercy.”), that is: “Athenians, do not enact these measures before you have overthrown the altar of Mercy.”]

The Epicureans were permitted to determine some true form of pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0467B] In the editions before Rigaltius, these words are placed only at the very end of the chapter, written thus: “But the Epicureans were permitted to determine some true form of pleasure, that is, equanimity and ample affairs.” But in the Fulda manuscript they alone are placed here, with these words added: “that is, equanimity.” Heraldus preferred to write: “To be sure, the Epicureans were permitted,” etc. Wouwer produced this reading from his manuscript: “But the Epicureans were permitted to determine some true form of pleasure, ἀταραξίαν καὶ ἀπραξίαν (“tranquility and freedom from public business”), that is, equanimity and rest from public affairs.”] How do we offend you if we choose other pleasures? If we do not wish to have learned how to be entertained, [Note: [Col. 0467B] Rhenanus and Gelenius: “if we do not wish to be entertained”; the Fulda manuscript: “if we do not wish most recently to entertain.” I do not know whether the text should be written: “if we do not wish to entertain ourselves most vainly” (compare *On Modesty* 1).] the injury, if any, is ours, not yours. But we reject what pleases you, and you take no delight in what pleases us.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0467] This note appears at the foot of column 470, but the callout letter, (i), has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0470D] “And now household elders.” This is the ancient reading of the best manuscripts and editions; in its place others, such as the Aldine editions and Rhenanus, preferred to put “and those subdued by age,” which I do not approve equally. I write the words with a hyphen, like those concerning a noble horse in Virgil, *Georgics* III.92, when it has grown old:

> This one too, when burdened by sickness or now more sluggish with years,  
> Fails: remove him from the stable, nor pardon his shameful old age.

The most elegant Andreas Schottus establishes this reading admirably against Canterus and others in *Observationes Humanae*, Book II, chapter 51. But if, with Junius, you prefer to understand the words simply of those who are “members of the household of faith,” from Galatians 6:10, a passage of Justin lies ready to hand. Thus in Book II, chapter 10, he calls Artaphernes, the paternal uncle of Artamenes and Xerxes when they were contending for the Persian kingdom, a “household judge,” just as our author says in chapter 1, “household testimony.” But I do not accept this interpretation. **HAV.**]

Thus, in order that the nations may withdraw from their prejudgment, he freely communicates to them the discipline of the Christian association, as they called it, and all but sets before our eyes the condition of the ancient Church: namely, how Christians were accustomed to assemble in one place; to whom, for whom, and for what they prayed; how they delivered the admonitions and declarations of Scripture; exercised moral censure; ordered the assembly; collected alms; and distributed them for the burial of the dead, the support of the needy, orphans, and retired elders, or the relief of shipwrecked persons and of those banished to the mines, islands, or prisons for the faith. [Col. 0467B–0468A]

He teaches that so great an affection is free from every stain and deserves the true title of love—a love which among the nations is only impure and feigned. Among them banquets are sumptuous, costly, lustful, and infamous; among Christians they are sober, moderate, chaste, and devout. Such a fellowship, therefore, should be called not a faction but a council.
