Their renderings give the recoverable sense while preserving the supplied Greek, with the material uncertainty in S000762 noted explicitly.; S000773 has the unusual recovered reading πάντοθε (“everywhere”), preserved and rendered as supplied.  

I shall now set forth the actual business of the Christian association, so that, having refuted its alleged evils, I may display its virtues. [Note: [Col. 0468B] Cod. Fuld. reads “so that the less” (*quo minus*).] We are a body united by a shared consciousness of religion, by the divine character of our discipline [Note: [Col. 0468B] “Truth,” Paris; “unity,” Fran.], and by the covenant of hope. We come together in an assembly and congregation so that, as though forming a body of troops, we may surround God with our prayers. [Note: [Col. 0468B] “We come together before God,” Rig.] Such force is pleasing to God. We pray also for the emperors, for their ministries [Note: [Col. 0468B] Fran. and Par. add “praying.”] [Col. 0468B] and authorities [Note: [Col. 0468B] “Ministers,” Fran. and Par.], for the condition of the age [Note: [Col. 0468B] The words “for the condition” are absent from the Lyons manuscripts and the editions of Gelenius, Havercamp, Semler, and Rigaltius], for public tranquillity, and for the postponement of the end.

We assemble [Note: [Col. 0468B] “We come together,” Paris.] for the recollection of the divine writings, [Col. 0469A] [Note: [Col. 0469B] “We come together for the recollection of the divine writings.” La Cerda has *cogimur*, that is, “we convene,” as he explains there. Justin Martyr has nearly the same things in *Apology* 2. All these passages, both Justin’s and Tertullian’s, are cited by Stephanus Durantus, book 2, *On the Rites of the Church*, chap. 18. LE PR.] if some feature of present circumstances compels us either to give warning in advance or to review the past. Certainly we nourish faith with holy words, raise up hope, establish confidence, and no less reinforce the discipline of the commandments amid assaults. [Note: [Col. 0469A] “Amid assaults,” Cod. Fuld., Haverc.] [Note: [Col. 0469C] “Amid assaults.” This reading of the Fulda manuscript is far better than the *inculcationibus* (“inculcations”) of the others. For it especially demonstrates the divine character of Christian discipline that even amid persecutions and attacks by the wicked—for this is how he uses *compulsare* and *compulsatio*—Christians depart in no respect from faith, hope, confidence, or the Lord’s commandments. Thus “of the commandments” means those which the Lord commanded us. If anyone nevertheless prefers *inculcationibus*, let him explain it with Salmasius, *On Interest Paid to Bankers*, p. 464, as follows: “We do not consider it enough to nourish faith by singing to God, to raise up hope, and to establish confidence in him—by all of which we testify that we seriously believe in him—but we also inculcate the commandments, which show what must and must not be done, concerning which see above, chap. I.” But all these things are included in our reading. HAV.]

In the same place there are also exhortations, corrections, and divine censure. [Note: [Col. 0469D] “Divine censure.” A notable passage against those who despise ecclesiastical excommunication, which was instituted by Christ and practiced from the earliest apostolic times. PAM.] For judgment too is delivered with great gravity, as among men certain that they stand in the sight of God; and it is a supreme anticipation of the future judgment if anyone has so transgressed that he is banished from participation in prayer, [Note: [Col. 0469D] “That he is banished from participation in prayer.” The discipline of the ancient Christians was truly grave and strict: by it they either excluded grave sinners entirely from the communion of the saints, or imposed onerous penalties for their offenses. Thus in Tertullian’s time public penance was scarcely, if at all, granted to adulterers, murderers, and idolaters, as is evident from *On Modesty*, chap. V; the matter is treated extensively by those who have expressly discussed penance and the penalties of clerics—Jean Morin, in his most learned book *On the Sacrament of Penance*, and Gabriel de l’Aubespine, a man deeply versed in every branch of ecclesiastical antiquity, in his *Ecclesiastical Observations*. The grades of penance were: first, Weeping, when the sinner, removed from the threshold and every covered part of the church, stood weeping and in mourning before the doors of the sanctuary, grasped the faithful as they entered, and begged them to pray for him, so that the scandal might be removed from the Church of God. [Col. 0470B] The second was Hearing, when they were permitted to stand among the catechumens at the entrance of the sanctuary. The third was Prostration, when they were allowed to enter, but only so as to prostrate themselves behind the ambo and then depart again with the catechumens. When these stages had been completed over a fixed period determined according to the magnitude of the scandal, they were admitted to Σύστασιν (“Standing”), or Standing, when they stood praying together with the faithful. They were not yet permitted to approach the sacred supper, however, but only when they were judged to have been fully reconciled to the Church. HAV.] assembly, and every holy fellowship.

Approved elders preside, each having obtained this honor not by payment [Col. 0470A] [Note: [Col. 0470B] “Approved elders preside.” There is a distinguished testimony concerning Alexander Severus in Spartianus: he wished provincial governors to be chosen in the same manner, saying that it was a grave matter that, although Christians and Jews did this when publicly presenting priests who were to be ordained, it was not done in the case of provincial governors, to whom both men’s fortunes and their lives were entrusted. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0470C] “Not by payment”—which God does not need, and by which the worthiest men are everywhere excluded from honor. Concerning the former, Lucian says in *Zeus Refuted*, p. 183: ὥστε οὐχ ὁρῶ ἀνθ` ὅτου ἀπαιτεῖτε τὸν μισθὸν ἐπὶ τῇ μαντικῇ (“Thus I do not see why you demand payment for prophecy”), that is, “I do not see why you should also demand payment for prophecy.” Concerning the latter there is the Constantinian law in the Theodosian Code, I, *On Provincial Governors*: “Let the judge’s curtain not be for sale, let entrance not be purchased, let the private chamber not be disgraced by bidding, nor access to the governor himself be had for a price.” HAV.] but by testimony, for nothing belonging to God has a price.

Even if there is a kind of treasury, its fund is not collected from a fee, as though religion had been purchased. [Note: [Col. 0469B] Thus the Put. codex and others, and Rhen.; Her. has *de oneraria*; Pam., *de ordinaria*; Rig. and Hav., *dehonoraria* (that is, dishonorable).] [Note: [Col. 0470C] “The fund is not collected from a dishonorable payment.” This is precisely how it reads in the oldest manuscript. “In our assemblies,” he says, “a fund is collected, but one which does not dishonor religion; nor therefore should our religion be called venal or purchased.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0469B] “Is collected,” Paris.] On the appointed day of the month, or whenever he wishes, and only if he wishes [Note: [Col. 0469B] “And only if he wishes” is absent from the Paris manuscript] [Note: [Col. 0470D] “Provided that he can. Provided that he wishes.” Justin: οἱ εὐποροῦντες δὲ καὶ οἰ βουλόμενοι κατὰ προαίρεσιν ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ὁ βοὺλεται δίδωσι (“Those who have means, and are willing, each give voluntarily whatever they wish from their own resources”). LE PR.] and only if he can, each person contributes a modest offering. [Note: [Col. 0469B] “Sets against,” Paris.] For no one is compelled; he contributes voluntarily. These are, as it were, the deposits of piety. For they are not spent on feasts, drinking-parties, or thankless gluttony, [Note: [Col. 0469B] The words “and only if he wishes” are absent from the editions of Rhenanus, Aldus, Gelenius, and Gangneius. In what follows, the Lyons codex has “and if he perhaps can”; the Agobardine codex, “and if only he perhaps can.” It would seem that the text should read: “either when he wishes, or provided that he can,” with the rest deleted.] but on feeding and burying the needy, on boys and girls destitute of means and parents, [Note: [Col. 0470B] The Fulda codex has: “For it is not spent from this source on feasts.”] and on elderly household dependants, [Note: [Col. 0470D] “Destitute of means and parents.” This is Suetonius’ expression in the *Life of Nero*: “He established annual stipends for each of the most noble senators who was destitute of family means.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0470B] Rhen., Gel., Ald., and Gangn. have “elderly persons subdued by age”; Hav., from the Fulda codex, adds “now inactive.”] as well as the shipwrecked, [Note: [Col. 0470B] “Shipwrecks,” Haverc., Cod. Fuld.] and any who are in the mines, on islands, [Col. 0471A] or in prisons, [Note: [Col. 0471B] “Or in prisons.” In *To the Martyrs*, chap. II: “Meanwhile let us compare the life of the world with that of prison, to see whether the spirit does not gain more in prison than the flesh loses; indeed, through the care of the Church and the brethren’s love-feast, the flesh does not lose even those things that are its due.” This follows Christ’s command in Matt. XXV.43–44. Thus our author again commends his little work *To the Martyrs* on this ground in chap. I: “Among the provisions for the flesh, blessed martyrs elect, which both our lady mother the Church supplies to you in prison from her breasts and individual brethren from their own resources, receive something also from us that may contribute to nourishing the spirit as well.” HAV.] provided only that they are there for the cause of God’s sect; these become the foster-children of their confession. [Note: [Col. 0471B] The Fulda codex adds “struggles.”]

Yet it is precisely this practice of love more than anything else that brands us with a mark of reproach among certain people. “See,” they say, “how they love one another”—for they themselves hate one another—“and how ready they are to die for one another”—for they themselves will be readier to kill one another. [Note: [Col. 0471C] “See,” they say, “how they love one another.” Christ said concerning the charity which he so greatly commended: “I came to cast fire upon the world, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” The surest effect of ardent love among true Christians, therefore, was that they so loved one another that each was entirely ready to die for the other. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0471B] Semler deletes “will be.”]

But as for our being designated by the name “brothers,” [Note: [Col. 0471C] Those who have acknowledged one Father, God, are both called and regarded as brothers. Christ, the Son of God, willed to become what man is so that man might become what Christ is, that is, a son of God. Christians therefore have God as their common Father in Christ, and we are fellow heirs with Christ, and heirs of God, although he is living. For there is an inheritance belonging to the living where the dead live and no one dies. By this sacrament of divine adoption Christ willed that the candidates for his Father’s kingdom should be called brothers, so that he might consecrate charity through the mystery of fraternal fellowship. He forbade, however, the ambitious use of the name “father” in the sense in which the Pharisees claimed it, lest any inequality oppress the most sacred brotherhood, or lest the majesty of the eternal Father be violated by any rivalry with divinity, that ancient fault of the human race. Yet the rule of this discipline by no means severs natural affections, since it was instituted by God so that charity might be admitted more fully, not less fully. Thus the Apostle says that he begot Onesimus in chains and commends him to his Philemon under the designation of “son.” That designation certainly implies a relation to a father. RIG.] I think they defame it for no other reason than that among them every name of blood relationship is a counterfeit maintained for show. [Note: [Col. 0471B] Thus Cod. Fuld. and the editions of Rig. and Hau.; others read: “But I think that they are mad for no other reason than that we call ourselves brothers” (Her.: “defame it because,” etc.).]

Yet we are your brothers as well, by the right of Nature, our common mother, although you are scarcely human beings because you are bad brothers. But how much more worthily are those called and regarded as brothers [Note: [Col. 0471D] “But how much more worthily brothers.” *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chap. XX: “The sharing of peace, the designation of brotherhood, and the mutual pledge of hospitality—rights governed by no other principle than the single transmission of the same sacrament.” And *To His Wife*, book II, chap. 9: “What a yoke is that of two believers, of one hope, one vow, one discipline, the same service! Both are brother and sister, both fellow servants, with no division of spirit or flesh.” Hence Christians long ago, to demonstrate that union of minds and fraternal affection, were accustomed to greet one another with a kiss. Among other witnesses there is Chrysostom, Homily XXX on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “For this reason the kiss was given to us, that it might be a spark and kindling of charity, that it might inflame affection, and that in this way we might love one another as brothers love one another and parents in turn love their children—indeed, far more intensely; for the former affections belong to nature, but these to grace.” The Fulda codex has “how much now.” If that reading is preferred, the text should be written *quanto nunc*. HAV.] who have acknowledged one Father, God; who have drunk one Spirit [Note: [Col. 0472B] “Have drunk the Spirit of holiness; have started with awe at the light of truth.” He speaks of drinking the Spirit and feeding upon light in a figure extremely common among Christians, who were accustomed to use even the terms of mortal life as figures of eternal life. An old epigram on Empedocles reads: εἰς δὲ πυρὸς κρατῆρας (“into the mixing-bowls of fire”) [Col. 0472C] ἐσήλατο, καὶ πίε τὸ ζῆν (“he leapt, and drank life”). RIG.] of holiness; and who, from the same womb of ignorance, have started with awe at the one light [Col. 0472A] of truth? [Note: [Col. 0472C] “Have started with awe.” A most beautiful metaphor. For just as the eyes of those who have long been in darkness, if you suddenly let in the sun, are accustomed to blink and, as it were, recoil in alarm, so also those who are drawn from the prison of darkness, death, and sin to the light of truth and of the Gospel are stricken in heart and tremble throughout, as happened to the distinguished Sergius Paulus in Acts XIV.12, and to the Apostle Paul himself when he was called to the faith in that marvelous vision narrated in Acts IX.6. Aldus therefore reads *expiraverint* in vain, and Barr. and Rhen., with Junius, *expiraverunt*. The reading *expaverunt* in Cod. L.B. and Rig. from Fuld. is also better than the *expaverint* of Pam., Heraldus, and La Cerda. Cod. Agob. has “have arrived,” which derives from a gloss. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0472B] “Have breathed their last,” Paris and Jun.]

But perhaps we are considered less legitimate precisely because no tragedy cries out concerning our brotherhood, [Note: [Col. 0472C] “No tragedy cries out.” He has in view the sons of Atreus and the Theban brothers; how popular these themes were can also be learned from chap. IX. Hence, because of his frequent repetition in tragedy, the poets call him:

[Col. 0472D] “Orestes, harried across the stages.”

The words in Minucius, p. 36, look in a very different direction: “You do not recognize one another as brothers, unless perhaps for parricide.” HAV.] or because we are brothers with respect to our family property, which among you generally dissolves brotherhood. Accordingly, we who are mingled in mind and soul have no hesitation about sharing property. Everything is held in common among us except our wives. We dissolve partnership in the one place in which other men alone practice partnership—men who not only make use of their friends’ marriages but also most patiently provide their own wives to their friends, following, I suppose, the discipline of their ancestors and wisest men, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, [Note: [Col. 0472D] “The Roman Cato,” who handed over his Marcia to Hortensius and took her back after Hortensius’ death. Lucan, book II.338, presents this remarkable speech of Marcia to her husband:

“While blood remained in me, while a mother’s strength remained,  
I fulfilled your commands, Cato, and in childbearing received two husbands.  
With womb exhausted and worn out by childbirth, I return,  
now to be handed over to no man”; and what follows.

Plutarch narrates the entire story in his *Life of Cato*. Hortensius had first asked Cato for his daughter Porcia, Bibulus’ wife but already the mother of two children, ὥσπερ εὐγενῆ χώραν κ (“as though a fertile field …”; the recovered Greek ends with an incomplete κ). τ (an isolated Greek letter from an unreadable fragment). λ (an isolated Greek letter from an unreadable fragment), that is, “as a fertile field for producing offspring.” When Cato replied that the woman whom he sought was not under his authority, he asked for and received Cato’s own Marcia. Diogenes Laërtius and Hesychius Illustrius tell a similar story concerning the philosophers Menedemus and Asclepiades: Menedemus married the mother and Asclepiades the daughter; when Asclepiades’ wife died, he took Menedemus’ wife, while Menedemus, because he governed the republic, married another woman, noble and wealthy. Nevertheless, since they shared a common household, Menedemus entrusted the management of the family property to his former wife. On Socrates, see shortly below at the words “Pimps,” etc. HAV.] who shared with their friends the wives whom they had married for the sake of having children begotten elsewhere as well—although I do not know whether the women were unwilling. [Note: [Col. 0473B] “And begotten elsewhere as well.” Just as Plautus says in the *Amphitryon* that to furnish a wife on loan is the same as leasing out a barren field to be dug. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0473A] “For” is absent from Paris.] For why would they care about chastity, when their husbands had so readily given it away? O example of Attic wisdom and Roman dignity! The philosopher and the censor are pimps. [Note: [Col. 0473A] “Pimps,” Havercamp.] [Note: [Col. 0473C] He confuses the Catos, as above he confused the Scipios. In Lucian’s very amusing dialogue entitled *The Lapiths*, Cleodemus objects to Zenothemis: Ἀλλ` οὐ μαστρωπὸς ἐγὼ τῆς ἐμαυτοῦ γυναικὸς ὥσπερ εἶ σὺ (“But I am not my own wife’s pimp, as you are”), that is, “And I am not my wife’s pimp, as you are.” I think he is alluding to Socrates, whose second wife Xanthippe is reported to have been rather freely shared. Indeed, in the *Auction of Lives* Lucian likewise makes Socrates the author of the Platonic doctrine; there Socrates presents to the buyer as his principal doctrine, insofar as it concerns wives: Δοκεῖ μηδεμίαν αὐτῶν μηδενος εἶναι μόνου, παντὶ δὲ μετεῖναι τῷ βουλομένῳ τοῦ γαρου (“It seems that none of them belongs exclusively to anyone, but that everyone who wishes may share in the marriage”; γαρου is an apparently corrupt recovered reading), that is, “It seems to me that no woman ought to belong privately to anyone, but that each should freely go to whoever desires her.” The Platonic philosopher also sets this forth quite ridiculously in *The Lapiths*.]

Why, then, is it surprising if so great a charity dines together? [Note: [Col. 0473A] Franeq. has “is violated”; Cod. Fuld., “dines together”; Cod. Agob., “is violated”; others, “is jointly violated.”] [Note: [Col. 0473C] “Dines together.” Rigaltius restored this excellent reading from the Fulda manuscript; before him Scaliger, correctly, in the margin of his book, and Junius had taught that it belongs with what follows. It can be illustrated from Suetonius, *Augustus*, [Col. 0473D] chap. LXX, where he writes of Augustus’ incontinence: “A private dinner of his also became notorious; it was commonly called δωδεκάθεος (*dōdekatheos*, “of the twelve gods”). At it the guests reclined dressed as gods and goddesses, while Augustus himself was adorned as Apollo. This is charged against him not only by Antony’s letters, which most bitterly list the names of each participant, but also by these very well-known anonymous verses:

“When first that table hired a producer for those players,  
and Mallia saw six gods and six goddesses,  
while Caesar impiously plays Apollo’s falsehoods,  
while he feasts upon new adulteries of the divinities,  
all the divine powers then turned away from the earth,  
and Jupiter himself fled his golden throne.” HAV.]

For you stigmatize our modest suppers not only as infamous for crime but also as extravagant. [Note: [Col. 0473B] “Also” is absent from the Paris manuscript.] It was of us, no doubt, that Diogenes said: “The Megarians buy provisions as though they were to die the next day, but build as though they would never die.” [Note: [Col. 0473D] “The Megarians.” Laërtius testifies in the following words that Empedocles used this saying of the Agrigentines: Ἀκραγαντῖνοι τρυφῶσι μὲν, ὡς αὔριον ἀποθανούμενοι, οἰκίας δὲ κατασκευάζονται, ὠς πάντα τὸν χρόνον βιωσόμενοι (“The Agrigentines live luxuriously as though they were to die tomorrow, but build houses as though they were to live forever”). Among the sayings of Diogenes the Cynic, however, he records that Diogenes said to τὸν πολυτελῶς ὁψωνοῦντα,

Ὠκύμορος δή μοι τέκος ἔσσεαι, οἶ άγοράζεις (“to one buying provisions extravagantly: ‘My child, you will indeed be short-lived, judging by what you buy’”; οἶ is a seemingly corrupt recovered reading), that is, “My son, you will not live long,” implying that he would soon die of hunger because he had pawned everything. [Col. 0474B] Thus the same writer also lists among Aristotle’s pithy sayings that most men are so frugal as though they were going to live forever, while others are so extravagant as though they were going to die at once: Τοὺς μὲν, οὕτω φείδεσθαι ὡς ἀεὶ ζησομένους, τοὺς δὲ, οὕτῳς ἀναλίσκειν ὡς αὐτίκα τεθνησομένους (“Some are so frugal as though they would live forever, while others spend as though they would die at once”). HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0473B] The words “but build … die” are absent from the Agobardine and Lyons manuscripts and from the editions of Rhenanus, Aldus, Gelenius, Barr., and Gangneius.]

But who more readily sees the straw in another’s [Col. 0474A] eye than the beam in his own? The air turns sour with so many tribes, wards, and divisions belching. [Note: [Col. 0474A] “Will become acrid,” Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0474B] “The air turns sour.” Sidonius Apollinaris, book III, epistle 12: “Hemmed in, a captive at the sides, by the rank and souring caves of their armpits.” Cicero, *Speech against Lucius Piso*, chap. XIII: “We stood for a little while amid the stench and smoke of your eating-houses, from which you drove us by answering in the most shameless fashion and belching in the most disgraceful.” Writers note that this happened because of the multitude of people in theaters and spectacles. Thus Eunapius of Sardis, in his *Aedesius*, remarks that Constantine the Great transferred inhabitants from everywhere to Constantinople πρὸς τοὺς ἐν τοῖς θεάτροις κρότους παραβλυζόντων κραπάλης ἀνθρώπων (“to court applause in the theaters from drunken men spewing up their debauchery”), that is, “and to catch applause in the theater from men drunken and vomiting up their debauch.” Hence our author too says in *On the Spectacles*, chap. XXVII: “Will you not therefore flee the seats occupied by Christ’s enemies, that chair of pestilence, and the very air brooding above it, polluted by criminal voices?” HAV.]

The Salii, when they are about to dine, will need a creditor. [Note: [Col. 0474C] “The Salii,” who held a most sumptuous banquet on the Kalends of March during the festival of the sacred shields. See Ovid, Horace, and others. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II.9, lists magnificent dinners of this kind.] Accountants used to calculate the cost of the tithes of Hercules and of the sacrificial feasts. [Note: [Col. 0474A] “And” is absent from Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0474A] “Stablemen,” Paris. The Agobardine and Lyons manuscripts and the edition of Rhenanus also have “stablemen.”] Let selections of cooks be proclaimed for the Apaturia, the Dionysia, and the Attic mysteries. [Note: [Col. 0474C] “The Attic mysteries.” He means the Eleusinian rites. From this it is evident that costly dinners were held there as well, a fact that may be noted as an addition to Meursius, who wrote a separate little book on those rites. HAV.] At the smoke of a banquet of Serapis, the *sparteoli* will be roused. [Note: [Col. 0474C] “The *sparteoli*.” Casaubon was the first to explain who these were, in his notes on Suetonius’ *Augustus*, chap. XXX, adducing the passage of an ancient scholiast on these words of Juvenal:

[Col. 0474D] “After setting out his hooks, the very rich Lucinus orders a cohort  
of slaves to keep watch by night.”

The scholiast notes there that the term was transferred from the military organization of the *sparteoli* at Rome, whose cohorts were accustomed to keep watches, with hooks and water, to protect the city “for their neighbors.” Here P. Pithoeus reads “because of fire” instead of “for their neighbors”; I should prefer “in their neighborhoods.” Casaubon there inquires into the origin of the name and thinks they were so called because they frequently carried ropes, or from tunics or shoes made of esparto grass. They might instead appear to have been so called from esparto vessels coated with pitch for holding water—*brandemmers*—with which they were equipped. These men were also called *matricarii*. The scholiast on Julian the Antecessor, Constitution XXIII, chap. 88, where he also explains the use of hooks: “Those whom we see running to fires and carrying sponges with iron implements, and other implements by which they can pass from wall to wall and thus extinguish the fire, are called *matricarii*.” Add Wouwer’s notes on Sidonius Apollinaris, book VI, epistle 8. HAV.]

Only the Christians’ dining room is called into question. Our supper reveals its nature by its name: it is called by the term that among the Greeks means “love.” [Note: [Col. 0474B] “Its own,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0474B] Thus it stands written in the Lyons codex; Cod. Fuld. has, “it was called by which,” etc.; the others have, “for it is called ἀγάπη (*agapē*, “love”), that which among the Greeks means love.”] [Note: [Col. 0474D] “It is called by the term that among the Greeks means love.” Rigaltius printed it thus, persuaded by the reading of the Fulda manuscript, which has this wording except that through a copyist’s error it reads “it was called by which.” But the complete text is found in MS. L.B. It is corrupt in Aldus: “it is called ἀγάπη (*agapē*, “love”),” etc.; in others: “for it was called—that ἀγάπη (*agapē*, “love”) which among the Greeks means love.” For here he wished not to state the name but to describe it. Mention of this term is frequent in Christian books. Tertullian himself, *On Baptism*, chap. IX: “When [Christ] teaches concerning the *agape*, he commends a cup of water offered to a brother among the works of love.” And *Against the Psychics*, chap. XVII: “Among you the *agape* boils in cooking pots, faith grows hot in kitchens, and hope lies in serving dishes.” On these *Agapae*, besides La Cerda, see Wouwer on Minucius, p. 41, and Elmenhorst there, p. 91; Photius and Balsamon on Canon II of the Council of Gangra; Justellus and Beveridge on the canons of Nicaea III, Trullo V, Ancyra XIX, Gangra IV, and the Second Council of Nicaea XVIII and XX; Dodwell, *Cyprianic Dissertations*; Valesius on Eusebius, p. 157; Suicer under ἀγαπητοὶ, ἀδελφὴ, συνείσακτος (*agapētoi*, “beloved”; *adelphē*, “sister”; *syneisaktos*, “a woman brought in as a companion”); and especially Ludovico Antonio Muratori in his *Greek Anecdotes*, pp. 185, 218 ff., who is adorned with a distinguished eulogy by Fabricius—who lists these writers—in his never sufficiently praised *Bibliographia Antiquaria*, p. 587. Johannes Fronto, chancellor of the University of Paris, also compared these *Agapae* with the ancients’ friendship-feasts with singular care in the first of his *Selected Letters*, published at Liège by Ebutonus in 1674, in duodecimo. Ultimately, however, they were abolished when, as commonly happens, they degenerated into luxury. Hence Nazianzen appears in his *Precepts to Virgins* to exhort them to avoid these and similar dinners. For he says in that poem, verse 166:

Πολλάκι μὲν συνἀγειρει ὁμόφροναι ἀλλήλοισί (“Often he brings together those of one mind with one another”) [Col. 0475C] Πνεύματί, καὶ φάος ἧλθεν, επωνυμίην τέ γε σεμνὴν,

Τὴν ἀγὰπην κᾶλέουσιν, ὑπηλυθεν αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα

Ἐκκραδίης ὲπί σάρκας ᾄγων πόθον ἐγγὺς ἐούσας,

Ἡ πῦρ, ήὲ πυρὸς σημήια λυγρὰ δὶδωσιν (“in spirit; and it came as light, bearing the venerable name they call *agape*; but afterward it crept in, leading desire from the heart toward the flesh close at hand, and produces either fire or grievous signs of fire”).

Εἰ τοι μὴ δὲ πυρός σημὴιον, ἀλλὰ τάχιστα

Πλήξεις εἰσορόωντας (“If indeed it is not a sign of fire, then very swiftly come blows for those looking on”; the recovered syntax is uncertain). ἑτοιμότεροι δέ τε πάντες

Εἶς κακίην τελέθουσι, ῥὸος δ` ἐπὶ πρηνὲς ὁδεὺει (“All become readier for vice, and the current travels headlong downward”). That is:

“Often he brought together in one place those equal in heart and mind,  
displayed the appearance of light, and assumed the honorable  
name of *agape*; soon, cunningly, he turns all  
love from the soul toward the neighboring flesh,  
and leaves either a flame or the most sorrowful marks of flame.  
Even though the flame itself should have impressed no marks,  
yet you yourself, swift, will strike with a deadly wound  
the breast of those who turn their eyes upon you.  
For we are all borne more readily toward vice,  
just as a very swift river flows down a slope.”

Augustine too condemned them and wished them abolished, Epistle LXIV. HAV.]

However great its cost, to incur expense in the name of piety is a gain, since by this refreshment we assist all the poor—[Col. 0475A] not in the manner in which among you parasites seek the glory [Col. 0476A] of an enslaved freedom, [Note: [Col. 0475A] “Also,” Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0475C] “Seek the glory.” Like that Gnatho in Terence, who wished to establish a sect so that, just as philosophers were called Platonists, and so forth, parasites might be called Gnathonists. Add Lucian’s *The Parasite*, a dialogue in which he extols that art with extraordinary praises. Nor is Diodorus of Sinope less extravagant in the *Heiress*, quoted by Athenaeus, p. 239:

Βούλομαι δεῖξαι σαφῶς

Ὡς σεμνόν ἐστι τοῦτο νενομισμένον,

Καὶ τὼν Θεῷν εὕρημα, τᾶς δ` ἄλλας τέχνας

Οὐδεὶς Θεῶν κατέδείξαν, ἀλλ` ἃνδρες σοφοί (“I wish to show clearly that this is regarded as venerable and as an invention of the gods; none of the gods revealed the other arts, but wise men did”).

Τὸ γὰρ παρασιτεῖν εὗρεν ὁ Ζεὺς ὁ Φίλιος,

Ὁ τῶν Θεῶν μέγὶσος ὁμολογουμένως (“For Zeus Philius, admittedly the greatest of the gods, invented living as a parasite”). That is: “I wish openly to prove that this invention is venerable, legitimate, and divine; that none of the other arts was discovered by the gods, but all by wise men. Philius Jupiter, by universal consent the greatest among the celestials, was the first to begin living as a parasite”; and what follows. *Affectant* means “eagerly seek”; the Latins used the word in this sense. Virgil, *Georgics* IV:

[Col. 0476A] “And seeks a path to Olympus.”

Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria*: “You see what route he is seeking.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0476A] “A freedom to serve,” Jun.; compare chap. 21.] binding themselves over to their bellies so as to be fattened amid insults, [Note: [Col. 0476A] “Of an enslaved freedom.” Though freeborn, they submit to servile treatment. Indeed, Chrysostom, on Matthew chap. XIV, Homily 49, compares those who hire such kitchen-smoke for themselves to base men and actors in this very weighty discourse: “Tell me, what is more bitter than to strike with one’s fists a man made in the image of God and take pleasure in this injury to one’s neighbor? Are you not ashamed to turn your house into a spectacle when it is filled with guests, and to imitate actors when you appear to be a freeborn and noble man?” The same golden mouth says in the same place: “But if you wish to obtain richer fruits from them, order them, when you have leisure, to read the divine Scriptures. They will more gladly oblige you in these things, by which both you and they are made more honorable, than in those Gnathonic performances by which you are all dishonored—you as an abusive drunkard, they as wretches enslaved to their bellies. For one who supports people for the purpose of abusing them does something worse than if he had killed them; but one who supports them for their profit and praise benefits them more than if he had rescued them from death.” Tertullian uses a word proper to the arena: this was the gladiators’ bond, or the terms to which they obligated themselves—to be burned, bound, and cut. Thus parasites, bound over to their bellies, also submitted to the condition of being struck with slaps, sandals, and dishes, spat upon, and subjected to every insult. Far different is the Christians’ covenant, concerning which Tertullian says in *To Scapula*, chap. I: “We neither recoil from nor fear the things we suffer from ignorant men, since we came to this sect having assuredly accepted the condition of its compact, so that, having bound ourselves over, we surrender even our lives to these contests.” Chrysostom again speaks against parasites among the pagans in the *Life of Babylas*: “Those among them who are wealthier force into the ranks of parasites men who through idleness are perishing from hunger; they feed these very men at their tables like dogs and stuff their shameless bellies with the remnants of wicked banquets, using them as they please.” HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0476C] “To be fattened amid insults.” Such a buffoon elegantly describes himself in verses of Aristophanes quoted by Athenaeus, book VI, p. 238:

Προσβαίνειν πρὸς οἰκὶαν δεῖ; κρίος (“Must a house be assaulted? I am a battering ram”).

Ἀναβῇναί τε πρὸς κλιμάκιον; Καπανεύς (“Must a ladder be climbed? I am Capaneus”).

Υπομένειν πληγὰς; ἄκμων καί κόνδυλος (“Must blows be endured? I am an anvil and a knuckle”). That is: “If an assault on a house is required, I am a battering ram; if ladders must be climbed, a Capaneus; if blows must be endured, an anvil and a knot.” In the same place Timocles praises him as wise:

[Col. 0476D] Ὀργὴν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἀγαθὸς· ἂν σκόπτῃς, γελᾶ (“He is good at bearing anger; if you mock him, he laughs”). That is: “He prudently restrains his anger; even if you mock him, he laughs.” See their bond in the same place, p. 289, in verses of Diodorus:

οἷς ἐπειδὴ προσερυγοι

Ραφανιδα καὶ σαπρὸν σὶλουρον καταφαγῶν,

Ἴα καῖ ῤόδ` ἔφασαν αὐτὸν ἠριϛηκέναι,

Ἐπειδὰν δ` ἀποπορδῃ μετὰ τινος κατακείμενος,

Τόυτῳ προσάγων τῆν ῥῖνα δεῖ οὺτῷ φράσαι,

Πόθεν τὸ θυμὶάμα τοῦτο λαμβάνεις; (“If someone belches upon them after eating radish and rotten catfish, they say that he has breakfasted on violets and roses; and whenever someone reclining beside another breaks wind, he must bring his nose close and say to him, ‘Where do you obtain this incense?’”). That is: “If anyone belches in their faces after eating radish or rotten catfish, they will say he has eaten a rose and violets; or if someone beside whom he is reclining breaks wind, he wishes to bring his own nose close and address him thus: ‘Where did you obtain this incense?’” But St. Chrysostom more wisely rejects such pleasures, on Matthew XVI, Homily 49: “Consider, I beg you, how many and how great are the things your flatterers accomplish for you. What benefit do they bring to you or your household? ‘They make the meal more pleasant,’ you will say. How can men who are struck with open hands and speak most disgracefully make anything pleasant?” HAV.] but in the manner in which, before God, there is greater regard for those of modest means. [Col. 0477A] [Note: [Col. 0477B] “But in the manner in which, before God.” “We do not therefore,” he says, “spend God’s gifts on thankless gluttony, but on feeding the needy, which we know is more acceptable to him.” Chrysostom beautifully says in the passage cited repeatedly: “I say these things not because I forbid food to be provided for them, but because I would not wish it to be provided for this reason. For nourishment takes its origin from mercy, not insult. Pity him; do not mock him. Feed him because he is poor; feed him because in him you feed Christ, not because he provokes laughter with diabolical words and ruins his own life.” HAV.]

If the occasion of the banquet is honorable, judge what the remaining order of its discipline is, [Note: [Col. 0477B] “For the sake of discipline, judge what it is,” Fran.] since it arises from a religious duty: it admits nothing base, nothing immodest. [Note: [Col. 0477B] “Is admitted,” Paris.] We do not recline before prayer to God is first tasted. [Note: [Col. 0477C] “Prayer to God is first tasted.” If even the pagans, as Arrian teaches us on Epictetus, book III, chap. 21, οὐδὲ σπείρουσιν ἄλλως, εἰ μὴ τὴν Δήμητρα ἐπι καλεσαμένος (“nor do they sow except after invoking Demeter”), do not sow their fields without first invoking Ceres, how much more is it improper for those about to receive the fruit of the field itself not to ask the blessing of the Lord God? Quintilian, *Declamation* CCCI, testifies that the pagans themselves did not neglect this: “You approached a table at which, when we begin to come, we invoke the gods.” The food of Christians, therefore, is sanctified by the word and invocation of the true God, 1 Tim. IV.4–5. For, as Chrysostom piously says in *To the People of Antioch*, Homily LXXIX: “A table beginning with prayer and ending in prayer will never fail, but will bring us every good thing more abundantly than a fountain; let us therefore not neglect so great a benefit.” Note the word “tasted first,” by which he suggests that prayer is spiritual food. HAV.]

As much is eaten as satisfies the hungry; as much is drunk as is beneficial to the chaste. They satisfy themselves as people who remember that they must worship God even during the night; they converse as people who know that the Lord hears them. After water for washing the hands [Note: [Col. 0477B] “Hand-washing water,” Jun.] and the lamps have been brought in, each person is invited into the midst to sing to God from the holy Scriptures or from his own composition, as he is able. [Note: [Col. 0477D] “Or from his own composition.” I interpret this as referring to hymns and songs composed by the more learned guests, while the former expression refers to psalms publicly received in the Church. I think the notable passage in Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, chap. V.19, should also be referred to this: λαλοῦντες ἑαυτοῖς ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὓμνοις καὶ ὠδαῖς πνευματικοῖς, ἄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ κυρίῳ (“speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord”). HAV.] From this the measure of his drinking is put to the test. Prayer likewise brings the banquet to an end. [Note: [Col. 0477D] “Prayer brings the banquet to an end.” Again, in the same passage, verse 20: εὐχαριστοῦντες πάντοθε ὑπὲρ πάντων ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί (“giving thanks everywhere for all things, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God and Father”; πάντοθε, “everywhere,” is the unusual recovered reading), so that Tertullian too appears to have had these words in view. Chrysostom also says in the passage cited: “It is therefore necessary for us to give thanks to God both when approaching the table and when leaving it. For one prepared to do this will never fall into drunkenness or insolence and will never be overwhelmed by debauch. With the expectation of prayer imposed upon his senses as a bridle, he will partake of everything set before him with due moderation and will fill both his soul and his body with abundant blessing.” And shortly afterward: “For it is absurd that our servants, if they receive from us some portion of the things set before them, should both thank us and depart with a blessing, while we, though enjoying so many good things, do not repay even this much honor to God.” HAV.]

From there we depart, not into bands for beatings [Note: [Col. 0478B] “Not into bands for beatings.” Πληκτισμῶν (“of brawls”), says Scaliger. Suetonius mentions this wantonness in *Nero*, chap. XXIV: “For he had been accustomed, on returning from dinner, to beat people, to wound those who resisted, and to plunge them into sewers.” And in *Otho*, chap. [Col. 0478B] and Hav. added the words enclosed in brackets from the single Fulda manuscript; but, after accepting them, Havercamp should properly have inserted “factious” or “an association” after “those that deserve condemnation.”]]—if anyone complains about it under the same designation under which complaints are made about associations. ## CHAPTER XL

Rather, it is they who are factious: after plotting against the deserving, they impute public calamities to the Christians, although even before this sect arose greater and still more dreadful disasters shook the world, while since its appearance calamities have begun to be fewer and lighter, since by its prayers it averts the punishments deserved from the divine Power, although those who rashly worship gods attribute the true God’s kindness to idols.

40. Lucan, concerning the Thessalian witch, book VI, 474:

> Standing with dust.

So many against one? Tell me, before Tiberius—that is, before Christ’s advent—how many disasters struck the world and the city! We read that Hiera, [Note: [Col. 0479D] **Before Christ’s advent.** Thus the complaint of the gentiles resembled that once made by the idolatrous Jews in Jeremiah XLIV.18: “For from the time when we ceased sacrificing to the Queen of Heaven and offering incense, [Col. 0480A] we have lacked everything and have been consumed by sword and famine.” And so they employed the saying which Augustine uses in another sense in Psalm XXXIII: “How long shall we suffer these things, worse and worse every day? The days of our parents were better.” To which he rightly replies: “Oh, if you were to question your parents themselves, they would likewise complain to you about their parents: ‘Our fathers were fortunate; we are miserable and have evil days.’” Jerome aptly says on Ecclesiastes VII: “Do not say, ‘Times were better than they are now’; virtues make the days good for the living, vices make them bad.” Lucretius, book II.1163, teaches that it is ingrained in human beings to compare ancient things with new and the past with the present:

> And now, shaking his head, the aged farmer sighs  
> That his great labor has too often fallen fruitlessly;

There the following, thoroughly corrupt verses—

[Col. 0480C] So read the Vossian parchments, now at Leiden, except that they have *it fails, he assails the foul*. That is, he accuses the age and attacks it with abuse as foul. In the final verse of the book, read from the same parchments *to the coffin*—that is, to burial and destruction—instead of *to the cliff*. HAV.], Anaphe [Note: [Col. 0480A] “Hierapolis,” Fran.] and Delos and Rhodes and Cos [Note: [Col. 0480C] **Hiera, Anaphe.** The only true reading of this corrupted passage seems to be that given here, or, as that most learned man Jacob Gothofredus also emends it from the books *To the Nations*, *Hiera, Nea, Anaphe*. For the reading *Hierapolis*, substituted by the editions of Pamelius, Rhenanus, and La Cerda, and Barraeus’ *Hieropolis*, is plainly false, since Tertullian is enumerating events that occurred before—not after—Christ was born and proclaimed. For in the cited passage of *To the Nations* he says: “Our era is not yet three hundred years old; how many disasters previously, throughout the whole extent of the world,” etc. Here Priorius absurdly displays his carelessness by restricting those disasters to the period of the Christians and their afflictions; in correcting the words that follow to [Col. 0480D] *Heria, Anaphe, and Delos*, he faithfully makes Gothofredus’ emendation his own. The Leiden manuscript has *Hyeramcipaeam*, as do almost several other codices; from their reading Junius conjectured *Hierem cepiam*, calling Pliny, *Natural History* V.31, to his aid. But the Aldine codex, as Rigault prints it, expressly has *Hierennapen*; and, what is more, the unique manuscript containing the books *To the Nations* gives exactly the same form there. The Putean manuscript has *Hierennapean*, the Agobardine *Hierantnapeam*, Bongars’ manuscript *Itherannapeam*. Thus the reading we have printed is the only true one. The Fulda codex has *Hierannanda penes*; beside this, in the margin of my book, Scriverius had written by conjecture: “We read that almost unutterable disasters befell Delos and Rhodes,” etc. But he is sufficiently refuted by Tertullian himself in *To the Nations*, book I, chapter 9: “Where then were the Christians, when Hierennape and Delphi,” etc.? Read *Hiera, Anaphe*, or *Napea*, as Salmasius also does in his notes on Solinus, p. 102, and Gothofredus before him. Both are believed to have grown from a submarine volcano and often to have been overturned from top to bottom. Compare the dissertation of D. Salies [Col. 0481B] in the *Proceedings of the Academy of Inscriptions and Literature at Paris*, vol. III. EDD.]—[Note: [Col. 0480A] “Con,” Paris.] islands—perished utterly together with many thousands of people. Moreover, an earthquake drank up the Corinthian Sea, [Note: [Col. 0481B] **And Cos.** Rigault correctly restored this reading, as did Salmasius, whom by all means consult at the passage cited above. Pamelius and others have *Coon*; Aldus and Rhenanus, *Con*; but the Leiden manuscript plainly has *Cho*. More cities could have been added whose destruction Lucretius recounts in those splendid verses on the origin and nature of earthquakes in book VI, including verse 583:

> What happened in Tyrian Sidon, and what befell Aegium  
> In the Peloponnese—how this outburst of air  
> Shatters cities, when an earthquake has arisen!

HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0481B] **An earthquake drank up the Corinthian Sea.** The commentators pass this over lightly, as though nothing here were obscure, ambiguous, or corrupt. Junius alone suspected something and emended it to “by an earthquake”—not very successfully, for it is not water that drinks up earth, but earth that drinks water; moreover, he does not state what the Corinthian Sea drank up through an earthquake. At first sight, Tertullian certainly seems to suggest not that some land was torn away by an inundation of the sea, but that the sea itself was swallowed into the depths when an earthquake opened a chasm in its bottom. This seems to be suggested still more clearly in *To the Nations*, book I, chapter 9, by the words: “When the Corinthian Sea was snatched away by an earthquake.” Lucian, in his dialogue with Charon near the end, under the character of Mercury, indicates that something similar happened in the Peloponnese itself, which the Corinthian Sea, or Gulf of Corinth, washes, in the case of the River Inachus: ἀποθνήσοκουσι γὰρ αἱ πόλεις ὥσπερ ἄνθροποι, καὶ τὸ παραδοξότερον, καὶ ποταμοὶ ὅλοι [recovered text contains apparent corruptions]. Ἰνάχου οὖν ουδἑ τάφος ἐν Ἄργει ἐτι καταλείπεται [recovered text contains apparent corruptions]. That is: “For cities, ferryman, die just as human beings do; and, what is far more astonishing, entire rivers also die, so that not even a memorial of the Inachus itself remains visible at Argos.” Many long ago believed that both this river and the Alpheus, swallowed through vast channels in the earth, emerged elsewhere; Strabo enumerates and refutes them about the middle of book VI. But, if the passage is considered more carefully, the same event seems to be indicated here that Strabo relates near the end of book VIII: εξαρθὲν γὰρ ὑπὸ σεισμοῦ τὸ πέλαγος κατέκλυσε καὶ αὐτὴν καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν τοῦ Ἐλικονίου Ῥοσειδῶνος [the recovered divine name is apparently corrupt]; that is: “For the sea, raised by an earthquake, overwhelmed both Helice and the temple of Heliconian Neptune.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XV [printed “XE”]:

> If you seek Helice and Buris, Achaean cities,  
> You will find them beneath the waters, and sailors still  
> Are accustomed to point out the submerged towns with their leaning walls.

These cities bordered the Corinthian Sea. Helice was twelve stades distant from the sea and was swallowed up two years before the battle of Leuctra, as Strabo relates. Thus the cause of its ruin was both earthquake and inundation: water rushed into the places fractured and shattered by the movement of the earth—which itself also disturbed the neighboring sea—and remained there in the channels thus hollowed out. Hence we now understand how [Col. 0482A] the earthquake—that is, the earth when moved—drank up the Corinthian Sea. More strictly one might read *drank in*, but *drank up* is stronger. The Leiden manuscript displays *went away*, as though one should read, “but the earthquake went away into the Corinthian Sea.” [Col. 0482B] Ovid most elegantly expresses this entire transformation of things in the passage just mentioned: how cities and lands are swallowed by waters, rivers by lands. The whole passage deserves to be reproduced here:

> I myself have seen what once was firmest land  
> Become sea; I have seen lands made from the sea.  
> Far from the ocean, marine shells have lain,  
> And an ancient anchor has been found on mountaintops.  
> The downward course of waters has made a valley  
> Where once was a plain, and a flood has carried a mountain to the sea.  
> Through drought, the marshy ground is parched into dry sands,  
> While places that endured thirst are wet with stagnant marshes.  
> Here nature has sent forth new springs, and there  
> Has closed them; and through ancient tremors of the earth  
> Many rivers leap forth, or else remain dried up.  
> Thus, where Lycus is swallowed by a chasm in the earth,  
> It rises far away and is reborn from another mouth.

See what follows in the same place; the passage is longer, but exceedingly charming. HAV.], and the violence of the waves severed Lucania from Italy [Note: [Col. 0482B] **Severed from Italy.** The Fulda editor deletes *Italy* with the Herault manuscripts; the Leiden and other manuscripts retain it. Rhenanus [Col. 0482C] and Herault have *severed*. Strabo, Mela, and all the geographers mention the event; so does Sallust, *Fragments of the Histories*, no. 297: “It is agreed that Italy was once joined to Sicily, but the intervening space was either overwhelmed by waters because of its low elevation or torn apart because of its narrowness.” HAV.] and banished it under the name of Sicily. These things surely could not have happened without injury to their inhabitants.

Where then were—not, I will say, the Christians who despise your gods—but your gods themselves, when the flood destroyed the entire world, or, as Plato thought, merely the plains? [Col. 0482A] For the very cities in which those gods were born and died [Note: [Col. 0481A] “Lingered and,” Fulda codex.], and even those which they founded, prove that they came after the catastrophe of the Flood. Otherwise those cities would not remain to the present day [Note: [Col. 0481A] “Others today,” Rigault, Havercamp.] unless they too were later than that catastrophe. Palestine had not yet received the Jewish swarm from Egypt, nor had the origin of the Christian sect yet settled there, [Note: [Col. 0482C] **Its origin had settled.** Here too, maintaining the metaphor, he speaks with the utmost propriety. For when young swarms of bees burst from their hives, they ordinarily choose a nearby tree and its branch—or, if that is lacking, some other elevated object—to which they attach themselves and on which they settle. An expert in the matter then sweeps and packs them into new hives, and so their owners’ estate increases. Virgil, that consummate devotee of every elegance, intended to indicate this, if only his commentators had sufficiently understood his verses from *Georgics* IV.20:

> Let a palm shade the entrance, or a great wild olive,  
> So that when the new kings first lead forth their swarms  
> In their own spring, and the youth released from the combs begins to play,  
> A neighboring bank may invite them to withdraw from the heat,  
> And a tree in their path may hold them in its leafy lodging.

[Col. 0482D] Add Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina*, book II.119:

> One might believe a swarm was pouring out  
> To plunder Hyblaean thyme, when the waxen kings  
> Move camp and, descending from the hollow belly of a beech,  
> The honey-bearing army hums over its chosen plants.

This can also illuminate Numbers XXII.5, where the king of the Moabites speaks of the immense multitude of Israelites as though of a swarm of bees: “Behold, a nation has come out of Egypt; behold, it has covered the face of the land and settles opposite me.” The Egyptians and Assyrians who would come against Judaea are also compared to swarms of bees or flies in Isaiah VII.18 and 10. HAV.], when a fiery rain burned up its neighboring regions [Note: [Col. 0482A] “And its borders,” Semler.], Sodom and Gomorrah. [Note: [Col. 0482D] **A fiery rain burned up Sodom and Gomorrah.** In *On the Pallium*, chapter 2, according to Salmasius’ reading: “Look toward Palestine, where the River Jordan serves as the boundary of territories: a vast wasteland, a bereaved region, and a field cultivated in vain. The earth still smells of the conflagration; [Note: [Col. 0483B] **The earth still smells of the conflagration.** This is utterly true and an ever-living example of divine vengeance. For not only does Lake Asphaltites, or the Dead Sea itself, exhale a pestilential vapor, but the surviving stones of the ruins burn when brought near a flame and exhale an exceedingly foul smell. All travel narratives attest it. Martin von Baumgarten, *Travels*, book II, chapter 12, reports “that there is an utterly foul odor there, a grim and almost infernal appearance, and that the taste [Col. 0483C] of the water is extremely salty, astringent with a bilious bitterness.” Burchard says: “The Dead Sea is always smoking and dark, like the mouth of hell. With my own eyes, together with several companions, I saw an utterly foul and evil vapor smoking from the Dead Sea.” Salignac and others say the same. Concerning the taste of the water, the most illustrious Prince Radziwiłł, having tested it himself, says in Epistle II, p. 96: “Its water is very thick and foul-smelling; when tasted drop by drop, as we did, it bites the tongue fiercely and powerfully infects the head with a heavy, pestilential odor.” For what I said about the stones, a remarkable testimony survives in Johann Jakob Ammann, *Journey*, part II, p. 131. Since he wrote in German, I have appended his words translated into Latin: “Meanwhile,” he says, “the Arabs—and some of our people as well—collected stones broken from the cliffs or lying scattered here and there, and set them alight with a small flame. They burn and catch fire like wood, producing thick smoke, but smell so strongly of sulphur and pitch that [Col. 0483D] one cannot remain nearby for long. The nearer one approaches the Red Sea, the more fiercely the stones burn in this manner. These cliffs and stones also have a very white appearance, as though sprinkled and coated with white ashes. When broken open, they appear gray and lurid within. Yet they are not entirely consumed by fire; once the pitch and sulphur have been consumed, they remain somewhat smaller than before, become entirely black, and go out of their own accord. They then burn no longer, as I myself proved, for I also brought away a small fragment of stone. The Arabs said that the cliffs and stones around the Red Sea possess this property for a journey of one hour, and nowhere else—something neither credible nor probable. I myself discovered only this: where the cliffs are sandy, the stones indeed smell strongly, but do not burn.” HAV.]

and if any fruits of trees there attempt to grow, [Note: [Col. 0483D] **If any fruits of trees there attempt to grow.** This is the true reading, confirmed by Herault together with Pamelius, [Col. 0484A] La Cerda, Aldus, and Rigault from the Fulda codex, and finally also by the Leiden and Agobardine manuscripts. Junius therefore should not say that Latinius correctly restored from the Vatican manuscript and all the codices *fruits arise*, which Pamelius had marked for deletion. For both *arise*, the reading also of Barraeus and Rhenanus, and *arise together*, which Mursius wants, are inept. Finally, Tertullian himself favors no other usage. Below, chapter 47: “while they attempt our doctrines,” where Wouwer and Rigault, reading “are contaminated,” do not heal the passage, which is sound, but contaminate it; for the author speaks in this manner elsewhere also. Gronovius the elder, in *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 22, emends *it attempts*, as though the sense were “if any tree attempts.” “Although,” he says, “the same meaning belongs to the common reading, provided that one understands the pronoun as neuter plural.” So he writes, and I do not disagree. Otherwise, it seems possible to refer the words both to fruits and to trees, so that *if any*—as has been sufficiently shown above—is equivalent to “if in any way,” just as Virgil’s *in some way* means “by any means.” What he presently says, *covered*, also seems to lead in this direction. One can also punctuate: “and if there are any fruits of trees there, they make the attempt only upon the eyes”; or “in whatever way fruits of trees there,” etc. Finally, the poem entitled *Sodom* must be cleansed here too. The common text reads:

> Even if any half-destroyed acres there attempt  
> The rich resources of autumn, at first they easily  
> Promise the eyes the finest pears, peaches, and every fruit,  
> Until they are plucked; for at once, when touched by the pointing finger,  
> The fruit dissolves into ash and becomes empty cinders.

Read, much more elegantly:

> Until they are plucked; for at once, at the touch of the pointing finger,  
> The deceit of the empty fruit dissolves into ash.

We emend it in this manner partly from the most excellent parchments, [Col. 0484C] partly by conjecture. For they had “at the touch of the pointer,” for which we have restored “of the pointing finger,” for “of the finger”—a familiar license among the ancient poets, of whom our author read Lucretius most diligently. But that whole little poem, a truly beautiful one, we shall someday, if God wills, publish as though restored to life from darkness. Meanwhile note that here too τὸ [uncertain: only this fragment was recovered, although the context expects a repeated verb meaning “they attempt”], “they attempt,” is emphatically repeated, and thus that the whole attempt is fruitless. HAV.] they exist only as far as the eyes are concerned; when touched, however, they turn to ash. [Note: [Col. 0483A] Rhenanus, Latinius, Gangnaeus: “arise”; and in the following manuscripts [Col. 0484A] Fulda, Agobardine, and Leiden: “are ashes.”] [Note: [Col. 0484C] **When touched, they turn to ash.** The Agobardine and Fulda manuscripts have “they are ash,” but the former is better, for the poem *Sodom* says:

> It dissolves into ash.

Among the ancients Josephus, Tacitus, Solinus, and Augustine affirm this. Add the travel narratives. Martin von Baumgarten testifies that the shore is full of reeds and rotten trees. Salignac likewise affirms that trees grow all around, but that because of the sea’s pestilential exhalation they can produce nothing fit to eat. One may see fruits fair in appearance but filled within with ashes and cinders. Burchard too writes in §39: “Below Engedi, beside the shore of the Dead Sea, there are indeed very beautiful trees, but when their fruit is torn open it is found to be filled inside with cinders and ash.” Hegesippus says still more in book IV of *The Destruction of Jerusalem*: he records trees most beautiful to the sight, which by their pleasing appearance arouse in observers the desire to eat; if one takes them, they fall apart and dissolve into ash, raising smoke as though they were still burning. Whether these reports are fictitious or the condition has changed over time, Prince Radziwiłł writes that none now remain. Nevertheless, the words of Ammann, praised above, deserve to be presented in Latin. He records that he saw trees, and that they certainly exist on the road to Jericho, though their appearance differs from the earlier description. Here are his words: “On the road,” he says, “we also encountered some trees—or rather shrubs—with abundant, widely spreading branches and very thorny, much like our buckthorn. From them hung most beautiful and luxuriant fruit, resembling in appearance the smaller reddish apples called *paradises*, very striking to behold. [Col. 0485B] I plucked some to eat, but their taste was utterly unappealing and disagreeable; within they were full of white seeds, like the seeds of our pomegranates. Since these shrubs were laden with fruit, I took some of the apples away with me. Some among them were dry and blackish; when broken, they crumbled into ash and scattered like cinders. When freshly plucked, however, they are not like this, but dry out over time like other fruits.” So he writes. [Col. 0485C] From this it appears that if those fruits remain too long on the trees, they decay in such a way that they dissolve into ash at a touch. HAV.]

Nor, at that time, did Tuscany and Campania complain about the Christians when fire from heaven consumed Volsinii [Col. 0485A] [Note: [Col. 0485C] **Volsinii.** Pliny, *Natural History* II.52: “Volsinii, the wealthiest town of the Etruscans, was entirely burned by lightning.” Most write *Volsinios*, but Aldus and Rigault have *Vulsinios*. The Leiden manuscript has *Ulsineos*, with *Ulscinios* written above it. This is also the common reading in *To the Nations*. HAV.] and fire from its own mountain poured over Tarpeii. [Note: [Col. 0485C] **Tarpeii.** All manuscripts and printed editions have *Pompeii*. Since, however, the author is now dealing with disasters that befell not only the whole world but Italy as well before the Christian name became known, one may rightly ask how a catastrophe that occurred only under Nero could be included here. Gothofredus indeed noted that the manuscript of *To the Nations* has not *Pompeii* but *Trapeii*, and he advises that the same name be restored here. For Tarpe was a city of Italy, according to Stephanus’ epitomator; if we possessed Stephanus complete, perhaps we should know of this disaster too, and certainly more about that city. I prefer this to acknowledging, with Gatalterus, a truly learned theologian, a lapse of memory in Tertullian. Consult that scholar on the similar passage of Antoninus, philosopher and emperor, book IV, §48, where he collected much relevant both to this and to the preceding material, which it is not proper to copy out. I believe that town was in Campania and was chosen because of such a disaster, which Tertullian could have learned about from writers still extant in his own age. For one who named Tarpeii in *To the Nations* hardly seems likely to have forgotten himself so quickly. It is agreed that this little work was written before the *Apology* and was, as it were, a preliminary draft of it. In *On the Pallium*, where Pompeii is also named, the reasoning is different: there he did not have to explain what occurred before the time of Christ, but collected events better known to the general public. Hence editors wrongly wished the same name to stand in this passage. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0485B] Semler deletes *and*, “already at that time.”] [Note: [Col. 0485B] Gothofredus restored *Tarpeii* from *To the Nations* I.9; the manuscripts read *Pompeii*.] No one at Rome yet worshiped the true God when Hannibal at Cannae [Note: [Col. 0485D] **Hannibal at Cannae.** Augustine, *City of God* III.16, Orosius, *Histories* IV.16, Paul the Deacon after him, and Ludovicus Vives in his notes on Augustine describe this battle at length. The catastrophe occurred in the year 240 from the founding of the city, when Aemilius Paulus and Publius Terentius Varro were consuls. PAM.—Nothing is more commonly encountered among writers than the battle of Cannae, in which the then consul Lucius Aemilius Paulus fell, and with him forty-five thousand Romans were lost. The slaughter was so great that Hannibal, the victor, measured its magnitude by the number of rings; some say there were three pecks of them. Livy asserts that there was only one, and even here [Col. 0486C] I have difficulty agreeing with him, for the number of slain Roman knights was not so great that there could have been a peck of rings—unless we heed Pliny, who says in book XXXIII that at the time of the Second Punic War the use of rings was common to both knights and plebeians. LE PR.] measured the rings of the Romans—the tokens of his slaughter—by the peck. All your gods were worshiped by everyone when the Senones seized the Capitol itself. [Note: [Col. 0485B] Paris: “poured forth.”] [Note: [Col. 0486C] **When they seized the Capitol itself.** Augustine, *City of God* II.22, and Orosius II.19 also reproach the gentiles with this catastrophe. The former, however, writes that geese prevented the Capitol from being captured; the latter says that, although the entire surviving youth had been enclosed by the siege on the Capitoline Hill, the Romans bargained to pay one thousand pounds of gold as the price of the Gauls’ withdrawal. Accordingly, the author must use *seize* here in the sense of *forestall* or *take unawares*, in the Plautine phrase from the *Rudens*: “You forestall me in speaking.” PAM.]

And it is just as well that, whenever adversity befell cities, the same disasters struck the temples as struck the walls, so that I may now prove from this that such events do not come from the gods, since they also happen to the gods themselves. The human race has always deserved ill of God: first, because it failed in its duty [Note: [Col. 0485B] Junius adds *toward*.] [Note: [Col. 0485B] Paris: “in duties.”] toward him. Although it understood him in part, [Note: [Col. 0486C] **Although it understood him in part.** They could have constructed this natural theology under the guidance of conscience and also through contemplation of all created things. Romans I.19; II.14–15; Job XII.7–10; Acts XVII.27; XIV.17; and elsewhere; and this εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους in Romans I.20. Hence our author says: “Nature being the teacher, the soul the pupil. Whatever the former taught or the latter learned was delivered by God, the teacher, namely, of the teacher herself.” Elsewhere he says: “God sent nature ahead as his servant, intending afterward to add prophecy.” Rhenanus corruptly reads: “in its duties, whatever things.” The word *him* is absent from La Cerda’s edition. HAV.], not only did it fail to seek him out as one to be feared, but more readily invented others for itself [Note: [Col. 0485B] Paris: “whomever.”] to worship. Then, by failing to inquire after the master of innocence and the judge and exactor of guilt, it became overgrown with every vice and crime. [Note: [Col. 0485B] So the Fulda codex. The common reading was: “it did not seek him out, but moreover invented others for itself to worship.” The Herault codices have: “invented whom it might worship”; Aldus: “might invent,” deleting what follows.]

But if it had sought him out, it would follow that it would know and acknowledge the one sought; that it would observe the one acknowledged; and that it would experience the one observed as favorable rather than angry. [Note: [Col. 0486B] Paris: “involved.”] [Note: [Col. 0486B] Junius: “it followed.”] [Note: [Col. 0486B] “It would follow that it would know” is absent from Paris.] It should therefore know that the same God is angry now who was always angry in the past as well, even before Christians were named. Since it enjoyed his benefits, produced before it fashioned gods for itself, why does it not understand that evils also come from him whose benefits it failed to recognize as his? It is guilty toward the one to whom it is also ungrateful.

And yet, if we compare the disasters of former times, lighter things happen now, since God gave Christians to the world. For from that time innocence has tempered the age’s iniquities, and intercessors before God [Note: [Col. 0486D] **Intercessors before God.** “Since,” he says, “among you—slaves of injustice and every evil—there have arisen those who act before God in the role of scapegoats or intercessors.” This is the true meaning. Hence the term is frequently applied to slaves in Plautus and others, including this passage from Terence’s *Self-Tormentor*, act V, scene 2:

> You have prepared neither an altar for yourself  
> Nor a scapegoat.

[Col. 0487C] Abraham was such an intercessor for the Sodomites, as would even those ten have been, had they been found. Genesis XVIII.32. HAV.] have begun to exist. [Note: [Col. 0486B] Junius deletes “and acknowledge.”] [Col. 0487A]

In short, when summer and winter hold back their rains [Note: [Col. 0487C] **Summer and winter hold back their rains.** The meaning is: when it rains neither in summertime nor in wintertime. A child may understand it thus: “When summer or winter holds back and abstains from rain.” Among the ancients the year was divided into only two parts, namely winter and summer; hence authors frequently use these two parts to mean the year, but not spring and autumn. LAC.] and the year becomes a source of anxiety, you, indeed—fed daily and about to dine again immediately, occupied with baths, taverns, and brothels [Note: [Col. 0487B] Regius: “while serving.”]—sacrifice rites for procuring rain to Jupiter, [Note: [Col. 0487C] **You sacrifice rites for procuring rain to Jupiter.** Rhenanus says that *aquilicia* were so called from drawing forth the waters, a rite performed in the great city. *Aquileges*, or water-diviners, were experts in searching out springs, named from *elices*, the heads and sources of springs. He calls the rites *barefoot ceremonies* because the people were ordered to invoke rain barefoot during public supplications. PAM.] proclaim barefoot processions to the people, seek the sky at the Capitol, and await clouds from paneled ceilings, turned away from God himself and from heaven.

We, however, dried up by fasts and contracted by every form of continence, [Note: [Col. 0487C] **Contracted by every form of continence.** Not as those who, like David’s Amnon, grow dry and wasted because pleasure is denied them, II Samuel XIII.4, but as those whom zeal for God’s house consumes. Nazianzen develops the thought in that passage as follows: τοὺς διὰ τὴν νέκρωσιν ἀθανάτους, τοὺς διὰ λύσιν θεῷ συνημμένους, τοὺς ἔξο πώθου καὶ μετὰ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἀπαθοῦς ἔρωτος [recovered text contains apparent corruptions], that is, “immortal through mortification, joined to God through dissolution, estranged from desire, and seized by a divine love devoid of lust.” The same author, intending to commend to virgins a pallor pleasing to God, writes in his *Oration Against Women Overly Ambitious in Adornment*: “Namely, that you may assume pallor as your beauty, waste away through Christ’s labors, and wear yourself down by prayers and tears and by vigils lasting day and night.” Such was the great Athanasius. Looking upon him amid the outrage of the Arians, the same author concludes thus in *Oration XI, Against the Arians and Concerning Athanasius*: “Against whom have I brought in prostitutes—men almost devoid of flesh and blood?” And Christ himself says in the cited passage, verse 23: “I pass away like a shadow when it declines.” Finally, as our own proverb puts it, in accordance with that saying of Aristophanes in *Plutus* IV.4:

Διὰ δακτυλίου μέν οῦν ἐμού γ` ἂν διελκὑσαις [recovered text contains apparent corruptions]. [Col. 0488B] You could easily draw them through the middle of a ring. So that, in accordance with the line of Persius which may be understood from this, *Satires* VI.73, it may be said:

Let me retain a threadlike figure,

But let that sacrificial attendant’s belly quiver with fat.

Such people do occur; but these hypocritical Pharisees are only traffickers in reputation, in Matthew 6:16. Ἀφανίζουσι (“They disfigure”) [Col. 0488C] γάρ τἁ πρόσωτα ἀυτῶν (“for their faces”; the recovered Greek is corrupt), says the Savior. Aldus reads “besprinkled,” but wrongly. HAV.] Driven far from every fruit of life, rolling in sackcloth and ashes, we beat upon heaven with our resentment, we touch God, and [Note: [Col. 0487B] Perhaps “distress him.” Haverc.] when we have wrung mercy from him, Jupiter is honored by you, while God is neglected. [Note: [Col. 0487B] The words “by you, while God is neglected” are found only in the Fulda manuscript.]

## CHAPTER XLI

**SUMMARY.—Indeed, those very men who, scorning God, worship statues are the cause of the evils that occur every day. [Col. 0487B] For if their gods truly were Gods, they would not involve their own worshipers in the punishments of the Christians as well. But since he who truly is God sends evils upon both good and bad—upon the latter as punishment, upon the former as admonition—[Col. 0488A] he will not establish a distinction between the two before the severity of the eternal judgment. But if they persist in ascribing these evils to their own Gods because those Gods tolerate the existence of Christians, it follows that such Gods are unjust and ungrateful, since they wish their worshipers to be punished together with those who mock them.**

You, therefore, are a scourge [Note: [Col. 0488C] “A scourge to human affairs”: that is, calamitous and troublesome people, on whose account the world lacks public peace. Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.305:

> A ruinous war we citizens wage against the race of Gods  
> And unconquered men.

Here Servius explains “ruinous” as a place where there is no refuge because it lacks a harbor—that is, repose—where there is no haven. HAV.] to human affairs; you are the affliction of public interests, you are always the instigators of evils, among whom God is scorned and statues are worshiped. Surely it must be considered more credible that the one who is neglected should be angry [Note: [Col. 0488C] “That the one who is neglected should be angry.” This follows from the pagans’ own opinion. Thus, when Alexander attributed the killing of Clitus to the anger of the Gods, it occurred to him that the annual sacrifice had not been offered to Father Liber at its appointed time. Accordingly, since the killing had been committed amid wine and feasting, the anger of the God was manifest. Arrian tells the same story, IV.9. There is also a sufficiently ridiculous tale in that witty writer of Samosata, Lucian, who relates something similar about a statue of Hippocrates in the dialogue entitled *The Lover of Lies*. There Antigonus [Col. 0488D] the physician says: Κἀμοὶ, ὦ Εὔκρατες, Ἱπποκράτης ἐστί χαλκοῦς (“I too, Eucrates, have a bronze Hippocrates”), etc.; that is: “I too, Eucrates,” he says, “have a bronze Hippocrates, approximately a cubit high, who, as soon as the lamp is extinguished, goes all around the house, making a clatter, overturning boxes, mixing medicines, and upsetting the door—especially if we defer the sacrifice that we offer them every year.” HAV.] than those who are worshiped—or else, assuredly, those gods are utterly unjust if, on account of the Christians, they injure even their own worshipers [Note: [Col. 0488B] Perhaps: “than the one who is worshiped.” Haverc.] [Note: [Col. 0488B] But “assuredly” is the reading of the Fulda manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0488D] “They injure even their own worshipers.” This is utterly unjust, since, according to that well-worn maxim of the jurists, Digest V, *On Punishments*, it is better to let a guilty man go unpunished than to condemn an innocent one. Polybius too, Book V: Οὐ γάν ἑπ` ἀπωλεία δεῖ καὶ ἀφανισμῷ τοῖς ἀγνώμοσι πόλεμεν (“For one must not wage war against the unprincipled unto destruction and annihilation”; the recovered Greek is visibly corrupt), etc. “It belongs to good men, even when dealing with men of inferior character, not to wage a war of extermination, but only to the point that offenses are repaired and corrected; not to involve the innocent together with the guilty in a single punishment, but, for the sake of the innocent, even to spare the guilty.” Such too is Abraham’s argument addressed to God in Genesis 18:23. How much more ridiculous, therefore, are those Gods who destroy their own worshipers together with their enemies, [Col. 0489B] so that their vengeance accords with Lucretius II.1103:

> Often it passes over the guilty  
> And destroys the undeserving and innocent.

For, as Publilius Syrus rightly says, verse 836:

[Col. 0489C]

> It is ridiculous, from hatred of the guilty, to destroy the innocent.

See there further material relevant to this point. HAV.], whom they ought to separate from the punishments deserved by Christians.

“You can retort this,” you say, “against [Col. 0488B] your God as well, since he himself allows even his worshipers to be injured on account of the profane.” [Note: [Col. 0488B] Semler reads “allows.”] First accept his arrangements, and you will not make that retort. For he who has once appointed [Col. 0489A] the eternal judgment [Note: [Col. 0489C] “For he who has once appointed the eternal judgment.” The sense is that God, who once determined to judge for eternity when the end of the age arrives, does not anticipate before that time the discrimination between good and evil, in which the judgment partly consists. Therefore, the comma after “which is a condition of judgment” must not be neglected, as it has been in most editions. We have explained above the elegance and usage of the word “once.” HAV.] for after the end of the age does not bring forward [Note: [Col. 0489C] “Does not bring forward the discrimination.” This expression is highly exact and elegant; it means what elsewhere is called doing beforehand or anticipating. Lucan II.106:

> Nor, as his declining years approached, did the old man shrink  
> From bringing forward his final day.

Here the manuscript reading “to do beforehand” is more an interpretation than the true text. For in the same author Pompey says, VII.352:

[Col. 0489D]

> If they meant to give kingdoms to my father-in-law and prepare the world for him,  
> The Fates could have brought forward my old age.

That is: “The Gods could have anticipated me with death before this gray old age.” Again the same poet, in verse 51 of the same book:

> Each man longs to bring forward  
> His own fate and the public fate.

Finally, Book V.795:

> And they bring forward their grief,
