since, of course, the death had not yet been formally announced. HAV.] before the end of the age the discrimination that is a condition of judgment. Meanwhile, he is equally indulgent toward and reproving of the whole human race. [Note: [Col. 0489B] Franciscus, the Paris editions, and Rigault read “rebuking”; the Fulda manuscript, “assailing.”] He willed advantages to be shared with the profane and disadvantages with his own people, so that, through equal participation, we might all experience both his gentleness and his severity. Because we have learned these things in this way [Note: [Col. 0489B] The Fulda manuscript reads, “But we who learn”; the Lyon and Görres manuscripts and Pamelius’s edition, “because we have learned fairness” (Gelenius: “who have learned”), etc.] from him, we love his gentleness and fear his severity; you, by contrast, despise both. It follows that all the scourges of the age come from God upon us, perhaps as admonition, but upon you as chastisement.

Yet we are in no way injured: first, because nothing matters to us in this age except how quickly we may depart from it; and then because, if any adversity is inflicted, it is charged to your deserts. [Note: [Col. 0489B] Junius reads “it is charged to your deserts.”] [Col. 0489B] [Note: [Col. 0489D] “It is charged to your deserts.” Thus the Fulda manuscript; for the others do not acknowledge τὸ “it,” a reading I was unwilling to neglect, since it is appropriately placed. Zephyrus, Junius, and La Cerda vainly prefer “it is charged to our deserts,” contrary to the consensus of all the manuscripts. “We are not disturbed by these things,” he says: first, because we have no concern for this age, whether our poor little body fares badly or well; second, because we possess the great consolation afforded us by a good conscience—that you are the cause of such great anger on God’s part, since you neglect him, not we, who alone worship and observe him and offer him a sacrifice greater and richer than all your hecatombs: the sacrifice he himself commanded, prayer proceeding from chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and the Holy Spirit. These are nearly Tertullian’s own words above, Chapter XXX. Third, because we are more firmly confirmed in the divine character of our religion when we see fulfilled every day those things that we read were foretold long ago. HAV.]

But even if some evils graze us too because we are attached to you, we rejoice all the more in recognizing the divine predictions, which confirm, of course, our confidence and our faith in our hope. But if all your evils come upon you from those whom you worship, on our account, why do you persist in worshiping [Col. 0490A] beings so ungrateful and unjust, who ought rather to have helped and vindicated you to the grief of the Christians? [Note: [Col. 0490B] In all the old books except the Fulda manuscript, the additional words “whom they ought to separate from those who have earned the punishment of the Christians” are read; Rigault deleted them as inept in his edition.]

## CHAPTER XLII

**SUMMARY.—It is no less wrong to call Christians unprofitable for commerce, since they live both with the pagans and from them, mingle their labor and crafts with theirs, and sail, serve as soldiers, and trade together with them. Although they differ in certain ceremonies, renounce the spectacles, do not make supplication with incense, and do not throw contributions into the temples, they are nevertheless both human beings and citizens. They readily compensate for that trifling loss through other benefits, and especially by paying the public revenues faithfully when due, instead of defrauding them as the pagans do.**

[Col. 0490B] 42. But we are prosecuted under yet another charge [Note: [Col. 0490B] “Still,” in the Fulda manuscript.] of injury: we are said to be unprofitable in business. [Note: [Col. 0490C] “We are said to be unprofitable in business.” Hence, without doubt, Suetonius Tranquillus—quite hostile to the Christian sect—calls the distinguished Flavius Clemens, son of Flavius Sabinus, the emperor Vespasian’s brother, a man of the most contemptible inactivity, where he relates that Clemens was killed by his cousin Domitian, *Domitian* XV. Torrentius rightly noted this there as well. To the pagan in Minucius, p. 8, Christians are “a secretive, light-shunning nation, silent in public and talkative in corners.” Rhenanus here and the Leiden manuscript read “unprofitable in business.” The Fulda manuscript, however, reads “unprofitable to business,” approximately as below in Chapter XLVI: “what has now become known by use and from commercial dealings.” Heraldus, Barræus, Aldus, Pamelius, La Cerda, and Rigault too read “in business.” Tacitus charges them with hatred of the human race, *Annals* XV.44. They were called “unfruitful” with reference to their name, since it was more fitting that Christians should be “fruitful.” HAV.]

How can this be true of people who live with you [Note: [Col. 0490D] “Who live with you,” etc. Relevant here are the words in *On Idolatry* XIV: “It is permissible to live with the pagans, but not to die with them. Let us share in common activities; let us rejoice together from our shared nature, not from superstition. We are equal in soul, not in discipline; co-possessors of the world, not of error.” And in Chapter XVI of the same work: “As for the duties belonging to private and communal celebrations—such as the assumption of the plain toga, betrothals, weddings, and name-giving ceremonies—I think that no danger need be observed from the breath of idolatry that intervenes.” HAV.], sharing the same food, clothing, furnishings, and necessities of life? For we are not Brahmans [Note: [Col. 0490D] “Brahmans.” Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 172: Καὶ Βραχμᾶνας ἱστοροῦσιν ἕτεροι ἐν ταῖς ὕλαις διάγειν, φύλλοις τὸ σῶμα καλύπτοντας (“Others also relate that the Brahmans live in the forests, covering their bodies with leaves”); that is: “Other historians also relate that the Brahmans live in forests and clothe their bodies with leaves.” Pliny and Theophrastus teach that they lived there on the fruits of trees. From their description it is clear [Col. 0491B] that the fruit was what we call the coconut. Salmasius adduces the passage of Theophrastus in his notes on Solinus, p. 210, and emends it at the same time: Εστι δὲ καὶ ἕτερον δένδρον, καὶ τῷ μεγέθει μέγα, καὶ ἡδύκαρπον θαυμαστῶς, καὶ μεγαλόκαρπον, καὶ χρῶνται τροφῇ τῶν Ἰνδῶν οἱ σοφοὶ καὶ ἀπεχόμενοι (“There is also another tree, great in size, marvelously sweet-fruited and large-fruited; the sages of the Indians, who abstain, use it as food”); that is: “There is another tree of marvelous height, producing large and very sweet fruits. The sages of the Indians, who abstain from ordinary foods, live on these.” Here that very great scholar corrects οὐκ ἀμφεχόμενοι (“not clothed”), that is, “not clothed”; but there is no need for that correction, for οἱ ἀπεχόμενοι (“those who abstain”) plainly signifies here those whom the Hebrews call, with the same sense and a very similar term, Nazirites, whose manner of life agreed in many respects with the practice of the Gymnosophists. HAV.] or Indian [Note: [Col. 0489B] The Fulda manuscript reads “confirmed, as recognizing.”] [Col. 0491A] Gymnosophists, forest-dwellers and exiles from life. [Note: [Col. 0491B] “Exiles from life.” Junius spoils the elegance of this passage through incorrect punctuation. Tertullian calls them “exiles from life,” just as below, Chapter XLVII, he calls the inactive Epicurean god “a nobody in human affairs.” Thus in our Publilius the stork, unable to endure winter, is called “a bird exiled from winter” in Petronius; and those infants reared by Psammetichus in seclusion, apart from human intercourse, are described as “utter exiles from the human voice” in Tertullian, *To the Nations* I.8. HAV.]

We remember that we owe gratitude to God, the Lord and Creator. [Note: [Col. 0491A] Franciscus and the Paris editions read “the Lord God and Creator.”] We reject none of the fruit of his works; we merely exercise restraint, so that we do not use it immoderately or wrongly. Accordingly, we live in this world not without your forum, not without your meat market, baths, shops, workshops, inns, fairs, and other commercial dealings. [Note: [Col. 0491C] “And other commercial dealings.” Christians were therefore more tolerable even than the schools of philosophers, whose foolish wisdom the pagans not only tolerated but admired. Lucian notes this in his *Demonax*, whom he said to resemble Socrates in learning and Diogenes in frugality, though with conduct that was human, not doglike and ostentatious: οὐ παραχαράττων (“not altering”), he says, τὰ ἐς τὴν δίαιταν (“the things pertaining to his manner of life”). ὡς θαυμάζοιτο (“so that he might be admired”), etc. “Yet he did not ostentatiously alter what pertained to his manner of living in order to purchase popular admiration and make those with whom he associated fix their eyes upon him. Rather, he employed the same manner of life as others, without being infected by even the slightest philosophical arrogance; he maintained social relations with others and readily obeyed the common laws of the state.” HAV.]

We sail with you, serve as soldiers with you, till the soil, and trade. In the same way, we join our crafts with yours and make our labor available for your use. How we can seem unprofitable to your business, [Col. 0492A] when we live both with you and from you, I do not know.

But even if [Note: [Col. 0491D] “But if I do not frequent your ceremonies.” Christians utterly rejected, of course, those ceremonies that pertained to the worship of idols. *To the Martyrs* XI: “Do not, by mingling with them, participate in the nations’ solemn days.” And *On Idolatry* XIII: “On this point I will first consider whether a servant of God ought to share in such practices even with the nations themselves, whether in clothing, food, furnishings, or any other form of their rejoicing.” There he is not dealing with common business transactions, in which Christians were not unprofitable, as is clear from the beginning of this chapter, but with matters pertaining to superstitions; for he continues shortly afterward: “There are certain days which, among some, discharge an obligation of honor, and among others an obligation of payment. ‘Now, therefore,’ you say, ‘I shall receive what is mine or repay what belongs to another.’ If men have consecrated this custom to themselves from superstition, why do you, who are a stranger to all their vanity, participate in celebrations involving food sacrificed to idols, as though the day itself had been prescribed for you, so that you could not, [Col. 0492B] without observance of the day, pay or receive what you owe another person or what another person owes you?” The Fulda manuscript reads “even if your ceremonies”; the Leiden manuscript, “but the ceremonies held jointly,” as though the text should read “joint ceremonies,” that is, those that other nations celebrate together with you. HAV.] I do not frequent your ceremonies, I am nevertheless a human being on that day too. I do not bathe near nightfall [Note: [Col. 0491A] Franciscus reads, “I am not bathed at dawn.”] [Note: [Col. 0492B] “I do not bathe near nightfall.” La Cerda read: “I am not bathed near nightfall.” The Saturnalia were celebrated in December for five or seven days. It was a pagan superstition to believe that the day was observed religiously if they began it at dawn. LE PR.] during the Saturnalia, lest I lose both night and day. Yet I bathe [Note: [Col. 0492B] “Yet I bathe.” Since the Saturnalia fell during the coldest period of the year, health would necessarily be endangered if bathing took place very early in the morning. Hence bathing was appropriately undertaken in the bathhouse after exercise. LAC.] at a proper and healthful hour, one that preserves my warmth and blood. [Note: [Col. 0491A] Thus the Fulda manuscript; all the others read: “I am not bathed at dawn during the Saturnalia—yet I bathe at a respectable hour,” etc.] I can grow cold and pale after bathing when I am dead.

I do not recline at table in public during the Liberalia, because beast-fighters customarily dine their last meal there; [Note: [Col. 0492B] “Beast-fighters.” La Cerda noted that the Greeks call them παραβόλους (“recklessly daring men”), that is, men of reckless daring. Correctly; for Apuleius too, in the passage cited by Heraldus, characterizes them as men of desperate fearlessness. [Col. 0492C] Add that in Latin they were also called *parabolarii*. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* VIII: “Those born under the constellation of the Dog will be hunters, arena-fighters, *parabolarii*, and men who fight wild beasts in cages before the eyes of the people.” Beroaldus vainly disturbs this passage in his notes on Apuleius by reading *pyrobolarii*. The word παραβάλλειν (“to throw before”) was used of food thrown to wild beasts, as Henri Estienne confirms from the examples he adduces; and in Athenaeus παραβληθεὶς ζώοις (“having been thrown to the beasts”) means “thrown to the beasts.” Estienne likewise explains παραβάλλεσθαι (“to expose oneself”) as “to approach danger with reckless daring.” Homer, *Iliad* I:

Ἀεὶ ἐμὴν ψυχὴν παραβαλλόμενος πολεμίζειν (“always casting forth my life to fight”)

that is, “always casting forth my life to fight.” This may illustrate the Hebrew phrase “to place one’s life in one’s hand,” 1 Samuel 28:21, where the witch confesses that she has incurred the most immediate danger to her life; compare verse 9. The lexicographer also rightly derives the origin of this meaning in the word παρὰβολος (“recklessly daring”) [Col. 0492D] from the fact that a man who undertakes an act with a certain conspicuous and reckless daring seems to act as though he were hurling himself beyond all bounds. The same force of meaning occurs in παραπίπτειν (“to rush forward”) in Polybius II.13, where it is related of Philopoemen that he saw his mercenaries fleeing and the enemy, excessively eager for battle, advancing beyond the proper ground, so that the enemy appeared abandoned by them—which was certainly exceedingly rash. His words are: ἅμα τὸ παραπεσεῖν τοὺς διώκοντας καὶ τὸν τόπον γενέσθαι ἓρημον (“at once the pursuers rushed forward and the place became deserted”). Since that same verb occurs only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 6:6, its meaning must also be drawn from this sense, so that it signifies that reckless daring of the Jews who, though seeing and recognizing Jesus, the Messiah, the goodness of the Gospel, and the marvelous progress of God’s kingdom in the world, nevertheless relapse into their own depraved and carnal opinions. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0492A] Thus Rigault and Havercamp; others read “the last,” others “before the first.”] yet wherever I dine, I dine from your supplies. [Note: [Col. 0492A] In the Agobardine and Lyon manuscripts, a question mark is read after “I dine”; but perhaps it should be placed after “wherever,” while “I recline” should be excluded.]

I do not buy a crown for my head. [Note: [Col. 0492D] “A crown for my head.” He discusses this subject extensively in the little book entitled *On the Soldier’s Crown*. See [Col. 0493B] also the commentators on Minucius, Sirmond on Sidonius I.1, and Joachim Johann Mader, *On Crowns*, found in volume VIII of Graevius’s *Roman Antiquities*. Nazianzen acknowledges other flowers belonging to Christians and a sweeter crown made from them, *Oration II against Julian*: Ἔχω καὶ ἂνθη (“I too have flowers”), he says, πάντων ἐαρνῶν εὐανθέστερα τε καὶ μονιμώτερα (“more luxuriantly blooming and more lasting than all spring flowers”), etc.; that is: “I too have flowers, more blooming and fragrant than all the flowers of spring, gathered from that field which the Lord has blessed with holy and sweet-smelling pastors and teachers, and with pure and distinguished persons of the common order. With these I wish to be crowned and to triumph after I have fought the good fight.” HAV.] What concern is it of yours how I use the flowers once I have bought them? [Col. 0493A] I think they are more pleasing [Note: [Col. 0493B] “I think they are more pleasing when free.” Thus Rigault from the Fulda manuscript. Others read “that it is more pleasing.” “I therefore do not wish,” he says, “to place an unwelcome weight upon my head.” Lucretius, Book III, teaches that these garlands were sometimes quite large and heavy:

> And they shade their faces with crowns.

[Col. 0493C] And Horace, *Odes* I.4:

> Now it is fitting to bind the gleaming head with green myrtle,  
> Or with a flower borne by the loosened earth.

HAV.] when free and unbound and wandering everywhere. Yet even if they are bound into a crown, we recognize a crown by our noses; let those who smell through their hair look to it. [Note: [Col. 0493A] “To be” is absent from the Fulda manuscript and from Rigault and Havercamp.] [Note: [Col. 0493C] “Those who smell through their hair.” Diogenes Laertius, on Diogenes the Cynic: τῳ μύρῳ τοὺς πόδας ἀλειψάμενος ἒφη ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς κεφαλῆς εἰς τὸν ἀέρα ἀπιέναι τὸ μύρον, ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν ποδῶν εἰς τὴν ὄσφρησιν (“Having anointed his feet with perfume, he said that perfume from the head passes into the air, but from the feet reaches the sense of smell”); that is: “Anointing his feet with perfume, he said that perfume applied to the head rises into the air, but from the feet it reaches the sense of smell.” HAV.]

We do not attend the spectacles. Yet if I desire the things sold at those gatherings, [Note: [Col. 0493C] “Sold at those gatherings.” From this it is clear that traders were accustomed to gather there, which is especially natural because those events attracted the greatest crowd of people. The pagans complained that Christians neglected this opportunity, although they themselves suffered no loss from it, since the necessities of life could be obtained from the customary workshops and shops. HAV.] I shall more gladly obtain them from their own proper places. [Note: [Col. 0493A] The Fulda and Lyon manuscripts, Rhenanus, and Pamelius read “more freely.” The Fulda manuscript reads, “I shall obtain them from their own, from their proper places”; in that wording the traces of a glossator are quite evident. Others read “to obtain”; others, “let them be obtained”; [Col. 0494A] others, “let it be obtained”; others, “I obtain.”]

We certainly do not buy incense. If the Arabias complain, [Note: [Col. 0493C] “If the Arabias complain.” They could not complain, for Christians too used incense when circumstances required it. [Col. 0493D] *On the Soldier’s Crown* X: “And if the smell of some place offends me, I burn something from Arabia, but not with the same rite, clothing, or equipment employed before idols.” HAV.] let the Sabaeans know [Note: [Col. 0494A] Franciscus and the Paris editions read “let them know.”] that more and dearer of their merchandise is expended in burying Christians [Note: [Col. 0493D] “In burying Christians.” For, in order to testify to their sure hope of resurrection—which Paul illustrates by comparison with seed cast into the earth and decaying there, 1 Corinthians 15—they did not permit their dead to be cremated. The emperor Julian, Epistle XLIX, counts this care for funerals among the causes of that sect’s growth. Indeed, they even embalmed the dead with spices, as may be evident from this passage. After La Cerda, Ouzel gathered together, in his usual fashion, much material on this subject from Tertullian and others in his notes on Minucius, p. 63. Petrus Bellonius treats embalmed burial expressly in *Observations* II.47 and in his three books *On the Admirable Excellence of the Works of the Ancients*, found in volume VIII of Gronovius’s *Thesaurus*. So too Athanasius Kircher in his *Oedipus*, Joseph Lauzon in *On the Laying-Out and Embalming of the Dead among the Ancients*, and others. HAV.] than in fumigating the gods.

“Certainly,” you say, “the revenues of the temples are daily falling into bankruptcy; [Col. 0494A] scarcely anyone now throws in a contribution.” [Note: [Col. 0494B] “Scarcely anyone now throws in a contribution.” Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II.909:

> The final complaint, deplored with grief by the ambassador, is  
> That grain is denied to Pallas’s hearths, or that the very contributions  
> Supplying the Virgins and their chaste choirs are withheld,  
> And the Vestal fires are cheated of their customary expenditure.

See our observations above on Chapter XIII at the words: “Religion goes begging around the taverns.” Contributions were also customarily given to other gods and on other occasions. Thus, when Romans laid aside the bordered toga and assumed the toga of manhood, a silver coin was paid in the temple of the goddess Juventas for their fortunate advancement, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus testifies, Book IV. Pupils gave their teachers the *Minerval*, a contribution so called as though consecrated to the goddess, a practice our author condemns in *On Idolatry* X: “He consecrates the very first payment of a new pupil to Minerva’s honor and name, so that, even if he is not actually defiled by any idol, he may still be said verbally to partake of food sacrificed to an idol and be avoided as an idolater.” HAV.]

We cannot, you see, provide assistance both to needy human beings and to your needy gods, nor do we think that anything should be bestowed upon any but those who ask. Finally, let Jupiter stretch out his hand and receive it, [Note: [Col. 0494C] “Let Jupiter stretch out his hand.” Hollowed, of course, as beggars do. Balsamon on Photius’s *Nomocanon*: Τοῦ αἰτοῦντος καὶ λαμβάνοντος ἐγγὺς ἵσταται ὁ Χριστὸς, συγκυλαίνων τούτῳ τὴν χεῖρα (“Christ stands near the one who asks and receives, cupping his hand together with him”); that is: “Christ stands nearest to the one who asks and receives, extending his hollowed hand together with him.” On this custom one should certainly consult the very learned Casaubon’s note on Suetonius XCI, where it is related that Augustus, lest he provoke Nemesis through excessive good fortune, following a nocturnal dream begged a contribution from the people every year on a fixed day, presenting his hollowed hand to those offering coins. There the same scholar proves from many examples that this was a mark of rapacity and greed, while more honorable persons received money in the fold of their garments. Thus coins of Titus Vespasian, Domitian, and others attractively depict men receiving the donative or distribution in an outstretched cloak or garment rather than by hand. The same image appears on a coin of Hadrian bearing the inscription **ENRICHER OF THE WORLD**. Suetonius also relates an amusing story about Vespasian in his life, Chapter XXIII: “When ambassadors announced that a colossal statue of no moderate cost had been publicly decreed to him, he ordered them to erect it immediately, displaying his hollowed hand and saying that the base was ready.” Hence Seneca writes to his Lucilius in the preface to Book VI of the *Natural Questions*: “Add now a spirit unconquered by gifts, and a hand never held out to profit amid so great a contest of greed.” Tibullus censures his mistress’s greed:

> With hollowed hand she continually demands her price.

Diogenes, in Laertius, denied δεῖν τᾶς χεῖρας ἐπὶ τοὺς φίλους ἐκτείνειν συγκεκαμμένοις τοῖς δακτύλοις (“that hands ought to be extended toward friends with the fingers bent”); that is, “that hands ought to be extended to friends with the fingers bent.” Aristophanes vividly described Jupiter himself and the gods in this manner, where Phidolus refuses to give or contribute anything to the common fund because he is accustomed only to receive. *Women in Assembly*:

Καὶ γὰρ οἱ Θεοί,


Γνώσει δ` ἀπὸ τῶν χειρῶν τε καὶ ἀγαλμάτων (“For the gods do so too; you will know it from the hands and the statues”; the recovered syntax differs from the surrounding Latin’s “hands of the statues”) [Col. 0495B] Ὅταν γὰρ εὐχώμεθα διδόναι τἂγαθὰ,


Ἔϛηκεν ἐκτείνοντα τὴν χεῖρ` ὑπτίαν,


Οὐχ ὥς τι δώσοντ`, ἀλλ` ὅπως τι λήψεται (“For when we pray that they give blessings, one stands extending an upturned hand, not as though about to give something, but so as to receive something”; Ἔϛηκεν is corrupt or uncertain in the recovered text).

[Col. 0495C] That is: “Indeed, the Gods act in the same way. This can be learned even from the hands of their statues; for when we pray that they bestow blessings upon us, they stand extending an upturned hand—not as though they intend to give anything, but in order to receive.” HAV.] since meanwhile our mercy spends more street by street than your religion does temple by temple.

But the other revenues will thank Christians for faithfully paying what is due, because we refrain from defrauding another person. Thus, if an account were made of how much the public treasury [Note: [Col. 0494A] The Fulda manuscript and Havercamp read “the public treasury”; the others, “the revenues.”] loses through the fraud and falsehood of your declared assessments, [Col. 0495A] it could readily be calculated that the complaint concerning this single category is compensated by the advantage secured in all the other accounts. [Note: [Col. 0495B] The Fulda manuscript reads: “compensation for the complaint concerning one category in return for the security of the other accounts.”] [Note: [Col. 0495C] “The complaint concerning this single category is compensated by the advantage secured in all the other accounts.” The sense is that Christians show such honesty in paying the just assessments imposed in the name of the public revenues and the state that the slight loss suffered by temple revenues because Christians do not worship there should readily be disregarded—especially since the very people who complain of this crime by Christians commit far greater sacrileges every day when they consider it profitable to defraud the public revenues by every means. Here the Fulda manuscript reads: “the complaint concerning one category is compensation for the security of the other accounts.” The words “concerning one category” do not appear in the Leiden manuscript. HAV.] [Note: [Col. 0495B] Heraldus restored the passage in this form on the authority of the manuscripts. It formerly read: “I shall plainly confess who may complain. For if perhaps anyone—may be able” (others: “are able”; others: “might be able”).]

## CHAPTER XLIII

**Yet those who can truly complain about Christians are pimps, procurers, assassins, poisoners, magicians, and the like; and to be unprofitable to such men is itself a great profit. Even this loss, however, is exchanged for a better gain, since Christians both drive demons out of them and worship God on their behalf, and since, being such people as they are, Christians engage in no revolutionary activities aimed at the destruction of the state.**

43. I will plainly confess who, if anyone, can truly complain of the unproductiveness of Christians. First will come pimps, procurers, pimps’ water-boys, [Note: [Col. 0496B] The Fulda manuscript reads “soothsayers”; the Lyon manuscript, “egarioli”; Scriverius’s manuscript, “petty adulterers.”] [Note: [Col. 0496B] The words “because perhaps you do not believe” are absent from the Fulda manuscript, and Rigault deleted them from his edition.] [Note: [Col. 0495C] “Bath-attendants.” According to Festus, the servants of pimps were called *aquarii*, a name derived from fetching the water required for the bath. As Turnebus observed, *Adversaria* IV.12, they were called *aquarioli* with a contemptuous diminutive, as though they were the vilest of all men. PAM.], then assassins, [Col. 0495B] poisoners, magicians, likewise soothsayers, [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Soothsayers.” They were so called either from fates and speaking, as though *farioli*, or from breathing; for they were accustomed to breathe out or exhale the mortal soul so that they might receive the divine one. Hence, as Donatus notes on Terence’s *Phormio*, they uttered the sound **OE**, which conveys the force of exhaling. You should note, however, that among men this name is used whether you call them soothsayers or fanatics; among women, however, they are called “truth-speakers,” because they profess true knowledge of divination. LAC.], haruspices, and astrologers. To be unprofitable to these is a great profit.

And yet whatever loss your affairs suffer through this sect can assuredly be compensated by some advantage. [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Can assuredly be compensated by some advantage.” Here *praesidium* signifies profit, goods, or property. The author of the *Querolus*, which is customarily appended to some editions of Plautus: “Shall they carry my paternal property from the house with my own hands?” In the same work: “What benefit are thieves and robbers to me?” “So that, if you have any hope or property, they may bring it all together.” Again: “You have carried off my property and concealed the ashes.” The word occurs frequently in writers of the later age. HAV.] How highly do you value—I do not now say those who drive demons out of you; I do not now say those who spread prayers [Col. 0496A] before the true God on your behalf as well, because perhaps you do not believe this [Note: [Col. 0496B] The words “because perhaps you do not believe” are absent from the Fulda manuscript, and Rigault deleted them from his edition.]—but people from whom you can fear nothing?

## CHAPTER XLIV

**It should therefore rightly be reconsidered how great a loss the state suffers from the slaughter of so many innocent and deserving people. This can be demonstrated from the daily records and indictments of those in custody: among so many offenders there is found no criminal who is also a Christian.**

44. Yet no one considers that loss to the state, as great as it is real; no one weighs that injury to the citizen body, when so many of us righteous persons are expended, [Note: [Col. 0496B] “So many righteous persons are expended.” This is a metaphor drawn from household expenses. He speaks similarly in *On the Spectacles* XIX: “that they may be expended so credulously.” [Col. 0496C] Again, *On Idolatry* VI: “not the life of a beast expended, but your own life.” Through a printer’s error, the Rigault and Priorian editions give “are hindered.” HAV.] when so many of us innocent people are paid out.

We now call your own records as witnesses—you who preside each day over the trial of prisoners, you who settle the indictments by your sentences. [Note: [Col. 0496C] “You who cancel the indictments by your sentences.” The name, age, appearance, and charge of every prisoner—all of which were called *elogia*, indictments—were written on tablets and presented to the judges, who adjusted each man’s punishment according to his indictment. Hence, when the indictments of prisoners were once presented to Gaius Caligula and happened to mark a bald man as the first and another as the last in the series, that foolish emperor jested in a most serious matter, where no deliberation could have been too lengthy: without inspecting anyone’s indictment, and merely standing in the middle of the portico, he ordered the prisoners to be led away “from the bald man to the bald man.” Suetonius, *Life of Caligula* XXVII. HAV.]

So many offenders [Note: [Col. 0496B] The Fulda manuscript reads “How many.”] are listed by you under indictments for various crimes. What assassin among them, what cutpurse, [Note: [Col. 0496C] “Cutpurse.” The meaning of the word is known from Festus: it signifies a thief who searches purses. The Latin-Greek glosses likewise render *mantica* as πήραν (“a bag”). Hence those monks who walked about equipped with a bag were called [Col. 0496D] “bag-carrying.” Matthew Paris, who lived in the year 1248: “so that that bag-carrying monk might go on pilgrimage.” HAV.] what temple-robber, [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Temple-robber.” One who strips temples of their ornaments and votive offerings; hence they were protected by guards. See above, Chapter XXIX. HAV.] or corrupter, [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Corrupter.” How this word should be understood is clear from Chapter XLVII. I cite part of the Attic sentence against Socrates: “He is pronounced a corrupter of the young.” HAV.] or robber of bathers [Note: [Col. 0496D] “Robber of bathers.” Such men are frequently mentioned by the ancients. Plautus, *The Rope*, Act II, Scene III.51:

> A man who goes to bathe  
> In the baths, even when he carefully watches his clothing,  
> Still has it stolen; for he mistakes which of them he ought to watch.  
> The thief easily sees whom he is watching; the guard does not know who the thief is.

Apuleius, *The Golden Ass* IX: “But you, respectable robbers, in the course of petty and servile thefts, creep timidly through bathhouses and old women’s rooms, searching for plunder.” Catullus, Poem XXX:

> O best of bathhouse thieves,  
> Father Vibennius, and you, his pathic son.

Diogenes the Cynic in Laertius: ἰδὼν ἰματιοκλέπτην ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ, Ἐπ` ἀλειμμάτιον ἢ ἐπ` ἂλλο ἰμάτιον (“Seeing a clothing-thief in the bathhouse, he said, ‘Are you going for a little ointment, or for another garment?’”); that is: “Seeing a thief of clothing in the baths, he said, ‘Are you going for a little ointment, or for another garment?’” Our author, *On Idolatry* V: “I suppose bathhouse thieves too live by their hands”; and *On Flight in Persecution* XIII, among “shopkeepers, butchers, bathhouse thieves, gamblers, and pimps.” Gloss: “Bathhouse thief”: βαλανοκλέπτησ (“bathhouse thief”; the recovered final σ is preserved). Perhaps the following passage of Aristophanes also pertains to this, *Frogs*, Act IV, Scene II:

κᾁκβὰς, τινὰ λωποδυτῆσαι (“and, going out, to strip someone of his clothing”);

that is: “and, going out, to strip someone of his clothing.” In the same way, Petronius introduces a naked young man who had lost his clothes. Chrysostom, *On Virginity*, also disparages more costly adornment on the ground that both in bathhouses and in temples there are women ready to steal it. Wealthier bathers were therefore compelled to bring servants with them to guard their clothes. Martial XII.70:

[Col. 0497C]

> Though lately a little house-slave carried linen cloths for the sick,  
> And a one-eyed old woman sat over the poor cloak.

Ovid, *The Art of Love* III.539:

> While outside a guard watches over the girl’s tunic,
Let many baths contend in furtive pleasures.

But woe to those poor fellows if, through insufficient vigilance, anything was stolen from them. Hence that slave in Petronius, chapter XXX: “Stripped of his clothes, he threw himself at our feet and began to beg us to save him from punishment; his offense, he said, was not so serious as to place him in danger, for the steward’s clothes, which had been stolen from him in the bath, had scarcely been worth ten sesterces.” Add here Wouwer’s note. These clothes were deposited in the changing room, and theft was punished capitally, as is evident from the books of the jurists. Aristotle gives the reason; since Junius merely indicates the passage in passing, I shall not object to transcribing it in full. In *Problems*, Section XXIX, no. 14, he discusses the matter as follows: Διὰ τί ποτε ἐὰν μέν τις (“Why is it that, if someone …”). ἐκ βαλανείου κλέψῃ (“steals from a bathhouse …”), etc.; that is: “Why is one who has stolen from the baths, or from the wrestling school, or from the marketplace, or from some such place, punished with death, while one who steals from a private house pays twice the value of the theft?” And he answers: ἢ ὅτι ἐν μὲν ταῖς οἰκίαις, φυλάξαι (“Or is it because, in houses, [it is possible] to guard …”), etc.; that is: “Is it because in houses we can guard property more effectively? For there is both a strong wall and a key, and all the members of the household take care that domestic possessions are kept safe. But in baths and other public places it is easy for anyone to perpetrate the crime, for the person who has put down his belongings has nothing adequate for guarding them except his eyes. Thus an opportunity for theft is afforded even if he turns his gaze aside for a moment. Therefore the legislator, judging that people could not adequately guard their own property, imposed a law containing the severest threat: no one who committed theft in public places would be allowed to live.” [Col. 0497D] He then continues: ἔτι δὲ εἰς μὲν τὴν οἰκίαν (“Furthermore, into the house …”), etc.; that is: “Likewise, in a house it rests with the owner himself whom he wishes to admit and against whom, as less trustworthy, he wishes to take precautions. But one who has put something down in the baths is not permitted to prevent anyone either from entering or, once inside, from laying down his garment there with the intention of stealing; rather, [Col. 0498A] as each pleases, the cloaks of those who will steal and of those who will suffer loss lie promiscuously in the same place.” Hence he rightly concludes that the penalty restraining thieving hands in that [Col. 0498B] place must be extremely severe. HAV.]—is that same person also enrolled as a Christian? Or when Christians are brought forward under their own designation, [Col. 0497A] who among them is also such a person as so many criminals? Your people always keep the prison seething [Note: [Col. 0498B] “The prison always seethes.” Our Minucius, p. 40: “In short, the prison always seethes with people from your number.” Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, chapter I: “The prison is indeed the Devil’s house, in which he keeps his household.” And in the same work, chapter II, he says “breathes out,” corresponding to “seethes” here: “There it breathes out sorrow, but you are a sweet fragrance.” Note here the carefully chosen words in each instance and the author’s very great care. HAV.]; your people always make the mines groan [Note: [Col. 0498B] “The mines groan.” He speaks with great exactness, for that labor is severe, and frequent sighs are drawn there through exhaustion. This punishment is described by Plautus, *The Little Carthaginian* IV.ii.8, *The Captives* III.v.65, and especially V.iv.1:

> I have often seen many torments depicted  
> As taking place in Acheron; but in truth no Acheron equals  
> The place where I was, in the stone quarries. There, yes there, is truly the place  
> Where weariness must be driven from the body by every kind of toil.

[Col. 0498C] Thus Lucretius also makes farmers exhausted by hard labor sigh; these are his verses, book II, 1163:

> And now the aged ploughman, shaking his head, sighs  
> Ever more frequently that his great labor has fallen fruitlessly.

HAV.]; your people always fatten the beasts [Note: [Col. 0498C] “The beasts are fattened.” In place of *always*, the Fulda manuscript wrongly has *also*. He speaks of those who, because of their crimes, were either thrown to beasts or ordered to fight with them. The extraordinary cruelty and inhumanity of Caligula is noted by Suetonius, book IV, chapter 27: “When livestock for fattening the wild beasts prepared for a show was becoming too expensive, he designated condemned criminals to be butchered.” But Christians too were condemned to the mines and thrown to beasts. I answer: not always, for they rather frequently enjoyed peace under the emperors. Nor were they cast to the beasts under the same indictment as assassins, cutpurses, and the like. HAV.]; from your people the providers of public shows always feed their herds of criminals [Note: [Col. 0498C] “From your people the providers of public shows always feed their herds of criminals.” “From your people,” whom he called sacrilegious above. Hence Quintilian in *The Gladiator*: “I lingered among sacrilegious men, incendiaries, and murderers—the one glory gladiators possess.” He said “herds” because the madness of those who sponsored the games sometimes produced several thousand pairs. Particularly useful for illustrating this passage are the words of Plutarch in his *Crassus*, where he relates that the gladiator Spartacus, who raised that exceedingly grave war against the Romans, broke out of Lentulus’s gladiatorial school with his companions. His words are: Λέντυλου τινος Βατιάτου μονομάχους ἐν Καπυῃ τρέφοντος (“When a certain Lentulus Batiatus was maintaining gladiators at Capua …”), etc.; that is: “A certain Lentulus, surnamed Batiatus, maintained a large household of gladiators at Capua. Most of them originated from Galatia and Thrace and had been compelled to practice the gladiatorial profession, not because of any crime they themselves had committed, but solely through the buyer’s impiety.” HAV.]. No one there is a Christian unless he is this alone [Note: [Col. 0497A] “Unless he is a Christian and absolutely nothing more.” Fran., Paris.], or, if he is something else as well, he is now no Christian [Note: [Col. 0498D] “Now no Christian.” Thus Aldus, the Fulda and Agobard manuscripts, and Rigaltius. Others transpose the words to “not now.” Below, chapter XLVI: “But someone will say that even some of our own people depart from the rule of discipline: they then cease to be regarded among us as Christians.” Minucius, p. 40: “There is [Col. 0499B] no Christian there, unless he is either accused on account of his religion or a fugitive.” [Col. 0499C] It should be written with a hyphen, as in chapter II, “a Christian-again”; likewise “a Christian-only.” HAV.].

## CHAPTER XLV

The innocence of Christians proceeds not from fear of man [Col. 0498A] but from reverence for God. By his instruction they have received the most perfect laws and learned to forestall every evil at its very origin, reserving themselves holy and inviolate for God as judge.

45. We, therefore, alone are innocent. What wonder, if we must be? Indeed, we must be. Having been taught innocence by God, we both know it perfectly, as revealed by a perfect teacher, and guard it faithfully, as [Note: [Col. 0497A] Thus the Agobard manuscript, Pamelius, Junius, Rigaltius, and Havercamp. But the Fulda manuscript reads: “enjoined by God, a teacher who cannot be scorned.” Barraeus: “entrusted by [Col. 0498A] a steward who cannot be adorned.” Aldus: “as something entrusted by an inconceivable steward.” Rhenanus and Heraldus: “entrusted by a steward who cannot be scorned.”] entrusted by an inspector who cannot be scorned. But human judgment [Note: [Col. 0499B] The Fulda manuscript reads “human teaching”; in the following passage Rhenanus and Aldus read “human condemnation.”] has handed innocence down to you, and human dominion has likewise commanded it; consequently, your system of discipline is neither complete nor sufficiently formidable to attain the truth of innocence. How great is human wisdom for demonstrating what is truly good [Note: [Col. 0499B] “Such is the wisdom of man for demonstrating what is truly good.” Fran., Paris.]? How great is human authority for exacting it? The former is as liable to error as the latter is to contempt. And so, which command is more comprehensive: “You shall not kill,” or “You shall not even be angry”? Which is more perfect: to forbid adultery, or to restrain even the solitary lust of the eyes? Which is more refined [Note: [Col. 0499C] “Which is more refined?” A person is not sufficiently trained in virtue if only wrongdoing is forbidden him, unless evil speaking is forbidden as well. More clearly: one who merely abstains from wrongdoing will still be untrained in virtue, for he must also abstain from evil speaking. Understand the following statements similarly: for a person to be instructed in virtue, he must abstain not only from injury, but even from the shadow of injury and from everything that entails a return of injury. LAC.]: to forbid wrongdoing, or evil speaking as well? Which is more fully instructive: not to permit injury, or not even to allow injury to be repaid in kind [Note: [Col. 0499C] “Or not even injury in return.” That is, not to inflict an injury, but also not to repay one. Thus in book II *Against Marcion*: “God prohibits retaliation”; and in book IV: “Christ restrains even retaliation for an injury.” RIG.—“To allow injury in return.” He uses this expression most elegantly for “to repay an injury.” Virgil, *Aeneid* II, verse 432:

> I call you to witness that, when you fell, I did not shun the weapons  
> Or any reprisals of the Greeks.

[Col. 0499D] Here Servius talks nonsense. For the “reprisals” that he swears he did not avoid are not alternations in the fighting, as Servius explains, but wounds and slaughter: just as he himself had inflicted these on the Greeks, so, if it had been his fate to fall, he had not refused to suffer them himself in battle. HAV.]? Provided, however, that you know that your own laws, which appear to advance toward innocence, borrowed their pattern from the divine law as the more ancient [Col. 0499B] law [Note: [Col. 0499B] “As almost the more ancient.” Aldus reads “as the more ancient pattern”; Rhenanus, “from the pattern of the more ancient”; Fran., “as more ancient patterns”; the Leiden manuscript, “as more ancient forms.”]. We have already spoken of the age of Moses. But how great is the authority of human laws, when it may befall a man both [Note: [Col. 0500B] Fran. reads “even if he may escape them”; Junius, “even escape them.”] to escape them and, in most offenses, to remain concealed [Note: [Col. 0500B] Fran. reads “he might remain concealed”; Semler, “for one remaining concealed.”], and sometimes to despise them because of the intention [Note: [Col. 0500B] “Through involuntariness.” Semler.] or necessity of offending [Note: [Col. 0499C] “To despise them because of the involuntary nature or necessity of the offense.” I follow Rigaltius and explain that human laws, in comparison with divine laws, possess no authority. This is shown in three ways: first, because it is often possible to escape punishment; second, because the law frequently does not see the offender, and therefore his crime remains hidden; third, because their force is sometimes despised when an involuntary sin is alleged as a pretext for an act to which people were driven by force and necessity. With divine laws the matter is far otherwise. To these three points he will now add a fourth: the brevity of punishment and thus the fact that death need not be so greatly feared, whereas under divine laws punishment extends through immeasurable eternity. Add Rigaltius, who illustrates this with examples. HAV.—“For one offending through involuntariness or necessity.” [Col. 0500B] “Involuntariness,” that is, accident. Marcianus provides an example of such an offense in law XI, *On Punishments*: when a weapon cast at a wild beast during a hunt killed a man; “necessity,” when one could not otherwise protect one’s own life. Let us suppose, then, that Sempronius cast a weapon at a wild beast while hunting, and with that weapon killed not the beast but an enemy who happened to be passing by. Sempronius will rejoice at his fortunate error, because by that accident he took his enemy’s life with impunity. Yet it was with impunity before Caesar, not before Christ. For by his approval or ratification he made voluntary the blow that was involuntary in its origin and purpose. The same must be said if Titius killed a madman who had named him heir in his will before going mad and who attacked him when Titius could not otherwise protect his own life. He will rejoice inwardly that he has deprived the testator of the power to change his will during lucid intervals; and by that joy, before Christ, he willingly killed the man whom, before Caesar, he appears to have killed unwillingly and under compulsion of necessity, since Christ’s discernment is far more powerful and perfect than Caesar’s. RIG.], when account is also taken [Note: [Col. 0500B] Semler adds “of.”] of the brevity of any punishment whatsoever, which will not continue beyond death? Thus [Col. 0500A] Epicurus too [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Thus Epicurus too.” Lucretius, describing his doctrine in most brilliant verses, enlarged and multiplied his error by the greatness of his own genius, especially in book III, which must be read cautiously and with the mind forearmed. There:

> We may know that there is nothing for us to fear in death,  
> That one who does not exist cannot become wretched, and that it makes not the slightest  
> Difference whether he had never at any time been born,  
> Once immortal death has taken away his mortal life.

HAV.] depreciates every torment [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Depreciates torment and pain.” This word does not savor of Golden Latin; it appears to have been adopted from Tertullian’s usage and manner. He uses it again in book IV *Against Marcion*. Sidonius Apollinaris also used it in *Bargus*: “Their pigments, depreciated, disfigure the figures”; likewise in letter 10 of book II, and Symmachus, letter 41 of book VIII. LE PR.] and pain, declaring a slight pain contemptible and a great one of no long duration. But we, who are examined under God, the observer of all things, and who foresee eternal punishment from him, rightly take precautions for innocence—we alone—both because of the fullness of his knowledge, the difficulty of finding concealment, and the magnitude of the torment, which is not of long duration but everlasting. We fear him whom even the man who judges those who fear will himself have to fear: we fear God, not the proconsul.

## CHAPTER XLVI

He next meets those who suppose that Christians do not derive their wisdom from God but regard their faith and hope as a kind of philosophy, weighing in each the same classes of virtues. He shows them how far the name “philosopher” sinks below “Christian,” since philosophers are found to be ignorant of the truth and guilty of every crime, whereas Christians understand God and, to the amazement even of their enemies, are as far removed as possible from every kind of wickedness.

46. We have taken our stand [Note: [Col. 0500D] “We have taken our stand, I think.” The expression is drawn from military practice, where men, standing firm, defended the position they had occupied. [Col. 0501B] Thus above, at chapter IV, we noted that our author frequently uses formulas derived from that source, and there we explained the use of this verb. Barraeus and the Leiden manuscript read “we have established.” I do not approve; rather, with the Fulda manuscript and the rest, I write “we have taken our stand.” Akin to this is the statement in *On the Shows*, chapter XIII: “We have sufficiently completed, I think, our orderly account of which people, and in what ways,” etc. HAV.], I think, against the allegation [Note: [Col. 0500B] Semler reads “threatened allegation.”] of every crime, an allegation that demands the blood of Christians. We have demonstrated our whole position and [Col. 0501A] the ways in which we can prove that it is as we have shown: namely, from the trustworthiness and antiquity of the divine writings, and likewise from the confession of spiritual [Note: [Col. 0501A] Rigaltius reads “spiritual.”] powers. Who will dare to refute us [Note: [Col. 0501A] The Fulda manuscript and Havercamp read “Let someone come forward who will dare to refute us.”], not through verbal artifice, but by the same method by which we have established our proof concerning the truth? [Note: [Col. 0501A] The Fulda manuscript and Havercamp read: “Let someone come forward who will dare to refute us”; [Col. 0501B] Rigaltius approved the reading “he will not dare to resist the truth,” with the word “let someone come forward” removed. In the following passage the same editor deleted the words *dum u. m. v. nostra*.] But while our truth is being made manifest to each person, unbelief meanwhile, though forced to acknowledge the goodness of this sect—which has already become known through practical experience [Note: [Col. 0502A] Rigaltius reads “already through experience.”] and intercourse—does not, of course, consider it a divine institution, but rather a kind of philosophy. “The philosophers,” it says, “advise and profess the same things: innocence, justice, patience, sobriety, chastity. Why [Col. 0502A], then, since we are compared with them in respect of discipline, are we not likewise placed on an equal footing with them in respect of freedom and immunity for that discipline? Or why are they, as our equals, not also compelled to perform duties whose omission places us in danger [Note: [Col. 0502A] The Fulda manuscript reads: “Why are we not therefore placed on an equal footing in diligence and immunity of discipline? Or why are they, our equals, not compelled,” [Col. 0502B] etc.]? For who compels a philosopher to sacrifice, or to swear an oath, or to display useless lamps at midday [Note: [Col. 0501B] “Useless lamps at midday.” He looks back to what he said in chapter XXXV: “Nor do we encroach upon the daylight with lamps,” lest anyone suppose that the deed of Diogenes is meant, concerning which see *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 1: “For that little dog Diogenes sought to find a man by carrying a lamp about at midday.” HAV.]? [Note: [Col. 0502B] Fran., Paris read “to bring forth.”] On the contrary, they openly demolish your gods [Note: [Col. 0501B] “They openly demolish your gods.” Lucian aims at this in all his works, but especially [Col. 0501C] in *Zeus Tragoedus*. Yet he is composed wholly of mockery. But what of the ancient philosophers? Cicero says of Speusippus in book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “He held that there was a certain force by which all things are governed, and that it was animate,” wishing to tear from people’s minds the knowledge of the gods. But what Cicero himself thought of his gods is especially clear from his censor Lactantius. In book II of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 3, he writes: “Cicero understood that the things worshiped by men were false. For although he had said many things capable of overthrowing religions, he nevertheless says that they ought not to be discussed before the general public, lest such a discussion extinguish the religions publicly adopted.” HAV.], and even denounce your superstitions in treatises that you applaud. Very many also bark against rulers [Note: [Col. 0501C] “They bark against rulers.” The Cynics in particular considered this a matter of glory. The Cynic Isidorus rebuked Nero in a loud voice as he passed by because, as Suetonius relates in book VI, he sang well of Nauplius’s misfortunes but managed his own good fortune badly. Aristotle had once warned Callisthenes, whose tongue was too free, of his fate, as Laertius reports:

Restoration notes: S000828/E008 contains the uncertain recovered spelling “προϛεἰναῖ.”; S000833/E013 contains the uncertain recovered spelling “ἀσπαϛικὸν.”; S000851/E031 contains the uncertain recovered initial spelling “Κοὶ.”; S000858/E038 contains apparently corrupt or uncertain characters in “ἱὰς” and “Ἀϛρολόγων”; they have been preserved verbatim.; S000858/E038 contains the apparently corrupt or uncertain reading “ἱὰς”; the character “ϛ” in “Ἀϛρολόγων” has also been preserved verbatim.  

Ὠκύμορος δή μοι τέκος ἔσσεαι, οἷ ἀγορεύεις. [Col. 0501D] That is: “When you speak such things to me, my son, I fear you may not long survive.” Nor did Anaxarchus’s harsh temper go unpunished. After Alexander had received him at a splendid banquet and asked him about the dinner, he is said to have replied: Πάντα πολυτελῶς. ἔδει δὲ λοιπόν κεφαλὴν σατράπου τινὸς παρατεθεῖσθαι. ἁποῤῥίπτων πρὸς τὸν Νικοκρέοντα. That is: “Everything was magnificent; but the head of some satrap ought now to be added”—as he looked toward Nicocreon. Easily foremost among all these was Diogenes, who, when a tyrant asked him what sort of bronze would be best for casting his statue, dared to answer: “The kind from which Harmodius and Aristogiton were cast.” These men, of course, were tyrannicides and were honored with statues for that reason. Hence he is called “the little bitch” by Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 1.

Some admired the remark he addressed to Alexander as an expression of freedom, but others rightly deride it, and Chrysostom censures it in his book *Against the Gentiles*, or *On Saint Babylas*. His words are:

“You will say, ‘But the philosopher displayed great freedom of speech before the king.’ Let us therefore see what that excellent freedom was, and whether it too is [Col. 0502B] emptier than the tricks of his barrel. What, then, was it? When the Macedonian was setting out with his army against the Persians and earnestly urged the philosopher to tell him whether he needed anything, he replied, ‘Nothing,’ except that he asked the king not to stand between him and the sun; for it happened at that moment that the philosopher was warming himself in the sun’s rays.”

He therefore attacks this folly as follows:

“Will you not here be overwhelmed with shame? Will you not cover your eyes and face? Will you not depart from here and bury yourselves in the earth—you who take pride in precisely those things of which you ought to be ashamed? How much better it would have been for him to take some clothing, moderately thick, and proceed to some useful work, and also to ask the king for something that would be of use, than to sit dressed in a torn cloak, warming himself in the sun’s rays [Col. 0502C] like tiny nursing infants, whom their nurses, after bathing and anointing them, place in the very spot where the philosopher was then sitting, begging the favor of a wretched old woman.”

To this point pertains the wise counsel of Elihu in Job 34:18: “Would anyone say to a king, ‘You are Belial,’ and to princes, ‘You are ungodly’?” Indeed, οὐ πολλῆς τῆς πραγματείας δεῖ τριβώνιον, etc.; that is: “For it is no great undertaking to put on a threadbare garment, hang a wallet from one’s neck, carry a staff in one’s hand, and shout—or rather, bray or bark—and curse everyone,” as Lucian says in *The Runaways*. A little later in the same work he says of these same dogs: Οἱ τὸ μὲν χρήσιμον, etc.; that is:

“But what is best by nature in dogs—such as vigilance, love for their master, and memory—they do not imitate at all. Instead, they diligently practice barking, gluttony, robbery, lust, flattery, wheedling, and attendance at tables.”

To them applies the Homeric phrase cited there, παρῳδεῖ: “For these are the laws by which they swear.”

The same Lucian says in *The Auction of Lives*: Α δὲ μάλιστα δεῖ προϛεἰναῖ, ταῦτά εστιν [The recovered spelling “προϛεἰναῖ” is uncertain.], etc.; that is:

“Above all, you must possess the following qualities: you must be shameless [Col. 0502D] and bold, and abuse everyone indiscriminately, kings and private persons alike. In this way everyone will turn his eyes upon you and suppose you courageous. You should also have a barbarous voice and a discordant sound, one that appears wholly like a dog’s.”

See what follows there. HAV.]

—while you endure them. And they are rewarded with statues and salaries more readily than they are sentenced to the beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0502B] *Salutariis*, Franequer edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0502D] “With statues and salaries.” Aldus, Rhenanus, Heraldus, Junius, the Codex Agobardinus, La Cerda, and Rigaltius read thus. Those salaries were indeed sufficiently generous, as may be gathered from Lucian. In *The Eunuch* he says: Συντέτακται μὲν, ὦ Πάμφιλε, ὡς οἶσθα, ἐκ βασιλέως μισθοφορά τις, etc. In Latin these words mean:

“You know, Pamphilus, that a salary—and by no means a small one—was established by the emperor for each class of philosophers: namely, for the Stoics, Platonists, and Epicureans, and along with these also for the Peripatetics, so that the compensation was equal for each sect. When any one of them dies, however, someone else must be appointed in his place, approved by the votes of the leading men. Moreover, that compensation was neither a trifling thing, as the poet says, [Col. 0503A] nor a matter of sport, but ten thousand pieces of money each year, which they receive to teach the young.”

A little later in the same work: καὶ πρέποντα ταῖς μυρίαις, ἃς χρὴ παρὰ βασιλέως ἀποφέρεσθαι, that is, “and that he should not appear unworthy of those ten [Col. 0503B] thousand drachmas which were to be received from the emperor.”

The Leiden manuscript, however, reads *solariis*, a reading which, La Cerda testifies, had already occurred to Lipsius; he explains it as referring to taxes levied on buildings erected upon public ground. In this sense it is related in Eunapius of Sardis, in his life of Prohaeresius, that the emperor Julian assigned taxable and tribute-paying lands to learned men so that they might be exempt from burdens. “Ἓμέτρει μὲν,” he says, “γὰρ ὁ Βασιλεὺς τὴν γῆν τοῖς Έλλησιν εἰς τὸν φόρον, ὅπως βαρύνοιντο.” But how can philosophers be said to be rewarded with *solaria*, that is, with taxes or ground rent, when they are freed from the necessity of paying them? For I think that is what La Cerda means.

I therefore explain *solaria* as those sunny places where wealthier persons warmed themselves and, after being anointed, dried themselves in the sun. They adorned such places with statues, and thus he rightly joins *solaria* with statues. One might also read *larariis*. Capitolinus says in *Antoninus the Philosopher*: “He showed so much honor to his teachers that he kept golden images of them in his household shrine.” Lampridius says of Alexander Severus: [Col. 0503C] “In his household shrine, in which he kept the deified emperors—though only the best of them, chosen out—and holier souls, among whom were Apollonius and, according to what a writer of his own times says, Christ, Abraham, Orpheus, and gods of that sort, as well as portraits of his ancestors.”

Men of princely rank evidently had two household shrines: the first containing deified persons, and the second learned and great men. The same writer says a little later in the same place: “He called Virgil the Plato of poets, and kept his image together with a likeness of Cicero in his second household shrine, where he also kept Achilles and other great men. But Alexander the Great he consecrated among the Deified and the Best in the greater household shrine.” Among all the prodigies that preceded Tacitus’s death, Vopiscus says in his *Florianus*: “In the household shrine all the gods fell down, whether because of an earthquake or some other accident.”

Pamelius reads *salutariis*, beside which Scaliger wrote ἀσπαϛικὸν (“greeting” or “salutatory”; recovered spelling uncertain). Our author below, in the final chapter, says: “And yet you cast statues for all of them, engrave inscriptions upon images, and incise titles.”]

But deservedly so: for the philosophers are not [Col. 0503A] called Christians. The name “philosophers” does not put demons to flight. Why should it, when philosophers rank demons immediately after the gods?

[Note: [Col. 0503A] *Deputant*, Franequer edition.]

Socrates’ expression is, “If the demon permits.” Even when he showed some perception of the truth by denying that the gods existed, he nevertheless ordered, at the very end, that a cock be sacrificed to Aesculapius.

[Note: [Col. 0503C] “He nevertheless ordered, at the very end, that a cock be sacrificed to Aesculapius.” Did that jewel published by my teacher Jacobus Gronovius, volume II of the *Gorlaean Dactyliotheca*, no. 229, intend to teach us this? There an old man—perhaps Socrates himself, for the forehead is sufficiently bald—sacrifices a cock upon an altar. Add *Thesaurus Palatinus*, no. 202. Something involving cocks and a Socratic face is also frequently found upon the Abraxas gems collected by Chifflet and inserted by Gronovius among the Gorlaean gems. Compare volume II, nos. 316–317.

Aesculapius appears in Choul with remarkable ornamentation: besides the serpent wound around his staff, the god may be seen wearing a radiant crown, as the son of Apollo; the little image held in his left hand is his daughter Hygieia, while the cock at his feet, in marvelous agreement with the Gorlaean design, illustrates this passage of our Tertullian.]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] “He ordered at the very end.” At the end of the *Phaedo*, Plato relates the following about Socrates after he had drunk the poison: καὶ ἐκκαλυψάμενος, ἐνεκεκάλυπτο γὰρ, εἶπεν· ὃ δὴ τελευταῖον ἐφθἑγξατο· ὧ Κρίτων, ἔφη, τῷ Ἀσκληπίῳ ὀφείλομεν ἀλεκτρυόνα· ἀλλὰ ἀπόδοτε, καὶ μὴ ἀμελήσατε; that is:

“And when he was already covered—for he had covered his head—he uttered his final words. ‘Crito,’ he said, ‘we owe a cock to Aesculapius. Pay it, and do not neglect it.’”

Hence Lucian says that he died without even paying Aesculapius the cock: ἔπιεν ἄθλιος τοῦ [Col. 0504B] κωνείου, μὴ δὲ τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα τῷ Ἀσκληπίῳ ἀποδεδωκώς, as his words run in *Twice Accused*. Theodoret investigates the reason for this saying in *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 109, and writes: ἐγὼ δὲ οἶμαι καὶ Σωκράτην, etc.; that is:

“I think that Socrates, the son of Sophroniscus, ordered a cock to be sacrificed in order to refute the charge brought against him, since Anytus and Meletus had accused him of denying the existence of the gods.”

Tertullian ridicules this and other things concerning Socrates in *On the Soul*, chapter 1:

“But if Socrates was therefore the wisest of men according also to the testimony of the Pythian demon—which was, of course, rendering a service to its own associate—how much worthier is the assertion of Christian steadfastness and wisdom, before whose inspiration the entire power of demons yields? This wisdom, from the school of heaven, is freer in denying the gods of this age: it does not betray its principles by ordering any cock to be rendered to Aesculapius; it does not introduce new demons, but drives out the old; it does not corrupt the young, but trains them in every good form of modesty. Consequently, for the name of truth it endures the unjust sentence not merely of one city but of the whole world—a truth whose achievement is, indeed, the more arduous in proportion as it is fuller. Thus it does not swallow death from a cup under the appearance of pleasure, but drains it from the gibbet and the living pyre through every device of cruelty. Meanwhile, in this darker prison of the world, among its own Cebeses and Phaedos, if anything concerning the soul must be examined, it directs the inquiry according to the rules of God.”

He also touches upon the cock in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 10: “For I too sacrifice a cock to myself, no less than Socrates did to Aesculapius.”

Theodoret is seriously mistaken when he investigates the reason for the Socratic cock as though it were to be sacrificed to Apollo. For our Tertullian, who was in a position to know, adapted it to his own argument. Those who had recovered from illness customarily sacrificed a cock or chicken to Aesculapius, as is apparent from the engraving on the Gorlaean gem. This is also why a cock is added to him among the other ornaments in Choul’s very remarkable representation, which Sextus Pompeius Festus describes as follows under the word “Island”:

“A temple was built to Aesculapius on the island because the sick are sustained by physicians chiefly with water. [Col. 0504D] Serpents are under his guardianship because that creature is exceedingly vigilant, a quality especially suitable for guarding a sick person’s health. Dogs are employed in his temple because he was nourished at a bitch’s teats. He carries a knotted staff because it signifies the difficulty of the art. He is crowned with laurel because that tree furnishes a very great number of remedies. Chickens are sacrificed here.”

The reason Socrates wished a cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius is therefore clear: he had now recovered and was about to depart from this frail and diseased existence for a better life—punished in the judgment of his enemies, but brought to completion in his own. Valerius Maximus speaks elegantly in the same way of Theramenes, book III, chapter 2. HAV.]

I believe this was done in honor of his father, because Apollo had proclaimed Socrates the wisest [Col. 0504A] of all men. O thoughtless Apollo! He bore witness to the wisdom of a man who denied that the gods existed.

To the degree that truth is fiercely hated, the man who presents it sincerely gives offense; but one who falsifies it and merely affects it wins favor under that very name among the persecutors of truth—since even its mockers and despisers—

[Note: [Col. 0503A] *Odio*, Franequer and Paris editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0503A] Rigaltius theatrically deleted the words enclosed in parentheses and those following. The [Col. 0504A] Lyon manuscript reads *quam inclusores et corruptores*; another reading is *qua illusores et corruptores*.]

—theatrically affect the truth, [Col. 0507A] and by affecting it corrupt it, since they seek glory.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] “Theatrically.” The Fulda manuscript incorrectly reads *inimici*; the Codex Agobardinus, *inimicae*. In the Leiden manuscript the copyist was unable to make it out, writing only the letter M and leaving a blank space.

Philo Judaeus censures such people in his book *That the Worse Is Wont to Attack the Better*, in these words: Πεφύκασι δὲ οἱ σοφισταὶ πολεμίοις χρῆσθαι ταῖς ἐν αὐτοῖς δυνάμεσι, etc.; that is:

“For nearly all sophists are accustomed to have their own faculties set at variance with one another, since their words oppose their thoughts and their counsels oppose their words, without any agreement between them. By their discourses they charm our ears with accounts of how social a thing justice is, how greatly temperance benefits everyone, how highly courage is approved, how immense a profit is derived from piety, and how salutary the other virtues are. Conversely, they say that injustice is a turbulent thing, intemperance disease-producing, impiety abominable, and all other wickedness ruinous. Yet they do not cease to think contrary to their own words. After singing the praises of prudence, temperance, justice, and piety, they then display the greatest folly and wantonness and behave unjustly and impiously; in a word, they are discovered to confound and subvert every divine and human law.”

Our author therefore aptly says that philosophers act a mime, since they appear to be one thing outwardly while being another within, and thus sometimes become ridiculous when their vices are exposed. Apply to them Lucian’s statement in *The Cock*: Εἶτ` ἐπειδὰν πέσωσιν, ὅμοιοι μάλιστα φαίνονται τοῖς τραγικοῖς ὑποκρίταις, etc.; [Col. 0505B] that is:

“When they fall down, they appear very like tragic actors. For many, as may be seen, while they are playing Cecropses, Sisyphuses, or Telephuses, wear diadems, swords with ivory hilts, streaming hair, and cloaks interwoven with gold. But if one of them—as frequently happens—stumbles and falls in the middle of the stage, he certainly provokes laughter among the spectators: his mask is crushed together with the diadem itself, while the actor’s real head is bloodied and his legs are largely exposed, so that one can now see how wretched are the cloths of his undergarment and how grotesque the buskins he has put upon his feet, since they do not fit the size of the foot.”

Lucian frequently and wittily ridicules the same thing in the *Dialogues of the Dead*, in the dialogue of Charon and Mercury. There, once the theatrical disguise has been laid aside, everything about the philosopher appears ridiculous. But let us hear Lucian himself. Mercury says to that little-bearded fellow: Κατάθου σὺ τὸ σχῆμα πρῶτον εἶτα καὶ ταυτὶ πάντα. Ὦ Ζεῦ, ὅσην μὲν τὴν ἀλαζονείαν κομίζει, ὅσην δὲ ἀμαθίαν, καὶ ἔριν, καὶ κενοδοξίαν, etc.; [Col. 0505C] that is:

“First put off this costume, and then all these things too. O Jupiter, what arrogance he carries, what ignorance, what a mass of contentiousness and empty glory, how many dubious questions, thorny disputes, and tangled thoughts! Indeed, how many futile labors, no small number of delusions, how much nonsense and inquisitiveness! But, by Jupiter, he also carries this gold with him, as well as pleasure, shamelessness, anger, luxury, and softness; for these do not escape my notice, although you carefully conceal them. Cast away your lies too, and your pride, and that opinion by which you suppose yourself superior to everyone else. For if you board with all these things, what five-banked galley could hold you?”

After these have been cut away, his beard trimmed, and his eyebrow shaved, flattery is also removed: Ἓν ἔτι τὸ βαρύτατον ὑπὸ μάλης ἔχει. Τί, ὧ Μένιππε; Κολακείαν ὦ Ἑρμὴ, πολλὰ ἐν τῷ βιῳ χρησιμεύσασαν αὐτῷ; that is:

“He still carries one very heavy thing under his arms.

“Mercury: What, Menippus?

“Menippus: Flattery, Mercury, which was of great use to him while he lived.”

A little later, when the same philosopher, weeping childishly, is asked the reason and answers that he weeps because he had believed the soul immortal, Menippus mocks him, says that he is lying, and presents the true causes of his grief, namely: ὅτι μηκέτι δειπνήσει πολυτελῆ δεῖπνα, etc.; that is:

“Because he will no longer have such sumptuous dinners; nor will he go out at night, secretly wrapping his little cloak around his head so that no one sees him, and visit all the prostitutes in succession; nor in the morning will he deceive young men with his wisdom and receive money from them. These are the things that grieve him.”

Lucian also describes their conduct in *Twice Accused*, p. 228: Ἑώρα γὰρ οἶμαι, etc.; that is:

“For she saw, I suppose, that those who habitually say much about enduring and bearing hardships privately cultivate pleasure; that they boast like young men to this extent, but at home live in accordance with the precepts of pleasure; and that they are ashamed if they are caught relaxing their firmness in any respect and betraying their profession.”

Likewise in *The Runaways*: Ἃ μὲν [Col. 0506A] γὰρ ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις, δρῶσι, etc.; that is:

“It would take a long time to recount what they do at banquets and how they become drunk. And they do these things—just imagine!—while they themselves denounce drunkenness, adultery, luxury, and greed. You will therefore find nothing more mutually contradictory than their words and deeds.”

He adds: Οἷον κολακείαν μίσειν φασί, etc.; that is:

“For example, they say that flattery is hateful to them, although they could surpass Gnathonides and Struthias in it; and they exhort others to speak the truth, although they themselves cannot even move their tongues without lying. In words they all hate pleasure, and Epicurus is their enemy; but in practice they will do anything for its sake. Moreover, in the vehemence of their anger, their agitation over the slightest matters, and their readiness to become enraged, they surpass newborn infants. They therefore provoke no little laughter among the spectators when their bile boils up for any reason whatever and they are seen turning livid, displaying in their appearance shamelessness and impotence of mind. Their mouths are filled with foam—or rather, with venom.”

I think τὸν Στρυθίαν (“Struthias,” masculine accusative) should be restored: both were present, not the woman. He continues—for this too is exceedingly ridiculous—as follows: Μὴ σύγε ἐκεῖθι τύχοις, etc.; that is:

“Do not be there when that foul flood is poured forth: ‘By Hercules, I do not wish to possess gold or silver. An obol is enough for me to buy lupines, while a spring or stream will provide my drink.’ Yet a little later they demand not obols or a few drachmas, but entire fortunes, so that a merchant might be loaded with as great a burden as philosophy brings them in profit. Then, after they have scraped together enough to satisfy themselves and secured their livelihood, they cast aside that wretched little cloak and sometimes buy estates, soft garments, long-haired boys, and entire houses, bidding a long farewell to Crates’ wallet, Antisthenes’ cloak, and Diogenes’ barrel.”

He also describes the same men excellently in the *Necromancy*. Theodoret likewise sharply censures the life of Socrates in *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, p. 174, where among other things he says: Κοὶ ὁ Σωκράτης δὲ [The recovered initial spelling “Κοὶ” is uncertain.], etc.; that is:

“Socrates, too, does not command us to beware of every persuasion and enticement to the point that we should not eat when hungry or drink when thirsty; he does, however, command us wholly to avoid the kisses and glances of beautiful persons, since they infuse a venom worse than that of scorpions and venomous spiders. But these are mere words, lacking deeds and actions.”

For in the same place he shows that Socrates constantly frequented the gymnasia in order to feed his eyes upon a shameful spectacle, and that at drinking parties he remained awake through the night after the others had become exhausted, together with many additional details taken from ancient authors now lost, Aristoxenus and Porphyry.

There is also somewhere in Appian a very notable passage about philosophers to this effect, but at present it does not come to mind. In Laertius too, Diogenes rebuked those who praised the just because they despised money, yet strove to imitate the wealthy. Not even Marcus, that excellent emperor and philosopher, could entirely escape his detractors, who smeared him with a similar stain. Julius Capitolinus says: “They charged him with having been insincere and not so straightforward as he appeared, or as either Pius or Verus had been.”

Finally, Martial writes against a sodomite who pretended devotion to philosophy, [Col. 0506D] book IX, epigram 77:

> Of Democrituses, Zenos, and Platos past explaining,  
> Of all that bristles grimly in shaggy portraits,  
> You speak as though Pythagoras’ successor and heir;  
> No lesser beard hangs down from your chin.  
> But—what is shameful even in the hairy, and too late for goatish men—  
> You gladly take something stiff in your soft buttocks.  
> You who know the grounds and weight of every sect,  
> Tell me, Pannychus: what school teaches being circumcised?

Thus the old saying is entirely true: the man who advances in learning but declines in morals declines more than he advances. In Lucian’s *Lapiths*, after the philosophers’ ridiculous fight, the man who speaks as follows rightly concludes: Ἐν ὅσῳ δὲ ταῦτα ἐγίνετο, etc.; that is:

“While this was taking place, Philo, I turned various thoughts over in my mind. One conclusion was readily at hand: there is no value in a man’s learning the disciplines unless he also adjusts the conduct of his life to what is best, since I saw how ridiculous in their actions those men made themselves who surpassed others in words.”

Such a man is Zeno, who in Laertius is publicly proclaimed by decree at Athens to be a true philosopher, since he was ἐπ` ἀρετὴν καὶ σωφροσύνην παρώρμα, πρὸς τὰ βέλτιστα παράδειγμα τὸν ἴδιον βίον ἐκθεὶς ἃπασιν: “a man who, because he strives toward the things that are best, presents his own life to everyone as a model consistent with his words and teaching.”

Eunapius relates in his preface that Porphyry and Sotion gathered from every source the history and lives [Col. 0507B] τῶν φιλοσόφων ἀνάγων “of those who had truly practiced philosophy.” Epictetus also deservedly condemns those philosophers who are ἄνευ τοῦ πράττειν, μέχρι τοῦ λέγειν, that is, “men of words alone, without deeds.” HAV.]

[Note: [Col. 0507B] “Since they seek glory.” Hence our author calls the philosopher “an animal of glory” in *On the Soul*, chapter 1; and in *On Repentance*, chapter 1: “The philosophers, indeed, who are regarded as creatures of some wisdom.” Others read, “of animal wisdom.”

But Plato described the wise man in book XI of the *Republic*: ἄνδρα ἁπλοῦν καὶ γενναῖον, κατ` Αἰσχύλον, οὐ δοκεῖν, ἀλλ` εἶναι ἀγαθὸν ἐθέλοντα, etc.; that is:
