“A straightforward and noble man who, as Aeschylus says, desires actually to be good, but by no means to appear so. For I think that the desire to appear good must be removed altogether. If he appears just to men, honors and gifts will pursue him. It will therefore remain uncertain whether he is such a man for the sake of rewards and dignities.”

Sallust thus describes Cato, who preferred to be good rather than to appear so: accordingly, the less he sought glory, the more he attained it. *Catiline*, chapter 54. Theodoret, however, maintains that this description can apply to no one better than the Christian. In *Cure of the Greek Maladies*, discourse XII, p. 170, after quoting those words of Plato, he adds: Καὶ ταῦτα δὲ ὡσαύτως, etc.; that is:

“These words apply especially to our athletes. For they do not perform their right actions and fight courageously in the manner of Antisthenes, Diogenes, and Crates, for the sake of empty glory, but with regard for moral goodness alone.” HAV.]

Christians necessarily seek the truth and present it without corruption, since they care for their salvation. Thus we are not equaled even in knowledge—

[Note: [Col. 0507A] *Conscientia* (“conscience”), Franequer and Paris editions.]

—or in discipline, as you suppose. [Col. 0508A] For what of that Thales, the foremost of the natural philosophers—

[Note: [Col. 0508B] “The foremost of the natural philosophers.” This encomium is bestowed upon him by the following verses, which Diogenes Laertius reports were inscribed upon his statue in the *Life of Thales*:

Τόν δε Θάλην Μίλητος ἱὰς θρέψας, ἀνέδειξεν


Ἀϛρολόγων πάντων πρεσβύτατον σοφία [The recovered “ἱὰς” is uncertain or corrupt; “ϛ” in “Ἀϛρολόγων” is retained as recovered.].

They translate them thus:

> This Thales, whom the Milesian land that nurtured him—]

Restoration notes: E033/S000891 is textually incomplete: the recovered Greek ends with καί τῶν. The incomplete ending is explicitly represented without supplying an unsupported noun.; E036/S000894 preserves only the recovered Greek initial Υ of an already identified corrupt name; the remainder cannot be reconstructed from the supplied source.; E036/S000894 preserves only the recovered Greek initial Υ of an already identified corrupt name; the remainder cannot be reconstructed from the supplied packets.  

She herself produced an astrologer of the first rank. He is there called the most ancient. Much is said about him [Col. 0508C] there, and in Herodotus and others. Cicero says of him, *Academic Questions*, book IV, chapter 118: “Thales, one of the Seven, to whom, they say, the other six yielded first place.” Thus Scaliger emends *consensisse primos*. HAV.] Did he give Croesus, when he questioned him about the divinity, any certain answer [Note: [Col. 0508C] **About the divinity, a definite answer.** How far, nevertheless, he was able to advance under nature’s guidance may be read in Laertius. There his opinion is: Πρεσβύτατον τῶν ὄντων, Θεός, ἀγέννητον γάρ. That is: “The most ancient of all things that exist is God, for he is ungenerated.” Stobaeus repeats this in precisely the same words, *Physical Eclogues*, book I, chapter I: Θάλης ἐρωτηθεὶς τί πρεσβύτατιν τῶν ὅντων, ἀπεκρίνατο, Θεὸς, ἀγέννητον γάρ, that is: “When Thales was asked what was the most ancient of all things, he answered, ‘God, for he is ungenerated.’” Likewise in Laertius, when asked τί τὸ Θεῖον, “What is God?” he answered: Τὸ μήτε ἀρχὴν ἔχον μήτε τελευτὴν, “That which lacks beginning and end.” What others maintained is evident from the example of Melissus, concerning whom Laertius and Hesychius write: ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ Θεῶν ἔλεγε, μὴ δεῖν ἀποφαίνεσθαι, μὴ γὰρ εἶναι γνῶσιν αὐτῶν. That is: “He said that nothing should be determined concerning the gods, [Col. 0508D] for there is no manifest knowledge of them.” HAV.] after repeatedly frustrating him with delays for deliberation? [Note: [Col. 0508D] **Time for deliberation.** Properly, among the Romans, *to request leave* meant to seek permission from the princeps or commander to depart from and remain absent from the city or army because of some necessary cause. Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter XXIX: “When a man of praetorian rank, from his retreat at Anticyra, which he had sought for the sake of his health, repeatedly requested that his leave be extended, Caligula ordered him killed and added: ‘Bloodletting is necessary for one whom hellebore has failed to benefit for so long.’” From this it was transferred to every kind of delay and postponement. HAV.] Any Christian artisan [Note: [Col. 0508D] **Any artisan.** Eunapius of Sardis, the admirer of the sophists, says almost the same of his Chrysanthius in his *Life*: Ὡς ἔδοξε κοινωνήσας καὶ τοῖς Θεοῖς τὸ ἔργον περιφανῶς, ὡς κᾂν ἰδιώτην καί βαναυσόν διακρῖναι τὰ σημεῖα, that is: “He appeared to communicate so manifestly with the gods that any uneducated, sedentary craftsman from among the common people could easily pass judgment upon prodigies.” HAV.] both discovers and [Note: [Col. 0508A] *We are equaled*, MS. Leiden.] [Col. 0509A] demonstrates God, and from this also establishes in actual fact everything that is sought in God [Note: [Col. 0509A] *From God*, Semler.], although Plato [Note: [Col. 0509A] **Although Plato declares.** In the *Timaeus*, p. 28 C, Stephanus edition: Τὸν μὲν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς, εὑρεῖν τε ἔργον, καὶ εὕροντα εἰς πάντας ἀδύνατον λέγειν, that is, in Chalcidius’s translation: “It is as difficult to discover the maker and father of the universe as it is, once he has been discovered, impossible to proclaim him worthily.” See the many testimonies in Elmenhorst, p. 44, on those words of Minucius, p. 21: “Accordingly, in the *Timaeus*, God is for Plato, by his very name, the parent of the world, the craftsman of the soul, and the maker of things heavenly and earthly; and Plato declares beforehand that it is both difficult to discover him, because of his exceedingly great and incredible power, and, once you have discovered him, impossible to speak of him publicly.” The Leiden codex reads: “also affirms it in actual fact, although Plato establishes,” etc. HAV.] declares that the maker of the universe is neither easy to discover nor, once discovered, easy to explain [Note: [Col. 0509B] **To explain to everyone.** A letter of Thales to Pherecydes survives in Laertius, in which he does not wish him to discuss this subject openly before everyone. It begins thus: Πυνθάνομαί σε πρῶτον Ἰώνων μέλλειν, etc.; that is: “I hear that you are preparing to be the first of the Ionians to discourse openly among the Greeks about divine matters. Yet perhaps you will more rightly read what you have written among friends than release it indiscriminately to anyone, when it will bring them no benefit.” Minucius likewise says of the Christians, after citing those words of Plato: “These things are almost the same as our own. For we both know God and call him the parent of all, and we never proclaim him publicly unless questioned.” This is to be understood in accordance with those words of the Savior, Matthew 7:6: Μὴ δότε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσὶ, μηδὲ βάλητε τοὺς μαργαρίτας ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθην τῶν χοίρων. From this also his resolute silence, both in Caiaphas’s court and in Pilate’s presence, should be elucidated: he answered them concerning his divinity and kingdom only when put under oath and duly questioned; Matthew 26:63 and 27:11, 14. HAV.] to everyone.

Moreover, if we challenge them concerning chastity [Note: [Col. 0509A] *If we are challenged*, Rhenanus, Rigaltius.] [Note: [Col. 0509C] **If we challenge them concerning chastity.** Since at the beginning of this chapter he had said that the philosophers both recommend and profess the same things—innocence, justice, patience, sobriety, and chastity—he now refutes them one by one, preserving the measured structure of his discourse when he says: “if we challenge them concerning chastity,” “if I make my defense concerning integrity,” “if I contend concerning modesty,” “if I engage concerning equanimity,” “if I make a comparison concerning good faith,” and finally “if I take my stand concerning sincerity.” Pamelius and others here read *provocemus*, “let us challenge,” but Rhenanus and Rigaltius emend it to *provocemur*, “let us be challenged,” which accords less well with the remaining clauses. It would be better to read *provocem*, “if I challenge.” But what is the philosophers’ continence like? Hear Lucian in *The Runaways*: [Col. 0509D] Οἱ δὲ μάλα σεμνοὶ, etc.; that is: “Although these men appear exceedingly chaste and severe outwardly and in public, if they obtain a handsome boy or a beautiful woman, or have any hope of doing so, it is better to remain silent about what they do. Some even corrupt and carry off the wives of their own hosts, like that Trojan Paris—because, I suppose, the women themselves desire to philosophize.” Hear also Chrysostom, *Oration on Saint Babylas*: “But the man of Sinope, you say, was temperate and lived a continent life, since he would not even endure lawful marriage. But add, I beg you, the manner of his temperance and continence. You, however, will certainly not add it, since you would more willingly deprive him of the praise of temperance than disclose the manner of his temperance, so infamous indeed and filled with profound disgrace was he. I might at this point run through the absurdities of the others as well, their foolish and empty pursuits, and finally their obscenity. For where, I ask, is it useful not to abstain from tasting human semen? This is what the Stagirite did. What advantage is there in intercourse with mothers and [Col. 0510A] sisters? Yet the philosopher who led the Stoa sanctioned this by law. I might also run through the head of the Academy and his disciple, and likewise demonstrate that those who inspire still greater admiration were more obscene than those whom I have named. I might strip bare the obscene love of boys, which they counted as part of honor and philosophy, by exposing every allegory—were it not both that our discourse would thereby become rather long while we are hastening on to other matters, and that the customs of all of them are more than sufficiently refuted when the custom of one has been exposed.” HAV.], I read part of the Attic judgment pronounced against Socrates as a corrupter of the young [Note: [Col. 0509A] On the authority of the Fulda codex, Rigaltius and Havercamp read: “Socrates is pronounced a corrupter of the young”; the others: “pronounced against Socrates as a corrupter of the young” [Col. 0510A], or “Socrates pronounced.”] [Note: [Col. 0510B] **He is pronounced a corrupter of the young.** This is the reading of the excellent Fulda codex, which Rigaltius adopted; for the others read less elegantly: “I read part of the Attic judgment pronounced against Socrates as a corrupter of the young.” The Leiden edition reads “Socrates pronounced.” Our author likewise says of Socrates in *On the Soul*, chapter 1: “corrupting youth”; and so the ancients commonly say. See Lucian in *The Auction of Lives* and *The Eunuch*, and also in the *Dialogues of the Courtesans*, Dialogue X; Theodoret, *Cure of the Greek Affections*, pp. 174–175. There were nevertheless some who absolved the philosopher of this charge and said that he loved the beautiful because, from the beauty of their limbs and countenance, he sought to discern virtue of soul and nobility of character. Nonnus also inclines to this view in his exposition of Gregory Nazianzen’s Oration XLVIII, the second against Julian. The gem in volume II of Gorlaeus’s *Dactyliotheca*, no. 314, pertains to this, as some believe. HAV.]. [Col. 0510A] A Christian does not alter even the female sex [Note: [Col. 0510A] “A Christian does not alter even a woman’s sex,” Fulda codex and the editions of Rigaltius and Havercamp.]. I know too of the courtesan Phryne, rutting in response to the ardor of Diogenes as he lay on top of her [Note: [Col. 0510A] *Passion*, Franeker, Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0510C] **Phryne, rutting in response to the ardor of Diogenes as he lay on top of her.** At a banquet, she accommodated the Cynic cynically. LAC.]. I hear also that a certain Speusippus of Plato’s school died in the act of adultery [Note: [Col. 0510C] **Died in the act of adultery.** This is false, if the surviving writers are to be trusted. Thus Joseph Scaliger writes to Eusebius, p. 125, that in this passage of Tertullian either there is a μνημονικὸν σφάλμα (“memory error”), or else, he says, the man who persuaded him of this was an impostor. For Speusippus died at a very advanced age ἐξ ἀθυμίας (“from despondency”). The death of others enumerated by Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chapter 13, was nevertheless not dissimilar: “Cornelius Gallus, a man of praetorian rank, and Titus Haterius, a Roman knight, died during intercourse.” And Valerius Maximus, book IX, chapter XII: “This man’s death was courageous, theirs utterly ridiculous. For Cornelius Gallus, a man of praetorian rank, and Titus Haterius, a Roman knight, expired during the act of love.” As is his custom, he wisely adds: “Yet what purpose does it serve [Col. 0510D] to mock the fate of men who were carried off not by their own lust, but by the condition of human frailty? Since the end of our life is exposed to various hidden causes, things which do not deserve it sometimes assume the title of the ultimate cause of death, though they coincide with the time of death rather than summon death itself.” Speusippus, nevertheless, is described by Laertius as ἡδονῶν ἣττων, “devoted to pleasures.” HAV.]. A Christian is born a male for his wife alone.

Democritus, by blinding himself [Note: [Col. 0510D] **Democritus, by blinding himself.** Vincent of Beauvais, *Doctrinal Mirror*, book V, chapter 98: “Tertullian also reports that the philosopher Democritus blinded himself because he was unable to look at women without lust.” And again, chapter CLXXV: “Hence Aulus Gellius reports of the philosopher Democritus in his book *Attic Nights* that he was an Abderite by nationality and exceedingly wealthy; leaving his entire patrimony to his fellow citizens, he went to Athens and there tore out his own eyes, regarding them, presumably, as an impediment to noble studies, so that his thoughts might be more vigorous. Liberius, however, says [Col. 0511A] that he tore out his eyes so that he would not see wicked citizens prospering. [Col. 0511B] Tertullian says that he blinded himself because he could not look at women without lust.” He adds on his own account: “Moreover, he deservedly tore out his own eyes, since as a magician he devised darkness for human eyes.” HAV.], because [Col. 0511A] he could not look at women without lust and felt pain if he had not possessed them, acknowledges his incontinence by attempting to correct it. But the Christian sees a woman with his eyes intact; in his mind he is blind to lust.

If I make my defense concerning integrity, behold Diogenes, with muddy feet, trampling Plato’s proud couches in another kind of pride [Note: [Col. 0511B] **Diogenes, Plato’s proud, etc.** Jerome, *Against Jovinian*: “Although Plato was wealthy, and Diogenes trampled his couches with muddy feet, he chose the Academy, a country house far from the city, not only deserted but also unhealthy, so that he might have leisure for philosophy and so that the impulses of lust might be broken by the care and persistence of diseases. Hence several of his disciples also gouged out their own eyes.” For *deculcat*, “tramples,” the Fulda codex has *decalcat*. HAV.]. The Christian is not proud even toward a poor man.

If I contend concerning modesty, behold Pythagoras among the Thurians [Note: [Col. 0511B] **Pythagoras among the Thurians.** Thus Rigaltius, Heraldus, Rhenanus, and the Aldine edition; some read *Tyrians*. Among the various accounts of Pythagoras’s death was the view that he was burned through the violence of his opponents while seeking sovereign power. See Laertius and Athenagoras. Arnobius, book I: “Pythagoras of Samos, on the unjust suspicion that he sought sovereignty, was burned alive in a temple.” I read *inusta*, “burned in,” or *injusta*, “unjust.” HAV.], and Zeno among the people of Priene, aspiring to tyranny; but the Christian does not aspire even to the aedileship [Note: [Col. 0511C] **But Christians do not aspire even to the aedileship.** In the same place the Aldine edition wrongly reads: “the Christian truly does not even aspire to citizenship.” He does not name the aedileship without reason, since access to it was open even to the common people, and duties not particularly extensive appear to have belonged to it, such as the magistracy of a district and similar offices. Martial writes of Oracilius’s ridiculous ostentation and ambition, book X, epigram 79:

> Torquatus was consul; that man was a district magistrate,  
> Yet in so great an honor he appeared no less to himself.

HAV.].

If I engage concerning equanimity, [Col. 0512A] Lycurgus wished ἀποκαρτέρησιν (“to starve himself to death”) because the Laconians had amended his laws; the Christian gives thanks even when condemned.

If I make a comparison concerning good faith, Anaxagoras [Note: [Col. 0511C] **Anaxagoras denied a deposit to his guests.** This is quite correctly the reading of the Fulda codex, whose collation, made by Franciscus Modius and copied by Scioppius, Junius had appended to his notes. Although Heraldus and La Cerda could have used it, they repeatedly neglected to consult it, publishing with the others *enemies* instead of *guests*, a reading that is exceedingly absurd beside ours. Rigaltius, who alone knew how to use that excellent collation in his edition, transposed the words thus: “denied it to his guests.” Why he did so, I do not know. Aristotle touches upon the injustice of this offense in *Problems*, section XXIX, question 2, and explains why it is more serious than denying a loan: πρὸς γὰρ τῇ ζημίᾳ, καὶ τὴν πίστιν παραβαίνει, that is: “For besides the loss, good faith is disregarded”; and ὁ μὲν οὖν ἔδωκε ὡς [Col. 0511D] φίλῳ, ὀ δὲ ἀπεστέρησεν ὡς ἐχθρόν: “For the former entrusted his own property as to a friend; the latter denies it as an enemy.” Lucian relates something similar of Hermodorus the Epicurean in *Icaromenippus*: Καὶ γὰρ αὗ κᾀκείνους ἑώρων. Ερμόδωρον μὲν τὸν Επικουρεῖον, χιλίων ἓνεκα δραχμῶν ἐπιορκοῦντα. That is: “For among them I saw Hermodorus the Epicurean committing perjury over a thousand drachmas.” But nothing is recorded concerning Anaxagoras, nor do the commentators offer anything. I do not doubt, however, that the following passage, likewise from Lucian’s *The Lapiths*, pertains to him. It corresponds exactly to the words of our Tertullian, while further teaching that this crime was committed against his own disciple. Cleodemus says there: Οὐδὲ τοῦ ξένου μαθητοῦ λαβὼν τουφὸδιον παρακαταθὴκας ἐπειτα ὤμοσα κατὰτῆς Παλλιάδος μὴ εἰληφέναι. That is: “Nor did I afterwards swear by Pallas that I had not received the traveling money which my disciple, my guest, had entrusted to me.” See Ezekiel, chapter 18:12, and Laertius on Pittacus and Plato. HAV.] denied a deposit to his guests; the Christian is called faithful even by outsiders.

If I take my stand concerning sincerity, Aristotle disgracefully caused his intimate friend Hermias to yield his place [Note: [Col. 0511A] Perhaps *his bed*, Haverkamp.] [Note: [Col. 0512A] **Disgracefully caused Hermias to yield his place.** La Cerda cites from Laertius the account given by Aristippus that Aristotle received Hermias’s concubine from him, though he himself admits that it scarcely pertains to this passage. Otherwise Lucian could have had this in view, or certainly alluded to it, when he writes in *The Lapiths*: Σὺ δὲ, τὴν Σωστράτου γυναῖκα τοῦ μαθητοῦ ἐμοίχευσας, ὧ Κλεόδημε. “But you, Cleodemus, debauched the wife of your disciple Sostratus.” That this Hermias held a very intimate place in Aristotle’s friendship is clear from Athenaeus, in whose book XV, chapter 16, the philosopher is accused of impiety because he had rendered divine honor to this Hermias, celebrating his memory with a hymn as though he were one of the gods. But Athenaeus, defending Aristotle, demonstrates that it was not a hymn but a drinking-song, and appends the poem itself, in which virtue is addressed and these words occur concerning Hermias, whom he compares with Hercules, Achilles, and Ajax:

Σᾶς δ` ἕνεκ` φιλίου μορφᾶς


Καὶ Ἀταρνέως ἔντροφος


Ἡελίου χήρωσεν αὐγᾶς.

Τὸν γὰρ ἀοίδιμον ἔργοις [Col. 0512C] Ἀθάνατόν τέ μιν αὐξήσουσι Μοῦσαι


Μνημοσύνης θογατέρες,


Διὸς ξενίου, σέβας αὔξουσαι


Φιλίας τε γέρας βεβαίας.

That is: “For the sake of your lovely form, the ward of Atarneus deprived himself of the light of the sun. The Muses, daughters of Mnemosyne and Zeus the Guardian of Guests, will adorn him, renowned and celebrated for his deeds, with everlasting praise, extolling reverence for hospitality and the rewards of steadfast friendship.” In the same place these words of Aristotle are cited: Οὐ γὰρ ἄν ποτε Ερμεία θύειν ὡς ἀθανάτῳ προαιρούμενος, ὡς θνητῷ μνῆμα κατεσκεὑαζον, καὶ ἀθανατίζειν τὴν φύσιν βουλόμενος ἐπιταφίοις καὶ τιμίαις ἐκοσμήσατο. That is: “For Hermias, as an immortal, I did not resolve to sacrifice; as a mortal, I built him a tomb; but, desiring to make his fame immortal, I honored him with a funeral encomium and eulogy.” Yet in the Leiden manuscript there is a monstrous reading, *Herimantra putriculo excedere fecit*. I have not yet been able to grasp its meaning. Or should one rather read: “He disgracefully caused Hermias to yield his bed”? Laertius confirms this. HAV.]; the Christian does not harm even his enemy.

The same Aristotle, rather than governing Alexander, flatters him as disgracefully [Note: [Col. 0512D] **Rather than governing Alexander.** The same codex reads *the king*, but [Col. 0512D] wrongly. His teacher, he says, ought rather to have governed Alexander’s fierce youth with the bridle of modesty than to assent to him like a courtier and increase his mental derangement. Arrian, *The Expedition of Alexander*, book IV, chapter IX, p. 164 of Gronovius’s edition, offers us a notable example of such flattery by the wise men of the age. There, when Alexander was indignant and angry with himself over the abominable murder of Cleitus, Arrian says: Εἰσὶ δὲ οἱ λέγουσιν Ἀνάξαρχον τὸν σοφιστὴν ἐλθεῖν, etc.; that is: “Some write that the sophist Anaxarchus was summoned to console him and came to him. Finding him lying down and groaning, he smiled and said that Alexander did not know why the ancient sages had depicted Justice seated beside Zeus: namely, because whatever Zeus decrees must be regarded as justly done. Therefore, whatever a great king did ought to be considered just, first by the king himself and then by all other mortals.” By this remark, they say, he then brought Alexander some small measure of consolation. But Arrian himself admirably [Col. 0513A] adds: Κακὸν δὲ μέγα ὡς ἐγώ φημι ἐξέργάσασθαι Ἀλεξάνδρῳ, etc.; that is: “For my part, I judge Anaxarchus to have been the author for Alexander of an error greater than the former one, if he represented that as the opinion of a wise man: namely, that a king ought not, with the greatest care and discrimination, to do what is just, but that whatever the king might do, of whatever kind, ought to be considered just.” How closely they associated Aristotle with this fault is clear from Lucian’s comparison of him with this Anaxarchus in *The Parasite*: Εὐριπίδης μὲν γὰρ, ὅτι Ἀρχελάῳ μεχρι τοῦ θανάτου παρεσίτει, καὶ Ἀναξαρχος Ἀλεξάνδρῳ, πάντως ἐπίϛασαι. Καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης δὲ τῆς παρασιτικῆς ἤρξατο μόνον, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τεχνῶν. That is: “You know perfectly well that Euripides acted as a parasite at the court of Archelaus until his death, and Anaxarchus at that of Alexander. Aristotle, however, only made a beginning in the parasitic art, as he did in the other arts.” He bites at the philosopher because, while desiring to know and teach everything, he excelled perfectly in nothing. Yet this same man, though skilled in courtly arts, vainly warned his kinsman Callisthenes to restrain his fierceness of spirit lest he hasten his own doom, since he did not know how to deal with Alexander, as we explained above. HAV.] as Plato [Col. 0513A] put himself up for sale to Dionysius for the sake of his belly [Note: [Col. 0513C] **As Plato to Dionysius, etc.** The sense is, and can be no other: Aristotle courted Alexander’s favor as disgracefully as Plato courted the delicacies and dinners of Dionysius. La Cerda and Rigaltius were therefore right to cut down the old reading, “Plato by Dionysius,” although it occurs in all the manuscripts and editions. Lucian, *The Parasite*: Ὁ δὲ Πλάτων ὑμῶν ὁ γενναιότατος, etc.; that is: “That most noble Plato of yours also came to Sicily for this reason. After being the king’s parasite for a few days there, he failed because he was unsuited to the occupation. Then, after returning to Athens, applying himself with great zeal, and preparing himself, he undertook a second voyage to Sicily. There, after dining for a few days, he again failed through inexperience.” Lucian says that several writers affirmed this. Gregory Nazianzen also reproaches him for this reason in his second oration against Julian. It is also known from Laertius what Plato whispered to Diogenes and what Diogenes answered Plato. HAV.].

Aristippus, clad in purple, carouses beneath an impressive appearance of dignity [Note: [Col. 0513C] **Aristippus in purple, etc.** Many have mentioned this luxury, including Gregory Nazianzen in his *Song of the Swan* and others. Laertius described his life at length. Lucian too, that scourge of the philosophers, wittily marked it out. Thus in *The Auction of Lives*:

**JUPITER:** Summon another, that Cyrenaic dressed in purple and wearing a crown.

**MERCURY:** Come, everyone, pay attention. This is an expensive article and requires wealthy purchasers. This is a pleasant life, a thrice-blessed life. Who desires delights? Who will purchase the most luxurious of men?

**BUYER:** Come here, you, and say what you know, for I shall buy you if you prove useful.

**MERCURY:** Do not disturb him, my good man, and do not question him. He is drunk and therefore will not be able to answer you; as you see, his tongue is faltering.

**BUYER:** What sane person would purchase so corrupt and immoderate a slave? How strongly he smells of all those perfumes! And with what a slippery and irrational gait he walks! But at any rate, Mercury, tell me what arts he possesses or what he is accustomed to practice.

**MERCURY:** In short, he is an excellent banqueter and drinking-companion. Indeed, together with a flute-girl, he would be highly suitable for performing shameless and lascivious dances before some amorous and dissolute master. As for other things, he knows how to prepare sweetmeats and is thoroughly practiced in arranging [Col. 0514B] delicacies. In brief, he is an artisan of pleasure. He was educated at Athens and served the tyrants of Sicily, by whom he was highly prized.

Lucian likewise says of the same man in *The Parasite*: Καὶ οὗτος μέντοι κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον, etc.; that is: “At that age he too lived at Syracuse, serving as a parasite at the court of Dionysius. There he was approved above all other parasites, since he possessed exceptional skill in this art beyond the rest, so much so that Dionysius sent his cooks to him every day to learn from him.” This man certainly appears to have cultivated the art worthily. Accordingly, in *The Double Indictment*, Lucian introduces Virtue and Pleasure, or Luxury, contending over him. Virtue says there: Ἐμὸς γάρ ἐστιν Ἀριϛίππος, ὡς δηλούσιν οἱ λόγοι καὶ τὰ ἔργα. That is: “Aristippus is mine, as his discourses and deeds demonstrate.” Luxury replies: Οὐμενοῦν, ἀλλ` ἐμὲ, τὴν Τρυφὴν· ἐμὸς γὰρ ὁ ἁνὴρ, ὥς ἐϛιν ὁρᾷν ἀπὸ τῶν ϛεφάνων, καὶ τὴς πορφυρίδος, καί τῶν [the recovered fragment ends here]. That is: “By no means; he is mine—for it is proper that I, Luxury, should speak first. That man is mine, as is evident from his crowns, purple clothing, and perfumes.” Justice, sitting as judge, then says: Μἡ φιλονεικῆτε [Col. 0514C], etc.; that is: “Do not contend, for this case also will be postponed until Jupiter renders judgment concerning Dionysius. His case seems similar to this one, so that if Pleasure wins, Luxury will also have Aristippus; but if the Stoa wins, he will be awarded to Virtue.”

These things were said for amusement, but Epiphanius seriously calls Aristippus γαυρίμαργος καὶ φιλήδονυς, that is, “devoted to gluttony and pleasures,” in his work *Against Heresy* LXXX. Hence Lactantius says, *Divine Institutes*, book III, chapter 8: “I do not think Aristippus even deserves an answer. No one doubts that, since he always looked to bodily pleasure and served nothing but his belly and sexual desire, he was not a human being. For he lived in such a way that nothing distinguished him from a beast except the single fact that he could speak.” HAV.], and Hippias is killed while laying plots against his city [Note: [Col. 0514C] **Hippias.** There was a philosopher of this name whom Cicero, *On the Orator*, book III, recalls as highly expert not only in every branch of learning but also in every craft. Xenophon likewise praises him at length in the *Memorabilia*, book IV, and Lucian in his *Hippias*. But nothing of this kind is recorded concerning him. Did Tertullian, then, confuse him with Hippias, the son of Pisistratus, concerning whom Cicero writes to Atticus: “The wicked Hippias, son of Pisistratus, who died in the battle of Marathon while bearing arms against his fatherland”? Justin also relates the matter in book II, chapter 9. Yet this was more open warfare than a plot laid against the city. Either, therefore, that Hippias of Elis died in this manner while plotting against his city, according to certain writers whom Septimius had the opportunity to read, or else some other person is meant whose name has been corrupted. Indeed, witnesses attest that the Fulda manuscript had Υ [only this initial of the corrupt name is recoverable]chthias, and I myself observed *Jethiclias* in the Leiden codex. It may therefore have been one of Pythagoras’s followers, very many of whom died under charges of that crime. Iamblichus, chapter XXXVI, certainly mentions among them Euthycles of Rhegium, a name very close to the manuscript readings; others could have written it *Euthiclias*, whence it was corrupted into *Jethiclias*. HAV.].

No Christian has ever attempted this on behalf of his own people, even when they were dispersed with every kind of atrocity. But someone will say that even among us certain men depart from the rule of our discipline. In that case they cease to be regarded by us as Christians; whereas those philosophers, despite such deeds, continue among you in the name and honor of wisdom. What, then, [Note: [Col. 0513A] The Leiden codex, Aldine edition, Rigaltius, and Havercamp read: “Then what”; perhaps it should be written: “And so what,” etc.] is there in common between a philosopher and a Christian—a disciple of Greece and a disciple of Heaven, a trafficker in fame and one in salvation [Note: [Col. 0513A] All editions before Rigaltius read *life*; the Fulda codex reads *and of the salvation of life*.], an operator in words and an operator in deeds, a builder and a destroyer of things [Note: [Col. 0513A] All editions except that of Rigaltius read *and of things*. But Tertullian appears to have written either *of gods*, [Col. 0514A] as A. Neander conjectured, or *of idols*.], a falsifier of error and a restorer of truth, its thief and its guardian? [Note: [Col. 0514A] Editions before Rigaltius read: “a destroyer, a friend and enemy of error, a falsifier and restorer and expresser of truth, and its thief and guardian?”].

## CHAPTER XLVII

[Col. 0515A]

**ARGUMENT.** Indeed, if anything sound or resembling truth is found in the writings of the philosophers, all of it was borrowed from the more ancient law of God, which the Christians possess uncorrupted. Yet each philosopher corrupted and altered it according to his own capacity and inclination. This therefore establishes no equality between the two groups, but shows instead that their diverse sects fell away into innumerable errors from the single truth which Christians possess in its more ancient form.

**47.** For the established antiquity of divine literature [Note: [Col. 0515B] The common reading is: “More ancient than all, unless I am mistaken? Still,” etc. Rhenanus, Gangneius, and Heraldus: “Truth is more ancient than all [unless I am mistaken], and this assists me,” etc.; Gelenius: “A guardian more ancient than all, unless I am mistaken? And this,” etc. But Rigaltius and others rightly deleted these words as foreign to this passage.] continues to assist me [Note: [Col. 0515B] **The established antiquity of divine literature.** “Here too,” he says, “the supreme antiquity of Divine Scripture serves my purpose. In chapter XIX above we showed that even your most ancient writers were born several centuries after its authors. From them, evidently, your philosophers derived everything in which they show any true wisdom; but, measuring it by the limits of their own intellect, they disfigured it in manifold ways.” HAV.], so that it may readily be believed to have been the treasury of every later wisdom. And if I were not now restraining the bulk of this volume, I would also digress into this proof. What poet, what sophist, has not drunk from the fountain of the prophets? From that source, therefore, the philosophers watered the thirst of their intellect. Indeed, because they possess certain things belonging to us, for that reason they compare us with them [Note: [Col. 0515B] These words, which Rigaltius had deleted, were restored by Havercamp from the Fulda codex. The others read: “so that, because they possess things belonging to us, they compare us with them.”].

For this reason, I suppose, philosophy was also expelled by law [Note: [Col. 0515B] Havercamp added *by law* from the Fulda codex.] from certain cities—I mean by the Thebans [Note: [Col. 0515C] **By the people of Thebes.** Since this is the unanimous reading of both the Fulda and Leiden manuscripts, I do not doubt that Tertullian intended it thus, although others have *by the Thebans*. The Fulda manuscript soon afterward likewise has “both by the Spartans and the Argives,” where others have “by the Spartans and the Argives” in different forms. Indeed, even at Athens itself the philosophers were once compelled to go into exile, when, by a decree of Sophocles son of Amphiclides, every school was prohibited except those approved by the Senate and the people. Diogenes Laertius bears witness to this in the *Life of Theophrastus*, not far from the beginning. He says of Theophrastus: Τοιοῦτος δὲ ὢν, ὅμως ἁπεδήμησε, etc.; that is: “Although he was such a man, he too withdrew for a time, as did the other philosophers. For Sophocles son of Amphiclides had proposed a law that no philosopher should preside over a school unless the Senate or the people had decreed it; anyone who acted otherwise was to suffer capital punishment.” But it is added in the same place: Ἀλλὰ αὖθις ἐπανῆλθον εἰς νέωτα, etc.; that is: “They returned again the following year, however, after Philo brought a prosecution against Sophocles. At that time the Athenians repealed the law, fined Sophocles five talents, and decreed that the philosophers might return.” Casaubon there adduces these words of Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book XIII: Καὶ Σοφοκλῆς, ὅστις ψηφίσματι ἐξέλασε πάντας φιλοσὁφους τῆς Ἀττικῆς. That is: “And Sophocles, by whose decree all the philosophers were expelled from Athens.”

But should you wish to pass over into Italy, you may see that they were driven even from the city of Rome; for the very words of the legal decree still survive in Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XV, chapter XI, and Suetonius, *On Illustrious Rhetoricians*, at the beginning. Seneca refers to this when censuring the morals of his age in the *Consolation to Helvia*, chapter X: “Apicius lived within our own memory. In that city from which philosophers had once been ordered to depart as corrupters of the young, he professed the knowledge of the cookshop and infected the age with his teaching.” HAV.], the Spartans, and the Argives.

While they strive after our teachings [Note: [Col. 0516B] “While they strive after our teachings,” Franeker; “while our teachings are contaminated,” Rhenanus, Wouwerius; “for our teachings are contaminated,” Rigaltius.] [Note: [Col. 0515D] **While they strive after our teachings.** Learned men disturb the sense in various ways by attempting to connect these words with what precedes. [Col. 0516B] They think Tertullian means that philosophy was expelled from certain cities while the philosophers dreamed up doctrines resembling those of the Christians, something he has already said once. The simple and true sense is therefore this: philosophers, men devoted solely to fame and eloquence, corrupt Sacred Scripture [Col. 0516C] and the knowledge of God when they wish to know something of our doctrine. A full stop must therefore be placed after *Argives*, and the sense is plain. The Aldine edition read “while they strive after your teachings,” through the usual error. The Agobardine codex reads “while they strive after ours, and men of glory,” etc., thus opening the way to the correct punctuation. Wouwerius and Rhenanus read “while our teachings are contaminated”; hence Rigaltius reads “while they are contaminated toward our teachings,” which Scriverius praises in the margin of my copy and adopts. Pamelius and La Cerda read “while they strive after ours.” More correctly, the manuscripts of Puteanus, Fulda, and Heraldus, as well as the Leiden manuscript, read “while they strive after our teachings.” There is an almost similar expression in chapter XL: “and if any fruits of trees there strive forth merely as far as the eyes.” HAV.]—being men devoted to fame [Note: [Col. 0516C] **Men of fame, etc.** “A philosopher is an animal of fame and a slave offered for sale to rumor,” says Tertullian elsewhere. Augustine, Letter 56: “slaves of empty fame.” Thus the arrogance of the sophists, which the Homer of the philosophers calls κλεπτίκη σοφία (“thieving wisdom”), is repeatedly branded among the Fathers and the ancients. LE PR.], as we have said, and lusting only after eloquence—if they encountered anything in the ordered contents of the sacred writings [Note: [Col. 0516B] Rigaltius deleted *inserted in religious matters*.], they took it from there [Note: [Col. 0516B] Rigaltius inserted the words *took it from there* on the authority of the Fulda codex.] and turned it to their own purposes, in accordance with the aim of their curiosity [Note: [Col. 0516B] Franeker adds *works*.]. They did not believe sufficiently that these things were divine to refrain from falsifying them, nor did they understand them sufficiently, since at that time they were still clouded over [Note: [Col. 0516B] *Sublime*, Rhenanus.], being obscure even to the Jews themselves, to whom they appeared properly to belong.

For even where there was some simplicity of truth, human captiousness, scorning faith, wavered all the more [Note: [Col. 0516B] *Altered*, Rhenanus.] [Note: [Col. 0516D] **Wavered.** The old editions of Barré, Aldus, Rhenanus, Heraldus, and Pamelius, as well as the Leiden codex, read *altered*. La Cerda, departing from Junius, also defends this reading in his notes. But Junius rightly emended *altered* to *wavered*, and the Fulda and Agobardine manuscripts and Rigaltius himself read no differently. Just as those philosophers, lusting only after fame and eloquence, did not understand what was clouded and concealed from them, so too they did not dare trust what was sufficiently clear in itself, being accustomed to sophistical trifles and philosophical wrappings; accordingly, they confused everything. Tertullian speaks elegantly in *To the Nations* II.2: “For at other times too the simplicity of truth generally wavers in faith through captiousness.” HAV.]; by this means they confused into uncertainty even what they had discovered with certainty.

For they merely discovered God, but did not discuss him as they had discovered him [Note: [Col. 0516D] **Not as they had discovered him.** The sense here is somewhat obscure. Having drawn some knowledge of God from the sacred Scriptures, they did not teach God in accordance with those Scriptures, as they ought to have done, nor did they direct the people back to them. Instead, they sought glory as though they had investigated the divinity through their own efforts. Nor did they agree very closely with one another in their very knowledge of God, since some maintained one thing and others another. In this they show that they departed from truth, which is simple and one. I do not know how it happened that this entire passage is absent from the edition of Rigaltius which I use, contrary to all the manuscripts. HAV.]; instead, they dispute over his quality, nature, and dwelling place [Note: [Col. 0517A] **They dispute over his dwelling place.** Some maintain that he is everywhere in such a way that all things are simultaneously parts of the divinity. Lucan held this impious opinion, book IX, line 582:

> God’s dwelling is wherever earth, sea, air,  
> Heaven, and virtue are. Why seek the gods beyond?

].

Restoration notes: S000911 reads λόγος ἀτενης, which is grammatically possible but does not fit the surrounding reference to crested cocks; it has therefore been preserved verbatim and marked as apparently corrupt.; S000911 reads λόγος ἀτενης, a grammatically possible phrase that does not fit the surrounding reference to crested cocks; the recovered reading is therefore preserved verbatim and explicitly marked uncertain or corrupt.  

> Jupiter is whatever you see, wherever you move.

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, chapter 103, concerning the god of the Epicureans: “But let God indeed be, as you wish, the likeness and image of a human being. What is his dwelling? What his seat? What his location?” Then, after saying that every living creature has its own place in which it dwells, he continues in chapter 104: “I ask, therefore, first of all, where your god lives.” The same author, in Book II of the same work, proceeds thus: “He represented the gods as translucent and permeable, and placed their seat, as though between two exercise-grounds, between two worlds, for fear of their collapse.” HAV.]

Some assert that he is incorporeal, others corporeal [Note: [Col. 0517B] **Some assert that he is incorporeal, others corporeal.** Lucian, in the passage cited: Ἔτι δὲ, οἱ μὲν, ἀσώματόν τι, καὶ ἅμορφον ἡγοῦντο εἶναι τὸ Θεῖον. Οἱ δὲ, ὡς περι σώματος αὐτοῦ διενοοῦντο. That is: “Moreover, some thought that the divine power was something incorporeal [Col. 0517C] and formless; others imagined that it possessed a body.” HAV.], as do respectively the Platonists and the Stoics [Note: [Col. 0517A] “As both the Platonists and the Stoics,” Fran., Paris.]; some say that he consists of atoms, others of numbers [Note: [Col. 0517A] “Just as,” Fran., Paris.], as Epicurus and Pythagoras respectively taught; others of fire, as Heraclitus thought. The Platonists, moreover, hold that he cares for the world; the Epicureans, by contrast, that he is idle [Note: [Col. 0517C] **The Epicureans, by contrast, that he is idle.** Lucretius describes the nature of this ridiculous divinity in Book I, line 57, and Book II, line 646:

> For every nature of the gods must necessarily  
> Enjoy immortal existence in the highest peace,  
> Removed from our affairs and separated far away.  
> For, free from every grief and free from dangers,  
> Mighty in its own resources, needing nothing from us,  
> It is neither won by good deserts nor touched by anger.

Gods of this sort could not fail to provoke laughter in sensible and wise men. Hence Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “The gods care for nothing, neither themselves nor others, but are mere outlines and do nothing.” Seneca too, in that very witty *Apocolocyntosis*, speaking of Claudius, says: “Only tell us what sort of god you wish this fellow to become: Ἐπικουρεῖος Θεὸς (“an Epicurean god”) he cannot be, οὒτε αὐτος πρᾶγμα ἕχει, οὕτε ἅλλοις παρέχει.” Cicero translates this in Book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “That which is eternal and blessed neither has any business of its own [Col. 0517D] nor causes any for another.” Best of all, finally, is the witty Lucian, whose words in the *Icaromenippus* are: Εἶτα καὶ προνοεῖν τῶν καθ` ἡμᾶς πραγμάτων οὐ πᾶσιν ἐδόκουν οἱ Θεοὶ, αλλὰ ἦσάν τινες, οἱ τῆς συμπάσης ἐπιμελείας αὐτοὺς ἁφιέντες, ὥσπερ ἡμεῖς εἰωθαμεν ἀπολύειν τῶν λειτουργιῶν τοὺς γεγηραπότας. οὐδὲν γὰρ ὅτι μὴ τοῖς κωμικοῖς δορυφορήμασιν ἐοικότας αὐτοὺς εἰσάγουσιν. That is: “Furthermore, not all believed that the affairs of mortals were a concern to the gods; rather, there were some who freed them from every care—as we are accustomed to release those worn out by age from their duties—and represented them as no different from the attendants customarily introduced in comedies.” He aptly compares them to δορυφορήμασιν κωμικοῖς (“comic attendants”), because they were mute characters, to whom neither any speech nor any notable action was assigned onstage. HAV.], inactive [Note: [Col. 0517D] **And inactive.** The Fulda and L.B. manuscripts read “and unoccupied.” That saying of Hilary of Poitiers on Psalm 63 remains true: “Furthermore, he who removes from God the care of human conduct will come to know God as the judge of the eternal kingdom.” HAV.], [Col. 0518A] and, so to speak, a nobody in relation to human affairs [Note: [Col. 0518A] “Unconcerned with human affairs,” Wouwer.].

The Stoics, however, place him outside the world [Note: [Col. 0518A] **The Stoics, however, place him outside the world.** The philosophers did indeed ask whether God sits and watches his work or handles it; whether he is spread around it from without or implanted throughout it; whether the world is immortal or must be counted among things perishable and born only for a time. These are Seneca’s words in *On the Happy Life*, chapter 31, which, like much else in that passage, [Col. 0518B] bears upon the present chapter. But that placement of God outside the world should be ascribed not to the doctrines of the Stoics but to those of the Epicureans. For Seneca gives this splendid description of God according to the Stoics in the preface to his *Natural Questions*: “He alone is all things; he encompasses his work both without and within.” But those wretched triflers cast God outside the world. Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book IV, chapter 19: “You, Epicurus, make God defenseless; you have taken from him every weapon and all power, and, lest anyone should fear him, you have cast him outside the boundary”—as the great commentator correctly emends *fear* to *boundary* there, comparing these passages from Book VII of the same work: “One man charges the gods with neglecting us; another casts them outside their own world”; and Letter 90: “I do not speak of that philosophy which placed the citizen outside his country and the gods outside the world.” Where, then? I do not know—in certain intermundane spaces, at which Cicero wittily glances in Book II of *On Divination*: “He represented the gods as translucent and permeable, and placed their seat, as though between two exercise-grounds, between two worlds, [Col. 0518C] for fear of their collapse.”

But it is worth sending the reader to Justus Lipsius, *Physiology of the Stoics*, Book I, final chapter, or chapter 21, where he criticizes this passage of Tertullian and defends the Stoics with numerous testimonies. I do not know whether Lucian had this philosophical opinion in view, or instead wished to censure the Christians, when he rants forth these impieties in the *Icaromenippus*, p. 276 of the Benedictine edition: Οὓς καὶ μάλιστα ἐθαύμαζον θεὸν μέν τινα τεχνίτην τῶν ὃλων ἐφιστάντας οὐ προτιθέντας δὲ οὒτε ὃθεν ἥκων, οὒτε ὃπου ἑστὼς ἕκαστα ἐτεκταίνετο. That is: “I especially marveled at them because, although they established a certain God as the craftsman of all things, they did not also add either whence he had come or where he stood while each thing was being fashioned.”].

The Platonists place him within the world, so that, after the fashion of a helmsman, he remains within that which he governs. They likewise differ over whether the world itself was created or uncreated, and whether it will perish or remain [Note: [Col. 0518C] **So that, after the fashion of a helmsman, he remains within that which he governs.** Boethius, Book III, meter 9, alluding to this:

> O you who govern the world by everlasting reason,  
> Sower of earth and heaven.

[Col. 0518D] And more clearly, Book IV, meter 6:

> Meanwhile the exalted Creator sits,  
> And, governing all things, turns the reins:  
> King, Lord, fountain and source,  
> Law and wise arbiter of justice.  
> The things that motion drives onward  
> He checks, drawing them back, and steadies their wandering;  
> For unless, recalling them inward to straight courses,  
> He compels them again into interwoven circles,  
> The things now held by stable order,  
> Torn from their source, would fall apart.];

[Note: [Col. 0518D] **Likewise, whether the world itself was created or uncreated, and whether it will perish or remain.** See Seneca in the passage just cited. Besides many philosophers, the distinguished poet Manilius thought that the world was eternal, lacking both end and beginning, in Book I of the *Astronomica*:

> This form remains eternal and most like the gods;  
> Nowhere does it have a beginning, nor an end within itself,  
> But remains the same throughout and equal in every part.

The same author, in the same place:

> [Col. 0519B] But the world remains unharmed and turns all its contents,  
> Which length of days does not increase, nor age diminish;  
> Motion does not run through a single point, nor does its course grow weary.  
> It will always be the same, because it always was the same.  
> Our fathers saw no other world, nor will their descendants  
> Behold another.

But apart from Sophocles—whose memorable extract you have in Grotius’ collection entitled *Extracts from the Greek Tragic and Comic Poets*, p. 145—Lucan, Book I, line 72, Ovid, and others, Lucretius demonstrated beyond refutation, with most excellent arguments and verses, that the world once arose and would one day perish, Book V, line 94:

> The threefold nature of these things, the three bodies, Memmius,  
> Three forms so unlike, three structures of this kind,  
> One day will give to destruction; and the mass and fabric of the world,  
> Sustained through many years, will fall.

[Col. 0519D] See what follows there. Yet Lucian too could not refrain from extracting laughter from this quarrel among the philosophers, in the *Icaromenippus*, p. 276 of the Benedictine edition: Πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἡ περὶ τοῦ κόσμου, etc. That is: “For, first, opinions concerning the world differ: to some it appears ungenerated and imperishable; others have dared to state both who its craftsman was and how it was constructed.” What follows there is thoroughly impious. In the same dialogue, p. 273: Οὐ γὰρ εἶχον εὑρεῖν οὐδ` ὅπως ἐγένετο, οὒτε τὸν δημιουργὸν, οὒτε ἀρχή, οὐθ` ὃτε τὸ τέλος ἐστὶν αὐτοῦ. That is: “For I could discover neither how it had been made, nor by what craftsman, nor what its beginning or end was.”].

[Col. 0519A] So too they differ concerning the condition of the soul: some maintain that it is divine and eternal, others that it is dissoluble. Each has introduced or reshaped it according to his own opinion.

Nor is it surprising that the Old Testament was perverted by the ingenuity of philosophers. From their seed, certain men have adulterated this recent provision of ours [Note: [Col. 0519D] **This recent provision.** The New Testament. RIG.] with their own opinions, turning it into philosophical doctrines [Note: [Col. 0519D] **This recent provision.** Elsewhere he calls the Christians’ sect a new one, since it dates from Tiberius, in whose age this law began to be unfolded. LAC.], and from the one way they have cut many crooked and inextricable paths [Note: [Col. 0519B] “Many and inextricable paths,” Semler.].

I have suggested this lest anyone, observing the diversity of this sect, should think that in this respect also we are on a level with the philosophers, and should infer the truth from the diversity of defenses [Note: [Col. 0519D] **And should judge the truth from the diversity of defenses.** This passage is generally read in this way, though scarcely any other passage is so corrupt. What grain of sound sense does it contain? La Cerda explains it thus: “When they see the truth defended by many along different paths.” Is that so, learned sir? Do the Marcionites, Gnostics, Valentinians, and similar refuse of humanity defend the truth in any way? Nothing could be more absurd. Let us therefore see what the printed books and manuscripts supply.

Aldus: “so that from the truth of the defenses he may vindicate the truth.” Rhenanus: “so that from the truth of the defenses he may vindicate the truth.” Heraldus, Pamelius, and La Cerda: “and from the diversity of defenses he may judge the truth.” But La Cerda in his notes reads *vanity* with Wouwer. The L.B. manuscript agrees with Heraldus, except that, with Rhenanus—as the Agobardinus codex also does—it prefers “vindicate.” Finally, the excellent Fulda manuscript presents this reading: “may vindicate the defection from the truth,” Junius noted. This reading is entirely correct. I too accept it, for its sense is excellent: “Lest anyone,” he says, “charge us with having defected from the truth, which is one, because there are [Col. 0520D] so many different opinions among us.” Tertullian denies this, because those who disagree with us are no longer ours, but adulterers expelled from our school. See the end of chapter 46.] [Note: [Col. 0519B] Thus Heraldus, Pamelius, La Cerda, Rigaltius, Havercamp, Aldus, and Rhenanus: “so that from the truth of the defenses he may vindicate the truth.” Wouwer reads “vanity”; the Fulda codex, “may vindicate the defection from the truth.”].

We dispose of our adulterators quite readily by laying down that the rule of truth is that which comes from Christ and was transmitted through his companions; these various later commentators will be shown to have arisen considerably after them. Everything opposed to [Col. 0519B] truth has been constructed out of truth itself, with spirits of error producing this rivalry [Note: [Col. 0520D] **With spirits of error producing this rivalry.** Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book III, chapter 10, says that the devil plunged deceived and deluded souls into ruin when, transforming himself into an angel of light, he promised purification of the soul through those whom they call τελετὰς (“rites” or “mysteries”), by a manifold contrivance of lying signs and wonders. How the ancient serpent obscured the various mysteries of the Church of God for the wretched pagans must certainly be seen in Casaubon’s very learned work, *Exercises on the Annals of Baronius*, Exercise XVI, chapter 43, and in the same author’s note on Persius, Satire V, line 129.].

From them adulterations [Note: [Col. 0519C] “By adulterations,” Havercamp from the Lyon codex.] of this kind were suborned against the saving discipline [Note: [Col. 0520B] “Arisen,” Fran., Paris.]; from them certain fables were also introduced which, through their similarity [Note: [Col. 0520B] “Dissimilarity,” Fran., Paris.], might weaken faith in the truth—or rather might claim it for themselves [Note: [Col. 0520B] Rhenanus, Aldus, and Heraldus: “or even, if they could, might overthrow it”; the Fulda codex: “or might rather seize the same faith for themselves.”]—so that someone might therefore think that Christians should not be believed because neither poets nor philosophers are believed; or, for that very reason, might instead think that poets and philosophers should be believed because Christians are not.

Thus we are also ridiculed for proclaiming that God will judge. For the poets and philosophers likewise place a tribunal in the underworld. If we threaten with Gehenna, which is a subterranean treasury of hidden fire reserved for punishment, we are similarly laughed to scorn. For among the dead there is likewise the river Pyriphlegethon [Note: [Col. 0520C] “Among the dead,” Havercamp from the Fulda codex.]. And if we name Paradise [Note: [Col. 0520D] **And if we name Paradise.** Tertullian was in error in believing that the souls of the saints are preserved in Paradise until the day of Judgment. LE PR.], a place of divine delight appointed to receive the spirits of the saints, separated from knowledge of the common world by a kind of wall belonging to that fiery zone, belief in the Elysian Fields has forestalled us.

Whence, I ask you, have the philosophers or poets obtained things so very similar to these? From nowhere but our mysteries. If from our mysteries, as the earlier ones, then ours are the more trustworthy and more deserving of belief, since even their images find credence. But if they come from their own conceptions, then our mysteries will be regarded as images of later things—something the nature of reality does not allow; for [Col. 0520B] a shadow never precedes its body, nor an image the truth.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**ARGUMENT.—It is also remarkable that people believe philosophers when they teach incredible things, yet condemn things more credible among Christians. He develops this point with great clarity through the resurrection and restoration of the flesh, or human body, set against the brutish transmigration of souls taught by Laberius and Pythagoras.**

Come now: if some philosopher should affirm, as Laberius says [Col. 0521A] [Note: [Col. 0521B] **As Laberius says.** He was a writer of mimes, mentioned also by our author in *On the Pallium*, chapter 1, by Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*, Book II, and by Gellius, Book XI, chapter 9. More concerning him may be found in Crinitus’ treatment of Decimus Laberius. Minucius alludes to the same man in these words: “That opinion is worthy of the function of a mime.” Crinitus himself reproduces the actual passage of Laberius in *On Honorable Learning*, Book II, chapter 3:

> And I hear many evils even from good men,  
> Through that doctrine by which the philosophers transform us after death,  
> And now from a mule make a man, from a woman a snake,  
> And from different things make various other things.

PAM.] in accordance with the opinion of Pythagoras, that a man is made from a mule and a female snake [Note: [Col. 0521A] “A male snake,” Fran.] from a woman [Note: [Col. 0521B] **A female snake from a woman.** Junius and Rigaltius correctly read thus, as does the Agobardinus codex; others read “a male snake.” But the ancients were fonder of the feminine form, which is also more appropriate here beside “woman.” Lucilius the satirist, in Nonius Marcellus:

> Now he will be torn apart in the middle, just as the Marsian tears apart female snakes  
> With his song.

Turpilius, in the same author: “He seized the female snake with his teeth”; and Varro, in the *Eumenides*:

> Why do you hesitate whether you are now long-tailed monkeys,  
> Or female snakes, or beasts? Or [corrupt text] at Athens?

In this passage perhaps he too is ridiculing the Pythagorean doctrine; for, as the fragments show, in that part of the satire the conversation over dinner concerned philosophers. This becomes still clearer if, with my countryman Ausonius Popma, you refer those last, manifestly corrupt words back to Greek letters and restore the passage thus:

> Or female snakes, or beasts ἐν κεφαλῇ (“on the head”),

in which λόγος ἀτενης [uncertain or corrupt reading; literally, “unremitting discourse”], so that the subject is crested cocks, who also appear as Pythagorean philosophers in Lucian’s *Micyllus*. HAV.], and should twist every argument toward that opinion by the power of eloquence [Note: [Col. 0521A] “Distort,” Semler.], would he not win assent [Note: [Col. 0521A] “Feeling,” Aldus, Rhenanus.] and implant even a conviction that one ought to abstain from animals? Would someone not therefore be persuaded of this, lest by chance he serve beef taken from one of his own great-grandfathers [Note: [Col. 0521C] **Lest by chance he serve beef taken from one of his own great-grandfathers.** The remark is sufficiently ridiculous; and, had he been composing verse, he might have expressed it thus:

> And when you give the limbs of slaughtered cattle to your palate,  
> Know and perceive that you are chewing your own parents.

[Col. 0521D] Yet perhaps *to perceive* should be read in place of *perceive*. The verses are Ovid’s, though adapted to the present subject, since he wrote not “parents” but “farmers” (*Metamorphoses*, Book XV, line 141). But behold, in the same passage Pythagoras himself speaks appropriately in this fashion, at line 173:

> Therefore, lest piety be conquered by the belly’s craving,  
> Refrain—I prophesy—from driving kindred souls away  
> By impious slaughter, lest blood be nourished upon blood.

HAV.].

But if a Christian promises that from a man a man will return, and from Gaius Gaius himself [Note: [Col. 0521D] **From Gaius, Gaius himself will return, as he promises.** Gaius the jurist is used as an example referring to individual cases. *Repromittere* means to promise by a bare pledge and guarantee, without giving security. It has other meanings; see Schardius. PAM.], immediately his bladder complains [Note: [Col. 0521A] “Immediately his bladder complains” is added by Havercamp from the Fulda codex.] [Note: [Col. 0521D] **Immediately his bladder complains.** Here, as frequently elsewhere, the excellence of the Fulda codex is evident; without it, this could not have been imagined even in a dream. You will certainly search for it in vain in all the other editions and manuscripts. In those parchments the passage is framed thus: “promises that he will return, immediately there the bladder is sought for, and with stones,” etc. Whoever added the note to the collation—whether Modius, Scioppius, or Junius—wrote: “One must read ‘the bladder is sought for’; that is, as though it were distended with wind and their breast were being most violently tortured.” So far his note.

But this seems to me to be a proverbial expression derived from small boys who, their bladder being filled with urine, can no longer endure the need to urinate and therefore often cry out from fear of the rod. So, on hearing this Christian discourse, they immediately leave the lecture hall as though driven by the need to urinate. Rigaltius passed over the passage without leaving any indication in his notes. We have a not dissimilar proverb concerning an unpleasant thing: *Men zeu er de koude pis van krygen.* HAV.], and he will be driven out by the people with stones—or, at the very least, with fists [Note: [Col. 0521A] “Slaughters,” Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0522B] **Or, at the very least, with fists.** The ancient parchments read “assemblies.” One must certainly read “fists”; and he very cleverly used *caestus* for the calloused fists of the common rabble, [Col. 0522C] having in mind that passage of Juvenal:

> …and, beaten to pieces with fists, he begs  
> To be allowed to return from there with a few teeth.

(*Satire* 3.)

Septimius therefore says: if some Christian, happening to address the people in a crowd, speaks of the resurrection of bodies and declares that Gaius or Sempronius—the very Gaius and Sempronius themselves—will rise again, he will think the people have treated him well if he is driven out merely with fists and not with stones. Tertullian himself, *Against Marcion*, Book IV, p. 568, says that stoning is characteristic of popular gatherings and an unarmed riot; and in *To the Nations*, Book II, he says that a stone is a common and canine weapon. RIG.].

[Col. 0522A] As though the whole line of reasoning that supports the return of human souls into bodies did not itself require that they be recalled into the same bodies, since to be recalled is to be what they formerly were [Note: [Col. 0522C] **The whole line of reasoning that supports.** I explain it thus: as though the entire force of the arguments by which the return of human souls and their migration into other bodies is established and defended did not bind even more strongly if it were affirmed that souls are recalled to their own respective bodies. We learn that the verb “to support” is used in this sense [Col. 0522D] from *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 17: “Before everything, however, the reasoning that supported it must be commended.”

Since the entire order of the wording has been taken by me from the Fulda codex, it is fair that the common reading should also be supplied. It runs thus: “If any principle supports the return of human souls into bodies, why should they not return to the same substance, since this is what it means to be restored: to be what one formerly was? They are no longer the same beings that they were, because they could not be what they were not unless they ceased to be what they had been.” Then, after the omission of material that appears more fully in the Fulda manuscript, there follows: “Much,” etc. In Junius’ edition, after “they were,” the following is also inserted: “unless they cease to be what they were not.” It is evident that what we have maintained is true: Tertullian published his *Apologeticum* twice. HAV.].

For if they are not what they once were—that is, if they are not clothed in a human body, and that very same body—they will no longer be the same souls that they were. Moreover, if they are no longer the same, how will they be said to have returned? If they have become something else, they will not be the same [Note: [Col. 0522D] **If they have become something else, they will not be the same.** For if the soul of Euphorbus puts on the body of Pythagoras, that man is no longer Euphorbus but Pythagoras. Thus the whole man has not returned, because a man consists of soul and body. [Col. 0523B] It is pleasing to add the opinion of the golden-mouthed one, the great Chrysostom. In Homily I, *On the Resurrection*, he says: “Moreover, if the body does not rise, the human being does not rise. For the human being is not the soul alone, but body and soul. If, therefore, the soul alone rises, half the living creature rises, and thus not the whole. Nor is resurrection properly predicated of the soul. Resurrection belongs to that which has fallen and been dissolved. The soul, however, is not dissolved, but the body.” HAV.]; or, if they remain the same, they will not be from somewhere else [Note: [Col. 0521A] Thus Havercamp from the Fulda codex. In earlier editions the passage was printed as follows: “If any principle supports the return of human souls into bodies, why should they not return into the same substance, since this is what it means to be restored: to be what one formerly was? They are no longer the same souls that they were, because they could not be what they were not unless they ceased to be what they were not, unless they ceased to be what they had been.” From this variation in the text Havercamp likewise conjectures that Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* was published twice.].

We would need much joking and leisure [Note: [Col. 0522A] Thus Wouwer from a manuscript, and Rigaltius. Pamelius and others: “jokes arising from [Col. 0522B] leisure”; Gelenius: “jokes and leisure”; Havercamp: “jokes arising from leisure.”] if we wished to play wantonly with this aspect of the matter: who would seem destined to be transformed into which beast [Col. 0523A] [Note: [Col. 0523A] Thus it is read in the Fulda codex, a reading approved by Heraldus, Rigaltius, and Havercamp. In [Col. 0523B] the other editions: “Who, I ask [Rhenanus: ‘ever’], has seen a beast transformed?”] [Note: [Col. 0523B] **Who would seem destined to be transformed into which beast.** The old printed editions, such as those of Aldus, Barraeus, and Pamelius, and the L.B. manuscript, read: “Who, I ask, [Col. 0523C] has seen a beast transformed?” Rhenanus reads “ever,” absurdly. But Wouwer emended from an old codex to “would wish,” as though a woman were asked whether she wished to be a hen or a cow, and a man whether he wished to be a sparrow, a bull, or a beetle.

But the Fulda reading, embraced by Scioppius and Rigaltius and also confirmed by Heraldus from his own manuscripts, is better: “would seem.” Not only Latinius and Junius, from the manuscripts of Puteanus and Ursinus, but also the Agobardinus codex assent to it. Thus a warlike, avaricious, timid, or pleasure-loving man would be asked into what animals he wished his soul to migrate after the death of his body.

Micyllus provides an apt example. Having been rich in a dream and never ceasing to remember that golden vision, he asks what he himself had once been, and is taught by his companion, his cock, that he had been an Indian ant of the sort that digs out gold—as Lucian jokes in *The Cock*. Indeed, that Pythagorean soul, when it once more put on a human being, ought to have rendered him very similar to its former companion. How far the son of Mnesarchus himself differed from the son of Panthous and the others is shown by Tertullian in his customary manner—that is, humorously—in *On the Soul*, chapter 31:

“Behold, it is sufficiently evident that Euphorbus had a military and warlike soul, even from the very glory of his consecrated shields; but Pythagoras was so sedentary and unwarlike that, avoiding the wars then raging in Greece, he preferred the quiet of Italy. He was devoted to geometry, astrology, and music, and was alien to the interests and disposition of Euphorbus. Moreover, that Pyrrhus busied himself with deceiving fish; Pythagoras, by contrast, would not even approach them, since he abstained from animals. Aethalides and Hermotimus had even cast beans among the common foods; but Pythagoras taught his disciples that they must not even pass through bean fields. How, then, are the same souls recovered, when they will be shown to be the same neither in character, practices, nor diet?” HAV.].

But to return more closely to our defense: we maintain that it is surely far more worthy of belief that a human being will return from a human being [Note: [Col. 0523D] **That a human being will return from a human being.** Minucius, p. 38: “Moreover, who is so foolish or brutish as to dare deny that, just as a human being could first be formed by God, so he can be formed anew?” See Elmenhorst’s note there. A very similar passage of Chrysostom on Paul’s First Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter 4, Homily VII, is also relevant: “If there are Greeks [Col. 0524B] who doubt these things, we shall tell them countless examples. What examples? There are some among them who send souls down into plants, shrubs, and dogs. Tell me, which is easier: to receive one’s own body or another’s?” HAV.]: any person may return in place of any person, provided that he returns as a human being, so that the same quality of soul is restored to the same condition [Note: [Col. 0524B] **So that the same quality.** This too is counted among Tertullian’s errors, because he seems to attribute a bodily form to the soul; or, if he is speaking of the form of the human being, the passage must still be read cautiously, as though he did not sufficiently understand that the same human being would rise again in the same form. Yet he explains himself shortly afterward when he says: “But we shall be the same people who now exist, and not others afterward, because they must in every respect suffer the judgment of God.” These words are absent from Puteanus’ book. PAM.], even if not to the same outward form. Certainly, because the rationale of restoration is its appointment for judgment, necessarily the very same person who once existed will be presented, so that he may receive from God judgment for his good or contrary deserts.

Bodies too will therefore be presented again, because the soul alone, without stable matter—that is, flesh—is incapable of suffering anything [Note: [Col. 0524C] **Because the soul is incapable of suffering anything**, etc. In passages where he discusses the soul, he must be read cautiously. He says that the souls of the wicked suffer nothing after death while separated from the body. This must be numbered among Tertullian’s errors, unless the Magdeburg theologians object, for they list it among his doctrines. LE PR.]; and souls did not earn what they must suffer in every respect under God’s judgment without the flesh, within which they performed all their actions.

“But how,” you ask, “can dissolved matter be presented again?” Consider yourself, human being, and you will find faith in the fact. Think again about what you were before you existed: surely nothing, for you would remember it if you had been anything. You, therefore, who were [Col. 0524A] nothing before you existed, and who become that same nothing [Note: [Col. 0524C] **Become that same nothing.** Both our author and Minucius must be read cautiously here as well. For we are not nothing after death, nor do we cease to exist; rather, he seems to be alluding to the fact that a dead human being is not a human being. PAM.] when you cease to exist—why should you not be able once again to come into existence from nothing, by the will of that very same author who willed that you should exist from nothing?

What new thing will happen to you? You who did not exist were made; when you once more do not exist, you will be made. Explain, if you can, how you were made, and then demand to know how you will be made again. And yet you will surely be made more easily into what you once were, since it was equally not difficult for you to be made into what you had never previously been.

God’s powers will, I suppose, be doubted—God who composed this vast body of the world from what had not existed, no less than from the death-like vacancy and emptiness, and imposed order upon it [Note: [Col. 0523B] Wouwer thus emended the manuscripts’ reading “imposed the text,” with the assent of [Col. 0524A] Rigaltius and Havercamp.]; who animated it with the spirit that animates all souls; and marked it [Note: [Col. 0524C] **And marked it through the world itself.** He not only created the world from nothing and animated it, but also marked out within it many examples of the resurrection of living beings, so that these might serve as testimony to the nations. What these are he relates in what follows. LAC.] through the world itself [Note: [Col. 0524B] “And the world itself,” Fran.] as an example of human resurrection, for a testimony to you.

Light, slain every day, shines again [Note: [Col. 0524C] **Light, slain every day, shines again.** On this and what follows, see Elmenhorst’s diligence. In his notes, p. 100, on those words of Minucius derived from our author, p. 39—“The sun sinks and is born; the stars fall and return,” etc.—he has amassed much material. There is also a notable passage in Epiphanius, who does not permit me to be ἀσύμβολον (“without corroborating testimony”). In the *Ancoratus*, p. 595 of my Greek edition, he writes: Καὶ ἡ κτίσις πᾶσα διαῤῥήδην αὐτοὺς ἐλέγχει ὑποφαίνουσα καθ` ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἀναστάσεως τὸ εἶδος, etc. That is:

“And the whole creation openly refutes them, displaying every day the likeness of resurrection. For the day dies, and through sleep we represent the condition of the dead. The day rises, awakening us and demonstrating the sign of resurrection. Fruits are plucked, and the condition of things is cut down, so that in this way an image of our departure is set forth beforehand. The earth is sown and germinates, because things broken after the reaping rise again. The locust dies when it buries in the earth a certain cast-off product of itself; and after a time the earth restores what was buried. The seeds of fruits are sown and first die, then reach perfection; for unless they have died, they are not brought to life.”

He then continues in this fashion: Σφραγῖδας ἐν ἡμῖν ὁ [Col. 0525B] Θεὸς ἐποίησε διὰ τῶν ὀνύχων, δέκα καὶ δέκα ἀναστάσεως μαρτυρούσας, etc. That is:

“God has made tokens in us through our ten fingernails and ten toenails, which bear witness to the hope of our resurrection. He has also declared our resurrection, as it were, through the crown of our hair. For what appears to be a dead body in us—namely, our hair—sprouts again whenever it is cut. Countless further examples could be given to assure unbelievers. Yet neither the wood pigeon, a little bird, nor the dormouse, a little animal, has persuaded them. The latter dies for six months, and the wood pigeon for forty days, and each comes to life again after its appointed time. Scarab beetles, when near death, hide themselves in a ball of dung, burying and interring such a ball in the earth; and thus they are found to come to life again from their own moisture.” HAV.], and darkness likewise, in its turn, succeeds by withdrawing; the stars, though dead, come to life again [Note: [Col. 0525B] “Come to life,” Fran.]; [Col. 0525A] the seasons begin when they end; fruits are consumed [Note: [Col. 0525B] “Are brought to completion,” Fran.] and return; seeds assuredly rise more fruitfully only after they have decayed and dissolved. All things are preserved by perishing; all things are formed anew from destruction.

You—human being—even your mere name [Note: [Col. 0525C] **Even your mere name.** Horace, Ode IX:

> Many are called by Lydia’s name.

Virgil, *Aeneid* II, line 89:

> …and we too possessed some name and glory.

Nepos, at the end of his *Miltiades*: “a noble name.” Chrysostom truly says, on Psalm 143, concerning the excellence of this creature: “A human being is a great thing”; for he adds that humanity received governance over the whole creation. Manilius too, Book IV, concerning the human being:]

The recovered wording has been preserved without conjectural correction.; S000919 is grammatically corrupt; its approximate rendering follows the sense supplied by the adjacent Latin explanation.; S000922 contains the corrupt recovered form ϛρεύγεσθσι; it is preserved verbatim and rendered according to the sentence’s contextually supported sense.; S000925 is an infinitive meaning “to contend nobly,” although the surrounding syntax expects a name or designation; it is preserved without conjectural correction.; In S000928, the second occurrence of Anaxarchus’s name is recovered as the apparently corrupt Ἀνάξαρκον; it is preserved and explicitly noted.  

Each is an image of God in miniature.

And what follows there. HAV.], if you understand yourself, or learn from the inscription of the Pythia [Note: [Col. 0525C] “Or learn from the inscription of the Pythia.” He has in view that famous inscription at Delphi, upon the doors of Apollo’s temple, which is sufficiently well known: ΓΝΩΘΙ ΣΕΑΥΤΟΝ (“KNOW YOURSELF”). The Codex Agobardinus and the Aldine edition are therefore wrong in reading “saying the lord of all,” etc.; and Rhenanus, “you will be called lord,” etc. The Fulda manuscript also has: “you will learn God, the lord of all who die,” where the copyist supposed that God alone was here called lord—for that is either what he wrote or what he intended—of all who die and rise again. But see our note immediately below [Col. 0525D]. I also laughed at the ingenuity of a certain bard who dared to translate—or rather pervert—this little work into the Dutch language.
