He interprets it as though he had read: “You, man, are only—if you understand your own, or learn from the inscription of the Pythia—the lord,” etc. The name “man,” he says, means something like “earth”; and he interprets “the inscription of the Pythia” as “a name,” adding in his notes that in Greek speech it signifies stench and putrefaction. But it is well that I have resolved to rescue so exacting an author from those utterly defiled hands by means of a new and accurate translation—if only the printers and purchasers permit it—since, having already completed a translation of the two books *To the Nations*, I have also made considerable progress on this *Apology*. HAV.], you are lord of all things that die and rise again [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Lord of all things that die and rise again.” That is, “you who are lord,” etc.—namely, of those creatures which I have just said die and come back to life, all of which are either under the yoke of man or serve his needs. Chrysostom, on Genesis 1:28, Homily IX: “God made man ruler of everything upon the earth, and [Col. 0526B] nothing upon earth is greater than man; rather, everything is under his power.” The same author, on Genesis 4, Homily XXI: “For just as God, who is the founder and maker of all things, holds sovereignty over all things, both visible and invisible, so too, when he formed this rational animal, he wished it to be distinguished by authority over all visible things.” Again, in the sermon *That Adam Was Set Above Every Creature*: “Especially since God, the same craftsman, was going to hand over to this same man his own power over the entire fabric, so that the one whom he intended to make a secondary governor after himself he might also make full and perfect, possessing within himself both the dignity by which he would excel and the power by which he would rule all living creatures; serving him alone, by whom all things had been subjected to him, so that he might rule the world, serve God, look up to the Creator, compel creation to obey him, and perceive that he owed to the Lord as much dominion over himself as he himself demanded from creation.”

But since [Col. 0526C] I take very great delight in reading Chrysostom and am affected by it beyond belief, allow me to attach to these another passage from his *Exposition of Psalm IX*, where he shows that this dominion in man was indeed diminished after sin, yet was left sufficiently great for man’s benefit and by divine providence. His golden words are:

“If, however, he took away some small part, this too was an act of his providence. Before disobedience man ruled the beasts; after disobedience, however, something was taken away from this power. For even now he rules them by certain arts, though with fear and trembling. He neither removed the whole dominion nor left it whole, but permitted those creatures which were necessary to him for nourishment and exercise to remain subject; those that are more savage, however, he did not treat in the same way, so that through his struggle with them man might be reminded of the ancient sin of Adam, the first parent. Hence even from the fact that they are not wholly subject to us, great profit comes to us. For how would it help us if we had the lion subdued to our power and domesticated? What benefit would it bring us if we had the leopard tame? Nothing except arrogance and pride. He therefore permitted these creatures to be exempt from our rule; but those useful to us he made tame: the ox that plows, the sheep that clothes the nakedness of our body, beasts of burden suited to carrying goods that may be imported or exported, and birds and fish so that our table might be more plentiful.”

He illustrates the matter by a comparison:

“For just as one who disinherits a son does not deprive him of everything, but only of some part, so that he may correct himself, so also does God. Indeed, it is not even so, but rather the reverse. For a man who disinherits another deprives him of the greater share and leaves the smaller; God, however, left the greater share and deprived him of only a tiny portion, and that for his benefit, lest all the other creatures should easily overpower him.” HAV.], will you die for the purpose of perishing? Wherever you have been dissolved, whatever material has destroyed, swallowed up, abolished, or reduced you to nothing, it will restore you. Nothingness itself belongs to him to whom the whole belongs.

“Then,” you say, “we shall always have to die and always rise again.” If the Lord of all things had so ordained, you would unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0526B] Havercamp conjectures *ingratiis*, “unwillingly.”] [Note: [Col. 0526D] “You would unwillingly experience the law of your condition.” *Ingratis*, for which others read *ingratiis*, means: “Even against your will, you would experience the law of your condition.” RIG.] experience the law of your condition. But as matters stand [Col. 0526A], he has ordained no differently from what he proclaimed.

The same principle which composed the universe out of diversity, so that all things should consist in unity from mutually opposed substances—from void and solid, animate and inanimate, comprehensible and incomprehensible, light and darkness, life itself and death—has likewise woven the age together under an appointed and differentiated condition: this first part, which we inhabit, flows from the beginning of things through temporal duration toward its end; but the next part, which we await, extends into infinite eternity.

Therefore, when the end and the intervening boundary [Note: [Col. 0526D] “Therefore, when the end and the intervening boundary, which stands open between them, has arrived.” [Col. 0527B] The meaning of this somewhat obscure passage is as follows: when the appointed time and that final boundary which lies between the temporal and the perpetual age—called by the Apostle Paul ἄτομος καὶ ῥιπὴ ὀφθαλμοῦ (“an indivisible instant and the twinkling of an eye”) (First Epistle to the Corinthians 15:52)—shall arrive, so that even the form of the world itself, which is as temporal as the age and time itself and which until now, like a thick veil or immense wall, prevents the enjoyment of eternity, may pass away and be changed, then the entire human race will be restored, etc. Septimius’s sentence might perhaps be better punctuated thus: “Therefore, when the end and boundary—the intervening one which stands open between them—has arrived.” HAV.], which stands open between them, has arrived, so that even the form of the world itself, equally temporal, may be transformed—the form which has been stretched before that ordering of eternity like a curtain [Col. 0527A] [Note: [Col. 0527C] “Has been stretched before it like a curtain.” Above, chapter XVI, concerning the veil of the sanctuary: “Even the sight of the rest was forbidden by a curtain stretched before it.” Here he may have had in view Virgil, who in Book II, line 604, represents Venus speaking thus to her son Aeneas:

> Look—for all the cloud which now, drawn over your sight,  
> Dulls your mortal vision and, damply gathering round it,  
> Darkens it, I shall remove.

Homer had preceded him; in that author, *Iliad* V, line 127, Pallas speaks thus to Diomedes:

> Ἀχλὺν δ` αὖ τοι ἀπ` ὀφθαλμῶν ἕλον ἢ πρὶν ἐπῆεν,

Ὅφρ` εὖ γινώσκῃς ἢ μὲν Θεὸν ἢδὲ καὶ ἄνδρα

“I have taken from your eyes the mist that formerly lay upon them, so that you may clearly distinguish both god and man.”.

That is: “I have removed from your eyes the mist which formerly obstructed them, so that you may clearly distinguish both man and god.” Eunapius of Sardis speaks in nearly the same manner in a similar story about the disciples of Iamblichus, p. 25:

> ὡς ἐνοχλοῖ ἡ μὲν αὐτῶν πολλάκις μικρὸν εἶναι φάσκοντες (“perhaps because their less acute sight was impeded”—the recovered Greek is grammatically corrupt, so the rendering is approximate).

That is, “because perhaps their less acute vision had been impeded.” And in a true history, in response to Elisha’s prayers [Col. 0527D], God opened the servant’s eyes so that he might see the heavenly hosts (2 Kings 6:17). Relevant here also is God’s promise, desirable to all nations, in Isaiah 25:7: “And upon this mountain the Lord will abolish the covering of the face, and the veil with which all nations are covered.” HAV.]—then the entire human race will be restored, to settle the account of whatever good or evil it earned in this age, and thereafter to receive its payment throughout the boundless perpetuity of eternity [Note: [Col. 0527B] “And thereafter to perish into the boundless perpetuity,” Fr.].

And therefore there will no longer be death, nor resurrection again and again; rather, we shall be the same people that we are now, and no others afterward: the worshipers of God will be with God forever, clothed over with the proper substance of eternity; but the profane and those who are not wholly devoted to God will be in the punishment of an equally perpetual fire, which from its own nature possesses a divine supply, namely, of incorruptibility [Note: [Col. 0527B] Hav.: “and those who are not wholly devoted to God, in the punishment [Rig.: into the punishment] of an equally perpetual fire, possessing [Rig.: they possessing] from its own nature, namely, a divine supply of incorruptibility”].

The philosophers too know the difference between secret and ordinary fire. Thus the fire which serves human use is far different from that which appears in God’s judgment, whether drawing forth thunderbolts from heaven [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Whether drawing forth thunderbolts from heaven.” That is, eliciting them, and thus drawing a fiery sword, as it were, out of the clouds as from a sheath. So Virgil in *Aeneid* I.48 represents Ajax, son of Oileus, as pierced through the breast by a thunderbolt as though by a sword:

> Him, breathing flames from his transfixed breast,  
> She caught up in a whirlwind and impaled upon a sharp rock. HAV.], or belching up from the earth through the summits of mountains [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Or belching up from the earth through the summits of mountains.” In chapter XL he joined these together as punitive fires: “When Vulsinii was deluged from heaven, and Pompeii from its own mountain.” He calls the waves of flame which are driven with a great whirlwind within volcanic mountains, belched up, and burst outward “summits.” The ancients used both *vortex* and *vertex*. Lucretius VI.296:

> When it has split it, immediately that fiery  
> Vortex falls.

The same author, I.294:

> Sometimes in a twisting vortex  
> They seize them and carry them spinning in a swift whirlwind. HAV.];

for it does not consume what it burns, but restores it while expending itself. Thus [Col. 0527B] the mountains remain forever burning, and the person who is touched by fire from heaven [Col. 0528A] remains intact, so that no other fire can thereafter reduce him to ashes [Note: [Col. 0528B] “So that no other fire can thereafter reduce him to ashes.” Either Minucius understood this passage as though Tertullian were intimating what experience teaches, namely, that bodies struck by lightning appear unharmed, when he writes, p. 39: “Just as the fires of thunderbolts touch bodies but do not consume them.” The Gallic translator understood it in the same way. Or else he departed from the opinion which our author appears either to defend or to have in view. For when he says, “remains intact, so that no other fire can thereafter reduce him to ashes,” he may appear to teach that corpses struck by lightning cannot be consumed by fire. Thus the ancients denied that the hearts of those who had taken poison could be burned. Pliny XI.37: “It is said that the heart cannot be burned in those who died of cardiac disease or were killed by poison.” Certainly there survives a speech of Vitellius in which he convicted Piso of that crime, using this argument: he publicly declared that the heart of Germanicus Caesar could not have been burned because of the poison.

And perhaps from that Etruscan discipline came Numa’s law quoted by Festus under the word *Occisum*: “IF JUPITER’S THUNDERBOLT HAS KILLED A MAN, DO NOT LIFT HIM ABOVE THE KNEES”; and in the same place: “IF A MAN SHALL HAVE BEEN KILLED BY LIGHTNING, NO FUNERAL RITES OUGHT TO BE PERFORMED FOR HIM.” For they were buried where they had been struck by lightning and were not cremated like other corpses; the place was sacred and was called a *bidental*. [Col. 0528D] Persius, Satire II.27:

> You lie there grimly, a *bidental* to be avoided amid the groves.

There the highly learned notes of Casaubon may be consulted, as may those of Scaliger on Festus under the word *Bidental*. One may add Jacob Nicolaus Loensis, *Miscellanies* III.17, who shows from Euripides and Statius that this was unknown to Greek custom.

Or finally, with this rite in view, the author may have meant that one killed by lightning, and thus by heavenly fire, was safe from the flame of the funeral pyre because he was not cremated but buried, as were all Christians, who refused to be placed upon a pyre, as is clear from chapter XLII: “The Sabaeans know that more and dearer merchandise of theirs is expended in burying Christians than in fumigating the gods.” But I do not adopt this interpretation. HAV.].

And this will be a testimony to eternal fire; this will be an example of the perpetual judgment that nourishes its punishment. Mountains burn and endure: what, then, of the guilty and the enemies of God?

## CHAPTER XLIX

**ARGUMENT.—It is therefore absurd that the same thing should be praised and admired in philosophers, but hated and persecuted in Christians. Even if their opinion be false, since it nevertheless conduces to upright living, it ought to be assigned to ridicule rather than punishment. Yet the populace exults in those punishments—absurdly indeed, since these punishments are a joy to Christians, who would rather be unjustly harassed and condemned than fall away from God.**

These are the things [Note: [Col. 0528B] “These,” Rig., Haverc.] which in us alone are called presumptions, but in philosophers and poets are called the highest knowledge and marks of genius [Col. 0528B]. They are prudent; we are foolish [Note: [Col. 0528D] “They are prudent; we are foolish.” Arnobius, Book I: “And those who revere Fauns, Fatuae, the Genii of cities, Pans, and Bellonas appear to you shrewd, wise, and most prudent, deserving no reproach whatever. [Col. 0529C] We are declared dull, stupid, foolish, obtuse, and brutish because we have surrendered ourselves to God, by whose command and judgment everything that exists has its being and is fixed immovably in the perpetuity of his decree.” The same author, Book II: “Thus you do not consider it utterly unjust to ride us down and mock us as though we were uttering stupid and brutish things. Why are we judged by you to be brutish and stupid?” Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 13: “Why, therefore, are we commonly regarded as stupid, vain, and foolish, when we follow a master who is wise even by the confession of the gods themselves?” HAV.]; they are to be honored, [Col. 0529A] we ridiculed—indeed, more than that, punished.

Let what we defend now be false and deservedly called presumptions; nevertheless, it is necessary. Let it be foolish; nevertheless, it is useful, since those who believe it are compelled to become better through fear of eternal punishment and hope of eternal refreshment. It is therefore not expedient that things which it is expedient to presume true should be called false or considered foolish [Note: [Col. 0529B] “And it is expedient,” Fran.]. Things that are beneficial may under no designation whatsoever be condemned [Note: [Col. 0529B] “Things that are altogether beneficial,” Fran., Paris.]. Consequently, in your case the presumption is precisely this: condemning beneficial things. Such things therefore cannot be foolish; and certainly, even if false and foolish, they are nevertheless harmful to no one. For they are similar to many other things on which you impose no punishment—vain and fabulous things, unaccused and unpunished because harmless.

But errors of this kind—if errors they indeed are—must be judged with ridicule [Note: [Col. 0529B] Rig.: “But in matters of this kind, then, if indeed so, it must be judged in laughter,” etc. Hav. deleted the word *enim*. Heraldi’s manuscripts have: “But in matters of this kind, then, if indeed so, it must be judged fit for ridicule”; and he himself preferred to write [Col. 0529C]: “But if in matters of this kind there is error, it must indeed be judged with ridicule,” etc. The Fulda manuscript: “as harmful: equally, then, if indeed so, it must be judged into ridicule.” Ald., Rhen., and Gangn.: “But in matters of this kind, if indeed so, it must be assigned to mockery,” etc. The Frankfurt edition [Col. 0530B]: “But if in matters of this kind there is error, it must be punished with ridicule,” etc. Gelenius: “But an error of this kind, if it is indeed one, must be assigned to mockery, not punished with swords and beasts.” We have not hesitated to write *errores*, “errors,” instead of *error*, so that both “of this kind” and “must be judged” may have something to which they refer.], not with swords, fires, crosses, and beasts.

At the injustice of this cruelty not only does this blind populace exult [Col. 0529B], but even some among you boast, men who seek popular favor from injustice—as though everything you can do against us were not subject to our own choice. Certainly, if I wish, I am a Christian; therefore you will condemn me only if I wish to be condemned. But since you cannot do to me what lies within your power unless I wish it, what you can do is now a matter of my will, not of your power.

Consequently, the populace rejoices vainly in our persecution, for the joy which it claims for itself is ours, since we would rather be condemned than fall away from God. On the contrary, those who hate us ought to grieve [Col. 0530A], not rejoice, when we have obtained what we chose [Note: [Col. 0530C] *Elegimus*, Fran.].

## CHAPTER L

**But although Christians expose themselves to torments and willingly cast away their lives, they do not do so after the manner of the gentiles, for whom despair and an itch for glory prepare this path of contempt for pain and death, but after the manner of a most courageous soldier, who undertakes war although he does not love it, and rejoices in victory although he trembled in achieving it. It must therefore be admitted that theirs is true steadfastness, which reveals itself in deeds, not words; seeks favor with God, not praise among men; and through contemplation and the example of its own unshaken resolution daily produces more people to embrace it than ever emerged as disciples from all the schools of all the philosophers, captivated by the blandishments of words.**

“Then,” you say, “why do you complain that we persecute you, if you wish to suffer, when you ought to love those through whom you suffer what you wish?” We certainly wish to suffer [Note: [Col. 0529C] “We certainly wish to suffer.” The Fulda manuscript deletes the final word, and it can be absent. Relevant here are the words of chapter I: “What sort of evil is this, whose accused rejoices, whose accusation is his prayer, and whose punishment is victory?” And *To Scapula*, chapter I: “We rejoice more when condemned than when acquitted.” The same work, chapter II: “For far be it from us to resent suffering the things we desire.” And in the final chapter: “Your cruelty is our glory. Take care only that, through the very fact that we endure such things, we may not appear to break out for this sole purpose: to prove precisely that we do not fear these things but voluntarily summon them.” “For far be it,” he says in *On Patience*, chapter VIII, “that there should be such pollution in a servant of Christ that a patience prepared for greater trials should fail in trivial matters.” HAV.], but in the same manner in which no one willingly [Note: [Col. 0530C] Thus Rig. and Hav. on the authority of the Fulda manuscript. The others: “in which also a soldier suffers war. For no one willingly,” etc.] suffers war, since it is necessary both to tremble and to incur danger [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Since it is necessary both to tremble and to incur danger.” Nature, of course, is so constituted that, when the actual battle and risk to life have arrived, a certain horror assails even the bravest, since that day

> Οὐ μῆν ἔς γε χορὸν κέλετ` ἐλθέμεν, ἀλλὰ μάχεσθαι (“Surely it does not bid us come to the dance, but to fight”),

that is, “does not bid one come to dance, but to fight,” as Homer has it in *Iliad* XV.508. This is elegantly taught by Lucan in his description of that decisive battle between Caesar and Pompey, Book VII.467:

> Yet numbness bound every breast,  
> And chilled blood gathered in their vitals, struck by natural affection;  
> Entire cohorts held their long-prepared javelins  
> In outstretched arms,

when, as the same author says there at line 128,

> Fierce spirits beat upon their own breasts  
> With uncertain strokes. On many a face is the pallor  
> Of approaching death, an image most like their fate.

For Στρατιώτης ἐν χερσὶν ἔχων μάχην, πῶς οἶδεν εἰ ζήσεται; τοσαῦται τῶν θανάτων εἰσὶν ὁδοί (“How does a soldier with battle in his hands know whether he will live? So many are the paths to death.”), that is, “Who, when just about to enter battle, can be certain that he will survive, when a soldier has so many paths to death?” as Charmides, unable to endure his passion, says in Achilles Tatius, Book IV.];

nevertheless he fights with all his strength [Note: [Col. 0530D] “Nevertheless he fights with all his strength.” For, as Ajax suitably says in Homer, *Iliad* XV.808:

> Βέλτερον ἢ ἀπολέσθαι ἕνα χρόνον, ἠὲ βιῶναι,

Ἢ δηθὰ ϛρεύγεσθσι ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊότητι

“It is better either to perish once or to live than to be worn away for a long time in dreadful combat.” (The recovered form ϛρεύγεσθσι is corrupt.),

that is, “It is better either to perish once or to live than to be consumed for a long time in grievous battle.” There, since

> The coward and the brave alike must fall,

according to Cato’s oracle in Lucan IX.583, cowards who flee often perish shamefully, while the brave both live and conquer. Cicero speaks finely in *Tusculan Disputations* II: “As happens in battle, when a cowardly and timid soldier, as soon as he sees the enemy, throws away his shield and flees as fast as he can, and for that very reason perishes, sometimes even without a wound, while nothing of the kind happens to the man who stood his ground; so those who cannot endure the appearance of pain cast themselves down and thus lie afflicted and dispirited, whereas those who resist [Col. 0531B] very often depart victorious.”

The same author praises greatness and steadfastness of spirit in Trebonius, of whom he says in *Philippic* XI, chapter VI, that he endured Dolabella’s cruelty and the butchery of his body bravely and patiently. He adds: “Great praise—and in my judgment the greatest of all. For it belongs to a wise man to consider beforehand everything that can happen to a human being and, if it occurs, to bear it calmly. It certainly shows greater prudence to take precautions that nothing of the kind occur; but it shows no less courage to bear it bravely if it does.” HAV.];

and the man who complained of the battle rejoices when victorious in battle, because [Col. 0531A] he obtains both glory and spoil [Note: [Col. 0531B] “Because he obtains both glory and spoil.” Menedemus, reproaching his son much too harshly in Terence’s *The Self-Tormentor*, Act I, Scene I, says among other things:

> At your age I did not devote myself to love,  
> But left this place for Asia because of poverty; and there  
> I found both wealth and glory in the arms of war.

The glory of Christian service is to please God; its spoil is to live [Col. 0531C] forever, as immediately follows. Indeed, “the accusation is his prayer, and the punishment victory,” as he said in chapter I. The Codex Agobardinus: “who both glory.” HAV.].

For us, the battle is that we are summoned before tribunals, so that there, at the risk of our lives, we may contend for the truth. Victory, moreover, is to obtain that for which you contended. That victory possesses both the glory of pleasing God and the spoil of living forever.

But we are struck from the account [Note: [Col. 0531C] “But we are struck from the account, certainly when we have obtained.” We die in battle, he says, and this you object against us. But it is honorable to die for one’s country—which for us is heaven, chapter I.

> Οὐ γὰρ ἀεικὲς ἀμυνομένῳ περὶ πὰτρης

Τεθνάμεν

“For it is no disgrace to die while defending one’s fatherland.”.

This is Hector’s noble utterance in Homer, *Iliad* XV.496: it is honorable even for victors to die, and thus τὸν ἀγῶνα τὸν καλὸν ἀγωνίζεσθαι (“to fight the good fight”), as Paul testifies of himself in 2 Timothy 4:7. For those who had shown themselves brave and had fallen after winning a glorious victory for their country were called καλῶς ἀγωνίζεσθαι (“to contend nobly”; the recovered infinitive does not fit the surrounding phrase “were called”) by the Lacedaemonians, as is well known from Aelian VI.6:

> Οἱ δὲ καλῶς ἀγωνισάμενοι καὶ ἀποθανόντες θάλλοις ἀνεδοῦντο, καὶ κλάδοις ἐτέροις, καὶ δι` ἐπαίνων ἤγοντο (“Those who had contended nobly and died were crowned with olive shoots and other branches and conducted with praises.”).

That is: “Those who had shown themselves brave and had fallen were crowned with olive and other branches and borne along with praises.”

Chrysostom speaks excellently [Col. 0531D] in his sermon *On the Imitation of the Martyrs*: “In short, in the Christian contest, either the surviving soldier returns happily from battle after overthrowing the enemy, or, by dying, he conquers the enemy as victor. For he conquers happily who after victory does not know how to be conquered.” For, as Prosper says in his *Epigrams*:

> No crown may be hoped for by one who does not contend.  
> The palm by which glory is won comes only at the end.

The term *obducere* is correctly taken from accounting, namely, “to strike from the account,” like *expungere*. Because copyists did not understand this, they corrupted the passage; hence the Fulda manuscript has: “but we are certainly killed.” The printed editions, except those of Rigaltius and Junius, also punctuate it wrongly: “But we are certainly struck from the account, when,” etc. So above, chapter XLVI: “While an account is struck from the goodness of this sect.” HAV.], certainly when we have obtained our object. Therefore we have conquered when we are killed; in short, we escape when we are struck from the account.

Although you may now call us “faggot-men” [Note: [Col. 0531D] “Faggot-men and half-axle men.” Why Christians were so called he explains in the following words: “because, bound to a stake made from half an axle, we are burned within a ring of faggots.” For all the manuscripts, Belgian [Col. 0532B] as well as Gallic and Vatican, consistently read this; and there has been added the conjecture by which it is thought more idiomatic Latin to read *semiaxarios* and *axis*, instead of what had previously been printed, *semissarios*, while Crinitus long ago, in *On Honorable Learning* I.13, read *semissios*, and each understood it as “half an *as*.” PAM.] and “half-axle men” [Note: [Col. 0531A] Ald.: *semassios*; Rhen., Gangn., and Barraeus: *semissios*; Gelen.: *semissarios*; Cod. Lugd.: *semarios*; Fuld.: “faggot-men [Col. 0532A] and half-axle men.”], because, bound to a stake made from half an axle, we are burned within a ring of faggots. This is the attire of our victory; this is our palm-embroidered robe [Note: [Col. 0532B] “This is our palm-embroidered robe.” That palm-embroidered tunic, so famous among the Romans, was the garment of those celebrating a triumph, called “palm-embroidered” from the palm branches woven into it. The faggots with which our predecessors were burned, however, and the axle to which they were bound were the attire of the Christians’ triumph: that was the procession in which they flew upright into heaven. LE PR.]; in such a chariot we celebrate our triumph.

It is therefore natural that we do not please you, the vanquished; for this reason we are considered desperate and lost [Col. 0532A]. But among you this desperation and ruin, when undertaken for the sake of glory and fame, raise aloft the standard of courage.

Mucius willingly left his right hand upon the altar: what sublimity of spirit! Empedocles [Note: [Col. 0532B] Empedocles, whom he wittily mocks in *On the Soul*, chapter XXXII, where he discusses Pythagorean transmigration: “But Empedocles, since he had raved that he was a god, for that reason, I suppose, disdained to remember himself as any of the heroes. ‘I was a shrub and a fish,’ he says. Why not rather a gourd, so tasteless, and a chameleon, so puffed up? Evidently, like a fish, lest he rot under the conditions of some burial, he preferred to roast himself by throwing himself into Etna.” LE PR.] gave his entire self to the fires of Etna at Catana: what vigor of mind! A certain foundress of Carthage gave herself to the funeral pyre rather than to a second marriage: what a proclamation of chastity! Regulus, lest one man should live in exchange for many enemies, suffered crosses throughout his entire body: what a brave man, a victor even in captivity [Note: [Col. 0532C] “What a brave man, a victor even in captivity!” That is the praise assigned to him by Cicero in *On Duties* III.99. There the history of his ill-fated courage is related: “When Marcus Atilius Regulus, during his second consulship, had been captured in Africa through an ambush—Xanthippus the Spartan serving as commander and Hamilcar, Hannibal’s father, as commanding general—he was sent under oath to the Senate, on the condition that, unless certain noble Carthaginian prisoners were returned, he himself would return to Carthage. When he arrived at Rome, he saw the appearance of advantage, but judged it false, as the event makes clear. It consisted in remaining in his native country, living in his own home with his wife and children, regarding the calamity he had suffered in war as a common hazard of military fortune, and retaining the rank of consular dignity. Who would deny that these things were advantageous? What do you think?” He immediately adds: “Greatness of spirit and courage deny it.”]!

When Anaxarchus was being pounded with a pestle like barley groats [Note: [Col. 0532A] Thus the Fulda manuscript, Ald., Rig., and Hav.; others: “to destruction.”], he said: “Pound, pound [Note: [Col. 0532C] “Anaxarchus, when like…” Famous is the saying of Anaxarchus in Laertius, Book IX. When he was being pounded [Col. 0532D] by Nicocreon σιδηροῖς ὑπέροις (“with iron pestles”) with iron hammers because Nicocreon had heard that he himself deserved to be served up as a meal, the philosopher is said to have declared with full courage:

> πτίσσε τοῦ Ἀναξάρχου θύλακον, Ἀνάξαρκον δὲ οὐ πτίσσεις (“Pound Anaxarchus’s sack; you are not pounding Anaxarchus.” The recovered second spelling of the name, Ἀνάξαρκον, appears corrupt.).

“Pound Anaxarchus’s little sack, for you are not pounding Anaxarchus.” LAC.], the sack of Anaxarchus [Note: [Col. 0532D] “The sack of Anaxarchus.” Elegantly expressed: for while being pounded like barley groats or barley, he likewise declares that nothing else is happening to him than happens to barley—namely, that the divine inner particle, the vigor of the mind, remains unharmed, while only the perishable husk is broken and scattered. For this is what he called his little body, within which that element was in no way afflicted. Marcus Antoninus calls it τὸ ἔνδον ἐγκεκρυμμένον (“the thing hidden within”) in Book X; Iamblichus, θεῖος ἄνθρωπος (“the divine man”); Stobaeus, in his *Physical Extracts*, τὸ ἡγεμονικὀν μέρος (“the governing part”); and finally Philo Judaeus, in *On the Preliminary Studies*, ἄνθρωπος ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ, κρείττων ἐν χείρονι, ἀθάνατος ἐν (“a man within a man, the better within the worse, the immortal within”) [Col. 0533B] θνητῷ (“the mortal”). To these should be added the incomparable commentary of Isaac Casaubon on Persius, Satire V.129:

> But if within, and in the diseased liver,  
> Masters arise.

From this one understands Paul’s highly learned expression when he writes in Romans 7:24, Τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου (“Who will deliver me from this body of death?”), as well as the words read in verse 23. After the example of this Anaxarchus, *sack* and *little sack* were commonly used for the mortal body. I have seen examples in Lindenbrog’s notes on Virgil’s *Catalecta*, p. 301; Elmenhorst’s notes on Arnobius, p. 66; and Lydius’s *On Military Affairs*, p. 77. To these may be added the following passage from Gregory Nazianzen, *On the Different Ways of Life* [Col. 0533C]: “Yet Gregory will no longer be a companion to the Emperor as he was before, gratifying his belly somewhat, reclining sad and silent among the banqueters, scarcely drawing breath, and eating in a servile fashion.” HAV.]; for you are not pounding Anaxarchus [Col. 0533A] [Note: [Col. 0533C] “For you are not pounding Anaxarchus.” The same Gregory of Cygnus, in his poem *On Humility of Soul*: “Or shall anyone behold the pounding of Anaxarchus’s hands in the mortar, as though he were not present, while he nevertheless ordered his own skin-bag to be pounded violently, as though he himself remained unpounded, so that he might be seen to be no one [reading uncertain]?” Concerning Zeno, Diogenes Laertius—to whom he attributes this—writes:

> Ἤθελες, ὧ Ζὴνων, καλὸν ἤθελες, ἄνδρα τὑραννον

   Κτείνας, ἐκλῦσαι δουλοσύνας Ἐλέαν

“You desired, O Zeno—you desired a noble thing: by killing the tyrant, to free Elea from slavery.”.

Ἀλλ` ἐδάμης, δὴ γάρ σε λαβὼν ὁ τύραννος ἐν ὅλμῳ

   Κόψε. τὶ τοῦτο λέγω; σῶμα γὰρ, οὐχί δὲ σε. That is: “You nobly wished, O Zeno, by killing the tyrant to free Elea from servitude. But he was overcome: for the tyrant, having seized you, [Col. 0533D] crushed you in a mortar. What am I saying? Not you, but your body.” Nonnus, in the passage cited above, says of Epictetus: “His leg was bound in fetters by the Macedonian tyrant. Afterwards, when the tyrant wished to release him and asked him, ‘Would you like me to release you, Epictetus?’ he said, ‘Why? Am I bound?’” By these words, of course, he meant that his soul had by no means been bound. Accordingly, it is not the body that is called the man, but the soul. HAV.]: O the magnanimity of the philosopher, who even jested about such an end of his own! I pass over those who bargained for glory with their own sword or some other milder kind of death. For behold, even contests in torture are crowned by you. The Attic courtesan [Note: [Col. 0533D] **The Attic courtesan.** This prostitute, who was closely associated through her lyre-playing with Harmodius and Aristogiton, did not betray their plans for tyrannicide, although tortured by the tyrants to the point of death. Therefore the Athenians, wishing to hold her in honor, yet not to seem to have celebrated a prostitute, made an image of the animal bearing her name; and, so that the reason for the honor might be understood, they forbade the artist to add a tongue to the work. PAM.], when the executioner was already exhausted, at last spat her chewed-off tongue into the face of the raging tyrant, so that she might spit out her voice as well and be unable to betray the conspirators even if, once overcome, she had wished to do so. Zeno of Elea, when asked by Dionysius what philosophy afforded, answered, “Contempt for death”; subjected to the tyrant’s scourges [Note: [Col. 0533B] Thus Gelenius and Rigault; the Fulda codex and Havercamp’s edition read: “to become insensible through contempt for death,” etc. Rhenanus and Heraldus read “by insensible [Col. 0534B] scourges”; others: “insensible to scourges,” etc. We have adopted the word *subjected* from the Fulda codex; the common reading is *exposed*.], he attested his maxim even unto death. Certainly the scourging of the Spartans, made still more bitter under the eyes of relatives who even encouraged them, confers upon their house (6) [Col. 0534A] as much honor for endurance as the quantity of blood they shed. O permissible glory, because it is human—a glory which, for its contempt for death and every kind of cruelty, is charged neither with ruinous presumption nor with desperate conviction; for which it is permitted to suffer as much for one’s country, one’s land [Note: [Col. 0533D] **For one’s country, one’s land.** Since the Fulda manuscript usefully supplies us with the addition “for one’s land,” Rigault ought not to have rejected it—not to mention the others, [Col. 0534B] who did not even deign to inspect such excellent material. For in this way each item corresponds to another: Mucius, Regulus, and Zeno to country; the Spartans, and perhaps Zeno himself, to dominion; the Attic courtesan to friendship; Empedocles and Anaxarchus to human glory. But to “land” corresponds Queen Dido, who, having measured out an immense area with an ox-hide, deceived the Africans; for she herself was Tyrian. She was not merely fleeing marriage with Iarbas, but foresightedly took care that Carthage should be sought under that guise, as is splendidly evident in the marriage of Arsinoë and Ptolemy in Justin, book XXI, chapter 3. HAV.], dominion, or friendship as it is not permitted to suffer for God! And yet upon all of them you lavish statues [Note: [Col. 0534B] **Statues.** By these antiquity sought protection for itself unto eternity. Hence Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.34, recounts the ingenious device of Phidias: “But why mention poets? Even craftsmen wish to be ennobled after death. For what did Phidias do? He enclosed a likeness of himself upon Minerva’s shield, since he was not permitted to inscribe his name.” There is a notable passage of Eusebius in book I of the *Life of Constantine the Great*, chapter 2: “Human nature, frail and transitory in its lot, devised a consolation: by producing images it thought that it honored the memory of its ancestors with an honor that would endure—partly through an outline in painting, smeared with wax, and partly by contriving from sculpted and carved, motionless material a likeness insensible to movement.” HAV.], you inscribe images [Note: [Col. 0534C] **You inscribe images.** These are still everywhere visible upon marbles, gems, and the sacred relics of the ancient age. Hence Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXV, chapter 2, thus foretold the fate of Varro’s work [a mortal work, alas, and one that experienced the laws of mortality], in which he included images or descriptions of illustrious Romans: “By the invention of this gift he made even the gods envious, since he not only bestowed immortality, but also sent it throughout all lands, so that they might everywhere be present and capable of being enclosed.” HAV.], and you carve titles [Note: [Col. 0534D] **And you carve titles for eternity.** That architect therefore employed a cunning design to perpetuate his own name: on the proud structures of the Egyptians he carved his name and the dedication of the work into a harder material; over this, after it had been coated and concealed with plaster, he inscribed the king’s name. He readily foresaw that when the more fragile material fell away, the king’s memory would be erased, while his own would endure. Eusebius, in the same passage: “There are those who have believed that pillars and inscribed stelae confer an everlasting commendation upon the virtue of those whose names they bear.” Hence Cicero, *Philippic* XIV, chapter 33, thus celebrates the consuls Pansa and Hirtius, who were slain for the Republic: “A monument, therefore, will be erected with magnificent workmanship, and letters will be carved upon it as everlasting witnesses of divine courage; and the most grateful discourse concerning you will never fall silent among those who either see your monument or hear of it. Thus, in accordance with the mortal condition, you have attained immortality of life.” HAV.] for eternity; to the extent that you can through monuments, you yourselves in some fashion bestow resurrection upon the dead. Yet anyone who hopes for the true resurrection from God, if he suffers for God, is mad.

But carry on, worthy governors—you will be far better in the eyes of the people if you sacrifice Christians to them. Torture us, rack us, condemn us, grind us down: your injustice is the proof of our innocence. For that reason God permits us [Col. 0535A] to suffer these things. Indeed, only recently, by condemning a Christian woman to a pimp [Note: [Col. 0535A] **By condemning a Christian woman to a pimp.** The Fulda manuscript corruptly reads: “You thought it preferable for a Christian woman to be condemned to a lion rather than to a lion, and you have confessed,” etc. Barrée reads: “by shouting for a pimp” [Col. 0535B]. This too was one of the acclamations of the raging populace, as Ferrarius teaches in *On the Ancient Acclamations*, book VII, chapter 18. It was certainly the greatest possible outrage against chaste women, one which they would have preferred to redeem with a thousand deaths. Not without reason, therefore, does Nazianzen launch the weapons of his eloquence when, in his *Oration against the Arians and concerning Himself*, he reproaches the raging Arians with an almost similar inhuman and criminal act: Παρθένων, he says, αἰδὼς καὶ σεμνότης ὂψεις ἄνδρων μηδὲ σωφρόνων φέρουσα· σὲ δὲ τῖς ἡμῶν ῃσχυνε καὶ καθύβρισε μέχρι τῶν ἀθεάτων, καὶ ἀσεβῶν ὂψεσι προύθηκε θέαν ἐλεεινὴν καὶ τοῦ Σοδομιτικοῦ πυρὸς ἁξίαν, εῶ γὰρ θανάτους λέγειν τῆς αἰσχύνης ἀνεκτοτέρους, that is: “O modesty and chastity of virgins, which cannot bear even the sight of respectable men, which of us dishonored you—even down to those parts which it is impious to behold—and exposed you as a pitiable spectacle to the eyes of the impious, an offense to be avenged with the fire of Sodom? For I pass over the killings, which were more tolerable than this disgrace.” John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, book III, chapter XIII: “Yet it was long ago determined by the Fathers that chastity cannot be taken away unless corruption of the mind precedes. For, as the great Augustine asserts, what the body suffers violently without preceding lust should be called affliction rather than corruption. Chastity can therefore be preserved where corruption can only be voluntary: namely, in the integrity of the mind, where chastity can be preserved forever.” That is, as our author says on another matter in *On Monogamy*, chapter XV: “Surely she is more capable of excuse who fell in battle than she who fell in the bedroom; she who succumbed on the rack than she who did so in bed; she who yielded to cruelty than she who yielded to lust; she who was overcome groaning than she who was overcome panting with desire.” HAV.] rather than to a lion, you confessed that among us the stain upon chastity is regarded as more atrocious than every punishment and every death. Yet not even the most exquisitely devised form of your cruelty accomplishes anything: it is rather an enticement to our sect. We become more numerous [Note: [Col. 0535C] **We become more numerous whenever we are reaped by you.** The Fulda manuscript also reads *p. e.* What wonder, then, if you hear that apostate Julian, *Letter* XXIII, calls Constantius πολυκέφαλον ὕδραν, “a many-headed hydra”? For there is also a very large bronze coin of Herculius Maximianus in the treasury of the Christian queen, upon which he is seen, like Hercules, [Col. 0536A] as victor fighting the hydra πολυκεφάλου, with the inscription **TO HERCULES THE SUBDUER**. A remarkable gold coin of Diocletian, his partner in the empire and in hatred against [Col. 0536B] the Christians, is also presented by Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, p. 838; on it, with an equally mendacious title, the abolition of the Christian religion is celebrated. There stand the three Fates, with the inscription **TO THE VICTORIOUS FATES**. Theodoret, Discourse IX, *On the Laws*, p. 127: καὶ κορυβαντιῶντες καὶ λυττῶντες, etc.; that is: “And so, tossing their heads in their fury after the manner of the Corybantes, driven onward by madness, and employing a great many artifices and stratagems, they did not dissolve the laws of the fishermen, but by attacking them rendered them far stronger. They were found to be altogether like those who desire to extinguish a flame but foolishly pour oil upon it, thereby making it burn more fiercely. For these men too, by undertaking war against piety, made the strength of pious truth more manifest. And just as that bush which Moses once saw was not consumed by the heat of the fire, so neither did hostile weapons consume the Christians when they were assailed by the wars of the impious. Rather, just as, when woodcutters cut down a forest, far more shoots spring from the roots than the branches that are cut away, [Col. 0536C] so too at that time, when many of the pious had been killed, far more people came daily to the teaching of the Gospel; and the blood of those slaughtered bodies became irrigation for new plants emerging in the Church.” Immediately afterward Junius’s edition wrongly reads *of blood*. HAV.] whenever we are reaped by you: the blood of Christians is seed [Note: [Col. 0536C] **The blood of Christians is seed.** Christians cannot be diminished by persecutions, because, if their blood is seed, the more of it that is poured out, the greater the promised yield of the faithful—just as a plentiful harvest is the preparation for a more abundant crop. LAC.].

Many among you exhort people to endure pain and death, as Cicero does in the *Tusculan Disputations*, Seneca in the *Fortuitous Events*, Diogenes, Pyrrho, and Callinicus. Yet their words do not find as many disciples as [Col. 0536A] Christians do by teaching through deeds. That very obstinacy which you reproach is a teacher. For who is not shaken by contemplating it and driven to inquire what lies within the matter? Who, after inquiring, does not join us? Who, after joining us, does not desire to suffer, so that he may purchase the whole grace of God, and secure every pardon [Note: [Col. 0536C] **That he may secure every pardon.** Similar is the statement of St. Cyprian, Letter 52, to Antonianus, where he says that martyrs immediately attain the glory of faith, immediately receive the reward of courage, and are immediately crowned by the Lord. This passage should accordingly be noted against the error of those who are not ashamed to say that the crown of righteousness, and therefore of martyrdom as well, is to be deferred until the Day of Judgment. PAM.] from him by payment of his own blood? For all offenses are forgiven for this work. Hence it is that at that very moment we thank you for your sentences: such is the rivalry between the divine and the human order that, when we are condemned by you, we are absolved by God.

*John Lawrence Mosheim’s Inquiry concerning the Date of Tertullian’s Apology and the Beginning of the Persecution under Severus.*

[Col. 0535]

# JOHN LAWRENCE MOSHEIM’S INQUIRY CONCERNING THE DATE OF TERTULLIAN’S APOLOGY AND THE BEGINNING OF THE PERSECUTION UNDER SEVERUS

[Col. 0535D] § I. The great usefulness of inquiries of this kind is demonstrated. The occasion for the present inquiry.

[Col. 0536D] § II. A twofold classification is established of the differing opinions on this subject.

[Col. 0537A] § III. Namely, first are presented those who maintain that the *Apology* was written after the year 200. Against them.

§§ IV, V, VI. It is shown by many arguments that the afflictions of the Christians under SEVERUS began before he issued specific decrees for that purpose.

§ VII. Dodwell’s subtleties are examined in particular.

§ VIII. Those who say that the *Apology* appeared after the death of SEVERUS are refuted. After this,

§ IX. We proceed to the other class: those who, although they concede that it was composed before the year 200, nevertheless disagree about the year.

§ X. The exposition of our own opinion begins, and it is shown first that the work was written under SEVERUS. Then,

§ XI. That it was written after the disturbances of ALBINUS. The year in which it may correctly be placed.

§§ XII, XIII. It is shown by new arguments that those disturbances began in 196 and were suppressed in 197, and the opposing arguments are plainly dissolved. After this,

§ XIV. Judgment is given in favor of the year 198, and this opinion is carefully confirmed from a famous passage of TERTULLIAN.

[Col. 0537B] § XV. Conclusion.

## § I

If the sure knowledge of the times at which the ancient teachers committed their books to writing had always been sought by learned men with an eagerness and diligence proportionate to its evident usefulness, I do not doubt that sacred history would today abound in far fewer difficulties and would be furnished with a more orderly arrangement. But our ancestors, who first wiped away the filth of barbarism, labored rather to restore the utterly prostrate condition of letters than to render them distasteful to themselves and others through what they considered minute details. A different mind indeed belonged to those who followed those divine restorers and who, with Scaliger, Baronius, Petavius, Calvisius, and others leading the way, are known to have made great progress in these studies. [Col. 0537C] Yet both the age of our fathers and our own have produced men of the highest distinction in this field: Noris, Pagi, Lloyd, Dodwell, Tillemont, Nourry, and many members of the Benedictine family who edited the writings of the Fathers. Although I detract nothing from the praises due to any of them, I nevertheless do not deny that they left many things undone; that they treated many subjects more learnedly than successfully; and that many matters, because they burned with zeal for a sect or excessively favored some novel opinion, were entangled rather than unraveled. If no other testimonies to this fact existed, the very writings in which they attack one another and the books in which they repeatedly establish new calculations would themselves speak.

Especially in the history of the calamities through which the earliest of our brethren passed, it would have been of great [Col. 0537D] benefit if the dates of the books which we understand to have been presented on their behalf to emperors and provincial governors, and of the other writings composed while those persecutions were raging, had been carefully determined. For in this way we would possess a surer and fuller knowledge of the sequence of events, the magnitude of the evils inflicted, the number of confessors, and the unconquered strength of mind displayed by those most holy men. No one whose judgment has reached maturity can fail to recognize the remarkable utility which such knowledge can afford in every case.

I certainly wonder that, when Henry Dodwell—a man otherwise worthy of immortality—was perhaps with good intentions expelling whole armies of martyrs from the sacred commonwealth, none of those who came forward against him exercised himself in this arena. [Col. 0538A] Yet from this arena something could have been obtained than which nothing can be more certain or more useful for breaking down such boldness. So long as the words of the Fathers conflict with passages in other authors, an opportunity for escape will almost always be available. If no other refuge is at hand, either some stigma is branded upon the witnesses or some new kind of criticism is summoned to bring aid to a desperate cause. But if the intervals of time are carefully marked, and the order of successive events diligently explained, one must either incur the disgrace of brazen effrontery or else renounce one’s error.

In truth, learned men have been wanting in this cause: whether because they fled from the vexation inherent in such business, because they did not perceive its exceptional advantage clearly enough, or finally because they thought that they should take account not so much of the circumstances as of the events themselves. There were indeed some, [Col. 0538B] I admit, who chose to undertake part of this labor. Yet I do not know how it happened that they acquitted themselves either too carelessly or too unsuccessfully. It may have been haste, weariness, partisan zeal, or something else I cannot identify; but it is certain that there was something which caused them sometimes to reckon their calculations very badly.

For these reasons, although I feel myself far inferior to them, I began some time ago to form the plan of rolling this stone, and I conceived the idea of a new history of the Christian afflictions—one that would be distinguished, among other things, particularly by a more diligent notation of dates. A specimen was provided not long ago by our *Dissertation on the Date of Athenagoras* [Note: [Col. 0538D] It appears in the theological, historical, and philological library published at Bremen, vol. II, fascicle.], and a reading of it will attest that I inflicted considerable [Col. 0538C] damage upon the arguments of the celebrated Dodwell. Although thorny, the labor also enjoyed the good fortune of not displeasing those whose authority carries the greatest weight with me and whom all prudent men acknowledge as discerning judges of these matters.

I have therefore resolved now to test my strength again and to attempt whether I might, with the same dexterity, discover the date of the celebrated *APOLOGY* left to us by TERTULLIAN, the most ingenious of the Fathers. I was moved to impose this burden upon myself sooner than I had intended by the most elegant edition of that *APOLOGY*, which we owe to the labors of Sigibert Havercamp, a man of extraordinary learning and among my closest friends. When I saw it endowed with such brilliance, fortified with such varied and elegant learning, and splendid and spotless in every part, [Col. 0538D] I immediately wished above all that not only this work but also the more important books of the other Fathers might appear in the same dress. For I judged that, if a great part of the weariness associated with these studies were removed in this fashion, sacred antiquity would no longer be found almost abandoned and bereft of cultivators.

There was nevertheless something I missed in so polished a work: namely, an inquiry into its date and circumstances. I understood, indeed, that the most learned man promised to meet this desideratum also in the preliminary material to be prefixed to TERTULLIAN’s remaining books against the nations (*Preface*). [Col. 0539A] Yet so far was I from resting content with these promises that they instead spurred me to relieve him of this burden. For I immediately reasoned with myself as follows: “The wait for the works he is preparing will be shorter if even a very small part of the labor is transferred to someone else.” Added weight was given to these reflections by the encouragement of that excellent man, which drove me, still hesitant, to complete what I was attempting. Why say more? I immediately set aside my other work, applied my hand to this labor, and committed to paper what I present here.

It will now be for you to judge, most learned HAVERCAMP, whether my little effort is worth enough to allow you to dispense with the trouble of composing a new dissertation of this kind. But if my work should please you less, you will approve my intention—I know your fairness. And what was that intention? To serve the interests of learning, to explain the history [Col. 0539B] of the evils heaped upon the Christians under the emperor SEVERUS, and—if you permit this addition—to leave you somewhat freer to complete other works. Though perhaps rash in a man who is not exceedingly learned, it is nevertheless honorable. If I deserve less well of letters and of TERTULLIAN, I can in no way appear to have deserved ill of you. The common people, of course, judge plans by their outcome; good men judge them by their motive.

## § II

When, as was proper, I surveyed what learned men before me had thought about this same matter, I found it entirely abandoned by some and handled with little skill by others. Generally speaking, I saw disagreements and divisions of opinion reigning here as well. I heard something asserted by certain men, but in such a way that they forgot to provide reasons. I observed others sitting more diligently over their calculations, [Col. 0539C] though their efforts were not attended by equal success. I saw that very many men of great name had preferred to follow leaders rather than torment themselves over these reckonings.

Even this variety of opinions moved me to examine which one accorded with the truth. I shall attempt to cast as much light upon the matter as its intricate nature permits, and for that reason I shall first establish two classes of opinion. Let the year 200 of the era be the boundary separating the two. One class, therefore, will comprise those who seek the birth date of our book before that year or in that year itself. The other will comprise those who judge that it was composed after the completion of that two-hundredth year. I shall discuss the latter first, since it is both further removed from the truth and more easily refuted. [Col. 0539D] The former, whose arguments demand greater labor and must be drawn from the very hidden places of history, I shall reserve for later.

## § III

[Col. 0539D] Among those whom we have said must be heard first, let William Cave, a man of the greatest reputation and industry, give his opinion. He contends for the year 202. “It seems more probable to me,” he says (*Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 42b, Geneva ed.), “that it was written during the sixth persecution, about the year 202, when SEVERUS forbade anyone to become a Christian under a severe penalty.” To this he adds certain things by way of proof which I would repeat if I had any desire to harass that good man. One part tends to show that the Christians’ peace was indeed disturbed during SEVERUS’s reign; another shows that the evils inflicted upon them were not slight. [Col. 0540A] Yet since all these points have never been called into doubt by anyone, I am wholly at a loss to understand how they confirm the date he undertook to defend.

It would therefore have been better to omit the conclusion he appends: “Accordingly, we can assign the birth year of this work to no other epoch with a greater appearance of truth.” Its foundation is situated not in everything he had premised, but in this point alone: that before the year 202 SEVERUS did not trouble the Christians’ fortunes by his decrees. How slippery and infirm this is will soon become evident. TERTULLIAN certainly wrote when the brethren were already beset on every side by evils. Nevertheless, that is not sufficient unless it is also demonstrated that he did not take pen in hand before the emperor’s edicts were promulgated. If the contrary can be shown, [Col. 0540B] this entire computation is to be valued at nothing.

Nor did the learned man attend to this point: even if his arguments possessed great force, the date of the book would nevertheless have to be deferred rather to the year 203. For only when everything had already been ablaze for some time with the slaughter and punishment of Christians did our author emerge as the defender of his sect. It is therefore not sufficiently credible that this defense was committed to writing at the very beginning of the calamities, in the same year in which they arose.

Henry Dodwell, however, was not remote from Cave’s view. For although, so far as I know, he nowhere states openly what he thinks about the date of the *APOLOGY*, nevertheless what he intended can be gathered without any dispute from his discussion of the persecutions of Christians under SEVERUS. He persuades himself that before the year 202 no one had disturbed the peace [Col. 0540C] of the sacred assembly, and he endeavors to establish this by certain arguments which we shall presently examine (*Cyprianic Dissertations*, XI, § 41, p. 68, Bremen ed.). Thus it befitted one to whom nothing seemed less tolerable than an abundance of martyrs.

If, therefore, as is beyond doubt, TERTULLIAN addressed the governors of the provinces only after the calamities had begun to increase, it is also certain, according to Dodwell’s opinion, that this was done after the year 202 or toward its close. And why is there any need for conjecture? More explicit words of the learned man are available: “Hence,” he says (*Dissertation* cited, § 42, p. 69), “at precisely this time”—he is speaking of the year 202—“or perhaps even somewhat later, there appeared that new representation, as TERTULLIAN calls it, of the Christians’ God, with this inscription: ‘The Christians’ God, *onochoites*, with ass’s ears, [Col. 0540D] one hoofed foot, carrying a book, and wearing a toga.’” The passage to which he appeals is found in the *APOLOGY* (chapter XVI, p. 169 of the edition of the celebrated Havercamp, which I use throughout), the work presently under discussion. What could show more clearly that Dodwell agreed with Cave and others about the date of the book?

Today this man’s opinion concerning the small number of martyrs has spread more widely and taken possession of the minds of very many learned men. There can therefore be no doubt that this opinion concerning the date of the *APOLOGY* has become fixed in many minds. Yet since their leaders have been identified, I do not think it necessary to review them at greater length here.

I turn instead to Antoine Pagi, who, although he spent almost his entire life among chronological calculations, nevertheless committed himself to the same opinion. [Col. 0541A] When he composed his *Hypatic Dissertation*, no one judged better than he did, for he expressly pronounced in favor of the year 198. Hear his words (*Hypatic Dissertation*, part II, chapter III, § 12, p. 117; Lyon, 1682, quarto):

> TERTULLIAN composed his *APOLOGY* in the year 198, when SEVERUS celebrated his quinquennalia and departed from Rome, for which reason he addressed it to the Roman magistrates. For although no edict against the Christians had yet been promulgated by that emperor, Plautianus nevertheless, by whose authority everything at Rome was conducted, was beginning to persecute the Christians.

It is certainly excellent that he recognizes that no law against the Christians had then been enacted by the emperor. What he adds about Plautianus he owes to a conjecture of Baronius (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. II, at the year 200, nos. VII–VIII, p. 198; Cologne ed., 1624, folio), [Col. 0541B] which he himself later demolished (*Critique on the Annals of Baronius*, vol. II, at the year 199, no. IV, p. 92). His proof is vague and overly general, and could also fit other years in which we know that Severus was absent from the city. But let it have been altogether too weak: I nevertheless wish the learned man had persisted in that opinion.

When correcting Baronius, however, he judged that he must reject it and transferred the date of the *APOLOGY* to the year 205. “The persecution of the Christians,” you hear Pagi say (at the year 199, no. VI, p. 93), “was not decreed before the year 202. Therefore, since Tertullian wrote his *Apology* while persecution had already been raging everywhere for a long time, as is gathered from the *Apology* itself, that most excellent work was published much later—namely, as one may conjecture, in the year 205, when Antoninus celebrated the tenth anniversary [Col. 0541C] of his imperial power and when the persecution raged more fiercely.”

No one ever changed his mind under worse auspices. While wishing to correct another man’s slighter error, he polluted himself with a graver one. I know, indeed, that when our author composed his work, nations estranged from the worship of the true Deity were raging against the Christians. But what conclusion follows from this? “Therefore the book was written after Severus issued his decrees.” As if he had been so ignorant of events as not to know that our brethren had often been tortured under the authority of previously enacted laws. Or, if this fact had been less clearly known to him, as if this very *Apology* could not have taught him that it happened at that time. But I shall now discuss this matter more fully.

## § IV

We have seen that those who wish the book to have been committed to writing after the year 202 were chiefly misled by [Col. 0541D] their belief that the Christians’ affairs remained entirely peaceful until that year. This conviction arose from their having learned from many testimonies that, in the year I have named, decrees against the Christians were proposed by SEVERUS. The weakness of this reasoning was evidently not apparent to them: “In the year 202 SEVERUS enacted laws against the Christians; therefore they could not have been persecuted before that time.”

I am readily willing, however, to except Dodwell here, since he also took refuge in other subtleties because he perceived that no protection for his position lay in this argument. Since matters stand thus, there will be no surer way to refute these men than to demonstrate that, long before the emperor’s laws were enacted, very many evils had already weighed upon the Christians’ necks.

This whole issue was passed over by Thierry [Col. 0542A] Ruinart, who undertook to correct Dodwell. He bears it heavily and with great vexation that Dodwell compresses the entire affliction into the span of a single two-year period (*Preface to the Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, section II, § 12, p. 48, Wetstein ed.). Yet he adduces against him only more general considerations, for which the latter might perhaps have found parallels had he sought them. You will look in vain for the more diligent investigation and precise notation of dates which the nature of the matter uniquely demands.

Pagi applied greater industry, since he possessed extensive knowledge of these matters (*Critique on the Annals of Baronius*, vol. III, at the year 201, no. VII, p. 2, and at the year 207, no. III, p. 7). Nevertheless, he could not touch this point because, as I have shown, he did not differ from his opponent in assigning the beginning of the affliction. [Col. 0542B] He was therefore occupied solely in demonstrating that from the year 202 until the death of SEVERUS peace was not restored to the holy assembly.

What he and many others left unattempted, I shall now undertake to complete. We are not at present concerned with the precise year that gave rise to these evils. It will be possible to derive it without great difficulty from what we shall establish beyond doubt concerning the date of the *APOLOGY*. My sole purpose here is to demonstrate that, before the year 202—in which I concede that SEVERUS’s decrees against the Christians were published—an immense mass of afflictions had been inflicted upon them.

Let our own TERTULLIAN hold first place among the witnesses. Let him give testimony from the very book whose date we are determining here. It appeared—as no one denies—when Christians were already being put to death by the most cruel punishments. [Col. 0542C] Yet in more than one passage he explicitly indicates that nothing at all had then been heard concerning edicts of the emperor.

I now pass over a conjecture, though I deny that it deserves contempt: namely, that the work’s being addressed to the governors of the provinces is evidence that they alone, and not the emperor, were the authors of the evils. The matter will be decided by more evident testimonies.

Let this be the first (chapter XXXV, p. 300):

> Nor are there any who more loudly demand the Christians than the common people. Plainly, the other orders, in proportion to their rank, are religious out of loyalty: nothing hostile breathes from the senate itself, from the equestrian order, from the camps, or from the palaces themselves.

I certainly do not know what could make more evidently for our position. He excludes the palaces themselves, in which the emperor resided with his sons, from the number of the Christians’ enemies. [Col. 0542D] With what effrontery could he have written this if the laws already possessed authority for persecuting Christians?

The entire discussion concerning laws found in chapters IV, V, and VI confirms the same point clearly. The Christians’ opponents advanced the laws which commanded that they be treated with cruelty. But what laws? Those recently issued? By no means. They were continually invoking edicts enacted by emperors now dead, which they said they were not permitted to violate. The acute author splendidly meets these feeble little arguments. Before everything else, he demonstrates by reasoning that no law is so sacred that it must not immediately be abolished if it contains any injustice. He then shows that this principle is not lacking in examples, since the Romans had removed all authority from even the most ancient decrees once they recognized their injustice, and SEVERUS himself [Col. 0543A] had abrogated the Papian law.

“Do not you also,” he says (chapter IV [the source prints “XV”], p. 49), “daily, as experience casts light upon the darkness of antiquity, prune and cut down that entire old and squalid forest of laws with the new axes of imperial rescripts and edicts?” Observe, however, which laws are under discussion. They are ancient laws, as is evident, to which he opposes new ones.

He proceeds to the authors of the laws against the Christians (chapter V, p. 56), all of whom he contends were marked by the infamy of shameful and criminal acts and were exceedingly like Nero. I do not inquire how widely this assertion extends. It is enough for me that it makes clear that he did not regard SEVERUS as belonging to the number of those who had enacted decrees against the Christians. The logic of the matter itself is witness to this. For who would be so foolish as to persuade himself [Col. 0543B] that a wise man would have attacked the laws by this argument if it were established that the man who then possessed supreme power had bound himself by the same crime? A charming defender indeed—one who would number the emperor whose mind he wished to soften among the vilest of mortals, surpassed by none in wickedness!

On the contrary, our author praises SEVERUS several times and calls him the most steadfast of emperors (chapter V, p. 52). So far was he from thinking that Severus had ordered the sword to be drawn against the brethren.

But let TERTULLIAN explain himself, as he addresses the Romans in these words (chapter V, p. 62):

> Yet from among all the emperors since then down to the present—men wise in divine and human matters—produce a single assailant of the Christians.

Who is that “present” emperor? SEVERUS, I think. Yet he denies that Severus should be numbered [Col. 0543C] among the assailants of the Christians. What could be clearer?

I pass over the famous passage from the same dissertation (chapter V, pp. 63, 65):

> What kind of laws, then, are these, which only the impious execute against us—which no Hadrian, no Vespasian, no Pius, no Verus enforced?

There are manuscripts which read *Severus* here. But I agree with you, most learned Havercamp, and with the distinguished men who, with you and through the benefit of better manuscripts, restored *Verus* for us. Although Dodwell disapproves of this reading (*Cyprianic Dissertations*, XI, § 44, p. 69), he nevertheless could not deny that the names Severus and Verus are frequently confused in ancient monuments.

§ V.—These are the arguments that the *Apologeticus* itself supplies in support of our position; I do not see what [Col. 0543D] can be answered to them. Let another passage of TERTULLIAN now follow, taken from another of his books—namely, the one he sent to the martyrs confined in prison. It is beyond doubt that the martyrs meant here must be those who had been arrested during the reign of SEVERUS. To strengthen them, he presents the following as his final argument (*To the Martyrs*, ch. IV, p. 468 of the *Works*):

> Everyone can endure, even for a human being’s sake, what he hesitates to endure for God’s sake. In this regard, let even the present times serve us as evidence: how many persons, and of what distinction, meet ends unexpected in view of their birth, rank, physical condition, and age, for a human being’s sake—either at his own hands, if they have acted against him, or at the hands of his adversaries, if they have stood by him.

I could immediately point out here that it is sufficiently apparent [Col. 0544A] that TERTULLIAN did not wish to make the emperor, whom he here calls “a human being,” the author of the evils inflicted upon those martyrs. Otherwise he would have written, “for the sake of that human being who is torturing you.” I set this reasoning aside, however, and consider the event itself to which these words refer. They commemorate the slaughter of many men distinguished by rank and merit. Let anyone who thinks that these words can be applied to anything other than the execution of those whom SEVERUS butchered on the occasion of the Gallic war stirred up by ALBINUS be counted ignorant of the history of SEVERUS. This was the time when innumerable and eminent persons, contrary to every expectation, were being hurried off to death because they were thought to have favored ALBINUS. Hear Spartianus (*Life of Severus*, ch. XII, pp. 177–178, Obrecht’s ed.):

> After innumerable men of ALBINUS’ party had been killed, among whom [Col. 0544B] were many leading men of the state and many illustrious women—

is this not precisely what TERTULLIAN says?—

> all their property was confiscated and augmented the treasury. Then many nobles of the Spaniards and the Sualli were put to death.

Immediately afterward, the same author adds a fairly long list of the most noble men deprived of life in those disturbances (ch. XIII, pp. 178–179). Capitolinus (*Life of Clodius Albinus*, ch. XII, p. 217) and Herodian (*Histories*, book III, ch. VIII, p. 147, Boecler’s ed.) may be joined to him. What, indeed, could explain TERTULLIAN more clearly? Nor, on the other hand, is there any doubt that ALBINUS, who is hinted at here, employed the same savagery, especially after he perceived that SEVERUS was laying the plots against him that Capitolinus describes (*Life of Albinus*, chs. VII–VIII, p. 211f.). Anyone who weighs this [Col. 0544C] must find it hard to accept that someone should nevertheless assert that Christians were not harassed under SEVERUS before A.D. 202. ALBINUS’ uprising, as I shall shortly show, fell in A.D. 196, and his defeat in A.D. 197. It makes no difference whether the passage is understood of the one year or the other. For it will in either case prove that illustrious Christian martyrs had existed under his rule long before the decrees of SEVERUS were promulgated.

TERTULLIAN’S *Scorpiace* could supply me with certain other evidence. But I now intend to summon another witness, Clement of Alexandria. Eusebius long ago reported that Clement composed his *Stromata*, which are still read today, during the reign of SEVERUS (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. VI, p. 208). The earlier books in particular seem to have been written shortly after the beginning of his reign, when COMMODUS had not long [Col. 0544D] been dead. For in the first book, in which he establishes a chronological reckoning, he proceeds no further than the death of COMMODUS. Ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγῶνος ἐπὶ τὴν Κομόδου τελευτῆν, ἔτη ἑκατὸν ἐνδέκα (“From the first contest to the death of Commodus, one hundred and eleven years”). “From the first contest, moreover, to the death of COMMODUS there are one hundred and eleven years” (*Stromata*, book I, p. 402, Potter’s ed.). Here he stops—a clear indication that COMMODUS had died not long before he wrote these things.

For my present purpose, it is enough that Clement unquestionably published these writings before A.D. 202. When the evils suffered by the Alexandrians had been increased by the emperor’s decrees, that excellent man was in exile and spent his time chiefly in Palestine and Syria. Learned men have correctly observed this, following Jerome (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. XXXVIII, p. 111, Fabricius’s recent ed.) [Col. 0545A] and drawing upon Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. XI, pp. 212–213). No one would readily say that he could have devoted himself to so laborious a work during that turbulent and calamitous period. The very celebrated Dodwell himself, who often cuts down his own vines, acknowledged this and demonstrated by several arguments in two places that these *Stromata* were written long before A.D. 202 (*Dissertation III on Irenaeus*, § XXVII, p. 276f.; and *Dissertation on the Primitive Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, ch. XV, § IV, p. 209).

We have therefore obtained precisely what we most needed. We have the defendant’s own confession. If Clement wrote when SEVERUS’ reign was not yet far advanced, it is established that those who deny that the harassment of Christians began before A.D. 202 are guilty of error. For the slaughter and punishment of the brethren were daily before his eyes as he wrote. Behold what he says: [Col. 0545B] ἡμῖν δὲ ἄφθονοι μαρτύρων πηγαὶ ἑκάστης ἡμέρας, ἐν ὁφθάλμοις ἡμῶν θεωρούμενοι, παροπτωμένων, ἀνασκινδυλευομένων, τὰς κεφαλὰς ἀποτεμνομένων (“Among us, however, springs of martyrs abound every day—martyrs seen before our own eyes, being roasted, impaled, and beheaded”). (*Stromata*, book II, p. 494):

> Among us, however, springs of martyrs overflow daily—martyrs seen by our own eyes, who are burned, tortured, and beheaded.

Let those who deem it glorious to follow Dodwell’s precepts answer here, and above all let them reconcile the man with himself. COMMODUS met his fate, as schoolboys know, on the night separating the years 192 and 193. Suppose Clement wrote his first book three years after his death, in A.D. 195. Suppose again—though this is scarcely probable—that nearly two years intervened between the first and second volumes of the *Stromata*. [Col. 0545C] Nevertheless, already in A.D. 197 we shall find at Alexandria a fine company of those who, under Clement’s own observation, met a bloody death for the SAVIOR.

Here one may indeed marvel at Baronius’ acumen, for on account of these words of Clement he asserts that Clement’s books were composed after the tenth year of SEVERUS:

> Moreover, since it is established that in the books of the *Stromata* themselves mention is made of the persecution of Christians then in progress, it is necessary to affirm that he wrote after the tenth year of SEVERUS.

(*Annals*, vol. II, at A.D. 196, no. XXII, pp. 278–279.) A judgment unworthy of the author of the *Annals*! That most illustrious man forgets what he himself was shortly to maintain: that already in A.D. 198 injuries had been inflicted upon the Christians at Plautianus’ instigation. In this respect he commits a twofold error: [Col. 0545D] he makes both the sufferings of the Christians more recent than he himself thought and Clement’s books more recent than the circumstances permit.

§ VI.—I do not know whether it deserves to be added to these arguments that already in antiquity it was believed that Christians had been persecuted under SEVERUS long before A.D. 202. Those who do not strip the traditions of their forefathers of all credibility will not entirely despise this observation.
