I shall therefore produce Paulus Orosius, a writer of the fifth century, who relates that SEVERUS was grievous to the Christians before ALBINUS attempted a revolution—that is, in A.D. 196 at the latest (*Histories*, book VII, ch. XVII, p. 542, Mainz, 1615, octavo). These are his words, which Treculphus of Lisieux, a historian of the [Col. 0546A] ninth century, repeated without changing a single word (*Chronicles*, vol. II, book II, ch. XXIV, p. 488, Geneva ed., 1597, octavo):

> In the fifth persecution after Nero, he tortured the Christians, and very many of the saints throughout the different provinces were crowned with martyrdom. Heavenly vengeance immediately followed upon this profane presumption of Severus against the Christians and the Church of God. For Severus was at once swept—or rather dragged—back from Syria into Gaul for a third civil war. He had already waged one at Rome against Julianus and another in Syria against Pescennius; the third was being stirred up by Clodius Albinus, Julianus’ associate in the murder of Pertinax, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul.

He says, therefore, that the divine Power willed ALBINUS to disturb the peace of the empire because SEVERUS had acted unjustly toward the Christians. I certainly am not one who thinks Orosius a writer of the highest reliability. Nor do I make all [Col. 0546B] that he relates here my own. I wish him to serve only as a witness that, in his time, the opinion I defend was commonly accepted. If any credence is due to narratives handed down to us from our forefathers, no one will doubt that some must also be due to this one. I would immediately have cast aside a man whose superstition had been all too manifest if he had said that savagery toward the Christians was the cause of absolutely all the wars, including those waged against Julianus and Niger. As it is, I do not wholly disdain him, since he proceeds more scrupulously and does not always dream of the brethren’s punishments whenever he sees the whole world blazing with war.

§ VII.—I believe that what I have argued thus far is endowed with such clarity and evident force that anyone who should henceforth [Col. 0546C] attach himself to the opposing side would be unjust to himself. If the matter required it, I could have produced far more evidence; since it in no way demands this, I reserve it for another occasion. Thus all the arguments that the celebrated Dodwell, perhaps not without exertion, contrived in support of his position collapse.

He first attempts to wrest TERTULLIAN from us. For he understood that in the *Apologeticus* SEVERUS is excluded from the number of those who had laid violent hands upon Christians, although he does not even touch the altogether striking passages that we have examined. What, then, do you suppose he infers from this? Look and marvel: that the emperor’s decrees had indeed already been proposed at that time, but had not been conveyed to those regions in which TERTULLIAN lived (*Cyprianic Dissertation* XI, § 44, p. 69). Plainly, he strives with all his might to diminish the magnitude of the Christians’ sufferings. But what a lifeless [Col. 0546D] dream! It will perhaps not please even those who are ignorant of the condition of the Roman Empire.

Yet Ruinart is no less lifeless in refuting him; if ever there was a place where he seems to have been amid Gallic snows, it is here (*Preface to the Acts of the Martyrs*, sect. II, §§ 44–45, p. 46C). By hastily heaping together certain passages, he shows that the persecution extended far and wide. But what has this to do with Dodwell’s sophistry? Dodwell did not deny this; rather, he ventured to contend that the persecutions were not equally savage in all provinces, because the laws issued by the emperor had not reached them all. Unless I am mistaken, I have more securely rescued TERTULLIAN from this distortion.

I then adduced two further testimonies which, even if all the passages from the *Apologeticus* could be evaded—which is plainly impossible—[Col. 0547A] would nevertheless show that Christians had been tortured before the year he specifies. The suspicion for which the learned man contends is groundless. Yet let it stand, if anyone wishes. Other evidence still remains that is not exposed to this device. With these points unmoved, the arguments that the same author advanced to assign the beginning of all the afflictions to A.D. 202 will likewise fall (*loc. cit.*, § XLI, p. 68). They come down to two heads. He says that the pagans had lacked both leisure and an opportunity to attack Christians. The weakness of each contention is readily apparent when they are compared with what I have written. Let us nevertheless grant the learned man leave to speak:

> Previously there was no leisure, whether for the emperor himself, for the governors of the provinces, or for the common people and magistrates of the cities, whom peace from foreign enemies at least generally turns toward that wanton savagery.

I scarcely doubt that he was thinking of something else [Col. 0547B] when he wrote thus. What connection, I ask, is there between these propositions: “The Romans were entangled in war,” and “The Christians experienced no evils”? Either I understand nothing, or there is none. Amid the very clash of a most serious war, VALERIAN inflicted endless troubles upon the Christians. This will become clearer if we consider more distinctly the wars of that period. In those years the emperor was occupied with military service in the eastern regions and in Gaul. Let there have been peace there, as I shall concede for the moment, in the more divine assembly; but what impediment did this place in the way of the governors of other provinces, or of the common people, preventing them from summoning Christians before the courts? What is better known than that crimes are never more immune from punishment than when wars are laying everything waste? Finally, what is more commonplace than that [Col. 0547C] custom of the pagans by which they never created greater miseries for Christ’s disciples than when the Roman world was oppressed by military and other calamities? When asked what the cause was, the petty sacrificers confidently cried that all blame rested with the Christians. Arnobius reports their words (*Against the Nations*, book I, p. 16, Heraldus’s ed.):

> The gods are neglected, and there is now the greatest scarcity in the temples; the ancient rites lie open to mockery, and the most venerable ceremonies of former times have perished through the superstitions of new religions.

Hence those tears; hence their renewed frenzies whenever new disturbances arose. There was therefore no reason why the very distinguished Sébastien Tillemont—a man otherwise with few equals in this field—should have thought this argument of Dodwell’s so excellent that he ought to repeat it as his own (*History of the Emperors*, vol. III, part I, p. 146, [Col. 0547D] Brussels ed.). It is so far from proving anything that it instead affords some aid to the opposing side.

Still feebler is the second argument, that there had been no opportunity to mistreat Christians:

> At least no occasion presented itself that might stir the emperor’s anger against the Christians, since they had been neither Niger’s supporters nor Albinus’ supporters, as TERTULLIAN says.

I spare my words here, because I think nothing could have been said more thoughtlessly. Were emperors, then, never hostile to the Christian cause unless some Christians had attached themselves to men who were stirring up civil wars? Not even schoolboys would tolerate that. Nor is the principal question here whether SEVERUS himself raged against the Christians before A.D. 202. Although for him, and for others, the very name of Christian [Col. 0548A] was occasion enough. “For this reason we are tortured,” says our TERTULLIAN (*Apologeticus*, ch. II, p. 35), “when we confess; we are punished when we persist; and we are acquitted when we deny, because THE BATTLE IS OVER THE NAME.”

§ VIII.—More has been said than I had intended against those who contend that the *Apologeticus* was not produced before A.D. 202. Yet it has not been excessive, since in this way some light has been added to sacred history and the period of the Christians’ persecution under SEVERUS has been more carefully established.

I now proceed to those who prefer to go still further and maintain that the book appeared after SEVERUS’ death, after A.D. 210. These men are more easily excused, since their purpose is not so much to minimize the Christians’ sufferings as to extend them also into the beginning of CARACALLA’S reign. Nevertheless, they are far inferior to the others in the quality of their arguments, whose force here is almost nonexistent. The chief of this school [Col. 0548B] is the great Joseph Scaliger, and I am not at all surprised that his authority proved a snare to some. He says (*Notes on Eusebius’ Chronicle*, in the *Thesaurus of Time*, p. 229, last ed. of Alexander More):

> I doubt whether he wrote the *Apologeticus* under SEVERUS, since he says: “Only yesterday SEVERUS, most steadfast of emperors, repealed the Papian laws”; he seems to speak of a dead man.

For my part, I am not so acute as to see what compels these words of TERTULLIAN to be interpreted of a dead SEVERUS. He is praised. But who denies that living persons are commonly adorned with praise? The word “yesterday” is employed. But why must it therefore be understood of SEVERUS’ past reign, as though TERTULLIAN had compared it to a single day? You, most learned Havercamp, have correctly observed that it can be understood of a time not long past [Col. 0548C] (*Notes on the Apologeticus*, p. 287). I add that it must be so understood, unless we wish the most learned of the Fathers to have written nonsense. On Scaliger’s view, he would have meant: “SEVERUS, while he was still alive, repealed the Papian laws.” Silence, indeed! The Romans perhaps needed to be instructed that the emperor had not bestowed this benefit from the underworld. Accordingly, let “yesterday” here mean nothing other than “not long ago.”

Nevertheless, the very celebrated Peter Allix approved this argument of Scaliger’s and based upon it in particular his own opinion that the *Apologeticus* was not committed to writing before A.D. 211 at the earliest (*Dissertation on the Life and Writings of Tertullian*, with other works; Paris ed., 1680, quarto). How incautiously this was done is, I think, evident. The same author added [Col. 0548D] two other reasons for this computation. Although they have already been briefly refuted by the celebrated Dupin (*New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. I, pp. 107–108, second ed.), my plan requires that I examine them again here.

He says first that it is evident that our work was composed after the book *On Prescriptions*, because in the *Apologeticus* TERTULLIAN pointed to that work, as it were, with his finger. This is not the place to discuss the date of the book *On Prescriptions*. For the meantime I shall adopt the opinion of Cave (*Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 43) and others, that it was published about A.D. 207. We need only see how the very distinguished Allix proves that this book is mentioned in the *Apologeticus*. The passage he produces is this (ch. XLVII, p. 519):

> But we readily PLEAD AGAINST our adulterators [Col. 0549A] that the rule of truth is that which comes from Christ and was transmitted through his companions, while these various commentators will be shown to be considerably later.

You see the learned man’s remarkable reasoning: TERTULLIAN used the word “plead by prescription”; therefore he referred to the book *On Prescriptions*. His argument will have some force only when he has shown that, before our author wrote about prescriptions, the word “prescribe” had been unheard of among the Romans.

He continues by saying that TERTULLIAN refers to the eclipse of the sun observed at Utica in A.D. 210. I am undone if he speaks the truth. But a man who thinks this can be elicited from the words he cites is excessively ingenious. Hear them (*Apologeticus*, ch. XX, p. 390):

> Even the functions of the seasons and the duties of the elements depart from their courses; even the order of nature is disturbed by monstrosities and portents.

Where [Col. 0549B] is the eclipse of the sun here? Where is Utica? I think he is speaking of the seasons of the year producing crops neither sufficiently early nor very well. But let us concede what is false, that something is said here of the darkening of the sun: by what means will it be demonstrated that the eclipse which occurred in A.D. 210 is indicated here?

§ IX.—At last we have thus arrived at those who acknowledge that the *Apologeticus* was written either before A.D. 200 or in that very year, and whom we recognized above as friendlier to the truth. They do not pursue the same course, but diverge in various directions. Some favor A.D. 196 (Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 42); their reasons, for my part, are unknown to me. I showed above that PAGI once chose A.D. 198.

Caesar Baronius wishes the book to have appeared in A.D. 201 according to his customary reckoning—that is, in A.D. 199 according to the common era, which, as is well known, prevails [Col. 0549C] in investigations of this kind (*Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. II, at A.D. 200, no. VII, p. 198; at A.D. 201, no. XXVII, p. 307, no. XXXVI, p. 310). He judges that when SEVERUS marched against the Parthians—which he supposes without reasons to have happened in this year—Plautianus, left at Rome as praetorian prefect, violated the Christians’ peace. For this reason he thinks that TERTULLIAN, then present in the city, as he supposes, wished by this book to repel those dangers. Anton Pagi has already removed the conjecture concerning Plautianus, proving that he went to Asia with SEVERUS (*Critique of Baronius*, vol. II, at A.D. 199, no. IV, pp. 92–93). The *Apologeticus* itself refutes Baronius’ contention that, when TERTULLIAN wrote, only the Christians living at Rome were being tortured; for it is certain that the work is addressed to the governors [Col. 0549D] of the provinces. The date of the Parthian war will be carefully discussed below.

The year 200 was chosen by very many, and those among the most learned men. Among them is JACQUES PAMÈLE (*Life of Tertullian*, prefixed to his edition of the *Works*), if we believe John Forbes of Corse (*Historical-Theological Instruction*, book VII, ch. VII, § 16, p. 320, vol. II of the *Theological Works*), who says he follows him; Baronius, however, draws Pamèle into his own camp. There is also the most diligent Tillemont (*History of the Emperors*, vol. III, part I, p. 94), although elsewhere (*Chronology*, at the end of vol. III of the *History*, p. 1221) he is uncertain whether it should better be placed in A.D. 201. There is L. E. Dupin (*Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. I, p. 91), and a good many others whose names I think it of little use [Col. 0550A] to enumerate here.

Some of these merely state their opinion and omit their reasons. For it is generally the fate of this work of ours to lie neglected and abandoned. The most diligent derive their evidence from the same passage that we shall call to our aid. They differ in assigning the events in question to their respective years—namely, the Parthian war and ALBINUS’ movements. Accordingly, nothing will contribute more to completing this inquiry than for me both to disclose and establish my own position. Once this is done, it can no longer be obscure what room could remain for the arguments of others.

I intend, however, to proceed methodically and by stages. The more general considerations will come first, and for the sake of those who date the book after SEVERUS, it will be demonstrated that it was written during his reign. A more specific inquiry will follow, and every impediment [Col. 0550B] will be removed by indubitable arguments. In the last place, the precise year will be considered.

§ X.—That TERTULLIAN composed this work during the reign of SEVERUS is shown both by certain passages I have already indicated above and by the one I shall now recite. “Moreover,” he says (ch. V, p. 294), “from all the emperors since then down to the present day, WHO ARE VERSED IN DIVINE AND HUMAN WISDOM, produce a single persecutor of the Christians.” He counts the man who was then administering the affairs of the empire among rulers versed in divine and human wisdom—that is, skilled in both kinds of law and in literature. Except SEVERUS, and there will be no emperor to whom these words apply. Either COMMODUS or CARACALLA must be named, the former of whom ruled the world before him, the latter after him. For PERTINAX [Col. 0550C] and JULIANUS, who held this eminence for only a few days after COMMODUS’ death, do not enter into consideration here. But what manner of men, I ask, were those whom I have named? Wise neither in divine nor in human matters, endowed with manners more truly bestial than human, thoroughly learned in crimes, not literature.

SEVERUS, by contrast, had devoted much time to learning the arts. Spartianus calls him “sufficiently devoted to the studies of philosophy and eloquence, and even excessively desirous of learning” (*Life of Severus*, ch. XVIII, p. 154). Dio praises his zeal and diligence, although he was not particularly capable of putting into practice what he had conceived in his mind. This, I think, is the meaning of the words I shall transcribe (book XXVI [sic], in the *Peirescian Excerpts*, edited by Henri Valois, p. 740, Paris, 1634, quarto): [Col. 0550D] παιδείας μὲν γὰρ ἐπεθύμει μᾶλλον ἢ ἐπετύγχανε, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ πολυγνώμων μᾶλλον ἢ πολυλόγος ἦν (“For he desired learning more than he attained it, and therefore was more a man of many opinions than of many words”). For VALESIUS’ translation does not satisfy me in every respect: “More devoted to learning than proficient in it,” and so forth. Who could doubt that such a ruler could rightly be numbered among the learned? But there is no need of a longer proof. The fact itself places it beyond all doubt that this work was committed to writing under no emperor other than SEVERUS.

§ XI.—We have identified the emperor. From what has already been said, we next know that not all the years of his reign must be considered, but only those numbered from A.D. 193, when he assumed it, to A.D. 200. This cycle of eight years, therefore, will now occupy us. Yet no small portion of it will immediately be removed if we demonstrate that the book was written after the civil war stirred up by ALBINUS [Col. 0551A] in Gaul. This will be done with the aid of the following passage, which I present.

While that ingenious man contends that the members of the Christian sect had never plotted anything against the lives of rulers, he exclaims among other things (ch. XXXV, p. 300):

> Whence came the Cassiuses, the Nigers, and the ALBINUSES? Whence those who besiege Caesar between the two laurels? From Romans, unless I am mistaken—that is, from non-Christians.

In this passage he recalls to the governors’ memory the past calamities of the empire and enumerates the dangers from which the emperors had happily escaped. Among these he mentions in particular the uprising stirred up by ALBINUS. Accordingly, nothing more is required for certain knowledge than to inquire in what year those Albinian attempts were suppressed.

§ XII.—But here, indeed, is a new circuit. Those whose great authority in these matters very few fail to recognize disagree. Yet only a single year separates them. Some favor A.D. 197; others A.D. 198. Since we regard it as a matter of conscience not to omit anything pertaining to the examination of the whole question, we shall show by indubitable arguments which view ought to be held. This will be done all the more willingly because the whole dispute over the year of the *Apologeticus* depends upon this question.

The former opinion is the widespread one, defended by most compilers of the fasti (see Onofrio Panvinio, *Consular Fasti*, p. 241, Heidelberg, 1588), Caesar Baronius (*Annals*, vol. II, at A.D. 199, no. I, p. 293), Francesco Mezzabarba (*Imperial Coins*, p. 271, Milan, 1683), the celebrated Tillemont (*History of the Emperors*, vol. III, part I, pp. 72 and 404), and a good many [Col. 0551C] others. If these men had fortified their reasons with greater diligence, they would doubtless have preserved them inviolate and secure. They would have fortified them, I think, if they had imagined that anyone would be bold enough to overturn and reject them. I profess without any hesitation that I adhere to them. Before dismantling the apparatus of those who think otherwise, I shall set out the reasons for this decision. Once the foundations of our computation have been indicated, it will be easier to judge what value should be assigned to the other.

First of all, I wish it to be observed that the Albinian war did not last long, but began in one year and was concluded in the next. By great and hurried marches SEVERUS flew from the East into Gaul. The enemy, ALBINUS, was also at hand immediately. Without delay they engaged, and in several skirmishes—not, indeed, [Col. 0551D] very great ones—contended for control of the state. At the beginning the battle was fought with uncertain fortune, and ALBINUS had already been raised to the hope of victory. But shortly afterward, in the fatal and decisive battle near Lugdunum on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, victory fell to SEVERUS and destruction to ALBINUS. All the writers we possess testify that all these events were accomplished within a brief period and were not prolonged beyond a second year. Nor do I see anything that can be objected in any way.

Now hear why I hold these two years to have been 196 and 197. I shall bring three arguments into the field. There is no one who calls, or could call, into doubt that PESCENNIUS NIGER, SEVERUS’ other rival, was defeated and deprived of life in A.D. 194. [Col. 0552A] Not long afterward SEVERUS sent assassins into Gaul to remove ALBINUS from the way, so that he might no longer have a partner in imperial rank. Besides Herodian (*Histories*, book III, ch. V, p. 133 in my edition), SEVERUS’ own letter to ALBINUS, which he had entrusted to the assassins for delivery to him, confirms this in Capitolinus (*Life of Clodius Albinus*, ch. VII, p. 212). Even a cursory inspection of it can show that it was written at least a year after NIGER’S death. When the outcome did not answer the emperor’s expectation and the prepared plot was uncovered, ALBINUS immediately took up arms against SEVERUS. On receiving this news, Severus thought no time should be given to repose; gathering at once what forces he could, he hastened toward Gaul with incredible speed and with all his characteristic vehemence, [Col. 0552B] and attacked ALBINUS. He was unwilling even to wait for the capture of Byzantium. Αὐτὸς δὲ (“But he himself”), Herodian says of him (*Histories*, book III, ch. VI, p. 139), τῆς ὁδοῦ εἴχετό, μηδεμίαν ἀνοχὴν ἀναπαύλης διδοὺς μήτε ἑορταῖς μήτε καμάτοις, κρύους καὶ θάλπους ὀμοίως καταφρόνων (“kept to the road, allowing no respite for rest either for festivals or because of hardships, equally disregarding cold and heat”). He himself traveled without interruption, paying little regard either to feast days or to any hardships, equally enduring cold and heat.

Anyone who considers this haste cannot but determine that A.D. 196 marked the beginning and A.D. 197 the end of the Albinian war. I shall concede that the conspirators were dispatched by SEVERUS in A.D. 195. I shall add that they were detected in the crime when that year was nearly over. Finally, I shall say that SEVERUS was informed of the matter when A.D. 196 had already begun. Within not very many days the emperor, utterly intolerant of delay, who ran [Col. 0552C] rather than traveled, could have reached Gaul after receiving this news.

We shall prepare another supporting argument from the duration of the siege of Byzantium. Dio Cassius writes that this city was besieged by SEVERUS for a period of three years, ἐπὶ ὅλον τριετῆ χρόνον (“for a full period of three years”). (*History*, book LXXIV, p. 845, Frankfurt ed., 1606). All the circumstances of the event—as I see Tillemont had already observed (*Note XIV on Severus*, vol. III, *History of the Emperors*, part I, pp. 401–402)—require these words to be interpreted not of a completed cycle of three years, but only as indicating that the siege continued during three successive calendar years, although perhaps it began as the first was ending and was completed as the third began. This manner of speaking is very familiar to the Greeks. [Col. 0552D]

I shall not dispute to which year its beginning ought to be assigned, whether A.D. 193 or A.D. 194. It is enough that we owe to Dio the further information (*History*, book LXXIV, p. 844) that the city was surrounded by troops before NIGER had yet been killed. He fell in A.D. 194. Accordingly, whether the end of A.D. 193 is preferred, as some do, or the beginning of A.D. 194, we have prevailed in either case. Yet I do not deny that those who choose A.D. 194 are by far more correct, and for many reasons. The capture therefore falls in A.D. 196. But at the time when he marched to meet ALBINUS, the city had not yet been reduced to the emperor’s power, according to Herodian (*History*, book III, ch. VI, p. 139). Indeed, he appears already to have been on the road to Gaul when the news of the recovered city was brought to him. [Col. 0553A] If, therefore, the recovery of Byzantium and the expedition against ALBINUS occurred in one and the same year, and that year must necessarily be A.D. 196, it follows altogether that the battle of Lugdunum was fought in A.D. 197. If you advance to A.D. 198, you will simultaneously admit that the siege of Byzantium lasted four years, which is established by Dio to be utterly false.

The argument I shall present last is the strongest. A great mass of inscriptions in Gruter and others, and a great quantity of coins in Biragius, teaches that SEVERUS’ elder son, ANTONINUS, afterward called CARACALLA, was adorned with the title Augustus in A.D. 198. Moved by this evidence, learned men—though they dispute the day and month (see Anton Pagi, *Critique of Baronius*, vol. II, at A.D. 198, no. VII, p. 90; Heinrich Noris, *On the Decennial Vows of the Emperors*, p. 91; S. Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, vol. III, part I, note XIX on Severus, p. 406)—do not doubt the correctness of the year, and advise that Spartianus, who says this occurred in A.D. 200, in CARACALLA’S thirteenth year (*Life of Severus*, ch. XVI, p. 182), must be set aside. I do not trouble myself with the grounds on which they criticize him; I conjecture that perhaps he should be understood to refer not to the title Augustus, but to that of *Imperator*, which the soldiers bestowed upon ANTONINUS. I both embrace the position itself and acknowledge that it is exposed to no doubts.

It also lends excellent aid to our computation at this point. It is clear from the historians that this honor was paid to CARACALLA in the year following the battle of Lugdunum. Herodian teaches that it happened at Rome shortly [Col. 0553C] before the Parthian expedition (*History*, book III, ch. IX, p. 148); Spartianus, as they say, that it happened in the East. I pass over other arguments. Both positions agree on the year 198, when the emperor marched against the Parthians. If, therefore, in A.D. 198, when the Parthian war was already imminent, ANTONINUS was saluted as *Imperator*, it cannot in any way be denied that ALBINUS died in A.D. 197.

§ XIII.—I indeed think these arguments are so constituted as to demonstrate that the common position concerning ALBINUS’ defeat is absolutely certain. If the matter demanded it, I would be concerned to add others. I now think it better to inquire what moved those who preferred to leave the well-trodden path. Their arguments are slight; nevertheless, they must not be omitted.

Let Denis Pétau hold the first place. [Col. 0553D] He assigns the beginning of the siege of Byzantium to A.D. 195. For this reason it also became necessary, since that siege continued for three years, for him to say that A.D. 197 was the year in which SEVERUS left the East and A.D. 198 the year in which he defeated ALBINUS (*Doctrine of Times*, book XV, p. 693, Paris ed., 1627). The error is clear, provided only that it be observed that its source lies in his wrongly assigning the beginning of the siege of Byzantium to A.D. 195. He was impelled to do this by the following consideration: he believed that while NIGER was still alive, SEVERUS could not have devoted himself to an undertaking of such magnitude as this siege. The learned man could have learned the contrary from Dio, as I have already indicated. Let the beginning of the siege of Byzantium therefore be recalled, with Dio, to its true year, A.D. 194, and [Col. 0554A] the facts themselves will compel Pétau to become reconciled with us (compare Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, vol. III, note XVI on Severus, p. 404).

Restoration notes: S000950 reads νίμαις, apparently a corruption of νίκαις (“victories”).; The ending μεξεισ in S000953 is corrupt but evidently denotes “unions” or “intercourse.”; S000958 reads λλὰ, apparently lacking the initial ἀ of ἀλλὰ.; S000961–S000962 form one question divided between consecutive English markers; the translation preserves that division without duplicating content.; S000953 contains several corrupt spellings, especially its final μεξεισ, but the phrase clearly denotes Oedipal intercourse.; S000958 contains the irregular reading μίσοις ἅξια, and λλὰ apparently lacks the initial ἀ of ἀλλὰ; the contextual meaning remains clear.; S000961–S000962 form a single question divided between consecutive English markers; the two replacements preserve the division and represent the question exactly once.  

Henry Noris indicates that he supported the same opinion (*Dissertation on the Decennial Vows of the Emperors*, p. 93, Padua, 1686), but he does not disclose his reasons. I see that he cites Spartian, who, so far as I know, said nothing of the kind. I therefore turn at once to Antoine Pagi, whose express purpose was to establish this date (*Critique of Baronius*, at the year 198, no. V, p. 89). For Tillemont is mistaken when he says that Pagi agrees with him [Note: [Col. 0554D] *History of the Emperors*, vol. III, p. 408: “Father Pagi, who, like us, places Albinus’ defeat in 198.”]. The sum of his arguments—which I collect into one place from their remarkably scattered presentation—is this: Severus’ Quinquennalia were celebrated at Rome, without any dispute, in the year 198; but Herodian relates that immediately after the battle at Lyons he hastened to Rome with immense speed [Col. 0554B] and, as soon as he arrived, presented those Quinquennalia. Therefore, if the emperor entered Rome shortly after Albinus was killed—whose defeat no one denies occurred on the nineteenth day of February—and if no delay, or only a slight one, intervened between this return of his to the city and the Quinquennalia, then it is beyond doubt that the killing of Albinus and the Quinquennalia must belong to the same year.

If I did not know how easy it was for him to slip in such matters, I should certainly be surprised that such feeble little arguments could have proceeded from so learned a man. What displeases me about them generally is that he thus assigns three years to the Albinian disturbances, contrary to all credibility. He admits that arms were taken up in 196. Elsewhere he censures Petavius, [Col. 0554C] who, because of the opinion that he shared with Pagi, had preferred the following year (*Dissertatio Hypatica*, Part II, ch. XII, p. 221). Yet he does not perceive that by this means he falls into snares far more difficult than Petavius’, since, despite every opposing consideration, he prolongs that war into a third year.

There is also another difficulty that weighs upon this opinion. Severus’ journey to the East for the Parthian expedition—which the learned man concedes took place in the same year, 198—is joined with those Quinquennalia and his return to the city. But this conflicts with the testimony of every author, who presents these events in such a way that Severus’ return to Rome from Gaul must without any doubt be assigned to one year, and his departure to subdue the Parthians to another.

What am I to say of his particular arguments, [Col. 0554D] not one of which can support itself even slightly? I shall examine each one distinctly. It is entirely uncertain that Severus presented the Quinquennalia in 198. The celebrated Pagi himself repeatedly emphasized this rule: Quinquennalia, Decennalia, and festivals of that kind were celebrated indiscriminately, sometimes as the fifth year began, sometimes as it ended (*Dissertatio Hypatica*, Part II, ch. II, § V, p. 87). I am not unaware that he placed it upon an unstable foundation—namely, the opinion, of which he was the principal author, that emperors always assumed consular rank at solemnities of this kind. Yet otherwise the rule is not so devoid of its own strength as some [Col. 0555A] persuade themselves. Examples survive both of those who presented these games at the beginning of the fifth or tenth year and of those who did so at its end. Among the former is Constantine the Great, whose first day of his thirtieth year, 25 July, is known to have been distinguished by the ceremonies of the Tricennalia.

Let us apply this to Severus’ years, and we shall see that he could have presented those spectacles to the people either in 197 or in 198. He was placed at the head of the empire perhaps around the middle of 193. It matters little to know the day and month, about which others dispute (see Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, vol. III, Note VII on Severus, p. 393). Meanwhile, I shall follow Pagi himself, who thinks that this occurred on the Ides of May (*Dissertatio Hypatica*, Part II, ch. XII, p. 220). Thus the fifth year of his reign will have begun in May 197. What argument, then, can be advanced that demonstrates invincibly that he gave the Quinquennalia not in 197, when [Col. 0555B] Severus’ fifth year began, but in 198, when it ended? For it is certain that either was possible.

The condition of the remaining arguments is worse still. It is false that Herodian says that the emperor presented to the people immediately after his arrival in the city the gifts that Pagi calls the Quinquennalia. Let us hear the man’s own words (*Histories*, Book III, ch. VIII, p. 145): Ὁ δ` οὖν Σεβῆρὸς εἰς τὸ τοῦ Διὸς τέμενος ἀνελθὼν, καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς τελέσας ἱερουργίας, ἐπανῆλθεν εἰς τὰ βασίλεια, καὶ τῷ δήμῳ προὒθηκεν ἐπὶ ταῖς νίκαις μεγίστας νομὰς, τοῖς δὲ στρατιώταίς ἐπέδωκε χρήματα πλεῖστα, ἄλλα τε πολλὰ συνεχώρησεν ἃ μὴ πρότερον εἶχον (“Severus, then, went up to the precinct of Jupiter and, after performing the remaining sacred rites, returned to the palace; in celebration of his victories he presented the people with very great distributions, gave the soldiers a vast sum of money, and granted many other privileges that they had not possessed before”). Politian translates it thus:

> But after he entered the temple of Jupiter and performed all the customary sacrifices, he returned to the palace and bestowed a great largess upon the Roman people in honor of the victory, distributed money to the soldiers, and at the same time granted them many other things that they had never received before.

I look here for a mention of the Quinquennalia, but in vain. I do indeed hear Pagi say: “These novel favors were tokens of Severus’ Quinquennalia.” But what an unfortunate conjecture! As though the people could not have been presented with things of that kind at times other than the Quinquennalia. And what prevented you, most learned Pagi, from seeing those words of Herodian, ἐπὶ ταῖς νίμαις (“in celebration of the victories”; νίμαις is apparently corrupt, probably for νίκαις)? Severus exercised this generosity because of the victory won over Albinus, not on account of the fifth anniversary of his reign—games of which Herodian afterward speaks separately.

He is no less mistaken in saying that it is apparent from Herodian [Col. 0555D] that the emperor hastened to Rome immediately after Albinus’ defeat. Herodian does indeed say that, when he was making for Rome, πολλῷ τάχει (“with great speed”) he traveled. But he does not record that this journey immediately followed the slaughter of Albinus (*loc. cit.*, p. 145). Rather, he relates that Severus did not return to Rome before he had put Britain’s affairs in order, settled Gaul, and exacted punishment from the great host of Albinus’ friends. These were matters of such importance that much time was undoubtedly consumed in accomplishing them.

We therefore now affirm that nothing is more certain than that the Albinian disturbances were quelled in 197 [Note: [Col. 0555D] Yet I do not agree here with Baronius, who, for reasons unknown to me, although he concedes that Albinus was defeated in 197, nevertheless denies that Severus returned to Rome before 198. *Annals*, vol. II, at the year 200, no. I, p. 296. Everything conflicts with this opinion and confirms that the emperor returned to the city perhaps after the middle of 197. I pass over the fact that, in Adolf Occo’s *On Coins*, p. 849, certain indications occur on coins that this emperor’s arrival took place in the fourth year of his tribunician power.], once their instigator had been killed.

[Col. 0556A] § XIV.—And thus I proceed to the remaining matters without stumbling, and the year of our *Apologeticum* can more easily be established. I therefore declare without hesitation that in 198 Tertullian wished to come to the aid of his brethren in their distress. The passage that supports this opinion is as follows:

> But those who are now daily being exposed as accomplices or applauders of criminal factions—the gleaning left after the harvest of parricides—with what very fresh and luxuriant laurels did they cover their doorposts? With what very lofty and brilliant lamps did they clear the gloom from their vestibules? With what very elegant and sumptuous couches did they divide up the forum for themselves? They did so not to celebrate public rejoicings, but to proclaim their own wishes at another’s solemnity and to inaugurate the exemplar and image of their hope, changing the name of the prince in their hearts. Those who consult astrologers, haruspices, augurs, and [Col. 0556B] magicians concerning the life of the Caesars likewise neglect the same duties.

(*Apologeticum*, ch. XXXV, p. 458.)

This illustrious passage did not escape Baronius, nor did it pass Tillemont by. But neither man—if I may say so without diminishing such great scholars—was able to use it correctly, because they erred in other matters. Baronius saw something of the truth and correctly advised that it should be interpreted of the slaughter of Albinus’ surviving adherents (*Annals*, at the year 200, no. III, p. 198). Yet he could not correctly determine the book’s date, because he held that Severus returned to Rome in 198 and that war was not finally carried against the Parthians until 199.

Tillemont, however, whose astonishing industry I otherwise acknowledge, incautiously understood the passage of Niger’s followers, whom Severus persecuted at Plautianus’ prompting when he was already threatening the Parthians, as Spartian [Col. 0556C] reports (*Life of Severus*, ch. XV, p. 181). He therefore held that the *Apologeticum* was composed in 200 or 201 [Note: [Col. 0556D] *History of the Emperors*, vol. III, p. 94, at the year 200: “One of Severus’ occupations in the East was to make new searches for Niger’s supporters and, as Tertullian says concerning this, to glean after the harvest.”]. And yet I do not even understand why this learned man thinks that the slaughter of Niger’s adherents—which Spartian places at the beginnings of the Parthian war—occurred after the exceedingly difficult siege of the city of Hatra itself.

If we carefully examine Tertullian’s passage, we shall easily resolve the matter. It is plain who the “parricides” are in it: namely, those who had aided Albinus, when he was aspiring to the imperial power, either by deed or counsel. Cicero had long before expressed the opinion (*Philippic* II, ch. XIII, p. 446, vol. II of the works, Gruter’s edition) that men of this kind were even worse than parricides, since, as he adds, it is more atrocious to kill the father of one’s country than one’s own father. But by far the greater part of these men, whether truly guilty [Col. 0556D] of that crime or falsely regarded as such, had subsequently been executed both in Gaul and at Rome, apart from those who had openly taken up arms. Herodian and Spartian may be consulted here. And this is what Tertullian calls the “harvest.”

A certain gleaning, as the emperor at least believed, still remained. [Col. 0557A] The suspicious prince, who was at the same time greedy for money, although everything had already been restored to tranquility, nevertheless dragged certain men, as it were, from their hiding places, saying that they had plotted against him, and therefore ordered them to be hurried away to death. Tertullian was writing while that “gleaning,” as he calls it, was under way. To know when Severus searched for the remnants of the rebels is therefore to know the very year of the *Apologeticum*.

Tertullian himself indicates that this occurred after certain solemnities held at Rome, during which these enemies of the emperor had made a great but insincere show of rejoicing. He does not add how much time intervened. It is nevertheless apparent that it should not be understood as very long. There is also a passage in another of his books that, for the present point, explains this one, as it were (*To Scapula*, Book I, ch. I, p. 552 of the works):

> Christians could never be found among the Albiniani, the Nigriani, or the Cassiani; rather, they were those very men who until the day before had sworn by their guardian spirits and who had both vowed and offered sacrifices for their welfare.

[Col. 0557B] This ingenious man is speaking of the same matter as in the passages we are expounding. What, then, prevents the word “the day before,” which denotes a brief interval, from being applied to both passages?

But what were those public rejoicings to which he refers? Unless I am mistaken, he is indicating the Quinquennalia. It is true that when Severus entered Rome after Albinus had been killed, everything resounded with rejoicings and applause (see Herodian, *Histories*, Book III, ch. VIII, p. 145). Nor would it damage our argument if anyone said that this public rejoicing was indicated here. Yet I consider it much more probable that the reference is to the Quinquennalia, both for other reasons and because Tertullian implies that vows for the emperor’s safety were then made: “But to proclaim their own wishes at another’s solemnity,” and the rest.

What, indeed, is better known than that this custom was observed especially at the Quinquennial games? What is more celebrated than these inscriptions on coins: **VOTA DECENN. SUSCEP.**? Herodian undoubtedly touches upon these ceremonies when, besides the gift that the emperor had presented to the people upon his return to Rome, he commemorates another generosity of this kind shortly before the Parthian expedition: νομάς τε μεγαλοφρόνως ἐπεδίδου, ἐπετέλεσε δὲ καὶ ἐπινικίον ἀγῶνα, τοὺς παντάχοθεν μούσης τε ὑποκρίτας, καὶ ἀνδρείας μαθήτας μεταπεμψάμενος (“He bestowed distributions with great munificence and also celebrated a victory contest, summoning from every quarter performers in the arts of the Muses and practitioners of athletic prowess”) (Book III, ch. VIII, p. 147).

> He also gave most lavish distributions and instituted a contest, summoning performers and athletes from every quarter.

Spartian reports the same thing (*Life of Severus*, ch. XIV, p. 150), in these words: [Col. 0557D]

> He then set out for the Parthian war, after presenting a gladiatorial show and giving a largess to the people.

See how amicably these two agree, and how aptly each reports that a solemnity of great munificence preceded the Parthian expedition. Had the most celebrated Tillemont attended to these facts, he would undoubtedly have arranged the matter differently. He thinks the passage refers to the followers of Pescennius Niger whom Severus hunted down in Syria. But Tertullian introduces men who had been present at Roman spectacles. Such were not Niger’s followers who lay concealed in Syria.

I care little whether the emperor proclaimed these festive days in 197 or 198. My only task is to show that the blood of those believed to be Albinus’ followers was shed anew when he was on the point of invading the Parthians. Even if no witness could be produced, my computation would nevertheless remain certain, since I could commend Tertullian as equivalent to them all. Spartian, however, is conveniently at hand and reports that the auspices of the new war were polluted by human slaughter (*Life of Severus*, ch. XIV, p. 180):

> Amid these events—while he was preparing himself for a new war and presenting the people with games to watch, concerning which and other matters the author had spoken above—he killed many on either true or fabricated charges. Most were condemned because they had made jokes; others, because they had remained silent; others, because they had said many things figuratively—so that the emperor might truly live up to his name, being truly both Pertinax and Severus.

I also refer to this point the words that follow a little later, which, in my opinion, do not pertain solely to the persecution of Niger’s adherents in the East [Col. 0558B] and should be compared with Tertullian’s final words:

> He also killed many on the pretext that they had consulted Chaldeans or prophets concerning his safety, especially anyone whom he suspected of being fit for imperial rule.

The matter is settled. By universal agreement, Severus set out against the Parthians in 198. Then, after the Quinquennalia had been presented, when he was breathing nothing but battles and the slaughter of Parthians, there occurred that gleaning of rebels of which Tertullian speaks. It can therefore no longer be doubted that the *Apologeticum* was composed in the same year.

We may now also identify the first year of the calamities inflicted upon Christians under the reign of Severus. They had already endured the fury of their enemies for some time when our author spoke on their behalf. Certainly, he nowhere speaks of wounds inflicted only recently, but of evils that had already become inveterate. [Col. 0558C] This shows that, if their miseries are not to be traced back still earlier, they must at the very least be reckoned from the preceding year, 197.

§ XV.—You now have what I resolved to communicate to you concerning the date of Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*. For my part, I have striven according to my abilities to give these arguments both strength and clarity; whether I have attained either must be left to the judgment of others. If some obscurity still adheres to them, you will consider that this is due less to my fault than to that of the subject itself. Investigations of this kind have the peculiarity that they always carry some of their native grime along with them. Nor are they written for those serving their first campaigns, but for those who have already attained some standing among learned citizens and are not ignorant of either kind of history or of critical studies. What appears exceedingly obscure to the former usually presents [Col. 0558D] no difficulty to the latter.

If fate permits, and if my labor is not entirely without supporters of its own, I intend to proceed along this path. I shall discuss the rest of Tertullian’s works with not merely the same diligence, but shall also treat his life—considerably more carefully than I see has been done thus far—in a separate book, to which I shall append certain dissertations on his works.

For a long time, the more learned have desired a new edition of them. And no one would more willingly than I have taken this burden upon himself, had such a lot in life fallen to me that I could believe myself capable of duly discharging it. Since this has been denied me, I have nevertheless resolved, by the method I have described, to render service not so much to this particular field as to sacred and civil history itself.

Henry Dodwell, a man of immortal memory, undertook [Col. 0559A] a work of this kind (on his life, written by Francis Brokesby, see La Roche, *Bibliothèque Anglaise*, vol. I, part I, pp. 86–87). Death prevented him from bringing it to completion. For my part, I greatly doubt whether his learning would have been matched by equal candor and maturity of judgment.

We possess a life of Tertullian by Pierre Allix; but if I say that it is less than perfect and carefully wrought, I shall not depart from the truth. Let the points that we have considered from it in this dissertation serve as a sample. Neither I, nor perhaps all who live outside France, have seen the life of Tertullian by Pierre-Thomas du Fossé, which Dupin testifies was published without the author’s name (*Bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. XVIII, p. 258). The palm therefore still lies in the midst, and, if I live, I shall strive to claim it for myself. I am not a man unaware that I am far inferior in learning to those whom I have named. Yet I promise—perhaps too boldly—that I shall surpass Dodwell in love of truth, and the others in assiduity and diligence.

## Two Books *To the Nations*

[Col. 0559]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, *TO THE NATIONS* (C)

## BOOK I

[Col. 0559B] **1.** The evidence of your ignorance, which refutes injustice even while defending it, is readily at hand: all who previously shared your ignorance and shared your hatred cease to hate as soon as it happens that they come to know; when they cease to be ignorant, they even become themselves what they had hated, and begin to hate what they had been. Thus you daily groan over the growing number of Christians. You cry out that the city is besieged; that there are Christians in the countryside, in the fortresses, and on the islands; and you lament as though it were a loss that every sex, every age, and, finally, every rank is passing over from you.

Yet even this does not move your minds to consider whether some hidden good may be present. You are not permitted to suspect more correctly; you have no desire to investigate more closely. At this point alone human curiosity [Col. 0559C] grows torpid. You love to remain ignorant of what others rejoice to have discovered. You prefer not to know because you already hate, as though you knew for certain that, if you came to know, you would no longer hate. And yet, if no cause for hatred is found, it will certainly be best to abandon your former injustice; but if the cause is established, nothing will be taken away from your hatred, which will instead be increased all the more by the knowledge of its justice—unless, perhaps, you are ashamed to be corrected or reluctant to be excused.

I know perfectly well the answer with which you usually confront the evidence of our proliferation. You say that a thing is not thereby prejudged to be good merely because it converts a great many people and draws them to itself. I know the mind’s tendency to change, even toward the worse. How many deserters are there from a good life? How many fugitives to depravity? Many, certainly—and now even more, in keeping with the extremity of the times.

But the comparison fails to correspond. For evil is so universally recognized [Col. 0559D] that not even the guilty themselves—those who pass over to evil and turn aside from you into depravity—dare to defend evil as good. They regard shameful deeds as objects of fear, and impious deeds as objects of shame. In short, they are eager to remain hidden, avoid appearing in public, tremble when caught, and deny when accused. Even under torture they do not readily or invariably confess; certainly, when condemned, they grieve. For they reproach in themselves what they had become: [Col. 0560B] they attribute their passage from innocence to an evil disposition, or else to fate. So unwilling are they to regard the evil as their own, because they cannot deny that it is evil.

But what comparable conduct do Christians display? [Note: [Col. 0559D] “But Christians.” Christians, compelled by no force, declared themselves Christians and gloried exceedingly in that fact. Thus in the *Apologeticum*, ch. I: “If he is denounced, he glories; if he is accused, he does not defend himself; when questioned, he confesses, even voluntarily; when condemned, he gives thanks.” But those who confessed it voluntarily were not for that reason condemned or treated as defendants. LE PR.] No one is ashamed; no one repents, except of what he formerly was. If he is denounced, he glories; if he is dragged away, he offers no resistance. If he is accused, he does not defend himself; when questioned, he confesses; when condemned, he glories. What kind of evil is this, in which the nature of evil ceases to exist?

**2.** In this matter you yourselves even judge contrary to the established method of investigating crimes. For when guilty men who have been brought before you deny the offense, you press them with tortures toward confession; but Christians, who confess voluntarily, you crush with tortures toward denial. What great perversity is this: [Col. 0560C] that you oppose confession, alter the function of torture, and compel a defendant who could escape freely to deny against his will? You who preside over the extraction of truth seek a lie from us alone, so that we may say that we are not what we are. I suppose you do not want us to be evil, and therefore eagerly strive to exclude us from that name.

To be sure, you batter [Note: [Col. 0559D] Le Prieur reads: “batter.”] and torture all other men so that they may deny that they are what they are said to be. Yet when they deny, you do not believe them; when we deny, you believe us at once. If you are certain that we are utterly criminal, why are we treated by you differently from criminals even in this?

I do not mean merely that you grant us no opportunity either to answer the accusation or to refuse it; for you are ordinarily not hasty in condemning men who have neither been accused nor defended. But, for example, if an inquiry is held concerning a murderer [Note: [Col. 0560D] Rigault conjectured: “is consulted.”], the case is not immediately struck from the record, nor is the investigation satisfied, once he has confessed to the name of murderer. Although you are slow to believe those who confess, you additionally demand the attendant circumstances: how often he committed murder, in what places, with what spoils, accomplices, and receivers—so that nothing whatever belonging to the criminal may remain concealed and nothing may be lacking to the truth required for judgment.

But in our case, although you charge us with more numerous and more atrocious crimes, you draw up briefer and slighter records. [Col. 0561A] I suppose you do not wish those whom you wish utterly destroyed to be burdened with charges, or you do not think it necessary to investigate what you already know. This, then, is all the more perverse if you compel those of whom you possess the greatest certainty to deny. Indeed, what would have accorded better with your hatred—once the proper judicial procedure had been set aside—would have been to strive by your own zeal not for denial, lest you release those whom you hate, but for confession of each individual crime, so that your hostility might be more fully satisfied by the accumulation of punishments, as it was determined how many times each man had already celebrated those banquets and how often, in the darkness, he had committed the incestuous acts of the onslaught.

What of the fact that, to eradicate the race, the investigation ought to have been extended and the questioning prolonged to include accomplices and accessories? The child-slaughterers [Note: [Col. 0561C] “The child-slaughterers and cooks, and the very dogs that acted as groomsmen, should have been brought forward.” They were, of course, accused of three crimes: impiety, Thyestean feasts, and incestuous intercourse. Thus Athenagoras: τρία ἐπιφημίζουσιν ἐμῖν ἡγκλήματα· ἀθεότητα, Θυέστεια δεῖπνα, Οἰδιποδείοι μεξεισ (“They impute three crimes to us: atheism, Thyestean banquets, and Oedipal intercourse”; several recovered spellings are corrupt, but the sense is clear). For the pagans used to say that Christians, when they assembled, customarily killed an infant; that, after eating its flesh and drinking its blood, they entered into a covenant with one another; and that after the banquet they coupled promiscuously with any women whatever. It was furthermore customary, they said, to employ dogs tied to the lampstands, which, when a morsel was thrown to them, overturned the lamps; once the lights had been extinguished, they claimed that the crimes of those most shameful couplings then took place. LE PR.] and the cooks and the very dogs [Note: [Col. 0561D] “And the very dogs that acted as groomsmen.” In the *Apologeticum*, those who are here called “groomsmen” are called “pimps”—the overturners of the lights. RIG.] that acted as groomsmen should have been brought forward; then the matter would have been properly corrected [Note: [Col. 0561D] “Then the matter would have been properly corrected.” Only then would the procedure of investigation have been just and lawful, if the child-slaughterers, cooks, and so forth were brought forward. The same commentator.].

The spectacles, too, would have acquired an added attraction. With what eagerness people would gather in the amphitheater [Col. 0561B] if some man who had devoured a hundred infants were going to fight! But such horrifying and monstrous charges are laid against us. Surely they ought to have been brought to light, lest they appear incredible and public hatred against us grow cold. For many people moderate their belief in such allegations, recoiling from the notion that nature should seek a wild beast’s food, though intercourse with humankind has barred it from belonging to the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] “Recoiling from the notion that nature should seek a wild beast’s food, though intercourse with humankind has barred it from belonging to the human race.” We have thus restored what appears in the Codex Agobardinus without any meaning. For it has been corrupted as follows: “Honoring nature to seek a wild beast’s food, which intercourse with humankind has barred.” Tertullian says that such horrifying and monstrous charges are laid against us that many moderate their belief in them—that is, do not give credence to such things—recoiling from the idea that nature should seek a wild beast’s food: namely, that human beings are so born and constituted as to seek and desire a wild beast’s food; that their nature is so bestial that they willingly feed upon human flesh, which is the nature of wild beasts. But intercourse with humankind has barred that nature of beasts—that is, beasts themselves—from the human race. From where, then, were these humans born, this race of beasts? He said “a nature that seeks,” in the Greek manner, meaning something so made and born that it seeks. The same commentator.]

**3.** You, therefore, who are otherwise the most diligent and persistent investigators of far lesser crimes, abandon that diligence in the face of such horrors, surpassing every form of impiety. You neither accept confession—though judges must always labor to obtain it—nor arrange an investigation—though those who condemn must always take counsel from it. It is now apparent that every accusation against us is directed not against any particular crime, but against the name.

Indeed, if the truth of the crimes were established, the names of the crimes themselves would be applied to those condemned, and the sentence against us would be pronounced in this form: “It is decreed that this murderer, or incestuous person, or whatever else we are alleged to be, be led away, crucified, or given to the beasts.” But your sentences [Col. 0562A] record nothing except that someone has confessed to being a Christian. No name of a crime appears—unless the name itself is the crime. For this is in reality the whole basis of the hatred against us.

The name [Note: [Col. 0562C] “The name is the issue.” Since the pagans suffered from a shortage of crimes by which to oppress the Christians, they accused the name itself. Tertullian says much about this here and previously in the *Apologeticum*. For at that time Christians were ὑπὸ συκοφαντῶν σφαττόμενοι (“being slaughtered by false accusers”), as Athenagoras says in his *Apology for the Christians*. They were summoned to court and condemned on account of the name alone, for no inquiry was made whether Christians had committed any evil, as the same author says: ἀλλ` εἰς τὸ ὄνομα, ὡς εἰς ἀδὶκημα (“but against the name, as though against a crime”). The charge was drawn up; for no Christian had been detected in any criminal act: οὐδεὶς ἀδικῶν Χριστιανὸς ἐλήλεγκται (“no Christian has been proved guilty of wrongdoing”). Everywhere only the name was considered and treated as a crime: οὐδὲν δὲ ὄνομα, ἐφ` ἑαυτοῦ καὶ δι` αὑτοῦ, οὐ πονηρὸν οὒτε χρηστὸν νομίζεσθαι (“no name, considered in and of itself, is to be deemed either evil or good”), and earlier: οὐ γὰρ τὰ ὀνόματα μίσοις ἅξια, λλὰ τὸ ἀδίκημα δίκης καὶ τιμωρίας (“for names are not deserving of hatred, but wrongdoing is deserving of judgment and punishment”; μίσοις ἅξια is textually irregular, and λλὰ apparently lacks the initial ἀ of ἀλλὰ). Thus Athenagoras throughout the opening of his *Apology*. LE PR.] is the issue: some hidden force assails it through your ignorance, so that you are unwilling to know for certain what you are certain that you do not know for certain. Thus you neither believe allegations that are not proved nor wish to investigate them, lest they readily be proved false [Note: [Col. 0561C] Havercamp corrects: “lest they be proved false,” etc. In what follows, read “is answered or denied”—“is recited.”], so that a hostile name may be punished under a presumption of crimes. Indeed, to make us abandon the hostile name, we are compelled to deny it; then, when we have denied, we are released with complete immunity for our past acts. We are no longer bloodstained or incestuous, because we have relinquished that name.

But while this reasoning is demonstrated in its proper place, disclose the basis upon which you proceed in your assault upon the name. What is the name’s crime, what its offense, [Col. 0562B] what its fault? For you are barred from alleging crimes that no ordinance [Note: [Col. 0562D] “No ordinance directs.” That is, no command. Below, p. 51: “Nero’s ordinance.” RIG.] directs you to allege, no proof [Note: [Col. 0562C] Rigault reads “production of evidence.” In what follows, write “is answered or denied”—“is recited.”] establishes, and no sentence enumerates. What is presented to the governor, what is investigated concerning the defendant, what is answered or denied, what is recited from the council’s deliberation—that I recognize as the charge.

Therefore, as regards the merit of a name—if names can incur any guilt, if words can be accused—I think that no complaint can be brought against a word or name unless it either sounds barbarous, conveys something ill-omened or indecent, or otherwise displeases the hearer when it is pronounced. These are the crimes of words or names, just as barbarism, solecism, and an excessively tasteless figure are faults of words and speech.

But the name “Christian,” so far as its meaning is concerned, is interpreted from “anointing.” Even when it is incorrectly pronounced by you as “Chrestian” (for you are not even clearly certain of the name itself), it is still formed from “sweetness” or “goodness” [Note: [Col. 0562D] “From sweetness or goodness”: from sweetness, *Christianus*; from goodness, *Chrestianus*. RIG.]. Thus in innocent human beings you detain even our innocent name, which is neither awkward [Col. 0563A] [Note: [Col. 0563] This note appears at the foot of column 563, but the callout number (1) has not been printed in the text.] [Note: [Col. 0563C] Le Prieur conjectures: “Others, whom,” etc.] upon the tongue, nor harsh to the ears, nor harmful to a person, nor hostile to the country, but Greek, like other names, melodious, and pleasant in its meaning. Surely names are not to be punished by sword, cross, or beasts.

**4.** But you say that the sect is punished under the name of its founder. First, it is certainly a proper and customary rule for a sect to be designated by the title of its founder, since philosophers too receive their names from their founders—the Pythagoreans and Platonists [Note: [Col. 0563C] “Pythagoreans and Platonists.” He had said earlier in the *Apologeticum*: “Are not philosophers named from their founders—Platonists, Epicureans, Pythagoreans?” Thus Christians regarded it as glorious to be called by the name of their leader. Hence Chrysostom, concerning the blessed Lucian: ποίας εἶ πατρίδος; Χριστιανός εἰμι, φησί (“‘What country are you from?’ ‘I am a Christian,’ he says”). τί ἔχεις ἐπιτήδευμα; Χριστιανός εἰμι (“‘What occupation do you have?’ ‘I am a Christian’”). τίνας (“‘What…’”) [Col. 0563D] προγόνους; ὁ δὲ πρὸς ἅπαντα ἔλεγεν, ὅτι Χριστιανός εἰμι (“‘…ancestors do you have?’ But to every question he replied, ‘I am a Christian’”). “What is your religion?” “I am a Christian.” “What art do you profess?” “I am a Christian.” “Who are your ancestors?” To every question he replied, “I am a Christian.” LE PR.]—just as physicians are called Erasistrateans and grammarians Aristarchians. Accordingly, if a sect is evil because its founder is evil, it is punished as an offshoot of an evil name.

And yet this would be rashly presumed. It was first necessary to examine the founder so that the sect might be known, rather than to preserve an opinion of the founder from an inspection of the sect. But now, since you necessarily remain ignorant of the sect because you are ignorant of its founder—or fail to examine [Col. 0563B] the founder because you do not examine the sect—you strike at the name alone, as though in it you were apprehending both the sect and the founder, whom you do not know at all.

And yet philosophers have complete liberty to pass over from you to a sect, a founder, and a name of their own; and no one stirs up hatred against them when they publicly and openly bark all the bitterness of their eloquence against your morals, rites, worship, and ways of life, with contempt for the laws and without regard for persons—so that some even hurl their freedom of speech with impunity against the emperors themselves.

But philosophers only affect the truth, which is most burdensome to the world, whereas Christians possess it. Those who possess it therefore give greater offense, because one who affects it makes a mockery of it [Note: [Col. 0563D] “Because one who affects it confines it.” In the *Apologeticum*: “corrupts it.” RIG.], while one who possesses it defends it. In short, Socrates was condemned precisely because he had approached the truth more closely by destroying your gods. [Col. 0563C] Although the Christian name did not yet exist on earth at that time, the truth was nevertheless always condemned.

Accordingly, you will not deny that he was wise, since even your Pythian god had borne witness to him: “Of all men,” it said, “Socrates is the wisest” [Note: [Col. 0563D] “Of all men,” it said, “Socrates.” It is commonly known that Socrates was judged the wisest of all mortals by Apollo’s oracle: Ἀνδρῶν ἁπάντων Σωκράτης σοφώτατος (“Of all men Socrates is the wisest”). Hence Valerius Maximus, Book III, ch. 4: “Socrates was judged the wisest not only by human consensus but also by Apollo’s oracle.” And Salvian, Book VIII of *On the Governance of God*: “Nevertheless, Apollo the Pythian spoke against himself, and truth proved superior; for when he pronounced Socrates the wisest of men, he denied that he himself was a god.” Socrates, indeed, was summoned to trial by the Athenians and condemned to death because he held wrong opinions concerning the gods. Worthy of attention are the words of [Col. 0564C] Minucius Felix: “Yet if there is a desire to philosophize, let whoever among you is great enough imitate Socrates, the foremost figure in wisdom, if he can. Whenever that man was questioned about heavenly matters, his well-known answer was: ‘What lies above us is no concern of ours.’” The same commentator.].

Truth defeated Apollo, causing him to pronounce judgment against himself. [Col. 0564A] For he confessed that he was not a god by affirming that the man who denied the gods was the wisest. Yet among you Socrates is regarded as all the less wise because he denied the gods, although he was wise precisely because he denied them.

In the same fashion you also customarily say of us: “Lucius Titius is a good man—except that he is a Christian”; and similarly of another: “I am surprised that Gaius Seius, a respectable man, has become a Christian.” In the blindness of their folly, they praise what they know, censure what they do not know, and corrupt what they know by means of what they do not know. It occurs to no one that a man may be good and prudent precisely because he is a Christian, or a Christian because he is prudent and good, although it is more humane to judge hidden things from manifest ones than to prejudge manifest things from what is hidden.

They had formerly known certain men, before they bore this name, as vagrants, worthless, and depraved. They marvel at their sudden reform, and yet they know how to marvel rather than how to understand. Others contend with such obstinacy that they fight against their own advantages, which they might derive from association with people bearing this name.

I know more than one husband who was formerly anxious about his wife’s conduct and could not endure even mice [Note: [Col. 0564C] “Not even mice creeping in.” When Septimius wrote this, he had in mind the line of Juvenal: “Aware of his own testicle, from which the mouse flees.” RIG.] creeping into the bedroom without a groan of suspicion. Yet when he discovered the cause of her new diligence and unaccustomed confinement [Note: [Col. 0564D] “Unaccustomed confinement.” Having now become a Christian, she scarcely set foot outside the house but attended to domestic affairs, as though she had imposed confinement upon herself, whereas formerly she had wandered here and there, roving and unrestrained in lust. The same commentator.], he offered his wife every [Note: [Col. 0564D] “Every indulgence to his wife.” He touches upon the customs and exceedingly corrupt morals of the pagans, among whom the husband pretends to be wrapped and buried in deep sleep, as though drunk, and, as Juvenal has it, Satire I:

> Trained to gaze upon the paneled ceiling,
> Skilled also to snore over his cup with wakeful nose.

Here he says that nothing of this kind occurs among Christians. **LE PR.**] he offered his wife complete forbearance, renounced jealousy, and preferred to be the husband of a prostitute rather than of a Christian woman. He himself was permitted to change his nature for the worse, but he did not permit the woman to be reformed for the better. A father disinherited a son about whom he had ceased to complain. A master sent to the workhouse a slave whom he had otherwise found indispensable. As soon as anyone has learned that a man is a Christian, he prefers him guilty. For the discipline is itself made conspicuous by its own character, and [Col. 0564C] we are betrayed by nothing other than our goodness. If even the wicked [Note: [Col. 0564D] **The wicked shine forth through their own wickedness.** They become conspicuous, are pointed out, and are designated by name. **RIG.**] shine forth through their own wickedness, why are we alone, contrary to the ordinances of nature, marked out as utterly wicked because of our goodness? For what distinguishing marks do we display except, first, wisdom, by which we do not worship the frivolous works of human hands; self-restraint, by which we abstain from what belongs to another; chastity, which we do not defile even [Col. 0565A] with our eyes; compassion, by which we bend over the needy; truth itself, by which we give offense; and liberty itself, for which we know how to die? Whoever wishes to understand who the Christians are must necessarily use these as his criteria.

### 5

As for what you therefore say—that Christians are utterly wicked and disgraceful in avarice, luxury, and depravity—we shall not deny that some are so. Even this is sufficient testimony to our name: if not all are such, nor even the majority. In a body, however whole or pure you may wish it to be, some mole must sprout, or a little wart rise, or a freckle stain it. No refinement so thoroughly purges even the serenity of heaven that it is not marked by the wisp of some little cloud. A small blemish seen upon the forehead, upon some particular part, serves as an example of how the whole is clean: [Col. 0565B] the greater portion of goodness uses a little evil as testimony to itself.

Yet when you prove that some of our people are wicked, by that very fact you prove that they are not Christians. Ask to which sect the wickedness is to be assigned. In your own conversations, whenever you speak against us, you say: “Why is that man a cheat, if Christians are self-restrained? Why is he cruel, if they are compassionate?” To such a degree you bear witness that such men are not Christians, when you retort by asking why those who are called Christians are such men. There is a great distance between the charge and the name, between opinion and truth. For names too have been instituted in such a way that they have their own boundaries between being called something and actually being it. How many, after all, are called philosophers, yet do not fulfill the law of philosophy? All bear a name derived from their professions. Let those who disgrace the truth with the surface of a word deceive the name by the excellence claimed for their profession. Those who [Col. 0565C] are called something are not immediately what they are called; because they are not what they are called, they are called it in vain and deceive those who subject the reality to the name, whereas the standing of the name ought to accord with the reality.

And yet people of this kind neither assemble nor share fellowship with us, having become yours again through their offenses; for we do not mingle even with those whom your violence and cruelty have compelled to deny the faith. Unwilling deserters of the discipline would, of course, be more easily retained among us than willing ones. In any case, you call those people Christians without cause whom Christians themselves deny—Christians who do not know how to deny themselves [Note: [Col. 0565D] **Who do not know how to deny themselves.** For they were prepared to die for one another, for their brothers; and the pagans marveled at this steadfastness of mutual love. Hence the words in the *Apologeticum*: “See,” they say, “how they love one another, and how they are prepared to die for one another.” **RIG.**].

### 6

Whenever your conscience is constrained and hemmed in by these propositions and by our answers, which truth supplies from its own resources, it becomes the silent witness of its own ignorance; and in your agitation you take refuge at a certain little altar, [Col. 0565D] that is, in the authority of the laws: namely, that they surely would not punish [Col. 0566A] this sect unless its deserts had been established in the judgment of the lawgivers.

What, then, prevented those deserts from being established in like manner before the executors of the laws, since, in the case of all other crimes that are similarly forbidden and punished by the laws, the penalty is suspended unless an inquiry is first made? For example, the law identifies a murderer or an adulterer, yet the circumstances of the offense are still investigated, even though the general nature of the deed is known to everyone. The laws punish a Christian. If there is some deed committed by a Christian, it ought to be brought to light; no law forbids investigation. Indeed, investigation acts in the interests of the laws. For how will you observe a law by avoiding what the law forbids, if the diligence needed for avoidance is taken away through your failure to recognize what you are to observe?

No law owes the consciousness of its own justice to itself, but to those from whom it seeks obedience. Besides, a law is suspect if it does not wish to have itself proved. Thus the laws are rightly regarded as just against Christians, and as worthy of reverence and observance, only so long as what they persecute remains unknown. Once they are understood, they are rightly found to be utterly unjust and are spat upon, together with their swords, crosses, and lions. An unjust law is entitled to no honor. Yet I suppose the injustice of certain laws is admitted, since every day you moderate their harshness and viciousness by new legal opinions and enactments.

### 7

“From where, then,” you say, “did so widespread a report about you obtain currency—a report whose testimony may perhaps have sufficed for the lawgivers?” Who, I ask, guaranteed its trustworthiness either to them at that time or to you thereafter? It is rumor. Is this not rumor:

> Rumor—an evil than which no other is swifter  
> (*Virgil, Aeneid* IV.174)?

[Note: [Col. 0565D] **Is this not rumor?** In the seventh chapter of the *Apologeticum* he had described rumor as frivolous, deceitful, and unjust; here he repeats the same points, as though once again exposing its falsity. You might think Tertullian had Martial in view, who in Book VII, epigram 5, speaks as follows concerning Domitian’s return:

> No certain authority is present, but every voice announces this;
>
> I believe you, Rumor: you are accustomed to speak the truth.

The point, of course, is that he should detect and [Col. 0566D] convict him of falsehood together with rumor. Plutarch should be read in *Roman Questions*, question 5: διὰ τί τοῦς τεθνᾶναι φημισθέντας ἐπὶ ξένης ψευδῶς, κᾄν ἐπανέλθωσιν, οὐ δέχονθαι κατὰ θύρας, ἀλλὰ τῷ κεράμῳ τροσβαίνοντες εἴσω καθιᾶσιν ἀυτούς; (“Why do they not receive through the doors those falsely reported to have died abroad, even if they return, but instead go up onto the roof and lower them inside?”), since rumor is ἀθυρόστομος (“unrestrained of mouth”); or, as Nicetas Choniates has it in his *Andronicus*, αθυρόγλωττος (“unrestrained of tongue”). Thus in *Thebaid* 3 rumor is said to be capable of reporting deeds done and undone, and in Claudian, *Against Eutropius*, Book II:

> Now wandering Rumor shakes the pallid court
>
> With crowded terrors. ]

Why is it an evil, if it is always true and not, for the most part, more mendacious [Note: [Col. 0565D] Rigault, with Havercamp’s agreement, emends to *mendacior*, “more mendacious.”] [Col. 0566C] [Note: [Col. 0566D] **Not for the most part by falsehood.** Thus the Agobard manuscript reads. We shall emend by restoring the letter that has fallen out: “Not for the most part more mendacious.” **RIG.**]?
