Even when it brings a true report, it does not cease from its passion for lying, but interweaves falsehoods with truths, adding, subtracting, and confusing them by variation.

What of the fact that its condition is such that it persists only while it lies? It lives only so long as it proves nothing; once it has been substantiated, it falls away and, as though it had discharged its office of reporting, expires. From that point onward, the thing itself is possessed and the thing itself is named. No one says, for example, “They say this happened at Rome,” or, “Rumor has it that he obtained the province by lot”; rather: “He obtained the province by lot,” and, “This happened at Rome.” No one names rumor unless he is uncertain, because no one is certain through rumor but through knowledge; no one believes rumor except a fool, because a wise person does not believe what is uncertain.

However widely rumor has spread in its self-promotion, it must at some point have arisen from a single mouth. [Col. 0566D] From there it creeps, as it were, along the offshoots of tongues and ears, [Col. 0567A] and the rumors obscure the little flaw in its origins, so that no one reflects on whether that first mouth sowed lies—as often happens, whether from a disposition toward rivalry, from the judgment of suspicion, or even from the novel pleasure of lying. But it is well that time reveals everything, as your own maxims and proverbs testify, and nature itself, which is so ordered that nothing remains hidden, even what rumor has not betrayed.

See what sort of betrayer [Note: [Col. 0567C] **What sort of betrayer.** Here he calls *prodicia* what in the *Apologeticum* he calls an informer. “You bring this informer forward against us,” he says, “who has to this day been unable to prove what she once spread abroad and, over so long a period, strengthened into accepted opinion.” **RIG.**] you have suborned against us: what it once reported and over so long a time strengthened into belief, it has been unable to prove to this day.

This name arose under the emperor Augustus [Note: [Col. 0567D] **Under the emperor Augustus, etc.** Christ the Lord was born while the emperor Augustus held power; under the reign of Tiberius he suffered the punishment of death. But under the emperor Nero a most severe persecution arose, in which, of course, Saints Peter and Paul were put to death. **LE PR.**]; its discipline shone forth under Tiberius; under Nero its condemnation gained force. From this alone you may assess it by the character of its persecutor: if that emperor was pious, the Christians were impious; if he was just and chaste, the Christians were unjust and incestuous; if he was not a public enemy, we are public enemies. The condemner himself demonstrated what sort of people we are, for he surely punished what was opposed to himself. And yet, when all the others had been erased, this decree of Nero alone endured—just, ultimately, because it was unlike its author.

Thus our age [Note: [Col. 0567D] **Thus our age is not yet 250 years.** From the birth of Christ to Severus, under whom Tertullian lived, not yet 250 years had elapsed. For Severus died at York in Britain, through the intrigues of his elder son Caracalla, around the year of Christ 211, and he reigned for almost eighteen years; hence it is clear that fifty years of the Christian era had not yet elapsed [sic]. **Idem.**] is not yet 250 years old. So many wicked men in the meantime; so many crosses [Note: [Col. 0567D] **So many crosses attained divinity, etc.** The savagery of Tiberius is censured here; such was his cruelty and thirst for shedding blood that Constantine Manasses in his *Annals* calls him “mud mixed with blood,” πηλὸς αἵματι πεφυρμένος (“mud mingled with blood”). [Col. 0568D] **LE PR.**] have attained divinity, so many infants have been slaughtered, so many loaves stained with blood, so many overturnings of lamps, so many aberrations of marriage—and still rumor alone passes judgment upon Christians.

Rumor does indeed have a great foundation in the defect of the human disposition: it lies more successfully about bitter and atrocious things. For the more inclined you are to malice, the more receptive you are to believing evil; indeed, false evil is more readily believed than true good. Yet if [Col. 0567C] injustice had left any place for prudence among you, justice would surely have demanded, in order to test the credibility of rumor, that you examine from whom rumor could have been given to the populace, and thus to the entire world. Not, I suppose, by the Christians themselves, since the obligation of silence is owed by the very form and law of all mysteries—how much more in the case of mysteries whose disclosure would not in the meantime escape human punishment, but would incur immediate execution?

If, therefore, they are not their own betrayers, it follows that the informants are outsiders. I ask you: from where do outsiders obtain their knowledge, when even lawful and [Col. 0568A] legitimate mysteries guard against every outsider’s witnessing them? Unless notorious mysteries have less contempt for outsiders. Yet outsiders are more suited both to honor and to fabricate such things . . . The curiosity of members of the household has stolen knowledge through cracks and crevices.

What if members of the household betray them to you? All of us are betrayed by no one more readily [than by members of our households]—how much more so if there is so great an atrocity that, by the justice of its indignation, it breaks every bond of familiarity! Could the mind have contained what it abhorred, or the eye what it dreaded? This too is astonishing: that the man who sprang forward with so strong a right of impatience should be eager to accuse but not to prove, and that the man who heard should not also [Note: [Col. 0567C] Rigault: “not also prove—and not see.”] take care to see. For the informer’s reward is equal if he proves what he has reported, and the hearer’s if he also believes for himself what he hears.

“Then,” you say, “it was first reported and brought forward; it was heard and inspected, [Col. 0568B] and from that point it was entrusted to rumor.” This certainly surpasses all astonishment: that something continually committed should have been detected only once—unless we have now ceased to perform such things. Yet we are still called by the same name, are still reckoned under the same charges, and overflow in number day by day. The [Note: [Col. 0568C] Rigault reads *quod*, “the fact that.”] more numerous we are, the more people there are to hate us; hatred increases as its material increases. As the multitude of the accused grows, why does the multitude of informers not likewise grow?

As far as I know, our way of life has also become better known. You know even the days of our assemblies; accordingly, we are both besieged and overwhelmed, and we are arrested in the very secrecy of our gatherings. Yet who has ever come upon a half-eaten child [Note: [Col. 0568D] **Has ever come upon a half-eaten child.** By various arguments he wards off the impiety imputed to Christians, and by his eloquence prevents that charge of infanticide from adhering to them. It ought to be very well known that this slander was derived from the infamous rites of Saturn customarily performed in Africa, in which infants were sacrificed. Prudentius, Book II, *Against Symmachus*:

> The rites of Saturn smoke with the slaughter of infants,
>
> And the savage altars resound with their lamentable wailings.

Nothing is more frequently encountered in Lactantius, Minucius, and the others. Tertullian himself has the following against the Gnostics: “But indeed the world has permitted the Diana of the Scythians, the Mercury of the Gauls, or the Saturn of the Africans to be appeased with a human victim.” **LE PR.**]? Who has discovered marks of teeth in the bloodied bread? Who, when sudden light burst into the darkness, recognized any unclean [Col. 0568C]—so as not to say incestuous—evidence? If we purchase immunity from being dragged into public on such charges by paying a reward, why are we also overwhelmed? We could even avoid being dragged out altogether. For who either sells or purchases the betrayal of a crime without the crime itself?

But why should I disparage outside spies and informers, when you cast against us allegations that would have to be published with the loudest outcry by us ourselves—either as soon as they were heard, if they were disclosed beforehand, or after they were discovered, if they were hidden in the meantime? Without doubt, it is the custom for those who wish to be initiated first [Col. 0569A] to approach the master or father of the rites. Then he will say: “You need an infant who is still wailing [Note: [Col. 0569D] The manuscripts read *vagetur*, “wanders.”], to be sacrificed, and a quantity of bread to be broken into its blood; in addition, lampstands for the dogs tied to them to knock over, and morsels of food for those same dogs [Note: [Col. 0569D] *Apologeticum* 8: “morsels which make them strain toward overturning the lights.” Havercamp considers that the word *extendant*, “make them strain,” ought either to be restored or understood here.]. But you also need a mother or sister.”

What if none are available? I suppose you will be unable to become a properly constituted Christian. Tell me, do they endure having these things, announced by others, betrayed? The procedure is different: they must not know them [Note: [Col. 0570D] Rigault: “The procedure is different. They must not know them, etc.”]. The business of deceit is first carried through; the feasts and marriages are set before them while they are ignorant. For previously they had never heard anything about the Christian mysteries. Yet afterward they must necessarily learn of them, if only because preparations must be made for others whom they introduce.

Besides, how absurd it is that the profane person should know what the priest does not! They therefore keep silent and, having accepted it, endure it; [Col. 0569B] they let nothing of the tragedy of Thyestes or Oedipus break forth and do not bring it before the people. [The following text is uncertain and lacunose:] “trust in servants and teachers and in those more powerful than themselves, bites already learned . . . they seize.”

If nothing of this kind is proved, one must suppose it to be some great unknown thing, whose price consists in the endurance of such atrocities. Wretched and pitiable nations, behold, we set before you the promise of our discipline. It promises eternal life to those who follow and preserve it; contrariwise, it threatens the profane and its rivals with eternal punishment in eternal fire. For both outcomes the resurrection of the dead is proclaimed. We shall consider the credibility of these claims when they are set out in their proper place; meanwhile, believe them as we do.

For I wish to know whether you are prepared to enter through such crimes, as we allegedly do. [Col. 0569C] Come, whoever you are: plunge your blade into the infant; or, if that is another man’s duty, then merely watch the soul die before it has lived. At least catch the fresh blood in which you are to soak your bread; feast upon it gladly. Meanwhile, as you recline at table, count the places where your mother or sister has taken her couch. Mark them carefully so that, when darkness rushes in—evidently putting each person’s diligence to the test—you do not blunder by assaulting a stranger. You will have committed sacrilege unless you commit incest.

When you have discharged all these obligations, you will live forever. I desire your answer: do you value eternity so highly? No—precisely for this reason you do not believe it. And even if you came to believe it, I deny that you would wish it; and even if you wished it, I deny that you could do it. Why, then, should others be able, if you are unable? Why should you be unable, if others are able? What price do you wish immunity and eternity to exact? Do they seem to us things to be purchased at absolutely any cost? Or do Christians have [Col. 0569D] different rows of teeth, cavities [Col. 0570A] for torches, and different sinews for the lust of incest?

No, I think not. For it is enough that truth alone distinguishes us from your position. We are called a third race: some kind of Cynopenae [Note: [Col. 0570D] Rigault reads *Cynopennae*; but compare *Apologeticum* 8.] [Note: [Col. 0569D] Some *Cynopennae*, or Sciapods? Pamelius, followed by Lacerda, reads *Cynophane*, and thus the meaning is: “Do we have dogs’ faces or canine shamelessness, so that we can so readily watch a homicide or infanticide?” Voweren reads “Cyclopes,” but Desiderius Heraldus has *Cynopennae*. **LE PR.**], or Sciapods, or some underground Antipodes [Note: [Col. 0569D] **Underground Antipodes.** In the book *On the Soul*, p. 334, he said, “Animals living underground.” **RIG.**].

### 8

If there is any rationality here—at least among you—I should like you to produce the first and second races, so that the third may thus be established. Psammetichus indeed thought that the question of the first race had been investigated by his ingenuity [text uncertain]. For it is said that he entrusted newborn infants, separated from human intercourse, to a nurse to be reared; and for this very purpose he had cut out the nurse’s tongue, so that, being wholly exiled from the human voice, they would not shape their speech from hearing it, but by uttering speech of their own accord would identify as the first nation the one whose sound nature dictated.

Their first utterance was reported as *Bekkos* [Note: [Col. 0569D] **[Col. 0570B] Their first utterance was reported as *Bekkos*.** The reading *Pactos* found in the Agobard manuscript is corrupt. For in Herodotus and others who handed this story down to Septimius, it is written Βέκκος (*Bekkos*). Likewise in Galen, Book II, *On Differences*, ἀλλ` εἰ καὶ Βέκκος ἐθέλεις τὸν ἄρτον καλεῖν, ὥσπερ οἱ Φρύγες, οὐδὲν ἡμῖν διαφέρει (“But even if you choose to call bread *Bekkos*, as the Phrygians do, it makes no difference to us”). **Idem.**] [Note: [Col. 0570D] The manuscripts read *Pactos*. Compare Herodotus 2.2.]; its interpretation is the Phrygian word for “bread.” From this the Phrygians are held to be the first race.

But this will be one of the vanities of your stories that we must examine, and not idly, since we are eager to demonstrate that your faith is devoted to vanities rather than to truths [Note: [Col. 0570D] Write: *vanitatibus potiusquam veritatibus*, “to vanities rather than to truths.”]. Is it credible at all that, after such a member had been cut away, after the very organ of the soul had been laid waste and surely severed at the root, and after the throat—dangerously wounded even from the outside—had been mutilated, with putrefaction then flowing back into the vital organs and nourishment finally ceasing for some time, the nurse’s life could have continued?

Come now, suppose she survived through Philomela’s remedies . . . although more judicious interpreters understand that Philomela herself was rendered mute not by the cutting out of her tongue, but by the blush of shame. If, therefore, the nurse survived, [Col. 0570C] she could have poured forth some dull and inarticulate sound or ringing noise, without any modulation of the lips, her mouth open and her tongue numb, forced from her throat alone. The infants may then have imitated it more readily because it was their only sound and, having little tongues of their own, produced it with somewhat greater modulation; thus they may have stumbled by chance [Note: [Col. 0570D] **They may have stumbled by chance upon some interpretation.** That is, by a random impact of the tongue against the opposing wind or air they produced a sound to which some interpretation could be given. **Idem.**] upon some interpretation.

Let the Phrygians now be the first race; the Christians, however, are not therefore the third. For how many other successions of nations came after the Phrygians? Indeed, reflect whether those whom you call the third race might occupy the first place, since there is no nation that is not Christian. Thus, whatever nation is first is nonetheless Christian. Ridiculous madness! You call us the newest and name us the third.

“But we are reckoned the third race with respect to religion, not according to racial classification: Romans first, Jews second, and then Christians.” Where, then, are the Greeks? Or, if they are counted among Roman [Col. 0570D] superstitions, seeing that [Col. 0571A] Rome solicited even the gods of Greece (chapter 6), where at least are the Egyptians, who themselves, so far as I know, possess a peculiar and curious religion?

[Note: [Col. 0571] This note appears at the foot of column 571, but the callout number (1) has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0571C] Write: *Hiera, Anaphe* (or *Napea*) *et Delos*, etc. Compare [Col. 0571D] *Apologeticum* 40.]

Moreover, if those in third place are so monstrous, what must those who precede them in first and second place be considered?

### 9

But why should I marvel at your absurdities, when malice and stupidity, incorporated and conjoined by their natural form, have intervened under the same proprietor [Note: [Col. 0571D] **Rome solicited the gods of Greece.** The Romans imitated the Greeks in everything, even in their errors and vices. If any superstition was born or exalted in Greece, it immediately flew to Rome, where it was received with great popular applause. They also “solicited”—that is, summoned—the divinities and vanities of barbarians; thus Cybele, the mother of the gods, flew of her own accord from Pessinus to Rome. **LE PR.**] of error?

Indeed, since I do not marvel, I must enumerate them, so that in recognizing them you yourselves may marvel at the depth of the folly into which you fall when you insist that we are the causes of every public disaster or injury. If the Tiber has overflowed, if the Nile has not overflowed, if the sky has stood still, if the earth has moved . . . [text lost] has devastated, if famine has afflicted, immediately the cry of everyone is: “Christ’s . . . [text lost].” As though they had too little, or nothing else, to fear!

[Col. 0571B] What, then? I suppose that, because we despise your gods, we provoke these missiles from them. As we stated above, our age [Note: [Col. 0571D] **Under the same proprietor of error.** He means the Evil One, or Satan, that great wholesale dealer in fraud and malice. **RIG.**] is not yet three hundred years old. How many disasters before that span of time fell throughout the whole world upon individual cities and provinces? How many foreign and civil wars? How many plagues, famines, fires, chasms, and earthquakes has the age recorded?

Where were the Christians when the Roman state furnished so many narratives of its own sufferings? Where were the Christians when Hierenappe [Note: [Col. 0571D] **Our age is not yet, etc.** Just above he had said, “Not yet 250 years”; here, correctly, “Not yet three hundred years.” Yet within so brief a period so many disasters occurred, and so great a slaughter of Christians was inflicted in every part of the world, that those who consider the matter with too little attention regard it as wholly incredible. **LE PR.**], Delphi, Rhodes [Note: [Col. 0572D] **Hierennape.** For *Hierenape*, just as above *Cynopenne* for *Cynopene*. **RIG.**], and Crete—entire islands—perished together with many thousands of people? Or when, as Plato recalls, an area larger than Asia or Africa was submerged in the Atlantic Sea? When fire from heaven overwhelmed Vulsinii, and fire from its own mountain overwhelmed the Tarpeian district? When the Corinthian Sea was snatched away by an earthquake? When [Col. 0571C] a deluge destroyed the entire world?

Where, then, were—not Christians, the despisers of the gods, I will not say that—but your gods themselves? The places, towns, and cities in which they were born, lived, and were buried, and even those they founded, prove that they came after that disaster. Otherwise those places would not have survived to the present day, unless they were subsequent to that disaster.

But you take no care to reread and reconsider the testimony of the ages, since it has been reported to you differently—especially lest you pronounce your gods utterly unjust for harming even their own worshipers because of those who despise them. For you prove yourselves to be mistaken if you present gods who do not distinguish you from the deserts of the profane.

But if, as one or another . . . says, they are angry with you too because you neglect [Col. 0572A] our eradication, then their weakness and insignificance have been conclusively established. For they would not be angry with you for failing to inflict punishment if they themselves were able to execute it—although on other occasions you also admit this point, whenever you appear to avenge them through our punishment. One thing is defended by another greater than itself [Note: [Col. 0572] This note appears at the foot of column 572, but the callout letter (f) has not been printed in the text.] [Note: [Col. 0572D] **One thing is defended by another greater than itself.** Thus it is plainly read in the oldest manuscript. He wrote *abaliud* in the same form as the Greeks Ἔξαλλον (“from another”). *Abaliud* is that which is related to another thing, from which it is distinct: as God is distinct from man; man is distinct from God. **RIG.**] [Note: [Col. 0572D] **And Delphi and Rhodes.** He treated this subject in the relevant chapter of the *Apologeticum*; see what he says there and the annotations upon it. I do not know whether the text ought to be corrected to “Hiera and Anaphe” for *Hierenappe*, and “Delos” for “Delphi.” For Ammianus, Book 17, says: “As in Asia Delos emerged, and Hiera, and Anaphe, and Rhodes.” **LE PR.**].

### 10

Let the gods therefore be ashamed to be defended by a human being. Pour forth now every poison; hurl every weapon of slander against this name. Henceforth I shall not cease to repel them. Afterward, however, they will be blunted by an exposition of our entire discipline. For now I shall tear those very charges from our body and turn them back upon you; I shall show those same wounds of crime sunk into you, so that you may fall by your own swords and javelins [Note: [Col. 0572C] Rigault: *admenta*, that is, javelins.].

First of all, [Col. 0572B] consider again and again whether we share with you the very charge you direct against us as a general accusation: separation from the institutions of the ancestors. For behold, I recognize that antiquity has been corrupted in you throughout every aspect of life and discipline—indeed, not merely corrupted but destroyed. As for the laws, it has already been said above that day by day you bury them beneath new legal opinions and enactments. As for the remaining ordering of human conduct, it plainly lies open how far you have changed from your ancestors in mode of life, dress, equipment, food itself, and even speech itself.

You reject what is former as rancid. Antiquity is everywhere excluded from business and public duties; your own authority has cast down the entire authority of your ancestors. To be sure—and this is more disgraceful for you—you are always praising ancient customs, yet you nonetheless reject them. By what perversity [text lost] ought the customs of your ancestors to be proved to remain among you, when you reject the very things you approve?

But [Col. 0572C] I shall also show that the very practice you appear most faithfully to preserve and defend as handed down from your ancestors—the matter in which above all you arraign us as transgressors, and from which all hatred of the Christian name is inflamed, namely the worship of the gods—is destroyed and despised by you just as much as by us. Or rather, not just as much: for there is no reason for us to be regarded as despisers of the gods, because no one despises what he knows does not exist at all. What exists can be despised; what is nothing suffers nothing. Therefore, if gods exist for anyone, they must suffer contempt from those people. You are burdened all the more heavily because you believe they exist and yet despise them, worship and spurn them, honor and provoke them!

This may be recognized even from the following consideration. First, since different people among you worship different gods, you necessarily despise those whom you do not worship. [Col. 0573A] Preference for one cannot exist without insult to another, nor can any choice be constituted without [Note: [Col. 0573C] From *Apologeticum* 13, correct to “without rejection.”] rejection. Whoever accepts one from among many has despised the one he does not accept. But so many gods, and such great ones, cannot be worshiped by everyone. Thus you despised them from the very beginning, since you were evidently unafraid to establish matters so that they could not all be worshiped.

Yet those wisest and most prudent ancestors, whose institutions you claim not to renounce—especially as embodied in your gods—are themselves also discovered to be impious. I am lying if they did not once decree that no emperor should dedicate a temple he had vowed in battle before the senate had approved it, as happened to Marcus Aemilius, who had vowed one to the god Alburnus. For it is surely an utterly impious—indeed, an utterly insulting—act to place [Col. 0573B] the honor of divinity at the discretion and pleasure of human judgment, so that a god is not a god unless the senate has permitted him to be one.

The censors have often razed temples without consulting the people. Certainly the consuls, by authority of the senate, expelled Father Liber [Note: [Col. 0573D] **Certainly Father Liber.** Almost all writers testify that the rites of Bacchus were once abolished and suppressed: Saint Augustine, Book VI of *The City of God*; Livy, Book XXXIX; and others. I shall add here a passage from Cicero, Book I of *On the Laws*: “What, then,” he says, “will Iacchus do, and our Eumolpidae, and those august mysteries, if we abolish nocturnal rites?” **LE PR.**], together with his cult, not only from the city but from all Italy. Moreover, Serapis and Isis [Note: [Col. 0573D] **Moreover, Serapis and Isis.** Arnobius makes almost the same objection in Book II: “What? Did you not admit the Egyptian divinities named Serapis and Isis into the number of your gods only after the consulships of Piso and Gabinius?” Lucan had also said:

> We have received your Isis into Roman temples,
Restoration notes: E001/S000971: The recovered form δίφφαξ is lexically uncertain or corrupt; its contextual sense appears to be a couch or seat.; E004–E005/S000974–S000975: The recovered Greek is grammatically irregular, but the two consecutive fragments are represented separately and together convey the complete cited statement.; E010–E011/S000980–S000981: These form one continuous expression split across two English markers; each marker translates a distinct portion without duplication.; E012/S000982: Several recovered spellings or accents appear corrupt, but the sentence’s overall meaning is sufficiently clear.; E001/S000971: The recovered form δίφφαξ is uncertain or corrupt; the contextual sense is a seat or couch.; E004–E005/S000974–S000975: The recovered Greek is grammatically irregular, but the consecutive fragments together preserve the entire cited statement.; E010–E011/S000980–S000981: These are consecutive portions of the single expression ἤλαυνε εἰς τὴν μητέρα; the two replacements divide its meaning without duplication.; E012/S000982: Several recovered forms or accents appear corrupt, especially τῳ, προιέσθαι, ὃταν, and ἀπόστησωσι, though the sentence's overall meaning remains recoverable.  

[Col. 0574D] “And the demigod dogs, and the sistra commanding mourning.” From these passages an explanation of the present passage may be gathered. Ibid.] Varro records that Harpocrates and Anubis also were barred from the Capitol, and that their statues were cast down by the Senate and restored only through the violence of the populace. Yet even the consul Gabinius, on the Kalends of January, when he had scarcely approved the victims, preferred the Senate’s censure to the onslaught of the assembled populace because he had made no provision concerning Serapis and Isis, and he forbade altars to be established. You have, therefore, among your ancestors—though not the name, at least the Christian disposition—which disregards the gods. If only you yourselves [Col. 0573C] had preserved unimpaired the honor due to those whose religion had been injured! But I find that both superstition and impiety have advanced from among you in concert. For how much more irreligious are you shown to be? The private gods whom you call Lares and Penates by domestic consecration you also trample upon by domestic license,

[Note: [Col. 0574D] **By domestic license, etc.** What chiefly demonstrates the emptiness of those fictitious gods is that the ancients used to sell, auction, and alter their gods, as he said in *Apology* 13, “sometimes changing Saturn into a cooking-pot, Minerva into a ladle, according to inclination or necessity.” Ibid.]

selling and pawning them according to necessity and whim. Sacrilegious insults of this sort might indeed be more tolerable, were they not now all the more insulting for being petty. Yet the complaints of private and domestic gods are assisted by the consolation that you treat the public gods more shamefully and insultingly. First of all, those whom you have entered upon the auction list and subjected to the publicans [Col. 0574A]

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Havercamp, emending from *Apology* 13: *subditatis*.]

you put up for sale every five years among your revenues. Thus the Serapeum, thus the Capitol, is bid for, knocked down, and leased—

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Havercamp, emending from *Apology* 13: “the divinity is leased under the same cry,” etc.]

under the same auctioneer’s cry and the same quaestor’s exaction. But lands burdened with tribute are cheaper, and persons assessed for taxation less honorable; for these are the marks and penalties of captivity.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] The manuscript has *captivitate notae poena*. Rigaltius: *captivitatis notae*; but the word *poenae* must not be deleted. Cf. *Apology* 13.]

Yet the gods who are more heavily taxed are more holy—or rather, the more holy they are, the more heavily they are taxed. Majesty is turned into profit; commerce is advertised under the name of religion;

[Note: [Col. 0574D] “Commerce is advertised under the name of religion”; or, “Religion through commerce.” RIG.]

sanctity begs to be leased. You demand payment for the temple site, for entrance to the sanctuary, for offerings, and for the doors. You sell the whole divinity: it may not be worshiped free of charge. In short, more is spent upon the publicans than upon the priests.

The insult inflicted by taxing the gods had not been enough—an insult, of course, to be measured by the contempt involved [Col. 0574B]—and you are not content to have withheld honor from the gods unless you also cheapen whatever honor you do give them by some indignity. For what, in fact, do you do to honor them that you do not equally provide for your dead? You build temples for the gods, and temples likewise for the dead; you build altars for the gods, and altars likewise for the dead; you inscribe words upon them with the same titles;

[Note: [Col. 0574C] Thus Rigaltius. Semler (or Schütz): “altars, with letters inscribed upon them under the same titles.”]

you impart the same forms to their statues according to each person’s craft, occupation, or age: an old man is fashioned as Saturn, a beardless youth as Apollo, a virgin as Diana; a soldier is consecrated as Mars, and an ironworker as Vulcan. It is therefore no wonder if you slaughter for the dead the same victims as for the gods and burn the same perfumes. Who could excuse this insult, which reckons the dead together with the gods, however it does so?

[Note: [Col. 0574D] Havercamp, emending from *Apology* 21: *utut mortuos*, “however it reckons the dead.”]

Even priesthoods and sacred apparatus have been assigned to kings: sacred carriages, chariots, ceremonial couches for seated and reclining banquets . . . festivals [Col. 0574C]

[Note: [Col. 0574D] Rigaltius: “and festivals and games.”]

and games.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] **Sacred carriages, chariots, ceremonial couches for seated and reclining banquets.** The text must be read and supplied as follows: “such as sacred carriages and chariots, ceremonial couches for seated and reclining banquets, festivals, and games.” Festus indicates that *solisternium* derives from the spreading of a *solium*. The ancients said *solium* and *soliar*. And in the Glosses of Philoxenus we read: *Soliar*, δίφφαξ (“a seat or couch”; the recovered word is uncertain). In others: Σελλάστρωσις (“the spreading of couches”), *Sellisternium*. Ibid.]

Plainly, because heaven lies open to them! Yet this too is not without insult to the gods: first, because it was unfitting that others should be numbered among those who had been granted divinity after death; secondly, because Proculus, the witness of the one received into heaven, would not have perjured himself so freely and openly before the people unless he despised those by whom he swore—as he himself did, and as did those who permitted him to perjure himself. For they themselves agree that those by whom they swear are nothing; indeed, they additionally reward him for publicly despising the avengers of perjury—although among you every man is innocent of perjury. [Col. 0575A]

[Note: [Col. 0574D] The manuscript has: “although among you perjury, which each . . . is.” Havercamp, from *Apology* 25: “as though among you heedlessness of perjury, which each . . . is.”]

[Note: [Col. 0575D] **Although among you every man is innocent of perjury.** For who ought to be held guilty of perjury where there is no religion of a false divinity? The Agobardine codex reads: “although among you, as regards perjury, because every man may purify himself.” From this someone might conjecture that the text should read: “Although among you how few are innocent of perjury?” Augustine, *City of God*, Book III: “Amid utterly corrupt morals, the ancient custom of taking oaths was preserved for this purpose—not that fear of religion might restrain them from crimes, but that they might add perjury also to their other crimes.” RIG.]

Indeed, by now the danger of swearing by the gods has vanished,

[Note: [Col. 0575D] **The danger of swearing by the gods has vanished.** Among the Gentiles it was more tolerable if someone no longer swore by the divine power of their gods than if he refused to swear by the emperor’s name or fortune. Hence Christians were sometimes solicited to swear—not by the gods or by Jupiter’s stone, but by Caesar’s fortune—as we have also demonstrated from Eusebius in the *Apology*. LE PR.]

since greater religious weight is attached to swearing by Caesar; and this itself contributes to the obscuring of your gods. For those who perjured themselves by Caesar would be punished more readily than those who did so by any Jupiter.

[Note: [Col. 0575C] Havercamp corrects: “by some petty Jupiter.”]

But contempt is more honorable, possessing a certain glory of pride; for it sometimes proceeds even from confidence, from a secure conscience, or from a natural elevation of spirit. Ridicule, however, the more wanton it is, is the more conspicuously marked by the sting of insult.

Recognize, therefore, what mockers of your divinities you are found to be. I say nothing of what you are like in sacrificing: you slaughter every emaciated and diseased animal; from the fat and sound ones you offer only the superfluous parts,

[Note: [Col. 0576C] Rigaltius: *supervacui*; cf. *Apology* 14.]

which are useless for eating—the little heads, hoofs, and the plucked-out portions of feathers and bristles—and whatever else you would not have kept at home either. [Col. 0575B] I omit the things done by vulgar or sacrilegious gluttony, which will seem almost consonant with the religion of your ancestors. Yet even the most learned and weighty men—insofar as they believe that weight and wisdom derive from learning—always prove the most irreverent toward your gods; nor has literature served them except to bring shameful, empty, or false charges against the gods.

I shall begin with your Homer himself,

[Note: [Col. 0576C] **I shall begin with Homer himself.** The ancient Gentiles believed that they possessed nothing more illustrious than their Homer, who nevertheless writes very many absurd, empty, and false things about the gods. Ibid.]

from whom comes every wave and all the sea;

[Note: [Col. 0576D] **From whom comes every wave and all the sea.** “From whom, as from a perennial spring, the lips of poets are watered with Pierian waters.” RIG.]

the more honor you add to him, the more you have taken away from your gods by magnifying one who made sport of them. We still remember Homer. He, I suppose, is the man who treated divine majesty according to the human condition, imbuing the gods with human accidents and passions; who set them, divided by partiality, against one another in something like gladiatorial contests; who wounds Venus with a human arrow; who detains Mars in chains for thirteen months, perhaps to perish; who relates that Jupiter nearly suffered the same treatment at the hands of the heavenly host; who wrings tears from him over Sarpedon;

[Note: [Col. 0576D] **Over Sarpedon.** These things occur in Homer, *Iliad* 16, where Jupiter, looking upon Sarpedon, addresses Juno and reveals the supreme grief he drew from his impending death:

Ὤμοι ἐγῶν, ὅτε μοὶ Σαρπήδονα φίλτατον ἄνδρων,

Μοῖρ` ὑπὸ Πατρόκλοῖο Μενοιτιάδαι δαμήναι (“Alas for me, that Sarpedon, dearest to me among men, is fated to be slain by Patroclus, son of Menoetius!”).

These, like countless other things, are unworthy not only of a god or hero, but of a brave man. LE PR.]

or who most foully depicts him lusting after Juno, his desire being commended by the recollection of his mistresses. Thereafter, what poet, on the authority of his chief, has not behaved insolently toward the gods, either by disclosing truths or inventing falsehoods? And did the tragic or comic poets spare them, so as not to proclaim beforehand the hardships and punishments of a god? [Col. 0576A]

I say nothing of the philosophers, whom the pride of their austerity and the hardness of their discipline render secure against every fear, while some breath of truth also raises them against the gods. Thus Socrates too, in insult to them, swears by an oak,

[Note: [Col. 0576C] Rigaltius reads “Hera,” but *Apology* 14 shows that “goat” should be written.]

a dog, and a goat.

[Note: [Col. 0576D] **He swears by an oak, a dog, and a wild beast.** Others have “a goat,” as we read in the *Apology*. He also used to swear by a goose and a plane tree: ἢ (“or”) (thus) Σωκράτην ὃμνύεν τὸν κύνα καὶ τὸν χῆνα καὶ πλάτανον (“Socrates used to swear by the dog, the goose, and the plane tree”). Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, Book III. Ibid.]

For even if he was condemned for that reason, since the Athenians later repented of the condemnation and even punished his judges, the testimony of Socrates is restored; and I can retort that what is now condemned in us was approved in him. Diogenes too made some jest about Hercules; and the Diogenes of the Roman pen, Varro, introduces three hundred Joves—or perhaps we should say Jupiters—without heads.

Other talents devoted to wantonness also furnish your pleasures through the dishonor of the gods. Examine among yourselves the sacrilegious charms of the Lentuli and Hostii: is it the mimes or your gods whom you laugh at in their tricks and jests? You also receive with great pleasure dramatic compositions that portray every foul deed of the gods. Their majesties are violated before you in an impure body. A person infamous and deprived of civil standing wears the likeness of any god whatever. The Sun mourns his son destroyed by lightning while you rejoice; Cybele sighs for a disdainful shepherd while you feel no shame; and you endure the singing of Jupiter’s eulogies.

Plainly, you are still more religious in the gladiatorial arena, where, over human blood and the pollution of punishments, your gods likewise dance, supplying plots and stories for the execution of criminals—or else the gods themselves are punished as criminals. [Col. 0576C] We have often seen Attis, the god from Pessinus, castrated; and a man being burned alive had assumed the role of Hercules. We have laughed, too, at the mockery of the gods in the midday spectacle, in which Dis Pater, Jupiter’s brother, conducts the funerals of gladiators with a hammer, and Mercury, winged upon his bald pate,

[Note: [Col. 0576D] **Winged upon his bald pate.** With a winged cap.]

and fiery upon his caduceus,

[Note: [Col. 0576D] **Fiery upon his caduceus.** The serpents entwined about the staff flickered their fiery little tongues. RIG.]

tests with a cautery bodies already lifeless [Col. 0577A] or merely feigning death.

Who could continue to investigate every single instance? If these things disturb the honor of divinity, if they raze the summit of majesty, they must certainly be judged expressions of contempt—both on the part of those who perpetrate such acts and of those who receive them in this way. Therefore I do not know whether your gods may have more cause to complain of you than of us. . . . On the other hand, you flatter them and buy them off when you commit some offense; and, finally, you are free to act against those whom you have willed to exist, whereas we wholly turn away from them.

### 11

Nor are we accused under this name merely of abandoning the common religion, but also of introducing a monstrous superstition. For, as some of you have dreamed, an ass’s head is our god. Cornelius Tacitus gave rise to this suspicion. In the fourth book of his *Histories*, [Col. 0577B] where he arranges his account of the Jewish war, he begins with the origin of that people and, having argued as he pleased both about that origin and about the name of their religion, relates that the Jews, while on an expedition through desolate places and suffering from a lack of water, escaped by employing as guides to a spring

[Note: [Col. 0577D] Havercamp rightly directed that this be written instead of the common reading, “from springs”; cf. *Apology* 16.]

some wild asses, which were thought to be seeking water after feeding. Thus, out of gratitude for this, the Jews worshiped the image of a similar beast. From this, I suppose, it was presumed that we also, as relatives of the Jewish religion, are initiated into the same image.

Yet the same Cornelius Tacitus—that most loquacious purveyor of lies—forgetting his own assertion, relates later that Pompey the Great, after defeating the Jews and capturing Jerusalem, entered the temple, searched it, and found no image there. Where, then, would that god have been? Surely nowhere more than in so memorable a temple, especially one closed to everyone except the priests, who would have no reason to fear an outsider.

But why should I defend myself, when for the present I profess a provisional admission of everything that can equally be transferred to you? [Col. 0577C] Let our god be believed to have some asinine personage: will you really deny that you have the same things among yourselves? Indeed, you worship entire asses together with their Epona, and every beast of burden, herd animal, and wild beast, which you similarly consecrate along with their stalls. And perhaps you charge us with this as a crime because, among the worshipers of them all, we worship only the ass. But whoever asserts that we are priests of the cross will be our fellow devotee.

### 12

The essential character of a cross is that it is a sign made of wood. Among yourselves also you worship what is of the same material, though with an effigy upon it. Although yours has a human figure, so too does ours have its own proper form. Let the outlines be disregarded, provided that the essential character is one; let the form be disregarded, provided that the wood itself is the god’s body. [Col. 0577D–0578A] But if a difference arises on this point, how far removed from the upright post of a cross are Attic Pallas and Pharian Ceres, who are represented without form by a rough stake and by a mere shapeless little piece of standing wood?

[Note: [Col. 0577D] **A part of the cross, and indeed the greater part, etc.** Crosses are left to us, crosses are fixed up for us; yet from this the greatest honor redounds to us. Among the ancient Christians, indeed, the cross was always employed in everything, and its sign was impressed before all actions. Tertullian himself, *On the Soldier’s Crown*; Cyril, *Catechesis* 4: Ποιεῖ δὲ τοῦτο τὸ σημεῖον, ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων, καθήμενος, κοιταζόμενος, ἐξανιστάμενος, λαλῶν, περιπατῶν, ἁπαξαπλῶς ἐν παντὶ πράγματι (“He makes this sign while eating and drinking, sitting, reclining, rising, speaking, and walking—in short, in every activity”). “Make that sign while eating and drinking, sitting, reclining, standing, speaking, walking—in a word, on every occasion.” Basil the Great, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27, places it among the unwritten apostolic traditions. LE PR.]

Every piece of timber fixed upright in a straight position is a part of a cross, and indeed its greater part. But the entire cross is charged against us, including, of course, its crossbeam and that projecting seat.

[Note: [Col. 0578D] **Including that projecting seat.** The seat of the cross was a shorter stake driven into the middle of the upright. He calls it the “projection of the seat” because this stake, upon which those crucified sat, projected from the middle of the upright for use as a seat. Ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ξύλον ὡς κέρας, καὶ αὐτὸ ἔξεχον, ἐφ` ὧ ἐποχοῦνται οἱ σταυρούμενοι (“A piece of wood fixed in the middle like a horn and itself projecting, upon which those being crucified sit astride”), says Justin in his *Dialogue Against Trypho the Jew*. Irenaeus, Book II, chapter 42: “The very structure of the cross has five extremities and summits: two lengthwise, two breadthwise, and one in the middle, upon which rests the person fixed by nails.” This middle stake is called in the book *Against the Jews* “the unicorn planted in the middle.” RIG.]

You are, indeed, the less excusable because you have dedicated a mutilated and truncated piece of wood, while others have consecrated one complete and fully constructed.

For the rest, your religion of the complete cross is itself complete, as I shall demonstrate. You are also unaware that this origin came to your gods from that gibbet. For every image—whether carved from wood or stone, cast from bronze, or produced from any other richer material—must first be preceded by the sculptor’s hand. The modeler first sets up a wooden cross, because the position of our body itself contains the silent and hidden line of a cross: the head rises above, the spine extends straight, the shoulders slope . . . If you set a man upright with his hands extended, you have made the image of a cross. [Col. 0578B]

Upon this beginning, then, and as it were upon this framework, clay is laid over it, gradually completing the limbs and constructing the body; and the form that was chosen for the clay is imposed upon the cross within. From there, by compass and leaden molds, the preparation of the image is transferred into marble, earthenware, bronze, or whatever material it was decided should become a god. From the cross comes the clay, and from the clay the god: in a certain fashion the cross passes through the clay into the god. You therefore consecrate the cross from which the consecrated object begins.

The following may serve as an illustration. From the kernel of an olive, the stone of a peach, or a grain of pepper placed beneath the earth, a tree rises into branches, foliage, and the form of its kind. If you transplant it, or use one of its branches to produce another shoot, to what will that which arises from the stock be attributed? Surely to that grain, stone, or kernel. For since the third stage will be ascribed to the second, and the second equally to the first, the third is thus carried back to the first through the second. [Col. 0578C]

There is no need to argue the matter longer, since by a natural rule every kind whatsoever refers its lineage to its origin; and to the degree that a kind derives its lineage, its origin is implicated in that kind. If, therefore, in the lineage of your gods you worship an origin in crosses, this will be the kernel and primordial seed from which the forests of your images are propagated.

Now to manifest examples:

[Note: [Col. 0578D] Rigaltius: *At manifesta*; Verias and Havercamp: *ad manifesta*.]

you venerate Victories as divinities, and indeed as divinities the more august because they are the more joyful. What better raises them upon a framework

[Note: [Col. 0578D] Havercamp: *contignatione*, “framework.”]

than crosses, which are in a manner the internal structure of trophies? [Col. 0578D–0579A] Thus in its Victories the religion of the camp also worships crosses: it adores standards, swears by standards, and prefers the standards to Jupiter himself. Yet that display of images and all that ornamentation of gold are merely necklaces upon crosses. Likewise, in the *cantabra* and banners, which the military guards with no less sanctity, those hanging cloths are the garments of crosses. You are ashamed, I suppose, to worship unadorned and naked crosses.

### 13

Others, certainly with more refinement, think that the sun is the Christian god, because it has become known that we pray toward the region of the east

[Note: [Col. 0579D] **That we offer prayer toward the east.** It is most certainly true that Christians were accustomed to offer their prayers facing east. The reason for that custom was this: Christ the Lord, when placed upon the cross, faced west; hence Christians, as though fixing their eyes upon Christ, turned themselves toward the east. St. Jerome on chapter 6 of the prophet Amos: “In the mysteries we first renounce him who is in the west and who dies for us together with our sins; and then, turned toward the east, we enter into a covenant with the Sun of Justice and promise that we will serve him.” Profane people and Gentiles, who were wholly without the truth, likewise turned toward the east, but because they falsely believed the rising sun to be their god. LE PR.]

or celebrate the day of the Sun with rejoicing. Do you do any less? Do not many of you, affecting an act of worship, sometimes move your lips toward the sunrise even when adoring the heavenly bodies? It is certainly you who have also admitted the Sun into the register of the seven days and selected its day above the others: on that day you either abstain from bathing, postpone it until evening, or devote yourselves to leisure and feasting. Yet in doing this you yourselves deviate from your own religions toward those of strangers. [Col. 0579B] For Jewish are the festivals, Sabbaths, “pure meal,” Jewish rites of lamps, fasts with unleavened bread, and prayers upon the shore—all of which are certainly foreign to your gods. Therefore, to return from my digression: you who reproach us with the sun and its day should acknowledge your proximity to us. We are not far removed from your Saturn and your Sabbaths.

### 14

A new rumor concerning our God has now been put forward. Quite recently a thoroughly abandoned man in this city—also a deserter from his own religion, a Jew only by the loss of his skin,

[Note: [Col. 0579D] **Certainly even more so after the bites of beasts, to which he hired himself.** Tertullian himself in *To the Martyrs*: “How many idle men does a passion for arms hire out to the sword? Certainly they even descend to the beasts out of affectation, and consider themselves more handsome because of their bites and scars.” RIG.]

and certainly even more of a Jew after the bites of beasts, to which he hires himself and by which he is now daily stripped over his whole body—carried about a picture directed against us with this inscription: “ONOKOITĒS.”

[Note: [Col. 0579C] It is apparent from *Apology* 16 that ὀνοκοίτης (“one who lies with an ass”) should be written. Rigaltius both here and in the *Apology* writes *Onochoetes*.]

It had the ears of an ass, was dressed in a toga, carried a book, and had one hoofed foot. And the crowd believed the Jew. For what other race is the seedbed of slander against us? Thus throughout the whole city ὀνοκοίτης (“ass-bedfellow”) is proclaimed. [Col. 0579C]

Yet even this charge—so foreign, unsupported by the authority of antiquity, and weakened by the character of its author—I shall gladly accept out of eagerness to turn it back upon you. Let us therefore see whether on this point too you are caught in our company. For it makes no difference what the form is, provided that we tend misshapen images. Among you are gods with dogs’ heads and lions’ heads; gods horned like oxen, rams, and goats; goat-begotten or serpentine gods; and winged gods, with [uncertain OCR: “plantmerleta”] upon forehead and back. [Col. 0580A]

[Note: [Col. 0580D] **Winged, with a sole upon forehead and back.** The exemplar reads, incorrectly, “winged, flat upon forehead and back”; it should read: “with a sole upon forehead and back.” For he is describing Mercury. Ibid.]

Why, then, do you single out our one unique figure for censure?

### 15

More ass-bedded gods are found among you. If we meet on equal terms in the matter of gods, it follows that there is no difference between us in sacrifice or sacred rite either, so that the comparison may be completed under another category.

Do we propitiate or initiate by infanticide? If the facts have slipped from your memory, you will recognize in due order what rites you have conducted through human slaughter and what through infanticide. For now we postpone many points, lest we appear to treat the same matters everywhere. Meanwhile, as I have said, equivalence is not lacking from another direction. For although we [kill infants] in one way,

[Note: [Col. 0580D] **For although we do so in one way.** We are infanticides, when we are said to slaughter infants for our sacrifices; you are infanticides when you kill newborn infants at your pleasure. We do so, as you say, for our religion; you for your pleasure. You indeed kill infants in a different way from that in which we are said to kill them; nevertheless, you kill them. Therefore, inasmuch as you kill them, you are equally infanticides. RIG.]

you too are nevertheless infanticides in no different sense:

[Note: [Col. 0580D] **You too are nevertheless infanticides in no different sense.** He turns against the Gentiles the charge of infanticide and other outrages; they accused the Christians of acts of which they themselves were conscious, and which only the Gnostics were said to perpetrate. LE PR.]

although the laws forbid you to kill children after birth, no laws are more openly and securely evaded with impunity, under the awareness of all and the tablets of a single . . . [text defective]. [Col. 0580B] Nor do you differ on the ground that you do not kill them according to sacred ritual or for a god. On the contrary, you are harsher in this: you expose them to cold and hunger, or to beasts . . . [text defective], or drown them through a more lingering death in water. And if anything . . . more dissimilar is done among you, add to it the manner in which you cast out your own offspring . . . and the deficiency will be supplied. Indeed, whatever is lacking in the comparison will be heaped beyond measure upon you.

But we are said to sacrifice that victim of impiety . . . Since this practice is likewise recognized among you—where it has been set forth more appropriately—we are not far separated from your voracity, if yours is lustful whereas ours is cruel; perhaps we are united by the natural principle according to which savagery always agrees with lust.

### 16

Yet what less do you do—indeed, what do you not do in greater measure? Is it a small thing that you gape after human entrails, merely because you devour people alive and full-grown? Is it a small thing that you lick human blood because you draw forth blood that is yet to be? Is it a small thing that you feed upon an infant because you drain an entire premature infant?

We have reached the hour of the lamps, the service of the dog, and the devices of darkness. At this point I fear that I must yield. For what comparable thing shall I find among you? But now praise the prudent design of our modest incest: we have contrived a counterfeit night so that we might defile neither daylight nor true night; [Col. 0581A] we have thought that even earthly lights ought to be spared; we also deceive our own conscience, for whatever we do willingly we only suspect ourselves of doing!

Your own incestuous acts, by contrast, enjoy their freedom in every daylight and every night, under the consciousness of the entire sky. And what turns out still more happily for you is that, although you openly mingle in incest beneath the witness of the whole heavens, you alone remain ignorant of it; whereas we, even in darkness, can recognize our crimes.

Ctesias indeed reports that the Persians freely unite with their mothers, both knowing what they do and feeling no horror. That the Macedonians too openly do what they approve is evident. For when Oedipus first entered their stage with his eyes put out, they greeted him with laughter and mockery. The tragic actor, dismayed, removed his mask and said, “My lords, have I displeased you?” The Macedonians answered: “No; you yourself performed beautifully. Either the writer was utterly foolish if he invented it, or Oedipus was utterly mad if he acted thus.” And from that time one would say to another, ἤλαυνε (“he drove”), “said εἰς τὴν μητέρα (“into his mother”).” [Col. 0581B]

[Note: [Col. 0581C] Cf. *Apology* 9.]

But how small a stain upon the whole world is one or two nations! We, of course, have infected the entire sun and polluted the whole Ocean! Produce, then, some nation free from the circumstances that draw the entire human race into incest. If any people lacks sexual intercourse itself and the necessity of age and sex—not to mention lust and luxury—that people will be free of incest. If any people has been removed from the human condition by some peculiar nature, so as to be exposed neither to ignorance, error, nor chance, that people alone will be able to answer the Christians with greater assurance.

Consider, then, lust tossed among errors and winds, and see whether any peoples are lacking whom the broad shoals and rough waters of error drive into this crime. [Col. 0581C] First of all, when you expose your infants to the mercy of strangers or give them for adoption to better parents, you forget how much material for incest is supplied and how much opportunity is opened to chance. Plainly, disciplined men of greater severity, or men giving deliberate consideration to events of this sort, abstain from lust wherever they may be, at home or abroad, so that neither the scattering of seed nor the ubiquitous leaps of lust may unknowingly produce children whom their own parents—or others—may later encounter . . . even when moderation based upon age has been excluded by lust. [Col. 0582A]

As many adulteries as there are, as many violations, as many forms of public prostitution . . . whether under a stationary or itinerant title, so many are the minglings of blood, so many the joinings of kindred, and so many the lines of descent leading from them to incest. Hence such streams of plots flow to mimes and comedies; hence that tragedy of just this kind recently broke forth.

Under Fuscianus,

[Note: [Col. 0581C] **Under the prefect Fuscianus.** I know of Fuscianus, a man of senatorial rank and a fellow student of the philosopher-emperor Marcus Antoninus. Julius Capitolinus mentions him in his *Marcus Antoninus* and his *Pertinax*, reporting that he was prefect of the City and an upright man. Lampridius, in his *Commodus*, says that he was consul a second time. Mention of Fuscianus, legate of Numidia, occurs in law 7, *On the Liability of Legacies*, which contains Trypho’s reply in accordance with the constitution of the deified Pius addressed to Tuscius Fuscianus. RIG.]

prefect of the City, after sentence had been passed for the punishment of an accused man, a child’s journey beyond the door, occasioned by the accidental negligence of his attendants, was diverted by passersby, and he disappeared from his home. A petty Greek had seized him from the threshold—or “entering,” in the Greek manner.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] **In the Greek manner.** Julian Caesar explains this custom in a certain headless tract in Petavius’ edition, page 157: ὤσπερ οἱ τὰ παιδία τοῦ πλακοῦντος ἐξαπατῶντες, τῳ καὶ δὶς καὶ τρὶς προιέσθαι πείθουσιν ἀκολουθεῖν ἑαυτοῖς· εἶθ` ὃταν ἀπόστησωσι πόῤῥω τῶν οἰκιῶν, ἐμβάλλοντες εἰς ναῦν ἀπέδοντο (“Just as those who deceive children with cake persuade them to follow by offering it to them two and three times; then, when they have drawn them far from their homes, they put them aboard a ship and sell them”; several recovered spellings are uncertain, but the overall sense is clear). RIG.]

[Note: [Col. 0581C] Rigaltius emended this corrupt passage by writing *reatus*, “an accused man,” in place of the common *senatus*, “Senate,” and deleting the word *intrans*, “entering.”]

Thereafter, his appearance having changed with the age he spent in Asia, he was brought back to Rome for sale. [Col. 0582B] His unsuspecting father bought him and made sexual use of him as a Greek. Then, as is your practice, the master consigned the young man to an estate and to chains. There his former tutor and nurse had long been suffering punishment. The whole case was brought before them, and they related their respective outcomes to one another: they said that their foster child had disappeared in childhood; he said that he too had disappeared as a child, but that, as it happened, he had been born in Rome of an honorable family. Perhaps he also disclosed certain identifying marks.

Then, by the will of God, so that so great a stain might be cast in the teeth of the age, a spirit shakes them in daylight.

[Note: [Col. 0582D] **A spirit shakes them in daylight.** The exemplar reads, “The Spirit of God shakes by day,” which makes no sense. The word “God” occurs immediately before and ought not to occur here; it seemed right to write, “A spirit shakes them in daylight.” Ibid.]

The dates correspond with his age; the eyes also recollect something in his features; certain distinctive marks upon his body are reviewed. The masters—or rather, now the parents—are driven to conduct an inquiry with all the diligence warranted by so great a disclosure. The slave dealer is investigated

[Note: [Col. 0582D] **The slave dealer is investigated.** It should be observed here that *venaliciarius* does not mean a merchant but a dealer in slaves. For *mangones* are not properly called merchants, because slaves offered for sale are not included under merchandise; merchandise is distinguished from saleable slaves, and markets from slave marts, in law 1 of the Code, *On Fairs and Markets*. Slaves for sale are not properly classified as movable property, for although the thing is sold, the person is not delivered—this being a standard exception among the jurists. The term “merchandise,” however, applies only to movable things, as stated in Digest 6g, *On the Meaning of Words*. [Col. 0583D] LE PR.]

and, unhappily, is found. When the crime is disclosed, the parents cure themselves with a noose. The prefect assigns their property to the son who has so disastrously survived—not as an inheritance, but as payment for violation and incest.

This single example was enough for the public shame of crimes of this kind lying hidden among you. Nothing happens only once in human affairs, though it may indeed be discovered only once. [Col. 0583A] I suppose you are bringing charges concerning the mysteries of our religion; yet even your practices that are not mysteries are equal to ours.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] **After sentence had been passed for the punishment of an accused man.** Here we have allowed something to conjecture. The exemplar reads: “After sentence had been passed for the punishment of the Senate.” This is plainly corrupt. For what could that mean: “a tragedy after sentence had been passed for the punishment of the Senate”? And why does he mention Fuscianus, prefect of the City, if punishment had been decreed by the Senate? Indeed, nothing here was punished either by the Senate or by the prefect of the City.

I therefore establish first that the preceding passage should be punctuated thus: “Hence such streams of plots flow to mimes and comedies. Hence this also—recently a tragedy of the following kind—broke forth”: that is, this stream of a comic plot which had previously been such a tragedy. He then begins to narrate the tragedy, a plainly pitiable event:

“Under Fuscianus, prefect of the City, after sentence had been passed for the punishment of an accused man”—some criminal, obviously, while the populace was hurrying to the spectacle—“a child’s journey beyond the door, occasioned by the accidental negligence of his attendants, was diverted by passersby, and he disappeared from his home.”

That this must be understood of a boy six years old or thereabouts is made probable even by the fact that he remembered having disappeared in childhood, then, his appearance having changed with age, having been brought back to Rome and, when already a young man, having been consigned to chains.

The story should therefore proceed thus: “His journey beyond the door, occasioned by the accidental negligence of his attendants, was diverted by passersby, and he disappeared from his home.” In the same manuscript codex there follows: “A petty Greek had seized him from the threshold—or ‘entering,’ in the Greek manner,” so that this final word, “entering,” appears to be an interpretation of what preceded, “from the threshold.” If we have established this, it will at the same time be established that there is no reason by which the words we have enclosed in brackets, so that they may be removed, can be defended. The story should therefore continue thus: “A petty Greek had seized him, in the Greek manner. Thereafter, his appearance having changed with the age he spent in Asia,” etc. Finally, he may have said “his age in Asia” to mean the period of life passed in Asia.]

Restoration notes: S000983 reads μήκῶν, normally “poppy,” which does not fit the stated identification of the Greek term for a mocking grimace; the recovered reading has therefore been preserved and flagged as contextually uncertain.; S000984 appears textually corrupt or malformed; its context supports the sense “masters of arms,” but the recovered Greek has been preserved verbatim and the rendering marked uncertain.; S000983 reads μήκῶν, normally “poppy,” which does not fit the stated identification of a Greek term for a mocking grimace; the recovered reading is preserved and marked uncertain.; S000984 appears corrupt or wrongly divided. Its context supports the sense “arms instructors,” but the recovered Greek is preserved verbatim and the rendering marked uncertain.  

17. As for your charges of obstinacy or presumption, whatever instances you put forward, not even these stand apart from a shared comparison [Note: [Col. 0583D] “Not even these stand apart from a shared comparison.” An emendation may seem readily available: “They stand apart from a shared comparison.” But I believe that Tertullian wrote *adcommunionem* in this way. For he is fond of compounds of this kind: *adstudendum*, *adsacrificium*, *adlaederentur*. Here, therefore, he says that not even those things which you object to us *absistunt adcommunionem comparationis*, that is, “prevent the shared comparison from presenting itself.” RIG.]. The first charge of obstinacy is that which they establish as a second religion, namely Caesar’s majesty—because we are called irreligious toward the Caesars and, since we neither propitiate their images nor swear by their guardian spirits, are named enemies of the people. Indeed, let that be so, although it is from among you nations that there daily emerge Caesars bearing the titles Parthicus, Medicus, and Germanicus. At this point let the Roman nation consider among whom the unsubdued and foreign nations are to be found. Yet you conspire with our own people against our own people. We certainly recognize [Col. 0583B] Roman loyalty toward the Caesars. No conspiracy has ever broken out; no blood of Caesar [Note: [Col. 0583C] Thus Hav.; the manuscript has “of blood.”] has left its mark in the senate or even in the palaces themselves [Note: [Col. 0583D] “Or even in the palaces themselves.” He indicts the Romans for their cruelty toward their own emperors: they stabbed their rulers in the royal residence, in their palaces, and in the Senate itself, although no sedition was ever stirred up by Christians, nor had they ever appeared eager for revolution. LE PR.]; no imperial power has been usurped in the provinces. Syria still breathes with the odors of corpses; the Gallic provinces still do not wash themselves clean in their own Rhône. But I pass over crimes of madness, since not even these admit the name “Roman.” I shall confront the sacrileges of vanity, and review the irreverence of the native-born nation itself: the festive lampoons known to the statues [Note: [Col. 0584C] “Known to the statues.” By placards affixed or hung upon statues. RIG.], and those sometimes oblique sayings and curses issuing from the assembly, which echo in the circus. If not in arms, at least in speech you are always rebels. But it is another matter, I suppose, not to swear by Caesar’s guardian spirit. For the legal standing of perjurers is doubtful, since you do not even swear faithfully by your own gods. [Col. 0583C] But we do not call the emperor a god; for at this, as the common saying goes, we make a mocking grimace [Note: [Col. 0584C] “As the common saying goes, we make a mocking grimace.” A *sanna* is a form of derision produced by twisting the mouth and face, or by a particular configuration of the fingers or hands, or by a movement of the lips without any word. *Sanna* in Greek is μήκῶν (“poppy”; the recovered reading is uncertain here, since it does not fit the stated Greek term for a mocking grimace). That these *sannae* and distortions of the mouth were employed to frighten crying children is evident from Arnobius, book V: “Were mortals of that age and time so empty of heart and devoid of all reason and sense that, like little children and infants, they were restrained from wicked actions by the utterly monstrous grimaces of masks, by mocking faces, and even by bogeymen?” Hence men who were ridiculous more by their facial expression than by wit or sharp sayings were called *sanniones*. There was also a particular kind of *sanna* called “the stork,” when, namely, a stork’s neck was represented with the hands. Much may be read about *sannae* and mockeries in many authors, including Persius, Satires 1 and 5. LE PR.].

18. No: it is you who call Caesar a god and thereby mock him, by calling him what he is not; and you speak ill of him, because he does not wish to be what you call him—for he prefers to live rather than become a god. The remainder of our obstinacy you place under this heading: [Col. 0584A] that, because of our hardness and contempt for death, we do not shrink in spirit from your swords, your crosses, your beasts, your fire, or your tortures. Yet all these things learned among your earlier and greater ancestors not merely to be despised, but also to be valued as great praise and virtue. How many men, and what great men, have voluntarily faced the sword! I am weary of recounting them. As for the novelty of the cross, your Regulus willingly consecrated it—the intervening words *numerosae abstrusae* are textually uncertain. The queen of Egypt made use of her own beasts. Dido herself had taught the Carthaginian woman, who at her homeland’s final crisis was more steadfast than her husband Hasdrubal, to rush into the flames. An Attic woman also exhausted the tortures by refusing to answer the tyrant; finally, lest either her body or her sex give way, she spat out her own chewed-off tongue—the entire instrument of a confession eradicated at the root. But you reckon these things to your people as glory, and to ours as hardness. Then destroy the glory of your ancestors, so that you may destroy us as well. Be content, for the present, even to detract from your forebears’ praise, lest you grant us a place in it. Perhaps in their case the character of those times, belonging to a sturdier antiquity, demanded sterner dispositions; but now the tranquility of peace has produced gentler dispositions and the minds of men even toward outsiders [Note: [Col. 0584D] “Even toward outsiders.” In the *Apologeticum* the Christian is likewise called “an outsider to loyalty.” RIG.].... “Therefore,” you say, “compare yourselves with the ancients; in your case we must prosecute with hatred what we do not approve, because it is not found among us.” Then answer each instance individually. I do not demand examples bearing the same name. If, plainly through contempt for death, the sword made legends of your ancestors, surely it is not from love of life that you hire yourselves out by the sword to gladiatorial trainers, but you give military service the name of death [Note: [Col. 0584D] “But you give military service the name of death.” For you call gladiatorial trainers “masters of arms” and ὁ πλοδιδασκαλοις (a corrupt or wrongly divided reading, apparently “arms instructors”), although the word is derived from *laniena*, “butchery.” The same.]. If some woman’s death by beasts is celebrated, every day, in the midst of peace, you freely go to the beasts of your own accord. If no Regulus among you has yet contracted for the cross, that engine for fastening the body, nevertheless fire, once despised, has now broken forth [Note: [Col. 0584D] “Has broken forth.” It blazed up and passed through every limb, which was burned. The same.], since quite recently someone hired himself out to be clothed in an incendiary tunic and to proceed in it as far as a designated spot. If a woman defied the scourges, quite recently a man likewise traversed and retraced the course among the beast-fighters [Col. 0585A] [Note: [Col. 0585C] “Among the beast-fighters.” In the book *To the Martyrs*: “among the hunters’ bullwhips.” RIGALT.], to say nothing of Spartan glory [Note: [Col. 0585C] “To say nothing of Spartan glory.” Thus in Petronius, Eumolpus says: “And I, for my part, endured three lashes with Spartan nobility.” LE PR.].

19. Thus far, I suppose, concerning the dreadful obstinacies of Christians. Since we share these with you, it remains for us to compare the ridiculous traits of the respective persons; although all our obstinacy is built upon convictions. For we presume the resurrection of the dead. Hope of resurrection produces contempt for death. Laugh, then, as much as you please at those utterly stupid minds which die in order to live. But so that you may laugh more easily and guffaw more freely, take up a sponge—or, meanwhile, use your tongue—and erase for the moment your own writings, which likewise affirm that souls will return into bodies. Yet how much more acceptable is our presumption, which maintains that they will return into the same bodies! How much more vain is the tradition handed down to you, that a human spirit will return in a dog, a mule, or a peacock! We likewise proclaim a judgment appointed by God after death according to each person’s deserts. You assign this to Minos and Rhadamanthus, while in the meantime rejecting the more just Aristides. By that judgment, we say, the wicked will pass eternity in everlasting fire, while the devout and innocent will pass it in a pleasant place. Among you also ... the condition of Pyriphlegethon and Elysium is arranged no differently. Nor do only mythmakers and poets sing such things; philosophers too [Note: [Col. 0585C] “Philosophers too.” Not only the poets, to whom license to invent everything was granted, introduced those vain dreams and ravings of an empty brain; philosophers did so as well, and indeed philosophers of the greatest nations, such as Plato, who defended metempsychosis. LE PR.] affirm the return of souls and the apportionment of judgment. How long, then, most unjust nations, will you fail to recognize—indeed, will you go on execrating—your own? If there is no difference between you and us, if we are one and the same, since you do not hate what you yourselves are, then instead give us your right hands, exchange [Col. 0585C] kisses, mingle embraces: bloodstained with bloodstained, incestuous with incestuous, conspirators with conspirators, the obstinate and vain with their equals. Together we have injured the divine powers of the gods; together we provoke their indignation. You too possess a third kind, though not one belonging to a third rite, but to a third sex [Note: [Col. 0586C] “You too possess a third kind.” Alexander Severus, according to Lampridius, said that eunuchs were a third kind of human being, who ought neither to be looked upon nor employed by men, but scarcely even by noble women. RIG.]. That kind, compounded from man and woman, is more suitably joined to men and women. Or is it perhaps by our very association that we offend you? Equality is accustomed to furnish material for rivalry. Thus the potter envies the potter, the craftsman the craftsman.

Indeed, now, at the conclusion, a feigned confession brings conscience back to the truth and to steadfastness in the truth—for all these charges will belong to us alone and are refuted by us alone, against whom they have been brought—through recognition, that is, of the opposing side, from which informed knowledge both inspires deliberation and governs judgment. Your own maxim, after all, is that no one should judge a case [Note: [Col. 0586C] “That no one should judge a case.” The laws of justice require that a case be argued before judgment is rendered. Hence in Seneca, *Medea*, act II, scene 2, Medea addresses Creon thus:

> He who decides anything without hearing the other side,  
> Though his decision be just, was himself unjust.

LE PR.], unless both parties have been heard. By neglecting this only in our case, you satisfy the defect of your nature: so that what you do not refute in us, you ... in others; or the offenses whose guilt you remember in yourselves, you cast upon others.... You will be busier in deed, chaste toward outsiders and incestuous toward yourselves, bolder abroad and submissive at home. This is injustice: that we who know should be judged by the ignorant, and we who are guiltless by the guilty. Remove the speck from your eye—or rather, the beam from your eye—so that you may draw the speck from another’s [Note: [Col. 0585C] Havercamp, in his emendation at *Apologeticum* 39: “Remove the beam from [Col. 0586C] your eye, so that you may draw the speck from another’s.”].
