Reform yourselves first, so that you may punish Christians—except that, once reformed, you will not punish them; indeed, you will be Christians; indeed, if you become Christians, you will have been reformed. Learn what you accuse in us, and you will not accuse it. Examine what you do not accuse in yourselves, and you will accuse it. From this too there lies open before you—as far as we have been able to open it through these few little books—an examination of error and a recognition of truth. Condemn the truth, if you can, but only after examining it; [Col. 0586C] and approve error, if you think fit, but only after discovering it. But if it is laid down for you in advance that you must love error and hate truth, why should you not know what it is that you love and hate?

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585D] 1. Now, pitiable nations, our defense desires to engage with you concerning your gods, challenging your own conscience to judge whether they are truly gods, as you wish, or falsely so, as you do not wish to know. For this is the material of human error, fashioned by its artificer, lest [Col. 0586D] ignorance of error [Note: [Col. 0585D] “Ignorance of error ...”: “be removed,” [Col. 0586D] or something similar, must be supplied. RIG.] ... so that you may be all the more guilty. Eyes stand open and do not see; ears gape and do not hear; the heart, though beating, is stupefied; the mind does not know what it recognizes. In short, if such perversity could be dispelled by a single preliminary objection, the proclamation would be readily accomplished: since all [Col. 0587A] these gods were instituted by human beings, not ... from this the credibility of true divinity would collapse, because nothing that had at any time begun could justly be regarded as divine. But there are many things by which the tenderness of conscience is hardened into the callousness of voluntary error. Truth is besieged by a mighty host [Note: [Col. 0587D] “Truth is besieged by a mighty host.” Since Christians could not be defeated unless they were overwhelmed by falsehood, the nations, so far as they could, suppressed the truth and defended their own cause, though it was desperate, with endless words and slanders. Truth scarcely needs any testimony or clamor of words: ἀπλοῦς ὁ μῦθος τῆς ἀληθείας ἔφυ (“the account of truth is simple by nature”). This verse of Euripides from the *Phoenissae* is cited by the emperor Julian in Oration 7, and Julian himself adds σκιαγράφιας γάρ φησι τὸν ψευδῆ καὶ ἄδικον δεῖσθαι (“for he says that the false and unjust man needs shadow-painting”), words likewise adduced from the same passage of Euripides. So too Aeschylus in Stobaeus; Theodoret, book 1 of the *Therapeutic*; Basil of Caesarea, Oration 14; and Symeon the Chancellor, Oration 1. LE PR.]; yet it is secure in its own strength. And why not? Whomever [Note: [Col. 0587D] “Whomever.” The exemplar reads “whatever.” RIG.] it wishes, it takes from among its very adversaries as allies and protectors for itself, and casts down that entire multitude of assailants [Note: [Col. 0587D] “Multitude of assailants.” The book of Agobard reads “assailing multitude.” We have already observed, at *Apologeticum* 25, “Greece the conqueror,” that this reading can be defended. But here the slip was so easy [Col. 0588D] that wishing to follow the old hand in a mark of no importance is not free from superstition. RIG.].

It is against these things, therefore, that we must contend: against the institutions of the ancestors, the authority of received customs [Note: [Col. 0588D] “The authority of received customs.” Things long since accepted put forward the authority of public consensus. The same.], the laws of rulers, and the arguments of the wise; against antiquity, custom, and necessity; against examples, prodigies, and miracles—all of which have strengthened that counterfeit divinity. Accordingly, in proceeding step by step through your own commentaries, which you have taken from every kind of theology, and since among you the authority of writings is greater in matters of this kind than that of realities, I have chosen, for brevity’s sake, the works of Varro [Note: [Col. 0588D] “The works of Varro.” Lest he seem to evade the issue, and in order to bind the Gentiles by every pledge, he examines their own testimonies and the authors most highly approved among them—namely Varro, the most learned of all Romans. LE PR.], who, having commented on divine matters from all the compilations of earlier times, presented himself to us as a suitable target. If I ask him who introduced the gods, he designates either philosophers, peoples, or poets. For he divided the classification of gods into three kinds: one is physical, which the philosophers discuss; another mythical, which circulates among the poets; and a third national, which the several peoples have each adopted for themselves. Therefore, since the philosophers have pieced together the physical kind by conjectures, the poets have drawn the mythical kind from fables, and the peoples have arbitrarily presumed the national kind, where is truth to be placed? In conjectures? [Col. 0587C] But their conception is uncertain. In fables? But their account is shameful. In acts of adoption? But the adoption is indiscriminate and municipal. In short, among the philosophers all is uncertain because it varies; among the poets all is unworthy because it is disgraceful; among the peoples all is indiscriminate because it is voluntary.

Now divinity, if you examine the true kind, is by definition such that it is neither inferred through uncertain arguments, nor contaminated by unworthy fables, nor judged by indiscriminate acts of adoption. For it must be held to be as [Col. 0588A] it is: certain, unimpaired, and universal, because it plainly belongs to all. Otherwise, what God am I to believe in? One whom conjecture appraised, history vaunted, or a city chose? It is far more honorable to believe in no one at all than in one who is doubtful, shameful, or adopted.

2. But the authority of the natural philosophers pleads its case as the chattel of wisdom. Certainly it is the pure wisdom of philosophers [Note: [Col. 0588D] “The pure wisdom of philosophers.” That which savors of nothing Christian and nothing divine. RIG.], whose weakness is attested by this initial diversity of opinions, arising from ignorance of the truth. But what wise man is devoid of truth, if he is ignorant of God, the father and lord of wisdom and truth itself? ... Elsewhere there is the divine pronouncement of Solomon (Prov. IX. 10; Ps. XI. 10): “The beginning of wisdom,” he says, “is fear of God.” Now knowledge is the source of fear [Note: [Col. 0588D] “Now knowledge is the source of fear.” From that passage of Solomon he argues with perfect truth in order to establish the deity. Among the Gentiles it was commonly said, “Fear first made gods in the world”.... At that time there was scarcely anyone who did not think and speak in this way. LE PR.]; for who will fear what he does not know? Thus he who has feared God, having attained knowledge and truth concerning all things, will obtain full and perfect wisdom.

Philosophy, however, did not clearly succeed in this. For although, through its curiosity to inspect literature of every kind, it may seem to have made incursions even into the divine Scriptures, as being more ancient, and to have taken certain things from them, nevertheless ... as [Note: [Col. 0588D] “Nevertheless ...” The lacuna appears to require completion as follows: “Nevertheless, inasmuch as they believe, they prove that they either despised everything or did not believe everything.” LE PR.], they prove that they either despised everything or did not believe everything.... For elsewhere too the simplicity of truth, through over-scrupulousness ... [Note: [Col. 0587C] Havercamp, at *Apologeticum* 47: “frequently.”] wavers in faith; and thus, when the lust for glory was added, they altered it into works of their own ingenuity, through which even what they had discovered passed into uncertainty, and a flood of arguments was produced from one or two drops of truth. For when they had merely found it, they did not set it forth as they had found it, but began to dispute about its quality [Note: [Col. 0588C] Rigault: “they found—the quality”; compare *Apologeticum* 47.], its nature, and even its location: the Platonists make God the caretaker, arbiter, and judge of affairs; [Col. 0588C] the Epicureans make him idle and inactive—and, so to speak, no one at all; the Stoics place him outside the world, the Platonists within it. Since they had not admitted him completely, they could neither know nor fear him, nor therefore become wise: they had plainly strayed from the beginning of wisdom, that is, fear of God.

There survive testimonies to how thoroughly the philosophers were both ignorant and doubtful concerning Divinity. When Diogenes was asked what goes on in heaven, he said, “I have never gone up there.” [Col. 0589A] Again, when asked whether gods existed, he said, “I do not know—except that it is expedient that they should.” Thales of Miletus, when Croesus asked what he thought about the gods, requested several successive periods for deliberation and finally gave no answer. Socrates himself, as though certain, denied the existence of those gods. The same Socrates, as though certain, ordered that a cock be sacrificed to Aesculapius. And therefore, when philosophy is found to be so uncertain and inconsistent in defining God, how could it ... determine the ... of him whom it did not clearly grasp? We are speaking of the world.... For they force it into the physical kind of theology: ... they have handed down gods in such a way that Dionysius the Stoic divides the gods into three classes. One kind, he holds, is manifest, such as the sun and moon ...; another does not appear, such as Neptune; the remaining kind is said to have passed from humanity into divinity, such as Hercules and Amphiaraus. [Col. 0589B] Arcesilaus likewise presents a threefold form of divinity: Olympians, Stars, and Titans; from Heaven and Earth, and from these, through Saturn and Ops, came Neptune, Jupiter, Orcus, and the rest of the succession. Xenocrates the Academic makes two divisions: Olympians and Titans, who derive from Heaven and Earth. Most Egyptians believe in four gods: the Sun and Moon, Heaven and Earth. Democritus suspects that the gods arose together with the remaining celestial fire; Zeno holds that nature is fashioned after its likeness. Hence Varro too makes fire the soul of the world, so that fire governs everything in the world just as the soul does in us. But that is utterly vain. For “when it is in us,” he says, “we are alive; when it has departed, we die.” Therefore, when fire departs from the world in lightning flashes, the world too dies.

3. With these matters thus disposed of [Note: [Col. 0589D] “With these matters thus disposed of.” After that crowd of philosophers, who either thought most wrongly about God or abolished the gods altogether, he argues with the strongest reasoning from the very matter under inquiry—namely the origin of the gods, immortality, creation, and so forth. LE PR.], we see that this physical theology was suborned for the purpose of maintaining that the elements are gods, although it alleges that other gods were also born from them—for gods could be born only from gods. Since we shall examine these more fully in their proper place among the poets’ myths, nevertheless what must meanwhile be discussed concerning them, insofar as it pertains to the present class, and what must be drawn from the present class concerning them ... we are going to show: namely, that those said to have been born from the elements can in no way be regarded as gods. Thus it will already have been prejudged from this point that the elements are not gods, since those said to have been born from the elements are not gods. Likewise, by demonstrating that things which have come into being are not gods, we shall prepare the way for that class of their offspring, showing that those whose parents—that is, the elements—are not gods cannot rightly be defended as gods. It is a settled principle that a god is born from a god, just as no god is born from what is not a god.

Therefore, since this world contains the elements—to deal summarily with the whole before treating its parts, for whatever its condition is, the same will certainly be the condition of its elements and members—it must either have been instituted by someone, according to Plato’s humane view, or by no one, according to the hardness of Epicurus. And if it was instituted, then, since it has a beginning, it will also have an end, so that at one time it did not exist before its beginning and at some time will not exist after its end. It certainly cannot be regarded as a god when it lacks the substance [Col. 0590A] of divinity, that is, eternity, which is understood to be without beginning and end. But if it was not instituted at all and is therefore to be regarded as a god, because, like God, it admits neither a beginning nor an end of itself, how does anyone assign generation to the elements which they wish to make gods, when the Stoics deny that anything is born to God? Again, how do they wish those whom they report as born from the elements to be regarded as gods, when they deny that God is born?

Accordingly, whatever is true of the world will be ascribed to the elements—I mean heaven and earth, the stars and fire—which Varro has vainly proposed should be believed to be gods and the parents of gods, contrary to the denied generation and birth of God. Varro also declared heaven and the stars to be living beings. If that is so, they must also be mortal, in accordance with the nature of a living being; for although it is agreed that the soul is immortal, this will be permissible only for the soul itself, [Col. 0590B] not also for that to which it is attached, namely the body. No one, moreover, will deny that the body is mortal, since we both touch these things and are touched by them, and see that actual bodies fall from them. Therefore, if, once account of the soul has been set aside, the condition of bodies is mortal, the elements certainly are not gods.

And yet why do the elements seem to Varro to be living beings [Note: [Col. 0590D] “And yet why do the elements seem to be living beings?” He touches here upon Varro, who had taught that the elements were living beings because they moved. He charges him with ignorance in this matter, for Varro ought to have sought the mover and risen by the force of reason to that first principle. LE PR.]? Because they move. And lest the counterargument be proposed that many other things move—wheels, wagons, and other machines—he anticipates it of his own accord by saying that they were believed to be living beings because they moved by themselves, with no mover or driver appearing outside them, as there plainly appears to be someone who propels a wheel, turns a wagon, or regulates a machine. Therefore, unless they are living beings, they do not move by themselves. Yet in alleging that the agent does not appear, Varro shows what he ought to have sought: [Col. 0590C] namely, the artificer and arbiter of the motion. For it does not immediately follow that something does not exist merely because, since we do not see it, we do not believe it exists. On the contrary, what is not seen must be investigated all the more deeply, so that we may know the nature of what is seen. Otherwise, if only those things which appear are believed to be gods because they appear, how do you also accept as gods those who do not appear? But if those who do not exist appear to exist, why should there not also exist those who do not appear? I mean the mover of celestial things.

Let them, then, even be living beings because they move by themselves, and let them move by themselves because they are moved by no other; nevertheless they are not immediately gods because they are living beings, nor therefore because they move by themselves. Otherwise, what prevents all living beings, since they move by themselves, from being regarded as gods? ... Such folly, to be sure, is permitted to the Egyptians.

[Col. 0590D] 4. Some say that they were called gods for this reason: because θέειν (“to run forward”) and σείεσθαι (“to be moved”) mean “to run forward” and “to move.” Certainly that term is not expressive of any majesty, for it was formed from running and motion, not from the designation of divinity. But since even that one God whom we worship is called θεὸς (“God”), although neither any motion nor any running on his part is apparent—because he is not visible to anyone—it is manifest that this term ... adopted and proper, because by its very nature [Col. 0591A] it was devised for divinity.... Given the subtlety of its interpretation, it is more plausible that they were called θεοὺς (“gods”) not from running and motion, but through a loan from the title of the true God, so that those whom you had likewise fabricated as gods you might call θεοὺς (“gods”). Finally, proof of how much this is so is available in the fact that you commonly call all your gods θεοὺς (“gods”), including those in whom no function involving running or motion is discerned. Accordingly, if those who are equally θεοὺς (“gods”) are equally motionless, both the interpretation of the term and the opinion of divinity shaped from running and motion are abandoned and annulled.

But if this name is proper and simple to divinity, and no derivative interpretation of it is found in that God, then, as to the other things which you wish to be gods, show that there is also among them a partnership in the relevant quality, so that a fellowship of the name may rightly be established by community of substance. Now that ΘΕΟΣ (“GOD”), by this fact alone, [Col. 0591B] that he is not manifest, is exempt from comparison with those things which are manifest to sight and sense. But for sense it is sufficient that there is testimony proclaiming the difference between the hidden and the manifest. If the elements are openly displayed to everyone, while God, by contrast, is displayed to no one, how will you be able to bring the things you see into comparison with that aspect which you have not seen? Since, therefore, you have no means of joining them by sense ... by reason, why do you join them by a word, so that you may join them also in power?

For behold, Zeno too [Note: [Col. 0591D] “For behold, Zeno too.” He means Zeno of Citium, that distinguished philosopher who was presented by the Athenians with a golden crown and honored by them with a magnificent tomb, as Diogenes Laertius relates; this was sanctioned by public decree, and the decree was inscribed by the public scribe upon two columns. LE PR.] separates the world’s matter from God, or says that God passed through it as honey passes through honeycombs. Matter and God are therefore two terms and two things. In accordance with the distinction between the terms, the things too are separated, and the condition of matter follows its designation. But if matter is not God, as even its designation lays down in advance, how will the things that exist within matter—that is, the elements—be regarded as gods, since members cannot be something different from the body ...?

But what have I to do with physical arguments? One ought to have ascended ... from the condition of the world, not descended through uncertainties.... According to the Platonic form, he assembled it as square and angular ... yet made it round with a compass, so that it struggles to be believed a headless sphere. But Epicurus, who had said, “What is above us is no concern of ours,” nevertheless himself desires to inspect the sky and finds the sun’s disk [Note: [Col. 0591D] “The sun’s disk one foot wide.” Among the problems proposed and solved by Zeno’s disciples is numbered εἰ ὁ ἥλιος τηλικοῦτός ἐστι ἡλικὸς φαίνεται (“whether the sun is as large as it appears”), “whether the sun is as large as it appears.” They proposed the same concerning the moon, for they had drawn from their teacher many doctrines in physics and other fields that were alien to common opinion. LE PR.] one foot wide. Plainly, frugality was still practiced even in heaven. Finally, as ambition advanced, even the sun extended its reach; thus the Peripatetics declared that disk to be larger.

I ask you: what wisdom is there in the lust for conjecture? What does idleness prove when, with such presumptuous assertion, it is adorned by the artifice of affectedly morose eloquence? [Col. 0592A] Deservedly, therefore, did Thales of Miletus [Note: [Col. 0592D] “Deservedly, therefore, did Thales of Miletus....” He is called the chief of the natural philosophers in *Apologeticum* 46, because he is said to have been the first to debate physical and celestial matters. As for his having been mocked by an Egyptian, it is reported in this passage; Laertius, however, says that he was rebuked by an old woman in these words: Σὺ γὰρ, ὧ Θαλὴ, τὰ ἐν ποσὶν οὐ δυνάμενος ἰδεῖν τὰ ἐπὶ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ οἴει γνώσεσθαι (“For you, Thales, unable to see the things at your feet, think that you will know the things in heaven”). “You, Thales, though you can scarcely see what is at your feet, think that you can know heaven.” It is certain, however, that Thales excelled the ancients in astronomy, as is proved by the epigram inscribed upon his portrait. LE PR.], while examining the whole sky and walking with his eyes fixed upon it, fall into a well.... He was greatly mocked by that Egyptian: “You could discern nothing on earth,” he said; “do you think that the sky is for you to examine?” Accordingly, by a figure, his fall marks ... plainly those who exercise a senseless curiosity ... nature, before seeking its artificer and governor, into emptiness ... would possess.

5. Why, then, do we not turn to a somewhat more humane [Note: [Col. 0592D] “Why, then, to a somewhat more humane....” The sequence of the discourse requires “do we turn,” or something similar; and the following lacuna appears to require completion with “simple knowledge.” LE PR.] ... opinion, which appears to have been derived from the common sense of all and from simple knowl... [Note: [Col. 0591D] Le Prior supplied: “do we turn—from kinship.”]? For Varro too recalls it, saying that belief in the divinity of the elements arose, furthermore, because absolutely nothing could be born, nourished, or advanced toward human life and the sowing of the earth without their support; indeed, neither bodies nor souls themselves [Col. 0592B] could have been adequately sustained without the balanced mixture of the elements. By this mixture the habitation of the world is furnished, bound together by the conditions of its circles, except where extreme cold or heat has denied habitation to human beings.

Accordingly, the following are believed to be gods: the sun, which enriches the day from its own resources, brings crops to maturity with its heat, ... and preserves the year through its seasons; the moon, the solace of nights and the guardian of months through its governance; likewise the stars, certain marks for noting changes of time; finally, heaven itself, beneath which are all things; earth, upon which are all things; and whatever among them acts in concert for human advantages. Nor is belief in divinity thought to belong to the elements merely because of their benefits, but also because of the contrary things which customarily occur as though from their wrath and offense: lightning bolts, hailstorms, scorching heat, pestilential winds, floods, and openings and movements of the earth. And they are rightly believed to be gods, it is said, because their nature must be honored in prosperity and feared in adversity, as being mistress, plainly, of helping and harming.

Now if people feel this way in ... intercourse, they do not likewise offer thanks or direct complaints to the things themselves by which they are helped or harmed, but to those under whose direction and power the operation of those things proceeds. For in your pleasures you do not award the prize-crown to the pipes or lyres, but to the artist who regulates the pipes and lyre by the power of harmonious skill. Likewise, when someone is in ill health, you do not remember gratitude toward the wool, antidotes, or poultices themselves, but toward the physicians through whose labor and skill the remedies are effective. Again, in adversity, those who are pierced by iron do not accuse the sword itself or [Col. 0593A] the spear, but the enemy or robber. And those whom ... [Note: [Col. 0593C] Rigault supplies: “And those whom roofs crush do not blame the tiles,” etc.] do not charge the tiles or roofing-slabs, but their age; just as shipwrecked people do not impute their disaster to rocks and waves, but to the storm. Rightly so. For it is certain that whatever happens must be ascribed not to that through which it happens, but to the one by whom it happens, because the author of the deed is the one who determined both that it should happen and through what it should happen.

And in all matters there are these three headings: what exists, that through which it exists, and the one by whom it exists; because the one who wills that something should come to be is prior, and then that which can accomplish it must be found. Thus in other matters you act rightly by considering the author. But in physical matters your rule, by which you judge wisely in other things, operates contrary to nature: you remove the supreme rank of the author and regard the things that happen, not the one by whom they happen.... Thus it comes about that you believe the powers and ... of the elements to be ... although they are forms of service and functions.

In this investigation we are not tending toward any other ... of the artificer within and the lord, but toward the service of the elements ... the works of theirs which you make into powers. But gods do not serve; therefore, those things which serve are not gods. Or let them show that such things ordinarily occur, so that freedom may be established from license for indiscriminate action, dominion from freedom, and divinity understood from dominion. For if they remember that all these things above us, according to fixed courses, lawful progressions, proper intervals, and equal alternations, occur in the likeness of a law—with times revolving and the successions of seasons being carried out—then from the very observance of their conditions, the fidelity and constancy of their operations, ... and the careful ordering of changes and the remembrance of recurring things, let them persuade you that some dominion presides over them, to which the entire business of the world appears to render obedience as it advances [Col. 0593C] toward the benefit and ... of the human race [Note: [Col. 0593D] Gothofredus: “benefit or increase”? Havercamp, at [Col. 0594C] *Apologeticum* 13: “benefit and injury”?]. For one cannot say that these elements perform and regulate these things for themselves and arrange nothing for humanity’s sake, when you defend the divinity of the elements precisely because you perceive yourself either helped or harmed by them; for if they provide for themselves, you owe them nothing.

Restoration notes: E008/S001004: The recovered form γηκωεῖς appears corrupt; “earth-born” is inferred from the immediate context.  

6. Come now, do you concede that divinity must not only pursue its course without servitude, but above all stand unimpaired, and must neither be diminished, interrupted, nor corrupted? Otherwise all its blessedness is gone, if ever it suffers anything. Yet behold, even the stars perish, and testify that they have perished. The moon too acknowledges [Note: “[Col. 0593D] *The moon too acknowledges.* He is referring here to eclipses of the sun and the moon’s travails; for the moon has its periods of increase from the new moon, or *neomenia*, to the full moon, and of decrease from the full moon to the new moon. LE PR.”] how much [Col. 0594A] she has lost when she recovers it. Indeed, you are accustomed to observe her greater losses in a mirror of water, so that I may no longer believe any . . . . that which magicians know. The sun himself also has often been assailed by eclipse. Invent whatever explanations you please for celestial mishaps: a god will not consent either to become less or to cease to exist. Let the defenses offered by human learning therefore look to themselves—teachings that, by the artifice of conjecture, counterfeit wisdom and truth. For in other matters nature is such that the person who has spoken better seems to have spoken more truly, rather than that the person who has spoken more truly has spoken better.

7. But anyone before whom the matter is examined will surely say that it is more probable that those elements are ruled by someone than that they act of their own accord . . . therefore things subject to someone are not gods. Yet if one must err in this matter, it is better to do so simply than, like the natural philosophers, elaborately. But if we turn to mythic . . . [arts] [Note: “[Col. 0594C] Le Prior supplies: *to the mythic arts*.”], mortality now errs more excusably in the physical system by ascribing divinity to things in which it thinks divinity is perceived through a position, force, and magnitude surpassing man; for what is above man you may believe to be near to God.

But, to pass to the mythic system, which is assigned to the poets, I do not know whether so great . . . . . . . . . to our mediocrity, or so confident on the evidence of divinity . . . . . . . . as the African Mopsus and the Boeotian Amphiaraus [Note: “[Col. 0593D] *And the Boeotian Amphiaraus.* Amphiaraus was the father of Alcmaeon, who at his command killed his mother Eriphyle; seized with monstrous madness conceived from that crime, he wandered about erratically and out of his mind. But when he reached one of the Echinades islands, he was freed from his madness in accordance with an oracle’s response. Hence St. Basil, writing to the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus: πάντως γὰρ οὐδὲ (“For certainly not even”) [Col. 0594D] Ἀλκμαίων Εχινάδας εὗρων, ἔτι τὴς πλάνης ἠνήσχετο (“Alcmaeon, upon finding the Echinades, endured his wandering any longer”). Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 20 at the funeral of the blessed Basil, testifies that those heroes and gods were defended by the audacity of fables. LE PR.”]. For this class must now be touched upon briefly; an account of it will be given in its proper place.

Meanwhile, that these at least were human beings is plain even from the fact that you do not consistently call them gods, but heroes. What, then, are we contending? If divinity had to be assigned to the dead, surely it ought not to have been assigned to such persons? Behold, with the same freedom of presumption you disgrace heaven with the tombs of your kings. Would you not have been satisfied to honor all those approved for justice, courage, piety, and every such virtue with the consolation of this kind of consecration, while swearing that you would even be mocked for regarding them as such? Yet, on the contrary, you strip the impious and the disgraceful even of the former rewards of human glory: you mutilate their decrees and titles, pull down their images, and restrike their coinage. [Note: “[Col. 0594D] *You restrike their coinage.* That is, after melting it down, you stamp it with the image of another prince. For rejected coins, because they had no value and were useless in commerce, were carried to those who had the responsibility and authority to melt and strike gold, silver, and bronze. Dio, book 60, reports that Claudius’s coins were treated in this way. But he was indignant that statues of Mnester, after being melted down, were recast by Messalina’s order. He was an actor with whom she was desperately infatuated. The following words from Arrian’s *Discourses of Epictetus* show that Nero’s coins were treated in the same way: τίνα ἔχει τὸν χαρακτῆρα τοῦτο τὸ τετράσσαρον, Νέρωνος (“Whose stamp does this four-assarion coin bear?” “Nero’s.”). ᾿Ρίψον ἔξω· ἀδόκιμόν ἐστι, σαπρόν (“Throw it out; it is unacceptable, rotten.”). RIG.”]

Will that Observer of all things, the Approver—indeed, the Giver—of good things prostitute indiscriminately the dispensation of his great indulgence, and will human beings be permitted to show greater care and justice in distributing divinities? Will the attendants of kings and princes be purer than those of the supreme God? Yet you shudder at and turn away from vagabonds, exiles, . . . . . . the infirm, those born in sordid circumstances, [Col. 0595A] those disgracefully brought up; but, on the contrary, you bring forth laws against the incestuous, adulterers, abductors, and even parricides. Should one laugh or be angry that beings are believed to be gods who ought not even to be human beings?

But in that mythic class which the poets transmit, how uncertainly you behave where the shame of conscience and the defense of shame are concerned! For whenever we reproach your gods with their wretched . . . ., disgraceful, or atrocious deeds, you defend the poets’ allegations . . . . . . as fabulous; whenever such poetry is passed over in silence, you not only do not shrink from it, but actually honor it and regard it as belonging among the indispensable arts. Indeed, through this initiator into literature you cultivate the studies of liberal education. Plato held that the poets, as accusers of the gods, should be banished, and certainly that Homer himself, though crowned, should be expelled from the city. But since you receive and retain them, why do you not believe them when they disclose such things about your gods?

Therefore, if you believe the poets, [Col. 0595B] why do you bestow praise upon liars and fail to guard against offending those whose disparagers you honor? To be sure, faith is not to be demanded from poets. But when you say that the gods were made after death, do you not confess that they were human beings before death? What wonder, then, if those who were human beings are defiled by human misfortunes, crimes, or fables? You do not believe the poets, although you have arranged certain sacred rites in accordance with their accounts. Why is the priest of Ceres abducted, if Ceres did not suffer such a thing? Why are other people’s children sacrificed to Saturn, if he spared his own? Why is the male organ cut off for the Idaean goddess, if no youth, rendered more hateful to her by the grief of frustrated lust, was castrated? Why do the women of Lanuvium not taste the Herculean *polluctum* [Note: “[Col. 0595D] *The Herculean polluctum.* Hercules’ *polluctum* was a tenth part of foods, which was given to Hercules. In Plautus, ‘to offer Hercules a tenth part as a *polluctum*.’ They plainly thought that this rendered people blessed and fortunate. Likewise in Plautus, ‘to provision *pollucibiliter*,’ that is, splendidly and sumptuously; hence a *pollucibilis* dinner. LE PR.”], if it was not because of women . . . . . .?

The poets certainly lie—but not because such deeds were committed by . . . human beings who were lacking, nor because they ascribed divine . . . . to divinity; meanwhile it has seemed more credible to you that they were gods, but not gods of such a kind, than that they were of such a kind, but not gods.

8. There remains that national class of gods among the peoples, whom private acquaintance teaches to have been adopted by caprice, not through knowledge of the truth. I therefore understand God to be known everywhere, present everywhere, ruling everywhere, to be worshiped by all and propitiated by all. Yet when even those whom the whole world worships in common fail [Col. 0596A] the proof of true divinity, how much more do those whom not even their own fellow citizens know? For what adequate authority preceded a theology of this kind, which even fame has abandoned?

How many are there who know by sight or hearing Atargatis of the Syrians, Caelestis of the Africans, Varsutina of the Moors, Obodas and Dusares of the Arabs, Belenus of Noricum, or those whom Varro lists: Delventinus of the people of Casinum, Visidianus of the people of Narnia, Numentinus of the Athenians, Anchari[a] of the people of Asculum, and—whom I should have mentioned beforehand [Note: “[Col. 0595C] Rigaltius: *I should have mentioned beforehand*.”]—Nortia of the people of Volsinii? Not even the dignity of their names distinguishes them from human surnames. I laugh enough also at the gods who are the municipal councilors of each town, whose honor is confined within their own walls.

How far this freedom of adopting gods has advanced is shown by the superstitions of the Egyptians, who even worship their own particular beasts, . . . crocodiles [Col. 0596B] and their serpent. It is a small matter if they have also consecrated a man. I mean the one by whom no longer Egypt or Greece alone, but the whole world . . . . . . the Africans swear; concerning whose identity what may be conjectured is set forth in our writings, as seems probable.

For that Serapis was once a certain Joseph [Note: “[Col. 0595D] *That Serapis was once a certain Joseph.* Rufinus, *History*, book 2, where he speaks of the statue of Serapis: ‘Some report that the image was fashioned in honor of our Joseph because of his distribution of grain, by which he relieved the Egyptians in time of famine.’ From the fact, therefore, that among Christians Serapis was a figure of Joseph, and Joseph a figure of Christ, the emperor Hadrian seems to have been led into error in a certain letter in which he wrote from Egypt to the consul Servianus: ‘Those who worship Serapis are Christians, and those who call themselves bishops of Christ are devoted to Serapis.’ The same Joseph, because he was Sarah’s great-grandson, is called Serapis by Julius Firmicus. RIG.—*For that Serapis.* We have noted elsewhere that Isis and Serapis were idols held in veneration by the Egyptians. Here I add only that the denunciation of Egyptian impiety found in Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 24, clearly embraces all these matters and was composed in the manner of that blessed Father. LE PR.”] . . . . . belonged to the race of the holy, younger than the rest of his brothers, but more exalted . . . . . . . . . Sold into Egypt by those same brothers through envy, he served in the household of the king of the Egyptians [Note: “[Col. 0596D] *In the household of the king of the Egyptians.* Rather, in the household of Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch, unless we say that the eunuch himself belonged to the king’s household. But throughout the following account of Joseph, Tertullian departs a second and a third time from what Moses transmitted in Genesis 41; and in the book *Against the Jews*, chapter 5, he treated the history of Abel and Cain with insufficient care. LE PR.”], Pharaoh. He was desired by the less-than-chaste queen; but because he would not comply, he was accused by her in turn and was put in prison by the king. There, by interpreting certain men’s dreams correctly, he revealed the power of his spirit.

Meanwhile the king also wished him to explain certain terrifying dreams, after the men whom he had summoned had been dismissed. From prison Joseph instructed him about the measures to be taken; he disclosed the dream to the king: the seven exceedingly fat, luxuriant cattle signified the abundance of as many years; the latter seven, equally unfit cattle signified the scarcity of the following seven years. He therefore advised that stores should be laid up from the former abundance against the coming famine. The king believed him; the outcome of events proved that a prudent and holy man is always indispensable. Pharaoh therefore placed him over all Egypt, both to provision it with grain and thereafter to administer it.

They called him Serapis from the mound [Note: “[Col. 0596D] *This Serapis from the mound.* He seems to mean a heap and pile, which the Greeks call Σωρὸν (“a heap”): namely, a pile of grain, represented in the form of a bushel measure. Rufinus: ‘The bushel placed upon his head indicates that life is furnished to mortals through the abundance of crops.’ Julius Firmicus: ‘The bushel by which he had distributed grain to the hungry and to purchasers was placed upon his head.’ LE PR.”] with which his head was adorned. The bushel-shaped mound seals the memory of the grain distribution, and the ears of grain by which it is marked all around show that the care of crops rested upon his head. For this reason they also dedicated beneath his right hand the dog whom they assign to the underworld, because the oppression [Note: “[Col. 0597C] Le Prior remarkably changed this reading to *oppressed*.”] of the Egyptians lay beneath his hand. [Note: “[Col. 0597C] *Because the oppression of the Egyptians lay beneath his hand.* The manuscript reads: ‘because the oppression of the Egyptians lies beneath his hand.’ The correction *oppressed* was readily available. For nothing seems to me to be missing; or, if anything was erased at the end of the line after the word ‘his,’ it can have been nothing other than ‘to be,’ or something of that kind. Tertullian uses *oppression* for the affliction that was to oppress Egypt, as the Latin version of Genesis 41 has it. So too in *Scorpiace*, chapter 3: ‘The hand was upon them for evil, and they were grievously oppressed.’ LE PR.”]

They add Pharia, whom the derivation of the name shows to be the daughter of King Pharaoh; for at that time Pharaoh, among his other honors and rewards, also gave him his daughter in marriage. But because they had undertaken to worship both beasts and human beings, they combined both forms in a single Anubis. In him that quarrelsome nation might more properly be seen to have consecrated tokens of its own nature and condition: resisting its own kings [Note: “[Col. 0597C] *Resisting its own kings.* He says *recontrans*, which writers near his own age expressed as *contrarians*. What Septimius says here of the Jews, Lampridius says exactly of Gallic dispositions in his *Alexander Severus*: ‘Gallic dispositions, being as they are hard and backward, are often troublesome to emperors.’ RIG.”], abject before foreigners, and indeed slaves even in gluttony and filth . . . . .

[Col. 0597B] 9. In accordance with the threefold arrangement . . . . of divinity, we have set out either the better-known or the more notable examples, so that it may now appear that sufficient answer has been made concerning the physical class, the poetic class, and the nations. And since every superstition [Note: “[Col. 0597C] Rigaltius: *substitution*.”] has built up authority for itself—not now from the philosophers, poets, or peoples by whom it was transmitted, but from the ruling Romans by whom it was appropriated—we must now enter upon another breadth of human error; indeed, we must cut down a forest which, having sprung from seeds of superstition conceived on every side, overshadowed the childhood of vice. [Note: “[Col. 0598C] The manuscript has ‘childhood with vices’; Rigaltius, ‘childhood of vice.’”]

Varro, moreover, divided the gods of the Romans into two classes: uncertain and select. What vanity! For what had they to do with uncertain gods if they possessed certain ones—unless [Col. 0598A] they wished to adopt Athenian follies? For at Athens too there is an altar inscribed: “To Unknown Gods.” Does anyone, then, worship what he does not know? Then, if they possessed certain gods, they ought to have been content with them and not desired select gods. In this too they are found irreligious. For if gods are selected like bulbs [Note: “[Col. 0597D] *For if gods are selected like bulbs.* This statement of Tertullian is criticized by Augustine at the beginning of book 7 of *The City of God* as wittier than it is true. ‘For I see,’ he says, ‘that even from among the select some are selected for something greater and more excellent; therefore the fact that certain gods were selected from among many does not constitute a reason for censuring them. Rather, we must consider who they are and for what purpose they appear to have been selected.’ If examined more carefully, this criticism may perhaps be judged subtler. For Septimius certainly did with great clarity what Augustine directs us to consider—who those gods were and for what purpose they were selected—both in his celebrated *Apology* and in these books *To the Nations*. But here he rightly laughs at Varro’s selection of gods, since no one should be called, or can be, God unless he alone is omnipotent, eternal, immeasurable, and indefatigable. If you give him a companion or a deputy, you have plainly made the arrangement superfluous and useless, and indeed altogether unbecoming to divinity. By this first argument our Septimius routs the multitude of gods; next he says that Varro is irreligious in selecting the chief gods from the multitude, for he did this not without injury to the rest, whom he indeed regarded as gods, but as inferior in dignity or power. These therefore may complain not only of neglect but also of injured divinity against the man who dared to pass judgment concerning gods—as though one were not a god unless a human being favored him. This plainly amounts to regarding gods as mushrooms . . . ‘Nature is best in meadow mushrooms; others are ill trusted,’ says Horace. What else did Varro intend with his ‘select’ gods, except that in those selected the nature of divinity was best, while the others were ill trusted? As for the examples Augustine adduces to confirm his criticism, it must be considered whether they are applicable to divinity, or to God, whose peculiar attribute is to be one and alone. Thus soldiers are selected to become centurions; from among the faithful, some are chosen to become overseers; from among stones, some become cornerstones; yet the rest are not therefore said to be rejected, because the rule governing all these things is that they are distinguished by rank and authority. But to be God admits no degrees of more and less. RIG.”], those who are not selected are pronounced rejected.

We, however, recognize two classes of Roman gods: common and peculiar—that is, those whom they share with everyone, and those whom they themselves invented. And are these perhaps the gods called “public” and “foreign”? For the altars teach this: that of the foreign gods at the shrine of Carna, and that of the public gods on the Palatine. Since the common gods are included in both the physical and mythic classes, those categories have already been dealt with. Concerning the peculiar gods something must be said . . . . Let us marvel at the Romans, that third class of hostile gods . . . . because no other nation devised so much superstition for itself. [Col. 0598B] . . . . We arrange them into two categories, some adopted from human beings, others conceived from other sources.

Since, therefore, the same coloring of consecrating the dead, supposedly for their merits in life, is available to them, we too must offer the same answer: not one of these was of such great worth. They believed Aeneas to be a dutiful father, though never a glorious soldier, since he was disabled by a stone. As ordinary and dog-like as that weapon was, so dishonorable was the wound! But Aeneas is also found to have been a traitor to his country [Note: “[Col. 0598D] *But Aeneas was also a traitor to his country.* That Aeneas who is ‘pious’ in Virgil is here called a traitor, and the reason is immediately added: because he abandoned his burning homeland, and Dido, the widow of King Sychaeus. The remaining matters in the following passage are treated at length in *Apology*, chapters 25 and 50. LE PR.”], as was Antenor. Even if they refuse to accept this as true, Aeneas certainly abandoned his companions while his country was in flames, intending to subject himself to a Punic woman [Note: “[Col. 0598D] *Intending to subject himself to a Punic woman.* Below: ‘to be reckoned beneath a Punic woman.’ RIG.”]. She did not accompany her husband Hasdrubal when, with the cowardice of Aeneas, he supplicated the enemy; instead, she took her children with her, understanding that form and fatherland were to be held not in flight but in the flames of burning Carthage, and cast herself down into them as into the embrace of her dying country.

“Pious” Aeneas saved one boy and a decrepit old man, while abandoning Priam and Astyanax. Yet he ought to be all the more detestable to the Romans, who swear that, for the safety of their rulers and their rulers’ households, they will act against their own children, spouses, and every pledge dear to them. Vulcan knows that the son of Venus is being consecrated and tolerates it, and Juno permits it.

If bearers of their parents [Note: “[Col. 0599D] *If bearers of their parents.* In Agobard’s book the reading is, ‘if the twice-enclosed of their parents.’ Perhaps Septimius wrote ‘in turn bearers of their parents’: that is, those who in turn carry their parents, now burdened with old age, by whom they themselves were carried. Aeneas is said to have done this. RIG.”] sit in heaven, why were not the Argive youths rather regarded as gods, since, yoked in place of draft animals, they drew their mother farther than human custom required, so that she would not commit sacrilege in the sacred rites? Why is that daughter not rather a goddess, since she was more dutiful, nourishing with her own breasts her father, who was wasting away from hunger in prison? What other glorious deed did Aeneas perform, except that he was nowhere to be seen in the Laurentian battle? Again, perhaps, in his customary fashion, he fled from the battle like a deserter.

Romulus likewise became a god after death. If he was a god because he founded a city, the title of god extends even to women who founded cities. Romulus, to be sure, both killed his brother and treacherously abducted other men’s maidens. He is therefore Quirinus because at that time their parents cried out in complaint through him.

What did Sterculus [Note: “[Col. 0599D] *Sterculus.* The old spelling is *Stercolus*. RIG.”] do to deserve divinity? If he was diligent in assisting fields with manure, Augeas supplied more dung. If Faunus, the son of Picus, was driven contrary to right and divine law [Note: “[Col. 0599D] *Was driven beyond right*: contrary to right and divine law. RIG.”] by mental derangement, it would have been more fitting to cure him than to consecrate him. If Faunus’s daughter excelled in chastity, so that she did not even associate with men, whether because of barbarism, awareness of her deformity, or shame at her father’s madness, how much more worthy of being the Good Goddess was Penelope, who, though living among exceedingly importunate suitors, maintained and defended her besieged chastity? There is also Sanctus, who obtained a shrine from King Plotius because of his hospitality. Ulysses too might have supplied you with one additional god from the most humane Alcinous.

10. I hasten to more disgraceful matters. Your authors were not ashamed to publish the story of Larentina [Note: “[Col. 0599D] Rigaltius: *Laurentia*; compare *Apology* 13.”] [Note: “[Col. 0599D] *Your authors were not ashamed concerning Laurentina.* She was the same shameless woman as that Flora from whom the Floralia took their name. The critics differ here: some read *Laurentina*, or *Laurentia*; others *Larentia*; others again distinguish between Flora and Larentia, relying on the testimony of Minucius Felix, who says: ‘Indeed, both Acca Larentia and Flora, shameless prostitutes, must be reckoned among the diseases and gods of the Romans.’ LE PR.”]. She was a prostitute for hire—whether as the nurse of Romulus, and therefore a she-wolf because she was a prostitute, or as the mistress of Hercules, and that of a Hercules already dead, that is, already a god.

For they report that his temple-keeper happened to be playing at dice alone in the shrine. To provide himself with the fellow player whom he lacked, he began a game in which one hand played in the name of Hercules and the other in his own person, on the condition that, if he himself won, he would receive from Hercules’ offerings a little dinner and a little prostitute; but if Hercules—that is, the other hand—won, he would furnish the same things to Hercules. The hand of Hercules won—and this too might have been added to his twelve titles. [Col. 0600A] The temple-keeper paid Hercules the dinner and hired the prostitute Larentina. The fire—which is the Sun—ate the dinner, and the . . . . . . . altar of Hercules himself consumed it. Larentina slept alone in the shrine . . . . . . and boasted, as though after a brothel-game, that in her dreams she had discharged her duty to Hercules; and she could indeed suffer it in a dream while contemplating it in her mind.

As she left the shrine early in the morning, a certain young man—the “third Hercules,” as they say—desired her, and to himself . . . . . . . . . . . . . . s . . . . . . . . . . . . . this had been said to her by Hercules, surely . . . . . . . . . . . . . should be taught. For it was not permitted with impunity . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . also writes the same; soon afterward she, because . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . had followed through Hercules, a field . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . divinity also to her daughters, whom, as themselves . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . property from Larentina dignified the gods of the Romans . . . . . . . . . . . alone among so many wives was dear to Hercules, for she alone was rich . . . . . . . . . . or Ceres, who pleased him when dead.

With so many examples and your . . . . . . . . . . . . who could not [Col. 0600B] have been declared a god? Finally, who raised a dispute against the divinity of Antinous because Ganymede was more beautiful [Note: “[Col. 0600D] *Because Ganymede was more beautiful.* This is one of the common delusions of the ancients concerning their Jupiter; hence Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 10:

> Since the king of the gods burned with love  
> For Phrygian Ganymede, something was found  
> Which Jupiter preferred to be rather than what he was.

Our author brings this objection, like many others here, with good reason. LE PR.”] or dearer to his lover . . . . [Note: “[Col. 0599D] Gothofredus filled these gaps as follows: ‘was dearer to his lover?—you force down. Everywhere others ascend in this way.’ Havercamp, on *Apology* 13: ‘to his lover? It is plain among you—you force down. Everywhere catamites ascend in this way.’”]? Among you, heaven for the dead and a road from the underworld to the stars are forced open. Everywhere . . . . . . . . . . ascend. Do not imagine that you greatly surpass your kings.

Not content to assert as gods those who were formerly seen, heard, and touched, whose likenesses were portrayed, whose deeds were recorded, and whose memory was handed down, they demand as gods and solemnly establish certain incorporeal, inanimate shades and names derived from things. They divide the entire condition of the human being among individual powers, beginning with conception in the womb: as though there were a certain god Consevius who presides over sexual sowings, and Fluviona, [Col. 0600C] who . . . . . . . the infant in the womb; then Vitumnus and Sentinus, through whom the infant receives life and sensation . . . . .; thereafter Diespiter, who brings the child to birth.

When first . . . . . . . . . . . and Candelifera, because women gave birth by candlelight, and those who . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . were called. Children born in the wrong position . . . . . . . . . . are the province of the Carmentes Prosa . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . and from speech Farmus, and from other . . . . . . . . . . . . . . supplies . . . for guarding against . . . . . . . . . . rix and Albana, and one Rucinia. It is remarkable . . . . . . . . . . not to have been provided for.

Then for the taking of the first food . . . . . . . . . . . . Potina and Eluda; and for setting the infant on its feet, Sta . . . . . . . . . do, Abeona, and Domiduca; and they have Edea . . . . . . . . and evil. Likewise, for the will, Volumnus and Voleta . . . . . . . . . Paventina; for fear, Pavor; for hope, Venilia; for pleasure, Volupia; for . . . . . . . ence, [Col. 0600D] Praestitia; likewise, from action, Peragenor; from counsels, Consus; Juventas for new wearers of the toga; [Col. 0601A] for men now grown, Fortuna Barbata . . . . . . . I shall speak of nuptial matters.

Afferenda is appointed for the bringing of dowries . . . . . . . dor, and Mutunus and Tutunus [Note: “[Col. 0601D] *Mutunus and Tutunus.* Names fabricated from ‘Mine’ and ‘Yours’ amid the embraces of Venus. RIG.”], and the goddess Pertunda, and Subigus, and Prema . . . . . Spare human modesty, shameless gods! No one intervenes between the struggling newlyweds . . . those whose desire it is rejoice outside and blush. [Note: “[Col. 0601D] Havercamp supplies: ‘Spare human modesty—no one intervenes; those themselves whose,’ etc.”]

12. And how far must I discuss gods . . . because it must be explained what sort of gods you have received, how much of a master you will have . . . . Whether I should laugh at the vanity or reproach the blindness is exceedingly uncertain. For how many gods, and which ones, am I to bring forward? The greater, or the lesser as well [Note: “[Col. 0601D] *The greater, or the lesser as well?* No one doubts that there were greater and lesser gods. It is likewise clear that there were twelve great gods. Here I do not know whether they are the same as those discussed in *On the Shows*, chapter 8: ‘Before these stand three altars to three sets of gods—the Great, the Powerful, and the Strong; they think these are also the Samothracian gods.’ Gregory of Nazianzus the Theologian, against the emperor Julian, holds that religion was once derived from the Samothracians, besides the profane, and says θρησκεύειν παρὰ τῶν θρηκῶν (“to practice religion” from the Thracians) was derived. Perhaps what Varro has in *On the Latin Language*, book 4, will be relevant to this. LE PR.”]? The old, or the newcomers as well? Males, or females too? Unmarried, or also mar . . . . .? Craftsmen, or the idle as well? Rural, or urban? Citizens, or foreigners?

For there are so many families, so many nations, that they require a conscientious enumeration . . .; they cannot be surveyed, distinguished, and described, so that the more extensive the subject is, the more it must be compressed by us. Therefore, in this class we maintain one proposition: to demonstrate that all of them were human beings. This is not so that you may learn the fact, for you behave as though you had forgotten it, but by way of briefly reconsidering the first origin of their race from the very rationale for despising them.

For there is an origin of the entire posterity. That origin of your gods is marked, I think, by Saturn. Even if Varro reports Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva as the most ancient gods, we must not forget that every father is older than his children: Saturn older than Jupiter, and Caelus older than Saturn; for Saturn was born from Caelus and Terra. Yet I pass over the origin of Caelus and Terra. They were unmarried and childless for a long time before they became spouses and parents. They plainly had to grow through a long age to such stature. [Col. 0601C] Finally, at the same time the voice of Caelus began to grow insolent and Terra’s breasts to become stony, they married one another. I suppose either Caelus descended to his bride or Terra ascended to her bridegroom!

Terra nevertheless conceived by Caelus and bore Athos, and Athos bore Saturn—by a marvelous process. Which of his parents did he resemble? Yet she did give birth. Certainly before Saturn they produced no one, except afterward one Ops; then procreation ceased. Saturn, for his part, castrated Caelus while he slept. We read that Caelus was of the masculine gender; otherwise how could he be a father unless he were male? But how was the castration to be performed? He had a sickle: this . . l . . . For Vulcan, the worker in iron, did not yet exist.

Terra, though widowed while still of youthful age, postponed marrying another. Nor did Caelus have . . . . . Yet the Sea embraces her, but smells of brine . . . . accustomed to waters. Thus [Col. 0601D] Saturn was the only male child of Caelus and Terra. But when he reached puberty, he was joined to his sister. There were not yet any laws prohibiting incest or punishing parricide. And so he devoured his male children—better he than wolves, if he had exposed them; plainly he feared that one of them might have learned from his father’s sickle.

When Jupiter was soon born and removed from him, Saturn swallowed a stone pretending to be the infant. Secure for a long time through this device, he was finally overcome and deprived of his kingdom by the son who, having not yet been digested, had grown to maturity in darkness. Caelus and Terra, with the poets acting as midwives, produced this patriarch of your gods for you.

But certain people think themselves clever when, by allegorical argument, they interpret Saturn in terms of natural philosophy: that he is Time, and that Caelus and Terra are therefore his parents, since they themselves have no parents; that he therefore bears a sickle because all things are cut apart by time; and that he therefore devours his own children because he consumes back into himself everything produced from himself. They also summon the testimony of his name: that he is called *Cronius* in Greek, as though *Chronos*. Likewise they derive the Latin word from sowings . . . . so that those who conjecture that he is the progenitor say that through him the seeds of heaven are carried down into the earth. They join Ops to him because seeds bring the aid of seeing and because seeds emerge through work.

What, I ask, do you make of this transference . . . .? Either Saturn existed, or Time. How is Saturn . . . . how Time? For you cannot make him both: corporeal in the one respect . . . . sea. What prevented Time from being worshiped in its own quality? . . . . of a human being, or the fable of a human being, or the servant of a human being in its own form, not in the form of Time . . . . What is the purpose of this interpretation except to color disgraceful materials with counterfeit arguments? Saturn is not therefore . . d . . . Time; nor, when you make him Time, do you now wish him not to have been a human being.

Plainly . . . . Saturn is recorded in the ancient accounts as having lived on earth with human attributes. Anything that never existed at all can be imagined as incorporeal; where there is truth, there is no room for invention. But since it is agreed that Saturn lived, you transform him in vain. You are not permitted to defend as either a god or Time one whom you will not deny to have been a human being.

The record of Saturn survives everywhere in your literature. We read it in Cassius Severus, in Cornelius Nepos and Tacitus, and among the Greeks also in Diodorus and the other collectors of hoary antiquity. No more trustworthy traces . . . . than those marked in Italy itself. For after many lands and Attic sojourns, he settled in Italy—or Oenotria, as it was then called—having been received by Janus, or Janes, as the Salii [Note: “[Col. 0602D] Rigaltius’s edition: ‘as others call him.’ Compare *Apology* 10: ‘as the Salii maintain.’”] call him. The mountain he had inhabited was called Saturnian; [Col. 0602D] the city whose boundaries he had marked out remains Saturnia to this day; finally, all Italy [Note: “[Col. 0602D] *Finally, all Italy.* That Italy was called Saturnia is clear from Ennius:

> . . . . . Saturnian was  
> Its name, from which the land was widely called Saturnian.

And from Ovid, *Fasti*, book 1:

> From that time the name Saturnia long remained for the nation.

That the city was called Saturnia and was founded by Saturn is attested by Virgil, *Aeneid* 8: ‘Saturn founded this city.’ LE PR.”] was called Saturnia after Saturn.

With such a witness as the land that now rules the world, even if Saturn’s origin is disputed, it is nevertheless agreed from his conduct that he was a human being. Thus, if Saturn was a man, he was undoubtedly born from [a human being]—indeed, precisely because he was a man, he was certainly not born from heaven and earth. [Note: “[Col. 0603D] Thus restored here from *Apology* 10.”] But since his parents were unknown, it was easy for some to call him the son of those whose child everyone may be thought to be. For who, out of reverence, does not call heaven and earth father and mother? Or was it because of the human custom by which unknown persons who appear unexpectedly are said to have come from heaven?

Accordingly . . . . always needy . . . . suddenly [Note: “[Col. 0603D] Havercamp corrects from *Apology* 10: ‘Accordingly, since Saturn was always a stranger and appeared suddenly everywhere,’ etc.”], the custom everywhere arose of calling him heaven-born. For we also commonly proclaim people of uncertain ancestry “sons of the earth.” [Note: “[Col. 0603D] *We proclaim them sons of the earth.* Those whose origin is unknown or uncertain are called both Sons of the Earth and γηκωεῖς (“earth-born,” apparently a corrupt recovered reading). LE PR.”]

I say nothing of the condition of antiquity, in which . . . uncultivated [Note: “[Col. 0603D] Read: ‘in which the eyes and minds of human beings were so uncultivated at that time that’—others read ‘and’—etc.”] were the eyes and minds of human beings at that time that they were moved as though by something divine at the sight of any unfamiliar man, much more of a king, and indeed the first king.

I shall linger still upon Saturn, because I shall thereby prepare a summary treatment of the others, once the discussion of their beginnings has been satisfied. Nor shall I omit the more important testimony of the divine writings, to which greater credence is due because of their superior antiquity. For the Sibyl existed before all literature. I mean that Sibyl [Note: “[Col. 0604D] *I mean that Sibyl.* Long afterward Juvenal and countless others with him said that Sibyl was genuine and truthful:

> Believe that I am reciting to you a leaf of the Sibyl.

LE PR.”], the true prophetess of truth [Note: “[Col. 0604D] *The true prophetess of truth.* Arrian, *Epictetus* 3, concerning Apollo: Ὣστε μάντις εἶναι καὶ πηγὴ τῆς ἀληθείας (“so that he is a diviner and a source of truth”). RIG.”], whose titles you have transferred to the prophetesses of demons.

In a verse of six feet she sets forth, to this effect, the lineage of Saturn and his deeds: “In the tenth generation of humankind after the flood befell those of former times, Saturn, Titan, and Japhet reigned, the most powerful sons of Terra and Caelus.” If therefore any credibility attaches to writings even older than your . . . . authors, and for that very reason closer to . . . . of that age, it attaches to this account.

[Col. 0603C] 13. Enough concerning Saturn and his lineage . . . . it is [established] that they were human beings. We possess, as a summary, a preliminary objection concerning their origin applicable to the rest, lest we wander through them one by one. The character of the descendants is shown by the founders of the race: mortal beings from mortals, earthly beings from earthly beings; generation is linked with generation; marriages, conceptions, and births followed their course; native homes, kingdoms, monuments . . . . Those who cannot deny that they were born should believe that they died; those who acknowledge that they died should not think them gods. But manifest facts have their own force; those whom from the beginning they did not . . . . divinity, by asserting that they were made gods after death, as Varro and those who dreamed along with him do. Here, therefore, I take my stand . . . . into this title and divine rank, as into the senatorial order, . . . . your . . . . you must now concede [Col. 0603D] some supreme ruler . . . . with the power of choosing, as though he were Caesar; nor can anyone give precedence to others unless he himself holds dominion. But if they could make themselves gods after death, . . . . [Col. 0604A] they chose to be of an inferior condition from the beginning; or, if there is no one who made them gods, how will they be said to have been made, when they could only have been made by another? Thus no room is left you for denying that there is some proprietor of divinity.

Let us therefore examine the reasons for admitting mortality into heaven. I believe you will put forward a twofold account of these: either some preeminent being does this so that he may have supports, defenses, or even ornaments for his exalted station; or the necessity arising from merits . . . . each person worthy. No other supposition is possible. No one . . . . by choosing someone does so either for a reason not his own or not that person’s. But neither . . . . does such power belong to a divine being that, evidently, he should . . . . make, if such humanity is imposed upon one who needs the service or assistance of certain persons—and dead persons at that; all the more astonishingly, [Col. 0604B] since he could have appointed other immortals for himself. Nor will one inquire any longer about . . . . who compared human things with divine. The safer . . . . opinion must be examined: whether God remembers . . . . attributes, if to men of former times . . . . must be reconsidered. Because since then no one worthy . . . . if there can now be no room. With such great . . . . antiquity must evidently have deserved it.

Therefore, whether antiquity deserved it . . . . let whoever asserts that it did deserve it set forth its merits. If anything in the cradle . . . . of mortality counts as a vote for divinity, you have received the incestuous . . . . Ops and Saturn as brother and sister. A secretly begotten infant . . . . worthy of both a human roof and a human breast, and deservedly . . . . such evils awaited him. At length, when grown, [he dealt with] a father of whatever kind . . . . the most prosperous king, of the golden age, of course, under whom want and toil . . . . and peace rested, under whom no farmers [Col. 0604C] subdued the fields, . . . . the earth bore its produce without anyone asking. But he hated his incestuous father . . . . the castrator . . . . Yet see: he too unites with his sister, so that I might think this was first said to him: τοῦ πατρὸς τὸ παιδίον (“the father’s child”). As dutiful a father as he was a dutiful son . . . . if conduct was then governed by laws, Jupiter deserved to be divided between two sacks . . . . Who would doubt, once lust had been strengthened by incest, that he would diffuse it into lighter offenses—that is, . . . . and debaucheries? Concerning him poetry thus made sport.

Just as, when public notice has been given concerning a runaway slave, we are accustomed, by questioning about his occupation, to advertise it for misuse . . . . ? [Note: [Col. 0604D] Havercamp, on *Apologeticum*, ch. 2: “Just as, when public notice has been given concerning a runaway slave, we are accustomed, by questioning about his occupation, to advertise it for misuse?”] At one time, by representing him in forms suited to the price of his lust . . . . whether he assumed the form of a bull or paid the price of a bull, and whether, as a shower of gold, he broke through the entrance to the chambers . . . . with money; at another time, in likenesses corresponding to the acts themselves . . . . the one who carried off [became] . . . ., the one who had sung, a swan. So far are these things from being fables about deeds . . . . whether or [Col. 0604D] not wanton . . . . of human beings, whom . . . . long since dismissed from belief through incredibility . . . . need not be treated by us at greater length. For if the people, fashioned after their own kings and progenitors, [Col. 0605A] possessed the same . . . . nature, elsewhere authority demanded a likeness of morals . . . . how much worse is one who is not better? For by a private title you call Jupiter “Best” . . . . and Virgil’s “Jupiter Most Just” is “Best.” Accordingly, incestuous toward his own, unchaste toward strangers, impious, unjust—one to whom fable left no notable infamy . . . . he was not worthy to become a god.

14. But since they maintain that others were admitted separately from among human beings into divinity, and that a distinction must be made between gods by birth and gods by creation, according to Dionysius the Stoic, I shall add something about that class also. Concerning Hercules himself . . . . the sum of the reply is whether he was worthy of heaven and divinity; for thus, in proportion to . . . . merits, do they award divinity? If because of his valor, in that he resolutely . . . . wild beasts, what is so memorable about that? Do not men condemned to the games, or even to . . . . the degradation of the arena, [Col. 0605B] bring together very many in one place, and indeed dispatch them with greater zeal . . . . ? If because he traversed the world, for how many wealthy persons has pleasant . . . ., or the mendicancy that serves philosophers, accomplished the same thing? They do not remember that Asclepiades the Cynic, with a single little cow—on whose back he rode and by whose udder he was sometimes nourished—brought the whole world beneath his eyes. If . . . . he also went to the lower regions, who does not know that the road to the lower regions lies open to every . . . . ?

That famous Pompey . . . . very many . . . . who did not [offer] other victims . . . . one single lamb at Byrsa in Carthage . . . . Why, then, is this credited to Scipio rather than to Hercules? Add instead to the titles of Hercules . . . . of women, of wives, and the pregnancies of Omphale, and, because of the loss of a handsome boy, . . . . the abandoned expedition of the Argonauts. Add to his glory, after his shame . . . ., his fits of madness as well; hire out those arrows that [Col. 0605C] slew his sons and wife . . . . At that time he might more worthily have cast himself upon the funeral pyre, because of his grief at sharing . . . . He who, because of his wife’s wantonness, was ensnared by poisons, [did so] more through fear . . . . that he might die an honorable death.

You lift this man from the pyre into heaven . . . . by the same facility with which [you raised] another, consumed by both fire and divine power: one who devised a few . . . . inventions and was said to have recalled the dead to life . . . . a son, as human as he was Jupiter’s grandson and Saturn’s great-grandson . . . . illegitimate, with an uncertain father, as Socrates of Argos reported . . . . a foundling, reared more shamefully than Jupiter—on a dog’s teat, evidently . . . . No one can deny it: he was swallowed up by a thunderbolt. Jupiter was wicked if the thunderbolt was his [Note: [Col. 0605D] Rigault corrects: “Jupiter was wicked if the thunderbolt was his.”], impious toward his grandson, jealous of an artisan. But indeed . . . . did not conceal his . . . ., his greed and avaricious desire for profit . . ., by which he brought the living to death rather than the dead . . . . through the corrupt practice of medicine for sale.

[Col. 0605D] His mother also is said to have died by the same fate; deservedly . . . . she who had produced such a beast . . . . burst into heaven by, as it were, the same staircase. And yet the Athenians will know how to sacrifice to gods of that sort. For they make funeral offerings to Aesculapius and his mother among the dead—as though they did not also worship their own Theseus: a . . . . god who abandoned his savior upon a foreign shore, through the same forgetfulness—indeed, madness—that caused his father’s death.

15. It would be a long task to recount those also whom you buried among the stars and audaciously deified . . . . Thus, I suppose, Castor and Pollux, Perseus, and Erigone were worthy of heaven, just as . . . . satiated by Jupiter. But why wonder? You have transferred even dogs, scorpions, and crabs into heaven.

I defer discussion of those whom in oracles . . . . and here the testimony of the divine, since you wish even the gods to be arbiters of sorrow . . . . the god who strips the soul of the body, whom you condemned by refusing to permit him to be enclosed within the walls. Likewise Caeculus, who deprives the eyes of sensation . . . . Orbana, who extinguishes offspring into childlessness, and [the deity] of Death itself . . . . To pass over the rest, you regard even the city’s localities, or the places themselves, as gods . . . . father, and the goddess Arquis and Lana, and the Septimontium of the hills [Col. 0606B] [Note: [Col. 0605D] “And the Septimontium of the hills.” He has the same thing in *On Idolatry*, ch. 10: “Even the collecting of New Year’s gifts, and the Septimontium, and the winter solstice,” etc. It was a certain Roman festival, as we have noted elsewhere, named after the [Col. 0606D] seven hills; it fell in the month of December, and on this day New Year’s gifts were customarily collected in honor of the city’s foundation. LE PR.]. . . . Those who have altars or shrines in those same places make them [gods]; besides . . . . they live in another’s place or in rented lodgings.

I say nothing of Ascensus . . . . and Levicola [Note: [Col. 0605D] Rigault corrects this to *Clivicola*.], named from slopes; I say nothing of the gods Forculus, named from doors, Cardea, from hinges, and Limentinus, belonging to thresholds—or whatever other gods are worshiped among their neighboring . . . . doorkeepers. For what is remarkable in that? They even have gods in brothels, in kitchens, and in the depths of prison; in . . . . therefore their own . . . . and among the other gods of the Romans, to whom the duties of the whole of life are distributed in such a way that there is no need of the other gods.

Indeed, since those whom we identified above are assigned privately to the Romans and are not readily known abroad, how have they wished them to preside over all these things throughout the whole human race, and how do they operate in every nation, where their subjects lack not only reverence for them but [Col. 0606C] even knowledge of them? But, they say, certain persons revealed fruits and necessities of life.

16. I ask you: when you say that those persons discovered them, do you not acknowledge that the things discovered existed first? Why, then, do you not honor the author whose gifts these are, but transfer authorship to their discoverers? . . . when he had discovered it, surely he gave thanks to the author; surely he perceived him to be God . . . . the service of the founder, by whom the discoverer himself was also established . . . . that the things might be discovered.

No one at Rome knew the green fig . . . . Cato brought one into the senate, so that he might demonstrate how near the hostile province now was, the destruction of which he continually urged. Gnaeus Pompey [brought] the cherry from Pontus [Note: [Col. 0606D] Read: “the first to bring it from Pontus to Italy,” etc.; compare *Apologeticum* 11.2.] . . . . and made it generally known in Italy. The heralding of divinity might have accrued to me through new fruits among the Romans . . . . This is as vain as [Col. 0606D] regarding even . . . . inventions as gods.
