If the inventions of our age were compared with them . . . . consecration would more worthily have belonged to later generations than to earlier ones . . . . antiquity has not persisted in all the arts, since daily practice instructs innovation; and therefore those whom you sanctified because of their arts . . . . you challenge by the very arts themselves and find them surpassed by rivals.

[Col. 0607A] 17. Finally . . . . you do not deny to their founders all those whom antiquity wished to be gods; posterity . . . . of superstitions . . . . presumption, to which . . . . we owe; evidently it was for this reason that the Romans . . . . became lords of the whole world: because by their observance of religious duties they deserved dominion . . . . they prevail over . . . . Surely Sterculus . . . . this empire . . . . or of the Romans distinct . . . . rather to a foreign . . . . founders and destroyers . . . . and they were buried. Thus, no doubt, . . . . forgetting that Idaean cave . . . . a most foul odor. Is not [that] preferable to the whole Capitol . . . . so that that land rather should rule . . ., with beloved Samos set aside, and surely so that the offerings of the descendants of Aeneas might be burned . . . .

> Here were her arms,  
> Here was her chariot; even then the goddess both strove and cherished the hope  
> That this should be the kingdom ruling the nations, if only the Fates permitted.

[Note: [Col. 0608C] Virgil, *Aeneid* I.20 ff.]

Poor goddess: she had no power against the Fates. Yet [Col. 0607B] they did not decree enough Roman honor for her—as much as for Larentina—when they surrendered Carthage to them. If these gods are to be compared in power . . . . For Jupiter ruled Crete, Saturn Italy, and Isis Egypt . . ., and many are reported to have served even them. And so . . . . he makes men, and, though surrendered into Admetus’s service, Roman citizens . . . . his worshiper Croesus, by deceiving him with ambiguous oracles . . . . feared steadfastly to foretell the true god . . . . driven from his kingdom . . . . by the power of ruling also to protect, as it were, their own cities . . . . they might have been able. If they had strength to provide for the Romans, why did Minerva not defend Athens from Xerxes? Or why did Apollo not rescue Delphi from the hand of Pyrrhus? Let those who lost their own cities be credited with preserving the city of Rome!

If Roman religiosity deserved this—yet was not superstition sought out only [Col. 0607C] after supreme rule, when their affairs had already increased? [Col. 0608A] Even if Numa introduced the sacred rites, your affairs were not yet being deceived by images or temples. 28 A frugal religion and a poverty-stricken superstition: makeshift altars, filthy vessels, and the odor . . . . from them, while the god himself was nowhere . . . . more religious than their ancestors, because religious. Yet how . . . . religion and the Romans’ profoundly deep concern for the gods could be seen [to have produced] their empire, when it was sanctified rather through injury done to the gods? Unless I am mistaken, every kingdom or empire is gained by wars and enlarged by wars. Moreover . . . . and the gods of a city. For the slaughter of walls and temples is the same, the killing of citizens and priests is equal, and the plundering of profane and sacred property is identical. The Romans committed as many acts of sacrilege as they won trophies; they celebrated as many triumphs over gods as over nations. The images remain captives, and surely they perceive . . . . they do not love . . . . [Col. 0608B] But because they perceive nothing, they are injured with impunity . . . . they are injured; they are worshiped in vain. Therefore those whose supremacy . . . . matured cannot appear to have grown through the merits of religion . . . . since they grew by injuring religions.

All nations possessed dominion at their appointed times: the Assyrians, the Medes, the Persians, the Egyptians . . . . or it was in the hands of certain peoples; yet those who lost it were not without religions and worship, and after a delay granted by favorable gods . . . . almost universal dominion passed away. The lot of the ages thus rolls onward . . . . Ask who arranged the changes of the ages. The same being distributes kingdoms and has now gathered that total dominion into the hands of the Romans, as though it were money exacted under many accounts and collected into a single treasury. [Note: [Col. 0608C] Virgil, *Aeneid* I.20 ff.] What he has determined concerning it is known to those nearest to him.

## The Book *On the Testimony of the Soul*, Against the Nations

[Col. 0607]

# The Book of Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullian, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, Against the Nations

[Note: [Col. 0607D] The treatise *On the Testimony of the Soul* is connected with the *Apologeticum* and the books *Against the Nations*. For in it he develops and pursues at greater length the argument for religion that he had advanced in *Apologeticum*, ch. 17: namely, that the soul naturally recognizes, almost against its will, that there is only one God and that there is another life after this one has passed. He demonstrates this from a perception implanted in the soul by nature and so deeply engraved upon it that nothing can erase it; so much so that it slips out even from the unwary soul, as when one thoughtlessly exclaims, “God willing,” “Whatever shall please God,” “May God be with me,” and so forth. These expressions presuppose that the soul is imbued with knowledge of God, just as the fear of death implanted by nature, the desire to commend one’s name to immortality, and compassion for the dead presuppose that there is a life other than this one. Since these perceptions of the soul are naturally implanted in individual human beings, they must flow from God. See what Tertullian develops with great wit in this short treatise. LUMP.] (C)

## Argument

After the most abundant harvest of writers [Col. 0607D] who had pleaded the cause of the Christian religion, Tertullian had entered the arena, as is evident from the *Apologeticum* and the two books *Against the Nations*. Yet, since he seemed to have done nothing to advance that cause, he began this little book *On the Testimony of the Soul*, so that he might assail the enemies of the Christians through a new kind of combat, tear [Col. 0608C] from their minds the perverse opinion they had conceived, and place the [Col. 0608D] Christian cause in safety. He had laid, as it were, the foundations of this work in chapter 17 of the *Apologeticum*; here, however, he pursues more fully what he had touched on there only in passing, and demonstrates especially that God is one and that the soul has a state of existence after death.

## Chapter I

Great curiosity [Note: [Col. 0608D] “Great curiosity.” A word commonly used in the Middle Ages; Vopiscus in his *Aurelian*: “Perhaps these things may seem frivolous and excessively trivial to someone, [Col. 0609C] but curiosity rejects nothing.” Casaubon says in his notes on Vopiscus that *periergia*—a word having the same meaning as *curiositas*—was made the handmaid of philology by Martianus Capella; he also adduces certain other things concerning Aristaeas, a most ancient writer. LAC.] and a far greater memory [Col. 0609A] are required for the study [Note: [Col. 0609D] “Required for the study.” A work that must be studied with great curiosity and a still greater memory. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0609C] *Adstudendum*, Rigault.], if anyone wishes to extract from the most widely accepted writings of philosophers, poets, or any other teachers of secular learning and wisdom [Note: [Col. 0609C] “Of learning and wisdom,” Rigault.] testimonies to Christian truth, so that its rivals and persecutors may, from their own proper instruments, be convicted both of their error against themselves and of their injustice toward us.

Certain persons [Note: [Col. 0609D] “Certain persons indeed.” He alludes to those who wrote against the nations before him, especially the Greeks—for St. Jerome, in his catalogue, lists him as the second of the Latin writers after Apollonius. I mean Quadratus, Aristides, Justin the Philosopher, Athenagoras [printed “Anaxagoras”], Melito, Theophilus of Antioch, Apollinaris, Tatian, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and Miltiades. He inserted some of their material almost word for word into his *Apologeticum*, to which he also seems to allude here without naming it. PAM.] indeed [Note: [Col. 0609C] “May be convicted: and certain persons indeed,” Junius.], in whom both the labor of former literary culture and curiosity and the sustained power of memory remained, have composed works among us after this fashion [Note: [Col. 0609C] “Against the nations,” Rigault.]. They recall and call to witness, for the purpose of reproach, the origins, traditions, and arguments of opinions [Note: [Col. 0609D] “And arguments of opinions.” It appears that this should be read “and the arguments of opinions”; afterwards the words *quae recognosci* should be separated, and *re cognosci* written as two words. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0609C] “For the reproach both of origins and of traditions and of opinions—the arguments,” Junius and Latinus; “a reason and an origin in each particular,” Rigault.], through which it may be recognized [Note: [Col. 0609C] *Re cognosci*, Le Prior.] that we have undertaken nothing either novel or monstrous for which the common and public literature does not also lend its supporting testimony, whether we have cast out [Col. 0609B] some error or admitted some principle of justice.

Yet the obstinacy of human unbelief has not inclined to trust even its own teachers, who are otherwise highly approved and select, whenever they stumble upon arguments supporting the Christian defense. Then poets are vain, when they portray [Note: [Col. 0609C] *Absignant*, Junius.] the gods through human passions and fables; then philosophers are obtuse, when they knock at the doors of truth. [Note: [Col. 0609D] “They knock at the doors of truth.” I have also seen this expression in that letter of the great Pope Clement to [Col. 0610C] James, the Lord’s brother, where, speaking of those who are not yet Christians, he says that they are “outside.” LAC.] A man will be regarded as wise and prudent only so long as he has made pronouncements close to Christianity; but if he should aspire to any prudence or wisdom—whether by spurning religious ceremonies or by convicting the world—he is marked out as a Christian. [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Is marked out.” This word, here and often elsewhere, is used in a bad sense. Jerome, *On Suspect Cohabitation*: “The fingers of all will point you out,” that is, [Col. 0610D] they will disgrace you. LAC.]

Therefore, from now on we shall have nothing to do with the literature and learning of a perverse felicity, which is believed when it speaks falsely [Note: [Col. 0609C] “When its falsehood is believed,” old manuscript, Rigault.] rather than when it speaks truly. Let them see to it whether any have pronounced upon the one and only God. Indeed, nothing at all is recorded that a Christian might acknowledge, [Col. 0610A] lest he be able to reproach them with it. For even what has been recorded [Note: [Col. 0609C] “May have been recorded,” Junius, Rigault.] is neither known by all, nor do those who know it trust that it is established. So far [Note: [Col. 0610C] “So greatly,” Junius.] are people from assenting to our writings, to which no one comes unless he is already a Christian.

I summon a new testimony—indeed, one better known than all literature, more discussed than all learning, more widely published than every edition, greater than the whole human being: that is, all that constitutes a human being. Stand forth in the midst, O soul [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Stand forth in the midst, O soul.” An address in person to the soul, from which he demands testimony against the nations; he persists in this through the end of chapter 4. Below, in the book *On the Soul*, he recounts at great length the various opinions of Epicurus and other philosophers concerning the soul, which he treats here briefly. I shall say only this: when he wrote these words, the author had not yet fallen into error concerning the soul’s propagation or corporeality. PAM.]: whether you are a divine and eternal thing according to most philosophers—in which case you are all the more truthful [Note: [Col. 0610C] “You will lie,” Latinus and Ciaconius.]—or whether you are by no means divine, since you are mortal, as Epicurus alone thinks—in which case all the more you must not [Note: [Col. 0610D] “All the more, you must not lie.” The copies read, “you will not have to.” He addresses the soul: “If,” he says, “you are a divine and eternal thing, you are all the more truthful, since falsehood is shameful and unworthy of God. If you are by no means a divine thing, all the more you must not lie by giving testimony in God’s favor, since you have no relation to him.” RIG.] lie [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Being under no obligation,” Wouwer, Rigault.]; whether you are received from heaven or conceived from earth; whether you are formed from numbers or atoms; whether you begin together with the body [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Are begun,” Junius; “begin,” Rigault.] or are introduced after the body; from whatever source [Note: [Col. 0610C] “From there,” Rigault.] and in whatever manner [Col. 0610B] you make the human being a rational animal, most capable of sensation and knowledge.

But I do not summon you as one formed in schools, trained in libraries, and belching forth the Attic wisdom acquired [Note: [Col. 0610C] *Academicis*, Paris.] in academies and porticoes [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Fed upon,” Rigault.] [Note: [Col. 0610C] “Belching forth,” Wouwer.]. I address you as simple, uncultivated, unpolished, and ordinary—the kind possessed by those who possess you alone, that very soul whole and entire from the crossroads, the street corner, and the workshop. I need your inexperience, since no one believes even the little experience you possess. I demand those things that you bring with yourself into the human being [Note: [Col. 0610C] “With yourself to the human being,” Rigault.], those things that you have learned to perceive either from yourself or from whatever author you have.

You are not, so far as I know, Christian; for the Christian soul is customarily made, not born. [Note: [Col. 0610C] “You are accustomed,” Wouwer, Rigault.] [Note: [Col. 0610D] “You are not accustomed to be born Christian.” The soul is, of course, regenerated through faith, just as bodies are generated by parents, as Cyril of Jerusalem has it in *Catechesis* 1. Tertullian himself said in *Apologeticum*, ch. 18, “Christians are made, not [Col. 0611D] born,” words copied by blessed Jerome and found in his letter to Laeta. I note here that some read “it is customary,” not “you are accustomed.” LE PR.] Yet Christians now demand testimony from you—a stranger against your own people—so that [Col. 0611A] your own people may at least blush before you because they hate and ridicule us for those things of which they now hold you to be conscious.

## Chapter II

We find no favor because we proclaim the Lord [Note: [Col. 0611D] “We find no favor because we proclaim God.” Rigault reads “God” with Pamelius; nevertheless, Lacerda has “Lord,” supports his reading from the manuscripts, and adduces many passages in which it is used. LE PR.] by this sole title as the one and only, from whom are all things and under whom are all things. Give testimony, if this is what you know. For we hear you also, openly and with all the freedom that is denied to us, declaring both at home and abroad: “What God shall grant,” and, “If God wills.” By that utterance you both signify that someone exists and acknowledge that all power belongs to him, since you look to his will; at the same time you deny that the others are gods by calling them by their proper names—Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Minerva. For [Note: [Col. 0611C] “For” absent from Rigault.] you confirm that he alone is God whom alone you call simply “God,” so that, even when you sometimes call those others gods, you appear to employ a title belonging to another, as though borrowed.

Nor are you ignorant of the nature of the God whom [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Which,” Rigault.] we proclaim: [Col. 0611B] “God is good” [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Good,” Rigault.], “God does good”—these are your own words. Certainly, you say this, “but man is evil,” of course [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Certainly you add this: ‘But man is evil,’ of course,” Rigault.], indirectly and figuratively reproaching him by means of the contrary proposition: man is therefore evil because he has departed from the good God.

Likewise, because every blessing of goodness and kindness that rests with God is among us the supreme sacred principle of discipline and conduct, you pronounce “May God bless you” as readily as [Note: [Col. 0611C] “In Christian fashion,” others.] a Christian must. But when [Note: [Col. 0611C] “When you turn the blessing of God into a curse,” Junius, Rigault; “into” is absent from Latinus, the Venetian edition, Rhenanus, Pamelius, and Semler, who read: “when you turn that curse into the blessing of God.”] you turn the blessing of God into a curse [Note: [Col. 0611D] “But when into a curse.” Pamelius wrongly has: “But when you turn that curse into the blessing of God”—wrongly, I say, for no curse has preceded, as Latinus notes; his is the reading that I follow. LAC.], by that same declaration you acknowledge, in agreement with us, that all his power over us is established.

There are some who, although they do not deny God [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Deny,” Rigault.], nevertheless do not regard him as an observer, arbiter, and judge. It is precisely in this respect that they reject us most of all, since we pass over to this discipline through fear of the judgment proclaimed—thus [Col. 0611C] honoring God [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Dishonoring,” Junius.], while they release him from the cares of observation and the burdens of punishment and do not ascribe even anger [Col. 0612A] to him. [Note: [Col. 0611D] “To whom they do not ascribe even anger.” Perhaps this tends toward Tertullian’s error, by which he elsewhere makes God corporeal and therefore subject to passions—unless we understand God’s anger improperly, as other Fathers do, to mean God’s vengeance. PAM.]

“For if God,” they say, “grows angry, he is corruptible and subject to passion. Moreover, whatever suffers and is corrupted can also undergo destruction, which God cannot undergo.” Yet these same people elsewhere acknowledge that the soul is divine and bestowed by God, and so fall into the testimony of the soul itself, which must be turned back against their former opinion. For if the soul is either divine or given by God, it undoubtedly knows its giver. And if it knows him, surely it also fears him, since he is, after all, so great an author [Note: [Col. 0611D] “And so great an author, after all”—that is, the one by whom it has been increased and filled with so many benefits.]. Does it not fear him whom it would rather have propitious than angry?

Whence, then, comes the soul’s natural fear of God, if God does not [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Will not,” Rigault.] know how to be angry? How is one feared who cannot be offended? What is feared but anger [Note: [Col. 0612C] “What is feared but anger?” Anger, he says, is to be feared, since its nature is such that it overturns nature. For this reason Nicetas David, in his *Life of Ignatius, Bishop of Constantinople*, calls it παράφυσιν (“a state contrary to nature”), as though contrary to nature, and ἒκστασιν (“displacement from one’s natural state”), that which corrupts nature. LAC.]? Whence comes anger, unless from punishment? Whence punishment, unless from [Note: [Col. 0612C] “God’s” absent from Rigault.] God’s judgment? Whence judgment, unless from power? Whose [Col. 0612B] power is supreme, unless God’s alone?

Hence, therefore, your consciousness, O soul, supplies you both at home and abroad—while no one mocks or forbids you—with the proclamations: “God sees all things,” “I entrust it to God,” “God will repay,” and “God will judge between us.” Whence do you have this, though you are not Christian? And [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Indeed,” Junius, Rigault.] you generally say it even when bound with Ceres’ ribbon [Note: [Col. 0612D] “Bound with Ceres’ ribbon.” They adduce Ceres’ crown of grain in vain, since Tertullian says that she was ribboned. For it was customary to place ribbons upon the head, according to Pliny, book XVIII, ch. 5. LAC.], clad in Saturn’s scarlet cloak, and wrapped in the linen of the goddess [Note: [Col. 0612C] “And of the goddess” absent from Rigault.] Isis [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Covered with linen,” Junius.] [Note: [Col. 0612D] “And wrapped in Isis’ linen”—that is, in a cloak, so that Saturn’s was scarlet and Isis’ linen. For there was also a women’s cloak. The copy reads: “And wrapped in the linen of the goddess Isis.” We have thought that the word “goddess” was added by those who believed that the name Isis, as though insufficiently familiar, required some explanation. For why should Isis be called “goddess” rather than Ceres, Juno, or Minerva, who are here called simply by their own names? RIG.—“Wrapped in Isis’ linen.” The goddess called Ceres by the Romans is Isis among the Egyptians. LE PR.]?

Indeed, in the temples themselves you implore God as judge while standing beneath Aesculapius, entreating Juno in bronze [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Gilding in bronze,” Rigault.], and fitting Minerva’s helmet upon her with dark molds [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Minerva,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0612C] “You shoe,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0612C] “With ovens,” Paris; “of meal,” Rigault.] [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Fitting Minerva’s helmet upon her with dark molds,” Junius.]; and you call none of the gods present to witness. In your own forum you appeal to a judge from elsewhere; in your own temples you tolerate another god. O testimony of truth, which among the very demons makes a witness [Note: [Col. 0612C] “Makes you a witness,” Junius.] for the Christians!

## Chapter III

Indeed, why do we affirm [Note: [Col. 0612C] “When,” Rigault.] that they are demons? Surely it is not as though we do not also prove it, since we alone drive them out of bodies. [Note: [Col. 0612D] “Since we alone drive them out of bodies.” Thus in *On the Soul*, p. 304: “Christian power alone exposes that most destructive force.” Yet Irenaeus, book II, ch. 5, affirms that Jews also performed this, even after we were grafted, like a wild olive shoot, into their olive tree. RIG.]

Some adherent of Chrysippus [Col. 0613A] [Note: [Col. 0613C] “Some adherent of Chrysippus.” The use of *aliqui* for *aliquis* is thoroughly Tertullianic. Chrysippus the philosopher—concerning whom he speaks more fully below in *On the Soul*—appears to have mocked demons in a book, apparently *On Divination*, which Lactantius cites in book I. PAM.] mocks both their existence [Note: [Col. 0613B] “Their existence” absent from Rigault.] and their enduring our abhorrence; your curses answer him. You call a person a “demon” because of uncleanness, malice, insolence, or any stain that we attribute to demons, or because he is suitable [Note: [Col. 0613C] “And,” Wouwer.] to the necessity of hatred. [Note: [Col. 0613C] “Troublesome,” Rigault; “suitable for hatreds,” Junius.]

Finally, in every [Note: [Col. 0613C] “Vexation,” Paris.] act of aversion, rejection, and detestation you pronounce the name Satan [Note: [Col. 0613C] “Finally, in every act of aversion you pronounce the name Satan.” Was the name Satan, then, used by Greeks or Latins who were not yet Christians? Certainly not. Rather, they said *Malum*—“the evil!”—a familiar interjection among comic writers when expressing aversion to, rejection of, or detestation of something. Terence, in the *Eunuch*: “Who, the evil, is the other?” Plautus, in the *Epidicus*: “What, the evil, is this shamelessness?” Among Christians, however, “the Evil One,” used absolutely, stands for Satan; and in this passage Tertullian in turn has placed “Satan” for “the evil.” RIG.], whom we call the angel of malice, the maker of every error, the corrupter of the whole world. Through him the human being was deceived from the beginning, so that he transgressed God’s command and was therefore delivered over to death; thereafter he infected the whole race from his own seed and made it the transmitter of his own condemnation as well.

You therefore perceive your destroyer. And although Christians alone—or whatever sect belongs to the Lord—have known him, you nevertheless know him too, because you hate him.

Restoration notes: S001012 begins with an anomalous Ρ before ὁ; it has been preserved exactly, while the translation follows the otherwise clear phrase and its Latin context.  

## CHAPTER IV

Now, as regards that more necessary opinion of yours, insofar as it concerns your very condition [Col. 0613B], we affirm that you remain after life has been brought to its close, and that you await the day of judgment; and that, according to your deserts, you are destined either for torment or for refreshment, each everlasting.

[Note: [Col. 0613C] “Insofar as,” Junius.]

[Note: [Col. 0613D] “And according to his deserts,” etc. The author of the book *On Faith*, p. 43: “Each one of us will have an individual resurrection according to the deserts of his faith and life, whether to refreshment or to burning.” See the comments on that passage of Septimius: “Even for a slight offense, the delay of resurrection having been paid,” p. 338. RIG.—This is a passage in support of the merits of works, of which there are several elsewhere. Here again, indeed, is an obsolete word: *passionalis*, “liable to suffering.” PAM.]

To undergo these things, your original substance must necessarily return to you, together with the material and memory of the same human being, because you could experience neither evil nor good without the flesh’s capacity for suffering, and there could be no rationale for judgment without the presentation of the very person who merited the suffering imposed by judgment.

That Christian opinion, although far more honorable than the Pythagorean, which does not transfer you into beasts; although fuller than the Platonic, which restores to you also the endowment of the body; although more welcome than the Epicurean, which defends you from annihilation—nevertheless, because of its own name, it is reckoned merely vanity, stupidity, and, as they say, presumption [Col. 0614A].

[Note: [Col. 0613C] “More serious.” Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0613C] *Suum* is absent from Latinus and Rigaltius; *solum*, Latinus and Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0613D] “Is reckoned presumption.” Resurrection was described by this name among the gentiles. For Christians, honored with this glorious title, were called “presumptuous.” Thus Apuleius, book IX, tore at a Christian woman: “Then, despising and trampling upon the divine powers, in place of an established religion she feigned, with sacrilegious presumption, a God whom she proclaimed to be the only one,” etc. LAC.]

But we are not ashamed if our presumption is shared with you. For first, when you remember someone who has died, you call him “poor wretch”—not, surely, because he has been snatched away from the good of life, but because he has already been assigned to punishment and judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0614B] “Not as one snatched away from the good of life,” Latinus.]

[Note: [Col. 0614C] “Because” is absent from Junius; “as one snatched away from the good,” Rigaltius.]

At other times, however, you call the dead “secure.” You thereby acknowledge both the hardship of life and the benefit of death. Moreover, you call them secure whenever you go outside the gate to the tombs, making a funeral offering on your own behalf with provisions and delicacies, or return from the tombs the worse for drink.

[Note: [Col. 0614C] “Outside the gate.” It was formerly provided and forbidden at Rome, even by the laws of the Twelve Tables, that no one should be buried or cremated within the city. Hence Juvenal, Satire 1:

> I shall try what may be permitted against those  
> Whose ashes are covered by the Flaminian and Latin Ways.

LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0614C] “And *mattyae*,” Junius.]

[Note: [Col. 0614D] “With provisions and *matteae*.” It is certain that *matteae* here means those funeral banquets customarily held at tombs; but it appears that *mattyis* should be read. For in Athenaeus Ματτύη πᾶν τὸ πολυνελὲς ἕδεσμα (“*Mattya* means any sumptuous dish”), that is, *mattya* means any sumptuous dish. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0614D] “You go to the tombs.” He says that those who went outside the city to the tombs to make funeral offerings “went away.” RIG.]

But I demand your sober opinion. You call the dead “poor wretches” when you speak from your own mind, when you are far away from them. For at their banquet you cannot reproach them with their lot as though they were present and reclining at table with you; you must flatter those on whose account you live more festively [Col. 0614B].

[Note: [Col. 0614C] “Their” is absent from Rigaltius; Latinus adds “when.”]

[Note: [Col. 0614C] “More lavishly,” Ciacconius.]

Do you therefore call someone who feels nothing a poor wretch? What of the fact that you curse him as though he could feel, when you recall him under the sting of some grievance? You pray that the earth may lie heavy upon him and that his ashes may suffer torment in the lower regions.

[Note: [Col. 0614D] “You pray that the earth may lie heavy.” Pliny, book XI, where he speaks of the Earth: “Whose divine power, last of all, may we in our anger never invoke as heavy upon those who are now no one—as though we did not know that she alone never grows angry with humanity.” “Those who are now no one” means the dead. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “I speak of the dead, who are no one.” RIG.—This formula, “May the earth lie heavy upon you,” is proverbial, as is the other near the end of this chapter, “He has now departed and must return,” which even now remains in common German speech. PAM.]

Likewise, on the favorable side, when you owe someone gratitude, you pray for refreshment for his bones and ashes, and desire that he may rest well in the lower regions. If there is no capacity for suffering in you after death, if there is no persistence of sensation, if, in short, you yourself are nothing once you have left the body, why do you lie against yourself, as though you could suffer something further? Indeed, why do you fear death at all, if there is nothing for you to fear after death, in that respect in which nothing is to be experienced after death?

[Note: [Col. 0614C] I would prefer: “If you are nothing, what is there for you to fear after death?”]

[Note: [Col. 0614D] “In that respect in which nothing is to be experienced after death?” This particle always signifies a part or place, as in “on what side,” “in what place.” Therefore: Why do you fear death if nothing is to be feared after death, in that place or respect in which nothing is to be experienced after death? LAC.]

For even if it can be said [Col. 0615A] that death is feared not because it threatens anything, but because it cuts off the benefit of life, nevertheless, since at the same time you also escape the far more numerous hardships of life, you dispel the fear by gaining the weightier share; and the loss of good things is no longer to be feared, since it is compensated by another good, namely peace from hardships.

[Note: [Col. 0614C] “It can be said,” Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “Anything further,” Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “Escape,” the Venetian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “By that gain,” Junius.]

That which frees us from everything fearful is not itself to be feared.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] “It is not to be feared,” etc. St. Chrysostom, Homily 21 *To the People*, teaches that nothing in death is to be feared, since we are tending toward a better and more desirable life, καὶ πάσης ἀπηλλάγμενην ἀνωμαλίας (“and freed from every vicissitude”). So too Seneca, Epistle 102: “Therefore look fearlessly upon that decisive hour: it is the last not for the soul, but for the body.” LE PR.]

If you fear departing from life because you know it to be very good, then certainly you ought not to fear death, which you do not know to be evil. But since you do fear it, you know it to be evil. Yet you would not know it to be evil—and therefore would not fear it—unless you knew that there was something after death that makes death evil and causes you to fear it.

Let us now leave aside the natural form of the fear of death. No one should fear what he cannot escape. I engage the question from the other side: the hope of a happier state after death. For a desire for fame after death is innate in almost everyone [Col. 0615B]. It would take too long to recount the Curtii and the Reguli, or the Greek men whose innumerable eulogies celebrate their contempt for death for the sake of posthumous fame.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] “It would take too long to recount.” The history of the Curtii and of Regulus, who met death for their country, is too well known to require fuller treatment. He afterwards called fame “posthumous” metaphorically, meaning fame that endures after death. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0615D] “The Curtii.” This is the man who devoted himself to the gods of the dead for the salvation of his country. For when the earth had sunk into an immense chasm in the middle of the Forum, and the Romans had received the answer that the breach would not close unless one of the nobles cast himself into it, Curtius sacrificed his life for his country. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “Eulogies,” Junius.]

Who today does not strive so earnestly to ensure that his memory will be frequented after death, preserving his name either by works of literature, by the simple praise of his character, or by the ambitious magnificence of his very tomb?

[Note: [Col. 0616D] “Preserve his name.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, has almost the same concerning Caieta, Aeneas’s nurse:

> And now your honor preserves your resting place, and your name marks your bones  
> In great Hesperia—if that is any glory.

LE PR.]

How, then, can the soul today aspire to something that it wishes to possess after death, and prepare so earnestly for what it will use after its departure, if it knows nothing of what comes afterward?

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “The soul,” Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “Which,” others.]

But perhaps people are more certain of sensation after your departure than of a resurrection at some future time, for presuming which we are branded presumptuous. Yet this too is proclaimed by the soul. For if someone asks about a person long since dead as though he were alive, the ready answer that comes immediately to hand is: “He has now departed, and must return” [Col. 0615C].

[Note: [Col. 0615C] Rigaltius adds “about.”]

[Note: [Col. 0616D] “He has now departed.” The ancients said “he has lived,” “he has departed,” or “he has departed to the majority,” in place of “he is dead”; and in Festus too *abitio*, “departure,” is used for death. LE PR.]

## CHAPTER V

These testimonies of the soul are as simple as they are true; as commonplace as they are simple; as universal as they are commonplace; as natural as they are universal; as divine as they are natural. I do not think [Col. 0616A] they can appear frivolous or insipid to anyone who reflects upon the majesty of nature, from which the soul’s authority derives. As much as you grant to the teacher, so much you will adjudge to the pupil. Nature is the teacher, the soul the pupil. Whatever the former has taught or the latter has thoroughly learned was delivered by God, who is, of course, the teacher of the soul’s own teacher.

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “I think,” Rigaltius.]

What the soul can divine concerning its first institutor, it is for you to assess from the soul that is within you.

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “Is within you,” Rigaltius.]

Feel her, who causes you to feel! Reflect upon her as a prophetess in presentiments, a diviner in omens, and one who foresees events. Is it astonishing that, being given by God to humanity, she knows how to divine? It is equally astonishing if she knows him by whom she was given. Even when deceived by the adversary, she remembers her author, his goodness, his decree, her own end, and that of the adversary himself. Is it therefore astonishing that, being given by God [Col. 0616B], she sings the same things that God has given his own people to know?

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “And” is absent from the Paris edition.]

But one who has not thought that eruptions of the soul of this kind constitute a teaching of nature, secretly entrusted to a consciousness both connatural and inborn, will instead say that, through opinions scattered widely among the people, the practice of published writings has established and virtually hardened this manner of speaking into a habit.

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “Outburst,” Wouwer.]

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “And” is absent from Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “Secretly entrusted,” Wouwer.]

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “Published,” Junius.]

Certainly the soul is earlier than the written word, speech earlier than the book, sensation earlier than the pen, and the human being himself earlier than the philosopher and the poet.

[Note: [Col. 0616D] “Certainly the soul is earlier than the written word.” Since this passage calls the soul’s utterance “Tradition” a little later, it can very well be applied to the authority of ecclesiastical Traditions, since these precede all books and the pen, that is, all literature. PAM.—“The soul is earlier than the written word.” Antony the Great, according to Athanasius in his *Life*, employed the same argument against certain philosophers. LAC.]

Are we then to believe that before literature and its dissemination human beings lived mute, without utterances of this kind? Did no one speak of God and his goodness, no one of death, no one of the lower regions? Speech, I suppose, went begging—or rather could not exist at all—because even then those subjects were absent without which, even today, speech cannot be [Col. 0616C] happier, richer, or wiser. This would mean that things now so readily available, so constant, so close at hand, and in some fashion born upon the very lips, did not exist in former times, before letters sprouted in the world and before Mercury, I suppose, had been born.

And from where did the very system of letters obtain the ability to know and disseminate in spoken use things that no mind had ever conceived, no tongue uttered, and no ear received [Col. 0617A]?

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “Did it obtain? From where did it know?” Junius.]

But since the divine Scriptures, which are in our possession or that of the Jews—into whose wild olive tree we have been grafted—precede secular literature by far more than merely some modest period, as we have demonstrated in the proper place to establish their credibility, then even if the soul borrowed these utterances from writings, it must surely be believed to have borrowed them from ours, not from yours. For earlier writings are more potent in instructing the soul than later ones, which were themselves waiting to be instructed by those earlier writings.

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Into whose olive tree we have been grafted from the wild olive,” Latinus and Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Were waiting to be instructed.” That is, they were awaiting it. RIG.]

Even if we concede that the soul was instructed from your writings, the tradition nevertheless belongs to its first and principal origin; and whatever you happened to receive from our writings and hand on is wholly ours. Since this is so, it matters little whether the soul’s consciousness was formed by God [Col. 0617B] or by the writings of God. Why then do you wish, O human being, to maintain that these things came forth from the human opinions of your writings and entered the callousness of common usage?

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Into the callousness of common usage.” He means custom, which through long use has drawn over itself, as it were, a callus.]

## CHAPTER VI

Believe, therefore, your own writings; and from our records believe all the more in the divine writings; but from the judgment of the soul herself believe nature in the same way. Choose which of these you regard as the more faithful sister of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Faithful,” Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Regard as the sister of truth.” That is, which comes nearer to the truth, τῆς ἀληθέιας ἀδελφήν (“the sister of truth”). LE PR.]

If you doubt your own writings, neither God nor nature lies. That you may believe both nature and God, believe the soul; thus it will come about that you believe yourself as well. She is certainly the soul whom you value in proportion to how much she makes you what you are; to whom you belong entirely; who is everything to you; without whom you can neither live nor die; and for whose sake you neglect God.

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “As highly,” Junius.]

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “For whose sake you neglect God.” That is, you fear becoming a Christian lest, together with us, you lay down your soul—that is, your life—for the name of Christ. RIG.]

For since you fear becoming a Christian [Col. 0618A], confront her: why, while worshiping another, does she name God? Why, when she identifies spirits that are to be cursed, does she call them demons? Why does she call heaven to witness, yet use the earth in imprecation? Why does she serve in one place, but appeal to an avenger in another? Why does she pass judgment on the dead? Why does she possess the words of Christians, whom she wishes neither to hear nor to see? Why did she either give those words to us, or receive them from us? Why did she either teach or learn them?

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Why does she call heaven to witness?” Macrobius, book III, chapter 9, and Servius on *Aeneid* III note that the ancients, according to the character of the deities, sometimes looked downward and sometimes upward. *Contestari* means to summon someone openly as a witness. Cicero, *Against Verres*: “Calling gods and human beings to witness.” Cicero likewise uses *contestata* in *On Divination*: “For whom would authority, attested and sealed by the most illustrious records, not move?” *Detestor*, however, means “I curse” and “I abominate.” LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0617D] “Why does she serve in one place, but appeal to an avenger in another?” He alludes to what he said above in chapter 2: “Finally, in the very temples you implore God as judge.” Here, however, he suggests that God is invoked by them not merely as judge but also as avenger—that is, as redeemer and champion—as our Reynardus explains more fully in chapters 8 and 9 when citing this passage in connection with the laws of the Twelve Tables. PAM.]

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Nor,” Rigaltius.]

Hold suspect the agreement of proclamation amid so great a disagreement of conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “You have,” Junius and Rigaltius.]

You are foolish if you assign utterances of this kind to the Latin language alone, or to Greek, languages considered closely related to one another, and on that basis deny the universality of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0618C] “Which are considered closely related to one another.” Pliny writes that the fact that the ancient Greek letters were almost the same as those that are now Latin is evidence of this. PAM.]

The soul does not fall from heaven for Latins and Argives alone. Among all nations, “human being” is one name: there is one soul but various voices, one spirit but various sounds; each nation has its own language, but the substance of language is common.

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Among all nations there is one human being but a various name,” Junius and Rigaltius. “Among all nations there is a various name,” Wouwer.]

God is everywhere, and God’s goodness everywhere; the demon is everywhere, and the curse upon the demon everywhere; the invocation of divine judgment everywhere; death everywhere, and consciousness of death everywhere, and testimony everywhere [Col. 0618B].

[Note: [Col. 0618C] “God is everywhere,” etc. “He is present everywhere and fills all things,” Ρὁ πανταχοῦ παρὼν καὶ πάντα πληρῶν (“present everywhere and filling all things”; the anomalous initial Ρ is preserved as recovered), says St. Chrysostom, Oration 2 *Against the Jews*. LE PR.]

Every soul, by her own right, proclaims what we are not permitted even to mutter. Deservedly, therefore, every soul is both guilty and a witness: guilty of error to the same degree that she is a witness to truth. And she will stand before the courts of God on the day of judgment, having nothing to say:

“You proclaimed God, yet did not seek him; you abominated demons, yet worshiped them; you appealed to God’s judgment, yet did not believe it existed; you anticipated punishments in the lower regions, yet took no precautions against them; you understood the Christian name, yet persecuted the Christian.”

[Note: [Col. 0618C] “Nor,” Wouwer and Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0618D] “And she will stand before the courts of God,” Rhenanus; and *stabilis*. Nothing should be changed. “Before the courts of God” means before the palaces of God, unless perhaps the expression relates to sheep and *caulas Dei*, “the folds of God,” should be read; nevertheless, nothing should be changed. LAC.]

[Note: [Col. 0618C] “Having nothing to say, but hearing it said: ‘You proclaimed God,’” Junius.]

# Book to the Martyrs

[Col. 0619]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIANUS TO THE MARTYRS

[Note: [Col. 0619B] This book—or rather address—to Confessors, whom he calls “Martyrs” according to the ancient manner of speaking, was written around the year 197, in the judgment of the distinguished Naesselt. Tertullian was then still wholly Catholic, and it was approximately the time when Severus had launched an inquiry against those who had followed the parties of Niger and Albinus, as these words of Tertullian himself suggest (*To the Martyrs*, chapter 6): “In this matter, indeed, let even the present times serve you as evidence of how many persons, and of what kind, undergo deaths unexpected in view of their birth, rank, physical condition, and age, for the sake of a human being—either at his own hands, if they acted against him, or at the hands of his adversaries, if they stood for him.”

This book is an ardent exhortation to the Martyrs. In it he vigorously stirs and encourages those who were held in chains for the sake of the Christian religion to constancy in the faith and cheerfulness in enduring the squalor of prison and the punishments threatening them. Above all, however, he urges them to peace—the peace that those who did not possess it from the Church sought from the martyrs.

[Col. 0619C] At the beginning he praises the devotion of the faithful, who supplied bodily nourishment to the Martyrs in prison. He then exhorts the Martyrs themselves not to wish to grieve the Holy Spirit, but to preserve him in such a way that they maintain peace and concord with one another—the peace which those who did not possess it in the Church customarily entreated from the Martyrs in prison. “And therefore you ought, for that very reason, to possess, foster, and preserve it among yourselves, so that perhaps you may also be able to confer it upon others” (ibid., chapter 1).

From Tertullian’s words learned men conclude that he composed the present treatise while in communion with the Catholic Church. For after becoming a Montanist he held all these things in derision, as is clear from *On Modesty*, chapter XXII, and *On Fasting*, chapter XII.

In order to give the Martyrs courage to endure the squalor of prison, Tertullian proposes that the world itself is more truly a prison; and immediately he enumerates the benefits flowing from their detention in prison, arguing thus: “You have been separated from the world itself—how much more from the age and its affairs? … You do not see alien gods; you do not encounter their images; you do not participate, by the very fact of mingling with them, in the nations’ solemn days; you are not lashed by foul odors; [Col. 0620B] you are not struck by the shouting of the spectacles or by the cruelty, frenzy, or shamelessness of those celebrating them; your eyes do not fall upon places of public lust. You are free from scandals, temptations, evil recollections, and now even from persecution. Prison affords the Christian what the wilderness afforded the Prophets.… Let us remove the name ‘prison’ and call it ‘retirement.’ Although the body is enclosed and the flesh detained, all things lie open to the spirit. Wander in spirit, stroll in spirit, setting before yourself not shaded tracks or long colonnades, but that road which leads to God. As often as you walk upon it in spirit, so often you will not be in prison. The leg feels nothing in the stocks when the mind is in heaven” (ibid., chapter II).

Afterwards he attempts to rouse the Martyrs still further to patience and constancy by an argument drawn from the obligation, contracted in baptism, of serving as soldiers in God’s service. “Let prison now,” he says, “be troublesome even to Christians. We were summoned to the army of the living God at the very time when we responded to the words of the oath. No soldier comes to war with luxuries, nor does he proceed from the bedchamber to the battle line.… [Col. 0620C] Even in peace they learn by labor and hardships how to endure war.… Everything is achieved through sweat, lest bodies and spirits take fright when passing from shade to sunlight, from sunlight to the sky” (ibid., chapter III).

Finally, so that the Confessors may not allow themselves to be overcome by the severity of tortures, he adduces the examples of gentile men and women who bravely endured torture and death from the motive of vain glory alone (ibid., chapters IV and V). In the judgment of the very learned Dupin, nothing is more forceful in this brief address or better suited to move the emotions (Dupin, *Bibliothèque des auteurs*, vol. I).

In treating this subject, Tertullian was afterwards imitated by the blessed Cyprian in his book *On the Exhortation and Praise of Martyrdom* and in his letters to the Martyrs and Confessors.

Moreover, almost all learned men believe that Septimius addressed this discourse to martyrs held captive in some town under Carthaginian jurisdiction, or even in Carthage itself, on account of these words: “Finally, it awaits the judgments not of the Proconsul but of God” (Tertullian, *Treatise to the Martyrs*, chapter II). For the *Notitia Imperii* makes very frequent mention of the Proconsul of Africa. LUMP.]

(C)

[Col. 0619A]

## SUMMARY

With the fifth persecution under Severus now immediately threatening, Septimius wrote this short work, in which he exhorts the martyrs to constancy in the faith and cheerfulness in undergoing the squalor of prison and the decrees of the judges. Above all, however, he invites them to the peace that those who did not possess it in the Church sought from the martyrs.

## CHAPTER ONE

Among the provisions for the flesh, blessed martyrs-elect, which both our lady mother the Church supplies to you in prison from her own breasts and individual brethren from their own resources, receive something also from us that may serve to nourish the spirit as well.

[Col. 0620A]

[Note: [Col. 0620C] “Blessed martyrs.” That is, “worthy of praise.” Tertullian adorns the martyrs with this epithet, as shortly afterwards, “First of all, therefore, blessed ones,” and below in *To the Martyrs*. He also applied it above to Eleutherius, the Roman pontiff and martyr, after his death. Cyprian repeatedly calls them “most valiant and most blessed,” and in one place “most valiant and most faithful.” RHEN.]

[Note: [Col. 0620A] Others omit “elect” as superfluous.]

[Note: [Col. 0619A] “Works,” Rhenanus, Franeker, and Paris.]

For it does no good for the flesh to be fattened while the spirit goes hungry. Indeed, if that which is weak is cared for, that which is weaker must likewise not be neglected.

[Note: [Col. 0619A] August Neander emends “weaker” to “stronger.”]

I am not so important a person as to address you; nevertheless, even the most accomplished gladiators are exhorted from a distance not only by their own trainers and overseers, but also by any uninstructed and superfluous persons, since suggestions shouted even by the crowd itself have often proved useful.

First of all, therefore, blessed ones, do not grieve the Holy Spirit (Eph. IV, 3), who entered the prison with you. For if he had not entered with you then, you would not be there today. And therefore take care that he remain there with you, so that he may lead you from there to the Lord.

Prison is indeed the devil’s house, in which he confines his own household. But you entered prison for this purpose: that you might trample upon him even in his own house. For you had already encountered and trampled upon him outside. Let him not therefore say: “They are in my domain; I shall tempt them with contemptible splinters”—with passions or dissensions among themselves [Col. 0621A].

[Note: [Col. 0621B] “Hatreds,” Franeker; “fastings,” Rhenanus; for “contemptible,” Junius prefers “useful”; Rigaltius restored “splinters.”]

[Note: [Col. 0621B] “Privations,” Rhenanus.]

[Note: [Col. 0621B] “They are in my domain; I shall tempt them with contemptible hatreds.” Pamelius attests that this was the Vatican manuscripts’ reading. But no Christian will agree that hatreds existed among the martyrs themselves, and contemptible hatreds at that. Moreover, if Tertullian related that there were hatreds among the martyrs, he certainly added a futile and frivolous reproach concerning passions and dissensions. For what hatreds exist without passions and dissension? Indeed, Satan’s stratagem would have been exceedingly feeble: “The martyrs who have been driven into prison are in my domain; I shall therefore tempt them with contemptible hatreds.” Whom does he not tempt every day with hatreds of this kind—even when they are not in his domain, even outside prison? I therefore do not see how the Vatican reading can be defended.

In editions published before Pamelius the text read: “I shall tempt them with contemptible fastings, privations, or dissensions among themselves.” But no satisfactory sense can be derived from that either. For what sane person ever spoke of “contemptible fastings”? Or why should we suspect any fasting here, amid the provisions for the flesh which our lady mother the Church was supplying to these very martyrs in prison from her own breasts? This is stated most explicitly at the beginning of this work, and it also sufficiently refutes Rhenanus’s interpretation, which applies the word “privations” to a scarcity of provisions. Therefore, neither do those pre-Pamelian editions solve the difficulty.

Whoever copied the Dijon manuscript pointed toward the source of the truth. For there the reading is: “I shall tempt them with contemptiblesplinters, privations, or dissensions among themselves.” Let us separate what has wrongly been joined, and we have the author’s genuine reading: “I shall tempt them with contemptible splinters.”

Tertullian had heard that among the martyrs there were certain seeds, not of hatred, but of apostasy and dissension. Some perhaps argued that the authority of the Scriptures did not prohibit them from using money paid to extortioners to avert their chains and death itself. He therefore exhorts them to take particular care that Satan not devise plots against them, turning over in his mind the following thoughts: “I once tempted human beings when they were not in my domain—namely, when they were in paradise—and tempted them with the most excellent fruit of a certain divine tree. Those people today, who are in my domain—namely, in prison—I shall also tempt, but with contemptible splinters.”

It is as though he said: “Formerly, when humanity was tempted in paradise, a temptation of great magnificence had to be employed—namely, the desire for the fruit that would make gods out of human beings. But now I shall tempt those placed in my domain, since they are in prison and the kingdom of darkness, with trifles and rubbish: for example, fear of some momentary distress, or the desire to prolong for a few years a life that dies day by day. Finally, I shall set them against one another and harass them with dissensions.”

These are Satan’s readily available weapons, lying close at hand, as though made from worthless brushwood and the combustible splinters of trees. *Scidiae* or *scidia*, whence also *discidia*, “divisions,” are σχίδακες, κλάσματα ξύλων (“splinters, fragments of wood”), cheap cuttings from felled trees. Vitruvius, book II, chapter 1: “They stop up the gaps with splinters and mud.” RIG.]

Let him flee from your sight; let him shrink back and hide in his lowest depths, benumbed like a serpent charmed or smoked out. Let him not fare so well in his own kingdom that he sets you against one another; rather, let him find you fortified and armed with concord, because your peace is war against him.

Some who did not possess that peace in the Church were accustomed to entreat it from the martyrs in prison. And for that reason too you ought to possess it among yourselves, foster it, and preserve it, so that perhaps you may be able to confer it upon others as well.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] “That peace some,” etc. These words must first be understood of peace or reconciliation with the other Christians and with God. For the custom had grown up that those detained in prison by the tyranny would give certificates, upon request, to believers undergoing penance; with the aid of these they obtained the peace of God and entered into communion with the other brethren.

These statements also contribute very greatly to the authority of indulgences, whose perhaps excessive facility Cyprian once criticized. In the last century the Council of Trent, convened against the heresy that had sprung up under the pretext of abuses concerning indulgences, confronted both the heresy and the abuse. It confronted the heresy by defining that it belongs to the Church to grant indulgences—for the blessed Paul once granted them to Alexander and Hymenaeus. It confronted the abuse by desiring that moderation be applied in granting them, in accordance with the ancient and approved custom of the Church, etc.; Session 25, Decree on Indulgences. It thereby refers us to the ancient canons of councils, such as the many canons of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Carthage, Agde, etc. LE PR.]

## CHAPTER II

Let the other impediments of the mind have accompanied you only as far as the threshold [Col. 0621B] of the prison, as did your parents. From that point you were separated from the world itself—how much more from the age and its affairs?

Do not let the fact that you have been separated from the world dismay you [Col. 0622A].

[Note: [Col. 0621B] “From the world” is absent from Rigaltius.]

For if we reflect that the world itself is more truly a prison, we shall understand that you have gone out of prison rather than entered one. The world possesses deeper darkness, which blinds the hearts of human beings. The world puts on heavier chains, which bind human souls themselves. The world breathes forth fouler impurities: human lusts. Finally, the world contains more defendants—namely, the entire human race. In short, it awaits the judgments not of the Proconsul but of God.

[Note: [Col. 0622B] “Prisons,” Rigaltius.]

[Note: [Col. 0622B] “Imbues,” Semler.]

[Note: [Col. 0622D] “In short, it awaits the judgments not of the Proconsul but of God.” *Sustinet* means “awaits.” RIG.—Permit us to doubt the interpretation of the learned men who have won some reputation for themselves in this field. Almost all of them believe that the captives were held in some town under Carthaginian jurisdiction, or even in Carthage itself, because of the word “Proconsul”; for, they say, the *Notitia Imperii* makes very frequent mention of the Proconsul of Africa. Yet no one is unaware that magistracies were changed according to the emperors’ pleasure. LE PR.]

You may therefore consider yourselves, blessed ones, perhaps transferred from prison into a place of safekeeping. It has darkness, but you yourselves are light. It has bonds, but you are free for God. A foul odor is breathed forth there, but you are an odor of sweetness. A judge is awaited, but you are going to judge the judges themselves (Wis. III) [Col. 0622B].

[Note: [Col. 0622B] Rhenanus adds “concerning the judges.”]

Let the person who sighs for the fruit of this age be sorrowful there. Even outside prison, the Christian renounced the age; in prison, he renounces prison too. It makes no difference where you are within the age, since you are outside the age [Col. 0623A]. And if you have lost some of life’s pleasures, it is a commercial transaction to lose something in order to gain greater things.

[Note: [Col. 0623C] “You have lost,” Junius.]

I say nothing yet about the reward to which God invites the martyrs. Meanwhile, let us compare the very modes of life of the age and of prison, and see whether the spirit does not gain more in prison than the flesh loses. Indeed, through the Church’s care and the brethren’s love-feast, the flesh does not even lose the things that are its rightful due; and the spirit gains in addition those things that are always beneficial to faith.

You do not see alien gods; you do not encounter their images; you do not participate, by the very fact of mingling with them, in the nations’ solemn days; you are not lashed by foul odors; you are not struck by the shouting of the spectacles or by the cruelty, frenzy, or shamelessness of those celebrating them; your eyes do not fall upon places of public lust. You are free from scandals [Col. 0623B], temptations, evil recollections, and now even from persecution.

Prison affords the Christian what the wilderness afforded the prophets (Mark I). The Lord himself more frequently dwelt in retirement, so that he might pray more freely and withdraw from the age (Luke IV). Finally, it was in solitude that he displayed his glory to his disciples (Matt. XVII; Mark IX; Luke II; 1 Peter 1).

Let us remove the name “prison” and call it “retirement.” Although the body is enclosed and the flesh detained, all things lie open to the spirit. Wander in spirit, stroll in spirit, setting before yourself not shaded tracks or long colonnades, but that road which leads to God.

[Note: [Col. 0623C] “Shaded tracks.” With trees arranged in a long row on either side. LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0623C] “Setting before yourself,” Franeker and Paris.]

As often as you walk upon it in spirit, so often you will not be in prison. The leg feels nothing in the stocks when the mind is in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] “The leg feels nothing in the stocks.” Here *nervus* is a kind of wooden device pierced by many holes, which tyrants used to torture the martyrs, so that their legs, forced apart and dislocated, would be broken. This kind of punishment is called ξύλον (“wood,” here a wooden instrument of restraint) by certain Greeks, but by many of the more ancient writers κᾶλον (“wood,” likewise referring to that instrument of restraint); the two terms signify the same thing. Scaliger also taught me that defendants at Athens were called ἐγκαλοσκελεῖς (“those whose legs were confined in the stocks”). LE PR.]

[Note: [Col. 0623C] “When the hand,” Semler.]

The mind carries the whole person about and transfers him wherever it wishes (Matt. VI): “Where your heart is, there also will your treasure be” [Col. 0623C]. Therefore let our heart be where we wish to have our treasure.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 0623] This note appears at the foot of column 624, but the callout number has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0624C] “Blessed—about to undergo,” Rhenanus.]

Restoration notes: E014/S001030: The recovered word ἰδίδης appears textually irregular, although the surrounding Latin securely supports the sense “from one’s own judgment.”; E014/S001030: The recovered form ἰδίδης is textually irregular, but the surrounding Latin securely supports the meaning “from one’s own judgment.”  

Is prison, then, now to be irksome even to Christians [Col. 0624A]? [Note: [Col. 0623C] Thus Rig.] We were called to the service of the living God from the very moment when we responded to the words of the sacramental oath. [Note: [Col. 0623C] “We respond,” Seml.] No soldier comes to war amid luxuries, nor does he proceed from the bedchamber to the battle line, but from tents pitched and fastened down, [Note: [Col. 0623D] “But from tents.” I follow Rhenanus, who says that tents are unfolded when they are stretched out in camp and drawn tight and tied with cords to stakes fixed in the ground, lest they collapse when disturbed by the wind. LE PR.] where every hardship, discomfort, and unpleasantness is to be found. Even in peace they already learn, through toil and [Note: [Col. 0623C] “There is toil,” Rhen.] privations, how to endure war: by marching under arms, running over the field, constructing a trench, and compacting the shield formation. [Note: [Col. 0624C] “Drying,” Rhen.; “making dense,” Lacerda; “sitting down,” or “sweating,” others.] [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Compacting the shield formation.” Thus the old books read; others, however, wrongly have “sweating” or “sitting down.” Livy, book XLIV: “After forming a square column, with shields packed closely above their heads—the front ranks standing, the second somewhat lowered, the third and fourth still more, and the last even resting on their knees—they made a sloping shield formation like the roofs of buildings.” Lucan, III:

[Col. 0624C] Yet valor, roofed beneath a compact shield formation,

Approaches the enemy walls.—RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0624C] “Compacting the shield formation.” Of all readings, this one of Rigault, “compacting,” seems best to me, for I think it must be understood of the shield formation, which was made by [Col. 0624D] closely packed shields. Junius has “sweating,” perhaps his own conjecture, which is not to be despised. Rhenanus has “drying”; others, “sitting down”; others, “sweating”; Lacerda emended it to “making dense.” LE PR.] Everything costs sweat, lest bodies and spirits become terrified: from shade to sun, from sun to frost [Note: [Col. 0624C] “From sun to frost,” Latinus; “from sun to frost,” Jun.], from tunic to breastplate, from silence to shouting, from repose to tumult. Accordingly, blessed ones, regard whatever hardship there is here as training for the virtues of spirit and body. You are about to enter the good contest [Note: [Col. 0624C] “End,” Rigault.], in which the contest-master [Col. 0624B] is the living God; the superintendent of the training ground, [Note: [Col. 0624D] “The superintendent of the training ground is the Holy Spirit.” He elegantly calls the Holy Spirit the superintendent of the training ground, for martyrs owe their steadfastness to his aid. Accordingly, he said above of the Holy Spirit: “For if he had not now entered with you, neither would you be there today.” *Xystarches* means the presiding officer of the *xystus*, or training ground. RHEN.] the Holy Spirit; the crown, eternity; the prize, angelic substance, citizenship in heaven, glory for ever and ever. Therefore your trainer [Note: [Col. 0624D] “Therefore your trainer is Christ.” Here he takes *epistates* to mean the master who presides over athletes, for Tertullian is employing this metaphor. Among the Athenians, the man who presided over ten men holding daily command is called ἐπιστατης (“overseer”) by Demosthenes; elsewhere, in the battle line, ἐπιστάς (“one standing close by”) and παραστὰς (“one standing beside”), “those standing close by” and “those standing beside,” are so called in Aelian, as Gaza of Thessalonica most elegantly translates them. RHEN.] is Jesus Christ, who anointed you with the Spirit and led you out onto this contest-ground. Before the day of the contest, he willed to separate you from a freer condition and subject you to harsher treatment, so that your strength might be reinforced. Athletes, of course, are likewise set apart for stricter discipline, so that they may devote themselves to building strength. They are restrained from luxury, richer foods, and more pleasant drink. They are constrained, tormented, and wearied: the more they have labored in their exercises, the more they hope for victory. And they, says the Apostle (1 Cor. 9), do so in order to obtain a corruptible crown; we are to obtain an eternal one. Let us interpret the prison [Col. 0624C] as our training school, so that, well exercised in every hardship, we may be led forth to the stadium of the tribunal; for virtue is built up by hardship but destroyed by softness.

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0624] This note appears at the foot of column 625, but the callout number (4) has not been printed in the text.] [Note: [Col. 0625C] “When it is absent,” Pam.]

We know from the Lord’s admonition that the flesh is weak [Col. 0625A] but the spirit ready. We must not, therefore, flatter ourselves because the Lord agreed that the flesh is weak. For that very reason he first said that the spirit was ready, [Note: [Col. 0625C] Franeq. adds “was.”] in order to show what ought to be subject to what: namely, that the flesh should serve the spirit, the weaker serving the stronger, so that from it the flesh itself [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Itself,” Fran., Paris., Rig.] might also receive strength. Let the spirit converse with the flesh about their common salvation, thinking no longer about the privations of prison but about the contest and battle itself. The flesh will perhaps fear the heavy sword, the lofty cross, the savagery of wild beasts, the supreme punishment of fire, and every ingenuity of the executioner in devising tortures. But the spirit should set before itself and the flesh the fact that these things, though bitter, have nevertheless been endured with equanimity by many, and indeed voluntarily sought for the sake of fame and glory—and not by men alone, but also by women, so that you too, blessed women, [Col. 0625B] may answer worthily to your sex. It would take too long to enumerate the individuals who, led by their own inclination, [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Led by their own inclination.” Admirably said, for a true martyr ought not to follow his own leading but God’s: he must not kill himself, but fall when God wills it. LAC.] have killed themselves with the sword. Among women, a ready example is Lucretia, who, after suffering the violence of rape, drove a knife into herself in the sight of her relatives, so as to procure glory for her chastity. [Note: [Col. 0625D] “So as to procure glory for her chastity.” It was not love of chastity but weakness arising from shame. Augustine, *The City of God*. RIG.] Mucius [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Mucius [burned] his right hand.” Tertullian undoubtedly thinks that Mucius lost his life from the wound to his burned right hand, something I have not seen in any writer; for he places him in the catalogue of those who killed themselves by a voluntary death. LAC.] burned his right hand upon the altar so that fame might preserve this deed of his. Philosophers did less: Heraclitus, [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Heraclitus.” He, as Rhenanus observed, suffered from dropsy; and since the man was accustomed to obscure expressions, he asked the physicians whether they could make drought out of rain. When they disregarded him, thinking that they were being mocked, he finally wished to aid himself and had his swollen body covered with cattle dung. This is found in Laertius. PAM.] who burned himself after being smeared with cattle dung; likewise Empedocles, who leapt into the fires of Mount Etna; and Peregrinus, who not long ago threw himself upon a funeral pyre. Women too have despised fire: Dido, [Note: [Col. 0625C] “When,” Rhen.] so that she would not be forced to marry after the death of her dearly beloved husband; likewise the wife of Hasdrubal, who, when Carthage was already burning and she saw her husband as Scipio’s suppliant, hurled herself with her children into the conflagration of her homeland. Regulus, the Roman commander, [Col. 0625C] captured by the Carthaginians, refused to allow himself alone to be exchanged for many Carthaginian prisoners; he preferred to be returned to the enemy and, packed into a kind of chest pierced on every side from without by nails, experienced as many crosses. A woman willingly exposed herself to wild beasts—and indeed to asps, serpents more dreadful than a bull or bear—which Cleopatra let loose upon herself lest she fall into the hands of her enemy.

But fear of death is not as great as fear of tortures. [Note: [Col. 0625C] “As great as that of torture. And so she did not yield to the executioner,” etc., Jun.; “and so neither did she yield,” Latin.] And so, did that Athenian courtesan yield to the executioner [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Of the executioner,” Seml.] [Col. 0626A]—she who, being privy to a conspiracy and therefore tortured by the tyrant, neither betrayed the conspirators and at last spat her chewed-off tongue into the tyrant’s face, so that they might know that the tortures were achieving nothing even if they continued further? For the ceremony that is today the greatest among the Lacedaemonians, διαμαστίγωσις (“flogging”) [Note: [Col. 0626D] Διαμαστίγωσις (“flogging”), that is, flogging. He also mentions it near the end of the *Apology*. RHEN.], that is, flogging, is well known. In that rite all the noblest young men are scourged before the altar, while their parents and relatives stand by and exhort them to persevere. For it will be reckoned an honor and a glory of still greater title if the life yields to the blows before the body does.

Therefore, if earthly glory has such power over bodily and spiritual vigor that men despise sword, fire, cross, beasts, and tortures for the reward of human praise, I can say that those sufferings [Col. 0626B] are slight in comparison with obtaining heavenly glory and divine recompense. If glass is worth so much, [Note: [Col. 0626D] “If glass is worth so much, how much is a pearl worth?” The form of a proverb. Jerome to Laeta: “If glass is worth so much, why should a pearl not be of greater price?” Likewise to Demetrias, and again to Salvina. It is used to express the immense inequality and distance between things. For who but a madman compares glass with a pearl? LAC.] how much is a pearl worth? [Note: [Col. 0626C] “If glass is worth so much, how much is a true pearl worth?” Rhen.] Who, then, would not most willingly pay as much for the true as others pay for the false?

## CHAPTER V

For now I omit the motive of glory. Mere affectation too, and a certain sickness of mind among men, has trampled underfoot all these same trials of savagery and torment. [Note: [Col. 0626D] “Affectation among men.” Those things that appeared to be done with somewhat greater religious devotion by the pagans were attributed to affectation as though to some disease, so that the deed was judged feigned and performed merely for display, not as true virtue. LAC.] How many idlers does a taste for arms hire for the sword? [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Perhaps he calls,” Jun.] They certainly descend even to the beasts out of sheer passion and think themselves more handsome for their bites and scars. Some have even hired themselves out to the flames, to complete a fixed distance in a burning tunic. [Note: [Col. 0626D] “In a burning tunic.” That tunic was smeared with pitch and bitumen; in former times the holy martyrs were clothed in it before being cast into the fire. It is called the “tormenting tunic” by Martial, epigram 25 of book 10, and Juvenal, Satire 8:

“. . . that one may punish with the tormenting tunic.” RIG.] Others have walked between the hunters’ whips with backs capable of enduring the utmost. Blessed ones, it was not without reason [Col. 0626C] that the Lord permitted these things in the world: they serve both to exhort us now [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Then,” others.] and to confound us on that day, if we shrink from suffering for truth unto salvation what others have deliberately sought for vanity unto destruction.

## CHAPTER VI

But let us set aside these examples of steadfastness arising from affectation. Let us turn to contemplation of the human condition itself, so that such cases too may instruct us if there are things that must be faced steadfastly, since they commonly befall even the unwilling. [Col. 0627A] For how often have fires burned people alive! [Note: [Col. 0627A] “For how often have fires burned people alive!” He omitted the most acute torments of certain diseases and fevers, whose fires are often more hideous than those inflicted by tyrants and certainly more prolonged. Arrian elegantly observed this in his work on Epictetus, book II: Οὐδέποτε οὐδεὶς τύραννος ἓξ μησί τινα ἔσφαξε, πυρετὸς δὲ καὶ ἐνιαυτῷ πολλάκις (“No tyrant ever killed anyone for six months, but a fever often does so even for a year”). In the same place he says that it makes no difference by what road one arrives at death. Indeed, if we love truth, that road is shorter by which the tyrant orders one to be led. RIG.] How often have wild beasts devoured people both in their own forests and, after escaping from their cages, in the midst of cities! [Note: [Col. 0627B] “And in the midst of cities, after escaping from their cages.” Here I am reminded [Col. 0628A] of two savage she-bears kept by the emperor Valentinian, whose cages he used to place beside his bedchamber. One was named Golden Mica, the other Innocence. They mangled many mortals while the emperor laughed and took pleasure in this cruelty. The authority is Ammianus Marcellinus, book 39. RHEN.] How many have been killed with the sword by robbers, or even upon the cross by enemies, after first being tortured and indeed exhausted by every form of outrage! [Note: [Col. 0628A] “Exhausted by every form of outrage.” Here you hear a word characteristic of Tertullian: it means that no outrage was omitted that they did not suffer. RHEN.] There is no one who cannot suffer for the sake of a human being [Col. 0628A] what he hesitates to suffer for the sake of God. In this respect, let even the present times serve us as evidence: how many and what kinds of persons meet with ends unforeseen in view of their birth, rank, physique, and age, for the sake of a human being—either at that person’s own hand, if they acted against him, or at the hands of his adversaries, if they stood on his behalf.

# The Book *On the Shows*

[Col. 0627]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, *ON THE SHOWS* (C)

## NOTE

[Col. 0627B] The distinguished Noesselt has demonstrated that Tertullian wrote the books *On the Shows* and *On Idolatry* on the occasion when shows were being produced not only at Rome but also throughout the provinces because of Severus’s return and the victory he had won over Albinus. [Col. 0627C] Some indeed conjecture that Tertullian composed the book *On the Shows* during his Montanist period, because in it he appears to support those who sought revelations (Tertullian, *On the Shows*, ch. 29). But who does not know that the martyrs of the catholic Church themselves sought revelations from God, as may be seen in the acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity (XXXV, Ruinart, *Acta sincera*, p. 87)? These were read publicly in the assemblies in the time of St. Augustine (Augustine, Sermon 280).
