Add that St. Cyprian expressly asserts that confessors were often warned in a vision of their approaching martyrdom (Cyprian, Epistles XI and XVI).

However that may be, Tertullian’s purpose in this treatise was certainly to call Christians, including catechumens themselves, away from the shows [Col. 0627D] by demonstrating how shameless such entertainments are, how contrary to true piety and the sincere worship that we owe to God, and how hostile even to those who have renounced the pomp of the world, its pleasures, and idolatry. First, he removes two plausible arguments of the pagans. The first is that so great an outward gratification of the eyes or ears presents no obstacle to religion in the mind and conscience, and that God is not offended by a human being’s enjoyment. The second is that Christians, a race ready for death, are trained for this obstinacy by the renunciation of pleasures, so that they may despise life more easily once its bonds have, as it were, been cut away. He then rejects another ridiculous pagan objection: that everything serving the theater—earth, stones, lions, bodily strength, and the charms of the voice [Col. 0628B]—was created by God and therefore ought not to be rejected.

Against the objection of certain Christians who asserted that attendance at the shows is nowhere expressly forbidden in Holy Scripture, he sets those words of the royal Prophet: [Col. 0628C] “Blessed is the man who has not gone into the council of the impious, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.” He then adds that believers are bound to flee from them because, when they entered the water, they professed the faith and attested with their own mouths that they had renounced the devil and his pomp and angels. He affirms that games and shows belong to idolatry, from which he demonstrates that they derived their origin; and he reviews the names of the games, their idolatrous apparatus, their superstitious venues, and their arts. In discussing the circus, he says that although it was filled with idols and superstitious emblems, Christians could nevertheless enter it without fault outside the time of the shows, just as they might enter the temples themselves if their reason for entering were free from blame.

From the circus he passes to the theater, particularly consecrated to Venus and Bacchus; from there to [Col. 0628D] athletic contests, each dedicated to its own deity; and finally to the gladiators, who owed their origin to funeral processions. These last shows belonged to the amphitheater. But besides idolatry, the principal reason, he also recalls still other reasons why Christians must avoid the shows: namely, the danger of losing the Holy Spirit amid the agitation of our passions; the loss of time, so precious to a Christian; and insults, curses, slanders, and abuse. For there everything shameful that was concealed elsewhere with the greatest care was publicly brought forth. He shows how repugnant it is to sound reason eagerly to seek at the shows what shame and horror forbid us to see or commit in the rest of life’s intercourse.

Then [Col. 0629A] he proceeds: it is not expedient to see an image of those things that one is not permitted to do; yet in tragedy you present dreadful crimes to the spectators’ eyes, and in comedy, wantonness. It is not fitting for a human being endowed with reason to be cruel and savage; therefore it is likewise not fitting to delight in a dreadful sight in which people are slaughtered, even if those killed deserved death for their crimes. It is insane to esteem highly an art whose practitioners are excluded from the society of respectable people because of the mark of infamy. He next rebukes the insolence of masked performers and recalls God’s curse directed against men who would assume women’s clothing, for men in feminine dress played women’s roles on the stage.

Afterward he shows once again that the use of the shows is contrary to baptism and that the gentiles themselves customarily distinguished Christians by their rejection of the shows. [Col. 0629B] Finally, he adduces two examples of Christians punished for frequenting the shows. He then exhorts Christians to pass their lives here amid groaning while the gentiles immerse themselves in pleasures, and to desire nothing more than to depart from this world in order to come to God. Wishing to show what pleasures and entertainments befit Christians, Tertullian writes: “What greater pleasure is there than loathing pleasure itself, than contempt for the whole world, than true liberty, than an unblemished conscience . . . than that you trample upon the gods of the nations, that you expel demons, that you perform cures, that you seek revelations, [Col. 0630A] that you live for God?” These are the pleasures, these the shows of Christians: holy, perpetual, and free of charge. Finally, he exhorts them diligently to contemplate the contests of the martyrs, the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, his approaching advent, the Last Judgment, the eternal punishments of the impious, and the rewards of the good. LUMP.

## CHAPTER ONE

Servants of God, learn what the state of faith is, what the rationale of truth, and what the rule of discipline that, among the other errors of the world, also takes away [Note: [Col. 0629D] “What the state of faith is.” It is evident that this book was written not only for those already Christians but also for catechumens, whom the author customarily calls “Hearers.” This is clear both from these words, “Servants of God, learn, you especially who are drawing near [Col. 0629C] to God,” which refer to catechumens, and from these: “Acknowledge, you who have already testified and confessed that you have drawn near,” which refer to those already baptized, who had given testimony to the faith at baptism. PAM.] the pleasures of the shows. [Note: [Col. 0629C] “The pleasures of the shows.” This is assuredly what blessed Athanasius said in his homily *On the Sower*: θεατρομανεῖς ἡδονάς (“theater-crazed pleasures”). LE PR.] This applies to you who are now especially drawing near to God; and you who have already testified and confessed that you have drawn near, acknowledge it, lest anyone sin either through ignorance or through dissimulation. For so great is the force of pleasures that it both prolongs ignorance until an opportunity arises [Note: [Col. 0629C] “That it prolongs ignorance until an opportunity arises.” So great, he says, is the force of pleasures that it does not allow its subject to be taught that a Christian must avoid the shows for as long as there remains hope of an opportunity to see them. Augustine complains in Psalm 80 that the Christians of his own age suffered from this madness: “There are many who do not live worthily of the baptism [Col. 0629D] they have received. For how many baptized people today have preferred to fill the circus rather than this basilica!” LE PR.] [Col. 0630B] and corrupts the conscience into dissimulation.

To both tendencies, perhaps even now, the opinions of the pagans offer someone enticement; [Note: [Col. 0629B] “Which,” Seml.] in this case they customarily argue against us as follows: So great an outward gratification of the eyes or ears presents no obstacle [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Presents no obstacle to religion.” The verb is used for “to hinder” and “to be an obstacle.” It is exactly what Seneca, Epistle 115, calls *obstrigillant*, and what the Synod of Tricastina, writing to Pope Nicholas, calls *obdicere*. I wished to note these two words as peculiar usages. LAC.] to religion in the mind and conscience [Note: [Col. 0629B] Fran. adds “your”]; nor indeed is God offended by human enjoyment, which it is no crime to experience at its proper time and place, provided that fear and honor toward God remain intact. Yet this is precisely what we are preparing to demonstrate: how these things [Note: [Col. 0629B] “Those things,” Rigault.] are incompatible with true religion and true obedience toward the true God.

There are those who suppose [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Christians, a race ready for death.” Arrian, on Epictetus, book IV, ch. 7, attributes the obstinacy of Christians in meeting death for Christ’s name not to madness but to custom and habituation: Ὑπὸ μανίας μὲν δύναται τις οὓτως διατεθῆναι πρὸς ταῦτα, καὶ ὑπὸ ἔθους οἱ γαλιλαῖοι (“Someone may indeed be disposed toward these things in this way through madness, and the Galileans through habit”). We acknowledge such a custom and know that it must be preserved with the greatest constancy. Indeed, we shall not deny that it is madness, but a holy madness, a more vehement inspiration of the divine Spirit that drives his people in their ardor. The pagans attempted to tarnish the glory of this constancy by calling it obstinacy; indeed, among their proverbs for things least to be expected [Col. 0630B] they used to say: Θᾶσσον ἄν τις τοὺς ἀπὸ Μωυσοῦ καὶ Χριστοῦ μεταδιδάξειεν (“One would sooner teach the followers of Moses and Christ otherwise”), “Someone would sooner make them unlearn Moses and Christ.” Galen used this in book III *On Differences of Pulses*. Augustine too, in book XIX of *The City of God*, [Col. 0630C] records Apollo’s oracle, which answered Porphyry when he asked by what means he might call his wife back from Christianity: “He would more easily imprint letters upon a most rapid river, or fly through the air.” RIG.—“Christians, a race ready for death.” As though ἐπιθανατίους ῥιψοκινδύνους, παραβόλους, παρακεκινδυνευμένους (“those marked for death, reckless risk-takers, venturesome, and having put themselves in danger”). Paul, in Philippians ch. 2, says of Epaphroditus: μέχρι θανάτου ἤγγικε, παραβολευσάμενος τῇ ψυχῇ (“he came near to death, having risked his life”). For so it is read in a very ancient manuscript, where the Latin version also has: “Having risked himself concerning his life.” The author of that version hesitated whether he should say, “having risked his life” or “having risked himself concerning his life.” In the same sense, the author of the *Tripartite History*, book XI near the end, [Col. 0630D] called an artisan *parabolus*: “Let the artisan, the risk-taker, fight the cruel beast.” This is what Socrates, *History* 7, had expressed as παραβολευσάμενος (“having exposed himself to danger”). Epaphroditus and other Christians must by no means be thought to have despised their lives as though, rash, ruined, and desperate through mere obstinacy, they sought death: κατὰ ψιλὴν παράταξιν (“out of mere defiance”). Marcus Antoninus thought this in book XI of *His Life*. Rather, with supreme judgment, reason, and prudence they were always entirely ready to meet death bravely for the name of Christ, that is, for the truth of the Christian faith: ἀπὸ ἰδίδης κρίσεως, λελογισμένως, καὶ σεμνῶς (“from one’s own judgment”—the recovered ἰδίδης is textually irregular—“rationally and with dignity”). RIG. “A race ready for death.” Rigault says much on this passage about the word παραβολευσάμενος (“having exposed himself to danger”). To it may be added this statement of Hesychius: Παραβολευσάμενος, εἰς θὰνατον ἑαυτὸν ἐκδούς (“Having exposed himself to danger: having given himself over to death”). Phrynichus should likewise be read in his *Selection of Attic Words* under the word παραβόλιον (*parabolion*, “a risk or venture”). We have said something on this matter in the notes to the *Greek-Latin Glossary*, p. 141, col. 1, line 19. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0630B] “Suppose,” Rigault.] that Christians, [Note: [Col. 0630B] “A Christian,” Seml.] a race ready [Col. 0631A] for death, are trained for this obstinacy [Note: [Col. 0631D] “For this obstinacy.” The author commonly uses the word *obstinacy* in a favorable sense, for steadfastness, just as Tacitus, book IX, speaks of “obstinacy in loyalty.” PAM.] through the renunciation of pleasures, [Note: [Col. 0631D] “Through the renunciation of pleasures.” A doctrine circulated among gentile philosophers, those great managers of pain’s avoidance, that pleasures must be renounced before death so that death might be free from pain. Seneca presents this philosophical doctrine in Epistle 27. The gentiles therefore thought that this injunction was practiced among Christians through their renunciation of the shows, so that they might thus be better prepared to endure death without pain. LAC.] so that they may more easily despise life once its bonds have, as it were, been severed, and may not desire what they have already made superfluous [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Superfluous,” Jun., Paris.] to themselves; [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Had made,” Jun.; “have made,” Rigault.] thus it is supposed to have been determined with this design and from human foresight rather than by divine prescription. Evidently, even those who persisted amid such great pleasures found it distressing to die for God. Yet even if this were so, the steadfastness of so great a discipline owed obedience to so fitting a plan. [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Yet even if this were so, obedience,” etc.; thus Junius punctuates.]

## CHAPTER II

Now, indeed, there is no one who does not also put forward the claim that all things were established by God and assigned to humanity (Gen. 1), as we ourselves proclaim, and that all are therefore good, being the works of a good author; [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Good, as all things belonging to a good author,” Rig.] that among these must be reckoned all the things from which shows are furnished—for example, a circus [Note: [Col. 0631C] “A horse,” Rigault.], [Col. 0631B] a lion, bodily strength, and the charms of the voice. Accordingly, nothing that consists of God’s own creation can be regarded as alien or hostile to God, [Note: [Col. 0631C] “To God,” Paris., Rigault.] nor must God’s worshipers avoid [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Must suppose,” Paris.; “nor must reckon as a fault,” Rigault.] what is not hostile to God, since neither is it alien to him. Certainly the very structures of the venues—the stones, cement, marble, and columns—are God’s things, which he supplied as the furnishing of the earth; and the acts themselves are performed beneath God’s sky.

How wise an advocate human ignorance thinks itself, especially when it fears losing something of this sort from the joys and fruits of the world! Indeed, you will find more people whom the danger to pleasure, rather than the danger to life, turns away from this sect. For even a fool does not dread death, since it is owed; even a wise man does not despise pleasure, since it is so great, [Note: [Col. 0631C] “As something to be enjoyed,” Jun.] [Col. 0631C] because for fool and wise man alike there is no other charm in life than pleasure.

No one denies—because no one is ignorant of what nature spontaneously suggests—that God is the creator of the universe and that the universe is both good and made subject to humanity. But because they do not know God thoroughly, knowing him only by natural right and not also through intimacy, from afar and not close at hand, [Col. 0632A] they must necessarily be ignorant of how he commands or forbids the things he established to be used; [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Commands the things he established to be used,” Rigault.] and at the same time they must be ignorant of what rival stands on the opposing side [Note: [Col. 0631C] “What rival power stands on the opposing side,” Rigault.] to corrupt the uses of divine creation, because one cannot know either the will or the adversary of one whom one knows so little.

We must therefore consider not only by whom [Note: [Col. 0631D] “From whom,” Wouw., MS., Rigault.] all things were established, but also by whom they have been perverted. In this way it will become apparent by whose power [Note: [Col. 0632C] “For what use,” Rigault.] they were established, if it becomes apparent whose they are not. [Note: [Col. 0632C] “If it becomes apparent for what they were not,” Rig.] There is a great difference between corruption and integrity, because there is a great difference between the founder and the falsifier. Besides, every kind of evil that [Note: [Col. 0631D] “Which even the pagans both prohibit and affirm as unquestionable.” “Affirm” here means “assert”—namely, assert them to be evils, and indeed unquestionable ones; that is, evils that not even any pagan doubts to be evils. RIG.] even the pagans both prohibit and affirm to be unquestionably such consists of works of God. [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Unquestionably,” Seml.] Do you wish [Note: [Col. 0632C] “You see,” Jun.] murder to be accomplished by iron, poison, or magical bindings? [Col. 0632B] [Note: [Col. 0631D] “Magical bindings.” He uses *devinctiones* for binding spells, which he discusses more fully in the book *On the Soul*. Here [Col. 0632D] Gelenius’s correction, “did the author provide these things for the killing of a human being?” in place of “the author is in the killing,” is excellent. From a manuscript, a little below, I read “the perpetrator of crimes” in place of “the author”; for the human being is not their author—the Devil is their falsifier. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0632C] “To be accomplished,” Rig.] Iron is as much a thing of God as herbs and angels are. Yet did their author provide these things for killing a human being? On the contrary, he destroyed every form of homicide by one principal commandment: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20).

Likewise, who placed in the world the gold, bronze, silver, ivory, wood, and every kind of material appropriated for making idols, if not God, the author of the world? Yet did he do so in order that these things should be worshiped in opposition to himself? On the contrary, idolatry is in his judgment the supreme offense. [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Offense,” Rigault.] What is not God’s that offends God? But when it gives offense, it ceases to belong to God; and when it has ceased to belong to him, it gives offense.

The human being himself, the perpetrator [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Author,” Paris., Rig.] of every crime, is not merely God’s work but also his image; [Note: [Col. 0632D] “Is the image of God.” Understand the writer’s meaning: he says that the human being is both God’s work and God’s image—his work because of the body, his image because of the spirit. Therefore he immediately adds that the human being defected in both body and spirit. The words must therefore not be confused, for the human being is called God’s image only because of the spirit. Zeno of Verona, Sermon 2 on Genesis. LAC.] and yet in both body and spirit he has defected [Note: [Col. 0632C] “And yet in body and spirit has ceased,” Rig.] from his founder. For we did not receive eyes for lusts, [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Lust,” Rig.] [Col. 0632C] nor [Note: [Col. 0632C] “And,” Rig.] a tongue for evil speech, ears as a receptacle for evil speech, a throat for the sin of gluttony, [Note: [Col. 0632D] “A throat for the sin of gluttony.” “The sin of gluttony” is known only to ecclesiastical writers, meaning intemperance of appetite or gluttony, but not to secular writers. He spoke similarly in *On Fasting*: “Adam sold salvation for gluttony,” and in book I *Against Marcion* of the companions of gluttony, namely lust and luxury. PAM.] a belly for satiety in gluttony, [Note: [Col. 0632D] “Association,” Jun., from an MS., Rig.] genitals for the excesses of shamelessness, hands for violence, or feet for a wandering life. Nor, I think, was the spirit implanted [Col. 0633A] in the body so that it might become a workshop of plots, frauds, and iniquities.

For if God, the exactor of innocence, hates all wickedness and so much [Note: [Col. 0633B] “So much,” Wouw., MS., Rig.] deliberately contrived evil, he certainly did not create the things he fashioned for the outcome of the works he condemns, [Note: [Col. 0633C] “Did not create them for the outcome of the works.” This passage should be noted against Calvin, who in the *Institutes*, book III, chs. 22, 23, and 24, maintains that God created the greater part of the world for damnation and destruction by a simple decree of his will, as the Swiss themselves objected to him. PAM.—“For the outcome of the works.” I do not approve Pamelius, who here took *exitum* to mean destruction. The sense is entirely complete: the word must be related to the perverse use of things, and thus everything coheres; it must not be related to ruin, for Tertullian is not discussing that. LAC.] although those same works are carried out by means of the things he created, since this is the whole ground of condemnation: the perverse use of creation by created beings. [Note: [Col. 0633B] “By created beings” is absent from Rig.]

We, therefore, who have come to know the Lord [Note: [Col. 0633B] “God,” Rig.] and also discern his rival— [Note: [Col. 0633C] “We, therefore, who, having come to know God, have also discerned his rival.” We have changed nothing in this sentence, because [Col. 0633D] we found it so constituted in the Codex Agobardinus. Even if the reading of Fulvius Ursinus’s codex appears more convenient: “We, therefore, who, having come to know God, have also discerned his rival, and, having discovered the founder, have at the same time detected the falsifier as well, ought neither to wonder nor to doubt that, since that power of the falsifying and rival angel cast the human being himself—God’s work and image, the possessor of the whole universe—down from integrity at the beginning, it also changed the human being’s entire substance, which had been established in integrity together with him, into perversity together with him and in opposition to the founder,” etc. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0633B] “Have discerned,” Rig.] we who, having discovered the founder, have at the same time detected the falsifier as well—ought neither to wonder nor to doubt that, since that power [Note: [Col. 0633B] “For him,” Paris.; “power” absent from Paris.] of the falsifying and rival angel cast the human being himself—God’s work and image, the possessor of the whole universe—down from integrity at the beginning, [Note: [Col. 0633B] Wouw., MS. add “that the entire.”] it changed his entire [Col. 0633B] substance [Note: [Col. 0633B] Rig. adds “which had been established in integrity together with him.”], together with him, into perversity [Note: [Col. 0633C] “Might change,” Wouw., MS.; “changed,” Rig.] and in opposition to the founder, so that through the very substance whose grant to the human being rather than to itself it had resented, it might both make the human being guilty before God and establish its own dominion.

## CHAPTER III
Equipped with this awareness [Note: [Col. 0633C] *Instructa*, Rig.] against the opinion of the pagans, let us turn rather to the objections of our own people [Note: [Col. 0633C] *Retractatus*, Wouw., MS.]. For the faith of some—whether simpler or more scrupulous—demands scriptural authority for this renunciation [Col. 0634A] of spectacles [Note: [Col. 0633D] “Demands scriptural authority.” Cyprian, *On Spectacles*, says that Christians likewise asked the question in this way: in his words, “Where, they say, are these things written? Where are they forbidden?” He then adds passages of Scripture, wrongly interpreted, upon which they relied in defending spectacles; after these he adds: “At this point I would say that it would have been far better for them to know no literature at all than to read literature in this way.” LAC.], and places itself in uncertainty because abstinence of this kind is not expressly and specifically enjoined upon the servants of God.

Certainly nowhere do we find it explicitly laid down, in the same manner as: “You shall not kill; you shall not worship an idol; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not commit fraud” (Exod. 20): “You shall not go to the circus [Note: [Col. 0633C] “You shall not go into the circus,” Rig.]; you shall not go to the theater; you shall not watch a contest or a gladiatorial show [Note: [Col. 0634B] *Exspectabis*, Rig.].” But we do find that the first utterance of David also applies to this particular case: “Blessed,” he says (Ps. 1), “is he who has not gone into the council of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor [Note: [Col. 0634B] “Nor sat in the seat of pestilences,” Rig.] sat in the seat of pestilences” [Note: [Col. 0634C] “In the seat of pestilences.” The learned Clement of Alexandria has the same interpretation in Book III of the *Paedagogue*. For when he employs this passage of the royal prophet and infers that Christians are forbidden every kind of spectacle, he adds: Οὐ δὲ άπεικότως τὰ στάδια καὶ τὰ θέατρα καθέδραν λοιμιῶν προσέιποι τις ἂν, “Nor would one unreasonably call stadiums and theaters a seat of pestilences”, “Nor would one be wrong to call theaters and spectacles the seat of pestilence.” LE PR.].

For although he appears to have proclaimed that righteous man blessed [Note: [Col. 0634C] “For although he appears to have proclaimed that righteous man blessed.” He means Joseph of Arimathea, whom Luke says was a good and righteous man and had neither taken part in nor consented to the Jews’ counsel against Christ. The author of the *Commentaries on the Psalms*, Preface to Psalm 1: [Col. 0634D] “Tertullian, in his book *On Spectacles*, asserts that this Psalm may be understood both of Joseph, who buried the Lord’s body, and of those who do not assemble at the spectacles of the Gentiles.” Some ascribe those *Commentaries* to Jerome. They have, however, been inserted among the works of Bede. RIG.], because he did not participate in the council and assembly [Note: [Col. 0634B] “And sitting,” Rig.] of the Jews deliberating about the denial of God [Note: [Col. 0634B] “About killing the Lord,” Rig.]; nevertheless divine Scripture is always distributed broadly [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Nevertheless divine Scripture is distributed broadly”—“from the abundance of the divine store,” as he says *Against the Valentinians*. RIG.] wherever discipline is also supported in accordance with the meaning of the matter presently at issue. Thus here too the saying [Note: [Col. 0634B] “This saying,” Wouw., MS.] is not irrelevant to the prohibition of spectacles.

For if he called the few Jews of that time “a council of the ungodly” [Note: [Col. 0634D] “The Jews a council of the ungodly.” Those most wretched people were branded with this miserable designation. Thus Augustine too, Epistle 54, calls the Jews ungodly; John Chrysostom, Oration 2 against them, gives them ἀσεβέιαν, “impiety”; and the Council in Trullo, canon 1, δυσσέβειαν, “ungodliness”. Dionysius of Alexandria calls them faithless. And John Chrysostom, in the passage cited, calls them παράνομον πολιτείαν, “a lawless way of life”, and below, ἐναργεῖς καὶ μιαρους, “manifest and polluted”. LAC.], how much more so such a vast assembly of the pagan people! Unless pagans are godly, less sinful, and less hostile to Christ than the Jews were then? The remaining details also correspond [Note: [Col. 0634B] Rigalt reads: “What of the pagan people? Are they less ungodly, less sinful, [Col. 0634C] less hostile to Christ than the Jews were then? What? Do not the remaining details also correspond?” Wouw.’s written codex: “As regards the remaining details, they correspond.” Latinus and Junius prefer: “In which the remaining details also correspond.”]. For at spectacles one both stands “in the way”—they call the gangways [Note: [Col. 0634D] “For they call the fastenings of the belts ‘ways.’” The most learned Salmasius collected many noteworthy observations about all matters pertaining to the circus in his *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, [Col. 0635C] p. 895. RIG.] the fastenings of the belts around the circuit [Note: [Col. 0635C] “And the fastenings of the belts.” The belts were barriers, or leather bands decorated with bosses, by which the benches of the Roman equestrians who sat in the covered part of the auditorium were secured. These belts were fastened by hooks or certain buckles. For this reason Themistius, indicating the luxury of the theater in an oration, said ὁ κόσμος τῶν περιστύλων τοῦ θεάτρου, “the ornament of the theater’s colonnades”, “the ornament of the theater’s colonnades”; it is in this sense that it is called feminine. EDD.]—[Col. 0635A] and the divisions between the common people along the slope. The place situated on a curve for sitting together is itself also called a “seat.”

Accordingly, conversely, unhappy is he who has gone into any council whatever of the ungodly, stood in any way whatever of sinners, and sat in any seat whatever of pestilences. Let us understand as stated generally what can also receive a particular interpretation. For some things pronounced particularly also have a general meaning [Note: [Col. 0635D] “For some things pronounced particularly.” A rule most useful for understanding Holy Scripture. Moreover, blessed Jerome noted in more than one place in his commentaries on the prophets that what is said to the Israelites is said to everyone. PAM.]. When God admonishes or rebukes the Israelites concerning discipline, he surely addresses everyone (Exod. 12); when he threatens destruction against Egypt and Ethiopia, he establishes a precedent against every sinful nation [Note: [Col. 0635D] “He establishes a precedent against every sinful nation.” He also discusses this passage *Against the Jews*: “Thus Egypt,” he says, “is sometimes understood as the whole world,” etc. RIG.]. Thus every sinful nation is called Egypt and Ethiopia (Isa. 14 and elsewhere), from the particular to the general—just as, conversely, with reference to the origin of spectacles, he calls every spectacle a council [Col. 0635B] of the ungodly, from the general to the particular.

## CHAPTER IV

Lest anyone think that we are merely arguing, I shall turn to the principal authority of our own seal. When we enter the water and profess the Christian faith in the words of its law, we testify with our own mouths that we have renounced the devil, his pomp, and his angels. What will be the supreme and [Note: [Col. 0635C] “And,” Rigalt.] principal thing in which the devil, his pomp, and his angels are reckoned to consist, if not idolatry? From it comes every unclean and wicked spirit, so to speak—for there need be no more at length on this subject.

Therefore, if it is established that the entire equipment of spectacles consists of idolatry, it will indubitably have been established in advance that the testimony of our renunciation at baptism also extends to spectacles, since they are enslaved to the devil, his pomp, and [Col. 0635C] his angels, namely through idolatry. We shall recount the origins of each kind, by which [Note: [Col. 0635C] “From which,” Junius.] [Col. 0636A] they grew up from their cradles [Note: [Col. 0635C] *Incunabulis*, Rigalt.] in the world; then the titles by whose names some of them are called; then the preparations, and the superstitions with which they are furnished; next [Note: [Col. 0635C] “Then,” Rig.] the places, and the presiding deities to whom they are dedicated; and next [Note: [Col. 0635C] “Next” absent from Rig.] the arts, and the authors to whom they are assigned. If any of these things does not pertain to an idol, it will pertain neither to idolatry nor to our abjuration.

## CHAPTER V

As for their origins, since these are more obscure and unknown to most of our people, it was necessary to investigate them more deeply and from no other source [Note: [Col. 0635D] “More deeply and from no other source.” Thus the books printed hitherto read: “To most of our people, more deeply.” Agobard’s copy reads: “Since they are more obscure and unknown to most of our people, of the art.” Perhaps *actis* should be read, as if he had said that the origins—that is, the historical records—of Roman or Gentile affairs were more obscure and unknown to most Christians. But the common reading, “more deeply and from no other source,” is by no means displeasing.], than the documents of pagan [Note: [Col. 0635C] “Ethnic,” Rig.] literature. Many authors exist who have published commentaries on this subject.

They transmit the origin of the games as follows. The Lydians, migrants from Asia, settled in Etruria, as Timaeus relates, under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, who had yielded to his brother in a dispute over the kingdom. Accordingly, in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, they also instituted spectacles in the name of religion. From there the Romans summoned performers and borrowed from them the occasion and the designation, so that the games were called *ludi* after the Lydians [Note: [Col. 0636C] “So that the games were called *ludi* after the Lydians.” Here he enumerates various kinds of games that have been explained at length by a great many authors. The Lupercal games were instituted first in honor of Pan and later in honor of the she-wolf who nursed Romulus. The Liberalia were in honor of Liber, or Bacchus. The Consualia—called by others the circus games—were in honor of Neptune. [Col. 0636D] The Cerealia were in honor of Ceres, and the Equiria in honor of Mars; the latter games were so named from the horse races held in the Campus Martius. LE PR.].

But even though Varro interprets *ludi* from *ludus*, that is, from play—just as they also called the Luperci’s rites “games” because they run about in play—he nevertheless regards this play of young men as belonging to feast days, temples, and religious observances. The derivation of the word no longer matters, since [Note: [Col. 0636C] “While,” Rig.] the cause of the thing itself is idolatry. For even when the Liberalia were commonly called simply “games” [Note: [Col. 0636D] “The games were commonly called Liberalia.” Those who said that all games were indiscriminately called Liberalia did not understand this passage; I know many such interpreters, especially Heraldus, Book I, Digression, ch. 28. Nothing could be more absurd. Could the Consualia, Equiria, Tarpeia, or Robigalia, I ask, be called Liberalia? Away with the notion. No one said or heard such a thing. Those who impose it upon Tertullian wrong that most learned man. He locates this indiscriminate use of the name solely in the fact that the Liberalia, Consualia, and other rites of this kind are also called simply “games.” Thus the word *ludus*, “game,” is shared by all idolatrous festivals, for all these are called games. Therefore he immediately adds: “Hence the games called Consualia.” From this it is clear that not only the name “game,” but also the thing signified by “game,” was enslaved to demons; for this is what Tertullian wishes to prove. LAC.], they manifestly proclaimed honor to Father Liber. They were first held for Liber by country people because of the benefit they ascribe to him for revealing the gift of wine.

Hence came the games called the Consualia, [Col. 0636C] which [Note: [Col. 0636C] “By which,” Junius.] originally honored Neptune; for they also called him Consus [Note: [Col. 0636C] “Call,” Rig.]. Next Romulus named the Equiria [Note: [Col. 0636C] Rig. adds “which?”] for Mars. [Col. 0637A] Yet they also defend the ascription of the Consualia to Romulus [Note: [Col. 0637C] “By Romulus,” Junius.], because he dedicated them to Consus, the god, as they maintain, of counsel: namely, the counsel by which he then devised the abduction of the Sabine maidens as wives for his soldiers. An excellent counsel indeed—and even now regarded among [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Among,” Rig.] the Romans themselves as just and lawful, not to say before God.

For this too contributes [Note: [Col. 0637C] “For this too,” Rig.] to the stain upon its origin, lest you suppose good something whose beginning came from evil: from shamelessness, from violence, from [Note: [Col. 0637C] “From violence, from hatred.” Wowerius judged that the text should be emended thus, and I have nothing more consonant with the author’s intention or approaching more closely to these traces of the old text: “from violence, by another god.” LAC.] hatred [Note: [Col. 0637C] “From shameless violence, by another god,” Fran.], from a fratricidal founder, a son of Mars. Even now an altar to that Consus lies buried in the circus, underground by the first turning-posts, with an inscription of this kind:

> CONSUS, MIGHTY IN COUNSEL; MARS, IN WAR; THE LARES, IN ASSEMBLY [Note: [Col. 0637C] An old copy has: “The Lares, mighty in *coillum*.” The word is Greek: Κοίλῳ, “in the hollow”, “in the hollow, inner chamber.” Festus attests that the ancients called *caelum* “*coum*.” Scaliger reports that in an ancient manuscript of Festus he read this passage from Ennius: “—to fill the hollow of heaven with terrors.” Thus first *coum*, “hollow,” κοῖλον, “hollow”; then *coilum* or *coillum*, the inner chamber of a house where the Lares were worshiped. From this word *coillum* therefore come *coillinus* and *coilinus*, and thence *incoilinus*, also *inquilinus*, “tenant.” LAC.] POWERFUL [Note: [Col. 0637C] “NECK,” Rig.].

At that altar the public priests sacrifice on the Nones of July; on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0637C] “The fifteenth day before the Kalends of September,” Junius.], the Flamen Quirinalis [Col. 0637B] and the virgins sacrifice.

Next the same Romulus instituted games for Jupiter Feretrius on the Tarpeian Hill; Piso relates that they were called the Tarpeian and Capitoline games. After him Numa Pompilius held games for Mars and Robigo [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Held” absent from Rig.]. For they also fashioned Robigo [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Robigo,” Wouw., MS.] as a goddess [Note: [Col. 0637D] “For they also fashioned Robigo as a goddess.” Just as Robigus was a god, so Robigo was also a goddess who was supposed to avert crop-rust; similarly, they had made Paleness a goddess, and Fever too. Sacred rites were customarily performed for this goddess so that rust would not destroy the crops. LE PR.]. Next came Tullus Hostilius, then Ancus Marcius, and the rest. Suetonius Tranquillus—or the authors from whom Tranquillus drew—sets forth which men, how many, in what order [Note: [Col. 0637C] “And the rest likewise in order,” Fran.], and for which idols instituted games. But these examples will suffice to establish the guilt of their origin in idolatry.

## CHAPTER VI

To the testimony of antiquity is added the posterity that followed it, displaying the character of the games’ origin in the titles of the present time as well. By these titles it was marked for which [Col. 0638A] idol and for which superstition the games of each [Note: [Col. 0637C] Others read: “of each.”] of the two classes [Note: [Col. 0637D] “The games of the two classes.” Some read “of each”; this is unsatisfactory. Pamelius’ explanation is certainly preferable: he says that the author spoke with reference to only two classes of games, those of the circus and those of the theater. For these alone he includes in the preceding chapter. LAC.] were intended: the Megalensian [Note: [Col. 0637C] Rig. adds “for.”] [Note: [Col. 0637D] “Megalensian,” “Megalesia”: “They are so called from the Greeks,” says Varro, Book V of *On the Latin Language*, “because, according to the Sibylline books, she was brought at the request of King Attalus of Pergamum from Pessinus, where stood the Megalesion, the temple of that goddess—the Great Mother, I mean, of the gods—from which place she was conveyed to Rome.” Hence also the Megalensian [Col. 0638C] games. PAM.] and Apollinarian games, likewise the Cerealia, Neptunalia, Latiaria [Note: [Col. 0638D] “Latiaria.” They were sacred to Jupiter Latiaris, whom Suetonius mentions in his *Caligula*, as do other authors everywhere. I think Pamelius mistaken in referring these games to gladiators; Tertullian would thus wander from his argument, since he confines the games covered in the preceding chapter and this one solely to the stage and circus, as is evident from chapter 10 of this work. LAC.], and Floralia, are celebrated publicly. The remaining games derive the causes of their origin from the birthdays and solemn occasions [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Solemnities,” Rig.] of kings, public good fortune, and municipal calendars [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Festivals,” Wouw., MS.] of superstition [Note: [Col. 0638C] “And superstitions,” Paris, Junius.] [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Of origin” absent from Rig.].

Among them, shows funded by legacies also offer funeral tribute to the memories of private persons, this too in accordance with ancient institution. For from the beginning games were reckoned under two headings: sacred and funeral [Note: [Col. 0638D] “Sacred and funeral.” The sacred games were those he discussed above, namely the Megalensian, Apollinarian, and so forth; the funeral games are those he is about to discuss, since in assemblies of that sort funeral offerings were made to the dead. LE PR.]; that is, games for the gods of the nations and games for the dead. But as far as we are concerned, it makes no difference to idolatry under what name and title a thing reaches the same spirits whom we renounce [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Renounced,” Wouw., MS.], whether they conduct them for their dead or [Note: [Col. 0638C] “For the dead. It will be permissible,” Rig.] for their gods. Consequently, since they conduct rites for [Col. 0638B] their dead as for gods [Note: [Col. 0638C] “They do,” Junius; “consequently, they do them for the dead,” Rig.], the status of each division is one and the same: one idolatry, and one renunciation on our part directed against idolatry.

## CHAPTER VII

Since, therefore [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Therefore” absent from Rigalt.], the origin of both classes of games is common, and their titles are common because they arise from common causes, it follows [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Likewise,” Rigalt.] that their apparatus too must be common, deriving from the general guilt [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Native,” Junius from the MS.] of idolatry, their foundress. But the equipment of the circus games—those to which the name *pompa*, “procession,” properly belongs—is somewhat more pompous. The procession goes before them [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Going before,” Rig.] and itself proves [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Proves,” Rig.] whose it is: by the sequence of images, the train of statues, the chariots, the sacred carriages [Note: [Col. 0638D] “The chariots, the sacred carriages.” Chariots were secular vehicles, whereas the *thensae* were sacred ones. Sinnius—or, as it is clear from Lactantius that one should read, Sisinnicus—Capito says, according to Festus, that a *thensa* is the vehicle in which the accoutrements of the gods are conveyed to the sacred couch in the circus during the circus games; it was made both of ivory, as in Licinius’ *Barbatus*, and of silver. PAM.], the *harmamaxae* [Note: [Col. 0638D] “*Harmamaxae*.” Junius distinguishes the *harmamaxa*—or *armamaxa*, as others write it—from the British chariot, the covered carriage, and the four-wheeled carriage, because others confuse it with them. He says that it was properly a carrying-pole borne by men’s hands or shoulders, in the manner [Col. 0639D] of the sedan chairs mentioned by Suetonius and the litters mentioned by Seneca. Thus Tertullian passes from chariots drawn by beasts of burden and from sacred carriages drawn by ropes to *harmamaxae* carried by men’s shoulders, which thereby attested their devotion to the sacred rites of the circus. LAC.], [Col. 0639A] the seats, the crowns, and the divine accoutrements.

Moreover, how many sacred rites and sacrifices precede, intervene, and follow; how many colleges, priesthoods, and official bodies are set in motion—the inhabitants of that city in which the assembly of demons has taken its seat know well [Note: [Col. 0639D] “That city in which the assembly of demons has taken its seat.” He means Rome and the Capitol. In the *Apology*, p. 7, he calls the Capitol the senate-house of the gods, where, of course, their synod meets; compare chapter 6 of the same *Apology*. RIG.]. Even if these things are administered in the provinces with less care because their resources are smaller, nevertheless all circus games everywhere must be assigned to that place from which they are sought and are defiled by the source from which they are taken. For both a slender stream from its spring and a small shoot from its branch preserve the quality of their origin.

Let its extravagance or frugality answer for how [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Which,” Paris; both words absent from Rig.] it offends God. Whatever the character of the circus procession, even if it carries around only a few images, idolatry resides in even one; and if it draws only one sacred carriage, it is nevertheless Jupiter’s wagon. Any idolatry, though meanly equipped or [Col. 0639B] only modestly affluent [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Both splendid,” Latinus; “but splendid,” Paris.], is splendid when assessed by the gravity of its crime.

## CHAPTER VIII

To continue according to my plan with the places as well: the circus is dedicated principally to the Sun. His temple stands in the middle of the space, and his image gleams from the temple’s summit, because they did not think [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Did not think,” Rig. and Petrus Ciacconius.] that one whom they possess in the open air should be consecrated beneath a roof. They maintain that this spectacle was first held by Circe and was presented in honor of the Sun, her father, as they claim [Note: [Col. 0639C] “As they claim” absent from Rig.]; from her they also argue for the derivation of the circus’s name. Certainly [Note: [Col. 0639C] “They argue cleverly. Certainly,” Junius.] the sorceress performed this business for those whose priestess she was: the demons and angels, of course.

How many instances of idolatry, then, do you recognize in the very arrangement of the place? Every single ornament of the circus is a temple. They ascribe the eggs to the honor of the Castors [Note: [Col. 0639D] “The eggs to the honor of the Castors.” Alciatus, Book IV of the *Parerga*, final chapter, was the first to note from Livy, Dio, and Cassiodorus that the circuits of the racecourse were marked by eggs in the circus. Varro also alludes to this in Book I of *On Agriculture*. PAM.], since, in believing that they were hatched from an egg, they do not blush at Jupiter as a swan [Note: [Col. 0639D] “Since, in believing that they were hatched from an egg, they do not blush at Jupiter as a swan.” Thus reads Agobard’s old copy, except that it doubled a syllable, *decus cygno*, which is *de cucno* or *de cycno*. RIG.]. They dedicate the dolphins to Neptune [Note: [Col. 0639C] “The columns disgorge dolphins for Neptune.” Juvenal, *Satires* 6: “She consults in front of the goals and the columns of the dolphins.” Septimius says that the columns disgorge dolphins as though emitted from the bellies of the columns through pipes and channels. [Col. 0640D] RIG.]. The columns [Note: [Col. 0640C] “The columns disgorge,” Rig.] support the Sessiae, named from sowing; the Messiae, from harvests; and the Tutelinae, from the guardianship [Note: [Col. 0640C] “Guardianship,” Rig.] of the crops. Before these are three altars, serving three sets of gods: the Great, the Powerful, and the Strong. They consider these same gods to be the Samothracians.

The enormous obelisk [Note: [Col. 0640D] “The enormous obelisk.” Pliny discusses it in Book XXXVI, chapter 9: “The obelisk which the divine Augustus erected in the Circus Maximus was hewn by King Semneserteus, during whose reign Pythagoras was in Egypt, and measures 125¾ feet, apart from its base of the same stone. The one in the Campus Martius, made by Sesostris, is nine feet shorter.” PAM.], as Hermateles affirms, was prostituted to the Sun. Its inscription, from which its registration too is derived, is an Egyptian superstition. The assembly of demons would have been left cold without its own Great Mother; she therefore presides there beside the water-channel. Consus, as we have said, lurks underground at the turning-posts. They also made the Murtiae into an idol [Note: [Col. 0640C] “That formerly made it the Murtia,” Latinus; “Murtiae. These also,” Rig.]. For they regard Murtia as the goddess of love [Note: [Col. 0640D] “Murcia the goddess of languor,” Rigaltus reads. Augustine, *City of God* IV.16: “They called Murcia the goddess who would not move beyond measure and who made a person, as Pomponius says, *murcidus*—that is, excessively idle and inactive.” RIG.—“Murcia the goddess of love.” Turnebus, Book XXII of the *Adversaria*, ch. 17, was remarkably mistaken: he reads “Murtia the goddess of marble.” Since this seemed unusual to him, he corrected it to “the goddess of languor,” saying that it referred to Murtia, the goddess of sluggards mentioned by Arnobius. The true reading is “of love,” with Pamelius; the matter should be illustrated from Pliny, Book XV, ch. 29, where he discusses Venus Myrtea or Murtia. LAC.], to whom they vowed a temple in that part of the circus.

Observe, Christian, how many unclean names [Note: [Col. 0640C] “Divinities,” Junius.] have taken possession of the circus. A religion occupied by so many spirits of the devil is foreign to you.

With regard to places, however, there is occasion for reconsideration, so that we may anticipate a certain question. “What, then,” you say, “if I go to the circus at some other time? Shall I be in danger of defilement?” There is no absolute prohibition concerning places. For not only may the servant of God enter those very meeting places for spectacles without endangering discipline, but even temples themselves, provided only that he is compelled by an ordinary reason that does not pertain to the specific business or function of that place.

Besides, the streets, the forum, the baths, the stables, and even our own houses are not altogether free from idols; Satan and his angels have filled the whole world. Yet we do not fall away from God merely because we are in the world, but only if we touch any of the world’s crimes. Accordingly, if I enter the Capitol or the Serapeum as one who sacrifices and worships, I shall fall away from God, just as I would by entering the circus or theater as a spectator. Places do not contaminate us by themselves; rather, what is done in those places does so, and by those deeds, as we have argued, the places themselves are also contaminated: we are contaminated by contaminated things [Note: [Col. 0640C] “They are contaminated,” Rig.]. [Col. 0640C] We therefore recall to whom places of this kind are dedicated in order to demonstrate that the things done in those places belong to those to whom the places themselves are dedicated.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0641A]

Now let us consider the art by which the circus games are presented. In former times horsemanship [Note: [Col. 0641C] “In former times horsemanship was conducted simply.” Agobard’s copy reads: “In former times horsemanship was conducted simply from horseback.” “Formerly simple,” that is, it was once conducted simply, namely through an unadorned interest in skilled riding, before any solemn observance of equestrian games had been consecrated to demons. Some utter fool added “from horseback,” because he imagined that in this way he was giving such a fine interpretation of Septimius’ word “formerly.” Isidore was certainly more cautious here: “For horsemanship,” he says, “was formerly conducted simply.” RIG.] was conducted simply from horseback [Note: [Col. 0641C] “From horseback” absent from Rig.], and its ordinary use was certainly not guilty. But when it was forced into the service of the games, it passed from a gift of God into the service of demons. Accordingly, this form of display is assigned to Castor and Pollux, to whom Stesichorus teaches that horses were allotted by Mercury. But Neptune too is equestrian; the Greeks call him ἵππιον, “Hippios,” that is, “Equestrian”.

As for teams [Note: [Col. 0641C] “As for teams” absent from Rigalt.], they consecrated four-horse chariots to the Sun and two-horse chariots to the Moon. But [Note: [Col. 0641C] “Certainly,” Rigalt.] also:

> Erichthonius first dared to yoke four horses to a chariot  
> And, swift, to stand victorious upon the wheels.

Erichthonius, son of Minerva and Vulcan—and indeed born from lust spilled upon the earth—is a demonic portent; indeed, he is the devil himself, not a serpent. But if [Col. 0641B] Trochilus [Note: [Col. 0641C] “Acrophilus,” Paris.] the Argive invented the chariot, he first [Note: [Col. 0641C] “To Juno of his native land,” Wouw., MS., Latinus.] dedicated this work of his to Juno [Note: [Col. 0641D] “To Juno this work of his.” Pamelius reads “first to Juno”; others, “to the first Juno”; but Johannes a Wouweren corrected it from a manuscript to “to Juno of his native land.” Perhaps, since Juno was Argive and Trochilus was Argive, he first consecrated that work to the goddess of his people. Isidore may have suffered a lapse of memory, for he understands these statements not of Trochilus but of Erichthonius. LE PR.].

If at Rome Romulus was the first to exhibit a four-horse chariot, I think he too was enrolled among the idols, if he is identical with Quirinus. Since four-horse chariots were produced by authors of this sort, they deservedly clothed their charioteers in the colors [Note: [Col. 0641D] “They clothed them in the colors of idolatry.” By the “colors of idolatry” he means colors dedicated to idols. The charioteers’ four factions were distinguished by the same number of colors: they consecrated the Red faction to Mars, the White to the Zephyrs, the Green to Mother Earth, and the Blue to the Sky. RIG.] of idolatry. At first there were only two [Note: [Col. 0641C] “And they clothed the charioteers in the colors of idolatry. At first [Col. 0642C] there were only two horses,” Wouweren; “for at first there were only two horses,” Rigalt.], white and red [Note: [Col. 0641D] “White and red.” Where “red” is read here and twice afterward, Gagnaeus—and likewise Isidore—read “rose-colored.” But it is clear, even from the words “red for summer, because of the redness of the Sun,” that our reading is correct. For since Martial ascribes two horses to the Sun, Xanthus and Aethon, and ξανθός, “yellow” in Greek signifies reddish-yellow and therefore also red, this supports the reading. Much the same is indicated by the four names of horses in Ovid—Pyrois, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon—and those in Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I—Erythraeus, Actaeon, Lampos, and Philogeus. For Pyrois and Erythraeus also signify red, if we consider their Greek derivation. PAM.]. The white was dedicated to winter because of its gleaming snow; the red to summer because of the Sun’s redness. But afterward, as both pleasure and superstition advanced, some consecrated the red to Mars and others the white to the Zephyrs; the Green [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Green,” Latinus.] to Mother Earth or spring [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Spring.” Agobard’s codex reads “true.” Cassiodorus, *Variae* III.51: “The Green faction accords with verdant spring.” RIG.]; and the Blue to the sky and sea, or to autumn. But since every form of idolatry is condemned [Col. 0642A] by God, that form too is surely condemned which is profaned by the elements of the world [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Worldly,” Junius.].

## CHAPTER X

Let us pass to matters of the stage. We have already shown that they share a common origin and corresponding titles, in accordance with the designation “games” itself from the beginning and with their administration in conjunction with equestrian displays. Their apparatus too is shared, in the part that pertains to the stage: for the procession advances from temples and altars, and from that ill-fated incense and blood [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Incense and blood.” Flutes belonged to the stage, trumpets to the circus; similarly, incense refers to the stage and blood to the savagery of the circus. LE PR.], amid flutes and trumpets, under the direction of two utterly defiled masters of ceremonies—an undertaker and a diviner of entrails. Thus, as from the origins of the games we passed to the circus games, we now proceed from there to the theatrical games, beginning with the vice [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Beginning,” Latinus, Rig.] of the place.

The theater is properly the sanctuary of Venus. Indeed, it was in this way that this kind of structure made its way into the world. For the censors often [Note: [Col. 0642C] “The censors used especially to destroy theaters just as they were springing up.” [Col. 0642D] He himself says in the *Apology*, ch. 6: “They immediately destroyed theaters springing up to corrupt morals.” RIG.—“For the censors often.” It is quite certain that theaters at Rome were once temporary structures. The law provided that they should not be permanent because of the corruption of morals. Indeed, in our Tertullian’s *Apology*, ch. 6, theaters are said to arise for the corruption of morals. No one can doubt that the same practice was observed among the Athenians: before theaters became permanent, they were called temporary, for this is what ἰκρία, “temporary wooden stands” means. Thus: Ὣστ` εὐθὺς εἰσίοντες, ἀπὸ τῶν ἰκρίων


ὑποβλέπουσ` ἡμᾶς, “So that, as soon as they enter, they look askance at us from the stands”. Aristophanes in Τεσμ, an abbreviated title of the *Thesmophoriazusae*. LE PR.] destroyed the theaters as soon as they were being erected again [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Being erected?” Junius; “springing up,” Rig.], taking thought for morals. They naturally foresaw that morals faced grave danger from wantonness. Thus from this very fact their own judgment, which supports our position, may serve as testimony to the pagans; and even the precedence of human discipline may add weight to our discipline.

Accordingly, Pompey the Great [Note: [Col. 0642D] “Pompey the Great.” There is a wholly similar passage in Book VI, *On the Pallium*, where he speaks of Alexander the Great and calls him “inferior only to his glory.” Here, then, you have Pompey and Alexander—each was called “the Great”: the former inferior to his theater, the latter to his glory. LAC.], inferior only to his theater, after constructing that citadel of every disgrace, feared that censorial censure might one day attach to his memory. He therefore placed a temple of Venus above it and, when summoning the people to its dedication by edict, called it not a theater but a temple of Venus: “beneath which,” he said, “we have placed tiers of seats for spectacles.” [Col. 0643A] Thus he covered a condemned and condemnable structure with the title of a temple, and made a mockery of discipline by means of superstition.

But Venus and Liber suit one another. Those two demons are confederated and sworn together: the demons of drunkenness and lust. Thus the theater of Venus is also the house of Liber. For they properly called certain other theatrical games the Liberalia: besides being devoted to Liber—these are the Dionysia among the Greeks—they were also instituted by Liber. And Liber and Venus plainly exercise patronage over the arts of the stage as well, over those things that are private and peculiar to the stage: bodily gesture and bodily looseness. For they sacrificed effeminacy to Venus and Liber [Note: [Col. 0643C] “Through gesture and bodily bending they sacrifice effeminacy to Venus and Liber,” Paris; “Through gesture and bending of the body they sacrifice to the effeminacy of Venus and Liber,” Rigalt.]: dissolved, the one through sex [Note: [Col. 0643C] “The one through sex, the other through looseness, dissolved.” That is, to Venus dissolved through sex and to Liber dissolved through excess. Both are dissolved: she through sex, he through looseness. RIG.], the other through looseness [Note: [Col. 0643C] “Excess,” Wouw., MS.] [Note: [Col. 0643C] “The one through sex, the other through looseness.” They are, of course, dissolved and διαλελυμένοι, “dissolute”. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* XI: “With a flowing gait they feigned themselves women.” ὑγρόν, “flowing” is βάδισμα, “gait” in Clement of Alexandria. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0643C] “For the dissolved,” Paris, Rig.].

Whatever is performed by voice, melodies, instruments, and lyres [Note: [Col. 0643C] “Letters,” Paris, Junius.] has Apollos, Muses [Note: [Col. 0643D] “Apollos and Muses.” From this too the preceding reading, “lyres,” is confirmed: for a lyre was joined to Apollo’s image; the seven-stringed lyre was attributed to the Muses; music itself was named after them; and therefore every kind of musical mode, whether vocal or produced by the other instruments. The same things are rightly attributed to Minervas and Mercuries, since they are traditionally regarded as the parents of all the arts. See more in Georgius Gyraldus, *On the Gods of the Gentiles*. PAM.], Minervas, and Mercuries as its owners. You will hate, [Col. 0643B] Christian, the things whose founders you cannot but hate.

Now we wish to offer a further observation concerning the arts and concerning those whose [Note: [Col. 0643C] “Of which,” Junius.] founders we execrate by name. We know that the names of the dead are nothing, just as their images themselves are nothing [Note: [Col. 0643C] “And,” Rig.]. But we are not ignorant of those who operate and rejoice under those names and beneath the images that have been instituted, and falsely claim divinity: namely, wicked spirits, demons.

We see, therefore, that the arts too are dedicated to the honors of those who inhabit the names of their founders [Note: [Col. 0643C] “Of them” absent from Rig.], and that arts whose founders [Note: [Col. 0643C] “Vendors,” Junius.] are regarded as gods for this very reason are not free from idolatry. Indeed, as far as the arts are concerned, we ought to have laid down an even deeper preliminary principle: that the demons, foreseeing from the beginning for their own benefit, among the other defilements of idolatry, those of spectacles as well—by which they might call humanity [Col. 0643C] away from God and bind it to their own honor—also inspired the talents for arts of this kind. For the thing destined to come into their possession would not [Col. 0644A] have been appropriated beforehand [Note: [Col. 0644C] “Procured,” Rig.] by others. Nor would they at that time have produced it through any other people than precisely those in whose names, images, and histories they had determined that the deception of consecration would conduct its business on their behalf [Note: [Col. 0644C] “They themselves would conduct,” Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0644C] “They determined,” Paris.].

## CHAPTER XI
To complete the sequence, let us also undertake a reconsideration of the contests. Their origin is related to that of the games. Hence they too were instituted as sacred or funerary observances, and are held either for the gods of the nations or for the dead. Accordingly, their titles are: the Olympian games for Jupiter [Note: [Col. 0644C] “Titles” is absent from the Paris edition.] [Note: [Col. 0643D] The Olympian games for Jupiter. Although some may think that we would be wasting our leisure if we traced the origin of these games, I shall nevertheless say in passing that the Olympic Games were first celebrated when Aeschylus was archon of the Athenians, and that Coroebus of Elis emerged as victor in them. The Nemean games are held in honor of Hercules, who killed the lion in the Nemean forest. The Isthmian games was the name given to gymnastic games that were first celebrated in Arcadia and later on the Isthmus [Col. 0644C] of Corinth; they were sacred to Neptune. LE PR.], which at Rome are the Capitoline games [Note: [Col. 0644A] At Rome, the Capitoline games; for Apollo, the Pythian games. In all the books the text reads: “the Capitoline games; likewise the Nemean games for Hercules,” etc. Junius restored the text by inserting “for Apollo, the Pythian games,” which was missing. For why would he omit one of the four principal games? It is therefore credible that these words were erased by ignorant copyists who, since they did not understand in what sense Tertullian had spoken of the Capitoline games, deleted “for Apollo,” thinking that the Apollonian rites were the same as the Capitoline. LAC.]; likewise the Nemean games for Hercules [Note: [Col. 0644C] “The Capitoline games; for Apollo, the Pythian games; for Hercules, the Nemean games,” Jun.], the Isthmian games for Neptune; the other contests are funerary [Note: [Col. 0644C] “Various contests of the dead,” Pam.]. What wonder, then, if the apparatus of the contests is defiled by idolatry—with profane crowns, priestly presidents, ministers belonging to sacred colleges, [Col. 0644B] and, finally, with the very blood of bulls?

To complete the account with respect to the place: in that common venue for the college of the musical and Minerval arts, of the Apollonian arts, and even of the martial arts, they vie around the stadium by combat and trumpet-call [Note: [Col. 0644C] “Let them vie,” Seml.]; that place is certainly a temple, and indeed the temple of the very idol whose solemnities it celebrates. Moreover, the disciplines of the Castors, the Herculeses, and the Mercuries have also handed down the gymnastic arts.

## CHAPTER XII

There remains the examination of that spectacle most highly esteemed by the most distinguished men [Note: [Col. 0644D] “There remains the examination of that most distinguished and most favored spectacle.” This is in every respect the wording of the ancient exemplar. When he is about to speak of the Circus—that is, of gladiators and drivers of horses—he says: “There remains the examination of that spectacle which is customarily most favored even by the most distinguished men.” Or should we emend it thus? “There remains the examination of that most distinguished and most closely enclosed spectacle.” He may have called the spectacle “most closely enclosed” because in the Circus and amphitheater it is enclosed all around by the largest possible ring of people. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0644C] “Of that most unworthy spectacle,” but Jun.; “most distinguished,” Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0644C] “The examination of the spectacle called a *munus*,” Jun., from a manuscript.]. It is called a *munus* from “duty” [Note: [Col. 0644D] It is called a *munus* from “duty.” Just as the game itself is called a *munus*, so its producer is called a *munerarius*, and in Florus a *munerator*, where he speaks of Spartacus. See Lipsius. But do not suppose that Tertullian is deriving an etymology; for that would be utterly foolish. He merely says that it is called a *munus* from “duty,” [Col. 0645C] in the same way that Suetonius was called Tranquillus because his father was called *Lenis*. So Vitruvius was called Pellio, if you believe Alciatus, not Pollio as is commonly read; and he was called Pellio because he had previously been a *cerdo*, a craftsman. It is therefore merely a certain manner of deriving a name from a meaning. LAC.], since “duty” is also called a *munus*. The ancients believed that by means of this spectacle they were performing a duty toward the dead, after, as more civilized men, they had tempered it with cruelty. For in former times, since it was believed that the souls of the departed were appeased by human blood, they would purchase captives or slaves of an evil disposition [Note: [Col. 0645B] “Or of an evil condition,” Rig.] and sacrifice them at funerals. Later it was decided to veil impiety with pleasure. And so, after equipping certain men with such weapons as they then possessed and training them as best they could—only so that they might learn to be killed—they would then, on the appointed day of the offerings to the dead, expend them at the tombs [Note: [Col. 0645C] “They expended them at the tombs.” This can be explained simply as meaning that they gave or supplied gladiators to fight at the tombs; but it is more correct to understand *erogabant* as “they expended them,” that is, consumed them upon the funeral pyre. For the verb *erogo* is used with reference to the pyres of the dead. This explanation can be supported by the verses of Virgil, book 10:

> Here he seizes four young men alive, and as many whom Ufens rears,  
> to sacrifice them as offerings to the shades  
> and drench the flames of the pyre with captive blood.

LAC.]. Thus they consoled death with murders.

This is the origin of the *munus*. But gradually it advanced to a degree of popularity equal to its cruelty, because the sword did not sufficiently satisfy pleasure [Note: [Col. 0645C] “The pleasure of wild beasts was not sufficiently satisfied,” Paris, Lat., Rig.] unless human bodies were also torn apart by wild beasts. What was sacrificed to the dead was, of course, accounted part of the rites paid to deceased relatives. That kind of rite is therefore idolatry, since idolatry too is a kind of rite paid to the dead [Note: [Col. 0645C] “Idolatry is a kind of rite paid to the dead.” Certainly idolatry is the genus embracing all idolatrous worship, if you include both the living and the dead. But if the discussion concerns only the dead, whom the idolatry of the Gentiles for the most part acknowledged—for Jupiter, Mars, Neptune, and all the other gods were dead men—then rites paid to the dead are the genus, and idolatry the species. For since such rites comprise all worship rendered to the dead, there can be no doubt that this worship may be either idolatrous or non-idolatrous. LAC.]. Both the one and the other minister to the dead. Demons, moreover, dwell in the idols of the dead.

Let us also consider the titles. Although this form of exhibition has passed from honors paid to the dead to honors paid to the living—I mean quaestorships and magistracies, flaminate offices [Note: [Col. 0645C] “Flamens,” Rig.], and priesthoods—nevertheless, since the dignity attached to the name remains implicated in the crime of idolatry, whatever is administered in the name of that dignity must also share the stains of that from which it derives its grounds. We shall interpret in the same way the apparatus that must be reckoned part of the ceremonial display of those very honors: the purple robes, fillets, headbands, and crowns; and finally the public addresses and edicts [Note: [Col. 0645D] “Finally the public addresses and edicts.” Livy speaks similarly in book 2: “By a public address,” he says, “and by an edict he gave assurance that no one should keep a Roman citizen bound or confined.” It therefore appears that before the presentation of a gladiatorial show, either during the sacrifice or shortly thereafter, various public addresses were delivered and edicts—as I might say with Tacitus—were issued to the people; these were frequently also proclaimed against Christians. PAM.], and the porridge served on the preceding day [Note: [Col. 0645D] “And the porridge served on the preceding day.” Arnobius, book 7, ridicules the customary food of the gods—porridge and cakes—saying that he thinks they need wine in their sacrifices so that their food may rot and be digested more easily. Much earlier in the same book he says: “What are *fritilla*”—for so I read, from *frit.*, instead of *fitilia*—“what is grain; what are *gratilla*,” etc. PAM.]. These do not exist without the devil’s procession or without an invitation to demons.

Why, then, should I complete my denunciation of that dreadful place [Note: [Col. 0646B] “Horrifying,” Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0646C] “What shall I say in concluding about that horrifying place, which not even perjuries can endure?” He means the Circus, as though men intending to perjure themselves could not endure the horror of that place. That is, they would be terrified by the horror of the place and would therefore go to the Capitol to commit perjury. For the solemnities of oath-taking were held on the Capitol, not in the Circus. And Pliny’s statement is very well known: “Others deceive on the Capitol itself and swear falsely by Jupiter the Thunderer.” Finally, they worshiped Romulus himself, consecrated through the perjury of Proculus, on the Capitol. The words of Septimius that follow confirm our interpretation: “For the amphitheater is consecrated to more numerous and harsher divinities than the Capitol.” RIG.], which not even perjuries can endure? For the amphitheater is consecrated to more numerous and harsher divinities [Note: [Col. 0646C] “Names,” Fran., Paris.] than is the Capitol, the temple of all demons. As many unclean spirits sit gathered there as the place holds human beings. And, to conclude regarding its arts: we know that Mars and Diana [Note: [Col. 0646D] Mars and Diana. He sets forth the amphitheater’s twofold spectacle: namely, the gladiators, over whom Mars presided, and the hunt, or contest with wild beasts, over which Diana presided. Thus Claudian, on the consulship of Manlius Theodorus:

> Let Latonia favor the amphitheater’s procession.

LE PR.] preside over its two kinds of games.

## CHAPTER XIII

I think we have sufficiently completed the sequence, showing in how many ways, and by what means, spectacles incur idolatry, both through their apparatus and through their locations. As for the sacrifices, we are indeed certain [Note: [Col. 0646C] “By which we are certain,” Fran.] that they are in no respect compatible with us, who have twice renounced idols [Note: [Col. 0646D] “Who have twice renounced idols.” First in the church, beneath the hand of the presiding bishop, shortly before baptism; then in the baptismal water itself, when about to enter the water. For such was the custom of the ancients, as we learn from *On the Crown*, chapter 3.], 1 Cor. 8. This is not because an idol is anything, as the Apostle says, but because the things they do, they do to demons, which dwell, of course, in the consecrated images either of the dead or of those forms that they suppose to be gods.

Therefore, since both kinds of idols are of one and the same condition, inasmuch as the dead and the gods are one, we abstain from both kinds of idolatry. We reject tombs no less than temples; we acknowledge neither kind of altar [Note: [Col. 0646D] “We acknowledge neither kind of altar.” In the temples of the Greeks there were two altars, one larger and the other smaller. The former, situated in the middle, was called ἁγαία τράπεζα (“holy table”); the latter, on the left, was called πρόθεσις (“prothesis”), as Symeon, archbishop of Thessalonica, wrote in his book on the temple, priesthood, and mysteries. LAC.], Acts 20; 1 Cor. 10; we adore neither kind of image. We do not sacrifice; we do not perform rites for the dead; nor do we eat anything sacrificed or offered to the dead, because we cannot eat both the supper of God and the supper of demons. If, then, we free our throat and belly from defilements, how much more do we abstain with our more august parts—our eyes and ears—from pleasures sacrificed to idols and to the dead? Such things are not processed in the intestines but digested in the spirit and soul themselves, whose purity pertains more to God than does the purity of the intestines.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0647]

Now, setting aside the term “idolatry” [Note: [Col. 0647C] “Now, setting aside the term idolatry.” That is, temporarily omitting and suspending the term “idolatry.” RIG.], which as the sole ground of the matter ought to be sufficient for renouncing spectacles, let us proceed, by way of superabundance, to treat the matter from another line of reasoning. We do so especially on account of those who flatter themselves [Col. 0647A] that this abstinence has not been expressly enjoined by name, as though a ruling were not sufficiently pronounced even upon spectacles [Note: [Col. 0647C] “Upon letters,” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 0647C] “As though we did not pronounce,” Rig.] when the desires of the world are condemned. For just as there is a desire for money, rank, gluttony, lust, or glory, so too there is a desire for pleasure; and spectacles are also a species of pleasure. Desires, I think, when named in general, contain pleasures within themselves; and pleasures, understood equally generally, are specifically extended to spectacles as well.

Moreover, we have reported above concerning the condition of places that they do not defile us in themselves, but through the things done in them. Once they have imbibed defilement through those things, they then spit it back upon others [Note: [Col. 0647C] “And then they spit it back upon another,” Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0647C] “And then they spit it back otherwise.” RIG.) The Codex Agobardinus reads: “And then they spit it back otherwise.” He used *altero* adverbially, just as *alio* is used and, near the end of book 2 of *To His Wife*, *alterutro*. Festus likewise says that *alteras* was formerly used in place of the adverb *alias*. On these defilements of places, see above, chapter 3. RIG.].

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0647B] Let the principal charge of idolatry, then, be as we have said [Note: [Col. 0647C] “This, therefore, will be, as we have said,” Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0647C] “Idolatry,” Rig.]; let us now set all the remaining qualities of the things themselves against the things of God [Note: [Col. 0647C] “All things opposed,” Franeq.] [Note: [Col. 0647D] “Let us set all things against the things of God.” We have restored the text thus from the Codex Agobardinus. “Let us set,” he says, “the things of the spectacles against the things of God.” Note the expression “the things of God” for divine or Christian discipline. *Contra ferre* means to set against, oppose, compare, bring into conflict, or bring together. RIG.].

God has commanded that the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0647D] “God has commanded that the Holy Spirit...” He is undoubtedly alluding to Eph. 4: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed on the day of redemption. Let all bitterness and wrath and indignation and clamor and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice”; he thereby indicates that the preceding words are explained by those that follow.]—being by the goodness of its own nature tender and delicate—be treated with tranquility, repose, and peace, Eph. 4, and not disturbed by frenzy, bitterness, anger, or grief. How can this Spirit have any agreement with spectacles? For no spectacle is without a disturbance of the spirit. Where there is pleasure, there is also passionate interest, through which, of course, pleasure acquires its savor. Where there is passionate interest, there is also rivalry, through which that interest acquires its savor. Furthermore, where there is rivalry, there are frenzy, bitterness, anger, grief [Note: [Col. 0647D] “Anger and grief.” Pliny, book 7, chapter 7, recounts a remarkable example of this matter: “All Pompey’s elephants,” he says, “attempted to break out, not without distressing the people, though they were enclosed by iron bars. But when hope of escape was lost, they sought the compassion of the crowd by an indescribable demeanor; they made supplication, lamenting themselves with a kind of wailing. So great was the people’s grief that the entire crowd, forgetting the commander and the lavish entertainment devised for his honor, rose up weeping and called down upon Pompey dreadful punishments, which he soon suffered.” PAM.], and the other things arising from them that are incompatible with Christian discipline.

[Col. 0648] For even if someone enjoys the spectacles with moderation and propriety, as befits the condition of his dignity, age, or even natural temperament, he nevertheless is not of an unmoved mind [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Is of an unmoved mind,” Jun.] or without a silent passion of the spirit. No one approaches pleasure without emotion, and no one experiences emotion without its attendant vicissitudes. [Col. 0648A] Those very vicissitudes are the incitements of emotion. But if emotion ceases, there is no pleasure; and that man is already guilty of vanity in going to a place where he gains nothing. Yet I think vanity too is alien to us.
