What of the fact that, by placing himself among people whom he does not wish to resemble, he passes judgment upon himself and certainly confesses himself to be one who condemns them? It is not enough for us that we ourselves do no such thing, unless we also refuse to associate with those who do such things. “If you saw a thief,” he says, Ps. 49, “you ran together with him.” Would that we did not have to dwell together with them even in the world! Nevertheless, we are separated from them in worldly practices, because the world belongs to God, but worldly things belong to the devil.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0648B] Since frenzy, therefore, is forbidden to us [Note: [Col. 0648C] “By frenzy,” Jun.], we are removed from every spectacle, even from the Circus, where frenzy properly presides. Look at the people coming to the spectacle already in a frenzy, already tumultuous, already blind, already inflamed by their wagers. The praetor is too slow for them; their eyes continually roll toward his urn and its lots. Then they hang in suspense upon the signal; one cry proceeds from one common madness. Recognize [Note: [Col. 0648C] “I recognize,” Rig.] madness from its vanity. “He has dropped it!” they say [Note: [Col. 0648C] “He has dropped it,” they say. Budé’s opinion is attractive: he maintains that this was the signal for setting the charioteers in competition. This is confirmed by Suetonius, *Life of Nero*, chapter 22; Martial, book 12; and Juvenal, Satire 22. Cassiodorus certainly proves our interpretation true, *Various Letters*, book 3, letter 51, to Faustus, prefect of the praetorium: “The napkin,” he says, “which is customarily used to give the signal at the circus games, became customary through the following incident. When Nero prolonged his luncheon and the people, eager to see the spectacle, as usual demanded that it begin quickly, he ordered the napkin he used for wiping his hands to be thrown from the window, so as to grant liberty to the contest they demanded. From this arose the custom that the display of the napkin should be regarded as the sure promise of the circus frenzies.” PAM.], and they announce to one another what everyone saw simultaneously. I seize upon this as evidence of their blindness [Note: [Col. 0648D] “I seize upon this as evidence of their blindness.” That is, I charge them with blindness. He then explains the blindness. RIG.]: they do not see what it really is. They think it is a napkin that has been dropped; but it is the maw of the devil cast down from on high [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Hurled headlong,” Paris, Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Figure,” Seml.] [Note: [Col. 0648D] “But it is the maw of the devil cast down from on high.” We have reproduced the reading of the most ancient codex. Previously it read: “the figure of the devil cast down from on high,” with a blunted point. For he alludes to what the sacred Scriptures relate concerning Satan, whom God drove headlong from heaven into Tartarus. Septimius therefore denies that the napkin which the praetor customarily dropped as a signal is really a napkin. He says, rather, that it is the Devil himself, who opens out as wholly maw, wholly gulf, wholly abyss, [Col. 0649C] and rages, poured throughout the entire Circus, and savages it monstrously. RIG.—“The devil cast down from on high.” Thus in the book *On the Soul*, p. 319: “He will have seen Satan cast down from heaven.” RIG.].

From that point they pass into frenzies, violent passions, [Col. 0649A] and dissensions, and into everything that is unlawful for priests of peace. From there come curses and insults without justice, as well as votes of hatred [Note: [Col. 0649C] “Without the justice of hatred; even votes,” Rig.] and love without merit. For what of their own are those who are not their own going to obtain from what they do there—unless perhaps the one thing through which they cease to be their own? They are saddened by another’s misfortune and delighted by another’s good fortune. Whatever they desire and whatever they abhor is alien to them; thus their love is idle and their hatred unjust.

But perhaps it is more permissible to love without cause than to hate without cause. God certainly forbids hatred even when there is cause, since he commands enemies to be loved. God does not permit cursing even when there is cause, since he directs us to bless those who curse us, Matt. 5; Mark 7; Rom. 13. But what is more bitter than the Circus, where they spare not even their rulers or their fellow citizens? If any of those passions by which the Circus rages are anywhere compatible with the saints, they will also be permissible in the Circus. But if they are permissible nowhere, then they are not permissible in the Circus either.

## CHAPTER XVII

Similarly, we are commanded to put away all immodesty [Note: [Col. 0649C] “Similarly, we are commanded to put away all immodesty.” In this the eloquent writers imitate him: Blessed Cyprian, Epistle 2 and *On Spectacles*, chapter 5; Lactantius, book 6, chapter 20; Augustine, *The City of God*, book 2, chapters 4–13. [Col. 0649D] Here the author alludes to Mark 7, from which he cites the rest near the end of this chapter: “The things that proceed from a man, those defile a man,” etc.; and perhaps also to Rom. 13: “Not in chambers and immodest acts.” PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0649C] “Similarly, we are commanded not to love all immodesty,” Rig.]. In this way, then, we are also separated from the theater, which is the private consistory of immodesty, where nothing wins approval except what wins no approval elsewhere. Thus the highest favor it enjoys is chiefly composed of filthiness: filthiness enacted in gesture by the Atellan performer [Note: [Col. 0649D] “The Atellan performs in gesture.” The Atellan players are very well known from the city of Atella, an ancient town of the Oscans. In that city there was once an excellent amphitheater; see Jerome, Epistle to Sabinianus. LE PR.]; filthiness represented by the mime even through women, driving their sex beyond the bounds of modesty [Note: [Col. 0649D] “Driving their sex beyond the bounds of modesty.” A Greek expression: leading the sex far away from modesty; establishing it outside the boundaries of modesty. RIG.—“Driving their sex beyond the bounds of modesty.” I have referred this to the baring of bodies, for female mimes were often naked in the theater. Valerius Maximus, book 3, speaking of the Floralia, says that while Marcus Porcius Cato was watching these games, the people were ashamed to demand that the female mimes be stripped. When Cato learned this from Favonius, his dearest friend, who was sitting beside him at the games, he left the theater [Col. 0650C] so that his presence would not impede the customary practice of the spectacle. LAC.], so that women blush more readily at home than on the stage; and finally filthiness suffered in his own body from boyhood by the pantomime so that he may become an artist.

The prostitutes themselves, victims of public lust, are also brought forward upon the stage, more wretched in the presence of women, from whom alone [Col. 0649C] they had remained hidden. They are paraded before the faces of every age and every rank; their place, their price, and their identifying notice are publicly proclaimed even to those who have no need of them. I pass over the rest—things that ought to have remained hidden in darkness and in their own dens, lest they contaminate the daylight. Let the senate blush; let every order of society blush. Let those very destroyers of their own modesty, trembling at bringing their gestures into daylight and before the people, blush once a year [Note: [Col. 0650C] “Let them blush once a year”: at the Floralia, of course, which Ovid, *Fasti* 5, says were customarily celebrated by the multitude of prostitutes. At those games the wantonness of the prostitutes, who were always shameless at other times, was greater and their jokes more unrestrained. At other times they put off modesty in their chambers and vaulted brothels, but here they did so in full public view. “Let them tremble,” he says, “at daylight and the people, and let them blush at least once a year.” RIG.].

But if all immodesty must be abominated by us, why should we be permitted to hear what we are not permitted to speak? Since we know that buffoonery and every idle word are judged by God, why should we equally be permitted to see things that it is disgraceful to do? Why should things that defile a person when uttered by the mouth not be thought to defile a person when admitted through the eyes and ears, since the ears [Note: [Col. 0650D] “Since the ears are attendants upon the spirit.” Thus Cicero calls the senses the mind’s attendants. Gregory of Nyssa, in his book *On the Perfect Form of the Christian*, δεχομένης τῆς ἀκοῆς τὴν ὑφήγησιν (“the hearing receiving instruction”), “the ears receiving commands, as being subject to the spirit.” Here note the passage in Jerome, book 1 *Against Jovinian*, where he says that the five senses were kings and princes of the world before the advent of Christ; yet Jesus so subjected them that he killed them outright. To this matter he adapts a passage of Scripture. LAC.] and eyes are attendants upon the spirit, and the spirit, whose attendants are defiled, cannot be kept pure? You therefore have the prohibition of the theater in the prohibition of immodesty.

## CHAPTER XVIII

If, moreover, we reject the teaching of secular literature as something accounted foolishness before God, that also provides us with a sufficient rule concerning those kinds of spectacles that fill with secular literature the sportive or competitive [Note: [Col. 0650D] “Competitive stage.” No one should doubt that these words must be understood of actors and pantomimes. In Hesychius ἀγωνισταί (“contestants”) are ὑποκριταί (“actors”), that is, mimes. This chapter and the next expose the impunity of the ancients; hence I am greatly astonished that Christian men have labored so intensely not only to disclose this depravity in their commentaries but also to expound it to many. LE PR.—“Competitive stage.” Although at first sight this may still seem to pertain to the theater, comedies and tragedies eventually began to be performed even at the Olympian games and at the contests held every five years in the stadium after the Greek fashion—to which the phrase “because of Greece’s leisure” refers. PAM.] stage [Note: [Col. 0650C] “Stage,” Jun.].

But if [Note: [Col. 0650C] “Because,” Fran., Oberth.] tragedies and comedies are performers [Note: [Col. 0650C] “Promoters,” Fran., Oberth.] of crimes and lusts—bloody and lascivious, impious and extravagant—then the commemoration of no atrocious or vile deed is any better than the deed itself. What is rejected in action must not be received in speech either.

If you also insist that the stadium is mentioned in the Scriptures, you will certainly carry your point. But you will not deny that the things done in the stadium are unworthy of your sight [Note: [Col. 0650C] “Of sight,” Jun.]: blows with fists and heels, slaps, every insolent assault of the hand, and every kind of battering of the human face [Note: [Col. 0650C] “Of the more humane,” Fran.]—that is, of the divine image. You approve nowhere of futile races, javelin-casting, and still more futile leaps. Nowhere will you take pleasure in strength that is either injurious or vain, nor in the cultivation of an artificial body that surpasses God’s own workmanship. And because of [Note: [Col. 0651C] “That have surpassed because of,” Fran.] Greece’s leisure, you will hate fattened men [Note: [Col. 0651C] “Fattened men.” He means athletes or wrestlers, who were customarily fed with the utmost care by gymnasium-directors so that they might be renowned for possessing the greatest strength in contests. The Greeks, enjoying the leisure of public security, were exceedingly devoted to such contests. For these were the evils they suffered [Col. 0651D] from prolonged peace. Septimius called them “fattened men,” just as Varro and Martial call oxen and hens “fattened,” meaning plump and well-fed. Thus in *On Repentance*, p. 147: “the enormous fattening of well-fed birds.” RIG.].

The wrestling-school too is the devil’s business [Note: [Col. 0651D] “The wrestling-school too is the devil’s business.” The *palaestra*, says Isidore, derives either from άπὸ τῆς πάλης (“from wrestling”), that is, wrestling, or from άπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν (“from *pallein*,” ‘to shake’), that is, the movement of a violent fall, because in wrestling, when they seize one another around the middle, they strike one another heavily, and among the Greeks this is called πάλλειν (“to shake”). He is correct, as are those who derive it from ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν (“from *pallein*,” ‘to shake’), that is, the movement of the urn, because they wrestled after being chosen by lot. For πάλλειν (*pallein*) means to brandish, shake, and allot. PAM.]. The devil struck down the first human beings, Gen. 3. The very posture is the serpent’s power: tenacious in seizing, twisting in binding, fluid in slipping away. You have no use for crowns; why do you hunt after pleasures arising from crowns?

## CHAPTER XIX

We shall now expect [Note: [Col. 0651C] Fran. adds “that.”] the repudiation of the amphitheater from the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0651C] Fran. adds “we should seek.”], Gen. 9; Exod. 20; Matt. 6. If we can contend that cruelty, impiety [Note: [Col. 0651D] “If cruelty, if impiety.” He alludes to Scriptures forbidding cruelty, impiety, and savagery. Foremost among these are Gen. 9: “Whoever sheds a man’s blood, for that man’s blood shall his own be shed”; then the commandment of the Decalogue, Exod. 20, “You shall not kill”; corresponding to it is the Lord’s discourse [Col. 0652C] on the mountain, Matt. 6, and very many other passages. PAM.], and savagery have been permitted to us, let us go to the amphitheater. If we are such as we have been taught to be, let us delight in human blood.

“It is good when the guilty are punished.” Who but a guilty person would deny this? And yet an innocent person cannot rejoice in another’s punishment, since it is more fitting for an innocent person to grieve that a human being like himself has become so guilty that he must be expended so cruelly. But who guarantees to me that it is always the guilty who are sentenced to the beasts or to some other punishment, and that innocence too is not subjected to it [Note: [Col. 0651C] “That innocence is not,” Paris.], whether through the vengeance of the judge, the weakness of the defense, or the pressure of interrogation?

How much better it is, therefore, not to know when the wicked are punished, lest I also know when the good perish—if indeed they have any taste for goodness [Note: [Col. 0652C] “Lest I also know when the good perish, if indeed they have any taste for goodness. Certainly, gladiators who are innocent come to the games,” etc. He speaks of pagans who are condemned to the beasts by the sentences of pagan magistrates. He therefore says: “But who guarantees to me that it is always the guilty who are condemned, and that the innocent are not sometimes condemned as well? How much better, therefore, not to know when the wicked are punished, lest I also know when the good perish.” But here, lest some Christian object, “Then there are good men among the pagans,” he corrects himself: “If indeed they have any taste for goodness,” he says—that is, “if there is indeed any savor of goodness in people who do not belong to Christ!” [Col. 0652D] He then adds: “Certainly, gladiators who are innocent come to the games to become victims of public pleasure.” Now he does not call them “good,” but only “innocent,” because they have not been condemned but come voluntarily to the games. RIG.]. Certainly, gladiators who are innocent come to the games to become victims of public pleasure. As for those who are condemned to the games, what sort of correction is it that, for a lesser offense, they should advance into the rank of murderers?

But I have made these replies to the pagans. Far be it from a Christian to require any longer instruction about turning away from a spectacle of this kind. Yet no one can fully describe all these things unless he is still watching them; I would rather fail to complete the account than retain the memory.

## CHAPTER XX

How vain, then—indeed, how desperate—is the argument of those who, unquestionably as an evasion intended to admit pleasure [Note: [Col. 0651C] “By an evasion,” Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0652C] “For pleasure,” Jun.], allege that no mention of abstinence from it is specifically [Note: [Col. 0652C] Fran. adds “or locally.”] laid down in the Scriptures that directly forbids a servant of God to attend gatherings of this kind.

I recently heard a novel defense [Note: [Col. 0652C] “I recently heard a novel defense by a certain lover of games.” Thus in *On Baptism*: “I have heard, with the Lord as witness, a claim of this kind,” etc. RIG.] from a certain lover of games [Note: [Col. 0652D] “A certain lover of games.” In the same way he said “your lovers of games” in *On the Soldier’s Crown*. Rhenanus correctly interprets the phrase there as referring to those Christians who still delighted in the attractions of spectacles, or in the pleasantness of games. PAM.]. “The sun,” he says, “and indeed God himself, looks down from heaven and is not contaminated.” Certainly the sun casts its rays even into a sewer [Note: [Col. 0652C] “Turned aside,” Jun., from a manuscript.] and is not defiled. Would, however, that God saw none of the crimes of human beings, so that we might all escape judgment! But he sees robberies; he sees falsehoods, adulteries, frauds, idolatries, and the spectacles themselves. Therefore we shall not look at them, lest we be seen by him who sees all things.

You compare, O man [Note: [Col. 0652C] “You should compare,” Seml.], the accused and the judge: the accused, who is guilty because he is seen; the judge, who is judge because he sees. Do we therefore devote ourselves to frenzy outside the boundaries of the Circus as well, to immodesty outside the doors of the theater, to insolence outside the stadium, and to mercilessness outside the amphitheater, merely because God has eyes even outside the vaulted chambers, tiers [Note: [Col. 0652D] “Outside the tiers.” That there were tiers in the Circus is evident from Suetonius. Hence, according to Livy and Pliny, came that law of Otho that no one possessing less than 400,000 sesterces should watch from the fourteen tiers; Pliny elsewhere calls it the Julian theatrical law. PAM.], and awnings [Note: [Col. 0652D] “And awnings.” So the Codex Agobardinus reads. This word appears to denote the coverings used in theaters [Col. 0653C] and amphitheaters for ornament and to exclude the burning rays of the sun. These were sometimes purple, a color with which the finest wool—as is likely—was dyed, such as the wool from Apulia. Martial: “Apulian fleeces of the first quality.” Hence the awnings were also called *Apularia*. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0652C] Wouw. corrects it to Ἐπαυλίας (*Epaulias*).]? We are mistaken: what God condemns is excused nowhere and never. What is always and everywhere unlawful is nowhere and never lawful. This is the integrity of truth [Note: [Col. 0653C] “The integrity of truth.” Truth ought to be incorrupt; it is also sometimes granted the name of virginity. Hence heretics are said to traffic in or corrupt the truth, τὴν ἀλήθειαν καπηλεὺειν (“to traffic in the truth”), canon 2 of the Council in Trullo, [Col. 0653D] where the canons both of the Apostles and of earlier councils, to which adherence is decreed, are enumerated. LE PR.], the fullness of discipline owed to it, the constancy of fear, and the fidelity of obedience: not to alter one’s sentence or vary one’s judgment. That which is truly good or evil cannot be something different. All things are fixed under the authority of God’s truth.

## CHAPTER XXI
Restoration notes: S001064 is orthographically uncertain; its apparent sense is “unhewn” or “uncouth.”; S001075 ends in apparently corrupt ΩΜ, represented verbatim.; S001076 is corrupt and has only been given a tentative contextual rendering.; S001064 has an uncertain recovered spelling; its apparent sense is “unhewn” or “rough.”; S001075 ends in the apparently corrupt characters ΩΜ, which have been preserved.; S001076 is corrupt, so its contextual rendering is tentative.  

The pagans [Note: [Col. 0653D] The pagans, among whom there is no fullness of truth. This is what we explained above: “If, nevertheless, they perceive what is good.” RIG.], among whom there is no fullness of truth, because God is not their teacher of truth, interpret evil and good according to whim and desire: what is good in one place is evil in another, and what is evil in one place is good in another. Thus it happens that a man who in public will scarcely lift his tunic even under the compulsion of his bladder will not exult in the circus [Note: [Col. 0653B] *Strip himself*, Wouw. MS.] except by displaying all his shame before everyone; and one who [Note: [Col. 0653B] *So that one who*, Wouw. MS.] guards his virgin daughter’s ears from every [Col. 0653B] filthy word himself conducts her to the theater to hear those utterances and see those gestures; and one who, in the streets, either restrains or denounces a man conducting a quarrel with his fists himself casts his vote for more serious combats in the stadium; and one who shudders at the corpse of a man who has died according to the common law of nature himself leans over from above in the amphitheater and gazes with the most enduring eyes upon bodies that have been gnawed and torn apart [Note: [Col. 0653D] *And torn apart.* Understand this little expression, and at the same time grasp the incredible atrocity of the gladiatorial spectacle. The victorious gladiator commonly used to repeat his blows so often that he tore the wretched loser into pieces and divided him by a horrible mangling. Lactantius bears witness to this cruelty: “Indeed, the spectators even order those who have been struck down and lie prostrate to be struck again, and their corpses to be torn apart with blows, lest any of them deceive the spectators by feigning death.” These words occur in book VI, chap. 20. LAC.], and befouled in their own blood. Indeed, one who comes to the spectacle to approve the punishment of a murderer himself compels an unwilling gladiator to commit murder with whips and rods; and one who demands a lion for every particularly notorious murderer himself seeks for a savage gladiator the wooden sword and bestows the felt cap [Note: [Col. 0653D] *Seeks the wooden sword and the felt cap.* The wooden sword and felt cap were tokens of freedom: gladiators who had fought successfully in the arena were presented with a *rudis*, that is, a wooden sword or larger staff, and were called *rudiarii*. LE PR.] as a reward; but when the man has been finished off [Col. 0654A] [Note: [Col. 0654C] *But when the man has been finished off, he seeks the spectacle even of his face*: that is, he wishes also to look upon the face and countenance of the dying man. RIG.], he seeks the spectacle even of his face [Note: [Col. 0653B] *Of love*, Fran., Paris, Oberth.], more gladly recognizing at close quarters the man whom he wished [Note: [Col. 0653B] *Whom he did not wish*, Cod. Wouw.] to have killed from a distance—and all the more cruel if he did not wish it [Note: [Col. 0653B] *If he wished it*, Cod. Wouw.; *if he did not wish it*, Rig.].

## CHAPTER XXII

What wonder is there in this unequal inconsistency of men who mingle and interchange the status of good and evil through the inconstancy of their perception and the variability [Note: [Col. 0653C] *Variability* in the accusative, Paris.] of their judgment? For the very performers [Note: [Col. 0654B] *Authors*, Seml., Oberth., Leop.] and managers of spectacles deprive the charioteers, stage performers, athletes, and gladiators [Note: [Col. 0654C] *Gladiators.* The gladiatorial contest, like the amphitheater, was called κατ` ἐξοχὴν (“preeminently”) from the sand. For although sand was strewn in the places of other games, the name itself was applied only to the amphitheater. Barraeus, however, explains it very badly: “Chariot-workers and sand-workers: the former were those who repaired the chariots, the latter those who carried sand into the amphitheater.” That is not so; he means charioteers and gladiators. LAC.], those objects of utter madness [Note: [Col. 0654B] *Most loving*, Fran.; *most beloved*, Cod. Wouw.], beneath whom men lay down their lives [Note: [Col. 0654B] *Their paltry lives*, Fran., Oberth.] [Note: [Col. 0654D] *Beneath whom men lay down their lives, and women—or even those men—their bodies.* He means gladiators, loved to the point of madness by both men and women: by men, even those of noble rank, who descended into the arena; and by women of the highest nobility—and indeed also by men—who sacrificed their chastity through love of some utterly base murmillo or retiarius. The sixth satire of Juvenal supplies examples of this madness. RIG.], and women—or even those men—their bodies, for whose sake they commit the very things they condemn. They degrade them on account of the very profession [Note: [Col. 0654B] *Part*, Fran.] which [Note: [Col. 0654B] *Which* in the ablative, Rig.] they esteem highly [Note: [Col. 0654B] Fran. adds *and diminish*]; indeed, they openly condemn them by disgrace and diminution of civil status [Note: [Col. 0654D] *And diminution of civil status.* This is a phrase used by the jurists, among whom Digest, book IV, title 5, concerns those whose civil status has been diminished. PAM.], barring them from the municipal council, the rostra, the senate, the equestrian order, and all other offices and certain distinctions alike. [Col. 0654B] What perversity! They love those whom they punish; they disparage those whom they approve. They esteem the art highly but brand the artist. What sort of judgment is it that a man should be disgraced because of those very things through which he earns favor? Indeed, what a great confession of the evil nature of a thing, when its authors [Note: [Col. 0654B] *Its performers*, Wouw. MS.], though they are held in the highest favor, are not without a mark of disgrace!

## CHAPTER XXIII

Since, therefore, human reflection, even when the favor accorded to pleasure protests against it, judges that such men must be condemned—deprived of the advantages of rank and cast upon a kind of rock of infamy—how much more does divine justice punish practitioners of this sort? Will that charioteer please God, who disturbs so many souls, ministers to so many frenzies [Note: [Col. 0654D] *Minister to so many frenzies, so many states.* He notes the frenzied enthusiasm of the ancients for charioteers or drivers, by which the minds of spectators were very often divided by opposing wishes, some favoring the Green faction and others the Blue; hence various movements and various states of mind were produced according to the varying course of the race. We therefore retain the reading published by Rhenanus and Pamelius, [Col. 0655C] for the mutilated wording of the Agobard manuscript is of no assistance here: “Minister to so many frenzies, so many states, like a pimp.” Cassiodorus: “The Green passes by: part of the people mourns; the Blue takes the lead, and the more powerful multitude of the city is afflicted. Though gaining nothing, they insult one another passionately; though suffering nothing, they are grievously wounded; and they descend to empty contests as if they were laboring over the condition of an endangered fatherland.” RIG.], and so many states of mind, crowned like a priest, or, being clad in a faction’s color, like a pimp—the man whom the devil has adorned to be swept away in his chariot in opposition to Elijah? Will that man also please Him [Note: [Col. 0655C] *Also* is absent from Rigalt.], who alters his face with a razor? Faithless toward his own face, not content to make it resemble Saturn, Isis, and Liber, he further exposes it to the insults of slaps, as though mocking the Lord’s commandment. Evidently the devil also teaches one patiently to offer one’s cheek to be struck (Matt. VI). So too he raised the tragic actors upon buskins, because no one can add one cubit to his stature (Luke XII): he wishes to make Christ a liar. And now, as to the very work of masks and impersonations, I ask whether it pleases God, who forbids every likeness to be made—how much more the likeness of His own image. The author of truth does not love falsehood (Exod. XX): with Him, everything [Col. 0655B] that is feigned is adultery. Accordingly, He will not approve one who falsifies voice, sex, and age and affects loves, angers, groans, and tears, since He condemns all hypocrisy. Moreover, when in the Law He prescribes that anyone who dresses in women’s clothing is accursed [Note: [Col. 0655D] *Who dresses in women’s clothing.* The blessed Cyprian also inveighs against this in epistle 61, to Euchratius; and canon 62 of the Council in Trullo forbids a man to use women’s clothing, or a woman men’s clothing, or anyone to assume comic, satirical, or tragic characters. LE PR.] (Deut. XXII), what judgment will He pronounce upon the pantomime, who is elaborately fashioned even in feminine ways [Note: [Col. 0655D] *Who is elaborately fashioned even into a woman.* That is, he is most carefully effeminized in voice, gesture, and gait, so that, when dancing stories about women, he may be taken for a woman. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0655C] *Uses*, Wouw. MS.]?

Surely that practitioner of fist-fighting, too, will go unpunished? For he received such scars from the boxing gloves, such calluses on his fists, and such cauliflower growths on his ears [Note: [Col. 0655C] *Rough*, Latin.] from God together with his created form [Note: [Col. 0656C] *When he was fashioned*, Rig.]. It was for this reason that God fashioned his [Note: [Col. 0656C] *Their*, Rig.] eyes: that they might fail under blows. I say nothing of the man who puts another man between himself and a lion, lest he be too little a murderer [Note: [Col. 0655D] *Lest he be too little a murderer, who afterward cuts the same man’s throat.* When gladiators had been matched, the people would sometimes demand a lion. Once the lion had been released, the gladiator in immediate danger would, by whatever art he could, place his fellow combatant before himself through an adroit withdrawal or sidestep. It very often happened, however, that this second gladiator, after the encounter with the lion had ended successfully, was matched again in a renewed gladiatorial engagement with that first man and had his throat cut by him. For this reason Tertullian calls that first man “not too little a murderer,” that is, a murderer twice over: once, of course, when he put a man between himself and the lion; and again when he afterward cut the throat of the very man by whose body he had shielded himself. In short, the man who cuts the throat of his savior is no small murderer. RIG.]—[Note: [Col. 0656C] Pam. and Seml. add *than*.] who afterward cuts that same man’s throat.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0655C] In how many more ways shall we argue to the end that nothing assigned to the spectacles is pleasing to God [Col. 0656A] or fitting for God’s servants [Note: [Col. 0656C] *For a servant of God*, Rig.], since we have shown that everything was instituted for the devil and furnished from the devil’s possessions? For whatever is not God’s, or displeases God, belongs to the devil. This will be the devil’s pomp, which we renounce in the seal of faith. But we ought not to participate, by deed, word, sight, or observation, in what we renounce. Moreover, do we not renounce and annul the seal when we annul its attestation? Does anything remain, then, but for us to demand an answer from the pagans themselves? Let them now tell us whether Christians may attend a spectacle. Yet it is chiefly from this very thing—the rejection of spectacles—that they recognize a man as having become a Christian. Thus a man plainly denies who he is when he removes the mark by which he is recognized. What hope remains, then, for a man of this sort? [Col. 0656B] No one crosses over into the enemy’s camp unless he has thrown away his own arms, abandoned the standards and military oaths [Note: [Col. 0656C] *Standards and military oaths.* This is drawn from military service, as are the other expressions in this treatise. Fulbert of Chartres, epistle 41. LAC.] of his commander, and made a compact to perish along with them.

## CHAPTER XXV

Will such a man think about God at that time, stationed in a place where there is nothing of God? He will, I suppose, have peace in his mind while contending on behalf of a charioteer; he will learn chastity while transfixed by mimes. Indeed, at every spectacle no greater stumbling block will present itself than the more elaborate adornment of the women and men themselves: their very agreement, their very alliance or disagreement over their respective favorites [Note: [Col. 0656D] *Their very alliance or disagreement over their favorites fans into flame sparks of lust arising from intercourse.* Accordingly, the teacher of the *Art* also instructs this, book I:

> Make it your earnest care to ask whose horses are entering;
>
> And without delay, whoever he may be whom she favors, favor him, etc.

RIG.] fans into flame sparks of lust arising from intercourse [Note: [Col. 0656D] *From intercourse.* These words must be joined with what follows, not with what precedes; therefore observe our punctuation. Junius explains *commercium* as επιμιξίαν (“intermingling”), for formerly, according to Velius Longus, *commercium* was said to derive from *commiscere*, “to mingle,” through an interchange of letters. That etymology is pertinent here, for sparks of lust arise from promiscuous association. This is illustrated in Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book III, chap. 2, and book II, chap. 7. LAC.] [Note: [Col. 0656D] *Fans sparks into flame.* The Agobard manuscript has “lashes,” a reading not to be despised, although Tertullian himself, *Against the Valentinians*, said, “fire fanned by bodies.” Virgil, however, said that sparks leap from the eyes, and in leaping they seem to lash them. RIG.]. In short, no one approaches a spectacle without first thinking of seeing and being seen.

But while the tragic actor is shouting [Note: [Col. 0656D] *But while the tragic actor is shouting.* Tragic actors made it their practice to speak in an extremely expansive and declamatory manner. Heraldus illustrates this in his notes on Arnobius, book 7, from Crantor, who, according to Diogenes, said that tragic actors had a voice ὰπελέκετον (apparently “unhewn” or “rough”; the recovered spelling is uncertain); and from Demosthenes, who reproaches Aeschines with φωνασκίας έπίδειξιν (“a display of vocal training”). For Aeschines had practiced acting. LAC.], will that man be pondering the cries of some prophet [Col. 0656C]? Amid the melodies of an effeminate actor, will he compose a psalm to himself? And while the athletes are in action, [Col. 0657A] will he be saying that one must not strike back (Matt. V)? Will he be capable of being reminded of mercy while transfixed by the bites of bears and the sponges of the net-fighters [Note: [Col. 0657C] *The sponges of the net-fighters.* He calls the nets “sponges,” since they were so adapted for combat that, when cast upon an opponent, they spread themselves out and, immediately contracting, drew in the man thus caught—not so that he might be captured alive, but so that he might be pierced by the retiarius’s prop or trident. Such, perhaps, was the net in which Pittacus enveloped and seized the pancratiast Phrynon and killed him in single combat. Σπόγγον (“sponge”). The Greeks used the terms παρὰ τὸ σπᾴν (“from σπᾴν, ‘to draw’”) and σφόγγον (“sponge”), the latter of which comes closer to the word σφίγγειν (“to tighten”), both expressions being suitable to the contest of the retiarii. For the retiarii are σπαστικοὶ πρὸς αὐτούς (“those who pull them toward themselves”).—*The sponges of the net-fighters.* I pass over what Rigaltius has adduced. The retiarii customarily used sponges to wipe away blood flowing from wounds. LE PR.]? May God avert from His own people so great a craving for deadly pleasure.

For what a thing it is to go from the Church of God [Note: [Col. 0657D] *For what a thing it is to go from the Church of God.* The grave complaint of that most holy man Augustine, on Psalm 39, testifies that this perversity endured even into his age: “With what great crowds the churches are filled! The walls are packed; they press upon one another in the crush; they almost suffocate themselves by their multitude. Yet once again, if there is a mime, these very same people run to the amphitheater.” And on Psalm 50: “If by chance they become frightened in the Circus itself for some reason, they immediately sign themselves and stand there bearing upon their forehead that from which they would withdraw if they bore it in their heart.” RIG.] into the church of the devil—from heaven, as they say, into the mire! To exhaust in applauding an actor those hands that you have raised to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0657D] *Those hands that you have raised to God.* He grieves that hands raised to God are employed in an idolatrous matter. The great Athanasius makes the same complaint in his *Apology against the Nations*, where he grieves that members dedicated to God serve in attendance upon idols; among other things he also adduces hands that were made for the stretching out of prayer toward God. Some think that Tertullian’s words—among them Stephanus Durandus, *On the Rites of the Church*—must be understood of raising the hands in adoration of the body of Christ when it is elevated during Mass. LAC.]! From the mouth with which you uttered “Amen” over the Holy Thing [Note: [Col. 0658C] *From the mouth with which you uttered “Amen” over the Holy Thing.* By “the Holy Thing,” understand the mystery, the sacrament, the Body of the Lord. For each of the faithful, when receiving from the presiding minister the morsel of the Eucharist offered to him with the words, “THE BODY OF CHRIST,” would say, “AMEN,” which means, “So be it.” Augustine, *Sermon to the Newly Baptized on the Sacrament*: “If, then, you are the body and members of Christ, your mystery has been placed upon the Lord’s table: you receive the Lord’s mystery. To that which you are, you answer ‘Amen,’ and by answering you subscribe to it. You hear, therefore, ‘THE BODY OF CHRIST,’ and you answer, ‘AMEN.’ Be a member of Christ’s body, so that the Amen may be true.” Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book IV, chap. 5: “The priest says to you, ‘THE BODY OF CHRIST,’ and you say, ‘AMEN,’ that is, ‘True.’ Let the heart hold what the tongue confesses.” Cornelius, bishop of Rome, in the epistle quoted by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 31, rightly censured the sacrilegious intention of Novatus, because he demanded an oath against the Roman pontiff from the brethren of his party as they received the Eucharist, in place of the solemn formula by which “Amen” was answered to the minister who presented the sacrament and said, “The body of Christ.” ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰπεῖν λαμβάνοντα τὸν ἄρτον έκεἰνον, τὸ ἀμήν (“instead of saying ‘Amen’ when receiving that bread”). RIG.], to bear witness to a gladiator—to say εἰς αἰῶνας απ` αἰῶνος (“for ages, from eternity”) [Note: [Col. 0657B] Ἀπ` αἰῶνος (“From eternity”) is absent from Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0658D] ΕΙΣ ΑΙΩΝΑΣ ΑΠ` ΑΙΩΝΩΜ (approximately “FOR AGES, FROM ETERNITY”; the final ΩΜ is corrupt). In the Agobard manuscript only ἙΙΣ ΑΠ` ΛΙΩΝΟΣ (a corrupt reading, apparently “for/from eternity”) is read. Others read, “to say it to anyone at all except God and Christ.” Tertullian is noting what Dio relates was acclaimed to Commodus: ΝΙΚΑΣ ΝΙΚΗΣΕΙΣ ΑΠ` ΑΙΩΝΟΣ (“YOU CONQUER; YOU WILL CONQUER, FROM ETERNITY”), book LXXII. RIG.] to anyone at all except God and Christ!

## CHAPTER XXVI

Why, then, should people of this sort not also become accessible to demons? For an instance did occur, with the Lord as witness, [Col. 0657B] of the woman [Note: [Col. 0658D] *Of the woman.* This example is exceedingly celebrated and commonly in everyone’s mouth. I would suspect that the woman in question was possessed by a demon because she had perhaps gone to the spectacles without consulting her husband, or against his will. For this would be a cause for repudiation, as may be read in book 5 of the Code, title 17, *On Repudiations*. LE PR.] who went to the theater and returned from it with a demon. Thus, during the exorcism, when the unclean spirit was being pressed as to why it had dared to attack a believer, it replied, “I acted with perfect constancy and justice: I found her on my own ground.” It is also established that another woman, on the night of the day when she had listened to a tragic actor, was shown a linen cloth in a dream, while the actor was named in reproach, and that she did not remain in this world beyond the fifth day. How many other proofs, assuredly, have emerged concerning those who fell away from the Lord by entering into communion with the devil at spectacles! For no one can serve two [Col. 0658A] masters (Matt. VI; 2 Cor. VI; Ecclesiasticus XXXIII). What has light to do with darkness? What have life and death to do with one another?

## CHAPTER XXVII

We ought to hate these assemblies and gatherings of pagans, if only because there the name of God is blasphemed; there lions are demanded daily against us; from there persecutions are decreed; from there temptations are dispatched. What will you do when caught in that surging tide of impious acclamations? It is not as though you could suffer anything there at the hands of men, for no one recognizes you as a Christian; but consider what is happening concerning you in heaven. Do you doubt that at the very moment when you are in the devil’s church [Note: [Col. 0657B] “When the devil rages against the Church,” Cod. Wouw., Rig.], all the angels look down from heaven and mark each individual—who uttered the blasphemy, who listened to it, who placed his tongue and who his [Col. 0658B] ears at the devil’s service against God? (Ps. I). Will you not, then, flee the seats of Christ’s enemies, that chair of pestilences [Note: [Col. 0658B] *Pestilential chair*, Fran.], and the very air that hangs over it, violated by wicked voices?

Let some things there be sweet, pleasant, simple, or even honorable. No one mixes poison with gall and hellebore; rather, he injects that evil into seasoned and well-flavored dishes, and especially into sweet ones. So too the devil imbues the deadly thing he prepares with the things of God that are most pleasant and acceptable. Whatever there is of strength, honor, sonority, melody, or subtlety, regard it just as though it were drops [Col. 0659A] of honey from a poisonous little frog [Note: [Col. 0659C] *Drops of honey from a poisonous little frog.* As if someone were to press a honeycomb together with the lungs of a toad; for then honey mingled with poison would drip from it—honey indeed, but poisoned. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 0659C] *From a little sweet cake*, Fran.; *from a lucunculus*, Jun.] [Note: [Col. 0659C] *From a poisonous little frog.* Juvenal, in the first:

> Who, intending to offer her thirsty husband mellow Calenian wine,  
> Mixes a toad into it;

[Col. 0659D] and in the seventh:

> But now the matter is conducted by the slender lung of a toad;

and in the third:

> Never the entrails of frogs.

“I have examined.” RIG.—*From a poisonous little frog.* Thus Johannes Wover reads from an old manuscript. Junius thinks *lucunculum* should be read, for that word would be derived from *lucuns* and would be a ὐποκοριστικόν (“a diminutive”) word; it would denote a kind of sugared confection and dessert. Afranius speaks of it in the *Brothers*:

> He attends to the baker; why not to the pastry-cook,  
> So that he may send little sweet cakes to his brother’s son?

La Cerda’s annotations upon this word are slight, apart from what is found in the most learned Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XVIII, chap. 20. LE PR.]. Do not value the appetite for pleasure as highly as the danger concealed by its sweetness.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Let his own guests be fattened on sweets of this sort; both the places and the times and the one who invites them are his. Our banquet and our wedding feast have not yet come. We cannot recline at table with them, because neither can they with us. The matter is arranged by turns. Now they rejoice; we struggle (John XVI). “The world,” He says, “will rejoice; you will be sorrowful.” Let us therefore mourn while the pagans rejoice, so that when they begin to mourn, we may rejoice—lest, if we rejoice together now, we should also mourn together then. You are overdelicate, Christian, if you desire pleasure in this world as well; indeed, you are exceedingly foolish if you consider this [Col. 0659B] pleasure.

Certain philosophers [Note: [Col. 0659C] *Indeed*, Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0659D] *Certain philosophers.* He touches upon the Epicureans, who placed the highest good in pleasure. LE PR.] have given this name to repose and tranquility; in it they rejoice, in it they are occupied, and in it they even glory. Yet you sigh to me for turning posts [Note: [Col. 0659D] *You sigh to me for turning posts.* “Every contest,” says Cassiodorus, *Variae Lectiones*, book III, chap. 51, “is completed in seven circuits, after the likeness of the recurring week. The turning posts themselves, corresponding to the decans of the Zodiac, possess three summits apiece, which the swift four-horse chariots traverse in imitation of the sun.” PAM.], stage scenery, dust, and arenas. Tell me, if you please: can we not live without pleasure, we who ought to die with pleasure? For what other desire do we have than that which the Apostle also had—to depart from the world and be received with the Lord (Phil. I)? Where our desire is, there is our pleasure also.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Now, if you think [Note: [Col. 0659C] *Now suppose*, Rig.] that this span of life must be spent amid delights, why are you so ungrateful that you do not consider sufficient, or even acknowledge, the many great pleasures bestowed upon you by God? For what is more delightful [Col. 0659C] than reconciliation with God the Father and Lord, than the revelation of truth, than the recognition of errors, than forgiveness for so many former crimes? What greater pleasure is there than disgust with pleasure itself, contempt for the whole world, true freedom, an uncorrupted conscience, a sufficient life, and no fear of death; than the fact that you trample upon the gods of the nations, expel demons, effect cures, seek revelations, and live for God?

These are the pleasures, these are the spectacles of Christians—holy, everlasting, and free of charge. In these interpret for yourself the games of the Circus [Note: [Col. 0660C] *The games of the Circus.* He excellently adapts to Christian conduct the things that pertained to the circus. LE PR.]: gaze upon the course of the world; behold the passing times; count the laps; await the turning posts of consummation; defend the companies of the churches; rise at God’s signal; stand upright at the angel’s trumpet; glory in the palms of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0659C] *Of the martyrs*, Rig.]. If the teachings of the stage [Note: [Col. 0660C] *Of knowledge*, Rig.] delight you, we have enough literature, enough verses, enough maxims, enough songs as well, enough voices—not fables, but truths; not artifices [Note: [Col. 0660D] *Not artifices.* I explain this as tricks and frauds, but with reference to the strophes and odes of dramatic performance, to which antistrophes and antodes are opposed. Yet, as I have said, the meaning here is “frauds”; Charles Paschal also understands this passage in that way in *On Crowns*, book I, chap. 11. LAC.], but simplicities.

Do you also wish for boxing and [Col. 0660B] wrestling? They are at hand—not slight, but numerous [Note: [Col. 0660C] “Not a few at once,” Rig.]. Behold shamelessness cast down by chastity, treachery struck down by faith, cruelty crushed by mercy, insolence overshadowed by modesty [Note: [Col. 0660C] *Foreshadowed*, Par., Rig.]. Such are the contests among us, in which we ourselves receive the crown [Note: [Col. 0660D] *We ourselves receive the crown.* Who does not know the athletic crowns of the stadium? Indeed, from these alone crowns were called κᾳτ` έξοχήν (“preeminently”). To pursue the matter would be idle, indeed tiresome. Hence Jerome, book II *Against Jovinian*, when seeking correspondences of expressions, gives crowns to wrestlers in the same way that he gives a harbor to sailors and a triumph to combatants. LAC.]. Do you also desire something involving blood [Note: [Col. 0660D] *Do you also desire something involving blood?* He contrasts the blood of Christ the Lord, shed to recover the salvation of us all, with bloody pleasures and spectacles. LE PR.]? You have Christ’s.

## CHAPTER XXX

But what a spectacle is now close at hand: the coming of the Lord, now beyond doubt, now majestic, now triumphant! What exultation of the angels that will be! What glory of the saints as they rise again! What a kingdom of the righteous will follow! What a city, the new Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0660D] *What a city, the new Jerusalem!* This perhaps pertains to the error of the Millenarians, as does what he adds concerning so many births of the world. PAM.]!

Yet other spectacles remain: that last and eternal day of judgment, unanticipated by the nations and mocked by them, [Col. 0660C] when the great antiquity of the world and its many births will be consumed in a single fire. How vast will that spectacle be [Note: [Col. 0660D] *How vast will that spectacle be!* How many and how great will be the things presented for contemplation in that spectacle! RIG.]! What shall I admire? At what shall I laugh? Where shall I rejoice, where exult, as I behold so many mighty kings [Note: [Col. 0660C] “Beholding so many kings,” Rig.] who were proclaimed to have been received into [Col. 0661A] heaven [Note: [Col. 0661B] *Received into heaven.* He indicates pagan apotheoses. A notable example occurs in Herodian, speaking about Severus, who lived in Tertullian’s age. Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2; and it is established from Suetonius and Dio that at the funerals of Augustus and afterward of Drusilla the same thing was solemnly affirmed by men of senatorial rank. LAC.], groaning together in the lowest darkness with Jupiter himself and with the very witnesses who attested their divinity? Likewise, provincial governors, persecutors of the Lord’s name, melting in flames fiercer than those with which they themselves raged against Christians, as those flames leap upon them? And besides them, those wise philosophers blushing before their disciples as they burn together [Note: [Col. 0661B] *As they burn together.* He foretells this evil for the pagans, who thought there would be no resurrection. It is not so: you will rise again, but to punishment. LAC.]—the disciples whom they persuaded that nothing pertains to God, and to whom they affirmed either that souls do not exist or that they will not return to their former bodies? And the poets also, trembling not before the tribunal of Rhadamanthus or Minos, but before that of the Christ whom they did not expect?

Then the tragic actors will be more worth hearing, being naturally more vocal in their own calamity. Then the actors will be more worth recognizing, far more loosened through the fire [Note: [Col. 0661B] *Actors far more loosened through the fire.* Actors are “loosened” because, effeminized by softness and wantonness, they almost flow more freely than women. But they are “more loosened through the fire” because their limbs melt under its burning. RIG.]. Then the charioteer will be worth watching, glowing entirely red [Note: [Col. 0661B] *Red*, Rig.] upon his fiery wheel [Note: [Col. 0661C] *The charioteer glowing entirely red upon his fiery wheel.* He alludes to the Red faction of the drivers. RIG.]. Then the athletes will be worth contemplating, hurled not in gymnasia [Note: [Col. 0661C] *Not in gymnasia.* “The place of athletic games,” says Isidore, book 18, chap. 17, “was called a gymnasium, where athletes exercised and the speed of runners was tested. It was so called because young men exercised naked. Hence it happened that the exercise grounds of almost all arts are called gymnasia.” PAM.], but in fire—except that not even then would I wish to look upon them, since I would prefer to direct my insatiable gaze toward those who [Col. 0662A] raged against the Lord.

“This is he,” I shall say, “the son of the carpenter or the prostitute [Note: [Col. 0661B] *Of a male prostitute*, Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0661C] *The son of the carpenter or the prostitute.* Jerome, *Epistle to Heliodorus*: “This is he, the son of the workman and the prostitute.” These were the taunts of the Jews against the most holy and immaculate Virgin, to be expiated in flames filled with the thickest sulfur. Satanic words of this sort are found in Theodoret, book III, chap. 11, spoken by Felix, prefect of Gaza under Julian Caesar: ἰδοὺ ἐν τόιοις σκεύεσιν ὑπηρετεῖται ὁ Μαρίας υἱός (“Behold, with such vessels the son of Mary is served!”), which the *Tripartite History* renders in Latin: “Behold the vessels with which the son of Mary is served!” In the same author, where the martyrdom of Hormisdas is discussed, the tyrant says, “Deny the son of the carpenter.” RIG.—*The son of the carpenter or the prostitute.* I cannot readily assent to this reading of Rigaltius, nor to the other, *male prostitute*, which La Cerda adduces from Jerome in both places. For learned jurists long ago observed that a *quaestuaria* is a woman who gains profit or earnings from her body; thus in the Glossary *quaestuaria* is πρακτικὴ πορνη (“a prostitute by profession”). LE PR.], the destroyer of the Sabbath, the Samaritan and demoniac. This is the man whom you purchased from Judas; this is he who was beaten with a reed and with fists, dishonored with spittle, and given gall and vinegar to drink. This is the man whom the disciples secretly stole away so that he might be said to have risen again—or whom the gardener removed [Note: [Col. 0662C] *Or whom the gardener removed.* This irony appears to ridicule one of those heretics who deny that Christ truly suffered—namely Marcion, his teacher Cerdo, and, before them, Basilides and Simon Magus. PAM.], lest the crowds of people passing by should damage his lettuces [Note: [Col. 0662B] *Should cause damage*, Rig.] [Note: [Col. 0662C] *Lest the crowds of people passing by should cause damage to his lettuces.* Therefore, when sacred buildings were erected—among the ancients they were generally established on a boundary where the limits of three or four estates met—each proprietor contributed a definite measure of land from his own field to that sacred place and put in writing how much he had contributed, so that on the feast day the fields of private persons might suffer no disturbance from the people crowding in. Aggenus notes this on Frontinus, *On the Boundaries of Fields*. RIG.].”

To enable you to behold such things and exult in such things, what praetor, consul, quaestor, or priest will furnish them from his own liberality? And yet even now, in a certain manner, we possess these things, represented through faith by the imagination of the spirit. Moreover, what are those things which neither eye [Col. 0662B] has seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man? They are, I believe, more delightful than the circus, both auditoria, and every stadium.

# The Book on Idolatry

[Col. 0661]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN ON IDOLATRY (C)

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0661D] After his treatise *On Spectacles*, Septimius composed another, *On Idolatry*, in which he proposes, discusses, and resolves various cases of conscience—if it is permissible to speak thus. For there were indeed some who labored under such great ignorance that they thought no one was polluted by the crime of idolatry except those who either burned incense to idols, offered them sacrifices, or were initiated into their mysteries or profane priesthood (chap. 2). He therefore defines idolatry as follows: “Every attendance and service concerning an idol; and it makes no difference,” he says, “whether a modeler shapes it, a sculptor carves it, or an embroiderer weaves it; nor does its material matter—whether an idol is formed of plaster, colors, stone, bronze, silver, or thread” (chap. 3). He adds that God forbids an idol both to be made and to be worshiped (chap. 4). From this he says that Christians may not [Col. 0663A] manufacture idols or sell them to those who will worship them, even when they have no other means of livelihood (chap. 5). He also forbids the construction of a temple, altar, shrine, or house in honor of idols (chap. 8). He even forbids trade in goods that pertain to idolatry (chap. 11); one must also abstain from feast days, even extraordinary ones (chap. 13); slaves may not serve as ministers of idolatry (chap. 18); nor is military service lawful when one must serve beneath the devil’s standard (chap. 19). He condemns and execrates every oath such as “By Hercules” and “By Fidius,” as well as the curse “May Jupiter be angry with you,” and the response that follows it, “No, with you.” Nevertheless, discrimination is needed in reading through this treatise: for nearly all the propositions Tertullian lays down here as general principles are true, but not everything [Col. 0663B] that he deduces from them is true. LUMP.

## CHAPTER I
The chief crime of the human race, the supreme guilt of the age, the entire ground of judgment, is idolatry. For although each offense retains its own particular character, although each is also assigned to judgment under its own name [Note: [Col. 0663D] “Each under its name,” Junius], it is nevertheless entered in the account under the crime of idolatry. Set aside the titles; examine the deeds [Note: [Col. 0663D] “Examine the deed,” Junius, Latinus]: the idolater is also a murderer. Do you ask whom he has killed? If it adds anything to the fullness of the indictment, not a stranger or an enemy, but himself. By what treachery? By his own error. With what weapon? An offense against God. With how many blows? As many as his acts of idolatry. Whoever denies that the idolater has perished will deny that the idolater has committed murder. Accordingly [Note: [Col. 0663D] “Likewise,” Paris], you may recognize adultery [Col. 0663C] and fornication in the same man: for he who serves false gods is undoubtedly an adulterer against the truth, because every falsehood is an adulteration. Thus he is also plunged into [Note: [Col. 0663D] “Into” is absent from Rigault] fornication. For who can minister to unclean spirits without going about defiled and debauched (Ezek. 23)? Indeed, Holy Scripture uses the term “fornication” in its reproach of idolatry.

The nature of fraud, I suppose, is that someone takes what belongs to another or denies another what is owed to him; and certainly fraud committed against a human being bears the name of a most serious crime. But idolatry defrauds God, denying Him His own honors and conferring them upon others, so that it joins insult to fraud. And if fraud, fornication, and adultery alike bring death, then in these respects too [Note: [Col. 0663D] “Now in these respects alike,” Junius] idolatry is not absolved from the charge of murder.

After crimes of this kind, so destructive, [Col. 0663D] so devouring of salvation, all the others as well, though in some fashion arranged separately in their own right, display their character in idolatry. In it are also the lusts of the world. For what solemn observance of idolatry is without ostentatious display in its ceremonial and adornment? In it are wantonness and drunkenness, since such solemnities are attended chiefly for the sake of feasting, gluttony, and lust [Note: [Col. 0663D] “Are attended,” Rigault]. In it is injustice. For what is more unjust than that which does not know the Father of justice? In it also is vanity, since its whole rationale is vain; in it is falsehood, [Col. 0664A] since its whole substance is false. Thus it comes about that everything is found in idolatry, and idolatry in everything.

But there is also another consideration: since all offenses savor of opposition to the Lord, and nothing that savors of opposition to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0664D] “God—God,” Rigault] fails to be assigned to demons and unclean spirits, to whom idols are enslaved, whoever commits an offense undoubtedly commits idolatry; for he does what pertains to the owners of idols.

## CHAPTER II

But let all the names of crimes withdraw into the particular characteristics of their deeds; let idolatry remain what it is in itself. A name so hostile to God is sufficient unto itself, as is so abundant a substance of crime, which extends so many branches and spreads forth [Note: [Col. 0664D] “Diffuses,” Wouwer manuscript] so many veins, that this subject has now especially been undertaken: in how many ways we must guard against the breadth of idolatry. For in manifold ways it overthrows the servants of God, not only when unrecognized but also when willfully disregarded.

Most people suppose that idolatry should be understood simply in these ways alone: if someone burns incense, sacrifices, presents a sacred feast, or binds himself to some sacred rites or priesthoods. This is as though someone supposed that adultery should be reckoned only in kisses, embraces, and actual carnal intercourse, or that murder should be accounted only in the shedding of blood and the taking of life (Matt. 5:22). Yet we know how much more broadly the Lord defines these things: when He designates adultery even in lust, if anyone has fixed his eye lasciviously and stirred his soul impurely (ibid.); when He judges murder to exist even in a word of curse or abuse [Note: [Col. 0664D] “Indicates,” Junius], and in every [Col. 0664C] impulse of anger, and in neglect of charity toward a brother. Thus John teaches that whoever hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15).

Otherwise both the devil’s ingenuity in malice and that of the Lord God [Note: [Col. 0664D] “The Lord,” Junius] in discipline, by which He arms us against the heights [Note: [Col. 0664D] “Breadths,” Wouwer manuscript, Rigault] of the devil (Matt. 5; cf. Rev. 2:24), would consist in something trivial, if we were judged only for those offenses which even the nations have decreed should be punished [Note: [Col. 0664D] “If for these,” others]. How will our righteousness abound beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, as the Lord prescribed, unless we have perceived the abundance of its opposite, that is, injustice? But if idolatry is the head of injustice, our first task is to fortify ourselves against the abundance of idolatry by recognizing it not only in its manifest forms.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0664D]

At one time in the past there was no idol. Before the artisans of this monstrosity had burst forth, there were only temples and empty shrines, just as traces of antiquity remain in certain places to the present day. Idolatry was nevertheless practiced—not under that name, but in that deed. For even today it can be practiced outside a temple and without an idol.

But when the devil brought into the world the makers of statues and images and representations of every kind, [Col. 0665A] that primitive business of human ruin acquired both its name from idols and its further development. From that time onward, every art that in any way produces an idol became the head of idolatry. For it makes no difference whether a modeler shapes it, an engraver carves it, or an embroiderer works it out in thread; nor does its material matter—whether an idol is formed of plaster, pigments, stone, bronze, silver, or thread. For since idolatry can be committed even without an idol, it certainly makes no difference, when an idol is present, what sort it is, of what material or of what form [Note: [Col. 0665C] “Or of what form,” Junius], lest anyone suppose that only something consecrated in human form is to be regarded as an idol.

For this purpose an explanation of the word is necessary: εἶδος (“form”) in Greek signifies “form”; from it, by diminution [Note: [Col. 0665C] “Diminution,” Junius, from the manuscript], εἴδωλον (“little form,” hence “idol”) was derived, and likewise furnished us with the term “little form.” Therefore every form or little form demands to be called an idol. Hence [Col. 0665B] all servitude and service surrounding every idol is idolatry. Hence also every maker of an idol is guilty of the same single crime—unless the people committed only a little idolatry because they consecrated for themselves the image of a calf and not of a human being.

## CHAPTER IV

God forbids an idol both to be made and to be worshiped. Inasmuch as the making of what can be worshiped comes first [Note: [Col. 0665C] “By as much as its being made precedes.” This is a most noteworthy passage, so that you may know that images of the true God were never prohibited by natural law. Thus, from every age beginning with Adam himself, an image of God could be made so that it might be worshiped. Tertullian is to be commended here for this opinion, for he establishes parity of time in both cases. Just as in no age could that be made which could not be worshiped, so in every age that could be made which could be worshiped. But whether it was forbidden to the Jews by written law is disputed: Vasquez, one of the two most weighty doctors of this age, affirms that it was prohibited; Suárez denies it. Finally, insignificant as I am, I remain undecided. LAC.] so much the more must it first not be made, if it may not be worshiped. For this reason—namely, to root out the very material of idolatry—the divine law proclaims (Exod. 32; Lev. 26:1; Deut. 5:8): “You shall not make an idol” [Note: [Col. 0665D] “You shall not make an idol.” He translated literally, together with the Vulgate translator, the Seventy. The Greek is εἴδωλον (“idol”), as it is also in blessed Cyprian, chapter [—] of Book I, *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*. By that rendering the true sense of this passage is explained; the Author treats it more fully in Book II *Against Marcion*, where he interprets this passage of Scripture as concerning images containing the substance of idolatry. Moreover, he expresses in one phrase “and the things in the sea,” where others correctly translate from the Greek: “and whatsoever things are in the waters beneath the earth.” PAM.]. And, joining to it (Exod. 20:8), “nor a likeness of the things that are in heaven, and on earth, and in the sea,” He prohibited the servants of God throughout the entire world from arts of this kind.

Enoch had previously [Note: [Col. 0665C] “For this” added by François] foretold [Note: [Col. 0665C] “Enoch” is absent from Paris] [Note: [Col. 0665D] “Enoch had previously foretold.” The Book of Enoch entitled *The Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs* is often cited by Origen, Procopius, Tertullian, and others. It contains many prophecies about the crimes and punishments of the Hebrews, and among them this one concerning the propagation of idolatry throughout the whole circuit of the earth. Commonly circulated too was the account [Col. 0666C] of the two columns: one of stone, which would withstand water; the other of brick, which would withstand fire; in which this man’s books were enclosed. LAC.] that demons and the spirits of the apostate angels would turn all the elements, the entire contents [Note: [Col. 0665C] “Wealth,” Junius, Ciacconius] of the world—whatever is contained [Col. 0665C] in heaven, sea, and earth—to idolatry, so that they might be consecrated as gods in opposition to the Lord. [Col. 0666A] Human error therefore worships everything except the Creator of all things Himself. Their images are idols; the consecration of images is idolatry. Whatever idolatry commits must necessarily be charged to every maker of every kind of idol.

Finally, the same Enoch condemns beforehand in his threat both the worshipers and the makers of idols. And again [Note: [Col. 0665C] “Condemns utterly: I swear,” Junius]: “I swear to you, sinners, that repentance has been prepared for the day of bloodshed [Note: [Col. 0666C] “Bloodshed and,” Junius] and destruction. You who serve stones, and who make images of gold and silver, wood and stone and clay, and who serve phantoms and demons and infamous spirits [Note: [Col. 0666C] “Infamous,” Paris, Junius; “insane,” Wouwer manuscript] [Note: [Col. 0666C] “And infamous spirits.” In the codex of Fulvio Orsini it reads “insane”; but in the Codex Agobardinus, “infamous.” RIG.—“Infamous spirits.” I think the apostate spirits are here called “infamous.” The name “deserter” is taken from military service, and a soldier who deserted was infamous, as may be seen [Col. 0666D] in Law I, Digest, *On Those Who Are Marked with Infamy*. LE PR.], and every error without knowledge—you will find no help from them.”

[Col. 0666B] Isaiah, however, says (Isa. 44:8): “You are not witnesses whether there is a God besides Me.” And those who fashion and carve did not then exist; they are all vain, making what pleases themselves, things which will not profit them. And then follows that entire pronouncement in which he denounces both the makers and the worshipers, whose conclusion is (Isa. 44:20): “Know that their heart is ashes, and they err” [Note: [Col. 0666C] “Earth,” Rigault] [Note: [Col. 0666D] “Know that their heart is ashes, and they err.” This passage must certainly be restored in this way in place of the utterly corrupt reading “and earth.” For the words are very similar because of the same letters, and in Greek it is καὶ πλανῶνται (“and they err”). PAM.—“Know that it is ashes,” etc. Isaiah does not say this; does Tertullian therefore falsely attribute it to him? No, he explains him. Isaiah says that men were so foolish that they burned half a piece of wood to warm themselves and to bake bread and meat, while from the remainder of the wood they made a god for themselves and worshiped it. Tertullian therefore says in the person of Isaiah that the heart of the gods is ashes, because the middle and principal portion of the tree was turned to ashes. Thus the “heart” of Septimius and the “middle” of Isaiah are the same. LAC.], and no one can deliver his own soul.”

Likewise David says there [Note: [Col. 0666C] “Thus,” Junius], “And let those who make them become [Note: [Col. 0666C] “The makers” added by Junius, Paris, Rigault] like them” (Ps. 113:8) [Note: [Col. 0666D] “And let those who make them become like them.” Since otherwise the repetition of the same thing would be superfluous, we have omitted “the makers.” For in the book *Against the Gnostics* he reads nothing other than: “Those who make them shall be like them.” LAC.]. And why should I, a man of scant memory, supply anything further? Why should I recall anything more from the Scriptures? As though the voice of the Holy Spirit were insufficient, or there were any need for further deliberation over whether the Lord has cursed and condemned first the very makers of those things whose worshipers He curses and condemns.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0666C]

We shall certainly answer more forcefully the excuses [Col. 0667A] of makers of this kind, whom it is never fitting to admit into the house of God, if anyone understands that discipline. First comes the customary objection: “I have no other means by which to live” [Note: [Col. 0667C] “I have no other means by which to live.” This sufficiently indicates that many were accustomed to lapse from the faith because of necessity; Canon II of the Council of Nicaea concerns those who would lapse even apart from that necessity. LAC.]. It can be struck down more sternly: “Then you have a means by which to live. What have you to do with God, if you live on your own terms [Note: [Col. 0667C] “Let there be force according to your own laws” [reading uncertain], Wouwer Codex; “It becomes … according to your own laws” [corrupt reading], Fulvio Orsini]?”

Then there is the fact that they even dare to argue from the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0667C] “They dare to argue.” The people who display this audacity in twisting the Scriptures are called by Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, χαμαιλέοντες (“chameleons”), little creatures in whom change is innate. See his letter prefixed to the Nicene Synod. Note the expression of Theodoret, Book I of the *History*, chapter IV, ταῖς γραφαῖς ἐμπαροινοῦτες (“raving drunkenly against the Scriptures”). He is speaking of heretics—those, namely, who dare to inflict violence upon the sacred Scriptures, who seem, as though in a drunken frenzy, to rave against the sacred writings. LAC.], saying that the apostle declared that each person should remain as he was found (1 Cor. 7:20). By that interpretation, then, we can all remain in our sins. For none of us [Note: [Col. 0667C] “For” is absent from Paris] was found to be without sin (1 Cor. 4), since Christ descended for no other reason than to liberate sinners.

They likewise say that the same apostle commanded, following his own example (1 Thess. 4:11), that each person should work with his hands for his livelihood. If this precept is defended with respect to all handiwork, [Col. 0667B] I suppose bathhouse thieves too [Note: [Col. 0667D] “Bathhouse thieves.” The Codex Agobardinus has “thieves and bath attendants.” Rigault emends it to “thieves and gamblers,” for gambling too is practiced with the hands. If anyone nevertheless wishes to retain “bathhouse thieves,” there is no objection. For in his book *On Flight*, our Author also spoke of “thieves of the baths.” Indeed, he added, “and gamblers.” In the *Apologeticum*, p. 496, one finds “the robber of bathers.” RIG.—Pamelius has “bathhouse thieves,” which reading I think correct, for thus Catullus: “O finest of bathhouse thieves.” These, of course, were thieves against whom guards were stationed in the baths to protect clothing; those guards were called *capsarii*. But if they too had committed theft, they were summoned to court before the prefect of the watch, as in the law *Nam salutem* III, Digest, *On the Office of the Prefect of the Watch*. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 0667C] “Thieves and gamblers,” Rigault] live by their own hands, and robbers themselves use their hands to obtain a living. Likewise, counterfeiters certainly forge their criminal documents not with their feet but with their hands. Actors, however, labor for their livelihood not with their hands alone, but with all their limbs [Note: [Col. 0668C] “Labor for their livelihood with all their limbs.” He means pantomimes. RIG.].

Let the Church, therefore, lie open to all who sustain themselves by their hands and their own work, if there is no exception for arts which the discipline of God does not accept [Note: [Col. 0667C] “Did not accept,” François].

But someone says in opposition to the prohibition against making a likeness (Num. 21): “Why, then, did Moses make a bronze image of a serpent in the wilderness?” A separate category belongs to figures prepared in advance for some hidden dispensation—not in derogation of the law, but as representations of their own underlying subject [Note: [Col. 0668C] “Bestowal,” Semler] [Note: [Col. 0668D] “Representations.” Something that would serve posterity as a sign, figure, or enigma. RIG. “Of their own underlying subject”: that is, of the thing signified—namely, the Lord’s cross. RIG.]. Otherwise, if we interpret these things as adversaries of the law do, do we too, like the Marcionites, attribute inconsistency to the Almighty? They [Col. 0667C] destroy Him in this way as mutable, because He forbids in one place and commands in another [Note: [Col. 0668C] “To the Almighty? Because they,” Wouwer manuscript].

But if anyone willfully ignores that the image of the bronze serpent, suspended in that manner, signified the figure of the Lord’s cross [Note: [Col. 0668D] “Signified the figure of the Lord’s cross.” He treats this more fully in the book *Against the Jews* and in Book III *Against Marcion*. PAM.], which was to free us from serpents—that is, [Col. 0668A] from the devil’s angels—by hanging up the devil himself, that is, the serpent, slain upon it; or whatever other interpretation of that figure has been revealed to worthier persons; provided that the apostle affirms (1 Cor. 10) that all things then happened to the people figuratively, it is well that the same God who by law [Note: [Col. 0668C] “And by law,” Paris, Junius] forbade a likeness to be made commanded, by an extraordinary precept, a likeness of the serpent [Note: [Col. 0668C] “Ordered to be made,” Latinus; “introduced,” Junius; “prohibited,” François].

If you observe the same God, you have His law (Exod. 20:4): “You shall not make a likeness.” If you also look to the command concerning the likeness subsequently made, then imitate Moses yourself: do not make any image contrary to the law unless God has commanded you too.

## CHAPTER VI

Even if no law of God had forbidden us to make idols, even if no voice of the Holy Spirit threatened the makers of idols [Col. 0668B] no less than their worshipers, we would infer from our very sacrament that arts of this kind are opposed [Note: [Col. 0668D] “Are opposed to the faith.” For its meaning, read what is written concerning the five martyrs who suffered because they refused to make statues of idols. These accounts are contained in the *Life of the Four Crowned Saints*. Certainly, they suffered because they considered this art opposed to the faith. LAC.] to the faith. For how have we renounced the devil and his angels if we make them? What repudiation have we declared against those—not merely with whom, but from whom we live? What conflict have we undertaken against those to whom we are bound for the sake of our maintenance [Note: [Col. 0668D] “For the sake of our maintenance.” What he called “livelihood” in the preceding chapter he expresses circumlocutorily here; he uses the same word in this sense in Chapters VIII and XII. PAM.]?

Can you deny with your tongue what you confess with your hand? Destroy in word what you construct in deed? Proclaim one God when you create so many? Proclaim the true God when you make false ones?

“I make them,” someone says, “but I do not worship them.”

As though the reason why he does not dare to worship them were different [Note: [Col. 0668C] “Another,” François] from the reason why he ought not to make them—namely, offense against God in either case. Indeed, you do worship them, you who make it possible for them to be worshiped. You worship them, moreover, not with the spirit of some utterly worthless sacrificial odor, [Col. 0668C] but with your own spirit; not at the cost of an animal’s life, but of your own life. To them you sacrifice your ingenuity; to them you pour out your sweat as a libation; for them you kindle your skill. You are more to them than a priest, since through you they have a priest. [Col. 0669A] Your diligence is their divinity [Note: [Col. 0669B] “Name,” Venice].

Do you deny that you worship what you make? But those for whom you slaughter this richer, more gilded [Note: [Col. 0669C] “A more gilded and greater victim.” Festus says that *hostia* is so called from *hostire*, “to strike.” Others derive it from *hostes*, “enemies,” because such victims were customarily sacrificed after a victory, as Festus himself says elsewhere.
