He alludes, moreover, to those victims which were adorned with gold and were therefore called “gilded”; for the horns of cattle intended for sacrifice were commonly gilded. PAM.—“And a greater victim.” A greater victim or sacrificial animal is a bull, ox, or cow; a lesser one is a sheep, goat, or pig. This distinction is more certain than the claim that greater sacrificial animals are called *victimae* and lesser ones *hostiae*. You should also know that among the former the bull is the greater, and among the latter the sheep. LAC.] and greater victim—your salvation—do not deny it.

## CHAPTER VII

All day long the zeal of faith will plead its case on this subject, groaning that a Christian [Note: [Col. 0669C] “From idols into the Church.” The learned men Pamelius and La Cerda have compiled at great length the names given by the ancients to the house of God; after their harvest no gleaning remains. The first to assail the Church, or the assembly of Christians, was that Eustathius who said that churches ought to be despised. The Synod of Gangra [Col. 0669D] assembled against him and struck him with its thunderbolt in Canon V. He was followed by the Patarenes, against whom constitutions of Pope Honorius III and Emperor Frederick II remain. The Waldensians, Wycliffites, Hussites, and others also imitated these most wicked examples. Though sufficiently condemned together with Eustathius, they vainly object with Acts 17: “God does not dwell in temples made by hand.” One need only read what follows to silence these utterly shameless little men: namely, “nor is He worshiped by human hands, as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives all things to all,” etc. LE PR.] comes from idols into the Church, from the adversary’s [Note: [Col. 0669D] “To come from the adversary’s workshop into the house of God.” These words do not seem to belong to Tertullian, but to some glossator commenting on what precedes: “to come from idols into the Church.” RIG.] workshop into the house of God [Note: [Col. 0669B] “From the hostile workshop into the house of God,” Semler]; that he raises to God the Father hands that are the mothers of idols; that with those hands he adores [Note: [Col. 0669D] “To adore with those hands.” For they worshiped with hands raised, lifted, and spread toward God. RIG.] what outside is adored in opposition to God [Note: [Col. 0669D] “Which outside are adored in opposition to God.” The hands that were the mothers and makers of idols were adored by pagan [Col. 0670C] worshipers of idols. For what was a statue or idol before the artisan’s hand was applied to it except brute matter, which the skilled artisan’s hand carved into the likeness of some deity? Septimius speaks splendidly in his book *On the Resurrection*: “The hands of Phidias,” he says, “which fashioned the Olympian Jupiter from ivory, are adored; and what had been a beast, and a most senseless one at that, is now the supreme divinity of the age—not because the elephant was so great, but because Phidias was.” RIG.]; and that he brings those hands to the body of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0670C] “Brings his hands to the body of the Lord.” This passage concerns the custom by which the Eucharist was delivered into the hands, a custom attested for their own times by blessed Cyprian (*On the Lapsed*), blessed Cornelius (*To Fabius of Antioch*), blessed Dionysius of Alexandria (*To Pope Xystus*), blessed Ambrose (*Address to Emperor Theodosius*), Jerome (*To Theophilus*), etc. EDD.], though they bestow bodies upon demons.

Nor is this enough. Let it be considered too little if they receive from other hands what they defile [Note: [Col. 0669B] “May defile,” Wouwer manuscript]; they themselves [Note: [Col. 0669B] “Themselves” feminine, François] also deliver to others what they have defiled. Makers of idols are admitted into the ecclesiastical order. O crime! The Jews laid hands upon Christ once; these men assail His body every day. O hands that ought to be cut off! Let them now consider whether it was said figuratively: “If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off” (Matt. 18:8). What hands deserve more to be cut off than those by which [Note: [Col. 0669C] “Than those by which,” Junius] the Lord’s body is made to stumble?

## CHAPTER VIII

There are also many branches of other arts which, although they do not touch the manufacture of idols, nevertheless provide those things without which idols can do nothing and so fall under the same crime [Col. 0670A] [Note: [Col. 0670C] “Provide”: complete, adorn. RIG.]. For it makes no difference whether you construct or adorn, if you have furnished a temple, an altar, or its shrine; if you have beaten out gold leaf [Note: [Col. 0670C] “If you have beaten out gold leaf.” If you have beaten gold leaf from a mass of gold to overlay a bronze statue. RIG.], made its ornaments, or even constructed its house. Work of this kind is the greater, because it confers not an image but authority.

If the necessity of earning one’s livelihood is stretched this far [Note: [Col. 0670B] “Is pleaded,” Wouwer manuscript, Rigault, Leopold; “is regarded,” Junius], these arts have other branches that can provide the means of livelihood without departing from discipline—that is, without making an idol [Note: [Col. 0670B] “Fabrication,” Paris, Junius]. The plasterer knows both how to repair roofs and apply plaster, to seal a cistern [Note: [Col. 0670D] “To seal a cistern.” Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 23, indicates that this too is the work of a plasterer. Yet I myself think one should certainly read *ligare*, “to bind,” rather than *liare*, “to seal.” But I have been unwilling to alter the old reading, in case, like many others, it is a word peculiar to Tertullian that has now become obsolete. PAM.], extend moldings [Note: [Col. 0670D] “Extend moldings.” He seems to call the arches of temples or roofs themselves, when coated with plaster, *cymatia*, a word derived from κυματία (“waves”), that is, an inundation of waters, because those arches keep out the inundation of rainwater. PAM.—“Moldings.” That these are all ὑπεροχάς (“projections”), that is, projections on buildings, is both stated by Hesychius and readily inferred by anyone who has read Vitruvius. Pamelius therefore unjustly restricts this word to the arches of roofs and temples. For they are projections curved in the manner of a wave. In the Suda they are called λυσεῖς (“curves” or “bendings”); Vitruvius calls them *simae* from their shape. LAC.], and encrust walls with many other ornaments besides images [Note: [Col. 0670B] “Decorate,” Paris, Junius, Rigault, Rhenanus].

The painter, the marble-worker, the bronze-worker, and every engraver likewise knows that the scope of his art is certainly much broader and far easier. For one who draws a figure can paint a panel much more easily. One who carves Mars from linden wood can construct a cupboard much more quickly. There is no art that is not either the mother or a near relative of another art. Nothing stands free of another [Note: [Col. 0670D] “Nothing stands free of another.” Horace:

[Col. 0671C] Thus one thing  
Calls for another’s aid and joins with it in friendship. RIG.].

There are as many veins of art as there are human desires. But there is a difference in wages and payment for labor. Accordingly, there is also a difference in the labor itself. A smaller wage is compensated by more frequent employment. How many walls require images? How many temples and shrines are built for idols? But how numerous are houses, official residences, baths, and apartment buildings? Stage shoes and sandals are gilded every day; Mercury and Serapis are not. Let that suffice for the artisans’ profit. [Col. 0671A] Luxury and ostentation are more frequent [Note: [Col. 0671C] “Let them suffice—are more frequent,” François] than every superstition. Ostentation will demand dishes and cups more readily than superstition; luxury too supplies wreaths more often than solemn observance does.

Since, therefore, we encourage artisans toward those branches of their crafts which do not touch either an idol or the things belonging to an idol, although the same objects are often shared by human beings and idols, we must also take care that nothing from our hands is requested by anyone, with our knowledge, for the service of idols. If we permit this and do not employ the remedies now customary [Note: [Col. 0671C] “So customary,” Semler], I do not think that we are free from the contagion of idolatry, when our hands are found—knowingly—to be engaged in the service, honor, or use of demons.

Rigaltius.] member of the same order of the dead.

[Col. 0673C] Rigaltius.] up for sale through the laying-on of hands—[Col. 0673A] was cursed by the apostles and cast out of the faith (Acts VIII.20). One whose finger or measuring-rod abuses heaven cannot hope for the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER X

Inquiry must also be made concerning elementary-school teachers [Col. 0674A] and the other professors of letters—or rather, there must be no doubt that they are connected with idolatry in many forms. First, they are obliged to proclaim the gods of the nations, to recite their names, genealogies, myths, and every honorific distinction belonging to them; then to observe their solemn days and festivals, since these provide their income.

What schoolmaster [Note: [Col. 0673D] *What schoolmaster, without a tablet of the seven idols.* The earlier reading was: “What schoolmaster, if not the record offices of idols, will nevertheless attend the Quinquatria?” This makes no sense. The old reading, already noticed by Barraeus and now also confirmed by the manuscript of Agobard, was entirely correct. It runs as follows: “What schoolmaster without a tablet of the seven idols will nevertheless attend the Quinquatria?” But for the meaning to be evident, punctuation must be supplied: “What schoolmaster is without a tablet of the seven idols?” Then, not as a question but as an assertion: “Nevertheless, he will attend the Quinquatria.” Or, if the question is placed at the end, one must necessarily read as we have printed it: “What schoolmaster, though without a tablet of the seven idols, will nevertheless not attend the Quinquatria?” Thus, whichever way one reads it, the sense will be the same: [Col. 0674B] there is no schoolmaster who does not have in his school or classroom a tablet of the seven idols—that is, the seven planets: the Moon, Mars, Mercury, and the others, from which the names of the days of every week derive. Or, if anyone is found without a tablet of this sort, he will nevertheless be an attendant at the Quinquatria. What use this tablet or register of seven days had among schoolmasters is not worth investigating more diligently. Perhaps it prescribed or indicated what had to be assigned to or recited by pupils on each day. Juvenal, *Satires* VII:

> Nothing suits the Arcadian youth, whose wretched head  
> Is filled for me with dread Hannibal every sixth day.

On that day, evidently, the sum of the whole week was collected. On the seventh day, rest and leisure. Tertullian himself, in Book I of *To the Nations*, chapter XIII: “You surely are the people who have admitted the sun into the register of seven days and selected that day above the others, on which you either refrain from bathing, postpone it until evening, or make provision for leisure [Col. 0674D] and a meal.” Rigaltius.], though without a tablet of the seven idols, will nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0673B] Thus it is written in the manuscript of Agobard. Rhenanus: “What schoolmaster, if he does not attend the records of idols.” Rigaltius: “will nevertheless not attend.” Latinus: “nevertheless not.” Junius preferred: “Will he not nevertheless attend the Quinquatria?” [Col. 0674B]] attend the Quinquatria? [Note: [Col. 0674D] *Will nevertheless attend the Quinquatria.* The Quinquatria, or Quinquatrus—the rites of Minerva—derive their name from the conjunction of five days. Ovid likewise summons schoolmasters to these rites in Book III of the *Fasti*:

> Nor, you throng deprived of the fee owed your stern master,  
> Despise him: he attracts new pupils.

Rigaltius.]

He consecrates the very first payment of a new pupil to the honor and name of Minerva, so that, even if he is not [Note: [Col. 0674B] *So that, if*, Paris edition.] personally profaned to some idol, he may nominally be said to partake of a thing sacrificed to an idol. [Note: [Col. 0674D] *May nominally be said to partake of a thing sacrificed to an idol.* In the common editions there follows: “Let him be avoided as an idolater.” This does not appear to be Tertullian’s, even though in the manuscript of Agobard it is found as: “It is avoided as idolatry.”] What less pollution is there in the fact that his earnings are dedicated to the names and honors of an idol? The Minervalia are as much Minerva’s as the Saturnalia are Saturn’s, and even little slaves must celebrate the latter when the Saturnalia occur. [Col. 0674B] New Year’s gifts must also be solicited, as well as the seven-coin fee, and all the customary payments for midwinter and the festival of dear kinship must be demanded. The school must be crowned for Flora; [Note: [Col. 0674B] *Of Flora*, Franeker edition.] [Note: [Col. 0674D] *The school must be crowned for Flora.* At the Floralia, that is, the sacred rites of Flora.] priestesses and aediles offer sacrifice, and when special holidays are proclaimed, [Note: [Col. 0674B] *In sacred buildings to Ceres*, Rhenanus.] the school [Note: [Col. 0674D] *When special holidays are proclaimed, the school is honored with holidays.* Thus reads the old copy. Previously the absurd reading was “the school of Ceres.” He calls them “proclaimed holidays” because they were neither fixed nor regular, but announced by proclamation—namely, proclaimed by the aediles or priestesses on account of certain sacrifices.] is honored with holidays. The same thing occurs on an idol’s birthday: the whole pomp of the devil is attended. [Col. 0675A] Who will think these things appropriate to a Christian [Note: [Col. 0675C] *Who will think these things appropriate to a Christian.* That is, to every Christian, pupil as well as teacher. For he says that a pupil who must learn letters from a pagan teacher can be excused; but that a Christian who, after pledging his faith to Christ, becomes a schoolmaster and teaches letters through frequent readings of the poets cannot be tolerated, because of the pollutions of the idols, which he nevertheless appears to approve by expounding and explaining them. [Col. 0675D] Rigaltius.], unless he also thinks them appropriate to one who is not a teacher?

We know that it can be said: “If God’s servants are not permitted to teach letters, neither will they be permitted to learn them. And how could anyone be trained in ordinary human prudence, or in any understanding or activity whatever, when [Note: [Col. 0675C] *For which*, Rigaltius.] literary education is the instrument of every part of life? How can we reject secular studies, without which divine studies are impossible?” Let us therefore consider the necessity of literary education. Let us recognize that in one respect it cannot be admitted, and in another it cannot be avoided. It is more allowable for believers to learn letters than to teach them. For the rationale of learning and teaching is different.

If a believer teaches literature permeated [Note: [Col. 0675C] *Permeated*, Wouwer, manuscript.] by the proclamation [Note: [Col. 0675C] *Proclamations*, Rigaltius.] of idols, then without doubt, while teaching, he commends them; while transmitting the material, he affirms them; while recalling them, he bears testimony to them (Exod. XXIII.13). By this very designation he authenticates them as gods, although [Col. 0675B] the law forbids, as we have said, the pronouncing of gods (Exod. XX) and the application of that name to vanity. From this, faith in the devil is first built up at the very beginnings of education. Ask whether one who catechizes about idols [Note: [Col. 0675D] *One who catechizes about idols.* From this the Author’s position is apparent: in the preceding discussion he is not speaking of the mere utterance of the gods and their names, but of catechizing and proclamation and honorific mention. Let no one twist this against me who may perhaps think me rather lengthy in explaining these matters. But let the reader remember that I write these annotations not for the learned, but especially for the uneducated. Pamelius.] commits idolatry.

But when a believer learns these things, if he already understands what he is, he neither receives nor admits them; much more so if he does not yet [Note: [Col. 0675C] *Long since*, Venice edition, Semler.] understand. Or when he begins to understand, he must first understand what he first learned—that is, concerning God and the faith. Accordingly, he will reject those things and will not receive them. He will be as safe as one who knowingly accepts poison from an ignorant person but does not drink it. Necessity is reckoned to this person as an excuse, because he cannot learn otherwise. It is as much easier not to teach letters than not to learn them as it is easier for the believing pupil not to take part in the other pollutions arising from the schools’ public and particular solemnities than for the teacher not to attend them.

## CHAPTER XII

We wrongly flatter ourselves concerning the necessities of human subsistence if, after our faith has been sealed, we say: [Col. 0678A] “I have nothing by which to live.” For here I shall give a fuller answer to that abrupt objection: it is made too late. The matter ought to have been considered beforehand, following the example of that most prudent builder [Note: [Col. 0677D] *That builder.* *Aedifex* is used for a builder, not only of houses but of any structure whatever; and shortly afterward *defunctus* does not mean “dead,” but one who fails in the work he has begun. Pamelius.] who first calculates the cost of the work in relation to his resources, lest, having begun, he should later be ashamed when they fail. [Note: [Col. 0678C] *Having failed*, Franeker edition.]

But even now you have the sayings of the Lord and examples which deprive you of every excuse. What do you say? “I shall be in need.” But the Lord calls the needy blessed. “I shall have no food.” But he says, “Take no thought for food.” And for clothing we have the example of the lilies. “I needed property.” On the contrary, everything must be sold and distributed to the needy. “But provision must be made for children and posterity.” No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the work. “But I was bound by a condition of service.” [Note: [Col. 0677D] *But I was bound by a condition of service.* We emended this from the manuscript of Agobard, in which the text reads: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the work and I was bound by a condition of service.” It is clear that it must be punctuated as we have printed it. A *conditionalis* is a slave assigned and bound to a specified condition: Law VII, *On the Law of the Treasury*; “conditional clerks,” in the Theodosian Code, *On Accountants, Clerks*, etc. [Col. 0678C] Rigaltius.] No one can serve two masters. [Col. 0678B]

If you wish to be the Lord’s disciple, you must take up your cross and follow the Lord—that is, your distresses and sufferings, or simply your body, which is in the form of a cross. [Note: [Col. 0678C] *Which is in the form of a cross.* We judge that this was the ancient reading, and the traces still visible in the old copies support it. For in them it is written thus: “Or simply the body, which is in the form of Xps.” If we possessed copies of the original exemplars from which Agobard ordered his own to be transcribed, the origin of the corrupt reading would be evident. Meanwhile, one may suppose that in the most ancient copies it was written, “which is in the form of Xis”; since this symbol denoted a cross, it easily passed into “Xps,” which means Christ. Barraeus also testifies that it was written this way in his copy. What Tertullian says here—that our body is in the form of a cross—he explains still more clearly in Book I of *To the Nations*, chapter 12: “In our body itself, through a silent and hidden line, lies the configuration of the cross: the head which rises up, the spine which is held upright, the joining of the shoulders . . . If you set up a man with his hands outstretched, you will have made the image of a cross.” [Col. 0678D] Rigaltius.]

Parents, spouses, and children will have to be left for God’s sake. Do you hesitate about crafts, trades, and professions even for the sake of children and parents? It was already demonstrated to us then that both those dear to us and our crafts and occupations must be abandoned for the Lord, when James and John, called by the Lord, leave both their father and their boat; when Matthew is raised up from the tax-office; when even delaying to bury one’s father was too slow for faith. None of those whom the Lord chose said, “I have nothing by which to live.”

Faith does not fear hunger. [Note: [Col. 0678D] *Faith does not fear hunger.* Jerome always esteemed Tertullian highly, for he took many maxims from him, among them this one. Thus, in his letter to Heliodorus: “Do you think about food? But faith does not fear hunger.” Arator, Book II of the *History of the Apostles*, said:

> For faith does not know how to fear dangers.

La Cerda.] It knows that hunger too must be despised for God’s sake [Col. 0679A] no less than every kind of death. It has learned not to regard life; how much less, then, the means of living? How few have fulfilled these things! But what is difficult with men is easy with God.

## CHAPTER XIII

Let us nevertheless take comfort in the gentleness and mercy of God in such a way that we do not grant concessions to necessity even as far as associations with idolatry. Rather, let us avoid every breath of it, like a pestilence, even from afar—not only in the matters which we have already set forth, but throughout the whole succession of human superstition, whether devoted to its gods, the dead, or kings, since it pertains to the same unclean spirits: sometimes through sacrifices and priesthoods, sometimes through spectacles and things of that kind, and sometimes [Col. 0679B] through feast days.

But why should I speak about sacrifices and priesthoods? Concerning spectacles and pleasures of that kind we have already filled a volume of their own. What must be reconsidered here concerns feast days and other extraordinary solemnities, which we sometimes ascribe to our self-indulgence and sometimes to our timidity, sharing with the nations in idolatrous [Col. 0680A] matters contrary to the discipline of the faith.

On this matter I shall first take my stand: whether a servant of God ought to participate with the nations themselves in things of this kind, whether in dress, food, or any other form of their rejoicing. “Rejoice with those who rejoice, and mourn with those who mourn,” was said by the apostle concerning the brethren, as an exhortation to unanimity (Rom. XII.15). But as regards these matters, light has no communion with darkness, nor life with death; otherwise we annul what is written (2 Cor. VI.14; John XVI.20): “The world will rejoice, but you will mourn.” If we rejoice with the world, it is to be feared that we shall also mourn with the world. But let us mourn while the world rejoices, and afterward, when the world mourns, we shall rejoice (Luke XVI.19). Thus Lazarus too [Note: [Col. 0679B] *Eleazar*, Paris edition and others.] [Note: [Col. 0679B] *Thus Lazarus too.* “In the manuscript of Agobard, *Eleazar*, not *Lazarus*, is written everywhere. So too in Prudentius, *Hymn on Burial*:

> Hidden in the bosom of the holy old man
Restoration notes: S001098 has the recovered spelling θύπα, which is anomalous, but the surrounding text explicitly establishes the intended meaning as “door”; the recovered form is therefore preserved.  

He will recline where Eleazar is. RIG. Thus Lazarus also is in Abraham’s bosom in the lower regions. From [Col. 0679C] the Lord’s words to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise”; from Abraham’s words concerning Lazarus to the rich man clothed in purple; from John’s vision of the souls of the martyrs beneath the altar; and from Paul’s words in 1 Thessalonians, chapter 4, most of the ancients held the opinion that in the lower regions there are receptacles for the souls of the righteous and the wicked while they await the day of divine judgment. Meanwhile, however, the righteous enjoy peace, rest, and refreshment, while the wicked, by contrast, are tormented by imprisonment, fires, and Gehenna. The receptacles of the righteous are indeed in a subterranean recess, but built far above the lower abysses of the wicked; between the two, moreover, is fixed a chasm of insuperable depth.

Since, therefore, Tertullian held this opinion, there is nothing surprising here in his placing both Lazarus and Abraham’s bosom in the lower regions. For in the same sense, in his book *On the Soul*, he says that Christ’s soul, after departing from his crucified body, descended to the lower regions in order to make the patriarchs possessors of himself. Others, with the same faith, also believed that paradise was in the lower regions—the paradise which [Col. 0679D] Christ appointed for the thief; for by the word “paradise” is meant a garden, meadow, or any other place of pleasant refreshment, where the patriarchs, Abraham, Jacob, Lazarus, that believer who had been a thief, and also the souls of the martyrs rest in tranquility.

As for the martyrs, our Septimius seems to have thought in this way in the *Scorpiace*, when he says that their souls beneath the altar feed upon patience and, clothed in a white robe, make use of their glory. It is as though that place beneath the altar, ὑποκάτω θυσιατηρίου (“beneath the altar”), revealed to John, signifies by the name “altar” the earth upon which the bodies of the martyrs lay after being sacrificed, as though upon an altar; from there their souls were carried by angels into subterranean places of delight, where they await the resurrection and the kingdom of God. A delay so slight—even if it lasts many years—is by no means burdensome to the saints because of their worldly confidence in eternal glory.

Nevertheless, what Septimius taught in his book *On the Resurrection* [Col. 0680B] shows that he was not very consistent in this opinion. For after proving that every soul is sequestered in the lower regions until the day of the Lord, he immediately exempts the souls of the martyrs from that arrangement, saying that they will lodge in paradise, not in the lower regions. By these words he certainly denies that paradise is in the lower regions, even though in his book *On the Soul*, following Irenaeus’s opinion, he had said that Christ himself underwent the form of human [Col. 0680C] death in the lower regions, and that those who did not think the souls of the faithful worthy of the lower regions were excessively proud. “Servants above their lord,” he says, “and disciples above their master, if they disdain perhaps to receive in Abraham’s bosom the consolation of awaiting the resurrection.” From these things, therefore, we gather that people in that age were still very uncertain and doubtful about these matters.”

Thus far Rigault. The remaining claims that he added, apparently to weaken the Catholic doctrine of Christ’s descent into the lower regions, are devoid of truth and savor of heresy. Against this commentator it will suffice to set what Noël Alexandre asserted in his *Dissertation on the Creed of Faith*: “That Christ’s soul descended into the lower regions—that is, into the place theologians call the Limbo of the Fathers—not merely in power and operation but in reality and presence, is a dogma of faith, confirmed by the testimony of Sacred Scripture and the unanimous agreement of the Fathers. Both the Greek and the Latin Fathers concur in asserting this same Catholic dogma.” (*Complete Course of Theology*, [Col. 0680D] vol. VI, p. 239 ff.). See also the profession of the Catholic faith (*Complete Course of Theology*, vol. I, p. 1000).

Since Rigault cited Rufinus in support of his own opinion, as though Christ’s descent into the lower regions were not read in the creed of the Catholic Church, it is especially appropriate to reproduce the very words expressed by Rufinus himself concerning the Apostles’ Creed: “Crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried, HE DESCENDED INTO THE LOWER REGIONS.” (*Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, attributed to Rufinus, among the works of St. Cyprian, Pamelius’s edition, p. 544). EDD.]

having obtained refreshment in Abraham’s bosom in the lower regions; by contrast, the rich man, placed in fiery torment—they balance the alternating lots of evils and goods by a corresponding retribution. [Col. 0680B] [Note: [Col. 0680B] “It is recompensed,” Paris.]

There are certain days for gifts [Note: [Col. 0680D] “Days for gifts, which in some cases discharge a claim of honor.” The pagans had days for gifts and days for New Year’s presents. Tertullian himself says on the next page: “Gifts circulate, New Year’s presents resound.” RIG.], which in some cases discharge a claim of honor and in others a debt of payment. Specify the form in which [Note: [Col. 0681C] “The form in which,” Rigault.] you wish others to deal with you. [Note: [Col. 0681D] “Specify the form in which you wish others to deal with you; for why should you also remain concealed?” Choose, he says, the rule under which you wish others to deal with you: Christians may be known or unknown among pagans. For when you observe the pagans’ solemn days among them, you will cause yourself to remain concealed and the pagan to suppose that you are not a Christian; and this is deceit which contaminates your conscience by the very fact that it induces ignorance of the truth. RIG.] For why should you also remain concealed, when you contaminate your conscience through another person’s ignorance? If it is not unknown that you are a Christian, you are being put to the test and are acting against another person’s conscience as though you were not a Christian. Indeed, even if you have dissembled [Note: [Col. 0681C] “And you will be passed over in silence,” Paris, Rigault.], once tested, you stand condemned. Certainly, whether in this direction or that, you are guilty of being ashamed of God (Matt. 10:32; Luke 9:26). “But whoever has been ashamed of me before men, I too will be ashamed of him,” he says, “before my Father who is in heaven.”

## CHAPTER XIV

But many have now persuaded themselves that indulgence must be granted if, on some occasion, [Col. 0681B] they do what the pagans do, lest the Name be blasphemed. [Note: [Col. 0681C] “On some such occasion,” Franeker, Rigault.] Now the blasphemy that we must altogether avoid is, I think, this: if one of us gives a pagan just cause for blasphemy through fraud, injury, insult, or some other ground for a legitimate complaint, in which the Name is deservedly assailed, so that the Lord too is deservedly angry. [Note: [Col. 0681C] “The Lord is angry with him,” the first and only Leopold edition.]

But if the words, “Because of you my name is blasphemed” (Rom. 2:24), were spoken of every blasphemy, [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Woe, because of whom,” Paris, Junius, Pamelius; “because of you,” Leopold.] we all perish, since the whole circus assails the Name with its wicked acclamations and without any just cause. Let us cease to exist, and it will no longer be blasphemed! On the contrary, let it be blasphemed while we abide by the rule, not while we deviate from the discipline; while we are approved, not while we are rejected. O blasphemy [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Because of blasphemy,” Franeker.] akin to martyrdom, [Col. 0681C] which bears witness that I am a Christian at the very time that I am detested because of it! It is a blessing of the Name, a curse occasioned by the preservation of discipline.

“If,” he says, “I wished to please men, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). Yet the same apostle elsewhere (1 Cor. 10:33) commands us to take care to please everyone: “Just as I,” he says, “please everyone in all things.” Surely he pleased men by celebrating the Saturnalia and the January Kalends? Or was it by modesty and patience, by dignity, by kindness, and by integrity? Likewise, when he says, “I became all things to all people, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9:22), did he become an idolater to idolaters, a pagan to pagans, or worldly to the worldly?

Even though he does not prohibit us from associating with idolaters, adulterers, and other criminals, saying (1 Cor. 5:10), “Otherwise you would have to leave the world” [Note: [Col. 0681C] “You would have to leave,” Paris, Petit, Rhenanus, Rigault; “you would have left,” Semler, Ciacconius.], he certainly does not thereby loosen the reins of association so that, because we must live and mingle [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Mingle,” Paris.] with sinners, we may therefore also sin with them. [Note: [Col. 0682C] “Therefore also sin together,” Rigault.] There is the intercourse of life, which the Apostle permits; here there is sinning, which no one permits. It is lawful to live with pagans; it is not lawful to die with them. Let us live with everyone; let us rejoice together by communion of nature, [Col. 0682B] [Note: [Col. 0682C] The Agobard and Paris manuscripts read: “We are equal in soul, not in discipline.”], not of superstition. We are equal in soul, not in discipline; co-possessors of the world, not of error.

But if we have no right to share in such things with outsiders, how much more wicked is it to practice them among brethren! [Note: [Col. 0682C] “For them to be practiced,” Junius.] Who can tolerate or defend this? The Holy Spirit reproaches the Jews for their own solemn days: “Your Sabbaths,” he says, “and new moons and ceremonies my soul hates” (Isa. 1:14). Yet among us—to whom Sabbaths, new moons, and festivals once beloved by God are foreign—the Saturnalia, the January festivals, the Brumae, [Note: [Col. 0681D] “And the Brumae.” He means the winter festivals called the Brumalia. They were held in honor of Bacchus, the inventor of winepresses and presses, around the month Lenaeon—that is, our January. Among the Greeks those festivals were also called Ambrosia; what the Romans called Brumalia the Greeks called Ambrosia, for Dionysus among them is Brumus. In this interpretation Pamelius, following Lilius Giraldus, may have gone astray. Tzetzes discusses this word at length in his scholia on book II of Hesiod’s *Works*. LE PR.] and the Matronal festivals [Note: [Col. 0682D] “And the Matronalia.” The celebration of these festivals occurred on the Kalends of March; their solemnity concerned mothers and matrons. O how much more faithful the nations are to their own sect! They claim no Christian solemnity for themselves—neither the Lord’s Day nor Pentecost. What is to be thought about this practice too? If it is an honor paid to an idol, then honor paid to an idol is unquestionably idolatry. If it is done for a human being’s sake, let us remember that all idolatry exists for the sake of a human being. Let us remember that all idolatry is worship directed toward human beings, since it is established even among the nations themselves that the gods of the nations were formerly human beings. Therefore, it makes no difference whether this superstition is rendered to men of an earlier age or of the present one. [Col. 0683B] Idolatry was condemned not because of the persons who are set before us, [Note: [Col. 0683C] “Set beside us,” Latinus, Rigault, Franeker, Junius, Leopold; the others read “set before us.”] but because of those condemned services, which pertain to demons.

“The things that are Caesar’s must be rendered to Caesar” (Matt. 22)—well that he added, “and the things that are God’s to God.” What, then, belongs to Caesar? Obviously, the things about which the question was then raised: whether the tax ought to be paid to Caesar or not. For that reason the Lord also asked that a coin be shown to him and inquired whose image it bore. When he heard, “Caesar’s,” he said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” [Note: [Col. 0683D] “And the things that are God’s, to God.” Note this very acute exposition by Tertullian, which he draws out of Christ’s words. For just as the coin must be given to Caesar because it bears Caesar’s image, so the human being must be given to God because the human being is God’s image. LAC.]; that is, render Caesar’s image, which is on the coin, to Caesar, and God’s image, which is in the human being, to God—so that you render money to Caesar, but yourself to God. Otherwise, what will belong to God if everything belongs to Caesar?

“Then,” you say, “are lamps before the doors and laurels upon the doorposts an honor paid to God?” Certainly not as an honor to God, but as an honor to the one who is honored as a god by services of this kind, so far as the matter is outwardly apparent, while the operation reaching the demons remains hidden. [Col. 0683C]

For we ought to be certain—even if some are ignorant of it through lack of secular learning—that among the Romans there are gods even of doors: Cardea, named from the hinges; Forculus [Note: [Col. 0683C] Rigault’s manuscript has *foriculum* or *foreculum*.], from the doors; Limentinus, from the threshold; and Janus himself, from the doorway. And we certainly know that, although these names are empty and fictitious, nevertheless, when they are drawn into superstition, they attract demons and every unclean spirit to themselves through the bond of consecration. Otherwise demons have no individual names; rather, they find a name where they also find a pledge.

Among the Greeks also we read of Apollo θυραῖον (*Thyraion*, “of the doorway”) [Note: [Col. 0683D] Apollo Thyraeus. For in Greek θύπα (“door”; recovered spelling preserved) means “door.” Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 9, supplies the explanation. The words of the scholiast on Sophocles’ *Electra* pertain to this: when Sophocles calls Phoebus *prostaterios*, the scholiast says, προστατήριε, ὂτι πρὸ τῶν θυρῶν ἵδρυται, “O guardian, because he is stationed before the doors.” Aristides too, in his hymn to Minerva, mentions Apollo προπυλαίου (*Propylaios*, “of the gateway”). LAC.] and Antelii [Note: [Col. 0684D] “And the Antelii demons.” Rhenanus, in *On the Crown*: Among the Greeks the Antelii are gods dedicated to doors. Accordingly, as regards honors paid to kings or emperors (Rom. 13:7), we have a sufficiently definite rule: in accordance with the Apostle’s command, we ought to be entirely obedient, subject to magistrates, rulers, and powers—but within the limits of discipline, so long as we are kept separate from idolatry. [Note: [Col. 0684C] “Exalts,” Rigault.]

[Note: [Col. 0684C] “From discipline,” Junius.] For rather than incur that danger, he no more feared the king’s lions than the others feared the king’s fires.

If you have renounced temples, do not make your door a temple. ## CHAPTER XVI

But with regard to the duties connected with private and shared solemnities [Note: [Col. 0685B] “Shared.” Just as solemnities appropriate to only one person are called private, so those appropriate to two people—such as weddings and betrothals—are called shared. LAC.], such as the assumption of the plain toga, [Note: [Col. 0685B] “Such as the plain toga.” Which toga he means here he soon makes clear, first by the words “the clothing of manhood,” and then by the words “the toga is also called manly”: namely, the toga that boys assumed at seventeen years of age after laying aside the *praetexta*. It is also called “plain”—as Budé testifies—because it was neither embroidered, triumphal, nor bordered. Cicero mentions the same toga in book IX of his letters to Atticus, when he writes that he gave his own Cicero the plain toga. PAM.], betrothals, weddings, and naming ceremonies, [Note: [Col. 0685C] “Such as naming ceremonies,” etc. Here, in his usual manner, he attacks the ridiculous superstition of the pagans, who drew either a good or a bad omen from the day on which a child was named. That day was the seventh day of the week, although Lacerda writes that this occurred on the tenth day. The Latins called it the *lustricus* day, while the Greeks called it ἀμφιδρόμα (*Amphidromia*); the same day was called *Nominalia* because of that celebration. On this matter see the admirable Scaliger on Festus and Ausonius, Casaubon on Persius’s second satire, and Cicero, *Philippic* 13. LE PR.], I think that no danger need be perceived from the breath of idolatry that intervenes. For the causes for which the service is rendered must be considered. I think that these causes are pure in themselves, since neither the clothing of manhood, nor a ring, nor marital union derives from the honoring of any idol.

Indeed, I find no clothing cursed by God except female clothing on a man (Deut. 22:5): “For accursed,” he says, “is everyone who puts on women’s garments.” The toga, however, is even called “manly.” [Note: [Col. 0685C] “The toga, however, is even called manly.” For it is called the *toga virilis*, not simply a toga. RIG.] God no more prohibits the celebration of marriages [Col. 0686A] than the giving of a name. But sacrifices are attached to these occasions.

Suppose I have been invited, [Note: [Col. 0685C] “Suppose I have been invited, and let there be no designation of participation in sacrifice.” We have corrected this passage, most corrupt in all the printed books, from the Agobard manuscript. We shall easily prove through explanation that the correction is entirely sound. Christians subject to pagan rule very frequently encountered reasons to hesitate and deliberate whether, and to what extent, their labor or services were owed to pagan authorities when those authorities commanded or summoned them, without danger of idolatry.

For example, in the household or retinue of a governor or proconsul there may be slaves and freedmen, attendants, secretaries, copyists, and heralds, among whom are Christians; and certain solemn occasions may arise on which appointed festivals and sacrifices are customarily celebrated. The governor orders certain preparations belonging to these solemnities. What course will a Christian take here? Will he obey the man giving the command? Then he will be a supporter and servant of idolatry. Will he refuse obedience? Then he will be defiant toward authority.

God certainly abominates every form of worship of idols. Yet he also confirms the rights of rulers and authorities, allows no Christian defiance, and indeed compels everyone to perform the duties of obedience. In this case Tertullian establishes the distinction that, as regards honors paid to kings or emperors, Christians have a sufficiently definite rule: in accordance with the Apostle’s command, they ought to be entirely obedient, subject to magistrates, rulers, and powers—but within the limits of discipline, so long as they are kept separate from idolatry.

But with regard to the duties connected with private and shared solemnities, such as the assumption of the plain toga, betrothals, weddings, and naming ceremonies, “I think,” he says, “that no danger need be perceived from the breath of idolatry that intervenes. For the causes for which the service is rendered must be considered.” He then raises the objection: “But sacrifices are attached to these”—that is, to betrothals, naming ceremonies, and other solemnities of this kind.

He immediately resolves the objection by assuming the person of a Christian slave or freedman whom a pagan master ordered to attend or appear before himself or his son while offering sacrifice on the solemn occasion of assuming the plain toga or of a betrothal. “Suppose I have been invited,” he says, “provided that the performance of my duty and labor cannot be regarded as participation in sacrifice”—that is, as administration of, participation in, or consent to sacrifice. Let him make use of my labor and service as much as he pleases.

He immediately qualifies this wish: “I wish that ‘as much as he pleases’”—as though he said: I wish that the words I have just spoken, “as much as he pleases,” could be detached from my duty or labor, so that the pagan master would no longer summon any Christian to these solemnities, and we would not be able to see things that it is unlawful for us to do. But because Satan has so enveloped the world in idolatry, it will be lawful to be present on certain occasions that require us to serve a human being, not an idol.

He then concludes his position: “But otherwise”—that is, without the indulgence allowed by this distinction—“what will believing slaves or free persons, as well as officials, do when they attend masters, patrons, or governors who are sacrificing?” The occasion for corrupting this passage was the failure to understand the expression *ad sacrificii*. For those ignorant of its meaning altered it and wrote *in sacrificiis* in its place. The phrase “designation of *adsacrificium*” is not meaningless, just as one finds “by reason of *admilitia*” in the sole law *On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect*.

Arcadius says that, since among the ancients supreme power was entrusted to dictators for a limited period, they chose masters of the cavalry for themselves, who, joined to them and sharing in their responsibility “by reason of *admilitia*,” exercised the second-highest authority after them. So it is read in the Florentine Pandects, not, as commonly, “by reason of military service.” The masters of the cavalry served alongside the praetorian prefects, and their responsibility was called *admilitia* because they had been added and joined to the responsibility of the praetorian prefects.

Likewise, in sacrifices those were said to *adsacrificare* who were present with the sacrificer because of the sacrifice, and who assisted the person performing the rites by advice or expense. The “discharge” of duty and labor means their payment and performance. RIG.] and let the discharge of my duty and labor bear no designation of participation in sacrifice, [Note: [Col. 0685B] Thus Rigault corrected it; in the other editions, μηδὲν ὑγιές (“nothing sound”).] however much he pleases. [Note: [Col. 0686B] “What then? If he pleases. I wish indeed that not even,” Semler.] I wish that “however much he pleases” did not apply, and that we could not even see the things it is unlawful for us to do! Certainly, if I am summoned to a priesthood or sacrifice, I will not go, for that is a service belonging specifically to an idol; nor will I perform any function of that kind by advice, expense, or any other labor. If I attend because of the sacrifice, I shall be a participant in idolatry; if some other cause associates me with the person sacrificing, I shall be merely a spectator of the sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XIX

In this chapter the question of military service, which stands between rank and power, might also seem to have been settled. But the present inquiry is whether a believer may enter military service, and whether someone in military service may be admitted to the faith—even a common soldier, or anyone of lower rank [Col. 0690B] [Note: [Col. 0690B] “Also,” Wouw. MS.] who is under no necessity of offering sacrifices or passing capital sentences.

There is no compatibility between the divine and the human oath of service, the standard of Christ and the standard of the devil, the camp of light and the camp of darkness. One soul cannot be indebted to two masters, God and Caesar (Matt. 22; Exod. 3; Exod. 28; Matt. 3; Exod. 17; Luke 3; Matt. 8; Matt. 26). Moses carried a rod, and Aaron a clasp; [Note: [Col. 0690C] **And Aaron a clasp.** He means the golden hooks by which the ephod and breastplate were fastened together, just as by “strap” he means John the Baptist’s leather belt. PAM.] John too is girded with a strap; Joshua the son of Nun leads an army; and the people waged war—if one chooses to trifle with the question.

But how will he wage war— [Note: [Col. 0690C] **But how will he wage war—indeed, how will he serve as a soldier even in peace, without the sword that the Lord took away?** Those who, even outside wartime, remain armed at stations and garrisons, or appear under arms before the emperor and the other authorities to carry out orders, are said to “serve as soldiers in peace.” The discipline of the early Christians was that those whom the faith found in any branch of military service should, in accordance with John’s command, remain in their service. But it scarcely occurred that those who had not served before embracing the faith enlisted afterward; indeed, most who had been soldiers before the faith laid down both belt and sword after they had been converted to the faith. For this reason too Christians were objects of hatred and ridicule to pagans, as though they were inactive and cowardly, and ultimately enemies of the Roman Empire. Since they suffered greatly under this odium, it was eventually thought best to moderate so abrupt and precipitous a policy, so that, once peace had been granted to the Church by the pagans, Christians too might serve together with pagans. Hence Septimius himself, refuting in the *Apologeticum* the charges of cowardice made against Christians, says: “We sail with you, and we serve as soldiers.” And the third canon of the Council of Arles is very explicit in support of this view: “Concerning those who cast away their arms in peacetime, it has been decided that they be excluded from communion.” But our Septimius, both in *On the Crown* and here in *On Idolatry*, in keeping with his natural austerity, denies to all Christians—even when the Church is troubled by no persecutions—every kind of military service and every use of the sword. RIG.] indeed, [Note: [Col. 0690C] “Now?” Jun.] [Col. 0691A] how will he serve as a soldier even in peace [Note: [Col. 0691C] **How will he serve as a soldier even in peace?** That is: how will a Christian become entangled in worldly cares? ## CHAPTER XXI

It is an act of timidity, however, when another person binds you by an oath or some invocation of his gods, and you remain silent lest your allegiance be understood. For by remaining silent you equally confirm their majesty, on account of which you will appear to be bound. What difference does it make whether you confirm the gods of the nations by calling them gods or by hearing them so called? Whether you swear [Note: [Col. 0691C] “He swears,” Paris.] by idols or acquiesce when another adjures you by them?

Why should we not recognize the stratagems of Satan, who contrives to accomplish through the mouths of his own what he cannot accomplish through ours, introducing idolatry into us through our ears? Certainly, whoever he is, he binds you in either a friendly or hostile encounter. [Note: [Col. 0692C] “You,” added by Latinus.] If hostile, you have already been summoned to battle, and you know that you must fight. If friendly, how much more confidently will you transfer your answer to the Lord, so as to dissolve the obligation by which the Evil One was seeking, through that man, to attach you to the honor of idols—that is, to idolatry. Every acquiescence of this sort is idolatry. You honor those in whose name an obligation has been imposed upon you and to whom you have rendered compliance.

I know a certain man—may the Lord forgive him—who, when someone said to him publicly in a quarrel, “May Jupiter be angry with you,” answered, “No, with you.” What else [Note: [Col. 0692C] “What other thing,” Latinus.] would a pagan who believed Jupiter to be a god have done? Even if he had not returned the curse through that same god, or through [Col. 0692C] any being like Jupiter, he had confirmed Jupiter as a god by showing, through cursing in return, that he took it as an outrage to have been cursed by him. For why should you be indignant at being cursed through one whom you know to be nothing? [Note: [Col. 0692C] “Cursed through one whom you know to be nothing,” Wouwer MS.] If you rage, you thereby affirm that he exists, and your fear will be a profession of idolatry. [Note: [Col. 0692C] “Idolatry,” Lat.] [Col. 0693A] How much more, when you return the curse through Jupiter himself, do you render Jupiter the same honor as the man who provoked you? In such a case, however, the believer ought to laugh, not rage; indeed, in accordance with the command, he ought not even to curse in return by God, but rather to bless by God, so that you may both destroy the idols, proclaim God, and fulfill the discipline. [Note: [Col. 0693C] **Discipline.** In this author this word always signifies not merely discipline, but a stricter discipline, as it also does in innumerable passages of Cyprian. LAC.]

## CHAPTER XXII

God sees [Note: [Col. 0693C] “I did it. But God sees,” Wouw. MS.] that I did it on his account; he equally sees that I was unwilling to show that I had done it on his account, and that I have in a sense made his command into a thing offered to an idol.

Many say: “No one ought to advertise himself.” Yet, I think, neither ought anyone deny himself; for whoever conceals his identity when, in any circumstance, he is taken for a pagan, denies it. [Note: [Col. 0693D] **For whoever conceals it denies it.** A notable passage against dissemblers and, in a manner, certificate-holders of every age, who think themselves excused if, in place of an oath demanded contrary to the faith and Christian religion, they perform something else by some form of dissimulation. ## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0693C] But there is a certain form of this kind, consisting in deed and word, double-edged [Note: [Col. 0693C] “In deed and in words—pointedly,” Rig.] and dangerous on both sides, although it flatters you as though it were free of either, since the deed is not seen because the spoken word is not apprehended.

Those who borrow money [Col. 0694A] from pagans, secured by pledges, give sworn security and thereby deny the faith. [Note: [Col. 0693D] **Under pledges of trust they give sworn security, and so deny that they knew.** A pagan creditor gave money to a Christian borrower under pledges and an oath. When the documents of the fiduciary contract had been drawn up, it was prescribed which estates were to be pledged, and further what oath was to be sworn. It was necessary to swear according to what the creditor, in his own superstition, wished to be sworn to him. The Christian did not swear with his tongue, but signed the tablets that witnessed the oath required by the creditor. The question is whether he is liable to the charge of idolatry. The debtor denies liability on the ground that he signed the instrument of security or trust without investigating or understanding what had been prescribed in place of the oath. [Col. 0694C] Tertullian, on the contrary, says that he is liable. “For when you gave security,” he says, “you knew.” That is, you knew that the pagan creditor had lent you money on condition that you give security both through pledges and through an oath. And since you knew, you certainly willed it. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 0694C] **They give sworn security.** Not only jurists, but other Latin authors everywhere call similar documents or bonds [Col. 0694D] *cautiones*, “securities,” and say that the parties *cavent*, “take security,” because we thereby take precautions for ourselves and are rendered secure when we make a loan. [Note: [Col. 0694D] **They deny that they knew.** The following words show this reading to be entirely correct: “For when you gave security, you knew; since you knew, you certainly willed it.” RIG.] They wish, of course, to recognize denial only in a time of persecution, at a tribunal, and before the governor. PAM.]

“I wrote,” he says, “but said nothing: it is the tongue, not the written letter, that kills.” Here, then, [Note: [Col. 0693C] “I therefore,” Wouw. MS.] I appeal to nature and conscience: to nature, because the hand can write nothing—even if the tongue remains motionless and silent while the words are dictated—that the soul has not dictated, although the soul itself may have dictated to the tongue either what it conceived on its own or what was handed down by another. Now, lest it be said, “Another dictated it,” I appeal here to conscience: does the soul accept what another dictated, and transmit it to the hand whether the tongue accompanies the act or sits idle?

And rightly did the Lord say that sin is committed in the mind and conscience. “If,” he says, “desire [Note: [Col. 0694D] **If, he says, desire.** Since I have thus far been unable to find these exact words in Holy Scripture, it seems to me that he condensed the passage of Ecclesiasticus 5: “Do not follow the desire of your heart in your strength, and do not say: ‘How was I able, or who will subject me to judgment for my deeds?’ For God, who exacts vengeance, will exact it.” Or rather, he alludes to the passage so often cited from Matthew 5: “Whoever looks at a woman,” etc. PAM.] or malice has risen into a person’s heart, you are held liable as though for the deed” (Matt. 5:28). [Col. 0694B] [Note: [Col. 0694C] “Is held liable,” Wouw. MS.] You therefore gave security for what clearly rose into your heart, something you cannot contend either that you did not know [Note: [Col. 0694C] “He cannot,” Semler.] or that you did not will. For when you gave security, you knew; since you knew, you certainly willed it. You are implicated [Note: [Col. 0694C] “And you are,” Seml.] both in deed and in thought, and you cannot exclude the greater offense by the lesser, [Note: [Col. 0694C] “The greater,” Lat., Jun., Rig., Leop.; “the hand,” Rhen., Franeq., Semler.] saying that, in giving security for what you do not perform, you merely commit falsehood.

“Still, I did not deny, because I did not swear.” On the contrary, even if you had done nothing of this kind, you would nevertheless be said to swear if you consented. A silent voice in the stylus and a mute sound in letters are of no avail. Indeed, Zechariah (Luke 1), when punished with a temporary loss of voice, passed beyond his disabled tongue; [Note: [Col. 0694D] **He passes beyond his disabled tongue.** He does not wait upon a tongue that has been fettered and rendered idle. RIG.] with his hands he dictates from his heart and pronounces his son’s name without his mouth. He speaks with the stylus; his hand is heard upon the wax, clearer than every sound, and the letter more vocal than every mouth. Ask whether a man has spoken when he is proved to have spoken.

Let us pray to the Lord that no necessity of such a contract may beset [Col. 0695A] us. And if it should so happen, may he give the brethren the means to perform a work of charity, [Note: [Col. 0695B] **May he give the brethren the means to perform a work.** Pamelius very correctly explains this of almsgiving. For the verb *operari*, “to work,” means “to give alms,” perhaps because almsgiving holds the chief place among the good works bestowed upon the brethren. Hence Cyprian entitled a book *On Works and Almsgiving*, where he frequently presses this point. LAC.] or give us the steadfastness to break off every necessity, lest those written denials, acting in place of [Note: [Col. 0695C] **Letters acting in place of our mouth.** Cyprian imitated this in his letter to Rogatianus: “I send these letters to your ears and eyes to take my place.” RIG.] our mouth, be produced against us on the day of judgment, sealed with the seals no longer of witnesses but of angels. [Note: [Col. 0695B] **Sealed with the seals no longer of witnesses but of angels.** By *advocati* he means those who lent a friend their presence by affixing their seals, subscribing, and giving testimony. Thus Varro, *On Agriculture* II.5: “But you, Murrius, come as my witness while I pay the asses at the festival of Pales, so that, if they later claim them from me, you may be able to bear witness.” RIG.]

## CHAPTER XXIV

Amid these reefs and bays, these shoals and straits of idolatry, [Note: [Col. 0695C] **The straits of idolatry.** Peter Chrysologus agrees, *Sermon* 21, explaining that the reefs, bays, and straits past which the Lord’s ship—that is, the Church—sails are both the external masses of the nations that buffet her like waves and the internal, swollen surges of the heretics that rush upon her and rage. LAC.] faith sails under the impulse of the Spirit of God, [Note: [Col. 0695C] **Sailing under the impulse of the Spirit of God.** This word, peculiar among others to our author, has caused me to agree with Sixtus of Siena that the poems *Genesis* and *Sodom*, which after Morel and Fabricius I attributed to St. Cyprian, are Tertullian’s. PAM.—**Sailing under the impulse of the Spirit of God.** I do not sufficiently understand what Pamelius means here, for the verb *velificari* is common and occurs everywhere among writers of the Golden Age of Latin, in approximately this sense. LE PR.] safe if cautious, secure if vigilant. [Note: [Col. 0695B] “If attentive,” Rigalt., from the manuscript of Fulvius Ursinus.] [Note: [Col. 0696B] **Secure if attentive** (see variant reading). The final chapters of this little work are missing from the Agobard manuscript; for that reason we have followed here the manuscript of Fulvius Ursinus. Rhenanus’ editions read, “Secure if thunderstruck.” This is by no means to be rejected. For thus he says in the book *On Flight in Persecution*: “But when is God more trusted, unless it is when he is more feared, in a time of persecution? Then the Church is thunderstruck.” RIG.]

But when one has been cast out, the depth cannot be swum; when one has struck it, the shipwreck cannot be escaped; [Note: [Col. 0696B] **The shipwreck cannot be escaped when struck.** Lucifer of Cagliari used the phrase “inextricable darkness” in the book *On Despising Death for Christ*. RIG.] when one has been swallowed, the submersion in idolatry allows no breath. Every wave of it chokes; every whirlpool of it sucks down to the underworld. [Note: [Col. 0696B] **Sucks down.** I have no doubt that what Tertullian wrote about submersion, choking waves, and a devouring whirlpool was said with reference to Charybdis—that is, from extensive knowledge of this nautical peril. See my note on *Aeneid* III at the words:

> It sucks the waves into the abyss.

LAC.]

Let no one say, “Who will be able to take precautions so securely? We shall have to leave the world,” as though it were not worth leaving the world rather than remaining in it as an idolater. Nothing [Col. 0695B] can be easier [Col. 0696A] than precaution against idolatry, if fear of it holds the foremost place. Every necessity is less than so great a danger when compared with it.

For this reason the Holy Spirit, when the apostles deliberated, relaxed the bond and yoke for us, so that we might be free to avoid idolatry. This will be our law, to be administered the more fully because it is so unencumbered: the law proper to Christians, by which pagans recognize and test us. This must be set before those approaching the faith (Isa. 33; Matt. 7; Phil. 3; Luke 10), and impressed upon those entering the faith, so that those approaching may deliberate, those who observe it may persevere, and those who do not observe it [Note: [Col. 0695B] “Those who do not observe it,” absent from Rig.] may renounce themselves. [Note: [Col. 0696C] **May renounce themselves.** May cease to be Christians. RIG.]

For we shall see whether, according to the type of the ark (Gen. 7), [Note: [Col. 0696B] “Archetype,” Fran.] [Note: [Col. 0696C] **According to the type of the ark.** Here he uses “type” for what elsewhere he calls example, image, figure, sacrament, mystery, likeness, enigma, parable, memorial, allegory, mirror, comparison, shadow, and cloud. Jerome, *Against Jovinian* II: “Wine is a type of the blood of Christ.” LAC.] both raven and kite and wolf and dog and serpent will be in the Church; but certainly the idolater is not found in the type of the ark. [Note: [Col. 0696B] “In the archetype,” Fran.] No animal was made a figure of the idolater. What was not in the ark must not be in the Church. [Note: [Col. 0696C] **What was not in the ark must not be in the Church.** This concluding exclamation is far more obscure than what precedes it. Meanwhile, he seems to mean this: since animals of every kind were in Noah’s ark—clean animals seven by seven and unclean animals two by two—but acts of idolatry were excluded, it follows that what was not in the ark must not be in the Church. For this author teaches in *On Baptism* that the ark bore the figure of the Church. PAM.]

# The Book to Scapula

## APPENDIX TO THE APOLOGETIC BOOKS

[Col. 0697]

# THE BOOK TO SCAPULA (C)

## EDITORIAL NOTICE

[Col. 0695]

[Col. 0695D] Although, as nearly everyone admits, this book *To Scapula* was written after the author’s adoption of Montanism, we have nevertheless thought it should be placed immediately after the preceding works composed before Tertullian’s lapse, both because of their connection in subject matter and perhaps because of a certain chronological relation, as may be seen in the dissertation of D. Le Nourry printed below. EDD.

## ARGUMENT AND SYNOPSIS

[Col. 0697A] Scholars disagree concerning the date of the book *To Scapula*. Pamelius and Baronius taught that it was published by Tertullian in the year 203; others place it under Emperor Heliogabalus, in 217. It seems more probable, however, that this occurred in the intervening period, around the year 212, when Caracalla was ruling alone after his father’s death. Hence Tertullian mentions only one emperor in that book:

> We therefore honor the emperor in the manner permitted to us and advantageous to him, as a man second after God;

and again:

> Thus we also offer sacrifice for the emperor’s welfare—but to our God, who is also his God.

That Tertullian wrote this after the prolonged persecution that occurred under Severus’ reign is evident from his enumeration of five proconsuls who had persecuted the Christians and had themselves fallen into various calamities. By their example he exhorts Scapula to take care for himself, particularly since certain portents were seen at Carthage as soon as Scapula entered the province and condemned the Christian Mavilius of Hadrumetum to the beasts:

> In your case too we hope it was only an admonition, that after you had condemned Mavilius of Hadrumetum to the beasts, this affliction immediately followed.

[Col. 0697B] He relates what that affliction was in these words:

> Moreover, from last year’s rainfall it became evident what the human race had deserved—namely, that the flood of old also occurred because of human unbelief and iniquity. Those who saw them know what was threatened by the fires that very recently hung above the walls of Carthage throughout the night; those who have hardened themselves know what the recent thunderclaps proclaimed. All these are signs of God’s imminent wrath, which we must, by every means we can, both announce, proclaim, and pray may for the present remain local; for in its own time those who interpret its examples otherwise will experience it as universal and final. That sun too, at the assembly in Utica, when its light was wholly extinguished, was so truly a portent that it could not have suffered this from an ordinary eclipse, since it stood in its own altitude and station. [Col. 0697C] You have astrologers.

Then, to deter Scapula from shedding Christian blood, he recounts what other governors suffered:

> We must grieve that no city will escape unpunished for the shedding of our blood. Thus, under the governor Hilarianus, when people had cried out concerning the grounds of our cemeteries, “Let there be no burial grounds,” their own threshing-floors ceased to exist, for they did not gather their harvests.

After some matters related elsewhere, he adds:

> We can likewise set before you the ends of certain governors who at the close of their lives remembered that they had sinned by persecuting Christians. Vigellius Saturninus, who was the first here to wield the sword against us, lost his sight. Claudius Herminianus in Cappadocia, indignant that his wife had passed over to this sect, treated the Christians cruelly; afterward, when he alone in his governor’s residence was ravaged by plague [Col. 0697D] and seethed alive with worms, he would say, “Let no one know, lest the Christians rejoice in hope.” Later, recognizing his error in having caused some by torture to fall away from their resolution, he died almost a Christian. Caecilius Capella, at that catastrophe in Byzantium, cried out, “Christians, rejoice!” But even those who seem to themselves to have escaped unpunished will come to the day of divine judgment.

[Col. 0698A] He also adds examples of governors who dealt more mildly with Christians:

> How many governors, both firmer and more cruel, have turned a blind eye to cases of this kind! Cincius Severus, for example, himself provided Christians at Thysdrus with a way to answer so that they might be released. Vespronius Candidus released a Christian, as though he were merely a turbulent man, to satisfy his fellow citizens. Asper, after subjecting a man to mild harassment and immediately causing him to give way, did not compel him to perform the sacrifice; beforehand, in the presence of the advocates and assessors, he declared that he regretted having become involved in this case. Pudens too, when a Christian was sent to him, perceived from the written charge that the man had been subjected to extortion and released him; he tore up the charge and refused, in accordance with the imperial mandate, to hear a man’s case without an accuser. All these matters can be suggested to you both in an official capacity and by those same advocates who have themselves received benefits [Col. 0698B] from Christians, although they shout whatever they please. For one man’s clerk was delivered when a demon was casting him headlong; so too were the relative and the young child of certain others. And how many respectable men—to say nothing of common people—have been cured either of demons or diseases!

Next he relates the example of Emperor Severus, who had been cured by a Christian man through anointing with oil:

> Severus himself too, the father of Antoninus, remembered the Christians. For he sought out the Christian Proculus, surnamed Toparcion, the steward of Evodias, who had once cured him with oil, and kept him in his palace until the man’s death. Antoninus too knew him very well, having been reared on Christian milk.

Finally he warns Scapula to cease his investigation of Christians, lest all Carthage be filled with Christian blood:

> What will Carthage itself suffer when you decimate it, when each person recognizes among those there his own relatives and household companions; when perhaps he sees there men even of your own order, [Col. 0698C] matrons, and all the most prominent persons, as well as relatives or friends of your own friends? Spare Carthage, if not yourself; spare the province, which, upon witnessing your severity, has been made liable to extortion by both soldiers and each person’s enemies.

He says this because, once it became known that a governor was hostile to Christians, pagans were accustomed to attack them in bands with great fury, plunder them, and put them to death. He further observes in these words that persecution does not extinguish the Christian religion, but rather propagates it:

> Yet this sect will not fail; you should know that it is built up all the more whenever it seems to be cut down. For everyone who beholds such endurance is struck by some uneasiness and kindled to investigate what the cause may be; and when he has learned the truth, he himself immediately follows it.

Thus far Tertullian [Col. 0698D] *To Scapula*. LUMP.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0697D]

We neither shudder nor tremble with fear at the things we suffer from the ignorant, since we came to this sect having assuredly accepted its condition and entered into a covenant that we would approach these contests after pledging even our lives, desiring to obtain what God promises in return and fearing to suffer what he threatens against a contrary way of life. Finally, we contend against all your savagery, even breaking forth to meet it voluntarily, [Col. 0698D] and we rejoice more when condemned than when acquitted.

Therefore, we have sent this little book not because we fear for ourselves, but because we fear for you and for all our enemies, much more our friends. [Note: [Col. 0697D] “Not yet,” Rhen.] For by our discipline we are commanded to love even our enemies and to pray for those who persecute us, so that this goodness of ours may be perfect and peculiar to us, not common to all. To love friends belongs to everyone; to love enemies, however, belongs only to Christians.

Since, therefore, we grieve at your ignorance, pity human error, foresee [Note: [Col. 0698D] “And,” absent from Rig.] future events, and see their signs daily being held out before us, [Note: [Col. 0699C] “See them being displayed,” conjecture of Jun.] we must break forth, at least in this manner, to set before you those things that you are unwilling to hear openly. [Note: [Col. 0699C] **Those things that you are unwilling to hear openly.** These words plainly attest that this book of petition was not delivered into Scapula’s hands, but merely sent. LE PR.]

## CHAPTER II

We worship one God, whom you all know naturally, at whose lightning and thunder you tremble [Note: [Col. 0699C] “We tremble,” Rhen.], and at whose benefits you rejoice. You yourselves also suppose the others to be gods, though we know them to be demons. Nevertheless, it belongs to human right and natural liberty that each person should worship whatever he has thought fit; one person’s religion neither harms nor benefits another. Nor is it the part of religion to compel religion [Note: [Col. 0699C] “Nor is it the part of religion to compel religion.” Lest someone perhaps twist this passage in favor of license for sects, note that the Author’s judgment, at the beginning of the *Scorpiace*, is utterly opposed to their liberty. PAM.], which ought to be embraced voluntarily, not by force, since even sacrificial victims are required to be offered from a willing mind. Thus, even if you compel us to sacrifice, you will render no service to your gods: for they will not desire sacrifices from the unwilling—unless they are contentious; but a god is not contentious. [Col. 0699B] Indeed, he who is the true God bestows all his gifts equally upon the profane and upon his own. Therefore he has also appointed an eternal judgment upon the grateful and the ungrateful.

Yet us, whom you regard as sacrilegious, you have never caught even in theft, much less in sacrilege. But all who despoil temples [Note: [Col. 0699C] Others read *dispoliant*.], swear by the gods, and worship those same gods are not Christians, and yet they are caught committing sacrilege. It would take too long to recount in what other ways all the gods are mocked and despised by their own worshippers. In the same way we are defamed with respect to the majesty of the Emperor [Note: [Col. 0699C] “With respect to the majesty of the Emperor.” On the charge of violating majesty, see the Law in the Questions, D., *Ad legem Juliam majestatis*, and examine that whole title. La Cerda cites the law *Meminisse*, but ought to have explained what that law is. LE PR.]; yet Christians could never be found among the adherents of Albinus [Note: [Col. 0699C] “Yet never adherents of Albinus or Niger.” Claudius Albinus, as Spartianus writes, rebelled in Gaul against the emperor Severus. He was defeated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, near Tinurtium; and his corpse, after already being dismembered before his own house, was thrown into the river Rhône. Pescennius Niger met a not dissimilar fate: proclaimed emperor by the Syrian legions against Severus, he was at last killed by the latter near Cyzicus. Avidius Cassius, however, of the family of the Cassii who had conspired against Gaius Julius, laid plots against the emperor Lucius Verus; he was ultimately killed, not at the emperor’s command, though the emperor did not forbid it. Hence Tertullian calls those privy to these rebellions adherents of Albinus, Niger, and Cassius, as he does in the *Apology*: “Whence,” he says, “came the Cassii, the Nigri, and the Albini? Whence those who besiege Caesar between the two laurels?” RHEN.], Niger, or Cassius. Rather, the very men who, right up to the previous day, had sworn by their guardian spirits [Note: [Col. 0699D] “But the very same men who swore by their guardian spirits.” So too in the *Apology*. Indeed, all those men, right up to the moment when their impiety broke forth, were both performing rites for the emperor’s safety and swearing by his Genius, some outside and some within. Moreover, from this custom of swearing by the Genii of the Caesars, I see that the later practice among Christian rulers of swearing by the king’s safety or that of his children arose. [Col. 0700C] It is nevertheless certain that this was severely prohibited in the laws of the Franks. RHEN.], who had both offered [Note: [Col. 0700C] “Had effected,” Rhenanus.] and vowed victims for their safety, and who had often condemned Christians, were discovered to be their enemies.

A Christian is no one’s enemy, much less the Emperor’s. Knowing him to have been appointed by his God, he must necessarily love, revere, honor him, and desire his safety together with that of the whole Roman Empire, for as long as the world shall stand. For so long will the Empire stand. We therefore honor the Emperor in the manner that is both permitted to us and beneficial to him: as a man second to God, who has received whatever he is from God [Note: [Col. 0700C] Fran. and Rigaltius add *et*.], and is inferior to God alone. This is what he himself will desire. For in this way he is greater than all, while being inferior to the one true God; thus he is also greater than the gods themselves, since they too are under his authority.

Accordingly, we also sacrifice for the Emperor’s safety [Note: [Col. 0700C] “We sacrifice as God has commanded, with pure prayer, without incense, without a victim.” Thus in the book *On Repentance*: “To know food and drink in their purity,” that is, with bread and water alone. Thus Juvenal:

> Where kings observe the sabbath festivals with bare feet.

That is, with uncovered feet. Accordingly, “with pure prayer” means with prayer alone and unadorned, issuing from a holy and innocent mind. The nations offered lifeless things or brute beasts, incense or oxen, to vain gods. Christians offer to the true God a rational soul uttering praises and thanks to God. Athenagoras explicitly explains this in that embassy on behalf of the Christians addressed to Antoninus and Commodus, also citing the words of Paul in which he describes the victim: θυσίαν ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐάρεστον τῷ θεῳ, τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν (“a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, the rational worship”) [Col. 0700D] ὑμῶν (“of you”).
