Tertullian himself says in the *Apology*: “I offer to God a rich and greater victim, which he himself commanded: prayer proceeding from chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and the Holy Spirit.” And in Book IV, chapter 1, *Against Marcion*, on the passage from Malachi, “A pure offering is offered to my name”: “namely, simple prayer from a pure conscience.” And in chapter 9 he says that a man ought to offer a gift to God at the temple, namely prayer and thanksgiving in the Church, through CHRIST JESUS, the universal priest of the Father. Minucius Felix, after saying, “We have no shrines or altars,” adds: “A good disposition, a pure mind, and a sincere judgment are an acceptable victim. These are our sacrifices; these are God’s sacred rites.” Finally, Justin, against Trypho the Jew, testifies that our Eucharistic rites are accomplished by pure prayer, or by prayer alone. RIG.], but to our God and his; and in the manner [Col. 0700B] God has commanded—with pure prayer. For God, the Creator of the universe, has no need of any odor or blood [Note: [Col. 0700D] “Of any odor or blood.” Here he contrasts pure prayer with odor or blood. And indeed we [Col. 0701C] do not sacrifice to God with odor or blood, but with pure prayer. For a sacrifice is sacrificed or offered only through prayers and invocation. PAM.]. These things are the food of demons. But we not only reject demons; we also refute them, expose them daily, and drive them out of human beings, as is known to very many.

Thus we pray all the more for the Emperor’s safety, asking it from him who is able to grant it. And it can surely be sufficiently evident to you that we act according to the discipline of divine patience, since, although so great a multitude of people—almost the greater part of every city [Note: [Col. 0700C] “Greater” is absent from Rhen.]—we conduct ourselves in silence and modesty, perhaps better known individually than collectively, and recognizable by nothing other than the reformation of our former vices. Far be it from us to resent suffering what we desire, or to devise for ourselves any vengeance that we await from God.

## CHAPTER III

Nevertheless, as we said above, we cannot but grieve that no city will escape unpunished for shedding our blood [Note: [Col. 0701C] “That no city will escape unpunished.” Hence the saying of the martyr Cyprian: “Never,” he says, “does the crime of the impious rise against our name without divine vengeance immediately accompanying it.” RHEN.]. Thus, under the governor Hilarianus [Note: [Col. 0701B] “Governor” is absent from Rhen.], when they had shouted concerning the grounds of our burial places, “Let there be no burial grounds” [Note: [Col. 0701C] “Let there be no burial grounds.” He means cemeteries, for he is playing upon the word. When the man had shouted, “Let there be no *areae*,” he meant burial grounds; when Tertullian in turn says, “Their threshing floors did not exist,” he means threshing floors for grain. *Area* is also used for a cemetery by Pontius the Deacon in the *Acts of Cyprian*: “He was buried in the grounds of Candidus the procurator.” The ancients, indeed, called cemeteries *arenariae* and *areae*, as I. Bulengerus testifies in chapter 42 of Book III, *On Temples*. LAC.], their own threshing floors did not exist: for they did not gather in their harvests.

Moreover, what the human race deserved through last year’s rainfall [Note: [Col. 0701B] “Rains,” Rhenanus.] became apparent—namely, that the Flood also in former times [Note: [Col. 0701B] “Namely, and in former times,” Junius.] had occurred because of the unbelief and iniquities of human beings. Those who saw the fires that recently hung by night over the walls of Carthage know what they threatened; and those who hardened themselves know what the former thunderclaps proclaimed. All these are signs of the impending wrath of God, which we must, in whatever way we can, both announce and proclaim, while praying that it may meanwhile remain local [Note: [Col. 0701B] “And pray that meanwhile it may be local,” Junius.]. For those who interpret its examples otherwise will experience it as universal and final at its appointed time.

For that sun also, in the district of Utica [Note: [Col. 0701D] “In the district of Utica.” Utica was an African town of Roman citizens, famous for Cato’s death, as recorded by Pliny. Africa appears, moreover, to have been divided into judicial districts, like Spain, which, according to Pliny, was divided into seven districts in its nearer province, just as Baetica was divided into four. He also calls these “judicial” districts, because the inhabitants of each nearby town pleaded their cases there. Districts of this kind are represented today among Christians, as far as ecclesiastical cases are concerned, by towns distinguished by episcopal sees. Accordingly, understand “the district of Utica” as the territory subject to the jurisdiction of the people of Utica. RHEN.], lost almost all its light; and this was so great a portent that it could not have suffered this by an ordinary eclipse, being positioned in its own altitude and house [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Positioned in its own altitude.” In speaking of a certain eclipse of the sun, not ordinary but prodigious, he uses astrologers’ terminology: the sun was positioned, as people now like to say, above or at least outside the lunar node. EDD.]. You have astrologers.

We can likewise set before you the ends [Col. 0702A] of certain governors who, at the end of their lives, remembered that they had sinned by persecuting Christians. Vigellius Saturninus [Note: [Col. 0701C] Others: M. Gellius Saturninus. Pamelius: Valgius Saturninus. Junius: Vitellius Saturninus.], who was the first here to wield the sword against us, lost his sight. Claudius Lucius Herminianus [Note: [Col. 0701C] Others: Cl. Luc. Hierominianus; others: Lucius Hieronymianus. [Col. 0702B] Vatican 3: Lucius Gerominianus. Junius suspects that *Livius Geminianus* should be read.] in Cappadocia, resenting his wife’s conversion to this sect, treated Christians cruelly. Then, alone in his residence and wasting away from plague [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Alone in his residence.” A *praetorium* is a suburban villa, which differs from a country villa in elegance and splendor. Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter 37, and *Augustus*, chapter 72. RHEN.], and swarming with worms while still alive [Note: [Col. 0702C] “Swarming with worms.” Jerome, in the *Life of Hilarion*: “The sandy region boiled forth a multitude of serpents and venomous creatures.”] [Note: [Col. 0702B] “Skin,” Junius.], he used to say, “Let no one know, lest [Note: [Col. 0702B] Pamelius inserted *spe*, against the judgment of Rigaltius.] the Christians rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0702C] Rhenanus adds: “or in the hope of a Christian woman” [reading uncertain].]. Later, having recognized his error—because by tortures he had caused some to fall away from their resolution—he died almost a Christian.

Caecilius Capella, during that Byzantine catastrophe [Note: [Col. 0702C] “During that Byzantine catastrophe.” He uses *exitus* in the sense of destruction, as in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “No one has yet mourned Babylon’s destruction”; and in the book *Against the Jews*: “Christ’s *exitus*,” that is, his death. RIG.], cried out, “Christians, rejoice!” [Note: [Col. 0702C] “Christians, rejoice!” *REJOICE* was the formula for proclaiming exultation. We also learn this from a gold coin of Maximian Caesar, on which two Victories support a pillar bearing the inscription: “REJOICE, ROMANS.” [Col. 0702D] Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, near the end: “Rejoice, whatever nations there are.” Martial XI.62. RIG.]. But even those who seem to themselves [Note: [Col. 0702C] “To you,” Rigaltius.] to have escaped unpunished will come to the day of divine judgment.

For you also we desire that it should have been only a warning [Col. 0702B] when, after you had condemned Mavilus of Hadrumetum [Note: [Col. 0702C] “Of Hadrumetum” or “Hadrumetine,” Latin.] to the beasts, this affliction immediately followed; and now, for the same reason, the appeal of blood has arisen [Note: [Col. 0702D] “And now, for the same reason, the appeal of blood.” Immediately after condemning Mavilus, Scapula began to be tormented by the agony of an extremely acute illness. He was again being afflicted by it at the very time when Septimius wrote this, because of his renewed cruelty toward the Christians. Christian blood had cried out to God and interrupted the delays of divine patience. Petilianus the Donatist fought against the Catholics with similar examples, though for a very different cause, as may be seen in Augustine’s disputation. For Petilianus dared to make this terrible assertion: “But, to pass over the rest, observe in your own examples how very many emperors and judges of yours perished while persecuting us.” RIG.]. But remember hereafter [Note: [Col. 0702D] “But remember hereafter.” That is, concerning the future—namely, that eternal vengeance, far more dreadful, remains. RIG.].

## CHAPTER IV

We are not frightening you, for neither are we afraid; but I wish that by warning μὴ θεομαχεῖν (“not to fight against God”) we might be able to save everyone. You can both discharge the duty of your jurisdiction and remember humanity, especially because you too are beneath the sword. For what more is commanded you than to condemn guilty persons who confess, but to send those who deny back to torture? You see, therefore, how you yourselves act contrary [Col. 0703A] to your instructions, since you compel those who confess to deny. You thereby acknowledge that we are innocent, since you are unwilling to condemn us immediately upon our confession. But if you strive to crush us [Note: [Col. 0703C] “To choose us,” Rigaltius.], then it is innocence that you are attacking.

How many governors, both more resolute and more cruel, have turned a blind eye to cases of this sort! Cincius Severus, for example, who at Thistrus [Note: [Col. 0703D] “At Rhysdrus,” Rigaltius.] himself supplied Christians with the means [Note: [Col. 0703D] “Who himself supplied at Thistrus.” An entirely contrary practice seems to have been observed: those who wished the accused to be ruined led him into a trap by every means and artifice and by repeated questioning. Pamelius reads *Tiristi*, or *Tiristi*; La Cerda, *Thristri*. LE PR.] of answering so that they could be released; Vespronius Candidus, who released a Christian rather than satisfy his fellow citizens, on the ground that the affair would be riotous [Note: [Col. 0703D] “To satisfy his fellow citizens, on the ground that he was merely disorderly.” That Vespronius Candidus warned his fellow citizens, who were demanding a certain Christian’s death, that he would indeed gladly satisfy their wishes, but foresaw that the matter would bring disorder upon the community. RIG.]; Asper, who, after subjecting a man to slight harassment and seeing him immediately give way, did not compel him to perform a sacrifice, having first declared among the advocates and assessors that he regretted becoming involved in this case [Note: [Col. 0703D] “Regret” is absent from Rhen.].

Pudens also released a Christian sent before him when he perceived from the indictment that the man had been subjected to extortion [Note: [Col. 0704D] “When his extortion was perceived.” That is, his harassment. Tertullian himself says below, near the end of this book: “Spare the province, which, after seeing your determination, has been made liable to extortions both by the soldiers and by each person’s own enemies.” RIG.—*Concussio* is the fraudulent accusation of some raging scoundrel, not the legitimate pleading of a prosecutor. LE PR.]. He tore up that same indictment [Col. 0703B] and declared that, in accordance with his instructions, he would not hear a man’s case without an accuser [Note: [Col. 0703D] “Man” is absent from Rhen.].

All these things can be suggested to you both by virtue of your office and by those same advocates [Note: [Col. 0703D] “Of the same man,” Junius, from the Vatican manuscript.], who themselves have received benefits from Christians, even though they shout whatever they please [Note: [Col. 0703D] Rhen. adds *et*.]. For one man’s secretary, when he was being thrown from a height by a demon, was delivered; so too were the relative and the little boy of certain others. And how many respectable men—to say nothing of the common people—have been healed either of demons or of illnesses!

Even Severus himself, the father of Antoninus, was mindful of Christians. For he sought out the Christian Proculus, surnamed Torpacion, the steward of Euhodea [Note: [Col. 0703D] Rhenanus conjectured *Euboea*. In the old manuscript: *Euhodae*. Pithoeus corrected it to *Euodi*, which pleases Rigaltius. He also notes that Scaliger, in his *Observations on Eusebius*, defends the reading [Col. 0704C] *Euodiae*.], who had once cured him with oil; and he kept him in his palace until the man’s death. Antoninus too knew him very well, having been reared on Christian milk [Col. 0703C] [Note: [Col. 0704D] “Knew that he had been reared among Christians,” Dijon manuscript; *christiano*, Paris.]. Moreover, although Severus knew that women and men of the most distinguished rank belonged to this sect, he not only did them no injury but even honored them with his testimony, and openly resisted the people when they raged against us.

Marcus Aurelius too, during the German campaign, obtained rain in that drought from God through the prayers of Christian soldiers. When have droughts not also been driven away by our kneeling and fasting? Then even the people, acclaiming the God of gods [Note: [Col. 0704D] Rhen. adds *et*.], who alone is mighty [Note: [Col. 0704D] Others read “you are able.”], bore witness to our God under the name of Jupiter.

Besides [Note: [Col. 0704D] “Because of,” Rhen.] these things, we do not deny a deposit entrusted to us; we violate no one’s marriage [Col. 0704A]; we treat orphans dutifully; we bring relief to the needy; and we return evil for evil to no one. Let those who falsely claim our sect answer for themselves; we ourselves also reject them. Who, finally, complains [Note: [Col. 0704D] “Inquires,” Rigaltius.] of us under any other designation? What other charge does a Christian face except that of his sect? Though it is called incestuous and cruel, no one has proved this in all this time.

For such innocence, for such uprightness, for justice, chastity, fidelity, truth, and the living God, we are burned—something that neither the sacrilegious, nor public enemies, nor even so many persons guilty of treason are accustomed to suffer [Note: [Col. 0704D] “Publicii, but not,” Latin.]. Even now this name is persecuted by the governor of the legion and by the governor of Mauretania, though only with the sword, just as it was commanded from the beginning that persons of this sort should be punished. But greater contests are followed by greater rewards.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0704B]

Your cruelty is our glory. Only take care lest, through the very fact that we endure such things, we seem to burst forth for this sole purpose: to prove precisely this—that we do not fear these things but voluntarily summon them.

When Arrius Antoninus was vigorously conducting a persecution in Asia, all the Christians of that city presented themselves before his tribunal in a body. After ordering a few of them to be led away, he said to the rest [Note: [Col. 0704D] “Then,” Rhenanus.], ὧ δεῖλοι, εἰ θέλετε ἀποθνήσκειν, κρημνοὺς ἢ βρόχους ἔχετε [Note: [Col. 0704D] Ω δεῖλοι, κ. τ. λ. That is: “O wretched people, if you wish to die, you have precipices and nooses.” EDD.].

If it should be resolved to do the same here, what will you do with so many thousands of people—with so many men and women, of every sex, every age, and every rank, offering themselves to you? How many fires and how many swords will be required? What will Carthage itself suffer when you decimate it—when everyone recognizes among them his own relatives and members of his household [Col. 0704C], when he sees among them perhaps men and matrons of your own order, and persons of the highest standing, as well as either relatives or friends of your own friends?

Spare yourself, then, if not us; spare Carthage, if not yourself; spare the province, which, after seeing your determination, has been made liable to extortions both by the soldiers and by each person’s own enemies. We have no master except God alone. He is before you and cannot be hidden; but you can do nothing to him. Those whom you suppose to be your masters, moreover, are themselves human beings who will one day die.

Yet this sect will not fail. You should know that it is built up all the more when it appears to be cut down. For everyone who observes such great endurance [Note: [Col. 0705A] “Awaits,” Rhen.], struck by some scruple [Col. 0706A] [Note: [Col. 0706A] In Rhen. and Junius.], is kindled to inquire what lies behind it; and when he has learned the truth, he himself immediately follows.

*Dissertation on the Apology of Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullian, the Two Books to the Nations, and the One Book to Scapula, by Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, priest and monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Congregation of Saint Maur.*

[Col. 0705]

# DISSERTATION ON THE *APOLOGY* OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, THE TWO BOOKS *TO THE NATIONS*, AND THE ONE BOOK *TO SCAPULA*

(BY DOM NICOLAS LE NOURRY)

PRIEST AND MONK OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT, OF THE CONGREGATION OF SAINT MAUR

## CHAPTER ONE

### Analysis of the *Apology*, and Who the Tertullian Named in Its Title Was

[Col. 0705B]

### ARTICLE ONE

#### Analysis of the *Apology*

When Tertullian saw, with no slight grief of mind, that Christians were being persecuted and killed by the pagans with such injustice that they were permitted neither to defend themselves openly nor to be heard publicly by the judges, he undertook to plead their cause before the governors of the Roman Empire through the hidden power of written works.

First, therefore, he complains most gravely that all Christians were regarded and tortured by pagans who neither knew them nor wished to know them, contrary to every [Col. 0705C] law of equity and nature, and with an utterly implacable hatred. Indeed, the public testimony to this ignorance all the more clearly convicted the pagans of wrongdoing because, as soon as people learned what the Christian religion was and what kind of religion it was, they immediately abandoned the worship of false gods and embraced it throughout the whole world.

Nor should it be said that they were then being led into evil. For it is the disposition of an evil person to seek hiding places, overwhelmed by shame and fear. A Christian, by contrast, even when condemned and tortured by every kind of torment, glories, rejoices, and exults in his profession (chapter 1).

Furthermore, if a Christian is guilty of sacrilege, incest, homicide, or any other crime, as the pagans babbled [Col. 0705D], why is he condemned by them, contrary to divine and human laws, without any accusation of a crime, without a witness, without any prior examination of a single circumstance, of the time, or of accomplices, but solely on the prejudgment attached to the name?

Pliny, therefore, moved by this injustice, asked the emperor Trajan what should be done with Christians who had been convicted of absolutely no crime or offense except an obstinate determination to persevere in the worship of God and Christ and in their own discipline. But he received no other answer from Trajan than that they were not to be sought out, yet, if brought before the judges, ought to be punished. What, I ask you, could be more unjust than a law that forbids Christians to be sought out on the ground that they are innocent, yet commands them to be condemned as guilty (chapter 2)?

[Col. 0706B] In addition, divine and human laws provided that no one guilty of any crime whatsoever should ever be subjected either to punishment or to judicial torture except in order that he might confess his crimes. Christians, by contrast, were tortured so that they would deny both the crimes of which they were usually accused and the fact that they were Christians. The battle, therefore, concerned the Christian name alone. And certainly the sentence pronounced against them by the judges from the tablet, omitting the specification of any crime, declared nothing other than that Christians were condemned.

Yet the pagans sinned all the more gravely against the most sacred laws because they repeatedly acknowledged that the conduct of Christians was chaste and holy, and that those among their own pagan population who adopted the name of the Christian faith [Col. 0706C] always became better people. Nevertheless, they raged with no less cruelty against these converts than against all the others, because they had assumed the Christian name.

“But,” the pagans used to say, “the name of their founder displeases us.” What, then, Tertullian replies, can be hateful in the name of Christ? Is it not derived from pleasantness or kindness? What is there in it that is more deserving of hatred than the very names of philosophers, physicians, or cooks, transmitted by their founders and received by others? Finally, the name of no sect ought to be considered evil or hateful unless it is first certainly ascertained and proved what evil exists within that sect itself (chapter 3).

[Col. 0706D] The pagans insisted that the enactment of laws issued by the emperors bound them to persecute and destroy Christians. “But this exception,” Tertullian says, “is utterly inept.” For no one is bound by any unjust law that either prohibits what is good or commands something iniquitous. Yet such were the laws enacted against the Christians.

Moreover, the pagans could not deny that many laws issued by their own legislators and by others likewise subject to human weakness were afterward corrected, curtailed, or repealed by others because they appeared harmful or useless. Were not the laws of Lycurgus corrected by the Lacedaemonians? Were not the Papian laws concerning the begetting of children either corrected or rendered obsolete by the emperor Severus? Was not the law concerning the cutting of debtors into [Col. 0707A] pieces altered? Nor is this surprising. For laws are commended neither by antiquity nor by the dignity of their author, but by equity alone. Yet no law was ever more unjust than that which commanded Christians to be condemned merely because of their name, without their case having been heard (chapter 4).

Tertullian demonstrates that this law was not only new and unjust but also tyrannical from the following consideration. During the reign of Tiberius, when the Christian name began to be disseminated through various parts of the world, Tiberius, having heard of Christ’s miracles, wished him to be enrolled among the gods. Although he did not accomplish this because of the senate’s opposition, he nevertheless persisted in his opinion and threatened danger to the accusers of Christians.

Among his successors, Nero was the very first—alas, what an impious and criminal man!—to rage against Christians with the imperial sword [Col. 0707B]. Domitian, no less cruel than Nero, attempted the same thing, but quickly restrained his own efforts. Marcus Aurelius stood far apart from both of them: when rain had been obtained from heaven through the prayers of Christian soldiers, he ordered that those who accused Christ’s followers should be punished more severely. Before him, Trajan, without issuing any law, prohibited Christians from being sought out. Nor does any law or decree of the emperors Hadrian, Vespasian, Pius, or Verus against them survive. Thus only the worst, most wicked, and most impious emperors raged against them (chapter 5).

Tertullian then, in order to close off to the pagans every foolish line of argument based upon the institutions and laws of their ancestors, makes it plain to everyone by a brief induction [Col. 0707C] that they themselves had overthrown the laws and more sacred statutes concerning expenditure, canvassing for office, abstinence from wine, divorce, and the worship of the gods.

Roman consuls expelled Liber and his mysteries from Rome and all Italy, just as Piso and Gabinius, likewise consuls, expelled Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates from the Capitol and the council chamber of the gods; these deities were subsequently restored by the Romans only after returning from exile. Finally, all the pagans had renounced the customs of their forefathers in clothing, food, furnishings, wealth, and even language itself. They therefore reproached Christians in vain for trampling down and overthrowing the authority of their ancient fathers, which they themselves had destroyed as boldly as they had done so with impunity (chapter 6).

From there our Author passes to the false and fabricated abominable [Col. 0707D] crimes of the Christians. He refutes them in such a way as to demonstrate with the utmost clarity that the Christians were as entirely innocent of them as the pagans were actually guilty.

First, Christians had long been defamed as though, in the manner of wild beasts, they devoured the flesh of a child whom they had killed and then, after the lights had been extinguished by the activity of dogs, wallowed most foully in every kind of sexual violation and incest. Yet nothing could have been easier than to convict Christians of such great crimes, if those crimes were really perpetrated by them. For their enemies and foes were always as numerous as the Jews, the soldiers, the household servants, almost all their wives, and even the pagans who continually persecuted them. Yet none of these ever learned of such deeds, much less disclosed them [Col. 0708A] or sold silence about them to the Christians for any price.

And indeed, who could have revealed these crimes? Certainly not the Christians, who concealed their mysteries no less scrupulously than did the pagans. Nor the pagans, who, being completely excluded from the Christians’ assemblies, could undoubtedly not know what was done in them. “But these things,” they said, “were spread by common report.” Yet what is more insubstantial than rumor? Since it always arises from envy, hatred, suspicion, or the pleasure of deceiving others, it persists only as long as it lies (chapter 7).

Tertullian insists that those crimes were so horrible that no one ought ever to have believed them or could ever have committed them. Christians promised their followers eternal happiness. Who could bring himself [Col. 0708B] to believe that they promised it to a person who killed an infant, ate bread dipped in its fresh blood, and afterward polluted himself by unspeakable incest? Indeed, no one could ever be persuaded that these things could be done by a pagan who possessed any sense of shame and humanity.

Nor should you say that the candidates for the Christian religion were deceived by others. Who could have deceived them? The father of the sacred rites, perhaps, or another person by whom they were instructed? But by what fraud, by what deceptions, could he teach them what they had to do in order to perpetrate those accursed crimes? Nevertheless, grant, if you will, that these things were committed by them. Why, after they had finally learned of and performed those acts, did they never complain of the fraud practiced upon them, but all [Col. 0708C] remained so steadfast in the horrible doctrine handed down to them? Did they fear that they would be punished if they revealed these things? On the contrary, they would thereby have won the favor of the pagans. But they preferred to perish rather than live beneath such a consciousness of guilt (chapter 8).

With the same ease with which Tertullian clears the Christians of such great crimes, he shows that the pagans were thoroughly convicted of the same or entirely similar offenses. In Africa, infants were openly sacrificed to Saturn—who did not spare his own sons—down to the first proconsulate of Tiberius, and secretly thereafter. The Gauls were accustomed to sacrifice older persons to Mercury, the Taurians their guests to Diana, and the Romans bestiarii—who were nevertheless human beings no less than the others—to Jupiter in the public games.

Moreover, others, with no less cruelty, deprived infants of life either by abortion or by exposing them after birth to imminent death [Col. 0708D]. To this is added the fact that not only did certain nations, like Catiline, ratify a compact by shedding their own blood, but the Scythians were also said to eat human beings. The priests of Bellona were consecrated with their own blood; and gladiators, like those suffering from epilepsy, drank the blood of other human beings killed in the arena.

Others also, at public spectacles, ate the flesh of a stag that had lain in human blood, or of a boar that had bloodied a human being, or the stomachs of a bear that still belched forth the entrails of people killed in those games. Finally, in a still more horrible crime, which ought never even to be named, they swallowed the substance of a human being. Christians, by contrast, recoiled [Col. 0709A] from every kind of cruelty; and even amid the cruelest tortures it was unlawful for them to taste either animal blood, anything strangled, or carrion offered to false gods (chapter 9).

What reason, moreover, did the pagans have for charging Christians with incest, of which the most criminal Jupiter had furnished an example and of which the Persians were guilty? The Macedonians too were suspected of the same crime, for they mocked the actor who, while performing the tragedy of Oedipus, lamented that his own mother had been violated by him.

What more need be said? Wicked pagans, accustomed to sexual violations, blindly inflicted sexual outrage even upon their own children, who had formerly been exposed and were no longer recognized by them. Christians, by contrast, either persevered in the state of virginity or always abstained from every transgression after marriage.

[Col. 0709B] From the false and fictitious secret crimes of the Christians, Tertullian passes to those that the pagans charged were manifest and public. The chief of these was the charge of sacrilege and violation of the divine majesty, brought against them because they utterly denied all worship to the gods.

Tertullian does not deny that this would undoubtedly be a great crime if those whom the pagans worshipped were truly gods. But the consciousness of the pagans themselves bore witness that they were not gods but mere human beings. If anyone should still dare to resist, he would immediately be refuted by innumerable testimonies from their own writers, who identify the places where those fictitious gods were born, where they lived their mortal lives, and where, after those lives ended, they were buried.

[Col. 0709C] Since it would have taken too long to enumerate every one of these gods by name, our Author demonstrates the point by the example of Saturn, the first of all the gods. For all writers on antiquity assert that Saturn was truly a man who, after many journeys, was received in Italy with Attic hospitality by Janus or Ino, and gave the name Saturnian to the mountain and city he inhabited and to all Italy.

This was declared no less plainly by the tablets first fashioned by him there and by the coin stamped with an image, on account of which he is said to preside over the treasury. He was therefore a human being, not the offspring of heaven and earth, as some have fabricated. Who, then, would dare deny that all the other gods who derive their origin from him were human beings as well (chapter 10)?

Nor does Tertullian allow the reply that these men [Col. 0709D] were enrolled among the gods only after their death. For no human being can confer divinity upon himself. If, therefore, it was given to anyone either before or after death, he must certainly have received it from another, more powerful God. Yet there was never any reason whatever why that supreme God should make certain men gods after their death. For he has never needed anyone’s assistance, whether in creating the world or in doing anything else. Indeed, rain, the heavenly lights, the stars, thunder, lightning, and the various kinds of crops came into being before all the fictitious gods of the gentiles. Indeed, the first of all human beings was created only after everything necessary for his life. Liber, Ceres, Bacchus, and Minerva, therefore, were no more made gods [Col. 0710A] for discovering crops than Lucullus was for bringing cherries from Pontus to Italy.

Nor can it be said with any better reason that divinity was bestowed upon human beings on account of their merits and virtues. For it follows from this that there is some supreme god who dispenses divinity to those who deserve it. Moreover, the gentiles were compelled to admit that their gods had been wicked, impious, criminal, and thoroughly depraved men, and that others like them were rightly and deservedly condemned by men of good character. Grant, however, that they were upright; they were nevertheless no better than Socrates and Aristides, no braver than Themistocles and Alexander, no more fortunate than Polycrates and Sulla, no richer than Croesus and Crassus, no more eloquent than Demosthenes and Cicero, no wiser than Cato, and no more equitable than Scipio. Why, then, did the pagans leave the latter [Col. 0710B] in the underworld while raising the former to heaven as gods (chap. 11)?

But say further: who are these gods of the gentiles? “I see absolutely nothing in them,” says Tertullian, “except the names of dead men. I hear nothing but fables, and I recognize sacred rites established on the basis of those fables.” What, moreover, of the fact that their images, fashioned from the material of ordinary vessels and implements—or even from those very vessels and implements—were finally made gods by a sacrilegious consecration? Who, furthermore, does not see that while those beautiful images are being made they suffer the same things as Christians do when tortured by the gentiles? For they are made from metals, while Christians are condemned to the mines. They are placed upon crosses and stakes, scraped with claws, and burned with fire; and by all these methods [Col. 0710C] Christians are removed from the world. They differ from them, however, in this: the images are at first without a head, whereas the Christian’s head is finally cut off after he has been most unjustly condemned. Moreover, Christians are banished to islands in which, as no one is unaware, almost all the gentiles’ gods were born and died. Nor could they answer that these things were merely Christian insults against the gods, since Seneca attacked those same gods with many expressions far more bitter. Christians therefore rightly refused to worship those images of the gods which, defiled by kites, mice, and spiders, are neglected, mocked, and destroyed by the gentiles themselves.

Indeed, different men worshiped different gods, and no one could be a god without a decree of the Senate. Each man, according to his need or his power, [Col. 0710D] pledged, sold, or converted his household gods, now into a ladle, now into a cooking pot. Their public gods, meanwhile, they held subject to tax in the auction room and offered for sale beneath the spear and at the proclamation of the public crier. Nor is this at all surprising. For the holier the gods, the more heavily taxed they were. The mendicant religion of the pagans went round the taverns and charged a high fee for admission to some temple.

But come now: in what way, I ask, did the pagans honor their gods? Precisely as they honored dead emperors; indeed, they paid those emperors while alive the same honor as they paid their dead gods. In the same fashion they also venerated the prostitute Larentina, Simon Magus, some god of Synedus or other, and impure Junos, Cereses, and [Col. 0711A] Dianas. What greater insult, therefore, could any human being offer to the ancient gods (chaps. 12, 13)?

Were the gods not also held in no less derision by those who sacrificed all the vilest things to them and stole a third part of the tithes owed to Hercules? Did not others proclaim in their books, to the gods’ very great disgrace, that they had fought among themselves over the Trojans or Achaeans; that Venus had been wounded; that Mars had almost wasted away in chains; that Jupiter had been delivered from some monster and was now weeping, now shamefully in heat? The poets, moreover, sing of Apollo serving Admetus and Neptune serving Laomedon, while Pindar tells of Aesculapius being punished with a thunderbolt. Furthermore, tragedians continually sing of the gods’ miseries and errors. Among the philosophers, [Col. 0711B] Socrates, although he swore by the oak, the goat, and the dog, was nevertheless condemned to death because he was destroying the gods. But after rescinding his condemnation, they finally rendered him splendid testimony. Lastly, a certain Diogenes mocked Hercules, and Varro introduced three hundred Jupiters (chap. 14).

Tertullian presses the point further: in the gentiles’ comedies and tragedies are represented an adulterous Anubis, a male Moon, a scourged Diana, Jupiter’s testament, and three hungry Herculeses. The actors also exhibited the Sun in mourning, Cybele sighing for a disdainful shepherd, Jupiter’s epitaph, and the judgment of Juno and Minerva; and finally, in those performances, some utterly infamous person represented the likeness of a god, while a body rendered effeminate by ridiculous art represented Minerva or Hercules. [Col. 0711C] Nor should one expect anything better from the amphitheater. There the part was played of the castrated Attis, of Hercules burning, of Mercury testing the dead with a cautery amid the noonday spectacles, and of Jupiter’s brother dragging away the corpses of dead men with his hammer. Tertullian omits many other things of this kind and reproaches the gentiles because within the gods’ temples, between the very altars, and in the booths of priests and temple-keepers they arranged adulteries and conducted procuring. Who, then, he asks, were guilty of offending the divine majesty: those who treated their gods with such derision, or the Christians, who denied that these were gods and who, for that reason, did not know their temples by day and, if it could have been done, would have stripped them bare entirely (chap. 15)?

But the pagans objected in reply that Christians worshiped an ass’s head [Col. 0711D] as a god. Yet this, says Tertullian, is sheer fantasy, for which Cornelius Tacitus gave occasion when he falsely recorded that the Jews had consecrated the likeness of this animal because, when they were suffering from thirst in Egypt, certain wild asses had shown them a spring. But the slander of this utterly mendacious writer became perfectly evident when Pompey entered the Jews’ temple and found no image there. Yet the more false this was, the more certainly true it was that all beasts of burden and geldings, together with their Epona, were worshiped and honored by the gentiles.

Nor did they reproach Christians with the worship of Christ’s cross on any better grounds. For what could they condemn in it? Did they not have on public display the Attic Pallas and the Pharian Ceres, [Col. 0712A] which could not be distinguished from the upright post and timber of a cross? Furthermore, in the images of their own gods, in victories, trophies, military standards, the cloths of banners and cantabra, or in their inner ornaments and robes, they worshiped crosses set beneath them.

Others suspected, somewhat more plausibly, that the Christians’ God, like that of the Persians, was the Sun. But this false suspicion arose because those same Christians prayed to God while facing the sun and indulged in rejoicing on the day of the Sun, or the Lord’s Day. Yet this was certainly all the less deserving of the gentiles’ censure because they had devoted Saturn’s day to idleness and feasting.

Lastly, our author derides a certain Jew, [Col. 0712B] plainly an utter scoundrel, who, being an animal-fighter, displayed during the circus games most recently held in that city, he says, a placard on which the Christians’ God was carried around depicted with ass’s ears, hoofed on one foot, carrying a book, and wearing a toga, with this ridiculous inscription: “The Christians’ God, Onochoetes.” But just as false and mendacious as this picture was, so true was it that the gentiles worshiped gods composed of the limbs of human beings and beasts (chap. 16).

Lest the gentiles should thereafter slander the Christians’ true doctrine through willful ignorance and their customary shameless lies, Tertullian expounds it with the utmost brevity and sincerity as follows. “The God whom we worship,” he says, “is one, who created the whole universe out of [Col. 0712C] nothing as an adornment of his majesty. Although he is known, he is nevertheless invisible, inestimable, immeasurable, and known only to himself as great as he is.” That this one true God really exists is demonstrated both by the world and by all the other things which he commanded to come into being by his word, ordered by reason, and established by his power. Indeed, this is also most clearly confirmed by the testimony of our soul, Christian by nature, which, in whatever condition of infirmity, error, or depraved lust it may be, when it recovers its senses or returns to itself, cries out not to gods but to one God and invokes him as judge (chap. 17).

No less evident an argument for the divine existence is drawn from the sacred books of the Old Testament, which were written by men filled with the divine spirit and who [Col. 0712D] confirmed their writings by various genuine miracles. Aristaeus, moreover, testifies that these books, first composed in the Hebrew language, were translated into Greek with the utmost fidelity by seventy Jews under the direction of Ptolemy Philadelphus and with the approval of Menedemus. At that time they were still preserved in Ptolemy’s library, written in Hebrew and Greek characters; and the Jews read them publicly every Sabbath. There could therefore be no doubt about their truth and integrity (chap. 18).

Their antiquity, moreover, vindicates their very great authority. For the archive of one Prophet—that is, the books of Moses—is older than the other writings of the gentiles, than their gods, temples, oracles, and sacred rites, indeed than all Greek [Col. 0713A] characters and most nations and cities. For Moses, a contemporary of Inachus, far surpasses in antiquity not only Homer and the fall of Priam, but also the most ancient Danaus. The other prophets, though later than Moses, nevertheless precede the Greek sages, lawgivers, and historians by no short interval of time. Since, however, it would take too long to set forth something whose proof is easiest for everyone, Tertullian omitted this demonstration, while nevertheless indicating the sources and citing various writers from whom that antiquity of Sacred Scripture can become perfectly evident to anyone (chap. 19).

Moreover, he derives its supreme authority not only from this antiquity, but especially from the fact that it is wholly divine. For its authors, inspired by the divine spirit, [Col. 0713B] foretold the destruction of the world and many other things which we know actually occurred. We should therefore not doubt the other things that were likewise foretold by them. It must accordingly be held as settled and certain that there exists only the one God proclaimed everywhere by them, and that the Christian religion, which rests upon these books of theirs, is true (chap. 20).

But then the gentiles rose up and cried out that this religion of the Christians was new, since they differed utterly and completely from the Jewish religion both in name and in rites. Tertullian answers them, however, that the Jews flourished in the highest prosperity so long as they earned God’s favor by their remarkable righteousness and the faith of the patriarchs. But after trampling upon his laws and falling into the gravest crimes, as punishment [Col. 0713C] they were scattered and wander about, homeless exiles from heaven and country, so that they were not even permitted to greet their own homeland by setting foot upon it. Yet not only were these things foretold by their sacred prophets, but also that another people would arise, to whom God would transfer greater favor than he had given them. Christ is the judge and teacher of this chosen people, likewise foretold by those same prophets. And he, not wholly unknown to the philosophers Zeno and Cleanthes, is God’s λόγος (“Word”), word, reason, wisdom, and true Son. For he was begotten not in the manner of human beings or manufactured gods, but as a ray from the sun, so spirit from spirit and light from light; he did not withdraw from the source, but proceeded from it in such a way as not to be separated from the substance of his Father, from whom he is another in measure, not in number, [Col. 0713D] in degree, not in condition, and is altogether one God with him. Then, at the appointed time, having descended into a virgin, he became a man united with God.

Neither the gentiles, who had fabricated other similar tales, nor the Jews, who knew that he had been promised by their prophets, could dismiss these things as old wives’ fables. For the Jews erred in this: because they did not understand what was said in those sacred Scriptures about his first and second coming, they denied that he had already come to us. Their blindness, perversity, and wickedness, moreover, were so great that they accused of magic him who, by performing miracles, openly showed himself to be the λόγον (“Word”) of God. But when he drew very many to himself through his heavenly teaching, they became exasperated, delivered him to Pontius Pilate, [Col. 0714A] and by the violence of their votes extorted from him the sentence that Christ should be affixed to the cross, as he had foretold. When he died, there occurred an altogether extraordinary eclipse of the sun, recorded in their archives by those same Jews, who did not know that it had been announced by the prophets. His body was then laid in a tomb by them. But when on the third day he miraculously rose again, they spread the story that it had been stolen by his disciples. He, however, withdrew from the crowds after returning to life; and after associating with certain disciples for forty days, he instructed them in the doctrine to be disseminated everywhere, and thereafter ascended into heaven surrounded by a cloud. Pilate, who at that time was a Christian in conscience, reported all these things to Tiberius, who indeed would have believed in Christ had he not been Caesar and ruled over pagans. But the fiercer Jews most cruelly harassed the disciples of Christ [Col. 0714B] as they preached the doctrine entrusted to them by him; and Nero was the first to shed their blood at Rome.

Tertullian, moreover, firmly asserts that this is the true summary of Christian doctrine and that the gentiles cannot deprive him of credibility. For Christians were thoroughly persuaded that it had never been lawful for anyone, and much less for themselves when explaining the tenets of their religion, to lie. What evil, then, could there be in their religion and worship, when they openly declared that they worshiped God through Christ? Did not the Jews venerate God through Moses, the Greek gentiles through other men, and the Romans, initiated by Numa Pompilius, through their superstitions? The question that should rather have been asked was whether Christ’s divinity is true, through knowledge of which [Col. 0714C] a human being is reformed for the better (chap. 21).

Christians also believed that demons exist, not unknown to philosophers—especially Socrates and Zeno—to poets, or to magicians, and invoked by the common people when cursing or wishing evil upon others. These are of a spiritual substance, as are the angels; but having fallen into sin, they have plotted humanity’s destruction from the beginning of the world. Endowed with spiritual powers as well as a spiritual substance, they not only corrupt crops and human health, but also disturb the human mind with depraved impulses and turn it away from the thought of divinity. Because by their native swiftness they are everywhere in a single instant and know God’s dispositions, they emulate divinity by stealing divination. Moreover, they pronounce ambiguous oracles, cure those whom they have injured, perform false miracles through various [Col. 0714D] deceptions, produce apparitions, defame the souls of the dead, strike down children to elicit an oracular utterance, send dreams, and by their agency goats and tables were accustomed to divine. Yet the pagans, who ascribed all these things to their gods, were acknowledging beyond doubt that those gods were demons.

Nor could they answer that their gods should be judged not from what happened in profane places, but only from what happened in their temples. For the madness of one who hurls himself down from a tower consecrated to these gods does not differ from that of another who throws himself from the roof of a neighboring house. Nor is the insanity of one who cuts his arms and genitals in honor of a goddess any different from that of another who cuts his own throat. But if these arguments, [Col. 0715A] says Tertullian, appear of little weight, other arguments demonstrate most conclusively that the gods of the gentiles and demons are the same. Let someone be brought forward who is suffering from a god, who inhales over altars and conceives a divine presence; let the virgin goddess who promises rain come forth; let the god Aesculapius be brought into the midst to heal some dying man: then, if each and every one of these does not, when questioned by a Christian, confess that they are demons, Tertullian permits that the blood of that same Christian be shed immediately. Yet nothing is simpler, clearer, and more effective than this demonstration. Either the demon will lie, and is not a god; or it will speak the truth, and consequently the gods really are demons. Whoever, therefore, says that these things are done by the gods must assert that they are subject to Christians and, consequently, [Col. 0715B] that their status as gods is as false as the Christian religion is true. For all this power arises from the name of Christ, by which demons, when adjured by Christians, are compelled not only to depart from the human bodies they possess, but also to confess that they are not gods but unclean spirits, already condemned because of their wickedness; that there is only one God; and that the things said shortly before about Christ are therefore true (chaps. 22, 23).

Tertullian therefore rightly concludes from these arguments that Christians are wrongly accused of offending the divine majesty. For even if it were established that the gentiles’ gods were true gods, they themselves, like Plato, believed that supreme power belonged to one—namely Jupiter—and the offices to the rest. What wrong, then, were Christians committing when they worshiped and venerated one supreme God, just as other people [Col. 0715C] acknowledged a single emperor? Was this less lawful for them than it was for every individual, city, and province to have some god of its own and peculiar to itself? Yet some, with no one opposing them, privately worshiped Jupiter; others, Faith; the Egyptians, birds and beasts; the Syrians, Astarte; and so the rest, each his own god. In a word, everyone was permitted to worship whomever he wished except the true God. But was not this rather the greatest crime against the divine majesty of which they falsely accused Christians? And certainly it was all the greater, the more cruelly they sought to compel Christians to worship false divinities and utterly to deny the true God and creator of all things (chap. 24).

The Romans nevertheless objected that, as a reward for their piety and religion [Col. 0715D] toward their gods, they had received dominion over the whole world. “What then?” says Tertullian. Had they obtained it from their native and household gods, such as Sterculus, Mutunus, and the prostitute Larentina? Who would believe it? Or from foreign and immigrant gods, who should have been more concerned to protect their own homeland than Rome? Yet Cybele, after being brought to Rome, was so little concerned to announce the death of Emperor Aurelius to her great priest, the archigallus, that she calmly allowed him to offer his arms and impure blood for the safety of this emperor, who had already departed this life eight days earlier. By what reasoning, moreover, did Jupiter so patiently endure his own Crete, where he was born, died, and was buried, to be shaken by the Roman fasces? [Col. 0716A] Could Juno calmly endure Carthage, once so dear to her and preferred by her to Samos, to be destroyed by the Romans so that they might extend the boundaries of their empire more widely? Yet if matters really stand thus, why did the Romans pay her less honor than they paid Larentia, that most debauched she-wolf?

Moreover, several of their gods, such as Saturn and Jupiter, had reigned. From which Roman god, then, did they receive their kingdom? Was it from some Sterculus? Who but a fool would dare say so? There were also many kings who had never worshiped either the Roman gods or any others. Finally, Roman dominion grew before Roman religion. For before Numa Pompilius established empty superstitions at Rome, and before there were any images of the gods among them, the Latins had had many [Col. 0716B] kings. The Romans, therefore, says Tertullian, were not religious before they were great; and so they were not great because they were religious.

But he presses the point still more sharply: “How,” he asks, “did these men invade the kingdoms of others?” Certainly not by piety or religion, but by wars and victories, and consequently by the indiscriminate slaughter and ruin of walls and temples, priests and citizens, sacred and profane things. Is this, then, the piety on account of which the gods both gave dominion over the world to the Romans, who injured them, and took it away from others who worshiped their own gods with no less piety? Finally, before the foundations of Rome were laid, there reigned not only the Babylonians, Medes, Egyptians, Assyrians, and Amazons, but also the Jews, who rejected and despised all the gods of the Romans and the other gentiles. [Col. 0716C] It is not, therefore, the gods of the Romans or of other nations who dispense kingdoms, but that one omnipotent God alone, to whom, says our author, belong the world that is ruled and the human being himself who rules. It was therefore not the Christians who worshiped him, but the Romans and other gentiles, who were convicted of the crime of offending the divine majesty, because they not only worshiped false gods but also attempted by every kind of torture to compel those same Christians to worship them (chaps. 25, 26).

Those pagans who possessed greater clemency tried to persuade the Christians at least not to refuse so obstinately, and at such certain risk of death, to sacrifice to the gods, while preserving in their hearts their resolve to worship the true God. But this counsel of false compassion was inspired in them by the fraud and cunning of the demons, who, fearing the Christians’ power, [Col. 0716D] wage war against them with implacable hatred. They regard it as no small consolation in their own forecondemnation if they can sometimes weaken the Christians’ constancy and injure them. Christians therefore resist them and are persuaded that they never triumph more gloriously over the demons’ malice than when they are condemned for their steadfast profession of faith (chap. 27).

Furthermore, the pagans, through the impious deceits and arts of the demons, wished not only to force Christians against their will into worshiping the gods—a worship that must either be wholly free and voluntary or be no worship at all—but also to sacrifice to those same gods for the emperor’s safety. Therefore, because they avoided making these sacrifices, they accused them of a crime greater [Col. 0717A] than offending the divine majesty. Why should they not, since they feared the living emperor far more than their dead gods, and would therefore more readily swear falsely by all the latter than by the emperor’s genius? Yet what is more contrary to right reason than to sacrifice to gods for the safety of a human being—a safety which they can neither give nor preserve? For how, Tertullian presses, will they preserve others when they cannot protect their own temples and statues without the guards of Caesar’s soldiers? What, moreover, of the fact that many temples and gods depend upon Caesar’s nod and will? Christians therefore prayed for the emperor’s safety, with far better right, not to those false gods but to the true, living, and eternal God. For even the emperors themselves, if they are of sound mind, desire the favor of him from whom they have [Col. 0717B] their humanity, their life, and their rule over other human beings. For their safety, therefore, their prosperity, their longer life, and the long duration of their empire, Christians poured forth prayers with hands outstretched and head uncovered, without a prompter beforehand—prayers arising from chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and the Holy Spirit. But they did not offer, as did the pagans, grains worth a single as, nor the tears of an Arabian tree, nor the blood of an ox wasted by disease or age, nor a filthy conscience, nor victims slaughtered by the most vicious priests. Tertullian therefore challenges the pagan governors, if it could ever be right, to torture, rack, and kill Christians while they pray to God in this manner for the emperor’s safety (chaps. 28, 29, 30).

How sincere was the spirit, and how free from feigned flattery [Col. 0717C]—which could have profited them against the pagans who charged them with this—when Christians thus prayed to almighty God, Tertullian demonstrates from the fact that in their sacred writings, which they did not conceal, everyone is commanded to pray to God not only for his enemies but also, by name, for the emperors themselves. He adds that they had another reason, or rather necessity, for praying for the emperors and the stability of the Roman Empire: namely, that the end of the world, which was destined to perish together with it, might be delayed. Accordingly, they willingly swore by the safety of the emperors, but by no means by their genii, whom they were accustomed to drive away by adjurations (chaps. 31, 32).

Furthermore, says our author, the Christians’ piety and religious duty toward the emperor were all the greater because they knew with greater certainty that he had been chosen and [Col. 0717D] appointed by the true God. They could therefore obtain the emperor’s safety from this God all the more readily because by these prayers they acknowledged that the emperor was less than God. It was unlawful for them to call the emperor a god, since he is a human being and, while triumphing, is reminded of his human condition. Indeed, Emperor Augustus did not wish to be called lord. And rightly so, for there is one Lord of all, including the emperor—namely, almighty God. Finally, how could the emperor, while still alive, be called by the name of God, which the pagans did not bestow upon Caesars before their apotheosis (chaps. 33, 34)?

With the same ease and clarity with which Tertullian had thus far proved that Christians were not guilty of offending human majesty, [Col. 0718A] he shows that they could not on that account be called public enemies by the pagans because they did not celebrate the Caesars’ festivals in the pagan manner. For who but an impious man would deny that these observances should be conducted with great moderation, propriety, sobriety, and chastity? Yet the gentiles celebrated them with the utmost wantonness, drunkenness, shamelessness, riotous running about, insults, and laurels and lamps hung like brothel signs at the doorposts of houses. In addition, while celebrating these solemn festivals, they did not spare the emperors themselves: while insincerely wishing them many years of life, they were at the same time considering the creation of another, new emperor.

Nor does our author allow the reply that these are merely the desires of the blind and ungrateful mob, not of others. [Col. 0718B] For Cassius, Niger, and Albinus, the emperors’ bitterest enemies, were not plebeians; nor were the others, more audacious than Sigerius and Parthenius, who besieged Caesar between two laurels; nor, finally, were those men who were then daily recognized as accomplices in these criminal factions. Yet these very men made sacrifices for the emperors’ safety, swore solemnly by their genius, and celebrated their festivals like everyone else. Astrologers, haruspices, augurs, and magicians likewise rendered the same duties, while by demonic arts they inquired into the Caesars’ future death and desired it to be near (chap. 35).

The loyalty, piety, and religious duty owed to emperors therefore do not consist in these observances, which were often seen to be performed by their enemies, but in those habits and works of a good mind which one renders to emperors and to everyone else [Col. 0718C] indiscriminately, expecting no reward except from God. Christians performed these duties, for they are commanded to wish or do evil to no one, to think evil of no one, to hate no one, to love their enemies, and, when injured, not to repay like with like. This was indeed observed by them so diligently that, although pelted with stones by the mob, burned with fire by the fury of others, or exhumed from their graves by Bacchanalian frenzies, they never wished to avenge the many grave injuries inflicted upon themselves or their brethren. Yet they could have exacted vengeance for them, either secretly with a few small torches or openly with greater military forces than the pagans possessed. For, dispersed throughout the whole world, they had filled cities, towns, camps, and everything except the temples of the gods. And even if they could have mustered smaller forces, for what war [Col. 0718D] were those not ready and fit who willingly allowed themselves to be slaughtered for professing their religion? Grant also, if you wish, that they were unarmed. Yet they could very easily have avenged themselves merely by deserting or separating from the gentiles. For their multitude was so great that, had the gentiles been left to themselves, they would have been appalled at their own desolation and would have had more enemies than citizens. Finally, it would surely have sufficed for Christian vengeance if they had not driven the demons from the possessed bodies of the pagans. By granting the gentiles this single and very great protection, they therefore showed that they were enemies not of the human race, but of error, as we have thus far proved (chaps. 36, 37).

Our author then passes to another, no less shameless slander, by which Christians were accused of the false crime of unlawful association. For what, he asks, [Col. 0719A] is an unlawful faction except an association of men who disturb cities and kingdoms out of ambition for office or glory? Yet Christians, driven by no ambition, had always renounced the assemblies and public affairs of the gentiles, just as they had the pleasures of the circus, theater, arena, and other spectacles. Yet surely, by rejecting these things, they caused the pagans no loss or injury, just as they did not when Christians sometimes pursued other pleasures that the pagans in turn rejected (chap. 38).

Moreover, to show everyone still more plainly that Christians did nothing with the turbulent spirit of an unlawful faction, but everything solely from a disposition of true religion and piety, Tertullian briefly and sincerely describes what was done in their [Col. 0719B] assemblies. There, he says, they did violence to God by pouring forth prayers for the emperor and the authorities, for the stability of the world and the peace of affairs, and for delay to be imposed upon the final end of the world. Then the divine Scriptures were read, by which they might nourish the faith of those present, raise their hope, and establish their confidence. Exhortations, corrections, and divine censure for some grave sin followed. These assemblies were presided over by approved elders, who had obtained this honor not by payment but by merit. On one day each month, everyone voluntarily contributed a modest sum according to his means, to support all kinds of needy persons, the aged, children, exiles, those consigned to prisons, and others condemned to the mines. The pagans therefore strove in vain to defame this mutual charity of the Christians, by which they called one another brothers, [Col. 0719C] united as they were by true religion, and shared their goods with others—goods by which the pagans’ mutual affection was invariably divided. For the Christians held everything in common except their wives, whereas the pagans, while keeping everything else, shared their wives with their friends, as did Socrates and Cato.

Tertullian continues: the Christians’ supper, he says, was not lavish and costly like that of the Megarians or the others censured by him there, but was rightly and deservedly called by the Greeks ἀγάπη (“love”) and by the Latins “affection.” It begins with prayers, and afterward everyone eats and drinks with such moderation that they remember that God must be worshiped throughout the night. After water for the hands and the lights have been brought, each person is invited, as he is able, to sing something to God from [Col. 0719D] the sacred Scriptures. Others, conversing among themselves, know that the Lord is listening. Finally, prayer ends the banquet just as it began it, and afterward everyone departs not in the turbulent and wanton manner of the pagans, but with the utmost modesty. From these practices, thus explained, Tertullian concludes that unlawful and condemnable factions existed not in the Christians’ assemblies, but in those of the gentiles themselves.

Nor did the latter have any better right to cry out that these same Christians were the authors of all public calamities. For before their name had been heard, several islands named by our author were swallowed up either by the waves of the sea or by earthquakes. It is also established that previously, before any Roman [Col. 0720A] gods existed, the whole world perished in a universal flood, not merely a flood of the plains, as Plato supposed. Moreover, before the Jews migrated into Egypt, and thus long before Christ founded his religion, avenging fire had consumed Sodom and Gomorrah, Volsinii, and Pompeii. No one is unaware, moreover, that the Romans were routed in the battle of Cannae and that the Capitol was captured by the Senones when the Romans worshiped their own gods and no Christians worshiped the true God. Finally, the same devastation and ruin of cities and temples had occurred before. Yet these things could not be ascribed to the manufactured gods whose temples they were, but to the impiety of the human beings who worshiped them and who, either ignorant or contemptuous of the true God, the source of every good, had defiled themselves with every kind of vice and crime. [Col. 0720B] To this is added the fact that, from the time when Christ’s religion arose, public calamities of this kind were undoubtedly lighter. For the innocence of its followers tempered the iniquity of the age. And indeed, whenever some calamity oppressed the world, the gentiles vainly wearied their false gods with their customary rites, whereas the Christians obtained the mercy of the true God through continence, fasting, and other acts of repentance. It was therefore not these worshipers of the true God, but the gentiles who despised him, who were the cause of public calamities (chaps. 39, 40).

Tertullian further insists that their gods are most unjust if, because of the crimes of the Christians, they afflict and destroy them with such great evils. Nor does he allow this weapon to be turned against the Christians, whom God permitted to be overwhelmed by the same calamities as the Gentiles. For, as he himself declared, God will not distinguish the just [Col. 0720C] from the unjust until the final judgment after the end of the world. He therefore willed that, in this course of human life, all things should be common to all: adversities serving as admonition for the good, but as chastisement for the wicked. Moreover, Christians were harmed by no adversities, since nothing was more desirable to them than to depart from this world. Whatever affliction shook them, they renewed their hope and confidence through the predictions of the divine Scriptures. The Gentiles, by contrast, having no consolation from their gods in adversity, either in this life or in the life to come, plainly worshipped gods who were unjust and ungrateful (ch. 41).

What, moreover, could be more absurd than another complaint made by the Gentiles against the Christians, in which they protested that Christians were unproductive and useless to the commonwealth? For they were not [Col. 0720D] Brahmans or forest-dwellers, but everywhere engaged in every kind of commerce with those same Gentiles; and, excepting only the latter’s superstitious ceremonies, they so combined their crafts and services that they lived both with them and from them. “But the revenues of our temples,” the Gentiles said, “are diminished.” “For whom?” asks Tertullian. “For your beggar-men and beggar-gods?” Do Christians not always bring assistance to those who ask it, and does not their mercy distribute more street by street than the Gentiles distribute temple by temple? As for all other taxes, those same Christians pay them with as much good faith as the Gentiles use dishonesty in evading them (ch. 42).

But who, our author continues, complained that Christians were useless? Was it not pimps, procurers, bath-house attendants, assassins, poisoners, magicians, [Col. 0721A] and other men of the same stamp? Yet to be unproductive for them is itself a gain. Besides, if Christians caused any loss to the commonwealth, they more than adequately compensated for it by expelling demons from the bodies of the Gentiles themselves. But the Gentiles killed Christians with a cruelty as great as the injury they thereby did to the commonwealth, although the Christians’ innocence ought to have been evident to everyone, if only from the fact that, while the prisons were full of criminals, no Christian was found there except solely on account of his name (chs. 43, 44).

The integrity of their lives and morals is proved not only by this fact, but also by their divine laws, which far surpass all human laws in sanctity and authority. For the latter forbid homicide, the former [Col. 0721B] anger; the latter adultery, the former lust; the latter wrongdoing, the former evil speech. The latter command that injury be avenged, while the former forbid repaying injury in kind. To this is added the fact that everything approved in the human laws of the Gentiles was drawn from the divine statutes of the Christians. Moreover, it is plainly established that the authority of the latter is greater than that of the former, because a human law can easily be broken, whether because offenders can conceal themselves and feel compelled to sin, or because punishment is brief and cannot be inflicted beyond death. But absolutely nothing can be hidden from God, who exacts eternal punishments from all who are conscious of crimes. What wonder, then, if—as has already been demonstrated—the Christians who feared him possessed such great innocence, while the Gentiles who feared the proconsul displayed such depravity [Col. 0721C] (chs. 45, 46)?

“But our philosophers,” they said, “professed the same innocence, justice, patience, sobriety, and chastity as the Christians.” If that is so, Tertullian replies, why are so many philosophers, who spurned the superstitions of the Gentiles, praised and rewarded with statues and stipends, while Christians are tortured and killed for precisely the same reason? Was Socrates—who made use of the services of a demon that continually attended him, and who sacrificed to Aesculapius—better than Christians, who put demons to flight and expel them? Is the knowledge of Thales, who when questioned about God gave no answer, or of Plato, who said that God is difficult to discover and describe, greater or better than that of any Christian artisan, who has found God and immediately explains who he is [Col. 0721D]? Is the chastity of Christians, who preserve continence or desire no woman except a wife, less or worse than that of Plato, corrupter of young men; of Diogenes, desperately enamored of the prostitute Phryne; of Speusippus, who died in adultery; or of Democritus, who blinded himself lest he look upon women with corrupted eyes? And what modesty was there in Diogenes, who trampled Plato’s pride with another kind of pride, or in Pythagoras and Zeno, who aspired to tyranny? What equity was there in Lycurgus, who killed himself because his laws had been amended? Why say more? Is not Aristotle remembered for having shamefully expelled Hermias from his position, just as he flattered Alexander? Is not Plato remembered as having sold himself for the sake of his belly, Aristippus for his dissipation, [Col. 0722A] and Hippias as having been killed in an ambush which he himself had prepared for another? But the Christian, utterly removed from all these things, has never attempted anything of the kind. For if anyone departed from the rule of discipline, he thereby ceased to be a Christian.

The Gentiles therefore boasted in vain that their philosophers were equal to Christians in knowledge. For those very philosophers, like the poets and sophists, had indeed drawn many teachings from the sacred fountains of our divine Scripture; but, despising its simplicity and its language, which was then obscure, they corrupted those teachings with their own perverse opinions. From this sacred Scripture they learned that there is only one God; but the Platonists taught that he is incorporeal, the Stoics that he is corporeal, Epicurus that he arose from atoms, Pythagoras that he arose from numbers, and Heraclitus that he arose from fire. In the same way, [Col. 0722B] Plato affirmed his divine providence, which Epicurus denied. Some considered him to be outside the world, others to be situated within it. For the same reason, their opinions varied concerning the origin and duration of the world and the nature of the human soul. Nor should it be objected that the recent teaching of Christ was also adulterated by certain Christians. For these, says Tertullian, are heretics, and against their errors we prescribe the most certain rule of truth, which has been transmitted to us by the disciples of Christ himself.

Furthermore, through the malicious cunning and wicked prompting of demons, the Gentile philosophers and poets devised certain fables, so that, through a false resemblance to the truth handed down in the sacred Scriptures, other men would place their faith in them rather than in the Christians, whom they hated. [Col. 0722C] Thus they invented a tribunal in the underworld, the river Pyriphlegethon, and the Elysian Fields, because they had learned from our people that there would be a final judgment of all humanity, eternal punishments for the wicked, and everlasting happiness for the devout in paradise. But who does not know that our writings, as the more ancient, should be believed rather than the more recent writings of others, just as the archetype should be believed rather than its image (ch. 47)?

And certainly the complete restoration of our bodies is far truer than the Pythagorean transmigration of souls. For no one will ever deny that a human body can be reconstituted by him from whom the soul is falsely imagined to have received the power to migrate from one body into another. But that migration of souls is plainly fictitious, since no one has ever [Col. 0722D] recognized that he had been transformed into a beast. Moreover, in this passage of the soul from one body into another, one part of the human being remains alive while the other always remains dead. Yet the whole human being must necessarily return to his former life, so that he may receive God’s final judgment concerning the good or evil deeds he performed in this life. What of the fact that the soul can suffer nothing without the body, although it nevertheless merited nothing apart from it? Nor should you say that this can never be done by anyone. For he who, when you did not exist, created you, like the whole world, from nothing, can assuredly reconstitute you entire, just as you were, after you have ceased to exist. Finally, light, darkness, the stars, the fruits of the earth, seeds, and very many other things revive; how much more will man return [Col. 0723A] to life—man who, if he knows himself according to the oracle of the Pythia, is lord of all things that die and rise again? Wherever, therefore, or in whatever manner, he has been reduced to nothing, he will be recalled to life by the power of him to whom nothingness belongs, just as does the whole.

“Must one therefore,” someone will argue, “always die and rise again?” Certainly, says Tertullian, if it had so pleased God. But he who created all things from diverse and contrary realities plainly willed that dead human beings should be raised once to their former life at that intervening point of time which, at the end of the world, lies between this temporal age and the eternity that will follow.

Then the worshippers of God will obtain the reward of eternal happiness, just as the profane and wicked will be tormented in everlasting fire. Examples of this fire, [Col. 0723B] wholly different from our earthly fire, are furnished to us by lightning bolts and perpetually burning mountains. Although the philosophers acknowledged these things, and others did not reject them, they nevertheless mocked this opinion of the Christians. Grant, however, if it pleases God, that it is false. Yet surely the very hope of eternal punishment or reward is useful and necessary for everyone. Whatever that hope may be, Christians were still not for that reason to be savaged with swords, beasts, crosses, and fires while the populace exulted. The Gentiles, therefore, displayed an utterly foolish eagerness and gloried in the punishments of men who, choosing condemnation rather than falling away from God, celebrated an immortal triumph (chs. 48, 49).

But the Gentiles again cried out even more violently that Christians had no cause for complaint if they suffered voluntarily. Our author replies to them that Christians suffer in the manner of soldiers who, although they pray to be spared the dangers of war, nevertheless fight with all their strength and ultimately rejoice when they obtain spoil, victory, and glory. [Col. 0723C] For the Christians’ victory possesses the glory of pleasing God and the spoil of eternal life. In this glorious contest, the very instruments by which they are tortured become for them the attire of victory, the palm-embroidered robe, and the triumphal chariot.
