Thus they could not be called desperate or ruined by Gentiles who not only extolled with the highest praises the courage and constancy amid torture and the cruelest death of Mucius, Empedocles, Dido, Regulus, Anaxarchus, the Attic courtesan, Zeno of Elea, the Laconians, and others, but also adorned them with statues, images, and inscriptions, effecting a kind of recall from death to life [Col. 0723D] and an eternity of glory. So far, therefore, is the Christian—who expects from God, for whom he suffers, a true eternity—from being mad, that by this very fact he proves his own innocence and the unjust cruelty of the Gentiles. Did not those same Gentiles, by condemning a Christian woman to a pimp rather than to a lion, openly confess that she and other Christians considered the stain upon chastity more dreadful than every kind of torture and even death itself? Yet their savagery profited the Gentiles not in the least, since the blood of the martyrs was the seed of Christians, through which their number continually increased in a marvelous fashion. Indeed, by their death they made far more disciples than Cicero, Seneca, Diogenes, [Col. 0724A] Pyrrho, and Callinicus, who exhorted their followers to endure pain and death. For the Gentiles first admired the Christians’ unconquered constancy. Then they recognized the cause of such constancy and the truth of the Christian religion. Once they had recognized it, they embraced it without delay and were inflamed with a marvelous ardor for martyrdom, by which not only are all sins forgiven, but the entirety of God’s grace is also purchased. They therefore gave thanks for the judgments of the Gentiles, by which they were condemned but absolved by God (ch. 50).

## ARTICLE II. It Is Shown That Tertullian Is the Author of This Book; Who He Was; What His Native Country Was; Who His Parents Were; and in Whose False Religions He Was First Instructed

It is certainly established, and has hitherto been the common opinion of all, with no one dissenting, [Col. 0724B] that Tertullian is the true and genuine author of this *Apologeticus*. Yet if anyone desires certain arguments in support of this opinion, it is not difficult to satisfy him abundantly. For besides numerous manuscript codices of both earlier and more recent date, in which this very book is inscribed with Tertullian’s name, Eusebius—whose reliability in this matter ought to be suspect to no one—after transcribing certain words from this book, added in the same place: Ταῦτα Τερτυλλιανὸς, τοὺς Ῥωμαίων νόμους ἡκριβωκὼς ἀνὴρ, τὰ τε ἄλλα ἔνδοξος, καὶ τὸν μάλιστα ἐπὶ Ῥώμης λαμπρῶν, ἐν τῇ γραφείσῃ μὲν αὐτῷ τῇ Ῥωμαίων φωνῇ, μεναβληθείσῃ δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἑλλάδα γλώσσαν ὑπὲρ Χριστιανῶν ἀπολογίᾳ (“These things Tertullian—a man thoroughly versed in Roman law, otherwise distinguished as well, and among the most illustrious at Rome—says in his apology on behalf of the Christians, written by him in the Roman tongue but also translated into Greek”) (Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. II, ch. 2, p. 41). Rufinus translated this into Latin as follows: “[Col. 0724C] Tertullian, a man thoroughly versed in Roman laws and institutions and exceedingly renowned among our writers, says these things in his *Apologeticus*, which he writes against the Gentiles on behalf of our faith” (Ruf., bk. II, ch. 2). This is certainly not a bad translation, if he had not omitted certain words that should have been rendered into Latin thus: “afterward translated into the Greek language.” Eusebius, therefore, and Rufinus himself as well, were persuaded that this book had been composed by Tertullian. The same Eusebius, mentioning Tertullian by name, transcribed still more from this same book (Euseb., bk. III, ch. 23, p. 91), and elsewhere added: Εἴληται δ` ἡμῖν ἡ ἲστορία ἐξ ἧσ ἀνωτέρω δεδηλώκαμεν τοῦ Τερτυλλιανοῦ ῥωμαικῆς ἀπολογίας, ἧς ἡ ἑρμηνεία τοῦτον ἔχει τρόπον (“We have taken the narrative from Tertullian’s Roman apology, which we identified above; its translation is as follows”). “Moreover, from Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, composed in Latin, which we mentioned above, this narrative has been taken by us” [Col. 0724D] (*ibid.*, ch. 35, p. 105). Thus Valesius rendered Eusebius’s Greek words into Latin. Finally, in yet another book, when similarly quoting the words of our Tertullian, he prefaced them with the following (*idem*, bk. V, ch. 5, p. 169): Μάρτυς δὲ τούτων γένοιτ` ἂν ἀξιόχρεως ὁ Τερτυλλιανὸς τῇ ῥωμαϊκῇ συγκλήτῳ προσφωνήσας ὑπὲρ τῆς πίστεως ἀπολογίαν ἧς καὶ πρόσθεν ἐμνημονεύσαμεν, τήν τε ἱσθορίαν βεβαιῶν σὺν ἀποδείξει μειζονι, καὶ ἐναργεστέρᾳ (“Tertullian would be a trustworthy witness to these things: he addressed to the Roman senate an apology on behalf of the faith, which we have also mentioned previously, confirming the account with greater and clearer proof”). “But Tertullian also,” as Valesius translates, “is a competent witness to the same matter in the *Apologeticus*, which he composed in the Latin language for the defense of our faith and addressed to the senate of the city of Rome, and which we also mentioned above; there he confirms this account with a stronger and clearer argument.”

[Col. 0725A] In addition, Jerome says in his letter to Magnus (Jerome, Epist. 83, to Magnus, p. 656): “What is more learned than Tertullian, what more acute? His *Apologeticus* and his little books against the Gentiles embrace all the learning of the age.” But there is no need to heap up further evidence for a matter so certain and evident, unless one wishes to bring light to the noonday sun itself.

Before, however, we proceed to examine this book in our customary manner, it is worthwhile to investigate who its author was. First, then, these four names of his are transmitted, with no one yet disputing them: Quintus, Septimius, Florens, Tertullianus. No one should be troubled by this multitude of names. For many people were designated by just as many names, so that they might be distinguished from other members of their clan and family. The first [Col. 0725B] was the *praenomen*, by which the person upon whom it was conferred could be distinguished from all his brothers. For, as Varro has taught us, “*praenomina* were established as individual designations for practical use, by which clan names might be distinguished: from numbers, such as Prima, Secunda, Tertia, Quarta; among men, Quintus, Sextus, Decimus; and similarly from other circumstances, when there were two or more Terentii, in order to distinguish them they were marked by some individual designation—for example, one born in the morning was called Manius; one born by daylight, Lucius; and one born after his father’s death, Postumus” (Varro, bk. III, *On the Latin Language*, p. 126).

The *nomen* was the clan name, or one derived from the clan from which a person traced his origin. The *cognomen*, which many do not distinguish from the *agnomen*, was given so that, when several persons of the same [Col. 0725C] name belonged to a single family, it might be known from which branch each had been born. Some, however, believe that the *agnomen* was so called because it was added to the three names already mentioned on account of some illustrious deed, some virtue, a defect of character, a bodily mark, or another similar reason. Sigonius, Onuphrius Panvinus, and others discuss these matters more fully (Sigon., *On Roman Names*, ch. 5; Onuphr., *On Roman Names*, §§ 13 and 16).

Tertullian’s *praenomen*, therefore, was Quintus, undoubtedly because he was born fifth in order among his brothers. His *nomen* was Septimius, as he himself indicates in the words with which he concludes the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “To those who read these things in good peace, preferring truth to custom, may peace and grace from our Lord Jesus overflow together with Septimius Tertullianus, whose little work this is” [Col. 0725D] (Tertull., *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 17). He bore the name Septimius because he sprang from the Septimian clan. Since, however, there were several men of this family, the cognomen Florens Tertullianus was added to him—unless the *agnomen* is shown to be distinct from the *cognomen* and to have been added to him for some particular reason, as we have noted.

Yet although he possessed four names, he is nevertheless called simply Tertullian by Eusebius, as we have already seen, and by Jerome and others, as we shall observe more than once below. And under that single name his *Apologeticus* is also inscribed in our manuscript codices.

Jerome teaches us in what province and city he was born [Col. 0726A] in these words: “Tertullian . . . of the province of Africa, of the city of Carthage” (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115). Hence in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* he is called “Tertullian the African” (*Chronicle of Eusebius*, at the year of Christ 208), and by Optatus, “Tertullian the Carthaginian” (Optatus, bk. I, *On the Schism of the Donatists*, p. 8). But what need is there of further witnesses, when Tertullian himself indicates his native country in these words, which we read in the *Apologeticus* under discussion? “In Africa infants were openly sacrificed to Saturn down to the proconsulship of Tiberius . . . as witnessed by the military force of our own country, which performed that very service for that proconsul” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 9). Moreover, in another book, which he addressed to the Carthaginians, he testifies that he was born at Carthage. [Col. 0726B] There he reproaches them for the fault of forgetfulness because, although they had formerly used the battering ram in wars: “Yet,” he says, “when the last days of their native city approached, and the Roman ram now dared to assault walls once its own, the Carthaginians immediately stood amazed at it as a novel and foreign contrivance” (*idem*, *On the Pallium*, ch. 1). Can it not be inferred from this passage that in these words he designates his own native country no less clearly than that of those whom he addresses?

Tertullian was therefore undoubtedly born at Carthage, his father being, as Jerome says, a proconsular centurion; or, as we read in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, “he was the son of a proconsular centurion.” The proconsul’s centurions and soldiers, however, were not held in great honor, since they were his attendants and customarily performed menial services (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115; [Col. 0726C] *Chronicle of Eusebius*, at the year of Christ 208).

Born of this father and his other, now unknown, Gentile forebears, Tertullian imbibed their abominable superstitions with his mother’s milk and afterward openly professed them. For when he discusses the true doctrines of the Christians, he addresses those same Gentiles thus: “We too once laughed at these things; we were of your number: Christians are made, not born” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 18). In another book, moreover, he laments in these words the blindness and ignorance of the true God under which he then labored: “Repentance, as men of this kind—such as we ourselves once were—blind and without the Lord’s light, know it merely by nature, is a certain passion of the mind which arises from dissatisfaction with a previous judgment” (beginning of *On Repentance*, ch. 1).

[Col. 0726D] At that time, therefore, as learned men have observed, being deprived of the light of the true God and of the Christian religion, he delighted in profane spectacles. For of these he said somewhere: “I prefer not to give a full account rather than to remember” (*On the Spectacles*, ch. 19). Indeed, he confesses, not without anguish, that he had fallen into shameful sins of the flesh: “For I know,” he said, “that I did not commit adulteries in one kind of flesh, nor then”—read *now*—“strive for continence in another kind of flesh” (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 59). He declares no less openly that he had repented of his other sins: “You, a sinner like me—indeed, less than me. For I acknowledge my own preeminence in transgressions” (*On Repentance*, ch. 4). And again later: “Since I am a sinner of every mark, born for nothing [Col. 0727A] except repentance, I cannot easily remain silent on that subject” (*On Repentance*, ch. 12). Yet no one will doubtless find it surprising if a Gentile man who worshipped adulterous gods, and gods worse than adulterers, wished to follow their examples, as Chaerea does in Terence (*Eunuch*, act III, scene 5, v. 43). But as much pleasure as these crimes once gave Tertullian while he was a Gentile, so much horror did they afterward cause him when he professed the Christian religion, as is evident from his books, and especially from this *Apologeticus*.

## ARTICLE III. By What Considerations Tertullian Was Led to the Christian Religion, and When He Professed It

[Col. 0727B] If anyone asks by what considerations Tertullian was impelled to embrace the faith of Christ, he will hear from George of Amiens, the Capuchin, that there were three: the innocence of the Christians, the excellence of sacred Scripture, and the Christians’ marvelous power over demons (George, *Vindication of Tertullian*, part II, questions 1 and 2). Yet, however weighty these considerations may be, he destroys them with the same hand by which he had established them. For he immediately added that Gentiles and Jews—such as Ulpian and Suetonius, Josephus and Philo—and other very learned men, having weighed these considerations with minds no less attentive than Tertullian’s, could not be led to profess the Christian religion. He therefore supposes that Tertullian, while still wavering and fluctuating, was impelled by some [Col. 0727C] singular and divine vision to give his name to the Christian religion. But from where, I ask, did George learn that those proofs of the Christian religion were examined and weighed by the Gentiles and Jews whom he mentions with as much attentiveness, fairness, and sincerity as by Tertullian? From where, moreover, did he learn that Tertullian was granted that singular vision, without which, despite the strongest possible arguments, he could never have been led to the Christian religion? Is it thus permissible for a Christian and religious man, by a mere and extremely slight conjecture, to weaken the force and strength of those arguments by which, as we shall show below, the truth of the Christian religion is demonstrated most invincibly? But that learned man had doubtless not paid sufficient attention to these words of Tertullian in the [Col. 0727D] *Apologeticus* concerning the endurance of the martyrs: “Who is not stirred by contemplating it to inquire what the reality within the matter may be? Who, once he has inquired, does not join us? Once he has joined us, he longs to die” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50)? And again, he concludes another book thus: “Anyone who witnesses such great endurance is struck by some uneasiness and is kindled to inquire what the cause may be; and when he has learned the truth, he himself immediately follows it” (*To Scapula*, final chapter). But if any Gentile who was neither wholly obstinate nor an unfair evaluator of matters, having thus recognized the truth of the Christian religion, embraced it, how much more readily would Tertullian, who far surpassed others in mental acuteness and fairness?

What of the fact that he was especially [Col. 0728A] an eyewitness of the Christians’ power over demons, or was at least so firmly persuaded of it that he challenged the Gentiles to test it publicly, and declared that the blood of those Christians should be shed unless the demons adjured by them confessed that they were not gods? “But what,” he says, “is more manifest than this operation, what proof more trustworthy? The simplicity of truth stands openly before us” (*idem*, *Apologeticus*, ch. 23). He therefore regarded the force of this argument and experience as fully established, and believed that no one could resist it unless utterly blinded by false prejudices.

No less evident to him was the authority of sacred Scripture, in which, he says, “whoever approaches will find God; whoever also endeavors to understand will be compelled to believe” (*ibid.*, ch. 18). Did he not, therefore, find God there, [Col. 0728B] recognize the false gods of the Gentiles, and discover that the Christian religion was true? For this truth shone with such great light that it was immediately received by all who were not blinded by voluntary obstinacy. But I would have you hear him recount these things himself: “It is a testimony of ignorance, which, while excusing injustice, condemns it: for all who formerly hated because they did not know the nature of what they hated, as soon as they cease to be ignorant, also cease to hate. From these persons Christians are made, assuredly upon ascertainment of the truth; and they begin to hate what they had been and to profess what they had hated” (*ibid.*, ch. 1). But surely, if so many Gentiles, by Tertullian’s own admission, became Christians through all or any one of these considerations, how much more did he, to whom the falsity of the Gentiles’ religion and the truth of the Christian religion were so clearly established? To reject the former and [Col. 0728C] embrace the latter, therefore, he had no need of the divine vision invented by George.

It is not so easy to say when he gave his name to the Christian religion. Pamelius believed that the book *On the Pallium* was published by him in the year of Christ 195, immediately after he had been initiated into the Christian religion. But this writer’s opinion regarding the date of this book is false; more expert scholars now believe it was written much later, namely after his defection from the Catholic Church and around the year 211.

The beginning of his profession must therefore be investigated in another way. We learn from Jerome that he published a treatise on the troubles of marriage “while he was still a young man” (Jerome, [Col. 0728D] bk. I, *Against Jovinian*, p. 157). Although Jerome said that he had written playfully on this subject in his youth, he nevertheless exhorts the virgin Eustochium to read this work, just as he exhorts her to read other works of Cyprian, Damasus, and Ambrose: “And now,” he says, “I give the same advice: if it pleases you to know from how many troubles a virgin is free and by how many a wife is bound, read Tertullian’s book addressed to a philosopher friend” (*idem*, Epist. 18, to Eustochium, p. 37). Yet it may not unreasonably be doubted whether this book, which we lost long ago, was composed by Tertullian as a Gentile or as a Christian. But to whom, someone will object, will it appear plausible that Jerome wished to be the adviser and advocate of a Christian virgin’s reading this work, just as she was to read the books of Cyprian, Damasus, and [Col. 0729A] Ambrose, if he had seen in it anything contrary to the established laws of the Christian religion? And how could Tertullian have composed such a book unless he had been fully instructed in those same laws? Yet, by his own testimony, no one recognized the Christian religion and its laws without immediately wishing to profess it. Moreover, Jerome recorded this further fact concerning him: “He remained a presbyter of the Church”—that is, the Catholic Church—“until middle age” (*idem*, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115), and therefore until before he was infected by the heresy of Montanus. Then Jerome added in the same place: “He is said to have lived to a very advanced age,” namely to his eightieth year, or, if you prefer, his ninetieth. He therefore remained an orthodox presbyter until approximately the fortieth year of his life. [Col. 0729B] Yet he does not appear to have been elevated to this sacred order either for the first time then or immediately after professing the Christian religion. He therefore appears to have become a Christian from a Gentile while still a young man. Let all who are expert judge how much weight this entire argument carries.

## ARTICLE IV. On Tertullian’s Marriage and His Supreme Love of Continence; on His Priesthood; Whether, After Becoming a Presbyter, He Lived with His Wife in the Manner of Married Men and Did Not Distinguish Those Initiated into Sacred Orders from the Laity; What Manner of Life He Followed and How Harsh His Character Was; How and When He Fell into the Heresy of the Montanists; and in What Year of His Life and of Christ He Brought His Long Life to an End

[Col. 0729C] Tertullian certainly had a wife, and she was a Christian, as is most clearly demonstrated by the two books he wrote to her. Writers of our own age, however, dispute whether he, while still a Gentile or already a Christian, married her while she was a Gentile or a Christian. For at that time it was indeed customary among Christians, as Tertullian himself testifies, to contract marriages with Gentile women; and no trace exists in his writings or those of others by which it can be determined whether, after already taking a wife, he entered the camp of Christ. But if it can be inferred from what we said a little earlier that he swore allegiance to the laws of Christ while still a young man, can it not also be concluded from this that he married afterward? For once he had become a Christian, he always burned with too great a zeal for observing Christian law [Col. 0729D] to take any woman in marriage except a Christian. And indeed, in the books addressed to his wife already cited, he endeavors to persuade her that, if he should depart this life first, she should either remain in widowhood or marry a Christian man if she wished to be bound by a second marriage. Is it not altogether probable that he himself obeyed the laws which he prescribed for his wife? But we leave these conjectures to the judgment of others.

Tertullian undoubtedly lived with his wife in the ordinary manner of married couples when he addressed to her the books just commended. For he exhorts her as follows to preserve continence in widowhood if he should die first: “What we have not been able to attain in marriage, let us pursue in widowhood. The opportunity which removes what necessity commanded must be embraced” [Col. 0730A] (Tertull., bk. I, *To His Wife*, ch. 7). For why would he have addressed these words to her if he and his wife had always abstained from the customary use of marriage? Yet no one can fail to understand from this how greatly Tertullian was always inflamed with zeal for continence and chastity.

It ought to appear less surprising to everyone that he exhorts his wife to continence in these books, if the opinion of certain heterodox and Catholic writers concerning the time when they were written is true. They suspect that he published them when his own age was advancing, while his wife’s was still flourishing and vigorous. They therefore suppose that in them he drew up, as it were, the tablets of his testament. But they offer no other argument for their opinion except these words of Tertullian, which are read at the beginning of the first [Col. 0730B] book as follows: “For we are occupied with secular affairs, and we desire provision to be made for each of us. If we make arrangements for such matters, why should we not all the more provide for our posterity in divine and heavenly matters, and, as it were, bequeath in advance as a legacy an admonition and exposition of those things which are assigned from immortal goods and from the inheritance of heaven?” (*ibid.*, ch. 1). But because, as Rigaltius advises us, the word *talibus* (“for such matters”) is read twice in the Agobard manuscript, he wished it to be emended and read: “we arrange testamentary tablets for such matters”; and from this he infers that these books were composed by Tertullian in the manner of a testament, when he was already far advanced in age (Rigalt., note 1 on this book).

But even if the matter were so, have wills never been made and sealed by human beings except when their age was already advancing? Has no prudent [Col. 0730C] man, especially a Christian, ever reflected—while still in the flower of youth—upon death, which is always uncertain, and upon drawing up his will? Tertullian certainly had still greater reason to think about making it at any period of his life, because, with the Gentiles then raging against Christians, he could not have been unaware that his life was in daily danger. Could not he also, always inflamed—as we have said—with so great and singular a love of continence and chastity, have exhorted his wife at any period of his life to preserve it if she should ever become a widow? Moreover, if she was still vigorous, as they say, when Tertullian was engaged in publishing these books, can it be concluded from an invented meaning of some of his words that he was old or decrepit? Nor should those be heard who object that several things occur in [Col. 0730D] these books by which Tertullian reveals that his mind was already inclined toward the Montanists. Is it merely because he exhorts his wife to continence? But did not the apostle Paul himself also exhort Christians to the same virtue? It is enough for us that they concede that, when Tertullian wrote these books to his wife, he had not yet fallen into the error of the Montanists. For until middle age, as Jerome, whom we have cited, testifies, he was a presbyter of the Catholic Church. He therefore composed those books long before his old age.

But just as Tertullian’s marriage is established, so it likewise seems beyond doubt that he was ordained to the sacred order of the presbyterate. For Jerome [Col. 0731A] and the author of the book *On the Heresy of the Predestinarians* unhesitatingly call him a presbyter of the Church (Jerome, *Catalog. of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115; *Predestination*, ch. 26, p. 28). Alix therefore subscribed all the more readily to Rigault’s aforementioned opinion concerning the books written by Tertullian to his wife when he was already advanced in age, because he thought it could be inferred from them that Tertullian himself, after becoming a presbyter, continued to live with his wife in the customary marital fashion. But this opinion rests both on an utterly ruinous foundation, as we have noted, and on the false prejudices of the Calvinist heresy. And certainly, the greater the zeal for continence with which Tertullian burned, as we have often said, the less probable it is that, after he had been enrolled in the order of presbyters, he failed to follow in the footsteps of the other priests of the Latin Church [Col. 0731B], who abstained from their customary relations with their wives. For one would find very few—at most two or three—who acted otherwise. No one, however, will ever demonstrate by any reasoning that Tertullian set before himself the examples of these latter men for imitation rather than those of the former.

But perhaps some opponent of sacred orders or other will ask us why Tertullian, if he was a presbyter, at one point counted himself among the laity. For in the book *On Prayer* he says: “We, above all, are men of no particular station” (Tertullian, *On Prayer*, ch. 14). Yet even if this were, as they suppose, the meaning of these words, nothing can be concluded from them against Tertullian’s priesthood. For it is not certain whether, when he wrote this, [Col. 0731C] he was not still among the body of the laity.

Some will doubtless object to us that he abolished every distinction between laity and clergy when he spoke of both in the following manner: “Whence come bishops and the clergy? Are they not taken from among all? . . . But when we exalt ourselves against the clergy, then we are all one; then ‘He has made us all priests to God and the Father.’ When we are challenged to match the discipline of priests, we lay aside our mitres and become unequal.” So indeed he writes in the book *On Monogamy* (idem, *On Monogamy*, ch. 12). Similarly, in another work, *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, he says: “The authority of the Church has established the distinction between the order and the people, and the honor sanctified through the assembly of the order; so much so that, where there is no assembly of the ecclesiastical order, you both offer and baptize, and you are a priest for yourself alone” (idem, *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 7).

[Col. 0731D] But no one is unaware that, when he wrote these things, he had already imbibed the errors of the Montanists, following which he added in the same place: “But where there are three, there is the Church, even though they are laymen” (*ibid.*). Accordingly, in the manner of those in error, either he was inconsistent with himself, or he understood the word “priest” not in its proper and narrower sense but in an improper and broader one, just as it is used more than once by John in the words to which he appears to allude: “He made us a kingdom and priests to God and His Father” (*Apocalypse*, ch. I, 6). And again later: “You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (*ibid.*, ch. V, 10). For Tertullian himself, although he was then a follower of Montanus, speaks thus in another book: “Today there is among us [Col. 0732A] a sister who has received gifts of revelations, which she experiences in the Church during the Lord’s solemn rites through ecstasy in the Spirit. . . . After the rites have been completed and the congregation dismissed, as is her custom, she reports to us what she has seen” (Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 9). Yet there he plainly distinguishes himself from the people, or from the entire body of the laity.

He lived a private and solitary life; and he himself testifies that, having cast aside the common garment of all and assumed the philosophers’ cloak, he withdrew from the turmoil of public affairs. For these are his words, spoken under the fictitious persona of his cloak itself: “I owe nothing to the forum, nothing to the Campus, nothing to the senate-house; I keep watch over no office, I preoccupy no rostra, I attend no praetoria; I do not sniff at the drains; I do not worship the railings, I do not wear down the benches, I do not disturb the laws, I do not declaim lawsuits, I do not judge, I do not [Col. 0732B] serve as a soldier. I have withdrawn from the people. My sole business is with myself; I care for nothing else except not to care” (idem, *On the Pallium*, ch. 5).

His morals, moreover, were as chaste and holy as they were unquestionably harsh and severe. He was not merely a follower of stricter discipline, but also its most ardent defender and advocate, even beyond the established bounds of equity. It seems by no means improbable that, deceived by the false appearance of severity that the Montanists presented, he plunged headlong into their heresy. But while the innate harshness of his character inclined him in that direction, the false visions and predictions of certain women imbued with the poison of that heresy drew him into it. Finally, Jerome says that “through the envy and insults of the clergy of the Roman Church, he fell away to the doctrine of Montanus, and [Col. 0732C] in many places he mentions the New Prophecy, but especially in works against the Church” (Jerome, *Catalog. of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115).

Thus he spent the first part of his life—which was undoubtedly the longer—in the Catholic Church, but the second, by a lamentable misfortune that can never be sufficiently deplored, among the Montanist heretics. For, as Jerome continues: “He remained a presbyter of the Church until middle age” (*ibid.*). In the same place that most learned writer adds that he flourished chiefly under the emperor Severus and Antoninus Caracalla and, as tradition reports, lived to extreme old age. If, however, we place our confidence in the more expert writers of our own time, he was born around the year of Christ 160 and died around the year 245. No one, moreover, will deny that the course of his life extended beyond its midpoint; yet, by spending its [Col. 0732D] final part in defending the absurd errors of heretics, he harmed both himself and a great many others. Hence Jerome, whom we have already commended, rightly says: “In Tertullian we praise his genius; we condemn his heresy” (idem, book III, *Apology Against Rufinus*, p. 463). But we must discuss his genius somewhat more fully.

## ARTICLE V. On Tertullian’s genius and manifold learning; whether he was a jurisconsult and the same person as Tertyllianus; on his style and manner of writing, and the celebrity of his name

In the severity of his morals and manner of life, Tertullian followed [Col. 0733A] the innate impulses of a genius that was indeed exceedingly acute and ardent, but no less harsh and vehement. Jerome therefore calls him “a man of acute and vehement genius” (Jerome, *Catalog. of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115). Yet even if Jerome had passed over this in silence, the harsh and impatient character of his genius shines forth everywhere throughout his writings. What wonder, then, if he was often unable to keep himself within the proper bounds of patience, gentleness, and moderation? Indeed, with a spirit as sincere as it was penitent, he openly confessed that he was not fully endowed with the virtue of patience. For he begins his book on that very subject with these words:

> I confess before the Lord God that it was quite rash of me, if not even shameless, to dare to compose a work on patience, since I am wholly incapable of practicing it, being a man [Col. 0733B] possessed of no good quality. For when men undertake to demonstrate and commend some matter, they ought first to be found administering that matter themselves, and to direct the force of their admonition by the authority of their own conduct, lest their words blush for the failure of their deeds.

(Tertullian, *On Patience*, ch. 1.)

But although he was not always able to temper the more violent impulses of his mind through the virtue of patience, he certainly possessed a genius most aptly suited to the easy attainment of any branch of knowledge. How greatly he abounded in every kind of learning may be inferred from these words of Vincent of Lérins:

> As Origen among the Greeks, so among the Latins this man must readily be judged the foremost of all our writers. For what man was more learned than he? Who was more practiced in divine and human affairs? With a certain marvelous capacity of mind, he embraced all philosophy, every sect of the [Col. 0733C] philosophers, the founders and defenders of those sects, all their disciplines, and the entire variety of histories and branches of study. Did he not excel in a genius so weighty and vehement that he proposed scarcely anything to himself for conquest that he did not either break through by acuteness or crush by force? Moreover, who can adequately recount the praises of his discourse? It is knit together by some such compelling necessity of reasoning that it drives to agreement with itself those whom it has been unable to persuade. Almost as many words as it contains, so many judgments; as many thoughts, so many victories. The Marcions know this, the Apelleses, the Praxeases, the Hermogeneses, the Jews, the Gentiles, the Gnostics, and all the others whose blasphemies he overthrew, like thunderbolts, with the many great masses of his volumes.

(Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory*, I.)

[Col. 0733D] Yet with such great praises he undoubtedly exalts that universal learning of Tertullian with which, above all, he everywhere sprinkled the books he wrote in defense of the Christian religion and orthodox doctrines. Hence, besides Eusebius and Rufinus, whom we have already cited, and many others, Jerome calls him “a most learned man” (Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, p. 285, and Letter 83, *To Magnus*, p. 656), than whom there was nothing more learned or acute. Jerome unhesitatingly declares that this brilliance shines forth in the very *Apologeticum* now under discussion, as well as in his other treatises against the Gentiles. It would therefore be an entirely useless labor to prove by the testimonies of distinguished writers of every age—as could readily be done—a fact of which no one is ignorant and which the author’s own writings make most manifest to all. [Col. 0734A]

Yet we cannot pass over a particular kind of learning that Eusebius praised in Tertullian with these words: “Τερτουλλιανὸς τοὺς Ῥωμαίων νόμους ἡκριβωκὼς, ἀνὴρ τά τε ἄλλα ἔνδοξος καὶ τῶν μάλιστα ἐπὶ Ρώμης λαμπρῶν” (Eusebius, book II, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 2, p. 41); that is, in Valesius’s translation: “Tertullian was highly skilled in Roman law and the most celebrated among Latin writers.” Long before Valesius, Rufinus had anticipated him in almost the same manner: “Tertullian,” he says, “was a man highly skilled both in Roman laws and institutions, and very distinguished among our writers” (Rufinus, book II, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 2). But those who think it can be concluded from this that our Tertullian [Col. 0734B] was a jurisconsult by profession, and that he was the very same Tertyllianus who actually taught and interpreted the laws publicly, are far from the truth. For the two are sufficiently distinguished by their own respective names. Moreover, who does not know that someone may be thoroughly versed in Roman jurisprudence and law even though he never professed their study in public schools? Eusebius therefore praises there not Tertullian’s profession, but his complete knowledge and expertise in Roman law.

His expression did not equal his great learning. But if you desire fair and competent judges on this subject, here you have the judgment of Lactantius, who is called the Christian Cicero: “Septimius Tertullianus was skilled in every kind of literature, but in expression he was not very fluent, was less polished, and was exceedingly obscure” (Lactantius, book [Col. 0734C] V, *Divine Institutes*, ch. 1, p. 459). Nor should you say that Lactantius is speaking there of Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* and his other books written against the pagans rather than of his remaining works. For Jerome expresses the same judgment concerning all his compositions in these few words: “Tertullian is rich in maxims, but difficult in expression” (Jerome, Letter 49, *To Paulinus*, p. 567). There is no one who does not immediately perceive the faults noted by both men: his difficult, unadorned, and rather obscure discourse.

Others criticize the uneven variety of the arguments he employs. For, they say, among arguments of the greatest weight and utterly invincible force, he sometimes mingles several others devised by the acuteness of his rapid genius, which are of the slightest [Col. 0734D] importance or plainly of none at all.

But almost everyone admits that this faulty manner either of speaking or of arguing, wherever it occurs, is softened and repaired, as though by some marvelous compensation, by the brilliant gravity of his maxims and the supreme force and weight of his other arguments. Indeed, if you wish to hear again Vincent of Lérins, whom we have already cited and who was by no means an incompetent judge, he says: “His discourse is knit together by some such compelling necessity of reasoning that it drives to agreement with itself those whom it has been unable to persuade. Almost as many words as it contains, so many judgments; as many thoughts, so many victories.” For precisely this reason, as the author of the Eusebian *Chronicle* used to say: “He is celebrated in the discourse of all the Churches” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the year of Christ 208). [Col. 0735A] By “Churches” he means not only those of the West but also those of the East. For some of his books, on account of the great value placed upon them, were translated into Greek, as we noted shortly before, and were read by Greeks no less eagerly than by Latins.

Cyprian, moreover, valued them so highly that he called Tertullian his master and was unwilling to let a single day pass without reading one of his books. As a witness to this exceedingly constant reading, we have Jerome, whose trustworthiness is beyond all question and who relates as follows from whom, and with what certainty, he learned this:

> I myself saw a certain Paulus, an old man of Concordia, a town in Italy, who said that, when he himself was quite young, he had seen at Rome the secretary of the blessed Cyprian, who was already advanced in age. He said that this secretary was accustomed to relate to him that Cyprian never allowed a single day to pass without reading Tertullian [Col. 0735B], and frequently said to him: “Give me the Master,” meaning Tertullian.

(Jerome, *Catalog. of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115.)

Indeed, he plainly asserts that sufficient evidence for this is supplied by Cyprian’s own books. For he wrote to Pammachius and Oceanus in these words: “The blessed Cyprian uses Tertullian as his master, as his writings prove; and although he delights in the genius of that learned and ardent man, he does not follow Montanus and Maximilla with him” (idem, Letter 42, p. 342). Nor is there any doubt that very many others, like Cyprian, repeatedly read through Tertullian’s books. For concerning him we again read the following recorded by Jerome: “He wrote many volumes which, because they are known to many, we omit” (Jerome, *ibid.*). [Col. 0735C] But how could they have been so well known to them unless they had read them again and again?

## CHAPTER II. On the date of the *Apologeticum*; to whom it was addressed and dedicated; whether it was originally inscribed with the author’s name; what its title and subject are; by whom it was divided into chapters and chapter summaries prefixed; with what acclaim it was received; by whom it was translated into Greek; and in what style it was composed

## ARTICLE I. At what time Tertullian published the *Apologeticum*

It is beyond all doubt that Tertullian, as we have already shown, is the true and genuine [Col. 0735D] author of this *Apologeticum*. But there is no general agreement about when he composed it. For George of Amiens thinks that it was published by Tertullian in the first years of the emperor Severus, that is, shortly after the year of Christ 193 (George, *Vindiciae Tertulliani*, part III, § 1, p. 20), when Severus began to govern the Roman Empire. He attempts to confirm his opinion from the fact that he thinks that, where Tertullian speaks of the surviving gleaning of parricides who had brought death upon emperors, he was referring to the killers of Pertinax (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35). But because he saw that the name of Albinus, which is read there in Tertullian’s text, was opposed to this opinion, [Col. 0736A] he declares that it was interpolated and transferred to this passage from the book *To Scapula* (idem, *To Scapula*, ch. 2). Thus he wished to cut through the knot of the difficulty by excising a single word. But by what reasoning, pray? By none at all, and contrary to the authority of all the manuscript codices. Once the foundation of that empty opinion has therefore been overthrown, the opinion itself must necessarily collapse entirely. Indeed, its falsity will become still clearer from what will presently be said.

Scaliger and Alix, however, thought that this book appeared in public only after the death of the same emperor Severus, which occurred in February of the year of Christ 211. Yet they provide no reason for their opinion except that they suppose these words of Tertullian—“Only yesterday Severus, the most steadfast of emperors [Col. 0736B], excluded the Papian laws” (idem, *Apologeticum*, ch. 4)—cannot be understood except of an emperor already dead. Does the adverb “yesterday,” then, indicate that he was dead rather than still living? Moreover, Severus is there adorned with the glorious title “most steadfast emperor.” But how could Tertullian have decorated him with this encomium except before he had aroused, by public edicts, a dreadful persecution against the Christians? Yet he is said to have initiated it near the end of the year of Christ 202. Tertullian must therefore be said to have completed this book before that year, and consequently before the emperor’s death. The same point could be proved no less certainly by these words of his: “No Severus enacted laws against the Christians,” which are read in certain manuscript and printed codices of this *Apologeticum* [Col. 0736C] (*ibid.*, ch. 5). Since, however, other editions and our seven manuscript codices read “No Verus enacted them,” we have judged that these words, which will be discussed again later, should not be pressed beyond what is proper.

Alix nevertheless insists that Tertullian appears to allude to his own book *On the Prescriptions Against Heretics* [Col. 0736D] where, in the *Apologeticum*, he argues against them as follows: “We readily prescribe against our adulterators that the rule of truth is that which comes from Christ and was transmitted through His companions, to whom these various later commentators will be proved to be subsequent” (*ibid.*, ch. 47). But can this argument against innovators and corrupters of Christian doctrine be employed by no one except the author of a book *On the Prescriptions Against Heretics*? Moreover, if he intended there to aim at that book, why does he not indicate it in clearer words, rather than using terms which, as others think, can be understood either of a book still to be composed or of one already written? Finally, the learned do not agree about when Tertullian published this book *On the Prescriptions*. The more expert critics judge that he published it before he had defected from the Catholic Church.

Nor, we think, will anyone be moved by Alix’s further objection that Tertullian appears to indicate an unusual eclipse that occurred in the year of Christ 210 (*ibid.*, ch. 20). For the chapter of the *Apologeticum* that he cites contains no indication or suggestion whatever of any particular and unusual eclipse. [Col. 0737A]

Others therefore think that this book was composed by Tertullian while Severus was ruling the Roman world. For he would not have adorned him with the encomium “most steadfast emperor,” as we said shortly before, unless he were still reigning and had not yet openly raged against the Christians. Moreover, when he later discusses traitors, persons guilty of *lèse-majesté*, and public enemies, he says: “Whence came the Cassii, the Nigri, and the Albini?” (*ibid.*, ch. 35)—men, namely, who had contended with the legitimate emperors for supreme imperial power. But after the emperor Pertinax was killed in May of the year 193, Gaius Pescennius Niger assumed the purple and imperial power in Pannonia, and Cassius Clemens joined his party. [Col. 0737B] Niger, however, was defeated by Severus; and after his forces had been routed in a third battle, he attempted in vain to secure his safety by flight. For he was killed by those who pursued him as he fled, toward the end of 194 or the beginning of 195. After this Severus made war upon Albinus, whom he had deceived with false blandishments so that the number of his enemies would not increase. At last, in a battle fought near Lugdunum, Albinus was broken and routed at the beginning of the year 197 and is said to have taken his own life.

Yet even then the civil war was not entirely ended. Supporters of that faction survived, concerning whom our Tertullian says in the same place: “But even those who are now daily revealed as the associates and applauders of criminal factions are a surviving gleaning after the vintage” (*ibid.*, ch. 38). Aelius Spartianus [Col. 0737C] explains this more clearly in the following manner: “Indeed, many who remained loyal to Albinus after his death were defeated in war by Severus” (Spartianus, *Life of Severus*, p. 323, col. 1). Severus therefore took harsh vengeance for Albinus’s revolt: many were killed, his family was also extinguished, and Severus, angered against the people and the senators, came to Rome. Then, after recounting Severus’s various journeys, Spartianus adds: “Meanwhile, at the instigation of Plautianus, he pursued the remnants of Pescennius’s party, so far as even to prosecute some of his own friends as though they had plotted against his life” (*ibid.*, same page, col. 2). From these latter words some think it may be inferred that Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* appeared not only after the remnants of the traitors whom he discusses had been destroyed, but even after the killing of Plautianus, who was put to death at Caracalla’s command in the year of Christ 204 or 205.

[Col. 0737D] In confirmation of this opinion, the following words of the same Spartianus concerning this emperor could also be adduced: “He also killed many on the charge that they had consulted Chaldaeans or prophets concerning his safety, especially anyone whom he suspected of being suitable for imperial power, since his own sons were still young, and because he either believed or heard that this was being said by those who predicted imperial power for themselves” (*ibid.*). For Tertullian said in the same chapter cited by us: “Those who consult astrologers, haruspices, augurs, and magicians concerning Caesar’s life perform the same services”—namely, at the solemn festivals of the emperors (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35).

It cannot indeed be denied that this argument [Col. 0738A] would carry no little weight if the pagans who desired the imminent death of the emperors had only once consulted magicians and others skilled in the art of divination concerning the safety of the emperor Severus alone. Yet Tertullian clearly indicates that such consultation had been proposed and repeated more than once. Furthermore, if we consider more attentively his words about those same seditious factions—“But even now . . . they are revealed daily”—can it not rightly be inferred that he speaks of them as not yet entirely extinguished, but at most lulled into inactivity and no longer daring to raise their heads? Severus therefore did not yet appear to have entered into open enmity with Plautianus. Yet in the year 204 Plautianus gave his daughter Plautilla in marriage to Caracalla, the son of that same Severus. [Col. 0738B] In the following year, however, according to Herodian, fearing the manifest boldness and madness of his son-in-law Caracalla, who then hated his wife, he attempted by plots to seize Caracalla’s imperial power (Herodian, book III, *Life of Severus*, p. 244 ff.). But when these were uncovered, Caracalla ordered him to be killed in the presence of his father Severus. Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* therefore appears to have been written before this year, though not long before it. For why would he have spared the name of Plautianus rather than those of Albinus and the other traitors? Tertullian therefore composed this book after the year 197, when Albinus laid violent hands upon himself, and before 204 or 205, when Plautianus was killed.

It nevertheless seems probable to some that the book came from Tertullian in the later year, when the tenth anniversary of Antoninus Caracalla’s [Col. 0738C] Caesarian rule was celebrated and the fire of the persecution aroused against the Christians blazed more fiercely. For Tertullian discussed these matters several times in this *Apologeticum* (ch. 2). Moreover, although he mentions several laws enacted against the Christians by other emperors, he mentions none enacted by Severus. Did Tertullian not therefore publish this *Apologeticum* before Severus promulgated his edicts against them?

But although in this book he inveighs most bitterly against the pagans, who celebrated the solemn festivals of the emperors with rites no less impious than superstitious, he is not discussing the solemnities of Caracalla rather than those of Severus and the other emperors. As for the persecutions of Christians and the laws written against them, we readily concede that Severus truly favored them at the beginning [Col. 0738D] of his reign. Tertullian himself is a witness to this favor and supplied the following reason for it: “Even Severus himself,” he says, “the father of Antoninus, was mindful of the Christians” (Tertullian, *To Scapula*, ch. 4). “For he sought out the Christian Proculus, surnamed Torpacion, the steward of Euhodia, who had once cured him by means of oil, and kept him in his palace until his death. Antoninus too knew him very well, having been reared on Christian milk.” We also acknowledge that the *Apologeticum* makes no mention of a law enacted against the Christians by that same Severus.

Yet we do not think it can therefore be concluded with certainty that it was published after Caracalla began to rule alone in the year 211, when, during his reign [Col. 0739A], the pagans were already raging and rioting most cruelly against all Christians. For the pagans’ fury against them was so great that the bare and empty pretext of the ancient laws sufficed for them to torture Christians of every sort at all times. Nor is this rashly invented by us. For our Tertullian addresses those same Gentiles in these words:

> How often do you rage against the Christians, partly obeying your own inclinations and partly the laws! How often, even without waiting for you, does the hostile mob attack us in its own right with stones and fires! In the very frenzy of the Bacchanals they do not spare even dead Christians, but tear them from the repose of burial, from what is in a sense the asylum of death—some already altered, some no longer whole—and cut them apart and drag their pieces about.

(Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 36, p. 459.)

A little earlier he had said: “Nor are there any greater ravagers of Christians than the mob” (idem, [Col. 0739B] ch. 35, p. 451)—that blind and frenzied mob, namely, which was driven to harass and kill Christians by its own frenzy and, as it were, innate madness, not by any prescription of the laws. To this is added the fact that the pagans laid upon them the cause of every public disaster. Whenever some disaster occurred, therefore, they immediately cried out, as Tertullian again testifies: “The Christians to the lion!” (*ibid.*, ch. 40).

Yet we seem to hear someone who will still insist that these and many other things in this *Apologeticum* could not have been described by our author so long as the emperor Severus favored the Christians and had enacted no law against them. But if our author mentions no law enacted by Severus, others think that this was done deliberately, so that he would not further provoke the spirit of the emperor, who was then [Col. 0739C] still living, but might more readily recall him to a sounder frame of mind.

These, then, are the considerations upon which the differing opinions concerning the date of this book rest. But after carefully weighing them, if this latter opinion seems to you preferable to the others, it must be admitted that the book was published after the persecution against the Christians had been stirred up by Severus himself—not, indeed, in 197 or 198, as some vainly suppose, but in 202, when Severus actually enacted laws against them and was, as Eusebius says, in the tenth year of his reign (Eusebius, book VI, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 2, p. 101 ff.).

But if anyone judges that the supports of this opinion are not sufficiently strong, he certainly will not deny that, from the points we noted shortly before [Col. 0739D], it may rightly be inferred that this book of Tertullian was published by him sometime after the death of Albinus, that is, after the year of Christ 197, as we have observed. Since Tertullian indicates in the same place that the greater assaults of that faction had been repressed and that only certain remnants of them survived, it must therefore be concluded that the date of this book appears to be assignable to the year 199, or rather 200.

Finally, someone will object that Tertullian at that time, as has often been said, had not reached his forty-fifth year. Yet the supreme learning that shines forth marvelously and everywhere throughout this *Apologeticum* appears to require a more advanced age. Rather, others reply, it required the aid from above of divine light and grace. Moreover, Tertullian was endowed with so excellent and penetrating a genius that by the fortieth year of his life he could without difficulty have become imbued with this very learning—and even greater learning—and filled this entire book with it.

## ARTICLE II. To which governors and presiding officials Tertullian dedicated this *Apologeticum*

The more openly and clearly Tertullian declared at the very beginning of the *Apologeticum* that he addressed it “to the governors of the Roman Empire presiding in a public and elevated place, almost at the very summit of the city” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 1, p. 257), the more vigorously the learned dispute over who these presiding officials were and [Col. 0740B] to what city they belonged. Among very many, indeed, the opinion had long prevailed that the Roman Senate was signified by these words. Others, however, later thought that the presiding officials of Carthage were designated, while still others thought that all the governors throughout the whole Roman Empire were meant.

The supporters of the first opinion rely on the very words of Tertullian that we have cited. For they think that no city other than Rome is indicated. And certainly, they say, what else can that public and elevated summit of the city be except the Roman Capitol, which Tertullian judged should be called by a circumlocution rather than by its own name? Could not the following passage, which we read written by him concerning the eclipse of the sun that occurred when Christ died, also be advanced in confirmation of this opinion: “You have the account of that cosmic catastrophe [Col. 0740C] preserved in your secret archives” (*ibid.*, ch. 21)? For what are those archives if not the records or archives and repositories of the Romans in which public documents were stored? For there he relates that Pilate reported to the emperor Tiberius not only this eclipse but also all the extraordinary events that had occurred before and after Christ’s death. Who would not readily concede that Tiberius ordered these things to be deposited and preserved in those same archives, which Tertullian challenges the Romans to examine?

What Tertullian stated more obscurely, Eusebius reported more clearly in these words, which are enveloped in no obscurity: “Tertullian composed his Apology τῇ ῥωμαϊκῇ συγκλήτῳ προσφωνήσας to the Roman Senate” (Eusebius, book V, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 5, p. 169). They also think that no little [Col. 0740D] strength is added to this opinion by the fact that Tertullian spent a long time at Rome. For Eusebius again left the following account of him in writing for posterity: “καὶ τῶν μάλιστα ἐπὶ Ῥώμης λαμπρῶν. And he was very celebrated at Rome” (idem, *ibid.*, book II, ch. 2, p. 41). To this may also be added Jerome (Jerome, *Catalog. of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 53, p. 115), who testifies that Tertullian was harassed by the envy and insults of the Roman clergy. Where could that have occurred except while he was living at Rome?

But nothing, others say, prevents Tertullian from having been stung by the barbs of envy and slander even while he was living at Carthage. For intercourse between Romans and Carthaginians was so frequent that the reputation for supreme learning and [Col. 0741A] doctrine that Tertullian had earned could have been assailed by the envious clergy of the Roman Church. Indeed, Eusebius appears to them to have referred to nothing other than this reputation in the words cited immediately above. Nor does he thereby indicate any residence of Tertullian in the city of Rome, but rather the very great celebrity of his name and reputation among the Romans on account of his exceptional learning and writings.

Others might nevertheless insist that absolutely no one can deny that he came to Rome at least once. For who would dare deny what Tertullian himself asserted most explicitly? “We have seen at Rome the nobility of gemstones blushing before matrons because of the disdain shown for them by the Parthians, Medes, and the rest of their own Gentile women, among whom they are held almost solely for display” (Tertullian, book I, *On the Apparel of Women*, ch. 6). Yet just as he could go to Rome once [Col. 0741B], so he could go there repeatedly and remain there. Others will reply quite rightly: But how can Tertullian’s other journeys to this city be proved, or that he was actually staying there when he composed the *Apologeticum*?

For this reason many think that it was certainly published at Carthage and presented to the presiding officials of that city. For from the opening of the work, as we have already seen, he calls them those “presiding in a public and elevated place at the summit of the city” (idem, *Apologeticum*, ch. 1, p. 259). Again, elsewhere he says: “In that city”—that is, the city in which he was composing his *Apologeticum*. Yet Rome was not called a *civitas* but *Urbs*, “the City,” and was customarily designated by that name alone by antonomasia. Are these not his very words: “The consuls, by authority of the Senate [Col. 0741C], expelled Liber . . . not only from the City but from all Italy” (*ibid.*, ch. 6, p. 305).

Then Tertullian himself indicates quite clearly that he was absent from Rome at that time. For after the words just cited from him he said: “Behold, in that most religious city of the earlier Aeneadae”—that is, Rome—“there is indeed a Jupiter” (*ibid.*, chap. 9, p. 317). You see that he calls it a *city* and signifies by the words “in that city” that he was distant from it. Moreover, where he enumerates the ancestral and indigenous gods of certain nations, he says: “I have, I think, set forth the Roman provinces, but not the Roman gods belonging to them, because they are no more worshipped at Rome than those who, throughout Italy itself as well, are enrolled by municipal consecration” (*ibid.*, chap. 24). Yet surely, if he had dedicated this book to the Roman senate, he would not have used the words “Roman,” [Col. 0741D] “Romans,” and “at Rome,” but rather “your,” “yours,” and “by you.” Nevertheless, he spoke in the same manner elsewhere also (*ibid.*, chap. 21, p. 392; chap. 35, p. 451).

They further insist that in this book no mention is made of the Roman senate, but that, just as at the beginning the “chief authorities” and “governors” are addressed, so at the end too the “governors” are addressed. You have already heard his earlier words; now I would have you hear the later ones: “But go on, worthy governors—you will be much better in the people’s eyes if you sacrifice Christians to them” (*ibid.*, chap. 50, p. 530). By that title, however, he does not address Roman senators or magistrates, but other governors and chief authorities in the city and province where he was living—namely, Africa and Carthage.

[Col. 0742A] What, moreover, of the fact that, after showing that human victims were sacrificed to the gods among various peoples and among the Romans themselves, and that human blood was tasted in Catiline’s conspiracy, he then added: “I range too far afield: today, here”—that is, in the very city where he was writing these things—“blood caught in the palm from the slashed thigh of those consecrated to Bellona, and given as food, marks them” (*ibid.*, chap. 9, p. 321)? Who, they will say, does not therefore see that he openly distinguishes his own city from Rome?

Finally, he contrasts Christians, “who fear God, not the proconsul,” with the pagans (*ibid.*, chap. 45). The pagans therefore feared the latter, but certainly not the former. A proconsul, however, held this highest magistracy not at Rome but in the provinces. Yet the other supports of the preceding view, by which we showed that Roman rulers [Col. 0742B] were addressed, are neither destroyed nor weakened by these arguments.

Accordingly, a third opinion, intermediate between the two thus far explained by us, is held by those who think that this *Apologeticum* was directed by Tertullian not merely to the governors of one city or province, but to those of the entire Roman Empire, as widely as it extended. If this can be proved, the advocates of the other opinions will easily be able to reconcile their positions. Whether it is true, however, must be investigated by us more carefully, because its defenders have not demonstrated it with sufficient precision. First, then, it is certain that this book was sent and presented not to governors individually named, but to governors in general. For if some had been addressed by their own names, and no others besides them, there could have been no dispute or controversy. For once they had been named in this manner, the case would surely have been settled and complete.

[Col. 0742C] Next, everyone admits that Roman governors are addressed in this book, and not merely once. For why should that be denied which has already been proved and is again confirmed by these words: “That I may look to those rulers of the nations: Numa Pompilius was a man” (*ibid.*, chap. 21)? Yet he addresses not only these governors, but the Quirites and even the Roman common people themselves in this way (*ibid.*, chap. 35): “I call upon the Quirites themselves, the native populace of the seven hills”—that is, of the city of Rome—“to say whether the Roman tongue spares any emperor of its own.” Yet, you will say, it is one thing to address certain people in one’s book and another to send and dedicate one’s book to them. Quite right. But why, [Col. 0742D] I ask you, did he address all the Roman governors, the Quirites, and the common people by their own names, unless he knew for certain that his book was to be sent to them?

Yet we have shown clearly enough that not only Roman governors but others also are addressed in this book of Tertullian. For the arguments set out in defense of the second opinion prove no less plainly that this book was written for others as well as for the Roman senate or Roman governors.

To this may be added that our author, in this *Apologeticum*, just as in the two books *To the Nations*, pleads the common cause of all the Christians who existed throughout the world. Therefore, just as he sent those books to all nations, to whom will it not seem most probable that he sent the *Apologeticum* to all [Col. 0743A] the governors of the Roman Empire?

Nor should you say that he also wrote, in defense of the Christians, another “little book,” as he himself calls it, which he directed *To Scapula*, placing that man’s name at its head. For why, I ask you, did he inscribe upon this little book which you raise as an objection the proconsul’s proper name? Why does he everywhere signify in it that he is writing specifically to him? Why, on the contrary, did he nowhere insert the name of any single individual or of certain governors into the *Apologeticum*, a much weightier and longer book? Is not the reason precisely that he judged that the *Apologeticum* should be written generally to all pagan governors? And this certainly appears to be the sense of the opening words of that book: “If it is not permitted to you, chief authorities of the Roman Empire” [Col. 0743B]—that is, you who throughout the Roman Empire are the chief men, leaders, and governors—“in an open and elevated place, on” (this last particle is lacking in all our manuscripts and in the older printed editions) “almost the very summit of the city”—that is, to those presiding over each city. For there he spoke indefinitely: “Chief authorities of the Roman Empire, who preside for the judgment of others in an open and elevated place, upon the very summit of any city whatsoever.” This interpretation, and the third opinion, has at least this advantage: it easily removes the difficulties proposed by the advocates of the other positions and reconciles those differing positions themselves. For from this it is easy to understand why he sometimes addressed certain governors and at other times different ones in this book, which he was writing at Carthage. We have, moreover, set out all the arguments for those three opinions, whether proposed [Col. 0743C] by others or added by us, in our candid and straightforward manner, so that everyone may readily recognize which carry greater and weightier force and embrace the opinion they judge the truer.

## ARTICLE III. Whether Tertullian Inscribed His Own Name upon This *Apologeticum*; Its Title, Subject, Division into Chapters, and Chapter Summaries

Learned writers of our age debate whether Tertullian placed his own name at the head of this book. To some it seems more probable that he suppressed it, since at the very beginning he openly complains that the path to a public defense [Col. 0743D] was barred to him and to other Christians. For these are his exact words: “If, finally, as has very recently occurred, hostility against this sect, overactive through private informations” (our manuscripts and the better printed codices read “judgments”) “has barred its defense” (in certain printed editions the words “has barred the way” are added), “let truth be permitted to reach your ears at least by the hidden path of silent letters” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 1, p. 259). If, therefore, Christians were not permitted to defend their cause publicly and before judges, how much less was Tertullian permitted to do so, when he attacked the errors of the pagans so vehemently, lest by disclosing his name he rashly expose his life to certain and unavoidable danger? For at that time he had not yet assumed the proud and more audacious spirit of the Montanists, but was obedient [Col. 0744A] to the precepts of the Catholic Church, by which every Christian was forbidden voluntarily to expose himself to dreadful torments and the cruellest death.

“But what,” others say, “if, inflamed with a desire for martyrdom, he feared torture and death for the confession of Christ all the less because he desired them the more ardently? What also if he was fully persuaded that his name could not long remain hidden from others, but that his distinctive style of speaking would immediately make it plain to everyone?” Although, therefore, he did not dare present himself openly before the judges, he could nevertheless prefix his name to the hidden “path of silent letters,” as he himself calls it, since he could not conceal it for long. Nor does there appear to be any reason why he should have [Col. 0744B] withheld his name from the title of this book rather than from those of his other works *To the Nations* and *To Scapula*.

But whatever judgment may be made concerning whether Tertullian’s name was concealed or expressed, no one should have any doubt that it at least did not long remain unknown to Christians. For it was not unknown to Eusebius or Lactantius, who cited this book, as we have seen, without concealing his name. They therefore had at hand certain copies of this book, undoubtedly transcribed in Tertullian’s own time, in which his name had been placed at the head. In our two most ancient manuscripts its title is: “Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*”; and at the end these words are read: “Here ends the *Apologeticum* of Quintus Tertullian.” In all the other codices as well, both manuscript and printed, this book is entitled either *Apologeticum* or *Apologeticus*. [Col. 0744C] The authenticity of this title is proved not only by their testimony, but also by that of Lactantius, by whom the book is called *Apologeticus*, and of Eusebius, by whom it is cited in these Greek words (Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, chap. 4, p. 470; Eusebius, passage cited above): ὑπὲρ Χριστιανῶν ἀπολογία, that is, “an apology and defense of the Christians.” To cite more authorities in support of a matter so certain and well established would be as tedious for us as it would be burdensome to others.

Short as this title is, however, it embraces the subject of the entire book. For in it Tertullian undertook the defense of the Christians and demonstrates plainly that, contrary to every prescription of every natural, divine, and human law, they were condemned and killed by the pagans merely on account of their name, without their case [Col. 0744D] ever being heard, although the pagans themselves were guilty of all the crimes of which they falsely—indeed, most falsely—accused those Christians. From what has been explained more fully in the analysis of this book presented by us, it therefore follows most clearly that its whole subject is expressed by that title.

Although this very book is divided into various chapters in all printed editions and even in the most ancient manuscripts, that division did not originate with Tertullian. For who, however slightly learned, does not perceive at first glance how inaccurate and imperfect it is? [Col. 0745A] So many of those who prepared new editions of the book were convinced of this that they did not hesitate to alter that division. We think no one disapproves of their attempt. Yet no one will deny that they have not yet attained their goal and that this book may still be divided into chapters more satisfactorily.

Moreover, if it is certain that this book was not divided into chapters by Tertullian, it is assuredly far more certain that the summaries or arguments of those chapters were not composed by him. In books written by any ancient hand, they are so inept and so disorderly that nothing worse could have been produced. Accordingly, those responsible for the later editions of this *Apologeticum* endeavored to amend them. Their correction was indeed not altogether useless, but it was not so complete that they do not still require more careful revision.

## ARTICLE IV. With What Applause This Book Was Received; by Whom It Was Translated into Greek; in What Style It Was Written; and Whether Tertullian Properly Discharged the Office He Undertook as Defender of the Christian Religion

[Col. 0745B]

This book was certainly received and read with the highest applause and common approval of all Christians, Greek as well as Latin. To prove this we need no witness other than Eusebius, who recorded that it was held in such esteem among the Greeks that they translated it into their native language. For it is cited by him in precisely these words: “Τερτουλλιανὸς … ἐν τῇ γραφείσῃ μὲν αὐτῷ τῇ Ῥωμαίων φώνῃ, μεταβληθείσῃ δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἑλλάδα γλῶτταν, ὑπὲρ Χριστιανῶν ἀπολογίᾳ” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chap. 2, p. 41): “Tertullian … in the *Apology*, which was indeed composed by him [Col. 0745C] in Latin, but was afterwards translated into Greek.”

Certain writers of our age, however, distinguished for their learning, disagree among themselves concerning the author of this Greek translation. Some think it was Eusebius himself. Others deny this. For when Eusebius transcribed from this book several things which Pliny had reported to Tiberius concerning Christ’s miracles, he omitted many things that would nevertheless have greatly served his purpose. But this argument is not of great weight. That argument seems weightier which observes that several other testimonies taken from this book by Eusebius were not translated into Greek with sufficient accuracy. Yet it matters little to the Church to know who translated this book into Greek. [Col. 0745D] We, however, are more readily persuaded that it had been rendered into Greek before the time of Eusebius, when tyrants were raging against the Christians with a fiercer heat of persecution. For he seems to signify to us, not altogether obscurely, that he himself had not read this book before it was circulated in the Greek language. However the matter may stand, it is certainly clear from this how highly this *Apology* was esteemed by Greek readers.

“But what,” someone will say, “did not Lactantius pronounce a very different judgment upon it in these words? ‘Septimius Tertullian was skilled in every kind of literature, but in expression he was lacking in ease and polish and was very obscure. Hence he did not attain sufficient celebrity either’”—that is, fame and praise (Lactantius, book V of the *Divine Institutes*, chap. 1, p. 459). [Col. 0746A] But whoever raises this objection should, I ask, attend to what we said above: first, that Lactantius praises the universal learning of our Tertullian (above, chap. 1, art. 5). Second, when he said that Tertullian did not attain sufficient celebrity, this should not be understood as though he had pleaded the cause of the Christians with arguments of insufficient force, but as referring to his difficult, unpolished, and highly obscure diction and expression. And surely we think that no one who has so much as touched this book with the tips of his lips will fail immediately to admit that it is strewn with frequent thorns of words alien to good Latin, with ruggedness and rough places, and is often wrapped in great obscurity. Yet we also believe there is no one who will not admit that, even if Tertullian in this [Col. 0746B] book does not charm and delight his readers with verbal graces, elegance of language, and the sweetness of polished and refined discourse, he nevertheless strikes them with the marvelous sharpness of his style and the gravity of his thoughts; and that almost all his arguments possess such force and weight that the more equitable are convinced by them, while the more obstinate are crushed and overwhelmed. Yet we cannot conceal that, sometimes carried away by the impulse of his harsher temperament, he employed certain arguments that many consider weak or even false. Below, however, we shall demonstrate that they have not attended carefully enough to how much he aimed at brevity in this book, and that many things they regard as false are in fact found to be true if they are attentively compared with other matters that he himself explains more fully elsewhere.

[Col. 0746C] Yet one may, not altogether without justification, miss in this book a better arrangement and order of the arguments, which would have cast greater light upon the entire work and enabled Tertullian more easily to win the reader’s goodwill and approval.

But someone will still object to us with Lactantius, who pronounced this judgment upon the same *Apologeticum* of Tertullian: “Although Tertullian fully pleaded the same cause of the Christians in the book entitled *Apologeticum*, nevertheless it is one thing to reply to accusers—which consists solely in defense or denial—and another to give systematic instruction, as we do, in which the entire sum of the doctrine must be contained” (Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, chap. 4, p. 470). For he declares that two things should have been done by those who undertook the defense [Col. 0746D] of the Christian religion against the pagans. The first was to reply to those who charged the Christians with many crimes. The second was so to expound and demonstrate the doctrine of the Christian religion that anyone might be fully and perfectly instructed in it. He admits that the first part of this case was fully pleaded by Tertullian, but certainly not the second. Tertullian, however, considered it sufficient for his purpose to overthrow the foolish accusations of the pagans, who charged Christians with every most grievous crime, and to vindicate their innocence and integrity of morals. How soundly he demonstrated this will become evident to everyone from the analysis of this book already given and from what will be said below.

Moreover, he did not leave the instruction and explanation of Christian [Col. 0747A] doctrine entirely untouched.
