For he explains its principal heads briefly indeed, but with such sincerity and candor that everyone may readily understand that nothing is more consonant with both divine institutions and right reason, as we shall show later. Lactantius doubtless desired a longer exposition and proof of these teachings. But in our earlier dissertations we showed that this complaint is not entirely justified (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 2, art. 2; and *on Lactantius*, chap. 3, art. 2).

# CHAPTER III. The Manuscript Codices and Editions of This *Apologeticum*, and the Paraphrases, Scholia, and Observations of Various Writers upon It

## ARTICLE I. The Various Manuscript Codices of This Book

[Col. 0747B]

Many manuscript codices of the *Apologeticum* published by our Tertullian have indeed survived down to our age. Beatus Rhenanus mentions two, with whose aid he prepared an edition of this and of Tertullian’s other books. The first was preserved at the Transjuran monastery of Payerne, and the second in the library of the monastery of Hirsau. Both abound in so many—and almost entirely the same—errors that one appears to have been copied from the other. Sigismund Gelenius obtained another, a very ancient codex of Tertullian’s works and, as he himself says, one of excellent quality, [Col. 0747C] from the monastery of Masmünster; but he has not explained clearly enough whether this *Apologeticum* is one of the books of Tertullian missing from that codex. Three additional codices of the same works exist in the Vatican Library. Alanus Copus, supplied with these by the most illustrious Cardinal Sirleto, collected their readings differing from the printed editions and transmitted them to Pamelius, who used them in preparing a new edition of Tertullian’s works. But three further copies were supplied to Pamelius himself: two from the monasteries of Saint-Amand and Saint Bavo, and a third, an English codex, in the possession of the Englishman John Clement. Yet neither Pamelius nor anyone else has informed us of their quality or antiquity.

[Col. 0747D] In our own France other manuscript codices of these books from every period are found, several of which seem inferior to none in venerable antiquity or elegance of script. One of these, formerly belonging to the brothers Dupuy, is preserved in the library of our Most Christian King. Another was owned by Jacques Bongars. Desiderius Heraldus corrected his separate edition of the *Apologeticum* against both.

Nicolas Rigault, however, complains with no slight indignation that the first and genuine, highly accurate copies of Tertullian’s works had long ago been so corrupted by those unable to understand the language of this African writer that scarcely any hope remained of restoring the true text. [Col. 0748A] Yet he admits that his edition received a great accession of light and distinction from variant readings collected and published by Rhenanus, and from other, better readings collected and published by Fulvius and Junius. He further informs us that he had at hand the aforementioned codex of the brothers Dupuy, another belonging to Pierre Pithou, and the variant readings of the Fulda codex, copied, as he says, from the original in a volume belonging to the most illustrious Monchal, Archbishop of Toulouse. With the aid of these codices, and especially of these readings sent to him, he boasts that he corrected the text of the *Apologeticum* in 250 places. But he remained entirely silent as to the quality and antiquity of those two codices and of the original from which the Fulda readings had been excerpted.

We, however, obtained not only those first two [Col. 0748B] codices, but also several others, whose character and quality must be explained. The first, the Dupuy codex, appears to more expert judges to have been copied in a most beautiful hand around the year of Christ 900. It contains only Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* and, as we have said, is preserved in the library of our Most Christian King under the number 3971. The most illustrious Abbé Le Tellier, with his customary great kindness, ordered Nicolas Clément to make it available to us.

The second, as we have said, once belonged to Pierre Pithou and was given to the college of the Reverend Fathers of the Oratory of Jesus at Troyes. It was preserved in their library and, through their altogether exceptional kindness, was sent to us. Men more practiced in examining ancient codices judged from the form of its characters that it was written around the eleventh [Col. 0748C] century. But it is marred throughout by various errors due to the ignorance of the first scribe; another, more learned hand either corrected them or indicated that they required correction by adding obeli and marginal notes.

Several treatises of Tertullian were transcribed in that codex, and an index of them appears on its first page. This *Apologeticum*, however, was omitted from the index. There therefore appears to be room for suspicion that it was written out later by some scribe after the other books. For that index was written by the same hand as the other books. But the man who subsequently copied the *Apologeticum* was more ignorant than the others and unacquainted with the Latin language, and he left the frequent errors with which that codex abounds throughout. It also displays a different system of word abbreviation from that visible in the other books. [Col. 0748D] Nevertheless, certain sufficiently competent judges of ancient handwriting think that this book, like the others, was written by the same scribe. The codex does not, however, contain the entire *Apologeticum*, but only as far as the beginning of the thirtieth chapter; the remainder, constituting a quarter of the whole book, is wholly lacking.

The third manuscript codex was supplied to us by the most illustrious Achilles de Harlay, a man beyond all praise. After presiding for many years over the Parlement of Paris with truly admirable knowledge of law, equity, integrity, and other eminent virtues, he resigned that dignity with as much fortitude of spirit as universal regret, and died while always maintaining the same constancy of life. That codex, in elegance [Col. 0749A] of script, is not inferior to the Dupuy codex, nor does it seem to us to have been copied a hundred years later. Yet we find in it most of the same readings, both good and bad, as in the latter.

The fourth and fifth codices belong to the Colbert Library and are marked with the numbers 989 and 5,271. The older seems to have been committed to writing about 700 years ago, and the more recent no earlier than 400 years ago. Charles Duchesne, the distinguished custodian of that library, made both codices available to us at the command of the most illustrious Abbé Colbert.

We also received variant readings from two other manuscripts. The first belongs to the monastery of Murbach, at the end of which these words are read: “Pray for the lord abbot of Murbach.” [Col. 0749B] This was Bartholomew of Andlau, who was placed in charge of that monastery in 1455 and thereafter, and wished the very numerous manuscripts collected from everywhere to be marked with the same subscription. These words appended to the *Apologeticum* were written in a much more recent hand than the *Apologeticum* itself, which appears to have been written six or seven hundred years ago. One of the monks of that monastery excerpted its various readings with the greatest diligence, down to the smallest detail, and sent them to us; we owe no small thanks to his kindness.

The other manuscript whose readings differing from the printed editions were sent to us is one of those with which the most illustrious Abbé Giusto Fontanini enriched his library at Rome. He is sufficiently known for his learning [Col. 0749C] and should never be named by us without due praise. He supplied this codex to our Claude Devic, who, although devoted to more important studies, arranged for the variant readings he had extracted from it to be conveyed to us.

We carefully collated the five aforementioned codices—the Dupuy, Pithou, Harlay, and the two Colbert codices—with the edition prepared by Rigault. From this collation we collected a great many variant readings which he had, often without giving any reason but, as it seems, repeatedly on his own authority, either wholly cut away or altered. For he admits that he used only two codices, as we have said, those of Dupuy and Pithou, together with the variant readings from Fulda. But those readings [Col. 0749D] were found in a volume quite foreign to their original setting, and Rigault could not know by whom or with what diligence they had been collected. Nor did he ascertain—or at least he informed no one—of what quality and age that Fulda codex was, on whose authority he altered Tertullian’s text for the most part. For after newly and carefully collating the Dupuy and Pithou codices and the others mentioned, together with the variant readings of still others, we clearly observed that they are altogether opposed to Rigault’s corrections. Who would say that the doubtful reliability of a single Fulda codex should be preferred to the authority of so many others, both better and older? But lest anyone think that less credence should be given to us than to him, some examples of amputations and alterations of this kind [Col. 0750A] must be presented.

Thus, in the first chapter of the *Apologeticum*, only the following is read in Rigault’s edition: “All who formerly hated because they were ignorant cease at once to be ignorant,” etc. (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 1, p. 262). But in our manuscripts and the earlier editions: “All who formerly hated because they did not know what it was that they hated cease at once to be ignorant,” etc. Do you see that the words “what it was that they hated” were rejected by Rigault? Nor should you say that they were omitted by the printers. For then you would charge Rigault with the highest negligence, one that cannot be pardoned in anyone placed in charge of an edition of a work of this kind. Later, no more than this appears in the same edition of Rigault: “Venus wounded by a human arrow, Mars,” etc. (*ibid.*, chap. 14). But in the same printed books and manuscripts: “Venus [Col. 0750B] wounded by a human arrow because she wished to snatch away her son Aeneas, who had nearly been killed by the same Diomedes; Mars,” etc. Is this too, then, to be attributed to the printers’ carelessness or haste? But if Rigault thought that these words had intruded into the text from the margin or elsewhere, why did he not inform us of this addition? But come, and you will recognize other passages similarly cut away from our author’s text. Elsewhere, according to our codices, Tertullian had left it written: “I shall indeed call the emperor ‘lord,’ but in the ordinary sense” (*ibid.*, chap. 34). Rigault, however, saw fit to remove the last three words. Not much later Tertullian has: “So far is it from being proper for the emperor to be called God, not only,” etc. Yet in the same older copies it is written: “So far is it from being proper for the emperor to be called that which cannot be believed, [Col. 0750C] not only,” etc. Who therefore removed the words “which cannot be believed” from the text, if not the man who thought them useless and superfluous?

What of the fact that the following words of Tertullian were not merely excised but transposed by him: “The Epicureans were permitted to establish some truth concerning pleasure. How do we offend you if we presuppose other pleasures? If we are unwilling to know how to take delight, the injury is ours, if perhaps not yours. But we reject what pleases you, and our pleasures do not delight you” (*ibid.*, chap. 38). In the other, older printed and manuscript codices, however: “How do we offend you if we presuppose other pleasures? If we wish to know how to take delight, the injury is ours—if perhaps ours, not yours. But we reject what pleases you, and our pleasures do not delight you. Yet the Epicureans were permitted [Col. 0750D] to establish some truth concerning pleasure, that is, equanimity of mind, and the ample affairs of the Christian woman” [the final phrase is textually uncertain]. The last word, “Christian woman,” however, is not found in the printed editions. What then? Merely because of this single word, perversely added by a careless scribe, was anyone entitled to alter, distort, and mutilate Tertullian’s text? In the same manner, however, Rigault elsewhere deleted these words of Tertullian: “We touch God” (*ibid.*, chap. 40).

If you desire yet another example of alterations of this kind, it need not be sought far away. For not much later, in the same text of Tertullian, he altered the words of the editions and manuscripts, “I do not bathe at dawn,” and ordered that it be written: “I do not bathe toward night.” [Col. 0751A] Many other passages of this book, similarly interpolated and badly mutilated by Rigault, could easily be produced. But we have judged that their enumeration should now be omitted, lest the same points be repeated. For those of greater importance will indeed have to be treated below when occasion is given. We had resolved to present at the end of our dissertation absolutely all the variant readings of this book excerpted either by us or by others. But because one of our associates, who is diligently laboring to prepare an edition of all Tertullian’s books, asked that this province be entrusted to him, we judged that his very reasonable wishes should be satisfied. We therefore consider it sufficient for our purpose to indicate in this dissertation the principal and noteworthy words of Tertullian that have been corrupted, interpolated, excised, and altered, so that his meaning and opinion may [Col. 0751B] more readily be understood by everyone.

## ARTICLE II. The Various Editions of This *Apologeticum* and of Tertullian’s Other Books

One could find very few works of the ancient Fathers of the Church that have been printed more often than this *Apologeticum* and the other writings of Tertullian. It was published not only together with them, but also separately. For it alone emerged from the printers’ workshop into public light through the zeal and care of Giovanni Battista Egnazio.

Another edition of this *Apologeticum* was produced at Paris in 1613 through the labor and effort of Desiderius Heraldus, who appended to it, as we noted in its proper place, the *Octavius* of Marcus Minucius [Col. 0751C] Felix (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, chap. 2, art. 3).

Before and after that time, however, the *Apologeticum* was published with either most or all of Tertullian’s other works. To review briefly the principal editions of these works: Beatus Rhenanus first arranged for them to be printed at Basel in 1521, and then in 1528. Other editions based upon these were published in precisely the same manner in 1525, 1536, and 1538; another, prepared through the efforts of Sigismund Gelenius, appeared before the public in 1562. Then, in 1580, René Laurent de la Barre provided us with another edition, in which Tertullian’s treatises were corrected by comparing, as he says, old and recent copies. [Col. 0751D] No edition of these books, however, was reproduced more often than the one which, under the care of Jacobus Pamelius, was brought into public light in 1579. For it was reprinted in various cities of Europe in 1579, 1584, 1596, 1597, 1599, 1608, 1616, 1627, 1658, 1662, and 1664.

Furthermore, Luis de la Cerda, chief professor of theology among the Reverend Fathers of the Society of Jesus, published most of Tertullian’s works with new labor and care; but he omitted in particular those written by Tertullian against Marcion and against the Catholic Church. He nevertheless comprised the works he published in two volumes, which issued from the press in 1624, 1630, and 1641.

In 1634, Nicolas Rigault likewise arranged for all Tertullian’s works, comprised in one volume, to be published through new [Col. 0752A] study and in new type. But as regards the *Apologeticum* now under discussion, we have already observed that he altered, transposed, and even wholly excised many passages from the text of our African writer at his own pleasure and on his own authority.

In the following year, 1635, however, another edition subsequent to that of Rigault emerged from the printers’ workshop at Paris. Its editor, making no use of any further manuscript, wished Tertullian’s books *On the Pallium* and the *Apologeticum* to be reprinted according to Pamelius, but all the rest according to Rigault’s text. Yet the author of the preface goes completely astray in thinking that the books *On the Pallium* and the *Apologeticum* as edited by Rigault were so perfect that they might seem to have been presented by him to the public [Col. 0752B] for the first time. For, from what we noted a little earlier and shall note later, who does not see that this book was in many places corrupted rather than corrected by Rigault? Nevertheless, in 1641 that entire edition was again printed by the printers exactly as it had been prepared by Rigault.

Moreover, the editions that followed these were thereafter prepared on the authority of no manuscript codex, but only of Rigault’s edition. The first of them was overseen by Georges d’Amiens, a Capuchin friar. He divided it into three volumes, of which the first was published in 1646, the second in 1648, and the third in 1650. He prefixed to the entire work the striking title *Tertullian Revived*, just as though he had recalled the works of that most learned African from death to life. There is certainly [Col. 0752C] no need for us to interpose our judgment concerning this title and the edition as a whole, since very many others have delivered theirs abundantly, and that by no means a highly favorable one. Nevertheless, certain learned men judge that it contains several things by no means undeserving of praise, as will be stated shortly.

Finally, Philippe Le Prieur presided over the second edition of all Tertullian’s works after Rigault, completing it in 1664. But he added nothing new to it except a brief little dissertation on Tertullian’s life and blemishes, a text not interrupted by an inconvenient mass of notes, and new printers’ errors.

## ARTICLE III. On the Scholia, Paraphrases, Notes, and Observations of Various Authors on Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*

[Col. 0752D]

Many writers distinguished by varied learning, who devoted their attention to publishing Tertullian’s books or were engaged in some other undertaking, attempted by means of their observations, scholia, paraphrases, and commentaries either to explain and elucidate, or to confirm, the more obscure or particularly noteworthy passages of that *Apologeticum*. First, Beatus Rhenanus prefixed to his edition of this book an outline, though one far briefer than was fitting. He thought, however, that this brevity could be remedied by adding new chapter summaries, as they are called, through which he endeavored to correct others presented in the manuscripts. In addition, in that same—albeit very brief—outline of the book, [Col. 0753A] he attempted to cast some light upon a very few of its obscure passages.

Afterward François Zephyrus, having observed how useful this book could be to everyone, and wishing to prevent young students from being deterred from reading it by the obscurity of its language and by passages corrupted through scribal negligence, composed and published a paraphrase of it. In this paraphrase—which is indeed rather awkwardly intermingled with Tertullian’s text—he endeavors to explain several passages difficult to understand and to remove various impediments caused by obscurity. Moreover, Pamelius valued this paraphrase so highly that he judged it should be inserted into our Author’s text in precisely the same manner as in the preceding edition.

Nevertheless, this very paraphrase was wholly and completely rejected by others who subsequently presided over various editions [Col. 0753B] of this book, and especially by Luis de la Cerda. But lest anyone should ever be able to complain of this omission, that learned man published a new interpretation of the Tertullianic text. He also appended his own notes to the individual chapters. Although otherwise deserving of praise, these notes make it difficult to read the text itself without continually interrupting the reader’s attention. But many also complain of certain useless and overly lengthy notes and of digressions foreign to Tertullian’s purpose. Others, nevertheless, praise them and rank them above all others published thus far. They therefore find fault with them only because he did not correct Tertullian’s text against manuscript codices; because he did not publish all his works; and because, in keeping with his learning, he did not explain and confirm [Col. 0753C] the teachings of the Christian religion transmitted by him.

After Heraldus published this *Apologeticum* of Tertullian, he appended a book which he calls a commentary, though he composed it solely of notes entirely disconnected from one another. To avoid straying too far in them from Tertullian’s purpose, however, he added two books of digressions, in which he strives to smooth out Tertullian’s difficult and rugged passages. In all of these the author’s secular learning can be discerned, but one would look in vain for an explanation of the sacred and more obscure dogmas of the Christian religion transmitted by Tertullian. He also left untouched several other matters that undoubtedly required explanation and confirmation.

[Col. 0753D] Laurent de la Barre likewise published many observations on all of Tertullian’s works, which he states that he excerpted from those in which Beraldus, Alciatus, Crinitus, Turnebus, Vetranius, Homanus, Cujacius, and others attempted in scattered places to explain certain expressions of Tertullian that were difficult to understand. But because these matters pertain to grammar, he there appended Rhenanus’s notes, which he indicates that he had first corrected himself, since they had not escaped the censure of the Romans and Spaniards. But because he added very few of his own, and those extremely brief, and gave scarcely any to this *Apologeticum*, one can readily see what should be expected from him on theological matters.

Pamelius’s annotations on this [Col. 0754A] and Tertullian’s other books are therefore held to be of greater value. For, as they say, they are sprinkled with no small measure of sacred and secular learning, which can be useful to readers. Yet they fault them because Pamelius too frequently departs from his subject, amassed much that is useless, and, by interposing Zephyrus’s paraphrase, as we have said, interrupted Tertullian’s text, which in this and his other books he ought, with the aid of better codices, to have restored, if possible, to its original integrity.

Rigault therefore scorned and set aside all of these and wrote new notes and observations on this *Apologeticum* and Tertullian’s other works. Yet because he omitted, altogether without justification, very many observations originating with learned men, these were again made public in a single volume [Col. 0754B] published in 1635. They were collected from Pamelius, Latino Latini, Beatus Rhenanus, Jean Mercier, Edmond Richer, Théodore Marcile, Johann Wouwer, and Gabriel de L’Aubespine, Bishop of Orléans.

Certain learned men were persuaded that, if this volume were joined to Rigault’s published edition of Tertullian’s works, the latter would be more perfect than all the rest. But aside from the fact that this volume of notes omits the no less useful notes and explanations of others, such as La Cerda, what, I ask you, can be expected of Rigault, who, in correcting Tertullian’s text, took care neither to read nor to follow either the very manuscript codices he had at hand, as we have said (preceding Article), or any others? Moreover, in writing his notes he displayed no small [Col. 0754C] audacity, which he was compelled to excuse in his preface. But one would find very few people who find his excuse wholly acceptable.

Less rash, indeed, but no more approved are the extremely long observations heaped up to the point of nausea by Georges d’Amiens. For into them he thrust everything that he had gathered for another purpose and, it appears, for public sermons. Some nevertheless admit that they contain useful material, especially in the chapter scholia that he presents on the page facing Tertullian’s text.

Finally, Le Prieur selected various observations by learned men—Rhenanus, Pamelius, La Cerda, Salmasius, L’Aubespine, and certain others—and from time to time interspersed among them [Col. 0754D] some devised by himself. But these are of such little importance that scarcely anyone can be found who has approved them. Nevertheless, he deserves some measure of praise for having all these observations and notes printed in the lower margins of the pages without any interruption of Tertullian’s text. For in this way better provision was made for the reader’s convenience. But who will ever pardon the fault of negligence in a man who, undertaking to reprint Tertullian’s works in new type, compared no manuscript codex whatsoever with the printed editions, but followed Rigault’s edition alone, word for word?

From what we have thus far discussed concerning so many and such varied editions of Tertullian’s works, [Col. 0755A] who will not admit with us that there is absolutely none that can deservedly be called perfect and complete in every respect? He will therefore undoubtedly render good service to the republic of letters who, being thoroughly imbued with sacred and secular learning, prepares a new edition of the *Apologeticum* and Tertullian’s other works. But before all else, its text must, with the utmost fidelity and diligence, be reviewed and corrected against French, Italian, German, and English manuscript codices and the early editions. For there still survive several codices of excellent quality, at least of the *Apologeticum*, which no one has thus far compared with the printed editions. But if he faithfully presents the variant and noteworthy readings excerpted from them, it will be possible to render a more certain judgment concerning Tertullian’s true and genuine text.

# CHAPTER IV. On Tertullian’s Two Books *To the Nations*

[Col. 0755B]

## ARTICLE I. Analysis of the First Book *To the Nations*

In the two books *To the Nations*, Tertullian once again pleaded the cause of the Christians, and he quite clearly divided each book into two parts. In the first part of the first book, he shows that Christians, though neither heard nor permitted a defense, were harassed, condemned, and most cruelly killed by the gentiles on the basis of the falsest and most unjust prejudgments (Book I, ch. 1 and following). In the second part, however, he makes it plain to everyone that the crimes of which Christians were accused were entirely false and that the gentiles themselves were in reality guilty of them (ch. 9 [Col. 0755C] and following). In the first part of the second book, he demonstrates how empty and absurd is the threefold theology of the pagans devised by Varro, which he calls physical, mythical, and popular or gentile (Book II, ch. 1 and following). In the second part, however, he demonstrates that the gods of the Romans are false and entirely fictitious (ch. 9 and following). But these matters must be explained somewhat more clearly.

First, therefore, he censures the pagans because they persecuted Christians with implacable hatred, although they were utterly ignorant of who and what Christians were and had never wished to know. For as soon as they had come to know them, they immediately ceased to hate them and willingly embraced the Christian religion. Nor could this be denied, as their daily complaint concerning the multiplied number of Christians loudly proclaimed. Our Author does not permit it to be objected that they had changed for the worse, as sometimes happens. For the profession of the Christian religion bears no mark of evil: no one is either ashamed of it or regrets it, and everyone rejoices and glories in it (Book I, ch. 1).

But if Christians had committed any crimes, the pagans surely ought to have compelled them by interrogation and torture to disclose them. Yet, on the contrary, by immediately believing those who either voluntarily denied their designation or were forced to deny it, they also had to admit that nothing evil could be found in their religion. Furthermore, judges were bound by their own laws to question those accused of any crimes concerning what, of what kind, and how serious those crimes were, [Col. 0756A] who their accomplices and harborers were, and finally to state these matters expressly in the written sentence of the condemned. But nothing of the kind was ordinarily done in the condemnation of Christians, nor was anything pronounced in their sentence except the name “Christian.” The name alone, therefore, was the crime; yet this very name signifies nothing barbarous, ill-omened, or dishonorable, but either anointing or at least sweetness or goodness, since even the gentiles corruptly called them *Chrestians* (chs. 2–3).

But those who alleged that they hated the Christian sect solely because of its founder’s name were plainly witless (ch. 4). For they did not hate the Platonists or Pythagoreans because of the name of Plato or Pythagoras, nor physicians because of the name of Erasistratus, nor grammarians because of that of Aristarchus. Who also does not know that it is wrong to hate any sect unless one first observes [Col. 0756B] what there is in it deserving hatred? Yet the pagans neither knew the Christian sect or its founder nor wished to learn about them. Moreover, according to their own practice, any pagan was permitted to embrace whichever philosophical sect he wished, even one hostile to the state and its rulers. They also harassed only those philosophers who, by teaching the truth in part, spurned their gods. Thus indeed they condemned Socrates, although he had been proclaimed by Apollo’s oracle the wisest of all mortals. It is therefore no wonder if the truth engendered their hatred of Christians. But observe, I ask, the frenzy of their deranged minds. They admitted that all who had renounced the worship of false gods and enrolled themselves in the Christian religion had become better people. Yet for this name alone [Col. 0756C] they raged more cruelly against them and preferred them to be guilty and wicked rather than Christian.

The pagans, however, objected that some Christians were thoroughly wicked and ruined by vices and crimes (ch. 5). But these, Tertullian says, were very few; and, like blemishes on a body, they thereby showed the excellence of their sect. Whoever they were, and however many, they—just like philosophers who disgraced their own sect by shameful deeds—were true deserters, Christians in name alone, indeed unworthy of that name.

The gentiles insisted that the Christian sect was truly evil, since it had been condemned by the emperors’ laws (ch. 6). But did not, our Author replies, the same just laws of the emperors and others establish that no one was ever to be condemned unless he had first [Col. 0756D] been duly convicted of some crime? Why, then, did the pagans condemn Christians without either hearing or convicting them? Were not many exceedingly unjust laws likewise enacted by the lawgivers of those same pagans, and afterward amended or rendered obsolete? Finally, an unjust law, such as that enacted against Christians, requires no honor or obedience.

Nor could the pagans insist that the laws against Christians had been enacted by men who had learned of their crimes through common and popular report. For is not rumor, by the admission of those same pagans, an evil than which none is swifter? Yet it lives only so long as it remains uncertain, false, and mendacious. For where a matter is certain, there rumor ceases. Its origin must therefore be investigated, and [Col. 0757A] one must await time, which reveals all things. But from the very beginning of the Christian religion, who ever discovered, exposed, or disclosed the infanticides, incest, and other crimes alleged against Christians in their assemblies? Was it the Christians themselves? But they concealed their mysteries in profound silence, nor could they, had they been conscious of such horrendous crimes, disclose them without endangering their lives. Was it the gentiles? Certainly not. For although they kept Christians under daily surveillance in their assemblies, no one ever discovered these things, nor did any member of their households, corrupted by money, ever testify that he had either seen or concealed them.

Moreover, Christians promised eternal happiness to their followers who diligently observed Christ’s laws. But tell me, I ask, could it appear credible to anyone not utterly insane [Col. 0757B] that it had ever been promised to those who perpetrated such great crimes? No gentile endowed with even the slightest sense of humanity would ever have dared to commit them. Therefore neither would any Christians, who shared the same nature as other human beings and were neither Cynopenae, Sciapods, nor Antipodes (ch. 7).

Who would not laugh at the pagans, who endeavored to prove that Christians were later than the Phrygians and other nations by the ridiculous tale of a boy reared by a mute nurse and uttering, as the first sound of his voice, βέκκοις (“bekkois,” interpreted as “bread”)? For who does not know that the Christian people, which derived its origin from the Jews, is more ancient than the others? Yet even if it were more recent than others, it was nevertheless a third nation after the Greeks and Romans, and was not addicted to the most inhuman superstitions (ch. 8).

[Col. 0757C] The pagans insisted that Christians, because of their contempt for the gods, were the authors of every disaster and must therefore be exterminated (ch. 9). But by various examples Tertullian demonstrates that the world had been disturbed and overwhelmed by the gravest calamities—such as inundations of water, fire from heaven, and the universal flood—before the pagans themselves had fashioned their gods and before the cities in which those gods were born, dwelt, and buried had been founded. What of the fact that afterward these eminent gods could not rescue their worshippers from other disasters?

In the second part of this book, our Author shows that the gentiles themselves were conscious of the very crimes of which they vainly attempted to accuse Christians. [Col. 0757D] For those who unjustly complained that the Christians had repudiated the ancient but impious rites had themselves departed from their ancestors’ laws, institutions, and customs in worship, diet, and even speech, and had rejected the antiquities that they could never praise highly enough.

Furthermore, Christians could not have despised gods whom they knew not to exist. The pagans, however, utterly spurned those whom they advertised as true gods and claimed to worship. For after scorning and repudiating many, they honored only certain ones selected by themselves. Were not the god Alburnus, Liber, Serapis, Harpocrates, and Anubis also contemptuously expelled by the senate, and their statues overthrown? What could be more insulting to the gods than that they could not be worshipped [Col. 0758A] without a decree of the senate? What more ignominious than for any private individual to pawn his household gods, while public gods were auctioned beneath the spear? What more shameful than to charge a fee for the temple site, its approach, doorposts, and doors? What greater disgrace to the gods than to consecrate an old man in Saturn, a beardless youth in Apollo, a soldier in Mars, and a smith in Vulcan; than to make dead men equal to the greatest gods; than to punish those who swore falsely by the gods, but not those who did so by Caesar’s genius; or than to sacrifice to them all the worst parts of the victims? Finally, what could be more unworthy of the gods’ majesty than for Homer and other poets to sing with impunity of Venus wounded, Mars bound, Jupiter assailed by other gods, weeping, indulging his lust, and enumerating his own adulteries? Why say more? Were not these same gods mocked [Col. 0758B] in the theaters and in the comedies of the Lentuli and Hostii, where, to universal applause, mimes and actors played the utterly ridiculous part of Cybele’s sighing shepherd, or sang of Jupiter’s glories and disgraces? Were not the gods defamed by depraved men who in the arena represented Attis castrated, Hercules burned, Dis conducting the gladiators’ funerals, and Mercury examining the dead? Who, then, will deny that gods of this sort were far more despised and mocked by the very gentiles who fashioned them than by Christians (ch. 10)?

Come now: the pagans, deceived by the mendacious Tacitus, falsely asserted that Christians worshipped the head of an ass (ch. 11). But the gentiles themselves actually worshipped whole asses together with their Epona, and consecrated [Col. 0758C] beasts together with their mangers. By what reasoning, moreover, did they charge Christians with a crime for worshipping Christ’s cross, when they themselves revered the Attic Pallas and Pharian Ceres, whose forms did not differ from the upright beam of a cross? Did they not also place their gods upon part of an upright cross, while upon complete crosses they placed figures of Victory, *cantabra*, *siphara*, and military standards, which they held in the highest honor (ch. 12)?

Some of them wrongly supposed that Christians worshipped the Sun because they prayed to their true God with their faces turned toward that same Sun and indulged in spiritual rejoicing on the Lord’s Day (ch. 13). Yet these shameless slanderers could not deny that it was the custom of the pagans to pray to their fabricated gods in a similar fashion and to dedicate to them one day of the week, which they celebrated on the day nearest the Lord’s Day, according to a rite far different from that of the [Col. 0758D] Jews.

Tertullian then inveighs sharply against a certain beast-fighter, an apostate from the Jewish religion, who carried around in the Circus a picture of the Christians’ God in the form of an ass, with this inscription: *Onochoetes* (ch. 14). For the further that image departed from the truth, the more certain it was that the pagans worshipped horned gods, goat-born gods, and gods altogether resembling monsters.

Nothing more false could likewise have been invented than that Christians killed an infant amid their sacred mysteries and drank its blood. Yet it was plainly established that the pagans, contrary to their own laws, slaughtered newborn infants, or with the utmost cruelty exposed them to be killed by the injuries of the open air, [Col. 0759A] or drew out their blood and devoured premature infants whole (ch. 15).

What, indeed, could be more shameless than for Christians to be accused of wholly fictitious nocturnal incest by those who could not deny that pagan Persians openly had intercourse with their own mothers, and who praised and encouraged with great applause Oedipus when he represented that crime in the theater? Indeed, these very men frequently mingled in infamous incest with their own children, whom, as we have said, they had exposed as infants and no longer recognized (ch. 16). Lest anyone object that this was invented without evidence, our Author confirms it by a well-known example that occurred during Fuscianus’s term as prefect of the City, a considerable time before he wrote these books.

He proceeds and makes it plain that Christians were vainly proclaimed public [Col. 0759B] enemies by the pagans because they did not worship the images of the Caesars or swear by their genius (ch. 17). For he clearly shows that those rebellious nations conquered by the emperors, which had procured for them the surnames Parthicus, Medicus, and Germanicus, were justly charged with this very crime. Were not the Romans also public enemies who conspired against their emperors and recently killed them in their palaces in Gaul? Must not those also be called public enemies who assailed them with every kind of insult at the circus games, or in defamatory placards hung upon their statues? Finally, who were the public enemies: the Christians, who refused to call the Emperor a god, or the gentiles, who against their conscience and not without mockery called him a god, [Col. 0759C] and, swearing by his genius, did not shrink from perjury?

Moreover, they imputed a new crime to Christians: namely, their marvelous constancy in enduring every kind of torture for the truth of their religion (ch. 18). But with what effrontery and audacity, I ask? For they themselves extolled with the highest praises Regulus, who was the first to end his life by the punishment of the cross; the queen of Egypt, who ended hers through the bite of beasts; and Hannibal’s wife, who, like Dido, ended hers by voluntary fire. Did they not also praise the Attic woman who, after the bitterest torments, spat her tongue at the tyrant rather than betray a secret? Did they not likewise account it praiseworthy in gladiators to be killed by one another or by beasts, in certain men to let themselves be burned alive, and in the Laconians steadfastly to endure being beaten and mangled [Col. 0759D] with scourges?

Yet surely the Christians’ unconquered fortitude under horrendous tortures was all the more praiseworthy because, unlike the pagans, they endured them not to pursue the empty glory of men, but because they most certainly expected the future resurrection of bodies, God’s final judgment, and an eternal reward according to their deserts (ch. 19). Nor were they to be hissed off by the pagans because of this expectation, since the latter asserted that human souls would migrate even into other bodies, including those of beasts; that there would be a future judgment of Minos and Rhadamanthus; and that afterward the impious would pass eternity in fire, but the pious would pass eternal life in a pleasant place.

[Col. 0760A] Finally, from what has thus far been argued, Tertullian concludes that even if Christians had been guilty of all the crimes of which they were falsely accused, they nevertheless ought not to be punished and harassed by pagans who are proved actually to have committed the same things (ch. 20). Finally, even if Christians had declared themselves guilty of those crimes, the pagans should nevertheless have investigated with the utmost diligence whether the charges were true and should have heard and examined lawful witnesses to and accomplices in those crimes. But they refused to observe these provisions of their own laws, lest, once the Christians’ innocence had been recognized, they should love those whom they had resolved to hate and remove from their midst. Thus, through voluntary ignorance, they loved their own errors and hated the truth.

## ARTICLE II. Analysis of the Second Book

[Col. 0760B]

In the second book, likewise divided into two parts, Tertullian shows that the gods of the gentiles are false and that their forms of worship are depraved and to be rejected (Book II, ch. 1). However firmly they may appear to be established by ancestral authority, their falsity is so manifest that it is most readily recognized by all who have not voluntarily blinded themselves. Therefore, to break their unyielding obstinacy, Tertullian first refutes what Varro—easily foremost in learning among all the men of his age—had set forth in his books on religion. There he distinguishes three classes of gods: the first physical, or that of the philosophers; the second mythical, or that of the poets; and the third gentile, or that of the peoples. But the first, says [Col. 0760C] our Author, rests upon uncertain conjectures, the second upon mere fables, and the third upon ridiculous adoptions of gods and an insane and utterly shameful cult. All these things, therefore, are false, while everyone’s opinion concerning the true God ought to be one and shared, and their consensus unanimous.

For there was the greatest disagreement among the physicists or philosophers concerning God’s nature, which arose from nothing other than their ignorance of him (ch. 2). They therefore professed wisdom in vain, since its beginning is the fear of God. But how could they have feared him when they did not know who or what he was? Yet it was easy for them to know this true God from our Sacred Scriptures. But, led by a blind lust for glory, they corrupted with various sophistries what they had drawn from these pure fountains, and consequently split into various factions. [Col. 0760D] The Platonists taught that all things were governed by God’s providence; the Epicureans, by contrast, wholly and completely denied it. The same Platonists asserted that God was situated within the world, but the Stoics that he was outside it. Diogenes admitted that he did not know what was happening in heaven or who the gods were; while earlier Thales of Miletus could make absolutely no reply when Croesus questioned him about the gods. Socrates did not, indeed, believe that they existed, yet ordered that a rooster be sacrificed to Aesculapius.

Why say more? Dionysius divided the gods into three classes: first, those that fall within our sight, such as the sun and moon; second, others that are unseen, such as Neptune; and third, others who were deified [Col. 0761A] from among human beings, such as Hercules and Amphiaraus. Arcesilaus likewise devised a threefold but different class of gods, namely the Olympians, the Stars, and the Titans. Xenocrates, however, admitted only the latter two, just as most Egyptians admitted no more than the sun and moon, heaven and earth. Democritus suspected that all the gods arose together with the heavenly fire, which Zeno held nature to resemble. Hence Varro taught that the soul of the world was fire, since when it is extinguished we die.

All these opinions, however diverse they may be, seem to conspire toward this one conclusion: those philosophers thought there were no gods other than the elements of the world or things arising from them (ch. 3). Tertullian, however, demonstrates that these are the dreams of men who are awake. [Col. 0761B] For God exists from himself, unbegotten and eternal, having no beginning and never to have an end. But the elements are parts of the world, which Plato admits was created, and which Epicurus alone dreamed was uncreated.

Moreover, if the world and the elements are gods, they must be living beings, and by this very fact are mortal and devoid of divinity. Nor should Varro be heard when he prattled that they were indeed living beings, but ones that move of themselves and should therefore be regarded as immortal gods. For however these elements may be moved, they are certainly corporeal; and therefore, since they can be destroyed, they cannot be gods. Furthermore, even if they moved themselves, they nevertheless received the principle of their motion from another, who, although unseen, is the first author of all motions and therefore the true and only God.

[Col. 0761C] Nor does Tertullian permit the objection that the Greek name Θεός (“God”) is in fact derived from the running and motion with which the elements are endowed (ch. 4). For the true designation of God does not signify some quality visible to our eyes, as running and motion are, but supreme majesty and substance. What of the fact that many pagans proclaimed a great number of their gods to be motionless? Moreover, no one will ever deny that the elements are composed of matter, something that God’s utterly simple nature cannot admit. And indeed Zeno separated the world’s matter from God and supposed that he passed through it as honey passes through the comb. But I should like you to say by what reasoning the natural philosophers asserted that the world and the elements contained within it were gods. For Plato judges this world itself to be spherical and without a head. Epicurus, however, used to say, [Col. 0761D] “What is above us has nothing to do with us,” and babbled that the sun was only a foot across; the Peripatetics, by contrast, thought it far larger than the whole terrestrial globe. Is it not, therefore, the height of madness to fashion gods of this kind? Finally, Thales of Miletus fell into a well while scrutinizing the heavens. What does that fall indicate except the vanity of the natural philosophers’ curiosity, since, after fruitlessly investigating the nature of things, they failed to know its true craftsman, almighty God?

Varro insisted that divinity should be attributed to the elements because they either bind human beings to themselves through the greatest benefits or oppress them with hardships (ch. 5). Tertullian, however, replies that the elements are merely instruments of prosperous or adverse circumstances and that the true [Col. 0762A] God, whom they serve, is their author. For just as a sick person’s cure is to be attributed not to the medicines but to the physician, and a person’s death not to the sword or spear but to the robber or enemy, so prosperous and adverse events must be ascribed not to the elements but to God, the equitable judge of deserts. It is also evident that the elements diminish, perish, and are ruled by someone (ch. 6). But the true God can neither be diminished nor undergo anything, and he rules and governs all things.

Tertullian passes from there to the second class of gods, which Varro chose to designate the mythical class, or that of the poets (ch. 7). The poets imagined that these gods were heroes who, after passing through the mortal life of human beings, obtained the reward of divinity through their illustrious deeds. Following this utterly pernicious example, the Romans [Col. 0762B] likewise proclaimed their kings to be gods, while others perjured themselves. But who, I ask you, had those gods of the poets been? Human beings, certainly, born from a sordid or criminal origin, who throughout the course of their lives wallowed in every kind of crime. For this reason Plato judged that the poets, and Homer himself, should be expelled from the state as shameless accusers of the gods. Indeed, when the gentiles—shameless as they were—were reproached by Christians for such great infamy among their gods, they answered nothing except that these were mere fables of the poets. But although they loudly declared that they did not believe the poets, they not only venerated the gods fashioned by them—Ceres, the Idaean Mother, Saturn, and Hercules—but also performed horrendous sacrifices to them. Who, then, will not admit that these gods of the poets were worshipped and vaunted by the gentiles [Col. 0762C] with the greatest impiety?

Certainly no less senseless was the third class of gods, which Varro taught was gentile or popular (ch. 8). For these gods were none other than those whom certain peoples had adopted according to their own whim and caprice, and whom others could distinguish neither by sight, nor by hearing, nor even by name. Tertullian lists as such Atargatis, Caelestis, Versutina, Obodas, Dusares, Belenus, Delventinus, Visidianus, Numentinus, Ancharia, Praeveris, and Nortia. He thinks that by the same license the Egyptians, who worshipped beasts, regarded and honored the patriarch Joseph as a god under the name Serapis. He therefore rightly concludes from what has been said that those gods of the peoples are utterly false, since the one true God, present everywhere [Col. 0762D] and Lord of all, is equally to be worshipped and adored by everyone.

In the second part of this book he specifically assails and overthrows the gods of the Romans (chap. 9). Varro, however, perversely divided them into uncertain, certain, and select gods. For who, our author asks, unless he is mad, honors a god who is uncertain and doubtful? But whoever has and venerates certain and select gods plainly despises and rejects the others. That division of the gods is therefore inept; they might have been distinguished somewhat better into common and particular gods. Yet the first, or common, gods are the same as the public and imported gods, who are included within the physical or mythical class of gods mentioned and refuted by us shortly before. There remain, therefore, [Col. 0763A] only the particular gods of the Romans, who either had been taken from conquered enemies and carried off to Rome, or were the Penates and Lares, whom each person worshiped in his own private house and with a peculiar rite. But all these were human beings who, on account of certain outstanding deeds, were made gods after death by a plainly senseless consecration. Yet what, Tertullian asks, were the merits of one of them—for example, Aeneas? Was it his devotion to his father and son? But either he betrayed his own country, as Antenor did, or, by abandoning it in flames and leaving Priam and Astyanax behind, he failed to imitate the Punic woman who cast herself with her sons into the fires of her burning homeland. Was he better than the Romans who swore, for the safety of their emperors, against their children and wives? Moreover, if he earned any merit by carrying his father on his shoulders, did not the Argive [Col. 0763B] youths bear their mother like draft animals, lest she incur guilt in the sacred rites? If he nourished his father, did not a certain daughter, with greater filial devotion, offer her breasts to her father when he had been imprisoned? They, therefore, were more worthy of divine honors than the cowardly and fearful Aeneas, who was never seen again after the battle at Laurentum. Did Romulus likewise merit the honor of divinity, when he killed his brother and abducted the maidens of others? Did Hercules, for removing Augeas’s dung; Penelope, for chastity; Sanctus, for hospitality, deserve to obtain the rights of divinity any more than Sterculus, the daughter of Faunus, or Ulysses?

What, moreover, is to be said of other, far more shameful gods? What divinity, I ask you, is there in Larentina, [Col. 0763C] a public prostitute and the nurse of Romulus? What of the woman who, after being violated by the custodian of Hercules’ temple following a ridiculous game, boasted that she had been embraced by Hercules himself, though he was already dead? Who could patiently endure the infamous Antinous being regarded by the Romans as a god? Yet they devised other gods no less shameful, whom they most foolishly proclaimed to preside over marriage and the procreation of children. Such are Consevius, Fluvionia, Vitumnus, Sentinus, Diespiter, Candelifera, Prosa, Farmus, Albana, Runcinia, Potina, Edula, Abeona, Domiduca, Volumnus, Voleta, Paventina, Venilia, Volupia, Praestitia, Peragenor, Consus, Juventa, Fortuna, Barbata, Afferenda, Mutunus, Tutunus, Pertunda, Subigus, Prema, and others whose functions even the slightest sense of modesty [Col. 0763D] forbids one to designate by their proper names (chaps. 10, 11).

Furthermore, in order to cut down all the gods of the Romans together and at one stroke, Tertullian attacks their very origin, which Varro begins with Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, but which must be traced back to their parent Saturn (chap. 12). Yet Saturn—much less his sons—could never have been a god: he was said to have been born of Caelus, or Chronos, and Earth, and to have castrated his father. Nor should it be said that these things are to be explained allegorically of time and the fertility of the earth. For the most distinguished writers—Cassius Severus, Cornelius Nepos, Tacitus, Diodorus, and others—assert in the clearest terms that Saturn was in fact a man who, after traveling through various parts of the world, was received in Oenotria, or Italy, and gave his own name to the mountain and city where he had established his abode, as well as to all Italy. [Col. 0764A] But because he had arrived as if unexpectedly and his parents were unknown, he was said to have fallen from heaven. Moreover, lest the pagans dare to mutter any objection, Tertullian confirms this with the testimony of the Sibyl accepted by them.

Accordingly, since no room for doubt remains that Saturn was a man, it is securely inferred from this that those whom the pagans acknowledged to have sprung from him and afterward to have died and been buried were in reality human beings (chap. 13). But dead human beings cannot be gods unless they received their divinity either from themselves or from others. They do not, however, possess it from themselves. For they would not have allowed themselves first to have been human beings, subject to so many and such great human weaknesses. Nor were they endowed with supreme divinity by anyone else, unless by one more powerful than all the other fictitious gods, [Col. 0764B] who must therefore alone be called the true God. Furthermore, no reason whatever can be assigned why the true God should have made others gods—not, certainly, so that they might serve as an aid or adornment to him, for almighty God needs no assistance or embellishment. Nor did he make certain human beings gods because of their merits. For what did Saturn merit, who devoured his own children; or Jupiter, who was rescued from his father’s fury, committed adultery with his sister, and is said to have assumed the forms of a bull, a shower of gold, a swan, and others, so that he might commit further rapes and adulteries more safely? Human beings of this kind, so impious and criminal, therefore never merited divinity.

Nor are those gods whom Dionysius the Stoic distinguishes into native and made gods (chap. 14). For Tertullian overthrows this utterly senseless opinion by the single example of Hercules, which is nevertheless entirely [Col. 0764C] sufficient. Hercules was not worthy of divinity because he killed wild beasts, since more of them are killed by gladiators; nor because he traversed the world, for Asclepiades the Cynic and many philosophers roamed through every region of the whole world with greater toil in their mendicancy. Is he therefore a god because he went down to the underworld? But to which of them is the way open? Let us proceed, if you please. Did not that eminent Hercules violate women? Did he not desert the Argonauts’ expedition because a boy had been lost? Was he not ensnared by the poisons of his wanton wife, and, after lighting a pyre, did he not bring about his own death? What sane person, therefore, would believe him to be a god? In what manner, likewise, could Aesculapius be proclaimed a god, when, as Socrates of Argos relates, he was born of an uncertain father and, on account of his skill in medicine, was struck by Jupiter’s thunderbolt, as his mother also had been? [Col. 0764D] Yet the Athenians worship him and his mother, as Thesca does [the reading “Thesca” is uncertain].

Nor are the Castors, Perseus, Erigone, Jupiter’s catamite—that is, Ganymede—any more worthy of heaven and divinity; nor are the dogs, scorpions, and crabs that the Romans transferred to the stars. Who, indeed, could hear without laughter the names of those gods whom the Romans believed to have been placed over certain locations in cities and houses? For they are called Viduus, Caeculus, Orbana, Arguis, Lana, Ascensus, Levicola, Forculus, Cardea, Limentinus, and others appointed over each particular function of life. But if these, known almost to the Romans alone, had been gods, [Col. 0765A] there would have been no need whatever for all the rest (chap. 15).

“But we are plainly ungrateful,” the Romans said, “if we deny divine honors to those who discovered for us the necessities of life.” Then, says Tertullian, those honors ought to be bestowed upon Cato, who first brought a fresh fig to Rome, and Pompey, who first brought cherries there. But nothing is more futile than this reasoning. For the discoverer of fruits is not their author and creator; the true God is. And certainly new arts are discovered daily by human beings, yet no one would say that their inventors are gods (chap. 16).

The Romans insisted that by their piety and religion toward the gods they had merited dominion over the whole world. “Is that so?” Tertullian asks. Did the shameful Sterculus extend the boundaries of the Roman Empire? Did Jupiter, forgetting the cave of Ida, Crete his homeland, and the most pleasant fragrance of his nurse, prefer the Capitol to them? Did [Col. 0765B] Juno, utterly forgetful of Carthage, which she had once preferred even to Samos, wish it to be overthrown by the Romans? But these and other unwarlike gods had no power against the fates, nor could they defend their cities and provinces against the arms of their enemies.

Moreover, the Roman Empire had been founded before there were any images, worship, or sacred rites of the gods, all of which were afterward introduced by Numa Pompilius. That empire therefore grew through wars, and consequently through equal slaughter of priests and citizens, equal destruction of sacred and profane things, and as many sacrileges as trophies and triumphs. Finally, who does not know that the kingdoms of the Assyrians, Medes, [Col. 0765C] Persians, and Egyptians were utterly overthrown, although they worshiped their gods with no less piety than did the Romans? Therefore God alone, one and almighty, apportions kingdoms—not the gods of the Romans or of other nations, who are demonstrably as artificial as the religions of those who worship them are false and vain (chap. 17).

## ARTICLE III

### It Is Shown by Various Weighty Arguments That Tertullian Is the Author of These Books, and the New Opinion of Hoornbeek, Who Denies This, Is Refuted

Jerome has attested for us that, in addition to the *Apologeticum*, Tertullian published other books *To the Gentiles*, concerning which he wrote to Magnus in these words: “Who is more learned than Tertullian? Who more exact? His *Apologeticum* and his books *Against the Gentiles* embrace all the learning [Col. 0765D] of the age” (Jerome, Epistle 83, *To Magnus*, p. 656). Who, moreover, does not see that the books with which we are concerned are designated here and distinguished from the *Apologeticum*? For although in the Agobard manuscript, which will be discussed below, they are entitled *To the Nations*, who will deny that this title has the same meaning as *To the Gentiles*?

To this may be added Augustine, who, in refuting an opinion of our Tertullian, cited these books under his name, though somewhat obscurely: “I do not assert,” he says, “what Tertullian perhaps said more wittily than truly: ‘If gods are selected like onions, then certainly the rest are judged rejected’” (Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, chap. 1, p. 162). We know, indeed, that some have thought his *Apologeticum* to be cited there. But others were so persuaded that no books other than [Col. 0766A] those *To the Nations* were cited there that they wished to correct their text from it. And indeed we shall show later that Augustine there had our author’s books *To the Nations* in view rather than the *Apologeticum*.

Furthermore, these books are more than once inscribed with Tertullian’s own name in the ancient Agobard manuscript. For on its second page we read: “Here are the books of Tertullian: *To the Nations*, Book I. Likewise *To the Nations*, Book II.” At the end of the first book also: “Tertullian’s *To the Nations*, Book I, ends. Book II *To the Nations* begins.” Moreover, on its first page the copyist of this manuscript wrote in larger letters: “A book offered at the altar of Saint Stephen in fulfillment of the vow of Agobard, bishop.” Now this, they say, is Agobard himself, archbishop of Lyons, who flourished in the age of Charlemagne and his sons, and at the beginning of the ninth century. [Col. 0766B] Thus the manuscript was copied at that time from another, undoubtedly more ancient manuscript, in which—and doubtless in many others likewise—these books similarly bore Tertullian’s name at their head. It was therefore the common opinion, not only in Agobard’s age but also in earlier centuries, that Tertullian was the author of these books *To the Nations*.

But even if we lacked an argument of such force, the subject matter of these books, their age, and above all their style and mode of composition, together with their very close affinity with the *Apologeticum*, demonstrate that they proceeded from Tertullian. For from the analysis of them already presented by us, it is most clearly evident that their writer is wholly intent upon making it plain to everyone that Christians were most unjustly persecuted by the pagans contrary to the prescriptions of all laws, and were falsely accused of crimes of which the gentiles themselves were in fact guilty. [Col. 0766C] These books were therefore written in Tertullian’s own age, when the pagans still raged against the Christians with fury as blind as it was unrestrained. Finally, nothing is said in them, whether concerning the Christians or the gentiles, that does not accord with Tertullian’s age and point to his very period.

The distinctive style of these books also, and their unusual manner of expression and vocabulary, plainly show that Tertullian is their true father. For his peculiar and characteristic diction, unlike that of all others, shines forth everywhere throughout them and is very quickly detected by any reader. Moreover, there repeatedly occur in them not only the same distinctive and unusual words of Tertullian as in the *Apologeticum*, [Col. 0766D] but even whole identical sentences. Nor is it necessary to prove by a lengthy induction something so readily apparent and which will become manifest to everyone from what is said later. Does not so great an affinity and connection between the two works demonstrate clearly enough that they were composed by one and the same writer—namely, Tertullian?

We are therefore astonished at a certain more recent author, a man certainly of great reputation among his own people, who boldly declares that it does not at all appear to him that Tertullian was in fact the author of these books. But on what weighty arguments, do you suppose? On scarcely any others than those very grounds by which they are especially vindicated to him: “It does not appear to me,” he says, “that Tertullian is the author; the style and subject matter are not his, [Col. 0767A] though they are nearly the same as in Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, from which they were rather drawn and fashioned in imitation of him, perhaps by some rival or devoted student of Tertullian” (Hoornbeek, *On the Theology of the Fathers*, book I, chap. 1, §10, p. 106). A novel and astonishing mode of argument indeed! The style, that learned man says, and the subject matter of the *Apologeticum* and of the books *To the Nations* are the same; therefore these books were composed not by Tertullian but by his rival or devoted student. What if we were similarly to conclude from this that the *Apologeticum* was composed not by him but by his rival or student? Will he perhaps answer that other writers assign that book to Tertullian? But we too have just shown that the books *To the Nations* are likewise ascribed to him by others.

Furthermore, that learned man admits with us, [Col. 0767B] as he cannot deny, that the style of these books and of the *Apologeticum* is the same. Yet neither he nor anyone else will ever deny that Tertullian’s style and mode of speaking are so characteristic and peculiar to him that scarcely anyone, if indeed anyone at all, could ever imitate them. Should it not therefore be concluded from this, as the more expert critics are accustomed to do, with far greater right, that the same Tertullian was in fact the father of all three books?

Hoornbeek further insists that their subject matter and argument are the same. But what follows from that? Could the same Christian author not compose two different works on the same subject—especially in defense of the Christian religion, which was persecuted by the pagans with as much injustice as savagery—or, by revising what he had written, rework, correct, enlarge, or abridge it? [Col. 0767C] Certainly the man who raises this objection against us will never deny it. For he himself, like everyone else, openly admits that Tertullian is the true author of the book *To Scapula*. Yet in that book the argument is the same as in the *Apologeticum* and the two books *To the Nations*—namely, the cause of the Christians, who were most unjustly persecuted—though it is treated more briefly. Moreover, the books *To the Nations* were addressed to persons other than those addressed by the *Apologeticum* and the book *To Scapula*. What of the fact that we shall demonstrate a little later that many more matters are treated in the *Apologeticum* than in the books *To the Nations*, and conversely? Finally, we shall show that Tertullian was compelled by cogent reasons to write these books after the *Apologeticum*.

Hoornbeek nevertheless presses the point that the author of the first book *To the Nations* said that two hundred years had not yet elapsed since the birth of Christ, [Col. 0767D] whereas in the book *On Monogamy* he says approximately one hundred and sixty (Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, chap. 3). But he strives in vain to confirm very slight arguments by another far slighter one. For even if it were established that no scribal error underlies the copying of the numerals, and if it were certain that the beginning of those years was reckoned from Christ himself, it still could not be concluded from this that the books *To the Nations* must be denied to Tertullian. For in the first of these very books we read: “Our era is not yet 250 years old” (the same, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7). And not much later: “As we stated above, our era is not yet three hundred years old” (ibid., chap. 9). Would you therefore say that this book was not published by one and the same author? What [Col. 0768A] sane person ever argued in that way? Who does not see that the same writer, who was not acting as a chronographer, could in fact say both that two hundred years had not yet elapsed since Christ, and elsewhere that approximately 160 years had elapsed? But we would certainly be ashamed and weary of refuting so vain and singular an opinion, were it not that some later writers seem to have subscribed to this new author whom they extol with great praises.

## ARTICLE IV

### At What Time These Books Appeared in Public

The precise time at which Tertullian devoted himself to composing these books *To the Nations* is neither readily nor easily stated. Certain chronological marks and indications nevertheless present themselves in them. For in the first [Col. 0768B] book we read of a sentence passed shortly before by Fuscianus, prefect of the City, against a certain father who had exposed his newborn son and, after some time had elapsed, bought and violated him without any longer recognizing him (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 16). Now Capitolinus mentions Fuscianus, prefect of the City, whom Pertinax immediately succeeded (Capitolinus, *Life of Pertinax*, shortly after the beginning). Pertinax was made emperor at the beginning of the year 193 and was killed after approximately three months. Tertullian must therefore be said to have published these books not long after the death of Pertinax.

Nor should you object that in the same book he wrote: “Our era is not yet 250 years old,” that is, from the rise of the Christian religion (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7). For afterward he also wrote: “As we stated above, [Col. 0768C] our era is not yet three hundred years old” (ibid., chap. 5). Nothing at all certain or established can therefore be concluded from this. He doubtless preferred to assign the larger number of years so as to afford the pagans no occasion for caviling. Moreover, what certainty can be gathered from those two so disparate numbers, “not yet 250 years” and “300”? If, however, you wish to infer anything from them, you must first determine to what year Tertullian assigned the beginning of the Christian era.

Some therefore think that the date of these books can be recognized with greater certainty from other words of his, in which he addresses the pagans thus: “From among you nations there daily arise Caesars, and men styled Parthicus, Medicus, and Germanicus” (ibid., chap. 17). But these words, they say, refer to Caracalla, [Col. 0768D] who, after defeating the Germans and Parthians, was distinguished with the surname Germanicus and Parthicus in the year 216. This would not be a bad argument if these honorific surnames had been given to Caracalla alone.

The following words of our author therefore indicate the date of these books more clearly: “Syria still breathes with the odors of corpses; the Gauls still wash themselves in their Rhône” (ibid.). For Pescennius Niger and Clodius Albinus are undoubtedly designated there: after they had revolted from the emperor Severus, the former was routed and slain with his forces in Syria, the latter in Gaul. These events, which are mentioned in Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* as well, occurred in the year 194 or 195, or rather in 197, as we explained more fully above [Col. 0769A] (above, chap. 3, art. 2). Tertullian must therefore be said to have published these books *To the Nations*, as also the *Apologeticum*, shortly after that year.

Some, however, infer from his following words—“The character of the times demanded the harder temperaments of the vigor . . . of antiquity; but now the tranquility of peace produces gentler temperaments” (ibid., chap. 18)—that this statement was made by him when the Christians, at the beginning of Severus’s reign, enjoyed the desired tranquility of peace and leisure. But Severus stirred up persecution against them by edicts issued in the year 202. Therefore, they say, Tertullian had composed these books before that date.

It must, however, be observed that with these words he introduced the pagans as wrongly objecting that the temperaments of their ancestors had been harder, since they were better prepared than the people of his own age to endure patiently even the most bitter [Col. 0769B] tortures, whereas the tranquility of peace and leisure had made the latter’s temperaments gentler. If, however, you maintain and prove that these very words of our author must be understood of the true peace of the Christian Church, we shall readily agree with you. Nevertheless, no one will deny that it can be inferred more securely from what has been said above that these books *To the Nations* and the *Apologeticum* appeared in public not long after the year 197. Which of them, however, appeared first is another controversy among the learned, which we must now examine.

## ARTICLE V

### Whether These Two Books *To the Nations* Were Written Before or After Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*

[Col. 0769C] Those who think that the two books *To the Nations* were written after the *Apologeticum* attempt to establish their opinion by three arguments. First, they suppose that the *Apologeticum* was published around the year 200 and at the beginning of the persecution stirred up by the emperor Severus against the Christians, whereas the books *To the Nations* were published when Caracalla’s reign was already advanced and after that emperor had received the titles Parthicus and Germanicus. But we have already shown that the foundation of this latter assertion concerning Caracalla is thoroughly unstable.

Their second argument is that the defense of the Christians, which comprises the whole subject both of the *Apologeticum* and of the books *To the Nations*, is treated more fully in the latter than in the former. But we shall demonstrate later how little resemblance to truth this conjecture bears.

[Col. 0769D] They derive their third argument from words and sentences that occur in other books which Tertullian published after his defection to the Montanists—as though other expressions similar to these were not also found in his other books, and especially in the *Apologeticum*, where they admit that far more expressions identical to those in the books *To the Nations* occur.

As weak as these arguments are, so compelling do other considerations appear to us, which can be drawn from the books *To the Nations* themselves. For in them Tertullian promises more than once that he will explain many things elsewhere. Yet, lest some complain that anything doubtful and uncertain is being advanced, we shall not press the words that Tertullian added immediately after proving that Christians were persecuted solely on account of their name: “But while this reasoning is demonstrated in its proper place, [Col. 0770A] set forth the rationale by which you proceed in attacking the name” (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 3). For there he does not expressly promise that the matter will be treated by him later, but appears to us to signify that he has sufficiently explained the matter itself.

Yet in clearer words he certainly pledges that elsewhere he will institute a longer discussion of the future resurrection of bodies and of the eternal rewards or punishments of human beings after death. For he speaks in this manner: “We shall consider the credibility of these matters when they are arranged in their proper place” (ibid., chap. 7), that is, when they are disposed and prepared to be committed to writing. But where did he arrange and set this forth against the follies of the pagans? Certainly not in these books *To the Nations*, but toward the end of his *Apologeticum*, which one might say with good reason [Col. 0770B] he had in mind rather than any other book (the same, *Apologeticum*, chaps. 48 and 49).

Then, when he refutes other slanders of the pagans, who loudly declared that Christians were the cause of every public disaster, he says: “Later they will be blunted by an exposition of our entire discipline” (the same, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 10). Tell me, I ask, where did he expound this Christian doctrine in order to dispel these accusations of the gentiles? Certainly not in these books *To the Nations*, but in several chapters of the *Apologeticum*, as is evident even from the analysis of that book which we gave above (the same, *Apologeticum*, chap. 17, 18, and following).

Furthermore, he promises that he will at some point prove false the teachings concerning God not only of the pagan poets but also of those who profess the art of divination: “For the outline [Col. 0770C] of this kind,” he says, “must now be touched upon; its rationale will be given in its proper place” (the same, *To the Nations*, book II, chap. 5). In what book, then, did he give that rationale by which the pagans’ foolish accusations might be refuted? Was it not in the *Apologeticum*, where we read it explained at length (the same, *Apologeticum*, chaps. 21 and 22)?

Why say more? When he again checks the audacity of the gentiles, who most shamelessly charged the Christians with infanticide, he addresses them in these words: “If you have forgotten what you have accomplished through the slaughter of human beings and through infanticides, you will review it in its proper order. For now we defer many matters, lest we appear to treat the same things repeatedly everywhere” (*To the Nations*, book II, chap. 15). You plainly see two things expressly stated there by our author. First, that he himself would demonstrate more fully that the gentiles [Col. 0770D] were guilty of homicide and infanticide. Yet nowhere does he demonstrate this more fully than in the *Apologeticum*.
