Second, he openly declares that he had deferred many matters to be more fully elucidated by him elsewhere, lest he repeat and treat them again in other books. But where, I ask, did he discuss these matters against the gentiles more abundantly than in the *Apologeticum*?

Who, therefore, after accurately weighing all that we have reported, will not acknowledge that Tertullian, while writing these books *To the Nations*, referred us to his *Apologeticum*, which he was then contemplating composing (above, chap. 3, art. 1)? The books *To the Nations*, therefore, were published by him before the *Apologeticum*. But from the date we have assigned to the latter, it may be inferred clearly enough that, in order to fulfill his pledge to write the *Apologeticum*, he did not allow [Col. 0771A] a long interval of time to intervene, nor could he endure any delay before pleading the cause of the Christians before their governors, judges, and magistrates, just as he had done before all nations, and making their innocence clear to everyone. If, therefore, the *Apologeticum* was sent forth into public around the year of Christ 200, as we have said, these two books *To the Nations* had been published shortly before (ibid.).

## ARTICLE VI

### On the Subject of These Books, and Whether It Is Treated More Fully and Perfectly in Them Than in the *Apologeticum*

In the preceding article we cited several words of Tertullian in which he attests that he had omitted several matters from these books *To the Nations* which he had resolved to explain more fully in the *Apologeticum*. [Col. 0771B] But these words plainly contradict the opinion of those who contend that the subject of these treatises is handled more abundantly, more perfectly, and in a better order in the books *To the Nations* than in the *Apologeticum*. For by some reasoning unknown to me, they had persuaded themselves that the author’s keen, vehement, and acute genius, and his fiery acumen, flashes everywhere throughout these books, but that, swept along by its violent impetus, he wrote many things that were not sufficiently considered, polished, or refined. Yet this opinion plainly collapses if, as we have seen, the *Apologeticum* proceeded from him after the books *To the Nations*.

Furthermore, it is established that several matters of truly great importance are discussed in the *Apologeticum* which are omitted from the books *To the Nations*, although certain things are conversely found in these books [Col. 0771C] and not at all in the former. In order that these matters may become plainer and more evident to everyone, we have thought it proper to present an index of the chapters in which the same matters are treated. From this each person will readily judge in what respects these books differ from one another.

## INDEX OF CHAPTERS

### In Which the *Apologeticum* and the Books *To the Nations* Agree with One Another

| Book I *To the Nations* | *Apologeticum* |
|---|---|
| Chapter 1 | Chapter 1 |
| Chapter 2 | Chapter 2 |
| Chapter 3 | Chapters 2 and 3 |
| Chapter 4 | Chapters 3 and 46 |
| Chapter 6 | Chapter 4 |
| [Col. 0771D] Chapter 7 | Chapters 7 and 8 |
| Chapter 8 | Chapter 8, not the whole of it |
| Chapter 9 | Chapters 40 and 41 |
| Chapter 10 | Chapters 12, 13, 14, and 15 |
| Chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14 | Chapter 16 |
| Chapters 14, 15, and 16 | Chapter 9 |
| Chapter 17 | Chapter 35 |
| Chapter 18 | Chapter 50 |
| Chapter 19 | Chapters 47, 48, and 49 |

| Book II *To the Nations* | *Apologeticum* |
|---|---|
| Chapter 12 | Chapter 10 |
| Chapter 17 | Chapter 25 |

You see clearly from this index that the first book *To the Nations* agrees with the *Apologeticum*, [Col. 0772A] excepting its fifth chapter, in which an argument drawn by the pagans from certain evil Christians is refuted, and the final chapter, which is the conclusion of the whole book. The second book *To the Nations*, however, is divided into seventeen chapters, fifteen of which have nothing in common with the *Apologeticum*. In the first eight of these fifteen chapters, Tertullian attacks Varro’s fictitious threefold class of gods—physical, mythical, and plebeian—while in the latter seven he assails and overthrows the gods promoted by the Romans.

Of the fifty chapters of the *Apologeticum*, indeed, not even half agree with the two books *To the Nations*. It differs from them in the remaining chapters, in which Tertullian explains and asserts how true the teachings of the Christians are, [Col. 0772B] how chaste and incorrupt their morals, how pious and holy their solemn assemblies, and how religious their gatherings. But there is nothing about these things in the books *To the Nations*. In a word, these books demonstrate the innocence of the Christians, which was most unjustly assailed, and the injustice, depravity, corruption, and perversity of the pagans’ religion—and nothing more. In the *Apologeticum*, however, all these things are treated, and in addition the holiness and truth of the Christian religion. Who, therefore, can deny from this comparison of the books that their subject is explained and demonstrated far more fully and perfectly in the *Apologeticum* than in the books *To the Nations*?

## ARTICLE VII

### On the Title of the Books *To the Nations*; Why They Were Written by Tertullian and to Whom They Were Addressed; on Their Sole Manuscript, Their Various Editions, and the Notes and Observations of Certain Scholars upon Them

[Col. 0772C]

We observed that these books are entitled *To the Nations* in the Agobard manuscript (above, this chap., art. 3), but are cited by Jerome under the name of books *To the Gentiles*, although the two titles have the same meaning. Nevertheless, because those to whom these books are addressed are called by Tertullian himself “nations,” “wretched nations,” or “nations to be pitied,” the inscription prefixed in the Agobard manuscript certainly appears preferable (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 1, and book II, chap. 1).

Some, however, think it possible to infer from this title that these books were addressed to the common people and populace of the pagans, while the *Apologeticum* was addressed to their magistrates, [Col. 0772D] judges, and rulers. As regards the *Apologeticum*, indeed, this is certain and beyond controversy. Yet what prevents the two books *To the Nations* from having been written to absolutely all pagans, both peoples and judges and governors? Does Tertullian not assail in them not only the gentile populace but also the judges who, contrary to the prescribed form of equity and all laws, condemned Christians undefended and unheard? May it not therefore be said that Tertullian, when he beheld this injustice and extreme cruelty of the pagans, first addressed these books *To the Nations*—that is, to gentiles of every kind—in order to recall them, if possible, to a sounder mind? But because he had accomplished nothing, or certainly very little, he then sent his *Apologeticum* specifically to the [Col. 0773A] judges and governors, in order to compel them to examine the Christians’ cause and not to condemn the innocent without hearing it. Let impartial judges of these matters weigh and pronounce how much force these arguments possess.

As numerous and common as manuscripts of the *Apologeticum* are, so rare are manuscripts of these books *To the Nations* (above, chap. 2, art. 1). For only one survives for us, which Agobard, as they say and as we have already noted, archbishop of Lyons, had offered at the altar of Saint Stephen. But that manuscript has been so damaged in most of its margins by mold, filth, or rainwater that the final letters of its lines can no longer be read. Accordingly, in passages that are frequently corrupt, unless a more accurate manuscript is discovered, [Col. 0773B] a healing hand cannot be applied, nor can the author’s meaning be fully perceived.

In that ancient manuscript, moreover, the entire work was written in a single continuous text and without any division into chapters. James Gothofredus, however, divided it into various chapters and added chapter descriptions and summaries. Rigaltius omitted these, retaining only the chapter division, indicated in the margin merely by his own numerals. Everyone is therefore free to alter this division of the chapters and their descriptions, if he judges it appropriate.

Gothofredus was the first of all to arrange for these books to be printed separately in 1625, in precisely the form in which they are transcribed in the aforementioned codex of Agobard. Later, Rigaltius published them together with Tertullian’s other works, asserting that he had corrected them seventy-eight times. [Col. 0773C] He would certainly have done us a service, however, had he deigned to say whence he obtained all these corrections. For he did not derive them from the sole codex of Agobard, which Rigaltius appears never to have read, though Gothofredus printed it with the utmost fidelity. To omit numerous examples, within the words *suo amatori apud vos* he left a blank space, just as Gothofredus had, as though something were missing (Tertull. lib. II. *ad Nat.*, cap. 10). Yet nothing is missing in the manuscript codex, and everything is sound and complete. He therefore did not examine this codex, but only Gothofredus’s edition of it. Accordingly, from Gothofredus’s conjectures, which the latter had deliberately appended in his notes, Rigaltius drew what he calls his emendations; and these, together with many others devised by himself—sometimes well, but more often badly—he boldly thrust into the text of these books [Col. 0773D] as though they were his own. It would certainly take too long to present them all here; one of our own scholars seriously intends to reproduce them in a new edition of Tertullian’s works. We shall nevertheless note below, in more appropriate places, several of the more important ones. Finally, concerning the latest edition of these books, prepared by Priorius, we have nothing further to say, since he followed the Rigaltian edition step for step (*κατὰ πόδας*).

Moreover, those whom we have mentioned as editors of the books *To the Nations* wrote notes and observations upon them. Gothofredus published more than the others; in these he attempts to explain scribal errors and Tertullian’s words, even when they are sometimes not particularly obscure, or to confirm them by similar statements of Tertullian himself and of other authors. [Col. 0774A] Fewer notes were written by Rigaltius, in his own customary manner, about which we have said enough above. Priorius had these reprinted and added to them one note taken from Pamelius and others of his own devising. Learned men have more than once declared how much weight they carry.

## CHAPTER V. On Tertullian’s Book *To Scapula*

### ARTICLE I. Analysis of This Book

Tertullian addressed this book—or rather, this petition—to Scapula, proconsul of Africa, in order, if it were at all possible, to deter him from torturing and mangling Christians in defiance of every law, human and divine (Tertull. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 1). First, [Col. 0774B] however, he declares that he wrote this petition not because he feared for the Christians, who endured punishments willingly and cheerfully, but because he feared for their pagan enemies, whom, on this ground alone, those same Christians were bound to love and for whom they were bound to pray to God. He therefore considered it his duty to make clear to everyone that Christians were wholly innocent and that the pagans themselves were in reality guilty of precisely the class of crimes for which they falsely reproached the Christians.

For Christians do not worship fictitious gods, as the pagans do, but the one true God, whom all people know naturally and revere. Christians, therefore, ought not to be compelled to worship another, since it is no part of religion to compel religion. Nor can any of those who are represented as gods desire sacrifices [Col. 0774C] from the unwilling. Christians, therefore, are accused wholly without justification of impiety, sacrilege, theft, or sedition because they refuse to worship the gods. The pagans, by contrast, strip the temples of their own gods with impunity and treat those gods with contempt and ridicule.

What, moreover, of the fact that, during the seditions of Albinus, Niger, and Cassius, pagans alone were found who at that very time swore by the emperors’ guardian spirits, immolated victims for their safety, and offered sacrifices? Christians, however, are enemies of absolutely no one, much less of the emperor, whom they know to have been appointed by God, and whom they therefore sincerely honor and wish to remain safe and unharmed together with the entire Roman Empire. Nevertheless, they do not revere him in the pagan manner as a god, but because he is greater than all false gods and inferior only to the true God, [Col. 0774D] whom they therefore entreat for his safety with a daily sacrifice of prayer. Furthermore, although the multitude of those same Christians is exceedingly great, individuals are nonetheless scarcely recognized except by their modesty, silence, and correction of their former vices (cap. 2).

Tertullian says that Christians do not endure the punishments inflicted upon them by the pagans with a restless or impatient spirit, for they await vengeance from God. They do, however, grieve that signs of that vengeance, now imminent, have already been sent beforehand: namely, the harvests lost recently under the governorship of Hilarianus, excessive and untimely rains, nocturnal fires hanging over the walls of Carthage, unusual thunder, and an altogether extraordinary eclipse of the sun. Vigellius Saturninus, who was the first to order Christians [Col. 0775A] to be killed in Africa, was deprived of his eyesight. In Cappadocia, too, Claudianus Herminianus died of plague, with worms erupting from him, although through an all-too-late repentance he had almost become a Christian. Finally, when Caecilius Capella, during the Byzantine departure or destruction, had cried out in mockery of the Christians, “Rejoice,” he paid the penalty for his shameless cruelty. If any governors of this kind escaped punishment, they will be punished at God’s final judgment. Scapula, therefore, our author says, had reason to fear, because shortly before that Byzantine destruction he had condemned Mavillus of Hadrumetum to the beasts (cap. 3).

He nevertheless earnestly warns Scapula that he recalls these things not because he himself fears anything, nor in order to terrify Scapula, but because he desires everyone [Col. 0775B] to be saved. He consequently exhorts him to comply with the laws, which direct that no accused person be punished unless he has confessed his crimes or has been convicted of them. He then sets before him the examples of Cincius Severus, Vespronius Candidus, Asper, and Pudens, who had refused to condemn innocent Christians. Scapula’s advocates, upon whom Christians had certainly conferred benefits of no small importance, could suggest to him how he might imitate these men. For Christians had not only expelled demons from the advocates’ clerk and from another of their relatives, but had also miraculously healed others afflicted by diseases.

Indeed, when the emperor Severus, father of Antoninus, who had been brought up on Christian milk, had once been similarly healed by oil given to him by Proculus Torpacion, a Christian and procurator of Euhodia, he not only retained him in his palace until the day of his death, [Col. 0775C] but also never harmed the most distinguished women and men who were likewise followers of the Christian religion, and resisted the populace when it openly raged against Christians. Marcus Aurelius, too, during his German expedition, obtained by the prayers of Christians rain that was absolutely necessary for his army; and Christians had obtained it for others in a similar circumstance.

What, then, could be more unjust than to order that Christians, who devote diligent attention to every virtue, should not merely be struck down by the sword, as they were by the governors of the legion and of Mauretania under the prescription of the ancient laws, but should even be burned alive? Tertullian, however, openly declares that Christians desire these punishments more than they fear them. For when Arrius Antoninus was raging more cruelly against them, and all the Christians in a city of Asia voluntarily presented themselves to him, [Col. 0775D] he replied: “If you wish to perish, you have cliffs or ropes.” What, then, will Scapula do with the almost innumerable Christians of Carthage? What will he do with members of his own rank, or with relatives and friends who will voluntarily offer themselves to him to be killed? Tertullian therefore exhorts him to spare Carthage and the province, which he has made subject to extortions by soldiers and by each person’s enemies. For God alone is the Christians’ master; he existed before Scapula and cannot suffer any harm from human beings. Scapula’s masters, by contrast, are human beings who will one day die. Finally, whatever he may do, the Christian sect will not fail, for it grows even when it appears to be cut down. Whoever investigates and learns why Christians so steadfastly [Col. 0776A] endure every kind of torture then comes to know the truth and embraces their religion (cap. 4).

### ARTICLE II. It Is Shown That Tertullian Is the Author of This Book; the Reasons That Impelled Him to Publish It After the *Apologeticum* and the Books *To the Nations*; When He Wrote It; and Certain Pagan Proconsuls and Prefects Who Treated the Christians Either More Cruelly or More Leniently

Everyone acknowledges, with a truly great and unanimous consensus, that Tertullian is the genuine author of this book. Indeed, who would dare deny what the book itself, in its entirety, openly attests? For it contains the same style of expression as the *Apologeticum* and the books *To the Nations*, [Col. 0776B] the same distinctive forms of speech peculiar to Tertullian, the same unusual words, and generally the same arguments in defense of Christians against the pagans. Just as the *Apologeticum* and the books *To the Nations* were sent either to all pagans or to their governors, so it is entirely clear that this book was addressed to Scapula, prefect of Carthage and of all Africa, whom Tertullian attempted to dissuade from torturing and slaughtering wholly innocent Christians.

But someone may ask what need Tertullian had to write, besides the *Apologeticum* and the books *To the Nations*, another treatise or book against the pagans and on behalf of Christians. We answer that the monstrous cruelty of Scapula, governor of Africa, against Christians compelled him to present not exactly a book, but a petition. [Col. 0776C] For although Severus, who became emperor in the year of Christ 193, greatly favored Christians during the first years of his reign, nevertheless, after Cassius, Niger, and Albinus had been defeated and after his solemn entry into the city of Rome in 197, his attitude completely changed. For then, with his initial approval, or at least without his prohibition, the terrible persecution of Christians began to revive. Subsequently becoming still more hostile, he enacted new laws against them in 202; by the authority of these laws, Eusebius says, martyrdoms occurred everywhere throughout the Churches. Accordingly, the surge of this most cruel persecution ravaged Africa no less than the other provinces (Euseb. lib. VI. *eccles. Hist.* cap. 2. pag. 201. Hieronym. *Catalog. scriptor. eccl.* § 54. pag. 115).

[Col. 0776D] Tertullian, ever concerned for the safety of Christians, had published the *Apologeticum* and the books *To the Nations* before these laws were issued, as we have said; and the pagans’ fury against the Christians, however fiercely kindled, should undoubtedly have been calmed by reading them (Euseb. ibid. cap. I. pag. 201). But absolutely no weight of reasoning, even if clearer than the noonday sun, could extinguish that fury or prevent Christians in Africa from being mangled under the utterly unjust laws enacted by Severus. Tertullian therefore further presented this petition to Scapula, proconsul of that province, so that by both the very great weight of his arguments and the notable domestic examples of other governors and even emperors, [Col. 0777A] he might dissuade him from harassing and torturing Christians.

This book, moreover, supplies us with several arguments by which it is quite clearly established that it was written after the emperor Severus’s persecution of Christians had begun. For it presents examples of certain governors who, having at that time subjected Christians to various punishments, had already paid the penalty for their cruelty. Tertullian begins with Hilarianus as follows: “Under the governorship of Hilarianus, when they had shouted concerning the grounds of our burial places, ‘There must be no burial grounds,’ their own threshing floors ceased to exist; for they did not gather their harvests” (Tertul. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 3). Here, by a by no means wholly inept antithesis, he contrasts an *area*, meaning an empty place or barren field in which the dead were buried, [Col. 0777B] with an *area*, or threshing floor, on which crops are threshed and beaten out. Thus he said that at the very time when the pagans were raging more fiercely against Christians and shouting that grounds for burying them must be denied, those same pagans lacked harvests and grain to thresh upon their own threshing floors. He openly asserts that this barrenness occurred while Hilarianus was governor of Africa. Now from the Acts of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicitas—which were published as true and genuine by several editors and, finally, by the Bollandist associates and by our Theodoric Ruinart—we learn that these most holy martyrs were exposed to the beasts by order of the procurator Hilarianus, “who at that time,” as we read there, “had received the power of the sword in place of the deceased proconsul Minutius Firmianus” (Bolland. 7. *Martyr.* pag. 633 et seqq. Ruinart. *Act. Martyr.* cap. [Col. 0777C] 85 et seqq.). Some think that they received the crown of martyrdom in 202; others in 203; and others in 205, undoubtedly after the persecution had been stirred up by the emperor Severus. Tertullian himself, moreover, recorded the following concerning Perpetua in another book: “Perpetua, that most courageous martyr, in a revelation on the day of her passion saw there in paradise only her fellow martyrs” (Tert. lib. *de Anim.* cap. 55). We also learn from Augustine, who frequently mentions her and Felicitas, that the feast day of them both was celebrated annually in Africa. Is it not sufficiently and clearly established from this that they won the palm of martyrdom in Africa while Hilarianus was discharging the office of proconsul (Augustin. serm. 280 et seqq. pag. 1134 et seqq.)?

Tertullian subsequently says: “Vigellius Saturninus, [Col. 0777D] who was the first here to wield the sword against us, lost his eyesight” (Tertull. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 3). He is thought to have been the proconsul of Africa who, in the year 200—or, as others prefer, 205—condemned Speratus and the other Scillitan martyrs at Carthage to be beheaded. For we read this recorded in the acts of their martyrdom, which were first published by Baronius as true and authentic and were subsequently enlarged and corrected by our Ruinart (Bar. ad ann. Christ. 202, § 2 et seqq. Ruinart. *Act. Mart.* p. 77 et seqq.). When Tertullian added that Saturninus was the first in Africa to wield the sword against Christians, it must undoubtedly be understood to mean after the persecution had been stirred up by the emperor Severus. For it seems entirely beyond dispute [Col. 0778A] that several had previously been put to death. Tertullian’s meaning, therefore, is that Christians were tortured by Saturninus before they were tortured by Hilarianus, and consequently that, when listing here the prefects of Africa who were the Christians’ executioners, he does not follow chronological order.

Less certain, therefore, seems the opinion of those who have supposed that Cincius Severus, Vespronius Candidus, Asper, and Pudens are named there by our Tertullian after Hilarianus and Saturninus in the same order in which each man was proconsul of Africa (Tertullian. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 4). For he mentions them because they treated the Christians with as much leniency as the others treated them with cruelty. Why, then, should he be said to have observed chronological order in naming the former rather than the latter? Moreover, there is room to doubt whether these men [Col. 0778B] were governors of Africa, for after Hilarianus and Saturninus, those most dreadful torturers of Christians, he added Claudius Herminianus, prefect of Cappadocia. If anyone should nevertheless prove that our author presents the true sequence of their African proconsulates, we shall readily assent to him.

In any case, he placed these examples of more merciful governors before Scapula’s eyes for no other reason than that, after the laws against Christians had been enacted by the emperor Severus, the governors of Africa were raging and reveling against them with greater bitterness (Ibid. cap. 3). For besides the aforementioned Saturninus and Hilarianus, Scapula himself, as our author testifies in the same passage, had not only condemned Mavillus of Hadrumetum to the beasts; but Christian Africa, because Scapula either did not restrain it or gave the order, had also, he says, [Col. 0778C] been made subject to extortions by soldiers and by each person’s enemies (Ibid. cap. 4). Although we cannot determine in what year the aforementioned proconsuls governed Africa, it can nevertheless be gathered from the preceding discussion that this book *To Scapula* was published by Tertullian after the emperor Severus’s persecution of Christians had begun.

It therefore remains to inquire whether it was published immediately after the fire of that persecution had been kindled or after it had been extinguished. Some think that it appeared publicly after the year 210 and the death of the emperor Severus. For Tertullian, they say, speaks there of a certain eclipse of the sun in this manner: [Col. 0778D] “At the assembly in Utica, the sun, with its light almost extinguished, was so portentous that it could not have suffered this from an ordinary eclipse, being situated in its own *hypsoma* and domicile” (Ibid. cap. 3). This eclipse, they say, occurred in the year of Christ 210, on the eleventh day of April, at the very hour of noon. Others, however, consider the entire foundation of this opinion altogether unstable. For those authors identify an ordinary eclipse of the sun, whereas Tertullian identifies one that was entirely extraordinary and that, as he says, had been a portent. For at that time the sun, he says, was in its own *hypsoma*, that is, at its summit, height, and highest point. This is what the Greek word *ὕψωμα* (*hypsōma*) means. No eclipse can occur while the sun is situated there; it suffers one only when it passes near the nodes that occur at the dragon’s head and tail. [Col. 0779A] Although our Tertullian may have been wholly unacquainted with the science of astrology, it can nevertheless be gathered from his words that this eclipse of the sun was not an ordinary one, but so extraordinary that the astrologers, to whom he refers us, could not deny it.

Scaliger therefore sets that argument aside and thinks this book was composed after the death of Caracalla, when Elagabalus was already reigning, having been made emperor in May of the year 218. For Tertullian speaks of Severus, as we have seen, in these words: “He kept the Christian Proculus . . . . . . in his palace until his death; Antoninus Caracalla knew him very well” (Tertull. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 4). But no sane person, Scaliger says, would think that this was said while Antoninus Caracalla was still alive (Scalig. [Col. 0779B] *animadv. in Chron. Euseb.* pag. 129).

Those whose minds are sound and unimpaired, however, do not recognize soundness in Scaliger’s reasoning here. For what prevents the young and adolescent Caracalla from having known Proculus and from still being alive when Tertullian committed these things to writing? Moreover, Tertullian employs the verb “had known” because Proculus, and not Caracalla, was then actually dead. No further hearing, therefore, should be given to those who, relying upon this invalid argument of Scaliger, yet departing slightly from his opinion, suspect that this book was published in the year 217, when Macrinus reigned. For once the foundation of this opinion has been overturned, the opinion itself also collapses.

Those who date this [Col. 0779C] book shortly after the year 211, when Severus is said to have laid down both his life and his imperial power at York in England in the month of February, therefore appear to come closer to the truth. For Tertullian undoubtedly speaks of him in this book when he says: “Severus himself also, the father of Antoninus Caracalla, was mindful of the Christians” (Tert. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 4). Why, they ask, is he called the father of Antoninus unless he had already departed this life and his sons Caracalla and Geta had succeeded in his place? Does not our author subsequently allude to them as already reigning when he asserts that Scapula had masters in his cruelty against the Christians? After Severus’s death, or certainly not long thereafter, when Tertullian saw that the fury of Scapula and others against Christians had abated, he appears to have presented this petition to him. [Col. 0779D] For he did not consider that it should be presented while Severus—whose extreme clemency toward Christians during the first years of his reign he had praised, as we have seen—was raging atrociously against them until his death. But once Severus had died, it is more probable that Tertullian immediately seized the opportunity offered to him to deter the proconsul Scapula from persecuting Christians.

### ARTICLE III. On the Manuscript and Printed Copies of This Book, the Observations of Various Scholars upon It, and Certain Variant Readings and Notes

Several codices of this little book are mentioned. The first is the Gorze codex, which Rhenanus used for his edition of it. Another is called the Angelicus, and three Vatican codices [Col. 0780A] are also mentioned. Gelenius revised and corrected earlier editions of this little book according to the authority of the former, and Pamelius according to that of the latter. Rigaltius further testifies that he had seen another in the possession of Pierre Belin, S.C. of Dijon, whose readings differing from those of the printed editions had come into the hands of Pierre Pithou.

This book is said never to have emerged alone from the printers’ workshops into public view, but always together with Tertullian’s other works. There have therefore been as many editions of this book as of those works. Since we have already discussed these editions at some length, there is no need to repeat that discussion now. Rigaltius followed Pamelius everywhere; Pamelius, as he says, corrected the old editions from three Vatican codices. For although Rigaltius lays claim to the Dijon codex, he noted only [Col. 0780B] a single variant reading from it, which he entirely rejected. It occurs where in all editions we read these words of Tertullian concerning Proculus: “Whom Antoninus Caracalla also knew very well, having been brought up on Christian milk” (Tertull. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 4). The Dijon codex, however, reads: “whom Antoninus knew to have been brought up among Christians.” This signifies that Proculus, rather than Antoninus Caracalla, had been brought up on Christian milk.

Rigaltius rejects this reading of the Dijon codex, however, because those words of Tertullian must refer to Antoninus. Spartianus relates that when Antoninus, as a seven-year-old boy, heard that a boy who was his playmate had been severely beaten on account of the Jewish religion, he for a long time refused to look upon either his own father, the boy’s father, or those responsible for the beating (Spart. [Col. 0780C] *in Vit. Carac.* pag. 331. col. 1). By the term “Jewish religion,” however, Spartianus means the Christian religion, since pagans confused the two. We may add, if one pleases, that Proculus had been called a Christian by Tertullian himself shortly before. There was therefore no need to repeat this with the words “brought up among Christians,” which appear sufficiently corrupt in the Dijon codex.

Furthermore, at the beginning of this book, in Pamelius’s and subsequent editions, we read: “We, indeed, are not frightened . . . . . since we have come to this sect after accepting the condition of its compact, so that, having pledged even our lives, we enter into these contests” (Tertull. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 1). But the earliest editions had read: [Col. 0780D] “We, indeed, are not frightened . . . since we come to this sect, having accepted its condition, having previously made a compact with our life and pledged ourselves, into these contests.” Laurentius de la Barre alone testifies that he corrected these words from the Gorze codex. But he should have transcribed the words of the old editions in full in his notes, so that everyone might more easily recognize whether they had been correctly amended, for they do not appear to be altogether devoid of meaning. In any event, Tertullian there uses the verb *auctorari*, as he does elsewhere: “Some,” he says, “have pledged themselves to the flames” (Tertull. lib. *ad Martyr.* cap. 5. p. 158). The verb *auctorare* means to bind oneself either for pay or by an oath. In the first words of Tertullian, this verb is taken in the latter sense; in the second, in the former sense. If, however, you require this to be proved to you by the testimony of certain authors, first [Col. 0781A] hear Cicero: “The very wage,” he says, “is the bond of servitude” (Cicer. lib. II. *de offic.* p. 274. lin. 4). Suetonius, moreover, relates that Tiberius Caesar gave a gladiatorial show “for an enlistment bounty of one hundred thousand” (Sueton. lib. III. § 7). Seneca also said: “I gave him over to the ghosts and ordered him to be placed among the newly enlisted gladiators” (Senec. *lud. de morte Claud.* p. 919). Soldiers bound by the military oath are frequently called *auctorati*, and those discharged from it *exauctorati*, by Livy and other authors. We shall note below the other variant readings of this book as occasion presents itself.

The same men who wrote notes and observations on the *Apologeticum* wrote upon this book as well, and in the same manner. The same judgment, therefore, that we expressed above must be passed upon all of them. Nothing further need be added, [Col. 0781B] except that, in connection with these words of Tertullian *To Scapula*: “When you had condemned Mavillus of Hadrumetum to the beasts, this affliction immediately followed” (Tertull. lib. *ad Scapul.* cap. 3), Rigaltius thinks that an attack of some extremely painful illness is denoted, with which Scapula himself was again afflicted on account of his repeated cruelty against Christians, as Rigaltius says. For Tertullian immediately added: “And now, from the same cause, there is an appeal of blood”; that is, as Rigaltius likewise believes, the blood of the Christians had cried out to God and interrupted the delays of his divine patience. But our author did not say a single word—not even the least—about a first or second illness of Scapula. Indeed, if he had once and then again suffered from an extremely painful illness, as Rigaltius would have it, Tertullian would have pressed him much more forcefully on that basis, [Col. 0781C] so that he might more easily be restored to a sounder mind. But passing this over, he insists and presses him with the examples of other governors and proconsuls who had paid the penalty for their cruelty against Christians. We shall therefore be more readily persuaded that those words of Tertullian must be referred to the destruction of Byzantium, which he mentions in the same passage, through which the pagans openly confessed that they had been punished by God for their most unjust cruelty against those same Christians.

Rigaltius seems to have departed less from the truth where, in Tertullian’s words “Proculus, procurator of Euhodia” (Ibid.), he approves Pithou’s emendation, who suspected that *Evodi* should be read. But these observations, whether those of Rigaltius or of others, must be discussed more fully below.

## CHAPTER VI. New Observations on Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, the Two Books *To the Nations*, and the Single Book *To Scapula*, in Which It Is First Shown That the Christian Religion Is Supported by the Sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament; How These Scriptures Came to the Christians, the Successors of the Jews; and How Great Their Authority Is

[Col. 0781D]

### ARTICLE I. How Tertullian Shows That the Christian Religion, Introduced into the World During the Reign of Tiberius, Is Supported by the Sacred Scriptures of the Jews; and That Christians, Although They Differ from Those Same Jews in Name, in the Use of Certain Foods, in Feast Days, and in Circumcision, Were Nevertheless Truly Substituted in Place of the Jews, Who Were Driven from Their Native Land on Account of Their Crimes

[Col. 0782A] Tertullian had no other purpose in the books with which we are concerned than, in pleading the cause of the Christians, to demonstrate that their religion was true and that of the pagans false, and that the pagans were in reality guilty of all the crimes of which they falsely accused those same Christians. But because he does not treat these matters with sufficient distinction and orderly arrangement, and because numerous difficult questions arise, we shall endeavor, to the best of our ability, to reduce them to a better order and to examine and explain them in our customary manner.

Tertullian acknowledges that the Christian religion is not especially ancient, since it was founded by Christ the Lord during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, before whose time the name of Christians had never been heard. “The registration,” he says—that is, the origin and beginning—“of this discipline, as we have already stated, dates from Tiberius” (Tertullian. [Col. 0782B] *Apologet.* cap. 7). Earlier he had said: “Tiberius, in whose time the Christian name entered the world” (Ibid. cap. 5). If anyone desires to know where and when it was first introduced, he will learn from the Acts of the Apostles that Paul and Barnabas taught a great multitude in the Church at Antioch, “so that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch” (Act. cap. XI. 25). Hence our Tertullian says in another book: “Our era does not yet number two hundred and fifty years,” and subsequently: “Our era does not yet number three hundred years” (Tertull. lib. *ad Nat.* cap. 5 et cap. 9). Indeed, in the *Apologeticum* he says: “We are of yesterday,” that is, we were born not long ago, but, as it were, only yesterday in comparison with others. There he wished to warn us that it occurred not without a great miracle [Col. 0782C] that Christians, although they had arisen so few years before, had filled every place throughout the whole world, with the sole exception of the pagans’ temples (Idem, *Apolog.* cap. 37).

Yet although the Christian religion, by the admission even of its adherents, was, as Tertullian says, so new that it “belongs to the time of Tiberius”—this is how he speaks (Ibid. cap. 21)—that is, although it was introduced into this world, as we have just said, during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, it is nevertheless certain that it is supported, as he further says, by the most ancient “documents of the Jews,” that is, by the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament. It is not only founded upon them, but those Scriptures now belong no less to the Christians than they formerly did to the Jews. [Col. 0782D] For a little earlier our author had written: “The archive of a single prophet,” that is, the books of Moses, “surpasses the books of all others by many centuries; in it appears to have been deposited the treasure of the entire Jewish mystery, and consequently of ours as well” (Ibid. cap. 19); in our manuscript codices the reading is, “and consequently now of ours as well.” By these words Tertullian plainly signifies that the divine treasure of our mystery, just as formerly that of the Jews, is truly deposited in this and the other books of the Old Testament.

The pagans objected, however, that this was an empty and absurd presumption and boast on the part of Christians, who wished to conceal themselves “under the shelter of a most renowned religion” (Idem, cap. 21) and to defend the impious worship that they rendered to a crucified man. For, they said, there was a great discrepancy between Christians and Jews, [Col. 0783A] not only in name but also in the actual facts. First, just as no one was unaware how great the antiquity of the Jews was, so absolutely no one was ignorant that Christ was a man whom the Jews themselves, not long ago, as we have just observed, condemned and subjected to the punishment of the cross. Second, they disagreed among themselves in “distinctions of diet,” that is, in certain kinds of food from which the one group abstained but which the other consumed. Third, they differed in their observance of feast days, which was entirely different among the two groups. Finally, they differed in the very “mark,” or, as Minucius Felix says, the “bodily sign,” which the Apostle calls “the sign of circumcision” and “the seal of the righteousness of the faith in uncircumcision” (Minut. Felix, pag. 376. Paul. *Epist. ad Rom.* IV. cap. 4). Yet all these things [Col. 0783B] ought to have been common to Christians and Jews if they were devoted to the same God.

This line of argument against Christians was not new, whether on the part of pagans or of Jews. For Justin Martyr, in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, presses it in the name of the pagans as follows: *Εἰ δὲ τὶς φάσκοι τῶν προχείρως ἀντιλέγειν εἰθισμένων, μὴ ἡμῖν τὰς βίβλους ταύτας, ἄλλα Ἰουδαίοις προσήκειν, διὰ τὸ ἔτι νῦν ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς αὐτῶν σώζεσθαι, καὶ ματὴν ἡμᾶς ἐκ τούτων φάσκειν τὴν θεοσέβειαν μεμαθηκέναι λέγοι* (Justin. martyr. *Cohort. ad Graec.* pag. 14): “But if one of those who are accustomed rashly to contradict us should object that these are not our books but those of the Jews, and should say that through vanity we boast of having drawn our religion from them.” In another book, moreover, he introduces a Jew making the same objections to Christians as Tertullian does, as follows: *Ἐκεῖνο δὲ ἀποροῦμεν μάλιστα, εἰ ὑμεῖς εὐσεβεῖν λέγοντες, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὀιόμενοι διαφέρειν, κατ` οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ἀπολείπεσθε, οὐδὲ διαλλάσσετε ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν τὸν ὑμέτερον βίον, ἐν τῷ μήτε τὰς ἑορτὰς, μήτε τὰ σάββατα τηρεῖν, μήτε τὴν περιτομὴν ἔχειν, καὶ ἔτι ἐπ` ἄνθρωπον σταυρωθέντα τὰς ἐλπίδας ποιούμενοι*. (Idem *Dialog. cum Tryph.* pag. 227). [Col. 0783C] “This certainly is what we find most astonishing when we consider the matter: that you, who boast of the true religion and wish to excel other human beings, differ from them in nothing and in your manner of life do not differ from the nations, since you neither observe feast days nor Sabbaths, nor possess circumcision, and, furthermore, place your hope in a crucified man.”

Tertullian therefore replies that the Jews once possessed very great favor with God because of the exceptional righteousness [Col. 0783D] and faith of their “original founders” (Tertullian. *Apologet.* cap. 21), that is, of the earliest patriarchs from whom they derived their origin. Hence they were then prosperous and flourished, as he says, both in the greatness of their race and in the loftiness of their kingdom. But their descendants, he continues, “puffed up by confidence in their fathers,” deviated from discipline in a profane manner, spurned God’s warnings, and, trampling upon his laws, rushed headlong into every kind of vice. But the God whom they despised in his goodness they experienced as a severe judge. This is most clearly proved by their present condition, in which, our author says, “scattered, wandering, and exiles from their own sky and soil, they roam throughout the world without man or God as king” (Ibid.). Cyprian excerpted this entire passage from his master and even borrowed some of his very words in the following manner: [Col. 0784A] “At first the Jews possessed favor with God. Thus were they righteous in former times; thus did their ancestors obey religious ordinances. Hence both the loftiness of their kingdom flourished and the greatness of their race arose. But afterward they became negligent, undisciplined, and proud, and, puffed up by confidence in their fathers, they lost the favor given to them when they despised the divine commands. How profane their life became and what offense they incurred by violating religion they themselves also testify: though silent in speech, they confess it by their fate. Scattered and wandering, they roam about, fugitives from their own soil and sky, and are driven from one alien lodging to another” (Cyprian. *de idolor. vanit.* pag. 15). But we have already quoted these things in our dissertation on the book of Minucius Felix, who thereby refutes the obstinacy of Caecilius [Col. 0784B] (*Dissertat. in Minut.* cap. 6. art. 3).

But not only do the Jews wander and roam here and there throughout the whole world; they are not even permitted, Tertullian continues, “under the status of foreigners to greet their native land, even by setting foot upon it” (Tertullian, loc. cit.). And when in another book he argues expressly against those same Jews, he openly asserts further that this was not merely not permitted to them, but actually forbidden, just as it had been foretold long before by the sacred prophet, namely Isaiah. Hear, I pray, his words:

> We observe that now no one of the race of Israel has remained in the city of Bethlehem; and since it has consequently been forbidden that any Jew should remain within the borders of that region, this too would be something fulfilled through the Prophet: “Your land is desolate; your cities are burned with fire,” that is, what [Col. 0784C] befell them in time of war (Isaiah 1:7); “foreigners will consume your country in your sight, and it will be desolate and overthrown by alien peoples.” And elsewhere it is thus said through the Prophet: “You will see the King with glory,” that is, Christ performing mighty works in the glory of God the Father, “and your eyes will see the land from afar” (ibid. 33:17). Because, in accordance with your deserts, after the conquest of Jerusalem you were forbidden to enter your land, you have been permitted only to see it with your eyes from afar.

(Idem, *lib. adv. Judae.*, cap. 13.) That earlier passage of Isaiah is likewise cited by Cyprian for the same reason (Cypr., lib. I *adv. Judae.*, § 6, p. 22).

Moreover, that prediction and the subsequent prohibition against entering their homeland are confirmed by the author of the Eusebian *Chronicle* in these words:

> The Jewish war that was being waged in [Col. 0784D] Palestine came to an end, the affairs of the Jews having been utterly crushed. From that time onward permission to enter Jerusalem was also taken from them, first by the will of God, as the Prophets had foretold, and then by Roman prohibitions.

(Euseb., *Chron.*, at the year of Christ 135.)

Earlier, moreover, Justin Martyr cites the same earlier prophecy of Isaiah as Tertullian concerning the expulsion of the Jews from their homeland (Justin, *Cohort. ad gent.*, p. 14); and, after adducing yet another, immediately adds: And that it is guarded by you, so that no one may be there, and death has been ordained against any Jew caught entering it. “You know very well both that precautions are taken and watch kept lest any of you should be there, and that capital punishment has been established against a Jew who enters it” [Col. 0785A] (Justin, *Apolog.* 1 *pro Christian.*, p. 84). Jerome, however, says: “After the final devastation, public laws were also posted, and the Jews were forbidden to enter the land from which they had been expelled” (Jerome, on Isaiah 6:11, p. 65). And again elsewhere: “No Jew is permitted by law to enter the land and city once holy” (Idem, on Ezekiel 18:16, p. 617).

If, however, you ask at what time and by which emperor that law was enacted, you may learn from Eusebius, who relates that in the twelfth year of the emperor Hadrian, after the overthrow of the city of Betthera, situated not far from Jerusalem: From that time onward, the entire nation was wholly forbidden by a legal decree and the ordinances of Hadrian to set foot even upon the land around Jerusalem, so that they might not behold from afar their ancestral [Col. 0785B] soil, Hadrian having so commanded, as Aristo of Pella records. “The entire nation of the Jews was forbidden to set foot in the region surrounding Jerusalem, so much so that they were not even permitted to look upon their native soil from afar, as Aristo of Pella writes” (Euseb., *Hist. eccl.*, IV.6, p. 118). But by Hilary’s time the severity of this law had been somewhat relaxed, as he indicates in these very words:

> Indeed, even now they are barred by an edict of the Roman emperor from entering that same city. And when they remember that the Holy of Holies is desolate, the prophecies silent, the sacrifices of atonement absent, and all the dignity of the Levitical ministry disfigured, they now turn back and, afflicted by hunger for the word of God and for saving food, are accustomed to walk around the city as a consolation for their present miseries.

(Hilary, *Tract. in Psalm.* LVIII, § 7, p. 130.)

[Col. 0785C] But that unhappy people could not enjoy even this meager consolation for their miseries without payment; they were compelled to purchase it. I should like you to hear Jerome, a most substantial witness to this fact:

> To the present day the faithless tenants . . . are forbidden to enter Jerusalem; and, so that they may be allowed to weep over the ruin of their city, they purchase the privilege—for those who once purchased the blood of Christ now purchase their own tears. . . . Tears are still upon their cheeks, their arms are bruised, their hair disheveled, and the soldier demands payment so that they may be allowed to weep longer.

(Jerome, on Zephaniah 1:15, p. 1655.)

Yet it was not only these things that had been foretold, as stated above, by the sacred voices of the prophets. The same voices, Tertullian says, always insisted that it would come to pass that, “in the last courses of the age, God would choose for Himself, from every nation and people [Col. 0785D] and place, worshipers much more faithful, to whom He would transfer a grace that was indeed fuller because of their capacity for the discipline of its author” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, cap. 21). In our manuscripts we read *eadem* rather than *eaedem*, and *auctioris* rather than *auctoris*, not altogether badly. Cyprian excerpted this, like the preceding material recalled by us shortly before, in much the same fashion:

> God had foretold beforehand that, as the age declined and the end of the world was now drawing near, He would choose for Himself from every nation and people and place worshipers much more faithful and of better obedience, who would draw indulgence from the divine gifts—the indulgence that the Jews, though they had received it, lost by despising religion.

(Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 15.) Neither author there indicates what those oracles [Col. 0786A] of the sacred seers were; but Tertullian cited some in another book, Cyprian more of them, and Lactantius still later, as we have demonstrated in the appropriate place (Idem, *Adv. Judae.*, cap. 12; Cyprian, lib. I *Adv. Jud.*, § 11, p. 23; *Dissertat. in Lactant.*, cap. 10, art. 1).

Thus Christians, “grafted from a wild olive into the Jews’ olive tree,” as Tertullian continues to put it, and substituted in their place, came to share with those same Jews the treasury of the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament (Tertullian, *De testim. animae*, cap. 5). Earlier, moreover, the holy martyr Justin had firmly asserted that the teaching handed down in the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament belonged to Christians, to whom those Scriptures were transmitted by [Col. 0786B] the Jews themselves, not without divine providence (Justin, *Cohort. ad gent.*, p. 14).

Although these books became common to Jews and Christians, it does not thereby follow that Christians were obliged to accept all the rites prescribed in them. For Christ quite rightly abolished many of them, such as sabbaths, feast days, circumcision, and the like, which had been prescribed for carnal Jews. For all these things were shadows and figures, and were given as a sign; as Tertullian clearly demonstrates in another book, they were bound to vanish and become obsolete at the advent of the reality, that is, of Christ (Tertullian, *Adv. Judae.*, caps. 3 and 4).

Thus the Christian religion, although introduced into the world by Christ during the reign of the emperor Tiberius, was nevertheless substituted for the Jewish religion, received its divine Scriptures as though by hereditary right, and, as we have said, was supported and sustained by them. But this will become clearer still after we have examined, in our customary manner, what our Tertullian maintains concerning those same sacred Scriptures of the Jews, or of the Old Testament.

## ARTICLE II. When and how the books of Sacred Scripture, first written in Hebrew, were translated into Greek by seventy-two translators; whether they worked in separate cells; with a discussion of Aristeas, Ptolemy Philadelphus, Pisistratus, their libraries and those of the Attalid kings, and Demetrius of Phalerum, the most highly approved of grammarians

Tertullian observes that from the beginning God sent [Col. 0786D] men distinguished for justice and innocence, who both recognized and proclaimed Him to be the one God (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, cap. 18). They taught that all things had been created by this one God; that man had been formed from the earth; that the succession of the seasons had been ordered; that signs of His divine majesty had been displayed; that laws had been established for morals and the proper conduct of life; and that, when the age had run its course, all men were to be raised again to life and judged, so that according to their deserts they might be visited with either eternal punishment or eternal happiness. But there in Tertullian’s text we read these words: “What rules He has determined for winning His favor, which you do not know or have abandoned.” These seemed so obscure and corrupt to Heraldus that he did not venture to pronounce any judgment upon them. Rigault, however, was not so timid: contrary to the manifest testimony of all the manuscript and printed copies, [Col. 0787A] he wished to write the particle *qui* in place of *quas*, and then *quas* in place of *quae*, though he supplied no reason. We will nevertheless readily acknowledge that this conjecture does not appear altogether unsuccessful; but it lacks the support of any manuscript whatsoever. Heraldus, later grown bolder, suspects that *prodacto* should be substituted for *producto*, that is, “consumed and completed.” He attempts to prove his emendation from other passages of Tertullian where *prodactum* is read with the same meaning. He could also have cited the fifth book of our Tertullian against Marcion, where the same word is similarly employed. But what can one do when all the manuscripts protest, and when an author uses barbarous and improper words? [Col. 0787B] Whatever his manner of speaking may have been, he plainly signifies by it the end and termination of the world (Idem, *Adv. Marcion.*, V.6).

Those men whom he calls distinguished for piety and justice were not only “preachers,” as he says, but are also called “prophets” from their office of foretelling, or announcing future events (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, cap. 18). Furthermore, they performed mighty works, or miracles, to establish belief in the divinity. Finally, they were “flooded with the divine Spirit”—these again are his own words—that is, they were so filled with it that it flowed and poured out beyond themselves.

All the marvelous things performed by them above the order of nature, and all the things foretold under the inspiration of the divine Spirit, “remain,” Tertullian says again, “in the treasuries of writings” (ibid.). But of what writings, I ask you? [Col. 0787C] Doubtless of none other than Hebrew writings. For in the same passage he relates that Ptolemy Philadelphus received from the Jews, who had formerly been Hebrews, the books written in their “own native characters” (ibid.), or in the Hebrew language, because, as he continues, “the prophets had always addressed them” (ibid.). Thus the books of Moses and the other sacred seers, written in the Hebrew language, had remained among the Hebrews and Jews, who certainly preserved them whole and uncorrupted with the utmost care.

But lest so great a treasure should always lie hidden among them alone, it was communicated first to the Greeks and then [Col. 0787D] to other nations through the celebrated translation of the seventy-two elders. Hence Tertullian says: “Nor do these sacred writings now lie hidden” (ibid.). That is how the text stands in Rigault’s edition. In the older printed editions and in our manuscripts, however, the adverb *now* is absent—and not entirely without good reason. For Tertullian signifies that they had ceased to lie hidden not merely in his own time, but from the very time of the Greek translators, as we have said.

He explains when and how this Greek translation of the sacred books was prepared by them as follows. When Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, wished to enrich his library with a collection of every kind of book, [Col. 0788A] at the suggestion of Demetrius of Phalerum he requested and obtained from the Jews their sacred codices written in Hebrew, together with seventy-two men who translated them into Greek. Our Author then added in the same place: “The philosopher Menedemus also, a champion of Providence” (wrongly, in one Vatican manuscript, “a judge of the province”), “regarded them with admiration because of their agreement in judgment” (ibid.). But among the learned writers of our age there is no small disagreement over what is meant by the last words, “regarded them with admiration because of their agreement in judgment.” Some believe that they signify that Menedemus shared their opinion concerning divine providence governing all things. But Tertullian, others say, is not there discussing this providence of God, but only the Greek translation of the sacred Scriptures. [Col. 0788B] To what purpose, then, would he have inserted a reference to divine providence? They therefore think Tertullian’s meaning to be this: Menedemus examined the completed Greek translation of Sacred Scripture and perceived with admiration that it had been made in exactly the same manner through the translators’ common agreement. He was thus a champion and witness of divine providence, testifying openly that, by its wholly marvelous guidance, the Hebrew text of Scripture had been rendered into Greek by those translators in precisely the same manner.

But this, you will say, could not have occurred unless the translators had been placed separately in different cells and each had translated the Hebrew text into Greek. Yet that opinion concerning their separate cells is false. But what follows from that, if Tertullian followed earlier writers [Col. 0788C] who, after Justin Martyr, as we have shown elsewhere, consistently defended this opinion about the translators’ cells (*Apparatus*, vol. I, book II, diss. 2, cap. 7, § 5, pp. 390 ff.)? Is this not why Menedemus is called by him “a champion of Providence”: because he regarded these translators with admiration for their agreement in judgment, since, separated from one another, they translated the sacred Scriptures into Greek in one and the same manner?

But, someone will object, does not divine providence shine forth sufficiently in the fact that those translators, working together, rendered them into Greek in the same manner? Who does not know how difficult they are to understand, and that it must indeed seem marvelous that, in translating them into Greek, so many translators held one and the same judgment? [Col. 0788D] Yet who will deny that divine providence would have shone forth far more marvelously if they composed their translations separated from one another?

You will insist that these separate cells of the translators are not only indicated in obscure words, but that Aristeas is also cited as a witness, though he said nothing about them. It may be answered, however, that Tertullian’s words were sufficiently clear to people of his own age, and that he supplied only one authority because this belief concerning the translators’ distinct cells was then common and regarded as virtually beyond doubt. Who, moreover, will deny that he relates more things than are contained in Aristeas’s narrative? Whether this was in fact Tertullian’s opinion, we shall gladly hear you pronounce. We have discussed elsewhere [Col. 0789A] the history of Aristeas, the various opinions of learned men concerning it, and Menedemus (Idem, book I, diss. 2, cap. 1, pp. 223 ff.; and book III, diss. 2, cap. 3, art. 5, p. 922).

Philadelphus, moreover, who arranged for the Greek translation of Sacred Scripture, is called by Tertullian not only “most learned,” but also “most sagacious in all literature”; here, certainly, a substantive corresponding to the adjective “most sagacious” must be understood (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, cap. 18). This seems to be nothing other than “investigator” or “researcher,” for sagacity is said to be directed toward discovery or investigation. Philadelphus’s sagacity “in all literature” was therefore his most diligent search everywhere for all books written on any subject whatever. [Col. 0789B] Our Author says that, out of the highest zeal to preserve them, he had assembled a library from every kind of literature; Eusebius speaks similarly in his *Chronicle* (*Chron. Euseb.*, at the year 1734). With how great a number of books it was furnished we shall show in the following article. If anyone asks who Pisistratus was, whose zeal in this matter Tertullian says Philadelphus emulated, he may learn from these words of Aulus Gellius: “The tyrant Pisistratus is said to have been the first to make books of the liberal disciplines publicly available for reading at Athens.” There is frequent mention among various writers—Laertius, Pausanias, Thucydides, Aelian, Valerius Maximus, and others—of the tyranny of Pisistratus, which, as Herodotus relates, he recovered three times. We treated that tyranny of Pisistratus in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*. We further read in the cited Pausanias that [Col. 0789C] the poems of Homer had once been scattered, and that Pisistratus collected them, thereby producing, as Aelian says, the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*. But it is better to hear Cicero:

> Who in those same times was more learned, or whose eloquence was better furnished with literature, than Pisistratus? He is said to have been the first to arrange the books of Homer, previously confused, in the order in which we now possess them. He was not, indeed, beneficial to his fellow citizens, but he flourished so greatly in eloquence that he excelled in letters and learning.

(Gellius, *Noct. Att.*, VI.17, p. 393; Herodotus, II, §§ 59 ff.; Laertius, *Life of Solon*, §§ 53 ff., 65 ff.; Pausanias, I, pp. 3 and 21; Thucydides, *Hist.*, VIII, p. 446; Aelian, *Var. Hist.*, VIII.13; Valerius Maximus, I, § 2; VIII.9, *External Examples*, § 2; *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 1176; Pausanias, [Col. 0789D] VII, p. 235; Aelian, *Var. Hist.*, XIII.14; Cicero, *De orat.*, III, p. 194, line 37.)

Tertullian, however, does not venture to declare with certainty whether Philadelphus really emulated Pisistratus’s zeal in establishing so rich a library; he said only “I think,” that is, as seemed more probable to him. Yet if Vitruvius, who flourished in the age of Augustus Caesar, is to be believed, Ptolemy Philadelphus imitated in this endeavor the Attalid kings. I should like you to hear his words:

> When the Attalid kings, led by their great delight in philology, had established an excellent library at Pergamum for the common enjoyment, Ptolemy likewise, impelled by boundless emulation and eager zeal, strove with no less industry to establish one in the same manner at Alexandria. [Col. 0790A]

(Vitruvius, preface to book VII.) But others accuse him of error in this matter. For, they say, the Alexandrian kings were earlier than the Attalids. Yet nothing can be concluded from this against our Tertullian’s conjecture. Pisistratus and several others praised by Athenaeus and Epiphanius had established libraries, and Philadelphus could have imitated them (Athenaeus, *Deipnos.*, I, p. 3; Epiphanius, *De ponderibus et mensuris*, p. 166).

Furthermore, even if Tertullian’s opinion were certain, he is nevertheless lashed by Scaliger for having adorned Demetrius of Phalerum with no title other than “the most highly approved of grammarians.” “Indeed,” he says, “Demetrius’s gifts were little known to Tertullian” (Scaliger, notes on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, at the year 1724, p. 133). Why so? By mentioning certain gifts of Demetrius, did he [Col. 0790B] deny the others? And who would believe Scaliger even on oath? Did Suetonius not somewhere remind us that grammarians were initially given the name “men of letters,” because they were able to say or prove something acutely and knowledgeably (Suetonius, *De illustribus grammaticis*, § 4, p. 821)? Tertullian praised Demetrius by precisely this name because he was discussing the administration of the library entrusted to him by Philadelphus. To whom could it better have been assigned than to the most highly approved of grammarians—that is, a man endowed with varied learning, who knew all books and their value exceedingly well?

## ARTICLE III. In which library of Philadelphus the books of Sacred Scripture were deposited; where that library was constructed; how many books it contained; whether it was wholly consumed by fire; how the sacred codices reached the Christians; and the Jews’ tax-paid liberty to read them publicly

[Col. 0790C]

After Tertullian had woven together that entire account of the codices of Sacred Scripture, whether copied in Hebrew or in Greek, he immediately relates where all those codices were preserved: “Today,” he says, “they are displayed in Ptolemy’s library at the Serapeum, together with the Hebrew texts themselves” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, cap. 18, p. 19). By these words he plainly declares that these Hebrew and Greek books of the Old Testament had been deposited in the Serapeum, that is, the temple of Serapis constructed at Alexandria. For Chrysostom expressly declares that they had been placed by this Ptolemy Philadelphus in the temple of Serapis, “in the temple of Serapis” [Col. 0790D] (Chrysostom, *Orat.* 1 *Adv. Judae.*, vol. I, p. 394, Morel ed.). Yet in that complex, which in magnificence yielded only to the Capitol, as Gellius and Ammianus Marcellinus report, there were doubtless several buildings separated from one another (Gellius, *Noct. Att.*, VI, final chapter). In some one of these, a single or double library of Philadelphus was housed. For our Author, in the words just cited, mentions several libraries, as does Ammianus Marcellinus, who, after describing the magnificence of the Serapeum, continues thus:

> In it were libraries beyond valuation; and the concordant testimony of ancient records says that seven hundred thousand volumes, assembled through the vigilant exertions of the Ptolemaic kings, were burned during the Alexandrian war under the dictatorship [Col. 0791A] of Caesar, while the city was being plundered.

(Ammianus Marcellinus, XXII.16, p. 343.)

Athenaeus, however, mentions only one. After listing certain men famous for amassing books, he says: “King Ptolemy among us, surnamed Philadelphus, purchased them all and arranged for their transfer, together with those he had bought at Athens and Rhodes, he transferred them to beautiful Alexandria into the beautiful Alexandrian library” (Athenaeus, *Deipnos.*, I, p. 3). Similarly, the author of the Eusebian *Chronicle* says: “Ptolemy Philadelphus caused the divine Scriptures to be translated from the Hebrew language into Greek speech by seventy translators; he kept them in the Alexandrian library that he had assembled for himself from every kind of literature” (Euseb., *Chron.*, at the year 1734).

Epiphanius, however, although he identifies two libraries, differs [Col. 0791B] from our Tertullian and Ammianus Marcellinus in asserting that the books of Sacred Scripture were placed in the Brucheion, while the translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion were placed in the smaller Serapeum. For he concludes his account of their Greek translation with these words: The books, translated into Greek, were deposited in the first library, which had been built in the Brucheion. Still later another library was established in the Serapeum, smaller than the first and called its daughter; in it were deposited the translations of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the others, after the two hundred and fiftieth year.

> Those books, translated into Greek, were deposited in the first library, which was founded in the Brucheion. Afterward another library was established in the Serapeum, far smaller than the former [Col. 0791C] and called its daughter; into it the editions of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and others were gathered after 250 years.

(Epiphanius, *De ponderibus et mensuris*, § 11, p. 168.) You see clearly that in this he agrees with the others in asserting that there was a double Alexandrian library, but differs in wishing one to have been founded in the Brucheion and the other, the smaller, in the Serapeum. Whether his opinion alone should be preferred to the others is for you to judge.

If you extricate yourself from this difficulty, you will immediately encounter another, far greater one. For Tertullian speaks of the Greek codices of the Old Testament as though they were still preserved and extant in that Alexandrian library in his own time. Ammianus Marcellinus, on the contrary, as we have seen, expressly [Col. 0791D] asserts that this very library was burned in the Alexandrian war under Caesar’s dictatorship (Marcellinus, XXII.16, p. 344). Aulus Gellius likewise attests that nearly seven hundred thousand volumes were then burned by auxiliary soldiers (Gellius, *Noct. Att.*, VI.17, p. 394). Dio too seems to support them, saying that Achillas came directly to Alexandria, that various battles were fought by him against Caesar the dictator, and that many fires occurred: The storehouses of both grain and a great many excellent books were burned, as is reported, “and that the storehouses or chambers containing grain and a great many excellent books were burned, as is reported” (Dio, *Roman History*, XLII, p. 228).

Moreover, Epiphanius recorded that the library [Col. 0792A] situated in the region of Alexandria called the Brucheion was deserted in his time (Epiphanius, *De ponderibus et mensuris*, § 10, p. 166). Yet, as we have seen, he had said that the codices of Sacred Scripture were deposited in it. Therefore, if this library was deserted—and all the more if the Alexandrian libraries had already been burned in Caesar’s age—how, I ask you, could Tertullian say: “Today they are displayed in Ptolemy’s library at the Serapeum, together with the Hebrew texts themselves, and the Jews read them publicly” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, cap. 18)? Some answer that there were at least two libraries there. One, they say, could have burned, while the other, in which those books had been deposited, remained entirely intact. But this answer plainly conflicts with Epiphanius himself, who asserts that the library [Col. 0792B] in which these books had been stored no longer existed in his time. Others therefore answer that, even if this and all the other Alexandrian libraries were burned, not all the books were consumed, and the Hebrew and Greek codices of Sacred Scripture were rescued from the fire.

In confirmation of this opinion one may adduce the testimony of Seneca, and after him Paulus Orosius, who record that only four hundred thousand books were then consumed (Seneca, *De tranquillitate animi*, cap. 9, p. 663; Orosius, VII.15). Yet if we believe Marcellinus and Gellius, previously cited by us, seven hundred thousand books had been deposited in that library. Three hundred thousand, therefore, were withdrawn from the flames. Doubtless, then, [Col. 0792C] these Hebrew and Greek volumes of Sacred Scripture were among that number, God so providing.

What of the fact that Chrysostom firmly asserts that the Greek translation of the prophetic books was preserved down to his own time in the Serapeum, or, as he puts it, the temple of Serapis? These are his Greek words: Καὶ μέχρι νῦν ἐκεῖ τῶν προφητῶν αἱ ἐρμηνευθεῖσαι βίβλοι μένουσι (“And to this day the translated books of the prophets remain there”) (Chrysostom, *Orat.* 1 *Adv. Judae.*, p. 595, vol. I).

Furthermore, even if someone should clearly prove, against this opinion of Chrysostom and others, that those codices were burned, he still could not deny that copies of them had been multiplied before that fire, and that several Hebrew copies had been transcribed by the Jews and Greek copies by others, and carefully preserved. [Col. 0792D] There can indeed be no room for doubt that many reached the Christians. For not a few Greek testimonies are found cited in the books of the New Testament.

Furthermore, Hebrew copies were preserved with the greatest diligence by those same Jews. For our Tertullian said of those living in his own time: “The Jews read them publicly; the liberty is tax-paid; it is open to all every Sabbath.” Do you hear how clearly he affirms that the Jews, assembling in their synagogues every Sabbath, publicly and in everyone’s hearing read these sacred codices written in their native tongue? This custom had indeed become established from ancient times, both before and after Christ the Lord. [Col. 0793A] For concerning Paul and his companions it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: “Passing through Perga, they came to Antioch in Pisidia and, entering the synagogue on the Sabbath day, sat down. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, Paul, at the Jews’ request, addressed them” (Acts 13:14 ff.). Later you will find these words committed to writing in the same book: “From ancient times Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him in the synagogues, where he is read every Sabbath” (ibid. 15:21). This assuredly could not have happened unless the Jews already possessed these codices and devoted the greatest care to preserving them uncorrupted and wholly intact.

But what, you will ask, does Tertullian mean when he says that the Jews’ liberty to hold their assemblies every [Col. 0793B] Sabbath and read their books there was tax-paid? Some believe that these words designate permission granted to them by Philadelphus, provided that they paid a modest annual tax. But by what argument will it be proved that this tax was exacted by Philadelphus, who valued the sacred books of the Old Testament so highly and had heaped the greatest gifts upon their translators? It therefore seems far more probable to others that Tertullian is referring to the tribute imposed upon the Jews by the Roman emperors in order that they might be permitted to assemble each Sabbath according to their custom. Some think that the following words of Suetonius, dealing with the emperor Domitian, should be understood of this tribute:

> Besides all the others, the Jewish tax was exacted with the utmost severity. Informers denounced to its collectors those who either lived a Jewish life within the city without formally professing it, or, concealing their origin, [Col. 0793C] had not paid the tributes imposed upon that nation.

(Suetonius, book VIII, *Life of Domitian*, § 12.) But there he signifies that the Jews had to pay a tax in order to purchase the free profession of their sect, though it had then been increased rather than imposed for the first time. For in Dio’s epitome Xiphilinus relates that, after Jerusalem had been captured, the emperor Titus ordered the Jews who professed their ancestral laws to pay two drachmas annually to Capitoline Jupiter (Xiphilinus, epitome of Dio, *Life of Vespasian*, p. 318). Do you wish to hear his Greek words? Here they are: Καὶ ἀπ` ἐκείνου δίδραγμον ἐτάχθη τοὺς τὰ πάτρια αὐτῶν ἔθη περιστέλλοντας τῷ Καπιτωλίῳ Διῒ κατ` ἔτος ἀποφέρειν (“And from that time those observing their ancestral customs were ordered to pay two drachmas annually to Capitoline Zeus”).

They think, moreover, that Juvenal alluded to this tribute in the following verses:

> [Col. 0793D] Now the grove and shrine of the sacred spring are rented  
> To Jews, whose furniture is a basket and some hay.  
> For every tree has been ordered to pay a fee to the people,  
> And the wood begs now that the Muses have been expelled.

(Juvenal, *Satire* 3, lines 13 ff.)

This is therefore rightly called by Tertullian a “tax-paid liberty,” because they could not convene their assemblies or publicly read in their synagogues their sacred codices, most carefully preserved wherever they had been dispersed, unless the tribute had first been paid. From these Jews, therefore—their bitterest enemies—the Christians had received those codices of the Old Testament, about whose truth and integrity no person of sound mind will ever entertain doubt. For, as the ancient author of the book *Against Five Heresies*, once attributed to Augustine, rightly argues against the pagans:

> [Col. 0794A] The Jew has in his bookcase the codex in which these things are found written. My enemy is my witness. Ask him yourself; open it, read, believe.

(Augustine, *Appendix*, vol. VIII, *Against Five Heresies*, cap. 7, p. 9.)

The Christians therefore possessed these books exactly as they had been transmitted to them by the Jews. For they could not alter anything in their text without immediately being convicted of falsehood by the Jews, their enemies, who read them daily. Let us now investigate with our Tertullian what and how great their authority is.

## ARTICLE IV. How Tertullian demonstrates the authority of Sacred Scripture from its very great antiquity; what are the substances and materials of the ancient style; cities renowned for their histories; and hoary records

[Col. 0794B]

Tertullian openly vindicates the supreme authority of Sacred Scripture by a twofold argument. The first he derives from its very great antiquity, which we have discussed repeatedly in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*; the second from its divinity, or from the divine Spirit under whose inspiration all its books were committed to writing. He presses the former argument against the pagans all the more willingly because, acknowledging its force and weight, they endeavored thereby to defend and confirm their own religion, false though it was.
