For he addresses them all in these words: “Among you, it is virtually a religious principle to assert credibility on the basis of dates” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, cap. 19); that is, you contend that your religion and the worship of false gods are defended by their antiquity.

[Col. 0794C] Yet if this argument carries any weight, you cannot detract from the credibility of our Scriptures. For, Tertullian says, “the repository of a single prophet” (that is, the books of Moses) “surpasses in age all the substances and materials . . . of every ancient literary work of yours” (ibid.); that is, absolutely all your compositions and their subjects. Indeed, he says, it even surpasses their “origins,” that is, their beginnings and causes; their “orders and channels,” that is, the courses and conduits through which they have reached you.

Moreover, by their antiquity they precede most nations, which arose afterward, and cities distinguished in their histories and hoary in their records. So the text stands in our manuscript codices and older editions, except that in them *causas* is written in place of *canas*. Rigaltius, however, whom others subsequently followed, retained the word *canas*, but [Col. 0794D] deleted the preceding *historiarum*, apparently on his own authority. For neither he nor the others gave any reason for this omission. They were doubtless persuaded that there was here a very serious violation of the rules of grammar, ἀμάρτημα (“error”), in which a substantive noun is used for an adjective, and an adjective for a substantive. But is this not a Graecism employed more than once by authors of the better Latin style? Did not Horace say: “Blameless in life and pure of crime”? The meaning of our Author, therefore, is that the Hebrews are older than cities which were distinguished by historical monuments and by hoary records, that is, by accounts which, through their gray age and antiquity, displayed an origin older than that of all the rest. Thus Theophilus [Col. 0795A] of Antioch had likewise said that the same Hebrews were older than the cities that were most famous among the Egyptians (Theoph., Book III *To Autolycus*, p. 130). We shall not conceal, however, that in another book of Tertullian the text reads: “Those who collected the gray antiquities” (Tertull., Book II *To the Nations*, ch. 12). But only a single manuscript codex of that book survives, whereas there are very many of the *Apologeticus*. Whatever conclusion you adopt, however, the meaning will always be the same. Furthermore, our Author uses the word *memoriae* for *monumenta*, as may readily be confirmed from Augustine (August., *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, ch. 4, p. 519, vol. VI). Tertullian himself again used it in the same sense in the book just cited: “Saturn is numbered in the ancient records as having possessed human nature upon earth” (Tertull., [Col. 0795B] Book II *To the Nations*, loc. cit.).

Then in the *Apologeticus* he added that the books of Moses were, by their age, earlier even than “the very forms of letters, the signs and guardians of things” (Idem, *Apologeticus*, ch. 19); that is, they were written in characters and letters that were plainly the most ancient of all. For shortly before, he had written that they had been inscribed in Hebrew letters, which he regarded as certainly older than any others whatever. He adds that letters are the guardians of things, inasmuch as they preserve the things themselves and their history from destruction. But these matters are explained more fully by Josephus; may you not begrudge reading in his book the words that are somewhat too lengthy to be quoted here (Joseph., beginning of Book I *Against Apion*, p. 1034 ff.).

Finally Tertullian added: “And I think that we are still [Col. 0795C] saying too little: your very gods, I say, the temples themselves, and the oracles and sacred rites” (Tertull., loc. cit.); that is, the books of Moses are far older than the gods, temples, oracles, and sacred rites of the gentiles. For he considers the origin of the gods, as we shall say below, to be traced back to Saturn. It is therefore no wonder that he declares these gods to be later than the books of Moses. But by these words, “we are still saying too little,” he seems to reproach the pagans for advertising their gods and their worship as older than the books of Moses, as ignorantly as falsely.

## ARTICLE V. How clearly Tertullian proved the antiquity of the books of Moses from the age of Moses, who was contemporary with Inachus and preceded Danaus by several centuries, as well as the fall of Troy and Homer; with a discussion of Manetho, Berossus, Iromus or Hieronymus, and Josephus

[Col. 0795D]

Certainly no one will deny that the antiquity of the books of Moses can be proved in no clearer way than from the age of Moses himself. Accordingly, relying upon the testimony of ancient writers, Tertullian explains in the following words when Moses lived and whom he preceded: “He was,” he says, “contemporary with Inachus of Argos; by almost four hundred years—for seven years are wanting—he preceded Danaus, himself regarded among you as most ancient; by about a thousand years he preceded the fall of Priam; I might even say, by more than five hundred years, Homer” (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 19). First, therefore, he teaches [Col. 0796A] that Moses was contemporary with Inachus. But in the first volume of our *Apparatus* we showed that this was the common opinion of ancient writers down to Eusebius, an opinion which some have also attempted to defend in the present century (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 385, 531, 836, 909, and 1342). Our Author confidently affirms that he had many guarantors and patrons of his opinion. And lest anyone should think that he asserted this without evidence, he names these very persons individually and by name, as we shall see shortly.

Moreover, supported by the authority of these writers, he asserts that Moses preceded Danaus by 393 years. But consider, I ask, whether Tertullian drew this from Josephus, whom he there cites after the other writers. For after Josephus [Col. 0796B] had recounted the chronology of the Egyptians published by Manetho, he concluded it with these words: Οἱ καλούμενοι ποιμένες ἡμέτεροι πρόγονοι τρισὶ καὶ ἐννενήκοντα καὶ τριακοσίοις πρόσθεν ἔτεσιν, ἐκ τῆς Αἰγύπτου ἀπαλλαγέντες, τὴν χώραν ταύτην ἐπῴκησαν, ἢ Δαναὸν εἰς Ἄργος ἀφικέσθαι, καὶ τοι τοῦτον ἀρχαιότατον Ἀργεῖοι νομίζουσι (“Those called the Shepherds—our ancestors—after being delivered from Egypt, inhabited this country three hundred and ninety-three years before Danaus came to Argos, although the Argives regard him as most ancient”). “Those who were called the Shepherds, that is, our ancestors, after being delivered from Egypt, inhabited this province three hundred and ninety-three years before Danaus came to Argos, although the Argives regard him as most ancient” (Joseph., Book I *Against Apion*, p. 1041). In copying the text of Theophilus of Antioch, therefore, who cites the same Manetho, a scribe doubtless seems to have erred when he wrote that the Hebrews departed from Egypt πρὸ ἐτῶν τριακωσίων δεκατριῶν (“three hundred and thirteen years before”) three hundred and thirteen years [Col. 0796C] before Danaus came to Greece (Theoph., Book III *To Autolycus*, p. 131). For Theophilus, as is evident from what has been said, had doubtless written τριακοσίοις καὶ ἐννενήκοντα τρισὶ (“three hundred and ninety-three”), three hundred and ninety-three. But it was easy for a not sufficiently skilled scribe to write ἐννενήκοντα (“ninety”) in place of δέκα (“ten”). Nevertheless, we shall await the judgment of others concerning this conjecture. Yet from these words of Theophilus you will readily understand why Tertullian called Danaus most ancient among the pagans.

Then he continues: “Moses,” he says, “preceded the fall of Priam, that is, the destruction of Troy, by approximately one thousand years” (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 19). Here again he follows in the footsteps of Josephus, who asserts that the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt was so ancient [Col. 0796D] ὡς ἐγγύς που προτέραν αὐτὴν τῶν Ἱλιακῶν ἔτεσι χιλίοις (“so that it was nearly one thousand years earlier than the Trojan War”) “that it preceded the Trojan War by nearly one thousand years” (Joseph., Book I *Against Apion*, p. 1042). Both added the adverb “approximately,” and certainly not without reason. For, as we have seen elsewhere, opinions concerning this interval of time vary greatly. Yet whichever opinion may be nearer the truth, it is more certain than certain that Moses was far more ancient than the period of Troy (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 1345, 1347 ff.).

There is still greater disagreement concerning the age of Homer, whom our Author declares to have flourished five hundred years or more after that same fall of Troy, and consequently 1,500 or more years after Moses. These divergent opinions of writers are reviewed by Tatian [Col. 0797A] (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, pp. 166 ff.), by Eusebius, who reproduced his words (Euseb., Book X, *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 11, pp. 492 ff.), and also by Clement of Alexandria (Clem. Alex., Book I, *Stromata*, pp. 326 ff.), as well as by other ancient and more recent authors who, whether expressly or while treating another subject, undertook discussions concerning the ancient writers, or concerning chronologists and poets, and specifically concerning the life or age of Homer himself. We too have discussed these disagreements among authors elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 1278, 1347 ff.).

But at whatever time Homer flourished, it is plainly established, as Josephus correctly argues, that among the Greeks there is no written composition older than the works of this poet (Joseph., Book I *Against Apion*, p. [Col. 0797B] 1034). Indeed, if you believe the same Josephus, Homer’s poems were not committed to writing but recited in song; and since they were afterward collected by others from memory alone, many inconsistencies are found in them. In addition, shortly before this Josephus had said that other nations boasted that they had received the earliest use of letters from the Phoenicians and Cadmus, as we have also noted elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 385 ff.). Yet no one, Josephus continues, will be able to exhibit any writing preserved from that ancient period, whether in temples or in public monuments. The books of Moses, therefore, preceded all the rest by a long interval of time—indeed, of centuries.

Nothing, says our Author, was easier to prove (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 19). But because this [Col. 0797C] would have been a rather lengthy undertaking and could not be done without a very great digression from his purpose, he therefore judged that it should be deferred. Whether by these words he promises another work on the subject, and whether he fulfilled that promise, who would dare confidently to assert? Yet lest anyone say that he had advanced the claim rashly, he openly shows everyone the sources and the writers by whom it can be clearly proved. First, indeed, he cites the most ancient archives or repositories of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Phoenicians, in which their writings or books were deposited. He calls these nations by name because, according to Josephus (Joseph., ibid.), the Greeks acknowledged that the most ancient tradition of events was preserved among them. But since this investigation might still have seemed most difficult, “their fellow countrymen,” he says, “must be summoned, through whom [Col. 0797D] knowledge was supplied” (Tertull., ibid.). Properly speaking, *municipes* were those who, having been admitted into Roman citizenship, enjoyed the privileges of Romans. But he uses the name loosely to mean inhabitants of the same region. For he names both the nations and their writers individually: from the Egyptians, Manetho; from the Chaldeans, Berossus—both cited by Josephus, as we shall shortly note; and from the Phoenicians, Iromus, king of Tyre, who must be discussed more fully later. If these were insufficient, he adds their followers: Ptolemy of Mendes, who, according to Clement of Alexandria (Clement of Alexandria, Book I, *Stromata*) and, after him, Eusebius (Euseb., Book X, *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 12, p. 497), was a priest and [Col. 0798A] set forth the deeds of the kings of Egypt in three books; likewise Menander of Ephesus, by whom, Josephus (Joseph., Book I *Against Apion*, p. 1042) and Theophilus of Antioch attest, the acts and history of the kings of Tyre were written (Theoph., Book III *To Autolycus*, p. 132). To these he joins Demetrius of Phalerum, likewise cited by Josephus, and three others—King Juba, Apion, and Thallus—whom we have discussed in the first volume of our *Apparatus* and in the preceding dissertations.

Finally: “And the one who,” says Tertullian (Tertull., loc. cit.), “confirms or refutes these writers is the Jew Josephus, the defender of Jewish antiquities,” namely, in the books of the *Jewish Antiquities*, which are still in everyone’s hands. Yet Josephus does not confirm or refute these writers, as our Author expresses it, only in those books [Col. 0798B], but also in the other books, *Against Apion*, which we have already cited (Joseph., Book I *Against Apion*, pp. 1039 ff., 1043 ff.). For in these he reproduced a number of passages from the books of the Egyptians—namely, from Manetho the Egyptian—and of Berossus the Chaldean, from whom came treatises on astronomy and Chaldean philosophy.

There is therefore greater difficulty concerning the third writer, whom Tertullian styles “Iromus the Phoenician, king of Tyre.” For in our manuscript codices and the editions earlier than Rigalt’s, the reading is: “Hieronymus the Phoenician, king of Tyre.” But because it was thought that there had been no king of Tyre named Hieronymus, editors preferred to write *Iromus* in the text of Tertullian. They gave no reason for this correction, however, apart from certain words [Col. 0798C] drawn from the fragments of Menander published by Scaliger. Yet with far better right they should have cited Theophilus of Antioch, by whom not only those same Greek words are quoted (Theoph., Book III *To Autolycus*, pp. 131 ff.), but who also calls him Ἱέρωμος Τυρίων βασιλεὺς (“Hieromus, king of the Tyrians”), “Hieromus, king of the Tyrians.” He attests that this was the man who had written many letters to Solomon, while Solomon had in turn written to him—letters said to have been preserved among the Tyrians. Yet it cannot be inferred from this that the king committed anything concerning the antiquity of the Hebrews to writing.

May it not also be inferred that the name Hieronymus should be read in Tertullian’s text from the fact that Josephus, in the first book of the *Jewish Antiquities*, where he discusses the long lives of the earliest patriarchs, wrote the following after mentioning, just as our Author does, Manetho and Berossus: [Col. 0798D] Μώχος καὶ Ἑστιαῖος, καὶ πρὸς αὐτοῖς ὁ αἰγύπτιος Ἱερώνυμος, οἱ τὰ φοινικὰ συνταξάμενοι, συμφωνοῦσι τοῖς ὑπ` ἐμοῦ λεγόμενοις (“Mochus and Hestiaeus, together with Hieronymus the Egyptian, who composed accounts of Phoenician affairs, agree with what I have said”). “Mochus, Hestiaeus, and Hieronymus the Egyptian, who treated the affairs of the Phoenicians, agree with us” (Joseph., Book I, *Antiquities*, ch. 4, p. 11). He placed this Hieronymus among those who had left some written account concerning the longer life of Noah and the earlier patriarchs. Yet in the first book *Against Apion*, he observes that Hieronymus was one of those writers who, in composing histories, made no mention of the Jewish nation (Idem, Book I *Against Apion*, p. 1050): Ἱερώνυμος γὰρ οὐδαμοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἱστορίαν (“For Hieronymus nowhere in his history”) [Col. 0799A] ἐμνημόνευσε, καί τοι σχεδὸν ἐν τοῖς τόποις διατετριφὼς (“made mention of us, although he had spent time in almost those very places”). “For Hieronymus makes absolutely no mention of us in his history, although he was brought up almost in those very places.” He therefore admits that Hieronymus passed over the affairs of the Jews in that work, although they were not unknown to him. But there Josephus contrasts him with Hecataeus, by whom, he attests, a history concerning the Jews was published. Hieronymus could therefore, in a history or work on another subject, have introduced some discussion of their lives, just as he did concerning those who lived to a great age.

But although Hieronymus may have related either a few things or many concerning Moses and the Jews in some book, by what reasoning can it be proved that he was king of Tyre? Did Tertullian therefore suffer some human lapse here, or were his words corrupted by copyists, or must he be understood, like [Col. 0799B] Theophilus of Antioch, as referring to the letters of the Tyrian king to Solomon? Consider, therefore, which possibility seems more probable to you, or whether you can discover a better one.

## ARTICLE VI. On the age of the other sacred seers after Moses, finger gestures used for reckoning, and census records to be compared

Concerning the age of our other sacred seers after the death of Moses, Tertullian (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 19) thus pronounces against the pagans: “Although the other prophets are subsequent to Moses, the very last of them are nevertheless found not to be later than the earliest of your wise men, lawgivers, and historians.” Yet there he certainly employs several improper modes of expression (Book *On the Resurrection* [Col. 0799C] of Christ, ch. 45; Book *Against Valentinus*, ch. 35). First, he said *posthumant*, that is, “they lived after the death of Moses”; in this sense he wrote *posthumat* and *posthumatum* elsewhere. Second, those whom he here called *extremissimos*, he elsewhere called *postremissimos omnium*, “the last of all.” Third, he called them *retrosiores*, that is, “later and more recent.” But although he employs these obsolete and barbarous expressions, his meaning here is nevertheless clear: our other prophets indeed lived after the death of Moses, but the last of them all are not later than the Greek wise men, lawgivers, and historians.

Furthermore, he proves his opinion by no argument other than setting forth the names of several authors: either because the gentiles could not dispute or resist their public authority, or because it would have taken too long to reproduce every one of their testimonies in this book, in which he wished brevity to be observed. If anyone nevertheless asks that the point be confirmed by at least some testimony, let him hear Theophilus [Col. 0799D] of Antioch arguing as follows (Theophilus of Antioch, Book III *To Autolycus*, pp. 132 ff.): “Zechariah,” he says, “is reckoned the last of the prophets, and he reached the reign of King Darius. But Solon the Athenian, the most ancient lawgiver, is said to have lived in the reigns of Cyrus and Darius. The other prophets, therefore, are older than the other lawgivers, and Moses much more so, since he flourished before the Cretan Jupiter and, as we have said, before the Trojan War itself.” Nor was Theophilus content merely to have said this; rather, by presenting there a very brief chronology, he endeavors to demonstrate it.

[Col. 0800A] Josephus, however, speaks as follows about the age of the historians (Joseph., Book I *Against Apion*, p. 1034): Οἱ μέν τοι τὰς ἱστορίας ἐπιχειρήσαντες συγγράφειν παρ` αὐτοῖς, λέγω δὲ τοὺς περὶ Κάδμόν τε τὸν Μιλήσιον, καὶ τὸν Ἀργεῖον Ἀκουσίλαον, καὶ μετὰ τοῦτον εἴ τινες ἄλλοι λέγονται γένεσθαι, βραχὺ τῆς Περσῶν ἐπὶ τὴν ἑλλάδα στρατείας τῷ χρόνῳ προέλαβον (“Those who attempted to compose histories among them—I mean Cadmus of Miletus, Acusilaus of Argos, and any others said to have lived after him—preceded the Persian expedition against Greece by only a short time”). “Those who attempted to write histories among them”—that is, among the Greeks—“namely Cadmus of Miletus and Acusilaus of Argos, and whoever else is said to have existed after him, preceded the Persian expedition”—that of Cyrus and Darius—“by only a short time” (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 1165 ff., 1355 ff.). We have discussed the wise men of Greece and their age in the first volume of our *Apparatus*. We have treated the period of Moses and the other prophets not only in the same cited passage of our *Apparatus*, [Col. 0800B] but also in the preceding dissertation on the works of Lactantius (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. II, arts. 1 and 2).

Finally, Tertullian informs us that, in order correctly to determine the periods of all those prophets and pagan writers (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 19), one must sit down with many documents—that is, books and chronologies—together with the finger gestures used for reckoning. But what, someone will ask, are those reckoning gestures of the fingers, and to what purpose do they serve? We answer, therefore, that they are nothing other than gestures and movements of the fingers by which the ancients were accustomed to count years or other things. For Juvenal sang concerning the years of the long-lived Nestor (Juvenal, Satire 10, v. 240):

> Fortunate indeed was he who through so many ages  
> Deferred his death, and now counts his years upon his right hand.

[Col. 0800C] Pliny, moreover, relates that a statue of Janus had been made with its fingers arranged in such a manner as to indicate the number of 365 days (Pliny, Book XXXIV, *Natural History*, ch. 7, p. 182). We likewise read in Jerome (Jerome, Book I *Against Jovinian*, p. 146): “The number one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right, and with the same fingers, indeed, but not with the same hand by which brides and widows are indicated on the left, it forms a circle and displays the crown of virginity.” But long before him, Apuleius, when discussing the age of Pudentilla (Apul., *Apology*, II, after the middle, p. 375), wrote: “If you had said thirty years instead of ten, you could have seemed to err through the gesture used in calculation, by opening the fingers that you ought to have curved into a circle. But when you increase by half those forty years which, more easily than the other numbers, are indicated with an outstretched palm [Col. 0800D], you cannot have erred through the gesture of your fingers—unless perhaps, supposing Pudentilla to be thirty years old, you counted two consuls for each year.” Tertullian therefore signifies that greater leisure and a longer digression from his undertaking would be required in order to calculate by those finger gestures the age of so many writers and prophets.

But besides this and the other difficulties of counting years (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 19), “the census records of the Greeks,” he says, “must also be compared.” No one fails to see that the word “books” or “codices” is to be understood there. He calls those books “census records” in which official acts and annals of events had been recorded by scribes and public notaries, or by others. We, however, call these books [Col. 0801A] diaries, and, by the more common designation, public registers of scribes.

But although Tertullian briefly set forth so many arguments to prove the antiquity of sacred Scripture, whoever nevertheless declares that he does not understand their weight and strength seems to have wished to blind himself. Accordingly, we cannot conclude this entire discussion better than with these words of Tertullian himself to the gentiles in another book (Tertull., *On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 5): “But since the divine Scriptures that are in our possession, or in that of the Jews—into whose olive tree we, the wild olive, have been grafted—precede secular literature by no merely slight span of time, as we demonstrated in the appropriate place in establishing their credibility, then, even if the soul borrowed these utterances from writings, it must certainly be believed [Col. 0801B] to have borrowed them from ours, not from yours; because earlier writings are more powerful in instructing the soul than later ones, which themselves had to be instructed by the earlier. Even if we grant that it was instructed from yours, the tradition nevertheless belongs to the original source; and whatever you happened to take and transmit from our writings is entirely ours.” Finally, in the *Apologeticus* he further addresses the same pagans as follows (Idem, *Apologeticus*, ch. 45, p. 499): “You should know that even your own laws, which appear to advance toward innocence, borrowed their form from the divine law, as the more ancient.” And certainly in other dissertations of ours we have shown abundantly that pagan writers drew many things from our sacred books, which they thoroughly corrupted with their perverse errors. But there is no one who cannot readily understand from what has been said how correctly our Tertullian proved [Col. 0801C] their antiquity. Let us now proceed to explain their authority.

## ARTICLE VII. How Tertullian demonstrates that the authority of sacred Scripture is divine, and that the pagans cannot plead ignorance of it

Tertullian derives the supreme authority of sacred Scripture not from its antiquity alone, but especially from the fact that it is divine—that is, committed to writing by men who were inspired by the divine Spirit and who certainly foretold the future (Ibid., ch. 20): “For,” he says, “the truth of prediction is a sufficient testimony of divinity.” No one could deny this, not even the gentiles themselves, who attempted to establish from it that their gods were true gods, [Col. 0801D] because they supposed that future events had been foretold by them. Christians, however, weakened the force of this argument as employed by the gentiles for no other reason than that predictions of this sort, made by fictitious gods, were either false or contrived through the arts and deceptions of demons. For the one true God alone, or prophets filled with his Spirit, can certainly foretell the future. Yet, says our Author, we see that very many things have already come to pass in precisely the manner in which they had been foretold by our sacred seers.

He proves this by a brief enumeration of these predictions (Ibid.). For now, as he says, “lands swallow cities,” just as was predicted by the sacred prophets; that is, cities have been absorbed and swallowed by sudden earthquakes [Col. 0802A] and fissures in the earth (Ibid.). Then: “Seas defraud islands”—islands, namely, which we see engulfed by the waves and storms of the sea (Ibid.). Furthermore: “Foreign and civil wars tear apart; kingdoms dash against kingdoms”; that is, wars split apart not only kingdoms, provinces, and cities, but also citizens, relatives by marriage, and those joined by blood (Ibid.). Moreover: “Famines and pestilences, every local disaster, and the populations of the mountains [an uncertain reading] devastate most things.” The reading in our copies and the old editions is better: “and frequent deaths generally lay waste” (Ibid.). For some strive in vain to defend the word “mountains” by contending that it signifies lions, bears, and other beasts of that kind, by which the mountains are frequented and the fields devastated. For our Author is speaking [Col. 0802B] of human deaths, which occur with the greatest frequency through pestilence, famine, and other disasters of this kind.

He continues: “The functions of the seasons and the duties of the elements stray beyond their proper course” (Ibid.); that is, the customary order of the four seasons of the year and the established order of the elements are thrown into confusion, which he expressed by the improper word “stray beyond their proper course.” Indeed, “The form of nature is disturbed by monsters and portents.” Some wish here to distinguish monsters from portents in such a way that monsters occur in human beings and animals, whereas portents occur in inanimate things. But they have doubtless failed to attend sufficiently to Cicero’s statement that notions of the gods were fashioned contrary to nature from “portents of human beings and cattle” (Cicero, Book II *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 215, line 45). And elsewhere: “Or do those things truly terrify us, if at some time something portentous is said to have been born either from a beast or from a human being [Col. 0802C]?” (Book II *On Divination*, p. 247, line 16). A portent, therefore, is no more said of inanimate things than of human beings and beasts, in which some member is manifestly malformed contrary to nature, or is superfluous, or is lacking. Yet if it should ever be proved to us from Tertullian’s words that a portent really is distinguished from a monster, we shall immediately yield.

Why say more? “The lowly,” he says, “are changed by elevation, and the exalted by humiliation” (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 20, p. 390); that is, the status and condition of human beings are so altered that they either fall from a lofty and supreme station to a lowly and most abject one, or, conversely, rise from the latter to the former. Finally: “Justice grows scarce and iniquity increases; concern for every good discipline grows sluggish”—among the pagans, namely, who hated [Col. 0802D] or despised the Christian religion. For later, as we shall see in the appropriate place, Tertullian himself made it manifest to everyone that justice, piety, holiness, and concern for every good discipline were cultivated and disseminated by Christians. Moreover, no one can deny that the disasters, calamities, and disturbances of affairs which our Author enumerates were truly foretold by our sacred seers, unless he has never read, even cursorily, the books of these men and of other historians or chronologists. As Augustine argues against Faustus the Manichaean: “We demonstrate the credibility of the prophets from those events which they sang would come and which are seen to have come” (August., Book XIII *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, ch. 7, p. 255, vol. VIII). But you may consult Augustine himself, who discusses these matters there [Col. 0803A] at greater length. The disasters of the world which Tertullian said had been predicted by our sacred seers will be treated with him below.

We cannot conceal, however, that future events are foretold in other, far clearer words of sacred Scripture. Such, indeed, are the many predictions concerning the coming Christ, his life, miracles, death, and return to life, which are carefully reported by our Author and by Lactantius, as we have shown in the preceding dissertation (Below, ch. 9, art. 2; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 8, arts. 1 and 2). But our Tertullian himself judged—and not without good reason—that the matters which he now mentions were sufficient to prove the divinity of sacred Scripture, so that there was no need of other examples or proofs.

[Col. 0803B] Nor could it be objected that these Scriptures were concealed by Christians and that pagans did not possess the same opportunity to read and examine them. For although it was a matter of the greatest religious importance to Christians to conceal their sacred mysteries from all others, and even from the catechumens themselves, they nevertheless neither hid nor could hide the books of divine Scripture. Accordingly, Tertullian thus addresses a pagan: “Examine the words of God, our writings, which we neither suppress ourselves, and which many accidents transfer to outsiders” (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 31, p. 446). Does he not by these words, “our writings,” designate in general all the books not only of the Old but also of the New Testament, which he elsewhere called the supplement of the old Instrument (Tertull., Book *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 20)? Christians therefore did not suppress these sacred writings; [Col. 0803C] and although they might have wished to conceal them, they were nevertheless transferred by various accidents to outsiders, that is, pagans.

Moreover, from the time of Philadelphus the books of the Old Testament had been translated, as we have said, from Hebrew into Greek and had come into the hands of those same pagans, who could read them and determine whether they saw the fulfillment of all the things foretold in them. Yet even if the gentiles, through carelessness or obstinacy, had not read these sacred books, Christians nevertheless demonstrated most clearly that the prophecies which we see predicted in them long beforehand were true. Finally, the prophets whose words are recorded in these books most invincibly established and confirmed both their words and [Col. 0803D] their teachings through marvelous powers and miracles, as was observed above. From the matters stated in this and the preceding articles, therefore, Tertullian correctly concludes that the authority of our sacred Scriptures is divine; for this reason he calls them “divine writings” and “holy words” (*Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 469), and asserts that the truth of our religion and its teachings is demonstrated with absolute certainty by the credibility and antiquity of these divine writings (Ibid., ch. 46, p. 501). Let us now endeavor carefully to investigate and examine what he transmitted and asserted in the books presently before us.

# CHAPTER VII. On God and His Divine Perfections and Attributes, and on the Number and Nature of the Disagreements and Errors of the Pagan Philosophers Concerning Him

[Col. 0804A]

## ARTICLE I. An examination of the sixfold argument by which Tertullian demonstrates that God exists: namely, from the authority of sacred Scripture, the consensus of pagan philosophers, the works of God himself, the inward sense and conscience of the human mind, the infinite perfections of God, and the public and frequently repeated confession of demons adjured by Christians

Such is the perfection of the Christian religion that, in order to demonstrate its [Col. 0804B] truth and the falsity of every other religion, a mere, simple, and unadorned exposition of its doctrine, as Tertullian correctly says, is sufficient. For nothing occurs in it that does not plainly accord with the natural light common to all human beings and with right reason. Our Author sets forth its principal tenets, and he begins with that which is the foundation of all the rest: God himself, who is worshiped and adored by Christians.

He therefore shows plainly by various arguments that God exists and is one. First, he says, this is the very God whom nearly every individual page of our sacred Scriptures most openly asserts and proclaims to be the one God, with absolutely no other (Tertull., *Apologeticus*, chs. 17 ff., p. 375). But [Col. 0804C] we have already proved that the authority of that same sacred Scripture is divine. What it therefore proclaims so frequently and clearly concerning the one God who actually exists is certainly most true. For writers inspired by the divine Spirit, as we have seen, can neither lie nor ever lead us into any error.

If any pagan should refuse the labor of even briefly reading through some of the books of sacred Scripture, let him at least read their beginning and the first words of Genesis; there he will find most explicitly revealed what Tertullian said, namely, that there is only one God: “Who brought forth from nothing this entire mass, together with all its apparatus of elements, bodies, and spirits, by the word with which he commanded, by the reason with which he ordered it, and by the power by which he was able”—that is, by which he truly possessed the ability to create the world (Ibid.). [Col. 0804D] Minucius Felix, as we observed in another dissertation, borrowed some of these words, but omitted those which appear more obscure: “together with the apparatus of elements, bodies, and spirits” (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 21, art. 5). Yet these words signify nothing other than that the entire world, and all the things of which it is composed—namely, elements, bodies, and spirits—were created by almighty God, whose existence is therefore absolutely necessary.

Moreover, by these words Tertullian alludes not only to what was written at the beginning of Genesis, as we were saying, but also to other passages of sacred Scripture in which the divine seers proclaim that the heavens were established by the word of God and that the entire world was made from nothing [Col. 0805A] by his wisdom and power. But because Hermogenes and certain other heretics and pagans imagined that the world was made not from nothing but from preexistent matter coeternal with God himself, Tertullian therefore radically extirpates this false opinion with the invincible force of arguments in a special book composed against the same Hermogenes. But we have already explained elsewhere several arguments by which Lactantius destroys this error. Our Tertullian therefore correctly argues from this as follows: “There will be doubt, I suppose, about the powers of God, who imposed this vast body of the world, brought forth from what had not existed, no less than from the death of emptiness and nothingness, and animated by the Spirit who animates all souls” (Tertull., Book *Against Hermogenes*, chs. 8 ff.; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 21, art. 1; Tertull., *Apologeticus*, ch. 48, [Col. 0805B] p. 520).

You clearly hear that his argument is this: God created the world not from matter preexistent or coeternal with himself, but from nothing. Yet to create something from nothing—and, what is far greater, the entire world—is an act of supreme and infinite power. Therefore God, the almighty creator of the world, exists. This is Tertullian’s first argument, by which, from the authority of sacred Scripture—which no one, as we have said, not even a pagan, can gainsay—he correctly demonstrates that God really exists.

Before we proceed to the other arguments, however, it is worth observing that in the cited text of Tertullian Rigaltius arbitrarily removed the word *animarum* (“of souls”) [Col. 0805C] as superfluous, and wrote *composuit* (“composed”) in place of *imposuit* (“imposed”). For all the manuscript codices and earlier printed editions plainly oppose this correction, for which he gave no reason. Furthermore, could not our Author have used the verb *imposuit* loosely in order to express more forcefully what he had said before: that the world was created from nothing by God and, as it were, imposed upon the death of emptiness and nothingness? He could also have added the word *animarum* (“of souls”) for a certain emphasis, to signify more clearly that God is truly the animator and creator not only of bodies but also of souls.

Tertullian’s second argument is drawn from the common agreement of nearly all the Gentile philosophers. Although, as we shall show a little later, they disagree considerably with one another in defining the nature of God, nevertheless, willingly or unwillingly, they confessed that he truly exists [Col. 0805D] (Idem, cap. 47, pag. 516; below, this chapter, art. 4; Dissertat. in Minut. cap. 4, art. 1, and in Lactant. cap. 12, art. 1). But elsewhere we have discussed their opinion at length, and what we said there need not now be repeated.

Tertullian derives a third argument for the existence of the one God from his works. Just as no one, unless he is utterly foolish, can fail to acknowledge them, so no one can deny that the one God is their author. For the world, as Tertullian rightly says, was made by him “as an adornment of his majesty” (Tertullian. Apologet. cap. 17, pag. 375). What, then, is that “as an adornment of the divine majesty,” unless it means as a proof and argument of it, whereby, from the creation of the world, his divine [Col. 0806A] majesty and omnipotence are made manifest and known to everyone, even to those of duller understanding? Lactantius therefore expressly said afterward: “Who kindled the sun, the brightest and singular light for human affairs, as a proof of his unique majesty” (Lactant., lib. II divin. Instit. cap. 5, pag. 161). And certainly the sun was not created by some accident or by itself, being entirely devoid of reason. By its own light and splendor, therefore, it demonstrates that almighty God is its author. We have treated this argument in our dissertation on the books of Lactantius (Dissertat. in Lactant. cap. 12, art. 1).

Nor are the duller eyes of the human mind compelled to acknowledge God only because they are dazzled by the sun’s most brilliant light, but also by his other works: “So many and so great,” says Tertullian, “by which we are contained, [Col. 0806B] by which we are sustained, by which we are delighted, and by which we are terrified” (Tertullian. Apologet. cap. 17, pag. 376). For what else do so many and such great works proclaim, except that they were produced by the one God, who leads human beings to knowledge of himself either by benefits or by terror? And hence, indeed, he added a little later that the signs of his majesty were displayed through rains—undoubtedly those of the universal flood—and through fires, especially those by which the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah were consumed. By whom, I ask you, could these things have been done except by God, the most equitable judge, who exacted from impious and utterly wicked people the punishments due for their crimes?

There are yet other things by which, as Tertullian says, we are terrified: namely lightning flashes, thunderbolts, thunder, public calamities and storms, and other similar things. He seems [Col. 0806C] deliberately to have added these in order to meet the various subtleties of atheists, who object that thunderbolts which, for example, fall upon mountains, and other things of this kind, are wholly useless, and that no reason can be given why they occur. To these garrulous and impious people, who wish to serve depraved desires after scorning or suppressing the conscience of their minds, he replies that these things occur so that we may be terrified—that is, so that we may fear the true God who is their author, and through that fear, which elsewhere he demonstrates to be innate in human beings, acknowledge that he truly exists and can punish those same impious people and other criminals according to their deserts (Idem, lib. de Testimon. anim. cap. 2).

Moreover, we have shown elsewhere that, even if the infinite greatness of God and the cause of some of his works are not fully known [Col. 0806D] to the weak and purblind human mind, nevertheless his existence, and the end for which he made all things, are most manifestly demonstrated from his effects, which are unknown to no one. We are not now asking why or how all things are done or were made by him, but whether he himself exists and whether this is known from his works. In other dissertations of ours, moreover, we have clearly shown how certainly and evidently God’s existence is demonstrated from them, and how feeble is the argument of the pagans who denied it because God himself cannot be seen (Dissert. in Minut. cap. 5, art. 1, and cap. 6, art. 1).

Tertullian derives a fourth demonstration of God’s real existence from the inmost sense of the human soul, or [Col. 0807A] from its testimony and from the human conscience itself. “Would you have us,” he says, “prove it from the testimony of the soul itself? Although confined in the prison of the body, although surrounded by corrupt training, although deprived of vigor by lusts and desires, although enslaved to false gods, nevertheless, when it recovers its senses—as though from drunkenness, from sleep, or from some illness—and experiences its own soundness, it names God by this name alone, because this one true God is properly one, good, and great. And ‘Whatever God may grant’ is the voice of all; it also calls him to witness as judge: ‘God sees’; and ‘I commend it to God’; and ‘God will repay me’” (Tertull. Apolog., cap. 17, p. 376 et seq.). In this text of our author, however, Rigaltius, in his usual manner, altered and added certain things. First, on the sole, though perhaps not altogether unhappy, conjecture of Latinius, he wished the verb *patitur* to be corrected and written [Col. 0807B] *potitur*: that is, he says, “while it is possessed of a sound mind.” And certainly the noun *sanitas* is sometimes used for a sound condition of mind, while in good authors we read *potiri gaudia*, “to possess joys.” In two more recent manuscripts, however, *pascitur*, “is nourished,” is written. But what if Tertullian, speaking less classically, said *patitur sanitatem*, “it undergoes soundness,” namely a soundness not yet complete?

Whatever the case, Rigaltius seems on his private authority to have substituted for these words, “By this alone, because properly this one God is one, good, and great,” the following: “By this alone, because by the proper name of the true God: ‘God is great, God is good.’” But were not the words of the manuscripts sufficiently perspicuous, and no less clear than these? Yet suppose that they were more obscure: must hands therefore be laid upon the text of an ancient author, so that it may be corrected at pleasure and no longer remain his?

[Col. 0807C] Our Tertullian does not use this argument against the pagans only in this book, but also presses it more fully and forcefully throughout his book *On the Testimony of the Soul against the Nations*. There he teaches that this testimony of the soul itself is “better known than all literature, more discussed than all doctrine, more widely published than any edition, greater than the whole human being”—that is, the whole of what belongs to a human being (Idem, lib. de testim. anim. cap. 1). We have cited other words of his elsewhere and shown openly that the same argument was employed by Minucius Felix, Cyprian, Arnobius, and Lactantius, who, following in our author’s footsteps, overwhelmed all worshipers of false gods and all atheists by the force and weight of this argument (Dissertat. in Minut., cap. 2, art. 5, and cap. 3, art. 3; Dissertat. in Arnob. cap. 5, art. 1, and Dissertat. in Lactant. cap. 12, art. 1).

[Col. 0807D] We therefore judge that these matters should not be repeated here. We must examine only why he said that this natural invocation of God is the testimony of a soul “naturally Christian.” Is the soul, then, naturally Christian? Did he not say a little later: “Christians are made, not born” (Tertullian. Apologet. cap. 17, pag. 377; Ibid. cap. 18, pag. 378)? Elsewhere, moreover, he addresses the soul itself in this manner: “You are not, so far as I know, Christian; for you are accustomed to become, not to be born, Christian” (Idem, lib. de Testim. anim., cap. 1). But if a human being is not born but becomes Christian, then his soul is not naturally Christian. Yet Tertullian, who certainly did not contradict himself within a few lines, means by the earlier words nothing other than that a conception of the true God is naturally implanted in the human soul [Col. 0808A], and this is the foundation of the whole Christian religion. It does not, however, know all the other mysteries and teachings of that religion unless it is first instructed by others. In this way, therefore, Christians are made and are not born, although they naturally acknowledge and invoke the one God.

Would you have this proved to you from Tertullian himself? In writing *To the Nations*, he states that Father Liber, together with his sacred rites, was expelled from the city of Rome and from all Italy by authority of the senate, and that the statues of Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates were overthrown. From this, however, he draws the following conclusion: “You therefore have among your ancestors, if not the name, at least the Christian sect, which disregards the gods” (Tertull. lib. I ad Nation. cap. 10, pag. 573). Do you see that merely because of this deed he calls certain pagans by the name of the Christian sect [Col. 0808B]? In the same way, therefore, the soul could be called naturally Christian because, by the testimony of its own conscience and by a natural light and impulse, it acknowledges the one true God. But we have already observed that Minucius Felix advances statements wholly similar to these (Dissertat. in Minut., cap. 13, art. 4).

Rightly and deservedly, therefore, Tertullian concludes from this, and from all the things he had proved thus far, as follows: “This is the sum of the offense of those who refuse to recognize him whom they cannot fail to know” (Apol., c. 17, pag. 376). The conclusion of Cyprian, his pupil and follower, is wholly the same: “And this is the sum of the offense: to refuse to acknowledge him whom one cannot fail to know” (Cyprian., lib. de idolor. Vanit., pag. 15). For no one can plead ignorance of God, whom one is compelled to acknowledge by so many arguments and by the inmost sense of heart and soul [Col. 0808C]. It is therefore a very great offense—indeed, the greatest of all offenses—to refuse to recognize God, who cannot be unknown to anyone unless he is utterly witless and insane.

A fifth demonstration of what is called the divine existence is contained in these words, by which our author draws his conclusion from the infinite perfections of God: “For this reason,” he says, “God is true and so great” (Ibid.). Does he not argue in the following manner? By the name “true God” is understood one whose perfections are infinite and than whom nothing greater or more perfect can be conceived; for he would not be the true God if he were not so great. But he who embraces infinite perfections within himself assuredly has from himself both the fact that he exists and the power to grant existence and being to others. For since the sequence of all created things [Col. 0808D] is such that later things received from earlier ones the origin by which they exist, there had to be, before all time, someone who received his existence from no one but rather possessed it from himself, and who bestowed upon every created thing all the perfections with which it is endowed. But he is true precisely because he is so great. In his book *Against Marcion*, moreover, from the supreme perfection of God he concludes that God is unique, so that he would not exist if he were not one. I should like you to hear what his argument is:

“Since God is the supreme greatness, our truth has rightly pronounced: ‘If God is not one, he does not exist.’ We do not say, ‘If he is not one, he does not exist,’ as though we doubted that God exists; rather, because we trust that he exists, we define him as being that which, if he is not, he is not God—namely, the supreme greatness. [Col. 0809A] Moreover, the supreme greatness must necessarily be unique; therefore God also will be unique: he is not otherwise God unless he is the supreme greatness, nor otherwise the supreme greatness unless he has no equal, nor otherwise without an equal unless he is unique” (Idem., lib. I advers. Marcion., cap. 3).

A sixth and final demonstration proving that God exists was furnished to Tertullian by the supreme and marvelous power of Christians to expel demons, against which even the most obstinate pagan could not utter so much as a murmur. For very often demons, adjured by Christians in the name of Christ, were not only expelled from the persons whom they possessed, but were also compelled openly and publicly to confess that neither they nor the others worshiped by the pagans were gods, but that only one God existed, whom the disciples [Col. 0809B] of Christ worshiped. “But this entire confession of theirs,” says Tertullian, “by which they deny that they are gods and by which they answer that there is no other God besides the one to whom we are bound, is sufficiently effective to repel the charge of having violated especially the Roman religion,” which worshiped not the one true God, but false gods indeed (Tertullian. Apologet., cap. 24, pag. 416). For all the pagans were assuredly obliged to believe demons when they confessed the truth against themselves, since they believed them when they lied. For no one, as he rightly argues, “lies to his own disgrace, but rather to his own honor. Credence is more readily accorded to those who confess against themselves than to those who deny in their own favor” (Ibid., cap. 23, pag. 415). So public a testimony could plainly be doubtful or suspect to no one. For that reason, our author [Col. 0809C] continues, it was accustomed “to make Christians out of pagans” (Ibid.). For what person could reject testimony so certain and clear, unless false prejudices or private interests had utterly deprived him of the light of reason? Rightly and deservedly, therefore, our author reproves the extreme injustice of the pagans, who accused Christians of violating the Roman religion and, contrary to conscience and to so many demonstrations of such great weight, strove by every kind of torture to compel them to worship false gods and deny the true God.

## ARTICLE II. On the perfections or attributes of God; in what sense Tertullian says that God is known to human beings although he is invisible, incomprehensible, and inestimable; and on the knowledge, wisdom, and eternity of this true and living God

[Col. 0809D]

Tertullian rightly infers that God is supremely perfect from the fact that the world and everything in it were created by him, as we saw in the preceding article (Tertullian. Apologet., cap. 11). “For that which perfected all things,” he says, “could not have been imperfect”; that is, because God exists from himself and made all other things, he must have absolutely nothing imperfect in him, but must possess every perfection whatsoever.

These perfections, however, are so great, and so far surpass the weakness of human understanding, that he is “invisible” (Ibid., cap. 17, pag. 375), says our author—that is, he cannot [Col. 0810A] be seen by human eyes. For, as he himself speaks in Exodus (Exod., cap. XXXIII, 20): “Man shall not see me and live.” Tertullian nevertheless adds, “although he is seen”; that is, although human beings, by the arguments and demonstrations set forth above (Art. super.), mentally see and know that he truly exists.

“He is also incomprehensible,” Tertullian continues (Tertullian., ibid.). For Clement of Alexandria acknowledges (Clem. Alexandr., lib. V Strom., pag. 548): Δῆλον μηδένα ποτὲ δυνάσθαι παρὰ τὸν τῆς ζωῆς χρόνον τὸν Θεὸν ἐναργῶς καταλαβέσθαι. No one can ever comprehend God clearly during the course of this life. By these words both authors mean that the infinite perfections of God cannot be fully and thoroughly comprehended by human beings living this mortal life through a clear and distinct idea and conception [Col. 0810B]. Yet he adds: “Although he is represented through grace.” But what is this grace if not that of Christ our Savior, who, having become man, taught human beings how they might understand both him and his divine Father to be the one true God? For, as the author of the Epistle to Diognetus writes, “No one has seen or perfectly known God” (Epist. Diognet., pag. 499, edit. Justin. Martyr): Αὐτὸς δὲ ἑαυτὸν ἐπέδειξεν· ἐπέδειξε δὲ διὰ πίστεως ᾗ μονῇ Θεὸν ἰδεῖν συγκεχώρηται. “But he revealed himself; and he revealed himself through faith, by which alone it has been granted to see God.” Did not both authors have in view those words of Matthew (Matth. XI, 17): “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him”? Or those words of John (Joan., cap. I, 18): [Col. 0810C] “No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known.”

Our author continues: “Inestimable, although he is estimated by human senses”; that is, human beings estimate him rightly in this respect, that they know him to be inestimable (Tertullian. Apologet., cap. 17, pag. 375). For he himself immediately added: “This is what enables God to be estimated: that he does not admit of estimation,” just as if he had said: We estimate God rightly when we confess that neither we nor any other human being can estimate him according to his worth.

If you ask him for the reason for all these statements, he will give it in the same place: “That which can commonly be seen, comprehended, and estimated is less than the eyes by which it is occupied, the hands by which it is defiled, and the senses by which it is discovered”; that is, whatever is commonly perceived by [Col. 0810D] bodily eyes, touched by hands, or falls under the other senses is less than all those senses and belongs to an order lower than God (Ibid.). “For that which is immeasurable,” as God is, “is known to itself alone” (Ibid.). By the term “immeasurable,” however, Tertullian does not mean precisely that which exists everywhere and in every place, but that which is infinite. For in this sense good authors speak of “immeasurable toil,” “immeasurable grief,” or “immeasurable desire.” God, therefore, being infinite, is known only by himself in the full measure of what he is (Ibid.). And thus, as our author again says, “the force of his greatness presents him to human beings as both known and unknown” (Dissertat. in Minut. Octav., cap. 5, art. 1; Dissert. in Lactant. cap. 13, [Col. 0811A] art. 1). For so great indeed is his greatness and the excellence of that divine nature that, although human beings know with absolute certainty that he exists, they nevertheless cannot grasp how great and of what character all his perfections are. But we have already discussed all these matters in our preceding dissertations.

Moreover, we observe that Tertullian asserts not only these so-called negative attributes of God, but also several others called affirmative attributes (Tertullian. Apologet., cap. 30, pag. 441). For he calls God true and living, and thus sets him in opposition to the false and dead gods of the pagans.

He then teaches that God is the observer of all things, whose fullness of knowledge is infinite and from whom absolutely nothing can ever be hidden by any difficulty of concealment [Col. 0811B] (Ibid., cap. 45, pag. 500). He proclaims this divine knowledge not only in the *Apologeticum*, but also in another book. For elsewhere we read these words committed to writing by him (Idem. lib. de Poenit. cap. 3): “Nor, if human mediocrity judges the deed alone because it is unequal to penetrating the hiding places of the will, should we therefore suppose that the will’s offenses are disregarded even under God. God is sufficient for all things. Nothing is removed from his sight, however the sin may be committed.” He therefore penetrates all the inmost and more deeply hidden recesses of the human heart, and accordingly knows perfectly all other things whatsoever.

With no less assurance he declares that God has been rational from eternity, since he brought forth the Word—as will be shown more fully below—the Discourse, *Sophia*, or Wisdom; and, having fashioned the world by word, reason, and wisdom, created it [Col. 0811C] from nothing. He therefore preceded all time and is eternal (Idem, Apologet., cap. 17, pag. 375; cap. 11, pag. 332).

Elsewhere, indeed, he confirms this in the following words (Ibid., cap. 26): “He who existed before time and made the age, the body of times.” Here the noun “body” is used for a collection of several things and an assembled multitude. Thus one speaks of the body of a city or commonwealth. Of Christians, moreover, our author himself says: “We are a body.” His meaning, therefore, is (Ibid., cap. 39): “God made the age, the body of times”; that is, he caused the world to consist of the complete collection of times (Ibid., cap. 18, pag. 377). For this reason he had previously said: “God arranged the age according to fixed arrangements and endings of times.” But he could not have done this unless, as he himself says, he had existed before all [Col. 0811D] time and was therefore eternal. Nor should you doubt that this is the meaning of the one who elsewhere wrote in the name of the Christians (Ibid., cap. 30): “We invoke the eternal God.” There he proclaims him not only eternal, but also almighty, in whose power all things are placed.

## ARTICLE III. It is shown that Tertullian truly believed God to be spirit and to possess nothing corporeal, and contrary arguments are answered

What has thus far been explained concerning so many and such great perfections and attributes of God manifestly demonstrates that they are supreme, and that God possesses from himself alone, and [Col. 0812A] from no other, whatever he is. But if nothing accrues to him from another, if his perfections are infinite, and if they can never be circumscribed by anyone, his nature is undoubtedly most simple and therefore spiritual and wholly free from every corporeal composition. He therefore has no body, since a body is necessarily composed of parts and can consequently be dissolved and is imperfect. But what need is there to prove this teaching of our author by argument? Did he not proclaim it most openly in these words (Tertullian. Apologet., cap. 21): “We have declared him to be God; as his proper substance we designate spirit”? And a little later: “For God also is spirit.”

I would not have you reply that by the word “spirit” he there understands some body, albeit one far more subtle than other bodies. [Col. 0812B] For in the same place he says that the Word, Discourse, and Son of God proceeded from the bosom of his eternal Father, “spirit from spirit, and God from God” (Ibid.). Yet that eternal bringing-forth by God, prior to every created body, can plainly admit nothing corporeal. For it is God’s own thought and intelligence, which must be entirely incorporeal and purely spiritual. Tertullian therefore truly believed God the Father and his Son to be spirit, possessing absolutely nothing of body or of matter, however subtle.

Nevertheless, some protest against this and object to us that Tertullian taught that whatever exists is either a body or nothing, and that nothing intermediate between the two can be assigned. For these are his very words: “Everything that exists is a body of its own kind. [Col. 0812C] Nothing is incorporeal except that which does not exist” (Idem, lib. de Carne Christi, cap. 11). This proposition of his is undoubtedly universal, and accordingly he expressly defines whatever exists—whether God or anything else—as being a body by the very fact that it exists. Since, therefore, he proved by so many arguments, as we have seen, that the one true God exists, he assuredly believed him to be truly corporeal.

But what need is there, others will say, for this or any other argument? Does he not speak of God himself in this manner? “Who will deny that God is a body, even though God is spirit? For spirit is a body of its own kind, in its own form. But even all those invisible things, whatever they may be, have before God both their own body and their own form, through which they are visible to God alone” (Idem, liber adv. Prax., [Col. 0812D] cap. 7).

Yet however universal his first proposition may be, he nevertheless distinguishes some substance intermediate between body and nothing: one that is spiritual, and a spirit distinct from body. Indeed, in the *Apologeticum* with which we are dealing, he said that this mass of the world was created by God “with its whole apparatus of elements, bodies, and spirits” (Idem, Apologet. cap. 17). But what need was there to add “spirits” if he had believed body and spirit to be one and the same? Will you perhaps reply that by “bodies” are meant dense and coarser bodies, while by the word “spirits” more subtle and extremely fine bodies are meant? But these are merely different qualities of bodies, which [Col. 0813A] could adequately have been designated by the word “bodies” alone. By the word “spirits,” however, he undoubtedly seems to signify not qualities of bodies but something distinct from every body.

What of the fact that in another book he wholly and completely distinguishes a spiritual thing from a corporeal one? For when discussing the sins and offenses of a human being, who, as he says, consists of body and spirit, he openly declares that “some offenses are carnal, that is, corporeal, while others are spiritual” (Idem, lib. de Poenit. cap. 3). Then a little later: “Hence they are called spiritual and corporeal, because every offense is either enacted or conceived. That which is in the deed is corporeal, because the deed, like a body, is capable of being both seen and touched. That which is in the mind, however, is spiritual, because spirit [Col. 0813B] is neither seen nor touched. From this it is understood that not only offenses of deed but also offenses of will must be avoided.” He therefore acknowledges that sins are of two kinds: namely corporeal sins, which are perpetrated by the body with no resistance from the mind and will, and other sins belonging to the spirit alone, which are committed by thought and will alone, without any service of the body. Indeed, he also teaches that there are other acts proper to our soul which are in no way dependent upon its body, and for which not only punishment but also reward is due (Idem, lib. de Anim., cap. 58). Yet he considered these good or evil acts of the soul alone, deserving reward or punishment, to be neither body nor nothing, but something intermediate. He therefore thought that some things are solely spiritual and not at all corporeal.

[Col. 0813C] As regards that second proposition of his concerning God, does he not, as we have said, expressly affirm that God’s Son is his own wisdom, internal word and discourse, or intelligence, which is entirely incorporeal and wholly spiritual? How, then, can this be so unless God is wholly incorporeal and spirit? Furthermore, it is quite sufficient that he admits some spiritual substance intermediate between body and nothing. For if there is any such substance, who will deny that God is such above all?

You will nevertheless insist that he recognizes nothing third between the corporeal and incorporeal. For he argues against Hermogenes as follows: “Unless I am mistaken, every thing must necessarily be either corporeal or incorporeal—even if for the moment I concede that there is something incorporeal among substances alone [Col. 0813D], though substance itself is the body of each thing. Certainly, after the corporeal and incorporeal there is nothing third” (Idem, ad Hermog., cap. 35). Yet there he undoubtedly seems to admit incorporeal things rather than deny them. For there, as has been said, he refutes Hermogenes, who babbled that matter, although truly existing, was both corporeal and incorporeal. Tertullian, in order utterly to overturn this fiction of a vain opinion, divides every thing into corporeal and incorporeal. He thus acknowledges that something is incorporeal. And if anything is incorporeal, God certainly is so before all else.

You may perhaps urge that this division did not seem wholly complete to Tertullian himself. For he does not pronounce it absolutely, but, [Col. 0814A] without asserting anything, concedes gratuitously and for the moment to his adversary that some substance is incorporeal, although it is nevertheless the body of the thing itself. He therefore thought that nothing existed except the corporeal. But observe, I ask, that he is concerned only with the meaning of this word “body.” In the same place he explains with sufficient clarity what he understood by this word: “Substance itself,” he says, “is the body of each thing.” He therefore thinks that by the word “body” the substance of each thing is signified. Yet there is no one who does not acknowledge that there is absolutely no intermediate or third thing between substance and nothing itself. And what wonder is it if he thought the term “body” should be understood as the substance itself of each thing, since the apostle Paul sets this very word “body” in opposition to shadows and figures and said that it is that which is the thing itself and the truth? For he writes in the following manner concerning the figures of the Old Testament [Col. 0814B] (Paul. ad Coloss., II, 17): “Which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ”; that is: These ceremonies are nothing other than shadows, but their body—the thing itself and the truth—is Christ, in whom they are fulfilled.

For this reason, in those passages of our Tertullian which have been objected against us, where he said that every substance is a body or that whatever exists is a body, he did not without deliberation add “of its own kind”; that is, the substance is of its own kind, whether corporeal or spiritual.

But someone will insist that, even if this were most clearly proved, it might nevertheless be questioned whether Tertullian at one time thought God to be a body and afterward changed his mind and opinion. For Augustine speaks of him in this manner [Col. 0814C] (August., lib de Genes. ad litter., cap. 26, pag. 273):

“Tertullian believed the soul to be a body for no other reason than that he could not conceive it as incorporeal; and therefore he feared that it would be nothing if it were not a body. Nor did he wish to think differently about God. Yet because he was indeed acute, at times he is overcome by the truth when it presents itself, contrary to his own opinion. For what could he have said more truly than what he states in a certain passage: ‘Everything corporeal is passible’ (Tertul. lib. de Anim. cap. 7)? He ought therefore to have changed the opinion by which a little earlier he had said that even God is a body. For I do not think that he was so foolish as to believe that even the nature of God is passible, so that Christ might now be believed passible and mutable not only in the flesh but also in the Word itself, through which all things were made—a thought far from the Christian heart.”

[Col. 0814D] Petavius, however, disagrees with Augustine and does not think that Tertullian contradicts himself or changed his opinion concerning a corporeal God, although he believed every body to be passible but the nature of God to be in no way passible (Petav. tom. I, Theolog. dogmat., cap. 1, § 5 et seqq.). For the passions that he attributes to a corporeal thing, Petavius says, are of one kind, while those attributed to God—that is, other movements and affections—are of another. For when Marcion denied that there was a movement of anger in God and objected that, if God were ever angry, he would be liable to corruption and death, Tertullian himself replied that the passions, movements, feelings, and affections of the mind in God and in man are indeed called by the same names, but are as different in each as substance and body differ from one another. For he addresses Marcion in these words [Col. 0815A]:

“Distinguish the substances and distribute to them their respective feelings, as different as the substances require, although they may appear to share their names” (Idem, lib. II advers. Marcion., cap. 16) . . . . “As great as the difference between the divine body and the human body under the same names for their members, so great will be the difference between the divine and human mind, although under the same names for their members; the corruptibility of human substance makes these as corruptive in man as the incorruptibility of the divine substance makes them incorruptive in God.”

Petavius therefore infers from this that Tertullian thought there was a body both in God and in man, just as there were passions or sensations, movements, and affections, but with this difference: that in man they are corruptive, whereas in God they are incorruptive. Nothing therefore prevents God, [Col. 0815B] he says, from having a body according to Tertullian’s opinion, a body which he thought not passible but incorruptive. But consider, I ask, whether Petavius fully perceived the sense in which Tertullian understood the term “passible,” which he excludes from God. For by it Tertullian seems to signify nothing other than that which carries with it something imperfect and mutable. Did Augustine not therefore rightly say that Tertullian either contradicted himself or changed his opinion when he asserted that God is a body and that every body is passible? For God is supremely perfect and is endowed with the highest simplicity and every kind of perfection. He can therefore have absolutely nothing imperfect. Thus the supreme perfection of God and body conflict with one another and cannot exist together in God.

[Col. 0815C] Moreover, although Petavius had proved that Tertullian did not fall into any contradiction, that most learned man nevertheless acknowledges that what Augustine reported in another book in order to excuse Tertullian is of greater importance (August., lib. de Haeresib., cap. 86, pag. 25):

“Tertullian might in some fashion be thought to have regarded the divine nature and substance itself as a body whose parts could or should be conceived as some greater and others smaller, as is the case with all things that we properly call bodies . . . But he could, as I have said, have been thought to call God a body for this reason: because he is not nothing, is not emptiness, and is not a quality of body or soul, but is whole everywhere, divided by no intervals of space, and yet remains immutably in his own nature and substance.”

It will perhaps seem surprising to some who do not sufficiently know [Col. 0815D] Augustine’s modesty why he does not dare fully to affirm that this was truly Tertullian’s opinion, but says only that it can in some fashion be thought to have been so. For we have already shown that Tertullian declared with sufficient clarity that by the term “body” he understood substance, which exists in some manner and is opposed to nothing. Furthermore, we have observed that he divides substance into corporeal and incorporeal—that is, wholly free from every body and purely spiritual. But if he ever thought that even one such substance existed, he was certainly persuaded that God is spirit and by far more excellent than all others. And surely his supreme perfections and his infinite cognition and knowledge of all things, so clearly vindicated by Tertullian, as we observed a little [Col. 0816A] above, can possess nothing corporeal whatsoever. For no body, however fine; no matter, however agitated by motion; and no atoms, however joined together by collision, can produce knowledge of any thing, much less of all things. Tertullian therefore could not have attributed a body or anything corporeal to God unless, as we have seen, by this word he understood a substance of its own kind—that is, divine and spiritual. But further light will be cast upon these matters by what will be said in the following chapter concerning the divinity of Christ, and afterward concerning angels and demons and the human soul.

## ARTICLE IV. How many and of what kind were the disagreements of the Gentile philosophers concerning God: of Thales, or Simonides, who, when questioned about him, could give no answer; of the Platonists, who taught that he cares for all things; of the Epicureans, that he cares for nothing; of the Platonists, that he is within the world; of the Stoics, that he is situated outside it; of Plato, that he is the creator of the world; and of Pythagoras, that the world is uncreated; and whether Tertullian correctly explained their opinions

[Col. 0816B]

Although the Gentile philosophers, either by natural reason or from the sacred Scriptures, as Tertullian says, recognized—or could without much difficulty have recognized—that there is only one God (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47), they nevertheless never ceased fighting among themselves, whether through the vice of vainglory or a passion for disputation, over the very nature, character, and dwelling-place of God. “For what certain answer,” [Col. 0816C] in the words of our author, “did Thales, that chief of the natural philosophers, give to Croesus when he questioned him about the Divinity? None at all; rather, though repeatedly granted time for deliberation, he disappointed him” (*Ibid.*, ch. 46; and bk. II *Ad Nationes*, ch. 2). But Cicero, and Minucius Felix, who, as we have seen elsewhere, follows him, attributed this to Simonides and the tyrant Hiero (*Dissertat. in Minut.*, ch. 3, art. 2). Nor should you reply that some corruption underlies Tertullian’s text. For he calls Thales the chief of the natural philosophers (*Ibid.*, ch. 4, art. 1, vol. I; *Apparat.*, p. 1119 ff.), that is, the first of those who, as we have also shown, instituted disputations on natural subjects. To determine, however, whether Tertullian’s opinion is truer than that of Cicero and Minucius, the respective ages of Thales, Simonides, and Croesus must be investigated. [Col. 0816D] According to Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, in the year 1266 Thales of Miletus is recognized as a natural philosopher. Under the year 1465, however, “the events related of Croesus—how he tested the oracles—occurred at this time.” Two years afterward, Thales dies. Thus, as Scaliger observes, two men named Thales are recorded: the earlier, a natural philosopher in the age of Lycurgus and Orpheus; the later, said to have flourished almost two hundred years afterward, in the time of Croesus (Scaliger, notes on Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, p. 74). Yet Tertullian speaks of Thales, the chief of the natural philosophers, who, being two centuries older than Croesus, could not have lived at the same time as he did and consequently could not have answered him.

Simonides, however, is said in the same Eusebian *Chronicle* to have lived in the year 1531. For there we read: “Pindar [Col. 0817A] and Simonides are regarded as distinguished lyric poets.” Later, under the year 1542, Hiero, whom Minucius Felix mentions, exercised the tyranny at Syracuse after Gelon. Thus, by as much as the earlier Thales is separated in time from Croesus, Simonides is said to have been close in time to Hiero. The cited question and answer concerning the Divinity therefore fit Simonides better than Thales, the chief of the natural philosophers. Moreover, Minucius’ opinion seems still more probable because it is supported by Cicero’s authority.

Nor should you say that Eusebius’ *Chronicle* contains many errors in assigning the dates of illustrious men; for whatever those errors may be, no one will deny that the times of Thales the natural philosopher and Croesus are farther separated from one another than would permit them to be said to have lived together. Nor is there any reason [Col. 0817B] for you to insist that the recorded answer properly suits Thales, a philosopher and chief of the natural philosophers, but by no means Simonides, who, as we have seen elsewhere, devoted himself to poetry (*Dissertat. in Minuc. Octav.*, ch. 3, art. 2; and vol. I, *Apparat.*, p. 1284). For among the Gentiles poets were counted among theologians.

Finally, relying upon Cicero’s testimony, Minucius could correct Tertullian’s opinion concerning the first Thales and Croesus, even though, as we have observed, he excerpted many things from Tertullian’s books. And indeed, how could this Thales, when questioned about the Divinity, have dared give no answer, when—as we have noted elsewhere, following the same Cicero—he taught, as confidently as falsely, that water was the beginning of all things, and that God was the mind that formed all things from water (Cicero, bk. I *De Natura* [Col. 0817C] *Deorum*, p. 199; *Dissertat. in Minut.*, ch. 4, art. 1; and *in Lactant.*, ch. 12, art. 1)? No one has shown us that he ever doubted this opinion or ever changed it.
