Furthermore, if anyone proves that this answer about God should be attributed to the second Thales, he will show that these words must be deleted from Tertullian’s text: “chief of the natural philosophers.” But whoever the philosopher was who gave that answer, who will call into doubt that he asserted it? He therefore openly confessed that the Divinity was unknown to him.

In the second book *Ad Nationes*, however, Tertullian placed Diogenes before Thales. When asked what happens in heaven—these are Tertullian’s own words—he said: “I have never ascended into heaven” (Tertullian, bk. II *Ad Nationes*, ch. 2). Likewise, when asked whether gods existed, he answered: “I do not know, [Col. 0817D] except that it is expedient that they should”; that is: I do not know, but it is useful and expedient for everyone that gods should exist. This is not very far removed from the former answer, which Laertius reports was given by Diogenes the Cynic to a man discoursing on celestial matters: Ποσταῖος πάρει ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ “When did you come down from heaven?” (Laertius, bk. VI, *Life of Diogenes*, §39). But consider, please, whether the following answer of the same Diogenes to Lysias the druggist, who asked whether he believed that gods existed, is farther removed from the second: Πῶς οὐ νομίζω, ὅπου καὶ σε θεοῖς ἐχθρὸν υπολαμβάνω “How could I not believe it, when I regard you as an enemy of the gods?” (*Ibid.*, §42). Laertius nevertheless warns us in the same place that this saying is attributed to Theodorus, who was undoubtedly surnamed “the atheist,” as we have observed more than once. Yet if you contend that the statements which our Tertullian [Col. 0818A] ascribes to Diogenes were written by another man of the same name, but an atheist, we do indeed have Aelian, who, as some say, numbered Diogenes the Phrygian among this band of wicked men (Aelian, bk. II *Varia Historia*, §31). But besides the fact that our edition of Aelian’s books reads “Dionysius the Phrygian,” no one has indicated to us where this Diogenes, or Dionysius, uttered the words cited by our author.

There was, however, the greatest variety and disagreement among the other philosophers’ opinions about God. “Some,” says Tertullian—namely, the Platonists—“assert that God is incorporeal” (*Apologeticus*, ch. 47, p. 515). Would you like a witness to be produced? Here is Cicero, who introduces Velleius speaking thus about Plato: [Col. 0818B] “But as for his wish that God should be without any body, what the Greeks call ἀσώματον, it is impossible to understand what such a thing could be” (Cicero, bk. I *De Natura Deorum*, p. 200, l. 13). Laertius relates the same concerning this chief of the philosophers: “He holds,” he says, “that the soul, like God, is incorporeal ἀσώματον εἶναι” (Laertius, bk. III, *Life of Plato*, §77). Plutarch, Eusebius, Apuleius, and others agree with Laertius (Plutarch, bk. I *De Placitis Philosophorum*, ch. 7, p. 881; Eusebius, *Oration of Constantine*, p. 200; Plato, vol. III, pp. 27–28; and elsewhere Apuleius, *On God*).

However true this opinion may be, it was nevertheless rejected by other Gentile philosophers. For Velleius in Cicero, as we were just saying, maintained that it was impossible to understand what or of what kind that which is called incorporeal [Col. 0818C] might be (Socrates; Cicero, loc. cit.). Nor could the other philosophers explain what the true idea and notion of an incorporeal thing is.

“But the Stoics,” our author continues, “proclaimed that God is corporeal” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47 [the printed “515” appears corrupt]; vol. I, *Apparat.*, bk. III, diss. 1, ch. 11, art. 2; *Dissertat. in Minut.*, ch. 4, art. 10). We have discussed elsewhere this opinion of the Stoics, which, because of their contradictions, is not free of difficulties. We have also cited several authors who testify that they really did fall into this error.

Tertullian continues: “Some—namely Epicurus and his followers—chattered that God consists of atoms; others, such as Pythagoras, of numbers; others, like Heraclitus, of fire” (Tertullian, loc. cit., [Col. 0818D] vol. I, *Apparat.*, p. 435; *Dissertat. in Minut.*, loc. cit.; *Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 12, art. 1). All these men believed that these were the first principles of all things and that the gods were nothing other than these, as we have observed elsewhere more than once.

We have no less clearly proved that the philosophers held various and mutually opposed opinions concerning divine providence, as Tertullian calls it. “For the Platonists,” he says, “proclaimed that he takes care of things; the Epicureans, by contrast, that he is idle and inactive and, so to speak, a nonentity in relation to human affairs” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47; and bk. II *Ad Nationes*, ch. 2). If you desire more concerning Plato, go to Laertius, and you will hear him say: οἴεται καὶ θεοὺς ἐφορᾷν τὰ ἀνθρώπινα. [Col. 0819A] “He holds that the gods both observe and care for human affairs” (Laertius, bk. III, *Life of Plato*, §78). There is no need to cite many others, since Plato himself asserted this repeatedly (Plato, *Phaedo*, vol. I, p. 62, after the middle). For in one place he says that God cares for us no differently than for his own property and possession: Τὸ θεόν τε εῖναι τὸν ἐπιμελουμένον ἡμῶν, καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐκείνου κτήματα εἶναι (the same, bk. X *Laws*, p. 285). Elsewhere, however, he confidently asserts that the first madness is to deny the gods, and the second to assert that they have no care for men: Τὸ δεύτερον ὄντας οὐ φροντίζειν ἀνθρώπων (*Ibid.*, p. 899 ff.). But afterward he pursues this at greater length and refutes and overthrows that mad error (*Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 14, art. 1). Yet the error of Epicurus and his followers is utterly absurd, as we [Col. 0819B] have demonstrated.

For this reason our author added shortly afterward that the Platonists’ opinion concerning God’s dwelling-place was that he resides within the world, remaining, after the manner of a governor, within that which he governs (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47; and bk. II *Ad Nationes*, ch. 2). And indeed Plato determines and proves that this world is constantly governed according to a fixed and established order by a certain marvelous mind and wisdom, which is God himself (Plato, *Philebus*, vol. II, p. 28 ff.). In another of his books, however, we read that God, the governor of the universe, after the world and all things had been created, let go the reins by which it was governed and returned, as it were, to his watchtower (the same, *Politicus*, p. 272 ff.). But afterward, lest the world, buffeted by various storms and evils, [Col. 0819C] should be utterly dissolved, he resumed its helm and, taking anxious charge of it, arranged and governs the parts of that same world.

Against this opinion of the Platonists, however, the Stoics proclaimed, as Tertullian says, that God is situated outside the world and, like a potter, turns this mass from without (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47; and bk. II *Ad Nationes*, ch. 2). But there is considerable room for doubt as to whether this was in fact the Stoics’ position. For Zeno, their leader, and his followers, as may be learned from Laertius and Plutarch, believed God to be a mind that reaches and penetrates all things (Laertius, bk. VII, *Life of Zeno*, §§138, 147; Plutarch, bk. I *De Placitis Philosophorum*, ch. 7, p. 882). We have also observed elsewhere that this [Col. 0819D] really was their opinion. By what reasoning, then, could our author so confidently affirm that the Stoics taught that God, like a potter, is situated outside the entire mass of the world fashioned by him (vol. I, *Apparat.*, p. 780; Lipsius, bk. I *Psychologia Stoica*, diss. 31, p. 565, vol. IV)?

Lipsius cuts rather than unties the knot of this difficulty. For without hesitation he charges Tertullian here with the error of attributing to the Stoics something they had neither said nor even thought. Did Tertullian truly err, then? Was he ignorant of, or had it slipped his mind, what the Stoics taught concerning the divine mind permeating the whole world? Certainly not. For in another book he committed these words to writing: [Col. 0820A] “The Stoics hold that God coursed through matter as honey does through the combs” (Tertullian, *Adversus Hermogenem*, ch. 44). He should therefore have been charged with contradiction rather than forgetfulness or ignorance. But the contradictions of the Stoics were undoubtedly greater than Tertullian’s; Plutarch exposed them in entire books, and we have noted them elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 21, art. 2). Could this not therefore have been attributed to their contradictions rather than his?

But what if Seneca, himself a Stoic, suggests to us a way of removing this contradiction? For he speaks about God in this manner: “What is God? The mind of the universe. What is God? The whole of what you see and the whole of what you do not see. Only thus is his own greatness, than which nothing greater can be conceived, restored to him, if [Col. 0820B] he alone is. He embraces all his work, both within and without” (Seneca, preface to bk. I *Naturales Quaestiones*, p. 793). Does he not signify by these words that God is both within and outside the world, because he is greater than all his work? But if this was the Stoics’ opinion, it had two parts. What, then, if Tertullian mentioned only one part in order to oppose the Stoics to the Platonists?

It can nevertheless be objected that this same opinion is attributed by Seneca himself to the Epicureans, whom for that reason he sharply rebukes and assails: “You, Epicurus,” he said, “make God unarmed. . . . You have cast him beyond fear” (others prefer to read, “beyond the boundary”). “Thus you have him enclosed by some vast and inexplicable wall, and separated from contact with and sight of mortals; you have no reason to fear him. He has no means either of bestowing benefits [Col. 0820C] or of doing harm. Abandoned in the interval between this heaven and another, without living creature, without man, without anything, he escapes the wreckage of worlds falling above and around him, neither hearing prayers nor taking thought for us” (the same, bk. IV *De Beneficiis*, ch. 19, p. 79). In one of his letters too he rejects and condemns the same error of theirs in this way: “I am not speaking of that philosophy which placed the citizen outside his country, the gods outside the world, and surrendered virtue to pleasure” (the same, *Epistle* 79, p. 71), namely, Epicurean philosophy. He therefore testifies that this false opinion belonged not to the Stoics but to the Epicureans.

“Can it not, then,” someone will say, “be concluded from this testimony of Seneca that Tertullian’s text should be emended, and that ‘Epicureans’ should be written there in place of [Col. 0820D] ‘Stoics’?” Certainly—if that is proved by some sufficiently valid argument. But the Stoics did not have a single position concerning God; rather, as we have said, there was a very great variety of opinions. If some of them, such as the aforementioned Seneca, imagined God in some manner situated beyond the limits of the world, who will ever deny that this was sufficient for Tertullian? For he could omit the Epicureans, whom the Gentiles despised, and mention the Stoics. Nevertheless, whatever the genuine reading of Tertullian may be, the weight and force of his argument will remain the same. For from it, and from all that has been discussed thus far, it will be clearly apparent to anyone how deservedly he asserts that it was as difficult for all the philosophers to define the nature, character, and dwelling-place of God [Col. 0821A] as it was ready and easy for even a Christian of the lowest station to do so.

This is further confirmed by the authority of Plato, easily the chief of them all, who, as Tertullian himself recalls and as we have more than once observed, openly professed that “the maker of the universe is not easy to discover, and, once discovered, is difficult to describe to everyone” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46; Plato, *Timaeus*, p. 28). Consequently his followers, as our author says in another book, “could neither know nor fear him whom they had not fully accepted, nor therefore become wise,” since they strayed from the beginning of wisdom, that is, fear of God (vol. I, *Apparat.*, p. 948; *Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.*, ch. 4, art. 2). But any Christian discovers him and, in actual fact, also ascribes to him that which is sought in God (Tertullian, bk. II *Ad Nationes*, ch. 2): [Col. 0821B] namely, that he is one, omnipotent, infinite, the creator of the world, and such that nothing greater or better can be conceived. Therefore the Christian fears him and is far wiser than those who were wiser than the other philosophers.

Finally, no slight difficulty still attaches to those words of Tertullian by which he noted another disagreement among the philosophers concerning God as creator of the world: “This entire body of the world,” he says, “whether unbegotten and unmade according to Pythagoras, or begotten and made according to Plato” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 11, p. 332). For just as certain as it is that this was Plato’s opinion concerning the created world, as we have shown elsewhere, so false does it seem that Pythagoras taught that it was unbegotten and unmade. [Col. 0821C] For in that same place we observed that Lactantius emphatically declares that all philosophers down to Epicurus, and the Pythagoreans by name, consistently asserted that the world was made and created (*Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 21, art. 2). Indeed, Plutarch declares most explicitly that Pythagoras and Plato held the same opinion on this subject. Here are his Greek words: Πυθαγόρας καὶ Πλάτων γενητὸν ὑπὸ Θεοῦ τὸν κόσμον. “Pythagoras and Plato held that the world was made by God” (Plutarch, bk. II *De Placitis Philosophorum*, ch. 4, p. 886). What then? Did Tertullian err here too, and must it be said that either he or a copyist wrote the name Pythagoras in place of another? Or rather, because this celebrated philosopher is reported by the same Plutarch, Laertius, Theodoret, and others to have taught that unity is the [Col. 0821D] principle of all things and that all things come from numbers, did our author infer from this that the world, like unity and numbers, was neither begotten nor made (the same, *ibid.*, bk. II, ch. 3; Laertius, bk. VIII, §25; Theodoret, discourse 2 *On the Principle*, p. 489)? But if the matter stands thus, the authors cited by us will undoubtedly be convicted of error. Can it therefore be said more probably that Pythagoras, in the manner of men in error, did not remain of the same opinion? I would have you weigh these matters and pronounce judgment.

Far truer and more certain, therefore, is what our author taught: that the world was created by God from nothing, “by the word with which he commanded, by the reason with which he arranged it, by the power with which he was able” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 17, [Col. 0822A] and ch. 21). This was indeed repeated by him and transcribed by Minucius Felix, as we have observed elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.*, ch. 2, art. 5). But let us now, if you please, examine carefully what Tertullian teaches concerning this Word of God.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Divinity of Christ

### ARTICLE I. On the Various Names of the Son of God, and How Clearly Tertullian Teaches That the Attributes of the True and Supreme God Belong to Him, and That He Is One Eternal God with His Father

To make plain to everyone what the Word, Reason, Speech, and Son of God are, Tertullian [Col. 0822B] teaches that God and the Word, the Son of God, can each be considered in two ways. Both may be considered before God himself founded the world or any creature, or when the world had been created by him. Concerning both before the creation of the world, however, he establishes the following as entirely certain:

“Before all things God was alone, being himself his own world, place, and everything. He was alone, however, because there was nothing else external besides him. Yet not even then was he alone, for he had with him that which he had within himself, namely his own Reason. For God is rational, and Reason was first in him, and thus all things were from him. This Reason is his consciousness. The Greeks call it λόγον, a word by which we also designate Speech. And therefore, through the simplicity of translation, it is now customary among us to say that Speech was in the beginning with God, [Col. 0822C] although it is more fitting that Reason be regarded as prior; because God was not ‘speech-bearing’ from the beginning, but rational even before the beginning, and because Speech itself, since it consists in Reason, shows Reason to be prior as its substance. Nevertheless, even so, it makes no difference. For although God had not yet sent forth his Speech, he nonetheless possessed it within himself together with and in Reason itself, silently thinking and arranging with himself the things which he was soon to utter through Speech. For in thinking and arranging with his Reason, he made it into Speech, which he treated by means of Speech” (Tertullian, *Adversus Praxean*, ch. 5).

We have quoted this passage entire, though somewhat lengthy, because every part of it deserves singular attention and examination.

First, then, he declares that before the beginning, [Col. 0822D] that is, from all eternity and consequently before the world was created, God was both alone and not alone. Before the creation of the world he was alone, being himself his own world, place, and everything, because he had nothing external besides himself. Yet even then he was not alone, because he had his own Reason. For before the beginning, or from all eternity, he was rational, since God cannot be God unless he is endowed with consciousness and reason.

Second, that divine and eternal Reason of God, he says, the Greeks call λόγον, undoubtedly because John wrote at the beginning of his Gospel: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος (John 1:1). For Tertullian himself cited these words in Latin thus: “In the beginning was the Speech . . . and the Speech was with God, and the Speech was God” (Tertullian, *Adversus Hermogenem*, [Col. 0823A] ch. 20). In his time, however, a custom had become established among Latin speakers of calling the Son of God *Sermo* (“Speech”), although it would have been better for them to render that Greek term λόγος as *Ratio* (“Reason”). We have discussed this translation where we showed that Lactantius transcribed this passage of Tertullian (*Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 16, art. 2).

Third, he advises us why the Greek term λόγος ought to be translated into Latin as “Reason” rather than “Speech.” God, he says, was rational before the beginning, but not yet “speech-bearing,” because he possessed Reason within himself but had not yet sent forth Speech outside himself. Yet because from eternity he possessed Speech within himself just as he possessed Reason, Tertullian granted everyone freedom to use either name, Reason or Speech, as one pleased. [Col. 0823B] The Son of God, however, is called by him not only Speech, Reason, and Word, but also *Sophia*, or Wisdom (Tertullian, *De Carne Christi*, ch. 18; *Adversus Hermogenem*, ch. 18).

Moreover, in his *Apologeticus*, and afterward Lactantius, as we have seen in its proper place, informed us that this Logos (λόγον) was recognized by Zeno, a Gentile philosopher, who proclaimed it to be the maker of the universe (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 21; *Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 16, art. 1). Our author adds: “Cleanthes gathers it into the Spirit, which he affirms to be the permeator of the universe” (Tertullian, loc. cit.; vol. I, *Apparat.*, p. 782; *Dissertat. in Minuc. Oct.*, ch. 4, art. 1; and *Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 12, art. 1). This Cleanthes was a disciple of Zeno, [Col. 0823C] as we have noted elsewhere, where we also explained what his opinion concerning God was, from which the account given by Tertullian appears to have been derived.

Now, from Tertullian’s statements concerning the Word, Speech, and Reason of God, explained in this manner, it can certainly be inferred that he was entirely persuaded that this interior Word of God is as eternal as his Father himself, who indeed brought him forth from eternity, though only within himself. The eternity of the divine Word must, however, be treated more fully below (below, art. 8 ff.). For first we must most carefully elucidate and expound our author’s true and genuine opinion concerning his supreme divinity.

First, then, he teaches that all the names and attributes of his eternal Father [Col. 0823D] belong to this divine Word and Son of God:

“The names of the Father—God Almighty, the Most High, Lord of Hosts, King of Israel, He Who Is—insofar as the Scriptures teach thus, we say also belonged to the Son, and that the Son came under these names, always acted under them, and thus manifested them in himself to men. ‘All things of the Father,’ he says, ‘are mine.’ Why not the names also? Therefore, when you read ‘God Almighty,’ ‘the Most High,’ ‘God of Hosts,’ ‘King of Israel,’ and ‘He Who Is,’ see whether the Son also is not indicated by these: Almighty in his own right, as the Speech of Almighty God and as he who received authority over all things; the Most High, as exalted at the right hand of God, as Peter proclaims in Acts; Lord of Hosts, because all things were subjected to him by the Father; King of Israel, because the lot of that nation fell peculiarly to him; likewise He Who Is, since [Col. 0824A] many are called sons who are not” (Tertullian, *Adversus Praxean*, ch. 17).

By what words, I ask you, could the supreme divinity of Christ, the Son of God, be declared and asserted more clearly? Who can possess all these attributes of the true and supreme God except the supreme God, one with the eternal Father? What of the fact that Tertullian not only affirms that each and every one of these belongs to the Speech and Son of God, but also proves it and endeavors to confirm it by various arguments? He was therefore persuaded that the Son of God is one and the same God with his Father.

Nor let some Arian or Socinian, whoever he may be, rise up and object that Tertullian does not correctly prove how those divine attributes belong to the Son of God. For we are not now investigating how strong and firm his arguments are—although this is very easy to prove—[Col. 0824B] but what opinion he wished to prove. Yet from his own words it is most evident that he and all the other orthodox Christians of his age held it as entirely certain that the Word and Son of God is true God, and that those who thought otherwise—such as Praxeas, against whom he disputes there—were altogether in error.

Accordingly, elsewhere he professes most explicitly that this Speech and Son of God is equal to his Father, and elsewhere that he is not less than him: “For,” he says, “making that Father equal to himself, from whom by proceeding he became the Son” (*Ibid.*, ch. 7). Later: “The same Son of God, by saying, ‘I and the Father are one,’ shows that there are two whom he makes equal and joins together” (*Ibid.*, ch. 22). Again, [Col. 0824C] in another book: “And the Speech, God, who, being established in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as robbery” (the same, *De Resurrectione Carnis*, ch. 6). You have heard how clearly he asserts that the Son of God is equal to his Father; now hear how he proclaims that he is not inferior: “He says that all things were delivered to him by the Father. You may believe this if Christ belongs to the Creator, to whom all things belong, because the Creator delivered all things to a Son not inferior to himself—the things he created through him, namely through his own Speech” (the same, *Adversus Marcionem*, ch. 25). Yet if the Son of God is not inferior but equal to his Father, he is undoubtedly true God with him. For he is also called by the same Tertullian, as we have just seen, the Most High and Almighty. Yet there cannot be two Most High and Almighty beings, just as there cannot be two gods. For [Col. 0824D] elsewhere, as we have noted, he had said that God is one precisely because he is supreme, and therefore, he says, “If God is not one, he is not God” (preceding chapter, art. 1).

But if anyone desires more, let him consult Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, with which we are dealing. There, after a brief exposition of Christian doctrine concerning the Son of God, Christ the Lord, he addresses the Gentiles in these words:

“Investigate, therefore, whether this divinity of Christ is true. If it is such that, once it is known, a person is reformed toward the good, it follows that every other divinity discovered is false—above all that which” (our manuscript codices and the printed editions add “by every means,” which Rigault removed) “lurking beneath the names and images of dead men, establishes belief in its divinity by certain signs, miracles, and oracles” (the same, [Col. 0825A] *Apologeticus*, ch. 21).

In what way could the true and supreme divinity of Christ ever have been asserted and proclaimed more openly and confidently? For Tertullian openly asserts that it is as true as every other divinity recognized and introduced by the Gentiles is false. Indeed, he cries out that the divinity of Christ is so true that it follows from this that the divinity of all others is false, including that of the demons, who, lurking beneath the names and images of the dead, established belief in their divinity by signs, miracles, and oracles; that is, they tried to persuade everyone that these signs, miracles, and oracles were performed by their own divine power and that they themselves were true gods. Who, then, does not see that through this opposition between true and fictitious divinity, Tertullian declares the true and supreme divinity of Christ?

[Col. 0825B] Nor did he think it enough to say this there; shortly afterward he further addresses the same Gentiles with these words: “You cannot say that Christ is a man of the common condition” (*Ibid.*, ch. 23). For he will come at the end of the world “as the power of God, and the Spirit of God, and the Speech, and the Wisdom, and the Reason, and the Son of God.” Thus, openly and boldly, in the hearing and before the eyes of the fiercest enemies of the Christian name, he pronounces and testifies that Christ is the Speech, Wisdom, and Reason of his eternal Father, by which he is his Son from eternity. Accordingly, he explicitly affirms that in Christ there are two natures, of God and of man, and that he is as truly God as he is truly man.

### ARTICLE II. How Explicitly Tertullian Asserts That the Eternal Father and His Son Have One and the Same Substance and Nature, Although the Person of Each Is Distinct

[Col. 0825C]

Just as explicitly and consistently as Tertullian taught that the Son of God is one and the same God with his Father, so too he asserted that both have one and the same substance and nature, but distinct persons. For he said this not once but repeatedly, especially in his *Apologeticus*, where he discusses the generation of the Word, or Son of God, as follows:

“We have learned,” he says, “that this Logos (λόγον) was brought forth from God, and by being brought forth was begotten, and therefore was called the Son of God, and God, from the unity of substance. For God too is Spirit; and when a ray is extended from the sun, it is a portion from the whole, but the sun will be in the ray, because it is a ray of the sun, and the substance is not separated but extended. [Col. 0825D] So too, Spirit from Spirit, and God from God, as light kindled from light. The matrix of the substance remains whole and undiminished, even though you derive from it several offshoots of its qualities. Thus, what proceeded from God is God and the Son of God, and the two are one. Thus, as Spirit from Spirit and God from God, he was made second in number by mode, in degree but not in condition, and went forth from the matrix without withdrawing from it” (*Ibid.*, ch. 21).

Thus he declares simply and sincerely to the Gentiles what Christians believed concerning the nature and generation of the divine Word, and consequently of the Son of God. How sincere this explanation is becomes clear from the fact that, if he could have concealed or dissembled anything, he certainly would not have said it in a public book which he offered to all the Gentiles and even to the rulers of the Roman Empire. [Col. 0826A] But the truer and more certain this exposition is, the more carefully it must be examined by us.

First, then, he says: “We have learned that this was brought forth from God.” But whence, I ask, had he and the other Christians learned this? Surely from no other source than the sacred Scriptures and a sure and constant tradition from the Apostles down to his own time. Elsewhere he cites many passages of the same sacred Scripture on this matter, especially in his book against Praxeas, a supporter of the Patripassian heresy. There also he excellently teaches that this is “the rule of our faith, which has come down from the beginning of the Gospel and is older than any heretics.” “It is established,” he says, “that whatever is first is true, and whatever is later is false” (Tertullian, *Adversus Praxean*, ch. 2). Therefore certain [Col. 0826B] most foolish men wrongly advertised the claim that the doctrine concerning the Logos (λόγου) and the Son of God was unknown to the Apostles and their first disciples, and that only in the second century of the Church was it drawn from the opinions of the philosophers and received by Christians. For if any alteration had been made in a principal article of the Christian faith, it ought to have struck the mind of everyone, and especially that of Tertullian. That highly learned man flourished at the end of the second century and the beginning of the third, and therefore could not have been ignorant of how certainly this common doctrine of all had been transmitted from the Apostles down to his own time.

Second, he teaches that the divine Word is Spirit from Spirit, because it is God’s Word, Reason, and Speech (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 21). For, as he says elsewhere: “We understand Spirit under the name of Speech; so too we recognize Speech under the name of Spirit. For Spirit [Col. 0826C] is the substance of Speech, and Speech the operation of Spirit, and the two are one” (the same, *Adversus Praxean*, ch. 26). He therefore held that the Speech, or Word, and Son of God is spirit and a wholly spiritual reality, distinct from every kind of matter and from everything corporeal. This opinion of his is confirmed by the fact that in the same place he declares him to be Spirit from Spirit, that is, brought forth and begotten by the spirit and thought of his eternal Father (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 21). For the bringing-forth of divine thought not only admits nothing corporeal; he who is brought forth is also one God with his Father, by whom he is brought forth. Yet why need this be proved by us when Tertullian asserts it most explicitly in these very words: [Col. 0826D] “What proceeded from God is God and the Son of God, and the two are one, and God from God” (*Ibid.*)?

Third, Tertullian affirms that he is one God with God the Father by unity of substance, and consequently that the substance of both is one and the same (*Ibid.*). For the substance, he says, is not separated from his Father but extended, since “we have learned,” as he further expresses it, “that this was brought forth from God, and by being brought forth was begotten” (*Ibid.*). But because he thus proceeded from him and was begotten, he is distinguished from him in person, just as his substance is not separated from that of his Father. For the person of the Father and of the Son of God cannot be the same. Yet the substance of both is the same, since he is one God with the Father by unity of substance, from which [Col. 0827A] he is not separated but extended (*Ibid.*). For he did not withdraw from this substance, as from a matrix, but went forth from it; and thus the two are one and the same God.

Nor does he confirm it only there, but also in his book *Against Praxeas*, in these words: “We have given the reason why they are not called two Gods or two Lords, but why the Father and the Son are two; and this not from a separation of substance, but from the dispensation, since we declare the Son indivisible and inseparable from the Father, another not in condition but in degree; and although he is called God when named individually, he does not thereby make two Gods, but one, by the very fact that he is entitled to be called God from the unity of the Father” (Tertull., *Against Praxeas*, chap. 19). You see indeed how explicitly he asserts there, as elsewhere, that the Son of God is another than his Father, not in condition but in [Col. 0827B] degree—that is, not in nature but in person, a person distinguished as second in order—and that by this distinction they are indeed two, or two persons distinct from one another, but cannot be called two Gods, because the substance of both is the same, and therefore both are one God (*ibid.*, chap. 2).

Nor should you say that the term “person” is passed over there in silence. For it is sufficiently implied by this distinction between Father and Son. Since he said that the nature of both is one, it is solely in person that they can be distinguished and be two. Moreover, the term “person” is employed in the same *Against Praxeas* in the very sense in which we now use it, as will be most evident from the passages cited below.

But he maintains and defends this doctrine of a distinct [Col. 0827C] person of the Son and the Father, yet one substance of both, not only against Praxeas but also against another heretic, Valentinus. There were indeed two errors of Valentinus, which he described in these words: “Valentinus distinguishes and separates his *probolae*, that is, his divine emanations, and places them so far apart that an Aeon does not know the Father” (*ibid.*, chap. 8). He refutes the second of these errors, concerning an Aeon that does not know the Father, by the authority of John the Evangelist: “Among us,” he says, “the Son alone knows the Father, and he himself has disclosed the bosom of the Father.” Then he overthrows Valentinus’s first error concerning separated divine emanations in these words, which bear more directly upon our purpose: “The Word is always in the Father, as he said: ‘I am in the Father’; and always with God, as it is written: ‘And the Word was with God’; and never separated from the Father, or other [Col. 0827D] than the Father, because ‘I and the Father are one.’” From this he concludes that this Word and Son of God is distinct from his Father, because he proceeded and was brought forth from him, but is not separated from him, since the nature of both is one. Indeed, shortly afterward he added: “The Son is another than the Father, not by diversity but by distribution; another not by division but by distinction, because the Father and the Son are not the same, being different from one another even in measure” (*ibid.*). But I would now have you observe that the Son of God is said by him to be both another than the Father and not another: another than the Father in person, namely, but not another in substance, because this substance is plainly the same in both.

Since, therefore, the Son is distinct from his Father, because there are two persons in one and the same substance, he rightly [Col. 0828A] wrote of the same Son of God in the *Apologeticum*: “In measure,” just as he said against Valentinus, “he made an alternate number; in degree, not in condition.” But Rigaltius, contrary to the testimony of our manuscripts and of all previously edited codices, wished to correct the former words there as follows: “Another in measure, not in number” (Idem, *Apologet.*, chap. 21). Nevertheless, he gave no reason for this emendation. Did he therefore think, as it appears, that by altering the author’s words in this way he would preserve his antitheses more accurately? But it is unquestionably wrong to alter the text of an ancient author on the slightest conjecture, and much more so, by a perverse alteration, to twist his meaning into another that is plainly opposed to it, and into the very error that he attacks. For Tertullian, as has been abundantly proved, teaches most openly [Col. 0828B] that the Son of God is another than his Father in measure and degree, or in person, but one and the same in substance, and therefore that there are two distinct persons, yet one God. The two persons, therefore, distinct from one another, make an alternate number.

Furthermore, as we shall see in the following article, he openly declares with the whole Catholic Church that there are three persons in the most holy Trinity. He therefore rightly and deservedly said that the Son of God makes an alternate number with his Father. For we have already heard him say: “The Father and the Son are not the same in measure,” that is, in that mode of emanation by which the Son proceeded from the Father (Idem, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 8). The Son therefore makes an alternate number with the Father; that is, each of them, Father and Son, alternately and in turn [Col. 0828C] makes up the number of two persons. That this is Tertullian’s meaning may quite reasonably be gathered from these words of his in the same book: “The Father makes the Son, and the Son the Father. And those who are made from one another can in no way be made by themselves for themselves, so that the Father should make himself a Son to himself, and the Son himself a Father to himself. . . . The Father must have the Son in order to be Father, and the Son the Father in order to be Son” (*ibid.*, chap. 10). Do you hear how clearly he teaches that the Father and the Son are so related to one another that the Father with the Son, and in turn the Son with the Father, make an alternate number?

But because the difference between human beings and God is infinite, he therefore asserts without the least hesitation that the Son of God is another than the Father in degree, but not in condition; that is, by his generation he is another in degree, [Col. 0828D] or second in order (*ibid.*, chap. 2), inasmuch as he is begotten by the Father, but not another in condition—that is, not in substance and nature, which is one and the same in him and in his Father. But new light will certainly be shed upon these statements of his by what he taught concerning the divinity of the same Son and of the Holy Spirit, and concerning the sacred mystery of the Trinity, which must now be unfolded and explained by us.

## ARTICLE III. How explicitly Tertullian explains and defends the orthodox doctrine concerning the divinity of the Son of God and of the Holy Spirit, and concerning the sacred mystery of the Trinity

Tertullian maintains and defends the Catholic doctrine concerning the supreme [Col. 0829A] divinity of the Son of God and of Christ the Lord, not only in the passages we have cited but also in many others, with equal firmness and clarity. But because in these he also asserts and proclaims no less explicitly the Catholic dogma concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit and the mystery of the most holy Trinity, we have judged that it should be set forth separately in this article. First, therefore, against the Patripassian Praxeas, who babbled that God the Father and the Son were the same, he declares that the following must firmly be believed concerning the mystery of the Trinity, namely, the three divine persons and their one and the same nature: “Let the mystery of the economy be preserved,” he says, “which arranges the unity into a Trinity, setting forth three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three, however, not in condition but in degree; not in substance but in form; not in power but in aspect; yet of one substance, one condition, [Col. 0829B] and one power, because there is one God, from whom these degrees, forms, and aspects are reckoned under the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (Tertull., *Against Praxeas*, chap. 2). No one fails to understand that by the term “condition,” as we noted in the preceding article, the same thing is signified as the substance and nature of God; while by the terms “degree,” “form,” and “aspect” are signified the divine persons, their order, and their mode of existence. He therefore manifestly teaches that there are three persons of the most holy Trinity, who admit of number without division, but that their substance is one and the same.

Afterward he sets forth and confirms this doctrine—and, as he himself says, this rule—of the Catholic Church at greater length, in the following manner: “The Trinity, flowing down from the Father through interwoven and connected [Col. 0829C] degrees, does not disturb the monarchy and preserves the condition of the economy. Hold everywhere to this rule which I have professed, by which I testify that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable from one another, and thus you will recognize both what is said and how it is said. For behold, I say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Every simple or perverse person wrongly takes this statement as though it expressed diversity and, from diversity, implied the separation of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. I say this, however, of necessity, since they contend that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are the same, flattering the monarchy against the economy: the Son is another than the Father, not by diversity, nor another by division, but by distinction, because the Father and the Son are not the same, being different from one another even in measure” (*ibid.*, chap. 9). Could the true and Catholic [Col. 0829D] doctrine concerning the sacred mystery of the Trinity be explained more clearly or better? For our Author openly, and against the errors of heretics, professes that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons distinct from one another, yet without diversity, division, or separation, because their substance is one. And he asserts that this is the rule of orthodox faith, handed down in the sacred Scriptures, received from the forefathers, and to be maintained by all.

Therefore, not content to have said this once or twice, he afterward repeats and reinforces it: “We,” he says, “who by the grace of God examine both the times and the causes of the Scriptures, being disciples especially of the Paraclete, not of men, define the Father and the Son as indeed two, and now as three [Col. 0830A] with the Holy Spirit, according to the principle of the economy, which produces number, lest, as your perversity infers, the Father himself be believed to have been born and to have suffered—which it is not permissible to believe, since it has not been handed down in that way” (*ibid.*, chap. 13). When he wrote these words, he had already defected from the Catholic Church to the errors of the Montanists and had imbibed the absurd fiction of a false Paraclete. Nevertheless, he explicitly asserts and maintains a sound and orthodox faith concerning the mystery of the Trinity. Who, therefore, will deny that this principal doctrine of the Christian religion is true, when he defended it so consistently, in whatever state he was and throughout his whole life, and testified that it was attacked only by those who were plainly in error?

Indeed, we previously read this written by him: “How can it be that God should appear to suffer division and dispersion [Col. 0830B] in the Son and the Holy Spirit, who have obtained the second and third places and are such sharers in the Father’s substance, when he does not suffer these among so great a number of angels, who are moreover so alien from his substance?” (*ibid.*, chap. 3). You surely understand with what clarity he again declares that the Father is so distinguished in person from the Son and the Holy Spirit that the Son and the Holy Spirit hold the second and third places. Yet he plainly and absolutely contends and affirms that there is no division or dispersion among them, but that they share the same substance—a substance that is one in them, whereas in the angels, however perfect, it is divided and separate.

But what he not only declares most openly but also proves by the authority of sacred Scripture, [Col. 0830C] and especially by these words of John the Evangelist, “I and the Father are one,” undoubtedly requires no explanation. For after citing them, he continues as follows (*ibid.*, chap. 22): “Here, therefore, the foolish—indeed, the blind—wish to take their stand, failing to see, first, that ‘I and the Father’ signifies two; next, that the final word ‘are’ cannot refer to one person, because it is spoken in the plural; and then because it says, ‘we are one’ in the neuter, not ‘we are one’ in the masculine. For if he had said, ‘we are one’ in the masculine, it might have assisted their opinion. For the masculine ‘one’ appears to signify the singular number. Moreover, although the two are masculine in gender, he says ‘one’ with a neuter word, which pertains not to singularity but to unity, to likeness, to conjunction, and to the love of the Father. . . . By saying, ‘I and the Father are one,’ he shows that there are two, whom he makes equal and joins together.” Afterward he explains this more briefly, but [Col. 0830D] no less clearly and distinctly: “The connection of the Father in the Son, and of the Son in the Paraclete, produces three who cohere, one from another; and these three are one in the neuter, not one in the masculine, just as it was said, ‘I and the Father are one,’ with reference to unity of substance, not singularity of number” (*ibid.*, chap. 25).

Although he does not use the term “person” there, you could nevertheless have observed that he employed it in the preceding passage. But you will see it expressed still more distinctly where he again demonstrates, by various testimonies of sacred Scripture, that there are three persons in the most holy Trinity and only one nature. For he proves this from these words of Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. [Col. 0831A] I, 26); and from these others: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (*ibid.*, III, 22). From these he argues as follows: “Because the Son, the second person, his own Word, and the third, the Spirit in the Word, already adhered to him, he therefore spoke in the plural: ‘Let us make,’ and ‘our,’ and ‘us.’” Then shortly afterward: “Finally, the following Scripture distinguishes among the persons: ‘And God made man; in the image of God he made him.’ Why not ‘his own,’ if there was only one who was making and there was no one in whose image he was making him? But there was one in whose image he was making him, namely the Son, who, because he was to become a more certain and truer man, had caused man, who was then to be formed from clay, to be called his image—the image and likeness of the true.” And not long afterward: “I have already declared,” he says, “how you ought to understand the Son as another than the Father: in the designation of person, not of substance; for [Col. 0831B] distinction, not for division. Moreover, although I everywhere maintain one substance in three who cohere, nevertheless the necessity of the sense requires me to call him who commands another than him who acts” (Tertull., *Against Praxeas*, chap. 22).

Earlier, when in disputing against the same Praxeas he manifestly shows that the Son of God, who is his Wisdom and Word, is another than his Father, he introduces Praxeas arguing as follows: “‘Therefore,’ you say, ‘you grant that the Word is some substance, constructed by the imparting of spirit and wisdom’” (*ibid.*, chap. 7)? To this he answers in one word: “Certainly,” and thus freely confesses that it is true. He immediately gives this reason for it: “For you are unwilling that he should possess substantial existence in reality through the property of substance, so that he may be regarded as a certain thing and person, [Col. 0831C] and may thus, being constituted second from God, make two: the Father and the Son, God and the Word.”

We certainly should never finish speaking if we wished to transcribe and elucidate every single statement in which he asserts the sacred mystery of the Trinity against Praxeas as correctly as he does explicitly. Therefore, lest we become too lengthy, we shall add only those passages in which he further shows that there are three persons of one divinity in the most holy Trinity: “Christ,” he says, “finally commanded that they should baptize into the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—not into one, nor once, but three times, at each name into each individual person” (*ibid.*, chap. 27). That the substance and divinity of those three persons is one, he declared most explicitly not only in the passages [Col. 0831D] already cited, but also in another book, which no one doubts was composed by him while he was likewise following the Montanist heresy. For there he wrote: “The Church, properly speaking, is the Spirit himself, in whom is the Trinity, or three persons of one divinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (Idem, *On Modesty*, chap. 21).

Furthermore, from all that has thus far been discussed in this and the preceding article, it is sufficiently and, as we think, evidently concluded that Tertullian’s doctrine—whether as a Catholic or as a Montanist, that is, throughout the whole course of his life—concerning the supreme divinity of the Son of God and of the Holy Spirit, their possession of the same substance as the eternal God the Father, and their three distinct [Col. 0832A] persons, was wholly sound and plainly orthodox. It is no less evident that he was thoroughly persuaded that this principal dogma of the whole Catholic Church was founded upon the authority of sacred Scripture, and that it had been transmitted from the Apostles and their successors down to his own age by a sure and perpetual tradition. Finally, it is clear from what has been said that this doctrine was boldly defended by him not only against the heretics who denied it, but also against the pagans, the bitterest enemies of Christians, who most cruelly persecuted and killed them on account of this doctrine. Yet he could certainly have enticed the heretics more easily to his side if he had been able to admit that in the most holy Trinity there is only one person, and no plurality except in name. He could also have reconciled the pagans to himself and appeased their fury against the Christians if [Col. 0832B] he had said that there were three Gods, or at least one greater God and other lesser ones. Nor should you think that this is a gratuitous invention of ours, since Tertullian himself openly and explicitly professes it: “Moreover, if on the ground of our conscience,” he says, “by which we know that the name of God and Lord applies both to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we were to call them Gods and Lords, we should have extinguished our torches and would have been more timid even in facing martyrdoms, since an opportunity of escape would have lain open to us by immediately swearing by gods and lords, as do certain heretics whose gods are many” (*ibid.*, chap. 13). Tertullian, therefore, like other true Christians, preferred to experience every kind of torment and to be killed rather than in any way weaken or conceal this doctrine concerning the divinity of Christ himself and the mystery of the most holy Trinity, [Col. 0832C] which had been handed down to him by Christ and his disciples. There is therefore no room for doubt that this doctrine of Tertullian and the Catholic Church is true, since it was asserted in this manner by the sacred writers and was constantly and perpetually preserved and defended.

## ARTICLE IV. By what arguments Tertullian attempted to explain the divine and eternal generation of the Son of God, and why he, but not the Holy Spirit, is called the Son of God

It was not enough for Tertullian to maintain and defend his own doctrine, and that of the whole Catholic Church, concerning the supreme divinity of the Son of God and of the Holy Spirit in the manner we have seen (preceding article); he also attempted to explain [Col. 0832D] why the Word and Reason of God is his true Son and ought to be so called. He therefore openly declares to all that God, by the very fact that he is God, has always and from all eternity been rational (*ibid.*). Since, therefore, he cannot be without reason, from the same eternity he brought forth the Word—which Word, as we have noted, ought more properly in Latin to have been called Reason. That divine Word, however, is not an articulated voice like that of a human being, nor some sound of the mouth, struck air, and thus some empty and insubstantial thing; rather, “it possesses,” he says, “spirit as its own substance” (Tertull., *Apologeticum*, chap. 21). Because this was denied by the heretic Praxeas, Tertullian argues against him as follows and proves that this Word of God is a true [Col. 0833A] substance: “‘For what,’ you will say, ‘is a word except the voice and sound of the mouth and, as the grammarians teach, air struck, intelligible to hearing, but otherwise some empty, insubstantial, and incorporeal thing?’ But I say that nothing insubstantial and empty could have proceeded from God, since it was not brought forth from what is insubstantial and empty; nor could that which proceeded from so great a substance and made such great substances be devoid of substance. For he himself made the things that were made through him. How could that be nothing without which nothing was made? How could an insubstantial thing have produced solid things, an empty thing things that are full, and an incorporeal thing corporeal things? For although something can sometimes be made different from that through which it is made, nevertheless nothing can be made through what is empty and insubstantial. Is the Word of God, who is called the Son, who himself is also named God, an empty and insubstantial thing? ‘AND THE WORD WAS WITH GOD, AND THE WORD WAS GOD’” (Idem, *Against Praxeas*, [Col. 0833B] chap. 7)? By this argument, therefore, he shows that the Word—that is, the Speech and Reason of God—is not something insubstantial and empty, but a true substance.

Now this divine Word is a true substance precisely because he was brought forth by God. For “we say,” Tertullian declares, “that he was begotten by being brought forth, and therefore call him the Son of God.” Brought forth by his divine Father, he proceeded from the Father’s own intellect as though from a womb, and therefore he is begotten and is the true Son of God. For by this very generation he is not only like the Father, but the substance of both is also the same. For the Son of God, he says, “did not depart from the Father’s womb, but came forth from it.” Since he did not depart, he has the same substance as the Father; and because he proceeded from him, he is his Son (Idem, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 21).

[Col. 0833C] But let us hear Tertullian again, who elsewhere (Idem, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 8) asserts and confirms this by several testimonies of sacred Scripture: “By proceeding from him,” he says, “the Son was made the firstborn, as begotten before all things, and the only-begotten, as alone begotten from God, properly from the womb of his own heart—that is, his intellect—according as his Father also testifies: ‘MY HEART HAS UTTERED A MOST EXCELLENT WORD’ (Ps. XLIV, 2); and then, addressing him with joy in his person: ‘YOU ARE MY SON; TODAY I HAVE BEGOTTEN YOU’ (Ps. II, 7); and, ‘BEFORE THE MORNING STAR I BEGOT YOU’ (*ibid.*, CIX, 5). So too the Son in his own person professes the Father under the name of Wisdom: ‘THE LORD ESTABLISHED ME AS THE BEGINNING OF HIS WAYS FOR HIS WORKS’ (Heb., chap. I). ‘BEFORE ALL THE HILLS HE BEGOT ME’ (Prov., chap. VIII, 22).” And this [Col. 0833D] is the very reason why the Word, or Speech, of God—but not the Holy Spirit—is, and is called, the Son of God; and why, as Tertullian himself says, “he also properly received the name of Son”: both because that name is given to him in the sacred Scriptures, and because he was first begotten by his Father alone into the likeness of his nature, while the Holy Spirit proceeded from both, as will become evident to everyone from the words of our Tertullian soon to be cited (Tertull., *Against Praxeas*, chap. 8).

But although the Word of God proceeds eternally from his Father, or, as Tertullian himself says, “is derived from no other source than from the substance of the Father” (*ibid.*, chap. 4)—that is, arises from his thought and intelligence—he is nevertheless not thereby separated from him. For [Col. 0834A] the utterly simple substance of God cannot be divided, just as there cannot be several Gods. Therefore he says again: “Everything that proceeds from something must be second to that from which it proceeds; it is not, however, thereby separated. But where there is a second, there are two; and where there is a third, there are three. For the Spirit is third from God”—that is, from the Father and the Son—“just as the fruit from the shoot is third from the root” (*ibid.*, chap. 8). He teaches two things there which must certainly be observed with attentive care. First, he says that the Son of God is another than his Father and second in order, because he is the Father’s eternal Word, who proceeded from his intellect and thought, and is therefore his Son. Second, he says that the Holy Spirit is third because he proceeds from both Father and Son, just as the fruit arises third from root and shoot. But since there [Col. 0834B] he explains and defends against the heretic Praxeas not merely his own opinion but that of the whole Catholic Church, it certainly follows that this was asserted and defended by all orthodox Christians, and even by others not infected with the same or a similar error as Praxeas.

Some, however, object that Tertullian is not there treating the origin of the Holy Spirit, but the order of the persons of the most holy Trinity, in which the Spirit is placed third after the Father. But why, I ask, have those who argue thus omitted these subsequent words of our Author: “As the fruit from the shoot is third from the root, and the stream from the river third from the spring, and the point from the ray third from the sun; nevertheless, nothing is estranged from the womb from which it derives its properties”? Do these words not sufficiently show that he spoke not [Col. 0834C] only of the order of the Holy Spirit but also of his origin? For there, by these comparisons against Praxeas, he demonstrates that although the Son of God is not separated from his Father, he is nevertheless distinguished from him because he derives his origin from him. Then, passing from this to the origin of the Holy Spirit, he argues in precisely the same manner, as you see. He therefore discusses the origin of the Holy Spirit no less than that of the Son.

They nevertheless insist that Tertullian had previously declared most openly: “I think the Spirit originated from no other source than from the Father through the Son” (Idem, chap. 4). But attend, I ask, to how inconsiderately this is objected. For Hilary, as they admit, explicitly taught that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son when he wrote: “But if it were believed that there is a difference between receiving from [Col. 0834D] the Son and proceeding from the Father, it will certainly be judged one and the same thing to receive from the Son as it is to receive from the Father” (Hilary, *On the Trinity*, bk. 8, §20). Yet we read this written by the same Hilary: “From you”—namely, the Father—“through him”—the Son—“is your Holy Spirit.” A little later he prays to the Father as follows: “Grant me that I may worship you, our Father, and your Son together with you; and that I may be found worthy of your Holy Spirit, who is from you through your only-begotten Son” (*ibid.*, bk. 12, §§56–57).

But if Hilary said in the same Catholic sense both that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, why should Tertullian not have done so as well? Can the same manner of speaking be approved in one and condemned in the other? Both, therefore, rightly said both that the Holy Spirit [Col. 0835A] proceeds from the Father and the Son and that he proceeds from the Father through the Son. For the Son, as intermediate between the Father and the Holy Spirit, received his principle from the Father alone; and the Holy Spirit derives his origin from him and from the Father. Thus the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father through the Son, who, standing by his origin as an intermediary between them both, received from the Father that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him. Therefore this very procession is derived and traced in one and the same manner from both the Father and the Son.

Since, therefore, the Son is his Word and Speech, who proceeded from the Father’s intellect or thought as from a kind of womb, he is rightly his Son and only-begotten, and, as Tertullian said elsewhere, “properly received the name of Son” (Tertull., *Against Praxeas*, chap. 8). But the Holy [Col. 0835B] Spirit, because he proceeds from both, has never been called, nor ought he to have been called, the Son of either one of them or of both.

## ARTICLE V. Certain examples by which Tertullian attempted to explain the divine generation of the Son of God are set forth and examined

Since the divine generation of the Son of God far surpasses human comprehension and cannot readily be understood by it, our Tertullian therefore endeavored to explain and illustrate it by certain comparisons. But because these are not free from difficulties, they must be examined by us. First, then, he proposes them in the *Apologeticum* as follows: “When a ray is extended from the sun, it is a portion from the whole; but the sun will be in the ray, because it is a ray of the sun. The substance is not separated, [Col. 0835C] but extended: thus Spirit from Spirit and God from God, as light kindled from light. The source of the substance remains whole and undiminished, even if you borrow from it several offshoots of qualities. Thus also that which has proceeded from God is God, and the Son of God, and both are one”—supply: God (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 399). Elsewhere, however, he attempts to elucidate this still more fully by the same and other examples. Let us hear him, if you please: “God brought forth the Word, as even the Paraclete teaches, just as the root brings forth the shoot, the spring the river, and the sun the ray. For these forms too are *probolae*—that is, as he had said a little earlier, emanations—of the substances from which they proceed. Nor would I hesitate to call the shoot the son of the root, the river the son of the spring, and the ray the son of the sun; because every origin is a parent, and everything brought forth from an origin [Col. 0835D] is offspring; much more so the Word of God, who also properly received the name of Son. Yet neither is the shoot separated from the root, nor the river from the spring, nor the ray from the sun, just as the Word is not separated from God. Therefore, according to their pattern, I profess that I speak of two: God and his Word, the Father and his Son. For the root and the shoot are two things, but joined; the spring and the river are two forms, but undivided; and the sun and the ray are two shapes, but coherent” (Idem, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 8, p. 639).

But it must be carefully observed that these comparisons are offered by our Author not as wholly perfect, or as though they were entirely and in every respect similar to the divine generation of the Son. For he himself said, “Much more so the Word of God,” by which words he signifies that all these [Col. 0836A] comparisons are imperfect. And indeed, who does not know that they differ from it as greatly as the creature differs from the Creator? He therefore did not think that the generation of the Son of God could be fully explained by them, but used them so that we might understand it in some manner, according to the feeble powers of our intellect.

Furthermore, these examples are employed by him not in all respects, but only with regard to certain matters pertaining to the divine generation of the Son. For all of them tend only to show that although the Son of God proceeds from his Father, he is nevertheless not separated or divided from him. For since, as he says, the shoot proceeds from the root, the river from the spring, and the ray from the sun, and yet they are not separated or divided from one another but are joined together and cohere without any division, [Col. 0836B] the human intellect may thereby be led, according to its manifestly feeble powers, to know that although the Son of God proceeds from the Father, he is not separated from him, but is joined to him and remains wholly undivided from him in an infinitely more perfect manner than those corporeal things.

Thus, afterward, in order to confirm that the Son of God is not separated from the Father, although he came forth from him by divine generation, he introduces the Son himself speaking as follows: “I came forth from the Father, as the ray from the sun, the stream from the spring, and the shoot from the seed” (*ibid.*, chap. 22). Elsewhere he uses the same comparison of the sun and its ray solely in order to demonstrate that the name of God is not to be attributed to creatures, but to the eternal Father and his Son, whose substance is entirely one. It is better, however, to hear him state this himself: “I shall not,” he says, “call them Gods at all, nor Lords, [Col. 0836C] but shall follow the Apostle, so that if the Father and the Son are to be named together, I shall call the Father God and name Jesus Christ Lord. But when Christ alone is mentioned, I shall be able to call him God, as does the same Apostle: ‘From whom is Christ, who is,’ he says, ‘God over all, blessed forever.’ For I shall also call a ray of the sun, considered separately, ‘sun’; yet, when naming the sun to which the ray belongs, I shall not at once call the ray ‘sun’ as well. For although I shall not make two suns, I shall nevertheless number both the sun and its ray as two things and two forms of one undivided substance, just as I number God and his Word, the Father and the Son” (*ibid.*, chap. 13).

Nor did he stop there, but in again explaining that eternal generation of the divine Word he used another comparison. Although it is much [Col. 0836D] more perfect than the preceding ones, he nevertheless openly acknowledges that it too remains imperfect. It is drawn from a human being’s inward speech and word, and he argues thus: “Observe when you silently converse with yourself: this very act is carried on within you by reason, which meets you together with speech at every movement of your thought and every impulse of your perception. Whatever you think is speech; whatever you perceive is reason. You must speak it in your mind, and while you speak you experience speech as an interlocutor, in which resides that very reason by which, when you speak in thought, you are thinking, and through which, by speaking, you think. Thus speech is in some manner a second within you, through which you speak while thinking and through which you think while speaking; speech itself is another. How much more fully, therefore, does this take place in God, whose [Col. 0837A] image and likeness you also are reckoned to be, since even in his silence he has Reason within himself, and Speech within Reason?” (*ibid.*, chap. 5, p. 637). There he shows that God, who is rational by his nature, had Reason and Speech within himself from eternity, which he brings forth when he thinks and which is therefore another than himself, although the substance and nature of both are the same. Who would not readily concede that this could not have been proved more aptly and clearly than by this comparison with the inward word and speech of human beings? For in this, as he says, the human being is the image and likeness of God. Nevertheless, he admits that this very comparison is plainly imperfect, and that the Word of God is brought forth from God the Father in a far fuller and more perfect manner than the word of a human being is brought forth from the human being.

Furthermore, from what has thus far been said, it ought to be manifest to everyone [Col. 0837B] that Tertullian, whether a Catholic or a supporter of the Montanists, most consistently asserted the supreme divinity of the Son and Word of God. For, as we have seen, he openly teaches that the Son was begotten by the divine thought of his Father and that by this generation he is indeed another than the Father—that is, distinct in person—but by no means divided or separated from him, since the substance and nature of both are entirely one and the same. For God the Father, being rational from eternity, could never have been without thought; and therefore his Word, which is the same as his thought, must be consubstantial and coeternal with him. Is this not plainly the very same doctrine as that of the Council of Nicaea? For in its creed it is established that one must believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light [Col. 0837C] from light (or, as Tertullian says, *Apologet.* chap. 21, p. 399, “as light kindled from light”), true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

## ARTICLE VI. The arguments by which some endeavor to prove that Tertullian weakened the orthodox doctrine concerning the supreme divinity of the Son of God—because he said that the Son was a portion of the divine substance, which is wholly in the Father—are weighed and answered.

Although, as has been explained, Tertullian’s teaching on the supreme divinity and eternal generation of the Word and Son of God was entirely orthodox, certain persons—even defenders of this Catholic dogma—nevertheless boldly accuse [Col. 0837D] him of no slight error, but of the gravest. For if Petavius is to be believed, he surpasses the Arian heresy in impiety and absurdity (Petavius, vol. 2, *Theologia dogmatica*, book 2, chap. 5, p. 24). But that learned man was ultimately compelled to correct himself. Elsewhere, indeed, he acknowledges that not a few passages occur in the same Tertullian in which the force of the common teaching and dogma is apparent—a tradition that had permeated the minds of Christians (Idem, Preface to the cited volume, chap. 5). Nevertheless, he added there that orthodox faith in the Trinity is repeatedly bespattered in Tertullian’s writings with certain stains, which may have been daubed upon them through contamination by the foul Montanist heresy into which he defected. Yet although there he seems to mitigate rather than amend the severity of his judgment, [Col. 0838A] he is nevertheless not sufficiently consistent with himself. For he contends that the dogma of the Trinity was undermined not only in books written by Tertullian as a heretic, but also in others composed while he was still a Catholic. We, however, have sufficiently shown that this dogma was rightly asserted by Tertullian, whether Catholic or Montanist, and admirably defended against others who denied it.

Bull, however, branded this same Tertullian of ours, even where he argues against Praxeas, with another mark of censorious severity (Bull, *Defensio fidei Nicaenae*, sect. 3, chap. 10, nos. 5 and 11, pp. 403 and 416). For although he concedes that Tertullian thought rightly concerning the supreme divinity, eternity, and consubstantiality of the Son and Word of God—that is, the identity of his substance with the Father’s—he nevertheless appears to him to have mingled some dross into the golden veins, so to speak, of Catholic tradition, to have spoken quite absurdly, and to have trifled in the most august mystery of the Trinity and pursued foolish conceits. But who will readily persuade himself that Tertullian, a man of such gravity, trifles and talks nonsense about this mystery of the Trinity in the very book in which, by Bull’s own admission, he asserts and defends with all the powers of his mind that principal and greatest article of the Christian faith against the errors of Praxeas and other heretics? (Idem, ibid., § 2, chap. 7, no. 1, p. 150). And certainly we have already proved that the orthodox teaching is clearly taught and explained by him not only against Praxeas and other heretics, but also against the pagans, whom—as we have seen—he could easily have conciliated by concealing it.

[Col. 0838C] But lest we leave anything untouched, all those arguments brought against us by Petavius, Bull, and others must be examined. First, Petavius does not think it necessary to press the statement we read in our Author, that the Son, the Word of God, was brought forth by his Father and, as it were, embodied. For why should he press this? Have we not shown clearly enough that by the word “body” Tertullian understands nothing other than a substance of its own kind, a person, and a hypostasis? Nor have we shown any less clearly—and it will become still more evident from what remains to be said—that he most expressly asserted the Son of God to be pure spirit, proceeding from the understanding and thought of his eternal Father, and therefore incapable of having anything corporeal, or even the least corporeal admixture.

Petavius and others therefore think those statements [Col. 0838D] of far greater weight by which our Author appears to them to have denied that the substance of the eternal Father and of his Son is the same. For, they say, he openly teaches that the whole substance of God is in the Father, and only a certain portion of it in the Son. What, they say, could be clearer or more explicit than these words? “The Father is the whole substance, while the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, as he himself professes: ‘BECAUSE THE FATHER IS GREATER THAN I’” (John 14:28). Tertullian therefore believed, they say, that the whole substance of the Godhead is in the Father, as the greater, and that only a part and portion is in the Son, as the lesser (Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 9).

They press the point further from his assertion in the passage where he refutes the absurd error of Marcion, who babbled that the Father was born of the Virgin and had suffered: [Col. 0839A] “While not denying,” he says, “that his Christ, the Son and Spirit, is also the substance of the Creator, you must concede that those who did not know the Father could not have recognized the Son either, by reason of his being of the same substance, the fullness of which was not understood—much less its portion, certainly insofar as it shares in the fullness” (Tertullian, book 3, *Against Marcion*, chap. 6).

Finally, where he compares the generation of the Son of God with the sun and its ray, he speaks thus as well: “For God too is spirit; and when a ray is extended from the sun, it is a portion from the whole; but the sun will be in the ray, because it is the sun’s ray, and the substance is not separated but extended” (Idem, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 399). Petavius therefore concludes from all this that, in Tertullian’s view, the Son of God possesses not the whole divine substance but only a [Col. 0839B] portion of it, and consequently that the substance and nature of the eternal Father and of his Son are not the same.

But if that is how matters stand, Tertullian certainly contradicted himself in the most foolish fashion. For we saw in the preceding articles how often, how consistently, and how expressly he affirms that the substance in the Father and the Son is wholly one, undivided, and the same. But if the Son has only a portion or part of it, it is surely not the same in him as in the Father, but is divided from the whole as a part is (above, this chapter, art. 1). On the contrary, however, Tertullian, as we saw, committed these words to writing about him in another book against Marcion: “The Creator delivered all things to one who was not lesser than himself” (Idem, book 4, *Against Marcion*, chap. 25). But if the Son received only one portion of the divine substance from the Father, he is undoubtedly lesser through being deprived of the remainder. [Col. 0839C] Did Tertullian, then, both assert and deny that the Son of God is lesser than his Father? Who would believe this?

And what of the fact that in the passage against Marcion brought against us, the Son is indeed called a portion of the divine substance, but there is immediately added, “certainly insofar as it shares in the fullness”? But if he is a sharer, associate, and participant in the divine substance—which is most simple and, as we have observed that Tertullian himself says repeatedly, is not separated in him and the Father—he surely possesses it in its entirety.

Furthermore, if only a portion or some part of the divine substance is in the Son, the Father himself does not possess it entire. For a part of it will be in the Son and detached from the Father. In these words, therefore—“The Father is the whole substance, [Col. 0839D] while the Son is a portion”—an entirely evident contradiction will be found. For the whole of one and the same thing, especially a most simple thing, cannot be in one, and a part of it in another. Since no one, therefore, can convict Tertullian of so absurd a contradiction, what remains except to say that by the word “portion” he did not understand some part of the divine substance, which he most consistently affirmed can neither be divided nor separated?

In what sense, then, someone will ask, does he take the word “portion”? We shall readily allow it to be proved that it is taken in the same signification as partition, or participation and communication of the divine substance, which the Father derived into the Son. For in the very passage against Praxeas brought against us, the Son is called [Col. 0840A] “a derivation and portion of the whole,” and those words appear there to be synonymous. That derivation, however, is called a “portion,” or “partition,” because the Father communicated his whole substance to the Son in such a way that he nevertheless remained distinct from him in person. For since the persons of the Son and Father are distinguished from one another, and the Son received from the Father his own person together with the whole of that same divine substance, he is therefore called its “portion,” or “derivation.”

That this, moreover, is Tertullian’s true meaning may be gathered from another argument of his against the same Praxeas. For that heretic and others, who foolishly supposed the Father and the Son to be the same, contended that these words of Luke the Evangelist—“The Spirit of God will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you”—signified precisely the same thing as if he had said: “The Son of God [Col. 0840B] is God, and the power of the Most High is the Most High” (Luke 1:35 [the source reads “25”]). Tertullian attacks this heretical interpretation as follows: “If this,” he says, “had been the Evangelist’s meaning, he would surely have written: ‘God will come upon you, and the Most High will overshadow you’” (Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 26).
