But he did not write so; rather, by saying “the power of God”—not naming God directly, that is, in the nominative case—he intended a portion of the whole to be understood, which was to pass into the name of the Son. He therefore said that by these words, “the Spirit and power of God,” a portion is understood, because the name of God, taken not in the nominative but in the genitive case, signifies the portion—that is, the generation and derivation—of the Son from his Father. For by that derivation or generation, although he received the whole divine substance, his person is nevertheless not the same as the Father’s. Hence [Col. 0840C] our Author continues the discourse he had begun as follows: “Just as, therefore, the Word of God is not the very one whose Word he is, namely the Father, so neither is the Spirit, although he has been called God, nevertheless the very one whose Spirit he is called. . . . And therefore the Spirit of God is God, and the Word of God is God, because he is from God, yet he is not the very one from whom he is. But if he is God from God, as a substantial entity, he will not be the very God, but is God thus far: because he is from his substance, by which he is both a substantial entity and, as it were, some portion of the whole.”

Do you hear how the Son and Word of God is there openly denied to be “the God of God,” but is said, like his Father, to be true God? Yet although he is true God and his substance is the same as the Father’s, because he came forth and was begotten from the Father’s thought and intellection, he is distinguished from him in person. By this generation, however, he is called [Col. 0840D] “a derivation and portion of the whole”—that is, a partition and communication—but one by which, as Tertullian says, “he shares in the fullness”; that is, he possesses the whole and same substance and divinity of the Father from whom he arose.

Nor do we think those persons should be heard who will insist: if this is Tertullian’s meaning, then he takes the word “portion” in a wholly improper and entirely unusual expression. For Tertullian sprinkled his books, as no one fails to know and as we have often observed, with barbarous, improper, and unusual words and terms. For—to omit now the very many examples encountered everywhere in all his books—should he not, in this very *Apologeticum* about which we are disputing, which he addressed to pagan magistrates, have spoken more Latinate, elegantly, and correctly than in his other works? [Col. 0841A] Yet we have already noted, and shall still note, several barbarisms and improper and unfamiliar modes of expression in it. He employed the word “portion,” however, in the sense we have noted in order to refute more effectively Praxeas, who blathered that the Son was in no way distinguished from the Father in person.

## ARTICLE VII. Other arguments are answered by which it is objected that Tertullian denied the divinity of the Son of God, because he said that the Son was lesser than the Father, and that the Father was visible and the Son invisible.

They think another argument for Tertullian’s denial or undermining of the supreme divinity of the Son of God can be drawn from these words of his: “The Father is the whole substance, [Col. 0841B] while the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole, as he himself professes: ‘The Father is greater than I.’ By him he is also sung in the psalm as having been made a little lower than the angels. Thus the Father is other than the Son, insofar as he is greater than the Son” (Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 9). Does he not therefore, they say, openly signify there that the whole substance of the Godhead is in the Father, who is greater than the Son, and only some portion of it in the Son, who is for that reason lesser than he? Did he really say, however, that the Son was lesser than the Father, when, as we showed above, he asserted that the Son is equal to the Father, is made equal and equated with him, is joined to him, and is not lesser than him, because he himself had said: “I and the Father are one”? (above, this chapter, art. 1). Have we not discussed the statement he made before the words brought against us: “And never separated from the Father, or other than the Father, because: ‘I and the Father are one.’ This will be the projection [Col. 0841C] of truth, the guardian of truth, by which we say that the Son was brought forth from the Father, but not separated from him”? (cited book, chap. 8). Must he therefore be condemned for a nauseating contradiction such as could never be forgiven anyone? Was his mind ever so estranged from reason that he said the Son was lesser than his Father and not lesser, equal and not equal, one with him and not one—unless under different aspects? And certainly we have sufficiently proved how expressly he taught that there is in the Father and the Son one most simple nature and substance, which can neither be separated nor divided. But because Praxeas endeavored to infer from this that their person also was the same, our Author therefore shows that they are distinguished not in nature, but in person, because the Son was brought forth and begotten by his Father. Hence [Col. 0841D] immediately after the very words brought against us he added: “Thus too the Father is other than the Son, insofar as he is greater than the Son; insofar as the one who begets is other than the one who is begotten, the one who sends other than the one who is sent, and the one who makes other than the one through whom something is made. It is well that the Lord also used this word with respect to the person of the Paraclete, signifying not division, but arrangement: ‘For I will ask the Father,’ he says, ‘and he will send you another Advocate, the Spirit of truth.’ Thus he called the Paraclete other than himself, just as we call the Son other than the Father, so that he might show a third degree in the Paraclete, just as we show a second in the Son, for the preservation of the economy” (ibid., chap. 9).

He gives two reasons there why the Father is called greater and [Col. 0842A] the Son lesser. The first is that the Father sent the Son and the Son is sent by the Father. But this appears to concern the Son’s human nature, by which no one denies that he is lesser than his Father. The second is that the Son is begotten by his Father and received his divine nature from him. But by this generation he has the second degree and order after the Father, by which he can indeed be called lesser than him, but only, as Tertullian says, “for the preservation of the economy,” so that not division but arrangement is signified. Thus, on both those grounds, the Son could be called by him lesser than the Father and other than him, as one begotten by him.

Nor, I ask, should you reply that this explanation is not orthodox. For the ancient Fathers of the Church, even after the Council of Nicaea, interpreted in this very sense those words of Christ: [Col. 0842B] “The Father is greater than I.” Hilary, indeed—as vigorous a defender of Catholic teaching as ever there was—wrote without the least hesitation: “The Father is greater than the Son, but as Father than Son, by generation, not by kind. For he is the Son and came forth from him” (Hilary, *Tractate on Psalm 118*, § 17). We know, indeed, that the same words of John are elsewhere explained by him (Idem, book 9, *On the Trinity*, § 51), and by others also, of the human nature assumed by the Son of God. But it is enough for us that Hilary and several others later than the Nicene Synod, as we have noted elsewhere, also understood them of the divine generation of the Son of God himself, by which he is second in order after his Father (*Notes on Ambrose, On the Faith*, book 2). For it is established that nothing can be inferred from this against our Tertullian, who, since he did not contradict himself, is not without reason thought to have understood [Col. 0842C] the Evangelist’s words in this Catholic sense. And certainly he could interpret them thus all the more readily because he was less able to foresee the tasteless cavils of the Arians and was thereby more effectively refuting Praxeas’s tasteless error.

Nevertheless, they again object against us that Tertullian, in his books against Marcion, denied that the substance of the eternal Father and of the Son is the same (Petavius, vol. 2, *Theologia dogmatica*, book 1, chap. 5). For there he teaches that the Son was made and is visible, whereas the Father was neither visible nor made. He therefore thought their substance was different. To prove this, they bring against us these words of his: “We profess that Christ always acted in the name of God the Father; that it was he who from the beginning held converse and met with the Patriarchs and [Col. 0842D] Prophets—the Son of the Creator, his Word, whom by bringing him forth from himself he made Son, and thereafter set over his every arrangement and will, making him a little lower than the angels, as it is written in David; by which abasement he was also fitted by the Father for those very things that you censure as human, learning already from the beginning, already from that time, to be the man whom he was to become in the end. It is he who descends, he who questions, he who swears. As for the Father, the common testimony of the Gospel will attest that he was seen by no one . . . determining that the Father is invisible, in whose authority and name the one who was seen, the Son of God, was himself God” (Tertullian, book 2, *Against Marcion*, chap. 27).

But it must be observed that Tertullian is there arguing against Marcion, who, as he says in the same place, wrongly [Col. 0843A] proclaimed that the Creator was not the good God, since many things paltry, weak, and unworthy of God were proclaimed of him (ibid.). But Tertullian replies to this heretic that these lowly characteristics are indeed in Christ, though not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is man. He proves, however, that Christ truly is God because he always acted in the name of the Father, because it was he who spoke with the Patriarchs and Prophets, because he is the Word of God and the Son of the Creator. Yet this same Tertullian most consistently asserted that the Son and Word of God is true God and the Reason of his Father, by which the Father is rational from eternity. He therefore believed the Son’s eternity to be the same as the Father’s, and likewise his substance.

But, you will say, in the same place he wrote with sufficient clarity: “whom by bringing him forth from himself he made Son, and thereafter [Col. 0843B] set over his arrangement and will” (ibid.). Quite so. But is the Son there said to have been made at some point in time, or is his eternal generation denied? Certainly not. For Tertullian would then have confessed that there are two Gods: an eternal Father and a non-eternal Son, and thus would have fallen into the very error of Marcion whom he was attacking. When, therefore, he says that the Son of God was then made by his Father when he brought him forth from himself, his meaning plainly seems to be this: the Father made his Son when he brought him forth from himself—that is, from the matrix, as he calls it, and womb of his heart and intellect, or from his eternal reason, understanding, and thought; afterward, however, when he willed to create all things, he set him over his arrangement and will. But if anyone contends that by the words “from himself” is signified the same as “by sending him outside himself,” [Col. 0843C] his meaning will be: at the beginning of the world the Father brought the Son forth outside himself and made him, in that he made him manifest to creatures. For until the first creation of the world his divine generation, as we explained shortly before, lay hidden in the eternal bosom of the Father; at the beginning of the world it began to be recognized by rational creatures. Then, as our Author speaks and as we shall explain more fully below, his nativity was perfected and received a certain external completion.

Nor should you press the fact that the Father is called by him invisible, but the Son visible, and that the latter is therefore lesser than the Father and not properly called God. For nothing is more trivial or feeble than this argument. Indeed, in his book against Praxeas the same Tertullian openly declares: “The Father invisible because of the fullness of his majesty, [Col. 0843D] but the Son visible because of the measure of his derivation” (ibid., chap. 14). A little later, however: “We say that the Son too, in his own right, is invisible insofar as he is the Word and Spirit of God—by the condition of his substance even now—and insofar as he is God, Word, and Spirit; but visible before the flesh” (ibid.). He explains there in the following manner how the Son made himself visible before assuming flesh: “In former times God—that is, the Son of God—always appeared and was seen in a mirror and an enigma, in a vision and a dream, both by the Patriarchs and Prophets and even by Moses himself. And even if the Lord perhaps spoke face to face, nevertheless man would not see his face as it is, except perhaps in a mirror and an enigma. . . . . . . . Or was it indeed the Son who was seen, and was it thus his face? Yet this very thing was in a vision and dream, in a mirror and enigma, because the Word and Spirit cannot be seen except in an imaginary form” (ibid.).

[Col. 0844A] Who, after hearing these words of Tertullian, would not openly confess that he is so far from denying the Son’s divinity on the ground that the Father is called invisible and the Son visible, that he instead clearly proves from this against Praxeas that the same Son of God is true God, distinguished from his Father only by the measure of derivation—that is, by his person? Indeed, he even declares affirmatively that the same Son of God, insofar as he is Word and Spirit, was invisible in precisely the same manner as the Father. He nevertheless does not deny that before assuming flesh the Son presented himself to be seen by the Patriarchs; but in what manner, I ask? Only in a vision, he says, in a dream, in a mirror, in an enigma, and in what he calls an imaginary form.

[Col. 0844B] Perhaps there will be some who wonder that these objections are brought against the true teaching of our Tertullian concerning the divinity of the Son of God by Petavius, undoubtedly a most learned man (Petavius, vol. 2, *Theologia*, book 1, chap. 4). For he himself not only freely admits, but demonstrates from numerous testimonies of the Fathers of the Church, both before and after the Nicene Synod, that they most openly declared that the Son of God, although his divine nature, like the Father’s, cannot be seen, was nevertheless seen and beheld by the Patriarchs and Prophets, before he became man, under another, visible appearance (Idem, ibid., book 3, chap. 2, § 10 ff.). And what of the fact that Petavius himself considers it certain that not only the Son, but also the Father and [Col. 0844C] the Holy Spirit, appeared to human beings under an externally assumed appearance? From these points, duly proved, he concludes that the arguments the Arians drew from them against the Son’s divinity are utterly trivial and will be scorned by everyone. In our preceding dissertations, however, we showed that these visions in no way obstruct the supreme divinity of the Son of God, and why he rather than his Father should have presented himself to be seen by human beings (vol. 1, *Apparatus*, pp. 404, 593, and 689 ff.).

## ARTICLE VIII. It is shown once again how clearly Tertullian asserts the eternity of the Son of God; and the contrary arguments are dispelled by which some think it can be established that Tertullian taught that before the world was created the Son of God had no substance, and that his nativity was perfected when God undertook to create the world.

[Col. 0844D]

Having set forth and weighed in an equitable balance the force of those arguments by which Tertullian is wrongly accused of not acknowledging that the Father and the Son have the same substance, let us now come to those by which he is accused still more vehemently of having denied the eternity of the same Son of God. For if any credit is to be given to the most learned Petavius, in this respect Tertullian surpasses the Arian heresy in impiety and absurdity (Petavius, book 1, *Theologia dogmatica: De Trinitate*, chap. 5, p. 24). But if Tertullian himself rightly asserted, as we have seen, that the nature of the Son and the Father is the same, he undoubtedly believed the Son truly coeternal with his Father. [Col. 0845A] Anyone could readily perceive, from the passages we cited above and especially in the first article of this chapter, that this tenet of the Catholic faith is asserted and proclaimed by him in the clearest possible terms.

But let us now consider attentively, if you please, what he specifically determined concerning the Son’s eternity, and first how he defines the eternity of God: “What other origin,” he says, “does God have than eternity? What other origin does eternity have than always to have been and always to be, by the prerogative of having neither beginning nor end?” (Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chap. 4). There, as you see, he not only defines what eternity is, but makes it so proper to God alone that it can belong to no other. [Col. 0845B] Yet, as we showed above, he no less clearly and distinctly teaches and proves that the Son of God is true God, one and the same God with his Father. He was therefore persuaded that the Son’s eternity is the same as the Father’s.

Indeed, this is not only our argument but Tertullian’s own, by which he demonstrates the eternity of the Son of God most luminously. Hear, I ask, his words, and you will confess this with us: “God,” he says, “must be believed immutable and incapable of change of form, as being eternal. Transformation, however, is the destruction of the former state. For everything whatsoever that is transformed into another thing ceases to be what it had been and begins to be what it was not. But God neither ceases to be nor can be anything else; the Word, however, is God, and the Word is Lord, and abides forever by persevering in his own form” (Idem, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 27). This Word, moreover, is the Word and Son of God, who, as Tertullian immediately added, [Col. 0845C] was made flesh. Who, then, ever asserted his eternity in clearer words or by a clearer argument? Did Tertullian therefore build up there with one hand what he had elsewhere destroyed with the other? Yet some do not shrink from charging our Author with so great a paradox.

Petavius, indeed, objects against us that Tertullian taught no less certainly and evidently that the Son of God had no substance before the beginnings of the world, but received it from his Father when he undertook to create the world. Petavius was not alone in thinking this; some others too believed it could be established from the following words of Tertullian: “As soon as God willed to bring forth into their own substances and forms those things which he had arranged within himself together with the reason and discourse of Wisdom, he first brought forth the Word himself, having in himself the inseparable forms, Reason [Col. 0845D] and Wisdom, so that through him all things might be made, through whom they had been conceived and arranged—indeed, already made insofar as they were in the mind of God. For this alone was lacking: that they should also be known and apprehended outwardly, in their own forms and substances. Then, therefore, the Word himself also assumes his own form and adornment, sound and voice, when God said: ‘Let there be light’” (ibid., chap. 6). From this Petavius thinks it can be gathered that such was Tertullian’s opinion concerning the generation of the Son of God: that it was not eternal, but temporal. He adds further that shortly before Tertullian had said that God, who by his nature is rational, possessed Reason within himself from eternity, Λόγον (“Logos”), and the Word. But he contained this Word within himself, silently thinking and arranging with himself the things that he was [Col. 0846A] going to utter through the Word (ibid., chap. 5). At that time, therefore, this Word was only interior and did not yet subsist in himself. But when God began to fashion the world, he brought forth this Word and, by animating him, made him a substance and person. Tertullian therefore thought, they say, that the Son of God was not made before then.

But I truly do not know whether Petavius and the others who argue in this fashion paid sufficient attention to those words of Tertullian which immediately follow the very passages they bring against us: “This,” he says (ibid., chap. 6), “is the perfect nativity of the Word, when he proceeds from God, first established by him for thought under the name of Wisdom: ‘The Lord established me as the beginning of his ways.’ Thereafter begotten for effect: ‘When he prepared heaven, I was present with him’” (Proverbs 8:22 ff.). [Col. 0846B] “Thereafter, making him equal to himself, from whom by proceeding he was made Son; firstborn, as begotten before all things; and only-begotten, as alone properly begotten from God, from the womb of his very heart, in accordance with what the Father himself also testifies: ‘My heart has uttered an excellent word’” (Psalm 44:1).

For there he distinguished a twofold kind of nativity of the Son of God. The first, or first and properly so-called generation, is that by which the eternal Father brought forth Reason and the Word within himself before all creatures. The second, less properly so called, was his generation when the Father brought him forth at the beginning of the world—or, as our Author himself says, “begot him for effect,” that is, so that through him he might create all things. But the first generation was undoubtedly not ineffectual, and by it the Father begot a true Son. For as Tertullian says: “I may, without rashness, have established beforehand that even then, before the constitution of the universe, God was not alone, since he had in himself Reason, and in Reason the Word, whom he made second to himself” (ibid., chap. 5). [Col. 0846C] Who does not see, moreover, that Tertullian is there treating of the Word or Discourse of God before the creation of the world, while he was still within God his Father? Yet he clearly declares there that even then the Father was not alone, but had within himself this Word, distinct from his own person, whom he made second to himself and his Son—that is, whom he begot. Therefore before the constitution of the world, that is, from eternity, the Word or Son of God, as we observed above, had received his nature and substance from God the Father and was distinguished from the Father only in person.

[Col. 0846D] But the Father, Petavius argues, is said by Tertullian to have been, “before all things, God alone, because there was nothing external besides him” (Tertullian, cited passage). But we can scarcely, if at all, bring ourselves to believe that this is seriously objected by so learned and perspicacious a man. For Tertullian immediately added: “Yet even then he was not alone; for he had with him that which he had within himself, namely his Reason” (ibid.). Tertullian was therefore persuaded, as we showed above, that the eternal Father, before the world was created, or from eternity, both was alone and was not alone. For he was alone because he had nothing outside himself, but was not alone because he had within himself the Word, who is a person distinct from him and is his Son. We saw besides that the same Tertullian observed that the Greek term λόγον (“logos”) [Col. 0847A] ought to have been rendered in Latin as “reason” rather than “word”: “Because,” he says, “God was not discursive from the beginning, but rational even before the beginning; and because the Word himself also, subsisting in Reason, shows Reason to be prior as his substance” (ibid.). By these words he plainly signifies that the term λόγος (“logos”) can therefore be better rendered in Latin as “reason,” because God the Father was not “discursive” from eternity—that is, he had not brought the Word forth outside himself. Nevertheless, because he is rational by his very nature, he had Reason within himself from eternity, which is of the same substance as he, but is a second and distinct person, since the Father was not alone from eternity.

That this, indeed, is Tertullian’s true sense and meaning is established clearly from the fact that he is arguing there [Col. 0847B] against Praxeas, who babbled that the Son, the Word of God, was entirely the same as the Father and was not distinct from him. What, I ask, would he have gained against Praxeas if he admitted that the Son and Word of God did not subsist before the beginning of the world and was not a person distinct from the Father? By voluntarily abandoning the principal part of his case, he would have offered his throat to his adversary. But so far is he from conceding this that, on the contrary, he most consistently asserts that the Word of God was distinct from the Father before the creation of the world and from eternity, and was second to him.

But Petavius relents not at all and presses the point that Tertullian openly taught that the nativity of the Son of God was perfected when God created all things from nothing. Before then, therefore, he possessed neither origin, person, nor substance, [Col. 0847C] and consequently was not the Son of God (Petavius, vol. 2, *Theologia dogmatica*, book 1, chap. 5, p. 25). For these are his words in the passage cited, which we have already quoted (Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chap. 7): “This is the perfect nativity of the Word, when he proceeds from God, first established by him for thought under the name of Wisdom: ‘The Lord established me as the beginning of his ways.’ Thereafter begotten for effect: ‘When he prepared heaven, I was present with him’” (Proverbs 8:22, 27). Therefore, Petavius says, the nativity of the Son of God is said by Tertullian to have been perfected only when God created through him, who is his Word, both the world and all things.

But that most learned man could have observed that our Author distinguishes a twofold Word of God the Father. For the first is inward to him, [Col. 0847D] which the Greeks call ἐνδιάθετον (“inward”)‎; the other is external and brought forth, which they call προφορικὸν (“brought forth”) (Tertullian, cited passage). God the Father, Tertullian says, had arranged and conceived within himself, by that former inward Word, that he would create all things and bring them forth into their substances and forms. Then afterward, by sending this Word of his outside himself and outwardly, he created the universe. But we have already seen Tertullian assert, repeat, and inculcate that this inward Word was begotten by his Father from all eternity and, being therefore distinct from him in degree and order, is the second person of the most holy Trinity.

Why then, you will say, does he declare so openly that his birth was perfect not from eternity but at the beginning of the world, and that he then received his form, adornment, [Col. 0848A] sound, and voice? But shall we say that Tertullian descended into such madness as to suppose that the generation of the Son of God was at some time imperfect or merely begun, and that afterward it assumed form and adornment and was thus perfected and completed (ibid.)? He therefore called it imperfect not in that sense, but in the manner he himself explains in the same place: although it had been perfect from eternity, it nevertheless lay hidden within the bosom of God and was known to no one except God himself alone. But when, in creating the world, he brought forth this Word of his outside himself and, as it were, emitted him from the womb and matrix of his heart—as Tertullian likes to speak—then that eternal Word assumed sound and voice, and therefore an outward adornment and form. For then he was recognized by rational creatures. The noun *species* among good authors indeed has the same [Col. 0848B] meaning as the manifestation of some thing. And indeed, Nonius says that *species* derives from seeing. Therefore, when the Word of God, or the eternal Son of God the Father, was emitted outside him at the beginning of the world, he then received form and adornment, or sound and voice, and his birth was perfect—not, indeed, with respect to himself, but with respect to the creatures who recognized it.

No further hearing, therefore, should be given to those who again object that the same Tertullian said: “God was not possessed of Word from the beginning” (ibid., chap. 5). For he immediately added: “but God was rational even before the beginning; and because the Word himself also subsists in Reason, he shows that Reason to be prior, as his substance.” But if God was rational before the beginning, or from eternity, he also from eternity brought forth Reason, which, [Col. 0848C] as has often been said, is his Word and Son (ibid., chap. 8). Then afterward, he says, “this Word was constructed of spirit, and, so to speak, the body of the Word—that is, his substance—is spirit.” He acknowledges, however, that both, although they are one and the same, can in some manner be distinguished (ibid., chap. 26): “For spirit,” he says, “is the substance of the Word, and the Word the operation of the spirit, and the two are one.” But this Word of God the Father, or this very operation of his spirit, did not become known to creatures before the world was founded. The knowledge of this operation, or generation, of the Son of God is called by Tertullian his “perfect birth,” because what had previously been known to God the Father alone was then disclosed to rational creatures.

Petavius and others, however, still object to us these words of Tertullian concerning the same manifestation of the Son [Col. 0848D] (Petav., vol. II, *Theolog. dogmat.*, book I, chap. 5, p. 26; Tertull., *Against Praxeas*, chap. 12): “But in the preceding works of the world, how is it written? First, while the Son had not yet appeared: ‘And God said, Let there be light, and light was made’—the Word himself immediately being the true light which enlightens the man coming into this world, and through him the light of the world also. From then on, however, with the Word, Christ, assisting and administering, God willed things to be made, and God made them . . . through whom all things were made.” From this they conclude that it is there manifestly demonstrated that the Son and the Spirit, the second and third persons of the Trinity, did not subsist from eternity, but only when God willed to make the world and actually made it.

[Col. 0849A] But it must be observed that with these words Tertullian was answering the heretic Praxeas, who objected to Catholics that God, to whom nothing is impossible, could make himself both Father and Son at once. Tertullian readily acknowledges that all things could indeed be done by God, but that not everything he could do was done by him. Praxeas therefore had to demonstrate clearly that the Father had in fact made himself both Father and Son, or that the Son was none other than the Father himself. Tertullian, on the contrary, affirms all the more confidently that this can never be proved by Praxeas, because he so readily heaps up various testimonies of Scripture by which, he says, “among us the Father and the Son are demonstrated distinctly—distinctly, I say, not separately” (ibid., chap. 21); since the Son of God, as we have said so often, proceeded from the Father and is therefore [Col. 0849B] indeed distinct from him, but not divided or separated, because the substance of both is the same. Then, on the authority of the same Scripture, he shows that there are three persons of the Trinity joined by a simple unity. It was there that he uttered the words objected to us, and afterward concluded that all things were made through God’s Word, or through the Son of God, who is himself also God. Therefore, because he is God’s Word, he is distinguished from him and is called another “in the name of person,” he says, “not of substance; for distinction, not division.” But how is his substance one with that of the Father, and how is he one God with him, unless he existed from eternity, just as the Father did? Therefore, when he said that the Son of God had not appeared before the beginning of the world, he signifies plainly enough that the Son was then known to no creature. But when, as he says in the same place, it was first said, [Col. 0849C] “Let there be light,” light was immediately made and the true light appeared—that is, the Word of God—not indeed because he then existed for the first time and had not existed before, since he had been begotten from eternity, but because he who is the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world, then began to appear to men. So far, then, is this answer of our Tertullian from favoring Petavius and the others that it instead overturns their entire argument from its foundations.

We know, indeed, that his words are twisted by Bull into another sense. He admits that they are very obscure, but nevertheless suspects that they should be understood of the Son’s manifestation as follows: the Son of God, he says, insofar as he is eternal Reason and Wisdom, first began to appear when God began to dispose, order, and adorn by his wisdom the unformed and confused [Col. 0849D] matter of things. God’s Wisdom and Sophia had not yet shone forth from the confused and unordered mass of things called chaos. But it shone forth most clearly when the primeval light, as an image of the Son of God, who is the splendor of eternal light, illuminated matter and clothed each thing with its own form and adornment. Yet what seems to conflict with this interpretation is that the Word and Son of God shines forth no less from the creation of unformed and confused matter than from the creation of the primeval light, since through him every light and all other things were created. If, nevertheless, anyone should rightly prove that the explanation Bull offers of Tertullian’s words is true, we shall not greatly resist it, provided [Col. 0850A] that one can also infer from it that Tertullian acknowledged the eternal splendor of the light—that is, of the Son of God—and the eternal generation so constantly asserted and defended by him, as we have seen.

## ARTICLE IX. Another argument is resolved, derived from the fact that Tertullian seems to have said that there was a time when the Son of God did not exist

By another argument, drawn from Tertullian’s book *Against Hermogenes*, Petavius thinks it can still be proved that the eternity of the Son of God was entirely unknown to him. For our African author, as it seems to Petavius, declares most explicitly that there was a time when the Son of God did not exist. That learned man thinks that Tertullian asserts [Col. 0850B] the sheer and unadulterated fiction of Arius and his followers when he refutes the arguments of Hermogenes, who babbled that matter was coeternal with God. For that heretic attempted to demonstrate the eternity of matter from the fact that God had never not been Lord. But, he argued, God could not always have been Lord unless there had been matter of which he was always accounted Lord. Tertullian, however, refutes this argument of Hermogenes and denies that God was always Lord (Tertull., *Against Hermogenes*, chap. 3): “For ‘God,’” as he says, “is the name of the substance itself—that is, of divinity—whereas ‘Lord’ is the name not of substance but of power. He was therefore Lord only from the time when those things began to exist which God held in his power.” [Col. 0850C] He then continues as follows: “Because God is also Father, and God is Judge, he is not therefore always Father and Judge merely because he is always God. For he could not be Father before the Son, nor Judge before the offense. But there was a time when neither the offense nor the Son existed, the one to make him Judge, and the other to make him Father; so too he was not Lord before those things existed whose Lord he would be, but was only destined sometime to become Lord, just as Father through the Son and Judge through the offense, so also Lord through those things which he would make to serve him.” From this Petavius concludes that Tertullian clearly and plainly defines that there was a time when the Son of God did not exist.

Nor should it be answered that Tertullian is speaking not of God’s Son but of the son of any human being. For when he discusses God’s Sophia, or the Son of God himself, he cites and interprets concerning him these words of Proverbs (Prov. [Col. 0850D] VIII, v. 22 ff.): “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways; before the ages he established me for his works . . . Before the abyss I was begotten.” From them he argues as follows (Tertull., *Against Hermogenes*, chap. 18): “Let Hermogenes therefore acknowledge that God’s Sophia is proclaimed as born and created precisely so that we should believe nothing to be unbegotten and uncreated except God alone. For if that which was from the Lord and in him was not without a beginning—namely, his Sophia, born and created from the time when it began to be stirred in God’s thought for the ordering of the works of the world—much less can it be admitted that anything outside the Lord was without a beginning.” Here, they will say, Tertullian plainly asserts that Sophia, or the Son of God, was not without a beginning, but received one, and that [Col. 0851A] Sophia was then born and created when it began to be stirred in God’s thought for the ordering of the works of the world.

We have reported this entire argument and the complete words of our author lest anyone complain that we have concealed or omitted anything. Nor shall we conceal that these passages of Tertullian seem so obscure and difficult to some that they have thought nothing else should be answered to the argument drawn from them except these words of Jerome, with which Jerome answers Helvidius when the latter adduces the authority of this same Tertullian for another purpose (*Against Helvidius*): “Of Tertullian, indeed, I say nothing more than that he was not a man of the Church”—that is, that he fell into various errors of the heretics. But by this answer the knot of the difficulty is cut, not untied. For Tertullian wrote this [Col. 0851B] book while he was still a Catholic and a man of the Church. Moreover, even if he fell into various errors and, to use Hilary’s words, “although the man’s error detracted authority from writings otherwise worthy of approval” (Hilary, *Commentary on Matthew*, chap. V), we nevertheless demonstrated above that the Catholic doctrine of the divine and eternal generation of the Son of God was constantly asserted and defended by him, whether orthodox or heretical.

Perhaps, therefore, the response of others will appear more probable: they say that Tertullian, a man of extremely keen intellect, was carried somewhat further than was proper, in the not-unusual manner of disputants, during his very great contest with the heretic Hermogenes concerning the eternity of matter (Bull, *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, sect. 3, chap. 10, no. 4). For no one even moderately acquainted with reading his [Col. 0851C] books can fail to know that, in order to establish some proposition, he gathers arguments from every quarter, including even some that carried little weight. Therefore, they say, one should not judge from the cited words of this book what he thought about the eternal generation of the Son of God, but from other passages where, with a settled and tranquil mind, he explained his own doctrine—and that of the whole Church—concerning the supreme divinity and eternity of the Son of God, as we have seen.

But let us examine more carefully, if you please, whether in the passages objected against us he actually transgressed the limits of the true doctrine that he himself established. In the former passage he said that God was not always Lord, just as he could not be Father before the Son or Judge before the offense. Yet the question there concerned neither Father nor Judge, but only [Col. 0851D] Lord. They are therefore examples that he employs to refute Hermogenes. Examples involving any father or judge, whether created or uncreated, served his purpose equally well.

Granted, however—and let us concede, if you please—that he is speaking of the true God the Father and his Son: could he have denied that the Son was coeternal with his Father? Has it not been proved more than sufficiently how clearly and frequently he proclaimed that the Word, or Son of God, who is his Father’s Reason, was always in him and was never separated from him, and consequently is eternal? Accordingly, when he says that there was a time when he did not exist, he undoubtedly did not intend to deny his eternity, which he asserted and defended more frequently elsewhere.

[Col. 0852A] What, then, you will ask, is the meaning of his words, by which he seems so openly to deny it? You will readily persuade us that he intended nothing other than what he meant in the other words explained above, where he had said that the Son’s birth was perfect when God began to create the world. For although this Son of God had previously and from eternity been begotten, as we have shown, he had not yet come forth from the bosom or intellect of the eternal Father, as from his matrix, womb, and heart. Before the creation of things, therefore, neither his being the Son nor his having a Father was known. But when the Father emitted him outside himself, men then began to recognize his generation and that he truly was the Son of God. Therefore, in order to overturn more effectively Hermogenes’ frivolous argument drawn from the word “Lord,” Tertullian [Col. 0852B] thought it could be said that there was a time when men recognized neither that God was Father nor that his Son existed, because his generation and birth had not been ascertained and recognized by them. But when they recognized it, this generation was then perfect, as we saw him say. He therefore appears to be speaking of this perfect generation in the sense we have noted.

That this was indeed his meaning can be established from the cited words of Tertullian himself against Hermogenes: “His Sophia,” he says, “was born and created from the time when it began to be stirred in God’s thought for the ordering of the works of the world” (Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chap. 18); because this very Sophia, who, as he admits and as we have said, was always in God the Father, appeared to men as born from him and was manifested to them. For he did not say [Col. 0852C] that she then first arose and was begotten. Indeed, in this very passage, where he rejects the subtleties of Hermogenes, he most expressly proclaims that she arose from eternity: “If matter is necessary to God for the works of the world,” he says, “as Hermogenes thought, God possessed a matter far worthier and more suitable, not to be sought among the philosophers but understood among the prophets—namely, his Sophia. She alone, in short, knew the mind of the Lord. For who knows the things of God, and the things within him, except the spirit who is within him? But Sophia is spirit.” From this he concludes: “Who would not rather commend her as the source and origin of all things, a matter of matters not subjected to him, not different in state, not restless in motion, not formless in condition, but innate and his own, composed and beautiful, such as God could have employed, having need [Col. 0852D] of what was his own rather than another’s?” Who does not understand that Tertullian here asserts that God’s Sophia was begotten by her Father from all eternity; that she is spirit only, and God the Father’s counselor; that she is not different from him in state—that is, as we noted above, in substance—but is his own, was always inherent in him, and was the only thing, and no other, that he needed for the creation of the world, if indeed God can ever be said to have needed anything?

Having established these points, he answers Hermogenes, who babbled that God needed matter and that matter was therefore coeternal with him: “God’s Sophia is therefore also proclaimed as born and created, so that we should believe nothing unbegotten and uncreated except God alone” (ibid.). Thus he says that Sophia, or the Word and Son of God, is proclaimed to have been born at a certain time, [Col. 0853A] and to have begun to be stirred, according to the prophetic saying he cites: “My heart has uttered a most excellent word.” “And thus,” he says, “the Word of God, who is also his Sophia, was born,” because he then came and went forth from the bosom of his Father, in which he had lain hidden, begotten from eternity; and thus, as we have said, his birth was perfect, because it was then, and not before, disclosed and demonstrated to men. Moreover, just as this generation of the Son of God, so also the dominion—and indeed the fatherhood—of his divine Father began to be recognized by rational creatures at the beginning of the world, and God began to be called by the names of Father and Lord alike. Furthermore, that this is Tertullian’s meaning is established by the fact that he is there disputing against Hermogenes, who contended that God was not Lord from eternity unless he had matter outside himself of which [Col. 0853B] he truly was Lord. Yet although Tertullian may not have entirely extricated himself from every difficulty in this argument, no one can therefore rightly conclude that he denied the eternity and divine nature of the Son of God. For who does not know that certain doctrines most difficult to understand are asserted without hesitation by many who cannot entirely untie all the knots of the difficulties in which they are entangled? But we have shown most clearly how constantly, how explicitly, and without any verbal evasions Tertullian asserted and defended the eternity and divine nature of the Son of God. He proclaims it no less plainly elsewhere as well, as we shall see in the following chapter.

# CHAPTER IX. On Christ as God and Man

[Col. 0853C]

## ARTICLE I. On Christ’s human birth from a virgin, foretold by the sacred prophets; why he is said to be a man mingled with God; and why his advent upon earth cannot be rejected by the Gentiles, who had fabricated certain similar tales to destroy its truth

We have demonstrated sufficiently and abundantly, unless we are altogether mistaken, how true and orthodox was Tertullian’s opinion and doctrine concerning the supreme divinity of the Word, or Word and Son of God. But further light can be shed on these matters by what he taught concerning the same Son of God clothed in human flesh. To the Gentiles [Col. 0853D] he explains briefly, in this manner, what Christians believed concerning him: “This ray of God”—that is, the Son of God, who proceeded from his Father’s bosom like a ray from the sun—“as had always been proclaimed in ancient times” by the ancients, namely, the prophets, “descended into a certain virgin, and, fashioned as flesh in her womb, is born a man mingled with God” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 399). But in another book he expounded this in the following clearer words: “Accordingly, the derivation of each substance displayed him as man and God: on the one side born, on the other unborn; on the one side fleshly, on the other spiritual; on the one side weak, on the other exceedingly strong; on the one side dying, on the other living. This distinctive property of the conditions—the divine and the human—was duly assigned by the truth of each nature, with equal assurance regarding spirit and flesh: the miracles proved the Spirit [Col. 0854A] of God, the sufferings the flesh of man” (idem, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chap. 5). He therefore teaches lucidly that both the divine and the human nature were altogether perfect in Christ. No less openly does he declare that those two natures of Christ were not confused, but were so distinguished from one another that their properties are entirely different.

Accordingly, when in the *Apologeticum* he said, “He is born a man mingled with God” (passage cited above), he undoubtedly did not signify that his two natures were blended and confused, as the Eutychians later dreamed, but that they were coupled and joined to one another—as we have explained elsewhere—so that Christ is both true God and true man (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 17, art. 3).

He teaches, however, that Christ was made man [Col. 0854B] not in the ordinary manner of men, but “descended,” he says, “into a virgin,” who bore him without the agency of any man (*Apologeticum*, passage cited). But because this was extremely difficult to believe, or could be mocked by the pagans, Tertullian deliberately warns everyone that it had been foretold by the sacred prophets, whose authority, as we said above, can be undermined by no one. Hence he had said shortly before: “(Therefore he came who was foretold as destined to come from God to reform and illuminate it—the grace of the Jews transmitted to the Christians—namely, Christ, the Son of God.) The arbiter and master of this grace and discipline, the illuminator and guide of the human race, was announced as the Son of God; not, indeed, begotten in such a way that he should blush at the name of son or at his father’s seed . . . The Son of God has no mother through sexual misconduct; [Col. 0854C] even the one whom he seems to have had had not married” (ibid.). All these words, in precisely this form, are found in our manuscripts and in the old editions down to Rigaltius. But Rigaltius, whom others afterward followed, decided to cut away completely the first phrase of this passage, enclosed in parentheses. He nevertheless gave no reason for this excision—not even the slightest word. Yet even if this phrase appeared to him wholly useless and altogether improperly inserted into Tertullian’s text, the reader should at least have been notified of this addition.

Moreover, Tertullian’s meaning can be obscure to no one: he most manifestly declares that the Son of God descended into a virgin, from whom he received a human body. He said “virgin” because this Son of God, he says, [Col. 0854D] “has no mother through sexual misconduct; even the one whom he seems to have had had not married.” But if any woman became a mother without the stain of sexual misconduct and without marital intercourse, she certainly gave birth to Christ while preserving the integrity of her virginity. Yet by what reasoning, someone will ask, could it be said, “she had not married”? Do not almost all assert that she had actually married Joseph? Some answer that by the words “she had not married,” nothing else is signified than that Mary had not known a man. For she herself answered the angel: “How shall this be, since I know not a man?” (Luke 1:34). But they needed to prove who uses the verb *nubo* in this sense. Others approve the opinion—which they believe to be Jerome’s—that when Mary conceived Christ [Col. 0855A] she was Joseph’s betrothed, or, to use the Evangelists’ word, she had indeed been espoused to him, and married him after a short interval following the conception. But no one can disclose Tertullian’s meaning more certainly than Tertullian himself (Petav., vol. V, *Theolog. dogmat.*, book XIV, chap. 3, §10; Jerome, *Against Helvidius*). In his book *On the Flesh of Christ*, however, he wrote the following concerning the Virgin Mary: “Although she conceived as a virgin, in giving birth she married, by the very law of the body being opened,” which he there cites: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (idem, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chap. 23). You see plainly that he here takes the verb *nubere*, “to marry,” to mean the virgin’s delivery, by which her womb was opened. We are not now inquiring in what sense he said it was opened, a matter treated in our observations on Ambrose. For our present purpose it is enough [Col. 0855B] that the verb *nubere* is taken by him to mean the opening of a woman’s womb in childbirth (*Notes on Ambrose’s Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*). Just as we cannot deny that this is by no means the proper meaning of this verb, so certainly all must confess that Mary’s inviolate virginity is asserted by him most clearly (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, diss. 2, chap. 6, art. 9, p. 973). For he establishes and confirms this teaching not only in his *Apologeticum* but also in another book, as we have seen elsewhere, as something received by the universal Church of his time and previously by broad consensus. We discussed it in our preceding dissertations (ibid., book II, diss. 6, chap. 7, §5, p. 597; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 17, art. 3; vol. I, *Apparatus*, passage cited, and [Col. 0855C] book III, diss. 2, chap. 6, art. 4, p. 597 ff.; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 8, art. 1).

Tertullian further openly professes that this birth of Christ from a virgin and his advent upon earth were foretold by our sacred seers. But he remained entirely silent about what their oracles were in this book, in which he was aiming at brevity. He reported many, however, in his book *Against the Jews*, and others reported many in other books; we have already treated them in those same preceding dissertations of ours. Yet we cannot omit the testimony of Justin Martyr, which agrees excellently with Tertullian’s statements and confirms them wonderfully. For when that most holy martyr cites several predictions of the sacred prophets concerning Christ’s future advent, and especially this one of Isaiah, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” he there shows that this gave the pagans no opportunity to excuse their Jupiter, who had begotten several children in adulterous intercourse. For that prophecy of Isaiah—Σήμαινει οὐ συνουσιασθεῖσαν τὴν παρθένον συλλαβεῖν· εἰ γὰρ ἐσυνουσιάσθη ὑπὸ ὁτουοῦν, οὐκ ἔτι ἦν παρθένος· ἀλλὰ δύναμις Θεοῦ ἐπελθοῦσα τῇ παρθένῳ, ἐπεσκίασεν αὐτὴν, καὶ κυοφορῆσαι παρθένον οὖσαν πεποίηκε—means that a virgin was to conceive without sexual intercourse. For if she had consorted with anyone, she would no longer have been a virgin. But a power coming upon the virgin overshadowed her and, while she remained a virgin, caused her to carry a fetus in her womb (Justin, *First Apology*).

Even if no one should venture to declare with certainty that Tertullian was aiming at these words of Justin, no one can doubt [Col. 0856A] that Cyprian had regard to this passage of our Tertullian when he committed the following to writing: “The arbiter and master of this indulgence, grace, and discipline, the Word and Son of God, is therefore sent, who throughout earlier times had been proclaimed by all the prophets as the illuminator and teacher of the human race . . . He glides into the virgin, puts on flesh through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit: God is mingled with man” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*). He is said by Cyprian, as by Tertullian, to be “mingled,” not by a confusion of the two natures, divine and human, fabricated by the Eutychians, but because Christ, as we noted shortly before, has both perfect natures joined and coupled to his divine person.

Then our author, addressing the Gentiles themselves, demonstrates as follows [Col. 0856B] that these things cannot be rejected by them: “Accept for the moment this tale—or accept it as a tale; it is similar to your own—while we show how Christ is proved. Those among you who furnished rival tales beforehand for the destruction of this truth knew it” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 399). In our manuscripts, however, and in the editions before Rigaltius, the words after “is proved” are written differently, as follows: “and who among you furnished rival tales of this sort beforehand for the destruction of truth of this sort.” Why Rigaltius altered these words, you should expect no reason from him. Tertullian argues against the pagans as follows: You can object to me that what I have said about Christ, his birth from a virgin, and his human life is a mere tale. Yet even if I granted you that, [Col. 0856C] you should nevertheless not reject but accept it, since it is similar to the tales you have fabricated. For we show how Christ’s birth from a virgin is proved, and that there are several writers among you who furnished similar tales beforehand to destroy the truth. Tell me, then, I ask, whether the meaning of Tertullian’s words as transcribed in our manuscripts is any more obscure than it is in Rigaltius’s edition.

Moreover, Justin Martyr had previously argued against the same Gentiles in an entirely similar manner: Εἰ δὲ καὶ διὰ παρθένου γεγεννῆσθαι φέρομεν, κοινὸν, καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς τὸν Περσέα ἔστω ὑμῖν. “And when we proclaim that Christ was born of a virgin, let this too be something you have in common with us because of Perseus” (Justin, *First Apology*). For everyone knows the tale in which the Gentiles invented that [Col. 0856D] Jupiter, transformed into a golden shower, descended to Danaë and begot Perseus from her. In the same place the holy martyr mentions other pagan tales, which he shows to resemble what is truly narrated concerning Christ. Afterward he adds that such tales were celebrated by pagan poets under the prompting and through the deceits of demons, so that Christ’s wondrous deeds might be regarded as tales and poetic fictions.

There is no one who, even if we remained silent, would not understand how closely these things agree with Tertullian’s statements and how they confirm them. For he touched briefly not only on the single tale concerning Jupiter’s wicked intercourse with Danaë but also on several others in these words: “The Son [Col. 0857A] of God was announced as not begotten in such a way that he should blush at the name of Son or at his Father’s seed; he did not endure as his father a god who, through incest with a sister, violation of a daughter, or adultery with another man’s wife, became a scaly, horned, or feathered lover, or one transformed into gold. These are your names for the Jupiter of Danaë” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 396). Thus these words are read in our manuscripts and older printed editions, except that the latter placed a full stop after the name “Danaë” and read “gold” in place of “into gold.” But Rigaltius removed the name “Danaë” on his own authority, as is evident, and against the testimony of all the manuscript and printed copies. We discussed these transformations of Jupiter for the violation of virgins and women in our preceding dissertations, especially those on the books of Arnobius [Col. 0857B] (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 9, art. 4).

## ARTICLE II. The same advent of Christ upon earth cannot be denied by the Jews unless they are afflicted with blind obstinacy

After Tertullian had argued against the Gentiles in the manner we have explained, he then immediately proves that what Christians taught against the Jews concerning the advent of Christ the Lord was true. For he continues thus: “The Jews too knew that Christ was to come, since it was to them that the prophets spoke. For even now they await his advent, and there is no greater contention between us and them than their refusal to believe that he has already come. For since two advents of his were indicated—the first, which has already been discharged,” or accomplished and completed, “in the humility of the human condition; the second, which threatens at the close of the age, in the sublimity of manifested divinity,” that is, visible and manifest, “by failing to understand the first and hoping for the second, which was more manifestly proclaimed, they supposed there was only one” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 400). Cyprian, in his customary fashion, drank from this source of Tertullian and adapted it to his own use as follows: “The Jews too knew that Christ was to come. For he was always announced to them by the warnings of the prophets. But because a twofold advent of his was indicated—one in which he would perform the office and furnish the example of a man, the other which would confess him as God—by failing to understand the first advent, which secretly preceded in suffering, they believe only in the one that will be manifest in power” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*).

Both, therefore, acknowledge that Christ’s advent in the assumed flesh [Col. 0857D] of a man was real. For it was so openly foretold by the ancient sacred prophets, as we noted shortly before, that the Jews could not have been ignorant of it. But because Christ lived a mortal life in the humility of the human condition, the Jews stubbornly denied that he was the true Messiah and, swollen with pride, await another who is to come at the end of the world with the full glory of divine majesty. Elsewhere, however, we have shown that this error of the Jews was voluntary, and that it was utterly overthrown not only by our Tertullian and Cyprian but also by Lactantius (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 17, art. 5).

The cause of so great an error and so great a blindness among the Jews, Tertullian says, was their transgression, [Col. 0858A] as Isaiah had foretold. But our author himself must again be heard: “For their failure to understand Christ’s former advent—since they would have believed if they had understood, and would have attained salvation if they had believed—was the deserved consequence of their transgression. They themselves read it written thus: that they were punished by the loss of wisdom and understanding, and of the fruit of their eyes and ears” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 400). Cyprian once again followed closely in his tracks: “But the fact that the Jewish people could not understand this was the deserved consequence of their transgressions. They were so punished with blindness of wisdom and understanding that, being unworthy of life, they had life before their eyes and did not see it” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*).

Both were undoubtedly aiming at and tacitly citing these words of Isaiah: “You shall say to this people: Hear while hearing, and do not understand; and see a vision, and do not recognize it. Blind the heart of this people, make its ears heavy, and close its eyes, lest perhaps it see with its eyes and hear with its ears and understand with its heart and be converted, and I heal it” (Isa. 6:9–10). You will find these words cited not only in Matthew’s Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles, but also by John the Evangelist in this form: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and be converted, and I heal them” (Matt. 1:14; Acts 28:26; John 12:39–40). But we have already discussed in our dissertation on the books of Lactantius the Jews who were blinded by an utterly intolerable vice of obstinacy and who are therefore said to have been no longer able [Col. 0858C] to believe; and something further must still be said below in Article III (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 16, art. 2).

Nor did the Jews’ untamed and blind obstinacy stop here. Although Christ, by miracles hitherto unheard of, was making it most manifestly clear to everyone that he had come from the bosom of his eternal Father, they dared to attribute these miracles to magical arts. “Indeed,” Tertullian continues, “because they had presumed him to be merely a man on account of his lowliness, it followed that they regarded him as a magician on account of his power, since by a word he expelled demons from men, restored sight to the blind, cleansed lepers . . . . showing himself to be λόγον (“the Word”) of God, that is, that primordial Word, the first-begotten, supported by power and reason” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, [Col. 0858D] p. 400). So it stands in Rigault’s edition. In our manuscripts and the earlier editions, however, it reads: “showing himself to be,” or “showing himself [to be] the Word of God, that is, λόγον (“Word”), that”; and after the word “supported,” they add: “the same who by the Word both made all things and had made them.” But since the earlier words were transposed by Rigault, he ought at least to have given some reason why he deleted the latter ones. Did he reject them because there is a solecism there, or because he thought them useless? But what if the pronoun “the same” refers to λόγον (“the Word”)? Do we not read in John’s Gospel, “The Beginning, who also speak to you” (John, ch. 8, v. 25)? Is there any less of a solecism in these words than in Tertullian’s? Finally, the last words, which we read in all our manuscripts, [Col. 0859A] appear neither superfluous nor of little service to Tertullian’s purpose.

Rigault therefore showed greater diligence when, in the same place, he wished readers to be advised that in certain copies of our Author and of Cyprian the reading is indeed *magnum* (“great”), but that *magum* (“magician”) appears to be the more suitable reading. Quite rightly. For Tertullian later said: “Who, then, is this Christ with his story, if he is a man of ordinary condition, if a magician?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 20, p. 25). We have also observed that in the Harleian manuscript, where *magnum* occurs, two dots have been placed beneath the letter *n*, marking it as superfluous and to be deleted. Tertullian’s passage was transcribed by Cyprian as follows: “When Christ Jesus, in accordance with what had previously been foretold by the prophets, expelled demons from men by the command of his word and voice, [Col. 0859B] restored paralytics, cleansed lepers . . . . . the Jews, who believed him to be only a man on account of the lowliness of his flesh and body, regarded him as a magician because of the unrestrictedness of his power”—and in our Tertullian, “because of his power” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*). In the four more ancient manuscript codices of this work of Cyprian which we have obtained, however, the reading is *magnum*; in others, *magum*. Nevertheless, the latter reading seems preferable to the former, because both authors are discussing Christ’s divine power, by which he performed miracles almost without number and hitherto unheard of, which the most shameless Jewish slanderers had dared to ascribe to his magical arts. We have discussed in the preceding and other dissertations these miracles of Christ, by which he most clearly proved that he was the Son of God and, having assumed a human body, [Col. 0859C] lived a mortal life (Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 9, art. 2 ff.; ch. 18, art. 3).

## ARTICLE III. That Christ, as he himself had foretold, was driven to the cross by Pilate, procurator of Syria, through the violent votes of the Jews, and voluntarily yielded up his spirit with a word; concerning the eclipse of the sun at that time, recorded in the archives, and concerning Christ’s burial

Although so many and such astonishing miracles of Christ most conclusively demonstrate against the Jews, and against all others whatsoever, that he was truly God and man and lived among men, Tertullian nevertheless did not think this sufficient. For he proceeds and demonstrates no less clearly that this truth can be further established and confirmed [Col. 0859D] by other similar miracles performed by Christ before and after his death. Let us therefore follow him and hear him discoursing on Christ’s death:

“Because they were refuted” by “his teaching” (the manuscripts read *qua*, “by which”), he says, “the teachers and chief men of the Jews were so exasperated, especially because an immense multitude was turning toward him, that at last, when he had been brought before Pontius Pilate, who was then governing Syria on behalf of Rome, they extorted from him by the violence of their votes that he be delivered to them for the cross” (the manuscripts add “Jesus”) (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 400).

Cyprian borrowed this from our Author in such a way that he also excerpted some of his words: “Their teachers,” he says, “and chief men”—that is, those Jews whom he refuted by both teaching and wisdom—[Col. 0860A] “inflamed with anger and provoked to indignation, finally handed him over, after he had been detained, to Pontius Pilate, who was then governing Syria on behalf of Rome, demanding his cross and death by violent and persistent votes” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*). That both authors, and later Lactantius, so explicitly call Pilate procurator of Syria is not without difficulty; but we attempted to resolve it in our dissertation on Lactantius’s works. We also explained why the Jews are said to have been exasperated by Christ’s teaching—that is, made harsher—or, as Cyprian says, inflamed with anger and indignation: because he was dissolving and rendering obsolete their law (Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 18, art. 2).

Tertullian adds: “He himself had also foretold that they would act thus. This would be too little” (the pronoun [Col. 0860B] “this” is absent from the manuscripts), “if the prophets had not also foretold it long before” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 401). But Cyprian explains this somewhat more fully and clearly in these words: “He himself had foretold that they would do this, and the testimony of all the prophets had likewise preceded it, declaring beforehand that he must suffer, so that he might not merely experience death but conquer it” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*). Not merely one, but all the Evangelists have testified with the greatest possible unanimity how Christ foretold the death that the Jews would inflict upon him. We have shown elsewhere that it was also announced by the prophets of the Old Testament.

Then our Author continues: “And yet, fastened to the cross, he yielded up his spirit with a word, forestalling the executioner’s office” (Matt., ch. 20, vv. 18, 19; Mark, 10.35; Luke, 10, [Col. 0860C] 33 and 18.31; John, 3, 4 and 8; Acts 12.32; Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 8, art. 2; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 401). So Rigault indeed prints it. But observe here, as elsewhere, his truly remarkable diligence. For he noted no variant reading other than “and finally” in place of “and yet.” But in all our manuscript copies, as also in those previously printed, the passage reads: “And yet, fastened to the cross, he displayed many distinctive signs peculiar to his death. For with a word he voluntarily yielded up his spirit, forestalling the executioner’s office.” If all these words displeased Rigault, why did he remove them without giving any reason, including the word “voluntarily,” which is found in Cyprian, Tertullian’s intermediary and faithful interpreter, as follows: “Crucified, forestalling the executioner’s office, he voluntarily yielded up his spirit” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, [Col. 0860D]). Could Rigault not have understood from this that these were Tertullian’s own words, which Cyprian had undoubtedly read in his copy of this *Apologeticum*? Had he also forgotten, or could he have ignored, what we observed to have been written similarly by Lactantius: “Suspended and fastened, he cried to the Lord with a loud voice and of his own accord laid down his spirit” (Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 18, art. 3)? Observe in passing that the words “with a loud voice” mean the same thing as those of our Tertullian, “yielded up with a word.” Why, then, did Rigault scrape away other words of the same Tertullian, by which he wished to prove against the Jews and others that Christ, God and man, died of his own accord, as the miracles then performed by him demonstrated?

[Col. 0861A] What Tertullian and, later, Cyprian mean by saying “forestalling the executioner’s office” is explained more plainly and explicitly in these words of Lactantius: “When, fastened to the cross, he had laid down his spirit, the executioners did not think it necessary to break his bones, as their custom required” (Lactantius, bk. 4, *Divine Institutes*, ch. 26). Lipsius discusses this custom; if you please and have the leisure, you may consult him (Lipsius, bk. 2, *On the Cross*, ch. 14, p. 663, vol. 3).

Meanwhile, let us proceed and see what Tertullian adds about the dying Christ: “At the very moment,” he says, “when he was breathing his last, daylight was withdrawn while the sun marked the world. Those who did not know that this too had been foretold concerning Christ naturally thought it an eclipse” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 401). These words, and no more, are read in all the codices, both the earlier printed editions [Col. 0861B] and those written by any hand. But in his edition Rigault added: “failing to discover its cause, they denied it.” Thus he added these words to Tertullian’s text, just as he had removed quite a few words from it in many other places. From what source he took them he does not tell us, nor indeed can we conjecture. He used two manuscripts of this work, the Puteanus and the Pithoeanus, as well as variant readings from the Fulda manuscript. We have before us both the Puteanus, venerable for its antiquity, and the Pithoeanus; and these additional words do not occur in them. Rigault therefore ought to have stated whether they are found among the variant readings of the Fulda copy and why he preferred the authority of that manuscript alone to all the others.

We have discussed elsewhere the eclipse of the sun [Col. 0861C] next mentioned by Tertullian and its prediction (Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 8, art. 2). How greatly it struck not only the Jews but also the Gentiles may be inferred from these subsequent words of our Author: “And yet you have that event which befell the world recorded in your archives” (Tertullian, ibid.). These words are written thus in our manuscripts, as in Rigault’s edition. But who would not praise the singular diligence of that learned man, who there advised us that other editions have *archivis*, “archives,” in place of *arcanis*, “secret records”? He would nevertheless undoubtedly deserve greater praise if, after noting this and certain other similar readings of surely very little weight, he had not omitted many others of far greater importance. For *archiva* means precisely the same as *arcana*, which, on the testimony of Festus and Servius, are so called because they are secret and [Col. 0861D] closed, and everyone is barred from them (Festus, bk. 20, *On the Meaning of Words*; Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. 1, v. 266).

Our Author moreover asserts that this eclipse of the sun was recorded in the Gentiles’ secret archives because it and other events that occurred before and after Christ’s death were written down by public notaries or others and preserved in those same Gentiles’ archives. What these archives or secret records were—whether those of the Romans or of other Gentiles—may perhaps be gathered from what we shall say shortly concerning Pilate’s letter to the emperor Tiberius about Christ.

Meanwhile, however, we shall note that Rigault once again laid hands upon these subsequent words of Tertullian: [Col. 0862A] “The Jews took him down from the cross, placed him in a tomb, and surrounded it with the great diligence of a military guard” (ibid.). In our manuscript copies and the earlier printed editions, however, it reads: “Then the Jews . . . . . surrounded it with a large military force, with the diligence of a guard.” What harm was done there by the words “with a large military force”? Did not our Author thereby express more forcefully that the number of soldiers who guarded Christ’s tomb with the greatest diligence was not small? But let us proceed with the rest.

## ARTICLE IV. Concerning Christ’s return from death to life, his appearances in Galilee, his commissioning of the disciples to spread the Gospel, his ascension into heaven, and Pilate’s report of all these things to the emperor Tiberius; why the Caesars would have believed in Christ if they had not been necessary to the age

[Col. 0862B]

Tertullian continues and assures us that Christ foretold that on the third day after his death he would be recalled to life (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 401). Quite rightly, as we have explained elsewhere (Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 8, art. 2). Christ kept his promises and returned to life. After he had thus risen, in the words of our same Author, “nothing was found in the tomb except the grave-clothes of the tomb” (ibid.). In our manuscripts and other editions, the reading is “of the buried man,” and indeed more suitably. For *exuviae* is said primarily of human beings, and sometimes of beasts. Hence Lactantius says: “Nothing [Col. 0862C] was found in the tomb except the wrappings in which they had enclosed the enshrouded body” (Lactantius, bk. 4, *Divine Institutes*, ch. 29; Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 19, art. 2).

In that same dissertation of ours on Lactantius’s books, we also showed how he explained what Tertullian had said concerning Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection, to which the following is appended in the same place: “Nor did the risen Christ bring himself before the general public, lest the impious should be freed from error” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 402). There we demonstrated that this manner of speaking, employed not only by Tertullian and Lactantius but also by Cyprian and our sacred writers, is attacked entirely without justification by certain heterodox writers (Dissert. on Lactantius, place cited above, and ch. 17, art. 5).

[Col. 0862D] Tertullian next relates the following concerning Christ after he had been recalled to life: “He spent forty days with certain disciples in Galilee, a region of Judaea, teaching them what they were to teach” (Tertullian, ibid.). What, then? Did Christ spend that entire period in Galilee alone and with only some of his disciples? Did he not appear elsewhere and to all the disciples? But because Tertullian aimed at brevity in this book, he does not deny this; rather, he judged it sufficient to relate what was done in Galilee. Cyprian, however, though following him, wrote less restrictively and more generally: “He appeared to his disciples as he . . . . . had been . . . . . and remained for forty days, so that they might be instructed by him in life-giving precepts and learn [Col. 0863A] what they were to teach” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*). We have discussed these appearances of Christ and the teaching with which he imbued his disciples in other dissertations (Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 19, art. 3; and Dissert. on Caecilius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 4, art. 2).

In those same dissertations we also explained the meaning of these subsequent words of Tertullian: “Thereafter, when he had appointed them to the duty of preaching throughout the world, he was snatched up into heaven, enveloped by a cloud” (Tertullian, place cited). In our copies, however, and in others printed before Rigault, we read: “he was received into heaven.” Could Rigault not endure that form of expression? Why, then, did he not rather use these words of Cyprian: “He was raised into heaven, enveloped by a cloud” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*)? Would he not, if that were permissible, have [Col. 0863B] corrected the teacher better from the disciple? But authors must be left their own words. Otherwise, the genuine works of the ancient writers would be done for.
