Tertullian adds that Christ ascended into heaven “with far better grounds than your Proculuses among you Gentiles are accustomed to assert concerning the Romuluses” (Tertullian, place cited). Yet again, in those same manuscripts of ours and printed codices older than Rigault, the reading is: “with far greater truth . . . Proculuses are accustomed to assert concerning Romulus.” Who does not see that this is the preferable and genuine reading of Tertullian? For there he asserts that it is far truer that Christ ascended into heaven than that Romulus did, although “Proculuses”—that is, those who misuse Proculus’s perjury—are accustomed to affirm that they saw Romulus ascending into heaven.

Finally, our Author added: “Pilate reported all these things concerning [Col. 0863C] Christ to Caesar, then Tiberius, and was himself already a Christian according to his conscience. And the Caesars too would have believed concerning Christ if the Caesars had not also been necessary to the age, or if Christians could have been Caesars” (ibid.). Other words written by him earlier mutually shed light upon these. They are as follows: “Tiberius, when it had been reported to him” (our manuscripts and the old editions read “when there had been reported”) “from Syria-Palestine the things which” (Pamelius: “the fact which”) “had revealed there the truth of this divinity” (the same manuscripts and other earlier editions: “had revealed”), “referred it to the senate with the prerogative of his own vote. The senate rejected it because it had not itself approved it. Caesar remained of the same opinion and threatened danger to the accusers of Christians” (Tertullian, ibid., ch. 5, p. 291).

Eusebius transcribed this whole passage of Tertullian, [Col. 0863D] explicitly naming him. But he first relates that it had become customary for provincial governors to report to the emperor whatever new event occurred among them. “For this reason Pilate,” he says, “reported to the emperor Tiberius the resurrection of our Savior Jesus Christ, whose fame was celebrated throughout Palestine; he also indicated that he had heard of many other miracles performed by him, and how, after being restored once more to life, he was already regarded as God by very many. They say that Tiberius referred the matter to the senate, but that the senate spurned such a report—ostensibly, indeed, because it appeared that the senate’s authority had not been awaited in the matter, although there was an ancient law among the Romans that no one should be regarded as a god without a decree of the senate; but in reality because [Col. 0864A] the proclamation of the saving divine doctrine did not require human authority and assistance. Therefore, when the senate had rejected the report concerning the Savior, Tiberius nevertheless persisted in his former opinion and is said to have attempted nothing harsher against the teaching of Christ” (Eusebius, bk. 2, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 2, p. 40). Thus Valesius translated Eusebius’s Greek words, which, because they are somewhat lengthy, we do not transcribe here.

Eusebius then translated Tertullian’s words into Greek as follows: Τιβέριος οὖν ἀγγελθέντος αὐτῷ ἐκ Παλαιστίνης τοῦ δόγματος τούτου, ἔνθα πρῶτον ἤρξατο, τῇ συγκλήτῳ ἀνεκοινώσατο (“Tiberius, then, when this doctrine had been reported to him from Palestine, where it first began, communicated it to the Senate”). Δῆλος ὢν ἐκείνοις ὡς τῷ δόγματι ἀρέσκεται· ἡ δὲ σύγκλητος, ἐπεὶ οὐκ αὐτὴ ἐδεδοκιμάκει, ἀπώσατο (“making it clear to them that he approved the doctrine; but the Senate, since it had not itself approved it, rejected it”). Ὁ δὲ ἐν τῇ αὐτοῦ ἀποφάσει ἔμεινεν, ἀπειλήσας θάνατον τοῖς τῶν χρίστιανῶν κατηγόροις (“But he remained firm in his decision, threatening the accusers of the Christians with death”). Valesius rendered these in the same Latin words that, as we have seen, appear [Col. 0864B] in our codices and in editions before Rigault. In his notes, however, approving Rigault’s emendation, he judges the Greek words of Eusebius—or of another translator, as he himself supposes—to be corrupt. But if he had detected the changes made by Rigault in Tertullian’s text, he might perhaps rather have endorsed the Greek writer.

Whatever the case may be, Tertullian’s meaning is sufficiently clear from either reading, and no difficulty can arise concerning it except in the words by which Tiberius is said already to have been a Christian “according to his conscience.” For in the same place Tertullian said that the Caesars did not believe because they were Caesars. But there the verb “to believe” seems to mean nothing other than the public profession of the Christian religion. Tiberius was therefore a Christian according to his conscience, [Col. 0864C] but he did not dare to profess it openly.

But why, you will ask, did our Author add: “The Caesars would have believed if they had not been necessary to the age”? Rigault answers that this was said because, as we shall see below, they were persuaded that the world—which they did not wish to be destroyed so soon—would be overthrown together with the Roman Empire. But what necessity for the life of one Caesar or another can, I ask you, be inferred from this error? Could Tertullian not have meant that the Caesars were necessary to the age—that is, bound by such necessity to the customs of the age and of its peoples, and especially to its established religious institutions, that they could not undermine or change them without seditions and even the imminent danger of the overthrow of both their lives and the empire?

## ARTICLE V. That all the things said concerning Christ as God and man are true; that no one may lawfully lie about his religion; that Christians, without any ambiguity or dissimulation, openly and even amid the most dreadful tortures cried out that they worshiped God through Christ; and that this could not be condemned by the Jews, who worshiped God through Moses, nor by the Gentiles, who had learned through Orpheus, Musaeus, Melampus, and Trophonius to worship false gods

[Col. 0864D]

All the things which we have thus far seen written by Tertullian concerning Christ, whether as God and the Son of God or as true man, he affirms to be most true with such assurance that he leaves no room, [Col. 0865A] not even the slightest, for doubting them. For he addresses the pagans themselves as follows: “This is the order of our teaching; this is the account we have published of both our sect and our name, together with its author” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 403). By *census* he means an enumeration, review, and explanation. In this matter, he says, let no one suppose that there is anything else whatsoever which I have wished to conceal or dissemble. For nothing can be truer than what I have related, because, he says, no one may lawfully lie about his religion.

This principle had been planted so deeply in Christian hearts that they preferred to be tortured and killed by any of the most exquisitely devised torments rather than, when questioned about their religion, deny or dissemble anything—indeed, even merely their Christian name. Accordingly, Justin Martyr, as we have said elsewhere, similarly [Col. 0865B] told the Gentiles: “Consider, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ εφ` ἡμῖν εἶναι ἀρνεῖσθαι ἐξεταζομένους, οὐ βουλόμεθα ζῇν ψευδολογοῦντες (“that, although it is in our power to deny it when questioned, we do not wish to live by speaking falsely”) that it is in our power to deny it when we are questioned; but we do not wish to live falsely”—that is, we do not wish to live by lying about or disguising our religion (Justin, *First Apology to Antoninus*, p. 57; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 357). They considered it such a sacrilege to answer ambiguously when questioned about their religion that, as Tertullian himself also testifies, even those who most feared martyrdom preferred to be tortured and killed rather than, in confessing the three persons of the most holy Trinity, speak of several gods.

If you ask why every lie or any dissimulation whatsoever concerning religion is utterly condemned, Tertullian will answer that “he who says that he worships something other than [Col. 0865C] what he does worship denies what he worships, and transfers worship and honor to another; and by transferring it, he no longer worships what he has denied” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 403). But Rigault chose to delete the words “and honor.” Who will deny that they are not useless there? For worship and honor are not altogether synonymous; and even if they were, no one would deny that Tertullian could have used both. Yet this is of the least importance, except for noting Rigault’s audacity. Of far greater weight, certainly, is our Author’s reasoning: one who says, for example, that he worships Jupiter, while he worships another God, denies that Jupiter is a god, transfers the worship and honor of that same Jupiter to another, and thus, by transferring them, does not worship Jupiter himself, as he claimed, but denies that he is a god.

[Col. 0865D] Therefore we Christians, he says, casting aside absolutely all dissimulation, fraud, and ambiguity, openly declare—and, while you pagans torture us, cry aloud, lacerated and bloody—“We worship God through Christ” (ibid., p. 403 ff.), through whom, or under whose teaching, we learned who the true God is whom all ought to worship. “But Christ,” the pagans objected, “was a man.” Let it be so, Tertullian replies; Christians should not for that reason have been tortured and killed by the pagans, unless the latter condemned Jews, Greeks, and even Romans in the same manner. For “the Jews,” he says, “learned through the man Moses to worship God” (ibid., p. 23). In his books Moses taught them by what method and rites God ought to be worshiped by them.

[Col. 0866A] “Among the Greeks,” our Author continues, “Orpheus in Pieria, Musaeus at Athens, Melampus at Argos, and Trophonius in Boeotia bound men by initiations into the worship of false gods” (ibid.); that is, they tied and obligated them. We have shown elsewhere that the rites and festivals of Liber were introduced by Orpheus and were therefore called Orphic (Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 30, art. 3). In another place we cited the words of Diodorus Siculus, who relates that Hercules came to Athens to be initiated into the mysteries of the Eleusinian Mother, over which Musaeus, the son of Orpheus, was προεστηκώς (“standing at their head”), the presiding official, and thus taught how men were to be bound by them (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 35, p. 1280).

Moreover, as we noted in our dissertation on the works of Lactantius, [Col. 0866B] the same Diodorus Siculus committed to writing that Melampus brought from Egypt into Greece the orgies consecrated to Bacchus (Dissert. just cited; Diodorus, bk. I, *Library*, p. 61). He also appended a fabulous narrative concerning Saturn and the Titans and the passions of the gods, which, although it is not approved by everyone, nevertheless contributes not a little to our Tertullian’s purpose.

Trophonius, moreover, was said to be the son of Erginus—or rather of Apollo—whose oracle, as Tertullian says elsewhere, stood in Boeotia (Tertullian, place cited, and *On the Soul*, ch. 46). Pausanias, Lucian, Cicero, Philostratus, Erasmus, and others [Col. 0866C] cited by us in the preceding dissertation on the works of Arnobius have handed down much more concerning him and the temples of the gods, especially that of Apollo at Delphi, built by this same Trophonius (Pausanias, bk. 9, *On Boeotia*, p. 311; Lucian, *Dialogues of Menippus*, etc., p. 116 ff.; Cicero, bk. 1, *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 134; Philostratus, bk. VIII, *Life of Apollonius*, p. 420 ff.; Erasmus, *Adages*, cent. 1, adage 77; Dissert. on Arnobius, ch. 24, art. 2; Dissert. on Lactantius, ch. 30, art. 4). Who does not see that their testimony proves more than sufficiently that men were bound by that man, and by the others mentioned by Tertullian, through initiations into the gods instituted by other men? Finally, he added that Numa Pompilius burdened the Romans with most elaborate institutions. We have demonstrated how true this is.

Tertullian therefore rightly concludes from these things that Christ, even if he had been only a man, was no less entitled than they to devise some divinity [Col. 0866D] which he might teach men to worship. But Christ was not only man; he possesses true divinity together with his eternal Father, a possession, as our Author says, of his own, because it belongs to him just as it belongs to his Father (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 404). For he did not, like Numa Pompilius, civilize *rupices*—that is, woodland-dwellers, wild and barbarous men, as Tertullian himself explains elsewhere (the same, *On the Pallium*, ch. 4, and *On the Soul*, ch. 6)—by instilling terror of false gods; rather, he opened the eyes of the polished and urbanized to the knowledge of the true God—that is, gave them the ability to see or know the true God. For in the same sense he said elsewhere of the swallow: “It knows how to open the eyes of its chicks again with its own celandine” (the same, *On Repentance*, ch. 12). Therefore [Col. 0867A] Cyprian, imitating him in his customary manner, teaches, like Tertullian, that Christ’s disciples were dispersed throughout the world so that they might open the eyes of the blind and ignorant to the knowledge of the truth (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*). Indeed, Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon, wrote of him in his life: “The second birth had not yet opened the eyes of the new man with the full splendor of divine light” (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, near the beginning). Who, then, from what has thus far been discussed, does not perceive how justly Tertullian concludes that Christians were most unjustly tortured and killed by the pagans and Jews because, after recognizing the true God through Christ and professing his religion, they wished neither to deny nor even to dissemble either?

# CHAPTER X. Concerning Angels and Demons

[Col. 0867B]

## ARTICLE I. That the names of angels and demons were known to Gentile poets and philosophers, particularly Socrates and Plato, and also to magicians and to the common mass of uneducated people, who frequently used the name “demon” as a curse; why that name was so detestable; that all angels were created perfect by God, but the wicked corrupted themselves voluntarily; concerning their separation from God and their marriage with the daughters of men, from which a still more corrupt race of demons is said to have arisen

Tertullian passes to another doctrine of the Christian religion concerning angels and demons (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22, p. 404). He endeavors to explain it [Col. 0867C] with all the greater care because the pagans were more firmly persuaded that demons, lurking beneath the images and names of the dead (ibid., ch. 23, p. 404)—that is, of false gods—produced signs, miracles, and oracles “by which they contrived belief in their divinity” (ibid.); that is, by which the demons endeavored to persuade men that the gods worshiped by the pagans were true gods and, consequently, that their religion was true. We have already seen this error of the pagans, upon which their entire religion principally rested, rooted out by Minucius Felix, Lactantius, and others (Dissert. on Minucius, ch. 18, art. 1, and on Lactantius, ch. 20, art. 4). But because these writers drew many things from this book of our Author and from it, as from a pure spring, watered their little gardens, his opinion must therefore be examined by us with greater care.

[Col. 0867D] First, therefore, he teaches that angels and demons are certain spiritual substances whose names were not unknown to the Gentiles, whether poets or philosophers (place cited), as we have also shown elsewhere. Among the philosophers he specifically names Plato and Socrates, who had an attendant demon, “plainly,” he says, “dissuading him from the good” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22, p. 406). In another book he had said: “A demonic spirit found Socrates while he was still a boy” (the same, *On the Soul*, ch. 39, p. 341). We treated this demon of Socrates in the cited dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius and in the other works cited there (Dissert. on the *Octavius* of Minucius, ch. 18, art. 1). Moreover, in the same place we made clear that, as Tertullian further notes, magicians are witnesses to both names—that is, Angel and Demon [Col. 0868A] (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22, p. 405).

He further suggests another reason why demons were recognized not only by these people but by pagans of every kind: “Even the uneducated common people,” he says, “frequently use it as a curse” (ibid.). So Rigault; but two of our more recent manuscripts read “in use,” the more ancient manuscripts “in use for curses,” and the oldest editions “for use in curses.” Our Author’s meaning is that when the pagan common people spoke evil of others and cursed them, they were accustomed to call them demons or invoke the name of the Demon. For he continues: “For they also pronounce Satan, the prince of this evil race, in accordance with the soul’s own consciousness, [Col. 0868B] with the same word of execration.” In the old manuscript and printed codices, the reading is “of sacrament” rather than “of execration,” but this is undoubtedly due solely to copyists’ carelessness. For in another book Tertullian explains his meaning clearly enough:

“When we affirm that demons exist—surely as if we did not also prove it, since we alone drive them from bodies—some adherent of Chrysippus mocks us. Your own execrations answer both that they exist and that they endure the abhorrence expressed in your curse. You call a man a demon because of his uncleanness, wickedness, insolence, or any stain which we attribute to demons, or because he is troublesome enough to compel hatred. Finally, in every aversion, rejection, and detestation, you pronounce the name of Satan, whom we call the angel of wickedness, the author of every error, and the corrupter of the whole age” (the same, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 3).

It was therefore the pagans’ custom, when speaking evil of others [Col. 0868C] and cursing them, to call them demons, or to devote and execrate them with dreadful curses in the name of the Demon and Satan. If you desire another witness to this custom, you have Augustine, who further advises us that wherever the name Demon or Demons occurs in Sacred Scripture, it signifies evil spirits. Here are his very words:

“But we, speaking as Scripture speaks, according to which we are Christians, read that some angels are good and some bad, but never that good angels are Demons. Wherever this name is found in those Writings, whether they are called Demons or Demon-spirits, none but evil spirits are signified. And peoples everywhere have followed this custom of speech to such an extent that even among those who are called pagans and contend that many gods and demons ought to be worshiped, [Col. 0868D] scarcely anyone is so literate and learned that he would dare say in praise even of his own servant, ‘You have a Demon’; but if he wished to say this to anyone, he could not doubt that he would be understood in no other way than as intending a curse” (Augustine, bk. 9, *City of God*, ch. 19, p. 233).

He later added: “So detestable is the name of demons that we must by every means remove it from the holy Angels” (ibid., ch. 23, p. 236). Augustine, therefore, like our Tertullian, distinguishes a twofold class of angels: the one good, who are called Angels without qualification; the other the demons, whose detestable name always signifies evil spirits.

Why then, someone will ask, was that [Col. 0869A] name so detestable, and why was it always taken in a bad sense not only by Christians but also by gentiles? Do not Augustine himself and other Latin writers, as we have observed elsewhere (*Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 4), testify that the Greek term δαίμονες (*daimones*, “demons”) means the same thing, namely those knowledgeable and skilled in affairs? Moreover, Tertullian, in this book of the *Apology*, informs us that the name “demons” is the same as “genii”: “Do you not know,” he says, “that genii are called demons, and hence, in the diminutive form, *daimonia*?” And shortly afterward: “demons, that is, genii” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 32, col. 447). Elsewhere, moreover: “Genii are assigned to everyone, which is the name of demons” (Idem, *On the Soul*, ch. 39, col. 341). What, then, is so evil in that name, and so detestable to each and every person? It would indeed be well if they did not misuse their knowledge, skill, [Col. 0869B] and powers of intellect. But because, as we shall see later, they thoroughly abuse these things to torment and deceive human beings, it is surely no wonder if everyone detested this name and applied it to others in curses.

Although our Author has transmitted little about the good Angels in the *Apology*, he nevertheless distinguishes them from the evil ones, and the latter from demons, with sufficient clarity. Concerning the former, indeed, he says this, though very briefly: “How, from certain angels corrupted by their own will, a still more corrupt race of demons arose and was condemned by God together with the founders of the race and with the one whom we call its prince, is learned in due order from the Holy Scriptures” (Idem, *Apology*, ch. 22, col. 405). Yet in a few words he encompasses many things, which must not be reviewed so briefly or without certain [Col. 0869C] observations.

First, he declares that certain Angels were corrupted. He thus signifies that there were many others who were not corrupted, whom for that reason we call good, and whom we rightly and deservedly believe to be blessed because of their perseverance in the good. Second, those same Angels were endowed with free choice of the will, by which, through acting well or badly, they could merit reward or punishment. Third, some of them were corrupted and, through abuse of their free power, fell into certain sins for which they were condemned by God. Fourth, they had a prince, of whom he had said shortly before: “Satan, the prince of this evil race” (*Ibid.*). Elsewhere, moreover, he calls him an Angel “whom God, after the pattern of His good works, established as good and wisest of all; both by his original constitution, [Col. 0869D] according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, a good Angel, and by his own will corrupted” (Tertullian, bk. II, *Against Marcion*, ch. 10). Then further: “He was blameless from the day of his creation, created by God for good, as by a good Creator of blameless creations, adorned with all angelic glory, and placed in God’s presence as one good in the presence of the Good; but afterward he transferred himself into evil . . . . . . he himself no less having been established with free choice, as a spirit” (*Ibid.*, col. 462). Finally, he adds that this Satan fell from his exalted position through his own transgression, of which he himself was the author. We have treated him in our dissertation on the books of Lactantius (*Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 3).

What, however, was the sin of this Angel and of the other wicked angels whom he dragged to [Col. 0870A] their destruction? Tertullian explained it with complete clarity neither there nor in the *Apology*. In another book, however, he appears to indicate two of their sins in these words: “Let nothing be imputed to those angels except [others read: beyond] their rejection of heaven and marriage with flesh” (Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, ch. 4). Hence elsewhere he calls them “Angels who deserted God, lovers of women, and for that reason condemned by God” (Idem, *On Idolatry*, ch. 9). Does he not distinguish there a twofold sin of the angels: the first, whereby they rejected heaven and deserted God; and the second, their perverse love of women and marriage with flesh?

Concerning this second offense of theirs, moreover, he speaks as follows: “Those angels,” he says, “who rushed down from heaven to the daughters of men are condemned and appointed to the punishment of death, so that this disgrace too might attach to woman” [Col. 0870B] (Idem, *On the Apparel of Women*, ch. 2). But if disgrace attached to women because of this crime of the Angels, and if for that reason, as we have just seen stated by our same Author, the Angels were condemned, why then, someone will ask, does he call it simply “marriage with flesh,” rather than criminal fornication? To anyone who therefore asks this of us, we shall reply in these very words of Tertullian himself: “The sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. Here the Greek term for women carries the sense of ‘wives,’ because marriage is mentioned. When, therefore, it says ‘daughters of men,’ it manifestly indicates virgins who were still reckoned as belonging to their parents—for married women [Col. 0870C] are designated as belonging to their husbands—although it could have said ‘wives of men.’ Likewise, it does not call the angels adulterers but husbands, since they took the unmarried daughters of men, whom it had called ‘born’ above, thereby also signifying virgins: above, daughters born; but here, women married to angels” (Idem, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 7). He therefore calls it the marriage of the transgressing Angels because they took daughters of men who were not married but virgins, and for that reason the Angels themselves are not called adulterers.

Nevertheless, he did not consider this marriage lawful, but altogether unlawful and criminal, because of which disgrace attached to women and condemnation to the angels. Hence in another book he says: “The Apostle also knew,” he says, “that the spiritual wickedness of the Angels who were led into sin by the daughters of men had been at work in the heavens” (Idem, bk. V, *Against* [Col. 0870D] *Marcion*, ch. 18). But we have discussed this criminal marriage of the wicked angels with the daughters of men—or rather, indeed, their fornication—not merely once, both in our dissertation on the works of Lactantius and in the other places noted there (*Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, arts. 3 and 4).

In the fifth and final place, it remains to be observed that Tertullian asserted in the *Apology*, without any hesitation, that from the intercourse of those corrupted Angels with the daughters of men there arose a still more corrupt race of demons. Yet no fewer difficulties arise in this opinion than in the other opinion concerning the marriage of Angels with women. These difficulties are increased by what he determines concerning the nature of those same demons and of [Col. 0871A] Angels, whether good or evil. These matters must first be investigated by us, and others afterward.

## ARTICLE II. Whether Tertullian believed the nature of all Angels and demons to be spiritual; how great a difficulty arises in this matter from the origin of the latter from wicked angels and the daughters of men; concerning the envy of those same demons, by which they conspire to destroy the human beings to whom they are subject

Tertullian begins his discussion of Angels and demons with these words in the *Apology*: “We say that there are certain spiritual substances” (Tertullian, *Apology*, [Col. 0871B] ch. 22, p. 404). In the preceding article, moreover, we saw it stated of Satan, the most eminent of the Angels and an Archangel, as Tertullian himself says, that he was established by God with free choice “as a spirit” (Idem, bk. II, *Against Marcion*, ch. 7). The Creator, moreover, as he further writes (*Ibid.*, bk. III, ch. 9), made all Angels as truly spirits as He made His ministers a blazing fire (Psalm 103, v. 4; Hebrews, v. 7). He therefore never doubted that all Angels are spirits and that their substance is spiritual.

But it is disputed what he understands by the term “spirit”: whether a substance wholly distinct from every corporeal thing, or some extremely fine and subtle body that escapes all human sight. Nor, indeed, can we deny that this [Col. 0871C] dispute cannot easily be resolved by anyone. Nevertheless, we shall attempt to ascertain what can be stated with greater certainty about this opinion of our Tertullian.

First, therefore, it must be noted how he argues against the heretics who denied that Christ assumed a true body, and how he refutes their error. Those heretics inferred from the example of Angels, who are said once to have appeared to the patriarchs clothed in human flesh, that Christ’s flesh was neither real nor born. Tertullian, however, contends that the flesh of the Angels was not born, whereas Christ’s was, because it was not they but Christ who was born in order to be crucified and to die: “For it is agreed,” he says, “that the Angels did not bear flesh properly their own, being natures [another reading: *of a nature*] of spiritual substance, although perhaps of some kind of body, yet one of their own kind; they could, however, be transformed [Col. 0871D] into flesh for a time, so that they might be seen and might associate with human beings” (Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 6). He therefore acknowledges that these Angels assumed human flesh for a time. Although that flesh was real, it was nevertheless not their own flesh, because, as he affirms without hesitation, their substance is spiritual. But because either he himself or others thought it possible to doubt whether, as we noted above (supra, ch. 7, art. 3), there was anything intermediate between body and nothingness, he therefore added there, so as to leave no opportunity for quibbling: “although perhaps of some kind of body, yet one of its own kind.” It is just as if he had said: If someone more obstinately contends that absolutely every substance [Col. 0872A] is some kind of body, I shall not argue the point now, provided it be granted to me that angelic substance, if it perhaps is a body, is a body of its own kind. By the term “body,” however, as we saw elsewhere (*loc. cit.*), he means nothing other than any existing thing that is opposed to a nonexistent thing and to nothingness. May it not therefore be inferred, without absurdity, that he considered the nature of Angels to be purely spiritual, though it can nevertheless be called a body of its own kind because it is not nothing and truly exists?

By precisely the same argument he attacks the same error of Marcion: “All the more,” he says, “the Angels, who were not appointed to die for us, ought not to have taken on their brief use of flesh through birth, because they were not going to lay it aside through death . . . If the Creator makes the Angels [Col. 0872B] spirits, and His ministers a blazing fire, He makes them as truly spirits as He also makes them truly fire” (Tertullian, bk. III, *Against Marcion*, ch. 9). Do you hear how openly he declares that the Angels who were seen by the patriarchs in human form were as truly spirits as the human flesh they had assumed was real? That flesh was not properly their own, but was given to them by God for a brief time so that they might associate and converse with human beings. Their substance is therefore different from that of human beings: namely, spiritual, by which, being superior to human beings, they truly are spirits.

If anyone desires more, let him consult Tertullian’s book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, where he will be able to read these very words: “The Angels were at one time like human beings in eating and drinking and extending their feet for washing; for they had put on a human [Col. 0872C] exterior, while their inner substance remained intact” (Idem, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 62). What, however, was that proper substance and nature of the angels, concealed beneath a human appearance? He himself explains it in the same passage as follows: “Having become like human beings, the Angels undertook fleshly activity while remaining in the same substance of spirit” (*Ibid.*). By what clearer words, I ask you, could it have been expressed that the Angels truly are spirits, and that their spiritual nature admits absolutely nothing of matter or body?

What we have related thus far concerns the nature in which all Angels were created, which he quite openly asserts to be spiritual—had he not obscured this view, as though it were covered by a certain black mist and dense [Col. 0872D] darkness, through what he taught concerning wicked Angels and demons. For he calls all of them spirits, no less than the good Angels. Nor is this difficult to prove. For it has already been observed that he wrote in general of all Angels, both good and evil: “We say that there are certain spiritual substances.” Afterward, even more explicitly: “Every spirit is winged; such are both Angels and demons” (Idem, *Apology*, ch. 22, p. 404). Again: “Angels and demons, in substance the vilest spirits” (*Ibid.*, ch. 39, col. 468). The prince of the wicked Angels too, of whom we spoke in the preceding article, is called by him “a spirit of demonic and angelic constitution” (*Ibid.*, ch. 27, col. 433), that is, a spirit possessing the [Col. 0873A] dispositions and qualities of demons and Angels. But more will be said about this term below, in the following article.

What, furthermore, of the fact that, as we saw above (preceding article), the same Tertullian expressly pronounces that both this Satan and all the other wicked angels were created in the same manner as the good? Indeed, the demons themselves, he says, cannot deny that they are unclean spirits (Tertullian, *ibid.*, ch. 23, col. 410). Finally, he says that their subtlety and fineness are exceedingly great: by their swiftness they assail both substances of the human being, are everywhere in a single moment, and the whole globe of the earth is a single place to them. Moreover, he says: “Invisible and imperceptible, they appear in their effect rather than in their action” (*Ibid.*, ch. 22, p. 406). Do not all these things demonstrate quite manifestly [Col. 0873B] that Tertullian was persuaded that evil angels and demons, no less than good angels, were spirits?

Yet this view seems to be contradicted by what we noted above that he taught: that wicked angels polluted themselves through criminal intercourse with women, by which they begot demons. But someone might reply that the wicked Angels, just like the good, assumed human flesh, as we were saying shortly before, through which they could have intercourse with women. Yet another will immediately argue in reply that it must be proved from what source the wicked Angels took human flesh for some period of time. For although Tertullian openly pronounces more than once, as we have noted, that this flesh was given to the good Angels by God, no one can prove that he similarly [Col. 0873C] assigned it to the wicked Angels so that they might violate women.

Grant, nevertheless, that in some way or other, whether by their deceptions or by other impious arts, they put on such flesh: a greater difficulty certainly remains concerning the demons. For of what kind can those demons be as spirits, whom Tertullian supposes to have arisen from an unlawful union with unmarried virgins? How could there be begotten from them the finest, most subtle, invisible substances, surpassing the speed of birds, which penetrate the bodies and souls of human beings and are everywhere in a single moment? It certainly cannot be denied that this matter is enveloped in the greatest obscurity. For if Tertullian believed the demons to have some body, he undoubtedly did not consider it either human or fashioned in human form. [Col. 0873D] What, then? Did he think that they were certain monsters, neither angels nor human beings? Yet is that very idea not itself a monstrosity of absurd opinion? Nevertheless, Lactantius, as we observed in its proper place (*Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 4), appears to have drawn from this his opinion that the nature of demons is in some way intermediate between angels and human beings. Tertullian, however, at least in his *Apology*, defined the matter neither fully openly nor absolutely, but said that their nature was that which “is learned in due order from the Holy Scriptures” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 22, col. 403). It would indeed have been excellent if in his other books he had kept himself within these limits of true doctrine.

Besides, even if he held that the nature of demons was [Col. 0874A] equal neither to the angelic nor to the human, but something intermediate between the two, it must not therefore immediately be inferred that he denied Angels to be spirits. For if he attributed any body to demons, he thought it, as we have seen, to possess such fineness and subtlety that none greater could exist. He appears, moreover, to have been persuaded that the nature of good Angels was more excellent than that of demons. But in what manner, I ask you, can it be more excellent unless it is purely spiritual and possesses absolutely nothing corporeal? How much weight the arguments we have thus far presented have in proving this, we leave to others to judge. Yet no one, unless we are entirely mistaken, will deny that, if there is any error of Tertullian’s in all these matters, none is worse than that by which he attempts to explain the intercourse of the wicked angels with the daughters [Col. 0874B] of men and the generation of demons from it. But see, I ask, what was discussed on these matters in the preceding dissertation (*Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 5), and whether his opinion can thereby be brought back to the rules of truth.

No one, however, will doubt the truth of what he afterward relates concerning Satan and the demons. “Our Satan,” he says, “on account of his separation”—namely, from God—“and on account of his own sin, is a rival,” or an adversary and enemy, “and, because of God’s grace granted to Christians, is envious.” He has always attempted, through hidden inspiration and by suborning the gentiles, to persuade them to turn Christians away from the worship of the true God by every kind of torture and to compel them to worship false gods (Tertullian, *ibid.*, ch. 27, p. 432). For although “the whole power of demons and of a spirit of that kind is subject to us” (*Ibid.*, [Col. 0874C] col. 433), that is, the power of Satan . . . . yet “after the manner of convicts in rebellious workhouses, mines, or some such form of penal servitude, they break out against us Christians”; that is, they break out in the manner of those who, confined in workhouses and prisons, or condemned to mine metals or to some other form of penal servitude, oppose and resist their masters. Those whom these wicked demons were unable to bring to the worship of themselves and of false gods by violence and armed force, they attempted to suborn by every other kind of device, deception, fraud, and evil art. But what our Author has taught about them must be explained at somewhat greater length.

## ARTICLE III. How Tertullian shows that certain things which the pagans attributed to their gods as true miracles were accomplished by the arts and deceptions of demons

[Col. 0874D]

Tertullian certainly devotes much effort, and deservedly so, to explaining and exposing the “operation,” as he himself says, of demons (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 22, col. 405), that is, the devices, deceptions, tricks, frauds, and other evil arts by which they appeared to produce false miracles, oracles, and many other things outside the usual order of nature. For the pagans attributed all these things, which they believed to be real, to the power of their gods, and from this concluded that their gods were true and their religion true. Tertullian therefore strikes and utterly overthrows this last stronghold of theirs with a twofold argument, [Col. 0875A] as though with a double battering ram. First, he shows that those extraordinary deeds were produced not by their gods, as they supposed, but by the perverse arts of demons. Then he shows that those same demons, when adjured by Christians, openly confess that these things were performed by none other than themselves, who were not gods but demons only.

To demonstrate the first proposition more clearly, he lays down as certain (*Ibid.*)—what no one can deny—that the substance of demons, as we saw in the preceding article, is not only exceedingly subtle and fine, but that their powers are also spiritual and their swiftness so great that in a single moment they can be everywhere and penetrate every individual thing, even the very substance of a human being. Since they are thus constituted, therefore, “their [Col. 0875B] spiritual malice,” says Tertullian, “began from the beginning of the world for the destruction of humanity” (*Ibid.*), namely, when it deceived Eve and Adam as they lived their happy life in the earthly Paradise. By the same malice, they strive to lead other human beings into error and every kind of crime, and especially into idolatry and the worship of themselves under the name of false gods.

To begin with the miracles which the pagans attributed to their gods, our Author demonstrates in the following way that they were performed by demons. Equipped, he says, with such powers, both spiritual and invisible, they afflict unwary human beings with certain illnesses and drive them away with remedies either miraculously novel or even contrary, so that they are believed to have healed those whom, after removing only their harmful operations, they have ceased to injure. Hence [Col. 0875C] he ridicules them and their pretended miracles as follows: “They are benefactors indeed, even in the treatment of illnesses: for first they injure, and then prescribe remedies, miraculously novel or contrary, after which they cease to injure and are believed to have cured” (*Ibid.*, col. 409). Nor do they conspire to destroy human beings only by these afflictions inflicted upon and healed in the human body. Through their subtlety they also penetrate the very soul, and by stirring up savage lusts, madness, and frenzy, they lead human beings into any kind of crime (*Ibid.*). We have discussed these impious arts of demons elsewhere (*Dissert. on Minucius*, ch. XVIII, art. 2).

By the same subtlety, the demons put on phantoms, or the appearance of the Castors (Tertullian, *ibid.*), that is, Castor and Pollux; and by their innate speed they announced at Rome on the very same day the celebrated [Col. 0875D] Roman victory over King Perseus on which it had been won. We have related this elsewhere (*Dissert. on Minucius*, ch. 18, art. 2).

To this also pertain these few words of our Author, though they will appear obscure to many: “And the beard made red by a touch” (Tertullian, *ibid.*). Suetonius, however, explains them more clearly where he discusses the origin of the family of the Ahenobarbi: “The Ahenobarbi,” he says, “have as the founder both of their line and of their surname Lucius Domitius. It is related that, as he was returning from the countryside, the twin youths Castor and Pollux met him in a form more majestic than human and commanded him to announce to the Senate and people the victory of which there was still uncertainty. As proof of their majesty—namely, their divine majesty—they stroked his cheeks [Col. 0876A] so that they changed his hair from black to reddish and like the color of bronze. This distinguishing feature remained among his descendants, and a great part of them had red beards” (Suetonius, *Life of Nero*, §1). This is also confirmed by Plutarch (Plutarch, *Life of Paulus Aemilius*, vol. I, p. 268). Tertullian therefore said that the beard was “made red” because it was changed from black to red. For the sake of brevity, however, he records only this sudden and marvelous transformation of the beard, by which the other miracles that the pagans vaunted were also indicated with sufficient clarity.

He asserts that these things were accomplished by the spiritual capacities, powers, and deceptions of the demons (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*), as was also, he further says, the ship “moved by a girdle,” namely by Claudia the Vestal Virgin, [Col. 0876B] as we have already observed elsewhere (*Dissert. on Minucius*, ch. 17, art. 1). The pagans furthermore vaunted, as he continues (*Ibid.*), that water was carried in a sieve by Tuccia, another Vestal Virgin. By this miracle, as they supposed, she completely cleared herself of the charge brought against her of violated chastity—or, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus says (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, bk. II, *Roman Antiquities*, p. 128 ff.), of having extinguished the sacred fire. But concerning this story, whatever its character, Valerius Maximus has more, and you may consult him, as also Pliny, Augustine, and others (Valerius Maximus, bk. VIII, ch. 1; Pliny, bk. XXVIII, *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 157; Augustine, bk. X, *City of God*, ch. 16, p. 252).

Tertullian therefore asserts that these and other extraordinary deeds of this kind, which the pagans marveled at, were produced by the [Col. 0876C] art and deceptions of demons so that “stone divinities”—that is, images of the gods fashioned from stone—might not be believed to be false gods, and so that the true God might not be sought (Tertullian, *ibid.*). In our preceding dissertations, however, we have discussed these matters abundantly, and have there made clear by what reasoning Arnobius attempts to demonstrate their falsity (*Dissert. on Arnobius*, ch. 18, arts. 1 and 2). Minucius Felix and Lactantius, however, following Tertullian, show that these things were accomplished, as we have said, by the tricks and frauds of demons (*Dissert. on Minucius*, ch. 20, art. 2; *Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 7, and ch. 32, art. 4). We shall attempt in the following articles to clarify those points which are peculiar to Tertullian himself and which he specifically related.

## ARTICLE IV. How the demons attempted to steal knowledge of future events and, in the name of false gods, gave ambiguous oracles to certain persons, especially Pyrrhus and Croesus

[Col. 0876D]

“Foreknowledge and knowledge of future events,” says Cicero, “is a certain magnificent and salutary thing, if indeed there is any such thing, and is the nearest approach to the power of the gods that can be attained by mortal nature” (Cicero, bk. I, *On Divination*, p. 254). Nor was this unknown to the demons. Hence they wished in some way or other to claim this knowledge for themselves. For, as our Tertullian says with complete aptness, “They rival divinity while stealing divination” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 22, col. 408). Indeed, if [Col. 0877A] you trust him, nothing was dearer or of greater importance to them than this rivalry: “And what,” he says, “is a more carefully tended pasture for them than to turn a human being away from reflection upon the true divinity by the deceptions of false divination?” (*Ibid.*, p. 407). This is the reading in Rigault’s edition, for he thought that the words “for them” and “to turn away” should be referred to the demons. But in our manuscripts and the old editions we read “for it” and “that it may turn away,” which can certainly be referred to the aspiration of the demons noted there by Tertullian. The term “pasture” is used by him, as by our sacred Writers, for nourishment and food. For, to omit many passages from them, it is written in the twenty-second Psalm: “In a place of pasture, there He has settled me” (Ps. XXII, v. 20).

Our Author explained in the following manner how the demons attempted to steal divination: [Col. 0877B] “Through the subtlety of their intelligence they intercepted the dispositions of God, both when the prophets were preaching in former times and now when the readings of Holy Scripture resound” (Tertullian, *ibid.*, p. 408). Moreover, they “take,” that is, discern, certain “lots of the times,” or the future conditions and events of the times. We have explained these matters in our dissertation on the books of Lactantius (*Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 7).

In still another way they easily predict rain. For, Tertullian further says (*Ibid.*), “from their dwelling in the air, from the proximity of the stars, and from the interaction of the clouds, they possess knowledge of”—that is, they discern—“the preparations of the heavens, so that they also promise in advance the rains which they already perceive.” Pamelius wished to warn us here that he did not remember whether [Col. 0877C] the term “preparation” was found in other authors. But either he had not read, or did not remember having read, these words of Pontius in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “The second birth had not yet illumined the new man with all the splendor of the divine light, and already the mere preparation of light was overcoming the old and former darkness” (Pontius, *Life of St. Cyprian*, ch. 2). The term “preparation” is used there in Tertullian’s own sense, meaning arrangement, equipment, and preparation, as has already been observed (preceding article).

Our Author therefore says that the things being prepared in the higher region of heaven are discerned by the demons, from their dwelling in the air, through the interaction of the clouds. For he knew that Satan is called by the Apostle “the prince of the power of this air,” and demons “spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Epistle to the Ephesians, ch. 2, v. 2, and ch. 6, v. 12). Finally, [Col. 0877D] something must be said below concerning the rain announced in advance by them.

In the same way he further shows that the oracles of their gods, which the pagans vaunted so greatly, also proceeded from those same demons. Who is so blind that he cannot detect in them the customary frauds and malignant subtlety of demons all the more easily the more ambiguous they were? If anyone is unwilling to believe Tertullian, however, let him listen and consider how manifestly this is proved by him: “In oracles,” he says, “Croesus knows, and Pyrrhus knows, with what ingenuity they moderate their ambiguities to suit the events” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 22, p. 408). He therefore presents two celebrated examples of oracles, one given to Pyrrhus and the other to Croesus. How ambiguous and deceptive the first was Augustine made clear in these words: [Col. 0878A] “For the soothsayer said: ‘I say that you, Pyrrhus, can conquer the Romans’; and thus, whether Pyrrhus was conquered by the Romans or the Romans by Pyrrhus, the secure soothsayer could await either outcome” (Augustine, bk. III, *City of God*, ch. 17, p. 75). Deceptions and fraudulent snares of this kind cannot proceed from the true God, but from malignant demons, who, concealed beneath images of false gods through the subtlety of their nature, deceived human beings by these responses. We have discussed this deceptive response of the Pythian Apollo to King Pyrrhus in our dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius (*Dissert. on Minucius*, ch. 17, art. 3). The other response, given to Croesus, is certainly of the same kind. For Eusebius relates (Eusebius, bk. V, *Preparation for the Gospel*, chs. 21 and 22, p. 211 ff.) that this king of Lydia, [Col. 0878B] when he was considering making war upon the Persians, consulted the Delphic Apollo—whose temple he had adorned with boundless wealth and gifts—about the future outcome of this war, and received this entirely ambiguous response:

Χροῖσος Ἅλιν διαβὰς, μεγάλην ἀρχὴν καταλύσει.

“Croesus, having crossed the Halys, will overthrow a great power” (Herodotus, bk. I, ch. 65).

Eusebius afterward confirms this by the testimony of Oenomaus. But if that is insufficient for you, you may consult Herodotus, as well as Cicero, Bulenger, and others, who treat both Pyrrhus and Croesus (Cicero, bk. II, *On Divination*, p. 296; Bulenger, *On Oracles and Prophets*, ch. 6).

The following words of Tertullian likewise concern this same Croesus: “Moreover, the Pythian announced that a tortoise was being cooked with the flesh of a beast in the manner we described above: in a moment he had been in Lydia” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 22, p. 409). [Col. 0878C] Herodotus, whom we have already cited, recorded that Croesus sent messengers to consult various oracles of the gods and inquire what he himself was doing in Lydia. After receiving the individual responses, he approved none except that of the Delphic Apollo, who declared what Croesus was actually doing in this response: Χελώνην καὶ ἄρνα κατακόψας ὀμοῦ ἕψεε αὐτὸς ἐν λέβητι χαλκέῳ, χάλκεον ἐπίθημα ἐπιθείς. “He cut up a tortoise and a lamb together and cooked them in a bronze cauldron with a bronze lid placed over it” (Herodotus, bk. I, §48). Yet that demon did not learn by divine inspiration what Croesus was doing; rather, through his innate speed, Tertullian says, he flew to Lydia in a single moment and, returning with the same [Col. 0878D] speed, delivered to Croesus’s messengers in the name of Apollo the response just mentioned.

We have treated these and similar oracles, the ambiguous and deceptive responses of demons, and their cessation, not only in the cited dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius but also in our other dissertations (*Dissert. on Minucius*, ch. 30, art. 3; *Dissert. on Lactantius*, ch. 20, arts. 7 and 8, and ch. 32, art. 1). We think, however, that no one fails to understand from what has been said how greatly a certain more recent writer, as we observed elsewhere, departs from the opinion of Tertullian and the other most ancient Fathers of the Church, when he wrongly asserts that the ancient oracles of the gentiles were delivered not through these tricks and most wicked arts of demons, but through the frauds and deceptions of priests serving idols. [Col. 0879A] For although it were established that some proceeded from those priests, they nevertheless could not have produced nearly all of them, just as they could not produce the true miracles which must now be discussed.

## ARTICLE V. How Tertullian shows that, by the power and frauds of demons, those things are accomplished which magicians perform through itinerant conjuring tricks, by which the souls of the dead are dishonored, children are forced into delivering an oracular utterance, dreams are sent, and goats and tables divine; and that no one can reply that at least those things performed within the temples of the gods must be attributed to them

Tertullian presses the pagans still more sharply and makes it clear that those things which they supposed to have been produced beyond the order of nature by itinerant magicians were accomplished by the frauds and deceptions of demons. [Col. 0879B] And surely, how could those magicians accomplish anything by their accursed arts unless they possessed, Tertullian says, “the assisting power of angels”—namely, evil angels—“and demons once they had been summoned” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 23, p. 410)? For they do not possess in themselves that power which exceeds the ordinary strength of a human being, nor do they receive it from the supremely good God, who cannot be the author of evil deeds. They therefore received it from demons, who, through their malice, as we have said, attempt to lead human beings into every kind of crime. But Tertullian demonstrates this more clearly and fully in another book (Idem, *On the Soul*, ch. 57).

The magicians, therefore, having received from those demons the power to produce certain things beyond the customary order of nature, “play,” Tertullian says, “with mountebank tricks” [Col. 0879C] (Idem, *Apologet.*, c. 23, p. 411). But what, someone will ask, are these “mountebank tricks”? Some reply that they are so called because itinerant magicians, surrounded by a gathering or circle of spectators, entertain them with tales or tricks. Yet we shall more readily be persuaded that by these words Tertullian means nothing other than magical tricks. For when he refutes Marcion’s error concerning Christ’s illusory flesh, he says: “Therefore you ought now to have brought Christ down, not from heaven, but from some mountebank gathering—that is, a gathering of magicians—and not as God apart from man, but as a man who was a magician” (Idem, *De carne Christi*, c. 5). Elsewhere, moreover: “Another kind of magic, which operates through miracles . . . . . . Hence also Simon Magus, though now a believer, since he still entertained some thought of the mountebank [Col. 0879D] sect” (Idem, *De idololatria*, c. 9). What, however, does “mountebank sect” mean there except the sect of magicians? Yet somewhere, so that we may conceal nothing, he seems to distinguish magicians from mountebanks, where he argues against heretics as follows: “There have also been noted the dealings of heretics with very many magicians, with mountebanks, with astrologers, and with philosophers—men, of course, devoted to curiosity” (Idem, at the end of *De praescriptione haereticorum*, c. 43). But do you not see that there he is merely identifying various classes of people devoted to magical arts? Is not, therefore, his meaning here in the *Apologeticum* this: magicians play at many miracles by mountebank—that is, magical—arts; in other words, they fabricate them and falsely boast that they themselves perform them, and thus make sport of and deceive people?

[Col. 0880A] Furthermore, by those detestable arts “they produce phantoms and bring the souls of the dead into false repute” (Idem, *Apologet.*, c. 23, p. 410). We have already observed that he said the phantoms of the Castors were produced by demons (above, art. 3); now, however, he asserts that the phantoms, or fictitious likenesses, of other dead persons are represented by magicians through the artifice of demons. But in his book *On the Soul* he explains this more fully in these words: “In that kind of magic which is believed to tear souls already at rest from the lower regions and exhibit them to sight, no other power is more effective in deception; plainly because both a phantom is furnished and a body is counterfeited, nor is it a great thing for him to delude the external eyes when it is very easy for him to blind the inward vision of the mind. In short, the dragons produced from the magicians’ rods appeared as bodies to Pharaoh and the Egyptians; but [Col. 0880B] the truth of Moses devoured the falsehood” (Tertullian, *De anima*, c. 57, p. 355). He therefore contends that in these magical evocations there is nothing but the fraud, deception, imposture, and falsehood of demons. Indeed, in the same place he proves this by reasoning as certain as it is evident: “Unless I am mistaken, we prove this deception of an evil spirit lurking under the identities of dead persons from actual instances as well: in exorcisms it sometimes affirms that it is some man from among the subject’s relatives, sometimes a gladiator or a beast-fighter, just as elsewhere it claims to be a god—caring for nothing more than to shut out precisely what we proclaim, lest we readily believe that all souls are consigned to the lower regions, and so that it may disturb faith in judgment and resurrection” (*Ibid.*).

But why, you will ask, are the souls of the dead then said by him to be “brought into false repute”? Some think this was said because they are subjected to disgrace and insult. But we fear [Col. 0880C] that Tertullian employs this verb in another sense, namely, to fabricate and falsely exhibit. For in the same book he proves that men’s eyes are deceived and a falsehood is presented to their sight, “which brings a perfectly uniform colonnade into false repute as narrower at its end” (*Ibid.*, c. 17); that is, it exhibits it falsely and represents it by a deception. He then adds that there is no deception of the eyes and no falsehood when the causes themselves are freed from the false representation of the objects of correct vision. No one, however, would say that the verb *infamare* is used by him there for a blemish with which the colonnade is branded. Nevertheless, if anyone proves that in the *Apologeticum* it is used in this second meaning, just as in the passages just cited it is used in the first, we shall not venture to resist altogether.

Moreover, the magicians, he says, “dash boys into the utterance of an oracle” [Col. 0880D] (Idem, *Apologet.*, c. 23, p. 411). And so indeed the reading stands in our manuscripts and in the more recent printed editions, “among, etc.” [The text appears defective here.] Less correctly, however, the earliest editions read “draw forth.” For Apuleius attests that it was the common custom and practice of his time for magicians to employ boys or slaves to deliver oracles; enchanted by them, these boys collapsed, and for that reason were “dashed down” (Apul., *Apolog.* I, p. 340).

By the same fraud, Tertullian says, they “send dreams” (Tertull., *ibid.*; *Dissertat. in Minut.*, c. 20, art. 2; *in Arnob.*, c. 18, art. I; *in Lactant.*, c. 32, art. 4), dreams undoubtedly foretelling future events. But we have said more about dreams of this kind in our earlier dissertations.

[Col. 0881A] Nor were men alone accustomed to divine by this art of the magicians—or rather of the demons, who abused their services—but also, our author says, “goats and tables” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 22, p. 404). But what, I ask you, were these tables? Were they the sacred tripods, as the pagans babbled, from which the Pythias, the priestesses of Apollo, were accustomed to deliver their oracles? Virgil certainly sang of them (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. 3, v. 358):

> Trojan-born interpreter of the gods, who know  
> The powers of Phoebus, the tripods and laurels of Clarian Apollo, and the stars.

For Servius, commenting on these verses of the Poet, says: “The tripods were tables in the temple of Delphic Apollo, upon which the prophetesses of Phoebus prophesied” (Bulen., *De oraculis et vatibus*, c. 17 ff.). Those [Col. 0881B] tripods are known to everyone; if you desire to know more about them, you may consult Bulenger and others.

Nevertheless, because Tertullian appears there to have been speaking of things effected not through the agency of pagan priests but through that of magicians, if anyone proves that he is speaking of other tables, we shall assent without reluctance. Let him consider, however, that these words can be referred to the oracles of the gods no less than to the divining goats mentioned in the same place by Tertullian himself, which we discussed in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (tom. I, *Apparat.*, bk. I, c. 10, p. 772 ff.).

Since, moreover, Tertullian in this passage of the *Apologeticum* discusses the things done inside and outside the temples of the gods, he refutes those who objected that a distinction must be drawn according to differences of place, and that only those things customarily done in temples should be ascribed [Col. 0881C] to the gods (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 22, p. 407). “For when you pagans,” he addresses them, “raise these objections against us, you do not call them gods elsewhere”—that is, outside the temples (*Ibid.*); in other words, when you acknowledge that your gods neither exist nor act anywhere except in temples, by that very fact you declare them to be false gods. For the true God is everywhere.

Next, he says, the man who flies around the sacred towers of temples appears no differently “demented”—that is, as in Lucretius, Apuleius, and Lactantius (Lucret., bk. III, v. 396; Apuleius, *Apol.* I, p. 341; Lactant., bk. IV, *Divinae Institutiones*, c. 17, p. 441; Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 13, p. 343), insane, delirious, or out of his mind—than one who leaps across the neighboring roofs [Col. 0881D], or launches himself into the air by flying from roofs adjoining the temples. He therefore asserts that the madness is equal in the case of one who was said to have flown through the air by hurling himself from any sort of tower and in the case of another who did so from the towers of temples dedicated to false gods. I should like you to consider whether he was there referring, without naming him, to Simon Magus, whom he had mentioned earlier. Lucian, moreover, introduces Philocles asserting that he had seen a certain Babylonian who flew through the air (Lucian, *Dial. Philopseudes*, p. 831). Some add the example of a certain Hagarene trickster who, according to Nicetas Choniates, died after falling headlong while attempting to fly through the air from the highest tower of the Hippodrome. But from this example one can establish only [Col. 0882A] that it is not surprising if, in Tertullian’s time or earlier, rash tricksters attempted to fly in this manner.

He presses further that the frenzy and madness are equal in the case of one who cuts his genitals or arms and another who cuts his own throat (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 25, p. 421). The former was a Gallus or Archigallus, who was accustomed to cut his own limbs in the rites of the Mother of the Gods or of Bellona (*Dissert. in Minut.*, c. 20, art. 2, and *Dissert. in Lactant.*, c. 34, art. I). Tertullian speaks of this Archigallus a little later, while we have discussed him and the other Galli elsewhere: “And yet,” he says, “the outcome of the frenzy is comparable, and there is one and the same principle of incitement in them and in the man who cuts his own throat”—that is, who slaughters himself or drives his sword into his throat (Tertullian, [Col. 0882B] *ibid.*). In our manuscripts, however, *compara* occurs in place of *compar*; though this plainly seems corrupt, it is nevertheless not entirely without meaning of its own. Minucius Felix, as we have noted in the appropriate place, spoke somewhat differently but to the same purpose (*Dissertat. in Minuc.*, c. 20, art. 3): “The incitement of the demon is equal in them, but the manifestation of the frenzy is unequal.” For each uses the same argument against the pagans, by which they tear out their error by the roots. See the books of Cicero *On Divination* and Augustine *On the Divination of Demons*, which we cited in that dissertation.

From what has thus far been discussed, moreover, who does not see that Tertullian rightly draws this conclusion? If those things outside the usual order of nature which the gentiles attributed [Col. 0882C] to their gods were accomplished by the malignant arts, deceptions, and tricks of demons, then all these gods are false, the religion of those same gentiles is false, and that of the Christians is true. For the Christians worship the one omnipotent God, by whose power alone, superior to all others, true miracles can be performed.

## ARTICLE VI. By what argument Tertullian demonstrates that those who are thought to suffer from a god, who breathe upon altars, who conceive a divine power from the smell of burnt sacrifice, who labor by belching and pronounce oracles while panting—as well as the Virgin Caelestis, promiser of rains, and Aesculapius, who the other day supplied life to Socordius, Thenatius, and Asclepiodorus—when adjured by Christians openly answered that they were not gods but demons

[Col. 0882D] Tertullian indeed proceeds much further and, by an argument far more effective—one against which the pagans did not dare even mutter—demonstrates most evidently that all those miracles, oracles, and other things which they boasted had been performed by their gods beyond human powers were performed by the demons themselves, and consequently that those whom they called gods were in reality demons. For he proves this neither by the private authority of some man nor by reasoning devised by any human ingenuity, but by the gods’ own testimony, publicly given in the presence of any pagans whatever.

The substance of this entire argument is as follows (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 22, p. 405): by whatever demon or demons a man is driven [Col. 0883A], or whether he is agitated by their evil spirit, or the body of any man is besieged by them, those same demons are immediately expelled from all such persons solely by Christian adjuration and exorcisms, or merely by touch or breath. Yet at that time, although they were cast out unwillingly and not without the greatest disgrace, they were compelled openly and before all the pagans to confess that they were not gods, as the gentiles foolishly claimed, but mere demons, and that there was one God, whom the Christian faith worships and adores.

Since the matter is therefore thus, our Author rightly concludes from it (*Ibid.*, col. 405): “What is more manifest than this work? What proof is more trustworthy? The simplicity of truth stands in the midst.” For that public confession of the demons was either true or false and deceitful. If true, they must [Col. 0883B] undoubtedly be believed, and the pagans were obliged to confess that their gods were false and that the one whom the Christians venerate was the only true God. But if the demons were then lying, in the first place you will not easily persuade anyone of this. For everyone sometimes lies for his own honor, but never for his own disgrace and infamy. Furthermore, if they were lying and by that lie complied with the Christians, it follows with complete certainty that they possessed none of the divinity which the pagans vaunted. For the true God can neither lie nor comply with creatures to his own disgrace. Therefore that divinity is false which, as our Author says, “does something to its own disgrace for its rivals”—that is, which lies to its own disgrace for its enemies, the Christians, and by lying subjects itself to them (*Dissertat. in* [Col. 0883C] *Minut. Octav.*, c. 20, art. 3, and *in Lactant.*, c. 9, art. 2). How much force this argument possesses has been abundantly demonstrated in our preceding dissertations.

Accordingly, nothing remains to be explained except what occurs in somewhat obscure language in our Author’s text. There he boldly challenges the pagans to put to the test both this power of the Christians over demons and that public confession of demons denying that they were gods. How confidently he pronounces this you may learn from his very challenge (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 23, p. 24): “When adjured,” he says, “by Christians, if they do not confess themselves to be demons, shed the blood of that most impudent Christian on the spot”—that is, in that very place and at that very moment. [Col. 0883D] And lest anyone suspect any fraud or trickery, he demands for that test not some private place, or one suspect to the pagans, but a public place safe for them all (*Ibid.*). For he addresses them as follows: “Let someone be produced here before your tribunals who is known to be under the influence of a demon. When commanded to speak by any Christian whatsoever, that spirit will confess itself to be a demon as truly as elsewhere it falsely claims to be God.” In our manuscripts the reading is not “God,” but “Lord,” though the sense is no different.

He steadfastly asserts that this can be proved similarly not merely by this one test, but by any other test involving any person driven by a demon in any manner whatever. For he continues as follows (*Ibid.*): “Likewise let someone be brought [Col. 0884A] before the pagans’ tribunals from among those who are thought to suffer from a god, who, breathing upon altars, conceive the divine power from the smell of burnt sacrifice, who labor by belching, who pronounce oracles while panting. The Virgin Caelestis herself, promiser of rains; Aesculapius himself, revealer of medicines and, the other day, supplier of life to Socordius, Thenatius, and Asclepiodotus, who were about to die—all these, when adjured by Christians, will immediately confess themselves to be demons.”

Do you hear how many examples he advances, examples which the pagans could neither ever deny nor conceal in any way whatsoever? But because these statements, and particularly the latter ones, are covered by no small obscurity, let us endeavor to dispel it to the best of our ability. First, therefore, we shall observe that some light can be cast upon his preliminary statements by these verses of Virgil [Col. 0884B] (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VI, v. 77 ff.):

> But the prophetess, not yet enduring Phoebus, raves wildly  
> In the vast cavern, if only she can shake the mighty god  
> From her breast; all the more he wears down  
> Her frenzied mouth, subduing her fierce heart, and shapes her by constraint.

Commenting on the first verse, Servius says: “‘Not yet enduring’: because she could not yet give full utterance to the words of the oracles.” A prophet, therefore, is said to “endure a god” when, inspired by the divine power of some god for the purpose of delivering oracles, she labored, was tormented, subdued, and constrained until she had shaken it from her breast. Indeed, prophets of this sort, as the pagans themselves said, were filled with an extraordinary frenzy.

Those whom Tertullian next calls “persons breathing upon altars” are undoubtedly *harioli*, concerning whom Donatus says in his observations on Terence (Donatus, on [Col. 0884C] Terence, *Phormio*, act 4, scene 4, v. 27): “A *hariolus* is one who prophesies under divine inspiration; he is called *fariolus* from *fata* and *fando*, since F is substituted for H, and likewise H for F, in many expressions. Or is it because they imitate aspiration in breathing out? For they are accustomed to expel the mortal soul by their breath so that they may receive the divine. Hence they also uttered a sound of this kind, *OE*, because the sound *OE* conveys the force of breathing out.” Again, Maro, whom we have already praised, sang of the Sibyl (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VI, v. 45):

> They had come to the threshold, when the virgin said: “It is time  
> To ask the fates: the god—behold, the god!” As she spoke these words,  
> Before the doors, suddenly neither her face nor her color remained the same,  
> Nor did her hair remain arranged; but her breast panted,  
> And her fierce heart swelled with frenzy; she seemed larger,  
> And sounded no longer mortal, once she had been breathed upon  
> By the now nearer divine power of the god.

[Col. 0884D] Lucan likewise wrote of the Cumaean Sibyl as she attempted to prophesy (Lucan, bk. V, v. 91 ff.):

> Such was the Cumaean prophetess in her Euboean retreat;  
> Disdaining that her labor should serve many nations,  
> Proudly, from so vast a slaughter of destinies,  
> She selected Roman destinies with her hand; thus Phoenomoë,  
> Filled with Phoebus, labors. . . . . .  
>   
> . . . . . . . . . .  
>   
> Then for the first time foaming, frantic rage flows  
> From her mouth, with groans and murmurs clearly heard  
> Through her panting passage; then a mournful howl resounds  
> Through the vast caverns, and, the virgin now subdued,  
> Her final utterances ring out.

Accordingly, Cicero says (Cicero, *De divinatione*, bk. I, p. 274, line 35): “I believe there were also certain exhalations from the earth by which minds were inspired to pour forth oracles.” But we cited many other writers on these matters in [Col. 0885A] our dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius (*Dissertat. in Minut.*, c. 10, art. 2). Consider, I ask you, whether the following meaning of Tertullian may be gathered from them: prophets and soothsayers are thought to “suffer from a god” when, driven by him, they are tormented by heat and frenzy.

Those who “breathe upon altars,” moreover—that is, who blow and emit their breath upon the altars—conceive the *numen*, that is, the will and power of some god, from the *nidor*, that is, the odor of some thoroughly burnt victim. Next come those who, by belching—that is, by emitting belches and various panting breaths—strive to pour forth oracles and to belch them out and send them forth from their breast. But in our manuscripts and the earlier printed copies, *curantur* (“are cured”) is written in place of *conantur* (“strive”) (Tertull., *loc. cit.*). Its meaning may be that by belching and uttering an oracle they are said to be freed and cured of their labor [Col. 0885B] and torment. But the other reading appears preferable. For our author still seems to be speaking of people who are tormented and laboring, since he immediately adds: “Who pronounce oracles while panting” (*Ibid.*). The manuscripts and other editions printed before Rigault read “preface their utterances,” though with a meaning not very dissimilar. For he says that the god is then shaken out of them, as we have heard from Virgil and others, and that they pour forth oracles under the impulse of some god. But he demonstrates most clearly that all these things are done not by the operation of the true God, but, as has been said, by the deceptive tricks of demons. For when adjured by Christians, they were compelled to confess that they were demons, as we shall say again below.

Far more difficult to explain, however, are the words that follow. For who could readily say what [Col. 0885C] that “Virgin Caelestis” is whom he calls the “promiser of rains” (*Ibid.*)? Some think she is Juno, others Fortune, others Ceres, others Urania, and others Venus, because Herodotus, Pausanias, and Lucian mentioned Venus Urania, or Caelestis, and her temple (Herodot., bk. I, §§ 31 and 105; Pausanias, bk. I, pp. 14 and 17; Lucian, *dial. Mat. et musar.*, p. 973 [abbreviated title as in the source]). We, however, shall more readily be persuaded that Tertullian is there indicating Africa’s own local goddess, whom a little later he attests was worshiped in Africa (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 24, col. 416). For Augustine, certainly an eyewitness, recorded the following concerning that goddess: “In our youth we sometimes attended the spectacles and sacrilegious mockeries. We watched men seized by spirits, listened to musicians, and [Col. 0885D] delighted in the most shameful games presented to gods and goddesses—to the virgin Caelestis and Berecynthia, mother of all” (Augustine, *De civitate Dei*, bk. II, c. 4, p. 34). Again, later: “Where and when those consecrated to Caelestis heard precepts of chastity, we do not know. Yet before the very shrine where we saw that image installed, people gathered from every direction and, standing wherever each could find a place, watched with the closest attention the games being performed; their gaze alternated between the procession of prostitutes on one side and that virgin goddess being worshiped in supplication on the other, while obscenities were celebrated before her. We saw no modest mimes there, no more decorous performance; every service of obscenity was fulfilled. It was known what pleased the virgin divinity, and there was presented [Col. 0886A] what a matron, better instructed by the temple, might carry home” (*Ibid.*, c. 26, p. 56). He says still more about her elsewhere. But these passages prove more than sufficiently that among the Africans there was a temple of the virgin Caelestis, who was not only worshiped by them but, when invoked by them in a time of drought, promised rains and foretold that they would soon come. The opinion we propose is not so remote from the opinions of others that it cannot be reconciled with them. For that goddess was called by different names according to differences of place. If you desire a witness, here is Ambrose asserting it: “Her whom the Africans worship as Caelestis, the Persians as Mithras, and many as Venus, they worship under diversity of name, not diversity of divinity” (Ambrose, Epistle 18, *Against Symmachus*, § 30, p. 840).

The author then passes to Aesculapius, whom he [Col. 0886B] calls “the revealer of medicines,” and elsewhere “the one who first investigated remedies” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 23, p. 410, and *De corona*, c. 8; tom.
