I, *Apparat.*, p. 1192). In our earlier dissertations we showed by what reasoning the pagans ascribed the invention of medicine to him. But the clearer this point is, the greater indeed is the obscurity of the words that follow: “The other day,” he says, “supplier of life to Socordius, Thenatius, and Asclepiodotus, who were about to die” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 23, col. 24). It is astonishing how greatly these words have exercised the ingenuity of learned men. Yet this passage is certainly corrupt. For in our manuscripts, both those written by an older hand and those by a more recent one, the reading is: “The other day to those about to die” (or “to others who linger in dying”), “Socordius, Denatius, and Asclopiodotus is supplied.” In [Col. 0886C] editions older than Rigault’s: “At other times, supplier to those who linger in dying of Socordius, Denatius, and Asclepiodotus” (*Dissertat. in Arnob.*, c. 9, art. 2, and *in Lactant.*, c. 30, art. 5). Who does not see, however, that these variant readings increase the difficulty rather than remove it?

Some nevertheless suspect that these are expressions used by *agyrtae*, or tricksters, who falsely claimed to serve Aesculapius; they deem it better to pass over them in silence than to waste laughable and useless effort in explaining them. Others think they are the names of three men whose span of life Aesculapius was said to have prolonged shortly before. But this ought to be supported by at least some argument. Others, moreover, think that the three are names of herbs by which diseases could be driven away. For Pliny includes among various antidotes [Col. 0886D] *scordotin*, as he calls it, or *scordion* (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. II, c. 6, p. 395). Elsewhere he writes that this herb is useful for removing numerous diseases (Idem, bk. XXVI, c. 7, p. 451; c. 8, p. 471; and c. 10, p. 475). Yet what he says elsewhere certainly ought not to be omitted: “Against all these poisons and magical arts there will be, first, the Homeric *moly*, then *mithridation*, *scordotis*, and *centaurion*” (Idem, bk. XXV, c. 10, p. 412).

Some have thought that under the name *Asclepiodotus* Tertullian indicates *Asclepion*, about which we read the following transmitted in Pliny’s writings: “Panaces, by its very name, promises remedies for all diseases; it has numerous varieties, which are ascribed to gods. One, indeed, is surnamed *Asclepion*” (Idem, [Col. 0887A] *ibid.*, c. 4, p. 382), evidently after Aesculapius, the false god of the pagans, as its discoverer, or so named because of its efficacy.

The third name remains, and in explaining it everyone is at a complete loss. Those who read *Denatius* suppose that it denotes something customarily given to persons already at the point of death. Those who prefer to read *Thenatius* suspect that it signifies something else by which those breathing their last could be revived and, as it were, recalled from death to life. But these are mere conjectures, supported by no argument whatsoever.

Consider a little more attentively, therefore, I ask, whether these words of Julius Firmicus Maternus might cast some light on this obscure passage of our author: “Mercury, when positioned together with the sun at the horoscope, [Col. 0887B] will produce exorcists, and persons who free men suffering from an assault of demons by appropriate remedies, so that very great wealth accrues to them from those arts” (Jul. Firm., *Matheseos*, bk. III, c. 9). You plainly hear him speaking of Mercury, who was believed to cure with appropriate remedies men suffering from an assault of demons. May it not therefore be inferred from this that the remedies which Firmicus calls only generically “remedies” are called by Tertullian by their individual names, though these have been corrupted in his text—remedies by which exorcists made such by Mercury freed those afflicted by assaults of demons? For it is certain that throughout this entire passage Tertullian himself is speaking of persons driven by a demon whom certain men vainly attempted to cure by magical art. But the demon itself was immediately expelled from them when adjured by a Christian and was compelled [Col. 0887C] to disclose its name and confess the true God of the Christians. Nevertheless, if anyone suggests something better to us, we shall certainly not resist him.

Tertullian proceeds and steadfastly asserts that nothing is simpler or more trustworthy than this work of the Christians and the argument derived from it. For in it, he says, nothing can be suspected: “You will say that it is done by magic or some deception of that kind, if your eyes and ears permit you” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 23, col. 410). And thus Rigault did not hesitate to emend this passage of Tertullian without noting any variant reading. In the old editions, however, the text read: “Nothing . . . . . is done. You do not stand by what was said, if your eyes”; while in our two older manuscripts: “You say that nothing . . . . is done.” Then in other copies: “At the same time. You will not say, if your eyes,” etc. But however [Col. 0887D] difficult it may be to determine the genuine reading, it is nevertheless clear that our author’s meaning is evident. For he says that the pagans cannot either suspect or object that anything magical or deceptive is present in this Christian work, provided those same pagans are not blind and deaf through unconquered obstinacy. For they could easily see the simple manner in which the Christians acted and could also hear the demons confessing that they were not truly gods but unclean spirits, pre-condemned on account of their malice for the day of judgment together with all their worshipers and agents (*Ibid.*). Indeed, the demons themselves, while the pagans themselves listened, could not rebut, conceal, erase, or deny even the mark of their disgrace and condemnation. Therefore Tertullian [Col. 0888A] boldly challenges them to deny it sometime, if they ever can. “Let them refuse,” he says; our manuscripts read “They renounce,” while the ancient editions more correctly read “Let them renounce”—that is, though by an improper mode of expression, let them deny, reject, and disavow that they have been pre-condemned. But undoubtedly they could not deny it when, questioned and adjured by Christians, they were compelled to answer.

For how could they have denied that they were unclean spirits, when this ought to have been understood, as Tertullian says, “from their foods—blood and smoke and the stinking pyres of animals—and from the most impure tongues of the prophets themselves” (*Ibid.*)? Consult Augustine, if you please, and, if you have leisure, read what he related from Porphyry’s letter to Anebo concerning the impious and fraudulent arts of demons and [Col. 0888B] deceitful spirits (Augustine, *De civitate Dei*, bk. X, c. 11, p. 247 ff.). For there he writes that they rejoice in sacrificial odors, are enticed by victims—that is, slaughtered animals—and are compelled to do what men wish. You will also note other things there by which much of what we have thus far discussed concerning the tricks of those same demons can be confirmed and elucidated. Tertullian added that they are shown to be unclean spirits by the most impure tongues of the prophets themselves: either of those who breathed upon altars, as we said before, and were polluted by smoke and the blood of victims, or of those who were compelled by Christian adjuration to confess that the divine power they had conceived was not a god but a demon. Minucius Felix, moreover, used the word “polluted” when speaking of the statue of any false god: “It is polished,” he says, “by a polluted man” [Col. 0888C] (Minucius, *Octavius*, p. 307). And Prudentius later sang of Apollo:

> Soon, polluted, he wept for the man slain by the crooked discus.

Prudentius, *Hymn of St. Romanus*, v. 205.

## ARTICLE VII. How admirably Tertullian confirms the foregoing argument from the fact that demons were expelled in various ways from the bodies of the men whom they possessed, either by exorcists or by other Christians, whom they feared and hated and to whom they were subject; in what sense their condition is called desperate; and concerning the delay of punishment, by which they are said to possess the consolation of indulging their malignity

Tertullian presses the pagans still more sharply and makes plain to everyone how great was the Christians’ power to put demons to flight and drive them from the bodies [Col. 0888D] of possessed men, and how great their dominion over them: “For at our touch and breath,” he says, “seized by the contemplation and representation of that fire, they even depart from bodies at our command, unwillingly and in pain, and blushing in your presence” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 23, col. 410). The pagans therefore could certainly deny neither the demons’ weakness nor the Christians’ marvelous power over them by any reasoning, unless through an utterly hardened and invincible obstinacy; by that power the Christians demonstrated the truth of their religion more clearly than the noonday sun.

But someone will perhaps ask whether Tertullian is speaking there only of our exorcists. For when Cyprian writes to [Col. 0889A] Magnus about what was customarily done in his own time, he specifically attests that demons were put to flight by exorcists: “This is also done today, so that through exorcists the devil is scourged, burned, and tormented by a human voice and divine power” (Cyprian, Epistle 69 to Magnus, p. 187). “Did not Tertullian himself,” another will say, “also write these very words about the same exorcists in another book? ‘An example occurred, as the husband of the woman bears witness: she went to the theater and returned from there with a demon. And so, during the exorcism, when the unclean spirit was reproached for having dared to attack a believer, it said: “I acted consistently and most justly; I found her in my domain”’” (Tertullian, *De spectaculis*, c. 26). Did he not also say elsewhere: “With what mouth will a Christian incense-dealer—that is, one who burns incense to idols—if he passes through temples, spit and [Col. 0889B] blow upon the smoking altars for which he himself has provided? With what assurance will he exorcise his own fosterlings—that is, the demons to whom he provides his house as a storeroom? If indeed he has cast out a demon, let him not congratulate himself on his faith. For he did not cast out an enemy. He should easily have been able to obtain a favor from one whom he feeds every day” (Idem, *De idololatria*, c. 2).

Someone could indeed reply that in both those passages of Tertullian it is not exorcists who are named, but exorcisms or adjurations, which undoubtedly could be employed by all Christians. Yet no one can deny that demons were expelled from men’s bodies chiefly by exorcists, as Cyprian says, and that this was sufficient for our Author to prove the Christians’ power over those same demons.

[Col. 0889C] But he proceeds further, and in the cited passage of the *Apologeticum* he speaks generally of all Christians who cast out demons. For he unhesitatingly affirms that so great was the multitude of gentiles whom Christians freed from assaults of demons that, had this benefit been withdrawn, the Christians would have avenged themselves amply upon the gentiles for their monstrous cruelty. Here are his own words: “Who would snatch you away from those hidden enemies who everywhere ravage your minds and health—from assaults of demons, I mean—which we drive from you without payment or reward? This alone would have sufficed for our vengeance: that henceforth free possession of you should lie open to unclean spirits” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, c. 37, col. 460). Moreover, he wrote to Scapula in this manner: “And how many honorable men—for we say nothing of common people—have been cured either of demons or of illnesses?” (Idem, *Ad Scapulam*, c. 4). Who, however, will deny that these things were done not by exorcists alone but by all Christians? For the number of exorcists was then too small for them alone to have freed so great a multitude of men from assaults of demons.

Accordingly, when the pagans objected that Christians were wholly useless to the commonwealth, he refuted them thus: “At what value do you reckon those who now drive demons out of you?” (*Ibid.*, c. 43). And so indeed the text stands in our manuscripts. No less acceptable, however, is the reading of the ancient editions, “How many do you have?” and that of La Cerda’s edition, “When?” For Tertullian’s meaning is: If Christians [Col. 0890A] are useless to the commonwealth, at what value, then, do you estimate them, or at what price do you hold those who drive so many demons from you so often?

But what need is there of argument? Did he not himself declare it in the clearest words? “That spirit, when commanded by any Christian whatsoever to speak, will confess himself to be a demon as truly as elsewhere he falsely claims to be a god” (ibid., ch. 23). Did he not also write again to the same Scapula? “We not only reject demons, but also convict them, expose them daily, and expel them from human beings, as is known to very many” (the same, *To Scapula*, chs. 3–4). Yet who does not see that these things were said not only of exorcists but of all Christians? Very great, therefore, was the power not merely of exorcists but of all Christians over demons, [Col. 0890B] by which they very frequently cast them out of the bodies of pagans.

But if anyone should inquire whence, or by what name, they possessed this power, Tertullian will answer him: “All our”—that is, Christians’—“dominion and power over those demons derives its force from the naming of Christ,” or from pronouncing Christ’s name when they adjured the demons, “and from the recollection of those things which they expect to befall them from God through Christ the arbiter” (the same, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, p. 410). Some, however, though supported by the authority of no manuscript codex, think that *comminatione* (“threatening”) should be read, doubtless because demons were adjured by the living God, who will judge the living and the dead. But perhaps they did not sufficiently notice that shortly afterward Tertullian’s text speaks [Col. 0890C] of the “presentation” of that eternal fire with which the demons are to be punished—something equivalent to its recollection. See Eusebius recounting these things in his oration *In Praise of Constantine the Great*, and others whom we have cited elsewhere (Eusebius, *Oration in Praise of Constantine the Great*, ch. 16, p. 658 ff.; passage cited below).

Tertullian therefore rightly concludes from this: “The demons, fearing Christ in God and God in Christ, are subjected to the servants of God and of Christ” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, p. 410). But how did they fear them? “Through fear, as wicked servants do,” he says (ibid., ch. 27, p. 432), as we read in our manuscript codices. They therefore feared Christ and his disciples with servile fear. “And fear,” he continues, “breathes hatred”; or, as Minucius says, “through fear they secretly sow hatred of us” [Col. 0890D] (Minucius, *Octavius*, p. 255). The demons, therefore, were both subject to Christians and afraid of them, and for that reason hated them. Why should they not be afraid, since, as our author further says, “they are subdued by them, succumb to their own condition, and entreat at close quarters those whom they attack from afar” (Tertullian, ibid., ch. 27, col. 432)? But if they entreat them, fear them, hate them, and are subjected to them, then, when adjured by them, they surely did not lie; rather, as we have already said, they truly confessed that they really were demons and by no means gods, and that there is only one God. Moreover, our author says that so genuine a confession and so public a testimony customarily made people Christians and established and confirmed the truth of the Christian religion (ibid., [Col. 0891A] col. 23, p. 26). But we have treated these matters in our earlier dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 20, art. 3; *on Arnobius*, ch. 3, art. 1; *on Lactantius*, ch. 9, art. 2; ch. 16, art. 1; ch. 20, art. 7; ch. 33, art. 4).

But as we now hasten, in our customary manner, to explain other matters, someone may perhaps delay us and ask why our author said that the demons were “pre-condemned because of their wickedness,” and afterward added: “Their desperate condition, resulting from their pre-condemnation, counts as a consolation the enjoyment of their malignity in the meantime, owing to the postponement of their punishment” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 22, col. 404; ibid., ch. 27, p. 432). “What,” he will ask, “is this pre-condemnation of the demons, this postponement of punishment, and this consolation of enjoying their malignity?” For Tertullian himself had stated no less clearly, as we observed, that it is gathered from the sacred [Col. 0891B] Scriptures that the race of demons, together with the founders and prince of their kind, is not merely pre-condemned but condemned absolutely. Yet although the condemnation of the demons is certain, they do not yet suffer all the punishments due for their crimes. For even in the sacred Scriptures themselves they are said to have reproached Christ the Lord: “Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matt. 8:29). Augustine, however, explained this more clearly from the epistle of the apostle Peter: “That certain angels sinned,” he says, “and were thrust down into the lowest parts of this world, which is like a prison to them, and that they are reserved there for their final condemnation on the day of judgment, the apostle Peter shows most plainly, saying that God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, thrusting them into the prisons of infernal darkness, delivered them to be kept for punishment at the judgment” (Augustine, *City of God*, book X, [Col. 0891C] ch. 33, p. 293; 2 Peter 2:4). Yet this postponement and delay of the infernal darkness and of the fire reserved for them was a consolation of some sort in their pre-condemnation and desperate condition. For in the meantime they enjoyed their malignity, by which, as we have seen, they either induced Christians to worship themselves, or false gods, or caused those who refused to be tortured with the most cruel torments, even to death. But we have discussed elsewhere this consolation of theirs and the deferment of their punishment (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 20, art. 5).

# CHAPTER XI

## On the restoration of dead human beings to life, the final judgment of God, the eternal punishments of the wicked and rewards of the righteous, and the receptacles of souls before the last judgment

### ARTICLE I

#### By what arguments Tertullian proved that all dead human beings can be restored to life and will in fact be restored; whether souls stripped of their bodies, and without the bodies’ ministry, can do, suffer, grieve, and rejoice in anything

[Col. 0891D]

We must now pass to other doctrines of the Christian religion which Tertullian asserts and defends in his books against the pagans. One of these, and one worthy of our attention, is his constant teaching, supported by various weighty arguments, that absolutely all dead human beings are to be restored to life at the end of the world. [Col. 0892A] His first argument is drawn from the infinite power of God: “He who,” he says, “fashioned this great body of the world from what had not existed”—that is, from nothing (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 520)—or, as our codices and those printed before Rigaltius have it, “set it in place,” or created it, can certainly himself raise human beings “from the death of vacancy and emptiness”—that is, from death, or from emptiness and the deprivation of life—to a second life. For they constitute only one part of the world, which, it is agreed, “is animated by the spirit that animates all things.” Thus Rigaltius and later editors present this text of Tertullian. But our codices and the older printed editions read more correctly: “animated by the spirit that animates all souls.” Our author’s argument is indeed drawn, as they say, from the greater to the lesser, or from the whole, which [Col. 0892B] was made, to the part, which can therefore be remade. The world, he says, was animated or created by the Spirit of God, the animator of all souls; therefore that same Spirit of God can animate human beings again after their death—human beings animated not by the spirit of all, but only by their own—and restore them once more, not from nothing as before, but from destruction and from a life previously lost, to a second and identical life.

Moreover, this very power of God to raise dead human beings is demonstrated clearly by Tertullian not only from the creation of the entire world but even from the creation of the human being alone. For before he was created, the human being was nothing; otherwise he would remember having existed at least at some time. But if he was created by God from nothing, he can certainly be recalled from death by the same power and will of God [Col. 0892C] (ibid.). For no greater power is required for the first creation than for renewal and restoration. Nor should you inquire too curiously and importunately how this can be done: “For explain, if you can,” says Tertullian, “the manner in which you were made, and then ask in what manner you will be made” (the same, ibid.). For by the very power by which you were first made, you will afterward be remade. Accordingly, if you do not doubt the first making, you ought much less to doubt the second: “For surely,” as he further says, “you will more easily be made what you once were, since it was equally not difficult for you to be made what you once were not” (ibid.). We have heard Minucius Felix, Lactantius, and others argue in a similar manner in the foregoing dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 7, art. 2; and *on Lactantius*, ch. 29, art. 4).

[Col. 0892D] But if this lies entirely within God’s power, nothing remains to be proved except that he wills it and has signified that he truly wills it. Yet, as our author says, God “has ordained and proclaimed” this (Tertullian, ibid.), not merely once but repeatedly in the sacred Scriptures of the Old and especially of the New Testament. Nor is there any need to gather here their testimonies, which are everywhere readily available to all and which no one who has touched those Scriptures even lightly can possibly fail to know. Their authority, moreover, is most certain, as we demonstrated above (above, ch. 6, art. 3 ff.). It is therefore established that God both can and wills that absolutely all dead human beings be restored to the former condition of their life; and consequently there will certainly be [Col. 0893A] a universal return of them to life.

Tertullian presses the point further and demonstrates by another argument that it is altogether necessary for all dead human beings someday to return to life. The whole argument is contained in these words: “Certainly, because the purpose of restoration is the appointment of judgment, the same person who had existed must necessarily be presented, so that he may receive judgment according to his good or contrary deserts” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48). He therefore teaches that there is absolutely no room for doubt that all human beings must present themselves at God’s final judgment at the end of the world. But this cannot happen unless they return to life and receive from God a final sentence, and either reward or punishment, according to their good or evil deserts.

Our author, however, presses this argument much more fully [Col. 0893B] in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, where he argues as follows: “This will be the whole cause—indeed, the necessity—of the resurrection: namely, the appointment of judgment, most fully consonant with God. From the ordering of that judgment, consider whether divine adjudication must indeed preside over both substances of the human being that are to be judged, the soul as well as the flesh” (the same, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 14). For a human being certainly acts well or badly not with the soul alone but also with his body. Such is the partnership of the soul with the body that “in the flesh, with the flesh, and through the flesh is done whatever is done in the heart” (ibid., ch. 15), that is, in the soul. Indeed, even if the soul sometimes thinks by itself, this thought of its is scarcely ever without some interaction with the body: “For if the soul turns anything over,” says Tertullian, “the countenance supplies an indication; the face [Col. 0893C] is the mirror of every intention” (ibid.).

There is no need at present to investigate whether he truly believed that the soul can do absolutely nothing without interaction with the body and without its senses. For we have already said something about this opinion, and an opportunity to discuss it will arise immediately. For now, therefore, let it suffice to note that very many acts of the soul, as no one denies, are performed not without the ministry of the body and the senses. The human body is joined to the soul in such a way that it is certainly a participant in at least many good or evil deserts. The whole human being, therefore—that is, his body and soul—must be presented at the final and most equitable judgment of God, so that they may receive either punishment or reward for everything done in this mortal life.

Nor does our author allow anyone to object to him that the human [Col. 0893D] soul alone enjoys free choice of the will, while the body is driven into every action as an instrument. For the body is not an instrument foreign to the soul, but is so united to it that, just as it participates in the soul’s actions, so too it participates in its deserts. After the end of the world, therefore, it must be restored to life so that, by God’s just judgment, it may be punished or rewarded according to its deserts.

The third argument by which Tertullian endeavors to prove the future resurrection of the human being is not without difficulty and will appear false to many. For he argued in this manner (the same, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, p. 520): “Souls and bodies will therefore be presented again, because the soul alone cannot suffer anything without stable matter”—that is, the flesh. Can the soul, then, [Col. 0894A] suffer absolutely nothing without the flesh? “Yes,” someone will say, “Tertullian indeed believed this.” For in another book he addresses the soul in these very words (the same, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 4): “We affirm that you remain after the completion of life, await the day of judgment, and, according to your desert, are destined either for torment or for refreshment, each of them everlasting. To endure these, your former substance, and the matter and memory of the same human being, must necessarily return to you, because you can experience neither evil nor good without the flesh’s capacity for suffering, and there is no ground for judgment without the presentation of the very person who merited the suffering imposed by judgment.” Thus he affirms—not merely once, nor doubtfully, but insistently—and repeats that the soul can feel absolutely nothing without association with its body. He considered this [Col. 0894B] so true that he concludes from it that the dead human body will therefore return to life, because without it the soul can do nothing good or evil.

But withhold your assent for a little while, if you can. I would first have you turn your attention to what the same Tertullian argued in his books *On the Soul* and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, where he treats expressly and more fully both the dead body’s return to life and the soul’s capacity for acting and suffering. In the former book he asserts most explicitly and firmly that the soul, separated from the body, either suffers pain or is filled with joy. For all human souls remain in the underworld after death, “and, whether you will or not,” he says, “both punishments and refreshments are already found there.” Then, when someone objects that the soul must await the resurrection of the flesh, its partner in works, before it can grieve [Col. 0894C] or rejoice, he answers without hesitation that this is not necessary. For, as he puts it, “from its own resources it has enough for either category of suffering.” And certainly the soul by itself, without the ministry of the body, is sometimes tormented by anger or hatred; and sometimes, even while the body is afflicted, it seeks a secret joy for itself, as he confirms by the examples of Mucius, Zeno, and others (ibid.). Conversely, it sometimes grieves, is oppressed, and is tormented while the body remains unharmed. But if in this life, while bound to the body, the soul by itself is affected by joy or grief, how much more so when, after death, it is separated from the body and awaits the final judgment? Finally, some of its acts occur without interaction with the flesh, such as thoughts alone and bare acts of will, which divine judgment takes into account [Col. 0894D] (the same, *On the Soul*, ch. 17). From these considerations he draws the following conclusion: “Therefore it is most fitting that the soul, even without waiting for the flesh, should be punished for what it committed without the flesh’s participation; so too, for pious and benevolent thoughts in which it did not need the flesh, it will be refreshed without the flesh.” He taught the same things, and several others, in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, where he expressly demonstrates that human beings are altogether to be restored to life.

“What then,” you will ask, “did Tertullian contradict himself so absurdly?” But if you are willing to keep your judgment still suspended, you will see that he himself removed this apparent contradiction, although it is by no means slight. For in the same book *On the Resurrection* he repeats what he had said, [Col. 0895A] namely, that “souls are now tormented or comforted in the underworld, although naked, although still exiled from the flesh” (the same, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 17). But because some might object that it can be inferred from this that the soul is thus sufficient unto itself in its “capacity,” as he calls it, “for suffering and sensation,” and therefore does not need the flesh to be presented again, he responds to them as follows (ibid.):

> On the contrary, it will need the flesh to this extent—not because it cannot feel anything without the flesh, but because it must also feel together with the flesh. For insofar as acting is concerned, it is sufficient from its own resources; and so too for suffering. For acting, however, it is sufficient from its own resources only to a lesser degree. From its own resources it can merely think, will, desire, and determine; but to accomplish anything it awaits the service of the flesh. Thus for suffering also it demands the service of the flesh, so that through it it may suffer as fully as it was unable to act fully without it. Therefore, for those things for which it is sufficient from its own resources, it meanwhile pays the penalty—desire, thought, and will. [Col. 0895B] Moreover, if these were sufficient for the fullness of deserts, so that deeds were not also required, the soul would be entirely sufficient for the completion of judgment, being judged for those things in the doing of which it alone had been sufficient. But since deeds also are bound to deserts, and deeds are carried out through the flesh, it is no longer sufficient for the soul without the flesh to be comforted or tormented for the works of the flesh, even though it has members of its own; for these are correspondingly insufficient for it to feel fully, just as they are insufficient for it to act perfectly. Therefore, in whatever manner it acted, in that manner it also suffers in the underworld, tasting judgment first, just as it first introduced the offense; yet it awaits the flesh, so that through it it may also receive recompense for the deeds whose conception it entrusted to the flesh.

We have transcribed this entire argument [Col. 0895C] and response of our author, although it is rather long, because it not only completely resolves the difficulty proposed to us, but also yields several observations about the nature of the soul which should not be passed over without comment.

He therefore teaches that the naked soul, without partnership with the body, is truly either tormented or comforted in the underworld. Because, however, it could be objected to him from this that the soul is not a purely spiritual substance but a bodily one, or, as he himself says, possesses a “corporeity of its own,” he was unwilling to examine this more difficult question, lest he stray too long from his subject. Meanwhile, he concedes, though he does not expressly admit, that the soul has some kind of body and certain members peculiar to its own kind. Yet he asserts most explicitly that the soul has acts of its own which do not [Col. 0895D] depend upon the body at all, such as thoughts, acts of will, and desires. If, moreover, these acts—to note the point in passing—are altogether spiritual, he could much less deny that the soul itself is spiritual.

Since these are acts of the soul alone, it possesses from its own resources not only the capacity to act and suffer, but also that by which it can merit either reward or punishment. Once released from the body, therefore, it can and ought to be affected by either punishment or reward according to its deserts. For so long as it is united to the body, it always sins or earns merit first. After death, therefore, it must necessarily be affected by the punishments or rewards due to it, alone and before the body’s return. Tertullian was therefore convinced that the soul, once the bonds [Col. 0896A] of the body have been broken, suffers, is tormented, and is tortured. But because in this life it also committed many sins together with its body, it must therefore be reunited to its body, restored to life, so that it may be punished and tormented according to its deserts.

Once these points have been explained in this way, the alleged contradiction in Tertullian disappears. For he rightly said both that the soul truly suffers something without the body and that it can suffer nothing. Where he says that it can suffer nothing, the words “fully and perfectly” must be understood—that is, to the extent merited by its sinning together with the body. For with that with which it sinned, it must certainly also be punished. Tertullian therefore rightly proves from this the future restoration of the dead body to life, because the soul alone cannot suffer, namely, the full and perfect punishment which it jointly merited by sinning with the body.

[Col. 0896B] If you permit us to add anything further to these observations, we shall note that Ambrose, in the appropriate place, as well as Athenagoras, Minucius Felix, and Lactantius clearly proved by this very same argument—drawn from the punishments or rewards due to a human being who acts well or badly in this life—that the same human being will return to life; indeed, Lactantius also used it to demonstrate the immortality of our soul, as we have shown in our dissertations on their books (Ambrose, book II, *On Faith in the Resurrection*, § 12, p. 1147; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 475; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 24, art. 3, and ch. 29, art. 5; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 7, art. 2).

### ARTICLE II

#### By what examples, by what oracle of the Pythia, and by what philosophical opinion concerning the transmigration of souls Tertullian shows that all dead human beings whatsoever are to be restored to their former state of life, and how he answers the objections advanced

[Col. 0896C]

Although Tertullian demonstrated most clearly by the foregoing arguments that any human beings whatsoever can, by the will of almighty God, be raised from death, however incurred, he nevertheless endeavors to confirm this with several examples. Yet we must not conceal that these examples, since they are not entirely parallel, cannot furnish a perfect and in every respect complete demonstration of human resurrection. They can at least fittingly confirm that the pagans deny in vain that human beings can be restored to the former state of a life that has passed.

[Col. 0896D] Having offered these observations against more captious critics, we must hear Tertullian himself (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 520): “An example of human resurrection,” he says, “has also been marked out by God himself as testimony for you. The light, slain each day, shines again, and the darkness in turn withdraws and succeeds; the stars, having died, revive.” In our manuscript copies and the printed editions earlier than Rigaltius, the reading is *vivescunt*—that is, as is clear from Pliny, “they become alive” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XVII, ch. 10, p. 344). Our author continues: “The seasons begin when they end; fruits are consumed”—our manuscripts and printed codices have “are brought to completion”—“and return. [Col. 0897A] Seeds certainly spring up more fruitfully only after being corrupted and dissolved. All things are preserved by perishing; all things are re-formed from destruction” (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 12). He pursues these points with greater verbal splendor in another book; Minucius Felix does so more briefly, and Theophilus of Antioch more fully, as we have explained elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 7, art. 2).

Our Tertullian concludes his argument in these words (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 43): “You, human being—so great a name, if you understand yourself and how great you truly are, learning even from the inscription of the Pythia that you are lord of all things that die and rise again—will you die for the purpose of perishing?” He therefore says that the human being’s condition is no worse than that of the other things whose lord [Col. 0897B] he is, which die and rise again. The human being, therefore, has a far stronger claim than they do both to die and to rise again.

But someone will ask what that oracle of the Pythia cited by him was. Some answer that it is what he reports in that very passage: “Lord of all things that die and rise again.” Yet they have offered no argument proving that this was pronounced by the Pythia. Furthermore, he did not say in these words that he was reporting an oracle of the Pythia, but that from the oracle of the Pythia a human being could learn that he was lord of all things that die and rise again (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1170). To us, therefore, that oracle of the Pythia appears to be none other than this celebrated saying of Apollo: “Know yourself,” which we have discussed elsewhere. Tertullian, moreover, seems deliberately to have added [Col. 0897C] “even from the inscription of the Pythia,” because, as we noted in the same place, it had been inscribed upon the temple of Pythian, or Delphic, Apollo. “Why then,” you will ask, “did Tertullian write *Pythiae* (‘of the Pythia’), and not *Pythii* (‘of the Pythian’), the latter being a name by which Apollo was sometimes called?” If *Pythiae*, rather than *Pythii*, is to be read in his text, we shall answer that it is called “of the Pythia” because the Pythian prophetess customarily prophesied in that temple. For, to omit other authorities, this is expressed in the following verse of Lucretius (Lucretius, book V, v. 113):

> The Pythia, who speaks from Phoebus’ tripod and laurel.

Tertullian proceeds and, in order to break and ever more decisively refute the obstinacy of the pagans, presses them with the following *ad hominem* argument, as it is called. It is certain, he says, that they placed confidence in any philosopher [Col. 0897D] who attempted, through certain arguments proposed as ingeniously as elegantly, to defend Pythagoras’s empty opinion concerning the transmigration of souls. Indeed, none of them, deterred by the jibes of the biting Laberius, who mocked it, abstained from eating all animal flesh, “lest perhaps,” Tertullian further says, “he dine upon beef from some ancestor of his”—that is, lest in eating beef he should eat the soul of some ancestor, which he believed had migrated into the body of an ox (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 42). Tertullian did not think that so ridiculous an opinion needed to be refuted here (ibid.): “For,” he says, “we shall need many jokes and leisure if we wish to sport with this question of who might seem to be re-formed into what beast [Col. 0898A].” Rigaltius indeed reads thus; but our manuscript codices and the printed editions older than his have: “We shall also need many passages,” from which arguments to refute this error can be drawn, *ex otio*, or *otio* (“with ease”), just as Pliny wrote *ex facili* for *facile* (“easily”) (book III, epistle 3). Yet to many, *jocis* (“jokes”) will doubtless seem the preferable reading, since this utterly ridiculous opinion of Pythagoras and his followers ought to have been exploded with jokes rather than with more powerful arguments. The noun *jocis* is not unreasonably thought to accord better with the verb *lascivire* (“to sport”) than *locis* (“passages”) does (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 42). Nevertheless, shortly before this he had said that any philosopher could be overwhelmed by an immense weight of arguments if he affirmed, as Laberius says, that [Col. 0898B] according to the opinion of Pythagoras “a man is made from a mule, a snake from a woman” (the same, *On the Pallium*, ch. 1). These are verses of that poet of mimes, whom he mentions elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 7, art. 1), published by Crinitus, as we noted elsewhere:

> And now from a mule they make a man, from a woman a snake,  
> And from diverse things diverse other things.

Various writers, especially Cicero, Suetonius, both Senecas, Aulus Gellius, and Macrobius, frequently mention this Laberius, of whom Horace, among others, sang:

> Yet in conceding this, I would not grant the rest as well; for should I  
> Admire both the mimes of Laberius and his beautiful poems?

But such was the madness of the pagans and such their fury against [Col. 0898C] Christians that the Christian opinion, as our author rightly observes in another book, “although more honorable than the Pythagorean, which transfers you into beasts; although fuller than the Platonic, which restores to you also the endowment of the body; although more serious than the Epicurean, which defends you from destruction—nevertheless, solely because of the name ‘Christian,’ is accounted vanity, folly, and, as it is called, presumption.” Nor was it enough for the pagans to reject and scorn this Christian position, which was better than the others; rather, “the Christian who defends it will be driven out by the populace with stones rather than merely with boxing gloves”—these are further words of Tertullian in the *Apologeticum* (the same, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 42). But instead of *caestibus* (“boxing gloves”), our codices read *coetibus* (“assemblies”); that is, he will be expelled from meetings and gatherings. Tertullian indeed argues, and not badly, [Col. 0898D] from the greater to the lesser, as they say. The Christian, he says, who asserts that doctrine concerning the human being’s future return to life, will not only be expelled from the assemblies of the pagans, but, what is worse, will be overwhelmed with stones. Yet if *coestibus* is not very well written in Rigaltius’s edition, still worse is the reading *coedibus* (“slaughters”) found in the older editions, since slaughters are more cruel than stoning. We have treated the opinions of Pythagoras, Plato, and Epicurus noted by our author in our dissertations on the books of Minucius Felix and Lactantius (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 7, art. 1; and *on Lactantius*, ch. 34, art. 1).

Since Tertullian had attempted to support the human being’s return to life with the proposed examples of light and darkness, the stars and [Col. 0899A] seasons, fruits and seeds (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 45), the pagans argued from this: “Then it will always be necessary to die and always to rise again.” Yet this is plainly absurd. But first, Tertullian replies: “If the Lord of things had so ordained, you would experience, however unwillingly, the law of your condition” (ibid.). That is, because the true and omnipotent God is lord of all things, and consequently of death and life, he can certainly raise a dead human being to life not merely once, but as often as he wills. If, therefore, he had decreed various returns to life for the human being, the latter would experience that law unwillingly. Tertullian said *ingratis*, that is, involuntarily and against one’s will. For our author himself often used this word in that sense; indeed Cicero himself says: “What he does not owe must be extorted from him against his will and unwillingly.” And elsewhere: “They will gladly keep silent about what they can, but they will say unwillingly what necessity requires” (the same, ch. 4, col. 5; *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 19; *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 26, p. 300; Cicero, first speech *For Quinctius*, p. 9, line 2; and *Against Verres*, book IV, p. 163, line 15). Do you see that the words “gladly” and “unwillingly” are opposed to one another?

Secondly, Tertullian answers: “But as matters now stand, God has ordained no otherwise than he has proclaimed” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, p. 43)—namely, in the sacred Scriptures, as we noted above, where he proclaims that he has ordained for the human being to die once and rise once.

Finally, he answers that human beings therefore rise again so that, [Col. 0899C] “throughout the immeasurable perpetuity of eternity, they may receive what they have merited, whether evil or good, in this life” (ibid.). They must therefore be restored to life once. Afterward there will be neither death nor resurrection, but eternal life.

He next also meets the objections of those who customarily asserted that it was impossible for the very same human body—submerged in the deep and immeasurable sea, reduced to ashes, devoured by beasts and sometimes by human beings—ever to rise again: “For nothingness itself belongs to God, to whom the whole also belongs” (ibid.). For since God created all things from nothing, and is lord both of an existing thing and of a non-existing thing and of nothingness, he can certainly both make and remake anything whatsoever, in whatever manner pleases him. He therefore rightly concludes from this: “Wherever you have been dissolved, whatever material has destroyed, swallowed up, abolished, or reduced you to nothing, he will restore you” [Col. 0899D] (ibid.). But we have discussed this subject more fully in our preceding dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 7, art. 2; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 28, art. 4).

### ARTICLE III

#### At what time dead human beings will be raised to life and present themselves at God’s final judgment, and how Tertullian uses the pagans’ opinions concerning Minos and Rhadamanthus to confirm that everyone’s evil and good deserts will then be examined

After Tertullian had proved, by the weighty arguments we have set forth, the future return to life of every [Col. 0900A] dead human being, he immediately shows when all human beings are to rise again. “The Reason,” he says—that is, doubtless, the Word and Speech of God—“fashioned the world out of mutually opposing elements” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, col. 43), that is, elements contrary to one another; or, as he said in another book, “out of diverse substances, so that they might subsist in unity” (the same, *On the Pallium*, ch. 2). This same Reason willed time to flow from the beginning of this world and continually pass away until it reaches eternity, which stands opposite it. But between infinite and immeasurable eternity and finite time, it interposed a middle boundary, at which “the age” (*Apologeticum*, passage cited)—that is, the entire duration of this world—would end and infinite eternity begin. “At that final boundary of time and first boundary of eternity,” he says, [Col. 0900B] “the whole human race will be restored, in order to settle the account of whatever good or evil it has merited in this age” of its mortal life, “and thereafter to pay it throughout the immeasurable perpetuity of eternity” (ibid.). Thus the text stands in Rigaltius’s and the old editions and in our manuscript codices. But in some printed editions *deprehendendum* (“to be detected”) is read instead of *dependendum* (“to be paid”), while in others the reading is *exinde dependendum* (“thereafter to be paid”). In still others, moreover, this verb is omitted entirely. Nor does it appear especially necessary if the verb *expungendum* is taken here by Tertullian, as elsewhere and by other writers, to mean “to be paid in full.” But if he uses it to mean the rendering by human beings of the sum of their works, with their accounts to be reckoned and settled, then the verb *dependendum* must be retained, so that his meaning here is: absolutely all human beings will be restored so that [Col. 0900C] all the accounts of their good and evil deserts may be reckoned, examined, and settled, and they may then, throughout all eternity, pay and discharge what they merited during this life. Suetonius, moreover, appears to have used the verb *expungo* in this second sense when he wrote of the emperor Claudius: “When he reviewed the records of the panels” (Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, § 15)—that is, as some have observed, when he arranged and reckoned which members of the panels were to be retained among the number of judges. To this point they also refer these words of Papinian: “A man censured and restored in connection with desertion is deprived of his pay for the period during which he was a deserter” (*Digest*, book XLIX, title 16, law 15, *On Military Affairs*).

Restoration notes: E003/S001195 ends with the apparently truncated recovered form “δῶ”; it has been preserved verbatim and explicitly marked as truncated.; E003/S001195 ends with the truncated recovered form “δῶ”; it is preserved verbatim and marked as truncated in the replacement.  

Whatever may be the true and genuine reading of our author, he teaches with the utmost certainty that, in Christ’s final judgment, the merits of each individual will be weighed and carefully examined. [Col. 0900D] For Christ himself will come with all the glory and majesty of divinity, as Tertullian says, and also with a convulsion of the whole world, by which it will indeed be overthrown; with the terror of the world; and with the lamentation of all unbelievers and criminals, though not of Christians (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23, col. 25)—that is, of the faithful who have lived piously and virtuously. We have already discussed this final judgment elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 47, p. 42).

“But we are ridiculed by the pagans,” Tertullian continues, “for proclaiming that God”—whom he had previously called Christ—“will judge” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 47, col. 42). He judged, however, that this feeble mockery could be refuted in no more fitting way [Col. 0901A] than by citing their own doctrines: “For in like manner,” he says, “both poets and philosophers place a tribunal in the underworld” (*ibid.*). What that tribunal was he had explained in these words addressed to the pagans: “You laugh; let those demons also laugh with you. . . . Let them say this before the tribunal, if perhaps, in agreement with Plato and the poets, they have been allotted Minos and Rhadamanthus” (*ibid.*, ch. 23, col. 25). Since the tribunal of Minos and Rhadamanthus was very well known to everyone, he cites the poets collectively as witnesses, very many of whom, both Greek and Latin, had celebrated it in verse. Among the philosophers, however, he expressly names Plato, because he was readily acknowledged as the foremost of them all. Justin Martyr had argued in a similar way against the same pagans: Πλάτων δὲ Ῥαδάμαντον καὶ [Col. 0901B] Μίνω κολάσειν τοὺς ἀδίκους παρ` αὐτοὺς ἐλθόντας· ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ πρᾶγμά φαμεν γενήσεσθαι, ἀλλ` ὑπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ τοῖς αὐτοῖς σώμασι μετὰ ψυχῶν γενομένων, καὶ αἰωνίαν κόλασιν κολασθησομένων. “Plato likewise taught that Rhadamanthus and Minos would punish the unjust who came before them. We say that this very thing will indeed take place, but at the hands of Christ, when the same bodies are reunited with their souls and subjected to eternal torments” (Justin, *First Apology to Antoninus*, p. 57). Athenagoras later disputed against the pagans in the same way. The passages from Plato cited by him will be found in the *Gorgias* and the *Axiochus* (Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 12; Plato, *Gorgias*, vol. I, p. 124, and *Axiochus*, vol. III, p. 371).

If anyone wishes at least one of the poets cited by Tertullian [Col. 0901C] to be produced, we shall cite the two leaders of Greek and Latin poetry, Homer and Virgil. In the *Odyssey*, Homer sang the following about Erebus:

Ἔνθ` ἤτοι Μίνωα ἴδον, Διὸς ἀγλαὸν υἱὸν,


Χρύσεον σκῆπτρον ἔχοντα, θεμιστεύοντα νεκύεσσιν


Ἥμενον· οἱ δέ μιν ἀμφὶ δίκας εἴροντο ἄνακτα,


Ἥμενοι ἑσταότες τε κατ` εὐρυπυλὲς Ἄϊδος δῶ [the recovered final word is truncated]. (Homer, *Odyssey* Λ (Book 11), near the end)

> There I saw Minos, the splendid son of Jupiter,  
> Bearing a golden sceptre, dispensing laws to the dead,  
> Seated; while others around the king pleaded their causes,  
> Sitting or standing throughout the spacious house of Pluto.

Virgil, however:

> Nor were these dwelling places assigned without lot or judge:  
> Minos the inquisitor shakes the urn; he summons  
> The council of the silent and investigates their lives and crimes.  
> [Col. 0901D]

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI, v. 431 ff.)

Then afterward:

> Cnossian Rhadamanthus holds these most dreadful realms;  
> He chastises and hears their deceits, and compels each to confess  
> What crimes committed among those above, rejoicing in vain concealment,  
> He postponed expiating until a late death.

(*Ibid.*, v. 561 ff.)

But if the pagans, as Tertullian rightly argues, believed these poets and philosophers, far greater credence ought to be given to our sacred writers, who, filled with the divine Spirit, consistently proclaim that Christ himself, when this age has run its course—that is, when it has been completed and brought to an end—will judge his worshippers for the recompense of eternal life and the profane for fire equally perpetual and unceasing, [Col. 0902A] after all who have died from the beginning have been raised, restored, and mustered for the settling of the account of either kind of merit, whether good or evil. He now says “for the settling of the account,” doubtless in the same sense in which we saw him say previously “for settling the account.” For we have seen him write elsewhere: “We, whose account is settled under God, the observer of all things”—that is, who are examined and judged by God, who knows all things—“make provision against eternal punishment from him” (*ibid.*, ch. 45, col. 39); that is, we take precautions against it, or foresee that the wicked will be afflicted with eternal punishment. Therefore, by innocence and integrity of conduct, we prepare to meet him, lest we suffer the eternal punishments and everlasting torments of the impious. Accordingly, in Christ’s final judgment, everyone will render an account of his good or evil merits; and when these have then been examined and the final [Col. 0902B] sentence pronounced, the wicked will be punished with eternal fire, while the righteous will be granted the reward of everlasting felicity. We must now investigate what our author teaches about this eternal fire and reward.

## ARTICLE IV. On the eternal fire by which wicked and impious people will be tormented; how Tertullian asserts its eternity and confirms it by examples of fiery rivers, perpetually burning mountains, and a person struck by lightning; and why that fire is called eternal

What Christians had learned from the sacred Scriptures they openly proclaimed: that impious and wicked people would be tormented with eternal fire after their death. “But if,” says Tertullian, “we threaten Gehenna, which is [Col. 0902C] an underground treasury of eternal fire reserved for punishment, we are likewise laughed to scorn” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 47, col. 42). So indeed our manuscripts, the edition of Rigault, and other later editions read; the older editions, however, have the masculine *subterraneus*, as though it must refer to the noun “treasury.” Yet it can also refer to the noun “Gehenna,” always with the same meaning. Our author therefore teaches that Gehenna is an inexhaustible treasury of eternal fire, by which criminal people will be tormented after this life. The pagans, however, rejected this doctrine just as they would an old woman’s tale, with laughter and unrestrained mockery.

Yet this Christian doctrine was true; otherwise the pagans themselves, by whom the Pyriphlegethon, as our author says (*ibid.*), was proclaimed to be a river [Col. 0902D] among the dead, were equally deserving of ridicule. Thus he, and Arnobius after him, turns back against them the weapon they had cast (Arnobius, *Against the Pagans*, book III, p. 52). These are Arnobius’ words: “Do you dare to ridicule us when we speak of Gehennas and certain inextinguishable fires into which we have learned that souls are cast by their enemies and foes? Does Plato, in the volume that he composed on the immortality of the soul, not name Acheron, Styx, Cocytus, and Pyriphlegethon, in which he asserts that souls are whirled about, submerged, and burned?” Plato is rightly cited by him, for in the *Phaedo* he described those four rivers of the underworld, sufficiently well known to everyone, which the pagans had invented (Plato, *Phaedo*, vol. I, p. 112 ff.). Pyriphlegethon, however, is called Phlegethon by Virgil and other Latin poets. [Col. 0903A] Since the matter is sufficiently well known, it will be enough to cite some of Virgil’s verses:

> Gods who hold dominion over souls, and silent shades,  
> And Chaos, and Phlegethon, places lying far and wide in the silence of night.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI, v. 264 ff.)

And again afterward:

> Aeneas suddenly looks back, and beneath the cliff on his left  
> Sees broad walls, surrounded by a triple rampart;  
> Around them the Tartarean Phlegethon, a rushing river,  
> Rolls in torrents of flame and tumbles resounding stones.

(*Ibid.*, v. 543 ff.)

You may consult Prudentius and others, if you wish (Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, near the end). But however the pagans may have invented or believed these things, they certainly could not ridicule Christians, who, instructed by their divine writers, asserted that profane people and those [Col. 0903B] stained with crimes would, after this life, be punished by the torment of unceasing fire (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 45, p. 497). In the first dissertation of this volume we heard Minucius Felix argue against the pagans in the same way (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 7, art. 3).

But the pagans asked how fire could possibly be eternal and never be extinguished. Tertullian therefore replies that, by divine power, this fire possesses “a supply of incorruptibility” (Tertullian, *ibid.*). Nor could the pagan philosophers deny this, since they recognized two kinds of fire that were plainly different. The first, they said, was ordinary and public terrestrial fire, which people use every day. The other [Col. 0903C] was mysterious and far less common, “drawing lightning bolts from heaven,” as our author says, or rising from the earth, by which the mountains—namely Etna and Vesuvius—are burned yet endure and are not consumed. For this fire, as he says, “does not consume what it burns, but restores while it expends”; hence the perpetually burning mountains remain. We have discussed this fire elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 7, art. 3, and *on Lactantius*, ch. 29, art. 7).

Only two observations therefore remain for us to make. First, these examples of lightning and burning mountains are not employed by Tertullian and our other writers as though their fire were identical with the eternal fire of the underworld, but “as testimony,” he says, “to eternal fire, and as an example of the perpetual judgment that sustains punishment” (Tertullian, passage cited, p. 497). [Col. 0903D] Thus he adduces these things merely as testimony to and an example of another fire, which, kindled by divine power and preserved forever, will burn the impious throughout eternity without ever consuming them.

Second, in the same passage he proposes another, though more obscure, example in these words: “He who is touched from heaven”—namely, by lightning—“is preserved, so that he can no longer be reduced to ashes by any fire” (*ibid.*). There is considerable variation and disagreement among interpreters in explaining these admittedly difficult words. Some think that they allude to an ancient pagan law that prohibited anyone struck by lightning from afterward being subjected to any punishment. For Jupiter was said to have punished such a person sufficiently, however impious he might have been. Others think that our [Col. 0904A] author had in view what Pliny records in these words: “It is unlawful for a person killed in this manner to be cremated; religious custom has handed down that he should be buried in the earth” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, ch. 54, p. 209). But what, I ask, does this have to do with Tertullian’s purpose, when he is attempting by this example to establish that the bodies of certain persons struck by lightning remain so preserved that they can no longer be reduced to ashes by any fire?

Consider, therefore, whether he may not rather be alluding to what Plutarch committed to writing: that almost everyone knew that bodies touched from heaven were neither cremated nor buried by many people, but were left surrounded by an enclosure, so that, being free from decay, they might remain perpetually visible (Plutarch, *Table Talk*, book IV, question 2, p. 665). Later he says: ὁρᾷς, ὂτι καὶ τὸ κεραύνων πῦρ ἱερὸν ἡγούμεθα [Col. 0904B] καὶ θεῖον, ὅτι τὰ σώματα τῶν διοβλήτων ἄσηπτα πρὸς πολὺν ἀντέχοντα χρόνον ὁρῶμεν. “You know that the fire of lightning is called sacred and divine, because we see that the bodies of those touched from heaven resist decay for a long time” (*ibid.*, book VI, question 10, p. 685). Tertullian could have adduced this example, although it is not entirely perfect, in order to show and confirm that human bodies can be burned by eternal fire without ever being consumed by it.

If anyone wishes to know why Tertullian calls this fire “mysterious,” we shall answer that it was because he thought it hidden and concealed in the bowels of the earth. For in another book he explains both Plato’s view and his own concerning the place where the underworld is situated: “In the *Phaedo*, Plato describes the underworld as a kind of bosom of the earth, into which all the impurities of worldly filth flow together and, settling there, exhale, and, as though with the mire of their impurities, make the air breathed there denser and confined. We believe that the underworld is neither a bare cavity nor some open-air sewer of the world, but a vast space in a pit deep within the earth, and a depth hidden in its very bowels” (Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 54). [Col. 0904C] If anyone should further inquire whence he derived this opinion, he will quickly hear Tertullian’s own answer in the same place: “For we read that Christ spent the three days of his death in the heart of the earth”—that is, “in an inward and interior recess, covered over within the earth itself and enclosed inside it, and itself lying above still lower abysses . . . so that there he might make the patriarchs and prophets partakers of himself. You have reason, therefore, to believe that the region of the underworld lies beneath the earth” (*ibid.*, ch. 53). There [Col. 0904D] he again commends Plato, in the *Phaedo* already cited by us, so as further to refute the pagans by the authority of the foremost of their own philosophers.

## ARTICLE V. On the eternal blessedness of the saints; where they reside; whether they enjoy it immediately after death, or await it until the final day of judgment in certain abodes; and how Tertullian proves that the doctrines of the Christian religion recounted thus far cannot be rejected by the pagans, and that Christians ought not to be harassed and slaughtered for defending them

In the same way that eternal punishment by fire awaits evil and wicked [Col. 0905A] people, says Tertullian, so an everlasting reward for good works awaits the good and righteous. For after our dead body has been raised to life again, “We shall be the same persons that we are now, and not others afterward,” he says (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 48, p. 520), because, as was stated above, this very same body of ours will rise again. Then, he continues, “the worshippers of God will remain with God forever, clothed over with the proper substance of eternity” (*ibid.*); that is, they will be clothed over with the gift of immortality, which will subsist and endure eternally. He spoke of “the proper substance of eternity” (*ibid.*, ch. 49, p. 528), by which righteous people will enjoy not only immortality but perpetual felicity—or, as he himself puts it, “eternal refreshment and divine delight” (*ibid.*, ch. 47, p. 515).

[Col. 0905B] Yet however certainly and truly he asserts this, we just as readily discover his doubt and wavering judgment concerning the place where their souls, released from their bodies, will be received until the final judgment. First, in his *Apologeticum*, he says: “We call Paradise a place of divine delight, destined to receive the spirits of the saints, separated from the knowledge of the common world by a kind of wall of that fiery Zone” (*ibid.*). Some think that he was there referring to these words of Genesis: “And he cast out Adam, and placed before the paradise of pleasure cherubim and a flaming, revolving sword to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis III, last verse). Others deny this. For they cannot persuade themselves that “a wall of the fiery Zone” signifies the same thing as “a flaming sword.” They therefore [Col. 0905C] think that another fire is denoted, serving as the boundary of that more delightful place. Yet this opinion ought to have been supported by at least some reason. Until they produce one, therefore, we do not see what prevents Tertullian from having called that place “a place of divine delight” which in the cited words of Genesis is called “the paradise of pleasure.” For what inconsistency is there if he thought that the fiery sword signified the fiery Zone? But we have anticipated some discussion of this passage of Tertullian in the preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 22, art. 6).

A more certain judgment could be rendered on this matter if Tertullian’s short work *On Paradise*, which he testifies that he composed, were extant. For he himself referred us to it as follows: “You also have our short work *On Paradise*, in which we establish that every soul is sequestered in the underworld [Col. 0905D] until the day of the Lord” (Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 55), that is, until the general and final judgment. But from these very few words certainly arises no small difficulty. For even though he might be said to have distinguished Paradise from the underworld, he nevertheless teaches most explicitly that every soul—of the righteous, of course, as well as of the impious—is sequestered and reserved in that underworld until the final judgment. These things, however, will doubtless seem obscure and difficult to understand to many. We must therefore investigate what he determined about them in his other surviving works.

In his book *On the Soul* he draws the following from the Gospel: “In the underworld the soul of a certain person”—namely, the notorious rich man—“suffers pain and is punished in flame, is tormented in [Col. 0906A] its tongue, and implores assistance from the finger of a happier soul” (*ibid.*, ch. 7), namely, that of the poor man Lazarus. Nor does he permit the objection that this is a parable. For the added name of Lazarus indicates a real event; and even if it were a parable, it is itself testimony to the truth. Then he added: “What, then, is that which, after separation from the body, is transferred to the lower regions; which is detained; which is reserved until the day of judgment; to which Christ also descended in dying? I suppose it was to the souls of the patriarchs. But why, if the soul is nothing beneath the earth? . . . in the prison, the temporary lodging of the underworld, in the fire, or in Abraham’s bosom” (*ibid.*). He therefore teaches that the underworld is a subterranean place, and that Abraham’s bosom is there; that the soul of the wicked rich man was tormented there; that Christ descended there after his death; and that the patriarchs were awaiting him there. [Col. 0906B] Later he says: “Thus the rich man in the underworld has a tongue, and the poor man a finger, and Abraham a bosom. By these outlines the souls of the martyrs beneath the altar are also understood” (*ibid.*, ch. 9). Do the souls of the martyrs therefore also dwell there, beneath the altar and in the same underworld? This will be explained somewhat more distinctly below.

Meanwhile, let us continue to hear him speak. He says that Christ descended into the lower parts of the earth “so that there he might make the patriarchs and prophets partakers of himself. You have reason, therefore, to believe that the region of the underworld lies beneath the earth, and to repel with an elbow those who quite arrogantly consider the souls of the faithful unworthy of the underworld—servants above their Lord and disciples above their Master—disdaining, perhaps, to receive in Abraham’s bosom the consolation of awaiting the resurrection” (*ibid.*, ch. 55). Do you see that the same underworld is still [Col. 0906C] called Abraham’s bosom and the habitation of the patriarchs and prophets, where souls receive consolation from the hope of resurrection?

Finally, toward the end of the same book he introduces someone objecting to him: “Then all souls are in the underworld.” He immediately answers: “Whether you wish it or not, both punishments and refreshments are already there. You have the poor man and the rich man” (*ibid.*, ch. 58). Since he says “every soul,” therefore, he makes no exception.

Nor does he profess this belief only in that book; in another he confirms it quite clearly with these words: “For the example of Lazarus proved that even now souls are tormented and comforted in the underworld, though naked and still exiles from the flesh” (the same author, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 17). Moreover, concerning the martyrs themselves, he did not hesitate to write the following [Col. 0906D] in the *Scorpiace*: “Who are those sons of Zebedee, such blessed victors, if not martyrs properly so called? For the victories belong to those whose struggles they are, and the struggles to those whose blood they are. Meanwhile, however, the souls of the martyrs rest peacefully beneath the altar, sustain their patience by confidence in vengeance, and, clothed in robes, assume the white brightness of glory, until others also complete the company of their glory” (the same author, *Scorpiace*, ch. 12). Was it not, therefore, Tertullian’s opinion that the souls of all dead people whatsoever, stripped of their bodies, are reserved until the final day of judgment in the underworld, in Paradise, in Abraham’s bosom, and beneath the altar—different names by which he doubtless appears to have designated the same place?

[Col. 0907A] But wait, I ask, a little longer, and restrain yourself somewhat. For presently you will hear him distinguish three places corresponding to the three classes of souls, or of dead people—namely, the impious, the righteous, and the martyrs—and distinguish the underworld from Abraham’s bosom. For he refutes Marcion’s error concerning the receptacles of those souls by the authority of sacred Scripture, “which,” he says, “distinguishes the poor man’s Abraham’s bosom from the underworld. For the underworld is one thing, as I think, and Abraham’s bosom another. Indeed, it says that a great gulf lies between those regions and prevents passage in either direction. Nor would the rich man have raised his eyes—and that from afar—unless he were looking upward, and from far below across that immense distance of height and depth. . . . Accordingly, I call that region Abraham’s bosom, even though [Col. 0907B] it is not heavenly; nevertheless it is higher than the underworld and will meanwhile provide refreshment to the souls of the righteous, until the consummation of all things settles the account of the resurrection of all with the fullness of reward. . . . Why may it not be understood that Abraham’s bosom is a certain temporary receptacle for the souls of the faithful, in which an image of the future is already sketched and a certain bright prospect of both judgments is discerned?” (the same author, *Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 34).

Do you not now see how clearly he separates the underworld, where the souls of wicked people dwell and are tormented, from Abraham’s bosom, or the habitation of the righteous, where they, tasting beforehand the reward of eternal felicity, enjoy a temporary and preliminary delight and blessedness—or, as he calls it, refreshment? He asserts that this region, although it is not heavenly, is nevertheless far removed [Col. 0907C] from the underworld and situated much higher than it.

As for the souls of the martyrs, he appears to assign them a third place, namely Paradise itself. For these are his exact words concerning the souls of those martyrs: “How is it that the region of Paradise revealed to John in the Spirit, which lies beneath the altar, shows no souls with it other than those of martyrs? How is it that Perpetua, the most courageous martyr, in a revelation of Paradise on the day before her passion saw there only her fellow martyrs, unless it is because the sword that guards the gate of Paradise yields to none except those who have died in Christ, not in Adam? A new death for God, and an extraordinary one for Christ, is received in another and private lodging. Recognize, then, the difference between the pagan and the faithful person in death. If you fall for God, as the Paraclete admonishes, [Col. 0907D] not in soft fevers and beds, but in martyrdoms; if you take up your cross and follow the Lord, as he himself commanded, your blood is the whole key to Paradise” (the same author, *On the Soul*, ch. 55). Thus he indicates a third place, separate from both those already mentioned by us, which he calls the private lodging of the martyrs, of whom we shall speak below (*below*, ch. 15, art. 4).

Irenaeus had doubtless preceded him, and similarly explains his opinion concerning martyrs: “The Church,” he says, “in every place, because of the love it bears toward God, sends forward to the Father a multitude of martyrs in every age” (Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book IV, ch. 33, § 9, new ed., p. 272). But why, I ask you, to [Col. 0908A] the Father, unless so that they may obtain the reward of eternal felicity immediately after death?

Cyprian, Tertullian’s disciple, later subscribed to the opinion of both in these very words: “Blessed indeed are those among you who, journeying along the paths of glory, have already departed from the world and, having completed the course of courage and faith, have come to the embrace and kiss of the Lord, while the Lord himself rejoices” (Cyprian, letter 37, p. 73). Elsewhere he expressly affirms that martyrdom is a second baptism, which, as we depart from the world, immediately joins us to God. He then concludes his book with these words: “If persecution finds such a soldier of God, courage ready for battle cannot be overcome. Or if a summons comes first, the faith that was prepared for martyrdom will not be without reward. With no loss of time, the reward is rendered, with God as judge: in persecution the service, in peace the conscience, is crowned” (the same author, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 168; *ibid.*, p. 184). [Col. 0908B] He therefore did not think that the eternal glory and felicity of martyrs was postponed. Had he not also derived these things from his teacher and our author Tertullian, who similarly said that martyrdom is a second baptism by which martyrs are led directly to the divine throne? For he asserted that by unconquered patience and courage they are “brought forward for the experience of felicity, for the opportunity of a second immersion, for the ascent to the divine throne itself” (Tertullian, *On Patience*, p. 13). Elsewhere, as we shall see, he calls this second immersion a “second washing, by which all sins are forgiven and the fullness of God’s grace is purchased” (*below*, ch. 16, art. 3).

[Col. 0908C] But Tertullian’s opinion, like that of Irenaeus, appears not to have been the same concerning the souls of other righteous people. For Irenaeus handed down the following concerning them: After the death of the body, “They will depart,” he says, “to an invisible place appointed for them by God, and there they will remain until the resurrection, awaiting the resurrection, after which they will come into the sight of God” (Irenaeus, book V, ch. 31, p. 331). And do not be surprised, I ask you, if our Tertullian, like Irenaeus, remains uncertain and wavering in assigning dwelling places to souls released from the body, and does not always speak in the same way. For, as we have noted elsewhere, the opinions of other ancient Fathers of the Church were no more definite or consistent (*Admonition on Ambrose’s On the Good of Death*, vol. I, p. 385).

[Col. 0908D] Whatever our author’s opinion about these matters may have been, he rightly contends that it ought not to have been rejected by the pagans, whose belief, he says, “the Elysian Fields had preoccupied” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 47, p. 515), where they believed that the souls of the dead enjoyed delights. But since their opinion was not unlike the one he proposes, he says that theirs doubtless derived its origin from the Christian teaching. For that doctrine, and the other teachings of Christians, as was proved above (*above*, ch. 4, art. 4), are far older than the doctrines of the pagans. The pagans, therefore, had drawn their doctrines from the Christians, not the Christians from the pagans, and consequently ought to place no less faith in Christian teachings than in their own.

Moreover, even if that doctrine and all the other doctrines of the Christian religion that we have [Col. 0909A] reviewed thus far were entirely unlike and contrary to the opinions of pagan philosophers, among those philosophers, says Tertullian, they were called “products of the highest learning and distinguished intellects” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 49, p. 528)—or ought it rather to read “distinguishing marks of intellect,” that is, conspicuous signs and indications of intelligence? In any case, the sense will be exactly the same.
