Who, therefore, will not marvel that these most true teachings of Christians were called false by pagans who were not lacking in reason or intelligence, and, as our author further says, “foolish presumptions” (*On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 4)—that is, altogether vain and absurd divinations and conjectures concerning a doubtful matter?

Yet suppose, though it is utterly false, that they were wholly false: they were certainly harmful to no one; indeed, [Col. 0909B] they were useful and necessary to everyone. For all people are compelled to become better through fear of eternal punishment and hope of eternal life (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 49, p. 529). For whoever, as Athenagoras rightly teaches, is persuaded that the soul will perish together with the body, συναπόλλυσθαι τῷ σώματι καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν, dares every crime, μηδενὸς ἂν ἀπέχεσθαι τολμήματος (Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 39). But one who believes that, after being raised to life, he will render an account of all his sins at God’s final judgment is afraid to offend even in the smallest matters.

The pagans were therefore most unjust when they condemned Christians, the defenders of these doctrines, as though they were the most criminal of people and guilty of the gravest offenses. Our author therefore presses and assails them as follows: “But if in matters of this kind” [some editions add *error*, perhaps better as *in error*] “anything must indeed be judged worthy of laughter” or ridicule, Christians were not on that account to be most cruelly slaughtered [Col. 0909C] “with swords, fires, crosses, and beasts” (Tertullian, passage cited). Yet so far is there from being anything false underlying their doctrine that their altogether astonishing endurance amid so many and such terrible torments most invincibly demonstrated the truth of that doctrine and of the whole Christian religion, as has more than once been observed. But this is also plainly confirmed by the holy conduct, laws, and institutions of those same Christians, which must now be discussed.

## CHAPTER XII. It is shown who and what sort of people the Christians were, how they were distinguished from the pagans, and how much purer their conduct and how much better and holier their laws were than those of the pagans

[Col. 0909D]

### ARTICLE I. Who and what sort of people the Christians were in Tertullian’s time, how greatly they had multiplied, and how they were then distinguished from the pagans among whom they lived

Having explained the teachings of the Christian religion asserted by Tertullian, we must now investigate with him who and what sort of people their defenders, the Christians, were, and how they lived among the pagans. [Col. 0910A] It is therefore helpful to hear him speak about himself and the other followers of Christ: “We are a body,” he says (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 39, p. 431), just as the Apostle had previously written: “We, though many, are one body in Christ” (Epistle to the Romans XII, 5); that is, one society, congregation, and community composed of many people assembled together. If you ask how or on what basis they were assembled, he will answer you: “Through consciousness of religion” (Tertullian, passage cited); that is, because they were inwardly and most certainly convinced that the religion they all professed was true. In addition, they were joined “by unity of discipline” (*ibid.*), that is, by the one and the same, but most holy, body of teaching handed down by Christ and by the discipline of conduct. Finally, they were united “by a covenant of hope” (*ibid.*), that is, bound by covenant and associated [Col. 0910B] through the most certain hope of eternal life, which the true, sole, and omnipotent God promised them after this mortal life.

How greatly that Christian body had multiplied by the time of our Tertullian he himself certainly informs us (*ibid.*, ch. 1, p. 262). For at that time, as he relates (*ibid.*, ch. 37, p. 462), they had filled every place in the world: cities, islands, forts, towns, meeting places, military camps, tribes, municipal divisions, the forum, the senate, and the palace; and they had left the pagans nothing as their exclusive possession except their temples alone (*ibid.*, ch. 42, p. 491). They therefore mingled with them everywhere—in the forum, the provision market, the baths, shops, workshops, inns, fairs, and commercial dealings, which must be discussed below. Thus, dwelling together in mutual intermixture, they served as soldiers, worked the land, [Col. 0910C] engaged in commerce, and shared crafts and services through mutual dealings.

For this reason, in another book he addresses Scapula as follows: “What will you do with so many thousands”—the older editions read “ten thousand”—“people, so many men and women, of every sex, every age, and every rank, offering themselves to you? How many fires, how many swords will be needed? What will Carthage itself suffer when it is decimated by you, when each person recognizes among them his housemates; when he perhaps sees there men even of your own rank, matrons, all the foremost persons, and the relatives or friends of your friends?” (the same author, *To Scapula*, ch. IV). What more need be said? So great at that time was the number of Christians, not only in Carthage but everywhere throughout the world, that, “If so great a mass of people”—these are again [Col. 0910D] the words of Tertullian himself—“had broken away from you to some remote corner of the world, the loss of so many citizens, whatever their condition, would certainly have covered your dominion with shame; indeed, it would have punished it by the very abandonment. Without doubt you would have been terrified at your solitude, at the silence of affairs, and at a certain stupor as of a dead world; you would have asked whom you were to command. More enemies than citizens would have remained to you” (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 37, p. 463).

But we seem to hear someone whispering in our ears that there is some exaggeration by Tertullian here. For who, he will say, could ever be persuaded that the multitude of Christians was then so great? Yet with what effrontery, I ask, could this same Tertullian have asserted it so boldly in public books addressed not merely to Scapula alone, [Col. 0911A] the governor of Carthage, but to the Roman—or, if you prefer, African—governors, and even to the nations, that is, to all pagans, the bitterest enemies of Christians, unless it were entirely true? Did he not have to fear that, if convicted of falsehood, his case would collapse amid laughter and hisses? Yet if some obstinate person refuses to believe him, he surely will not refuse to credit Pliny the Younger, who had earlier written the following about those same Christians to Emperor Trajan: “Many people of every age, every rank, and both sexes are being summoned into danger, and will continue to be summoned. For the contagion of this superstition has spread not only through the cities, but also through villages and the countryside” (Pliny, letter 101, p. 376).

For this very reason, Tertullian further says, the pagans grieved that their number was so great and [Col. 0911B] publicly complained of it: “They cry out,” he says, “that the city is besieged; that Christians are in the countryside, the forts, and the islands; that people of every sex, age, condition, and now even rank are passing over to this name, and they grieve as though at a loss” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 1, p. 263). Will you still say, then, that this complaint of the pagans was invented or exaggerated by him? But in another book, addressing the pagans themselves, he repeats it in almost exactly the same words (the same author, *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 1).

Accordingly, since Christians had multiplied to such an extent, there is certainly no room for doubt that, mingled with the pagans, they shared with them a common manner of life. For, as Tertullian says, they lived among them with the same food and manner of dress—that is, food and clothing—the same equipment, [Col. 0911C] and the same necessities of life (Idem, *Apologet.*, chap. 42, p. 490). But did he not express it better, someone will say, in the book *To the Nations*, by the word *apparatus*, that is, style and adornment (Idem, book I *ad Nation.*, chap. 10)? Yet if this is the meaning of the noun *apparatus*, and if *instructus* is taken by him, as it is by Cicero (Cicero, book III, *de Orat.*, p. 181, line 37), to mean adornment, how could he have asserted that the Christians’ equipment was the same? Had he not, in the same *Apologeticum*, when censuring the luxury of the pagans, said: “In dress, food, equipment, wealth, you have renounced your ancestors” (Idem, *Apologet.*, chap. 6, p. 305)? It is established, however, by his own testimony, that the Christians’ frugality in all these matters was far greater. We shall therefore have little difficulty in being persuaded that, in the former passage, he was speaking of the things necessary for sustaining life, and which Christians, [Col. 0911D] like common people or the more modest pagans, used.

Yet certainly, although the Christians and pagans had the same food and clothing, and the same public manner of living and acting, Christians were nevertheless distinguished from them and could readily be recognized by their exceptional modesty, patience, and correction of their former vices. Nor was this unknown to the pagans, whom our author therefore addresses in these words: “It can be sufficiently evident to you that we act according to that discipline of divine patience, since so great a multitude of people—almost the greater part of every city—conduct ourselves in silence and modesty, perhaps better known individually than collectively, and [Col. 0912A] recognizable by nothing more than by the correction of our vices” (Tertull., book *ad Scapul.*, chap. 2).

Such, then, were the Christians at that time, whose number was greater than that of the pagans. Nor indeed is it surprising that, though mingled with the pagans, they pursued so pious and holy a manner of life, since they held nothing more venerable or dearer than obedience to those most holy laws which they knew had been given to them by God and Christ the Lord, and which were far superior to all human laws. It now falls to us to prove this point together with our author.

## ARTICLE II. How greatly the laws of the Christians surpassed all laws enacted by the pagans in their perfection and authority; with what diligence those laws were observed by those same Christians, who for that reason refused, even at the peril of their lives, to eat sausages swollen with blood that were offered to them by the pagans

[Col. 0912B]

Since the Christian religion was founded and established by the true God and his Son, all its laws must undoubtedly be most perfect. Therefore, in Tertullian’s time, Christians obeyed them with all the greater care because they knew with all the greater certainty that they had been enacted by the all-seeing and omnipotent God, who therefore can neither be deceived by anyone at all nor treated with contempt with impunity. Accordingly, our author openly declares to everyone: “Having been taught innocence by God, we know it in its perfection, as revealed by a perfect teacher, and we faithfully preserve it, as commanded by a judge who cannot be treated with contempt” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 45, p. 498).

[Col. 0912C] But the laws of the pagans, enacted by human beings alone, are manifestly imperfect and can be scorned, undermined, and violated by everyone with impunity. “For how great,” Tertullian continues—or, as our manuscripts read, “so great,” that is, so small and slight—“is the authority of a human being to exact” (Ibid.) faithful observance of the laws enacted by himself, when he can as easily be deceived as he can be held in contempt by everyone? For such is the weakness of human intelligence that no human being can foresee all those things which will always be good or evil for everyone else. And such is the malice of the wicked that very many of them have little difficulty in escaping the penalties imposed upon transgressors by any human law whatsoever.

Tertullian shows by several further examples that the laws of the Christians are far more perfect than those of the pagans. First, he says: “Which is more comprehensive” (Ibid.), [Col. 0912D] “to say, ‘You shall not kill,’ or to teach, ‘You shall not even become angry’?” (Matt. 5:21ff.). So it stands in all our manuscripts and early editions; but Rigaltius disliked the former words and ordered the text to be written: “Which was more comprehensively said?” He undoubtedly wished to make Tertullian speak more purely and correctly. But if human law, says Tertullian, prohibits adultery, divine law restrains even the solitary lust of the eyes (Ibid.). He said “solitary,” that is, alone, secret, and hidden. Thus Cicero asserts that virtue cannot be solitary, and that nature loves nothing solitary (Cicero, book *de Amicit.*, p. 43, lines 7 and 42). Divine law, therefore, prohibits not only adultery, as human law does, but also the secret [Col. 0913A] and hidden lust of the eyes.

Moreover, human law indeed prohibits wrongdoing but permits vengeance for an injury; divine law, however, forbids even abusive speech itself and the repaying of injury in kind (Tertullian, passage cited). How greatly that law excels human law has already been noted by us elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Minut.*, chap. 13, art. IV, and *Dissertat. in Lactant.*, chap. 26, art. 1ff.). Tertullian nevertheless does not deny that certain human laws are good, but contends that these were taken from the divine books of Moses and the other prophets, whose antiquity, as we saw above, he had previously demonstrated (Above, chap. 4, art. 4).

Not only is the perfection of divine law greater than [Col. 0913B] that of human law, but so too is its authority. For absolutely nothing is hidden from God; and, as we taught a little above, he chastises those guilty of violating his law with the eternal punishments they deserve (Ibid.). But it happens that the person who acts against human laws, as our author says, “usually remains concealed in his offenses, or scorns those laws because of his will or the necessity of offending” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 45, p. 497). Rigaltius, however, altered these words of our manuscripts and printed editions as follows: “For one offending through unwillingness or necessity.” But without indicating any variant reading from any manuscript, he merely observes that “through unwillingness” is the same as “by accident.” What, then, if Tertullian sets the words “through his will” in opposition to “or through necessity” (Ibid.)? Could not his meaning here be: A guilty person usually remains concealed when he sins either [Col. 0913C] through his own will or under some necessity?

Furthermore, he says, human laws are brought to ruin when people reflect upon the brevity of a punishment that cannot be inflicted by human beings beyond death. For this reason, he continues, Epicurus depreciates every torture and pain, declaring a moderate pain contemptible, but a great one not long-lasting (Idem, book I *ad Nation.*, chap. 10; book II *ad Uxor.*, chap. 3; book I *adv. Marcion.*, chap. 6; book *de Spectac.*, chap. 22; book *de Anim.*, chap. 24; book *de Fuga*, chap. 10). He frequently uses the verb *depretiat*, by which he meant nothing other than that one diminishes the value or magnitude of something. Cicero explains Epicurus’ maxim more clearly: “Let them bring out,” he says, “those Epicurean remedies for pain as though from a medicine chest: if it is severe, it is brief; if prolonged, it is slight.” Elsewhere [Col. 0913D] he says: “He consoles us for the magnitude of pain by its brevity, and for its duration by its slightness.” If you desire more, you may consult Laertius, Plutarch, and others (Cicero, book II *de Finib.*, p. 55, line 10, and book IV *Tuscul.*, p. 190, line 49; Laert., book 10 *de Vita Epicuri*, § 140; Plutarch, book *de Poet. audien.*, near the end, p. 36).

Since Christians therefore thoroughly understood the supreme perfection and authority of their laws, they obeyed them with such diligence that they preferred even to place their lives in danger rather than do anything that appeared contrary to any law. From the almost infinite number of examples by which this can be most clearly proved, we shall now take one that our Tertullian records (Vol. I, *Apparat.*, p. 680; *Dissertat.* [Col. 0914A] *in Minut.*, chap. 9, art. 1). The pagans had discovered that among those same Christians there was in force a law by which, as we have observed elsewhere, they were forbidden the blood of animals, meat from strangled animals, and carrion. Therefore, with the utmost pagan malice, “among their trials of Christians,” says Tertullian—that is, in order to test their faith and religion—“they offered sausages swollen with blood” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 9, p. 314). A *botulus*, says Festus, is a kind of sausage which, because of its connection, is so called from *boli* (Festus, book II *de Verbor. Signific.*). Martial also has these verses about it:

> The sausage that came to me in the midst of winter  
> Had arrived seven days before Saturn’s feast.

(Martial, book XIV, epigram 72.)

Accordingly, by offering these sausages, made from pieces of meat mixed with [Col. 0914B] animal blood, the pagans ascertained that those by whom they were rejected were truly followers of the Christian religion. By refusing them, the Christians made it plain to everyone that they preferred to undergo the peril of death rather than ever oppose their laws. Nor did they obey with the same diligence only this and the other laws of God and Christ, but also most of his counsels, although they were not bound by them. These matters, however, will become clearer to everyone from what must now be explained concerning their morals as reported by Tertullian.

## ARTICLE III. That the morals of the Christians were as chaste as those of the pagans were depraved; how great was the Christians’ love and charity toward all; why they called one another by the name of brothers and had all things except wives in common; and how, by contrast, the pagans violated the most sacred rights of brotherhood with impunity

[Col. 0914C]

To demonstrate the character and the piety and holiness of the Christians’ manner of life, our Tertullian compares their morals with those of the pagans and clearly shows that the former were as holy and chaste as the latter were depraved and corrupt. First, although Christians lived together with the pagans in the manner we have described, they were nevertheless joined by so strong a bond of charity and mutual love that even the pagans, their most bitter enemies, could not help admiring it. For why indeed would they not have admired what they recognized as excellent but were unable to imitate? [Col. 0914D] Therefore, by introducing them as speaking in the following manner, Tertullian reveals their mutual hatred just as he reveals the love of the Christians. He writes: “‘See,’ they say, ‘how they love one another’”—for the pagans themselves hate one another—“and how those same Christians are prepared to die for one another.” For the pagans themselves are more prepared to kill one another (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 39, p. 467). How greatly the pagans hated one another, and how prepared they were to kill one another, will become evident to everyone from what will be said below.

So great indeed was the Christians’ charity that, as we have already observed elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Minut.*, chap. 13, art. 4), they called one another brothers not only by the right of nature itself, by which they were also brothers of the pagans, [Col. 0915A] but by four further titles. First, because they acknowledged one God as Father, unknown to the pagans or repudiated by them. Second, because, imbued with the religion of Christ, they “drank one spirit of holiness” (Tertullian, passage cited). Third, because from the one womb of ignorance—in which, before recognizing the true God, they had lain so long in the foul darkness of idolatry—they started at the one light of truth. For they were astounded that they had not previously recognized their utterly absurd errors or the supreme God, whom, as we showed above (Above, chap. 5, art. 1), all were compelled, even against their will, to acknowledge by the light and prompting of their conscience alone.

Fourth and finally, they addressed one another by the name of brothers because, our author further says, “we are brothers in our family property” (Tertullian, Ibid.). [Col. 0915B] For they were accustomed to share this among themselves far more extensively than natural brothers did. In a word, says Tertullian (Ibid.), all things among them were entirely undivided and common.

At that time, therefore, they diligently observed—at least for the most part—what we read was handed down concerning the first Christians in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; nor did anyone say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32). Irenaeus also wrote in this manner concerning the Christians of his own age: “They, the Jews, held the tithes of their possessions as consecrated; but those who have received liberty—that is, Christians—assign all that belongs to them [Col. 0915C] to the Lord’s uses, giving their possessions cheerfully and freely—not lesser things, since they have the hope of greater things—just as that poor widow cast her entire livelihood into the treasury of God” (Irenaeus, book IV *contr. Haeres.*, chap. 18, p. 250, new ed.).

Cyprian, however, Tertullian’s disciple, complains in the following words about that charity of the Christians which had by then diminished—a matter to be discussed again below: “At that time they sold houses and estates, and, laying up treasures for themselves in heaven, offered the proceeds to the apostles to be distributed for the uses of the needy. But now we do not give even a tithe from our patrimony; and though the Lord commands us to sell, we rather buy and increase our possessions. Thus has the vigor of faith withered within us; thus has the strength of believers grown feeble” (Cyprian, book *de Unit. Eccles.*, p. 119ff.; Below, chap. 15, art. 2). In another book, [Col. 0915D] after again proposing the example of the first Christians, he does not ask his own people to sell their patrimonies and estates, but says: “The person who, though a possessor on earth, shares his revenues and produce with the brotherhood, being equitable and just in his gratuitous gifts, is an imitator of God the Father” (Idem, book *de Oper. et Eleemosyn.*, p. 208). Does not our Tertullian, then, likewise appear to be speaking of those same revenues from goods and estates, which, if not all, at least very many Christians shared with others with the utmost liberality?

The pagans were as far removed as possible from this liberality, since on account of their paternal property they broke every bond of brotherhood. For that reason, they greatly marveled that, as Tertullian again says, “no tragedy cries out concerning our brotherhood” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 39, p. 431). [Col. 0916A] For what is more frequent in tragedies than lamentations over brotherhood shattered by pagans? These are found especially, beyond the others, in the tragedy Seneca composed concerning Atreus and Thyestes. For who does not know that it represents the story, often celebrated by Horace, Ovid, and others, in which they imagined that Thyestes was deprived of his kingdom by his brother Atreus—whose wife he had violated—and was then served his own sons to eat at a banquet? Horace sang of this horrible tragedy:

> Let not Medea slaughter her children before the people,  
> Nor wicked Atreus openly cook human entrails.

(Horace, *de Art. poet.*, v. 185.)

Yet the pagans, more savage than the beasts themselves, watched this tragedy with the greatest [Col. 0916B] pleasure.

Christians, however, so abhorred spectacles of this kind, crimes, and greed for the possessions of others that, as we have said, they held absolutely nothing as separate except their wives. “For in this one matter,” says Tertullian, “we dissolve partnership, in which alone other people practice partnership” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 39, p. 431), namely by handing their own wives over to others or corrupting the wives of others. But we shall examine these matters in the following articles.

## ARTICLE IV. It is shown how great was the chastity of Christian spouses, and how certain it is that many persevered in the state of virginity until death; how far the pagans were removed from these morals, among whom Cato and Socrates gave their wives to their friends in marriage

[Col. 0916C]

The more stringent the law by which Christians knew that adultery had been forbidden them, the greater was the care with which they preserved the fidelity pledged in marriage. Therefore, “the most diligent and faithful chastity,” says Tertullian, “guarded all married Christians against illicit intercourse and against every transgression after marriage” (Ibid., chap. 9, p. 314). Nor need this now be proved by us at greater length, since no one can doubt it in view of what has been said elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Lactant.*, chap. 27, arts. 5 and 6) and what will be said below.

Yet not a few, desiring to do something beyond that divine commandment, were accustomed to remain in celibacy and virginity throughout the entire course of their lives. [Col. 0916D] But listen, I pray, to our author narrating these matters in his own words: “Some, far more secure, repel the whole force of this error against the rights of marriage by virginal continence—children grown old” (Tertullian, passage cited); that is, from the earliest age of childhood to extreme old age and the final breath of life, they preserved their virginity inviolate. For followers of true philosophy, says Eusebius (Eusebius, *Orat. de Laud. Constantin.*, chap. 17, p. 661), men who worshiped God, sacred women, and choirs of virgins had learned from Christ to devote themselves to perpetual chastity of mind and body even amid the dreadful storms of persecution. We have discussed this perpetual chastity and virginity of very many Christians in our preceding dissertations [Col. 0917A] (*Dissertat. in Minut.*, chap. 10, art. 1; *Dissertat. in Lactant.*, chap. 27, art. 6).

The pagans, however, were exceedingly far removed from this bodily chastity. “For they not only usurp the marriages of their friends,” says Tertullian, “but most patiently make their own wives available to their friends” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 39, p. 467). There he notes two outrages against chastity committed by the pagans. The first is that of adulterers, who defiled the marriage beds of friends and others. But that crime was extremely frequent, and Juvenal and other pagan poets inveigh against it as often as it deserves. Hence Jerome says: “Whatever causes tragedies to swell and overthrows households, cities, and kingdoms is the rivalry between wives and mistresses” (Jerome, book II *adv. Jovinian.*, p. 191).

[Col. 0917B] Their other crime, no less grave than the first, was that of those who prostituted the chastity of their own wives to their friends. Tertullian proves this by two examples, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, who were nevertheless regarded as the wisest men among those nations: “For these men,” he says, “shared with their friends the wives whom they had married for the sake of children, so that children might be begotten elsewhere”—that is, in a second but altogether unlawful and infamous marriage (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 39, p. 431).

Plutarch, in the *Life of Cato the Younger*, relates that he had received from Thrasea, and Thrasea from Munatius, Cato’s companion, the report that Hortensius, who was bound to Cato by friendship beyond all others, asked him to give him in marriage his wife Marcia, the daughter of Philippus, by whom Cato had already had several sons and who was then still pregnant (Plutarch, *Vit. Caton. minor.*, p. 770ff.). [Col. 0917C] Easily overcome by his friend’s entreaties, Cato granted her to him in the presence and with the approval of her father Philippus. But after Hortensius’ subsequent death, Cato took back his Marcia, whom Hortensius had left heir to his property. Therefore Caesar, as Plutarch expresses it, φιλοπλουτίαν προσφέρει καὶ μισθαρνίαν ἐπι τῷ γάμῳ “reproached him with avarice and with having received payment in the marriage” (Ibid., p. 784).

Appian reported the matter more briefly in these words: “When Cato had married Marcia, the daughter of Philippus, while she was a virgin, and she had become deeply beloved and already the mother of children they had in common, he yielded her to his friend Hortensius, who desired children and a fertile wife, things he had hitherto lacked, until, after she had become a mother by him as well, Cato received her back into his home as though she had been lent for use” (Appian, [Col. 0917D] book II *de Bell. civil.*, after the middle, p. 266).

We likewise read that Strabo wrote that among the Tapyri a law had been accepted whereby men, after having two or three children, gave their wives to others in marriage: καθάπερ καὶ Κάτων Ὁρτησίῳ δεηθέντι ἐξέδωκε τῆν Μαρκίαν ἐφ` ἡμῶν κατὰ παλαιὸν Ῥωμαίων ἔθος “Just as Cato also in our own age handed over his Marcia to Hortensius at his request, following the ancient custom of the Romans” (Strabo, book XI *Geogr.*, p. 265). Nor were there lacking poets who celebrated this deed of Cato in their verses, especially Lucan:

> Meanwhile, as Phoebus dispelled the icy darkness,  
> The doors sounded beneath a knocking; these doors holy Marcia,  
> Mourning, burst through after leaving Hortensius’ tomb,  
> Once a maiden joined to the bed of a better husband. [Col. 0918A]  
> Soon, when the price and payment of marriage had been discharged,  
> Already fruitful with three children, she was given to fill  
> Another household and to mingle two homes  
> Through the blood of their mother.

(Lucan, book II, v. 326ff.)

He then describes how Cato, after Hortensius’ death, had her again in a second marriage:

> No customary jests played, nor in Sabine fashion  
> Did the grave husband receive the festive gathering.  
> No pledges adorned the house; no relatives assembled.  
> They are joined in silence, content with Brutus as witness.  
> He did not remove the bristling hair from his solemn face,  
> Nor admit joy to his stern countenance.

(Ibid., v. 367ff.)

Finally, to pass over Augustine and others, Jerome argues as follows against Jovinian: “Cato married Marcia as his wife, but not as a virgin; rather, Marcia passed back and forth between Hortensius and Cato, and Marcia was able to live without Cato.” And again in the following book: “The nation of the Scots,” he says, “does not have wives of its own; and, as though it had read Plato’s *Republic* and followed Cato’s example, no woman among them is the exclusive wife of anyone, but, like cattle, they act wantonly as each pleases” (Augustine, book *de Fide et Operib.*, chap. 6, and book *de Bon. conjug.*, chap. 18; Jerome, book I *adv. Jovin.*, p. 188; Ibid., book II, p. 201).

Although there were several men distinguished by the name Cato, whose genealogy is presented by Aulus Gellius (Gellius, book XIII, *Noct. Att.*, chap. 19), it is nevertheless established from the authors cited that the Cato with whom we are dealing was Cato of Utica, who is therefore called the Younger because, as the same Gellius says, [Col. 0918C] he was the grandson, through his son, of Cato the Censor. Why then, someone will ask, is he called “Censor” by our Tertullian? For in that very passage he expressly wrote—our manuscripts reading *Lenones*, “panders”—“The pander is Socrates the philosopher, and the censor Cato” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 39, p. 467). Is there, then, in that passage a ἀμάρτημα lapse of his memory and an error?

It may be answered that Tertullian calls Cato a censor not by office, but in disposition and severity of morals. For Lucan, already cited by us, sang:

> These were the morals, this the unchanging school  
> Of stern Cato,

(Lucan, book II, v. 379), namely the Stoic school. The noun “censor” is also taken in this sense by Horace:

> But he who desires to have produced a lawful poem  
> Will assume, along with his tablets, the mind of an honorable censor.

[Col. 0918D] (Horace, book II, epistle 2, v. 379.)

And elsewhere, in the *Art of Poetry*:

> A censor and corrector of the younger men.

(*de Art. poet.*, v. 174.)

Moreover, that Cato, as Appian further testifies, was regarded as the gravest of all men and the most steadfast in his purpose, since he measured what was just and honorable not by the morals of the crowd but by upright and noble principles; or, as Lucan again sang:

> A worshiper of justice, a guardian of strict honor.

(Lucan, book II, v. 388.)

Yet that man, although a preacher of stricter discipline, nevertheless placed his own wife with his friend Hortensius in shameful procuration, [Col. 0919A] contrary to the rights and fidelity of marriage.

Our author accuses Socrates of the same crime. It is indeed certain that he had two wives simultaneously, namely Xanthippe and Myrrho, the daughter of a certain Aristides, or his granddaughter through a daughter. Yet the more this is demonstrated by the testimony of Athenaeus, Laertius, Plutarch, Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, and Theodoret, the more difficult it is to prove whether Socrates, no differently from Cato, truly shared his wife with his friends (Athenaeus, book XIII, beginning of the *Deipnosoph.*, p. 555; Laertius, book XII, *Vit. Socrat.*, § 26; Plutarch, end of *Vit. Aristid.*, p. 335; Jerome, book II *adv. Jovinian.*, p. 190; Cyril, book VI *advers. Julian.*, p. 186, and book VII, p. 226; Theodoret, [Col. 0919B] vol. IV, sermon 12, *de Virtut. act.*, p. 673). Consider, however, whether the knot of this difficulty may be untied sufficiently by what Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret have related (Cyril and Theodoret, passages cited): that Xanthippe, married by Socrates, was κοινωτέραν πως at one time rather common, and that by secretly having intercourse with her he fathered his son Lamprocles.

Moreover, concerning both Socrates and Cato, Tertullian added: “I do not indeed know whether they gave their unwilling wives to their friends in marriage.” For how could it have happened that these two wives were unwillingly given by their husbands to marry other men? Does not our author therefore seem to allude to Lucan’s words in which Marcia is represented, as we said, as addressing her husband Cato as follows?

[Col. 0919C]

> While blood and maternal strength remained in me,  
> I carried out your commands, Cato, and, fruitful, received two husbands.  
> With womb exhausted and worn out by childbirth, I return,  
> No longer to be handed over to any man. Grant me the bond  
> Of my former marriage inviolate; grant only the empty name  
> Of wedlock. Let it be permitted that upon my tomb be written,  
> “Marcia, wife of Cato,” lest in a distant age it be asked in doubt  
> Whether I exchanged my first marriage torches because I was cast out  
> Or because I was handed over.

(Lucan, book II, v. 234.)

For there she is said to have requested that, after Hortensius’ death, she be received by Cato into her former marriage. But she offers this reason for her request: that posterity might know she had not been rejected and repudiated by Cato himself, by whom she had been handed over to Hortensius. Yet she could have been handed over by him without being unwilling or resistant. Since, however, she had previously said, “I carried out your commands,” it can be inferred that against her own will she first left her husband and [Col. 0919D] accepted a second. Tertullian therefore does not improperly admit that the matter was uncertain to him. But however the matter may stand, Christians were far removed from this corruption of morals, since they always preserved intact, with the utmost zeal, the sacred rights of marriage established by God. But, if you please, we shall examine in the following article how he confirms this.

## ARTICLE V. How Tertullian demonstrates that the chastity of the Christians was very great and the incontinence of the pagans equally great: that Christians did not change into the female sex, whereas young men were corrupted by Socrates; that Christians preserved the fidelity pledged to their wives, whereas Aristippus desperately loved the prostitute Phryne and Speusippus perished in adultery; that Christians, with sound eyes but a blind mind, saw women, whereas Democritus blinded himself so that he would not desire them; and that the pagans, by condemning a Christian woman to a procurer rather than a lion, betrayed both their own intemperance and the chastity of Christians

[Col. 0919D]

[Col. 0920A] Let us follow our author and see how he continues the comparison he has begun between the chastity of Christians and that of pagans: “A Christian,” he says, “does not change even into the sex of a woman” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 46, p. 500). So indeed it stands in Rigaltius’ edition, and he observes that the words “into the sex of a woman” mean the same as “he changes into the female sex.” But neither he nor the others who followed him have indicated to us whence he took this reading. In our manuscripts, however, and in all the other printed editions, we read: “A Christian does not change even into the female sex.” [Col. 0920B] That is, to use the Apostle’s words, he is not “one who lies with males” (Paul, Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chap. 6, v. 10, and First Epistle to Timothy, chap. 1, v. 10).

For there our author sets Christians in opposition to Socrates, concerning whom he writes: “I read part of the Attic sentence against Socrates: he is pronounced a corrupter of young men.” But here again Tertullian’s text has been altered by Rigaltius; in our manuscripts and all other printed editions it stands as follows: “I read . . . that Socrates was pronounced a corrupter of young men” (Tertullian, passage cited). Why, then, should anything be altered there without the testimony of any manuscript whatsoever and contrary to the unanimous authority of all the books? Does not this form of expression convey clearly enough, and in good Latin, Tertullian’s true meaning: that the sentence of death passed by the Athenians upon Socrates was based in part on the fact that he was accused not only of denying the gods [Col. 0920C] but also of corrupting young men?

Certainly he is charged more than once with this unspeakable crime by Lucian, who in one place introduces him confessing his guilt (Lucian, *Vitar. Auctio.*, p. 193), and elsewhere accuses him of perjury, since he had sworn that he associated innocently with young men (Idem, book II, *Verar. histor.*, p. 397), although Hyacinthus and Narcissus openly testified that they had been shamefully loved by him. Athenaeus also charges him with an utterly disgraceful love for Alcibiades, as Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret later did (Athenaeus, book V, *Deipnosoph.*, chap. 19, p. 219; Cyril, book VI *in Julian.*, p. 137; Theodoret, sermon 12, *de Virt. Act.*, p. 672). Indeed, these two later writers affirm that he burned with detestable lusts.

But by whose testimony, you will ask, can it be proved that [Col. 0920D] he was condemned by the Athenians not only for scorning and rejecting the gods of the pagans, but also for this love of young men, which can never be sufficiently execrated? First, you have Plato, who recorded that Socrates was accused by Meletus of unlawfully and impiously corrupting the youth and, after denying the gods, introducing new ones. Laertius repeats the same charges. Xenophon, nevertheless, attempted to acquit him of both crimes, and especially the first (Xenophon, book I, *Memorabil.*, p. 711ff.), both because he cultivated continence with the utmost zeal and because he continually taught this virtue to his disciples. He does not deny, however, that Alcibiades and Critias, after being placed under his instruction, became corrupt [Col. 0921A] and utterly dissolute young men; but not, he says, until after they had departed from him.

Yet Xenophon may have written this with greater partiality toward Socrates than zeal for the truth. For if Socrates believed the gods of the pagans to be real and worshiped them, why was he afraid to imitate their deeds and crimes? Furthermore, although he may have preached continence in the public schools, were not pagan philosophers, as we have said elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Lactant.*, chap. 35, art. 4), accustomed to do privately and at home the very things they publicly condemned in their schools? Finally, Xenophon himself could not deny that Socrates was accused of a most shameful love for young men, and very many, as we have shown, were persuaded that he was in fact guilty of it. Who, then, will not readily persuade himself that mention of this crime also formed part of the sentence [Col. 0921B] passed against him?

Furthermore, our author says: “A Christian is born a man for his wife alone” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 46, p. 500). For he greatly abhorred every forbidden kind of immodesty and, as we have seen, always preserved fidelity toward his wife. By contrast, Tertullian says of the pagans: “I know Phryne the prostitute, in heat for the passion of Diogenes reclining above her.” In editions earlier than Rigaltius: “in heat for the passion of him reclining above her”; but in our manuscripts: “in heat for the passion of the one reclining above her.” There he censures the wholly ungovernable lust of Diogenes, who desperately loved Phryne. We read in Athenaeus, however, that Aristippus was rebuked by his slave because he gave an immense sum of money to Phryne, who rolled about with Diogenes [Col. 0921C] the Cynic for nothing (Athenaeus, book XIII, *Deipnosoph.*, p. 588). We have said something elsewhere, and more than once, about that Phryne, the most famous of prostitutes (Vol. I, *Apparat.*, p. 744; *Dissertat. in Arnob.*, chap. 20, art. 3).

Tertullian then says: “I also hear that a certain Speusippus of Plato’s school perished in adultery” (Tertullian, *Apologet.*, chap. 46, p. 500). We have observed elsewhere that this Speusippus was, as Laertius says, the son of Plato’s sister Potone, and Plato’s successor in the Academy (Vol. I, *Apparat.*, pp. 1131 and 1134; Laertius, book IV, *Vit. Speus.*, § 1). Yet according to the same Laertius he is said to have been ὀργίλος, καὶ ἡδονῶν ἥττων ἦν “irascible and devoted to pleasures” (Idem, Ibid.). Athenaeus likewise testified that he was not far removed from the pleasure-seeking Epicureans [Col. 0921D] and Cyrenaics, and that Dionysius the tyrant reproached him for his love of the prostitute Lasthenia (book XII, chap. 12, p. 546). Φιλήδονος ἦν καὶ Σπεύσιππος, ὁ Πλάτωνος συγγενὴς, καὶ διαδοχος τῆς σχολῆς Διονύσιος γοῦν, ὁ της Σικελίας τύραννος, ἐν τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐπιστολῇ κατὰ τῆς φιληδονίας αὐτοῦ εἰπὼν, καὶ φιλαργυρίαν αὐτῷ ὀνειδίζει, καὶ τὸν Λασθενείας τῆς Ἀρκαδικῆς ἔρωτα, ἥτις Πλάτωνος ἠκηκόει “Speusippus, Plato’s successor and kinsman, was also devoted to pleasure. Accordingly, Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, in his letter to him censures his pursuit of pleasure, reproaches him with avarice, and condemns his love for Lasthenia of Arcadia, who attended Plato’s lectures.” Yet this Lasthenia is earlier called by him σαρδικὴ, “of Sardis,” and by Laertius μαντινικὴ, “of Mantinea” (Laertius, book [Col. 0922A] *Vit. Platon.*, § 45, and book IV, *Vit. Speus.*, § 2).

Laertius reports two opinions concerning Speusippus’ death (Ibid., §§ 3 and 4). According to the first, worn out by paralysis, grief, and old age, he voluntarily brought death upon himself; according to the second, his life was taken from him by a violent eruption of lice. Therefore, when Tertullian says that he perished in adultery, he does not appear to mean, as some think, that he breathed his last when caught in adultery, but that he wallowed in adultery down to the time of his death.

Our author continues: “The Christian, though his eyes are intact, does not see women” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500). For thus we read this passage in the manuscript codices and in the editions of Rigault and later editors; but in the older printed editions: “The Christian, though his eyes are intact, sees a woman” [Col. 0922B]. Yet Tertullian’s meaning is readily understood to be this: although the Christian possesses sound and healthy bodily eyes, he nevertheless does not see women in such a way as to desire them in his mind. For he immediately added: “In his mind he is blind to lust” (*Ibid.*). He knew, of course, the law laid down by Christ: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt., ch. 5, v. 28). Therefore, in order that a true disciple of Christ may fulfill this precept, he sees women with his bodily eyes intact, but in the mind with which he might desire them he is blind and unmoved.

How great, by contrast, was the incontinence even of pagan philosophers Tertullian shows by the example of Democritus: “Democritus,” he says, “by blinding himself, because he could not look upon a woman without desire [Col. 0922C] and would suffer pain if he did not possess her, acknowledges his incontinence by the very act of correcting it” (Tertullian, *ibid.*). But there may be no slight reason to doubt both this voluntary blindness of Democritus and its cause. For Plutarch plainly and utterly denies that he extinguished his own eyes of his own accord so that they might not distract his mind or prevent it from dwelling upon things discernible by the mind alone (Plutarch, book *On Curiosity*, p. 521, vol. II). Cicero, moreover, appears to pronounce nothing certain about his blindness: “Democritus,” he says, “who—whether truly or falsely we might inquire—is said to have deprived himself of his eyes; certainly so that his mind might be distracted as little as possible from its reflections” (Cicero, book V, *On Ends*, p. 113, line 43). For if, as some think, the word “we might inquire” should there be deleted, and the reading should be “whether falsely,” he plainly signifies that he himself was [Col. 0922D] doubtful and undecided about that blindness of Democritus. But even if the word “we might inquire” proceeded from Cicero himself, nevertheless by the other expression, “is said,” he declares clearly enough that the matter could not be affirmed by him with certainty. Aulus Gellius, however, testifies that in the records of Greek history mention was made of Democritus, who voluntarily deprived himself of the light of his eyes so that the reflections of his mind in contemplating the principles of nature might be more vigorous and exact (Gellius, book X, *Attic Nights*, ch. 17, p. 541). He then immediately cites verses of Laberius describing another reason for this blindness which Democritus had brought upon himself, expressed by the poet in this line:

> That he might not see wicked citizens prosper.

[Col. 0923A] Jerome, without naming anyone individually, relates that certain philosophers tore out their own eyes so that they might not be distracted from the contemplation of philosophy, and might direct their entire thought toward purity of mind (Jerome, book II *Against Jovinian*, p. 203, and Epistle 55 to Abigaus, p. 589). Who, then, would not readily allow himself to be persuaded that Democritus was one of these philosophers, and perhaps the foremost?

Although, therefore, some appear to have doubted his voluntary blindness, we have nevertheless cited several witnesses to it. But certainly far fewer are found who report that this same Democritus deprived himself of his eyes so that he would not desire women. Yet I would have you consider whether the sophist Himerius, as preserved by Photius, did not indicate this in the following words: ἑκὼν δὲ ἑνόσει σῶμα Δημόκριτος [Col. 0923B] ἵνα ὑγιαίνῃ τὰ κρείττονα. “Democritus afflicted his body with a voluntary infirmity so that the better part might be sound” (Photius, *Bibliotheca*, cod. 243, p. 1087). For did he not, by this general manner of speaking, designate Democritus’s voluntary blindness, by which he wished to heal his mind, the better part of himself? However that may be, Christians certainly had no need of voluntary blindness of this kind, since, being blind in mind to desire, they not only cultivated with the greatest zeal the chastity prescribed by divine law, but very many also, as we said shortly before (*Supra*, this chapter, art. 4), were accustomed to persevere in the state of virginity throughout the whole course of their lives.

Finally, by a still recent example Tertullian proves that Christians were all the more solicitous to preserve chastity, the more shamelessly this virtue was violated by the pagans [Col. 0923C]. Hear, I ask you, the words with which he addresses and assails these enemies of chastity: “Most recently,” he says, “by condemning a Christian woman to a procurer rather than to a lion, you confessed that among us the violation of chastity is regarded as more dreadful than every punishment and every death” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530). Although that Christian woman is unknown to us, no one can nevertheless call into doubt that shortly before she had been condemned, by a most unjust and shameful judgment, to a brothel, where her chastity was to be overcome. Yet the vilest men made a mockery not merely of the chastity of one woman, but of that of many others. We think there is no one who has not read numerous examples of them in the *Acts of the Martyrs*.

## CHAPTER XIII

### How absurdly the pagans boasted that the other virtues of their philosophers were equal to those of the Christians, and how Tertullian demonstrates that the virtues of the latter were genuine and those of the former false

[Col. 0923D]

## ARTICLE I

### With what undeserved praises, statues, and salaries the pagans rewarded philosophers who voluntarily destroyed the worship of the gods, railed against rulers, and did not cast out demons—which they regarded as second only to the gods—although, contrary to right and justice, they killed Christians by every kind of torture merely because of their name

Our Tertullian compares not only the chastity of Christians and pagans, but all the virtues of both [Col. 0924A], and demonstrates that the virtues of the latter were corrupt and those of the former perfect. He conducts this comparison all the more carefully because the pagans used to cry out all the more insistently that the philosophers professed innocence, justice, patience, and sobriety equal to those of the Christians (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500). For, to omit many others, Celsus argued in the same way against the Christians (Origen, book I *Against Celsus*, p. 6). The Christian discipline, he said, introduced nothing new and nothing great in morals that had not been shared with the other ancient philosophers and handed down by them.

Tertullian therefore first refutes and demolishes the pagans’ objection by a general argument. If, he says, the morals of philosophers and Christians are the same, and their virtues the same [Col. 0924B], both must surely possess the same freedom to profess their religion. Why, then, are Christians, but not philosophers, compelled—as will be explained below (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*)—to sacrifice or swear by the gods, or “bring forth useless lamps at midday” (Rigault, contrary to the authority of the manuscript and printed codices, reads “prostitute”)? “Why,” our author continues, “do the philosophers openly destroy your gods and assail your superstitions even in their commentaries, while you applaud them?” Such, indeed, were Diagoras, Theodorus, and Nicagoras, whom we have discussed elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 23, art. 2, and *Dissertation above*, ch. 14, art. 1). But because he added “while you applaud them” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 14, p. 348), he perhaps appears more particularly to indicate Socrates, whom he had named both immediately and previously [Col. 0924C], as well as Epicurus, his follower and admirer Lucretius, and Cicero, by whom the pagan gods are utterly abolished in his books concerning their nature.

When our author added (*Ibid.*, ch. 46, p. 500), “They accuse your superstitions,” he undoubtedly had Seneca in view, whom he had cited earlier. “For you,” he says there (*Ibid.*, ch. 12, p. 337), “are the same men who approve a certain Seneca when he declaims against your superstition at greater length and with greater bitterness.” We have cited these words of Seneca elsewhere, and they must still be presented below in their proper place.

Furthermore, Tertullian continues (*Ibid.*, ch. 46, p. 500), “Most philosophers bark against rulers.” In one Vatican codex scholars have noted [Col. 0924D] the reading “tear to pieces”; but this is less satisfactory. For he appears deliberately to have said “bark,” and by this word to have censured the Cynics. According to Suetonius, the emperor Vespasian, when Demetrius the Cynic met him on the road after his condemnation and did not deign either to rise or to greet him, but even barked out something or other at him, contented himself with calling him a dog (Suetonius, book VIII, *Life of Vespasian*, §13). Xiphilinus relates that this same Vespasian, at Marcianus’s urging, sent the philosophers into exile, because not only that Cynic Demetrius but other philosophers as well publicly uttered many disgraceful things (Xiphilinus, *Epitome*, book X, p. 220 ff.). In private, however, he ordered the following to be written to Demetrius when the latter would not desist: “Although you do many things deserving of death, and I could therefore order you to be killed: [Col. 0925A] ἐγὼ δὲ κύνα ὑλακτσοῦντα οὐ φονεύω. Yet I do not kill a barking dog.”

Nor were the pagans content merely to tolerate such philosophers patiently and to praise them; rather, our author says, “they were very readily rewarded with statues and salaries” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 45, p. 497; *ibid.*, ch. 14, p. 348). Does he not there, without naming Socrates, indicate his golden image, which, as he noted above, the Athenians themselves—by whom Socrates had been put to death—later placed in a temple? If you ask to be shown statues of other philosophers, hear Juvenal castigating ignorant men who thought that they had sufficiently demonstrated a false learning by placing statues and images of philosophers in each of their libraries. Here are his verses:

> [Col. 0925B] First, the ignorant—although everything is full of plaster—  
> You will find a Chrysippus. For the most accomplished of these  
> Is he who buys a likeness of Aristotle or Pittacus  
> And orders an original Cleanthes to guard his shelf.[^c0099-1]

(Juvenal, *Satire* 2, v. 4 ff.)

[^c0099-1]: [Col. 0925D] That is, his library.

Ménage, moreover, reproduces several images of philosophers in his edition of Laertius.

A salary was also given to philosophers—that is, an allowance and wage, so called from salt, as Pliny observes (Pliny, book XXXI, *Natural History*, ch. 7, p. 809). Capitolinus indeed testifies that the emperor Antoninus ordered salaries and honors to be bestowed upon rhetoricians and philosophers throughout all the provinces (Capitolinus, *Life of Antoninus*, near the end). Lucian, however, recorded for posterity (Lucian, *The Eunuch, or Pamphilus*, [Col. 0925C] p. 535) that the emperor established μισθοφορά τις οὐ φαύλη a considerable salary, ἀλλὰ μυρίαι ten thousand coins, to be distributed among Stoics, Platonists, Epicureans, Peripatetics, and other philosophers, so that they might teach the young. Does not Augustine also say of these same philosophers, as well as of others, the following words, which contribute no little to our purpose (Augustine, book I, *City of God*, ch. 3, p. 4)? “The pagans are angry with us when we say such things about their gods, yet they are not angry with their own authors, whom they paid to learn by heart; and, in addition, they regarded the teachers themselves as most worthy both of a public salary and of honors.”

With what effrontery, then, or with what madness did they torture and slaughter Christians by every kind of punishment, while they tolerated their own philosophers with impunity, praised them [Col. 0925D], and rewarded them with great benefactions and prizes, although they advertised the morals and virtues of both groups as similar? Yet Christians were not merely equal to the pagans in virtue but far holier and more excellent, as we have demonstrated with irrefutable force.

Whence, then, so great a discrepancy in their judgments? Because the philosophers, as Tertullian rightly observes, “are not called Christians” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500). For it was with the greatest injustice that the pagans cried out that Christians deserved public hatred merely on account of their name, as has been said, and that they should be punished [Col. 0926A] with every kind of torture. Indeed, on account of their most devout manner of life they were all the more worthy of the same rewards and salaries with which philosophers were showered, since they very frequently cast demons out of the bodies of possessed persons solely by the name of Christ, as we have shown, but never by the name of any philosopher.

And indeed, how could demons be put to flight in the name of philosophers who thought them, as Tertullian continues, to be “second after the gods”—that is, as some understand it, nearest to the gods, or, as others prefer, who regarded them as gods? For Cicero wrote: “to judge concerning an absent person as concerning one who is present.” Suetonius, moreover, wrote of the emperor Claudius: “He gave to those absent as to those present” (Suetonius, book V, *Life of Claudius*, §15), that is, just as if they were present. But both explanations come down to almost the same meaning [Col. 0926B], although the latter appears preferable.

Whatever the case, Tertullian openly declares (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*) that the philosophers believed demons to be superior to them and to rule over them. They were therefore so far from being able to put them to flight that they actually obeyed them. For Socrates, our author continues, although he had been declared the wisest of all by the oracle of Apollo, as we have observed elsewhere (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 3, arts. 2 and 3; *ibid.*, and vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1115), was accustomed to say: “If the daemonic power”—supply “my”—“permits me to do this or that” (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*, and *Supra*, ch. 22). In this and other dissertations we have shown how he asserted that a demon had attended him from childhood, and that he never did anything without consulting it and receiving its approval (the same author, *Apologeticus*, [Col. 0926C] ch. 46, p. 500). Nevertheless, this same Socrates, when dying, ordered that a cock be sacrificed or slaughtered to Aesculapius. But because he had some taste of the truth, he denied that the gods existed. These matters have been explained by us in another dissertation (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 39, art. 1, and *Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, *loc. cit.*).

Furthermore, whether Socrates acknowledged the gods or denied them, he could certainly not put demons to flight or expel them from the bodies of the possessed, since, like the other pagans, he supposed them to be gods or beings nearest to the gods. But if Christians had been granted the power to confer so great a benefit upon the pagans, and if their morals and virtues were better than those of the pagans, then those same pagans could not, except in violation of all right and justice, kill the former [Col. 0926D] by every penalty and torture, while bestowing great praises and benefits upon the latter. But let us continue to follow Tertullian as he compares the virtues of the two groups individually.

## ARTICLE II

### How absurdly pagan philosophers—lustful for glory, pretending to teach the truth which they had found in Holy Scripture but corrupted in order to win popular favor, and driven into exile by the Spartans, Thebans, and Argives—were equated with Christians in knowledge and discipline

It is remarkable with what vain and foolish ostentation [Col. 0927A] the pagans objected that the knowledge, discipline, and wisdom of their philosophers were equal to those of the Christians (Tertullian, book II *To the Nations*, p. 585). For, as Solomon, cited by Tertullian, most rightly teaches concerning wisdom: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of God” (Ecclesiasticus, ch. 1, v. 16). These words are taken from the book of Ecclesiasticus, which our author and others, as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 11, art. 3), expressly attribute to Solomon. Yet even if the work were denied to him, the statement would be no less true. But how could pagan philosophers possess the beginning of wisdom through fearing a God whom they never acknowledged? Christians, however, truly knew and feared him, and were therefore endowed with this beginning of wisdom.

[Col. 0927B] Moreover, Christians, not only from this book but also from other books of Holy Scripture, as from divine and most pure fountains, necessarily pursue the truth from which this wisdom is drawn, says Tertullian, in order to provide for their eternal salvation (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500). Pagan philosophers, however, he says, “affect the truth, and by affecting it they corrupt it, since they seek glory” (*Ibid.*, ch. 47, p. 515). For nothing was more important to them than increasing by any means the renown of their name and reputation and of empty glory. For this reason he later calls them “men lustful only for glory and eloquence” (the same author, *On the Soul*, ch. 7), that is, exceedingly eager for them. In another book, however, he says: “The philosopher is an animal of glory.” Jerome undoubtedly borrowed these words from our author and subscribed to his judgment [Col. 0927C]: “The philosopher is an animal of glory and a base slave of popular favor and rumor” (Jerome, Epistle 54 to Pammachius, p. 585). Lucian, although himself a pagan, attacks these philosophers far more bitterly. For he openly asserts that they are a class of men ἀργὸν, φιλόνεικον, κενόδοξον, ὀξύχολον, ὑπόλιχνον, ὑπόμωρον, τετυφωμένον, ὕβρεώς ἀνάπλεων, καὶ ἵνα καθ` Ομηρον εἴπω, ἄχθος ἀρούρης: “idle, contentious, eager for glory, irascible, devoted to gluttony, foolish, ostentatious, insulting, and—to speak in Homer’s words—‘a useless burden upon the earth’” (Lucian, *Icaromenippus*, p. 739 ff.). He says still more in his dialogue *On the Sects* (the same Jerome, p. 284), where he testifies that he had received it as certain from everyone that the Epicureans were corrupted by delicacies and pleasures; that the Peripatetics devoted themselves to acquiring [Col. 0927D] and accumulating riches, and that some of them were excessively contentious; and that the Platonists were arrogant, swollen with excessive pride, and exceedingly desirous of glory: οἱ πλατωνικοὶ, he says, τετύφωνται, καὶ φιλόδοξοί εἰσι. We have assembled these statements here in anticipation of what our author is about to say. But we have already touched upon something of these matters in the preceding dissertation.

The philosophers, therefore, adulterated the truth with depraved opinions through a deceitful display of it, lest, if revealed, it offend the mad populace, and so that they themselves might obtain and pursue the false glory of empty learning. Indeed, Tertullian says: “In proportion as hatred burns against the truth, so he who presents it faithfully gives offense. But he who adulterates it wins favor under this very name [Col. 0928A] among the persecutors of the truth” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500). This, and no more, appears in the editions of Rigault and the other editions following it. In the older editions, however, as well as in our manuscript codices, after the word “adulterates” there is added “and affects”; and after the word “truth” one reads: “which”—the printed editions read “who”—“hostilely”—the printed editions read “mimically”—“the philosophers, mockers and corrupters, affect.” If you ask why Rigault excised all this, you will find no reason given by him. What then? Did he perhaps think the words too obscure and therefore to be removed? He would have been right if they had been his own words and not those of an ancient author—words which no editor ever had the right to suppress without giving a reason. But do they not yield this excellent sense? To the degree that truth is hated, the person who teaches it sincerely [Col. 0928B] offends others. But the person who adulterates it by affecting it thereby wins favor among its persecutors—the truth which philosophers affect as its mockers and corrupters. Accordingly, the pagan philosophers, like mimes imitating the words, deeds, and characters of others, affect and corrupt the truth they have recognized. Tertullian, however, appears to have said that philosophers affected the truth not “hostilely,” as is written in the manuscript codices through the carelessness of scribes, who turned the single initial letter *m* into the two letters *in*, but rather “mimically,” just as in another book he said that the soldier of Mithras is, as it were, a mime of martyrdom (the same author, *On the Crown*, near the end, p. 131).

He therefore admits that these same philosophers often recognized the truth: “For who among the poets,” he says, “who among the sophists, has not drunk from the fountain of the prophets? From there, therefore, the philosophers too watered the thirst of their intellect” [Col. 0928C] (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47, p. 515). Thus far the edition of Rigault agrees with the others and also with our manuscript codices; but in the latter the following words, removed by Rigault, are added: “So that they might compare what they possess from our writings with their own.” If these words escaped Rigault or erring printers, who would not wish that he had exercised greater diligence? But if he alone removed them on his own authority, who could excuse his audacity? For they contribute greatly to Tertullian’s purpose. He had undertaken to prove that pagan philosophers were compared with Christians in knowledge in an utterly perverse manner. He rightly demonstrates this by the fact that, in order to compare their own doctrine with ours, they had watered their little gardens, to use Cicero’s words [Col. 0928D], from the sacred fountain of the prophets (the same author, passage cited above, ch. 4, art. 4). Nor was this very difficult for them. For, as he himself says and as we have shown more than once, the sacred Scripture of the Old Testament is far more ancient than all the writings of the pagans. They therefore stole many teachings from our sacred books, as we have proved elsewhere, so that they might be believed equal to Christians in knowledge (*Supra*, ch. 6, art. 4 ff.; vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 384, 531, 909, and 1112 ff.).

But those philosophers, “lustful only for glory and eloquence,” says Tertullian, “if they encountered anything in the Holy Scriptures, once these had been arranged, diverted it, in accordance with the purpose of their curiosity, to their own works” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47, p. 515). But Rigault, despite the opposition of the manuscript and printed [Col. 0929A] codices, deleted the word “Scriptures,” and suspected that “arranged” was a substantive and signified the same thing as “books.” But this is wrong. For it is an adjective, meaning the same as “disposed and ordered,” or “explained and interpreted.” In the former sense Virgil said of the Sibyl:

> Whatever verses the maiden has written upon the leaves,  
> She arranges in order.

(Virgil, book III, *Aeneid*, v. 445.)

That is, Servius says, she orders and disposes them (Servius, *ibid.*, p. 295). Elsewhere Virgil uses it in the second meaning as well:

> . . . Thus Calchas expounds everything.

(Virgil, book II, *Aeneid*, v. 182.)

That is, as Servius again interprets it (Servius, *ibid.*, p. 233), he discloses the movement of the divine will or the future—that is, the order of the oracles—or orders and disposes it [Col. 0929B].

Rigault then wished the words “in accordance with the purpose” to be corrected and written “then transferred back for the purpose”; and finally, after adding the verb “transferred back,” he entirely excised the word “works,” without citing any codex. All the unpublished codices, however, and those printed before Rigault agree with us, except that in the older ones we read “ex improstituto” [a corrupt reading]. In later editions the preposition “from” was removed, and simply “for the purpose” was written. This is indeed better, but we do not venture to define what Tertullian’s true reading may be until some uncorrupted codex is found.

Nevertheless, his meaning appears without doubt to be this: if the philosophers drew anything true from the Holy Scriptures when rightly ordered and [Col. 0929C] explained, they diverted it, in accordance with the purpose of their curiosity—or their excessive zeal to explain those Scriptures badly—to their own works, that is, to the false opinions and popular errors of the common people. For since they did not believe the Scriptures to be divine, they thought that they had been granted the liberty to interpolate them and interpret them at will. Nor, since they failed to understand that the teachings of Scripture were veiled in obscurity and Jewish shadows, did they refrain from scorning its simplicity (Tertullian, *ibid.*, p. 515). Accordingly, what they found certain in them they rendered uncertain; and by rejecting truths or mixing falsehoods with them, they perverted them. But Clement of Alexandria says more about these matters, as we have noted in the proper place (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 871 and 113 ff.).

Tertullian further proves this point (Tertullian, [Col. 0929D] *Apologeticus*, ch. 47, p. 515) by the philosophers’ various opinions and errors concerning the nature, quality, and providence of God; the creation and duration of the world; the nature of the human soul, which some considered incorporeal, divine, and eternal, while others thought it dissoluble and corporeal; and its condition, punishments, and rewards after the destruction of the body. We have elsewhere analyzed and discussed all these various opinions of theirs (*Supra*, ch. 5, art. 4, and ch. 9, art. 1 ff.; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 12, art. 1 ff.; ch. 14, arts. 1 and 2 ff.; ch. 23, art. 1 f.; and ch. 28, arts. 4 and 6).

Nor does our author argue in this way against the pagan philosophers only in this *Apologeticus*, but also in the second [Col. 0930A] book *To the Nations*, where he further proves that the vanity and weakness of philosophical wisdom are most plainly demonstrated by the diversity of opinions, which arose from nothing other than ignorance of the truth: “For although,” he says, “through curiosity to examine every kind of literature they may appear to have made incursions even into the divine Scriptures, as being more ancient, and to have taken certain things from them” (Tertullian, book II *To the Nations*, ch. 2), nevertheless, scorning their simplicity and being driven besides by a lust for glory, they altered and adulterated the truth found in our sacred Scriptures.

“And hence,” as he says in the *Apologeticus*, “philosophy was also expelled by certain peoples—from the Thebans, Spartans, and Argives—when they are defiled by approaching our teachings” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 47, p. 515). So indeed [Col. 0930B] in Rigault’s and later editions. But in our manuscript codices and the older printed ones: “Hence, I think, also by certain peoples . . . the Spartans . . . while they attempt [to corrupt] our teachings”—wrongly, in some editions, “away from yours”—where “by imitation” must be understood, just as he said, “the fruits strive” (*Ibid.*, ch. 40, p. 478), supply “to become ripe.” Why, by whom, and through whose effort or negligence the word “I think” was omitted, and what harm it does there, no one has told us; just as you will readily persuade others that it is Tertullian’s. For elsewhere he uses this expression in that sense when discussing a matter about which he has no doubt at all.

As for philosophy’s expulsion by the pagans, Athenaeus relates (Athenaeus, book XI, ch. 12, p. 542, and book XIII, ch. 9, p. 160) that sophists and two Epicurean philosophers, Alcaeus and Philiscus, were expelled from their city by the Romans; all members of the same sect from their town by the Messenians [Col. 0930C]; all philosophers whatsoever from their respective kingdoms by Antiochus and Lysimachus; and from Attica by the Athenians under a public edict of Sophocles; and, finally, that philosophy and rhetoric were not admitted by the Lacedaemonians. Julius Pollux also mentions this decree of the Athenians, which he calls νόμος ἀττικὸς (“Attic law”) (Pollux, book XI, p. 427). He does not, however, say that it was issued by Sophocles, but merely mentions it. Laertius, however, openly supports Athenaeus, similarly asserting that Sophocles truly enacted a law forbidding anyone to preside over a philosophical school unless approved by the senate and people, on pain of death (Laertius, book V, *Life of Theophrastus*, §38). But who enacted that law and how it was enacted contributes either nothing or little to our purpose [Col. 0930D]; it is enough that philosophy was rejected by its command.

Aulus Gellius presents to us that decree of the senate and another as well, and adds a third enacted during the reign of Domitian, by which philosophers were banned not only from Rome but from Italy also, and for that reason Epictetus withdrew from there to Nicomedia (Gellius, book XV, *Attic Nights*, ch. 14). Suetonius likewise mentions this edict (Suetonius, book VIII, *Life of Domitian*, §10). Philostratus, however, added that such terror was thereby struck into the philosophers that, changing their dress, some fled to Spain, others to the deserts of Libya and Scythia, while others attached themselves to Domitian as advisers in his crimes (Philostratus, book VII, *Life of Apollonius*, p. 877). Finally [Col. 0931A], to omit more, we have noted elsewhere that Clement of Alexandria committed to writing that Greek philosophy perished as often as it was prohibited by the magistrates (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 823). Moreover, the philosophers deservedly suffered these punishments because they adulterated the truth and, as Tertullian says, “disputed about truth against the truth” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500). But blind desire and lust for human glory and popular favor hurled them headlong into so great an abyss of errors.

Christians, however, scorning the praises of men, “necessarily seek,” says Tertullian, “and preserve inviolate” the truth handed down in the Holy Scriptures, “since they care for their salvation” (*Ibid.*). Hence he properly concludes against the pagans whom he addresses: “We are not equated with you either in knowledge [Col. 0931B] or in discipline, as you suppose” (*Ibid.*). No comparison, therefore, could have been more unequal or perverse than that made by the pagans in equating both groups in knowledge and discipline. Nor did they advertise with any better right that their other virtues were equal and alike. This must now be examined together with our Tertullian.

## ARTICLE III

### How perversely the pagans contended that the moral integrity of their philosophers was equal to that of the Christians, although Diogenes trampled upon Plato’s pride with another kind of pride; how supreme was the modesty of the Christians, whereas Pythagoras and Zeno aspired to tyranny; how great was the Christians’ equanimity, whereas Lycurgus chose death by starvation; how faithfully Christians kept their word, whereas Anaxagoras denied a deposit entrusted to him by guests; and how remarkable was the Christians’ simplicity, whereas Aristotle displaced Hermias from his position and flattered Alexander the Great, Aristippus reveled in purple, and Hippias plotted against the state

[Col. 0931C]

If, together with our Tertullian, we pass to the other moral virtues of Christians and pagans, no less a difference can certainly be discovered between them than between those mentioned above. For if the contest concerns “moral integrity,” as he likes to call it—that is, uprightness of conduct, or, as it is commonly called, the virtue of humility—then behold, he says, “Diogenes, with muddy feet,” or, as he wrote elsewhere, “with filthy feet, tramples upon the proud couches of Plato with another kind of pride” [Col. 0931D] (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500, and *On the Pallium*, ch. 4). Does not Jerome appear to have had this passage of Tertullian in view when he said that Diogenes, with mud-covered feet, trampled upon the couches of the wealthy Plato (Jerome, book II *Against Jovinian*, p. 203; Laertius, book VI, *Life of Diogenes*, §26)? But before them both, Laertius relates that, while Diogenes was trampling upon Plato’s στρώματα (“couches”), he said πατῶ τὴν Πλάτωνος κενοσπουδίαν, “I trample upon Plato’s empty ostentation,” and that Plato replied to him: Ὅσον τοῦ τύφου διαφαίνεις, δοκῶν μὴ τετυφοῦσθαι, “How much arrogance you display, you who wish to appear swollen with no arrogance!” Or, as others report, Diogenes said: πατῶ τὸν Πλάτωνος τύφον, “I trample upon Plato’s pride,” to which Plato replied: ἑτέρῳ γε τύφῳ, “But with another pride.” As for why [Col. 0932A] our author said “with muddy” or “filthy” feet—or, as Jerome says, “mud-covered,” that is, stained with mud—you will learn from the same Laertius that the disciples led by this Diogenes went without shoes ἀνυποδήτους, while he γυμνοῖς ποσὶ χιόνα ἐπάτει trod upon the snow with bare feet. Although, therefore, he openly professed such great poverty, he was nevertheless no less inflated with the vice of pride and arrogance than the wealthy Plato.

Tertullian therefore properly opposes to those proud philosophers the Christian, “who is proud neither toward the poor, much less toward the rich” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 500; *ibid.*, ch. 25, p. 422). For among Christians, who were united, as we observed above, by the bond of brotherhood and the spirit of holiness, everything except wives was held in common [Col. 0932B], and there was no rivalry over superior rank or dignity.

Restoration notes: One extra English omission marker had no recovered foreign-script source and was removed. The recovered γνώριπον is probably corrupt for γνώριμον. Two Greek constructions span intervening source text or a column marker. The recovered ὃκ ἄγε represents the Latin ritual formula *hoc age*; its accentuation is uncertain.  

Then, if the question concerns modesty—which is the restrained moderation of the desires within the mind—Tertullian says (ibid., ch. 46, p. 500) that no comparison whatever can be drawn between Christians and gentiles. For, as he says, Pythagoras among the Thurians and Zeno among the people of Priene aimed at tyranny.
