We read in Laertius that Milo’s house, where Pythagoras was then staying, was burned by the people of Croton, τυραννίδος ἐπίθεσιν εὐλαβούμενοι (“fearing an attempt to establish a tyranny”) “because they feared his tyranny” (Laertius, Book VIII, *Life of Pythagoras*, § 38). Tzetzes and Iamblichus mention the kindling of this fire, by which they wished to burn Pythagoras alive, and the war waged against him and his disciples (Tzetzes, *Chiliad* 11, v. 67 ff.; Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, ch. 35, vol. I, *Apparatus*, [Col. 0932C] p. 1246 ff.). What, then, was the purpose of that fire and war, unless he was attempting revolution and plotting to seize tyrannical power—or unless, as Laertius says, others truly feared that he would attempt this?

We have already observed that Zeno of Elea, when the tyrant Demysius or Nearchus tortured him to force him to reveal some secret, doubtless concerning a conspiracy, spat his own tongue at the tyrant. We are well aware that some, such as Pliny and Valerius Maximus, attribute this strength of spirit to Anaxarchus, while others attribute it to Diomedon. But many others whom we cited in the passage just mentioned ascribe it to Zeno of Elea. One of these is Plutarch, who testifies that Zeno was Parmenides’ γνώριπον (“disciple” or “associate”; the recovered form is uncertain, probably corrupt for γνώριμον) “disciple” (Plutarch, Book I, *Against Colotes*, p. 1126), or, as others held according to Laertius, his son by birth or adoption; and that he was subjected to such torments by [Col. 0932D] the tyrant Demysius because he had laid a plot against him. Philostratus, however, says: Ζήνων ὁ Ελεάτης (“Zeno of Elea”) τὴν Νεάρχου τοῦ Μύσοῦ καταβαλὼν τυραννίδα, ἥλω, καὶ στρεβλωθεὶς, τοὺς μὲν ἑαυτοῦ ξυνωμότας ἀπεσιώπησεν· οἵ δὲ ἦσαν τῳ τυράννῳ βεβαιοι, διαβάλλων τουτους ὡς οὐ βεβαίους· οἱ μὲν ὡς ἐπ` ἀληθέσι ταῖς αἰτίαις ἀπέθανον· ὁ δ` ἐλεύθερα τὰ Μυσων ἤγαγε, τὴν τυραννίδα περὶ ἐαυτῇ σφήλας (“Having set about overthrowing the tyranny of Nearchus the Mysian, he was captured and tortured. He kept silent about his own fellow conspirators but accused those loyal to the tyrant of being disloyal. They died as though the accusations were true, while he brought freedom to the Mysians by bringing the tyranny down upon itself.”). “Zeno of Elea, attempting to overthrow the tyranny of Nearchus the Mysian, was detected; and, although subjected to various tortures, he did not betray his fellow conspirators. Instead, he falsely accused those whom he knew to be most loyal to the tyrant and thereby caused them to be condemned to death. He himself liberated Mysia by making the tyranny turn against itself” (Philostratus, Book VII, [Col. 0933A] *Life of Apollonius*, ch. 1, p. 320). For the citizens, making a sudden assault, overwhelmed the tyrant with stones, as Laertius says (Laertius, Book IX, *Life of Zeno*, § 27). Let us add this testimony of the Latin Cicero: “Zeno of Elea endured everything rather than disclose his accomplices in the destruction of the tyranny.” Elsewhere, however, Cicero simply reports that he was killed under torture (Cicero, Book II, *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 146, line 2; and Book III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 252, line 28).

But because several men bore the name Zeno, there is perhaps considerable reason to doubt whether the man whom Tertullian simply calls Zeno is Zeno of Elea, who is said not to have sought tyranny but rather to have wished to overthrow it. Yet one may answer that, while plotting against the tyrant, he was also considering how to seize his kingdom. [Col. 0933B] Moreover, since opinions concerning this Zeno’s death differed greatly, what wonder is it if Tertullian, following other authorities, reported something distinctive about him? In any case, if anyone points out another Zeno to us and proves more securely that he aimed at tyranny, we shall immediately concede the point. But Zeno must still be discussed later.

The Christian, by contrast, is as far removed as possible from that desire to rule and to invade the kingdoms of others, since, as Tertullian says, he does not seek even the aedileship—that is, any magistracy or public office. As Festus notes after Varro, an *aedile* was originally so called because he had charge of sacred and private buildings. But the name was afterward transferred to other magistracies (Tertullian, [Col. 0933C] *Apology*, ch. 46, p. 500; Varro, Book IV, *On the Latin Language*, § 14; Festus, Book XX, *On the Meaning of Words*, s.v. “Aedile”).

Next Tertullian says: “If I enter into comparison concerning equanimity” (our manuscripts written in an ancient hand, as well as the early editions, read *aequanimitate*), that is, concerning the balanced condition of a calm mind, “behold, Lycurgus stands ready before us: he chose death by starvation because the Spartans had amended his laws” (Tertullian, loc. cit.), as we explained above. But the Christian, as our author says, even when condemned by the gentiles on account of his religion, preserves the same equanimity at all times and gives thanks, as we shall show later (below, ch. 16, art. 3).

Our author continues: If, with respect to fidelity, which must always be maintained toward everyone, the Christian is compared with the gentile, “Anaxagoras denied to his guests the property entrusted to him.” Does he not there allude to the story of Pericles related by Plutarch? Pericles, accused of extortion, embezzlement, and expenditure of money that had been deposited with the Prytanes, anxiously expelled Anaxagoras from the city and sent him into exile in order to clear himself (Plutarch, *Life of Pericles*, p. 169, vol. I). But the Christian, Tertullian adds, “is called faithful even toward outsiders” (Tertullian, ibid.); that is, he always preserves inviolate the pledge he has given not only to his fellow Christians but also to all people outside their community. Ambrose discusses at greater length the faithful preservation of deposits by Christians in his work *On the Duties of Ministers* and in another book; there he says: “It makes no difference whether you forswear the deposit or regret [Col. 0934A] having returned it. In either case the peril to life makes fidelity uncertain” (Ambrose, Book II, *On Duties*, ch. 36, p. 105 ff.; and Book I, *On the Death of Satyrus*, § 3, p. 1144).

Moreover, Tertullian says, “if I take my stand upon sincerity,” the gentile sins against it all the more, the more the Christian strives to attain it. For “Aristotle shamefully caused his intimate friend Hermias to depart from his place” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 46, p. 500). If we believe Laertius, this Hermias was a eunuch and king of the people of Atarneus Ἀταρνέων τύραννος (“tyrant of the Atarneans”) (Laertius, Book V, *Life of Aristotle*, § 3). When Aristotle came to him, he so won his friendship that he obtained as his wife Hermias’ daughter—or concubine—whom he loved, as we have noted elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1152). As testimony to his wholly [Col. 0934B] grateful disposition, Aristotle is said to have sacrificed to the woman and to have written a hymn in honor of her and Hermias, on account of which he was accused of impiety (Athenaeus, Book XV, *Deipnosophists*, ch. 16, p. 696; Suidas, s.v.). But the more numerous the witnesses who confirm these facts, the more difficult it is to prove why and how Hermias was expelled by him either from his kingdom or from this life. Aristocles, a disciple of Aristotle himself, admits that Aristotle was assailed by many accusations, which he attempts there to refute (Aristocles in Eusebius, Book XIV, *Preparation for the Gospel*, p. 791 ff.). Yet, through an undoubtedly excessive partiality toward his teacher, he could certainly have concealed much. What, then, if this flattery by Aristocles was all the more suspect to Tertullian because he had learned more securely from another source that Aristotle had injured even [Col. 0934C] Hermias, his dearest friend? For Tertullian contrasts him with the Christian, who does not injure even his enemy (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 46, p. 500; ibid., chs. 31 and 37), in obedience to the divine precepts, as has often been observed, by which he is commanded to hate no one, not to repay injury in kind, to love his enemies, and to pray to God for them.

He continues: “The same Aristotle more shamefully flatters Alexander, whom he was to govern, than Plato is put up for sale by Dionysius” (ibid., ch. 46, p. 500). Some, to whom this phrase seemed rather obscure, think that *potitus* should be read there instead of *potius*. But this is futile and contradicts the evidence of all the manuscripts. For what if our author uses the adverb *potius* to mean “sooner,” “earlier,” or even “more,” so that his meaning is: [Col. 0934D] Aristotle, the tutor of Alexander the Great, as everyone knows, more readily and shamefully flattered him than Plato was wickedly put up for sale by the tyrant Dionysius? We have discussed Plato’s sale elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 554, 620, 1144; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 39, art. 10). It is no less certain that Aristotle flattered Alexander, whose ambition—to say nothing of his other vices—he not only failed to restrain but actually fostered and softened by the art of flattery: ταύτην μὲν οὖν (“this, then,” anticipating the continuation that follows), says Plutarch, τὴν φιλοτιμίαν αὐτοῦ παραμυθούμενος (“soothing this ambition of his”) (Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*, p. 668, vol. I).

Tertullian then continues: “Aristippus, clad in purple and beneath a great appearance of gravity, indulges in debauchery”; that is, he lived luxuriously and intemperately. Laertius records [Col. 0935A] that Dionysius ordered each person at a certain banquet to put on a purple garment and dance (Laertius, Book II, *Life of Aristippus*, § 78). Plato refused, but Aristippus readily put on the garment and began to dance, reciting the following verses, which Gregory Nazianzen and Suidas affirm to be by Euripides (Gregory Nazianzen, *Iambic Poem* 18, p. 209; Suidas, s.v. Ἀρίστιππος (“Aristippus”)):

> . . . . Καὶ γὰρ ἐν βακχεύμασιν  
> Ὁ νοῦς ὁ σόφρων οὐ διαφθαρήσεται (“For even amid Bacchic rites, the sober mind will not be corrupted”).
>
> . . . Nor amid the sacred rites of Liber  
> Is the chaste mind of the wise ever corrupted.

You may consult Gregory Nazianzen, who there compares the vices of other philosophers with the virtues of Christians (Gregory Nazianzen, loc. cit.). Moreover, speaking of the same Aristippus but suppressing his name, our Tertullian says elsewhere: “I hear that philosophy has even been practiced in purple” [Col. 0935B] (Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, ch. 4; the same, *Apology*, ch. 46, p. 500).

Finally, he added: “Hippias is killed while laying plots against the state; no Christian ever attempted this on behalf of his own people, although they had been scattered by every kind of savagery.” It is remarkable how corrupted the name of Hippias is in the manuscript codices. In our two older manuscripts it is read *Icthidias*; in two more recent Colbert manuscripts, *Icthiclias*; and in certain others, *Hidias*, which comes closer to *Hippias*, the reading presented in the printed editions. That our author is truly to be understood as speaking of Hippias can be confirmed by these words of Cicero: “The wicked Hippias, son of Pisistratus, who fell in the battle of Marathon bearing arms against his country” (Cicero, Book IX, *Letters to Atticus*, letter 12, p. 306). Herodotus, [Col. 0935C] Pausanias, Suidas, and others provide more information about him (Herodotus, Book I, § 61; Book V, § 93 ff.; Pausanias, Book I, p. 20; Suidas, s.v. Ἱππίας (“Hippias”)). But it is not so certain that this is the very man of whom Tertullian speaks as a philosopher, unless it can be proved that he devoted himself to philosophy.

Suidas mentions another Hippias, a sophist and philosopher, the disciple of Hegesidamus, who taught that the mind should be content with its own lot. Is this not the man who, as we have said elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1222), was greatly praised by Cicero and boasted that there was nothing in any art that he did not know? But if this man was the philosopher, neither Cicero nor Suidas has told us by what death he died. It will therefore undoubtedly seem more probable to many that Tertullian was speaking of the former Hippias, unless this philosopher’s [Col. 0935D] name was corrupted in his text by careless copyists.

But it is absolutely certain, as Tertullian added, that Christians never attempted anything against their country, although they were “scattered by every savagery” of the punishments inflicted upon them because of their religion—that is, torn apart and put to death (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 46, p. 500). For, taught by Christ, they imitated the simplicity of doves; harming no one, they strove to deserve well of everyone, even of those who slaughtered them with such cruelty.

Who, then, does not now easily see how rightly Tertullian (ibid.), after establishing his comparisons between gentile philosophers and Christians, concludes with these words: [Col. 0936A] “Accordingly, what similarity”—supply “do they possess” (some editions read: “What similarity, accordingly?”)—“is there between the philosopher and the Christian? Between the disciple of Greece,” where philosophers especially flourished, “and the disciple of heaven,” that is, of the true God and Christ? “What similarity is there between the philosopher, a trafficker in reputation,” or a creature of glory, as was said shortly before, “and the Christian, a trafficker in life” (Rigault’s edition and later editions read “salvation”)? “What between the philosopher, a worker only of words, and the Christian, a worker of deeds? What between the Christian, a builder of realities, and the philosopher, a destroyer? What do the philosopher, the friend of error, and the Christian, its enemy, have in common?” Rigault, however, excised these latter words on his own authority.

Then, in our unpublished manuscripts and the older printed editions, the text reads: “What similarity is there between the interpolator of truth and its restorer and expresser, between its thief and its guardian?” Rigault altered it as follows: [Col. 0936B] “The interpolator of error and the restorer of truth; its thief and its guardian?” But because that emendation rests on the authority of no manuscript, it was doubtless made by him because the words appeared rather obscure and insufficiently elegant. Yet what prevents us from declaring that the words as transcribed in our manuscripts are genuine, and that their meaning is this? The philosopher is an interpolator of the truth handed down in our Sacred Scripture because, by inserting his own errors, he gave it a new form. He is also its thief, since, as we have often said, he plucked many things from it and corrupted them. The Christian, however, is the restorer, expresser, and guardian of truth because he presents, expresses, and guards it entire.

Nor did Rigault restrain his hand there; he also removed these following words: [Col. 0936C] “Truth is more ancient than all of them, unless I am mistaken.” By what right he removed them is sufficiently clear from his other, more audacious corrections. Let it suffice for us to have noted the variant readings of Tertullian’s text, and how rightly he maintains that the Christians’ doctrine is far superior to that of the philosophers, and that their morals are purer and holier than those of any gentiles. We have already treated these comparisons in our dissertation on Minucius’ *Octavius* (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 13, art. 4).

# CHAPTER XIV

## On the Christians’ fasts, works of penitence, prayers, and solemn observance of the Lord’s Day, and how greatly they differed from the gentiles in all these matters

### ARTICLE I

#### How long and severe the Christians’ fasts were; how far removed from this severity of abstinence were the banquets and dinners of the Megarians, tribes, curiae, and decuries; the tenths and sacrificial feasts of Hercules; the Apaturia, Dionysia, and Attic mysteries; and the Serapic dinners, with a discussion of the *sparteoli* and the infamous parasites

[Col. 0936D]

Among the other virtues of the Christians, nothing shone more brightly than their care and solicitude—at once diligent and rigorous—to observe fasts, by which they differed from the gentiles no less than by their other virtues. For very often, and especially amid public calamities, they endeavored to entreat the divine mercy not only for themselves but also for their enemies, [Col. 0937A] not through a perfunctory observance but through the most rigorous practice of a stricter fast. Hear Tertullian himself: “We are parched by fasts,” he says—that is, exhausted and dried up, since at those times they ate only dry foods. For elsewhere he speaks of “late or dry foods,” and somewhat more explicitly: “We observe *xerophagies*, drying our food by excluding all meat, all gravy, and every more succulent fruit, so that we neither eat nor drink anything containing wine; we also abstain from the bath, in harmony with our dry diet” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, p. 478; *On Fasting*, chs. 1 and 13).

If you ask Epiphanius what this dry food and dry diet was, he will answer that it consisted of nothing but bread, salt, and water. [Col. 0937B] Throughout those days of fasting and *xerophagy*, as he calls them, Christians were not permitted to taste these foods—however unpalatable and lacking in savor they might be—at just any time of day (Epiphanius, *Exposition of the Faith*, § 22, p. 1015). Rather, “deferred from every fruit of life,” as our author again says—that is, from every kind of food (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, p. 487)—they took it only late, at the beginning of night. Nor is this our own explanation of these words, but that of Tertullian himself, who elsewhere says most clearly: “Abstaining from those things which, unlike certain heretics, we nevertheless do not reject but merely postpone” (the same, *On Fasting*, ch. 15); and thus “we prolong our fasts until evening.”

Indeed, according to Eusebius, Christ had taught his followers most willingly to abstain from food and wine for many days, to lead a hard and severe [Col. 0937C] mode of life, and had impelled an immense multitude not only of men but also of women to despise bodily nourishment and seek instead the rational food of divine readings (Eusebius, *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, ch. 17, p. 661). What wonder, therefore, if the same Tertullian says that they were “wasted by all that continence” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, p. 487), that is, so exhausted that their bodily strength failed?

But the gentiles’ dinners—prepared at lavish expense—their immoderate banquets, drinking parties, revels, and gluttonous feasts were utterly and completely at variance with this Christian frugality, abstinence from food, and fasting. First, Tertullian says, the intemperance of the Megarians is plainly rebuked by this saying of Diogenes: [Col. 0937D] “The Megarians buy provisions as though they were going to die the next day, but build as though they were never going to die” (ibid., ch. 39, p. 473). Yet if you trust Laertius, Empedocles said this of the people of Acragas (Laertius, Book VIII, *Life of Empedocles*, § 33); if Aelian, Plato said it of those same people (Aelian, Book XII, *Various History*, ch. 28); if Plutarch, Stratonicus lashed the Rhodians with this reproach (Plutarch, *On the Love of Wealth*, p. 525, vol. II). But who will deny that several people could have said and repeated it concerning several nations? Whoever these peoples were, they were exceedingly far removed from Christian sobriety and fasting.

Undoubtedly it was not concerning them but many others that our author added: “With so many tribes, curiae, and [Col. 0938A] decuries belching” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39, p. 473)—that is, exhaling excessive food and drink that could not be digested in the stomach—“the air turns sour.” But could this, you will ask, have been written without great hyperbole? Yet what, I ask you, prevents it from being said of the public banquets customarily set out on the forum, public squares, streets, and crossroads of cities during the solemnities of certain great days, especially those honoring emperors? For then individual cities, and indeed entire cities, presented the appearance of taverns and cookshops, as we shall see below. What wonder, then, if the air turned sour from the belching of such a multitude of people exhaling food that had been taken immoderately and remained undigested? Turnebus therefore thought in vain that by the word *curiae* Tertullian meant the banquets given by curiales [Col. 0938B] in the senate-house itself (Turnebus, Book XII, *Adversaria*, ch. 13). For Tertullian must undoubtedly be understood as referring to those public banquets.

Tertullian later says: “The Salii,” whom we have discussed elsewhere, “will need a creditor when they are about to dine” (Tertullian, loc. cit.), because no one was capable of paying their expenses immediately. If, however, you do not believe us (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 20, art. 3) and wish the point to be proved to you, hear these words of Festus: “The Salii were so called from dancing; because sumptuous dinners are set before them on every day and wherever they stay, any other dinners that are magnificent are also called ‘Salian’” (Festus, s.v. “Salii”). Hence Horace sang:

> Now is the time for drinking; now with unfettered foot  
> The earth must be struck; now was the time,  
> Companions, to adorn the gods’ couch  
> [Col. 0938C] With Salian feasts.  
> (Horace, Book I, Ode 27.)

He calls rich, highly exquisite feasts prepared at great expense “Salian.” The gods’ couch was burdened with them, and afterward they were devoured by the Salii. It was for precisely this reason, as Suetonius relates, that the emperor Claudius, “struck by the savor of a luncheon being prepared in the nearby temple of Mars, abandoned the tribunal, went down to the priests, and reclined at table with them” (Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, § 33). Apuleius, moreover, says that his horse had been filled with such an abundance of barley that it thought it had dined like a Salius (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book IV, after the middle).

The Salii, however, were priests of Hercules, concerning whom Tertullian adds: [Col. 0938D] “The accountants calculated the expense of the tenths of Hercules and of the *pollucta*” (the manuscript codices read *pollinctorum*); the same printed and other unprinted codices read “stable-keepers” instead of “accountants” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39, p. 473). *Pollinctores* were those who anointed the bodies of the dead and arranged funerals. But Tertullian does not appear to have spoken of them. Therefore *polluctorum* is the better reading, as can be confirmed by the following verses of Plautus, which shed no little light upon this passage:

> He must come here as quickly as possible,  
> So that I may offer a tenth part to Hercules.  
> (Plautus, *Stichus*, act II, scene 1, v. 80.)

For the gentiles, as our author had said above, consecrated a tenth part of their goods to Hercules, placed it upon his altar, and afterward [Col. 0939A] feasted magnificently. Hence the same Plautus says: “Purchase provisions lavishly for the sacrificial feast” (the same, *Mostellaria*, act II, scene 4, v. 11). Festus says: “To offer goods as a *polluctum* . . . spelt, meal, wine. To Hercules, however, they offered every kind of food as a *polluctum*” (Festus, s.v. “Pollucere”); that is, they offered a tenth part. On this tithe, sacrifice, and feast of Hercules, see Varro, Plutarch, and Macrobius, who also calls it a “lavish sacrificial dinner” (Varro, Book V, *On the Latin Language*, p. 58; Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 267; Macrobius, Book III, *Saturnalia*, chs. 12, 15, and 17).

The accountants who kept the accounts of cities and provinces, as is evident from the Theodosian Code, where an entire title concerns accountants, would calculate how great the expense of this dinner was. Our author therefore means that the expense of these dinners was so great that [Col. 0939B] only public accountants, accustomed to calculating the largest sums of expenditure, could scarcely reckon it. This reading is therefore preferable to “stable-keepers,” that is, innkeepers and tavern-keepers, who in their establishments were accustomed more easily to calculate expenses, whether great or small, incurred by their diners.

Tertullian continues: “At the Apaturia, the Dionysia, and the Attic mysteries a levy of cooks is proclaimed” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39, p. 473). The Ἀπατάρια (“Apaturia”) was a solemn festival celebrated annually by the Athenians for three days in the month of October. On the first day, the members of the tribes or associations enrolled in this solemnity dined sumptuously together. On the second day they sacrificed to Jupiter and Minerva. Finally, on the third day, they registered boys and girls in the curiae. [Col. 0939C] Herodotus recorded that Homer, invited by the associates to this dinner, actually reclined at their table. Elsewhere the same historian also mentions this festival (Herodotus, *Life of Homer*, § 29 ff.; and Book I, § 147), concerning which see also Pollux, Suidas, Petrus Castellanus, Joannes Fasoldus, and especially Joannes Meursius (Pollux, Book VI; Suidas; Castellanus and Fasoldus, *On Greek Festivals*; Meursius, *Festivals of Greece*, s.v. ἀπατούρια (“Apaturia”)).

The Dionysia, or διονύσια (“Dionysia”), were festivals celebrated by the Attic people in the eighth month in honor of Dionysus or Bacchus; they were also called the Bacchanalia. Tertullian called them both the Dionysia and the Attic mysteries, in order to signify that these were the same festivals for which the Athenians prepared dinners with such an abundance of the most delicate foods that more highly skilled cooks had to be selected to prepare them.

[Col. 0939D] Tertullian then returns to the Romans, who celebrated the festivals of Serapis with equal or even greater intemperance in dining: “At the smoke of a Serapic dinner the *sparteoli* will be aroused” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39, p. 473). The *sparteoli* were a certain class of soldiers who, according to an ancient commentator on Juvenal, kept watch at Rome for the protection of the city, equipped with hooks and water for extinguishing fires (Juvenal, Satire 14, v. 313). According to some, they were so called from their tunics and footwear, or more probably from the vessels made of esparto grass in which they carried water. But Suetonius, if Casaubon is to be believed, declared in the following words that they had been instituted by the emperor Augustus: “As a safeguard against fires, he devised nocturnal watches and a corps of [Col. 0940A] watchmen” (Suetonius, Book II, *Life of Augustus*, § 30).

Who, then, does not easily understand that Tertullian is speaking of these men, who, since they were common and lowly people and walked through the city at night, were aroused by the smoke of the sumptuous dinner laid out for the festival of Serapis and ran to it? These festivals and sacred rites, called the Serapia or Serapida, or the rites of Serapis or Isis, were customarily celebrated in the month of April. But we have discussed them in our preceding dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 22, art. 1).

Undoubtedly worse than the *sparteoli* were the parasites, the most disgraceful attendants at every table. They “aspire,” our author says, “to the glory of a servile liberty under contract” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39, p. 475); that is, as may be gathered from Cicero, Suetonius, [Col. 0940B] and others, for something like a stipend, price, or payment in return for having their bellies fattened amid insults (Cicero, Book I, *On Duties*, p. 372, line 3; Suetonius, Book III, *Life of Tiberius*, § 7). In another book he calls them “laborers for the belly, whom a patience inspired by the devil binds to insulting patrons through the subjection of their liberty” (Tertullian, *On Patience*, near the end, ch. 16). But Terence depicts this breed of utterly worthless men more vividly than anyone else. If you do not begrudge the trouble of consulting him, you will find there an explanation of whatever appears obscure in Tertullian’s words (Terence, *Eunuch*, act II, scene 2).

Christians utterly abhorred all these most intemperate and wanton dinners and banquets of the gentiles. They mortified their bodies with such long and rigorous fasts, as we have said, and their own [Col. 0940C] dinner was wholly frugal and exceedingly modest, as we shall show later.

### ARTICLE II

#### How different were the penitential works of the Christians and the gentiles: by the former the heavens were assailed with the sight of their misery, while the latter continually provoked the true God through impious superstitions

It was not enough for the Christians to placate God’s anger through so severe and austere an observance of fasts, not only amid public calamities but also on various other days. Rather, Tertullian says, “rolling in sackcloth and ashes” (*volvitantes* is incorrectly written in our two older manuscripts, through the misplaced addition of the letter *i*), “we batter heaven with the sight of our misery” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, p. 487). Thus, when they were about to entreat God, they rolled themselves in [Col. 0940D] sackcloth and ashes, just like others who performed public penance in the churches for some grave crime.

For the discipline of such persons, as our author relates elsewhere, “commands, with respect to their very clothing and food, that they lie in sackcloth and ashes, obscure the body with filth, and cast down the spirit with grief” (the same, *On Repentance*, ch. 9). And a little later: “One must dwell apart from gladness, amid the roughness of sackcloth, the horror of ashes, and the wasting of the face through fasting” (the same, ibid., ch. 11). Cyprian indeed exhorts the lapsed to repentance in these words: “One must pray more earnestly and make supplication; spend the day in mourning; pass the nights in vigils and weeping; occupy all one’s time with tearful lamentations; lie prostrate [Col. 0941A] and cling to the ground; roll in ashes, haircloth” (elsewhere: “in ashes and haircloth”), “and filth” (Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, near the end). That not only those guilty of a crime but others too performed penance of this kind is clear from one of Celerinus’ letters published among those of Cyprian. In it he testifies that he mourned his lapsed sister’s crime in this manner: “On account of her deeds, I spent—and to this day continue to spend—the joyful season of Easter weeping, day and night, tearfully in haircloth and ashes” (the same, Letter 21).

Thus the other Christians, although conscious of no crime, nevertheless “battered heaven with the sight of their misery,” as Tertullian says, through the acts and dress of public penitents (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, p. 487). If the word *invidia* carries any obscurity there, some light may be cast upon it by what he says [Col. 0941B] elsewhere concerning the gentiles themselves: “In certain colonies, by an annual rite, they are clothed in sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes, and display before their idols, as supplicants, the sight of their misery . . . a Ninevite cessation of business, I suppose.” Of our holy martyrs he says: “The souls of the martyrs beneath the altar cry out to the Lord with the spectacle of their suffering: ‘How long, Lord, will you not avenge our blood upon the inhabitants of the earth?’” (the same, *On Prayer*, ch. 5). He also calls their scars “provocative of Christ’s regard,” because they had desired to conquer (the same, *On Modesty*, at the end). Indeed, he similarly said of himself: “I prefer to bring the sight of my suffering before him”—that is, before God—“by perishing according to his will, rather than provoke his anger by escaping according to my own” (the same, *On Flight in Persecution*, ch. 10).

Why say more? Statius, when lamenting his father’s death, sang:

> [Col. 0941C] Surely I shall assail the other gods above and Tartarus  
> With a still greater display of grief.  
> (Statius, Book IX of the *Silvae*, *Lament for His Father*.)

Again, in the lament for his son:

> . . . Shall I not, with the horror of my grief, assail  
> The gods above themselves and unjust Tartarus?  
> Shall I not mourn you, dear boy?  
> (Ibid.)

It is clear that the word *invidia* in all these passages is not taken in its ordinary sense of hatred and ill will, or grief at another person’s prosperity. Such emotions neither apply to God nor touch or move him to mercy. Cicero indeed acknowledges that the word *invidia* is ambiguous: “This word,” he says, “is derived from looking too intently upon another person’s fortune, as in the *Melanippus*:

> [Col. 0941D] Who has cast an envious eye upon the flower of my children?

The Latin seems incorrect, yet Accius writes excellently: for just as we say ‘to see,’ so ‘to look enviously upon the flower’ is more correctly said than ‘to envy the flower.’ Custom forbids us, but the poet maintained his right and spoke more boldly” (Cicero, Book III, *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 151, line 10). What, then, if Tertullian used the word *invidia* in the same sense as Accius, to mean the beholding, sight, and appearance of the wretched condition and dress of the Christian penitents, by which they endeavored to touch and move the divine mercy (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, p. 487)?

We cannot deny that the gentiles also performed certain [Col. 0942A] works of penance amid public calamities, by which they thought they could bend and appease their gods. For at such times they proclaimed rites for obtaining rain, barefoot processions, laid aside the insignia of their magistracies and ranks, and did other things, all of which we shall discuss below (below, ch. 23, art. 4). But they wrongly invoked and entreated an artificial Jupiter and others who were not gods. Provoking the true God by those impious acts and superstitions, they could undoubtedly obtain nothing from him, just as they could obtain nothing from their false gods.

### ARTICLE III

#### How the Christians prayed to God without a prompter, with hands extended toward heaven, the head uncovered, the soul innocent, and facing east; and how differently the gentiles prayed to their gods and the Persians worshiped the sun

[Col. 0942B]

By the severe penitential labors we have described, Christians prayed to God not only at times of public calamity but also on individual days, especially on appointed days, both for themselves and for others, “without a prompter,” as our author says, “but from the innermost breast” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 30, p. 443). He deliberately said “without a prompter,” because it was the gentiles’ custom for someone to lead aloud all those who were praying and to prompt them beforehand. Some think that the following verses of Statius should be referred to this custom:

> Hence the fathers’ prayers are entrusted to you, and the noble youth  
> Is governed with you as prompter, while you recount the customs  
> And deeds of those who came before.  
> (Statius, Book V, *Silvae*, v. 488.)

[Col. 0942C] But that passage does not concern any prayers recited under the leadership of a prompter. Pliny comes closer to the matter in these words: “We have seen the highest magistrates offer supplication with prescribed prayers; and, lest any word be omitted or spoken out of order, one person reads in advance from a written text, another is assigned as a supervisor to listen attentively, and yet another is appointed to order that favor be shown with the tongues”—that is, that all remain silent (Pliny, Book XXVIII, *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 556).

If anyone objects that this passage treats of magical rites and of words then pronounced in advance, he certainly cannot deny that Plutarch speaks of the gentiles’ solemn prayers when he informs us that Numa Pompilius commanded that, whenever magistrates and priests performed any divine rite, a herald should precede them and cry out in a loud voice: “Attend to this!” ὁ κήρυξ πρόεισι μεγαλῃ (“the herald goes before them in a loud…”—continued after the column marker) [Col. 0942D] φωνῇ, ὃκ ἄγε (“voice: hoc age, ‘Attend to this!’”; ὃκ ἄγε represents the Latin ritual formula hoc age, though the recovered accentuation is uncertain) (Plutarch, vol. I, *Life of Coriolanus*, p. 225). By that cry, Plutarch says, he ordered everyone to direct their attention to the sacred rites and not to be interrupted by any work or business.

Juvenal also bears upon the point. Speaking of a woman who prayed to Janus and Vesta that Pollio might win, he sang:

> . . . She stood before the altar and did not think it shameful  
> To veil her head for a lyre-player, and repeated the words  
> Dictated to her, as custom requires.  
> (Juvenal, Satire 6, after the middle.)

If you have leisure and inclination, consult Brissonius in his book *On Formulas* (Brissonius, Book II, *On Formulas*, p. 68). Christians, however, admitted no such prompter, since they prayed to God not only with mouth and lips but from the breast, [Col. 0943A] and with the inward and sincere affection of the heart.

Restoration notes: In S001250, ωὐ appears corrupt; the syntax and context indicate οὐ (“not”), whose sense is represented in the translation.; In S001252, the recovered ἣ is syntactically anomalous and apparently represents ἢ (“or”); the replacement records this uncertainty.; The proposed mapping of S001245 and S001246 was reversed: the contexts show that E004 is the particle οὐ and E005 is the word πιαίνειν.  

Moreover, they prayed while looking up to heaven and with their hands, as Tertullian says, outstretched; or, as he puts it in another book: “We, however, not only raise them, but also spread them out, patterned after the Lord’s Passion” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 30, p. 441; idem, *On Prayer*, ch. 11), that is, in the manner and form of Christ affixed to the cross. We have discussed this custom of praying elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s Octavius*, ch. 12, art. 3). But because the pagans also used to pray to their gods in the same manner, as we have already shown, our Author therefore added, after the words “with hands outstretched,” “because they are innocent” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, loc. cit.). For the Gentiles raised in prayer hands polluted by impiety, idolatry, and other crimes; [Col. 0943B] Christians, however, raised toward heaven hands no less wholly clean and pure than their breast and mind.

They also prayed, Tertullian further says, with uncovered head, “because we do not blush” (*ibid.*). Here again he contrasts them with the Gentiles, whose custom it was to pray and sacrifice with covered head. Hear, I pray, Virgil’s verses concerning this rite:

> Indeed, when the fleets have crossed the seas,  
> And altars have been set up and you now fulfill your vows upon the shore,  
> Cover your hair, veiled in a purple mantle,  
> Lest amid the sacred fires, in the worship of the gods,  
> Some hostile face appear and disturb everything.  
> Let your companions retain this rite of sacrifice, and retain it yourself;  
> In this observance let your descendants remain pure.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book III, v. 403 ff.)

On these verses Servius makes the following observation: “It must indeed [Col. 0943C] be known that those sacrificing to all the gods customarily covered their heads, so that amid the religious rite something might not present itself to their wandering gaze; with the sole exception of Saturn, lest it appear to be an imitation of the deity, and of Hercules in his own temple, because he himself is represented with covered head, or because these altars were consecrated by Juno and Evander before the arrival of Aeneas” (Servius on the cited verses, p. 292). That exception sufficiently proves this to have been a rite and custom of the Gentiles, which they also observed when saluting and praying to the gods. Brissonius, whom you may consult, has more concerning it (*On Formulae*, book I, p. 140 ff.).

Christians, therefore, on the contrary, prayed with uncovered head, because they knew the Apostle’s saying: “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head” (Paul, 1 Corinthians 11:4). But someone will ask why Tertullian [Col. 0943D] did not adduce this reason from the Apostle, but instead said, “because we do not blush.” We shall answer that he appears to have given this reason because it was especially suited to his purpose. For there, as we have said, he contrasts Christians with the Gentiles. But the latter, as he adds in the same place, when sacrificing to false gods, as also when praying, brought, after all their pollutions, “even a filthy conscience” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 30, pp. 443, 445), contaminated with every kind of crime; and on its account, had any sense of shame remained in them, they ought perpetually to have been suffused with blushes. Christians, by contrast, offered to their almighty God prayer proceeding “from chaste flesh,” as we noted shortly before (art. above), “from an innocent soul, from the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0944A] (Tertullian, *ibid.*), as we explained at greater length in the preceding dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s Octavius*, ch. 12, art. 2; and *On Lactantius*, ch. 33, art. 1). So far were Christians from blushing when they prayed to God in this manner that, as our Author says: “While we are stretched out toward God, let claws tear us, crosses suspend us, flames lick us, swords cut off our throats, beasts leap upon us: the very posture of a Christian at prayer is ready for every punishment” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, loc. cit.). For the Christian was ashamed neither to profess his religion nor to pray to God. And they poured forth their prayers openly and in public synaxes not only with uncovered head but also with body prostrate, as we have shown in another dissertation (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 8, art. 2).

In addition, they prayed facing east, or, as [Col. 0944B] Tertullian puts it, “toward the region of the east” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 16, p. 369). Nor was this custom, which we have discussed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, diss. 2, ch. 8, art. 7, p. 1040), unknown to the pagans, who were likewise accustomed to pray in the same manner, though in a wholly and utterly perverse way. Hence our Author addresses them in these words: “Many of you, on occasion, with a pretension of worshipping even the heavenly bodies, quiver your lips toward the sunrise” (Tertullian, loc. cit.). He repeats the same statement in the first book *To the Nations* (book I, ch. 13, p. 579). If you seek a witness to this custom, you may hear Virgil singing as follows of Aeneas:

> He rises, and, gazing upon the dawning light  
> Of the ethereal Sun, duly lifts water from the river  
> In his hollow palms and pours forth such words to heaven.  
> [Col. 0944C]  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VIII, v. 68 ff.)

And in another book, concerning others performing sacrifices:

> They, turning their eyes toward the rising Sun,  
> Give salted grain with their hands, mark with the sword  
> The brows of the beasts, and pour libations from bowls upon the altars.  
> (Ibid., book XII, v. 72 ff.)

Servius, moreover, remarks upon these last verses: “He certainly did not mean that the sun was now rising, for it had long been daylight; rather, he followed the discipline of the ceremonies, so that he might say that one who was about to pray looked toward the east” (Servius, p. 676). Hence Latinus Pacatus, at the beginning of the panegyric that he delivered to Theodosius in his presence, said: “When engaged in divine rites, we turn our faces toward that region of heaven from which light has its beginning” (Pacatus, *Panegyric to Theodosius*, p. 246). Finally, to [Col. 0944D] pass over many others, Ovid sang concerning the goddess Pales:

> With these the goddess must be appeased; facing the sunrise,  
> Say these words four times, and wash your hands in living dew.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV, v. 365.)

Yet although this rite was common to Christians and Gentiles, the latter prayed to their gods facing east for reasons different from those for which the former prayed to the one true God. For the Gentiles, as Tertullian notes, did so “with the thoroughly wicked pretension, on occasion, of worshipping even the heavenly bodies” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 16, p. 371; and *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 13, p. 579). Since, therefore, they worshipped heavenly things—namely, the stars and planets—and thought them gods, they consequently turned themselves in prayer toward the sun, [Col. 0945A] the greatest and chief of them all.

Christians, however, prayed in this manner for very different reasons, and chiefly because they ought to look toward paradise, from which they had been expelled, and toward Christ the Lord, the Sun of righteousness. Cardinal Bona has reported several other reasons from various writers; they may readily be read in his books and need not be collected here (Bona, *On the Divine Psalmody*, ch. 6, § 3, p. 177). Nevertheless Origen, as we have observed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1040), candidly admits that no sufficiently compelling reason for this rite can be offered. Yet no one will easily be persuaded that Christians adopted it for no reason at all, since it was observed with such public and unanimous consent by all that [Col. 0945B] it was not unknown even to the pagans themselves. For from this some of them suspected, as our Author says, that the corporeal sun was the God of the Christians and was worshipped by them. But he crushes this absurd calumny in these few words: “We might perhaps be classed with the Persians, even though the sun we worship is not painted on linen, since we have it everywhere in its own shield” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 16, p. 369). It is well established that the Persians worshipped the sun, which they regarded as the true God. Witnesses to this impiety are Herodotus, Strabo, Justin the historian, and many others, whom, lest we repeatedly treat what others have already treated, we have not thought it necessary to name (Herodotus, book I, § 131; Strabo, *Geography*, book XV, p. 732; Justin, *Histories*, book I, ch. 10). No one, therefore, should think it strange if these worshippers of the sun [Col. 0945C] had it painted upon their shields, since soldiers customarily carried painted or sculpted images upon their shields. Indeed, if we believe Pliny, the very name *clypeus* was derived from this. He adds: “The origin of the custom, full of valor, was that the face of each person who had used a shield should be reproduced upon it. The Carthaginians regularly made both shields and images from gold and carried them with them in camp” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXV, ch. 3, p. 177). Who, moreover, is unfamiliar with what Homer sang in Greek verse about the shield of Achilles, and Virgil in Latin verse about the shield of Aeneas? (Homer, *Iliad* XVIII, v. 478 ff.; Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VIII, v. 925 ff.). In the same way, therefore, the Persians bore upon a shield the likeness of the sun, which they considered the greatest god.

Grant, you will say, and I concede that this truly was a Persian custom. But how can one infer from it [Col. 0945D] what Tertullian’s true meaning is? Some indeed interpret his words thus: the Persians paint the sun upon linen, whereas Christians have it upon their shield—that is, in that which is the eye of the world and like a shield; or, as others maintain, they behold the face of the sun as though upon a shield. But this explanation, surely more subtle than sound, without doubt never entered Tertullian’s mind. The simpler sense of his words, as is clear from the foregoing observations, appears to be this: the pagans falsely supposed that the sun was worshipped by Christians as it was by the Persians. For the Persians everywhere had upon their shields the fashioned and represented image of their sun-god, whereas Christians did not even have it painted anywhere upon linen.

## ARTICLE IV

### Why Christians joyfully kept the Lord’s Day, which the pagans had dedicated to the Sun, as a feast, and thus differed at only one point from the Gentiles and Jews who solemnly observed the Sabbath day

[Col. 0946A]

Another and surely no less serious error belonged to the Gentiles, who further supposed that Christians worshipped the sun as God because they joyfully observed the Lord’s Day, which the pagans had dedicated to the Sun. Tertullian therefore refutes and chastises them as follows: “Likewise, if we devote the day of the Sun—that is, the Lord’s Day—to gladness, we do so for a reason far different from religion or worship of the Sun” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 16, p. 371). He does not, indeed, state what that other reason was for which they celebrated the day gladly and [Col. 0946B] even festively. But Barnabas has supplied it for us: “For this reason,” he says, “we observe the eighth day—that is, the Lord’s Day—with gladness, the day on which Jesus both rose from the dead and, after appearing, ascended into heaven” (Epistle of Barnabas, § 15, p. 16). Justin Martyr beautifully confirms this, for, no less than Barnabas and our Tertullian, he openly declares that this day on which Christians customarily assembled was called the day of the Sun: “on the day called the Sun’s day on the day called the Sun’s day” (Justin, *First Apology*). It is designated by the same name in various laws of Constantine the Great, Valentinian the Younger, and Theodosius, upon which Gothofredus and others elsewhere have made many observations pertinent to our subject (Theodosian Code, laws 1 and 2, *On Holidays*, p. 118 ff.).

Sometimes it was also called “the Lord’s Day,” [Col. 0946C] “the Lord’s solemnities,” or simply “the Lord’s.” For our Tertullian left it written: “How shall we celebrate the Lord’s solemnities?” (Tertullian, *On Flight*, final chapter). Cyprian, moreover, wrote in his letter to the presbyters, deacons, and entire people: “Meanwhile he read for us on the Lord’s Day—that is, he inaugurated peace while dedicating the reading” (Cyprian, epistle 38, p. 57). And what, I ask you, is this reading other than that which, as we shall say in the following chapter, customarily took place in the public assemblies of Christians? But if you desire something clearer, hear Eusebius, who recorded that this custom of celebrating the Lord’s Day with a solemn rite derived from Christ the Lord: “He handed down that each week they should assemble together and celebrate as a feast the day called the Lord’s Day, and even their bodies to fatten, but their souls with divinely inspired teachings— [Col. 0946D] he prepared to rekindle. He commanded that, assembling together each week, they should keep the Lord’s Day as a feast and should not fatten their bodies but refresh their minds with divine precepts” (Eusebius, *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, ch. 17, p. 664). Valesius thus translates this passage of Eusebius; he does not doubt that, through a copyist’s carelessness, the particle οὐ (“not”) was omitted before the word πιαίνειν (“to fatten”), because τὸ πιαίνειν (“the fattening”) is not appropriate to Christians. Later Epiphanius committed the following to writing concerning the same celebration of the Lord’s Day: “The holy catholic Church itself regards every Lord’s Day as joyful, holds assemblies from early morning, and does not fast. The catholic Church has appointed every Lord’s Day festive and joyful, announces solemn assemblies in the morning [Col. 0947A], and observes no fasts” (Epiphanius, *Exposition of the Faith*, § 22, p. 105). Elsewhere he tells us that this custom originated with the apostles (idem, *Heresy of Arius*, § 6, p. 910). There is plainly no need to accumulate more concerning a matter known to everyone. It is enough to have proved to all that this day was rightly and deservedly instituted in honor of Christ, who was raised from the dead on this very day.

Tertullian therefore continues: “We stand next to those who assign Saturn’s day to idleness and feasting, though they too deviate from the Jewish custom, which they do not understand” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 15, p. 357). But he explained this more fully and clearly elsewhere, where he addresses the Gentiles in these words: “You assuredly are those who have even admitted the Sun into the register of the seven days and have selected its day from among them [Col. 0947B] as the day on which you refrain from bathing, or postpone it until evening, or attend to leisure or dining. You do this while yourselves deviating from your own religions toward others. For Jewish are the feasts, the Sabbaths, the ‘pure meal,’ the Jewish rite of lamps, the fasts with unleavened bread, and prayers on the shores—all of which are certainly alien to your gods. Therefore, to return from the digression: you who reproach us with the Sun and its day, acknowledge the proximity. We are not far removed from your Saturn and Sabbaths” (idem, *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 13, p. 579). But it is not easy to say whether these words, “prayers on the shores,” are genuine and uncorrupted (Philo Judaeus, *Against Flaccus*, p. 992D). For if Tertullian wrote them, it is still more difficult to say what they signify, and no one has attempted to explain them in his notes. Did our Author perhaps have in view certain [Col. 0947C] prayers of the Jews, which they customarily poured forth upon the banks of rivers or fountains before washing in their waters? He rebukes the Gentiles, however, because they charged Christians as a fault with keeping the Lord’s Day as a feast. For the Christians did not differ greatly from the Sabbaths of the Jews and the rite of the Gentiles themselves, who had also named one day of the week after the sun.

Moreover, as Philo Judaeus writes, although individual peoples and nations lived under their own distinct laws, there was nevertheless none that did not honor “did not honor that sacred seventh day, granting rest from labor and relaxation to himself and those near him, not only to the free but also to slaves—and indeed even to beasts of burden that sacred day recurring each week, which brings relief from labor and a holiday to the head of the household with his family, [Col. 0947D] not only the freeborn but also slaves, and even beasts of burden” (Philo, *Life of Moses*, book I, near the beginning, p. 657). We have another witness of the same nation in Josephus, who similarly declared: “There is neither a Greek nor a barbarian city, nor any nation, where the observance of the seventh day, on which we rest, together with fasts and the lighting of lamps, has not spread [the recovered ωὐ appears corrupt, apparently representing οὐ (“not”)]. There is no city of Greeks or barbarians, and no nation, to which the observance of the seventh day, on which we rest, has not extended, together with fasts and lighted lamps” (Josephus, *Against Apion*, book II, p. 1081). Finally, we have observed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, diss. 2, ch. 16, art. 1, p. 1117) that Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius prove by testimonies from various writers that the seventh [Col. 0948A] day of the week was sacred to Jews and Greeks.

It ought therefore to be certain to everyone from what has thus far been said, first, that Christians celebrated the day of the Sun, or Lord’s Day, for a reason and with a rite far different from those of Jews and Gentiles, of whom Lactantius also speaks, whatever some have said; and secondly, that Christians devoted this day to gladness—spiritual gladness, of course—because they gathered from every direction, as we have noted elsewhere from Justin Martyr (*ibid.*, p. 23), into the same place and held their sacred synaxis in the manner we have described. But our Tertullian has transmitted more concerning it, which must now be explained.

## CHAPTER XV

### On the Sacred Synaxes of Christians

## ARTICLE I

### For what reason Christians entered sacred assemblies; concerning the prayers poured forth there, and especially for the postponement of the end; concerning the reading of Sacred Scripture and exhortations; concerning the presidents—approved elders who obtained their honor not by any payment but by testimony

[Col. 0948B]

There was plainly nothing in the entire discipline and customs of Christians that the pagans assailed with harsher calumnies than their synaxes and solemn assemblies for celebrating the sacred mysteries. Tertullian therefore judged that the shameless audacity of their slanderers could be utterly restrained by no stronger argument than a sincere and straightforward exposition of what took place in those assemblies. He first explains [Col. 0948C] the end for which Christians gathered: “We come together,” he says, “into an assembly and congregation so that, as though forming a body of troops, we may surround God with prayers as we pray” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 467). Although these words occur verbatim in all our manuscripts and ancient editions, they appeared too lengthy and perhaps too obscure to Rigault. Therefore, contrary to the evidence of the older manuscript that he himself used, he wished only the following to be retained in the text: “We come together to God so that, as though forming a body of troops, we may surround him with prayers.” Yet he gives not even the slightest reason why he deleted so many words against the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts. Was Rigault, then, permitted to correct the book of so ancient a writer as though it were his own, according to his whim, and to remove and amputate from it whatever he pleased? Tertullian said, “We come together into an assembly and congregation,” [Col. 0948D] just as Cicero, after Terence, said, “We come together into the Piraeus” (Cicero, book VII, epistle 3 to Atticus, p. 275, line 8; Terence, *Eunuch*, act III, scene 4, v. 1), while Virgil sang:

> . . . All the valor of the allies comes together as one.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book X, v. 410.)

Thus assembled, Christians, as though forming a body of troops, surrounded and encompassed God from every side, so that, praying together, they might bend his divine mercy by their prayers. Nor did they exercise against him an unwelcome force: “For this force,” says our Author, “is pleasing to God” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 467)—the force by which Christians, through the united prayers of all, compelled him, as it were by a kind of violence, to lay down the fearsome weapons [Col. 0949A] of justice and not deny them the requested gifts of divine mercy.

They prayed in this manner not only for themselves but also, as he further says, “for the emperors, for their ministers, and for the authorities” (Tertullian, *ibid.*)—that is, for magistrates and governors, whether of cities or provinces, and for all whose service they employed in governing peoples; “for the condition of the age,” that is, of the empire, so that it might be firm and stable and not shaken by wars or seditions; and “for the peace of affairs,” so that all might always enjoy the desirable blessing of peace. For Christians knew what the Apostle had commanded: that “supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings [Col. 0949B] and all who are in high station, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). We have discussed elsewhere these prayers that Christians customarily poured forth for themselves and others in their synaxes (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 8, art. 2).

It is therefore worth observing here only what Tertullian added in the same place: that in these synaxes Christians further prayed to God “for the postponement of the end” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 467). What end, I ask you, was this if not that of the whole world, which they believed would be destroyed with the fall of the Roman Empire (idem, *To Scapula*, ch. 2)? Although this opinion, about which something must be said later (below, ch. 21, art. 1), is altogether false, from it we nevertheless understand [Col. 0949C] that Christians prayed for the continuance of the Roman Empire as often as they prayed for the delaying of the world’s end. For they had become thoroughly convinced—wrongly, indeed—that “the final termination of the age,” to use the very words of our Author, “is delayed by the continuance of the Roman Empire” (idem, *Apologeticus*, ch. 32, p. 447).

But as false as these things are, so true are those practices of the sacred synaxes of Christians that he records as follows: “We come together for the commemoration of the divine writings” (*ibid.*, ch. 39, p. 34), that is, for their reading and recitation. For in this assembly of the faithful, as Justin Martyr says: “τὰ ἀπομνημονεύματα (“the memoirs”) of the apostles, or the writings of the prophets, are read for as long as time permits [the recovered ἣ is apparently ἢ (“or”)]. The memoirs of the apostles, or the writings of the apostles, [Col. 0949D] are read for as long as time permits” (Justin, *First Apology*, no. 67); or, as Tertullian says: “if the character of the present times”—in which the pagans were raging against Christians with such cruelty—“compels us either to be forewarned or to review” (Tertullian, loc. cit.). By these sacred words they nourished faith, raised up hope, and established their confidence and assurance. By repeatedly reading and hearing the precepts of conduct handed down in them, they also made their discipline and manner of living rightly more steadfast.

The reading of Sacred Scripture was followed by “exhortations,” says our Author. Earlier Justin Martyr had said: “Then [Col. 0950A] when the reader has ceased, the president delivers in an address an admonition and exhortation to imitate these beautiful things. Then, when the reader has ceased, the president delivers an admonition by which he urges and exhorts the others to imitate such beautiful things” (Justin, *ibid.*). Thus he relates more explicitly what these exhortations were, by whom they were given, and for what reason.

These, Tertullian continues, were immediately followed by “rebukes and divine censure” (Tertullian, *ibid.*), which Justin Martyr omitted entirely, either for brevity’s sake or because they contributed little to his purpose. Origen, however, expressly declares first that the Christians of his own time devoted every effort to filling their assemblies and synaxes with intelligent persons, to whom everything excellent and divine that we possess was explained in popular sermons [Col. 0950B] and according to each person’s capacity (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book III).

Tertullian then immediately adds that those who were stained by sins, and especially by lust, were utterly expelled from those same assemblies (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 469). There were three classes of sins and crimes, as we shall show in the proper place, on account of which a sentence of excommunication was passed against the guilty, following the Apostle’s example (Paul, 1 Corinthians 5:3 ff.), and they were barred from entering the church. Nor could they be absolved until they had performed public penance for these crimes.

Beforehand, however, their sins had to be examined and ascertained with the greatest diligence. Hence, our Author says, “Judgment is conducted with great gravity, as among those who are certain of [Col. 0950C] the sight of God; and it is the supreme anticipation of the future judgment if anyone has sinned in such a way that he is banished from participation in prayer, assembly, and every holy fellowship” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 469). With the utmost care, therefore—a care greater than which there could be none—they investigated what the sins of the accused were and of what kind, and passed sentence upon those convicted as though they had God, the supreme judge of all, before their eyes. Such a sentence was therefore the greatest anticipation of the judgment to be pronounced by God at the very end of the world. For, as Cyprian later wrote to Pomponius: “Among the faithful servants of God, the proud and contumacious are slain with the spiritual sword of excommunication when they are cast out of the Church. For they cannot live outside, since the house of God is one, and no one can have salvation except in the Church” (Cyprian, [Col. 0950D] epistle 5, to Pomponius).

Tertullian continues: “The approved elders preside over these assemblies of Christians” (Tertullian, loc. cit.). He does not explain to us who these presiding elders were; just as here he calls them by this name alone, so in another passage, where he discusses the same synaxes, he calls them simply “presidents”: “The sacrament of the Eucharist,” he says, “both at the time of meals and as commanded to all by the Lord, we receive even at assemblies before dawn, and from the hand of none but the presidents” (idem, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 3). Justin Martyr likewise, as we saw shortly before, calls the president of each synaxis only προεστώς (“president”). But Tertullian himself, when discussing the administration of sacred baptism conferred in these same synaxes, [Col. 0951A] openly indicates who these presidents were. There we read his very words: “The chief priest, who is the bishop, has the right to confer baptism; then the presbyters and deacons, yet not without the bishop’s authorization, for the sake of the Church’s honor, by whose preservation peace is preserved” (idem, *On Baptism*, ch. 17). Bishops, therefore, presided over these and other synaxes of Christians, and, by their authority, presbyters and deacons.

Why, however, were they called “elders” by him? This may be learned from Cyprian’s words: “Long since, throughout every province and in each individual city, bishops have been ordained who are advanced in age, sound in faith, approved under oppression, and proscribed in persecution” (Cyprian, epistle 55 to Antonianus). You see there that bishops are called advanced in age, [Col. 0951B] and therefore elders. Did Tertullian not, then, designate by that name the bishops, at least very many of whom in his time were elders and advanced in years? Moreover, Cyprian says that they were “approved under oppression,” that is, approved through tortures steadfastly endured for the faith of Christ. Yet in another sense our Author calls them simply “approved”: namely, approved and elected by the suffrage of others because of the holiness of their lives. For he added in the same place: “They obtained this honor not by payment but by testimony. For no thing of God has a price” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 469 ff.). No one, we think, will deny that by the words “this honor” Tertullian designates the sacred orders of God’s ministers, which ought to be conferred upon approved and elected men for no payment whatsoever, however slight, but upon the certain and weighty testimony of religious [Col. 0951C] persons. If you seek the reason, receive it from Ambrose, in words entirely consonant with those of Tertullian: “You have the Lord’s command and the example of the prophet Elisha punishing Gehazi: to give ministry freely and not to sell it, but to offer it; for God’s grace is not assessed at a price, nor should one seek profit in the sacraments, but the service of the priest” (Ambrose, *Exposition of Luke*, book IV, § 52). And shortly afterward: “For the guilt of a ministry and grace sold is inexpiable: heavenly vengeance passes to one’s descendants” (*ibid.*, § 53). Later he confirms this by the example of Simon Magus (*ibid.*, book IX, § 19), from whom simony—so often condemned by the canons of the Church and the writings of the holy Fathers—received its name.

## ARTICLE II

### On the contribution that Christians offered in their synaxes; where it was deposited; whether their charity had grown cold in Tertullian’s time; and to whom and for what uses their gifts were distributed

[Col. 0951D]

Although in Tertullian’s time every simoniacal stain was utterly banished from the Church, nevertheless in that house to which Christians customarily flocked to hold their synaxes there was deposited “a kind of chest,” as he says, containing “no dishonorable sum, as though religion had been purchased” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 469). Thus indeed the text reads in two of our older manuscripts. But in two more recent Colbert manuscripts it reads “not from an honorarium.” [Col. 0952A] In old and some more recent printed editions it reads “not a burdensome sum.” Worst of all, in Pamelius’s edition, it reads “not an ordinary sum.” For, as will shortly be said, that sum was brought at least every month. Rigault therefore preferred the first reading to the others, both because it occurs in the oldest manuscript and because he thinks the word “dishonorable” signifies a sum that was neither venal nor, as Tertullian says, the price by which religion was purchased, and thus involved no dishonor. The two words “from an honorarium” were therefore less correctly fashioned by copyists from this word, unless by them you wish it to be signified that Christians, who utterly abhorred pagan ostentation, did not give this sum in pursuit of any human honor. But if you judge that the reading should be “not a burdensome sum”—one, namely, that was neither troublesome nor burdensome to Christians—this [Col. 0952B] reading can be supported no less than Rigault’s by Tertullian’s following words: “Each person deposits a modest contribution on the monthly day, or whenever he wishes, and only if he wishes and only if he is able. For no one is compelled; each contributes voluntarily” (*ibid.*). Thus the modest sum of money that each person offered according to his pleasure and means could carry neither great honor nor great burden. When he added that it was “not as though religion had been purchased” (idem, *ibid.*, chs. 13 and 42), by these words he censured the pagans, who, as he himself says and as we shall show below, held all sacred things for sale and demanded payment for them.

Tertullian next attests that this sum or contribution was given by Christians “on the monthly day” (*ibid.*, ch. 39, p. 469), that is, once each [Col. 0952C] month. Marcian explains a “monthly contribution” thus: “Those of limited means are permitted to contribute a monthly payment, provided that they assemble only once a month; the deified Severus also declared by rescript that this was to have application not in the City but in Italy and the provinces” (*Digest*, book XLVII, title 22, law 1). Tertullian was writing these words, as noted above, during the reign of this same Severus.

What then, someone will ask: had the charity of Christians grown cold at that time? Had the Apostle not written to the Corinthians: “Concerning the collections made for the saints, as I directed the churches of Galatia, so do you likewise. On the first day of the week, let each of you set something aside, storing up whatever has pleased him, so that collections may not be made only when I come” (Paul, 1 Corinthians 16:1–2)? Nor does he speak only there, but in almost [Col. 0952D] all his epistles, says Jerome, and command the churches of the Gentiles that every first day of the week—that is, on the Lord’s Day—all should contribute what is to be sent to Jerusalem for the relief of the saints (Jerome, book *Against Vigilantius*). The Apostle therefore commanded that these collections be made every Lord’s Day and that the money be deposited with certain persons until it was sent to the poor and to other wretched and needy persons. Justin Martyr also committed to writing that this custom was observed in his time, and that at each synaxis assembled on the day of the Sun, or Lord’s Day: “those who have means and are willing give, each according to his own judgment, whatever he wishes, and what is collected is deposited with the president. Those who possess more abundant means and are willing contribute, each according to his own judgment, whatever he thinks fit, and what is thus collected [Col. 0953A] is deposited with the president” (Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, no. 67).

If, therefore, in Tertullian’s age Christians disbursed this contribution only on a monthly day, and a modest one at that, had their compassion and charity not, as we noted before (above, ch. 12, art. 3), been considerably diminished and weakened? Nor does Cyprian, whom we cited there, conceal this fact; he complains as follows about the rather hard heart of a Christian matron toward the poor and wretched: “You are wealthy and rich, and you think that you celebrate the Lord’s Day, though you take no notice whatever of the contribution-box, though you come to the Lord’s assembly without a sacrifice, though you take a portion of the sacrifice that the poor person offered” (Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*). Yet although some persons at that time, seized by the vice of avarice, contributed nothing on that day, many [Col. 0953B] nevertheless bestowed numerous gifts for distribution to the poor, not only on the monthly day but, as Tertullian says, whenever they wished. For there he declares that Christian liberality was so great that “the exercise of such very great love brands us, in the eyes of certain persons”—namely, the Gentiles—“with the reproach, without doubt, of an excessive outpouring of money” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 39, p. 471).

How great that generosity and beneficence of Christians was you may further learn from Tertullian’s following words. He openly affirms that the money, “as a deposit of piety,” was disbursed “for feeding and burying the needy; for boys and girls destitute of means and parents; for elderly persons now confined to the household; likewise for shipwrecked persons; and if any are in the mines”—that is, condemned to the mines—“if any are on [Col. 0953C] islands”—that is, banished to islands—“or in custody,” that is, in prisons, “provided it is for the cause of God’s sect, they become dependents of their confession” (*ibid.*). That is, adherents of the Christian religion who had suffered these penalties for confessing it were supported with money liberally collected by Christians. Hence he begins his book *To the Martyrs* as follows: “Among the nourishment for the flesh, blessed designated martyrs, which both Lady Mother Church supplies to you in prison from her breasts and individual brothers from their own resources, accept something also from us that may serve to nurture the spirit as well” (idem, *To the Martyrs*, ch. 1). And shortly afterward: “The flesh does not lose what is its due, through the care of the Church and the love-feast of the brethren” (*ibid.*, ch. 2). Earlier Justin Martyr, whom we quoted, had said that with this money the president, with whom it had been deposited, assisted “ὀρφανοῖς (“orphans”) [Col. 0953D] and widows, those in need because of illness or some other cause, those who are in chains, and strangers who are sojourning orphans and widows, those in need because of illness or some other cause, those who are in chains, and strangers arriving from abroad” (Justin, *First Apology*, no. 67).

Eusebius also presents to us a fragment of a letter from Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, to the Romans, in which he praises their custom—originating from the very beginning of the Christian religion and enlarged by Soter, their bishop—whereby they relieved, through various kinds of benefactions, the poverty of Christians, including those living in other cities and those condemned to the mines (Euseb., *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, [Col. 0954A] chap. 33, p. 145). Indeed, Cyprian also wrote these words to the presbyters and deacons:

> As regards providing funds either for those who, having confessed God with a glorious voice, have been placed in prison, or for those who suffer as poor and needy yet nevertheless persevere in the Lord, I ask that nothing be lacking, since the entire sum that has been collected has been distributed there among the clergy for such contingencies, so that several of them might have the means to minister to the necessities and afflictions of individuals.  
> (Cyprian, epist. 5)

He also established in the following terms how the needs of the indigent were to be relieved by this contribution and these alms:

> But if such a person pleads destitution and the necessity of poverty, his need too can be relieved among the others who are supported by the provisions of the Church, provided, however, that he is content with more frugal but innocent [Col. 0954B] food.  
> (Idem, epist. 2, to Eucratius)

In this manner, then, and for this reason, the money offered in the synaxes and deposited with the clergy was distributed to the needy persons who have been named.

For this reason Tertullian extols so highly this charity of the Christians, through which they held everything in common except their wives, just as he inveighs against the pagans who, as we showed above, divided everything through avarice and insatiable greed (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 471). Nor is it surprising, he says, if such great charity is *conviolatur*—“is violated”—by men so avaricious and unimbued with the Christian religion, as the word is written in our older manuscripts and in the old editions; in the fourth, however, it is simply *violatur*, “is violated,” though always with the same sense. Yet Rigaltius, contrary to the evidence of all the manuscripts, printed *convivatur*, [Col. 0954C] that is, “Christian charity holds a banquet.” But this correction is supported by the authority of no manuscript. Moreover, Tertullian is speaking there of fraternal charity, so violated by the pagans that they branded the Christians’ little suppers, by which it was especially nourished, as extravagant. But these must now be discussed.

## ARTICLE III. On the supper given in the synaxes of the Christians and the prayers preceding it; and, against the shameless slanders of the pagans, a demonstration of how frugal, sober, and modest it was

The pagans knew very well that the Christians dined in their synaxes, but they certainly did not know with what great modesty, frugality, and piety this supper was furnished. Therefore, always inflamed with [Col. 0954D] their customary unbridled fury against those same Christians, “Besides branding our little suppers as criminal,” says Tertullian, “they censured them as extravagant” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 473). Thus this accusation had two counts. The first was that those suppers were infamous for crimes—namely, the murder of an infant, the dreadful eating of its flesh, and the most shameful incest. But our Author utterly overthrows this wholly false accusation, as we shall see below. The second charge, that of extravagance, he demolishes by a plain and entirely truthful account of that supper. Please do not find it burdensome, then, to hear him relate it and to examine his words carefully with us. He speaks as follows:

> Our supper reveals the rationale [Col. 0955A] of its name: it is called by what among the Greeks means love.

In the old editions the reading is: “It is called ἀγάπη (“love”), which among the Greeks means love” (Tert., *Apol.*, chap. 39, p. 473). Did the editors of those editions, then, add this Greek word, which scribes ignorant of Greek had not dared to write?
