Yet in another book it is found written in Latin, where Tertullian himself writes the following about martyrs sent to prison:

> The flesh does not lose what is its due, through the care of the Church and the *agape* of the brethren.  
> (Idem, *To the Martyrs*, chap. 2)

There, however, that noun is taken in its proper signification, for charity and love. Yet in his *Apologeticum*, as also in Origen (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book I), cited by us elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 715), the Christians’ supper is called by this name, because in it their mutual love [Col. 0955B] and charity were especially conspicuous.

That supper, therefore, given as a pledge of this love, could certainly not have been wanton or extravagant. Yet even if it had contained something lavish and costly, it should not therefore have been reproached by the pagans. For however costly it might have been, the needy were assisted by it. But, as our Author most aptly observes:

> It is a gain for piety to incur expense.  
> (Tertullian, *Apol.*, chap. 39, p. 473)

So far, however, were the Christians from incurring very great expense upon this supper that it was provided with the utmost frugality and modesty. Indeed, it admitted nothing intemperate or immoderate, or, as Tertullian says, “nothing base, nothing immodest” (Ibid., p. 477). Now the word *vile* is sometimes taken to mean sordid and abject, and sometimes also abundant; in this latter sense [Col. 0955C] Virgil said, “and the plentiful kidney bean” (Virgil, *Georgics* I, v. 257), that is, as Servius observes, abundant. For what is abundant is cheap, as in: “or loads [the table] with cheap fruits.” But if our Author took the word in this latter signification, his meaning will be that there was nothing superfluous or excessive in the Christians’ supper. It seems easier to us, however, to accept that the adjective *vile* is employed in the former sense, for sordid and abject. For he contrasts the Christians’ supper with the banquets of the pagans, into which infamous parasites, the basest of all men, were admitted, as he puts it, “to be fattened upon insults.” Nor was any immodesty seen in it; and it differed completely from the feasts of the pagans and the Bacchanals mentioned by him in the same place, matters that we have discussed elsewhere and must discuss again below.

[Col. 0955D] Moreover, “No one reclines at the Christians’ sacred table,” says Tertullian, “before a prayer to God is first tasted” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 477). He had already said earlier that they assembled in order to pray to and entreat God, as we observed. Here, then, he speaks of the prayers that they were accustomed to place before the supper. From Justin Martyr, however, we learn that they were poured forth after the reading of sacred Scripture and the presiding minister’s exhortation, but before the bread, wine, and water were offered.

Tertullian continues: “As much is eaten as the hungry can take” (Ibid.); this is indeed the reading of our manuscripts and of the old printed editions. It displeased Rigaltius, however, and on his own authority he wished *capiunt*, “can take,” to be written *cupiunt*, “desire,” [Col. 0956A] doubtless because he thought the meaning there was that no one was compelled to eat or drink more or less. But what if our Author’s meaning is that the hungry then ate not beyond due measure, as he himself says later (Ibid., chap. 42, p. 491), or improperly, but only as much as they could take to allay hunger moderately, so that they were led to take food and drink by necessity, not by pleasure? For he immediately added: “As much is drunk as is useful to the chaste” (Ibid., chap. 39, p. 477), that is, with such sobriety that chastity suffers no injury from it.

With this temperance in food and drink, therefore, “they are so satisfied,” he says (Ibid.), that is, they use them so temperately, “as those who remember that even during the night they must worship God.” Elsewhere we have made it manifest to everyone [Col. 0956B] (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 1, chap. 6, p. 712 ff.) that it was then an established custom and practice for Christians to rise during the night to pray to God. Therefore he wrote to his wife:

> Will you escape notice . . . when you rise even during the night to pray?  
> (Tertullian, *To His Wife*, book II, chap. 5)

Yet in that passage of the *Apologeticum* the discussion does not concern every night, but only those on which the feast days of the sacred synaxes were celebrated. Finally, during the supper, he says, the Christians “converse as those who know that God hears” (Idem, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 477) whatever they discussed among themselves concerning divine matters.

He adds further that hymns were afterward sung to God, and from this, he says, “it is proved how he who sang had drunk” (Ibid.), that is, with what sobriety [Col. 0956C] and temperance he had drunk. Who, from this entirely candid description of the Christian supper, would not understand how moderate, frugal, and devout it was?

## ARTICLE IV. On what was done after supper in the synaxes of the Christians; on water for the hands; on the lighting of lamps and the hour of the synaxes; on songs and hymns; on thanksgiving and the Christians’ departure

After the supper had been given and concluded in the manner we have explained, Tertullian relates three further things done by the Christians in these words:

> After water for the hands and the lamps, each person, according as he is able, is invited into the midst to sing to God either from the holy Scriptures or from his own composition.  
> (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 477)

First, therefore, [Col. 0956D] he noted the water for the hands, which was of course provided for washing them. This custom had become prevalent not only among Christians but also among pagans. Athenaeus relates that before and after supper the Greeks provided water for washing the hands, and that the first was called by the ancients κατὰ χειρὸς (“for the hand”), the second ἀπονίψασθαι (“to wash off”) (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book XI, chap. 18, p. 408; idem, book IV, chap. 1, p. 128, and chap. 2, p. 129). He confirms this with various testimonies from writers. Earlier, moreover, he published a fragment of a letter of Hippolochus, who had written that the guests, when filled with food, washed their hands. Lampridius likewise recorded that courses were served by Heliogabalus to parasites in such a way that they drank with each one and washed their hands as though they had eaten (Lampridius, *Life of Heliogabalus*, [Col. 0957A] p. 343). Thus the custom of washing the hands after supper, being decorous, was also observed by Christians. See Theodoret and others (Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chap. 18).

The two words of Tertullian that follow—“and the lamps”—will doubtless seem more difficult of explanation to many. We are certainly aware that some have noted that Wouwer’s manuscript reads “to the lamps”; but that manuscript alone should not be preferred to all the others. Our Author undoubtedly wished there to notify us that lamps were then lit, because the Christians assembled toward evening and ate supper after the day had already ended and after all the things we have related had been done. Thus these lamps were lit out of necessity and to dispel the darkness of night, as he indicates elsewhere (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, [Col. 0957B] chap. 7, p. 306). But we have already made some observations about them elsewhere and shall make further observations later (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 25, art. 2).

Someone, however, will doubtless object to us: If these Christian synaxes were convened toward evening and they began their supper at the commencement of night, why does Tertullian himself elsewhere call these assemblies “before dawn”? Why did he say in another book:

> We receive the sacrament of the Eucharist even at assemblies before dawn.  
> (Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chap. 3)

He testifies that they were called by no other name by Pliny the Younger in his letter to the emperor Trajan. For in it, as Tertullian himself reported, Pliny had written that he had discovered nothing in the rites of those Christians except “assemblies before dawn for singing to Christ and to God” (Idem, *Apologeticum*, [Col. 0957C] chap. 2, p. 273). Indeed, these assemblies are again called “nocturnal convocations” by Tertullian:

> Who will willingly endure his wife being taken from his side for nocturnal convocations, if occasion should require it?

And a little later:

> Will the husband not know what you taste in secret before all food, and indeed in the morning hours? And if he knows it to be bread, he will not believe it is the bread that it is said to be.  
> (Idem, *To His Wife*, book II, chap. 4)

In a similar manner Cyprian also wrote these words to Caecilius:

> Unless someone fears this in the morning celebrations, lest through the taste of wine he smell of the blood of Christ.  
> (Cyprian, epist. 63, to Caecilius)

In several other manuscripts, however, the passage reads as follows:

> Someone fears this, lest he offer wine, lest through the taste of the wine, with its fragrance spreading, the smell of wine should be detected by an unbeliever’s awareness in the morning hours, [Col. 0957D] and he should be recognized as a Christian, while we commemorate the blood of Christ in the offering of wine.

Some suppose that the knot of this difficulty can be untied by distinguishing two kinds of synaxes. One, they say, was that in which the Eucharist was received by fasting Christians very early in the morning. The other, they think, was the one under discussion, which they called the *agape* and which was ordinarily begun toward evening. But Socrates and Sozomen appear to tell against this answer, for they assert that Christians did not everywhere observe the same custom in holding their assemblies. They relate that in some Churches synaxes were held on the Sabbath, in others on Sunday; likewise, in some the sacred mysteries were received [Col. 0958A] toward evening by persons who had eaten, but in others before any food (Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 2, p. 287; Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 17, p. 735). If someone says that they are speaking of their own time rather than of the most ancient period, including the time of our Tertullian, he will neither prove this easily nor accomplish much by it. For Tertullian, no less than Justin Martyr, as is plain from what we noted above, argues against pagans who cried out, as falsely as audaciously, that utterly horrendous crimes were perpetrated in the synaxes of Christians. Does he not, then, speak plainly of all the synaxes, in which he briefly and truthfully sets forth what was done there? It is also certain that at certain solemnities, such as the feast of Easter, Christians kept vigil throughout the entire night. For Tertullian wrote to his wife:

> Who will calmly endure her spending the night away at the solemn observances [Col. 0958B] of Easter?  
> (Tertullian, *To His Wife*, book II, chap. 4)

But in the *Apologeticum* he discusses not only these but also other synaxes, which Christians were accustomed to prolong far into the night. There is therefore nothing to prevent their being called assemblies before dawn and nocturnal convocations.

Thirdly, Tertullian relates that after that Christian supper, “each person, according as he is able, is invited into the midst to sing to God either from the holy Scriptures or from his own composition” (Idem, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 477). Thus, after the table was removed, each person was invited to sing, in the midst of the whole gathering and circle, some hymn either taken from sacred Scripture or composed by his own talent in honor of God. Cyprian exhorts Donatus to join in singing psalms one day in the following [Col. 0958C] words:

> And since there is now holiday repose and the time is free, let us gladly spend what remains of this day, now that the sun is declining toward evening; nor let even the hour of the banquet be without heavenly grace. Let the sober banquet resound with psalms; and since your memory is retentive and your voice melodious, undertake this customary office. You will feed your dearest friends the more if we have spiritual hearing; let religious sweetness delight their ears.  
> (Cyprian, *To Donatus*, at the end)

If anyone objects that Cyprian is not speaking there about sacred synaxes, what will he achieve by that? For if psalms were sung at ordinary suppers, how much more ought they to have been sung in sacred synaxes? And certainly Pliny, cited by Tertullian himself (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 467), had written to Trajan, as we saw earlier, that he had detected no other [Col. 0958D] offense in the Christians’ assemblies before dawn except that they sang a hymn to Christ as to God. We have discussed these hymns elsewhere (*Apparatus*, vol. I, pp. 413, 656, and 658).

Moreover, the end of this banquet was such as its beginning had been. “For likewise,” says Tertullian, “prayer brings the banquet to an end.” Thus, when the singing of psalms, songs, or hymns was finished, the Christians again poured forth prayers to give thanks to God. “Finally, they depart from there”—the words are still Tertullian’s—“with the same care for modesty and chastity, as persons who have partaken not so much of a supper as of discipline” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 477), that is, a rule for living piously and holily, and the divine and spiritual teaching upon which they had been fed. [Col. 0959A] But we have dealt elsewhere with this modest, religious, and chaste departure of the Christians from the church (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 713).

## ARTICLE V. How the things said about the synaxes of the Christians may be confirmed from the assemblies of the Therapeutae

Philo the Jew, and Eusebius after him, recorded many things concerning the assemblies of the Therapeutae similar to what we have thus far seen done in the synaxes of the Christians. Since these accounts can shed mutual light upon one another, we think it will be unwelcome to no one, and perhaps not wholly useless to many, if by a brief account we set before everyone’s eyes what [Col. 0959B] was done by those Therapeutae. For whether they observed the Mosaic law, as Philo thinks, or the Christian law, as Eusebius believed, or both together, as certain more recent scholars have held, their rites can certainly give clear confirmation to what Tertullian reported concerning the Christians.

Philo the Jew relates that for these Therapeutae, whom Eusebius considers disciples of Mark the Evangelist, the seventh day of every week was festive and sacred, but especially the one that recurred after seven weeks (Philo, *On the Contemplative Life*, pp. 893, 899 ff.; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chap. 16 ff., p. 53 ff.). On that day they all, both men and women, assembled at a signal in one place, entered upon a banquet, and, raising [Col. 0959C] their eyes and hands to heaven, prayed that it might be pleasing to God. When the prayers were completed, they reclined according to each person’s rank, yet in such a way that the men occupied the right side and the women—nearly all of whom were virgins by their own choice—the left. Nothing was served at this banquet except bread for food, salt as relish, and, for those of more delicate taste, hyssop as seasoning; while everyone had water alone to drink, either cold or, for the elderly, warm, since they regarded wine as poison. Throughout the entire banquet there was the profoundest silence on the part of all, while only one person either proposed some question from the sacred Scriptures or resolved one that had been proposed.

Afterward the person presiding over the assembly led a hymn composed by himself or taken from the sacred prophets; each person followed him in his proper and fitting order, while the others [Col. 0959D] remained silent, raising their voices without distinction of sex only at the final refrain of the hymn. Then, when the table had been removed, they all arose and, led by the cantor, sang hymns in honor of God, now with one voice, now antiphonally, moving their steps sometimes forward, sometimes backward, or to the right or left, until finally they all formed a single chorus together. At last, after they had passed the night in this manner, they turned their faces and their entire bodies toward the east, prayed there for a happy and auspicious day, and each returned home.

It is no part of our present undertaking to determine whether these Therapeutae were Jews or Christians as well as Jews, or to settle the considerable dispute [Col. 0960A] that has arisen among the learned on this subject and that does not yet seem to us to have been resolved. For our purpose it is sufficient to note that Eusebius acknowledges that the things we have seen described by Philo were observed by Christians: καὶ μάλιστα τὰς τῆς μεγάλης ἑορτῆς παννυχίδας, καὶ τὰς ἐν ταύταις ἀσκήσεις, τούς τε λέγεσθαι εἰωθότας πρὸς ἡμῶν ὕμνους (“and especially the all-night vigils of the great feast, the exercises performed during them, and the hymns customarily recited by us”). “And especially the all-night vigils of the great solemnity, the pious exercises performed in them, and the hymns customarily recited by us” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chap. 17, p. 57).

Nor indeed should anyone object that Eusebius erred in taking these Therapeutae, who were actually Jews and professed the Jewish law, for Christians. For even if he did suffer some human error there, no one can deny that the sacred rites of the Christians observed in the Churches in his own and even the preceding age were known to him. Yet he plainly affirms that there were many [Col. 0960B] similar sacred exercises, rites, and vigils in the assemblies of the Christians and of the Therapeutae.

Moreover, from what has thus far been discussed concerning the supper and synaxes of those same Christians, the utterly shameless slander of the pagans—whereby they falsely asserted that these were both extravagant and infamous for horrendous crimes—ought to be entirely manifest to everyone. For so enormous and shameless a lie is utterly overthrown by Tertullian’s simple and truthful description of these synaxes, a description fully confirmed by others.

Furthermore, “since the good meet in these synaxes,” says our Author, “since the pious and the chaste assemble, it must be called not a faction but a *curia*” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 39, p. 477). It was not, indeed, an unlawful and seditious faction, such as that of the pagans was accustomed to be, as we shall say below; [Col. 0960C] rather, it was a *curia* in which, as Varro and Festus say, public care for sacred affairs was exercised (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book V, § 6; Festus, s.v. *Curia*), and which, to use Cicero’s words, was “the avenger of rashness and the regulator of duty” (Cicero, *For Flaccus*, p. 367, line 28). There, if anyone had previously sinned in any respect, he was chastised according to his deserts; and the presidents diligently taught and prudently regulated the pious duties of every individual. What, then, could be more absurd and false than to accuse those sacred congregations of being an unlawful faction, when Christians, as Tertullian rightly asserts, harmed no one and saddened no one except unto salutary repentance, as the Apostle says, if any had perhaps fallen through human frailty or a perverse disposition into some grave crime (Tertullian, loc. cit.)? [Col. 0960D] But certainly very few such persons were found. “For all the rest of us,” Tertullian further says, “when gathered in such holy synaxes, are the same as when dispersed; all together the same as each individually” (Ibid.): namely, upright, good, pious, and chaste, as we have thus far demonstrated more fully and as will be confirmed in the following article.

## ARTICLE VI. The argument of the pagans against the pious and chaste conduct of the Christians is refuted, an argument drawn from the fact that some Christians had fallen away from the discipline of morals, from doctrine, and from the Christian religion itself

Against what had been argued concerning the most holy synaxes and conduct of the Christians—matters that could not have been unknown to anyone—the pagans [Col. 0961A] audaciously rose up and objected to us, as Tertullian puts it, “that certain of our people depart from the rule of discipline” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 46, p. 513). Christians could depart from it in three ways: first, through certain crimes and corrupt conduct; second, through errors and heresy; third, through shameful desertion of the entire Christian religion itself and return to the impious worship of the gods.

As concerns the first, since the pagans’ grossly unjust detraction had been more than sufficiently refuted by what we have thus far related, Tertullian judged that nothing further or more specific needed to be said in the *Apologeticum*. In his book *To the Nations*, however, he examines and refutes that charge:

> But among you we are said to be the worst and most disgraceful in avarice, luxury, [Col. 0961B] and wickedness.  
> (Idem, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 5, p. 565)

Thus indeed they were accustomed to slander the Christians. But what does Tertullian reply?

> We shall not deny that some are.

Thus he admits and does not at all conceal that there were some Christians stained by certain crimes. But what follows from that against the rest, and much more against the Christian religion? Absolutely nothing, he says; indeed, this very fact does much to establish both its truth and its holiness. “For even this suffices,” he says, “as testimony to our name and to the perfect religion, if not all, if not the majority” are such (Ibid.). He gives the following fine and true reason:

> It is necessary that upon a body, however sound or pure you wish it to be, some mole (*aliqui*, for *aliquis*) should sprout, or a little wart arise, or a freckle blemish it.  
> (Ibid.)

[Col. 0961C] He indeed wrote *effruticet*, “should sprout,” just as in the book *On the Soul* he says that a human being is formed from two elements, “so that the two together may sprout forth as a human being from each substance” (Idem, *On the Soul*, chap. 27), that is, arise and grow. But this small blemish makes it more evident that the whole body is beautiful, healthy, and perfect. Thus certain—but very few—Christians, like a few moles upon their entire body and community, demonstrated more clearly the supreme perfection of the Christian religion.

Moreover, those Christians who strayed from the right rule were accustomed, according to the gravity of their offenses, to be admonished, rebuked, and chastised in the public synaxes, as we saw earlier (preceding article), and sometimes to be cut off and cast out like putrid members by the sword of excommunication? For this reason our Author wrote elsewhere to Scapula:

> We do not deny a deposit entrusted to us; we violate no one’s marriage; [Col. 0961D] we treat orphans dutifully; we relieve the needy; we return evil for evil to no one. Let those who falsely claim our sect look to themselves—those whom we ourselves reject.  
> (Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chap. 4)

He means those who, because of their crimes, had been cast out of the sacred assemblies of the Christians whose name they falsely claimed.

Others vaunted themselves as professing the Christian religion—namely, heretics—who, from the one way, as he says, of doctrine and truth, split off many crooked and inextricable paths and drove themselves and others headlong into the abyss of errors and heresies. But these, he says, arose “from the seed of the philosophers,” from whose “talents,” as he said elsewhere, “every heresy is animated,” [Col. 0962A] and elsewhere again, “heresies are suborned” (Idem, *Apologeticum*, chap. 47, p. 519; idem, *Against Marcion*, book I, chap. 13; *On Prescription*, chap. 7; idem, *Against Hermogenes*, chap. 8). For this reason philosophers are called by him more than once, and later by Jerome, “the patriarchs of the heretics” (Jerome, epist. 43 to Ctesiphon). And just as the philosophers distorted sacred Scripture of the Old Testament, as we observed above, so the heretics adulterated “this new-fledged equipment of ours”—that is, the books of the New Testament—“with their opinions toward philosophical propositions” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 47, p. 519); that is, they attempted to accommodate the doctrine handed down in the sacred books of the New Law to philosophical opinions. But by perversely mixing falsehoods with truths, [Col. 0962B] they departed from truth itself and adulterated the true teachings.

“But readily and plainly,” he continues, “we enter a prescription against our adulterators,” or, in other words, oppose an exception to these heretics who corrupt sacred Scripture, and refute them even by this argument alone: “that there is one rule of truth, which comes from Christ through his companions, to whom the various commentators will be proved considerably posterior” (Ibid., p. 519). He therefore defines most plainly that there is one sole rule of true religion, which was delivered to us by Christ and transmitted through his companions, the Apostles and first disciples, from whom we received it both in writing and orally. Whatever, therefore, the heretics devised that differed from this norm of tradition proceeded neither from Christ nor from his first disciples; it is manifestly false. For they will be proved later than these.

[Col. 0962C] But by whom, I ask you, will they be proved so? By Tertullian himself? If that is the case, in these words he promised his book *On the Prescriptions of Heretics*, where he actually proved it. But it is by no means agreed among scholars whether this book was published before or after the *Apologeticum*. Could he not, therefore, have said “they will be proved,” because it was exceedingly easy for anyone to prove it?

Moreover, he openly affirms that heretics, even before a public examination of their false opinions, are convicted of error by the very fact that those opinions are new and were handed down neither by Christ nor by his disciples, but were falsely contrived by the heretics themselves. Therefore elsewhere he promises to explain these matters more fully in his book *On the Prescriptions of Heretics*, as he states more clearly in these words:

> Another little book will maintain this position against the heretics, who are to be convicted [Col. 0962D] even without a reconsideration of their doctrines, because they are such on the grounds of a prescription of novelty.  
> (Idem, *Against Marcion*, book I, chap. 1)

The pagans, therefore, could draw absolutely no conclusion from the corruption of the heretics against the truth and excellence of the Christian religion. For, having been wholly cut off from the Catholic Church, they were Christians no longer except in name—indeed, not even in name. I would have you hear Tertullian himself speaking:

> If they are heretics, they cannot be Christians, since they do not derive from Christ what, in accordance with their own choice, they have followed, thereby assuming the names of heretics.  
> (Idem, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chap. 37)

For this reason the Christian emperors [Col. 0963A] wished them to be “called by the name of their own author, whose crime they imitated in deserting God” (*Theodosian Code*, title *On Heretics*, law 65, p. 190, vol. VI), or, as Constantine the Great said in Socrates, “that they should also be called by the name of those whose conduct they have followed” (Socrates, book I, chap. 9, p. 32). If you ask the reason, receive it from Cyprian:

> Just as the devil is not Christ, although he deceives in his name, so neither can that person be regarded as a Christian who does not remain in the truth of the Gospel and of its faith.  
> (Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*)

You see how strong against heretics of every kind is this argument drawn from prescriptions, or from the ancient tradition of Christ’s disciples. For Tertullian plainly demonstrates that the pagans could establish absolutely nothing against the perfection of the Christian [Col. 0963B] religion from the most wicked errors of those heretics, since they had so corrupted Christ’s true doctrine that they were considered unworthy even of the name of Christians.

Finally there was a third class of Christians, deserters and apostates from their faith, who had returned to the impious worship of the gods like dogs to their vomit. But the pagans vainly supposed that anything could be inferred from the guilt of these apostates against the Christian religion. For those who had violated the faith they had pledged to Christ were no longer Christians and could not be called by that name. Hence Tertullian addresses the pagans in these words:

> Such persons neither assemble nor share with us, having become yours again after their offenses, since we do not even mingle with those whom [Col. 0963C] your violence and savagery have driven to denial.  
> (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 5)

How true this is everyone will readily understand from the things that Cyprian and our other ancient writers repeatedly recorded concerning the lapsed, who had renounced the Christian faith under the threats and tortures of tyrants. But a more suitable occasion for discussing them will be given to us. Tertullian therefore rightly concludes, once again addressing the pagans:

> Without cause you call those men Christians whom Christians themselves disown—Christians who do not know how to deny themselves, that is, the faith of Christ.  
> (Ibid.)

For true Christians, assailed by the most dreadful torments of every kind, steadfastly maintained the truth of the Christian religion even unto the cruelest death and obtained the crown of martyrdom. But what our Author [Col. 0963D] has handed down concerning these most holy martyrs must now be explained.

# CHAPTER XVI. On Christian Martyrs

## ARTICLE I. By what and how various and horrendous tortures Christians were tormented and slaughtered by the pagans; and why they were called *Sarmenticii* and *Semaxii*

No virtue of the Christians doubtless shone more brightly than their utterly unconquerable patience, constancy, and courage in enduring punishments in defense of their religion. For the greater the pagans’ hatred of them because they despised and undermined pagan religions, the more cruel [Col. 0964A] were the afflictions and torments—hitherto devised by no one—with which they mangled and killed them. Tertullian enumerates many of their punishments, which we must not pass over without some observation. First, then, he says:

> Every day we are besieged, every day betrayed; most often we are overwhelmed in our very assemblies and congregations.  
> (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 7, p. 307)

Thus not a few but very many were overwhelmed, not rarely but very frequently, in their assemblies and elsewhere. Nor is this surprising. For the pagans, having cast aside all humanity, raged against them, partly in obedience to their own dispositions and partly to the laws. Indeed, Tertullian further says:

> How often, bypassing you—that is, the governors—the hostile mob attacks us on its own authority with stones and fires!  
> (Ibid., chap. 37, p. 461)

[Col. 0964B] That is, without awaiting any judicial sentence, the pagan rabble, in a blind assault, buried Christians beneath blows from stones or burned them alive.

To come, then, to each of their punishments: “At one time,” says our author, “we are banished to islands” (*ibid.*, ch. 12, p. 341); but this punishment of exile was certainly lighter than all the others. “At another time we are condemned to the mines” (*ibid.*, ch. 12, p. 341), that is, to excavate them with the greatest toil. Very many, moreover, were thrust into dreadful prisons to waste away from want and hunger, had not other Christians, as we said above, come to their aid. Tertullian, however, treats these matters more fully in his brief but excellent book *To the Martyrs* (the same, *To the Martyrs*).

Furthermore, he says, “the sides of Christians are scraped with claws” (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. [Col. 0964C] 12, p. 339). These claws were iron instruments fashioned like the claws of wild beasts, with which the pagans furrowed and tore apart the Christians’ sides. Hence he later said: “As we are stretched out toward God upon the rack, or doubtless upon some other similar machine, let the claws dig into us” (*ibid.*, ch. 30, p. 441). Prudentius likewise sang:

> Inflamed by these words, Asclepiades ordered  
> His body to be disembowelled, suspended aloft  
> Upon the rack, and stretched by hooks and claws.  
>   
> (Prudentius, *On Saint Romanus*, v. 107 ff.)

Tertullian continues: “We are driven to the beasts,” or are cast to them in the theatre so that they may devour us: “the beasts,” as he afterward described it, “leap upon us” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 12, p. 341; *ibid.*, ch. 30, p. 445). [Col. 0964D] How frequent this punishment of Christians was may be gathered from the fact that, whenever any public calamity occurred, the pagans immediately cried out, as he likewise testified, “The Christians to the lion!” (*ibid.*, ch. 40, p. 479). In another book, while censuring and condemning the assemblies of the pagans, he says: “There daily demands are made that lions be sent against us” (the same, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 27). Elsewhere again he declares that Christ’s enemies have already been placed beneath his feet, “though every assembly of the populace still cries, ‘The Christians to the lion!’” (the same, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 22). What more need be said? He warns the enemies of chastity that they need not fear that there will be no one to shout, “The Christians to the lion!” (the same, *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 12).

And this was precisely the cry raised against [Col. 0965A] Polycarp, as we learn from Eusebius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. IV, ch. 15, p. 32). Cyprian likewise wrote of himself: “Immediately upon the first outbreak of the disturbance, when the people had demanded me with violent shouting” (Cyprian, epistle 20). Pontius teaches us in the following words from his *Life* what they had demanded: “Especially since, by repeatedly renewed acclamations, he was demanded for the lion” (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, p. 4). I would therefore have you consider whether our Tertullian was also aiming at this when he said of the Roman populace: “None are more insistent in demanding the Christians than the mob.” For common people demanded and cried “The Christians to the lion!” far more frequently than others. If, however, you think that he is speaking there of any form of death demanded by them, and can establish this, we shall not offer much resistance. Meanwhile, however, let us pass to other [Col. 0965B] torments of the Christians.

“Some,” says our author, “were placed upon crosses” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 12, p. 339) and stakes; or, as he afterward said, “crosses suspend them.” “Others lay down their necks”; or, as he preferred to say elsewhere, “swords sever their throats” (*ibid.*, ch. 30, p. 445). Others, moreover, “are burned by fires,” or “fires lick them,” as we afterward read in his words (*ibid.*, loc. cit.).

In his book *On Modesty*, however, he explains these various kinds of punishment thus: “Imagine the martyr now beneath the sword, with his head already poised for the blow; imagine him upon the cross, with his body already outstretched; imagine him upon the stake, with the lion already let loose; imagine him upon the axle, with the fire already built up” (the same, *On Modesty*, ch. 22). Yet he declares that Christians were tormented not only by these tortures. For in another book [Col. 0965C] he mentions not merely “the heavy sword, the lofty cross, the fury of beasts, and the supreme punishment of fire,” but also “every device of the executioner in yet more monstrous torments,” which human ingenuity, more cruel than wild beasts, could contrive (the same, *To the Martyrs*). And so, in those few latter words, he indicated clearly enough that there was no kind of torment with which Christians were not then racked.

Since, however, the punishment of fire was more grievous than the others—or, as we have just seen him write, was the supreme punishment—the pagans demanded it against Christians more frequently. Hence, as we read there in our manuscripts, they called them, with sarcasm and mockery, *sarmenticii* and *semaxii* “now,” that is, in his own time (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 53). The old editions, however, read *semissii*; [Col. 0965D] while some would read *semassii*, and afterward *assis* instead of *axis*, as though Tertullian had meant to say that Christians were bound to a stake or pole of half an *as*. But in what sense? Surely not in the meaning you assert? Yet that is hardly probable. Beyond doubt, the reading of our manuscripts and of all the others, with only one exception—and that perhaps corrupt—appears preferable and genuine. For Tertullian himself, the best interpreter of his own meaning, immediately added: “because, bound to a stake of half an axle, we are burned amid a surrounding mass of brushwood” (*ibid.*). Thus he said that Christians were tied to a stake or pole and burned alive, brushwood having been piled all around them and set alight.

You will say that this is correct; but why is the stake called “half an axle”? Observe, I ask, that by the term *stipes* is meant, as Festus says, a piece of wood fixed in the earth (Festus, at the word *Stipes*). The term *axis*, as the same Festus notes, [Col. 0966A] has various meanings (the same, at the word *Axis*). Sometimes it is used for the northern region of the sky; sometimes for the rounded shaft about which a wheel revolves, whence poets occasionally use it for the whole chariot; and finally, for a sawn plank. Tertullian appears to use the term *axis* in the second sense and to signify that martyrs were sometimes bound and burned upon a whole axle, but more frequently upon a stake—that is, a piece of wood fixed in the earth—which was shorter by half than an axle. The pagans therefore insulted all Christians with the derisive name *semaxii*.

Yet the monstrous and utterly horrible cruelty and fury of the pagans [Col. 0966B] was not sated by such great and dreadful punishments. For, in the very frenzy of Bacchanals, “they do not spare even dead Christians,” says Tertullian; “but tear them from the repose of burial, from what is a kind of asylum of death—some when already altered, others when no longer whole—and cut them up and pull them apart” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 37). In another dissertation (Dissertation on Lactantius, ch. 10, art. 2), we disclosed with what savagery the pagans raged against the bodies of dead and buried martyrs.

## ARTICLE II. How the blood of the martyrs was the seed of Christians, and possessed greater power to persuade than Cicero, Seneca, Diogenes, Pyrrho, Callinicus, and other pagan philosophers and orators

[Col. 0966C] So far were the martyrs’ punishments that we have recounted—punishments that can scarcely even be heard without horror—from deterring other Christians from professing their religion that, made stronger by them, they drew more pagans to embrace it, and thus their number was continually increased. For when the pagans themselves had witnessed the martyrs’ many and great tortures and their altogether astonishing constancy, they were thereby induced to investigate more carefully the cause of such great courage; and when they had discovered and grasped it, they became Christians.

If anyone is unwilling to believe us, let him hear our Tertullian: “Who,” he says, “on beholding the supreme constancy of some martyr amid his torments, is not shaken by contemplating it and moved to inquire what truly lies within the matter? Who, once he has inquired, does not join us? Once he has joined us, who does not desire to die?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 535). [Col. 0966D] That is, once he has recognized and confessed the truth of that religion, he then desires to end his life through any tortures and punishments whatsoever. In his address *To Scapula* he likewise spoke these words: “Everyone who beholds such great endurance is struck by some misgiving and is kindled to inquire what is at issue; and when he has learned the truth, he himself immediately follows it” (the same, *To Scapula*, ch. 4).

Thus every Christian, after professing his religion, is inflamed with supreme zeal to preserve and defend it and is, says our author, “ready for every punishment” (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 30, p. 445). “For nothing,” he used to say, “matters to us in this age except to depart from it” (*ibid.*, ch. 41, p. 489). Yet he believed that he could never depart from it [Col. 0967A] with greater glory than when crowned through martyrdom.

Therefore, as he perceptively observes, “no one is ashamed” of having embraced the Christian religion, “no one regrets it, except plainly that he was not one earlier. If he is marked out, he glories; if accused, he offers no defense; when questioned, he confesses even of his own accord; when condemned, he gives thanks” (*Apologeticus*, ch. 1, p. 269). Nor should you suppose that he asserted this too boldly or rashly. For in another book he repeats it thus: “No one is ashamed, no one regrets it, except with respect to his former life. If he is marked out, he glories; if dragged away, he does not resist; if accused, he offers no defense; when questioned, he confesses; when condemned, he gives thanks” (the same, *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 1, p. 559).

No one, therefore, regretted being a Christian, but only that he had not been one earlier or sooner; and he was afflicted with the deepest grief for his former sins, [Col. 0967B] committed in the foul darkness of idolatry. Furthermore, if someone marks him out as professing the Christian religion and for that reason he is dragged before the judges’ tribunals, he offers no defense; if accused or questioned, he does not resist, conceal, or deny, but voluntarily and with glory “confesses” (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 46, p. 511); and, far stronger than Lycurgus, of whom we shall later speak together with Tertullian (below, ch. 14, art. 3), “when condemned, he gives thanks.” Hence he concludes his *Apologeticus* with these words: “We thank you for your sentences, pagans.” Why, then? “Because when we are condemned by you, we are acquitted by God” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 536).

In precisely the same manner, Lucius, according to Saint Justin, thanked Urbicus, who had condemned him: ὁ δὲ καὶ χάριν εἰδέναι ὡμολόγει (“and he acknowledged that he owed him thanks”) [Col. 0967C] πονηρῶν δεσποτῶν τῶν τοιούτων ἀπηλλάχθαι, γινώσκων καὶ πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα καὶ βασιλέα τῶν οὐρανῶν πορεύεσθαι (“knowing that he was being freed from such wicked masters and was going to the Father and King of heaven”). He professed that he owed him thanks because he was being freed from evil masters and passing to God, the Father and King of heaven (Justin, *Second Apology to the Senate*). But this, if it were necessary, could easily be established by almost countless examples.

It is therefore no wonder that the more cruelly the pagans mowed down Christians with the sword, the more numerous were those who sprang from their blood as from the most fertile seed. But hear, I pray, our author, who addresses the pagans themselves in precisely these words: “Nor does any refinement of your cruelty accomplish anything; it is rather an attraction to the sect. We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you. The blood of Christians is seed” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 535). Elsewhere he says: [Col. 0967D] “Nor will this sect fail; you may know that it is being built up precisely when it appears to be cut down” (the same, *To Scapula*, at the end).

Indeed, this very blood of the martyrs, shed with such courage and constancy, far surpassed in eloquence absolutely all pagans—whether philosophers or others—who had exhorted anyone to endure pain and despise death. For it was “more eloquent than Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*,” as Tertullian says (the same, *Apologeticus*, loc. cit.). The first book of those disputations, to use Cicero’s own words, is “on despising death; the second, on enduring pain; the third, on alleviating distress; the fourth, on the remaining disturbances of the mind; the fifth . . . . . . teaches that [Col. 0968A] virtue is self-sufficient for living happily” (Cicero, *On Divination*, bk. II, p. 248, line 14 ff.).

The martyrs’ blood was also “more eloquent than Seneca in the *Fortuitous Events*,” a work which we have elsewhere noted to be lost (Dissertation on Lactantius, ch. 10, art. 3) and to have been cited by Lactantius (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 13). In this book Seneca had discussed contempt for death.

That blood was also “more eloquent than Diogenes,” doubtless the Cynic, whom Tertullian himself describes in another book with these words: “A human affectation fashioned into the insensibility of canine equanimity” (Tertullian, *On Patience*, ch. 2). According to Laertius, he trained himself in every respect to endure hardships and wrote a book *On Death*, in which he doubtless exhorted others to bear it patiently (Laertius, bk. VI, *Life of* [Col. 0968B] *Diogenes*, §§ 23 and 80).

Moreover, the same blood, by its supreme power of expression, surpassed Pyrrho, who, as Stobaeus notes, taught that there was no difference between life and death (Stobaeus, discourse 120, p. 606). Laertius has more about him; consult that author (Laertius, bk. IX, *Life of Pyrrho*, § 91 ff.).

Finally, this blood possessed greater eloquence than Callinicus—that is, Suctorius—who is cited by Jerome (Jerome, prolegomenon to Daniel, p. 1073) and was not only a historian but also a sophist. He published various treatises listed by Suidas and Vossius (Suidas, at the word Καλλίνικος (“Callinicus”); Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, bk. II, ch. 13, p. 225), as well as several others. Tertullian had doubtless read one of these in which Callinicus discussed patience and contempt for death.

[Col. 0968C] The blood of the martyrs therefore possessed greater persuasive power than the most eloquent discourse of any of these or of any other pagan writers. Nor was this difficult for Tertullian to prove, but evident to everyone from the following irrefutable argument: “Their words,” he says, “do not find as many disciples as Christians do by teaching through their deeds”—that is, by shedding their own blood (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 535). We have already shown how greatly the number of Christians had multiplied by Tertullian’s own time. “Indeed,” he says in addressing the pagans, “that very obstinacy with which you reproach us is a teacher” (*ibid.*).

For Pliny the Younger, whom he had cited earlier (the same, *ibid.*, ch. 2, p. 271), uses this term “obstinacy” in his letter to the emperor Trajan, in which he wrote that he had found nothing among the Christians “except obstinacy in refusing to sacrifice” [Col. 0968D] to their false gods. He then added: “Nor did I doubt that, whatever the nature of what they confessed, their perversity and inflexible obstinacy certainly deserved punishment” (Pliny, bk. X, epistle 101, p. 375).

Thus the pagans called “perversity and inflexible obstinacy” that invincible constancy of the Christians by which they preferred to be tortured and slaughtered with every kind of rack and torment rather than offer even the smallest grain of incense to fictitious gods or deny or conceal their religion. That altogether astonishing courage was therefore a teacher which fully persuaded the pagans that our religion alone was true.

## ARTICLE III. How Tertullian refutes the pagans who objected that the complaint of the Christians whom they persecuted was unjust, since those who voluntarily hastened toward torments and death—which they could have avoided by concealing their religion—ought rather to have been called mad and desperate; and by what right he overturns this disparagement through the examples of Mucius, Empedocles, Dido, Regulus, Anaxarchus, the Spartan boys, the Attic woman, Cleopatra, and the wife of Hasdrubal

[Col. 0969A]

To excuse in some fashion their monstrous and dreadful cruelty toward the Christians, the pagans replied that no injury was done to those who wished to perish; indeed, Christians ought to love those through whom they obtained the death they desired [Col. 0969B] and sought. But Tertullian shows that this reply is wholly empty and futile. For the pagans demanded that the Christians worship false gods and deny that their own God alone was the true God. This they most steadfastly refused, since the matter lay within their own power and will; and “they preferred to be condemned rather than fall away from God” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 49, p. 528)—that is, rather than fall from his divine grace by denying God against the testimony of conscience and, having avoided punishments that would shortly end and committed a supreme crime, deservedly incur eternal punishments.

Thus they plainly wished to suffer with an unconquered and cheerful spirit, but “in the same manner,” says Tertullian, “as a soldier wishes for war” (*ibid.*). This is the reading in all unpublished and published manuscripts before Rigault, who, with his customary license, entirely removed the final word, *soldier*. Yet our author’s own argument plainly appears to require it. For he compares our most holy martyrs, contending for their religion before the tribunals of tyrants, with other soldiers who fight the enemies of the commonwealth in open warfare and hand-to-hand combat (*ibid.*).

“For the martyr’s contest,” as Tertullian and later Lactantius say, is one in which, “before the tribunals of judgment and at the risk of his life” (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 11, p. 491; Tertullian, loc. cit.), he fights not with an iron weapon in his hand but by unconquered patience, and wins a victory as certain as it is glorious. Yet no soldier willingly commits himself to battle, in which, because he is exposed to danger, he trembles with natural fear. But once he has been compelled to enter battle, he fights with all his strength and then rejoices when victory has been won.

In this manner, therefore, the martyr, fighting against tyrants, dreads the danger with the fear innate in everyone. Yet he is filled with such joy over the victory won that he not only wills but even loves the contest that he can no longer avoid, and fights the tyrants with all his strength. Tertullian therefore did not think that the time of martyrdom should be anticipated through heedless rashness; but whenever it was offered, with God so permitting, it was to be undergone with unconquered courage.

Some pagans, however, who were gentler than others and more favorably disposed toward the Christians, insisted that they were mad, since they could easily, “while preserving their intention within the mind” (Tertullian, [Col. 0970A] *Apologeticus*, ch. 27, p. 433)—or by a “mental reservation,” as they call it—sacrifice to the gods and thus depart unharmed. Yet under the deceptive appearance of humanity, these people were giving the Christians advice intended to exploit their credulity. This counsel, Tertullian continues, could have emanated from no source other than the devil, the father of lies, who was attempting to entrap those same Christians either by violence and cruelty or at least by cunning and deceit.

Thus, as we have shown above (above, ch. 9, art. 5; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 357), they considered it a supreme sacrilege ever to “lie about their religion” in any fashion whatsoever, as Tertullian says. Hence they preferred to experience any tortures, however dreadful, and to be slaughtered by them rather than by even the slightest [Col. 0970B] lie, concealment, or mental reservation pretend to worship any god whom they knew to be false.

“But if it was not the act of a madman,” the pagans said, “it was certainly that of a desperate man to expose himself to every kind of punishment and to an extremely cruel death, which could most easily have been avoided by casting two or three grains of incense into the fire.” We have already observed elsewhere (Dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius, ch. 12, art. 1; and Dissertation on Lactantius, ch. 10, art. 3) that the pagans called Christians “men belonging to a ruined and desperate faction,” because they despised and did not fear every torment and every most cruel form of death. We likewise saw there how others refuted this absurd accusation. But what does Tertullian say? “There is no despair [Col. 0970C] or ruin,” he says, “where victory is by no means doubtful, where there is a certain pledge of pleasing God, and where the reward of eternal happiness is secure” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530).

But come now: with what effrontery, I ask, could the pagans accuse our martyrs of wicked desperation because they met death for their true religion with a cheerful and willing spirit (*ibid.*)? Did not those very pagans adorn many of their own people, who had voluntarily allowed themselves to be killed by the most dreadful torments and a horrible death, not only with the highest praises but also with titles of eternal glory and with statues (*ibid.*)?

For, to pass over the great number of gladiators who, as we shall say below, repeatedly lost their lives after voluntarily exposing them to beasts, while those same pagans praised them, “Mucius,” says [Col. 0970D] our author, “willingly burned his right hand upon the altar so that this deed might become his title to fame” (the same, *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4). We have discussed this very deed of Mucius elsewhere (Dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius, ch. 6, art. 3).

“Did not Empedocles,” he also says, “give his whole self to the flames of the Catanian Etna?” The manuscripts incorrectly read “the Athenian flames of Athena.” For in another book already cited by us, we read his words: “He who leapt down into the fires of Mount Etna” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 49, p. 528; and *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4). Elsewhere he says: “Because Empedocles had raved that he was a god . . . . . lest he decay in a burial-place of some finer sort, he preferred to be roasted by hurling himself into Etna” (the same, *On the Soul*, ch. 32). [Col. 0971A] Earlier, Horace had sung:

> . . . . I shall tell, and recount, the death  
> Of the Sicilian poet: while Empedocles desires  
> To be regarded as an immortal god, he coolly  
> Leaps into blazing Etna.  
>   
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, v. 463 ff.)

If you desire more, consult Laertius, Lucian, Gregory of Nazianzus, and others (Laertius, bk. VIII, *Life of Empedocles*, § 69; Lucian, *Dialogue of Menippus*, p. 142; *Icaromenippus*, p. 731; and *Histories*, bk. II, p. 398).

Tertullian then says: “A certain foundress of Carthage gave her second marriage to the funeral pyre” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530). So read all our manuscripts, both unpublished and published. Thus some people vainly think that the reading should not be “a certain woman,” but “Elissa.” For Dido is so clearly designated by these words that there is no one who would not [Col. 0971B] recognize her immediately. Hence Jerome wrote somewhere in precisely the same manner: “I shall briefly touch upon the queen of Carthage, who preferred to burn rather than marry King Iarbas” (Jerome, epistle 91, to Ageruchia; and *Against Jovinian*, bk. I). Yet, like Tertullian, when recounting the same story elsewhere, he calls her by her own name (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 18, p. 584). But not even schoolboys studying grammar, who read Virgil every day, can be ignorant of these matters.

Our author continues: “Regulus, lest he alone should live in exchange for many enemies, suffers crosses over his whole body” (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530); or, as he preferred to phrase it in another book: “Your Regulus willingly inaugurated a new form of the cross, both manifold and hidden” (the same, *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4; and [Col. 0971C] *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 31). Elsewhere, however, he explained the matter somewhat more fully in these words: “Regulus, commander of the Romans, having been captured by the Carthaginians, when he had wished that he alone be exchanged for many Carthaginian prisoners, preferred to be returned to the enemy; and, confined in a kind of chest studded on every side externally with nails, he felt so many crosses” (the same, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530).

Thus he calls this most cruel form of punishment a “new form” of the hitherto unused, “manifold cross”—that is, one fitted with sharp nails projecting on every side—and a “hidden” cross (the same, *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 18, p. 584; and *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4), because, as Tubero testifies in Aulus Gellius (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. V, ch. 4), they shut him up in that chest every day amid black and profound darkness, until they exposed him to be scorched when the sun’s rays had grown intensely hot. [Col. 0971D] We have treated this punishment of Regulus elsewhere (Dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius, ch. 6, art. 3; and Dissertation on Lactantius, ch. 10, art. 3).

We have also explained what Tertullian added concerning Anaxarchus: “When, as an example to others, he was being pounded with a pestle as though he were barley-groats, he said, ‘Pound, pound the skin-bag of Anaxarchus; for Anaxarchus himself you do not pound.’” He used “skin-bag” there in the same sense in which Lucilius, cited by Nonius, wrote “little skin-bag” for the body (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1147; Nonius, *On the Meaning of Words*, ch. 2). Arnobius likewise says: “Nothing has been promised to us for this life, nor in the little skin-bag of this morsel of flesh” (Arnobius, at the end of bk. II *Against the Pagans*). Gregory of Nazianzus, however, wrote in Greek, τὸν αὐτοῦ θύλακον (“his pouch”) (Gregory [Col. 0972A] of Nazianzus, *Iambic Poem* 18), “his vessel and wineskin.”

Tertullian then returns to examples of women and says: “An Attic courtesan, when she had already exhausted her executioner, at last bit off her own tongue and spat it into the face of the raging tyrant, so that she might spit out her power of speech as well and thus be unable to betray the conspirators” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530). He reported the same thing, though in different words, in two other books (*To the Nations*, ch. 18, p. 584; *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4, § 17). Ambrose, however, calls her “one of the Pythagorean virgins” (Ambrose, *On Virgins*, bk. I, ch. 4, § 17). See, if you please, what we noted upon this passage of Ambrose and what we said about her in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*, where we observed that the name Leaena was given to her (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1250).

Far more difficult will appear what our author immediately [Col. 0972B] added: “Zeno of Elea, when Dionysius asked him what philosophy conferred, replied, ‘Contempt for death’; subjected to the tyrant’s scourges, he sealed his statement even unto death” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530). In our manuscripts, the word *impassibilis* (“incapable of suffering”) is read before “scourges,” while the old editions have *impassibilibus*. Rigault, however, excised this word as having been improperly added by an ignorant copyist. But what if Zeno is called *impassibilis* in the sense of “unconquerable,” as one who could never be overcome by any tortures?

Perhaps Rigault would have had better grounds for saying that in this text of our author the name Dionysius had been corrupted by copyists. For Laertius expressly testified that Zeno of Elea died around the seventy-ninth Olympiad (Laertius, bk. IX, *Life of Zeno*, [Col. 0972C] § 29). But Dionysius the Elder is said to have exercised his tyranny around the ninety-fourth. Zeno therefore could neither have been tortured nor killed by him. Accordingly, it is not entirely without reason either that Tertullian may be accused of a lapse of memory, or that careless copyists may be supposed, through a far from unusual error, later to have written “Dionysius” in place of “Nearchus,” “Demysus,” or “Diomedon.” For various writers, as we have shown elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1246), relate that Zeno of Elea was tortured and killed by one of these men.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that Zeno was questioned by him about an attempted tyranny, and not, as Tertullian says, about the benefit of philosophy. For what prevents the tyrant, while questioning him about those who were privy to the treason, from having asked what philosophy provided and taught, in order by this question to reproach him more bitterly [Col. 0972D] for that crime of treason?

Finally, Tertullian closes the ranks of pagans glorying in their endurance with these words in the *Apologeticus*: “Certainly the scourging of the Spartans, made more severe even under the eyes of relatives who encourage them, confers as much honor as the blood it sheds” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530). In his book *To the Nations*, however, he declares that he wishes to pass over this matter in silence: “Not to speak of Spartan glory” (bk. I, *To the Nations*, ch. 18, p. 584); yet he stings the pagans with no less sharp a barb.

But in *To the Martyrs* he wrote more clearly that this utterly inhuman custom had continued down to his own age: “Today,” he says, “among the Lacedaemonians, the greatest solemnity is διαμαστίγωσις (“scourging”), that is, a scourging. It is no secret at what rite, before the altar, [Col. 0973A] all the young men of noble birth are beaten with scourges, while their parents and relatives stand by and urge them to persevere. For it will be accounted an ornament and a glory, with a still greater title, if the soul rather than the body yields to the blows” (the same, *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4). But we have already related more about these matters in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1246).

He also produced the examples of two women in his book *To the Nations* (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 18, p. 584). The first is called by him simply “the Queen of Egypt,” namely Cleopatra, who made use of “her beasts”—that is, of the bite of an asp secretly brought to her—and thereby brought about her own death. In *To the Martyrs* he wrote of this more explicitly: “A woman willingly sought beasts—and indeed asps, serpents more dreadful than a bull or bear—which Cleopatra [Col. 0973B] let loose upon herself lest she fall into the hands of her enemy” (*To the Martyrs*, ch. 4).

But this deed of the notorious woman has frequently been celebrated by the historians Suetonius (Suetonius, bk. II, *Life of Augustus*, § 30), Plutarch (Plutarch, *Life of Antony*, p. 954), and others, as well as by poets. It will therefore suffice to cite these verses of Horace, which are especially suited to Tertullian’s purpose:

> She dared to look upon her fallen palace,  
> Serene of countenance and brave, and to handle  
> The rough serpents, that she might drink  
> Their black venom into her body;  
>   
> Fiercer because her death was resolved,  
> Scorning, no doubt, to be carried away  
> By savage Liburnian ships and, no humble woman,  
> Be led as a private captive in a proud triumph.  
>   
> (Horace, *Odes*, bk. I, ode 37, v. 25 ff.)

[Col. 0973C] The second woman was a Carthaginian, “more steadfast than her husband Hasdrubal at the final crisis of her country,” says Tertullian (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, bk. I, ch. 18, p. 584); or, as he said elsewhere, “when Carthage was already burning, upon seeing her husband as a suppliant before Scipio, she plunged with her children into the conflagration of her country” (the same, *To the Martyrs*, ch. 4). For when she learned, after Carthage had been captured, that Hasdrubal had obtained his life from Scipio and had abandoned her, she is said to have cast herself with her children into the fires of the burning city. See Valerius Maximus (Valerius Maximus, bk. III, ch. 2, Foreign Examples, § 8) and other historical writers.

By so many examples of both men and women, Tertullian rightly demonstrates that the Christians, who met with the most willing [Col. 0973D] spirit the death inflicted upon them by the pagans solely because of their religion, were wrongly accused by those pagans of madness and despair. For the pagans heaped the highest praises and titles of honor upon their own people whom we have thus far mentioned. Christian martyrs, however, were worthy of far greater honors, since they astonishingly allowed themselves to be racked by truly dreadful tortures not for the sake of acquiring the fleeting and empty glory of men, but to obtain eternal happiness. For they held it as wholly certain that through martyrdom they would attain everlasting blessedness. But this must be explained by us somewhat more distinctly.

## ARTICLE IV. How clearly Tertullian teaches that martyrdom is a second baptism, by which the whole grace of God is secured, all sins are remitted, and a battle is fought from which victorious Christians, adorned with the palm-embroidered robe, are carried into paradise in a triumphal chariot

[Col. 0974A]

Great indeed, as we have seen, and surpassing all praise, was the utterly invincible courage of the martyrs, by which they sealed the religion received from Christ with their own blood, as with a public seal. And they certainly shed it all the more willingly because they knew with greater certainty that through martyrdom they would obtain the whole grace of God and the forgiveness of all sins. For why did the Christian so ardently desire martyrdom? “That through it,” says Tertullian, “he may purchase the whole grace of God, and secure from him complete forgiveness by the payment of his own blood” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530). If you ask the reason, he will answer at once: “For all transgressions are forgiven to this deed.” In another [Col. 0974B] book, moreover, he teaches that it is a second baptism, through which the grace of God is bestowed and all sins committed before that most sacred washing with water are wholly and completely forgiven. But let us, if you please, continue to hear him speak for himself:

> We have indeed also a second washing, itself one and unique: namely, that of blood, that is, martyrdom, concerning which the Lord says: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized,” although he had already been baptized. . . . . . . He sent forth these two baptisms from the wound in his pierced side, so that those who believed in his blood might be washed with water, and those who had washed with water might also drink his blood. This is the baptism that both supplies the place of a washing not received and restores one that has been lost.

(Idem, *De Baptismo*, ch. 16.)

We have already seen this asserted by him above (above, ch. 11, art. 5), as it was also by his disciple Cyprian, who furthermore openly proclaims [Col. 0974C] in these words that the grace of this baptism is greater than that of the first:

> We have given the first baptism to believers; let us also prepare each one for the other, making known and teaching that this is a baptism greater in grace, loftier in power, more precious in honor—a baptism in which angels baptize, a baptism in which God and his Christ rejoice, a baptism after which no one sins any longer, a baptism that completes the growth of our faith, a baptism that, as we depart from the world, immediately unites us with God. In the baptism of water the remission of sins is received; in that of blood, the crown of virtues.

(Cyprian, *De Exhortatione Martyrii*.)

Elsewhere he puts it more briefly: “Can the power of baptism,” he asks, “be greater or more excellent than confession, than suffering, so that one confesses before men and is baptized in one’s own blood?” (Id., ep. 73, to Jubaianus.) He [Col. 0974D] repeats the same things elsewhere (Idem, epistle 55; *De Oratione Dominica*), and Augustine confirms them (Augustine, *De Civitate Dei*, book XIII, ch. 7), where he shows by various words of Holy Scripture that martyrdom has as much efficacy as if one were washed in the sacred font of baptism. There he also adds: “For what is more precious than a death through which all transgressions are forgiven and merits are increased more abundantly?” Ambrose, moreover, followed the footsteps of our Tertullian more closely:

> Is there not one baptism? There is one, which the Church here hands down through water and the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Lord Jesus says: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, which you do not know.” He had, of course, already been baptized in the Jordan, as the preceding words make clear; but let this be the baptism of suffering, by which each person is also [Col. 0975A] cleansed in his own blood.

(Ambrose, *Expositio in Psalmum CXVIII*, sermon 3, § 14.)

More on these matters may be read in the scholastic theologians (*In IV Sententiarum*, distinction 4; and in the *Summa* of St. Thomas, part III, question 66, article 11).

Christians were therefore thoroughly persuaded that they never celebrated a greater triumph over the demons, the enemies of their eternal salvation, than when pagans, incited by the demons’ malicious instigations, killed them for confessing Christ. “For we never triumph more completely over them,” says our Author, “than when we are condemned for our obstinacy in the faith” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 27, p. 434), or, as we said shortly before, for its steadfast and unconquered defense. What that Christian triumph is, and how glorious, he explains in this manner:

> It is a battle for us when, [Col. 0975B] accused because of our Christian profession, we are summoned before the tribunals of the pagans, so that there, at the risk of our lives, we may contend in defense of the truth of this same religion of ours.

“In this battle,” he says, “we conquer when we are killed. In short, we emerge victorious from this battle when we are led away” (*Ibid.*, ch. 50, p. 530), that is, when, led to punishment, we are destroyed and killed. For our Author appears there to have used the word *obducimur* in this sense, although elsewhere, as we shall see, he employed it with another meaning. Since Christians desired nothing more than to die and be slaughtered in defense of their religion, they assuredly conquered when they were killed. “For victory,” Tertullian continues, “consists in obtaining that for which you have contended” (*Ibid.*).

But in this contest the victors gained both glory and spoil, and indeed the greatest of all; for [Col. 0975C] that victory, as Tertullian says, “possesses both the glory of pleasing God and the spoil of living forever” (*Ibid.*). This spoil perhaps seemed all the greater and more welcome to him because, as we noted above (above, ch. 11, art. 5), he believed that the reward of eternal blessedness, deferred for other righteous persons, was bestowed upon the holy martyrs immediately after their death and departure.

Furthermore, those who celebrated so distinguished a triumph over the world and the devil did not lack the attire of triumphers, the palm-embroidered garment, and the chariot. But what, you may ask, were these insignia of the triumphant martyrs? Certainly nothing less than those of Roman generals and emperors. “For when we are burned alive upon the stake of half an axle, of which we spoke shortly before, this,” says Tertullian, “is the attire of our victory, this is our palm-embroidered garment; in such a chariot do we triumph” [Col. 0975D] (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 50, p. 530).

First, he there mentions the “attire of victory,” a term that generally signifies all the ornaments of victory or of triumphers: namely, the golden crown, the curule chair, the ivory staff, the painted toga, the palm-embroidered tunic, and other things frequently mentioned by various writers. For brevity’s sake, however, he passes over most of these ornaments and identifies only two: the palm-embroidered garment and the triumphal chariot. Livy, however, introduces Decius speaking of these and other honors as follows:

> To whom among gods or men can it seem improper to add the insignia of pontiffs and augurs to those men whom you have honored with curule chairs, the purple-bordered toga, the palm-embroidered tunic, the painted toga, and the triumphal crown—whose houses you have made conspicuous among [Col. 0976A] the others by fastening to them the spoils of enemies—and one of whom, adorned in the apparel of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, has been carried through the City in a gilded chariot and has ascended the Capitol?

(Livy, book X, § 7.)

He said “in the apparel of Jupiter” because triumphers, as Servius observes, “possess all the insignia of Jupiter, including the palm-bearing scepter. Hence Juvenal says, ‘in Jupiter’s tunic’” (Servius, on *Eclogue* 10, v. 27, p. 55). Elsewhere Servius speaks thus about the palm-embroidered garment and the chariot:

> It must be known that the curule chair was named from the chariot, because only those who had been carried in a triumphal chariot used it; just as the tunic is called *palmata*, which those who had won the palm from their enemies deserved to wear.

(Idem, on *Aeneid* II, v. 334, p. 637.)

Does he not imply there that it was so named because it was given to those who had deserved the palm? Others, however, think it was so called because palms were woven into it. [Col. 0976B] Martial has these verses concerning it:

> Go, companion, and deserve great triumphs unharmed,  
> And return the general of the palm-embroidered toga—but return him soon.

(Martial, book VII, epigram 1.)

If anyone desires more, let him consult Octavius Ferrari (Ferrari, *De Re Vestiaria*, book II, ch. 8), Aldus Manutius (Manutius, *De Toga Romana*), Lazarus Bayfius (Bayfius, *De Re Vestiaria*, ch. 10), and Albertus Rubenius (Rubenius, *De Re Vestiaria*, book I, ch. 21), who expressly discuss the triumphal chariot. In addition, concerning these and the other insignia and ornaments of triumphers, you may, if you wish and have leisure, consult Onofrio Panvinio’s book *De Triumpho* and Mader’s annotations upon it.

But the glory of the triumph of our martyrs was far greater and altogether extraordinary. For in the midst of the flames of burning [Col. 0976C] bundles of brushwood, scorched on every side as though clothed in a purple, palm-embroidered garment, and bound to the stake and post, they were borne thence as if in a triumphal garment and chariot—not to the Capitol, but to paradise, as we saw above (ch. 11, art. 5)—triumphing over the world, over tyrants, and over the devil.

# CHAPTER XVII

## By what arguments Tertullian demonstrates that Christians were harassed and slaughtered by the pagans with the greatest injustice and contrary to the prescriptions of all laws

### ARTICLE I

#### With what perversity the pagans hated and persecuted Christians, although Christians were entirely unknown to them and although they were unwilling to investigate who or what sort of people they were

[Col. 0976D] What we have thus far said concerning the truth and holiness of the Christian religion, its divine teachings and laws, the excellent morals of its followers, and the utterly invincible courage of the martyrs, demonstrates more than sufficiently that this religion alone is true, while all the others are false and must be utterly rejected. No greater injustice, therefore, can be imagined than that of the pagans, who, because Christians defended this religion of theirs, harassed, tortured, and killed them with the utmost and most dreadful cruelty, as we have seen. But our Tertullian, in order to defend the cause of these same Christians more precisely, undertook to demonstrate two further points: first, [Col. 0977A] that Christians were condemned by the pagans contrary to every natural, divine, and human law; second, that all the crimes of which they were accused were false, and that the pagans themselves were in fact guilty of them.

Let us therefore first see by what reasoning he proved the truth of the first proposition, and then we shall come to the second. “As the first ground of your injustice toward the name of Christians,” he says, “we lay before you, governors of the Roman Empire, the injustice of your hatred—an injustice that is aggravated and refuted by the very title that seems to excuse it: namely, ignorance” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 1; and *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 1, p. 559). Some editions read “hatred” in the nominative instead of “of hatred,” but incorrectly. For “the injustice of hatred” there signifies the same thing as “unjust hatred.” Tertullian therefore first indicts the injustice of the pagans, by which they hated [Col. 0977B] Christians before they knew who or what sort of people they were. For what greater perversity is there than to hate someone when you are wholly ignorant whether he deserves hatred or love?

Our Author plainly shows that the pagans had blazed up with this blind hatred against Christians from the fact that “all who formerly hated them because they did not know the nature of what they hated, as soon as they cease to be ignorant, also cease to hate” (*Ibid.*, passage cited). In Rigault’s edition the words “the nature of what they hated” (or, as some printed editions have it, “the nature of what they had hated”) are entirely omitted. By what right—whether on Rigault’s own authority or through a printer’s error—we do not know; but we know very well that they are found in subsequent and recent editions. That they are Tertullian’s genuine words is established clearly enough both by the common agreement of all the manuscripts [Col. 0977C] and by the Author’s own manner of thought. His argument is this: when the pagans learned who and what sort of people the Christians were, and what their piety and integrity were like, they immediately ceased to hate them. Therefore, they had hated them because they previously did not know who they were.

Although no one wholly deprived of the natural light of reason could deny this, Tertullian nevertheless presses the point and further refutes the pagans by the authority of Anacharsis, who explicitly pronounced that “those without practical wisdom who judge the wise are no less culpable than those without musical knowledge who judge musicians” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 1, p. 265). Laertius presents this philosopher’s maxim as follows: Θαυμάζειν δὲ ἔφη πῶς παρὰ τοῖς ἕλλησιν ἀγωνίζονται μὲν οἱ τεχνῖται, κρίνουσι δὲ οἱ μὴ τεχνῖται (“He said that he wondered how, among the Greeks, craftsmen competed, while those who were not craftsmen acted as judges”). “He said that he wondered how, among the Greeks, craftsmen competed, while those who were not craftsmen acted as judges” (Laertius, book I, *Life of Anacharsis*, § 103).
