Plutarch reports it somewhat differently: Ἔφη δὲ κἀκεῖνο θαυμάζειν ὁ Ἀνάχαρσις ἐκκλησίᾳ παραγενόμενος, ὅτι λέγουσι μὲν οἱ σοφοὶ παρ` ἕλλησι, κρίνουσι δὲ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς (“Anacharsis also said, after attending an assembly, that he wondered that among the Greeks the wise spoke, but the ignorant passed judgment”). [Col. 0977D] “Anacharsis said this when he had attended an assembly: that he wondered that among the Greeks the wise spoke, but fools passed judgment” (Plutarch, *Life of Solon*, p. 81). You see that all these words express the same opinion, stated only in somewhat different forms: namely, that it is wrong to pass any judgment upon matters one does not understand.

But far more wicked were the pagans, who hated Christians and condemned them for abominable crimes, although [Col. 0978A] they not only did not know what sort of people they were, but, with inflexible obstinacy, were never willing either to learn or to investigate. There was no other cause of this intolerable obstinacy and willful blindness than their fear that, by learning what the Christians’ manner of life was, they would be forced to admit that, after embracing the religion of Christ, they had become better people.

The pagans, however, boldly denied that the integrity of Christians who had abandoned the worship of the gods was genuine. “For,” they said, “something is not therefore good merely because it converts many people” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 1, p. 266), that is, because it transfers them from one profession to another. “And certainly,” they said, “how many are completely transformed from good to evil?” The ancient editions have *praeformantur*, while others and our manuscripts more correctly have *performantur*; or rather, perhaps, *reformantur*, if the authority of [Col. 0978B] some manuscript supported it. The pagans added: “How many deserters go over to perversity?” These are called deserters who flee to the enemy, or who during a truce migrate to those with whom no friendship exists. Yet these men, the pagans continued, having often been converted to perversity, assuredly became worse. Finally, pressing their argument more sharply, they cried out:

> A thing is certainly not to be prejudged as good because it converts a great many people and seizes them for itself. I know of changes of mind in the direction of evil. How many deserters from the good life! How many fugitives to perversity!

(*Ibid.*; and *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 1, p. 559.)

But Tertullian replies that no one denies this; rather, everyone freely admits that very many have also converted themselves from evil to good. Yet this, he says, is readily discerned from the nature of evil and good. For the inseparable [Col. 0978C] companions of evil are fear, shame, evasion, repentance, and lamentation. “Consequently,” our Author says again, “evildoers are eager to remain hidden and avoid appearing” (Id., *Apologeticus*, ch. 1, p. 267). Rigault removed these last two words on his own authority, evidently failing to notice that they are repeated in the book *Ad Nationes* (Id., *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 1, p. 559), as are the words that immediately follow in the *Apologeticus*:

> When discovered, they tremble; when accused, they deny; even under torture they do not readily or invariably confess; when condemned, they certainly grieve; they enumerate against themselves the impulses of an evil mind, yet attribute them either to fate or to the stars.

In the book *Ad Nationes*, however, these latter words are altered as follows: “For they reproach what they were; they attribute the passage of an evil mind from innocence either to themselves or to fate” (*Ibid.*, passage cited). But perhaps in that passage the two words “or to the stars” [Col. 0978D] fell out through a copyist’s pen. Georgius Ambianensis alone, guided solely by conjecture, rather boldly placed *deonerant* in Tertullian’s text instead of *dinumerant*. For his meaning is this: evildoers acknowledge, enumerate, and reproach themselves for the impulses of an evil mind; nevertheless, they impute and ascribe the guilt for them not to themselves but to the stars or to fate. We have already seen (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s Octavius*, ch. 6, art. 4) how widespread among the pagans was the false opinion that everything happened by fate. But absolutely none of these marks of evil just mentioned are found in the Christian, who, as we observed above (preceding chapter, art. 2), is neither ashamed of nor sorry for his religion, but, when accused and interrogated, confesses [Col. 0979A] that he is a Christian, rejoices, glories, and, when condemned, gives thanks.

Tertullian therefore rightly asks: “What evil is there in this, among Christians, which does not possess the natural characteristics of evil?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 1, p. 269). In our manuscripts, however, we read: “which the nature of evil does not possess otherwise”; perhaps not altogether badly, if the particle “than” is understood there, as is by no means wholly uncommon among good authors, giving this sense: “which has no other characteristics than those possessed by the nature of evil.” But to many it will undoubtedly appear that the letter *a* was duplicated there through the ignorance or error of copyists. Consider, nevertheless, whether the first reading might not be confirmed from the book *Ad Nationes*, where it is said more briefly but no less clearly: “What kind of evil is this in which the nature of evil is absent?” (Idem, *Ad Nationes*, book I, [Col. 0979B] ch. 1, p. 560.) Indeed, our Author adds that there must be a very great good in a thing “whose accused party rejoices, and whose accusation is his desire.”

He presses the pagans still more sharply (Idem, *Apologeticus*, ch. 1, p. 264) and openly demonstrates that there was nothing evil in Christians, who, having abandoned the worship of false gods and embraced the religion of Christ, had become better people, as we have said. Nor could this be unknown to the pagans themselves, whatever protests they might raise to the contrary. For they knew how great the number of Christians was throughout the whole world; they therefore grieved deeply and complained about it both frequently and publicly. Yet however they had come to know them, they had certainly seen that from evil and dishonorable people they had become good and honorable; from the unchaste, chaste; from the unjust and criminal, chaste [the source reads *eastos*, evidently *castos*], religious, [Col. 0979C] and diligently devoted to every virtue. And certainly, as Tertullian says, they thought “Caius a good man—except that he was a Christian” (our manuscripts read “Gaius Seius”) (*Ibid.*, ch. 3, p. 280; and *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 4, p. 564). They marveled that Lucius was wise, that this woman was chaste, this son obedient to his father, and this servant faithful to his master. They indeed marveled at these and other virtues of Christians, but could not tolerate the fact that these people were Christians.

“Who, then, can deny that those are rather the ones in error,” asks our Author, “who praise what they know, condemn what they do not know, and corrupt what they know by what they do not know?” (*Ibid.*). In all our manuscripts we read *irrumpunt*, “break into,” instead of *corrumpunt*, “corrupt”; but perhaps less correctly. For in the book *Ad Nationes* it is written: [Col. 0979D] “Through the blindness of folly, they praise what they know, condemn what they do not know, and vitiate what they do not know” (passage cited), which, as you see, is the same as “corrupt.” If, however, you prefer and approve the reading “break into,” we shall not wholly oppose it. For Lucan sang concerning rumor:

> An empty rumor also reached your descendants  
> And broke into the minds of the people.

(Lucan, book I, after the middle.)

Thus, with the utmost folly, blindness, and malice, the pagans praised the virtues of Christians that were known to them, but condemned those Christians because they did not know what their name signified. On the basis of this unknown name, moreover, they vitiated or corrupted their virtues, babbling that these were either nonexistent or false. Yet nothing is certainly more unjust [Col. 0980A] than to condemn something unknown to you on the basis of something you have ascertained, or to corrupt something you have recognized on the basis of something unknown. It was no less unjust, however, to condemn and kill Christians merely because of their unfamiliar name, while never wishing to learn and investigate what good or evil there was in them. Indeed, the pagans so greatly abhorred this investigation that their utterly unjust judges never wished to hear Christians when they were brought before their tribunals. This, moreover, was the second principal point of their extreme injustice, which must now be examined.

### ARTICLE II

#### With what injustice the pagans condemned Christians without allowing them to be heard or defended, merely because of their name, and killed them with the utmost cruelty

[Col. 0980B] Tertullian’s second argument against the unbridled violence of the pagans toward Christians is certainly no less forceful and important than the preceding one. It is drawn from the most certain rule governing judicial proceedings, a rule so thoroughly consonant with natural equity that, if it is disregarded, any judgment passed upon any person is utterly unjust, invalid, and null. This, as Tertullian perceptively observes, is the rule that forbids anyone to be condemned altogether undefended and unheard (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 2, p. 276). Fully convinced of the equity of this law, the pagans had ordained that anyone accused of any crime should have recourse both to his own voice, as our Author says, and to hired advocacy—that is, to patrons who, upon receiving a fee, [Col. 0980C] would defend his cause.

But they treated Christians accused of false crimes very differently. For they never granted them any opportunity to defend their innocence either by their own speech or through anyone’s advocacy. Nevertheless, as he perceptively argues, the same treatment should have been applied to the same culpability (*Ibid.*), or, as our manuscripts and ancient editions read, to the same charge (*Ibid.*). What, therefore, could be more unjust than to grant to a pagan what was just, while denying that very thing to a Christian?

Furthermore, according to the prescriptions of all divine and human laws, every person charged with any crime must not only always be heard and questioned, but inquiry must also be made—and [Col. 0980D] even extracted by judicial examination and torture—into the nature of the crime, its place and manner, its time, and who were the accomplices and those privy to it. The pagans did not deny that this was entirely equitable, for they diligently investigated all these matters whenever one of their own was accused by someone of any crime. Yet with the greatest injustice they dismissed and scorned all these things whenever the matter concerned “our indictments,” as Tertullian says (*ibid.*), that is, the denunciation and accusation of Christians. Our manuscripts therefore read *eulogiis*, that is, “commendations,” less satisfactorily—unless one can prove that he used that term ironically. Whatever the case may be, Tertullian’s meaning is plain and evident: so far were the pagans from ever investigating, in the manner equity required, [Col. 0981A] the crimes of which Christians, like everyone else, were accused, that on the contrary every investigation of them was forbidden to all judges.

For when Pliny the Younger asked the emperor Trajan what should be done with Christians, whose number was almost infinite, Trajan, says Tertullian, “replied that this class of persons should not indeed be sought out, but that, when brought forward, they ought to be punished” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 2, p. 273). Trajan’s own words in his letter to Pliny are these: “They are not to be sought out; if they are denounced and proved guilty, they are to be punished” (Pliny the Younger, book X, epistle 102, p. 377); that is, according to our Tertullian’s interpretation, if they are shown and proved actually to be Christians, they are indeed to be punished, but by no means [Col. 0981B] sought out. Eusebius cited this entire passage from Tertullian (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ch. 33, p. 106), interpreting in Greek the words we have quoted as follows: Τὸ τῶν χριστιανῶν φύλον μὴ ἐκζητεῖσθαι μὲν, ἐμπεσὸν δὲ κολάζεσθαι (“The Christian people are not to be sought out, but if encountered, are to be punished”). Rufinus rendered them into Latin: “Christians are not indeed to be sought; yet if any are encountered, they are to be punished” (Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, ch. 27). Tertullian therefore had no doubt that this edict pronounced that Christians were not to be sought out, but that as soon as they were brought before the judges and it was established that they were Christians, they were to be punished without any further investigation whatsoever. Nor was he wrong. For Trajan immediately added:

> Yet with this qualification: whoever denies that he is a Christian and makes this manifest by the act itself—that is, by supplicating our gods—[Col. 0981C] although he may have been under suspicion in the past, shall obtain pardon through repentance.

(Pliny, *ibid.*)

He therefore wished no crime of the Christians to be investigated by the judges; instead, merely because they had been brought forward and merely because of their name, he wished them to be punished without any further hearing, unless perhaps they denied that name of theirs and supplicated the false gods.

Tertullian therefore rightly exclaims: “O judgment entangled by necessity!” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 2, p. 273). He deliberately said “by necessity,” because Trajan could not explain it more clearly. Yet it is entangled because Trajan says, as our Author rightly argues (*ibid.*), that Christians must not be sought out, on the ground that they are innocent and guilty of no crime; nevertheless, he orders them to be punished as guilty persons privy to the gravest crimes. This same judgment, therefore, [Col. 0981D] “both spares and rages, overlooks and punishes” (*Ibid.*). For it makes a show of clemency by sparing Christians who were not brought before the judges, but rages against those who were brought forward, although innocent, ordering them to be punished merely because of their name.

Thus, in the entire case of the Christians, nothing else was demanded, as Tertullian further says, but “a confession of the name, not an examination of the crime” (*Ibid.*, p. 271), nor any defense of the accused. To condemn or acquit them, it was enough merely that they should either deny or confess their name—that is, that they were Christians.

He further demonstrates [Col. 0982A] how unjust this was, and how contrary to every divine, natural, and human law, from the judicial examinations that the laws command to be conducted by scourging and torture. For they ought to be employed for no other reason than that crimes may be uncovered and those accused of them may confess that they committed them. Indeed, all enactments of rulers—provided they are not tyrants—just decrees of the senate, and other laws that are not altogether unjust, command, in our Author’s words, “that the evil be brought to light, not concealed; that those who confess be condemned, not acquitted” (*Ibid.*, p. 276; and *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 2, p. 560). He wrote similarly to the judge Scapula: “What further instruction is given to you than to condemn the guilty who confess, but to send those who deny back to torture?” (Idem, *Ad Scapulam*, ch. 4.)

Nevertheless, contrary to this rule for judging defendants, prescribed with such great equity, the pagans [Col. 0982B] compelled Christians by the cruelest torments of judicial examination not to confess any crime, but to deny. They must therefore have been persuaded that the Christians were innocent and guilty of no crime, since they wished them to deny it—or else, which is wicked, they wished them, if they were guilty, to lie outright. For when tortured under examination, they confessed and openly cried out that they were Christians. But the pagans, although it was unlawful for them to torture other defendants further once they had confessed, ordered Christians to be tortured more savagely until they denied or were killed.

Tertullian therefore rightly presses them as follows:

> You see how you yourselves act contrary to your instructions, compelling those who have confessed to deny. You thus acknowledge that we are innocent, since you are unwilling to condemn us immediately upon our confession.

(Idem, *Ad Scapulam*, ch. 4.)

Certainly, through so great a violation of [Col. 0982C] their own laws, these men most manifestly condemned themselves. For they persecuted Christians without hearing or defending them, as though they were guilty of every crime against the gods, the laws, the emperors, morality, and nature itself. Therefore, while striving to force them through torture to deny such things, they assuredly confessed that those crimes were as false as the Christians’ innocence and integrity were supreme. Thus, in this dreadful persecution of those same Christians, there was nothing else, as Tertullian said, but “a battle over the Christian name” (Idem, *Apologeticus*, ch. 2, p. 279), in which those who denied were acquitted, while those who confessed were tortured.

Nor should you think that anything there was either invented or exaggerated by him. For precisely the same public protest had been made not only [Col. 0982D] by Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, and Tatian, as we have seen elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 351, 356, 471, and 523), but also by Melito, as Eusebius reports (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 26, p. 147). They openly complained that, although no name is good or evil in itself, Christians were nevertheless condemned merely on account of their designation, without their case ever being heard. Minucius Felix, as we showed above (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s Octavius*, ch. 8, art. 2), and Cyprian, as we shall say below, pierced the pagans with the same weapon, though turned somewhat differently.

Nor did the pagans take much care to conceal this extreme injustice, which they publicly proclaimed in the judgment issued against Christians on a tablet, such as Cicero [Col. 0983A] (*In Verrem*, book V, p. 179, line 19; oration 39, *Pro Rabirio*, p. 561, final line; oration 23, *Pro Flacco*, p. 369, line 47; oration 37, *In L. Pisonem*, p. 543) and others frequently mention. On this tablet, indeed, no crime of the Christians was recorded, as was done for others condemned to death, but only the name of Christian. “From the tablet,” Tertullian says in addressing them, “you read out that he is a Christian” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 2, p. 279), and nothing more. But since the matter stands thus, he continues, certainly: “If ‘Christian’ is the name of no crime, it is exceedingly absurd if the crime consists in the name alone” (Tertullian, *ibid.*). This is the reading in Rigault’s edition. In our manuscripts, however, it reads: “If the Christian is guilty of the name of no crime, it is exceedingly incestuous”—more recent editions have “uncertain”—“if the crime consists in the name alone.” [Col. 0983B] In some manuscripts and in printed editions earlier than Rigault: “If the Christian is guilty of no crime, the name is exceedingly hostile, if the crime consists in the name alone.” This appears to be Tertullian’s genuine reading; in other manuscripts the word “name” was transposed and the other word, “incestuous,” corrupted. For Tertullian’s meaning is that the Christian name was exceedingly hateful to the pagans, and that merely because of it, and for absolutely no other crime, they tortured and killed Christians so cruelly.

But no hatred of a name, Tertullian insists (*ibid.*, ch. 3, p. 281), can possibly be conceived unless it signifies something barbarous or inherently vicious, or unless hatred is directed toward unknown persons who are called by it. Yet the pagans could discover nothing [Col. 0983C] vicious in Christians, whom they were unwilling to hear even once. Nor was there anything barbarous in the name “Christian,” which, says Tertullian, “is derived from anointing” (*Ibid.*, p. 281). The ignorant pagans made not the slightest advance by prattling that they should be called *Chrestians*, not Christians. For this very name is derived from sweetness or kindness (*Ibid.*). We have discussed elsewhere the etymology of both names (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 17, art. 1).

### ARTICLE III

#### How absurdly the pagans alleged that Christians should be hated because of their own name or that of their founder, although no philosopher is said to hate Platonists, Epicureans, Pythagoreans, Stoics, or Academics; no physician, Erasistratus; no grammarian, Aristarchus; and no cook, Apicius—the founders of their respective schools—because of their name

[Col. 0983D] Since there is nothing clearer even than the noonday sun that the human intellect, blinded by the prejudices of false religion, does not attempt to obscure, it is certainly no wonder that the pagans tried by contentious arguments to evade or weaken the utterly invincible arguments advanced by our Author in defense of Christians. Nevertheless, those who were unwilling to hear Christians must themselves be heard, and their arguments, whatever they may be, must be examined.

They loudly asserted that there was no need to investigate the crimes of Christians, since all of them were comprehended in their one name. [Col. 0984A] But we have already shown that these crimes were utterly false. Yet suppose, if you can, that they were as true as they are false: should a murderer, or any other criminal, be condemned merely because of his name? Are not judges bound to hear him and to investigate where, when, how, and with what accomplices he committed the crime? Christians, however, were condemned contrary to these most equitable laws, as we have said. The judgment of the pagans was therefore utterly unjust (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 2, p. 279; and *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 6, p. 566).

The pagans nevertheless insisted: “The Christian sect is hated under the name, of course, of its founder” (*Ibid.*, p. 282). Should it not therefore have been examined whether that founder or his followers truly deserved to be hated? Tertullian [Col. 0984B] demonstrates most clearly that by this absurd argument the pagans cut themselves down with their own sword, as the saying goes. For they did not hate Platonists because of Plato’s name, Epicureans because of Epicurus’, Pythagoreans because of Pythagoras’, or Stoics because of Zeno’s (*Ibid.*). Yet these men, as we have shown elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, ch. 17, art. 1 ff., p. 1123 ff.), had been the founders of their respective schools. Tertullian then lists the Academics, whom he evidently distinguishes from the Platonists (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 3, p. 282). Should he therefore be said to have been speaking of Arcesilaus and Lacydes, the leaders of the Middle and New Academies, as we observed in the same place? Consider, I ask, and decide.

[Col. 0984C] He continues: did not physicians, he asks, derive their name from Erasistratus, who is called “a renowned physician” by Aulus Gellius (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XVII, ch. 11), and “the most renowned of the ancient physicians” by Macrobius (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book VII, ch. 15)? Strabo, moreover, attested that in Smyrna, in the time of his fathers, there existed an Erasistratean school of medicine (Strabo, *Geography*, book XII, p. 580). Plutarch (*Symposium*, book IV, question 1, p. 603; book VII, question 1, p. 698; and *Life of Demetrius*, p. 907), Pliny (*Natural History*, book XXIX, ch. 1, p. 663), Valerius Maximus (book V, ch. 7, § 1), and the author of the Eusebian *Chronicle* (*Chronicle of Eusebius*, at the year 1755) also made mention of this most celebrated physician.

[Col. 0984D] Finally, Tertullian says, cooks too were named after Apicius, whom elsewhere he numbers among the most extravagant cooks and whose seasonings he ridicules (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 3, p. 5; *De Pallio*, final chapter; and *De Anima*, ch. 33). From Athenaeus, moreover, we learn that this man was exceedingly wealthy in the age of the emperor Tiberius, but abandoned to luxury; that through the vice of his belly and appetite he squandered many myriads of coins; and that various kinds of cakes were called by his name (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae*, bk. I, ch. 1, p. 7). Seneca also says much about him, but we shall transcribe only these words, which bear more directly upon our purpose: “Apicius lived within our own memory; in that city from which philosophers were once ordered to depart as corrupters of the young, [Col. 0985A] he professed a science of his own and infected the age with his teaching” (Seneca, *De Consolatione ad Helviam*, ch. 10, p. 781). Elsewhere Seneca, like Pliny (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. IX, ch. 17, p. 308) and Jerome, recalled Apicius (Jerome, *Adversus Jovinianum*, bk. II), his gluttony, and his boundless appetite. Casaubon, moreover, identifies three men named Apicius, all infamous for the vice of gluttony (Casaubon on Athenaeus, bk. II, ch. 6, p. 22 ff.). In the preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 23, art. 4), we cited more than once the treatise on cookery published under the name of Apicius. You will not need great effort to persuade us that this is the man of whom Tertullian speaks.

[Col. 0985B] But whoever he may have been, no gentile ever said that a sect founded by anyone deserved hatred solely because of his name, or because of the names of the others whom we have reviewed, unless it had first been established that there was something evil in it. The gentiles, therefore, ought not to have hated the Christians either because of their own name or because of the name of their founder, unless they had first ascertained that they were wicked. Yet we have already shown that those same gentiles neither knew, nor wished ever to know or investigate, whether the Christians did anything that ought to be pursued with hatred and punishment.

On the contrary, however, it was entirely unknown to no one that Christians were immediately condemned merely under their designation, or solely on account of their name, by the proceedings and judgments of provincial governors before whom they had been brought. For, Tertullian said, we now call upon your own records—that is, the records of the judges—as witnesses that Christians are condemned by them for this name alone: [Col. 0985C] “You who preside each day over the trial of prisoners,” that is, of those committed to prison, “who conclude the indictments by your sentences” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 44, p. 496), or examine the accusations against defendants: has anyone among all of them been found to be an assassin or murderer? Any purse-snatcher (*ibid.*; cf. Festus, s.v. *Manticularius*), that is, one who stole money stored in other people’s purses? Any robber of bathers, or, as he says elsewhere, a thief of the baths, who stole the clothes or silver of people while they were bathing? Yet certainly all these were pagans (Apuleius, *Apology* 1, near the end), and among them you found no true follower of the Christian religion. “For it is not with our people,” Tertullian continues, “but with yours that the prison is always seething” (Plautus, *Captivi*, act IV, scene 2), and it is entirely filled with your criminal gentiles. [Col. 0985D] “It is with your people, too, that the mines are always sighing” (Tertullian, *De Fuga*, ch. 13)—namely, with those who, having been convicted of crimes, were compelled to dig in the mines. Finally, “it is with your people that the beasts are always fattened; it is from your people that the providers of public shows always feed their herds of criminals” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 44, p. 497). The providers of public shows, as we have already observed elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 13, art. 1; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 27, art. 1), were those who presented gladiatorial spectacles. They fed and maintained criminals who, after being condemned to the beasts, had to fight them. If the men were defeated, the victorious beasts were then fattened upon their flesh.

Accordingly, no Christian belonged to their number [Col. 0986A] because he had been thrown into prison or condemned to the beasts for any crime, but solely because of his name, which contained absolutely nothing evil. For Tertullian openly and emphatically declares: “No one there is a Christian unless it is for this alone, because of his name; or, if he is also guilty and convicted of something else”—that is, of some capital crime—“he is now no Christian” (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*), but an apostate and deserter from the Christian religion. Nothing, therefore, was more unjust or more contrary to divine and human laws than to condemn innocent Christians, never heard or permitted to defend themselves, solely because of their name, and to torture and kill them with punishments of every possible severity.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### How absurdly the gentiles objected that certain laws of their own bound them to harass and kill the Christians, although they themselves so often violated even the more sacred laws with impunity

[Col. 0986B]

### ARTICLE I

#### By what arguments Tertullian shows that no law or authority can compel any person to worship a god whom he knows to be false, or deprive anyone of the freedom to embrace the religion he believes to be true

The gentiles, driven into the greatest straits, sought refuge in the authority of their laws as though in their final stronghold. “We are bound,” they said, “by our laws, which command that Christians be harassed [Col. 0986C] and tortured even to death. In order to torture them, therefore, it is enough for us to know that they really are Christians; there is no further need to inquire who or what sort of people they are” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 3, p. 282). But Tertullian replies that this argument is empty and utterly absurd, and addresses the gentiles themselves as follows: “If through your laws you consider it lawful and necessary to condemn Christians without hearing or defending them, you profess violence and an unjust domination from the citadel” (*ibid.*); “from the citadel,” he says—that is, perhaps, from the elevated summit of the state itself (*ibid.*, ch. 1, p. 259), as he had said at the beginning of this book. For one who condemns any accused person without hearing his case and orders him to be killed is undoubtedly not discharging the office of an equitable judge, but exercising a most unjust domination and an intolerable tyranny.

[Col. 0986D] Yet, to break the obstinacy of the gentiles completely, he draws another argument from the fact that they granted every individual the freedom to worship any god whatever except the one true God. For after saying that one god was freely and lawfully worshipped by one person and another by someone else, he presses them as follows: “Take care that it does not contribute to an indictment of irreligion to take away freedom of religion and forbid the choice of a divinity, so that I may not be permitted to worship whom I wish, but am compelled to worship whom I do not wish” (*ibid.*, ch. 24, p. 418). Religious worship, he says, must be free and voluntary, and no one can ever be compelled by any person or any law to embrace a religion which he knows to be false: “For the performance of a divine rite,” as he later said, “requires a willing mind” (*ibid.*, [Col. 0987A] ch. 28, p. 435). If you ask for his reason, he will give you this: “It is a matter of human right and natural liberty that each person worship what he has thought proper; another person’s religion neither harms nor benefits anyone else. Nor is it the part of religion to compel religion, which ought to be undertaken voluntarily, not by force, since sacrifices too are demanded from a willing mind. Thus, even if you compel us to sacrifice, you will render no service to your gods. For they will not desire sacrifices from the unwilling, unless they are contentious. But God is not contentious” (the same author, *Ad Scapulam*, ch. 2).

You certainly hear with what weighty arguments our Author shows that it is contrary not only to human but also to natural right for anyone ever to be compelled by any force to adopt a false religion or the worship of a false god. For the religion of any person neither benefits [Col. 0987B] nor harms another, who is made neither better nor worse by his neighbor’s good or evil.

Next, God does not desire sacrifices from one who is unwilling and resistant, unless he is contentious—that is, unless he wishes to sow disputes and quarrels. But such a God can by no means be the true God. Indeed, Tertullian further says: “No one will wish to be worshipped by an unwilling person, not even a man” (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 418). For pretence and wicked hypocrisy are plainly to be condemned when someone outwardly feigns worship of one whom inwardly he despises and detests.

Moreover, such is certainly human frailty that a person offends the true God again and again. Yet he cannot appease Him except by a free and sincere conversion and repentance of mind, or by a sacrifice performed with the fullest freedom. [Col. 0987C] Therefore, without the greatest injustice, no one can compel me to sacrifice to Jupiter or to any other god whose favor or anger toward me I do not care about—much less if I have learned with absolute certainty that he was a man and no longer exists.

Tertullian presses the point further: “Let one person,” he says, “worship God, another Jupiter; let one stretch suppliant hands toward heaven, another toward the altar of Faith; let one, if that is what you think, count the clouds while praying, another the ceiling panels; let one dedicate his own soul to his god, another the soul of a goat” (*ibid.*). Ought not all these persons either to be tolerated or condemned by an equal right, without one rather than another being deprived of the liberty to worship whom he wishes?

But these words of Tertullian are not altogether clear and transparent, and there may perhaps be room to doubt whether [Col. 0987D] he is speaking only of the gentiles or of them together with the Christians, as many have thought. What if he should be said to have designated both groups and, in addition, the Jews? For he could have written of Christians and Jews: “Let one worship God”—that is, the one and almighty God—and of the pagans: “another Jupiter,” as no one fails to understand. Of the same Christians he could also have said: “Let one stretch suppliant hands toward heaven.” For, as we have seen (above, ch. 14, art. 3), they prayed to God with outstretched hands. Although a pagan might pray to his gods in a similar manner, Tertullian nevertheless seems to contrast him with the Christian when he says in the same place: “But let another”—namely, a gentile—“similarly stretch his hands toward the altar of Faith.” Our manuscripts read [Col. 0988A] *of Phidias*, but undoubtedly through a copyist’s error. Perhaps *of Fidius* would be a more tolerable reading, whom the gentiles, as Ovid sings, believed to be Jupiter’s son and a god (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. VI, § 4). Yet *of Faith* is correct, for Faith had a temple on the Capitol as a goddess, as we have observed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 866).

The subsequent words of our Author seem to concern the Jews: “Let one, if that is what you think, count the clouds while praying.” For Juvenal sang of these same Jews:

> Some, whose lot was to have a father who revered the Sabbath,  
> Worship nothing but the clouds and the divinity of heaven.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 16, v. 916.)

But why did Tertullian add: “if that is what you think”? Did he not wish by these words to designate those same Jews whom [Col. 0988B] the gentiles falsely believed to worship both the clouds and the heavens? Tertullian contrasts with him another, a gentile, who worshipped the ceiling panels—namely, of his temples—as we shall show below. He continues: “And let another,” he says—suppose, a Christian—“dedicate and consecrate his own soul to his God”; but, by contrast, “let another,” a pagan, “dedicate the soul of a goat to a false god.” For Virgil sings:

> Therefore we shall duly render Bacchus his proper honor  
> With ancestral songs, and bring platters and sacrificial cakes;  
> And, led by the horn, the sacred goat will stand at the altar.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. II, v. 393.)

And Martial:

> Harmful to the vine, at your rose-decked altars, Bacchus,  
> Stood the goat, about to die, a victim welcome to your rites.  
> (Martial, bk. III, epigram 24.)

Yet what prevents Tertullian from attributing all these things [Col. 0988C] not to Christians and Jews, but to gentiles alone? Did not Menoeceus, Codrus, and Curtius, whom we discussed in the preceding dissertation after Lactantius (Lactantius, bk. III, ch. 12, p. 370; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 10, art. 4), dedicate their souls to the gods? Aristophanes, moreover, portrays Socrates praying to and invoking the clouds (Aristophanes, comedy *Clouds*, act I, scene 3). The gentiles too prayed to their gods with hands raised toward heaven, as has been said. Tertullian therefore appears rather to be speaking of them alone, and his argument would thereby acquire greater force. “Quite right,” you will say, “were it not that he contrasts with Jupiter God, doubtless the true God, whom he afterward again names in the singular.” But what prevents him from having contrasted with Jupiter, the greatest god of the gentiles, any other god, whether of the greater or the lesser [Col. 0988D] nations? In whatever way his words are understood, he quite rightly concludes from them that the gentiles, contrary to every law and principle of justice, deprived Christians of the ability to worship the true God. For under their rule everyone else was permitted to worship not only Jupiter, but any false and ridiculous god whatever, with the sole exception of the one true God. With the same indulgence with which these impious men, in their cruelty, took from Christians the liberty to honor the true God, they allowed, in every city and province, as will be said below, any person to worship and adore whatever god he pleased, even if that god was wholly unknown to others.

But we now seem to hear someone whispering in our ear that Tertullian has there wandered completely from the road, [Col. 0989A] since by these arguments he seeks to prove that everyone ought to be granted the freedom to worship whatever god he wishes, whether true or false, and to choose a religion at his own discretion. Did Tertullian, then, truly lose his senses—he who, as we have seen, strives with all the powers of his intellect to demonstrate that the Christian religion alone is true and must be professed, while all the others are false and must be rejected; who plainly and thoroughly maintains that it is the greatest wickedness for a Christian to deny or even conceal his religion; who heaps every praise upon our martyrs precisely because they preferred to be tortured and killed by any of the most dreadful torments rather than burn three grains of incense to false gods, and because with altogether marvelous constancy they shed their blood in defense of their faith and religion? Had he thought otherwise, he would plainly have wasted his labor, and without any purpose, in composing his *Apologeticum* and other similar [Col. 0989B] books. His arguments, therefore, have no other aim than to demonstrate that no one can be compelled to abandon the true religion and embrace a false one, and that the gentiles were most unjust because they granted everyone freedom to worship any god, even one unknown to others, while depriving only the Christians, who worshipped the true God, of that freedom.

But someone else will ask us why Tertullian asserts so emphatically that religion is voluntary, when elsewhere he explicitly said: “It is proper for heretics to be compelled to their duty, not enticed. Their hardness must be overcome, not persuaded” (Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, ch. 2). Let him ask Rigaltius, however, how our Author wishes the hardness of heretics to be overcome and them to be recalled to their duty, [Col. 0989C] and he will hear: not by force or bodily coercion, but by the spiritual weapons of divine Scripture and by divine authority. And indeed Tertullian himself continues as follows: “And surely that will be adjudged sufficiently excellent which is proved to have been established and commanded by God.” Accordingly, he refutes and conquers them there with these weapons.

We may add that the case of heretics and that of gentiles is not the same. For whatever you may say ought to be determined concerning heretics, who acknowledged the true God but fell away from the Church through their errors and crimes, it was nevertheless never lawful for the pagans, as Tertullian rightly says, to drive Christians by torments and tortures to the veneration of false gods. [Col. 0989D] For no one is driven—or indeed even led—into error without guilt. But nothing prevents heretics from being recalled by legitimate authority to the truth which they abandoned.

### ARTICLE II

#### How foolishly the gentiles pleaded, when torturing and destroying Christians, that they were bound by certain imperial laws, although Lycurgus’ laws had themselves been amended—whereupon he brought about his own death by starvation—and other laws had been abrogated by the Romans, especially the Julian and Papian laws and those ordering debtors to be cut into two parts; and what those laws were

No one can ever be bound by any law, except a most unjust one, to worship a false god. [Col. 0990A] Yet, as Tertullian rightly says, “an unjust law has no claim to honor” (Tertullian, *Ad Nationes*, bk. I, ch. 6, p. 566), nor has it ever bound the conscience of any person. Christians, therefore, could not be compelled by any human law to worship fictitious gods. With what effrontery, then, could the gentiles object that they were bound by certain laws of their emperors to torture and kill Christians, when they could not deny that very many laws had been enacted by men of even greater authority—as we have already seen in the preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 28, art. 1)—in accordance with human weakness and the circumstances of their times, but that for this very reason they boldly and with impunity amended, despised, and trampled upon them? How could they have denied something known to everyone, not only through Cicero’s most certain testimony (Cicero, *De Legibus*, bk. I, p. 328, line 5 [Col. 0990B] ff.), but also through the constant experience of every age? It was therefore hardly necessary for Tertullian to prove it by various examples, and by far more than was appropriate. Nevertheless, because, as they say, excess does no harm, he assembled a great many laws enacted by various legislators and afterward either amended or rendered obsolete by their peoples, so that at last he might utterly silence the gentiles, who constantly and ad nauseam invoked against the Christians the authority of the laws enacted concerning them. We have therefore considered it our duty to follow all his footsteps and, to the best of our ability and in our customary manner, to elucidate the particular statements he made concerning the ancient laws of the gentiles, their authors, amendment, and abrogation.

He begins with the most ancient legislator, Lycurgus, [Col. 0990C] whose laws, he says, when amended by the Lacedaemonians, inflicted such grief upon their author that in retirement he passed judgment upon himself by starvation; or, as elsewhere he said in different words conveying the same meaning, “he chose *apokarteresis*” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 4, p. 286; and ch. 46, p. 512)—that is, he died by voluntary hunger and starvation. Why, I ask you, did the Lacedaemonians amend these laws unless because they judged them imperfect and neither useful nor suitable to themselves? Pausanias recorded that he took refuge in a certain village named Alpium after one of his eyes had been struck out by Alcander, who had disliked his laws (Pausanias, bk. III, p. 100). Valerius Maximus recounts this somewhat more fully in the following words: “Even the laws which Lycurgus devised for the public welfare could not protect him from encountering hostile [Col. 0990D] citizens. For he was frequently attacked with stones, was once expelled in a public frenzy, was even deprived of an eye, and at last was driven from his very homeland” (Valerius Maximus, bk. V, ch. 3, foreign example § 2). But both authors were silent about the kind of death by which he ended his life. Aelian writes that when Lycurgus wished to imbue the Lacedaemonians with justice, his eye was put out either by a stone hurled from ambush or by a blow from a staff (Aelian, *Varia Historia*, bk. XIII, ch. 23), as various writers had reported. More pertinent to our subject, however, he expressly cites Ephorus as a witness that Lycurgus died of hunger in exile. But Aelian did not say there whether this hunger was voluntary. Our Author, therefore, follows Plutarch more closely, for Plutarch explicitly writes that Lycurgus bound [Col. 0991A] the kings, senate, and citizens by oath to observe his laws diligently until he returned from Delphi (Plutarch, vol. I, *Life of Lycurgus*, p. 57). And so that they might not be released from the religious obligation of their oath, *ἐτελεύτησεν ἀποκαρτερήσας* (“he died by starving himself”); he caused his own death by starvation. Yet this did not prevent the Lacedaemonians from despising and abolishing not only their oath, but also his laws.

Our Author then passes to the Romans and addresses them in these words: “Do not you too every day, as experience illuminates the darkness of antiquity”—that is, taught by your own experience—“lop and cut down that whole old and squalid forest,” or infinite and obscure multitude of ancient laws, “with the new axes of imperial rescripts and edicts,” that is, with new rescripts of the emperors (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 4, p. 286)? [Col. 0991B] In the edition of Rigaltius and those following it, however, the reading is “clear and cut the soil”; but by what authority neither he told us, nor can we ascertain anything except that this reading conflicts with all the manuscripts and even with the Puteanus copy which he had before him. We are nevertheless aware that Tertullian wrote elsewhere: “He undertook to cultivate everything, to weed it and clear the soil, so that from it, as though from shoots and slips, peoples might be planted from peoples and cities from cities throughout every region of the world” (the same author, *De Pallio*, ch. 2). But who has ever been permitted to transfer a word from one book of an author into another in defiance of the protest of all the manuscripts? Whichever way one reads, our Author’s meaning is sufficiently clear: the bristling forest of ancient laws was cleared and pruned by new imperial edicts, through which many things were uprooted like [Col. 0991C] harmful weeds. The gentiles therefore boasted in vain, and with such clamor, of the authority of their laws against the Christians.

To demonstrate this point further, Tertullian immediately added: “Did not Severus, the most resolute of emperors, only yesterday, after so venerable an old age, set aside the utterly futile Papian laws, which compel the begetting of children before the Julian laws permit marriage to be contracted?” (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 4, pp. 286–287). He clearly teaches there that these Julian laws were amended by the Papian laws, but that both were abrogated by the emperor Severus. There were various Julian laws, so called after Julius Caesar. The Papian—or, more properly, Poppaean—laws took their name from Papius and Poppaeus, suffect consuls in the time of Caesar Augustus. Everyone readily concedes that Tertullian designates the Julian law concerning the marriage of the [Col. 0991D] orders. But Herold frankly confesses that he does not sufficiently understand how the Papian law compelled children to be begotten before the Julian law ordered marriage to be contracted (Herold, notes on Tertullian), while Antonio Agustín acknowledges that the matter is unknown to him (Agustín, *De Legibus*, ch. 18). Yet it is certain that, as Dio (Dio, *Roman History*, bk. IV, p. 256), Cornelius Tacitus (Tacitus, *Annals*, bk. III, before the middle), and Suetonius report (Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, § 34), this Julian law was revised by Caesar Augustus more severely than the others. For besides the rewards proposed for those who had begotten children, he imposed heavier penalties upon the unmarried and celibate, penalties which he was later compelled to mitigate because of the disturbance raised by those who resisted. [Col. 0992A] Suetonius further adds: “When he perceived that the force of the law was being evaded by the immaturity of betrothed girls and frequent changes of marriages, he shortened the period for having a betrothed and imposed a limit upon divorces” (Suetonius, *ibid.*). Can it not be inferred from the words “the immaturity of betrothed girls” that, because of the multitude of those previously destroyed in civil and other wars, the emperor Augustus decreed that maidens should marry even when they were not yet sufficiently grown or mature for a husband? If that is Suetonius’ meaning, the following appears to be Tertullian’s: the Poppaean law enacted that maidens be given in marriage at an earlier age, before they could have contracted it under the Julian law. And indeed we learn from Dio that the same Augustus decreed that a betrothal agreement should be void if the marriage were postponed beyond two years—that is, as [Col. 0992B] Dio himself says, the maiden whom a man wished to betroth should be ten years old and the marriage should not be deferred beyond two years (Dio, *Roman History*, bk. LIV, p. 609). But if a girl could be betrothed and marry in the tenth year of her age, she was therefore compelled, as Tertullian says, to bear children even though under the Julian law she could enter into marriage only in her twelfth year. See, if you please, the annotations of Gothofredus (Gothofredus, *Codex Theodosianus*, p. 226 ff.) and others on the third law concerning betrothals; and consider, I ask you, whether this interpretation of Tertullian’s words, or some other that you may devise, pleases you more.

[Col. 0992C] There can be no doubt, however, that the emperor Severus abrogated that part of both the Julian and Poppaean laws and assigned a time at which maidens might marry at a mature age. For Tertullian asserts that this was done “yesterday,” that is, in his own time. Furthermore, we learn from Marcian that something in the Julian laws was amended by the same Severus (*Digest*, bk. XXIII, title 2, law 19). Elsewhere we showed (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 18, art. 3, p. 1153) that Constantine the Great removed the penalties which those Julian and Poppaean laws had decreed against the unmarried and childless. But these developments occurred after the time of our Tertullian.

Finally, Rigaltius thinks that Tertullian called these laws “utterly futile” because Christians, believing that the end of the ages was imminent and yearning for mortal life to be exchanged for eternal life, not unreasonably regarded it as vain and foolish to think about begetting children. [Col. 0992D] But we have seen that those same Christians were accustomed to pray for a delay of this end. We shall therefore be more readily persuaded that our Author said this from his zeal for chastity and virginity, virtues which Christians cultivated with as much ardor as the gentiles held them in contempt and scorned them.

Tertullian then immediately continues: “In former times there were laws that men adjudged debtors should be cut into parts by their creditors. Yet by public consent this cruelty was afterward erased” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 4, p. 287). This was one of the most ancient laws, first included in the Ten and afterward in the Twelve Tables, which, according to Livy, amid the immense heap of laws accumulated one upon another, “are the source of all public and private law” [Col. 0993A] (Livy, bk. III, §§ 34–35). Aulus Gellius will teach you what that law was and in what words it was framed: in one place he gives its beginning (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. XV, ch. 13, p. 821), and elsewhere transcribes the whole of it as follows:

> FOR AN ACKNOWLEDGED DEBT AND FOR MATTERS ADJUDGED AT LAW, THIRTY DAYS SHALL BE ALLOWED. THEREAFTER THERE SHALL BE A LAYING ON OF HANDS. THE DEBTOR SHALL BE BROUGHT INTO COURT. UNLESS HE SATISFIES THE JUDGMENT, OR SOMEONE COMES FORWARD IN COURT TO GUARANTEE IT FOR HIM, THE CREDITOR SHALL TAKE HIM AWAY WITH HIM. HE SHALL BIND HIM EITHER WITH A THONG OR WITH SHACKLES WEIGHING FIFTEEN POUNDS, NOT LESS; OR, IF HE WISHES, HE MAY BIND HIM WITH HEAVIER ONES. IF THE DEBTOR WISHES, HE SHALL LIVE AT HIS OWN EXPENSE. IF HE DOES NOT LIVE AT HIS OWN EXPENSE, THE PERSON WHO HOLDS HIM BOUND SHALL GIVE HIM A POUND OF SPELT A DAY. IF HE WISHES, HE MAY GIVE MORE. ON THE THIRD MARKET DAY THEY SHALL CUT HIM INTO PARTS. IF THEY CUT MORE OR LESS, IT SHALL BE WITHOUT FRAUD.  
> (*Ibid.*, bk. XX, ch. 1, p. 1101 ff.)

[Col. 0993B] Fulvius Ursinus reproduced this same law, though with various readings (Fulvius Ursinus, notes on the cited book of Agustín).

Under this law, therefore, those burdened with debt were first granted a period of thirty days in which to find the money. Then they were bound and thrust into prison. On the third market day, or after another sixty days, they paid the penalty with their lives; and if there were several creditors, the debtor’s body was cut up and its several parts given to the several creditors. “Certainly nothing,” says Gellius, “is more savage than this, unless—as the facts themselves indicate—so great a cruelty of punishment was threatened with the intention that it should never be reached. For we now see many men assigned and bound because the worst men despise the punishment of bonds. I have neither read nor heard that anyone was cut apart in ancient times, since the savagery of that punishment [Col. 0993C] could not be despised” (Gellius, *ibid.*). You clearly see that this is the very law which Tertullian asserts was rendered obsolete and rejected by public consent. Quintilian too confirms this most plainly in the following words: “Some things are not praiseworthy by nature, but are permitted by law; thus, under the Twelve Tables, it was lawful for a debtor’s body to be divided among his creditors, but public custom rejected that law” (Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria*, bk. III, ch. 6).

[Col. 0993D] But if among the laws of the Twelve Tables—which even boys were once required to learn as the best of all laws, as Cicero says (Cicero, *De Legibus*, bk. II, p. 341, line 27)—there was something not only unworthy of praise, as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 26, art. 1), but altogether savage as well, how much more might this be true of other laws enacted by men solely for their own advantage! For no antiquity and no dignity of a legislator commends a law, but equity alone. No law, therefore, is more unjust than one by which a Christian is condemned solely because of his name, without his case ever being heard.

### ARTICLE III

#### An examination of how freely the gentiles violated the laws restraining excessive expenditure on dinners, household furnishings, and clothing; what those laws were, and what “hundred-as dinners” were; how boldly they overthrew other laws, especially that by which a patrician possessing ten pounds of silver was expelled from the senate; who that man was, and who were the freedmen who, while still breaking their scourges, scorned similar sumptuary laws

[Col. 0994A] Tertullian continues his argument. Against the gentiles, who raged against the Christians under the pretence of certain laws, he objects that they themselves were no more bound by those laws than the gentiles were by sumptuary laws which, with great equity and prudence, restrained expenditure on dinners, household furnishings, and clothing (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 4, p. 288), or, as he himself likes to say, “held expenditure and ostentation in check” (the same author, ch. 6, p. 205). Yet they had utterly overthrown those laws with such boldness that they could give Tertullian no answer when he asked them: “What has become of those laws which commanded that no more than one hundred asses be entered as the expenditure upon a dinner, and that no more than one hen be served, and one that had not been fattened?” Aulus Gellius relates that he had read in the miscellanies of Ateius Capito a decree of the senate by which the leading men of the state [Col. 0994B] were ordered to swear that at the Megalensian Games they would spend no more than one hundred and twenty bronze coins, or asses, on each dinner, apart from vegetables, spelt, and native wine; and that no more than one hundred pounds’ weight of silver should be used at a banquet (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. II, ch. 24). The Fannian law then provided that no more than one hundred asses should be spent during the Roman Games, the Plebeian Games, the Saturnalia, and certain other days; thirty asses on ten other days in each month; and finally ten asses on all remaining days. Later, the Licinian law permitted an expenditure of two hundred asses at weddings and thirty asses on other days, apart from fruit and vegetables. But afterward, when these laws had been effaced by neglect and age and many were gluttonously consuming their ample inheritances, the dictator Sulla enacted the Cornelian law, by which permission was granted to spend thirty sesterces upon a dinner on certain solemn feast days, and no more than three on other days. [Col. 0994C] In addition, the Aemilian and Antian laws further prescribed the expense of dinners and the kind and quantity of food. Finally, by the Julian law, which was enacted during the reign of Augustus, as we have said, these permitted expenses were greatly increased, yet in such a manner that the surge of unbridled luxury was restrained within certain limits. All these matters, explained by Macrobius (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. III, ch. 17) after Aulus Gellius (Aulus Gellius, *loc. cit.*), plainly establish and confirm the judgment of our Tertullian.

Nor did they show greater concern for the Fannian law already praised by us, which forbade more than one hen, and one not fattened, to be served at a dinner. [Col. 0994D] Pliny mentions this law and explains in the following words how the gentiles began to undermine it: “The people of Delos began to fatten hens. From this arose the pestilent practice of devouring plump birds basted in their own fat. I find this first singled out among the ancient restrictions concerning dinners, already in the law of the consul Gaius Fannius, eleven years before the Punic War: that no bird should be served except one hen, and one that had not been fattened” (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. X, ch. 50, p. 442)—*altilis* meaning plump and fattened, a term Juvenal uses without qualification (Juvenal, *Satires* 5, v. 117). “This provision was afterward carried over and passed through all the laws, and a means of evading them was discovered by feeding cockerels too upon food soaked in milk; prepared in this way, they are judged much more agreeable” (Pliny, *loc. cit.*). Concerning these [Col. 0995A] sumptuary and dietary laws, much more is said by Paulus Manutius (Paulus Manutius, *De Legibus Romanis*, ch. 18) and Antonio Agustín (Antonio Agustín, *De Legibus*, bk. I, ch. 18), whom we cited in another dissertation, where we heard Arnobius arguing similarly from these laws after Tertullian (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 9, art. 1).

How greatly, moreover, the pagans despised these excellent laws and regarded them as nothing you will learn from these further words of our Author: “I see also ‘hundred-as’ dinners, which must now be named from hundreds of sesterces” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 300). “Hundred-as dinners,” as Festus observes, were those upon which, under the Licinian law, no more than one hundred asses might be spent, apart from the produce of the earth—that is, one hundred asses, which were small bronze coins [Col. 0995B] (Festus, s.v. *Centenariae*), as we noted above. Our Author therefore signifies the immoderate increase in the expense of the old frugal dinner. For a dinner which previously had to be furnished at a cost of no more than one hundred asses had in his time come to be provided for one hundred sesterces. A sestertius, moreover, was worth two and a half asses. He used “one hundred sesterces” as a round figure, employing a definite number for an indefinite one, so that by opposing one hundred asses to one hundred sesterces he might censure the excessive cost of dinners. Who, indeed, even upon the most cursory reading of the lives of the Caesars written by Suetonius and other authors, does not perceive that during their reigns dinners were so extravagant that these historians, although trustworthy, can scarcely be believed? You therefore see with what ease the Romans amended and weakened their ancient and venerable laws, [Col. 0995C] even while babbling that they were bound by the most unjust rescripts against the Christians.

Tertullian then similarly declares that those laws had been overthrown which “removed from the Senate a patrician because he possessed ten pounds of silver, regarding it as a serious mark of ostentation” (Tertullian, loc. cit.). If anyone should ask us who that patrician was, we shall answer him in the words of Aulus Gellius: “Gaius Fabricius Luscinus and Quintus Aemilius Papus were censors at Rome, and they expelled from the Senate Publius Cornelius Rufinus, who had twice been consul and had been dictator; and as the reason for this censure they recorded that he had been found to possess ten pounds of wrought silver for the purposes of dining” (Gellius, bk. XVII, *Noctes Atticae*, ch. 2, p. 1005). You hear him note there precisely the same quantity of silver possessed by Rufinus as Tertullian does. But [Col. 0995D] what the former expressed as “for the purposes of dining,” Aulus Gellius elsewhere puts thus: “Because of the stigma of luxury,” he says, “since he possessed ten pounds’ weight of wrought silver” (ibid., bk. VIII, ch. 8, p. 289). We read precisely the same thing in Livy’s *Epitome* (Livy, *Epitome*, bk. XIV). Pliny, however, testifies that the same quantity of silver was spent upon household plate (Pliny, bk. XVIII, *Historia naturalis*, ch. 6, p. 447), while Valerius Maximus says it was spent upon silver vessels (Valerius Maximus, bk. II, ch. 6, § 4). It may perhaps not be tedious to hear his words, which are highly pertinent to our subject. They are these: “Every age has related, and every age hereafter will relate, how the censorship of Fabricius Luscinus refused to retain Cornelius Rufinus in the senatorial order, as a luxurious man setting an evil example, because, after having discharged two consulships and a dictatorship with the greatest distinction, he had acquired ten pounds of silver vessels.” [Col. 0996A] He then immediately added: “By my faith, the very letters of our age seem to me astonished when they are compelled to lend their service to recounting such severity, as though fearing that they may be thought not to be recording the deeds of our city. For it is scarcely credible that within the same sacred boundary ten pounds of silver should once have been both a fortune that provoked resentment and a poverty held in the greatest contempt.”

Does not Tertullian similarly indicate that this quantity of silver was spent by Cornelius Rufinus upon making or purchasing silver vessels? He justly rebukes the still greater luxury of the Romans in these following words: “I see that for serving dishes—that is, for carrying food to diners—it is too little if the silver mines have been drawn out only for senators, and not also for freedmen or men who are still breaking the whips” [Col. 0996B] (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 301). He therefore charges the pagans with the vice that not only senators but even freedmen, still “breaking the whips”—that is, men who had cast off slavery only a few days before—had been released into such luxury. Slaves, indeed, were customarily beaten with whips as a punishment peculiar to their condition. Hence Juvenal sang these verses concerning the slave Liburnus:

> Liburnus is said to have arrived late,  
> And is forced to pay the penalty for another man’s sleep;  
> This one breaks rods, that one grows red beneath the lashes.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 6, v. 490.)

In Terence, moreover, Simo threatens his slave Davus with whips and blows as follows:

> I shall have you scourged, Davus, and hand you over to the mill  
> Until you die.  
> (Terence, *Andria* 1, scene 2, v. 8.)

[Col. 0996C] But we shall treat the punishments of slaves more fully in the following dissertation. Yet if the luxury of those who had only just obtained their freedom was so great, judge from this how great that of others must have been. Hence the Pliny just cited says: “That an aged triumphator was censured by the censors on account of five pounds of silver now seems fabulous” (Pliny, bk. III, *Historia naturalis*, ch. 11, p. 69). By what reasoning, then, did the pagans dare to object that they were bound by unjust laws against the Christians, when they themselves had openly and with impunity overthrown those most equitable sumptuary laws?

## ARTICLE IV. With what license the pagans, in contempt of the laws that had destroyed newly established theaters, built many more, to which they flocked wearing cloaks for the sake of greater pleasure

[Col. 0996D] Tertullian proceeds to other laws by which provision had been made for chastity, moral decency, and modesty. He openly shows that these too had been overthrown by the pagans with just as much license as the recklessness with which they alleged that they were bound by other, plainly wicked laws enacted against the Christians: “For what,” he asks, “has become of those laws intended to correct vices, which immediately destroyed theaters as they arose to corrupt morals?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 299). Yet certainly the common opinion of nearly everyone, as Servius teaches (Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* II, v. 381; and *Aeneid* II, v. 737), was that the first theatrical games were instituted in honor of Bacchus, or Father Liber, and for that reason were called the Liberalia. How greatly human morals were corrupted by these games [Col. 0997A] there is surely no one who cannot readily understand from their utterly detestable indecency and obscenity, which we have discussed elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 17, art. 1, and on Lactantius, ch. 35, art. 1). If, however, anyone contends that our Author was speaking not only of these but also of other theatrical games formerly abolished, he will certainly have Cicero as a supporter, as well as Augustine, by whom Cicero is cited. These are Augustine’s own words:

“The Romans, although they were already oppressed by a harmful superstition which made them worship gods whom they saw to have wished theatrical obscenities to be consecrated to themselves, nevertheless, mindful of their own dignity and sense of shame, did not honor the actors of such plays after the custom of the Greeks. Instead, as Scipio says in Cicero: ‘Since they regarded the dramatic art and the entire stage as disgraceful, they wished that class of men not only to be deprived of the honors enjoyed by the other citizens [Col. 0997B] but even to be removed from their tribe by censorial censure’” (Augustine, bk. II, *De civitate Dei*, ch. 13, p. 40 ff.).

Augustine praises and approves this judgment of Cicero, thus cited, in these following words: “An excellent prudence indeed, and one to be counted among the glories of Rome; but I wish that Rome had followed and imitated itself.”

Thus these excellent laws did not remain in force for long. For Tertullian attacked the pagans as follows: “I see theaters too, neither single nor bare” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 301). They were not single, because after the earlier ones had been demolished they had erected far more of them throughout the world. He added “nor bare,” because people customarily flocked there dressed not in ordinary clothing but in the *paenula*, or cloak. “For,” he says, “lest shameless pleasure should grow cold even in winter, the Lacedaemonians were the first to devise for the games [Col. 0997C] the odiousness of the cloak.” In all the manuscripts and in the editions printed before Rigault, however, we read not “the odiousness of the cloak” but simply “the cloak.” Learned men have exercised their ingenuity to no small extent in explaining these obscure and perhaps corrupt words. Heraldus thinks that they may signify that the cloak devised by the warlike Lacedaemonian nation to keep off rain was adopted by the Romans so that they might watch the games more patiently. Tertullian, however, declares clearly enough that it was invented by those same Lacedaemonians not merely for military use but also for the games. Rigault, on the other hand, suspects that Tertullian is speaking ironically of cloaks as excessively heavy and burdensome and thus capable of producing aversion rather than pleasure. But why should Tertullian speak ironically in these words rather than in the others that precede and follow them? [Col. 0997D]

Because Tertullian therefore appears to speak without irony and affirmatively, Ferrari consequently believes that his memory failed him here and that he wrote *paenula* instead of *endromis* (Ferrari, pt. II, *De re vestiaria*, bk. II, ch. 1). The *endromis* was also a thick and shaggy garment, useful in the wrestling school—or rather after exercise in the wrestling school—no less than the cloak. To confirm his opinion Ferrari adduces these verses of Martial:

> This well-padded offspring of a weaver of the Sequani,  
> Which bears the foreign name “Lacedaemonian,”  
> A coarse thing, but not to be despised in freezing December,  
> We send you as a gift, an *endromis* from abroad,  
> Whether you rub yourself with sticky wrestling oil or play the warm game of *trigon*,  
> Or snatch with your hand the dust-covered *harpastum*.  
> (Martial, bk. IV, epigram 19.)

[Col. 0998A] Yet there appears to be no need whatever to alter by conjecture the word *paenula*, which is read consistently in all the copies. No one can doubt that the Romans attended public games wearing cloaks. Suetonius is our witness that the emperor Galba ordered those attending a certain solemn spectacle to keep their hands inside their cloaks (Suetonius, *Life of Galba*, § 6). In the *Epitome* of Dio, moreover, we read that the emperor Commodus commanded the senators to come to the theater for the last gladiatorial show he gave, Ἔν τε τῇ στολῇ τῇ ἱππάδι, καὶ ἐν ταῖς μανδύαις εἰς τὸ θέατρον εἰσελθεῖν (“to enter the theater both in equestrian dress and in cloaks”). “He ordered them to come into the theater wearing equestrian dress and cloaks” (*Epitome of Dio*, *Life of Commodus*, p. 295). They had never previously been accustomed to enter it in such attire unless the emperor had departed this life. [Col. 0998B] But μανδύη (*mandyē*, “cloak”) signifies a particular kind of cloak. Thus Lampridius says of the same Commodus: “Contrary to custom, he ordered them to come to the show wearing cloaks rather than togas” (Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*, p. 315).

Tertullian therefore rightly reproves the Romans, since, contrary to ancient custom, they wore the cloak when attending public games and spectacles, particularly in winter. For because the theaters then lacked roofs, they put on the cloak lest cold or rain harm them and so that they might watch the shameful acts performed there without any inconvenience. Thus, contrary to former customs, they had adopted for pleasure the cloak which soldiers wore solely from necessity. For concerning the soldier who professed the Christian religion before the tribune, Tertullian says: “He laid aside the exceedingly heavy cloaks” (Tertullian, *De corona*, ch. 1). Concerning this [Col. 0998C] garment, moreover, see Octavius Ferrari and Barthold Bartholin, who published special investigations of it, as well as others who wrote books on clothing.

Who, then, does not see with what recklessness the pagans cried out that they were compelled by the emperors’ most unjust laws against the Christians to persecute them, when with such boldness and impunity they utterly despised and spurned other, most equitable laws which commanded theaters to be completely destroyed because of their monstrous corruption of morals? Nor did they value many other excellent laws any more highly, as Tertullian teaches and as we shall show after him.

## ARTICLE V. An examination of the recklessness with which the pagans trampled upon laws commanding distinctions between the insignia of rank and birth and between the garments of matrons and prostitutes, or forbidding women to adorn themselves with gold except in the betrothal ring

[Col. 0998D]

Tertullian then proceeds to another class of laws overthrown by the pagans, laws which had once made most prudent provision for modesty and sobriety, especially among women. For the very men who so insolently invoked laws injurious to the Christian name calmly and cheerfully allowed other laws to be trampled underfoot—laws which did not permit the insignia of rank and honorable birth to be assumed rashly or with impunity (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 300). Who does not know that kings, senators, knights, and plebeians possessed different insignia and different garments by which they were distinguished from one another? To pass over very many examples [Col. 0999A], these are some further words on the subject from our Author himself: “What king displays the insignia of his power upon his shoulder rather than a diadem upon his head, a scepter in his hand, or some mark upon his distinctive garment?” (ibid., *Adversus Judaeos*, ch. 10).

An edict was also issued by Caesar Augustus forbidding anyone other than a senator henceforth to wear the purple garment that was then commonly assumed (Dio, bk. XLIX, *Roman History*, p. 459). Earlier, moreover, Julius Caesar, according to Suetonius, had restricted the use of litters, garments dyed with shellfish purple, and pearls to certain persons and ages and to certain days (Suetonius, *Life of Julius Caesar*, § 43). The author of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* explains this regulation concerning women as follows: “Women who had neither husbands nor children and were less [Col. 0999B] than fifty-five years old were forbidden to use litters and pearls” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, 1972).

There was also a great difference between the garments of matrons and those of prostitutes (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 301). Prostitutes, as Nonius noted, wore a more closely girded garment (Nonius, ch. 14, *De genere vestimentorum*). Hence Ulpian says: “If someone had addressed virgins improperly, yet they were dressed in the clothing of slave girls, he appears to offend less seriously, and much less so if the women were dressed in the clothing of prostitutes rather than of respectable married women” (*Digest*, bk. XLVIII, title *De injuriis*, etc., law 15).

How greatly women abused these garments, contrary to the institutions of their ancestors, learn from our Tertullian: “I see,” he says, “that no distinction in attire has been left between matrons and prostitutes” (Tertullian, loc. cit.). He says no more there, but in another book [Col. 0999C] he treats the subject more fully, continuing in this manner:

“Turn also to the women. You may behold what Caecina Severus forcefully impressed upon the Senate: matrons appearing in public without the *stola*. Finally, according to the judgments of the augur Lentulus, the punishment for one who had thus divested herself of her rank was the same as for fornication, because certain women had studiously abandoned the marks and guardians of dignity in their attire as impediments to the practice of solicitation. But now, in soliciting on their own behalf so that they may be approached more openly, they have renounced the *stola*, the *supparum*, the little sandal, the headdress, and even the litters and chairs in which, even in public, they were kept as though at home and in privacy” (ibid., *De pallio*, ch. 4).

In yet another book he attacks still more sharply the same abuse and the rejection of that distinction between the garments of respectable matrons and those of prostitutes. Hear him, I pray, as he speaks:

“How much more blasphemous it is if you who are called priestesses of chastity proceed adorned and painted after the fashion of the unchaste! Or what less do those most wretched victims of public lust possess—women whom laws once restrained from marital and matronly ornaments—but whom the wickedness of the age, continually increasing, has now placed on the same level as every most respectable woman, even to the point that they cannot be distinguished?” (ibid., bk. II, *De cultu feminarum*, ch. 12).

Then a little later:

“That Tamar who had painted and adorned herself was for that reason judged by Judah, on suspicion, to be offering herself for hire; and she was so concealed beneath her veil, the character of her attire falsely representing her as a prostitute, that he both desired her as a prostitute, addressed her as one, and made an agreement with her” (ibid.).

Jerome writes in a manner not unlike this: “Tamar deceived Judah under the guise of a prostitute” (Jerome, bk. I, *Adversus Pelagianos*). [Col. 1000A] Do you hear how ancient the laws distinguishing the garments of matrons and prostitutes were, and how freely the pagans violated them?

Nor did they pay greater heed to other laws which had provided for the modesty and sobriety of women. “In ancient times,” says Tertullian, “no woman knew gold except upon the one finger which her betrothed had pledged with the betrothal ring” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 302). No one is unaware that it was a very ancient custom for the bridegroom to send his bride a ring, called the betrothal ring, as a pledge of the future marriage. If, however, anyone desires at least one witness to this custom to be cited, let him hear Juvenal:

> Yet you arrange the meeting, the compact, and the betrothal  
> In our own day; already you are being combed by the master barber,  
> And perhaps you have given the pledge upon her finger.  
> [Col. 1000B] (Juvenal, *Satires* 6, v. 25 ff.)

Pliny testifies that in his day this ring was made of iron and had no gemstone: “Even now,” he says, “an iron ring is sent as a gift to the bride, and that without a gem” (Pliny, bk. XXXIII, *Historia naturalis*, ch. 1, p. 7).

By the age of our Tertullian, therefore, that wholly modest custom had already been changed, and a gold ring was given instead of an iron one.
