Later Isidore spoke in the plural of these same betrothal rings as follows: “Women did not use rings except those which a bridegroom had sent to a maiden, nor was she accustomed to have more than two gold rings upon her fingers. But now, because of gold, no part of a woman’s body is light or unburdened” (Isidore, bk. XIX, *Origines*, ch. 32). Did he not in these latter words have regard to the following words of Tertullian, by which, in the very passage [Col. 1000C] under discussion, he censures the luxury of women: “Now, because of gold, no part of a woman’s body is light” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 304)? Hence Ovid had previously sung:

> Do not come forth weighed down with gold sewn into your garments;  
> By such means you often drive away the wealth you do not seek.  
> (Ovid, bk. III, *Ars amatoria*, v. 172.)

Pliny is a further witness for us that he saw Agrippina, the wife of the emperor Claudius—that is, Nero’s wife [sic; the source reading is uncertain]—when Claudius was presenting a spectacle of a naval battle and she was sitting beside him, dressed in a military cloak woven entirely of gold, without any other material (Pliny, ibid., ch. 3, p. 39). This is confirmed both by Dio (Dio, bk. X, *Roman History*) and by Cornelius Tacitus (Tacitus, bk. XII, *Annals*, near the end). Anyone wishing to learn more about this luxury of Roman women should consult Meursius (Meursius, *De luxu Romano*, ch. 4 ff.), [Col. 1000D] Kobierzycki (Kobierzycki, bk. I, *De luxu Romano*, ch. 8 ff.), and, if he has leisure, what we have noted elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 792).

## ARTICLE VI. An examination of the severity with which women were formerly forbidden the use of wine, and of the impunity with which wives were killed by their husbands for violating that prohibition; of women’s later immoderate use of wine, on account of which they did not dare offer the customary kiss to their relatives; of the frequency of repudiating wives, a practice unknown in ancient times; and of the manner in which the pagans renounced their forefathers in speech and manner of speaking

Nothing was more worthy of the ancient integrity of the Romans [Col. 1001A] than that salutary severity by which the use of wine was so completely forbidden to women that, as our Tertullian relates, a matron’s own family starved her to death because she had unsealed the little chest containing the keys of the wine cellar. Under Romulus, moreover, a woman who had touched wine was killed with impunity by her husband Mecennius. “For this reason women were also required to offer kisses to their relatives, so that they might be judged by their breath” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 303). Pliny explains precisely the same matters, though not in the same order, more clearly:

“Women at Rome,” he says, “were not permitted to drink it”—that is, wine. “Among the recorded examples we find that the wife of Egnatius Mecennius was killed by her husband because she had drunk wine from a cask, and that Romulus acquitted him of the killing. Fabius Pictor wrote in his *Annals* that a matron was compelled by her family to die of hunger because she had unsealed a little chest in which were the keys to the wine cellar. Cato says that relatives therefore gave women [Col. 1001B] a kiss so that they might know whether they smelled of *temetum*. That was then the name for wine, whence also the word *temulentia*, drunkenness” (Pliny, bk. XIV, *Historia naturalis*, ch. 13, p. 142).

Who would not readily persuade himself that Tertullian could not have combined all these facts in precisely this way unless he drew them either from Pliny himself or from the same sources as Pliny? Valerius Maximus relates the story of the wife of Egnatius Mecennius somewhat differently, saying that because she had drunk wine she was killed by him without either an accuser or a reprover (Valerius Maximus, bk. VI, ch. 3, § 9), since everyone thought that she had suffered an exemplary punishment for violating sobriety (ibid., bk. II, ch. 1, § 5).

He had previously said that the use of wine was once unknown to Roman women because from it there is but one short step to unlawful sexual intercourse. Moreover, Cato is again cited by Aulus Gellius [Col. 1001C] as reporting that a woman who had either drunk wine or been caught in adultery was condemned in the same manner (Aulus Gellius, bk. X, *Noctes Atticae*, ch. 23, p. 557). Athenaeus, furthermore, not only mentions the Roman prohibition of wine to women, but adds that the wine cellar was not entrusted to them and that kisses were therefore offered by husbands and relatives so that they might detect by smell whether the women had actually drunk wine (Athenaeus, bk. X, *Deipnosophistae*, ch. 7, p. 429, and ch. 11, p. 440). We have already discussed this prohibition of wine (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 4, art. 1).

Yet contrary to this law, “because of wine,” Tertullian says, “no kiss is free” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 304). Various writers, and especially the satirical poets, inveigh against this vice of drunkenness. [Col. 1001D] But in so well-known a matter it will suffice to cite these verses of Juvenal, which plainly confirm what we have said in the preceding article not only about drunkenness but also about luxury:

> No crime or deed of lust has been absent since  
> Roman poverty perished. . . .  
>   
> . . . . . . . . . .  
>   
> Foul money first brought foreign morals among us,  
> And enervating riches shattered the age with shameful luxury.  
> For what does drunken Venus care?  
> She does not know the difference between groin and head,  
> She who bites into huge oysters already at midnight.  
> When perfumes, steeped in Falernian wine, foam;  
> When she drinks from a shell; when, through dizziness, the roof  
> Seems to move and the table rises beneath twin lamps.  
> Go now, and doubt what scornful sniff Tullia draws in,  
> Or what Maura says to the notorious Collacia,  
> When Maura passes the ancient altar of Chastity.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 6, v. 293 ff.)

[Col. 1002A] What more need be said? Our Author further reproaches the pagans because the ancient happiness of marriages had vanished—a happiness certainly sustained by morals—during which, for nearly six hundred years after the foundation of Rome, no household issued a bill of repudiation (Tertullian, ibid.). Do you wish this to be proved by certain Greek and Latin witnesses? The first shall be Dionysius of Halicarnassus, whose words are these: Ὁμολογεῖται ἐντὸς ἐτῶν εἴκοσι καὶ πεντακοσίων μηδεὶς ἐν Ῥώμῃ διαλυθῆναι γάμος· κατὰ τὴν ἑβδόμην ἐπὶ ταῖς τριάκοντα καὶ ἑκατὸν Ὀλυμπιάσιν, ὑπατευόντων Μάρκου Πομπωνίου, καὶ Γαίου Παπυρίου, πρῶτος ἀπολύσαι λέγεται τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα Σπούριος Καρουίλλιος ἀνὴρ οὐκ ἀφανὴς, ἀναγχαζομένος ὑπὸ τῶν τιμητῶν ὁμόσαι τέκνων ἕνεκα γυναικὶ μὴ συνοικεῖν· ἦν δ` αὐτῷ στείρα ἡ γυνή, ὃς ἐπὶ τῷ ἓργῳ τούτῳ, καίτοι δι` ἀνάγκην γινομένῳ, μισούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ δήμου διετέλεσεν (“It is agreed that within five hundred and twenty years no marriage at Rome was dissolved. In the seventh year of the 130th Olympiad, when Marcus Pomponius and Gaius Papirius were consuls, Spurius Carvilius, a man of some distinction, is said to have been the first to dismiss his wife. He was compelled by the censors to swear, for the sake of children, not to continue living with his wife; his wife was barren, and for this deed, although it was done under compulsion, he continued to be hated by the people”). “It is agreed [Col. 1002B] that for 520 years no divorce occurred. Only in the seventh year of the 130th Olympiad, when Marcus Pomponius and Gaius Papirius were consuls, is Spurius Carvilius, a man of some distinction, said to have been the first to dismiss his wife. He was compelled by the censors to swear that for the sake of having children he would not retain his spouse, for she was barren; and because of this act, although compelled by necessity, he was forever hated by the people” (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, bk. II, *Roman Antiquities*, p. 96).

The Latin writers Valerius Maximus and Aulus Gellius committed the same account to writing (Valerius Maximus, bk. II, ch. 1, § 4), except that Gellius, citing Servius Sulpicius as his authority, relates that it occurred in the 523rd year after the foundation of the city, when Marcus Atilius and Publius Valerius were consuls (Aulus Gellius, bk. IV, *Noctes Atticae*, ch. 3, p. 278). But there is certainly either here or elsewhere some error in his memory or that of a copyist. [Col. 1002C] For in another book he writes that it occurred in the 519th year after the foundation of the city, in which case the consuls must accordingly have been different, perhaps those named by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (ibid., bk. XVII, ch. 21, p. 1008).

The pagans had therefore utterly and completely departed from these equitable morals and laws. Among them, Tertullian says, repudiation “is now both the object of marriage and, as it were, its fruit” (Tertullian, ibid.). Nor should you suspect that there is any exaggeration on his part here. You will not distrust Seneca, in whom we read these words concerning repudiation:

“Does any woman now blush at divorce, after certain illustrious and noble women reckon their years not by the number of consuls but by the number of their husbands, and leave marriage in order to marry and marry in order to divorce? It was feared so long as it was rare; but because no public records”—that is, records drawn up by public notaries—“were made without a divorce, they learned to do what they so often heard of” [Col. 1002D] (Seneca, bk. III, *De beneficiis*, ch. 16, p. 53).

To this may also be added Juvenal, who attacks these exceedingly frequent divorces of wives in the following verses:

> She therefore commands her husband, but soon abandons this realm,  
> Changes houses, and wears out her bridal veils; then  
> She flies back and retraces her steps to the bed she had scorned.  
> She leaves the doors only lately adorned, the curtains  
> Hanging from the house, and branches still green upon the threshold.  
> Thus the number grows; thus there are eight husbands  
> In five autumns—a fact worthy of inscription on a tomb.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 6, v. 223.)

You hear how plainly he said that a single wife had, within five autumns—that is, five years—[Col. 1003A] eight husbands. Martial, moreover, sharply reproves a certain Telesina who, contrary to the enacted laws, had married ten times within a single month and had done so with impunity:

> Since the Julian law, Faustinus, was renewed for the people,  
> And Chastity was commanded to enter their homes,  
> Less than—or certainly no more than—the thirtieth day has dawned,  
> And Telesina is already marrying her tenth husband.  
> A woman who marries so often does not marry: she is an adulteress by law.  
> I am less offended by a more straightforward adulteress.  
> (Martial, bk. VI, epigram 7.)

Indeed, this wicked license of divorce was so unbridled that it could scarcely ever be restrained by any laws of the emperors, many of which still survive. What of the fact that they not only trampled upon so many excellent laws in the manner we have described, but also rejected the reverence owed to their ancestors? Tertullian therefore presses them by addressing them in these words: “In habit [Col. 1003B]—that is, clothing—in diet, furnishings, property, and finally in speech itself, you have renounced your forefathers” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 305). Again, in another book, he says: “It is plainly evident how greatly you have changed from your ancestors in manner of life, clothing, equipment, and diet itself,” as is clear from what has already been said. He added “and in speech itself.” Why also in speech and manner of speaking? “Because,” he says, “you banish the old-fashioned as rancid” (ibid., bk. I, *Ad nationes*, ch. 10, p. 572)—that is, you reject it as disagreeable, putrid, and foul-smelling.

## ARTICLE VII. An examination of the ancient decree forbidding the introduction of new gods without a senatorial decree, and of Metellus’s vow to build a temple in honor of the god Alburnus, which was declared invalid; and of how that decree was violated by the pagans, who most shamelessly restored Father Liber, Serapis, and Harpocrates with his Cynocephalus after they had been rejected by decree of the Senate

[Col. 1003C]

Tertullian presses the pagans still more forcefully and utterly overwhelms them. For he clearly shows that they despised and overthrew not only the more sacred laws concerning human affairs but also those concerning divine rites. But let us, if you please, hear him argue in his book *To the Nations*:

“Yet those exceedingly wise and prudent ancestors, whose institutions you do not know how to renounce, are themselves found impious, particularly in relation to your gods. I lie if they never decreed that no commander should dedicate a shrine which he had vowed in battle before the Senate had approved it, as happened to Marcus Aemilius Probus, who had vowed one to the god Alburnus. An utterly impious, indeed an utterly insulting, offense was surely committed in placing the honor of divinity at the discretion and caprice of human judgment, so that there should be no god unless the Senate had permitted him to exist” (Tertullian, bk. I, *Ad nationes*, ch. 10, p. 573).

But he states the matter more briefly in his *Apologeticum*: “There was an ancient decree,” he says, “that no god should be consecrated by a commander unless approved by the Senate. Marcus Aemilius knows this from the case of his god Alburnus. This supports our case, because among you divinity is weighed according to human judgment. Unless a god pleases a man, he will not be a god; man must now be propitious to God” (ibid., *Apologeticum*, ch. 5, p. 290). In certain older editions, however, instead of the words “Marcus Aemilius knows,” the reading is “as Marcus Aemilius”; [Col. 1004A] and Eusebius appears to have read it thus, for he presents these words of our Author translated into Greek as follows: Παλαιὸν ἦν δόγμα, μηδένα θεὸν ὑπὸ βασιλέως καθιεροῦσθαι, πρὶν ὑπὸ τοῦ συγγκλήτου δοκιμασθῆναι· Μάρκος Αἰμίλιος οὓτως περί τινος εἰδώλου πεποίηκεν Ἀλβούρνου (“It was an ancient decree that no god should be consecrated by a king before being approved by the senate; Marcus Aemilius acted thus concerning a certain image of Alburnus”) (Eusebius, bk. II, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 2, p. 41). Yet the meaning of both readings is plainly the same. These matters must therefore first be explained, and then we must examine how Tertullian argues from them against the pagans.

There may indeed be doubt as to what edict concerning the consecration of a god this was. We know that Cicero describes one in these words: “Let no one have gods separately; nor let anyone privately worship new or foreign gods unless they have been publicly adopted” (Cicero, bk. II, *De legibus*, p. 334, line 37). Tertullian, however, appears [Col. 1004B] to designate a different decree, since he mentions an *imperator*, a military commander. The law cited by Cicero was certainly far older than the Roman emperors. What, then, if we say that our Author uses the title *imperator* for the commander of an army, or for the consul who led it? Aemilius Probus, either unaware of this law or giving it no thought amid the doubtful fortune of battle, vowed that, if he conquered the enemy, he would consecrate a shrine to a god named Alburnus. From his own experience, however, he learned that this vow, made without a decree of the Senate, had been excessively rash. For the Senate prohibited the construction of the shrine, just as it later prevented Christ, as Tertullian says in the same place, from being declared God, although Tiberius strongly desired it.

Who this god Alburnus was is undoubtedly [Col. 1004C] no less difficult to say. He is very rarely mentioned among the ancients. From Virgil, however, we learn that in Lucania, beside the river Silarus, there is a mountain which he calls Alburnus in these verses:

> There is a grove beside the Silarus and Alburnus green with holm oaks;  
> Around it an insect flies in great numbers, whose Roman name is *asilus*,  
> Which the Greeks have translated as *oestrus*.  
> (Virgil, bk. III, *Georgics*, v. 146 ff.)

That mountain, however, had been consecrated after the custom of the pagans to some god who was given the name Alburnus, and Metellus could have vowed a shrine to him. Nor should you be surprised that this god is now unknown, for he was a local god. Such gods, as Servius observes, did not pass into other regions and were consequently scarcely known to anyone except the inhabitants of their own locality (Servius on *Aeneid* VII).

Tertullian [Col. 1004D] draws two arguments against the pagans from this. First, he most clearly concludes from it that the gods of the pagans were made according to the will and judgment of men, and that consequently no pagan deity could be a god unless he pleased a man. Yet it is the height of impiety to attribute divinity to anyone at human discretion. For the true God exists from himself and is omnipotent, and is therefore subject to no one, while all things are subject to him. The pagans, therefore, could by no law whatever—unless it were a most unjust law—decree that Christians must reject the worship of the true God and adore gods made by men, and that otherwise they should be killed without even being heard.

Second, Tertullian concludes from this that the ancient decree forbidding the introduction of new gods was violated by the pagans themselves, who [Col. 1005A] with equal license rejected gods who had once been made and restored those who had been rejected. For, as he says, “the consuls, by authority of the Senate, expelled Father Liber with his mysteries not merely from the city but from all Italy” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 304). He repeats this in another book in almost the same words (bk. I, *Ad nationes*, ch. 10, p. 573). Livy accurately relates this entire history: when, on what occasion, and how the consul Postumius uncovered the abominable and horrifying crimes committed at night in these execrable rites, and how for that reason they were utterly abolished and removed from Rome and all Italy by decree of the Senate (Livy, bk. XXXIX, §§ 9–19). Augustine therefore rightly says: “These things later displeased the more sound-minded Senate, which ordered them to be removed” (Augustine, [Col. 1005B] bk. VI, *De civitate Dei*, ch. 9, p. 156).

Conversely, our Author continues:

“Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates with his Cynocephalus were prohibited from the Capitol—that is, expelled from the assembly of the gods—and the consuls Piso and Gabinius, who were certainly not Christians, repudiated them and even overturned their altars, restraining the vices of shameful and idle superstitions” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 6, p. 305).

He treats this somewhat more fully in another book, where he also cites Varro as a witness in the following manner:

“Varro records that Serapis, Isis, Harpocrates, and Anubis were prohibited from the Capitol and that their statues were cast down by the Senate and rebuilt only through the violence of the populace. Yet when the consul Gabinius, on the Kalends of January, was scarcely able to approve the sacrificial victims before the assembly of the people because he had made no provision concerning Serapis and Isis, he valued the Senate’s censure more highly [Col. 1005C] than the violence of the crowd and prohibited the establishment of their altars” (ibid., bk. I, *Ad nationes*, ch. 10, p. 573).

But I should like you to observe how great was the pagans’ inconsistency and folly even in sacred matters. After they had with the fullest justice abolished these utterly shameful and wholly detestable mysteries of Serapis, they nevertheless restored them with the utmost impiety, as Tertullian promises later to demonstrate more fully. We have noted certain matters concerning both their destruction and their restoration in our dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s Octavius*, ch. 22, art. 1), and shall make further observations below.

Therefore, the pagans, who had thus rejected and restored their own gods, were never entitled to condemn and kill Christians who had neither been heard nor defended, [Col. 1005D] simply because they refused to deny and renounce the true God and their true religion. This is further confirmed by what we related in another dissertation (*Dissert. on Arnobius*, chap. 5, art. 1 ff.), where we disclosed the great audacity with which they despised, undermined, and abolished even the more sacred customs, laws, and institutions.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Laws Enacted against Christians, and the Emperors’ Hatred or Favor toward Them

### ARTICLE I. How Tertullian Shows That the First Laws against Christians Were Enacted by Nero, a Most Wicked Emperor, and Then by Domitian, Who Shared in Nero’s Cruelty, but Who Nevertheless Restored Those Whom He Had Banished

[Col. 1006A]

Tertullian demonstrated more than sufficiently how absurdly the pagans alleged that they were bound by their laws to harass and kill Christians, when they themselves violated or scorned with impunity the institutions, customs, and more sacred laws of their ancestors. For, as our Author says, they praised the ancients but lived each day in a novel fashion; and by excluding antiquity from their affairs and duties, they brought the venerable authority of their fathers to ruin (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 6, p. 305). But he did not think all this sufficient, and attacks the very head of the accusation. He therefore makes it manifest that the laws enacted against Christians were most unjust and were established by the worst and most criminal rulers. [Col. 1006B] No less clearly does he demonstrate that good and pious rulers either never raged against Christians or never ordered that violence be done to them. This he shows by a brief survey of the emperors from the beginning of the Christian religion down to his own time (Idem, *Ad Nationes*, book I, chap. 10, p. 572).

For when the Christian name began to become widely known throughout the world (Idem, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 290), the emperor Tiberius, as we observed above (supra, chap. 8, art. 4), wished to include Christ among the gods; and although the senate prevented him, he nevertheless persisted in his opinion. So far was he from enacting any law against Christians that, as Tertullian says, he even threatened their accusers with danger—that is, with punishment and execution [Col. 1006C] (Tertullian, ibid.).

Nor did our Author ever believe that the emperors Caligula and Claudius decreed anything against those same Christians. For in the same passage he added: “Consult your records; there you will find that Nero was the first to rage with the imperial sword against this sect when it was just then arising at Rome” (Tertullian, loc. cit.). We shall explain below why the first persecution of the Christians is said to have been stirred up by this emperor (*Dissert. on Lucius Caecilius*, book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chap. 6, art. 1). We shall therefore observe only that some have thought that by these words, “your records,” our Author designated either the *Annals* of Cornelius Tacitus or, more probably, Suetonius’ account of the life of Nero. For elsewhere he said: “We read the *Lives of the Caesars*: Nero was the first to stain the rising faith with blood” [Col. 1006D] (Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chap. 15). This conjecture does not, indeed, appear wholly inept. Yet what prevents us from supposing that by the term “record” he also meant the secret or public acts of the Romans, in which, as we noted above (supra, chap. 9, art. 3), extraordinary events were preserved in written form?

However the matter may stand, the Christian religion assuredly even glories in Nero, the most wicked tyrant of all, or, as Tertullian puts it, “such an inaugurator of our condemnation” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 293). For, having been condemned by him, it is thereby proved to be good and true. For, as he continues: “Anyone who knows him can understand that nothing but some great good was condemned [Col. 1007A] by Nero” (Idem, ibid.). But he pursues this point somewhat more fully in his book *Ad Nationes*: “Under Nero,” he says, “condemnation gained force, so that from this point you may weigh it by the character of the persecutor. If that ruler was pious, then Christians are impious; if he was just and chaste, then Christians are unjust and incestuous; if he was not a public enemy, then we are public enemies. That condemner demonstrated what sort of people we are, since he punished virtues that were, of course, rivals—that is, contrary—to his own most wicked morals. And yet, when all else had been erased, this one institution of Nero alone remained—just, no doubt, because it was unlike its author” (Idem, *Ad Nationes*, book I, chap. 7, p. 567).

The pagans could not, therefore, object to the Christians that they were bound by laws enacted by that most impious tyrant. For the first law sanctioned against them, enacted by one who led a life infamous for so many [Col. 1007B] and such horrendous crimes, certainly made manifest to everyone how chaste and innocent the Christians’ manner of life was. Furthermore, that most bitter enemy of all good condemned nothing but what was good and equitable. The pagans therefore could never be bound by his most unjust laws; and the Christians rightly and deservedly gloried in having been condemned by so impious a man. Finally, through his cruelty and crimes hitherto unheard of, he became so horrifying to everyone that all his monuments were erased and abolished. For, as Suetonius says, he was judged a public enemy by the senate and sentenced to be punished according to ancestral custom (Suetonius, book VI, *Life of Nero*, § 49). In Dio’s *Epitome* we read that the soldiers smashed and demolished his statues (Dio, *Epitome*, p. 196); and, if Plutarch is to be believed, the gladiator Spiculus, [Col. 1007C] after they had been dragged through the city, was buried beneath them in the forum and killed (Plutarch, *Life of Galba*, p. 1056).

But although the pagans rightly and deservedly rescinded all Nero’s acts and decrees, their blind fury against the Christians nevertheless caused Nero’s decree against them alone to remain when everything else had been erased. But Tertullian, mocking their madness, added: “Just, indeed, because unlike its author”—that is, it was as unjust as it was like the impious Nero himself and his other abominable deeds and laws.

Tertullian continues: “Domitian too had attempted it, a portion of Nero in cruelty; but, being also human, he readily suppressed what he had begun and even restored those whom he had banished” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 293). Eusebius reproduced all these words in Greek and cites another witness, Hegesippus, who recorded that Domitian, [Col. 1007D] after questioning certain relatives of Christ about their ancestry and the kingdom of Christ himself, enacted nothing harsher against them, but dismissed them free and, by issuing an edict, checked the persecution that had been stirred up against adherents of the Christian religion: καταπαῦσαι διὰ προστάγματος τὸν κατὰ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας διωγμόν (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chap. 20, p. 90). Finally, concerning both Domitian and Nero, our Author added: “Such have always been our persecutors: unjust, impious, shameful men, whom even you pagans have been accustomed to condemn, and whose condemned victims you have customarily restored” (Tertullian, ibid.).

In vain, therefore, and quite ineptly, those same pagans tried [Col. 1008A] to excuse their cruelty toward Christians under the empty pretext of edicts issued by these emperors. But we shall discuss both of those emperors, Domitian and Nero, and the persecution stirred up against the Christians, in another dissertation (infra, chap. 16, art. 3; *Dissert. on Lucius Caecilius*, chap. 6, arts. 1 and 2).

Moreover, if these two most wicked emperors sanctioned certain most unjust laws against the Christians, it is certainly established that the others who reigned in the interval between them, or after Domitian down to Tertullian’s age, either did not harass the Christians, favored them, or issued no edicts against them, but instead amended earlier ones. How certain this is, you will indeed recognize from these words of Tertullian, with which he challenges the pagans [Col. 1008B] as follows: “Of all the rulers from that time down to the present who possessed wisdom divine and human, produce any one who waged war upon the Christians” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 294). With what assurance, I ask, would he have dared to address the pagans so confidently, unless this had been entirely true? And certainly he had Melito, cited by Eusebius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chap. 26, p. 148), and several others, as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissert. on Lucius Caecilius*, chap. 6, art. 3), as supporters and advocates of his opinion, which he himself further confirms, as will be clear from the following articles.

### ARTICLE II. An Examination of Whether Marcus Aurelius Favored the Christian Religion Because Christian Soldiers Obtained from God, Not without a Great Miracle, Rain for His Army When It Was Dying of Thirst, and How He Did Not Remove the Penalties Imposed upon Those Same Christians, but Openly Rendered Them Ineffectual

[Col. 1008C]

The pagans abused the most unjust laws of the worst emperors in order to torture Christians with all the greater perversity because they knew with certainty that far better emperors of their own had either issued decrees in the Christians’ favor or had been their patrons and defenders. Tertullian calls these emperors by name, though without observing the chronological order of each. For he begins with Marcus Aurelius, whom he asserts to have been a protector of the Christians. Nor, he says, will anyone ever deny it: “If the letters of that most serious emperor are sought out, in which he testifies that the German thirst [Col. 1008D] was dispelled by rain obtained through the prayers of soldiers who happened to be Christians” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 295). It is indeed certain, and proved by the unanimous agreement of all, whether pagan or Christian, that these events occurred when Marcus Aurelius was drawing up his battle line to fight against the Germans and Sarmatians. For then his soldiers, who were dying of thirst, were revived by rain obtained from heaven. But someone may call into question whether it was obtained through the prayers of pagans or of Christians.

For several pagan writers attribute this rain to the prayer and piety of that same emperor. First among these we encounter Capitolinus, whose words concerning him are as follows: “By his own prayers he wrested lightning [Col. 1009A] from heaven against the enemy’s contrivance, while rain was obtained for his men when they were suffering from thirst” (Capitolinus, *Life of Marcus Antoninus*, p. 305). Themistius speaks more fully in a public oration to Theodosius: Ἀντωνίνῳ τῴ Ῥωμαίων ἀυτοκράτορι τοῦ στρατεύματος ὑπὸ δίψους αὐτῳ πιεζομένου, ἀναχὼν τὼ χεῖρε ὁ βασιλεὺς πρὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν· Ταύτῃ, ἔφη, τῇ χεῖρι προυτρεψάμην σε, καὶ ἱκέτυσα τὸν ζωῆς δοτήρα, ᾗ ζωὴν οὐκ ἀφελόμην, καὶ ὅυτω κατῄδεσε τὸν θεὸν τᾖ εὐχᾖ, ὥστε ἐξ αἰθρίας ἦλθον νεφέλαι ὐδροφεροῦσαι τοῖς στρατιώταις. “When the army of Antoninus, emperor of the Romans, was suffering from thirst, he raised his hand to heaven, saying: ‘With this hand I wished as a suppliant to appease you, and I prayed to the giver of life, since with it I have deprived no one of life.’ By that prayer he appeased the divine power, and immediately, when the sky had cleared, a great abundance of rain burst forth to quench the soldiers’ thirst” (Themistius, [Col. 1009B] Oration 15, *To Theodosius*, p. 191). He then immediately added that he remembered seeing a painting represented in a picture in which the emperor was depicted in the midst of the battle line and the soldiers were shown catching the rain in their helmets. Baronius, moreover, presented a representation of the column upon which that miraculous rain is seen being granted by Jupiter as giver of rain and wielder of thunder (Baronius, under the year of Christ 176, § 24).

In Dio’s *Epitome*, however, we read that a report had spread that Arnuphis, an Egyptian magician, invoked Mercury by certain magical arts, together with other demons who dwell in the air, and by their agency wrested forth this rain (Dio, *Epitome*, p. 274). Although Xiphilinus strives with all his might to accuse Dio of falsehood there (Xiphilinus, ibid., p. 275), Claudian, uncertain and doubtful in mind, nevertheless set out both opinions in these verses [Col. 1009C]:

> … Whether Chaldean spells, in a magician’s rite,  
> Armed the gods, or—as I believe—the whole  
> Service of the Thunderer was merited by Marcus’ character.  
> (Claudian, *On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius*, v. 357 ff.)

But this doubt of the pagans, also noted by Lampridius, arose from nothing other than their innate hatred of Christians and their customary flattery of their rulers (Lampridius, *Life of Heliogabalus*, p. 141).

For Eusebius quite rightly asserts that greater credence should be given to our own writers, who, as devotees of truth, committed the event itself to writing simply and candidly (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 5, p. 169). And lest anyone deny him credence, he cites two witnesses. The first is Apollinaris, who had recorded in writing [Col. 1009D] that Aurelius gave that legion of Christian soldiers the name “Thundering” for this reason: because it had obtained that rain by divine favor. But the pagans, doubtless seizing upon the occasion supplied by this cognomen, invented the claim that it had been brought about by Jupiter the Thunderer. The second witness praised by Eusebius is our own Tertullian, whose words from the *Apologeticus*, transcribed by us, he cited in Greek translation. But he could also have cited another of his books, in which he affirms no less clearly and confidently that this astonishing rain was granted by God in response to the Christian soldiers’ prayers. For he wrote as follows to Scapula, the pagan governor: “Marcus Aurelius, during the German expedition, obtained rains in that drought through the prayers made to God by Christian soldiers. When have droughts not also been driven away by our kneeling [Col. 1010A] and fasting? Then even the people, crying out to the God of gods, who alone is mighty, bore witness to our God under the name of Jupiter” (Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chap. 4). From these words, moreover, you may readily perceive that there is nothing at all surprising if pagan writers proclaimed that the miraculous rain had been granted by their Jupiter, since they were accustomed to attribute similar miracles, worked through the prayers of Christians, to that same Jupiter. But, as Tertullian very aptly observes, unwittingly and unwillingly they acclaimed our true and almighty God under the name of Jupiter.

Someone may perhaps ask why, in this latter passage, he pronounced so confidently that this rain was granted in response to Christian prayers, when in the *Apologeticus* he added the adverb “perhaps.” Did he at some point hesitate in doubt [Col. 1010B] on this matter, or was that adverb improperly inserted into his text? For it does not occur in Eusebius’ Greek text. Yet we do not dare assert this against the authority of the manuscripts. Is it not more probable, then, that the adverb belongs not to one who doubts but to one who mocks the pagans, who foolishly believed that this rain had been given by their fictitious Jupiter?

The matter would be more evident to everyone if the letters of the emperor Aurelius cited by our Author had come down to us. Some, however, suspect that they are those of which a copy is printed after the First *Apology* of Justin Martyr. But we have already noted that document to be spurious and adulterated (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 369).

From these words of Tertullian, “if they are sought out,” Scaliger thinks it may be inferred [Col. 1010C] that Tertullian had never read them (Scaliger, *Observations on Eusebius’ Chronicle*, at the year 2189). He attempts to establish this also by the testimony of Orosius. But how could Tertullian so confidently urge the pagans to read them unless he himself had read either the letters or what was written in them? Moreover, Eusebius concludes from these same words of Tertullian that these letters existed in Tertullian’s time: εἴσετι νῦν φέρεσθαι (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 5, p. 169). Why, then, Scaliger argues, did Eusebius not transcribe them in full with his customary diligence, if they truly existed at that time? But that objection is altogether feeble unless it is clearly proved that there is absolutely no document of this kind that Eusebius failed to transcribe. Scaliger, or anyone else, will never be able to prove this.

[Col. 1010D] Moreover, Marcus Aurelius, mindful of so great a benefit received from heaven through the prayers of Christians, showed them favor insofar as he could. For since he was unable wholly to suppress the exceedingly great fury of the pagans against the Christians, “Just as,” says Tertullian, “he did not openly remove the penalty from such persons, so in another way he openly rendered it ineffectual, even adding condemnation for the accusers, and indeed a more severe one” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 296). For he did not dare entirely to remove, relax, and remit the penalties that had previously been established against Christians by the laws of other emperors. Yet, in order to restrain the insolence of the pagans, who never ceased accusing them, he imposed upon these accusers other penalties, more severe than those imposed by Trajan, whom our Author cites in the same passage, as we shall shortly see; [Col. 1011A] and by this prudent compromise he protected the Christians for his part.

Moreover, Eusebius transcribed for us the complete text of a law addressed in the name of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus to the Council of Asia and issued in favor of the Christians, the concluding words of which are these: Εἰ δέ τὶς ἐπιμένοι τίνα τῶν τοιούτῶν εἷς πράγματα φέρων ὡς δὴ τοιοῦτον, ἐκεῖνος ὁ καταφερόμενος ἀπολελύσθω τοῦ ἐγκλήματος, καὶ ἐὰν φαίνεται τοιούτος ὥν· ὁ δὲ καταφέρων, ἔνοχος ἔσθαι δίκης. “But if anyone still persists in causing trouble for any of them on the ground that he is a Christian, the accused shall be acquitted of the charge, even if it is established that he is in fact a Christian. The informer himself, however, shall suffer punishment” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chap. 14, p. 127). We know, indeed, that some have thought this law to have proceeded not from Marcus Aurelius [Col. 1011B] but from Antoninus Pius. Yet if this opinion is true, it equally serves Tertullian’s purpose. For he also places this same Antoninus Pius among the good rulers who sanctioned no edicts against Christians (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 297).

Perhaps someone will ask us how Tertullian can extol in such praises Marcus Aurelius’ solicitude and favor toward Christians, when during his reign, as some think, the fourth persecution of the Christian Church arose, as we shall observe later (*Dissert. on Lucius Caecilius*, chap. 1, art. 3, and chap. 6, art. 3). But that very law cited immediately above supplies us with an answer. For although penalties were decreed in it against the accusers of Christians, the gods [Col. 1011C] of the pagans were nevertheless first praised. But this commendation increased rather than extinguished the raging frenzy of the pagans against them. What, moreover, of the fact that those same pagans were convinced that other laws issued against the Christians were not abrogated by these more recent ones? Besides, what could laws accomplish against the unbridled fury of a populace blinded by various superstitions and against the mad assaults of the mob? Were not almost innumerable martyrs, as Eusebius relates, most cruelly killed in these times in contempt of these laws (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 5, p. 153)? Nothing, therefore, should be inferred from this against Marcus Aurelius’ favorable disposition toward Christians, since he permitted what he could not prevent.

### ARTICLE III. An Examination of the Grounds upon Which Tertullian Asserts That the Laws Written against Christians Were Mitigated by the Emperor Trajan, but That No Laws against Them Were Enacted by Hadrian, Investigator of All Curiosities; by Vespasian, Conqueror of the Jews; by Pius; or by Verus—or Severus—the Emperors

[Col. 1011D]

Tertullian retraces his steps and passes from Marcus Aurelius to Trajan, who was earlier than he. Trajan, as Tertullian himself puts it, partially frustrated the laws enacted against Christians by forbidding Christians to be sought out (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 296). Earlier decrees of the emperors had ordered that they be sought out and punished; but Trajan, as we showed above (supra, chap. 7, art. 2), did indeed forbid their being sought out, while ordering that those who were brought before the authorities be punished.

[Col. 1012A] But his successor Hadrian established no law whatever against them, although he seemed bound to be more hostile to them than others. For he was, says our Author, “an investigator of all curiosities” (Idem, ibid., p. 297)—that is, wholly devoted to every kind of magical art. And, according to Xiphilinus, he was certainly reproached with the vice of being πριεργοτατος καὶ μαντείαις μαγγανείαις τε παντοδαπαῖς ἐχρῆτο: “exceedingly inquisitive, and practicing divination and every magical art” (Xiphilinus, *Epitome of Dio*, p. 262). Ammianus Marcellinus, moreover, when speaking of Julian the Apostate, says: “He was excessively devoted to the consultation of omens, so that in this respect he seemed to equal the emperor Hadrian, being superstitious rather than a lawful observer of sacred rites” (Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXV, chap. 4, p. 427). Nevertheless, says Tertullian, no law [Col. 1012B] against Christians was sanctioned by this Hadrian. Accordingly, Melito wrote in his *Apology* to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus that Nero’s and Domitian’s lack of judgment had been corrected by rescripts of subsequent emperors: Ἐν οἶς ὁ μὲν πάππος σου Ἁδριανὸς πολλοῖς μὲν ἀλλοις, καὶ Φουνδάνῳ δὲ τῳ ἀνθυπάτῳ τὴς Ἀσίας γράφων φαίνεται. “Among these, your grandfather Hadrian sent letters not only to many others but also to Fundanus, proconsul of Asia” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chap. 26, p. 148). Jerome further attests that, when Hadrian visited Eleusis and was initiated into almost all the sacred rites of Greece, a book in defense of our Christian religion was presented to him; it so greatly astonished everyone that his excellent intelligence brought a most severe persecution to an end (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, § 19, and Letter 83, *To Magnus*). But [Col. 1012C] the pagans, finding in the impious emperor’s many superstitions an opportunity to harass Christians with impunity, raged against them most bitterly, although he enacted no law against them and indeed afterward calmed the storm that had arisen.

Then our Author proceeds still farther backward from Hadrian to Vespasian, who likewise, he says, issued no edict against Christians, although he was “the conqueror of the Jews” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 5, p. 294), whom almost all pagans customarily confused with those same Christians. Who does not know that the Jewish nation was conquered by him, and that at Rome he celebrated a triumph over them together with his son Titus? That he issued no decree concerning Christians is attested by Eusebius, who recorded [Col. 1012D] that the second persecution after Nero was stirred up by Domitian: Καὶπερ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ Οὐεσπασιανοῦ μηδὲν καθ` ἡμῶν ἄτοπον ἐπινοήσαντος. “Although his father Vespasian had never attempted to inflict any injury upon us” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chap. 17, p. 88).

What more need be said? Pius also, who ruled long after Vespasian, Tertullian continues, neither approved nor signed any bloody laws against Christians (Tertullian, loc. cit.). For Melito, in the *Apology* already cited by us, addresses Marcus Aurelius in these words preserved by Eusebius: Ὁ δὲ πατὴρ σου, καὶ σοῦ τὰ σύμπαντα διοικοῦντος αὐτῷ, ταῖς πόλεσι περὶ τοῦ μηδὲν νεωτερίζειν περὶ ἡμῶν ἔγραψεν· ἐν οἶς, καὶ πρὸς Λαρισσαίους, καὶ πρὸς [Col. 1013A] Θεσσαλονικεῖς, καὶ πρὸς Ἀθηναίους, καὶ πρὸς πάντας Ἔλλήνας. “Your father also, during the time when you administered all affairs together with him, wrote to the cities that they were not to stir up disturbances against us—specifically to the people of Larissa, the Thessalonians, the Athenians, and finally to all the Greeks” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chap. 26, p. 148). Several learned men of our own age also think that he enacted, in favor of the Christians, the law which, as we noted a little above, others ascribe to Marcus Aurelius (preceding article).

The sixth and last of these more equitable emperors is named by Tertullian in these words: “No Verus impressed laws hostile to Christians” (Tertullian, loc. cit.); we must doubtless understand, “upon the public tablets, so that they might be promulgated.” But it is worth observing here [Col. 1013B] that these words, “No Verus,” are omitted in Eusebius’ text, which renders this passage of Tertullian in Greek (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chap. 5, p. 170). And certainly this same Verus, made co-ruler by Marcus Aurelius, reigned with him for nine years at most and died before him. For this reason, some suspect that this name was corrupted in Tertullian’s text and that “Severus” should be read. Pamelius, indeed, advises us that this reading is actually found in one Vatican manuscript and another at Liège. But because it is not read in all the other manuscripts, including those of better quality, we dare decide nothing against the authority of so many codices. Could not Tertullian also have mentioned him because, following the example of Aurelius, his colleague who had been adopted by him, he enacted no law against Christians and had devised nothing [Col. 1013C] against them?

Yet if anyone rather obstinately maintains that the name Severus was written there, we shall not strongly resist. For in another book Tertullian commends Severus’ singular inclination and benevolence toward Christians, all of whom—at least during the early years of his reign—he embraced because of a miracle performed for his benefit. But let us hear his words, if you please: “Severus himself,” he says, “the father of Antoninus Caracalla, was mindful of the Christians. For he sought out the Christian Proculus, surnamed Torpacion, the steward of Euhodias, who had once cured him by means of oil, and kept him in his palace until the man’s death. Antoninus too knew him very well, having been reared on Christian milk” (Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chap. 4). He thus informs us that the emperor Severus was miraculously [Col. 1013D] relieved of an illness by oil that Proculus had given him. And lest anyone either excessively obstinate or altogether unbelieving raise a doubt concerning so great a miracle, he specifies both Proculus’ surname and his office. He was called Torpacion, he says, and was the steward of Euhodias. But it is now exceedingly difficult to say who this person was.

In another book, however, Tertullian relates that the errors of the Valentinians were attacked not only by Justin Martyr, Miltiades, and Irenaeus, but also by Proculus, of whom he speaks as follows: “Our Proculus, the distinction of virginal old age and Christian eloquence; all of them, in every work of faith as in this one, I would wish to equal” (Idem, *Against the Valentinians*, chap. 5). But because [Col. 1014A] this book was composed by Tertullian after his defection to the Montanists, and Proculus is called “our Proculus,” some think it may be inferred that he was so called because he was attached to the same errors of the Montanists. Accordingly, they add that he is designated by these words of Jerome: “Gaius, under Antoninus the son of Severus, conducted a notable disputation against Proculus, a follower of Montanus” (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, § 19). But since this man was a Montanist, he certainly does not appear to have been the same as Proculus Torpacion. Moreover, the latter is called the steward of Euhodias, whereas the former was highly renowned for the distinction of his Christian eloquence.

But we learn from Dio’s *Epitome* that Evodus (Εὔοδον) was the tutor of Antoninus Caracalla, τοῦ τροφέος αὐτοῦ (Dio, *Epitome*, p. 333). Proculus could therefore have been the steward of this Evodus, or [Col. 1014B] Euhodias. For at this very time, as Tertullian says, he was residing in Severus’ palace, where Caracalla came to know him and, through his influence, was reared on Christian milk.

Moreover, whatever conclusion may be reached concerning this Proculus Torpacion, there is no room for doubt that Severus favored the Christians because his health had been restored to him in a wondrous manner. For he not only retained this Christian Proculus in his palace, but also, as Tertullian further asserts, “Severus, knowing that most distinguished women and most distinguished men belonged to this sect, not only did them no injury but even honored them with his testimony and openly resisted the populace when it raged against us” (Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chap. 4). He therefore truly favored the Christians, and not slightly, and showed himself to be not a secret but a public [Col. 1014C] patron and defender of them. Why, indeed, should he not have favored those from whom he had not only received the greatest benefit, but whose supreme loyalty toward himself he had also always experienced? For among the factions of Cassius, Niger, and Albinus which arose from the very beginning of his reign, as we saw above (supra, chap. 2, art. 1) and shall say again below, no Christian was ever found.

Nor should you say that this conflicts with what we stated above (ibid.), namely that a persecution against the Christians was stirred up by this same emperor Severus. For it was provoked not at the beginning of his reign, but after ten years and more. It is, however, established that until that time he favored the Christians to no small degree.

We think, moreover, that there is no fair judge of these matters [Col. 1014D] who will not readily understand from what has thus far been said how powerful is this argument of our Author, by whose weight he utterly overwhelms the pagans who claimed that they were bound by their laws to torture and destroy Christians. For he demonstrated that those laws were both most unjust and enacted by most unjust rulers. No less clearly did he disclose that they had been corrected and amended by several others endowed with uprightness and equity. Finally, those who enacted no law against the Christians were undoubtedly endeavoring to safeguard and protect them insofar as the injustice of the times permitted.

## CHAPTER XX. On Crimes of Injured Divine Majesty, of Which Christians Were Accused by Pagans Who Were Themselves Guilty of Them, as Falsely as Shamelessly

[Col. 1015A]

### ARTICLE I. How Invincibly Tertullian Demonstrates That Christians Were Undeservedly Accused of Infanticide—That Is, of Killing an Infant in Their Sacred Assemblies, Then Eating Its Flesh and Drinking Its Blood—and of Most Shameful Incest; and How He Utterly Overthrows the Pagans’ Empty Cavils, with Reference to Dog-Faced Men, Shadow-Feet, and Antipodes

No other pretext remained to the pagans for harassing and destroying Christians except to accuse them, by whatever means, of some capital [Col. 1015B] crime. But they had advanced to such a degree of fury and madness that they declared them guilty not merely of one enormity but of all crimes, and, as Tertullian says, enemies “of the gods, the emperors, the laws, morality, and the whole of nature” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 2, p. 277). But who, struck by this altogether horrendous accusation, would not immediately be stupefied? For how could Christians be guilty of so many and such great crimes when, as we have already demonstrated, they not only worshiped the one true God with the highest veneration, but also possessed the chastest morals and a most pious manner of life? So false an accusation therefore collapsed of itself. But because the Christian religion, as Tertullian puts it, “begs no indulgence for its cause” (ibid., chap. 1, p. 259), nor, as defendants commonly do, seeks any favor [Col. 1015C] or partiality, it therefore wishes and asks this one thing alone: that it be examined according to the stricter prescriptions of the laws. Accordingly, Tertullian undertakes to examine and refute individually all the charges brought against Christians, and demonstrates most manifestly that those same Christians were as falsely accused of these enormities as it was certain that the pagans were in truth guilty of them.

For what could be further from the truth than to charge with injured divine majesty those who, as we have said, always worshiped the true God both privately and publicly in their assemblies, and preferred to be killed by any of the most atrocious tortures rather than deny this one God or venerate false gods with even merely feigned and simulated worship? By contrast, the pagans were most evidently convicted of this supreme impiety, for they [Col. 1015D] worshiped fabricated gods, as we shall show below, whom they admitted to be infamous and defiled by every kind of most shameful crime.

Yet they never ceased crying out that Christians were guilty of offenses against the divine majesty because in their assemblies and amid their more sacred mysteries they most shamelessly polluted themselves with utterly abominable crimes. For, says Tertullian, they were called “most criminal on account of the sacrament of infanticide” (ibid., chap. 7, p. 306)—that is, the infant whom they were said to kill there and devour. Then, after that accursed banquet, they were said to be polluted by most shameful incest, because “the overturners of the lamps—the dogs, namely the procurers—provide the darkness and then also [Col. 1016A] the shamelessness required by impious lusts”; these too are words of our Author (ibid.). In our manuscripts and in the early editions, the word *then* is absent, nor does it seem very necessary there. Tertullian’s meaning, which he relates more briefly in another book, is this: after the lamps have been overturned and extinguished by dogs, darkness, performing the office of most impure procurers, provides the shamelessness required by impious lusts (Idem, *Ad Nationes*, book I, chaps. 15 and 16). These were the principal and capital crimes which the pagans, as we have noted elsewhere more than once (*Dissert. on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 8, art. 1 ff.), charged against Christians with as much long-continued shamelessness as the ease with which they were refuted and confuted by the ancient Fathers of the Church.

Our Tertullian, however, utterly overthrows [Col. 1016B] this false accusation by various cogent arguments. First, he addresses the pagans themselves in this manner: “You are forever saying that we are guilty of such great crimes; yet throughout the long time in which this has been said, you have not taken care to uncover, investigate, and disclose them” (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chap. 7, p. 307). Yet no one should be condemned before being convicted of a crime: “Therefore either uncover them,” he says, “if you believe them, and convict the Christians of these crimes, or do not believe them, because you have not uncovered them” (ibid.). Indeed, through this deliberate concealment and negligence, a presumption is established (ibid.), and by the surest prior judgment the Christians’ innocence and supreme moral integrity are proved: because “you yourselves do not dare to uncover” (ibid.) those crimes of which you accuse them as falsely as rashly, although their case has never, as we have seen, been heard before you condemn, torture, and kill them.

[Col. 1016C] Moreover, the perversity of the pagans was all the greater because they could very easily and readily investigate and ascertain whether those crimes attributed to the Christians were true. “The origin of that teaching,” says Tertullian—that is, the beginning of this Christian teaching disseminated throughout the world—“dates from Tiberius” (ibid.); or, as he states more explicitly in another book: “Under the emperor Augustus this name, ‘Christians,’ arose; under Tiberius its teaching dawned.” Yet certainly, because the Christian religion is true, “it began together with hatred of itself”—these too are his own words—“as soon as it appeared, it was an enemy.” In our manuscript codices, however, the reading is “it is an enemy”; that is, from the very time when it began and appeared to the world, it was hostile and hateful to everyone; and “it had as many enemies as there were outsiders” (the same author, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 307), that is, absolutely everyone except the Christians themselves. For, as Tertullian further says, [Col. 1016D] their enemies were, first, “the Jews, from rivalry peculiar to themselves,” or from their envy of them, with which they were always inflamed because Christ had abolished their ancient rites; then “the soldiers, from extortion” (the same author, *Apology*, chap. 7, p. 308), which, as some understand it, means through the insidious accusations of men driven to frenzy, but, more properly, through cruel harassment; and finally even “the Christians’ own household members, by their very nature” (ibid.), since, impatient with their own condition, they customarily plotted against their masters and never ceased attempting to harm them.

“We are therefore besieged by all these persons every day,” Tertullian continues; “every day we are betrayed; very often we are seized in our very assemblies [Col. 1017A] and congregations” (ibid.); or, as he said elsewhere in addressing the pagans themselves: “You know even the days of our gatherings; and so we are both besieged and seized, and detained in our most secret congregations” (the same author, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 568). The pagans therefore could not have remained unaware of what Christians were accustomed to do in them.

But who, our Author argues (Tertullian, *Apology*, loc. cit.), ever came upon an infant wailing in this fashion while it was being killed by Christians? Who, after finding the Christians eating its flesh and drinking its blood, preserved for the judge to inspect their bloody mouths—like those of Cyclopes and Sirens—not even wiped clean? Who ever discovered upon their wives any filthy [Col. 1017B] traces of the adultery committed a little earlier in those same assemblies (ibid.)? In another book he pressed these points in other words as follows: “Who ever came upon a child half eaten? Who detected marks of teeth upon the bloodstained bread? Who, when sudden light burst into the darkness, observed anything filthy—to say nothing of incestuous?” (the same author, *To the Nations*, book I, loc. cit.). In the *Apology*, however, he alluded to the twofold fable of the Cyclopes and the Sirens. For both Greek poets, such as Homer (Homer, *Odyssey* VIII, past the middle), and Latin poets, such as Virgil (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book III, v. 617 ff.), represented the Cyclopes as one-eyed men who devoured their guests. No less familiar is the fable of the Sirens, who lulled sailors with the sweetness of their song and cast them into the sea (Pliny, *Natural History*, book X, chap. 49, p. 441).

[Col. 1017C] Tertullian therefore argues as follows: the Christians had as many enemies as there were pagans, Jews, soldiers, and household servants, by whom they were daily besieged and seized even in their own synaxes. If, therefore, they had perpetrated so many and such horrible crimes in them, they could very easily have been detected by so many enemies so fiercely hostile to them. And yet, out of the almost countless number of those enemies down to that time, not one had ever discovered the slightest trace of any crime. Therefore the charges brought against the Christians by their wicked slanderers were utterly false (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 569).

Nor could these men, however shameless, reply that witnesses to these crimes had ever been corrupted by the Christians with money or payment. For, says Tertullian, “who, after discovering such deeds, [Col. 1017D] concealed or sold them, even while dragging the persons themselves away?” (the same author, *Apology*, chap. 7, p. 308). That is, it could not have happened that any pagan, after learning of these crimes of the Christians, either concealed them of his own accord or, while dragging the Christians before the tribunals of the judges, sold his knowledge for some price and then became completely silent. In another book, however, he expresses this in other—and consider whether clearer—words as follows: “If by payment we prevail upon pagans who have witnessed our crimes to prevent us from being brought before the public and condemned as the persons they actually know us to be, why are we seized when no one has accused or convicted us? Can we not, after corrupting the witnesses with gold, also avoid being brought to trial altogether? For who, whether witness or judge, sells the betrayal”—that is, the disclosure and accusation—[Col. 1018A] “of some horrible crime without the crime itself, which might at some later time be discovered and punished by another; or who, being privy to it, buys back the secret?” (the same author, *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 568).

Thus it had never been proved by anyone’s testimony that Christians were guilty of these crimes. For who, as Tertullian insists, could ever have disclosed them? Certainly not the Christians themselves. For if it was unlawful for pagans to disclose their Samothracian and Eleusinian rites, how much more were Christians bound to keep silent about their divine mysteries (Tertullian, *Apology*, loc. cit.; and *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 568)? If, therefore, they were concealed by the Christians themselves in the profoundest silence, “whence,” asks Tertullian, “did foreign pagans obtain knowledge of them, when even pious initiations always exclude the profane and dispense with witnesses, unless the impious have less fear?” [Col. 1018B] (ibid., loc. cit.). In our better manuscript codices and in most of the early editions, we read “even impious initiations.” And this is perhaps not a bad reading. For Tertullian could thus have argued, as they say, from the lesser to the greater: if the impious initiations of the pagans must be concealed, how much more the sacred and pious initiations of the Christians—unless impious pagans, by divulging them, had less reason to fear for themselves than Christians did.

Our Author presses the matter further, and demonstrates by the following argument that these execrable crimes could neither be committed nor believed by anyone. Christians who lived piously were promised a blessed eternity after this life. But what Christian, or what person about to be initiated into the Christian religion, could ever have been persuaded that it might be obtained by so many and such great crimes? [Col. 1018C] Could even one pagan who was not wholly insane ever have believed a man, even one of the highest authority, who said such things—or, if you prefer, swore to them—and with such ready credulity have allowed himself to be polluted by such atrocious abominations? Yet if pagans can neither believe nor perpetrate these things, how much less can Christians, whose nature is no different from that of other human beings (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 8, p. 312; and *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 569)? For, says Tertullian, “they are not Cycopennae or Sciapods”; or, as he writes in another book, “some Cynopennae, or Sciapods, or some antipodes from beneath the earth” (the same author, loc. cit., pp. 312 and 569). The first of these, if Ctesias, whom Pliny cites, is to be believed, “were called Monocoli,” he says, “and had a single leg, with marvelous speed in leaping; they were also called Sciapods because, in the greater heat, they lay upon the ground on their backs [Col. 1018D] and protected themselves with the shadow of their feet” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chap. 2, p. 11). On these see also Solinus (Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chap. 52, p. 80), Augustine (Augustine, *City of God*, book XVI, chap. 8, p. 422), Suidas (Suidas, under V. Σκιάποδες), and Apollodorus as cited by Tzetzes (Tzetzes, *Chiliades* 7, v. 662 ff.). The Cynopennae, however, are called “Cyclopes” in some printed editions and “Cynophanes” in others, but contrary to the authority of our manuscript codices. Vossius thinks that *Cynopanes* should be read, in Greek κυνοπάνες, “horned dogs” (Vossius, notes on Mela, *On the Situation of the World*, book III, chap. 9). Salmasius, however, approves the reading *Cynopennae* found in those same codices of ours, deriving it from the Greek word κυνοπεῖναι: “as though,” he says, “suffering from canine hunger” (Salmasius, notes on Solinus, [Col. 1019A] p. 1005). This certainly suits Tertullian’s purpose, since he is there speaking of Christians who were falsely accused by the pagans of eating the flesh of a murdered infant and suffering from hunger worse than a dog’s. But who these beings were is of little importance to know. For our Author is speaking of monsters which everyone freely acknowledges to have been entirely fictitious.

What, then, someone may ask: did he regard the antipodes also as monsters of this kind? Yet no mention of them is found in the *Apology*, but only in the book *To the Nations*. Did he not name them there because he himself, like many others whom we have named elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 21, art. 6), had persuaded himself that there could be no antipodes unless they walked, as was said, with their feet turned opposite to ours? Certainly [Col. 1019B] they are rejected by him as nothing other than monstrous, false, and fictitious men in these words: “Or some persons sprung up like mushrooms from the earth beneath the ground, who possess a nature different from that of the people of our earth.” But Christians were far removed from the savagery of these and other monsters; they differed from other human beings like ourselves only in surpassing them in humanity and charity. They could therefore never have been induced, under any appearance whatsoever of piety and religion, to eat the flesh of an infant whom they themselves had killed, and afterward to pollute themselves with fornications, adulteries, and incest.

The pagans, nevertheless, struck blind by obstinacy, insisted that either the Christians, being excessively credulous, or at least novices in their religion had been deceived and deluded. But nothing more foolish or absurd could be imagined. For it was the custom among Christians that those about to be initiated should be taught by the father of the sacred rites—that is, by the bishop or one of his deputies—what they must do to prepare for those rites, or what was to be done in them. But with what effrontery could a bishop or anyone else have said to a novice or a Christian: “When you come to the sacred synaxes, you will need an infant, still tender, one who knows nothing of death, who will smile beneath your knife, with which you will cut his throat; likewise bread, with which you may collect the juicy blood”—or, as it is better expressed in another book, “the fresh blood” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 8, p. 313; and *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 569). “You will also need dogs which, after a morsel has been thrown to them, will extinguish the lights; and finally you will need your sister and your mother, with whom in the midst of the darkness you will commit sexual violation.” But tell us, please: with what ears could any Christian [Col. 1019D] or novice have listened to these things? Could he do so without horror? Ought he not at least to have feared the laws, in which, as Cicero observes, it had been ordained: “Let the pontiffs punish incest with the ultimate penalty” (Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, p. 335, line 15)? But if he thought he could evade this penalty through the Christians’ deception or influence, how was it that, when questioned by pagan judges, he preferred to be tortured with the cruelest torments and killed rather than confess crimes against which his conscience utterly rebelled? Such things are plainly credible to no sane person, nor will anyone ever be persuaded that they could have occurred.

The pagans insisted that they had learned by report that the Christians were in fact guilty of the aforesaid crimes. But, Tertullian replies, this answer is utterly foolish [Col. 1020A] and futile (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 7, p. 309; and *To the Nations*, book I, chap. 7, p. 566). For they could not deny the truth of what the most celebrated poet sang:

> Rumor—an evil swifter than any other.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book IV, v. 174.)

For rumor is merely the name given to an uncertain matter, and it very often arises either from a disposition toward rivalry—that is, envy—or at the prompting of suspicion, meaning a suspicion invented without cause, or from the pleasure of lying. Arising, therefore, from so corrupt a source and from the mouth of only one person, it generally lies; or, if it ever reports anything true, it even then adds something, subtracts something, or alters something. It remains vigorous only so long as it proves nothing. For once the matter is proved, rumor ceases by that very fact and disappears. [Col. 1020B] A wise man therefore rightly places no trust in it, and all the less when it alone is the informer and messenger of wholly secret crimes which no person in possession of his faculties either dares or is able to commit. We have observed elsewhere that this reply of Tertullian is fully confirmed by Minucius Felix in fewer, indeed, but no less effective words (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 8, art. 2). Finally, Tertullian added that rumor, as swift as it is mendacious, ought not to be believed, but that the truth must be investigated, because, as a proverb current among the pagans declared, “Time reveals all things” (Tertullian, ibid., p. 310). Aulus Gellius (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XII, chap. 11) cited this adage as celebrated in the following verses of Sophocles:

[Col. 1020C] Πρὸς ταῦτα, κρύπτε μηδὲν, ὡς ἅπανθ` ὁρῶν

Καὶ πάντ` ἀκούων, πάντ` ἀναπτύσσει χρόνος.

> Moreover, nothing is hidden, since time, seeing all  
> And hearing all, reveals everything.

Seneca, however, says: “Some falsehoods bear the appearance of truth. Time must always be allowed: the day discloses the truth” (Seneca, *On Anger*, book II, chap. 540). Erasmus, however, assembles more material concerning this proverb, and you may consult him (Erasmus, *Adages*, chiliad 2, century 4, adage 17). But what announces falsehoods under the appearance of truth more frequently than rumor? The pagans therefore ought not to have relied, in harassing the Christians, upon its testimony alone, which, if not false, was at least uncertain; rather, they ought to have allowed time for the Christians’ case to be examined and the truth ascertained.

## ARTICLE II. How invincibly Tertullian demonstrates that the pagans were themselves guilty of the homicide of which they falsely accused the Christians, since in Africa they sacrificed infants to Saturn down to the proconsulship of Tiberius, and since this custom continued in secret, although Saturn’s priests, suspended from the trees that shaded his temple, paid the penalty with death, as attested by the soldiery of our native country

[Col. 1020D]

Nothing more shameless can be conceived than falsely to accuse another of a most grievous crime of which the accuser himself is openly proved guilty. Yet such were the pagans, who most shamelessly charged the Christians with infanticide and incest. For “this very thing,” as Tertullian says in addressing them, [Col. 1021A] “is perhaps what led you to believe other things about us” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9, p. 314)—namely, that the far more grievous crimes we have recounted were committed by us. But he deliberately added “perhaps” there, because he had said shortly before that the crimes with which they charged the Christians were so atrocious that scarcely any person could have believed them, unless they themselves had done something similar. First, however, he shows in various ways that they were murderers, because “in Africa,” as he says, “infants were openly sacrificed to Saturn down to the proconsulship of Tiberius, who exposed those very priests upon the same trees that shaded their temple, upon crosses consecrated to their crimes, as is attested by the soldiery of our native country, which carried out that very task for that proconsul” (ibid. ff.). Concerning this detestable sacrifice of infants, contrary to every law of nature itself, [Col. 1021B] we have made many observations in our earlier dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 9, art. 2; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 34, art. 3). It remains, therefore, for us now to examine individually those points peculiar to our Tertullian.

First, then, he relates that this most cruel custom persisted down to the proconsulship of Tiberius. Some, however, have suspected that the passage should read “down to the proconsul of Tiberius”; that is, some proconsul either sent by the emperor Tiberius or himself surnamed Tiberius, who was entirely different from and later than the emperor Tiberius. But since this emendation, whatever its worth, was insufficient, they added another, and thought that what followed should be read “as attested by the military service of our father”; that is, as they conjectured, Tertullian’s father, [Col. 1021C] who was proconsul after the death of Tiberius Caesar. But they first ought to have proved that Tertullian’s father bore Tiberius as his personal name. Moreover, all the codices, both printed and manuscript, contradict this conjecture.

But what prevents us from believing that the emperor Tiberius prohibited that most dreadful sacrifice of infants in Africa? Did not Pliny record that in the year 647 from the foundation of the City, when Gnaeus Lentulus and Publius Licinius Crassus were consuls, a senatorial decree forbade the sacrifice of a human being? But because this most savage custom nevertheless persisted afterward among the Gauls, “the principate of Tiberius Caesar,” he says, “abolished their Druids. . . . . . [Col. 1021D] Nor can it adequately be estimated how much is owed to the Romans, who abolished monstrosities in which it was considered most religious to kill a human being, and even most beneficial to eat one” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXX, chap. 1, p. 728). Do you hear that in this most impious sacrifice the pagans not only killed human beings but even ate their flesh? Yet Tiberius Caesar is said to have abolished it in Gaul and elsewhere. Why, then, should he not also have done so in Africa, as Tertullian so expressly declares? If, moreover, a similar example can contribute anything toward confirming this opinion, Josephus supplies one for us (Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book XVIII, chap. 4, p. 622). For he attests that the same Tiberius demolished the temple of Isis and had its statue cast into the Tiber because Paulina, a noblewoman, had been violated in that temple of Isis through the wicked artifices of the priests by the young Decius Mundus, who was pretending to be the god Anubis. [Col. 1022A] Why, then, would he have spared the still more horrible sacrifice of infants to Saturn in Africa, rather than in Gaul, as we have said, and in other regions?

But by what reasoning, you will ask, did Tertullian say “down to the proconsulship of Tiberius”? Had Tiberius been proconsul in Africa before he held the government of the Roman Empire? But what, I ask you, prevents him from having been appointed proconsul of Africa and sent there by Augustus Caesar, or even earlier? If, however, someone should properly prove that Tertullian must be understood as referring to another Tiberius, a proconsul of Africa, we shall readily agree with him.

Tertullian further added that the most cruel priests of Saturn were, by command of the same Tiberius, exposed upon the trees of that temple which had shaded so many crimes. [Col. 1022B] For trees were planted around pagan temples and consecrated to the particular god of each temple. Passing over other witnesses, Apuleius recorded the following concerning a certain shrine: “She sees splendid offerings and strips of cloth embroidered with gold, fastened to the branches of trees and to the doorposts, which, together with an acknowledgment of the favor received, bore witness to the name of the goddess to whom they had been dedicated” (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VI, shortly after the beginning, p. 92). You see, therefore, that gifts were hung upon these trees and that the name of the god to whom the temple was dedicated was affixed to them. But from these trees that shaded Saturn’s temple, says our Author, were made votive and consecrated crosses upon which those most inhuman priests were suspended and compelled to end their lives by strangulation. Whether this is the true meaning of Tertullian’s words, [Col. 1022C] which have exercised the ingenuity of scholars to no small degree, I should like you to consider, or else to offer us a better interpretation. Yet you will doubtless acknowledge with us that some light may be shed upon this passage by the following verses of Ausonius, in which he sang of Love suspended from the trunk of a myrtle:

> In the mournful grove the best-known myrtle is chosen,  
> Hateful because of a god’s punishments. There once Proserpina,  
> Scorned by Adonis, tormented him in remembrance of Venus.  
> Upon the lofty trunk of this tree they suspend Love,  
> His hands bound behind his back and bonds tightened  
> Around his feet; as he grieves, they afflict him with punishment  
> Without restraint.  
> (Ausonius, *Idyll* 2, v. 55 ff.)

Furthermore, lest anyone should doubt the punishment inflicted upon those priests of Saturn, our Author calls as witness the soldiery of his native country, which “carried out,” he says, “that very task for the proconsul Tiberius” (Tertullian, *Apology*, [Col. 1022D] chap. 9, p. 315). By these words he doubtless means the soldiers of Africa who were then serving under the proconsul Tiberius and, while performing their duty, saw the priests suspended and strangled upon those trees. The pagans were indeed terrified by their example, but not entirely overcome. For they no longer dared openly to sacrifice infants to Saturn; “but now,” says Tertullian, “this sacred crime continues in secret” (the same author, ibid.). Thus, armed against their innocent children under the appearance of false piety, they did not cease to slaughter them secretly and in concealment, in contempt of the laws of their emperors.
