And so Saturn, “who did not spare his own children,” as our Author says and as we have seen elsewhere (ibid.; and *Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, [Col. 1023A] chap. 9, art. 2), did not abandon his former cruelty, but desired the children of other men still to be sacrificed to him.

Therefore, even if Christians had killed some infant in their synaxes—although this was utterly false—they ought not on that account to have been accused and condemned by pagans who, with the most savage inhumanity, sacrificed their own children as victims which they believed most pleasing to Saturn.

## ARTICLE III. It is shown that the Gauls were likewise guilty of homicide, since they sacrificed human beings to Mercury; as were the Taurians, who sacrificed them to Diana; likewise the Romans, who in the city of the descendants of Aeneas drenched Jupiter with human blood at their games; and others, who wrung the breath from their newborn children in water or exposed them to a death by no means entirely uncertain; and how greatly Christians abhorred every homicide, since they were not even permitted to destroy what had been conceived in the womb while the blood was still being formed into a human being

[Col. 1023B]

Tertullian proceeds and demonstrates that the pagans were guilty of parricide and homicide. For, he says, persons “older than infants were also slaughtered in the Gauls’ rites to Mercury”; and he repeats this in another book (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9, p. 316; and *Scorpiace*, chap. 7). We have made many observations elsewhere concerning this utterly execrable sacrifice (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 9, art. 2), where we also explained more clearly what he immediately adds: [Col. 1023C] “I leave the Taurian fables to their own theaters” (ibid.); or, as he himself says in another book: “Nothing glows there but savagery, namely that which furnished the tales about the sacrifices of the Taurians” (Tertullian, loc. cit.; and *Against Marcion*, book I, chap. 1), who, of course, sacrificed their guests to Diana.

He continues: “Behold, in that most religious city of the pious descendants of Aeneas there is indeed a Jupiter”—namely, Jupiter Latiaris—“whom at their circus and gladiatorial games they drench with human blood.” Elsewhere we read that he wrote: “In Latium, down to the present day, human blood is given to Jupiter to taste in the midst of the City; yet no one reconsiders the matter, or fails either to assume some reason for it or to presume upon the inestimable will of his god” (the same author, *Apology*, chap. 9, p. 317; *Scorpiace*, chap. 7). Who does not see that by the names “most religious city” [Col. 1023D] and “pious descendants of Aeneas,” he designates the Romans with considerable irony? For they boasted that they derived their origin from Aeneas, whom Virgil everywhere calls “pious father.” But who could have been more impious and less religious than those Romans who, at games and spectacles consecrated to Jupiter Latiaris, their “best and greatest” god, watched with eyes not merely dry but joyful as gladiators killed one another, or were horribly torn apart and killed by the beasts against which they fought? We have discussed elsewhere both this cruel homicide and this cruel spectacle (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 8, art. 2).

The pagans replied that blood was indeed shed on those occasions, [Col. 1024A] but it was the blood of men who were either beast-fighters or condemned criminals put to death (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9, p. 321). The former, as they said, were the vilest of men, who hired themselves out for profit and voluntarily offered their services to kill beasts. The latter, however, were compelled, because of their crimes, as will be said below, to fight against beasts by sentence of the judges. Therefore, the pagans said, there was nothing wrong in the slaughter of such men.

But Tertullian easily and quickly overturns that empty evasion (ibid.). For the beast-fighter, however vile and however much the lowest dregs of society, is nevertheless no less a human being on that account, and his life is taken by the same homicide as that of a richer man. But if a criminal has been condemned to death, certainly the more wicked he is, the more unworthy he is to be sacrificed to Jupiter; or, to use Tertullian’s own words: [Col. 1024B] “It is all the more shameful because it is the blood of an evil man” (ibid.) that is poured out in honor of the highest god, as they called him. For this reason Tertullian there exclaimed, not without wit, in mockery of the pagans and their Jupiter: “O Christian Jupiter!” (ibid.). For Jupiter was the cause and author of the homicide of which Christians were falsely accused, and by that title alone was he the son of his father Saturn, who had devoured his children—the son, that is, of his father’s cruelty, to which his own was similar.

Tertullian presses further and asserts that the crime of those who killed their newborn children was greater than that homicide. Would you like to hear him pressing and addressing the pagans? Here are his very words: “Surely it is more cruel when you wring out their breath in water, or expose them to cold, hunger, and dogs.” But you will ask why he calls extinguishing the breath of infants in water a more cruel kind of death. [Col. 1024C] Some reply that philosophers, joined by Servius, taught that the human soul is fiery and is therefore extinguished in water, or reduced to nothing, with greater difficulty (Servius on Virgil’s *Aeneid*, book I, v. 95). They think that this can be proved to be truly the cruelest of all deaths from the following verses of Ovid:

> I do not fear death; it is the manner of death that is pitiable:  
> Remove shipwreck, and death will be a gift to me.  
> (Ovid, *Tristia*, book I, elegy 2, v. 57 ff.)

But the poet sang this because of his desire for burial, of which one who died by shipwreck would be deprived. As for the philosophers, although some believed the human soul to be fire, others certainly thought it to be water, others a body, others breath, and others something else, as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 23, art. 2). [Col. 1024D] Moreover, Tertullian did not have one philosopher’s opinion in view rather than another’s.

Thus, in our judgment, there is little substance in the answer of those who, by investigating the rationale of Tertullian’s words more curiously than was proper, looked for a knot in a bulrush. For he speaks of infants whose breath is extinguished in water in no other manner than he speaks of those exposed to cold, hunger, and dogs. He maintains that the killing of all these infants is more cruel than that of other persons because infants exposed to certain death were entirely deprived of every means of defense by which others might protect themselves, and therefore were killed more cruelly than older persons. That this is Tertullian’s meaning is indicated with sufficient clarity [Col. 1025A] by his following words: “For even a more advanced age would choose to die by the sword” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9, p. 319). For it would prefer to be killed by a single stroke of the sword rather than in the prolonged and lingering manner inflicted upon those pitiable infants. We have discussed this exposure of infants, and the force of this argument, in our dissertation on Minucius Felix’s *Octavius* and in the passages cited there (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 9, art. 12).

Moreover, every kind of homicide was so strictly forbidden to Christians that, in Tertullian’s words, “they were not even permitted to destroy what had been conceived in the womb while the blood was still being formed into a human being” (Tertullian, loc. cit.); that is, while the fetus in the mother’s womb had not yet received human form. For not all the members of the human body are formed at the same time, nor is the soul immediately infused into the fetus, but only many days after conception, as the philosophers believe and as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 27, art. 2; and chap. 40, art. 6). [Col. 1025B] Yet if it was unlawful for Christians to induce abortions of this kind, how much more unlawful was it for them to kill any human beings! Who, then, would not be indignant that they were so rashly charged with homicide by pagans who so frequently killed other human beings with the utmost cruelty, as has already been said and remains to be said?

## ARTICLE IV. How certainly Tertullian asserts that human blood was drunk by pagans at public games dedicated to Jupiter, by those who sought a remedy for epilepsy, and by others who, like Catiline, entered into a compact with certain persons; likewise that in Africa those consecrated to Bellona were marked by drinking blood, and that others committed a crime still more execrable than these

[Col. 1025C]

With the same evident proof by which Tertullian demonstrated that nothing was more false than the charge that Christians drank the blood of an infant killed while they celebrated their sacred mysteries, he shows with equal certainty that pagans were in fact guilty of so great a crime. For at the Latin Games, which we discussed in the preceding article, “they drench him,” says Tertullian, “with human blood” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9, p. 317); or, as he writes in another book: “In Latium, down to the present day, human blood is given to Jupiter to taste in the midst of the city of Rome” (*Scorpiace*, chap. 7). The unknown author of the book *On the Public Shows*, printed after the works of Cyprian, [Col. 1025D] describes how that impious sacrifice was customarily performed: “What need is there,” he says, “to pursue the matter further, or to describe the monstrous kinds of sacrifices at the games? Among these, a human being is sometimes made the victim through the murderous robbery of a priest, when blood, still hot, is received from his throat into a bowl and, while it yet boils, is cruelly cast into the face of the idol as though offered for it to drink” (author of the book *On the Public Shows*). We have discussed this sacrifice, as absurd as it was cruel, in our dissertation on Minucius’ *Octavius* (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 9, arts. 3 and 4), where we also dealt with those who, when suffering from epilepsy, sought a cure by drinking the blood of men killed at these spectacles. For these persons, as Tertullian says, “[Col. 1026A] at a public show in the arena carry away with greedy thirst the fresh blood of criminals whose throats have been cut, treating epilepsy” (Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 9, p. 321). Who, unless savage and ironhearted, would not shudder to preserve his own life by such a remedy and by the cruel death of other human beings?

Not far removed from their inhumanity were those savage peoples who struck and confirmed compacts among themselves by drinking blood drawn from their own limbs. Tertullian cites Herodotus as a witness to this plainly barbarous custom in the following words: “Read whether it is not reported somewhere—by Herodotus, I think—that certain nations contracted an alliance by tasting blood drawn from one another’s arms” (ibid. ff.). By these words, “by Herodotus, I think,” he indicates clearly enough that he was quoting the matter from memory, [Col. 1026B] and so was not entirely certain whether it had been recorded by Herodotus himself or by another writer. Nevertheless, he could certainly have cited Herodotus, for in his first book he relates the following about the Lydians: Ὃρκια δὲ ποιέεται ταῦτα τὰ ἔθνεα, τὰ πέρ τε ἕλληνες, καὶ πρὸς τούτοισι ἐπεὰν τοὺς βραχίονας ἐπιτάμωνται ἐς τὴν αἰμοῤῥοίην, τὸ αἷμα ἀναλείχουσι ἀλλήλων. “These nations make compacts with one another, both in other respects according to the custom of the Greeks and by bloodying their arms with self-inflicted wounds and licking one another’s blood” (Herodotus, book I, § 74). In another book, however, he says of the Scythians: Όρκια δὲ, ποιεονται Σκύθαι ὧδε πρὸς τῶν ἂν ποιέωνται· ἐς κύλικα μεγάλην κεραμίνην οἶνον ἐγχέαντες, αἷμα συμμίσγουσι τῶν τὰ ὅρκια ταμνομένων, τύψαντες ὑπέατι, ἣ ἐπιταμόντες μαχαίρῃ σμικρὸν τοῦ σώματος· καὶ ἔπειτα ἀποβάψαντες ἐς τὴν κύλικα ἀκινάκεα [Col. 1026C] καὶ οἰστοὺς, καὶ σάγαριν, καὶ ἀκόντιον· ἐπεὰν δὲ ταῦτα ποιήσωσι, κατεύχονται πόλλα, καὶ ἔπειτα ἀποπίνουσι αὐτοί τε οἱ τὸ ὅρκιον ποιευμένοι, καὶ τῶν ἐπομένων οἱ πλείστου ἄξιοι. “The Scythians make compacts with anyone in the following manner: after wine has been poured into a large earthenware cup, they mingle with it the blood of those making the compact, striking with a knife or cutting a small part of the body with a sword. They then dip into the cup a scimitar, arrows, an axe, and a javelin. When they have done this, they bind themselves by many words of imprecation; afterward, not only those who have made the compact drink the wine, but also the companions who hold the highest rank” (the same author, book IV, § 70).

Tertullian could therefore have invoked this ancient writer without hesitation as an authority for his position, and with all the greater right because he has Lucian as a supporting witness [Col. 1026D] (Lucian, *Dialogue Toxaris, or On Friendship*, p. 630). For Lucian attests that the Scythians allowed blood from their cut fingers to drip into a cup, dipped the points of their swords into it, and drank together; and that in this manner they established a compact which no one was thereafter permitted to dissolve. Concerning certain peoples neighboring the Axiacae, Pomponius Mela recorded the following: “They love wars and slaughter; and it is the custom of warriors to drink, directly from his wounds, the blood of the first man they kill. . . . . . Even their compacts are not bloodless. Those who make the agreement wound themselves; when they have mixed the blood thus drawn, they taste it. They regard this as the surest pledge of enduring fidelity” (Pomponius Mela, *On the Situation of the World*, book II, chap. 1, p. 27).

[Col. 1027A] In addition, Cornelius Tacitus, when speaking of the compact between Rhadamistus and Mithridates, says: “It is the custom of kings, whenever they enter into an alliance, to clasp right hands, bind their thumbs together, and fasten them tightly with a knot. Then, when the blood has flowed into the extremities, they draw blood with a slight cut and lick it from one another. This compact is held secret, as though consecrated by their mutual blood” (Cornelius Tacitus, *Annals*, book XII, past the middle).

Why say more? Valerius Maximus writes the following about Sariaster, or Tigranes the Younger, who deserted his father and went over to Pompey the Great, and then defected from Pompey back to his father: “Sariaster formed an agreement with his friends against his father Tigranes, king of Armenia, in such a manner that they all drew blood from their right hands and drank it from one another” (Valerius [Col. 1027B] Maximus, book IX, chap. 11, foreign examples, § 3).

Nor were the more civilized Romans far removed from this barbarity and these savage customs. For “something of the same kind,” says Tertullian, “was tasted under Catiline as well” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 321), namely when he conspired against the Republic, as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.* ch. 9, art. 4).

Moreover, that custom, wholly devoid of humanity, flourished not only in the profane assemblies of the pagans but also in their sacred gatherings, and not merely among barbarous peoples remote from Tertullian, but in Africa itself, and at the very time when he was writing this *Apologeticum*. For of those initiated into the mysteries of Bellona he speaks as follows: “Today, in this very place, blood caught in the hollow of the hand from a slashed thigh, and given for consumption, marks those consecrated to Bellona” (Tertullian, ibid.). [Col. 1027C] Yet in all our manuscript copies, instead of *sacratos . . . esui*, we read *sacratus . . . et sui*. But these words make no sense. In editions older than Rigault’s, the reading is *sacratus . . . et suis datus signatis*. But scarcely any better sense can be made from that. This passage of Tertullian is therefore corrupt, and to repair it some wish *haustui* (“for drinking”) to be read instead of *et sui*, or *et suis*, or *esui*. And this can indeed be said of blood caught in the hollow of the hand more aptly than *esui* (“for eating”). Nor would we strongly resist this conjecture, provided that you also show that *sacratus* must still be emended to *sacratos*. For Minucius Felix (*Minut. Octav.*), who drew many things from this book, expressed Tertullian’s meaning in these words, where, like Tertullian, he objects to the pagans that “Bellona imbues her sacred rite [Col. 1027D] by the drinking of human blood.” See what we have noted in our dissertation on his book (*Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.* ch. 9, art. 4, and ch. 20, art. 3).

Furthermore, so that the pagans might be made still more ashamed—if that were ever possible—of accusing Christians of a false crime, he reproached them, in decent language as the matter required, with another appalling crime. But it must neither be named by us, much less explained, although the satirical poets make it sufficiently evident and assail it everywhere (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 323, and bk. I *Ad Nationes*, ch. 15, p. 580).

## ARTICLE V. It Is Shown How Gladiators, Scythians, Massagetae, and Derbices Ate Human Flesh, and How, After Embracing the Christian Religion, They Abandoned These Savage Customs

[Col. 1028A]

Tertullian proceeds and makes it plain to everyone that the pagans not only drank human blood but also fed upon human flesh. First, after the spectacles had ended, the gladiators, he says, “dine on dishes of wild beasts taken from the arena” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 322); that is, while dining they ate the flesh of the wild beasts they had shortly before killed in the circus. But those beasts had only just devoured the raw flesh of men whom they had slaughtered in those same spectacles and could not yet have digested it. Accordingly, those most cruel [Col. 1028B] gladiators sought out, as our Author says, “the containers of the very bears, still suffering indigestion from human entrails” (ibid.). So indeed it stands in Rigault’s edition; but in the earlier editions, instead of the word *cruditantes*, we read *trucidantibus*, plainly in error. In our manuscripts and in other codices, however, the reading is consistently *cruditantibus adhuc de visceribus humanis*, that is, while the human entrails were still raw and not yet digested in the gut and belly of the bears that had devoured them. Yet who would dare determine with certainty whether this is the true reading without the aid of some more accurate codex? Whatever the reading may be, it is sufficiently clear that Tertullian meant nothing other than that the gladiators sought and ate the flesh of bears that shortly before had devoured human entrails and flesh, which were therefore still undigested in their stomachs.

[Col. 1028C] But, you will say, is not the noun *alvei* also corrupt, and should not *alvi*, the receptacles of food, rather be written? Not unreasonably, provided that you say Tertullian used the better part to signify the whole and support this emendation with at least one codex. For not merely the guts of bears, but other parts of their flesh as well, were customarily eaten, as may be gathered from the words of Apuleius, in which he describes the most magnificent preparations for a gladiatorial show: “We carried to our lodging a she-bear,” he says, “which surpassed the others in bodily bulk, as though it were to be prepared for food” (Apuleius, bk. IV, *Metamorphoses*, p. 59). What, then, prevents us from retaining the reading common to all the codices, *alvei*, by which are meant the vessels [Col. 1028D] in which the flesh of bears, only partially cooked, was contained—the flesh which the gladiators eagerly sought and ate? Hence Tertullian concludes: “Consequently, a man belches up the flesh of a bear that had fed upon a man” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 323), by whom it had shortly before been killed.

But far more savage than these gladiators were undoubtedly others, of whom he does not speak quite so affirmatively, but only in this manner: “It is also said that among certain pagan Scythians every deceased person is eaten by his own people” (ibid.). Yet he could certainly have pronounced this without hesitation. For from Strabo we learn that guests were sacrificed by the Scythians, who ate their flesh and used their skulls in place of drinking cups [Col. 1029A] (Strabo, bk. VII, *Geography*, p. 298). Then, a little later, he records the following concerning the Massagetae, either Scythian peoples or their neighbors: θάνατος δὲ νομίζεται παρ` αὐτοῖς ἄριστος, ὅταν γηράσαντες κατακοπῶσι μετὰ τῶν προβατείων κρεῶν καὶ ἄναμιξ βρωθῶσι “They consider the best kind of death to be when those worn out by old age are cut to pieces together with sheep’s flesh and devoured along with it” (ibid., p. 513). Strabo is followed by Eusebius, who added the Derbices to the Massagetae and related that both peoples sacrificed the parents whom they held most dear when they were already exhausted by age, and used their flesh as though it were the most sumptuous banquet (Eusebius, bk. III, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, ch. 4, p. 11). If you desire something expressed more clearly, consult Pliny (Pliny, bk. VI, *Natural History*, ch. 17), and Solinus, who follows him (Solinus, ch. 15, p. 34); they explicitly [Col. 1029B] affirm that the Scythians were anthropophagi, feeding upon human bodies. From Herodotus too you will learn that the Melanchlaeni, so called from their black clothing, lived according to Scythian customs and were accustomed to eat human flesh (Herodotus, bk. IV, §107). To this may be added Mela, whom you may hear narrating the following: “Just as the Essedones furnish drinking cups from the heads of their parents, so they furnish them from the heads of their bitterest enemies. Among the anthropophagi, the very banquets themselves are prepared from human entrails” (Mela, bk. II, *De Situ Orbis*, ch. 1, p. 27).

Furthermore, Eusebius, already cited by us, asserted in the same place that as soon as the Massagetae and Derbices professed the Christian religion, they abandoned these savage and inhuman customs (Eusebius, loc. cit.). Moreover, in our dissertation on the book of Minucius Felix (*Dissertat.* [Col. 1029C] *in Minut. Octav.* ch. 9, art. 2), and in the other passages cited there, we have shown that Christians were never cognizant of or guilty of this anthropophagy, but that pagans alone were so in actual fact.

## ARTICLE VI. How Clearly Tertullian Shows That Christians Were Most Falsely Accused of Secret Incest in Their Sacred Assemblies, Whereas the Pagans Openly and Repeatedly Defiled Themselves with It, Following the Example of Jupiter

We have already made clear to everyone by what arguments, and by arguments of what force, our Tertullian utterly crushed the altogether senseless calumny of the pagans, by which they most shamelessly lied that Christians defiled themselves with infamous incest in their assemblies. For how could they have wished to pollute their sacred mysteries with incest [Col. 1029D] so frequently repeated, when, as we have shown elsewhere, they observed with the greatest zeal either the chastity of marriage prescribed to them by Christ or perpetual virginity, although this was not commanded? Yet such was the shamelessness of the pagans that they most falsely charged them with the crime of secret incest, although in fact it was perpetrated by the pagans themselves not only in secret but “in every light,” as Tertullian says, “and every night, and with the whole sky as witness” (Tertullian, bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 16, p. 581), as boldly as it was done with impunity. Why indeed should they not have perpetrated so great a crime, when, as he with perfect justice presses them, “Jupiter himself taught” them (idem, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 325), that is, taught them by his own example to commit incest? For who does not know how truthfully Athenagoras [Col. 1030A] (*Legatio pro Christianis*) and other Fathers of the Church objected to these same pagans what was openly proclaimed by their writers: that this same Jupiter had begotten children by his own mother and by his daughter Core, or Proserpina? Who, moreover, has touched even superficially the books published by the profane poets without immediately recoiling in horror when they introduce Juno boasting that she was at once the sister and wife of that same Jupiter? Yet, μιμητὰς θεῶν says Justin Martyr, καλὸν εἶναι πάντες ἡγοῦνται “Everyone considers it noble to be an imitator of the gods” (Justin, *Apology* I). Even if the pagans had denied that they had actually imitated him, they nevertheless could not have held it as a fault in Christians to do what they admitted had been done by Jupiter, whom they called the supreme god. We have discussed these crimes of his more than sufficiently in our preceding dissertations. [Col. 1030B]

The Persians, moreover, imitated that supreme—or rather supremely impious—Jupiter; Ctesias, says our Author, testifies that “they have intercourse with their own mothers” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 325). Our older manuscript codices present the form *Chteseas*, while in the book *Ad Nationes* it is written *Thesias* (bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 16, p. 581). We have treated the name Ctesias and that abominable Persian crime in our other dissertations (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1259, and *Dissert. in Arnob.* ch. 24, art. 2; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1239, and *Dissert. in Minut.* ch. 20, art. 2).

Tertullian then concludes from the following that the Macedonians had fallen under grave suspicion of incest, or even proof of it: “Because,” he says, “when they first heard [Col. 1030C] the tragedy of Oedipus, seeing the anguish caused by incest, they said ἔλαυνε εἰς τὴν μητέρα” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 325). It is astonishing how corruptly and variously these Greek words are written in our manuscripts and in other printed codices. For in three of the older ones the reading is ΕΛΛΥΝΕ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΑΛΙΓΕΕΡΑ or ΤΗΝ ΛΛΙΓΕΡΛ; in two others, *elline eistena ligera*; in the first Basel edition of 1512, ἔμεεν εἰς τὴν μετέρα. In the second, of 1528, only *emene* is written in Latin characters, and the other words are omitted. Finally, in the book *Ad Nationes* the reading, likewise in Latin letters, is *Elaune ten metera*. Those Greek words were therefore corrupted by scribes ignorant of Greek, and one cannot easily say what Tertullian actually wrote.

Gothofredus, however, who was the first to have these books printed, [Col. 1030D] has no doubt whatever that this latter reading of the Agobardinus codex is the true one, and that Tertullian himself wrote it in Greek letters: ἔλαυνε εἰς τὴν ματέρα. Rigault, by contrast, asserts that the ancient codices read ἔλαυνε εἰς τὴν μητέρα. But he ought to have indicated which codices these were, and whether they differed from ours. For apart from the codices already noted and read by us, he possessed no other, but only certain Fulda readings that were not entirely reliable. But what judgment can you make concerning the true reading of Greek words corrupted by scribes unless you have sound codices at hand? Consider, nevertheless, whether Tertullian’s meaning is expressed by these Latin words: “Come, advance against your mother.” For [Col. 1031A] when Oedipus, a warrior king, was brought upon the stage and represented as weeping over the incest he had unknowingly committed with his mother, the Macedonians, mocking the weeping of this warlike king, assailed him with this taunt: “Come, advance against your mother,” as though he were about to subdue some metropolis. That this was the meaning of our Author may perhaps be inferred, not implausibly, from his book *Ad Nationes*, where he explains the matter more fully in these words: “When Oedipus first entered the stage of those Macedonians, his eyes destroyed, they received him with laughter and mockery. The tragic actor, dismayed, drew back his mask and said, ‘Surely, my lords, I have not displeased you?’ The Macedonians replied: ‘No, you indeed performed beautifully’” (the manuscript codex reads *beautiful*). From this, however, he argues as follows: “Either the writer was utterly frivolous, if he invented it, or Oedipus utterly mad, if he did it; and thereafter you used to say one to another, *elaune ten matera*” [Col. 1031B] (Tertullian, bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 16, p. 581). You clearly hear Tertullian recounting that the masked Oedipus was at first received by the Macedonians with laughter and mockery, though they later acknowledged that he did not displease them; and then, conversing among themselves, they uttered these words to one another in turn: *Elaune ten metera*. If these words are genuine, they signify that one Macedonian said to another: “Drive, goad, spur, thrust your mother on, and imitate Oedipus.” For in that sense the verb ἐλαύνω is used by Aristophanes (Aristophanes, *Electra*, vv. 735 and 740), Homer, and other Greek writers. Whatever word Tertullian may have used, through it he not unjustly charges the Macedonians with incest, since they either praised it in Oedipus or, following his example, urged one another to perpetrate it.

[Col. 1031C] Finally, he proves that not only the Macedonians but all other pagans as well were cognizant of this shameful act, from the fact that, as we have said, they exposed their newborn children. For the parents did not later recognize those children whom they had earlier exposed to the mercy of strangers, nor were they recognized by them. It therefore frequently happened that, through this ignorance, those lustful parents inflicted rape and incest upon their own children (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 9, p. 526, and bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 16, p. 582). Tertullian proves this by an especially disastrous example that occurred in Rome shortly before he wrote the books *Ad Nationes* and, as it appears, during the reign of Commodus. For at that time, as he says, Fuscianus was prefect of the City, when a certain boy, having gone beyond the threshold of his father’s house, was carried off by [Col. 1031D] a certain petty Greek and taken to Asia. When the boy had grown older, he was brought back to Rome, where his own father, no longer recognizing him, violated him. Later his parents recognized him by certain marks on his body and, Tertullian says, “treated themselves with the noose.” Fuscianus assigned their property to the boy, “not as an inheritance,” as Tertullian says, “but as payment for rape and incest” (idem, bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 16, p. 582).

There does, however, appear to be room for doubt whether that wicked father was condemned not only by Fuscianus but also by the senate. For the beginning of this story reads as follows in the Agobardinus codex: “Such a tragedy broke out when Fuscianus was prefect of the City, after the senate’s punishment had been adjudged. Through the accidental negligence of his attendants, having advanced on his way beyond the door, [Col. 1032A] he was dragged away by passers-by and lost to his home. The petty Greek who had reared him, or had seized him from the threshold in Greek fashion, entered. Thence he was removed” (ibid., etc.). But several scribal errors are exposed there. First, Rigault was so persuaded that *reatus* (“guilt”) should be read there instead of *senatus* (“senate”) that he inserted it into Tertullian’s text itself. Second, he removed from it the words “The man who had reared him” and “or from the threshold”; and besides this he thinks the word “entered” should also be removed. He gives the following reason for the first emendation: if this case had been adjudged by the senate, it ought not subsequently to have been adjudged by Fuscianus. The reading should therefore rather be: “when Fuscianus had adjudged the punishment of guilt.” This conjecture indeed seems quite probable. Yet what if something is missing there, and Tertullian intended to signify that Fuscianus’s sentence [Col. 1032B] had been approved by the senate? But Rigault himself has not told us why he wholly removed from our Author’s text the words “The man who had reared him.” Are they so useless there that they ought to have been amputated without warning anyone? Did he not later say, “the foster-child in boyhood”? Finally, he suspects that “or from the threshold” and “entered” should be removed because the latter is an interpretation of the former. But let others judge these matters. For our part, if room were given for conjecture, we would suspect that instead of the words “having advanced on his way,” the reading should be “the boy having advanced,” since it is of course the boy who is under discussion there, and his boyhood is mentioned shortly afterward.

However corrupt this passage may be, the history of this abominable incest is no less certain. Tertullian therefore rightly concludes from it that there were many other parents guilty of the same crime [Col. 1032C] who, because it remained hidden, escaped the punishments due for so grave an offense. Who, moreover, will deny that not only from this story but also from the many other examples we have reported (*Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.* ch. 10, art. 2), the pagans are most clearly convicted of the incest of which they accused Christians with a most shameless falsehood? Let us now, therefore, proceed to their other no less false accusations.

## ARTICLE VII. How Absurdly the Pagans Alleged That Christians Worshipped the Head of an Ass; Who Gave Occasion for This Fable; With What Shamelessness a Certain Jewish Scoundrel Carried About a Picture of That Ass with an Utterly Ridiculous Inscription; and How Truly Those Same Pagans Worshipped Whole Asses and Other Beasts, Either Living or Depicted

[Col. 1032D]

By another calumny, no less serious than the rest, the pagans vainly attempted to defame Christians as though they worshipped, as Tertullian says, “an ass’s head” as a god. But this, he says, was merely the dream of wakeful and envious men who strove by every means to slander Christians. He does not deny, however, that Cornelius Tacitus gave occasion for this false accusation. For as rashly as falsely he had written in his histories that when the Jews, wandering through the vast deserts of Arabia, were suffering from thirst, they were shown springs of water by certain wild asses and quenched their thirst with them; therefore, in testimony of their gratitude, as he asserted, they consecrated an image of an ass. [Col. 1033A] And because the Christian religion was closely related to the Jewish, the pagans therefore invented the story that Christians too worshipped the head of an ass (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 365 ff., and bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 11, p. 577). Elsewhere, however, we have utterly demolished this most senseless accusation, both insofar as it concerns Jews and insofar as it concerns Christians (*Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.* ch. 11, art. 1).

It remains, therefore, for us to examine a particular occurrence described by our Tertullian in two books as follows: “Quite recently, a new representation of our God was publicly displayed in this city, when a certain criminal hired to evade the beasts exhibited a picture with an inscription of this kind: THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONOCHOETES. He had ass’s ears, one hoofed foot, [Col. 1033B] carried a book, and wore a toga” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 372). In another book, however, he explains this somewhat more fully: “Now rumor has supplied an account of our God. For quite recently, in this city, a certain utterly depraved man, a deserter even from his own religion, a Jew only by the loss of his foreskin—though even more so because of the bites of the beasts, to which he hires himself out and by which he is now flayed over his whole body every day as he goes about—displayed against us a picture bearing this public inscription: ONOCHOETES. He had ass’s ears and wore a toga with a book, with one hoofed foot” (idem, bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 14, p. 579).

First, then, he said that this happened recently, that is, a short time before he composed both books, and “quite recently in this city,” in which he was residing. There is therefore no room to doubt the truth of this occurrence. [Col. 1033C] Second, its author was a certain Jew, a deserter from his own—that is, the Jewish—religion, who was then a Jew only by the loss of his foreskin, that is, solely by circumcision, while professing the impious worship of the pagans. But this was an utterly depraved man, convicted by public judgment of several crimes and therefore condemned to the beasts, so that he would fight them in his appointed turn. Yet because he was sometimes permitted to be absent from that combat, he voluntarily hired himself out each day to evade the beasts—that is, to escape their attacks and bites by fighting them—in order to make a greater profit. For, as Cassiodorus very aptly observes: “A detestable occupation, an ill-fated contest: to wish to contend with wild beasts, which a man cannot doubt he will find stronger than himself. His sole confidence, therefore, lies in deceiving them; his only consolation in trickery. [Col. 1033D] If he does not deserve to escape the beast, he may sometimes be unable even to find a burial” (Cassiodorus, bk. V, *Variae*, epist. 42, p. 94). Such was that circumcised Jew, of whom Tertullian says that, in addition to circumcision, “he is now flayed over his whole body every day”; that is, each day he received many wounds from the bites of beasts. But men of this kind were called *bestiarii*, concerning whom we discussed matters shortly above (*supra*, ch.).

Accordingly, at the public games that scoundrelly pseudo-Jew, in order to mock the Christian religion, carried about the utterly ridiculous image described by Tertullian, bearing the inscription: THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONOCHOETES (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 372); or, as the name appears in our manuscripts [Col. 1034A] and others, *Onochitis*; in others, *Onochorsitis*, or *Onochortissis*, or *Onochotasis*; in the old editions, *Onychites*; and finally, in some, Ὀνοχήλος (*Onochēlos*). In the unpublished copy of the book *Ad Nationes* and in other printed copies, however, this name is written in three ways: first, *Onocholtes*; second, *Onochoites*; and third, *Onochoete* (idem, bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 14, p. 579). But the very variety and discrepancy of the readings of this single name make it clear that it is corrupt. Hence several learned men have labored considerably to repair it. Some think that *Onochoetes* should be read, so that the word would mean an ass who was a teacher and priest of sacred rites, by whom others were to be initiated. Others prefer *Onochorsites*, from an ass’s head; others, *Onocoites*, that is, of asinine origin and lineage. Still others propose *Onotacoustes*, in Greek Ὀνωτακούστης (*Onōtakoustēs*). [Col. 1034B] But why should we labor to discover this single word in the inscription when the *Apologeticum* states that the two Latin words *Deus Christianorum* (“God of the Christians”) preceded it? What if that latter name was invented by the criminal jester and later corrupted by scribes? What if, moreover, it is some common Punic name, now wholly obsolete? Ought not the explanation given by our Author of this name and picture to suffice for us? “He had,” he says, “ass’s ears, one hoofed foot, carried a book, and wore a toga.” In the book *Ad Nationes* he expressed this in different words, but words signifying exactly the same thing.

That depicted ass, moreover, was clad in a toga and carried a book, plainly in mockery [Col. 1034C] of the Christians, who held the sacred Gospels in the highest honor and were accustomed to carry them with them and read them publicly in their assemblies.

But the Christians and Tertullian laughed at that monstrosity of divinity, which had arisen from the mind of the impious scoundrel, and at its name and form. Why should they not have laughed at it, since it was, as he says, “deprived of the authority of antiquity and weakened by the character of its author” (idem, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 373, and bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 14, p. 579)?

Nor indeed should anyone object to us that the Gnostics had not strayed so far from this, since long before, as we observed after Epiphanius (Epiphanius, *Haereses* 26, p. 91; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 244; *Dissertat. in Minut.* ch. 11, art. 1), they had imagined Sabaoth to be the seventh of the Aeons and the creator of heaven and earth, and some babbled that he bore the form [Col. 1034D] of an ass, others that of a pig. For this ridiculous image of Sabaoth was entirely different from the hideous figure of the Christians’ God that the most wicked and disgraceful traitor to the Jewish religion had most foolishly devised.

Perhaps the white ass approached it more closely, which, as Suidas relates (Suidas, s.v. Ζήνων) and as we have noted elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Minut.*, loc. cit.), a certain Zeno of Alexandria, a deserter from the Jewish religion, is said to have led through the Jewish synagogue on the Sabbath. Yet even if it were proved that this was done before Tertullian’s time, it nevertheless differed greatly from the picture that the pseudo-Jew carried about in mockery of the Christians’ God, not in a synagogue but [Col. 1035A] at the pagans’ public spectacles. Yet it could not altogether absurdly be said that one of these scoundrelly pseudo-Jews gave the other the occasion to do these things.

Although both those monstrosities of divinity were utterly detestable, the pagans nevertheless could not completely and absolutely reject either of them without immediately condemning themselves for wickedness and madness. For Tertullian proves this clearly in the words with which he addresses them: “You will not deny that all beasts of burden, and whole asses together with their Epona, are worshipped by you” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 365). Again, in the first book *Ad Nationes*: “Indeed, you worship whole asses, together with their Epona; and you consecrate all beasts of burden, cattle, and wild animals alike, together with their mangers.” Therefore he presses them thus: “But those pagans [Col. 1035B] ought immediately to have worshipped that composite name invented by the Jew” (bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 11, p. 577), “because they have accepted gods with mixed canine and leonine heads, gods horned like goats and rams, goats from the loins downward, serpents from the legs downward, and birds at the feet or back” (idem, *Apologeticum*, ibid.). Similarly, in his book *Ad Nationes*: “Among you are gods with dogs’ heads and lions’ heads; gods horned like oxen, rams, and goats; gods goat-begotten or serpentine; and winged at the feet, forehead, and back” (bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 14, p. 579). We have explained all these matters in other dissertations and have heard Minucius disputing against the pagans in a similar fashion (*Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.* ch. 14, art. 2, and *Dissertat. in Arnob.* ch. 20, art. 1).

But Tertullian cuts them down with their own sword as follows. [Col. 1035C] If, he says, you charge it as a fault against us that we worship the head of an ass as God, you certainly prove yourselves far more wicked. For you declare to be gods, and actually worship, not only the head of an ass or certain parts of beasts, but whole asses and very many other entire beasts as well. What greater folly, I ask you, can there be than for someone to be accused of a single crime by another who admits himself guilty of the same crime and of several still graver ones? But these things, says Tertullian, are superfluous. For just as it was certain that beasts were worshipped by the pagans, so it was false that Christians worshipped an ass’s head or asses. They worshipped one supreme God, who created all things and can neither be seen nor comprehended by anyone.

## ARTICLE VIII. How Thoughtlessly the Pagans Charged Christians with the Worship of Christ’s Cross, Although They Themselves Worshipped Every Kind of Cross in the Images of Their Gods, in Trophies, Standards, and the Adornment of Military Ensigns; Of What Parts Tertullian Thought Christ’s Cross Was Composed; Why He Called the Draperies of the Cross *Siphara*, and How a Person with Outstretched Hands Presents the Figure of the Cross

[Col. 1035D]

The pagans further charged that Christians had injured and violated the supreme majesty of God by their religious worship of the cross upon which Christ had been affixed. But by what reasoning, do you suppose, did Tertullian refute this accusation, repeated by them again and again? By none other, certainly, than by turning against the pagans themselves [Col. 1036A] the weapon they had hurled. For he remains silent on whether Christians actually worshipped that cross and shows merely, by various arguments, that the pagans were altogether thoughtless in reproaching them for such worship, since they themselves everywhere venerated crosses of every kind.

What then, you will say? Did he by some deceptive silence deny or conceal that Christ’s cross was honored by his disciples? By no means. For why could he have denied or concealed this, when he admits that at nearly every action of their lives they fortified their foreheads with the sign of the cross? Why, I ask, did they so frequently place that sacred sign upon their foreheads unless they were fully persuaded that it afforded them some protection and was worthy [Col. 1036B] of their veneration (Tertullian, *De Corona*, ch. 3, and bk. II, *Ad Uxorem*, ch. 5)? But concerning this most ancient custom of worshipping Christ’s cross we have argued at greater length against the heretics in our other dissertations (*Dissertat. in Minut.* ch. 11, art. 3; *in Lactant.* ch. 19, art. 1; and *in Lucil. Caecil.* ch. 5, art. 2). Tertullian therefore could not deny something that in his day was practiced daily by all Christians and was also sufficiently well known to the pagans themselves (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 366).

Accordingly, to those who objected to the worship of Christ’s cross he gave no reply other than this very brief one: “Whoever thinks us devotees of the cross will be our fellow-worshipper”; or, as in another book: “Whoever declares us priests of the cross will be our fellow-worshipper” (idem, [Col. 1036C] bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 12, p. 578). The noun *consecraneus*, as is noted in the ancient glosses, means the same as “companion in sacred rites.” He therefore openly asserts that the pagans were utterly thoughtless in daring to accuse Christians of this superstitious and impious worship because they venerated Christ’s cross, when the pagans themselves worshipped a great many crosses.

Before examining the arguments by which he endeavors to prove this, however, we must observe what he said the form of Christ’s cross was. “The whole cross,” he says, “is attributed to us, namely with its yard and with that projecting seat” (ibid., bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, loc. cit.). He thus teaches us that Christ’s cross was entire and complete, since it was composed of three parts: [Col. 1036D] an upright piece of wood; the yard, or another transverse piece of wood; and the seat, or small support, attached to and projecting from the cross. Elsewhere we have observed (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 597) that a controversy arose among the learned over whether that support, or projecting piece of wood, was placed beneath the entire body of the crucified man or beneath his feet alone. But since our Tertullian calls it a “seat,” by this name he undoubtedly indicates clearly enough that it was positioned in the middle of the cross and that the crucified man’s body rested upon it, lest by its heavier weight it slip downward or fall when the hands were torn. Some think that this seat is designated by these words of our same Tertullian in another book: “The outer horns of the cross; for even on a ship’s yard, which is part of a cross, the extremities are called horns, while [Col. 1037A] the middle stake of the upright belongs to the unicorn” (Tertullian, *Adversus Judaeos*, ch. 2). They admit, however, that this passage is not entirely uncorrupted and that it therefore cannot be determined with certainty whether the latter words instead denote the upright wood of the cross. But it seems beyond doubt that he calls Christ’s cross entire and complete, composed of both the upright and transverse pieces of wood and the seat.

In order to curb the rashness of the pagans who reproached Christians for worshipping this cross, he shows by accumulated arguments that the pagans worshipped not only many other entire crosses but even parts of crosses. For, as he says, “Attic Pallas and Pharian Ceres, who stand forth without an image as a rough stake and an unshaped piece of wood, are no different from the upright post of a cross” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, [Col. 1037B] ch. 16, p. 366). He repeats this in almost the same words in the book *Ad Nationes* (bk. I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 11, p. 577). But in our manuscript copies the reading is *Ceres Fariam*; in the earlier printed editions, *Ceres Farrea*. This reading pleases several scholars because they think this name was given to Ceres because she is said to have discovered spelt and grain. Others prefer the reading *Pharia*, or *Faria*, as in the book *Ad Nationes*. For they suppose that Ceres was called by that epithet because she was worshipped on Pharos, the island of Egypt. We have made some observations about her in our dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius Felix (*Dissertat. in Minut.* ch. 14, art. 4).

More than once in other dissertations (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 734 ff., and *Dissertat. in Arnob.* ch. [Col. 1037C] 20, art. 1), we have noted that before the pagans fashioned the images of their gods in human form, some regarded and worshipped as gods a scimitar, others a sword, blade, or spear, some a stone, and others a rough piece of wood or an unworked stake. This custom persisted longer among certain peoples. Tertullian appears to indicate that even in his own time there still existed an image of Pallas in the region of Attica and one of Ceres on the island of Pharos that consisted merely of a rough stake and an unshaped piece of wood without any figure. This can certainly be confirmed from the material we have reported in the dissertations cited above. The pagans, therefore, in worshipping such a stake fixed in the ground as a sacred divinity, were unquestionably worshipping part of a cross.

Restoration notes: E009/S001318: The recovered expression πρός τε οὗς appears corrupt; it has been preserved verbatim and rendered cautiously from context as referring to speaking into the person’s ear.; E009/S001318: The recovered expression πρός τε οὗς appears corrupt; it is preserved verbatim and, in light of the supplied Latin and English contexts, rendered cautiously as referring to speaking into the person’s ear.  

[Col. 1037D] They also venerated complete crosses in the images of their gods that represented the human form. For these could not be fashioned by modelers and craftsmen unless clay or some other material were first actually laid upon supports arranged in the form of a complete cross. Tertullian therefore rightly says: “We have said that the origin of your gods is derived by the modelers from the cross” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 366). Earlier he had said: “First the clay begins to shape the image” (*Ibid.*, ch. 12, p. 340), that is, begins to form it, being built upon the cross and stake. Again, in another book:

> Upon this beginning and, as it were, framework, clay is woven over it; little by little it completes the limbs, constructs the body, and imposes upon the cross within it whatever form was desired for the clay. . . . From [Col. 1038A] the cross it passes, in a manner, to clay, and from clay to a god: the cross passes through the clay into a god. You therefore consecrate the cross, from which the process of consecration begins.

(Book I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 12, p. 578.)

We have already discussed these matters in our dissertation on the book of Minucius Felix (*Dissertat. in Minut. Octav.*, ch. 4, art. 12), as well as trophies, *cantabra*, and standards. For the same reason our Author adds all these words: “Those *siphara* of the standards and *cantabra*” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 369). Now *sipharum*, or *sypharium*, *supparus*, and *supparum* were names given to various kinds of garment and covering—for example, the coverings of ships and of the theater. But there, as is sufficiently clear, Tertullian uses the word for a covering of military standards placed upon a cross, whether wooden or made of some other material. For immediately [Col. 1038B] afterward he says: “These *siphara* are the robes of the cross” (*Ibid.*); that is, they are the garments and coverings by which the cross was veiled or covered. By the name *sipharum*, therefore, he denotes the cloth hanging from the transverse part of the cross, with which standards and *cantabra* were adorned. He consequently mocks the pagans in these words: “I commend your diligence. You were unwilling to consecrate naked and unadorned crosses” (*Ibid.*). Likewise, in another book: “Those *siphara* are the garments of crosses. You are ashamed, I suppose, to worship unadorned and naked crosses” (Idem, Book I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 12, p. 579).

He presses the point further: “You worship Victories, although in trophies crosses are the inward structure of the trophies” (Idem, *Apologeticum*, loc. cit.); that is, they underlie the trophies. In another book, however, he puts it somewhat differently: “You venerate Victories as divine powers, and indeed as more august the more joyful they are; with . . . [Col. 1038C] what better might they raise aloft? Crosses will be, in a manner, the inward structure of the trophies” (Idem, *Ad Nationes*, loc. cit.; the text is defective at “with . . .”). It is certainly established that Victory was placed by them among the number of goddesses. Since this fact is scarcely unknown to anyone, it will suffice to prove it by these words of Cicero:

> What of the temple of Concord, of Liberty, and of Victory? Because the power of all these things was so great that it could not be governed without a god, the thing itself acquired the name of a god.

(Cicero, Book II, *De Natura Deorum*, p. 223, line 5.)

Concerning Victory and her image, Claudian composed these verses:

> Victory herself would open the sacred halls to the commander.  
> O maiden rejoicing in the green palm and clad in trophies,  
> guardian of the Empire, who alone can heal  
> wounds and teach men to feel no toil.

(Claudian, Book III, *De Laudibus Stilichonis*, v. 204 ff.)

Her image therefore shone upon trophies, that is, upon the captured [Col. 1038D] spoils of enemies, which were placed upon the top of a stake erected in the form of a cross and customarily carried in solemn procession. Thus, by worshiping Victory not only in her temple but also upon these trophies, the pagans worshiped the cross as well. For, as Minucius Felix says, “Victorious trophies imitate not only the form of a simple cross but also that of a man affixed to it” (Minucius, p. 287).

But let us follow Tertullian as he presses the argument still more sharply:

> The religion of the Romans is wholly a religion of the camp: it venerates the standards, swears by the standards, and places the standards before all the gods. All those distinguished structures supporting images are necklaces of crosses.

(Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 367.)

So indeed the text stands in our handwritten codices and in the older editions. But Rigault removed the word “Romans” [Col. 1039A] there without giving any reason. We nevertheless suspect that his reason was that, in the book *Ad Nationes*, Tertullian repeats the same statement while omitting the word “Romans”:

> In its victories the religion of the camp also worships crosses; it adores the standards, swears solemnly by the standards, and places the standards before Jupiter himself. But that structure supporting images, and the entire adornment of gold, are necklaces of crosses.

(Idem, Book I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 12, p. 579.)

Rigault, however, does not appear sufficiently to have noticed that the word “Romans” could be omitted in this book, which was addressed generally to all nations, but not in the *Apologeticum*, which was sent to all governors and especially to the Roman ones. Among the Romans, moreover, the custom of worshiping military standards had become so firmly established that, according to Suetonius, Artabanus, king of the Parthians, when he came to Caligula’s legate, “worshiped the eagles and Roman standards and the images [Col. 1039B] of the Caesars” (Suetonius, Book IV, *Life of Caligula*, §14).

Why it is called the religion of the camp, and why it swore by its standards, may be understood from these words of Seneca:

> The first bond of military service is religious obligation, love of the standards, and the sacrilege of deserting them; afterward all other things are easily demanded and commanded of those who have been bound by oath.

(Seneca, Epistle 95, p. 305.)

The first of these, therefore, was the military oath by which soldiers pledged themselves to service. Schelius discusses it more fully in his notes on Polybius (Schelius, ch. 1, *De Sacramento*), as do Brissonius (Brisson., beginning of Book IV, *De Formulis*), Justus Lipsius (Lipsius, Book I, *De Militia Romana*, dialogue 6, p. 26), and others. But in addition to this oath, the soldiers also swore by their standards. Thus Lucan represents a centurion swearing to Caesar by them:

> [Col. 1039C] . . . By the ten standards fortunate for the camp,  
> and by all your triumphs over every enemy, I swear.

(Lucan, Book II, v. 278.)

Nor is this surprising, since, as we learn from Cornelius Tacitus, they regarded their standards and eagles as “the peculiar divinities of the legions” (Tacitus, Book II, *Annals*, near the beginning, p. 20; cf. Lucan, Book II, v. 370). Elsewhere, speaking of Antonius suppressing a mutiny, Tacitus says:

> Then, turning toward the standards and the gods of war, he prayed that they would cast that madness and discord upon the armies of the enemy instead, until the mutiny died away.

(Idem, Book III, *Histories*, near the beginning, p. 180.)

Dionysius of Halicarnassus speaks still more clearly: Σημεῖα τιμιώτατα Ῥωμαίοις ταῦτα ἐπὶ στρατείας καὶ ὥσπερ ἰδρύματα θεῶν ἱερὰ νομίζονται (“These standards are held in the highest honor by the Romans on campaign and are regarded as sacred, like images of the gods”). “Nothing in the Roman army is held in greater veneration than the standards, nor are they judged less sacred than the images of the gods” (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book VI, [Col. 1039D] *Roman Antiquities*, p. 375).

Tertullian therefore added that the religion of the camp “places the standards before all the gods” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 16, p. 368), because soldiers venerated them, like their banners, with greater devotion than all their other gods. Perhaps there will be someone who thinks that by these words Tertullian meant that, in the army and on the battlefield, military standards were carried by the standard-bearers before the statues and images of the gods. But the former meaning appears more consistent with his words and intention. For in another book he said: “It places the standards before Jupiter himself, even though he is the greatest of their gods” (Idem, Book I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 12, p. 579).

[Col. 1040A] “But all those distinguished structures supporting images,” he says, “are necklaces of crosses.” Some have wished to advise us that certain manuscripts there read *in signis* (“upon the standards”) rather than *insignes* (“distinguished”), and this is by no means entirely absurd, since military standards are the subject under discussion. Yet because *insignes* is found in far more numerous manuscripts of better quality, we do not dare reject this reading. Nothing, however, can be drawn in confirmation of this reading rather than the other from the book *Ad Nationes*, where Tertullian omitted the word and added: “That structure supporting images and the adornment of all the gold are necklaces of crosses” (*Ibid.*).

Some indeed think that the word *suggestus* is used there for clothing and ornamentation, but they should have proved this. For what if it is understood as the very act of raising up or carrying beneath [Col. 1040B] these images, which hung from the upper portion of a spear or elongated piece of wood and were the necklaces and ornaments of the crosses, since the crosses were veiled and adorned by the images placed above them? In any event, we have already discussed all these matters in our dissertation on the *Octavius* of Minucius Felix (*Dissert. in Minut.*, ch. 12, art. 4), where we also showed that a man with his hands outstretched, as our Author finally says, displays in his own person the image of a cross (Tertullian, Book I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 12, p. 578).

But we seem to hear someone object that this argument of Tertullian is altogether weak. For the pagans, he will say, when worshiping the images of their gods, their standards, trophies, Victories, and any other things of this kind, gave no thought at all to the crosses that lay beneath or covered them. Yet [Col. 1040C] he should observe that the argument of Tertullian and the other defenders of the Christian religion rests upon that pagan belief according to which they thought the images and standards of their gods to be true gods. They therefore worshiped those objects in their entirety and all their parts, among which the crosses were principal elements. For they thought that a god was made not only from the image’s form, appearance, and character, but also from its material; and they customarily venerated the whole object as composed of all its parts. We must therefore say that the crosses lying beneath the cloths and necklaces of the military standards, no less than the other parts of those same standards—parts of which perhaps they were not then thinking explicitly—were honored by them with religious worship.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On the Crimes of Treason Against Human Majesty of Which the Pagans Wrongly Endeavored to Accuse the Christians

[Col. 1040D]

### ARTICLE I  
#### How clearly Tertullian shows that Christians were undeservedly accused of treason against human majesty, since with their whole devotion they prayed—not to false gods, but to the true and almighty God—for the emperor’s safety and prosperity and for the continuance of the Roman Empire, which Tertullian and many others thought would come to an end together with the whole world

We have thus far set forth and explained all the arguments by which Tertullian demonstrates with perfect clarity [Col. 1041A] that the Christians were falsely and most shamelessly accused by the pagans of treason against the divine majesty, although those very accusers were themselves manifestly guilty of it on many counts. We must now examine the considerations by which, in a similar manner, he shows that the pagans were actually conscious of treason against human majesty, although with the greatest rashness they still did not hesitate to accuse the Christians of this crime. For, to use his words: “We have come to the second charge, that of injuring the more august majesty” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 28, p. 436), namely, the majesty of the emperors. Their majesty is called “more august” because the pagans, as we shall shortly explain, were far more afraid to injure the majesty of a living emperor than that of Jupiter and the other dead gods.

But the Christians, while honoring the emperor with due [Col. 1041B] reverence, prayed for his safety not to dead and fictitious gods, but to the true and living God, from whom those emperors had actually received supreme power, second only to His, the enjoyment of life, and everything they themselves were (*Ibid.*, ch. 30, p. 441).

For from this sole and almighty God, in their daily prayers, the Christians implored for those same emperors, as Tertullian says, “a long life, a secure empire, a safe household, brave armies, a faithful senate, an upright and peaceful people, and whatever a man and a Caesar may desire” (*Ibid.*); that is, whatever the emperors could desire for their private lives and imperial dignity in accordance with the laws of equity and justice. Other eminent defenders of the Christian religion proclaimed this no less emphatically. Θεὸν μὲν μόνον (“God alone”), Justin Martyr used to say, [Col. 1041C] προσκυνοῦμεν, ὑμῖν δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα χαίροντες ὑπηρετοῦμεν, βασιλεῖς καὶ ἄρχοντας ἀνθρώπων ὁμολογοῦντες, καὶ εὐχομένοι μετὰ τῆς βασιλικῆς δυνάμεως, καὶ σώφρονα τὸν λογισμὸν ἔχοντας εὐρεθῆναι (“we worship; but in other matters we gladly serve you, acknowledging you as emperors and rulers of men and praying that, together with imperial power, you may be found to possess sound judgment”). “We worship God alone, and in other matters we serve you, acknowledging that you are emperors and rulers of men, while praying at the same time that you may be found to possess sound judgment together with imperial power” (Justin, *Apology to Antoninus*, p. 64). At the end of his embassy on behalf of the Christians, Athenagoras openly declares that those same Christians prayed to God for the imperial rule of Augustus, that it might increase more and more, that everything might befall him according to his desire, and that his son and heir might succeed him in his place (Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 40). But there is no need to pursue more fully matters that are sufficiently known to everyone. [Col. 1041D]

We have also made clear to all (above, ch. 14, art. 3) with what sincere devotion of mind, what innocent soul, and what humble and abject posture of body they endeavored to obtain these things from their almighty God by both private and public prayers. We shall therefore add nothing further except what Tertullian wrote to Scapula, a pagan governor:

> We also honor the emperor, in the manner permitted to us and beneficial to him: as a man who comes from God, second . . . . Accordingly, we offer sacrifice for the emperor’s safety, but to our God and his, and in the manner God has commanded—with pure prayer. For God, the Creator of the universe, has no need of any odor or blood. These things are food for demons.

(Tertullian, *Ad Scapulam*, ch. 2.)

[Col. 1042A] Nor could the pagans reply that these Christian wishes for the emperor’s safety were false and deceitful, or that their prayers were fraudulent and uttered only with the lips so that they might not undergo the punishments they deserved. For by this futile response the pagans, as Tertullian says, conceded that the Christians really did offer prayers to their God for the safety of the emperors (Idem, *Apologeticum*, ch. 31, p. 446). But who has ever proved that those prayers proceeded only from the lips and not from the innermost disposition of the heart?

Tertullian plainly proves that they were entirely sincere from the fact that our sacred Scriptures—which, as we have shown, were not unknown even to the pagans—command each and every Christian “as an overflow of kindness, even to pray to God for his enemies and to ask blessings for his persecutors” (*Ibid.*). Who does not see [Col. 1042B] that by these words he designates this commandment of Christ:

> You have heard that it was said: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.

(Matthew 5:43 ff.)

By these words Christ commands Christians no longer to hate their enemies, as the Jews did, but, in the overflowing abundance of Christian kindness, to love them, do good to them, and pray to God for their persecutors and slanderers with the intimate and sincere affection of the heart.

“But who,” Tertullian continues, “are more the enemies and persecutors of Christians than the emperors, against whose injured majesty we are brought under accusation”—that is, accused (Tertullian, loc. cit.)? Elsewhere he uses this verb more than once (*Ibid.*, ch. 35, [Col. 1042C] p. 454). Above, for example, he had said: “We are arraigned as guilty of sacrilege and treason.” Below he says: “We are arraigned for a second sacrilege against the majesty that is second, namely, after God.” This is a jurists’ term and means the same as being summoned before a court. Under the law laid down by Christ, therefore, Christians were bound to supplicate God for the emperors and their safety, however hostile those emperors might be and however much they might persecute them.

What is more, under another law given by the Apostle, Christians were required to petition God expressly “for kings, rulers, and powers, that all things might be peaceful” (*Ibid.*, ch. 31, p. 446). In those few words, while leaving Paul’s name unspoken, Tertullian encompasses what Paul wrote to Timothy and what we have already cited (above, ch. 12, art. 1):

> I therefore beseech, [Col. 1042D] first of all, that supplications and thanksgivings be made for all men, for kings and all who are in high position, that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity.

(Paul, First Epistle to Timothy 2:1 ff.)

Tertullian does not prove this solely by the authority of sacred Scripture and the law imposed upon Christians, but also by an argument against which no one could so much as mutter:

> When the Empire is shaken, and its other members are shaken with it, we too, although we are regarded as strangers to the disorders, are nevertheless found somewhere within the disaster.

(Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, loc. cit.)

Yet in Rigault’s edition the word *aestimemur* (“we are regarded”) was removed there, contrary to the evidence of our codices and editions. [Col. 1043A] Whether this was due to the printers’ carelessness or to Rigault’s own authority, we do not know; but we certainly have no doubt that our Author correctly included it. For earlier, as we have seen, he asserted that Christians were everywhere intermingled with pagans in every aspect of public life. Nevertheless, they were regarded as strangers to the pagans’ disorders because they were entirely alien to their mysteries and superstitious worship. In other respects they lived together with the pagans, and therefore, when the Empire was shaken, they too necessarily suffered the shock. Consequently they prayed to God with calm and wholehearted sincerity for the peace of the Empire and the safety of the emperors, not only privately but also publicly in their assemblies, as we observed above (above, ch. 15, art. 1).

What is more, if we believe Tertullian, a still greater necessity [Col. 1043B] demanded that Christians offer these prayers sincerely (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 32, p. 447). Their minds had been pervaded by the belief that various portents then foretold the imminent end of the world, but that, as we have already observed (above, ch. 15, art. 1), the world would not be destroyed before the Roman Empire was overthrown. They therefore prayed for the Empire’s continuance and that the end of the world, which they did not wish to experience, might be delayed. Yet although that Christian belief was not true, as we saw above (*Dissertat. in Lactant.*, ch. 29, art. 1 ff.), it nonetheless proves with equal certainty that in sincere prayers they petitioned God both for the safety of the emperors and for the peaceful continuance of their empire.

### ARTICLE II  
#### Christians were undeservedly accused of treason against human majesty because they refused either to sacrifice to the gods of the pagans for the emperor’s safety or to pray to gods who could protect neither their own temples nor themselves, and could neither bestow nor preserve the emperor’s safety—which the almighty God alone could do, and from whom the Christians could obtain it by their prayers

[Col. 1043C]

By so many weighty arguments it has been sufficiently demonstrated that Christians, who prayed daily to God for the emperors’ safety with their whole hearts, were not guilty of injuring their majesty. What, then, could the pagans oppose to this except wholly feeble arguments and absurd quibbles, which collapse of themselves and fall utterly to pieces? Nevertheless, so that we, like our Tertullian, may leave nothing untouched, they must be examined, so that it may become still more evident [Col. 1043D] to everyone with what great injustice those same Christians were harassed and oppressed because of their religion.

The pagans therefore objected that Christians were proved guilty of treason against human majesty because they stubbornly refused to sacrifice to the pagans’ false gods for the safety of the emperors or to pray to them. But to whom, Tertullian asks, should such sacrifice be offered (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 29, p. 438)? Surely to those who can bestow safety upon any person, including emperors. Yet the pagans’ gods could bestow it neither upon emperors nor upon any human being. For those gods were either demons and, as was said above, the vilest spirits, lost and condemned; or rather they were dead men, as [Col. 1044A] the pagans knew from their own consciousness and as we shall demonstrate below. Christians therefore could neither hope for the emperors’ safety from either kind nor ought they to seek it from them.

For how could those false gods bestow safety when they had never been able to protect either themselves or their own temples and images from thieves or from the injuries of time? To preserve them, therefore, they required the sentries of soldiers, as our Author says—that is, their guardianship by day and night. The author of the Epistle to Diognetus fully supports Tertullian when he justly and deservedly reproaches the pagans as follows: Τοὺς μὲν λιθινοὺς καὶ ὀστρακίνους σέβοντες ἀφυλάκτους, τοὺς δὲ ἀργυρέους καὶ χρυσοὺς ἐγκλείοντες ταῖς νυξὶ, καὶ ταῖς ἡμέραις φύλακας παρακαθίσαντες ἳνα μὴ κλαπῶσιν (“You venerate those of stone and pottery though they are unguarded, but those of silver and gold you lock away at night and station guards beside them during the day, lest they be stolen”). “You venerate gods of stone and [Col. 1044B] pottery that have no guardians; but those of silver and gold you lock away at night and appoint guards over during the day, lest they be stolen” (Epistle to Diognetus, near the beginning, p. 495).

Tertullian therefore rightly declares that such guard duty is forbidden to a Christian soldier:

> Will he stand guard over temples that he has renounced, and dine where the Apostle does not approve? Will he defend at night, leaning and resting upon his javelin, those whom during the day he has driven away by exorcisms—namely, the demons and gods of the pagans?

(Tertullian, *De Corona*, ch. 11.)

Other editions read “upon the *lunchus*,” or lance, with which Christ’s side was pierced. You certainly see by what method the pagans stood guard and kept watch for their gods. Yet these guardians, however vigilant, could not prevent the pagans’ temples and images from being plundered and carried off, or [Col. 1044C] from becoming objects of ridicule and contempt to very many. Nevertheless, the pagans were thoroughly persuaded that these images either were their gods themselves or were at least their dwelling, seat, and habitation. We have made numerous observations on these matters elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Arnob.*, ch. 20, art. 5; and *in Lactant.*, ch. 35, art. 5), and shall speak of them again below.

Suppose, if you wish, that the pagans did not believe these images to be gods, but only to represent them. What will you gain from this? For it is established that these very gods of the pagans, whoever they were, depended upon the emperor’s will and judgment. Many of them, as we demonstrated above, experienced this very thing. Indeed, several gods, as Tertullian said, “had Caesar angry with them” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 29, p. 439), because he had forbidden not only the construction of their shrines and statues but even their being regarded as gods. [Col. 1044D] Nothing, however, could be more absurd than to seek the emperor’s safety from gods subject to the emperor, who were more capable of obtaining their own safety from him than he was of obtaining his from them. Tertullian therefore addresses the pagans in these words: “But you are irreligious, for you seek that safety where it does not exist; you ask it from those by whom it cannot be given” (*Ibid.*, p. 440). So the text reads in our codices and in the old editions. Rigault, however, contrary to the authority of them all, ordered *religiosi* (“religious”) to be printed, doubtless because he thought the pagans were there being called religious ironically. But is it permissible, because of this conjecture, to alter an author’s text on one’s own authority—especially when both readings have the same meaning?

Again, Tertullian demonstrates that Christians were more concerned than the pagans for their emperor’s safety [Col. 1045A] (*Ibid.*, ch. 33, p. 448), since they knew with certainty that he had been chosen by their true God. “For from the same source,” he says, “he has his power as he has his spirit and life” (*Ibid.*, ch. 30, p. 442). He had recognized this not only by the light of nature, but also from our writers inspired by the divine Spirit (Idem, Book I, *De Praescriptionibus*, ch. 2). For in the book of Wisdom, as Tertullian says, Solomon addresses kings themselves as follows: “Power was given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High” (Wisdom 6:4). Paul, moreover, wrote to the Romans: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God” (Romans 13).

Tertullian therefore rightly and deservedly concludes from this: “Caesar is more truly ours, since he was appointed by our God” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 33, p. 448), than he belonged to any gods of the pagans, who could never [Col. 1045B] make anyone a Caesar or emperor. Consequently, by praying to his God, by whom the emperor was appointed, the Christian contributes more to the emperor’s safety than does the pagan by praying to his fictitious gods, who cannot confer even the smallest benefit upon either the emperor or any other human being.

### ARTICLE III  
#### How vainly the pagans objected that Christians were guilty of treason against human majesty because they refused to swear by the emperor’s Genius, although they nevertheless swore by his safety, albeit in a manner entirely different from that of the pagans

The pagans persisted in arguing that Christians were shown to be guilty of offending Caesar’s majesty because they refused to swear by the emperors’ Genii; or, as our Author says elsewhere: [Col. 1045C] “We are called irreligious toward the Caesars because we neither propitiate their images nor swear solemnly by their Genii” (Tertullian, Book I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 17, p. 583).

According to Festus (Festus, Book XX, *De Significatione Verborum*, s.v. “Genius”), the pagans called “Genius” not only the god of each particular place, but also the god who possessed the power of directing everything that was to be done. In confirmation of this belief he cites these words of Aufustius:
