> Genius is the son of the gods and the father of men, from whom men are begotten; and therefore he is called my Genius, because he begot me.

Servius somewhere observes that the ancients called the natural god of each place, thing, or person its Genius; and elsewhere that the *Manes* are called by Virgil the Genii allotted to everyone together with life (Servius on Book I of the *Georgics*, p. 85, and Book VI of the *Aeneid*, p. 440). Varro also, as cited by Augustine (Augustine, Book VII, *De Civitate Dei*, ch. 13, p. 172), had said that the Genius was the god [Col. 1045D] appointed over, and possessing the power of, the generation of all things. More is said concerning Genii by Lipsius (Lipsius, Book I, *Physiologia*, ch. 19, p. 554 ff., vol. IV), Natalis Comes (Natalis Comes, Book IV, *Mythologia*, ch. 3), Vossius (Vossius, Book I, *De Origine et Progressu Idololatriae*, ch. 18), and others, as well as by us in our earlier dissertations.

What we touched upon briefly there demonstrates more than sufficiently that the pagans were persuaded that the emperor’s Genius was his own particular god, by whom they thought he had been begotten and was governed. It is therefore unsurprising that they swore by it and accused Christians who refused to swear of treason.

But the Christians, although very frequently provoked by the pagans to take this impious oath—sometimes by flattery, [Col. 1046A] sometimes by threats and tortures—never consented to take it. Do you wish this to be demonstrated by an example? Eusebius is at hand, who relates more than once that the most holy martyr Polycarp was challenged by the proconsul to swear by Caesar’s Genius: Ὄμοσον (“Swear”), he said, τὴν Καίσαρος τύχην (“by Caesar’s Fortune”) (Eusebius, Book IV, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 15, p. 132). But Eusebius continues that the proconsul received from him no answer except this: “You pretend not to know that I am a Christian, to whom that oath is completely and utterly forbidden.”

We are not unaware that the Greek word τύχη (*tychē*, “Fortune”) signifies Fortune, but Caesar’s Fortune is meant there—the Fortune that the pagans believed to be governed by his Genius. We discussed this pagan oath, and its refusal by Christians, in our earlier dissertation on the [Col. 1046B] *Octavius* of Minucius (*Dissert. in Minut. Octav.*, ch. 12, art. 3).

Christians therefore detested every oath sworn by the Genii of emperors, since those Genii either did not exist or were demons subject to those very Christians, who adjured them in Christ’s name and cast them out of the bodies of those whom they possessed (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 32). It was therefore not lawful for Christians to swear by beings over whom they possessed supreme power. Moreover, pagans who swore by Caesar’s Genius very frequently perjured themselves. For traitors and perjurers habitually broke the loyalty they had pledged to Caesar by this oath (Idem, Book I, *Ad Nationes*, ch. 17, p. 583). Who, then, is guilty of treason: one who is implicated in an impious oath or infamous perjury, or another who steadfastly refuses to take that most unjust [Col. 1046C] oath (above, ch. [number omitted], art. [number omitted])?

Thus, in rejecting this oath, Christians were all the less guilty of treason against human majesty because they all the more willingly swore by the emperor’s safety, which, our Author says, “is more august than all the Genii,” as we explained shortly above (*Ibid.*). As a witness to this oath we have Athanasius, who wrote to the emperor Constantius concerning Syrianus, doubtless a Christian: Μαρτυρομένος τὴν σὴν σωτηρίαν (“Having called your safety to witness”), “having called your safety to witness” (Athanasius, *Apology to Constantius*, p. 310, vol. I), he promised that he would cause no further disturbance but would report the matter with far greater solemnity to his piety.

At the Conference of Carthage, moreover, the count Marcellinus bound himself by the same oath in these words:

> Whether I participate in judging this matter with another or alone, [Col. 1046D] I promise that I shall judge nothing except what the examined representations of the parties have been able to demonstrate and what the assurance of truth has discovered—by the wondrous mystery of the Trinity, by the sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation, and by the safety of the aforementioned princes, Honorius and Theodosius.

(*Collatio Carthaginensis*, after Optatus’s book, p. 481.)

You certainly see how weighty this oath was, since in a celebrated assembly of bishops it was joined with two other oaths than which nothing could be more sacred. Numerous examples of this oath, whether in public or private affairs, and confirmed by the laws of the emperors, occur frequently and are sufficiently accessible to all (Theodosian Code, law VIII, *De Pactis et Transactionibus*). Nothing therefore need be added by us except [Col. 1047A] that the custom of taking this oath is extremely ancient. For in sacred Scripture (Genesis 42:15–16), the patriarch Joseph is said twice to have sworn by Pharaoh’s safety.

Basil, however, wished to caution us that, although this bears some appearance of an oath, it is not properly called an oath, but is rather a means by which a matter may more easily be made persuasive to its hearers (Basil, Homily on Psalm 14, §2). Yet Tertullian openly declares that Christians swore by the emperor’s safety because “we desire,” he says, “that he whom God has willed should be safe, and we regard this as a weighty oath” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 32, p. 447).

You therefore understand how great a difference there was between Christians and pagans when they swore in this manner. By this public religious oath, Christians affirmed that they [Col. 1047B] sincerely desired and prayed for the safety of the emperor whom God had placed over them. Pagans, however, with impious flattery declared that the emperor—whose death they desired—was God and a participant in true divinity. Horace was certainly both a witness to and a participant in such wicked adulation, for he wrote these verses to Caesar Augustus, as we have noted elsewhere (*Dissertat. in Minut.*, ch. 12, art. 3):

> While you are present, we bestow timely honors upon you,  
> and set up altars at which men must swear by your name.

(Horace, Book I, Epistle 1, vv. 15–16.)

### ARTICLE IV  
#### Christians were wrongly accused by the pagans of treason against human majesty because they refused to call the emperors gods; how the emperor himself was reminded of his frailty amid the greatest glory of a triumph; how Caesar Augustus refused the title of god and lord; how emperors were called lords by Christians in the ordinary sense of the word; and how it was unlawful for pagans to call an emperor a god before his death and apotheosis

[Col. 1047C]

There was certainly no greater perversity than that of the pagans, who brought an accusation of treason against the Christians because they entirely refused to call the emperors gods or to confer divine honors upon them. For, as Tertullian acutely argues: “He who calls him a god denies that he is an emperor. Unless he is a man, he is not an emperor” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 33, p. 449). For who can deny that an emperor begotten by a human father and mother cannot be God, who must necessarily be altogether eternal? Christians, therefore, who rightly detested the most shameful flattery of the pagans in calling their emperors gods, could not on that account be prosecuted by anyone for treason against human majesty.

Indeed, by the celebrated example of an emperor celebrating a triumph, Tertullian most plainly convicts the pagans who customarily called him a god of a most disgraceful falsehood. For at this highest summit of human glory—or, as Tertullian expresses it, “in the most exalted chariot of his triumph”—he is reminded of his frailty. For someone behind him whispers: “Look behind you; remember that you are a man” (*Ibid.*). Tertullian does not say who it was that gave this reminder, doubtless because the person was then as well known to everyone as he is known to few today. Tzetzes, however, calls him an attendant, slave, [Col. 1048A] and public servant. For concerning the triumphal chariot and this admonisher he wrote:

> Καὶ πῶς ἐπὶ τοῦ ἅρματος δημόσιος οἰκέτης,

Ὄπισθεν τοῦτον ἴσταται τὸν στέφανον ἀνέχων,

Καὶ λέγων τούτῳ πρός τε οὗς· καὶ τὸ κατόπιν βλέπε

(“And how, upon the chariot, a public servant stands behind him, holding up the crown and saying to him—apparently into his ear—‘Look also at what is behind you.’” The recovered words πρός τε οὗς appear corrupt and are uncertain.) And how, in the chariot, a public servant  
> stands behind him, holding up the crown  
> and saying into his ear: “Look at what is behind you.”

(Tzetzes, *Chiliades* 13, §461.)

Pliny, however, calls him a physician of envy and glory:

> Hanging beneath the chariot of those celebrating triumphs, he defends them as a physician against envy; and a similar remedy of the tongue commands them to look back, lest Fortune, the executioner of glory, be appeased behind them.

(Pliny, Book XXVIII, *Natural History*, ch. 4, p. 570.)

But if this passage of Pliny is sound and complete, it means that the envy customarily aroused [Col. 1048B] in others by those celebrating triumphs—or the vice of vainglory by which the triumphators themselves could be bewitched—was cured by the remedy of the attending slave’s tongue, as he reminded the triumphator of his human condition. For elsewhere the same Pliny explicitly said that the triumphator’s crown was held up by a slave (*Ibid.*, Book XXXIII, ch. 1).

But because in the former passage Fortune is called the executioner of glory, perhaps for this reason Isidore conceived the idea that the monitor was not a slave but an executioner: “Those celebrating triumphs,” he says, “were touched by an executioner, so that, having been raised to so great an eminence, they might be reminded of human mediocrity” (Isidore, *Origins*, book XVIII, ch. 2, p. 156). But without doubt he is more appropriately called simply a companion by Jerome—the man who, amid the acclamations of the people, whispered into the triumphator’s ear the words recalled by Tertullian. For he wrote to Paula: [Col. 1048C] “As men celebrated triumphs in the chariot, a companion remained close behind them, saying at every acclamation of the citizens: ‘Remember that you are a man’” (Jerome, epistle 22, *To Paula*). Yet if an emperor amid so magnificent a triumphal procession had to remember his humanity, how much more throughout the whole course of his life. Christians therefore could not call any emperor God, since, as Tertullian rightly says, they did not know how to lie, nor did they dare to mock him (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 449).

He presses the point further: Augustus, although the organizer of the Roman Empire, which had already been founded by Julius Caesar, did not wish even to be called “lord,” much less “god” (*Ibid.*, ch. 34, p. 450). If you desire a witness to this moderation, we shall summon Suetonius, who handed down the following concerning [Col. 1048D] the same Augustus: “He always recoiled from the title ‘Lord’ as from a curse and a reproach. When, as he watched the games, the line was delivered in a mime, ‘O just and good Lord!’ and everyone, exulting as though it had been said of him, loudly expressed approval, he immediately checked their unseemly demonstrations with hand and countenance; and on the following day he rebuked them in a most severe edict. Thereafter he did not permit himself to be called ‘lord,’ even by his children or grandchildren, either seriously or in jest, and he forbade such flatteries even among them” (Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, § 53).

But someone will rise in opposition and cite to us another witness, Cornelius Tacitus, who also committed to writing that various rumors were spread after the death of the same Augustus, and that he had left nothing remaining of the honors due to the gods, since he had wished himself to be worshiped in temples, and in the likeness of divine powers, through flamens and priests (Cornelius Tacitus, *Annals*, book I, near the beginning). [Col. 1049A] Yet an answer can certainly be made to him in other words of Suetonius: “Although he knew that temples were customarily decreed even to proconsuls, he accepted them in no province except in the joint name of himself and Rome. In the city itself, indeed, he most obstinately refused this honor” (Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, § 52). Thus, even if he permitted the practice that must be discussed later, it is nevertheless no less certain that he rejected the title “lord,” which his successors seized upon most eagerly. For Pliny the Younger, although a pagan, openly asserted in his Panegyric to the emperor Trajan that the time had passed when cowardly flatterers fawned upon the emperor as upon a god and divine power: [Col. 1049B] “For we speak,” he says, “not of a tyrant, but of a citizen; not of a lord, but of a father” (Pliny, *Panegyric to Trajan*, beginning). Christians therefore had all the greater reason for refusing to call the emperor God, because, as our Author says, this is a title belonging to the one true God alone (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 34, p. 449), as we have observed elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 12, art. 1).

Because, however, long usage had already established the practice of attributing the name “lord” to emperors and others, Tertullian accordingly says: “Certainly I shall call the emperor ‘lord,’ but in the ordinary manner of speech, when I am not compelled to call him Lord in place of God” (Tertullian, *ibid.*). But Rigault removed these two words, *voce communi* (“in the ordinary manner of speech”), both because he had learned that they were not found in the Fulda manuscript and because, in his view, they have the flavor of a note taken from the margin. [Col. 1049C] Yet those words occur in all our copies and in others, whether printed or manuscript. Moreover, there is no room for doubt that several of them surpass the Fulda manuscript in antiquity. How, then, could those words have been intruded from the margin into the text? Do they not also produce an excellent sense, one consistent with the Author’s purpose? “I call the emperor ‘lord,’” he says, “when I am not compelled by that name to acknowledge him as God, but when I utter that name in the ordinary manner of speech, or in the common meaning in which a son customarily addresses his father, a slave his master, and other men one another.” How ordinary and popular this form of address was you may learn even from Martial alone:

> You know that you were born of a slave-woman, and you admit it ingratiatingly  
> When, Sosibianus, you call your father “lord.”

[Col. 1049D] And elsewhere:

> When I call you “lord,” Cinna, do not be pleased with yourself:  
> I often greet my slave in just the same way.

(Martial, book I, epigram 82.) But it would be thoroughly wearisome to prove at greater length things so commonplace and everywhere familiar to everyone. In this vulgar and ordinary sense, therefore, our Author continues, I call the emperor “Lord”; but otherwise I am free in relation to him and am not his slave. “For my Lord,” he says, “is the one God, almighty and eternal, the same who is also the Lord of the emperor himself, and whom consequently both he and all other men ought to serve” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 34, p. 449).

Our Author further acknowledges that the name “father” is far more pleasing [Col. 1050A] than “lord,” because the latter is a name of power, the former of dutiful affection. Accordingly, from what has now been said he draws this conclusion: “So far is it from being proper for the emperor to be called god—which cannot be believed—not only by most disgraceful but also by pernicious flattery, but as if, while having one emperor, you were to call another one so” (*Ibid.*). Yet these words, “which cannot be believed,” undoubtedly appeared useless to Rigault, who excised them contrary to the testimony of every manuscript, whether printed or unpublished. Was it therefore lawful for him, on his own authority, to cut out from Tertullian’s text everything that seemed superfluous to him? Is not this the sense of the passage? The emperor ought to be the father of his country, and this name is far more pleasing than “lord.” You ought not, therefore, to call the emperor God, since it cannot be believed that he is God. For [Col. 1050B] by this most disgraceful and pernicious flattery you signify that you have another emperor who is not God but a man, a man who commands you, another man.

Finally, if the pagans had adhered to their own laws and customs, it was not lawful for them to call any emperor a god except after his death and apotheosis, that is, his enrollment among the gods by decree of the senate, as we saw above. For, says Tertullian, “it is a curse to call Caesar a god before his apotheosis” (*Ibid.*). Herodian, more accurately than the others, described the solemn ceremony of this apotheosis, first reminding us that it was Roman custom for emperors to be consecrated by their successors and thus declared to have been enrolled among the gods (Herodian, *History of His Own Times*, p. 540). Before that, therefore, no one was permitted to call them gods. [Col. 1050C] For this reason Cornelius Tacitus concludes the fifteenth book of his *Annals* with these words: “Divine honor is not accorded to a prince before he has ceased to live among mortals” (Tacitus, *Annals*, book XV, at the end). Tertullian therefore rightly says in another book: “But we do not call the emperor a god. For on this point, as people commonly say, you jeer. Indeed, those of you who call Caesar a god mock him by saying what he is not, and you curse him because he does not wish to become what you call him; for he would rather live than become a god” (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 18, p. 583). For because he could become a god only after his death, he certainly preferred to live rather than lay down his life and afterward become a god—or rather, be adorned with this wholly mendacious title. Christians therefore could not, without the greatest injustice, be called guilty of treason against human majesty or public enemies [Col. 1050D] merely because they refused to call the emperor God. For that title belongs solely to him who is not a man but eternal and immortal.

## CHAPTER XXII  
Christians are neither public enemies nor factious persons; rather, the pagans who accused them of these crimes are such.

### ARTICLE I  
Christians are not public enemies: although they could very easily have done so, they never wished to avenge the injuries inflicted upon them by the pagans—whether by secretly setting fire to the city, openly declaring war, separating themselves from those same pagans, who were fewer in number, or refusing to cast demons out of possessed bodies.

With as much rashness as the pagans babbled that Christians were guilty of treason against [Col. 1051A] human majesty, so with equal shamelessness they accused them of being public enemies and enemies of the whole human race. Nothing more rank than this slander could ever have been devised. For by divine law (Matt. 5:39; Luke 6:28) they were forbidden, as Tertullian says (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 36 ff., p. 460; and *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 17, p. 583), to wish evil upon anyone, to do evil, speak evil, or think evil of anyone, and to repay an injury in kind. They obeyed these precepts with the greatest exactness, as is evident from what we previously said about their most holy morals (above, ch. 12, art. 1 ff.). They were therefore not public enemies—indeed, not enemies of any human being at all, much less of the emperor and of the entire human race. And certainly, although they were tortured with every kind of insult [Col. 1051B] and torment by emperors and other pagans, not one of them was ever found among the very many, to be discussed shortly, who had conspired against those same emperors and the commonwealth.

Yet this was not to be attributed to the weakness or powerlessness of those same Christians. For they could have avenged the injuries done them by the pagans, not only secretly and through concealed stratagems, but openly and in outright warfare. They could have done so secretly, since “even one night,” as Tertullian says, “could, with a few little torches, furnish abundant opportunity for vengeance” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 37, p. 462); that is, amid the silence of a dark night, they could have set cities on fire with a very few torches purchased at minimal cost. “But far be it,” he continues, “that a divine sect should be avenged by human fire, [Col. 1051C] or should grieve to suffer that by which it is tested” (*Ibid.*); or, as he himself wrote to Scapula: “Far be it that we should resent suffering the things we desire, so that we might contrive some vengeance ourselves, when we await it from God” (same author, *To Scapula*, ch. 2). He therefore offers three reasons why Christians refused secretly to avenge their offenses, although it was easy for them to do so. First, because theirs is a divine sect, whose laws forbid vengeance, and they considered it a sin not to obey them. Second, they awaited that vengeance from their almighty God, the most just punisher of crimes. Third, they most willingly endured all the torments inflicted upon them by the pagans, because they knew that these did not harm them but tested whether they were worthy of an eternal reward.

[Col. 1051D] For these reasons alone, and not from any weakness or powerlessness, they abstained from taking vengeance upon their pagan enemies. For nothing was easier or more readily available to them. We have shown above (above, ch. 12, art. 1) that they had filled every place throughout the whole world, with the sole exception of the temples of the false gods, and that their number was far greater than that of the pagans. What, then, could have prevented them from declaring war, defeating the pagans, and inflicting deserved punishments upon them when defeated (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 37, p. 462)? Yet suppose, if you wish, that they were inferior to them in both numbers and resources: were they thereby less fitted to wage war and conquer their enemies? Did the pagans not acknowledge that they did not fear death [Col. 1052A] (*Ibid.*)? Surely the less they feared it, the more fiercely they would have fought despite every uncertain turn in the outcome of war, and thus could have exacted the penalties due from their enemies. But, bound by their religion, they never wished to attempt it, whether armed or unarmed.

Furthermore, they had no need of any war or violence to obtain vengeance (*Ibid.*, p. 463). For separation and withdrawal from the pagans would have sufficed. The latter, then astounded at their isolation, would have had more enemies than citizens, and certainly very few people to govern: “For now,” says Tertullian, “you have fewer enemies in comparison with the multitude of Christians ([almost all citizens; almost all citizens ought to be accounted Christians; and you preferred to call them enemies of the human race rather than of human error])” (*Ibid.*). So indeed the passage stands in our [Col. 1052B] manuscripts and in printed editions older than Rigault’s, except that in some of them *habendo* is read in place of *habendos*, and these final words, “rather than of human error,” have been cut away. But Rigault, with still greater boldness, excised everything that we have ordered to be enclosed in brackets. Yet he said not a single word about so extensive an excision. Did he therefore suppose that the reason for it was known to everyone because Tertullian said shortly afterward: “You preferred to judge us enemies, though we are plainly not enemies of the human race, but rather of error” (*Ibid.*)? But was an author never permitted to draw the same conclusion in the same words from two arguments? Tertullian concludes that the pagans preferred Christians to be judged enemies not of error but of the human race, because they had failed sufficiently to observe [Col. 1052C] that Christians would leave them more enemies than citizens, first by withdrawing from them and, second, by refusing to cast out demons, as will soon be said. He deliberately said “citizens,” because, as we have seen, by sharing a common life with them they were their fellow citizens.

But someone may perhaps object that this entire argument of Tertullian rests upon an intolerable exaggeration of the number of Christians. We ask such a person, however, what benefit could Tertullian have gained from an ill-timed hyperbole? For there he addresses the pagans, who were not ignorant of the number of Christians and who, had he been convicted at once of lying, would have denied him credibility in everything else. Furthermore, we showed above (above, ch. 12, art. 1) how true are the things that he stated so expressly both there [Col. 1052D] and elsewhere concerning the immense number of Christians.

Finally, by another argument he demonstrates how easily Christians could have avenged themselves. They alone, he says, had the power to cast demons out of the possessed bodies of pagans, as we saw previously (above, ch. 8, art. 6; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 37, p. 463). But if they had not driven them out, “this alone would have sufficed for our vengeance”—these are his own words—“that a vacant possession should thereafter lie open to unclean spirits” (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*). Rigault, however, solemnly advises us there that he learned from others that the Fulda manuscript has *pateretis* instead of *pateret*. You will doubtless marvel at the extraordinary diligence of a man who notes, upon the testimony of others, this variant reading of such slight importance, while entirely omitting the preceding one [Col. 1053A] and others of far greater importance, even though they are supported by the authority of all the manuscripts. Yet the word *pateretis*, he says, has the flavor of Tertullian’s style. Do all the other readings he omitted have less of the flavor of that style? Surely no one, not even Rigault himself, would dare seriously to affirm it. Moreover, the common reading of every book except the Fulda manuscript is no less Tertullianic, and produces the same sense: if Christians did not put demons to flight, the bodies of the pagans would lie open to them at will, like vacant property.

What means of avenging themselves could have been more prompt and readily available than this? But they so abhorred every act of vengeance that they preferred to expel demons from the bodies of their pagan enemies—and thus benefit them—rather than fail to expel those demons and so fail to benefit them. [Col. 1053B] The pagans were therefore most ungrateful when, making light, as Tertullian says, of so great a protection, they clamored that Christians, who were so necessary to them, were public enemies of the human race (*Ibid.*).

### ARTICLE II  
How absurdly the pagans charged Christians with being public enemies because they did not celebrate the imperial festivals as the pagans did: by bringing hearths and couches out into public, feasting street by street, transforming the city into the likeness of a tavern, turning the ground into mud with wine, running about in crowds toward acts of violence, shamelessness, and the enticements of pleasure, and fastening laurels and lamps to the doorposts of their houses as though these were new brothels.

[Col. 1053C] Since Christians utterly abhorred every act of vengeance and rendered good service to everyone, with what demented fury, you will ask, did the pagans so boldly shout that they were public enemies? For no reason at all, save one that was plainly absurd, as you will understand from these words of Tertullian: “Christians are therefore public enemies because they do not utter toward the emperors honors that are empty, deceitful, and rash; because, as men of true religion, they celebrate even their festivals with conscience rather than with wantonness” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 452). Thus the whole of that enormous crime of the Christians was that they observed the imperial festivals only according to their own pious and holy rite, and not according to the utterly corrupt rite of the pagans.

If anyone first desires to know what those festivals were, he must remember that they are called by our Author himself [Col. 1053D] “the solemn days of the princes,” and “the vows and rejoicings of the Caesars” (*Ibid.*), which were customarily celebrated at various times. For every year, on the third day after the Kalends of January, “vows are undertaken for the safety of the princes,” as Gaius says (*Digest*, book L, title 16, law 233); or, as Tertullian himself wrote, “at the beginning of the year, at the beginning of the month” (Tertullian, *To His Wife*, ch. 6). They were also observed annually on the emperor’s natal day, that is, the very day on which he had been made emperor, and especially in the fifth, tenth, fifteenth, and twentieth year thereafter. These festivals were called quinquennial, decennial, quindecennial, and vicennial. We have touched briefly upon them in another dissertation (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. 11, art. 3), [Col. 1054A] where you will find cited Pagi (Pagi, *Hypatic Dissertation*, part 2, ch. 2) and others who discuss them at greater length.

During those festivals the pagans prayed to their fictitious gods for the safety of the emperors and citizens, for the eternity of the empire and its flourishing condition, as has been observed by Pliny (Pliny the Younger, letters 36, 37, 101, 106, and *Panegyric to Trajan*, after the midpoint), Brisson (Brisson, *On Formulae*, book II, p. 110), and others. Christians, therefore, who worshiped the one true God, and who could offer the emperors only true honors prescribed by the sacred laws of their religion, did indeed celebrate their festivals, though not, of course, with the same wantonness as the pagans but “with conscience,” as Tertullian says (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 452); that is, with a true and sincere disposition of mind, [Col. 1054B] in the manner they knew God required. Hence he says elsewhere: “As regards the honors due to kings and emperors, we have sufficiently prescribed for us that in every act of obedience, according to the Apostle’s precept, we ought to be subject to magistrates, princes, and powers—but within the limits of our discipline, insofar as we remain separate from idolatry” (same author, *On Idolatry*, ch. 15).

He thus acknowledges that the imperial festivals were celebrated by Christians according to this law of the Apostle, and with prayers poured out to God, as we saw above, for the emperor and empire from the innermost affection of the heart. They were not celebrated in the pagan manner, concerning which, as he says in addressing the pagans themselves, “neither moderation, nor reverence, nor chastity permits such a manner of demonstrating your loyalty and sincerity ([but the opportunity for pleasure, rather than a worthy motive, has persuaded you to adopt it])” (same author, [Col. 1054C] *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 454). Everything you see enclosed in brackets in this text was completely removed by Rigault and his followers, contrary to the testimony of the printed and unpublished manuscripts. Yet you will find no reason given by them for this excision, unless by their silence they wished to indicate that these words seemed to them to have been added by some unskilled scribe. But who will believe them when they remain silent in this way? The common agreement of all the manuscripts clearly proves that these are Tertullian’s genuine words. Furthermore, his entire genius and manner of expression can readily be discerned in them. Their sense is this: Christians are proclaimed enemies of the emperors and of the commonwealth because they do not observe the imperial festivals in the pagan manner, a manner which neither moderation, nor reverence, nor chastity permits them to adopt; [Col. 1054D] and which the opportunity for pleasure, rather than a worthy motive for demonstrating loyalty and sincerity toward the emperors, persuaded those same pagans to celebrate. He thus openly asserts that in these solemn festivals the pagans possessed no loyalty or sincerity. For at that time they made utterly false vows for the emperors’ safety, although they wished those emperors to die soon and often, as we shall see in the following articles.

He also rightly complains that three virtues—moderation, reverence, and chastity—were then utterly destroyed. For what could be more contrary to these virtues than to hold magnificent and splendid banquets, not secretly in private homes but openly and publicly in the streets—banquets polluted by the intoxication, [Col. 1055A] drunkenness, impurity, wantonness, lust, and other crimes of the feasters? But, if you please, let us hear Tertullian himself: “A grand duty,” he says, “of those pagans observing those imperial festivals was, to be sure, to bring hearths and couches out into public” (*Ibid.*). The older editions read “choruses,” but “couches” is undoubtedly better. For there he speaks of public banquets at which the pagans reclined at table. Hence he adds shortly afterward: “With couches as ornate and sumptuous as possible they divided the forum among themselves” (*Ibid.*). They therefore spread so many couches in the forum, and with such magnificence, that they seemed to have divided and filled it among themselves.

But because the forum, however large it might be, was not sufficient for everyone, others feasted “street by street” (*Ibid.*), that is, in every quarter of the city, on the public roads and at the crossroads. [Col. 1055B] Consider, then, I ask, whether the following words of Cicero do not contribute something to understanding this custom. He openly reports that Apronius had ordered couches to be spread for himself in the middle of the forum, and that he was accustomed every day to feast not only in public but at the public expense, while music played at those feasts and the largest cups were served (Cicero, *Against Verres*, book III, p. 136, line 43). Cornelius Tacitus also recorded somewhere that “nothing anywhere delighted the emperor Nero so much as arranging banquets in public places and using the entire city as though it were his house” (Tacitus, *Annals*, book XV, before the midpoint, p. 127). The pagans, believing that everything was permitted to them on these imperial feast days, were then accustomed not only to use the entire city as though it were a house, but, as Tertullian says, “to efface the city beneath the appearance of a tavern” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 452), [Col. 1055C] so that the entire city bore the appearance of a shop and an inn. There are some who, by way of explanation of this passage, adduce these verses of Martial:

> Barber, innkeeper, cook, and butcher keep to their own thresholds;  
> Now it is Rome; recently it was one great shop.

(Martial, book VII, epigram 60.) But others judge that Martial uses the word *taberna* there not for an inn but for a market, or a place where goods were customarily sold. Whichever meaning is adopted, it is certain that the pagans displayed such intemperance, shamelessness, and wantonness in these public banquets that they not only gorged themselves with food but, as our Author says, “made mud with wine” spilled through the middle of the city streets [Col. 1055D] and mixed with the earth (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 452). One might then see intoxicated and drunken men running about in crowds toward acts of violence, shamelessness, and the enticements of lust; or, as he says later (*Ibid.*, ch. 39, p. 477), “into bands of beatings”—men who struck others with blows and whips—and “into companies of running about,” that is, groups who ran throughout the whole city in the manner of Bacchants. How great the intemperance in these public banquets was may be inferred from what Seneca wrote concerning private ones: “You see those same men gazing from their couches upon their eating house, delighting their ears with the sound of voices, their eyes with spectacles, and their palates with flavors. Their entire body is stimulated with soft and gentle fomentations; and [Col. 1056A] lest their nostrils meanwhile remain idle, the very place in which funeral rites are performed for luxury is perfumed with various scents” (Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, ch. 11, p. 624). For if such were their private banquets, how much more so the public feasts held in honor of the emperors, at which they believed even more atrocious and shameful acts were permitted to them.

Rightly and deservedly, therefore, did Christians utterly detest these things as unworthy of any person in whom even the smallest remnant of shame and true religion remained. Thus they observed those festive and solemn days of the Caesars chastely and soberly. Keeping far away from the corrupt customs of the pagans, “we do not,” says our Author, “shade our doorposts with laurels, nor break into the daylight with lamps” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 451). For hidden traitors, in order more safely to conceal their hatred and hostility toward the emperor, [Col. 1056B] then decked their doorposts with the freshest laurels bearing the most branches, and clouded their vestibules with the tallest and brightest lamps (*Ibid.*). Why he uses this last verb may be understood from these verses of Persius concerning Herod:

> The days of Herod have come, and every window,  
> With lamps arranged in rows, has spewed a greasy cloud.

(Persius, satire 5, near the end.) Concerning the same lamps and the laurel with which the doorposts of houses were adorned, Juvenal has these verses:

> All things gleam; the doorway has raised long laurels  
> And celebrates the festival with early-morning lamps.

(Juvenal, satire 12, v. 96 ff.) Tertullian gives the following reason why Christians utterly rejected these superstitions: “Every day they light lamps for those who have no light”—namely, the light of true religion—“and fasten to their doorposts laurels that will later burn, over which flames hang threateningly; to them belong both testimonies of darkness and omens of punishment” (Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, ch. 15), [Col. 1056C] namely, of the eternal fire by which impious men are to be punished after this life. Then he addresses the Christian thus: “If you have renounced temples, do not make your doorway the temple”—that is, of some false god (*Ibid.*). For Ovid sang concerning the temple of Jupiter:

> Yet why is the doorway veiled with laurel placed upon it,  
> And why does the shady tree encircle the august house?  
> Is it because this house has earned perpetual triumphs,  
> Or because it has always been loved by the Leucadian god?  
> Is it because the house itself is keeping festival, or because it makes all things festive?  
> Or is this the sign of peace that it bestowed upon the earth?

(Ovid, *Tristia*, book III, elegy 1, v. 41 ff.) [Col. 1056D] This reason alone was therefore sufficient for Christians to reject this profane rite. But Tertullian suggests another: “If you have renounced brothels, do not clothe your house with the appearance of a new brothel” (Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, *loc. cit.*). For not only laurels but also lamps were customarily hung at the doors of these infamous houses. Hence the following complaint of a door in Propertius:

> I do not complain that I am wounded by the nocturnal brawls of drinkers,  
> Or that I am often struck by unworthy hands;  
> Nor do I lack shameful garlands to hang upon me,  
> And torches always lying as signs for those shut out.

(Propertius, book I, elegy 16.) Tertullian therefore earnestly warns his wife [Col. 1057A] that it is lawful neither for her nor for any Christian woman, “at every royal festival, to come forth from a doorway crowned with laurel and illuminated with lamps, as from a new council chamber of public lusts” (Tertullian, *To His Wife*, ch. 6). Hence in his *Apologeticum* he rightly concludes that it is neither honorable nor lawful, “when a public solemnity demands it, to clothe your house with the appearance of some new brothel” (same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 451).

We do not think that any person of sound mind can fail to understand from what has thus far been said that certain heterodox persons wholly and completely abuse this testimony of the Author when they infer from it that Christians are forbidden to use wax candles and lights in their churches. For he is not there discussing these, concerning which we have written above (ch. 15, art. 4, and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. [Col. 1057B] 25, art. 2), but other candles and lights customarily employed in a profane and pagan rite. Yet from this it is very clearly established that Christians were not public enemies of either the commonwealth or the emperors merely because they celebrated the latter’s festivals in their own pious manner, and not according to the utterly condemnable and detestable manner of the pagans.

### ARTICLE III  
It is shown that the pagans were in fact public enemies of the emperor, whom they openly assailed with taunts and abuse, to which the Tiber and the school of beasts bore witness; and that they always desired the spectacle of one new Caesar after another, even while acclaiming him: “May Jupiter add years to you from our years.”

[Col. 1057C] Tertullian was not content to demonstrate more clearly than daylight itself that Christians were not public enemies either of the emperor or of the commonwealth; rather, he openly and clearly showed that the pagans themselves had offended in precisely the same class of wrongdoing for which they censured others without the least justification. Nor does he summon foreign or far-removed witnesses. “I call upon,” he says, “the Quirites themselves, the Romans, the native populace of the seven hills”—that is, the common people of the city of Rome—“to answer whether the Roman tongue spares any Caesar” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 35, p. 454); that is, whether it spares him the taunts, jeers, abuse, and insults with which they assailed their emperors. “The Tiber and the school of beasts,” he says, “bear witness” to so many insults (*Ibid.*). But what, someone will ask, could this testimony of the river Tiber have been? [Col. 1057D] Some reply that this name designates the sailors dwelling on the riverbank, fierce and insolent men who, in times of scarcity and grain shortage, were accustomed to inveigh against Caesar himself with the most wanton speech. But this explanation will scarcely commend itself to anyone, nor does it appear consistent with Tertullian’s thought. Others suppose that by the name “Tiber” is denoted a bridge or some place from which slanderers and detractors were cast into the Tiber; but that is perhaps no better. You will therefore more easily persuade us that Tertullian is alluding to certain statues placed in public locations at Rome and on the bank of the Tiber, upon which biting pamphlets of this sort were posted. For elsewhere Tertullian himself says: “I shall arraign the sacrileges of vanity, and examine the irreverence of the native people themselves, and the witty pamphlets known to the statues, and those indirect remarks sometimes uttered by the council, [Col. 1058A] and the curses that resound in the circus: if you are not rebels in arms, you are always rebels in tongue” (same author, *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 17, p. 583). Does he not indicate there in other words those two things that he calls “the Tiber” and “the school of beasts” in the *Apologeticum*? For witty pamphlets insulting the emperor were hung upon statues that had been placed in public locations, doubtless near the Tiber. Hence the Tiber could be called a witness to these witty and insulting remarks.

As for the school of beasts, perhaps there will be some who think that this name designates their cage, upon whose door were inscribed the witty and pointed sayings with which they stung the emperors. [Col. 1058B] But what if the “school of beasts,” or perhaps “of beast-fighters,” is understood as the whole circus, concerning which we have just heard Tertullian say: “The curses of the circus resound”? For scarcely anywhere else were the pagans accustomed to injure their emperors with greater license, more bitter taunts, or more scurrilous sarcasm. Do you wish this fact, although sufficiently well known, to be proved by some examples? Hear these words of Suetonius concerning Caesar Augustus, though he was an excellent prince: “Once, on a day of games, the entire populace both took as an insult against him and approved with the loudest assent a verse delivered on the stage concerning a *gallus* of the Mother of the gods beating a drum” (Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, § 68):

> Do you see how the wanton fellow governs the world with his finger?

Afterward, concerning the emperor Tiberius: “His anxious mind was further tormented by various reproaches from every quarter, since every condemned man, without exception, flung every kind of abuse at him either to his face or through pamphlets placed in the orchestra” [Col. 1058C] (same author, book III, *Life of Tiberius*, § 66). Julius Capitolinus, moreover, relates the following concerning the emperor Verus: “He took such an interest in the circus games that he frequently both sent and received letters to and from provincials concerning them. Finally, even when present and sitting with Marcus, he endured many insults from the supporters of the Blues because he acted most disgracefully against them” (Julius Capitolinus, *Life of Verus*, p. 306). But what need is there to pursue at greater length events that occurred so often?

Tertullian presses the point: If some window into the human heart and mind lay open through which its innermost thoughts might be examined, we should then certainly recognize with what ardent wishes they all desired “the spectacle of a new Caesar, and yet another new Caesar”—that is, the frequent death of one Caesar and the choice of another, who would preside over the distribution of a largess [Col. 1058D] (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 35, p. 455). Some, however, would prefer the reading *praesiderantis* (“of one presiding”), but this rests on a slight conjecture and conflicts with the authority of the manuscripts. For Tertullian means that the pagans were always longing for the spectacle of a new Caesar who would preside over the distribution of a *congiarium*, or gift—usually one of money—to the populace or soldiers, or would order it distributed in his presence. It was indeed customary for newly elected Caesars, or those who sought election, to lavish gifts of this kind upon the people. Many examples of this largess may be found everywhere in the writers of Roman history. If anyone nevertheless desires some, we shall select a few of them.

On the day after Claudius had been carried off by the soldiers to imperial power—seized rather than elected—“he allowed the armed men,” Suetonius says, “to swear allegiance to his name before the assembly, [Col. 1059A] and promised fifteen thousand sesterces to each of them, being the first of the Caesars to pledge the loyalty of the soldier by means of a reward as well” (Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, § 10). After Claudius died, “Nero was brought into the camp”—these are the words of Cornelius Tacitus—“and, after a preliminary address suited to the occasion, he was acclaimed emperor upon promising a donative modeled upon his father’s generosity” (Tacitus, at the end of Book XII of the *Annals*). Spartianus, moreover, attests that Hadrian gave the soldiers a double largess at the beginning of his reign (Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, shortly after the beginning); and Lampridius records other gifts bestowed by Macrinus when he proclaimed Antoninus Diadumenus emperor (Lampridius, beginning of the *Life of Antoninus Diadumenus*). Anyone for whom these examples are insufficient may consult Robertellus (Robertellus, *De Commodis Praemiis Donativisque Militum*), Pancirolus (Pancirolus, *Notitia Imperii Orientalis*, [Col. 1059B] chap. 74), and others. The pagans, therefore, always impelled by gain, desired the death of the reigning Caesar so that they might more frequently receive a donative, and longed for the spectacle of a new Caesar—though he too was soon to die.

Our Author presses the point still further: at the very time and in the very hour when they acclaimed:

> May Jupiter add to your years from our years,

they were all the more eagerly desiring this spectacle and the Caesar’s death. But in our manuscripts and the older printed editions we read, with the metrical form broken:

> From . . . . . may Jupiter add years to you.

(Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 35, p. 456.) However it may be read, Tertullian there intimates that this acclamation of the pagans was feigned and altogether mendacious, since at that very time they desired the Caesar’s death with their whole hearts. Nor does there seem to be any room for doubt that, [Col. 1059C] with a similar falsehood, Ovid acclaimed Caesar Augustus with a similar falsehood in this verse:

> May he increase the dominion of our Leader, and increase his years.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, Book I, v. 611.)

Yet if this acclamation of the pagans was entirely feigned, it is evident that Ambrose’s prayer for the emperor Valentinian, though already dead, was utterly sincere: “Nor do I deny that he died at an untimely age, whom we would have wished to sustain with portions of our own lives, so that he might live from our years, since he could not fulfill his own” (Ambrose, *On the Death of Valentinian*, § 43, p. 1186). We observed long ago that Ambrose was alluding here to the solemn formula of acclamation noted by Tertullian. Furthermore, we frequently read many similar acclamations, in which the pagans appeared to wish the Caesars a long life, in the books of those who wrote the lives of the emperors Commodus, Pertinax, [Col. 1059D] Probus, Balbinus, and others. One may also consult Brissonius (Brissonius, Book I, *De Formulis*, p. 95 ff.) and Bernardino Ferrari’s first book on acclamations and applause (Ferrari, Book II, *De Acclamationibus*, chaps. 19, 20 ff.). In any event, Tertullian rightly concludes from what has been said that the pagans who made wishes of this kind for the emperor’s imminent death were in fact public enemies both of him and of the commonwealth, as will be further apparent from what must be said in the following article.

## ARTICLE IV. That the greater enemies of the emperors were the pagan traitors—the Cassii, Nigri, Albini, and others—who beset Caesar between two laurels; who practiced wrestling in order to squeeze his throat; who broke into the palace, more daring than all the Sigerii and Parthenii; who were daily revealed as accomplices and applauders of criminal factions; and, finally, who consulted astrologers, haruspices, augurs, and magicians concerning the emperors’ lives, and offered prayers for their safety that were as false as those of the Christians were sincere

[Col. 1060A]

If the pagans who demanded the death of Caesars and emperors with such impious wishes were guilty of violating human majesty, other rebels and cowardly traitors undoubtedly sinned against them far more gravely—those who had either deserted their side or, after attempting to deprive them of life, sought to seize despotic power. Among their number undoubtedly belonged those mentioned by Tertullian [Col. 1060B] (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 35, p. 457): the Cassii, Nigri, and Albini—that is, Cassius Clemens, Pescennius Niger, and Albinus—who, as we saw above (above, chap. 2, art. 1), contrived to usurp the imperial power of the emperor Severus. They were therefore public enemies and guilty of violating human majesty.

Those too are plainly convicted of the same crime who, to continue in Tertullian’s words, “beset Caesar between two laurels” and “practice wrestling in order to squeeze his throat” (Tertullian, passage cited). He seems to be speaking with tolerable clarity about the emperor Commodus, against whose life plots were laid more than once. First, Pompeianus—or Quadratus, as others maintain—plotted against his life in a certain narrow entrance, as we read in the Epitome of Dio (Dio, *Epitome*, p. 284); or, [Col. 1060C] as Ammianus Marcellinus says, in the seating area of the amphitheater (Marcellinus, Book XXIX, p. 550); or, as Herodian relates, at the entrance to the amphitheater, in a dark place (Herodian, *History*, Book I, p. 472). Now, if laurels were planted at this entrance to the amphitheater, it is not difficult to understand why Commodus is said to have been beset between two laurels. But because stricter critics do not readily accept this, Rigaltius thought that these words of our Author designated the laurel grove which, according to Herodian (the same, ibid.), was planted with various trees and with beautiful, luxuriant laurel, and to which Commodus withdrew upon his physicians’ advice while a plague was raging at Rome. This interpretation might perhaps not be wholly inappropriate, had Herodian not said that the plot against Commodus was prepared not there, but at the entrance to the amphitheater. Some therefore suspect [Col. 1060D] that by “laurels” are meant two palaces of Commodus, between which the conspirator attacked him. For the laurel, as Pliny observes, was the doorkeeper of the Caesars (Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XV, chap. 30). Consider, I pray, which of these three explanations pleases you more, and we shall gladly hear your verdict. Whatever the explanation may be, it follows most evidently that this man who plotted against Caesar’s life was a public enemy.

The following words of Tertullian can undoubtedly be explained more easily: “Those who practice wrestling in order to squeeze his throat” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 35, p. 457). For a second plot was laid against the same Commodus, in which he was strangled by Narcissus, “an athlete,” as Xiphilinus says (Dio, *Epitome*, p. 384 ff.); or, [Col. 1061A] as Herodian writes (Herodian, *History*, Book I, p. 486 ff.), by Narcissus, a bold and vigorous young man; or, as Aurelius Victor relates (Aurelius Victor, *Life of Commodus*), by a very powerful athlete; or, as Lampridius attests, “by the athlete with whom he customarily trained” (Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*, p. 315), who compressed his throat.

Tertullian adds that other pagans too are public enemies and guilty of violating majesty: those “who break into the palace” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 35, p. 457)—namely, the rebellious assassins by whom the emperor Pertinax was cruelly killed, as Herodian (Herodian, *History*, Book II, p. 598), Capitolinus (Capitolinus, *Life of Pertinax*, p. 318), and Xiphilinus (Dio, *Epitome*, p. 390) committed to writing. But these men, says [Col. 1061B] our Author, were “more daring than all the Sigerii and Parthenii” (Tertullian, passage cited), by whom, that is, the emperor Domitian was killed, as we have shown elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, chap. 6, art. 2). Accordingly, nothing remains for us to observe except that these words of Tertullian do not appear entirely uncorrupted. For our older manuscripts have *tot Sigeriis* (“so many Sigerii”), while some editions have *Stephanis* (“Stephani”), undoubtedly because Suetonius (Suetonius, Book VIII, *Life of Domitian*, § 17), without mentioning Sigerius at all, relates that Domitian was first wounded by Stephanus and was afterwards killed by Clodianus, Parthenius, and Saturius. But it is difficult to say why the name of Sigerius should have been omitted there, since he is expressly mentioned not only by Xiphilinus (Xiphilinus, Epitome of Dio, p. 335), but also by Martial in these two [Col. 1061C] verses:

> Ten times you retrace the palaces upon the sacred slope,  
> And sound the measures of Sigerius and Parthenius.

(Martial, Book IV, epigram 79.)

Let Heraldus’s conjecture therefore be dismissed: at first he suspected that *Sergiis* should be read in Tertullian’s text, and later, after better consideration, as he himself says, *Chaereis* or *Corneliis*. For these readings are opposed by the authority of our better-quality manuscripts, confirmed by the testimony of Martial and others.

Tertullian further asserts that those too are public enemies “who are now daily revealed as accomplices or applauders of criminal factions” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 35, p. 458). We have indeed already observed above (above, chap. 2, art. 2) that these words [Col. 1061D] designate the confidants and supporters of Albinus’s faction, who had conspired to destroy the emperor Severus. There too we more fully elucidated what our Author added: “Those also discharge the same duties who consult astrologers, haruspices, augurs, and magicians concerning the lives of the Caesars” (Tertullian, passage cited). For why did they consult them with such curiosity, unless because they were thinking about the Caesars’ future death, which they certainly wished would occur in a short time? For he immediately said: “Counsel is not sought concerning loved ones”—that is, blood relatives and parents—“in the same spirit as concerning masters” (Tertullian, passage cited, p. 459), whom we do not sincerely love. Regarding the former, he says, there is “the anxious concern of blood”—that is, concern for those to whom [Col. 1062A] we are joined by blood, and whom we desire to remain safe; but the concern arising from slavery is different, since every slave longs, once his master has been removed, to cast off its yoke as quickly as possible. Yet you must not suppose that Tertullian approves the first kind of consultation, concerning the welfare of relatives. His sole meaning is that the latter consultation, concerning the death of the Caesars, is far worse than the former. Indeed, he utterly and completely condemns every consultation of magicians, since such practices were, as he says (ibid.), handed down by deserting angels, as we saw above, and forbidden by God (above, art. 5).

Moreover, who would not shudder at the monstrous perfidy of all these men, who, even up to the very outbreak of their impiety, “performed sacred rites for the emperor’s safety . . . so that they might now declare their own wishes on the occasion of another’s solemnity”—namely, [Col. 1062B] that of the emperor—“and inaugurate the pattern and image of their own hope, changing the prince’s name in their hearts” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 33, p. 459)? That is, while uttering prayers wholly feigned for the emperor’s safety, but sincere prayers for his death and for his immediate successor, they named the former merely with their lips but the latter in their inmost hearts. What could be more detestable than such perfidy?

We therefore cannot sufficiently marvel at the audacity of the pagans, who, though so many examples showed them to be public enemies guilty of violating majesty, most shamelessly accused the wholly innocent Christians of this crime. For among so many rebels and public enemies no Christian was ever discovered. Hence our Tertullian wrote the following to Scapula, governor of Africa, in response to the charge: “We are defamed in matters concerning the emperor’s majesty. [Col. 1062C] Yet Christians could never be found among the Albinians, the Nigrians, or the Cassians. Rather, those very men who, up until the day before, had sworn by their guardian spirits, as we showed above, who had both offered and vowed sacrifices for their safety, and who had often condemned Christians, were discovered to be their enemies. A Christian is no one’s enemy, much less the emperor’s; knowing him to have been appointed by God, he must love, revere, and honor him, and wish him safe together with the whole Roman Empire” (the same, *To Scapula*, chap. 2). But we have sufficiently explained these matters above.

Thus the Christians’ prayers for the safety of the emperors were as sincere as those of the pagans were false, and the Christians treated the emperors with as much devotion and honor as the pagans pursued them with hatred. For, says our Author, “the dutifulness, religion, [Col. 1062D] and loyalty owed to emperors does not consist in observances of this kind, which hostility can employ rather as a veil for itself” (the same, *Apologeticum*, chap. 36, p. 460)—that is, observances beneath whose shadowy mask of false piety religion can conceal a perfidious and hostile disposition. Rather, “dutifulness and religion reside in those morals through which civility must be manifested as truly toward the emperor as toward everyone else.” This is the reading of the Wouwer manuscript and some more recent editions. In the older editions and in our manuscripts, however, the reading is: “in those morals which divinity commands, as truly . . . toward everyone else,” etc. (ibid.). Surely the authority of so many older and better-quality manuscripts carries greater weight than that of the single Wouwer manuscript? [Col. 1063A] Nor should you say that the term *civility*, by which the fellowship and concord of citizens is signified, is more suited to Tertullian’s purpose. For he is speaking of conduct commanded by God, through which religion and dutifulness must be displayed toward the emperor and all others. From this it is demonstrated still more evidently that Christians, who regarded it as impious not to obey the laws of their God, honored the emperor with sincere intent, and consequently were neither public enemies nor guilty of violating human majesty.

## ARTICLE V. What unlawful factions are, and how greatly the pious manner of life of Christians differs from them—Christians who were undeservedly called factious because they shunned the pleasures of spectacles and pursued pleasures as lawful as those in which Epicureans and others indulged, though other pleasures were forbidden

[Col. 1063B]

The implacable hatred of the pagans against the Christians could never be appeased by any arguments, however powerful; instead they cried out more and more that the Christians’ faction, being altogether opposed to both the emperors and the commonwealth, must be torn out by the roots. Tertullian intimates with tolerable clarity that the word *faction* may be understood in either a good or a bad sense (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 38, p. 464). Festus likewise says: “*Factio* and *factiosus* were originally honorable terms. Hence we also speak of the factions of actors and chariot teams. Nowadays, however, sedition and armed violence are called by the name of faction” (Festus, *On the Signification of Words*, chap. 2, s.v. *Factio*). The factions of the circus, which the pagans did not consider evil, are also mentioned frequently in the books of Suetonius (Suetonius, Book V, *Claudius*, § 5, [Col. 1063C] and Book VIII, *Domitian*, chap. 7), Cassiodorus (Cassiodorus, Book III of the *Variae*, epistle 41, p. 56, col. 2), and others, as well as in various inscriptions.

Tertullian therefore castigates the pagans in these most forceful words: “Accordingly, with no less leniency, this sect of the Christians should have been reckoned among lawful factions, since it commits nothing of the kind that is usually feared from unlawful factions” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 38, p. 464). Heraldus, however, conjectures, against the protest of all the manuscripts, printed and handwritten alike, that the reading should be “unlawful,” not “lawful factions.” Tertullian meant nothing else, he says, than that the opinion of certain pagans seemed more lenient because they believed the Christian sect to be prohibited by the laws promulgated against factions, though they erred [Col. 1063D] in placing this sect among the number of unlawful factions. But what can one venture against the unanimous agreement of all the manuscripts? What, moreover, if the particle *nec* has been transposed, or should be taken with the term “lawful,” so that the meaning of our Author here is: The pagans falsely cried out that Christians were public enemies. Nor did those treat them much more leniently who enrolled them among factions that were not lawful, with which they had nothing in common, and by which nothing of the kind is committed that is usually feared from unlawful factions (ibid.).

Let us now consider how he proved that the sect of the Christians was not unlawful. “The reason for prohibiting factions,” he says, “clearly consists in provision for public propriety, lest the community be split into parties” (ibid.). In the older [Col. 1064A] printed editions we read “in provision and public propriety.” But that reading is less satisfactory, since our Author declares the reason for prohibiting factions to be that provision should be made for and regard paid to public propriety. *Propriety* is defined by the Latin orator as follows: “The knowledge of assigning to their proper place those things which are to be done or said. And so it appears that order and arrangement will have the same force . . . since this propriety, as we interpret it, is, as I said, knowledge of the suitability of times appropriate for action” (Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 370, line 47 ff.). It seems that the term *propriety* was taken in this sense by our Tertullian, who accordingly asserts that evil factions were forbidden lest the community be split into parties through the disturbance of the order of things to be done or said at their proper place and time. For this division and [Col. 1064B] dissension “disquiets,” as he puts it—or disturbs—*comitia*, that is, general assemblies of all the orders, and *concilia* (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 38, p. 464), that is, an assembled part of them. For Laelius Felix, cited by Aulus Gellius, says: “One who commands not the entire people, but some part of it, to be present commands the holding not of *comitia*, but of a *concilium*” (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book XV, chap. 7, p. 847). It also disturbs the *curiae*, through which, as Varro observes (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book IV, p. 51), the priests formerly attended to divine affairs and the senate to human affairs; it disturbs *contiones*, whether understood as the public speeches of advocates or as the gatherings of people convened to hear them; finally, it disturbs public spectacles—the circus and other public games, as we were saying shortly before.

But all these things, Tertullian continues, were especially [Col. 1064C] to be feared at the time “when they had already begun to keep for hire the venal and mercenary service of their violence” (Tertullian, passage cited), in order to stir up disturbances and seditions against the emperor, as we have observed. For conspirators against him drew other desperate men into their faction with payment and wages.

Nothing of this kind, or even the smallest thing resembling it, was to be feared from Christians. First, nothing was done in their public assemblies except what was pious and holy; and there, as elsewhere, they prayed to God with all their hearts for the emperors, for the tranquil condition of the empire, for their enemies, and for everyone else (ibid., chap. 39, p. 468). We have already demonstrated all these matters abundantly (above, chap. 14, art. 3, and chap. 21, art. 1).

Second, since they utterly abhorred all ambition and desire for offices [Col. 1064D] and honors—or, to use our Author’s words, “since we are cold toward every ardor for glory and office, we have no need of assemblies” (Tertullian, ibid.)—that is, no need to attend the assemblies of the pagans just mentioned, where offices, magistracies, and the insignia of honors were customarily bestowed upon the covetous and ambitious. Moreover, “aloof from public affairs, we recognize only one commonwealth for all humankind—namely, the world,” which we desire to be tranquil and peaceful. Thus, inclined no more to one party than to another, we stand far removed from every turbulent, seditious, and unlawful faction whatsoever.

Furthermore, Christians [Col. 1065A] wholly and utterly shunned and detested the public spectacles of the pagans, which were extremely frequent incitements to faction. For these have no other origin than superstition, as he says—that is, the impious worship of false deities—as he himself demonstrates more fully and individually in another book. Hence in his *Apologeticum* he rightly draws this conclusion: “We have nothing to do, in speech, sight, or hearing, with the madness of the circus, the shamelessness of the theater, the savagery of the arena, or the vanity of the exercise-ground.” Thus all the manuscripts and ancient editions read; but Rigaltius and his followers removed the words “in speech, sight, or hearing.” Whether rightly, I appeal to you as judge. For those words are genuine and were added by him with the greatest deliberation, to show that Christians avoided these spectacles because, beyond the crime of idolatry, they regarded it as impious to take pleasures unlawful to speak of, see, or hear (Tertullian, [Col. 1065B] passage cited, and *On Spectacles*, chaps. 6, 7 ff.). How harmful and pestilential those pleasures were you may learn from these words of his, by which he elsewhere calls them “the solemn pleasures of the raging circus, the savage enclosure, and the lascivious stage” (the same, *Against Marcion*, Book I, chap. 27). Elsewhere: “Even a believer perishes when he slips away to a spectacle of charioteering frenzy, gladiatorial bloodshed, theatrical foulness, and gymnastic vanity” (the same, *On Modesty*, chap. 7). But more about these matters may be found in his book *On Spectacles*, and in this and other dissertations of ours.

The pagans nevertheless objected [Col. 1065C] that, by that very fact, the Christian sect ought to be prohibited and condemned: Christians spurned the assemblies of other people and avoided, as they would a public plague, the amusements of public spectacles, which the emperors and the older human laws favored. But Tertullian replies to them: Let these pleasures be as lawful as they are impious. “How do we offend you,” he says, “if we claim and pursue other pleasures? What, indeed, if we refuse to know how to be amused and reject every kind of pleasure? Surely the injury is ours, if perhaps it is not yours” (the same, *Apologeticum*, chap. 38, p. 467)—that is, we inflict loss only upon ourselves and by no means upon you, unless perhaps it is also to your loss that you devote yourselves entirely to such impious pleasures.

Nor should you press the objection that “we reject what pleases you” (ibid.). We do not deny it; indeed, we glory in it. But what concern is that of yours? Do not our pleasures likewise fail to delight you? If, then, you reject our lawful and chaste enjoyments, why should we not be permitted to reject yours, which are altogether lustful [Col. 1065D] and utterly unworthy of a human being endowed with reason?

Tertullian continues and confirms the point by the example of the Epicureans, which he sets forth in these exact words of our manuscripts: “The Epicureans were permitted to determine some true form of pleasure—that is, equanimity of mind—and extensive Christian occupations” (ibid.). The ancient editions have the same reading, except for the final word *christianae* (“Christian”), which no one of sound judgment will deny was added through the carelessness of scribes. Rigaltius, however, as we noted above (chap. 3, art. 1), retained only these words: “The Epicureans were permitted to determine some true form of pleasure”; moving them from their proper place, he placed them before the words: “How do we offend you?” He wished us to understand that he had learned of this emendation from those who had seen the Fulda manuscript. But even if matters stand thus, [Col. 1066A] should the authority of the single Fulda manuscript for that reason have been preferred to all the others, many of which are far older? If the term *christianae*, as we have said, is removed as superfluous, do not those words accord very well with our Author’s purpose and thought?

For his argument proceeds in this manner: Why should Christians not be permitted to pursue the pleasure they consider honorable, when the Epicureans were permitted to choose that which affords equanimity—or rather evenness and tranquility—of mind, disturbed by no unpleasant agitation and by no extensive occupations? For, Cicero said, “the highest [Col. 1066B] pleasure, as Epicurus holds, is to feel no pain” (Cicero, *On Ends*, Book I, p. 45, line 28); or, as Theodoret relates, it is that pleasure which excludes every kind of care and disgust, and consequently extensive occupations (Theodoret, sermon 12, *On the Blessed Life*, p. 675). If this is indeed Tertullian’s meaning, then his text should read *nec* (“nor”), not *et* (“and”), “extensive occupations,” unless by that expression he understood occupations which by their extensiveness cause no disturbance of mind. We have, moreover, discussed that opinion of Epicurus and his followers elsewhere, more than once. From all these considerations Tertullian rightly concludes that the sect of the Christians, who rejected the unlawful pleasures of the pagans, was not an unlawful faction that ought to be prohibited, but was indeed excellent and superior to all others. By contrast, the pagans were plainly factious and seditious, since, as we saw [Col. 1066C] in the preceding articles, they openly assailed their emperors with scurrilous wit, abuse, and insults, wished for their death, conspired against them, and laid violent hands upon them.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That Christians Are Not the Cause of Public Calamities

## ARTICLE I. What the public calamities were of which the pagans complained, as frequently as falsely, that Christians were the authors, and how Tertullian refutes them

We observed in our earlier dissertations (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 6, arts. 1 and 2) that no accusation was repeated more often than that by which the pagans complained that Christians were the cause, as [Col. 1066D] Tertullian says, “of every public calamity and every popular affliction.” We would indeed be weary of reheating once again cabbage so often reheated, by refuting anew this utterly foolish argument, if the pagans had ever repented of pressing it so ineptly. But these madmen, raging with monstrous hatred against the Christians, believed that they could devise scarcely anything more suitable than this calumny for destroying Christians (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 40, p. 479, and Book I *To the Nations*, chap. 9, p. 571). Let us therefore follow our Tertullian and attempt to elucidate whatever distinctive or somewhat obscure point he made in setting forth and overthrowing it.

He begins with the Romans as follows: “If the Tiber [Col. 1067A] rises to the walls” (ibid.); or, as he says in another book, “if the Tiber has overflowed”—that is, if by excessive flooding it has harmed the walls of the City and even the fertility of the lands. Conversely, “if the Nile does not rise to the fields” and inundate them with its customary flood—or, as Virgil sings:

> . . . does not fertilize them with black sand.

(Virgil, *Georgics*, Book IV, v. 290.)

Furthermore, our Author adds, “if the sky has stood still”; or, as he says later, “when summer and winter weather suspend the rains” (Tertullian, passage cited). If you ask what he denotes there by the word “sky,” we shall answer you in the words of Tullius: “This sky in which clouds, rains, and winds gather” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book II, p. 122, line 14). If the rains do not flow down from this sky at the proper season of winter or summer and render the earth fertile—which [Col. 1067B] Cyprian, following Tertullian, expressed thus: “When you say that very many complain because prolonged clear weather suspends the rains and showers”; and elsewhere: “when clear weather suspends rain from the clouds” (Cyprian, treatise *To Demetrianus*; and *On Mortality*)—likewise “if the earth has moved,” and towns have collapsed from its unusual motion or people have been swallowed by its chasms, as we shall soon see; finally, “if famine and plague” (here “rage and spread” must be supplied); or, as he says more clearly elsewhere, “if famine has afflicted” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 40, p. 480, and Book I *To the Nations*, chap. 9, p. 571): amid all these public calamities, says Tertullian, the cry is raised with one voice by all the pagans, “The Christians to the lion!” (the same, *Apologeticum*, ibid.). The final word, however, which is found in our manuscripts [Col. 1067C] and ancient editions, was lopped off by Rigaltius. Yet even if it is absent, it must certainly be understood. That acclamation, which we discussed above, was customarily made chiefly in the circus. By that cry alone, however unjust it might be, Christians were seized and immediately exposed to be devoured by lions and other wild beasts. Tertullian derides and rejects it in only these three words: “So many to one!” (ibid.), just as if he had said: “Good heavens! Do you think that the almost infinite multitude of Christians, as we observed earlier, could have been exposed to a single lion and devoured by it?”

After this he demonstrates [Col. 1067D] by weighty arguments that nothing more false could have been devised than the claim that Christians were the authors of public or other calamities: “For before Tiberius,” he says—that is, before Christ’s advent—“what great calamities struck the world and its cities” (ibid.)? He did not say “before Tiberius” in the sense that Christ had not come into this world earlier, but that his advent was manifested to the world when, during Tiberius’s reign, he performed miracles and founded his Church. For in the book *To the Nations* he says: “Under the emperor Augustus this name arose; under Tiberius his teaching shone forth” (the same, Book I *To the Nations*, chap. 7, p. 567). Accordingly, he later said: “Our era is not yet three hundred years old; how many calamities, before that span, struck the whole world, individual cities, and provinces? How many foreign and civil wars? How many plagues, famines, fires, chasms, and earthquakes has the age set down? [Col. 1068A] Where then were the Christians, when the Roman state supplied so many histories of its sufferings” (ibid., chap. 9, p. 571)? Since we cannot pass over without some explanation the examples by which he demonstrated these claims, let us proceed, if you please, to expound them individually.

## ARTICLE II. How Tertullian demonstrates that Christians are not the authors of public calamities, because before Christ’s birth Hiera, Anaphe, Delos, Rhodes, and Cos were destroyed by numerous inundations and earthquakes, along with many thousands of people; likewise the greater part of Asia or Africa, and the Corinthian Sea was drained dry; Sicily was severed from Lucania and became detached from Italy; and all human beings perished in a cataclysm that affected not merely the plains but the whole world

[Col. 1068B]

No more powerful argument can certainly prove that Christians were not the authors of public calamities than the many examples of such events that occurred before Christ’s birth. And yet no one who has touched the histories of ancient times even with the tips of his fingers can fail to know how frequently almost all writers have mentioned them.
