It therefore seemed scarcely necessary for Tertullian to collect many examples of this kind, unless he judged that they had to be advanced in order to crush the pagans’ obstinacy. We must therefore examine them, both because of the variant readings of the manuscripts, by which proper names have been deformed, and because of certain difficulties that may cause trouble for some readers.

[Col. 1068C] The first example is presented in Rigaltius’s edition in these words: “We read that the islands Hierannape, Delos, Rhodes, and Cos perished together with many thousands of people” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 45, p. 36). In our copies, however, the reading is: *Hierananpeam, et Delon, et Rhodon, et Cho*; with the exception of one copy, in which *Hierant pean* appears; the Bongars manuscript has *Iherrapean*; one Vatican manuscript, *Hieramapeam*; another Vatican manuscript likewise has *Hiera Niepaeam*; the Fulda manuscript, *Hierearranda penes*; and the editions before Rigaltius, *Hierapolis*, but incorrectly. For that city is not reported to have fallen before the beginnings of the Christian religion. You can certainly see how greatly, and for how long a time, this passage has been corrupted. In the book *To the Nations*, however, [Col. 1068D] the reading is plainly: “The islands Hierennape, Delphi, Rhodes, and Crete perished together with many thousands of people” (the same, Book I *To the Nations*, chap. 9, p. 54, Rigaltius’s edition). But these words neither remove nor even lessen the difficulty. Nor are these words of the same Tertullian in another book any more sound: “Delos, Rhene, and Samos no longer exist” (the same, *On the Pallium*, chap. 2). For many wish *Harenae* to be read there in place of *Rhene*, although Pliny (Pliny, *Natural History*, Book IV, chap. 12, p. 456) and others mention the island of Rhene. Let us therefore see whether we can borrow from elsewhere some light for explaining that obscure and corrupt passage of Tertullian.

The first author who presents himself to us is Pliny, cited just above, where he discusses places from which the seas had withdrawn and islands that had emerged [Col. 1069A]: “The famous islands of Delos and Rhodes,” he says, “are recorded as having emerged long ago. Later, smaller ones emerged: Anaphe beyond Melos; Nea between Lemnos and the Hellespont; Hanelo between Lebedos and Teos; Thera and Therasia among the Cyclades, in the fourth year of the 135th Olympiad; and, among the same islands 130 years later, Hiera, also called Automate” (Plin., lib. II ibid., cap. 87, pag. 236). To this may also be added Ammianus Marcellinus, where he investigates the causes of earthquakes: “Brasmatiae,” he says, “which violently heave up the ground, thrust forth enormous masses, as Delos, Hiera, and Anaphane emerged in Asia” (Marcell., lib. XVII, cap. 7, pag. 456). Do you see that Delos and Rhodes are mentioned in these passages, just as they are by Tertullian himself? Is there not therefore room to suspect that, from the other two islands, Hiera and Anaphe, as Pliny writes [Col. 1069B], or Hiera and Anaphane, as Marcellinus writes, the corrupt word *Hierannapen* was produced by ignorant copyists? We shall, however, readily yield to anyone who offers a better suggestion.

There remains the last island named by Tertullian: Co, or Cho, as in our manuscripts and in the already cited first book *To the Nations*; or Coro, as in the old editions; or Coon, as in Heraldus’s edition. Pamelius, however, thinks that it should be corrected to Coo, because we read in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*: “On the island of Cos very many things collapsed in an earthquake” (Chron. Euseb., ad. 38 ann. August.). Perhaps not altogether wrongly, for Strabo mentions the island Κῶς (Cos) (Strab., lib. II Geogr., pag. 124, et lib. X, pag. 489), as do others. But some have advised us that the text of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* reads “in [Col. 1069C] Cyprus,” and they endeavor to confirm this by Seneca’s testimony. Finally, some have suspected that Tertullian wrote Cea, and they think that this emendation can be supported by these words of Pliny: “More than thirty miles were suddenly torn away from the island of Cea, carrying off a great multitude of people” (Plin., lib. II Natur. Hist., cap. 92, pag. 239). Would this conjecture not gain some additional strength from the fact that the same Pliny later observes that Cos was called Cea by Staphylus (Ibid., lib. V, cap. 9)? But this will doubtless be established more securely if it can be proved that Tertullian had Pliny’s books in view.

He certainly appears to have been aiming at Pliny when he said: “Plato records that a land greater than Asia or Africa was taken away by the Atlantic sea” (Tertullian., Apologet., cap. 40, pag. 481). And again in another book: “Plato records that an Asia or Africa of greater extent was submerged in the Atlantic sea” (lib. I ad Nation., cap. 9, pag. 571). For we have seen that the same Pliny wrote: “It carried lands away altogether—first of all, where the Atlantic sea now lies, over an immense extent, if we believe Plato” (Plin., lib. II Hist. natur., cap. 90, pag. 238). The passage of Plato cited by both is found in his *Timaeus* (Plato., Tim., tom. III, pag. 25), as we have observed elsewhere (Dissertat. in Arnob., cap. 6, art. 3). Yet even if Tertullian had never thought of Pliny when writing these things, this nevertheless confirms no less strongly what he repeats elsewhere, that a Libya or Asia was leveled beneath the Atlantic sea.

But let us follow him still further, unless you think it has already been sufficiently proved by so many examples [Col. 1070A] that Christians were not the cause of public calamities, and unless you are weary of having it proved by still others. He proceeds and says: “An earthquake drank up the Corinthian Sea” (Tertullian., lib. de Pall., cap. 2); and in the book *To the Nations*: “The Corinthian Sea was carried away by an earthquake.” Some think that he was alluding there to the destruction of the cities Helice and Bura, concerning which Pliny again says: “The sea swallowed Helice and Bura in the Corinthian Gulf, traces of which are visible in the deep” (Plin., lib. II Natur. Hist., cap. 92, pag. 239). If you desire more, consult Strabo (Strab., lib. I Geogr., pag. 59), Pausanias (Pausan., lib. VII, pag. 212 et 231), Seneca (Senec., lib. VI Natur. Quaest., cap. 23, pag. 893), and, passing over others, Ovid, who sang:

[Col. 1070B] If you seek Helice and Bura, Achaean cities,

You will find them beneath the waters; and even now sailors

Are accustomed to point out the sunken towns with their lofty walls.

(Ovid. *Metamorph.* lib. XV, v. 293, etc.)

But a little earlier he composed these verses, not indeed about cities but about the lands named by our Author:

I myself have seen what once had been most solid earth

Become sea; I have seen lands made from the sea;

And marine shells lay far from the ocean,

And an ancient anchor was found on the highest mountains.

See, if you please, what we noted on Arnobius in the preceding dissertation (Dissertat. in Arnob., cap. 6, art. 3). But someone will object that these things do not suffice for Tertullian’s purpose unless it is shown by some argument that the Corinthian Sea was, as he says, carried away and drunk up by an earthquake. Yet Callisthenes, already cited by [Col. 1070C] us after Seneca, will fully satisfy him, for he teaches that cities and lands can easily be swallowed by overflowing waters when air, slipping through hidden openings, shakes the earth (Senec., lib. VI natur. Quaest., cap. 85, pag. 895). For then a chasm is formed in which everything is consumed. Hence the same Seneca said again: “A violent convulsion engulfed the two cities Helice and Bura.” But Bura and Helice were cities of the Peloponnesian, or Corinthian, isthmus, which could not have been submerged by the waters without the Corinthian Sea being swallowed in a similar event. Yet it was not swallowed in its entirety, but produced the double sea of which Ovid says:

And the isthmus that separates the waters of the twin sea.

(Ovid. epist. 12, v. 104.)

[Col. 1070D] And Lucan:

. . . As the slender isthmus

Which cuts through the waves and separates the twin sea,

And does not permit the straits to meet; should the land recede,

The Ionian Sea would break against the Aegean. . . .

(Lucan. lib. II, v. 99.)

Moreover, what Tertullian added is far easier for everyone to understand: “The violence of the waves cut Lucania away from Italy and banished it under the name of Sicily” (Tertullian. *Apologet.* cap. 40, pag. 481). In another book, however, he speaks at somewhat greater length: “Once a side of Italy, battered by the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian seas, was intercepted through its middle and left Sicily as its remnant; while that entire region of rupture, forcing back the contentious meeting of the seas into narrow confines, gave the sea a new defect—not that of spewing out shipwrecks, but of devouring them” (Idem, [Col. 1071A] lib. de Pall. cap. 2). These things have indeed been handed down to memory by many geographers, poets, and others. Ovid, in the same passage cited a little above, sang of Zancle, one city of Sicily:

. . . Zancle also is said to have been joined

To Italy, until the sea swept away their boundaries

And thrust the land back with an intervening wave.

(Ovid., lib. XV *Metamor.* v. 290.)

Lucan, whom we have also commended, sang the same thing more than once concerning the whole of Sicily (Lucan. lib. II, v. 543, et lib. III, v. 58 et seqq.), as did Virgil in these verses:

These places, once convulsed by violence and vast destruction—

So greatly can the long passage of time alter things—

Are said to have burst apart, when previously both lands

Had been one; the sea came violently between them and with its waves

Cut the Hesperian side away from Sicily, and flows

[Col. 1071B] Between fields and cities drawn apart by a narrow channel.

(Virgil., lib. III *Aeneid.*, v. 414 et seqq.)

After citing these verses, Seneca added: “Thus, by this inundation celebrated by the greatest poets, Sicily was cast away from Italy” (Senec., lib. IV natur. Quaest., cap. 29, pag. 898). See Pliny (Plin., lib. II natur. Hist. cap. 87, pag. 235), Statius (Stat., lib. III *Thebaid.* et lib. I *Sylvar.*), Silius Italicus, Cluverius, and others.

Why say more? Before Saturn and all the other gods of the gentiles there occurred the cataclysm which, as Tertullian says, destroyed the whole world, or, as Plato thought, only the level country (Tertullian. *Apologet.*, cap. 40, p. 481). More briefly in the book *To the Nations*: “A cataclysm destroyed the whole world” (lib. I ad Nation. cap. 9, p. 571); but more fully in another book: “Even now,” he says, “the sea’s shells [Col. 1071C] and trumpets travel abroad upon the mountains, desiring to prove to Plato that even the heights were afloat” (Idem, lib. de Pall. cap. 2). No one fails to understand that he is speaking there of the universal flood described in the sacred book of Genesis (Genes., cap. VI et VII). He censures Plato there because Plato thought that the waters of this flood had not reached the highest mountain peaks, to which, as he fancied, a great many shepherds fled and, unlike the others, did not suffer shipwreck (Platon. tom. II, lib. III de legib. pag. 677; et tom. III Tim. pag. 22). Our Author refutes this false opinion from the fact that shells and trumpets were found upon mountains—or *buccina*, as Pliny says, who observes in the same place that this is a smaller kind of shell shaped like a horn or trumpet (Plin., lib. IX natur. Hist. cap. [Col. 1071D] 36, pag. 340, et cap. 33, pag. 328). But a little earlier we cited Ovid, who testifies that shells and an anchor had been found on the highest mountains. Yet at the time of that universal flood Saturn and the other gods afterward invented by the gentiles did not yet exist, as is clearly demonstrated by the cities founded by them, or in which they were born and died—or, as the book *To the Nations* says, were born, remained, and were buried (Tertullian. loc. cit.). We have discussed these matters, and the origin of the gods and of idolatry, in the preceding dissertations, and something more will be said below.

## ARTICLE III

### On the disasters that were caused before the beginnings of the Christian religion by heavenly fire and by human arms; on Sodom and Gomorrah, which were burned, and their land, where fruits attempt to grow and then turn to ashes when touched; on Volsinii and Pompeii, or the Tarpeians, consumed by fire; on the disaster at Cannae, after which Hannibal measured the slaughter of the Romans by a bushel of rings taken from them; and on the Capitol occupied by the Senones

[Col. 1072A]

Tertullian passes to other disasters caused by heavenly fire and by human arms, and says: “A fiery rain burned Sodom and Gomorrah” (Tertullian. *Apologet.* cap. 40, p. 482), before the Israelites migrated from Egypt into Palestine, and consequently many centuries before the Christians, who arose from them, came into the world. The destruction of both these cities is confirmed by the most certain testimony of Holy Scripture [Col. 1072B] (Genes. cap. XIX, v. 24). But even if that testimony were lacking, an unmistakable indication of that disaster would be supplied by the land itself, which, to use Tertullian’s favored manner of expression, “still smells of burning; and if any fruit of the trees there attempts to appear so far as the eyes are concerned, it nevertheless turns to ashes when touched” (Tertullian., loc. cit.). So indeed it reads in our manuscripts and in others. Some, however, wrongly read “arise and are seen.” For there is an ellipsis, and one must understand there: “attempts to ripen.” In another book, however, he says: “Impiety deserved rains of fire. Sodom survives to this day, and no Gomorrah; everything is ashes, and the neighboring sea, together with the soil, lives a death” (Idem, lib. de Pall. cap. 2). Josephus, however, relates that the remnants of the divine fire were still visible there, together with the outlines of five towns and ashes reborn from fruits which, although resembling edible fruit, dissolve into smoke and ashes when touched by the hands [Col. 1072C] (Joseph. lib. V de Bello Judaico. cap. 5, pag. 892). Augustine even asserts that this is corroborated by the authority of gentile writers (August. lib. XXI, de Civit. cap. 3, pag. 629). If anyone wishes one of them to be cited, we can readily supply Cornelius Tacitus, whose words are these: “Not far from there”—that is, from the Dead Sea—“are plains said once to have been fertile and inhabited by great cities, but to have been burned by bolts of lightning; traces remain, and the ground, scorched in appearance, has lost its productive power. For everything that springs up of itself or is sown by hand, whether it grows into grass or flower or reaches its customary form, black and empty, vanishes as though into ashes” (Tacit. lib. V *Histor.* paulo post init.). But as a gentile man ignorant of Holy [Col. 1072D] Scripture, he suspects that this failure of the fruits to mature arises from the exhalation of the lake, by which the air spread over the land is first corrupted and then corrupts the land. Solinus erred no less, for he similarly attributes this effect of divine vengeance to the heavenly sun alone, by which he relates that this land was struck:

“At a great distance from Jerusalem a grim gulf opens, which the black earth, reduced to ashes, attests was struck from heaven. Two towns are there, one named Sodom and the other Gomorrah. Although the fruit produced near them has the appearance of ripeness, it cannot be eaten. The mere envelope of its outer skin confines sooty ash within; when pressed even by a light touch, it exhales smoke and collapses into drifting dust” (Solin. *Polyhist.*, cap. 35, pag. 65).

[Col. 1073A] Tertullian afterward says: “Nor were Tuscany and Campania at that time complaining about Christians, when fire from heaven overwhelmed Vulsinii, and fire from its own mountain overwhelmed Pompeii” (Tertullian. *Apologet.*, cap. 40, p. 485). Again, in another book: “From a cloud of this kind Tuscany also burned ancient Vulsinii, while Campania—so that it might place greater hope in its mountains—lost Pompeii” (lib. de Pallio, cap. 2). But these passages are not without their difficulty. For in the book *To the Nations* we read: “Fire from heaven overwhelmed Vulsinii, and fire from its own mountain overwhelmed the Tarpeians” (Idem, lib. I ad Natio. cap. 9. pag. 54). Those who are called Tarpeians there are called Pompeians in the other two books, although Tertullian appears to be speaking about the same peoples. But Pompeii was at no slight distance from the Tarpeians, who inhabited the Tarpeian, one of Rome’s seven hills [Col. 1073B]. Virgil sings of this hill:

Hence he leads him to the Tarpeian seat and the Capitol,

Golden now, but once rough with woodland thickets.

(Virgil., lib. VII *Aeneid.* v. 347.)

And again later:

Manlius, guardian of the Tarpeian citadel, stood

Before the temple at its summit and held the lofty Capitol.

(Ibid. v. 652.)

There is no need to cite Ovid (Ovid. lib. I *Fastor.*, v. 79) and others on so well-known a matter.

Pompeii, however, was a town on the coast of Campania: “Not far,” says Pliny, “with Mount Vesuvius overlooking it and the river Sarnus washing its shores” (Plin. lib. III natur. Hist. cap. 4. pag. 327). Pomponius Mela supports Pliny in these words [Col. 1073C]: “Within sight of Mount Vesuvius are Pompeii, Naples, and Puteoli” (Mel. de Sit. orb. lib. II. cap. 4, § 65). Strabo (Strab. lib. V Geogr., pag. 247) and other geographers relate the same things. Seneca, moreover, described not only the location of this city but also its destruction:

“We have heard that Pompeii, a celebrated city of Campania, at which the Surrentine and Stabian shores meet on one side and the Herculanean shore on the other, while the sea, led in from the open, surrounds it, subsided in an earthquake, and that all the adjoining regions were afflicted. This earthquake occurred, indeed, in the winter, on the Nones of February, in the consulship of Regulus and Virginius” (Senec., lib. VI natural. Quaest. cap. 1. pag. 881).

Finally, Cornelius Tacitus uses fewer words where he writes of the emperor Nero: “A large [Col. 1073D] part of Pompeii, a celebrated town of Campania, collapsed in an earthquake” (Tacit., lib. XV *Annal.* long. post init.). But these accounts do not entirely serve Tertullian’s purpose, for he asserts that the destruction of this city occurred not by an earthquake but by fire, and not during Nero’s reign but before the time of Christ. Therefore, if anyone demonstrates that he was speaking not of the town of Pompeii but of the Tarpeian citadel, destroyed by heavenly fire, we shall not protest greatly. But observe, I ask you, that the city of Pompeii was situated upon another mountain than Vesuvius. Yet if it was at some time burned by flames erupting from that Mount Vesuvius, before the Christian religion was proclaimed, could this not have been noted by our Tertullian as an extraordinary event?

[Col. 1074A] There is less difficulty concerning Vulsinii, or Volsinii, whose people he elsewhere called the Volsinians (Tertullian. *Apologet.* c. 24, p. 421), as we shall say below (Infr. cap. 27. art. 2). For Juvenal sings of them:

Who fears, or ever feared, the fall of chilly Praeneste,

Or of Volsinii, set among wooded ridges?

(Juvenal., satir. 3, v. 181.)

Their town is called Οὐλσίνιον (Volsinium) by Strabo. Pliny records in precisely as many words that it was overwhelmed by fire, as Tertullian says: “Volsinii, the most renowned town of the Etruscans, was burned by lightning” (Plin., lib. II natur. Hist., cap. 52. pag. 207). He is silent there, however, as to when this occurred; but nearly everyone is persuaded that both authors must be understood to refer to the same fire, which occurred before the rise of the Christians.

[Col. 1074B] Tertullian presses the matter still further and, by another example very well known to all, challenges the gentiles as follows: “No one at Rome yet worshiped the true God when Hannibal, at Cannae, measured his slaughter by the bushel through the rings of the Romans” (Tertull. *Apologet.*, c. 40, p. 485). For who does not know of the battle of Cannae, after which the victorious Hannibal, as Livy relates, ordered the gold rings to be poured out in the vestibule of the senate-house? Their heap was so great that some authors say that, when measured, they filled three and a half bushels. The report nearer the truth maintained that there was no more than one bushel (Liv., lib. XXIII, § 12). But even if there had been only one bushel, it undoubtedly suffices for these rings to have been measured by a bushel, as our Author says. Pliny, however, writes that three bushels of rings were sent by Hannibal to Carthage (Plin., lib. XXXIII natur. Hist., cap. [Col. 1074C] 1. pag. 12), and Augustine says the same (August., lib. III de Civit. cap. 19).

But here we cannot remain silent about the fact that, in Rigault’s edition, contrary to the authority of our manuscripts and of the old editors, *per* was omitted from Tertullian’s text and *caede sua* was written. As to his reason, Rigault was entirely silent. For what reason could he have had? Is Tertullian’s style not sufficiently evident there, and is this not his meaning: after his victory Hannibal did not count individually the number of Romans killed in battle, but measured it by a bushel through their rings? Hence Augustine, already commended by us, says:

“He sent three bushels of gold rings to Carthage, so that they might understand that so much Roman rank had fallen in that battle that it was more readily comprehended by measurement than by number; and from this it was thought that the slaughter of the remaining multitude—necessarily more numerous in proportion as it was lower in rank, namely the men who lay without rings—should be estimated rather than counted” [Col. 1074D] (August., loc. cit.).

But do not begrudge the effort of consulting this book of Augustine, where, like our Author, he argues against the gentiles from this and other disasters.

Another Roman disaster was assuredly more ancient, but no less celebrated and well known to all, when, as Tertullian again writes, “the Senones occupied the Capitol” (Tertullian. *Apologet.*, cap. 40), or, as we read in our manuscripts, “had occupied it.” But what, you will say, does he mean when he says, “occupied”? Do not Livy (Liv. lib. V, § 41 et seq.), Augustine (August., lib. II [Col. 1075A] de Civit. cap. 22. pag. 51), and certainly a great many others consistently assert that the Capitol was by no means stormed by the Senones, but only Rome was captured by them? Nothing is more certain. Consequently, the verb “had occupied” is understood there to mean “had kept under siege.” Yet at that time Saturn and the other gods of the gentiles, as Tertullian says, were worshiped by all, both besiegers and besieged. Christians, therefore, who did not then exist, could not have been the authors either of this calamity or of the others that we have related thus far.

## ARTICLE IV

### How clearly Tertullian shows that Christians were not the authors of public calamities, since, when these threatened, they implored the mercy of the true God through the harsh labors of repentance; but that the gentiles were, since, while drunkards and while the baths, taverns, and brothels remained in operation, they sacrificed rain rites to Jupiter, proclaimed barefoot processions to the people, and awaited clouds from paneled ceilings

[Col. 1075B]

When the gentiles asked who, if not the Christians, the most bitter enemies of the gods, could be the cause of public disasters, Tertullian replies that responsibility for them must be cast upon the gentiles themselves alone (Tertul. *Apologet.* c. 40, p. 487). For, he says: “The human race has always deserved ill of God,” the true and only God, for two reasons. First, “as neglectful of him whom, although it understood him in part, it did not seek” (Ibid.); that is, although by the light of nature alone it had at least partially recognized that he truly existed and that there could be no other God, it did not trouble to investigate further who he was, and consequently did not render to him the duties and honors that were his due [Col. 1075C].

Second, that same human race also invented other gods for itself to worship. Therefore, by no longer “seeking the master of innocence” (Ibid.) and the avenger of crimes, but abandoning him, it plunged headlong into idolatry and every kind of wickedness. Thus the gentiles found God—whom they could have had as their gracious protector by acknowledging him and worshiping him as was fitting—angered by their crimes. It was not the Christians, therefore, who always worshiped the true God with due service and pious works, who were the cause of public calamities, but the ungrateful race of the gentiles themselves, which spurned him and most grievously offended him through idolatry and other crimes. Tertullian reinforces this entire argument by what Christians and gentiles respectively did when a disaster had arisen or was imminent [Col. 1075D]. For when, as he says, “the summer and winter seasons suspend their fruitful rains,” as we said a little above (Ibid.), and the rains especially desired; and “the year is a cause for anxiety,” whether sterility is feared for it—or, as he himself says elsewhere, “when the sky is stunned and the year grows dry” (Tertull., *Apolog.* loc. cit. et lib. de Jej., c. 16)—then Christians, by fasts and the other most severe labors of repentance which we discussed above (Supr., cap. 14. art. 1 et 2. cap. 15. art. 1), wrested an answer from God’s infinite mercy by a violence pleasing to him. This indeed brought it about, as he rightly and deservedly observes (Tertullian. *Apologet.* cap. 40), that from the time when Christians tempered the iniquities of the age by holiness of life and these pious works, the troubles by which people had formerly been afflicted and tormented were much [Col. 1076A] lighter.

By contrast, when some particularly frightening calamity was imminent or had arisen, the gentiles provoked the true God by feasting, drunkenness, fornication, adultery, and the impious invocation of false gods. “For then,” Tertullian says in addressing them, “having eaten every day and about to dine immediately, while the baths, taverns, and brothels remain in operation, you sacrifice rain rites to Jupiter” (Ibid.). These are his exact words in our manuscripts, except that they read *cauponiis*, a term used by the historian Justin, though he added *artibus* (Justin. lib. I). We read the same in the old editions of the same *Apologeticum*, except that they have “having worked in taverns”; but other editions read better, “while the taverns remain in operation,” that is, supplying their service [Col. 1076B]. Rigault, however, citing no manuscript and doubtless acting entirely on his own authority, completely deleted the preceding words: “having eaten every day and about to dine immediately.” Is an editor, then, permitted to correct—or rather corrupt—his author’s text without offering any reason? For Tertullian contrasts the Christians with the gentiles and shows the very different ways in which each group sought to avert an impending public calamity. “Then,” he says, the Christians, “begrimed with sackcloth and ashes,” took no food throughout the entire day. The gentiles, by contrast, did not wait for the hour of dinner, but tasted food beforehand, being about to dine more lavishly in the taverns. Afterward they were refreshed by the pleasure of the baths and wallowed in every kind of fornication in the brothels.

They also provoked the true God by another crime of idolatry [Col. 1076C]. For, having rejected him, they “sacrificed rain rites to Jupiter.” According to Festus, an *aquilicium*, or *aquaelicium*, is so called when rainwater is drawn forth by certain rites, as once occurred—if the account is believed—when the *manalis* stone was led into the City (Fest. cap. 20. de verbor. Signif. ad v. Aqualicium). If you ask what that *manalis* stone was, the same Festus will answer you: “They called *manalis* a certain rock that stood outside the Capene Gate beside the temple of Mars. When, because of excessive drought, they dragged it into the City, rain immediately followed; and because it made waters flow, they called it the *manalis* stone” (Idem. ad. v. Manualis). Thus, during a drought, when they dragged this stone from the temple of Mars, they performed rites for Jupiter—doubtless Jupiter Pluvius, or Pluvialis, who is called ὑέτιος (“Rain-bringing”) by Pausanias (Pausan. lib. II. pag. 61. lin. 44), and ὄμβριος Ζεύς (“Rainy Zeus”) [Col. 1076D] by others. Hence Tibullus sang the following of Egypt:

Because of you, your land asks for no rains,

Nor does its parched grass supplicate Jupiter Pluvius.

(Tibull. lib. I, eleg. 7. v. 25 et 26.)

In addition to this, the gentiles proclaimed barefoot processions to the people during that time of drought. For they had a custom of approaching the temples barefoot on certain festive or solemn days. Ovid celebrates the Vestalia in these verses:

By chance I was returning during the festival of Vesta, by the way

Where the New Way is now joined to the Roman Forum.

I saw a matron descend this way with bare foot.

I was silently astonished and halted my step.

(Ovid., lib. VI *Fastor.* § 9.)

After the body of the deceased emperor Augustus was burned [Col. 1077A] in solemn procession, “the leading men of the equestrian order,” as Suetonius relates, “wearing tunics, ungirded, and barefoot, gathered the remains and deposited them in the mausoleum” (Sueton. lib. II, in Vit. August. § 100). Some have further thought that Juvenal had this rite in view where he sang the following about the Galli, priests of the Mother of the Gods:

. . . Then, naked and trembling, she will burst forth

Across the proud king’s entire field upon bloodied

Knees. . . .

(Juvenal. satir. 6, v. 466.)

Seneca likewise committed this to writing: “When someone shaking a sistrum lies at another’s command, when someone skilled in cutting his own arms makes his forearms and shoulders bleed with poised hand, when some woman crawls along the road on her knees and howls” (Senec., lib. de Vit. beat., cap. 27, [Col. 1077B] pag. 640). But here, like Juvenal, he discusses those who proceeded on their knees rather than those who went barefoot into the temple to pray to their gods. The cited words of Ovid therefore apply more closely to Tertullian’s purpose.

Thus proceeding barefoot, the gentiles “came to the Capitol,” Tertullian says—that is, to the temple of Capitoline Jupiter—and there “sought a rain-bearing sky,” and awaited “from the paneled ceilings” a cloud heavy with fruitful rains: that is, from the paneled ceiling of the very temple in which they wrongly believed their supreme Jupiter dwelt.

Although our Author said there that, during this very time of calamity, no crime of intemperance or lust was omitted by them, he nevertheless testifies [Col. 1077C] in another book that some displayed a certain appearance of repentance, not only going barefoot but also laying aside the insignia of their offices. For in another book he says: “When the sky is stunned and the year grows dry, barefoot processions are proclaimed, the magistrates lay aside their purple, turn the fasces backward, prescribe a prayer, and repeat the sacrifice” (Tertull. lib. de Jejun. cap. 16).

But through these works of idolatry they could plainly obtain nothing either from their gods, who did not exist, or from the true and omnipotent God, who alone is the giver of every good. Who, then, does not now understand how true and certain is the conclusion of our Tertullian when addressing the same gentiles: “You, therefore, are the burdensome ones in human affairs; you are guilty of public misfortunes; you are always the enticers of evils, among whom God is despised [Col. 1077D] and statues are worshiped” (Idem. *Apologet.* cap. 41. pag. 488). Some editions read: “always the summoners.” For in the height of impiety you worship false gods and statues and reject the true God, who deservedly chastises impious and criminal people with public calamities. The gentiles themselves, therefore, truly were the authors of public calamities, and certainly not the Christians, who, worshiping the true God, could assuredly obtain from him what they requested.

## ARTICLE V

### An examination of the reasons given by Tertullian why God permits Christians to be afflicted by public calamities, and why those reasons cannot apply to the gentiles

Overwhelmed by the most grievous weight of so many and such powerful arguments [Col. 1078A], the gentiles, with astonishing obstinacy, were never willing to yield, but endeavored in every possible way to turn against the Christians the weapons that the Christians had hurled at them. If Christians, they said, are not truly the authors of public disasters, why does their God, if he is omnipotent and just, so calmly permit them to be tormented, harmed, and oppressed by the same calamities as other guilty and criminal people?

Tertullian replies that this weapon was being hurled back by the utterly leaden and blunt hand of purblind men who were entirely ignorant of the eternal dispositions of the supreme God (Tertull. *Apologet.* cap. 41). For at the supreme judgment after the end of the world, God will distinguish the good from the wicked and will treat them according to their deserts, with either everlasting punishments or rewards. In the meantime, however, he willed the advantages and disadvantages of this life to be common to all [Col. 1078B], “so that,” Tertullian says, “all might experience, through an equal participation,” either his gentleness or his severity, and might love the former and fear the latter (Ibid.). Public calamities, therefore, served as a reminder of duty to Christians, but as punishment for crimes to the gentiles. Nor could the latter insist that this was wrongly invented by the Christians themselves. “For these things,” he continues, “we have learned from God himself” (Ibid.); that is, from the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments (Matth. cap. V. v. 45, et cap. XIII. v. 49, et cap. XXV. v. 32 et seqq.), whose supreme authority he had demonstrated, as we saw above (Supr. cap. 8. art. 1 et 5).

Second, he replies that Christians were not afflicted by any adversities in this world, but rather rejoiced in them (Tertull. loc. cit.), since they had nothing more pleasing or dearer than to depart from this world so that they might more quickly attain [Col. 1078C] that eternal happiness which they knew with absolute certainty had been promised to them, and to no others, by the most certain divine oracles. The gentiles, however, could never similarly weaken the force of this argument, which applied to them alone. For if their gods oppressed the world with public calamities because of the Christians, their enemies, those gods allowed their own worshipers to be involved in the same disasters only at the cost of ingratitude. “They ought,” as Tertullian rightly says, “to have separated them from what the Christians deserved” (Tertull. ibid.). After presenting the reasons that we have expounded in favor of those same Christians, he addresses the gentiles in these words:

“But if all your evils come upon you from those whom you worship, on our account, why do you persist in worshiping beings so ungrateful and unjust, who ought rather to have assisted and defended you, to the distress of the Christians”—our manuscripts read “in the distress”—“whom they ought to separate from what the Christians deserved?” [Col. 1078D] (Ibid.).

You see that these latter words are repeated twice. Rigault therefore removed them entirely from his edition as having been added out of place, contrary to the authority of all the manuscripts, whether printed or handwritten. But what, I ask you, prevented Tertullian, while arguing against the gentiles, from repeating, after the reasons adduced to prove it, the same words with which he had stated his thesis?

But these matters, someone will say, are not so important as knowing how he could infer that, if the gods of the gentiles possessed any sense of gratitude and justice, they ought to have separated the gentiles [Col. 1079A] from the Christians in public calamities. But he correctly infers this because the gentiles had no certain reason whatever to hope that, after departing from this life, they would receive from their gods—who did not exist—an eternal reward for their virtues. Christians, however, as we have said, most certainly expected that reward from their omnipotent God. The gentiles therefore ought not to have worshiped these gods if they were persuaded that they were being afflicted by them with public calamities because of the Christians. For if those gods could confer nothing after death upon their own worshipers, who in this life had suffered public calamities because of others, they were utterly ungrateful and unjust—or certainly powerless, and consequently altogether devoid of divinity. Tertullian therefore rightly concludes that the worshipers of these gods, and certainly not the Christians, were the authors of public calamities [Col. 1079B]. Elsewhere we have clearly shown (Dissert. in Arnob. cap. 6. art. 4 et seqq.) how this accusation, repeated by the gentiles as often as it was foolishly, was refuted by Arnobius, and how Minucius Felix and Lactantius demonstrate that the arguments of those who attempted thereby to undermine divine providence were utterly feeble and futile (Dissert. in Minut. cap. 6. art. 3, et in Lactan. cap. 14. art. 3). But let us now proceed to the final argument of those same gentiles against the truth of the Christian religion.

# CHAPTER XXIV

## How absurdly the gentiles complained that Christians were useless to the commonwealth and therefore ought to be exterminated

### ARTICLE I

#### How Tertullian proved that Christians were not Brahmans, nor Indian gymnosophists, nor forest-dwellers, but were exceedingly useful to the commonwealth

[Col. 1079C]

The pagans, leaving no stone unturned against the Christians, further objected that they were wholly useless to the commonwealth and, for that reason alone, ought to be utterly exterminated. But they, says Tertullian, are neither Brahmans nor Indian Gymnosophists, forest-dwellers and exiles from ordinary life (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42). But who, someone may perhaps ask, were those Brahmans and Gymnosophists? Were they the same people, or peoples distinct from one another? For Apollonius of Tyana and Damis, cited by Philostratus (Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, bk. III, ch. 4, p. 119, and bk. VI, ch. 4, p. 265), assert that [Col. 1079D] the Brahmans were inhabitants of India and that, as he says elsewhere, the γυμνούς (“naked men”), or Gymnosophists, inhabited a hill not far from the banks of the Nile. Jerome, however, speaks in one place of the Brahmans of India and the Gymnosophists of Egypt (Jerome, Epistle 57, to Laeta, and bk. I *Against Jovinian*); elsewhere, both he and other authors whom we cited in another dissertation call them the Gymnosophists of India (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 19, art. 1, p. 1160 ff.). In the same place, moreover, we noted that there were at least two kinds of them. If anyone should further prove that they established dwellings not only in India but also in Egypt, he will easily reconcile Tertullian with the other authors praised by Philostratus. In any event, they, like the [Col. 1080A] Brahmans, lived apart from other human beings and pursued an extremely harsh manner of life and abstinence from food, which we explained in the passage already cited.

But the Christians’ abstinence was very different, as our Tertullian rightly asserts: they received with thanksgiving the foods given them by God, though always observing the laws of temperance. “For,” he says, “we do not reject any fruit of God’s works; we certainly exercise restraint, lest we use them beyond measure or wrongly” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42). Nor were these same Christians inhabitants of forests or, like the Brahmans and Gymnosophists, “exiles from ordinary life” (*ibid.*), wholly separated from association with other human beings. For they lived intermingled with the pagans in towns and cities, as we have already said, and everywhere joined them in common [Col. 1080B] activities—in the forum, the market, fairs, fields, baths, and shops (*ibid.*)—not wine shops, to be sure, but buildings which, as Festus says (Festus, s.v. *Tabernacula*), were constructed from planks and, according to Nonius, served popular use (Nonius, s.v. *Taber.*). They also practiced their crafts in workshops open to anyone and stayed in *stabula* (Tertullian, *ibid.*), either inns and lodgings where guests and travelers were received, or rather dwellings and the private homes of certain people, such as farmers, of which Virgil sings:

> He seeks the lofty roof of the dwelling, and from its highest ridge  
> Sounds the shepherd’s signal.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VII, v. 512.)

And thus the Christians, says our Author, “shared the habitation of this age” [Col. 1080C] or, as our manuscripts read, “lived together in this age.”

For this reason he presses the pagans themselves as follows: “We too sail with you, and with you” (this latter phrase is absent from our manuscripts) “we serve as soldiers, farm, and trade; accordingly, we mingle our crafts and make our services available for your use” (the manuscripts and editions before Rigaltius read “our work”), and thus by reciprocal labors we assist one another. And all these things brought the greater benefit to the entire commonwealth in proportion as the number of those same Christians was then greater, as we saw above. Nothing, therefore, could have been devised more remote from the truth than the claim that Christians were useless to public affairs.

## ARTICLE II. That no harm was inflicted upon the commonwealth by Christians who did not attend the pagans’ ceremonies, did not bathe at dawn during the Saturnalia but at the proper hour, and did not recline at public banquets during the Liberalia, as was customary for beast-fighters eating their last supper

[Col. 1080D]

However clearly and certainly Tertullian demonstrated that Christians were of the greatest benefit to public affairs, the pagans nevertheless did not hesitate to protest that they were unproductive for the commonwealth because, scorning all their ceremonies and the more sacred rites of their religion, they absolutely refused to take part in them. But although Tertullian concedes this, he utterly denies that Christians were therefore of no use or advantage to the commonwealth. [Col. 1081A] He therefore addresses any pagan as follows: “If I do not attend your ceremonies, I am nevertheless a human being on that day too” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42)—one who, as was just said, by living together with the pagans and combining my crafts with theirs, supplies you and others with the many things necessary for your life and for human society, so that everyone derives the greatest benefit from my labors.

No one can fail to admit that this wedge utterly demolishes the wholly foolish accusation of the pagans. Nevertheless, Tertullian goes beyond what is sufficient and makes it evident to everyone through several examples that, even if Christians did not attend the pagans’ mysteries, either no harm was thereby brought upon public affairs or, if any was brought, it was abundantly made good by them from another source. [Col. 1081B]

But let us, if you please, hear him begin with the pagans’ Saturnalian festivities: “I do not bathe,” he says, “at dawn during the Saturnalia, lest I lose both night and day” (*ibid.*). And this is indeed how these words appear in our manuscripts and older printed copies. Rigaltius, however, rejected the adverb “at dawn” and ordered the text to read, “I bathe toward night”; but he offers us sheer nonsense, contrary to the genuine text (the same author, *On Idolatry*, ch. 10) and thought of our Author. To make this more readily recognizable, everyone should observe that the festival of the Saturnalia, as Tertullian himself elsewhere, Varro (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. V, p. 51), and Festus (Festus, s.v. *Saturnia*) attest, was instituted in honor of Saturn, whom they regarded as guardian of the fields. [Col. 1081C] Livy discloses its origin and the appointed day of its celebration in these words: “By then it was the month of December; a sacrifice was offered at the temple of Saturn in Rome, a lectisternium was commanded, the senators spread the couch, and a public banquet was held; throughout the City the cry ‘Saturnalia!’ was raised by day and night, and the people were ordered to keep and observe that day as a festival forever” (Livy, bk. II, § 1). Macrobius (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, chs. 8 and 10), and later Lipsius (Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 3, vol. III), debated whether these rites were held for only one day or for seven consecutive days, as they consider more probable. At that time, according to Lucian (Lucian, *Dialogue on the Saturnalia*, p. 1021), it was forbidden to conduct any serious private or public business; instead, people drank, became drunk, shouted, played, contended at dice, sang naked, [Col. 1081D] danced with lascivious movements of the body, sometimes plunged into water with faces smeared with soot, and admitted their servants to the banquet, just as Accius sang in these verses transcribed by Macrobius:

> The greater part of Greece, and Athens most of all,  
> Perform rites to Saturn, which they call the Cronia;  
> And when they celebrate the day, throughout the fields and nearly all the cities  
> They feast in gladness and each attends to his own servants.  
> The same custom has likewise been handed down from there to us:  
> That servants then feast there together with their masters.  
> (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 7.)

It is therefore no wonder that Christians condemned these abominable acts of idolatry, wantonness, drunkenness, and the other detestable practices which we have enumerated from the writers cited above, and refused to lose night and day [Col. 1082A] celebrating such impious festivals. “For this reason,” says Tertullian, “I do not bathe at dawn during the Saturnalia” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42, p. 482), in order to prepare myself to perform those rites. For who does not know that it was the custom of the pagans to bathe before a banquet? Christians, however, did not believe it permissible to prepare themselves at dawn, when winter was raging, in an untimely bath for the celebration of those abominable banquets and mysteries.

Yet they thereby brought no harm upon public affairs. “For I bathe,” says our Author, “at an honorable and healthy hour.” Rigaltius preferred “the proper” to “an honorable hour,” but against the protest of all the manuscripts. Could not our Author have said that Christians did not reject baths, but went to bathe at an honorable and healthy hour—namely, the hour at which everyone customarily bathed consistently with [Col. 1082B] decency and health? In winter, according to Pliny, this was the ninth hour, and in summer the eighth (Pliny, bk. III, Epistle 1, p. 90), or, as others observe, from noon until evening. Horace sang:

> But when the fiercer sun warned me, weary as I was, to go and bathe,  
> I flee the hours of the raging constellation.  
> (Horace, bk. I, Satire 6, v. 125.)

Does Tertullian not therefore appear to designate the midday hour, which in December, when the Saturnalia were held, was honorable and healthy, “so that,” he says, “it may preserve my warmth and blood”? “I do not bathe,” he continues, “at dawn on these cold days of the impious Saturnalia, since after the bath I can stiffen and grow pale when I am dead.” By these words he undoubtedly alludes [Col. 1082C] to another ancient custom, that of washing dead human bodies, and perhaps to these verses of Virgil concerning the funeral of Misenus:

> Some prepare hot water and cauldrons seething over the flames,  
> And wash and anoint the cold body.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VI, v. 217 ff.)

Servius, in his comments on these verses, cites the following line composed by Ennius:

> A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquinius.  
> (Servius, p. 411.)

Tertullian therefore says that he can indeed stiffen and grow pale in that bath after death, but that while alive he does not wish to anticipate it with the untimely winter bath with which the Saturnalia began. Although this reasoning is merely natural, it stung the pagans all the more sharply [Col. 1082D] because of the absurdity of their objection that Christians were useless to the commonwealth because they rightly fled from and execrated this bath and the impious ceremonies that followed it.

He next passes to the Liberalia, that is, the days and games dedicated to Liber or Bacchus, as follows: “During the Liberalia I do not recline at table in public” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42, p. 492). If you ask him the reason, you will find it given in another book in these words: “Since the games were indiscriminately called Liberalia, they manifestly proclaimed the honor of Father Liber. For they were first held for Liber by country people because of the benefit which they attribute to him, the gift of wine having been revealed” (the same author, *On the Shows*, ch. 5). We have indeed discussed this matter more than once. Since, therefore, these festivals [Col. 1083A] were celebrated in honor of a false god, not without idolatry and other crimes—especially gluttony and drunkenness—they were an object of the greatest horror to Christians. Our Author added: “During the Liberalia I do not recline at table in public, as is customary for beast-fighters eating their last supper” (the same author, *Apology*, loc. cit.). This is how we read it in the Puteanus manuscript and the first Colbert manuscript, but the Harleian and second Colbert manuscript have “the last” in a different grammatical form. Junius suspects that the text should read “toward the first hour,” because, he says, the beast-fighters, whom we discussed above, fought at midday. Bulenger, however, dismisses this conjecture not without laughter (Bulenger, *On Hunting in the Circus*, ch. 34), because beast-fighters fought not only at midday but also in the morning. For what could be clearer than these words of Suetonius concerning the emperor Claudius? [Col. 1083B] “He took such delight in beast-fighters and the midday spectacles that he would go down to the show even at first light and, when the people had been dismissed at noon, remain seated” (Suetonius, bk. V, *Life of Claudius*, § 34). Seneca likewise says: “In the morning men are exposed to lions and bears; at noon, to their own spectators” (Seneca, Epistle 70, p. 295). Do you wish to hear other, no less transparent words of his? Here they are: “By chance I came upon the midday spectacle, expecting some entertainment.... In the morning men are exposed to lions and bears; at noon, to their own spectators. They are ordered to be exposed to those who will kill them after they themselves have killed, and they reserve the victor for another death” (*On Anger*, bk. III, ch. 43, p. 583). Again, elsewhere: “Recently, in the school of the beast-fighters, one of the Germans, while being prepared for the morning spectacle, withdrew” (the same author, Epistle 7, pp. 172–73). Finally, he repeatedly calls them the “morning spectacles” of the arena (*On Anger*, [Col. 1083C] ch. 43, p. 583). It would not be difficult to gather many other passages here; but since these suffice, we shall add nothing except this poem of Martial:

> Recently seen in the morning arena,  
> Mucius.  
> (Martial, bk. X, Epigram 25.)

Nothing, therefore, should be changed in Tertullian’s text. He aptly calls the beast-fighters’ meal their “last,” or final, supper, because, since they were to fight the next day with other gladiators or wild beasts, they ought to have expected death rather than victory. For, as the Seneca already cited warns, “the outcome for those who fight is death” (Seneca, Epistle 7, p. 173). Even if some escaped unharmed, they nevertheless did not dare hope for this and believed that on the preceding day they were eating their last supper. From the author of the [Col. 1083D] *Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*, moreover, we learn that this meal was called the “free supper,” doubtless because it was extremely lavish and the gladiators gorged themselves on foods set before them at will.

Christians therefore rightly rejected those public banquets, since they were given in honor of Bacchus and with intemperance. Yet no harm thereby came to public affairs. “Wherever I dine,” Tertullian thus addresses any pagan, “I dine from your provisions”—that is, from food which I have been accustomed to purchase from your fellow pagans in any public place not consecrated to false gods.

## ARTICLE III. How foolishly the pagans objected that Christians were unproductive for the commonwealth because they did not buy garlands, attend spectacles, or purchase incense, although they consumed more and costlier goods purchased from the Sabaeans in burying the dead than the pagans did in offering fumes to their gods

[Col. 1084A]

The use of garlands was undoubtedly frequent in Tertullian’s time, since the pagans had a particular complaint about its rejection by Christians, as though this inflicted great harm upon the commonwealth. But he answers any pagan as follows: “I do not buy a garland for my head—but what concern is that of yours?” For what harm thereby comes upon public affairs? Plainly none. “I use purchased flowers,” he says, “but I think them more pleasing when free, loose, and wandering in every direction” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42, p. 493), rather than bound into a garland. For the fragrance of flowers is perceived not by the hair [Col. 1084B] but only by the nostrils. We have treated these matters more fully in another dissertation, where we further showed that Christians rejected the use of garlands of this kind because it derived its origin from idolatry (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 13, art. 3).

The pagans insisted that Christians inflicted great harm upon the commonwealth by not attending public spectacles (Tertullian, loc. cit.). It was, to be sure, a great evil to flee things which Tertullian proves in another book to have arisen “from the general guilt of idolatry, their mother” (the same author, *On the Shows*, ch. 7). In other dissertations, moreover, we noted that these spectacles were polluted not only by idolatry but also by many other crimes, from which Christians rightly fled no differently than from a public plague. [Col. 1084C] What loss to the public good, therefore, resulted from this? A great one indeed, said the pagans. For those spectacles continued for a long time; spectators therefore bought at the entrance of the amphitheater many kinds of food with which they could refresh themselves from time to time. Christians, accordingly, incurred none of these expenses.

“But if we buy nothing there,” says Tertullian, “whatever is sold at those gatherings, should I desire it, I shall more gladly obtain from its proper places” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42, p. 493). Certain old editions read, “I obtain”; some more recent ones, “they will be obtained.” The reading “I shall obtain,” found in our manuscripts and the other editions, is better. Nothing was therefore lost to the public good if [Col. 1084D] Christians purchased in other places lawful for them the things sold at the pagans’ unlawful gatherings.

Nor, whatever those same men might still allege, does the commonwealth suffer loss “if,” says Tertullian, “we do not buy incense” (*ibid.*), which the pagans burned to false gods. For this was wholly forbidden to us, and the price of incense was too small for the pagans ever to have had reason to complain of such a loss. “For the Arabians,” he continues, “have better grounds for complaint.” But if the Arabs have any complaint about the failure to sell their more costly incense, the “Sabaeans,” he says, “will know,” or will answer on our behalf, “that their merchandise, of greater quantity and value, is expended in burying Christians than in fumigating the gods” (*ibid.*). Concerning Sabaean incense Virgil writes:

[Col. 1085A]

> India sends ivory, the soft Sabaeans their incense.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. I, v. 57.)

And in another book, concerning Venus:

> ...where she has a temple, and a hundred altars glow  
> With Sabaean incense.  
> (The same author, *Aeneid*, bk. I, v. 420.)

Servius notes the following on these verses: “The Sabaeans are peoples near Syria and Arabia, called Sabaeans ἀπὸ τοῦ σέβεσθαι (“from worshiping”) politically, because incense, with which we placate the gods, grows among them.”

Tertullian, moreover, spoke not only of this Sabaean incense, concerning which Pliny records a great deal (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. VI, ch. 28, p. 726), but also of their other wares, or spices, as will become evident from what follows. Indeed, there was such an abundance of these in their region [Col. 1085B] that, as Strabo relates (Strabo, *Geography*, bk. XVI, p. 776), they used cinnamon, cassia, and other sweet-smelling substances of this kind as brushwood and material for making fire. We likewise read in Pliny: “The Sabaeans cook their food with incense wood” (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. XII, ch. 17, p. 32). But our Tertullian, not only in his *Apology* but also in another book, openly declares that Sabaean incense was used by Christians chiefly in burying the bodies of the dead: “Bodies,” he says, “treated with preserving spices, are set apart for burial, mausoleums, and monuments, from which they will come forth into a second life when the Lord commands” (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 27). Elsewhere, and more closely to our present purpose, he says: “Let the pagans see whether the same wares—I mean incense [Col. 1085C] and the other imported goods used for sacrifice to idols—also serve human beings as medicinal ointments, and serve us besides for the consolations of burial” (the same author, *On Idolatry*, ch. 11).

Let it be so, someone will argue, and let it be held demonstrated more clearly than the noonday sun that Christians used Sabaean incense, the most precious of all, in burying the bodies of the dead. Could Tertullian nevertheless assert without great hyperbole that the Sabaeans sold a greater quantity and value of their incense for Christian burials than to the nations for fumigating their gods? Did not a great many pagans, he will say, burn Sabaean incense to their gods with a full and lavish hand? But whoever makes this objection ought to observe that these people were richer than others and far fewer in number than the poorer majority, [Col. 1085D] who offered incense with only three fingers or incense worth a single *as*, as will be said below (below, ch. 29, art. 2). In addition, we have observed that the multitude of Christians was greater than that of the pagans. If Christians therefore embalmed the bodies of their dead with Sabaean incense, the Sabaeans must have sold them more incense for this pious office than they sold to the pagans, the greater part of whom customarily gave their gods only a very few grains of cheaper, ordinary incense.

## ARTICLE IV. How undeservedly the pagans complained that the revenues of their temples had been dwindling since the Christians arose, although Christians did not have enough to supply both their gods and their human beggars, and paid their taxes with as much care as the same pagans used deceit in evading them; that no one could complain of the unproductiveness of Christians except infamous pimps, procurers, bathhouse-panders, assassins, poisoners, magicians, haruspices, soothsayers, and astrologers; and that, if Christians had perhaps inflicted any harm upon the commonwealth, they made it good elsewhere with interest

[Col. 1086A]

Although what we have thus far related is clear and evident to everyone, it could not restrain the blind assaults of the pagans or extinguish their unbridled fury against the Christians. For they still shouted everywhere with a great clamor that the Christians had arisen for the destruction of the commonwealth. Ever since their religion was disseminated throughout the world, they said: “The revenues [Col. 1086B] of our temples are daily becoming insolvent” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42, p. 493), that is, are gradually diminishing. For every Christian, as Tertullian himself admits, was forbidden to “undertake the management of temples or administer their revenues” (the same author, *On Idolatry*, ch. 17). Since the number of Christians was greater than that of pagans, as we have frequently said, far fewer people were consequently paying the revenues of the temples.

But even if matters were so, the pagans ought to have remonstrated not only with the Christians but also with their own adherents. For Tertullian asks them: “How few now cast a contribution?” (the same author, *Apology*, loc. cit.). A *stips*, moreover, was a stamped coin. “For,” says Varro, “when they give *asses* to gods with treasuries, they call it a *stips*” [Col. 1086C] (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, near the end). Hence Ovid sang:

> The people contributed bronze; from it Metellus built  
> The shrines, he says: hence the custom of giving contributions remains.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. IV, § 3.)

If the pagans, therefore, did not give contributions to the temples, they certainly harmed them no less than the Christians did.

The pagans persisted, and, as Arnobius says, diviners, soothsayers, prophets, and others [Col. 1086D] bitterly lamented the emptiness of their temples (Arnobius, *Against the Pagans*, bk. II), and that even paltry contributions could not be extorted from their very few clients. We know that Pliny the Younger wrote in his letter to the emperor Trajan that temples and solemn rites had begun to be frequented again in his time. For these are his exact words: “It is certainly sufficiently established that the temples, which had by now been almost deserted, have begun to be frequented, that the solemn rites long discontinued are being resumed, and that victims are everywhere on sale, though until now a buyer was very rarely found” (Pliny, bk. X, Epistle 101, p. 376). His admission that the temples and sacred rites of the pagans had been almost deserted is entirely true. But in adding that they had begun to be frequented again, he ineptly flattered Trajan, whose clemency he wished to extol by fair means or foul. For as the number of Christians increased, pagan temples were less frequented and fewer revenues were paid.

Tertullian therefore freely admits this and answers the pagans [Col. 1087A] that, however great that loss might be, it was abundantly repaid by Christians. “For we do not have enough,” he says, “to bring aid both to human beings and to your beggar gods” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42, p. 494)—that is, all our goods and all our resources do not suffice to bring aid to your beggars, both gods and human beings, whom we have discussed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 784). Although, therefore, we cast no contribution into the treasury of your temples, into which it is sacrilege for us to enter together with you, elsewhere we much more frequently and abundantly bestow it upon anyone who asks (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 20, art. 30). “For,” he says, “our compassion spends more street by street”—that is, gives more to all who beg throughout the streets and roads of the cities—[Col. 1087B] “than your religion does temple by temple” (Tertullian, loc. cit.), that is, than it gives in each of your temples.

Moreover, Christians paid the taxes imposed by the emperors with much greater care and better faith than the pagans. “Indeed,” he says, “the taxes will thank the Christians, who faithfully pay what is due, because we refrain from defrauding another of his property” (*ibid.*). For they knew Christ’s command: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matt. 22:21). Hence Justin Martyr openly said to the pagans: “Φόρους καὶ εἰσφορὰς τοῖς ἐφ` ὑμῶν τεταγμένοις πανταχοῦ πρὸ πάντων πειρώμεθα φέρειν. Indeed, we strive everywhere, above all others, to pay taxes and assessments to the collectors appointed by you” (Justin, *Apology to Antoninus*). The pagans, however, defrauded those taxes to such a degree that, “if an account is taken,” [Col. 1087C] in Tertullian’s words, “of how much is lost to the taxes through the fraud and falsehood of your declarations, it may readily be reckoned that the complaint concerning one category is compensated by the advantage furnished under the other accounts” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 42, p. 495). Here the term “declaration” certainly means the public disclosure or statement of all the property which each person possessed. But this does not remove the entire difficulty of this rather obscure phrase, which more acute interpreters explain in two ways. Some think Tertullian’s meaning to be this: if one considers how much harm the pagans bring upon the commonwealth through “the fraud and falsehood of their declarations” (*ibid.*), or through a false declaration of their property, it will at once be recognized from this category or this single example that such harm is greater than whatever benefit [Col. 1087D] they confer by other means. Others explain Tertullian’s meaning thus: Christians pay taxes with as much care and good faith as the pagans employ fraud and falsehood in evading them; and this single example fully establishes that the pagans’ complaint about the uselessness of Christians is most unjust, because Christians paid taxes more accurately than all others, and, if they brought any harm from another quarter, it was abundantly compensated by the advantage of the other considerations that have been indicated. Now, if Tertullian is not there comparing the pagans with the Christians, the first interpretation seems preferable, for from it one gathers that they complained entirely undeservedly of the harm these brought upon the commonwealth, since they conferred another and greater benefit. But if he there compared Christians and pagans [Col. 1088A] with one another, you may, so far as we are concerned, prefer the second exposition.

Furthermore, to press the pagans more closely, our Author (the same author, *ibid.*) freely concedes to them that certain persons could be found among them who complained of what he calls the Christians’ “unproductiveness.” But who, good God, were these men? Certainly none other than abandoned men, infamous for their vices and crimes, whom it is of the highest benefit to the commonwealth neither to please nor favor. He divides them into three classes. The first consisted of the most disgraceful ministers of abominable lust, whom he calls pimps, procurers, and bathhouse-panders. Cicero mentions the first two when inveighing against Verres: “Let there be silence concerning his nocturnal bacchanals and vigils; let no mention [Col. 1088B] be made of pimps, gamblers, and procurers” (Cicero, *Against Verres*, bk. II, p. 68, line 3). The distinction between pimps and procurers was that the former brought women who did not resist to fornication, while the latter brought unwilling women. Hence Horace sang:

> “Once she has praised you,” says the fornicator, “beware lest she ask more;  
> Hand easy Penelope over to the better man. Do you think  
> One so virtuous and modest can be procured?”  
> (Horace, bk. II, Satire 5, v. 75 ff.)

The *aquarioli* were of the same sort; according to Festus, this was the name given to “the sordid attendants of shameless women” (Festus, bk. XX, *On the Meaning of Words*, s.v. *Aquarioli*). Hence Apuleius mentions “the embittered *aquariolus* of his shameless and meretricious wife” (Apuleius, *Apology*, before the middle, p. 366). Men of this most filthy kind [Col. 1088C] carried water to women for washing away filth. But consider, please, whether the emperor Commodus should be enrolled in this most impure herd of men; Lampridius has recorded the following about him: “He lived together with gladiators and carried water as a pimp’s servant” (Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*). Some, however, hold that the term *aquariolus* means a bath attendant who guarded the clothes of bathers and acted as a pander. Hence Martial sang:

> When the bath attendant, once the lamp is extinguished, admits you  
> Among the tomb-haunting adulteresses.  
> (Martial, bk. III, Epigram 62.)

But the complaint of such men about the unproductiveness and uselessness of Christians was certainly a commendation and proclamation of both the Christians’ virtue and their usefulness.

[Col. 1088D] Nor can any different judgment be passed upon the assassins, poisoners, and magicians who make up Tertullian’s second class (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 43). For these lay snares for the lives of others and very frequently took them away. Assassins were so called from the *sica*, or shorter sword, which they carried to kill people by ambush. How frequently others were secretly and treacherously killed by these savage men you may learn from these few words of Cicero: “These are everyday things: daggers and poisons” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. III, p. 251, line 15). But to come nearer Tertullian’s times, Cyprian says: “Hence poisoners, hence assassins, as swift to sin as they are free from punishment after sinning” (Cyprian, book *To Demetrianus*).

[Col. 1089A] It is now evident why those who administer poison to others, prepare it, or sell it are next called poisoners by our Author. Magicians, who are assigned the third place in this class, were undoubtedly not unlike them. For by diabolical arts, maleficent practices, and deceptions they sought to harm others and kill them. These are the persons whom Horace marks in the following verses:

> What witch, what great god, with Thessalian poisons,  
> Will be able to release you?  
> (Horace, bk. I, Ode 27, vv. 21–22.)

Finally, Tertullian places in the third class haruspices, soothsayers, and astrologers (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 43), whom Arnobius, cited by us shortly above, calls empty diviners. For by their detestable arts, frauds, and deceptions they advertised that they could [Col. 1089B] foretell the future. The soothsayers, or *farioli*, whom we discussed above, pretended to prophesy by divine inspiration, and the haruspices by inspecting sacrificial victims. Terence, however, stings both with the barbs of these verses:

> A hen crowed; the soothsayer forbade it.  
> The haruspex prohibited beginning any new  
> Business before midwinter.  
> (Terence, *Phormio*, act IV, scene 4.)

Cicero certainly spared neither these nor the others when he wrote: “Μαντικὴ your art, which in Latin is called divination, by which we would be steeped in such great superstition if we wished to listen to you: haruspices, augurs, soothsayers, prophets, and diviners would have to be cultivated by us” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. I, p. 203, line 36). But these matters have been discussed elsewhere and will again be discussed later.

[Col. 1089C] That criminal band, hostile and wholly destructive to the commonwealth, is completed by the astrologers. “The common people,” says Aulus Gellius, “call ‘astrologers’ those who should be called ‘Chaldaeans’ by their national designation” (Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. I, ch. 9). Earlier, Cicero had explained their art and profession in these words: “Named not from their art but from the name of their people, they are thought, through long observation of the stars, to have created a body of knowledge by which it could be predicted what would happen to each person and under what destiny each was born” (Cicero, *On Divination*, bk. I, beginning, p. 255, line 4). Hence Juvenal:

> Your nativity is known to the astrologers.  
> (Juvenal, Satire 14, after the middle.)

But this same Cicero [Col. 1089D] calls them and their science “monstrosities of the Chaldaeans,” and warns us that Eudoxus, their leader, recorded in writing that “the Chaldaeans are by no means to be believed in their prediction and description of each person’s life from the day of birth” (Cicero, *On Divination*, bk. II, p. 291, line 49). To omit much else, our Tertullian asserts without hesitation in another book that evil angels, or demons, were the teachers of this impious art, and then adds: “Let the astrologers be expelled, like their angels: disciples and teachers suffer the same penalty of exile” (Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, ch. 9). Suetonius relates that these astrologers were driven from the City and Italy by the emperor Vitellius and were afterward condemned to death (Suetonius, bk. VII, § 14). But earlier, according to Tacitus, [Col. 1090A] decrees of the senate had been issued concerning this exile of the astrologers (Tacitus, *Annals*, bk. II, before the middle). Finally, Ulpian records many things concerning them and may be consulted (Ulpian, *On the Office of the Praetor*, bk. VII).

These, then, were the men of the three classes who complained that Christians were useless to the commonwealth because they abhorred their abominable works and brought them no profit. “But to be unprofitable to the most abandoned men,” says Tertullian, “is undoubtedly a great profit to the commonwealth” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 43).

Finally, he demonstrates by this further argument that Christians were of the greatest benefit to the pagans: “How many do you have”—the old editions read “how many” in the accusative, Lacerda “when”—“I do not mean those who now cast demons out of you; I do not mean those who also lay prayers before the true God on your behalf, because perhaps you do not believe it, but simply those from whom you can fear nothing?” (*ibid.*). Rigaltius, however, on his own authority and contrary to the testimony of the manuscript and printed copies, removed the words “because perhaps you do not believe it” as superfluous or displeasing to him. But what harm, I ask you, was done by those words, through which the Author signifies that the pagans were by no means persuaded that Christians prayed to the true God on their behalf? Yet this, he says, was as certain as it was plainly established that demons had been cast by Christians out of the bodies of those same pagans, as we have most evidently proved.

How highly, then, Tertullian argues, do you pagans value—that is, at what price do you estimate—this surely very great benefit which Christians confer upon you? [Col. 1090C] By that fact alone, were they not assuredly of the greatest benefit to you, as we said above (supra, chap. 22, art. 1)?

But he presses the matter further and, turning back upon the pagans the weapon they had aimed at Christians, plainly demonstrates that they themselves inflict the greatest harm upon the commonwealth. For since, as we have said more than once, the number of Christians was far greater than theirs, did not the commonwealth assuredly suffer the greatest loss from those very men through whose cruelty so many righteous Christians, as our Author says, “we are expended,” that is, consumed and killed? For it was in this sense that the Latin translator of Paul’s epistles wrote: “But I will most gladly expend, and myself be expended besides, for your souls” (Paul, Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chap. XII, 15). Tertullian further adds: [Col. 1090D] “When we innocents are expended” (Tertullian, *On Prescription*, chap. 2). Pamelius, indeed, would prefer *erodimur*, “we are consumed”; but our Author uses the verb *erogare*, “to expend,” too frequently for it to be believed, against the evidence of all the manuscripts, that the word is corrupt there. It is therefore used there with the same meaning as when he said elsewhere that fever had been appointed “for expending a man.” And indeed a man is expended by a fever whose outcome is death. Elsewhere he also wrote that gladiators who had learned how to be killed were expended on the appointed day of the funeral rites (*On the Shows*, chap. 12). Finally, concerning the fire of hell, as we have observed (supra, chap. 11, art. 4), he said: “While it expends, it restores.”

Moreover, what, I ask, could have resulted in greater harm to the commonwealth than, contrary to human and divine [Col. 1091A] laws, to persecute countless Christians—not only useful to the commonwealth by their very numbers, but also excellent citizens, venerable for the integrity of their conduct and life, enemies of no one, guilty of no crime—merely, as we demonstrated above (supra, chap. 14, art. 3), on account of their name, and to torture and kill them with every kind of exquisitely devised torment? The pagans, therefore, for this reason alone, were certainly inflicting a great evil upon the entire commonwealth. Christians, by contrast, assuredly brought no evil upon it; or, if anything ever done by them could be pointed out, it was certainly repaired by them from other sources, in various ways, and with ample interest.

Thus far, then, we have expounded and elucidated each and every argument by which Tertullian demonstrates the truth and holiness of the Christian religion, its sincere [Col. 1091B] teachings, and the utterly unjust persecution of Christians. It therefore remains now to examine how he proved the religion of the pagans to be false.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Arguments by Which Tertullian Demonstrates That the Religion of the Pagans Is False, and That All Their Gods Are False

### ARTICLE I. How Clearly the Falsity of the Pagans’ Religion Is Demonstrated from the Truth of the Christian Religion; from Demons Cast Out of the Bodies of the Possessed; from the Certain Testimony of Human Conscience; from the Superior and Better-Known, but Entirely False, Divinity of Saturn, Who Was a Man and, After Being Received by Janus in Italy, Gave His Name to the City He Had Staked Out and to All Italy, Which Had Previously Been Called Oenotria; and Likewise from the Testimony of Thallus, Cassius, and Nepos; and How It Therefore Follows That the Divinity of Jupiter and the Other Gods, Vaunted by the Pagans, Is Also False

[Col. 1091C]

The very arguments by which, as we have seen, Tertullian invincibly asserted and vindicated the truth of the Christian religion utterly overthrow all the gods and superstitious religions of the pagans. For if Christ’s divinity is true, as our Tertullian acutely observes, it follows that every other belief found to be contrary to it must be pronounced false (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 404). Moreover, we have demonstrated most clearly with him (supra, chap. 7, art. 1) that there can be only one God, and consequently that all the others, however many the pagans could invent, are false.

[Col. 1091D] Nor have we demonstrated any less clearly (supra, chap. 8, art. 1) that demons were cast out by Christians from the bodies they possessed, and that the demons were then compelled openly to confess that they were not gods, as the pagans believed, but unclean spirits; that the one proclaimed by the Christians was the only God; and that Christ was His Power, Wisdom, Reason, and Son, by whose name and power they were put to flight.
