There was therefore no need for Tertullian (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 23) to accumulate many further arguments by which he might prove more fully that the pagans’ gods were wholly imaginary and fictitious, and consequently that their religion was false. But so that those same pagans might at long last, if possible, feel utter shame for the impious worship of their gods and for their perverse religion, [Col. 1092A] he employs various further arguments to make it perfectly evident to everyone that such manifest marks of that false religion can be detected that whoever fails to perceive them must wish to blind himself completely.

First, therefore, he calls their very conscience as a witness against the pagans. Constrained by it, they were compelled to confess, as we saw above, that there is one God, and that all those whom they called and worshipped as gods had in reality been men. But if any wicked man had dared to resist the most certain testimony of his own conscience, he was plainly refuted by the voiceless indeed, but most eloquent, outcry of all the cities in which these gods, as we have observed more than once (supra, chap. 7, art. 1), were born, lived, died, and were buried. Since, however, their multitude [Col. 1092B] was infinite, and it would take too long to enumerate them individually or even call them by their names, Tertullian attacks their very chief and the origin best known to all (*ibid.*, chap. 11, p. 12 ff.; chap. 29, p. 438; and book II *To the Nations*, chap. 1).

He therefore presses and addresses the pagans as follows: “Before Saturn there is no god among you: from him derives the census of the whole divinity, or at least of its superior or better-known part” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 332; and book I *To the Nations*, chap. 12, p. 578). He said “the superior or better-known” (*ibid.*), or, as in our handwritten copies, “and better-known,” which is not at all amiss. For he indicates that he derives the beginnings of the gods not from the first origin of idolatry—which, as we have seen elsewhere, is obscure and is not assigned identically by everyone (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 717 ff.; and dissertation [Col. 1092C] above, chap. 30 ff.)—but from the very divinity of Saturn, who was held to be superior to and better known than all the other gods. What wonder is it that he should begin with Saturn, when Varro, who had composed so many books about his gods, vaunts Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva as the most ancient of all the gods (Tertullian, book II *To the Nations*, chap. 12)? Yet Jupiter was said to have been begotten by Saturn, who was therefore more ancient than he. Tertullian did not think that he should begin with Saturn’s parents, Heaven, or Chronus, and Earth, both because Saturn, their only son, was better known than they and all the other gods and was believed to be superior, and because these accounts and fables of the poets concerning his origin from Heaven and Earth are ridiculous inventions. He was indeed imagined to have been born from them because his parents were unknown. For, as Tertullian says, in ordinary human usage those whose origins are unknown, or who appear unexpectedly, are said to have descended from heaven (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 10, p. 331; and book II *To the Nations*, chap. 12), [Col. 1092D] just as the common people call those whose lineage is uncertain “sons of the earth.” But we have explained all this in our preceding dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 15, art. 1; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 30, art. 1, and chap. 31, art. 2).

Moreover, in the same place we made it clear to everyone how rightly Tertullian asserted that Saturn had been a man, who, after many expeditions, reached Italy and, after being received there by Janus, “the mountain,” he says, “which he inhabited was called Saturnian; the city which he had staked out remains Saturnia to this day.” In the old edition and another [Col. 1093A] more recent one we read *debellaverat*, “he had conquered”; but *depalaverat*, “he had staked out,” is Tertullian’s word (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*). For when disputing against Hermogenes concerning the creation of the world, he says: “God completed all His works in due order, first staking out, as it were, the world with its elements still uncultivated” (the same, *Against Hermogenes*, chap. 29). Again, against Marcion: “As for his affirmation that he is a wise architect, we find this to mean the one who marks out the divine discipline received from the Creator” (the same, book V *Against Marcion*, chap. 6). Accordingly, he said that the city had been “staked out” by Saturn, that is, founded or established by setting up stakes, or, as others prefer, fortified with stakes. They attempt to support their explanation with these words of Hermas: “When he had staked out the vineyard” (Hermas, book III, similitude 5, § 2, p. 61).

[Col. 1093B] Tertullian then continues: “Saturn settled there, received by Janus,” or *Jane* (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 10); our manuscripts have *Janae*, “as the Salii maintain.” In two of our copies written in a more recent hand, however, and in the first book *To the Nations*, where the same material is repeated, we read: “Even if others call him” (book I *To the Nations*, chap. 12, p. 578); perhaps better, “as others call him.” For what purpose would the Salii be mentioned there? Was it either by them alone or by them first that Saturn was said to have been named after Janus, rather than received by Janus? But we leave this to the judgment of others.

After Saturn had established the dwelling given him by Janus, “all Italy,” says our Author, “was called Saturnia after Oenotria” (Tertullian, *ibid.*); and in the book *To the Nations*: “All Italy was named after Saturn.” Virgil plainly [Col. 1093C] teaches in the following verses that Italy was first named Oenotria:

> There is a place the Greeks call by the name Hesperia,  
> An ancient land, mighty in arms and in the richness of its soil.  
> Oenotrian men inhabited it; now report has it that their descendants  
> Called the nation Italy after the name of their leader.  
> (Virgil, book I of the *Aeneid*, v. 534 ff.)

Not content to have sung this only once, he repeats it in the same words in another book (book III, v. 163 ff.). See Servius’ annotations on these verses, Antiochus as cited by Strabo (Strabo, book III of the *Geography*, p. 254), and others. Italy, therefore, named after Saturn, was previously called Saturnia, as is evident from these verses of Ovid:

> I remember that Saturn was received in this land;  
> He had been driven by Jupiter from the celestial realms.  
> Hence for a long time the name Saturnia remained with the nation;  
> The land was also called Latium because the god lay hidden there.  
> (Ovid, book II of the *Fasti*, § 3, v. 235.)

[Col. 1093D] For this reason it is called by the poets, as we have seen (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 16, art. 1), the Saturnian soil and land, and by Virgil, where he sang:

> Hail, great mother of crops, Saturnian land!  
> (Virgil, book II of the *Georgics*, v. 174.)

Do not all these things prove clearly enough that Saturn was a man? Tertullian further confirms this, both in the *Apologeticum* and in the second book *To the Nations*, by the testimony of Diodorus, Thallus, Cassius Severus, and Cornelius Nepos, whom we have discussed elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, final chapter, art. 2; and *On Lactantius*, chap. 31, art. 3). Yet we may first offer an observation of some relevance: in the former book the name is written Cassius [Col. 1094A] Severus. There were two distinguished men of that name. One, as we read in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, was an outstanding orator (*Chronicle of Eusebius*, at the year 2047), who was sent into exile during the reign of the emperor Augustus. The other was the poet of Parma, one of those who, together with Brutus, killed Julius Caesar; concerning him Lilius Giraldus (Giraldus, Dialogue IV, *On the History of Poets*, p. 160), Vossius (Vossius, *On Latin Poets*, chap. 2), Scaliger (Scaliger, on the cited *Chronicle of Eusebius*), and others (Fabius, book X; and Seneca, epistle 79) provide more information. Both, moreover, are called Cornelius Severus by some. But in Tertullian’s text the cognomen *Severus* was perhaps added; it is omitted, as we have seen elsewhere, by Minucius Felix and Lactantius. For the things he relates about Saturn seem to have been transmitted in writing by Cassius [Col. 1094B] Hemina rather than by Cassius Severus, as we have also noted. In Tertullian’s book *To the Nations*, too, a careless copyist wrote: “The Cornelii Nepotes and Tacitus.” For what purpose would Tacitus be mentioned there, when no mention of him is made in the *Apologeticum*, or by Minucius and Lactantius (*Dissertation on Minucius*, final chapter, art. 2)? Should we not read there, as in their books, “the Greek Thallus”?

Whatever judgment those more expert in the matter may pronounce—and we shall always abide by their judgment—Tertullian affirms without hesitation that no author can be found or cited by any pagan who ever denied that Saturn was a man, who received both life and a kingdom from another man, and who therefore cannot be God (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 10, p. 331; and book II *To the Nations*, chap. 12, p. 578). For the true God, as we have often said [Col. 1094C] (*Dissertation on Minucius*, final chapter, art. 2), exists from Himself alone and is therefore almighty: He created men and all other things, rules over all, and dispenses all kingdoms.

After this Tertullian says: “Enough now concerning Saturn” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 10, p. 331), to demonstrate, even to someone rather dull and obstinate, that his divinity is altogether false. He deliberately added there, “though in few words.” For in the second book *To the Nations* he demonstrates its falsity by various arguments (book II *To the Nations*, chaps. 7 and 16), which have been explained in our earlier dissertations and need not be repeated here.

Furthermore, if Saturn neither was nor could have been a god, because he was a man like other men, much [Col. 1094D] more are Jupiter, his son, and almost the whole host of countless others devoid of divinity, since it is established that they originated from the same Saturn, or at least after him (the same, *Apologeticum*, chap. 10, p. 333). For who does not know that Jupiter, whom the pagans called the best and greatest god, was said to have been born from the union—or rather the incest—of that same Saturn with his sister Ops, or Rhea? When grown, however, after driving out his father, he seized the latter’s kingdom and, assuming, as Tertullian says, the forms of a scaly creature, a horned creature, a feathered creature, and a shower of gold, begot children through infamous debaucheries and adulteries (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 21, p. 396; and book II *To the Nations*, chap. 13).

Who, then, after weighing all these matters, which we have elucidated in our other dissertations (*Dissertation on [Col. 1095A] Minucius*, chap. 15, art. 1; *Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 11, art. 4; and *On Lactantius*, chap. 3, art. 1 ff.), could ever deny that he was not a god, but a wicked man who had cast off every sense of humanity and shame?

### ARTICLE II. How Preposterously the Pagans Vaunted That Their Gods Had Been Made Gods After This Mortal Life by Another, Superior Dispenser of Divinity; That There Is Only One God, Who Had Created the World Before All the Gods of the Pagans, and the Crops Before Ceres, Bacchus, and Minerva; and That the Discoverers of Those Crops Could No More Be Called Gods Than Lucullus, Who First Brought Cherries into Italy, and Cato, Who First Brought in the Green Fig

[Col. 1095B] The pagans indeed admitted—what they could never deny—that Saturn and the others whom they had dreamed to be gods had in reality been men; but with Varro they maintained that divinity was bestowed upon them after they had duly completed the service of this mortal life (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 335). Yet in vain they attempted to defend their absurd opinion with another, still more absurd invention. For men could not become gods after their death unless either by their own power or through some other god more powerful than they. But both alternatives are false. They themselves certainly did not possess the power to confer divinity upon themselves when dead. For if they had ever possessed such power, they would never have been men subject to the weaknesses and vices of mortals. Our Author gives this reason for it: “They would never have been men, since they possessed, that is, a power superior [Col. 1095C] to the frail human condition” (*ibid.*). For only the Son of God, God from eternity, lived a mortal life after assuming human nature, though in a wholly wonderful manner and without any stain of vice or sin.

Nor could the fictitious gods of the pagans receive divinity from anyone else unless he were greater and more powerful than they; or, to use Tertullian’s words to the pagans: “You must concede that there is some higher God and a certain dispenser of divinity” (*ibid.*). The term *manceps* is used by writers of more polished Latin for one who publicly contracts for, sells, or purchases something. But here it seems rather to be used by our Author for a sort of guardian, administrator, and superintendent of divinity (the same, *On Idolatry*, chap. 1; and [Col. 1095D] *On Modesty*, chap. 14); in this sense the superintendents of baths and other things are called *mancipes* in the Theodosian Code (Theodosian Code, sole law *On Mancipes*, vol. V, p. 183). But whoever says that Saturn and other dead men received their divinity from some other dispenser of it thereby openly confesses that they are not gods. For it is altogether necessary that the true God exist from Himself alone and be eternal.

Moreover, no one, unless he is plainly foolish, would ever say that anything was done by the almighty and supremely wise God without reflection, rashly, and without cause. Yet absolutely no cause can be assigned why He should share His divinity with dead men (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 333). Only a twofold [Col. 1096A] cause could be—or rather could have been imagined—for this. First, because God needed their services and assistance; second, because through their outstanding deeds and virtues they merited divinity. But both are proved more false than falsehood itself.

For what assistance from either dead or living men has almighty God ever needed? Was it perhaps for creating the world? But any pagans who assert this will find Pythagoras opposed to them in the matter (*ibid.*, p. 13), for, as we saw above (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 21, art. 2), he proclaimed that the world was uncreated. Yet although the world was in reality created, as Plato and other philosophers rightly taught, as has also been noted, the true God, whose power is infinite, nevertheless needed no one’s assistance whatsoever [Col. 1096B] in making it.

What of the fact that it is established that, before Saturn and any of the other pagan gods, rain, as Tertullian says, had fallen from heaven, the heavenly bodies (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*)—namely, the sun and moon—had shone, and the lights—that is, the stars—had flourished? For in another book he wrote: “Heaven had flourished with lights; the sun had exulted all the more with its rays” (book IV *Against Marcion*, chap. 42). What assistance, then, could Saturn or anyone else have given God in creating the world, when they arose long after the sun, moon, and stars? Tertullian adds that before all the gods of the pagans “thunder had bellowed, and Jupiter himself had feared those lightning bolts which you place in his hand” (or, as in the older printed and unprinted copies, “impose upon him”) (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 334). And indeed, since [Col. 1096C] it is certain that thunder had bellowed before Jupiter existed, no one should doubt that, through the fear innate in all human beings, he was afraid, at least the first time, of thunderbolts he had never heard before. Tertullian therefore rightly and deservedly ridicules the pagans, who babbled that flashes of lightning and thunderbolts were in Jupiter’s hand and were hurled by him, although they had not been made by him.

But he presses still more forcefully: nothing imperfect is made by the Almighty, and therefore the world was created by Him complete in every respect. He had therefore created everything necessary to sustain human life before any of the pagan gods and before all men. Accordingly, says Tertullian himself, after man had been created, nothing could be introduced as having been provided and given for “containing” man—that is, preserving him and preventing him from dying—or for supporting, that is, sustaining, nourishing, [Col. 1096D] and restoring him (*ibid.*). But these words of his must not be pressed so literally that he is believed to have said that after man was established nothing could be created by God by which human life might be preserved and sustained. For he meant nothing other than that everything without which human life cannot be preserved had been created by God before any human beings were established, and much more before Saturn and Jupiter and all the other gods of the pagans. He therefore concludes from this as certainly as he does clearly that the true God needed no one’s assistance in making the world. No gods, therefore, were made for this reason.

He further insists that every crop had abounded from the earth before [Col. 1097A] Liber, Ceres, and Minerva, indeed “before that first man” (*ibid.*), namely Saturn, whom the pagans babbled was the superior and first of all the gods, as we said a little above. Here he chastises the pagans, who believed that Liber was enrolled among the gods because of the discovery of wine, Ceres because of grain, and Minerva because of the olive tree. For these crops necessarily had to be created before they could be discovered. But only He by whom they were created and established is God. Nor should one press the objection that Lucretius, speaking of these matters, used the verb “establish,” when he sang:

> For Ceres is said to have established crops for mortals,  
> And Liber the liquid of the vine-born juice,  
> Although life could remain without these things,  
> As some peoples are reportedly living even now.  
> (Lucretius, book V, v. 14 ff.)

[Col. 1097B] For the poet is speaking there of things discovered by the skill and ingenuity of certain persons. He therefore used “establish” in no other sense than “discover.” If anyone maintains that he said “establish” because Bacchus and Ceres were said to have taught the method of making bread from crops and wine from grapes, we shall not object very strongly. But he will gain not the slightest advantage from this. For it is wholly sufficient for us that it is more certain than certainty itself that no crops were created by Bacchus, Ceres, and Minerva. No one can either become or be a god because crops were pointed out or discovered by him.

Nor should anyone thereafter be heard who dares to object that the discovery of crops was of such great benefit to human beings that, on account of this benefit alone, Ceres, Bacchus, and Minerva deserved to be numbered among the company of the gods. [Col. 1097C] For this reasoning has already been sufficiently refuted. Then again, if it were of any importance, Lucullus too ought to have become a god, since he was the first, as Tertullian says, to introduce cherries (the manuscripts read *cerasia*) from Pontus into Italy (Tertullian, *ibid.*). From Pliny, moreover, we learn that in the year 680 from the founding of the city, after the victory over Mithridates, cherries were brought by this Lucullus from Pontus into Italy (Pliny, book XV of the *Natural History*, chap. 25, p. 207), or, as Jerome says, from Cerasus in Pontus (Jerome, epistle 23 to Eustochium, p. 60), from which they derived their name. On the authority of these distinguished men, therefore, another passage of Tertullian in the second book *To the Nations* must be corrected, where we read: “Gnaeus Pompey introduced from Pontus . . . . . into Italy” (Tertullian, book II *To the Nations*, chap. 16).

[Col. 1097D] Tertullian further insists that the green fig was not known at Rome before Cato brought it before the senate (*ibid.*). This whole history, moreover, was related by the already cited Pliny (Pliny, book XV of the *Natural History*, chap. 18, p. 198). From it, as from the preceding account, Tertullian concludes that the pagans are unjust: they placed Ceres, Bacchus, and Minerva among the number of their gods because of crops discovered by them, yet left among the dead Lucullus and Cato, who had brought into Italy and Rome other fruits previously unknown there. But we pursued these matters more fully in our other dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 14, art. 2; *On Arnobius*, chap. 9, art. 2; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 30, art. 5), where we refute those same pagans who babbled that human beings had been made [Col. 1098A] gods after their deaths because of benefits conferred upon other human beings.

### ARTICLE III. With What Great Folly the Pagans Vaunted That Saturn, Jupiter, and Others Had Been Made Gods on Account of Their Merits and Illustrious Deeds, While Others More Excellent Than They Were Left among the Dead—Namely Socrates, Aristides, Themistocles, Alexander the Great, Pompey, Polycrates, Sulla, Croesus, Crassus, Demosthenes, and Cicero; and How It Is Shown That, by the Same Reasoning by Which the Pagans Ascribed Divinity to Their Gods, They Ought to Ascribe It to Lais, Phryne, Larentia, and to the Caesars Themselves, Whether Dead or Living

The second reason the pagans gave for bestowing divinity upon dead men was drawn from their merits and [Col. 1098B] outstanding deeds, by which, they boldly vaunted, those men had attained it. Yet whoever seriously affirmed this was compelled, as Tertullian rightly observes, to admit that there is some “deifying God” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 333), that is, one who makes others gods because of certain illustrious deeds. That preeminent God must therefore weigh the merits of others in the most equitable balance of justice and reward them with the due recompense through His omnipotence. But divinity belongs to this supremely just and omnipotent being alone, and He cannot give it to anyone distinct from Himself, whether by nature or through any merits whatsoever. For supreme divinity cannot be divided, and, as we have often said, either God is one or there is none.

But come, tell us, I pray, what virtues and outstanding [Col. 1098C] merits Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, and the others possessed by which they could have merited divinity. Did not the pagans openly proclaim and insolently boast that those gods had lived lives infamous and defiled by debaucheries, adulteries, and every kind of most grievous crime and outrage, as we have demonstrated elsewhere (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 12, art. 1 ff.)? Grant, nevertheless, that they were adorned with as many and as great virtues as the vices by which they were stained; why, then, Tertullian asks, when these were raised to heaven and endowed with divinity, were others equal to them in virtue, and even more excellent, left among the dead (Tertullian, *ibid.*)? For no pagan, however reckless in daring, could deny what is most clearly proved by the examples of illustrious men whose exceptional and singular virtues the pagans themselves extolled with the highest praises.

[Col. 1098D] For, to review the examples proposed by Tertullian (*ibid.*), what pagan god was wiser than Socrates, who was pronounced the wisest of all mortals by the oracle of Apollo cited by us elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, chap. 3, art. 2)? Yet so far was he from being called a god that he was actually condemned by the judgment of the Athenians. “Whenever I read Plato,” Cicero used to say, “I am accustomed to weep over his death” (Cicero, book III *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 252, line 29). We discussed that death of Socrates in our preceding dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 3, art. 2; and *On Lactantius*, chap. 14, art. 1), and something further must be said a little later (infra, chap. 26, art. 4).

What pagan god was more just than Aristides (Tertullian, [Col. 1099A] *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 336), “by whom,” as Valerius Maximus says, “the justice of all Greece is measured” (Valerius Maximus, book V, chap. 3, § 3, foreign examples)? For this reason he is called by Cicero, antonomastically, “Aristides the Just” (Cicero, book III *On Duties*, p. 339, line 7), and in Greek by Plutarch Ἀριστείδης ὁ δίκαιος (“Aristides the Just”) (Plutarch, vol. I, p. 318; and vol. II, p. 186). Nevertheless, the pagans not only denied him the divinity granted to other, utterly unjust men, but, through a faction of wicked men, he was ordered to leave his homeland, as the same Valerius Maximus testifies. He immediately adds: “Happy Athens, which after his exile was able to find anyone who was either a good man or a lover of herself, since holiness itself then departed with him” (Valerius Maximus, *loc. cit.*).

What warlike god was more distinguished in military glory than Themistocles (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, [Col. 1099B] p. 336)? Yet although he performed brilliantly in the many military exploits that Thucydides (Thucydides, book I of the *Histories*, p. 62 ff.) and Plutarch (Plutarch, *Life of Themistocles*, p. 113 ff.) recorded for posterity, and although he had rendered his homeland “illustrious, secure, wealthy, and foremost in Greece,” as Valerius Maximus again says (Valerius Maximus, book V, chap. 3, foreign examples, § 3), he found it utterly ungrateful. For, falsely accused of treason, he fled first to Argos, thence to Corcyra, afterward to Admetus, king of the Molossians, and then to Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes. At last, in exile, having drunk bull’s blood, as some think—or poison, as more numerous authorities relate—he flew from the bonds of the body as though from a prison.

What pagan god, our Author continues, was more exalted [Col. 1099C] than Alexander and Pompey? For each man’s achievements in arms and war earned him the surname “Great.” Yet no one who has even lightly handled the books written by Quintus Curtius and Plutarch about their lives can possibly be ignorant of the unhappy end by which both departed this life. Nevertheless, no less than Mars, Romulus, and others, they had merited the reward of divinity by their outstanding deeds.

Moreover, what pagan god was more fortunate than the Greek Polycrates and the Roman Sulla (Tertullian, *loc. cit.*)? For many, as Sallust says, doubted whether Sulla was braver or more fortunate (Sallust, *The Jugurthine War*, chap. 17). Plutarch further attests that after celebrating his triumph, when he had recounted before the assembly the deeds he had performed as bravely as successfully, Sulla ordered that he be surnamed [Col. 1099D] “the Fortunate” (Plutarch, *Life of Sulla*, vol. I, p. 453 ff.). But these achievements did not lead him to divinity. Corrupted by indulgence, he ended his life through a disease of lice. The good fortune of Polycrates, however, is described in these words of Valerius Maximus: “All his undertakings were received upon a smooth course; his hopes grasped the certain fruit of the thing desired; his vows were made and at the same time fulfilled; to will and to be able stood on equal terms” (Valerius Maximus, book VI, chap. 8, § 5, foreign examples). And indeed he enjoyed such success that when he threw a ring of enormous value into the sea to test his good fortune, it was later found in a fish that had been caught. As witnesses of this and his other successes you have Strabo (Strabo, book XIV of the *Geography*, p. 657), Herodotus (Herodotus, book III, [Col. 1100A] § 39 ff.), and a great many others. Yet he completed the course of so many and such great successes not by receiving the title of divinity, but, as Valerius Maximus again records, by suffering the punishment of the cross.

Why say more? No pagan god was richer than Croesus and Crassus (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 337). Concerning the first, Ovid sang:

> Who has not heard of the wealthy Croesus’ opulence?  
> (Ovid, book IV, *From Pontus*.)

Concerning Crassus, however, Cicero says: “He maintained that no amount of money was great enough for one who wished to be foremost in the commonwealth, unless he could support an army from his own revenues” (Cicero, book I *On Duties*, p. 354, line 3). Hence arose the proverb, “Richer than Croesus and Crassus,” concerning which you may read more in Erasmus (Erasmus, [Col. 1100B] *Adages*, chiliad 1, century 6, adage 74). Yet Croesus, defeated and captured by Cyrus, was compelled to endure slavery, “the last,” Cicero says, “of all evils,” and to serve him (Cicero, *Philippic II*, p. 606, line 12). See Herodotus (Herodotus, book I, § 86 ff.), Thucydides, Justin the historian, and others. Who likewise does not know of the unhappy slaughter of Crassus, after he had been routed and defeated by the Parthians together with the greater part of the Roman army, and whose severed head was subjected to mockery? Plutarch relates much concerning him in his life (Plutarch, *Life of Crassus*, vol. I, p. 564 ff.); you may consult him, as also Florus, Velleius Paterculus, Justin the historian, and other writers of Roman history.

What pagan god, moreover, Tertullian says, ever surpassed the Greek Demosthenes or the Latin Cicero in eloquence? [Col. 1100C] But what was the reward of such great Greek and Latin eloquence, utterly unknown to no one? Certainly not divinity, but a most unhappy end by cruel death. Since these facts are sufficiently known to everyone, let it now suffice to prove them with the following five verses of Juvenal, who, after singing of Crassus and Pompey, wrote:

> He begins to desire the eloquence and fame of Demosthenes or Cicero,  
> And desires them throughout the whole festival of Minerva,  
> Whoever still reveres Minerva, purchased for a single coin,  
> . . . . . . . . .  
> But each orator perished through his eloquence; in each case  
> The generous and overflowing fountain of genius delivered him to death.  
> (Juvenal, *Satire* 10, v. 113 ff.)

Who, then, Tertullian argues, would not be indignant with the pagans? For they left so many men who excelled so greatly in virtue and merit among the dead, yet babbled that so many other wicked and thoroughly depraved men had been proclaimed gods after their deaths because of certain [Col. 1100D] illustrious deeds (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 11, p. 337).

He presses them still further (*ibid.*, chap. 13, p. 347), saying: “What were the virtues and merits of the goddess Larentina?” Was she not a public prostitute? We have certainly proved this sufficiently elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 18, art. 1; and *On Lactantius*, chap. 32, art. 1). Would you perhaps call the Junos, the Cereses, and the Dianas more chaste? But the pagans themselves, as we have demonstrated in the preceding dissertations, publicized their unbridled lust and shamelessness. For this reason our Author thus ridicules the mad impiety of the pagans who worshipped these goddesses: “I should wish you at least to worship Lais and Phryne among your Junos, Cereses, and Dianas” (Tertullian, [Col. 1101A] *Apologeticum*, chap. 13, p. 347). Lais, moreover, publicly practiced the harlot’s trade; of her Propertius writes:

> The house of Lais at Ephyra was not so filled  
> At whose door all Greece lay prostrate.  
> (Propertius, book II, Elegy 6, vv. 1–2.)

She admitted no one unless she had received the sum of money she demanded. And because she lived at Corinth, there arose that proverb expressed in Horace’s verse:

Not every man has the fortune to go to Corinth. (Horace, Book I, Epistle 17, v. 36.) Moreover, Sotion, cited by Aulus Gellius (Gellius, Book I, *Attic Nights*, chap. 8, p. 37), relates that Demosthenes replied that he would not purchase repentance at so high a price. We have made some observations about her elsewhere (Vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1241); and, if you wish for more, consult Pausanias (Pausanias, Book II, p. 42), [Col. 1101B] Athenaeus (Athenaeus, Book XIII, chap. 6, p. 587), Ovid (Ovid, Book I, *Amores*, Elegy 5, v. 12), and others. Callistratus, moreover, cited by the same Athenaeus, informs us that Phryne, still mentioned by Tertullian, was so wealthy that she promised to rebuild the walls of Thebes if this inscription were added: Ἀλεξανδρὸς μὲν κατέσκαψεν, ἀνέστησε δὲ Φρυνὴ ἡ ἕταιρα. Alexander indeed built them, but Phryne the harlot rebuilt them (Athenaeus). But we have made further observations about her elsewhere (Vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 550 and 744, and *Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 22, art. 3).

Finally, in order to pierce the pagans with a sharper goad, our Author asks them why they made gods of the worst men, men far inferior to the other illustrious figures whom we have reviewed. Was heaven ever closed, he asks, so that excellent men could not [Col. 1101C] thereafter enter it? Why, then, did they later open it to their Caesars, not only when dead but even while alive, though ruined and debauched by every kind of vice? Will your gods, he continues, credit this to you, O pagans—indeed, will they congratulate you—that their own masters are made their equals (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 13, p. 347)? You plainly perceive that he is jesting and that he calls the emperors the masters of the gods, because, as we have already said, it lay within their power either to make new gods or to remove those already made. It is no less evident how forcefully he demonstrates that the pagans could have invented nothing more senseless than the claim that men became gods because of certain merits or some extraordinary exploits.

## ARTICLE IV. The fictitious threefold class of gods devised by Varro is refuted: physical or natural; mythical or fabulous; and national, or civil and popular

[Col. 1101D]

In order to eradicate the pagans’ errors concerning their gods, Tertullian, in the second book of his *To the Nations* (Tertullian, Book II, *To the Nations*, chap. 1 ff., p. 64 ff.), refutes everything that Varro had taught about them in the sixteen books *On Divine Matters* cited by Augustine (Augustine, Book IV, *City of God*, chap. 2, p. 147). He thought that Varro should be refuted by name because he was regarded as the most acute and learned of all writers, as we have shown in the appropriate place (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, final chap., art. 3).

Varro had distinguished a threefold pagan theology, [Col. 1102A] or class of gods. The first was physical or natural, which the pagan philosophers attempted in vain to establish in their schools and in almost innumerable treatises. For these are Varro’s words as quoted by Augustine:

> The philosophers have left many books in which this is discussed: who the gods are, where they are, of what kind and character, from what time they have existed, whether they have existed from eternity, whether they are made of fire, as Heraclitus believes; of numbers, as Pythagoras holds; or of atoms, as Epicurus holds—and likewise other things which ears can more readily endure within the walls of a school than outside in the forum.

(Augustine, Book VI, *City of God*, chap. 5, p. 150.)

But these disagreements and controversies among the philosophers concerning the gods demonstrate with the greatest clarity that their opinions concerning their gods were utterly false and absurd.

[Col. 1102B] Varro called the second class of gods mythical or fabulous. “For *mythical*,” Augustine says, “is derived from fables, since μῦθος in Greek means a fable” (*Ibid.*). This class, however, had been invented by poets who celebrated the gods’ births, rapes, adulteries, and every other abominable deed. Nevertheless, Varro himself, as Augustine again testifies (Augustine, Book IV, chap. 32, p. 112), openly admitted that the ancestors, or ancient Romans, believed those who proclaimed the gods’ horrifying crimes and marriages, because the mass of the uneducated populace was more inclined toward these poets than toward the natural philosophers. Who, however, would not detest the very great impiety of both parties? For the peoples seriously worshipped these gods, however infamous and ridiculous. Others, wiser than they, were incited by the wicked deceits [Col. 1102C] and frauds of demons either to mislead the unwary minds of the common people in religion itself, which is the highest of all concerns, or to allow them to be misled.

The third class of theology or gods is called civil, that is, belonging to citizens and peoples: namely, those gods whom peoples had adopted for themselves according to their whim and caprice. Yet apart from the fact that this class of gods is plainly reducible to the second and fabulous class, as Augustine, whom we have already cited, teaches (Augustine, Book VI, chap. 7, p. 153), what could be more absurd than to believe in those gods whom a blind and insane populace imagined to have been enrolled among the gods after they had passed through the course of this mortal life in every kind of crime, as we have often said?

Our Tertullian [Col. 1102D] and, afterward, Augustine utterly overthrow that threefold class of gods by arguments of various weight (Augustine, Book VI, chap. 5 ff., p. 150 ff.). It is therefore unnecessary for us now to explain individually the matters examined and elucidated by so great a teacher (Augustine, Book IV, chap. 31 ff., and Book VIII, chap. 1 ff., p. 162 ff.). Moreover, if any difficulty arises in them, it has been smoothed away to the best of our ability in this and our other dissertations.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How clearly Tertullian shows from the pagans’ own literature and writings that all their gods are false

## ARTICLE I. How Tertullian demonstrates that the gods of the pagans are false from the literature through which they were trained for prudence and liberal duties, and were taught of the gods’ various battles with one another, Venus wounded, Mars long confined in chains, Jupiter freed from a monster, or weeping over Sarpedon’s fall, or rutting with desire for his sister; likewise the servitude of Apollo and Neptune, Aesculapius struck by lightning, and from the poets’ tragedies—particularly those of Lentulus and Hostilius—and other works ridiculing the Moon as male

[Col. 1103A]

Such is the nature of error that it does not remain consistent with itself for long, and even destroys itself precisely when it raises its head more boldly. It is therefore unsurprising that the pagans overthrew the divinity bestowed upon dead men in the very place where they should have established it most firmly. For nowhere should it have been explained more clearly and distinctly than in the literature by which [Col. 1103B] young men were trained, as Tertullian says, for prudence (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 14, p. 351), which, according to Cicero, consists in knowledge of things good and bad and of things neither good nor bad; and for liberal duties (Cicero, Book III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 245, line 15), which, Terence says, it is altogether proper for a freeborn and well-bred man to know (Terence, *Eunuchus*, act III, scene 2, v. 24). Yet in this literature, as our Author puts it, what mockeries do I find by which they brought the divinity of their gods into disrepute?

If anyone asks what this literature and these compositions are, we shall reply that the poems of Homer are designated by that name. For the matters which our Author relates in the same passage were drawn from that poet. But if anyone wishes to have this point confirmed by some authority, behold, [Col. 1103C] Minucius Felix is at hand. After reviewing those various mockeries of the gods from the poems of Homer, whom he calls by name, he continues as follows:

> By these and similar inventions and more pleasing falsehoods, the minds of boys are corrupted; clinging to the same fables, they grow up until they reach the strength of mature age, and miserably grow old in the same opinions.

We have, however, attempted to explain these matters more fully in the preceding dissertation on this book of Minucius (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 17, art. 4).

Let us now consider, if you please, how Tertullian proves these points:

> I shall begin with your own … beginning, its source and the whole expanse; the more honor you add to him, the more you take away from your gods by magnifying the man who made sport of them.

(Tertullian, Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 575.)

These words are written in this form [Col. 1103D] in the Agobard manuscript and in Gothofredus’s edition; Gothofredus thinks that the missing words there should be supplied as follows: “I shall begin with your own study, from which comes all the material and the whole expanse.” Rigaltius, however, without giving any reason and as though certain of the true reading of Tertullian, wished the text to read: “I shall begin with your Homer himself, his wave and the whole expanse.”

But this conjecture should have been supported by at least some argument. It nevertheless appears sufficiently probable to us that Tertullian, who is speaking of pagan literature, cites a particularly famous writer of theirs, to whom the more honor the pagans paid, the more they detracted from their gods by praising him. That writer is without doubt Homer: both because, as we have seen elsewhere, [Col. 1104A] he is the oldest of all writers, and because they valued his writings so highly that, as we were just saying, young men were educated through them for prudence and liberal duties. If, however, someone more discerning demonstrates that Tertullian meant another writer, we shall gladly hear him. Yet observe, I ask you, that Homer himself is called by name in these subsequent words of our Author:

> We still remember Homer. He, I think, is the man who treated divine majesty in terms of the human condition, imbuing the gods with human accidents and passions.

(*Ibid.*)

That is, representing them as corrupted by every human emotion and vice, even the foulest.

And indeed, that leader of the Greek poets everywhere defiled his books with these disgraces of the gods. Our Author, so as not to be too lengthy, selected several examples. The first is the episode in which Homer celebrates [Col. 1104B] the gods as having met in combat with one another on behalf of the Trojans and Achaeans, like matched pairs of gladiators (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 14, p. 351); or, as the book *To the Nations* puts it: “He set them against one another, divided by their partisan favor, in something like gladiatorial pairs” (Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 575). But who does not know how often Homer sang in the *Iliad* of these battles of the gods, and, as Tertullian continues (*Ibid.*), of Venus wounded by a human arrow, Mars nearly wasted away in chains, Jupiter at one moment freed through the efforts of some monster, at another weeping over Sarpedon’s fall, and now, after the most obscene manner of swine, rutting and burning with lust for his sister and wife Juno, while recounting to her his shameful love for his mistresses?

Here, however, it should be observed in passing that Rigaltius’s edition reads simply: “Venus wounded by a human arrow.” Our manuscripts and the older printed editions, however, read:

> Venus wounded because she wished to rescue her son Aeneas, nearly killed by the same Diomedes. Mars, etc.

[Col. 1104C] Rigaltius does not explain why he removed these words, but he doubtless judged that they had been added by some copyist for the sake of explanation and later intruded into the text. For they do not occur in the book *To the Nations*, where the same things are repeated. Nor is it easy to say why the words “by the same Diomedes” were added there, since he had not previously been mentioned. Yet because these words are present in very many of the oldest manuscript copies, they ought not to have been cut away without prior notice, as we said above (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, chap. 17, art. 4). Moreover, we have indicated and explained elsewhere (and in the *Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 12, arts. 1 and 3) [Col. 1104D] the passages of Homer which Tertullian appears, with good reason, to have cited concerning that Venus, Jupiter, and Mars.

In like manner, we have also shown in the same dissertations with what great reproaches and insults other poets pursued their gods. For, not without great disgrace to them, they had imagined, as Tertullian again notes (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 14, p. 352), Apollo tending the flocks of King Admetus, Neptune contracting to perform building work for Laomedon, and Aesculapius struck by Jupiter’s thunderbolt, just as Pindar also sang.

The gods were exhibited to even greater mockery and disgrace, as Tertullian continues (Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576, and Book [Col. 1105A] II, chap. 14), and as we have also observed elsewhere (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 14, art. 1), on the stages and in the tragedies and games of the pagans. For with what abuse and insults, I ask you, were they not harassed by the performers of comedies and tragedies? Their titles alone, and their plots alone, made this sufficiently evident to everyone. Tertullian reviews a few of them (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15, p. 358), namely, Anubis the adulterer, Diana scourged, the will of the dead Jupiter, three hungry Herculeses held up to ridicule, and the male Moon. What then, you will ask? Was the Moon counted as masculine among the titles of comedies? Indeed so. For many pagans foolishly held the conviction that at least some of their gods were both male and female (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 27, arts. 3 and 4, [Col. 1105B] and the other passages cited there). Servius, commenting on the following verse of Virgil, in which he introduces Aeneas speaking thus while Ilium burns—

> I descend, and with a god as my guide, make my way  
> Through flames and foes. . . . . . .

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book II, v. 632),

makes these observations:

> According to those who say that divinities participate in both sexes. For Calvus writes:
>
> “And the mighty god Venus.”
>
> Likewise Virgil:
>
> “Nor was a god absent from the erring right hand,”
>
> although it was either Juno or Allecto. There is also in Cyprus an image of a bearded Venus.

(Servius, p. 252.)

If you desire other witnesses, Macrobius will give you several; he observes that in the cited verse of Virgil one must read “god,” not [Col. 1105C] “goddess” (Macrobius, Book III, *Saturnalia*, chap. 8, p. 329). He proves this not only by the words of Calvus already cited by Servius and by the image of the bearded Venus, but also by the testimony of Aristophanes, who calls her ἀφρόδιτον (*Aphroditon*, the masculine form of “Aphrodite”)“, and of Laevinus, who worshipped her whether she was male or female. He adds that Philochorus asserted that she was the same as the Moon, to whom men sacrifice in women’s clothing and women in men’s clothing.

Even closer to Tertullian’s purpose is Spartianus’s report that the emperor Caracalla came to Carrhae for the sake of the god Lunus (Spartianus, *Life of Caracalla*). There he reminds us of a point committed to memory by all the most learned and especially observed by the people of Carrhae: the man who thought the moon female would always be subject to women, whereas the man who believed it a male god [Col. 1105D] would rule his wife and suffer no feminine plots.

What wonder is it, then, if poets composed tragedies in mockery of the gods and inscribed them with ridiculous titles referring to the gods? Our Author names two of these poets, Lentulus and Hostilius (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15, p. 358, and Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576), but mention of them rarely occurs in other writers. Yet in another book Tertullian said of this same Lentulus:

> The boxer Cleomachus … now deserving to be crowned among the Novian fullers, and deservedly commemorated by the mime-writer Lentulus in the *Catinenses*.

(Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chap. 4.)

There he expressly calls Lentulus, whom Jerome also mentions (Jerome, Book II, *Apology Against Rufinus*), a mime-writer, or author of a play [Col. 1106A] to which he had prefixed the title *Catinenses*. A little later, however, our Author cites the pronouncements of Lentulus the augur (Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chap. 4). But this man was different from the mime-writer. There is therefore greater reason to doubt whether the latter is the mime-writing poet whom Juvenal sharply rebukes in these two verses:

> Nimble Lentulus, too, performed the *Laureolus* well—  
> In my judgment, worthy of a real cross.

(Juvenal, Satire VIII, v. 184.)

For although no one denies that the *Laureolus* was a play, some nevertheless suspect that the word “performed” indicates that it was acted by Lentulus the actor, rather than committed to writing by a poet of that name. But what if he was both actor and poet, and both wrote and performed it? Moreover, the play was not performed by only one [Col. 1106B] actor. Why, then, is Lentulus alone named, unless he had also committed it to writing?

Mention of Hostilius the mime-writer is still less frequent in the books of others. Yet, if Priscian is to be trusted, Hostilius, following the example of Ennius, published annals of the Roman people in concise language. He could therefore also have written comedies. If anyone offers us better information about him and Lentulus, he will do us a very welcome service.

## ARTICLE II. How clearly Tertullian demonstrates that the gods of the pagans are false from the scripts of actors, by whom there were represented through voice, gesture, movement, and song the Sun mourning his son, Cybele sighing after a shepherd, Jupiter’s eulogies, the judgment of Juno, Venus, and Minerva, and the disgraceful representation of Minerva and Hercules

[Col. 1106C] Tertullian passes to the actors and openly shows that their gods were treated with no less mockery by these performers than by the poets. “The actors’ scripts,” he says, “depict all their foulness” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15, p. 359), and express it through voice, facial expression, bodily movements, costume, and insignia. Who, indeed, does not know that the actors, about whom Valerius Maximus has transmitted more information (Valerius Maximus, Book II, chap. 4, § 4), were performers of tragedies and comedies who represented the characters of gods and others?

But why, someone will ask, did Tertullian not only here but also in another book say, not “actors,” but “the scripts of actors” (Tertullian, Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576)? What are these actors’ scripts? Some have thought that “sides” should be read there, but this is mere conjecture, supported by the authority of no manuscript. [Col. 1106D] What if, by the term “scripts,” he meant the things exhibited by the actors’ voices and bodily movements, but first committed to writing and letters by the poets? For, as Augustine says:

> What, in comparison with this evil, are Mercury’s thefts, Venus’s wantonness, and the rapes and obscenities of the others, which we would bring forward from books if they were not sung and danced daily in the theaters?

(Augustine, Book VII, *City of God*, chap. 26, p. 182.)

By whom were they sung and danced, if not by the actors, after they had been committed to writing by the poets?

Tertullian offers the following examples of acts performed by those actors to the insult and utmost disgrace of their gods: “The Sun mourns his son cast down from heaven” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. [Col. 1107A] 15, p. 359). Our parchment manuscripts and editions older than Rigaltius read “cast down from heaven,” doubtless referring to Phaethon, whose story is well known. Nevertheless, in the first book *To the Nations* we read: “The Sun mourns his son destroyed by lightning” (Tertullian, Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576). This applies to Aesculapius, as we observed in the preceding article. Yet because we saw that Aesculapius was already mentioned in the *Apologeticum*, it may be inferred that Phaethon is meant there and Aesculapius in the book *To the Nations*.

An actor also represented “Cybele sighing after the disdainful shepherd,” namely Attis. We have seen this story described by Minucius Felix (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, chap. 20, art. 2; and *Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 26, art. 1), and by Arnobius, who accordingly [Col. 1107B] reproaches the pagans thus:

> Does the Great Mother become calmer and milder if she sees the ancient story of Attis revived by the actors?

(Arnobius, Book VII, *Against the Pagans*.)

Earlier he had said:

> The Great Mother loved him. If as a grandson, like a grandmother, the matter is innocent; but if as the theaters proclaim, it is an infamous and destructive love.

(Arnobius, Book V.)

Tertullian continues and rebukes the pagans with these words: “You endure the eulogies of Jupiter being sung” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15, p. 359), and in the book *To the Nations*, “the eulogies being set to music” (Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576)—that is, Jupiter’s censures and disgraces being expressed in comedies by actors’ voices and gestures and by the modulation of flutes, just as they were celebrated in the *Amphitryon* and surely in very many other similar works.

“You also endure Juno, Venus, and Minerva being judged by a shepherd” (Tertullian, [Col. 1107C] *Apologeticum*, *ibid.*), namely Paris, who was raised among shepherds on Mount Ida and called a shepherd; his judgment concerning these goddesses is unknown to no one. We shall therefore add nothing except what Augustine aptly and altogether appropriately said for our purpose:

> Although the quarrels or judgments concerning several gods may be false, including that of the three goddesses who are said to have contended before Paris as judge for preeminence in beauty in order to obtain the golden apple, nevertheless, in order to appease with games the gods who delight in these charges, whether true or false, they are sung and danced amid theatrical applause.

(Augustine, Book XVIII, *City of God*, chap. 10, p. 495.)

Thus, our Author says, the majesty of the gods was violated and prostituted while the pagans not only did not blush (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15, p. 359), but even applauded, as Rigaltius’s edition reads; our [Col. 1107D] parchment manuscripts, the old editions, and the book *To the Nations*, however, read “rejoiced” (Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576).

Tertullian presses the point (*ibid.*):

> What of the fact that the image of your god clothes a most disgraceful and notorious head?

Our manuscripts and old editions include “itself”; other manuscripts read “a disgraceful head.” In the book *To the Nations*, however, we read:

> A notorious and mutilated head is clothed by the image of any god whatsoever.

That is, a disgraceful actor notorious for his crimes represents the image of any god whatsoever. He adds:

> An impure body, trained by effeminacy for that art—

that is, “a shameless female mime represents some Minerva, or a still more impudent male mime represents Hercules” (*ibid.*); that is, he exhibits the shameful deeds of either on the stage. What person [Col. 1108A] of sound mind does not see that the divinity of these gods vaunted by the pagans was plainly and utterly overthrown by these performances of the actors, by the applause and delight of the spectators, and by all those tragedies and comedies, about which we have discussed more extensively in the preceding dissertation and in the other places cited there (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 27, art. 3)?

## ARTICLE III. How greatly the pagans, assuming the person of the gods in the arena, ruined their divinity by representing Attis castrated, Hercules burning alive, Mercury testing the dead with a cautery, Jupiter’s brother conducting away the corpses of gladiators with a hammer, and others arranging adulteries and acts of procuring in the temples, by which they degraded the majesty of the gods

[Col. 1108B] Tertullian descends from the actors’ theater into the arena, as he himself puts it, and does not find the pagans any more religious there (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15, p. 361; and Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576). They distinguish three sections of the seating area—or rather, its three parts—as we learn from Cicero (Cicero, *On Old Age*, p. 412, line 37, and *On Friendship*, p. 422, line 13), Suetonius (Suetonius, Book II, § 44), Servius (Servius on Book V of the *Aeneid*, v. 340, and Book VIII, v. 635), and others. The highest was where women sat; the middle, where the people sat; and the third, where men of higher rank sat and watched the public games. Tertullian, however, like Ammianus Marcellinus (Marcellinus, Book XIX, p. 550), uses the word *cavea* to designate the amphitheater’s arena, in which gladiators fought. For in his book *To the Nations* he wrote:

> You are [Col. 1108C] more religious in the gladiators’ arena, where, over human blood and over the defilements of punishment, your gods dance in like manner, supplying plots and stories for the punishment of criminals—or else criminals are punished in the roles of the gods themselves.

(Tertullian, Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576.)

In the *Apologeticum* he writes similarly:

> In the arena, where, over human blood and over the defilements of punishment, your gods dance in like manner, supplying plots and stories to criminals, except that criminals themselves also often assume the roles of your gods.

(Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15, p. 361; and Book I, *To the Nations*, cited above.)

By these words he means that after a gladiatorial contest a pantomime, having assumed the mask and character of some god, descended into the arena and danced over the bodies of those who had been killed or were breathing their last—criminals, that is, those who, after being condemned for their crimes, were forced to fight with wild beasts. [Col. 1108D] Say, then, how beautiful and pious it was for one impersonating a god to perform the office of an executioner or to mock the corpses of condemned men killed by beasts.

No one should suppose that our Author invented or exaggerated this, for he testifies that he had often seen it with his own eyes: “We have seen on occasion,” he says (Tertullian, *ibid.*); and in the book *To the Nations*: “We have often seen Attis castrated,” that god from Pessinus, a city situated on the frontier of Greater Phrygia beneath Mount Agdistis, where Attis was said, according to Pausanias, to have been buried. Furthermore: “The man who was burning alive,” he says, “had assumed the role of Hercules” (Pausanias, Book I, p. 4). What else did he mean by these words than that in those cruel spectacles condemned and criminal men, having taken the appearance either of Attis [Col. 1109A] or of Hercules, represented Attis castrated and Hercules burned alive? We have treated both in our dissertation on the books of Arnobius (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, chap. 14, art. 2, and chap. 18, art. 1).

What more need be said? “We laughed,” Tertullian continues, “amid the sportive cruelties of the midday gladiators” (Tertullian, passage cited), whom we discussed above, at “Mercury”—a man wearing a mask of Mercury—testing with a cautery, or red-hot iron, whether some fraud lay concealed in the dead, that is, the slain gladiators, and whether they were truly dead.

“We have also seen,” he continues (*ibid.*), “Jupiter’s brother,” namely Pluto, “conducting away the corpses of the gladiators with a hammer,” or, as the book *To the Nations* reads, “conducting their funeral procession with a hammer”—namely, into the *spoliarium*, where defeated gladiators who had received a mortal wound were killed if any breath remained in them. [Col. 1109B] Hence Seneca wrote: “Do you suppose anyone is so eager for life that he would prefer to have his throat cut in the *spoliarium* rather than in the arena?” (Seneca, Epistle 94, near the end, p. 384.) Elsewhere he says more about the midday gladiators (Epistle VII, p. 172), as does Suetonius (Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, § 34, and *Caligula*, § 26 ff.). See them, as well as Lampridius (Lampridius, *Life of the Emperor Commodus*), concerning the *spoliarium*, into which gladiators were dragged with a hook.

One is moved to wonder at certain scholars who wish Tertullian’s text here to read: “We have also seen him conduct them to Jupiter’s brother” (Johannes Argotus, *Notes on Onuphrius Panvinius, On the Games of the Circus*, chap. 2), as though he had said: “We have seen the same Mercury, who not only tested the gladiators’ corpses [Col. 1109C] with a cautery but also conducted them with a hammer to Pluto, Jupiter’s brother—that is, to the underworld.” For they do not appear to have paid sufficient attention to these words of the same Tertullian in the book *To the Nations*:

> Dis Pater, Jupiter’s brother, conducts the gladiators’ funerals with a hammer; Mercury, feathered upon his bald head and provided with a fiery wand, tests with a cautery bodies already lifeless or feigning death.

(Tertullian, Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576.)

He therefore distinguishes the offices of both: that of Mercury, who tested whether the gladiators were dead, and that of Pluto, who conducted the dead, or their funeral processions, into the *spoliarium*. For he is speaking of things customarily done at gladiatorial games. Otherwise, Mercury was said to conduct souls to Tartarus with his caduceus or wand, as Virgil sings of him:

> Then he takes his wand: with it he summons pale souls  
> From Orcus, sends others beneath gloomy Tartarus,  
> Gives sleep and takes it away, and unseals eyes in death.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book IV, v. 242 ff.)

[Col. 1109D] The pagans, moreover, mocked their gods not only in public spectacles and in the arena, but even in their temples, where surely, if anywhere, divine honors ought to have been paid to them. For there, Tertullian says, adulteries could be seen being arranged, acts of procuring negotiated between the altars, and lust discharged—that is, expressed and satisfied—most often in the very lodgings of temple attendants and priests, no differently than in brothels, beneath those same sacred ribbons, caps, and purple robes, while incense burned (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, [Col. 1110A] chap. 15).

Do not, I ask you, regard his testimony as suspect. For Juvenal, although a pagan, could not endure such great crimes and reproached them with the utmost indignation in these verses:

> For lately, as I recall, the shrine of Isis and the Ganymede  
> Of Peace, and the secluded palace of the imported Mother,  
> And Ceres—for in what temple does a woman not prostitute herself?

(Juvenal, Satire 9, v. 22 ff.)

Indeed, he had previously said:

> Or rather, at the sanctuary of Isis the procuress,  
> She arranges her hair.

(Satire VI, vv. 4–5.)

But we have already said more about these matters in our other dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 13, art. 1; and *On Lactantius*, p. 27, art. 1 and 34). Who of sound mind would not willingly agree with Tertullian, who, from [Col. 1110B] all these things explained in this and the preceding articles, correctly concludes that the pagans themselves utterly ruined and completely overthrew all the divinity of their gods, whom they wished Christians and others to acknowledge and worship?

For so many and such great insults, disgraces, and mockeries of the gods, he says, “disturb the honor of divinity”; that is, they trouble it and do not allow it to remain undisturbed and secure. Indeed, “they degrade the summits of majesty” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 15; and Book I, *To the Nations*, chap. 10). Thus the word is written in our manuscripts and in all editions published before Rigaltius. But he considered the meaning of the verb *obsoletant* wholly inappropriate and wished it corrected to *adsolant*, which, following Gothofredus, he judges to mean “they cast down to the ground and earth.” He readily admits that the first book of our Author’s *To the Nations* reads: “They cast down the summit of majesty” (Tertullian, passage cited). But what prevents Tertullian from having employed one verb in one book and another in the other?

[Col. 1110C] Whoever objects that the meaning of *obsoletant* is utterly inappropriate has surely failed to notice that the same Tertullian said elsewhere: “Most would perish again after salvation who had worn out their wedding garment” (Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chap. 6). Does the verb not have the same sense in this book as in the *Apologeticum*? If, then, it seems utterly inappropriate, why, I ask you, did Rigaltius alter it in this book but preserve it in the other? It therefore ought not to have been changed on the testimony of the single Fulda manuscript, even if it is found there, since so many other copies of older and better character openly disagree with it. It is sufficient that *obsoletant* is a genuine word of Tertullian, which Fortunatus also used in precisely the same sense (Fortunatus, *Life of St. Albinus*, § 1): they abolish, invalidate, and render obsolete.

Our Author’s meaning, therefore, is this: when the pagans harass their gods with so many insults, reproaches, and injuries in every place, sacred and profane alike, yet nevertheless wish them to be worshipped and adored, they invalidate and destroy with one hand the divinity which with the other [Col. 1110D] they vainly endeavor to establish.

## ARTICLE IV. By what arguments Tertullian disclosed that the gods of the pagans were mocked and rejected by philosophers, particularly Socrates, Diogenes, and Varro

No one, whoever he may be, can object to us [Col. 1111A] that the pagan philosophers showed greater reverence toward their gods than did the other common people (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 14, p. 353). For nearly all were so estranged from acknowledging the true God, or from proclaiming him once acknowledged, that Tertullian thought it superfluous here even to call them by name. He appears to have passed them over here because elsewhere, as we have shown (above, chap. 5, art. 4), he had sufficiently and openly demonstrated their vain and utterly absurd opinions concerning God.

Nevertheless, in this very passage he names Socrates specifically, and not without reason. For, as we observed earlier (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, chap. 3, art. 2), he had been declared by Apollo’s oracle the wisest of all mortals. Yet although he was regarded as so wise, [Col. 1111B] “to insult the gods,” Tertullian says, “he swore by the oak, the goat, and the dog” (Tertullian, passage cited). Rigaltius wished us to be informed that the words “and the dog” are absent from the Fulda manuscript; it is surely sufficient, however, that they are found in all the others. In the book *To the Nations*, a copyist erred by writing “mistress” in place of “goat” (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, chap. 10, p. 576). Elsewhere we have related more concerning this oath of Socrates and openly shown that various writers report it in various forms, but never without contempt and injury toward the gods (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, chap. 30, art. 1).

Tertullian further adds that Socrates was condemned to death by the Athenians because he destroyed the gods, but that they were at last so moved by repentance for their unjust condemnation that, he says, “they afterward punished Socrates’ accusers” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 14, p. 354): [Col. 1111C] namely, Melitus with death and Anytus with exile; and they placed a golden statue of Socrates in the temple (Plato, *Apology of Socrates*, Vol. III, p. 390). Yet we read that Laertius recorded: Χαλκῆς εἰκόνος ἐτιμήσαντο, “they honored him with a bronze, not a golden, statue” (Laertius, Book II, *Life of Socrates*, § 43).

Casaubon and Menagius therefore wish “bronze” to be restored in Tertullian’s text, and the latter is surprised that Rigaltius made no mention of this emendation. But Rigaltius is surely less deserving of surprise here, where he follows the common reading of all the manuscripts, than in very many other places where, contrary to their manifest testimony, he altered and corrupted Tertullian’s authentic text.

Since, therefore, Socrates, by denying the gods of the pagans, had aroused the hatred of the Athenians [Col. 1111D] against himself, Tertullian immediately added: “Clearly, of old”—that is, “always”—“truth has been hated.” Yet someone may, not wholly without reason, call into question whether these words, “that is, always,” were subsequently inserted into this text. For why, he will ask, would Tertullian have explained the adverb *olim* by these words? Could he not have said more simply: “Truth is always hated”? Moreover, the adverb *olim* is used by Virgil to signify any time whatever, where he sings: “Now for you, ever exceedingly strong” (Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. II, v. 100; and *Aeneid*, bk. VIII, v. 391); that is, Servius says, “at all times.” Later the same poet writes: “No otherwise than thunder is wont,” that is, as Servius again observes: “As it is accustomed to occur. For it is not an adverb of time” (Servius, [Col. 1112A] p. 511). But could Tertullian not have said that truth was hated by men of old—namely, in the time of Socrates, of whom he was speaking—and in his own time also, and thus always? Whatever judgment you may reach, Tertullian concludes from this that hatred of truth is so great that the Athenians hated it in Socrates when he overthrew their fictitious gods. We discussed his condemnation and death above, in the earlier dissertations cited there (above, ch. 25, art. 3).

Tertullian joins two other philosophers to Socrates (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 14, p. 355), one Greek, Diogenes, and the other Roman, Varro. But many may perhaps wonder why, in his testimony against the pagans, both here and in the first book *To the Nations*, he argues as follows: “Diogenes,” he says, “makes some jest or other at Hercules”; [Col. 1112B] in the other book, “he jested” (bk. I, *To the Nations*, ch. 10, p. 576). For, they will object, is this argument of such importance that it deserved to be repeated? If Tertullian did not know what jest Diogenes made at Hercules, what could he infer from it against the false gods of the pagans? And who is this Diogenes? Since that is difficult to say, some suspect that *Diagoras* should be read. He, because he lacked a fire on which to cook his dinner, is said to have asked a statue of Hercules to cook it for him as his thirteenth labor. But absolutely all the manuscripts oppose this emendation. Yielding, therefore, to their authority, we are readily persuaded that Tertullian calls him Diogenes the Cynic, just as in the same passage he calls Varro a Cynic. For who does not know how greatly Hercules is mocked by this very Cynic Diogenes in Lucian’s *Dialogues* [Col. 1112C] (Lucian, *Dialogues of the Dead*, 56, p. 137; and *Old Authors*, p. 190)? There is, moreover, that epigram of Ausonius in which Diogenes is said, not without humor, to have made Hercules the founder of his school:

> I am the first founder of the Cynic school. What reasoning is this?  
> Alcides is said to be much earlier.  
> Once, with Alcides as my teacher, I was second;  
> Now I am the foremost Cynic, and he a god.

(Ausonius, *Epigram* 26.)

Is that not the “some jest or other” by which Tertullian attests that the divinity of Hercules was mocked by Diogenes? If, however, you show that he was referring to some other mockery recorded by Lucian or another author, we shall not oppose you. Moreover, although he called it “some jest or other,” since it was nevertheless not unknown [Col. 1112D] to the pagans, he properly drew an argument from it against their gods (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 24, art. 4).

Someone may perhaps doubt whether the other philosopher, whom he calls “Varro the Cynic,” is the man whose learning the pagans, as we have seen, heaped with such great praise, and who had composed so many books on religions. For did he too dare to jest about the gods? Why not? Do we not read in our author’s books *To the Nations*: “Varro, a Diogenes of the Roman pen, introduces three hundred Joves, or Jupiters” (our manuscripts have *Jupiteros*), “without heads” (Tertullian, bk. I, *To the Nations*, ch. 10, p. 576)? But how could he introduce so many Joves without ridicule? Did not Minucius Felix, undoubtedly following our Tertullian, say that there are “as many monstrous forms of Jove [Col. 1113A] as there are names”? See what we have observed elsewhere on these words (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 2). Some, moreover, think that Varro said these things in his *Menippean Satires*; why not in his other books on the religion of the pagans, of which there were so many? But wherever he said them, the false divinity both of Jove and of the others is thereby most clearly demonstrated. This was indeed so thoroughly accepted by those in whom some spark of uprightness and fairness still remained that, as we saw above (above, ch. 18, art. 9), they utterly rejected Father Liber, Serapis, and Harpocrates together with his Cynocephalus. Yet, after setting aside all the other false divinities, they assuredly ought to have worshiped the one almighty God.

# CHAPTER XXVII

## Other arguments of Tertullian by which he demonstrates that the gods of the pagans are false and nonexistent are examined

[Col. 1113B]

### ARTICLE I

#### How impious was the license of provinces and cities, and especially of the Egyptians, to adopt particular gods for themselves; how improbable are the things reported by Tertullian concerning the patriarch Joseph; whether the Egyptians called and worshiped him as a god under the name Serapis; and by what warrant Tertullian calls Astarte the god of Syria, Dusares that of Arabia, Belenus that of the Norici, Caelestis that of Africa, and their own petty kings the gods of Mauretania

Another very evident proof of false religion is surely the license granted to cities and peoples [Col. 1113C] to adopt and worship any god whatever, often unknown to the others. But, our Tertullian says, many provinces and cities of the pagans worshiped gods adopted at whim, not from a knowledge of the truth, whether gods rejected by others or unknown to them (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 417; and bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8). There he particularly reproaches the Egyptians, who, as we have shown in our other dissertations (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 34, art. 2, and the passages cited there), in a superstition as impious as it was absurd, not only consecrated sheep and other beasts, but even condemned to death those who killed any such god. Having received this freedom to adopt them, the Egyptians, Tertullian says, so abused it that they made the patriarch Joseph a god under the name Serapis (Tertullian, [Col. 1113D] passage cited). But there he confuses many things, and indeed to such a degree that it seems astonishing how a man exceptionally well versed in the sacred Scriptures should offer us several assertions plainly opposed to them.

First, Joseph, he says (Tertullian, bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8), was younger than his other brothers—he ought to have excepted Benjamin—and, after being sold in Egypt, served in the household of Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians. But in the book of Genesis (Gen. 37:18, 36; 39:1 ff.) we read that he was sold to the Midianites, and by them to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and commander of the soldiers, whom he actually served until he was cast into prison. Unless, therefore, you prove that this Potiphar, whom Josephus calls πετεφρὴς (Petephres) (Josephus, bk. II, *Jewish Antiquities*, ch. 3, [Col. 1114A] p. 39 ff.), belonged to Pharaoh’s royal household, this opinion of Tertullian appears false. Nor is what he adds any truer: that Joseph was desired by the less than chaste queen and was for that reason thrust into prison at the king’s command. For it was not the queen, but Potiphar’s wife, as is related in the same sacred book, who solicited him to adultery; and it was the deceived Potiphar who cast him into bonds. Tertullian further asserts that Joseph received in marriage the daughter of King Pharaoh, whose dreams he had explained. But sacred Scripture (Gen. 41:50) and Josephus the historian (Josephus, passage cited) give us the more certain information that the patriarch Joseph married Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis.

Finally, some judge the following addition by our author to conflict with the truth handed down in those same books of Genesis and [Col. 1114B] Josephus: “Joseph taught the ways of release from prison; he disclosed the dream to the king” (Tertullian, bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8). For he had been released from prison when he interpreted the king’s dreams. Yet could Tertullian not have indicated by these words the dreams of Pharaoh’s two eunuchs, which Joseph actually explained in prison and which afterward furnished the occasion for his interpretation of Pharaoh’s own dreams? Moreover, the things contrary to sacred Scripture that Tertullian reports were written only in the book *To the Nations* and were wholly omitted from the *Apologeticum*. Who would dare determine the reason for this omission—whether it was because he recognized that they were not altogether true? Besides, he had perhaps drawn them from corrupt sources, unless you can show that copyists, as so often elsewhere, erred in transcribing the proper names in this [Col. 1114C] book.

Vossius therefore considers more probable (*On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. I, ch. 29) what Tertullian further relates: that after Joseph supplied them with grain in a time of famine, the Egyptians ordered a bull to be reared by the priests as a memorial and symbol of so great a benefit; this bull they honored first with civil and then with divine worship. It is, indeed, agreed that the same Egyptians made the bull into the god Apis, and thence Serapis, concerning whom see Rufinus (Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. II, ch. 23) and our discussion elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1090). A very celebrated statue of this Serapis was also fashioned at Alexandria, concerning which the same Rufinus says: “A grain measure was placed upon his head, and he is said to have been fashioned in honor of our Joseph, because of the measurement of the grain [Col. 1114D] with which he relieved the Egyptians in the time of famine.” The Suda supports Rufinus (Suda, s.v. Σαράπις (Sarapis)), although neither could deny that others held different opinions.

From the Egyptians our author passes to other peoples, who with no less license had adopted for themselves particular gods unknown to others, and especially to the Romans: “For how many are there,” he says, “who know by sight or hearing which god belongs to each province and city—such as Astarte of Syria?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 418; our manuscripts have *Adstartes*); in the book *To the Nations*, “Atagartis of the Syrians” (bk.
