II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8). This reading can be confirmed by these words of Pliny: “But for the Syrians, Magog. There is the marvelous Atagartis, called Derceto by the Greeks” (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. V, ch. 23, [Col. 1115A] p. 577). Strabo, moreover, says of Hierapolis: “ἐν ᾗ τιμῶσι τὴν Συρίαν θεὸν τὴν Ἀταργατίν, in which they worship Atargatis, the Syrian goddess” (Strabo, *Geography*, bk. XVI, p. 748). But later he wrote: “Ἀταργατὴν δὲ τὴν Ἀθάραν, Δερκέτω δ` αὐτὴν Κτησίας καλεῖ, they called Atargatis Athara, whom Ctesias called Derceto” (ibid., p. 785). By others, however, she was called Astarte, as by Minucius Felix, who had read this name in our Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, as he had many other things. See Vossius (*On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. I, ch. 28) and, if you please, what we have annotated on that passage of Minucius (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 14, art. 1).

Just as this was the goddess of Syria, so, Tertullian says, Dusares was that of Arabia (Tertullian, passage cited); but in the second book *To the Nations* the name is given differently, *Obodanedussiren*. They think that this [Col. 1115B] name was corrupted by an unskilled copyist who made one name out of the two, Obodas and Dusares. They attempt to confirm their opinion by the authority of Eusebius, by whom, they say, these Arabian gods were mentioned, although they indicate neither his words nor the book. Vossius has more about both those gods and is readily accessible to anyone (Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. II, ch. 8, p. 178). Belenus was also the native god of the Norici, our author says (same author, ibid., ch. 24, p. 419); but these names were also corrupted in our manuscripts as *Nori Cibelenus*, and in some printed editions as *Tibelenus*. Vossius suspects that he is the god whom they called Tybelinus, whom the ancient Saxons called Tebilenus, and the Slavs Zerneboch. But is it not far more probable that Tertullian [Col. 1115C] is speaking of the god Belenus, whom the people of Aquileia, as Julius Capitolinus (Capitolinus, *Life of Maximinus*, p. 361, col. 2) and Herodian (Herodian, *History*, bk. II, p. 612) have recorded, held in the highest honor and believed to be the sun? Gruter, moreover, presents various inscriptions dedicated “To the God Belenus,” set up by Augustus Caesar (Gruter, vol. I, *Inscriptions*, pp. 26–27). Indeed, he is proclaimed by Ausonius as the god of the people of Bordeaux in more than one poem (Ausonius, *On the Professors of Bordeaux*, poem 4, §145; and poem 10, §154). Belenus was thus worshiped not only by the Norici, peoples of Germany, but also by others. Tertullian perhaps named them specifically because he knew that they honored this god above the rest (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 420). Nevertheless, if you can show that he meant some more obscure god of the Norici or of another nation, we shall readily agree with you.

Nor did he omit his native land: “Caelestis of Africa”; and in the book *To the Nations*, “Caelestis of the Africans” (bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8), concerning whom we discussed above (above, ch. 18, art. 6). [Col. 1115D] Moreover, Mauretania was a region of the same Africa, concerning which he immediately adds: “Mauretania, its own petty kings.” But Minucius Felix and Lactantius name Juba, whom the inhabitants of this province honored specifically with divine worship. Consult, if you wish, what was discussed in our dissertations on the books of both authors (*Dissertation [Col. 1116A] on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 16, art. 2; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 30, art. 2).

### ARTICLE II

#### On other gods unknown to the Romans who were worshiped in the provinces and cities of Italy, such as Delventinus of the people of Casinum or Crustumerium, Visidianus of the people of Narnia, Ancaria or Ancharia of the people of Asculum, Nursia or Nortia of the people of Volsinii, Valentia of the people of Ocriculum, and Juno, who among the Faliscans received her surname in honor of Father Curis

Tertullian continues his argument and passes from provinces more distant from Rome to Italy: “Throughout Italy itself,” he says, “gods are also registered by municipal consecration” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, [Col. 1116B] p. 420), though the Romans did not worship them. So great, indeed, was the blindness and license of the inhabitants of each city that they not only possessed gods unknown to others, but gods whose very names, as he says, “do not differ in dignity from human surnames” (same author, bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 2). But just as they bore the name of a human being, so it is manifest that they lived a human life and therefore were not gods. He enumerates several of them (ibid.); and so that no opportunity might exist for anyone to detract from his credibility, he cites Varro as a witness, undoubtedly in those books which, according to Augustine (*City of God*, bk. VI, ch. 3, p. 148), he published *On Divine Matters*.

At the head of this troop of obscure gods is placed “Delventinus of the *Casianienses*” (Tertullian, passage cited), or, as our older handwritten manuscripts and others have it, “of the *Casianenses*”; the older printed editions have “of the Crustuminians,” [Col. 1116C] and certain later editions, *Belventinus*. Varro says that Casinum, a town of Campania, was first held by the Samnites, who sprang from the Sabines, and afterward by the Romans (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. VI, p. 77). Pliny (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. III, ch. 4, p. 229) and Silius (Silius Italicus, bk. XII, v. 525) mention that town, and its name occurs in various inscriptions published by Gruter (Gruter, pp. 136, 151). If, however, someone should prefer to read “of the Crustuminians” there, he may support his opinion with these verses of Virgil:

> . . . Nor does the same shoot  
> Belong to Crustumian and Syrian pears.

(Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. II, v. 88.)

For Servius observes on this passage: “Crustumian pears are red on one side, taking their name from the town Crustumium.” [Col. 1116D] Pliny describes the territory of Crustumerium and its location in these words: “Within thirteen miles of the city, separating the territory of Veii from that of Crustumerium, then the territory of Fidenae, and the Latin territory from the Vatican” (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. III, ch. 5, p. 323). But shortly before this he had mentioned another Crustumerium (ibid., p. 322), whose location is now unknown. If we must yield to the authority of the better and older manuscripts, Tertullian meant the town of the Casinians (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 420; and bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8), which they believe to be what is now Monte Cassino.

Next he says: “Visidianus of the Narnians.” Pliny, when enumerating the towns and peoples of Umbria, says: “The Narnians, whose town was formerly called Nequinum” [Col. 1117A] (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. III, ch. 14, p. 365). And indeed we read in Livy: “The other consul, Apuleius, laid siege to the town of Nequinum in Umbria. The place was difficult of access and precipitous on one side, where Narnia now stands” (Livy, bk. X, §9). It took its name from the river Nar, which flows past it, as you will understand from these words of Strabo: “Νάρνα δι` ἧς ῥεῖ ὁ Νάρ ποταμὸς, Narnia, through which the river Nar flows” (Strabo, *Geography*, bk. V, p. 227). The Narnians are also commemorated in various inscriptions in Gruter (Gruter, p. 174, inscr. 4; p. 388, inscr. 2; p. 460, inscr. 4).

Furthermore, “Ancharia of the people of Asculum”; in the book *To the Nations* and our manuscript copies: *Ancharia* (Tertullian, passage cited). Pliny, however, says: “The colony Asculum, the most renowned city of Picenum” (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. III, [Col. 1117B] ch. 13, p. 362), in whose name many inscriptions survive in Gruter (Gruter, p. 465, inscr. 1 and 10; p. 371, inscr. 1; p. 427, inscr. 1). Strabo, however: “Ἀσκλον τὸ πικηνὸν (Asculum of Picenum).” But there is another Asculum, a town of Apulia, very famous for the defeat of Pyrrhus. Our author undoubtedly speaks of one of the two, unless you prove that the same goddess was worshiped in both. Someone may perhaps think that it can be inferred from these verses of Lucan about Lentulus that Tertullian is speaking of the former:

> . . . Lentulus is driven  
> From the Asculan citadel.

(Lucan, *Pharsalia*, bk. II, v. 150.)

For some observe that *Esculea* and *Asculea* were used interchangeably; why not also *Aesculea*, whence the Aesculani of whom we are now speaking?

[Col. 1117C] Turnebus, moreover (Turnebus, *Adversaria*, bk. XVII, ch. 24), suspects that Ancharia is the goddess from whose madness men possessed by frenzy were called *ancarii*. He attempts to establish this by two verses of Lucilius cited by Nonius (Nonius, s.v. *Quiritare*):

> This same man will roar from among our ranks and raise a howl,  
> Rushing about like an *ancarius* and loudly shrieking.

In our edition of these verses we indeed read: “This man, I say . . . like an arena-fighter.” But this is undoubtedly corrupt and contrary to the rules of meter. Nevertheless, this is a mere conjecture of Turnebus and still requires some other proof. In the book *To the Nations* the name *Anchariam* appears, followed by *et quam praeverint*. Considering this corrupt, editors wished to substitute *et quam praeverim*; but they gave no reason for the emendation, which seems no better than the adulterated text. We therefore prefer to await the aid of another manuscript rather than indulge in various conjectures.

It will thus be easier to prove what Tertullian adds: “Nursia of the people of Volsinii” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 421); but in the book *To the Nations* (bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8, p. 71) and in our unpublished manuscripts, *Norcia* and *Nortia*, or, as Lipsius notes on the passage of Tacitus soon to be cited, *Neurscia*. Livy more than once mentions the people of Volsinii (Livy, bk. V, §31; bk. IX, §21), who are also so called in an inscription published by Gruter (Gruter, inscr. 1, p. 385). But Tertullian himself elsewhere, as we [Col. 1118A] observed (above, ch. 23, art. 3), calls them *Volsinii*, as do Propertius (Propertius, bk. IV, elegy 2, v. 2) and Pliny (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. II, ch. 52, p. 287; bk. III, ch. 4, p. 322), who testify that this was a very wealthy city of the Etruscans, now under the dominion of the supreme pontiffs.

That Nortia was their goddess we learn from these words of Livy already cited: “Cincius, a careful authority on monuments of this kind, affirms that at Volsinii nails, marking the number of years, can be seen driven into the temple of Nortia, an Etruscan goddess” (Livy, bk. VII, §3). Juvenal too sang the following concerning her:

> . . . The same people, if Nortia [Note: [Col. 1118D] In some editions, *Nursia*.] had favored the Etruscan,  
> If the aged prince, feeling secure, had been overwhelmed,  
> Would at this very hour proclaim Sejanus  
> [Col. 1118B] Augustus.

(Juvenal, *Satires*, X, v. 70 ff.)

Furthermore, “Valentia of the people of Ocriculum,” Tertullian says (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 421). Ocriculum, or Ocriculi—Strabo’s Ὀκρίκλου (Ocriculum) (Strabo, *Geography*, bk. V, p. 227)—is a city on the borders of Umbria, not far from Rome, and is now called Otricoli. It is mentioned by Pliny (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. III, ch. 4, p. 323; ch. 14, p. 365), Livy (Livy, bk. IX, §41), and others, especially geographers. That Valentia actually was the goddess of the people of Ocriculum you will recognize from this ancient inscription in Gruter (Gruter, p. 2, inscr. 12):

> FOR THE SAFETY OF THE DEPARTURE AND RETURN OF OUR MOST SACRED LORD . . . TI. AUG., A SHRINE OF THE ASSEMBLY OF THE GODS AND GODDESSES, AUG. N., FOLLOWING A VISION OF THE GODDESS VALENTIA, S. P. E. C. [The unresolved source abbreviations are retained.]

[Col. 1118C]

What more? “Nortia of the people of Sutrium,” our author says (Tertullian, passage cited). But Sutrium, Livy says, “a city allied with the Romans, was like the gateway of Etruria” (Livy, bk. IX, §32; bk. VI, §3). He had already mentioned it earlier, and it also occurs in various inscriptions presented by Gruter (Gruter, pp. 254, 302, 305, 481). It lies twenty-four miles from the city of Rome, as Marsus noted on these words of Silius Italicus: “the roofs of Sutrium” (Silius Italicus, bk. VIII, v. 408). See Erasmus on the proverb “As though they were going to Sutrium” (Erasmus, *Adages*, chiliad 4, century 4, adage 52, p. 841). The goddess of this city’s inhabitants, moreover, was, as Tertullian says, Nortia. But previously, as we have seen, he had said “Nortia of the people of Volsinii.” Was [Col. 1118D] the same goddess, then, goddess of both peoples? Is he not enumerating particular gods proper to each city? Yet it was undoubtedly for this reason that, as we have noted, some wished the former name to be written a little differently. Against this emendation, however, stand not only all our manuscripts, but also the passage of Livy cited by us. But because Volsinii and Sutrium were cities of Etruria, and this goddess is called a goddess of Etruria by Livy, she could have been the goddess of both cities. If anyone should show that there were two goddesses called by different names, we shall willingly subscribe to his opinion.

Tertullian closes the troop of these municipal and local gods [Col. 1119A] with these words: “Among the Faliscans, in honor of Father Curis, Juno also received her surname” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24, p. 421; and bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8). Falisca, moreover, was a city of Etruria situated between Mount Ciminus and the Tiber. The colony of the Faliscans is mentioned in Pliny’s books (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. III, ch. 4, p. 320) and in Gruter’s inscriptions (Gruter, p. 288, inscr. 1), but more frequently in the histories of Titus Livy (Livy, bk. V, §§17, 18, 26; bk. VII, §17, etc.) and in these verses of Virgil:

> These hold the Fescennine ranks and the Aequian Faliscans;  
> These hold Soracte’s heights and the Flavinian fields,  
> Lake Ciminus with its mountain, and the groves of Capena.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VII, vv. 695 ff.)

You will find similar things celebrated by Silius Italicus (Silius Italicus, [Col. 1119B] bk. VIII, vv. 406 ff.). Juno, moreover, as no one fails to know, had many surnames, of which one, according to Festus, was *Curis*. If anyone asks why she was so called, let him hear Servius: “Juno has many names: she is *Curetis*, because she uses a chariot and spear” (Servius, on *Aeneid*, bk. I, v. 6). If he wishes, let him also hear Festus Pompeius: “*Curis* is the Sabine word for spear. . . . They called Juno *Curitis* because they believed her to carry a spear” (Festus, s.v. *Curis*). But just as these writers favor our Tertullian when he asserts that Juno was surnamed *Curris* or *Curetis*, so they oppose him when they openly state that this surname was not given to her in honor of Father Curis, but was derived from the spear, which the Sabines called *curis*, or from the chariot, as Servius implies. Servius, however, is criticized by some who consider the former [Col. 1119C] etymology of this name the truer.

What then? Can it be answered that Juno derived this surname from the spear, but that the Faliscans afterward conferred it upon her in honor of Father Curis? But who, you will ask, is that Father Curis? Ovid teaches us that Romulus was so called when he sings:

> The next day is vacant, but the third is named for Quirinus;  
> He who holds this name was Romulus before:  
> Whether because a spear was called *curis* by the ancient Sabines,  
> And the warlike god rose from his weapon to the stars;  
> Or because the Quirites bestowed the name upon their king;  
> Or because he had joined Cures to the Romans.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. II, §13.)

But not only Romulus: the name had previously been conferred upon Janus, as Macrobius attested in these words [Col. 1119D]: “In sacred rites we invoke Janus Junonius, Janus Quirinus . . . ‘Father,’ as though father of the gods; ‘Junonius,’ as though presiding not only over the entrance of January but over that of every month. All the Kalends are under Juno’s dominion. . . . ‘Quirinus,’ as though parent of wars, from the spear that the Sabines call *curis*” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 9). Janus thus had various names, three of which bear upon our purpose. The first is *Father*; the second, *Quirinus*, derived from *curis*, or “spear”; and the third, *Junonius*, as though he were the beginning and entrance both of January and of all the months. Can this not confirm Tertullian’s statement that Juno received her surname *Curis*, or *Curitis*, from Father Curis, who was also called Junonius? [Col. 1120A] Let others, however, judge this conjecture.

Moreover, according to the variant readings of our manuscripts, Tertullian’s words can bear two meanings. For if you read there, as in our handwritten copies and Rigault’s edition, “Among the Faliscans, in honor” (MSS: “in the honor”) “of Father Curis, Juno also received her name,” the meaning will be: “The goddess of the Faliscans is Juno, who obtained her designation *Curitis* in honor of Father Curis.” But if we read with the other editions, “Among the Faliscans, Father Curis is held in honor, from whom Juno received her surname,” these words will signify that divine honors were rendered by the Faliscans to Father Curis, from whom Juno was surnamed. But if he is speaking of the honor of Father Curis, why, I ask, is Juno—who has plainly nothing to do [Col. 1120B] with that matter—mentioned there? Do not those approach Tertullian’s meaning more closely who prove that he must be understood as referring to Juno Curitis, whom the Faliscans worshiped as the particular goddess of their city? You, however, weigh the matter and decide which reading and interpretation is the truer.

Someone may perhaps confront us and object that Tertullian here suffered a human lapse, since he so expressly affirms that the Romans rendered no divine honor to these gods of the provinces and cities whom he has named thus far (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24). For had not the Capitol previously been called by him “the senate-house of demons”? Are these not also his words in another book: “The amphitheater is consecrated by more numerous and harsher names than” (*quam* is absent from the older printed editions) “the Capitol is the senate-house of all the gods” (same author, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 12)? Did not Rome, as Leo I says, serve the errors of all nations and adopt their gods (Leo, sermon on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul)? The Romans therefore worshiped the gods of every nation. Yet although the matter is so, they worshiped all of them only collectively, not individually by name. For they could not even enumerate them, much less honor and invoke them! Tertullian, however, is discussing local and particular gods whom the inhabitants of cities and provinces were accustomed to worship as their own fellow citizens and to invoke by their own names.

What wonder, then, if most of them are now unknown to everyone, such as Delventinus and Visidianus, named in [Col. 1120D] the *Apologeticum*, and Numentinus or Numertinus of the Athenians—or rather of the Aternians—in the book *To the Nations* (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 24; and bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 8)? For knowledge of these and other local gods, whose number was infinite, was taken from us long ago. Yet our author’s argument is no less forceful on that account. From what has thus far been said, he most justly concludes that the pagans were exceedingly unjust: although they had the power to worship, according to their own pleasure and whim, any false god unknown to other nations, they did not permit Christians to adore the true God.

# CHAPTER XXVIII

## With what great folly the Romans boasted that by their piety toward the gods they had merited dominion over the whole world

[Col. 1121A]

### ARTICLE I

#### How false it is that the Romans merited dominion over the whole world by their piety toward the gods Sterculus, Mutinus, Larentia, Cybele, Jupiter, Juno, and others, who ought to have defended their own native lands rather than the Romans, and who were all subject to fate

We have seen the false religion of the pagans, who worshiped wholly fictitious gods, so overthrown by Tertullian with so many arguments of such great weight that no one, if he is of sound mind, seems capable of resisting them. But [Col. 1121B] because such is the obstinacy of most men in error that they never wish to confess themselves defeated, the pagans still rose up in opposition and objected to us, as Tertullian says, that “the Romans, in proportion to the merit of their most scrupulous religious observance, were raised so high that they took possession of the world” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 25, p. 422; and bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 17); that is, by their great piety and religious devotion toward their gods they merited and obtained dominion over the whole terrestrial globe. “These gods therefore exist,” they said, “and ought to be honored by all men.” This entire argument, which we have explained more fully elsewhere (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 16, arts. 2–3), our Tertullian not unjustly considers entirely frivolous and devoid of weight. Nevertheless, so as not to provide the pagans even the slightest occasion for muttering, he refutes and demolishes this argument, such as it is, with various answers.

For the gods of the Romans, he says, were either native and peculiar to them or foreign and adopted. Can it be said that the boundaries of the Roman Empire were extended by the former? “To be sure, this recompense”—these are the words of Tertullian mocking this opinion—“was entered to the Romans’ credit by the gods. Sterculus, Mutinus, and Larentina advanced the empire” (Tertullian, passage cited). In the older printed books, *si* is read in place of “to be sure,” but with entirely the same meaning, though in a less elegant expression. He names the vilest and plainly most infamous of the Roman gods there, so that he might sting the pagans, who most foolishly vaunted the power of their gods, with the sharper barbs of irony. Sterculus, as Tertullian teaches elsewhere, [Col. 1121D] was diligent in assisting the fields with manure (same author, bk. II, *To the Nations*, ch. 9). But we have previously discussed him, as well as the most shameful Mutinus and Larentina, whom Tertullian calls “a public prostitute,” both above and in our earlier dissertations (above, ch. 25, art. 3; *Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 17, art. 2; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 32, arts. 1–2). No one in possession of his faculties will ever dare seriously to affirm that the boundaries of the Roman Empire were extended by such infamous native gods. Nor were they extended by Rome’s other domestic and particular gods. For the power, excellence, and holiness of the true God, just like his nature, cannot exist in diverse forms in a plurality of beings. Yet no one has ever said that the aforementioned infamous gods, or the other domestic gods of the Romans, possessed the same nature and omnipotence, excellence and holiness, as [Col. 1122A] almighty God. They are therefore not gods and could not have brought any increase whatever to the Roman Empire.

It remains, then, that the greatness of the Roman Empire increased through the aid and power of foreign gods. Yet this opinion is no less wholly devoid of every appearance of probability than the preceding one. For, besides the argument just advanced: “I would not suppose,” as Tertullian rightly says, “that foreign gods wished to favor an alien nation more and to surrender to men from across the sea the native soil in which they were born, raised, ennobled, and buried” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 23); that is, that they favored their own native and nurturing land less than the Romans, who came from overseas and were foreigners. By what vice of an ungrateful disposition could they have delivered their native soil to be laid waste by the Romans [Col. 1122B] and subjected to their rule?

But, to make this clearer by some examples, he says: “Let Cybele—the daughter of Heaven and Earth, the wife of Saturn, and the Great Mother—see to it whether she loved the city of Rome in remembrance of the Trojan race, her own native people, of course, whom she had protected against the arms of the Achaeans; and whether she foresaw that she would pass over to her avengers, whom she knew would subdue Greece, the conqueror of Phrygia” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 424). To understand the force of this argument, it must be recalled that some think Cybele was surnamed from Mount Cybelus in Phrygia. No one doubts that her celebrated image was located at Pessinus, a city of Phrygia, and was afterward installed at Rome with the greatest pomp, as we have said elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 19, art. [Col. 1122C] 1; *On Arnobius*, ch. 20, art. 2; and *On Lactantius*, ch. 31, art. 3).

Tertullian then argues from this as follows: Did Cybele love the Romans on account of Aeneas, who came from Troy, a city of Lesser Phrygia, and was therefore her fellow countryman, because after he had been rescued from the burning of Troy and the arms of the Achaeans, they traced their origin back to him? Did she, moreover, despise her own native land and prefer the Romans to it because she foresaw that her image would be transferred to Rome and that Greece—the conqueror of her native Phrygia—would be conquered by the Romans? Why, then, did she allow Phrygia, where she was worshipped with the highest honor, to be taken by the Greeks? Yet grant, if you wish, that she allowed this. But how could she have foreknown that she herself—or, what amounts to the same thing, her image—would one day be carried from Pessinus to Rome? For she foresaw this no more than she foresaw the day on which the emperor Marcus Aurelius died at Sirmium. Indeed, Tertullian says, either she did not know it, or she sent very tardy messengers to her chief priest, the archigallus, who, on the sixth day after that emperor’s death, made an offering for his welfare of impure blood drawn from his own arms. Christians therefore rightly and deservedly ridiculed such a goddess, either ignorant of the future or cruel, who permitted not only the blood of her archigallus to be wrongly shed, but also her own native country to be utterly destroyed. She could therefore have rendered the Romans no assistance in extending the boundaries of their empire without displaying an unjust and ungrateful disposition.

[Col. 1123A] Nor should Jupiter have embraced them with any greater zeal and favor (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25). Could he have forgotten that cave on Mount Ida in the island of Crete, where the pagans proclaimed that he had been born and buried? Had his love of country been transformed into hatred, so that he allowed his own Crete, as Tertullian puts it (*ibid.*), to be shaken by the Roman fasces and arms? Had the brazen instruments of the Corybantes also slipped from his memory, whose clash and din frustrated the most savage cruelty of his father Saturn, who wished to devour him? Finally, had he willfully buried in oblivion the exceedingly pleasant odor of his nurse there (*ibid.*)?

Many, however, are uncertain who that nurse was and what her most pleasant odor was. Some suspect that in these words Tertullian alludes to [Col. 1123B] the horn of Amalthea, from which nectar and ambrosia flowed. But this suspicion is undoubtedly groundless. For the subject is Jupiter’s nurse, whom some believed to be the she-goat Amalthea, others the Nymphs, or daughters of Melissus, king of Crete. Accordingly, if our Author followed the latter opinion, the odor of the Nymphs, who were said to have nourished Jupiter with honey and milk, could rightly be called exceedingly pleasant. But if, as is more probable, he had the former in view, he is ironically assailing the foolish divinity of Jupiter, who had sucked the milk of a foul-smelling goat and could not forget that most repulsive odor. Yet if he always remembered her and his native Crete, he ought to have preferred Crete to the Capitol, and to have given dominion over the whole world to the Cretans rather than to the Romans. We have discussed elsewhere his birth, nurses, upbringing, and tomb [Col. 1123C] (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 2).

What, then, of Juno, this Jupiter’s sister and wife? Would she, Tertullian asks, have wished the Punic city of Carthage to be destroyed by the race of the sons of Aeneas (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 427; and bk. II *To the Nations*, ch. 17), that is, by the Romans? Did she not prefer that beloved city of hers to Samos, where she had been brought up or married to Jupiter, as is evident from these verses of Virgil, quoted by our Author only in part and without naming their author?

> One city more than all lands Juno is said  
> To have cherished, even setting Samos second. Here were her arms,  
> Here was her chariot; that this should be the ruling power  
> Over the nations, if somehow the Fates permit, the goddess even then both strove and cherished.

[Col. 1123D] (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. I, v. 19 ff.)

Yet that wretched wife and sister of Jupiter, Tertullian continues, however greatly she loved Carthage, could not prevent its being overthrown by the Romans. For she had no power against that city’s fatal destiny. Nor is this at all surprising, because, our Author continues, “Jupiter himself plainly stands subject to Fate” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 428). Is not that declaration confirmed quite openly by the Delphic Apollo’s response to the messengers of Croesus, which Herodotus reported in these very words: τὴν πεπρωμένην ἀδύνατά ἐστιν ἀποφυγεῖν καὶ θεῷ “Even for a god it is impossible to escape the lot appointed by Fate” (Herodotus, bk. I, § 91).

Concerning Jupiter himself, Cicero (Cicero, bk. II *On Divination*, p. 281, line 44) and Homer, [Col. 1124A] whom he cites (Homer, *Iliad* 16, v. 434; and *Odyssey* 3, v. 137 ff.), pronounce as follows: “Nothing occurs outside Fate.... Homer holds this view when he represents Jupiter lamenting that he could not rescue his son Sarpedon from death.” The same is signified by that Greek verse expressing the thought:

> What has been prepared to happen surpasses even supreme Jupiter.

Seneca likewise says: “Whatever it is that has commanded us to live thus and die thus binds the gods by the same necessity. An irrevocable course carries human and divine things alike. That very founder and ruler of all things did indeed write the Fates, but follows them; he always obeys, though he commanded only once” (Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 5, p. 501). Hence that Greek proverb, Ανάγχῃ οὐδὲ θεοὶ μαχόνται: “Not even the gods resist necessity.” See Erasmus’s observations on this proverb [Col. 1124B] and Lipsius’s on the words of Seneca just cited. See also Vossius (Vossius, bk. II *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, ch. 44, p. 276 ff.), and, if you wish, what we have remarked in our work on Minucius Felix concerning Fate, and in the following discussion concerning Jupiter and Juno (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 6, art. 3; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 31, art. 4).

If, therefore, Juno and Jupiter himself and all the gods are subject to Fate, as the pagans admit, they undoubtedly could never have granted any increase to the Roman Empire. For if Fate is more powerful than Jupiter and all the gods, the pagans, says Tertullian (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 428), ought surely to have bestowed greater honors upon the Fates, which surrendered Carthage to them, than upon Juno and that utterly prostituted she-wolf Larentina, [Col. 1124C] whom we discussed a little earlier. It is therefore false that by their great devotion toward Juno, Jupiter, and their other gods, whether native or imported, the Romans merited dominion over the whole world.

## ARTICLE II

### The Empire Was Not Given to the Romans Because of Their Devotion to the Gods, Since It Had Been Founded Before Numa Instituted the Various Rites—Here Explained—for Worshipping Those Gods, Before Images of the Gods Had Been Made, and Before There Was Any God at Rome

By still other weighty arguments Tertullian demonstrates (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 429) that the Romans could not have received their empire, or any extension of its boundaries, from any one of their gods or from all the [Col. 1124D] others together. For it is certain that several gods of the Romans—Saturn, Jupiter, and others—attained supreme royal power. Tell me, then, if you please, from what other gods whom they worshipped did they receive it? Was it given to Saturn by that thoroughly contemptible Sterculus whom we mentioned a little earlier? But he lived after Saturn. No pagan could ever say which other god gave Saturn his kingdom. Yet there is no better reason for saying that it was granted to the Romans by some god.

Moreover, their empire had been founded before the worship of the gods was established at Rome. For with Numa, says Tertullian (*ibid.*), began [Col. 1125A] “superstitious curiosity,” that is, religion and superstition—the depraved and perverse solicitude expended upon false gods. But for what reason do you suppose it was instituted by him? Consult Livy (Livy, bk. I, § 19 ff.), Eutropius (Eutropius, bk. I, *Breviary*, p. 64), and other writers of Roman history, and they will answer you: in order that he might restrain and refine the fierce and warlike dispositions of the Romans through fear of religion and the gods.

But what, pray, were those first rites of Roman religion? “At that time,” says our Author, “divine worship among the Romans did not yet consist either of images or of temples,” as we have explained elsewhere, where we investigated the origin of temples and images (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 430 ff.; and bk. I *To the Nations*, ch. 17, p. 583; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, bk. III, [Col. 1125B] dissertation 1, chs. 7 and 8, p. 717 ff.).

At that time, moreover, there were no “Capitols contending with heaven,” as he continues (*ibid.*, p. 28); that is, the Capitoline temple had not yet been constructed, so magnificent that it seemed to raise its summit as far as the heavens. Nor should you suppose this an exaggeration born of a mind excessively hostile to the pagans. For Martial, himself a pagan, sang the same thing in these verses:

> Nor the innermost shrine of the Capitoline Thunderer,  
> Nor the temples that gleam nearest to their own heaven.

(Martial, bk. II, Epigram 51.)

Silius Italicus likewise:

> She too, where the ancient royal house we faithfully revere now stands,  
> Will set golden Capitols upon the Tarpeian rock,  
> And the pinnacles of the temples will touch our heaven.

(Silius, bk. III, v. 620.) [Col. 1125C]

If you wish, you will readily find more material related in the books of Alexander Donatus and others on the city of Rome (Donatus, bk. II *On the City of Rome*, ch. 4 ff.).

Where, then, someone will ask, was divine worship conducted at that time? On “makeshift altars of turf,” says Tertullian (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 430; and bk. II *To the Nations*, ch. 17), that is, altars erected hastily, suddenly, and as occasion happened, as one may learn from Cicero (Cicero, bk. II *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 228, line 12) and Apuleius (Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, beginning). The vessels with which the service was performed, our Author says, were “squalid and still Samian”; that is, they were then made of clay and soft earth. We have discussed these elsewhere (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 30, art. 2).

Tertullian added (Tertullian, passage cited): [Col. 1125D] “And the smell from them,” as we read in both of his works, the *Apology* and the second book *To the Nations*. In our manuscripts, however, one of these two words has, as frequently happens, been written as a single word: *exillis*. From this perhaps Rigaltius wished to emend it to *exilis* (“meager”), by a conjecture not altogether infelicitous, though he ought to have offered at least some reason for it. It can be supported by the fact that in the same place Tertullian asserts that the rites of Roman religion were then poor. Yet the two words *ex illis* (“from them”) can also refer to the Samian vessels to which they are appended. We therefore dare determine nothing concerning this variant reading.

Moreover, because in Numa’s time there were no images of the gods among the Romans—indeed, [Col. 1126A] because he had forbidden them to be made, as we have shown elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 733 and 1227 ff.)—Tertullian inferred from this: “And God himself was nowhere.” For he seems to have been wholly persuaded, as we shall see in the following chapter, that the opinion had spread throughout the minds of the pagans that there were no gods other than their images, or that the divinity of the gods resided in them.

You therefore see how rightly he concludes from what has been said: “Thus the Romans were not religious before they were great, and consequently they were not great because they were religious” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 430). For their empire had been founded and established before either they had gods or, at least, worshipped and adored them with so many superstitious rites and such an empty display of ceremonies. Yet surely they needed an equal measure of the gods’ aid and support both for extending that empire and for laying [Col. 1126B] its foundations—aid which it is nevertheless manifest they never possessed. But this is demonstrated by Tertullian even more clearly through other arguments, which we must examine.

## ARTICLE III

### The Empire of the Romans Was No More Given or Extended by Any Gods of the Pagans Than Were the Empires of the Babylonians, Medes, Egyptians, Assyrians, Amazons, and Jews, Who Reigned Before Those Same Romans; That the Romans Extended the Boundaries of Their Empire by Impiety and Sacrilege; and That the Existence of Any of These or the Other Pagan Gods Cannot Be Proved by Any Miracles, Divinations, or Oracles Whatever

[Col. 1126C] It is indeed certain, and the Romans themselves openly admitted it, that earthly kingdoms are instituted, granted, and dispensed by someone. But that power can belong only to him alone who created all things. Accordingly, none of the Roman gods ever gave any kingdom to their worshippers or to others. And surely, before their Pontiffs, Quindecimvirs, Salii, Luperci, and Vestals—whom we have discussed elsewhere—and before all the ministers of the Roman gods, indeed before any gods were worshipped at Rome, the kingdoms of the Babylonians, Medes, Egyptians, Assyrians, and Amazons had been established and, as everyone knows, flourished with great power and glory (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 26, p. 432; and bk. II *To the Nations*, ch. 27, p. 583).

It is therefore evident that these nations received the power to reign neither from the Roman gods nor from those whom they themselves worshipped: [Col. 1126D] not from their own gods, who could not defend those by whom they were held in the highest honor; nor from the Roman gods, who had not yet been fashioned and by whom the Romans believed the empires of those nations to have been overthrown. We have already seen (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 18, arts. 4 and 5) how Minucius Felix employed this argument against the pagans.

But to make the point clearer by certain examples, Tertullian presses them: “Why did Minerva not defend Athens from Xerxes, or why did Apollo not rescue Delphi from the hand of Pyrrhus?” (Tertullian, bk. II *To the Nations*, passage cited). For no pagan god either at Rome or anywhere else was adorned with such great divine honor as Minerva [Col. 1127A] at Athens, where her renowned image, known to everyone, stood. Nor was any god honored with greater worship than Apollo at Delphi, where he was believed to issue oracles celebrated throughout the whole world. Nevertheless, neither Apollo rendered Delphi safe from the arms of its enemies, nor Minerva Athens. How, then, could gods, whether foreign or native, extend the boundaries of the Roman Empire? Were they more powerful than the other gods? But the true God must be omnipotent and therefore can only be one: he who grants and dispenses kingdoms.

Come now, and let us follow Tertullian as he presses his case (same author, *Apology*, ch. 26, p. 432). The Jews, he says, had their own kings, whom they would possess even now, had they not bloodied their hands with the dreadful parricide against Christ. [Col. 1127B] Yet these same Jews utterly despised the gods of the Romans. They did not, therefore, merit their kingdom through devotion to those gods. The Romans, moreover, having made a treaty with these enemies of their gods, honored their God with slaughtered victims and endowed his temple with gifts and offerings. With what eyes, I ask you, could those gods look upon the treaties, sacrifices, and gifts made by the Romans to the true God and to their own adversary? Ought these things not to have inflamed their wrath rather than their inclination to enlarge the boundaries of the Roman Empire?

Furthermore, it is absolutely certain that kingdoms are seized and invaded by men through arms and victories (*ibid.*, ch. 25, p. 431). Yet these things cannot generally occur without cities being overthrown and, consequently, temples and walls alike being destroyed, priests and citizens alike being slain, [Col. 1127C] and sacred and profane property alike being carried off and plundered. Thus, says Tertullian (*ibid.*), the Romans committed as many sacrileges as they erected trophies carried to Rome from the sacred and profane spoils of captured cities; they celebrated as many triumphs over gods who could not protect their own countries and the cities in which they were worshipped as over nations. They had as much booty as there still remain at Rome images of captive gods.

The term *manubiae* (“spoils”), which we have discussed elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 16, art. 2; and *On Lactantius*, ch. 31, art. 4), appears there to be used by Tertullian for spoils which the Romans carried back with them to Rome from captured cities. Chief among them were images of the gods, which they customarily installed in temples and thereafter adored. The Roman Empire therefore increased not through any devotion or religious observance toward the gods, [Col. 1127D] but through impiety, crimes, and sacrileges.

By what reasoning, then, our Author continues, do those gods permit themselves to be worshipped by their enemies, the Romans, and give an empire without end to men whose injuries, rather than their acts of worship, they ought to have requited? In our manuscripts and various editions, especially the older ones, the reading is *adolationes*, or *adulationes* (“flatteries”), as it occurs differently written by others. Some, however, have preferred *adorationes* (“acts of worship”), so that this noun may correspond to the preceding verb *adorari* (“to be worshipped”). But what if Tertullian meant that the gods could not patiently endure flatteries—that is, the empty blandishments of their worship—offered by those who flattered them at the very time they were devastating everything through impiety and sacrilege? Whichever reading you decide upon, [Col. 1128A] it must be admitted that nothing more absurd can be imagined than that the Romans enlarged the boundaries of their empire through devotion to the gods, although they had extended those boundaries through wars and victories, and consequently not without injury and insult to those very gods.

By most of the same arguments of Tertullian against the Roman gods that we have expounded thus far, Minucius Felix utterly demolished the fictitious divinity of those same powers, as we showed in our first dissertation (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 16, arts. 2 and 3).

Yet the Romans and all other pagans insisted that their gods were true gods, since by astonishing signs, miracles, predictions, oracles, divinations, and certain deeds which seemed to surpass all the powers of created things, [Col. 1128B] they had time and again proved their divinity and omnipotence. And certainly these things, which they believed to have been performed outside the customary order of nature, had so bewitched their eyes and minds that they were altogether persuaded they must be attributed to the power of the gods alone. But Tertullian shows that this argument is advanced and pressed only by those who were ignorant of the true cause of those effects.

Once empty prejudices had been set aside, they could have recognized that all these things had been done through the extraordinary agility of demons, their evil arts, deceits, frauds, and impostures, by which these lying and impure spirits wholly deluded unwary men. To this is added the fact that the pagans could not deny that many deeds resembling the extraordinary acts of their gods, as they supposed them to be, had been performed by men devoted to magic, [Col. 1128C] through the deceits and frauds of the same demons. Who, then, unless he were mad, would say that these men were therefore true gods? We have attempted above to elucidate and disclose the nature and weight of the arguments by which Tertullian proved this point (above, ch. 8, art. 3 ff.). In earlier dissertations we also explained these and many others besides (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, ch. 16, art. 1 ff.; *Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 18, art. 1 ff.; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 32, art. 4), by which other defenders and champions of our religion uprooted this pagan opinion and argument.

# CHAPTER XXIX

## On the Images, Statues, and Representations of the Gods

## ARTICLE I

### By What Arguments Tertullian Demonstrates That Images of the Gods Should Not Be Worshipped: There Were None at Rome Before Numa Pompilius, Nor for a Long Time Thereafter; They Were Made from the Same Material as Cheap Vessels; Through a Ridiculous Consecration They Changed Their Destiny; Fashioned by Artisans, They Were Subjected to Various Insults by Beasts and Men; and Beasts Were Most Absurdly Assigned to Liber, Cybele, and Caelestis

[Col. 1128D]

Since it has been demonstrated more than sufficiently that the gods of the pagans are false and nonexistent, [Col. 1129A] it necessarily follows that their images, statues, and representations are empty things, deserving no honor whatever. For what can the image of a false god be except false? It is therefore never worshipped and adored without great impiety. Tertullian, however, refutes and assails this error of the pagans with certain particular arguments, which must now be explained by us.

We have already heard him say that no images or representations of the gods were made at Rome during the reign of Numa Pompilius or before his age (preceding chapter, art. 1). For “at that time,” he says, “the talents of the Greeks and Tuscans had not yet flooded the City with the fashioning of images” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 430). Here he seems to allude to the opinion of Tatian, as we observed elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 543), and of others who believed that the Tuscans were the inventors of pottery and [Col. 1129B] of fashioning images from clay and earthenware. Yet these images of the gods were not brought to Rome immediately after Numa Pompilius died. For, as Varro—cited by Augustine—and Clement of Alexandria testify, the Romans worshipped their gods without images for one hundred and seventy years or more. But we have discussed these matters in the already cited volume of our *Apparatus* (*ibid.*), and have shown there in addition that Numa forbade any image or representation to be made.

Throughout that entire period, therefore, in which the Romans lacked them, “God himself,” says Tertullian, “was nowhere” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 430). Why, except because the pagans had persuaded themselves that the images of the gods were in actual fact their gods? Indeed, Clement of Alexandria, whom we have also cited elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, [Col. 1129C] p. 734), confidently asserts that in those later times the pagans fashioned the gods whom they worshipped. Tertullian had therefore said elsewhere that the gods were valued by those same pagans according to the temples in which their images had been placed (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 10, p. 330; and ch. 25, p. 427). Elsewhere he calls those same images of the gods, which the Romans, as we said before, carried to Rome in triumphal procession, “captive gods.” But it is superfluous to prove at greater length what he everywhere assumes as certain and what will appear more clearly from what is about to be said.

With what great blindness, however, the true God, he says, is despised by the pagans, while the statues of those same gods are worshipped (same author, *Apology*, ch. 41, p. 488)! [Col. 1129D] For what was there to be discerned in them except that their materials were “sisters of common vessels and utensils,” or that they were made from those same vessels and utensils, “as though changing their destiny by consecration, while the license of art transformed them” (*ibid.*, ch. 12, p. 339)? He thus openly declares that the materials of the images—that is, the woods and metals of which they were made—were the same as those of the vessels and utensils destined for common, and sometimes exceedingly base, human use. Thus they had changed their destiny and lot, first at the will and whim of the craftsmen by whom they were fashioned, and then by the ridiculous consecration upon receiving which at last they were worshipped by the pagans as true gods. But we have pursued these matters at greater length elsewhere (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 19, art. 4), [Col. 1130A] and made plain how insane and absurd this pagan opinion is.

For what greater disgrace can there be than to pursue with divine honor gods who, Tertullian says, “trace their rank from metals” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 12, p. 339)—where we must undoubtedly understand “originated and were made”? For Juvenal used the verb *censeri* in this same sense when he sang:

> What do pedigrees accomplish? What profit is there, Ponticus,  
> In tracing one’s rank through a long lineage? . . .

(Juvenal, *Satire* 8, v. 1.)

Moreover, whether these images of the gods were to be made from metals depended upon the decision of the emperor, who owned those metals (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 29, p. 439). According to his nod and will, therefore, those gods were made [Col. 1130B] or rejected. How many insults, besides, do they undergo in being fashioned and manufactured by artisans? First, says Tertullian (*ibid.*, ch. 12, p. 339), “they are built upon a cross and a stake”; next they are shaped with axes and cut with large saws, while with rasps—that is, files—they are polished smooth. What of the fact that before the lead, he adds, the glue, and the *gomphoi*, in Greek γόμφους, or nails by which they are joined together, the gods are headless? (Varro, bk. VI *On the Latin Language*, p. 54.) Does he not signify by these words that the head of the image was made separately, afterward set upon its body, and fastened to it with nails?

But these “distinguished gods,” as he calls them (Tertullian, passage cited, p. 339), or images animated by no breath of life, do not feel these indignities. For statues and cold images, most like dead men, [Col. 1130C] are no more affected by the dishonor of their manufacture than by the worship and homage of those who adore them. To this is added the fact that “kites, mice, and spiders,” he says, “understand this insensibility of the images” (*ibid.*), since they nest in those statues with impunity and defile them with their droppings. Thieves and other impious men understood it even more readily, for these images could never be safe from their thefts and insults without guards of imperial soldiers. But we have elucidated these matters in our earlier dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 21, art. 1; *On Arnobius*, ch. 22, art. 3; and *On Lactantius*, ch. 33, art. 5).

Against this the pagans clamored that these were impious expressions and sacrilegious insults. “But gnash your teeth,” our Author says to them, “and foam as much as you wish; assuredly these outcries will do you no good. For you have at some time heard [Col. 1130D] a certain Seneca, whom you cannot contradict, arguing against your superstition in more numerous and more bitter words” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 12, p. 339). We have indicated what these words of Seneca were in another of our dissertations, where we also cited this passage of Tertullian (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 33, art. 3). Yet even if Seneca had remained silent, our Author’s argument is no less valid: the pagans could indeed foam against it in rage, but could not break its force.

Who, then, will not deplore the blind impiety of those who, so that greater veneration might be shown to their gods, or images, “assigned beasts,” says Tertullian, “to Liber, Cybele, and Caelestis” (Tertullian, *Apology*, [Col. 1131A] ch. 12, p. 339), that is, to the chariots in which they were represented as riding? Liber’s chariot was drawn by tigers, as may be learned from Ovid (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, final fable; and *The Art of Love*, v. 560) and many others. It will therefore suffice to cite these verses of Virgil:

> And Liber, who, victorious, turns the yokes with vine-leaf reins,  
> Driving tigers down from Nysa’s lofty summit.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VI, v. 779.)

Cybele’s chariot, however, was carried by lions, as Lucretius sings:

> Her the learned poets of the Greeks in ancient times sang  
> As driving paired lions from her seat upon a chariot,  
> Teaching that the great earth hangs within the expanse of air  
> And that earth cannot rest upon the earth.

(Lucretius, bk. II, v. 600 ff.)

Diodorus Siculus writes that lions and leopards [Col. 1131B] were placed beside this goddess’s image because she was said to have been nourished by them (Diodorus, bk. III of the *Library*, p. 135).

The third goddess to whose chariot beasts were yoked is called *Caelestis* by Tertullian, as it is written in our manuscripts, though some others read *Cereri* (“to Ceres”). Now Ceres was indeed called Caelestis, and her chariot was carried by serpents, as Ovid confirms in these verses:

> . . . The fertile goddess yoked twin serpents  
> To her chariot and curbed their mouths with bridles,  
> And was carried through the air midway between heaven and earth.

(Ovid, bk. V of the *Metamorphoses*, final fable.)

Yet not Ceres alone, but Venus also was surnamed Caelestis, and they babbled that her chariot was drawn by swans and doves. If you ask for a witness, Ovid is again at hand:

[Col. 1131C]

> Carried in her light chariot through the midst of the air,  
> Cytherea had not yet reached Cyprus on swans’ wings.

(*Ibid.*, bk. X, final section.)

And later:

> And through the light air she rode, borne by yoked doves.

Finally, the chariot of Juno, who was also called Caelestis, was drawn by horses, as Homer and Virgil attest, and by peacocks, as others testify. For Ovid again sang:

> . . . Saturn’s daughter, in her well-fitted chariot,  
> Enters the clear upper air with painted peacocks.

(Ovid, bk. II of the *Metamorphoses*, shortly before the end.)

It is therefore as difficult to say what Tertullian signifies by the name *Caelestis* as it is easy to prove that beasts were, as Tertullian says, assigned by the pagans to their gods or their images. Yet no person of sound mind [Col. 1131D] will ever deny that nothing is more absurd than seriously venerating and worshipping such images as true gods or as endowed with divine power.

## ARTICLE II

### How Absurdly the Pagans Said That Images Were Their Gods, Although Very Many Worshipped Certain Gods Unknown to Others and Adopted by Themselves, or Pawned and Sold Their Household Gods and Exchanged Them for the Cheapest Vessels, or Offered Public Gods for Sale at Auction, and Considered Those Gods Holier Who Were More Heavily Taxed and Sold at a Higher Price

Tertullian could not patiently endure the pagans [Col. 1132A] who, willfully closing their eyes to the light of right reason, which shone more brightly than the noonday sun, contended with extraordinary obstinacy that the images, statues, and representations of false gods must be retained and worshipped. For in place of a reason, he says, there was only that foolish outcry: “These are gods to us” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 13, p. 344). But these were mere words by which they were wholly condemned on their own judgment.

For they could not deny that no one could be named and honored as a god without the Senate’s approval, as we saw above (ch. 18, art. 9). Nevertheless, it lay within the power of any pagan to choose or reject whatever god he wished, or whatever image of a god pleased him. Thus, a god accepted by one person was rejected by another at his pleasure. Yet this could not be done without injury to the rejected god, [Col. 1132B] or, as Tertullian himself says in addressing them: “Since some of you worship some gods and others worship others, you certainly offend those whom you do not worship. Preference for one cannot proceed without insult to another” (Tertullian, passage cited).

Some think that Augustine had these words in view where he censures and refutes this entire argument as follows: “I do not say what Tertullian says, perhaps more wittily than truly: ‘If gods are selected like onions, then surely the rest are judged rejected.’ I do not say this. For I see that even from among selected persons some are selected for some greater and more distinguished purpose; as in the army, when recruits have been chosen, from among these too some are chosen for some greater military task.... There is no need to go through many examples when the matter is obvious. Therefore, it is not because certain gods have been selected from among many that either the writer who recorded this, their worshippers, [Col. 1132C] or the gods themselves ought to be censured; rather, one must consider who these are and for what purpose they appear to have been selected” (Augustine, bk. VII *City of God*, ch. 1, p. 162).

It may perhaps be answered, however, that Augustine is there speaking of the pagans’ select gods, while Tertullian, in the cited passage, is discussing images of gods of every kind. But others will object that the pagans, as we have said, believed those very images to be their gods. Moreover, although they did not always speak of both in the same way, Augustine’s argument against Tertullian nevertheless seems no less forceful. Yet it cannot be denied that its weight is far greater if Augustine had in view what our Author argued at greater length in the books *To the Nations* against Varro’s opinion concerning the select gods themselves (Tertullian, bk. II *To the Nations*, ch. 9), and especially these words of his: “If the pagans had certain gods, [Col. 1132D] they ought to have been content with them and not to desire select gods. In this too they are detected as irreligious. For if gods, as you wish, are selected, those who are not selected are declared rejected” (*ibid.*). Some were so persuaded that Augustine was referring to this passage that, following him, they boldly restored the noun *bulbi* (“onions”) in this text in place of the verb *vultis* (“you wish”).

Someone will nevertheless insist in reply that Tertullian, even though he discusses images of the gods in the *Apology*, drew from those things which the pagans believed to be gods the same conclusion as he drew in the book *To the Nations* concerning the select gods themselves: “The status of each god depended upon the Senate’s estimation. No one was a god unless a man, [Col. 1133A] when consulted, had wished him to be one” (same author, *Apology*, ch. 13, p. 344). But he must observe that these words do not denote select gods, but the images of gods of every kind, which the pagans, as Tertullian added in that same place, could pawn, sell, exchange, and break at pleasure. Yet this could not occur without their disgrace and dishonor, especially when one was rejected and another chosen. Can it not also be said that the force of the argument Tertullian drew from this rests in the fact that whatever gods are imagined must either be omnipotent or be no gods at all? But from among several omnipotent beings one cannot be chosen as stronger than another, although this may certainly be done among recruits and soldiers.

But if this entire line of argument seems altogether weak to you, take from him another, which you will doubtless [Col. 1133B] acknowledge to carry greater weight. It is established, he says, that all the images of the pagans—or, what amounts to the same thing, all their gods—were either domestic and private or common and public. The first were called Lares and Penates, which each person used to keep at home and worship according to a particular rite (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 344, and book I *Ad Nationes*, ch. 10). Tibullus has these verses about the Penates:

> But may it be my lot to honor my ancestral Penates  
> And render monthly incense to the ancient Lar.

(Tibullus, book I, elegy 3, v. 33.)

We may add, if one wishes, these lines published by Virgil:

> Within are fifty maidservants, whose task in long succession  
> Is to lay out the provisions and honor the Penates with flames.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book I, v. 707.)

[Col. 1133C] Juvenal, for his part, sang of the Lares:

> O humble Lares who are ours, whom I am accustomed to adorn  
> With a little incense, or meal, or a slender garland.

(Juvenal, satire 9, near the end.)

There is no need to gather here the many other things repeatedly celebrated by the pagans about both, in prose and verse. Yet such was those same pagans’ fickleness of mind and such their impious contempt for their gods that, against those whom they had long worshiped, as Tertullian says, they exercised “domestic authority by pawning, selling, and altering them—sometimes making a cooking pot out of Saturn, a drinking vessel out of Minerva” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 344). Thus, just as the pagans fashioned images, or gods, out of vessels intended for the basest uses, as we saw above, so afterward [Col. 1133D] they fashioned other vessels out of these images, or pawned or sold them. From Saturn, or an image of Saturn, they would sometimes make a *cacabŭlum*, that is, a small *cacabum*, which, according to Varro, was a vessel in which they cooked food; from it they derived the name *cacabum* (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV, § 27). A *trulla*, however, was a drinking vessel, as is clear from these verses of Horace:

> He who on feast days was accustomed to drink Veientan wine  
> From a Campanian *trulla*.

(Horace, book II, satire 3, v. 143.)

This is also confirmed by Juvenal (Juvenal, satire 3, v. 112). Sometimes, however, others seem to use the word for a vessel into which the burden of the bowels was discharged, as we showed in another dissertation (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, final chapter, final article), [Col. 1134A] but we shall be more readily persuaded that Tertullian took it in the former sense, since in the same place he spoke of a vessel used for preparing food. We have said something about the *trulla* and *cacabŭlum* in the dissertation cited.

Furthermore, there were two reasons why these gods, or images, were altered, pawned, and sold by the pagans. The first, says Tertullian, was “as each god has been worn and battered through long worship” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 344). Thus they rejected a god eaten away or disfigured by age, or exchanged it for another. The second reason was: “As each of the gods found domestic necessity more sacred.” So indeed Rigault; but in the Froben edition: “And each one the master.” Better in the other editions [Col. 1134B] and in all our unpublished copies: “As each master”—that is, the master of that god and image—“has found a more sacred domestic necessity” (p. 345). But what, someone will ask, does the word “more sacred” mean there? Some reply that Tertullian meant nothing other than that the poor owner sold this god because his own need and poverty seemed more sacred to him than his god. For they think an extreme and most urgent necessity is called “more sacred,” just as Livy calls the treasury “more sacred,” because, he says, it “was reserved for the final emergencies” (Livy, book XXVII, § 10). Cicero might also have been cited, who wrote to Atticus that it had been decreed that they should withdraw money from the “more sacred treasury” (Cicero, book VIII, letter 20 to Atticus, p. 284, line 5).

Yet would the man stray entirely from the point [Col. 1134C] who said that the adjective “more sacred” refers not to “necessity,” but to “god”? For the more sacred the pagans supposed a god to be, the more dearly they sold it. Indeed Tertullian himself says in that same place and in the book *Ad Nationes*: “The more sacred the gods, the more heavily taxed” (Tertullian, *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10). But whether the god—or rather the pagans’ necessity—is designated by this term “more sacred,” Tertullian rightly reproaches them in these words: “The private gods whom you declare to be Lares and Penates through domestic consecration, you trample underfoot by domestic license, selling and pawning them according to need and inclination” (*ibid.*, p. 55).

They valued their public gods no more highly; as he continues, they “dishonored them equally under public law” (the same author, [Col. 1134D] *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 345, and *Ad Nationes*, book I, passage cited)—indeed, they treated them still more disgracefully and insultingly. For each person sold his private gods at his own discretion, certainly, but did so privately; their public gods, however, they sold publicly, since they held them in the *hastarium* as taxable property (*ibid.*). According to Turnebus (*Adversaria*, book XXVIII, ch. 5), the *hastarium* was the place where the property of proscribed persons was sold. Rigault, however, thinks the term signifies the *liber hastarius*, a record book or register of taxes, which were customarily auctioned to contractors every five years beneath a spear and at the herald’s proclamation. And indeed our author says: “Those whom you have entered in the *hastarium*, you auction to tax-farmers under . . . every five years, proscribed among your revenues” (Tertullian, [Col. 1135A] *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10; text materially defective).

But Tertullian undoubtedly appears to signify both of these. For he says that public gods were transferred to that place where, like the other possessions of proscribed persons, after first being recorded in the public register, they were kept for five years until sold publicly; and thus “under the same spear,” as he says, “under the same notation of the quaestor, their divinity is auctioned off.” Could not *hastarium* have taken its name both from that spear and from the quaestor’s notation or register?

Whatever the case, these gods were considered not only saleable but also taxable, says Tertullian, because some tax or tribute was paid for their five-year stay in the *hastarium* (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 344). With how much disgrace and reproach, then, I ask you, [Col. 1135B] were those wretched gods afflicted? If you ask how people went there to sell and buy them, Tertullian will answer: “Thus one goes to the Capitol; thus to the vegetable market” (the same author, *ibid.*). Some printed editions less correctly have “if . . . if” in place of “thus . . . thus.” For in the book *Ad Nationes* we read: “Thus one goes to the Serapeum; thus to the Capitol” (*Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10, p. 55). That is, the *hastarium* was leased for storing and selling gods in the same manner and subject to the same tax as the Capitol, the Serapeum, and the vegetable market. No one could enter those temples, or sell anything in the vegetable market, without paying the tax. Therefore, he concludes, “the more heavily taxed, the more sacred—indeed, the more sacred, the more heavily taxed” (*ibid.*); that is, the more sacred a god was judged in the pagans’ false opinion, [Col. 1135C] the greater the price and tax demanded for its stay in the *hastarium* and its sale.

If someone should now ask us who those public gods were, we shall reply that they were chiefly of three kinds. Some were placed in temples; others were either manufactured or bought and imported; others, finally, were openly carried around through streets and squares, as we noted above (above, ch. 24, art. 4). The first were customarily taxed and sold merely because of their age; the second and third at the pagans’ discretion. Did not those who branded their gods with such infamy openly confess, even against their will, that neither they nor their images were gods or worthy of any divine honor?

### ARTICLE III. How perversely the pagans consecrated Simon Magus, like their other gods, by means of a statue of a holy god; how they represented them all in the same dress and with the same insignia as belonged to their age, craft, and occupation before death; and how they erected equivalent statues to their emperors, whether dead or alive—and why nothing can be inferred from this against the sacred images of Christians

[Col. 1135D]

Tertullian’s final argument against the insane worshipers of images is not altogether free of difficulty. Let us therefore listen to him a little longer as he rebukes the pagans in these words: “With what effrontery,” he says, “do you worship Junos, Cereses, and Dianas”—that is, images of those and of your other goddesses and gods—[Col. 1136A] “when you consecrate Simon Magus with a statue and an inscription as a holy god?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 347).

We observed that Justin Martyr reported that, in the reign of Claudius, a statue was erected to this Simon Magus on the Tiber Island between the two bridges, bearing the inscription: “To Simon, the holy god” (*Simoni sancto deo*) (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 6). Cyril of Jerusalem supports the most holy martyr (Cyril, catechesis 6, p. 157), saying that it was erected by the same emperor Claudius; and Eusebius (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, p. 52) unhesitatingly affirms that it was erected by the Romans. To cite other witnesses here would be as easy as it would be superfluous. Everyone indeed concedes that this was the common opinion of the ancient writers.

Recent critics, however, boldly assert that this opinion [Col. 1136B] rests upon a gross error which, originating with Justin himself, who was utterly ignorant of Latin, subsequently spread through the minds of the rest. For when, they say, he had persuaded himself that the statue of the god Semo Sancus Fidius was the same as that of Simon Magus, all the others incautiously agreed with him, since he himself had been deceived by a false resemblance of names.

What then? Did everyone do so, including not only those who knew Greek but those who knew Latin, and even those who came to Rome after Justin Martyr? Did none of them detect this error, or warn anyone of it once he had recognized it? Because in recent times a statue of Semo Sancus was found, does it necessarily follow that in Justin’s time there was no statue of Simon Magus? What of the fact that Augustine bears explicit witness that Simon Magus himself had images made of himself and of Helen the prostitute, [Col. 1136C] which, he says, “he offered to his disciples for worship and had erected at Rome as images of gods by public authority” (Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 1, p. 6)? But if he erected these images at Rome, could not one of them still have existed in Justin’s time? What, then, prevents the conclusion that that holy martyr and others after him either saw one of them or were informed that others had seen it?

But suppose, if you please, that Justin, Augustine, and very many others were mistaken; Tertullian’s argument against the statues of the gods nevertheless remains no less valid. Everyone at least admits that an image of Semo Sancus was erected at Rome. But it was no less impious to worship the image [Col. 1136D] of this false god than the image of Simon Magus. Moreover, Tertullian says that in statues of the gods “the dress is the same, the insignia are the same; and as were the age, craft, and occupation of the dead man, so is the god” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 347). What could be more absurd than that, as he wrote in another book, “an old man is fashioned in Saturn, a beardless youth in Apollo, a virgin in Diana, a soldier is consecrated in Mars, and an ironworker in Vulcan” (the same author, *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10)? Who, on seeing them, would not immediately perceive that they had been human beings, formerly engaged even in lowly crafts, and thus could never have been gods? It was therefore an act of the highest impiety to worship their statues and images as those of gods.

Finally, these same pagans erected temples not only to these and their other ancient [Col. 1137A] gods, but also to their dead emperors, and sometimes to emperors still living, as we shall say shortly; in those temples their images were placed and worshiped with the same honor as the rest of their gods. What greater impiety could there be than to adore and venerate as a true god the image of a living or dead man, who while alive had often been defiled by every kind of crime? Yet this detestable superstition belonged not only to an insane and ignorant rabble, but also to others who possessed the greatest ability and authority. For Pliny wrote the following to the emperor Trajan concerning himself and certain persons who denied that they were Christians: “When, with me leading them, they invoked the gods and offered incense and wine in supplication to your image—which for this purpose I had ordered to be brought in with the images of the divinities—[Col. 1137B] and moreover cursed Christ, none of which, it is said, those who are truly Christians can be compelled to do” (Pliny, book X, letter 101 to Trajan). It is certainly no wonder that true Christians utterly and absolutely refused an act that could not be performed without incurring the gravest guilt of idolatry.

The pagans, therefore, must no longer be heard when they objected to us that help was given them by such statues and images of the gods, especially the ancient gods, that oracles were delivered from them, or that some supposed miracles were performed. For do not the things we have said about these gods or images demonstrate more clearly than the noonday sun that nothing—much less miracles—could be performed by them? Moreover, Tertullian, as we saw above, plainly shows that if anything appeared to have been done by them outside the customary order of nature, it [Col. 1137C] was to be attributed to the evil arts, deceptions, and frauds of demons, who, lying concealed, as he puts it, “beneath the prostitution of images and the consecration of human names” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 27), deceived the unwary minds of the pagans. But we have discussed these matters sufficiently above (above, ch. 10, art. 3 and following).

Nor is there any reason for some heretic to snarl in our ear or shout openly that from what has thus far been elucidated after Tertullian one may conclude that he condemned absolutely all sacred images of Christians. For he discussed none other than images of false gods, which, as has been sufficiently proved, cannot be worshiped without the vice of sacrilegious impiety (Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, ch. 5). Nor will another person have any stronger grounds [Col. 1137D] for insisting that elsewhere he firmly declared that every kind of statue and image was forbidden by the divine law of Moses. For in the same place he asserts no less clearly that by God’s command Moses himself made images or statues of the bronze serpent, the Cherubim, and others, which for that reason entailed no corrupt worship or idolatry. He therefore judged that images which have no affinity with the impious worship of idols are not to be condemned. These matters, however, have been explained more fully in the first volume of our *Apparatus* and in other earlier dissertations of ours (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 748; *Dissertation on Minucius’s Octavius*, ch. 29, art. 1 and following; *Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 22, art. 1 and following; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 34, art. 1 and following). If those discussions are compared with what we have related here, [Col. 1138A] they will cast and receive fresh, reciprocal light upon one another.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Temples and Sacrifices of the Pagans

### ARTICLE I. With what great impiety the pagans built temples and altars to their gods and to dead and living emperors; how they exacted payment for the temple site, the entrance, the doors, and the doorposts; and with what unspeakable crimes they polluted those same temples, which Christians did not frequent even by day

By the same arguments with which Tertullian demonstrates that images and statues of false gods are opposed to true religion, he demonstrates that their temples also must not be built. [Col. 1138B] For it has never been permissible to construct temples to a false god, much less to a dead or living human being as though he were the true God. Who, then, could calmly endure those pagans who had erected temples—or, as Tertullian calls them, shrines and altars—not only to fictitious ancient gods but also to their dead and living emperors? For this reason he addresses and mocks them with these words: “You worthily assign the honor of divinity to deceased emperors, since you also award it to them while living”; or, as he added in another book, “you establish priesthoods, sacred apparatus, sacred carriages, chariots, *solisternia*”—that is, seats and thrones—“and even *lectisternia*” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13, p. 344; *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10). Lest anyone doubt that those temples were consecrated to these new gods, the pagans themselves took care to inscribe upon the thresholds and altars conspicuous [Col. 1138C] titles naming the gods to whom they were dedicated.

If anyone should wish examples of temples dedicated to emperors to be produced, here are Suetonius’s words about Julius Caesar: “He allowed honors surpassing the elevation of a human being to be decreed to him: temples, altars, images, a sacred couch beside the gods, flamens, and Luperci” (Suetonius, book I, § 76). Indeed, this insane impiety of the pagans went so far that Valerius Maximus dared to pray to this same Julius Caesar in these words: “Having venerated your altars and your most sacred temples, divine Julius, I pray that, with your divine power propitious and favorable, you will allow the misfortunes of such great men to find concealment under the shelter and protection of your example” (Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. 6, § 13).

The emperor Augustus was indeed more restrained. According to Suetonius, although he knew that temples were customarily decreed even to proconsuls, [Col. 1138D] he accepted them in no province unless they were dedicated jointly in his own name and that of Rome (Suetonius, book II, § 52).
