Yet he nevertheless accepted temples that could not be accepted without injury to the true and supreme God. Much more blameworthy, therefore, were others who founded these and other temples in the name either of an emperor or even of the commonwealth. What, then, must be said of Domitian and other most criminal emperors who, as the writers of Roman history relate, ordered themselves to be called gods and temples to be built to them? No one of sound mind will deny that this was the supreme crime of impiety.

But observe, I ask you, how blind and unbridled [Col. 1139A] were the obstinacy, impiety, and avarice of the pagans. A temple or sacred shrine is certainly built to any god for no other reason than that it may be frequented by all; its entrance should therefore be easy, voluntary, and free for everyone. Nevertheless, just as the pagans, with supreme injustice, strove to compel Christians by every kind of punishment to enter them, so, with the grossest avarice, they barred their fellow pagans from them unless a price was paid. Through them, indeed, absolutely no one was permitted to enter any temple for free; rather, from every entrant, says Tertullian, they exacted “payment for the ground of the temple and for entrance into the sacred place” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 13), that is, for entry into the sacred building. The term “ground” there designates the place upon which the sacred building had been constructed. Cicero clearly explains this in the following words: [Col. 1139B] “They change their ground”—that is, “they change their residence and place” (Cicero, speech 12 *For Caecina*, p. 241). Elsewhere he says: “They could not previously have changed this citizenship without changing the ground of this city” (speech 36 *For Cornelius Balbus*, p. 519, line 38).

Tertullian therefore spoke somewhat more obscurely in the first book *Ad Nationes* when he said that the pagans extorted payment “for the doorposts, for the doors of the temples to be opened to each person” (Tertullian, *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10). Gothofredus thinks that the word *stipitibus* (“doorposts”) is corrupt and that *stipibus* (“contributions”) should be read, because Tertullian himself wrote in the *Apologeticum*: “How few now cast in a contribution?” (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 42). But the former words concern people entering a temple, while the latter concern those who have already entered. Rigault therefore did not do badly to retain the word *stipitibus*, [Col. 1139C] although he ought to have offered some reason for his opinion. We, for our part, may readily be persuaded that by the word *stipitibus* Tertullian meant either stones or perhaps the gods Terminus placed before the doors of temples, which really were called *stipites*, as we demonstrated from verses of the ancient poets in the other dissertations cited (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 19, arts. 2 and 17; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, p. 32, art. 2). For there he appears to distinguish the doorpost, the door, and the entrance of the temple, so that, by distinguishing them, he might attack the pagans’ avarice and impiety more sharply. Yet what can one dare to determine with certainty if the word is corrupt and no better manuscript is found?

Moreover, besides these sordid practices of intolerable avarice, the pagans polluted the same temples of their gods with procuring [Col. 1139D] and adulteries, as was observed above (ch. 26, art. 4) with our Tertullian (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 15), as shamelessly as they did with impunity. How, then, could they believe that their gods inhabited temples that were so very often disgraced by such outrages and crimes?

It is therefore no wonder if Christians, says Tertullian, “do not know these temples even by day” (Tertullian, passage cited); that is, they did not visit them during the day, much less by night, which was privy to such great crimes. Yet if they ever entered, perhaps “they too would despoil them, if they worshiped them,” as he says; that is, if Christians could ever have entered these temples as the pagans did, they undoubtedly would have stripped them bare, like the tyrant Dionysius [Col. 1140A] and others whom we have mentioned elsewhere—not, as those men did, from avarice, but because of the crimes and sacrileges perpetrated in them. We have discussed the temples of the pagans and also of the Christians more fully in our cited dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 12, art. 2; *On Arnobius*, ch. 21, art. 1; and *On Lactantius*, ch. 33, art. 1).

### ARTICLE II. With what guilty conscience and how much avarice the pagans sacrificed to their gods, offering grains of incense worth one as, two drops of undiluted wine, the blood of a rejected ox longing to die, and victims exhausted, consumptive, and diseased, along with hooves, little heads, and scraps plucked from feathers and bristles; and how they withheld the tithe owed to Hercules

[Col. 1140B]

The piety and religious devotion of the pagans in their sacrifices was certainly no greater than in their temples; nor was their avarice and greed for gain any less. For when sacrificing to their gods, after all their other defilements they also offered, says Tertullian, “a filthy conscience” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 30), that is, one contaminated by all the crimes noted shortly before and throughout this dissertation. If you wish to know what kind and quantity of incense they burned, our author will answer you: “grains of incense worth one *as*, and tears of the Arabian tree” (*ibid.*)—that is, grains of incense not indeed from Saba, which fetched a higher price, but Arabian incense, which was bought at the lowest price. Indeed, these avaricious men took no more grains of this incense, however common it might be, [Col. 1140C] but only three, as we observed above (above, ch. 24, art. 3; and *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 35, art. 2), grasped with fingers that could certainly hold very few.

But what, someone will object: did not very many people burn whole heaps, even of costly incense, with a full hand, as Tibullus sang in these verses?

> Juno of the birthday, receive the sacred heaps of incense  
> Which the learned young woman gives you with tender hand.

(Tibullus, book IV, elegy 6.)

Did not Martial also sing:

> I consumed the false sacrificial meal and heaps of incense;  
> The flocks diminished while ewe after ewe fell.

(Martial, book VII, epigram 53.)

But these are undoubtedly poetic exaggerations; and Martial is speaking there of the interpretation of dreams. [Col. 1140D] Who does not know that those who wish to learn the future and, above all, obtain what they desire, spare no expense? It is no less certain that only the rich—and very few of them—burned a great quantity of incense or more costly incense to their gods, and then only when pressed by some necessity or seeking to catch at whispers of empty renown. Almost all the rest gave three or four grains of incense and, as Tertullian adds, “two drops of undiluted wine” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 30)—that is, as little incense and wine as they could. With what frame of mind they did so you will learn from these verses of Ovid about an old woman sacrificing:

> She also drips in wine—whatever wine is left;  
> She herself or her companions drink it, though she herself drinks more.
>
> [Col. 1141A] “We have bound hostile tongues and unfriendly mouths,”  
> She said as she departed, and the old woman went out drunk.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, book III, § 15.)

With precisely the same vice of avarice, the pagans sacrificed victims that were certainly neither fat, nor choice, nor sound, but, as Tertullian further says, “the blood of a rejected ox longing to die” (Tertullian, passage cited). Some more fastidious critics would have the word written there as not “ox” but “man,” because only a man can wish for death. But this is mere captiousness against the common agreement of all the manuscripts. Who does not see that our Tertullian said this metaphorically of an ox so wasted by old age, emaciation, and consumption that, if it were possible, it would prefer death to life? Hence Tertullian himself had already addressed the pagans in these words: “You slaughter every victim that is exhausted, consumptive, and mangy . . . [Col. 1141B] things which at home you would have assigned even to boys, or slaves, or dogs” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 14, and *Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10).

Yet by law they were obliged to sacrifice whole, excellent, and becoming victims to their gods, a law which Cicero reported in these very words: “Let them take care that the victims offered to each divinity are becoming and pleasing to that divinity” (Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, p. 334, line 46). According to Vitruvius, as quoted by Macrobius, these were called *eximiae* (“choice victims”), either because they were “taken out” (*eximuntur*) from the herd or because, being of exceptional appearance, they were selected as offerings to the divine powers (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, ch. 5). Hence, according to Pliny, there was a custom of inspecting and selecting victims. Virgil recalls this custom in the verse:

> [Col. 1141C] . . . They sacrifice, according to custom, selected two-year-old sheep.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book IV, v. 57.)

For, as Servius perceptively annotates there: “It was customary for sheep to be selected for sacrifice which lacked nothing,” as in the sixth book of the same poet, where he sings again:

> Now it would be best to sacrifice from an untouched herd  
> Seven bullocks and as many selected two-year-old sheep, according to custom.

(The same author, book VI, v. 38 and following.)

And just as Virgil repeats the same thing, Servius again observes upon these verses: “‘According to ancient custom,’ which he omitted as though known to everyone: that is, they must have neither a pointed tail, nor a split tongue, nor a black ear. By this he teaches that ‘untouched’ is one thing and ‘selected’ another.”

The pagans, therefore, contrary to the law given and the custom received, offered all the worst things and the blood, [Col. 1141D] as was said, “of a rejected ox”—that is, one disapproved and rejected by their ancient law and custom. If some of them did in fact sometimes select the best victims as commanded, they certainly did not present them whole and untouched, but only certain and inferior parts of them, such as “little heads,” says Tertullian, that is, heads. For in another book he calls the chameleon’s head a *capitulum* immediately adjoining its back, “for it lacks a neck” (Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, ch. 3), the neck being the posterior part of the throat. Thus *capitulum* is there used by him for the chameleon’s entire head.

After keeping the better portions of the victims, therefore, they sacrificed the head and “the hooves and scraps of feathers” (the same author, *Apologeticum*, ch. 14)—or, as he says elsewhere, [Col. 1142A] things “plucked off beforehand” (*Ad Nationes*, book I, ch. 10)—along with other parts which masters and heads of households would have assigned to their slaves, or even to their dogs. But if anyone should clearly prove that Tertullian has said something there “hyperbolically” (ὑπερβολικῶς), we shall not resist him greatly. Nevertheless, no one can deny that he rightly reproached the pagans for sacrificing inferior victims to the gods and for taking away the better part of fat and whole victims and reserving it for their own uses.

Nor did the avaricious impiety of the pagans stop here. For they did not shrink from withholding the tenth part of their property owed to Hercules. Tertullian therefore addresses and rebukes them in these words: “Of Hercules’ tithe, you do not place even a third part upon his altar” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 14). But Cicero openly testifies [Col. 1142B] that the whole of this tithe had to be paid by them (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 253, line 22). It was surely for this reason that Plautus introduces a certain Gelasinus speaking thus:

> I must come here as quickly as possible,  
> So that I may offer a tenth part to Hercules.

(Plautus, *Truculentus*, act II, scene 2.)

Do not, I ask you, doubt that this poet means the full tenth of one’s property. For elsewhere he said that from it a slave could easily determine how much gold his master possessed. Here are his very verses:

> But I should like to know how much gold the master deducted for himself  
> And how much he gave back to his father.
>
> If he is thrifty, he made Hercules a participant in the share:  
> He gave him the tenth part and took nine for himself.

(The same author, *Bacchides*, act IV, scene 4.)

[Col. 1142C] Plutarch gave various explanations of this custom and institution, which anyone may easily read in his works (Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, question 13, p. 267, vol. II). But the pagans, little concerned about this duty of their religion, subtracted whatever they could with impunity from this tithe and did not pay even a third of it. How true this was you will further learn from these verses of the same Plautus:

> Just now, from this provision money, from a single mina, I reduced  
> Five coins; I withheld Hercules’ share for myself.

(Plautus, *Truculentus*, act II, scene 7.)

Tertullian therefore mocks the pagans as wittily as he does justly and deservedly: “I praise your wisdom all the more, because you rescue something from what was lost” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. [Col. 1142D] 14). He rightly called “lost” what was given to false gods and divine powers.

With what reason, then, with what effrontery, did the pagans strive, with a cruelty greater indeed than that of beasts, to compel Christians to worship and sacrifice to their gods? Even if they had believed them to be true gods; even if they had honored them with worship as sincere as it was false; even if they had sacrificed to them whole, selected, and altogether excellent victims—nevertheless nothing was more unjust or perverse, nothing more contrary to human and divine laws and to the laws of nature itself, than to condemn Christians without allowing them a defense or hearing them, solely on account of their name, and to kill them with the most exquisite tortures that could be devised by the ingenuity of a man [Col. 1143A]—or rather, of a demon. But these most cruel and unjust men feared that, if Christians were heard, they would demonstrate so clearly the truth of their own religion and the falsity of the others that no one could ever contradict them. How easy and readily available this was to all of them has been most clearly proved throughout this dissertation.

[Col. 1144A] Moreover, throughout it we have attempted, in their respective places, to explain whatever difficult, obsolete, and barbarous words occur in these books of Tertullian which we have endeavored to elucidate and illustrate. We have therefore not thought it necessary to reproduce a new index of them here.

## Second Series: Dogmatic Books Written Before the Author Embraced Montanism

*On Prayer. On Baptism. On Repentance. On Patience. To His Wife, Two Books. On the Dress of Women, Two Books.*

### The Book *On Prayer*, with the Notes of Panciroli, Muratori, and Various Others

[Col. 1143]

## THE BOOK *ON PRAYER* OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN (C)

### Prolegomena

[Note: [Col. 1143A] From the third volume of the *Anecdota* which Lodovico Antonio Muratori extracted from manuscripts in the Ambrosian Library and published at Padua in the year 1715.]

[Col. 1143A] We count very many of Tertullian’s books as printed, but few as surviving in manuscript in libraries. Hence it has come about that even now we do not possess his works reproduced in print with the greatest accuracy: some have appeared publicly in a mutilated state, disfigured by hideous wounds; certain works are also missing which we know Tertullian published, and which, we equally suspect and lament, have been wholly snatched from us by time’s devouring power. [Col. 1144A] The book *On Prayer* has not thus far enjoyed better fortune. John Gagney, a Parisian theologian, was the first of all to publish it at Paris from a very ancient manuscript, in the year of Christ 1545—but by no means complete, and deprived of its splendid conclusion. Nor, for want of manuscripts, did the editions that followed bring assistance to this one. Rigault alone observed that the old manuscript contained the book in a mutilated form; after adding merely a few lines at the end, he left the remedy for others to administer.

When, therefore, I came upon [Col. 1145A] an ancient manuscript of the Ambrosian Library in which those passages absent from the others could be read, I immediately added them to my *Anecdota*, as gems especially welcome to the republic of letters. For whatever was committed to writing by Tertullian—certainly the most learned man of his age—and especially whatever he wrote while in the Catholic camp, is highly valued by all students of ecclesiastical matters, as is evident even to beginners.

The Ambrosian manuscript, however, did not begin the little work with the exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, as we have it in the printed editions, but with the material that follows such an exposition, under this title: “Here begins Tertullian’s work on various necessary matters.” Then the first chapter, whose opening is “By means of the brevity of a few words,” etc., was headed as follows: “Recapitulation.” “That we may add something further” was the title [Col. 1145B] of the following chapter. The remaining chapters likewise bore their own titles, which we have judged should also be retained in this edition of ours.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] Hence the new editors likewise thought that readers would be greatly pleased if, after the annotations of the most illustrious Panciroli and Muratori, they appended notes selected from Rigault, Pamelius, La Cerda, Albaspinaeus, and Priorius.]

Moreover, we have chosen to adorn and elucidate this little work with such annotations, so that what highly learned men have provided for Tertullian’s other books may not be lacking here, and so that certain overly delicate readers may not complain of the darkness and the harsh, iron style of this author and thereby be deterred from reading him. Indeed, among the ancient Christian authors you could point to none upon whom the illumination of learning and scholia seems more necessary to cast than upon Tertullian; for I do not know whether obscurity in expression could in any way have been avoided by him, or whether he cherished it as a delight.

When I had arranged all these matters to the best of my ability, it occurred to me that scholars would not find it unwelcome if I appended to [Col. 1145C] my notes those also which Guido Panciroli, a jurist of Reggio, had written upon the same book *On Prayer*. I hoped all the more readily that my plan would meet with approval because I observed that the illustrious man’s chief concern had been placed in explaining Tertullian’s obscure meanings, whereas I, by contrast, had set myself rather to elucidate the historical and learned remains contained in this little book.

It is, however, to be regretted that no one has yet arisen in Italy who, for the glory of our nation, has taken care to publish Panciroli’s remaining commentaries on Tertullian. We have scarcely a brief mention of them in Thomasinus’s *Life of Panciroli*, in Dupin, William [Col. 1146A] Cave, and a few other writers; indeed, they scarcely knew that any part of them survived. That labor of the very celebrated Panciroli certainly deserved a better fate, for he won for himself an eminent place among learned men through distinction not only in jurisprudence but also in sacred and secular learning.

And indeed I think—as Possevino also thought in his *Apparatus*—that those very abundant commentaries upon Tertullian which Beatus Rhenanus, Pamelius, La Cerda, Salmasius, and other most learned men published prevented Panciroli’s from appearing. Those whose responsibility it was to enhance Panciroli’s posthumous reputation evidently thought that they would expend labor to little advantage if they served the same dishes to the palates of scholars. But Tertullian is not an author who is satisfied with a few interpreters; and since his more recent [Col. 1146B] interpreters were by no means deterred by the efforts of the earlier ones from bringing forth their own, why should this ill-considered fear have dislodged Panciroli’s admirers from so noble a plan?

It can readily happen that, when several different intellects unite in explaining a single author, his mind and writings become clearer day by day and are freed from the darkness arising either from the antiquity of the times, the carelessness of copyists, or the author’s austerity. Although these things may truly be said of each of the ancients, they must be affirmed especially of Tertullian, whom, after the labors of so many interpreters, we still find obscure.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] Hence the new editors likewise thought that readers would be greatly pleased if, after the annotations of the most illustrious Panciroli and Muratori, they appended notes selected from Rigault, Pamelius, La Cerda, Albaspinaeus, and Priorius.]

At the same time that Pamelius was engaged in explaining Tertullian, Panciroli also left us complete commentaries upon all of Tertullian’s writings published down to his own death. [Col. 1146C] Their autograph manuscript lies concealed at Reggio Emilia, his native city. I happened to see and copy only a transcript of it, written with the greatest accuracy and preserved in his library by Father Giovanni Battista Cattaneo, an ornament of the Franciscan Order of the Observance, as they call it. And since by his favor it came about that I could draw whatever I pleased from that manuscript work, I have decided to present here also the letter prefixed to those same commentaries; from it what Panciroli accomplished upon Tertullian will become evident. He therefore writes as follows:

## PANCIROLI’S PREFACE TO THE READER

[Col. 1145]

[Col. 1145D] I consider my arrival at Turin from Padua to have been fortunate chiefly for this reason: among the other highly learned men whom I found there, foremost of all I encountered Vincenzo Lauro, bishop of Mondovì and apostolic nuncio of Our Holy Lord Pope Gregory XIII to the Most Serene Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, and a cardinal versed in every branch of learning. By judging me worthy of his private conversations, he continually made me more learned; and just as Marcus Tullius [Col. 1146D] Cicero used to leave the side of Quintus Mucius Scaevola more learned than before (*Laelius*, or *On Friendship*), so I departed richer after drawing no small amount from his deeply learned conversations. At one time he would recount events performed since the foundation of the world; at another he would bring forth the mysteries of philosophy, explain [Col. 1147A] certain obscure authors, correct a corrupt reading from approved copies, or, in accordance with his pious purpose, interpret some passage from Holy Scripture.

Because he took marvelous delight in Tertullian’s writings (St. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Tertullian”) and, like another Cyprian, had him in his hands every day, he was deeply grieved to find him so obscure that at times no meaning could be extracted from him. But since he was overwhelmed by the many affairs pressing upon him as bishop of Mondovì from his own jurisdiction and, as the supreme pontiff’s legate, arising everywhere—either entrusted to him from Rome or emerging from the Subalpine regions—he had no leisure to explain this author and sought someone else who might be equal to undertaking so great a burden.

He saw that, to interpret a man imbued with every branch of learning and thoroughly skilled in the [Col. 1147B] Greek language and in history, there was need of a scholar acquainted with many subjects, especially civil law, since Tertullian himself, as Eusebius writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 2, was a jurist who everywhere inserted in his writings many things drawn from civil law. But although there was no lack of other learned men who could have performed this task more exactly, he expected more from me than I could bear and considered me suited for this office. For when he observed that I had long taught civil law at Padua and for several years at Turin, and since he had not yet recognized the slenderness of my abilities, he was misled, I suppose, by the public office of teaching entrusted to me and judged me fit to undertake so great a burden, as one who could interpret not only this jurist in my capacity as an interpreter of law, [Col. 1147C] but also many of his more obscure passages.

He therefore first offered me this province; and when I refused once and again, he persisted and finally, by his authority, prevailed upon me to accept the commission. I certainly perceived that, as a man of rather slight learning, I lacked many things necessary for explaining so great an author; that a moderate knowledge of the laws did not suffice to elucidate the many matters he derived from recondite histories, philosophy, medicine, and Holy Scripture; and that my time, entangled in numerous affairs of the courts, did not permit it. But when I said that I could not do it, he believed that I was unwilling:

> What could I do? I was not free to leave his service,  
> Nor was it right not to acknowledge gods so manifestly present.

[Col. 1147D] (Virgil, *Eclogue* 1.)

I was therefore not permitted to resist him, and by obeying I preferred that he should investigate my ability rather than my willingness, and rebuke my weakness rather than my obstinacy.

I consequently placed my neck beneath the yoke and began to undertake in my spare hours what neither my strength allowed nor my time conveniently permitted. But while accommodating him, I fear that what happened to Servius Galba may happen to me: while a private citizen he was judged worthy of imperial power, but once made emperor he appeared unequal to it (Tacitus, book I of the *Histories*, or book XVII of the *Annals*). I too fear that, whereas in silence I seemed to him to know something, in speaking I shall be revealed to everyone as most ignorant. Whatever the outcome may be, however, I wished, by accepting the commands imposed upon me, to test under his authority what I could accomplish. [Col. 1148A]

I found Tertullian obscure in his style, as both Lactantius Firmianus and St. Jerome indicate (Lactantius Firmianus, *Divine Institutes*, V.1; St. Jerome, Epistle 13 to Paulinus), because he either wishes omitted words to be understood, employs unusual expressions, or even fashions a novel phraseology for himself. To assist readers, I compiled a special index of these, so that everyone might see in what sense he takes particular expressions or words.

Since corrupt manuscripts, however, present an even greater difficulty, I emended many passages—but only from things which the same author often repeats or which St. Jerome and others after him quote. On my own initiative I did not dare to change anything beyond a letter or syllable. I preferred that meanings should remain ambiguous rather than that false or alien meanings should be introduced, and that something should be missing rather than corrupted. [Col. 1148B] Nevertheless, I left nothing entirely untouched; and amid great obscurities I thought it better that my ability should be put at risk than that readers should be sent away confused.

Protogenes, although an excellent painter, could not depict the foam of a panting horse, though it was a trivial detail; in anger at his art he struck a sponge laden with every color against the painting and applied it to the animal’s lips, thereby producing by chance what he desired (Pliny, XXXV.10). In the same way, while enveloping the author’s mind in numerous interpretations, I thought it possible that by some effort I might perhaps attain some part of his meaning. The philosophers judge that Averroes accomplished this in commenting on Aristotle, and our own writers judge that Angelo degli Ubaldi did so in explaining Justinian’s *Novellae*, which had been badly translated into another language.

I have also narrated from approved authors all the histories which [Col. 1148C] Tertullian touches upon rather than relates, wherever necessary, so as to leave no one any ground for uncertainty. Among these, the books *On the Soldier’s Crown*, *To the Martyrs*, *On the Dress of Women*, *On the Shows*, and the *Apologeticum*, but especially the little work *On the Pallium*, caused me no small trouble. Some have explained certain matters from these works; but what they and I myself have accomplished will be for others to judge. In any case, passing over all the slighter matters and those which seemed easy, I explained only the difficult ones; and, altering Tertullian’s own order, I divided his works into three parts according to their diversity of subject matter, for the benefit of students.

If I have assisted readers in any respect, I shall ascribe it to God, the true light of all; if otherwise, I shall charge it to my own weakness and to the indulgence of the man who chose a poor interpreter. [Col. 1148D] We certainly possess in Tertullian an author who is great, a teacher of the ancient rites of the Church, and worthy to be read by all. He also refutes the errors of more recent heretics when he frequently teaches that the Eucharist is the true body of Christ—concerning which, however, no one ever doubted or could have doubted before Berengar—admonishes that confession (*exomologesis*) of sins must be made, indicates that offerings were customarily made for the dead, proclaims the authority of the Roman see, and confirms that the souls of the dead are purified by fire, as well as fasts and other similar matters which it would take too long to enumerate. But madmen are not readily persuaded by arguments or authorities. You will therefore receive these modest lucubrations of mine kindly and interpret them equitably and favorably. Farewell.

## THE BOOK ON PRAYER

[Note: [Col. 1149D] Among the outstanding qualities of the Lord’s Prayer, this is plainly marvelous and divine: although it can be grasped by humble and limited minds, it nevertheless satisfies minds that are lofty and most capacious. For the former it is a familiar, daily formula of prayer; for the latter, moreover, a compendium of the entire Christian discipline. The ancient Fathers vied with one another in proclaiming this pledge of heavenly grace. No one explained it more learnedly than Tertullian; no one demonstrated with holier reverence that it should be honored by posterity. He gave his little book the title *On Prayer*, a title as excellent as it is simple, since it signifies the Christian prayer dictated by the Son of God himself. Petitions presented to the emperor were customarily drafted with the assistance of a jurist. Our heavenly jurist, our Lord Jesus Christ, composed for us our petitions to God. RIG.]

## SUMMARY

[Col. 1149]

[Col. 1149A] That golden little book was certainly written by Tertullian while he was still a Catholic. Indeed—if you wish to except his exhortation *To the Martyrs*—it was, in the judgment of Dom Lumper, the first fruit of that great intellect, now coming to life again in its newly acquired faith. It concerns partly dogma and partly morals and discipline.

In its first part, our Septimius—the first of all writers known to us to do so—lucidly explains the Lord’s Prayer and presents in it the doctrine of the entire Gospel gathered together as though in the mirror of a compendium. Many after him traveled this same well-worn road, and Cyprian in particular, manifestly his disciple in this matter, followed him wholly. In the latter part, by an exceptionally rare exposition given the antiquity of the period, he indicates especially in what manner one should participate in sacred rites, and which practices of prayer should either be omitted [Col. 1149B] or diligently performed.

The principal headings of the first part are as follows:

1. How great is that prayer which was delivered by the Word of God and the Reason of God, the word of reason and the reason of the word, Our Lord Jesus Christ. Chapter 1.

2. Next its opening is examined, in which the Father is acknowledged, the Son is invoked in the Father, and not even Mother Church is passed over. Chapter 2.

3. Then each petition is separately explained. In the first, we too, as candidates for the company of angels, ask for God’s heavenly glory and for his name to be sanctified in us. Chapter 3. In the second, we pray that his will may be done in us, who are heaven and earth. Chapter 4. [Col. 1149C] In the third, moreover, we must hasten to the embrace of our hope, the desire of Christians, the confusion of the nations, and the exultation of the angels. Chapter 5. The fourth admits a threefold explanation: first concerning ordinary bread; then concerning Christ, as the bread of believers; and finally concerning the Eucharistic body of Christ. Chapter 6. The fifth then implores God’s clemency. Chapter 7. The sixth and seventh, finally, pray for the removal of temptation and evil. Chapters 7–9.

The latter part, however, is manifold, though it may without very great difficulty be reduced to these three divisions:

1. What things fruitfully prepare the soul before prayer: namely, remembrance of the commandments and, above all, the duties of charity; and a free concentration of the mind, by which the Spirit’s inexpressible groanings are drawn forth to the Father. Chapters 10–15.

2. What may be omitted either before or after prayer: namely, washing the hands, removing one’s cloak, or sitting down. Chapters 16–17.

3. What practices are fitting or must necessarily be performed: namely, the raising of the hands; the lowering of the face and voice; the kiss of peace; the station at the altar after the Lord’s body has been received and reserved; the modest attire of women and the veiling of virgins; the practice of bending the knees; the place of prayer and its more solemn hours; the antiphonal singing of psalms; and the devout *agape*, crowned with a procession of good works and conducted to God’s altar amid psalms and hymns. Chapters 16–28. To this densely packed and marvelously rich store of ancient rites is added, as a crowning conclusion, an ornate and very ample description of the power and effect of prayer. Chapter 29. [Col. 1150C] THE EDITORS.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1149C]

The Spirit of God,

[Note: [Col. 1149C] **The Spirit of God.** Not only here but elsewhere too Christ is called the Spirit of God by Tertullian, as may be seen in *Apologeticum*, chapter 21; *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 10, book III, chapters 6 and 16, and book IV, chapter 21; and *Against Praxeas*, chapter 26. The designation certainly sounds improper to our ears now, but it was incautiously employed by certain ancients who did not have before their eyes the heresies that arose afterward. Lactantius Firmianus especially held this view, according to St. Jerome’s testimony in his letter to Pammachius and Oceanus *On the Errors of Origen*: “Lactantius,” he says, “in his books, and especially in the letters [Col. 1149D] to Demetrianus, wholly denies the substance of the Holy Spirit; and, by a Jewish error, says that he is referred either to the Father or to the Son, and that the sanctification of each person is indicated under his name.” Jerome repeats the same statement in his commentary on chapter IV of the Epistle to the Galatians. It would therefore seem beyond doubt that Tertullian errs here too. Yet because in other books he distinguishes the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son with the greatest clarity, calling him the third divine being of the Godhead and the third name of majesty, [Col. 1150C] I therefore think that he called Christ the Spirit of God because he believed that, in a general sense, God was said to be spirit, as the apostle John writes: “God is spirit.” L. A. MURATORI.

—**The Spirit of God.** Before interpreting the Lord’s Prayer, he states who taught it. It was Christ, whom he calls by several names: for he is Spirit, by which he performed miracles; the Word of God; and Reason, or Wisdom, which came into the world, as he adds below. Tertullian likewise says in chapter 17 of the *Apology*: “What we worship is one God, who from nothing brought forth this entire mass, together with its whole equipment of elements, bodies, and spirits, by the word with which he commanded, [Col. 1150D] the reason with which he arranged, and the power with which he was able, as an adornment of his majesty.” G. PANCIROLI.]

and the Word of God, and the Reason of God,

[Note: [Col. 1150D] **The Word of God and the Reason of God.** The Greek term *Logos* (Λόγος), a proper name of the Son of God among the Greeks, has had several Latin renderings: *Verbum* (“Word”), *Sermo* (“Word” or “Discourse”), and *Ratio* (“Reason”). The ancient writers of the Church used these Latin names interchangeably to signify the same thing. We now prefer to translate it as “the Word.” MURATORI.]

and [Col. 1150C] the word of reason and the reason of the word,

[Note: [Col. 1150D] **The word of reason, and the reason of the word.** Whoever wishes to measure the language of the ancients by modern usage will be surprised that Tertullian here bestows upon God [Col. 1151B] the Father too the designation of Word and Reason. But because the term *logos* (τοῦ λόγου) is ambiguous and signifies reason, thought, mind, and understanding, in that sense the designation both of *Logos* (τοῦ Λόγου) and of reason and word was made common to the Father as well. Therefore the Son was called by some of the Fathers *Logos from Logos* (Λόγος ἐκ Λόγου), “Word from Word”; and St. Irenaeus, book II, chapter 48, calls the Father *logon* (λογόν), or word, and mind, writing as follows: “For God, being wholly Mind and wholly Logos, speaks what he thinks and thinks what he speaks. [Col. 1151C] For his thought is Logos, and Logos is Mind; and the Mind that encompasses all things is the Father himself.”

But by whatever terms the Father and the Son may be called, inadequate and ambiguous terms for the Godhead are excused by the magnitude and majesty of the ineffable reality, provided that it is agreed that we distinguish the Son from the Father and proclaim one essence and nature in them and in the Holy Spirit. St. Ambrose held this position most admirably in *On the Divinity of the Son*, chapter 5. We wish to reproduce his words so that it may be evident that not only Tertullian but other ecclesiastical writers also designated both the Father and the Son by the names Word, Reason, Discourse, and Spirit. “This, then,” he says, “is the rationale of the name: that in the Father and the Son you should believe unity of substance, although you cannot define the reality itself, which is ineffable; so that, whether you say Light from Light, Word from Word, Spirit from Spirit, or Lord from Lord—whatever you say concerning him—[Col. 1151D] you may nevertheless believe the Father and the Son to be of one essence.” See also St. Irenaeus, book II, chapter 48. PAM.]

John too had taught his disciples to pray; but everything belonging to John was being prepared in advance for Christ, until, when Christ himself had increased—as the same John foretold, saying that he must increase while John himself must decrease (John III.30)—the whole work of the forerunner, together with his spirit, passed over to the Lord. For this reason the words in which John taught them to pray are not extant, because earthly things yielded to heavenly things. “He who is from the earth,” he says, “speaks earthly things; and he who is present from heaven speaks the things he has seen” (John III.31). And what belonging to the Lord Christ is not heavenly—including also this discipline of prayer?

Let us therefore consider, blessed brethren, his heavenly Sophia (σοφία, “Wisdom”),

[Note: [Col. 1152B] **Let us therefore consider, etc.** What are these three precepts—or rather counsels—concerning prayer which Tertullian enumerates here and in what follows? You will understand at a glance from the Gospel of John, chapter VI, verse 6 [sic; the quotations are from Matthew VI.5–7], where Christ, [Col. 1152C] the divine Sophia, or Wisdom, speaks in these words: “And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in synagogues and at street corners, so that they may be seen by men.” Here is the first precept: namely, that we flee ambition in praying, as though God could hear and see us only in public, and that we trust that both the sight and hearing of almighty God are present even under roofs and in hidden places; this pertains to a person’s faith.

Christ then continues: “But when you pray, enter your chamber, and after closing the door pray to your Father in secret.” Here is the second precept, as Tertullian explains it: that we offer our devotion to him alone whom we trust hears and sees everywhere; this concerns the modesty of faith.

The divine Teacher then continues: “But when you pray, do not speak at length like the Gentiles; for they think they will be heard because of their many words.” This is the third precept: namely, to speak with Tertullian, that we should not suppose the Lord must be approached with a column [Col. 1152D] of words, since we are certain that he looks after his own of his own accord. MURATORI.

—**Let us therefore consider.** This is the third element of which prayer consists: Sophia, who teaches us the manner of praying. For in this he commands two things: first, that we pray secretly and in a hidden place; secondly, that we pray briefly, as is found in Matthew, chapter VI: “When you pray, enter your chamber and, with the door closed, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. But when you pray, do not speak at length as the Gentiles do; for they think that they are heard because of their many words.” G. PANCIROLI.]

In those passages Tertullian considers the Church to exist in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but principally in the Holy Spirit. From this he concludes that the Spirit and the Church are mentioned here in the Lord’s Prayer when we say, “Our Father”; for whoever invokes the Father appears also to implore the divine power of the Son and of Mother Church, or the Holy Spirit. For in the Son and the Father the Mother is recognized, from whom the names both of Father and of Son are established. Thus under one [Note: [Col. 1154D] “Thus under one class,” etc. Tertullian begins the Lord’s Prayer in this way: “Father, who art in heaven.” The word *our* is omitted, although it is found in one manuscript. That Tertullian omitted it, however, seems sufficiently suggested by his explanation; for by this indefinite name he shows not only that we are designated as sons of God, but also affirms that the divine Son is invoked there, since his name is tacitly signified when the general designation “Father” is expressed. Moreover, Tertullian says that, once mention has been made of Father and sons, the name of the Church must also be understood; for there is no father without sons, nor sons without father and mother. Although this mode of argument is fallacious when applied to divine things, it nevertheless seems to have pleased Tertullian with reference to us, the sons of God: whenever we are called sons, we are to understand, besides God our Father, also the Church our mother, who through Christ begot us for God. Thus by the one designation “Father” we honor God together with his own—that is, God the Father, his eternal Son, and Mother Church. We also remember the commandment, since Christ, as Matthew attests, declared that we should call no one on earth father except him whom we have in heaven.

We cannot readily embrace what the most learned Albaspinaeus has advanced concerning the name “Church” used here. For that most distinguished man thinks that by this word Tertullian signifies the Holy Spirit, because in *On Baptism*, ch. 6, he affirms that the Church is constituted in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and in *On Modesty*, ch. 21, he has the following: “For the Church itself, properly and principally, is the Spirit himself, in whom is the Trinity of the divinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He gathers together that Church which the Lord placed in the three.” Albaspinaeus then says: “In those passages Tertullian considers the Church to exist in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but principally in the Holy Spirit. From this he concludes that the Spirit and the Church are mentioned here in the Lord’s Prayer when we say, ‘Our Father.’ For whoever invokes the Father appears also to implore the divine power of the Son and of Mother Church, or the Holy Spirit; and thus under one name—namely, that of the Father—the three persons are enumerated.”

But I would not wish an explanation of the present passage to be sought from the book *On Modesty*, since it seems certain to me that by “Holy Spirit” there he meant none other than the heresiarch Montanus. In order that Tertullian might assent to Montanus’s ravings, he imagined that the Church was properly and principally constituted in him; indeed, with a most amusing notion, he judged that Montanus himself was the Church. By contrast, since until now it has been believed, on St. Hilary’s testimony, that the book *On Prayer* was written by Tertullian while he was Catholic, I do not know how we could properly shed light upon this book by adducing the follies and fantasies of another book. But even if we say that the Church is constituted in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—which I do not deny could rightly be said—not even so shall we extricate ourselves from these circumlocutions, as will be evident to anyone who considers the matter seriously. MURAT.]

In the *Apology*: “Clothed in sackcloth and ashes, by our importunate entreaties we beat upon heaven.” In *On Flight in Persecution*: “He is Lord, he is powerful; all things are his. “Or, in the parched land of Memphis, could they bring

The most learned Pamelius explained this last sense, proving from it that, according to Tertullian’s judgment, the body and blood of Christ are truly contained in the sacrament of the Eucharist. Besides the passages Pamelius adduces, other words of Tertullian may be cited which prove the same still more clearly. In book 5 *Against Marcion*, ch. 8, he writes: “Accordingly, through the sacrament of the bread and cup we have already proved in the Gospel the reality of the Lord’s body and blood against Marcion’s phantom.” The impious Marcion thought Christ’s flesh was not real but phantasmal and merely apparent. If, therefore, the reality of the Lord’s body and blood is proved through the sacrament of the bread and cup, who does not understand that the true and substantial body and blood of Christ are present in the august sacrament? Other passages may be gathered from the remaining books against Marcion.

Then in *On Idolatry*, ch. 7, note the following: “At this point the zeal of faith will make its plea, groaning that a Christian comes from idols into the Church, from the adversary’s workshop into the house of God; raises to God the Father hands that are mothers of idols; worships with those hands which outside are worshiped against God; brings to the Lord’s body those hands which provide bodies for demons,” etc. There he inveighs against Christian makers of idols who received Christ’s body—as was the custom of those times—with the same hands with which they fashioned idols. See also ch. 14 of the book *Against the Jews*.

Accordingly, the words “his body is accounted to be in the bread”—the verb *censetur* means the same as “is” among the jurists—indicate that under the name of bread we ask for Christ’s life-giving body, so that in asking for bread we ask for the Lord’s sacrament and inseparability from Christ’s body. —“Then because his body is in the bread.” Whoever carefully attends to these words will never say that the author passed over to the opinion of the adversaries. Here it should be noted that he establishes a distinction between Jesus insofar as he nourishes the faithful and believing, and the same Jesus himself existing in the Eucharist. For after explaining why Jesus is the bread of those who confess him and believe in him, he introduces yet another manner in which Christ himself is also bread. He therefore distinguishes here those two breads and the twofold manner of nourishment. There would have been no need to do so if Christ were received in the Eucharist by faith alone, just as he is received by faith alone by those who believe in him and his Gospel.

Moreover, he speaks for the most part in terms proper to jurists, among whom *censetur* has the same meaning as “is.” ALBASP.

Now in the Scriptures “debt” is a figure for offense [Note: [Col. 1162B] “Now debt.” The word “debt” signifies an offense and is its type, figure, and signification, because just as a debt is exacted from a debtor in court unless it is remitted, so too is an offense. PANCIROL.

—“Now in the Scriptures ‘debt’ is a figure for offense.” Tertullian observes that “debt” in the Scriptures is a figure for offense because an offense is similarly owed under judgment and exacted by it, and does not escape the justice of exaction unless the exaction is waived. This seems consonant with Aristotle’s teaching in *Ethics* 5 that some transactions are voluntary and others involuntary. One who sells something enters into a transaction with the purchaser and is bound by actions arising from purchase and sale, through a voluntary contract. One who commits a crime enters into a transaction with the law, so that he becomes liable, even unwillingly and against his will, to the penalty which the law has assigned to the crime.

Thus we are debtors to God, since by our daily offenses we despise God’s commands; under that title we owe penalties that are by no means light. Nor do we possess the means to make satisfaction to his immeasurable and infinite majesty, since in ourselves we are of no value. God, therefore, our creditor, pursues us, although undeserving, with such beneficence that he teaches us the means by which we may be set free. “Forgive,” he says, “and you will be forgiven.”

Does one human being offend another? Whatever passes between them is assuredly human. How small is what is owed; how small what is forgiven! But does a human being offend God? On one side the human being is the debtor; on the other God is creditor and avenger. The contest is altogether as unequal as divine things are different from human ones.

And so God puts on humanity, to set off our accounts against his own. He deals with us under our laws and allows a debtor to be assigned to him. Those who have inflicted injuries upon us are our debtors. We assign our debtors to God whenever we forgive our debtor the satisfaction owed to us on account of offenses, in such a way that we wish it also to be forgiven him by God. Then in heaven an *acceptilatio*—a formal discharge of debt—takes place, through which God in turn cancels our debts toward him.

Therefore that debtor is richer and wealthier before God who has suffered more injuries, for he has more debtors of his own whom he can assign to God his creditor. What if we have no debtor? The answer that Nicolas Le Fèvre had noted in his papers on Augustine is satisfactory: “Although a will disposed toward forgiveness is sufficient for God, the searcher of hearts, how much richer and safer is that debtor who is able not only to free his creditor in intention, but actually to pay what is demanded from him.” Those who inflict injuries upon us enable us to do this by making themselves our debtors. With what ready and eager hearts, therefore, ought we—I do not say merely to spare, but even to thank—those who supply us with the means of balancing our grave debts with him with whom no one can balance accounts! RIG.], because it is likewise owed to judgment and exacted by it, and does not escape the justice of exaction unless the exaction is waived, just as the master forgave that servant his debt (Matt. 5:25).

And when Peter had asked whether his brother must be forgiven seven times, he said: “Rather, seventy-seven times” (Matt. 18:22), so that he might reform the law for the better, because in Genesis vengeance was reckoned [Note: [Col. 1163C] “Vengeance was reckoned.” That is, enacted. For when Lamech had killed a man—that is, Cain—he said in Genesis ch. 4: “Sevenfold vengeance will be given for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech.” Some interpret this to mean that anyone who killed Cain would be avenged seven times. But St. Jerome, Epistle 125 to Damasus, question 1, understands that Cain was not to be released until the seventh generation, which occurred when he was killed by Lamech; for then he was released from his trembling, the punishment he suffered here.

But Lamech’s sin—that is, the sin of the whole world and of the blood that was shed—was released seventy-seven times, that is, in the seventy-seventh generation, in which Christ appeared and freed the whole world from its crimes; for he was the seventy-seventh generation from Adam, in Luke ch. 3.

Tertullian, however, understands the text to mean that the sin of Cain was to be avenged seven times, and the sin of Lamech seventy-seven times. By the new law too it was commanded, in Matthew ch. 18, that sin should be forgiven just as often—that is, seventy-seven times. But there a finite number is placed for an infinite one, and it signifies that forgiveness must always be granted, as St. Jerome, book 3 of the *Commentary on Matthew* ch. 18, and others interpret it. G. PANCIROL.] sevenfold for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech (Gen. 4:24).

## CHAPTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 1167C] Title in the Ambrosian manuscript: “On the Washing of Hands.”]

Moreover [Note: [Col. 1167C] *Moreover, what reason is there?* Here he teaches that hands are not to be washed with water but kept clean from wicked deeds. G. PANCIROL.—*Moreover, what reason is there?* etc. The washing of the hands, and sometimes indeed of the whole body, customarily preceded prayer not only among Christians but also among pagans and Jews. Some evidently believed that, once the body had been washed and especially the hands cleansed—which generally contract dirt more readily—the soul too was washed and purified from the stains of guilt. But both reason and religion counseled that a person ought to approach God with a pure and purified soul. I shall prove that this custom prevailed among the gentiles by citing the most ancient witness of all. Homer, namely, presents Penelope to us in the *Odyssey* washing herself with water before her prayers. Her son Telemachus likewise:

> Ξεῖρας νιψάμενος πολιῆς ἁλὸς εὔχετ᾽ Ἀθήνῃ.

“Having washed his hands in the gray sea, he prayed to Athena.”

“His hands washed in the sea, he thus adores Pallas.” [Col. 1167D]

Macrobius, moreover, says in *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 1: “It is established that one about to perform sacrifices to the gods above is purified by washing the body.” In the same place Macrobius supplies other examples of this rite from Virgil. Lactantius Firmianus likewise ridicules those same pagans who suppose that they have sacrificed piously if they have washed their skin, as though any rivers could wash away the lusts enclosed within the breast, or any seas purify them. Pseudo-Aristeas, in his book *On the Seventy Translators*, attests that the Jews had the same custom: “After consulting the king,” he says, “they withdraw to various places and, as is the custom of all Jews, first wash their hands in the sea and then pour out prayers to God.” See Spencer, *De Legibus Hebraeorum*, book III, dissertation 3, chapter 3.

This custom afterward passed to Christ’s faithful, and perhaps some believed it had been commanded by the Apostle himself in 1 Timothy, chapter II, where he orders us χεῖρας ὁσίους ἐπαίρειν, “to lift pure hands” to heaven, as though the Apostle were speaking also of the external purity and washing of the hands as a sign of inward purity. [Col. 1168B] For this reason the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 32, says:

> Πᾶς πιστὸς ἢ πιστὴ ἕωθεν ἀναστάντες ἐξ ὕπνου, πρὸ τοῦ ἔργου ἐπιτελέσαι, νιψάμενοι προσευχέσθωσαν.

“Every Christian man or woman, rising from sleep in the morning, before performing any work, should wash the hands and pray to God.”

This will appear still more clearly to anyone who considers that basins, fountains, and vessels were anciently placed in the courtyards of churches so that the faithful might wash their hands before approaching to pray. St. Paulinus, in his letter to Severus:

> Gleaming in the holy court, a fountain flows with water for the servants  
> And washes the hands of those entering . . . .

Chrysostom in several places, and especially in homily [Col. 1168C] 57, volume V, page 390, attests to the same fact in these words:

> Κρήνας εἶναι ἐν ταῖς αὐλαῖς τῶν εὐκτηρίων οἴκων νενόμισται, ἵνα οἱ μέλλοντες εὔχεσθαι τῷ Θεῷ πρότερον ἀπονιψάμενοι τὰς χεῖρας, οὕτως αὐτὰς εἰς εὐχὴν ἀνατείνωσιν.

“It has been established that there should be fountains in the courtyards of houses of prayer, so that those wishing to pray to God may first wash their hands and only then extend them in prayer.”

Consult the same author in homilies 82 and 108, volume VI, and homily 43 on 1 Corinthians. Elsewhere, however—namely in homily 6 on 1 Timothy—Chrysostom himself ridicules this external rite of washing when it is not accompanied by inward purity of heart, and calls it γέλωτα καὶ λῆρον, παίγνια καὶ παίδων ἀθύρματα, “laughter and nonsense, games and children’s playthings.” This is also Tertullian’s position as he rebukes those who undertake prayer with their hands washed but their spirit filthy. Among certain Eastern peoples, moreover, and especially among the followers of Muhammad, this custom remains in force even in our own times. MURAT.]

what reason is there for undertaking prayer with the hands indeed washed, [Col. 1168A] but the spirit filthy? The hands themselves require spiritual purity, so that they may be lifted up pure from falsehood, murder, poisonings, idolatry, and all the other stains which, though conceived in the spirit, are carried out by the operation of the hands. These are the true purities, not those which most people superstitiously observe, taking water for every prayer, even with a bath of the whole body.

PANCIROL.—*But we extend the form derived from the Lord’s Passion.* Pamelius printed: “We, however, do not merely raise but also extend them, shaping them according to the Lord’s Passion, and while praying we confess Christ.” The reading “we also extend them, shaping them from the Lord’s Passion” might indeed be accepted. Yet the reading of the Agobardine manuscript appears truer: “But we extend the form derived from the Lord’s Passion.” The sense of either reading will, however, remain sufficiently obscure and ambiguous unless the rationale of the rite then in use is explained.

First of all, it must be noted that those who understand *modulantes* here as though it meant “singing” or “chanting psalms” are seriously mistaken. For since the subject is private prayer, which Tertullian says should be performed with a subdued and lowered voice, there was no need for musical melodies. We interpret *modulatum* as “image,” namely the figure or posture of a person praying. We therefore “extend the form derived from the Lord’s Passion”; that is, in prayer we do not merely raise our hands but also extend the pattern, the model—or, as Tertullian says, the *modulatum*—which our Lord Jesus Christ displayed when his hands were extended upon the cross. This rite is still observed among us today when the Lord’s Prayer is recited in public worship. In praying thus we confess Christ, because during prayer we profess by that very gesture that we are Christians, conforming our body to the figure of Christ crucified. Tertullian himself says in book I of *To the Nations*: [Col. 1170C] “If you set a man upright with his hands extended, you will have made the image of a cross.” Maximus of Turin, homily II *On the Lord’s Cross*: “Even the very posture of a man, when he lifts his hands, depicts a cross. We are therefore commanded to pray with hands raised, so that by the very gesture of our limbs we may confess the Lord’s Passion.” What Maximus calls “by the very gesture of our limbs,” Tertullian would have called “by the very configuration of the body.” So too in *On the Soul*, chapter 32, where he discusses the transference of souls into other bodies, he says: “Nor are they equal to the dimensions of bodies”; that is, they do not correspond to their measure, size, or capacity. In this sense the earlier Latin writers had spoken of “the extent of a field” and “measuring oneself by one’s own measure and foot.” RIGALT.] its form [Note: [Col. 1170A] *Modulantes*, “shaping,” in Semler and Leopold, from Pamelius’s edition.]; and as we pray, we confess Christ.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Note: [Col. 1174C] Title in the Ambrosian manuscript: **On Raised Hands and the Countenance.**]  
[Note: [Col. 1173A] Chapter XIII in other editions.]

Yet if we worship with modesty and humility, we shall commend our prayers to God all the more—not even with our hands raised too high [Note: [Col. 1174C] **Not even with the hands raised too high.** To raise the hands toward heaven and toward God when prayers are being poured forth was a most ancient custom, practiced not only by the Jews but also by the pagans. Furius Camillus, in Livy, book V, chapter 21: “He is said to have prayed, raising his hands toward heaven.” Marius likewise, when making vows to the gods in Plutarch, “νιψάμενος τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ πρὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνασχών”—“after washing his hands and raising them toward heaven.” I pass over other witnesses, especially the foremost of the Latin poets in books II and XII of the *Aeneid*, contenting myself with Aristotle, who says in *On the World*: “πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἀνατείνομεν τὰς χεῖρας εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν, εὐχὰς ποιούμενοι”—“All human beings raise our hands toward heaven when offering prayers.”

Moreover, this most ancient rite appears to have passed from the Jews to the pagans [Col. 1174D], rather than from the pagans to the Jews, since, as is stated in Exodus 17:11, Moses himself prayed with his hands raised toward heaven: “And when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but if he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed.” We also read in Psalm 133: “Raise your hands toward the holy places,” etc. The same may be gathered from Psalm 140 and from Lamentations 3:41.

Furthermore, it is evident from the Apostle’s command or admonition in chapter 2 of the First Epistle to Timothy that Christians were accustomed, and indeed obliged, to pray with their hands raised toward heaven. For he says: “I desire men to pray in every place, raising pure hands.” Clement of Alexandria, book VII of the *Stromata*, attests to this custom when he writes: “While we pray, we raise our hands toward heaven”—“τὰς χεῖρας εἰς οὐρανὸν αἴρομεν.”

I refrain from citing others, since even in our own age Christian priests raise their hands when about to pray to God, both in the ecclesiastical liturgy and in the celebration of the sacred rites. They do not, indeed, raise them too high, but moderately and properly, as Tertullian requires in this passage—that is, without lifting them above the shoulders [Col. 1175A]. Whether I should call this priestly rite a raising or an extension of the hands [Col. 1175B], I do not know. It is at least certain that among Christians in antiquity both practices were indiscriminately followed in prayer: the hands were either raised or spread out in the form of the cross. ## CHAPTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 1175D] Title in the Ambrosian manuscript: **On the Kiss.**]  
[Note: [Col. 1175A] Chapter XIV in other editions.]

Another custom has now gained force [Note: [Col. 1175D] **Another custom has now gained force.** Some, when fasting or during Lent, do not wish to kiss their brethren after the prayer has been completed; Tertullian reproves them. G. PANCIROLI.—**Another custom has now gained force.** We have emended what follows partly by conjecture and partly on the authority of the Agobardine manuscript. Tertullian condemns a custom that had already gained force among Christians at that time: many persons, on days when they subjected themselves to a private fast, did not conclude the prayer offered with their brethren [Col. 1176A] with the peace and did not seal it with the kiss of peace. He says that this is the “seal of prayer,” just as above in this book he called prayer “consigned,” that is, completed and finished [Col. 1176B].

He does not inquire into the cause of this corrupt custom, nor do I see any cause commonly advanced except that they might say that the kiss contained an element of cheerfulness foreign to the sadness and mourning of a fast. The profane suggested another cause, namely the bad breath of a fasting mouth; hence Martial, in epigram 4 of book IV, says that Bassa smells of:

> The fasts of Sabbath-keepers,  
> And the breath of sorrowful defendants.

But it hardly seems credible that the softness of so delicate a stomach existed in those stout hearts of the nearly apostolic age, when even mere women did not shrink from embracing and kissing the filth of martyrs in prison and wounds flowing with gore in the contest. What then? The same poet indicates that even among pagans the kisses of legacy-hunters were so unavoidable and importunate, in book IX, epigram [Col. 1176C] 99:

> There is no escaping kissers, Bassus:  
> Neither a painful ulcer nor shining pustules,  
> Neither a repulsive chin nor filthy scabs,  
> Nor lips smeared with greasy salve,  
> Nor the drip of a frozen nose will help.

Leaving aside, therefore, the cause of that superstition so peevish that those fasting believed it unlawful to perform the duty of kissing, Tertullian censures the custom, chiefly on the ground that peace should especially be exchanged with the brethren when prayer rises more commendably. The subject itself indicates that this is certainly how the text must be read, not, as Pamelius edited it, “when it rises more commendably with prayer.” For the question was not whether peace should be exchanged with the brethren after prayer had been offered, but whether it should be exchanged by one who had prayed in church with the brethren on days when he had voluntarily undertaken a private fast. Tertullian teaches that it should especially be exchanged at that time, “when prayer rises more commendably” [Col. 1176D], namely, when borne aloft by the vehicle of fasting. Basil says in his homily *On Fasting*:

> Νηστεία προσευχὴν εἰς οὐρανὸν ἀναπέμπει, οἱονεὶ πτερὸν αὐτῇ γινομένη πρὸς τὴν ἄνω πορείαν.  
> “Fasting sends prayer up to heaven, becoming, as it were, a wing for its upward journey.”

And Tertullian himself, in his book *On Fasts*, says that through fasting a richer prayer is sacrificed to God. Accordingly, a Christian who practices private fasts during public prayers should be all the more willing at that time to employ the kiss by which peace is exchanged with the brethren with whom he has celebrated the prayer, since he hopes that his prayer will be more pleasing and commendable to God, so that, through the benefit of Christian communion, even the brethren who are not fasting may participate in the fasting person’s observance. RIGALTIUS.]: after offering prayer with the brethren, those who fast withhold [Note: [Col. 1176D] **They withhold the kiss of peace.** Nothing is more widely known among the learned than that Christians were accustomed to greet one another with the kiss of peace and invite one another to concord and peace during public prayers and sacred rites, and indeed also on the roads and in private houses. It is therefore called the “seal of prayer” by Tertullian, because Christian prayers and almost all the sacraments of the ecclesiastical rite were concluded by this sign of peace [Col. 1177A], as though by a seal [Col. 1177B] of brotherhood.

Yet a custom and opinion had gained force among some that the kiss should be withheld from the brethren after prayer whenever they themselves were observing a fast voluntarily and out of private devotion. Tertullian refutes their practice and opinion by several arguments, showing that prayer is not complete without the kiss; indeed, it is more fitting to join peace to prayer when the prayer rises to God more commendably through fasting. He also adds that this conflicts with the Lord’s command by which we are ordered to conceal our fasts; for those whose abstention from the kiss revealed that they were fasting did not conceal them. What sort of sacrifice is it from which one departs without peace [Note: [Col. 1177D] **What sort of sacrifice is it from which one departs without peace?** By “sacrifice” here I understand prayer together with participation in the body of Christ; its conclusion and seal was the kiss of peace, the holy kiss.

In the common editions the following words occur: “Whatever the reason may be.” This does not appear defensible, since a little later the Author introduces the concession (*παρομολογία*): “But even if there is some reason.” The oldest manuscript reads: “Whatever the prayer may be, it will not be preferable to the observance of the command”—an obvious corruption. From this it appears that Tertullian wrote: “Whatever the observance may be, it will not be preferable to the observance of the command” [Col. 1178A], in this sense: however severe or perfect the austerity of a fast, or of any observance we have imposed upon ourselves [Col. 1178B], it will not be more commendable than the observance of the Lord’s command by which we are ordered to conceal our fasts. For those who, on account of private fasts, abstained from the kiss of peace after celebrating prayer with the brethren proclaimed by that very rejection of the kiss that they were fasting.

Thus far, therefore, Tertullian shows that abstention from the kiss is superstitious in those who fast: first, because there is no reason for abstaining; and then because, by rejecting the kiss, they proclaim their fasts, which God willed to be concealed. He adds: “But even if there is some reason, nevertheless, lest you become guilty in respect of this command”—namely, the command to conceal a fast—“you may defer the peace at home, if perhaps you are among persons from whom the fast cannot be completely concealed.”

So great was the Fathers’ concern for charity that they preferred to tolerate many rites adopted on an unsound rationale rather than provide, through a severe censure, even the smallest occasion for schism. Such was the Christian *συγκατάβασις*—accommodation—of that age. Accordingly, Tertullian supposes that the rite which he taught above should be abolished can be defended by some rationale; at the same time he prescribes a method of observing the rite while preserving the Lord’s command [Col. 1178C], namely, that those fasting may, after prayer with their household and close associates, abstain from the kiss of peace. For in this way, although they abstain from the kiss out of regard for the fast, they will nevertheless by no means disclose the fast, since no one knows of it except those from whom domestic circumstances make concealment impossible.

He confirms the plausibility of this excuse by the example of the fast which common and public religion sanctioned on the day of Passover—by which he means the day of the Lord’s Passion. For each year, when the day returned on which the Bridegroom was taken away, the Church had resolved to suspend the custom of kissing as a sign of widowhood and desolation, yet without any concern to conceal the fast, since anyone could disclose without ostentation what he had to do together with everyone else.
