PANCIROLI.—**So too on the day of Passover.** That “Passover” must here be understood as the day of the Passion, or the final Friday of Lent, which we call sacred on the Preparation, is sufficiently shown by the mention of the public fast then observed. The Author himself says [Col. 1179A] in chapter 10 of *Against the Jews*: “The Passover is the Passion of the Lord”;  and he uses the word in this sense elsewhere. Accordingly, on the Friday of the Preparation, Christians abstained from the kiss of peace in Tertullian’s age, a practice also preserved in the ecclesiastical liturgy in our own times. The ancient Rituals attest the same, and Berno, chapter 7 of *Matters Pertaining to the Mass*, among other writers, supplies the reason for this custom: “On the Preparation,” he says, “we abstain from the kiss because of the example of Judas the traitor, who betrayed the Lord Jesus Christ with a kiss of feigned peace.” MURATORI.—**So too on the day of Passover, when there is a common and, as it were, public religious observance of fasting.** By this very argument it appears to be proved that, in Tertullian’s age in Africa, a complete or full fast was neither common nor public except on the day of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 1179A], and that on that day and during that fast the prayers of the sacrifices and the kisses of peace were omitted. Yet on certain days throughout the remainder of the year voluntary or private fasts—proper to each person according to his devotion—were extremely common. These were full fasts, extended until evening, but those observing them nevertheless assembled for the prayers of the sacrifices and the kisses of peace.

There were, moreover, appointed days [Col. 1179B] on which assemblies were proclaimed at the tombs of the martyrs. There the faithful, fasting from sunrise onward and occupied with prayers, exhortations, and interpretations of the sacred readings, remained—but not beyond the ninth hour. At the ninth hour, after the Eucharist and the kisses, the assembly and the fasts were concluded. Such at that time were the *stations*; such was the Christians’ military discipline.

Meanwhile, even on the days of the stations, the private and voluntary fasts of which I have spoken were by no means prohibited, even if those private fasts were complete and continued until evening, whereas the station fasts lasted only until the ninth hour and were, by comparison with the former, like half-fasts. But some who privately practiced such an observance [Col. 1179C] considered it contrary to religion to break their observance or fast before evening; for that reason they did not approach the Eucharist, which was distributed at the ninth hour.

Tertullian says that this scruple can be tolerated by the same *συγκατάβασις*—accommodation: those observing a complete private fast may nevertheless take part in the half-fasts of the stations and, after receiving the Lord’s body at the ninth hour, may depart from the station together with the others but reserve the sacred morsel until evening, the conclusion of their personal fast. In this way both would be preserved: participation in the sacrifice and the fulfillment of the duty.

Yet he appears to take insufficient precaution against the danger which he most strongly warned must be avoided: namely, that they not become guilty in respect of the command by which we are ordered to conceal our fasts. For once they have received and reserved the Lord’s body, they are recognized as fasting—unless we say that it was such a widespread custom either to eat the portions of the Eucharist received in the churches or to carry them home reserved for private consumption [Col. 1179D] that even those engaged only in the fasts of the stations would eat or reserve them as they saw fit.

Certainly, the safer interpretation is that of one who rigorously establishes Tertullian’s proposition: that a devout act of obedience to God, such as fasting, is not dissolved by the Eucharist. For, as the most holy Nicene Fathers profess, we do not receive much bread or wine, but a little, so that we may understand that we receive it for sanctification, not for satiation—“οὐκ εἰς πλησμονὴν, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς ἁγιασμόν,” “not for fullness, but for sanctification.” Furthermore, those final words about Christian stations being performed after the military model are cited with quite inadequate consideration by Isidore, *Origins* VI, and no more suitably or judiciously by Rabanus. RIGALTIUS.], we rightly [Col. 1179A] set aside the kiss [Note: [Col. 1179D] **We rightly set aside the kiss.** Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, in book I, chapter 17, of *Observations on the Rites of the Ancient Church*, was led by these words of Tertullian to the opinion that Christians in antiquity omitted the kiss of peace on those days for which a full and complete fast had been proclaimed and prescribed. For if—as he reasons—the kiss was not employed on Good Friday because the fast was common to everyone and there was no imminent danger of ostentation in disclosing that one was fasting when one fasted with everyone else [Col. 1180A], then Christians always abstained from the kiss whenever the fast was solemn and common. I shall not reproduce his words at length.

But I fear that this most learned man did not grasp Tertullian’s meaning and the ancient custom of the Church. First, Saint Ambrose and the most ancient liturgies attest that the kiss of peace was employed in Christian assemblies on every fast day and during Lent itself, except only on its final days. Second, since it is certain that neither priests nor people customarily approached the celebration of the unbloody sacrifice without the kiss, and since it is also well established that the sacrifice was customarily performed on many fast days, who does not understand that Christians employed the kiss even on days of public fasting [Col. 1180B]? “What sort of sacrifice,” Tertullian had just said, “is it from which one departs without peace?” But since, according to the common rite of the Church, the sacrifice was by no means offered on the final two days of Lent, it is no wonder that Christians then dispensed with the kiss.

From this passage of Tertullian, therefore, Albaspinaeus should, as I have begun to suspect, have reasoned differently: namely, that in Tertullian’s age, at least in the African churches, a common and public religious fast was observed only on the last two days of Lent, while throughout the rest of the year and even during Lent itself Christians were free either to practice fasting or to forgo it. Hence, even if we were to grant—which I certainly do not venture to affirm—that fasting alone was the reason why the kiss of peace was omitted on the Preparation and the vigil of the Lord’s Resurrection, nevertheless, since in Tertullian’s view no public fast was held on any other days of the year, omission of the kiss must have been restricted to those two days of Lent alone [Col. 1180C].

Albaspinaeus could therefore truly have said that Christians abstained from the kiss on those days when a complete and full fast was prescribed. Yet according to Tertullian’s meaning he should have added that there were no more than two such days in the whole year, and that on the remaining days the kiss of peace was employed, although people fasted out of private devotion.

Since, however, almost everyone is persuaded that at least the Lenten fast, as instituted by apostolic tradition, was religiously observed by all Christians even in the earliest centuries of the Church, and that no one abstained from it without fault, I may easily appear to interpret Tertullian with boldness and rashly conjecture that there were once only two public fast days during Lent. But Tertullian himself will stand for me. After he had fallen into the heresy of Montanus, he wrote the following against the *Psychics*—the spiteful name by which he called Catholics—in chapter 2 of his book *On Fasting* [Col. 1180D]:

> Certainly they—the Psychics or Catholics—believe that in the Gospel those days were appointed for fasts on which the Bridegroom was taken away, and that these alone are now the lawful days of Christian fasting, the antiquated legal and prophetic observances having been abolished.

He then continues:

> Accordingly, for the rest, one must fast without distinction, by choice and not by command of the new discipline, according to the circumstances and reasons of each person. The Apostles also observed this practice, imposing no other yoke of appointed fasts to be undertaken in common by everyone.

Here you have the opinion and practice of the Catholics, at least in Africa, at that time. Following the Lord’s command, they fasted only on the two days when the Bridegroom was taken away: namely, when Christ the Bridegroom was placed upon the cross and laid in the tomb, just as the ancient Christians were accustomed to interpret the words of Mark 2 and Luke 5. On the other days Christians did indeed observe fasts, but by choice, not by command.

For although Lent was observed by Christians even in those times [Col. 1181A], and everyone held it certain that it had its origin in apostolic tradition, as could easily be shown by many testimonies of the ancients, nevertheless the observance of this complete fast had not yet been established by law and command—or at least had not yet gained force in all the churches. The fasts of the Four Seasons, other fasts, and several points of discipline, although flowing from apostolic tradition itself, were not immediately received throughout the whole Church of God, nor made binding by command. This was accomplished gradually through councils and through the decrees of the Fathers, and especially of the Roman pontiffs, so that fasts which once depended upon individual choice [Col. 1181B] are now observed with a concordant religious practice and by command.

The same Tertullian again bears witness in chapter 13 of the same book *On Fasting* that, besides Passover and apart from those days on which the Bridegroom was taken away, Catholics fasted not by the law of a command or by compulsion, but by choice. From this we may perhaps infer why Tertullian disapproves the custom of those who, when fasting, shrank from the kiss of peace: by disclosing that they were engaged in fasting, they exposed their modesty to danger, since it was uncertain whether the other brethren were fasting on the same day. Tertullian appears, however, to permit and praise this omission of the kiss only at Passover and on those days when the Bridegroom was taken away—that is, on the Friday of the Preparation and on Holy Saturday. MURATORI.], taking no care to conceal [Col. 1181A] [Note: [Col. 1181A] “To kiss” is wrongly read in the Frankfurt and Paris editions.] what we do together with everyone [Note: [Col. 1181B] **What we do together with everyone.** Namely, fasting. G. PANCIROLI.].

Similarly, [Note: [Col. 1182A] “Similarly,” Semler.] [Note: [Col. 1181C] “Similarly also on station days.” It has been stated in *On Fasting*, ch. 10, n. 91, that a “station” was an assembly of Christians held on certain days for the purpose of prayer, and that Catholics prolonged these stations until the ninth hour, Montanists until nightfall. G. PANCIROLI.—“On station days.” What stations were has been very fully explained by others; I shall therefore be content with a few remarks. Hermas, *The Shepherd*, book III, Similitude 4: “‘What,’ said the Shepherd, ‘is a station?’ And I replied: ‘A fast.’” In fact, by the term “stations” ecclesiastical writers meant nothing other than a fast observed by Christians, so that stations of every kind were sometimes called fasts. For when the faithful fasted, they customarily gathered in the sacred buildings at daybreak and remained there until the ninth hour, devoting themselves to prayer and the contemplation of divine things; hence the name “stations” later became attached to fasts. Some scholars nevertheless debate whether stations differed from fasts. [Col. 1181D] For my part, I think there was a certain distinction only when the term “strict station” was used. For then only the fasts of Wednesday and Friday were meant, and accordingly the stations continued until the ninth hour, as we have said, whereas fasts were prolonged until evening. It is uncertain, moreover, whether Tertullian here means fasts of every kind, or only those observed on Wednesdays and Fridays. I would more readily adopt the latter view. Whence, therefore, came the pagans’ hatred of them and the charges against them as impious, on the ground that they had neither temples nor altars and did not sacrifice? “Do you suppose,” says Minucius, “that we conceal what we worship if we have no temples and altars?” Just as Malachi, ch. I, called it “the table of the Lord” where in the same passage he had called it an altar, so here Septimius calls the table of Christ an altar. From it, namely, the body of Christ was received, in bread and wine consecrated by holy prayers in memory of the Lord’s Passion. Thus Paul, in 1 Corinthians 10, after saying that the bread which we break is a participation and communion in the body of Christ, which God willed to be handed over and sacrificed for us, adds that those who eat the victims become participants in the altar. He then warns the Corinthians that if, while they are dining among pagans, something is set before them [Col. 1182D] which is said to have been sacrificed to idols, they must take no portion of it; for they cannot be participants in the Lord’s table and in the table of demons. This precept, by applying the word “table” to pagan sacrifices, signifies that among the faithful the table of Christ is equivalent to an altar; and that the Jews who understand according to the flesh become participants through their sacrifices only in the altar, *thysiastērion* (θυσιαστήριον), the victim, namely, being consumed by flames, whereas Christians become participants in the *thysia* (θυσία), the sacrifice itself, namely, the body of Christ. And here our Septimius says that the morsel received by a Christian is participation in the sacrifice. Indeed, the Christian himself is reckoned as the Lord’s altar, to be steeped in blood—but Christ’s blood. This same author of ours, when restraining the faithful from spectacles and the circus, says: “Do you also desire some blood? You have Christ’s.” Finally, Chrysostom too, addressing his hearers as though in Christ’s own words, says: “If you desire blood, do not redden the altar of idols with the slaughter of irrational animals, but redden my altar with my own blood” (*Ei haimatos epithymeis*, φησί, *mē ton tōn eidōlōn bōmon tō tōn alogōn phonō, alla to thysiastērion to emon tō emō phoinisse haimati*; Εἰ αἵματος ἐπιθυμεῖς, φησί, μὴ τὸν τῶν εἰδώλων βωμὸν τῷ τῶν ἀλόγων φόνῳ, ἀλλὰ τὸ θυσιαστήριον τὸ ἐμὸν τῷ ἐμῷ φοίνισσε αἵματι). From this passage of Tertullian, namely, the opinion of certain recent heretics is refuted, who think it unlawful to preserve the body of the Lord after the sacred rites have been completed. Yet that what is now done in the Catholic Church was also done in ancient times is most plainly proved not only by these words of Tertullian, but also by Cyprian and other very ancient writers; it would be superfluous to repeat the testimonies which others have adduced. Secondly, since Tertullian here mentions only the reception of the body, and since we understand that the one body was customarily carried home and reserved, we may learn that it was once sufficient for Christians to partake of Christ’s body; and that this practice, preserved by the Catholic Church and confirmed by countless other ancient documents, is wrongly condemned by recent heretics. MURATORI.]

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 1184D] Title in Muratori’s codex: “On Virgins.”] [Note: [Col. 1184B] Chapter XVI in other editions.]

But what is variously observed among the Churches must be reconsidered as uncertain: whether virgins ought to be veiled or not. [Note: [Col. 1184D] “But what is observed indiscriminately.” He had said that it is absolutely certain from the Apostle’s precept that women’s garments and ornaments ought to breathe modesty. He now says that the uncertain question—whether virgins ought to be veiled—must be treated. For some allowed virgins to be unveiled in the temple and at sacred assemblies; others, however, thought that a veil was necessary for them also, as for other women, for the sake of modesty and by authority of the apostolic precept. MURATORI.] [Note: [Col. 1184B] “But that,” Semler, Leopold.] For those who grant virgins exemption of the head [Note: [Col. 1184D] “Exemption of the head.” Those who grant virgins a bare head and exemption from the veil. MURATORI.] appear to rely upon the fact that the Apostle did not name virgins specifically, but declared that women were to be veiled; and did not designate the sex by saying “females,” but a condition within the sex by saying “women” (1 Cor. 11:5). [Note: [Col. 1184D] “The Apostle did not name virgins specifically,” etc. “But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her own head; for it is one and the same as if she were shaven” (*Pasa de gynē proseuchomenē ē prophēteuousa akatakalyptō tē kephalē kataischynei tēn kephalēn heautēs; hen gar estin kai to auto tē exyrēmenē*; Πᾶσα δὲ γυνὴ προσευχομένη ἢ προφητεύουσα ἀκατακαλύπτῳ τῇ κεφαλῇ καταισχύνει τὴν κεφαλὴν ἑαυτῆς· ἓν γὰρ ἐστιν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ τῇ ἐξυρημένῃ). These are the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians, ch. XI, v. 5, which our Vulgate translator renders thus: “Every woman praying or prophesying with her head unveiled [Col. 1185B] disfigures her head, for it is the same as if she were made bald.” Those who contended that virgins had by no means been commanded [Col. 1185C] to pray veiled in the temple fashioned the following argument from the Apostle’s own words: If the Apostle had resolved to command this, he would not have used the word *gynē* (γυνή), which in Latin means “woman,” for *gynē* is commonly used only of married females. He would rather have said *thēleia* (θήλεια), the term by which Greeks designate all females, both married and unmarried; or he would also have added *parthenous* (παρθένους), that is, “virgins.” Therefore in that passage the Apostle signified not the whole sex, but a condition and part of the female sex, namely married women. Indeed, in the same Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. VI [sic; 1 Cor. 7:34], he himself distinguished virgins from women, saying: *memeristai de hē gynē kai hē parthenos* (μεμέρισται δὲ ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος), “the woman and the virgin are divided.” Tertullian addressed to himself a similar argument not only here, but also in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, which he later wrote in the school of Montanus. There he says in ch. 4: “It is objected to us that the Apostle made no mention of virgins where he prescribed concerning the veil, but named only women; whereas, if he had wished virgins also to be covered, he would have made a declaration concerning virgins as well as women, [Col. 1185D] just as, he says, in the passage where he treats of marriage he declares what is to be observed concerning virgins also. Accordingly, they are not included in the law of veiling the head, since they are not named in this law; indeed, they are thereby shown to be unveiled, since those who are not even named are not commanded.” MURATORI.]

For if he had named the sex by saying “females,” he would have made an absolute [Col. 1185A] ruling concerning every woman. But when he names one condition of the sex, he separates the other by leaving it unmentioned. For, they say, he could either have named virgins specifically as well, or, more concisely, females in general.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Note: [Col. 1185B] Chapter XVII in Leopold’s edition.]

Those who make such a concession ought to reconsider the status of the word itself—what “woman” means from the very first pages of the sacred writings; for they will find that it is the name of the sex, not of a rank within the sex. Indeed, God called Eve, who had not yet known a man, both “woman” and “female” (Gen. 2:23): “female,” insofar as it designates the sex generally; “woman,” insofar as it designates a particular rank of the sex.

> **Note [Col. 1185D]: Eve, who had not yet known a man, etc.** To show that Tertullian understands married and unmarried females alike by the term γυνή (*gynē*, “woman”), he adduces an example from Genesis 2:23. There, speaking of Eve, God says, according to the Septuagint translators: αὐτὴ κληθήσεται γυνή, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς ἐλήφθη, “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man”—as Tertullian himself most aptly translates elsewhere, following the version of the Seventy. The Vulgate translator, however, has: “She shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from man.” The divine writer had also said above: “The Lord God fashioned the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman,” εἰς γυναῖκα, “into a woman.” In both places Eve, although still a virgin and not yet having known a man, [Col. 1186B] is called γυνή, “woman.” Therefore this word does not signify a rank of the sex, that is, the order of married women, but the female sex generally; and hence [Col. 1186C] both virgins and married women are commanded by the Apostle to be veiled. —MURAT.

Thus even then, while Eve was still unmarried, the designation “woman” belonged to her, and that designation [Col. 1185B] was thereby made common to the virgin also. Nor is it surprising if the Apostle, being moved by the same Spirit by whom all divine Scripture—including the book of Genesis—was composed, used the same term, writing “woman,” a word which, by the example of unmarried Eve, applies also to a virgin.

The remaining arguments, finally, carry no weight. For by the very fact that he did not name virgins—just as in another passage, where he teaches about marriage—he sufficiently declares that what was said concerned every woman and the entire sex, and that no distinction was drawn with respect to the virgin, whom he does not name at all.

> **Note [Col. 1186B]: “Divine matters,” Murat.** This makes no sense.

> **Note [Col. 1186C]: Thus in another passage.** He refers to the same First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 7, verse 34, where Paul speaks as follows: “The unmarried woman and the virgin thinks about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.” If, says Tertullian, the Apostle had wished to distinguish unmarried women from married women when commanding women to be veiled, he would have distinguished them by some term, just as he did where he truly wished to distinguish them. It is therefore apparent that both married and unmarried women were comprehended under the single designation “woman,” or γυνή, when Paul did not wish to distinguish them. Tertullian answers in the same way in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 5. —MURAT.

For he who remembered elsewhere to distinguish—where, of course, the difference required it, distinguishing each kind by its own designation—when he does not distinguish, by failing to name the two separately, intends no difference to be understood. Moreover, in the Greek language, in which the Apostle wrote his letters, it is customary to call females γυναῖκες (*gynaikes*, “women”) rather than θήλειαι (*thēleiai*, “females”).

> **Note [Col. 1186C]: Rather than females.** That is, *in preference to* “females.” This is an elegant Hebrew mode of expression, also employed by Tertullian elsewhere. —MURAT.

Therefore, if this word is commonly employed as the name of the sex, being used in translation for the term “female,” he named the sex when he said γυναῖκα (*gynaika*, “woman”). But the virgin too is included within the sex.

There is also the explicit pronouncement: “Every woman,” he says, “who prays and prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head” (1 Cor. 11:5). What does “every woman” mean, if not every age, every rank, every condition? By saying “every,” he excepts no woman—just as neither man nor the obligation concerning veiling; for in the same way he says “every man” (ibid.). [Col. 1186B]

> **Note [Col. 1186C]: Just as neither man nor the obligation concerning veiling.** In the cited First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11, verse 4, the Apostle says: “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head.” But below he adds: “A man indeed ought not to cover his head.” Paul therefore says that it is disgraceful for any man whatsoever to be covered when he prays; and by naming every man he means all males, of whatever rank, age, or condition. Thus under the designation “every woman” he comprehends all females—virgins, married women, and widows alike. No one, however, will doubt that these words have been corrupted in our text. They might perhaps be restored, or at least some light may be shed upon them, if we also quote what Tertullian reports in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 8:
>
> “The Apostle says, ‘Every woman.’ What is ‘every,’ unless every kind, every rank, every condition, every dignity, every age? For ‘every’ is whole, complete, and lacking in no part of itself. The virgin, moreover, is a part of woman. Likewise, concerning the man who is not to be veiled, he says ‘every.’ See: two different names, man and woman; each is ‘every.’ Two laws corresponding to one another: on the one side veiling, on the other uncovering. Therefore, if by the expression ‘every man,’ the name ‘man’ is common even to one who is not yet a man—to the unbearded male—and since that name is common by nature, the law of not being veiled is also common to him who is a virgin among men,” etc. —MURAT.

Just as, therefore, in the male sex, under the designation “man,” even the unbearded youth is forbidden to be veiled, so also in the female sex, under the designation “woman,” even the virgin is commanded to be veiled. In each sex alike, the younger age should follow the discipline of the older; otherwise let male virgins also be veiled, if female virgins are not veiled, since the former too are not expressly bound by name. Let “man” and “unbearded youth” be different things, if “woman” and “virgin” are different things.

He says, of course, that she ought to be veiled “because of the angels” (ibid.), since the angels fell away from God on account of the daughters of men. Who, then, would contend that only women—that is, women already married and deprived of virginity—are objects of desire, unless perhaps virgins are not also permitted to excel in beauty and to find lovers? [Col. 1187A]

> **Note [Col. 1187B]: And deprived of virginity, objects of desire.** A word seems to me to be missing here, such as “kindle the fires” or something similar, so that the sense would be: Can only married women who lack virginity kindle the desire of angels and men? Are virgins not also allowed to excel in bodily beauty and find lovers for themselves? —MURAT.

Indeed, we see that they did not desire virgins alone, since Scripture says “the daughters of men” (Gen. 6:2), although it could have named “the wives of men,” or “females” without distinction.

> **Note [Col. 1187B]: Indeed, we see.** Indeed, says Tertullian, the angels appear to have desired virgins rather than married women, since Scripture testifies in Genesis 6:2: “The sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” Thus it was not the wives of men, nor females without distinction, who were sought by the sons of God—or by angels, as Tertullian interprets them, though I do not inquire how soundly—but virgins, women who were “free,” that is, not yet married. Therefore I think Tertullian’s passage should read: “Indeed, we see that they desired virgins alone.” Below too, no one will deny that “wives” should be read instead of “wife.” The same passage of Genesis is treated by Tertullian in the aforementioned *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 7. —MURAT.

Furthermore, the statement “And they took them as wives” (ibid.) supports this point, because those who are free are taken as wives. Concerning women who were not free, Scripture would have spoken differently. Thus women are “free” both through widowhood and through virginity: so completely, by naming the sex generally as “daughters,” Scripture blended the individual kinds within the genus.

> **Note [Col. 1187C]: Thus women are free.** That is, women are said to be “free” when they are either virgins or widows. —MURAT.

Likewise, when he says that nature itself teaches that females are to be veiled, since it assigned hair to women as a covering and an adornment, has not the same covering and the same honor of the head been assigned to virgins [Col. 1187B] as well?

> **Note [Col. 1187C]: Likewise, when he says, etc.** In the same chapter 11 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, verse 14, the Apostle says: “Does not nature itself teach you that, if a man lets his hair grow, it is a disgrace to him? But if a woman lets her hair grow, it is a glory to her, since hair has been given to her as a covering.” Therefore, since hair has also been given by nature to virgins as a covering, they too ought to use a veil. —MURAT.

If it is disgraceful for a woman to be shorn (1 Cor. 11:6), it is equally so for a virgin. Therefore, where one and the same condition of the head is assigned, one and the same discipline of the head is also required, even for those virgins whom childhood protects; for she has been called “female” from the beginning. Finally, Israel too observes this practice.

> **Note [Col. 1187D]: Finally, Israel too observes this practice.** Tertullian elsewhere also testifies that it was customary for Jewish women to walk with covered heads—namely, in chapter 4 of *The Chaplet*, whose words are: “Among the Jews the covering of their women’s heads is so established a custom that they are recognized by it.” He then adds the examples of Rebecca, still a virgin, who went veiled to her bridegroom, and of Susanna, who, when brought to trial, was covered with a veil according to the custom of the other Hebrew women. He repeats similar statements in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 11. Rabbi Nathan, in the *Arukh*, also mentions a certain thin veil with which women’s heads were customarily covered. —MURAT.

But even if Israel did not observe it, our law, enlarged and supplemented, would claim this addition for itself. Let it be excused for imposing a veil upon virgins also.

> **Note [Col. 1187D]: But even if Israel did not observe it.** Although Jewish virgins might not have had the custom of veiling their heads, such a practice would nevertheless have to be observed under the law of Christians; for in the New Testament the old laws have been both enlarged and supplemented. —MURAT.

For the present, let the age which does not yet know its own sex retain the privilege of innocence. For both Eve and Adam, when knowledge came to them, immediately covered what they had come to recognize.

> **Note [Col. 1188B]: For the present, let the age which does not yet know its own sex.** From this it is clear that girls who had not yet attained the use of reason were permitted to appear with uncovered heads. Tertullian calls this “the privilege of innocence.” But in those who had grown toward adolescence, as nature changed, discipline too properly had to change. See Tertullian himself in the cited chapter 11 of *On the Veiling of Virgins*. —MURAT.

> **Note [Col. 1088B]: Covered.** I read *texerunt*, “covered,” as in Genesis 3:7, rather than *texuerunt*, “wove.” —MURAT.

Certainly, in those whose childhood has changed, age ought to be as generous toward discipline as it is toward nature. For they are disclosed as women both in their bodily members and in their functions. No one is a virgin from the time when she is capable of marrying, since age in her has already married its own husband, that is, time.

But some woman has vowed herself to God. [Col. 1188B] From that moment she transforms the arrangement of her hair and changes her entire attire into that of women.

> **Note [Col. 1188B]: But some woman has vowed herself to God.** That from the very infancy of the Church there were virgins who dedicated their virginity to Christ can be shown most clearly both from several passages of Tertullian in the aforementioned *On the Veiling of Virgins* and from this chapter. One may therefore marvel either at the blindness of some people in a manifest matter, or at their audacity in condemning a practice approved by the usage of so many centuries; for they deny either that this custom flourished in the ancient churches of the Christians or that it should be praised in more recent churches. Yet here we read that certain women vow themselves to God and that this holy institution is practiced through God’s grace. Below he says: “You have married Christ; you have delivered your flesh to him. Conduct yourself according to the discipline of your husband”—that is, Christ. “If Christ commands the brides of others to be veiled, how much more surely his own.” To these add what the most learned Pamelius says in his preface to the same book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. In a matter sufficiently established, I refrain from citing further testimonies of the ancients. —MURAT.

> **Note [Col. 1188C]: From that moment she transforms the arrangement of her hair.** We have said that when virgins dedicated their chastity, they “transformed” their hair. I do not think Tertullian means by this expression that their hair was cut; for the author himself states that it is disgraceful for virgins also to be shorn: “If it is disgraceful for a woman to be shorn,” he says, “it is equally so for a virgin.” He repeats the same statement in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 7. I am well aware that in some regions consecrated virgins were accustomed to lay aside their hair, particularly in Syria and Egypt, as Jerome testifies in Letter 48 to Sabinianus, together with other records. But nowhere do I find that such a custom prevailed in Africa during at least the first three centuries of the Church. I therefore judge that nothing else is meant here than the modest arrangement of the hair which virgins began to observe when they dedicated themselves to Christ.
>
> In antiquity, virgins customarily went about with their hair loose and free. But as soon as they bound themselves in marriage, their hair was gathered and arranged, so that they passed into the sober dignity of matrons. Those, therefore, who married a divine bridegroom were rightly to show that they were married to God by hair that was arranged, restrained, and transformed; and by changing all their attire into that of women—that is, by clothing themselves in matronly garments—they were to be counted among matrons or married women. Other virgins, however, who were being raised in hope of worldly marriage, scarcely beyond childhood, “turn their hair, and with a rather wanton pin fasten up their tresses, parting their hair from the forehead and openly professing their womanhood.” These [Col. 1189B] are Tertullian’s own words in chapter 12 of *On the Veiling of Virgins*. Yet when, in chapter 11, he says, “Look at that virgin of yours already married, in soul through expectation and in flesh through transformation,” I do not know whether this adds darkness to the present passage or whether those words should be corrected from this one. If anyone wishes to understand “transforming the hair” here as referring to the aforementioned wantonness of virgins in arranging, fastening, and parting their hair, let him show that in this passage Tertullian is not speaking about virgins dedicated to God. —MURAT.

Let her therefore affirm the whole and fulfill the whole character of a virgin: what she conceals for God’s sake, let her cover completely. [Col. 1189A]

> **Note [Col. 1189B]: Let her therefore affirm the whole.** That sacred virgins are being discussed here is made more convincing to me by these words. For the sense is: If, from the time when she dedicated her virginity to God, a virgin ought to restrain the freedom of her hair and display sobriety in her clothing, why does she afterwards present herself with uncovered head to be seen in the sacred assemblies of the people? Let her therefore show herself altogether married to Christ and preserve the whole modesty of a sacred virgin, completely overshadowing the virginal head which she conceals for God’s sake. —MURAT.

It is our concern to commend to God’s knowledge alone what God’s grace accomplishes, lest we receive from human beings the recompense we hope for from God. Why do you uncover before God what you cover before human beings? Will you be more modest in public than in the Church?

> **Note [Col. 1189C]: Why do you uncover before God?** See what Tertullian considered utterly intolerable. Virgins consecrated to Christ went about in public with veiled heads just like matrons, but not in church. Tertullian does not believe that those virgins were free from the fault of ostentation: as though glorying in themselves, they appeared to boast of their own virtue before the other virgins, advertising that divine grace had chosen them to make a vow of continence. Some answered that they did this so that by their example they might encourage others to make the sacred vow of virginity; but Tertullian says that not even this was free from the danger of ambition. —MURAT.

If it is God’s grace and you received it, “why do you boast,” he says, “as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Why do you judge others by displaying yourself? Or do you invite others to the good by your own glory? Yet you yourself run the risk of losing it if you boast, and you compel others toward the same dangers. What is assumed out of a passion for glory is easily chosen.

Veil yourself, virgin, if you are a virgin; for you ought to blush. If [Col. 1189B] you are a virgin, do not endure many eyes. Let no one marvel at your face; let no one perceive your fiction. You successfully pretend to be married if you veil your head.

> **Note [Col. 1189D]: You successfully pretend to be married.** It is established that all married women, in obedience to the Apostle, covered their heads with a veil both in public places and in sacred buildings. This was therefore a mark of married women. Since sacred virgins wished to be regarded as married to Christ, they used in public the same garments, ornaments, and veils as matrons and women married in the world; in the Church, however, they removed the veil to distinguish themselves. Tertullian therefore says: “Let no one marvel at your face; let no one perceive your fiction.” That is, he calls it a fiction—though certainly a pious one—to pretend that they were married when they were still virgins. If sacred virgins had also used a veil in church, no one would have distinguished them from married women; and virgins could successfully pretend to be married only if they veiled their heads everywhere. —MURAT.

Indeed, you will not seem to be pretending; for you have married Christ and delivered your flesh to him. Conduct yourself according to the discipline of your husband. If he commands the brides of others to be veiled, how much more surely his own. [Col. 1190A]

> **Note [Col. 1189D]: Indeed, you will not seem to be pretending.** Tertullian corrects himself for having said that sacred virgins simulated marriage: for they had truly married Christ and dedicated their bodies to him, and therefore ought to attend the divine offices with veiled heads, in the manner of married women. He says the same in chapter 16 of *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “Fulfill the attire of a woman, so that you may preserve the state of virginity. Pretend outwardly something of what is within, so that you may display the truth to God alone. Yet you are not pretending to be married; for you have married Christ, you have delivered your flesh to him, you have betrothed your maturity to him. Walk according to the will of your bridegroom. It is Christ who commands both the brides of others and married women to be veiled: surely, much more his own.” I therefore have no doubt that Tertullian is speaking here not about all virgins but only about those dedicated to Christ, from the words “But some woman has vowed herself to God” down to the following words, “But let no one suppose.” —MURAT.

[The text is corrupt:] But let no one suppose that [the matter] is to be influenced by the practice of each predecessor.

> **Note [Col. 1190C]: But let no one suppose.** I perceive that an error lies hidden in these words, but I do not dare repair it. Perhaps *uniuscujusque*, “of each person,” should be read. The sense, however, is that the custom of virgins who went before ought not to be adduced as a reason. —MURAT.

Many consign their judgment to another’s custom, and add to it their own constancy, so that they may not be compelled to be veiled.

> **Note [Col. 1190C]: Many consign their judgment to another’s custom.** Here too I think the words are corrupt. I would prefer to read *multae*, “many women.” He says that numerous virgins, so that they might not be compelled to be veiled in the church, defended themselves by appealing to the custom of preceding virgins, considering themselves sufficiently prudent if they did what those women had consistently done. —MURAT.

> **Note [Col. 1189B]:** Muratori already understood that this passage was corrupt, and that it would not be adequately restored by writing *uniuscujusque et multae*, “of each person, and many women.” A. Neander emended it to: *Institutionem unusquisque*, “Let each person [regard] the institution.”

Certainly, voluntary virgins ought not to be prohibited, since they cannot deny that they too are virgins; they are content to abuse their reputation, secure in their conscience before God.

> **Note [Col. 1190C]: Certainly, those acting voluntarily.** I would interpret it as follows. It is altogether necessary for women bound either by worldly marriage or by marriage to Christ to be veiled. But women who practice voluntary virginity until they obtain a husband should not be absolutely forbidden to uncover their heads; they should merely be admonished to embrace the better counsels of discipline, although they sometimes pretend that they are virgins. We are compelled to explain the corrupt text by conjectures alone. —MURAT.

Concerning those, however, who are said to be betrothed, I can confidently pronounce and affirm beyond my measure that they ought to be veiled from the day when they first trembled at contact with a man’s body through a kiss and the joining of right hands.

> **Note [Col. 1190D]: Concerning those, however.** Nevertheless, Tertullian thinks that women who are called voluntary virgins ought to be veiled from the day on which they were betrothed to men and began to prepare themselves for future marriage. He contends that they differ in no respect from women already married. He makes similar statements in chapter 11 of *On the Veiling of Virgins*. We have said that betrothals among Christians were customarily performed by the giving of a kiss and the joining of right hands. Moreover, the matters presented briefly in this chapter were afterwards treated more fully by Tertullian himself in the frequently mentioned book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. —MURAT.

For everything in them has already entered into marriage beforehand: age through maturity, flesh through age, spirit through consciousness, modesty through the experience of the kiss, [Col. 1190B] hope through expectation, and mind through willing. Rebecca is a sufficient example for us (Gen. 24:65): when her bridegroom was pointed out to her, she was veiled for marriage merely through becoming aware of him.

## CHAPTER XXIII

> **Note [Col. 1191B]:** Title in Muratori’s manuscript: *On Bending the Knee.*

> **Note [Col. 1191B]:** Chapter XVIII in Leopold’s edition.

[Col. 1191A]

Prayer also suffers variation in the observance concerning the bending of the knee, because of a certain few who abstain from kneeling on the Sabbath.

> **Note [Col. 1191B]: They abstain from kneeling on the Sabbath.** The practice of bending the knees in prayer is exceedingly ancient. We have examples in 1 Kings 8:54; Luke 22:41; Acts 7:60, 20:36, and 21:5. Indeed, Eusebius of Caesarea calls this practice distinctive of Christians in *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 5, where he says that Christian soldiers prayed γόνυ θέντας ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν κατὰ τὸ οἰκεῖον τοῖς χριστιανοῖς τῶν εὐχῶν ἔθος, “placing the knee upon the ground, according to the custom of prayer peculiar to Christians.” Some, however, abstained from bending the knee on the Sabbath, although the other churches maintained the contrary practice. Tertullian held the latter opinion and for that reason [Col. 1191C] wished this diversity of ritual to be removed. I think it certainly was removed, since among the ancients I encounter no one who forbids bending the knees on the Sabbath.
>
> The same opinion nevertheless pleased later Greeks, as John the Monk attests in the *Canonical Collection* appended to Morinus’s books *On Penance*. It contains the following: τὰς πάσας σαββατοκυριακάς, καὶ ἑορτὰς δεσποτικάς, καὶ δωδεκαήμερον, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ Πάσχα ἡμέρας ἕως τῶν ἁγίων πάντων μὴ γονυκλινεῖν ἐν ταῖς εὐχαῖς, “On every Saturday and Sunday, on the feasts of the Lord, during the twelve-day festival, and likewise on the days from Easter until the feast of All Saints, it is not permitted to bend the knees in prayer.”
>
> In book III of the *Greco-Roman Law*, where Luke the Patriarch is discussed, no. 9, we also read: οἱ ἀποστολικοὶ κανόνες κολάζουσι τὸν ἐν τῷ τυχόντι σαββάτῳ, ἢ τῇ κυριακῇ γονυκλιντοῦντα, ἢ νηστεύοντα, “The Apostolic Canons punish anyone who bends the knee or fasts on any Sabbath or Sunday.” Although this little Greek is mistaken—for no such provision is found in the Apostolic Canons—it is nevertheless evident that [Col. 1191D] many centuries after Tertullian this custom had again become established in the East. —MURAT.

Since this disagreement is currently pleading its case most forcefully among the churches, the Lord will give his grace so that they either yield or employ their own opinion without scandal to others.

We, however, as we have received the practice, ought on the Lord’s Day alone, the day of the Resurrection, to guard ourselves not only from kneeling but from every posture and duty expressive of anxiety, postponing even our business so that we may give no place to the devil.

> **Note [Col. 1191D]: On the Lord’s Day alone.** The same statements are made in *The Chaplet*, as things received from the storehouse and authority of tradition: “On the Lord’s Day,” he says, “we regard it as unlawful to fast or to worship on our knees. We rejoice in the same immunity from Easter Day until Pentecost.” This practice was then common among Christians. Therefore, when some departed from it, the Fathers of the First Council of Nicaea thought it proper to settle the matter in its final canon, lest the churches disagree on it. St. Hilary, in the Prologue to the Psalter; St. Jerome, chapter 4 *Against the Luciferians*; the author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, among the works of St. Justin, question 113; St. Basil, chapter 17 of *On the Holy Spirit*; St. Augustine, Letter 119; Cassian; Germanus of Constantinople; Balsamon; Zonaras; [Col. 1192B] and not a few others mention the suspension of kneeling both on every Lord’s Day and on the days from Easter to Pentecost. —MURAT.

We do the same throughout the season of Pentecost, which we observe as the same solemnity of exultation.

> **Note [Col. 1192B]: But from every posture of anxiety.** A verb such as “to abstain” seems to me to be missing here. Since bending the knee and fasting expressed sadness and penitence, Christians abstained from that practice on the Lord’s Day, which was a day of exultation. —MURAT.

> **Note [Col. 1192B]: Which we discharge as the same solemn period of exultation.** We have said that Christians did not bend their knees during Pentecost either. I do not know whether it should be read: “which is the same solemnity of exultation, we discharge.” In *On Patience*, Tertullian uses *expunxit* for “performed”; in chapter 5 of *On the Flesh of Christ*, *dispuncta est* for “was completed”; and in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, *expunget* for “will accomplish.” In *Against the Jews* he likewise says: “Let us therefore *discharge* the order we have begun,” that is, let us complete it. Thus *tantumdem dispungimus* here signifies nothing other than “we perform and complete the same.” —MURAT.

For the rest, who would hesitate to prostrate himself before God every day, at least during the first prayer with which we enter the daylight?

> **Note [Col. 1192C]: At least during the first prayer.** The ἑωθιναί (*heōthinai*), or morning prayers, are famous among the ancients. On them consult the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 34; Chrysostom’s homily on Psalm 109 and elsewhere; and Basil’s *Longer Rules*, question 37—to omit others. —MUR.

During fasts and stations, however, no prayer is to be celebrated without kneeling [Col. 1191B] and the other customary expressions of humility. For we do not merely pray, but also make supplication and satisfaction to God our Lord. Concerning the times of prayer, nothing whatever has been prescribed, except, of course, to pray at every time and in every place. [Col. 1192A]

> **Note [Col. 1192C]: At every time.** He alludes to chapter 2 of the Epistle to Timothy, where Paul says: “I desire, therefore, that men pray in every place.” But he makes no mention of time. —MURAT.

## CHAPTER XXIV

> **Note [Col. 1192C]:** Title in Muratori’s manuscript: *On Place.*

> **Note [Col. 1191B]:** Chapter XIX in Leopold’s edition.

But how are we to pray in every place (1 Tim. 2:8), when we are forbidden to pray in public? “Every place,” he says, means every place which opportunity or even necessity might require. For what was done by the Apostles is not regarded as contrary to the precept: in prison, with the guards listening, they prayed and sang to God; likewise Paul, who celebrated the Eucharist aboard ship in the presence of everyone.

> **Note [Col. 1192C]: In the case of Paul.** It would seem that the reading ought to be “or by Paul.” He is referring to Acts 27:35. For when Paul was aboard ship, he took bread, gave thanks to God in the sight of all, broke it, and began to eat. —MURAT.

## CHAPTER XXV

> **Note [Col. 1192C]:** Title in Muratori’s manuscript: *On Time.*

> **Note [Col. 1192B]:** Chapter XX in Leopold’s edition.

Concerning time, however, the external observance even of certain hours will not be without purpose. I mean those common hours [Col. 1192B] which mark the divisions of the day: the third, sixth, and ninth, which are found to be more solemn in the Scriptures.

> **Note [Col. 1192C]: The third, sixth, and ninth.** Different authorities established different times to be devoted to prayer. The author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VII, chapter 34, says that prayer should be offered six times daily: around dawn, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, in the evening, and around cockcrow. Chrysostom, in his homily on Psalm 109, likewise teaches that prayer should be offered six times, though he does not employ the same division of hours. St. Basil determines that prayers are to be poured out to God seven times a day.
>
> Clement of Alexandria, however, in *Stromata*, book VII, praises this division of hours but adds other observations not to be disregarded: “Some establish fixed and definite hours for prayer, such as the third, sixth, and ninth. But the person endowed with knowledge prays throughout his entire life, as he strives through his prayers to live in communion with God.”
>
> Tertullian elsewhere, namely in *On Fasting*, chapter 10, again assigns the third, sixth, and ninth hours to prayer and confirms his opinion by the same examples. Maimonides, in *On Prayer and the Priestly Blessing*, chapter 1, states that in the synagogue prayer was likewise practiced three times every day. St. Cyprian, in *On Prayer*, and St. Jerome, in his letters to Laeta and Demetrias, testify that the same was customarily done three times in the Church of God. —MURAT.

The Holy Spirit was first poured out upon the assembled disciples at the third hour (Acts 2:15). On the day when Peter experienced the vision of the universal community in that vessel, he had gone up to the upper room at the sixth hour for the purpose of praying (Acts 10:9). The same Peter, together with John, was going to the temple at the ninth hour, where he restored the paralytic to his health (Acts 3:1).

Although these observances stand simply, without any command requiring them, it may nevertheless be good to establish a certain presumption which both enforces a reminder to pray and, as though by law, sometimes wrenches us away from our business for such a duty. Thus, as we also read that Daniel observed—surely from the discipline of Israel (Dan. 6:10)—we should worship no fewer than three times a day, being debtors to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

This is in addition, of course, to the prescribed prayers [Col. 1193B] which, without any reminder, are owed at the coming of daylight and of night.

> **Note [Col. 1193C]: In addition, of course, to the prescribed prayers.** He means the morning and evening prayers prescribed by law. Chrysostom speaks of them in Homily 22 on the Epistle to the Hebrews. See also Cyprian, the final chapter of *On Prayer*, where he says that one must necessarily pray in the morning and at the setting of the sun. —MURAT.

It is also fitting for the faithful neither to take food nor to enter the bath before prayer has intervened. For the refreshments and nourishment of the spirit must take precedence over those of the flesh, and heavenly things over earthly things.

## CHAPTER XXVI

> **Note [Col. 1193C]:** Title in Muratori’s manuscript: *On the Departure of Brethren.*

> **Note [Col. 1193C]:** Chapter XXI in Leopold’s edition.

Do not allow a brother who has entered your house to depart without prayer. “You have seen,” he says, “a brother; you have seen your Lord”—especially if he is a stranger, lest perhaps he be an angel.

> **Note [Col. 1193C]: You have seen, he says, a brother.** These words appear to be quoted from the sacred Scriptures, but I do not know what passage is intended. What is clear is that he is referring to Hebrews 13:2, where the Apostle, commending hospitality, says that people have sometimes received angels as guests. His words are: “And do not forget hospitality, for through it some, having received angels as guests, were unaware.” [The transmitted Latin is corrupt; it appears to record *latuerunt* (“were unaware”), with *placuerunt* (“pleased”) as a variant.] He alludes to the angels who presented themselves as guests to Abraham and Lot.
>
> Hence St. Ambrose, in *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 5, says: “How do you know whether you may receive God when you think you are receiving a guest? Abraham, while offering hospitality to travelers, received God and his angels as guests. Even when you receive a guest, you receive God,” etc. Ambrose repeats the same in *On Duties*, book II, chapter 21. But something may be missing from Tertullian’s words. —MURAT.

Nor should the visitor himself, once received by the brethren, place earthly refreshments before heavenly ones.

> **Note [Col. 1193C]:** “Once received” should be written instead of “removed.” —LEOP.

For immediately your faith will be judged. Or how will you say, in accordance with the command, “Peace to this house” (Luke 10:5), unless you also exchange mutual peace with those who are in the house? [Col. 1194A]

## CHAPTER XXVII

> **Note [Col. 1193D]:** Title in Muratori’s manuscript: *On Appending a Psalm.*

> **Note [Col. 1194C]:** Chapter XXII in Leopold’s edition.

Those who are more diligent in praying are accustomed to append “Alleluia” to their prayers, as well as psalms of the kind whose closing phrases those who are present may answer.

> **Note [Col. 1193D]: Alleluia in their prayers.** Others have already treated sufficiently the antiquity and repeated use of this word in sacred prayers. St. Augustine mentions it in his works on Psalms 106 and 110; St. Ambrose in the *Apology for David*; Sozomen in book VII, chapters 15 and 19; as do St. Paulinus, St. Jerome, Isidore, Sidonius, and others. It passed from the Jews to the Christians, for it is frequent in the Psalms of David; and we learn from St. Gregory, book II, Letter 63, that it was once used especially in the Church of Jerusalem. —MURAT.

> **Note [Col. 1194C]: Whose closing phrases they may answer.** I would wrong the reader’s learning if, after the most learned and deeply devout Cardinal Bona, I wished to discuss the very ancient practice of psalmody and of either reciting or singing the Psalms of David. Whoever wishes to be fully satisfied should consult his book *On Psalmody*. Here I merely observe in passing how ancient was also that practice whereby psalms are recited antiphonally in choir and in other ecclesiastical supplications. —MURAT.

And certainly every institution is excellent which is suitable for setting something before God and honoring him—bringing forward a prayer enriched to fullness as though it were the finest sacrifice.

> **Note [Col. 1194C]: A prayer enriched to fullness.** Just as Cicero spoke of a “meager prayer,” although in another sense, so Tertullian calls a prayer “enriched to fullness” when it joins prayers with the recitation of psalms. This is the finest, the well-fattened victim which we bring to the divine altar. —MURAT.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

> **Note [Col. 1194C]:** Chapter XXIII in Leopold’s edition.

For this is the spiritual sacrifice that has abolished the former sacrifices. “What use have I,” he says, “for the multitude of your sacrifices? I am sated with burnt offerings of rams; and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and [Col. 1194B] goats I do not desire. For who has required these things from your hands?” (Isa. 1:11). What God has sought, therefore, the Gospel teaches: “The hour will come,” he says, “when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23). “For God is spirit” (2 Cor. 3:17), and therefore he seeks worshipers of this kind. We are the true worshipers and the true priests, who, praying in spirit, sacrifice in spirit the prayer proper to God—the acceptable prayer which, indeed, he sought and which he provided for himself. This prayer, devoted from the whole heart, [Note: [Col. 1194D] **Devoted from the whole heart.** To prayer, which he calls a spiritual sacrifice, he attributes each quality that belonged to fleshly victims: namely, that it be vowed to God from the whole heart, fed, carefully prepared, whole, clean, and crowned. MURAT.] fed upon faith, carefully prepared with truth, made whole by innocence, cleansed by chastity, and crowned with *agape*, [Note: [Col. 1194D] **Crowned with agape.** Although the name *agapae* almost always signifies those banquets that the first Christians customarily celebrated in their sacred assembly for the relief of the poor and as a communion of mutual love, nevertheless the Fathers sometimes used this word to signify the Eucharist itself and the unbloody Sacrifice. Nor in former times was the administration of the Lord’s Body and Blood separated from the *agapae*. Tertullian seems to have understood it in the former sense in the *Apology*, ch. 39: “Our supper,” he says, “shows its nature by its name. For it is called ἀγάπη (*agapē*), which among the Greeks means love.” In the book *To the Martyrs*, ch. 2, he likewise calls it “the *agape* of the brethren.” From this, moreover, it is evident that the *agape* was customarily celebrated [Col. 1195B] after prayer, since it is called the crown of prayer. I appended an investigation concerning the abolition of the *agapae* to the unpublished poems [Col. 1195C] of St. Gregory Nazianzen. MURAT.] we must conduct with a procession of good works, [Col. 1195A] amid psalms and hymns, to God’s altar; it will obtain all things [Note: [Col. 1195C] **It will obtain all things for us.** These words should have been joined to what precedes: namely, “we must conduct the prayer, the spiritual sacrifice, to God’s altar; it will obtain all things for us from God.” MURAT.] for us from God.

## FINAL CHAPTER

[Note: [Col. 1195C] Title in Muratori’s manuscript: **On the power and affection of prayer.** “And affection”: I think *effectu* (“effect”) should be written, for what follows supports this. MURAT.]

For what has God denied to prayer coming from spirit and truth, when he himself requires it? We read, hear, and believe how many proofs there are of its efficacy. Prayer in ancient times delivered men from fires, wild beasts, and starvation, even though it had not yet received its form from Christ. But how much more fully [Note: [Col. 1195C] **But how much more fully, etc.** In commending the power and efficacy of Christian prayer, he seems to anticipate the objections of certain persons who did not see miracles being worked through prayer like those which, as we have learned, were performed under the old law. He therefore answers that Christian prayer produces, not indeed precisely those prodigies, but others no less great. I think the reading should be: “It not only stations the angel of dew, etc., but also equips those who patiently endure, etc.,” so that the sense is: not only those miracles that the synagogue obtained are obtained by the prayers of Christians, but other and even greater ones as well, since it is a far greater prodigy patiently to endure torments that are felt than to be delivered from torments. Both the preceding and the subsequent words and examples seem to support this interpretation. However much we may conjecture from a corrupt manuscript, it is certain that Tertullian is recounting extraordinary prodigies obtained from heaven through praying Christians. MURAT.] does the prayer of Christians pray! It does not station the angel of dew [Note: [Col. 1195D] **The angel of dew.** He calls the angel who preserved the three young men in the furnace, as though they had been drenched by a dewy shower, the “angel of dew.” In the same way, of course, he gave other angels names derived from some deed or office. Above he mentioned the “angel of prayer”; he recalls angels appointed over marriage in book II of *To His Wife*, final chapter; the “angel of baptism” in *On Baptism*, [Col. 1196C] chs. 5 and 6; and he names the angel charged with forming the human being in the womb in *On the Soul*, ch. 37. MURAT.] amid the flames; it does not close lions’ mouths; it does not transfer the farmers’ meal to the hungry; nor does the grace commissioned for this purpose avert any sensation of suffering. Rather, it equips those who endure patiently, who feel and who grieve, with the power of endurance; it enlarges grace through courage, so that faith may know what it receives from the Lord, understanding what it suffers for [Col. 1195B] God’s name.

Prayer in former times also inflicted plagues, routed enemy armies, and withheld the benefits of rain. [Note: [Col. 1196C] **Withheld the benefits of rain.** Since an error plainly lies hidden here, we may explain it to mean that prayer was the cause of beneficial rains not falling from heaven upon the enemies’ fields. MURAT.] But now the prayer of righteousness turns aside all God’s wrath; it keeps watch on behalf of enemies and makes supplication for persecutors. Is it any wonder that prayer knows how to force down the waters of heaven, when it was also able to obtain fire? Prayer alone conquers God. But Christ willed that it should perform no evil. He conferred upon it every power for good. And so [Col. 1196A] it knows nothing except how to call back the souls of the dead from the very road of death, restore the weak, heal the sick, cleanse the demon-possessed, open prison doors, and loose the chains of the innocent. The same prayer washes away offenses, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, consoles the fainthearted, delights the magnanimous, guides travelers, calms waves, strikes robbers with astonishment, feeds the poor, governs the rich, raises the fallen, supports those who are falling, and keeps those who stand steadfast.

Prayer is the wall of faith, our arms and weapons against [Note: [Col. 1196C] **Against the man, etc.** These words ought in truth to have been said of the devil, who always prowls about seeking someone to devour. But by what right would Tertullian have called him a “man”? The author therefore seems to me to be speaking of pagan rulers, who took every care and watched for every opportunity to harm the Christian commonwealth. MURAT.] the man who watches us from every side. Therefore let us never go unarmed. By day let us remember our station; by night, [Note: [Col. 1196C] **By night let us remember the vigil.** I would be doing what has already been done if I wished to commit anything to writing about the antiquity of vigils in the Church of God. Yet this passage of Tertullian will contribute considerably to proving it more clearly. I cannot, however, pass over the self-assurance of those who write that the institution of vigils arose from necessity and was preserved during the first three centuries of the Church. For since, they say, Christians could not assemble during the day for fear of pagans, it consequently happened that they held their gathering at night, keeping vigil in prayer and divine praises. But what is more evident than that Christians also assembled at church during the daytime, even in the first three centuries after Christ’s birth? This is sufficiently proved by what I have briefly, and others more fully, noted concerning the stations. MURAT.] the vigil. Under the arms of prayer let us guard the standard of our Commander; let us await the angel’s trumpet.

All the angels, too, were praying. Every creature prays. Cattle and wild beasts pray, [Col. 1196B] and they bend their knees; emerging from stalls and caves, they look up to heaven with no idle [Note: [Col. 1196D] **With no idle mouth.** It should be written *non otioso* or *non otiosae*. MURAT.] mouth, quivering [Note: [Col. 1196D] **Quivering.** If Tertullian indeed wrote this, I would explain the word in this way: they endeavor with their breath to move their mouths to praise and pray to God. MURAT.] as they move it with their breath. Even birds, when they now rise, lift themselves toward heaven; in place of hands they spread out the cross of their wings and utter something that seems to be prayer. What more, then, need be said about the duty of prayer? Even the Lord himself prayed—to whom be honor and power for ever and ever.

# The Book on Baptism

[Col. 1197]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, ON BAPTISM, AGAINST QUINTILLA (C)

## Argument

QUINTILLA HAD SPREAD THE HERESY OF THE CAIANITES AT CARTHAGE AND TAUGHT THAT WATER WAS NOT NECESSARY IN BAPTISM. IN THIS TREATISE TERTULLIAN, WHO WAS STILL A CATHOLIC, ATTACKS THIS ERROR. THE TREATISE IS DIVIDED INTO TWO PARTS: THE FIRST PART CONCERNS THE DOCTRINE OF THE NECESSITY AND EFFICACY OF BAPTISM; IN THE SECOND PART, SEVERAL DISCIPLINARY QUESTIONS CONCERNING BAPTISM ARE DISCUSSED.

### I

The excellence of the water of Baptism, chs. I, II, III. The matter and power of Baptism, IV. The effects of Baptism, V, VI. The customary anointing after Baptism, VII. The imposition of hands after Baptism and its significance, VIII. Figures of Baptism, IX. Whether John’s baptism was heavenly or earthly, X. The necessity of Baptism for salvation, XI.

### II

Whether the Apostles were baptized, XII. At what time the law of Baptism began to bind, XIII. Whether St. Paul baptized, XIV. The unity of Baptism, XV. The baptism of blood, XVI. The minister of Baptism; whether women may baptize, XVII. At what age of life Baptism should be conferred, XVIII. The time for conferring Baptism, XIX. Dispositions for Baptism, XX.

SCHRAM.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1197A] Happy is the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1197A] **Happy is the sacrament.** This first chapter is nothing other than a preface to the entire work. Since no one has ever doubted that Baptism is a sacrament, we shall cite only a few passages from Tertullian—and this not only in the sense in which *sacramentum* is understood as an oath, as the following passage from *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. XI, must be understood: “Do we believe that a human sacrament may be superimposed upon the divine?” but also properly, as a divine mystery and a sacrament of the Church. Such is this passage from book IV *Against Marcion*: “Nor elsewhere admit those who have been joined and the sacrament of Baptism”; and that passage from *On the Soul*: “Of the most secure and safest sacrament”; likewise *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 2: “The same sacraments of the washing”; and below, *On Baptism*, ch. 5: “Do unclean spirits not also brood over waters elsewhere without any sacrament?” Compare *On Idolatry*, ch. 6; *Against Marcion*, book I; and below, *On Baptism*, chs. 4, 12, and 13. EDITORS, from Pamelius.] of our water, [Note: [Col. 1197B] **Of our water.** Against Quintilla, who denied the necessity of water in Baptism, the Author bursts forth with this opening expression and overthrows the heresy, later revived among the Seleucians and Herminians and thoroughly refuted by blessed Philastrius and St. Augustine, but nevertheless reheated once again by certain followers of Calvin who, stiff-necked and slow of heart, revive these worn-out ravings. EDITORS, from the same.] by which, once washed clean [Note: [Col. 1197A] “Because those washed clean,” Fran.] from the sins of our former blindness, we are set free unto eternal life. [Note: [Col. 1198A] **Unto eternal life.** The fruit of Baptism is the remission of sins, by which we are rendered acceptable to God and made participants in eternal life. LE PR.] This treatise will not be useless, instructing both those who are just now being formed and those who, content simply to have believed without investigating the grounds of the traditions, through ignorance bear a faith that is untested yet liable to trial. [Note: [Col. 1198A] **Through ignorance bear a faith that is untested yet liable to trial.** The mind of Septimius is sought in vain unless we restore the words, as we seem to do by this emendation: *In tentatum probabilem fidem per imperitiam portant*. He uses *tentatum* for “temptation.” Those who are content simply to have believed, without investigating the grounds of the traditions, through ignorance carry into temptations a faith that is “liable to trial,” not without danger—that is, one to be tested with an uncertain outcome. RIG.]

[Col. 1198A] And indeed, quite recently a certain most venomous viper here, belonging to the Caianite heresy, [Note: [Col. 1198B] **A viper belonging to the Caianite heresy.** Jerome, Letter 43 to Oceanus: “And the Caianite heresy rises against me, and the long-dead viper lifts its crushed head.” RIG.—**A certain woman belonging to the Caianite heresy.** He speaks of Quintilla, from whom came the Quintillianist heretics, who were also called Pepuzians because she spread her poison especially at Pepuza. Before she joined Montanus’s party, she denied Baptism altogether; for after becoming devoted to Montanus, she admitted it as Montanus did. LE PR.] has carried away very many people by her doctrine, chiefly by destroying Baptism. Entirely in accordance with her nature: for vipers, [Note: [Col. 1197A] Others read “wild beasts.”] asps, and even basilisk-serpents generally seek dry and waterless places. But we little fishes, after the pattern of our ἸΧΘΥΣ (*Ichthys*, “Fish”), [Note: [Col. 1198B] **But we little fishes, after the pattern of our ἸΧΘΥΣ, Jesus Christ.** Compare what we previously touched upon concerning this symbol in Dr. Lumper’s preliminary dissertation, p. 150. Now, since I intend to put out and loosen the net somewhat more freely into the deep, I should like, under the illumination of the torches of the ancient Fathers and more recent scholars, to investigate the two chief meanings of this symbol: the one relating to Baptism, the other to the Eucharist.

The first reason Christians were called “little fishes” after the pattern of our ἸΧΘΥΣ, Jesus Christ, derives from the life-giving water of Baptism. “For since,” says the most learned Mamachi in *Origins and Antiquities of the Christians*, book I, ch. 1, §6, p. 54, “our ancestors understood that we are regenerated in the water of Baptism unto a new and spiritual life, they drew a likeness from fish, which are born in [Col. 1199B] water and cannot live without water, and gave the name ‘little fishes’ to all who had been baptized and embraced the Christian religion.”

There was also the fact that they read in the Gospels that the Apostles had been called by Christ fishers of men, and that the Church was compared to a dragnet gathering fish of every kind. Clement of Alexandria therefore urged Christians in the *Paedagogus* that those who wore rings should have the figure of a fish engraved upon them, lest they forget their origin: Αἱ δὲ ἔσφραγίδες ἡμῖν ἔστων . . . ἢ ἸΧΘΥΣ—“And let our seals be … a FISH” (book III of the *Paedagogus*, Oxford ed., p. 289). Hence the same Theosophist sang in his sacred and exceedingly elegant hymn to Christ the Savior (*ibid.*, p. 312):

> Fisher of mortals,  
> fishing from the sea of wickedness  
> those who are being saved—  
> pure fish [Col. 1199C]  
> from the hostile wave—  
> baiting them with sweet life.

The ancient Christians were all the more readily induced to use this symbol because, when the heat of persecution made it urgently necessary to conceal the token by which they distinguished themselves both from one another and from pagans, the Greek word ἸΧΘΥΣ seems to have appeared from the earliest infancy of Christianity. It was perhaps discovered by Asian neophytes living at Smyrna or Ephesus, in this region especially fertile in riddles, acrostics, and cryptic poems—whether deliberately or by God’s favor. The word is formed from the initial letters of the Greek titles “Jesus Christ, Son of God, our Savior.”

To this point belong very many testimonies of the Fathers, among which one of St. Augustine deserves praise above all (*City of God*, book XVIII, ch. 23): “If you join the first letters of these five Greek words, ἸΗΣΟΥΣ, ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ, ΘΕΟΥ ΥΙΟΣ, ΣΩΤΗΡ—meaning in Latin JESUS [Col. 1199D] CHRIST, SON OF GOD, SAVIOR—you obtain ἸΧΘΥΣ, that is, FISH. By this name Christ is mystically understood, because in the abyss of this mortality, as though in the depth of waters, he was able to remain alive—that is, without sin.” Compare the same author on Psalm 64; *Various Questions* 61.1–2, vol. I, p. 80; III, 1961; Sermons 249 and 270, vol. V, no. 205, §1, Appendix; Gregory Nazianzen, Sermon 37, otherwise 31, at the beginning; St. Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenian*, book III, Lyons ed., vol. 4, p. 351; Jerome, Letter 7 to Chromatius; Letter to Rufinus; on Matthew 14; on Ezekiel 29 and 37; on Hosea 4; on Zephaniah 1; on Habakkuk 1; St. John Chrysostom, Sermon on Andrew; St. Paulinus, Letter 13; St. Eucherius, *Spiritual Formulae* IV, ed. Fathers of Lyons, vol. 6, p. 831; St. Prosper, *On the Promises*, part II, ch. 39; St. Gregory the Pope, Homily 11 on the Gospels, Venice ed., vol. V, pp. 183–84.

Let the charming and pious words of honey-flowing [Col. 1200A] Ambrose serve as a crowning flourish (*Hexaemeron*, book V, chs. 6–7): “You are therefore a fish, O man! Hear that you are a fish: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like,’ etc. There are therefore good fish and bad; the good are preserved for a reward, the bad are immediately burned. The net does not entangle the good fish but raises it up; the hook does not destroy and kill it, but drenches it in the blood of a precious wound.… Therefore, O good Fish, do not fear Peter’s hook: it does not kill but consecrates.… Leap above the waves, O man, because you are a fish. Let not the waves of this age overwhelm you. If there is a tempest, seek the deep; if calm, play among the waves; if a storm, beware the rocky shore, lest the raging surge [Col. 1200B] dash you against a rock.”

There remains, however, another meaning of the symbolic fish, perhaps more sublime and profound, since it reaches the summit of divine things—namely, the most holy Eucharist. From this arises the second reason the ancient Christians took pleasure in calling themselves fishes. For by him through whom they were reborn they were also fed.

Anyone who turns even hastily through the sacred records of the Gospel must necessarily notice that Christ twice multiplied loaves as a figure of the sacrament, and twice after the Resurrection ate food with his disciples, and that fish was nowhere absent, as another evident symbol of the sacrament. Were I not afraid that this note, already perhaps too long, might grow beyond measure, I could hardly refrain—favored by this new light and guided by that most prolific interpreter of antiquities—from reviewing the countless monuments scattered here and there, especially glass, ivory, bronze, and earthenware vessels once used in sacred rites, upon which the most evident signs show [Col. 1200C] that one fish, two fish, or several fish constituted a manifest figure of the Eucharist.

Within the narrow limits of these brief observations there is scarcely room to refer the reader to the works throughout which the arguments for our position are scattered. See, therefore, if you please or have leisure: Boldetti, *Observations on the Cemeteries*, pp. 516, 163, 208, 198; Astadoni, Dissertation 22 on the Fish; Calogera, *Collection*, vol. XLI, p. 281; Bottari, plates XIX, XX, XXIII, XXXI, XXXVI, XXXVII, XL, XLIX, LI, LIX, LXVII, LXXXIII, etc.; Ciampini, *Ancient Monuments, Especially Those Containing Mosaic Works*, vol. II, p. 26; Fortunio Liceto, *Hieroglyphics*, Padua, 1653, no. 54, p. 390; Montfaucon, *Antiquity Explained*, III, 71.

Finally, an immense forest of testimonies could readily be added from Latin or Greek Fathers of the ancient or medieval period, whom it will suffice to indicate briefly: Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book III, p. 787, Oxford; Athanasius, *Questions on Sacred Scripture* 44; Severian of Gabala, sermon from a Vatican manuscript in Bottari, *Underground Rome*, vol. III, p. 20; St. Paulinus, Letter XIII, Roman ed., p. [Col. 1200D] 397; St. Peter Chrysologus, Sermons 47 and 55; the Venerable Bede on John 21 and Luke 24; Albert the Great, Commentary on John 17; St. Isidore in Albert’s *Mariale*, book IX, ch. 4; St. Thomas, Commentary on John 21; Cornelius a Lapide on Habakkuk 1:14 and Ezekiel 29:4 and 47.

At another time, kindly Reader, I should like you to be referred back here so that we may undertake the intricate but closely connected dispute over the Sibylline acrostic. Now, as I am about to leave you, I wish to warn you that a certain mystical conjecture by the otherwise most learned Gerard Vossius concerning this saying of Tertullian is of no weight—namely, that there lies concealed in it an obscure pagan slander against Christians. J. Kortholdt very effectively dispelled it in the study entitled *The Pagan Slanderer, or On the Calumnies of the Gentiles*, Lübeck, 1703. EDITORS.] our Jesus Christ, are born in water [Note: [Col. 1198A] “May be born,” Paris.] and are saved in no other way than by remaining in [Col. 1199A] the water.
