Thus that most monstrous Quintilla, who did not even have the right to teach soundly, [Note: [Col. 1199A] “Sound,” Junius.] [Col. 1200A] knew exceedingly well how to kill the little fishes by taking them out of the water. [Note: [Col. 1200D] **Who did not even have the right to teach soundly.** That is, she did not even have the right to teach sound and true doctrine, much less perverse, adulterated, heretical doctrine. [Col. 1201C] Thus at the beginning of book II *To His Wife*: “But if you understand soundly,” that is, truly. He therefore says that Quintilla did not even have [Col. 1201D] the right to teach soundly, because the office of teaching is masculine and indeed priestly, just as are baptizing and offering sacrifice. He explained this admirably in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. RIG.]

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1201A]

But how great is the power of perversity to undermine faith or prevent its reception altogether, when it attacks faith by means of the very things of which faith consists! Nothing so hardens human minds as the simplicity of God’s works as seen in their performance and the magnificence promised in their effect. Thus here too, because with such simplicity—without pomp, without any novel ceremonial equipment, and finally without expense—a man is lowered into water [Note: [Col. 1201C] “Water,” Junius.] and immersed while a few words are spoken, and rises again little or no cleaner, the attainment of eternity is consequently deemed incredible. [Note: [Col. 1201D] **Is consequently deemed incredible, etc.** This too was Quintilla’s error: she thought it incredible that Baptism should confer eternal life. For this reason he called her a viper of the Caianite heresy, because she departed to some extent from the impious doctrines of the Caianites. For they, as St. Jerome teaches in Letter 43 to Oceanus, dared to say that there were certain sins which Christ could not wash away through the shedding of his blood and which had put down such deep roots in our souls that they could not be torn out. LE PR.]

I am lying if, conversely, the solemn or secret rites of idols do not build up their own credibility and authority by means of display, apparatus, and expense. Alas, wretched unbelief, which denies [Note: [Col. 1201C] Others read “denies” in the third person.] God his own proper attributes, [Col. 1201B] simplicity and power! What then? Is it not also marvelous that death should be washed away by a bath? Yet it should be believed all the more if it is disbelieved precisely because it is marvelous. For what ought divine works to be like, if not beyond all wonder? We too marvel, but because we believe. Unbelief, however, marvels and does not believe: it marvels at simple things as though they were empty, and at magnificent things as though they were impossible.

And grant, indeed, that the matter is as you suppose: the divine declaration has sufficiently anticipated both objections: [Note: [Col. 1201C] “Precedes,” Paris.] “God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound its wisdom” (1 Cor. 1:27), and “Things exceedingly difficult for human beings are easy for God” (Matt. 19:26). For if God is both wise and powerful—which even those who pass him by do not deny—he has rightly established the materials of his operation in the opposites of wisdom and power, that is, in foolishness and impossibility. For every power derives its occasion from the things by which it is challenged.

## CHAPTER III

Mindful of this declaration as a rule barring objection, we nevertheless examine how foolish and impossible it is to be re-formed by water. What, then, [Col. 1202A] has this material merited, that it should serve as the instrument of so great a favor? I suppose the authority of the liquid element must be demonstrated. Yet abundant authority is available, and indeed from the beginning. For water is one of those things which, before all the world’s equipment, still unformed in appearance, rested with God: “In the beginning,” he says, “God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible [Note: [Col. 1201C] Others read “visible”; compare *Against Hermogenes*, ch. XXIII.] and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God [Note: [Col. 1201C] “Of the Lord,” Paris; compare *Against Hermogenes* XXIII.] [Note: [Col. 1201D] **The Spirit of God.** Thus Pamelius, who strikes out “of the Lord,” thinking that he has emended the text according to Tertullian’s more customary phrase and the Greek and Hebrew texts. Those considerations would not move me to alter the text or keep me from casting Tertullian’s vote in favor of the Vulgate, which translates “of the Lord” [Col. 1202C] and sometimes does so where the Greek has Θεοῦ (*theou*, “of God”). Nevertheless, I was led to retain Pamelius’s reading because Tertullian, in *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 3, said that in Genesis God was not called “Lord” until the world had already been completed and the human being formed. He therefore did not read “the Spirit of the Lord,” but “of God.” LAC.] was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:1–2).

You have, O man, first of all reason to venerate the age of the waters, because their substance is ancient; then their dignity, because they were the seat of the divine Spirit, at that time more pleasing, of course, than the other elements. [Note: [Col. 1202D] **More pleasing, of course, than the other elements at that time.** He prefers water to the other elements, especially as they then existed in a dreadful condition, taking care lest some philosophically minded critic accuse him of a physically less accurate assertion, since nearly all assign primacy to fire. Although Plutarch hesitates somewhat, he composed an entire treatise entitled *Whether Water Is Worthier than Fire*, in which he gives water precedence on numerous grounds and quotes Pindar, *Olympian Ode* 1: ἄριστον μὲν ὕδωρ, “Water is best.” LAC.] For darkness was still entirely shapeless, without the adornment of the stars; the abyss was gloomy; [Note: [Col. 1202D] **The abyss was gloomy.** By the name “abyss” he signifies the fiery seat of the world, not a mass of water, which here he calls by no means gloomy but joyful. LAC.] the earth was unprepared; and heaven was crude. Water alone—the liquid that is always perfect material, joyful, simple, and pure of itself—offered itself as a worthy vehicle [Note: [Col. 1201C] Others read *vectabulum*, which Junius prefers in *On the Soul*, ch. 53.] beneath God.

What of the fact that thereafter the ordering of the world was in some manner regulated by waters and established by God? [Note: [Col. 1202C] Others add “by God.”] For in order to suspend the heavenly firmament, he made it by dividing the waters at the midpoint; and in order to disclose the dry land, [Note: [Col. 1202C] Junius reads “divide.”] he accomplished this by separating the waters (Gen. 1). Then, when the world had been ordered through its elements and inhabitants were to be given to it (Prov. 8), the waters were the first to be commanded to bring forth living creatures. The primal liquid was the first thing to produce that which lived, so that it should not be surprising if, in Baptism, waters know how to give life. [Note: [Col. 1202D] **So that it should not be surprising if, in Baptism, waters know how to give life.** “To give life,” that is, to restore to the human being the eternal life from which he had fallen through sin. RIG.]

For the work of fashioning [Note: [Col. 1202C] Rigault and the Venetian edition read “molding.”] the human being himself was likewise completed with the cooperation of waters. Earth supplied the material, but it was not workable unless moistened and succulent; the waters, which before the fourth day had been separated into their own station, had tempered it into mud by means of the moisture that remained. [Note: [Col. 1202C] Others read “temper.”]

If I were now to pursue all, or many, of the things I could recount concerning the authority of this element—how great its power or favor, how many its capacities and offices, how great the service it renders the world—I fear I might seem to have gathered praises of water rather than arguments concerning Baptism. Yet thereby I would teach all the more fully that there should be no doubt that God has caused the material which he arranged throughout all his works and [Col. 1203A] deeds to obey him also in his own sacraments; that what governs earthly life [Note: [Col. 1203B] “Eternal life,” Franeker.] also provides for heavenly life.

## CHAPTER IV

But it will be enough to have outlined in advance those matters in which we also recognize the first rationale of Baptism—that original one, by which, even then, through its very disposition, it foreshadowed a figure of Baptism: that the Spirit of God, who from the beginning was borne over the waters, would re-form those immersed in them. [Note: [Col. 1203B] Franeker reads: “which even then—over the waters—would re-form those immersed.” Rigault reads: “was borne above, destined to remain over the waters of those being immersed.”]

The Holy Spirit was assuredly borne over something holy; or else that which bore him borrowed holiness from him who was borne above it. For every underlying material must necessarily take on the quality of that which hangs above it—especially corporeal matter taking on the quality of spiritual substance, which by the subtlety of its nature can readily penetrate and settle within it. Thus the nature of the waters, sanctified by the Holy One, itself conceived the power to sanctify.

Let no one say: “Surely we are not immersed in the very same waters that existed then [Note: [Col. 1204B] “Now,” Franeker; “themselves,” Rigault.] in the beginning?” Not in precisely the same waters, certainly, except insofar as the genus is one, [Note: [Col. 1203C] **The genus is one.** He preserves the terminology of law, not the elementary teaching of Porphyry; for interpreters of law call a species a “genus,” and an individual a “species,” so that “human being” and “horse” are genera, while Titius and Bucephalus are species. Thus Julian, law LIV, *Digest*, *On Verbal Obligations*, and Ulpian, law XXX, *Digest*, *On Legacies*. See Boerius on the military, forensic, and legal discipline of topics. Gothofredus, however, on law LIV, attempts to draw Aristotle into agreement with Julian and the jurists. He thus notes that Aristotle called species τελευταῖα γένη ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀτόμοις, “the last genera above individuals,” and individuals ἔσχατα εἴδη, “ultimate species.” Yet this will seem to dialecticians a less than logical assertion. By ἔσχατα εἴδη, “ultimate species,” which they themselves render “lowest species,” they understand not individuals but those universal, essential things which are predicated only of several things differing in number, such as “human being”; thus they contain beneath themselves no other species, but only individuals. They call the lowest genus that which truly is a genus but is predicated of several things differing only in species, so that it can by no means contain another genus beneath itself but is instead subordinated to the other genera. LAC.] while the species are many. Now what has been attributed to the genus also flows over into the species.

Accordingly, it makes no difference whether someone is washed in the sea or a pool, a river or a spring, a lake or a basin; nor is there any distinction between those whom John immersed in the Jordan and those whom Peter immersed in the Tiber. [Note: [Col. 1203D] **It makes no difference whether someone is washed in the sea or a pool; nor is there any distinction between those whom John immersed in the Jordan and those whom Peter immersed in the Tiber.** No one has said greater things about Christ’s Baptism than Paulinus said concerning John’s baptism in his *Poem on John the Baptist*:

> Proceed, then, to the holy waters of the pure Jordan, etc.

And yet these words of Tertullian mean only that in the matter of Baptism there is no difference among waters, nor is one more excellent than another. Therefore, it makes no difference whether someone is washed in the sea or a pool, a river or a spring, a lake or a basin. For the Tiber, in which Peter immersed people, conferred no more salvation than the Jordan, in which John did; nor was the chance water encountered on the road, in which Philip baptized the eunuch, for that reason either more or less salutary. This is certainly most true. For waters, whatever their kind, do not sanctify; rather, all waters, when God in three Persons has been invoked, receive the sacrament of sanctification, and through them God sanctifies the human being. Septimius says only this. RIG.—**Peter immersed people in the Tiber.** Peter, then, was at Rome at some time—a fact Calvin dared to deny, or at least to put forward as doubtful. Tertullian, who lived near those times and was a diligent observer of Christian affairs, leaves the matter in no doubt here and in *On Prescription*. LE PR.]

Nor did that eunuch whom [Col. 1204A] Philip immersed along the road in water encountered by chance consequently receive more or less salvation. Therefore all waters, by virtue of the ancient prerogative of their origin, receive the sacrament of sanctification when God is invoked. For the Spirit immediately comes upon them from heaven and remains over the waters, sanctifying them from himself; and thus sanctified, they absorb the power of sanctifying. [Note: [Col. 1204B] Wouwer’s old manuscript appends to these words: “in place of filth, may be washed away by the waters.” Wouwer thinks the text should read: “they absorb, so that offenses too, in place of filth, may be washed away by the waters.”]

The likeness, however, corresponds to the simple act: since we are defiled by offenses as though by filth, we are washed clean by waters. But offenses do not appear upon the flesh, since no one carries upon his skin a stain of idolatry, [Note: [Col. 1204C] **Of idolatry, fornication, or fraud.** These are the principal offenses which, at the very beginning of *On Idolatry*, he calls crimes destructive and devouring of salvation. In the same place he adds murder—which he omitted here—because murderers commonly bear the stains of a killing they have committed upon some part of their own body. RIG.] fornication, or fraud. Rather, persons of this kind are filthy in the spirit, which is the author of the offense. For the spirit rules and the flesh serves; nevertheless they share the guilt between them—the spirit because of its command, the flesh because of its service. Therefore, when the waters have in some manner been medicated [Col. 1204B] through the intervention of the angel, the spirit is bodily washed clean in the waters, and the flesh is spiritually cleansed in those same waters.

## CHAPTER V

But the foreign nations, strangers to all understanding of spiritual things, ascribe power to their idols through the same efficacy; yet they deceive themselves with widowed waters, [Note: [Col. 1204C] **But they deceive themselves with widowed waters.** Waters, that is, widowed of the angel and the Holy Spirit, and therefore barren. But upon our waters the Spirit comes from heaven, sanctifying them from himself; and thus, once sanctified, they conceive the power of sanctifying and consequently give birth—namely, to Christians, human beings destined for eternal life. Paulinus, Letter XII to Severus:

> Into this river the Holy Spirit descends from heaven.
and weds the sacred waters to the heavenly font, etc. RIG.] waters, deceive themselves. For they too are initiated into certain sacred rites by a bath—those of some Isis or Mithras—and they even carry forth their gods themselves for washings. [Note: [Col. 1204D] **They even carry forth their gods themselves for washings.** Blessed Augustine expressly relates this concerning the rites of the Mother of the Gods (*The City of God*, book II, ch. 4): “We took delight,” he says, “in the most shameful games presented to gods and goddesses. Before the litter of the heavenly goddess and Berecynthia, mother of all the gods, on the solemn day of her washing, things were publicly sung by the most depraved actors such as, I will not say the Mother of the Gods, but not even the mother of those very actors ought to hear.” And shortly afterward: “What are acts of sacrilege, if those were sacred rites? Or what is defilement, if that was a washing?” On this passage Ludovicus Vives relates that on the day before the Ides of April the Mother of the Gods was carried with great pomp by the Galli to the river Almo, [Col. 1205C] which joins the Tiber not far from the City, and that her image was customarily washed there at the confluence of the two rivers. He derives this from Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book I; [Col. 1205D] Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV; and Prudentius, *On the Martyr Romanus*. He also cites Giraldus, *On the Gods of the Gentiles*, Syntagma 4; Vibius Sequester, addressed to his son Virgilianus; Ammianus, book XXIII; Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica*, book VIII; and Claudian. EDD., from Pamelius.]

Moreover, they everywhere purify country houses, homes, [Col. 1205A] temples, and entire cities by sprinkling water carried around them; certainly, at the Apollinarian and Eleusinian games [Note: [Col. 1205C] *Pelusian*. Fran., Corbinian.] [Note: [Col. 1205D] **At the Apollinarian and Eleusinian games.** This is the reading in Ursinus’s manuscript; the common reading is *Pelusian*. And rites of the sun, or of Mithras and Serapis, certainly appear to be meant here. Capitolinus relates that Marcus Antoninus excluded ordinary Pelusians from these rites of Serapis. RIG.] they are baptized. And they presume that they do this for regeneration and impunity for their perjuries.

Likewise, among the ancients, anyone who had stained himself with homicide purified himself with cleansing water. [Note: [Col. 1205D] **Anyone who had stained himself with homicide purified himself with cleansing water.** The story is well known—on the testimony of Giraldus, cited above—and indeed nothing is more familiar among the authors: anyone who had stained himself with homicide washed and purified himself and his clothes twice seven times with cleansing water, generally at rivers. He adds that Pausanias speaks, in the *Attica*, of Theseus’s similar purification for killing the sons of Pallas, and, in the *Corinthiaca*, of the purification of Apollo [Col. 1206C] and Diana after the slaying of Python; likewise Herodotus, book II, concerning Adrastus.]

Therefore, if they flatter themselves that waters possess this power from nature alone [Note: [Col. 1205C] “Water possesses it from nature.” Fran., Corbinian.], because water is by its own material character suited to washing as a preliminary to purification, how much more truly will waters furnish this through the authority of God, by whom their entire nature was constituted? If they think that water is endowed with healing power by religion, what religion is more excellent than that of the living God? Once we recognize him, here too we recognize the devil’s zeal [Note: [Col. 1205C] “We know.” Rig.] in emulating the things of God, since he too practices baptism among his own. What similarity can there be? The unclean one cleanses; the destroyer delivers; the condemned one absolves. Evidently [Col. 1205B] he will destroy his own work by washing away [Note: [Col. 1205C] *Deluens*. Jun.] the sins that he himself inspires.

These things, indeed, have been set down as testimony against those who reject the faith, if they do not believe at all in the things of God while believing in imitations of them practiced by God’s rival. Do not unclean spirits also, on other occasions and without any sacrament, brood over waters, affecting that hovering of the divine Spirit in the beginning (Gen. I)? Every gloomy spring knows this, and every remote stream, and the pools in bathhouses, and channels in houses, and cisterns and wells, which are said to snatch people away—namely, through the power of a harmful spirit. For those whom waters have killed, or afflicted with madness or terror, are called “drowned,” [Note: [Col. 1206C] *Apopnictos* (“choked/drowned”). Wouw.] “water-maddened,” and “hydrophobic.”

Why have we related these things? So that no one may find it too difficult to believe that a holy angel of God is present to temper waters for human salvation, when an evil angel [Col. 1205C] frequently engages in profane commerce with the same element for human destruction. [Note: [Col. 1206C] “The profane one—frequents.” Fran., Corbinian.]

If the intervention of an angel in waters seems novel, an example anticipated what was to come. An angel intervened and stirred the pool of Bethesda (John V); those who suffered from illness watched for it. For if anyone had been first to descend into it, after the bath he ceased to suffer. This figure of bodily healing [Col. 1206A] foretold spiritual healing, according to the pattern by which bodily things always precede as figures of spiritual things. Therefore, as God’s grace advanced among humankind, more was added to the waters and to the angel: they who used to heal bodily defects now heal the spirit; [Note: [Col. 1206C] “More was added to the waters, which healed bodily defects; now by the spirit,” etc. Wouw.] they who used to accomplish temporal salvation now restore eternal salvation; they who once a year delivered one person now preserve whole peoples every day, death being destroyed through the washing away of sins. Once the guilt is removed, [Note: [Col. 1206C] **Once the guilt is removed, the punishment too is removed.** Paulinus, in the passage cited above, on the baptism of John:

> He washed away believers’ sins with the waters poured upon them,  
> And freed humankind from fear, remitted punishments,  
> And quenched fire with waters. RIG.]

the punishment too is removed. Thus the human being is restored to God according to his likeness (Gen. I), who in the beginning had been made according to God’s image: the image is reckoned to consist in outward form, the likeness in eternity. For he receives again that Spirit of God which he had then received from God’s breath, but afterward lost through sin.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1206B] It is not that we obtain the Holy Spirit in the waters; rather, once cleansed in the water [Note: [Col. 1206D] **But once corrected in the water, under the angel, we are prepared for the Holy Spirit.** He speaks of the angel of baptism, just as in the book *On Prayer* he speaks of the angel of prayer. RIG.] under the angel, we are prepared for the Holy Spirit. Here too a figure preceded (Matt. III). EDD.] directs the ways for the Holy Spirit who is to come, through the washing away of sins, which faith obtains, sealed (Matt. XXVIII) in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit (ibid., XVIII).

For if every word shall stand by three witnesses, how much more—since through the blessing we have the same arbiters of faith whom we also have as guarantors of salvation—does even the number of the divine names suffice for the confidence of our hope? [Note: [Col. 1206D] **For the confidence of our hope, the number of the divine names.** For the blessing was given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. RIG.] But since both the attestation of faith and the pledge of salvation [Col. 1206C] are guaranteed under three, mention of the Church is necessarily added; for where the Three are—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—there is the Church, which is the body of the Three.

## CHAPTER VII

Thereafter, having emerged from the bath, we are thoroughly anointed [Note: [Col. 1206D] **Having emerged from the bath, we are thoroughly anointed.** On the forehead, as we learn from Prudentius’s *Psychomachia*:

> After the seals were inscribed with oil upon the forehead, through which  
> The royal ointment and perpetual chrism were given. RIG.]

with a blessed anointing, in accordance with the ancient discipline [Note: [Col. 1206D] **In accordance with the ancient discipline.** That is, the Jewish discipline. RIG.], by which men were customarily anointed to the priesthood with oil from a horn. Thus [Col. 1207A] Aaron was anointed by Moses (Lev. XVIII); hence Christ is so called, from *chrism*, which means anointing. [Note: [Col. 1207B] **Which means anointing.** *Chrism* has several meanings among writers: some mean confirmation, which in the Latin Church is administered by the bishop alone; others mean the anointing performed when an infant is baptized. This passage refers to the latter anointing, which is performed by the priest on the crown of the head, whereas the former, or confirmation, is performed by the bishop on the forehead. For precisely this reason, a famous controversy concerning the anointing rite of bishops and presbyters arose incidentally between Petrus Aurelius and Jacobus Sirmondus, S.J.; anyone may have recourse to it to understand the matter fully. LE PR.] (1 Sam. XV). This anointing furnished the Lord with his name and was made spiritual, because he was anointed with the Spirit by God the Father, as in Acts: “For truly they gathered together in this city against your holy Son, whom you anointed” (Acts IV.27).

So too in us the anointing runs over the flesh [Note: [Col. 1207B] **In us, over the flesh.** The oil gently passing through and permeating the flesh or body. RIG.], but produces spiritual benefit; just as the act of Baptism itself is bodily, in that we are immersed in water, while its effect is spiritual, in that we are freed from sins.

## CHAPTER VIII

Next the hand is imposed, [Note: [Col. 1207B] **The hand is imposed.** The imposition of hands was once common in the Church’s rites, and almost nothing was done without an imposition of hands. It is nevertheless entirely certain that by the sacrament of the imposition of hands is meant confirmation, or *cheirotonia* (χειροτονία, “laying on of hands”), which for St. Clement is *bebaiōsis tēs exomologias* (βεβαίωσις τῆς ἐξομολογίας), “confirmation of the confession.” The imposition in question here is this one. LE PR.] invoking and inviting the Holy Spirit through the blessing.

Indeed, human ingenuity is permitted to summon spirit into water [Note: [Col. 1207C] **Human ingenuity is permitted to summon spirit into water.** He means hydraulic organs, such as are described by Vitruvius in book X of *Architecture* and by Hero in the *Pneumatics*. RIG.—**To summon spirit into water.** Vitruvius, on Ctesibius’s machine: “With the air compressed by pressure from that liquid.” LE PR.], and, after combining the two by applying hands from above, [Col. 1208A] [Note: [Col. 1207C] **By applying hands from above.** Vitruvius: “When the keys, touched by the hands, continually drive forward and draw back the slides, alternately closing and opening the apertures, they cause voices to sound in numerous varieties of musical modulation.” RIG.] to animate it with another kind of spirit so as to produce such brilliance of sound; [Note: [Col. 1207C] **To animate it with another kind of spirit so as to produce such brilliance of sound.** The machine is said to be animated when the musician’s fingers modulate the air [Col. 1207D] condensed by pressure into the water and combined with it, so that it emerges in a very brilliant sound articulated into manifold variety. Septimius calls this “another spirit,” namely, one trained and articulated. RIG.] yet shall God not be permitted, through holy hands, to modulate spiritual sublimity in his own instrument? [Note: [Col. 1207D] **In his own instrument.** He calls the human being God’s instrument. RIG.]

But this too comes from an ancient sacrament, in which Jacob blessed his grandsons by Joseph, Ephraim [Note: [Col. 1207B] *Efrem*. Fran., Corbinian.] and Manasseh (Gen. XLVIII.14), laying his hands upon their heads and crossing them over; [Note: [Col. 1207B] “Blessed.” Others, perhaps better, read “blesses,” with Corbinian not dissenting.] and indeed he so inclined them crosswise over one another [Note: [Col. 1207D] **And indeed he so inclined them crosswise over one another that they represented Christ.** Hands inclined crosswise make a *chiasmus*, that is, the shape of the letter X, which among the Greeks might signify the name of Christ. But since it is agreed that all nations, not merely the Greeks, were to be called to blessing by Christ, hands inclined crosswise certainly would not have portended any Christian mystery to the other nations, among whom the shape of that letter is not in use. Tertullian’s words must therefore be understood as meaning that the hands inclined crosswise represented the cross, or Christ fixed to the cross—not Christ simply, that is, Christ’s name. [Col. 1208B] For the form of the cross could portend Christ among all nations, for whom salvation was to come through his cross. RIG.] that, by representing Christ, they already then portended the blessing that was to come in Christ.

Then that most holy Spirit willingly descends from the Father upon bodies that have been cleansed and blessed (Matt. III.16); he rests upon [Note: [Col. 1208B] “And upon.” Jun., Corbinian.] the waters of Baptism, recognizing, as it were, his former seat, and descends upon the Lord in the form of a dove. [Note: [Col. 1208B] **He descends upon the Lord in the form of a dove.** At this point our Septimius contributes not a little to the symbolic subject, and it will not be irrelevant to review individually the several features of the Dove described by the Author and at the same time compare them with the monuments of the ancient Christians.

1. On the testimony of Sacred Scripture, the nature of the Holy Spirit is declared in the form of a Dove (Luke III.22; Mark I.10; Matt. III.16; John I.32). Cf. Bottari, *Explanation of the Paintings and Sculptures of Subterranean Rome*, plate XV, vol. I, p. 66; Aringhi, *Subterranean Rome*, book III, ch. 22, p. 517.

2. Christ himself, hidden under the Eucharistic Sacrament, [Col. 1208C] is represented by a Dove, because in ancient times the body of Christ was customarily preserved in a vessel bearing the form of a Dove. Cf. the *Life of Basil* written by pseudo-Amphilochius, ch. 2, no. 3, p. 943, vol. II; the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*, month of June; Bottari, cited passage, plate XIX; Aringhi, I, 339; II, 309, 337; Boldetti, *Observations on the Cemeteries*, 560, 375, 164, 371, 874.

3. Moreover, as the Fathers observed, the Dove is a sign of purity and simplicity of conduct, and of love, peace, chastity, prudence, contemplation, and a gentle, humble, and innocent spirit. Hence Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, ch. 6: “The dove,” he says, “is a simple and joyful animal, not bitter with gall, not savage in biting, not violent in tearing with its claws; it loves human dwellings and knows the fellowship of a single home; when they breed, they rear their young together; when they travel, they remain together in flight; they pass their lives in shared companionship; they acknowledge the harmony of peace with the kiss of the beak; they fulfill the law of unanimity in all things. This is the simplicity that must be known [Col. 1208D] in the Church; this is the love that must be maintained, so that the affection of the brotherhood may imitate the Doves.” Compare Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book I, ch. 5, p. 106, vol. I, Oxford ed.; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Illuminative Catecheses* XVII–XVIII; Augustine, *Against the Epistle of the Foundation*, ch. 4; and the others cited by Ph. Buonarroti, *Observations on Some Fragments of Ancient Glass Vessels*, p. 154 ff.; Aringhi, book VI, ch. 25, p. 607; Boldetti, book I, ch. 7, p. 24; Bottari, III, p. 78, plate CXV.

4. Nor is it unusual in paintings and carved stones for the Apostles to be represented under the figure of Doves. Paulinus of Nola, Epistle XXXII to Severus, p. 202, discussing the paintings and mosaic works of the basilica of St. Felix constructed by him, says:

> The cross, in a radiant globe, is encircled by a crown;  
> The crown of that crown is the apostles,  
> Whose figure is in the choir of doves.

[Col. 1209C] And on the cross that stands in Rome at the top of the apse of the Basilica of St. Clement, twelve doves rest upon the cross, signifying the Apostles. A reproduction of this cross appears in Bosio, book VI, *On the Triumphal Cross*; Gretser, *Work on the Cross*, book I, ch. 33; Bottari, vol. I, p. 118.

5. Finally, the ancient Christians everywhere adorned themselves with the same symbol, in order to spur themselves more vigorously to imitate the Dove. Another celebrated passage of Paulinus of Nola occurs in the same epistle:

> You will make us too, O Christ, doves pleasing to you.

[Col. 1209D] And a little earlier:

> The lofty cross is encircled by the ring of a flower-bearing crown,  
> And reddens, dyed with the Lord’s outpoured blood;  
> And the heavenly Doves that rest above the sign  
> Proclaim that God’s kingdoms lie open to the simple.

“The dove alone,” says the excellent Boldetti, in the cited passage, p. 23, “is very often seen painted in the chapels and tombs of the cemeteries, and also carved.... This was undoubtedly done because those first believers ... represented in this innocent bird charity, simplicity, groaning, compunction, purity, and innocence.” Cf. Mamachi, *Origins and Antiquities of the Christians*, book I, ch. 1, §9, pp. 66–69. EDD.]

Thus the nature of the Holy Spirit was declared through an animal of simplicity [Col. 1209A] and innocence, [Note: [Col. 1209D] **Through an animal of simplicity and innocence.** No one is so ignorant of the subject as not to recognize that these words designate the dove, because of its innocence and whiteness. Some theologians also affirm that the dove which flew down upon the head of Christ the Lord when he was baptized in the Jordan [Col. 1210C] was white. Thus Nonnus of Panopolis calls it *mimēma peleiados* (μίμημα πελειάδος), “an image of a dove”; *peleias* (πέλειας) is a white dove, called in Latin *livia* from its whiteness or livid hue. LE PR.] since the dove even physically lacks gall. Hence he says: “Be simple as doves” (Matt. X.16), and even this is not without the evidence of an antecedent figure.

For just as after the waters of the flood, by which the ancient iniquity was purged—after the Baptism, so to speak, of the world—the dove, herald of the heavenly wrath’s appeasement, was released from the ark and announced peace to the earth, returning with an olive branch (Gen. VIII.11), a sign which is also displayed among the nations to signify peace; [Note: [Col. 1210C] **Is displayed to signify peace.** What is better known than this peaceful hieroglyph? Thus the *patres patrati*, the fetial priests and ambassadors of peace, carried a branch of leafy olive as a symbol of peace. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> And in his hand he held forth a branch of the peace-bearing olive.

Silius, book III:

> Holding forth in his right hand a branch of the whitening olive. LAC.]

so by the same arrangement, after our former sins, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies down (Luke III) upon the earth—that is, upon our flesh emerging from the bath—and brings God’s peace, having been sent from heaven, where the Church is the ark prefigured. [Note: [Col. 1210D] **Where the Church is the ark prefigured.** Almost every one of the Fathers asserted that the ark was a type of the Church: Jerome, Cyprian, and others; Augustine, *On Baptism*, book V, final chapter. Tertullian’s words must be carefully noted, lest he exclude the visible Church on earth; for the dove of the Holy Spirit comes to the Church on earth with the peace of his grace. Therefore, when he says “sent from heaven,” he by no means connects this with “upon the Church,” since the Church is also on earth, but with the word “prefigured.” For in God’s sight the Church militant on earth, shaken by the flood of persecutions, bears the figure of the ark and of the blessed in heaven enjoying secure tranquillity, as Cyprian explains. LAC.]

But the world sins again, [Note: [Col. 1209C] “Has sinned.” Fran.] and therefore Baptism is ill compared with the flood. [Note: [Col. 1210D] **Therefore Baptism is ill compared**, etc. It appears that one should read, “To which evil Baptism may be compared with the flood.” RIG.] [Col. 1209B] Accordingly, it is destined for fire, as is also the person who renews his sins after Baptism, so that this too must be understood as a sign for our admonition.

## CHAPTER IX

How many supports of nature, how many privileges of grace, how many solemn rites of discipline, figures, preliminary constructions, and prayers have established the religious significance of water!

First, when the people, freely [Note: [Col. 1209C] “Freely” is absent from Fran.] delivered from Egypt (Exod. XIV), escaped the power [Note: [Col. 1209C] “Free from Egypt, the power,” etc. See the manuscript of Wouw.] of the Egyptian king by passing through the water, the water extinguished the king himself together with his entire army. What figure is more evident in the sacrament of Baptism? The nations are delivered from the world through water, and they leave behind in the water the devil, their former ruler, overwhelmed.

Again, water is healed from the defect of bitterness and restored to its proper [Note: [Col. 1209C] “Use.” Jun., Lat.] sweetness [Col. 1210A] by Moses’ wood. That wood was Christ, healing from himself the most unwholesome channels of the formerly poisoned and bitter nature—namely, the waters of Baptism (Exod. VII; Num. XX; 1 Cor. X). [Note: [Col. 1210C] Wouwer punctuates: “the channels; the most unwholesome waters of Baptism.”]

This is the water that flowed for the people from the rock that accompanied them. For if the rock is Christ, we undoubtedly see that water [Note: [Col. 1210C] “Waters,” manuscript of Wouw.; “water,” Jun.] is blessed for Baptism in Christ. How great is the grace of water in the presence of God and his Christ, for the confirmation of Baptism!

Christ is never without water. Indeed, he himself is baptized in water (Matt. III, X, XIV, XXVII; John III, IV, VII, XIII, XIX). When summoned to a wedding, he inaugurates the first rudiments of his power with water. When he speaks, he invites the thirsty to his everlasting water. When he teaches concerning love, he approves a cup of water offered to a brother [Note: [Col. 1210C] “Father,” Paris; others, “a poor person.” See the manuscript of Wouw., Rig.] among the works of affection. [Col. 1210B] At a well he recovers his strength; he gladly walks upon water and crosses it by boat; he ministers water to his disciples. The testimony of Baptism persists as far as the Passion: when he is handed over to the cross, water intervenes—the hands of Pilate know it; when he is wounded, water bursts from his side—the soldier’s lance knows it.

## CHAPTER X

We have spoken, so far as our modest ability permitted, concerning all the things that construct the religious significance of Baptism. Now I shall proceed, equally as far as I can, to its remaining condition, addressing certain minor questions.

The Baptism proclaimed by John [Note: [Col. 1210D] **The Baptism proclaimed by John.** The orthodox know that there is a distinction between the Baptism of Christ and that of John; hence the Council of Trent, session 7, canon 1. LE PR.] already at that time gave rise to a question proposed by the Lord himself to the Pharisees: whether that Baptism was heavenly or earthly (Matt. XXI). They were unable to answer consistently concerning it, since [Col. 1211A] they did not understand because they did not believe (Isa. VII). As for us, in proportion to the small measure of our faith, we are able to judge with a correspondingly small measure of understanding that this Baptism was indeed divine by command, though not also by power. For we read that John was sent by the Lord to this office, which nevertheless remained human in its condition.

For it furnished nothing heavenly, [Note: [Col. 1211C] **For it furnished nothing heavenly, but ministered in advance to heavenly things.** In this way, although those baptized in John’s water [Col. 1211D] did not receive the Holy Spirit, they were nevertheless prepared for the way of salvation in the name of our Lord who was to come. For Paul says in Luke, Acts XIX.4:

*Iōannēs men ebaptise baptisma metanoias, tō laō legōn: eis ton erchomenon met’ auton hina pisteusōsi, toutestin eis ton Christon Iēsoun. Akousantes de ebaptisthēsan eis to onoma tou Kyriou Iēsou* (Ἰωάννης μὲν ἐβάπτισε βάπτισμα μετανοίας, τῷ λαῷ λέγων· εἰς τὸν ἐρχόμενον μετ’ αὐτὸν ἵνα πιστεύσωσι, τουτέστιν εἰς τὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν. Ἀκούσαντες δὲ ἐβαπτίσθησαν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ): “John indeed baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Christ Jesus. And when they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.”

Paul therefore perfected those thus baptized: he imposed his hands upon them, and immediately the Holy Spirit came upon them. Luke certainly appears to suggest this meaning. But the Latin translator rendered the passage in such a way that those who had already received John’s Baptism are understood to have been baptized again. Hence Cyprian and Augustine too agree that these persons were indeed baptized again. It has not yet been possible for us to conjecture why Septimius refrained from using this argument, the strongest of all on either side of the question he had proposed. Jerome, however, uses it against the Luciferians and supports the translator. RIG.]

but ministered in advance to heavenly things, being appointed, that is, over repentance, [Note: [Col. 1211D] **Being appointed, that is, over repentance.** Destined to preach repentance through the commission of that Baptism [Col. 1212C] by which people might obtain remission of their crimes through repentance. LAC.] which lies within human power. [Note: [Col. 1212C] **Within human power.** And therefore John’s Baptism did not conduce to the remission of sins; for it lay within the power of those baptized to obtain remission through repentance—although by God’s grace—even if they had not received John’s Baptism. LAC.]

Finally, the teachers of the Law and the Pharisees who refused to believe did not practice [Note: [Col. 1211C] “Do.” Gelenius and others.] repentance either. But if repentance is human, its Baptism must necessarily have been of the same condition; otherwise, if it had been heavenly, it would also have given the Holy Spirit and remission of sins. But no one forgives sin or grants the Spirit except God alone (Mark V). Even [Col. 1211B] the Lord himself declared that the Spirit would not descend otherwise unless he himself first ascended to the Father (John XVI). What the Lord was not yet conferring, the servant certainly could not furnish.

Indeed, afterward in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1212D] **In the Acts of the Apostles**, etc. He means chapter XIX of Acts, which has exercised the minds of many. LE PR. See Tournely, *Course of Theology*, *On Baptism*, question 1, article 5. EDD.] we find (Acts XIX) that those who possessed John’s Baptism had not received the Holy Spirit, of whom they had not even heard. Therefore, that which did not provide heavenly things was not heavenly (John I). Even that which had been heavenly in John—the spirit of prophecy—so utterly failed after the whole Spirit had been transferred to the Lord that he afterward sent men to inquire whether the very one whom he had proclaimed and pointed out when he came was indeed he (Matt. II).

Thus the Baptism of repentance was being administered as a kind of candidate for the remission and sanctification that were to follow [Col. 1211C] in Christ. For the fact that he preached “a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins” was an announcement of a future remission. Repentance indeed comes first, and remission follows; this is what it means to prepare the way. But the one who prepares does not himself also complete the work; rather, he arranges for it to be completed by another. [Col. 1212A]

John himself professes that heavenly things are not his but Christ’s, saying: “He who is from the earth speaks from the earth; he who comes from above is over all” (John III.31). Likewise, he said that he baptized in repentance alone, [Note: [Col. 1211C] “Likewise, that he baptized himself in repentance alone.” Fran., Corbinian.] but that one would soon come who would baptize in spirit and fire (Luke III.16). This was because true and steadfast faith in the water [Note: [Col. 1212D] **True and steadfast faith in the water, by which one is baptized for salvation.** One must certainly write: “True and steadfast faith is baptized with water for salvation.” Reason persuades us that Tertullian wrote it thus, and what follows bears witness to it. RIG.] is baptized for salvation, but feigned and feeble faith is baptized with fire [Note: [Col. 1212D] **Is baptized with fire for judgment.** This is Tertullian’s custom: whenever fire is mentioned, he immediately seizes the occasion and directs it toward that final judgment of the Lord. Others, however, understand John’s statement that one would soon come who would baptize in spirit and fire as referring to the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost. RIG.] for judgment.

## CHAPTER XI

“But look,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1211C] “They say.” Paris.] “the Lord came and did not baptize.” For we read: “And yet he himself did not baptize, but his disciples did” (John IV), as though [Note: [Col. 1212C] “As though.” Paris, Jun., Corbinian.] John had proclaimed that he would himself baptize with his own hands (Luke III).

This is certainly not to be understood in that way; rather, the statement was made simply, according to ordinary usage. For example: “The emperor issued an edict,” or “the prefect beat someone with rods.” Does the emperor himself post it? Does the prefect himself administer the beating? The person for whom the service is performed is always said to perform the act. Thus “He will baptize you” must be understood to mean “You will be baptized through him” or “into him.”

But let no one be disturbed by the fact that he did not himself baptize. For into what would he have baptized? Into repentance? Why, then, would he have needed a forerunner? Into the remission of sins, which he granted by his word? Into himself, whom he concealed through humility? Into the Holy Spirit, who had not yet descended from the Father? Into the Church, which the Apostles had not yet established?

Therefore, his disciples baptized as ministers, just as John had previously baptized as a forerunner, with the same Baptism as John’s—lest anyone suppose it was with another, since no other existed except, later, Christ’s Baptism. At that time this could certainly not be given by the disciples, [Col. 1212C] since the Lord’s glory had not yet been fulfilled, nor had the efficacy of the bath been established through his Passion and Resurrection. For neither could our death be dissolved except through the Lord’s Passion (Rom. VI), nor could life be restored without his Resurrection. [Note: [Col. 1212C] “His rising.” Paris.]

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 1213A]

When, however, it is laid down that salvation belongs to no one without Baptism—above all on the basis of that declaration of the Lord who says, “Unless someone is born of water, he does not have life” (John 3)—there arise scrupulous, or rather rash, reconsiderations on the part of certain people: how, under this rule, can salvation belong to the Apostles, whom we do not find baptized in the Lord, apart from Paul? Indeed, since Paul alone among them put on the Baptism of Christ, either judgment has already been given concerning the peril of the others, who lack the water of Christ, so that the rule may stand; or the rule must be rescinded, if salvation has also been appointed for the unbaptized. As the Lord is my witness, I have heard arguments of this kind—lest anyone think me so perverse that, from the mere wantonness [Note: [Col. 1213C] “Wantonness,” Rigalt.; Fran.] of my pen, I gratuitously stir up matters that cause others scruple [Note: [Col. 1213C] “That causes,” Fran.]. And now, [Col. 1213B] as best I can, I shall answer those who deny that the Apostles were baptized.

For if they had undergone John’s human baptism, but desired the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 1213C] “But desired the Lord’s.” So that, reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, they might have eternal life. For that necessity proclaimed in John 3—“Unless someone has been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into [Col. 1213D] the kingdom of God”—must be understood of Christ’s Baptism. The author therefore answers those who, because they said that the Apostles had not been baptized, called their salvation into question or were altogether doubtful about it. He begins by arguing against those who expressly denied that the Apostles had received Christ’s Baptism; and Tertullian does not deny this in the present chapter. But he abstains from that question and seeks only to establish that their salvation must not be doubted, even though they had not been initiated by Christ’s Baptism—a Baptism which, in the preceding chapter, he denied that the Apostles had received before Christ’s resurrection. For, according to Tertullian, Christ did not baptize them; nor had the sacrament of Baptism which they themselves could administer yet been instituted, as the same Tertullian proves. He does not discuss whether they were baptized after Christ’s resurrection, nor does he incline to either side. His sole purpose in this chapter is that salvation belongs altogether to the Apostles, whether they were baptized or remained unwashed; and, taking the opportunity, he proves that they received John’s Baptism, [Col. 1214C] but prudently remains silent about the Lord’s. Consequently, the title which Pamelius prefixed to this chapter—“That the Apostles appear to have been baptized”—plainly shows that he entirely missed the author’s meaning. Hence the most illustrious Baronius, at the year 31, [Col. 1214D] no. 4, although he does not explain himself fully, and Bellarmine, *On Baptism*, book I, chapter 25, received too little illumination from the testimony of our African in this chapter when they sought to prove that the Apostles had been baptized with Christ’s Baptism. LAC.], inasmuch as the Lord himself had defined that there was one Baptism [Note: [Col. 1213C] “Was defining,” variant reading, Wouw.], when he said to Peter, who was unwilling to be washed [Note: [Col. 1213C] “Willing,” Junius, Corbinian.], “He who has once washed has no need to do so again” [Note: [Col. 1214D] “He who has once washed.” These words appear to speak of Baptism as not to be repeated. LE PR.] (John 13:6)—something he certainly would not have said at all to one who had not been baptized—this is the express proof against those who deprive the Apostles even of John’s Baptism, in order to destroy the sacrament of water.

Can it appear credible that the way of the Lord had not then been prepared in those persons—that is, through John’s Baptism—who were being appointed to open the way of the Lord throughout the entire world? The Lord himself, who owed no repentance, was baptized; was it not necessary for sinners? What then? Were others not baptized [Note: [Col. 1213C] “What therefore,” Junius; “that others were not baptized,” variant reading, Wouw.]? Not, however, Christ’s companions, but the rivals [Col. 1213C] of the faith—the teachers of the Law and the Pharisees. Hence it is also suggested that, since those who opposed the Lord refused to be baptized, those who followed the Lord had been baptized and did not share the judgment of his rivals—especially when the Lord to whom they adhered had exalted John by his testimony, saying [Col. 1214A] that no one among those born of women was greater than John the Baptist (Matt. 11:11).

Others, plainly enough under considerable strain, introduce the claim that the Apostles then fulfilled the equivalent of Baptism when, in the little boat, they were sprinkled and covered by the waves (Matt. 8); and that Peter himself, when walking upon the sea, was sufficiently immersed (Matt. 14). In my opinion, however, it is one thing to be sprinkled or overwhelmed by the violence of the sea, and another to be baptized according to the discipline of religion. Moreover, that little boat displayed a figure of the Church, because upon the sea—that is, in the world—it is disturbed by waves—that is, by persecutions and temptations—while the Lord, through his patience, is as though asleep (Matt. 8), until, awakened in the last times by the prayers of the saints [Note: [Col. 1214D] “Awakened in the last times by the prayers of the saints, he stills the world.” That is, by this petition: “May your kingdom come.” RIG.], he stills the world and restores tranquility to his own.

Now, whether they were baptized in some manner or remained unwashed—so that the Lord’s statement (John 13) about one washing, spoken in the person of Peter [Note: [Col. 1214D] “About one washing, spoken in the person of Peter.” Historically it was said to Peter: “He who has been washed has no need,” etc. LE PR.], may pertain only to us—it is nevertheless rash enough to pass judgment concerning the salvation of the Apostles, because [Note: [Col. 1213C] “Because not to them,” variant reading, Wouw.] the privilege of their first calling, and thereafter of their inseparable intimacy [Note: [Col. 1214D] “Inseparable intimacy.” The Apostles are called companions and members of Christ the Lord’s household, and *homōrophioi hetairoi* (ὁμωρόφιοι ἑταῖροι), “companions under the same roof,” by Nonnus of Panopolis in his paraphrase of John. LE PR.], could have conferred upon them a shortened equivalent of Baptism [Note: [Col. 1214D] “The privilege of intimacy could have conferred a shortened equivalent of Baptism.” In that manner, namely, in which the legal authorities themselves teach that sometimes, through the speed with which actions are joined [Col. 1215C] to one another, one action is concealed within another. RIG.].

I think they followed him [Note: [Col. 1213C] Junius emends: “Thereafter, the privilege of inseparable intimacy with [Col. 1214C] him could have conferred a shortened equivalent of Baptism. I think,” etc. Rigalt.: “Could have, when they, I think, followed,” etc. Leopold: “Could have conferred a shortened equivalent of Baptism. I think they followed.”] who promised salvation to everyone who believed. “Your faith,” he said, “has saved you”; and, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Mark 10)—to one who believed, certainly, yet had not been baptized. If such faith was lacking in the Apostles, I do not know whose faith is genuine. At a single word of the Lord, one of them arose [Note: [Col. 1214C] “Arose,” feminine form, Wouw.] and abandoned the tax booth (Matt. 9); another left his father, his boat, and the craft by which he supported his life [Note: [Col. 1214C] Fran. adds “who”]; another disregarded his father’s funeral rites; and he fulfilled that supreme [Note: [Col. 1214C] “That supreme command of his,” Fran., Corbinian.] command of the Lord—“Whoever prefers father or mother to me is not worthy of me” [Col. 1214C] (Matt. 10:37)—before he had heard it.

## CHAPTER XIII

Here, therefore, those most criminal men raise questions. “Baptism,” they say, “is therefore unnecessary for those for whom faith is sufficient, for even Abraham pleased God by no sacrament of water, but only by that of faith” (Gen. 15). But in every matter later things determine the conclusion, and what follows prevails over what came before. Granted that in former times, before the Lord’s passion and resurrection, salvation came through bare faith. But when faith was enlarged by the requirement of believing in his nativity, passion, and resurrection, an enlargement was added to the sacrament: the seal of Baptism [Note: [Col. 1215C] “The seal of Baptism, in some manner the garment of faith.” Even the Stoics knew that the faithful are perfected by Baptism. Thus Arrian speaks most explicitly, *Epictetus* XI, 9: Ὅταν δὲ ἀναλαβῇ τὸ πάθος τὸ τοῦ βεβαμμένου, καὶ ἡρημένου, τότε καὶ ἔστιν τῷ ὄντι, καὶ καλεῖται Ἰουδαῖος: “But when he assumes the disposition of one who has been baptized and has made his choice, then he both truly is and is called a Jew.” RIG.], which is, in a certain sense, the garment of the faith that formerly was bare and possessed no power apart from its own law.

For the law of baptizing was imposed and its form prescribed: “Go,” he says, “teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). The definition joined to this law—“Unless someone has been reborn of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5)—bound faith to the [Col. 1215B] necessity of Baptism. Accordingly, from that time onward all who believed were baptized. Then Paul also, when he believed, was baptized (Acts 9:6). And this is what the Lord had commanded during that affliction of blindness: “Rise,” he said, “and enter Damascus; there it will be shown to you what you must do” (*ibid.*)—namely, be baptized, which alone was lacking to him. Otherwise, he had sufficiently learned and believed that the Nazarene was the Lord, the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XIV

But concerning the Apostle himself they object that he said, “For Christ did not send me to baptize” (1 Cor. 1:17), as though Baptism were abolished by this argument. Why, then, did he baptize Gaius and Crispus and the household of Stephanas (*ibid.*)? And although Christ had not sent him to [Col. 1215C] baptize, he had nevertheless commanded the other Apostles to baptize. [Col. 1216A] But these words were written to the Corinthians in view of the circumstances of that time (*ibid.*), because schisms and dissensions were arising among them, while one attached himself to Paul and another to Apollos. For that reason the peaceable Apostle, lest he seem to claim everything for himself, said that he had not been sent to baptize, but to preach. For preaching comes first; baptizing comes afterward. If preaching came first, I think [Note: [Col. 1215C] “To baptize. But let preaching have come first. I think,” etc., codex Wouw.] that one who was permitted to preach was also permitted to baptize [Note: [Col. 1215C] “I think, however, that one who was permitted to preach was also permitted to baptize.” The rule of faith is preached or taught; then faith is sealed by Baptism. RIG.].

## CHAPTER XV

I do not know whether anything further is debated in the controversy over Baptism. I shall, however, take up again what I omitted above, lest I appear to have broken off the train of thought then pressing forward.

For us there is altogether one Baptism, both according to the Lord’s Gospel (John 3) and according to the Apostle’s letters (Eph. 4), since [Col. 1216B] there is one Lord, one Baptism, and one Church in heaven. But as to what rule is properly to be observed with regard to heretics, one may rightly reconsider the matter; for the declaration was issued to us [Note: [Col. 1215C] “For the declaration was issued to us.” This seems exceedingly obscure to Pamelius, yet it is not so very obscure. The sense is: In the Gospel and in Paul one Baptism is prescribed; but [Col. 1215D] who will decide whether this is to be observed in relation to heretics, since what has been issued and promulgated in Holy Scripture is directed to us Catholics? Nor is there any reason for Pamelius to remain uncertain whether Tertullian means that Baptism cannot be conferred by heretics or cannot be received by them, since he must mean both when he says that they do not possess Baptism.—“For the declaration was issued to us”: namely, what he said in the preceding clause, “For us there is altogether one Baptism.” This rule was issued to us, both from the Lord’s Gospel and from the Apostle’s letters, not to heretics. Among us—that is, among Catholics—it has been issued, made manifest and explicit, what must be observed by us in the discipline of Baptism; heretics, however, have no share at all in our discipline. We must not recognize among them what was issued to us and commanded to us. See Baronius, year of Christ 217, no. 8. LAC.].

Heretics, however, have no share at all in our discipline; the very withdrawal of communion certainly bears witness that they are outsiders. I am not bound to recognize among them [Note: [Col. 1216C] “To know,” Rigalt.] what has been commanded to me, because we and they do not have the same God, nor one Christ—that is, the same Christ. Therefore neither is there one Baptism [Note: [Col. 1215D] “Therefore neither is there one Baptism,” etc. Some think that Cyprian, Tertullian’s disciple, derived from this the error [Col. 1216C] of baptizing again those who had been baptized by heretics. Yet if the present author is rightly explained, perhaps no suspicion of error will remain. For many considerations suggest that a defect in what they call the matter may be understood here, or even a defect in the form, since St. Cyprian taught nothing of the kind. Hence canon 19 of the Council of Nicaea decreed that those who took refuge in the Church from the Paulianists should be baptized afresh. LE PR.], because it is not the same. Since they do not possess it rightly, they undoubtedly do not possess it at all; and what is not possessed cannot be counted [Note: [Col. 1216C] “What is not possessed cannot be counted.” In the Church there is one Baptism. Unity, however, is not a number, but the principle of number. Since, therefore, heretics are outside the Church, there is no Baptism among them; [Col. 1216D] consequently there is not even one Baptism, because what does not exist cannot be counted or supply a beginning to number. This was Tertullian’s opinion, which his disciple Cyprian maintained rather obstinately against Stephen in several letters. Yet perhaps he ought especially to be excused because the crimes of heretics in those times were such that they were in some respect guilty of violating the most holy Trinity; since the Trinity was not intact among them, and therefore was no Trinity at all, they could neither possess nor give anything that seemed to savor of Christ’s Baptism. RIG.]. Thus they cannot receive it either, because they do not possess it [Note: [Col. 1216D] “Thus they cannot receive it either, because they do not possess it.” The matter is expressed more clearly in Cyprian: “But we say that those who come from there are not rebaptized among us, but baptized; for they receive nothing there, where there is nothing.” RIG.].

But this subject has already been more fully set out by us in Greek [Note: [Col. 1216D] “Set out in Greek.” You see that Tertullian made a preliminary treatment of this subject in Greek, as he did in others—a point many have observed. LE PR.]. We therefore enter the washing once; sins are washed away once, because they ought not to be repeated. The Jewish Israel, however (Mark 7), [Col. 1217A] washes daily [Note: [Col. 1217B] “The Jewish Israel washes daily because it is daily defiled.” Thus in the book *On Prayer*: “Although Israel may wash all its members [Col. 1217C] every day, it is nevertheless never clean. Certainly its hands are always unclean with the blood of the prophets,” etc. RIG.—“The Jewish Israel.” For there is now also a Catholic Israel, just as there is a Catholic Jerusalem. LE PR.], because it is daily defiled (Heb. 6). It was precisely to prevent this practice among us as well that the rule concerning one washing was established. Happy is the water that washes once, that is no object of sport for fishermen, and that, being unclean through the continual recurrence of filth, does not again defile those whom it washes.

## CHAPTER XVI

We do indeed also have a second washing, itself one: namely, that of blood. Of this the Lord says, “I have a Baptism with which to be baptized” (Luke 12:50), although he had already been baptized. For he had come through water and blood (1 John 5:6), as John wrote, so that he might be baptized by water and glorified by blood, and accordingly might make us called by water (John 19) and chosen by blood.

He sent forth these two baptisms [Note: [Col. 1217C] “These two Baptisms.” The author’s meaning is that we first need the Baptism of water so that afterward we may drink the blood which flowed from the pierced side—that is, become participants in the Eucharist. LE PR.] from the wound in his pierced side [Col. 1217B] [Note: [Col. 1217B] The manuscripts read: “Accordingly, to make us by water.” Semler and the Franeker edition: “Accordingly, so that he might make us—chosen, he sent forth these—. Because those,” etc. With Leopold, we have adopted Wouwer’s emendation approved by Rigalt. The same applies in what follows: “This is the Baptism,” namely that of blood, or martyrdom, “which supplies the washing—and restores it.”], because those who believed in his blood were to be washed with water, while those who had washed with water were also to drink blood [Note: [Col. 1217C] “Those who had washed with water were also to drink blood.” This passage concerns the twofold Baptism of water and blood. Septimius says that both flowed from the wound in the pierced side, so that we who believe in Christ’s blood may be washed with his water; and, when cleansed by the benefit of such saving water, may also drink the cup of martyrdom for Christ’s name fearlessly and steadfastly whenever occasion arises. For he says that this Baptism is so efficacious that it both supplies the washing when it has not been received and restores it when it has been lost. These words must undoubtedly be understood of martyrdom. RIG.]. This is the Baptism that both supplies the place of the washing when it has not been received and restores it when it has been lost.

## CHAPTER XVII

To conclude this little subject, it remains to offer an admonition also concerning the rule for giving and receiving Baptism. The right of giving it belongs to the chief priest, who is the bishop [Note: [Col. 1217C] “The chief priest, who is the bishop.—For the sake of [Col. 1217D] the honor of the Church, which, when preserved, preserves peace. Otherwise, even laypeople possess the right.” There is a similar passage in the book *Exhortation to Chastity*. From both passages Jerome gathered what he says against the Luciferians: that Baptism is a priesthood. For it is written, “He made us a kingdom and priests to his God and Father”; and again, “A holy nation, a royal priesthood.” To the same point pertains what Septimius noted at the beginning of this little work: that those who have come out of the washing are anointed with blessed anointing, according to the ancient discipline by which they customarily were anointed into the priesthood with oil from a horn. The same Jerome, against those same heretics, borrowing the words of our Septimius as well, discusses the bishop’s honor and power and calls him the chief priest. Before Jerome, the author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments* had done the same, question 101: “That by ‘presbyter’ a bishop is understood,” he says, “Paul the Apostle proves when he instructs Timothy, whom he ordained a presbyter, regarding what sort of [Col. 1218B] person he ought to appoint as bishop.” He then adds: “For what is a bishop except the first presbyter—that is, the chief priest?” [Col. 1218C] And it certainly follows that the chief priest is the person set over not merely the people of priests—that is, laypeople endowed with the priesthood or sacrament of Baptism—but also presbyters and deacons. Indeed, he is called chief priest because, in addition to the priesthood of Baptism, he possesses the priesthood of order or honor, which order or honor is the highest in the Church. Augustine, *City of God*, book XX, chapter 10, says that bishops and presbyters are now properly called priests in the Church: “But just as we call all Christians such because of the mystical chrism, so we call all of them priests, because they are members of the one Priest.” Finally, since every Christian, even a layperson, is everywhere called by Tertullian and others an altar of God and a temple of God, and is said to offer and sacrifice to God praises, thanksgivings, fasts, and alms; and since he also plays the part of one expressing assent to the bishop or presbyter who formulates the prayers of the sacrifices by answering “Amen,” which means “Let it be done,” in this sense even Christian laypeople are called priests. RIG.].

Next come the presbyters and deacons, though not without the bishop’s authorization [Note: [Col. 1218D] “Not, however, without the bishop’s authorization.” The same is taught by Clement, *Constitutions* VIII, chapter 46, and St. Ignatius, *To the Smyrnaeans*: Οὐκ ἐξόν ἐστι χωρὶς τοῦ ἐπισκόπου οὔτε βαπτίζειν, οὔτε προσφέρειν: “It is not permitted apart from the bishop either to baptize or to offer the sacred rites.” LE PR.], for the sake of the Church’s honor. When that is preserved, peace is preserved. Otherwise, even laypeople possess the right. For what is received equally may be given equally—unless bishops or presbyters or deacons are now called “learners” [Note: [Col. 1217B] “Were called speakers,” Latinus. “Are called speakers,” Franeker, [Col. 1218B] Paris.]—and the Lord’s word ought not to be hidden from anyone. Accordingly, Baptism too, being equally a possession of God, may be administered by all [Note: [Col. 1218D] “Being equally a possession of God, may be administered by all.” A similar passage concerning the honor of bishops and presidents occurs in the book *On the Crown*. RIG.].

But how much more does the discipline of reverence and modesty rest upon laypeople, since this responsibility belongs to their superiors [Note: [Col. 1218D] “Since this responsibility belongs to their superiors”: namely, bishops, presbyters, and deacons. RIG.], so that they may not assume for themselves the office dedicated to the bishop [Note: [Col. 1218B] “Bishops,” variant reading, Wouw.]—the episcopate [Note: [Col. 1218B] Leopold thinks that this word was written in the margin by some copyist and inserted into the text. Junius: “Office. Rivalry for the episcopate,” etc.]. Rivalry is the mother of schisms. “All things are permissible,” said the most holy Apostle, [Col. 1218B] “but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. 6 and 10). Let it suffice, then, that you exercise the right in cases of necessity [Note: [Col. 1218B] Rigalt. omits “that.”], wherever a condition of place, time, or person compels it. For then the resolution of the person bringing assistance [Note: [Col. 1218D] “The resolution of the person bringing assistance.” This signifies the confidence of the helper, who, conscious of his right, assists a person in peril without doubt or hesitation; that is, such conduct is admitted, accepted, and praised. By “resolution” he means boldness. He might have said “to assist resolutely,” in the same form in which he will shortly say “to learn resolutely,” and in the book *On Patience*, “he did not resolutely denounce.” RIG.] is accepted when the circumstances of the person in peril are urgent. For he will be guilty of the loss of a human being if he has neglected to provide what he freely could [Col. 1219A] [Note: [Col. 1219B] “For he will be guilty of the loss of a human being if he has neglected to provide what he freely could.” How can he be guilty of the loss of a human being when, in what follows, he says that those who understand the weight of Baptism should fear receiving it more than delaying it, and that unimpaired faith is secure of salvation? He does not contradict himself. For anyone who has neglected to give Baptism to a person desiring it amid a sudden and violent danger is guilty of that person’s loss. For, so far as it lay with him, he destroyed the person for whom, through either inhuman negligence or ill-timed diffidence, he did not hasten to procure the saving washing. But one who with his whole heart and mind desired to become a Christian was, through faith, made for Christ what Christ granted to faith; and he who was lost through a wickedly delaying human being is saved by the most generous saving God. RIG.].

The presumption of a woman [Note: [Col. 1219A] “Of women,” Franeker.] who has usurped the right to teach will certainly not also produce for her a right to baptize—unless some new beast should arise similar to the former one, so that, just as the one abolished Baptism, another might confer it by herself [Note: [Col. 1219C] “So that another might confer it by herself”: that is, so that she herself might baptize. RIG.].

But if writings wrongly attributed to Paul [Note: [Col. 1219C] “But if writings wrongly attributed to Paul.” He means the writing entitled *Acts of Paul*, long since classified among the apocrypha. Eusebius mentions it, *History* III, chapter 19. We have emended this passage from Ursinus’s book, for the name of Thecla had undoubtedly crept into the text from some marginal note. Her story, of the same stamp as those Pauline writings, still circulates under the name of Basil of Seleucia. In the age of our Septimius, writers of such fables were expelled from whatever position they held in the Church. RIG.—“But if writings attributed to Paul,” etc. Here Rigalt.’s manuscript struck out “the example of Thecla,” which occurs in almost all the others and has exercised the commentators. I think these words crept into the text from the margin. Yet lest Thecla’s story be altogether unknown, it should be noted that most regard it as apocryphal, although Baronius defends it in his notes on the martyrology. It runs as follows: When the virgin Thecla heard Paul preaching [Col. 1219D] at Iconium, she rejected the young man to whom she had been betrothed in marriage. Her mother denounced her daughter to the judges as a Christian. By the sign of the cross and Paul’s prayers she overcame innumerable tortures and finally gained the martyr’s palm. All these things up to this point are true; but other things are doubtful—namely, that she became a nun and received a veil from blessed Paul. The spurious “Damascenus VI” drew these things from Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, as he did certain other matters of this kind concerning the souls of Falconilla and Trajan, supposedly delivered by the prayers of Thecla and Gregory. LE PR.—Thus far the Catholic authors, whose arguments contain more indignation than persuasion. Having considered them, the upright, sober-minded, and more judicious Grabe, a most learned man from the Protestant ranks, offers the following observations. Until we produce the *Acts of Paul and Thecla* themselves, it will be sufficient to oppose them to the harsher disdain of our own people: “From this,” he says, “it is indeed established that this little book was falsely inscribed with Paul’s name. Yet the question still remains [Col. 1220B] whether the story of Thecla narrated in that book was a mere fable invented by that presbyter—as though no such most holy virgin and martyr ever existed, or did and suffered those things for the Christian faith which she is said to have learned from Paul. Certainly Tertullian’s words do not establish this; they establish only that the book of that Asiatic presbyter was wrongly attributed to Paul. Those who claim that it is wrongly related therein that Thecla herself exercised the office of teaching and baptizing are mistaken. Indeed, if you examine this very feature more deeply, does it not attest the antiquity of these Acts? For a writer of a later age would scarcely have included it; nor would any later person have attributed such a thing to the female sex, or introduced either the Apostle Paul assigning that sacred office or Thecla exercising it. These things agree better with the earliest times and are sufficiently consistent with the history of the churches of Asia. For it is gathered from Paul’s words to Timothy, whom he left at Ephesus in Asia, that certain women in those churches arrogated to themselves the power of preaching in the Church. He writes: ‘Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I do not permit a woman to teach’ (1 Tim. 2:11–12). Why, I ask, did Timothy need this instruction unless women in the Ephesian Church were aspiring to this sacred office? Likewise, in another Asiatic church—namely, Thyatira—a woman, Jezebel, was teaching and calling herself προφῆτιν, ‘a prophetess,’ which is condemned (Rev. 2:20). This Asiatic presbyter who wrote the *Acts of Paul and Thecla* likewise appears to have been a patron of women of this kind who preached in the churches; and for that reason he was rightly deposed from his rank by St. John, as Tertullian and Jerome have recorded” (*Spicilegium of the Holy Fathers*, vol. I, pp. 88, 94, and 334). Thus far the learned Grabe. He also observes that Jerome called not Thecla’s story, but the story of the baptized lion, a fable. That fable is not found in our text of the Acts; consequently, it may rightly be judged that the holy Father either was entirely unacquainted with these Acts or encountered a corrupted copy of them. EDD.] defend the example of Thecla [Note: [Col. 1219A] “But if writings wrongly attributed to Paul—the writing [Col. 1219B] of Thecla,” etc., manuscript Wouw. “The example of Thecla” was deleted after Rigalt. by the Paris, Venetian, Semler, and Leopold editions.] as authorization for women to teach and baptize [Note: [Col. 1220D] “As authorization for women,” etc. That is, authorization both to teach and to baptize. He said “as authorization,” just as he says “for confidence,” “for communion,” etc. RIG.], let them know that in Asia the presbyter who composed that writing, as though adding something of his own to Paul’s title [Note: [Col. 1220D] “As though adding something of his own to Paul’s title”: that is, as though from his own resources he were adding something to Paul’s titles and glory, something resembling an accumulation. RIG.], when convicted and having confessed [Note: [Col. 1220D] “When convicted and having confessed.” Jerome added: “when convicted before John.” RIG.] that he had done it from love of Paul, departed from his office.

For how close to the faith would it appear that the man who did not even permit a woman to learn [Note: [Col. 1220A] Others read “to teach.”] with self-assertion should give a woman the power of teaching and baptizing [Col. 1220A] [Note: [Col. 1220D] “Did not even permit a woman to learn with self-assertion.” That is, women should seek to learn with modesty. “Not to learn with self-assertion” means not to inquire imperiously or question obstinately. Thus in the book *On Patience*: “He did not even resolutely denounce his betrayer.” RIG.]? “Let them be silent and consult their husbands at home” (1 Cor. 14).

## CHAPTER XVIII

Moreover, those whose office it is know that Baptism is not to be entrusted indiscriminately. “Give to everyone who asks of you” has its own subject matter, since it pertains specifically [Note: [Col. 1220A] “Accordingly,” variant reading, Wouw.] to almsgiving. Rather, this command must be considered: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Luke 6), nor “cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6) [Note: [Col. 1220B] “Your pearl,” Paris; “and cast your pearl before swine,” variant reading, Wouw.]; and, “Do not readily lay hands upon anyone, lest you share in another’s sins” (1 Tim. [Col. 1221A] 5:22; Acts 8).

If Philip baptized the eunuch so readily, let us reflect that the Lord’s manifest and explicit favor had intervened. The Spirit had commanded Philip to proceed [Note: [Col. 1221C] “To continue,” variant reading, Wouw.] upon that road.
