Has the guilt of the deed. RIG.] cancels the effect. Since the power of this will is so great [Note: [Col. 1232D] “Since the power of this will is so great, why should it not, by satisfying itself with its own consolation, count as the deed?” Thus Rhenanus edited it. But I think the reading of the ancient manuscript should be retained as follows: “Since the power of this will is so great that, by satisfying itself with its own consolation, it counts as the deed, it will therefore be punished as the deed.” I interpret it thus: one who contaminates a woman not his own by looking at her with desire has already committed adultery in his heart, because his mind, through the imagined presence of pleasure, possesses what it desired. Rightly, therefore, does a will whose power is so great that through it the mind delights in an imagined enjoyment count as the deed and receive punishment as the deed. RIG.], [Col. 1233A] that, satisfying itself with its own consolation [Note: [Col. 1233C] “Why” in Franequer, Paris, and Rigaltius.] [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Satisfying itself with its own consolation.” Through the will, the mind has inwardly done and obtained what it pleased; therefore it now enjoys and is satisfied by this consolation. What remains belongs not to the mind but to the body. RIG.], it counts as the deed, and therefore will be punished. It is utterly vain to say, “I willed it, yet did not do it.” On the contrary, you ought to carry it out because you will it—or else not even will it, since you do not carry it out. But you pronounce judgment by the confession of your own conscience. For if you desired what was good, you would have been eager to accomplish it; moreover, just as you do not accomplish the evil, neither ought you to have desired it. Whichever position you take [Note: [Col. 1233C] “Whichever way you turn,” in Latinius and Junius.], you are bound by guilt, because you either willed evil or failed to fulfill the good.

## CHAPTER IV

For all sins, therefore [Note: [Col. 1233D] “For all sins, therefore.” He is speaking of the first repentance. Pamelius, failing to notice this, creates some inexplicable confusion, and it is unclear why he confounds the first repentance with the second. For he must grant me that this passage contributes nothing to particular repentance, and consequently nothing to the confession and remission of all sins, since the first repentance is being discussed; for, I say, no one denied that absolutely all sins are erased. ALBASP.], whether committed in the flesh or in the spirit, in deed or in will, the same God who appointed punishment through judgment also promised pardon through repentance, saying to the people: “Repent [Note: [Col. 1233C] “May it repent you,” in Wouwer’s manuscript.], and I will save you” (Ezek. 18:21, 23). And again: “As I live,” says the Lord, “I prefer repentance to death.” Repentance, therefore, is life [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Repentance, therefore, is life.” The Lord says, “I prefer repentance to death,” opposing repentance to death. But what is more truly opposed to death than life? Therefore repentance, as the opposite of death, is life. RIG.], since it is preferred to death.

You, sinner, like me—indeed, less a sinner than I [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Indeed, less a sinner than I.” Whatever catechumens had deserved or done before the washing was thought to have been done more from the impulse of nature than from deliberate will, as the Author in *On Modesty*, St. Cyprian—or whoever gave us the tract *On the Washing of Feet*—Hermas, and Justin affirm. For this reason he says that the catechumen has sinned less than he. ALBASP.], for I acknowledge my own preeminence in sins—seize it, embrace it, as a shipwrecked man trusts some plank [Note: [Col. 1234C] “Some plank.” When the Fathers say that repentance is the second plank after shipwreck, this must be understood of the second repentance, undertaken after baptism, not of the first, which was not the second but the first plank. ALB.—“Some plank.” Albaspinaeus rightly observed that “second plank” is said only of the second repentance, that undertaken after baptism. The first repentance, by which believers approached baptism, was called the ship; when that was wrecked, the second repentance remained as a plank in the shipwreck. LE PR.]. It will raise you up [Note: [Col. 1234D] “Will raise up.” Thus it is read in the ancient copies. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1233C] “Will wash thoroughly,” in Franequer.] when you are submerged beneath the waves of sin and carry you onward into the harbor of divine mercy. Seize the opportunity of unexpected felicity, so that you who formerly were, in God’s sight, nothing but (Isa. 40:15; 64:8; Dan. 2; Ps. 1:3; Jer. 19:11; Matt. 3) a drop from a bucket, dust from the threshing floor, and a little vessel of the potter, may henceforth become that tree which is planted beside waters, remains evergreen in its leaves, and bears fruit in its season—a tree that will see neither fire nor axe.

Repent of errors [Col. 1233C] once the truth has been found; repent of having loved what God does not love, since not even we ourselves permit our servants [Col. 1234A] not to hate the things by which we are offended [Note: [Col. 1233C] Rhenanus incorrectly reads “to know.”]. For the principle of obedience is established in likeness of mind. To enumerate the goodness of repentance would furnish an expansive subject, one to be undertaken with correspondingly grand eloquence [Note: [Col. 1233C] “For,” in Junius.]. We, however, within our limitations, insist upon this one point: what God has commanded [Note: [Col. 1233C] “Commands,” in Franequer, Paris, and Rigaltius.] is good—indeed, supremely good. I consider it presumptuous to debate the goodness of a divine command. For we ought not to obey merely because it is good, but because God [Note: [Col. 1234C] “Commands,” in Rigaltius.] has commanded it. For the rendering of obedience, the majesty of divine power comes first: the authority of the one commanding takes precedence over the benefit of the one serving.

Is it good to repent, or is it not? Why reconsider the question? God commands it. Yet he [Note: [Col. 1234C] “But he,” in Rigaltius.] does not merely command it; he also exhorts us. He invites us to salvation by offering it as a reward (Ezek. 33:11) [Note: [Col. 1234C] “Of salvation,” in Petrus Ciacconius; “by salvation,” in Rigaltius.], swearing—even saying, “As I live”—because he desires to be believed. [Col. 1234B] O blessed are we [Note: [Col. 1234C] Semler omits “we.”], for whose sake God swears! O most wretched are we if we do not believe even the Lord when he swears! Therefore, what God commends so earnestly, what he attests even after the human fashion under oath, we ought both to undertake and to preserve with the utmost seriousness, so that, by remaining within the assurance of divine grace, we may likewise be able to persevere in its fruit and benefit.

## CHAPTER V

What I mean is this: the repentance which, through God’s grace, has been revealed and prescribed to us, and which restores us to favor with the Lord, once recognized and embraced, must never thereafter be annulled [Note: [Col. 1234C] “To annul,” in the Venetian edition.] by a repetition of sin. No pretext of ignorance [Note: [Col. 1234D] “Pretext of ignorance.” The Gentiles, or hearers, wished their sins to be forgiven on the sole ground that they had not known what was best to do. Those who had been instructed in Christ’s commandments could not use that excuse; from this it will also be evident that this entire chapter concerns hearers and catechumens. ALBASP.] now comes to your defense, when, after acknowledging the Lord, accepting his commandments, and finally performing repentance for your sins, you restore yourself once more to sin [Note: [Col. 1234C] Thus . . . in Leopold. “You will restore,” in Semler, Franequer, Paris, and Rigaltius.] [Note: [Col. 1234D] “You restore yourself once more to sin.” Most foolish is the man who fights against his own advantages and demands to be restored to a worse condition. RIG.]. [Col. 1234C–1235A] To precisely the degree that you are separated from ignorance, you are joined to obstinacy. For if you had repented of your sin because you had begun to fear the Lord, why did you choose to undo what you had done for fear’s sake, unless because you ceased to fear? Nothing but obstinacy overturns fear.

Since even those who do not know the Lord [Note: [Col. 1235C] “Since even those who do not know the Lord.” This passage also argues against those new evangelicals who say that since the time of the Apostles our ancestors lived in perpetual ignorance and yet were excused from guilt. Particularly supportive of the Author’s position are the very frequent sacrifices ordered for sins of ignorance in Leviticus 4 and 5 and Numbers 15, which are also discussed in Hebrews 9. Then, in the New Testament, Acts 2, blessed Peter says to those whom he knew to have sinned through ignorance: “Repent and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out.” Hence the uniform opinion of all the Fathers is that ignorance—what modern theologians call crass ignorance—excuses no one from guilt; yet their ignorance would undoubtedly have been of this kind if these men spoke the truth. PAM.] are protected by no exemption from punishment [Note: [Col. 1235C] “From punishment,” in Franequer, Paris, and Rigaltius; “unto punishment,” in Semler.], because it is not permissible to remain ignorant of God, who has been set openly before us and can be apprehended even from the heavenly blessings themselves, how dangerous it is [Note: [Col. 1235C] “How much more,” in Junius.] to despise him after knowing him! Moreover, a person despises him when, after receiving from him an understanding of good and evil, he resumes what he understands must be avoided and what he had already avoided, thereby insulting his own understanding—that is, God’s gift. He rejects the giver when he abandons the gift; he denies [Note: [Col. 1235C] “The benefactor,” in Junius.] the benefit when he does not honor it. [Col. 1235B] How can he please the one whose gift displeases him? Thus he appears not merely obstinate toward the Lord, but ungrateful as well.

Furthermore, he sins not lightly against the Lord who, after renouncing God’s rival, the devil, through repentance and thereby subjecting him to the Lord, raises him up again by returning to him and makes himself the devil’s exultation, so that the Evil One may rejoice against the Lord once more, having recovered his spoil. Does he not—though it is dangerous even to say it, yet must be stated for edification—prefer the devil to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1235C] “Put forward,” in Semler.]? For one who has known both seems to have made a comparison and, after judging, to have pronounced that one the better whose possession he has chosen to become again. Thus the man who, through repentance for his sins, had begun to make satisfaction to the Lord will make satisfaction to the devil [Col. 1235C–1236A] through another repentance—a repentance of his repentance [Note: [Col. 1235C] “Will make satisfaction,” in Semler.] [Note: [Col. 1235D] “Through another repentance—a repentance of his repentance.” Pliny, *Letters* 7.10: “It remains to be seen whether the province again comes to approve what it is said to have condemned, and repents of its repentance.” RIG.]; and he will be all the more hateful to God, the more acceptable he is to God’s rival.

But some say [Note: [Col. 1235D] “But some say.” This passage is also worthy of note against the new heresy of certain people—from which even the Calvinists do not dissent—who think it sufficient to retain their religion in heart and mind, although they involve themselves and even communicate in the practices and mysteries of the Catholics’ religion, which is contrary to their own. PAM.] that God is satisfied if he is revered in heart and mind, even if this is less fully done in action. Accordingly, they sin while preserving fear and faith: that is, they violate marriages while preserving chastity and mix poison for a parent while preserving filial piety. So they too will be thrust into hell with their pardon preserved, while they sin with their fear preserved. A prime example of perversity: because they fear, they sin! Presumably they would not sin if they did not fear. Therefore, whoever does not want God offended should not reverence him at all—if fear of offending him provides a defense. But such dispositions have customarily sprouted from the seed of hypocrites, whose [Note: [Col. 1236C] “Enmity,” in Franequer and Paris.] inseparable friendship is with the devil [Note: [Col. 1235D] “Whose inseparable friendship is with the devil.” The reading is entirely correct and ought not to have been disturbed. For the discussion concerns the class of hypocrites, whose repentance is never faithful—those, namely, whose friendship with the devil is inseparable—and who therefore always return to his camp. RIG.], and whose repentance is never faithful.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1236B]

Whatever our limited capacity [Note: [Col. 1236C] “Whatever our limited capacity,” etc. Tertullian appears here to teach that catechumens, whom he calls recruits, sometimes prolonged their repentance until baptism. For because they understood perfectly well that all sins were erased by baptism, they extended the time before undertaking repentance as far as they could, and therefore did not “complete” repentance—that is, they did not carry it through. In this interpretation I differ somewhat from Rigaltius; for *includere* means πληρῶσαι, “to fulfill,” and τελειῶσαι, “to complete.” LE PR.] has attempted to suggest concerning repentance, once undertaken and thereafter perpetually maintained, applies indeed to all who are devoted to the Lord, as all petition for salvation by seeking to earn God’s favor [Note: [Col. 1236C] “All,” in Paris and Junius.]; but it bears especially upon these novices [Note: [Col. 1236C] “These novices.” Shortly afterward he will call these novices “hearers” and speak of “the recruits among the hearers.” RIG.—“These novices.” Note that catechumens were so called, whence perhaps the terminology of monastic discipline still retained today was taken, according to which novices in religious orders are like hearers and catechumens. LAC.]. They are only now beginning to water their ears with divine discourses; like young animals still fresh from birth, their sight not yet perfected, they crawl uncertainly. They do indeed say [Note: [Col. 1236C] Thus all editions except Leopold, which reads: “say that they renounce.”] that they renounce their former ways [Note: [Col. 1236D] “Renounce their former ways”: that is, idolatry and the affairs of secular life. RIG.], and they undertake repentance [Note: [Col. 1236D] “Undertake repentance.” Those who give in their names among the hearers are said to undertake repentance. RIG.—“Undertake repentance.” It should especially be noted that “to undertake repentance” is the proper expression for those who entered upon repentance, whose first approach itself was called its undertaking. Heraldus noted, in book 1, chapter 4 of his *Digressions*, that this was the proper expression for those entering upon repentance, but proved it by no evidence. LAC.], yet neglect to bring it to completion [Note: [Col. 1236D] “Yet neglect to bring it to completion”: namely, through baptism, which is also called the sealing. And he himself will shortly say, “the bar of immersion having been shut.” Repentance and faith, therefore, are completed when they are brought to baptism, just as Gaius said that actions were “included in a trial” when they were brought to trial, law 139, *On the Rules of Law*. Moreover, those who renounce their former ways reluctantly neglect to complete repentance, as though the full sum of their misdeeds, which they wish to have sealed by baptism, had not yet been made up. RIG.].

[Col. 1236C–1237A] For the very end of desire incites them to desire something from their former ways—just as fruit, when it is already beginning to age into sourness or bitterness, nevertheless still flatters its own attractiveness in some part. Moreover, every fault of delay and evasion with respect to repentance is introduced by presumption upon immersion [Note: [Col. 1237C] “Presumption upon immersion”: confidence that pardon will be obtained through baptism. RIG.]. For, certain of the indubitable pardon of their sins, they meanwhile steal the intervening time and make for themselves a furlough [Note: [Col. 1237C] “Make for themselves a furlough.” Hearers were taught not only how grave and dangerous it was to sin and to have God angry with them, but also that all former sins were forgiven in baptism; hence Tertullian says that such teaching gives some people boldness and security in sinning. ALBASP.] for sinning, instead of an education in not sinning.

How absurd, moreover, how unjust, not to complete repentance and yet to await the pardon of sins—that is, not to present the price [Note: [Col. 1237C] “That is, not to present the price.” It had been provided by the Law of the Twelve Tables that the seller’s property should not pass to the buyer unless the latter had paid the price, § *The Seller*, *Institutes*, *On the Division of Property*; this was borrowed from Attic law. Plautus in the *Asinaria* calls it “Greek credit”; Ausonius in his *Letters* says, “Greek, not in good faith.” Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book 12, chapter 18. ALBASP.] and yet to reach out one’s hand for the merchandise [Note: [Col. 1237B] “Payment,” in Rigaltius.]! For the Lord has determined to award pardon at this price; he offers impunity for redemption by this compensation of repentance. If, therefore, those who sell first test the coin over which they bargain, to ensure that it is neither carved away, nor shaved, nor counterfeit [Note: [Col. 1237C] “Neither carved away, nor shaved, nor counterfeit.” Under the Cornelian Law concerning forgery, a person is punished if he has partly shaved, partly colored, or counterfeited gold coins, law 8, *On the Cornelian Law concerning Forgery*; there the authors of the *Basilica* seem to have read “encircled,” not “colored.” For they said: Οἱ τὰ νομίσματα ξέοντες ἢ περικόπτοντες, “those who scrape or clip coins.” RIG.], do we believe that the Lord will first put repentance to the test when he is about to grant us so great a recompense [Note: [Col. 1237B] “Merchandise,” in Latinius.]—namely, everlasting life?

But let us postpone for a moment the question of repentance’s genuineness. Will it become evident, I suppose, that we are reformed [Note: [Col. 1237B] “It will be permitted,” in Rhenanus.] when we are absolved? By no means. Rather, it is while pardon is still pending that punishment is kept in view; while we still do not deserve to be delivered, in order that we may become able to deserve it [Note: [Col. 1237D] “While we still do not deserve to be delivered, in order that we may become able to deserve it.” These words must be carried through in one breath, without any punctuation. Tertullian is discussing the progress of penitents. “And when,” he says, “shall we who have undertaken repentance be regarded as reformed? When we are absolved, after obtaining the washing and being granted the water? By no means,” he says; “but when, while pardon is pending, we keep in view the punishments appointed for the offenses of our former life; while we still do not—I will not say do not deserve to be delivered, for who would ever dare reckon his merits before God?—but while we still do not deserve in order that, through the divine mercy thus bestowing from its own resources, we may become able to deserve.” RIG.]; when God threatens, not when he pardons.

For what slave, after being changed by manumission into a free person [Note: [Col. 1237D] “A slave changed by freedom.” The rite of manumission involved a turning around, the sign of a change. Hence the passages:

> For whom a single turn  
> Makes a Roman citizen;

[Col. 1238C] and:

> In the turning of a moment  
> Marcus Dama emerges.

And those who become Christians from pagans are said to be converted—to the true God, namely, service to whom alone is true freedom. RIG.], holds his thefts and flights against himself? What soldier, after being discharged from his camp, is anxious about his disciplinary marks [Note: [Col. 1238C] “Is anxious about his disciplinary marks.” He means the military brands by which a soldier is marked for military offenses—for example, if he has overstayed leave, deserted, been seditious, and so forth. He will use the same metaphor of himself near the end of this work, calling himself a sinner bearing every mark. RIG.]? The sinner must bewail himself before pardon, because the time of repentance [Note: [Col. 1237B] “The same,” in Franequer and Rigaltius.] is the time of danger and fear.

Nor do I deny that the divine benefit—that is, the abolition of sins—is in every way assured to those about to enter the water; but to succeed in reaching it, one must labor. For who would provide even a single sprinkling of ordinary water to a man of such faithless repentance [Note: [Col. 1238C] “For who would provide even a single sprinkling of ordinary water to a man of such faithless repentance?” Such was the sprinkling of the devotees of Isis, which he describes more openly in *On Baptism*: “They purify country houses, homes, temples, and entire cities by sprinkling water carried around them.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1237B] “Sprinkling,” in Junius from a manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 1238C] “Even a single sprinkling of ordinary water.” Of common, profane water. “A man of such faithless repentance,” he says, “no one would deem worthy—I will not say of a cupful, but not even of a single drop—of common water”; so far would he be from wishing to bring him to baptism. Those who understand these words as baptism by sprinkling engage in splendid trifling; for wherever he speaks of baptism he says “washing,” “to dye,” “to immerse,” “to be washed,” “to be submerged,” and “immersion,” which assuredly do not signify sprinkling. Nevertheless, the Church’s kindness is not on that account to be blamed, which later appears to have established that, under the pressure of necessity, people might be made Christians at least by sprinkling with water. For Cyprian, in his second letter to Magnus, proves from the sacred writings that water of sprinkling is a purification, and that no one ought to be troubled because the sick appear to be sprinkled or poured upon, rather than baptized. RIG.]? It is indeed easy to approach by stealth and mislead with your declarations the official set over this matter [Note: [Col. 1237B] “Purpose,” in Semler. “The official set over,” in Wouwer’s manuscript and, more correctly, Rigaltius.] [Note: [Col. 1238D] “To mislead with your declarations the official set over this matter.” He means the presbyter placed in charge of administering the washing, whom in *On Baptism* he calls “the angel who arbitrates baptism.” RIG.]. But God watches over his treasury and does not allow the unworthy to slip in.

[Col. 1238B] What, finally, does he say? “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Luke 8:17). However great the darkness you heap over your deeds, God is light. Some, however, think as though God were obliged to provide even the unworthy with what he has promised, and so they turn his generosity into servitude. But if he forgives us the bond of death [Note: [Col. 1238B] A. Neander thinks that these words should be transposed, so that the text reads: “But if he does it under necessity, he therefore does it unwillingly; he forgives the bond of death.” Yet the difficulty of the passage is removed by placing a question mark after “does.”] [Col. 1239A] [Note: [Col. 1239C] “Forgives the bond of death.” He grants remission of the written bond of death—that is, sin. For obligations also arise from offenses and misdeeds. Paul said in Colossians 2: “Having erased the handwritten bond against us in its decrees” (ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ’ ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον τοῖς δόγμασιν). Tertullian himself says in *On Modesty*: “For he also releases, liberating man through the washing after forgiving him the handwritten bond of death.” RIG.] under compulsion, does he therefore act unwillingly? For who guarantees [Note: [Col. 1239C] “Promises,” in Junius.] that what he has granted unwillingly will remain? Do not many afterwards fall away? Is not that gift taken away from many? These, of course, are the people who slip in, who, having entered upon faith in repentance [Note: [Col. 1239C] “Who, having entered upon faith in repentance.” That is, they begin to believe that they must repent, and yet they do not truly repent; for catechumens or recruits were taught nothing before they were taught to repent of their former life. ALBASP.], build a house destined to collapse upon the sand.

Let no one, therefore, flatter himself because he is enrolled among the recruits of the hearers [Note: [Col. 1239D] “Among the recruits of the hearers.” I do not think he means catechumens; for properly speaking those were called catechumens who, thoroughly taught and instructed in Christ’s law, prayed and possessed a right to baptism—although I am not unaware that recruits, hearers, and catechumens were sometimes designated by one and the same name—and who had almost completed their first repentance. Rather, he means recruits and novices who were taught the first elements of Christian law. ALBASP.], as though even now he were permitted to sin. As soon as you have known the Lord, fear him; as soon as you have beheld him, revere him. Otherwise, what difference does it make that you have known him, when you persist in the same things to which you formerly devoted yourself in ignorance? What separates you from the perfected servant of God [Note: [Col. 1239C] “The Word of God,” in Junius from manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 1239D] “From the perfected servant of God.” They were initiated by undertaking repentance; they were perfected through baptism, anointing, and the Eucharist. RIG.]? Is there one Christ for the immersed and another for the hearers? Is there a different hope or reward, a different dread of judgment, a different necessity of repentance?

That washing is the seal of faith; and that faith begins from, and is commended by, the faith of repentance [Col. 1239B] [Note: [Col. 1239D] “And that faith begins from repentance.” They did not approach baptism unless fully instructed in matters of faith—that is, concerning God’s majesty and power and the matters contained in the Gospels, with the single exception of the mystery of the Eucharist; nor were they baptized until they had sworn that they believed all these things. Their faith began from repentance because, namely, they were not to be judged to believe God and to magnify and fear him unless they considered him worthy that they should make satisfaction to him for their former conduct and, by repentance, wash away the sins they had once committed against him and his law. ALBASP.]. We are not washed in order that we may cease to sin, since we have already been washed in heart. For this is the hearer’s first immersion [Note: [Col. 1240C] “The hearer’s first immersion,” etc. By this immersion the Christian who thinks rightly is bound throughout his whole life to God, his mind turned away from idolatry, sexual immorality, and murder. RIG.]: unbroken fear; thenceforth [Note: [Col. 1239C] “As regards,” in Rigaltius.], as far as your perception of the Lord extends [Note: [Col. 1240D] “Thenceforth, as far as your perception of the Lord extends.” Devoted to the Lord, below. RIG.], sound faith and a conscience that has once embraced repentance.

Otherwise, if we cease to sin only after the waters, we put on innocence from compulsion, not voluntarily [Note: [Col. 1240D] “From compulsion, not voluntarily.” At baptism they swore in solemn words that they would never sin; then they renounced the devil and his pomp; finally, if they sinned after baptism, they were restrained by ecclesiastical discipline. For this reason he says, “from compulsion.” ALBASP.]. Who, then, excels in goodness: the person who is not permitted to be evil, or [Note: [Col. 1240C] “Or whether,” in Franequer and Rigaltius.] the person to whom being evil is displeasing? The one who is ordered to be free of crime, or the one who delights in being so? Therefore let us not even turn our hands away from theft unless the strength of locks resists us; nor restrain our eyes from lust for sexual immorality unless we are obstructed by guards over bodies—if no one devoted to the Lord will cease to sin unless bound by immersion. If anyone thinks in this way, I do not know [Col. 1239C] whether, once immersed, he is more grieved that he has ceased to sin than rejoiced that he has escaped.

Accordingly, hearers [Col. 1240A] ought to desire immersion, not presume upon it. For the one who desires it honors it; the one who presumes upon it is arrogant. In the former, modest restraint appears; in the latter, insolence. The former is diligent; the latter negligent. The former desires to deserve it; the latter promises it to himself as a debt. The former receives; the latter seizes. Whom would you judge more worthy, if not the more reformed? Whom more reformed, if not the more fearful, and therefore the one who has performed true repentance? For he remained afraid to sin, lest he should not deserve to receive it. But the presumptuous man, because he promised it to himself and was therefore secure, could not fear; thus he did not complete repentance either, because he lacked repentance’s instrument—fear. Presumption is a share of shamelessness: it presses its claim upon the giver as a petitioner and despises him as the giver. And so it sometimes deceives. For it promises something to itself before it is due, and the one who is to provide it is always offended by that.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 1240B]

May it be granted, Lord Christ, that your servants speak or hear about the discipline of repentance only up to this point: the point up to which hearers ought not to sin either. May they henceforth know nothing of repentance and require nothing from it. I am reluctant to append mention of a second—indeed now a final—hope, lest, by discussing the remaining aid of repentance, we appear to display further room for sinning. Far be it from anyone to interpret the matter as though the way to sin still lies open to him because the way to repentance lies open, or as though the abundance of heavenly mercy should produce license for human rashness. Let no one become worse because God is better, sinning as often as [Col. 1240C] he is pardoned [Note: [Col. 1240D] “Sinning as often as he is pardoned.” Who would not infer from these words that the Church’s doors always stood open to penitents, since he says that Christ pardons as often as one sins? Pamelius too has no hesitation in affirming from these words that the Church always granted pardon to sinners, and that if anything is encountered in the authors about a second and final repentance, it must all be understood of public repentance. To confirm this, he accumulates many passages from the authors which it would serve no purpose to explain, since our undertaking is merely to teach what Tertullian means here and how his words are to be understood. These words, “as often as he is pardoned,” therefore, you should not understand as though there were another opportunity for repentance after the second repentance. He meant nothing more than this: although some hope of pardon remains after baptism and a second and final repentance is granted, one must nevertheless not sin again after baptism. For in hundreds of passages—not to mention this chapter—he says that only one pardon remains after the washing, and no distinction between private and public treatment of graver crimes is found in those earliest times. Thus “as often” and “so often” are rightly spoken of the two pardons, so to speak, and the corresponding two sets of sins—namely, those remitted before and after baptism. Yet I would not dare affirm either that this was the opinion of the universal Church or that this custom was observed in absolutely all churches. ALBASP.].

In any case, his opportunities for escape will come to an end if there is no end to his offending. We have escaped once; henceforth [Col. 1241A] let us never again expose ourselves to dangers [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Henceforth let us never again expose ourselves to dangers.” “Henceforth” means “never hereafter.” RIG.], even if we seem likely to escape a second time. Most people, once delivered from shipwreck, thereafter divorce themselves from both ship and sea [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Divorce themselves from both ship and sea.” For, says Rhenanus, as in Publilius the mime-writer: “He wickedly accuses Neptune who suffers shipwreck a second time.” The expression is charming when he says that they “divorce themselves from both ship and sea,” borrowing the metaphor from those who send a bill of divorce to a wife. Similarly, in *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 4, he spoke of a “divorce from heaven.” PAM.], and honor God’s benefit—their salvation, namely—by remembering the danger. I praise their fear; I cherish their modest restraint. They are unwilling to burden divine mercy a second time; they dread appearing to trample upon what they have obtained. With surely wholesome anxiety, they avoid experiencing again what they once learned to fear. Thus the restraint of rashness is an attestation of fear. And human fear is honor paid to God.

Yet that most obstinate enemy never allows his malice to be idle. Indeed, he rages most fiercely precisely when he perceives a person to have been fully liberated [Note: [Col. 1241C] By baptism, namely.]; he is most greatly inflamed while he is being extinguished. He must grieve and groan when pardon of sins has been granted, so many works of death in a person [Col. 1241B] have been destroyed, and so many records of his former condemnation have been erased. He grieves that Christ’s servant, who had been his sinner, will judge him and his angels. And so he watches, attacks, and besieges, to see whether he can strike the eyes with carnal desire, ensnare the mind with worldly allurements, overthrow faith by fear of earthly power, or turn it aside from the sure path by perverse traditions [Note: [Col. 1241C] Others read “conditions”; Pamelius found this in three manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 1242D] “By perverse traditions.” Three manuscripts read “conditions.” Yet the former pleases me more, so that he is arguing against the Montanists, who were turning the faithful from the sure path by their perverse traditions concerning the impossibility of repentance after baptism. Moreover, from his addition of “perverse,” it is clear that the Author does not attack all traditions. But he treats these more fully in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, where he approves many traditions of the Church. PAM.]. He is never at a loss for scandals or temptations.

God, therefore, foreseeing these poisons of his, although the door of forgiveness had been closed and the bar of immersion shut, still permitted something to remain open. In the vestibule he placed [Note: [Col. 1242D] “In the vestibule he placed.” It was the custom and rite for penitents to remain in the church’s vestibule; he alludes to this. ALBASP.] a second repentance, to open for those who knock—but now only once, because it is now the second time; never again thereafter [Note: [Col. 1242D] “Never again thereafter.” Therefore there was only one repentance after baptism. ALBASP.], because the most recent occasion had proved fruitless. Is not this one further opportunity enough? You possess something you now [Note: [Col. 1241C] “Not” is absent from Rigaltius.] did not deserve; for you had lost what you had received. If the Lord’s indulgence grants you the means to restore what you had lost, be grateful for the repeated benefit, to say nothing of its enlargement. For it is a greater thing to restore than to give, since it is more wretched to have lost [Note: [Col. 1242D] “It is more wretched to have lost,” etc. It is far more wretched to lose by sinning the salvation you received in baptism than never to have received it at all. ALBASP.] than never to have received at all.

Yet the spirit is not immediately to be cut down and overthrown [Col. 1242A] by despair if someone has become liable to a second repentance. By all means let him be ashamed to sin again, but let him not be ashamed to repent again; let him be ashamed to come into danger a second time, but not to be delivered a second time. Let no one be ashamed: for a recurrent illness, the medicine must be repeated. You will show yourself grateful toward the Lord [Note: [Col. 1241C] “To the Lord,” in Semler.] if you do not refuse what the Lord offers you. You have offended, but you can still be reconciled. You have someone to whom you may make satisfaction—and one who is indeed willing.

## CHAPTER VIII
If you doubt this, unfold what the Spirit says to the Churches (Rev. 1–3). He charges the Ephesians with having abandoned their love; he reproaches the Thyatirans with fornication and the eating of things sacrificed to idols; he accuses the Sardians [Note: [Col. 1241C] “Sardios” Paris, Fran.] of works not brought to completion; he rebukes the Pergamenes for teaching perversities; he chastises the Laodiceans for trusting in riches. And yet he admonishes them all to repent [Col. 1242B]—under threats, to be sure. But he would not threaten the unrepentant if he did not forgive the repentant. This might be doubtful, had he not demonstrated elsewhere too this lavish outpouring of his clemency. Does he not say (Jer. 8:4; Hos. 6:6), “Will not one who has fallen rise again, and one who has turned away turn back?” He it is indeed, he it is who prefers mercy to sacrifices [Note: [Col. 1242C] “Sacrifice” Fran.]. The heavens and the angels who are there rejoice over a person’s repentance (Matt. 9:13). Come now, sinner, take heart: you see where rejoicing occurs over your return [Note: [Col. 1242C] “Return” was absent from Rhen.].

What do those arguments from the Lord’s parables mean for us? The woman lost a drachma, searched for it, found it, and invited her friends to rejoice: is this not an image of the restoration of a sinner? One little sheep belonging to the shepherd [Note: [Col. 1242C] “To the shepherd” Rigalt.] also strays; although the one was not dearer than the flock, that one is sought, that one is longed for [Col. 1242C] in place of all the rest, and at last it is found and carried back upon the shoulders of the shepherd himself, for it had suffered greatly in its wandering.

Nor shall I pass over that most gentle father, who calls back his prodigal son and gladly receives him when he repents [Note: [Col. 1242C] “Repentance” Seml.; “repentance” Fran., Paris, Rigal.] after his destitution; he slaughters the choicest calf and adorns his joy with a banquet. Why should he not? [Col. 1243A] For he had found the son whom he had lost; he perceived as dearer the one whom he had gained. Who are we to understand that father to be? God, of course: no one is so truly a father, no one so tenderly devoted. Therefore he will receive you as his son, even if you have squandered what you received from him, even if you return naked, because you have returned; and he will rejoice more over your return than over another’s sobriety—but only if you repent [Note: [Col. 1243B] “You” added by Jun.] from the heart; if you compare your hunger with the plenty enjoyed by your father’s hired servants; if you leave the pigs, that unclean herd; if you seek your father again, even though he is offended, saying, “I have sinned, Father, and I am no longer worthy to be called yours.”

Confession lightens offenses [Note: [Col. 1243B] “Offense” Paris.] [Note: [Col. 1243C] “So greatly does it lighten.” These words are not to be understood of public and particular confession, but of the confession by which the sinner accuses himself before God. ALB.] as greatly as concealment makes them heavier. For confession is the counsel of satisfaction; concealment is the counsel of obstinacy.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1243B] Therefore, the more narrowly restricted is the business of this second and only repentance, the more laborious is its proof [Note: [Col. 1243B] Paris, Fran., and Rigalt. add “is”]: it must not merely be brought forward in the conscience [Note: [Col. 1243B] “Be preferred” Fran., Paris, Rigalt.; “be endured” P. Ciaconius.], but must also be administered through some outward act. This act, which is more commonly expressed and employed under its Greek name, is *exomologesis* (ἐξομολόγησις) [Note: [Col. 1243C] “It is exomologesis.” Since we shall say at greater length what exomologesis is, and prove the matter at greater length, it will suffice here to say that auricular confession is not meant by it, but rather the acts by which penitents demonstrated to others the sincerity of their repentance. ALBASP.]. Through it we confess our offense to the Lord—not, indeed, as though he did not know it, but insofar as satisfaction is arranged by confession, repentance is born from confession, and God is appeased by repentance.

Accordingly, exomologesis is a discipline for prostrating and humbling a person, prescribing [Col. 1244A] a mode of life [Note: [Col. 1243C] “Anointing,” Dijon codex.] calculated to entice mercy. With regard also to dress and [Note: [Col. 1244B] Junius too reads thus; others add “it commands concerning food,” which is absent from Rhen. The word “commands” is missing from Rhen.’s edition, but was afterwards added by him from the Gorze codex.] food, it commands one to lie in sackcloth and ashes [Note: [Col. 1243C] “To lie in sackcloth and ashes.” “Clothed in goat-hair cloth and covered in ashes,” as he himself will say in the book *On Modesty*. In the harshness of sackcloth and the horror of ashes—as Paulinus, writing to Pneumatius, describes sackcloth a little later here:

> If only heavy sackcloth with its bristling covering should clothe the mourner,  
> covering and pricking him with goat-bred hairs.

RIG.]; to obscure the body with filth; to cast down the spirit with mourning; to exchange the things by which one sinned for sorrowful treatment. Furthermore, it commands one to know food and drink only in their plain form [Note: [Col. 1243C] “To know food and drink only in their plain form.” Elsewhere he said, “with mere bread and water,” that is, plain or alone, without any other [Col. 1243D] foods and without seasonings. Thus, in *To Scapula*, “we sacrifice with pure prayer,” that is, without perfumes, without blood, without incense, without a victim—that is, with bread and water. In the same sense the comic poet Alexis said ἄρτον καθαρόν, “pure bread,” in *The Tarentines*, where he jokes in most elegant verses about the diet of the Pythagoreans:

> Πυθάγορ᾽, οἴμοι, καὶ λόγοι  
> λεπτοί, διωμιλευμέναι τε φροντίδες  
> τρέφουσ᾽ ἐκείνους· τὰ δὲ καθ᾽ ἡμέραν, τάδε·  
> ἄρτος καθαρὸς, εἷς ἑκατέρῳ, ποτήριον  
> ὕδατος· τοσαῦτα ταῦτα.

> Pythagoras—alas!—and subtle arguments  
> and finely spun reflections nourish them;  
> but their daily provisions are these:  
> plain bread, one loaf for each, and a cup  
> of water—this and nothing more.

On the frugality of the Pythagoreans, that familiar line of Juvenal is relevant:

> From which you could provide a feast for a hundred Pythagoreans.

RIG.], not, of course, for the stomach’s sake but for the soul’s. For the most part it commands one to nourish prayers with fasts; to groan, weep, and cry out day and night to the Lord your God [Note: [Col. 1244B] “His” Rig.]; to cast oneself at the feet of the presbyters [Note: [Col. 1243D] “To cast oneself at the feet of the presbyters.” See how they rolled themselves before the priests in order to confess their sins and obtain forgiveness for them, say the interpreters, together with Baronius, Bellarmine, and Maldonatus in their controversial works. Although I acknowledge this rite to be very ancient, it nevertheless cannot be proved from these words. For when penitents stood before the doors of the church, as the priests and the rest of the faithful passed by, they testified to their repentance with every possible sign of a sorrowing spirit: they did not spare their tears, persisted in entreaties, rolled themselves on the ground, and omitted none of the other acts belonging to repentance that might stir mercy, so that they might recover peace. The author describes this rite when he says “to cast oneself at the feet of the presbyters”; therefore these words have nothing to do with auricular confession. ALBASP.]; to kneel before God’s beloved [Note: [Col. 1244C] “To kneel before God’s beloved.” I would think that by “God’s beloved” the martyrs are to be understood. Penitents were accustomed to ask them to restore them to the Church and to grant them some remission of penance. Hence our Tertullian says in the *Exhortation to the Martyrs*: “That which some who do not possess it—namely peace—have been accustomed to request from the martyrs.” In this way they secured greater leniency from the presbyters and the other Christians. What La Cerda adduces to prove that “God’s beloved” means the presbyters seems irrelevant; for those passages, whether from Eusebius, Gregory Nazianzen, or others, must be referred to the words “to cast oneself at the feet of the presbyters.” LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 1244B] “Altars” Seml.]; and to commission all the brethren to carry the embassy of one’s supplication.

All these acts constitute exomologesis: that it may commend repentance; that it may honor the Lord through fear of danger; that, by itself passing judgment upon the sinner, it may discharge the function of God’s indignation; and that by temporal affliction [Note: [Col. 1244C] Others read “affliction.” This reading, however, is not very sound.] it may—I will not say frustrate, but cancel—eternal punishments. Thus, when [Col. 1244B] it casts a person prostrate [Note: [Col. 1244D] “It casts a person prostrate.” For penitents rolled themselves at the knees of the brethren. RIG.], it raises him up all the more; when it makes him filthy, it renders him all the more cleansed; when it accuses and condemns him, it absolves him. Insofar as you have not spared yourself, to that same degree God—believe it—will spare you.

## CHAPTER X

Yet I presume that most people either evade this work, as though it were the public exposure of themselves [Note: [Col. 1244D] “As though it were the public exposure of themselves.” After baptism, serious offenses were always punished through public penance, and for this reason were sometimes openly disclosed. For the rest, I do not agree with the interpreters or with Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 56, who wish these words to be understood of auricular confession rather than of a public act of penance; for throughout this entire chapter the subject is the public confession of sins and public penance. ALBASP.], or postpone it from day to day, more mindful of shame than of salvation. They resemble those who, when disease has been contracted in the more private parts of the body, avoid the knowledge of physicians [Col. 1245A] and so perish together with their embarrassment.

It is intolerable to shame, evidently, to make satisfaction to the offended Lord and to be restored to the salvation one has squandered [Note: [Col. 1245C] “Squandered salvation”: utterly ruined by prodigal shamelessness in sinning. RIG.]. Truly, you are a fine modest fellow: spreading your brow wide for sinning, but drawing it down when it comes to pleading for pardon! I make no room for embarrassment when I profit more from its loss [Note: [Col. 1245C] “Indeed” Latinus and Jun.], when it itself somehow exhorts a person by saying, “Pay no attention to me; it is better that I should perish through you.”

Certainly, the danger posed by shame is then burdensome, if ever, when it lies among people ready to insult one with ridicule, where one person is exalted by another’s downfall, where one climbs over the person who has been laid low. But among brothers and fellow servants, where hope, fear, joy, grief, and suffering are shared—because the spirit is shared, from a common Lord and Father—what else do you suppose these people to be [Note: [Col. 1245C] “Your own” Seml., Leop.; “these people” Rig., from the Dijon codex.] [Note: [Col. 1245C] “What else do you suppose these people to be than yourself?” Thus it is read in the Dijon codex, and I consider it entirely correct. RIG.] than yourself? Why do you flee from those who share your misfortunes [Note: [Col. 1245C] “Those who share your misfortunes.” The blessed Pacianus expressed this passage as follows: “Do not be afraid of those who share your misfortunes. No body rejoices at the suffering of its own members; rather, it grieves together with them and works together toward a remedy. In one and another person there is the Church, but in the Church there is Christ; and therefore one who does not conceal his sins from the brethren, aided by the tears of the Church, is absolved through the prayers of Christ.” PAM.], [Col. 1245B] as though they were people who would applaud your fall?

The body cannot rejoice at the suffering of one member: it must grieve as a whole and labor together toward a remedy. In one and another person there is the Church, but the Church is Christ. Therefore, when you stretch yourself out at the knees of the brethren, you touch Christ, you entreat Christ. Likewise, when they shed tears over you, Christ suffers, Christ entreats the Father. What the Son asks is always readily obtained.

What a great advantage the concealment of an offense evidently promises to shame! If we withdraw something from human knowledge, shall we therefore conceal it from God as well? Are human estimation and God’s knowledge to be compared so closely? Or is it better to be secretly condemned than openly absolved [Note: [Col. 1245D] “Than openly absolved.” They were indeed absolved publicly and in a full assembly of the Church. Yet it is not sufficiently clear to me that these words should be understood of sacramental absolution. I would rather conjecture that “openly absolved” was said of the final exomologesis, which seemed exceedingly burdensome and full of shame. For what shame or embarrassment could there have been in that absolution? But in the final exomologesis many things occurred that could not be endured without shame. First, they were led by the bishop from the threshold into the middle of the church; there, prostrate at his feet, they begged forgiveness for their sins; with the prayers and tears of the whole brotherhood they solicited grace and mercy; and finally, while remaining in that same condition—that is, lying on the ground—they were released from their sins. All this seemed so burdensome to many that they preferred to remain in guilt rather than be released from it in this way. ALBASP.]?

“It is wretched to come to exomologesis [Col. 1245C] in this fashion!” [Note: [Col. 1245D] “It is wretched to come to exomologesis in this fashion!” This is a formula used by people recoiling from something: “It is wretched!” Thus Horace: “It is wretched to be caught.” Here, therefore, someone recoiling from the more austere form of repentance says, “It is wretched to come to exomologesis in this fashion!” Tertullian answers him: “For it is through evil that one comes to wretchedness,” and so forth—that is, through sin. And evil things are what lead us to wretchedness. RIG.]. No: it is through evil that one comes to wretchedness [Note: [Col. 1245C] “To wretchedness” Fran., Paris, Rigalt.; “loving, if he should come” [Col. 1246C] Seml.; “an arrival was intended” Rhen., less satisfactorily.], [Col. 1246A] but where repentance must be performed, the evil abandons the wretched person [Note: [Col. 1246C] Fran. ends here.], because the act has become salutary. It is wretched to be cut, burned with a cautery, and tormented [Note: [Col. 1246C] “Tortured” Fran., Rig.; “distressed” Seml.] by the biting action of some powder. Yet remedies that heal through unpleasantness excuse their offensiveness by the benefit of the cure, and commend the present injury by reason of the advantage that will follow.

## CHAPTER XI

What if, besides the shame they consider preferable, they also dread physical discomfort, because they must live unwashed, filthy, and apart from gladness [Note: [Col. 1246C] “Apart from gladness.” Penitents were not permitted to enjoy any kind of pleasure, not even baths. ALBASP.], amid the harshness of sackcloth, the horror of ashes, and the wasting of the face through fasting [Note: [Col. 1246C] “The wasting of the face through fasting.” For through fasting the natural vigor of the face and form fades away. He alluded to Matthew [Col. 1246D] 6:16: Ἀφανίζουσι τὰ πρόσωπα αὐτῶν, “They disfigure their faces.” They walk about with a faded countenance. RIG.]?

Are we, then, properly to supplicate for our offenses dressed in scarlet [Note: [Col. 1246D] “In scarlet.” By scarlet, says Rhen., he means a garment dyed with scarlet. Martial:

> You give scarlet and violet robes to your beautiful mistress.

Scarlet dye is commonly called *granum* in Latin, translating the Greek term τοῦ κόκκου, “of the berry.” PAM.] and Tyrian purple [Note: [Col. 1246D] “And Tyrian purple.” Tyrian, says the same commentator, denotes a garment made of Tyrian purple. Ovid:

> Or if she is dressed in Tyrian robes, you will praise her Tyrian garments.

He also notes that *cedo* is here to be understood as “give.” PAM.]? Give me a needle for parting the hair, powder [Col. 1246B] for polishing the teeth [Note: [Col. 1246D] “And powder for polishing the teeth.” He has used the verb *elimare*, “to file smooth,” most aptly, for *limus* is the name given to that rough coating, or that filth, adhering to the teeth. Besides powder, however, the ancients used dentifrice. See Apuleius in the *Apology*. LE PR.], and some forked implement of iron or bronze for digging around the nails. If there is any artificial sheen, any forced redness, press it upon the lips or cheeks. Besides this, seek out more delightful baths in a garden or seaside retreat; add to your expenditure; procure an enormous quantity of fattened fowl; clarify wine until it has reached old age. And when someone asks to whom you are lavishing these things [Note: [Col. 1246D] “To whom you are lavishing these things.” We emended the text thus, following the traces of the old reading, “Why should you lavish your soul?” RIG.], say: “I have sinned against God, and I am in danger of perishing eternally. And so now I am anxious, I waste away, and I torment myself, in order to reconcile to myself the God whom I injured by sinning.”

Yet those who go about campaigning to secure public office are neither ashamed nor reluctant to strive through hardships of soul and body—and not only hardships, but every kind of humiliation—in pursuit of their ambitions. [Col. 1246C] What degrading forms of dress do they not affect? What [Col. 1247A] entrance halls do they not occupy with their nocturnal greetings, even before they have eaten? They diminish themselves at every encounter with any person of higher rank; they are conspicuous at no banquets and join no drinking parties, but live as exiles from the happiness of freedom and gladness. And all this for the fleeting joy of a single year [Note: [Col. 1247C] “For the fleeting joy of a single year.” For the consulship, says Rhen., was an annual magistracy, as were certain other offices. Moreover, *volaticum* is an ancient word meaning “inconstant,” used also by Cicero in book II of *To Atticus* and in *On the Response of the Soothsayers*, chapter 43. PAM.].

Do we hesitate to endure, when eternity is at stake, what the pursuit of axes and rods endures? Shall we cease to offer to the offended Lord that chastisement of food and dress which pagans impose upon themselves although they have injured no one at all? These are the people of whom Scripture makes mention: “Woe to those who bind their offenses as with a long rope” [Note: [Col. 1247C] “Woe to those who bind their offenses,” etc. No one recognized the passage, although it is Isaiah 5: Οὐαὶ οἱ ἐπισπώμενοι τὰς ἁμαρτίας ὡς σχοινίῳ μακρῷ, “Woe to those who draw their sins along as with a long rope.” But Tertullian never read the Latin text, which has, “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity,” while the Septuagint has, “Woe to those who bind their offenses as with a long rope.” The matter is otherwise with the “rope of contemplation”; read book IV [Col. 1247D] *Against Marcion* and the book *Against the Jews*. LAC.].

## CHAPTER XII

If you shrink from exomologesis, consider in your heart [Col. 1247B] Gehenna, which exomologesis extinguishes for you; and first imagine the magnitude of the punishment, so that you may not hesitate to obtain the remedy. What must we suppose that treasury of eternal fire to be, when certain little vents from it arouse such blows of flame that neighboring cities either no longer exist or daily expect the same fate for themselves? The loftiest mountains burst apart through the internal offspring of fire; and what proves for us the perpetuity of the judgment is that, although they burst apart and are devoured, they are nevertheless never exhausted. Who will not consider these present punishments of the mountains to be images of the judgment that threatens? Who will not agree that such sparks are certain missiles and practice darts [Note: [Col. 1247D] “Practice darts”: sporting darts. RIG.] from some great and immeasurable furnace?

Therefore, since you know that, against Gehenna, after those first defenses of the Lord’s immersion, there still remain secondary resources in exomologesis, [Col. 1248A] why do you abandon your salvation? Why do you delay undertaking what you know will heal you? Even mute and irrational creatures recognize at the proper time the remedies divinely assigned to them. A stag pierced by an arrow knows that it must be healed with dittany, in order to expel from the wound the iron and its barbs, which prevent its withdrawal [Note: [Col. 1247D] “The iron and its barbs, which prevent its withdrawal.” He means a barbed dart which, once it has penetrated a wound, cannot be drawn back or pulled out unless the wound itself is torn open with a new wound. RIG.]. The swallow, if she has blinded her chicks, knows how to give them eyes again [Note: [Col. 1247D] “To give eyes”: that is, to restore their eyes. He used this same verb in *On Modesty* and in the *Apology*; this is evidence for me that this little book is Tertullian’s. ALBASP.] by means of her own celandine.

Will the sinner, knowing that exomologesis was instituted by the Lord for his restoration [Note: [Col. 1247D] “For his restoration”: for the sake of his restoration. RIG.], pass it by (Dan. 4)—the exomologesis that restored the Babylonian king to his kingdoms? For a long time he had sacrificed repentance to the Lord, performing exomologesis through seven years of squalor, with his nails grown wild like a lion’s and the neglect of his hair displaying the horror of an eagle [Note: [Col. 1247C] Some add “in the manner of an eagle.”]. Ah, what harsh treatment [Note: [Col. 1248C] “Of harsh treatment.” I suspect that Tertullian wrote *maletractationis* as a single word, since Turnebus, book II, chapter 20, says that what many call *malatractio* is called *maletractatio* by Arnobius, as a single word, in book IV *Against the Nations*. It is evident that Arnobius imitated Tertullian’s writings. Among rhetoricians too, *maletractatio* is written as a single word. LAC.]! The man whom human beings shuddered at [Col. 1248B], God was receiving.

By contrast, however, the Egyptian ruler who pursued God’s people—once afflicted and long denied to their Lord—rushed into battle after so many demonstrations of the plagues; and when the sea, which had permitted passage to God’s people alone, was divided [Note: [Col. 1247C] “Division” Rig.], he perished when its waves rolled back (Exod. 14). For he had rejected repentance and its ministry [Note: [Col. 1248C] “Repentance and its ministry, exomologesis.” Exomologesis was administered to a sinner admitted to repentance. Once it had been duly completed, if the bishop, presbyters, and people judged that satisfaction had been made, he was restored to the Church. RIG.], exomologesis.

Why, then, should I go on concerning these two planks, as it were, of human salvation [Note: [Col. 1247C] “I” Fran., Paris; “two” Fran.] [Note: [Col. 1248C] *Pharis* Pam.] [Note: [Col. 1248D] “These two planks, as it were, of human salvation.” Others read *Pharis*, but they do not tell us whether they derive that reading from ancient books or from conjecture. “Planks, as it were,” however, comes closer to the traces of the old reading, *quasi plane*. RIG.], attending more to the business of my pen than to the duty of my conscience [Note: [Col. 1248C] “Should I attend?” Latinus.]? For since I am a sinner bearing every mark of sin, born for nothing except repentance, I cannot readily remain silent about that which even Adam himself—the first both of the human race and of offense against the Lord—restored by exomologesis [Note: [Col. 1248D] “Adam restored by exomologesis.” This is directed against the heretic Tatian, whose heresy maintained that Adam could not attain salvation, as is clear from the book *On the Prescription Against Heretics*. PAM.] to his own paradise, does not keep silent.

# The Book on Patience

[Col. 1249]

# THE BOOK OF QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN ON PATIENCE. (C)

## Synopsis

[Col. 1249] The treatise *On Patience*, which many believe was composed around the year 200, while Tertullian was still a Catholic—an opinion embraced especially by the most learned Tillemont, D. Cellier, and P. Dominicus Schram—is a distinguished exhortation, written with great eloquence, to embrace patience, I might almost say to endure martyrdom. It is as though, when Septimius was writing these things, a new tempest were already threatening and the sufferings of Christians were about to be renewed.

Whatever is to be held as settled concerning that matter [Col. 1250], or whatever the time or crisis in which this little book was composed, no reason is omitted in it by which Christians might be stirred to patience and deterred from impatience. For at the threshold of the work, after the author has, as though laid prostrate in public, disclosed his own weakness and lack of self-command, and has briefly described patience with great praise, he proceeds to touch upon each motive to be proposed for embracing it, namely:

I. God’s patience toward us. | II. |

II. Christ’s patience. | III, IV. |

III. The origins of impatience and its evils, as detected in the devil himself. | V. |

IV. Faith to be proved by patience. | VI. |

V. Temporal things consequently despised. | VII. |

VI. Injuries borne with equanimity. | VIII. |

VII. Grief arising from the loss of one’s loved ones moderated. | [Col. 1250] IX. |

VIII. The desire for vengeance extinguished. | X. |

IX. The enemy’s provocations now rendered ineffectual. | XI. |

EDD.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1249A]

I confess before the Lord God that I have ventured quite rashly, if not even shamelessly, to compose a work on patience, though I am utterly incapable of practicing it [Note: [Col. 1249B] “I am” Paris.], being a man possessed of no good quality [Note: [Col. 1249B] “A man possessed of no good quality.” Almost everywhere he speaks of himself in the most abject terms. Thus, in the book *On Repentance*: “You, then, a sinner like me—or rather less than I, for I acknowledge my own preeminence in offenses—seize upon it in this way.” And in book II of *On the Dress of Women* [Col. 1250B]: “May God permit me to rebuke this very thing, since I am indeed to be rebuked in every respect”; and in the same work: “Would that I, most wretched man,” etc. RIG.]. For when people undertake to demonstrate and commend any subject, they ought first to be found themselves engaged in its practice, and to direct the steadfastness of their admonition [Note: [Col. 1249B] “Commendation” Latinus.] by the authority of their own conduct, lest their words blush at the deficiency of their deeds.

And would that this blushing brought some remedy, so that shame at not exhibiting what we are proceeding to recommend to others might become our instructor in exhibiting it! Yet there is such an insupportable greatness in certain good things, just as there is in certain evils, that divine inspiration’s grace alone brings about our ability to apprehend and practice them. For whatever is supremely good belongs supremely to God, and none but he who possesses it dispenses it, as he deems each person worthy.

Thus it will be at least a consolation to discuss what it is not granted us to enjoy, after the fashion of the sick, who, though deprived of health, cannot refrain from speaking about its blessings. So I, most wretched man, always sick with the fevers of impatience, must sigh after, invoke, and plead for the health of patience that I do not possess, whenever I remember and ponder, in contemplation of my weakness, that the good health of faith and the soundness of the Lord’s discipline do not readily come to anyone unless patience sits beside him. Patience has been so placed at the head of the things of God that no one who is a stranger to patience can fulfill any commandment or accomplish any work pleasing to the Lord.

Even those who live blindly [Note: [Col. 1250B] “Blind” Rhen., Fran.] honor its excellence by calling it the highest virtue [Note: [Col. 1250B] “Even those who live blindly.” This is the reading of Fulvius Ursinus’s codex. Others read “who live blind things,” which may rightly seem more in keeping with Tertullian’s manner, as in Juvenal:

> Those who pretend to be Curii and live Bacchanalia.

RIG. In the same way the blessed Cyprian used the same Hellenism in the book *On the Good of Patience*: “We who do not speak great things, but live them,” as though he had said: Οὐ λαμπρὰ μὲν λέγομεν, ἀλλὰ ζῶμεν, “We do not merely speak splendid things, but live splendidly,” using the adjective for the adverb λαμπρῶς. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 1250B] “May honor” Fran., Paris.]. Philosophers [Col. 1251A], indeed, who are regarded as creatures possessing some degree of wisdom [Note: [Col. 1251B] “Carnal” Wouw., MS.], place so high a value upon patience that, although they disagree among themselves through the diverse whims of their schools and rivalries of opinion, nevertheless, united in their regard for patience alone, they have entrusted to this single virtue the peace of their studies. They conspire in its favor and enter into alliance over it; they [Note: [Col. 1251B] “To it” Fran., Paris.] [Note: [Col. 1251C] “They pursue it.” So the ancient copies have it. RIG.] pursue it [Note: [Col. 1251B] “It” absent from Rigalt.] with one accord in their aspiration to virtue; every display of wisdom they advance on the basis of patience. It is a great testimony to patience that it promotes even the vain disciplines of the world to praise and glory. Or is this instead an injury, when a divine thing is rolled about amid secular arts? But let them see to that: soon they will be ashamed when their wisdom is destroyed and disgraced together with the world.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1251B] The authority for our practice of patience is conferred not by a human affectation [Note: [Col. 1251B] “Affection” Paris.] fashioned through the insensibility of canine equanimity [Note: [Col. 1251C] “Not a human affectation.” Thus from three manuscripts instead of “affection”; for St. Cyprian uses a very similar expression, as even Rhenanus notes. PAM.] [Note: [Col. 1251C] “Fashioned through the insensibility of canine equanimity.” He means Cynic or Diogenic endurance. Cyprian, an imitator of Tertullian, quotes this passage in the book *On the Good of Patience*. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 1251C] “Fashioned through insensibility.” For the patience of Diogenes was closer to brutish insensibility than to human endurance. [Col. 1251D] LAC.], but by the divine ordering of a living [Note: [Col. 1251B] “Living” Paris.] and heavenly discipline, which assigns it to us [Note: [Col. 1251D] “But of a living and heavenly discipline,” etc. For *diligat*, “esteems,” we once thought *dirigat*, “directs,” should be written; we have now changed it to *delegat*, “assigns”—not wrongly, as we think. *Delegare* means to enjoin or entrust something; thus in book II *Against Marcion*. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 1251B] Others read “directs”; Rhen. reads “esteems.”], showing God himself as the example [Col. 1252A] of patience.

For first of all [Note: [Col. 1251B] Junius punctuates thus: “the example. For first of all, he who scatters the bloom,” etc.], he scatters the dew [Note: [Col. 1251B] “Bloom” Rhen.] of this light equally over the just and the unjust [Note: [Col. 1251D] “He who scatters the dew of this light.” Cyprian too expounds this passage delightfully in the cited book *On the Good of Patience*. RHEN. Others, such as La Cerda, read “bloom.” — “‘The bloom of light.’ The flower of light is fire. Lucretius, book IV: ‘eyes blossoming with flames’; and book I: ‘they shone with the flower of flame.’ Statius, *Thebaid* I: ‘the doorposts blossoming with mysterious light.’ Tertullian, *Apology* 2: ‘the lights blossomed.’ John Chrysostom, Homily 10 *To the People of Antioch*: Τὰ ποικίλα τῶν ἄστρων ἄνθη, ‘the many-colored flowers of the stars.’ I discussed further examples in my commentary on book VII of the *Aeneid*. The manuscripts have ‘dew of light,’ perhaps because he scatters it; but I change nothing.” LAC.]. He allows the duties of the seasons, the services of the elements, and the tributes of the whole creation to come equally to the worthy and the unworthy [Note: [Col. 1251B] “Allows them to come equally” Paris.]. He endures the most ungrateful nations, which worship the playthings of their crafts and the works of their own hands; which persecute his name together with his household [Note: [Col. 1251D] “His name together with his household, persecuting.” I gladly restore what Rhenanus published and the manuscript copies confirm: “His name and his household, persecuting.” By “name” he means the Christian name, and by “his household” [Col. 1252C] the household of Christ—that is, Christians. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1252B] “His household” Rhen.; “the Christian name together with the household of Christ” Jun.]; and among which luxury, greed, injustice, and malice grow more insolent every day [Note: [Col. 1252B] “Grow into” Wouw., MS., Rig.]. Thus his own patience works to his own disadvantage, for many do not believe in the Lord precisely because they have so long failed to perceive him as angry with the world.

## CHAPTER III
And this, indeed, [Note: [Col. 1252B] “Indeed” is absent from the Paris edition.] may perhaps be regarded as a manifestation of divine patience seen from afar, as something belonging to the heights above. But what of that patience which was openly present among human beings on earth and was, so to speak, grasped by the hand? [Col. 1252B] God suffers himself to be born in his mother’s womb and waits; once born, he endures growing to maturity; and when grown, he is in no haste to be acknowledged, but even subjects himself to indignity [Note: [Col. 1252B] Christ suffers himself to be conceived and waits in the womb, according to the law of nature, until he is born and comes into this light. Moreover, he subjects himself to indignity through the work of a craftsman, as in Mark. JUN.] [Note: [Col. 1252C] “But even subjects himself to indignity.” His face, because of its deformity, was exposed to reproaches and insults. Thus, in *On the Pallium*, he used “the indignity of his countenance” to mean deformity of face; and in *Against the Jews* he says that Christ was not even attractive in appearance. Likewise, in Book III *Against Marcion*: “Whatever that little body may have been, since it had an appearance and since it was seen—if it was inglorious, if ignoble, it will be my Christ; for such was the appearance and aspect in which he was announced.” Septimius evidently wished the words in Isaiah, “We saw him, and he had neither beauty nor comeliness,” to be understood not merely of the time of his Passion but of the native formation of his body, so that because of his deformity he seemed fashioned for insults; and accordingly he says that Christ subjected himself to indignity. Likewise, in *On the Flesh of Christ*: “So far was his body from possessing even human attractiveness.” “Even if the prophets among us had been silent about his ignoble appearance, his sufferings and indignities themselves speak: the sufferings, [Col. 1252D] indeed, attest human flesh, and the indignities an unattractive one. Would anyone have dared even to graze a novel body with the tip of a fingernail, or to defile with spittle a face that did not deserve it? He who had come to be crucified for us with the punishment of a slave had also assumed the form of a slave, not an εἶδος ἀξιόν τυραννίδος, ‘an appearance worthy of sovereignty.’” Origen, Book VI *Against Celsus*: Ὀμολογουμένως τοίνυν γέγραπται τὰ περὶ τοῦ δυσειδὲς γεγονέναι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ σῶμα, κ.τ.λ., “It is therefore admittedly written that the body of Jesus was unattractive,” etc. Augustine on Psalm 43: “As a man, he had neither beauty nor comeliness; but he was beautiful in form insofar as he is fairer than the sons of men.” And on Psalm 118: “The Bridegroom himself was beautiful, not in flesh but in power.” On Psalm 127: “He is that Bridegroom than whom nothing is more beautiful, who appeared as though hideous in the hands of his persecutors; of him Isaiah had said a little earlier: ‘And we saw him, and he had neither beauty nor comeliness.’ Is our Bridegroom therefore hideous? Far be it. For how would the virgins have loved him who sought no husbands on earth? He therefore appeared hideous to his persecutors. And unless they had thought him hideous, they would not have assailed him, beaten him with scourges, crowned him with thorns, or [Col. 1253C] dishonored him with spittle. But because he appeared hideous to them, they did these things to him; for they did not possess the eyes by which Christ might be seen as beautiful,” etc. Finally, our Septimius, in Book III *Against Marcion*, explains David’s words, “Fairer in form than the sons of men,” by saying: “For although in David he is mature in beauty above the sons of men, this is in that allegorical condition of spiritual grace, when he is girded with the sword of the Word, which truly is his beauty, comeliness, and glory. But in bodily appearance, in the same prophet, he is even ‘a worm and not a man, the disgrace of mankind and the contempt of the people.’” I heard Jacques Sirmond, a man of exceptional piety and learning, relate that he had seen an ancient bronze coin, struck—as [Col. 1253D] he believed—under Constantine. Its engraving displayed a face that was rather deformed and terrible, and on the reverse a temple with the inscription ANACTACIC, that is, Ἀνάστασις, “Resurrection.” This would seem scarcely capable of indicating anyone other than Christ, who on the third day restored the temple—that is, his body—which death had destroyed and dissolved, by taking up his life again. Accordingly, those are very far mistaken who say that the face of Christ is the one Fulvio Orsini attributes to Titus Quinctius Flamininus (*Images of Illustrious Men*, 126). On this subject see Janus Rutgersius, *Various Readings*, Book I, chapter 1. What the Jews say in John, indicating that Christ’s age was approaching fifty years, seems to relate to the sorrowfulness of the Lord’s countenance: on a face lacking beauty, whose features were confused by that very deformity, they naturally reckoned far more years than he actually had. RIG.], and he is baptized by his own servant [Note: [Col. 1252B] “Is baptized”: Franeker edition.], and [Col. 1253A] repels the tempter’s assault with words alone [Note: [Col. 1253D] “Repels the tempter’s assault with words alone.” We may easily restore this passage, corrupted by faulty punctuation, as follows: “And he repels the tempter’s assault with words alone, when from being Lord he becomes teacher, instructing man to escape unto salvation, namely, to obtain pardon for an offense, once trained in patience. He did not contend, he did not cry out,” etc. Christ repelled Satan’s temptation with words alone, and indeed with words cited from Scripture. The Lord could by divine power and a nod have thrust him down to the depths of Tartarus; but he preferred to act as a teacher and to refute the one who cited Scripture maliciously by the simple truth of Scripture. Tertullian then transferred from Satan to man the occasion supplied by that phrase, “from being Lord he becomes teacher,” and immediately added, “instructing man to escape unto salvation.” He is everywhere accustomed to seize such opportunities. RIG.], when [Note: [Col. 1253B] “Then”: Latinus.] from being Lord he becomes [Note: [Col. 1253B] “May become”: Franeker edition.] teacher, instructing man to escape unto salvation, [Note: [Col. 1253B] The Dijon manuscript reads: “instructing man to escape absolute death” (Pithou’s manuscript: *absolutem*), “namely, to obtain pardon for an offense, once trained in patience.” Orsini’s manuscript: “instructing man to escape death; toward the pardon, namely, of the accustomed offense, once trained in patience.” Three Vatican manuscripts, according to Pamelius, and the Franeker edition: “instructing man to escape death, for salvation, namely, to come when patience has been offended, once trained.” Rhenanus: “instructing man to escape death, absolutely, namely, to obtain pardon for an offense, once trained in patience.” Rigault and Semler omitted “death.”] [Note: [Col. 1254C] “Instructing man to escape unto salvation.” Here the ancient books disagree greatly among themselves. Pithou’s oldest manuscript has: “Instructing man to escape absolute death; namely, to obtain pardon for an offense, once trained in patience.” The Dijon manuscript: “Instructing man to escape absolute death; namely, to obtain pardon for an offense, once trained in patience.” Orsini’s: “Instructing man to escape death; toward the pardon, namely, of the accustomed offense, once trained in patience.” Three Vatican manuscripts, according to Pamelius: “Instructing man to escape death, for salvation, namely, to come when patience has been offended, once trained.” Rhenanus published: “Instructing man to escape death, absolutely, namely, to obtain pardon for an offense, once trained in patience.” RIG.] namely, to obtain pardon for an offense, once trained in patience [Note: [Col. 1254B] Manuscripts 42, 2, and 3. Leopold preferred to read: “death unto salvation,” etc.]. He did not contend, he did not cry out, nor did anyone hear his voice in the streets; he did not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoking flax (Isa. 42). For the prophet had not spoken falsely; rather, this was the testimony of God himself, who placed his Spirit in the Son together with all patience (John 13; Matt. 9; Luke 9; Luke 17; Matt. 14; Matt. 26; Isa. 53; Matt. 29; John 18; Matt. 26; Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19).

He refused no one who wished to attach himself to him; he disdained no one’s table or roof.
