He himself supplied the water for washing his disciples’ feet [Note: [Col. 1254B] “But rather”: Franeker and Paris editions.] [Note: [Col. 1254D] “He himself supplied the water for washing his disciples’ feet.” This reading of Orsini’s manuscript was preferred because likewise, in *On Baptism*, we find: “He supplies water to those learning.” Yet the reading found in Pithou’s manuscript, “But rather, he himself for washing,” etc., can also be defended, and not without reason. For here the subject is only the service; there, the water. RIG.]. He did not spurn sinners or tax collectors. He was not even [Note: [Col. 1254B] “Even”: Franeker and Paris editions.] angry with [Col. 1253B] the city that had refused to receive him, though his disciples had wished heavenly fires to be brought down upon so insulting a town. He healed the ungrateful and yielded to those who plotted against him. This would be too little if he had not even kept his betrayer with him and refrained from steadily [Note: [Col. 1254B] “Insistently”: Junius.] pointing him out.

But when he is betrayed, when he is led like a beast to sacrifice—for in this way he no more opens his mouth than a lamb under the power of its shearer—he to whom, had he wished it, legions of angels would have come from heaven at a single word, [Col. 1254A] did not approve even the avenging sword of a single disciple [Note: [Col. 1254B] “One leading him out”: Rhenanus, Franeker, and Paris editions.] [Note: [Col. 1254B] “As an avenger”: Franeker and Paris editions.]. The Lord’s patience was wounded in Malchus. Accordingly, he both cursed the works of the sword for the future and, by restoring to health the man whom he himself had not injured, made satisfaction through [Note: [Col. 1254C] “Ah!”: Rhenanus.] patience, the mother of mercy.

I pass over the fact that he is crucified, for this was why he had come. Yet was there also need of insults for the death he had to undergo? But before departing, he wished to feast richly upon the delight of patience. He is spat upon, scourged, mocked, clothed in shameful garments, and crowned with things still more shameful. Wondrous is the faithfulness of his equanimity. He who had determined to lie concealed in the form of a human being imitated nothing of human impatience. From this above all, Pharisees, you ought to have recognized the Lord: no human being would have carried patience of this kind to completion.

Such and so great are these proofs. Their very greatness is, among the nations, a reason for rejecting the faith, but among us a ground and structure [Note: [Col. 1254C] Others read “instruction.”] for it. They demonstrate clearly enough—not merely through the Lord’s words when he gives commands, but also through his sufferings [Note: [Col. 1254C] Junius adds “in”; Rigault reads “by enduring sufferings.”] when he endures—that, for those to whom it has been granted to believe, patience is God’s nature [Note: [Col. 1254D] “Patience is God’s nature.” For, as Augustine says, even God’s weakness arose from power (*City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 9). RIG.], the effect and excellence of a certain innate property.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, if we see that every upright and well-disposed servant conducts himself in accordance with his master’s character—since [Col. 1255A] the art of earning favor is obedience, while the discipline of obedience [Note: [Col. 1255C] Rigault reads “to obey.”] is compliant submission—how much more must we be found to have a character conforming to the Lord! [Note: [Col. 1255C] On the authority of three Vatican manuscripts, Pamelius reads: “obedient according to the Lord.”] We are, of course, servants of the living God, whose judgment upon his own does not turn upon fetters or the cap of freedom [Note: [Col. 1255C] “Not upon fetters or the cap.” Fetters were the marks of slavery, just as the cap was the mark of freedom. Hence the coin of Brutus was distinguished by a cap and two daggers, by which he signified that he had restored freedom to his country. I omit mentioning here that Anacharsis the Scythian—and thus a slave—assumed the πῖλος, “cap,” in the gymnasia. LE PR.], but upon the eternity either of punishment or of salvation. To avoid that severity, or to invite that generosity, we need as great a diligence in obedience as are the things which severity threatens or generosity promises.

And yet we exact obedience not only from human beings held down by slavery [Note: [Col. 1255C] “Held down by slavery.” That is, from slaves who labor with great exertion and effort. The author of the *Poems against Marcion*, Poem 3:

> Afflicted, he preferred to bear the people’s toils  
> With neck bowed beneath the burden . . .

[Col. 1255D] And:

> For the fatherland, which bends beneath the toil of war.

RIG.], or from those who under any other legal title owe us obedience, but even from cattle and wild beasts, understanding that they were provided and handed over by the Lord for our use [Note: [Col. 1255D] “Provided by the Lord for our use.” He alludes to Genesis 1: “Have dominion over the fish of the sea,” etc.; likewise Genesis 9: “Let fear and dread of you be upon every living creature,” etc. PAM.]. Will those whom God subjects to us, then, be better than we are in the discipline of obedience? Those who obey us do, after all, acknowledge us. Yet we hesitate to listen to the only one to whom we are subject—namely, the Lord. But how unjust, and even how ungrateful, it is not to repay to the one through whose indulgence you obtain something from others the very thing you obtain from them!

There is no need to say more about the obedience owed and displayed by us to the Lord God. Recognition of God understands sufficiently what duty rests upon it. Yet lest we seem to have introduced obedience as a foreign subject, obedience itself also derives from patience. No impatient person obeys; nor does anyone who is patient fail to delight [Note: [Col. 1255C] “Fail to”: present in the Franeker and Paris editions.] [Note: [Col. 1255C] Rigault reads “resists.”] in obedience.

God, the Lord, demonstrator, and recipient of every good thing, displayed patience in himself. Who, then, could discuss [Note: [Col. 1255C] “Conceal”: Franeker and Paris editions.] his good at length? [Note: [Col. 1255D] “Who could discuss his good at length?” That is: Who has ever spoken adequately of his good? In Tertullian, *retractare* means to treat, debate, or discuss. Yet all the ancient copies read: “Who would think to conceal or keep silent within himself concerning his good?” This should not have been altered, for it can readily be explained in that way. RIG.] [Col. 1256A] Who, likewise, could doubt that every good, because it belongs to God, must be pursued with one’s whole mind by those who belong to God? Through these considerations both the commendation and the exhortation concerning patience have been established in an unencumbered form [Note: [Col. 1255D] “In an unencumbered form.” This is a phrase of the jurists: “to be readily ascertainable.” Hence Ulpian’s expression in *Digest*, “If He Should Doubt,” on sureties: “Since the reckoning of the entire debt is not readily ascertainable.” Similarly, “in the concise form of a preliminary objection.” PAM.] and, as it were, in the concise form of a preliminary objection [Note: [Col. 1255D] “In the concise form of a preliminary objection.” In law *praescribo* has three meanings, all of which can suit Tertullian. First, *praescribere* means to prescribe or determine beforehand, as “a time prescribed by the testator,” that is, predetermined. Therefore, since God has valued this virtue so highly, you have briefly prescribed and predetermined for you what you ought to think about it. The second meaning is that whereby someone who has acquired another’s property through prescription protects himself against every attempted lawsuit with this one word alone. Thus, one who has pleaded prescription strikes down and takes away every action against himself and kills any lawsuit whatsoever. What, then, is more concise than this word? You therefore have a concise formula by which to strike down those who attack patience, if you say only: “It is the Lord’s virtue.” By this word you will take away every action, just as those do who have pleaded prescription. The third and proper meaning is this: in law a *praescriptio* is an exception or preliminary plea, and *praescribere* means to make an exception or oppose a preliminary plea and so exclude the plaintiff. In this sense, one who defends himself in court and transfers the charge to his adversary when refuting it is said “to plead against” his adversary. Therefore, you have a concise formula with which to plead against your opponents. What is that formula? “It is God’s virtue; God values it greatly; God displayed it in himself.” LAC.] [Note: [Col. 1256C] The Franeker and Paris editions read “has been established.” Rigault reads: “concerning patience, it has been established in the concise form of a preliminary objection.”].

## CHAPTER V

Nevertheless, it is not pointless for the discussion of matters necessary to faith to proceed, because neither is it fruitless. Loquacity in edification is never shameful—if indeed it ever is shameful. Accordingly, if the discourse concerns some good thing, the subject requires that the contrary of the good also be reviewed. For you will make it clearer [Note: [Col. 1256D] “You will make it clearer.” This genuinely belongs to the “illuminations” of the rhetoricians. Therefore I do not listen to those who invent some connection with baptism here. I know that baptism is called illumination, as Paul also attests; but it is foolish to divine some reference to baptism here. LAC.] what is to be pursued if you correspondingly set forth what is to be avoided.

Let us therefore consider impatience: whether, just as patience was born and found in God, so its opposite was born and found in our adversary, so that from [Col. 1256B] this it may appear how fundamentally it is opposed to faith. For what was conceived by God’s rival is certainly no friend to the things of God. The discord between the things is the same as that between their authors. Moreover, since God is supremely good and the devil, by contrast, supremely evil, they testify by their very opposition that neither favors [Note: [Col. 1256C] Wouwerius’s manuscript reads “to favor.”] the other; consequently, nothing good can seem to us to have been spoken by the evil one any more than anything evil by the good one [Note: [Col. 1256C] The Franeker and Paris editions and Rigault read “produced.”].

I therefore discover the birth of impatience [Note: [Col. 1256D] “The birth of impatience.” He calls the origin or beginning of impatience its “birth.” Thus, in Book I *Against Marcion*, he spoke of “the birth of recognition,” and in *On the Pallium*, of “the birth of the world.” RHEN.] in the devil himself, at the very time when he impatiently endured the Lord God’s subjecting all the works he had made to his image, that is, to man (Gen. 3). For he would not have grieved if he had endured it, nor would he have envied man if he had not grieved. Thus [Note: [Col. 1256C] “Therefore.”] he deceived him because he had envied him; [Col. 1257A] he envied him because he had grieved; he grieved because he had certainly not borne it patiently.

I decline to inquire what that angel of perdition was first, evil or [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Or” is absent from Rigault.] impatient, since it is plain that either impatience began together with malice, or malice from impatience; that they then conspired together and grew up inseparably in the one bosom of their father. But having learned by his own experience what assistance in sinning was supplied by the very passion he had first felt and through which he had entered upon transgression [Note: [Col. 1257C] Rhenanus reads: “through which he had first transgressed”; Pithou’s manuscript: “he had first entered upon transgression.”] [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Would assist”: Franeker and Paris editions and Wouwerius’s manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Instructed”: Wouwerius’s manuscript.], he enlisted that same passion in his crime by thrusting it upon man.

The woman, immediately approached by him, was—I may confidently say—through that very conversation breathed upon by his spirit infected with impatience. So thoroughly was this so [Note: [Col. 1257C] Wouwerius’s manuscript reads: “so thoroughly that never.”] that she would never have sinned at all if she had preserved patience within [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Within” is absent from the Franeker and Paris editions and Rigault.] the divine prohibition [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Had guarded beforehand”: Franeker edition and Rhenanus.].

What of the fact that she could not bear being the only one approached? Before Adam, who was not yet her husband and did not yet owe her his ears, [Col. 1257B] [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Did not yet owe her his ears.” He alludes to the mutual debts spouses owe each other, which even the Apostle wished to be discharged in good faith, so that a spouse owes an ear to a spouse who addresses and petitions him. RIG.] she was too impatient even to remain silent, and made [Note: [Col. 1257C] Semler reads “toward.”] him the transmitter [Note: [Col. 1257D] “And she makes him the transmitter of what she had imbibed from the evil one.” The ancient copies read, corruptly, “toward the transmitter toward him.” Yet this shows what must be regarded as the genuine text: “she makes him its co-transmitter.” Satan, he says, had approached Eve alone and had breathed upon her alone with a spirit infected by impatience. But she, too impatient even to remain silent, poured Satan’s depraved suggestion into her Adam. Thus she herself became the channel of sin into Adam, and thereafter made him the co-transmitter of the same sin—that is, its agent and partner in transmitting sin into their common posterity. RIG.] of what she had imbibed from the evil one [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Makes?” Latinus and Junius; “and” is absent from Wouwerius’s manuscript.].

Thus another human being perishes through another’s impatience; and presently he himself also perishes through his own impatience, committed in both directions—toward God’s warning and toward the devil’s deception [Note: [Col. 1257D] “And toward the devil’s deception.” He means the deception by which the devil had circumvented Eve; Adam should have refuted it. *Circumscribere* means “to deceive.” In Cicero too, “to circumvent the senate” means to deprive the senate of its authority, the metaphor being taken from craftsmen or surgeons, who first draw a line around what they intend to cut away. And truly our first parents were circumvented by the devil, through whose cunning they were [Col. 1258C] cast out of Paradise and condemned to exile, with every right of possession taken away from them. RHEN.], since he could not endure preserving the former and refuting the latter.

Hence came the first judgment, from the same source as the origin of sin. Hence God began to be angry, from the point at which man was led to offend. Thence came the first patience in God, whence came the first indignation. Content then with a curse alone, he restrained himself from the violence of punishment against the devil. Or what crime before this [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Or what crime before this”: Junius. “What crime”: Ciacconius. [Col. 1258C] CIAC.] act of impatience is imputed to man? He was innocent, God’s close friend, and an inhabitant of Paradise. But once he yielded [Note: [Col. 1258C] Others read “once he succumbed”; Junius does not approve.] to impatience, he ceased [Note: [Col. 1258C] Rhenanus reads “ceases—ceases.”] to have the mind of God and [Col. 1257C] ceased to be capable of enduring heavenly things.

Thereafter [Note: [Col. 1258D] “Thereafter man was given over to the earth.” The author himself says in *On the Pallium*: “Clothed in skins, he is given over to the world as though to a penal mine.” RIG.] man, given over to the earth and cast out from God’s sight, began readily to be appropriated [Note: [Col. 1258C] Junius reads “to be occupied for use.”] by impatience for everything that would offend God [Note: [Col. 1258D] “Began readily to be appropriated by impatience.” Properly speaking, those to whom the right of possession belongs “appropriate” a thing. Thus impatience, as though it now possessed man, readily drew him to whatever would offend God. RHEN.]. [Col. 1258A] For immediately impatience, conceived from the devil’s seed, through the fecundity of malice begot wrath [Note: [Col. 1258C] Junius reads “wondrous.”] as its son, and trained what it had brought forth in its own arts [Note: [Col. 1258C] Latinus reads “educated.”]. For what had plunged Adam and Eve themselves into death taught their son also to begin with homicide (Gen. 4).

I should attribute this to impatience in vain if Cain, that first murderer and first fratricide, bore with equanimity and without impatience the Lord’s rejection of his offerings [Note: [Col. 1258C] Rhenanus reads “to the Lord.”], if he was not angry with his brother, and if, finally, he killed no one. Since, therefore, he could not have killed unless angry, nor have become angry unless impatient, what he did through wrath shows that it must be referred to that by which wrath was prompted.

And these, indeed, [Note: [Col. 1258C] “And these, indeed” is absent from Rhenanus and the Franeker edition.] were, so to speak, the cradle of impatience while it was still an infant. As for the great growth it soon achieved, there is no cause for wonder. For if it was the first to sin, it follows that, because it was first, [Col. 1258B] it is therefore also the sole matrix of every sin, pouring out from its own fountain the various veins of crimes.

Homicide has already been discussed. Yet although it was brought forth by wrath at the beginning, whatever causes it afterward [Note: [Col. 1258C] “Later”: Franeker and Paris editions and Rigault.] discovers for itself, it refers them to impatience as to its own origin. For whether someone commits that crime because of enmity or for the sake of plunder, first he must become unable to endure either his hatred or his greed. Whatever compels him cannot achieve its end without its own impatience. Who has entered upon adultery without impatience of lust? And if among women that sale of chastity is compelled by a price, it is certainly governed by an inability to despise gain.

These are the principal [Note: [Col. 1258D] “These are the principal sins.” Not unlike this is St. Cyprian in *On the Good of Patience*, chapter 5: “Adultery, fraud, homicide—each is a mortal crime.” Meanwhile, it should be noted that, whereas St. Augustine and other later writers understand *delicta* as lesser sins, Tertullian uses the word generically for every kind of sin; when, however, he treats of the graver sins, he adds “principal,” “capital,” or “mortal.” PAM.] sins in the Lord’s sight. To state the matter briefly, every sin must be attributed to impatience. Impatience is the evil of being unable to bear good. No one is unchaste without being impatient of chastity, dishonest without being impatient of honesty, impious without being impatient of piety, or restless without being impatient of rest. For anyone to become evil, he must be unable to persevere in good.

Why, then, should such a hydra [Note: [Col. 1258C] Junius reads “exedra”; Paris, “exhedra”; Rhenanus, “exedra.”] [Note: [Col. 1258D] “Such a hydra.” Rhenanus interpreted this passage as referring to an *exedra*; we have nevertheless preferred to follow others, who explain *excetra* as a serpent, or as the hydra conquered by Hercules. LE PR.] [Col. 1259A] of sins not offend the Lord, who condemns evil things?

Is it not evident that Israel itself always sinned against God through impatience, beginning when, forgetful of the heavenly arm by which it had been delivered from Egyptian afflictions, it demanded of Aaron gods to serve as its leaders, and poured out its contributions of gold into an idol (Exod. 17)? For it had impatiently endured the delays—necessary though they were—of Moses’ meeting with the Lord [Note: [Col. 1259C] “It had impatiently endured the delays.” The final word is not found in Pithou’s manuscript, so that in this clause the preceding word “contributions” appears to need repetition: that is, “contributions of Moses with the Lord.” RIG.].

After the edible rain of manna [Note: [Col. 1259C] “After the edible rain of manna,” etc. He speaks of the manna granted to the Hebrews as they wandered in the wilderness, and then of the abundance of water that Moses obtained from the Lord. Countless familiar passages on this subject occur both among pagan and sacred writers. We said something about these matters in our observations against the Pre-Adamites; here [Col. 1259D] I shall add Salvian, Book I *On the Governance of God*: “The heavens dripping with heavenly food, waters leaping from the rocks.” This is poetic enough. LE PR.], after the watery attendance of the rock, they despaired of the Lord because they could not endure three days’ thirst. For this impatience too is reproached in them by the Lord. And lest we roam through every individual instance: by sinning through impatience, they invariably perished.

How, moreover, did they lay hands upon the prophets [Note: [Col. 1259C] Rigault reads “hands upon the prophets.”] except through impatience with hearing them (Acts 8; Wisd. 2)? And upon the Lord himself, through impatience [Col. 1259B] even at seeing him [Note: [Col. 1259D] “Through impatience even at seeing him”: through envy; for a person who is envied is not seen patiently or gladly, and those who envy commonly hate the very existence of that person. Thus Christ was hateful to the Jews, and “Pilate knew that he had been handed over to him by the Jews through envy.” RIG.]. But if they had entered upon patience, they would have been delivered.

## CHAPTER VI

Patience is indeed that which both follows faith and precedes it (Gen. 15). Thus Abraham believed God and was reckoned [Note: [Col. 1259C] Junius reads “reckoned,” in the accusative.] righteous by him [Note: [Col. 1259D] “Was reckoned righteous by him.” In Abraham there is a typological attestation of faith. The author himself indicates here that this pertains to no faith other than a living faith, when he adds: “But patience proved his faith”; and a little later: “faith illuminated by patience.” You have an entirely similar passage in St. Cyprian, Letter 63. PAM.]. But patience proved his faith when he was commanded to sacrifice his son—not, I would say, as a testing of his faith, but as a typological attestation [Note: [Col. 1259D] “But as a typological attestation”: that is, an example, figure, sacrament, or mystery. RIG.]. For God already knew the man whom he had reckoned righteous. Abraham both heard patiently so grave a command—one whose completion did not please the Lord—and, if God had wished it, would have fulfilled it. Deservedly, therefore, was he blessed, because he was also faithful; deservedly faithful, because also patient.

Thus faith, illuminated by patience, when it was sown among the nations [Col. 1259C] through the seed of Abraham, which is Christ (Gal. 3), and [Col. 1260A] brought grace in addition to the law, placed patience, its assistant, at the head of the law that was to be enlarged and fulfilled, because patience alone had formerly been lacking from the teaching of righteousness.

For in former times they demanded an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, and repaid evil with evil at interest (Exod. 21; Deut. 19). Patience was not yet upon the earth, because faith was not yet here either. Meanwhile, of course, impatience took advantage of the law’s opportunities. This was easy while the Lord and teacher of patience was absent [Note: [Col. 1259D] “And teacher.” Ignatius the Martyr, in his letter to the Smyrnaeans, says that the faithful were instructed by the Father through the Son: Πατέρα διὰ αὐτοῦ ὑμᾶς σοφίσαντα, “the Father who made you wise through him.” Gregory of Nyssa, in his work *On the Perfect Form of the Christian*, speaking of Christ: ὁ τῷ σῷ βίῳ δι’ ἑαυτοῦ νομοθετῶν τὸ μακρόθυμον, “he who through himself prescribed patience as the law for your life.” LAC.].

After he arrived [Note: [Col. 1260C] “After he arrived.” I believe Jerome had the same matter in view in his letter to Marcella, where he says: “He who becomes angry judges himself not to be a Christian.” Why? Because Christ and the new law have now removed anger, which formerly was not so strictly forbidden. Cyprian likewise said: “Patience itself directs our conduct, so that we may keep to the way of Christ while walking by means of his endurance.” LAC.] and shaped the grace of faith with patience, it was no longer permitted even to provoke another by a word, nor even to say “Fool!” without danger of judgment. Anger was prohibited, tempers restrained [Note: [Col. 1259C] Latinus and Junius read “extinguished.”], the insolent hand checked, and the tongue’s poison removed. The law gained more than it lost, when Christ said (Matt. 5:44): “Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, and pray for your persecutors, [Col. 1260B] that you may be children of your heavenly Father.”

You see what Father patience acquires for us. In this principal command the whole discipline of patience is gathered up, since we are not permitted to do evil even where it would be deserved [Note: [Col. 1260C] The Franeker edition reads “of the tongue”; Pamelius, on manuscript authority, reads “of faith,” and Junius approves.] [Note: [Col. 1260D] “We are not permitted to do evil even where it would be deserved.” This is the reading of the oldest copies, and there can be no doubt that Tertullian wrote it thus, as Rhenanus also published and very correctly explained it. Under the law of the Gospel it is not permitted to return evil for evil or to do evil to those who have deserved evil, though they might otherwise deserve retaliation and evil might therefore be done to them “deservedly,” that is, justly and meritoriously. RIG.].

## CHAPTER VII
Now, as we run through the causes of impatience, the other precepts too will answer to them in their proper places. If the mind is aroused by a loss of property, it is admonished in almost every passage of the Lord’s Scriptures to despise the world; nor is there any greater inducement to contempt for money than the fact that the Lord himself is found possessing no riches. He always justifies the poor and condemns the rich beforehand [Note: [Col. 1260D] “Condemns the rich beforehand”—as though in anticipation of the Last Judgment. RIG.]. Thus, by his contempt for opulence [Note: [Col. 1260C] “Of losses,” Wouwer’s MS.] [Note: [Col. 1260D] “Thus the loss of patience,” etc. The sentence is obscure; it appears that it should be understood and punctuated as follows: “Thus the Lord furnished beforehand for patience the loss”—understand, “of property”—“the loathing of opulence, the contempt of riches”; the phrases are appositional. The sense would thus be: the Lord was the first to show that the loss of property must be endured patiently, since he teaches that riches are to be despised. In this way the clause that follows will cohere suitably. RHEN.], he furnished patience beforehand against loss, demonstrating [Col. 1260C] through the rejection of riches that their losses also [Col. 1261A] [Note: [Col. 1261C] “Their losses also,” etc. By *injuries* he means losses or diminutions, when something of our property [Col. 1261D] is lost. He could have said *losses*, but preferred a novel term. RHEN.] are to be reckoned as nothing. Therefore, what we have no need at all to seek—because the Lord did not seek it either—we ought not to endure reluctantly when it is diminished or even taken away.

Through the Apostle, the Spirit of the Lord declared covetousness to be the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10). Let us not interpret it as consisting only in desire for what belongs to another; for even what seems to be ours belongs to another: nothing is ours, since all things belong to God, to whom we ourselves also belong. Accordingly, if, when afflicted by loss, we react impatiently [Note: [Col. 1261C] Thus Rigault and Semler. “We shall be impatient,” Paris and Leopold.], grieving over the loss of what is not [Note: [Col. 1261C] “What is not ours,” Rigault.] ours, we shall be detected as close relations of covetousness. We seek another’s property when we reluctantly endure the loss of another’s property [Note: [Col. 1261C] Franeker adds “grieving.”]. Whoever is aroused by impatience at loss, preferring earthly things to heavenly, sins directly against God. For, on account of a worldly possession, he disturbs the spirit that he received from the Lord [Col. 1261B]. Let us therefore willingly [Note: [Col. 1261C] “Willing,” Franeker and Rigault.] lose earthly things and preserve heavenly things. Let the whole world perish, provided that I gain patience.

Anyone who has resolved not steadfastly to endure some trifling loss through theft, violence, or even negligence—I do not know whether he could easily or sincerely lay hands upon his own property for the sake of almsgiving. For how can one who cannot bear at all to be cut by another apply the knife to his own body [Note: [Col. 1261C] “To his own body,” Rigault.]? Patience amid losses is training in giving and sharing. One who does not fear to lose is not reluctant to give. Otherwise, how will a man who has two tunics give one of them to the naked, unless he is also the same man who can offer his cloak as well to one who takes away his tunic (Matt. 5)? How shall we make friends for ourselves from mammon [Col. 1261C] (Luke 16), if we love it so greatly that we cannot bear its loss? We shall perish along with what has perished. What do we find here, where we possess only so as to lose [Note: [Col. 1261D] “What do we find here, where we possess only so as to lose?” He alludes to Christ’s words in Matt. 10:39: “He who finds his soul will lose it, and he who loses his soul for my sake will find it.” RIG.]?

It belongs to the Gentiles to meet every loss with impatience, for they perhaps place monetary property [Note: [Col. 1261C] “Money,” Franeker.] before their souls. Indeed [Note: [Col. 1262C] “What,” Latinus.], they do so when, in their lust for gain, [Col. 1262A] they undertake the profitable perils of commerce at sea; when, for money’s sake, they do not hesitate to undertake even in the forum anything that carries the risk of condemnation; when, finally, they hire themselves out to the arena and the camp [Note: [Col. 1261D] “When, finally, to the arena and the camp.” He means the gladiatorial school, whose master was called the *lanista*; by “camp,” military service. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 1261D] “They hire themselves out.” This was a most disgraceful custom of acquiring profit; for even men born to respectable station, when they had fallen into poverty, hired and bound themselves to the gladiatorial arena. Seneca mentions this custom in Epistle 87: “Whether he hires himself out to the sword or to the knife.” No wonder: for what will poverty not bring about? On this, see Cyril of Alexandria, Homily 5, *On the Paschal Festivals*. LAC.]; and when they turn brigand along the road, adopting the habits of beasts [Note: [Col. 1261D] “They turn brigand along the road, adopting the habits of beasts.” Pithou’s codex reads, “through the way into those mindful.” These are traces of the true reading, which we think was something like this: “Through trackless places [Col. 1262C] they turn brigand after the manner of beasts.” Thus Tertullian himself in *On the Soul*: “Because it too has cast to the beasts those whom it has slaughtered in forests [Col. 1262D] and trackless places.” “Into the habits of beasts” means “after the manner of beasts,” “in the way of beasts.” RIG.]. But in accordance with the difference between them and us, it is fitting for us to surrender not life for money, but money for life, whether voluntarily in giving or patiently in losing.

## CHAPTER VIII

In this world we carry our very soul and body exposed to every injury, and we submit patiently to that injury; shall we be hurt by the relinquishment of lesser things [Note: [Col. 1262C] “By the tasting,” Latinus, Pithou, and Rigault. They judge that one could write “concerning liberation.” Latinius emended it to “concerning libation.”] [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Shall we be hurt by the relinquishment of lesser things?” The old books most consistently preserve the reading *minorum*, “of lesser things,” that is, of money. *Deliberatione*, however, appears to have been used with the force of *liberatione*, “relinquishment.” It is also a tenet of Christian philosophy that riches are counted among impediments. In the same sense it might also be read: “Shall we be hurt at being freed from lesser things?” This also commended itself to Pithou. RIG.]? Far be such a stain from a servant of Christ: that patience, prepared for greater trials, should fail in trivial matters [Col. 1262B].

If anyone has tried to provoke you with his hand [Note: [Col. 1262C] “To be provoked,” Rhenanus.], the Lord’s admonition [Note: [Col. 1262D] “The Lord’s *monela*.” He uses *monela* from *monere* (“to admonish”) for “admonition,” just as *sequela* comes from *sequi* (“to follow”). RHEN.] is at hand: “To him who strikes you,” he says (Matt. 5:39), “on the face, turn the other cheek also.” Let wickedness be wearied by your patience. Whoever [Note: [Col. 1262C] “Whoever,” Franeker, Paris, and Rigault.] dealt that blow, being bound over to pain and disgrace, is beaten more severely by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Is beaten more severely by the Lord”—by a counterblow, or by the rebound of divine vengeance. RIG.]. By enduring, you strike that wicked man more heavily; for he will be beaten by the one for whose sake you endure.

If the bitterness of a tongue breaks out in a curse or insult, look to the saying (Matt. 5:12): “When they curse you, rejoice.” The Lord himself was accursed under the Law (Deut. 21:23), and yet he alone is blessed (Gal. 3:13). Therefore, let us servants follow the Lord and patiently suffer curses [Col. 1262C], so that we may be blessed.

If I hear with insufficient composure some insolent or wicked remark directed against me, I must either repay bitterness in kind or be tormented by silent impatience. Therefore, when, having been cursed, I have struck back [Note: [Col. 1262C] “With a curse,” Franeker and Paris; “accursed,” Wouwer’s MS.], how shall I be found to have followed the Lord’s teaching, by which it is handed down (Mark 7:15, 18) that a person is defiled not by the uncleanness of vessels [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Not by the uncleanness of vessels.” What is read more than once in Matt. 15, *κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον* (“defiles the person”), Tertullian translates as *communicat* (“makes common”), just as Aurelius Augustine also read it. *Κοινοῖν* means “to make common.” And because the Jews call what is impure “common,” it came about that *κοινοῖν*, or “to make common,” means for them “to defile,” as the Old Latin version of the Gospels has it in certain manuscripts, especially ours. Erasmus very elegantly translates it “to render impure.” RHEN.], but by those things that [Col. 1263A] issue from the mouth [Note: [Col. 1263C] Others read “to be defiled.”]? Likewise (Matt. 12), that the guilt of every vain and superfluous word remains upon us? It follows, then, that what the Lord restrains us from doing, he also admonishes us to endure calmly when done by another.

Here, now [Note: [Col. 1263C] Junius adds “also.”], is the pleasure of patience. For every injury, whether inflicted by tongue or hand, when it encounters patience, will be canceled by the same outcome [Note: [Col. 1263D] “Will be canceled by the same outcome.” *Dispungere* means to delete and erase; the metaphor is taken from wax tablets containing names, on which entries that have been settled are struck through and erased with a stylus. For the jurist Ulpian teaches that this verb pertains to accounts when he says, “To strike through is to compare receipts and expenditures,” *Digest*, *On the Meaning of Words*. RHEN.] as some missile hurled [Note: [Col. 1263C] “Against a rock,” Junius.] against a rock of utterly steadfast hardness [Note: [Col. 1263D] “As some missile.” Here he takes *librare* to mean “to hurl with great force,” imitating Virgil, *Aeneid* IX: “He was poising the missile from beside his ear.” Otherwise its proper meaning is quite different: “to weigh.” PAM.], and blunted. For it will fall there, its effort vain and fruitless, and sometimes, rebounding against the one who launched it, it will rage back with reciprocal force.

Indeed, a person injures you precisely so that you may suffer, because the offender’s profit lies in the pain of the injured party. Therefore, when by not suffering you destroy his profit, he must himself suffer from the loss of his profit. Then you depart not merely uninjured [Note: [Col. 1263C] “You will depart,” Rhenanus.]—which by itself is enough for you [Col. 1263B]—but, beyond that, delighted by your adversary’s frustration and defended by his pain. This is the usefulness and pleasure [Note: [Col. 1263C] “Will,” Rhenanus.] of patience.

## CHAPTER IX

Not even that species of impatience arising from the loss of our own people is excused, where some affection pleads in defense of grief [Note: [Col. 1263C] “Assertion,” Rhenanus; perhaps: “affection pleads in defense of grief.”]. For precedence must be given [Note: [Col. 1263C] “We shall set before ourselves,” Wouwer’s MS.; “must be preferred,” Rhenanus.] to regard for the Apostle’s injunction, when he says (1 Thess. 4): “Do not grieve over anyone’s falling asleep, as the nations do who have no hope.” And rightly so. For, believing in Christ’s resurrection, we believe also in [Note: [Col. 1263C] “In” is absent from Junius.] our own, for whose sake he both died and rose again.

Therefore, since the resurrection of the dead is certain, grief over death is idle, and so is impatience with grief. Why, then [Note: [Col. 1264C] “For,” Franeker.], should you grieve if you do not believe that one has perished [Col. 1263C]? Why should you endure impatiently the temporary withdrawal [Col. 1264A] of one whom you believe will return? What you think to be death is a departure. One who goes ahead is not to be mourned, though certainly he is to be missed. That longing too must be governed by patience. For why should you bear immoderately the departure of one whom you will soon follow?

Moreover, impatience in such cases both casts an evil omen upon our hope and betrays the faith. And we injure Christ when we do not calmly accept those summoned by him, as though they were to be pitied. “I desire,” says the Apostle (Phil. 1), “now to be received [Note: [Col. 1263D] “I desire,” says the Apostle, “to be received.” The common text very properly has “to be dissolved,” for the Greek is *ἀναλῦσαι* (“to depart”). La Cerda defends this interpretation, “to be received,” with an ingenious but insufficiently true explanation. Septimius follows this version elsewhere, as in chapter 28 of *On the Spectacles* and chapter 5 of Book I of *To His Wife*. LE PR.] and to be with the Lord.” How much better [Note: [Col. 1263D] “How much better displays the desire of Christians.” One must repeat from the preceding words: “than the nations who lack hope.” RIG.] does this display the desire of Christians? Therefore, if we impatiently grieve that others have attained this desire [Note: [Col. 1264C] Junius punctuates: “How much better does it display the desire? Therefore, the desire of Christians,” etc.], we ourselves do not wish to attain it.

## CHAPTER X

There is also another supreme spur to impatience: the lust for vengeance [Col. 1264B], which serves the interest either of glory or of malice. But glory is certainly vain, and malice is never anything but hateful to the Lord—especially in this instance [Note: [Col. 1264C] Franeker adds “when.”], when, provoked by another’s [Note: [Col. 1264C] “By another’s,” Franeker.] malice, it sets itself above him in exacting vengeance [Note: [Col. 1264C] “Sets itself above him in exacting vengeance.” To establish oneself as superior in vengeance will be to conduct oneself like a ruler and to arrogate to oneself the authority of a judge. LAC.], and, by repaying wickedness, doubles what was done only once.

Among those in error [Note: [Col. 1264D] “Among those in error”—among the heathen. Thus, “with the truth” means “with Christ.” RIG.], vengeance appears to be a consolation for pain; with the truth, it is certainly convicted of malignity [Note: [Col. 1264C] “Certainly,” Wouwer’s MS.; “certain,” Rhenanus.] [Note: [Col. 1264D] “It is certainly convicted of malignity.” Rhenanus printed: “With the truth, it is convicted of certain malignity.” The emendation “a contest is convicted of malignity” is attractive. Augustine confirms this emendation and appears to have had Septimius’s words before his eyes when he wrote thus on Psalm 36: “Contend with the evil man, but in goodness; for this is the true contention, or rather the salutary contest: that one should be good against an evil man, not that there should be two evil men.” RIG.]. For what difference is there between the provoker and the provoked, except that the former [Note: [Col. 1264D] “The former is found first in wrongdoing.” For to render evil for evil, or *ἀνταποδοῦναι* (“to repay”), what else is it than *ἀντιδικῆσαι δεύτεραν* (“to retaliate a second time”)? Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII.] is found first in wrongdoing and the latter afterward? Yet each is guilty before the Lord of injuring a human being—the Lord who both forbids and condemns every [Note: [Col. 1264C] “Every” in the feminine, Franeker and Paris.] wicked deed.

There is no consideration of order in wrongdoing; position does not separate what similarity joins. It is therefore commanded without qualification [Note: [Col. 1264D] “It is therefore commanded without qualification.” Indeed, Ambrose, Sermon 10, says that this is the sum of Christian discipline: “For this is the sum of our Christianity: that we repay mutual love to those who love us and patience to those who injure us.” LAC.] that evil is not to be repaid with evil (Rom. 12). An equal deed [Col. 1264C] has equal desert [Note: [Col. 1264C] “Also has desert,” Wouwer’s MS.]. How shall we observe this [Col. 1265A] if, having first been scorned [Note: [Col. 1265C] “If, having first been scorned, we shall not be engaged in the scorn of vengeance?” Thus it is read in Ursinus’s codex. Others read, “If, being scornful, we shall not be engaged in the scorn of vengeance,” with a very feeble sense. Accordingly, we read: “If we have harmed the one scorning us with the scorn of vengeance.” We are scorned by an adversary who hates us; if we hate and scorn him in turn, we have now scorned the one who scorned us, repaid evil with evil, and failed to observe the Lord’s precept. In this passage Septimius said “to harm the one scorning,” just as he says “to harm the one being born” in *On the Exhortation to Chastity*. RIG.], we do not engage in scornful vengeance [Note: [Col. 1265B] “Being scornful, in scorn,” Rhenanus.]?

What honor, moreover, shall we offer as a sacrifice to the Lord God if we arrogate to ourselves the decision concerning our defense? We—mere wineskins [Note: [Col. 1265B] “Corrupt,” Rhenanus.], earthen vessels—are gravely offended when our little servants take vengeance upon fellow servants on their own authority; and those who offer us their patience, mindful of their lowliness and servitude and cherishing their master’s right to honor, we not only approve, but also grant them more ample satisfaction than they would have presumed to take for themselves. Is this uncertain for us in the Lord, who is so just in assessing and so powerful in accomplishing? Why, then, do we believe him to be judge, if we do not believe him also to be avenger?

He promises us this in return, saying (Deut. 32): “Vengeance is mine [Note: [Col. 1265C] “Vengeance is mine.” Consider the passage of Gregory of Nyssa in his letter to Flavian, where, speaking of an injury done to him, he first states that the insolence of the enemy must not be pardoned, but rather that his pride must be beaten down and his empty arrogance restrained. After saying this, so that the reader might suppose Gregory about to aspire to avenge himself, he splendidly confounds his readers by adding: *ὅπως δ’ ἂν γένοιτο θεῷ μελήσει*, “But how that is to be done will be God’s concern.” That is, the injury done to me has God as its avenger; I entrust it to him who hears my complaints. LAC.], and I will avenge”; that is: “Give patience to me, and I will reward patience.”

For when he says (Matt. 7) [Col. 1265B], “Do not judge, lest you be judged,” does he not demand patience? For who will refrain from judging another except one who will patiently forgo defending himself [Note: [Col. 1265C] “Being defended,” Rhenanus; Junius prefers “to be defended.”]? Who judges for the purpose of pardoning [Note: [Col. 1265C] “Would judge,” Franeker.]? And even if he does pardon, he has nevertheless provided for the judge’s impatience [Note: [Col. 1265C] “Patience,” Latinus.] and has taken away the honor of the sole judge, that is, God [Note: [Col. 1265D] “He has nevertheless provided for the judge’s impatience.” That is, he has employed the impatience of the person judging, or prosecuting an injury, in a judicial action. He has provided against his impatience over the injury by undertaking legal action concerning it, even if he did not pursue it to completion. He has furnished security for impatience, as though the vengeance deposited with God were at risk; and by that security he has taken away the honor of the sole judge, that is, God. Tertullian said *cavere impatientiam* (“to furnish security for impatience”) in the same construction in which Ulpian and Scaevola say *cavere chirographum* (“to secure by a written bond”), Book V, *Digest*, *Commodatum*, and Book LXXXIX, *On Payments and Releases*; that is, “to secure by means of a written bond.” Thus *cavere* [Col. 1266C] *impatientiam* means “to secure by means of impatience,” to provide vengeance for oneself through impatience at an injury. RIG.].

How many disasters of this sort impatience is accustomed to incur [Note: [Col. 1265C] “Accuse,” Rhenanus.] [Note: [Col. 1265C] “Had been accustomed,” Rhenanus.]! How often has self-defense been regretted! How often has its insistence become [Note: [Col. 1266C] “Its insistence became worse than its causes.” It pressed its claim more sharply and harshly than was fair. There was no cause underlying such savage and atrocious or obstinate insistence. It exacted more than any law conceded to pain. RIG.] worse than its causes [Note: [Col. 1266B] “Was found,” Rhenanus.]! For nothing undertaken in impatience knows how to be carried through without violence; and nothing done violently fails either to give offense, to collapse, or to rush headlong to ruin.

Now, if your defense is too slight, you will go mad; if too abundant, you will be burdened. What have I to do [Col. 1266A] with vengeance, whose measure I cannot govern because of my impatience with pain? But if I devote myself to patience [Note: [Col. 1266C] “If I devote myself to patience.” *Incubare* means “to sleep upon”; the metaphor is taken from precious things that, lest we lose them, we place beneath ourselves for safekeeping even while we sleep. Cyprian, *On Almsgiving*: “Why do you brood alone over your riches?” Tertullian similarly uses it in *On the Prescription* [Col. 1266D] and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. RHEN.], I shall not suffer pain; if I do not suffer pain, I shall not desire vengeance.

## CHAPTER XI

After setting forth, as best we could, these principal materials of impatience, why should we wander among the rest? The things at home, the things abroad [Note: [Col. 1266D] Broad and diffuse is the operation of evil. Thus in *On Idolatry*, chapter 2, he said that the devil’s ingenuity does not remain within narrow bounds and that Christians are armed against the devil’s breadth. RIG.]? Broad and diffuse is the operation of evil [Note: [Col. 1266B] Others punctuate: “The operation. Of evil.”]: manifold are the incitements of the spirit that hurls its darts, now very small, now very great. But you may despise the small because of their insignificance and yield to the greatest because of their overwhelming force [Note: [Col. 1266C] “Abundance,” Paris.]. Where the injury is smaller, there is no necessity for impatience [Note: [Col. 1266C] “Patience,” Latinus.]; but where the injury is greater, there patience [Note: [Col. 1266C] “Of patience,” Franeker and Paris.] is the more necessary remedy for injury [Note: [Col. 1266D] “There the more necessary.” An unusual comparative. Thus he used *necessarius* in the neuter in *On the Flesh of Christ*: “As though,” he says, “they brought something necessary.” RHEN.].

Let us therefore strive to endure what is inflicted by the evil one, so that the rivalry of our composure may frustrate [Col. 1266B] the enemy’s zeal. But if we ourselves bring certain things upon ourselves, whether through imprudence or even deliberately, let us equally submit with patience to what we impute to ourselves. And if we believe that some things are struck upon us by the Lord, to whom should we show patience more than to the Lord? Indeed [Note: [Col. 1266C] “Who moreover,” Junius.], he teaches [Note: [Col. 1266C] “It is fitting,” Latinus.] us in addition to give thanks and rejoice in the honor of divine chastisement. “Those whom I love,” he says, “I chastise.”

O blessed servant, whose correction the Lord pursues! With whom he deigns [Note: [Col. 1266D] “With whom he deigns to be angry.” Splendidly said; for God’s acts of anger toward us proceed from his sheer condescension and mercy, so that we may be corrected. The wife of Julian the Apostate, a pious and holy woman, when she saw her impious husband punished by God, said to him, as recorded in Theodoret, Book III, chapter 12: *οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν ἔγνως τίς ὁ παρὰ σοῦ πολεμούμενος, εἰ τῇ συνήθει μακροθυμίᾳ χρησάμενος ταύτας σοι θεηλάτους πληγὰς οὐκ ἐπήγαγεν*—“Indeed, you would never have known who it was whom you attacked, had he, employing his customary forbearance, not inflicted upon you these divinely sent blows.” LAC.] to be angry, whom he does not deceive by withholding admonition!

From every side, then, we are bound to the duty of exercising patience. From whatever quarter the occasion for that duty comes upon us—whether through our own errors, the evil one’s snares, [Col. 1267A] or the Lord’s admonitions [Note: [Col. 1267C] “Whether through our own errors, the evil one’s snares, or the Lord’s admonitions the occasion comes upon us.” We intervene against our errors or the evil one’s snares when we oppose them—not by consenting, but rather by avoiding them. Thus formerly a tribune interposed his veto against decrees of the senate. But we intervene in the Lord’s admonitions when we obey them. RHEN.]—great is its reward: blessedness, of course.

For whom did the Lord call blessed, if not the patient, when he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5)? Certainly no one is poor in spirit unless he is humble; and who is humble unless he is patient? For no one can subject himself without first possessing patience for the very act of submission.

“Blessed,” he says, “are those who weep and mourn.” Who endures such things without patience? Accordingly, consolation [Note: [Col. 1267C] “To such people consolation and laughter are promised.” *Advocatio*, Greek *παράκλησις*, means “consolation.” Thus “words of consolation”; “to console the languishing,” that is, to comfort [Col. 1267D] the sick; “consoler of the poor.” RIG.] and laughter are promised to such people.

“Blessed are the gentle.” By this designation the impatient certainly cannot be reckoned at all. Likewise, when he marks peacemakers with the same title of blessedness and calls them sons of God, can the impatient have any affinity with peace? Only a fool would think so [Note: [Col. 1267C] “This,” Franeker and Paris; Junius prefers “this.”].

And when he says, “Rejoice and exult whenever they curse and persecute you [Col. 1267B], for your reward is very great in heaven,” he certainly does not promise that reward to the impatience of exultation, because no one has exulted [Note: [Col. 1267C] “Will exult,” Franeker and Paris.] amid adversities unless he first despised them, and no one will despise them unless he has practiced patience.

## CHAPTER XII

As for the discipline of peace, which is most pleasing to God, what man wholly born to impatience will forgive [Note: [Col. 1267C] “Forgives,” Rhenanus.] his brother even once—not to say seven times, but even [Note: [Col. 1267C] “Or,” Latinus and Junius.] seventy-seven times (Matt. 18)? Who, while arranging a settlement with his adversary (Luke 6; Matt. 5), will resolve the matter by agreement [Note: [Col. 1267D] “Will resolve the matter by agreement”—that is, by a settlement, an amicable compact. RIG.], unless he first cuts away his heart’s pain, hardness, bitterness—the poisons, of course, of impatience?

How will you forgive, and be forgiven, if through the absence of patience you cling to an injury? [Col. 1267C] No one whose mind is enraged against his brother will complete his offering [Col. 1268A] at the altar unless, by first being reconciled to his brother, he has returned to patience. If the sun sets upon our anger, we are in danger. We are not permitted to remain without patience for even a single day.

But since patience governs every form of saving discipline (Eph. 4), what wonder is it that it also ministers to repentance, which is accustomed to assist the fallen? When a marriage has been severed for that cause which permits either the man or the woman to be sustained in continued widowhood, patience waits [Note: [Col. 1267D] “It desires this, entreats this.” Patience not only waits and desires, but even wrests forth repentance—that is, it compels those whom it thus calmly tolerates to repent, so that they may eventually enter upon salvation. And because he adds, “which is accustomed to assist the fallen,” he appears to be speaking of Christians, whether men or women, who join themselves in marriage to heathens. Here it sometimes happened that a Christian wife at last persuaded her heathen husband to continence, which he embraced and maintained; the woman, meanwhile, performed repentance and expiated her former deed before the Church according to the rite of that time. And this is what follows: “How much good it confers upon both! It does not make the one an adulterer; it corrects the other.” RHEN.], desires, and entreats [Note: [Col. 1268C] “Exhorts this,” Paris.] for the repentance of those who will one day enter upon salvation. How much [Note: [Col. 1268C] “Salvation? How much,” etc., Junius.] good it confers upon both! It does not make the one an adulterer [Note: [Col. 1268C] “An adulterer it does not,” Franeker, Paris, and Junius.] [Note: [Col. 1268C] “It does not make the one an adulterer.” Thus Rhenanus in his final edition; thus Pamelius; thus others. But the oldest copies read, “It does not send the one to another,” which we are readily led to believe is Tertullian’s own style. When a marriage, he says, has been severed on account of adultery, patience intervenes and confers very much good upon both: it does not “send the one”—that is, the spouse who has repudiated the adulterous spouse—“to another” marriage. That is certainly the sense: “It does not send,” “does not dispatch,” “does not permit to go.” So in *On the Pallium*: “Which makes its way from Libya to that man,” that is, “comes.” RIG.]; it corrects the other.

Thus, in those examples from the Lord’s holy parables, patience is also present. The shepherd’s patience [Note: [Col. 1268D] “The shepherd’s patience”—that is, Christ’s, who is the most patient shepherd. Ignatius the Martyr, *Letter to the Philadelphians*: *ποιμένος πραοτάτου*, “of the gentlest shepherd.” Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 1, among Christ’s praises, also has this. Likewise, in Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 6, Christ is called the merciful shepherd, and he ascribes to him pastoral discipline and gentleness. LAC.] seeks and finds the wandering sheep. For impatience would readily have despised a single one [Col. 1268B]. But patience undertakes the labor of the search, and the patient bearer additionally carries the abandoned sinner upon his shoulders.

The father’s patience also receives that prodigal son, clothes him, feeds him, and defends him against the impatience of his angry brother. Therefore, the one who had perished is saved because he entered upon repentance. Repentance does not perish [Note: [Col. 1268C] “Did not perish,” Junius.], because it has found patience.

For love is the supreme mystery of faith, the treasure of the Christian name [Note: [Col. 1268D] “Love is the supreme mystery of faith”—because it alone comprehensively (*συλλήβδην*) displays in itself all the Christian virtues. RIG.]. The Apostle commends it with all the power of the Holy Spirit; but by whose discipline is it instructed, if not patience’s?

“Love,” he says, “is great-souled” [Note: [Col. 1268D] “Love,” he says, “is great-souled.” Tertullian renders the Pauline word *μακροθυμεῖ* (“is patient”) as *magnanimis est*, “is great-souled,” a phrase unusual in Latin; but he is accustomed to speak in his own fashion. Cyprian, an imitator of Tertullian but of purer style, says, “Charity is great-souled.” He likewise rendered *μακροθυμίαν* as “greatness of soul” in *On Almsgiving*. Others prefer “long-suffering” and “long-sufferingness.” RHEN.]. Thus it assumes patience.

“It is beneficent”; patience does no evil.

“It does not envy”; that certainly is patience’s own property.

“Nor does it savor insolence” [Col. 1268C]; it has drawn modesty from patience.

“It is not puffed up; it does not trample others” [Col. 1269A] [Note: [Col. 1269C] “Does not act insolently,” Franeker and Paris.] [Note: [Col. 1269C] “It is not puffed up; it does not trample others.” La Cerda explains this of the pride of those who arrogate too much to themselves and trample upon others. Others read “has not acted insolently.” Erasmus translates it not badly as “is not brazen,” that is, as he interprets it from certain Greek scholia, “does not exalt or display itself.” LE PR.]; for that does not belong to patience.

“It does not seek its own,” since it offers its own [Note: [Col. 1269C] “But offers,” Latinus.], provided that it benefits another.

“It is not provoked”; otherwise [Note: [Col. 1269C] “Otherwise indeed,” Latinus.], what would it have left for impatience?

Therefore, he says, “Love sustains all things, tolerates all things”—certainly because it is patient. Rightly, then, it will never fail; for the other things will be made void, will be brought to an end. Tongues, forms of knowledge, and prophecies are exhausted [Note: [Col. 1269C] “Will be exhausted,” Junius.]; faith, hope, and love remain: faith, which Christ’s patience introduced; hope, for which human patience waits; love, which, with God as teacher, patience accompanies.

## CHAPTER XIII

Thus far, finally [Note: [Col. 1269C] “Only,” Junius.], we have treated patience as simple and uniform, and as established only in the soul. Yet that same patience also labors in many ways in the body to win the Lord’s favor [Col. 1269B], since it was manifested by the Lord himself in the strength of the body as well; for the governing soul readily shares the things brought in by the spirit [Note: [Col. 1269C] “Unconquered,” Wouwer’s MS.] with its dwelling.

What, then, is the activity of patience in the body? First of all, the affliction of the flesh, an appeasing victim offered to the Lord through the sacrifice of humiliation: when it offers the Lord squalor together with straitened nourishment [Note: [Col. 1269C] “When the straitness,” Wouwer’s MS.], content with simple food and a drink of pure water; when it joins fasts to these; when it becomes habituated to ashes and sackcloth [Note: [Col. 1269D] “It becomes habituated to ashes and sackcloth.” That is, through custom it renders repentance familiar to itself and, as it were, natural. The metaphor is taken from trees that, when grafted and budded into other trees, become accustomed to food and nourishment drawn up and attracted through the trunk. LE PR.].

This patience of the body commends prayers and strengthens supplications; it opens the ears of Christ God [Note: [Col. 1269C] “Of Christ and God,” Junius.] [Note: [Col. 1269D] “It opens the ears of Christ God.” It renders God kindly and accessible to us, so that he does not close his ears to our petitions and prayers. LE PR.], disperses severity, and draws forth mercy (Dan. 4). Thus that Babylonian king, after offending the Lord and being exiled from human form amid seven years of squalor and filth, by sacrificing the patience of his body both recovered his kingdom [Col. 1269C] and—what is more desirable for a human being—made satisfaction to God.

Now, if we set forth the higher and happier degrees of bodily patience, that same patience also provides for holiness the continence [Note: [Col. 1270C] “Continence,” Petavius and Ciacconius.] of the flesh (Matt. 19). It preserves the widow, appoints the virgin, and raises the voluntary eunuch [Col. 1270A] to the kingdoms of heaven. What proceeds from the virtue of the soul is perfected in the flesh.

Finally, the patience of the flesh does battle in persecutions. If flight presses upon us, the flesh struggles against the hardships of flight. If prison too bears down [Note: [Col. 1270C] “Comes beforehand,” Franeker.], the flesh is in chains, the flesh in the wooden stocks [Note: [Col. 1269D] “The flesh in the wood”—in wooden fetters. Thus in Acts 16: *τοὺς πόδας αὐτῶν ἠσφαλίσατο εἰς τὸ ξύλον*, “he secured their feet in the wood.” The Vulgate rendered it in Latin: “He fastened their feet in the stocks.” RIG.], the flesh upon the ground [Note: [Col. 1269D] “The flesh upon the ground”—in solitude, in the sorrow of desolation; [Col. 1270C] or on the bare earth, upon naked flint. The same.], both in that poverty of light and [Note: [Col. 1270C] “Patience,” Rhenanus.] in that deprivation of the world [Note: [Col. 1270C] “In that deprivation of the world”—in destitution of all things. *Ἐν ἐρημίᾳ* (“in abandonment”), which Arrian, in his book on Epictetus, most elegantly calls *κατάστασίς τις ἀβοηθήτου*, that is, “the condition of a person bereft of aid.” RIG.].

But when it is led forth to the trial of blessedness, to the opportunity of a second immersion [Note: [Col. 1270D] “To the opportunity of a second immersion”—of a second baptism, that is, martyrdom. RIG.], to the very ascent to the divine throne, nothing avails more there than patience of the body. If the spirit is willing but the flesh weak without patience (Matt. 26), where is the salvation of the spirit and of the flesh itself?

Yet when the Lord says this of the flesh, declaring it weak, he shows what is needed to strengthen it—namely, patience against every apparatus intended to overthrow or punish [Note: [Col. 1270D] “To punish the faith”—that is, to exercise and test it by punishments and torments. RIG.] the faith [Note: [Col. 1270C] “Prepared,” Paris.]—so that it may most steadfastly endure blows [Col. 1270B], fire, the cross, beasts, and the sword: the things that the Prophets and Apostles conquered by enduring them.

## CHAPTER XIV
By the powers of this patience Isaiah is sawn apart, yet he does not cease speaking of the Lord. Stephen is stoned, yet asks forgiveness for his enemies (Acts 7). O most blessed, too, was that man who fully discharged every form of patience against every power of the devil: neither the driving away of his flocks, nor the loss of all that wealth in livestock, nor his children taken from him by the single onslaught of a collapsing house, nor, finally, the torment of his own body by ulceration [Note: [Col. 1270C] *Wounding*, Rhenanus] drove him away from the patience and faith owed [Note: [Col. 1270C] *Devoted*, Rhenanus] to the Lord—the man whom the devil struck down with all his might, but in vain (Job 1)! For all those sufferings did not divert him from regard for God; instead, he stood as an example and testimony for us that patience must be exercised [Col. 1270C] in spirit as well as flesh, in mind as well as body [Note: [Col. 1270C] *Perpetuated*, Junius], so that we may succumb neither to the loss of worldly possessions, nor to the loss of our dearest ones, nor even to bodily struggles [Note: [Col. 1270D] “As though in that man God constructed a bier for the devil.” So the ancient books. A *feretrum* is a νεκροφορεῖον (*nekrophoreion*), “a bier on which a dead man is carried out.” Job is therefore said to have been a bier for the Devil because all Satan’s assaults were so utterly crushed and slain upon the body of the most patient Job. RIGALTIUS].

What a bier [Note: [Col. 1270D] “In that man a bier,” etc. Among the instruments of a triumph is the *feretrum*, the frame on which the triumphal display is carried. Understand this as that upon which the devil was displayed in triumph, while God erected the trophy. For by divine grace Job conquered the devil, never yielding to impatience—as though he were saying: [Col. 1271C] “What a trophy over the devil God erected!” Formerly the arms of conquered peoples were carried about in the triumphal procession and afterward suspended; he therefore speaks aptly: “What a standard!” RHENANUS] God [Note: [Col. 1270C] The editions of Franeker and Paris add *over*] constructed for the devil in that man (Job 2)! [Col. 1271A] What a standard he raised over the enemy of his glory, when that man, at every heap [Note: [Col. 1271C] *Bitter message*, Franeker, Paris] of messages [Note: [Col. 1271C] “At every heap of messages.” So also the ancient books, and correctly; for those many grievous things were reported to Job all at once: “While he was still speaking,” says Scripture; then again, “While he was still speaking,” etc. RIGALTIUS], brought nothing from his mouth except thanks to God; when he cursed his wife, already exhausted by his misfortunes and urging him toward wicked remedies. What then? God was smiling [Note: [Col. 1271C] “Whom was God mocking?” Junius]. What then? The evil one was being torn apart, while Job scraped away with great composure the unclean discharge overflowing from his ulcer; while, as though in play, he called the little creatures bursting forth [Note: [Col. 1271C] “The little creatures bursting forth.” I do not see why Pamelius could object to this on the ground that scarcely any mention of little creatures occurs anywhere in the whole book. For that was the miracle of his patience: [Col. 1271D] when his whole body had dissolved into putrefaction and swarmed everywhere with worms. It is hardly surprising if Tertullian speaks in this way. LE PRIEUR] back from there into the same cavities [Note: [Col. 1271D] “Into the same cavities and feeding grounds of his misshapen flesh.” We have emended the text thus, following traces in the ancient copies, in which *reformasse* is read. He called Job’s flesh *reformosa*, “misshapen,” because it was deformed by ulcers and swarming with worm-infested pus. RIGALTIUS] and feeding grounds of his misshapen [Note: [Col. 1271C] *Perforated*, Franeker, Paris; others: *reformed*, *dug up again*, or *pierced again*; *ant-infested*, Junius] flesh [Note: [Col. 1271D] “Misshapen flesh.” Thus Rigaltius. Formerly the text read “dug up again” and “pierced again”; but Rhenanus corrected it to “perforated”—perhaps better, since his body was pierced everywhere and was, as it were, a sieve, to use a Plautine expression. LE PRIEUR].

And so that champion of God’s victory, having blunted every missile of temptation with the breastplate and shield of patience, soon recovered [Note: [Col. 1271C] *Recovered*, as modifying *integrity*, Rhenanus] from God the wholeness of his body and possessed in double measure [Note: [Col. 1272C] *Redoubled*, Franeker, Paris; *a hundredfold*, Rhenanus] what he had lost. And had he wished his children also to be restored [Note: [Col. 1271D] “And had he wished his children to be restored, he would again have been called a father.” “Rather,” they say, “he was called a father again”; for Scripture expressly relates: “He had seven sons and three daughters.” He did indeed—but they were born after Job’s restoration. He did not receive back the same children taken from him by the single onslaught of a collapsing house, nor was he again called father by them. He therefore willingly endured bereavement of these children, lest he should live without some occasion for patience.

“But if they were not restored, how will the truth of the same Scripture stand, when it declares that God increased twofold everything Job had possessed?” We readily assent to the opinion of those who attribute the examination of Scripture with so scrupulous a balance to the vice of captious curiosity. Yet it may most conveniently be said that the first seven children were not numbered among the other things restored because they had not perished like those other things, but were understood to live eternally with God, in glory, for Job himself. RIGALTIUS], he would again have been called their father. But he preferred that they be returned to him on that Day. Confident thus in the Lord, he deferred so great a joy; he endured so [Note: [Col. 1272C] *Then*, Junius; *already*, Wouwerius manuscript] willing a bereavement, lest he should live without some occasion for patience.

## CHAPTER XV

Thus God is a fully adequate trustee of patience. If you deposit an injury with him, he is the avenger; if a loss, he is the restorer; if pain, he is the physician; if death, he is the one who raises the dead. How great is the privilege of patience, that it should have God as its debtor! And deservedly so. For it protects everything pleasing to him; it intervenes in support of all his commandments. It fortifies [Col. 1272A] faith, governs peace, assists love, teaches humility, awaits repentance, assigns confession (*exomologesis*), rules the flesh, preserves the spirit, bridles the tongue, restrains the hand, tramples down temptations, drives away stumbling blocks, consummates martyrdoms, consoles the poor, moderates the rich, does not overburden the weak [Note: [Col. 1272D] “Does not overburden the weak”: it does not oppress the feeble or weigh him down with a burden. RIGALTIUS], does not exhaust the strong [Note: [Col. 1272D] “Does not exhaust the strong”: it does not drain the robust man’s strength. RIGALTIUS], delights the believer, invites the gentile, commends the servant to his master and the master to God, adorns the woman, and approves the man. It is loved in a child, praised in a young man, and revered in an old man; in every sex and at every age it is beautiful.

Come now, let us also apprehend [Note: [Col. 1272C] *May you apprehend*, Junius] its image and bearing. Its face is tranquil and calm, its brow pure and contracted by no wrinkle of grief or anger; its eyebrows are likewise relaxed into a cheerful expression, its eyes cast down through humility, not unhappiness. Its mouth is sealed with the dignity of silence. Its complexion is such as belongs to those who are untroubled and innocent. Its head frequently moves in menace against the devil, while it smiles. Moreover, its garment is white around the breast and pressed against the body, since it neither billows nor becomes stained [Note: [Col. 1272C] *Nor is disturbed*, Rhenanus].

For it sits upon the throne of that most gentle and most mild Spirit, who is not massed into a whirlwind, nor darkened by cloud, but is open and unalloyed in tender serenity—the Spirit whom Elijah saw at the third manifestation [Note: [Col. 1272D] “Whom Elijah saw at the third manifestation.” He is his own best interpreter in book 4 *Against Marcion*, chapter 23, where he says of God’s clemency: “Such a one, surely, was even less likely to burn human beings; for at that time also he said to Elijah, ‘The Lord is not in the fire, but in the gentle spirit.’” In both places he refers to the story of Elijah in 3 Kings 10, and says that patience sits upon the throne of the most gentle and mild Spirit, whom Elijah saw at the third manifestation. For three manifestations present themselves there to Elijah: in the first and second, an angel of the Lord brings commands to Elijah; in the third, the Lord himself addresses his prophet, not in the wind that shatters rocks, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but after the calm and gentle breeze. Septimius therefore says that patience sits in that gentle Spirit of tender serenity, open and unalloyed. RIGALTIUS]. For where God is, there too is his foster-child, namely patience (Matt. 17). Accordingly, when the Spirit of God [Col. 1273A] descends [Note: [Col. 1273B] “Accordingly, when the Spirit of God descends,” etc. The sense is: when the Spirit of God descends into any Christian, patience also descends with him as his inseparable companion. He must therefore be received with his companion. If we do not receive her with the Spirit, do we suppose that the Spirit will always wish to remain within us? Indeed, I do not know whether he will remain even for a short while. For without his companion and attendant he will everywhere and always labor in distress and perplexity; whatever the devil inflicts, he will be unable to endure alone, lacking his auxiliary—namely patience, the mightiest instrument of endurance. RIGALTIUS], inseparable patience accompanies him [Note: [Col. 1273A] *Her. If we receive her with the Spirit*, Wouwerius manuscript. Junius prefers: “Patience accompanies him. If we receive her with the Spirit,” etc.]. If we do not [Note: [Col. 1273A] *We*, Franeker, Paris] receive her together with the Spirit, will he always remain within us? Indeed, I do not know whether he will persevere much longer [Note: [Col. 1273A] “Indeed, I do not know whether anyone will persevere long without his companion,” Junius; “always: indeed, I do not know whether he will persevere long without his companion and attendant. In every place and at every time he must be distressed,” Rhenanus]. Without his companion and attendant, he must be distressed in every place and at every time. Whatever his enemy inflicts, he will be unable to endure alone, lacking the instrument of endurance.

## CHAPTER XVI

Such is the rationale of patience; such is its discipline; such are the works of patience that is heavenly and true—that is, Christian [Note: [Col. 1273A] “Such are the works of heavenly and true, that is, Christian patience,” Rigaltius]—not like that earthly patience of the gentiles, which is false and shameful. For the devil, so that in this matter also he might rival the Lord, as though they were altogether on equal terms—except that the very difference between evil and good is matched by an equal greatness [Note: [Col. 1274A] *In greatness*, Junius]—has also taught his own followers their peculiar patience. I mean the patience that subjects husbands who sell themselves for a dowry, or [Col. 1274A] trade in procuring [Note: [Col. 1273B] “Trade in procuring.” This too is an expression of the jurists; for, according to Ulpian, concerning those branded with infamy (*c. l. athletas*), a man practices procuring if he has kept slaves for prostitution, and likewise if he conducts this trade through free persons—add, in accordance with the author’s meaning, through his wife. PAMELIUS], to the authority of their wives; that, in hunting after the estates of the childless [Note: [Col. 1273C] “Hunting after the estates of the childless.” The assiduity of legacy-hunters is very well known: they flattered the childless and unmarried with gifts and every kind of service, so that they might be named heirs. Cicero treats of them in the *Paradoxes*. Blessed Jerome treats of the same persons in Letter 2, addressed to Nepotian: “I hear, moreover, of the shameful servitude of certain men toward childless old men and women. They bring them the chamber pot, besiege their bed, and receive with their own hands the purulence of the stomach and the phlegm of the lungs,” etc. See the whole letter in volume I. LE PRIEUR.—“Which, in hunting after the estates of the childless”: he marks the will-hunters whom Juvenal attacks in his twelfth Satire. RHENANUS], endures every labor of compulsory attendance under a pretense of affection; and that which binds the laborers of the belly [Note: [Col. 1274B] “Laborers of the belly.” He calls “laborers of the belly” both parasites and followers of other men’s tables, who care for nothing more than satisfying their belly, and those who surrender themselves to the patronage of the rich, to be subsequently abused by them. RHENANUS.—“Laborers of the belly”: parasites, whom Lucilius also calls “Bellies”:

> Live, gluttons, eaters, live, you bellies.

Tertullian himself says in the *Apology*: “Among you, parasites make a glory of enslaving their freedom, under contract to fatten their bellies amid insults.” Hence he presently calls those who invite parasites “insulting patrons.” And among the comic poets the parasites themselves are called “sons of the lash” and “hard heads”; while their hosts’ tables are ungenerous, as in Juvenal’s *Satires*. RIGALTIUS] to insulting patronage [Note: [Col. 1274A] “To insulting patrons,” Wouwerius manuscript; “to insulting patrons,” Rigaltius] by subjecting their freedom for the sake of gluttony [Note: [Col. 1274A] *Gluttony*, Wouwerius manuscript; both words are absent from Rigaltius].

The nations know such exercises of patience, and they appropriate the name of so great a good for shameful practices: they live patiently enduring rivals, rich men, and hosts [Note: [Col. 1274C] “Patiently enduring rivals, rich men, and hosts.” By “those enduring rivals” he means husbands who sell themselves for a dowry; by “those enduring rich men,” legacy-hunters who plot after the estates of childless rich persons; and by “those enduring hosts,” parasites, who fed at their hosts’ tables amid the grossest insults. RIGALTIUS], yet impatient of God alone. But let that patience look to itself [Note: [Col. 1274C] “But let it look to its own affairs”: let the patience of the nations—which endures rivals, rich men, and most insulting hosts—look to itself. RIGALTIUS] and to the patience of its ruler [Note: [Col. 1274C] “Its ruler”: Satan. RIGALTIUS] [Note: [Col. 1274A] “Let its rulers see to their own patience,” Franeker], which the fire below [Note: [Col. 1274C] “The fire below”: the hidden treasury of fire beneath the earth. RIGALTIUS] awaits.

But as for us, let us love the patience of God, the patience of Christ. Let us repay to him the patience that he himself paid out [Note: [Col. 1274A] *Defended*, Rhenanus] for us. Let us offer patience of spirit and patience of flesh, since we believe in the resurrection [Note: [Col. 1274A] *Who believe the resurrection*, Junius] of flesh and spirit.

# TWO BOOKS TO HIS WIFE

[Col. 1273]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, TO HIS WIFE [Note: [Col. 1273D] The Franeker edition adds: *On Single Marriage*] (C)

## BOOK ONE
