[Col. 1273D] **SUMMARY.—**Whether warned by advancing age or illness, or because he was now about to bid farewell to worldly affairs so that he might profess Christian discipline more rigorously and be raised to the heights of the sublime priesthood, Tertullian drew up for his wife what were, as it were, the tablets of a will—namely these two books. In the first he urges his wife, should he himself depart to the Lord before her, to abstain [Col. 1274D] from a second marriage; in the second he instructs her, should she wish to marry, to unite herself only with a Christian man. Such is the outline of the whole work.

## CHAPTER I

I have judged it fitting [Note: [Col. 1273D] “I have judged it fitting” was absent from Rhenanus’s first edition], my fellow servant most beloved by me [Note: [Col. 1274D] Thus Franeker, Paris, and Rigaltius; Semler deletes *by me*] in the Lord, to provide even now for what course you must follow after my departure from this world, should I be called before you, and to entrust to your faith the charge that you observe what has been provided. For we take sufficient care over worldly affairs and wish provision to be made for us both [Note: [Col. 1275A] Thus, on the authority of the Codex Agobardinus, Rigaltius emended this passage: “we wish provision to be made—such matters—such matters—we arrange.” Wouwerius: “If concerning such matters we arrange.” Semler, following the first edition: “we wish—such matters—we arrange.” The others: “and such matters we arrange,” or “if such matters we arrange”]. If in such matters we draw up testamentary tablets [Note: [Col. 1275B] “In such matters we draw up testamentary tablets.” Tertullian, presbyter of the church of Carthage, admonished by his now advancing age, composed two books for his still-living wife, as though they were the tablets of a will. In the first he entrusts to the faith of his most beloved wife the charge that, should he himself first depart to the Lord, she abstain from a second marriage; in the second he directs that, if she decides she cannot abstain, she should marry only a Christian. Thus in the first book he prefaces his counsel by saying that such care is most worthy of a Christian. For almost everyone anxiously and solicitously makes provision for his own human and mortal affairs and draws up tablets concerning them, which he desires to be most carefully observed. But if people take such precautions over things momentary and perishable, why should they not wish all the more to make provision for their heirs concerning divine and immortal goods? “For,” he says, “we take sufficient care over worldly affairs and wish provision to be made for us both. If we arrange such matters, why should we not all the more provide for our heirs concerning divine and heavenly things?” So the common editions. Others preferred, “If we arrange concerning such matters.” Agobard’s manuscript preserved traces of the genuine reading: “We wish provision to be made for us both—such matters—such matters—we arrange,” etc. It was an easy error to write *talibus* (“such matters”) for *tabulis* (“tablets”), through the reverberation of the preceding word. We have therefore edited the passage thus: “We wish provision to be made for us both; in such matters we draw up tablets. Why should we not all the more provide for our heirs concerning divine and heavenly things?” RIGALTIUS], why should we not all the more provide for our heirs concerning divine and heavenly things, and in a sense bequeath in advance a legacy—the admonition and exposition of those things that are allotted from immortal goods and from [Note: [Col. 1275B] *From* is absent from other editions] the inheritance of heaven? May God grant that you be able to receive this trust of my admonition [Note: [Col. 1275C] “That you be able to receive the whole.” This trust of my admonition [Col. 1275D] and faith. He alludes to the legal capacity of husband and wife to receive an entire inheritance, which was permitted only in certain cases under the Julian and Papian laws. Title XVI among the fragments of Ulpian concerns this matter. He also alluded to the same laws in the book *On Monogamy*: “It is otherwise if they believe that proceedings before Christ too are governed by the Julian laws, and suppose that the unmarried and childless cannot receive an entire inheritance under God’s testament.” RIGALTIUS] and faith in full [Note: [Col. 1275B] Others insert *and*]. To him be honor, glory, splendor, dignity [Note: [Col. 1275B] Others add *and*], and power [Note: [Col. 1275B] *And* is added], now and for ever and ever. Amen.

I therefore instruct you, with all the continence of which you are capable, to renounce marriage after my departure. In that respect you will confer nothing upon me, except that you will benefit [Col. 1276A] yourself. Moreover, Christians who have departed this world are promised no restoration of marriage on the day [Note: [Col. 1275B] *Day*, other editions] of resurrection, since they are transformed into angelic character and holiness. Consequently no anxiety [Note: [Col. 1275D] “Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh.” In the common editions the text reads: “Christians who have departed this world are promised no restoration of marriage on the day of resurrection, since they are transformed into angelic character and holiness. Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh—or the Lord’s declaration—the woman whom they represented as having married seven brothers in succession will offend none of her many husbands on the day of resurrection, nor does anyone await her in order to put her to shame. The Sadducees’ question yielded to the Lord’s declaration.” This reading almost buries and stifles Tertullian’s meaning. For the words “Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh” are left incomplete. Moreover, “or the Lord’s declaration” is plainly intrusive and does not agree with what follows. And the sequel, “the woman whom they represented as having married seven brothers in succession will offend none of her many husbands on the day of resurrection,” bears very little savor of Tertullian’s style.

Agobard’s manuscript shows that these words are corrupt, although it is not itself free of errors. It reads: “Christians who have departed this world are promised no restoration of marriage on [Col. 1276C] the day of resurrection, since they are transformed into angelic quantity and holiness. Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh comes, and now the day of resurrection of husbands will offend that woman whom seven brothers successively—nor does anyone await her in order to put her to shame.” The text of this very ancient copy sufficiently warns us that the true and genuine text was corrupted by spurious additions, and indeed resolves part of the corruption. The remainder, it seems to me, may be distinguished and resolved if we read the latter sentence thus: “Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh will offend even that woman of seven husbands on the day of resurrection, nor does anyone await her in order to put her to shame. The Sadducees’ question yielded to the Lord’s declaration.”

Tertullian says that this instruction to his wife not to marry again by no means proceeds from the bitterness of a husband inflamed with jealousy, aggrieved that after his death his wife might perhaps seek another husband. No insult arising from this could reach the dead man, since Christians who rise again are promised [Col. 1276D] no restoration of marriage. Among immortals the function of the sexes will then be idle and useless; here it was temporarily granted to mortals as consolation for mortality and for the propagation of offspring.

To confirm this opinion, he advances Christ’s own testimony. When the Sadducees asked Christ, in a question maliciously devised as a trap, what would happen in the resurrection of bodies to a certain woman who had been the wife of seven husbands—that is, who, after six husbands had been carried to the grave, married a seventh, so that, widowed six times, she had contracted a seventh marriage—he refuted the malice of the question with the simplest reply: among human beings endowed with angelic holiness there would then be no mention of marriage. Consequently she had no reason to fear her seven husbands, lest any of those many husbands, aggrieved as though by rivals on the day of resurrection, should molest his former wife and cast her repeated marriages in her teeth as a disgrace. Thus, with the aid of the ancient book, Tertullian’s true and genuine meaning [Col. 1277C] is most excellently established. It will be worthwhile to refashion at the same anvil rather more of the following text; when compared with the edition of Pamelius, its marked superiority will be apparent even without my saying so. RIGALTIUS] arising from jealousy of the flesh will, even with reference to that declaration of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1275B] The common text: “Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh. Or the Lord’s [Col. 1276A] declaration.” Semler: “Or with reference to that declaration—the woman whom seven [Col. 1276B] brothers successively represented as having married—to disclose in marriage—no one will offend so many husbands on the day of resurrection.” Codex Agobardinus: “Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh comes; even that woman whom seven brothers successively—the day of the resurrection of husbands will offend,” etc. From this Rigaltius ordered only the following to be retained: “Consequently no anxiety arising from jealousy of the flesh will offend even that woman of seven husbands on the day of resurrection”], offend the woman whom they represented as having married seven brothers in succession: she will offend none of her many husbands on the day of resurrection, nor does anyone await her in order to put her to shame. The Sadducees’ question yielded to the Lord’s declaration.

And do not suppose [Note: [Col. 1276B] *Do not*, Semler] that, out of painful apprehension of an insult, I am already now suggesting to you the counsel of widowhood because the integrity of your flesh ought to be reserved for me. No resumption of dishonorable pleasure will then take place between us. For God promises his people nothing so frivolous and filthy. But you may consider fully [Note: [Col. 1277B] *Examine fully*, other editions] whether what we advise is beneficial to you, or to any [Col. 1277A] other woman who belongs to God [Note: [Col. 1277C] “A woman who belongs to God”: that is, a Christian woman. RIGALTIUS].

## CHAPTER II

We certainly do not deny that the union of man and woman was blessed by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1277B] *God*, other editions], and was devised, as we know [Note: [Col. 1277B] “As a nursery for the human race,” Rigaltius], for the human race, the replenishment of the world, and the ordering of temporal life, and was thereafter permitted—yet only one such union. For Adam was Eve’s one husband, and Eve his one wife: one woman, one rib.

It is true that among our ancestors and the patriarchs themselves it was lawful not merely to marry, but even to enter marriages in several forms; there were concubines as well. But although this passed over figuratively [Note: [Col. 1277B] *A figure*, Junius, Franeker; *figuratively*, Rigaltius] into the synagogue and the Church [Note: [Col. 1277B] “Intervened in the synagogue as the Church,” Rigaltius], nevertheless—to interpret it simply—it was necessary to institute practices that would afterward deserve either to be cut away or to be moderated. For the law was going to supervene; the grounds for fulfilling the law had to run in advance. The same [Note: [Col. 1277C] *For the same*, Franeker, Paris; *likewise*, Rigaltius] Word of God was soon to come to the law’s aid by introducing spiritual circumcision. Thus, through the unrestricted license [Note: [Col. 1277C] “Unrestricted license”: multiple marriages permitted indiscriminately. RIGALTIUS] of that time, material was furnished in advance for the subsequent reforms, whose excesses the Lord afterward cut away by his Gospel and then, at the ends of the age, the Apostle either excised where redundant or arranged where disordered.

## CHAPTER III

Yet I would not for that reason have begun by discussing the freedom of antiquity and the correction [Col. 1278A] of later times, or have laid the foundation for claiming that Christ came to separate marriages and [Note: [Col. 1277C] *And* is absent; *abolish*, Rigaltius] destroy unions, as though I were here and now prescribing an end to marrying. Let those answer for it who, among their other perversities, teach that the flesh made one from [Note: [Col. 1277C] *In*, other editions] two must be separated [Note: [Col. 1277C] “Among their other perversities.” He refers to the Marcionites; for with Marcion, as he writes in book 1 against him, the flesh is not baptized unless it is virginal, widowed, unmarried, or has purchased baptism by divorce. RHENANUS]. They deny him who borrowed the woman from the male and then joined the two bodies—taken from a common share in the same substance—back into one through the compact [Note: [Col. 1277C] *Computation*, Rigaltius] of marriage.

In short, we nowhere read that marriage is altogether forbidden, since it is, of course, a good. Yet we learn from the Apostle what is better than that good: although he permits marriage [Note: [Col. 1277C] “Although he permits marriage.” Marriage is permitted on account of weakness, but abstinence is considered preferable to it; thus St. Ambrose, book 1 *On Virgins*: “She who marries is not censured; she who abstains is praised.” And Blessed Jerome, on the Apostle’s words, “But if you take a wife, you have not sinned,” says: “For it is one thing not to sin, another to do well.” LE PRIEUR], he gives preference to abstinence—the former because of the snares of temptation, the latter because of the constraints of the times. Once the rationale of each pronouncement is examined, it is readily discerned that the power to marry was granted to us by necessity; [Col. 1278B] and what necessity supplies is itself thereby depreciated. For, after all, Scripture says, “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9). What sort of good, I ask you, is one commended by comparison with an evil? Marriage is better only because it is worse to burn. Yet how much better it is neither to marry nor to burn!

Even [Note: [Col. 1277C] Semler and Leopold include *even*; others omit it] in persecutions [Note: [Col. 1277D] “Even in persecutions it is better, by permission, to flee from one town than, when arrested, to deny.” The well-known judgment of Paul writing to the Corinthians is that it is better to marry than to burn. Tertullian argues and contends that it is far better neither to marry nor to burn. To prove this, he employs a comparison with another maxim, which teaches that in persecutions it is better for a Christian to flee than to deny Christ; to this he immediately adds that it is far better neither to flee nor to deny.

This passage circulates in the printed copies in so corrupted a state that the force of the argument, being insufficiently understood, appears to droop. Pamelius printed it thus: “In persecutions it is better, by permission, to flee from town to town than, when compressed and twisted, to deny. But what blessedness is that—to escape the confession of blessed testimony for this reason, lest one deny? I can say: what is permitted is not good. Why must I die? If I weep, it is good; if I fear. What is permitted has a suspect reason for its permission.”

This passage greatly tormented Rhenanus, and he printed it in the following form, probably because the manuscripts pointed that way: “It is better, by permission, to flee from town to town than, when compressed and twisted, to deny—and by that fact it is blessed. Or what do those who deny lose by the confession of blessed testimony? I can say: what is permitted is not good. Why [Col. 1278D] must I die, if when I weep it is good; if I fear. What is permitted has a suspect reason for its permission.” These words are undoubtedly devoid of good sense.

Let us see whether the author’s meaning can be recovered with the aid of our manuscript. It reads: “In persecutions it is better to flee from a town than, when arrested and twisted, to deny; and therefore more blessed are those able to depart through the blessed confession of testimony. I can say that what is permitted is not good. Why must I die, if when I weep it is good? But if I fear what is permitted, it has a suspect reason for its permission.” So reads Agobard’s manuscript throughout. It too requires some assistance, but very little, in my opinion, as follows: “Even in persecutions it is better, by permission, to flee than, when arrested and twisted, to deny; and yet more blessed than that are those able not to fail in the blessed confession of testimony. I can say: what is permitted is not good. What then? I must die. If I weep, what is permitted is good. [Col. 1279C] But if I fear what is permitted, it has a suspect reason for its permission.”

Tertullian says that when Christians are sought by a tyrant in order to make them defect, they are indeed permitted to provide for their safety by flight, and that it is better to avail themselves of the permission and flee than to be arrested and driven by torture into apostasy. He then adds that it is far better to stand firm, await and endure the tyrant, hooks, and crosses, and not violate the sacramental pledge of faith given to Christ.

The stern censor continues and obstructs the flight he had said was permitted. “I can say,” he declares, “that what is permitted is not good. What then? The sword hangs over my neck, the furnace blazes, the instruments of torture crack: I must die. If, cowardly with weeping and wailing, [Col. 1279D] I beg to be spared torture and death, what is permitted—namely flight—is good. But if I fear the very thing that is permitted, because conscience dictates that flight from so blessed a death is unbecoming to a Christian, the very fact that my mind does indeed suggest permitted flight, though not without fear of disgrace, sufficiently proves that the reason for that permission is suspect: namely, a spirit insufficiently courageous and insufficiently tenacious of faith—the fault of weakness, for which evil flight was granted as a remedy. Thus, if it was good for someone to flee so as not to fall into the fault of weakness, it would certainly have been better not to flee, but, once arrested, bravely to endure torture and not deny.” RIGALTIUS] it is better [Note: [Col. 1278B] Thus the Codex Agobardinus supplied the text to Rigaltius, with the words “by permission” omitted; Rigaltius nevertheless restored: “and yet more blessed than that are those who—do not fail in the confession.” Rhenanus: “when compressed and twisted, to deny, and by that fact it is blessed. Or what do those who deny lose by the blessed testimony?” Pamelius: “But what blessedness [Col. 1278C] is that—to escape the confession of blessed testimony for this reason, lest one deny? I can say: what is permitted is not good. Why must I die? If I weep, it is good; if I fear. What is permitted—reason”], by permission, to flee from town to town than, when arrested and tortured, to deny. And therefore more blessed are those who are able to depart through the blessed confession of testimony. I can say: [Col. 1279A] what is permitted is not good. What then? I must die. If I weep, it is good; but if [Note: [Col. 1279B] “But if I fear,” Rigaltius] I fear, what is permitted has a suspect reason for its permission. But what is better, no one has permitted, because it is unquestionable and evident by its own purity.

Certain things are not therefore to be sought merely because they are not forbidden, even though in a manner they are forbidden when others are preferred to them; for preferring higher things [Note: [Col. 1279B] Semler correctly conjectures that *higher things* was written instead of *higher*.—*And*, Franeker and Rigaltius; *of the weak*] is a dissuasion from weaker things [Note: [Col. 1279B] *Lower things*, Franeker, Rigaltius]. A thing is not good merely because it is not evil; nor is it therefore not evil [Note: [Col. 1279B] “It is not therefore good, nor is it therefore not evil,” Venetian edition] because it does no harm. Rather, that is plainly [Note: [Col. 1279C] *Fully*, Semler] the prior good which not only does no harm but, in addition, does benefit. Accordingly [Note: [Col. 1279C] *For*, Semler; “Accordingly, that,” Franeker, Paris; Rigaltius], you ought to prefer what benefits to what merely does no harm. For every contest strives toward first place; second place has consolation, but not victory.

[Col. 1279B] If we listen to the Apostle, then, “forgetting what lies behind, let us stretch forward” [Note: [Col. 1279C] Others add *and*] “to what lies ahead,” and let us pursue the better gifts [Note: [Col. 1279C] *Donatives*, other editions]. Though he does not lay a snare upon us [Note: [Col. 1280B] “Thus, even if,” Rigaltius], he shows what is beneficial when he says (1 Cor. 7:34): “The unmarried woman thinks about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about how she may please her husband.” Nowhere, moreover, does he permit marriage in such a way that he would not rather have us strive after his own example. Blessed is the one who shall prove to be like Paul [Note: [Col. 1279D] “Blessed is the one who shall prove to be like Paul.” These words prove that Blessed Paul lived unmarried; this, moreover, is entirely certain in Tertullian’s writings, for, with the exception of Blessed Peter, all the apostles were continent, as is evident from the book *On Monogamy*. LE PRIEUR].

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 1280A]

But we read that the flesh is weak, and from this we flatter ourselves all the more lavishly; yet we also read that the spirit is strong. For both are stated in a single passage. Flesh is earthly matter, whereas spirit is heavenly. Why, then, being more inclined toward excuse, do we plead the things within us that are weak, but fail to uphold those that are stronger [Note: [Col. 1280B] “Strong,” Fran., Par.]? Why should earthly things not yield to heavenly ones? If the spirit is stronger than the flesh, because it is also nobler, it is through our own fault that we follow the weaker [Note: [Col. 1280B] “The weaker things,” Fran., Paris.].

For when marriage has been dissolved [Note: [Col. 1280B] “From marriage,” Rig.], two kinds of human weakness make marriage seem necessary. The first, and indeed the most powerful, comes from the lust of the flesh; the next from the desire of the world. But both must be rejected by the servants of God, who renounce both sensuality and ambition. The lust of the flesh pleads the claims of youth [Col. 1280B], demands the harvest of beauty, and delights in its own disgrace. It says that a man is necessary for the female sex, whether [Note: [Col. 1280B] Or, Jun.] for the sake of authority and consolation, or so that [Note: [Col. 1280C] “Or so that,” Fran.] she may be safe from malicious rumors.

Against these counsels of the flesh, set the examples of our sisters whose names are known to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1280C] “Whose names are known to the Lord.” The expression frequently occurs in ancient martyrologies: “And other saints, whose names God knows.” LE PR.]. They allow no occasion of beauty or youth, after sending their husbands on before them, to take precedence over holiness [Note: [Col. 1280C] “Under no pressure arising from beauty or youth, they prefer holiness to husbands,” Fran., Parisin.; “no beauty … holiness,” Semler; “with husbands permitted,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1280C] “They allow no occasion of beauty or youth, after sending their husbands on before them, to take precedence over holiness.” After refuting the opinion of those who, under the pretext of human weakness, favored second marriages all too readily, Tertullian gives his wife counsels against that very weakness, as though they were amulets—or rather *victory-charms* (νικητήρια). “When marriage has been dissolved,” he says, “two kinds of human weakness make marriage seem necessary. The first, and indeed the most powerful, comes from the lust of the flesh; the next from the desire of the world. But both must be rejected by the servants of God, who renounce both sensuality and ambition. The lust of the flesh pleads the claims of youth, demands the harvest of beauty, and delights in its own disgrace; it says that a man is necessary for the female sex, whether for the sake of authority and consolation, or so that she may be safe from malicious rumors. Against these counsels of the flesh, set the examples of our sisters whose names are known to the Lord, who, under no pressure arising from beauty or youth, prefer holiness to husbands.”

This was the reading in the editions published up to now. Hence someone might say that this argument of Tertullian against second marriages, drawn from the examples of women “who, under no pressure arising from beauty or youth, prefer holiness to husbands,” is invalid. For what wonder is it if ugly women and those already old persevere in widowhood? They are chaste because no one has asked them; indeed, it would be an extraordinary example if any woman afflicted by this misfortune were to find another husband.

But the Author’s own hand, most attentive to the precision of his style, wrote otherwise. The ancient manuscripts have: “Against these counsels of the flesh, set the examples of our sisters whose names are known to the Lord, who allow no occasion of beauty or youth, after sending their husbands on before them, to take precedence over holiness.” He uses the examples of women whose husbands have already been received into heaven. For by “those sent on before,” he means husbands who went before their wives to God and died before them. Such women, I say, although beautiful and still flourishing in youth after their husbands have been received into heaven, nevertheless do not put forward beauty or youth as an excuse, nor do they allow themselves to be flattered by them; instead, they preserve the integrity of their flesh in honor and remembrance of their one marriage.

Tertullian continues: “For they prefer to marry God; for God they are beautiful, for God they are maidens; with him [Col. 1281D] they live, with him they converse,” etc. RIG.]

For they prefer to marry God. For God they are beautiful; for God they are maidens. With him they live, with him they converse; him they engage with by day and by night. They assign their prayers [Col. 1281A] to the Lord as their dowries, and from him, whenever they desire, they obtain his favor as though it were a husband’s gifts [Note: [Col. 1281B] “Dowry-gifts,” others.]. Thus they have secured for themselves the Lord’s eternal good [Note: [Col. 1281B] “The Lord,” Jun.; “the Lord’s good gift,” Rig. For *humabis* (“you will bury”), perhaps *domabis* (“you will subdue”)?], and already on earth, by not marrying, they are counted as members of the angelic family [Note: [Col. 1281D] “They are counted as members of the angelic family”: as though already translated into the angelic condition, as above and in Book I, *On the Apparel of Women*: “For the same angelic substance is also promised to you at that time.” RIG.].

Exercise yourself in continence, in emulation of such women. By spiritual affection you will bury that carnal desire, erasing the temporal and fleeting desires of beauty or youth by compensating for them with opposing goods [Note: [Col. 1281B] “Compensating,” or “you will compensate,” Rhen.; “compensating,” Paris.; “you compensate things that must be destroyed,” Semler.].

Furthermore [Note: [Col. 1281B] Semler omits this.], this worldly desire has as its motives glory, greed, ambition, and lack of means. Through these it contrives a supposed necessity of marrying, promising, of course, heavenly things: to rule in another’s household, to settle upon [Note: [Col. 1281B] “To brood over,” Rig.] another’s wealth, and to extract adornment at another’s expense—an expense that you do not feel is being incurred for [Col. 1281B] you [Note: [Col. 1281C] “Expense … to consume,” without “for you,” Rig.].

Such things must be far from the faithful, who have no anxiety about sustaining life—unless we distrust God’s promises, care, and providence [Note: [Col. 1281C] “Care and providence” are absent from other copies.]. He clothes the lilies of the field [Note: [Col. 1281C] “He clothes the field with such grace,” Rig.]; he feeds the birds of heaven without any labor on their part; he forbids anxiety about tomorrow, food [Note: [Col. 1281C] Semler deletes “and clothing.”], and clothing; and he pledges that he knows what each of his servants needs—not, indeed, the weight of necklaces, the burden of garments, a great many Gallic [Note: [Col. 1281D] “A great many Gallic.” The exemplar reads *Non calligos multos* instead of *gallicos*. Blemishes of this sort appear not infrequently in manuscripts through transposition of letters. Thus a little later, on this very page, one finds *legibus locuntur* (“they speak by laws”) instead of *legibus coluntur* (“they are honored by laws”); and *de calonica gloria* instead of *de Laconica gloria*. Accordingly, one must read here: “a great many Gallic bearers, nor Germanic ones.” From this arose the reading seen in Rhenanus’ editions, “Gallic faces.” I know that the reading said to be found in certain manuscripts, “Gallic [Col. 1282C] mules,” may seem attractive, because in the following book, when discussing the same precept, Septimius says: “From whom, unless from the Devil, are they to seek a husband capable of providing a litter, mules, and attendants of extraordinary height?” But since many other things from this book are likewise treated differently there, and since a multitude of Gallic and Germanic bearers suits a woman’s ceremonial display, I think the reading of the Agobard exemplar should be retained: “not a great many Gallic bearers, nor Germanic ones.” For Clement of Alexandria also writes in Book III of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 4: καὶ φοράδην βαστάζοντες Κελτοὶ πολλοί, “and many Celts carrying [her] in a litter.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1281C] “Gallic mules,” others; “a great many Gallic,” Rigalt.], nor Germanic bearers, which inflame the splendor of marriage—but sufficiency, which befits modesty and chastity.

Assume, I beg you, that you need nothing if you attend upon the Lord; indeed, assume that you possess everything if you possess the Lord. Consider all his [Note: [Col. 1282B] “If you possess the Lord, whose are all things: heavenly,” Jun.] heavenly things [Col. 1282A], and you will despise earthly things. Nothing is necessary for a widowhood formally pledged before God except perseverance.

## CHAPTER V

People do indeed add to their motives for marriage anxiety about posterity and the intensely bitter pleasure of children. But among us this too is hateful [Note: [Col. 1282B] “Among us it is superfluous,” Rig.]. For why should we eagerly desire to bear children whom, once we have them, we hope to send on before us—namely, in view of the impending distresses [Note: [Col. 1282C] “In view of the impending distresses.” So above: “Because of the distresses of the times.” RIG.]—since we ourselves desire to be removed [Note: [Col. 1282B] “Shaken free,” Jun., from the Vatican manuscripts.] from this most wicked world and received by the Lord, as indeed the Apostle himself desired?

Offspring is certainly necessary to a servant of God! For we are sufficiently secure concerning our own salvation [Note: [Col. 1282B] “For we are sufficiently secure concerning our own lot to have leisure for children,” Jun.] [Note: [Col. 1282B] “For” is absent; “our own things, if we are secure,” Semler.] that we can devote ourselves to children. We must seek out burdens [Note: [Col. 1282D] The burdens of children are especially troublesome to us. Thus in the book *On the Exhortation to Chastity* he spoke of “the troublesome burden of children.” “Men,” he says, “are compelled by laws to beget them.” The same author.—“We must seek out burdens that are honored by laws”: by the right granted for three children. Juvenal, *Satire* IX:

> You have the privileges of a parent; because of me you are named as heir,  
> You receive every legacy, and also the agreeable lapsed bequest.  
> Many advantages besides will be joined to those lapsed bequests,  
> If I complete the number—if I make it three.

RIG.], burdens which even the profane among the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 1282B] “By very many,” Rigalt.] avoid, which are honored by laws, and which are assailed by acts of parricide [Col. 1282B] [Note: [Col. 1282D] “Assailed by acts of parricide”: by abortifacients, once the conception has been dissolved by drugs. Thus in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins* he said, “infants for some time attacked by their mothers.” The same commentator.]. To us [Note: [Col. 1282C] “Indeed,” Rig., with “certainly” omitted.] they are especially troublesome, in proportion as they are dangerous to faith.

For why did the Lord pronounce woe upon pregnant and nursing women (Matt. 24:19; Luke 21:23), unless because he testifies that the encumbrances of children will be an impediment on that day of mobilization? [Note: [Col. 1282C] Rig. adds “these things.”] He will certainly charge this to marriage [Note: [Col. 1282C] “Are charged,” Rig.]. But it will not concern widows: ready for action, they will spring forward at the first trumpet of the angel. They will freely endure every affliction and persecution, with no burden of marriage heaving in the womb or at the breasts.

Therefore, whether one marries [Note: [Col. 1282C] Others read “she marries”; Semler, “let her marry.”] for the sake of the flesh, the world, or posterity, none of these supposed necessities pertains [Note: [Col. 1282C] “Applies,” Rig.] to God’s servants [Col. 1283A]—as though it were not enough for us [Note: [Col. 1283C] “For us,” Lat.] to have succumbed to any one of them once and, by a single marriage, to have atoned for every such desire! Let us marry every day, and let us be found marrying on that day [Note: [Col. 1283C] Rig. adds “of fear”], like Sodom and Gomorrah.

For surely they were not conducting only marriages and commerce there. But when he says, “They were marrying and buying” [Note: [Col. 1283C] “They were marrying and buying.” Pamelius and La Cerda charge him here with a lapse of memory. For he writes concerning Gomorrah and Sodom what Christ Jesus said concerning the days of Noah in Matthew 24: “For as they were in the days before the flood, eating and drinking and giving in marriage.” The same scholars also say that the Author erred here, for in the Gospel’s account of Noah’s times there is no mention of people buying. LE PR.], he identifies the most conspicuous vices of the flesh and the world [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Detaining,” Semler.], which especially draw people away from divine discipline: the one through the pleasure of wantonness, the other through the desire [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Greed,” Rig.] to acquire.

And yet [Note: [Col. 1283C] “And nevertheless,” Rigalt.] that blindness then was held to be far removed from the end of the world [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Was held to be far removed from the end of the world.” This confirms what we observe elsewhere: that Christians in Tertullian’s age believed the end of the world to be near. RIG.]. What, then, will happen if the things that were once detestable in the Lord’s sight now keep us from these divine disciplines? “The time,” he says, “has been shortened; it remains that those who have marriages should conduct themselves as though they had none.”

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1283B] But if those who have marriages [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Those who have must efface,” Fran., Paris.] ought to efface what they have, how much more are those who do not have one forbidden to seek again what they do not have? Thus a woman whose husband has departed from the world [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Had from worldly possessions,” Semler; “departed,” Fran., Par., Rig.; “thereafter, repose.”] should thereafter impose peace upon her sex by abstaining from marriage [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Should join abstinence,” Fran.]. Many Gentile [Note: [Col. 1283D] “Many Gentile women.” Jerome uses this argument toward the same end in his letter to Salvina, adducing the example of the queen of Carthage, who, once widowed, declares in the great Poet:

> He who first joined me to himself took away my love;  
> Let him possess it and preserve it with him in the tomb.

Likewise in the letter to Furia. He treats the same argument in the letter to Gerontia, where he adds to the queen of Carthage the widow of Hasdrubal, who threw herself into the fire lest she suffer the loss of her chastity. Trebellius speaks of the Gentile Calpurnia in the *Thirty Tyrants*. LAC.] women honor the memory of their dearest husbands [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Spare,” Semler.] in this way.

When something seems difficult, let us recount others who undertake more difficult things [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Because that seems difficult,” Lat.]. How many there are who seal their flesh immediately after the washing of baptism! [Note: [Col. 1283D] “How many there are who seal their flesh immediately after the washing.” So in Book II of *On the Apparel of Women*: “For do not many also act in this way and seal themselves for eunuchhood?” RIG.] How many likewise, by mutual consent, abolish between themselves the marriage debt [Col. 1284A], becoming voluntary eunuchs from desire for the kingdom of heaven! If abstinence is endured while the marriage remains intact, how much more when it has been taken away! For I believe it is more difficult to relinquish what remains intact than not to long for what has been lost.

Is continence for God’s sake, after her husband’s death, altogether hard and arduous enough for a holy woman [Note: [Col. 1283C] “Holy seed,” Semler.], when Gentile women endure both virginity and widowhood in the priesthood of their Satan? At Rome, those women who tend the image of that unquenchable fire, tending the omens of their own punishment together with the dragon [Note: [Col. 1284C] “With the dragon, tending” is absent from the Agobard manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 1283D] “Tending the omens of their own punishment together with the dragon.” The codex of Agobard reads: “At Rome, those women who tend the image of that extinguishable fire are assessed, together with it, on the basis of virginity, as omens of their punishment.” This might indeed be explained by supposing that he calls the fire of Vesta an omen of the punishments awaiting the wretched Vestals, together, of course, with the unquenchable fire that God has prepared for worshipers of idols.

Yet, to conceal nothing, I prefer the edition of Pamelius, which had previously been that of Rhenanus, who also represented the manuscripts faithfully: “tending the omens of their punishment together with the dragon.” Thus the Vestals are understood to tend that supposedly unquenchable fire of Vesta together with the dragon—that is, Satan, the guardian of the prison, vomiting forth everlasting fire. So in the book *On Idolatry*: “Let them therefore light lamps every day, though they have no light. Let them fasten to their doorposts laurels that are afterward to burn, over which flames hang. To them belong both the testimonies of darkness and the omens of punishments.” In the same sense he says in Book II of *On the Apparel of Women*: “With the flame-colored covering of the head,” he says, “they take an evil and most wretched omen for themselves.”], are assessed on the basis of virginity.

At the town of Aegium, a virgin is chosen by lot for Juno of Achaea [Note: [Col. 1284D] “For Juno of Achaea.” We have written “of Achaea,” for Aegium is a town of Achaea where Juno was worshiped, as Pliny and others attest. Jerome mentions this Juno on the basis of this passage in his letter to Gerontia; the widely circulated editions of that letter read “and of Achaean Juno.” RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 1284C] “Of Achaea,” Semler, Franequer, Paris, Jun.; “of the Heights,” others.]; and the women who rave at Delphi know nothing of marriage.

Furthermore, we know that widows attend upon the African Ceres, induced to forsake marriage by the harshest possible oblivion [Note: [Col. 1284C] “Of marriage,” Paris; “of marriages,” Jun.]. For although their husbands remain [Note: [Col. 1284C] Perhaps “with their husbands consenting,” Lat.; “with their husbands unwilling,” Rig.] forever [Note: [Col. 1284C] “Meanwhile,” Lat.], they not only withdraw from their marriage bed [Note: [Col. 1284C] “From the bed” is absent in Rig.], but even [Col. 1284B] introduce other women into their own place for their husbands—who naturally laugh at them—while every form of contact, even the kisses of their children, is taken away. Yet, while this arrangement continues, they persevere in such a discipline of widowhood, one that excludes even the consolations of holy affection [Note: [Col. 1284C] “Holy,” Jun.].

The devil commands these things [Note: [Col. 1284C] “Commands his own,” Rigalt.], and he is obeyed. Through the continence of his adherents, he plainly challenges the servants of God, as though the priests of Gehenna also practiced continence on equal terms [Note: [Col. 1284C] “As though on equal terms. For the priests of Gehenna also practice continence,” Rhen.; Rig. and the Agobard manuscript likewise divide the sentence after “equal terms.”] [Note: [Col. 1284D] “The priests of Gehenna also practice continence.” Thus we emended it from those ancient manuscripts of Agobard. “Of Gehenna” means “of Satan, of idolatry.” RIG.]. For he has discovered how to destroy human beings even through the pursuit of good practices; and to him it makes no difference whether he kills some by sensuality and others by continence.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 1285A]

Continence has been disclosed to us by the Lord of salvation as an instrument of eternity, as a testimony of faith, as a commendation of this flesh—which must be presented to the garment of incorruptibility that will come upon it—and for enduring the will of God to the very end.

Beyond these things, I urge you to reflect that no one is taken from the world except by God’s will [Note: [Col. 1285B] Franequer and Parisin. add “except.”], if not even a leaf falls [Note: [Col. 1285B] “Falls down,” Jun., Cod. Wouw.] from a tree without God’s will. The very one [Note: [Col. 1285B] “Therefore the one,” Cod. Wouw.] who brings us into the world [Note: [Col. 1285B] “Brings us into the world.” This is an ill-omened and wholly funereal verb; from it comes *inferiae mortuorum*, “offerings to the dead.” That is, when we are born, we are not so much born as brought into the body as into a place of custody—or rather, into a tomb. He opposes to this the verb *educo*, “to lead out,” for death is true life, which frees us from prison and leads us out of the tomb. LAC.] must also be the one who leads us out.

Therefore, when a husband has died by God’s will [Note: [Col. 1285B] “Husband” is absent from Semler’s edition.], the marriage too expires by God’s will. Why would you restore what God has ended? Why do you disdain the freedom offered to you [Col. 1285B] by taking on the slavery of marriage a second time? “Are you bound,” he says (1 Cor. 7:27), “to marriage? Do not seek release. Are you released from marriage? Do not seek a bond” [Col. 1286A] [Note: [Col. 1285B] The words “Are you released … a bond” are absent from Semler’s edition.].

For although you do not sin by marrying again, he nevertheless says that affliction of the flesh follows (ibid., vv. 10, 28). Why, then, should we not cherish [Note: [Col. 1285B] “As much as we can, let us cherish,” with the negation omitted, Lat., Rig.] the capacity for continence as much as we can? As soon as it comes to us [Note: [Col. 1286B] “When,” Lat.], let us drink it in, so that what we could not accomplish in marriage we may pursue in widowhood. We must embrace the opportunity that removes what necessity had imposed.

How much second marriages detract from faith [Note: [Col. 1286B] “Of faith” is absent from Semler’s edition.], how much they obstruct holiness [Note: [Col. 1285C] “For the Apostle’s injunction also declares how much second marriages detract from faith and how much they obstruct holiness. In two Epistles, to Timothy and Titus, Paul prescribes among the qualifications of a bishop that he be the husband of one wife. But by Tertullian’s age the discipline had already become established that a man who had married another wife after the death of the first ought neither to be nor to be called the husband of one wife. Thus a man was called *digamus*, twice-married, if he had a second wife in marriage, even if he enjoyed only one at a time and did not have two marriages simultaneously in effect.

Septimius says that this was instituted by the Apostle, and no other interpretation of the apostolic command was to be expected from so great an opponent of marriage. Yet from the commentaries of Chrysostom, Theodoret, and even Jerome, we learn that distinguished men in the Church, and indeed men close to Tertullian’s own age, were unwilling to support this interpretation. For they held that the Apostle meant only that a bishop should be chosen who faithfully preserves the sanctity of marriage with his one wife. [Col. 1285D] RIG.] of the Church’s discipline [Note: [Col. 1285D] “Second marriages.” He certainly inveighs vehemently against second marriages, and in this matter he appears to agree with the ancient Fathers. For blessed Jerome, in his letter to Gerontia, calls second vows fornication and whoredom. Read the same author’s book *Against Helvidius* and his letter to Salvina. Athenagoras said: εὐπρεπὴς μοιχεία δεύτερος γάμος, “A second marriage is respectable adultery.” I omit Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book I, final chapter; Hilary on Psalm 131; canon 18 of the First Council of Toledo; and countless other passages, in order to add, from profane literature, this one from Book I of the *Anthology*, to the disgrace of Christians in the eyes of so many most holy Fathers:

> Εἴ τις ἅπαξ γήμας πάλι δεύτερα λέκτρα διώκει,  
> Ναυηγὸς πλώει δὶς βυθὸν ἀργαλέον.

> If one who has married once again pursues a second marriage bed,  
> Shipwrecked, he sails twice into the grievous deep.

LE PR.]—the Apostle’s injunction declares, since he does not permit the twice-married to preside [Note: [Col. 1285D] “Does not permit them to preside.” Presbyters and bishops presided, whence they were called “presidents.” In *On the Soldier’s Crown*, speaking of the Eucharist, he says: “Nor do we receive it from the hand of anyone other than those who preside.” He is alluding to Titus 1, “the husband of one wife.” RHEN.

“Does not permit the twice-married to preside.” In chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, the most blessed Apostle requires a bishop or presbyter to be the husband of only one wife, or monogamous. That is, if anyone through natural weakness has been able to succumb to this fault, the first marriage is pardoned; but if he contemplates a second marriage, let him be deprived of every ecclesiastical office. [Col. 1286C]

Among the pagans, as Plutarch reports in his *Roman Questions*, it was an accepted principle that ζηλωτὸς ὁ πρῶτος γάμος, ὁ δὲ δεύτερος ἀπευκταῖος: “The first marriage is to be esteemed, but the second rejected.” What judgment should be made about Christians, if this was the Gentiles’ opinion? For when a δεύτερος πλοῦς, “second voyage”—or “second counsels,” as our Author has it here in the following book—is permitted by the Church, the saying must be understood thus: πορνείας παραμυθία ὁ δεύτερος γάμος, οὐχὶ ἐφόδιον εἰς ἀσέλγειαν, “Let a second marriage be a remedy for fornication, not a provision for wantonness,” as St. Basil writes in Epistle 117 to Diodorus.

Hence Apostolic Canon 17 prohibits bigamists from becoming bishops, presbyters, or members of the ecclesiastical order: οὐχ ὅλως καταλόγου ἱερατικοῦ, “not at all of the priestly register.” In the following canon, ὁ χήραν λαβών, “one who has married a widow,” is excluded from the same rank. Gratian agrees with this teaching, Distinction 33, chapter *Si quis post accept.* LE PR.], and since it does not permit a widow to be chosen for the order [Note: [Col. 1286B] “For ordination,” Semler.] unless she has been the wife of one man. For the altar [Note: [Col. 1286B] “The threshing floor,” Jun.] of God must be presented pure [Note: [Col. 1286C] “For the altar of God must be presented pure.” We observed above that a Christian person is called an altar of God, from whose heart prayers are borne to God. Here, however, in a certain exceptional sense, he calls the leaders of the ecclesiastical order the altar of God, since they bear the Church’s vows to God and through them the Christian Church customarily offers the sacrifices of prayers to God.

What, then? If, after his wife has died, the survivor marries another, with whom, dearly beloved, he lives harmoniously and chastely, will the altar of God not be pure? Jerome therefore rightly said that no one who has read the Apostle would deny that Tertullian’s opinion was contrary to the Apostle. RIG.].

[Col. 1286B] The whole Church is described as white through holiness [Note: [Col. 1286D] “That whole bright-robed order of the Church is marked out by holiness.” It must be emended, as it stands in the manuscripts: “That whole bright-robed order of the Church is enrolled on the basis of holiness.” He used “the bright-robed order of the Church” to denote rank, as in the book *On the Crown*, “the bright-robed order of martyrdom”; and in the *Scorpiace*, “the bright-robed order of glory.” Augustine likewise uses “the bright mass” for the splendid multitude of martyrs in Sermon 112, where, speaking about those who believe in the name of God, he says: “This is the first cause of the martyrs; this is the bright mass of martyrs. If the cause is bright, the mass also is bright.” “Mass” was used of a multitude in number, and “bright” of the splendor of the cause. Thus Tertullian himself, in Book IV *Against Marcion*, uses “the bright-robed order of salvation” for the glory of salvation; and in Book V, “the Pharisaic bright-robed order” for the ostentation and pride of the Pharisees. RIG.].

The priesthood of widowhood [Note: [Col. 1286B] “Of celibates,” Rigalt.] has also been celebrated [Col. 1287A] among the nations, evidently in imitation by the devil. It is forbidden for the king of the age, the chief pontiff [Note: [Col. 1287C] “The chief pontiff.” He means the *Flamen Dialis*, who was called not only chief pontiff but also king, because he was the arbiter of divine and human affairs. Tertullian, *Exhortation to Chastity*, final chapter. LAC.], to marry again. How greatly holiness pleases God, since even his enemy imitates it—not, certainly, as one allied to anything good, but as one who imitates the things pleasing to the Lord God in order to insult him!

## CHAPTER VIII

For the honors of widowhood [Note: [Col. 1287B] “Of widowhoods,” Semler.] before the Lord, the matter is settled by his single saying through the Prophet: “Deal justly [Note: [Col. 1287B] “Deal justly,” singular, Semler.] with the widow and the orphan, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord.”

The Father of all has undertaken to protect [Note: [Col. 1287B] “To protect. The Father of all”; see Semler.] those two classes of persons to the same degree that they are exposed to human contempt [Note: [Col. 1287B] “Destitute of human aid,” Rig.] and therefore to divine mercy. See how one who has done good to a widow is regarded as an equal; see how highly the widow herself is valued, since her champion has reasoned with the Lord [Note: [Col. 1288C] “Her champion with the Lord.” An *assertor* is an avenger who claims someone for freedom; here it means a patron who undertakes to protect a person. RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 1287B] “Will reason,” Franequer, Parisin.; “will reason with the Lord,” Rigalt.]!

I do not think so much has been granted to virgins, although in them unimpaired integrity and complete holiness will see the face of God from close at hand. Yet the widow possesses something more laborious, because it is easy not to seek what you do not know and to reject what you have never desired. More glorious is the continence that feels its own right and knows what it has experienced. A virgin may be regarded as happier, but a widow as more laborious: the former because she has always possessed what is good, the latter because she has discovered what is good for herself. In the one, grace is crowned; in the other [Col. 1288A], virtue.

For some things belong to divine generosity, others to our own exertion. Those bestowed by the Lord are governed by his grace; those sought by a human being are accomplished through diligence. Strive, therefore, for the virtue of continence—and modesty [Note: [Col. 1288B] Rig. omits “modesty”]—which provides for chastity; for diligence, which has no dealings with trifles; and for frugality, which despises the world [Note: [Col. 1288B] “Mirror,” Rig.].

Pursue companionship [Note: [Col. 1288B] “Companions and conversations,” Rig.] and associations worthy of God, remembering that verse sanctified by the Apostle:

> Bad company corrupts good morals.

## CHAPTER IX

Talkative, idle, wine-bibbing, and inquisitive companions are especially harmful to a resolution of widowhood. Through talkativeness, words hostile to modesty creep in; through idleness, they lead one away from seriousness [Note: [Col. 1288B] “They lead away from truth,” Fran.; “they introduce complacency,” Jun., Paris.]; through drunkenness, they insinuate every kind of evil; through inquisitiveness, they convey rivalry in lust.

No woman of this kind knows how to speak [Note: [Col. 1288C] “Was unwilling,” Rig., incorrectly.] of the good of having one husband. For their god, as the Apostle says, is their belly (Phil. 3:19), and likewise those parts that are near the belly.

These things I now commend to you, dearest fellow servant. They have indeed been treated more fully after the Apostle, but they will also serve as consolation to you, because, if events turn out so, you will keep my memory present in them.

# BOOK II

[Col. 1287]

## [SUMMARY]

[Col. 1287C] **SUMMARY.—**This book has nearly the same subject as the preceding one, except that the Author, mindful of human frailty, exhorts his wife that, if she should ever contemplate a second marriage, she should abstain from marriage with Gentiles, as something unlawful, resembling fornication, harmful to faith, inclining toward unbelief, and alien to the Church’s sacrament of marriage, which is magnificently described. EDD.

[Col. 1287D] The first book, therefore, teaches:

I. That marriage, instituted by God, is one, chapters 1–2.  
II. That abstinence is better than marriage, chapter 3.  
III. Examples of continent widows, chapter 4.  
IV. That it is not expedient to enter a second marriage for the sake of having children, chapter 5.  
V. Examples of persons abstaining from marriage, chapter 6.  
VI. That second marriages are less pleasing to God, chapter 7.  
VII. To these he adds, as a conclusion, a eulogy of widowhood.

[Col. 1288D] In the second book it is established:

I. That marriage with a Gentile is forbidden, chapters 1–2.  
II. That it is unclean, like fornication, chapter 3.  
III. That it is an impediment to the duties of true religion, chapter 4.  
IV. That it encourages Gentile rites, chapter 6.  
V. But that in the Church marriage is a great and holy sacrament, which the Church brings about, the offering confirms, the blessing seals, the angels announce, and the Father ratifies, chapter 8. EDD., from D. SCHRAM.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1287D]

1. Most recently, my dearest fellow servant in the Lord, I discussed as well as I could what course a holy woman [Col. 1288D] ought to follow when, by whatever circumstance, she has been deprived of marriage.

> **Note [Col. 1287D]: “A holy woman.”** Rhenanus very properly observed [Col. 1288D] that by “holy women” Christians are meant here; for you will find this word used several times [Col. 1289C] in that sense by this author. The earliest Christians were also called “saints,” in accordance with the Apostle’s words in 1 Cor. 7: “Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.” Saint Luke has the same usage (Acts 9:32): “As Peter passed through all the regions, he came down to the saints who lived at Lydda”; and blessed Paul again, in 2 Thessalonians, chapter 1: “To all who are in Rome, called to be saints.” In former times bishops too were indiscriminately called “Most Holy”; but from antiquity the Supreme Pontiff alone has retained this title for himself. LE PR.

Now let us turn to secondary counsels, out of regard for human weakness, since we are warned by the examples of certain women who, when divorce or the death of a husband offered them an opportunity for continence, not only cast away the opportunity for so great a good, but even in marrying again refused to remember the rule that they should marry preferably “in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:39).

> **Note [Col. 1289C]: “Divorce.”** Thus Christian wives too, when their marriage had been dissolved by divorce, sometimes married another man without waiting for the former husband’s death. Consequently, they were not wives of one husband. Nor were those men husbands of one wife who, after repudiating one wife, married another. In the Apostle’s judgment, persons of this kind were considered less qualified for ecclesiastical orders or honors, since their example was not sufficiently blameless or temperate. For although such marriages were not forbidden by the laws, they were nevertheless not free from reproach; nor did a man seem likely to govern the Church successfully when his own marriage had turned out so unsuccessfully, or to preserve faithfully his goodwill toward the Christian people when he had by no means preserved it toward his wife. These are the words of Chrysostom in his interpretation of Paul’s Epistle to Titus: Ὁ γὰρ πρὸς τὴν ἀπελθοῦσαν μηδεμίαν φυλάξας εὔνοιαν, πῶς ἂν οὗτος γένοιτο προστάτης καλός; τίνα δὲ οὐκ ἂν ὑποσταίη κατηγορίαν; Ἴστε γὰρ ἅπαντες, ἴστε ὅτι εἰ μὴ κεκώλυται παρὰ τῶν νόμων τὸ δευτέροις ὁμιλεῖν γάμοις, ἀλλ’ ὅμως πολλὰς ἔχει τὸ πρᾶγμα κατηγορίας: “For how could a man who preserved no goodwill toward the wife who departed become a good leader? And what accusation would he not incur? For you all know—yes, you know—that even if association in a second marriage is not prohibited by the laws, the matter nevertheless remains open to many accusations.” LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 1289D]: “But even in marrying again they refused to remember the rule.”** He does not accuse them of violating the rule because they had married another while the husband who had dismissed them was still alive, but because they had married a pagan and had taken their marriages outside the Church. LE PR.

And so my mind is troubled lest I, who recently exhorted you to perseverance in single marriage and widowhood, should now, by mentioning the ready availability of marriage, cause you to slip down from higher things.

> **Note [Col. 1290C]: “Lest now, by mentioning marriage, I remove your safeguard against a downward slope.”** In the preceding book he had advised his wife to abstain from a second marriage. Now, when about to discuss that same marriage—should necessity for it arise—as something to be contracted only with a Christian, he says that he fears the indulgence of this secondary exhortation may make it seem that he has abandoned the austerity of the first, or greatly relaxed it, although he still earnestly desires it to be observed. “And so my mind is troubled,” he says, “lest I, who recently exhorted you to perseverance in single marriage and widowhood, should now, by mentioning marriage, cause you to slip down from higher things.” Thus the editions of Rhenanus and Pamelius. But Agobard’s manuscript gives the final clause in words better suited to Tertullian’s meaning: “lest I remove your safeguard against a downward slope”; that is, lest the removal of caution become, as it were, a downward slope for you. [Col. 1290D] “I fear,” he says, “lest this mention of second marriage amount to removal of the prohibition and thereby make the road to second marriage slope downward.” By *proclivium* he means the danger of slipping, which is certainly more immediate on a slope. A downward slope, or *proclivium*, appears to be created by the removal of caution whenever the barriers are taken away or the handles by which one might have held fast and taken care are cut off. LE PR.

But if your judgment is sound and complete, you certainly know that you must observe what is more advantageous.

> **Note [Col. 1290D]: “But if your judgment is sound and complete, certainly this must be observed there: what is more advantageous” (according to the variant reading).** We have corrected many things here at the suggestion of Agobard’s manuscript. Tertullian says to his wife: If your judgment is sound and perfect, then in this mention of marriage you must pursue what is more advantageous—namely, abstinence from a second marriage. But because I know that this undertaking in life is arduous and difficult, I have decided to sit down and pause, and to make some interval in my writing while I gather myself for the counsel that follows. I would not, indeed, have reported even on this matter to you had I not discovered a difficulty [Col. 1291C] greater than I had foreseen in my preceding discourse. He then shows that a woman sins more seriously by marrying a pagan than by entering a second or third marriage. Immediately afterward he makes assertions about Christians who seek marriage outside the Church and expresses grave indignation. LE PR.

But because this is difficult, not without compelling circumstances, and this highest purpose in life [requires?] supreme assistance—the text is corrupt here.

> **Note [Col. 1289B]:** Rigaltius thought that, on the basis of Agobard’s codex, he had restored the corrupt passage as follows: “Now, by mentioning marriage, I may remove your safeguard against a downward slope. But if your judgment is sound and complete, certainly this must be observed there: what is more advantageous. Because—compelling circumstances—this highest purpose in life, I paused.”

Nor would I have had reason to write to you about this matter also, had I not perceived that my anxiety was the more serious.

> **Note [Col. 1289B]:** Rigaltius reads: “in that matter.”

For the greater the continence of the flesh that sustains widowhood, the more pardonable its failure may appear; difficult things readily obtain pardon. But the more practicable it is to marry in the Lord, since this lies within our power, the more blameworthy it is not to observe what one can.

Furthermore, with regard to widows and unmarried women the Apostle advises that they remain as they are, when he says, “I desire all to persevere after my example” [Col. 1290A] (1 Cor. 7:7). But concerning marriage in the Lord, when he says “only in the Lord,” he no longer advises but expressly commands. Therefore it is especially in this matter that, unless we obey, we are in danger; because one may neglect advice with impunity more readily than a command, since the former comes as counsel and is proposed to the will, whereas the latter descends from authority and binds by necessity: there it is liberty, here contumacy, that appears to commit the offense.

> **Note [Col. 1289B]:** Wouwer’s codex reads: “because advice too,” etc. Rigaltius: “because his own things—someone may neglect with impunity,” etc. Perhaps one should write: “because you may indeed neglect advice with impunity, but by no means a command.”

## CHAPTER II

Accordingly, when in these days a certain woman took her marriage away from the Church—that is, joined herself to a pagan—and I recalled that others had done this previously, I was amazed either at the women’s own wantonness or at the dereliction of their advisers, since no Scripture grants permission for such an act.

Do they perhaps, I asked, flatter themselves with that passage in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 7:12–14), where it is written: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to the marriage, let him not dismiss her; likewise, if a believing woman is married to an unbeliever and finds her husband agreeable, let her not dismiss him; for the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife by the believing husband; otherwise your children would be unclean”?

> **Note [Col. 1290B]:** Rigaltius reads “of the brethren.”

> **Note [Col. 1290B]:** Rigaltius and Pamelius read *consentaneum*; Semler, *consentanea*.

Perhaps, by understanding this admonition simply as referring to believers already joined in marriage, they think that it is also lawful to marry unbelievers.

> **Note [Col. 1290B]:** The first edition of Rhenanus reads “movement” rather than “admonition.”

> **Note [Col. 1290B]:** Rhenanus reads “found”; Franeker and Paris, “enjoined.”

> **Note [Col. 1290B]:** Semler reads “to be understood.”

> **Note [Col. 1290B]:** The Franeker and Paris editions read “they think it is to be understood.”

> **Note [Col. 1291C]:** Rigaltius emended the passage here in this way. Others read: “perhaps they think it is to be understood simply of believers bound” (variant: “enjoined”; variant: “found”), “and that it is also lawful to marry unbelievers. Those who interpret it thus—God forbid,” etc.

God forbid that anyone who interprets it in this way should knowingly deceive himself. It is, rather, manifest that this passage of Scripture designates believers whom God’s grace finds already in a pagan marriage, as the words themselves show: “If any believer,” it says, “has an unbelieving wife.” It does not say, “takes an unbelieving wife.” It shows that the man is already living in marriage with an unbelieving woman and is afterward converted by God’s grace, and that he ought to persevere with his wife—clearly so that no one who has attained faith should think that he must separate from a woman who has now, in a certain sense, become alien and foreign to him.

Indeed, the Apostle also adds the reason: that we are called by the Lord in peace, and that an unbeliever may be won by a believer through the practice of marriage.

> **Note [Col. 1291C]:** Rigaltius reads “to the Lord God.”

The conclusion itself also confirms that this is how the passage must be understood: “As each person,” he says, “is called by the Lord, so let him persevere” (1 Cor. 7:15–17). But it is pagans, I think, who are called—not those who are already believers.

For if he had made an absolute pronouncement concerning a believer before marriage, he would have permitted the saints to marry indiscriminately. Yet if he had permitted that, he would never have appended a pronouncement so different from and contrary to his own permission, saying: “A woman is free when her husband has died: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”

> **Note [Col. 1291D]: “A woman is free when her husband has died.”** Here he paraphrastically renders “falls asleep” as “dies.” In both Greek and Latin the Apostle has: “But if her husband sleeps,” a phrase most familiar in Scripture. PAM.

Nothing here is open to reconsideration; for the Apostle forestalled what might have been reconsidered: lest we misuse his statement, “let her marry whom she wishes,” he added, “only in the Lord”—that is, undoubtedly, to a Christian.

> **Note [Col. 1291C]:** Apart from Rigaltius, the others read: “concerning that which might have been discussed.”

> **Note [Col. 1292C]:** In both places Rhenanus reads “Christ” in the manuscripts; Rigaltius, “the Spirit.”

Thus that holy Apostle, who prefers widows and unmarried women to persevere in chastity, and who exhorts us by his own example, prescribes no other form for entering marriage again except “in the Lord.” Only on this condition does he permit the loss of continence: “Only,” he says, “in the Lord.”

> **Note [Col. 1291D]: “Unmarried women in chastity.”** *Integritati* is ablative, not dative. Accordingly, this case takes both endings in all nouns. For *caput* indisputably forms the ablative *capite*, and yet Virgil said:
>
> *Capiti tremit aerea cassis*  
> “The bronze helmet trembles upon his head.”
>
> And *latus* forms the ablative *latere*, yet the same poet said:
>
> *Includunt caeco lateri*  
> “They enclose it within the hidden flank.”
>
> There he used *capiti* and *lateri* for *capite* and *latere*. So too *ruri* and *vesperi* are commonly used for *rure* and *vespere*. LAC.

> **Note [Col. 1291D]: “Only, he says, in the Lord.”** Our Septimius was so rigorous an observer of Christian discipline that in some matters he may appear, if it is permissible to say so, to have sinned through excessive holiness. Evidence of that fault will be found in his explanation of Paul’s admonition, which teaches that a widow possesses the freedom to marry whom she wishes, provided that she marry in the Lord: ἐλευθέρα ἐστίν, ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι, μόνον ἐν Κυρίῳ, “she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.” By that qualification, “only in the Lord,” he says that “to a Christian” is undoubtedly meant. [Col. 1292D] Chrysostom interpreted this more gently and indulgently, taking “in the Lord” to mean μετὰ σωφροσύνης καὶ κοσμιότητος, ἐπὶ παιδοποιΐᾳ καὶ προστασίᾳ, μὴ διὰ πάθους ἐπιθυμίας: “with chastity and propriety, for the begetting and upbringing of children, not through the passion of desire.” All these things may occur even with a pagan, provided his life outside the sphere of religion is blameless. But our Tertullian insists inflexibly: “Only to a Christian.” RIG.

The word “only” added weight to his law. Whatever tone and manner you use to pronounce this declaration, it is burdensome: it both commands and advises, enjoins and exhorts, entreats and threatens.

> **Note [Col. 1292D]: “And entreats and threatens.”** Tertullian presses the point and weighs the Apostle’s language carefully. Clement of Alexandria’s *Paedagogus*, book III, chapter 8, agrees with him: τὰ μὲν παρήνεσε, τὰ δὲ ὠνείδισεν, “in part he advises, in part he reproaches.” LE PR.

It is a strict, unencumbered judgment, eloquent in its very brevity. Such is the custom of the divine voice: that you understand at once and obey at once.

> **Note [Col. 1292D]: “A strict, unencumbered judgment.”** Pamelius read with Rhenanus “an unqualified and explicit judgment”; Rigaltius’ reading is better and clearer. LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 1292C]:** Rhenanus and Pamelius read: “It is an unqualified and explicit judgment, fruitful in its very brevity. Such is its custom. Divine wife, obey at once. For who else could—the Apostle have foreseen?”

For who could fail to understand that the Apostle foresaw the many dangers and wounds to faith involved in marriages of the kind he prohibits, and that he sought, first of all, to guard against the pollution of holy flesh by pagan flesh?

Someone will say at this point: “What difference, then, is there between a man who, while living in a pagan marriage, is chosen by the Lord, and one who was already a believer—that is, before his marriage—such that they are not equally required to guard their flesh, when the latter is barred from marriage with an unbeliever while the former is commanded to persevere in it? If we are polluted by a pagan, why is the former not separated, just as the latter is not bound?”

I shall answer, if the Spirit grants it, by alleging before all else that the Lord regards it as preferable for a marriage not to be contracted than for it to be entirely dissolved. Thus he prohibits divorce except on account of fornication, but commends continence. The former man, therefore, is under a necessity to persevere; the latter, moreover, has the power not to marry at all.

Then, if according to Scripture those whom faith finds already in a pagan marriage are not polluted precisely because the others are also sanctified along with them, undoubtedly those who were sanctified before marriage cannot sanctify foreign flesh if they mingle with it, since faith did not find them in that flesh. God’s grace sanctifies what it finds. Thus what could not be sanctified is unclean; and what is unclean has no share with what is holy, except to pollute it from its own uncleanness and kill it.

## CHAPTER III

Since these things are so, it is established that believers who enter marriages with pagans are guilty of fornication and must be barred from every communion of the brotherhood, on the authority of the Apostle’s words that one must not even take food with a person of that kind (1 Cor. 5:11).

Or shall we produce the marriage documents concerning that union before the Lord’s tribunal and plead that the marriage was duly contracted? Is what he himself forbade not adultery? Is what has been prohibited not fornication? Does the admission of an alien man violate God’s temple less, or mingle Christ’s members with an adulteress’s members less?

> **Note [Col. 1292D]: “Shall we produce the marriage documents on that day before the Lord’s tribunal and plead what he himself forbade?”** There were evidently women who married non-Christian husbands and nevertheless believed that they were marrying “in the Lord”—that is, in just and lawful marriages, undertaken for the sake of seeking children rather than lust. But Tertullian strips away these pretexts and turns to his wife: “It is not enough,” he says, “to have married properly and lawfully and to have preserved the fidelity of marriage in holiness. Nor, when you plead your case before the Lord’s tribunal, will it benefit you at all to produce the marriage documents; for by pleading the documents you will be pleading a marriage with an unbeliever, and by your own plea you will condemn yourself for the sin that the Lord commanded you through the Apostle to avoid. What, then, do you think is forbidden by the words ‘only in the Lord’? Fornication? Adultery? Those are forbidden under another provision of the law, not this one. A Christian, whether man or woman, is a temple of God. A Christian woman who marries a non-Christian man allows God’s temple to be contaminated and polluted—indeed, more shamefully than an adulteress does. For admitting an alien man violates that temple less, does it? It mingles Christ’s members with an adulteress’s members less, does it? I want you to know this and weigh it diligently again and again. We are not our own, but were bought at a price—and indeed with God’s blood. Therefore, in injuring this flesh, we injure God directly, because we injure his flesh, flesh redeemed by his blood.” This was certainly Tertullian’s meaning. RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1293]:** These words, “and plead that the marriage was duly contracted,” found in Wouwer’s manuscript, are absent from Rigaltius’ edition.

As far as I know, we are not our own, but were bought at a price. And at what price? With God’s blood. Therefore, in injuring this flesh, we injure him.

> **Note [Col. 1293D]: “As far as I know, we are not our own.”** The old copy reads, “as he may know.” One should write either “as you know” or “as far as I know,” a formula very commonly used by Tertullian. RIG.

What did that man recently mean who said that marrying an outsider was indeed an offense, but a very small one, when, quite apart from injury to the flesh that belongs to the Lord, every voluntary offense against the Lord is serious? The greater one’s power to avoid it, the more heavily one is burdened with the guilt of contumacy.

Let us now review the other dangers and wounds to faith which, as I said, the Apostle foresaw—things exceedingly troublesome not only to the flesh but also to the spirit itself. For who can doubt that faith is daily worn away by intercourse with an unbeliever? “Bad conversations corrupt good morals”; how much more do life together and inseparable familiarity do so?

Every believing woman must necessarily attend to the Lord. And how can she serve two masters—the Lord and, in addition, a pagan husband? For by attending to the pagan she will furnish pagan things: appearance, elaborate coiffure, worldly adornments, more shameful endearments, and even the stained secrets of marriage. Among the saints, by contrast, the functions of sex are discharged modestly and temperately, with the honor due to necessity itself, as though beneath God’s eyes.

> **Note [Col. 1293D]: “Appearance, elaborate coiffure.”** By “elaborate coiffure” understand a structure of piled-up hair, an edifice by which, in Juvenal 6, a woman “builds her head high.” RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1293D]: “Among the saints, the functions of sex,” etc.** We have already discussed this word; here, however, by “the functions of sex” he means ἁγνὴν ἀναστροφήν, “a most chaste manner of life,” as in blessed Peter’s First Epistle, chapter 3. LE PR.

> **Note [Col. 1293D]: “As though beneath God’s eyes, modestly and temperately.”** Jerome expresses the same view in his commentary on Titus, chapter 2: “So that with modesty and shame, and as though under the necessity of sex, she may render the debt to her husband rather than herself demand it from him, and may believe that she performs the works of childbearing before the eyes of God and the angels.” RIG.

## CHAPTER IV

But let her see how she renders her duties to her husband. She certainly cannot satisfy the Lord in accordance with the rule when she has at her side a servant of the devil, an agent of his own master for obstructing the pursuits and duties of believers.

If a station-fast is to be observed, her husband arranges a visit to the baths on that very day. If fasts must be kept, her husband holds a banquet on that same day. If she must go out in procession, never is some household occupation more certain to arise.

> **Note [Col. 1294B]: “The husband arranges a visit to the baths on that very day.”** The old copy reads “permits.” RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1294B]: “If she must go out in procession.”** He notes the ancient rite of going forth, or public supplication, in the Church; and this passage is important for confirming many rites. One cannot but marvel at the negligence of the Magdeburg writers, who relate the rite of going forth, or processions, to the Montanist heresy, although elsewhere they admit that Tertullian wrote this book before he gave his allegiance to Montanus’ heresy. I do not know whether Albaspinaeus mocks them quite safely when they understand these words as referring to the rite of going forth; he has, I think, pierced the eyes of crows. LE PR.

For who would allow his wife, for the sake of visiting the brethren, to go from street to street around other people’s huts, especially the poorer ones? Who would gladly endure her being taken from his side for nocturnal gatherings, should that be necessary? Who, finally, would without anxiety tolerate her spending the night away during the solemnities of Easter? Who would let her go, without suspicion of his own, to that Lord’s banquet which they defame? Who would allow her to crawl into prison to kiss a martyr’s chains? Or indeed to meet one of the brethren for the kiss? To offer water for the feet of the saints? To seize upon, long for, and keep in mind something from their food or drink?

> **Note [Col. 1294C]: “From street to street.”** The old copy reads “along the roads.” RIG.
