> **Note [Col. 1294C]: “To that Lord’s banquet.”** Toward the end of this book he will say “God’s banquet.” In both places he appears to mean what Paul in 1 Corinthians 11 called Κυριακὸν δεῖπνον, “the Lord’s Supper,” when he rebuked the Corinthians for approaching the Lord’s meal as though it were their own—τὸ κυριακὸν ἰδιωτικῶν ποιήσαντες, “making the Lord’s meal a private affair”—because the more powerful or wealthy alone seized and consumed the eucharistic offerings, without waiting for poorer people or admitting them to a share. This was certainly not to eat the Lord’s Supper, which, because it is the Lord’s body, ought to have been treated worthily. But those who did not regard the other believers, however poor, as brethren treated it most unworthily, being devoid of charity as well as humility, and consequently guilty concerning the Lord’s body and blood because they so shamelessly seized for themselves what belonged to all in common. Jerome appears to interpret the matter in this way.
>
> Theodoret, however, preferred to refer it to the *agapae*, which were celebrated on solemn days after the Lord’s Supper. On that interpretation, the Apostle introduced mention of the Lord’s Supper to rebuke the pride or gluttony of the wealthy Corinthians, so that he might strike down all the more forcefully the shamelessness of those who, immediately after the Lord’s Supper—in which they themselves had shared equally with all the poorest as their brethren—at once assumed such arrogance at the *agapae* that they seized the food first, without calling the poorer people to share or waiting for them. This was evidence that the Lord’s Supper had been celebrated most unworthily—that is, faithlessly and wrongly.
>
> But if the weight of this interpretation perhaps impels us so far [Col. 1295B] that we judge that here too our Septimius calls the *agapae* “God’s banquet” and “the Lord’s banquet,” scarcely any reason for this designation will be more probable than that the *agapae* were called “the Lord’s” because Christians assembled for them on the Lord’s days.
>
> “That Lord’s banquet which they defame”—that is, the pagans. Tertullian himself says in the *Apology*: “Besides defaming our little suppers as criminal, you also denounce them as extravagant.” And on the following page of this very book, where he speaks of the pagan husband of a Christian woman: “Will the husband not know what you secretly taste before all other food? And if he learns that it is bread, will he not believe it to be that bread of which the story is told?”—that is, bread saturated with the gore and blood of a slaughtered infant. Tertullian himself says in the *Apology*: “We are said to be utterly criminal because of the sacrament of infanticide and the food derived from it, followed by incest after the banquet.”
>
> That man of Cirta in Minucius spun out a tale from both slanders, with all the greater shamelessness because the letters of Pliny the Younger to the emperor Trajan had established that it was false. For after conducting an investigation, Pliny states that he discovered from deserters of the Christian religion, who had even cursed Christ, that Christians did indeed customarily assemble to take food, but food of an ordinary and innocent kind.
>
> It should also be observed that, amid all the charges and insults brought by those who accused Christians of impiety because they possessed no altars and offered no sacrifices, and amid so many betrayals by faithless brethren, no one appeared who charged Christians with eating the flesh and drinking the blood of their God and Lord, although in their eucharistic rites they testified that they did so. RIG.

If a brother should arrive from abroad, what hospitality is there for him in another man’s house? If anything must be given to someone, the granary and store cupboard are locked.

## CHAPTER V

But some husbands tolerate our practices and do not object. This, then, is the offense: that pagans know our practices; that we are under their knowing observation; and that whatever we do is done by their indulgence.

> **Note [Col. 1295B]:** Rigaltius reads: “But someone tolerates our practices and does not object. This—under the knowing observation of the unjust,” etc. Variant: “of the just.”

A man who tolerates them cannot say that he does not know. Or, if the matter is concealed from him because he does not tolerate it, he is feared. But since Scripture commands both that we act for the Lord without another’s knowing observation and that we act without constraint upon ourselves, it makes no difference on which side you offend: either under your husband’s knowing observation, if he knows and tolerates it, or in conflict with yourself, while you avoid him because he will not tolerate it.

“Do not,” he says, “cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them and then turn and overthrow you as well” (Matt. 7:6). Your pearls are the distinguishing marks of your daily conduct. The more carefully you endeavor to conceal them, the more suspicious you make them and the more objects of wariness for pagan curiosity.

> **Note [Col. 1296B]:** Rigaltius reads “liable to be caught.”

Will you escape notice when you sign your bed and your little body with the cross, when you reject something unclean by blowing and spitting, and when you rise even during the night to pray? Will you not appear to be practicing some kind of magic?

> **Note [Col. 1295C]: “Something unclean while blowing.”** Thus, very properly, the old copy. By “something unclean while blowing,” he means some offensive smoke or stench by which the nostrils of a passing Christian woman might happen to be struck and offended by the fumes from a smoking altar. RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1296B]:** Rigaltius reads: “you drive away what is unclean by blowing.”

Will the husband not know what you secretly taste before all other food? And if he learns that it is bread, will he not believe it to be that bread of which the story is told? How will anyone who knows nothing of these things tolerate their meaning without concern, without suspicion that the bread is poison?

Some do tolerate them—but in order to trample upon and mock women of this kind, whose secrets they preserve for the danger they believe may arise, should they themselves happen to be offended.

> **Note [Col. 1295D]: “Some tolerate them, but in order to trample upon and mock women of this kind,” etc.** He shows what dangers threaten and what wounds are inflicted on faith by the unequal marriage of a Christian woman to a pagan. Through their very daily life and intimate cohabitation, the Church’s sacraments—which would better remain concealed between Christian spouses—come before profane eyes, thereby giving advantage-seekers opportunities for harassment and slander.
>
> For how could a woman not sometimes be detected by her husband when, at every forward movement and advance, every entrance and departure, when dressing and putting on her shoes, at the baths, at meals, at the lighting of lamps, on going to bed, and on taking a seat, she wears down her forehead with the sign of the cross? Or when, abhorring the smell or stench of a smoking altar, she blows it away and spits? Or, finally, when she rises during the night to attend gatherings before dawn and sing hymns to Christ as God? Will he not interpret these things as curses, spells, and magical incantations?
>
> Will he not know when you consume the Eucharist preserved at home? Will he not inquire more curiously what you secretly taste before all other food? And if he learns that it is bread, will he not immediately reflect that it is the bread said to be stained with the blood of infanticide? This was the slander that especially afflicted Christians at that time.
>
> Let us grant that someone may be found who suspects nothing concerning magical arts, the slaughter of infants, the consumption of raw flesh, or bloodstained bread, but simply does not know the reasons for the practices mentioned above—the sign, the blowing, the gatherings before dawn, and the bread preserved with special care. Do you think there is such a man who would tolerate these unknown things without concern? Even if he suspects nothing about that frenzied and barbarous bread, he will still suspect something about poisoned bread and begin to fear that, instead of a matron, he has married a poisoner.
>
> Yet some men tolerate all these things without concern or suspicion of poison. But they tolerate them in order to crush their wives and hold them up to ridicule, preserving their secrets for this use: to have some means of creating danger for them if they should happen to incur suspicion of adultery, often falsely entertained.
>
> They tolerate them and, once they have investigated them, disclose them themselves, either to shake the Christian faith from their less steadfast wives or, in the case of the more steadfast, to extort their dowry. For there were women who gave extortioners and informers considerable sums of money to avoid denunciation. Nor were there lacking husbands who employed advantage-seekers and suborned informers, with whom they bargained, under fictitious claims, for a share of the money. By that “subjection of a claim”—that is, by putting forward a creditor—they often plundered the dowries of Christian wives through a most disgraceful bargain as the price of silence.
>
> For if a wife brought an action over a defrauded dowry, she was immediately placed in danger of her life for being a Christian by the informers whom her husband had put forward and suborned. Thus the husband himself, the spy who had cunningly investigated Christian secrets through the opportunity afforded by marriage, became arbiter of the dispute. Unless the wife was entirely prepared to die, she was compelled either to betray the faith she had pledged to Christ or to lose her dowry. This was certainly what Tertullian meant.
>
> Those who think that no question mark should be placed after the words, “And if he learns that it is bread, will he not believe it to be that bread of which the story is told?” are mistaken; for the clauses that precede and follow are interrogative in the clearest possible sense. Tertullian is therefore asking a question there also. Does it really seem possible for a Christian woman who has married a pagan to conceal the Christian mysteries so successfully that, when she keeps the Eucharist at home, he will not inquire what she religiously preserves? “And if he learns that it is bread,” Tertullian says, “will he not believe it to be that bread of which the story is told”—that is, the bread defamed by the common people? RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1297B]: “Whose secrets they preserve for the danger they believe may arise, should they happen to be offended.”** By “the wives’ secrets” he means that pagan husbands do not betray their wives when they are engaged in Christian sacred rites. Thus pagan husbands preserve their wives’ secrets for the danger they believe may arise—that is, for the danger they believe threatens the Christian name when, as they hope, persecution flares up—so that they may betray them at that time if, through some hurt to their feelings arising from any source, they should desire their wives’ destruction. RIG.

> **Note [Col. 1297B]: “Should they happen to be offended.”** That is, if some hurt to their feelings happens to arise; if there is some quarrel, injury, complaint, offense, harm, lawsuit, or danger. Hence those expressions of affection in tomb inscriptions: “FROM WHOM HE SUFFERED NO GRIEF”; “FROM WHOM HE HAD RECEIVED NO PAIN”; “WITH WHOM HE LIVED WITHOUT ANY DISPUTE”; “WITHOUT ANY QUARREL”; “WITHOUT ANY HURT TO THE FEELINGS”; “WITHOUT RANCOR”; and other expressions of this kind. RIG.

They tolerate women whose dowries they make the price of their silence by bringing an accusation based on the Christian name—women who, of course, must litigate before an arbiter who is himself their spy. Most women, failing to foresee this, have departed either after their property was extorted from them or after losing their faith.

> **Note [Col. 1297A]:** Rigaltius reads: “Some tolerate them—preserve them, should they happen to be offended. They tolerate women whose dowries, by subjection of the name,” etc.

> **Note [Col. 1297A]:** Thus Wouwer’s codex. Rigaltius reads “have been accustomed to acknowledge”; the others, [Col. 1298A] “have reviewed.”

## CHAPTER VI
She dwells [Note: [Col. 1297C] “God’s handmaid dwells amid the labors of others.” Thus we emended what, before the discovery of Agobard’s manuscript, was read as “amid the household gods of others”—a thoroughly corrupt reading. For if by *lares* he meant a dwelling, there is no reason why a husband’s house should be considered foreign to his wife. If by *lares* he meant the household gods, it would be absurd to reproach a Christian for worshiping other people’s household gods rather than her own, since she acknowledges none as her own. But he rightly reproaches a Christian woman who, although she is God’s handmaid, dwells amid the labors of others, when she ought to be occupied with her own. Christians have their proper labors, and pagans theirs. The Author indicates the latter labors: running about and occupying oneself with the worship of demons; providing, arranging, and carrying out different sacrifices under their various names—some for Jupiter, some for Mars, some for Ceres; taking part in the emperors’ ovations and solemnities at the beginning of the year and the beginning of the month; fastening laurel to the door and lighting lamps. These labors are altogether foreign to Christians. But there are others proper to Christians, which Tertullian himself [Col. 1297D] describes: attending stations, observing fasts, going forth, keeping vigil through the Paschal solemnities, crawling into prison to kiss the martyrs’ chains, meeting one of the brethren for the kiss, and offering water for the saints’ feet. RIG.]—God’s handmaid amid foreign household gods—and among them she will be buffeted by the fumes of incense at every honor paid to demons [Note: [Col. 1298A] Rigault: “amid the labors of others—at every name of demons”], at every solemnity of kings, at the beginning of the year and the beginning of the month. And she will go out through a door crowned with laurel [Note: [Col. 1297D] “And she will fall forth through a door crowned with laurel and illuminated with lamps, as though from a newly established haunt of public lusts.” Among the pagans it was customary, at times of public rejoicing, not only to fasten laurels to the doors of their houses but also to light lamps during the day. Christians abhorred this as something dedicated to the honor of profane divinities, as an affront to nature and reason, and finally as the sign of some new brothel. Our Septimius says in the *Apologeticum*: “Why, on a day of rejoicing, do we not shade our doorposts with laurels, nor violate daylight with lamps?” He adds the reason mockingly: “It is an honorable thing,” he says, “when a public solemnity demands it, to dress your house in the appearance of some new brothel.” And again: “For who compels a philosopher to sacrifice, or to prostitute useless lamps at midday?” It is in this sense that Canon XXXVII of the Council of Elvira prohibits the faithful from lighting lamps publicly—that is, during the day, according to pagan custom; and Canon XXIV of the Second Council of Arles deprives of communion a bishop who permits even unbelievers in his territory to light torches. Canon XXXIV of Elvira also forbids candles to be burned in a cemetery during the day, lest the spirits of the saints be disturbed. Lactantius explained why the spirits of the saints might be disturbed by such observances in a very harsh denunciation of pagan ritual, Book VI, chapter 2. Nevertheless, the use of wax candles even during the day subsequently began in the Church; nor was there lacking, among the holiest and most learned men, Jerome, who contended against Vigilantius that such a rite, if it could not be approved, should at least be excused and tolerated. One may therefore marvel that this man of keen intellect, inflamed by the heat of controversy, after commending the example of the woman who anointed Christ’s feet, did not turn his Vigilantius into Judas Iscariot. The same Jerome testifies that it was the custom of the churches throughout the East to light lamps during the reading of the Gospel even while the sun was shining: “Certainly not to dispel the darkness, but to demonstrate a sign of joy.” This explanation shows the rite to be all the more pagan, since the signs that the nations used even in their more wanton and wicked rejoicings were adapted to the most sacred readings of the Gospels. Septimius would therefore say in this instance also that by lighting lamps in the Church during the day we make ourselves equal to the pagans, and that such things and others of this kind are rightly censured because they are celebrated before idols; for so he himself says. Jerome, however, held that those very things were indeed to be detested because they were then performed for idols, but that now, because they are dedicated to God and to God’s martyrs, they are to be praised. And so I stop here. (On the contrary, Rigault continues his arduous journey of innovation and submits the use of candles lit during the day to the tribunal of Nature and the scrutiny of Reason. We too submit it—to the most ancient tradition of all nations no less than of the whole Church, as may be seen in the published discussions of the matter by [Col. 1298D] Father Lebrun, *Explanation of the Prayers and Ceremonies of the Mass*, preliminary treatise, art. V. Cf. Fortunatus Scacchus, *Three Repositories of Sacred Oils and Chrism*. EDD.)] and illuminated with lamps, as though from a newly established haunt of public lusts. She will recline at table with her husband in clubs, often in taverns; and at times she will minister to the unrighteous, though once accustomed to minister to the saints. Will she not recognize in this a prejudgment of her own condemnation, when she attends upon those whom she was destined to judge? Whose hand will she long for [Note: [Col. 1298D] “Whose hand will she long for?” The common editions read: “From whose hand will she long?” Shortly afterward: “where are the supports of faith from the interspersing of the Scriptures?” The common editions have: “from the understanding of the Scriptures.” It makes no difference which reading we choose. “To long for a hand” and “to long for something from a hand” mean the same. Thus above, when he enumerates a Christian’s duties: “to offer water for the saints’ feet; to seize, long for, and keep in mind something from the food and from the cup.” These things pertain to the Christians’ *agapae* and are signs of vehement love, such as poets everywhere describe—although theirs are generally wanton and shameful desires of forbidden lust, whereas these are holy tokens among the saints of mutual affection and brotherhood. By them Christians declared that, because of Christ’s name, they were wholly united with one another in the highest fidelity and sought, desired, and yearned with all their heart and mind for their Lord and one Father, God, together with the Holy Spirit. RIG.]? From whose cup will she partake? What will her husband sing to her, or she to her husband? Let him hear—yes, let him hear—something from the theater, the tavern, the eating-house! What mention of God will there be? What invocation of Christ? Where are the supports of faith from the interspersing of the Scriptures? Where the refreshment of the spirit? Where the divine blessing? Everything is foreign, everything hostile, everything condemned, sent by the Evil One to wear salvation away. [Col. 1299A]

## CHAPTER VII

If these things can also happen to those [Note: [Col. 1299B] “If these things can also happen to those,” etc. Against Tertullian, who so bitterly condemned the marriages of Christian women with pagans and enumerated their dangers, it was objected that, in a pagan marriage, if one spouse should at some point be called to the Christian faith, precisely the same things would have to be feared; yet the marriage was not dissolved on that account—indeed, the Apostle’s most explicit words took care to forbid its dissolution. He therefore adds: “These things can also happen to those who, having attained faith while in a pagan marriage, remain in it. Nevertheless, they are excused, because God found them in those very circumstances; they are commanded to persevere, they are sanctified, and they receive the hope of gaining the other spouse. If, therefore, such a marriage is valid before God, why should it not also prosper, so as not to be assailed in the same way by pressures, constraints, and impediments, since it already possesses, on one side, the protection of divine grace? For the spouse from among the pagans, called to some heavenly virtue by proofs of divine favor, is also an object of fear to the pagan, so that the latter is less inclined to spy. The pagan has perceived mighty works, has seen proofs, and knows that the spouse has been made better. Thus through fear that pagan too is a candidate of God. Persons of this sort, in whom God’s grace has established familiarity, are more easily won.” We have transcribed this entire period from Agobard’s book because it exhibits the Author’s meaning more clearly. He is discussing a pagan marriage and, by designating the more excellent sex, examines arguments common to both. “We have shown,” he says, “the many disadvantages, dangers, and losses facing Christians who seek marriage with pagans. These can also happen to those who, having attained the Christian faith while in a pagan marriage, remain in it. Nevertheless, these are excused because divine grace found them amid the very dangers of marriage; they are commanded to persevere, they are sanctified, and they receive the hope of gaining the other spouse.” He then proceeds to show that a marriage of this kind already possesses the protection of divine grace on one side. Indeed, that calling from paganism to Christian discipline is an indication of divine favor and strikes fear into the pagan, so that the pagan spies less, plots less, and objects less, having perceived the miracles of the sudden change and knowing that his wife has become better since becoming a Christian. Thus he too, through such fear and reverence, becomes a candidate for Christ. [Col. 1300B] There is an allusion to that saying of David: ἀρχὴ σοφίας φόβος κυρίου, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” He then adds the distinction concerning a woman who, already a Christian, marries a pagan: “But,” he says, “it is another matter to descend voluntarily and willingly into what is forbidden. Things that offend God are certainly introduced by the Evil One.” RIG.] who, having attained faith while in a pagan marriage, remain in it, nevertheless they are excused, because God found them in those very circumstances; they are commanded to persevere, are sanctified, and receive the hope of gaining the other spouse. If, therefore, such a marriage is valid before God, why should it not prosper, so as not to be assailed in the same way by pressures, constraints, impediments, and defilements [Col. 1299B], since it already possesses on one side the protection of divine grace? For that woman from among the pagans, called to some heavenly virtue by proofs of some divine favor [Note: [Col. 1299B] Thus A. Neander emended this passage. Rigault’s reading, which we have followed in the other particulars, is excellent: “that man from among the pagans who has been called is an object of fear to the pagan”], is also an object of fear to the pagan, so that he objects to her less, knows less, and spies less. He has perceived mighty works [Col. 1300A], seen proofs, and knows that she has been made better. Thus through fear he too becomes a candidate of God. Persons of this sort, in whom God’s grace has established familiarity, are more easily won.

But it is another matter to descend voluntarily and willingly into what is forbidden. Things that do not please the Lord certainly offend the Lord and are certainly introduced by evil [Note: [Col. 1299B] Leopold, “introduce themselves into evil.”]. This will be the sign of it [Note: [Col. 1300C] “This will be the sign of it: that the Christian name pleases only the worse sort.” This, I think, is how the passage should be read, not the common “only suitors.” In the manuscripts I find: *Solis et itioribus*, which is corrupt. Among the pagans some were better than others. Thus in the *Scorpiace*: “So that you might suppose him a brother, or a pagan of the better sort.” But just as some were better, so some were also worse. Tertullian therefore says that things which offend God are introduced by the Evil One; and that this is made evident by the fact that, among pagans, those especially seek marriage with Christian women whose lives are worse and more shameful and who are counted among the worse sort. The Evil One, or Satan, incites these men to overthrow a Christian girl’s faith through such a marriage. “That is why,” says Tertullian, “pagans are found who do not shrink from such women”—that is, Christian women—“so that they may destroy them, carry them off, and exclude them from the faith.” “Only the worse sort”: just as Septimius says that among the pagans some are worse than others, so Augustine said that among Christians some are better than others. Thus in Book VIII of *The City of God*, chapter 27, where he discusses banquets at the memorials [Col. 1300D] of martyrs: “This,” he says, “is certainly not done by the better Christians, and in most regions there is no such custom.” RIG.]: the Christian name pleases only the worse sort [Note: [Col. 1300B] Rhenanus and others: “This will be a sign, so that only”; “because it pleases only suitors,” etc.]. That is why men are found who do not shrink from such women, so that they may destroy them, carry them off [Note: [Col. 1300B] Rhenanus: “that they may openly raise them up” (first edition: “openly encourage them”), “that they may seize them”], and exclude them from the faith. You have the reason why you should not doubt that no marriage of this kind proceeds prosperously: it is arranged by the Evil One but condemned by the Lord.

## CHAPTER VIII

Regarding this, let us ask whether it is just—as though we were truly examiners of divine judgments. Even among the nations, do not all the strictest masters and those most tenacious of discipline forbid their slaves to marry outside the household? [Col. 1300B] This is, of course, lest they stray into licentiousness [Note: [Col. 1300D] “Lest they stray into licentiousness.” The old copy reads “in licentiousness,” which I should prefer to retain. “Stray,” namely, from their master’s house. RIG.], abandon their duties, and reveal their master’s affairs to outsiders. Moreover, have they not decreed [Note: [Col. 1300D] “Have they not moreover decreed that those who persist in relations with the slaves of others,” etc. He means the Claudian senatus consultum concerning women who had joined themselves to slaves belonging to others. Julius Paulus composed *Sentences* on this senatus consultum, which Cujacius inserted from the Besançon manuscript into Book XXI of his *Observations*. The first *Sentence* sufficiently illuminates Tertullian’s passage: “If a freeborn woman and Roman or Latin citizen joins herself to another person’s slave, and if, despite the master’s opposition and formal warning, she persists in the same union, she becomes a slave.” RIG.] that those who persist in relations with the slaves of others after their masters’ formal warning are to be claimed for slavery? [Note: [Col. 1300D] “To be claimed for slavery, those who are with the slaves of others.” Thus reads Agobard’s copy, and thus other ancient books. Yet it is not recorded that the Claudian senatus consultum provided that a free man who entered into union with a female slave should become the slave of the woman’s master. Nor is there any mention of a free man in the *Sentences* of Paulus. But even if the senatus consultum had at some time also applied to free men, so that it had to be corrected by laws of Diocletian and Alexander found under the titles *On a Claim to Free Status* and *Common Provisions on Successions*, some emendation would still be needed here. We would have to say, “those are to be claimed for slavery who have persisted in relations with the female slaves of others,” not “those who are with the male slaves of others.” For elsewhere, and especially in this book, Septimius uses the word “female slaves.” I would therefore gladly agree with those who read, “women are to be claimed for slavery who have persisted in relations with the male slaves of others,” did I not know that our Septimius, writing hastily, sometimes observed such distinctions of sex less carefully. RIG.] Shall earthly disciplines be regarded as more severe than heavenly precepts? Shall pagan women who unite themselves to outsiders lose their freedom, while our women unite themselves to the devil’s slaves and remain in their own status? They will, of course, deny that the Lord has given them the same formal warning through his Apostle.

What cause of this madness shall I arraign [Note: [Col. 1301C] “What cause of this madness shall I arraign?” *Detineam*, “shall I accuse.” Thus Book I *To the Nations*: “For what such thing shall I arraign in you?” RIG.], if not the weakness of a faith always prone to desire worldly pleasures? This is indeed detected especially among the more affluent. For the more a wealthy woman is puffed up by the title of matron [Note: [Col. 1301B] Semler, from the first edition: “some woman is named a fellow matron.” Rhenanus, on the authority of the Gorze manuscript: “some woman is both a matron, puffed up by the title”; “the more capacious a house she requires for her burdens”], the more capacious a house she requires for her burdens, as a field over which her ambition may run. Churches are contemptible to such women. A rich man is hard to find in the house of God, and if there is one, it is hard to find him unmarried. What, then, are they to do? From whom but the devil are they to seek a husband capable of providing a sedan-chair, mules, and hairdressers of foreign stature? A Christian, even a wealthy one, might perhaps not provide these things.

I beg you, set before yourself the examples of the pagans. Very many women, both noble by birth and blessed with wealth, are everywhere joined there to lowborn [Note: [Col. 1301C] “Everywhere they are joined there to lowborn and ordinary men.” “There,” that is, among the pagans. Thus above: “Certainly that must be observed there.” “There,” that is, in contracting marriage. RIG.] and ordinary men, discovered for purposes of extravagance or castrated for sexual license [Note: [Col. 1301B] Another reading: “to the very worst of the lowborn—men eagerly sought”; another, “awaited”; Rigault, “castrated.”] [Note: [Col. 1301D] “Or selected for sexual license.” Women have greater license when there is no need for an abortifacient. Jerome called it “secure lust” in Book I *Against Jovinian*: “A eunuch, castrated for prolonged and secure lust.” Juvenal, *Satire* VI:

> There are women whom unwarlike eunuchs and ever-soft  
> Kisses delight, and the hopelessness of a beard,  
> And the fact that there is no need for an abortifacient.

Martial, *Epigrams*, VI.67. RIG.]. [Col. 1302A] Some give themselves to their own freedmen and slaves, despising the judgment of everyone, provided they have men from whom they fear no impediment to their freedom [Note: [Col. 1302B] The words from “Some” through “freedom” are absent from Rigault’s Venetian edition.].

Yet a Christian woman is ashamed to marry a faithful man of lesser means, though she will become richer in a poor husband! For if the kingdoms of heaven belong to the poor (Matt. 5:3), because they do not belong to the rich, a rich woman will find more in a poor man and will be endowed with a greater dowry [Note: [Col. 1302B] Rigault: “She will find. She will be endowed with a greater dowry from the goods of him who is rich in God. Let her be,” etc.]. Let her be his equal on earth, she who perhaps will not be so in heaven.

## CHAPTER IX

One must doubt, inquire, and deliberate again and again whether the man to whom God has entrusted his wealth is fit to receive an incoming dowry. How could we ever adequately recount the happiness of that marriage which the Church arranges [Note: [Col. 1301D] “Which the Church arranges”: namely, when Christians do not remove their marriages from the Church; when both parties come together as Christians; when a Christian woman seeks as her husband a Christian who has been recognized in the Church for the integrity of his Christian conduct, with the Church’s superiors either giving their consent or being informed. RIG.], the offering confirms [Note: [Col. 1301D] “And the offering confirms”: when the marriage, arranged by the superiors of the Church, as Septimius said, is presented to the Church on a solemn day to be blessed by the common prayers of the faithful amid the prayers of the sacrifices. Justin relates in *Apology* II that new Christians, after obtaining the saving waters, were presented to the Church of the faithful: μετὰ τὸ οὕτως λοῦσαι τὸν πεπεισμένον καὶ συγκατατεθειμένον ἐπὶ τοὺς λεγομένους ἀδελφοὺς ἄγομεν ἔνθα συνηγμένοι εἰσὶ κοινὰς εὐχὰς ποιησόμενοι ὑπέρ τε ἑαυτῶν καὶ τοῦ φωτισθέντος, “After thus washing the person who has been convinced and has given his assent, we lead him to those called brethren, where they are assembled to offer common prayers both for themselves and for the person who has been enlightened.” RIG.], the blessing seals [Col. 1302B] [Note: [Col. 1302C] “And the blessing seals”: when the spouses have been presented, the Church blesses them with prayers formally addressed to God, εὐφημίαις καὶ εὐλογίαις, “with acclamations and blessings,” which is the seal of the sacrament. The integrity of the marriage bond is a concern worthy of Christian statesmen, since the union of male and female is the foundation of every family and thus of the entire commonwealth, and the origin of civil life. Therefore, lest indiscriminate lust confound public ordinances, laws had to be imposed that would create lawful marriages and consequently lawful and legitimate children, so that those who united contrary to the commandments of those laws would receive no aid from any effect or benefit of civil law for their unions. And it was fitting that political laws be completed by Christian sacraments, so that marriages would not be recognized until the spouses had been presented and publicly announced in the Church before the pastors and the people, so that the faithful—already thoroughly known to one another through their frequent exchanges of prayer and thanksgiving—might bless the marriage of believers and pray for its welfare. This ancient form of the Church knew nothing of clandestine marriages, which a wandering and unrestrained license to roam outside one’s own churches and to divorce introduced a little later. RIG.], the angels announce [Note: [Col. 1302D] “The angels announce.” He indicates that angels are witnesses of the sacrament of marriage. In the book *On Prayer* he says that they are present at Christians’ prayers, and in the book *On Baptism* that they are witnesses of baptism. RIG.], and the Father ratifies [Note: [Col. 1302D] “The Father ratifies”: the Father who is in heaven. RIG.]? For even on earth children do not marry rightly and lawfully without their fathers’ consent.

What a yoke is that of two believers, of one hope, one discipline, and the same service! Both are brother and sister, both fellow servants; there is no separation of spirit or flesh. Indeed, they are truly two in one flesh; where there is one flesh, there is also one spirit. Together they pray, together they prostrate themselves [Note: [Col. 1302D] “Together they pray, together they prostrate themselves.” Thus in Book III *Against Marcion*: “to commend prayer with hands beating the breast and the face rolling upon the ground”; and in *On Modesty*: “Let that man mourn, let him roll upon the ground, who knows both what he has lost and what he will recover if he sacrifices repentance to God.” Likewise in the *Apologeticum*: “But we, withered by fasting, rolling in sackcloth and ashes, assail heaven with reproach.” RIG.], and together complete their fasts, each teaching the other, each exhorting the other, each sustaining the other [Note: [Col. 1303A] Thus Rigault; others: “each leading the other, each exhorting the other. In the Church,” etc.]. Both alike are in the Church of God, alike at God’s banquet, alike in hardships, persecutions, and times of refreshment [Note: [Col. 1303A] With the exception of Rigault, others read: “alike in the Church of God, alike in God’s marriage, alike in hardships, in refreshment”]. Neither conceals anything from the other; neither avoids the other; neither is burdensome to the other. The sick are visited freely, the needy supported; alms are given without torture [Note: [Col. 1303A] “Alms without torture.” When the pagan husband of a Christian woman noticed that something was missing from his property, perhaps portioned out by his wife to Christ’s poor, he often raged to such a degree that he ordered his wife’s slaves to be tortured. But when both are Christians, there are then alms without torture. RIG.]; sacrifices are offered without misgiving [Note: [Col. 1303B] “Sacrifices without misgiving.” Even a pagan husband of the better sort would scarcely allow his Christian wife to attend Christian sacrifices without grumbling, suspicion, or misgiving, because of the horrible crimes that pagans most slanderously alleged concerning Christian gatherings. Thus above: “Who, finally, will tolerate without anxiety her spending the night away at the Paschal solemnities? Who will let her go without suspicion to that Lord’s banquet which they defame?” But when both are Christians, each is free to attend the sacrifices without the other’s misgiving or suspicion. RIG.]; daily religious observance proceeds without impediment [Note: [Col. 1304A] “Daily religious observance without impediment.” He means the *diligentia* that in the *Apologeticum* he calls “the most diligent religiosity,” that is, the assiduous and solicitous observance of discipline or religion. Thus in *On the Prescription of Heretics*: “Where there is fear of God, there is honorable gravity and vigilant diligence,” etc. RIG.]. There is no furtive signing, no trembling thanksgiving, no silent blessing. Psalms and hymns resound between the two, and they challenge each other as to who can sing better to their God.

Seeing and hearing such things, Christ rejoices. To these he sends his peace. Where two are, there he too is; and where he is, the Evil One is not. These are the things that the Apostle’s voice, in its brevity [Note: [Col. 1304A] Another reading: “in its kindness.”], has left us to understand. Suggest these things to yourself if need be; by them turn yourself away from the examples of certain women. Believers are not permitted to marry otherwise [Note: [Col. 1304B] “Believers are not permitted to marry otherwise; it is not expedient.” Canon VI of the First Council of Arles: “Concerning faithful girls who are joined to pagans, it has been resolved that they be separated from communion for some time.” And Canon XV of the Council of Elvira: “Because of the abundance of girls, Christian virgins must by no means be given in marriage to pagans, lest an age swelling in the bloom of youth be dissolved in adultery of the soul.” He speaks of “adultery of the soul” concerning a Christian wife who, as though seduced by the procuring enticement of her pagan husband’s exhortation, divorces Christ for Satan. RIG.]; and even if it were permitted, it would not be expedient [Note: [Col. 1304A] Rigault: “for believers to marry: it is not expedient.”].

# TWO BOOKS ON THE ADORNMENT OF WOMEN

[Col. 1303]

# QUINTUS SEPTIMIUS FLORENS TERTULLIAN, *ON THE ADORNMENT OF WOMEN* [Note: [Col. 1303D] *On the Adornment of Women*. Until now editions of Tertullian have presented us with one book *On Women’s Dress* and another *On the Adornment of Women*. We have entitled both *On the Adornment of Women*, following the authority of the very ancient Agobard manuscript, in which, although only half of the first book has been preserved, the second concludes intact as follows: “Here ends Book II of *On the Adornment of Women*.” From this it is manifest that the first book preceded under the same title. Both are also cited thus in the catalogue of books: *On the Adornment of Women*. RIG.] (C)

## BOOK ONE

### [ARGUMENT]

[Col. 1303C] **ARGUMENT.—** Since the emperors’ most savage edicts against Christians threatened them with death hanging over them daily, Tertullian, already inclining toward Montanism, composed two books *On the Adornment of Women*. His purpose was to prepare more readily for martyrdom even those Christian women who did not shrink from imitating pagans in bodily adornment and luxury. In these books he shows that they adorn a body which at every moment they ought to be willing to lose for Christ. Hence in them he writes a bitter repudiation of feminine finery.

After prefacing a few remarks about women’s fall in Eve and the extreme humility consequently incumbent upon them, he shows that feminine adornment was instituted by a demon and describes the vanity of gold, silver, and gems glittering upon [Col. 1303D] clothing.

[Col. 1304C] Then, in the second book, he vigorously asserts that women who love ornament hate chastity; that no adornment befits God’s handmaids except simple cleanliness; that one must not glory in the flesh except when it is torn for Christ; and, finally, that cosmetics and pigments, curling irons and eye paints, little stones upon garments, and variegated colors must be avoided entirely, lest a body occupied by chains of pearls and emeralds leave no place for the sword.

EDITORS, FROM D. SCHRAMM.

## CHAPTER I

If as much faith dwelt upon earth as the reward awaiting it in heaven is great, not one of you, dearly beloved sisters [Col. 1304D], after she had come to know the living God and had learned about her own condition—that is, the condition of woman—would have desired a more cheerful mode of dress, to say nothing of a more glorious one. Rather, she would live in mourning garments and affect a neglected appearance, carrying Eve herself about in her person, grieving and repentant. She would thereby atone more fully, through every habit of satisfaction, for what she derives from Eve—I mean the disgrace of the first transgression and the odium of humankind’s perdition:

> In pains and anxieties you shall bear children [Note: [Col. 1305C] Semler: *paries*, “you shall bear.”], woman; your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule [Note: [Col. 1305C] *Dominatur*, “he rules,” in the Paris edition.] over you.  
> (Gen. 3:16)

And do you not know that you are Eve? God’s sentence upon that sex lives on in this age; therefore her guilt must necessarily live on as well. You are the devil’s gateway. You are the unsealer of that tree. You are the first deserter of the divine law. You are she who persuaded [Note: [Col. 1305C] Semler: “advised.”] him whom the devil was not strong enough to attack. You so easily shattered man, the image of God. On account of what you deserved—that is, death—even the Son of God had to die. And does it enter your mind to adorn yourself over your tunics of skins?

Come now: if from the beginning of creation the sheep of Miletus had been shorn, the Seres had spun from trees, the Tyrians had dyed, the Phrygians had embroidered, and the Babylonians had woven; if pearls had gleamed white and thunderstones flashed [Note: [Col. 1305D] “Thunderstones flashed.” The *ceraunia* is a gem, white and gleaming red, so called as though from thunder, for κεραυνός means “thunderbolt.” Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 9: “Among the white gems is also the one called *ceraunia*.” The neuter *ceraunium* is also used; St. Jerome, *Letter to Demetrias*: “with the flames of thunderstones.” LE PR.]; if gold itself had already emerged from the earth accompanied by greed; if even a mirror [Note: [Col. 1305C] Junius: “from a mirror.”] had already been permitted to lie so greatly—then even this Eve, expelled from paradise and already dead, would, I suppose, have desired these things [Note: [Col. 1305C] “Had been permitted; this Eve had desired,” in François; Semler, following Rhenanus: “desired.”].

Therefore, even now, if she desires to live again, she ought neither to seek nor to know the things that she neither possessed nor knew when she was alive. All these things are accordingly the impedimenta of a condemned and dead woman, arranged as though for the pageantry of her funeral.

## CHAPTER II
[Col. 1305C] For those who instituted these things are themselves reckoned among the condemned, destined for the punishment of death: namely, those angels who rushed down from heaven to the daughters of men, so that this disgrace also might attach to woman. For when they disclosed to a far more inexperienced world certain materials that had rightly been concealed and many arts that had not rightly been revealed [Col. 1306A]—inasmuch as they had uncovered the working of metals [Note: [Col. 1305D] “Inasmuch as they had uncovered the working of metals.” In the excerpts of George Syncellus, the following is taken from Book I of Enoch: “Exael, the tenth of the rulers, taught them to make swords and breastplates and every implement of war, and to work the metals of the earth” (Ἐξαὴλ ὁ δέκατος τῶν ἀσχόντων ἐδίδαξεν ποιεῖν μαχαίρας καὶ θώρακας καὶ πᾶν σκεῦος πολεμικὸν, καὶ τὰ μέταλλα τῆς γῆς). RIG.], disclosed the properties of herbs [Note: [Col. 1305D] “The properties of herbs and the powers of incantations.” In the same place: “drugs, incantations, wisdom, and means of release from spells” (φαρμακείας, ἐπαοιδίας, σοφίας καὶ ἐπαοίδων λυτήρια). RIG.], made public the powers of incantations [Note: [Col. 1305C] Others read “promulgated,” which Junius prefers.], and marked out every species of esoteric inquiry, extending even to the interpretation of the stars [Note: [Col. 1305D] “The interpretation of the stars”: astrology (ἀστροσκοπίαν). RIG.]—they bestowed particularly and, as it were, peculiarly upon women this equipment of feminine glory [Note: [Col. 1305D] “Equipment of feminine glory”: “adornment for women” (κοσμία ταῖς γυναιξίν). RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1305D] “Feminine glory.” He censures the affected splendor of women who, although Christians, nevertheless went about no less elaborately dressed and adorned than pagans; for that creature is especially fond of adornment (φιλόκοσμον) and proud. LE PR.]: the brilliance of the little stones [Note: [Col. 1306D] “The brilliance of the little stones”: “and the choice stones” (καὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς λίθους). RIG.] with which necklaces are variegated; rings of gold with which arms are encircled; dyes made from coloring matter [Note: [Col. 1306D] “Dyes made from coloring matter”: “polishing and beautifying” (τὸ στιλβεῖν καὶ τὸ καλλωπίζειν). RIG.] with which wool is colored [Note: [Col. 1306C] Junius reads “cheeks.”]; and that very black powder by which the outlines [Note: [Col. 1306C] Junius reads “outer corners.”] of the eyes are extended.

What sort of things these are [Note: [Col. 1306C] Others read, “what they presently are.”] can already be determined from the character and condition of their teachers: sinners could neither reveal nor provide anything conducive to integrity; lovers, nothing conducive to chastity [Note: [Col. 1306C] Junius reads “lovers” rather than “adulterers.”]; spirits who deserted God, nothing conducive to the fear of God. [Col. 1306B] If these are to be called teachings, bad teachers must necessarily have taught badly. If they were rewards for lust, no reward for a shameful act is honorable. But what was so important about revealing these things—or about bestowing them [Note: [Col. 1306C] Franeker and Rigault read “or”]? Was it that women could not please men without materials for splendor and devices for beauty, although, while still uncultivated, unadorned, and—so to speak—raw and rude, they had moved angels? Or [Note: [Col. 1306C] Franeker and Rigault read *anne*; Junius, *an ne*.] would their lovers have seemed mean and insultingly parsimonious if they had bestowed nothing upon the women they had enticed into marriage?

But it is impossible to suppose that women who possessed angels could desire anything more [Note: [Col. 1306D] “Nothing more.” This is his own idiom: “My priests marry no more.” RIG.]; they had, of course, made a magnificent marriage. In truth, those who must sometimes have reflected upon the place from which they had fallen and, after the heated moments of their lusts, sighed for heaven, rewarded that very good which women possessed—their natural [Col. 1306C] beauty—as the cause of evil, so that their own happiness might not profit them, but that, dragged down [Note: [Col. 1306C] Franeker, Paris, and Rigault read “dragged down”; Wouwer, “conquered.”] from simplicity and sincerity, they might arrive together with those angels at an offense against God. They knew for certain that every kind of ostentation, ambition, and studied effort to please through the flesh is displeasing to God.

These, indeed, are the angels [Note: [Col. 1306D] “These are the angels,” etc. The holy Fathers often touch upon this rite of renunciation, by which those about to enter the waters of baptism declared under the hand of the presiding minister that they renounced the devil. Basil, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*: “to renounce Satan and his angels” (ἀποτάσσεσθαι τῷ σατανᾷ καὶ τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτοῦ). So too Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, Book II, chapter 2, calls this renunciation an *apotagē* (ἀποταγήν), and says that it was customary for the one making the renunciation to blow three times against Satan. LAC.] whom we are to judge [Col. 1307A]; these are the angels whom we renounce in the baptismal bath. These, surely, are the things through which they deserved to be judged by man. What, then, will their possessions do [Note: [Col. 1307B] Franeker and Rigault read “do.”] in the presence of their judges? What fellowship is there between those who will condemn and those who are to be condemned? [Note: [Col. 1307C] “What fellowship is there between those who will condemn and those who are to be condemned?” It is as though he were forbidding Christian women every association or conformity with pagan women. For when that excessive cultivation and splendor were censured, they offered nothing else in their defense except the necessity of conducting business and dealing with pagans. Yet here, although he does not condemn such dealings when kinship, the necessity of one’s office, or something similar sometimes required them, he forbids the condemnable splendor of pagans in a Christian woman. LE PR.] The same, I think, as between Christ and Belial.

With what confidence shall we ascend [Note: [Col. 1307B] Junius reads “shall we ascend,” future tense.] that tribunal to pronounce judgment against those whose gifts we covet? For the same angelic nature is also promised to you then, the same sex [Note: [Col. 1307C] “For the same sex is promised to you as to men.” That is, none. Thus Ovid, in Jupiter’s banquet in the story of Philemon, after saying that all the food was served in earthenware, says: “Afterward a mixing bowl, engraved in the same silver, is set before them”—that is, in no silver, for the mixing bowl too was earthenware. Thus Tertullian says here that women received into heaven will have the same sex as men—that is, none, since men too will not retain their own. Both will be stripped of their sex: they will be like angels, neither a male angel nor a female angel. So he himself says in *Against the Valentinians*. In both places, however, by the term “sex” he means the functions of the sexes, not their natural bodily forms. For in his book *On the Resurrection* he demonstrates that they will return to their own bodies. RIG.] as men, and the same privilege of judging [Note: [Col. 1307D] “The same sex, the same privilege of judging, is promised.” Under civil law the function of judging is counted among the duties of men, from which it was decided that women should be excluded. But in God’s presence, since among human beings who are now heavenly there are no longer any functions of the sexes, a common privilege of judging is granted in the shared glory of the saints—whether to one formerly a man or formerly a woman—in accordance with the prerogative of holiness and blessedness. RIG.]. Therefore, unless we have already prejudged the matter here by condemning beforehand their possessions, which we are then to condemn in them, they instead will judge and condemn us.

## CHAPTER III

I know that the Scripture of Enoch, which assigned this order of events to the angels [Col. 1307B], is not accepted by some because it is not admitted into the Jewish archive [Note: [Col. 1307D] “Nor is it admitted into the Jewish archive.” That is, into that canon of Scripture which was preserved in the temple of the Hebrew people through the diligence of successive generations of priests. Augustine interprets it thus in Book XV, chapter 23 of *The City of God*. Likewise in Book XII *Against Faustus*, where he says of the Jewish nation: “What else is that nation today but a kind of record keeper for the Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony in support of the Church, so that we may honor through the sacrament what it announces through the letter?” And on Psalm 56: “The Jew carries the book from which the Christian may believe. They have been made our copyists, just as servants customarily carry books behind their masters, so that the former grow weary from carrying while the latter profit from reading.” And on Psalm 58: “They possess the books in which Christ was prophesied, and we possess Christ.” What Augustine says about servants carrying books behind their masters must be understood of book-box bearers, who are mentioned in Book III *On Those Manumitted by the Rod*: “If he is a foster-brother, tutor, or book-box bearer—that is, one who carries books.” Juvenal:

> Whom the keeper—a household slave of the narrow book-box—follows.

RIG.]. They suppose, I think, that because it was composed before the Flood it could not have survived that catastrophe of the world, which destroyed all things.

If this is their reasoning, let them remember that Noah, Enoch’s own great-grandson, survived the Flood. By reason of his family connection and hereditary tradition, he had surely heard and remembered both the favor enjoyed by his great-grandfather in God’s sight and all his prophecies, since Enoch had charged his son Methuselah with nothing other than transmitting knowledge of them to his descendants. Therefore Noah could undoubtedly have succeeded [Col. 1308A] to the commission of proclaiming them, especially since he would not otherwise have remained silent either about the providence of God, his preserver, or about the glory of his own house.

Even if the matter did not stand so readily upon this basis, another consideration would uphold the authority of that Scripture. Noah could equally well have reconstituted through the Spirit a work destroyed by the violence of the Flood, just as, after Jerusalem had been destroyed in the Babylonian conquest, it is agreed that the whole corpus of Jewish literature [Note: [Col. 1308D] “The whole corpus of Jewish literature.” It is agreed that the Old Testament was restored by Ezra and that certain things were altered or added by him or by Joshua, such as the accounts of Moses’ death and burial. LE PR.] was restored through Ezra.

But since Enoch also prophesied of the Lord in that same Scripture, nothing whatever that pertains to us should be rejected by us [Note: [Col. 1307B] Junius punctuates as follows: “should be rejected; because it pertains to us. And we read … to be inspired.”]. And we read that “every Scripture suitable for edification is divinely inspired” (2 Tim. 3:16). It may now be thought [Note: [Col. 1308B] Semler places “afterward” here.] to have been rejected [Note: [Col. 1308B] The same editor reads “rejected,” accusative.] by the Jews for precisely the same reason as almost all the other writings that proclaim Christ. Nor indeed is it remarkable [Col. 1308B] that they did not accept certain Scriptures that spoke of the one whom they were not going to accept even when he spoke in their presence. To this is added the fact that Enoch [Note: [Col. 1308D] “To this is added the fact that Enoch possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude.” Jerome observes in his commentary on Ephesians 5 that Paul too cited certain things from apocryphal writings. Jerome himself also relates from the Book of Enoch the story of the angels descending upon Mount Hermon to the daughters of men, in his *Commentary on Psalm 13*—“not,” he says, “as an authority, but as a commemoration.” And in his letter to Laeta, on the education of her daughter, he says that apocryphal works may be read, not for the truth of their doctrines but out of reverence for their signs. Likewise, in his commentary on Titus 1: “Those who think that one must accept an entire book because someone has used part of that book seem to me also bound to receive among the Scriptures of the Church the apocryphal Enoch, from which the Apostle Jude placed a testimony in his epistle, as well as many other things that the Apostle Paul spoke from hidden writings.” RIG.] possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude (Jude 14).

## CHAPTER IV

For the moment, let no mark of prior condemnation be branded upon feminine display on account of the fate of its authors. Let nothing be imputed to those angels except their rejection of heaven and their marriage to flesh. Let us examine the qualities of the things themselves, so that we may also detect the designs of the desire directed toward them.

[Col. 1309A] A woman’s outward presentation comprises two forms [Note: [Col. 1309C] “A woman’s outward presentation comprises two forms: cultivation and adornment.” On account of this distinction, two titles would suit these two books: this one, *On the Cultivation of Women*—that is, on gold, gems, and clothing; the following one, *On the Adornment of Women*—that is, on care of the hair and skin, etc. RIG.]: cultivation and adornment. By “cultivation” we mean what they call a woman’s *mundus* or finery; by “adornment,” what ought to be called a woman’s *immundus* or defilement. The former is reckoned to consist in gold, silver, gems, and clothing; the latter, in the care of the hair, the skin, and those parts of the body that attract the eyes. Against the one we bring the charge of ambition; against the other, of prostitution. From this point, then, servant of God, you may see what among these things accords with your discipline, since you are governed by principles of a different kind—namely, humility [Note: [Col. 1309B] Others read “humanity,” less correctly.] and chastity.

## CHAPTER V

Gold and silver, the chief materials of worldly cultivation, must necessarily correspond to the place from which they come: the earth, of course, rendered all the more glorious because, amid the death-dealing workshops [Note: [Col. 1309C] “Death-dealing workshops.” For condemned persons were sentenced to labor in the mines, and Christians were often among them. Of these the martyr Cyprian says in Letter 25, Book III: “In the mines, the body is not cherished with a bed and mattress. Limbs exhausted by labor lie upon the ground. Unwashed, the members grow squalid, deformed by neglect and filth. Bread there is scanty; those who freeze lack clothing; the hair of the half-shorn head bristles,” etc. RHEN.] of the accursed mines, lamented under penal labor [Note: [Col. 1309D] “Lamented under penal labor”: watered by the tears and lamentation of the condemned. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1309C] Franeker reads “assigned.” There is no need.] [Note: [Col. 1309D] “Penal labor.” Thus Cyprian speaks of “the dreadful prison and the deathly darkness of the place of punishment”; likewise, “the squalor of the prison and the horror of the penal enclosure.” And in *To Donatus*: “He persists in clinging tenaciously to punishment with its wailings.” RHEN.], the fugitive from the mine [Note: [Col. 1309D] “From instruments of torture into ornaments.” Here he elegantly joins contraries, the first member being further commended by paronomasia. Hence Ambrose’s remark: “But you, blessed virgins, who know such things as instruments of torture rather than ornaments.” RHEN.] leaves behind the name of earth in the fire and is transformed thereafter from instruments of torture into ornaments, from punishments into pleasures, from disgrace into honors [Note: [Col. 1309D] “The fugitive from the mine.” As though, having been condemned to the mine, it had escaped from there. Here one may observe a splendid contest of wit between our Septimius and the words of Pliny at the beginning of Book XXXIII. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1309D] “The fugitive from the mine.” Understand this of bracelets or necklaces. You will find this manner of speaking in the law *aut damnum*, Digest, *On Penalties*: “And that a fugitive from labor [Col. 1310C] in the mines,” etc.; the law is speaking of a severe punishment. And in the law *milites*, Digest, *On Military Affairs*: “because he is a fugitive from custody, not a deserter from military service.” LE PR.].

Yet iron, bronze, and the other cheapest materials share the same condition of terrestrial origin and mining labor; consequently, the substance of gold and silver cannot be judged any nobler than they are by nature. But [Note: [Col. 1309C] Latinius reads “What.”] if gold and silver derive their glory from the quality of their use, then iron and bronze possess it to an even greater degree. Their utility has been so ordered that they both provide human affairs with a greater number of services, and more necessary ones, and nevertheless, in their own turn [Note: [Col. 1310B] Semler reads “their service.”], put gold and silver to use for more legitimate purposes. Rings too [Note: [Col. 1310C] “Rings too.” On that practice of wearing rings, see Clement of Alexandria in the summary of the Christian life near the end of Book III of the *Paedagogus*. LE PR.] are made of iron; and the memory of antiquity still preserves certain little vessels for food and drink made of bronze. Never mind whether the insane abundance of gold and silver has also descended to filthy implements [Note: [Col. 1310B] Others read “among filthy implements.”].

Certainly no field is cultivated by the labor of gold, and no ship is joined together by the strength of silver. No mattock [Note: [Col. 1310C] The Venetian edition and Semler read “nothing.”] drives gold into the earth; no nail forces silver into planks. I pass over the necessities of the whole of life, which rest upon iron and bronze, since those rich materials themselves could neither be dug again from the mines nor brought into any form of use without the effective strength of iron and bronze [Note: [Col. 1310C] Franeker and Latinius read “cannot be serviceable.”]. We must therefore now consider whence so great a dignity attaches to gold and silver, when they are preferred to materials that are both related to them in origin [Note: [Col. 1310C] “Related in origin.” He calls those materials related which belong to the same class and have the same origin—namely, the bowels of the earth. RIG.] [Col. 1310B] and superior in utility.

## CHAPTER VI

And those little stones that combine pride with gold—what else am I to interpret them as but little stones and pebbles, tiny fragments of the same earth [Note: [Col. 1310C] “Tiny fragments of the earth.” To lower the value of little stones and gems, he calls them crumbs of the earth. Thus in Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, Book II, chapter 12, they are called “the vomitings of a foreign sea and scrapings of the earth” (ἀπεξενωμένης θαλάσσης ἐκβράσματα· καὶ τῆς γῆς ἐκψήγματα). LE PR.], and yet necessary neither for laying foundations, raising walls, supporting pediments, nor compacting roofs [Note: [Col. 1310D] “Or compacting couches.” He is speaking of African roofs and those of eastern regions, which resemble what we call terraces. The Germans call them *terras*, as though *terracium*. RHEN.]? They have learned to build up only this female stupefaction [Note: [Col. 1310C] Agobard’s manuscript reads “formerly.”] [Note: [Col. 1310D] “They have learned to build up only this female stupefaction.” Septimius says that the little stones and pebbles which women customarily value against gold are useless for the practical needs of buildings and can build nothing except women’s pride. That is, women, raised up by pride, appear stunned and rigid, like statues placed and fixed for spectacle and admiration. Latin authors call astonishing things *stupenda*, and use *stupere* for “to marvel.” Juvenal: “No one marveled more at the turbot.” Our Septimius transferred the meaning of this verb to foolish pride. Thus he will call glory vain and stupefied. So in Book I *Against Marcion*: “The Marcionites build up their stupefaction with a raised brow.” So in Book II *To the Nations*: “Attic stupefactions.” So Cyprian, Letter 42: “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to his doctrine, he is puffed up with stupefaction.” RHEN.], because they are laboriously polished so as to gleam, cunningly mounted so as to sparkle, and anxiously pierced so as to hang; and they and gold lend each other reciprocal enticement.

But [Note: [Col. 1311C] Others insert “And.”] if ambition fishes anything from the British or Indian sea, it is a species of shellfish whose taste, I do not say is no more agreeable than purple shellfish or oyster, but not even than a large mussel. For it is as fruits of the sea that I know shellfish. But if that shell develops some swelling within itself [Note: [Col. 1311C] Semler and Rhenanus read “demands.”], it ought to be regarded more as its disease than as its glory. And although it is called a pearl, it must nevertheless be understood as nothing other than a certain hard and rounded wart belonging to that shell.

They say that gems are also extracted from the foreheads of dragons, just as there is a certain stony substance in the brains of fish. This too was lacking [Note: [Col. 1311C] Junius and Rigault read “was lacking.”] to a Christian woman—that she should make herself more ornate by means of a serpent! In this fashion she will tread upon [Note: [Col. 1311C] “Thus she will tread upon the devil’s head.” From this it is evident that Tertullian read Genesis 3 as follows: “And she shall crush your head.” RIG.] the devil’s head, while from his head she constructs ornaments for her own neck or even her own head [Note: [Col. 1311C] Others read the singular, “an ornament.”].

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 1311B]

All these things derive their attractiveness solely from rarity and foreign origin. Indeed, within the bounds of their native countries they are not held in such esteem. Abundance is always insulting to itself [Note: [Col. 1311C] “Insulting to itself.” Above he said that our Lord treated himself with contempt. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1311C] Pamelius reads “itself,” nominative.]. Among certain barbarians, because gold is native and plentiful, they keep prisoners in workhouses bound with gold and burden criminals with riches, making them wealthier in proportion to their wickedness. At last it has truly been discovered how even gold may not be loved.

We have also seen at Rome the nobility of gems blushing before matrons at the disdain shown them by the Parthians, Medes, and their other native peoples [Col. 1312A] [Note: [Col. 1311C] Junius distinguishes the sentence with a full stop.], except that they are scarcely regarded even as objects of display [Note: [Col. 1311C] Others read “ostentation.”]. Emeralds lie hidden in rings [Note: [Col. 1311C] Semler reads “girdles”; Pamelius, “individual settings.”] [Note: [Col. 1311D] “Emeralds lie hidden in rings.” So reads Agobard’s manuscript. By “rings” he means necklaces. He himself said above: “rings of gold with which arms are encircled.” RIG.]; the sword alone, beneath the fold of its wearer’s garment, knows the cylinders upon its sheath; and pearls set in boots seek to emerge from the mud. In short, nothing [Note: [Col. 1312C] Semler omits “nothing.”] they possess is so richly jeweled as that which ought not to be jeweled, if it does not appear—or appears precisely so that it too may be shown to be treated with neglect.

## CHAPTER VIII

Likewise, even their slaves wear the distinction of colored garments. They also misuse for wall hangings, in place of paintings, Tyrian, hyacinthine, and those royal fabrics that you laboriously unravel and refashion. Among them purple is cheaper than red ocher.

For what rightful honor can garments possess through the adulteration [Col. 1312B] of wrongful colors? [Note: [Col. 1311D] “What rightful honor can garments possess through the adulteration of wrongful colors?” He censures the luxury of women who introduced into garments colors not native to the fleece or wool—namely, purple, hyacinth, and scarlet. He calls these wrongful colors and adulterations. “What God did not produce,” he says, “does not please him.” Then, with a smile: “Unless, perhaps, he was unable to command purple and sky-blue sheep to be born.” He next continues seriously: “If he was able, then he did not will it; what God did not will may not be fabricated.” This is also a notable and most powerful argument applicable to graver matters. He therefore concludes that colors which wool does not possess as its own are wrongful and consequently adulterous. He soon explains the argument and says that wool of this kind, steeped in colors not its own, lends garments a wrongful honor. Garments dyed with a foreign and ostentatious color possess a wrongful honor, splendor, or brilliance that does not pertain to Christian decency and modesty. RIG.]

What God did not himself produce does not please him—unless, perhaps, he was unable to command purple and sky-blue [Note: [Col. 1312C] So the oldest manuscript reads; others have “airy.” Rigault reads “sky-blue.” Rhenanus read “spring-green,” from the Greek ἐαρινά; so too Franeker and Paris. Others read *arinas*. Junius interprets both readings as referring to a green color.] sheep [Note: [Col. 1312C] “Unless, perhaps, he was unable to command purple and sky-blue sheep to be born.” This is exactly how the oldest manuscript reads, not *aerias*, as was printed until now. By *aerinae* sheep he means sheep of the color of the sky, a color Ovid praises as particularly attractive in women’s garments. After mentioning Tyrian murex, Ovid immediately adds:

> Since so many colors have appeared at a lower price,  
> What madness is it to carry one’s fortune upon one’s body?  
> Behold the color of the sky, when the air is free of clouds  
> And the warm south wind does not stir the waters into rain.
] to be born? If he was able, then he did not will it; and what God did not will may certainly not be fabricated. These things, therefore, which do not come from God, the author of nature, are not naturally excellent; they are thus understood to come from the devil, the corrupter of nature. For they cannot belong to anyone else if they do not belong to God, because things that are not God’s must necessarily belong to his rival; and no one besides the devil and his angels is God’s rival.

But if the materials come from God [Note: [Col. 1312D] “But if the materials come from God, it does not immediately follow that products of this kind made from them do also.” After that most severe censor has proscribed hyacinthine, purple, and sky-blue garments, and other instruments of luxury of that kind, under a harsh condemnation, he answers the objection of those who repeatedly asserted that all the things he attacked so vehemently had been created by God, just like everything else; that those marvelous colors were made from the juices of plants and the secretions of shellfish; and that plants and shellfish were rightly counted among the things created by God and created for the sake of human beings. He therefore dissolves the sophistry by making a distinction. He acknowledges that the materials come from God—plants, I mean, and shellfish, their juices, and those famous secretions of shellfish. But he denies that the use and enjoyment of those things comes from God when they are converted into preparations for wickedness and luxury. He proves this by the example of spectacles—the circus, the arena, and the stage. A human being may indeed look upon or praise horses, panthers, and the voice as things created by God and as divine gifts. Yet it does not immediately follow that the use made of those things comes from God—for example, the use of horses for the insane factions in the circus, of panthers or lions for foul disembowelments and savage slaughters, or of stage performers’ voices for empty or indecent stories. These things do not come from God, any more than idolatry does, even though the incense, wine, and fire through which idolatry is performed were created by God. “But,” he says, “if the materials come from God, it does not immediately follow that products of this kind made from them do also; for all those profane pleasures of worldly spectacles, just like idolatry itself—as we have published our own volume about them—consist of things belonging to God,” etc. RIG.—“About them” (another reading has “about those things”), “his own volume”: namely, the book *On the Spectacles*. EDD.], it does not immediately follow that products of this kind made from them do also [Note: [Col. 1312C] Latinius proposed another text: “But if the materials come from God, it does not immediately follow that a product of this kind lies hidden in everything; the question is whence it comes.”]. For all [Col. 1313A] those profane pleasures of worldly spectacles—as we published a volume specifically about them—and even idolatry itself consist of things belonging to God. Yet a Christian ought not on that account be affected by the frenzies of the circus, the atrocities of the arena, or the obscenities of the stage merely because God gave the horse, the panther, and the voice to humankind. Nor will a Christian practice idolatry with impunity merely because incense [Note: [Col. 1313C] “Incense is God’s creation.” Incense was created by God. Here “creation” means a created thing. RIG.], wine, the fire that consumes [Note: [Col. 1313C] “The fire that consumes”: that devours the victims. RIG.], and the animals made into victims are God’s creation, since the very material that is worshiped also belongs to God.

Thus, therefore [Note: [Col. 1313B] Rhenanus reads: “Thus neither here, therefore—excused; alien to God, so that—of glory, the world.” Junius reads similarly. Semler reads: “Thus, I say, also concerning the use of the materials, an evaluation descending from God is for that reason excused.”], with respect to the use of materials, an evaluation descending from God [Note: [Col. 1313C] “Thus, therefore, with respect to the use of materials, an evaluation descending from God.” Here too we have allowed some room for conjecture, but in such a way that the reasoning ought to remain sound before judges who are not unfair. Tertullian calls the use of things created by God an “act,” when we do something with them, when we employ them for some act or action of whatever kind. Materials, or created things, have a twofold evaluation—that is, they are assessed and valued from two different perspectives. A Christian, for example, will assess a horse differently from a pagan. A Christian will use a horse to support the weakness of nature or age; to arrive more promptly for the celebration of sacrificial offerings or for administering or hearing the word of God; to assist a brother in distress more swiftly; or to arrange more conveniently for a man wounded by robbers to be carried to an inn. But a pagan will buy a horse at a higher price than a tutor and will take greater care over its training than over his son’s, so that it may race around the turning posts in the circus with practiced bends, outrun its opponent, and seize the palm—with no other result than that it is exalted by the shouts of a maddened populace:

> Conspicuous in flight before the rest, and first to raise dust upon the plain.

Tertullian therefore says that one and the same material, one and the same animal, possesses two utterly different evaluations. The former, which we have illustrated in the Christian, is a truly praiseworthy and holy evaluation descending from God; the latter, which we have illustrated in the pagan, is foreign, alien, and adulterous. “And the evaluation,” he says, “descending from God therefore accuses and condemns the evaluation alien to God, as guilty, namely, of worldly and thoroughly un-Christian glory.” RIG.] accuses what is alien to God, as guilty, namely, of worldly glory.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1313B] For whatever things [Note: [Col. 1313B] The Venetian edition reads “certain things.”] have been distributed by God as materials [Note: [Col. 1313B] The Venetian edition reads “of the sea.”] throughout the several lands and each individual region are foreign to one another, mutually rare among strangers, but among their own people are rightly either desired or neglected [Note: [Col. 1313B] Others read “and among.”] [Note: [Col. 1313B] Others read “their own.”] [Note: [Col. 1313B] Junius reads “rightly thus.”], as the case may be, because the passion for glory is not so intense toward objects that leave those at home cold.

But from the distribution of possessions that God arranged as he willed [Col. 1314A], rarity and foreign origin—always finding favor among outsiders—arouse [Note: [Col. 1314B] Junius reads “excite.”] a desire to possess, simply because people do not have what God placed elsewhere. From this another vice develops: the desire to possess without moderation; for even if something ought perhaps to be possessed, moderation is nevertheless required.

This will be ambition [Note: [Col. 1314B] Rhenanus and Semler read “was.”], and from this its very name must be interpreted [Note: [Col. 1314B] “Must be” is absent from other editions.]: it is born when desire circles about (*ambiente*) within the mind, aspiring to glory—a grand aspiration, of course, commended, as we have said, not by nature or truth, but by the mind’s diseased passion, desire. And [Note: [Col. 1314B] Latinius reads “As.”] so it is with the other vices of ambition and glory. In this way it inflames the prices of things, so that it may inflame itself as well. Does not [Note: [Col. 1314B] Rhenanus, Latinius, and Rigault read, “For does not desire become so much greater …?”] desire become greater in proportion to the greatness it has conferred upon what it desires?

From [Note: [Col. 1314B] Semler omits “from.”] [Col. 1314B] the smallest jewel boxes a great patrimony is brought forth. Ten times one hundred thousand sesterces are strung upon a single thread [Note: [Col. 1314C] “Ten times one hundred thousand sesterces are strung upon a single thread.” He means pearls, which women wear upon a thread after they have been pierced.
