Scaevola speaks of “a string of pearls” in Law 26 on the Falcidian Law. Ulpian’s Law 27 on the Aquilian Law concerns pearls upon a string. RIG.]. A tender neck carries woodland estates and islands [Note: [Col. 1314B] Others read “carries around.”]; the delicate skin of the ears spends an entire account book of loans; and the left hand plays, upon each separate finger, with the contents of a separate moneybag [Note: [Col. 1314B] “Upon” is absent from Franeker and Rigault.]. Such are the powers of ambition: to make one tiny female body carry the principal [Note: [Col. 1314D] “The principal of such vast interest-bearing sums.” He speaks of the “principal of interest-bearing sums,” just as Scaevola speaks of “the principal of an account book” in Law 34, *On Legacies*, Book III. The “principal of interest-bearing sums” is the original sum or capital; the Greeks call it οὐσία, κεφάλαιον, and ἀρχαῖον. Thus on the following page he will say, “the whole substance of the faith”; in *Against Praxeas*, “the whole substance of the question”; and in *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, “You will acquire a great substance of holiness.” RIG.] of such vast interest-bearing sums.

# BOOK II

[Note: [Col. 1315C] So many passages of this book were altered by Rigault on the authority of the Agobard manuscript that it appears to have been made almost a new work. Accordingly, in the following pages we have recorded the principal textual variation in such a way that we attribute the new recension to Rigault and use Semler’s name to indicate the received text. LEOPOLD.]

[Note: [Col. 1315C] In this second treatise *On the Cultivation of Women*, many subjects from the first are treated more fully, and not a few new ones are presented to greater practical effect; all are filled with a more sublime Christian spirit. Matters hitherto polluted by errors are restored to their native splendor in such a way that they ought to be regarded as almost new. Nevertheless, certain points in the corrections themselves must be examined closely, since only the most attentive readers will distinguish them. It will therefore be worthwhile to provide an index. RIG.]

[Col. 1315]

## [SUMMARY]

[Col. 1315A] **SUMMARY.—**This book has almost the same subject as the preceding one, except that it censures the care of the hair and skin more particularly.

I. He teaches that the chastity befitting God’s female servants, by which they differ from pagans, consists wholly in simple cleanliness. Chapter I.

II. Excessive attention to pleasing through adornment opens the way to temptations and places those who look upon it in danger. Chapter II.

III. One must not glory in the flesh unless, when it has been mangled for Christ, it has endured so that the spirit may be crowned in it. Chapter III.

IV. Beauty will offer no spectacle to a believing husband, but will be an object of suspicion to an unbelieving one. Chapter IV.

V. God the craftsman is censured by those who anoint their skin with cosmetics, stain their cheeks, and smear their eyes. Chapter V.

VI. Those who, like German and Gallic women, change their hair with saffron dye [Col. 1315B] or attach curling arrangements made from another person’s hair make an evil omen for themselves and reserve destruction for themselves. Chapters VI–VIII.

VII. The colors of garments, works of gold, and precious stones come not from God but from sinful angels. Chapters IX–XI.

VIII. Indeed, Scripture establishes that the enticements of beauty are associated with bodies offered for prostitution. Chapter XII.

IX. Finally, their works ought to shine; they must cast away the luxuries by which the strength of faith can be rendered effeminate, since in the age of the Christians especially their lives were then passed amid the sword.

**THE EDITORS, FROM PAMELIUS.**

## CHAPTER ONE
Servants of the living God, my fellow servants and sisters, by that right which I am reckoned to share with you, I—the very least [Col. 1316A]—indeed by my right of fellowship in service and brotherhood, venture to address you, [Note: [Col. 1315D] *Postremissimus* (“the very least”). A superlative used by Gellius. Rigault later reads *equidem meo jure* (“indeed by my own right”), that is, by the right that belonged to him to write to women, since he was their brother and fellow servant. LE PR.—Perhaps it would be better to read: *Et quidem meo jure* (“And indeed by my own right”). EDD.] [Note: [Col. 1315C] Semler: *postremissimus omnium, qui de meo jure—ad* [Col. 1316C] *nos verba ista facere, non utique affectationi* (Rigault: *affectionis*) *sed*, etc.: “the very least of all, who by my own right—to address these words to us, certainly not for ostentation” (Rigault: “of affection”), “but,” etc.] certainly not out of affectation, but acting out of affection in the cause of your salvation.

That salvation—not only women’s, but men’s also—is established chiefly in the manifestation of chastity. For since we are all a temple of God, because the Holy Spirit has been brought into us and consecrated there, chastity is the keeper and high priest of that temple, [Note: [Col. 1316C] Rigault: “the female keeper and high priestess.”] permitting nothing unclean or profane to be brought into it, lest the God who inhabits it, offended by the defiled dwelling, abandon it. [Note: [Col. 1315D] “Which permits nothing unclean or profane.” Cyprian the martyr transferred this into his own treatise: “And let us take care,” he says, “that nothing unclean and profane be brought into the temple of God, lest, being offended, he abandon the dwelling which he inhabits.” RHEN.]

But our present subject is not chastity itself, for the urgent divine commandments everywhere are sufficient to enjoin and exact it, [Note: [Col. 1315D] “For the enjoining and exacting of which,” etc. The passages of Scripture by which chastity is enjoined may be seen in the books *On Chastity*, both the Author’s and St Cyprian’s. Rhenanus, however, notes that the phrase “for me to rebuke” is expressed in the dative case, that is, “worthy of my rebuke.” I, however, from three Vatican manuscripts, read: “But indeed they persist,” for “let them persist”; and “of their beauty and luster,” with Latinius—that is, displaying the same beauty. PAM.] but the matters pertaining to chastity, namely, how you ought to conduct yourselves. For most women—may God indeed permit me to rebuke this [in all things deserving rebuke]—[Col. 1316B] either in simple ignorance or in bold dissimulation conduct themselves as though chastity consisted solely in the integrity of the flesh and avoidance of fornication, and as though nothing further were required inwardly concerning the regulation of dress and adornment. But they persist in their former pursuits of beauty and luster, [Note: [Col. 1316C] Wouwerius. Rigault deleted “But indeed they persist in their former.”] displaying the same appearance of themselves [Note: [Col. 1316C] Thus Wouwerius; Semler: “displaying the same presentation of themselves”; Rigault: “displaying the same outward surface.”] as the women of the nations, who lack consciousness of true chastity, because there is nothing true in those who do not know God, the guardian and teacher of truth. [Note: [Col. 1316C] “The women of the nations.” What am I to say of these? Are they chaste? The Angylae—a nation—compel their women during the first nights of marriage to submit to adulteries, and afterward bind them to chastity by laws, as Solinus relates in his *Polyhistor*. It would take too long to speak of the rest. LAC.]

For even if some chastity can be believed to exist among the Gentiles, it is manifestly so imperfect and unformed that, although inwardly it may to some extent act with self-restraint, it nevertheless dissolves itself in freedom of dress, [Col. 1317A] perversely desiring among the Gentiles that very thing whose outcome it avoids. [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Nevertheless dissolves itself in freedom of dress.” The most ancient copy reads: “It dissolves itself into freedoms of outward display.” This may be explained without difficulty if one understands *ambitus* here as what Tertullian himself called the “outward surface” above: namely, the body and the ornaments of the body, which surround and clothe the mind. He is discussing Christian chastity and shows that it ought to be more perfect than Gentile chastity. He therefore says that Gentile chastity is so perverse that, although the mind steadfastly perseveres in its resolution never to violate chastity, chastity itself nevertheless so dissolves and breaks itself amid liberties of cultivating and adorning the body that it seeks the thing whose actual result it avoids—that is, it seeks to please and delights in drawing the sighs of young men after it, although it is unwilling to yield to the lust of another which it has itself aroused. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1317B] Semler: “It dissolves itself because of the truth” (another reading: “because of the vanity”) “of the Gentiles, seeking consolation,” etc.]

How many women, after all, do not even desire to please strangers? How many do not wish to paint themselves for that very purpose, and then deny that they have been desired? [Note: [Col. 1317C] “How many women, after all, do not even desire to please strangers?” How many chaste Christian women are there today, he asks, who are so austere and seriously chaste that they do not even desire to please strangers? Who do not take care to have themselves painted and adorned, if only to please them? How many, finally, are there who would wish to deny—or who would not be ashamed to deny—that they had ever been desired? Gentile chastity, though, is such that women do not actually sin, yet present themselves in such attire as to seem to want what they do not want; they walk in such a way that by their very gait and dress they do not refuse what shameless women promise. [Col. 1317D] He then presses the point: “What wonder? Everything that does not belong to God is perverse.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1317D] “Who do not wish to paint themselves for that very purpose.” Here he denounces the cosmetics and rouge that women used to give themselves luster; and in doing so, as Clement of Alexandria says in *Paedagogus* III.2, they seem to censure the Maker of all things for not having bestowed sufficient beauty. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 1317B] Rigault: “Who do not take care to have themselves painted for that very purpose—and deny” [Col. 1317C] “that they have been desired?”]

And yet this also is characteristic of Gentile chastity: not to sin, yet to wish to; or even not to wish to, yet not to refuse. What wonder is it? Everything that is not from God is perverse. Let those women, then, who do not possess the whole good, see how readily they mingle even what they do possess with evil. It is necessary for you to turn away from them in your manner of walking also, as in other matters, since you ought to be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect.

## CHAPTER II

You who are perfect—that is, Christian and chaste—should know that the desire to be desired must not merely be avoided, but [Col. 1317B] even abhorred. [Note: [Col. 1317C] Rigault: “Since perfect—that is, Christian—chastity,” etc., omitting the remaining words.] First, because the pursuit of pleasing through beauty does not arise from an unblemished conscience, since we know that beauty is naturally an invitation to lust. Why, then, do you arouse that evil against yourself? Why do you invite that to which you profess yourself a stranger?

Then, because we ought not to open a path to temptations. Sometimes—may God keep this far from his own—they accomplish their purpose by persistence; at the very least, they disturb the spirit through scandal. [Note: [Col. 1317D] Rigault reads: “At the very least, they raise a scandal in the spirit.” They shake and disquiet the spirit. For the faithful, or saints, possess the Spirit of God. Accordingly, if they admit anything arising from evil, they disturb the Spirit of God; for the sake of a worldly thing, they shake the Spirit they received from the Lord. Broad and extensive is the operation of evil, hurling manifold provocations at the spirit. Thus Tertullian himself speaks in the books *On Patience* and *On the Shows*: “God,” he says, “commanded that the Holy Spirit, as being tender and delicate because of the goodness of his nature, be treated with tranquillity, gentleness, quiet, and peace.” For this reason it pleased the Fathers of the Council of Elvira that candles should not be lit in a cemetery during the day, canon XXXIII: “For the spirits of the saints must not be disturbed.” They are disturbed by a profane and Gentile rite. At night, indeed, I think this would have been burdensome or troublesome to no one, since it is plainly necessary both for the assistance of light and as a testimony to chastity. We shall make some observations about candles and lamps lit during the day at Book II, *To His Wife*, on the words: “And she will proceed from a doorway crowned with laurel and lit with lamps, as though from a new council chamber of public lusts.” RIG.]

We ought indeed to conduct ourselves with such holiness and with the whole substance of faith that, assured and secure concerning our conscience, we desire this state to continue in us—yet without presumption. [Col. 1318A] For one who presumes fears less, takes fewer precautions, and is exposed to greater danger. [Note: [Col. 1317C] Rigault: “For one who presumes now fears less; one who fears less takes fewer precautions; one who takes fewer precautions is exposed to greater danger.”] Fear is the foundation of salvation; presumption is an impediment to fear. [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Presumption is an impediment to fear.” Prosper of Aquitaine discusses this argument—how necessary the fear of God is for attaining salvation—in Book III, chapter 11, of *The Contemplative Life*. There he also speaks of fear in opposition to presumption, as Tertullian does here; for he says that people cease to fear God when enticed by the hope of presumed impunity. LAC.]

It is therefore more advantageous that we hope we cannot sin than that we presume we cannot. For by hoping we shall fear; by fearing we shall take care; by taking care we shall be safe. Conversely, if we presume, neither fearing nor taking care, we shall hardly be safe. One who acts as though secure is not vigilant and does not possess sure and firmly grounded security. But one who is vigilant will truly be able to be secure. Let the Lord, indeed, in his mercy, take care of his own servants, so that they may even be happily permitted to presume upon his goodness toward them.

But why should we be a danger to another? Why should we bring lust upon another—a lust which, if [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Which, if God, by enlarging the law, does not distinguish in punishment from the deed of fornication, I do not know whether she who has been the cause of someone’s perdition will go unpunished.” Christ enlarged the law when he said: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you: Everyone who looks upon a woman to lust after her,” etc. RIG.] the Lord, by enlarging the law, does not distinguish in punishment from the deed of fornication, [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Not by enlarging the law.” Thus in the book *On Prayer*: “Thereafter the Lord openly, enlarging the law, ranks anger against a brother together with murder.” In the same sense he said in the book *On Monogamy*: “Those things which concern righteousness not only remain preserved, but are also enlarged.” RIG.] [Col. 1318B] [Note: [Col. 1318B] The Agobardine manuscript reads: “As though God, by not enlarging the law, does not distinguish lust in punishment from the deed of fornication.”] I do not know whether she who has been the cause of someone’s perdition will go unpunished. For he perishes at once in your beauty if he lusts after it; [Note: [Col. 1318B] Rigault: “as soon as he lusts after your beauty”; he also deleted [Col. 1318C] the words that follow and accepted the reading “he lusted after.”] he has already committed in his mind what he desired, and you have become a sword to him. [Note: [Col. 1318D] “You have become a sword to him.” Cyprian, in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*: “So that, even if you yourself do not perish, you nevertheless cause others to perish, presenting yourself as a sword and poison to those who see you.” RIG.]

Though you may be free of guilt, you will not be free of reproach. [Note: [Col. 1318C] Rigault: “a sword to him, so that, even if you are free of guilt, you will not be freed from reproach.”] It is as when a robbery has been committed on someone’s estate: the crime indeed does not touch its owner, [Note: [Col. 1318C] Rigault: “will not touch”; Semler: “does not bind him, yet the property,” etc.] but while his land is marked by the disgrace, he too is sprinkled with infamy. Are we to paint ourselves so that others may perish? Where, then, is: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”; “Do not care only for your own concerns, but also for another’s”? [Note: [Col. 1318C] Semler: “Do not care for your own concerns.”] No declaration of the Holy [Col. 1319A] Spirit should be directed and applied only to the matter immediately at hand, and not to every occasion of usefulness. [Note: [Col. 1319C] Semler: “can be.”]

Since, therefore, both our own cause and that of others are involved in the pursuit of most dangerous beauty, you should now know that you must reject not only the apparatus of fabricated and elaborately produced beauty, [Note: [Col. 1319C] Semler: “lust”; François du Jon: “desire.”] [Note: [Col. 1319C] “The apparatus of elaborately produced beauty.” These words must be understood not only of the hair, but of the adornment of the entire body; by *suggestus* understand “apparatus.” LE PR.] but must even obscure natural attractiveness through concealment and neglect, making it correspondingly troublesome to the assaults of the eyes. For although beauty is not to be accused—as a bodily felicity, as an addition to God’s handiwork, as a kind of elegant garment of the soul— [Note: [Col. 1319D] “As an addition to God’s handiwork.” Cyprian the martyr, *On the Dress of Virgins*: “Because God’s work, his production and handiwork, must in no way be adulterated.” RHEN.] [Note: [Col. 1319C] Thus Gelenius and the Frankfurt edition; Rigault: “a good garment”; Semler: “good clothing.”] it must nevertheless be feared because of the injury and violence of spectators. [Note: [Col. 1319C] Rigault: “violent pursuit, which,” etc.] Even Abraham, the father of faith, feared this because of his wife’s beauty and, by falsely calling Sarah his sister, redeemed his safety through dishonor. [Note: [Col. 1319D] “And falsely called Sarah his sister.” The manuscript reads: “And Isaac falsely called Rebecca his sister.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1319C] The Agobardine manuscript: “And Isaac falsely called Rebecca his sister.”] [Note: [Col. 1319D] “And falsely called Sarah his sister.” This passage has exercised the ingenuity of many. Those who had undertaken a defense of lying truly misuse this passage and twist it to their own meaning. On this matter St Augustine should be consulted in the book *On Lying, to Consentius*, and Book XXII *Against Faustus*. LE PR.]

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 1319B]

Now let the dignity of beauty not be feared; let it be considered neither burdensome to its possessors, nor ruinous to those who desire it, nor dangerous to those associated with it—not exposed to temptations, not surrounded by scandals. It is enough that it is unnecessary to God’s angels. [Note: [Col. 1319D] “God’s angels”: the faithful, the saints. RIG.] For where chastity is present, beauty is idle, because the proper use and fruit of beauty is sensual indulgence—unless someone supposes there to be another harvest from bodily attractiveness.

Let those women display the beauty given to them and seek beauty not given to them, who suppose that, when they furnish it to another, they are also furnishing to themselves what is demanded from beauty. [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Let those women display the beauty given to them and seek beauty not given to them, who suppose that they are also furnishing to themselves what is demanded from it, because they furnish it to another.” These words are to be read with the intonation of a question, as if he said: “Should not Christian women be ashamed to increase the natural attractiveness of their beauty, or, if it is lacking, to supply it by art and falsehood—women who suppose that they are also furnishing to themselves what is demanded from that beauty, namely, the kindling of more violent lust and thereby the destruction of the soul, because they furnish it to another?” Certainly, if they are truly Christian, they will think about themselves in no other way. RIG.—As it seems to me, however, there is no question here, but what rhetoricians call a concession: Tertullian concedes that only those women may concern themselves with beauty who wish to furnish the works of the flesh no less to themselves than to another. EDD.]

Someone will say: “What, then? Once sensual indulgence has been excluded and chastity admitted, is it not permissible merely to enjoy the praise of beauty and glory in the body’s good?” [Note: [Col. 1319C] Rigault: “Once chastity has been admitted, is praise of the body, its glory, permissible?”] Let whoever finds it helpful see to glorying in the flesh. For us, however, there is first of all [Col. 1319C] no pursuit of glory, because glory has the character of self-exaltation. But self-exaltation is incompatible with those who profess humility according to God’s ordinances. [Col. 1320A] Next, if all glory is vain and stupefied, how much more the glory that exists only in our flesh! [Note: [Col. 1320D] “If all glory is vain and stupefied.” He uses *stuporata* in the sense of foolish and dull. In this sense Catullus said: “This fool of mine sees nothing, hears nothing.” Tertullian himself, in the preceding book, where he speaks of precious stones and pebbles, says: “They knew only how to build up this stupefaction of women.” RIG.]

Even if there is something in which we should glory, we ought to desire to please in the goods of the spirit, not in the flesh, because we are followers of spiritual things. Let us rejoice in the things in which we labor; let us gather glory from those things from which we hope for salvation. Certainly, the Christian will glory even in the flesh—but when it has endured being torn apart for Christ, so that the spirit also may be crowned in it, not so that it may draw after itself the eyes and sighs of young men.

Thus, since beauty is altogether useless in you, you rightly should disdain it if you do not have it, and neglect it if you do. If a holy woman is naturally beautiful, let her not thereby become an occasion of sin; if she does, she certainly ought not to ignore her beauty, but even to obstruct it. [Note: [Col. 1320C] Rigault: “If holy women are naturally beautiful, let there not thereby be an occasion of sin; but if there is, she certainly ought not to assist it, but even to obstruct it.”]

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 1320B]

Speaking to you as though to Gentiles, by a Gentile precept common to everyone: you ought to please your husbands alone. [Note: [Col. 1320D] “You ought to please your husbands alone.” I do not recognize here the irony that Rhenanus supposes. I think the meaning is that Tertullian, forgetting his stricter discipline, permits women to go about somewhat more adorned, provided that they do so with no other intention than to please their husbands. For Clement of Alexandria likewise seems to make this concession, *Paedagogus* III, to those who have married less continent husbands. LE PR.] But you will please them precisely to the extent that you take no care to please others.

Be assured, blessed women: no wife is unattractive to her husband. She pleased him sufficiently when she was chosen, whether commended by her character or her beauty. Let none of you suppose that, if she moderates her personal adornment, she [Note: [Col. 1320C] We have thought that the pronoun *se* (“she”) should be inserted here. LEOP.] will incur her husband’s hatred and aversion. Every husband demands chastity. A believing husband, moreover, does not require beauty, because we are not captivated by the same goods that the Gentiles consider such; an unbelieving husband, on the other hand, even regards it with suspicion, if only because of that wicked opinion of the Gentiles concerning us. [Note: [Col. 1320C] Rigault: “from that wicked opinion concerning us.”]

For whom, then, are you nurturing your beauty? If your husband is a believer, he does not demand it; if [Col. 1320C] a Gentile, he does not trust it. [Note: [Col. 1320C] Rigault: “If for an unbeliever, he does not believe it to be innocent.”] Why are you eager to please either one who suspects you or one who does not desire it?

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1321A]

These things are certainly not suggested to you in order to commend an altogether crude and savage appearance; [Note: [Col. 1321C] Rigault: “These things should not be suggested in favor of a crude,” etc.] nor are we recommending the virtue of filth and foulness, [Note: [Col. 1321C] Semler: “concerning the body’s good, filth—but concerning foulness we advise.”] but proper measure, balance, and rightness in caring for the body. [Note: [Col. 1321C] “Rightness in caring for the body.” Thus, in the book *On the Pallium*, he used “the rightness of the pallium” to mean a pallium that fitted well and sat well; and above, “an unjust color.” RIG.] One must not go beyond what simple and sufficient cleanliness desires, beyond what is pleasing to the Lord.

Those women sin against him who smear their skin with cosmetics, [Note: [Col. 1321C] Rigault: “press upon.”] stain their cheeks with redness, and daub their eyes with soot. [Note: [Col. 1321C] “Their eyes with soot”: with antimony, *platyophthalmon* (πλατυόφθαλμον, “eye-enlarging cosmetic”). Thus above: “that same black powder by which the corners of the eyes are extended.” RIG.—“They extend their eyes with soot.” Perhaps the reading is *perlinunt* (“smear thoroughly”). He means the *kalliblepharon* (καλλιβλέφαρον, “eyelid beautifier”), which they used for the beauty of the eyelids. In Petronius, a boy adorns his mistress’s head with a topknot and even draws out her eyebrows from a cosmetic box. Martial, Book IX, epigram 38: “And may you lie hidden, put away in a hundred cosmetic boxes.” Juvenal: “He extends the eyebrow, stained with damp soot, with a slanting needle.” Philostratus praises his wife in a letter because she did not dye her cheeks with rouge and was numbered not among painted women but among the truly beautiful. In Clement of Alexandria and the ancient writers, as found in Athenaeus, Book XV, *ophthalmous hypographesthai* (ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑπογράφεσθαι, “to outline the eyes”) is the practice under discussion here. LE PR.] [Note: [Col. 1321C] Thus the Frankfurt edition and others; Semler: “gather”; Rigault: “extend.”]

Plainly, God’s handiwork is displeasing to them. [Note: [Col. 1321D] “God’s handiwork.” Cyprian: “God’s work, his production and handiwork, must in no way be adulterated.” RIG.] In their own persons they refute and censure the Craftsman of all things. [Note: [Col. 1321C] Rigault: “In their own persons they plainly accuse themselves.”] [Note: [Col. 1321D] “They censure the Craftsman,” etc. The love of adornment (*philokosmia*, φιλοκοσμία) was so displeasing to Tertullian that he did not hesitate to assert that the devil was its craftsman. For since what is born is God’s, it follows that what is added artificially is the devil’s work. He also warns that injury is done to God when his work is adorned with alien rouge and borrowed luster. LE PR.] For they censure him when they correct his work, when they add to it—taking, of course, those additions from a rival craftsman, namely, the devil. [Note: [Col. 1321C] Rigault: “those additions. He is the devil.”]

For who would teach people to alter the body except the one who also transfigured the human [Col. 1321B] spirit by wickedness? He undoubtedly devised contrivances of this kind so that, in us, he might in a certain manner lay hands upon God. [Note: [Col. 1321C] Rigault: “so that in you it may appear that you are in a certain manner laying hands upon God.”] [Note: [Col. 1322C] “Might lay hands upon God.” Cyprian: “They lay hands upon God when they strive to remake and [Col. 1322D] transfigure what he formed.” RIG.]

What is born is God’s work; therefore, what is fabricated is the devil’s business. [Note: [Col. 1322C] Rigault: “what is imposed” (*emplattetai*, ἐμπλάττεται, “is molded upon”).] How criminal it is to superimpose Satan’s contrivances upon God’s work! Our servants borrow nothing from our enemies; soldiers desire nothing from the enemy of their commander. For to request something for your use from the adversary of him in whose power you are is transgression. Will a Christian receive the help of that evil one in any matter? I do not know whether the name “Christian” will continue to belong to such a person. For that person will belong to the one by whose teachings he desires to be instructed.

How alien these things are to your disciplines and professions, how unworthy of the Christian name: to bear a fabricated face when all simplicity is enjoined upon you; to lie in your appearance when you are not permitted to lie [Col. 1321C] with your tongue; to seek [Note: [Col. 1322D] “To seek what has not been given.” The old manuscript: “what is not yours.” RIG.] what has not been given, [Note: [Col. 1322C] The Agobardine manuscript: “what is not yours.”] when you are commanded to practice abstinence from what belongs to another; to commit adultery in your appearance, [Col. 1322A] when your pursuit is chastity! [Note: [Col. 1322C] Rigault: “when abstinence from another’s property is handed down to you? To commit adultery in your appearance, when your pursuit should be chastity?”] Believe this, blessed women: how will you preserve God’s commandments when you do not preserve his lineaments in yourselves?

## CHAPTER VI

I see some women turning their hair yellow with saffron. They are even ashamed of their own nation because they were not born German or Gaulish; thus they transfer their homeland to their hair. [Note: [Col. 1322C] Rigault: “thus they now transform their hair.”] They take a bad—indeed, the worst—omen for themselves from their flame-colored heads, [Note: [Col. 1322D] “They take the worst omen for themselves from their flame-colored heads.” Thus, Book I *To His Wife*: “They handle the image of that unquenchable fire, the omens of their own punishment.” Cyprian: “With an evil foretoken of things to come, you already take the fiery color of your hair as an omen for yourself.” Jerome to Laeta: “Do not dye your hair red, thereby taking for yourself some omen of the fires of Gehenna.” RIG.] and they consider beautiful what they defile.

Moreover, the force of the chemicals burns damage into the hair and reserves destruction for the brain; so too does the constant application of any unadulterated moisture, while the heat of the sun—desirable for giving life and dryness to the hair—does harm. [Note: [Col. 1322D] “The sun’s heat, giving life to the hair.” *Animando* means “coloring,” as in Lucretius’s “animated crops” and Arnobius’s “animated entrails.” RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1322C] Rigault: “the heat does harm.”] What beauty is there together with injury? What loveliness together with uncleanness?

Will a Christian woman heap saffron [Col. 1322B] upon her head as though upon an altar? For whatever is customarily burned as an offering to an unclean spirit may seem a sacrifice unless it is applied to the proper, necessary, and healthful uses for which God’s creation was provided. But the Lord says: “Which of you can make black hair white, or white hair black?” (Matt. 5:36). And so they refute God: “See,” they say, “instead of white or black, we make it yellow—more winning in charm”—although women who regret having lived to old age even attempt to make white hair black.

What audacity! The age once desired in their prayers causes them shame; [Note: [Col. 1322D] “The age once desired in their prayers causes them shame.” Quintus Serenus:

> Those who are ashamed of long life, whom sacred old age  
> Offends, desire to conceal their hastening gray hairs  
> And counterfeit black hair with deceitful dye, etc.

RIG.] the theft is confessed, [Note: [Col. 1322C] Rigault: “is accomplished.”] the youth in which we sin is sighed after, and the occasion for gravity is tampered with. Far be such folly from the daughters of wisdom. The more old age strives to be concealed, the more it will be revealed. [Note: [Col. 1322C] Rigault: “will be retained.”]

This is [Col. 1322C] our eternity, derived from the youthfulness of the head. [Note: [Col. 1322C] Rigault: “the true eternity derived from the youthfulness of the hair.”] This is the incorruptible eternity we are always to put on for the house of the Lord, [Col. 1323A] which *akakia* (ἀκακία, “innocence”) promises. [Note: [Col. 1323B] Rigault: “We have this incorruptibility to put on over ourselves for the new house promised by the Monarchy.”] [Note: [Col. 1323B] “We have this incorruptibility to put on over ourselves for the new man promised by the Monarchy.” Or, if it is preferred—and I certainly prefer it—“for the new house promised by the Monarchy.” We have emended the text in this way according to the traces of the ancient reading visible in Agobard’s manuscript, which are as follows: “We have this incorruptibility always to put on for the new while which the Monarchy promises.” He is indignant with Christian women who, being excessively occupied with bodily adornment, gave too little thought to the Apostle, who calls us to a far more excellent glory of our bodies before God. He alludes to Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 15 and 2 Corinthians 5, which command Christians to hope confidently in the resurrection, which will clothe mortal bodies with immortality. For then the souls of the blessed will return to their bodies as though to new dwellings—dwellings now eternal, clothed over with immortality as with a new garment, never to be worn away by any subsequent age. He therefore says that old age is concealed in vain: the more it is suppressed, the more it breaks forth; the more it is concealed, the more it is exposed. Then, at once indignantly and mockingly, he says: “This is true eternity, derived from the youthfulness of the hair! This is the incorruptibility we have to put on over ourselves for the new house promised by the Monarchy.” By “Monarchy” he means God, the Best and Greatest, the unity of the most holy Trinity, in the sense in which he very frequently used that word in his disputation *Against Praxeas*. This is the most certain text of this extremely corrupt passage. Nor am I now influenced by the reading of the Dijon or Pithou manuscript that has hitherto been received in all editions: “for the house of the Lord promised by the acacia.” Pliny and the medical writers do indeed describe the acacia as a kind of thorn in Egypt, Cappadocia, and Pontus, whose juice or gum possesses so great a power of thickening that it serves the tanners’ workshops in place of gall; it was also adopted for women’s cosmetics, for tightening loose skin and producing wrinkles, and even for dyeing the hair: *dynamin echei styptikēn, melainei de kai trichas* (δύναμιν ἔχει στυπτικὴν, μελαίνει δὲ καὶ τρίχας), “it has an astringent power and also blackens the hair,” says Dioscorides. Marcellus, too, mentions acacia among the preparations commonly prescribed in his time for blackening and curling the hair. But these things agree sufficiently with neither the Apostle’s meaning nor Tertullian’s. Still less am I influenced by what Rhenanus, Pamelius, and others attempted concerning innocence—which the Greeks call *akakia* (ἀκακία)—for they were deceived by the corruption of a somewhat ancient manuscript. RIG.]

You make excellent speed toward the Lord; you hasten admirably to depart from this most wicked age—you to whom it is ugly to draw near to your end. [Note: [Col. 1323B] Latinius: “toward the end.” Rigault: “to approach the end.”]

## CHAPTER VII

For what does so laborious an elaboration of the head contribute to salvation? [Note: [Col. 1323B] Rhenanus, from the Gorze manuscript: “adorning”; others: “arranging.”] Why is your hair not permitted to rest—now bound up, now loosened, now raised, now flattened? Some delight to constrain it into curls; [Note: [Col. 1323B] Another reading: “into ringlets.”] others, without virtuous simplicity, delight to let it escape loose and flying.

In addition, you fasten upon yourselves all manner of monstrous structures of stitched [Note: [Col. 1324B] “All manner of monstrous structures.” Understand this of the wig or small hairpiece that both men and women used because of the thinness of their hair, with other people’s hairs added to it. It was so skillfully glued to the head that the hair appeared natural rather than borrowed. On this, Juvenal, *Satire* 6:

> But concealing black hair beneath a yellow wig.

LE PR.] and woven hairpieces: now shaped like a cap, as though a sheath for the head and a covering for the crown; now built up backward upon the neck. [Note: [Col. 1323B] Semler: “You preserve it without virtuous simplicity. In addition—of fine,” [Col. 1324B] etc. The words “stitched and woven” are absent from Rigault’s edition.]

It is remarkable that this does not openly contend against the Lord’s commandments [Col. 1323B]. It has been declared that no one can add to her stature. You certainly add to your weight by building upon your necks certain round buns or shield-bosses. [Note: [Col. 1324C] “Certain round buns.” Other manuscripts have *collyridae*. A *collyris* is a kind of cake, round in shape, so that it appears to be the same as the boss at the center of a shield. Juvenal, *Satire* 6:

> But when she is plastered over and treated  
> With so many cosmetics, and her face receives poultices  
> Of cooked wheat flour and wet dough, will it be called a face or an ulcer?

The great Scaliger read “bosses of the eruptions,” that is, bubbles and blisters in the leather that was put on. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1324B] Rigault: “certain coils,” etc. Others: “certain round buns—and shield-bosses.” Scaliger: “the bosses of eruptions” (*pampholygas*, παμφόλυγας, “blisters”).]

If you are not ashamed of the monstrosity, be ashamed [Col. 1324A] of the defilement: do not fit the castoffs of another’s head—perhaps unclean, perhaps guilty and destined for Gehenna—to a holy Christian head. Indeed, drive away all this slavery to adornment from a free head.

You labor in vain to appear adorned; in vain you employ every highly skilled architect of hairdressing. [Note: [Col. 1324C] “Every highly skilled architect of hairdressing.” Such persons were called by the special name *cosmetae*. The ancient glosses: *kosmētēs* (κοσμήτης), “adornment-worker, adorner.” Juvenal: “The *cosmetae* lay down their tunics.” Girls were also employed for this purpose, for in the glosses we likewise read *kosmētrias* (κοσμητρίας), “female adorners.” Ulpian, in the law *Item legato*, *On Legacies* III, where he discusses the things said to be prepared for the wife’s benefit: “Likewise included in the legacy are slaves—for example, litter bearers who carried only the lady of the household; likewise other slaves, perhaps girls with whom women adorn their hair”—for so, it seems, the text should be read. RIG.—“Architects of hairdressing.” The word *structor*, used absolutely, is applied to various occupations: sometimes to an arranger of dishes, as Servius says, and in Petronius’s *Dinner of Trimalchio*: “The arranger had placed upon it food properly suited to the subject”; sometimes to a carver of dishes, as Juvenal, *Satire* 5:

> Meanwhile, lest any indignity be lacking, you watch the carver  
> Dancing and gesticulating with his flying  
> Knife until he completes everything his master prescribed;  
> And indeed it makes no small difference  
> With what gesture the hares, and with what gesture the hen, is cut.

LE PR.]

God commands you to be veiled, I believe, so that the heads of some of you may not be seen. And [would that I, most wretched man,] on that day of Christian exultation [might raise my head even among your heels!] [Note: [Col. 1324B] The words enclosed in brackets appear to have been improperly inserted by an overzealous copyist.] [Note: [Col. 1324D] “Among your heels.” Wondrous humility!] I shall see whether you rise again with white lead, purple rouge, and saffron, and with that whole circumference of the head; whether the angels lift you up, painted in that fashion, into the cloud to meet Christ.

If these things are good now and belong to God, they too will meet the bodies as they rise again and will recognize their proper places. But nothing can rise again except the flesh and the spirit [Col. 1324B] alone and pure. Therefore, the things that do not rise again in flesh and spirit stand condemned, because they do not belong to God. Abstain today from things condemned. Let God see you today as he will see you then.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 1325A]

Clearly, then, I—both a man and a rival sex—am now driving women away from their own possessions. [Note: [Col. 1325C] “I am driving women away from their own possessions”—as though from their dowries, from their own proper goods: dress and ornament. RIG.] Are certain things also being taken away from us, in consideration of the seriousness that must be observed [Note: [Col. 1325C] Rigaltius, from the Agobardine codex: “of the gratuitous duty to be undertaken.” Latinus: “of the seriousness to be undertaken.”] [Note: [Col. 1325C] “They are undertaken in consideration of seriousness.” Tertullian intimates that men who sought to please the other sex by indulgence in luxury or by their own artificial enhancements of beauty could deservedly be censured no less severely than women, since they owed seriousness to God, who is present. EDD.], because of the fear owed to the Lord? For in men because of women, just as in women because of men, the desire to please is implanted by a fault of nature; and this sex too acknowledges its own artificial enhancements of beauty: trimming the beard more closely, plucking it [Note: [Col. 1325C] “Plucking it.” He attacks that excessive affectation of beauty and youth [Col. 1325D] by which they pulled out their hairs with tweezers so as to appear smoother—something that could readily be censured even among our own people. LE PR.], shaving around it [Note: [Col. 1325D] “Shaving around it.” Rigaltius reads this very well, whereas the others commonly read “surrounding it,” in the interpretation of which they become astonishingly perplexed. Lacerda and Pamelius learnedly adduce a great many things to explain the corrupt reading. LE PR.], arranging the hair, even coloring [Note: [Col. 1325C] Rigaltius: “and bleaching.”] gray hair, removing every fresh growth of down from the whole body, marking it out [Note: [Col. 1325C] Rigaltius: “staining it.”] also with a woman’s pigment, smoothing the rest with the roughness of some powder, and then consulting a mirror at every opportunity and anxiously inspecting oneself. Yet, once God has been known and the desire to please removed, all those things are rejected, through renunciation of luxury, [Col. 1325B] as idle and as hostile to chastity. [Note: [Col. 1325C] Rigaltius: “through an occasion for luxury, all these things are rejected as idle or hostile.” [Col. 1326C]] For where God is, there is chastity; there is seriousness, its helper and companion. How, then, shall we practice chastity [Note: [Col. 1325D] “Chastity without its equipment.” Chastity is better equipped when it has seriousness as its companion. RIG.] without its equipment, that is, without seriousness? And how shall we employ seriousness in maintaining chastity unless severity is displayed in the face, in dress, and in the whole person’s appearance?

## CHAPTER IX

For this reason you must likewise concern yourselves, with regard to clothing and the remaining encumbrances of your adornment [Note: [Col. 1325D] “And the remaining encumbrances of your adornment.” By “encumbrances” he here means all that equipment of feminine finery which is like a kind of baggage. Thus in the preceding book: “Therefore all these things are condemned, and are the encumbrances of a dead woman, as though prepared for the pomp of a funeral.” RHEN.], with cutting away and striking down excessive splendor. [Note: [Col. 1325D] “Striking down excessive splendor.” For expressing elegance, the word *nitor* (“splendor”) is especially apt, as Casperius testifies in his notes on Statius and Horace: “from being polished he becomes rustic”; Statius, in the *Exhortation to Crispinus* [Col. 1326C] and in the *Silvae*; likewise Martial. Or he says this because of lovers of women, for it is customary in Latin to call lovers of this sort *nitidi* (“polished” or “shining”). Plautus, *Casina*: “Since I fell in love with Casina, I shine more”; and Juvenal: “They are called cheerful and polished.” Taubmannus noted this. But whence “striking down”? Perhaps from an approaching wind that lays all the little flowers upon the ground? I would believe so, since Cicero says in *On Duties* II: “All artificial things fall away gently, like little flowers.” This trope is found in the Epistle of James, chapter 1, where it says, καὶ τὸ ἄνθος αὐτοῦ ἐξέπεσε, “and its flower fell.” I therefore think Tertullian took the metaphor from this. LAC.] For what advantage is there in presenting a face that is indeed sober, unencumbered, and possessed of a simplicity worthy of divine discipline, but occupying the other parts of the body with the ragged excesses [Note: [Col. 1326D] “The ragged excesses of displays,” etc.—that is, with things various and excessive. He uses this word elsewhere too. RHEN.] [Col. 1325C] of displays and luxuries, as though we were not abusing them? For, he says, the fashion [Col. 1326A] of this world is passing away. [The supplied text is disordered here; “the fashion of this world is passing away” appears displaced from its later scriptural context.]

It is easy to discern how closely these displays serve the business of lust and clamor against the disciplines of chastity: they prostitute the charm of beauty by associating it with finery; indeed, if they are absent, they render it ineffectual and unpleasing, as though it had been disarmed [Note: [Col. 1326C] Semler: “adorned.”] and shipwrecked. Conversely, if beauty is lacking, the support of splendor supplies charm, as it were, from its own resources. Finally, splendor and distinction of dress summon away even ages that are already at rest and have withdrawn into the harbor of modesty [Note: [Col. 1326D] “Into the harbor of modesty.” The metaphor is taken from ships that withdraw from the open sea into a safe anchorage. RHEN.], and they disturb seriousness with desires, the allurement of dress evidently compensating for the coldness [Note: [Col. 1326D] “The allurement of dress compensating for the coldness of age.” He says that women whose age is now cooling care for and adorn their bodies with such effort that they arouse desire for themselves; and if the coldness of age has extinguished anything, the wantonness of luxurious dress provokes and rekindles it. RIG.] of age.

Therefore, blessed women, first take care not to admit clothing and finery into yourselves as procurers and panderers. Then, if considerations of [your own] wealth, birth, or former rank compel any of you to go forth with such display, [Col. 1326B] take care at least, now that you have attained wisdom, [Note: [Col. 1326C] Rigaltius: “take care to restrain yourselves from this sort of evil, lest you appear not to have attained wisdom.”] to restrain yourselves from conduct of this sort, lest you exercise license with completely loosened reins under the pretext of necessity. For how shall we be able to fulfill the humility that we Christians profess [Note: [Col. 1326C] Rigaltius: “that our people profess, will you be able to fulfill”], unless we uproot the use of your riches or finery, which contribute to glory? But glory is accustomed to exalt, not to humble.

“Then shall we not use [Note: [Col. 1326D] “Then shall we not use our own possessions?” This is spoken in the person of women complaining that they are being driven away from their own possessions. RIG.] our own possessions?” Who forbids their use? Yet use them according to the Apostle, who warns us to use this world as though not using it, for the fashion of this world [Note: [Col. 1326D] “For the fashion of this world is passing away.” By *habitus* he means what Paul calls σχῆμα, “form” or “fashion.” RIG.] is passing away. “And those who buy,” he says, “must act as though they did not possess.” Why so? Because he had first said: “The time has been shortened” (1 Cor. 7:29–31). If, then, he shows that even wives themselves are to be possessed as though they were not possessed, because of the distress of the times, what are we to say of these vain accessories [Col. 1326C] belonging to them?

Do not many indeed act in this way and assign themselves to eunuchhood [Col. 1327A] for the sake of the kingdom of God (Matt. 19:12), voluntarily laying aside so powerful and certainly permitted a pleasure? Some [Note: [Col. 1327B] Rigaltius: “Do not some?”] forbid themselves even God’s own creation, abstaining from wine and animal foods [Note: [Col. 1327B] All except Rigaltius read “banishing themselves.”], whose enjoyment is attended by no danger or anxiety; instead, they sacrifice the humility of their soul to God through the chastisement of their diet as well.

You too, therefore, have made sufficient use of riches and luxuries; before your knowledge of the disciplines of salvation, you have sufficiently deducted the interest from your dowries. [Note: [Col. 1327C] “You have sufficiently deducted the interest from your dowries.” These words were extremely corrupt in the books published thus far. We have emended them from the Agobardine manuscript. He speaks, as it were, to the whole female sex: “You women, before Christ was named among humankind, made sufficient use of riches [Col. 1327C] and luxuries. You yourselves have sufficiently deducted and taken in advance the interest from your dowries—interest that ought to have accrued to your husbands’ advantage—and spent it on every kind of luxury and insane expense. You have sufficiently allowed the pleasurable fruits of the beauty with which you were endowed to be plucked. You have had your sport; it is enough. Now other times have arrived, and affairs of greater importance occupy you. Knowledge of the disciplines of salvation calls us elsewhere. Before the very beginning of the world, God appointed us to live in the last times, at the temporal extremity, that is, at the end of the ages—a time in which we must think not of earthly things that perish in a moment, but of heavenly things that endure forever.” RIG.] We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come. We were appointed by God before the world for the reckoning of the times [Note: [Col. 1327C] “At the temporal extremity,” as Rigaltius reads: in the last times, at the end of the age. He wished *extimatio* to be understood here in the sense in which he used *extimavit* in the book *On the Crown*: “He brought the contact to an end at the hands.” RIG.]; we are instructed by the Lord, so to speak, through chastising and castrating the age. [Note: [Col. 1327B] Rigaltius: “at the temporal extremity. And so, through chastisement...”] We are the circumcision of all things, both spiritual and carnal, for in spirit and flesh we circumcise worldly things. [Note: [Col. 1327B] Rigaltius: “for both in spirit and in flesh we are circumcised.”]

## CHAPTER X

To be sure, it was God who showed how to boil wool in the juices of herbs and the fluids of shellfish. [Note: [Col. 1327C] “The fluids of shellfish,” as the same editor reads. [Col. 1327D] Pliny not infrequently uses the word *saliva* for moisture and juice. Speaking of purple shellfish and murices, he says: “They exude a certain waxy viscosity.” RIG.] When he commanded all things to come into being, it had escaped his notice to order purple and scarlet sheep! It was God who devised workshops for garments so light and fine that they would be made heavy by their price alone; [Col. 1328A] God who produced such great works of gold for surrounding and setting off little stones; God who inflicted upon ears wounds laden with little weights [Note: [Col. 1327D] “Wounds laden with little weights”—from which the little weights of gems might hang. RIG.], and who valued so highly the tormenting of his own handiwork and the anguish of infancy then first experiencing pain, that from those scars in a body newly subjected to iron [Note: [Col. 1327D] “A body newly subjected to iron.” He calls it a body “born for iron” because, as soon as it is born, it is wounded with iron when the lower ears of infants are pierced. RIG.] there might hang some sort of beads—things which, indeed, the Parthians insert everywhere upon their own belongings [Note: [Col. 1328B] Rigaltius: “which the Parthians insert even upon their boots in place of bosses.”] in place of bosses. Yet pagan literature reports that gold itself, with whose glory you are preoccupied, serves one nation as chains.

Thus these things are good not by their true nature but by their rarity. Once crafts had been introduced through sinful angels [Note: [Col. 1327D] “Once crafts had been introduced through sinful angels.” In the excerpts of George Syncellus, the following material concerning crafts of this sort is read from the ninth book of Zosimus of Panopolis’ *Imouth, or Alchemy*, addressed to Theosebia:

> “The sacred writings, or books, say, O woman, that there exists a certain race of demons which has intercourse with women. Hermes too mentioned this in the *Physical Writings*, and virtually every discourse, both public and secret, has recalled it. The ancient and divine writings therefore say that angels desired women, and that after descending they taught them all the works of nature. For this reason, having given offense, they remained outside heaven, because they taught humankind all things evil and of no benefit to the soul.”

The sacred Scriptures report, O woman, that a certain race of demons had intercourse with women. Hermes too recalls this in the *Physical Writings*, and nearly every common and esoteric discourse imagines the same thing. Those ancient and divine Scriptures therefore relate [Col. 1328C] that women were desired by angels and learned every work of nature through intercourse with them. Consequently, the angels were cast down from heaven and remained in perpetual exile because they had taught humankind every wicked thing harmful to the soul. EDD., from Rigaltius.], who also disclosed the materials themselves, craftsmanship [Note: [Col. 1328C] “Craftsmanship”: labor, the price of handiwork. Irenaeus uses this word for toil and hardship, book II, chapter 19. RIG.], joined to rarity, created preciousness; and preciousness aroused in women the lust to possess costly things.

But if the same angels who revealed materials and allurements of this kind—I mean gold and shining stones—also transmitted the crafts for working them, and among other things taught the very use of *calliblepharum* [eye-beautifying cosmetic] [Note: [Col. 1328C] “The very *calliblepharum*.” This seems to be nothing other than purple pigment, which heightens beauty and charm in women. Some say that it is foam collected from boiling purple dye. See Pliny, book XXI, chapter 19, where he teaches that a rose-colored pigment is made from burned petals and from date stones, and also, in book XXVII, chapter 4, from beef marrow. LE PR.] and the dyeing of fleeces [Note: [Col. 1328B] From the words “Thus these things are good not by their true nature,” etc., we have followed Rigaltius’s recension, since what the others have printed cannot be understood. LEOPOLD.], and if they were condemned by God, as Enoch reports [Note: [Col. 1328C] “They were condemned by God, as Enoch reports.” Once again he cites the apocryphal Book of Enoch, which Jerome testifies that he had read. George Syncellus also copied from it certain chapters and shows that Paul himself likewise cited some things from the apocryphal books of Elijah, Moses, and Jeremiah. He then adds:

> “We have said these things, not because we wish to grant permission to read them indiscriminately—far from it. For many have been harmed by believing everything in them. Hence the holy Church of God and the choir of our God-bearing fathers forbade their being read in the same way as the rest of divine Scripture.”

Let these things have been said by us, not because we wish to hold to such books or use them without discrimination—far from it. Excessive credulity of this sort has harmed many. Hence the holy Church of God and the choir of our God-bearing fathers prevented their being read in the same manner as the remaining divine Scriptures. Concerning writings of this sort, the most learned Jerome long ago warned in his *Letter to Laeta*: “It must be understood that they are not by those whose names appear in their titles, that many corrupt things have been mingled with them, and that it requires great prudence to seek gold in mud.” RIG.], how shall we please God while delighting in the things of those who provoked God’s wrath and punishment?

[Col. 1329A] Suppose now that God foresaw these things and permitted them; suppose Isaiah (Isa. 3:18ff.) censures no garment dyed with shellfish, condemns no little moon-shaped ornament, and strikes down no grape-clustered arrangement [Note: [Col. 1329D] “Strikes down no grape-clustered arrangement.” By *botronatum* he means a heap of hair arranged in clusters. Hesychius: βοτρυδὸν, ἑτέρα τῆς ἑτέρας ἐχομενη, ὡς οἱ βότρυες τὰς ῥᾶγας ἔχουσι πυκνάς—“in clusters: one thing holding to another, just as bunches of grapes have their berries densely packed.” RIG.—“No grape-clustered arrangement,” etc. Rhenanus conjectures that it is a band binding the hair of the head, so called because it resembles a bunch of grapes. There is nothing like it in the Greek text of the Septuagint; it may therefore be a word used by the common people of that period to describe a woman’s head ornament. LAC.]. Nevertheless, let us not flatter ourselves like the pagans, imagining God only as the creator and not also as the inspector [Note: [Col. 1329D] “Inspector.” Thus Rhenanus reads. *Despector*, as more than once above, stands for *dispector*: one who takes care of and considers the things he has instituted. Thus also in the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “Nor,” he says, “were those most holy predecessors willing to overlook it among customs.” RHEN.] of what he has instituted.

How much better [Note: [Col. 1329C] Rigaltius: “more advantageously.”] and more cautiously shall we act if we assume that all things were indeed provided by God and placed in the world at that time so that they might now exist as things by which the discipline of his servants could be tested, and so that the proof of self-restraint might emerge through freedom of use. [Note: [Col. 1329C] Rigaltius: “so that experiments in self-restraint might proceed.”] Do not wise heads of households [Note: [Col. 1329D] “Heads of households.” The author uses this form against Varro’s judgment in book VII, according to which he should have said *patresfamilias*. Martial likewise, book I: “Quirinalis is a true head of a household.” PAM.] deliberately offer and permit certain things to their servants in order to test whether and how they use what is permitted—whether honorably and modestly [Note: [Col. 1329C] Rigaltius: “moderately.”]? And how much more praiseworthy is the person who [Col. 1329B] has abstained altogether, who has feared even the Lord’s indulgence? Thus the Apostle also says: “All things are permitted, but not all things build up” [Note: [Col. 1329C] Rigaltius: “are advantageous.”] (1 Cor. 10:23). How much more readily will one fear unlawful things if one is wary even of lawful ones?

## CHAPTER XI

What cause have you for going forth in more elaborate array, since you are removed from those occasions that require such things? For you do not make the rounds of temples, demand spectacles, or recognize the pagans’ feast days. It is for such gatherings, and for mutual seeing and being seen, that every display is brought out in public, so that either lust may ply its trade or glory grow insolent.

But you have no reason for going out that is not grave [Note: [Col. 1329D] “No reason for going out that is not grave.” [Col. 1330D] That is: no reason for going out that is not weighty, serious, and holy. RIG.]: either some sick brother is to be visited, or the sacrifice is offered [Note: [Col. 1330D] “The sacrifice is offered.” Thus he spoke of “the prayers of the sacrifices,” in which, namely, the eucharistic mysteries are offered to be shared by the faithful. RIG.—“Or the sacrifice is offered.” That this means the sacred rite of the Mass is clearer than to require demonstration, despite the impudence of Junius, who understands it generically as some prayers. See our Gretser in his notes against Junius, chapter 3. LAC.], or the word of God is administered. Any of these is a matter of seriousness [Col. 1329C] and holiness, one that has no need of extraordinary, carefully arranged, and flowing attire. [Note: [Col. 1329C] A. Neander emends: “extraordinary and flowing attire, but carefully arranged.”]

And if the necessity of friendships and obligations toward pagans calls you, why do you not go out clothed in your own armor—all the more when going among those alien to the faith? Let there be a distinction between the handmaids of the devil and those of God; let you be an example to them; let them be built up through you; let, as the Apostle says, God be magnified in your body (Phil. 1:20; 1 Cor. 6:20). God is magnified in the body through chastity, and certainly through attire appropriate to chastity.

But some say that his name may be blasphemed in us (Rom. 2:24) if we take anything away from our former clothing and finery. Then let us not take away our former vices either [Note: [Col. 1330C] Rigaltius deleted “from us also.”]; let us remain the same in morals if we remain the same in outward appearance, and then the nations truly will not blaspheme! What a dreadful blasphemy it is when someone says [Note: [Col. 1330C] Gelenius and others: “It is a blasphemy if someone says... she walks.” Rigaltius: “It is a blasphemy from which someone says... she walks.”]: “Since she became a Christian, she goes about more poorly dressed.” Will you fear appearing poorer now that you have become richer, and more squalid now that you have become purer? Ought Christians to walk according to the approval of the pagans, or according to God’s?

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 1330B]

Let us desire only that we not be a cause of justified blasphemy. Yet how much more blasphemous it is if you who are called priestesses of chastity go forth adorned and painted after the fashion of the unchaste! Or what do those most wretched victims of public lusts possess any less than you? Certain laws used to restrain them from the dress of matrons [Note: [Col. 1330C] Others: “married women.” Rigaltius: “marital ornaments.”] and from matronly ornaments; but now the wickedness of the age, daily increasing, has placed them on an equal footing with even the most respectable women, to the point that one may mistake the one for the other. Moreover, Scripture also indicates that the enticements of beauty have always been joined and owed to the prostituted body.

That mighty city which presides over seven mountains and many waters, when it merited from the Lord the designation of prostitute [Note: [Col. 1330C] Rigaltius: “presides over them and merited from the Lord the designation of prostitute. But with what attire,” etc.], in what attire is it presented as corresponding to its designation? It sits, of course, in purple [Col. 1330C] and scarlet, gold, and precious stone. How accursed are the things without which what was accursed and prostituted could not be described!

Because that Tamar (Gen. 38:14ff.) had painted and adorned herself, Judah therefore saw her and suspected that she was sitting there for hire. [Note: [Col. 1330D] “That Tamar was seen,” etc. “She was seen for hire”: that is, sitting there to make a profit, etc. The blessed Cyprian also cites this Scripture later to show that a woman ought not to adorn herself in a worldly manner, in these words: “Tamar covered herself with a cloak” (which the blessed Jerome also calls a *theristrum*) “and adorned herself; and when Judah saw her, he thought her to be a prostitute.” The author appears to understand the words “and he desired her” as meaning “he burned with desire for her.” PAM.—“Sitting there for hire.” Sitting is characteristic of women who are prostitutes. Concerning the same Tamar, Genesis 38 [Col. 1331C] says: “She covered herself with a veil and concealed herself, and sat at the gate of the eyes”; or, as the Vulgate has it, “Having changed her dress, she sat at the crossroads.” And Jeremiah, chapter 3: “See where you have not been prostrated; you sat by the roads.” For it was customary among the Hebrews for public prostitutes to occupy the roads. Hence Ezekiel 16: “At every head of the road you built the sign of your prostitution”; and again: “You built your brothel at the head of every road.” Hence also among the Romans prostitutes were called *prosedae*, of whom there is frequent mention, because they sat before their doors. Plautus in the *Poenulus*: “Streetwalkers, bakers’ mistresses, remnants of barley-women.” LAC.]

Indeed, because she was hidden beneath a veil while the character of her dress falsely represented her as a woman for hire [Col. 1331A] [Note: [Col. 1331C] “The character of her dress falsely representing her as a woman for hire.” He is perhaps censuring a certain woman who had become stuck in that mire, in the way that Juvenal, *Satire* 6, alludes to Messalina, [Col. 1331D] who, “naked with gilded nipples, stood falsely assuming the name Lycisca”—that is, she entered the chamber in which a foul prostitute had sat, falsely pretending that she made money from her body. LE PR.], her dress caused him to desire her as a woman for hire, address her as one, and bargain with her as one. [Note: [Col. 1331B] Rigaltius: “Indeed, because she lay hidden beneath a veil while the character of her dress falsely represented her as a woman for hire, he desired her as such, addressed her as such, and bargained with her as such.”]

From this we learn that provision must be made in every way against even unchaste encounters and suspicions. Why should the integrity of a chaste mind be stained in another person’s suspicion? Why is that hoped for in me which I reject? Why does my dress not proclaim my character, lest my spirit be wounded through my ears by shamelessness? [Note: [Col. 1331D] “Lest the spirit be wounded through the ears by shamelessness”—that is, by the shamelessness of insolent young men, who will dare to address you as unchaste when you are in such attire, and to assail and disturb your spirit with shameless speech; and thus through your ears they will wound your modesty. In this way a worldly matter shakes the spirit and moves it by scandal. The Council of Elvira: “The spirits of the saints are disturbed.” RIG.] One may be allowed to appear chaste; one certainly may not appear unchaste. [Note: [Col. 1331B] Rigaltius, from the Agobardine codex: “certainly unchaste, that is.”]

## CHAPTER XIII

Someone may perhaps say: “I have no need to be approved by human beings, for I do not seek human testimony. God is the inspector of the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7). We all know this. Nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1331B] Franciscus Junius conjectures: “We all know this; nevertheless, let us remember what [Col. 1331C] the same one,” etc.], let us remember what the same God said through the Apostle: “Let your probity [Note: [Col. 1331D] “Your probity before,” etc. He rendered literally the Greek expression used by the Apostle—a title by which he everywhere means Saint Paul the Apostle—at Philippians 4: τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ὑμῶν, “your forbearance,” for which our Vulgate translator paraphrastically has *modestia vestra*, “your modesty.” PAM.] appear before human beings” (Phil. 4:5). For what purpose, except that wickedness may have no access to you at all, and that you may be both an example and a testimony to the wicked?

Or what does “Let your works shine” mean? Or why did the Lord call us “the light of the earth” [Note: [Col. 1331D] “Or why did the Lord call us...” Since Matthew’s Greek text reads τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου, “the light of the world,” while κόσμος is nowhere used for “earth,” the author appears here too to have suffered a lapse of memory because “the salt of the earth” had shortly preceded it; otherwise he ought to have said “the light of the world,” just as one says “lights of the world.” PAM.]? Why did he compare us to a city established upon a mountain (Matt. 5:14), if we do not shine among those in darkness [Note: [Col. 1331C] Rigaltius: “shine in the darkness”; others: “shine among the darkness.”] and stand out among those submerged?

If you hide your lamp beneath a bushel, you must necessarily, after being abandoned in darkness, be run into by many. [Note: [Col. 1332C] “After being abandoned in darkness, you must necessarily be run into by many.” The common reading is “you will be assailed by many.” The Agobardine codex has “you will have enclosed.” One should write “you will be run into,” in this sense: it cannot happen otherwise than that many will stumble against you when you are left in darkness. The word *incursari* is ambiguous here, for a woman is also called *incursa* when she is overwhelmed by the blind assault of lustful persons. Thus Tertullian himself, *To the Nations* I: “How often had he committed incest in the darkness?” And: “Take careful notice, so that when darkness falls you do not go astray and assault a stranger.” And in the book *On Modesty*: “For it makes no difference whether someone assaults another man’s wife or a widow.” PAM.]

These are the things that make us lights of the world—our good deeds, of course. But the good, provided that it is true and complete, [Col. 1332A] does not love darkness; it rejoices to be seen and exults in being pointed out for what it is. [Note: [Col. 1332D] “At the very indications,” etc. Fabius, *Declamation* 19: “condemned by everyone’s denunciation.” PAM.] [Note: [Col. 1331C] Rigaltius: “exults at the very indications.”]

For Christian chastity, it is not enough to exist; it must also be visible. Its fullness ought to be so great that it flows out from the soul into the clothing and erupts from the conscience onto the outward appearance, so that it also examines externally, as it were, its own equipment—the equipment fitting for the perpetual maintenance of faith. Luxuries must be cast off, for their softness and fluidity can render the strength of faith effeminate.

Otherwise, I do not know [Note: [Col. 1332D] “Whether a hand accustomed to being surrounded by a *spathalium*.” A *spathalium* is a woman’s ornament, from σπαθᾶν, which signifies “to live luxuriously.” RHEN.] whether a hand accustomed to being encircled by a *spathalium* [bracelet] can endure becoming numb in the hardness of a chain. I do not know whether a leg that has delighted in a *periscelium* [anklet] [Note: [Col. 1332B] Rigaltius: “a leg delighted by an anklet,” etc.] will allow itself to be tightly confined in the stocks. [Note: [Col. 1332D] “I do not know whether a leg with an anklet.” Legs or shins were adorned with the *periscelis* or *periscelium*; the Greeks call the leg σκέλος. RHEN.] I fear that a neck occupied by necklaces of pearls and emeralds will not leave room for the sword.

Therefore, blessed women, let us rehearse harder things, and we shall not feel them; [Col. 1332B] let us relinquish more pleasant things, and we shall not desire them. Let us stand unencumbered against every violence, possessing nothing that we fear to leave behind. These things are the bonds that hold back our hope. Let us cast away earthly ornaments if we desire heavenly ones.

Do not love gold, in which the first [Note: [Col. 1332B] Rigaltius: “all.”] sins of the people of Israel are marked out (cf. Exod. 32:2ff.). You ought to hate that which destroyed the Jews [Note: [Col. 1332B] Rigaltius: “the fathers.”], that which they worshiped when they abandoned God. Even then gold was food for fire. [Note: [Col. 1332D] “Even then gold was fire.” In the preceding book he said of gold: “It left behind the name of earth in the fire.” Accordingly, gold already derives its being gold from fire. By mentioning fire, moreover, he continually alludes to the fire prepared for the punishment of the profane. RIG.] [Note: [Col. 1332B] Rigaltius: “that which was worshiped by those abandoning God. Even [Col. 1332C] (others: already) then gold was fire. But,” etc.]

In any case, the times of Christians are always—and now especially—passed not in gold but in iron. The robes of martyrdom are being prepared; supported by angels as bearers [Note: [Col. 1332C] Rigaltius: “the angels as bearers support them.”] [Note: [Col. 1332D] “Supported by angels as bearers.” That is, angels are expected to lift them into heaven to meet Christ. Thus Tertullian himself in the preceding book: “I shall see whether you rise with white lead, purple pigment, saffron, and that arrangement of the head, [Col. 1334A] or whether angels lift you, painted in such a fashion, into the clouds to meet Christ in the air.” RIG.].

Go forth now built up [Col. 1333A] with the cosmetics and ornaments of the prophets [Note: [Col. 1333A] Semler omits “of the prophets.”] and apostles: drawing whiteness from simplicity and blush from chastity; painting your eyes with modesty and your mouth with silence [Note: [Col. 1333A] Others: “and your spirit with silence.”]; inserting the word of God into your ears; fastening the yoke of Christ around your necks. Subject your head [Col. 1334A] to your husbands, and you will be sufficiently adorned. Occupy your hands with wool [Note: [Col. 1334A] “Occupied,” the Paris edition.]; plant your feet at home, and they will please more than if they were in gold. [Note: [Col. 1334A] Others: “you will please.”] Clothe yourselves in the silk of probity, the fine linen of holiness, and the purple of chastity. Painted in this fashion, you will have God as your lover.

# CORRECTIONS AND ADDITIONS
## Corrections and Additions

It should be noted:

1. That all the notes occurring throughout the *Apologeticum* which are not signed with an author’s name are to be referred to Havercamp’s continuous commentary.

2. That the variant readings cited in nearly every column from the Paris edition were taken from the first Paris edition, prepared by Sigismund Gelenius, 1566, with a very few exceptions, which the editors drew from Priorius’s Paris edition of 1664.

3. That, because of the excessive number of Tertullian’s works and the enormous bulk of both volumes, there was so little space available for indexes that the lexicon of Tertullian’s Latin could scarcely be placed at the end of the second volume; the very extensive index of all subjects, however, had to be deferred to the third volume, which it will conclude.

Col. 60 C, “Cassiodorum” [Cassiodorus, acc.], read: “Cassiodorus.” — 82 C, “when the eighteen years of St. Zephyrinus are included, there will be forty-two years,” read: “to these should be added the eighteen years of St. Zephyrinus; there will be forty-four years.” — 150 D, “sufficientia,” read: “Sufficientis.” — Same column, “adorned with the others,” read: “adorned, with the others.” — Ibid., “Siclis,” read: “Sigliis.” — 155 D, “Barinonensem,” read: “Barcinonensem” [of Barcelona]. — 166 A, “Tertullian,” read: “Tillemont.” — 174 D, “He has,” read: “you have.” — 201 A, “Apoca se,” read: “Apoc. a se.” — 281 B, “mandaciis,” read: “mendaciis” [falsehoods]. — 307 D, “adio,” read: “odio” [hatred]. — 338 D, “αῦ δε τὸ μυυαν,” read: “αὖ δ’ ἔτ’ ἔμυξαν” [“again they still snorted”; reading uncertain]. — 350 B, “In frac.,” read: “Infra c.” [below, chapter]. — 352 A, B, line 17 must be placed before lines 15 and 16. — 354 B, “of the goose of the eagle, of the dog of the cock,” read: “of the goose, of the eagle, of the dog, of the cock.” — 360 C, what pertains to Morell’s gem is to be deleted. — 367 D, “legabatur,” read: “legebatur” [was read]. — 368 D, “scopulis” [rocks], read: “scapulis” [shoulders]. — 373 B, “formem,” read: “formam” [form]. — 382 B, “nobis” [for us], read: “nos” [us]. — 397 D, “amen,” read: “tamen” [nevertheless]. — 401 C, “And the day should grow dark, Amos,” read: “the day should grow dark, Amos.” — Ibid., “erit” [will be], read: “Et erit” [And it will be]. — 407 D, “mullus, hominum,” read: “nullus hominum” [no human being]. — 413 D, “confu vocis et valentissione simo,” read: “confusione vocis et valentissimo” [by confusion of voice and by the most powerful …]. — 420 B, “sanctam,” read: “sancta.” — 437 D, “Casobonus … Claudi,” read: “Casaubonus … Claudio.” — 445 C, “liq.,” read: “lib.” [book]. — 446 D, “otantis,” read: “orantis” [of one praying]. — 461 D, “vivis,” read: “Vivis” [You live]. — 462 D, “potere,” read: “petere” [to seek]. — 463 A, “municipia,” read: “municipia.” — 465 B, “inicitiae qune im,” read: “inimicitiaeque” [and hostilities]. — 474 D, “pe-,” read: “per.” — 475 D, “μέγισος,” read: “μέγιστος” [greatest]. — 479 D, “ανίρους,” read: “ἀγρίους” [wild]. — 481 A, “creptam,” read: “ereptam” [snatched away]. — 483 B, “afferrit,” read: “asserit” [asserts]. — Ibid. D, “constae,” read: “confitae.” — 484 B, “sique,” read: “si qua” [if any]. — Ibid. C, “conantar … tenut,” read: “conantur … tenus” [they attempt … as far as]. — Ibid. C, “digitu,” read: “digiti” [of the finger]. — Ibid. C, “Ilium,” read: “alium” [another]. — 485 B, “promorunt,” read: “promorum.” — 487 B, “peccatorem” [sinner], read: “precatorem” [one who entreats]. — 488 D, “differamas,” read: “differamus” [let us postpone]. — 491 B, “Est est,” read: “est et” [is also]. — Ibid. ## The Following Additions Are to Be Made to the Literary Annals of Tertullian

[Col. 1335]

### Year 1702

The Blessed Cardinal Joseph Maria Thomasius published the first volume of his *Theological Institutions*, at the beginning of which he printed Tertullian’s book *On Prescriptions against Heretics*. Rome, quarto.

### Year 1769

When Anton Francesco Vezzosi, C.R., revised and republished those same *Theological Institutions of the Ancient Fathers* by the venerable Blessed Thomasius, the book *On Prescriptions* was once again issued under his supervision, enlarged with several notes displaying sound doctrine and exceptional learning. Rome, from the printing house of Marco Palearini. Quarto.

### Year 1840

Among certain principal minor works of ecclesiastical writers, [Col. 1336] Martin Joseph Routh, S.T.P., President of St Mary Magdalen College, Oxford, published two books by Tertullian—namely, *On Prayer* and *On the Prescription of Heretics*—and furnished them with notes both by others and by himself. He also augmented them with a new collection of readings, placed at the end and taken from an Ambrosian manuscript. Second edition, Oxford. It is regrettable that this excellent work did not come into our hands until the whole of this present work had been completed; nevertheless, we shall give it such notice as we can in the third volume, in the index.

### Year 1843

We are able to report only that, at the same time as this edition of ours is being committed to the press, another edition of Tertullian is likewise beginning to appear, edited by H. A. Woodham, Cambridge.

[Col. 1135] A very extensive analytical index will conclude the third volume.

**End of the First Volume.**
